metadata.programme_name: International Finance Facility for Immunisation (IFFIm)
metadata.quote: The International Finance Facility for Immunisation (IFFIm) is an innovative financing mechanism used to frontload donor pledges to fund Gavi’s immunisation programmes including Gavi 5.0 and the COVAX AMC. (D0005419.odt, Overview of IFFIm)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: April 2007–March 2027 (extended to March 2030 in 2022). (D0005419.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: IFFIm is a financial instrument that frontloads donor pledges by issuing vaccine bonds on international capital markets, enabling Gavi to access large volumes of future donor funding immediately for immunisation programmes. The UK's contributions are legally binding pledges that allow Gavi to accelerate vaccine delivery and save lives in poor countries without creating new liabilities on the UK's balance sheet.
what_objectives.q1_source: IFFIm raises money for Gavi by selling 'vaccine bonds' on the international capital markets. These bonds are backed by long-term legally binding pledges from donor governments. In this way, IFFIm is a flexible financing mechanism, accelerating the delivery of vaccines by making large volumes of future donor funding immediately available for Gavi programmes as and when needed. (D0005419.odt, Overview of IFFIm)
q3_expected_outputs: Vaccinate 300 million children (2021-25 strategic period)
Save 7-8 million lives (2021-25 strategic period)
Reduce the number of children who have never received a vaccine by 25% (from 9.7 million down to 7.3 million)
Frontload £300m for Gavi’s 5.0 activities (2021-25 period)
Deliver £139m to Gavi 2026-30 as the UK pays their commitment to IFFIm
what_objectives.summary: IFFIm is a financing mechanism that enables Gavi to frontload donor funding for immunisation programmes, accelerating vaccine delivery and saving lives in low-income countries. The UK's contributions are structured as legally binding pledges that do not appear as liabilities until paid, allowing flexible, long-term support for Gavi's objectives.
what_objectives.quote: The UK’s commitments to Gavi’s core mission through IFFIm provide Gavi with flexible support, and so contribute to overall UK objectives and results, as set out in the core Gavi business case (300871). Key performance measures in the 2021-25 strategic period are to: Vaccinate 300 million children; Save 7-8 million lives; Reduce the number of children who have never received a vaccine by 25% (from 9.7 million down to 7.3 million). (D0005419.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: IFFIm operates in a challenging financial market environment but has consistently delivered efficient frontloading of donor resources. The mechanism includes a 'grant payment condition' that reduces future payments if Gavi countries are in arrears to the IMF, indicating some financial risk exposure.
where_context.q5_source: All IFFIm contributions are subject to the ‘grant payment condition’ which means future payments may be subject to a percentage reduction if Gavi countries are in arrears to the IMF. (D0001188.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Exchange rate fluctuations affect the value of UK contributions, which are hedged to lock in future value. Financial market conditions impact IFFIm's ability to borrow at favorable rates, affecting the cost of frontloading funds.
where_context.quote: IFFIm receives contributions and issues bonds in a variety of currencies. The UK pays IFFIm contributions in GBP but it is subject to fluctuating exchange rates so these contributions are hedged to lock in future value at the point the grant agreement is signed. (D0001188.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (as the largest donor) and other Northern donors make legally binding pledges to IFFIm, which are then managed by the World Bank (as IFFIm’s Treasury Manager) to frontload funds to Gavi. Decision-making power over fund allocation lies with Gavi’s governance structures, which include both Northern and Southern representation but are ultimately influenced by major donors.

partner_organizations.name: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
partner_organizations.role: Recipient and implementer of immunisation programmes

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Treasury Manager for IFFIm (issues bonds and manages pledges)

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Largest donor to IFFIm, providing legally binding pledges

who_partners.quote: IFFIm raises money for Gavi by selling 'vaccine bonds' on the international capital markets. These bonds are backed by long-term legally binding pledges from donor governments. (D0005419.odt, Overview of IFFIm)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides legally binding pledges to IFFIm, which issues vaccine bonds on capital markets to frontload funds for Gavi. The UK's contributions are structured as grant agreements with the World Bank (IFFIm’s Treasury Manager), with payments made over multi-year periods. The mechanism allows Gavi to access funds immediately while the UK spreads its payments over time.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IFFIm is managed by the World Bank as Treasury Manager, which issues bonds backed by donor pledges. Gavi allocates the frontloaded funds to immunisation programmes globally. The UK FCDO monitors performance through annual reviews but does not manage day-to-day operations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IFFIm was established as a multilateral financing mechanism with the World Bank as Treasury Manager by design. The UK’s participation is through legally binding pledges to this existing structure, which was created to accelerate funding for Gavi’s immunisation programmes. No competition is mentioned as IFFIm is a pre-existing mechanism.
how_mechanism.quote: The FCDO will draw up a new legally binding grant agreement between the FCDO and the World Bank (IFFIm’s Treasury Manager). (D0001188.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Gavi’s governance structure includes a Board with representation from donor countries, implementing countries, and other stakeholders. IFFIm’s operations are overseen by the World Bank as Treasury Manager, with annual reviews conducted by the FCDO to monitor performance.
how_governance.quote: IFFIm scores consistently highly in FCDO annual reviews, achieving A+ in the last four reviews, demonstrating that IFFIm continues to be a highly effective and efficient financial instrument supporting Gavi’s ability to achieve equitable access to immunisation. (D0001188.odt, What are the expected results?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for Gavi’s immunisation programmes, and the IFFIm agreement enables funds to be used for any Gavi-approved immunisation programme. However, reallocation between components requires alignment with Gavi’s strategic priorities and is subject to the terms of the legally binding pledges.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The UK’s pledges to IFFIm are legally binding with fixed payment profiles, limiting flexibility to adjust priorities mid-programme. However, Gavi can allocate frontloaded funds based on evolving needs within its immunisation programmes.
how_flexibility.quote: Merging these programmes does not change the purpose for which the funds were allocated to Gavi through IFFIm. The IFFIm agreement enables the funds to be used for any Gavi approved immunisation programme. (D0005419.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (IFFIm Treasury Manager) → Gavi (implementer)
how_efficiency.quote: Payments will be due at the same time as our existing grant agreements. The FCDO IFFIm programme manager will make the additional payment at the same time as existing planned payments. (D0001188.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Preferred payment profile (2026-2029)
Option 2: Earlier payments starting 2025/26
Option 3: Extended payments beyond 2030
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (Option 1) was chosen because it aligns the end date of the UK’s legally binding IFFIm commitments with existing commitments, backloads funding to reduce pressure on earlier years, spreads funding beyond 2025/26, minimises the discounting ‘cost’, and avoids committing to Gavi beyond 2030 (the end of the Gavi 6.0 period). It also keeps the level of funding committed to Gavi 2026-30 below 10% of the 2021-25 commitment.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (avoiding overcommitment in stretched budget years)
flexibility (spreading payments over fewer years to reduce discounting costs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exchange rate fluctuations affecting the value of UK contributions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Contributions are hedged to lock in future value at the point the grant agreement is signed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial market conditions increasing the cost of borrowing for IFFIm
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFFIm has historically borrowed at below-donor cost of funds and maintains a buffer (25.9% of pledges) to protect lenders against adverse credit events.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Gavi countries falling into arrears with the IMF, triggering grant payment condition reductions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The grant payment condition is a standard feature of IFFIm contributions, and the UK accepts this as part of the mechanism’s risk-sharing design.

why_rationale.quote: In the recommended option 1, Gavi receive a total £439m 2022-30; £300m frontloaded in 2022-25 and £139m 2026-30 as the UK pay their commitment to IFFIm. UK contributions to IFFIm will total £461m. This is the preferred option because it brings the end date of our legally binding IFFIm commitments in line with existing IFFIm commitments; it backloads the funding, reducing the pressure on earlier years where existing commitments already take up considerable headroom; it spreads the funding beyond 2025/26; it minimises the number of years we spread the commitment over thereby reducing the discounting ‘cost’ and avoiding committing to Gavi beyond 2030 which is the end of the Gavi 6.0 period; and it brings the level of funding committed to Gavi 2026-30 below 10% of our 2021-25 commitment. (D0001188.odt, Table 1)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope of IFFIm and Gavi’s immunisation programmes requires a multilateral delivery structure, as no single country or regional partner could manage the scale or complexity of frontloading funds for worldwide vaccine delivery. The need for financial market access and bond issuance further necessitates the involvement of the World Bank as Treasury Manager.
q27_constraints_detail: Global immunisation goals require a multilateral partner (Gavi) with worldwide reach
Frontloading mechanism necessitates a Treasury Manager (World Bank) capable of issuing bonds on international capital markets
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The financing mechanism objective (frontloading donor pledges) determines the delivery structure: IFFIm must issue bonds backed by legally binding pledges, requiring a Treasury Manager (World Bank) and a multilateral implementer (Gavi) to allocate funds. The long-term, large-scale nature of the funding also necessitates annual oversight rather than more intensive management.
q28_linkages: Frontloading requirement → Need for bond issuance → World Bank as Treasury Manager
Global immunisation goals → Multilateral implementer (Gavi) with country-level partnerships
Legally binding pledges → Fixed payment profiles → Limited flexibility in fund reallocation
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The documents do not explicitly discuss equity vs. efficiency trade-offs. However, the mechanism’s design prioritises efficiency (frontloading funds at low cost) while relying on Gavi’s governance to ensure equitable access to immunisation. The UK’s burden share of results (~25%) reflects a balance between major donor influence and multilateral decision-making.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (financial market exposure, exchange rates, IMF arrears) is managed through annual reviews and the World Bank’s role as Treasury Manager, which provides stability. The ‘grant payment condition’ acts as a risk-sharing mechanism but does not require intensive oversight beyond standard annual reviews.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: No explicit capacity building is included, as IFFIm is a financing mechanism rather than a technical assistance programme. The roles of partners (World Bank as Treasury Manager, Gavi as implementer) are shaped by their existing capacities to manage bond issuance and global immunisation programmes, respectively.
intersections.quote: IFFIm is a flexible financing mechanism, accelerating the delivery of vaccines by making large volumes of future donor funding immediately available for Gavi programmes as and when needed. (D0005419.odt, Overview of IFFIm)

key_programme_risks: Exchange rate fluctuations reducing the value of UK contributions
Adverse financial market conditions increasing IFFIm’s cost of borrowing
Gavi countries falling into arrears with the IMF, triggering the grant payment condition
Discounting costs of future payments reducing the present value of pledges

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Contributions are hedged to lock in future value at the point the grant agreement is signed.
IFFIm maintains a buffer (25.9% of pledges) to protect lenders and has historically borrowed at below-donor cost of funds.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: IMF arrears triggering grant payment condition
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: This is a standard feature of IFFIm contributions, accepted as part of the mechanism’s design.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Discounting costs of spreading payments over many years
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The preferred payment profile minimises the number of years over which commitments are spread (2026-2029).

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: IFFIm has consistently scored A+ in FCDO annual reviews, demonstrating its effectiveness as a financing mechanism. Past performance shows it can deliver efficient frontloading even in challenging financial market conditions. Gavi’s strong track record (e.g., exceeding targets in Gavi 4.0) provides confidence in the mechanism’s ability to achieve results.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2022 addendum (D0005419.odt) consolidates multiple IFFIm programmes into one to streamline administrative and reporting procedures, based on lessons from parallel monitoring processes. The merger eliminates duplicate log frames and risk matrices while maintaining oversight of all components.
risks_lessons.quote: IFFIm scores consistently highly in FCDO annual reviews, achieving A+ in the last four reviews, demonstrating that IFFIm continues to be a highly effective and efficient financial instrument supporting Gavi’s ability to achieve equitable access to immunisation despite challenging financial market conditions. (D0001188.odt, What are the expected results?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: IFFIm can issue bonds against 74.1% of the present value of donor pledges, enabling Gavi to access £300m in proceeds from a £461m UK pledge (2021-25). The mechanism has frontloaded over £5bn for Gavi since inception, with the UK as the largest contributor.
financial_details.quote: IFFIm can issue bonds against a portion (74.1%) of the present value of donor pledges. This means that, in order for Gavi to receive £300 million in proceeds from IFFIm in the period 2021-25, the UK needs to contribute £461m over 2026-30. (D0001188.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: UNITAID (The International Drug Purchase Facility)
metadata.duration_text: Initial funding period – 2006/7 to 2007/8. Pending performance review in 2007/8, funding duration could extend to 2010/11.
metadata.quote: "To scale up access to treatment for HIV/AIDS, Malaria and Tuberculosis for poor people by funding programmes that (often through bulk international procurement) lower the price of quality drugs and diagnostics and accelerating the pace at which they are made available." (D0006737.odt, Project Headersheet)
metadata.duration_source: "Initial funding period – 2006/7 to 2007/8. Pending performance review in 2007/8, funding duration could extend to 2010/11." (D0006737.odt, Annex iii: Environmental Screening Note)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: UNITAID is a drug purchasing facility that channels long-term predictable contributions from donors into assured demand for drugs and diagnostics. Its mission is to scale up access to treatment for HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis by leveraging price reductions and accelerating availability of quality drugs.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UNITAID is a new international drug purchasing facility launched in September 2006. Its mission is ‘to contribute to scaling up access to treatment for HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis for people in developing countries by leveraging quality drugs and diagnostics price reductions and accelerating the pace at which they are made available.’" (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)
q3_expected_outputs: 125,000 children in 2007 will have access for the first time to Anti-Retro Virals (ARVs) for HIV-AIDS
100,000 HIV-AIDS sufferers will have access to 2nd line ARVs for the first time
$13 million in cost-efficient Artemisinin Combined Therapy (ACT) treatments will be provided to malaria sufferers in 2007
150,000 children in 2007 will be provided with paediatric TB treatments for the first time
New formulations for children under 5 will become available in 2008
Pricereductions achieved with partners (20% for pediatric ARVs, 20% for 2nd line ARVs, 10-40% for ACTs)
Decrease of delivery lead times for drugs
30 medicines prequalified by WHO
what_objectives.summary: UNITAID aims to improve access to affordable, quality drugs for HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis in developing countries through bulk procurement and price negotiations, with specific targets for pediatric treatments and second-line drugs.
what_objectives.quote: "UNITAID will fund paediatric ARVs for up to 125,000 children in 2007 across 34 countries... UNITAID will commit funds for scale-up of 2nd line ARVs to 70,000 patients in 26 countries... UNITAID will scale up existing Global Fund grants to provide up to USD 19 million for ACT treatments in eight countries by the end of 2007... UNITAID will provide appropriate-strength paediatric TB treatment for up to 150,000 children in 2007" (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: UNITAID is at a very early stage in its development and faces considerable risks to its successful operation, including poor coordination, poor selection of proposals, and governance issues. However, these are mitigated through a partnership approach and performance-based funding.
where_context.q5_source: "UNITAID is at a very early stage in its development and as such there are numerous risks to its successful operation." (D0006737.odt, Part 3: Risks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Failure to systematically fund sufficient supplies of injection devices has been identified by WHO as a key determinant of widespread reuse of syringes and needles. Poor logistics and storage practices can cause human or environmental harm, including use of out-of-date or inactivated drugs.
where_context.quote: "Failure to systematically fund sufficient supplies of injection devices has been identified by WHO as a key determinant of widespread reuse of syringes and needles in the absence of effective sterilization in immunization services." (D0006737.odt, Annex iii: Environmental Screening Note)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Executive Board includes representatives from founding countries (Brazil, Chile, France, Norway, UK), African and Asian countries, civil society networks, and WHO, indicating a balanced decision-making structure.
q10_capacity_building_details: support to WHO pre-qualification program to ensure speedy and efficient quality assurance of new products
improving effectiveness of supply of pharmaceutical delivery systems and related safety equipment
reinforcing hazardous healthcare waste management

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Host and Trustee for UNITAID, financial management, procurement oversight

partner_organizations.name: Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (GFATM)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for program implementation and scale-up

partner_organizations.name: Clinton Foundation HIV/AIDS Initiative (CHAI)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for market dynamics and procurement

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Partner for pediatric treatments and prequalification

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Brazil, Chile, France, Norway, UK
partner_organizations.role: Founding donors and Executive Board members

who_partners.quote: "UNITAID will work in close cooperation with and may eventually rely on organisations that have experience in procurement, price negotiation, shipment and handling, rather than be involved directly in procurement activities themselves." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: UNITAID uses a combination of long-term donor commitments (e.g., UK's 20-year pledge) and innovative funding mechanisms like solidarity contributions on air tickets. Funds are channeled through WHO as trustee, with procurement managed via partnerships with organizations like GFATM and CHAI.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNITAID has three main structures: an Executive Board (decision-making), a Consultative Forum (advisory), and a Secretariat (implementation). The Secretariat is lean (10-15 persons) and works with partners for procurement and delivery.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNITAID relies on existing organizations with experience in procurement and price negotiation, rather than competitive selection. Partners are chosen based on their expertise and alignment with UNITAID's goals.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNITAID will work in close cooperation with and may eventually rely on organisations that have experience in procurement, price negotiation, shipment and handling, rather than be involved directly in procurement activities themselves." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Executive Board is responsible for determining UNITAID’s objectives, approving financial commitments, and monitoring progress. It includes representatives from donor countries, recipient regions, civil society, and WHO. The Board reviews and approves all major decisions, including budget and work plans.
how_governance.quote: "The Board will be responsible for monitoring the implementation of approved recommendations... The UNITAID secretariat will prepare a report to support an annual work plan and budget that will be submitted for approval by the UNITAID Board." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated based on Board approval of proposals, with some flexibility to adjust based on performance and emerging needs, but major reallocations require Board approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: UNITAID’s strategy and interventions can be refined based on annual assessments and Board decisions, allowing for adjustments in response to performance and context changes.
how_flexibility.quote: "DFID’s continued support to UNITAID will be based on regular assessments of its performance. Our long term commitment will be managed after the first year of operation in three year tranches." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNITAID Secretariat → Implementing Partners (e.g., WHO, GFATM, CHAI)
how_efficiency.quote: "The administrative costs of UNITAID are estimated to remain below 3.0% of the expected revenues and to represent less than 5% of total expenditures." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

q24_alternatives_considered: in-country procurement systems (used by GFATM but deemed insufficient for volume and price reductions)
existing donor facilities (lack long-term assured funding)
Nordic bulk procurement models (limited in scope)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: UNITAID was chosen for its ability to provide long-term predictable funding, leverage monopsonistic buying power to reduce prices, and complement existing mechanisms like GFATM by focusing on international bulk procurement and assured demand.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (lower prices through bulk procurement)
risk mitigation (long-term funding reduces uncertainty for countries)
partner capacity (relying on experienced organizations like WHO and GFATM)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UNITAID may displace other sources of funding and become a funder of first resort, undermining existing systems.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Develop a clear policy on partnerships to ensure UNITAID complements rather than replaces other funding sources.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor coordination with Global Fund could lead to duplication or gaps.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Articulate a clear partnership agreement with GFATM to ensure complementarity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor selection of proposals could lead to inefficiencies and donor fatigue.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Develop an appraisal policy and criteria for selecting high-impact, high-quality projects.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Pooled procurement may not lead to expected price reductions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use strategic interventions to build on successful models and encourage best practices among partners.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (measurable health outcomes like treatments delivered)
equity (focus on low-income countries and vulnerable groups like children)
why_rationale.quote: "Securing long term financial resources for an international procurement mechanism is intended to provide developing countries with access to sustainable cost reductions... UNITAID is particularly suited to complement or support other innovative approaches such as Advance Market Commitments (AMCs) and Global Subsidies." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on low-income countries require UNITAID to rely on partners with existing procurement and logistics experience in developing contexts, limiting the pool of potential implementers to organizations like WHO, GFATM, and UNICEF.
q27_constraints_detail: need for partners with experience in procurement in low-income settings
requirement for compliance with WHO quality standards
logistical challenges in drug delivery and waste management
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of scaling up drug access through price reductions and accelerated delivery requires a multilateral, partnership-based structure to leverage existing procurement systems and avoid duplication.
q28_linkages: bulk procurement (WHAT) → need for experienced procurement partners (HOW)
price reductions (WHAT) → reliance on monopsonistic buying power via multilateral structure (HOW)
rapid delivery (WHAT) → use of existing logistics networks (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses the tension between achieving rapid, cost-efficient procurement (efficiency) and ensuring equitable access, particularly for children and marginalized groups. For example, pediatric formulations are prioritized despite higher costs, and at least 85% of funds are earmarked for low-income countries.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion (rapid scale-up vs ensuring access for vulnerable groups like children)
cost vs reach (lower prices vs ensuring quality and safety in logistics)
Northern expertise vs Southern ownership (reliance on multilateral partners vs local capacity building)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., governance challenges, coordination risks) leads to a milestone-based oversight structure with regular Board reviews and performance assessments to mitigate potential failures.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme, with UNITAID supporting WHO prequalification and training for healthcare waste management, which in turn shapes the roles of Southern partners in implementation and monitoring.
intersections.quote: "UNITAID will support the WHO pre-qualification program to ensure speedy and efficient quality assurance of new products in the identified UNITAID niches... UNITAID will have opportunities to promote good environmental policies and practices relevant to healthcare in the process of procuring, transporting, storing and use by end-user of medicines and diagnostics." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details and Annex iii: Environmental Screening Note)

key_programme_risks: Poor coordination of UNITAID activities complicates international systems
Poor selection of proposals leads to poor outcomes and donor fatigue
More pooled procurement does not lead to additional price reductions or delivery improvements
Other donors and institutions do not join UNITAID
UNITAID’s partnership with the Global Fund is not well defined, leading to delays
Poor governance leads to inefficient decision-making
UNITAID displaces spending from other sources without increasing overall resources
Delays in production of joint assessments delay donor support
UNITAID supports programmes with poor procurement systems, leading to financial losses
Political will of founder members diminishes over time

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor coordination of UNITAID activities complicates international systems
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Mitigated by a partnership approach that makes use of and helps to improve existing systems.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor selection of proposals leads to poor outcomes, promoting donor fatigue and undermining UNITAID’s potential
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Development of an appraisal policy will help.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: More pooled procurement and AMT does not lead to additional price reductions or delivery improvements
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strategic interventions to build on partners’ successful models and to encourage partners to replicate successful models and best practices.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Other donors and institutions do not join UNITAID
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demonstrating UNITAID’s added value and communicating its success to potential members will mitigate this risk.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNITAID’s partnership with the Global Fund not well enough set out leading to delays or poor implementation
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Current work on the partnership will help.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor Governance leads to inefficient decision making and poor effectiveness
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Current Board discussions on Governance arrangements will be critical.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNITAID displaces spending from other sources which does not lead to increased resources for the three diseases
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Mitigated by continuous attention to UNITAID’s additional nature and complementarity with other partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in the production of the joint assessment in 2007 which would delay subsequent donor support
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Ensure timely production of assessments through performance-based management.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNITAID supports programmes with poor procurement systems that result in loss of money through incompetence and/or irregularities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Applying appropriate due diligence to partners’ procurement cycle systems.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The political will of founder members diminishes over time along with their long term commitment, including the possibility that Air Passenger Levies do not survive domestic elections
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain momentum and produce some immediate results to safeguard commitment.

fcas_specific_lessons: Ensure that UNITAID programmes complement investment in pro-poor health system strengthening, as Global Health Partnerships can operate within (and exacerbate) systems that are far from pro-poor.
Address gender inequalities in access to treatment, as women and girls are disproportionately affected by HIV/AIDS, TB, and malaria in FCAS contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from GAVI’s central purchasing of Hib vaccines (which drove prices up) and GFATM’s procurement (which found few statistically significant relationships between order size and price reductions) highlight the need for careful market analysis and strategic intervention to achieve price reductions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: UNITAID’s approach includes regular performance assessments and adaptive management to refine its strategy based on lessons from implementation (e.g., the 2007 joint assessment will inform adjustments to the business model).
risks_lessons.quote: "UNITAID is at a very critical stage of its development, needing to set up internal capacities and systems as well as demonstrate success through its interventions on the ground, and faces considerable risks... We can mitigate these risks partly by positioning as a donor on the Executive Board, and UNITAID’s own performance will guide our future commitments." (D0006737.odt, Part 3: Risks)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UNITAID’s long-term funding model is designed to leverage additional contributions from other donors and innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., air ticket levies), with total estimated contributions rising from $53 million in 2006 to $346 million by 2010.
financial_details.quote: "The administrative costs of UNITAID are estimated to remain below 3.0% of the expected revenues and to represent less than 5% of total expenditures... At least 85% of UNITAID funds will be spent in low income countries." (D0006737.odt, Part 1: Project details)

metadata.programme_name: Poorest States Inclusive Growth Programme (PSIG)
metadata.quote: "Up to £65 million over 7 years (2012-2019) - £30 million for expanding access to financial services through technical assistance, and £35 million of returnable capital for promoting pro-poor investment in India’s poorest states." (4939477.odt, Project Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Up to £65 million over 7 years (2012-2019)" (4939477.odt, Project Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (£35m returnable capital for impact investing) with implementation research (testing microfinance models) and capacity building (women's empowerment). It aims to both deliver services (financial inclusion) and generate evidence on what works in pro-poor investment.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The project will support the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI)... to develop and expand two types of work in India’s poorest states: Component 1: Micro Finance and Women’s Empowerment; Component 2: Impact Investing" (4939477.odt, Project Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 12 million poor people reached with financial services (70% poor/borderline poor)
9 million people experience ≥33% income increase vs non-beneficiaries
5 million women report improved social status/mobility
£676m economic benefit to poorest states
£56m capital leveraged for SME investments
£10m increased disposable income for poor
Policy/institutional environment for responsible financial services
New institutions/models providing savings/loans/insurance
Private sector entities benefiting poor as producers/consumers
Improved women's financial literacy and health/nutrition awareness
what_objectives.summary: PSIG aims to catalyze inclusive growth in India's poorest states through two components: 1) expanding microfinance with women's empowerment, and 2) promoting impact investments that generate both financial returns and poverty reduction benefits.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact of the PSIG is ‘Poor and vulnerable people, especially women, in the low income states benefit from economic growth through enhanced private investment and better access to financial services’" (4939477.odt, Strategic Case - Impact and Outcome)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in India's poorest states with weak financial infrastructure but not active conflict. The document notes 'medium/manageable potential risk' in climate/environment sensitivity analysis (Category B).
where_context.q5_source: "On the basis of the Sensitivity Analysis, both options are categorised as Category B: Medium / manageable potential risk/opportunity" (4939477.odt, Appraisal Case - Climate and Environment Sensitivity Analysis)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory uncertainty after the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis created investor hesitation ('curtailment of lending to MFIs across the country'). Poor states attract only 20% of domestic/2.4% of foreign investment despite housing 50% of population due to perceived high risks. Weak infrastructure and bureaucracy rank among top business constraints (World Bank Doing Business Survey 2010).
where_context.quote: "Private investors generally perceive the risks of investment in these states to be too high... Eight of India’s major low income states house 50% of India’s population but account for only one fifth of domestic and 2.4% of foreign direct investments" (4939477.odt, Strategic Case - Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: SIDBI (Indian government-promoted institution) designs and implements both components with DFID providing funding and oversight. Investment decisions for Component 2 are made by SIDBI Venture Capital's Investment Committee (mutually agreed members).
q10_capacity_building_details: training women clients in financial/business practices
promoting women's health/nutrition awareness
recruiting specialist women's organizations
mentoring/building capacity of entrepreneurs (Component 2)
institutional strengthening of MFIs/SHGs
policy dialogue with regulators

partner_organizations.name: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer for Component 1 (Microfinance) and parent organization for Component 2

partner_organizations.name: SIDBI Venture Capital Limited (SVCL)
partner_organizations.role: Manager of Component 2 (Impact Investing Fund)

partner_organizations.name: Specialist women's organizations (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Facilitate women's empowerment discussions/training

partner_organizations.name: Local microfinance institutions (MFIs) and SHG Promoting Institutions (SHPIs)
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery partners for financial inclusion

partner_organizations.name: State/central regulators (RBI, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Policy dialogue partners

who_partners.quote: "SIDBI will be contracted to deliver component 1 subject to the commercial bid. Component 2 will be managed by SIDBI Venture Capital Limited (SVCL) - a wholly-owned subsidiary of SIDBI" (4939477.odt, Project Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Component 1 uses a contract with SIDBI (£30m for technical assistance). Component 2 provides returnable capital (£35m) to SVCL's impact investment fund, structured as equity/debt/guarantees with expected financial returns.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Component 1: SIDBI manages microfinance expansion as a contractor. Component 2: SVCL operates as an impact investment fund manager with an Investment Committee (joint DFID-SIDBI members) approving investments. DFID retains oversight through annual reviews and mid/end-term evaluations.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (SIDBI selected based on prior relationship)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: SIDBI was chosen due to its "leading role in SME development", prior successful DFID partnerships (CASHE/NMSPI programmes), and existing microfinance expertise. SVCL is its wholly-owned subsidiary specializing in developmental investments.
how_mechanism.quote: "SIDBI is a well respected Government-sponsored institution... It has played a leading role in Small and Medium Enterprise (SMEs) development... SIDBI has also pioneered the growth of the microfinance sector in India, primarily as a result of an earlier DFID funded project" (4939477.odt, Strategic Case - Fit with Priorities)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Component 2 investments require approval by an Investment Committee with mutually agreed members (DFID + SIDBI).
how_governance.q17_governance_details: Annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews by DFID; Investment Committee for Component 2; mid-term (year 3) and end-term reviews. M&E framework includes computerised MIS and independent evaluations.
how_governance.quote: "DFID will undertake annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews to assess progress, a mid-term review in year three, and an end-term review... An Investment Committee which reviews and approves investments, with members mutually agreed, will be established" (4939477.odt, Management Case & Component 2 details)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between states (e.g., 40% minimum in 3 focus states; up to 20% in developed states if beneficiaries are poor from target states) but require agreement on investment criteria. Support beyond 2015 subject to mid-term review.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Investment criteria and sector focus will be reviewed annually and adapted based on "changing context, emerging evidence and lessons". DFID can increase/decrease financial commitment based on performance.
how_flexibility.quote: "The overall approach will be reviewed and adapted based on changing context, emerging evidence and lessons... DFID will increase or decrease the overall financial commitment against this component based on performance" (4939477.odt, Component 2 & Financial Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → SIDBI/SVCL → end beneficiaries (no additional sub-grantee layer mentioned)
how_efficiency.quote: "Of the total budget of £65 million, £53m will be spent on programme delivery; £6m for monitoring and evaluation; and £6 million for management and advice" (4939477.odt, Project Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Commercially sustainable approaches with minimal donor funds (CHOSEN)
Option 2: Fully grant-funded approaches with subsidies
Option 3: Do nothing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 was selected for its higher value-for-money (BCR 2.02 vs 1.7 for Option 2), sustainability (services continue post-project), and market-distortion minimization. The economic appraisal showed it would reach more clients (12m vs 4m for Option 2) with lower costs per client (£2 vs £5).
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (catalytic capital for untested models)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Investment failures in Component 2 (some businesses may fail despite due diligence)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified portfolio approach; rigorous selection criteria; mentoring support to entrepreneurs; expectation that overall fund will provide net benefits.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on SIDBI as single implementer
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SIDBI's strong track record (prior DFID projects reached 12m clients); complementary World Bank project reduces overlap; performance-based funding adjustments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory changes affecting microfinance (post-Andhra Pradesh crisis)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Policy dialogue component; establishment of a think tank to monitor sector health; adherence to new RBI regulations.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 1... uses commercially sustainable approaches to provide development benefits, leverage private mainstream capital... This option scores highest on VfM (BCR 2.02), sustainability, and minimising market distortions" (4939477.odt, Appraisal Case - Comparison of Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's focus on India's poorest states (with weak financial ecosystems) necessitated partnering with SIDBI, an apex government-backed DFI with existing branches/networks in these regions. Local MFIs/SHPIs were required to have "grounded" knowledge of state-specific challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited pool of financial institutions operating in target states (only 20% of microfinance clients nationwide)
Need for partners with existing regulatory relationships (SIDBI sits on RBI's consultative panels)
Requirement for Hindi/regional language capacity in service delivery
Partners must navigate state-level bureaucratic variations (e.g., "inefficient bureaucracy" ranked as a top business constraint)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of financial inclusion + women's empowerment required a mixed delivery structure: 1) SIDBI's technical assistance for scalable microfinance models, and 2) SVCL's impact fund for flexible equity investments. The need for both rapid reach (12m clients) and adaptive learning (RCTs for women's components) shaped the combination of contract-based implementation and returnable capital.
q28_linkages: Women's empowerment goals → embedded capacity building in Component 1 (training/participatory learning)
Impact investing's "double bottom line" → fund manager structure for Component 2 (SVCL)
Policy influence objective → inclusion of regulators in governance/stakeholder dialogues
Evidence generation needs → allocation of £6m for M&E with control groups
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses balancing: 1) Speed vs inclusion: "cheaper more innovative operating models" to reach 12m clients while adding women's empowerment costs; 2) Risk vs reach: investing in "untested business models" in poorest states despite higher failure risks; 3) Cost vs depth: providing "comprehensive financial services" beyond micro-credit increases per-client costs but improves outcomes.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Higher per-client costs (£2 vs £1.80 in prior projects) due to adding women's empowerment components
Acceptance of some business failures in Component 2 to achieve "catalytic" market effects
Allocation of 45% of funds to financial inclusion (proven) vs 55% to impact investing (emerging)
Geographic focus on 8 states with 50% of India's poor but only 20% of microfinance penetration
intersections.risk_affects_management: The "medium/manageable" risk profile (Category B) led to milestone-based oversight (annual reviews + Investment Committee approvals) rather than intensive day-to-day management. Higher perceived risks in poorest states justified using returnable capital to "minimise distortions" and attract commercial follow-on investment.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: SIDBI's existing capacity (branches in target states, prior DFID projects) enabled it to take the lead role, while SVCL's specialized impact investing experience justified its fund manager position. The need to build MFI capacity shaped the technical assistance component, and women's low financial literacy (27% decision-making on healthcare) necessitated embedded training roles for partner NGOs.
intersections.quote: "The poorest states also lag behind other parts of India in access to private sector investment... Private investors generally perceive the risks of investment in these states to be too high... [Thus] DFID capital, which has a higher appetite for risk, [will] support the establishment and expansion of these businesses" (4939477.odt, Strategic Case - Context & Component 2)

key_programme_risks: Regulatory uncertainty post-Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis
Investment failures in early-stage businesses (Component 2)
Over-indebtedness of microfinance clients
Weak institutional capacity of local MFIs in target states
Political/economic instability in poorest states affecting investor confidence
Gender backlash (e.g., increased domestic violence with women's economic participation)
Climate/environmental shocks disproportionately affecting poor clients
Crowding out of commercial capital in Component 2 investments

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Policy dialogue with RBI/state regulators; establishment of a think tank to monitor sector health; adherence to new microfinance regulations.
Diversified portfolio; rigorous due diligence; mentoring support; expectation that successful investments will offset failures.
Responsible finance standards; client education; limits on multiple lending; adherence to RBI's microfinance guidelines.
Technical assistance to build institutional infrastructure; cheaper operating models; leveraging SIDBI's existing networks.
Participatory learning cycles addressing domestic violence; involving men in dialogues; monitoring social impacts via RCTs.
Promotion of climate-resilient products (e.g., weather insurance, cook stoves) and ESG safeguards for investments.
Additionality criteria (first/second-round investor only); tracking investment trends to avoid overlap; focusing on underserved segments.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh crisis: "A positive result was a review of regulations by India’s central bank" leading to improved responsible finance standards.

Need for "patient capital" in FCAS-like contexts: "Patient (returnable) capital is increasingly viewed as an effective tool to facilitate market-based solutions to poverty reduction since it minimises distortions and allows recycling of scarce philanthropic capital."

Importance of local grounding: "Locally grounded agencies like SIDBI... can utilise DFID capital, which has a higher appetite for risk, to support the establishment and expansion of these businesses."
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior DFID-SIDBI programmes (CASHE, NMSPI) demonstrated that: 1) Small donor funds (£12m) could catalyze microfinance expansion (6.6m clients at £1.80/client); 2) Technical assistance is critical for institutional infrastructure; 3) Women's empowerment components require structured inputs (RCTs showed improvements in neonatal mortality with participatory learning); 4) Leveraging mainstream loan funds is possible with viable MFI models.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added women's empowerment as a core component (not just financial access) based on evidence from SEWA Bank/Bangladesh studies showing 25-56% higher incomes for women clients; 2) Included ESG safeguards and climate-sensitive products (e.g., weather insurance) based on vulnerability assessments; 3) Structured Component 2 as returnable capital to address lessons on market distortions from grant-based approaches; 4) Expanded M&E budget to £6m (vs £1.2m in prior projects) to improve impact attribution.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID India has a good track record on promoting financial inclusion, having financed two successful all India programmes... These programmes have made a significant contribution to the evolution of the microfinance sector... However, the most populous and poorest states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, have not yet made significant gains... Some of these poorer states are now relatively better governed, and models of financial inclusion have since been established, which can be adapted and replicated" (4939477.odt, Strategic Case - Argument for DFID Intervening)

co_funding_partners.contribution: Up to 15% of Component 2 fund value from own resources

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Expected to leverage £5bn in loan funds (assuming 3 loans of INR 8,000 per beneficiary) and £56m in private capital for SME investments. Prior SIDBI-DFID projects leveraged £1.6-3x per £1m invested.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £35m (53.8%) returnable capital for Component 2; £30m (46.2%) technical assistance grants for Component 1
financial_details.quote: "Of the total budget of £65 million, £53m will be spent on programme delivery; £6m for monitoring and evaluation; and £6 million for management and advice... £30 million for expanding access to financial services through technical assistance, and £35 million of returnable capital for promoting pro-poor investment" (4939477.odt, Project Summary & Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Joint Global Health Trials Scheme
metadata.quote: "DFID will provide £36,000,000 over six years from 2014 to 2019 to the Joint Global Health Trials initiative in partnership with the Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Wellcome Trust." (3896966.odt, Intervention summary)
metadata.duration_source: "DFID will provide £36,000,000 over six years from 2014 to 2019 to the Joint Global Health Trials initiative in partnership with the Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Wellcome Trust."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to determine the efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness of health interventions in low- and middle-income countries. It also includes **capacity building** by encouraging partnerships between UK and developing country researchers and **implementation research** to test scalable health solutions. The goal is to improve health outcomes for the poor by generating robust evidence on what works.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DFID’s funding will support the best proposals to generate new knowledge about interventions that promise to contribute to the improvement of health in developing countries. Well conducted randomised controlled trials provide the opportunity to say definitely whether an intervention is or is not effective." (3896966.odt, Intervention summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Testing of new technologies for efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness
Better health in Africa and resource-poor Asia through proper assessment of healthcare interventions
Research focused on translational and implementation research relevant to developing countries (public health, health services, health systems)
Capacity development to strengthen the scientific research base (particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa)
Emerging publications and longer-term impacts (journal articles, patents, new products, policy influences)
At least 22 trials funded across Africa, Asia, and Latin America (malaria, TB, HIV, maternal/child health, neglected tropical diseases)
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds high-quality RCTs to generate evidence on effective health interventions in LMICs, with a focus on implementable results for major causes of mortality/morbidity. It combines research excellence with capacity strengthening and strategic partnerships.
what_objectives.quote: "The joint fund will deliver high quality and cutting edge research that will improve our understanding of what works to ensure evidence-based health systems, services and interventions." (3896966.odt, Expected results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in low- and middle-income countries with varying stability, including fragile contexts where health systems are weak. Risks include operational delays (e.g., ethics committees, drug imports) and financial overruns, but the partnership structure mitigates these through shared risk and robust MRC/Wellcome Trust systems.
where_context.q5_source: "Typical risks are for example, unanticipated delays caused by third parties, such as ethics committees, drug and placebo manufacturers, importing authorities, can create cost-overruns, and the findings from other trials which can affect the design and purpose of a trial after it has begun." (3896966.odt, Option A)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory hurdles (e.g., ethics approvals, drug imports) and weak institutional capacity in LMICs can delay trials and increase costs. Infrastructure limitations (e.g., lab facilities, supply chains) affect implementation of complex interventions. Data limitations may constrain the design or generalizability of trials.
where_context.quote: "In developing countries there are many unanswered questions about the efficacy, effectiveness, safety and cost-effectiveness of new (and some old) interventions, and clinical trials are the best way to address these." (3896966.odt, Why is UK support required?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **Joint Funders Review Committee** (comprising DFID, MRC, and Wellcome Trust) makes funding decisions, but the scheme explicitly allows **lead Principal Investigators (PIs) to be based in LMICs** (a departure from MRC’s standard rules). This enables Southern researchers to lead trials, with UK partners often providing technical/commercial expertise. The Wellcome Trust and MRC provide administrative/peer-review support, while DFID contributes strategic oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training through joint research partnerships
Mentorship via co-leadership of trials (Southern PIs with UK co-applicants)
Co-authorship on publications
Institutional strengthening (e.g., research units in Sub-Saharan Africa)
Use of MRC’s Researchfish system to track career progression of Southern researchers

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Development (DFID)
partner_organizations.role: Funder; strategic oversight; member of Joint Funders Review Committee

partner_organizations.name: Medical Research Council (MRC)
partner_organizations.role: Host institution; grant management; post-award oversight; peer review (adapted for LMIC PIs)

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder; leads Joint Funders Review Committee meetings; referee selection; due diligence on commercial/IP issues

partner_organizations.name: LMIC-based research institutions
partner_organizations.role: Lead or co-lead trials; implement interventions; data collection; local ethics approvals

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (e.g., GlaxoSmithKline, Gilead Sciences)
partner_organizations.role: Product donors (e.g., drugs for trials); technical partners (e.g., assays)

who_partners.quote: "The MRC have adapted their usual eligibility criteria and procedures to allow lead principal investigators (PIs) to be based either in the UK or in a developing country. In practice this means MRC eligibility applies but additionally for this scheme the lead PI can come from the developing country in which the study takes place." (3896966.odt, How is the JGHT scheme organised?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The scheme uses **competitive grants** awarded through annual calls for proposals. Funds are disbursed to successful applicants (UK or LMIC-based PIs) via the MRC’s grant management system, with joint oversight by DFID, MRC, and Wellcome Trust. Grants cover trial costs (e.g., personnel, interventions, monitoring) and are subject to milestone-based reporting.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **MRC hosts the scheme** and handles administration (calls, applications, post-award monitoring). The **Wellcome Trust leads the Joint Funders Review Committee** (scientific peer review, referee selection). **DFID provides funding and strategic oversight**. This tripartite structure leverages each partner’s strengths: MRC’s grant management, Wellcome Trust’s scientific rigor, and DFID’s development focus.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition ensures **high-quality, innovative proposals** are selected through rigorous peer review. The MRC/Wellcome Trust’s reputation attracts top-tier applicants, while the joint committee’s expertise (including Southern representation) ensures relevance to LMIC contexts. The process is designed to be **transparent and merit-based**, with acceptance rates around 10% for MRC/Wellcome Trust funding.
how_mechanism.quote: "The mechanism will improve funding decision processes by establishing a bespoke group of experts who will consider clinical trial applications in competition." (3896966.odt, What will we do?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Joint Funders Review Committee** includes representatives from DFID (Chief Scientific Adviser, Senior Health Adviser), MRC, and Wellcome Trust. It oversees: 1) Shortlisting of preliminary applications; 2) Referee and committee member selection; 3) Annual progress reviews; 4) Approval of supplements for cost overruns. Decisions are made collectively, with MRC/Wellcome Trust providing technical/scientific input and DFID ensuring alignment with development priorities.
how_governance.quote: "The Wellcome Trust lead on the administrative arrangements around the Joint Funders Review Committee meetings and supporting referee selection... DFID’s contribution is to provide financial resources and strategic oversight." (3896966.odt, How is the JGHT scheme organised?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between trials **with joint committee approval**, typically to address unanticipated delays (e.g., regulatory, supply chain) or emerging scientific opportunities. Supplements are awarded competitively from the scheme’s total allocation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted **annually** through the call specification, which is agreed jointly by DFID, MRC, and Wellcome Trust. This allows the scheme to respond to new evidence (e.g., trial results, WHO guideline changes) or shifting development needs (e.g., emerging diseases). However, major shifts require consensus among all three funders.
how_flexibility.quote: "The scope and definition of the scheme is contained in an **annual call specification** agreed between DFID, MRC and Wellcome Trust." (3896966.odt, How is the JGHT scheme organised?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **MRC/Wellcome Trust joint platform** → end-researchers (LMIC/UK PIs). The MRC and Wellcome Trust absorb management costs within their existing systems, minimizing overhead.
how_efficiency.quote: "As the percentage of DFID funding going to programme administration is less than 0.001% of our overall contribution, it is our view that the scheme still represents very good value for money." (4658834.odt, Amendment No. 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" counterfactual (no DFID investment in global health trials)
DFID funds specific RCT projects through competing organizations
DFID administers an in-house grants scheme
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **Joint Global Health Trials platform** was selected because it: 1) **Leverages £32M from MRC/Wellcome Trust** (total £68M pool); 2) Uses **tried-and-tested MRC/Wellcome Trust systems** (peer review, grant management); 3) **Shares financial/reputational risks** among partners; 4) **Encourages Southern leadership** via adapted eligibility criteria; 5) **Minimizes DFID’s administrative burden** (0.001% overhead); 6) **Aligns with DFID’s strategic priorities** (MDGs, neglected diseases). The alternative options were rejected due to higher costs, lower quality, or reduced leverage.
q25_decision_factors: speed (minimal setup time; annual calls predictable)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in trial implementation due to regulatory/commercial hurdles in LMICs (e.g., ethics approvals, drug imports).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Shared risk pool among funders; MRC’s experience with trial overruns; joint committee approval for supplements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Perceived imbalance in North-South power dynamics (e.g., UK institutions dominating bids).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit eligibility for LMIC-based PIs; Wellcome Trust/MRC’s global networks to encourage Southern applications; capacity-building embedded in trials.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High competition may exclude worthy but less polished Southern-led proposals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Wellcome Trust/MRC provide pre-application support; referee panels include Southern experts; emphasis on implementable results for LMICs.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (low overhead costs absorbed by MRC/Wellcome Trust)
why_rationale.quote: "Given the costs and benefits and the associated risks outlined above, the judgement is that **Option A (DFID continues to fund the Joint Global Health Trials scheme) is the best value for money option** because it... leverages funding from a number of sources for research; helps share the risk...; represents the most cost-effective option with one layer of management costs." (3896966.odt, Comparison of options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **LMIC operating context** constrains partner selection by: 1) Requiring partners with **local regulatory expertise** (e.g., ethics committees, drug imports); 2) Limiting eligible PIs to those based in **low/middle-income countries** (excluding high-income countries); 3) Prioritizing institutions with **existing research infrastructure** (e.g., labs, data systems) to mitigate implementation risks. This excludes many Northern-only institutions unless they partner with Southern leads.
q27_constraints_detail: Ethics/regulatory approvals in LMICs require local partners with navigational experience.
Weak institutional capacity in some LMICs necessitates partnerships with stronger Northern institutions.
Logistical challenges (e.g., supply chains for drugs) favor partners with in-country presence.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for high-quality RCTs** determines the platform structure by: 1) Requiring **rigorous peer review** (hence leveraging MRC/Wellcome Trust systems); 2) Demanding **shared risk management** (due to trial costs/uncertainty); 3) Necessitating **Southern PI eligibility** to ensure context-relevant research. The **focus on implementable results** drives the joint governance model (DFID + MRC + Wellcome Trust) to balance scientific excellence with development impact.
q28_linkages: RCTs’ high cost → Need for **leveraged funding** → Platform with multiple funders.
Need for LMIC relevance → **Southern PI eligibility** → Adapted MRC rules.
Complex trial risks → **Joint oversight committee** → Shared decision-making.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The scheme explicitly balances **equity** (Southern leadership, capacity building) with **efficiency** (leveraging MRC/Wellcome Trust’s high-competition systems). Trade-offs include: 1) **Higher administrative costs** to accommodate Southern PIs (e.g., due diligence for LMIC institutions) vs. **faster disbursement** through MRC systems; 2) **Inclusive eligibility criteria** (LMIC PIs) vs. **risk of lower success rates** if proposals lack polish; 3) **Longer review times** for complex Southern-led trials vs. **rigor of peer review**.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Open competition favors established institutions, but adapted rules enable Southern PIs.
Cost vs. reach: Leveraging MRC/Wellcome Trust systems reduces overhead but may limit flexibility for LMIC-specific needs.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern partners often provide technical rigor, while Southern partners ensure contextual relevance.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate-risk LMIC context** (regulatory delays, weak institutions) increases **oversight intensity**: milestone-based reporting, joint committee approval for supplements, and MRC’s trial monitoring systems. However, the **shared risk pool** among funders reduces the need for intensive DFID micro-management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives **shape partner roles** by: 1) Requiring **co-leadership models** (Southern PI + UK co-applicant) to transfer skills; 2) Embedding **mentorship** in trial design (e.g., joint protocols, co-authorship); 3) Using **MRC’s Researchfish system** to track Southern researchers’ career progression post-trial.
intersections.quote: "The MRC have adapted their usual eligibility criteria and procedures to allow lead principal investigators (PIs) to be based either in the UK or in a developing country... The expectation is that this will stimulate and encourage new partnerships between the best scientists in the UK and in developing countries." (3896966.odt, How is the JGHT scheme organised?)

key_programme_risks: Regulatory delays in LMICs (e.g., ethics committees, drug imports) causing cost overruns.
Findings from other trials mid-study requiring design changes.
Low capacity in some LMIC institutions to manage complex trials.
Private sector disengagement for neglected diseases (market failure).
Reputational risk if trials fail or have negative outcomes.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Shared risk pool among funders; MRC’s experience with trial overruns; joint committee approval for supplements.
Co-leadership with Northern partners; embedded training; MRC/Wellcome Trust pre-award support.
Public-private partnerships (e.g., GlaxoSmithKline donations in DART/ARROW trials); DFID’s focus on global public goods.
Rigorous peer review; joint branding; focus on implementable results to demonstrate impact.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts, **local partnerships** are critical for navigating ethics approvals and community engagement.
Flexible funding (e.g., supplements) is essential to adapt to **unpredictable delays** (e.g., conflict, epidemics).
**Simplified protocols** (e.g., DART trial’s reduced lab testing) can improve feasibility in resource-poor settings.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **first phase (2010–2012)** demonstrated that: 1) **Joint funding** reduces piecemeal support and accelerates trials; 2) **Southern-led trials** are viable with adapted eligibility; 3) **Predictable annual calls** allow teams to prepare stronger proposals. Examples like the **AQUAMAT** (artesunate for malaria) and **DART** (HIV treatment simplification) trials showed how RCTs can **change global practice** (e.g., WHO guideline updates).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Amended MRC eligibility** to allow LMIC PIs (previously UK-only). 2) **Added a full-time administrative assistant** (2014 amendment) to improve due diligence and M&E. 3) **Annual call specifications** to adjust priorities based on emerging evidence.
risks_lessons.quote: "The MRC’s independent Global Health Group (GHG) reviewed the scheme at its last meeting in November 2012. The group concluded that there remains a major global need for research that will deliver implementable interventions to target the major causes of mortality and morbidity in low and middle income countries... They concluded that there is likely to continue to be high quality, innovative proposals submitted to the scheme." (3896966.odt, Continuing the JGHT scheme)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The scheme leverages £32M from MRC and Wellcome Trust against DFID’s £36M, creating a total pool of £68M. This is a **1:0.89 leverage ratio** (£1 DFID : £0.89 partners).
financial_details.quote: "DFID will provide £36,000,000 over six years from 2014 to 2019... The Wellcome Trust and MRC are together willing to contribute up to £12,000,000 and £20,000,000 respectively... giving total available funds of up to £68,000,000." (3896966.odt, Intervention summary)

metadata.programme_name: Climate Public Private Partnership (CP3)
metadata.duration_text: Original project start date: 16/04/2010; no explicit end date mentioned in addendum, but original documents imply multi-year programme
metadata.quote: "The Climate Public Private Partnership (CP3) is an innovative joint initiative managed by the Department for International Development (DFID) and the Department for Business, Energy and Industry Strategy (BEIS), and funded through the UK’s International Climate Finance (ICF). Its aim is to catalyse increased investment from the private sector into low-carbon climate resilient (LCCR) projects in developing countries, in order to both support sustainable development and tackle climate change." (55795643.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 16/04/2010" (55795643.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CP3 is designed to catalyse private sector investment in low-carbon climate resilient projects in developing countries by acting as an anchor investor in private equity funds. It uses public funds to leverage private capital through equity investments and technical assistance, aiming to demonstrate commercial viability and reduce perceived risks for private investors.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Climate Public Private Partnership (CP3) is an innovative joint initiative... Its aim is to catalyse increased investment from the private sector into low-carbon climate resilient (LCCR) projects in developing countries, in order to both support sustainable development and tackle climate change." (55795643.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: £50 million equity investment in the IFC Catalyst Fund (global focus)
£60 million equity investment in Asia Climate Partners (Asia focus)
Technical Assistance Facility (Seed Capital Assistance Facility) supporting first-time fund managers in frontier markets
3,989 MW of renewable energy capacity created
8,758 jobs created
4.5 million tonnes of CO2 emissions avoided
US$9,164 million of public and private investment leveraged (73% from private sector)
100+ investments made through intermediaries
what_objectives.summary: CP3 uses public equity investments and technical assistance to catalyse private sector funding for low-carbon projects in developing countries, demonstrating commercial viability and reducing investment risks.
what_objectives.quote: "CP3 has made over 100 investments through its intermediaries, and its recent Mid Term Evaluation found that CP3 investments have produced a total of 3,989MW of RE capacity, creating 8,758 jobs, and avoiding 4.5m tons of CO2 emissions." (55795643.odt, Summary Information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in developing countries with market failures in climate finance, including information asymmetries and coordination problems, but does not focus on FCAS or high-conflict zones. The risks are primarily financial and market-related rather than security or political instability.
where_context.q5_source: "The problems are worse in the PE market for those investors... placing funds with a fund manager. The LP... want a fund manager with the expertise to make higher returns... in a new area like climate friendly investing in emerging markets, where managers lack track records, LPs can find it almost impossible to tell who to invest with." (3744949.odt, Market Failures section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: These constraints create barriers for private equity fund managers to raise capital and for investors to identify viable opportunities, slowing the growth of climate-friendly investments in developing countries. For example, lack of track records in climate investments makes it difficult for Limited Partners (LPs) to assess fund managers, and coordination problems delay project implementation due to unfamiliarity with new sectors like biomass or energy service companies.
where_context.quote: "In climate the issues are compounded by widespread publicity around investment failures and regulatory problems... in a new area like climate friendly investing in emerging markets, where managers lack track records, LPs can find it almost impossible to tell who to invest with." (3744949.odt, Market Failures section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK Government (DFID/BEIS) manages the programme and sets strategic direction, while implementation is carried out by international financial institutions (IFC, ADB) and private sector fund managers. Decision-making power rests with Northern institutions, though Southern partners (e.g., ADB, local fund managers) execute investments.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to first-time fund managers (Seed Capital Assistance Facility)
support for project pipeline development
knowledge sharing on environmental and social governance (ESG) standards
training and mentorship for emerging fund managers via IFC and ADB

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC) Asset Management Company
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager for the Catalyst Fund (global focus)
partner_organizations.location: Multilateral (headquartered in Washington D.C., operates globally)

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Co-manager of Asia Climate Partners fund (Asia focus)

partner_organizations.name: Robeco and Orix
partner_organizations.role: Co-managers of Asia Climate Partners fund

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)
partner_organizations.role: Administrator of the Seed Capital Assistance Facility (SCAF)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector investors (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies)
partner_organizations.role: Co-investors in CP3 funds
partner_organizations.location: Global (mix of Northern and Southern institutions)

partner_organizations.name: Monitoring and Evaluation agents (Integrity Global, Climate Policy Initiative, LTS International)
partner_organizations.role: Independent evaluators for programme performance

who_partners.quote: "The UK Government’s participation as an equity investor... will help accelerate movement of money into the developing country climate investment area and reduce perceived and actual investor risks." (3744949.odt, The UK Role section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: CP3 uses equity investments (£110 million) on pari passu (equal footing) terms with private investors to demonstrate commercial viability, combined with grant-based technical assistance (£20 million initially, later adjusted) to support first-time fund managers and project development. The equity investments are structured as limited partnership stakes in private equity funds.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through two primary equity funds (IFC Catalyst Fund and Asia Climate Partners) and a technical assistance facility (SCAF). Day-to-day operations are delegated to professional fund managers (IFC Asset Management, ADB, Robeco, Orix), while DFID/BEIS retain oversight and strategic control. The Seed Capital Assistance Facility is administered by UNEP.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct selection of IFC and ADB as multilateral partners)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IFC and ADB were selected due to their existing expertise in climate finance, private equity fund management, and regional presence in developing countries. The UK Government acted as an anchor investor to catalyse additional private sector participation, leveraging the multilateral institutions' credibility and networks.
