how_mechanism.quote: "The CP3 Platform will comprise three vehicles: The CP3 (Asia) Fund... managed by a private sector fund manager; The IFC Catalyst Fund (CF)... managed by the IFC Asset Management Company...; Technical Assistance and Project Development Facility (TAPDF)... opened as a new window in the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG)." (3744949.odt, Structure section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by DFID and BEIS in collaboration with monitoring and evaluation agents (Integrity Global, Climate Policy Initiative, LTS International). The addendum mentions a review process to rationalize the logframe and reporting structure, suggesting a governance mechanism for adaptive management.
how_governance.quote: "DFID and BEIS, in concert with the programme’s monitoring and evaluation providers will continue to assess the effectiveness of the programme on an ongoing basis." (55795643.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds returned from Asia Climate Partners (due to early end of investment period) were reinvested in other programmes, indicating some flexibility in reallocation. However, the core equity investments in IFC Catalyst Fund and technical assistance facility appear fixed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The addendum describes adjustments to the logframe, reporting indicators, and methodologies for additionality/attribution based on mid-term evaluation findings. This suggests an adaptive management approach where changes require approval but are implemented based on learning.
how_flexibility.quote: "The objective of this addendum is to rationalise the CP3 logframe and programme management approach to reflect how the programme has evolved over its lifetime... These changes will simplify the results and reporting process for the programme and focus on its key activities." (55795643.odt, Summary Information)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (DFID/BEIS) → Fund Managers (IFC/ADB/UNEP) → Sub-funds/Projects → End Investments (companies/infrastructure). The technical assistance facility adds a parallel layer for capacity building.
how_efficiency.quote: "The total UK support is now worth £51,061,207.94, due to the return of uninvested funds from Asia Climate Partners, which have been reinvested in other programmes." (55795643.odt, Additional Support section)

q24_alternatives_considered: pure grant financing (rejected due to lack of demonstration effect for private sector)
debt financing (considered but deemed less effective for early-stage, high-risk climate projects)
direct project investments (rejected in favor of fund-of-funds approach for scalability)
carbon credit mechanisms (not the primary focus of CP3)
guarantees (used by other ICF programmes but not central to CP3)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The private equity fund-of-funds model was chosen to address critical market failures in climate finance: 1) Information asymmetries (investors lack track records to assess fund managers), 2) Coordination problems (difficulty in bringing together equity, debt, and project developers), and 3) First-mover disadvantages in emerging markets. By acting as an anchor investor, the UK could signal viability to other investors, while the fund structure allowed for professional management and risk-sharing with private capital.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (leveraging £1 of public money to mobilize £7+ of private capital)
risk-mitigation (pari passu terms reduce perceived risk for private investors)
experience (IFC and ADB have existing climate finance portfolios)
speed (accelerating private sector entry into climate markets)
equity (focus on low-carbon development in emerging economies)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to attract sufficient private co-investors, leaving funds dominated by public money
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK's anchor investment and 'signalling effect' to attract pension funds and sovereign wealth funds; commercial fund management to ensure market-rate returns.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund managers lack expertise in climate sectors or emerging markets
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance facility (SCAF) to support first-time fund managers; IFC/ADB's existing networks and due diligence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market failures persist despite public intervention (e.g., regulatory changes, economic downturns)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified portfolio across regions and sectors; adaptive management via mid-term reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Perception of funds as 'too developmental' deterring private investors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Commercial fund structures with no public sector interference in investment decisions; focus on financial returns.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of public funds to leverage private capital)
efficiency (streamlined fund management via professional intermediaries)
effectiveness (measurable outcomes in CO2 reduction, RE capacity, jobs)
equity (focus on low-income countries and first-time fund managers)
why_rationale.quote: "The UK Government’s participation as an equity investor, even on commercial and pari passu terms... will help accelerate movement of money into the developing country climate investment area and reduce perceived and actual investor risks." (3744949.odt, The UK Role section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's focus on emerging markets with underdeveloped financial infrastructure (e.g., Asia, Africa) limits partner selection to institutions with regional expertise and risk appetite. For example, Asia Climate Partners required managers like ADB and Orix with local networks, while the Catalyst Fund's global scope allowed for broader participation but still prioritized experienced fund managers capable of operating in frontier markets.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited pool of fund managers with climate sector expertise in developing countries
Regulatory environments in target countries affect fund structuring (e.g., debt-equity ratios)
Need for partners with ability to navigate information asymmetries and agency problems
Preference for multilateral institutions (IFC, ADB) due to their existing relationships with governments
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of catalysing private sector investment required a delivery structure that could demonstrate commercial viability (hence equity funds on pari passu terms) while addressing market failures (hence technical assistance for first-time managers). The fund-of-funds model was chosen to achieve scale and diversification, while the UK's anchor role was essential to signal credibility to risk-averse institutional investors like pension funds.
q28_linkages: Need for demonstration effect → Equity investments on commercial terms
Market failures in emerging markets → Technical assistance facility (SCAF)
Global scope of climate challenge → Fund-of-funds structure for diversification
Private sector risk aversion → UK's anchor investor role and 'signalling effect'
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging private capital at scale) with equity considerations (targeting low-income countries and first-time fund managers). For example, the Seed Capital Assistance Facility provides concessional support to frontier markets where commercial returns are harder to achieve, while the main funds focus on viable projects that can attract private co-investors. The addendum notes adjustments to reflect the 'riskier nature of projects in frontier markets.'
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Faster mobilisation of capital in established markets (China, India) vs. slower progress in frontier markets requiring more technical assistance
Expertise vs. ownership: Reliance on Northern fund managers (IFC, ADB) for credibility vs. building Southern capacity through SCAF
Cost vs. reach: Higher transaction costs for smaller projects in low-income countries vs. economies of scale in larger markets
Financial returns vs. development impact: Commercial fund requirements may exclude highest-risk/highest-impact projects without technical assistance
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (market failures, information asymmetries) led to a milestone-based oversight structure with adaptive management features. For example, the mid-term evaluation triggered adjustments to the logframe and reporting indicators, while the early end of Asia Climate Partners' investment period prompted reinvestment of returned funds. The technical assistance component was expanded to address persistent coordination problems.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme design, with the Seed Capital Assistance Facility explicitly targeting first-time fund managers in frontier markets. This shapes partner roles by enabling local fund managers to participate in the platform, while the technical assistance from IFC/ADB helps emerging managers meet the commercial standards required by institutional investors.
intersections.quote: "The problems are worse in the PE market for those investors... placing funds with a fund manager. The LP... want a fund manager with the expertise to make higher returns... in a new area like climate friendly investing in emerging markets, where managers lack track records, LPs can find it almost impossible to tell who to invest with." (3744949.odt, Market Failures section)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient private sector co-investment, leaving funds undercapitalized
Failure of fund managers to achieve target financial returns, deterring future investors
Regulatory or policy changes in target countries (e.g., removal of feed-in tariffs)
Economic downturns increasing investor risk aversion
First-mover disadvantages in frontier markets delaying project pipelines
Perception of climate investments as high-risk/low-return
Coordination failures between equity, debt, and project developers
Limited additionality if private investors would have entered without public support

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK's anchor investment and signalling effect; commercial fund structures; targeted outreach to pension funds and sovereign wealth funds.
Selection of experienced managers (IFC, ADB); technical assistance for emerging managers; performance-based milestones.
Diversified portfolio across countries/sectors; adaptive management via mid-term reviews.
Long-term investment horizon; focus on infrastructure assets with stable returns.
Seed Capital Assistance Facility to support project development; knowledge-sharing platforms.
Demonstration of commercial viability through pari passu investments; transparency in reporting financial returns.
Technical assistance to streamline deal structuring; IFC/ADB's role in convening stakeholders.
Focus on frontier markets and first-time fund managers; methodologies to measure and report additionality.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The addendum highlights lessons from the UK's earlier £150m fund-of-funds initiative (2009), which failed to attract private co-investors due to its pure clean-tech focus and binary outcomes. CP3 addressed this by: 1) Combining infrastructure and cleantech investments for lower perceived risk, 2) Using established multilateral partners (IFC, ADB) for credibility, and 3) Structuring funds to offer clearer value propositions to private investors.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Rationalization of the logframe from 24 to 16 outputs to focus on key activities; 2) Adjustment of expected results to reflect actual investments by Asia Climate Partners; 3) Introduction of new methodologies for additionality and attribution based on mid-term evaluation; 4) Increased funding for the Seed Capital Assistance Facility to support higher-risk frontier markets; 5) Use of project-level data for more accurate leverage reporting.
risks_lessons.quote: "The UK Government launched a private sector fund of funds—with a £150m cornerstone investment... The fund reached first close in 2010 with £325m but this was seemingly comprised only of matched funding from the two fund managers. According to press reports only £5m was raised from the private sector... There are two or three apparent reasons as to why the fund failed to attract additional top level investment. First a pure clean tech fund is a much riskier play than a fund with a combined infrastructure and cleantech focus." (3744949.odt, What is the background or track record section)

co_funding_partners.partner: Private sector investors (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, etc.)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: US$9,164 million (£~7,100 million at 2020 exchange rates) of public and private investment leveraged, with 73% (US$6,690 million) from the private sector. This represents a leverage ratio of approximately £7 of external funding per £1 of UK public investment.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily uses capital investments (equity) with a smaller revenue component for technical assistance. The original structure included £110 million in equity investments and £20 million for technical assistance, later adjusted based on performance.
financial_details.quote: "CP3 has made over 100 investments through its intermediaries, and its recent Mid Term Evaluation found that CP3 investments have... leveraged US$9,164m of public and private investment, with 73% coming from the private sector." (55795643.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: Ideas to Impact
metadata.quote: "The Ideas to Impact programme was designed to stimulate technological innovations for addressing intractable development challenges, initially in the focal areas of energy, water and climate, and then increasingly in emerging 'frontier' technologies with broader applicability." (59650315.odt, Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: April 2014 – December 2023" (59650315.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (piloting frontier technologies), financing mechanisms (innovation prizes, crowdfunding), capacity building (Frontier Technology Futures), and implementation research (testing and scaling solutions). It aims to stimulate innovation for development challenges by testing various funding mechanisms and approaches to ensure technology ideas lead to real-world impact.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Ideas to Impact programme was designed to stimulate technological innovations for addressing intractable development challenges... It adopted a 'portfolio' approach, testing different funding mechanisms and approaches for ensuring technology ideas lead to a real-world development impact." (46841702.odt, Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 24 pilot projects to test frontier technologies
10 Frontier Technologies proven in field contexts
5 technologies picked up for private sector investment
2-3 country offices each year receiving technology engagement and strategy support
Matchmaking between 20 international innovators and DFID country challenges
Evidence and policy advice informing DFID programming
3 million people with access to assistive technologies (AT2030 component)
10 new disruptive assistive technologies catalysed
6 innovative service delivery models developed
30-50 new start-ups sparked
Establishment of an East Africa AT Innovation Hub
Double DFID’s initial investment through partner backing
Leverage £35m of new private investment in technologies and business models
what_objectives.summary: Ideas to Impact is a portfolio programme testing multiple innovation mechanisms (prizes, crowdfunding, frontier technology pilots) to stimulate technology solutions for development challenges, with a focus on scaling successful approaches.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme, approved in 2014, has focussed on enabling technology ideas and approaches to be translated into development impacts via a range of tools and approaches, including innovation prizes and challenges." (46841702.odt, The Ideas to Impact programme)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in developing countries facing challenges like resource scarcity, climate change, and economic volatility, but no explicit FCAS or high-risk contexts are mentioned. The focus is on technological innovation rather than conflict or fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "resources are becoming more scarce and expensive; climate change is threatening communities and livelihoods; population is growing, placing greater demands on the environment; the global economy is becoming more volatile, with more frequent shocks and stresses." (46841702.odt, Context and need for DFID intervention)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers may affect technology deployment (e.g., drone use in Tanzania required relocation to Rwanda). Infrastructure limitations (e.g., energy access, connectivity) constrain technology adoption. Climate risks (e.g., extreme weather) affect the applicability of solutions. Data limitations may hinder evidence generation for scaling.
where_context.quote: "The Lake Victoria Challenge (LVC) is a drone prize in collaboration with the World Bank... This prize was due to be delivered in Tanzania, however due to the Government of Tanzania rescinding their support of the challenge as hosts the challenge has been delayed by 4 months overall." (59650315.odt, Time extension)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by a UK-based consortium led by R4D, with decision-making resting in the Investment Committee (DFID SRO, Lead Adviser from EPIC, PFA, and delivery partners). Southern partners (e.g., country offices, local innovators) participate in implementation but not in strategic governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: Frontier Technology Futures (immersive experiences for DFID teams)
Country Innovation Ecosystem engagement (e.g., Bangladesh, Tanzania)
Training and matchmaking for local innovators (e.g., East Africa AT Innovation Hub)
Support to analytical and preparatory work on technologies for country teams
Mentorship through Livestreaming pilots and Scale/Pivot Fund

partner_organizations.name: Results for Development (R4D)
partner_organizations.role: Prime delivery partner (consortium lead)

partner_organizations.name: IMC Worldwide
partner_organizations.role: Former Frontier Tech Hub lead (transitioning to R4D)

partner_organizations.name: Energy for Impact
partner_organizations.role: Thematic lead (low carbon energy)

partner_organizations.name: Institute of Development Studies (IDS)
partner_organizations.role: Thematic lead (climate adaptation)

partner_organizations.name: InnoCentive
partner_organizations.role: Prize design expertise

partner_organizations.name: ITAD
partner_organizations.role: Research, evaluation, and learning

partner_organizations.name: Global Disability Innovation Hub
partner_organizations.role: AT2030 lead (transitioned to standalone programme)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Defence (MoD) - Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL)
partner_organizations.role: Innovative partnerships (UAVs, IoT, machine learning)

partner_organizations.name: DFID Country Offices
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation and co-financing (e.g., Zambia, Bangladesh)

partner_organizations.name: Local innovators/SMEs
partner_organizations.role: Technology pilots and scaling (e.g., energy access, AT solutions)

partner_organizations.name: International Development Innovation Alliance (IDIA)
partner_organizations.role: Cross-donor coordination and learning

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be delivered by a consortium led by Results for Development (R4D) through an extension of the existing accountable grant agreement with R4D. R4D will lead on the assembly of downstream partners, including bringing in innovation expertise and contracting expertise." (59650315.odt, Overall Programme Structure)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants (e.g., to R4D consortium), competitive challenge funds (e.g., Livestreaming pilots), and partnerships (e.g., MoD DSTL co-funding). The Frontier Tech Hub operates as a flexible platform reallocating funds between components based on demand.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured as an open platform with a central Frontier Tech Hub (led by R4D) managing six components: Livestreaming, Futures, Foresighting, Scale/Pivot Fund, Research/Learning, and Partnerships. An Investment Committee (DFID SRO, EPIC, PFA, R4D) oversees decisions, while a Programme Funded Adviser ensures coherence. Country offices and central teams propose and co-finance pilots.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not explicitly stated (R4D selected via extension of existing grant; downstream partners via competitive process)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: R4D was chosen based on its existing role in delivering the Innovative Partnerships strand (IDIA) and its capacity to convene global networks. Downstream partners are selected through competitive processes (e.g., Livestreaming calls) to ensure quality and alignment with DFID priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: "R4D will run a competition to appoint downstream partners with expertise in flexible contract management, lean and agile methodologies and innovation consultancy." (59650315.odt, Overall Programme Structure)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: An Investment Committee meets quarterly with DFID SRO, EPIC Lead Adviser, PFA, and delivery partners (R4D consortium). Decisions on Livestreaming pilots are proposed by DFID Pioneers (country/central staff) and approved within grant provisions, while Scale/Pivot funding requires Investment Committee approval.
how_governance.quote: "There will be an Investment Committee meeting every quarter that brings together the DFID SRO, Lead Adviser from EPIC, PFA and delivery partners where key decisions are made, and reporting updates are delivered to DFID." (59650315.odt, Governance Structure)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between Frontier Tech components (e.g., Livestreaming to Futures) based on demand. The Scale/Pivot Fund explicitly supports high-performing pilots to extend or retarget work. Additional thematic calls (e.g., climate tech, AI) can be launched if demand arises.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses 'lean impact' methodology with rapid sprints to test assumptions. Pilots can be stopped early if assumptions prove incorrect, with funds reallocated to Scale/Pivot. New focus areas (e.g., AI, gender) can be integrated into Livestreaming calls based on emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The Frontier Tech Hub uses agile and flexible methods of programme management in order to enable DFID to respond rapidly to demands and test technologies in a timely fashion... The Scale and Pivot Fund will allow extra resources for high-performing FTL pilots to complete additional sprints and experiments." (59650315.odt, Governance Structure)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → R4D consortium (prime) → downstream partners (e.g., tech providers, country offices) → end innovators/SMEs.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Hub uses 'agile' and flexible methods of programme management... approval for each sprint remains with the DFID Pioneer, within the original grant provision." (59650315.odt, Governance Structure)

q24_alternatives_considered: Counterfactual (do nothing)
Traditional R&D grants (direct funding to researchers)
Innovation prizes (focus of original programme)
Crowdfunding (tested via Crowd Power component)
Frontier Tech Livestreaming (scaled up in addendum)
Partnerships with MoD/DSTL (expanded in addendum)
Standalone AT2030 programme (transitioned from I2I)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The platform model was chosen to (1) build on the success of Frontier Tech Livestreaming (proven demand from DFID staff), (2) enable adaptive management via agile sprints, (3) leverage R4D’s convening power (e.g., IDIA network), and (4) consolidate fragmented components (prizes, partnerships, Futures) into a coherent offer. The open structure allows co-financing from country offices and other donors (e.g., DFA, IDIA members).
q25_decision_factors: experience (R4D’s track record with IDIA and innovation networks)
partner-capacity (Hub’s ability to matchmake tech providers with DFID needs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of efforts across multiple components (prizes, Futures, partnerships)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Consolidation under R4D-led platform with a Programme Funded Adviser ensuring coherence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low uptake from country offices or central teams
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand-driven design (e.g., Futures engagements tailored to office needs) and senior DFID buy-in.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on UK-based expertise limiting local ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FTx model (in-country Hubs) and capacity-building via Futures/ecosystem engagements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Difficulty scaling successful pilots into mainstream programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Scale/Pivot Fund and dedicated learning component to document pathways to scale.

why_rationale.quote: "This structure builds on the 'portfolio' approach of the original I2I programme... bringing together consortium partners with expertise in delivering the Frontier Tech programme, but also expands the approach... to bring in others who can bring specialist inputs on specific projects." (59650315.odt, Overall Programme Structure)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Regulatory environments (e.g., Tanzania’s drone restrictions) and infrastructure gaps (e.g., connectivity for IoT) limit the types of technologies that can be piloted and the partners who can deliver them. For example, the Lake Victoria Challenge had to relocate to Rwanda due to host country constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory barriers (e.g., drone laws in Tanzania)
Infrastructure limitations (e.g., energy access for off-grid tech)
Climate risks (e.g., extreme weather affecting technology deployment)
Local capacity gaps (e.g., need for Futures engagements to build country office skills)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to test a *portfolio* of innovation mechanisms (prizes, crowdfunding, frontier tech) drove the platform structure, while the focus on *scaling* successful pilots led to embedded components like the Scale/Pivot Fund and learning systems. The agile sprint methodology was adopted to match the experimental nature of the 'what works' objectives.
q28_linkages: Portfolio approach (mixed objectives) → Platform structure (flexible components)
Scaling focus → Scale/Pivot Fund and learning components
Frontier tech testing → Livestreaming pilots + Futures capacity-building
Cross-Whitehall collaboration → Innovative Partnerships with MoD
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) *efficiency* (UK-led Hub for rapid testing) with *equity* (FTx in-country Hubs, Futures engagements for country offices), and (2) *speed* (agile sprints) with *inclusion* (open Livestreaming calls, matchmaking with local innovators). The AT2030 component highlights tensions between global market-shaping (efficiency) and community-led solutions (equity).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UK Hub expertise vs. local ownership (addressed via Futures and FTx)
Rapid sprints vs. inclusive partner selection (mitigated by open calls)
Global AT market-shaping vs. community-led innovations (balanced in AT2030 design)
Flexible reallocation vs. predictable funding for Southern partners
intersections.risk_affects_management: Higher perceived risks in frontier tech testing (e.g., failure of pilots) led to intensive oversight via the Investment Committee and milestone-based sprint approvals, while regulatory risks (e.g., drone laws) required adaptive management (e.g., relocating the Lake Victoria Challenge).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The need to build DFID’s internal capacity (Pillar 6 of HT4D) shaped the Futures component (immersive training for staff) and FTx model (country-specific Hubs), while limited local innovator capacity led to matchmaking support via the Frontier Tech database.
intersections.quote: "The programme uses an internal challenge fund to draw out gaps, opportunities and 'first adopter' staff and advisors - allocating up to £100k to pilot new ideas in context, then the Frontier Tech Hub matchmakes each challenge with specialist technology providers." (46841702.odt, Frontier Technology Livestreaming)

key_programme_risks: Low demand from DFID country offices or central teams
Failure of pilots to generate scalable solutions
Regulatory barriers blocking technology deployment (e.g., drones, data privacy)
Over-reliance on UK-based expertise limiting local ownership
Difficulty transitioning successful pilots into mainstream DFID programmes
Partner attrition or lack of co-financing
Unforeseen climate or political shocks disrupting implementation
Limited capacity of local innovators to absorb frontier technologies

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demand-driven design (e.g., Futures engagements tailored to office needs) and senior leadership buy-in.
Agile sprints with 'go/kill' decisions; Scale/Pivot Fund for high-potential ideas; learning component to document failures.
Flexible relocation (e.g., Lake Victoria Challenge move to Rwanda); early engagement with governments.
FTx model (in-country Hubs); capacity-building via Futures; matchmaking with local innovators.
Dedicated Scale/Pivot Fund; learning on pathways to scale; integration with DFID country programmes.

lessons_from_previous: Success of Frontier Tech Livestreaming (24 pilots, 12 country offices engaged) demonstrated demand for agile testing.
Crowd Power’s leverage (£1 DFID → £5 crowd funding) informed Energise Africa’s design under TEA programme.
AT2030’s rapid transition to standalone programme showed potential for scaling innovation components.
Need for stronger learning systems to document failures and scaling pathways (addressed in addendum).
Value of cross-Whitehall partnerships (MoD DSTL) for leveraging expertise and co-financing.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Consolidation of components under R4D-led platform for coherence.
Introduction of Scale/Pivot Fund to address scaling gaps.
Expanded Futures component to build country office capacity.
FTx model to test country-specific delivery with co-financing.
Stronger learning component (e.g., Science of Scaling research with LBS).
Transition of AT2030 to standalone programme for focused delivery.
risks_lessons.quote: "The major success of the Frontier Technologies component has been the phenomenal interest and demand from within DFID, especially country offices... The programme has supported 18 pilots and 22 tech organisations in 12 technology areas... There was a very strong response from DFID staff and offices to the 4th Livestreaming Call with 24 applications." (59650315.odt, Programme Performance)

co_funding_partners.partner: MoD Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £1 DFID funding leveraged £1 in co-investment for Frontier Tech pilots; AT2030 expected to double DFID’s investment through partner backing; DSTL partnership unlocked £3.2m additional funding (£2.3m DSTL + £0.9m BEIS).
financial_details.quote: "DFID’s initial £900,000 investment into the DSTL is enabling us to help develop a UAV capable of carrying 150kg... Our investment is also funding other UAV systems... We are also benefiting from the technical and scientific expertise of the DSTL and a range of suppliers and Universities, who have previously not worked with DFID; our investment therefore represents good value for money." (46841702.odt, Innovative Partnerships)

metadata.programme_name: Gender, Growth and Labour Markets in Low Income Countries (G2LM|LIC)
metadata.duration_text: 13 years to the end of March 2024
metadata.quote: "The G2LM|LIC programme aims to address the research gaps and generate and disseminate high-quality knowledge on the dynamics and opportunities for greater female participation in labour markets in Low Income Countries (LICs)." (44585521.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "DFID has so far committed £12.5M in support to the current programme, which is due to run until the end of November 2020. Under this extension, DFID would commit an additional £12M bringing the total programme cost to £24.5M over 13 years to the end of March 2024." (44585521.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) about labour markets in LICs, with a strong emphasis on **policy influence** (informing policy decisions) and **capacity building** (strengthening institutions/skills). It also includes **implementation research** (testing/scaling interventions) through randomized evaluations and pilot studies.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The G2LM|LIC programme aims to address the research gaps and generate and disseminate high-quality knowledge on the dynamics and opportunities for greater female participation in labour markets in Low Income Countries (LICs). This will lead to more informed policy debates and better evidence-based policy making on how to maximise employment opportunities for both men and women in LICs." (44585521.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 18-20 research projects on gender, labour markets, and growth in LICs
20 Small Innovative Research Grants (SIRGs) piloting new approaches
Publication of academic journal articles (e.g., American Economic Review, Quarterly Journal of Economics)
44 working papers, 28 policy briefs, and 9 synthesis papers (existing outputs)
Development of open-access datasets (Global Jobs Dataset, Global Labour Market Policy Evaluations/RCT Database)
Capacity building through training programmes, annual conferences, and summer schools
Policy uptake plans for each research project, including direct engagement with policymakers
Improved data harmonization and accessibility for labour market research in LICs
what_objectives.summary: The programme generates high-quality evidence on labour markets in LICs, with a focus on gender dynamics, to inform policy and improve labour market outcomes. It combines research, data building, capacity strengthening, and policy engagement to create inclusive and efficient labour markets.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will continue to deliver a significant body of high-quality evidence from southern and northern experts that will shape and inform policy debate and the design of more gender inclusive and effective labour markets programme and policies." (44585521.odt, What are the expected results?)

countries_regions: Low Income Countries (LICs) in Africa and Asia
Specific countries mentioned: Kenya, Togo, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, India, Pakistan, Ethiopia, Ghana, Liberia, Malawi, Yemen, Syria, Libya, Somalia
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in LICs, which include fragile and conflict-affected states (e.g., Yemen, Syria, Somalia, Liberia). However, the overall risk is mitigated by working with established academic institutions and IZA's robust policies. The document explicitly states: "This is a low risk programme" (5773571.odt, Compliance with the Terrorism Act), but the inclusion of FCAS countries suggests a **moderate** risk profile.
where_context.q5_source: "This is a low risk programme. Whilst funds will be used by external researchers, these will predominantly be from established academic institutions and will be in accordance with the clear IZA policies and procedures which have been assessed by the due diligence." (5773571.odt, Compliance with the Terrorism Act)
q6_contextual_constraints: legal restrictions (e.g., discriminatory legislation against women)
infrastructure gaps (e.g., lack of public services affecting women’s labour participation)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Data limitations restrict the ability to conduct rigorous research (e.g., lack of gender-disaggregated labour data in LICs). Weak institutions and conflict in countries like Yemen and Somalia complicate implementation. Legal and cultural constraints (e.g., 90% of LICs have gender-based legal restrictions) directly affect labour market dynamics and require context-specific policy solutions.
where_context.quote: "Data availability is restricting the ability of the research community to undertake work on labour markets in LICs. Quality data in a format that is readily available to the research community is needed." (3718905.odt, Why labour market research in LICs?)

who_partners.q8_lead_institution_location: LMIC (Germany, classified as high-income but operating as a global network)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between DFID (UK) and IZA (Germany), with IZA leading research procurement and programme management. Southern researchers participate in research calls and capacity-building activities but do not hold governance roles in the Programme Management Group (PMG) or Independent Oversight Committee (IOC).
q10_capacity_building_details: training programmes in econometrics and research methods
Small Innovative Research Grants (SIRGs) for Southern and junior researchers
annual conferences and summer schools
co-authorship opportunities (48% of published papers co-authored by women)
mentorship through North-South research collaborations

partner_organizations.name: Institute of Labour Economics (IZA)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer, research procurement, programme management, data hosting

partner_organizations.name: DFID (now FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funder, co-governance (Programme Management Group), strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Southern researchers (e.g., from Kenya, India, Pakistan)
partner_organizations.role: Research grantees, co-authors, participants in capacity-building

partner_organizations.name: Independent Oversight Committee (IOC)
partner_organizations.role: Peer review of research proposals, strategic advice

partner_organizations.name: Advisory Board
partner_organizations.role: Guidance on research themes, policy linkages

partner_organizations.name: World Bank, African Development Bank, ILO, UN Women
partner_organizations.role: Policy uptake partners, data collaboration

who_partners.quote: "GLM|LIC has attracted and expanded the capacity of many Northern and Southern researchers, contributing to generate new knowledge on labour dynamics in LICs... 306 researchers have been contributing to GLM work so far, 22% being southern researchers." (44585521.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is implemented through a **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)** between DFID and IZA, which outlines joint financing, research specification, and supervision. This is not a traditional grant or contract but a **stakeholder partnership**, where IZA contributes 6% of the budget and DFID 94%. The MoU allows flexibility and shared decision-making.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IZA acts as the **fund manager** and programme secretariat, while DFID participates in governance through the Programme Management Group (PMG). Research is procured through **open competitive calls** managed by IZA, with oversight from an Independent Oversight Committee (IOC) and Advisory Board. The structure is designed to leverage IZA’s global network of labour economists.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (IZA was selected based on its unique global network and track record)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IZA was chosen because it is the "leading global think tank on labour economics" with a pre-existing network of 1,000+ researchers, policy links (e.g., World Bank, ILO), and experience in managing large-scale research programmes. The business case states: "IZA is the premier global research and policy think tank on labour economics... [with] access to the largest network of labour economists worldwide." (3718905.odt, Option 1 - IZA Partnership)
how_mechanism.quote: "The proposal is to formalize the partnership between DFID and IZA through a jointly-agreed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that sets out the project objectives, respective roles and responsibilities, financing and implementation arrangements." (3718905.odt, Commercial Case - Indirect procurement)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Programme Management Group (PMG)** is the executive body with 4 members (2 from DFID, 2 from IZA) and meets annually. The **Independent Oversight Committee (IOC)** (6 international experts, at least 50% from the South) reviews research proposals. The **Advisory Board** (gender/labour academics and practitioners) provides thematic guidance. The PMG has veto power over grant awards.
how_governance.quote: "The Programme Management Group (PMG) will be the programme’s executive decision-making authority... It will meet at least once a year and operate on a consensus basis... The PMG will define the strategic orientation of the programme and hold the right to veto grant awards." (3718905.odt, Management Case - Oversight)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research themes based on emerging priorities, but this requires approval from the Programme Management Group (PMG). The programme includes a **contingency mechanism** for delays (payment reductions for late deliverables).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research themes can be adjusted based on consultations with the Advisory Board and stakeholders. The programme’s Theory of Change was updated in 2018 to reflect a stronger gender focus, demonstrating adaptive management. However, major shifts require PMG approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme extension will deliver new research and improved understanding across the following five themes... These will be presented and fine-tuned by the Advisory Board and other stakeholders." (44585521.odt, What are the expected results?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IZA (implementer) → end-researchers (no additional intermediary layers)
how_efficiency.quote: "IZA will manage the funds for the programme as a whole... and will make quarterly funding claims on DFID. Funding claims will be based on statements of actual needs and previous funds utilisation." (3718905.odt, Financial Case - How funds will be paid out)

q24_alternatives_considered: Stand-alone DFID Labour Markets Programme (RPC model)
Funding through the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)
Direct procurement with DFID management
Counterfactual (do nothing)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: IZA was selected because it offers **unparalleled global reach** (1,000+ labour economists), **policy links** (World Bank, ILO, governments), and **cost efficiency** (94% of funds go to research). The partnership model allows DFID to leverage IZA’s existing infrastructure (e.g., data portal, peer review systems) without building new systems. The business case emphasizes: "IZA is the premier global research and policy think tank on labour economics... By tapping into the IZA network, DFID will be able to gain access to a unique network of labour economists and policy makers." (3718905.odt, How will we tackle the problem/gap?)
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (IZA’s track record and network)
risk mitigation (IZA’s established systems reduce implementation risks)
flexibility (open calls allow adaptive research priorities)
equity (explicit focus on Southern researchers and gender)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on IZA’s network may limit diversity of research perspectives.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Open competitive calls and requirement for North-South collaborations in selection criteria.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential capture of funds by Northern researchers.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit targets for Southern researcher participation (20% of publications) and Small Innovative Research Grants (SIRGs) for LIC researchers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of data portals post-programme.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IZA’s core funding covers long-term maintenance of the International Data Service Center (IDSC).

why_rationale.quote: "The IZA option appears to be the most appropriate, would support a global shift in labour market research in LICs and is the most cost-effective option for delivering the desired outputs and impact." (3718905.odt, Appraisal of options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on **Low Income Countries (LICs)** limits partner selection to organizations with existing networks in fragile/conflict states (e.g., IZA’s global reach was critical). Data limitations in LICs also require partners with capacity to build datasets (e.g., IZA’s International Data Service Center).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with FCAS experience (e.g., Liberia, Yemen)
Requirement for data expertise due to poor labour market data in LICs
Legal/regulatory constraints in LICs necessitate partners with local knowledge
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **evidence-generation objective** drives the open-partnership structure (to access global expertise) and competitive calls (to ensure quality). The **policy-influence goal** necessitates IZA’s policy networks (e.g., World Bank, ILO links). The **gender focus** requires embedded capacity-building (e.g., SIRGs for women researchers).
q28_linkages: Open competitive calls → High-quality research outputs
IZA’s policy networks → Effective policy uptake
Small grants for Southern researchers → Capacity building
Data harmonization → Long-term research sustainability
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (IZA’s low overhead, competitive procurement) with **equity** (20% Southern researchers, gender focus). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Open calls may slow procurement but ensure diverse participation. (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: IZA leads management, but Southern researchers are prioritized in grants.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Competitive calls (efficiency) vs. targeted Southern grants (equity)
IZA’s Northern leadership (expertise) vs. Advisory Board’s Southern representation (ownership)
Global data standards (rigor) vs. context-specific LIC adaptations (relevance)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (FCAS countries, data gaps) justifies **quarterly oversight** and milestone-based payments. For example, payment reductions for delayed deliverables mitigate implementation risks in fragile contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives (e.g., SIRGs, training) shape partner roles by requiring IZA to **actively recruit Southern researchers** and embed mentorship in research calls. The Advisory Board’s composition (50% Southern experts) ensures capacity needs inform governance.
intersections.quote: "The programme targets an area that is of critical importance to LICs... The existence of a large informal sector suggests that labour is under-utilized in LICs... We need better evidence on how to support labour markets to work effectively." (3718905.odt, Strategic Case) AND "The Small Innovative Grant Component... will help through 2 open competitive calls in testing new ideas and methodologies, run pilot studies... and provide seed funding for exploratory studies." (44585521.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

key_programme_risks: Weak data infrastructure in LICs limiting research rigor
Policy resistance to gender-inclusive labour reforms in conservative contexts
Implementation delays in fragile/conflict-affected states (e.g., Yemen, Somalia)
Over-representation of Northern researchers in competitive calls
Sustainability of data portals post-funding
Low uptake of research findings by policymakers

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dedicated data-building component (£240,000) to harmonize labour datasets and collaborate with World Bank/ILO.
Early engagement with policymakers in research design and tailored policy briefs (e.g., VoxDev, synthesis papers).
Payment reductions for delayed deliverables and close monitoring by PMG.
Small Innovative Research Grants (SIRGs) for Southern researchers and 20% Southern co-authorship target.
Policy uptake plans required for all grants, direct support to policymakers in focus countries.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible payment structures (e.g., milestone-based) are critical for FCAS operations.
Local partnerships (e.g., with African Economic Research Consortium) improve relevance in conflict zones.
Early engagement with governments (e.g., Liberia’s behavioural therapy programme) accelerates uptake.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2016 RAND review highlighted the need for **stronger synthesis and dissemination** to maximize policy impact. This led to the addition of **policy uptake plans** for all grants and a redesigned website. The programme also learned that **small grants** (SIRGs) effectively attract Southern researchers, prompting their inclusion in the extension.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added Small Innovative Research Grants (SIRGs) to increase Southern/young researcher participation.
Strengthened policy uptake tracking (e.g., direct support to policymakers).
Expanded data harmonization efforts based on identified gaps.
Increased gender focus in response to evidence gaps (renamed G2LM|LIC).
Added cross-cutting themes (e.g., fragile states, violence against women).
risks_lessons.quote: "A review of the programme by RAND in 2016... concluded that the programme had performed well and was supporting high quality and important work on labour market development in LICs. The analysis also identified the need to strengthen the uptake and dissemination work... This extension will respond directly to this." (44585521.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: IZA’s contribution (6%) leverages DFID’s funds by providing access to its global network, data infrastructure, and policy links without additional cost. The programme also collaborates with World Bank, African Development Bank, and Gates Foundation for data-sharing.
financial_details.quote: "Of the additional £12 million funds provided by DFID: 83.75% will be used to fund research activities, 7.8% will be routed towards uptake activities, and 8.45% will be used for general programme administration." (44585521.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

metadata.programme_name: The Global Agriculture and Food Security Programme (GAFSP)

quote.text: The Global Agriculture and Food Security Programme (GAFSP) is a $3bn global initiative, started in 2009 by the G7/8 and G20, in response to the global food price crisis. It works towards lasting food security in the poorest and most vulnerable countries through support to sustainable food and agricultural programmes.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: 2012/13-30 June 2031; New project end date (if applicable): 30 June 2034

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GAFSP is a multi-donor trust fund designed to channel funds to support sustainable food and agricultural programmes in low-income countries. It provides competitive, catalytic, and innovative public and private sector finance in response to country demand, aiming to fill gaps left by bilateral and multilateral programmes.

q1_source.text: GAFSP is a multi-donor trust fund set up in 2010 by signatories of the L’Aquila Food Security Initiative (AFSI) to provide an effective means of supporting country-led and strategic agriculture investment plans in low income countries.

q3_expected_outputs: 1.1 million new jobs on and off-farm
30 of the poorest countries building sustainable and resilient food systems
20% increase in income for an additional 10 million farmers
25% yield increase for an additional 10 million farmers through climate-resilient practices
All new projects including climate mitigation and adaptation approaches
Support for 6 million farmers (direct and indirect) through local currency lending pilots
Strengthened local food supply, food security, and nutrition in target countries
Reduced GHG emissions through sustainable farming practices
Increased farmer incomes and market access for up to 15,000 farmers in Madagascar (example)
Improved business and operational capacities for agribusinesses
Enhanced food safety and reduced food loss and waste
what_objectives.summary: GAFSP aims to improve food and nutrition security, raise incomes, create jobs, and promote sustainable agriculture in the world's poorest countries through a combination of public sector grants and private sector investments. The programme focuses on climate-smart approaches, gender equality, and supporting smallholder farmers.

quote.text: The overarching objective is to support the incomes, and food and nutrition security of those in low and lower middle income countries. The cross-cutting issues of gender, nutrition, climate change and fragile and conflicted affected states are integrated into GAFSP programmes.

countries_regions: World Bank IDA and IDA-blend countries (71 eligible countries as of FY2024)
Includes 36 countries affected by fragility, conflict, and violence

Specific examples: Madagascar, Bangladesh, Malawi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Zambia, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, Yemen, Cabo Verde, Côte d’Ivoire, Djibouti, Ghana, Lesotho, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, Honduras, Nicaragua, Fiji, Cameroon, Uzbekistan
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: GAFSP targets the poorest and most vulnerable countries, many of which are affected by fragility, conflict, and violence. The programme explicitly focuses on countries where food insecurity and malnutrition are worst, and where climate change and economic pressures exacerbate vulnerabilities.

q5_source.text: GAFSP is incentivising multilaterals to do more in very poor and fragile geographies, where food insecurity and malnutrition are worst, and where climate change as well as conflict and economic pressure affect countries most.

q6_contextual_constraints: infrastructure (limited rural infrastructure, e.g., roads, irrigation)
regulatory (complex business environments, lack of access to finance)
climate risks (vulnerability to climate change, yield losses up to 20% by 2030)
data limitations (lack of robust monitoring systems in some countries)
currency risk (lack of local currency lending options for agribusinesses)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The lack of local currency lending options prevents agribusinesses from accessing finance, as they cannot afford foreign exchange-denominated loans. Weak infrastructure and institutional capacity in target countries limit the effectiveness of interventions, while climate risks and conflict exacerbate food insecurity and poverty.

quote.text: There is agreement that there are billions of investment finance looking for deals in food and agriculture, including in low and middle/low-income countries and in fragile states. However, even those international donor-funded investors aiming to deliver a measurable development impact often cannot access the highest-impact options of smaller local businesses producing for local markets.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: GAFSP's Steering Committee includes donors, recipient governments, supervising entities, and civil society representatives from both North and South. Decisions are taken collectively by members, including governments from target countries.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for farmers on climate-smart practices
technical assistance to agribusinesses
advisory services to improve commercial viability of smallholders
institutional strengthening for producer organizations
support for women's involvement in decision-making and entrepreneurship
development of global public goods (e.g., GHG Food Loss Tool, Food Safety Platform)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Trustee, Coordinator, and Supervising Entity (Public Sector Window)

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Manager of Private Sector Window, investment and advisory services

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IADB)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO)
partner_organizations.role: Supervising Entity

partner_organizations.name: Recipient Country Governments
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partners, Steering Committee members

partner_organizations.name: Producer Organizations and Farmer Groups
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and direct recipients of advisory services

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Steering Committee members, advocacy and monitoring

quote.text: Its inclusive governance assembles donors, governments, supervising entities, farmers’ and CSOs from the north and south around the same table. Decisions in the Steering Committee are taken by members, including donors and governments.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: GAFSP uses a combination of grants (for public sector projects) and concessional finance (loans, equity, guarantees for private sector projects). The UK's contribution includes both core funding and specific allocations for climate finance and local currency pilots.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank acts as the Trustee and Coordinator, managing the overall fund and compliance. The IFC manages the Private Sector Window, while recipient countries choose from accredited supervising entities to implement projects. The Steering Committee oversees strategic decisions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Recipient countries select supervising entities from a pre-accredited list (World Bank, AfDB, ADB, IADB, IFAD, WFP, FAO). The IFC is the sole manager of the Private Sector Window, chosen for its expertise in private sector investments.

quote.text: As a source of financing and not an implementing vehicle, GAFSP uses experienced multilateral development partners, with the choice of partner made by recipients.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes donors, recipient governments, supervising entities, and civil society representatives. Decisions are made collectively, often using a no-objection 'silence' procedure. The UK co-chaired the Steering Committee until 2022 and remains an active member.

quote.text: The World Bank, as manager of the GAFSP overall Trust Fund, is responsible for ensuring compliance with the Bank’s financial and operational procedures; and maintaining up to date legal agreements between the Bank and each donor.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between public and private sector windows with Steering Committee approval, but specific allocations (e.g., climate finance, local currency pilots) have defined parameters.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: GAFSP has demonstrated flexibility in responding to crises (e.g., COVID-19) and can adjust project priorities through Steering Committee decisions. The UK's local currency pilot is an example of adaptive programming.

quote.text: GAFSP has flexed in times of need: it stepped up fast in 2020 and has responded well to the impacts of COVID-19, made worse by climate change and conflict.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (Trustee/Coordinator) → Supervising Entities/IFC → End Beneficiaries (farmers, agribusinesses)

quote.text: The World Bank, as manager of the GAFSP overall Trust Fund, is responsible for ensuring compliance with the Bank’s financial and operational procedures.

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to individual countries
Direct investments through DFID/FCDO channels
Other multilateral trust funds (e.g., IDA Private Sector Window)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: GAFSP was chosen for its unique ability to combine public and private sector financing under one mechanism, its inclusive governance structure, and its track record of leveraging additional funding (e.g., $6.5 of benefits for every £1 of UK funding). The programme's focus on climate-smart agriculture and gender equality aligned with UK priorities, while its demand-led approach ensured country ownership.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (high leverage of private finance)
partner capacity (World Bank/IFC expertise in agriculture and private sector)
flexibility (ability to respond to crises and adjust priorities)
equity (inclusive governance and focus on poorest countries)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between public and private sector windows
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot approaches to integrate the two windows, e.g., linking public and private investments in Haiti. UK influence through Steering Committee to improve coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Currency risk in local currency lending pilots
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of exchange rate buy-down mechanisms to reduce swap costs for clients, with ODA funds absorbing residual risk.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-subscription of funds leading to unmet demand
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Increased replenishment targets (e.g., $1.5 billion for 2021-25) and prioritization of poorest countries.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (use of multilaterals to reduce transaction costs)
effectiveness (measurable impacts on poverty and food security)
equity (focus on women, smallholders, and fragile states)

quote.text: The availability of competitive grant financing and concessional loans, equities and/or guarantees under one umbrella for agricultural development, make GAFSP unique. The two funding windows have not yet taken full advantage of this arrangement.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) limits the pool of implementing partners to multilaterals with experience in high-risk environments (e.g., World Bank, IFC, IFAD). Local currency constraints and weak financial sectors in target countries necessitate the use of blended finance and advisory services to de-risk investments.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS environments require partners with strong safeguards and risk management (e.g., World Bank/IFC)
Local currency risks prevent commercial lenders from serving agribusinesses, requiring ODA subsidies
Weak infrastructure in target countries limits the types of interventions possible (e.g., need for advisory services to prepare projects)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to support both public sector institutions and private agribusinesses determines the dual-window structure (public/private). The focus on climate-smart agriculture and gender requires embedded advisory services and monitoring frameworks. The demand-led approach shapes the competitive allocation of funds.
q28_linkages: Dual windows (public/private) reflect the need to support both institutional strengthening and market development
Advisory services are embedded to address capacity gaps in climate-smart practices and gender inclusion
Competitive calls for proposals ensure alignment with country priorities and demand
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging IFC's private sector expertise) with equity (targeting smallholders, women, and fragile states). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for inclusive projects (e.g., local currency pilots) versus the potential for greater impact on poverty reduction.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Competitive processes may delay disbursements but ensure fair access
Expertise vs. ownership: Use of multilaterals provides technical capacity but may limit local control
Cost vs. reach: Advisory services increase costs but are critical for supporting smallholders and women
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of target countries (FCAS, climate vulnerability) necessitates intensive oversight through the Steering Committee and robust M&E frameworks. The UK's role in co-chairing the Committee reflects the need for strong donor coordination in fragile contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with advisory services and training designed to strengthen the role of Southern partners (e.g., producer organizations, women farmers) in project implementation and decision-making.

quote.text: Through our co-chairing of the Steering Committee, including through its reform process and recent shocks and stresses, and then continuing to be a proactive donor that others look towards, we have successfully led efforts to improve the coherence between GAFSP support for governments and its lending to the private sector.

key_programme_risks: Fragmentation between public and private sector windows limiting synergies
Currency risk in local currency lending pilots
Over-subscription of funds leading to unmet country demand
Weak monitoring systems in some recipient countries
Climate and conflict shocks disrupting implementation
Limited access to finance for smallholders and women
Governance risks in fragile states

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pilot integrated projects (e.g., Haiti) and strengthen Steering Committee coordination. UK influence to align public/private sector strategies.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Currency risk in local currency pilots
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Exchange rate buy-down mechanisms using ODA funds to absorb risk. Pilot phase with limited initial investments.
Increase replenishment targets (e.g., $1.5 billion for 2021-25) and prioritize poorest countries. Use competitive calls to allocate funds transparently.
Strengthen M&E frameworks with donor support. Use World Bank's DIME and independent evaluations.
Build resilience into project designs (e.g., climate-smart agriculture). Flexible funding to respond to crises (e.g., COVID-19 response).
Advisory services and blended finance to de-risk investments. Targeted grants for producer organizations.

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for flexible funding mechanisms to respond to shocks (e.g., COVID-19, conflict)
Importance of advisory services to prepare projects in high-risk environments
Value of blended finance to attract private investment in fragile states
Critical role of civil society in monitoring and advocacy in FCAS
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2018 independent global evaluation highlighted the need for better coordination between public and private sector windows and stronger aggregate reporting on results. GAFSP 2.0 reforms addressed these gaps by improving the M&E framework and piloting integrated projects. The evaluation also confirmed the effectiveness of blended finance in reaching smallholders in low-income countries.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Stronger results and evaluation framework to track aggregate impact
Pilot projects to integrate public and private sector windows (e.g., Haiti)
Expanded advisory services to support smallholders and climate-smart practices
Local currency lending pilots to address financing gaps for agribusinesses
Increased focus on gender and nutrition in project appraisals

quote.text: An independent 2018 global evaluation confirmed a strong performance for GAFSP; its unique role in bringing together public and private sector finance for agriculture; and its success in ensuring public finance helps attract funding into high impact investments.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: GAFSP Private Sector Window projects leverage on average 1.9 times funding from IFC and 6.5 times in total financing, delivering £6.5 of benefits for every £1 of UK funding. Public sector grants have mobilized additional funding in recipient countries (e.g., $100 million in three countries in 2010).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The UK's £206 million contribution includes both capital (e.g., investments through IFC) and revenue (e.g., grants for public sector projects). Up to 40% of funding is classified as International Climate Finance (ICF).

quote.text: The UK will provide an additional £20 million to GAFSP in financial year 2024/25. 100% percent of GAFSP’s funding is classified as International Climate Finance (ICF), based on the programme’s track record of delivering climate-smart approaches.

metadata.programme_name: Global Development Innovation Ventures
metadata.quote: "£50 million over 5 years to create a stand-alone, market-facing organisation with the following objectives:" (5435489.odt, INTERVENTION SUMMARY)
metadata.duration_source: "£50 million over 5 years to create a stand-alone, market-facing organisation with the following objectives:" (5435489.odt, INTERVENTION SUMMARY)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (investment platform), implementation research (testing/scaling innovations), and capacity building (supporting innovators). It focuses on identifying, testing, and scaling cost-effective development innovations with rigorous evidence, while also creating a marketplace for co-investment between donors, foundations, and private investors.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Objective 1: Identify and support the development, rigorous testing, and implementation of innovations that deliver more development impacts, with fewer resources, and to scale-up those with evidence of successful results." (5435489.odt, INTERVENTION SUMMARY) AND "Objective 3: Through a ‘venture-style’ approach, stimulate collaboration between donors, foundations and the investment community to co-create and co-invest in innovations that have the potential to generate significant development impact and potentially commercial returns." (5435489.odt, INTERVENTION SUMMARY)
q3_expected_outputs: a rigorously tested portfolio of innovations with potential for cost-effective and transformational results at scale
new networks and partnerships with diverse stakeholders to maximize learning and sharing of innovation activities
a pipeline of commercially viable innovations for private sector investors and public sector initiatives
3.3 million cases of diarrhoea averted and 3,200 children’s lives saved in the first three years (Dispensers for Safe Water example)
155 villages reached with solar micro grids in Uttar Pradesh (Mera Gao Power example)
global deployment of CommCare mobile health platform in 10 countries
60% reduction in election fraud in Afghanistan and Uganda
50% reduction in insurance claims for dangerous driving in Kenya
5 million people provided with chlorinated water in Kenya, Uganda, and beyond
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to create a stand-alone organization that identifies, tests, and scales high-impact development innovations, while fostering collaboration between public, private, and philanthropic investors to maximize cost-effectiveness and transformational results.
what_objectives.quote: "The organisation will focus on: Creating a global focus on innovation for development; Developing innovations that deliver more development impacts, with fewer resources, and to scale-up those with evidence of successful results; Creating a marketplace to broker co-investment and collaboration between investors and innovators alike." (5435489.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in diverse contexts including fragile states (Afghanistan) and high-poverty regions (urban slums in Nairobi, rural Uttar Pradesh), but the overall approach is designed to manage risk through staged financing and rigorous evidence requirements. The document explicitly acknowledges that "innovation inevitably involves risk" but emphasizes portfolio-based risk management.
where_context.q5_source: "Innovation inevitably involves risk. In the private sector, a venture capitalist seeking the next big innovative breakthrough will expect as much as nine carefully chosen investments to fail for every one that succeeds." (5435489.odt, THE CHALLENGE) AND "The organisation will manage the inherent risks of developing radical solutions by: Isolating and incubating radical innovation development outside of DFID core business; Spreading financial risk; Adopting a ‘venture style’ approach to investment by staging funding in three phases." (5435489.odt, Managing Risk)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions in some countries limit the ability to design and implement innovations locally (e.g., "The new organisation will also identify innovations in countries where the institutions in the administrative public sector are too weak to design, develop and implement innovations."). Regulatory and political economy constraints affect the scaling of market-based solutions, while infrastructure gaps (e.g., lack of electrification) create demand for innovations like solar micro-grids. Data limitations are addressed through rigorous testing requirements to generate evidence where it is lacking.
where_context.quote: "The new organisation will also identify innovations in countries where the institutions in the administrative public sector are too weak to design, develop and implement innovations." (5435489.odt, Core principles of the organisation) AND "In rural Uttar Pradesh, Mera Gao Power (MGP) is reaching thousands of un-electrified homes with village-level solar micro grids." (5435489.odt, Lighting India with solar micro grids)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The organization is designed to be globally accessible, with decision-making power shared between Northern and Southern partners. The document emphasizes "open innovation" and user-led approaches, with beneficiaries and local innovators playing a key role in problem identification and solution development. The "Hubs & Spokes" model in developing countries further decentralizes decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to innovators
managerial capacity building
support for organizational effectiveness
strategy development
transition support from pilot to scale

partner_organizations.name: DFID (UK Department for International Development)
partner_organizations.role: funder and co-designer

partner_organizations.name: USAID (U.S. Agency for International Development)
partner_organizations.role: funder and co-designer (based on DIV model)

partner_organizations.name: Mera Gao Power (MGP)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (solar micro-grids)

partner_organizations.name: Sanergy
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (sanitation solutions)

partner_organizations.name: Dimagi
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (CommCare mobile health platform)

partner_organizations.name: Dispensers for Safe Water (DSW)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (chlorine dispensers)

partner_organizations.name: University of California, San Diego
partner_organizations.role: research partner (election fraud reduction)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector investors
partner_organizations.role: co-investors and scalers of innovations

partner_organizations.name: Foundations (e.g., Gates Foundation)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and adopter of innovations

partner_organizations.name: Local entrepreneurs (e.g., Sanergy franchisees)
partner_organizations.role: service providers and innovators

who_partners.quote: "The organisation will not specify eligible sectors, countries, or organisations; instead, applicants will compete on evidence of impact, cost-effectiveness, sustainability, and potential to scale." (5435489.odt, How it will work) AND "The organisation will embrace the concept of user-led innovation recognising that beneficiaries of aid and local citizens with deep contextual knowledge are a valuable resource for identifying problems, developing innovative solutions and providing feedback on impact." (5435489.odt, Core principles of the organisation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a staged financing model inspired by venture capital, with three stages: Stage 1 (seed funding up to $100k), Stage 2 (pilot funding up to $1M), and Stage 3 (scale-up funding up to $15M). Funding is milestone-based and contingent on evidence of impact. The organization can employ grants, equity, loans, and other instruments to manage risk and support innovators.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The organization acts as an open platform that sources innovations globally, appraises them through internal and external experts, and brokers investment opportunities to public and private investors. It provides technical assistance to innovators and manages a portfolio of investments at various stages. The structure is designed to be small, flexible, and autonomous, similar to DARPA, with outsourced support personnel to avoid bureaucratic burdens.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The open competition approach is chosen to maximize the diversity and quality of innovations, ensuring that the best ideas are selected based on rigorous criteria (impact, cost-effectiveness, scalability, and evidence). This aligns with the "open innovation" principle and avoids bias toward specific sectors or geographies.
how_mechanism.quote: "Applicants will be able to apply directly to any of the three stages of funding. Those who have received past awards must re-compete." (5435489.odt, How it will work) AND "The organisation will use a broad range of internal and external expertise to assess incoming proposals." (5435489.odt, How it will work) AND "The organisation will not specify eligible sectors, countries, or organisations; instead, applicants will compete on evidence of impact, cost-effectiveness, sustainability, and potential to scale." (5435489.odt, How it will work)

how_governance.quote: "The organisation will support the implementation of public agency funded innovations post award." (5435489.odt, Implementation) AND "Successful applicants will receive funding in instalments, based on their achievement of project milestones - predetermined targets that assess impact, cost-effectiveness, sustainability, and scaling potential." (5435489.odt, How it will work) AND "The suite of ‘prospectuses’ will provide the outcome of the appraisal and suggesting the optimal investment options (grants, loans, debt and equity). The organisation will provide technical assistance to applicants to support this process if the innovators require it. These innovation ‘prospectuses’ will then be open to bids from the market represented by the investment community." (5435489.odt, Brokerage)
