Banks do not lend ‘enough’ to SMEs in part because they are not able to assess the risks... The perception of risk is exacerbated by lack of collateral from SMEs and the collateral regime itself is not very sophisticated in many developing countries." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 7)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The IFC (a multilateral institution headquartered in Washington DC) manages the initiative and makes key decisions about fund allocation, partner selection, and programme adjustments. DFID acts as the anchor donor but defers to IFC's technical and operational leadership, with oversight through periodic reviews.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical support to PFIs in strategy and market segmentation
financial product development
credit risk management training
IT/MIS system upgrades
development of credit bureaus and collateral registries
training for women-owned SMEs and sustainable finance
environmental and social risk management

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: Partner Financial Institutions (PFIs)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient banks and NBFIs for SME lending (35-40 institutions)

partner_organizations.name: Development Finance Institutions (DFIs)
partner_organizations.role: Co-investors (e.g., KfW, EIB, OPIC, OFID, IDB) providing £325 million in risk-sharing capital

partner_organizations.name: DFID Country Offices (Nigeria, Mozambique, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers (£15 million) and local coordination

partner_organizations.name: G-20 SME Finance Challenge Winners (e.g., Entrepreneurial Finance Lab, Peace Dividend Trust, BIDweb)
partner_organizations.role: Technology solution providers for credit scoring, market access, and investment platforms

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Arab Fund, SIDA, Dutch government)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-financiers for future fund closings

who_partners.quote: "The Initiative will be managed and implemented by IFC to deliver the results agreed between IFC and DFID. The decision to go with IFC is based on strategic as well as commercial reasons... Partnership with IFC makes this Initiative rightly ambitious and technically cutting edge." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 12)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of (1) **grant funding** (£38m for risk-sharing, £29.8m for technical assistance) to IFC, (2) **co-financing agreements** with DFIs (£325m leveraged), and (3) **direct funding lines** to Partner Financial Institutions (PFIs) in liquidity-constrained markets. The risk-sharing facility operates as a catalytic fund where DFID's grants reduce the cost of capital for DFIs, enabling them to lend to PFIs at lower interest rates (LIBOR + 3-6% vs. LIBOR + 8-11% without DFID support).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IFC acts as the sole fund manager, responsible for selecting PFIs, disbursing funds, and monitoring results. DFID provides oversight through half-yearly progress reports, annual reviews, and a mid-term independent evaluation. The programme operates as a global facility with standardized products (risk-sharing, TA, technology grants) but allows country-level adaptation based on diagnostics (e.g., liquidity constraints vs. risk aversion).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IFC was selected as the implementing partner through a strategic (non-competitive) process due to its existing global network of 50+ SME-focused banks, technical expertise in risk-sharing facilities, and ability to leverage co-financing from other DFIs. The selection of Partner Financial Institutions (PFIs) is based on their willingness to address SME financing gaps in DFID priority countries, with a focus on sustainability and inclusion (e.g., women-led SMEs).
how_mechanism.quote: "We believe IFC has the experience, network and relationships with major DFIs, banks and financial institutions in our target countries to deliver such an initiative more cost-effectively and quickly than other alternatives... Using the IFC also allows us to pool risk and leverage resources from DFIs on a scale that would not be possible through the efforts of any single donor." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 10)

how_governance.quote: "IFC will provide half-yearly reports to DFID of progress against the indicators in the Logical Framework agreed with DFID... DFID will undertake annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews... and an independent mid-term review before end of year three (February 2015)." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 15-16)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Up to 20% of allocations can be transferred between components (risk capital, advisory services, technology) at the mid-term review, subject to DFID approval. Country-level flexibility is built in to adapt to liquidity constraints or risk aversion (e.g., direct funding lines vs. risk-sharing).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments based on mid-term review findings (e.g., scaling successful components, reallocating funds to frontier markets). Country pipelines can be revised if additional DFID Country Offices wish to co-fund. The technology component explicitly supports adaptive solutions (e.g., psychometric scoring tools can be tailored to local contexts).
how_flexibility.quote: "At mid-term review of the Programme, requests may be made to allow for the transfer of up to 20% transfer of allocations between the components based on need, subject to consultation with DFID and other donors." (3716779.odt, Output 3, Paragraph 47)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IFC (fund manager) → Partner Financial Institutions (PFIs)/SMEs
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID’s funding to the Initiative will comprise three components... IFC will provide half-yearly reports to DFID of progress against the indicators in the Logical Framework." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 11 and 15)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral country-level programmes (rejected due to lack of scale and higher design costs)
Direct DFID lending to SMEs (rejected due to lack of sustainability and bank capacity constraints)
Traditional credit lines (rejected as they fail to address risk aversion or build bank capacity)
Standalone technical assistance (rejected as less effective without risk-sharing)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The IFC-led global facility was chosen for its ability to (1) **pool risk and leverage co-financing** from DFIs at scale (£325m from DFIs vs. £38m DFID grant), (2) **address multiple constraints** (liquidity, risk aversion, infrastructure) through a combined risk capital + TA + technology approach, (3) **operate flexibly** across 15 countries with standardized products, and (4) **build on IFC’s existing network** of 50+ SME-focused banks. The platform model reduces design costs for DFID Country Offices and accelerates delivery compared to bilateral programmes.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage ratio of 1:8.5 for risk capital)
partner capacity (IFC’s global footprint and SME expertise)
equity (targeting women-led SMEs and frontier markets)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on IFC’s selection of PFIs may exclude innovative local banks without prior IFC relationships, limiting market diversity.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s oversight through annual reviews and mid-term evaluation includes assessment of PFI inclusivity and frontier market coverage.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk-sharing may incentivize PFIs to target less risky SMEs within the segment, reducing additionality.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maximum 50% risk-sharing cap and focus on underserved markets (e.g., 25% loans to women-led SMEs) to ensure additionality.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Technology solutions (e.g., psychometric scoring) may not be scalable in low-infrastructure FCAS.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot testing in 3-4 markets with mid-term review to assess adaptability before scaling.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: DFIs may prioritize less risky countries, reducing impact in frontier markets.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit target of 25% results from frontier markets and co-funding from DFID Country Offices in these regions.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leverage of £325m DFI funds per £38m DFID grant)
effectiveness (combined risk capital + TA addresses multiple constraints)
equity (targets for women-led SMEs and frontier markets)
why_rationale.quote: "The proposed Initiative is ambitious and technically cutting edge. It can pool risk and leverage resources from DFIs on a scale that would not be possible through individual country level initiatives... The Initiative also provides flexibility to respond to shifts in country and regional needs over the term of the programme." (3716779.odt, Strategic Case, Paragraph 35)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS and frontier market context (e.g., South Sudan, Liberia, DRC) limits partner selection to financial institutions with existing operations or high risk appetite, excluding many local banks. Weak financial infrastructure (e.g., lack of credit bureaus) necessitates reliance on DFIs/IFC with technical capacity to build systems, reducing opportunities for local intermediaries.
q27_constraints_detail: Frontier markets lack banks with SME lending experience, requiring reliance on international/regional PFIs
Conflict-affected areas have limited data for credit scoring, favoring DFIs with global risk assessment tools
High transaction costs in LICs make local NBFIs unviable without risk-sharing, benefiting larger PFIs
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to **scale SME financing sustainably** (WHAT) drives the **platform delivery structure** (HOW), as it enables risk-pooling across countries and leverages IFC’s existing PFI network. The **focus on frontier markets** (WHERE) requires a **flexible fund manager** (IFC) to adapt products (e.g., direct lending lines in liquidity-constrained markets vs. risk-sharing in others). The **technology component** (WHAT) necessitates **global partners** (e.g., G-20 Challenge winners) with scalable solutions.
q28_linkages: Combined risk capital + TA (WHAT) → Requires a fund manager (IFC) to coordinate both (HOW)
Frontier market focus (WHERE) → Needs adaptive products (e.g., liquidity support) and flexible allocation (HOW)
Job creation targets (WHAT) → Necessitates capacity building for PFIs to sustain lending (WHO)
Women-led SME targets (WHAT) → Requires gender-focused TA and monitoring (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (standardized products, IFC’s global scale) with **equity** (25% frontier market target, women-led SME focus). Trade-offs include: (1) **Higher transaction costs** in FCAS reduce leverage ratios compared to stable markets, (2) **Risk-sharing caps** (50%) limit additionality in less risky countries to ensure frontier market inclusion, and (3) **Technology solutions** prioritize scalability (e.g., psychometric tools) over deep localization.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scaling through IFC’s existing PFIs may exclude local banks in frontier markets.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led IFC management ensures technical rigor but limits Southern institutional strengthening.
Cost vs. reach: High TA costs for financial infrastructure (e.g., credit bureaus) reduce funds available for direct lending.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context necessitates **intensive oversight** (milestone-based reporting, mid-term review) and **flexible fund allocation** (20% reallocation between components). DFID’s role as anchor donor enables it to enforce equity targets (e.g., frontier markets) despite IFC’s commercial incentives.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme’s capacity-building objectives (e.g., credit risk training for PFIs) determine that **IFC must lead implementation** (due to its TA expertise) while **PFIs are limited to delivery roles**. Southern partners (PFIs) receive funding contingent on adopting IFC’s systems, reinforcing a Northern-led technical assistance model.
intersections.quote: "DFIs have been clear that the risk appetite of their own shareholders and their return on equity targets as well as competition for resources in better off countries limits their willingness to increase exposure in the SME markets without some buffer from additional grant financing... Our funding is aiming to draw the DFIs in to such a facility and to allow them provide their financing at a lower rate of interest than they would have otherwise done." (3716779.odt, Strategic Case, Paragraph 34)

key_programme_risks: PFIs may not sustain SME lending after DFID/IFC support ends ("additionality risk").
Frontier markets (e.g., South Sudan, DRC) may fail to attract sufficient PFIs due to high perceived risks.
Technology solutions (e.g., psychometric scoring) may not be culturally adaptable or scalable in low-literacy contexts.
DFIs may prioritize less risky countries, reducing impact in target frontier markets.
Credit bureaus and collateral registries may not be financially sustainable post-programme.
Macroeconomic shocks (e.g., global liquidity crunches) could reduce PFI participation.
Overlap with other SME programmes (e.g., EBRD, ADB) may lead to duplication or competition for PFIs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Risk-sharing is capped at 50% to ensure PFIs retain skin in the game; TA includes business model sustainability training.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low PFI participation in frontier markets
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Co-funding from DFID Country Offices (e.g., Nigeria, Mozambique) and explicit 25% frontier market target.
Pilot in 3-4 markets with mid-term review before broader rollout; focus on G-20 validated tools.
DFID’s anchor funding is contingent on frontier market inclusion; leverage ratios are higher for FCAS.
TA includes legal/regulatory framework development and stakeholder capacity building for long-term ownership.

fcas_specific_lessons: In conflict-affected countries, existing bank relationships increase entrepreneurship survival rates (Demirgüc-Kunt et al., 2009).
Post-conflict SMEs require simplified collateral systems (e.g., movable assets) due to weak property rights.
Liquidity constraints in FCAS necessitate direct funding lines alongside risk-sharing.
High SME failure rates in frontier markets require blended finance (grants + commercial capital) to incentivize PFIs.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past IFC programmes show that **advisory services combined with risk-sharing** achieve 76% success rates vs. 55% for standalone financing (IFC IEG, 2008). The **EU+EBRD SME Facility** demonstrated that regional platforms with standardized TA can train 7,300+ FI staff and disburse 100,000+ loans. However, **traditional credit lines** often fail to sustain lending after donor exit, highlighting the need for capacity building.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) **Risk-sharing caps** (50%) to avoid moral hazard, learned from IFC’s energy finance facilities where coverage declined as banks gained experience, (2) **Frontier market targets** (25%) to counter DFIs’ risk aversion, and (3) **Technology pilots** to test scalability before commitment, based on G-20 Challenge lessons.
risks_lessons.quote: "Experience from IFC’s programmes indicate that technical assistance/advisory services to banks without investment/risk sharing are much less likely to have the desired impact on the target market; the two pieces are highly complementary... A review of IFC’s 15 years of experience with risk-sharing facilities in sustainable energy demonstrated that... the leverage on each dollar of concessional lending has increased dramatically from $0.8 to $30 in the IFC’s most recent facilities." (3716779.odt, Strategic Case, Paragraphs 58-59)

co_funding_partners.partner: Development Finance Institutions (DFIs: IFC, KfW, EIB, OPIC, OFID, IDB)
Potential additional donors (Arab Fund, SIDA, Dutch government)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID’s £38 million risk capital component is projected to catalyse £325 million from DFIs, which will further leverage £1.6 billion in new SME lending (7:1 total leverage ratio). The advisory services component (£29.8m) is expected to generate £3.6 billion in additional lending through improved PFI capacity and financial infrastructure.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The £38 million risk capital component is structured as a revolving fund (recycled over 7 years via 2.3-year average loan tenures). The £29.8 million for advisory services and technology is grant-based revenue expenditure. DFID’s contribution is 100% revenue (grants); leveraged DFI funds include both capital (equity/mezzanine) and revenue (loans).
financial_details.quote: "DFID’s funding to the Initiative will comprise three components: (1) Risk Capital: A £38 million risk sharing fund... (2) Advisory Services: A complimentary £26.90 million Technical Assistance pool... (3) Technology-Based Solutions: A £2.9 million Technical Assistance pool... IFC projects that DFIs will put in roughly £325 million based on DFID’s funding of £38 million to this component." (3716779.odt, Intervention Summary, Paragraph 11)

metadata.programme_name: Impact Programme
metadata.quote: "The DFID Impact Programme was launched in 2012 to catalyse the markets for impact investment in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia." (5196727.odt, Introduction)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Dec 2012 - Dec 2025 (Dec 2028 after first extension)" and "New project end date: Dec 2035" (14346444.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Impact Programme is a financing mechanism designed to catalyse the market for impact investment in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. It provides patient capital through two funds (DIF and DIAF) to support enterprises that deliver both financial and social returns, benefiting poor and low-income people by improving access to affordable goods, services, and income-generating opportunities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The DFID Impact Programme was launched in 2012 to catalyse the markets for impact investment in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Impact investments are those which have both a financial and social return by benefitting poor and low-income people, improving access to affordable goods and services and income generating opportunities at the base of the pyramid." (14346444.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: £293m non-fiscal CDEL to scale-up the DFID Impact Acceleration Facility (DIAF) from £40m to £333m
£230m non-fiscal CDEL to scale-up the DFID Impact Fund (DIF) from £75m to £305m
£23m RDEL for additional technical assistance to DIF investees
£29.3m RDEL for additional technical assistance to DIAF investees
Reach at least 5 million low-income beneficiaries by 2035
Investments in over 100 enterprises in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
Increased local capacity, skills, and expertise to identify, develop, measure, and manage impact investments
Development of market infrastructure, including standardised metrics for measuring impact
Catalysing additional private capital into impact investment markets
what_objectives.summary: The Impact Programme aims to scale up impact investing in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia by providing patient capital through two funds (DIF and DIAF) to enterprises that deliver both financial and social returns. The programme focuses on improving access to affordable goods, services, and income-generating opportunities for low-income populations, while also building market infrastructure and local capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "The DFID Impact Programme was launched in 2012 to catalyse the markets for impact investment in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia." (5196727.odt, Introduction)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly targets fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) as part of its mandate. Both DIF and DIAF have invested in countries like Burma (Myanmar) and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which are classified as FCAS. The programme's exposure to FCAS is noted as 46% for DIF and 62% for DIAF and neighbouring countries, with investments in highly fragile states like DRC and Zimbabwe.
where_context.q5_source: "The existing mandate of DIAF and proposed mandate of DIF, enable the funds to invest in countries with higher risk than CDC is able to under its main mandate. As such we expect that DIF and DIAF will exceed CDC’s main balance sheet exposure to FCAS, which is greater than 50%... DIF has invested in Insitor (see paragraph 12d) which is active in Burma, while DIAF’s second investment was Virunga Hydropower (see paragraph 20b) in Eastern DRC." (14346444.odt, Fragile and Conflict Affected States)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates in regions with limited market information, ineffective regulatory environments, inadequate physical infrastructure, and restricted access to financial products. These constraints make it difficult to achieve market rates of return and increase perceived risks, leading to underinvestment. For example, West Africa’s GDP is twice as large as East Africa’s, but impact investing volumes are only two-thirds of those in East Africa due to these constraints.
where_context.quote: "In spite of West Africa’s GDP being twice as large as East Africa’s, impact investing volumes are only two third of those in East Africa." (14346444.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: CDC (UK-based) manages the funds and makes investment decisions, with oversight from DFID. Local partners, such as fund managers and enterprises in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, implement the investments but do not have primary decision-making authority over fund allocations or strategy.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
technical assistance
institutional strengthening

partner_organizations.name: CDC Group plc
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager for DIF and DIAF, investment decisions, technical assistance administration

partner_organizations.name: PwC (Programme Coordination Unit - PCU)
partner_organizations.role: Market building, programme coordination, technical assistance oversight

partner_organizations.name: Global Impact Investing Network (GIIN)
partner_organizations.role: Market building, research, advocacy, impact measurement standards (IRIS)

partner_organizations.name: Novastar Ventures
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager (DIF investee), early-stage equity investments in East Africa

partner_organizations.name: Injaro Agricultural Capital Holdings
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager (DIF investee), agricultural value chain investments in West Africa

partner_organizations.name: Energy Access Ventures Fund (EAV)
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager (DIF investee), renewable energy investments in Sub-Saharan Africa

partner_organizations.name: Insitor Impact Asia Fund
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager (DIF investee), early-stage equity investments in South Asia

partner_organizations.name: Africa Improved Foods
partner_organizations.role: DIAF investee, fortified food production in Rwanda and Ethiopia

partner_organizations.name: Virunga Hydropower
partner_organizations.role: DIAF investee, mini-hydro power generation in Eastern DRC

partner_organizations.name: LAB (Lafarge-Holcim joint venture)
partner_organizations.role: DIAF investee, soil-stabilized brick production in Malawi, Rwanda, Tanzania

who_partners.quote: "The key implementing partners in the programme are CDC, the Programme Coordination Unit (PCU – currently tendered to PwC) and its market building partners." (14346444.odt, What is the purpose of the project?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of funding instruments, including non-fiscal Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) for investments and Resource Departmental Expenditure Limit (RDEL) for technical assistance and programme management. The funds are structured as financial assets on DFID’s balance sheet, managed through Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) between DFID and CDC.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: CDC acts as the fund manager for both DIF and DIAF, with oversight from DFID. The Programme Coordination Unit (PCU), managed by PwC, coordinates market-building activities and technical assistance. A Technical Assistance Committee oversees the allocation of technical assistance funds to investees.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: CDC runs a competitive "Call for Proposals" process to select fund managers for DIF and DIAF. This ensures that DFID capital is allocated to the most effective and innovative fund managers who can demonstrate strong development impact potential and the ability to raise matching capital from private investors.
how_mechanism.quote: "We will ask CDC to run a competitive process to ensure that we achieve the best possible allocation of DFID capital. CDC will publicly announce a 'Call for Proposals' through the CDC website and other media." (5196727.odt, Competitive Selection for Funds)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DFID assists in monitoring and shaping the Impact Programme through its Quarterly Steering Committee, Quarterly Partner Meetings, and regular catch-up meetings with CDC and the PCU. The Steering Committee provides oversight and strategic direction for the programme.
how_governance.quote: "DFID assists in monitoring and shaping the Impact Programme through its Quarterly Steering Committee, Quarterly Partner Meetings and regular catch-up meetings with CDC and the PCU." (14346444.odt, What is the purpose of the project?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated based on milestones and performance. Additional tranches of funding are unlocked only if the existing portfolio meets investment policy requirements and 50% of committed funds have been deployed. This ensures ongoing control over value for money and need for capital.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in strategic themes and investment focus based on lessons learned and market evolution. For example, DIF’s mandate was extended to include investments in difficult geographies that cannot attract commercial capital, based on learning from DIAF’s wider mandate.
how_flexibility.quote: "Each tranche of additional funding would be unlocked in the event that the existing portfolio has met the investment policy and 50% of funds committed by DFID have been deployed." (14346444.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → CDC (fund manager) → Fund Managers/Investees (e.g., Novastar, Injaro) → End Beneficiaries (enterprises and low-income populations)
how_efficiency.quote: "Each tranche of additional funding would be unlocked in the event that the existing portfolio has met the investment policy and 50% of funds committed by DFID have been deployed." (14346444.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct investments by DFID without intermediation
Grant-based support for enterprises
Purely commercial investment without patient capital
Relying solely on existing DFIs and market actors
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The chosen modality of using CDC as a fund manager with a competitive selection process for fund managers was selected to address several key challenges: (1) the nascent stage of the impact investment market in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, (2) the need for patient capital to support early-stage, high-risk investments that commercial investors avoid, (3) the requirement to demonstrate additionality and catalyse private capital, and (4) the importance of building local capacity and market infrastructure. CDC’s expertise in development finance and its ability to manage higher-risk investments made it the partner of choice.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient deal flow
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Through market-building activities and the Programme’s market development work, sectors are made more viable, and pipelines are strengthened. The risk was initially assessed as medium likelihood and high impact but is now considered low likelihood due to demonstrated pipeline growth.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Investment/development outcomes do not justify scaling the pilot
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The initial assessment proved incorrect as both DIF and DIAF significantly exceeded expectations in their pilot phases, demonstrating strong development impact and financial viability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Confusion about the strategy of the UK’s DFI
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DIF and DIAF are being integrated into the UK’s approach to higher financial risk investment, which enhances clarity and coherence with CDC’s main mandate.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capital loss due to high-risk investments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversification across sectors, geographies, and deal types, combined with CDC’s active management and quarterly reporting, helps mitigate the risk of capital loss. The programme’s phased scale-up based on milestones also manages risk exposure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational burden of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) on investees and CDC
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme is implementing lean data approaches and aligning data collection to be both developmentally and commercially relevant, reducing the burden on investees.

why_rationale.quote: "DIF and DIAF play complementary roles to each another... Both funds have technical assistance available to them which is administered by CDC (overseen by a Technical Assistance Committee) of up to 10% of the size of their investments." (14346444.odt, What is the purpose of the project?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The geographic focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, including FCAS, constrains partner selection to those with experience and capacity to operate in high-risk, low-infrastructure environments. This limits the pool of potential fund managers and investees to those familiar with the regulatory, security, and market challenges in these regions.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited number of fund managers with experience in FCAS and difficult geographies
Regulatory and infrastructure challenges reduce the pool of viable investees
Need for partners with deep local knowledge and networks to navigate political and economic risks
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objective to catalyse impact investment markets and reach low-income beneficiaries determines the delivery structure. The need for patient capital and technical assistance to support early-stage, high-risk investments requires a fund-of-funds approach managed by an experienced DFI (CDC) with strong oversight and market-building components (PCU and GIIN).
q28_linkages: Objective to reach BoP populations → Requires intermediated investments through local fund managers
Need for market catalysation → Requires competitive selection and technical assistance to build fund manager capacity
Focus on difficult geographies → Requires flexible, patient capital and strong oversight structures
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between equity (inclusive partnerships, local ownership) and efficiency (speed, cost-effectiveness). For example, the decision to use CDC as a UK-based fund manager balances the need for strong oversight and risk management with the goal of building local capacity. The programme also notes challenges in gender lens investing, where the lack of fund managers with explicit gender focus limits the ability to directly target women and girls, despite the programme’s equity goals.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UK-based fund manager (CDC) ensures efficiency and risk management but limits Southern ownership
Competitive selection process ensures value for money but may exclude smaller, less experienced local fund managers
Focus on financial sustainability may limit the depth of impact in the most marginalized communities
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of investments in FCAS and early-stage enterprises increases the intensity of oversight, requiring quarterly reporting, milestone-based funding releases, and active management by CDC. The programme’s governance structure, including a Steering Committee and Technical Assistance Committee, reflects the need to closely monitor and mitigate risks associated with patient capital investments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme’s capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by embedding technical assistance and training within the fund management process. For example, DIF and DIAF provide up to 10% of investment values as technical assistance to investees, and the PCU coordinates market-building activities to strengthen local fund manager capacity. This ensures that partners like Novastar and Injaro not only receive capital but also support to improve their investment and impact measurement capabilities.
intersections.quote: "The existing mandate of DIAF and proposed mandate of DIF, enable the funds to invest in countries with higher risk than CDC is able to under its main mandate... DIF has invested in Insitor (see paragraph 12d) which is active in Burma, while DIAF’s second investment was Virunga Hydropower (see paragraph 20b) in Eastern DRC." (14346444.odt, Fragile and Conflict Affected States)

key_programme_risks: Capital loss due to high-risk investments in early-stage enterprises and FCAS
Insufficient deal flow in target regions, particularly outside of Kenya and South Africa
Limited investment activity in South Asia compared to Africa
Operational burden of M&E on investees and CDC
Confusion about the UK’s DFI strategy and the role of DIF/DIAF within it
Private capital mobilised for investment in basic services undermining local/national government capacity
Lack of additionality in investments
Failure to achieve demonstration effects for impact investing
Corruption or misuse of DFID funds
Technical assistance funds being misused post-subsidy
Deal execution taking longer than anticipated due to capacity constraints
Systemic shock to financial markets impacting CDC’s performance

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversification across sectors, geographies, and deal types; active management by CDC; quarterly reporting; phased scale-up based on milestones.
Market-building activities to generate pipeline; demonstrated growth in DIF and DIAF pipelines reduces likelihood.
Revising DIF’s mandate to enable greater access to South Asia; proactive outreach and capacity building in the region.
Lean data approaches; alignment of data collection with commercial and developmental needs.
Integration of DIF and DIAF into the UK’s approach to higher financial risk investment; clear communication of roles and objectives.
Due diligence ensures funds engage with local/national government stakeholders and follow ESG procedures.
CDC processes ensure additionality; nascent market makes it easier to demonstrate catalytic role.
Learning and insights strategy to disseminate best practices and track records from the programme.
CDC’s anti-corruption policies; annual external audits; immediate reporting requirements for any instances of corruption.
Policies and oversight by CDC and the Technical Assistance Committee; ongoing assurance from PwC.
Capacity building and technical support for first-time fund managers; realistic timelines and milestones.
Patient capital approach; focus on less globally linked markets; long-term investment horizon.

fcas_specific_lessons: Investments in FCAS require flexible, patient capital and strong local partnerships to navigate political and security risks.
Technical assistance is critical for building the capacity of investees in FCAS to manage risks and achieve sustainability.
Demonstration effects in FCAS can catalyse further investment by reducing perceived risks for commercial investors.
Local presence and hands-on management are essential for success in FCAS, given weak institutions and infrastructure.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The initial phases of DIF and DIAF demonstrated that patient capital can successfully catalyse private investment and achieve development impact in high-risk markets. Key lessons included the importance of technical assistance, the need for flexible investment structures, and the value of competitive selection processes to ensure additionality and value for money. The programmes also highlighted the challenges of gender lens investing and the need for further capacity building in this area.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Extension of DIF’s mandate to include investments in difficult geographies that cannot attract commercial capital, based on learning from DIAF’s wider mandate.
Increased focus on technical assistance and capacity building for fund managers and investees, based on demonstrated needs in early phases.
Phased scale-up of funding based on achievement of milestones to manage risk and ensure ongoing development impact.
Integration of DIF and DIAF into CDC’s broader approach to higher financial risk investment to enhance clarity and coherence.
risks_lessons.quote: "Both DIF and DIAF, as delivered by CDC, have piloted and helped to define our overall approach to higher financial risk investment... As our plans to use this tool increase, there is a large opportunity to build on success to date and scale up both funds." (14346444.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage at least 1:1 matched capital from private investors for DIAF investments. DIF has already demonstrated a mobilisation ratio of nearly 3:1, with £92m in third-party capital committed alongside £36.8m from CDC. The scale-up is expected to catalyse further private investment into impact markets in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes £523m in non-fiscal Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) for investments and £52.3m in Resource Departmental Expenditure Limit (RDEL) for technical assistance and programme management. The capital is deployed as patient investments in funds and enterprises, while RDEL covers operational and support costs.
financial_details.quote: "The following table sets out the additional funding required across non-fiscal CDEL for scaling-up investment and RDEL for TA... TOTAL ADDITIONAL: Non-fiscal CDEL £523m, RDEL £52.3m, TOTAL £575.3m." (14346444.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Macroeconomic Research in Low Income Countries (MRLIC)
metadata.quote: "Macroeconomic Research in Low Income Countries (MRLIC) is a strategic partnership between DFID and the International Monetary Fund (IMF)." (56217735.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: March 2012 – March 2020 (phases 1, 2 & 3)" and "New project end date (if applicable): March 2023" (56217735.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme focuses on producing high-quality, policy-relevant research (evidence generation) while also developing practical tools and frameworks (technology development) to improve macroeconomic policy-making in LICs. It includes capacity building through training and expanding the network of researchers, and aims to influence IMF policy and practice (policy influence).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The aim of MRLIC is that ‘Better macroeconomic policy-making in LICs leads to faster economic growth, job creation and poverty reduction in LICs’. This is delivered through the four core activities of this programme: Producing high quality, policy relevant research on macroeconomic issues affecting LICs; Ensuring these research products are used by IMF country teams and partner authorities; Strengthening engagement by senior IMF policymakers on issues affecting LICs; and Expanding the network of researchers and policymakers working on LIC macroeconomics." (56217735.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 32 working papers and 11 published papers (per phase)
2 books (per phase)
20 low-income country applications of models/frameworks in coordination with IMF country teams (per phase)
5 low-income country applications of models/frameworks in coordination with country authorities (per phase)
5 high-level policy conferences attended by senior IMF staff (per phase)
4 policy papers reflecting research results in IMF Board discussions (per phase)
12 commissioned research papers on thematic areas (per phase)
4 workshops for researchers/academics (per phase)
Development of toolkits (e.g., DIG, DIGNAR, MDAM models)
Training courses for IMF and central bank staff
Publicly accessible datasets and research outputs
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve macroeconomic policy-making in LICs through research, tool development, capacity building, and policy influence, with a strong focus on practical applications and uptake by policymakers.
what_objectives.quote: "The overarching objective of the project has been to improve understanding of the macroeconomics of low-income countries with a view to improving development outcomes." (56217735.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: LICs are vulnerable to shocks such as natural disasters, climate change, and economic instability, but the programme itself operates within the stable institutional framework of the IMF, mitigating operational risks.
where_context.q5_source: "LICs face external challenges that prevent them from growing in a sustained manner, including; natural disasters, dealing with the effects of climate change, and managing large labour flows (e.g. due to conflict)." (8092697.odt, Topic C - Building resilience)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and limited capacity in LICs make it difficult to implement research findings and use analytical tools. Data limitations constrain the ability to conduct robust empirical research, while climate risks and conflict create unstable environments for policy implementation.
where_context.quote: "Capacity to do macroeconomic research and use the evidence is very small, as is the capacity within LICs to use the evidence for better policy making." (3717399.odt, Why should DFID Intervene in macroeconomic research?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The IMF, a Northern-led multilateral institution, holds decision-making power, with input from DFID (UK) and external experts. LIC researchers and policymakers are engaged as collaborators and beneficiaries but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training courses for IMF and central bank staff
workshops for researchers/academics
expanding the network of LIC researchers
mentorship through collaborative research
development of toolkits for practical application

partner_organizations.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and research partner

partner_organizations.name: DFID (now FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Low-Income Country Central Banks and Governments
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and collaborators in research uptake

partner_organizations.name: External Academics and Researchers
partner_organizations.role: Commissioned research contributors

partner_organizations.name: African Regional Technical Assistance Centers (AFRITAC)
partner_organizations.role: Collaborators in training and technical assistance

who_partners.quote: "Implementation remains the responsibility of the IMF Macroeconomic Research in Low Income Country programme management unit, with a steering committee of IMF, DFID, and external experts." (8092697.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is governed by a Letter of Understanding (LoU) between DFID and the IMF, which outlines the terms of collaboration, funding disbursements, and project governance. This agreement allows for flexible funding while ensuring alignment with IMF policies and DFID priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed jointly by the IMF's Research Department (RES), Strategy, Policy & Review Department (SPR), and the Institute for Capacity Development (ICD), with oversight from a steering committee comprising IMF, DFID, and external experts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The IMF was selected due to its unique mandate, expertise in macroeconomic research, and existing policy networks in LICs. The partnership addresses market failures in procuring academic research, such as information externalities and incentive misalignment, by leveraging the IMF’s credibility and policy influence.
how_mechanism.quote: "A key rationale for partnering with the IMF relates to two potential market failures. The first relates to information externalities and second to principal agent or incentive compatibility inherent in the procurement of ‘academic’ research." (3717399.odt, Why a partnership with the IMF?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The steering committee includes representatives from DFID, the IMF, and external experts. It provides oversight, monitors progress, and ensures additionality of the research. For Phase 4, a programme advisory committee will be introduced to further engage senior IMF staff and external advisors.
how_governance.quote: "Governance would follow the lines of the original project. Implementation would remain a joint responsibility of RES (Andrew Berg) and SPR (Catherine Pattillo), under the guidance of Jonathan Ostry and Olivier Blanchard (RES) and Sean Nolan and Siddharth Tiwari (SPR), with a steering committee of IMF, DFID, and external experts." (5495067.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research topics based on emerging priorities, but major changes require approval from the steering committee to ensure alignment with programme objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in research priorities based on new evidence or policy needs, but changes are reviewed by the steering committee to maintain focus and relevance.
how_flexibility.quote: "The extension will allow the IMF to conduct and commission research on the themes that are of macro-critical importance in LICs. This research takes place across five topic areas... There will be opportunities to add and revise the specific work projects under each theme as opportunities arise." (56217735.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IMF (lead implementer) → end-researchers/contractuals
how_efficiency.quote: "The proposed additional UK support is £5,470,000 for a total project cost of £9,610,000." (5495067.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "TTF Fee (7%)" (5495067.odt, APPENDIX 2: PROPOSED BUDGET FOR PROJECT EXTENSION)

q24_alternatives_considered: In-house research programme (discounted due to lack of research skills and resources)
Short-term consultancy (discounted due to limited depth and uptake potential)
Medium-term outsourced research programme (preferred option)
Long-term outsourced research programme (discounted due to sunk costs and delayed delivery)
Research Council funding (discounted due to limited policy influence and coherence)
Competitive tender through RPC (Research Programme Consortia) (discounted due to risk of mission drift and limited capable institutions)
Appointing another academic institution (discounted due to delays and lack of policy networks)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The IMF partnership was chosen for its high-quality research capacity, strong policy networks, and ability to ensure research uptake in LICs. The direct award addressed market failures in academic research procurement, such as the misalignment between academic incentives and policy relevance, and leveraged the IMF’s credibility with LIC policymakers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High unit costs compared to other options
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The IMF committed to transparency in contracting and cost containment, e.g., through non-business travel for non-IMF staff.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited explicit competition in partner selection
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The IMF’s strong track record in research quality and policy uptake justified the direct award, with oversight from a steering committee to ensure value for money.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential for reduced additionality if IMF reallocates internal resources away from LIC research
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The IMF agreed to monitor and maintain its own resources devoted to LIC research, with the steering committee overseeing additionality.

why_rationale.quote: "In comparison to other options, partnership with the IMF have some weaknesses. Unit costs are higher and there is an absence of explicit competition. However, it is the preferred option primarily because of the quality of the IMF research staff and the strength of their policy networks and the scope to ensure evidence is used to improve LIC macroeconomic performance." (3717399.odt, How will we tackle the problem/gap?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on LICs, which face weak institutional capacity and limited data, constrained partner selection to organizations with strong macroeconomic expertise and existing networks in these countries. The IMF was uniquely positioned to address these constraints due to its mandate and experience working with LICs.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited macroeconomic research capacity in LICs
Scarce quality data on LICs for empirical research
Weak institutions in LICs to absorb and implement research findings
Need for policy-relevant research that can be directly applied by LIC policymakers
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for high-quality, policy-relevant research that could influence IMF operations and LIC policymaking determined the choice of the IMF as the lead partner. The IMF’s existing policy networks and credibility with LIC authorities were critical for ensuring research uptake, which shaped the collaborative delivery structure and governance model.
q28_linkages: Policy influence objective → IMF partnership (due to its policy networks)
Capacity building objective → Embedded training and toolkit development (to strengthen LIC institutions)
Research quality objective → IMF’s research department leadership (to ensure rigorous outputs)
Uptake and dissemination objective → Collaborative research design with IMF country teams (to integrate findings into policy advice)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between the efficiency of leveraging the IMF’s existing capacity (a Northern-led institution) and the equity goal of expanding LIC researchers’ involvement. While the IMF leads research and decision-making, efforts are made to include LIC researchers through workshops, commissioned papers, and training to build local capacity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: IMF’s established research capacity and policy networks enable rapid, high-quality output production.
Equity: Limited decision-making power for LIC researchers, though efforts are made to expand their participation through training and collaborations.
Cost: Higher unit costs for IMF-led research are justified by the expected policy impact and uptake.
Reach: The global scope of the programme allows for broad influence but may dilute focus on specific country needs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of LICs (e.g., economic instability, weak institutions) increases the need for intensive oversight and adaptive management. The steering committee’s quarterly reviews and the IMF’s policy networks help mitigate these risks by ensuring research remains relevant and applicable to evolving LIC challenges.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The limited capacity in LICs to conduct and use macroeconomic research shapes the IMF’s role as the primary researcher and trainer. The programme includes capacity-building activities (e.g., workshops, toolkits) to strengthen LIC institutions’ ability to engage with and apply the research findings over time.
intersections.quote: "The IMF has a mandate to promote macroeconomic stability among its member countries and therefore has strong incentives to align research with policy priorities and stated demands of regional departments within the Fund and Authorities in country." (3717399.odt, Why a partnership with the IMF?)

key_programme_risks: Limited additionality if IMF reduces internal resources for LIC research
High unit costs relative to other research options
Potential for research to be perceived as IMF-driven rather than LIC-owned
Challenges in ensuring uptake of research by LIC policymakers due to weak institutional capacity
Data limitations in LICs constraining empirical research quality
Risk of mission drift in research priorities without strong oversight

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The IMF committed to maintaining its own resources for LIC research and the steering committee monitors additionality.
Costs are justified by the IMF’s high research quality and policy influence, with transparency in contracting.
Collaborative research design with LIC policymakers and inclusion of LIC researchers in workshops and conferences.
Training and toolkits are developed to build LIC institutions’ ability to use research findings.
The IMF’s experience in LICs and use of case studies complement quantitative analysis.
Steering committee oversight and clear research specifications aligned with LIC policy needs.

fcas_specific_lessons: Research on state fragility has highlighted the need for tailored macroeconomic advice that accounts for weak institutions and conflict risks.
The programme has explored how financial inclusion and female labor force participation can mitigate shocks in FCAS.
Lessons from FCAS are integrated into broader research themes, e.g., public investment in fragile environments and the impact of fragility on economic growth.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme has evolved from funding IMF staff to join country missions to a model where country teams request and ‘buy into’ MRLIC expertise, improving efficiency and demand-driven research. The introduction of a programme advisory committee in Phase 4 aims to strengthen senior IMF engagement and external oversight.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 4 introduces a formalized process for selecting work projects, using senior IMF staff to prioritize and align research with emerging LIC challenges. The operational model has shifted to respond to demand from IMF country teams, increasing the relevance and uptake of research.
risks_lessons.quote: "The MRLIC programme has evolved over time. Initially it funded MRLIC staff to join IMF country missions, now IMF country and operational teams are requesting and ‘buying in’ analysis and expertise from MRLIC’s team members." (56217735.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged additional IMF resources and technical assistance funding (e.g., AFRITAC support for monetary policy work in Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Mozambique), extending the impact of DFID’s investment.
financial_details.quote: "The proposed additional support is £5.1m (£1.7m p.a.), bringing the total project cost to £19.84m." (56217735.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "TTF Fee (7%)" (5495067.odt, APPENDIX 2: PROPOSED BUDGET FOR PROJECT EXTENSION)

metadata.programme_name: Jobs and Incomes for Women
metadata.quote: The Jobs and Incomes for Women Research Programme aims at understanding and generating high-quality evidence on "what works, what does not and why" for government, donors and the private sector to address gender inequality and boost women’s economic and social empowerment in Sub-Saharan Africa. (S20305017.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: 27/03/2013 to 30/06/2023; New project end date (if applicable): 30/06/30 (S20305017.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is a combination of evidence generation (research to create new knowledge), policy influence (informing policy decisions), and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions). It conducts impact evaluations, disseminates knowledge, and supports the uptake and design of innovative, cost-effective, and scalable initiatives to improve women's economic and social empowerment.
what_objectives.q1_source: The Jobs and Incomes for Women Research Programme aims at understanding and generating high-quality evidence on "what works, what does not and why" for government, donors and the private sector to address gender inequality and boost women’s economic and social empowerment in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its research focuses on five thematic areas: agricultural productivity; firms and enterprises; youth employment and labour; social norms; and use and control of productive assets. (S20305017.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: 12 new high-quality impact evaluations of innovative development interventions
20 ongoing impact evaluations using World Bank resources
12 capacity building workshops and events
5 Junior Fellows and 4 Senior Fellows for African national researchers
2 major south-south learning events
Synthesis products for agricultural productivity, non-agricultural employment and entrepreneurship, and property rights/assets and agency
21 peer-reviewed journal articles, 85 working papers and policy briefs, and 3 synthesis reports (AFRGIL)
10 peer-reviewed journal articles and 35 working papers and policy briefs (SARGIL)
9 methodological validation studies on priority thematic areas (LSMS)
20 research papers on methodological validation studies (LSMS)
3 survey modules and tool packages developed and disseminated (LSMS)
3 new or updated guidebooks (LSMS)
Analysis using WBL’s 50-year panel dataset (WBL)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to generate robust evidence on effective policies and interventions to address gender inequality and boost women’s economic and social empowerment, focusing on agricultural productivity, entrepreneurship, youth employment, social norms, and productive assets. It combines research, capacity building, and policy influence to create scalable solutions.
what_objectives.quote: The impact objective of the programme is "to increase government, donor, and private sector uptake of effective policies that can address the underlying causes of gender inequality in Africa", particularly in terms of women’s economic and social empowerment, and through that promote development, poverty reduction, and growth. (S20305017.odt, Summary Information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in regions with fragile states and significant gender inequalities. For example, three of the countries in Sub-Saharan Africa are classified as fragile states, and the programme aims to address persistent gender gaps exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic and other crises.
where_context.q5_source: Three of these countries are classified as fragile states. (4058655.odt, Why a regional focus on Sub-Saharan Africa?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and data limitations affect the ability to collect robust evidence, particularly in fragile contexts. Social norms and conflict exacerbate gender inequalities, while climate risks impact women's economic opportunities and resilience.
where_context.quote: The Gender Lab, located in the Africa Region Gender Practice, distinguishes itself from other impact evaluation-based research institutions within and outside of the World Bank by maintaining a strong regional focus. The Gender Lab’s work is focused exclusively on Sub-Saharan Africa, where the Lab is currently working in 18 countries. Three of these countries are classified as fragile states. (4058655.odt, Why a regional focus on Sub-Saharan Africa?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by the World Bank with strong involvement from Southern researchers and policymakers. Decision-making is shared through regional GILs, which include local researchers and policymakers in their governance structures.
q10_capacity_building_details: fellowships and mentoring of African national researchers (5 Junior Fellows and 4 Senior Fellows)
capacity building workshops and events
south-south learning events
technical support and training for national statistical offices (NSOs) and local statisticians

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Africa Gender Innovation Lab - AGIL)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and research coordinator

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (South Asia Regional Gender Innovation Lab - SARGIL)
partner_organizations.role: Regional research and policy engagement

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (East Asia and Pacific Gender Innovation Lab - EAPGIL)
partner_organizations.role: Regional research and policy engagement

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Living Standards Measurement Study - LSMS)
partner_organizations.role: Data collection and methodological research

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Women, Business and Law - WBL)
partner_organizations.role: Data analysis and policy research

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Funding and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Local researchers and policymakers (various countries)
partner_organizations.role: Research collaboration and policy uptake

who_partners.quote: The World Bank is a major source of knowledge and finance for developing countries, and a key channel for advice and programming around women’s economic empowerment. (S20305017.odt, Why build on the World Bank and FCDO partnership?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Funds are channeled through the World Bank's Umbrella Facility for Gender Equality (UFGE), which pools resources from multiple donors to support gender-related research and policy initiatives. This allows for flexible allocation of funds across regions and themes while maintaining strategic alignment with the World Bank's gender strategy.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a network of regional Gender Innovation Labs (GILs) and specialized units (LSMS, WBL) within the World Bank. Each GIL is independently managed but collaborates closely with others, sharing knowledge and coordinating activities through the Federation of GILs and UFGE governance structures.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its established expertise in gender research, existing infrastructure (GILs, LSMS, WBL), and ability to leverage additional resources from other donors. The partnership builds on a decade of successful collaboration with FCDO.
how_mechanism.quote: FCDO’s support to the Regional Gender Innovation Labs (GILs), LSMS and WBL would be one of the only sources of funding to the World Bank on Gender and WEE research. (S20305017.odt, Why build on the World Bank and FCDO partnership?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each GIL has its own governance structure: AGIL has a Steering Committee with donor partners, academic experts, and sectoral experts; SARGIL has a Technical Advisory Committee (TAC); and EAPGIL has a Steering Committee. The UFGE is guided by the Donor Partnership Council (PC) and the World Bank’s Gender Leadership Council (GLC).
how_governance.quote: The World Bank’s Gender Group leads the global implementation of the WB’s new Gender Strategy and manages UFGE. The Gender Group and the UFGE Secretariat closely collaborate with, support, and disseminate the work of the GILs, WBL, and the gender-relevant work of the LSMS with internal and external stakeholders. (S20305017.odt, Coordination and Governance arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to specific components (AGIL, SARGIL, EAPGIL, LSMS, WBL) but can be adjusted within these components based on evolving research priorities and policy needs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in research priorities based on emerging evidence and policy demands, with approval from the relevant governance bodies (Steering Committees, TAC, UFGE).
how_flexibility.quote: The World Bank researchers are also well positioned to integrate their work with the Bank’s Global Practices, influencing programming and leveraging additional internal funds from operations to facilitate scale up of successful innovative interventions. (S20305017.odt, Why build on the World Bank and FCDO partnership?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (UFGE/GILs/LSMS/WBL) → Local researchers/policymakers
how_efficiency.quote: FCDO funds are currently provided through UFGE at the World Bank, which is operating until June 30, 2027, although we anticipate this will be extended to 2030 to align with the World Bank’s Gender Strategy. (S20305017.odt, What is the proposed approach?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Funding through the Knowledge for Change (KCP)
Adding to the Development Impact Evaluation (DIME) initiative
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UFGE mechanism was chosen for its ability to leverage the World Bank's existing infrastructure, regional focus, and strong alignment with the Bank's gender strategy. It allows for efficient coordination across regions and themes, with proven capacity to influence policy and scale up successful interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited flexibility in reallocating funds across regions/themes due to UFGE's structured allocation process.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular reviews and approvals by governance bodies (PC, GLC) to adjust allocations based on emerging needs and evidence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential for thematic drift without strong oversight.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear governance structures (Steering Committees, TAC) and alignment with the World Bank's Gender Strategy to maintain focus.

why_rationale.quote: Alternative arrangements (funding through the Knowledge for Change (KCP) or adding to the Development Impact Evaluation (DIME) initiative) have been considered but the lack of regional and thematic foci make these options less attractive, more prone to thematic drift with potentially less policy impact. (4058655.odt, Why a DFID and World Bank partnership?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The regional focus on Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and East Asia & Pacific requires partnerships with local researchers and policymakers who understand the specific gender challenges and policy environments in these regions. Fragile contexts and data limitations necessitate collaboration with institutions that have strong local presence and expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: Fragile states in Sub-Saharan Africa require adaptive and context-specific approaches.
Data limitations in many countries necessitate partnerships with organizations like LSMS that specialize in data collection and methodological research.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's focus on generating rigorous evidence to inform policy and practice determines the need for a networked delivery structure (GILs, LSMS, WBL) that can conduct impact evaluations, synthesize findings, and engage with policymakers across regions.
q28_linkages: The need for regional specificity and policy influence shapes the use of regional GILs as implementation partners.
The emphasis on data-driven policy solutions necessitates the inclusion of LSMS and WBL for data collection and analysis.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme balances the need for high-quality, rigorous research (efficiency) with the goal of inclusive partnerships and capacity building in the Global South (equity). This is operationalized through fellowships, south-south learning, and engagement with local researchers and policymakers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Investing in capacity building (e.g., fellowships, workshops) may slow down research outputs but ensures long-term sustainability and local ownership.
The use of regional GILs adds complexity to coordination but ensures that research is contextually relevant and policy-influential.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The presence of fragile states and high-risk contexts in the programme's geographic scope necessitates intensive oversight and adaptive management to ensure effective delivery and policy influence.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective that shapes partner roles, with local researchers and policymakers actively involved in research design, implementation, and policy uptake to ensure relevance and sustainability.
intersections.quote: By encouraging collaboration between the regional GILs, LSMS and WBL this extension would bring together evidence systematically and facilitate a stronger evidence base on common themes to influence policy. (S20305017.odt, What is the proposed approach?)

key_programme_risks: Limited availability of gender-disaggregated data in many countries
Policy resistance to gender-transformative interventions in conservative contexts
Fragile states and conflict affecting implementation and data collection
Ensuring uptake and scale-up of research findings by policymakers
Maintaining focus and coherence across multiple regions and themes

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Investment in methodological research and data collection through LSMS and WBL, including the use of AI technologies and innovative survey methods.
Engagement with policymakers through bilateral meetings, workshops, and synthesis reports to build evidence-based cases for gender equality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fragile states and conflict affecting implementation
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive management and close collaboration with local partners who understand the context, as well as leveraging the World Bank's experience in fragile settings.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Ensuring uptake and scale-up of research findings
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Active policy engagement, synthesis products, and a research uptake strategy to promote knowledge sharing and influence policy design.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Maintaining focus and coherence across regions/themes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strong governance structures (Steering Committees, TAC) and regular coordination meetings among GILs, LSMS, and WBL.

fcas_specific_lessons: The programme has demonstrated success in influencing World Bank operations in fragile contexts, such as Nigeria and Ethiopia, by providing just-in-time policy support during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Localization approaches, such as decentralized country labs in Nigeria and Ethiopia, have been effective in building local research capacity and engaging in policy dialogues.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Investing in AGIL has so far generated substantial value for money, with an estimated $170 influenced in development spending for every $1 spent on research/analytical work through AGIL. The programme has also successfully leveraged additional funding from other donors, such as Global Affairs Canada and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The extension includes new components on climate and gender, unpaid work and care, macroeconomics and gender, social protection, and reducing gender-based violence. It also expands the geographic scope to South Asia and East Asia & Pacific, and introduces innovative data collection methods and a helpdesk service for FCDO country teams.
risks_lessons.quote: Investing in AGIL has so far generated substantial value for money. The AGIL team track the volume of development programming inside and outside of the WB that their research has directly influenced, and hence increased the effectiveness of. Between 2013 and 2020, this is estimated at $6.4 billion of projects on three continents, with every $1 spent on research/analytical work through AGIL influencing $170 in development spending. (S20305017.odt, Results and Impact to date?)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other UFGE donors (Australia, Denmark, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United States, Canada, Germany, Latvia)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged over $100 million in additional resources from Global Affairs Canada and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and has influenced over $6.4 billion in development spending through its research and policy engagement.
financial_details.quote: FCDO has spent £21.7m to date and the programme is currently due to run until June 2025. Under this new extension, FCDO would commit an additional £28.1m to 2030, bringing the total funding for the programme to £48.95m. (S20305017.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: AgResults: Innovation in Research and Delivery
metadata.quote: "AgResults is a $145 million multi-donor initiative which designs and implements innovative payment-by-results ‘pull mechanisms’ to address market failures and stimulate either the adoption of proven agricultural technologies or Research & Development (R&D) for the development of new technology." (49628448.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original Start: June 2012", "Revised/Current End: March 2024", "New project end date (if applicable): March 2029" (49628448.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (pull mechanisms to stimulate private sector investment), implementation research (testing and scaling agricultural technologies), and evidence generation (evaluating cost-effectiveness and impact). It aims to address market failures in agricultural innovation by incentivizing private sector engagement through results-based payments, while generating rigorous evidence on what works.
what_objectives.q1_source: "AgResults is a $145 million multi-donor initiative which designs and implements innovative payment-by-results ‘pull mechanisms’ to address market failures and stimulate either the adoption of proven agricultural technologies or Research & Development (R&D) for the development of new technology. Incentives or prizes are awarded to competing businesses based on the verified achievement of pre-defined results and are intended to overcome existing markets failures that impede the development of sustainable commercial markets for agriculture technologies." (49628448.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Evidence of effect of AgResults on private sector involvement in development and spread of agricultural innovation and uptake of innovation by farmers
Evidence on the scale of any effect and their cost-effectiveness (relative to no intervention or traditional push mechanisms) of AgResults
Process reports providing lessons learned on how best to deliver AgResults
120,000 households reached with biofortified provitamin A maize in Zambia
Adoption of improved on-farm storage amongst at least 100,000 households, with 7% reduction in on-farm post-harvest losses
Adoption of Aflasafe™ to reduce aflatoxin contamination on 60,000 ha of smallholder farms
Development of a livestock vaccine and tools for control of Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR)
Environmentally friendly fertilizer products and processes developed and promoted
Evaluation of Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) vaccination project in East Africa
Evaluation of on-farm storage technology adoption in West Africa
Evaluation of solution-agnostic approach to improving rural incomes in Eastern Indonesia
what_objectives.summary: The programme uses pull mechanisms to incentivize private sector investment in agricultural innovation, while generating rigorous evidence on cost-effectiveness and impact through large-scale pilots and independent evaluations.
what_objectives.quote: "The additional £6m funding would support the objectives of the overall project in three ways. Firstly, it will enable impact evaluations to be carried out on three new projects for which funding for evaluation does not currently exist. Secondly, it will be used to generate learning and knowledge management products, and lastly provide technical assistance to support partners who want to employ the pull mechanism model." (49628448.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is described as innovative with a medium risk profile due to the weak evidence base for pull mechanisms in agriculture. Risks are mitigated through a portfolio approach and results-based payments that only disburse upon verified delivery.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risks to DFID are rated medium. This is a highly innovative programme, in an area where the evidence base is weak." (3538207.odt, Risk profile and mitigation)
q6_contextual_constraints: diverse and fractured state of agricultural markets
uncertainty of technology performance on marginal land
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Underdeveloped markets limit private sector investment and slow technology adoption. The fractured state of agricultural markets in developing countries creates uncertainty about the applicability of pull mechanisms. Environmental and climate risks (e.g., disposal of storage bags) require mitigation strategies in pilot design.
where_context.quote: "In many developing countries, private sector investment and slow technological innovation are limited by either underdeveloped or non-existent markets for agricultural inputs, services and outputs." (3538207.odt, What need are we trying to address?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Steering Committee, which includes DFID, BMGF, and other donors, makes funding decisions. Country-based pilot managers oversee implementation, suggesting a mixed decision-making structure with Northern donors and local implementers.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to partners adopting pull mechanisms
knowledge management products to disseminate lessons
gender analysis in project design

partner_organizations.name: DFID (now FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funder, leads evaluation component

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: funder, co-manages evaluation contract

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Financial Intermediary Trust Fund manager, secretariat procurement

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Australia, Canada, US
