partner_organizations.role: funders

partner_organizations.name: Abt Associates
partner_organizations.role: evaluator (incumbent)

partner_organizations.name: Country-based pilot managers
partner_organizations.role: implementation oversight, procurement of private sector delivery agents

partner_organizations.name: Private sector delivery agents
partner_organizations.role: technology development and delivery

partner_organizations.name: 3rd party verification agents
partner_organizations.role: independent verification of results

who_partners.quote: "The Agriculture Pull Mechanism Initiative is a multilateral initiative, launched under the G20. Finance will come from Australia, Canada, the US, the World Bank, and Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF). Funds will be channelled through a World Bank Financial Intermediary Trust Fund." (3538207.odt, Who will be implementing the initiative?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Funds are channeled through a World Bank Financial Intermediary Trust Fund. Payments to private sector actors are results-based (payment-by-results), with incentives or prizes awarded upon verified achievement of pre-defined outcomes. The evaluation component is managed through competitive contracts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The initiative operates through a multilateral platform with a Steering Committee (donors), a Secretariat (procured competitively), and country-based pilot managers. The World Bank acts as the financial intermediary, while DFID and BMGF co-lead the evaluation component.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The restricted competition for the evaluation contract balances speed (to align with project timelines) with quality, allowing DFID and BMGF to drive value for money while maintaining coherence with the existing evaluation framework.
how_mechanism.quote: "The Steering Committee would like to commission this third evaluation component, ensuring that the coherence of the evaluation framework and approach is maintained across all projects in the AgResults portfolio. BMGF have a particularly strong interest in the FMD evaluation... The £6m for this evaluation work will be channelled via the DFID-BMGF collaboration agreement allowing DFID to fund the contract whilst BMGF lead on the management of the contract... This will enable 3 specialist groups (including the incumbent) to bid competitively." (49628448.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes DFID, BMGF, and other donors. It approves funding decisions for new projects, oversees the Secretariat, and ensures alignment with the initiative's objectives. The committee also plays a role in screening and appraising pilot proposals.
how_governance.quote: "The Steering Committee as a whole is supportive of this concept, but have yet to identify an appropriate mechanism for taking forward this kind of TA support to other development partners." (49628448.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects based on Steering Committee decisions, as evidenced by the approval of new projects (e.g., FMD vaccination) using existing Trust Fund balances. However, reallocation requires committee approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The initiative allows for the addition of new projects (e.g., FMD vaccination, West Africa storage, Indonesia rural incomes) based on emerging priorities, but these require Steering Committee approval. The design of pull mechanisms is also adaptive, with lessons from earlier projects informing new ones.
how_flexibility.quote: "The AgResults Trust Fund has a balance of ~$30m available for Steering Committee funding decisions made on new projects. A new project, incentivising the development and distribution of an improved Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) vaccination in East Africa, was recently approved by the Steering Committee to start in November 2019." (49628448.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (Financial Intermediary Trust Fund) → Secretariat/Pilot Managers → Private Sector Delivery Agents/3rd Party Verifiers
how_efficiency.quote: "Incentives or prizes are awarded to competing businesses based on the verified achievement of pre-defined results." (49628448.odt, Summary Information)

q24_alternatives_considered: conventional push-based mechanisms (public sector-driven R&D with limited private sector engagement)
enabling mechanisms (subsidized venture capital, challenge funds, investment funds)
pull mechanisms (results-based financing to incentivize private sector)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Pull mechanisms were chosen to address market failures in agricultural innovation by leveraging private sector investment, which conventional push mechanisms had failed to achieve. The approach was selected for its potential to generate evidence on cost-effectiveness compared to traditional methods, while also aligning with DFID's strategic priorities around results-based financing and private sector engagement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Uncertainty over private sector response to incentives in fractured agricultural markets
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Portfolio approach with mixed-risk pilots; results-based payments ensure funds are only disbursed upon verified delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of designing appropriate incentive structures for diverse agricultural contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust peer review mechanisms and pilot-specific design work, including consultation with industry stakeholders.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential for market distortions or monopolies by a small number of private sector actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-qualification of products and anti-monopoly safeguards in pilot design.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3: Pull Mechanisms: Under this option, we would join the G20 multilateral initiative to develop pull mechanisms in Agriculture... This mechanism encourages collaboration and facilitates a variety of private and public sector actors to address a variety of market failures constraints... The evidence base for Options 2 and 3 is weak, as this is an emerging area of work. Developing the evidence base is one of the primary justifications for this business case." (3538207.odt, Assessing the strength of the evidence base for each feasible option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The underdeveloped and fractured state of agricultural markets in target countries (e.g., Africa) limits the types of private sector partners that can effectively participate. This necessitates careful pilot design to ensure technologies are accessible to smallholders and that incentives are structured to overcome market failures.
q27_constraints_detail: weak purchasing power of smallholders limits demand for new technologies
lack of access to output markets discourages private sector investment
diverse agro-ecological conditions require locally adapted solutions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to test pull mechanisms at scale (to generate robust evidence) requires a multilateral platform with significant donor coordination. The mixed portfolio of pilots (some high-risk, some proven technologies) shapes a flexible management structure that can adapt to different market contexts.
q28_linkages: Large-scale pilots (WHAT) → require multilateral funding and coordination (HOW)
Results-based payments (WHAT) → necessitate independent verification and robust M&E (HOW)
Private sector engagement (WHAT) → demands competitive selection processes and anti-monopoly safeguards (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between reaching the poorest smallholders (equity) and achieving rapid, cost-effective market development (efficiency). For example, prizes must be designed to avoid monopolies while still incentivizing private sector participation, and technologies must balance affordability for poor farmers with commercial viability for businesses.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of adoption vs. inclusion of marginalized farmers
private sector profitability vs. pro-poor pricing
standardized technologies vs. locally adapted solutions
intersections.risk_affects_management: The medium-risk profile of the programme (due to weak evidence base and market uncertainties) leads to intensive oversight through the Steering Committee, independent evaluations, and third-party verification. High-risk pilots are balanced with more proven interventions to manage overall portfolio risk.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme to ensure Southern partners (e.g., country-based pilot managers) can effectively oversee implementation and that private sector actors in LMICs can compete for incentives. Technical assistance is also provided to external partners adopting pull mechanisms.
intersections.quote: "If demand is uncertain among poorer sections of the population, there can be disincentives for scaling up where the poverty reduction priority is greatest. Additionally, companies do not find it profitable to invest in a portfolio targeted specifically at the needs of the poorest, who are often poorly connected to markets." (3538207.odt, Impact on smallholders, food security and gender)

key_programme_risks: Private sector may not respond to incentives as expected, leading to low adoption of technologies
Pull mechanisms may not be cost-effective compared to traditional push mechanisms
Market distortions or monopolies could emerge from prize competitions
Complexity of designing appropriate incentive structures for diverse agricultural contexts
Environmental risks (e.g., disposal of storage bags) may create unintended consequences
Political or regulatory barriers in target countries could hinder implementation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Portfolio approach with mixed-risk pilots; results-based payments ensure no payout without delivery.
Independent evaluations compare pull mechanisms to push mechanisms; Steering Committee reviews cost-effectiveness data.
Anti-monopoly safeguards in pilot design; pre-qualification of products.
Peer review mechanisms and stakeholder consultations inform pilot design.
Environmental considerations included in peer review; mitigation strategies built into implementation (e.g., bag disposal plans).

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the pneumococcal vaccine AMC in health suggest that pull mechanisms can succeed but require careful design tailored to specific market contexts. The AGPM builds on this by testing multiple mechanisms (e.g., prizes, AMCs) and emphasizing robust evaluation to generate transferable lessons.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addition of new projects (e.g., FMD vaccination, West Africa storage) reflects learning from earlier pilots. The emphasis on gender analysis in project design and the inclusion of technical assistance for external partners are also adaptations based on ongoing lessons.
risks_lessons.quote: "A number of important early lessons emerge from the AMC for pneumococcal... The specific product, market, industry and policy context matter to the design of the mechanism... Combinations of instruments may be required... to provide value enhancement to overcome uncertainty over whether investment costs can be recouped." (3538207.odt, Lessons from other sectors)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The initiative has leveraged additional private sector investment through results-based incentives, though the exact amount is not quantified in the documents. The multilateral structure also pools resources from multiple donors (total initiative budget: $145 million).
financial_details.quote: "DFID will provide an additional £6m to the £25m that was approved in 2012. This will bring our total support for the AgResults programme to £31m (a total of £13.5m for the evaluation component)." (49628448.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: MIGA’s Conflict-Affected and Fragile Economies Facility (CAFEF)
metadata.quote: The UK will provide up to £35m over five years to MIGA’s Conflict-Affected and Fragile Economies Facility (CAFEF) to support job creation and increase incomes for poor people in fragile states. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)
metadata.duration_source: The UK will provide up to £35m over five years to MIGA’s Conflict-Affected and Fragile Economies Facility (CAFEF) to support job creation and increase incomes for poor people in fragile states.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CAFEF is a multi-donor trust fund that provides political risk insurance (PRI) to encourage foreign direct investment (FDI) into fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS). The facility aims to catalyze private sector investment by reducing political risk, thereby supporting job creation, income growth, and poverty reduction in some of the world’s most insecure countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: Through the provision of political risk insurance (PRI), the facility will encourage foreign direct investment into some of the most insecure countries in the world. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

q3_expected_outputs.output: $550m of FDI into fragile and conflict-affected states
Over $150m of taxes and fees paid to governments of fragile and conflict-affected states
Over $110m local purchases supported in fragile and conflict-affected states
Over 590,000 customers reached by infrastructure projects
Over 5,300 direct jobs in fragile and conflict-affected states
Build the effectiveness of MIGA to work in fragile states, increasing its willingness to take more risk on its own balance sheet
Increase the conflict sensitivity of MIGA operations in FCAS, bringing in strengthened conflict analysis and sharing learning on this across the WBG
Catalyse and foster private sector investment in fragile and conflict-affected states and help develop a private reinsurance market

what_objectives.summary: CAFEF is a financing mechanism designed to reduce political risk for investors in fragile states, thereby increasing FDI, job creation, and economic growth. It combines insurance provision with market development objectives to create sustainable private sector activity in high-risk environments.
what_objectives.quote: The facility will encourage foreign direct investment into some of the most insecure countries in the world. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The facility targets countries on the World Bank Group’s Harmonized List of Fragile Situations, where poverty levels are far higher (54% living on less than $2/day) and conflict/weak institutions create significant barriers to investment. These countries are characterized by political instability, weak rule of law, and high vulnerability to violence.
where_context.q5_source: The facility will cover countries on the World Bank Group’s Harmonized List of Fragile Situations. This includes a number of DFID priority countries (DRC, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Zimbabwe, Afghanistan, Burma, Nepal, Yemen, OPTs). (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The three main challenges for businesses in FCAS are: (i) inadequate electricity supply; (ii) lack of access to finance; and (iii) political instability. These constraints deter both foreign and domestic investment, with only 7% of FDI to developing countries flowing to FCAS. Portfolio equity flows are virtually non-existent due to underdeveloped financial sectors, and domestic credit to the private sector is lower than in other low-income countries.
where_context.quote: The three main challenges that formal businesses themselves say they face in fragile states are: (i) an inadequate supply of electricity; (ii) lack of access to finance; and (iii) political instability. (Document: 5395216.odt, Context: violent conflict, fragility and poverty are inextricably linked)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: MIGA (a World Bank Group entity) manages the facility, with DFID and other Northern donors (CIDA, SIDA) providing funding and strategic oversight. Decision-making rests with MIGA’s governance structures, which include representation from member countries but are dominated by high-income shareholders.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening MIGA’s ability to operate in FCAS
increasing MIGA’s risk appetite for fragile states
conflict sensitivity training for MIGA operations
knowledge-sharing across the World Bank Group

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and facility manager; provides political risk insurance and underwriting

partner_organizations.name: UK Department for International Development (DFID)
partner_organizations.role: Primary funder (up to £35m); strategic oversight and performance monitoring

partner_organizations.name: Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder ($20m commitment)

partner_organizations.name: Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder ($30m in guarantees and $10m in cash)

partner_organizations.name: Export Credit Agencies (ECAs)
partner_organizations.role: Partners for reinsurance and risk-sharing

partner_organizations.name: Commercial banks and private insurance companies
partner_organizations.role: Reinsurance partners and transaction originators

who_partners.quote: CAFEF is a multi-donor trust fund housed by the World Bank Group’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA). (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides grant funding (up to £35m) to a trust fund managed by MIGA, which then uses these resources to underwrite political risk insurance (PRI) for private sector investments in FCAS. The facility combines donor contributions with MIGA’s own resources in a first-loss layer to leverage additional insurance capacity.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: MIGA manages the facility as part of its existing operations, leveraging its underwriting systems, guidelines, and global network. DFID and other donors provide oversight through performance monitoring and strategic direction, but day-to-day operations are handled by MIGA’s staff and systems.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: MIGA was selected due to its existing mandate, expertise in political risk insurance, and global reach. The facility builds on MIGA’s established processes and privileges (e.g., immunities) to enable rapid deployment in high-risk environments where other insurers are reluctant to operate.
how_mechanism.quote: CAFEF is a multi-donor trust fund housed by the World Bank Group’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA). It will provide PRI for cross-border investment and lending in FCAS through a $100 million first loss layer funded by donors and MIGA. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: MIGA selects and approves projects based on its underwriting criteria, with DFID’s role limited to high-level oversight and performance assessment. Sub-awards (insurance contracts) are allocated by MIGA to private sector investors meeting the facility’s additionality and development impact requirements.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: MIGA’s existing governance structures (e.g., Board of Directors) oversee the facility, with donor representatives (including DFID) providing input on strategic direction. The facility operates under MIGA’s standard policies but includes donor-specific reporting and evaluation requirements.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: DFID will conduct regular monitoring, a mid-term review, and an impact evaluation. The mid-term review will assess efficiency and effectiveness, potentially leading to adjustments in the facility’s design. MIGA provides periodic reports to donors on underwriting activity, claims, and development impacts.
how_governance.quote: We will determine whether the expected results have been achieved through regular monitoring, a mid-term review and impact evaluation. (Document: 5395216.odt, Monitoring and Evaluation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between countries/projects within the FCAS list based on demand and performance, but require DFID approval for additional contributions beyond the initial £20m. The facility’s revolving nature allows reused capacity over its lifetime.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The mid-term review may result in adjustments to the facility’s design or focus areas, subject to DFID’s approval. Learning from early transactions will inform refinements in underwriting criteria or target sectors.
how_flexibility.quote: We will assess the timing of further contributions approved within this business case based on need and performance and make a recommendation to the Head of Private Sector Department. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (DFID) → MIGA → private sector investors (end beneficiaries). The facility is managed directly by MIGA with DFID oversight, eliminating additional intermediary layers.
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: DFID’s initial contribution is upfront (£20m + £0.7m for evaluation), with further disbursements tied to performance. Insurance payouts to investors occur upon triggering events (e.g., political violence, expropriation) as defined in MIGA’s contracts.
how_efficiency.quote: We will make an initial contribution of £20m now. We will assess the timing of further contributions approved within this business case based on need and performance. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No DFID centralised support specifically to increase investment in FCAS beyond existing country office programmes.

Setting up a new entity to act as an intermediary between DFID and commercial insurers, subsidizing high-risk deals. This was rejected due to implementation challenges (e.g., lack of track record, high overheads, difficulty ensuring development impact).

Delivering the programme through UK Export Finance was discounted because it would restrict support to UK exports, limit geographical coverage, and potentially breach the International Development Act.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: MIGA was selected because it offers an existing, credible platform with global reach, established underwriting systems, and the ability to leverage donor funds to mobilize private reinsurance. The facility builds on MIGA’s mandate to operate in high-risk environments and can achieve scale through risk-pooling across multiple FCAS.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage of £35m to mobilize $400m in insurance capacity)
risk mitigation (MIGA’s experience in FCAS and first-loss layer structure)
partner capacity (MIGA’s existing systems and global network)
flexibility (revolving fund structure allows reused capacity)
equity (focus on poorest and most fragile countries)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited leverage if private reinsurers remain risk-averse
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The first-loss layer reduces reinsurer exposure, and MIGA’s engagement with ECAs and commercial partners aims to demonstrate viable markets over time.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low demand for insurance in FCAS due to perceived high costs or lack of awareness
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MIGA will work with export credit agencies and commercial banks to originate transactions and market the facility. Donor funds subsidize premiums to improve affordability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MIGA’s prudential limits restrict coverage in the most fragile states
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The facility aims to demonstrate successful investments to influence MIGA’s board to adjust country risk limits over time.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Difficulty ensuring additionality (projects that would have proceeded without CAFEF support)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: CAFEF will only support projects that meet strict additionality criteria, including proof that they could not be supported under MIGA’s standard business model.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (leverage ratio of 1:3 for donor contributions)
equity (targeting the poorest and most fragile countries)
why_rationale.quote: At this stage, therefore, we have eliminated this option [new intermediary entity]. For the appraisal case we have assessed the option of CAFEF against the counterfactual (‘do nothing’). (Document: 5395216.odt, Feasible options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk, fragile context of FCAS limits the pool of potential partners to those with specialized expertise and risk appetite. Most commercial insurers and DFIs avoid these markets due to political instability, weak institutions, and low profitability, leaving multilateral agencies like MIGA as the only viable implementers.
q27_constraints_detail: Few commercial insurers operate in FCAS due to high perceived risks and lack of data.
Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) like IFC and CDC have limited FCAS exposure (3% of portfolios) due to prudential limits.
Local banking partners are often unavailable in the most fragile states (e.g., Afghanistan, Sudan, Somalia), restricting financial intermediation models.
Security concerns and high operational costs deter many potential partners from engaging in FCAS.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of increasing FDI in FCAS requires a delivery structure that can (1) pool risks across multiple high-risk countries, (2) leverage multilateral immunities to operate in insecure environments, and (3) mobilize private reinsurance markets. This necessitates a centralized, multilateral approach (MIGA) rather than country-level or commercial models.

q28_linkages.mechanism: First-loss layer and MIGA’s balance sheet to absorb initial losses, lowering premiums for reinsurers.
Demonstration effect through successful underwriting, crowding in other investors and reinsurers.
Embedded learning and performance incentives tied to donor contributions.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leverage through MIGA’s global systems) with equity (targeting the poorest and most fragile states). While MIGA’s multilateral structure enables scale, it also centralizes decision-making in a Northern-led institution, potentially limiting Southern ownership. The trade-off is mitigated by focusing on countries where poverty levels are highest (54% living on <$2/day) and by embedding conflict sensitivity in MIGA’s operations.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Using MIGA’s existing systems enables rapid deployment but may sideline local institutions or Southern-led solutions.
The facility prioritizes projects that would not occur without CAFEF support, but this may limit the total volume of investments underwritten.
A multi-country approach improves efficiency but may not fully address unique constraints in individual FCAS (e.g., Somalia vs. DRC).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context necessitates intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, mid-term evaluation) and a structured approach to risk-sharing (first-loss layer, reinsurance partnerships). MIGA’s role as a multilateral insurer provides credibility but requires robust governance to ensure development impacts are prioritized over commercial returns.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme’s design, with MIGA’s increased exposure to FCAS intended to build its long-term ability to underwrite in these markets. This shapes partner roles by positioning MIGA as both implementer and beneficiary of institutional strengthening, while donors (DFID, CIDA, SIDA) focus on strategic oversight and performance incentives.
intersections.quote: Development actors face challenges working in fragile countries because of a lack of capacity, inappropriate systems and procedures, a lack of incentives to work in these states or staff that are unwilling to travel to these countries. (Document: 5395216.odt, The need for intervention)

key_programme_risks.risk: Low demand for political risk insurance in FCAS due to investor skepticism or lack of awareness.
Insufficient leverage of private reinsurance markets, limiting the facility’s ability to scale.
Political or security deterioration in target countries disrupts investments or increases claims.
MIGA’s prudential limits or board resistance prevent expansion into the most fragile states.
Difficulty demonstrating additionality (proving investments would not have occurred without CAFEF).
Limited development impact if investments are concentrated in extractives or fail to create local jobs.
Donor coordination challenges or shifting priorities reduce long-term commitment.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low demand for insurance in FCAS
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: MIGA will partner with export credit agencies, commercial banks, and multilateral providers to originate transactions and market the facility. Donor subsidies reduce premium costs for investors.
The first-loss layer (funded by donors) absorbs initial losses, making excess layers more attractive to reinsurers. MIGA will target 40% reinsurance participation on a portfolio basis.
Diversification across multiple FCAS and sectors spreads risk. MIGA’s existing claims experience shows FCAS do not generate disproportionately more claims than other developing countries.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: MIGA board resistance to increased FCAS exposure
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The facility will generate evidence on FCAS performance to inform board discussions on prudential limits. Successful transactions may demonstrate lower-than-expected risks.
Strict criteria require proof that projects could not proceed under MIGA’s standard model. Independent evaluation will assess additionality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited local job creation or poverty reduction
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Projects are screened for development impact, with targets for jobs (5,300 direct), local purchases ($110m), and tax revenues ($150m). Focus on non-extractive sectors (e.g., infrastructure) is encouraged.

fcas_specific_lessons: Political risk is the primary barrier to investment in FCAS, but actual claims rates are not significantly higher than in other developing countries. This suggests perceived risks exceed reality, creating opportunities for market-shaping interventions.
Local banking partners are often absent in the most fragile states (e.g., Afghanistan, Somalia), requiring alternative financial intermediation models or direct support to investors.
Conflict sensitivity must be integrated into investment processes, as traditional due diligence may overlook drivers of fragility (e.g., gender inequality, land tenure insecurity).
Reinsurers are more likely to engage in FCAS if first-loss layers or guarantees reduce their exposure. The facility’s 40% reinsurance target reflects this lesson.
Extractive industries dominate FDI in FCAS but create few jobs or local linkages. Diversifying into infrastructure and SMEs is critical for poverty reduction.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous MIGA facilities in FCAS (e.g., West Bank and Gaza, Afghanistan) had mixed success due to restrictive product designs and limited origination capacity. CAFEF addresses these by: (1) broadening sectoral focus beyond extractives; (2) embedding conflict analysis; and (3) leveraging MIGA’s global network for deal flow. The IFC’s experience shows that advisory work alone is insufficient—combining investment and technical assistance is necessary for impact.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expanded focus on infrastructure and job-creating sectors (beyond extractives) to align with poverty reduction goals.
Inclusion of conflict sensitivity requirements in underwriting criteria, informed by WBG’s World Development Report 2011.
Revolving fund structure to maximize reuse of capacity, addressing the limited scale of previous facilities.
Explicit targets for local economic impacts (jobs, taxes, local purchases) to ensure investments benefit host communities.
Stronger monitoring of additionality to avoid subsidizing investments that would have proceeded without CAFEF.
risks_lessons.quote: MIGA has developed a number of facilities in FCAS, including West Bank and Gaza, Afghanistan and Bosnia and Herzegovina, although these have met with varying degrees of success, partly as a result of constraints put on products offered and origination of investments. (Document: 5395216.odt, The need for intervention)

co_funding_partners.amount_usd: contribution to the $100m first-loss layer (exact amount not specified)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £35m DFID contribution (part of a $100m first-loss layer) is expected to mobilize $400m in total insurance capacity, supporting $550m in FDI. This represents a leverage ratio of approximately 1:11 (DFID funds to FDI mobilized).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The facility operates as a revolving fund, with donor contributions (capital) used to underwrite insurance contracts (revenue-generating through premiums). The first-loss layer absorbs initial claims, while reinsurance and premium income cover subsequent losses.
financial_details.quote: It is expected to mobilise three times that amount [$100m first-loss layer] in insurance capacity for projects, targeting a total underwriting capacity of $400 million. (Document: 5395216.odt, Introduction)

metadata.programme_name: Evidence for Development (E4D)
metadata.quote: "Evidence for Development (E4D) was established to help build the capacity of Government of Nepal (GoN) to generate and use evidence in order to support more effective action on poverty reduction and help Nepal to transition from dependence on aid." (50925332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: October 2015 – December 2020", "New project end date (if applicable): December 31, 2023" (50925332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening Nepal's National Statistics System and government institutions), evidence generation (data collection, surveys, and research), and policy influence (supporting evidence-based decision-making at federal, provincial, and local levels). It also includes a financing mechanism to extend and scale up existing work.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The objective of the cost and time extension is to scale up the results of the current E4D programme and to help the GoN and DFID Nepal adapt to new evidence requirements under Nepal’s new federal system." (50925332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened National Statistics System (NSS) with improved institutional framework, open government data, and survey calendars
Poverty and socio-economic indicators estimated at local level using geospatial and remote sensing data
Local government and ward census providing core data on service availability for 750 local governments and 6,000 wards
q3_expected_outputs.target: 750 local governments, 6,000 wards

q3_expected_outputs.output: Phone-based citizen engagement surveys for monitoring welfare indicators
Training of over 500 GoN staff (statisticians, policy makers, local officials) in data generation, analysis, and use
q3_expected_outputs.target: 500+ staff

q3_expected_outputs.output: Development of a national database/warehouse for improved data sharing across ministries
Implementation of District Planning Monitoring and Analysis System (DPMAS) with 25 rationalized indicators
q3_expected_outputs.target: 25 indicators (reduced from 81)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Portfolio-level Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) system for DFID Nepal
Synthesis of evidence into knowledge products (e.g., gender-based violence, planning processes, job creation)
Support to 2021 Nepal Population and Housing Census (preparatory phase)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2021 census

q3_expected_outputs.output: Open data ecosystem strengthened with increased capacity of civil society, media, and private sector to use data
Women in Data community expanded through D4D programme

what_objectives.summary: E4D aims to strengthen Nepal's capacity to generate and use evidence for poverty reduction and effective governance, focusing on adapting to Nepal's federal system by supporting data generation, analysis, and use at all government levels (federal, provincial, local) and fostering an open data ecosystem.
what_objectives.quote: "The objective of the cost and time extension is to scale up the results of the current E4D programme and to help the GoN and DFID Nepal adapt to new evidence requirements under Nepal’s new federal system." (50925332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal is categorized as moderate risk due to its transition to federalism, which presents both opportunities and challenges for data systems. The National Statistics System (NSS) is underfunded and lacks autonomy, while political pressures and data sensitivity (e.g., potential to highlight inequalities) pose risks to evidence-based decision-making.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall residual risk rating of E4D is currently Moderate and should remain so with the cost extension." (50925332.odt, Risk management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions (e.g., CBS's slow absorptive capacity and resistance to change) and political economy challenges (e.g., lack of funding for NSS, potential suppression of sensitive data) hinder evidence generation and use. Nepal's history of conflict and federal transition adds complexity, requiring adaptive approaches to data collection and dissemination.
where_context.quote: "The greatest overall risk is federalism, which presents both opportunities and risks. The National Statistics System was already unempowered and not particularly effective but with new pressures from local and provincial government the NSS and especially CBS needs to adapt to meet these new needs." (50925332.odt, Risk management)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between DFID Nepal (providing oversight and strategic direction) and Southern partners (World Bank, UNDP, The Asia Foundation, Development Initiatives), who lead implementation with local government counterparts. DFID retains approval authority for major changes but delegates day-to-day management to partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (technical and policy-relevance for statisticians, policy makers, local officials)
mentorship (embedded support to CBS, MoF, and local governments)
institutional strengthening (NSS reforms, DPMAS implementation, open data policies)
research grants (support for local data communities and innovation)
co-authorship (joint development of knowledge products and MEL frameworks)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance and capacity building for the National Statistics System (NSS), including support to CBS, provincial governments, and innovative data collection (e.g., big data, citizen-based surveys).

partner_organizations.name: UNDP
partner_organizations.role: Support to Ministry of Finance (MoF) for evidence-based policymaking, aid effectiveness, and Aid Management Platform (AMP) operations.

partner_organizations.name: The Asia Foundation (TAF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead of Data for Development (D4D) programme, focusing on open data ecosystems, local government capacity building, and digital literacy.

partner_organizations.name: Development Initiatives (DI)
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead of D4D programme, supporting data use by civil society, media, and private sector, and strengthening local data communities.

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA
partner_organizations.role: Support to CBS for the 2021 Population and Housing Census, including preparatory phase and conflict sensitivity analysis.

partner_organizations.name: Global Evaluation Framework Agreement (GEFA) or International Multi-Disciplinary Programme (IMDP)
partner_organizations.role: Procurement vehicle for the portfolio MEL component (competitive process planned).

partner_organizations.name: Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS)
partner_organizations.role: Primary GoN counterpart for statistical capacity building, data generation, and NSS reforms.

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Finance (MoF)
partner_organizations.role: Counterpart for aid effectiveness, evidence-based policymaking, and AMP management.

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration (MoFAGA)
partner_organizations.role: Counterpart for DPMAS implementation and local government data coordination.

partner_organizations.name: National Planning Commission (NPC)
partner_organizations.role: Apex body for strategic planning, monitoring, and evidence uptake.

partner_organizations.name: Local and provincial governments
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and co-implementers of data generation and use initiatives, including ward-level censuses and service delivery monitoring.

partner_organizations.name: Civil society, media, academia, and private sector
partner_organizations.role: Partners in open data initiatives, evidence use, and accountability mechanisms.

who_partners.quote: "Existing delivery partners: The above results will be delivered by extending or renewing the agreements of the existing suppliers: World Bank (MoU) for support to NSS; UNDP (MoU) for EDFC; and The Asia Foundation and Development Initiatives (AG) for D4D." (50925332.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with existing partners (World Bank, UNDP, TAF/DI) for extended work, and a competitive procurement process (via GEFA or IMDP) for the new portfolio MEL component. MoUs allow flexibility to adapt existing relationships, while competitive procurement ensures value for money for new components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID Nepal acts as the overall programme manager, with a Statistics Adviser as Senior Responsible Owner (SRO). Existing partners (World Bank, UNDP, TAF/DI) operate under MoUs with defined roles, while the portfolio MEL will be managed through a competitive contract. Regular coordination occurs through monthly informal meetings, quarterly formal reviews, and biannual partner workshops.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated for MoUs; competitive process for portfolio MEL (no ratio specified)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Existing partners were selected for extension due to their established relationships, technical expertise, and value for money (avoiding re-tendering costs). The portfolio MEL will use a competitive process (GEFA/IMDP) to ensure quality and innovation for this new component.
how_mechanism.quote: "Existing delivery partners: [...] This is the preferred commercial option compared to re-tendering for the following reasons: Understanding of data ecosystem [...]; Value for money: extending or renewing allows each component to save time and resources on inception and building up knowledge and contacts." (50925332.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Statistics Adviser (SRO) oversees the programme, with programme management support from the PET and EDT teams. The portfolio MEL will have a dedicated team reporting to the HR manager in PET. A Development Partners Statistics Coordination Group meets every 3-4 months for wider stakeholder engagement.
how_governance.quote: "Management arrangements: The current management arrangements for the programme will be maintained with the Statistics Adviser acting as SRO for E4D. [...] The portfolio MEL is expected to be quite labour intensive, especially in the early set up phase." (50925332.odt, Management arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components within the extended budget (e.g., £11m addition), but major changes require approval through annual reviews. The portfolio MEL is designed to repurpose existing programme data, indicating some flexibility in resource use.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive management, with annual reviews used to adjust logframes, indicators, and theories of change. The portfolio MEL includes a Shared Learning Agenda and reflection processes to enable responsive programming. However, significant changes require SRO approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "Annual Reviews: the Annual Review is due to be completed by October 12 each year, based on assessment of the annual reports and discussions with stakeholders." (50925332.odt, Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (World Bank/UNDP/TAF/DI) → Local government/CBS (no sub-grantees mentioned).
how_efficiency.quote: "Current budget: up to £6m from 2017 to December 2020; Budget extension: up to £3m from 2021 to December 2023" (50925332.odt, World Bank support section) [implies phased payments]

q24_alternatives_considered: Re-tendering for all components (rejected due to delays, cost, and loss of institutional knowledge)
Fully competitive procurement for extensions (rejected to maintain existing partnerships and avoid disruption)
Direct awards without competition (not mentioned but implied as an alternative for extensions)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (extending MoUs for existing partners + competitive procurement for new components) was chosen to balance (1) **value for money** (avoiding re-tendering costs and leveraging existing relationships), (2) **risk mitigation** (continuity with trusted partners in a complex federal transition), (3) **partner capacity** (existing partners have proven technical expertise and GoN relationships), and (4) **flexibility** (competitive process for innovative MEL component). The approach also aligns with DFID's adaptive management priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in implementation due to re-tendering (if competitive processes were used for all components).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Extending existing MoUs to maintain momentum while using competitive procurement only for the new portfolio MEL component.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on existing partners limiting innovation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Introducing a competitive process for the portfolio MEL to bring in new expertise and approaches.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between multiple partners (World Bank, UNDP, TAF/DI, etc.).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular partner meetings (monthly informal, quarterly formal) and a Development Partners Statistics Coordination Group to align efforts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks with CBS (e.g., requests for "bonuses").
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Channeling all funds through implementing partners (no direct access for CBS) and maintaining high-level dialogue with CBS/NPC management.

why_rationale.quote: "Existing delivery partners: [...] This is the preferred commercial option compared to re-tendering for the following reasons: Understanding of data ecosystem [...]; Value for money: extending or renewing allows each component to save time and resources on inception and building up knowledge and contacts; Reputation risk: re-tendering would result in delays in support." (50925332.odt, Approach to implementation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal's federal transition and weak institutional capacity (e.g., CBS's slow absorptive capacity, lack of NSS autonomy) constrain partner selection to organizations with existing GoN relationships and proven ability to navigate political and bureaucratic challenges. Local data needs and federal structures require partners with subnational reach (e.g., TAF/DI's work with provincial governments).
q27_constraints_detail: CBS's resistance to change and requests for "benefits" limit partner flexibility.
Federalism requires partners to engage with provincial/local governments, favoring those with existing subnational networks (e.g., TAF/DI).
Data sensitivity (risk of elite capture or conflict) necessitates partners with experience in inclusive, disaggregated data collection.
Limited GoN funding for NSS requires partners who can leverage additional resources (e.g., World Bank's technical assistance).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **subnational data generation** (due to federalism) shapes the delivery structure by expanding partnerships beyond Kathmandu (e.g., TAF/DI's role in provincial/local support). The **portfolio MEL's cross-cutting learning objectives** require a competitive, flexible mechanism (GEFA/IMDP) to synthesize evidence across programmes. **Capacity building at all government levels** necessitates a mixed structure (MoUs for institutional support + competitive procurement for innovative MEL).
q28_linkages: Federalism → Expanded partner roles to include provincial/local governments (e.g., TAF/DI's D4D extension).
Portfolio MEL's learning goals → Competitive procurement to ensure quality and innovation in synthesis.
CBS's weak capacity → MoU with World Bank for long-term technical assistance rather than short-term contracts.
Need for adaptive management → Annual reviews and flexible logframes to adjust to federal transition challenges.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (e.g., disaggregated data for marginalized groups, Women in Data initiatives) with **efficiency** (e.g., extending existing MoUs to avoid re-tendering delays). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid support to provincial governments (via existing partners) risks bypassing slower but more inclusive local processes. (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: World Bank/UNDP's technical leadership is paired with efforts to build local capacity (e.g., embedded training for CBS staff). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Competitive procurement for MEL aims to maximize value for money while ensuring high-quality synthesis.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Extending MoUs with existing partners prioritizes speed and continuity over potential innovation from new actors.
Portfolio MEL's competitive process balances cost efficiency with the need for specialized MEL expertise not available locally.
Focus on federal/provincial governments risks diluting resources for the most marginalized (e.g., remote wards), mitigated by targeted citizen engagement surveys.
Disaggregated data collection (e.g., by gender, ethnicity) increases costs but is critical for equity and conflict sensitivity.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., federalism challenges, CBS's weak capacity) drives **intensive oversight**, including monthly partner meetings, quarterly reviews, and embedded advisory roles (e.g., Statistics Adviser as SRO). High fiduciary risks (e.g., CBS "bonuses") lead to strict fund management (all payments via implementing partners).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Partners' roles are explicitly tied to capacity-building objectives: (1) **World Bank** leads technical assistance for NSS strengthening due to its global statistical expertise. (2) **TAF/DI** focus on local government and open data ecosystems, leveraging their grassroots networks. (3) **UNDP** supports MoF on aid effectiveness, aligning with its mandate. (4) **Portfolio MEL provider** will include national staff to ensure local ownership of learning processes.
intersections.quote: "The greatest overall risk is federalism, which presents both opportunities and risks. The National Statistics System was already unempowered and not particularly effective but with new pressures from local and provincial government the NSS and especially CBS needs to adapt to meet these new needs." (50925332.odt, Risk management)

key_programme_risks: Federalism transition disrupting data systems and creating unmet subnational demand (Major).
Slow absorptive capacity and resistance to change within CBS (Major).
Lack of GoN funding for NSS sustainability (Major).
Data sensitivity leading to elite capture or conflict (Moderate).
Fiduciary risks (e.g., CBS "bonuses", dummy consultants) (Major).
Reputational risk of DFID being seen to support elite interests (Moderate).
Failure to implement the Statistics Act or NSDS reforms (Major).
Limited traction in legislative/structural reforms for CBS autonomy (Major).
Political pressure to suppress disaggregated data highlighting inequalities (Moderate).
Coordination challenges between federal, provincial, and local governments (Moderate).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Develop a strategic plan to influence federal data agendas; extend support to provincial/local governments through TAF/DI and World Bank.
Maintain constant dialogue with CBS leadership; adapt partner workloads to ensure quality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of GoN funding for NSS
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Advocate for predictable GoN funding; use DFID resources to provide a platform for long-term sustainability.
Ensure disaggregation by gender, ethnicity, etc.; build requirements into all data collections; provide TA for conflict-sensitive analysis.
Channel all funds through implementing partners (no direct CBS access); maintain high-level dialogue with CBS/NPC on anti-corruption.
Prioritize disaggregated data to ensure inclusion of marginalized groups; transparent dissemination.
Advocate for reforms through DP Statistics Coordination Group; align with World Bank's NSS assessment.
Focus on capacity-building activities within DFID's control (e.g., training, IT systems) while influencing wider reforms.
Strengthen CBS autonomy through institutional reforms; engage with parliament and civil society for accountability.
Use Development Partners Statistics Coordination Group and regular partner meetings to align efforts.

fcas_specific_lessons: Federal transitions require adaptive, multi-level support (e.g., extending beyond Kathmandu to provincial/local governments).
In FCAS, data sensitivity can exacerbate conflicts; disaggregation and conflict-sensitive analysis are critical.
Weak institutions (e.g., CBS) need long-term capacity building paired with political advocacy for structural reforms.
Donor coordination is essential to avoid duplicative or conflicting support in fragile statistical systems.
Local ownership (e.g., via D4D's Women in Data community) enhances sustainability in volatile contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from annual reviews and field trips highlighted: (1) Urgent need to support subnational data demand post-federalism. (2) Importance of aligning individual E4D components into a cohesive portfolio (addressed via portfolio MEL). (3) Value of south-south learning and stakeholder engagement (e.g., EDFC's expanded focus). (4) Need for conflict-sensitive data collection (applied to 2021 census support).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The extension added: (1) **Subnational focus**: Broadened World Bank, TAF/DI, and UNDP support to provincial/local governments. (2) **Portfolio MEL**: Created to synthesize learning across DFID Nepal's portfolio. (3) **Conflict sensitivity**: Integrated into census support and data disaggregation requirements. (4) **Adaptive management**: Annual reviews now explicitly test theories of change and adjust logframes.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from Annual Reviews: Federalism and its impact on demand for data from local and provincial government has been highlighted [...]. The need to develop an approach to bring the individual products from across E4D together in a way that makes them greater than the sum of their parts." (50925332.odt, New evidence from ongoing monitoring)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages GoN's existing investments in data systems (e.g., CBS, MoF) and aligns with other development partners (e.g., World Bank's NSS assessment, UNDP's EDFC) to avoid duplication. The portfolio MEL is designed to repurpose data from across DFID Nepal's portfolio, maximizing efficiency.
financial_details.quote: "The original total budget for E4D was £15m from October 2015 to December 2020. This extension will increase the budget by £11m to a new total of £26m, with the end date extended by three years to December 2023." (50925332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: British International Investment (BII) Programme of Support in ODA eligible countries
metadata.quote: "British International Investment (BII) is the UK’s Development Finance Institution. BII makes investments in private companies in Africa and Asia in the form of equity and debt, either directly or via funds with the dual objectives to 1) achieve development impact and 2) generate a financial return." (D0003132.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 2015-2024" (D0003132.odt) and "New project end date (if applicable): September 2027" (D0003132.odt) and "New project end date (if applicable): 2028" (D0003303.odt)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme channels funds through British International Investment (BII), the UK's Development Finance Institution (DFI), to invest in private companies in ODA-eligible countries. The objective is to mobilize private sector investment, generate financial returns, and achieve development impact by supporting economic growth, job creation, and climate resilience.
what_objectives.q1_source: "BII makes investments in private companies in Africa and Asia in the form of equity and debt, either directly or via funds with the dual objectives to 1) achieve development impact and 2) generate a financial return." (D0003132.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: £10-12 billion investment programme over 2022-26
30% of investments qualifying as climate finance (over £3 billion)
Mobilisation of approximately £5 billion of private finance over the strategy period
160,000 new jobs created over 5 years
£6 billion in tax revenue generated over 5 years
125 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity generated over the strategy period
25% of investments qualified as having a positive impact on women using the 2X challenge indicators
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to deliver a £10-12 billion investment programme over 2022-26, with a focus on climate finance, job creation, and gender inclusion. It seeks to mobilize private finance, generate tax revenue, and produce electricity while ensuring 25% of investments benefit women.
what_objectives.quote: "The capital increase to BII and the associated grant funding will support a $10.5bn/£8bn programme of investments over 2022-2026 which will deliver impact across BII’s three strategic themes: Productive, Sustainable and Inclusive investments." (D0003132.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) such as Ukraine, which has suffered a 30.4% fall in GDP due to war, and Moldova, which faces significant economic instability due to its proximity to the conflict. Many target countries are classified as high-risk due to political instability, weak institutions, and economic volatility.
where_context.q5_source: "The scale of human suffering and damage to Ukraine’s infrastructure and economy caused by Russia’s war against Ukraine is immense. Ukraine suffered a 30.4% fall in GDP in 2022 and its fiscal deficit in 2023 (before considering international support) is projected to be around $38 billion." (D0003303.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and conflict in Ukraine and Moldova create significant operational challenges, including infrastructure damage, economic instability, and regulatory uncertainties. Weak institutions and political economy issues in many target countries increase investment risks and transaction costs, while climate risks and data limitations further complicate programme delivery.
where_context.quote: "The war has destroyed Ukrainian infrastructure on a monumental scale, and Russia’s deliberate targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure has been particularly devastating. The Kyiv School of Economics has estimated that, as of December 2022, total infrastructure damage amounted to $137 billion." (D0003303.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: BII, as a UK-based institution, holds decision-making power over investments and strategy, with oversight from FCDO as the shareholder. Local partners and investees in ODA-eligible countries implement projects but do not have direct control over investment decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance through BII Plus
advisory support to improve business integrity and ESG standards
training and support for investee companies to enhance productivity and sustainability

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: co-investment partner in Ukraine and Moldova

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: co-investment partner in Ukraine and Moldova

partner_organizations.name: Local financial institutions and private companies
partner_organizations.role: investees and implementation partners

who_partners.quote: "BII will partner with DFIs who hold current presence in the region to ensure that capital can be deployed effectively and BII benefits from their experience and market knowledge." (D0003303.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Financial Transactions (FT) for core investments and Fiscal Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) for concessional finance, including grants and blended finance. Promissory Notes (PNs) are issued to provide funding assurance for BII's investment commitments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: BII operates as an arm’s length body (ALB) from FCDO, with its own Board of Directors and investment committees. FCDO provides oversight through shareholder meetings and governance arrangements but is not involved in day-to-day operations or investment decisions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: BII, as the UK's DFI, is the designated implementer of the programme. Partner selection for co-investments is based on alignment with BII's strategic objectives, market presence, and ability to share risks, particularly in high-risk environments like Ukraine and Moldova.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO oversight and governance of BII is provided through its rights as a shareholder and represented in the Articles of Association, MOU and the 5-year investment policy (2022-26)." (D0003132.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: BII is governed by a Board of Directors, with the Chair and two non-Executive Directors appointed by FCDO. Investment decisions are delegated to Investment Committees (ICs) with internal and external members. FCDO exercises oversight through quarterly shareholder meetings and annual reviews but does not interfere in individual investment decisions.
how_governance.quote: "Oversight of BII operations is via quarterly and annual shareholder meetings chaired by DG Indo-Pacific. The annual shareholder meeting is attended by the Board." (D0003132.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated within the programme's strategic priorities, subject to approval by BII's governance structures and alignment with the Investment Policy. The use of Promissory Notes provides flexibility in timing and drawdown of funds.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: BII's strategy allows for adjustments in response to changing market conditions and emerging opportunities, particularly in climate finance and fragile states. However, significant changes require approval from FCDO and alignment with the overall Investment Policy.
how_flexibility.quote: "The capital increase will allow BII to invest: Up to £8 billion over 5 years for growth and catalyst investments in Africa and South Asia. At least 30% of total investments will be ICF." (D0003132.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BII → investees/partners
how_efficiency.quote: "BII’s operating cost framework for 2022-27 includes a commitment to keep costs up to 1.7% of Total Portfolio plus unfunded commitments at the calendar year-end." (D0003132.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: direct FCDO investment management
multilateral DFI partnerships
pure grant-based financing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: BII was chosen as the delivery mechanism due to its established track record as a DFI, ability to operate in high-risk environments, and capacity to mobilize private finance at scale. The arm’s length structure ensures commercial discipline while achieving development impact, and the use of blended finance allows for higher risk tolerance in fragile states.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk due to business integrity challenges in Ukraine and Moldova
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced due diligence and compliance with BII's Policy on Responsible Investing, including anti-corruption measures and routine screening against sanctions lists.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Underutilization of risk tolerance in concessional capital
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust governance processes for the Climate Innovation Facility and LIC Facility, including independent investment committees and alignment with DFI Blended Finance Principles.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Currency and political risks in FCAS
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of blended finance to absorb higher risks, partnership with experienced DFIs like EBRD and IFC, and strict adherence to BII's risk management framework.

why_rationale.quote: "BII’s approach to risk was reviewed in 2019. As a result of this review, BII strengthened their approach to risk by building out their risk management systems and recruiting personnel including a Chief Risk Officer." (D0003132.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk and FCAS context of Ukraine and Moldova limits partner selection to organizations with established presence and experience in these markets, such as EBRD and IFC. Local partners must meet BII's strict business integrity and ESG standards, reducing the pool of eligible investees.
q27_constraints_detail: security risks limit on-the-ground operations
weak institutions increase due diligence requirements
regulatory uncertainties require experienced partners
corruption risks necessitate enhanced compliance measures
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's objectives of mobilizing private finance and achieving development impact in high-risk environments determine the need for a flexible, arm’s length delivery structure. BII's dual mandate (financial return and development impact) requires a governance model that balances commercial discipline with strategic oversight by FCDO.
q28_linkages: climate finance targets require blended finance instruments
FCAS operations necessitate partnerships with experienced DFIs
gender inclusion goals shape technical assistance and investment criteria
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive partnerships and rapid delivery, particularly in FCAS like Ukraine. While BII aims to support local businesses and marginalized groups, the need for speed and risk mitigation often leads to partnerships with larger, more established entities (e.g., EBRD, IFC) rather than direct engagement with smaller local firms.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: faster deployment through DFI partnerships may exclude smaller local businesses
expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led governance ensures compliance but limits Southern decision-making
cost vs. reach: higher transaction costs in FCAS reduce the volume of investments that can be made
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of target countries (e.g., Ukraine, Moldova) increases oversight intensity, with quarterly shareholder meetings, enhanced due diligence, and strict compliance requirements. FCDO's 'no surprises' policy and regular audits reflect the need for tighter control in fragile contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building through BII Plus and technical assistance is embedded in the programme to strengthen local partners' ability to meet BII's standards. This shapes partner roles by enabling smaller firms and financial institutions to participate in BII-funded projects, expanding the programme's reach and impact.
intersections.quote: "BII will continue to operate against its high standards for Business Integrity and ESG responsibilities, as set out in its Investment Policy and Policy for Responsible Investing, and will ensure that investments in Ukraine and Moldova fully satisfy these standards." (D0003303.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Business integrity risks in Ukraine and Moldova due to high corruption levels
Currency and political risks in FCAS affecting financial returns
Underutilization of concessional capital due to limited investible opportunities
Slow deployment of funds in high-risk markets
Reputational risks for FCDO if BII fails to manage integrity risks adequately
Macroeconomic volatility in target countries impacting investment viability
Limited pipeline of bankable projects in LICs and FCAS
High operating costs in fragile states reducing programme efficiency

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Business integrity risks in Ukraine and Moldova
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strict adherence to BII's Policy on Responsible Investing, enhanced due diligence, and partnership with experienced DFIs like EBRD and IFC to leverage their local knowledge and risk management capabilities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Currency and political risks in FCAS
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of blended finance to absorb higher risks, diversification of portfolio across sectors and countries, and close monitoring through quarterly shareholder reviews.

Robust governance processes for the Climate Innovation Facility and LIC Facility, including independent investment committees and clear additionality criteria to ensure concessional capital is used where most needed.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Slow deployment of funds in high-risk markets
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Partnership model with EBRD, IFC, and other DFIs to accelerate deal flow and leverage their pipelines, combined with technical assistance to build investible projects.
BII's 'no surprises' policy, regular audits, and enhanced assurances on business integrity processes, with FCDO retaining oversight through quarterly shareholder meetings.
Flexible investment instruments (e.g., local currency financing, guarantees) and patient capital approach to accommodate economic fluctuations.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited pipeline of bankable projects in LICs and FCAS
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Upstream technical assistance through BII Plus and initiatives like ARIA to develop investible opportunities, combined with higher risk tolerance in the LIC Facility.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High operating costs in fragile states
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Concessional capital to cover additional transaction costs, focused sectoral approaches (e.g., financial services, infrastructure), and leveraging partnerships to share operational burdens.

fcas_specific_lessons: Enhanced due diligence and compliance measures are critical in FCAS to mitigate corruption and integrity risks.
Partnerships with multilateral DFIs (e.g., EBRD, IFC) are essential for effective risk-sharing and local market access in conflict-affected regions.
Blended finance is a necessary tool to absorb higher risks in FCAS and catalyze private sector investment.
Technical assistance and upstream project development are key to building a pipeline of bankable projects in fragile states.
Flexible financing instruments (e.g., local currency loans, guarantees) are required to address macroeconomic volatility in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases demonstrated the importance of a strong development impact framework to guide investments, the need for patient capital in fragile markets, and the value of DFI partnerships in mobilizing private finance. The 2017-2021 strategy highlighted the effectiveness of sector-focused approaches and the role of technical assistance in enhancing impact.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2022-2026 strategy incorporates a more rigorous development impact framework, expanded use of blended finance (e.g., Climate Innovation Facility, LIC Facility), and deeper partnerships with DFIs to address lessons from previous phases. The addition of concessional capital tools reflects learning on the need for higher risk tolerance in FCAS and LICs.
risks_lessons.quote: "BII’s 2022-26 strategy will maintain this risk appetite and scale of ambition, delivering on average over £1.6bn of investments each year. Core elements of the 2022-26 strategy are summarised below, These demonstrate the substantial degree of continuity in the key elements of this new strategy but also the significant number of areas where it has committed to greater ambitions." (D0003132.odt, BII’s 2022-26 strategy)

co_funding_partners.partner: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize approximately £5 billion of private finance over the 2022-2026 strategy period, including £2 billion for climate projects. This represents a leverage ratio of roughly 1:1.4 (£5 billion mobilized against £3.5 billion of BII capital increase).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is primarily capital expenditure (FT) for investments, with a smaller component of revenue expenditure (RDEL) for technical assistance and advisory services. The £3.5 billion capital increase is complemented by £40 million in RDEL for BII Plus and £250 million in FT for Ukraine expansion.
financial_details.quote: "The capital increase will allow BII to invest: Up to £8 billion over 5 years for growth and catalyst investments in Africa and South Asia. At least 30% of total investments will be ICF. Up to £500 million over 5 years to expand investments to the Indo-Pacific region, beginning with climate funds." (D0003132.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Capital Investment in Risk Pools (originally known as African Risk Capacity)
metadata.quote: "In March 2014, the Department for International Development (DFID), now the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), agreed support of up to £100m over 20 years to launch an African regional risk insurance pool and early response mechanism, African Risk Capacity (ARC)." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 13/03/2014–31/03/2034" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31/03/2044" (62196180.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily functions as a financing mechanism (risk insurance pools) but also includes significant capacity building (technical assistance for contingency planning) and technology development (Africa RiskView software). It aims to provide early response funding for natural disasters while strengthening African governments' risk management capabilities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ARC enables African governments to insure themselves against natural disasters... Buying insurance cover as a group reduces the costs of insurance for members... Technical assistance in disaster risk financing diagnostics and contingency planning also improves governments’ understanding of broader risk management options." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: £772m of cumulative coverage across 14 African countries by 2021
$65 million in insurance pay-outs disbursed since establishment
120 days for first contact to assist drought-affected communities (vs previous 210 days)
1.9 million people covered by ARC insurance policies by 2015 (target)
25 drought-vulnerable countries with contingency plans by 2034 (target)
$200 million of African public finance mobilized for climate change by 2034 (target)
Expansion to tropical cyclone, flood, and epidemic coverage models
Replica coverage for humanitarian first responders (e.g., $10.6m pay-out to START Network in Senegal)
what_objectives.summary: The programme establishes regional risk insurance pools to provide rapid disaster response funding while building African governments' capacity to manage climate risks through technical assistance and contingency planning support.
what_objectives.quote: "ARC is the first and only sovereign insurance pool in Africa, and the first in the world that links pay-outs to pre-approved contingency plans which direct funds quickly to pre-agreed response plans." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in climate-vulnerable regions including FCAS (Fragile and Conflict-Affected States) where governments may be unwilling or unable to lead responses. The addendum explicitly mentions expanding Replica coverage to FCAS like Somalia where country governments cannot respond effectively.
where_context.q5_source: "It is hoped that this precedent can be replicated in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where Governments are unwilling or unable to lead responses." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate change increases disaster frequency/severity while weak institutional capacity limits risk management. Competing budget priorities (e.g., COVID-19) reduce governments' ability to pay insurance premiums. In FCAS, lack of government capacity requires humanitarian actors to lead responses.
where_context.quote: "With competing demands on budgets and a hesitancy to move into insurance for the first time, in a still evolving field, governments often took out smaller policies which left large parts of the risk uninsured." (62196180.odt, Theory of Change)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ARC is governed by an African Union treaty with decision-making by African member countries through the ARC Agency's Conference of Parties and Governing Board. Donors (UK/Germany) provide capital but have limited governance roles as Class C members.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance in disaster risk financing diagnostics
