contingency planning support
peer review mechanisms for plan quality assurance
training on risk assessment and insurance mechanisms
post-pay-out audits and learning reviews

partner_organizations.name: African Risk Capacity (ARC) Agency
partner_organizations.role: Specialised Agency of the African Union overseeing technical assistance and quality assurance

partner_organizations.name: ARC Ltd (insurance company)
partner_organizations.role: Mutual insurance company underwriting policies and managing pay-outs

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Original secretariat host during design phase; continues as implementation partner

partner_organizations.name: Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF)
partner_organizations.role: Regional risk pool for Caribbean/Small Island States

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Catastrophe Risk Insurance Company (PCRIC)
partner_organizations.role: Regional risk pool for Pacific nations

partner_organizations.name: South East Asia Disaster Risk Insurance Facility (SEADRIF)
partner_organizations.role: Regional risk pool for ASEAN countries

partner_organizations.name: START Network
partner_organizations.role: Humanitarian NGO network receiving Replica coverage

partner_organizations.name: KfW (German Development Bank)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder with 50% burden share for ARC capitalization

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Trust fund administrator for PCRIC/SEADRIF; technical partner

who_partners.quote: "ARC Agency is a specialised Agency of the African Union established to provide technical assistance to African countries joining ARC as well as quality assurance, audit, and learning on delivery of pay-outs." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) Returnable capital investments (£90m non-fiscal CDEL) in insurance pools, and 2) Grants (£10m RDEL) for technical assistance. Capital is provided at 0% interest with 20-year return terms, while grants fund capacity building.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ARC is governed by African Union member states through the ARC Agency (intergovernmental body with Conference of Parties and Governing Board). ARC Ltd operates as a separate mutual insurance company. Donors (UK/Germany) participate as Class C members with limited governance rights.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ARC was established via an African Union treaty with member countries as Class A members. The UK/Germany joined as capital providers (Class C) through direct negotiation. Other risk pools (CCRIF/PCRIC/SEADRIF) were pre-existing World Bank-administered facilities.
how_mechanism.quote: "ARC Ltd was registered in Bermuda in November 2013. Its application for a full insurance licence is underway... A Board of Directors has been appointed (with 5 of a possible 7 seats filled)." (4643483.odt, Governance section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: ARC Ltd has a Board of Directors (7 seats) and ARC Agency has a Governing Board. Decisions on insurance underwriting, pay-outs, and contingency plan approvals require joint approval between ARC Agency (technical arm) and ARC Ltd (insurance company). Donors have observer roles but no voting rights on operational decisions.
how_governance.quote: "An agreed compliance policy sets out what will happen if a country fails to use the funds properly – including return of funds and suspension of Certificate of Good Standing (and therefore ability to participate in ARC) in the worst cases." (4643483.odt, Accountability section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The 2021 addendum allows reallocation of remaining £60m CDEL across four regional risk pools (Africa, Caribbean, Pacific, SE Asia) based on need and strategic fit, but requires IFD Director approval for each investment. Original ARC funds could not be reallocated outside Africa.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: New perils (e.g., floods, epidemics) can be added to insurance products with Governing Board approval. Contingency plans are reviewed annually and can be adjusted based on lessons from pay-out audits. The 2044 extension allows testing new products like public asset insurance.
how_flexibility.quote: "Expanding the scope of this business case would enable direct Financial Transaction investment into the Caribbean, South East Asia, and Pacific risk pools, as well as the African pool... Decisions will be taken over the next 1-3 years, based on the needs of each risk pool compared to its current reserves and client demands for expansion." (62196180.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ARC Agency/ARC Ltd (implementing partners) → Member countries (no sub-grantees; funds flow directly to governments)
how_efficiency.quote: "Pay-outs are made when satellite data indicates drought thresholds are crossed, with funds disbursed to pre-approved contingency plans. After responses, there is a full programme audit, beneficiary spot check and financial audit." (62196180.odt, Summary Information)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (counterfactual)
Bilateral country-level insurance schemes
Commercial insurance markets
Humanitarian appeal mechanisms (status quo)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The risk pool model was selected because: 1) It reduces insurance costs through regional risk diversification; 2) Enables faster pay-outs than humanitarian appeals (120 vs 210 days); 3) Incentivizes better risk management via contingency planning requirements; 4) Allows gradual transition to African ownership (premiums to replace donor capital); 5) Complements existing social protection systems.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (reduces basis risk via satellite data)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Basis risk (mismatch between pay-out triggers and actual losses)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Countries submit final implementation plans 1 month before pay-out to tailor activities to actual harvest failure levels. Pay-outs for less severe events can fund risk-reduction assets.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low country uptake due to budget constraints
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Premium subsidies through Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF) and technical assistance to demonstrate value. Pilot Replica policies for humanitarian actors in FCAS.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor dependency for capitalization
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: 20-year returnable capital structure with expectation that country premiums will sustain the pool post-2044. Exploring blended finance (Convergence platform) and private sector investors.

why_rationale.quote: "By pooling Africa’s risk of extreme weather, the countries will reduce the cost to each government of maintaining contingency funds or of buying insurance from the commercial markets... The benefit of an early response is currently estimated to be around US$3 for every US$1 spent when compared to traditional humanitarian response mechanisms." (4643483.odt, Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts limit government-led responses, requiring humanitarian actors (e.g., START Network) to take Replica policies. Climate vulnerability in Small Island States (Caribbean/Pacific) necessitates regional pools due to limited individual country capacity to absorb risks.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS governments unable/unwilling to lead → requires NGO partners
Small Island States' climate exposure → needs regional risk sharing
Weak contingency planning capacity → requires embedded technical assistance
Competing budget priorities (e.g., COVID-19) → limits premium payments
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid pay-outs (WHAT) drives the parametric insurance structure (HOW) with pre-approved plans. Capacity building objectives (WHAT) require embedded technical assistance teams (HOW) within ARC Agency.
q28_linkages: Early response requirement → parametric triggers + pre-approved plans
Risk pooling goal → regional multilateral structure
Capacity building needs → ARC Agency's technical assistance role
FCAS challenges → Replica policy for humanitarian actors
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) Including FCAS via Replica policies reduces efficiency (higher transaction costs) but improves equity; 2) Premium subsidies improve affordability for poor countries but require donor funds; 3) Strict contingency plan requirements ensure effective responses but may exclude weaker governments.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed (rapid pay-outs) vs inclusion (FCAS access)
affordability (subsidies) vs sustainability (donor dependency)
rigor (plan requirements) vs reach (excluding weaker governments)
intersections.risk_affects_management: High-risk contexts (FCAS/climate vulnerability) require intensive oversight: annual audits, beneficiary spot checks, and financial reviews for all pay-outs. ARC's Governing Board includes risk management committees to monitor basis risk and reinsurance strategies.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme's capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Requiring ARC Agency to provide technical assistance for contingency planning; 2) Mandating peer review mechanisms for plan quality assurance; 3) Using pay-out audits as learning opportunities to strengthen future responses.
intersections.quote: "An important secondary effect is the strengthening of the broader disaster risk ecosystem. As regional institutional structures, risk pools support coordination, development of political mechanisms, preparedness planning beyond insurance, and investment in reliable data and models." (62196180.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks: Basis risk (1 in 5 chance of mismatch between pay-outs and actual losses)
Low country uptake due to budget constraints (exacerbated by COVID-19)
Donor fatigue/funding gaps for capitalization
Political risks in FCAS limiting government participation
Reinsurance market volatility affecting premium costs
Climate change increasing frequency/severity of disasters
Weak institutional capacity in some member countries

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Final Implementation Plans submitted 1 month pre-pay-out to adjust activities; pay-outs for less severe events fund long-term risk reduction assets.
Premium subsidies via GRIF; Replica policies for humanitarian actors; technical assistance to demonstrate ROI.
20-year returnable capital; blended finance (Convergence platform); private sector engagement.
Replica policies for NGOs; adaptive products for public assets/infrastructure.
Expanding peril coverage (floods, epidemics); increasing capital reserves.

fcas_specific_lessons: Replica policies enable humanitarian responses where governments cannot lead (e.g., Somalia).
NGO partnerships require additional due diligence but expand reach in high-risk areas.
Flexible products (e.g., public asset insurance) better suit FCAS contexts than sovereign policies.
Premium subsidies are critical for FCAS participation but require long-term donor commitments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) CCRIF demonstrated that regional pools can achieve sustainability with proper capitalization (49 pay-outs totaling $200m since 2007). 2) PCRIC's slow growth highlighted the need for patient capital and gradual product expansion. 3) ARC's Performance Improvement Plans (2016-17) resolved early issues with reinsurance and quality assurance. 4) Premium subsidies proved essential for initial uptake but must be time-bound to avoid dependency.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Expanded from drought-only to multi-peril coverage (cyclones, floods, epidemics). 2) Added Replica policies for humanitarian actors. 3) Extended duration to 2044 to allow capital accumulation. 4) Incorporated gender targeting and beneficiary spot checks. 5) Developed public asset insurance products for critical infrastructure.
risks_lessons.quote: "The experience with the Pacific demonstrates the importance of long-term investment in the risk pools to enable sustainable growth, strategy development, and roll-out of new products... Additional capital will enable growth also in important new sectors such as infrastructure and public assets." (62196180.odt, Ongoing Learning)

co_funding_partners.partner: Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: $772m in cumulative coverage across 14 African countries with $103m in premiums paid (mix of national resources and donor subsidies). $65m disbursed in pay-outs to date. Additional leverage expected through blended finance (Convergence platform) and private sector investments.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £90m non-fiscal Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) for risk pool capitalization (returnable over 20 years) + £10m Resource Departmental Expenditure Limit (RDEL) for technical assistance grants.
financial_details.quote: "The total approved budget for this programme (up to £100m, including up to £90m in non-fiscal CDEL and up to £10m in RDEL) will not increase. This addendum is to expand the geographic scope for CDEL investments beyond Africa to the Caribbean, Pacific and South East Asia, if needed." (62196180.odt, Additional Support)

metadata.programme_name: Adolescence Research Programme GAGE
metadata.quote: "GAGE is a decade-long (2015–2026) mixed-methods longitudinal research and evaluation study." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "GAGE is a decade-long (2015–2026) mixed-methods longitudinal research and evaluation study." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GAGE is primarily an **evidence generation** programme (longitudinal research on adolescent well-being) with strong **policy influence** objectives (direct engagement with decision-makers) and **capacity building** (75% of researchers from Global South). It also includes **implementation research** through nested impact evaluations.
what_objectives.q1_source: "GAGE is a decade-long (2015–2026) mixed-methods longitudinal research and evaluation study... generates evidence on ‘what works’ to enable adolescent girls and boys emerge from poverty and fast-track social change..." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)

q3_expected_outputs.output: longitudinal datasets
q3_expected_outputs.target: 20,000 adolescents across 6 countries (2 cohorts: 10–12 and 15–17 years at baseline)

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy briefs and reports
q3_expected_outputs.target: country-specific and cross-country syntheses (e.g., on conflict, economic growth links)

q3_expected_outputs.output: participatory research outputs
q3_expected_outputs.target: with 4,500+ refugee/displaced adolescents

q3_expected_outputs.output: capacity-strengthened researchers
q3_expected_outputs.target: 75% of GAGE researchers from Global South

q3_expected_outputs.output: open-access data
q3_expected_outputs.target: publicly accessible longitudinal dataset

q3_expected_outputs.output: dissemination events
q3_expected_outputs.target: series in all GAGE countries + final conference

what_objectives.summary: GAGE combines **longitudinal research** (tracking 20,000 adolescents), **policy engagement** (direct uptake with national/international actors), and **capacity building** (Global South-led research) to generate actionable evidence on adolescent well-being in LMICs.
what_objectives.quote: "Rigorous, policy-relevant research on what works to enhance adolescent girls' capabilities... Effective research uptake. Knowledge and evidence are effectively communicated... Capacity strengthening... enabling researchers from the Global South." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)

countries_regions: Ethiopia (Africa, including Tigray and conflict-affected Afar)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Multiple countries are fragile/conflict-affected: Ethiopia (Tigray conflict), Lebanon/Jordan (Syrian/Rohingya/Palestinian refugees), and Rwanda (Congolese refugees). The addendum explicitly notes delays due to "conflict-affected northern Afar" and "spillover effects of the war in Gaza on Jordan and Lebanon."
where_context.q5_source: "Endline quantitative datasets for... Ethiopia (including in Tigray and conflict-affected northern Afar)... GAGE includes more than 4,500 refugee and internally displaced adolescents... The spillover effects of the war in Gaza on Jordan and Lebanon." (D0006485.odt, Expected Results and Summary Information)
q6_contextual_constraints: data limitations (e.g., delayed surveys due to COVID-19)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: COVID-19 halted data collection for 2 years, requiring a pivot to pandemic-related research. Budget cuts (57% in 2021/22, 42% in 2022/23) delayed endline surveys. Conflict in Tigray/Afar and refugee influxes (Syrian, Rohingya) disrupted fieldwork and added complexity to sampling.
where_context.quote: "GAGE faced critical challenges... (i) unable to continue planned research during COVID-19... (ii) faced budget reductions of 57% for FY 2021/22 and 42% in 2022/23... delayed the endline data collection." (D0006485.odt, Cost Extension Objective)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ODI (UK) holds the prime contract and manages the consortium, though 75% of researchers are from the Global South. Decision-making on research priorities and dissemination appears centralized, with ODI negotiating extensions and budget revisions directly with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for Global South researchers (75% of team)
youth researchers (direct involvement in data collection/analysis)
mentorship via quarterly management team reviews
co-authorship on publications
in-person writing workshops for final analysis

partner_organizations.name: Overseas Development Institute (ODI)
partner_organizations.role: consortium prime/lead

partner_organizations.name: Country-based research teams
partner_organizations.role: data collection/fieldwork
partner_organizations.location: Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Jordan, Lebanon, Nepal, Rwanda (LMICs)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF Office of Research
partner_organizations.role: partner for structural determinants analysis (from original 4277938.odt)

who_partners.quote: "GAGE’s capacity strengthening is aimed at enabling researchers from the Global South (including youth researchers), who have local insights and deeper relationships with local policymakers... Currently 75% of GAGE researchers are from the Global South." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO holds a direct contract with ODI as the prime, with fixed deliverables (e.g., endline datasets, policy briefs) and milestone-based payments. The addendum describes renegotiations for overhead increases (7% to 27%) and a 24-month extension, indicating a formal contractual relationship.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ODI acts as the prime contractor, managing a core team (Director, Operations Manager, regional directors) and country-based researchers. Sub-awards or partnerships (e.g., with UNICEF) are pre-defined, not open to competitive calls. The structure is hierarchical, with ODI negotiating all changes with FCDO.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The extension was awarded to ODI without competition due to (1) the longitudinal nature of the research requiring continuity of the same team, and (2) ODI’s existing relationships with national governments and stakeholders, which were deemed critical for data collection and uptake.
how_mechanism.quote: "ODI management would not agree to the previous terms... FCDO assessed that the best option was to renegotiate the fee margin with ODI... so that this long-term research study could be finalised with the same central team of researchers." (D0006485.odt, Cost Extension Objective)

how_governance.quote: "The GAGE management team meets quarterly to review progress in terms of deliverables and key plans." (D0006485.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are tied to specific deliverables (e.g., endline surveys, policy briefs). The extension was required due to rigid budget lines that couldn’t absorb delays from COVID-19 or budget cuts without formal renegotiation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme pivoted to COVID-19 research during the pandemic, but core longitudinal objectives (e.g., tracking the same 20,000 adolescents) remained fixed. Adjustments required FCDO approval (e.g., 24-month extension).
how_flexibility.quote: "GAGE was unable to continue planned research and data collection during the Covid-19 pandemic... they pivoted research instead to respond to the high demand for evidence on the immediate and longer-term impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic." (D0006485.odt, Cost Extension Objective)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ODI (prime) → country-based research teams (no sub-grantees mentioned).
how_efficiency.quote: "The GAGE programme will continue to operate at 7% margin (NPAC) until 30 November 2024 and... at 26% margin (NPAC) from 01 December 2024 to 30 November 2026... The average overheads over the lifetime of the programme would be 12.03%." (D0006485.odt, Additional Support)

q24_alternatives_considered: transferring the prime contract to another consortium partner
terminating the programme in November 2024
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Continuity of the **same research team** was deemed essential for longitudinal integrity (tracking 20,000 adolescents over 11 years) and **policy relationships** (trust with national governments). ODI’s institutional knowledge and existing contracts with country teams were considered irreplaceable.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (avoiding loss of 10 years of data)
value-for-money (12.03% average overhead within FCDO thresholds)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of longitudinal data integrity if the prime contractor changed mid-programme.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Renegotiated contract with ODI to ensure team continuity, despite higher overheads.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational damage to FCDO if the programme ended prematurely without endline data.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Approved 24-month extension to capture endline findings, despite budget constraints.

why_rationale.quote: "Ending before the objectives are fully achieved would be ‘catastrophic’ for the programme as it would not produce the evidence we are hoping it will... The cost-to-date would be wasted if the endline data are not captured and synthesised." (D0006485.odt, Implications of Not Extending)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Conflict and refugee contexts (Ethiopia, Lebanon, Jordan) **limited partner options** to organizations with existing field presence and trust in fragile areas. ODI’s pre-existing relationships with governments in FCAS countries (e.g., Ethiopia, Rwanda) were a key factor in its selection as prime.
q27_constraints_detail: conflict in Tigray/Afar restricted new partners from entering
refugee populations (Syrian, Rohingya) required specialized ethical/expertise capacities
COVID-19 travel restrictions favored incumbents with local teams
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **longitudinal research design** (tracking individuals over 11 years) necessitated a **closed consortium** to maintain consistency in methods/relationships. The **policy influence objective** required a prime (ODI) with direct FCDO access for uptake.
q28_linkages: Need for trust with adolescents → closed consortium with continuous teams
FCAS contexts → centralized management for security/ethics oversight
Policy engagement → UK-based prime (ODI) for donor coordination
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The **75% Global South researcher target** increased costs (training, coordination) but was justified for **local legitimacy** and **data quality**. The **26% overhead for ODI** (post-2024) was accepted to retain **institutional continuity**, prioritizing effectiveness over strict cost-efficiency.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: equity (Global South researchers) vs. cost (higher overheads for ODI)
expertise (ODI’s methodological rigor) vs. ownership (limited Southern decision-making on budget)
speed (delays from COVID/conflict) vs. inclusion (ensuring refugee/disabled adolescents were tracked)
intersections.risk_affects_management: High FCAS risk (Ethiopia, Lebanon) led to **intensive oversight** (quarterly reviews) and **centralized control** (ODI prime), despite efficiency trade-offs.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building objective** (75% Global South researchers) shaped ODI’s role as both **implementer** and **mentor**, blending delivery with training responsibilities.
intersections.quote: "GAGE’s capacity strengthening is aimed at enabling researchers from the Global South... who have local insights and deeper relationships with local policymakers... Currently 75% of GAGE researchers are from the Global South." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information)

key_programme_risks: Loss of endline data due to budget cuts/conflict (mitigated via extension)
Reputational risk to FCDO if programme terminated early (mitigated via renegotiation)
Ethical risks in FCAS contexts (e.g., refugee adolescents) (mitigated via participatory methods)
Data gaps from COVID-19 disruptions (mitigated via pivot to pandemic research)
Overhead cost increases post-2024 (mitigated via negotiated cap at £1.5m)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: 24-month costed extension approved to complete data collection.
Renegotiated to 26% overhead post-2024, capped at £1.5m total increase.
Adapted survey instruments for remote data collection where possible.

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-existing relationships with governments/NGOs in FCAS are critical for access (e.g., Ethiopia, Rwanda).
Refugee adolescents require tailored ethical protocols and participatory methods to ensure inclusion.
Conflict spillovers (e.g., Gaza war) can disrupt neighbouring countries (Jordan, Lebanon), requiring adaptive research designs.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The original **Global Girls Research Initiative** (4277938.odt) highlighted gaps in longitudinal evidence on adolescent girls, informing GAGE’s design. Lessons included: (1) need for **multi-cohort tracking** (hence 10–12 and 15–17 age groups), (2) **policy engagement** as a core component (not just research), and (3) **capacity building** to address Northern dominance in evidence generation.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **participatory research** with disabled/married girls (absent in 4277938.odt) and **refugee focus** (4,500+ displaced adolescents) based on gaps in earlier programmes. Extended to **11 years** (vs. 8 in 4277938.odt) to capture longer-term outcomes.
risks_lessons.quote: "GAGE is the largest longitudinal study on adolescents in LMICs... including more than 4,500 refugee and internally displaced adolescents... The spillover effects of the war in Gaza on Jordan and Lebanon... have meant that it has been necessary to nuance some of GAGE’s original assumptions." (D0006485.odt, Summary Information and Expected Results)

financial_details.quote: "The average overheads over the lifetime of the programme (i.e., from 2015–2027) would be 12.03%... The GAGE programme will continue to operate at 7% margin (NPAC) until 30 November 2024 and... at 26% margin (NPAC) from 01 December 2024 to 30 November 2026." (D0006485.odt, Additional Support)

metadata.programme_name: Tackling Maternal and Child Undernutrition in Zambia (Phase II)
metadata.duration_text: Original project start and end dates: Start date: November 2013, Original End date: 31 March 2023, Extended to 31 March 2025, with no-cost extension to March 2026
metadata.quote: The purpose is to contribute towards improved health and nutritional status of children under two years measured primarily by a reduction in stunting by 2021. (43740657.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: Start date: November 2013, Original End date: 31 March 2023, Extended to 31 March 2025, with no-cost extension to March 2026 (D0007050.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct nutrition interventions), capacity building (institutional strengthening), policy influence (advocacy for increased domestic spending), and financing mechanism (pooled fund management). It aims to reduce stunting through multi-sectoral coordination and evidence-based interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: The purpose is to contribute towards improved health and nutritional status of children under two years measured primarily by a reduction in stunting by 2021. [...] The programme will collaborate with other UK funded programmes in promoting nutrition messages so as to influence sustainable behavioural change across a wider population. (43740657.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Improve nutrition and health status of an additional 376,000 children and 300,000 pregnant and lactating mothers (total reach: over 1 million people)
Scale up Most Critical Days Programme to 24 out of 107 districts by 2021
Strengthen national nutrition response through improved maternal and child nutrition practices (e.g., increase from 37% to 65% in WHO Infant & Young Child Feeding guidelines compliance by 2021)
Reduce stunting from 40% (2014) to 31% by 2021
Reduce low-birth weight babies from 9.3% to 5% by 2021
Increase national budget allocation for nutrition from US$0.50 to US$17 per under-5 child per year by 2021
Deliver emergency cash transfers to 1 million drought-affected households (2024 addendum)
Provide timely treatment to children at risk of wasting in drought-affected areas (2024 addendum)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce chronic undernutrition (stunting) in Zambia through a multi-sectoral approach combining direct nutrition interventions, institutional capacity building, and policy advocacy, while adapting to emergencies like the 2024 drought.
what_objectives.quote: The objectives of the proposed costed extension are as follows: Improve nutrition and health status of an additional 376,000 children and 300,000 pregnant and lactating mothers; [...] Build on the results achieved to-date to scale up the interventions that worked best [...] (43740657.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's risk rating is moderate, with risks including lack of political leadership, weak NFNC capacity, and complex programme coordination. Zambia is not classified as FCAS but faces significant development challenges including high stunting rates (40%) and weak institutional capacity.
where_context.q5_source: The programme’s risk rating is moderate. (43740657.odt, Risk management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak NFNC capacity limits coordination across sectors; political economy challenges affect budget allocations for nutrition; climate risks (e.g., 2024 drought) disrupt food security; and limited nutrition data (e.g., surveys every 3-5 years) hampers real-time monitoring. The 2024 drought has caused 70% crop loss, exacerbating food insecurity and increasing stunting risks.
where_context.quote: NFNC, responsible for coordination of SUN and nutrition programme has weak capacity and authority for stewardship of multi-sectoral programme [...] Complexity of programme and limited capacity for grant management slows progress on smooth programme delivery. (43740657.odt, Risk and mitigation measures)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: National Food and Nutrition Commission (NFNC), Zambia
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between DFID/FCDO (funding and strategic oversight) and NFNC/GRZ (programme coordination and implementation). The SUN Steering Committee includes both donors and Zambian line ministries, with NFNC having a mandate for national coordination.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to NFNC and line ministries
training for district-level nutrition coordination committees
establishment of BSc and MSc nutrition courses at University of Zambia
support for institutional restructuring of NFNC
development of Zambia Nutrition Information System (ZamNIS)

partner_organizations.name: National Food and Nutrition Commission (NFNC)
partner_organizations.role: National coordination and leadership for nutrition; programme stewardship

partner_organizations.name: Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ) - Line Ministries (Health, Agriculture, Education, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of multi-sectoral nutrition interventions at district level

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Implementation support; management of SUN II programme (2017 onwards); down-stream partners (PLAN International, CARE, Save the Children, etc.)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Management of Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) for emergency cash transfers (2024)

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder; procurement of technical assistance and research facility

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (£8.5m committed)

partner_organizations.name: Germany (KfW Development Bank)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (£8.5m committed)

partner_organizations.name: Ireland (Irish Aid)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder; pooled fund contributor

partner_organizations.name: Sweden
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder; pooled fund contributor

partner_organizations.name: Palladium
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support for drought response (2024)

partner_organizations.name: Danish Refugee Council
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support for drought response (2024)

partner_organizations.name: PLAN International, CARE, Save the Children, World Vision, CRS
partner_organizations.role: Downstream partners operating in 17 SUN 2.0 districts

partner_organizations.name: FAO, WFP, WHO
partner_organizations.role: UN agency support to UNICEF-led implementation

who_partners.quote: The programme will be implemented in partnership with the Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ) and co-funded with the US, EU, Germany (KfW Development Bank), Ireland and Sweden. (43740657.odt, Is the programme coherent with wider international community and partner government response?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **pooled fund mechanism** (SUN Fund) for multi-donor contributions, managed by a contracted Fund Manager (e.g., CARE in pilot phase, re-tendered for scale-up). Emergency cash transfers (2024) are channeled through the **World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF)**. Technical assistance is procured separately (e.g., by USAID).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **SUN Fund** acts as a pooled funding platform with a **Fund Manager** (contracted by DFID) responsible for grant disbursements and a **Technical Assistance Provider** (contracted by USAID) for capacity building. A **SUN Steering Committee** (NFNC, line ministries, donors) provides oversight. For the 2024 drought response, the **World Bank MDTF** manages emergency cash transfers.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: DFID will return to the marketplace for contracting the Fund Manager using an **open tender route** to attract the largest possible number of bidders for fair competition. An early market engagement (EME) in September 2016 revealed a reasonable range of potential service providers.
how_mechanism.quote: DFID will return to the market place for contracting of the Fund Manager using an open tender route. This is preferred to the restricted route because we are unsure what the market looks like in terms of service providers with the right capacity and experience in fund and grant management. (43740657.odt, Commercial and Value for Money Considerations)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **SUN Steering Committee (SC)** comprises NFNC, involved line ministries, and donors. It meets quarterly to review work-plans, progress, and make recommendations. The **Fund Manager** and **Technical Assistance Provider** report to this committee, which provides strategic direction.
how_governance.quote: The SUN SC was constituted to maintain oversight and provide strategic direction on MCDP-SUN Fund activities. The SUN SC comprises NFNC, involved Line Ministries and donors. The committee meets on a quarterly basis to review work-plans, progress and make recommendations to improve programme quality and performance. (43740657.odt, Commercial and Value for Money Considerations)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated within the pooled fund mechanism based on approved annual costed work-plans and performance reviews, but require donor consensus. The 2024 drought response introduced emergency cash transfers as a new component, demonstrating adaptive flexibility.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities based on new evidence (e.g., dropping IMAM, Vitamin A, and Iron/Folic Acid supplementation in scale-up due to overlap with other programmes) and emergencies (e.g., 2024 drought response). Changes require approval from the SUN Steering Committee and donors.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme will continue to have in-built monitoring and evaluation processes. These generated the evidence used to inform changes introduced in this Addendum. (43740657.odt, Does the proposed level of risk to be taken fit with DFID’s risk appetite for this portfolio?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager (e.g., contracted service provider) → Line Ministries/NGOs (implementers) → Community volunteers (e.g., Nutrition Support Groups)
how_efficiency.quote: The programme management costs will be maintained within 11%. (43740657.odt, Commercial and Value for Money Considerations)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Expand coverage of direct/indirect nutrition interventions through contracted service providers (parallel to government)
Option 2: Option 1 plus supporting multi-sectoral response and capacity building (preferred option)
Option 3: Do nothing beyond phase 1 investments
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (multi-sectoral + capacity building) was chosen because it **aligns with Zambia’s national 1000 Most Critical Days Programme**, supports **government ownership** (critical for sustainability), and allows **leveraging of other donor funds** through the pooled mechanism. The platform approach also enables **flexibility to respond to gaps** (e.g., 2024 drought) and **strengthens NFNC’s coordination role** across sectors.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (NFNC and line ministries need strengthening)
equity (multi-sectoral approach addresses underlying causes of stunting)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of strong political leadership and commitment by Government to address undernutrition
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engage senior government nutrition champion (Vice President/First Lady); advocate for increased nutrition budget allocations; support NFNC to engage Ministries of Finance and Planning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: NFNC’s weak capacity and authority for multi-sectoral coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Push for enactment of revised NFNC Act; provide technical assistance for restructuring; increase NFNC visibility across line ministries.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of programme and limited grant management capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Separate Fund Manager and Technical Assistance roles; clarify accountability channels; develop strong ToRs for Fund Manager procurement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial mismanagement, fraud, or corruption
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fund Manager to propose risk management strategy; conduct routine spot-checks; milestone-based payments.

why_rationale.quote: The preferred Option 2 involving programme implementation through a pooled fund managed by a contracted service provider was approved, and remains valid for MCDP scale-up. The option is preferred as it helps the Government continue supporting the programme beyond the donor funding period. (43740657.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Zambia’s weak institutional capacity (e.g., NFNC’s limited coordination authority) and political economy constraints (e.g., low domestic budget allocations for nutrition) necessitate the use of a **pooled fund mechanism** with strong donor oversight (FCDO/USAID) and technical assistance. The 2024 drought further constrained partner selection to those with rapid emergency response capabilities (e.g., World Bank MDTF for cash transfers).
q27_constraints_detail: NFNC’s structural relationship under Ministry of Health prevents cross-sectoral autonomy
Limited government capacity delays implementation (e.g., slow disbursements)
Drought (2024) requires partners with humanitarian expertise (e.g., WFP for market tracking)
High stunting rates (40%) demand multi-sectoral partners (health, agriculture, WASH)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **multi-sectoral coordination** (addressing both direct and underlying causes of stunting) determines the **platform-based delivery structure** (SUN Fund with Fund Manager + Technical Assistance). The **scale-up requirement** (from 14 to 24 districts) necessitates a **pooled fund** to harmonize donor contributions and reduce transaction costs.
q28_linkages: Multi-sectoral objectives → Platform structure (SUN Fund with cross-sectoral Steering Committee)
Scale-up needs → Pooled fund mechanism (to leverage co-funding from US/EU/Germany)
Capacity gaps → Embedded technical assistance (separate from Fund Manager)
Emergency response → Adaptive use of World Bank MDTF for cash transfers
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (reaching rural, high-stunting districts) with **efficiency** (pooled fund reduces duplication). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid scale-up risks bypassing weaker government systems (mitigated by capacity building). (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: DFID/USAID manage funds, but NFNC leads coordination. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Dropping some interventions (e.g., Vitamin A) to focus on high-impact areas.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Pooled fund enables rapid disbursements but requires strong NFNC oversight to ensure equity.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern donors (FCDO/USAID) manage funds, while NFNC/GRZ lead implementation.
Cost vs. reach: Focus on 24 high-stunting districts (not nationwide) to maximize impact per pound.
Flexibility vs. control: Adaptive management (e.g., drought response) requires donor approval, slowing some decisions.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** leads to **quarterly oversight** by the SUN Steering Committee and **milestone-based payments** to mitigate financial risks. High climate risks (e.g., 2024 drought) triggered **intensive management** of emergency components (e.g., World Bank MDTF).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak NFNC capacity led to **separate Fund Manager and Technical Assistance roles** (instead of a single contractor). Capacity building for NFNC and line ministries is embedded to enable future **government ownership** (e.g., social cash transfer programme, now GRZ-funded).
intersections.quote: The challenge is compounded by the inherently complex nature of addressing malnutrition, which involves a range of different partners with varied interests. In the scale up phase, the fund management and technical assistance will be split and contracted separately. (43740657.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Lack of political leadership/commitment (e.g., delayed NFNC Act revisions)
Weak NFNC capacity for multi-sectoral coordination
Complex programme design slows implementation (e.g., grant management delays)
Financial mismanagement/fraud (e.g., weak procurement controls)
Climate shocks (e.g., 2024 drought increasing food insecurity)
Donor coordination challenges (e.g., aligning US/EU/Germany contributions)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Engage Vice President/First Lady as nutrition champion; advocate for budget increases via Ministry of Finance.
Technical assistance for NFNC restructuring; push for NFNC Act reforms to enhance authority.
Separate Fund Manager (disbursements) and Technical Assistance (capacity building); milestone-based payments.
Fund Manager to propose risk management strategy; routine spot-checks; hybrid contract with performance milestones.
Partner with Disaster Management Unit for emergency planning; promote climate-smart agriculture.
Formalize pooled fund via Joint Financing Agreement (JFA); quarterly SUN Steering Committee meetings.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 lessons included: (1) **Multi-sectoral coordination works** (e.g., linking health, agriculture, WASH). (2) **Government ownership is critical** (e.g., social cash transfers now GRZ-funded). (3) **Pooled funds reduce duplication** but require strong fiduciary controls. (4) **Local volunteers (e.g., Nutrition Support Groups) improve reach**. (5) **Flexibility is needed** to adapt to emergencies (e.g., 2024 drought response).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Changes from Phase 1 to Phase 2 include: (1) **Splitting Fund Manager and Technical Assistance roles** (previously combined under CARE). (2) **Formalizing the pooled fund** via Joint Financing Agreement (JFA). (3) **Dropping overlapping interventions** (e.g., Vitamin A, IMAM) to focus on high-impact areas. (4) **Adding emergency response mechanisms** (e.g., World Bank MDTF for drought cash transfers). (5) **Strengthening NFNC’s role** via capacity building and advocacy for legal reforms.
risks_lessons.quote: The design of the proposed costed extension draws on the learning from our pilot phase of work, in particular from the independent evaluation which provided valuable insights into how the programme can improve approaches to delivery and fiduciary risk management. (43740657.odt, Does the programme have sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust?)

co_funding_partners.partner: Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leveraged co-funding from USAID (£15m), EU (£8.5m), and Germany (£8.5m), with additional contributions from Ireland and Sweden. The pooled fund mechanism attracted multi-donor support, and the 2024 drought response unlocked World Bank emergency financing. GRZ’s in-kind contributions (staff time, office space) were valued at ~£1m/year, increasing over time.
financial_details.quote: The UK will invest an additional £19.6 million over 5 years to support programme scale up. It is anticipated that 75% of this will be for direct service delivery to address stunting and 25% will be for: programme oversight and management; GRZ institutional capacity strengthening; and monitoring and evaluation. (43740657.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Investing in Human Capital through Partnerships Beyond Aid

quote.programme_name: "Title: Investing in Human Capital through Partnerships Beyond Aid" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £25m" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.duration: "Start Date: 01 December 2019\nEnd Date: 30 December 2024" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.sector: "This programme will build government capacity to deliver quality health, education and social protection services to all." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 01 December 2019\nEnd Date: 30 December 2024" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **capacity building** (strengthening government institutions to deliver social services) and **policy influence** (supporting reforms in health, education, and social protection). It also includes elements of **implementation research** (testing efficiency reforms) and **service delivery** (through embedded technical assistance). The overarching goal is to enable Ghana’s self-reliance in financing and managing social services, aligning with the "Ghana Beyond Aid" agenda.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will build government capacity to deliver quality health, education and social protection services to all. It will do this by providing expert advice and support to the Ministries to plan, manage and finance these services more efficiently and effectively. [...] This will support Ghana to support itself by reducing the costs required by government to deliver these services; while at the same time improving the quality and equity of the services themselves." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: improved governance capacity, systems, and mechanisms within social sector ministries
strengthened sector financing (e.g., allocation, accessing alternative sources of financing) and PFM capacity
improved MoF policies and processes to drive PFM, procurement, human resourcing, VfM/efficiencies, and equity
increased capacity of CSOs to hold Government to account for equitable and effective delivery of quality social sector services
reduced disparity between poor-performing and best-performing districts in delivery of social sector services
q3_expected_outputs.target: by end of 2024

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased client satisfaction with social sector services
q3_expected_outputs.target: by end of 2024

q3_expected_outputs.output: improved domestic resourcing and utilisation of quality education, health, and other social services at primary level
q3_expected_outputs.target: by end of 2024

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to self-finance and deliver quality health, education, and social protection services by improving governance, public financial management (PFM), and accountability mechanisms. It combines technical assistance to ministries with support to civil society for demand-side accountability, ultimately reducing reliance on UK aid.

quote.objective: "The expected impact of this programme is self-reliance by Government in managing and financing the social sectors to deliver quality services to all. The expected outcome is greater accountability and more efficient, higher quality and equitable delivery of services by the Ministries and Agencies of Health, Education and Gender." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.outputs: "Outputs will be: [...] improved governance capacity, systems and mechanisms within social sector ministries to organise and deliver high quality services for all; strengthened sector financing [...] and PFM capacity; improved MoF policies and processes; and increased capacity of CSOs to effectively hold Government to account." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ghana is classified as a lower-middle-income country (LMIC) with stable politics but faces risks of economic reversals due to vulnerability to external shocks (e.g., commodity price fluctuations) and stalled poverty reduction. The programme’s risk rating is explicitly stated as "Moderate."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: data limitations (underutilization of data for decision-making)
accountability gaps (limited citizen demand for services)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak PFM systems lead to delayed disbursements and poor service implementation (e.g., only 50% of health budgets executed). Centralized HR management results in inequitable distribution of teachers/health workers (e.g., 20% of teachers placed in schools where they lack proficiency in the language of instruction). Limited use of data for policy decisions undermines equity and efficiency. Economic volatility risks reductions in social sector spending, disproportionately affecting marginalized groups.

quote.pfm: "Capital and goods and services budget execution in health has, for the past 3 years, been approximately 50% of the allocation." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section B)
quote.hr: "Centralised human resource (HR) management with limited ability to take into account local needs. [...] 20% of teachers are placed in schools where they are not fully proficient in the language of instruction." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section B)
quote.economic_risk: "Ghana’s vulnerability to external shocks became felt with deteriorating macroeconomic indicators. [...] A key risk is around Ghana’s macro-economic situation that could lead to reductions in government spend in the social sectors." (Document: 53885140.odt, Sections B and F)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes **Ghanaian ownership** with DFID/FCDO providing technical assistance and coordination. Decision-making is shared, with reforms driven by Government of Ghana (GoG) priorities and DFID supporting implementation. The technical assistance team is "largely national" with international experts brought in only where gaps exist.
q10_capacity_building_details: embedded technical assistance (mentoring, coaching, leadership development)
training for government officials (e.g., PFM, workforce planning)
institutional strengthening (e.g., MoF efficiency reforms, sector-specific systems)
peer-to-peer learning (e.g., HMG-GoG partnerships, twinning with UK institutions)
CSO capacity building (e.g., budget tracking, advocacy skills)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ghana (GoG) Ministries
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer (Health, Education, Gender, Finance)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: accountability and advocacy (monitoring budgets, service delivery)

partner_organizations.name: UK Government Institutions (e.g., Department of Health and Social Care, Government Partnerships International)
partner_organizations.role: technical partnerships (e.g., health research, education reform support)

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Partners (e.g., World Bank, USAID)
partner_organizations.role: coordination and complementary support (e.g., Global Finance Facility, GALOP)

partner_organizations.name: DFID/FCDO
partner_organizations.role: funding, oversight, and technical assistance coordination

quote.delivery_structure: "The programme will be delivered through partnerships with HMG institutions and expert technical assistance to Ministries; as well as some support to CSOs to hold the Government to account." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)
quote.ownership: "Government ownership – avoid external experts driving the agenda, rather get behind government priorities which fit with the programme." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section E)
quote.ta_team: "Using a mix of respected local and international experts – the TA team should be largely national with internationals only brought in if there is a clear need." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section E)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **grants** (for CSOs and specific reforms) and **technical assistance agreements** (for embedded support to ministries). Grants are likely milestone-based, while TA is delivered through flexible, iterative partnerships.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID/FCDO acts as the convenor and coordinator, working with GoG ministries, CSOs, and other UK/HMG partners. The structure is **adaptive**, with technical assistance tailored to emerging reform priorities and political opportunities. There is no closed consortium; instead, partnerships are formed based on needs (e.g., HMG-GoG twinning, CSO advocacy networks).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on **alignment with GoG priorities** and DFID’s strategic objectives. The programme emphasizes **government ownership** and **political buy-in**, so partners (e.g., ministries, CSOs) are pre-identified based on their role in Ghana’s social sectors. Technical assistance providers are chosen for their ability to deliver **embedded, flexible support**.

quote.instrument: "The programme will not provide Financial Aid for service delivery although it may provide some grants to government and others to deliver specific reforms." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)
quote.structure: "The programme will take an adaptive, iterative approach that is responsive to GoG needs and priorities. [...] It will necessarily involve identifying and exploiting opportunities for small strategic interventions that may only become evident during implementation." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.selection: "This approach comes with the risk of limiting its strategic impact by attempting to meet every request and losing focus. To mitigate this, the interventions will be selected on whether they fit under the three areas of the programme as well as meet criteria around: supporting self-reliance; going with the grain/political commitment; addressing barriers that are common across the sectors; filling a gap/a DFID niche; and expertise is available and appropriate." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly detailed, the programme implies a **steering mechanism** involving DFID/FCDO, GoG ministries, and potentially CSOs to align technical assistance with political priorities. The **Ministry of Monitoring and Evaluation (MoM&E)** and **Ministry of Planning (MoP)** are mentioned as oversight bodies for government plans, suggesting coordination at a high level.

quote.day_to_day: "DFID’s influencing role is vital – the TA team provide the technical expertise but DFID has influence in high level discussions with Ministries and with other donors." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section E)
quote.oversight: "The programme will be underpinned by ongoing political economy analysis to identify the most effective ways to leverage change and spot reform opportunities as they arise." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.governance_hint: "MoP ensures coherence across Ministries’ plans (including on the fit with SDGs) while MoM&E is mandated to monitor implementation of the plans." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section C)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on **emerging priorities** and **political opportunities**. The programme is designed to be **iterative**, with interventions scaled up or down depending on impact. Flexibility is a core principle, though reallocation requires alignment with the three programme areas (governance, PFM, MoF reforms).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a **Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA)** approach, allowing priorities to shift in response to real-time learning and political changes (e.g., elections). Technical assistance is **demand-driven** and adjusts to GoG’s reform agenda. The adaptive management is operationalized through ongoing political economy analysis and close DFID adviser involvement.

quote.reallocation: "The programme will take a flexible, iterative and politically smart approach. [...] It will be underpinned by ongoing political economy analysis to identify the most effective ways to leverage change and spot reform opportunities as they arise." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.adaptive: "This Business Case purposefully does not set out all of the programme’s interventions. This approach comes with the risk of limiting its strategic impact by attempting to meet every request and losing focus. To mitigate this, the interventions will be selected on whether they fit under the three areas of the programme as well as meet criteria around: [...] being responsive to arising needs." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **GoG Ministries/CSOs** (direct implementation). No intermediary layers are mentioned; DFID/FCDO works directly with government and civil society partners.

quote.layers: "The programme will be delivered through partnerships with HMG institutions and expert technical assistance to Ministries; as well as some support to CSOs." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)
quote.payment: "The programme will not provide Financial Aid for service delivery although it may provide some grants to government and others to deliver specific reforms." (implies milestone/performance-based disbursements) (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: Strengthening social sector systems through Technical Assistance (TA) to and HMG partnerships with Health, Education, and Gender Ministries and the Ministry of Finance (MoF).
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focused solely on supply-side reforms (government capacity building).

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Strengthening social sector systems through TA/HMG partnerships **and** supporting CSOs to hold government to account.
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Combines supply-side (TA to ministries) and demand-side (CSO accountability) interventions.
No new DFID support; risks reversal of humandevelopment gains and financing gaps.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 was selected because it **mitigates risks** associated with Option 1 (e.g., government rejection of reforms) by adding **demand-side accountability** through CSOs. This increases the likelihood of sustained impact, especially ahead of elections. The mixed approach aligns with DFID’s transition principles (e.g., strengthening governance and civil society) and Ghana’s "Beyond Aid" agenda, which requires both **efficient service delivery** and **citizen engagement**.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (CSO accountability reduces risk of government inaction)
political economy (elections in 2020 require demand-side pressure)
value for money (combining TA and CSO support leverages existing DFID investments)
equity (CSOs ensure marginalized groups are included)
flexibility (adaptive approach allows response to changing priorities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government may reject or not use technical assistance, limiting impact.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close DFID adviser involvement to ensure interventions are scaled based on impact; CSO advocacy to create demand for reforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: By responding to arising needs, the programme may miss opportunities for longer-term, transformational change.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Criteria for interventions include alignment with self-reliance goals and political commitment; adaptive management balanced with strategic focus.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Short-term political cycles (e.g., 2020 elections) may disrupt momentum.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early operationalization to demonstrate efficiency gains; CSO engagement to sustain pressure across administrations.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing systems rather than creating new ones)
equity (focus on reducing disparities for marginalized groups)

quote.why_chosen: "This option has the same impact and outcome as in Option 1 [...] but it makes the achievement of the outcome more likely by mitigating the risks around it. It is ensuring the programme does not just build capacity to deliver but also builds demand for those services." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.risk_mitigation: "Support to CSOs to hold government to account for spend and the quality of the outcomes will help mitigate both risks, particularly over the elections." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section F)
quote.vfm: "The programme contributes to S01’s Golden Thread (enhancing the social contract and the distributional effects of taxation; public sector reform and institutional capacity development; sustainable financing of critical pro-poor sectors)." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Ghana’s **political economy** and **institutional weaknesses** constrain partner selection by necessitating **embedded, government-owned reforms**. The need for **local credibility** limits the role of international partners to advisory functions, while **CSO capacity gaps** require targeted support to ensure effective accountability. The **election cycle** (2020) also shapes timing, favoring partners who can demonstrate quick wins.
q27_constraints_detail: Centralized HR systems require partners with **GoG relationships** to navigate bureaucratic hurdles.
PFM weaknesses demand partners with **local PFM expertise** (e.g., MoF, Auditor General).
CSO limitations (e.g., short-term funding cycles) necessitate **capacity-building components**.
Election timelines favor partners who can **operationalize quickly** and show visible results.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for systemic change** (e.g., PFM, workforce planning) determines the **embedded TA approach**, while the **focus on accountability** drives CSO partnerships. The **cross-sectoral goals** (health, education, social protection) require a **platform-like structure** to share lessons, and the **adaptive management** model is chosen to address **complex, interlinked barriers** (e.g., HR allocation affecting service quality).
q28_linkages: Systemic PFM weaknesses → **embedded TA in MoF** to drive efficiencies.
Need for equity → **CSO partnerships** to monitor disparities.
Cross-sectoral barriers (e.g., HR, data) → **shared learning across ministries**.
Political risks (elections) → **flexible, iterative delivery** to sustain momentum.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between **efficiency reforms** (e.g., wage bill rationalization) and **equity** (e.g., ensuring rural/northern regions retain services). It also balances **Northern expertise** (e.g., HMG partnerships) with **Southern ownership** (e.g., GoG-led reforms). The **speed of reforms** is traded off against **inclusive processes** (e.g., CSO engagement may slow implementation but improves sustainability).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: PFM reforms (e.g., reducing salary spend) risk disproportionately affecting marginalized groups unless mitigated by targeted CSO advocacy.
International TA provides specialized skills but must be "largely national" to ensure local buy-in.
Rapid efficiency gains (e.g., digitization) may exclude groups without access to technology; CSOs help bridge this gap.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., economic volatility, election cycles) justifies **embedded oversight** (e.g., DFID advisers, ongoing political economy analysis) rather than light-touch management. High fiduciary risks in social sectors (e.g., off-budget IGFs) necessitate **intensive PFM monitoring**.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **limited capacity of CSOs** shapes their role as **monitoring/advocacy partners** rather than direct implementers. GoG ministries’ **variable reform readiness** determines where TA is embedded (e.g., MoE’s ambitious agenda vs. MoH’s PFM challenges). **MoF’s weak scrutiny** of sector budgets leads to a focus on **building its analytical capacity** to drive efficiencies.

quote.context_constrains_who: "The programme will be delivered through partnerships with HMG institutions and expert technical assistance to Ministries; as well as some support to CSOs to hold the Government to account through effective monitoring of budgets and services." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary)
quote.what_how_link: "The programme is therefore taking a bottom-up approach and joining it with a top-down one. And it is also taking a cross-sectoral approach in order to both identify systemic problems and promote innovative solutions." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section D)
quote.equity_efficiency: "The programme will not provide Financial Aid for service delivery although it may provide some grants to government and others to deliver specific reforms. [...] Support to CSOs to hold government to account for spend and the quality of the outcomes will help mitigate both risks, particularly over the elections." (Document: 53885140.odt, Programme summary and Section F)
quote.risk_management: "This will be mitigated by close involvement by DFID advisers ensuring interventions are scaled up/down depending on impact underpinned by a flexible delivery model to allow this." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section F)

key_programme_risks.risk: Macroeconomic downturn reduces government spending on social sectors, reversing humandevelopment gains.
Technical assistance or partnerships fail to achieve impact due to government rejection or misalignment with priorities.
Election-related leadership changes disrupt reform momentum (e.g., wage bill rationalization).
CSOs lack capacity to effectively hold government accountable, limiting demand-side pressure.
Over-emphasis on responsiveness to emerging needs dilutes strategic focus on long-term systemic change.
PFM weaknesses persist, undermining efficiency gains (e.g., delayed disbursements, off-budget funds).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Macroeconomic downturn reduces social sector spending.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on efficiency reforms to mitigate budget cuts; "Leave No One Behind" programme ensures continued service access for the poorest.
Close DFID adviser involvement to scale interventions based on impact; CSO advocacy to create demand for reforms.
Early operationalization to demonstrate quick wins; CSO engagement to sustain pressure across administrations.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: CSOs lack capacity for accountability roles.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted capacity-building for CSOs (e.g., budget tracking, advocacy skills).
Interventions selected based on criteria: supporting self-reliance, political commitment, cross-sectoral barriers, DFID niche, available expertise.
Embedded TA to MoF to strengthen budget execution and scrutiny; regular fiduciary risk assessments.

lessons_from_previous.lesson: PFM reforms deliver results but require **long-term, iterative support** (e.g., Ghana’s slow but progressiven improvements noted in PEFAs).
**Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA)** principles are critical for institutional reforms (e.g., focusing on feasible, context-specific changes).
Successful capacity building requires **country ownership**, **mixed local/international expertise**, and **flexibility** to adapt to political opportunities.
**Demand-side and supply-side actors must work together** for sustainable reforms (e.g., CSO-government coalitions).
lessons_from_previous.source: International evidence on citizen engagement (Fox 2014, cited in document).

design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **direct service delivery** to **technical assistance** based on Ghana’s "Beyond Aid" commitment and DFID’s transition principles.
Inclusion of **CSO component** to address risks of government inaction (learned from past TA programmes where reforms stalled).
Adoption of **adaptive management** to respond to political economy changes (e.g., elections, economic shocks).
Focus on **cross-sectoral systemic issues** (e.g., HR, PFM) rather than siloed sectoral support, based on evidence of shared barriers.

quote.lessons: "Significant evidence points to the need for realism and flexibility in donor support. Initiatives to reform the whole ‘machinery’ of government are rarely successful. [...] Other evaluations have similarly emphasised the lack of real political commitment to institutional reforms which are often over-ambitious and unrealistic in their planned implementation period." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section E)
quote.design_changes: "DFID Ghana has therefore begun to reduce resources for direct service delivery [...] Under the objective of ‘building stronger institutions to help Ghana to move beyond aid’, DFID Ghana is shifting to supporting the Government of Ghana to make better use of its own resources in delivering social sector services." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section C)
quote.risk_mitigation: "PBA is therefore moderate risk. There is a high potential return given that the programme could allow Ghana to realise its vision of becoming self-reliant; and for DFID to exit Ghana responsibly." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section F)

co_funding_partners.partner: Government of Ghana (in-kind contributions via ministries)
Multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, USAID - complementary programmes)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **catalyze domestic resource mobilization** (e.g., improved PFM to free up government funds) and **coordinate with multilaterals** (e.g., World Bank’s GALOP, Global Finance Facility) to avoid duplication and fill gaps. No explicit leverage targets are stated.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £25m" (Document: 53885140.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.leverage: "DFID will need to work closely with these multilaterals to ensure complementarity of support and approach." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section C)
quote.co_funding: "The greater part of UK ODA spend in social sectors will come from multilaterals, in particular the World Bank who are starting new programmes in education (e.g. GALOP) and health (e.g. Global Finance Facility)." (Document: 53885140.odt, Section C)

metadata.programme_name: Anti-Corruption Evidence (ACE) Programme
metadata.duration_text: The programme’s new end date is 30 September 2025 (with a further option to 30 March 2027 if there is a requirement to manage further reductions in the annual ODA financial allocation).
metadata.quote: "Robust new knowledge and evidence on anti-corruption lead to development of and investment in more effective anti-corruption policies and programmes, including by FCDO and partners." (D0001416.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "The programme’s new end date is 30 September 2025 (with a further option to 30 March 2027 if there is a requirement to manage further reductions in the annual ODA financial allocation)." (D0001416.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The ACE programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) but also includes **policy influence** (informing policy decisions) and **implementation research** (testing/scaling interventions). It generates rigorous evidence on 'what works' in anti-corruption, illicit finance, and serious organised crime (SOC), while directly supporting FCDO and HMG policy teams to apply findings in real-world contexts.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Robust new knowledge and evidence on anti-corruption lead to development of and investment in more effective policies and programmes, including by FCDO and partners." (D0001416.odt, Summary Information) AND "ACE fills a unique gap in the research market with its overarching focus on being problem-led rather than starting with preconceived ideas about the ‘right’ tactics and solutions." (D0001416.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
q3_expected_outputs: High-quality primary research (e.g., 10+ projects under 'What Works' component)
Research-related dissemination (working papers, peer-reviewed articles, open-access books, conference presentations)
Evidence syntheses and rapid evidence reviews (commissioned in consultation with FCDO/HMG)
Capacity development for FCDO staff (targeted training, learning sessions, synthesis briefs)
Policy uptake tools (e.g., World Bank Pro-ACT procurement data portal, GIACE ‘Red Flags’ procurement projects)
Public datasets (quantitative/qualitative, via UK Data Service)
100+ academics engaged across global research network
Direct support to FCDO teams on programme design (SOASACE component)
what_objectives.summary: ACE generates operationally relevant evidence on anti-corruption, illicit finance, and serious organised crime (SOC) to inform FCDO/HMG policies and programmes. It combines rigorous research with direct policy engagement, testing 'what works' in real-world contexts while building capacity among researchers and policymakers.
what_objectives.quote: "ACE fills a unique gap in the research market with its overarching focus on being problem-led rather than starting with preconceived ideas about the ‘right’ tactics and solutions." (D0001416.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in contexts with systemic corruption, transnational crime networks, and political sensitivity (e.g., Russia/Ukraine, FCAS-like environments). Research topics directly challenge vested interests, including elites benefiting from corruption, and involve security risks for researchers (e.g., "instability and external risks to global research delivery").
where_context.q5_source: "All anti-corruption research is politically sensitive, with inherent risks (including of violence) to researchers." (8568845.odt, Political economy, risks and challenges) AND "The weaponisation of corrupt practices by kleptocratic regimes to undermine democratic resilience—with Russia’s war against Ukraine being just one example." (D0001416.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit fieldwork and researcher safety, particularly in Russia/Ukraine and FCAS-like contexts. Political economy constraints (e.g., elite resistance) hinder evidence uptake. Data limitations (e.g., clandestine nature of corruption) challenge measurement, while regulatory barriers (e.g., beneficial ownership transparency) affect cross-border research. Conflict zones (e.g., Ukraine) disrupt data collection and partnerships.
where_context.quote: "The potential risks to researchers are clear – combining the difficulties of any research in a FCAS with the specific risks associated with research that challenges powerful people benefiting from corruption." (8568845.odt, Political economy, risks and challenges) AND "Data leaks such as the Pandora papers in 2021 or the FinCEN files in 2020 highlight the complex and systemic nature of many forms of corruption, revealing transnational dependencies and vulnerabilities." (D0001416.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed and overseen by UK-based academic leads (University of Birmingham, SOAS, University of Nottingham) and FCDO, with Southern partners (e.g., local think tanks in Bangladesh, Nigeria) primarily engaged as sub-grantees or research collaborators. Decision-making rests with the UK-based Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and steering group.
q10_capacity_building_details: Targeted training and learning sessions for FCDO staff
Mentorship through the Senior Research Fellow (SRF) for Governance and Conflict
Co-authorship opportunities with Southern researchers
Research grants to Southern institutions (e.g., SOAS partnerships with local universities)
Institutional strengthening via embedded research uptake support

partner_organizations.name: University of Birmingham
partner_organizations.role: Lead for Serious Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Evidence (SOCACE) component; manages research grants and direct research

partner_organizations.name: Global Integrity (GIACE)
