partner_organizations.role: Lead for Illicit Finance and Corruption research; manages competitive research grants
partner_organizations.location: UK (professorial lead at University of Nottingham)

partner_organizations.role: Lead for corruption research in Nigeria, Bangladesh, Nepal; manages in-country partnerships

partner_organizations.name: Local research institutions in Bangladesh, Nigeria, Nepal
partner_organizations.role: Sub-grantees and research partners (e.g., sector-specific studies)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Collaborator (e.g., uptake of GIACE procurement 'Red Flags' tool)

partner_organizations.name: Home Office Joint Anti-Corruption Unit (JACU)
partner_organizations.role: Policy partner (advisory group member)

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (NCA)
partner_organizations.role: Stakeholder (engaged via HMG advisory group)

who_partners.quote: "Each component of ACE—SOCACE, GIACE, and SOASACE—will be delivered via an accountable grant, with University of Birmingham, Global Integrity and the School of Oriental and African Studies respectively." (D0001416.odt, Grant arrangements) AND "SOAS has developed excellent partnerships with Southern think tanks and universities." (D0001416.odt, Equity)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **accountable grants** for the three main components (SOCACE, GIACE, SOASACE), combined with **competitive research grants** sub-awarded by the leads. The British Academy partnership (original 'What Works' component) also used a grant mechanism. This hybrid approach allows for both direct research delivery and open competition.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees three parallel accountable grants (SOCACE, GIACE, SOASACE), each led by a UK university/NGO. These leads manage their own research portfolios and sub-grant competitions, with coordination via an FCDO Senior Responsible Owner (SRO), quarterly steering group, and HMG advisory group. The structure balances specialization (by theme) with cross-programme synthesis.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not explicitly stated; original RPC selection used open competition with ~5 shortlisted bidders (8568845.odt)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The **British Academy** was selected as a "partner of choice" for the 'What Works' component due to its reputation and "in kind" contributions (8568845.odt). The **RPC consortium** (now split into SOCACE/GIACE/SOASACE) was selected via open competition to ensure "transparency, competition to drive down costs, and innovation" (8568845.odt). Sub-grants use further competitions to "attract new entrants" and shape the research market.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID-British Academy partnership (‘what works’): we propose to establish a partnership and an accountable grant with the British Academy." (8568845.odt, Commercial Case) AND "A competitive procurement process will be used to select a new Research Programme Consortium." (8568845.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **ACE Steering Group** includes: FCDO SRO (senior governance adviser), FCDO deputy programme manager, FCDO Senior Research Fellow (SRF), and the three academic/programme leads (Birmingham, Nottingham/SOAS). It meets quarterly to review delivery, risks, and complementarity. A separate **HMG Advisory Group** provides policy input.
how_governance.quote: "Quarterly ACE steering group meetings will bring together the FCDO SRO, FCDO deputy programme manager, FCDO senior research fellow (SRF), and the three academic and programme management leads." (D0001416.odt, Coordination) AND "The ACESRO will draw together and facilitate contact amongst HMG colleagues and academics." (D0001416.odt, Coordination)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects within components (e.g., SOCACE shifting resources to high-potential research), but major changes require FCDO approval. The programme uses "modular" project designs to adapt to budget uncertainty.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities are adjusted via: 1) **Modular project designs** (allowing partial delivery if budgets shrink); 2) **Dynamic research strategy** (SRO terminates less fruitful projects); 3) **Consultation with HMG Advisory Group** (to align with emerging policy needs). The extension explicitly adds Russia/Ukraine and Indo-Pacific foci in response to geopolitical shifts.
how_flexibility.quote: "Using a portfolio management approach, the SRO will terminate less fruitful research, and direct more resources to those projects which emerge as highly successful." (D0001416.odt, Grant arrangements) AND "Calls for proposals will require researchers to design ‘modular’ projects to help balance ambition and rigour with the need to accept a degree of budget uncertainty." (D0001416.odt, Modular and sequenced calls)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Component Leads (Birmingham/GIACE/SOAS) → Sub-grantees/Researchers
how_efficiency.quote: "Bids will be prepared on the basis of maximum results proposed for a stated budget." (8568845.odt, Commercial Case) AND "The final number of projects and evidence reviews that will be delivered will depend on final budget allocations." (D0001416.odt, Modular and sequenced calls)

q24_alternatives_considered: Competitive small grants programme (managed by British Academy)
One large RPC (single consortium for all themes)
Four RPCs (separate consortia for each theme)
Hybrid model (open competition for ‘What Works’ + single RPC for other themes)
Do nothing (status quo)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **hybrid model** (Option 4) was selected to balance **diversity** (via open competition for 'What Works') with **coherence** (single RPC for interdependencies/private sector). The current structure (three accountable grants) evolved from this to: 1) **Specialise** by theme (SOCACE, GIACE, SOASACE); 2) **Retain competition** via sub-grants; 3) **Simplify FCDO management** (fewer partners than Option 3). The British Academy partnership was chosen for its "reputation for excellence" and ability to attract high-quality researchers (8568845.odt).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of coherence between components (due to separate accountable grants)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly steering group and HMG advisory group to align priorities; SRO synthesizes findings.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner capture of research agenda (e.g., academic leads prioritizing publication over policy relevance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO SRO and SRF embedded in governance; modular projects with policy-linked milestones.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs from managing multiple grants/sub-grants
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Standardized reporting templates; shared M&E framework across components.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication with other HMG anti-corruption initiatives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: HMG advisory group includes cross-departmental stakeholders (e.g., Home Office JACU, NCA).

why_rationale.quote: "Our recommended option is 4 – a hybrid approach." (8568845.odt, Options Analysis) AND "The hybrid approach would balance the advantages and disadvantages of options 1 and 2. Attracting new entrants and encouraging diversity in anti-corruption research would be addressed through the open competition for ‘what works’, while strategic coherence, and ensuring a reasonable management load for DFID, would be addressed by limiting the total number of partnerships to 2." (8568845.odt, Options Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **high-risk contexts** (e.g., Russia/Ukraine, FCAS-like environments) constrain partner selection by: 1) Limiting fieldwork to researchers with security clearance/experience; 2) Requiring partners with political economy expertise to navigate elite resistance; 3) Prioritizing UK-based leads (e.g., Birmingham, SOAS) for diplomatic cover and risk management. Data limitations in conflict zones also favor partners with existing local networks (e.g., SOAS’s Nepal/Bangladesh partnerships).
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks → Restricts fieldwork to vetted researchers
Political sensitivity → Requires partners with elite negotiation skills
Data scarcity → Favors partners with pre-existing local datasets/networks
Regulatory barriers (e.g., beneficial ownership) → Needs legal/expertise-heavy partners (e.g., GIACE)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for policy-relevant, operationally tested evidence** drives the hybrid delivery structure: 1) **‘What Works’** uses open competition to maximize diversity of methods/geographies; 2) **Interdependencies** (now split across SOCACE/GIACE) requires specialized consortia to handle complex, multi-sectoral research (e.g., SOC-growth-trade linkages); 3) **Private sector/SOC focus** necessitates UK-based leads (e.g., Birmingham for SOCACE) to engage HMG stakeholders (e.g., NCA, Home Office).
q28_linkages: Problem-driven research → Open competition for ‘What Works’
Transnational crime focus → UK-based leads (e.g., Birmingham) for HMG coordination
Sectoral depth (e.g., procurement, climate) → Thematic specialization (GIACE/SOASACE)
Policy uptake needs → Embedded FCDO SRF and advisory group
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid policy responses (e.g., Ukraine research) prioritize UK/Northern leads, limiting Southern ownership; 2) **Expertise vs. local relevance**: GIACE’s global finance focus relies on Northern academics, while SOASACE’s Bangladesh/Nigeria work embeds local partners; 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Competitive grants favor established institutions, though "50% of GIACE project PIs were women" (D0001416.odt) and SOASACE partners with Southern think tanks.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (e.g., GIACE’s illicit finance analysis) vs. Southern contextual knowledge (e.g., SOASACE’s Nepal climate work)
Competitive grants (efficient but may exclude smaller Southern institutions) vs. targeted capacity building (e.g., FCDO staff training)
Policy urgency (e.g., Russia/Ukraine research) vs. long-term Southern partnership development
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk profile** (transnational crime, elite resistance) intensifies oversight: 1) **Quarterly steering group** (vs. annual); 2) **Embedded SRF** to flag political sensitivities; 3) **Modular projects** to limit exposure if contexts deteriorate (e.g., Ukraine). FCAS experience led to dropping dedicated FCAS research in Phase 1, but Phase 2 adds conflict-sensitive methods (e.g., Nepal climate work).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded but uneven**: 1) **FCDO staff** receive direct training (e.g., SOASACE’s programme design support); 2) **Southern researchers** gain co-authorship/grants but decision-making rests with UK leads; 3) **Local institutions** (e.g., Bangladesh think tanks) are sub-grantees, not co-leads. The structure reflects a **‘capacity for uptake’** priority over **‘capacity to lead’**.
intersections.quote: "The consultation recommended that FCAS be a distinct research theme as the expertise required may be different, and in an open process FCAS are often relatively neglected." (8568845.odt, Responding to These Needs) AND "SOAS has developed excellent partnerships with Southern think tanks and universities." (D0001416.odt, Equity)

key_programme_risks: Slow policy uptake due to vested interests (e.g., elites benefiting from corruption)
Research delays in high-risk contexts (e.g., Ukraine, FCAS)
Limited Southern partner decision-making power
Overlap with other HMG anti-corruption initiatives (e.g., Home Office JACU)
Measurement challenges (e.g., quantifying illicit financial flows)
Reputational risk if research is perceived as politically biased (e.g., Russia/Ukraine)
Budget uncertainty due to ODA fluctuations
Loss of researchers in volatile contexts (e.g., conflict zones)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded FCDO Senior Research Fellow (SRF) to broker researcher-policymaker links; HMG advisory group to align research with policy cycles.
Modular project designs; prior approval from Heads of Mission (HoM) for fieldwork; security protocols for researchers.
SOASACE’s in-country partnerships (e.g., Bangladesh, Nigeria) co-design research; 50% of GIACE PIs are women.
HMG advisory group includes JACU, NCA, and Treasury; quarterly steering group reviews complementarity.
Use of big data (e.g., GIACE procurement ‘red flags’); political economy analysis to contextualize findings.
Modular projects; portfolio management approach (SRO reallocates funds to high-potential research).

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid standalone FCAS research components (Phase 1 dropped FCAS theme due to feasibility risks; Phase 2 integrates conflict sensitivity into broader themes).
Use local partnerships to navigate elite resistance (e.g., SOASACE’s Nepal climate work with national researchers).
Prioritize ‘political feasibility’ over technical solutions (e.g., ACE’s ‘political won’t to political will’ framework).
Leverage transnational research (e.g., GIACE’s illicit finance work) to reduce fieldwork risks in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Problem-driven > solution-led**: ACE’s shift from testing preconceived interventions to diagnosing specific corruption problems (e.g., procurement in Uganda) improved uptake. 2) **Political economy trumps technical fixes**: Research must address ‘why corruption persists’ (e.g., elite bargains) not just ‘how to stop it’. 3) **Hybrid delivery works**: Combining open competition (for diversity) with thematic RPCs (for coherence) balanced innovation and strategic alignment. 4) **Embedded policy links are critical**: The SRF role (seconded into FCDO) and HMG advisory group were added post-Phase 1 to improve relevance.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Added Russia/Ukraine focus** in Phase 2 (response to geopolitical shifts). 2) **Expanded Indo-Pacific/private sector themes** (aligned with FCDO’s economic security priorities). 3) **Incorporated ‘political will’ framework** (from SOCACE research) into FCDO’s Crime Sensitivity Framework. 4) **Modular project designs** (to handle ODA budget volatility). 5) **Stronger gender focus**: GIACE/SOASACE now require gender-disaggregated analysis in all research.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lack of political will is a significant challenge for tackling SOC, illicit finance and corruption: however, we need to stop using (lack of) political will as an excuse." (D0001416.odt, Lessons: D. Thinking and working politically) AND "The consultation recommended that FCAS be a distinct research theme as the expertise required may be different, and in an open process FCAS are often relatively neglected." (8568845.odt, Responding to These Needs)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme attracted £5m in non-ODA funding (NODA) from UK national security budgets, reflecting its dual development/security mandate (e.g., SOC/illicit finance research). No external co-funding from other donors was secured, but GIACE’s ‘Red Flags’ tool was adopted by the World Bank and governments of Uganda/Jamaica, indicating indirect leverage.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Not explicitly mentioned; budget primarily covers revenue (research grants, salaries, dissemination) with no capital infrastructure investments noted.
financial_details.quote: "The cost extension is up to £9,629,679 ODA and up to £5m non-ODA (NODA), which will bring the total project value to up to £32,000,000." (D0001416.odt, Summary Information) AND "The programme is envisaged to cover 3-4 countries, all of which will be DFID Tier One countries." (8568845.odt, Proposed scale of DFID funding)

metadata.programme_name: Mobile for Development (M4D): Strategic Partnership for Inclusion, Innovation and Scale
metadata.quote: "The purpose of the Mobile for Development programme (M4D) is to bring together the mobile ecosystem and the development sector to stimulate digital innovation to deliver sustainable business models and large-scale socio-economic impact for low-income people in developing countries." (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: October 2019 – March 2025", "New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2029" (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research on digital inclusion, climate action, and emerging technologies), technology development (supporting start-ups and digital solutions), capacity building (training and advisory support), policy influence (advocacy and engagement with governments), and implementation research (piloting and scaling innovative business models). It also includes a financing mechanism through the Innovation Fund.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme is improving climate resilience, livelihoods and access to opportunities for women and underserved groups, as well as mitigating climate change. This is being achieved by unlocking mobile-enabled innovation which deliver on the Global Goals, as well as improving people’s access to and use of digital and mobile services." (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 100 innovative, sustainable, and inclusive digitally-enabled business models launched (40 additional through this addendum)
105 innovators supported to scale in partnership with Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) (42 through this addendum)
240 million people benefited (an additional 100 million)
£360 million of additional funding crowded in (£150 million through this addendum)
32 instances where the programme contributes to policy on climate action, digital inclusion, and emerging technology
182 thought leadership pieces published (88 through this addendum)
933 GSMA-organised convenings where M4D messaging is shared (405 through this addendum)
113 mobile-based solutions supported and scaled (50 through this addendum)
280 partnerships catalysed with public and private sector stakeholders (116 through this addendum)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to leverage mobile and digital technologies to improve climate resilience, digital inclusion (especially for women and underserved groups), and access to economic opportunities. It focuses on scaling innovative business models, generating evidence, and advocating for enabling policies.
what_objectives.quote: "By catalysing end-to-end innovation, advocating for an enabling policy and regulatory environment, engaging private sector players and creating unique insights and research, M4D will empower underserved groups to access and use mobile and digital technologies to build resilience, leverage new opportunities, and enhance their livelihoods." (D0007332.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme scored a moderate climate risk, which is within expectations given it is designed to work in climate-vulnerable areas. The environmental risk is considered low, with appropriate safeguards in place for relevant environmental categories.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme scored a moderate climate risk, which is within expectations, given it is designed to work in climate vulnerable areas." (D0007332.odt, Climate and nature)
q6_contextual_constraints: digital divide (900 million fewer women than men using mobile internet in LMICs)
limited availability of data for emerging technologies (especially AI)
lack of relevant frameworks for privacy/ethics in AI
nascent funding ecosystem for digital entrepreneurs
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers and limited data availability hinder the scaling of emerging technologies like AI. The digital divide and climate risks disproportionately affect women and underserved groups, requiring targeted interventions. Nascent funding ecosystems make it challenging for entrepreneurs to pioneer digital business models.
where_context.quote: "There is a risk of entrenching the digital divide, with an estimated 900 million fewer women than men using the mobile internet in LMICs... LMICs face several barriers in scaling emerging technologies—especially AI—including insufficient availability of data, a lack of relevant frameworks especially around privacy/ethics, and the lack of local skills base." (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is governed by a Partnership Strategy Group that includes DFID/FCDO, other donors, GSMA leadership, and Mobile Network Operator (MNO) chairs. Decision-making is shared, with DFID/FCDO representatives present at key decision points and advisory roles in thematic areas.
q10_capacity_building_details: Mobile Internet Skills Training Toolkit (MISTT) to train people on mobile internet use (54 million people trained so far)
Technical assistance to innovators to build investment plans and improve gender reach
Capacity building for policymakers and regulators on emerging technologies (e.g., AI, privacy, ethics)
Advisory support to MNOs on digital inclusion, climate action, and gender equality

partner_organizations.name: GSMA
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: Mobile Network Operators (MNOs)
partner_organizations.role: Partners for scaling digital solutions, advisory support, and data sharing

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Primary funder, strategic oversight, and advisory support

partner_organizations.name: Local governments and regulators
partner_organizations.role: Policy engagement and enabling environment creation

partner_organizations.name: Social enterprises and innovators
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of Innovation Fund grants and technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Sida, BMGF, USAID, GIZ, Visa, NORAD)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funders and collaborators

who_partners.quote: "The London-headquartered GSMA will continue to provide the lead management resource and support to individual programme strands. FCDO funds will be managed by the GSMA Mobile for Development Foundation, a not-for-profit organisation that holds fiduciary governance." (D0007332.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme operates under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and GSMA, with FCDO providing core funding to the GSMA Mobile for Development Foundation. The Innovation Fund disburses competitive grants to external innovators, while the programme also includes research, advocacy, and market engagement activities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: GSMA acts as the lead manager, with FCDO providing oversight and advisory support. The programme includes a Partnership Strategy Group for strategic planning, independent Fund Panels for Innovation Fund allocations, and a GSMA Foundation Board for fiduciary governance. FCDO representatives are embedded at key decision points.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Innovation Fund uses competitive calls to select innovators, ensuring that the most promising and scalable solutions are supported. GSMA's role as a convener and its access to MNOs and the mobile ecosystem provide a robust pipeline for identifying high-potential partners.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO will fund five Innovation Fund rounds, which will support a total of 50 social enterprises with patient capital and technical assistance, de-risk their approaches and help them build a clear path to scale and commercial sustainability." (D0007332.odt, End-to-end innovation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Partnership Strategy Group includes FCDO and other core donors, GSMA leadership, and MNO chairs. It meets annually to agree on strategic plans and mid-year for course corrections. The Innovation Fund has independent Fund Panels with GSMA, FCDO, and external experts. The GSMA Foundation Board reviews progress three times a year.
how_governance.quote: "A Partnership Strategy Group, made up of FCDO and other core supporting donors, the Operator Chairs of the Programme Leadership Groups, and key members of the GSMA M4D leadership will meet once at the start of the year to agree an annual strategic plan and again half-way through the year to make any necessary course corrections." (D0007332.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes a break clause for March 2025 and allows for adjustments based on annual reviews and strategic planning meetings. Funds can be reallocated between components with approval from the Partnership Strategy Group.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be flexible and adaptive, with annual strategic reviews allowing for adjustments in priorities. The Partnership Strategy Group can approve changes to focus areas based on emerging evidence and FCDO priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will remain flexible and will strive to adapt or pivot to stay fully aligned with FCDO’s priorities and changes to the wider environment (political, economic, social, and technological changes)." (D0007332.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GSMA (lead implementer) → MNOs/social enterprises (sub-grantees)
how_efficiency.quote: "Overhead costs: £3.3m (10%)." (D0007332.odt, Table 1: The programme’s high-level budget)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The GSMA was chosen due to its unique position as a convener of the mobile ecosystem, its strong track record in delivering digital inclusion and climate resilience programmes, and its ability to leverage MNO partnerships for scaling innovations. The platform approach allows for flexibility, adaptive management, and the ability to crowd in additional funding from other donors and the private sector.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (GSMA's expertise and convening power)
flexibility (adaptive management and ability to pivot)
equity (focus on women and underserved groups)
risk mitigation (moderate risk profile with safeguards)
alignment with FCDO priorities (digital inclusion, climate action, emerging technologies)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of entrenching the digital divide if interventions do not reach the most underserved groups.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted focus on women, people with disabilities, and rural populations through specific initiatives like the Connected Women Commitment Initiative and digital skills training.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited scalability of emerging technologies (e.g., AI) due to data and regulatory barriers.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for policymakers on AI ethics and privacy, and partnerships with MNOs to leverage Mobile Big Data (MBD) for inclusive solutions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on MNO partnerships for scaling solutions, which may limit reach in areas with poor network coverage.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on areas already covered by mobile broadband (3 billion people) and advocacy for affordable mobile services.

why_rationale.quote: "By working with GSMA, FCDO is tapping into its subject matter expertise and thought leadership, its connections with the private sector (in particular MNOs) and its considerable convening power." (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's focus on climate-vulnerable areas and underserved groups (e.g., women, people with disabilities) shapes partner selection, prioritizing MNOs and innovators with strong local presence and commitment to inclusion. Regulatory barriers in LMICs also influence the choice of partners capable of navigating these challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Climate vulnerability requires partners with local expertise in resilience-building.
Digital divide necessitates partners focused on gender and disability inclusion.
Regulatory environments in LMICs limit the types of innovations that can be scaled.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's mixed objectives (research, innovation, policy influence, capacity building) require a platform-based delivery structure that can manage competitive funding (Innovation Fund), research dissemination, advocacy, and technical assistance. The need for adaptive management and flexibility is driven by the rapidly evolving digital and climate landscapes.
q28_linkages: End-to-end innovation objective → Platform structure with Innovation Fund and technical assistance.
Policy influence objective → Advocacy and convening role of GSMA with governments and MNOs.
Capacity building objective → Embedded advisory support and training tools (e.g., MISTT).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., targeting women, people with disabilities, and rural populations) with efficiency (e.g., leveraging MNO partnerships for scale). This includes trade-offs such as higher costs for inclusive design (e.g., handset affordability initiatives) versus the potential for broader reach through MNO networks.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusive design (e.g., for people with disabilities) may reduce speed but increases equity.
Targeting women and underserved groups requires additional resources but aligns with FCDO's equity priorities.
Scaling through MNOs balances efficiency with the risk of excluding areas with poor network coverage.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (climate vulnerability, digital divide) necessitates milestone-based oversight and adaptive management, with annual reviews and a break clause to mitigate risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include advisory support, training, and technical assistance. This ensures that innovators and MNOs can effectively scale solutions while addressing inclusion and climate resilience.
intersections.quote: "The programme will remain flexible and will strive to adapt or pivot to stay fully aligned with FCDO’s priorities and changes to the wider environment (political, economic, social, and technological changes)." (D0007332.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Entrenching the digital divide if interventions do not reach women and underserved groups.
Limited scalability of emerging technologies (e.g., AI) due to data privacy and regulatory barriers.
Climate shocks disrupting programme activities in vulnerable areas.
Dependence on MNO partnerships limiting reach in areas with poor network coverage.
Nascent funding ecosystems hindering the growth of digital entrepreneurs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted initiatives for women (e.g., Connected Women Commitment Initiative) and people with disabilities, with a focus on handset affordability and digital skills training.
Capacity building for policymakers on AI ethics/privacy and partnerships with MNOs to leverage Mobile Big Data (MBD).
Incorporate climate risk reduction measures into programme activities and focus on building resilience in vulnerable communities.
Advocacy for affordable mobile services and focus on areas already covered by mobile broadband.
Catalytic funding and technical assistance to de-risk early-stage business models and attract private investment.

fcas_specific_lessons: The programme scored a moderate climate risk, requiring adaptive management and safeguards for climate-vulnerable areas.
Lessons from previous phases highlight the need for flexible funding to respond to external shocks (e.g., pandemic, climate crises).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme has continuously scored A/A+ in annual reviews since 2013, demonstrating strong performance in digital inclusion, climate resilience, and leveraging mobile technology for development. Key lessons include the importance of adaptive management, the value of MNO partnerships for scaling, and the need for targeted interventions to close the digital gender gap.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Reinstated work on disability inclusion (discontinued in previous phase due to budget constraints).
Added focus on handset affordability and technology-facilitated gender-based violence.
Discontinued work on reducing mobile network coverage gaps (now 95% coverage) to focus on the 3 billion people not using mobile broadband.
Expanded Innovation Fund with stronger technical assistance to facilitate scaling.
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme has continuously scored A/A+’s in its Annual Reviews since FCDO and GSMA’s partnership began in 2013... The value for money offered by the programme has further improved since the approval of the original business case, due to M4D’s increased credibility, partnerships, investments, research and technical expertise." (D0007332.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: FCDO’s current funding for the M4D programme has leveraged a total of £29 million from other donors (Sida, BMGF, USAID, GIZ, Visa, NORAD). The addendum is expected to leverage an additional £40 million in co-funding.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: At least 1/3 of the programme’s funding is expected to be spent on the UK’s International Climate Finance, covering adaptation, mitigation, and nature objectives.
financial_details.quote: "We expect FCDO’s additional contribution to leverage £40 million co-funding from other funders... FCDO’s current funding for the M4D programme has leveraged a total of £29 million from Sida, BMGF, USAID, GIZ, Visa and NORAD." (D0007332.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Disaster Risk Insurance – Global Parametrics
metadata.quote: "This programme is designed to build resilience to natural disasters across the private and humanitarian sectors in developing countries through the provision and market development of risk transfer and risk insurance products." (58779222.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: November 2015 – November 2025" (58779222.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes a financing mechanism (Natural Disaster Fund) to channel funds and shape markets, while also implementing research and development of parametric insurance products. It includes capacity building through a Technical Assistance Facility and aims to demonstrate commercial sustainability of disaster risk insurance solutions in developing countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The UK will provide up to £37.1m of funding... DFID will help establish a start-up social enterprise, Global Parametrics (GP). GP will provide and commercialise insurance-like Financial Disaster Risk Management (FDRM) products..." (45411632.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "Establishment of a start-up social enterprise (Global Parametrics), to develop and distribute Financial Disaster Risk Management (FDRM) products... Seed funding of a Natural Disaster Fund (NDF)... Establishment of a Technical Assistance Facility..." (58779222.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
q3_expected_outputs: New entity Global Parametrics set up and incorporated (1 entity)
Commercially sustainable social enterprise established (1 enterprise)
FDRM solutions developed and marketed to non-state entities (3,776 million GBP potential origination by year 5)
Commercially sustainable NDF established (251 million GBP sum insured by year 5)
50 million beneficiaries covered by disaster risk financing products by November 2020
48% private risk capital drawn in by November 2019
13 clients implementing disaster risk management products by November 2020
Technical Assistance Facility supporting capacity building (regulators, stakeholders)
Improved FDRM in LMICs through targeted technical assistance
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to build private sector resilience to natural disasters in developing countries by creating a market for commercial disaster risk insurance through a social enterprise (Global Parametrics), a risk capital fund (Natural Disaster Fund), and technical assistance to strengthen regulatory and institutional capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "Its expected outcome is: A deepened market for commercial disaster risk insurance for the private sector in developing countries." (45411632.odt, Expected Results) AND "The expectation is that GP will finalise the structuring deals and NDF Notional pipeline with key transactions... providing greaterexposure for GP in demonstrating its proof of concept" (58779222.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in developing countries with high exposure to natural disasters where insurance penetration is lowest and disaster risks are most acute. The original business case explicitly rates the programme risk as 'High'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: High" (45411632.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Natural disasters... are among the key risks faced by the private sector in developing countries; but they are also among the least insured" (58779222.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory failures prevent recognition of insurance benefits, data limitations hinder robust risk modelling, weak institutions lack capacity to oversee products, and underdeveloped market infrastructure increases transaction costs. These constraints collectively prevent commercial insurers from entering disaster risk markets in developing countries.
where_context.quote: "Regulatory failures: Central banks, supervisors and credit rating agencies in developing countries can fail to recognise the benefits of insurance in off-setting risk... insurance regulation and laws in low income countries are inadequate for regulating insurance companies providing catastrophe insurance." (45411632.odt, Barriers to entry) AND "Data: Required data for robust risk modelling is frequently incomplete in developing countries." (45411632.odt, Barriers to entry)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID (UK) and KfW (Germany) hold board seats and provide all initial funding, with GP's management team (including founder Jerry Skees) making operational decisions. Southern partners (e.g., VisionFund, Aga Khan Agency) are clients/beneficiaries rather than decision-makers.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical Assistance Facility for regulators and stakeholders
Training on FDRM product use
Regulatory capacity building
Institutional strengthening for private sector entities

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of equity investments (£1.5m to GP, £25m to NDF), convertible loans (£6.4m + £1.8m extension to GP), and grant funding (£2.5m for Technical Assistance Facility, £1m for M&E, £700k for consultancy). The convertible loans automatically convert to equity upon raising Series A capital or default.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Global Parametrics (GP) is the single implementing entity responsible for developing FDRM products, managing the NDF, and delivering technical assistance. DFID and KfW/Blue Orchard provide funding and board oversight but do not manage day-to-day operations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GP was developed by Dr. Jerry Skees of GlobalAgRisk, who approached DFID in 2012 with a pre-existing business plan. DFID conducted due diligence but selected GP as the sole implementer without competitive bidding, given its specialized expertise in parametric insurance for LMICs.
how_mechanism.quote: "In 2012 DFID was approached by Dr. Jerry Skees of GlobalAgRisk... Skees presented the concept to develop a social enterprise, Global Parametrics (GP)..." (45411632.odt, What we will do) AND "DFID appointed Lion’s Head Global Partners (LHGP) to undertake a due diligence of Global Parametrics and their investment proposal..." (58779222.odt, The potential of the investment)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: GP has a board with representatives from DFID and KfW/Blue Orchard. The board oversees strategic decisions, including fundraising and major transactions. The NDF has both a development committee and an investment committee to attract ESG-focused funds.
how_governance.quote: "DFID will be represented on the GP board to increase its oversight of the programme." (58779222.odt, What is the approach to implementation?) AND "The NDF’s unique position of having both a development committee alongside an investment committee has been an attractive proposition for funds looking for transactions that satisfy Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) criteria." (58779222.odt, Mobilising Private Capital) AND "The disbursement deliverables and timetable will enable DFID to monitor progress. Disbursement will be staggered in three equal amounts associated with milestones..." (58779222.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are tied to specific milestones (e.g., hiring CFO, securing BMZ funding), but the programme has demonstrated flexibility in reallocating resources to address delays (e.g., extending runway for 18 months, adjusting hiring plans).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has adapted to delays by extending timelines, adjusting revenue projections, and reallocating funds to critical areas (e.g., technology platform strengthening). DFID approval is required for major changes, as seen in the £1.8m cost extension.
how_flexibility.quote: "As per the SMART rules, the business case and the logframe are considered living documents and changes may be needed as the situation changes and advances..." (45411632.odt, Evidence to demonstrate Impact and Outcome are achievable) AND "Both founding investors, DFID and KfW’s Climate Investment Fund... have agreed that providing GP with enough capital for 18 months of operation would enable GP to consolidate its business and drive a series A capital raise by March 2021." (58779222.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Global Parametrics (implementer) → [clients/beneficiaries in LMICs]. The Technical Assistance Facility and NDF are managed by GP as part of its core structure.
how_efficiency.quote: "Disbursement will be staggered in three equal amounts associated with milestones with a 60:40 split DFID to IIF..." (58779222.odt, What is the approach to implementation?) AND "Total support to the programme: £38.9m" (58779222.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (status quo)
Science & Data Company (standalone data provider)
Technical Assistance interventions (standalone capacity building)
MGA + Science + TAF (limited risk capital access)
Partnership with (re)insurers & TAF (unlikely to change market behavior)
New private (re)insurer & TAF (high costs, seen as competitor)
New public (re)insurer & TAF (challenging setup, lacks innovation incentives)
New hybrid social venture with risk capital, science, MGA, & TAF (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid social venture model was selected because it uniquely addresses all four critical market failures: (1) climate/seismic data provision, (2) innovative FDRM product design, (3) 'patient' risk financing, and (4) capacity building. Unlike alternatives, this model combines commercial sustainability with development impact, leverages DFID's catalytic funding to attract private capital, and avoids the free-rider problem by internalizing market-making costs. The structure also allows gradual transition of risks to commercial markets once proven.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (DFID's risk tolerance as anchor investor)
partner capacity (GP's 15+ years of experience in LMIC parametric insurance)
speed (catalytic effect to mobilize £227m private investment by year 6)
equity (focus on underserved LMIC private sector)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GP fails to reach commercially sustainable scale
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID's patient capital and staged funding tied to KPIs; technical assistance to build demand; leveraging DFID's signaling effect to attract private investors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Significant delays in GP’s establishment due to regulatory/legal approvals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-programme funding for legal/financial due diligence; DFID's active role in resolving post-approval clarifications (e.g., ODA eligibility).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lower than expected demand, distribution, and sales
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical Assistance Facility to build client capacity; targeted market research to identify viable clients; master policies to reduce transaction costs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FDRM contracts classified as (re)insurance rather than derivatives, increasing costs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with regulators through TAF; use of globally native risk models to demonstrate product validity; leveraging DFID's influence in regulatory dialogues.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: DFID encounters difficulties reaching agreement with KfW (platform host)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early engagement and alignment on investment terms; joint funding commitments (e.g., £3m co-investment with Blue Orchard).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational costs higher than expected
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Staged disbursements tied to milestones; cost extensions (e.g., £1.8m bridge funding) to cover shortfalls; focus on technology platform efficiency.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of DFID's catalytic £25m to leverage £227m private capital)
equity (focus on underserved LMIC private sector, gender-sensitive microfinance impacts)
why_rationale.quote: "Several options for an intervention that addresses these market failures were extensively reviewed in the KfW strategic plan provided to DFID by GlobalAgRisk in 2012... Option 8: New hybrid social venture w/ risk capital, science, MGA, & TAF... Comprehensive: Preferred Option. Addresses all key drivers of market failure and has ability to work alongside existing market players." (45411632.odt, What we will do) AND "The hybrid model was selected over alternatives because it alone could address the self-reinforcing constraints to FDRM growth in developing countries—assuming high entry costs, free rider risks, information failures, and market structure gaps—while maintaining commercial sustainability." (45411632.odt, Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk, low-insurance-penetration context of LMICs constrained partner selection to entities with specialized expertise in parametric insurance and risk modelling for developing markets. Traditional insurers/reinsurers were unwilling to enter these markets due to correlated risks, data gaps, and regulatory uncertainties, necessitating a bespoke social venture (GP) with DFID as anchor investor.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory failures in LMICs required a partner (GP) with experience navigating legal approvals (e.g., Peru’s forecast insurance).
Data limitations in LMICs necessitated a partner (GP/Enki) with globally native risk models flexible to sparse data.
Market infrastructure gaps demanded a partner capable of bundling small transactions (e.g., master policies).
High correlation of disaster risks in LMICs required a partner with diversified, patient capital (NDF structure).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to simultaneously address data provision, product innovation, risk financing, and capacity building determined the hybrid delivery structure. The commercial sustainability objective required a social enterprise (GP) with profit motives, while the development goal necessitated DFID’s catalytic funding and technical assistance. The staged funding (tranches tied to KPIs) reflects the need to prove concept before scaling.
q28_linkages: Data provision (WHAT) → Required in-house scientific arm (HOW: GP’s integration of Enki’s models).
Product innovation (WHAT) → Needed flexible, globally applicable parametric designs (HOW: GP’s native risk models).
Risk financing (WHAT) → Demanded patient capital (HOW: NDF with DFID’s £25m subordinated equity).
Capacity building (WHAT) → Required embedded TAF (HOW: standalone facility with £2.5m grant).
Commercial sustainability (WHAT) → Shaped milestone-based disbursements (HOW: KPI-linked tranches).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (serving underserved LMIC private sector) with efficiency (commercial sustainability). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher upfront costs for market-making vs. long-term private capital mobilization; (2) Slower initial ramp-up due to regulatory hurdles vs. sustainable market development; (3) DFID’s patient capital absorbing early losses vs. attracting private investors through proven track record.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Delays in operations (e.g., 18 months for Enki IP integration) slow initial impact but ensure robust, scalable solutions for LMICs.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led GP (with DFID/KfW board seats) ensures technical rigor but limits Southern decision-making power.
Cost vs. reach: High initial subsidies (£38.9m) enable coverage of 50m beneficiaries but require eventual commercial viability to justify costs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (FCAS/LMIC context) necessitates intensive oversight: milestone-based disbursements, DFID board representation, and independent due diligence (LHGP). The innovative, unproven nature of the model further increases management intensity (e.g., quarterly reviews in early years).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) GP’s role includes originating risk AND delivering TAF-supported training; (2) Southern partners (e.g., VisionFund) start as clients but are expected to graduate to independent FDRM users; (3) Regulators are engaged through TAF to create enabling environments, shaping their future oversight roles.
intersections.quote: "The cumulative effect of these market failures and obstacles is reflected in the failure of weather-index based micro-insurance products... to achieve sufficient scale and commercial viability to graduate from subsidised funding support." (45411632.odt, Barriers to entry) AND "The hybrid structure was essential to assume the high entry costs and free rider risks that deter traditional insurers, while the TAF addresses regulatory failures and institutional weaknesses." (45411632.odt, What we will do) AND "DFID’s funding (and its signalling effect) is vital to catalyse investment in GP... £25m of DFID investment in the NDF will catalyse £227m of 3rd party investment by year 6." (45411632.odt, Why is UK support required?)
