Significant delays in GP’s establishment due to regulatory/legal approvals (undermines investor confidence).
Lower than expected demand, distribution, and sales (requires additional financing).
Operational costs higher than expected (cash flow shortfalls).
FDRM contracts classified as (re)insurance, increasing transaction costs.
Difficulties in reaching agreement with KfW (platform host risk).
Highly correlated disaster risks in LMICs (volatility in profits/losses).
Free rider problem (competitors capturing benefits after GP proves market).
Data limitations in LMICs (robust risk modelling challenges).
Regulatory failures in target countries (licensing and product approval hurdles).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GP fails to reach commercially sustainable scale
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Staged DFID funding tied to KPIs; technical assistance to build demand; leveraging DFID’s signaling to attract private capital (e.g., Hanover Re, BMZ).
Pre-programme legal/financial due diligence; DFID’s active role in resolving regulatory clarifications; 18-month bridge funding.
Technical Assistance Facility to educate clients; master policies to reduce transaction costs; targeted market research.
Cost extensions (£1.8m); focus on technology efficiency; milestone-based disbursements.
Engagement with regulators via TAF; use of parametric triggers to distinguish from traditional insurance.
Early alignment on terms; joint funding commitments (e.g., £3m co-investment with Blue Orchard).
Globally diversified NDF portfolio; patient capital to absorb initial volatility.
First-mover advantages (e.g., Enki IP acquisition); DFID’s catalytic role to accelerate market entry.
Globally native risk models flexible to sparse data; partnerships with meteorological agencies.
Technical assistance to regulators; leveraging DFID’s influence in policy dialogues.

fcas_specific_lessons: Regulatory capacity in FCAS/LMICs requires upfront investment (e.g., TAF funding for approvals).
Data gaps in FCAS necessitate flexible modelling approaches (e.g., GP’s globally native models).
High disaster risk correlation in FCAS demands patient, diversified capital (e.g., NDF structure).
Local financial capability constraints require simplified products (e.g., master policies).
Political economy risks (e.g., currency controls) may delay transactions (e.g., BMZ funding staggers).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous attempts at disaster risk products (e.g., weather-index microinsurance) failed due to insufficient scale, high transaction costs, and lack of commercial sustainability. Lessons applied: (1) Bundling small transactions via master policies; (2) Patient capital to absorb early losses; (3) Technical assistance to address regulatory barriers; (4) Leveraging DFID’s catalytic role to attract private sector.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. Extended runway from 12 to 18 months based on slower-than-expected ramp-up. 2. Added £1.8m bridge funding to address cash flow shortfalls. 3. Staggered BMZ NDF contributions to align with GP’s deal pipeline. 4. Strengthened technology platform to reduce operational risks. 5. Formalized strategic approach to business development (dedicated sales teams per revenue channel).
risks_lessons.quote: "The greatest impact on GP’s funding requirements is associated with delays in initiating operations, followed by a lower than forecast rate of ramp up." (58779222.odt, Why the requirement for investment?) AND "Previous attempts to create disaster risk mitigation products have met with limited success. A number of self-reinforcing barriers have prevented the development of commercially sustainable disaster risk insurance business models." (45411632.odt, Why is UK support required?) AND "Over the past 12 months GP have undergone significant changes, including... a more formal strategic approach to business development... won the structuring mandate for an emerging markets parametric facility for the IFC." (58779222.odt, The potential of the investment)

co_funding_partners.partner: KfW Climate Investment Fund (via Blue Orchard)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: By year 6, DFID’s £25m NDF investment is projected to catalyse £227m in third-party private capital (equity and guarantees). As of 2019, the NDF’s $11.36m in risk mobilised $30m from Allianz ART for the Philippines cyclone programme. Hanover Re’s $50m matching commitment and BMZ’s €33m injection are expected to increase NDF capacity to $126m.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme combines capital investments (£8.2m loans + £1.5m equity to GP; £25m equity to NDF) with revenue-generating activities (management fees from NDF, structuring mandates) and grant funding (£4.2m for TAF/M&E). GP’s revenue streams include modelling fees, deal origination fees, and NDF management fees.
financial_details.quote: "DFID will contribute: up to £6.4m non-fiscal C-Del (convertible loan) and £1.5 fiscal C-Del (quasi-equity) for GP; £25 m non-fiscal C-Del (subordinated equity) in a Natural Disaster Fund (NDF); £2.5m in R-Del grant funding for a Technical Assistance Facility; and £1m R-Del for M&E and £700k R-Del for consultancy support." (45411632.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "In the base case projections, £25m of DFID investment in the NDF will catalyse £227m of 3rd party investment in the form of equity and guarantees by year 6." (45411632.odt, Why is UK support required?) AND "The NDF’s unique position... has been an attractive proposition for funds looking for transactions that satisfy Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) criteria." (58779222.odt, Mobilising Private Capital)

metadata.programme_name: India Infrastructure Equity Partnership Programme

quote.text: Upto £37.5 million over 10 years (2013-2022) as equity investments in infrastructure projects with poverty impact in the eight low income states of India

metadata.duration_source: Upto £37.5 million over 10 years (2013-2022)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling equity funds to infrastructure projects) with implementation research (testing private sector-led infrastructure models in under-invested regions). It aims to demonstrate viability of pro-poor infrastructure projects in India's eight low-income states while mobilizing additional private investment.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will directly support: i) At least 12 new private sector-led (including PPP projects) ii) At least £120 million additional private investment mobilised for pro-poor infrastructure services... The intervention has the potential to unlock capital flows into the target states and sub-sectors through its returnable capital approach and working with the private sector.

q3_expected_outputs.output: 12 new private sector-led infrastructure projects (including PPPs) reaching financial closure
£120 million additional private investment mobilised for pro-poor infrastructure services
280,000 people getting access to new/improved infrastructure services (electricity, sewerage, transport)
1,500 long-term jobs generated directly
3,000 short-term construction jobs generated
Technical assistance to improve project design and attract co-investors
Monitoring and evaluation framework including MIS system

what_objectives.summary: The programme uses returnable capital to catalyze private investment in pro-poor infrastructure (agricultural storage, clean energy, transport, urban services) in India's eight poorest states, combining equity investments with technical assistance to demonstrate viability and attract follow-on funding.

quote.text: The proposed programme is fully aligned with Secretary of State's November 2012 statement to Parliament on a new development relationship with India and also the March 2013 statement that outlined her vision for DFID support to economic growth, particularly, "unlocking the ability of entrepreneurs and business people in developing countries to themselves drive growth through their businesses being successful".

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The eight low-income states are perceived as more risky by investors due to political and execution risks, but have shown recent growth rates of 5-9.5% and improving business environments. The programme explicitly notes these states have 'higher political and execution risk' but are experiencing development-oriented political leadership.
where_context.q5_source: The reluctance of private sector to invest in these states/sectors is due to the perception of higher political and execution risk... Some poorer states have begun showing higher growth rates State GDP growth rates of between 5 and 9.5%...
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The constraints include: 1) Limited availability of local currency finance for infrastructure in low-income states; 2) High front-end costs and uncertainty in project development; 3) Lack of locally available capacity and skills; 4) Absence of systematic credit rating for infrastructure projects; 5) Difficulties with land acquisition and environmental clearances; 6) Challenges in setting fair tariffs that balance affordability with cost recovery. These constraints make it difficult to attract private investment to the target states and sectors.

quote.text: The market and institutional failures that discourage private investment into low income states, especially in some sub-sectors are: limited availability of local currency finance, particularly fresh equity from developers and banks utilising their infrastructure limits in more profitable sub-sectors in developed states; high front-end cost and uncertainty attached to project development, with multiple investors required to agree, leading to fewer deals; lack of locally available capacity and skills in both the public and private sectors; absence of a systematic approach to credit rating infrastructure projects; lack of rupee denominated guarantees; difficulties relating to policies, regulations, and institutions, with land acquisition and environmental clearances particular problems; difficulty setting fair tariffs that balance affordability for poorer customers against generating sufficient income to cover costs.
quote.source: 6159755.odt, Strategic Case: B. Infrastructure and growth

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The fund manager (SBICAP Ventures Ltd., an Indian entity wholly owned by State Bank of India) has primary decision-making authority over project selection and fund management, with DFID providing oversight and technical assistance. The document emphasizes working through 'GoI-sponsored intermediaries' and notes that 'SBI was identified as a strong potential partner based on its meeting the essential criteria of being a GoI-sponsored entity'.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to improve project design
strengthening environmental and social governance standards
monitoring and evaluation capacity building
knowledge generation to attract other investors

partner_organizations.name: SBICAP Ventures Ltd. (SVL)
partner_organizations.role: Fund Manager (primary implementer)

partner_organizations.name: State Bank of India Capital Markets Limited (SBICAP)
partner_organizations.role: Parent organization overseeing SVL

partner_organizations.name: State Bank of India (SBI)
partner_organizations.role: Co-investor (planning to invest £12 million) and strategic partner

partner_organizations.name: Government of India (GoI) sponsored institutions
partner_organizations.role: Policy linkage and potential co-investors

partner_organizations.name: DFID India
partner_organizations.role: Funder and technical assistance provider

partner_organizations.name: Potential co-investors (domestic DFIs, pension funds, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Expected to contribute additional capital at fund level

quote.text: For implementation of this option, DFID would need to work through a chosen financial intermediary and tailor the design elements of the equity option based on negotiations with the Partner. Of the possible partners considered for managing the equity partnership, DFID judged the proposal from SBI amongst the strongest... The prospective partnership was also the most likely to create additionality for DFID capital across the following elements: Financial (equity investment through the fund structure allows attracting private sector capital at the fund-level through co-investors such as domestic DFIs, pension funds etc. and at the project level as patient risk-capital), Design (an equity instrument enables DFID greater scope to influence project design to focus on smaller transaction size projects and use TA support to enhance the growth and/or poverty impact of projects)...

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses £36 million as returnable equity capital invested in an infrastructure-focused equity fund managed by SBICAP Ventures Ltd., combined with £1.5 million in technical assistance grants. The equity fund provides patient risk capital to infrastructure projects that would otherwise struggle to attract private investment, while the TA component supports project design, ESG standards, and monitoring/evaluation.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: SBICAP Ventures Ltd. (SVL) acts as the fund manager with operational autonomy, while DFID provides oversight through annual reviews and technical assistance. The structure allows for co-investment from other domestic and international investors at both fund and project levels. The fund targets smaller projects (£3-5 million average) in four pro-poor sub-sectors: agricultural infrastructure, energy services, transport, and urban services.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: DFID conducted a partner evaluation exercise with eight GoI-sponsored institutions. The selection was based on pre-agreed criteria including: i) demonstrated experience in financing projects in multiple infrastructure sub-sectors; ii) capacity to use financial instruments; iii) pipeline of potential investments in low-income states; iv) track record in these states; v) fit with DFID's pro-poor objectives; vi) quality of staff and systems; vii) experience in identified sub-sectors; viii) networks; and ix) understanding of additionality requirements. SBI/SBICAP scored highest on institutional mission, systems, sector experience, and ability to identify quality projects.

quote.text: To short-list the range of partnership options and better understand the capacity of partners to engage, DFID invited eight potential partners to set out their interests and capability in line with Government of India-sponsored criteria under the UK-India bilateral aid framework. A four-person DFID assessment team assessed proposals against pre-agreed and weighted criteria including: i) Demonstrated experience of financing projects in multiple infrastructure sub-sectors; ii) Capacity to use a variety of financial instruments; iii) Pipeline of potential investments in low income states; iv) Track record of deploying capital in low income states; v) Fit with DFID pro-poor objectives; vi) Quality of staff and systems; vii) Experience in identified pro-poor subsectors; viii) Good networks (project sponsors, financiers and investors) and ix) Understanding that DFID investments must be additional.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly named as a steering committee, the document describes a governance structure where DFID conducts annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews, a mid-term review, and an end-term review, with the fund manager (SBICAP Ventures) having operational control but subject to DFID's monitoring and evaluation framework. The partnership includes regular knowledge sharing and policy dialogue components.

quote.text: The project will have a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework including a computerised management information system (MIS). DFID will undertake annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews to assess progress, a mid-term review in year two, and an end-term review to assess whether the targets in the log frame have been achieved and the cost-benefit assumptions outlined in the economic appraisal have been confirmed.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The equity fund structure allows for reallocation between projects within the four target sub-sectors (agricultural infrastructure, energy services, transport, urban services) and eight states, but requires DFID approval for major strategic shifts. The technical assistance component appears more flexible for adaptive learning.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a technical assistance component designed to generate knowledge about what works best, with annual reviews that can feed into adjustments. The document notes that 'DFID will commission evaluations (up to £1m) to assess impact and attribution,' suggesting a learning-oriented approach. However, major changes would require DFID approval through the review processes.

quote.text: DFID will commission evaluations (up to £1m) to assess impact and attribution... The programme is expected to result in... generating knowledge about what works best and attract other investors into the eight low income states.
quote.source: 6159755.odt, Monitoring and Evaluation and Appraised Options

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO/DFID → Fund Manager (SBICAP Ventures) → Infrastructure Projects/Developers. The technical assistance component adds a parallel layer for monitoring and capacity building.

quote.text: Returnable capital will be provided as patient risk capital over a 10 year period to infrastructure projects that would otherwise not have been considered as attractive investment opportunities by private equity investors.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Provide £36 million as a credit top-up to existing partnership with IDFC as part of the India Infrastructure Debt Programme (plus £1.5m TA)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: IDFC indicated it would struggle to deploy an additional £36m within DFID's timescale, and the top-up could cause diminishing returns or competition with existing DFID credit line.
Would result in lost opportunity to accelerate equity investments in the eight low-income states and build local capacity, with about twelve projects either not coming up or being heavily delayed.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Other potential partners considered (CDC, PIDG, IDFC PE team, sector-focused GoI institutions)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: CDC had limited in-country presence; PIDG's InfraCo Asia had limited capacity to scale in India; IDFC PE team wasn't ready before 2014/15. SBI/SBICAP was judged strongest on GoI sponsorship, pro-poor mandate, systems, and ability to identify quality projects.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The equity fund modality was chosen because: 1) It allows attracting private sector capital at both fund and project levels through co-investment; 2) Provides greater scope to influence project design for smaller transactions (£3-5m average) in pro-poor sub-sectors; 3) Enables demonstration effects to catalyze further private investment; 4) Aligns with DFID's new returnable capital approach; 5) Leverages SBI's extensive branch network and GoI sponsorship to reach frontier districts; 6) Combines patient risk capital with technical assistance to address market failures in under-invested regions.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage ratio of 1:3.3 expected)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited pipeline of bankable projects in target states/sub-sectors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance component designed to improve project design and attractiveness; SBI's branch network used to identify potential projects; focus on smaller transaction sizes (£3-5m) that are currently under-served.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund manager's limited experience with pro-poor infrastructure sub-sectors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID's technical assistance will strengthen ESG standards and project design capabilities; annual reviews to monitor performance; SBI's co-investment (£12m) aligns incentives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Difficulty in attracting co-investors to high-risk states
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demonstration effect of initial projects; knowledge generation to share lessons; policy dialogue to address regulatory bottlenecks; DFID's involvement provides comfort to other investors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Execution risks in low-income states (land acquisition, environmental clearances)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on sub-sectors with simpler implementation (e.g., agricultural storage, off-grid energy); technical assistance to improve project preparation; working with state governments showing development orientation.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (focus on eight low-income states and pro-poor sub-sectors)

quote.text: The feasibility of partnering with SBI and the Fund Manager has also been judged on the basis of several months of detailed discussions between DFID and SBI/SBICAP involving: Exploration of investment parameters, a shared approach and SBI and SBICAP investing $20 million (or £12 million) of their own money into this infrastructure equity fund... The prospective partnership was also the most likely to create additionality for DFID capital across the following elements: Financial (equity investment through the fund structure allows attracting private sector capital at the fund-level through co-investors such as domestic DFIs, pension funds etc. and at the project level as patient risk-capital), Design (an equity instrument enables DFID greater scope to influence project design to focus on smaller transaction size projects and use TA support to enhance the growth and/or poverty impact of projects)...

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The context of India's eight low-income states (Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal) significantly constrained partner selection by: 1) Requiring GoI-sponsored intermediaries (limiting to Indian public sector entities); 2) Needing partners with existing presence/networks in these states (excluding many international players); 3) Demanding experience with smaller transaction sizes (£3-5m) that most infrastructure funds don't handle; 4) Requiring pro-poor sector expertise (agricultural storage, off-grid energy, etc.) that few financial institutions possess. This led to selecting SBICAP Ventures (SBI's subsidiary) as the only partner meeting all criteria of GoI sponsorship, local presence, appropriate systems, and pro-poor mandate.
q27_constraints_detail: Requirement for GoI-sponsored intermediaries (limited to public sector entities)
Need for existing networks in eight low-income states (excluded many international players)
Focus on smaller transaction sizes (£3-5m average) that most infrastructure funds don't handle
Requirement for experience in pro-poor sub-sectors (agricultural storage, off-grid energy, etc.)
Political and execution risks in target states requiring local knowledge
Limited pipeline of bankable projects in these regions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's objectives to 1) demonstrate viability of pro-poor infrastructure projects and 2) mobilize private investment in under-served regions directly shaped the delivery structure by: 1) Requiring an equity fund mechanism (rather than grants or debt) to attract co-investors; 2) Needing a local fund manager (SBICAP) with GoI sponsorship to navigate political/economic risks; 3) Incorporating technical assistance to improve project bankability; 4) Focusing on smaller transaction sizes (£3-5m) that align with the target sub-sectors; 5) Building in monitoring/evaluation to generate evidence for replication. The mixed financing (equity + TA) approach was specifically designed to address the market failures identified in the strategic case.
q28_linkages: Objective to attract private investment → Chose equity fund structure with co-investment potential
Focus on eight low-income states → Required GoI-sponsored partner with local networks (SBI/SBICAP)
Need to demonstrate viability → Incorporated technical assistance for project design improvements
Targeting smaller projects (£3-5m) → Selected fund manager experienced with this transaction size
Pro-poor sub-sector focus → Partner needed expertise in agricultural storage, off-grid energy, etc.
Knowledge generation goal → Built in comprehensive M&E framework with annual reviews
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses several equity vs. efficiency trade-offs: 1) Targeting eight low-income states with higher perceived risks reduces financial efficiency but aligns with equity goals; 2) Focusing on smaller projects (£3-5m) increases transaction costs but reaches underserved communities; 3) Including technical assistance (£1.5m) reduces funds available for direct investments but is necessary to improve project quality and attract co-investors; 4) Working through a GoI-sponsored entity (SBI) adds bureaucratic layers but provides critical local legitimacy; 5) The 10-year patient capital approach sacrifices immediate returns for longer-term development impact. The document frames these as necessary trade-offs to achieve the programme's pro-poor objectives while still aiming for financial sustainability through leverage (1:3.3 ratio).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Higher perceived risk in target states reduces financial returns but aligns with poverty reduction goals
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Mitigated through co-investment structure and DFID's risk capital

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Smaller project sizes (£3-5m) increase transaction costs but reach underserved communities
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Addressed through fund manager's existing networks and technical assistance

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Technical assistance component (£1.5m) reduces direct investment funds but improves project quality
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Justified as necessary to attract co-investors and generate knowledge

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: GoI-sponsored partner adds bureaucratic processes but provides local legitimacy
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Selected SBI for its robust systems and pro-poor mandate

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: 10-year patient capital sacrifices immediate returns for long-term impact
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Aligned with DFID's new returnable capital approach

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of operating in eight low-income states with perceived higher political and execution risks directly shapes the management intensity through: 1) Annual Output-to-Purpose Reviews (more frequent than typical for lower-risk programmes); 2) Mid-term and end-term evaluations to closely monitor progress; 3) Comprehensive M&E framework including computerised MIS; 4) Technical assistance component to address implementation challenges; 5) Focus on smaller, more manageable project sizes (£3-5m) rather than large-scale infrastructure. The oversight is designed to be intensive enough to manage risks while allowing operational flexibility.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives significantly shape partner roles by: 1) Making technical assistance a core component (£1.5m) to strengthen project design and ESG standards; 2) Selecting SBICAP Ventures partly for its ability to receive and implement capacity building support; 3) Including knowledge generation and dissemination as explicit fund manager responsibilities; 4) Building monitoring and evaluation capacity into both the fund manager and infrastructure developers; 5) Using the partnership to influence policy through lessons learned. The document positions capacity building as both an output (improving specific projects) and a mechanism (enabling the fund manager to better attract and manage investments).

quote.text: The key outcome of the programme is sustainable private sector supported pro-poor infrastructure projects delivered in the targeted sub-sectors in the eight low income states... The programme is expected to result in... generating knowledge about what works best and attract other investors into the eight low income states. The technical assistance component (£1.5m) is explicitly designed to improve project design, strengthen ESG standards, and build M&E capacity. The selection of SBICAP Ventures was based partly on their ability to absorb and implement this capacity building support while managing the equity fund.

key_programme_risks: Limited pipeline of bankable projects in target states/sub-sectors
Fund manager's limited experience with pro-poor infrastructure sub-sectors
Difficulty in attracting co-investors to high-risk states
Execution risks in low-income states (land acquisition, environmental clearances)
Political and regulatory uncertainties affecting project implementation
Market risks affecting revenue generation from infrastructure services
Currency and inflation risks affecting financial returns
Capacity constraints in state governments and local partners
Potential for project delays due to approval processes
Risk of not achieving leverage targets (£120m private investment mobilised)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance component to improve project design; leverage SBI's extensive branch network to identify projects; focus on smaller transaction sizes that are currently under-served

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fund manager's limited experience with pro-poor sub-sectors
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID's technical assistance to strengthen ESG standards; annual reviews to monitor performance; SBI's co-investment aligns incentives
Demonstration effect of initial projects; knowledge generation to share lessons; policy dialogue to address regulatory bottlenecks
Focus on sub-sectors with simpler implementation; technical assistance for project preparation; work with development-oriented state governments
Work through GoI-sponsored entity (SBI); build relationships with state governments; include contingency in project timelines
Target sub-sectors with clear demand (agricultural storage, off-grid energy); patient capital approach allows time for market development
Embedded technical assistance; focus on partners with existing systems (SBI); knowledge transfer as core objective

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts (though not FCAS), demonstrating initial success is critical to attracting follow-on investment - hence the focus on smaller, quicker-to-implement projects
Local sponsorship (GoI entities) provides essential legitimacy and risk mitigation in challenging environments
Technical assistance must be integrated with financial instruments to address both capacity and bankability issues
Monitoring systems need to be more intensive in higher-risk environments to track both financial and development outcomes
Policy dialogue becomes more important in regions with weak institutional capacity to address systemic bottlenecks
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The business case references several lessons from previous DFID programmes: 1) From West Bengal Municipal Development Fund: £6.3m DFID investment leveraged £74.3m (1:11.5 ratio) showing potential of blended finance; 2) From PIDG experience: systematic review noted that while additionality is hard to measure, DFI involvement provides comfort to other investors; 3) From MP Power programme: successful private participation in infrastructure service delivery; 4) General lesson that infrastructure projects require patient capital and technical support to become bankable in challenging contexts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes based on learning include: 1) Focus on smaller project sizes (£3-5m) that were identified as under-served in previous infrastructure funds; 2) Mixed instrument approach (equity + TA) addressing the need for both financing and capacity building; 3) Explicit knowledge generation component to address the evidence gap identified in systematic reviews; 4) Selection of a GoI-sponsored fund manager to navigate political risks that affected previous programmes; 5) Comprehensive M&E framework incorporating both financial and development metrics based on past difficulties in measuring additionality.

quote.text: DFID's experience in West Bengal through West Bengal Municipal Development Fund (WBMDF) showed that an investment of £6.3 million helped fund additional infrastructure projects worth £74.3 million (a capital leverage ratio of 1:11.5), in turn benefiting around 3 million city dwellers... PIDG documents suggest that its $55 million invested in India has attracted $1.5 billion from the private sector; although the systematic review noted earlier notes that how much 'additionality' this support generated is less clear. The proposed programme design addresses these lessons by: focusing on smaller transactions that can demonstrate viability; building in technical assistance to improve project quality; selecting a partner with both financial strength and pro-poor mandate; and creating a comprehensive monitoring framework to track both financial leverage and development impacts.
quote.source: 6159755.odt, Empirical evidence from relevant DFID programmes and Why DFID intervention is justified

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilise at least £120 million in additional private investment, representing a leverage ratio of approximately 1:3.3 (£120m private : £36m DFID equity).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £36 million (96%) as returnable equity capital; £1.5 million (4%) as technical assistance grants

quote.text: This Business Case proposes to commit up to £37.5 million: £36 million to an infrastructure equity fund investing in pro-poor infrastructure projects and infrastructure developers in the low income states. SBI is likely to co-invest £12 million into the infrastructure equity fund. £1.5 million to provide expertise that helps improve the design of infrastructure projects; improve the quality of environmental, social and governance standards on investments; conduct monitoring and evaluations that generate knowledge about what works best and attract other investors into the eight low income states... The programme will directly support: i) At least 12 new private sector-led (including PPP projects) ii) At least £120 million additional private investment mobilised for pro-poor infrastructure services

metadata.programme_name: Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF)

quote.programme_name: "DFID will provide £25million for a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF) over 2011/12-2016/17" (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.duration: "DFID will provide £25million for a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF) over 2011/12-2016/17" (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.sector: "Impact Evaluations of Interventions with clear human development outcomes" (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "DFID will provide £25million for a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF) over 2011/12-2016/17"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SIEF is a financing mechanism that funds rigorous impact evaluations (evidence generation), builds capacity on impact evaluation methods (capacity building), and disseminates findings to influence policy (policy influence). It operates through thematic clusters to address strategic evidence gaps in human development.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The funds will be spent on: 1. Impact Evaluations of Interventions with clear human development outcomes; 2. Capacity building on impact evaluation methods and implementation techniques; and 3. Dissemination and knowledge sharing of Impact Evaluation findings and results." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)

20 capacity-building workshops/events
dissemination products (policy briefs, peer-reviewed articles, meta-studies, web-based materials)

q3_expected_outputs.target: not quantified

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy workshops and external events
q3_expected_outputs.target: not quantified

what_objectives.summary: SIEF aims to generate rigorous evidence on what works in human development through impact evaluations, build capacity for conducting such evaluations, and ensure findings are disseminated to inform policy and programming globally.

quote.objectives: "The objective of providing funds for impact evaluations is to strengthen the effectiveness of DFID’s policies, programmes and partnerships globally by generating evidence where knowledge gaps exist, assessing innovative solutions to address developmental priorities, and helping to build and use evidence to inform key stakeholders of the impact of global development programmes." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.outputs: "It is expected that SIEF will deliver a minimum of 54 high quality impact evaluations of key development interventions focusing on human development outcomes. In addition, SIEF will deliver 20 capacity building workshops and events to improve understanding of impact evaluation techniques." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)

countries_regions: middle-income countries (if interventions target vulnerable populations with replication potential in LICs)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly targets fragile states and areas with weak evidence bases, where robust data collection is challenging. It also focuses on innovative delivery strategies (e.g., non-state partners) and complex interventions like health systems and nutrition, which inherently carry higher implementation risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Gaps in our knowledge base exist particularly where we are seeking to build the evidence base for innovative delivery strategies (e.g. non-state partners) or in areas of fragility where, by definition, robust evidence is hard to collect." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
q6_contextual_constraints: limited staff capacity (in DFID and partner organizations)
political economy challenges (e.g., scaling innovations in fragile states)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and fragility limit the ability to collect robust evidence, while limited DFID staff capacity constrains the management of evaluations. Data limitations in target regions (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia) affect the feasibility of rigorous impact evaluations, particularly for innovative or multi-sectoral interventions.

quote.constraints: "DFID’s ability to undertake impact evaluations has been constrained by limited staff capacity in spending departments and project-specific budgets that don’t always allow for impact evaluations across a portfolio of work." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.fragility: "Gaps in our knowledge base exist particularly [...] in areas of fragility where, by definition, robust evidence is hard to collect." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)

While Southern researchers and institutions can apply for funding and participate in capacity-building, decision-making authority rests with the World Bank and DFID (as the primary funder).

quote.structure: "DFID will provide £25million for a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF) [...] channelled through a World Bank executed Trust Fund." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.capacity_building: "SIEF will deliver 20 capacity building workshops and events to improve understanding of impact evaluation techniques." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.partners: "The activities will be open to all development partners, and SIEF will fund all costs associated with the workshops including participant travel and subsistence costs." (3744993.odt, Pillar 2)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: SIEF operates as a **Trust Fund** managed by the World Bank, combining: 1) **competitive grants** for impact evaluations (Pillar 1), 2) **block funding** for capacity-building activities (Pillar 2), and 3) **core funding** for dissemination (Pillar 3). Funds are disbursed in stages (seed funding → technical review → milestone-based tranches).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank acts as the fund manager, overseeing a **Steering Committee** (with DFID representation) that sets thematic priorities and approves evaluations. Operational management is decentralized: grantees (researchers/institutions) implement evaluations, while the World Bank handles financial administration, technical reviews, and compliance. Capacity-building and dissemination are centrally managed by the World Bank but delivered through open workshops.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: An open, competitive process was chosen to ensure rigor, quality, and transparency while avoiding excessive transaction costs. The two-stage process (initial proposal review → technical peer review) allows for efficient allocation of funds and reduces the risk of supporting poorly designed evaluations.

quote.instrument: "DFID will provide £25million for a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund (SIEF) [...] channelled through a World Bank executed Trust Fund." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.structure: "It is intended that SIEF will have an open, transparent and competitive process that assures rigor, quality and full consideration of all impact evaluation proposals [...] The funding would be allocated in two stages: Stage 1: Call for proposals and initial proposal review. Stage 2: Technical peer review of impact evaluation designs." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)
quote.selection: "To make the process more competitive and to avoid locking up funds in evaluations that look promising initially but fail to materialize, the funding would be allocated in two stages." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **SIEF Steering Committee** (comprising DFID and World Bank representatives) sets cluster priorities, approves funding windows, and monitors progress. It finalizes thematic areas, reviews proposals, and ensures alignment with DFID’s strategic goals. The Committee also oversees the addition of new clusters (e.g., social safety nets) and monitors the proportion of non-LIC evaluations.

quote.governance: "Through its Steering Committee, the SIEF will develop a cluster priorities related to key policy questions to determine potential areas to be funded over the period of SIEF (2011/12-2016/17), based on agreed criteria and existing evidence gaps." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)
quote.oversight: "Proposals that pass a technical peer review will have access to the first tranche of funding in the budget. Additional funds will be transferred based on achievement of subsequent milestones." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between thematic clusters if evidence gaps emerge or policy priorities change, but this requires Steering Committee approval. The addition of new clusters (e.g., social safety nets) is explicitly permitted with Committee approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Thematic priorities can be adjusted mid-programme if new evidence gaps are identified or policy needs evolve. For example, the document states that "DFID may increase funding to these thematic windows in the future if evidence gaps become apparent, or add windows that are deemed to fit with changing policy priorities." Adjustments require Steering Committee approval.

quote.reallocation: "DFID may increase funding to these thematic windows in the future if evidence gaps become apparent, or add windows that are deemed to fit with changing policy priorities." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)
quote.adaptive: "The Steering Committee will take a final decision over the clusters and their scope." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (fund manager) → grantees (researchers/institutions conducting evaluations).

quote.layers: "The funds will be spent on: 1. Impact Evaluations [...] channelled through a World Bank executed Trust Fund." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.payment: "Proposals that pass a technical peer review will have access to the first tranche of funding in the budget. Additional funds will be transferred based on achievement of subsequent milestones." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing
Develop a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund with 3ie
Develop a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund with World Bank
Develop a Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund within DFID
Embed evaluation in DFID programmes through existing work
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank was selected because: 1) **Proven capacity**: It already managed the Spanish Trust Fund for Impact Evaluation, demonstrating experience in running large-scale, multi-country impact evaluation programmes. 2) **Alignment with DFID priorities**: The World Bank’s geographic focus (66% of its impact evaluations in Africa/South Asia) and thematic expertise in human development matched DFID’s targets. 3) **Efficiency**: Leveraging the World Bank’s existing systems (e.g., technical review processes, training infrastructure) reduced setup time and transaction costs compared to building capacity within DFID or using 3ie (which was at full absorption capacity). 4) **Scalability**: The World Bank’s multilateral status allowed for global reach and attract co-funding from other donors.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging existing World Bank systems)
risk mitigation (World Bank’s experience in fragile contexts)
partner capacity (World Bank’s technical and administrative infrastructure)
speed (quick setup vs. building DFID internal capacity)
equity (global reach and inclusion of Southern researchers)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single multilateral partner (World Bank) could limit diversity of approaches or introduce bureaucratic delays.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Steering Committee (with DFID representation) ensures alignment with DFID’s priorities, and the open competitive process mitigates bias.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Transaction costs for grantees (e.g., complex World Bank procurement procedures) could deter Southern researchers.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SIEF funds all costs for capacity-building workshops (including travel/subistence) and provides seed funding to develop proposals, reducing barriers to entry.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of misalignment between World Bank’s institutional priorities and DFID’s strategic goals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Thematic clusters and priority research questions are finalized by the Steering Committee, and DFID policy leads approve initial clusters (e.g., maternal nutrition, education).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of £25m vs. potential programme savings)
effectiveness (generating rigorous evidence to improve MDG progress)
equity (inclusion of Southern researchers and focus on LICs)

quote.alternatives: "DFID has a strong programme of embedding evaluation into DFID’s human development programmes [...] However, DFID’s evaluation mainstreaming activities will take time to fully embed into programmes, and therefore DFID is unable to meet current need for evidence from its existing human and programme resources for evaluation." (3744993.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.rationale: "The World Bank’s geographic focus is broadly aligned with DFID. Out of the 184 impact evaluations in the World Bank’s current impact evaluation programme, 122 (66%) are in Africa and in South Asia." (3744993.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.risks: "Using a mixture of other evaluation providers for specific impact evaluations or specifically commissioned activities would create significant transaction costs for DFID and lose the coherence of the package of interventions, resulting in lower impact." (3744993.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on **fragile states and LICs** (where evidence gaps are largest) limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **experience in high-risk contexts** (e.g., World Bank’s existing work in fragile states), 2) **capacity to manage complex evaluations** (e.g., handling data limitations), and 3) **global reach** to support multi-country studies. Southern researchers in these regions often lack resources to compete without seed funding or capacity-building support, which SIEF explicitly provides.
q27_constraints_detail: Fragility/conflict (requires partners with experience in unstable contexts)
Data limitations (partners must have methodological expertise to handle weak data environments)
Weak institutions (need for partners who can build local capacity, not just conduct evaluations)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rigorous, multi-country impact evaluations** (WHAT) drives the choice of a **multilateral fund manager** (World Bank) with: 1) **technical review capacity** to assess counterfactual methodologies, 2) **global operational presence** to manage evaluations across regions, and 3) **thematic expertise** in human development. The **cluster-based approach** (grouping evaluations by theme) requires a centralized structure to coordinate synthesis and dissemination, which a single implementer (World Bank) can provide more efficiently than a decentralized model.
q28_linkages: Rigorous impact evaluations (WHAT) → Need for technical review processes (HOW: World Bank’s existing systems)
Multi-country scope (WHAT) → Requires a partner with global reach (HOW: World Bank’s presence in 72+ countries)
Capacity-building for Southern researchers (WHAT) → Necessitates open workshops and seed funding (HOW: Pillar 2’s inclusive design)
Policy influence (WHAT) → Demands dissemination to global stakeholders (HOW: Pillar 3’s communication strategy)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly acknowledges tensions between: 1) **Inclusivity vs. speed**: Open competitive calls ensure quality but may exclude smaller Southern institutions without seed funding (mitigated by SIEF’s provision of proposal development support). 2) **Southern ownership vs. Northern expertise**: While the World Bank (Northern-led) manages the fund, capacity-building targets Southern researchers, and evaluations must include local partners. 3) **Thematic focus vs. flexibility**: Clustering evaluations by theme (e.g., nutrition, education) improves coherence but may limit responsiveness to emerging priorities (mitigated by Steering Committee’s ability to add clusters).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion (competitive process may favor established institutions; seed funding mitigates this)
Expertise vs. ownership (World Bank’s technical leadership vs. Southern researcher participation)
Cost vs. reach (global dissemination is resource-intensive but maximizes policy impact)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk profile** (fragile states, innovative interventions) necessitates **milestone-based oversight** and a **two-stage funding process** to minimize losses from failed evaluations. The Steering Committee’s role in prioritizing clusters also ensures alignment with DFID’s risk appetite (e.g., focusing on areas with the largest evidence gaps).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **core objective of capacity-building** (Pillar 2) directly influences partner roles: 1) Southern researchers are not just grantees but **active participants in training and dissemination**, 2) The World Bank’s role extends beyond funding to **mentorship** (e.g., hands-on sessions, material development), and 3) Government officials in target countries are engaged as **stakeholders in workshops**, ensuring local ownership of findings.

quote.where_who: "Gaps in our knowledge base exist particularly where we are seeking to build the evidence base for innovative delivery strategies (e.g. non-state partners) or in areas of fragility where, by definition, robust evidence is hard to collect." (3744993.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.what_how: "SIEF will consist of three pillars: Pillar 1: Calls for proposals for prospective and rigorous impact evaluations [...] Pillar 2: Capacity building on impact evaluation methods [...] Pillar 3: Dissemination and knowledge sharing." (3744993.odt, Business Case)
quote.tradeoffs: "The activities will be open to all development partners, and SIEF will fund all costs associated with the workshops including participant travel and subsistence costs." (3744993.odt, Pillar 2)
quote.risk_management: "Proposals that pass a technical peer review will have access to the first tranche of funding in the budget. Additional funds will be transferred based on achievement of subsequent milestones." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

key_programme_risks: Limited evidence on the impact of impact evaluations themselves (uncertainty about whether findings will lead to policy changes).
Risk of low uptake of evaluation findings by policymakers (despite dissemination efforts).
Challenges in collecting robust data in fragile states and LICs (affecting evaluation quality).
Potential for evaluations to focus on "easier" interventions rather than the most strategic or innovative ones.
Transaction costs for grantees (e.g., complex World Bank procedures) deterring Southern researchers.
Risk of over-reliance on a single partner (World Bank) limiting diversity of approaches.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dissemination strategy includes targeted policy workshops, synthesis papers, and engagement with stakeholders at multiple levels (country, cluster, programme).
Prioritize evaluations with feasible methodologies (e.g., quasi-experimental designs where RCTs are not possible) and provide seed funding for pilot data collection.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Exclusion of Southern researchers due to resource constraints.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Fund all workshop costs (travel, subsistence) and provide seed funding for proposal development.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Misalignment between World Bank and DFID priorities.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Steering Committee with DFID representation finalizes cluster priorities and monitors alignment.
Technical review process prioritizes innovative, high-impact questions (e.g., multisectoral nutrition interventions, private school models).

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile states, **community-driven service delivery models** (e.g., for water/sanitation) may be more sustainable than government-led approaches (highlighted in the WASH cluster).
Evaluations in FCAS require **flexible methodologies** (e.g., mixed methods) to account for weak data infrastructure, as noted in the constraints section.
**Local ownership** is critical for sustainability; SIEF requires evaluations to include local researchers and interact with national datasets.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Spanish Trust Fund for Impact Evaluation** (World Bank) demonstrated that: 1) **Thematic clustering** of evaluations builds communities of practice and improves policy relevance. 2) **Training workshops** (2,000+ participants trained) significantly increase local capacity to design/manage evaluations. 3) **Milestone-based funding** reduces risks of non-delivery. SIEF adopts all three approaches.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Based on the Spanish Trust Fund’s experience, SIEF: 1) Uses a **two-stage funding process** (seed funding → technical review) to avoid locking up funds in non-viable proposals. 2) Explicitly includes **cost-effectiveness analysis** in all evaluations (a gap identified in earlier work). 3) Expands capacity-building to **regional and country-specific workshops** (beyond the Spanish Fund’s global training).

quote.risks: "There is limited evidence that impact is or will be feasible and achievable during the life of this project. [...] Influencing policy through research and evaluation takes a longer time horizon than the duration of the programme." (3744993.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.mitigations: "All impact evaluations will be required to develop an outreach/dissemination plan at proposal stage, which must include (at minimum) publication of research findings (final report), a short policy note and a dissemination workshop for in-country stakeholders." (3744993.odt, Pillar 3)
quote.lessons: "DFID’s support to the international objectives of ‘more’ and ‘better’ impact evaluations is well aligned with what Spanish Trust Fund has provided in the past in terms of strategic impact evaluations structured around clear policy questions and innovative approaches to building a stronger evidence base." (3744993.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.design_changes: "SIEF will consider a broad range of evaluation questions ranging from effectiveness and efficacy to implementation and long-term impacts, as well as multi-site or multi-country studies." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The World Bank’s existing infrastructure (e.g., technical review processes, training platforms) is leveraged, reducing setup costs. The document notes that other donors may add funds to SIEF’s thematic windows, but no specific co-funding amounts are mentioned.

quote.allocation: "Pillar 1: 62% of funds [...] Pillar 2: 13% of funds [...] Pillar 3: 15% of funds." (3744993.odt, Business Case)
quote.leverage: "Other donors may also add funds to these windows or add additional windows over the life of SIEF." (3744993.odt, Pillar 1)

It also includes a financing mechanism through the World Bank trust funds and direct support to government institutions.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme supports efficient, accountable and responsive delivery of public services through the modernisation of the Government’s Public Financial Management (PFM) systems and strengthening institutional capacity. (59863179.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to modernize Myanmar's PFM systems to improve public service delivery, increase transparency, and strengthen accountability. It focuses on tax administration, budget planning, and extractive industries governance, with recent adaptations to support COVID-19 economic recovery.
what_objectives.quote: The programme supports efficient, accountable and responsive delivery of public services through the modernisation of the Government’s Public Financial Management (PFM) systems and strengthening institutional capacity. (59863179.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Myanmar is characterized by ongoing ethnic conflicts, weak institutions, and a history of political instability. The programme explicitly mentions the peace process and ethnic armed groups as key contextual factors.
where_context.q5_source: The peace process is attempting to move from ceasefire areas to a political dialogue process addressing the root grievances of the ethnic groups. (4288104.odt, A. Context and need for a DFID intervention)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The peace process and fiscal decentralization negotiations create uncertainty. Weak PFM systems and low capacity impede service delivery. Political transitions (e.g., 2015 elections) affect reform momentum. Limited transparency and accountability mechanisms constrain progress.
where_context.quote: The peace process is attempting to move from ceasefire areas to a political dialogue process addressing the root grievances of the ethnic groups. Prioritised amongst these are the requirements for decentralisation and revenue sharing from natural resources in the ethnic areas. (4288104.odt, A. Context and need for a DFID intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank and DFID retain primary decision-making authority, with Myanmar government institutions (e.g., Ministry of Planning, Finance and Industry) as implementing partners. The programme is designed and overseen by Northern institutions, with Southern partners primarily in execution roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: Establishment of a PFM Academy (training civil servants)
Embedded advisors in Ministry of Planning, Finance and Industry
Technical assistance to State & Region governments
Support to Auditor General’s office and parliamentary committees
Mentorship through The Asia Foundation’s subnational programmes

partner_organizations.role: Subnational PFM and social accountability (AISR project)

partner_organizations.role: Parliamentary oversight and budget scrutiny

who_partners.quote: The proposed intervention would support the first phase of government’s PFM Reform strategy... co-financed by the WB who would provide IDA resources of $30 million (£19m) over 5 years, with Australia also considering funding. (4288104.odt, Component 1. The Public Finance Management Modernisation Programme)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses grants to the World Bank’s Multi-Donor Trust Fund (for PFM modernisation), direct grants to NGOs (The Asia Foundation, International IDEA), and contracts for technical advisors (e.g., strategic tax adviser). The World Bank acts as a financial intermediary for most components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank’s Myanmar Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) serves as the primary platform, with DFID as a key donor. The MDTF has a steering committee (with DFID representation) and an Institutional Strengthening Window for operational decisions. DFID retains oversight through quarterly reports and direct engagement with task teams.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its existing leadership in the PFM Sector Working Group, established relationship with the Myanmar government, and ability to leverage co-financing from other donors (e.g., Australia). The Asia Foundation and International IDEA were chosen based on their long-term presence and technical expertise in Myanmar.
how_mechanism.quote: A partnership between the UK and the WB is well placed to play a leading role in PFM in Burma... Working in partnership with the WB builds on this good coordination; it leverages the central position the WB has built up already as chair of the SWG and through its relationship with government. (4288104.odt, B. What are the costs and benefits of each feasible option?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The MDTF steering committee includes DFID, the Myanmar government, and other donors. Operational decisions for the Institutional Strengthening Window are made by donors and the World Bank, with quarterly reporting to DFID. The EITI Multi-Stakeholder Group (MSG) makes decisions for the EITI component.
how_governance.quote: The MDTF steering committee... makes overarching strategic decisions and receives a report biannually. The Institutional Strengthening Window... submits a quarterly implementation report to donors. (47410464.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with DFID approval, as demonstrated by the 2019 restructure to focus on subnational authorities and the 2020 COVID-19 response extension. The Strategic Support Fund allows adaptive use of resources for emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes mid-term reviews (e.g., 2018 evaluation) and explicit adaptive management mechanisms, such as the programme-funded DFID Economic Adviser role to support ‘adaptivemanagementframework’ development. The Theory of Change was revised in 2020 to incorporate COVID-19 response priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: The addendum would use existing governance structures which DFID has been central in reforming... We must also continue to focus on long term reform... It will be important to sustain our support in order to ensure a rapid economic bounce back. (59863179.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank MDTF (or direct partners like The Asia Foundation) → Myanmar government institutions. For EITI: FCDO → World Bank → EITI Multi-Stakeholder Group.
how_efficiency.quote: Funding under this window is expected to be disbursed in the 2020/21 and 2021/22 financial years upon evidence around advance of need. (59863179.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (continue sector-level engagement only)
UK-designed package independent of the World Bank
Funding only a subset of interventions (e.g., excluding social accountability or extractives)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank partnership was chosen for its existing coordination role in the PFM Sector Working Group, ability to leverage co-financing, and reduced transaction costs. The mixed delivery structure (World Bank + NGOs + direct advisors) allows for both technical depth (e.g., tax administration) and political engagement (e.g., parliamentary oversight).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on World Bank systems may limit Myanmar government ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded advisors (e.g., in MoPFI) and capacity-building components (e.g., PFM Academy) to transition skills to local institutions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex multi-donor coordination could slow decision-making
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Established governance structures (MDTF steering committee) and DFID’s central role in donor coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political transitions (e.g., elections) may disrupt reform momentum
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible programme design with adaptive management mechanisms (e.g., mid-term reviews, Strategic Support Fund).

why_rationale.quote: A partnership between the UK and the WB is well placed to play a leading role in PFM in Burma... Working in partnership with the WB builds on this good coordination; it leverages the central position the WB has built up already as chair of the SWG and through its relationship with government; and is efficient in terms of implementation costs. (4288104.odt, B. What are the costs and benefits of each feasible option?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with existing in-country presence and conflict sensitivity (e.g., The Asia Foundation’s long-term engagement in ethnic states). Political economy constraints require partners with government trust (e.g., World Bank’s role as SWG co-chair).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with experience in ethnic conflict areas (e.g., The Asia Foundation’s work in all 14 States/Regions)
Requirement for fiduciary assurance due to weak institutions (hence World Bank’s central role)
Limited local CSO capacity necessitates international NGO support (e.g., International IDEA for parliamentary oversight)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for whole-of-government PFM reform (not sector-specific) requires a multilateral platform (World Bank MDTF). Subnational focus (e.g., DAO support) necessitates partners with decentralized networks (The Asia Foundation). Extractives transparency demands a multi-stakeholder mechanism (EITI MSG).
q28_linkages: Whole-of-government PFM reform → Multilateral delivery (World Bank MDTF)
Subnational decentralization → Localized partners (The Asia Foundation’s AISR project)
Extractives governance → Multi-stakeholder oversight (EITI MSG)
COVID-19 response → Adaptive funding windows (IFI Grant Window)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging World Bank systems for fiduciary assurance) with equity (e.g., targeted support to ethnic states through The Asia Foundation). Speed of reform is traded off against inclusive engagement, as seen in the phased rollout of tax self-assessment systems.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: World Bank systems ensure efficiency but may reduce local ownership
Direct support to ethnic states (e.g., DAOs) increases inclusion but raises transaction costs
Embedded advisors (e.g., tax office) improve capacity but require long-term commitment
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (e.g., ethnic conflicts, military interests) increases oversight intensity (quarterly MDTF reports) and necessitates adaptive management structures (e.g., Strategic Support Fund).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Low local capacity (e.g., ‘Burmese government faces pervasive capacity constraints’) justifies the central role of international partners (World Bank, ODI) in technical areas, while capacity-building components (PFM Academy) aim to transition skills locally.
intersections.quote: The Burmese government faces pervasive capacity constraints, which in the absence of dedicated support... are likely to worsen... To enhance capacity in a sustainable way, the default option in programme implementation will be to build capacity of existing government staff. (4288104.odt, E. For each feasible option, what is the assessment of local capacity?)

key_programme_risks: Government commitment to reform may wane (e.g., post-2015 elections)
Capacity constraints in line ministries could bottleneck implementation
Extractives sector transparency may reveal politically sensitive interests (e.g., military-linked companies)
COVID-19 economic impact could derail fiscal stability
Ethnic conflicts may disrupt subnational reform rollout
Donor coordination challenges in multi-partner structures

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible programme design with adaptive management (e.g., mid-term reviews) and high-level political engagement (e.g., Ministry of Finance leadership in PFM-ERT).
PFM Academy for sustainable skills development and embedded advisors (e.g., Large Taxpayer Office support).
Multi-stakeholder EITI process to balance transparency with political realities.
IFI COVID-19 Grant Window to shape recovery lending and Strategic Support Fund for adaptive responses.

fcas_specific_lessons: PFM reforms in post-conflict contexts require sequencing aligned with peace processes (e.g., fiscal decentralization tied to ethnic negotiations).
Social accountability must be context-adapted, with slower progress expected in ethnic states.
Donor coordination platforms (e.g., PFM Sector Working Group) are critical in FCAS to avoid parallel systems.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2018 evaluation highlighted the need for adaptive management and sustained subnational engagement. The MSSP programme’s success in DAO governance reforms informed the AISR project design. EITI progress demonstrated the value of multi-stakeholder processes in sensitive sectors.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2019 restructure refocused on subnational authorities based on MSSP lessons. The 2020 COVID-19 extension added adaptive funding windows (IFI Grant Window, Strategic Support Fund) and a programme-funded Economic Adviser role for coordination.
risks_lessons.quote: A 2018 external evaluation of the PFM programme showed that this programme remained relevant to delivering PFM reform, the decentralisation agenda and improved extractives governance. The evaluation suggested strengthening the adaptive management processes of the programme in line with best practice. (59863179.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID’s £4.25m IFI COVID-19 Grant Window is expected to shape £1-2 billion in international finance, achieving a leverage ratio of 250:1 to 350:1. World Bank co-financing for PFM modernisation ($30m) leverages DFID’s £12m contribution.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes capital investments (e.g., PFM Academy facilities, IT systems like ITAS and CBS) alongside revenue support (e.g., technical assistance, advisor salaries).
financial_details.quote: DFID is providing £20m over five years (2014-2019)... The total cost of the first component is £35m ($55 million), of which DFID is contributing £12m, and the cost of the other two components combined is £8 million. (4288104.odt, B. What are the costs and benefits of each feasible option?)

metadata.programme_name: Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan (CSFP) - 2024-2025 Corporate Plan

quote.mission: "The Commonwealth Scholarship Commission in the UK (CSC) provides the main UK government scholarship scheme led by international development objectives." (D0005183.odt, Section 1)
quote.duration: "CorporatePlan2024-2025" (D0005183.odt, Title)

metadata.duration_source: "CorporatePlan2024-2025" (D0005183.odt, Title)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The CSC operates a scholarship and fellowship scheme that combines capacity building (training future leaders), research support (development-focused studies), and policy influence (aligning with UK international development priorities). It functions as both a financing mechanism (channeling funds to scholars) and a service delivery platform (providing educational opportunities).
what_objectives.q1_source: "By attracting individuals with outstanding talent and identifiable potential to become leaders and innovators on returning to their home countries, the CSC’s work combines sustainable development with the UK national interest." (D0005183.odt, Section 1)

q3_expected_outputs.output: scholarships and fellowships awarded
alumni profiles published
evaluation case studies
partnership funding
q3_expected_outputs.target: £4.5 million annually

q3_expected_outputs.output: gender balance
q3_expected_outputs.target: at least 45% female and 45% male candidates

what_objectives.summary: The CSC delivers a world-class scholarship programme that supports sustainable development across the Commonwealth by funding high-potential individuals to study in the UK, with a focus on equity, inclusion, and development impact.

quote.objectives: "The CSC’s objectives are: To provide an innovative world-class scholarship and fellowship scheme that delivers impact on sustainable development across the Commonwealth; To ensure that our programmes promote equity and inclusion, reward merit, and deliver widespread access, especially to those from disadvantaged backgrounds and underrepresented groups; To support and encourage cutting-edge research, innovation, and knowledge exchange throughout the Commonwealth." (D0005183.odt, Section 4)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in both stable and fragile contexts (including conflict-affected states), but has robust risk management frameworks and mitigation strategies in place. The CSC explicitly mentions working in "fragile and conflict-affected states" but does not classify the overall programme as high-risk.
where_context.q5_source: "High-quality graduates from Least Developed and middle-income countries (including fragile and conflict-affected states)..." (D0005183.odt, Appendix 2, multiple instances)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Fragile and conflict-affected states limit mobility for scholars, requiring alternative delivery models like Distance Learning and Split-site Scholarships. Climate risks are embedded as a cross-cutting priority, affecting programme design.

quote.fragility: "including fragile and conflict-affected states" (D0005183.odt, Appendix 2, repeated)
quote.climate: "To embed the cross-cutting priority issues of climate change and global health across the CSC’s communications, engagement, alumni, and evaluation programming" (D0005183.odt, Section 5)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The CSC (UK-based) makes all final selection decisions for scholarships and fellowships, though nominating agencies in Commonwealth countries identify candidates. UK universities and the British Council/ACU (both UK-based) manage operational delivery.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (Master’s/PhD programmes)
mentorship (Leaders for Sustainable Development programme)
institutional strengthening (collaboration between UK and Commonwealth universities)
professional fellowships (mid-career skills enhancement)
alumni engagement (post-award support and networking)

partner_organizations.role: lead sponsor and funder

partner_organizations.role: Secretariat and management functions
