quote.structure: "The CSC has no employees, contracting out its Secretariat and other management functions to two external bodies: The Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) and the British Council." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)
quote.decision_power: "the Act legislates that the Secretary of State may not give any direction for the selection or rejection of any particular person for an award or as a candidate for an award." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The CSC uses **block funding** from FCDO/DfE (core grant-in-aid) combined with **partnership agreements** (co-funding from UK universities and other stakeholders). Scholarships are awarded through a **competitive selection process** managed by the CSC, with funds disbursed to successful candidates via host universities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The CSC acts as a fund manager, overseeing scholarship allocations but outsourcing day-to-day administration to the ACU and British Council. UK universities deliver the actual education/training, while the CSC retains control over selection, monitoring, and strategic direction.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UK universities are directly engaged based on their capacity to host scholars and contribute co-funding (tuition waivers). Nominating agencies in Commonwealth countries are pre-selected based on their role in national education systems. The CSC does not run open competitions for partners but works with established institutions.

quote.instrument: "The CSC’s annual income and expenditure are incorporated in the overall accounts of FCDO, and the CSC account is held with the Government Banking Service." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)
quote.structure: "The CSC has no employees, contracting out its Secretariat and other management functions to two external bodies: The Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) and the British Council." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Commission** (15 members, including Chair) meets three times per year and is supported by specialist committees (Finance, Audit and Risk Management, Awards Policy, Evaluation and Monitoring). The **Audit and Risk Management Committee** reports directly to the Commission. Selection committees (comprising Commissioners) make final award decisions.

quote.governance: "The full Commission meets three times per year. It is supported in its work by specialist Committees, made up of Commissioners, which deal with Finance, Audit and Risk Management, Awards Policy, and Evaluation and Monitoring... Separate Committees of Commissioners are convened to handle the selection of scholarship recipients." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)
quote.oversight: "The CSC operates an Evaluation and Monitoring Programme which provides evidence of the impact of its work, through interviews and surveys of alumni and other stakeholders. The results of this programme influence the CSC’s decision-making processes." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The CSC reviews award types and nominations annually based on strategic priorities, allowing for adjustments in allocations across programmes/countries. However, reallocation requires Commission approval and is tied to evidence of impact.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The CSC embeds cross-cutting priorities (e.g., climate change) and can launch **Time-Limited Programmes** (e.g., 2024 theme: 'Entrepreneurship, Innovation and Job Creation') in response to emerging challenges. Adjustments are based on annual reviews of strategic priorities.

quote.reallocation: "Look forward, be dynamic and responsive by continuing to offer ‘Time Limited Programmes’ and reviewing award types and nomination allocations on an annual basis based on strategic priorities." (D0005183.odt, Section 4)
quote.adaptive: "To embed the cross-cutting priority issues of climate change and global health across the CSC’s communications, engagement, alumni, and evaluation programming" (D0005183.odt, Section 5)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → CSC (Commission/Secretariat via ACU/British Council) → UK universities → scholars

quote.budget: "Total Grant-in-aid to CSC: £28,676,000" (D0005183.odt, Appendix 4)
quote.overhead: "Efficient and streamlined administration is a critical element in our current strategy, which commits the CSC to ensure that its administrative costs do not account for more than 10% of total expenditure." (D0005183.odt, Section 6)
quote.layers: "The CSC has no employees, contracting out its Secretariat and other management functions to two external bodies: The Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) and the British Council." (D0005183.odt, Section 2)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The CSC’s delivery model was chosen for its **proven track record** (65 years of operation), **alignment with UK international development priorities**, and **ability to leverage partnerships** (UK universities, Commonwealth governments). The use of external Secretariat (ACU/British Council) ensures **cost efficiency** while maintaining **independent decision-making** (as legislated by the 1959 Act).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on UK universities for co-funding (tuition waivers) may limit programme scalability if contributions decline.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversify funding sources (e.g., HMG departments, external partnerships) and negotiate fee caps (e.g., £18,000 max for tuition).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex multi-layered governance (CSC → ACU/British Council → universities) could slow decision-making.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Streamlined administration (max 10% overhead) and annual budget reviews to ensure efficiency.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Equity goals (45% gender balance, disadvantaged backgrounds) may conflict with merit-based selection in some contexts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust selection criteria that consider personal circumstances alongside academic excellence, with transparent monitoring.

quote.rationale: "The CSC uses rigorous procedures to ensure that its programmes promote equity and inclusion, reward merit, and deliver widespread access, especially to those from disadvantaged backgrounds." (D0005183.odt, Section 1)
quote.vfm: "In everything we do, we aim to be... Efficient and accountable – by ensuring that our work delivers value for money, is effectively and proportionately reviewed, and that emerging findings are used in our future planning." (D0005183.odt, Section 1)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country scope (including fragile/conflict-affected states) necessitates **local nominating agencies** (rather than direct CSC recruitment) to identify candidates, given security/access constraints. Distance Learning and Split-site Scholarships were introduced to overcome mobility barriers in high-risk contexts.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict/fragility limits in-person study → requires Distance Learning/Split-site options.
Weak institutions in some countries → reliance on UK universities for quality assurance.
Data limitations → partner with local agencies for candidate identification.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **development-focused objectives** (e.g., SDG alignment, equity) shape the **delivery structure** by requiring: (1) **decentralized nomination** (via local agencies) to ensure reach; (2) **co-funding partnerships** (with UK universities) to maximize resources; and (3) **flexible award types** (e.g., Split-site, Distance Learning) to adapt to contextual constraints.
q28_linkages: Equity goals → decentralized nomination process (local agencies identify disadvantaged candidates).
Research impact focus → partnerships with UK universities for academic rigor.
SDG alignment → cross-cutting themes (climate, health) embedded in all programmes.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The CSC explicitly balances **equity** (e.g., 45% gender targets, support for disadvantaged backgrounds) with **efficiency** (e.g., 10% overhead cap, competitive co-funding). Trade-offs include: (1) **higher administrative costs** for monitoring equity outcomes; (2) **longer selection processes** to ensure inclusive reach; and (3) **limited scalability** in high-risk contexts due to safety/access constraints.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Transparent nomination processes slow selection but ensure fairness.
Cost vs. reach: Distance Learning Scholarships increase access but require additional IT/infrastructure support.
Expertise vs. ownership: UK universities provide academic rigor but may limit Southern institutional leadership.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (including fragile states) leads to **milestone-based oversight** (e.g., annual reviews, Audit and Risk Management Committee) and **flexible delivery models** (e.g., Split-site Scholarships to mitigate mobility risks).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives (e.g., Leaders for Sustainable Development programme) are **embedded in partner roles**: UK universities deliver training, while local nominating agencies identify high-potential candidates, ensuring skills transfer aligns with national priorities.

quote.constraints: "Strengthening resilience and response to crises" (D0005183.odt, Section 4, development theme) → "Distance Learning Scholarships... provide vital opportunities for online study to Scholars otherwise unable to benefit from a mobility Scholarship." (D0005183.odt, Section 5)
quote.tradeoffs: "Attract diverse talent to UK higher education institutions by considering personal circumstances in all applications to ensure that, all other things being equal, candidates from disadvantaged, marginalised or underrepresented backgrounds are chosen." (D0005183.odt, Section 4)

key_programme_risks: Reduction in co-funding from UK universities (affecting programme scale).
Geopolitical instability in Commonwealth countries (disrupting scholar mobility).
Failure to meet equity targets (e.g., gender balance, disadvantaged backgrounds).
Administrative inefficiencies due to multi-layered governance.
Reputation risk if development impact is not demonstrably achieved.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversify income sources (e.g., DfE contributions, external partnerships) and negotiate long-term fee agreements (e.g., 20% tuition waivers).
Expand Distance Learning and Split-site Scholarships; monitor country risks via Audit and Risk Management Committee.
Enhance outreach to underrepresented groups; provide additional support for disadvantaged applicants (e.g., application guidance, hardship funds).
Cap overhead at 10%; conduct annual reviews of administrative fees; benchmark against comparable schemes.
Strengthen Evaluation and Monitoring Programme; publish case studies and alumni profiles to demonstrate outcomes.

fcas_specific_lessons: Split-site and Distance Learning Scholarships are critical for **fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)** to ensure continuity of education.
Local nominating agencies in FCAS require additional support (e.g., training on transparent selection) to mitigate corruption risks.
Flexible award durations (e.g., 12-month Split-site periods) accommodate disruptions in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The CSC has learned that **co-funding models** (e.g., Shared Scholarships with UK universities) enhance sustainability, while **alumni engagement** (e.g., publishing impact profiles) strengthens long-term development outcomes. The 2023 audit of selection processes led to improved transparency in nominating agency practices.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Increased focus on **Distance Learning Scholarships** (from 205 awards in 2023/24 to 220 in 2024/25) to improve access.
Introduction of **Time-Limited Programmes** (e.g., 2024 theme on Entrepreneurship) to respond to emerging challenges.
Enhanced **alumni tracking** (e.g., 100+ profiles published) to better demonstrate impact.

quote.risks: "The CSC operates a risk management framework that overarches the full programme cycle and joins up risk management activity at Commissioner and Secretariat levels." (D0005183.odt, Section 7)
quote.lessons: "Innovations such as Shared Scholarships (jointly funded by UK universities), Distance Learning Scholarships, and Split-site Scholarships have facilitated this cost effectiveness." (D0005183.odt, Section 3)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The CSC mobilizes £4.5 million annually in matching contributions from UK universities (via tuition fee waivers and caps) and additional in-kind support (e.g., host contributions for Professional Fellowships).

quote.budget: "Total Grant-in-aid to CSC: £28,676,000" (D0005183.odt, Appendix 4)
quote.leverage: "Partnerships with UK universities will generate at least £4.5 million annually in matching contributions." (D0005183.odt, Section 5, KPIs)
quote.overhead: "commitment to ensure that its administrative costs do not account for more than 10% of total expenditure." (D0005183.odt, Section 6)

metadata.programme_name: UK Collaborative on Development Research (UKCDR)
metadata.quote: "UKCDR has a mission to amplify the value and impact of research for global development by promoting coherence, collaboration and joint action among UK funders." (D0005152.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Start 01/04/13 End 30/09/2025" (D0005152.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: UKCDR serves as a coherence mechanism for ODA-funded research across HMG departments, promoting collaboration, mapping research investments, and providing strategic coordination. It combines evidence generation (research mapping), policy influence (coherence mechanisms), capacity building (strengthening partnerships), and financing mechanism (coordinating ODA research funds).
what_objectives.q1_source: "UKCDR has a mission to amplify the value and impact of research for global development by promoting coherence, collaboration and joint action among UK funders. It covers a series of areas to map and make publicly accessible all UK ODA R&D and global COVID research, publish and promote good practice guidance, identify funding gaps and opportunities, better communicate the substantial and wide-ranging impacts of UK development research and support and report to the Strategic Coherence of ODA-funded Research (SCOR) Board." (D0005152.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Enhanced quality and usefulness of data on development research (MODARI database)
Climate Research Tracker development
Convening International Research for Development Funders Forum (IRDFF)
Reports on UK Secondary Benefits, Equitable Partnerships, and Funding Mechanisms
Completion of paper on continued funding for research in international development
Continuation of Funders Groups for information exchange and learning
International engagement at SSUNGA and Science Granting Councils Initiative meetings
Initiation of two new projects aligned with SCOR steers
Weekly newsflows and blog publications
what_objectives.summary: UKCDR acts as a strategic coordination platform to maximize the impact of UK ODA-funded research by ensuring coherence across government departments, mapping research investments, and promoting good practice in international development research.
what_objectives.quote: "The total DFID funding of phase 3 of UKCDR will be £2,111,935 from FY2017/18 to FY2021/22... The key objective of DFID’s cost and time extension under this addendum is to allow UKCDR to evolve and become a fit-for-purpose coherence mechanism that meets the core needs key HMG funders of science and research for international development." (15237653.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme focuses on coordination and coherence of ODA research funds without direct implementation in fragile contexts. Funds are managed through UK-based institutions with established systems.
where_context.q5_source: "This is a low risk programme. Funds are used to build coherence across HMG ODA-research programmes. No funds go through non-UK suppliers or to countries affected by conflict or fragility." (15237653.odt, Compliance with the Terrorism Act)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates within UK regulatory frameworks and relies on data availability from multiple government departments, which can affect the comprehensiveness of research mapping and coordination efforts.
where_context.quote: "The UKCDR is a non-entity, non-statutory, joint-venture; and is a collaborative of 14 UK Government departments and UK research funders and aims to maximise the impact of UK research investments on international development outcomes." (4189574.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The SCOR Board, composed of senior representatives from UK government departments and research funders, holds decision-making authority. Southern partners are engaged through research collaborations but do not have governance roles in UKCDR.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening capacity and building effective equitable partnerships with Southern research communities
Supporting more UK researchers working with developing country scientists
Improving research capacity in developing countries through member interventions

who_partners.quote: "UKCDR is a small organisation funded by FCDO, Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), United Kingdom Research and Innovation (UKRI) and the Wellcome Trust. Leaders of these organisations sit on the independently chaired SCOR Board which provides high level advice of xHMG ODA R&D and Wellcome Trust coherence." (D0005152.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: UKCDR operates through core funding contributions from multiple UK government departments and research funders, pooled to support the Secretariat's coordination and coherence activities. This allows for shared decision-making and collective action among funders.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UKCDR functions as a neutral platform with a small Secretariat that facilitates collaboration among 14+ UK government departments and research funders. The Strategic Coherence of ODA-funded Research (SCOR) Board provides high-level governance, while the UKCDR Officials Group manages operational decisions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UKCDR was established as a direct response to parliamentary recommendations (2006 House of Commons Science and Technology Committee) and has evolved through successive government endorsements. Its unique role as a cross-HMG coherence mechanism makes competition impractical.
how_mechanism.quote: "UKCDR is a unique organisation. There are no direct comparators or ‘competitors’; it is difficult – in the short-term impractical – either to outsource activities efficiently to other organisations or to ‘insource’ work by employing additional staff within government departments." (D0005152.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The SCOR Board is composed of senior representatives (Director/CEO/CSA-level) from FCDO, DSIT, DHSC, UKRI, and Wellcome Trust. It provides strategic oversight, while the UKCDR Officials Group (representatives from funding organizations) manages operational decisions. The Board is chaired by an independent Chairperson who reports to the Directors General for Policy in FCDO and DSIT.
how_governance.quote: "The SCOR Board will be a senior (Director, CEO, CSA-level) group made up of the budget holders who are the senior responsible owners and decision-makers for each major HMG ODA fund for science and research for development... The Board will be chaired by senior, independent Chairperson that reports to the DGs for Policy in DFID and BEIS." (15237653.odt, Establishment of a HMG Strategic Coherence of ODA-funded Research (SCOR) Board)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval from the SCOR Board and FCDO, as evidenced by the 2024/25 budget adjustments to account for inflation and changing priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme demonstrates adaptive management through regular reviews (e.g., SCOR Board reviews at year 2 and year 3 of Phase 3) and adjustments based on member needs. New projects can be initiated with SCOR Board approval, as seen with the two new projects planned for 2024/25.
how_flexibility.quote: "An independent evaluation of Phase 3 of UKCDR will be undertaken at year 3 (FY2019/20). This evaluation will be used by SCOR Board members to determine if Phase 3 remains fit-for-purpose and effective before agreeing to fund the final 2-years." (15237653.odt, Monitoring and Evaluation of Phase 3 of UKCDR)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UKCDR Secretariat (hosted by Wellcome Trust, employed by UKRI) → Research communities/implementers
how_efficiency.quote: "UKCDR Officials Group (representatives of funding organisations) has agreed to increase the total UKCDR budget from £712,000 to £753,500 in 2024/25... FCDO's contribution to core funding... was £292,000 and again for FY23/24 FCDO's contribution was for up to £292,000." (D0005152.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Delivery through another mechanism (rejected as impractical due to UKCDR's unique role and established membership)
Outsourcing activities to other organisations (rejected as inefficient)
Insourcing work by employing additional staff within government departments (rejected as impractical)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: UKCDR was chosen because it provides a unique, established platform for cross-HMG coordination of ODA research funds with proven value for money. Its neutral, non-statutory status enables effective collaboration among 14+ government departments and research funders, which would be difficult to replicate through alternative mechanisms. The platform approach leverages in-kind contributions (e.g., Wellcome Trust hosting) and shared funding to maximize impact.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of staffing capacity due to surges (e.g., Ukraine/Russia, Israel/Gaza roles)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funded extension to provide assurance to UKCDR staff and maintain operational continuity

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential withdrawal of members due to changing priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Account management system to ensure activities remain relevant to all members, with regular Board reviews

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Bureaucracy of collaboration slowing decision-making
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly officials meetings and Board Champions to maintain strategic focus

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Differing objectives among member organizations reducing willingness to collaborate
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified workstream portfolio reflecting multiple members' interests, with regular engagement

why_rationale.quote: "UKCDR is a unique organisation. There are no direct comparators or ‘competitors’; it is difficult – in the short-term impractical – either to outsource activities efficiently to other organisations or to ‘insource’ work by employing additional staff within government departments. All current funders recognise this and committed to an 18-month extension." (D0005152.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and UK-based coordination structure limit direct Southern partner involvement in governance, though the programme actively engages Southern research communities in collaborative projects and capacity-building initiatives.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory requirements for ODA compliance limit funding flows to non-UK entities
Need for cross-HMG coordination requires UK-based secretariat and governance
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for cross-government coherence in ODA research funding determines the platform-based delivery structure, as this enables neutral coordination among multiple funders with diverse priorities. The strategic long-term approach requires stable governance through the SCOR Board.
q28_linkages: Coherence objective → Platform structure with shared governance
Multi-funder engagement → Neutral secretariat hosted by Wellcome Trust
Policy influence goal → SCOR Board with senior government representatives
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (through UK-based coordination and shared funding) with equity considerations (through capacity-building initiatives and equitable partnerships with Southern researchers). The 2021 independent review confirmed strong performance in both areas.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UK-based governance for efficiency vs. Southern inclusion in decision-making
Shared funding model for cost-effectiveness vs. ensuring equitable resource allocation
Standardized processes for coherence vs. flexibility for diverse research needs
intersections.risk_affects_management: The low-risk profile enables light-touch oversight for routine operations, with intensive reviews reserved for major decisions (e.g., SCOR Board evaluations at years 2 and 3 of Phase 3).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by embedding Southern researchers in collaborative projects and providing training/mentorship, though governance remains Northern-led to ensure ODA compliance and coordination.
intersections.quote: "UKCDR programme does not explicitly target gender equality, though it focuses strongly on equity throughout research organisations and partnerships. Moreover, since 2018 UKCDR has played a lead role in respect of safeguarding in international development research." (D0005152.odt, Due regard to Gender Equality)

Decrease in member financial contributions
Broad remit leading to reduced strategic focus
Changing funder priorities or budget reductions
Reduced political traction for international development research
Differing objectives among member organizations
Competing initiatives reducing member engagement
Competitiveness between members

Key staff changes in member organizations
Inflation increasing operational costs

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular team meetings, minimum 2 months' notice period, and 6-monthly PPDR reviews
Account management system with proactive engagement and workstream reviews
Quarterly officials meetings and Board Champions to maintain focus
Account management and communications to demonstrate value of collaboration

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Loss of staffing capacity due to surges
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Funded extension to provide stability and continuity

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 independent review confirmed strong overall performance and considerable achievement, leading to a refreshed strategy. Lessons included the importance of maintaining neutral coordination, adaptive management through regular reviews, and embedding safeguarding in research partnerships.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 3 incorporated a more structured governance through the SCOR Board, increased funding for the SHED mechanism based on its proven value during emergencies (e.g., Ebola, Zika), and formalized DFID secondments to strengthen ODA research programming in other departments.
risks_lessons.quote: "In 2021 UKCDR commissioned an independent review of its performance... The review confirmed strong overall performance and considerable achievement, leading to a refreshed strategy." (D0005152.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case)

co_funding_partners.partner: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)
Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: In-kind contributions from Wellcome Trust (hosting, IT, meeting rooms) valued at ~£90k/annum and UKRI as employing organization help constrain costs. The platform leverages shared funding across 14+ members to maximize impact.
financial_details.quote: "UKCDR Officials Group... has agreed to increase the total UKCDR budget from £712,000 to £753,500 in 2024/25. This reflects – but does not fully compensate for – significant increases in salary and other costs during a recent period of high inflation. Accommodation and services continue to be provided by Wellcome; UKRI serves as the employing organisation. These inputs help to constrain costs." (D0005152.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Capacity for Economic Research and Policy in Africa (CERPA)
metadata.quote: "The project will start in April 2015 and end in March 2025." (D0007415.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 01/04/15 to 31/03/20" and "New project end date: 31/03/25" (D0007415.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **capacity building** for economic research and policy-making in Africa, with embedded **evidence generation** and **policy influence** components. It supports training of economists (MSc/PhD), research grants for junior/senior researchers, and policy engagement through seminars and publications. The goal is to strengthen African institutions' ability to produce and use economic research for evidence-based policymaking.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DFID will provide up to £14.30 million over five years to support **capacity development** for economic research and policy making in Africa... The project will support African economists to undertake PhD and Masters training... support post-doctorate researchers... and support the development of more senior African researchers through competitive research grants" (5350736.odt, Business Case and Intervention Summary). "The proposed impact of the programme is: **Improved evidence based policy making and investments in Africa**" (5350736.odt, Impact and Outcome).

q3_expected_outputs.output: 1,500+ MSc economics graduates trained (AERC)
110+ PhD students supported (AERC)
300+ developing country researchers supported (PEP)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 80 early-years researchers + 20 senior/Alumni researchers (2020-2025)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 80+ research publications (AERC)
100+ research projects funded (PEP)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 20 research teams (2020-2025)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 500+ economic policymakers trained (AERC)
27 African universities' capacity strengthened (AERC)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 27 (ongoing)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 100+ policy briefs (PEP)
2 Senior Policy Seminars (AERC)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2 per phase

q3_expected_outputs.output: 1 book synthesizing research (PEP)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1 (drawing from PAGE I and II)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Core funding from 15 African governments (AERC)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 15 by 2025 (up from 5 in 2015)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Gender parity in training (40% female participation)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 40% female participation in AERC training (up from 26% baseline)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to build **long-term capacity** for economic research and policy-making in Africa by training economists (MSc/PhD), funding research projects, and strengthening institutions (AERC/PEP). It combines **research production**, **policy engagement**, and **institutional development** to improve evidence-based decision-making in African governments, central banks, and research institutions.
what_objectives.quote: "The project will support African economists to undertake PhD and Masters training in economics across the continent; support post-doctorate researchers in the early stages of their careers, and support the development of more senior African researchers through competitive research grants, helping to establish a core of quality researchers across the continent." (5350736.odt, Business Case and Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **Low-Income Countries (LICs)** with **weak institutional capacity** but is not classified as FCAS. Risks are mitigated by working with established African-led institutions (AERC/PEP) that have strong track records and government linkages. The World Bank's 2013 Competitiveness Report notes "stalled gains in institutional quality" in some African economies, but the programme targets capacity-building to address this.
where_context.q5_source: "While the quality of economic decision making has improved in the continent over the last 10 to 15 years... deeper economic reform and better policies are needed in almost all DFID focus countries if the recent economic gains are not to be lost" (5350736.odt, Strategic Case). "The global competitiveness report concludes that overall the trends confirm Africa’s continuous but gradual improvement in the pillars of the Global Competitive Index (GCI). However, the report notes that while positive, the gains in institutional quality, infrastructure and macroeconomic stability have stalled across a number of African economies since 2010" (5350736.odt, Strategic Case).
q6_contextual_constraints: rapidly changing global economics curriculum standards
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions limit policy uptake of research; underfunding forces reliance on donor support; brain drain reduces retention of trained economists; curriculum gaps require updates to training programmes; gender disparities necessitate targeted scholarships; digital gaps slow adoption of blended learning.
where_context.quote: "Africa Capacity Building Foundation (ACBF) in the recent 2010 report highlights some of the economic and particularly **capacity challenges** for the continent... a trend analysis would underscore the centrality of **capacity as a key covariate of Africa’s development trajectory** over the last six decades, alongside slow and inequitable growth, and poor governance" (5350736.odt, Strategic Case). "The **recent external review** [of AERC] noted that **funding for AERC’s training programme has not kept pace with demand and with the rapidly changing nature of economics courses** provided at the top global universities" (D0007415.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?).

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with **African-led boards** (AERC/PEP Africa). DFID has a non-voting representative on both boards for advisory purposes only. Research agendas are set collaboratively with African policymakers and researchers, with Northern partners (e.g., PEP North America) providing technical support under Southern leadership.
q10_capacity_building_details: MSc/PhD training for African economists (AERC)
post-doctoral research grants with mentorship (PEP)
collaborative research between junior/senior African researchers
curriculum development for African universities
policy engagement training (e.g., PEP’s policy brief requirements)
institutional strengthening (e.g., AERC’s university partnerships)
gender-targeted scholarships and training
digital/blended learning expansion
Alumni tracking and network utilization

who_partners.quote: "AERC is a **leading African-led capacity building organisation** based in Nairobi... It is widely recognised as having been an important element in improving the ability of African Governments to make good economic policy making and growth choices" (5350736.odt, AERC section). "PEP Africa: **Consortium pour la Recherche Economique et Sociale (CRES)**, based in Senegal" (5350736.odt, PEP section). "DFID has a **permanent representative on the board of each institution** helping to represent DFID’s views on the board and helping to share experience and lesson learning across the two institutions" (D0007415.odt, Accountability and monitoring).

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides **core funding** to AERC and PEP to implement their strategic plans, supplemented by a **performance-based incentive tranche** (up to £300K/year per institution) tied to research quality metrics (e.g., publications in top journals). Funds are disbursed annually based on logframe milestones and REF-style quality assessments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: AERC and PEP operate as **independent African-led networks** with their own boards and strategic plans. DFID aligns its funding to these plans but does not manage day-to-day operations. A **DFID representative** sits on both boards in an advisory capacity. Technical support is provided for cross-institution learning (e.g., Alumni tracking).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AERC and PEP were selected based on their **30+ year track records** in African capacity-building, **Southern leadership**, and alignment with DFID’s strategic goals. The 2015 business case notes that both institutions had scored **‘A’ in annual reviews** and were recognized as **‘leading African-led’** organizations with unrivaled policy convening power.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID will provide **core funding** for each institution related to the logframe... The **performance tranche** will be linked to indicators of ‘quality research’... The funding for this will be as follows: **£300K per institution per year** (from year two) for high-quality outputs" (5350736.odt, Funding section). "The **preferred option** is direct support to AERC and PEP through a **joint programme**... Both institutions have been successful having scored **A’s during annual reviews**" (5350736.odt, Appraisal Case).

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Both AERC and PEP have **independent boards** with majority African representation. DFID has a **non-voting representative** on each board. Research sub-awards (e.g., PEP grants) are allocated via **competitive calls** assessed by peer review. AERC’s collaborative research uses a **proposal-based selection** with cost feasibility as a criterion.
how_governance.quote: "Both AERC and PEP submit **regular reports on expenditure** with their accounts audited by external auditors. **No issues** have been identified during the programme. Both institutions have **well-functioning boards** providing clear oversight to their programmes, finances and activities. DFID has representatives on both boards" (D0007415.odt, Accountability and monitoring). "AERC uses a **competitive process** for procuring research considering costs as part of this competitive assessment. This is in line with best practice and consistent with UK research councils" (D0007415.odt, Value for Money).

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated **within institutional logframes** (e.g., AERC shifting between training/research components) but require **board approval**. The performance tranche allows for additional resources if quality targets are met. Major reallocations between AERC/PEP would require DFID approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research themes can evolve (e.g., PEP’s 2020-2025 focus on climate employment impacts was added post-2015). Adjustments require **board sign-off** and alignment with DFID’s strategic objectives. The **incentive tranche** allows for adaptive improvements in quality.
how_flexibility.quote: "The **logframes will identify key output and outcome deliverables** for each institution. DFID will provide core funding for each institution related to the logframe" (5350736.odt, The programme approach). "PEP’s new strategic plan includes themes like **the employment impacts of climate change**, which was not a focus in 2015" (D0007415.odt, Component 2 – support to PEP).

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → AERC/PEP → (1) African universities/researchers or (2) policymakers. No additional intermediaries.
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID will provide **core funding** for each institution related to the logframe... **All the components will contribute to common Impact and Output statements**" (5350736.odt, The programme approach). "PEP has a **well-established system to monitor** the progress and administrative follow-up on all research grants... All grant payments are tied to the satisfactory delivery of outputs" (D0007415.odt, Value for Money).

q24_alternatives_considered: Counterfactual (no support to AERC/PEP)
Separate programmes for AERC and PEP
Joint programme for AERC and PEP (preferred option)
Funding through third parties: African Development Bank (AfDB), World Bank (WB), or Global Development Network (GDN)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen:
The **joint programme** was selected for **value for money (VFM)**, **reduced transaction costs**, and **synergies** between AERC/PEP. Key reasons:
1. **Proven track record**: Both institutions had scored ‘A’ in annual reviews.
2. **Southern leadership**: AERC/PEP are African-led with strong policy links.
3. **Catalytic effect**: DFID’s support leverages additional funding (e.g., AfDB, IDRC).
4. **Efficiency**: Joint monitoring framework reduces administrative burden.
5. **Quality focus**: Performance tranche incentivizes high-impact research.

Third-party options (AfDB/WB/GDN) were rejected due to **higher overheads** (e.g., GDN’s 13% fee), **less direct engagement**, and **uncertainty** (e.g., GDN’s future post-World Bank cuts).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on DFID funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: AERC/PEP are diversifying funding sources (e.g., African governments, AfDB, IDRC). AERC’s Central Bank Governors Forum raised $1M/year by 2020.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Quality variability in research outputs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Performance tranche (£300K/year) tied to REF-style quality assessments and publication in top journals.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited policy uptake of research
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: PEP requires policymaker involvement in research teams; AERC convenes Senior Policy Seminars with ministers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Brain drain of trained economists
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Training conducted in Africa with regional university partnerships to retain talent.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Currency/financial instability in Africa
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Core funding in GBP with local currency management by partners.

why_rationale.quote: "**Option 3 (joint programme) is the preferred option**. We set out below how the preferred option will work and provide a rating of the evidence that underpins it... **Direct support is the most appropriate option** with a combined programme significantly reducing DFID’s transaction costs and exploiting some economies of scale" (5350736.odt, Appraisal Case). "The **CERPA programme combining support to AERC and PEP still represents good value for money**. It is more cost effective to bring resource persons to the continent in order to upgrade the MSc and PhD programmes and to support research capacity building than take the students to Europe" (D0007415.odt, Value for Money).

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who:
The **African context** constrains partner selection to institutions with:
1. **Local legitimacy**: Must be African-led to ensure policy uptake (e.g., AERC’s alumni in governments).
2. **Regional reach**: Need pan-African networks to address continent-wide capacity gaps.
3. **Language/cultural alignment**: Training in local languages and contexts (e.g., AERC’s university partnerships).
4. **FCAS adaptability**: Experience operating in fragile settings (e.g., PEP’s work in LICs).

**Northern partners** (e.g., PEP North America) are limited to **technical support roles** due to context constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for African-led institutions to ensure policy relevance
Requirement for pan-African networks to reach multiple LICs
Language/cultural barriers favor local trainers
Weak local funding necessitates donor support but demands Southern ownership
Brain drain risks require in-continent training models
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
**Capacity-building objectives** shape the delivery structure through:
1. **Network model**: AERC/PEP’s pan-African networks enable continent-wide training and research collaboration.
2. **Mentorship layers**: Junior researchers paired with seniors (PEP) and students with global academics (AERC).
3. **Policy linkages**: Research teams must include policymakers (PEP requirement).
4. **Quality incentives**: Performance tranche tied to publication outputs.
5. **Institutional strengthening**: Core funding for AERC/PEP to develop internal systems (e.g., financial audits, Alumni tracking).
q28_linkages: Network structure (AERC/PEP) → enables pan-African reach for training/research
Mentorship requirements → build research capacity while ensuring quality
Policy engagement rules → ensure research uptake by governments
Performance incentives → align partner goals with DFID’s quality focus
Core funding → allows institutional development (e.g., AERC’s private sector partnerships)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
**Explicit trade-offs discussed**:
1. **Cost vs. quality**: Training in Africa is cheaper but requires curriculum upgrades to match global standards.
   - *Mitigation*: DFID funds AERC’s curriculum review and digital learning expansion.
2. **Speed vs. inclusion**: Competitive grants (PEP) ensure quality but may exclude weaker institutions.
   - *Mitigation*: AERC’s university partnerships build broader capacity.
3. **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: PEP’s global network provides mentorship but is led by African hub (CRES).
   - *Mitigation*: Southern researchers lead projects; Northern partners provide technical support.
4. **Gender equity vs. meritocracy**: Female participation targets (40%) require additional scholarships.
   - *Mitigation*: AERC provides extra grants to female researchers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Training in Africa (lower cost) vs. global standards (requires investment)
Competitive grants (higher quality) vs. inclusive access (risk of exclusion)
Global mentorship (expertise) vs. local leadership (ownership)
Gender targets (equity) vs. merit-based selection (efficiency)
intersections.risk_affects_management:
Higher risk context (LICs/weak institutions) → **more intensive oversight** via:
- Annual audits and board reporting.
- DFID representative on boards.
- Milestone-based funding releases.
- Performance tranche tied to quality outputs.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity-building objectives **define partner roles**:
- **AERC**: Focuses on **training and institutional strengthening** (university partnerships, curriculum development).
- **PEP**: Specializes in **post-doctoral mentorship and policy engagement** (grants + policymaker links).
- **DFID**: Provides **core funding + quality incentives** (not day-to-day management).
- **African governments**: Co-finance and **policy uptake** (e.g., Central Bank Governors Forum).
intersections.quote: "**Capacity building requires a long term commitment** and as such tends to be underfunded as the results are beyond the planning horizons of many donors... DFID’s commitment to fund ‘evidence for policy making’ positions us well to play a leading role in supporting long term economic capacity development" (5350736.odt, Business Case and Intervention Summary). "The **PEP ‘model’ complements the work of AERC** by providing a scheme to mentor junior post doctorate researchers through a competitive research grant process... PEP therefore provides the key ‘bridging’ mechanism by which economics graduates can apply for research grants" (5350736.odt, PEP section).

key_programme_risks: Underfunding of capacity-building due to long-term horizons (donor fatigue)
Brain drain of trained economists leaving Africa
Limited policy uptake of research findings
Quality variability in research outputs
Over-reliance on DFID funding (sustainability risk)
Currency/inflation risks in African economies
Gender disparities in economics training
Digital infrastructure gaps for online learning
Political instability in some African countries

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID’s long-term commitment (10 years) and performance incentives. AERC/PEP diversifying funding (e.g., African governments, AfDB, IDRC).
In-continent training (AERC’s university partnerships) and policy engagement (PEP’s government links).
PEP requires policymakers in research teams; AERC convenes Senior Policy Seminars with ministers.
Performance tranche (£300K/year) tied to REF-style quality assessments and top-journal publications.
AERC’s Central Bank Governors Forum raised $1M/year by 2020; PEP expanding partnerships (IDRC, World Bank).
AERC targets 40% female participation (up from 26%) via additional scholarships; PEP includes gender analysis training.
AERC investing in digitization and blended learning (2020-2025 plan).

fcas_specific_lessons: Long-term funding is critical in FCAS contexts where institutional capacity is weak (ACBF 2010 report).
Local ownership mitigates political risks (AERC’s African-led model).
Policy engagement must be embedded early (PEP’s requirement for policymakers in research teams).
Regional networks (AERC/PEP) help navigate country-specific fragility.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
1. **AERC (1988-2015)**: Alumni network is critical for policy impact (e.g., Central Bank Governors, Ministers).
   - *Change*: 2020-2025 plan includes **Alumni tracking system** and expanded visiting scholars programme.

2. **PEP (PAGE I)**: Early-career researchers need bridging to top-tier journals.
   - *Change*: 2020-2025 adds **Senior Research Programme** for Alumni to publish in top journals.

3. **Training gaps**: Curriculum not keeping pace with global standards.
   - *Change*: 2020-2025 includes **curriculum review** and **digitization**.

4. **Gender**: Female participation was 26% at baseline.
   - *Change*: Target increased to **40%** with additional scholarships.

5. **Policy engagement**: PAGE I had 33% direct policy impact.
   - *Change*: PAGE II requires **policymaker in every research team**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **AERC training upgrade**: Added curriculum review, digitization, and blended learning (2020-2025).
2. **PEP Alumni programme**: New Senior Research Programme to bridge gap to top journals.
3. **Gender targets**: Increased female participation goals (26% → 40%) with scholarships.
4. **Policy linkages**: PAGE II mandates policymaker involvement in all research teams.
5. **Private sector engagement**: AERC to expand partnerships with African businesses.
6. **Institutional strengthening**: Core funding for AERC/PEP to develop financial systems and Alumni networks.
risks_lessons.quote: "**Lessons from ACBF’s interventions** (2010): ‘Netting out the transitory effects of the ongoing global financial crisis... a trend analysis would underscore the **centrality of capacity as a key covariate of Africa’s development trajectory**’" (5350736.odt, Strategic Case). "**Independent review recommendations** [for AERC]: - Review of the curricula and assess whether it is keeping up with world frontier standards; - Speed up digitization and blended learning" (D0007415.odt, What are the expected results?).

co_funding_partners.partner: Central Bank Governors Forum (15 African central banks)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: AERC’s total 2015-2020 budget was $86.5M, with DFID contributing ~12.9% (£7M max). By 2020, AERC secured **$1M/year from African central banks** (up from $0 in 2015) and aims for **15 government funders by 2025** (up from 5 in 2015). PEP leveraged IDRC co-funding for PAGE II.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Primarily revenue (training/research grants), with minor capital for institutional systems (e.g., AERC’s Alumni tracking database).
financial_details.quote: "AERC funding support during 2015-20 is projected from the following main sources: ‘traditional’ core supporters (e.g. DFID, DANIDA, SIDA, NORAD, World Bank) – **70%** of total support; African governments – **17%**; New funders – 7%; Private sector – 1%" (5350736.odt, Funding section). "AERC has established a **Central Bank Governors Forum** in 2015 with a focus on raising resources for their MSc and PhD programmes. The Forum has increased funding allocations from zero to over **$1m/year in 2020**" (D0007415.odt, Component 1 – Support to AERC).

metadata.programme_name: J-PAL Post-Primary Education Initiative (Phase II) / Learning for All Initiative (LAI)
metadata.quote: "The Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) is a global research centre, anchored by a network of more than 220 education researchers at universities around the world, working to reduce poverty by ensuring that policy is informed by scientific evidence." (D0003933.odt, Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 30th January 2014 – 30th March 2023" and "New project end date: 30th March 2027" (D0003933.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through rigorous randomized control trials (RCTs) to identify "what works" in education interventions. It also includes **implementation research** (testing/scaling interventions), **policy influence** (disseminating findings to policymakers), and **capacity building** (training researchers and strengthening Southern research institutions).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The purpose of this FCDO partnership with J-PAL is to provide funding for research that rigorously tests the impact and cost-effectiveness of education interventions in low- and middle-income countries." (D0003933.odt, Information)
q3_expected_outputs: At least 68 RCTs in post-primary education (20 full-scale + 14 pilots in Phase I; 19 full-scale + 15 pilots in Phase II)
51 pilot research projects (£1.275m, £25k avg) and 29 full RCTs (£3.625m, £125k avg) in LAI phase
Scale-focused projects (adaptations: £60k; policy pilots: £160k; scale projects: £245k)
Policy briefs, evidence summaries, and synthesis papers (e.g., gender-focused analyses, cost-effectiveness reviews)
African Scholars Programme (proposal development: £8k; pilot RCTs: £60k)
Training for 600,000 adolescents annually via gender-sensitization curriculum (Punjab, India)
Reach 566,659 students in Peru via scaled returns-to-education programme
60 million children reached by Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) interventions (India/Africa)
10% of budget (£700k–£1m) for research management; 20% for evidence synthesis/dissemination
what_objectives.summary: The programme generates rigorous evidence on cost-effective education interventions (primary/secondary/vocational) through RCTs, scales successful models via government partnerships, and synthesizes findings into policy-relevant products. It expands to include climate-education nexus and foundational literacy/numeracy, with explicit focus on gender equity and Southern research capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "Research and research synthesis under the business case cost-extension will be focussed under three thematic areas...: Girls’ Education, Foundational Skills, Climate & Education." (D0003933.odt, Annex A)

countries_regions: India (Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in diverse contexts including FCAS (e.g., Iraq, Sierra Leone) and stable LMICs (e.g., India, Peru). Risks are mitigated through J-PAL’s affiliate vetting, ethical review boards, and government partnerships. The overall risk rating is "minor" per J-PAL’s risk matrix, but moderate due to multi-country complexity.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk rating of the programme is minor." (29395967.odt, Annex C) && "Personal risk to researchers... Bidders... require research to go through internal ethical review boards." (29395967.odt, Risk)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (e.g., teacher absenteeism in Madhya Pradesh)
political economy (e.g., gender norms limiting girls’ education in Bangladesh/India)
climate risks (e.g., flooding disrupting schools in Sub-Saharan Africa)
data limitations (e.g., lack of cost-effectiveness data in education policy)
regulatory (e.g., ethical approvals for RCTs in multiple countries)
conflict (e.g., operations in post-conflict Sierra Leone)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Gender norms in South Asia limit girls’ school participation (e.g., 22% reduction in child marriage via incentives in Bangladesh). Climate shocks disrupt 40M children’s education annually. Weak governance in Madhya Pradesh required adaptive follow-ups to improve pedagogy reforms.
where_context.quote: "Girls’ risk of early marriage and pregnancy increases in times of crisis as families... use negative coping mechanisms to survive." (D0003933.odt, Annex A) && "One of the key preliminary findings... was that there was no effect of the program on key indicators like teacher absenteeism." (29395967.odt, Annex A)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: J-PAL (MIT-anchored) leads research commissioning, proposal selection, and fund allocation. Southern partners (e.g., Pratham, IPA country offices) implement projects but require J-PAL affiliate status (vetted by Northern Executive Committee) to access funding. Government partners (e.g., Zambia Ministry of Education) co-design interventions but rely on J-PAL for technical leadership.
q10_capacity_building_details: African Scholars Programme (£160k): proposal development grants (£8k) and pilot RCTs (£60k)
Matchmaking conferences to pair Southern researchers with J-PAL affiliates
Technical training for government partners (e.g., Zambia Ministry of Education on negotiation skills curriculum)
Co-authorship requirements: 46% of Phase I papers included women; 9% Southern authors (target to increase)
Executive Education courses for FCDO officials and Southern researchers

partner_organizations.role: Lead research commissioning, fund management, and quality assurance

partner_organizations.name: Innovations for Poverty Action (IPA) country offices
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of RCTs in project countries

partner_organizations.name: Pratham

partner_organizations.role: Gender-sensitization curriculum (India)

partner_organizations.role: Curriculum integration (negotiation skills, sexuality education)

partner_organizations.role: Gender-sensitization curriculum rollout (6,250 schools)
