partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (foundational learning)

partner_organizations.name: King Philanthropies
partner_organizations.role: Funds King Climate Action Initiative (K-CAI)

who_partners.quote: "J-PAL’s network of country offices limits the amount of travel... When travel is necessary, J-PAL requires travel in economy class, modest accommodation..." (29395967.odt, Value for Money) && "The base of researchers from the Global South has already expanded threefold over the duration of PPE initiative." (D0003933.odt, Inclusion)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO provides core funding to J-PAL via an **Accountable Grant** (updated iteratively via addendums). J-PAL then re-grants funds to affiliates through **competitive research calls** (twice annually). Sub-grants require FCDO approval for DFID-priority countries. The mechanism combines block funding (for J-PAL operations) with project-specific grants (for RCTs).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: J-PAL acts as a **global platform** with regional offices (South Asia, Africa, LAC) and thematic initiatives (LAI, IGI, K-CAI). FCDO has a seat on the bi-annual research moderation board but delegates day-to-day management to J-PAL. Southern partners (e.g., IPA country offices) implement projects under J-PAL’s technical oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not stated (but "number of J-PAL affiliated researchers doubled in Phase I (from 72 to 143)")
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners must be J-PAL affiliates (vetted for RCT expertise) or "special invitees" nominated by affiliates. This ensures methodological rigor but limits Southern researcher access unless they collaborate with Northern affiliates. Government partners are selected based on alignment with FCDO priorities (e.g., girls’ education in Punjab).
how_mechanism.quote: "Bids are chosen by a selection board made up of high profile researchers and academics in addition to a DFID representative." (29395967.odt, Implementation) && "To be considered for affiliation, candidates must be nominated by other J-PAL affiliates and approved by J-PAL’s Executive Committee." (D0003933.odt, Inclusion)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Bi-annual **Research Moderation Board** includes J-PAL senior researchers, donor reps (FCDO on rotation), and technical advisors (e.g., FCDO Climate/Education Advisors for climate-education proposals). FCDO has **ultimate say** over sub-grants using UK funding. J-PAL’s Executive Committee (Northern-led) vets affiliate nominations.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO will have a representative on the J-PAL twice-yearly research round moderation boards and will have ultimate say over funding decisions related to subgrants using FCDO-funding." (D0003933.odt, Approach to Implementation) && "Grantholders will initially be required to respond to a ‘start up’ survey three months after they are awarded funding." (29395967.odt, Monitoring)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can shift between research themes (e.g., climate-education added in LAI) but require FCDO approval for major changes. Flexible funding pots (e.g., £100k for dissemination in Phase II) allow adaptive use. No-cost extensions require detailed justification.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research calls are adjusted based on emerging evidence (e.g., climate-education added post-Covid). Thematic focus shifts (e.g., from post-primary to primary/pre-primary in LAI) require FCDO sign-off. "Flex funding" (£130k in Phase II) supports unplanned policy uptake opportunities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The cost extension will enable the programme to work in a flexible and agile manner to commission and facilitate products, insights and partnerships." (D0003933.odt, Approach to Implementation) && "J-PAL has introduced close monitoring techniques to ensure that projects adhere to their initial timings." (29395967.odt, Risk)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → J-PAL Global (MIT) → [J-PAL Regional Offices/IPA Country Offices] → End Researchers/Implementers
how_efficiency.quote: "J-PAL will invoice DFID quarterly in arrears. They will also pay grantholders in arrears unless the grantholder has specified that they would be unable to undertake the research without some payment in advance." (29395967.odt, Financial Changes) && "10% of the programme funding will be allocated to indirect costs." (29395967.odt, Value for Money)

q24_alternatives_considered: New separate business case for Youth Initiative (rejected to "keep administration and management costs low")
Direct funding to multiple J-PAL initiatives (IGI, K-CAI) instead of LAI umbrella (rejected to ensure cross-sectoral synergy)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **platform model** (J-PAL as fund manager) was chosen for: 1) **Value for Money**: Leverages J-PAL’s existing affiliate network (760 researchers) and regional offices to minimize overhead (10% indirect costs). 2) **Risk Mitigation**: J-PAL’s rigorous affiliate vetting and ethical review processes reduce research quality risks. 3) **Flexibility**: Bi-annual research calls allow adaptive prioritization (e.g., adding climate-education post-Covid). 4) **Scaling Potential**: Government partnerships (52% of projects) enable policy uptake (e.g., TaRL reaching 60M children). 5) **Equity**: African Scholars Programme and gender-disaggregated data requirements address Southern inclusion.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (10% indirect costs; £125k avg per RCT vs £1m–£5m in health sector)
risk-mitigation (affiliate vetting; ethical reviews; government partnerships)
experience (J-PAL’s Nobel Prize in Economics; 64 full projects delivered)
partner-capacity (760 researchers; regional offices in Africa/Asia/LAC)
speed (quarterly invoicing; pre-payments for urgent projects)
equity (46% women authors; 9% Southern authors; African Scholars Programme)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Northern dominance in decision-making
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: African Scholars Programme (£160k) and target for Southern Co-PIs; Executive Committee promotes diversity in affiliate nominations.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on J-PAL’s affiliate network limiting Southern access
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: "Special invitees" mechanism (21 in Phase I) and matchmaking conferences to integrate non-traditional partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in government-led scale-ups (e.g., Madhya Pradesh pedagogy reforms)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close monitoring of timelines; no-cost extensions require detailed justification and updated budgets.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low response rate to research calls (e.g., Round 4 elicited few proposals)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: J-PAL uses regional offices and IPA country networks to "match" researchers with high-potential opportunities.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (indirect costs at 10%; staff paid below market rates)
efficiency (£125k avg per RCT; 34 evaluations in Phase II)
effectiveness (% of studies with policy impact; citations in World Bank reports)
equity (% Southern authors; gender-disaggregated data requirements)
why_rationale.quote: "An alternative option would be to utilise this cost-expansion for direct funding to two or more of these initiatives [IGI, K-CAI]. These objectives will be agreed at proposal stage and monitored through indicators in the FCDO Logframe." (D0003933.odt, Approach to Implementation) && "The smart solution is to extend the current PPE programme with JPAL to include youth and employment related issues." (8331604.odt, Objective)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts (e.g., Sierra Leone, Iraq) limit partner selection to organizations with existing in-country presence (e.g., IPA offices, Pratham). Gender norms in South Asia require local NGOs (e.g., Breakthrough) to implement sensitive interventions (e.g., gender-sensitization). Climate vulnerability in Sub-Saharan Africa necessitates partnerships with disaster-resilient institutions (e.g., government education ministries).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Sierra Leone → reliance on IPA’s established networks
Gender norms in India → Breakthrough NGO selected for school-based programmes
Weak governance in Madhya Pradesh → J-PAL’s process monitoring to track teacher absenteeism
Climate risks in Africa → K-CAI’s adaptive capacity focus in research calls
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **generalizable policy lessons** (e.g., TaRL’s scalability) drives the **platform structure** (J-PAL’s regional offices + thematic initiatives). **Government uptake requirements** (e.g., Zambia’s curriculum integration) necessitate **joint committees** (FCDO + J-PAL moderation boards). **Climate-education nexus** adds **cross-initiative collaboration** (LAI + K-CAI).
q28_linkages: Generalizable evidence → Platform model (J-PAL’s 760 affiliates)
Policy influence → Joint governance (FCDO on moderation boards)
Scaling focus → Government partnerships (52% of projects)
Climate focus → Cross-initiative funding (LAI + K-CAI)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions between **Northern efficiency** (J-PAL’s centralized management; 10% overhead) and **Southern equity** (only 9% Southern authors in Phase I). Trade-offs addressed via: 1) African Scholars Programme (£160k), 2) "special invitee" mechanism for Southern researchers, 3) Co-PI targets for Southern leadership. **Speed vs. inclusion**: Competitive calls favor established affiliates (Northern bias), but matchmaking conferences aim to onboard Southern researchers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Centralized management (efficient) vs. Southern ownership (equitable)
Affiliate vetting (quality control) vs. barriers for Southern researchers
Rapid scaling (e.g., TaRL) vs. context-specific adaptation needs
Northern-led synthesis (e.g., "Smart Buys" report) vs. Southern-authored papers (9%)
intersections.risk_affects_management: High-risk contexts (e.g., FCAS) increase oversight intensity (e.g., quarterly reports for Iraq projects). Moderate-risk settings (e.g., India) allow milestone-based monitoring. Climate-vulnerable regions (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa) trigger additional K-CAI technical reviews.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Southern partners with strong implementation capacity (e.g., Pratham, IPA) receive direct sub-grants, while those needing support (e.g., African Scholars) access proposal development funds. Government partners with high absorption capacity (e.g., Punjab) co-design interventions, while fragile states (e.g., Sierra Leone) rely on J-PAL for technical leadership.
intersections.quote: "The base of researchers from the Global South has already expanded threefold over the duration of PPE initiative... However, only 9% [of papers] were authored or co-authored by a researcher from a Southern institution." (D0003933.odt, Inclusion) && "J-PAL’s network of country offices limits the amount of travel... ensuring that a substantial portion of funds trickle down to organisations in the project country." (29395967.odt, Value for Money)

key_programme_risks: Poor quality research (mitigated via affiliate vetting and DFID representation on selection board)
Low response rate to research calls (mitigated via regional office outreach)
Personal risk to researchers (mitigated via ethical review boards)
Projects going off-track (mitigated via 3-month start-up surveys and no-cost extension justifications)
Northern dominance in authorship (mitigated via African Scholars Programme)
Government delays in scale-ups (mitigated via process monitoring, e.g., Madhya Pradesh follow-ups)
Climate shocks disrupting fieldwork (mitigated via K-CAI’s adaptive research designs)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: African Scholars Programme (£160k); targets for Southern Co-PIs; Executive Committee diversity requirements.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in government-led scaling (e.g., Shaala Sidhi in Madhya Pradesh)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Process monitoring data shared with government partners; adaptive follow-up schedules.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low Southern author representation (9% in Phase I)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Disaggregated data requirements; co-authorship incentives; proposal development grants for African researchers.
K-CAI’s focus on resilience metrics; cross-sectoral research with climate scientists.

fcas_specific_lessons: In Sierra Leone, IPA’s existing networks enabled rapid post-conflict research deployment.
In Iraq, quarterly reporting (vs. annual) was introduced due to security volatility.
Ethical review boards in FCAS contexts added layers of local approval to mitigate personal risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase I lessons led to: 1) **Start-up surveys** (3-month check-ins to flag delays early), 2) **Flex funding** (£130k for unplanned dissemination), 3) **Gender mainstreaming** (all projects now require gender-disaggregated data), 4) **Government co-design** (52% of projects now have government partners vs. 38% in Phase I).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **climate-education theme** post-Covid; expanded from post-primary to **primary/pre-primary** in LAI; introduced **replication studies** to test generalizability; increased **Southern researcher targets** (from 9% to ambitious new goals).
risks_lessons.quote: "As a result of DFID suggestions in Annual Reviews, J-PAL now require grantholders to report to them more regularly... This innovation has been so successful that it has now been rolled out to the other J-PAL Initiatives." (29395967.odt, Monitoring) && "The programme will also allow J-PAL to begin to fill evidence gaps around the ability of education systems to successfully adapt and become more resilient to the increasing likelihood of climate related disruption." (D0003933.odt, Objective)

co_funding_partners.partner: Douglas J. Marshall, Jr. Family Foundation

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £10 million in co-funding from 31 organizations (e.g., USAID, International Growth Center). Projects funded with FCDO funds attracted additional co-financing of US$12.95m and £686k. Five co-funding organizations received all/majority of their funding from FCDO, demonstrating catalytic effect.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue-focused: 70% to sub-grants (research/pilots/scale projects), 20% to evidence synthesis/dissemination, 10% to management. No capital expenditures mentioned.
financial_details.quote: "FCDO’s investment forms 44% of the total PPE funding... PPE funding has also been catalytic in allowing research at scale by crowding in additional resources." (D0003933.odt, Catalytic Effects) && "Roughly 70% [of £7m] will be spent on sub-grants generating research, 20% on evidence synthesis, dissemination and capacity building and 10% spent on management costs." (D0003933.odt, Additional Support)

metadata.programme_name: FCDO-ESRC Joint Research Fund on Raising Learning Outcomes (RLO)
metadata.quote: "Raising Learning Outcomes (RLO) is a joint programme between FCDO and ESRC to fund a portfolio of research on critical policy areas that currently constrain education systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) from translating resources into better learning." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 02/2014-03/2025", "New project end date (if applicable): 03/2025-12/2032" (D0006484.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through rigorous research on what works to raise learning outcomes, with a strong emphasis on **policy influence** by ensuring decision-makers access and understand the evidence. It also includes **capacity building** through equitable partnerships with Southern researchers and **implementation research** by embedding studies within government systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The aim of RLO is to provide policymakers and practitioners with concrete ideas on how to improve learning and understanding of how these ideas will translate to their specific context and institutions, and to demonstrably inform relevant policy and programme decisions." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 176+ journal articles, books, or book chapters (86% cited in other publications)
430+ conference abstracts, talks, or similar events
160+ non-academic outputs to reach policy and practitioner stakeholders
9 case studies evidencing demonstrable impact on policy or practice
Rigorous primary research that reaches academic and non-academic audiences
Data collection for secondary analysis, including longitudinal research on education
Synthesis products on key themes (e.g., teacher effectiveness)
Capacity building activities benefitting Southern researchers (90% of RLO1 grants reported such activities)
Detailed gender analysis in 50%+ of projects
what_objectives.summary: RLO generates rigorous evidence on "what works" to improve teaching and learning outcomes in LMICs, with a focus on teacher effectiveness, equity (especially gender and disability), and scalability. It bridges research and policy by embedding studies in government systems and ensuring uptake through dedicated impact support functions.
what_objectives.quote: "RLO2 will provide a valuable contribution to the UK government’s vision to see transformed education systems providing quality teaching and learning outcomes, as stated in the Development White Paper that received cross-party support." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in LMICs with challenging education contexts (e.g., high teacher absenteeism, weak accountability systems) but is not explicitly focused on FCAS or high-risk environments. The emphasis on government systems and political economy considerations suggests moderate risk.
where_context.q5_source: "Education systems are failing to deliver learning outcomes despite increasing investments... This suggests that many education systems cannot translate resources into learning effectively." (4221301.odt, Intervention Summary)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (education systems unable to translate resources into learning)
data limitations (scarce internationally comparable learning outcome data)
implementation challenges (scaling from NGO pilots to government systems)
cultural/social factors (how context interacts with reforms)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy factors (e.g., teacher union resistance) have blocked successful interventions from scaling (e.g., contract teachers in Kenya worked in NGOs but failed in government schools). Weak institutional capacity limits the ability to use evidence, and data scarcity hampers measurement of outcomes. Cultural contexts require adaptations to interventions.
where_context.quote: "A recent replication of an RCT of contract teachers in NGO schools in Kenya found identical positive effects in NGO schools but zero effect in government schools due to resistance from teacher unions." (4221301.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is jointly managed by FCDO and ESRC, with a mixed commissioning panel including academic experts, users, and practitioners from both Northern and Southern perspectives. Southern researchers co-lead 41% of funded awards, and the 30% cost cap for international co-leads is waived to enable more resources for Southern partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: 90% of RLO1 grants included capacity-building activities for Southern researchers
Small grants (up to £250k) target new researchers in the UK and partner countries
Equitable partnerships with Global South institutions (41% of RLO1 funding to Southern institutions)
Mentorship and training embedded in research projects
Programme-level support for Southern engagement and synthesis

partner_organizations.name: Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead delivery partner; responsible for research commissioning, grant management, and programme oversight

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder and strategic oversight; joint management with ESRC

partner_organizations.name: Institute of Development Studies (IDS) and University of Cambridge’s REAL Centre
partner_organizations.role: Impact Initiative for International Development Research (RLO1); support for research uptake and impact

partner_organizations.name: Global South research institutions (various)
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead or partner on 41% of funded awards; primary researchers in LMIC contexts

partner_organizations.name: Programme Research Lead (PRL)
partner_organizations.role: Builds collaboration and synergy across projects (RLO1)

partner_organizations.name: Overseas Development Institute (ODI)
partner_organizations.role: Programme-level communication and impact activities (mentioned in 4221301.odt)

who_partners.quote: "41% of funding awarded under RLO1 was to Southern institutions, and 90% of grants reported capacity-building activities benefitting Southern researchers." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)** between FCDO and ESRC to govern the joint funding arrangement. Research awards are disbursed as **grants** through open competitive calls managed by ESRC, with varying sizes (small: £250k; medium: £350k–£1M; large: up to £1M).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ESRC acts as the platform manager, responsible for delivering the programme (including research commissioning and grant management) on behalf of both funders. FCDO and ESRC jointly oversee programme support functions and strategic direction. A mixed commissioning panel (academics, users, practitioners) assesses proposals for rigour and policy relevance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition ensures high-quality, policy-relevant research and aligns with ESRC’s "gold standard" peer-review processes. The mixed panel (including practitioners) guarantees proposals are both academically rigorous and operationally feasible.
how_mechanism.quote: "ESRC is responsible for delivery of the programme, including leading on the commissioning and management of research awards, on behalf of both funders... Bids will be assessed by a mixed panel comprising both academic experts, users and practitioners." (D0006484.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is governed through joint FCDO-ESRC oversight, with ESRC handling day-to-day delivery. A mixed commissioning panel (academics + practitioners) assesses grant applications. The Impact Initiative and Programme Research Lead (RLO1) provided additional governance for synthesis and uptake, which will be replaced by a new support function in RLO2.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO and ESRC provide operational management of the programme and oversee delivery of programme support functions... The support function will deliver activities to support the existing conceptual and impact objectives of the programme." (D0006484.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between grant calls based on proposal quality (e.g., "If there were a number of suitable larger bids in the first call, the initial allocation could be increased"). However, the overall budget envelope is fixed, and reallocation requires joint FCDO-ESRC agreement.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research topics can evolve based on consultations with stakeholders (e.g., RLO2’s focus on "teachers and teaching" was refined after RLO1 lessons). However, major shifts require FCDO-ESRC approval, as seen in the delayed launch of RLO2 due to strategic reviews.
how_flexibility.quote: "The selection of research areas for future calls will depend on the response to the first call and further consultation with key stakeholders." (4221301.odt, Future call topics)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ESRC (platform manager) → Research grantees (no additional intermediary layers).
how_efficiency.quote: "A 4% slice of the combined ESRC and FCDO contributions to the programme is levied by ESRC to cover administrative staffing costs, which would not exceed £600K." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" (no DFID/FCDO investment in learning outcomes research
Direct funding of research by DFID/FCDO
Research Programme Consortia (RPCs)
Funding relationships with UK Research Councils (chosen option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Partnering with ESRC was selected for its **value for money**, **rigorous peer-review systems**, **multidisciplinary networks**, and **experience in research uptake**. ESRC’s reputation attracts high-quality proposals, and its existing structures reduce administrative costs for FCDO. The joint model also leverages additional ESRC funds (£10M in RLO2).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage of ESRC funds and reduced admin costs)
risk mitigation (ESRC’s robust selection and management processes)
past experience (successful DFID-ESRC collaborations in poverty/health)
partner capacity (ESRC’s networks and ‘gold standard’ reputation)
equity (ESRC’s waiver of the 30% cost cap for Southern co-leads)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in programme launch due to strategic reviews (e.g., RLO2 paused for ODA reviews and ESRC’s international investment strategy)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination between FCDO and ESRC to realign timelines and retain momentum (e.g., 2024 restart after 2022/23 pauses).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low Southern engagement in early phases (identified in RLO1 evaluation)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Waiver of ESRC’s 30% cost cap for Southern co-leads and explicit focus on equitable partnerships in RLO2 design.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited scalability of research findings (e.g., NGO-led interventions failing in government systems)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedding research within government systems from the design phase and requiring ‘Pathways to Impact’ plans for each project.

why_rationale.quote: "The proposed partnership with the ESRC represents significant value for money for DFID because: The ESRC has a strong appetite for engaging in education systems research and will invest additional resources in this area... ESRC grants are viewed as ‘gold standard’ in the research community, which will drive up the quality of research proposals submitted." (4221301.odt, Why should DFID fund this research?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s global scope and focus on LMICs require partnerships with Southern researchers to ensure contextually relevant evidence. However, weak institutional capacity in some LMICs (noted in RPC experiences) limits the pool of eligible Southern partners, necessitating capacity-building components.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited Southern research capacity (from RPC lessons)
Political economy barriers (e.g., teacher union resistance to reforms)
Data scarcity in LMICs (affects who can conduct rigorous research)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **policy-relevant, scalable evidence** drives the platform structure (ESRC’s open calls + mixed commissioning panel) and the focus on **government-embedded research**. The **interdisciplinary** and **equity** objectives shape the requirement for Southern co-leads and gender-disaggregated analysis.
q28_linkages: Policy relevance → Mixed commissioning panel (practitioners + academics)
Scalability → Embedding research in government systems
Equity focus → 41% funding to Southern institutions and gender analysis requirements
Interdisciplinary needs → Platform model to attract diverse expertise
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., waiving the 30% cost cap for Southern co-leads, 50%+ gender analysis) with efficiency (e.g., leveraging ESRC’s existing systems to reduce admin costs). The RLO1 evaluation highlighted that stronger Southern engagement initially slowed progress but improved long-term impact and relevance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion (delays to ensure Southern partnership)
Cost vs. reach (higher overhead for equitable grants but broader impact)
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership (mixed panels to balance rigour and context)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate-risk LMIC context (e.g., political resistance to teacher reforms) necessitates **milestone-based oversight** and **embedded impact support** to navigate implementation barriers. The RLO1 evaluation led to stronger synthesis and uptake functions in RLO2 to mitigate risks of low policy adoption.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is a **core objective** (not just an add-on), with Southern researchers co-leading 41% of awards and small grants targeting new LMIC researchers. This shifts Southern partners from passive recipients to active decision-makers in research design and delivery.
intersections.quote: "Waiving the 30% cost cap for Southern co-leads allows for more resources to support Southern researchers... 90% of RLO1 grants reported capacity-building activities benefitting Southern researchers." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

key_programme_risks: Low uptake of research findings by policymakers (mitigated by dedicated impact support functions)
Scalability challenges (e.g., NGO successes failing in government systems)
Delays due to strategic reviews (e.g., ODA pauses, ESRC’s international strategy)
Weak Southern engagement in early phases (addressed in RLO2 design)
Data limitations in LMICs (mitigated by secondary data analysis scoping)
Political resistance to teacher reforms (e.g., union opposition to contract teachers)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dedicated impact and synthesis support functions (e.g., Impact Initiative in RLO1, new function in RLO2) to translate findings for policymakers.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Scalability failures (e.g., NGO to government transition)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedding research in government systems from the design phase and requiring ‘Pathways to Impact’ plans.
Close FCDO-ESRC coordination to realign timelines (e.g., RLO2 restart in 2024 after 2022/23 pauses).
Waiver of ESRC’s 30% cost cap for Southern co-leads and explicit equity targets (41% funding to Southern institutions).
Scoping opportunities for secondary data analysis and longitudinal research.

fcas_specific_lessons: Political economy considerations are critical for teacher reforms (e.g., union resistance in Kenya).
Embedding research in government systems improves scalability but requires navigating bureaucratic barriers.
Local ownership (e.g., Southern co-leads) increases relevance but may slow initial progress.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: RLO1’s independent evaluation found that: (1) **Equitable partnerships** improved research relevance but required upfront investment; (2) **Impact support functions** (e.g., Impact Initiative) were key to policy uptake; (3) **Programme-level events** (e.g., annual workshops) strengthened cohort collaboration; (4) **Early-stage support** for researchers enhanced dissemination.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Reduction in RLO2 scale (from 3 to 2 grant calls) to match budget cuts, with proportional adjustments.
Stronger emphasis on **teachers and teaching** based on RLO1 findings and policy demand.
New impact/synthesis support function from the start of RLO2 (vs. mid-programme in RLO1).
Retention of successful elements: mixed commissioning panels, interdisciplinary focus, and gender equity requirements.
risks_lessons.quote: "The independent evaluation of RLO1... provided evidence that RLO1 largely exceeded original objectives. Findings and recommendations... have been collated into actionable next steps for RLO2, including stronger support for impact and synthesis and enhanced Southern engagement." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: ESRC doubled its initial £5M commitment to £10M for RLO2, and the programme attracts high-quality global academics due to ESRC’s reputation.
financial_details.quote: "The delivery mechanism of RLO maximises economy by leveraging the institutional expertise and infrastructure of ESRC. A 4% slice of the combined ESRC and FCDO contributions... is levied by ESRC to cover administrative staffing costs." (D0006484.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Sustainable Urban Economic Development Programme (SUED)
metadata.quote: "SUED will support market-driven growth in emerging towns and cities in Kenya that will ultimately help Kenya to exit from aid as a middle income country." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source: "SUED will provide £75m over 6 years (2016-2022)" (Document: 16865377.odt, "What support will the UK provide?")

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SUED combines financing mechanisms (£75m flexible facility), capacity building (technical assistance to local authorities), implementation research (testing urban economic interventions), and service delivery (infrastructure/value chain projects). The programme aims to catalyze private investment while directly improving urban planning and climate resilience.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SUED will provide £75m over 6 years (2016-2022) to support thriving and inclusive economic development... It will promote market-driven growth in intermediate towns and cities along economic growth corridors, creating trade networks that spur economic development that is resilient to climate change." (Document: 16865377.odt, "What support will the UK provide?")
q3_expected_outputs: Improved economic planning by 6-10 county authorities (£16.5m allocation)
Better business environment reforms in selected urban centres (£10.1m allocation)
Establishment of an Urban Investment Advisory Facility (UIAF) for PPP projects
Climate-resilient infrastructure investments in energy, water, and industrial estates (£23.6m)
Development of high-potential value chains (£17.6m) creating 2m jobs in 500,000 low-income households (water access target)
Technical assistance to county governments for urban economic planning
Public-private dialogue platforms in target corridors
Seed capital for 10-15 bankable urban projects (estimated)
Reduction of climate shock vulnerability by 0.5% of GDP through economic diversification
Support to 2-3 economic corridors (Northern Corridor and LAPSSET initially)
Gender-disaggregated data collection and women's representation (40% on Steering Committee)
what_objectives.summary: SUED aims to transform Kenya's intermediate cities into engines of inclusive, climate-resilient growth by combining infrastructure finance, value chain development, and institutional strengthening. The programme explicitly links urban economic planning with climate adaptation and gender inclusion to reduce poverty and fragility risks.
what_objectives.quote: "SUED will help Kenya’s expanding intermediate towns and cities along key growth corridors to attract more investment for crucial infrastructure and job-intensive value chain projects, ensuring these are inclusive for women and girls and resilient to climate change; and create more jobs and better livelihoods, particularly for young people." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Kenya faces political instability (2017 election cycle), corruption risks in flexible financing, and climate vulnerability (floods/droughts costing 2.4% GDP annually). The programme's 'major' risk rating reflects these compounded challenges in a devolved governance context with weak urban institutions.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall programme risk is rated as major. Kenya faces a threat of political instability, as SUED will be in place over a national and county election cycle in 2017." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Weather shocks are estimated to cost up to 2.4% GDP per year in Kenya" (Document: 16865377.odt, "Sustainable growth requires economic diversification that is climate resilient")
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (county-level urban planning capacity deficits)
regulatory (lack of bankable projects and PPP frameworks)
data limitations (lack of county-level urban economic data)
land tenure (informal settlements like Kibera with 1m+ residents)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak county capacity limits agglomeration economies along corridors, while infrastructure deficits (7.3% growth in intermediate towns vs 4.5% in Nairobi) and coordination failures between public/private sectors prevent investment in job-creating value chains. Climate shocks exacerbate rural-urban migration pressures, and political instability during elections could disrupt devolution processes.
where_context.quote: "County government finance deficits: While devolution decentralises service delivery, without increased county revenue, agglomeration economies along corridors and in centres will not develop." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Cross-sectoral constraints") AND "Public-private coordination failures: There is a lack of trust between the public and private sector. This limits scope for public-private partnerships (PPPs)." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Cross-sectoral constraints")

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID retains strategic oversight and approval authority, with county governments and private sector implementing operational activities under technical assistance. The Urban Investment Advisory Facility (UIAF) will be demand-led but require DFID validation for seed capital disbursements.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to county authorities for urban economic planning (£16.5m)
public-private dialogue training
climate-resilient infrastructure design support
gender-sensitive urban planning requirements
PPP project preparation mentorship
value chain development workshops for SMEs

partner_organizations.name: Government of Kenya (GoK)
partner_organizations.role: primary beneficiary and co-implementer (national/county levels)

partner_organizations.name: County Governments (6-10 selected)
partner_organizations.role: direct implementers of urban economic plans and infrastructure projects

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA)
partner_organizations.role: coordination of urban growth coalitions and investment matching

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM)
partner_organizations.role: value chain development and industrial policy dialogue

partner_organizations.name: Urban Investment Advisory Facility (UIAF) - to be established
partner_organizations.role: PPP project preparation and seed capital allocation

partner_organizations.name: Private sector firms (SMEs and multinationals)
partner_organizations.role: investors in climate-resilient value chains and infrastructure

partner_organizations.name: KenInvest
partner_organizations.role: investment promotion and public-private dialogue

partner_organizations.name: Technical Assistance providers (e.g., Adam Smith International)
partner_organizations.role: capacity building for county authorities

partner_organizations.name: Women's organizations (local)
partner_organizations.role: gender mainstreaming and safe infrastructure design

who_partners.quote: "SUED will work with the public and private sector to improve urban economic planning, business environment reforms, and developing bankable urban investments." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Private sector associations like KEPSA... can play a strong role in coordinating urban growth coalitions." (Document: 16865377.odt, Box 3)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The £75m programme uses a combination of: (1) direct grants for technical assistance to county governments, (2) a flexible Urban Investment Advisory Facility (UIAF) for PPP seed capital, and (3) potential reimbursement mechanisms for climate-resilient infrastructure. The UIAF operates as a demand-led fund manager for public/private projects.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID oversees the programme through a Programme Management Unit (PMU), with the UIAF acting as a semi-autonomous fund manager for infrastructure/value chain investments. County governments and private sector partners implement projects under technical assistance contracts, with KEPSA/KAM coordinating growth coalitions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme targets specific economic corridors (Northern/LAPSSET) and county towns based on growth potential and devolution priorities. Technical assistance providers were likely selected through DFID's existing frameworks (e.g., Adam Smith International), while private sector partners are chosen based on their investment commitments to value chains.
how_mechanism.quote: "The Facility [UIAF] will be flexible, adaptive and demand-led, working with both public and private actors. It will deliver climate-resilient infrastructure and value chain investments." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Main programme activities") AND "SUED will work with the public and private sector to improve urban economic planning..." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes DFID, GoK representatives, county governments, KEPSA/KAM, and at least 40% women. It oversees strategic direction and approves UIAF investments, with technical advisory support from climate/urban experts.
how_governance.quote: "Governance arrangements will ensure women are fairly represented, including at least 40% women on the programme’s Steering Committee." (Document: 16865377.odt, "How can SUED contribute to reducing gender inequality?") AND "The Facility will assist with the project preparation and seed capital for investments that are commercially robust and strategically targeted." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Main programme activities")

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The UIAF allows adaptive allocation between infrastructure/value chain projects based on demand, but requires Steering Committee approval for major reallocations. Technical assistance budgets are fixed by component (e.g., £16.5m for planning).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Political economy analysis is 'hardwired' into activities to enable adaptation to election-related shifts. The UIAF's demand-led design permits reprioritization of value chains/corridors with Steering Committee endorsement.
how_flexibility.quote: "SUED will seek to embed thorough political economy analysis into its intervention design and implementation..." (Document: 16865377.odt, Box 3) AND "The Facility will be flexible, adaptive and demand-led..." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Main programme activities")

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Programme Management Unit (PMU) → Implementing Partners (county governments/private sector/TA providers) → End beneficiaries (urban poor/youth/women)
how_efficiency.quote: "SUED will work with the public and private sector to improve urban economic planning..." (Document: 16865377.odt, Summary Sheet) implies layered implementation. Payment structure inferred from "seed capital for investments that are commercially robust" (Document: 16865377.odt, "Main programme activities").

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct infrastructure financing (rejected due to lack of county absorption capacity)
National-level policy reforms only (rejected as insufficient for local impact)
Focus on primary cities (Nairobi/Mombasa) only (rejected to avoid aggravating regional inequalities)
Pure private sector-led growth (rejected due to market failures in SME access to finance)
Standalone climate adaptation programmes (rejected for missing economic growth linkages)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (flexible UIAF + technical assistance + growth coalitions) was selected to: (1) address Kenya's devolution context by building county capacity while leveraging national systems; (2) mitigate corruption risks through demand-led, transparent PPP processes; (3) combine DFID's strengths in market systems (e.g., MAP programme) with climate finance (ICF); and (4) balance rapid job creation with long-term resilience through integrated corridor/value chain investments.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (political economy analysis and flexible UIAF design)
experience (DFID's prior work with KEPSA/KAM and corridor programmes like TMEA)
partner-capacity (targeting counties with highest growth potential)
equity (40% women on Steering Committee and gender-targeted interventions)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption in flexible UIAF financing
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Zero-tolerance policy with due diligence assessments, regular audits, and spot checks for all partners. Governance controls embedded in PPP project preparation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in corridor/city selection
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Transparency in growth coalition formation and Steering Committee approvals. Political economy analysis integrated into all activities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low county absorption capacity for technical assistance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased rollout starting with 2 corridors/6 cities, coupled with embedded mentorship and 'learning by doing' approaches.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector disengagement due to coordination failures
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: KEPSA/KAM-led public-private dialogue platforms with clear investment promotion strategies and de-risking instruments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks disrupting value chain investments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mandatory climate resilience criteria for all UIAF-funded projects and diversification across sectors (agro-processing, energy, textiles).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per job created in value chains)
effectiveness (jobs and incomes in climate-resilient sectors)
equity (gender/youth targets and ASAL region inclusion)
why_rationale.quote: "DFID’s wide experience in market development tells us that taking a systemic approach to sustainable economic development... ensures longer-term sustainability." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Key strategic choices") AND "SUED will take a climate-sensitive approach to urban economic development, diversifying from climate-dependent rural livelihoods to climate resilient, off-farm livelihoods." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Which type and size of cities and corridors should we target?")

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Kenya's devolution context and weak county capacity limit partner selection to organizations with: (1) existing county government relationships (e.g., KEPSA/KAM); (2) experience in ASAL regions (e.g., climate-resilient infrastructure providers); and (3) ability to navigate political economy risks (e.g., TA providers with corruption safeguards). The focus on intermediate cities excludes partners specialized in megacity informal settlements.
q27_constraints_detail: Devolution transition requires partners with subnational governance expertise
Climate vulnerability necessitates partners with green infrastructure experience
Corruption risks exclude partners without robust compliance systems
Youth unemployment crisis prioritizes partners linked to job-intensive value chains
ASAL region focus limits to partners with arid-zone operational capacity
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for integrated corridor/value chain development drives the mixed delivery structure: (1) UIAF's flexibility addresses the requirement to adapt to diverse city contexts; (2) technical assistance components respond to weak county planning capacity; (3) growth coalitions reflect the necessity for public-private coordination; and (4) gender mainstreaming is embedded across all mechanisms due to women's disproportionate urban poverty.
q28_linkages: Value chain objectives → UIAF's demand-led design for private sector engagement
Climate resilience goals → Technical assistance for green urban planning
Devolution context → Capacity building for county authorities
Youth employment targets → Focus on labour-intensive sectors (textiles, agro-processing)
Gender equity → 40% Steering Committee representation and safe infrastructure criteria
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) Balancing rapid job creation (efficiency) with gender/youth inclusion targets (equity) in value chain selection; (2) Prioritizing high-growth corridors (efficiency) while ensuring ASAL region coverage (equity); and (3) Flexible UIAF processes (efficiency) versus stringent anti-corruption safeguards (equity). The programme mitigates these by setting explicit targets (e.g., 2m water access beneficiaries) and embedding gender experts in technical assistance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Demand-led UIAF may favour established firms over women/youth-led SMEs without proactive targeting
Expertise vs ownership: Northern TA providers bring climate resilience knowledge but risk crowding out local institutions
Cost vs reach: High transaction costs for small-city projects reduce economies of scale compared to Nairobi-focused interventions
Risk vs innovation: Climate-resilient infrastructure requires untested technologies, increasing implementation risks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'major' risk rating drives intensive oversight: (1) election cycles trigger quarterly political economy reviews; (2) corruption risks necessitate embedded auditors in the UIAF; and (3) climate vulnerabilities require real-time monitoring of infrastructure projects. Oversight intensity varies by component—high for financial flows, moderate for technical assistance.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak county capacity shifts partners into mentorship roles (e.g., KEPSA providing 'learning by doing' support) and creates layered implementation (national TA providers → county teams → communities). The UIAF's design as a fund manager reflects the need to compensate for limited municipal project preparation skills.
intersections.quote: "SUED aims to formalise [growth coalitions] in a more transparent and market-driven manner in order to drive balanced growth in these emerging towns and cities that deliver widespread job opportunities..." (Document: 16865377.odt, Box 3) AND "The Facility will be flexible, adaptive and demand-led, working with both public and private actors." (Document: 16865377.odt, "Main programme activities")

key_programme_risks: Political instability during 2017 elections disrupting devolution processes
Corruption in UIAF financing or procurement (zero-tolerance policy)
Low private sector uptake of PPP opportunities due to coordination failures
Climate shocks (floods/droughts) damaging value chain investments
County absorption capacity limitations for technical assistance
Gender blind urban planning perpetuating exclusion
Youth unemployment fuelling extremism/migration despite job creation efforts
Land tenure conflicts stalling infrastructure projects
Over-concentration of growth in primary corridors (Northern/LAPSSET)
Failure to achieve 0.5% GDP reduction in climate shock vulnerability

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Political economy analysis hardwired into all activities; adaptive management protocols for election periods.
Due diligence assessments for all partners; regular audits and spot checks; zero-tolerance policy.
KEPSA/KAM-led investment promotion strategies; de-risking instruments for PPPs; public-private dialogue platforms.
Mandatory climate resilience criteria for UIAF investments; diversification across sectors/geographies.
Phased rollout; embedded technical assistance; 'learning by doing' approaches with mentorship.
40% women on Steering Committee; gender-sensitive urban planning requirements; women's organization partnerships.
Targeted value chains (textiles, agro-processing) with youth apprenticeship components; monitoring of job quality.
Participatory planning processes; legal support for informal settlement upgrading.

fcas_specific_lessons: Devolution creates both opportunities (local ownership) and risks (capacity gaps) - SUED's phased approach reflects lessons from Kenya's 2013 devolution launch.
Climate shocks in ASAL regions require integrated resilience planning - informed by DFID's prior work on drought responses.
Urban growth coalitions must formalize informal networks to reduce elite capture - builds on Kenya's experience with public-private dialogue failures.
Youth bulge in fragile contexts demands job-intensive interventions - SUED's value chain focus aligns with CVE (Countering Violent Extremism) strategies.
Corruption in high-risk environments necessitates layered safeguards - lessons from Kenya's Procurement Act implementation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme incorporates lessons from: (1) DFID's Market Assistance Programme (MAP) on agriculture-value chain linkages; (2) TradeMark East Africa (TMEA) on corridor development; (3) Beira Agricultural Growth Corridor Initiative (BAGCI) on integrated spatial development; and (4) Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Programme (KISIP) on inclusive urban planning.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations include: (1) shifting from primary cities to intermediate towns based on World Bank evidence about agglomeration economies; (2) embedding gender targets (40% Steering Committee) after ActionAid's urban violence studies; (3) adding climate resilience criteria to UIAF following AEA Group's cost estimates (2.4% GDP/year); and (4) prioritizing LAPSSET corridor based on GoK's agricultural potential mapping.
