q3_expected_outputs: High quality evidence on impact of agricultural interventions on nutrition/health (6m households reached)
Publications in peer-reviewed journals on agriculture-nutrition linkages
Technologies/products for nutrition improvement (biofortified crops, aflatoxin tools)
Technical assistance and capacity building at scale (e.g., BMGF-led A2NU partnership)
Rigorous evaluation designs (large-scale RCTs on agriculture-nutrition pathways)
Gender-disaggregated data on nutrition outcomes
Increased capacity of African/South Asian researchers (training, evaluators, practitioners)
what_objectives.summary: The programme generates evidence on agriculture-nutrition linkages while simultaneously scaling up technologies and building capacity, with explicit targets for household reach (6m) and policy influence.
what_objectives.quote: "The impact of this programme will be to contribute to: Improved food and nutrition security through effective agriculture interventions... We estimate that the joint efforts of DFID and BMGF will contribute to reach 6 m households with technologies and products that improve nutrition" (8372889.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in regions with transforming food systems and double burden of malnutrition (undernutrition + obesity), but no explicit FCAS classification. Risks are primarily related to evidence gaps and policy translation rather than conflict/instability.
where_context.q5_source: "Most low and middle income countries now have increasingly complex and globally-linked food systems... Little is currently known about the drivers of these changes in both the food system and individual food choice especially in poor countries" (8372889.odt, Strategic Case A)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Limited evidence on food choice drivers and agriculture-nutrition pathways hampers policy-making. Weak institutional capacity in target countries requires technical assistance. Climate risks affect agricultural productivity and food systems stability.
where_context.quote: "The lack of robust evidence hampers policy making to support healthy food systems and diets among poor people in poor countries... Developing countries increasingly demand technical advice to understand better the impact and potential of agriculture and food systems for improved nutrition" (8372889.odt, Strategic Case A)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: DFID and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Joint decision-making through co-funding and co-management arrangements, with BMGF managing day-to-day research delivery and DFID providing strategic oversight. Technical collaboration is explicitly bidirectional (e.g., DFID provides inputs to BMGF-led programmes in India).
q10_capacity_building_details: training for researchers/evaluators/practitioners (especially in Africa/South Asia)
technical assistance to countries for nutrition-sensitive agriculture
institutional strengthening through joint programmes (e.g., A2NU Consortium)
mentorship via collaborative research designs

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder, research manager, technical lead

partner_organizations.name: HarvestPlus
partner_organizations.role: implementation (biofortified crops scaling)

partner_organizations.name: International Potato Centre (CIP)
partner_organizations.role: implementation (orange-fleshed sweet potato)

partner_organizations.name: A2NU Consortium
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance in Africa

partner_organizations.name: CGIAR (A4NH)
partner_organizations.role: research on agriculture-nutrition-health

partner_organizations.name: Local researchers/institutions (Africa/South Asia)
partner_organizations.role: research implementation, capacity-building recipients

who_partners.quote: "The partnership will increase the scale and reach of our efforts in promoting agriculture that improves the nutrition and health status of the poor, maximizing the results attributable to DFID’s investment and representing excellent value for money. Collaboration, cooperation and co-funding will ultimately increase the cost-effectiveness of both DFID and BMGF investments... by sharing our complementary technical, management and organisational capacities" (8372889.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is a partnership agreement (extension of existing DFID-BMGF MoU) with co-funding arrangements. Includes grants for specific research programmes (e.g., large-scale RCTs) managed under BMGF’s financial/scientific cycles, plus technical collaboration on existing portfolios.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Joint DFID-BMGF oversight with BMGF managing day-to-day research delivery (e.g., large-scale studies, food choice research) and DFID providing strategic/technical input. Builds on existing MoU with expanded scope to include nutrition teams from both organizations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: BMGF is an "established and trusted funder and partner on agricultural research" with proven capacity to manage large-scale research. The existing partnership (2010–2015) delivered tangible outcomes (e.g., rust-resistant wheat, aflatoxin diagnostics), justifying expansion without competition.
how_mechanism.quote: "The arrangements whereby BMGF manage joint projects on DFID’s behalf were put in place after lengthy discussions... These arrangements, which were unique when they were introduced in 2011, have now become a blueprint for other parts of DFID engaging with BMGF and other private foundations" (8372889.odt, How are we going to manage this intervention?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Joint technical oversight by DFID and BMGF, with BMGF’s programme officers managing research execution. Existing MoU provides framework; addendum will cover new nutrition-focused collaboration. No formal steering committee mentioned, but regular portfolio reviews planned.
how_governance.quote: "DFID will work with BMGF on technical and strategic oversight... research will be managed directly by BMGF’s programme officers and technical specialists following their rigorous financial and scientific management cycle" (8372889.odt, How are we going to manage this intervention?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research components during the inception phase (first 2 years), with joint DFID-BMGF agreement. New initiatives (e.g., post-harvest loss, aflatoxin) will be determined based on portfolio reviews.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted through regular portfolio reviews (e.g., "Others will be determined over the next 2 years"). Requires mutual agreement, with BMGF managing operational adjustments and DFID providing strategic input.
how_flexibility.quote: "Others [research initiatives] will be narrowed down during the beginning of the partnership... Some of the research initiatives are already designed and ready to launch (eg large scale impact studies; food choice studies). Others will be determined over the next 2 years through on-going portfolio reviews" (8372889.odt, Expected Results)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BMGF (fund manager) → end-researchers/implementers (e.g., A2NU Consortium, HarvestPlus). No additional intermediary layers mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: "BMGF will not charge administrative fees or overhead, thus this partnership represents high value for money. It will entail extremely low transaction costs per unit of spend" (8372889.odt, Appraisal Case G)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Maintain existing CGIAR/A4NH funding (£120m, 10% to A4NH) without new agriculture-nutrition research. Risk of ineffective nutrition-sensitive investments.
DFID-managed competitive procurement for a consortium to deliver RCTs/food choice studies. High transaction costs and no BMGF leverage.
Co-funding with BMGF to address evidence gaps, building on successful 2010–2015 partnership. Low transaction costs, high technical capacity.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its **value for money** (leveraging BMGF’s technical/expertise without overhead costs), **risk mitigation** (proven track record of existing partnership), **speed** (avoids consortium setup delays), and **scalability** (BMGF’s ability to absorb management costs and attract co-funding). The business case explicitly states this represents "high value for money" with "extremely low transaction costs."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on BMGF’s management systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular joint portfolio reviews and DFID’s strategic oversight. Existing MoU provides legal framework for accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited competition may reduce innovation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: BMGF’s rigorous grant selection process and DFID’s technical input ensure quality. Open calls for specific research (e.g., food choice studies) maintain competitive elements.

why_rationale.quote: "The selection of Option 3 represents the best Value for Money... This option would allow DFID to utilise BMGF’s strong technical expertise, rigorous screening of grant applicants and in-house management of the research programmes. BMGF will not charge administrative fees or overhead, thus this partnership represents high value for money. It will entail extremely low transaction costs per unit of spend" (8372889.odt, Appraisal Case G)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on **Africa and South Asia** (regions with weak institutional capacity and data limitations) necessitates partnerships with organizations like BMGF that have **existing technical assistance platforms** (e.g., A2NU Consortium) and **local research networks**. The double burden of malnutrition in these regions requires partners with **multidisciplinary expertise** (agriculture + nutrition + health).
q27_constraints_detail: Limited local research capacity → requires BMGF’s technical oversight
Rapidly changing food systems → need for adaptive partners like CGIAR/A2NU
Gender disparities in agriculture → partners must integrate gender analysis (e.g., women’s productivity studies)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for large-scale RCTs and interdisciplinary studies** (WHAT) drives the choice of a **joint DFID-BMGF management structure** (HOW) to pool expertise and funding. The **policy influence objective** requires a **unified donor voice**, achieved through co-funding rather than separate consortia.
q28_linkages: Large-scale impact studies → require BMGF’s grant management capacity
Technical assistance at scale → leverages BMGF’s existing platforms (e.g., A2NU)
Gender-disaggregated data → necessitates partners with gender expertise (e.g., CGIAR)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses balancing **Northern expertise** (BMGF’s technical/management capacity) with **Southern ownership** (e.g., capacity building for African/South Asian researchers). Trade-offs include: **speed vs. inclusion** (direct award to BMGF accelerates delivery but limits competitive bids) and **global evidence vs. local relevance** (studies must be "long enough to detect changes in anthropometry" while addressing context-specific drivers of food choices).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Direct award to BMGF (efficiency) vs. open competition (equity)
Global research standards (rigor) vs. local adaptability (relevance)
BMGF’s technical leadership (expertise) vs. Southern institution ownership (sustainability)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (transforming food systems, weak evidence base) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and joint portfolio reviews rather than light-touch management. BMGF’s "rigorous financial and scientific management cycle" is cited as a mitigation for research quality risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles: BMGF-led programmes (e.g., A2NU) include technical assistance to Southern institutions, while DFID’s inputs (e.g., on India Grand Challenges) ensure Northern-Southern knowledge exchange. Southern researchers are positioned as **co-implementers** (e.g., data collection, local adaptation of technologies).
intersections.quote: "The partnership will increase the scale and reach of our efforts in promoting agriculture that improves the nutrition and health status of the poor... by sharing our complementary technical, management and organisational capacities... A portion of DFID funds (£100,000) will be set aside to evaluate the programmes funded under the partnership" (8372889.odt, Expected Results & Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Weak evidence base on agriculture-nutrition linkages may limit policy uptake
Double burden of malnutrition (undernutrition + obesity) complicates intervention design
Gender disparities in agriculture productivity may undermine nutritional outcomes
Rapid food system transformations outpace research/policy adaptation
Limited Southern institutional capacity to absorb technical assistance

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Large-scale RCTs and interdisciplinary studies to generate robust data; joint DFID-BMGF oversight ensures relevance.
Studies designed to capture both undernutrition and overnutrition outcomes (e.g., dietary diversity + anthropometry).
Explicit gender analysis in research designs; focus on women’s control over agricultural assets/income.
Adaptive management via portfolio reviews; inclusion of food choice drivers in research.
Embedded capacity building (training, technical assistance) and direct funding to Southern researchers.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The existing DFID-BMGF partnership (2010–2015) demonstrated success in delivering **tangible outcomes** (e.g., rust-resistant wheat, aflatoxin diagnostics) through co-funding. Lessons applied: 1) **Joint management reduces transaction costs**, 2) **BMGF’s technical oversight ensures quality**, 3) **Regular portfolio reviews enable adaptability**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Expansion from agriculture-only focus to **agriculture-nutrition-health linkages**; addition of **nutrition teams** to the partnership; increased emphasis on **gender-disaggregated data** and **Southern capacity building** based on prior gaps.
risks_lessons.quote: "The existing Strategic Collaboration is performing well, and continues to deliver a stream of tangible development outcomes such as improved rust resistant wheat varieties, new diagnostic tests for aflatoxin and milk spoilage and improved tools for cassava breeding... These arrangements... have now become a blueprint for other parts of DFID engaging with BMGF" (8372889.odt, How are we going to manage this intervention?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The partnership leverages BMGF’s existing investments in agriculture-nutrition (total ongoing DFID+BMGF investments = £182m). Co-funding attracts additional BMGF finance (e.g., $6m for large-scale studies) and technical resources (e.g., A2NU Consortium).
financial_details.quote: "BMGF will not charge administrative fees or overhead, thus this partnership represents high value for money... The cumulative on-going DFID and BMGF investments in nutrition-sensitive agriculture amount to £182m" (8372889.odt, Appraisal Case G & Strategic Case)

metadata.programme_name: Exiting Poverty in Rwanda (EPR)
metadata.quote: "The Exiting Poverty in Rwanda (EPR) Programme will provide support to the Government of Rwanda (GoR) to help create and scale up a more sustainable, self-financed and inclusive system for supporting the most vulnerable, helping the poor manage shocks and enabling more people to sustainably exit poverty." (54145050.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Start: September 2019, End: March 2024" (90000989.odt, Summary Information) and "New project end date (if applicable): 30 June 2027" (D0007006.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The EPR programme combines implementation research (testing graduation packages), capacity building (strengthening Rwanda's social protection systems), and service delivery (direct cash transfers and public works). It also includes policy influence through supporting Rwanda's new Social Protection Sector Strategic Plan.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will comprise of 1) non-budget support financial aid for vulnerability focused social protection instruments, graduation packages and shock responsive social protection, 2) Technical Assistance (TA) to the Social Protection Sector; and 3) Monitoring and Evaluation activities." (90000989.odt, Approach to Implementation)
q3_expected_outputs: 65,000 households (approximately 250,000 people) lifted out of extreme poverty per year by the last year of the programme
Lives of at least 4,800 children saved due to improved nutrition
Improved targeting of People with Disabilities
Increased level of climate-sensitive and shock responsive financing
Key elements of the new SP system introduced and used, with specific indicators on instruments targeting PwD
Domestic sector finance increased
Joint Sector Review (JSR) and SWG assessments of sector management, including progress against implementation of the SP-SSP action plan
Capacity Building: Number of people trained, number of sessions held, percent of tasks/responsibilities carried by MINELOC/LODA staff (as opposed to external TA or consultants)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce extreme poverty in Rwanda through a combination of direct support (cash transfers, public works), system strengthening (institutional capacity, shock responsiveness), and policy implementation (graduation packages, disability inclusion).
what_objectives.quote: "The intended EPR outcome is to enhance the resilience of vulnerable men, women and children and of the social protection system that helps sustain them." (90000989.odt, Project's Purpose)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Rwanda is ranked 65th globally on the Global Terrorism Index (2016) with a medium-low risk of terrorism that has been decreasing since 2012. The programme is rated as 'Major' risk overall, with concerns about civil and political rights but strong commitment to poverty reduction and economic rights.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall, we assess that the Government of Rwanda remains committed to the underlying principles of our partnerships sufficient to continue financial aid. Rwanda continues to demonstrate strong commitment to poverty reduction, economic and social rights, anti-corruption and sound public financial management. Commitment to civil and political rights and domestic accountability is limited and we remain particularly concerned about civil and political rights." (54145050.odt, Partnership Principles) and "This programme is considered to be at an extremely low risk of funding terrorism." (54145050.odt, Other Considerations)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate shocks (heavy rains, landslides) have destroyed assets/savings of 25% of VUP beneficiaries in the past year, requiring shock-responsive systems. Local government capacity is limited for rapid scale-up of programmes like expanded Public Works. Political constraints affect domestic accountability and civil rights engagement.
where_context.quote: "In the last 12 months alone, a quarter of all VUP beneficiaries have experienced severe shocks such as destruction of their homes and farmland due to heavy rains and landslides." (54145050.odt, Other Considerations) and "ePW programmes are small scale and localised and it is probable that the rapid pace of scale-up envisaged will exceed local government capacity and implementation would need to be scaled back." (54145050.odt, Option 1 Weaknesses)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Rwanda (GoR) - specifically MINALOC (Ministry of Local Government) and LODA (Local Administrative Entities Development Agency)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Government of Rwanda (GoR) leads decision-making on social protection policy and implementation, with FCDO providing financial aid and technical assistance. The Social Protection Sector Working Group (SPSWG), co-chaired by DFID/FCDO, facilitates coordination but does not override GoR authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for GoR staff (MINALOC/LODA)
institutional strengthening (evidence-based planning, sector management)
technical assistance for SP-SSP implementation
development of safeguarding frameworks (gender, disability, labour)
support for integrated social protection MIS (iSP-MIS)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Rwanda (GoR) - MINALOC
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer of social protection programmes (VUP, SP-SSP)

partner_organizations.name: Local Administrative Entities Development Agency (LODA)
partner_organizations.role: Manages flagship Vision 2020 Umurenge Programme (VUP) and public works components

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder and technical assistance provider (Investment Project Financing for NSDS and cPW)

partner_organizations.name: Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for programme extension

partner_organizations.name: FCDO-managed Technical Assistance Facility
partner_organizations.role: Provides TA for institutional capacity building and SP-SSP implementation

partner_organizations.name: Social Protection Sector Working Group (SPSWG)
partner_organizations.role: Coordination platform co-chaired by FCDO, includes UNICEF, FAO, WFP, and other DPs

who_partners.quote: "DFID co-chairsthe Social Protection-Sector Working Group (SPSWG) and is able to use this position to critically assess results and drive forward change processes to improve outcomes." (54145050.odt, Why a DFID Intervention?) and "A key component of FCDO’s support is therefore to the provision of technical assistance (TA) to support the implementation of GoR’s new social protection policy and strategic plan." (90000989.odt, Project's Purpose)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses (1) Non-Budget Support Financial Aid (NBSFA) earmarked for specific social protection instruments (£50.5m), (2) a Partnership Agreement/MoU with MINECOFIN governing the NBSFA, and (3) technical assistance contracts (£12m) managed directly by FCDO and originally planned to include a World Bank Executed Trust Fund (later dropped).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The GoR (MINALOC/LODA) implements social protection instruments directly with NBSFA, while FCDO manages a Technical Assistance Facility and coordinates with the World Bank and other DPs through the SPSWG. The programme includes both earmarked funds (for specific instruments) and flexible TA support.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Government of Rwanda is the sole implementing partner for social protection delivery, given its leadership role in the sector and the programme's alignment with the national SP-SSP. FCDO's TA providers are selected through a separate procurement process (not detailed in the documents).
how_mechanism.quote: "£50.5m of non-budget support financial aid to the GoR, earmarked to 4 areas" (54145050.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The programme will comprise of 1) non-budget support financial aid for vulnerability focused social protection instruments... 2) Technical Assistance (TA) to the Social Protection Sector" (90000989.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Disbursement-Linked Indicators (DLIs) govern 40% of the NBSFA, with payments made in arrears based on achievement of agreed indicators. The Joint Sector Review (JSR) and Social Protection Sector Working Group (SPSWG) assess progress.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Social Protection Sector Working Group (SPSWG), co-chaired by FCDO and GoR, serves as the primary governance body. It includes other development partners (UNICEF, FAO, WFP, World Bank) and meets regularly to review progress against the SP-SSP action plan.
how_governance.quote: "40% of this financial aid will be performance-based, with payments made in arrears subject to the achievement of disbursement-linked indicators (DLIs) focused on improvements to existing social protection instruments and the introduction of new instruments in line with GoR’s new social protection strategy." (54145050.odt, Intervention Summary) and "DFID co-chairsthe Social Protection-Sector Working Group (SPSWG)" (54145050.odt, Why a DFID Intervention?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for specific instruments (NSDS, eDS, PW, graduation), but the programme includes a ring-fenced budget for scaling up successful pilots. The extension to 2027 allows for prolonged piloting and learning.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme's theory of change is described as a 'living document' under continuous review. Adjustments are made based on emerging evidence (e.g., mid-term review recommendations to slow reform pace) and changing context (e.g., COVID-19 budget reductions).
how_flexibility.quote: "The theory of change is a living document and is under continuous review, considering changing context and new and emerging evidence." (90000989.odt, Key Changes) and "The mid-term review of EPR highlighted that the pace of reforms was too fast and recommended a more realistic plan for implementation." (D0007006.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Government of Rwanda (MINALOC/LODA) → Beneficiaries. The World Bank and TA providers operate in parallel but report to FCDO/GoR jointly.
how_efficiency.quote: "40% of this financial aid will be performance-based, with payments made in arrears subject to the achievement of disbursement-linked indicators (DLIs)" (54145050.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Focus only on improving VUP (£50m, 5 years) - expanding coverage of core instruments (eDS, ePW, cPW) without broader sector reforms.
Option 3: No further support to SP - full exit by DFID.
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (£64.5m, mixed approach) was selected because it (1) aligns with GoR’s ambitious SP-SSP to create a comprehensive, domestically financed system; (2) addresses both immediate poverty reduction (through transfers/PW) and long-term sustainability (through graduation and shock responsiveness); (3) builds on lessons from VUP while introducing innovations (e.g., climate-sensitive PW, disability grants); and (4) provides a responsible exit pathway for FCDO by strengthening GoR capacity.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (graduation packages and CTs are evidence-based 'best buys')
experience (10 years of DFID/GoR partnership on VUP)
partner-capacity (GoR’s track record and commitment to SP)
equity (focus on extreme poor, PwD, women, and shock-affected households)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with World Bank activities (e.g., both funding NSDS/cPW) leading to duplication or confusion.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear delineation of roles: FCDO focuses on sector strategy/policy and new instruments (e.g., DLG, shock responsiveness), while World Bank focuses on scaling existing VUP components. Joint coordination through SPSWG.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoR’s capacity to absorb rapid reforms (e.g., ePW scale-up, graduation pilots).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with extended timeline (to 2027), TA support for institutional strengthening, and mid-term review adjustments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Performance-based funding (40% DLIs) may delay disbursements if targets are missed.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Indicators aligned with GoR’s SP-SSP priorities; technical assistance to support achievement; flexibility in adjustment period.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political constraints (limited civil/political rights) affecting domestic accountability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on economic/social rights where GoR has stronger commitment; support to safeguarding frameworks; annual Partnership Principles assessments.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (evidence from VUP impact evaluations showing CTs/PW reduce poverty)
efficiency (performance-based disbursements, TA to improve implementation)
equity (targeting extreme poor, PwD, women, and climate-vulnerable regions)
economy (leveraging GoR’s increasing domestic financing for SP)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 2 takes advantage of the opportunity provided by the new SP policy and SP-SSP to expand the focus of DFID’s support to include both support to core SP instruments and to the establishment of a more sustainable, coherent and better-managed SP sector." (54145050.odt, Option 2 Summary) and "The mid-term review of EPR highlighted that the pace of reforms was too fast and recommended a more realistic plan for implementation." (D0007006.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The single-country focus (Rwanda) and GoR’s leadership in social protection necessitate a Southern-led implementation structure. Local government capacity constraints limit the pace of scale-up (e.g., ePW expansion) and require embedded TA. Political context (limited civil rights) shapes the focus on economic/social rights over governance reforms.
q27_constraints_detail: GoR’s institutional capacity (MINALOC/LODA) determines the feasibility of reforms (e.g., graduation pilots, shock-responsive systems).
Climate vulnerability (frequent shocks) requires adaptive, locally managed systems rather than rigid external models.
Political economy (strong GoR commitment to SP but limited civil rights) restricts partner roles to technical/advisory support.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (direct service delivery + system strengthening) require a hybrid structure: (1) NBSFA for GoR-led implementation of transfers/PW; (2) FCDO-managed TA for capacity building; and (3) SPSWG for coordination. Graduation packages (complex, multi-sectoral) need flexible piloting before scale-up, while CTs/PW use established systems.
q28_linkages: Direct service delivery (CTs/PW) → GoR implementation with performance-based funding (DLIs).
System strengthening (graduation, shock responsiveness) → FCDO TA + joint learning via SPSWG.
Policy influence (SP-SSP) → Aligned with GoR’s NST and co-designed through SPSWG.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting extreme poor, PwD, women) with efficiency (performance-based disbursements, TA for implementation). Trade-offs include: (1) slower scale-up of ePW to ensure inclusion of labour-constrained households (mostly women); (2) ring-fenced funds for disability grants despite higher per-household costs; and (3) shock-responsive systems that may require rapid reallocation of resources.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: ePW expansion is phased to avoid excluding women with caring responsibilities, despite delays.
Cost vs. reach: Disability Living Grants (DLG) target smaller households but address severe exclusion of PwD.
Flexibility vs. accountability: Performance-based funding (DLIs) ensures efficiency but requires adaptive management to avoid penalizing GoR for contextual shocks (e.g., climate events).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating (due to political constraints and climate vulnerability) justifies intensive oversight via DLIs, annual Partnership Principles reviews, and the SPSWG. Shock responsiveness is embedded in both programme design (climate-sensitive PW) and governance (flexible disbursements).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: GoR’s capacity gaps (e.g., in graduation pilots or MIS systems) shape the TA component, with FCDO providing embedded advisors (e.g., for iSP-MIS) and joint training (e.g., on safeguarding). The extension to 2027 reflects learning that capacity building takes longer than initially planned.
intersections.quote: "The programme has been developed in close consultation with the GoR. It supports the GoR’s own sector strategy and policy, with the clear objective of building sustainable capacity for implementation, planning, and financing." (54145050.odt, Coherence with International Community) and "The mid-term review of EPR highlighted that the pace of reforms was too fast and recommended a more realistic plan for implementation." (D0007006.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)

key_programme_risks: GoR’s capacity to implement reforms at pace (e.g., graduation packages, ePW scale-up).
Overlap/duplication with World Bank’s parallel SP programme.
Performance-based disbursements (40% DLIs) may delay funding if targets are missed.
Climate shocks eroding livelihood gains (addressed via shock-responsive SP).
Political constraints (limited civil rights) affecting domestic accountability.
Targeting errors excluding vulnerable groups (e.g., PwD, women with caring responsibilities).
Sustainability of poverty reduction gains post-FCDO exit.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GoR capacity gaps in implementing SP-SSP.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Extended timeline (to 2027), FCDO TA for institutional strengthening, and phased reforms based on pilot learning.
Clear division of labor: FCDO focuses on new instruments (DLG, shock responsiveness) and sector strategy; World Bank on scaling existing VUP components. Joint coordination via SPSWG.
DLIs aligned with GoR priorities; TA to support achievement; flexibility in adjustment periods.
Shock-responsive SP systems (expansion/contraction based on shock data), climate-sensitive PW in vulnerable regions.
New instruments (Disability Living Grant, expanded eDS for carers), improved targeting via Ubudehe revisions, and safeguarding frameworks.
Graduation packages to enable sustainable exits; increased GoR domestic financing (from 65% of VUP budget in 2017/18 to higher levels).

fcas_specific_lessons: Shock responsiveness must be embedded in SP systems (e.g., 25% of VUP beneficiaries experienced severe shocks in 12 months).
Local government capacity is a binding constraint for scale-up (e.g., ePW implementation risks exceeding absorptive capacity).
Political economy requires focusing on economic/social rights where GoR has stronger commitment, while cautiously engaging on governance issues.
Performance-based funding (DLIs) must balance accountability with flexibility to adapt to shocks (e.g., climate events).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from VUP (2008–2018) include: (1) CTs (DS) have larger poverty impacts than PW; (2) targeting errors and self-exclusion (e.g., women unable to participate in cPW due to caring responsibilities) require adaptive designs (e.g., ePW); (3) timely payments and predictable schedules improve outcomes; (4) linking SP to complementary services (e.g., health, nutrition) enhances graduation; and (5) public awareness campaigns reduce exclusion.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations in EPR design: (1) Introduction of ePW with flexible schedules for women/carers; (2) Nutrition-Sensitive Direct Support (NSDS) with health/nutrition conditions; (3) Disability Living Grant (DLG) to address exclusion of PwD; (4) shock-responsive mechanisms based on climate shock data; (5) extended timeline (to 2027) for realistic reform pacing; and (6) ring-fenced funds for scaling successful pilots.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from VUP include: (i) Direct Support (DS) has larger poverty impacts than Public Works (PW); (ii) targeting errors and self-exclusion (e.g., women with caring responsibilities) require adaptive designs; (iii) timely payments improve outcomes; and (iv) linking SP to complementary services enhances graduation." (54145050.odt, Strategic Case) and "The mid-term review of EPR highlighted that the pace of reforms was too fast and recommended a more realistic plan for implementation. Extension of the programme by fifteen months to end in June 2027 will allow the work plan for policy reforms to be prolonged." (D0007006.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages increasing GoR domestic financing for social protection, which rose from 25% of the VUP budget in 2012/13 to 65% in 2017/18, with projections for further increases. The World Bank’s parallel Investment Project Financing (IPF) loan ($80m) complements FCDO’s support.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The £50.5m NBSFA is primarily revenue expenditure (cash transfers, PW wages), while the £12m TA includes both revenue (training, advisory services) and capital (e.g., IT systems for iSP-MIS).
financial_details.quote: "£50.5m of non-budget support financial aid to the GoR, earmarked to 4 areas... £12m will be used to provide technical assistance to support the implementation of GoR’s new social protection policy and strategy." (54145050.odt, Intervention Summary) and "GoR’s focus on SP is also quite recent by comparison with countries like Kenya and Ethiopia and has, to date, focused very much on its flagship VUP programme... GoR’s expenditure as a proportion of GDP is commendable, but it is still much less in cash terms than other countries’ in the region." (54145050.odt, Strategic Case)

metadata.programme_name: AAWAZ II: Inclusion, Accountability, and Preventing Modern Slavery Programme

quote.text: The AAWAZ II programme works with government and local communities to promote the rights of children, women, youth, religious minorities and excluded groups to strengthen their control over their own development.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: January 1, 2018 - March 31, 2027

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The AAWAZ II programme combines capacity building (strengthening government institutions and community organizations), service delivery (direct support through AAWAZ Aagahi Centres), policy influence (legislative reforms on modern slavery and child protection), and implementation research (testing community empowerment models). It operates through both supply-side institutional strengthening and demand-side community mobilization.

q1_source.text: The programme has a particular focus on the issue of modern slavery, to which marginalised groups are extremely vulnerable. [...] The intervention will draw on the skills and capability of both the UN and a contracted supplier as part of a hybrid delivery model.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened national and provincial institutions
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: Technical assistance to Ministry of Human Rights, Provincial Bureaux of Statistics, Social Welfare Departments, and Commissions on Status of Women

q3_expected_outputs.output: 450 AAWAZ Aagahi Centres (citizens' advice bureaux)
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 450 centres across 45 districts

q3_expected_outputs.output: Community fora (45 District Fora + 2 Provincial Fora)
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 47 fora to raise demands for services

q3_expected_outputs.output: Trained community change agents
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 18,000 youth and 17,020 men/women as 'change makers' (from AAWAZ I, continued in AAWAZ II)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Pre-emption of community conflicts
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 22,000+ conflicts pre-empted (AAWAZ I baseline)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy/legislative reforms
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: Support for youth action plans, child labour surveys, birth registration systems

q3_expected_outputs.output: Digital literacy and hate speech mitigation
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 10,000 young people trained in digital literacy (from D0005910.odt)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Beneficiaries reached
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 13 million across KP, Punjab, and Sindh (D0004556.odt)

what_objectives.summary: AAWAZ II aims to create a more inclusive Pakistan by simultaneously strengthening government institutions (supply side) and empowering marginalized communities (demand side) to reduce modern slavery, gender-based violence, and discrimination against religious minorities. The hybrid model combines UN-led institutional reforms with community-level interventions delivered through local NGOs and the British Council.

quote.text: The programme aims to reach 7 million beneficiaries across the provinces of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Punjab [...] The programme will lead to: an increase in the capacity of selected government institutions to respond to and protect citizens, particularly women, youth and religious minorities; the empowerment of 4,500 communities through AACs to engage with government to demand better services and greater protection; a reduction in vulnerability within these communities to forms of violence and exploitation (such as forms of modern slavery).

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to high levels of violence, terrorism, and weak governance. The 2015 Global Peace Index ranks Pakistan 154th out of 162 countries, and it is among the top 4 countries most affected by terrorism. The programme explicitly notes risks of reputational damage from being perceived as 'anti-religious' or 'anti-state' and highlights the shrinking civic space for religious minorities.

q5_source.text: Pakistan is characterised by high levels of violence and insecurity, poverty, inequality, and deteriorating human rights [...] it lies 154th out of 162 on the Global Peace Index [...] and 4th out of 162 countries most affected by terrorism.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit operating space for partners and beneficiaries, particularly in conflict-affected areas. Weak institutions (e.g., low birth registration rates, lack of social security for bonded labourers) hinder service delivery. Political sensitivity around religious issues (e.g., blasphemy laws) constrains advocacy. Data limitations (e.g., no recent child labour surveys before 2016) affect evidence-based policymaking. The programme notes that 'space for civil society remains tight' and that 'violence is now a binding constraint to realising the potential of the next generation'.

quote.text: The current security situation could worsen and reduce the operating space for partners and political space for beneficiaries. Implementing partners will need to have contingency plans to deal with this scenario [...] Weak governance, weak institutions and a lack of accountability help drive exclusion and discrimination, which in turn increases vulnerability to exploitation/modern slavery.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-led by UN agencies (multilateral) and the British Council (UK), with significant decision-making power delegated to local NGOs and community structures. The hybrid model explicitly aims to balance Northern technical expertise (UN/UK) with Southern ownership (local CSOs, government institutions, and community fora).
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to government institutions (e.g., Ministry of Human Rights, Provincial Commissions on Status of Women)
Training of 18,000 youth and 17,020 men/women as 'change makers' (community leaders)
Establishment of 450 AAWAZ Aagahi Centres (local advice bureaux) managed by communities
Support for local academic institutions in research commissioning
Digital literacy training for youth (10,000+)
Sustainability planning for community structures post-programme

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Lead for institutional development (policy/legislation/data systems)

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA
partner_organizations.role: Lead for institutional development (gender-based violence, child protection)

partner_organizations.name: UNDP
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of digital safety/hate speech component (from D0005910.odt)

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: Lead for community engagement (AAWAZ Aagahi Centres, youth training, conflict prevention)

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Community-level implementation (district fora, change agents, service delivery)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Pakistan (Ministry of Human Rights, Provincial Commissions on Status of Women, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Policy reform and service delivery partner

partner_organizations.name: Oxford Policy Management (OPM)
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring and Evaluation

quote.text: The intervention will draw on the skills and capability of both the UN and a contracted supplier as part of a hybrid delivery model [...] We are aiming to reach 7 million beneficiaries. The programme will lead to: an increase in the capacity of selected government institutions to respond to and protect citizens, particularly women, youth and religious minorities; the empowerment of 4,500 communities through AACs to engage with government to demand better services [...] The programme will work with local organisations to build networks (for instance of trained youth and gender champions) and processes which should continue beyond the lifetime of this programme.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: (1) **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** with UN agencies (UNICEF/UNFPA/UNDP) for institutional components; (2) **commercial contracts** with the British Council for community engagement (later converted to MoU in D0004556.odt); (3) **accountable grants** for Sindh expansion (D0004556.odt); and (4) **direct MoU** with UNDP for the digital safety component (D0005910.odt). This hybrid approach allows flexibility in managing different components (institutional vs. community vs. digital).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a **hybrid model** with two parallel structures: (1) A **UN Joint Programme (UNJP)** led by UNICEF/UNFPA for institutional reforms, and (2) a **community engagement component** initially led by the British Council (later transitioned to MoU). The components are coordinated but maintain separate management structures, with FCDO overseeing both. Local NGOs and government partners are embedded in delivery, particularly for community-level activities.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UN partners (UNICEF/UNFPA) were selected based on their **existing relationships with government** and **technical expertise** in child protection and gender-based violence. The British Council was chosen for its experience in community engagement (building on AAWAZ I). For Sindh expansion, a **competitive call for proposals** was used to select a nonprofit implementer (D0004556.odt). The UNDP was directly engaged for the digital safety component due to its ongoing work under the ISF-funded Hate Speech programme (D0005910.odt).

quote.text: The intervention will draw on the skills and capability of both the UN and a contracted supplier as part of a hybrid delivery model [...] The UN agencies have a strong relationship with government and have provided assurance that the political will exists to achieve results. [...] We will procure a new contractor through a single contract for KP, Punjab and Sindh using the IMDP framework (D0003495.odt) [...] The current commercial contracts for the community engagement component will be concluded in September 2024. In parallel we will sign a MoU with the British Council for KP, Punjab (D0004556.odt).

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is governed through **regular coordination meetings** between FCDO, UN agencies, the British Council, and government partners. For the digital safety component, a **Steering Committee** with key ministries will deliberate on online regulation issues (D0005910.odt). Annual reviews and technical advisory inputs are explicitly mentioned, but no formal board structure is documented.

quote.text: We are in close contact with FCO colleagues on issues of modern slavery and exploitation/marginalisation more generally. We carry out joint meetings internally and externally, including with multilateral and government partners [...] A comprehensive communications strategy will be drafted in consultation with implementing partners during the inception phase [...] The programme will be monitored through a third-party monitor (OPM), with additional resources allocated for oversight of the digital safety component (D0005910.odt).

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, as demonstrated by the **£1.24m repurposing** from underspend to the digital safety component (D0005910.odt). The programme also adjusted budgets to extend operations in Sindh (£7.4m addition in D0003495.odt) and reallocated savings from M&E contracts to cover extension costs (D0001179.odt).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a **2-year break clause** in all contracts to allow adjustments based on performance or context changes (49846919.odt). Adaptive management is explicitly mentioned in response to COVID-19 delays (D0001179.odt) and political transitions (e.g., post-election reforms in D0003495.odt). The digital safety component was added mid-programme to address emerging online risks (D0005910.odt).

quote.text: This is a 5 year programme, with a 2 year break clause built in to all contracts/agreements to ensure that necessary adjustments to the intervention can be made in the light of changing priorities/political context [...] The extension will allow reasonable timeframe for advancing legislative and institutional reforms post-election (D0001179.odt) [...] We will re-align £1.24m of identified Aawaz II programme underspend to accommodate the new [digital safety] component (D0005910.odt).

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN/British Council (implementing partners) → Local NGOs/Community Structures (sub-implementers). For Sindh, an additional layer was added: FCDO → Nonprofit grantee → Local partners.

quote.text: The programme will utilise the opportunity for reforms after the general elections expected in 2023/24 [...] The forecast until the current end date (March 2024) is £9.6m. The remaining budget of £12.7m is available for programming during the extension period (D0001179.odt) [...] The total approved budget for this programme is £46.9m. The programme has spent £23.2m (49.27%) to date (D0004556.odt).

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Rely on existing DFID/UN programmes, deemed insufficient for transformational impact.
Focus solely on government institutions; rejected as unsustainable without community demand.
Focus solely on communities; rejected as ineffective without institutional capacity.
Chosen for its potential to create sustained impact by linking institutional reforms with community empowerment.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **hybrid delivery model** was selected to address the **multi-dimensional drivers of exclusion and modern slavery** (institutional, cultural, and individual levels). The rationale included: (1) **Value for Money**: Leveraging UN’s existing government relationships and British Council’s community engagement expertise; (2) **Risk Mitigation**: Balancing top-down policy influence with bottom-up legitimacy to avoid reputational risks; (3) **Flexibility**: Allowing adaptive management through break clauses and component-specific instruments (MoUs, contracts, grants); (4) **Equity**: Ensuring Southern ownership through local NGOs and community structures; (5) **Speed**: Building on AAWAZ I’s established networks (450 AACs, 4,500 communities).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational damage from being perceived as anti-religious/anti-state
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong government engagement and sensitive messaging, building on AAWAZ I’s positive experience.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner capacity limitations in high-risk areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Contingency plans for security scenarios and adaptive management structures.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of community structures post-programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investment in local ownership (e.g., Muqami Agahi Centres) and sustainability planning with government/CSOs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges in hybrid model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular joint meetings and third-party monitoring (OPM) to ensure alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political transitions disrupting reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Timing legislative pushes post-election (D0001179.odt) and flexible budget reallocation.

quote.text: Option 3: A multipronged approach combining both demand side and supply side outputs [...] By increasing political space at the community level, while simultaneously increasing the capacity at provincial and federal levels to be more responsive and accountable to the demands of marginalised communities, impact is likely to be significant and sustained [...] Options 1 and 2 were rejected as they do not respond to the multi-dimensional and interconnected ways in which inequality, exploitation and marginalisation are kept in place – namely at the individual, institutional and cultural levels, thus limiting impact.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** directly shapes partner selection: (1) **Security risks** limit the operating space for international partners, necessitating reliance on local NGOs for community access; (2) **Political sensitivity** around religious issues requires partners with established government relationships (e.g., UN agencies); (3) **Weak institutions** demand capacity-building-focused partners (e.g., UNICEF for child protection systems); (4) **Shrinking civic space** prioritizes partners with experience in conflict-sensitive programming (e.g., British Council’s AAWAZ I track record).
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks → Local NGOs essential for community access
Political sensitivity → UN agencies preferred for government engagement
Weak institutions → Technical partners (UNICEF/UNFPA) needed for systems strengthening
Shrinking civic space → Partners with conflict-sensitive experience prioritized
Regulatory environment → MoUs/grants used to navigate bureaucratic hurdles
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **dual objectives** (institutional reform + community empowerment) necessitate a **hybrid structure**: (1) **Policy influence goals** → UN-led component with MoUs for legitimacy; (2) **Community mobilization goals** → British Council/local NGOs with flexible contracts; (3) **Emerging digital risks** → UNDP added via direct MoU; (4) **Geographic expansion (Sindh)** → Competitive grants to identify local expertise. The **need for adaptive management** (e.g., post-election reforms, COVID-19 delays) also shapes the use of break clauses and reallocatable budgets.
q28_linkages: Institutional reforms (UN) → MoU instrument for government buy-in
Community empowerment (British Council) → Commercial contracts (later MoU) for flexibility
Digital safety (emerging risk) → Direct UNDP MoU for speed
Sindh expansion → Competitive grants to ensure local fit
Adaptive needs (COVID/elections) → Break clauses and budget reallocation
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are addressed: (1) **Local ownership vs. speed**: The programme balances local NGO leadership with UN/British Council’s existing networks to accelerate delivery; (2) **Inclusive partnerships vs. coordination costs**: The hybrid model adds management complexity but ensures marginalized groups (e.g., religious minorities, transgender communities) are reached; (3) **Southern capacity vs. Northern expertise**: Technical assistance (UN) is paired with community-led structures (AACs) to build local skills without displacing ownership; (4) **Flexibility vs. oversight**: Adaptive management (e.g., repurposing £1.24m for digital safety) is balanced with milestone-based monitoring to mitigate risks.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Local NGOs lead community work, but UN/British Council’s existing relationships enable faster scale-up.
Hybrid model (UN + British Council + local NGOs) increases management layers but ensures reach to religious minorities/transgender groups.
UN provides technical assistance while community structures (AACs) are locally managed to avoid dependency.
Break clauses and budget reallocation allow adaptability, but milestone-based monitoring maintains accountability.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight** in some areas (e.g., third-party monitoring for digital component, D0005910.odt) while allowing **flexibility in others** (e.g., adaptive management for COVID/election delays). High reputational risks lead to **strong government engagement requirements**, and security risks necessitate **contingency planning** for partners.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: (1) UN agencies focus on **institutional capacity** (e.g., training government officers on GBV response); (2) British Council/local NGOs build **community capacity** (e.g., 18,000 youth change agents); (3) The shift from commercial contracts to MoUs (D0004556.odt) reflects **increased trust in local partners’ capacity** post-AAWAZ I. Sustainability plans explicitly aim to transition community structures (e.g., Muqami Agahi Centres) to local management.

quote.text: The intervention will work with local organisations to build networks (for instance of trained youth and gender champions) and processes which should continue beyond the lifetime of this programme [...] The programme will continue and expand the networks established under AAWAZ I (for instance of trained youth and gender champions) and processes (such as community conflict maps) which should endure beyond the intervention [...] The extension will enable the BC to deliver results that will be otherwise missed due to budget cuts and to implement a sustainability plan for the community structures (D0001179.odt).

key_programme_risks: Reputational damage from being perceived as anti-religious or anti-state
Security deterioration limiting operating space for partners
Weak government capacity to sustain reforms post-programme
Shrinking civic space for religious minorities and women’s rights advocates
Political transitions disrupting legislative reforms
Sustainability of community structures (AACs) without long-term funding
Coordinating hybrid delivery model (UN + British Council + local NGOs)
Data limitations hindering evidence-based policymaking
Online hate speech and disinformation targeting vulnerable groups

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strong government engagement, sensitive messaging, and building on AAWAZ I’s positive track record.
Contingency plans for partners, adaptive management, and local NGO leadership in high-risk areas.
Technical assistance to institutions (e.g., Ministry of Human Rights), paired with community demand-generation.
Conflict-sensitive programming, legal literacy for marginalized groups, and digital safety interventions.
Timing reforms post-election (D0001179.odt) and flexible budget allocation.
Investment in local ownership (Muqami Agahi Centres), sustainability planning with government/CSOs, and exploring government funding post-programme.
Regular joint meetings, third-party monitoring (OPM), and clear division of roles (UN for institutional, British Council for community).
Digital literacy training, fact-checking tools (iVerify), and engagement with social media platforms (Meta, TikTok).

fcas_specific_lessons: Leverage existing local networks (e.g., AAWAZ I’s 4,500 communities) to navigate security and political risks.
Use hybrid instruments (MoUs + contracts + grants) to balance flexibility with accountability in volatile contexts.
Prioritize conflict-sensitive programming, including pre-emption of sectarian/interfaith conflicts (22,000+ conflicts pre-empted in AAWAZ I).
Invest in local conflict mapping and early warning systems to adapt to changing risks.
Align with government priorities (e.g., post-election reform windows) to ensure political buy-in.
Build redundancy into community structures (e.g., AACs continued during funding gaps via local benefactors).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: AAWAZ I’s success demonstrated that: (1) **Community structures can endure beyond funding** (e.g., AACs self-funded during gaps); (2) **Hybrid models work** in Pakistan’s context, combining UN legitimacy with local NGO reach; (3) **Conflict pre-emption is critical**, with 22,000+ conflicts addressed in AAWAZ I; (4) **Government engagement is essential** for sustainability, though slow; (5) **Flexibility is non-negotiable**, given Pakistan’s political and security volatility. The programme explicitly builds on these lessons, e.g., expanding AAWAZ I’s networks and using break clauses for adaptability.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **digital safety component** (D0005910.odt) in response to emerging online risks (hate speech, disinformation).
Extended to **Sindh province** (D0003495.odt) based on evidence of high vulnerability post-floods.
Shifted from **commercial contracts to MoUs** (D0004556.odt) to reflect increased trust in British Council’s capacity.
Incorporated **adaptive management** (break clauses, budget reallocation) based on AAWAZ I’s experience with political transitions.
Added **sustainability planning** for community structures (Muqami Agahi Centres) to address AAWAZ I’s gap-period lessons.

quote.text: The experience of AAWAZ I has been generally positive in this regard, with local implementing partners working sensitively and respectfully [...] During a recent short gap in funding while an extension phase was agreed, many of the citizens’ advice bureaux continued, seeking short term funding from local benefactors or self-funding [...] The intervention will build on the success of AAWAZ I, continuing to engender stronger relationships between citizens and state [...] The extension will allow reasonable timeframe for advancing legislative and institutional reforms post-election (D0001179.odt).

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UN agencies’ £2.294m contribution leverages longer-term multilateral investment in modern slavery and child protection, supporting a sustainable exit for FCDO (49846919.odt). The programme also mobilizes government resources (e.g., Punjab’s $50m bonded labour project) by aligning with national priorities.

quote.text: The total approved budget for this programme is £46.9m. The programme has spent £23.2m (49.27%) to date. The remaining budget of £23m is available for programming during the extension period (D0004556.odt) [...] The UN agencies will commit £2,294,000 to focus on modern slavery, leading to longer term investment in this space from multilateral partners (49846919.odt).

metadata.programme_name: Sub-National Governance Programme II (SNG II)
metadata.quote: "SNG II aims to improve public sector management in Pakistan. The programme works alongside the federal, provincial (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab) and local governments to build sustainable government institutions and improve the management of public finances." (D0003346.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 31/05/2018–23/08/2024", "New project end date (if applicable): 30 June 2026" (D0003346.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SNG II is a **capacity-building** programme focused on strengthening public financial management (PFM) and governance systems at sub-national levels in Pakistan. It also includes **implementation research** through piloting innovative governance approaches (e.g., digital solutions, disaster risk financing) and **service delivery** improvements by unblocking systemic governance challenges in health and education sectors. The programme directly supports reforms in planning, budgeting, revenue mobilization, and institutional effectiveness, while testing scalable innovations.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will work across four themes, all aimed at getting the right systems and resources in place for the effective functioning of government and the delivery of services. These are: Planning and reform [...] Budgeting and transparency [...] Fiscal space [...] Innovations, piloting and scaling up innovative approaches [...]" (50807182.odt, Theory of Change)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Public Financial Management (PFM) Reform strategies implemented in KP and Punjab
q3_expected_outputs.target: Improved PEFA ratings in agreed areas (alignment of recurrent/development budgets, transparency, reliability)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased budget execution rates
q3_expected_outputs.target: Year-on-year improvement across all departments

q3_expected_outputs.output: Provincial Own Source Revenue (OSR) mobilization plans
q3_expected_outputs.target: Two plans developed and implemented in KP and Punjab, generating additional PKR 135 billion (£598 million) in FY 2021-22

q3_expected_outputs.output: Social protection systems strengthened
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1.2 million unregistered people included in Punjab’s social welfare net; 10,378 women beneficiaries in flood-affected districts

q3_expected_outputs.output: Climate and disaster budget tagging system
q3_expected_outputs.target: Operationalized on government’s financial management system (e.g., PKR 112 billion allocated for disaster management in Punjab’s 2022-23 budget)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Service delivery pilots
q3_expected_outputs.target: Three pilots (solid waste management, own-source revenue mobilization) in selected local governments

q3_expected_outputs.output: Innovative approaches evaluated
q3_expected_outputs.target: At least 10 pilots documented and considered for government adoption

q3_expected_outputs.output: Prime Minister’s Strategic Reforms Roadmap
q3_expected_outputs.target: Designed and delivered focusing on economic recovery and energy

what_objectives.summary: SNG II aims to improve the effectiveness of state institutions in Pakistan by strengthening public financial management, planning, and service delivery systems at federal, provincial, and local levels. It combines systemic reforms (e.g., PFM, revenue mobilization) with adaptive support for crises (e.g., COVID-19 recovery, flood response) and pilots innovative governance solutions.
what_objectives.quote: "SNG II aims to improve the management of the public sector in Pakistan. The programme works alongside the federal, provincial (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa-KP and Punjab) and local governments to build sustainable government institutions and improve the management of public finances." (D0003324.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan is classified as a **Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS)** due to structural drivers of conflict, including elite capture of resources, youth bulge, urbanization, and radicalism. The programme operates in regions with historic insurgent presence (e.g., KP’s border with FATA) and faces risks from political instability, natural disasters (e.g., 2022 floods), and weak local government capacity.
where_context.q5_source: "Conflict and stability dynamics in Pakistan remain complex. The Joint Analysis of Conflict and Stability (JACS) identified that conflict and instability in Pakistan is the result of a series of structural drivers including a highly exclusive carve-up of power and resources, and the presence of structural socio-economic ‘stresses’, particularly Pakistan’s youth bulge, urbanisation, and a burgeoning middle-class with notable associations with radicalism." (50807182.odt, Conflict and fragility)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit access to certain districts and require conflict-sensitive programming. Political instability (e.g., 2022 no-confidence vote, delayed local elections) disrupts reform continuity. Weak institutional capacity at local levels (e.g., 43,000 new officials in KP with limited PFM experience) hampers decentralization. Climate risks (e.g., floods, monsoons) demand adaptive disaster response mechanisms. Data limitations (e.g., informal economy, unregistered populations) challenge evidence-based planning.
where_context.quote: "The programme will interact directly with the way in which resources are divided in Pakistan. The nature of the programme intervention means that it will require a strong approach to conflict sensitivity to ensure that it maximises its impact and does no harm." (50807182.odt, Conflict and fragility)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO (funding) / Oxford Policy Management (OPM) and UNDP (implementation)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between FCDO (strategic oversight), OPM/UNDP (technical delivery), and Pakistani government counterparts (e.g., Finance and Planning Departments in KP/Punjab/Sindh). The programme emphasizes **adaptive technical assistance** and **government ownership**, with local civil servants (e.g., deputy commissioners) playing key roles in implementation.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for government officials on PFM, planning, and disaster risk management
Mentorship for local governments (e.g., developing Annual Development Plans under new Local Government Acts)
Institutional strengthening (e.g., Punjab Social Protection Authority, KP Revenue Authority)
Knowledge transfer through pilot projects (e.g., e-procurement, climate budget tagging)
Guidelines for inclusive budgeting (e.g., engaging marginalized groups like women and people with disabilities)

partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider for KP and Punjab governments

partner_organizations.role: Primary counterpart for PFM, revenue, and service delivery reforms
