who_partners.quote: "The programme’s focus on governance and service delivery makes it a core DFID area of expertise and as such is best suited to delivery through DFID bilateral funds. However, there will be engagement with other HMG departments and cross-HMG funds, including the democracy and stabilisation programmes under the CSSF." (50807182.odt, Programme Design)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **contribution agreements** with UNDP and **contracts** with OPM/Delivery Associates. Funds are disbursed as **technical assistance** (not budget support) to government institutions, with payments tied to milestone-based delivery. The UNDP agreement includes a **results framework** and **VfM criteria**, while OPM operates under a performance-based contract.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme through two primary implementing partners: **OPM** (for KP/Punjab) and **UNDP** (for federal/PMO and Sindh). UNDP sub-contracts Delivery Associates for specific roadmap tasks. Quarterly steering committees with provincial governments review progress, and annual work plans are co-developed with counterparts. The structure is **closed** (no open calls for new partners) but **flexible** within the consortium.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not specified (but OPM was selected through a competitive process delayed by a legal challenge)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: OPM was selected based on its **proven track record** in SNG I (2013–2018), which scored ‘A+’ in annual reviews. UNDP was chosen for its existing relationship with the PMO (e.g., supporting the Strategic Roadmap unit) and its ability to coordinate with OPM. The selection prioritized **local expertise**, **government trust**, and **adaptive capacity** to respond to crises (e.g., COVID-19, floods).
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will require similar resources to those currently deployed by DFID for SNG. There is consequently confidence that there will be adequate capacity within the team." (50807182.odt, Quality Assurance) && "The existing contractual agreements with OPM and UNDP are ending in September 2023. Considering the protracted procurement process, initiating the amendments at the earliest will allow the team to extend the contract/agreements before their expiry." (D0003346.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Quarterly **steering committees** with provincial governments (KP and Punjab) review progress and adjust work plans. A **joint committee** (FCDO, OPM, UNDP) oversees federal-level reforms. The **Prime Minister’s Strategic Roadmap** is managed through a delivery unit within the PMO, supported by UNDP. Decision-making is **shared** between FCDO (strategic), implementers (operational), and government (prioritization).
how_governance.quote: "The programme is designed so that regular feedback on performance and dialogue with government and partners will allow outputs and indicators to be adjusted when appropriate to better address the overall theory of change." (50807182.odt, Flexibility) && "Progress against milestones is reported on a quarterly basis." (D0003324.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between **themes** (e.g., PFM, revenue, innovations) with government agreement, but require **FCDO approval** for major shifts (e.g., adding Sindh in 2023). The programme uses **annual work plans** (reviewed quarterly) to adjust activities based on context (e.g., floods, elections).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **adaptive management** through: 1) **Quarterly reviews** with governments to reprioritize activities; 2) **Innovation Challenge Fund** to test new approaches (e.g., e-governance, disaster risk financing); 3) **Pivots in response to crises** (e.g., COVID-19 recovery plans, 2022 flood response). The **Theory of Change** was revised post-COVID to include social protection and climate adaptation.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will establish annual work plans with government and then review these quarterly through formal steering committees with governments in KP and Punjab." (50807182.odt, Flexibility) && "SNG II helped both KP and Punjab plan for recovery, playing a central role in developing Punjab’s PKR 140 billion emergency package [...] and KP’s PKR 29 billion Azm-e-Nau economic recovery plan." (D0003346.odt, Changes to Original Business Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Implementing Partners (OPM/UNDP)** → **Government Counterparts** (no sub-grantees). UNDP sub-contracts Delivery Associates for specific tasks, adding a third layer in some cases.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Contribution Agreement [with UNDP] is agreed based on a robust results framework and value for money (VfM) criteria and progress against milestones is reported on a quarterly basis." (D0003324.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Contributions to existing World Bank governance programmes
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: World Bank focuses on **federal-level** audit/accounting/procurement, while SNG II targets **sub-national service delivery** and adaptive technical assistance.
SNG II prioritizes **supply-side reforms** (PFM, planning, revenue) to complement DFID’s demand-side programme (AAWAZ II).
Risk of eroding gains from SNG I and missing opportunities to consolidate decentralization reforms.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **closed consortium model** (OPM + UNDP) was chosen for: 1) **Proven track record**: OPM’s success in SNG I (A+ ratings, roadmap delivery); 2) **Government trust**: Existing relationships with KP/Punjab/PMO; 3) **Adaptive capacity**: Ability to pivot to crises (e.g., COVID-19, floods); 4) **Value for money**: Leveraging economies of scale (e.g., £48,000 return per £1 spent in Punjab); 5) **Risk mitigation**: UNDP’s robust procurement and fiduciary systems.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capacity developed may not be sustained post-programme.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Exit strategies embedded from design phase; focus on institutionalizing reforms (e.g., PFM Acts, social protection systems) and training mid-tier civil servants for continuity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Perception of UK interference.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme branded as **collaborative technical assistance**; high-level workshops co-hosted with governments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political instability disrupts reforms (e.g., 2022 no-confidence vote, delayed elections).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with **mid-tier civil servants** (more stable tenure) and **cross-party technical working groups** to ensure continuity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Uncertainty over local government structures (e.g., legal challenges in Punjab/Sindh).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on **deputy commissioners’ offices** (executive heads) as stable nuclei for district-level work.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High turnover of senior officials.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building targeted at **middle management** and **standard operating procedures (SOPs)** documented for continuity.

why_rationale.quote: "The programme’s level of risk is considered moderate. While it will likely work in some insecure areas – although districts are still to be selected – the experience from SNG is that good results can still be achieved in a challenging context. Political and delivery risks are partly mitigated through sound ongoing contextual analysis and a pragmatic approach to planning activities." (50807182.odt, Risk Appetite) && "The programme will not be uniformly UK Aid branded, as it is most effectively presented as the UK funding specialised technical expertise as part of a collaborative partnership." (50807182.odt, Communications Strategy)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **Local presence and trust** (e.g., OPM’s existing relationships with KP/Punjab); 2) **Conflict sensitivity expertise** (e.g., UNDP’s experience in crisis response); 3) **Ability to navigate political instability** (e.g., working with mid-tier civil servants). Security risks in KP/Sindh exclude partners without **in-country operational capacity**, while the need for **rapid disaster response** favors agile implementers like UNDP.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in KP/Sindh require partners with **local networks** and **conflict-sensitive approaches**.
Political instability demands partners who can engage **non-partisan technical counterparts** (e.g., civil servants).
Weak local government capacity necessitates **embedded technical assistance** (e.g., OPM advisors in Finance Departments).
Disaster response needs (e.g., 2022 floods) require partners with **emergency procurement systems** (e.g., UNDP’s frameworks).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (systemic PFM reforms + adaptive crisis response) shape a **hybrid delivery structure**: 1) **Long-term capacity building** (OPM for KP/Punjab) for PFM/planning; 2) **Agile crisis support** (UNDP for federal/Sindh) for floods/COVID-19; 3) **Innovation pilots** (e.g., e-governance) managed flexibly. The need for **government ownership** drives the **closed consortium** model, while **cross-province learning** (e.g., replicating KP’s Land Use Act in Sindh) requires centralized coordination (UNDP).
q28_linkages: Systemic PFM reforms → **OPM’s embedded advisors** in Finance Departments.
Crisis response (floods/COVID) → **UNDP’s rapid procurement** and PMO coordination.
Innovation pilots → **Challenge Fund** managed by implementers with government buy-in.
Social inclusion → **Gender-disaggregated data** requirements in all partner contracts.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid flood response in Sindh (2023) used existing UNDP systems (**efficient**) but limited local CSO engagement (**equity gap**). 2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: OPM (UK-based) leads technical PFM reforms (**efficiency**), while UNDP’s local hires ensure **government trust** (**equity**). 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Pilots in 6 districts (**targeted**) balance against province-wide systemic reforms (**scalable**).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.example: Sindh flood response (2023) prioritized **rapid UNDP-led support** over slower, participatory processes with local NGOs.
OPM’s **international PFM experts** accelerate reforms, but **local civil servants** lead implementation to ensure sustainability.
Innovation pilots in **3 districts** (e.g., Swat) test scalable models before province-wide adoption.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate-high risk profile** (FCAS, political instability) drives **intensive oversight**: 1) **Quarterly steering committees** with governments; 2) **Milestone-based payments** to implementers; 3) **Embedded advisors** in key departments (e.g., Finance, Planning). The **2022 floods** triggered a shift to **monthly check-ins** with Sindh counterparts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles through: 1) **OPM’s focus on mid-tier civil servants** (stable tenure for sustainability); 2) **UNDP’s training for deputy commissioners** (disaster response leaders); 3) **Joint development of SOPs** (e.g., flood preparedness drills) to institutionalize knowledge.
intersections.quote: "The programme’s focus on governance and service delivery makes it a core DFID area of expertise and as such is best suited to delivery through DFID bilateral funds. However, there will be engagement with other HMG departments and cross-HMG funds, including the democracy and stabilisation programmes under the CSSF." (50807182.odt, Coherence) && "SNG II will test these measures in mock exercises and drills in a small number of districts to identify where gaps exist in exercising effective risk governance." (D0003324.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks.risk: Reforms not sustained post-programme (e.g., PFM systems, revenue mobilization).
Political instability disrupts reform continuity (e.g., 2022 no-confidence vote, delayed local elections).
Low local government capacity hampers decentralization (e.g., 43,000 new KP officials with limited experience).
Climate shocks (floods, monsoons) divert resources from long-term reforms.
Perception of donor interference undermines government ownership.
High turnover of senior officials disrupts institutional memory.
Legal challenges to local government laws (e.g., Punjab/Sindh) limit district engagement.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Exit strategies embedded from design; focus on **institutionalizing reforms** (e.g., PFM Acts, SOPs) and training **mid-tier civil servants** (more stable tenure).
Engage **cross-party technical working groups** and **mid-level bureaucrats** (e.g., deputy commissioners) for continuity.
**Embedded advisors** in Finance/Planning Departments; **GIS units** for data-driven planning; **mock drills** for disaster preparedness.
**Climate budget tagging** (e.g., PKR 112 billion in Punjab 2022-23); **anticipatory measures** (e.g., KP’s Land Use Act for flood-prone areas).
Brand as **collaborative technical assistance**; co-host workshops with governments; avoid UK Aid branding in sensitive contexts.
Document **SOPs** and **knowledge repositories**; target **middle management** for capacity building.
Work with **deputy commissioners’ offices** (stable executive heads) and **provincial line departments** as fallback.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity is critical: Programme avoided **direct engagement in FATA** (security risks) but supported KP’s capacity to manage potential merger.
Adaptive management works: **Pivots to COVID-19/flood response** (e.g., Punjab’s PKR 140 billion emergency package) maintained relevance during crises.
Local ownership mitigates risks: **Government-led steering committees** and **co-developed work plans** reduced perception of external imposition.
Decentralization is fragile: **Recentralization trends** (e.g., KP’s 2017 LGA amendment) require flexible engagement at both provincial and local levels.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: SNG I (2013–2018) lessons applied in SNG II: 1) **Roadmap approach** (e.g., Punjab’s education reforms) delivers results when linked to **high-level political ownership** (e.g., Chief Minister’s office). 2) **GIS units** improve evidence-based planning (scaled from 6 districts in SNG I to province-wide in SNG II). 3) **Output-Based Budgeting** increases allocations (e.g., 19% rise in Punjab’s health/education budgets) but requires **spending efficiency** follow-up. 4) **Innovation pilots** (e.g., e-procurement) need **government buy-in** early to scale.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added **Sindh component (2023)** to address flood response gaps, replicating KP/Punjab models. 2) Expanded **social protection focus** post-COVID (e.g., Punjab’s informal worker registry). 3) Integrated **climate budget tagging** after 2022 floods. 4) **Extended timeline to 2026** to accommodate delayed procurement (legal challenge) and political transitions (2023 elections).
risks_lessons.quote: "The consequences of non-intervention are more significant. There is the risk that some reforms that SNG worked on over the past 5 years are not consolidated and the programme’s gains in terms of the functioning of provincial and district governments are eroded." (50807182.odt, Risks) && "SNG II helped both KP and Punjab plan for recovery, playing a central role in developing Punjab’s PKR 140 billion emergency package [...] and KP’s PKR 29 billion Azm-e-Nau economic recovery plan." (D0003346.odt, Changes to Original Business Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme’s support helped KP and Punjab generate **additional PKR 135 billion (£598 million)** in revenue and efficiency savings in FY 2021-22, equivalent to a **£48,000 return per £1 spent** in Punjab. This enabled increased spending on education (43% more) and health (21% more).
financial_details.quote: "In Punjab alone, this equates to a return of £48,000 for every £1 UK Aid spent, with 43% more spent on education and 21% more on health." (D0003324.odt, Achievement to Date) && "The total approved budget for this programme is £37 million. The programme has spent £14,318,037 million till the end of the financial year (FY) 2021-22 (38.6% of the overall programme budget)." (D0003346.odt, Financial Information)

metadata.programme_name: Montserrat Capital Investment Programme for Resilient Economic Growth (CIPREG)

quote.programme_name: "Montserrat Capital Investment Programme for Resilient Economic Growth (CIPREG)" (D0001167.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
quote.duration: "five years (2018-2023)" (D0001166.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.sector: "Strategic infrastructure development on Montserrat to support economic growth, enhance resilience against natural disasters and promote the role of the private sector." (D0001166.odt, Programme Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "The UK Government will provide up to £30 million over five years (2018-2023) for strategic infrastructure development on Montserrat" (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines infrastructure development (service delivery) with capacity building and private sector promotion. It aims to establish foundations for economic growth through capital investments while strengthening government capacity to manage projects and improve resilience against natural disasters.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The UK Government will provide up to £30 million over five years (2018-2023) for strategic infrastructure development on Montserrat, to support economic growth, enhance resilience against natural disasters and promote the role of private sector." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Fibre optic cable laid to Montserrat
Roads & bridges upgraded (including A1 road with underground ducting)
Power transmission and water supply distribution networks upgraded
Emergency shelters upgraded (internal facilities + new shelters)
Solid and liquid waste management improved (sewage treatment + recycling)
New hospital construction (primary/secondary care + acute mental health unit)
Airport runway resurfacing + night-time landing facility
Support for small-scale tourism infrastructure by private sector
Technical support for resilience in all programme components
Economic growth rate target

what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers capital infrastructure projects (roads, hospitals, utilities) while building government capacity and promoting private sector growth to achieve economic self-sufficiency for Montserrat.

quote.objectives: "The programme will support of GoM’s Economic Growth Strategy (EGS), thereby improving the island prospects for self-sufficiency by helping achieve the target economic growth rate of 3.5%." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.outputs: "The following outputs will be delivered under the programme: Fibre optic cable laid... Roads & bridges upgraded... Power transmission and water supply distribution networks upgraded..." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Montserrat faces ongoing risks from natural disasters (hurricanes/volcanic activity) and has limited institutional capacity, but is not classified as FCAS. The programme's risk rating is assessed as moderate by DFID's Overseas Territories Department.
where_context.q5_source: "Overseas Territories Department (OTD) assesses the risk of this programme to be moderate and therefore within DFID’s risk appetite." (D0001166.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The small population (≈5,000) limits human resource capacity for both government and private sector. Weak PFM systems create fiduciary risks. Hurricane vulnerability requires all infrastructure to meet resilience standards. Limited private sector reduces absorption capacity for challenge funds.

quote.constraints: "Montserrat is a small island state with limited capacity to support economic growth, and is at risk from natural disasters... The small private sector on island limits revenues from taxes, which impacts on GoM’s ability to undertake infrastructure development without UK assistance." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.PFM_risks: "AnumberofreviewsandassessmentshavetakenplaceofMontserrat’sPublicFinancialManagementsystemsoverthelastfewyears... Theseassessmentsandthereports...highlightedmanyweaknessesthatsuggestthatinvestmentsinMontserrathavetomanageasubstantialfiduciaryandcorruptionrisk." (D0001166.odt, Assessment of Financial Risk and Fraud)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Montserrat (GoM) with DFID/FCDO oversight
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared through a joint GoM-DFID Programme Board with DFID retaining veto power for critical decisions. The hybrid management model embeds technical assistance within GoM while maintaining DFID oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance embedded in GoM departments
training for local contractors via Public Works Department
procurement and project management capacity building
resilience technical support across all components
support for private sector enterprise development

partner_organizations.role: primary implementer (line ministries deliver projects)

partner_organizations.name: DFID/FCDO
partner_organizations.role: funding, oversight, and technical support

partner_organizations.role: technical assistance and programme management support (hybrid model)
