quote.partnership: "The programme will be monitored by a joint GoM-DFID Programme Board... DFID Core Team will have direct oversight of the programme delivery... GoM would be fully accountable and responsible for the implementation of its strategic priorities." (D0001166.odt, Management Case)
quote.capacity_building: "The proposed programme, in conjunction with GRID, and the TC component of Financial Aid, will further address the institutional reform and capacity building needs of GoM, providing a more favourable ground for the programme to achieve its outcomes." (D0001166.odt, Assessing Capacity)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct budget support to GoM (for smaller projects) and DFID-managed contracts (for larger/higher-risk projects). Funds are disbursed retrospectively against milestones via a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between GoM and DFID.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Hybrid model combining GoM-led implementation for smaller projects with a Managing Agent (MA) providing technical assistance for larger/complex projects. A joint GoM-DFID Programme Board oversees prioritization and monitoring, with DFID retaining veto power.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Managing Agent was selected via direct award due to limited market interest and GoM's positive progress in capacity building. The hybrid model was chosen to balance GoM ownership with DFID's need for assurance on value for money.

quote.selection: "TheappointmentofaManagementAgent...willbeundertakenbyDFID...followingpositiveprogressbyGoMandalackofinterestfromtheinternationalmarkettodeliverthiswork,thedeliveryapproachhaschanged." (D0001167.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The joint GoM-DFID Programme Board includes DFID (Programme Manager, Infrastructure Adviser, Economist), GoM (Financial Secretary, Accounting Officers), and the Managing Agent. It meets quarterly to monitor progress, set ambition levels, and approve project variations. A high-level DFID-FCO-GoM panel convenes bi-annually for strategic decisions.

quote.governance: "The programme will be monitored by a joint GoM-DFID Programme Board... It will meet quarterly (or if called on an ad-hoc basis)... The Programme Board will have complete control and oversight of the programme." (D0001166.odt, Management Case)
quote.oversight: "DFID Core Team will have direct oversight of the programme delivery... DFID Resident Representative and/or Programme Officer will continue to be observers on all GoM Public Procurement Board meetings and will have voting rights on all DFID funded capital projects’ procurements." (D0001166.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects with Programme Board approval, but major shifts require DFID veto. The programme is designed to "learn and adapt to changes in context" (D0001166.odt, Summary Sheet).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a "small change fund" for private sector support and technical assistance to adjust to emerging needs. Priorities can be revised through the joint Programme Board, with DFID retaining veto power for significant changes.

quote.flexibility: "The programme is designed to learn and adapt to changes in context, meeting newly identified infrastructure needs and changing management arrangements as required." (D0001166.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.adaptive: "A small change fund would support private sector development... The joint GoM and UKG (DFID and FCO) steering committee would ensure that programme priorities remain focused and implementation is monitored adequately." (D0001166.odt, Appraisal of Options)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO/DFID → Managing Agent/GoM → (sub-contractors for specific projects)

quote.layers: "DFID would be managing the payments and certification of MA Team work, while the MA Team would be jointly managed by a DFID-GoM panel." (D0001166.odt, Management Case)
quote.payments: "Funds will be provided to GoM from DFID’s OTD capital resources... The payments will be made under a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)... and will be paid retrospectively on a quarterly basis... on conditions of reconciled and up-to-date financial spend reports." (D0001166.odt, Financial Arrangements)

q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: Would lead to economic stagnation and increased future liabilities for UK aid.
Insufficient to achieve step-change in growth or resilience; past similar investments failed to deliver transformation.
Additional £8m unlikely to significantly alter growth projections; absorption capacity constraints.

q24_alternatives_considered.rationale: Balances GoM ownership with DFID assurance; addresses capacity gaps while maintaining focus on results.

q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: High fiduciary risk and lack of control over VfM due to GoM capacity limitations.
High cost and risk of MA not embedding in GoM systems, reducing local ownership.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The £30m hybrid model was selected because it: (1) provides sufficient scale to achieve Montserrat's 3.5% growth target; (2) includes technical assistance to address GoM capacity gaps; (3) balances local ownership with DFID oversight; and (4) allows flexibility to adapt to emerging needs while mitigating fiduciary risks through joint governance.
q25_decision_factors: flexibility (need to adapt to natural disasters and economic changes)
past experience (lessons from previous infrastructure programmes)
equity (ensuring benefits reach all communities, including gender/disability considerations)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoM capacity limitations leading to slow implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical assistance (MA team) and joint Programme Board oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs of hybrid model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of responsibilities (GoM for <£500k projects; DFID for larger ones) and annual performance reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Politicisation of MA team or projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Transparent prioritisation criteria and DFID veto power for major decisions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MA team perceived as external imposition
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fully embedded MA team working alongside GoM departments.

quote.rationale: "This option involves a much greater level of investment together with the requisite capacity support to GoM, through technical assistance, to be able to meet its economic growth and resilience needs... This is the preferred option." (D0001166.odt, Appraisal of Options)
quote.risks: "The key internal risks to the programme success are weaker than expected standard of public financial management and a failure to improve the existing procurement and project management procedures, resulting in poor value for money or slow project implementation." (D0001166.odt, Risks)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Montserrat's small size (≈5,000 population) and limited private sector constrain partner selection to mostly local/government entities with heavy reliance on DFID technical support. The island's vulnerability to natural disasters requires all partners to have resilience expertise, limiting the pool of qualified implementers.
q27_constraints_detail: Small population limits local contractor capacity
Natural disaster risks require specialised resilience expertise
Weak PFM systems necessitate DFID oversight
Limited private sector reduces absorption capacity for challenge funds
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for resilient infrastructure (WHAT) drives the hybrid delivery structure (HOW), combining GoM implementation with DFID/MA oversight to ensure quality. The economic growth objective requires both capital investments (delivered by GoM) and capacity building (delivered via embedded TA), shaping the mixed modality.
q28_linkages: Resilience requirements → hybrid management model (GoM + MA)
Economic growth targets → combination of capital projects + private sector support
Capacity gaps → embedded technical assistance
Fiduciary risks → DFID-led procurement for high-value projects
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (rapid delivery via MA) with equity (GoM ownership and local capacity building). Trade-offs include: (1) higher transaction costs for the hybrid model to ensure local embedding; (2) slower implementation to build GoM capacity; and (3) additional monitoring to ensure gender/disability inclusion.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Hybrid model slows implementation to build GoM capacity but ensures long-term sustainability.
MA provides technical expertise while embedded approach maintains GoM leadership.
Higher management costs for oversight ensure funds reach intended beneficiaries.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (natural disasters + weak institutions) justifies intensive oversight (quarterly Programme Board meetings, embedded advisors) and milestone-based payments to mitigate fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: GoM's limited capacity determines the hybrid structure: MA handles complex projects while GoM manages smaller ones, with technical assistance gradually transferring skills to local staff.

quote.context_who: "Montserrat is a small island state with limited capacity to support economic growth... The small private sector on island limits revenues from taxes, which impacts on GoM’s ability to undertake infrastructure development without UK assistance." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.what_how: "The programme will support of GoM’s Economic Growth Strategy (EGS)... through a combination of capital investments and technical assistance to address capacity gaps." (D0001166.odt, Intervention Summary)
quote.tradeoffs: "The construction industry employs a higher number of males than females... Training in construction is more likely to benefit boys, but gender equitable planning... will support gender equitable outreach." (D0001166.odt, Gender Analysis)

key_programme_risks: Weak public financial management leading to poor VfM
Natural disasters (hurricanes/volcanic activity) disrupting implementation
GoM capacity limitations causing delays
Limited private sector absorption capacity for challenge funds
Politicisation of project selection
High transaction costs of hybrid model
Currency exchange rate fluctuations increasing costs
Inflation exceeding budget allocations
Contractor failure to meet resilience standards
Low community buy-in for infrastructure projects

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded financial management technical assistance, joint Programme Board oversight, and milestone-based payments.
All infrastructure built to resilience standards; contingency funds; and flexible reallocation mechanisms.
Hybrid delivery model with MA support; gradual capacity transfer; and DFID veto for major decisions.
Phased challenge fund disbursement and technical support for business development.
Transparent prioritisation criteria with gender/disability inclusion requirements.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID programmes on Montserrat highlighted: (1) the need for embedded technical assistance to address capacity gaps; (2) the importance of resilience standards in infrastructure; (3) challenges with GoM-led procurement requiring DFID oversight; and (4) the value of joint governance structures to maintain focus.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The shift from a fully MA-led model to a hybrid approach (GoM + MA) reflects lessons about the importance of local ownership. The inclusion of a small change fund addresses past rigidities in responding to emerging needs.

quote.risks: "Weaker than expected standard of public financial management and a failure to improve the existing procurement and project management procedures, resulting in poor value for money or slow project implementation are the key internal risks." (D0001166.odt, Risks)
quote.lessons: "Previous experience on Montserrat also highlights significant implementation and delivery issues, which have been considered in the design of this programme." (D0001166.odt, Evidence Table)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme complements £14.4m from CDB for port infrastructure and €18.4m (≈£16m) from EU-EDF over 5 years, creating a total infrastructure investment package of ≈£60m when combined with CIPREG's £30m.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is capital-focused: "the vast majority of the work currently allocated as RDEL is of a non-recurrent nature and is designed to deliver capital projects" (D0001167.odt). All £30m was converted from RDEL to CDEL to reflect this.

quote.co_financing: "GoM has secured €18.4m of EU funding over 5 years under EDF-11... and £14.4m from the Caribbean Infrastructure Fund (CIF)... to extend the breakwater at Little Bay." (D0001166.odt, Summary of Options)
quote.capital_focus: "The objective of the addendum is to remove the split between RDEL and CDEL, changing all available budget to CDEL. As the vast majority of the work... is of a non-recurrent nature and is designed to deliver capital projects, it would be more appropriate for this to be managed as CDEL funding." (D0001167.odt, Objective)

metadata.programme_name: Trade and Investment Advocacy Fund (TAF2 Plus)
metadata.quote: "The Trade and Investment Advocacy Fund (TAF2+) helps improve compliance with and shaping of a free and fair global trading system through supporting developing countries in important trade negotiations, particularly in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) through technical assistance grants and logistical support to attend key negotiations meetings such as Ministerial Conferences." (D0006013.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 27/07/2016 to 30/06/2025" (D0006013.odt, Summary Information) and "New project end date (if applicable): 30 June 2026" (D0006013.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: TAF2+ primarily focuses on **capacity building** (strengthening skills and institutions in developing countries for trade negotiations) and **service delivery** (providing technical advice, logistical support, and legal assistance). It also includes elements of **policy influence** (shaping fairer trade agreements) and **financing mechanism** (channeling funds to support negotiations).
what_objectives.q1_source: "TAF2+ helps improve compliance with and shaping of a free and fair global trading system through supporting developing countries in important trade negotiations... through technical assistance grants and logistical support" (D0006013.odt, Summary Information) and "The programme will provide demand-led trade-related support through four windows: Negotiation Window, Strategic Window, Country Office Window, Institutional Support Window" (28249924.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased technical skills and coordination within developing countries’ trade and investment ministries
More effective participation of LDCs, LICs, LMICs, and Regional Economic Communities (RECs) in multilateral, regional, and bilateral trade negotiations and dispute settlement
Support to WTO accessions (e.g., Ethiopia, South Sudan, Somalia, Eritrea, Tuvalu, Timor-Leste, Kiribati)
Legal advice and training for WTO dispute settlement via the Advisory Centre on WTO Law (ACWL)
Pre-negotiation analysis, ratification, and pre-implementation strategy planning for trade agreements
Logistical support (flights, accommodation, subsistence) for attendance at key negotiations (e.g., WTO Ministerial Conferences)
Commissioned studies and knowledge products for DFID country offices (8 requests/year)
Support to the Enhanced Integrated Framework (EIF) Interim Facility for LDCs
Skills training for long-term capacity building (e.g., negotiation skills, trade analysis)
Funding to niche organizations (e.g., ACWL, International Institute for Sustainable Development)
what_objectives.summary: TAF2+ aims to level the playing field in global trade negotiations by providing demand-led technical assistance, logistical support, and capacity building to developing countries, particularly LDCs and ACP groups, to ensure fairer trade agreements and better harnessing of trade benefits for poverty reduction.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected outcome is that government ministries have better technical skills to be able to develop clear strategies, negotiation positions and steer subsequent wider related interventions. This should lead to (Impact) more developing countries effectively participating, to their advantage, in trade and investment negotiations with an ability to harness the benefits of those outcomes through meaningful strategies and wider donor co-ordination." (28249924.odt, Impact and Outcome)

countries_regions: DFID priority countries (28 countries, including 19 supported by TAF1)
Specific countries: Ethiopia, South Sudan, Somalia, Eritrea, Tuvalu, Timor-Leste, Kiribati, Gambia, Uganda, Malawi, Vanuatu, Sierra Leone, Burma (Myanmar)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a complex global trade environment with political and economic risks, but the overall risk rating is classified as 'moderate.' Developing countries face constraints like limited technical capacity and small delegations, but TAF2+ mitigates these through targeted support.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (28249924.odt, Summary Sheet) and "LDCs and developing countries have much smaller delegations and lack the technical capacity that developed countries can deploy" (D0006013.odt, Summary Information)
q6_contextual_constraints: lack of coordination within and across government ministries
complexity of WTO and investment dispute mechanisms
plurilateral negotiation challenges (new substantive issues and mechanisms)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Developing countries struggle to participate effectively in negotiations due to limited personnel (e.g., African countries average 2-3 officers for WTO committees), lack of financial resources for travel/logistics, and weak institutional memory. This leads to unequal representation, with LDCs making fewer submissions and focusing only on high-level meetings. The constraints also affect post-negotiation implementation, where ministries lack skills to harness trade agreement benefits.
where_context.quote: "An inability in some developing countries to participate effectively – to their advantage - in trade and investment negotiations and secure deals that are pro development... Where trade and investment deals are secured, some developing countries lack the ability to harness the benefits through meaningful strategies and wider donor co-ordination." (28249924.odt, Why is UK support required?) and "On average, most African countries had only two to three officers covering the WTO, yet the WTO runs more than four parallel committee meetings per day." (28249924.odt, Constraints that block developing countries)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Trade Policy Unit (TPU) - a tri-departmental unit (DFID, Foreign Office, Department for Business, Innovation and Skills)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Trade Policy Unit (TPU), based in the UK, manages the programme and selects implementing partners through competitive processes. Southern partners (e.g., ACWL, EIF) receive funding but do not lead decision-making or programme design.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical advice and skills training for trade negotiators
long-term advisory support and job-sharing with international advisors
pre-negotiation and pre-implementation strategy planning
institutional reforms in trade ministries
legal training via ACWL for WTO dispute settlement
knowledge products for DFID country offices
support to National Implementation Units (EIF)

partner_organizations.name: Advisory Centre on WTO Law (ACWL)
partner_organizations.role: Provides legal advice, training, and dispute settlement support to developing countries

partner_organizations.name: Enhanced Integrated Framework (EIF)
partner_organizations.role: Supports LDCs in trade strategy development and implementation

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Island Forum (PIF)
partner_organizations.role: Regional group receiving negotiation support (co-funded by Australia’s DFAT)

partner_organizations.name: International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD)
partner_organizations.role: Provides investment-related technical advice and arbitration support

partner_organizations.name: Fund Manager (contracted)
partner_organizations.role: Manages grant portfolio, allocates funds across windows, and oversees implementation

partner_organizations.name: DFID Country Offices
partner_organizations.role: Receive trade-related research and design support via the Country Office Window

partner_organizations.name: WTO Umbrella Grant recipients
partner_organizations.role: Regional and plurilateral negotiation groups (e.g., LDC Group, ACP Group)

who_partners.quote: "DFID will contract out £14 million of programme funds to external parties to deliver the services... The Trade Policy Unit (TPU) would be able to continue to draw on its tri-departmental expertise, its FCO and DFID networks and integrated policy and programming to deliver greater benefits." (28249924.odt, Intervention Summary) and "TAF2+ is the only programme supporting negotiations capacity building at the WTO... LDCs and developing countries have much smaller delegations and lack the technical capacity that developed countries can deploy, so TAF2+ support helps to level the playing field." (D0006013.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: TAF2+ uses a combination of **accountable grants** (for organizations like ACWL and EIF), **technical assistance grants** (for negotiation support), and **contracts** (for the Fund Manager). The programme also includes **logistical support** (e.g., flights, accommodation) as in-kind contributions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A **Fund Manager** is contracted to implement the grants portfolio, allocate funds across the four windows (Negotiation, Strategic, Country Office, Institutional Support), and oversee day-to-day delivery. DFID/FCDO retains oversight and approves major allocations. The ACWL and EIF are managed via separate accountable grant agreements (AGAs).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Fund Manager is selected through a competitive tendering process to ensure value for money and expertise in managing demand-led technical assistance. For the ACWL and EIF, DFID enters into direct AGAs based on their specialized roles and alignment with programme objectives.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID will contract out £14 million of programme funds to external parties to deliver the services. This excludes management fees which can only be determined during the competitive tendering process." (28249924.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The TAF2+ programme will be monitored through monthly financial reports, quarterly management reports and meetings with the fund manager and other implementing partners." (D0004080.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.quote: "The TAF2+ programme will be monitored through monthly financial reports, quarterly management reports and meetings with the fund manager and other implementing partners." (D0004080.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "DFID will work in consultation with the Fund Manager to ensure funds are used effectively." (28249924.odt, Negotiation Window)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be flexed and allocated across the various grants as required, but major reallocations (e.g., between windows) likely require FCDO approval. The programme has built-in contingency for in-year demands (e.g., COVID-19 response).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can respond to emerging needs (e.g., new plurilateral agreements, WTO accessions) but requires FCDO consultation for significant shifts. The Fund Manager has discretion to target funds based on demand and potential impact.
how_flexibility.quote: "Financial resources being flexed and allocated across the various grants as required." (D0004080.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The selected Fund Manager would be required to target funding at countries which demonstrated the most need and negotiations most likely to bring the highest return on economic growth and poverty reduction." (28249924.odt, Negotiation Window)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager → Beneficiaries (e.g., LDC/ACP groups, ACWL, EIF). Some components (e.g., ACWL) are directly managed via AGAs, reducing layers.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Fund Manager would be responsible for all activities except for the institutional window which would be managed [directly]." (28249924.odt, Overarching Costs) and "The programme will be monitored through... quarterly management reports." (D0004080.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (Option A)
Aid delivered through other organisations (Option B)
Business as usual: Phase two retains the current structure (Option C)
Enhanced and Integrated Trade and Investment Programme (Option D - chosen)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **Enhanced and Integrated Trade and Investment Programme (Option D)** was selected to address gaps in TAF1, including the need for **pre-negotiation and pre-implementation support**, **longer-term skills training**, and **better coordination with DFID country offices**. It allows for a **comprehensive package** combining trade and investment, cross-project synergies, and sustainable capacity building in DFID priority countries. The platform model also enables flexibility to respond to emerging needs (e.g., plurilateral agreements, WTO accessions).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (e.g., leveraging existing TPU expertise and networks)
risk mitigation (e.g., avoiding gaps in negotiation support during WTO Ministerial Conferences)
past experience (e.g., lessons from TAF1 on sustainability and skills transfer)
partner capacity (e.g., ACWL’s specialized legal expertise for dispute settlement)
flexibility (e.g., demand-led support for new agreements like the Environmental Goods Agreement)
equity (e.g., targeting LDCs and countries with limited alternative donor support)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UK implicated in advice or criticized for supporting non-UK interests
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Independent technical advice and tri-departmental oversight (TPU) to ensure neutrality and alignment with development goals.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Short-term support fails to build sustainable ministry expertise
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Longer-term advisory support, skills training, and pre-/post-negotiation engagement (Strategic Window).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination gaps lead to duplication or gaps
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fund Manager coordinates with other donors (e.g., EU, World Bank) and DFID country offices to align support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund Manager underperforms or misallocates funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly monitoring, milestone-based payments, and FCDO oversight of allocations.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (streamlined fund manager model with 2 organizational layers)
effectiveness (targeted support to LDCs/ACP groups with highest needs)
equity (focus on least-developed countries and gender-inclusive trade policies)
why_rationale.quote: "Option D: Enhanced and Integrated Trade and Investment Programme... would allow for cross project synergies and broader skills training... At the centre of this support would be a focus on sustainable and transformative change... through enhanced skills training and better co-ordinated approaches to trade policy." (28249924.odt, Option D) and "The UK has also provided funding to International Institute of Sustainable Development (IISD) which helps developing countries effectively participate in international investment negotiations and arbitrations... DFID has established a leadership role in supporting developing countries to integrate into global trade and investment negotiations." (28249924.odt, Why DFID should intervene)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope** and **WTO-centric focus** constrain partner selection to organizations with multilateral reach (e.g., ACWL, EIF) and expertise in WTO processes. The need to support **LDCs and ACP groups** limits partners to those with regional networks (e.g., Pacific Island Forum) or specialized legal/institutional capacity (e.g., IISD for investment disputes).
q27_constraints_detail: WTO’s complex legal and negotiation environment requires partners with specialized expertise (e.g., ACWL for dispute settlement).
LDCs’ limited resources and small delegations necessitate partners who can provide logistical and technical support at scale.
Geographic spread (global) favors multilateral or platform-based partners over single-country implementers.
DFID priority countries focus requires partners with existing in-country presence or DFID relationships.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The **demand-led, negotiation-focused objectives** determine the **platform-based delivery structure**: 
- **Four windows** (Negotiation, Strategic, Country Office, Institutional) reflect the need for flexible, targeted support at different stages (pre-negotiation to implementation).
- **Fund Manager model** enables rapid allocation of technical/financial resources to emerging needs (e.g., new plurilateral agreements).
- **Direct AGAs with ACWL/EIF** ensure specialized services (legal advice, LDC strategy support) are embedded.
q28_linkages: Negotiation support (WHAT) → Fund Manager model (HOW) for agile allocation across countries/groups.
Capacity building (WHAT) → Long-term Strategic Window (HOW) for sustainable skills transfer.
WTO dispute settlement needs (WHAT) → ACWL partnership (HOW) for legal expertise.
DFID country office integration (WHAT) → Country Office Window (HOW) for localized research.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting LDCs, ACP, and countries with no alternative donor support) with **efficiency** (using a single Fund Manager to avoid duplication). Trade-offs include: 
- **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid response to negotiations (e.g., MC13) vs. ensuring all LDCs benefit (mitigated by pre-allocated funds for LDC/ACP groups).
- **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led Fund Manager for efficiency vs. Southern capacity building (mitigated by long-term training and job-sharing).
- **Cost vs. reach**: Capped logistical support to maximize participation vs. budget constraints (mitigated by contingency funds).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (Fund Manager/TPU) vs. Southern ownership (e.g., ACWL’s role in legal advice).
Targeted support to DFID priority countries vs. global accessibility (mitigated by Negotiation Window for all LDCs/LMICs).
Short-term negotiation wins vs. long-term institutional reform (addressed via Strategic Window).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., political sensitivity of trade negotiations, capacity gaps in LDCs) drives **quarterly oversight** and **milestone-based payments**. High-risk components (e.g., WTO dispute settlement) use specialized partners (ACWL) with direct AGAs for tighter control.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 
- **ACWL**: Focused on legal training and dispute settlement skills.
- **EIF**: Strengthening National Implementation Units for LDC trade strategies.
- **Fund Manager**: Required to include skills transfer in all project proposals.
intersections.quote: "The programme would be split across four new distinct windows of support... The key services provided under TAF1 would remain at the core... Sustainability would be at the core of the window which would focus on long-term advisory support and skills training." (28249924.odt, Option D) and "LDCs and developing countries have much smaller delegations and lack the technical capacity that developed countries can deploy, so TAF2+ support helps to level the playing field." (D0006013.odt, Summary Information)

key_programme_risks: UK criticized for supporting non-UK interests in negotiations.
Trade agreements fail to reduce poverty or benefit women.
Short-term support does not build sustainable ministry expertise.
Poor coordination with other donors leads to gaps/duplication.
Fund Manager underperforms or misallocates funds.
Developing countries refrain from public-interest policies due to ISDS fears.
LDCs unable to participate in MC13 or other critical negotiations due to logistical/funding gaps.
EIF Interim Facility fails to preserve National Implementation Units during transition.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UK implicated in advice or criticized for non-UK interests
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Independent technical advice via ACWL and tri-departmental TPU oversight to ensure neutrality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Agreements do not reduce poverty or benefit women
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Gender-aware programme design, monitoring of gender impacts in agreements, and targeted support to women’s economic participation.
Strategic Window for long-term skills training, pre-/post-negotiation support, and institutional reforms.
Fund Manager aligns with EU, World Bank, and DFID country offices; regular coordination meetings.
IISD support for investment negotiation capacity and ACWL legal advice to strengthen defenses.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: LDCs miss MC13 due to funding gaps
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pre-allocated logistical support budget (£200k for MC13) and contingency funds.
Interim Facility funding to preserve National Implementation Units during successor programme design.

fcas_specific_lessons: Small delegations and limited technical capacity in LDCs require **pre-negotiation support** and **logistical assistance** to ensure participation (e.g., MC13 in Cameroon).
Conflict-affected or post-conflict countries (e.g., South Sudan, Somalia) need **flexible, rapid-response funding** to engage in negotiations.
Institutional memory gaps in FCAS contexts necessitate **longer-term advisory support** and **knowledge hubs** (e.g., commissioned studies for DFID country offices).
Gendered constraints in trade (e.g., women’s limited access to export opportunities) require **targeted capacity building** and **monitoring of gender impacts** in agreements.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
TAF1’s Mid-Term Review (2014) highlighted needs for: 
1. **Broader, longer-term skills training** (TAF1’s short-term support often did not lead to sustained capacity).
2. **Pre-negotiation and post-agreement support** (e.g., Uganda and Gambia projects struggled without groundwork).
3. **Better coordination within ministries** (e.g., investment agreement negotiators often unaware of trade commitments).
4. **Donor alignment** (TAF1’s comprehensive approach filled gaps left by fragmented Aid for Trade programmes).
5. **Gender integration** (limited attention to women’s roles in trade; TAF2+ includes gender-aware indicators).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
TAF2+ incorporated lessons by: 
- Adding a **Strategic Window** for pre-negotiation/post-implementation support.
- Extending skills training duration and emphasizing **job-sharing with international advisors**.
- Including **gender capacity gaps** in partner selection criteria.
- Creating a **Country Office Window** to institutionalize trade sensitivity in DFID programmes.
- Allocating funds for **WTO accessions** (e.g., Ethiopia, Timor-Leste) and **plurilateral agreements** (e.g., Environmental Goods Agreement).
- Direct AGAs with **ACWL and EIF** to ensure specialized services are sustained.
risks_lessons.quote: "The TAF1 review recommended that broader trade strategy planning, such as the formulation of consultative structures within the ministries, were essential to fully embedding the support provided... Long-term skills training would ensure donor interventions were sustained." (28249924.odt, Some developing countries lack broader and more sustainable approaches) and "The first key change to the Business Case is the increase in total value from £16m to £23m as well as the time extension of 15 months... The second key change... is the addition of a new component to fund the extension of Phase II of the EIF." (D0004080.odt, Key changes to the original business case)

co_funding_partners.partner: Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: TAF2+ secured additional funding from DFAT to continue support to the Pacific Island Forum (PIF), demonstrating donor coordination and resource mobilization. The programme also leverages multilateral partnerships (e.g., WTO, ACWL, EIF) to extend reach beyond bilateral UK support.
financial_details.quote: "The additional cost of the extension will be £7m, which will bring the total budget of the TAF2+ programme to £23m, an increase of 43.75%." (D0004080.odt, Additional and total support) and "The Fund Manager would be responsible for all activities except for the institutional window which would be managed [directly]... The total Programme Fund would be £14m excluding management fees." (28249924.odt, Overarching Costs)

metadata.programme_name: Supporting the Africa-led Movement to End FGM: Phase II
metadata.quote: "DFID will provide up to £35 million over a period of 5 years (starting April 2019) for a second phase of support to efforts to end Female Genital Mutilation (FGM)" (46360584.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "5 years (starting April 2019)" (46360584.odt, Programme Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing/scaling interventions), capacity building (strengthening grassroots organizations and activists), policy influence (supporting laws and policies), and service delivery (protection and care services). It aims to accelerate the abandonment of FGM through community-led social norms change, supported by enabling environments and global advocacy.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Building on significant learning and evidence generated by our first phase of investment in ending FGM, DFID will spend £35 million over 5 years to work innovatively to address FGM at scale... through three complementary and mutually reinforcing approaches: 1) Supporting and building the capacity of the Africa-led movement to end FGM... 2) Getting laws, policies and systems at multiple levels to work effectively to end FGM... 3) Generate the right data to guide interventions and measure change." (46360584.odt, What will we do?)
q3_expected_outputs: 24 million people pledged to abandon FGM (Phase I baseline)
6 countries introduced national budget lines for tackling FGM (Phase I baseline)
3 million girls and women received FGM protection and care services (Phase I baseline)
700+ grassroots activists and organizations built capacity (Phase I baseline)
4-6 strategic countries/regions for intensive community support (Phase II)
Global small-grants mechanism for grassroots organizations
Best practice guidance on integrating FGM interventions into existing development programmes
Improved data and measurement tools for FGM incidence and social norms change
Laws, policies, and national action plans implemented in focus countries
Media campaigns and global advocacy to amplify ending FGM messages
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to accelerate the abandonment of FGM by 2030 through a multipronged approach: intensive community support in 4-6 African countries, capacity building for grassroots movements, integration of FGM interventions into existing development programmes, and global advocacy. It builds on Phase I achievements (2013-2018) and addresses critical gaps in data, cross-border coordination, and scaling effective interventions.
what_objectives.quote: "The intended impact of this programme is a significant reduction of the practice of FGM in focus countries/regions by 2024. The intended outcome of this programme is the acceleration of positive change in social attitudes towards ending FGM in countries/regions in which the programme is operational." (46360584.odt, Impact and outcome)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in contexts where FGM is deeply rooted in social norms, often taboo, and involves sensitive cultural practices. Political and social resistance, weak enforcement of laws, and cross-border complexities increase delivery risks. The document explicitly states the overall risk profile as 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk profile for this second phase of programming is likely to remain ‘Major’. As with our first phase of investment, there are delivery and reputational risks associated with working on this issue." (46360584.odt, Does the proposed level of risk to be taken fit with DFID’s risk appetite for this portfolio?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security and political economy constraints limit access to some communities and require careful navigation of local power structures. Weak institutions hinder enforcement of laws and policies. Data limitations (e.g., reliance on self-reported FGM status with a 10-year lag) make real-time monitoring difficult. Social norms around FGM being taboo require culturally sensitive approaches, and cross-border practices necessitate coordinated regional strategies.
where_context.quote: "FGM is a deep-rooted practice... deeply embedded in many communities... Working to change social norms is extremely difficult... programming must therefore be highly context-specific... measuring social norms change is challenging... the programme will have to test new thinking on how best to do this." (46360584.odt, Risks and What are partners doing?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed to be "Africa-led," with DFID providing support and acceleration to locally driven efforts. Decision-making for community-level interventions and grassroots activities is explicitly devolved to Southern partners (e.g., grassroots organizations, activists, and civil society networks), while DFID retains oversight of strategic direction, funding allocation, and global advocacy.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for grassroots activists and organizations
mentorship through small-grants and network mechanisms
institutional strengthening of civil society coalitions
co-authorship of best practice guidance (e.g., integrating FGM interventions into development programmes)
research grants for operational research and data improvement

partner_organizations.name: Africa-led movement consortium (ALM)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver comprehensive support to communities, grassroots grants, media campaigns, and global advocacy

partner_organizations.name: UN Joint Programme on FGM
partner_organizations.role: Support laws, policies, and sectoral integration (health, education, justice)

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Support health sector integration and policy implementation

partner_organizations.name: Data and Measurement (DM) supplier
partner_organizations.role: Conduct in-depth data analysis and improve measurement tools

partner_organizations.name: Grassroots women’s organizations and activists
partner_organizations.role: Lead community-level change and hold governments accountable

who_partners.quote: "This programme will be the UK’s (and currently the world’s) largest donor investment in ending FGM... We will also test and produce best practice guidance on how to integrate ending FGM interventions into existing development programmes... We will catalyse these interventions through the use of media and campaigns to amplify and diffuse the process of change, and enhanced global advocacy." (46360584.odt, What will we do?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for the ALM consortium and DM supplier, selected through tendering) and partnerships with multilateral organizations (UN Joint Programme and WHO). Grassroots grants are likely sub-awarded through a competitive or participatory process managed by the ALM consortium.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through four distinct entities: 1) an ALM consortium (contract), 2-3) UN Joint Programme and WHO (partnership agreements), and 4) a DM supplier (contract). Each entity has a defined scope, with DFID coordinating overall strategy and approvals (e.g., co-creation phase outputs). The ALM consortium acts as a closed group for community-level and advocacy work, while UN/WHO handle policy and sectoral integration.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The ALM and DM components underwent a procurement process, implying open competition to select the most capable partners. The rationale emphasizes the need for context-specific expertise, adaptive management, and alignment with the programme’s principles (e.g., community-led, do no harm).
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will have four entities managing the implementation... 1) A consortium to deliver support to the Africa-led movement to end FGM (ALM)... 4) A supplier (tendered) to deliver work on data and measurement (DM). The ALM and DM components are approaching the end of the procurement process." (54075071.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes a co-creation phase where DFID works with partners to agree on interventions, followed by DFID approval of the final results framework. This suggests a steering committee or joint decision-making structure, though the exact composition is not detailed. Oversight is adaptive, with real-time monitoring and feedback loops.
how_governance.quote: "Once the contract is signed there will be a 6-9 month co-creation phase during which DFID will work with the ALM and DM suppliers to agree a schedule of interventions... This will be an adaptive programme, which will learn from testing interventions and measuring them in close to real-time. The final results framework... will be subject to DFID approval." (54075071.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., community support vs. advocacy) with DFID approval, as evidenced by the adaptive programming design and real-time monitoring. However, the closed consortium structure may limit flexibility between entities (ALM vs. UN/WHO).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme explicitly includes adaptive management with rapid feedback loops, real-time monitoring, and a co-creation phase to adjust strategies. Changes require DFID approval but are encouraged based on emerging evidence (e.g., "flexible programming approach with rapid feedback loops").
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will also commence with a 6-9 month co-creation phase... enabling DFID to work with our preferred partners to shape the context-specific elements of the programme... inbuilt monitoring, learning and flexibility is a significant design feature of this programme." (46360584.odt, Does the programme have sufficient flexibility?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ALM Consortium/UN/WHO/DM Supplier → Grassroots Organizations/Activists. The ALM consortium and DM supplier act as intermediaries, with sub-awards to local partners.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will have four entities managing the implementation... The ALM and DM components are approaching the end of the procurement process." (54075071.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral country programmes (e.g., Sudan, Somalia)
Multilateral-only approach (e.g., UN Joint Programme Phase III)
Direct funding to grassroots organizations without intermediaries
Regional cross-border programmes
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (consortium + multilateral + tendered supplier) was chosen to balance scale, flexibility, and local ownership. A centrally managed programme was deemed necessary to address global challenges (e.g., data gaps, cross-border issues) while allowing country-specific adaptation. The consortium model enables rapid testing of interventions, and the inclusion of UN/WHO leverages their policy influence and sectoral expertise. Grassroots grants ensure local leadership, aligning with the "Africa-led" principle.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (leveraging UN/WHO for policy work and consortium for innovation)
risk-mitigation (diversifying partners to spread delivery risk)
experience (building on Phase I lessons, e.g., cross-border focus)
partner-capacity (selecting entities with proven track records in social norms change)
equity (prioritizing Southern-led implementation and grassroots access)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating multiple entities (ALM, UN, WHO, DM) may create fragmentation or misalignment in strategies.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Co-creation phase and DFID’s oversight role to ensure integration; shared results framework.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Closed consortium structure could limit responsiveness to emerging local needs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adaptive management with rapid feedback loops and flexibility to adjust interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on intermediaries (ALM consortium) for grassroots funding may slow disbursement or dilute local ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity-building for grassroots organizations and tapered funding to encourage donor diversification.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (streamlined through four entities with clear roles)
equity (prioritizing high-prevalence, high-risk regions and marginalized groups)
why_rationale.quote: "A centrally managed programme... There remains a need to tackle and solve global challenges; such as those around data and measurement... test proof of concept for strategies to end FGM at scale... undertake much-needed global advocacy... This centrally managed programme is designed to help end FGM at scale but to also lay the foundations on which future country level programmes can be built." (46360584.odt, A centrally managed programme)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk, multi-country context limits partner selection to organizations with proven experience in navigating sensitive social norms, cross-border dynamics, and weak institutional environments. For example, the need for sub-national and cross-border approaches (e.g., Somalia-Ethiopia-Kenya) requires partners with regional expertise and trust in local communities. Security constraints in some areas may exclude less experienced actors.
q27_constraints_detail: Cross-border issues require partners with regional networks (e.g., ALM consortium).
Taboo nature of FGM necessitates culturally embedded partners (e.g., grassroots activists).
Weak institutions limit reliance on government partners alone, increasing need for civil society intermediaries.
Data limitations demand partners with research capacity (e.g., DM supplier).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The multipronged objective (community support + policy + data + advocacy) necessitates a mixed delivery structure. Intensive community work requires localized, flexible partners (ALM consortium), while policy influence leverages multilateral actors (UN/WHO). The need for real-time data and adaptive learning drives the inclusion of a dedicated DM supplier. Global advocacy and cross-border work justify a centrally managed, multi-entity approach rather than bilateral programmes.
q28_linkages: Community-level social norms change → requires grassroots-led consortium with sub-grants.
Policy and sectoral integration → requires UN/WHO partnerships for legitimacy and reach.
Data gaps → requires specialized DM supplier for technical expertise.
Scaling interventions → requires adaptive management and feedback loops across all entities.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (Southern leadership, grassroots access) with efficiency (centralized management, economies of scale). For example: 1) Grassroots grants ensure local ownership but may be slower than top-down approaches; 2) The ALM consortium provides coordination but adds a layer between FCDO and communities; 3) Cross-border focus maximizes impact but increases complexity. The co-creation phase and adaptive management are designed to mitigate these tensions.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Grassroots grants take time but ensure local relevance.
Expertise vs. ownership: UN/WHO bring technical skills but may overshadow local voices.
Cost vs. reach: Intensive community support in 4-6 countries limits geographic spread but deepens impact.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk profile drives intensive oversight (milestone-based, DFID approvals) and adaptive structures (real-time monitoring, feedback loops). For example, the co-creation phase and flexible funding are direct responses to the high uncertainty in social norms change.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is core to the programme’s design, shaping partner roles explicitly: 1) Grassroots organizations receive grants and training to lead community interventions; 2) The ALM consortium is tasked with strengthening civil society networks to hold governments accountable; 3) The DM supplier’s role includes improving local data capacity. This ensures Southern partners move from recipients to leaders.
intersections.quote: "Partners will be required to define and demonstrate these [principles] clearly in programme design and implementation... Supporting, enabling, facilitating and strengthening efforts to end the practice that are led from within affected communities and countries." (46360584.odt, Impact and outcome)

key_programme_risks: Social norms backlash: Resistance from communities or leaders to abandoning FGM, potentially undermining progress.
Political instability: Changes in government or conflict disrupting programme implementation (e.g., in Somalia or Sudan).
Data limitations: Inability to measure real-time progress due to reliance on lagged, self-reported data.
Partner coordination: Fragmentation among ALM consortium, UN, WHO, and DM supplier leading to misaligned strategies.
Reputational risk: Backlash from criticizing cultural practices or perceived external imposition.
Sustainability: Dependency on donor funding without long-term local ownership or government commitment.
Cross-border complexities: Legal or logistical barriers to coordinated action in regions like Somalia-Ethiopia-Kenya.
Medicalization of FGM: Laws or policies inadvertently driving the practice underground or into health settings.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Community-led approaches with structured packages of support, ensuring local ownership and gradual change. Use of influential individuals (e.g., faith leaders, teachers) to model abandonment.
Flexible programming with rapid adaptation to context changes; focus on sub-national regions with stable local partners.
DM supplier’s work to improve real-time measurement tools and analyze existing data for strategic insights.
Co-creation phase to align interventions; DFID oversight and shared results framework.
Africa-led framing, sensitivity to local terminology (e.g., using ‘cutting’ where appropriate), and unbranded campaigns in sensitive contexts.
Capacity-building for grassroots organizations; tapered funding to encourage diversified donor support; integration into existing development programmes (e.g., health, education).
Explicit focus on cross-border regions in programme design; partners with regional expertise and networks.
Supporting health sectors to enforce bans on medicalized FGM; monitoring shifts in practice patterns.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS (e.g., Somalia, Sudan), programme design must account for: 1) Sub-national variation in FGM prevalence and drivers; 2) Non-state actors (e.g., faith leaders, clan elders) as key influencers; 3) Rapidly changing security contexts requiring adaptive management.

Lessons from Sudan and Somalia programmes highlight the need for: a) Health sector engagement to address medicalization; b) Cross-border coordination to prevent displacement of the practice; c) Localized messaging to avoid backlash.
Phase I showed that in FCAS, intensive community support must be paired with high-level advocacy to create an enabling environment for change.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase I (2013–2018) demonstrated that: 1) Comprehensive, structured community support over several years is effective in changing attitudes and behavior; 2) Change must be community-led to be sustainable; 3) Laws and policies alone are insufficient without complementary social norms work; 4) Cross-border issues require explicit attention; 5) Flexible, adaptive programming is critical to respond to emerging opportunities or challenges. These lessons directly shaped Phase II’s design, including the focus on fewer countries for deeper impact, the grassroots grants mechanism, and the DM component to address data gaps.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase II adjustments based on Phase I lessons include: 1) Concentrating intensive efforts in 4-6 countries/regions (vs. 17 in Phase I) for greater depth; 2) Explicit cross-border focus; 3) Integrating FGM interventions into existing development programmes (e.g., WASH, health) to leverage their reach; 4) Enhanced data and measurement tools to address lagged indicators; 5) Greater role for WHO based on Sudan programme success; 6) Adaptive management with real-time feedback loops.
risks_lessons.quote: "Key recommendations from [Phase I] Annual Reviews... Develop a programme approach which optimises opportunities for achieving change at scale... Consider a more concentrated approach in fewer countries to achieve more deep-rooted change... Pay particular attention to cross-border issues... Adopt a flexible programming approach with rapid feedback loops." (46360584.odt, Box 5: recommendations for Phase II)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Phase I leveraged $4.4m in additional donor funding for grassroots activists and organizations. Phase II aims to encourage more donors through tapered funding and global advocacy, though specific leverage targets are not stated.
financial_details.quote: "DFID was the biggest donor to Phase II of the UN Joint Programme, so now that this programme has secured additional funding streams DFID has the option to pivot to a greater focus on complementary work... Both DFID and the UN Joint Programme are working towards the same long-term vision." (46360584.odt, What are partners doing?)

metadata.programme_name: Data and Evidence to Tackle Extreme Poverty (DETEP)

quote.text: "This research will help us to better understand the changing nature of extreme poverty; and use this to deliver DFID’s core business—support more effective strategies, policies and programmes for poverty reduction, in particular in fragile and conflict-affected states and situations (FCAS)."

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: April 2018", "End Date: April 2025" (90000585.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research on extreme poverty), implementation research (testing anti-poverty approaches), and policy influence (informing DFID strategies). It focuses on improving data, analyzing poverty drivers, and evaluating interventions in fragile contexts.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This research will help us to better understand the changing nature of extreme poverty; and use this to deliver DFID’s core business—support more effective strategies, policies and programmes for poverty reduction..." (90000585.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: better data and measures of extreme poverty
analysis of changing causes of poverty and structural drivers of poverty reduction
impact evaluations and operational research on effective anti-poverty programmes
operational recommendations (emerging from Year 2 for data/measures, Year 3 for trends/drivers and effective approaches)
innovative approaches tested in up to eight countries
q3_expected_outputs.target: 8 countries

what_objectives.summary: DETEP aims to generate evidence on extreme poverty in fragile contexts, improve data quality, and test interventions to inform DFID's poverty reduction strategies. It combines research, analysis, and implementation testing across three thematic areas.

quote.text: "The programme will have three themes: developing better data and measures of extreme poverty; analysis of the changing causes of poverty and structural drivers of poverty reduction; impact evaluation and operational research that identifies what programming approaches work best to drive poverty reduction in different contexts."

countries_regions: Up to eight DFID priority countries (seven DFID priority countries plus one other high-poverty country)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly targets fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), where 60% of the world's extreme poor are projected to live by 2030. These contexts are characterized by weak institutions, conflict, and high vulnerability.
where_context.q5_source: "the extreme poor—the 700m who live on less than $1.90 per person per day—are concentrated increasingly in contexts of fragility and conflict... DFID is committed to... targeting 50% of UK aid to FCAS." (90000585.odt, Programme Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Data limitations in FCAS require new methods (e.g., remote sensing, machine learning) to generate accurate poverty measures. Conflict and fragility make traditional survey methods unsafe or impractical, while weak institutions limit local capacity to collect/analyze data. Political economy constraints affect policy uptake.

quote.text: "In FCAS (as well as for the hardest to reach in more stable settings), governments and donors need measures of extreme poverty that are more accurate, precise, comparable, frequent and fine-grained than those currently available."

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank (for Theme 1) and Research Programme Consortium (for Themes 2-3)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led multilateral) manages Theme 1, while Themes 2-3 are delivered via a competitive consortium (composition unspecified). Decision-making power for Themes 2-3 depends on the selected RPC, but the document does not specify North-South balance.
q10_capacity_building_details: improving national and global measures of poverty (Theme 1)
training in data collection/analysis methods (e.g., remote sensing, machine learning)
support to DFID Country Offices for operational research

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Theme 1 (data and measures of extreme poverty)

partner_organizations.name: Research Programme Consortium (RPC)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Themes 2-3 (trends/drivers and effective approaches) via competitive tender

partner_organizations.name: Up to eight DFID Country Offices
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation and operational research

quote.text: "We recommend delivery through a new Research Programme Consortium (RPC), selected through a competitive tender for themes 2 and 3 (and a minor part of theme 1); and a partnership with the World Bank to deliver the larger part of theme 1."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Theme 1 uses a partnership agreement with the World Bank (likely a trust fund), while Themes 2-3 use a competitive contract with a Research Programme Consortium (RPC). The RPC is selected via open tender, implying a grant/contract hybrid.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Theme 1 is managed via a World Bank trust fund, while Themes 2-3 are delivered by a closed consortium (RPC) under a single contract. The RPC includes provisions for sub-grants or collaborations with Country Offices.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected for Theme 1 due to its global leadership in poverty measurement (e.g., Atkinson Commission). The RPC for Themes 2-3 is selected via open competition to ensure quality and value for money, with DFID retaining oversight.

quote.text: "We recommend delivery through... a partnership with the World Bank to deliver the larger part of theme 1... [and] a new Research Programme Consortium (RPC), selected through a competitive tender for themes 2 and 3."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The RPC contract includes provisions for regular review (implying a steering committee). World Bank financing uses a trust fund with options for shifting funds between workstreams, subject to DFID approval.

quote.text: "The RPC contract will have provisions for regular review to allow course correction. World Bank financing... will build in options that allow shifting funds and effort between workstreams when required by context and approved by DFID."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between workstreams within Theme 1 (World Bank) with DFID approval. The RPC contract allows course correction but does not specify budget flexibility.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Regular reviews enable adjustments to research priorities, but changes require DFID approval (e.g., shifting funds between World Bank workstreams).

quote.text: "World Bank financing... will build in options that allow shifting funds and effort between workstreams when required by context and approved by DFID."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) World Bank/RPC → (2) Country Offices/sub-grantees. The World Bank and RPC act as intermediaries, with Country Offices implementing locally.

quote.text: "Programme Value: £12 million" (explicit budget); payment structure inferred from "regular review to allow course correction" (milestone-based).

q24_alternatives_considered: direct grants to Country Offices
expanded use of existing DFID research hubs
sole reliance on multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank for all themes)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed model (World Bank + RPC) was chosen to (1) leverage the World Bank’s expertise in poverty measurement (Theme 1), (2) ensure competitive quality for Themes 2-3 via open tender, and (3) balance flexibility (World Bank trust fund) with accountability (RPC contract). The structure aligns with DFID’s risk appetite (minor/moderate) and need for both global standards (World Bank) and context-specific research (RPC).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (competitive tender for RPC)
risk mitigation (World Bank’s robust systems for Theme 1)
partner capacity (World Bank’s leadership in poverty data)
equity (focus on FCAS and marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: coordination gaps between World Bank (Theme 1) and RPC (Themes 2-3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular reviews and DFID oversight to ensure alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: delays in RPC selection via competitive tender
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased start (Theme 1 begins immediately with World Bank).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: limited Southern ownership in World Bank-led Theme 1
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnership with Country Offices for local implementation.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (focus on FCAS and marginalized groups)

quote.text: "The Business Case has been reviewed by... DFID’s external Research Advisory Group... We are confident that the research supplier market can deliver high quality research which can shape policy and practice."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts limit partner selection to organizations with (1) conflict-sensitive expertise, (2) capacity to operate in high-risk environments, and (3) experience with fragile data systems. This excludes many Southern institutions lacking such capacity, necessitating Northern/multilateral leads (e.g., World Bank).
q27_constraints_detail: weak local statistical capacity requires external expertise (e.g., World Bank for Theme 1)
security risks in FCAS limit fieldwork to partners with conflict experience
political economy constraints favor multilateral actors (perceived neutrality)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for (1) **global comparability** (Theme 1) drives the World Bank partnership, while (2) **context-specific testing** (Themes 2-3) requires a flexible RPC. The mix of **evidence generation** (Themes 1-2) and **implementation research** (Theme 3) necessitates both a multilateral standard-setter (World Bank) and an adaptive consortium (RPC).
q28_linkages: global poverty measurement standards → World Bank’s role
local operational research → RPC’s country-level focus
FCAS constraints → need for both robust systems (World Bank) and local adaptability (RPC)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between (1) **rapid delivery** (using established partners like World Bank) and **Southern ownership** (limited by FCAS capacity constraints), and (2) **cost efficiency** (competitive RPC tender) and **inclusive partnerships** (few Southern institutions can compete for large consortia).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion: World Bank’s existing systems enable quick start (Theme 1) but may sideline local actors.
expertise vs ownership: RPC’s competitive selection prioritizes technical quality, potentially excluding Southern-led consortia.
cost vs reach: Focus on FCAS increases per-capita costs due to security/data challenges.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** (FCAS + innovation) justifies **milestone-based oversight** (regular reviews) and **fund reallocation flexibility**, but stops short of embedded advisors (which would increase costs).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in all themes: Theme 1 strengthens national statistical systems via World Bank, while Themes 2-3 include training for Country Offices. However, **decision-making power** remains with Northern/multilateral leads due to FCAS constraints.

quote.text: "In FCAS... governments and donors need measures of extreme poverty that are more accurate, precise, comparable, frequent and fine-grained than those currently available... [requiring] innovation in the collection and analysis of socio-economic data."

key_programme_risks: data quality limitations in FCAS (affecting Theme 1)
political instability disrupting fieldwork (Themes 2-3)
coordination gaps between World Bank and RPC
limited Southern partner capacity to lead complex research
delays in operational research due to conflict (Theme 3)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of innovative methods (remote sensing, machine learning) and World Bank’s technical expertise.
Flexible funding (reallocation between workstreams) and partnership with Country Offices for local insights.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: coordination gaps between World Bank and RPC
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID oversight and regular reviews to align themes.
Embedded capacity building (training, institutional strengthening) via both World Bank and RPC.

fcas_specific_lessons: Prior experience shows traditional poverty surveys fail in FCAS; new methods (e.g., tablet-assisted surveys) are essential.
Conflict-affected areas require adaptive management (e.g., shifting funds between workstreams).
Local ownership in FCAS is constrained by weak institutions, necessitating multilateral intermediaries.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2016 Atkinson Commission highlighted gaps in global poverty measures, informing Theme 1’s focus. DFID’s past work in FCAS (e.g., Bilateral Development Review) showed that residual poverty is concentrated in marginalized groups, shaping Theme 3’s targeting.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added explicit focus on **urban poverty** and **within-household inequalities** (previously understudied).
Incorporated **behavioral science** approaches (e.g., ‘nudge’) based on evidence of uptake barriers.
Expanded use of **ICT tools** (remote sensing, machine learning) to address data gaps in FCAS.

quote.text: "The data and analysis that have underpinned progress in settings such as China and India are not well suited for the task ahead [in FCAS]... [requiring] measures of extreme poverty that are more accurate, precise, comparable, frequent and fine-grained."
"Programme Value: £12 million"

metadata.programme_name: BRILHO – Energy Africa Mozambique
metadata.quote: "To develop a stronger off-grid energy market with more companies with functional business models approaching commercial viability and with high potential for ongoing growth." (5634901.odt, Project Purpose)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: September 2016 – August 2022" and "New project end date: August 2023" (25058297.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: BRILHO combines financing mechanisms (Market Development Fund), capacity building (technical assistance to businesses and government), policy influence (Energy Africa Compact), and implementation research (testing business models). It aims to catalyze private sector investment in off-grid energy solutions while strengthening institutions and generating evidence for scale-up.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The proposed BRILHO Programme will be the main vehicle to deliver the UK’s Energy Africa campaign in Mozambique and to meet the UK’s commitments in the Energy Africa compact. BRILHO will provide support to government and non-state energy providers through a holistic and comprehensive set of interventions." (5634901.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "The approach is unchanged, although the focus (spread of funds) has shifted slightly away from the mini-grid intervention on the grounds that it may be easier to attract additional partner donor finance to this component." (25058297.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 750,000 people benefitting from improved cookstoves (ICS) (down from 1m)
750,000 people benefitting from solar home systems (SHS) or mini-grids for domestic use (down from 1m)
15,000 additional businesses supplied with off-grid renewable productive energy (down from 20k)
£20m of additional private funding mobilised for BRILHO interventions (down from £30m)
Technical assistance to Mozambican government institutions (FUNAE, MIREME)
Research outputs on policy/regulatory environment and market barriers
Demand activation campaigns for rural consumers
Establishment of a Challenge Fund for private sector grants/loans
Capacity building for private sector firms (business models, supply chain linkages)
what_objectives.summary: BRILHO aims to transform Mozambique's off-grid energy market by combining financial incentives for private companies, technical assistance to strengthen business models and government capacity, policy reforms to reduce barriers, and research to generate scalable solutions. The revised targets reflect a 30% budget reduction but maintain the core market-development approach.
what_objectives.quote: "The estimated programme targets have been reduced roughly in proportion to decrease in budget. The new targets are: i) 750 thousand people (down from 1m) benefitting from an improved cookstoves (ICS)..." (25058297.odt, What are the expected results?) AND "The programme will be a contribution to the UK’s international commitment to increase climate finance for developing countries to increase access to energy." (5634901.odt, Strategic Case)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique faces macroeconomic instability (hidden debt crisis), political conflict, and climate vulnerabilities (drought/El Niño), but the programme uses adaptive management to mitigate these risks. The overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (5634901.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Mozambique is facing a difficult future due to a combination of: i) drought and hunger from El Niño; ii) increasing politically-motivated conflict and violence; and iii) a macro-economic crisis exacerbated by the recent discovery of billions of dollars of secretly contracted state-backed debt." (5634901.odt, Strategic Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers (30-40% import tariffs, GMG laws) and weak logistics/mobile money infrastructure hinder private sector entry. Political instability and debt crises create macroeconomic uncertainty. Low rural purchasing power (<$100/year on energy) limits market viability. Portuguese language requirements exclude many regional players. Conflict in northern provinces disrupts supply chains.
where_context.quote: "Inadequate regulation/policies: fiscal barriers include import costs estimated as high as 30-40%. GMG tariff setting and laws prevent companies from generating and selling energy across property boundaries." (5634901.odt, Figure 1) AND "Limited logistics: lack of infrastructure, logistics and supply chain partners makes delivery and supply of goods challenging and/or expensive." (5634901.odt, Figure 1)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID designs the programme components (e.g., Challenge Fund windows, TA focus areas) and approves all major financial decisions, while Mozambican partners (FUNAE, private sector) implement activities under DFID oversight. The Service Provider (SP) manages day-to-day operations but reports to DFID.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to private sector firms (business models, legal/regulatory navigation)
institutional strengthening for FUNAE (policy advice, loan guarantees)
seconded experts to Mozambican government agencies
training for supply chain partners (mobile money, logistics)
research capacity support (Eduardo Mondlane University solar/biomass labs)

partner_organizations.name: FUNAE (Fundo de Energia)
partner_organizations.role: Government implementing agency for rural energy; receives TA to build capacity for private sector support and policy advice

partner_organizations.name: MIREME (Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy)
partner_organizations.role: Policy reform partner (Energy Africa Compact); co-leads National Electrification Strategy
