who_partners.quote: "TWFA will establish a Services Company Limited by Guarantee that will be staffed by professionals and will work with smallholder farmers providing technical assistance, extension services, and patient working capital." (17984722.odt, IMPLEMENTATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO provides an Accountable Grant to TWFA, which is disbursed quarterly based on activity and financial reporting. TWFA channels these funds to Services Companies (SCs) as zero-interest, patient capital loans to smallholder farmers. The SCs operate on a cost-recovery basis, with repayments from farmers once tea production begins.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by TWFA in partnership with private sector investors (Lipton and Luxmi) and philanthropic organizations (Gatsby). TWFA establishes and oversees Services Companies (SCs) co-owned with smallholder farmers. The SCs deliver all farmer-facing services, while TWFA provides management oversight and reports to FCDO.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TWFA was selected based on its institutional experience in tea production, including a successful partnership with DFID in Tanzania (Chai Kwa Maendeleo programme). The selection was also influenced by TWFA's ability to leverage private investment and its established relationship with Unilever/Lipton and Luxmi.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID will provide an Accountable Grant to The Wood Foundation Africa (TWFA)." (17984722.odt, IMPLEMENTATION) and "An Accountable Grant arrangement is an arrangement whereby a Not-for-Profit organisation approaches DFID and submits a project proposal in line with DFID objectives." (5694639.odt, OPTIONS ANALYSIS)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each Services Company (SC) has a board with representation from TWFA, smallholder farmers (minority positions), and in some cases, private sector partners. The SC boards oversee operations, financial management, and service delivery to farmers. TWFA provides management oversight through staff located in Rwanda.
how_governance.quote: "DFID disbursements to TWFA will be planned on a quarterly basis. Upon receipt and approval of the quarterly reports including the financial reports and a written disbursement request, the programme team will write a submission to the Economic Growth Team Leader." (17984722.odt, IMPLEMENTATION) and "The SCs provide agricultural support services to tea farmers... The SCs do not seek a profit and operate on a cost-recovery basis." (D0007182.odt, Annex A)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be flexed across financial years to meet internal targets or constraints, with philanthropic capital (TWFA/Gatsby) filling gaps. This flexibility has been a strength of the programme, allowing adaptation to funding uncertainty.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has adapted based on learning, such as increasing the focus on climate-smart agriculture and expanding to new areas (Nshili Kivu) based on farmer demand. Adjustments require approval but are facilitated by the flexible funding structure.
how_flexibility.quote: "A real strength of the SILTPR programme in recent years, as DFID/FCDO has faced funding uncertainty, has been the ability to flex funding across financial years... This is an advantage for BHCKigali, providing a helpful degree of flexibility within the programme portfolio." (D0007182.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TWFA → Services Companies (SCs) → Smallholder Farmers
how_efficiency.quote: "Disbursements... Upon receipt and approval of the quarterly reports including the financial reports and a written disbursement request, the programme team will write a submission to the Economic Growth Team Leader. His/her approval will trigger the payment to TWFA." (17984722.odt, IMPLEMENTATION) and "The amount [to farmers] is paid through farmers’ bank accounts... upon verification and approval of the quality and full completion of each phase of land preparation by the SC." (D0007182.odt, Annex A)

q24_alternatives_considered: Cooperative model (rejected due to poor quality of extension services and governance issues)
Factory-led extension services (considered but not chosen as the primary model)
Private service providers procured by factories (not selected as it risked deteriorating service quality)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The Services Company model was chosen because it addresses critical market failures in Rwanda's tea sector: lack of coordination among smallholders, absence of patient capital, and limited tea knowledge. The model leverages TWFA's experience in Tanzania and allows for professional management of extension services while ensuring farmer ownership and representation. It also enables the programme to attract private investment by mitigating risks for investors (Lipton/Luxmi).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (high leverage of private investment, $27m from Luxmi and €50m from Unilever/Lipton)
risk mitigation (addresses investor concerns about smallholder reliability)
past experience (successful Chai Kwa Maendeleo programme in Tanzania)
partner capacity (TWFA's ability to manage Services Companies and attract co-investment)
flexibility (ability to adapt to farmer needs and market conditions)
equity (inclusion of women, youth, and marginalized farmers)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Farmers may not repay loans, affecting SC financial sustainability
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Co-guarantor system where groups of farmers guarantee each other's loans and maintenance obligations. Payments are tied to greenleaf supply, and SCs operate on cost-recovery basis without profit motives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private investors (Lipton/Luxmi) may not fulfill commitments (e.g., factory construction)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close monitoring of investor activities and contingency planning for alternative off-takers of greenleaf. DFID's due diligence on Luxmi and Unilever's strong commercial incentives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor road infrastructure limiting tea transport (Component B)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot ropeway system to bypass poor roads, with GoR (RTDA) support and cost-sharing with private sector. Ongoing road maintenance by RTDA for main roads.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate change affecting tea viability (Component C)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Climate-smart agriculture practices, Rainforest Alliance certification, and carbon footprint reduction strategies. Minimum altitude for planting set higher to account for future temperature increases.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low farmer adoption of climate-smart practices
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Increased capacity building and incorporation of environmental management into Farmer Field School curriculum (response to evaluation findings).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging £27m private investment per £6.83m public funding)
efficiency (Services Company model reduces transaction costs compared to cooperatives)
effectiveness (expected 9-fold income increase for farmers over long term)
equity (targeting women, youth, and marginalized farmers, with 55% female workforce in agriculture)
why_rationale.quote: "The proposed cost extension offers high Value for Money from the perspective of: smallholder farmers who stand to witness vastly improved living standards... leveraging much needed Foreign Direct Investment... the value of increased exports... improved efficiency by increasing the size of the programme but maintaining the same number of DFID personnel." (17984722.odt, VFM) and "The model deemed to be the most suitable for ensuring high service quality delivery is a Services Company staffed by tea professionals providing services efficiently and directly to farmers, but which is at least partly owned by farmers." (5694639.odt, PARTNERSHIP)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The land constraints in Rwanda (small plot sizes and lack of large contiguous land) necessitate working with thousands of smallholder farmers, which requires a partner like TWFA with experience in coordination and extension services. The poor infrastructure (roads) in tea-growing areas limits the types of partners who can effectively operate, favoring those with local presence and ability to innovate (e.g., ropeways).
q27_constraints_detail: Land fragmentation requires a partner capable of coordinating thousands of smallholders (TWFA's Services Company model).
Poor roads in Rugabano necessitate partners with local operational capacity and willingness to pilot alternative transport (TWFA/ROS).
Climate vulnerability requires partners with expertise in climate-smart agriculture (TWFA's experience and Rainforest Alliance certification).
Shallow financial markets require partners able to provide patient capital (TWFA/Gatsby's zero-interest loans).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to support smallholder farmers in adopting tea production (a long-term, high-coordination crop) determines the use of Services Companies rather than cooperatives or direct factory management. The goal of leveraging private investment requires a structure that mitigates investor risks (hence TWFA's coordination role). The focus on climate resilience shapes the inclusion of climate-smart practices in Farmer Field Schools and carbon footprint assessments.
q28_linkages: Smallholder coordination needs → Services Company model (not cooperatives).
Private investment leverage → TWFA as intermediary to mitigate investor risks.
Climate resilience goals → Integration of climate-smart practices and carbon footprint analysis.
Income stability during transition → Patient capital and wage payments during crop switching.
Gender equity → Targeted inclusion of women in training, governance, and payments.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency by: (1) Using Services Companies to achieve economies of scale in extension services while ensuring farmer ownership; (2) Targeting women and youth in training and governance roles, which requires additional capacity-building efforts; (3) Providing patient capital to all farmers regardless of initial wealth, which increases costs but ensures inclusion. The co-guarantor system balances risk management with inclusive access to finance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Services Companies achieve economies of scale in extension services and input provision.
Equity: Additional costs for targeted inclusion of women (e.g., childcare support) and marginalized farmers.
Speed vs. Inclusion: Farmer sensitisation and registration take time but ensure broad participation.
Expertise vs. Ownership: Professional management of SCs ensures quality but requires capacity building for farmer governance.
Cost vs. Reach: Zero-interest loans increase programme costs but enable poor farmers to participate.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high initial risks (e.g., farmer default, investor pull-out) led to intensive oversight structures, including quarterly reporting, SC boards with farmer representation, and co-guarantor systems. The moderate risk profile of Rwanda (non-FCAS) allows for some flexibility in fund management but still requires robust mitigation measures like ropeways for transport risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The limited capacity of smallholder farmers shaped the design of Services Companies, which provide professional management while gradually building farmer governance skills. TWFA's capacity to attract co-investment (Gatsby, Lipton, Luxmi) enabled the programme to scale. The need for climate-smart capacity led to expanded training programmes in Component C.
intersections.quote: "The smallholder model is a significant risk in its own right. The capital investment associated with the development of a factory is substantial. The viability of the investment is dependent on the supply of greenleaf by smallholder farmers, a supply chain which investors in the factory lack direct control over." (5694639.odt, RISKS) and "The model deemed to be the most suitable for ensuring high service quality delivery is a Services Company staffed by tea professionals providing services efficiently and directly to farmers, but which is at least partly owned by farmers." (5694639.odt, PARTNERSHIP)

key_programme_risks: Expected yields and quality not realized due to climate or farming practices (affecting farmer incomes).
Private investors (Lipton/Luxmi) fail to fulfill commitments (e.g., factory construction).
Farmers unable to repay loans due to crop failure or market fluctuations.
Poor road infrastructure limiting tea transport and increasing costs.
Climate change reducing suitable tea-growing areas or affecting yields.
Exclusion of marginalized groups (landless, women, youth) from benefits.
Child labour risks in tea production without proper safeguards.
Low adoption of climate-smart practices by farmers.
Financial sustainability of Services Companies post-DFID/FCDO funding.
Political or regulatory changes affecting land use or tea pricing.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Expected yields and quality not realized
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Farmer Field Schools, climate-smart training, and close monitoring of farming practices. Rainforest Alliance certification to ensure quality standards.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Private investors fail to fulfill commitments
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Close monitoring of investor activities and contingency planning for alternative greenleaf off-takers. DFID's due diligence on partners.
Co-guarantor system, wage payments during transition, and patient capital structure. Farmers only repay once tea income begins.
Pilot ropeway system (Component B) to bypass poor roads, with GoR (RTDA) support. Ongoing road maintenance by RTDA and local contributions.
Climate-smart agriculture practices, higher minimum altitude for planting, and carbon footprint reduction (Component C). Rainforest Alliance certification.
Targeted inclusion strategies (e.g., lower fees, smaller land requirements for women), childcare support, and gender-disaggregated monitoring.
Strong safeguarding policies, electronic payments to named accounts, and monitoring systems.
Increased capacity building and integration into Farmer Field School curriculum (response to evaluation findings).
Cost-recovery model without profit motives, gradual transfer of ownership to farmers, and long-term business plans (20 years).
Close engagement with GoR and alignment with national tea strategy. Flexible funding to adapt to policy changes.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Chai Kwa Maendeleo programme in Tanzania (2009-2017) informed the Services Company model, including the importance of professional extension services, farmer ownership, and private sector partnerships. Early experience in Rwanda showed that farmers were unfamiliar with the TWFA model (preferring cooperatives), requiring greater sensitisation. Socio-economic surveys revealed the need for targeted inclusion strategies, especially for women and landless labourers. The first evaluation (2022) highlighted slow adoption of climate-smart practices, leading to increased capacity building in Component C.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. Increased focus on climate-smart agriculture in Farmer Field Schools (response to evaluation findings). 2. Expansion to Nshili Kivu (Component A) based on farmer demand and success in adjacent areas. 3. Pilot ropeways (Component B) to address persistent transport challenges identified in annual reviews. 4. Carbon footprint assessment and reduction strategies (Component C) in response to industry trends and evaluation recommendations. 5. Adjustments to loan amounts (increased to RWF 1m in 2024) to account for currency depreciation.
risks_lessons.quote: "A socio-economic survey for the Kibeho and Munini sectors has been undertaken with preliminary results expected to be available in February 2017. This will provide a better understanding of the socio-economic conditions... and will also inform the need for any complementary measures to address potential barriers to inclusivity." (17984722.odt, LESSON LEARNING) and "The first phase report was positive about SILTPR’s performance... The evaluation report noted as slow adoption rate of climate-smart agriculture (CSA) practices/technologies. SCON-N and ROS are responding to this through increasing capacity building for SHFs on CSA technologies." (D0007182.odt, Annex F)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged approximately $84 million in total investment, including: $27 million from Luxmi Tea Company over 10 years; over €50 million from Unilever/Lipton over 20 years; $16 million from TWFA in interest-free returnable capital; and $3.5 million from Nshili Kivu Tea Factory shareholders (Component A). This represents a leverage ratio of roughly $5 in private/philanthropic funding for every £1 of UK public funding.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes both capital expenditures (e.g., ropeway infrastructure in Component B, factory investments by private partners) and revenue expenditures (e.g., farmer training, extension services, and working capital loans). The ropeways (Component B) are a capital-intensive intervention ($2m from FCDO, $1m from TWFA/RTC), while Components A and C focus more on revenue spending for services and studies.
financial_details.quote: "The UK will provide additional financial support up to £6.83 million to The Wood Foundation Africa (TWFA) to work with smallholder farmers to plant and cultivate tea. The support will leverage investment from a new private Indian investor who would otherwise not invest in Rwanda." (17984722.odt, ADDITIONAL SUPPORT) and "DFID support to TWFA is leveraging more than $27m million investment from Luxmi over a ten year period to develop a factory and core estate." (17984722.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Digital Access Programme

quote.text: The Sustainable Development Goals include an ambition to provide universal and affordable access to the Internet for least developed countries by 2020. Meeting this goal is vitally important in ensuring that poor and vulnerable people are able to benefit from the significant development impact of the Internet and digital technologies, and to avert the substantial risk of widening inequalities resulting from digital exclusion.

metadata.duration_source: Timeframe: 2018–2023 (Phase 1 - Diagnostic & Phase 2 - Implementation)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Digital Access Programme aims to catalyse the development and scaling of inclusive business models for affordable Internet connectivity in marginalised communities, while also strengthening the enabling environment (regulatory frameworks, digital skills, cybersecurity). It combines implementation research (testing innovative models), capacity building (skills, governance), and policy influence (regulatory reforms).
what_objectives.q1_source: The Digital Access Programme will facilitate the market validation and roll-out of inclusive business models that adopt emerging innovations to widen basic Internet connectivity for poor and excluded people. [...] It will address issues of affordable basic connectivity, cyber-security, digital skills and inclusion, the regulatory and policy environment, and digital ecosystems.

q3_expected_outputs.output: validated inclusive business models for affordable connectivity
improved regulatory frameworks for digital access
enhanced cybersecurity resilience in partner countries
increased digital skills and inclusion (e.g., for women, PwD, rural populations)
crowded-in private/impact investment into validated models
q3_expected_outputs.target: £57.5 billion to £137.1 billion (leveraged finance over 10 years)

q3_expected_outputs.output: GDP growth from increased connectivity
q3_expected_outputs.target: £6.3 billion to £15.1 billion (direct primary benefits over 10 years)

q3_expected_outputs.output: people reached with digital access

what_objectives.summary: The programme tests and scales innovative models to expand affordable Internet access for marginalised groups (bottom 40% income, women, PwD, rural/remote areas), while strengthening the enabling environment through regulatory reforms, cybersecurity, and digital inclusion. It aims to catalyse market growth, reduce poverty, and generate secondary benefits for UK businesses in digital sectors.

quote.text: The Programme will be catalytic in nature, as it will facilitate key processes to address market failures and to induce systemic improvements. It will focus on interventions that can have a multiplier effect, in particular through future scale-up of viable innovative models for affordable access; and through its emphasis on research and learning that will build evidence and lessons for the UK to influence policy and practice on ‘digital for development’ in the international arena.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme acknowledges complexity in programme architecture (coordination across departments/countries) and risks of not delivering expected digital inclusion outcomes, but no explicit FCAS or high-risk context is mentioned. Risks are described as consistent with Prosperity Fund portfolio ambitions.
where_context.q5_source: Key risks include: Complexity of programme architecture raises the transaction costs of programme management and coordination across departments and countries. [...] Risks are consistent with other programmes in the portfolio and ambitions for the Prosperity Fund, and are within the PF’s and DFID’s risk appetite.
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers (e.g., spectrum licensing, taxation) and weak institutions hinder market entry and affordability. Infrastructure gaps (e.g., unreliable electricity, lack of supporting networks) increase costs. Social norms limit access for women/PwD, while low digital skills and literacy reduce demand. Rural/remote areas face geographic and economic barriers to connectivity.

quote.text: Traditional models of Internet access [...] are too expensive to be viable for poorer populations or in rural settings in lower-income countries. [...] Digital access is also inhibited by the absence of conducive regulatory environments, lack of locally-relevant and development-oriented content, as well as low levels of digital skills and inclusion.
quote.source: 54170779.odt, The need: addressing barriers to ‘digital dividends’ for development

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed and delivered by DFID (UK) in collaboration with FCO and DCMS, with country-level diagnostics and adaptations. Southern partners (governments, CSOs, private sector) are involved in implementation but decision-making rests with HMG departments.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to businesses/CSOs for model development
digitals skills training for marginalised groups (women, PwD, rural populations)
support to governments for digital service delivery (e.g., e-governance)
cybersecurity capacity building for national agencies
regulatory framework strengthening
institutional support for inclusive business models

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Development (DFID)
partner_organizations.role: lead department, programme design/delivery

partner_organizations.name: Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO)
partner_organizations.role: co-lead (Pillar 2: Trust and Resilience - cybersecurity)

partner_organizations.role: co-lead (Pillar 3: Sustainable Digital Ecosystems)

partner_organizations.role: funding management

partner_organizations.name: Government Digital Service (GDS)
partner_organizations.role: technical expertise for digital service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Partner country governments (Brazil, Indonesia, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa)
partner_organizations.role: implementation, regulatory reforms, digital service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Local tech sectors/private companies
partner_organizations.role: inclusive business models, digital ecosystems

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: digital inclusion, community networks, advocacy

partner_organizations.name: UK Tech Hubs (in partner countries)
partner_organizations.role: delivery mechanism for Pillar 3 (DCMS)

partner_organizations.name: Potential deliver partners (e.g., Andela, Livity, AkiraChix, Project Isizwe, Avanti, Mawingu)
partner_organizations.role: digital skills, connectivity models, ecosystem support

quote.text: The Programme will be delivered in three ‘pillars’, providing in every country a tailored mix of well-targeted technical assistance and funding in order to address supply- and demand-side barriers as well as systemic constraints to inclusive digital access: Pillar 1 – Models and Enablers (led by DFID); Pillar 2 – Trust and Resilience (led by FCO); Pillar 3 – Sustainable Digital Ecosystems (led by DCMS).
quote.source: 54170779.odt, What are the main programme activities?

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for innovation funding, technical assistance) and contracts (for service delivery, capacity building). Funding is channelled through HMG departments to implementing partners, with potential for sub-grants to local organisations.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by a cross-HMG team (DFID, FCO, DCMS) with dedicated staff in the UK and partner countries. Delivery is structured around three pillars, each led by a different department, with coordinated technical assistance and funding. Country-level diagnostics inform tailored interventions.

quote.text: The programme has been cleared by DFID’s Quality Assurance Unit and has been designed with significant input from international business leaders, academic experts, connectivity specialists (see Annex 7) and potential delivery partners.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme involves cross-HMG coordination (DFID, FCO, DCMS) with departmental SROs and Lead Advisers overseeing delivery. Country offices and Prosperity Fund committees provide alignment with partner government priorities. A dedicated HMG programme team manages implementation.

quote.text: Departmental SROs, Lead Advisers and respective teams are well placed to oversee and quality-manage the delivery the programme. Dedicated staffing resources in UK and partner countries are being put in place to ensure robust programme management and effective delivery and impact.
quote.source: 54170779.odt, Do the SRO and team have the capability and resources to deliver the Programme?

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed to be needs-driven and adaptive, with country-level diagnostics informing tailored interventions. However, reallocation between pillars or countries likely requires approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an initial diagnostic phase to tailor activities to each country context and includes mechanisms for continuous improvement based on evidence/learning. Flexibility is built in to respond to local needs and risks.

quote.text: The programme will take a flexible and needs-driven approach. It will use an initial diagnostic phase to tailor programme activities to each country context, identify and mitigate risks, and shape programme activity for maximum impact on prosperity and inclusion.
quote.source: 54170779.odt, What are the main programme activities?

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (via Prosperity Fund) → HMG departments (DFID/FCO/DCMS) → Implementing partners (e.g., Tech Hubs, CSOs, private sector) → [End beneficiaries].

quote.text: Dedicated staffing resources in UK and partner countries are being put in place to ensure robust programme management and effective delivery and impact.
quote.source: 54170779.odt, Do the SRO and team have the capability and resources to deliver the Programme?

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct bilateral aid (discounted due to lack of cross-sectoral integration)
Pure private-sector led models (discounted due to market failures in reaching poor/rural populations)
Standalone digital skills programmes (discounted due to need for holistic approach)
Traditional infrastructure investment (discounted as too costly for last-mile connectivity)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (cross-HMG collaboration with tailored country interventions) was chosen to address the multi-dimensional barriers to digital inclusion (technical, regulatory, skills, cybersecurity) while leveraging UK expertise in digital governance, cybersecurity, and inclusive business models. The catalytic approach aims to crowd in private investment and scale innovations beyond direct programme funding.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (catalytic effect to leverage £57.5-137.1bn in additional finance)
risk mitigation (cross-HMG expertise reduces implementation risks)
partner capacity (builds on existing UK strengths in digital sectors)
flexibility (adaptive programming responds to country contexts)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of cross-departmental coordination increases transaction costs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated HMG programme team and clear pillar division (DFID/FCO/DCMS leads)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Innovative models may fail to scale or attract private investment
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance to prove commercial viability and facilitate access to finance

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory reforms may stall due to political economy barriers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted support to governments and multi-stakeholder engagement

quote.text: The Programme will be catalytic in nature, as it will facilitate key processes to address market failures and to induce systemic improvements. [...] The cross-government approach of the programme will provide the appropriate expertise and policy leadership needed for the three pillars.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country scope and focus on marginalised groups (rural, poor, PwD, women) require partners with local presence and contextual expertise. Regulatory and infrastructure constraints in partner countries limit the types of organisations that can deliver connectivity solutions (e.g., need for spectrum licensing, local content adaptation).
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory environments require partners with policy influence (e.g., government agencies, multilateral orgs)
Rural/remote areas need partners with last-mile delivery capacity (e.g., community networks, local ISPs)
Digital skills gaps necessitate partners embedded in local education/CSO networks
Cybersecurity threats demand partners with government-level access (e.g., national agencies)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to test *inclusive business models* (Pillar 1) requires flexible funding instruments (grants for innovation, technical assistance for capacity building). The *cross-cutting* objectives (cybersecurity, digital ecosystems) necessitate a multi-pillar structure with specialised HMG leads (FCO for cybersecurity, DCMS for ecosystems). The focus on *scaling* validated models shapes the use of catalytic funding to attract private investment.
q28_linkages: Implementation research (testing models) → requires adaptive management and country diagnostics
Capacity building (skills, governance) → embedded in all pillars via technical assistance
Policy influence (regulatory reforms) → delivered through government partnerships and HMG expertise
Financing mechanism (crowding in investment) → structured via innovation grants and private sector engagement
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting bottom 40% income, women, PwD) with efficiency (scaling models via private sector). Trade-offs include: (1) *Higher transaction costs* from inclusive targeting vs. rapid scalability; (2) *Local adaptation* needs vs. standardised models; (3) *Long-term capacity building* vs. short-term connectivity gains. The design prioritises equity by mandating context-specific success criteria for inclusion.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: Diagnostic phase slows rollout but ensures targeting of marginalised groups
expertise vs. ownership: UK-led technical assistance balanced with local partner delivery
cost vs. reach: Subsidised models (e.g., urban WiFi hotspots) increase affordability but require ongoing support
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (complexity, innovation uncertainty) justifies milestone-based oversight and a dedicated HMG programme team. High flexibility in country adaptations is balanced with centralised quality assurance.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme’s theory of change: (1) *Businesses* receive technical assistance to develop scalable models; (2) *Governments* get support for regulatory/digital service reforms; (3) *CSOs* are funded to deliver digital inclusion. Southern partners’ roles expand as their capacity grows (e.g., from pilot implementers to scale-up leaders).

quote.text: The programme will focus on interventions that can have a multiplier effect, in particular through future scale-up of viable innovative models for affordable access; and through its emphasis on research and learning that will build evidence and lessons for the UK to influence policy and practice on ‘digital for development’ in the international arena.

key_programme_risks: Complexity of cross-departmental/HMG coordination increases transaction costs
Innovative models fail to achieve commercial viability or scale
Regulatory reforms stall due to political economy barriers
Private sector does not crowd in expected investment
Digital inclusion outcomes are not realised for target groups (women, PwD, rural)
Cybersecurity threats outpace capacity-building efforts
Partner country GDP growth does not materialise as projected
Programme benefits are captured by elites rather than marginalised groups

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dedicated HMG programme team; clear division of pillars by department; country-level diagnostics to tailor interventions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Market validation of innovative models fails
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance to refine business models; financing gap support to prove commercial viability; facilitation of links with investors.
Targeted support to governments for reforms; multi-stakeholder engagement (private sector, CSOs, academia).
Demonstrate viability through pilot results; reduce risk perception via blended finance; showcase UK expertise to attract partners.
Explicit targeting of marginalised groups via context-specific criteria; support to locally-relevant content and skills programmes.
National-level capacity building; baseline assessments; awareness-raising campaigns.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from the World Bank’s *Digital Dividends* report (2016), which highlighted the need for ‘analogue complements’ (skills, governance, competition) to realise digital benefits. It also incorporates findings on market failures in connectivity (e.g., Caribou Digital’s *Closing the Gap* report) and the role of inclusive business models in reaching poor populations.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The two-phase design (diagnostic + implementation) was added to ensure country-specific adaptations. The three-pillar structure (models, trust, ecosystems) reflects lessons on the multi-dimensional nature of digital exclusion. Explicit equity criteria (Annex 10) were developed to address risks of elite capture.

quote.text: The programme draws on recommended responses made in the 2016 World Bank’s World Development Report on ‘Digital Dividends’. [...] The catalytic nature of the Programme will spark organic growth of digital markets that can self-sustain after programme end.
quote.source: 54170779.odt, Is the Programme coherent with the wider international community?

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to crowd in £57.5–137.1 billion in private/impact investment and improved regulation impacts over 10 years, alongside £282.7–674.0 million in international business opportunities.

quote.text: The UK will provide up to £82.5m from the Prosperity Fund over five years (including a diagnostic and stakeholder engagement phase of up to one year, and up to four years of implementation). [...] Primary benefits through crowding in private finance and improved regulation and its impact on GDP could range between an estimated £57.5 billion and £137.1 billion over a 10-year period.

metadata.programme_name: Climate Smart Development for Nepal
metadata.duration_text: Original: 6th October 2016 to 6th July 2021; Extended: 31st March 2025
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to accelerate climate resilient and low carbon development in Nepal. It will help businesses to thrive in the context of increasingly severe floods, droughts and landslides under climate change." (D0001201.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Original 6th October 2016, 6th July 2021. (No cost extension to 31st March 2024 agreed 2019) New project end date (if applicable): 31st March 2025" (D0001201.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing climate resilience interventions), capacity building (strengthening government systems), policy influence (integrating climate change into national planning), and service delivery (direct support for renewable energy access and adaptation measures). It operates through both government systems and private sector engagement to achieve economic development goals.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will enhance the productivity of the economy through improved uptake of off-grid renewable energy technologies and improved energy efficiency of brick kilns." (5639308.odt, Project Purpose) AND "Support to government policy and institutional development and a strong focus on ‘learning by doing’ will ensure that the resilient and low carbon growth is sustained over the next decade and beyond." (5639308.odt, Project Purpose)
q3_expected_outputs: Improve the resilience of at least 700,000 poor and vulnerable people (especially women) to floods, landslides and droughts in the most remote districts of Nepal
Improve the resilience of businesses in 5 growing urban centres and 3 river basins through investments in urban planning, large scale irrigation systems, and flood management
Facilitate the connection of over 95,000 households to new clean and renewable energy and increase installed capacity of Renewable Energy Systems by 16MW
Develop an industry standard for ‘clean’ brick production and enable over half of the brick kilns in Nepal (at least 400) to adopt more efficient technologies
Launch the Mountains of Opportunities Investment Framework developed for the Hindu Kush Himalayas (HKH) to enhance green investments in Nepal at COP27
Nepal engages in the Green Grid Initiative, LEAF, REAP and AAC initiatives and increases clean power trade in the region
Development of the Green Resilient and Inclusive Development Action Plan framework with 14 other donors and $4.2Bn of investment to support climate action in Nepal
Effective climate support through LISP to improve the climate resilience of 1.2 million people
what_objectives.summary: The programme integrates climate resilience and low-carbon development into Nepal's economic planning, combining community adaptation, renewable energy expansion, policy support, and institutional strengthening to promote sustainable growth while protecting vulnerable populations.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will enhance the productivity of the economy through improved uptake of off-grid renewable energy technologies and improved energy efficiency of brick kilns." (5639308.odt, Project Purpose) AND "The cost and time extension will allow the CSD programme to achieve the following additional results: [...]" (D0001201.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal is ranked as the fourth most vulnerable country to climate change globally, with frequent disasters like floods and landslides. The programme operates in a context of weak institutional capacity for climate risk management and limited coordination across government ministries, but without active conflict or extreme fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (5639308.odt, Summary) AND "Nepal is highly exposed to climate change. It ranks as the fourth most vulnerable country globally." (D0001201.odt, Summary Information)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak government capacity limits climate finance absorption and policy integration (e.g., "Government of Nepal has started to develop climate change institutions, policies and finance mechanisms... but resilience is not yet meaningfully integrated into government planning"). Climate risks (floods, landslides) disrupt implementation, while poor data systems hinder evidence-based planning. Regulatory barriers include limited private sector investment in renewables due to subsidy distortions.
where_context.quote: "Whilst climate change is an emerging policy theme at the central level, interest and capacity is varied at the sector level. Sectoral policies and plans in water resource management, agriculture, energy and industry do not specifically address risks associated with climate change." (5639308.odt, Barrier 1) AND "The off-grid market is distorted by the Government’s subsidy policy, which some argue has created a barrier to private sector investment in the market." (5639308.odt, Barrier 3)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Nepal (Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Population and Environment, Alternative Energy Promotion Centre)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Government of Nepal leads policy and implementation decisions, with DFID/FCDO providing technical and financial support. Key components (e.g., NCCSP2, NREP) are delivered through Nepali government systems, with international partners (e.g., Mott MacDonald, DAI) providing contracted technical assistance under GoN oversight.

training (e.g., brick kiln owners in efficient technologies)
policy development (e.g., climate budget codes, NDC implementation)
knowledge sharing (e.g., Climate Change Knowledge Centre, COP advocacy)
