(5639308.odt, Programme Value) AND "NCCSP2 will continue to work with the GoN, MoFE and the local governments in the Karnali Province through a Mott MacDonald contract to support local adaptation action." (D0001201.odt, Implementation Approach)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **financial aid** (85% of budget) channeled directly to the Government of Nepal for implementation, combined with **contracts** for technical assistance providers (e.g., Mott MacDonald, DAI) and **accountable grants** for advocacy partners (e.g., British Council, ICIMOD). Financial aid is reimbursed to GoN after verification by technical assistants.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a **hub-and-spoke model**: FCDO provides oversight and funding, while the Government of Nepal leads implementation across components. Technical partners (e.g., Mott MacDonald for NCCSP2, DAI for NREP) deliver specialized support under GoN contracts. Advocacy and science components (ICIMOD, British Council) operate semi-autonomously but align with GoN priorities.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct awards to pre-selected partners)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **existing relationships** (e.g., DFID’s long-standing collaboration with GoN on NCCSP), **technical expertise** (e.g., Mott MacDonald’s experience in climate adaptation), and **alignment with government systems** (e.g., AEPC’s mandate for renewable energy). The addendum notes no competitive process for extensions, citing urgency of COP26 follow-up.
how_mechanism.quote: "The NCCSP builds on a long history of community governance in Nepal [...] The programme works through Government of Nepal systems to help communities develop Local Adaptation Plans of Action (LAPAs)." (5639308.odt, Community-Based Adaptation) AND "NCCSP2 will continue to work with the GoN, MoFE and the local governments in the Karnali Province through a Mott MacDonald contract [...]" (D0001201.odt, Implementation Approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Policy and Institutions Facility** includes a multi-stakeholder coordination mechanism (originally the MCCICC, though inactive). The addendum implies joint oversight by FCDO and GoN for component delivery, with technical partners (e.g., Oxford Policy Management) providing advisory support. No formal governance body is explicitly described, but annual reviews and portfolio-level MEL suggest structured oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The RMEL (Resilience, Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning) component [...] will be integrated into wider BEK monitoring to improve VFM." (D0001201.odt, Implementation Approach) AND "Investment funding is channelled through GoN financial systems as with funds spent for local adaptation actions reimbursed by FCDO to the Nepal Government’s Treasury after review by the Technical Assistance (TA)." (D0001201.odt, Implementation Approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, as demonstrated by the **repurposing of CSD funds for COVID-19 recovery** and COP26 activities. The addendum notes that unspent funds (e.g., £2.9m in the low-spend scenario) may be transferred to the Local Infrastructure Services Programme (LISP).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **‘learning by doing’** and adaptive management, with annual reviews informing adjustments. The addendum highlights shifts in focus (e.g., adding LISP support, COP26/27 follow-up) based on emerging priorities, though changes require FCDO sign-off.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexible support to government systems is needed to ensure sustainability of climate smart development." (5639308.odt, Policy and Institutions) AND "The cost and time extension are requested now so that commitments made at COP26 can be delivered and programmes can scale up to national level." (D0001201.odt, Timing)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Technical Assistance Providers (e.g., Mott MacDonald/DAI) → Government of Nepal → Local Governments/Private Sector
how_efficiency.quote: "Investment funding is channelled through GoN financial systems as with funds spent for local adaptation actions reimbursed by FCDO to the Nepal Government’s Treasury after review by the Technical Assistance (TA)." (D0001201.odt, Implementation Approach) AND "The programme will have a strong focus on building systems and institutions for the future and on learning to inform adaptive programme management." (5639308.odt, Programme Value)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct bilateral funding to GoN without technical assistance
Multilateral funding (e.g., through World Bank or UN agencies)
Standalone projects for each component (e.g., separate adaptation and renewable energy programmes)
Private sector-led implementation (e.g., for renewable energy)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **hybrid model** (GoN-led with TA support) was selected to: 1) **ensure government ownership** (critical for sustainability), 2) **leverage existing systems** (e.g., NCCSP’s LAPA framework), 3) **balance speed and inclusion** (TA providers accelerate delivery while GoN maintains control), and 4) **mitigate fiduciary risks** (reimbursement model with TA verification). The addendum emphasizes scaling successful pilots (e.g., LAPAs) nationally through GoN channels.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in GoN financial systems (NCCSP)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Reimbursement model with TA verification; clear risk mitigation plan monitored during implementation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market failure in renewable energy (NREP)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with investors during challenge fund design; government policy alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery delays due to local government restructuring
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Time extension and flexible planning to accommodate transitions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low private sector response to clean energy incentives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Revised subsidy policies and investor engagement (e.g., Green Investment Summit).

why_rationale.quote: "Support to government policy and institutional development and a strong focus on ‘learning by doing’ will ensure that the resilient and low carbon growth is sustained over the next decade and beyond." (5639308.odt, Programme Value) AND "The cost and time extension will allow the CSD programme to achieve the following additional results [...]" (D0001201.odt, Expected Results)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s **weak institutional capacity** and **climate vulnerability** necessitate GoN leadership with international TA support. The **remote geography** and **decentralized governance** (753 local governments) require partners like Mott MacDonald with local presence, while **political economy constraints** (e.g., subsidy distortions) limit private sector roles without policy reforms.
q27_constraints_detail: GoN’s limited absorption capacity → reliance on TA providers for implementation
Decentralization → need for partners with subnational reach (e.g., Mott MacDonald)
Subsidy distortions → exclusion of pure private sector models for renewables
Climate urgency → prioritization of partners with rapid scaling experience (e.g., ICIMOD for HKH work)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (adaptation + mitigation + policy) drive the **hybrid structure**: GoN leads policy/implementation (for ownership), while TA partners (e.g., DAI for NREP) handle specialized delivery. The **need for national scale-up** (e.g., LAPAs) requires GoN systems, while **private sector engagement** (e.g., brick kilns) necessitates market-facing partners like ICIMOD.
q28_linkages: Community adaptation goals → GoN-led LAPAs with TA support
Renewable energy targets → NREP’s challenge fund with private sector
Policy integration → PIF’s direct GoN advisory role
COP26 commitments → British Council/ICIMOD for advocacy
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **inclusion** (e.g., women-targeted adaptation, rural energy access) with **efficiency** (e.g., reimbursement model to mitigate fiduciary risks). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. reach**: Rapid COP26 follow-up (e.g., GGI) vs. slow GoN systems for LAPAs; 2) **Local ownership vs. expertise**: GoN-led implementation with high TA costs; 3) **Subsidy phase-out vs. access**: Gradual reduction of renewable energy subsidies to attract private sector while protecting poor households.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Reimbursement model (efficiency) vs. GoN ownership (equity)
Urban resilience investments (growth) vs. rural adaptation (poverty focus)
Subsidy phase-out (market efficiency) vs. affordable energy access (equity)
COP26 speed (global leadership) vs. local institutional strengthening (sustainability)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., GoN capacity gaps, climate shocks) justifies **intensive oversight** for fiduciary components (e.g., NCCSP reimbursements) but **lighter touch** for advocacy (e.g., ICIMOD’s regional work). COVID-19 delays led to **extended timelines** and **repurposed funds**, reflecting adaptive management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in all components: NCCSP2 strengthens local government adaptation planning; NREP develops private sector renewable energy markets; PIF builds GoN climate finance skills. Partners like Oxford Policy Management **co-deliver** policy work with GoN counterparts to ensure knowledge transfer.
intersections.quote: "Whilst two of the implementation modalities (components 1 and 2) follow on from existing programming, this programme makes a step change in focus – from livelihoods generating activities towards economic growth and work with the private sector." (5639308.odt, Programme Design) AND "The time and cost extension will allow the CSD programme to achieve the following additional results [...]" (D0001201.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks: Low GoN commitment/leadership on climate change (Major - External)
Local government restructuring delays (Major - External)
Natural disasters/conflict disrupting delivery (Moderate - External)
Failure to procure high-quality private sector partners (Minor - Delivery)
Gender risks (programme fails to target women/girls) (Minor - Delivery)
Fiduciary risks in GoN public financial management (Major - Fiduciary)
Market failure in renewable energy uptake (Moderate - Delivery)
Reputational risk from working in brick production sector (Moderate - Reputational)
COVID-19 delays (Added in addendum - External)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fiduciary risks in GoN financial systems
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Reimbursement model with TA verification; risk mitigation plan monitored closely.
Engagement with investors during challenge fund design; policy alignment with GoN.
Time extension and flexible planning.
GESI strategy integrated into LAPAs; women-targeted energy interventions (e.g., e-cooking microfinance).
Cost/time extension; repurposing funds for green recovery.

fcas_specific_lessons: Decentralization requires **subnational capacity building** (e.g., LAPA training for 753 local governments).
Climate finance absorption in FCAS contexts needs **simplified reimbursement models** with TA support.
**Policy ownership** (e.g., NDCs) must precede large-scale funding to avoid implementation bottlenecks.
Post-disaster (e.g., 2015 earthquake) **market-based recovery** (e.g., brick kiln upgrades) can align climate and livelihood goals.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **NCCSP phase 1** demonstrated that community adaptation (LAPAs) works but requires **scaling through government systems**. Lessons included: 1) **Local ownership** improves sustainability (100 LAPAs in 14 districts); 2) **Small-scale investments** need complementing with basin-level planning; 3) **Gender integration** in LAPAs increases resilience for women. The **National Rural Renewable Energy Programme** showed that **subsidy distortions** hinder private sector growth, informing NREP’s market-based approach.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Shift from livelihoods to economic growth**: Added urban resilience and private sector components (e.g., clean bricks, GGI). 2) **Scaling LAPAs nationally**: Integrated with LISP programme for 753 local governments. 3) **Adaptive policy support**: PIF added to help GoN access climate finance (e.g., GCF accreditation). 4) **COP26/27 focus**: New components for regional advocacy (HKH) and global initiatives (LEAF, REAP).
risks_lessons.quote: "The NCCSP builds on a long history of community governance in Nepal [...] The programme works through Government of Nepal systems to help communities develop Local Adaptation Plans of Action (LAPAs)." (5639308.odt, Community-Based Adaptation) AND "Lessons from NCCSP: Community-based adaptation to climate impacts is having positive results but investments are small scale. Larger investments are needed to have a transformational impact." (5639308.odt, Barriers to Climate Smart Development)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize private sector investment in renewable energy (e.g., through the Sustainable Energy Challenge Fund) and unlock international climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund). The GRID framework includes $4.2Bn from 14 donors for climate action in Nepal.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily funds **revenue expenditures** (e.g., TA contracts, reimbursements for adaptation actions) with some **capital investments** in renewable energy infrastructure (e.g., micro-hydro, solar systems) and flood management.
financial_details.quote: "Up to 85% of this money will be provided as Financial Aid to enable the Government of Nepal to take the lead on delivering results from the programme." (5639308.odt, Programme Value) AND "The additional budget of up to £8.5m is requested bringing the total for the programme to £58.5m." (D0001201.odt, Financial Implications)

metadata.programme_name: Building sustainable anti-corruption action in Tanzania (BSAAT)
metadata.quote: "To reduce the role of corruption as a barrier to poverty reduction in Tanzania." (20385572.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £13m over six years to help reduce the role of corruption as a barrier to poverty reduction in Tanzania." (20385572.odt, Narrative summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening criminal justice institutions), policy influence (supporting implementation of anti-corruption commitments), and implementation research (testing social norms interventions). It aims to reduce corruption as a barrier to poverty reduction through systemic reforms and behavioral change.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will spend funds on improving the capacity and coordination of the criminal justice system in corruption cases, improving integrity and governance in the private sector, and influencing social change through research and media." (20385572.odt, Narrative summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved capacity and coordination in the criminal justice chain
indicators: increase in mutual legal assistance and international cooperation
improved judicial processes for relevant cases

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved ethics and transparency in the private sector
indicators: law enforcement access to all beneficial ownership information
public access to beneficial ownership information in the extractives sector
improved monitoring of ethics and integrity in selected private sector forums

q3_expected_outputs.output: A change in social norms, expectations and behaviour in relation to corruption
indicators: other results to be identified during inception phase

q3_expected_outputs.output: Effective management information, learning and research produced
indicators: effective implementation of a monitoring and evaluation strategy

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce elite incentives for corruption through deterrence in the criminal justice system, increased private sector transparency, and social norms change, with quantifiable public sector savings and unquantifiable benefits to tax revenue and public services.
what_objectives.quote: "The impact of this intervention will be to reduce the role of corruption as a barrier to poverty reduction in Tanzania." (20385572.odt, Outputs section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as SEVERE risk due to the complex political economy of corruption in Tanzania, though risks are mitigated by strong political will under President Magufuli's administration.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: SEVERE" (20385572.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Corruption is systemic with elite capture of public resources, and institutions like the PCCB lack independence from the President's Office. The financial sector has vulnerabilities (e.g., FBME Bank's money laundering concerns), and fiduciary risks persist in procurement and audit systems. Political will is strong but potentially volatile, and Zanzibar's separate legal system adds complexity.
where_context.quote: "The political environment has become increasingly competitive. Corruption, driven by the availability of rents in the public sector, has filtered into critical sectors on a damaging scale." (20385572.odt, Context section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO retains decision-making authority, with the Government of Tanzania (GoT) as a crucial partner. The SRO (Senior Responsible Officer) is a DFID governance advisor, and day-to-day management may be procured commercially or staffed by GoT under DFID oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for criminal justice institutions (e.g., Special Division of the High Court, DPP, PCCB)
mentorship and management assistance to anti-corruption bodies
institutional strengthening of private sector associations (lawyers, accountants)
research grants for social norms studies
support to media and civil society for advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania (GoT)
partner_organizations.role: primary partner; recipient of capacity-building and coordination support

partner_organizations.name: Prevention and Combatting of Corruption Bureau (PCCB)
partner_organizations.role: direct beneficiary; receives technical and operational support

partner_organizations.name: Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP)
partner_organizations.role: direct beneficiary; receives management assistance to reduce case dismissals

partner_organizations.name: Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA)
partner_organizations.role: partner for tax compliance and beneficial ownership transparency

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (UK)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner via Institutional Integrity Partnership

partner_organizations.name: Tanzania Media Foundation
partner_organizations.role: partner for media training and public campaigns

partner_organizations.name: Private sector associations (e.g., lawyers, accountants)
partner_organizations.role: targets for ethics and transparency improvements

partner_organizations.name: Civil society organizations (e.g., Twaweza, REPOA)
partner_organizations.role: partners for research, advocacy, and social norms interventions

partner_organizations.name: EU Mission (potential)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (up to €7m) if administrative arrangements are agreed

who_partners.quote: "The Government of Tanzania (GoT) will be a crucial partner. UK assistance is needed for the GoT to implement commitments made at the London Anti-Corruption Summit in May 2016." (20385572.odt, Narrative summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of financial aid (grants) to GoT institutions and contracts for commercial procurement of management/technical assistance. The EU co-funding (if secured) would likely follow similar instruments under pooled financing.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID leads with a mix of direct funding to GoT institutions and commercially procured implementation support. A secretariat or programme team (either procured or GoT-staffed) manages day-to-day operations, with annual reviews to adjust activities. The EU may join as a co-funder under a separate agreement.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (GoT is pre-selected as primary partner)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The GoT is the primary partner due to its commitments at the London Anti-Corruption Summit and DFID's long-standing relationship with Tanzanian anti-corruption institutions. Other partners (e.g., media, private sector) are selected based on alignment with programme objectives and existing DFID programmes (e.g., STACA).
how_mechanism.quote: "The Government of Tanzania (GoT) will be a crucial partner. [...] There are options for how to deliver this programme, but in all cases the Government of Tanzania (GoT) will be a crucial partner." (20385572.odt, Narrative summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly detailed, the programme implies a steering mechanism involving DFID, GoT, and potentially the EU (if co-funding is secured). The SRO (DFID governance advisor) oversees implementation, with annual reviews to adjust activities.
how_governance.quote: "Monitoring and learning is a critical component and is separately budgeted for. [...] This programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through annual reviews, where decisions will be taken to scale activities up or down based on performance." (20385572.odt, Flexibility section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on annual reviews, but major shifts require approval. The programme is designed to scale activities up or down based on performance and context changes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an inception phase to finalize activities, and annual reviews allow for adjustments. Social norms and private sector components are explicitly designed to be responsive to new evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "This programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through annual reviews, where decisions will be taken to scale activities up or down based on performance." (20385572.odt, Flexibility section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) Secretariat/Programme Implementation Team (commercially procured or GoT-staffed) → (2) Direct beneficiaries (GoT institutions, private sector, civil society).
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through annual reviews [...] Management costs [are] at about 15%." (20385572.odt, Appraisal Case and Flexibility sections)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: Focus on criminal justice reform only
Option 2: Broader programme targeting criminal justice, private sector, and social norms
pros: better able to handle context changes
cons: more scoping needed for business/social norms

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: Additional EU funding for broader programme

pros: more space to focus on other priorities
cons: higher potential for gains to be reversed

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 was selected because it balances the need for a credible theory of change (addressing criminal justice, private sector, and social norms) with flexibility to adapt to Tanzania's political context. It leverages the UK's unique position post-London Summit and aligns with GoT priorities while mitigating risks of over-reliance on a single component (e.g., criminal justice alone).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on political will: A deterioration in GoT commitment could undermine progress, especially in criminal justice reforms.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual reviews to assess political commitment and adapt activities; diversification across private sector and social norms components to reduce dependency on GoT.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex management: Coordinating across criminal justice, private sector, and social norms requires significant oversight.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Separate budget for monitoring/learning; phased implementation with inception period to finalize activities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: EU co-funding transaction costs: Administrative burdens if EU joins as a co-funder.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Only pursue EU co-funding if administrative arrangements are deemed acceptable (e.g., no excessive reporting duplication).

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option is option 2. This is preferable to doing nothing or doing only a narrow range of activities around only criminal justice. A broader programme has a higher likelihood of achieving impact and is less susceptible to derailment because of a single issue." (20385572.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy of Tanzania constrains partner selection to institutions aligned with President Magufuli's anti-corruption drive (e.g., PCCB, DPP). Zanzibar's separate legal system (e.g., ZAECA instead of PCCB) and the need to avoid undermining GoT credibility limit direct engagement with some actors (e.g., branding restrictions for justice institutions).
q27_constraints_detail: GoT institutions must be primary partners due to Summit commitments and political momentum.
Zanzibar's separate legal system requires tailored approaches (not covered by PCCB).
Branding restrictions for justice/law enforcement to avoid perception of foreign influence.
Need for cross-HMG coordination (e.g., National Crime Agency) due to UK's strategic interests.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (criminal justice + private sector + social norms) necessitate a flexible, multi-component structure. Criminal justice reforms require direct GoT partnership and HMG expertise, while private sector and social norms components need adaptive, evidence-based approaches (e.g., grant-making facilities, research pilots).
q28_linkages: End-to-end criminal justice reform → requires direct institutional support (GoT partnership).
Private sector transparency → needs flexible funds for professional associations and beneficial ownership pilots.
Social norms change → demands responsive mechanisms (e.g., grant-making for local research).
Monitoring/learning → separate budget to track cross-cutting impacts.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (e.g., UK criminal justice advisors) with Southern ownership (GoT-led implementation). Trade-offs include: (1) Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to GoT enable rapid start-up but limit competitive selection. (2) Expertise vs. ownership: UK advisors provide technical skills, but GoT institutions must lead to ensure sustainability. (3) Cost vs. reach: EU co-funding could expand scope but adds transaction costs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Direct awards to GoT prioritize speed and alignment over competitive selection.
UK expertise (e.g., National Crime Agency) is critical for complex areas like financial investigations but risks perceived foreign influence.
Social norms components require local ownership but may have higher upfront costs for research/pilots.
EU co-funding could increase impact but complicates management (e.g., reporting duplication).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The SEVERE risk rating drives intensive oversight (annual reviews, embedded monitoring/learning budget) and flexible design (adaptive management). Political volatility in Tanzania necessitates frequent 'temperature checks' and contingency planning (e.g., diversified components).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with GoT institutions (e.g., PCCB, DPP) receiving embedded support (training, mentorship) to gradually take on leadership roles. Private sector and civil society partners are engaged through grants and technical assistance to build local ownership.
intersections.quote: "The political will has rarely been so conducive in Tanzania, and there are multiple commercial options for bringing in the needed skills and capability, learning lessons from previous programmes." (20385572.odt, Quality Assurance section)

key_programme_risks: Political risk: Deterioration in GoT commitment to anti-corruption (e.g., elite pushback, election cycles).
Institutional risk: Weak capacity in anti-corruption bodies (e.g., PCCB's slow performance, lack of independence).
Financial sector risk: Vulnerabilities to money laundering (e.g., FBME Bank case) and illicit financial flows.
Implementation risk: Complex coordination across criminal justice, private sector, and social norms components.
Reputational risk: Perception of foreign interference if UK support is overly visible in sensitive areas (e.g., justice institutions).
Sustainability risk: Limited GoT budgeting for anti-corruption institutions post-programme.
Data risk: Weak baseline data on corruption dynamics, especially gender-disaggregated impacts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Annual reviews to assess political will; diversified components (private sector/social norms) to reduce reliance on GoT; leverage President Magufuli's public mandate.
Embedded technical assistance; focus on systemic bottlenecks (e.g., case management, inter-agency coordination); build on STACA programme lessons.
Support to Financial Intelligence Units; alignment with FATF review processes; focus on beneficial ownership transparency.
Separate M&E budget; phased implementation; clear division of roles between criminal justice, private sector, and social norms teams.
Restrict branding for justice/law enforcement; emphasize GoT leadership in communications; focus on capacity-building narratives.
Strengthen GoT budgeting processes; advocate for long-term funding of anti-corruption institutions; document lessons for future programmes.
Invest in home-grown indicators (e.g., PCCB surveys); disaggregate data by gender/region where possible; partner with local researchers (e.g., REPOA).

fcas_specific_lessons: Leverage political momentum: President Magufuli's anti-corruption drive creates a unique window for reform, but progress must be institutionalized quickly to outlast his tenure.
Adapt to elite incentives: Corruption in Tanzania is elite-driven; deterrence requires a mix of criminal justice, financial transparency, and social norms change.
Local ownership is critical: Previous programmes (e.g., STACA) showed that sustainability depends on GoT institutions taking leadership, not donor-driven agendas.
Flexibility is essential: Annual reviews and adaptive management are necessary to respond to Tanzania's volatile political economy.
Zanzibar requires tailored approaches: The island's separate legal system (e.g., ZAECA) and distinct political dynamics necessitate specific strategies, not just mainland replication.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The STACA programme (2012–2016) demonstrated that: (1) Criminal justice reforms require end-to-end support (not just focusing on one institution). (2) Political will is volatile—gains can be quickly reversed without sustained pressure. (3) Social accountability mechanisms (e.g., media, civil society) are critical complements to state-led enforcement. (4) Procurement and fiduciary risks persist despite reforms. (5) Local data (e.g., PCCB's home-grown indicators) is more actionable than global indices (e.g., CPI).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Broader scope than STACA: Adds private sector and social norms components to address root causes of corruption, not just enforcement.
Flexible funding: Includes a separate M&E budget and adaptive mechanisms (e.g., annual reviews) to respond to context changes.
Focus on beneficial ownership: Directly addresses a London Summit commitment and a key gap in Tanzania's anti-corruption framework.
Gender disaggregation: Explicitly includes gender analysis in baseline surveys and M&E, learning from STACA's limitations.
EU co-funding option: Explores pooled financing to increase resources while maintaining DFID leadership.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID’s Strengthening Tanzania’s Anti-Corruption Action programme ran from 2012-2016 and worked closely with the relevant Tanzanian agencies. The relationships built up through this can be leveraged in this new programme, as can the lessons of an evaluation by U4 Christian Michelsen Institute and Research on Poverty Alleviation (REPOA)." (20385572.odt, Context section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage GoT commitments (e.g., London Summit pledges) and mobilize additional resources through EU co-funding (€7m, ~£6m). Asset recovery efforts (e.g., IPTL case) could also generate significant returns (potential £94m).
financial_details.quote: "The cost of the DFID programme is £13m over six years, discounted to £9.6m. [...] Management costs [are] at about 15%." (20385572.odt, Appraisal Case)

metadata.programme_name: UK-Ghana Partnership for Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET)
metadata.quote: The JET programme will help drive economic transformation in Ghana by supporting government to attract increased private investment and create high quality jobs in key industrial sectors. (D0000974.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: The UK will provide up to £20 million over 6 years to stimulate investment in four or five target sectors (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The JET programme combines capacity building (strengthening Ghana's industrial policy and investment promotion institutions), financing mechanism (leveraging private capital), and implementation research (testing sector-specific interventions). It aims to stimulate private investment in 4-5 industrial sectors to create 15,000 jobs and leverage £50M in private capital.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme will be the catalyst for a new strategic partnership between the Ghana and the UK. A partnership based on economic development, investment, trade and strategic political cooperation, in line with the UK’s Africa Strategy and with the GoG’s ‘beyond aid’ vision. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 15,000 formal jobs created within the programme target sectors
£50 million leveraged in additional private capital
Increased productivity of domestic firms in targeted sectors
Industrial policy development (technical assistance to national institutions)
Investment promotion and facilitation for investors in 4-5 target sectors
Increased engagement of domestic firms in sectors attracting investment
Addressing enabling environment gaps around investments (technical assistance for industrial parks, logistics, transport)
what_objectives.summary: JET aims to catalyze Ghana's economic transformation by supporting industrialization through private sector investment in 4-5 'backbone' sectors, creating jobs and diversifying the economy beyond commodities.
what_objectives.quote: Indicative result projections are that the programme will facilitate over £50 million of additional private sector investment and create 15,000 jobs. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ghana's economy remains at high risk of debt distress (70% debt-to-GDP ratio) and is vulnerable to commodity price shocks. The programme risk is categorized as 'Major' due to potential macroeconomic instability affecting investor confidence.
where_context.q5_source: Programme risk is categorised as Major, primarily due to context risks such as deterioration in Ghana’s macroeconomic stability which would have an adverse impact on investor confidence. (D0000974.odt, Risk)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Ghana's World Bank Doing Business ranking has fallen 12 places since 2016 (now 120th), and 70-87% of tax revenues are spent on wages and interest payments, severely constraining public investment. The government has limited resources to address industrialization gaps, requiring heavy reliance on private investment.
where_context.quote: Ghana’s performance in WB doing business has stagnated and fallen in recent years. Ghana is now ranked 120th in the World Bank Doing Business Index falling 12 places since 2016. (D0000974.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Cross-HMG Economic Development, Investment and Trade (EDIT) team
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme will be delivered by a contracted Technical Service Provider (TSP) with oversight from a separated DFID Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) and Lead Adviser roles. A Strategic Advisory Panel (SAP) will include UK Government, international experts, and key investors like CDC, ensuring joint decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to national institutions (Ministry of Trade, GIPC, Free Zones Board) to implement trade and investment frameworks
Business development and technology innovation support for domestic firms
Training for investment promotion agencies on sector prioritization and investor engagement
Support for developing special economic zones (SEZs) regulations and public-private partnership frameworks
Building technical/technological capacity within Ghanaian SMEs (e.g., industrial engineering, quality control)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ghana (GoG)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiary and co-designer; provides political leadership through a high-level reference group (Ministers of Trade, CEOs of GIPC, Free Zones Board, Export Promotion Authority)

partner_organizations.name: Ghana Investment Promotion Council (GIPC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead agency for investment promotion and facilitation within target sectors

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Trade and Industry (MoTI)
partner_organizations.role: Policy development and coordination for industrialization

partner_organizations.name: Ghana Free Zones Board
partner_organizations.role: Management of special economic zones and local content strategies

partner_organizations.name: Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA)
partner_organizations.role: Trade promotion and market access support

partner_organizations.name: DFID (now FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funding and strategic oversight; SRO and Lead Adviser roles separated for robust governance

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Trade (DIT)
partner_organizations.role: Trade promotion and UK business engagement

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCO)
partner_organizations.role: Diplomatic support and political cooperation

partner_organizations.name: CDC Group
partner_organizations.role: Advisory role and piloting an investment market information platform; potential co-investor

partner_organizations.name: Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG)
partner_organizations.role: Pilot initiative to generate infrastructure support in target sectors

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Collaboration on skills development and economic transformation programmes

partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer contracted to work with public/private stakeholders in 4-5 priority sectors

partner_organizations.name: Strategic Advisory Panel (SAP)
partner_organizations.role: Flexible, evidence-based decision-making body including UK Government, international experts, and investors

partner_organizations.name: DFID Invest Africa programme
partner_organizations.role: Advisory role and peer-to-peer learning with East Africa

who_partners.quote: Programme delivery will be primarily through a contracted specialised Technical Service Provider (TSP). To ensure robust oversight, quality assurance and risk management, it is proposed that the DFID Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) and Lead Adviser roles be separated. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will be delivered primarily through a contracted Technical Service Provider (TSP), with DFID providing upfront funding for a 6-year period. The contract includes performance-based milestones tied to investment leverage and job creation targets.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A contracted TSP will deliver the programme with oversight from DFID's separated SRO (compliance/influence) and Lead Private Sector Development Adviser (day-to-day management). The Strategic Advisory Panel (SAP) provides additional governance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The TSP was selected to ensure specialized technical expertise in investment promotion and industrial policy, with flexibility to adapt to Ghana's evolving priorities. The separation of SRO/Lead Adviser roles mitigates conflicts of interest.
how_mechanism.quote: Programme delivery will be primarily through a contracted specialised Technical Service Provider (TSP). (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Strategic Advisory Panel (SAP) includes UK Government representatives, international experts, and key investors (e.g., CDC). It facilitates flexible, evidence-based decision-making and aligns programme support with locally owned priorities.
how_governance.quote: A Strategic Advisory Panel (SAP) will facilitate flexible, evidence-based decision-making, bringing together the UK Government, international experts and key investors such as CDC. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme design allows resources to be allocated to industrial sectors where investments are being generated and to exit sectors where this is not the case. A portion of funds is reserved for rapid response to emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Target sectors can be adjusted based on investor interest and development potential, with approval from the SAP. The programme includes a 'demonstration effects' approach to capitalize on early wins.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme design allows resources to be allocated to industrial sectors wherein investments are being generated and to exit sectors where this is not the case. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Technical Service Provider (TSP) → End beneficiaries (GoG agencies, private sector firms)
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will be delivered by a small team of technical experts and investment advisers who will draw on practical support from global experts, including from the UK. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: GoG would struggle to implement industrialization plans due to fiscal constraints; limited donor support for sector-specific interventions.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: B: National capacity building programme for trade/investment promotion
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Direct support to GoG agencies (MoTI, GIPC, Free Zones Board) to improve investment promotion capacity, with embedded experts and training.
Targeted support in 4-5 priority industrial sectors to stimulate private investment, promote domestic firms, and address enabling environment gaps.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option C was selected for its ability to (1) work with both public and private sectors to stimulate investment; (2) influence sector selection and intervention priorities; and (3) create incentives for cross-HMG collaboration by focusing on private sector funding sources. The 'backbone' approach aligns with Ghana's growth pole theory and offers higher development impact by targeting sectors with scale potential.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (higher leverage of private capital per pound of ODA)
risk mitigation (diversifying beyond commodities reduces macroeconomic volatility)
partner capacity (builds on GoG's industrialization vision and UK's trade/investment expertise)
flexibility (allows sector adjustments based on investor interest)
speed (capitalizes on current window of pro-business government and investor appetite)
equity (targets formal job creation, including for women and youth)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of perceived UK commercial bias
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme design includes transparent selection criteria for target sectors and investors, with SAP oversight to ensure fairness.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoG ownership dilution due to third-party delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong GoG buy-in secured through high-level reference group; flexible funds reserved for emerging GoG priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow delivery due to coordination gaps
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Separated SRO/Lead Adviser roles and embedded technical experts to accelerate implementation.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per output compared to alternatives)
equity (disproportionate benefits for women and poor regions)
why_rationale.quote: Option C: Take a ‘backbone’ or ‘anchor’ focused approach to target support in priority industrial sectors... The benefits of this option are: (i) the ability of the programme to work with both the public and private sectors to stimulate private investment, promote domestic firms and address enabling environment gaps; (ii) the opportunity for the programme to influence the selection of target sectors and intervention priorities; and (iii) the incentives created by the programme for UK Government departments to work collaboratively. (D0000974.odt, Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Ghana's macroeconomic volatility (70% debt-to-GDP, 120th in Doing Business) and limited fiscal space (70-87% of tax revenues spent on wages/interest) constrain the pool of capable local partners. This necessitates a mixed delivery structure with international TSPs to fill technical gaps while building local capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited GoG resources for industrialization (only 20,000 acres of industrial land earmarked across 10 regions)
Weak domestic firm capabilities (Ghanaian manufacturing firms are 7x less productive than Kenyan peers)
Regulatory barriers (falling World Bank Doing Business rank, complex SEZ frameworks)
Investor skepticism due to historical reliance on commodities (oil/gas/cocoa account for 76% of exports)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to (1) stimulate private investment in 4-5 'backbone' sectors and (2) address both supply-side (firm capabilities) and demand-side (investor facilitation) constraints drives the mixed delivery structure. The TSP model was chosen to provide specialized expertise while the SAP ensures alignment with GoG priorities.
q28_linkages: Job creation targets (15,000 formal jobs) → Requires direct engagement with private sector firms → Justifies TSP's business development support role
Leverage goal (£50M private capital) → Needs investor facilitation → Drives inclusion of UKEF, PIDG, and CDC in governance
Industrial policy development → Requires MoTI/GIPC capacity building → Embedded technical experts in GoG agencies
Enabling environment gaps → Needs infrastructure/regulatory fixes → Partnership with World Bank and PIDG
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) speed/efficiency (using UK TSPs for rapid delivery) with (2) equity/inclusion (70% of funds earmarked for flexible response to GoG priorities and 30% for direct firm support). The 'backbone' sector approach prioritizes high-growth sectors while requiring 40% of facilitated investments to include local content provisions.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (UK TSPs) vs. Southern ownership (GoG reference group oversight)
Speed (contracting TSPs) vs. capacity building (embedded training for GIPC/MoTI)
Focus (4-5 sectors) vs. inclusivity (flexible funds for emerging priorities)
Commercial opportunities (UK firm engagement) vs. development impact (job quality standards)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk rating (due to macroeconomic volatility) drives intensive oversight through: (1) separated SRO/Lead Adviser roles; (2) quarterly SAP reviews; and (3) milestone-based payments to the TSP. The high-risk context also justifies reserving 15% of funds for rapid response to shocks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited GoG capacity (e.g., GIPC's weak investor aftercare) shapes the TSP's role to include hand-holding support for investors and brokerage between UK firms and Ghanaian SMEs. The programme's 60% budget allocation to technical assistance reflects this capacity gap.
intersections.quote: The programme design allows resources to be allocated to industrial sectors wherein investments are being generated and to exit sectors where this is not the case... Flexibility will be built in to enable target sectors to change as the context shifts. (D0000974.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic instability reducing investor confidence (linked to commodity price/exchange rate shocks)
Change in government (2020 elections) deprioritizing industrialization
Slow materialization of results leading to dwindling GoG support
Reputational risk from poor business practices among supported firms
Perception of UK commercial bias in sector/investor selection
Limited absorption capacity in GoG agencies (e.g., GIPC, MoTI)
Over-reliance on a few anchor investors in target sectors
Delays in industrial park development (only 3 of 10 regions have parks under development)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversify target sectors beyond commodities; include shock-responsive funds (15% contingency); align with IMF Extended Credit Facility reforms.
Secure cross-party buy-in through high-level reference group; document quick wins in first 2 years.
Front-load visible activities (e.g., Investment Summit in Year 1); use SAP to adjust interventions quarterly.
Due diligence framework for investor selection; mandatory ESG compliance for supported firms.
Transparent sector selection criteria published; SAP includes non-UK investors; track % of non-UK FDI leveraged.
Embed TSP experts in GIPC/MoTI; allocate 20% of budget to institutional strengthening.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Ghana's 2015 macroeconomic crisis (10% fiscal deficit, 40% cedi devaluation) informed the programme's shock-responsive design (e.g., flexible sector allocation).
Adaptation of World Bank SEZ models to Ghana's context (e.g., combining industrial parks with local content requirements).
Incorporation of 'demonstration effects' from East Africa (e.g., Ethiopia's apparel hub) to attract investors.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID programmes in Ghana (e.g., BEEP, ENGINE) showed that: (1) regulatory reforms alone are insufficient without private sector engagement; (2) SME support must be linked to specific value chains; and (3) UK-Ghana commercial ties require active brokerage (e.g., UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce involvement).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added: (1) explicit local content requirements (40% of facilitated investments); (2) gender-disaggregated job targets (10.3% of manufacturing jobs held by women); (3) SAP with investor representation to address previous coordination gaps.
risks_lessons.quote: The programme risk is categorised as Major, primarily due to context risks such as deterioration in Ghana’s macroeconomic stability... This is within DFID Ghana’s risk appetite given the very high potential returns and the need for a more ambitious approach to economic development. (D0000974.odt, Risk)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage £50 million in additional private capital (2.5x the £20M ODA investment) through: (1) investment facilitation in 4-5 sectors; (2) UKEF's increased exposure limit (from £375M to £1.1B); and (3) PIDG/CDC co-investments.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both capital expenditures (e.g., industrial park infrastructure development) and revenue support (e.g., technical assistance to GIPC), with ~60% allocated to direct firm/sector interventions and 40% to enabling environment improvements.
financial_details.quote: The UK will provide up to £20 million over 6 years to stimulate investment in four or five target sectors... Indicative result projections are that the programme will facilitate over £50 million of additional private sector investment. (D0000974.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Increasing renewable energy and energy efficiency in the Caribbean
metadata.duration_text: June 2015 - December 2025 (with consideration for extension to March 2028/9 by March 2025)
metadata.quote: "To increase the use of renewable energy and energy efficiency measures and to improve energy security in the Caribbean by supporting governments to build capacity and infrastructure to diversify their energy portfolio with an emphasis on homegrown, greener and cheaper RE and EE which is pivotal to their progress towards sustainable development." (D0005864.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: June 2015-March 2020. The programme had one cost extension in 2018 (increase from £17.35m to £19.35m) and time extensions to 31 March 2023 and 31 December 2025." (D0005864.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (channeling funds for geothermal and offshore wind development), implementation research (testing and scaling renewable energy interventions), and capacity building (strengthening institutions and skills in the energy sector). It also includes direct service delivery through energy efficiency retrofits and renewable energy installations.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will be extended to the broader ODA eligible Caribbean given potential location of selected OSW ‘lighthouse’ site. [...] To increase the use of renewable energy and energy efficiency measures and to improve energy security in the Caribbean by supporting governments to build capacity and infrastructure to diversify their energy portfolio with an emphasis on homegrown, greener and cheaper RE and EE which is pivotal to their progress towards sustainable development." (D0005864.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Exploratory geothermal well drilling in Grenada (15MW potential plant)
Caribbean Offshore Wind "lighthouse" project (50-100MW demonstration turbine)
Energy savings of 7,025.72 MWh/year from SEEC component
900 kW of solar photovoltaics installed
Geothermal production and reinjection wells in Dominica (10MW plant)
Exploratory geothermal drilling in St. Vincent & the Grenadines and St. Lucia
Construction of a 500 kW PV plant in St. Vincent & the Grenadines
Leveraged financing for 400 kW in solar PV at SMMEs in Grenada
Completion of energy audits of 83 public building sites across 6 countries
Energy efficient retrofits to 3 government buildings in St. Vincent & the Grenadines
Installation of 13,612 energy-efficient LED streetlights in Antigua & Barbuda and 7,380 in St. Vincent & the Grenadines
Capacity building of 319 individuals (255 males, 64 females) in solar PV installation, regulation, and energy planning
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform the Caribbean's energy sector by reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels through a combination of geothermal development, offshore wind demonstration, energy efficiency retrofits, and capacity building. It uses grant financing to de-risk investments and catalyze private sector participation while building local technical capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme has supported energy savings of 7,025.72 MWh/year and installed 900 kW of solar photovoltaics (PV) to date. The results include: geothermal production and reinjection wells in DOM which allowed them to negotiate for construction of a 10MW plant; exploratory geothermal drilling in SVG and SLU; construction of a 500 kW PV plant in SVG; leveraged financing for construction of 400 kW in solar PV at SMMEs in Grenada; completion of energy audits of public buildings (83 sites) in ANT, DOM, Grenada, St. Kitts & Nevis, SLU and SVG; energy efficient retrofits to three government buildings in SVG; installation of energy efficient LED street lighting in Antigua and Barbuda (13,612 streetlights) and SVG (7,380 streetlights); and capacity building of 255 males and 64 females in initiatives such as solar PV installation and regulation, negotiating power purchase agreements and energy planning." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in small island developing states with limited economies of scale, high vulnerability to climate shocks, and fiscal constraints that hinder debt financing. While not classified as FCAS, the region faces significant implementation challenges due to its geographic isolation and capacity limitations.
where_context.q5_source: "Caribbean SIDS continue to face increasing and more severe climate related shocks that often lead to significant setbacks and increase the cost and time of doing business. This and their geographical location, lack of economies of scale and human resource constraints for delivering transformative change in the energy sector means that they require considerable support and time to achieve planned project outcomes and impact." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The constraints have led to slower-than-expected implementation, with countries struggling to access affordable debt or take on additional financing despite grant funds being available. Climate shocks frequently cause setbacks, and the archipelagic geography creates logistical challenges for regional initiatives like offshore wind development.
where_context.quote: "The 2020 annual review assessed that while the Theory of Change holds true and we are already seeing results, the timelines for attaining planned outcome and impact indicators will be longer than projected in the programme design. This is mainly due to the specific context in Caribbean SIDS where even with the grant funds provided through FCDO and other development partners, countries continue to be challenged to access affordable debt and/or to take on additional debt due to national fiscal constraints." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank and Caribbean Development Bank (primary implementers)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between FCDO, multilateral partners (World Bank, CDB), and Caribbean governments, with technical oversight from UK-based entities like the Green Cities and Infrastructure Centre of Expertise. Southern partners (Caribbean governments and regional bodies like CCREEE) have significant influence over project priorities and implementation.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for geothermal strategy and regulation
training in solar PV installation (255 males, 64 females trained)
support for negotiating power purchase agreements
energy planning and regulatory capacity building
gender-sensitive consultations and social impact analysis
institutional strengthening for national development banks

partner_organizations.role: Implementation of geothermal components in Dominica and St. Lucia; management of ESMAP Multi-Donor Trust Fund

who_partners.quote: "We will use implementing partners that have successfully delivered under this programme, meet our due diligence requirements and are best placed for further energy delivery in the Caribbean. [...] The original programme has three components: £2.5m for the Sustainable Energy for the Eastern Caribbean (SEEC) in partnership with the European Union’s Caribbean Investment Facility and implemented by the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB) [...] £16.4m in support to geothermal development in the Eastern Caribbean [...] implemented by the World Bank." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grant agreements (for geothermal and offshore wind components), administrative arrangements with multilaterals (World Bank, CDB), and memoranda of understanding for the SEEC component. Funds are channeled through existing multi-donor trust funds (e.g., World Bank's ESMAP) and blended with concessional loans from partners like CDB.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through separate agreements with the World Bank and CDB, each overseeing distinct components. The World Bank handles geothermal development in Dominica and St. Lucia via the ESMAP Trust Fund, while CDB manages the SEEC programme and geothermal activities in St. Vincent & the Grenadines and Grenada. FCDO retains oversight through administrative agreements and disburses funds based on expenditure reports.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct award to existing partners)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on prior successful delivery under the programme, existing relationships, and their technical capacity to manage complex energy infrastructure projects in the Caribbean. The use of multilaterals (World Bank, CDB) reduces transaction costs and leverages their safeguards systems and regional expertise.
how_mechanism.quote: "The support to SEEC and to SVG geothermal development are being implemented by the CDB through separate Memoranda of Understanding with the FCDO, while DOM and SLU geothermal development are being implemented by the WB through separate Administrative Arrangements with the FCDO." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION) AND "We will use implementing partners that have successfully delivered under this programme, meet our due diligence requirements and are best placed for further energy delivery in the Caribbean." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Sub-awards for specific activities (e.g., energy audits, retrofits) are managed by CDB and World Bank according to their internal procedures, with FCDO oversight limited to high-level reporting and milestone reviews. For example, CDB disburses SEEC funds semi-annually based on expenditure plans, while World Bank manages geothermal funds through the ESMAP Trust Fund.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: No formal steering committee or board is mentioned. Governance relies on bilateral agreements between FCDO and implementing partners (World Bank, CDB), with FCDO conducting periodic reviews (e.g., annual assessments) and requiring partners to comply with their internal safeguards and procurement policies.
how_governance.quote: "Funds were disbursed to the WB using the existing ESMAP Trust Fund. In the case of the SEEC, funds are disbursed to CDB semi-annually based on expenditure, commitments and plans for the following 6-month period." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The 2020 annual review assessed that while the Theory of Change holds true and we are already seeing results, the timelines for attaining planned outcome and impact indicators will be longer than projected in the programme design." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within components (e.g., Dominica repurposed geothermal funds from plant construction to reinjection wells and substations), but major shifts require FCDO approval. The 2020 addendum notes that £12.1m disbursed to the World Bank remained undrawn due to delays, indicating some flexibility in timing but not purpose.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has adapted to context changes (e.g., COVID-19 delays, hurricane impacts) by extending timelines and reallocating funds (e.g., Dominica's geothermal component shift). New components (offshore wind, Grenada geothermal) were added based on emerging evidence, but these required formal addendums and approvals.
how_flexibility.quote: "The main change from the original business case is around how FCDO funds will be allocated in the Dominica Geothermal Project. The GoCD identified an alternate source of funds to construct the geothermal plant and has requested that FCDO funds be reallocated to finance the single re-injection well serving the Small Geothermal Power Plant (SGPP), an additional production well [...] and a high voltage transformer substation." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The proposed additional activities therefore do not represent a substantial change in the programme focus, in fact they align fully with the original outcome and impact." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (World Bank or CDB) → End Recipient (e.g., national governments, DGDC). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned beyond the primary recipients.
how_efficiency.quote: "Funds were disbursed to the WB using the existing ESMAP Trust Fund. In the case of the SEEC, funds are disbursed to CDB semi-annually based on expenditure, commitments and plans for the following 6-month period." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)

q24_alternatives_considered: Regional solutions (e.g., interconnection of electricity markets via submarine cables) - rejected due to high costs and lack of regional cooperation
Large-scale solar/wind/marine renewables - rejected due to intermittency concerns and grid limitations
Natural gas as a transition fuel - excluded because ICF funds cannot support fossil fuels
Allocation of entire budget to either small-scale renewables/EE OR geothermal - rejected as too high-risk; combined approach chosen for balance
Direct financing of geothermal plant construction (vs. exploratory drilling) - shifted to based on government requests and emerging needs
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery model (multilateral partners + direct government engagement) was chosen to balance risk, leverage existing platforms (e.g., ESMAP Trust Fund), and align with Caribbean governments' capacity constraints. Using the World Bank and CDB reduces transaction costs, provides safeguards, and enables blending with concessional loans. The phased approach (exploratory drilling → plant construction) de-risks geothermal investments, while the SEEC component ensures quick wins through energy efficiency.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (blending grants with loans to maximize impact)
risk mitigation (multilaterals manage high-risk geothermal drilling)
partner capacity (World Bank/CDB have regional expertise and safeguards)
speed (existing trust funds enable rapid disbursement)
flexibility (ability to adapt to government priorities, e.g., Dominica's reallocation request)
equity (focus on ODA-eligible SIDS with highest energy costs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in multilateral partner processes (e.g., World Bank Board approvals, safeguard compliance) stalling implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Time extensions granted (e.g., to December 2023 for World Bank activities) and close monitoring of milestone achievement. FCDO retains ability to reallocate undrawn funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of private sector interest in small-scale geothermal plants (e.g., Dominica's 10MW plant) reducing cost-effectiveness
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Grant funding used to de-risk exploratory drilling and negotiate favorable PPAs. FCDO funds catalyze additional financing (e.g., World Bank, EU, Italy co-investments).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Geopolitical tensions hindering regional offshore wind cooperation (e.g., country-specific interests vs. shared infrastructure)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Two-phase approach: pre-feasibility studies first to identify viable ODA-eligible sites before committing to construction. Collaboration with CCREEE and CDB to manage regional dynamics.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: CDB's implementation challenges (noted in earlier phases) affecting SEEC delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Semi-annual disbursements tied to expenditure plans and commitments. FCDO conducts annual reviews to assess progress.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks and fiscal constraints in Caribbean SIDS prolonging timelines
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible extensions (e.g., from 2021 to 2023/2025) and adaptive management to reprioritize activities based on context changes.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of ICF funds via multilaterals)
efficiency (leveraging existing trust funds and partner systems)
effectiveness (balancing quick wins from EE with long-term geothermal transformation)
equity (targeting countries with highest energy costs and lowest resilience)
why_rationale.quote: "The option of using all the allocated £17.4 million available for either a large programme on renewable energy and energy efficiency or a larger programme of geothermal support was discounted because the risk of failure was deemed too great. Small-scale renewables and energy efficiency measures are important quick wins but are unlikely to have a transformative impact. In contrast geothermal can provide base-load electricity but is a longer-term prospect with higher risks. A combined programme would allow us to balance technology type, risk, cost and the potential for impact, while also supporting progress towards a more diverse, resilient energy mix." (4885414.odt, Option A) AND "DFID can help address early stage high financial risks in geothermal development to make it more attractive for investors. [...] Our preferred option is to directly finance test drilling and provide technical assistance for improved geothermal strategy, policy and regulation." (4885414.odt, Recommended Approach)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Caribbean's small island context and fiscal constraints limit partner selection to multilaterals (World Bank, CDB) and regional bodies (CCREEE) with existing safeguards and concessional financing mechanisms. Local private sector firms lack capacity to manage high-risk geothermal drilling, and governments cannot absorb additional debt, necessitating grant-based support channeled through trusted intermediaries.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited local technical capacity for geothermal development → reliance on World Bank/CDB
High debt levels in Caribbean SIDS → need for grant (not loan) financing
Small market size → multilaterals required for economies of scale
Climate vulnerability → partners must have adaptive management experience
Regional fragmentation → CCREEE/CDB needed to coordinate cross-country initiatives
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to de-risk geothermal exploration (high upfront costs, uncertainty) drives the use of multilaterals with safeguards systems (World Bank) and phased funding (exploratory drilling first). The mix of quick-win EE measures and long-term geothermal transformation requires a dual structure: CDB for SEEC's rapid disbursements and World Bank for complex geothermal projects.
q28_linkages: High-risk geothermal drilling → World Bank's ESMAP Trust Fund (existing platform for risky energy projects)
Need for concessional blending → CDB's ability to combine grants with loans
Regional EE retrofits → CDB's multi-country programme management experience
Offshore wind's regional scale → CCREEE's coordination role for cross-border initiatives
Capacity gaps → embedded technical assistance from multilaterals and UK experts
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting high-energy-cost SIDS) with efficiency (using multilaterals to reduce transaction costs). Trade-offs include: (1) Northern expertise (World Bank, UK technical support) vs. Southern ownership (Caribbean governments lead priority-setting), and (2) speed (multilateral safeguards slow disbursement) vs. inclusion (ensuring gender-sensitive consultations and local capacity building).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Multilateral safeguards (efficient) vs. local adaptive needs (equitable)
Grant funding for SIDS (equitable) vs. leverage requirements (efficient)
Regional coordination (efficient) vs. country-specific priorities (equitable)
Technical assistance from North (efficient) vs. capacity building for South (equitable)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate-to-high risk profile (geothermal uncertainty, climate shocks) justifies intensive milestone-based oversight by FCDO, with semi-annual disbursements to CDB and structured World Bank trust funds. High risks in geothermal components lead to more rigorous due diligence (e.g., legal agreements for Dominica's transmission substation) compared to the SEEC's lighter-touch management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: CDB and World Bank provide technical assistance to strengthen Caribbean institutions (e.g., energy audits, PPA negotiations), while Caribbean governments and DGDC gradually take on more implementation responsibilities (e.g., Dominica's shift from FCDO-funded plant construction to self-financed construction with FCDO supporting ancillary infrastructure).
intersections.quote: "The risks to this programme overall are classified as medium. [...] There are higher risks in the geothermal component. These mainly relate to the uncertainty over the outcome of the exploratory drilling as it is possible that the resource will be unsuitable for further development. Other areas that will need active management include political, social and environmental risks." (4885414.odt, Risks) AND "The small island developing states of the Eastern Caribbean face a similar set of challenges in achieving an uninterrupted supply of energy at an affordable price. [...] High energy and transportation costs have contributed to the poor economic performance of the region and its declining competitiveness over the past decade." (4885414.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Unproven geothermal resources in exploratory drilling phases (St. Lucia, Grenada)
Delays in World Bank/CDB processes (e.g., Board approvals, safeguard compliance)
Limited private sector interest in small-scale geothermal plants (e.g., Dominica's 10MW plant)
Geopolitical tensions hindering regional offshore wind cooperation
CDB implementation challenges affecting SEEC delivery timelines
Climate shocks (hurricanes, pandemics) disrupting implementation
Fiscal constraints in Caribbean SIDS limiting co-financing or debt uptake
Regulatory and grid limitations for renewable energy integration
Gender imbalances in energy sector participation
Reputational risk for FCDO if funding gaps cause project cancellations

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased funding (exploratory drilling first); use of World Bank's ESMAP Trust Fund for risk-sharing; co-financing with other donors (e.g., Italy, EU) to spread risk.
Time extensions (e.g., to December 2023 for World Bank activities); semi-annual disbursements tied to expenditure plans; FCDO monitoring of milestone achievement.
Grant funding to de-risk exploratory drilling; FCDO funds catalyze additional financing (e.g., World Bank, EU co-investments); technical assistance to improve PPAs.
Two-phase approach (pre-feasibility studies first); collaboration with CCREEE/CDB to manage regional dynamics; focus on ODA-eligible sites.
Semi-annual disbursements tied to expenditure/commitment plans; FCDO annual reviews; capacity building for CDB staff.
Flexible extensions (e.g., from 2021 to 2025); adaptive management to reprioritize activities; grant funding to avoid increasing debt burdens.
Technical assistance for regulatory reform; capacity building for grid integration; pilot projects to demonstrate feasibility.
Gender-sensitive consultations; disaggregated data collection; targeted training for women in energy sector roles (e.g., 64 females trained in solar PV installation).
Time extensions to avoid project cancellations; proactive communication of UK's climate commitments; leveraging high-level political support.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Early phases demonstrated that Caribbean SIDS require more time and support than initially projected due to fiscal constraints, climate vulnerability, and limited economies of scale. The 2020 annual review highlighted the need for adaptive management and flexible timelines. Successful components (e.g., SEEC's energy audits) showed the value of blending grants with concessional loans, while geothermal delays underscored the importance of phased funding and risk-sharing with multilaterals.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. Extension of timelines (from 2020 to 2025) to accommodate SIDS' constraints. 2. Reallocation of Dominica geothermal funds from plant construction to ancillary infrastructure (reinjection wells, substations) based on government's alternate financing. 3. Addition of offshore wind component based on emerging regional potential and UK expertise. 4. Shift from direct FCDO management to multilateral implementation (World Bank, CDB) to reduce transaction costs. 5. Increased focus on capacity building (e.g., 319 individuals trained) to address technical gaps identified in early phases.
risks_lessons.quote: "The 2020 annual review assessed that while the Theory of Change holds true and we are already seeing results, the timelines for attaining planned outcome and impact indicators will be longer than projected in the programme design. This is mainly due to the specific context in Caribbean SIDS where even with the grant funds provided through FCDO and other development partners, countries continue to be challenged to access affordable debt and/or to take on additional debt due to national fiscal constraints." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The main change from the original business case is around how FCDO funds will be allocated in the Dominica Geothermal Project. The GoCD identified an alternate source of funds to construct the geothermal plant and has requested that FCDO funds be reallocated to finance the single re-injection well serving the Small Geothermal Power Plant (SGPP), an additional production well [...] and a high voltage transformer substation." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)

co_funding_partners.partner: Government of the Republic of Italy

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged co-financing from multiple partners: (1) CDB's own resources (€18 million in concessional loans) for SEEC; (2) World Bank's ESMAP Trust Fund for geothermal components; (3) Government of Italy, IADB, and EU contributions for Grenada geothermal drilling; (4) Private sector financing catalyzed by FCDO's de-risking of exploratory drilling. The offshore wind component aims to mobilize private sector investment through a demonstration "lighthouse" project.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes both capital expenditures (e.g., £34m for offshore wind turbine construction, geothermal drilling/infrastructure) and revenue expenditures (e.g., technical assistance, capacity building, M&E). The majority of funds are allocated to capital-intensive activities (geothermal drilling, renewable energy installations), with ~£445k (originally) for M&E reduced to £0 in later phases.
