financial_details.quote: "UK will provide up to £10m in CDEL for Grenada geothermal exploratory drilling and up to £34m (up to £5m RDEL and £29m CDEL) for an offshore wind “lighthouse” project from the UK’s International Climate Fund, increasing the total value of the programme to £63.35m." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The original programme has three components: £2.5m for the Sustainable Energy for the Eastern Caribbean (SEEC) [...] £16.4m in support to geothermal development in the Eastern Caribbean [...] £445k for monitoring and evaluation." (D0005864.odt, INFORMATION) AND "Since project initiation partners have agreed to conduct separate evaluations of the programme components and on the advice of EQUALS a decision was made not to pursue an impact evaluation within the current programme, the budget will therefore be reduced by £445,500." (60692415.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Central Asia South Asia (CASA-1000) Electricity Trade Project
metadata.quote: "This project will spend a total of up to £31 million over 3 years from FY2015/16 to FY2017/18." (D0003514.odt, Financial Details section)
metadata.duration_source: "This project will spend a total of up to £31 million over 3 years from FY2015/16 to FY2017/18."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The CASA-1000 project combines financing (to plug investment gaps), implementation (of electricity transmission infrastructure), and capacity building (through Community Support Programmes). It aims to facilitate cross-border electricity trade while ensuring local communities benefit directly through targeted support activities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Through this project, the UK (DFID) will provide £31 million to co-finance, with the World Bank Group (WBG) and other donors, the Central Asia South Asia (CASA1000) electricity trade project. This will include: £25 million capital grant funding to help plug the investment financing gap for one of the critical components of the project, a power converter station in Tajikistan; £6 million technical assistance (TA) to support the development and delivery of Community Support Programmes (CSPs) in Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Pakistan." (D0003514.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased cross-border energy transmission capacity (1300 MW of summer electricity surplus)
Improved private sector investment in the energy sector
Improved pro-poor growth through access to jobs and services (670 communities along the CASA-1000 corridor)
Reduced electricity shortages in Afghanistan and Pakistan (meeting one-fifth of Pakistan's unmet summer energy needs)
Economic boost for Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan from selling surplus hydropower (up to $200 million annually)
Community Support Programmes (CSPs) for 670 poor communities, including gender-specific interventions
Resettlement Action Plans (RAPs) to mitigate negative impacts on vulnerable groups
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to create a regional electricity market by transmitting surplus summer hydropower from Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan to energy-deficient Afghanistan and Pakistan, while ensuring local communities benefit through targeted support programmes.
what_objectives.quote: "The objective of CASA-1000 is to take 1300 MW of summer electricity surplus from existing hydroelectric plants in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan and provide it to consumers in electricity deficient Afghanistan and Pakistan." (D0003514.odt, CASA-1000 Electricity Trade Project section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The region is described as one of the least connected and most fragile in the world, with complex politics, security threats, and weak institutions. Afghanistan is explicitly in a post-conflict transition, and the project corridor crosses hostile, inaccessible terrain vulnerable to sabotage.
where_context.q5_source: "Central and South Asia is one of the least connected regions in the world and intra-regional trade is the lowest globally. Despite strong growth across Asia, economic growth and poverty reduction are uneven, with clear evidence that populations in parts of the region are missing out. In particular, power connectivity is low, resulting in energy being one of the key binding constraints to growth in the region. These trends are partly driven by weak economic cooperation across the region, underpinned by complex politics." (D0003514.odt, Context and evidence of need)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks include potential sabotage of transmission lines and difficult repairs in hostile terrain. Political tensions between upstream/downstream countries affect water resource management. Weak institutions in Tajikistan create fiscal risks, while local communities' lack of direct electricity access could create social tensions. The project must navigate complex regional politics and ensure buy-in from 670 poor communities along the corridor.
where_context.quote: "Security problems and geopolitical tensions will also have implications for the operation of CASA1000. The geographic location of the CASA1000 transmission line, while unavoidable, could expose the project to threats of sabotage and theft of equipment. The hostile and inaccessible terrain in some areas means that repairs will be difficult to carry out." (D0003514.odt, Geopolitical and security risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank Group (a Northern-led multilateral) retains approval authority for key decisions through a no-objection process, while day-to-day management is handled by national Implementing Agencies nominated by partner governments. DFID influences delivery through its relationship with WBG but ultimate decision-making rests with the multilateral.
q10_capacity_building_details: Community Support Programmes (CSPs) for 670 communities
Resettlement Action Plans (RAPs) with gender-specific protections
Vocational training for women in project areas
Community-led decision-making for local activities
Institutional strengthening of national transmission companies (e.g., Barki Tajik)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank Group (WBG)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer, fund administrator, and technical oversight

partner_organizations.name: Barki Tajik (Tajikistan National Transmission Company)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing Agency for converter station in Tajikistan

partner_organizations.name: Afghanistan Implementing Agency (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Project management for Afghanistan components

partner_organizations.name: Pakistan Implementing Agency (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Project management for Pakistan components

partner_organizations.name: Kyrgyzstan Implementing Agency (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Project management for Kyrgyzstan components

partner_organizations.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financier (€140 million)

partner_organizations.name: Islamic Development Bank
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-financier (contributions on hold)

partner_organizations.name: United States Government
partner_organizations.role: Co-financier ($15 million)

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-financier for converter station gap

partner_organizations.name: Owner’s Engineer (independent company)
partner_organizations.role: Contract administration and oversight

partner_organizations.name: Procurement Committee (representatives from all four countries + WBG)
partner_organizations.role: Oversight of joint contract packages

who_partners.quote: "Delivering through an International Financial Institution (IFI) (i.e. WBG) was found to be more effective and provide better value for money than delivering bilaterally or through other partners." (D0003514.odt, Discussion of options and early decisions)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a £25 million capital grant (for the converter station) and £6 million technical assistance (for Community Support Programmes), both channeled through a WBG-administered multi-donor trust fund (MDTF). The MDTF allows harmonized procurement and financial management under WBG systems.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank Group acts as the fund administrator and lead implementer, with day-to-day delivery managed by national Implementing Agencies (IAs) in each country. A Procurement Committee (with representatives from all four countries + WBG) oversees joint contracts, while an independent Owner’s Engineer monitors implementation. DFID’s role is primarily as a co-financier with oversight rights via a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The WBG was selected due to its established role as the primary donor for CASA-1000, its track record in regional connectivity projects, and its ability to navigate complex political dynamics. Delivering through WBG was deemed more effective than bilateral channels to avoid duplication and leverage existing systems.
how_mechanism.quote: "Delivering through an IFI (i.e. WBG) was found to be more effective and provide better value for money than delivering bilaterally or through other partners for the following reasons: [...] The WBG is the primary donor supporting CASA-1000 and has been instrumental in the design and implementation of the project to date." (D0003514.odt, Discussion of options and early decisions)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Inter-Governmental Council (IGC), established in 2008, steers the project with a Secretariat. A Procurement Committee (with representatives from all four countries + WBG) oversees contract awards, while the WBG retains approval authority for key decisions. DFID participates in regular reviews via the MoU but does not have direct decision-making power.
how_governance.quote: "In August 2008, the countries entered into a formal inter-governmental agreement to set up an Inter-Governmental Council (IGC) and an associated Secretariat to steer the development of the project. [...] This Committee will oversee the development and issuance of all procurement documentation, management of the pre-qualification process, evaluation of proposals and preparation of bid evaluation reports, and award of contracts to DS&I contractors." (D0003514.odt, Procurement and implementation arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for specific components (converter station vs. CSPs) and require prior agreement for reallocation. DFID’s contribution is conditional on the remaining financing gap being filled before disbursement.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The project has fixed infrastructure deliverables (e.g., converter stations, transmission lines) with little flexibility to adjust core components. However, Community Support Programmes (CSPs) allow some adaptability to local needs through community-led decision-making.
how_flexibility.quote: "DFID financing would be agreed with a condition that the [remaining financing] gap must be filled before the first planned DFID disbursement." (D0003514.odt, Option 2)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank Group (MDTF) → Implementing Agencies (e.g., Barki Tajik) → Contractors/Communities
how_efficiency.quote: "The MoU will include the broad objectives and parameters of the project as set out in the Theory of Change and will set out the arrangements for the two windows of support (TA and Investment). [...] Disbursement schedules will be linked to realistic expenditure profiles for the project and reviewed annually." (D0003514.odt, Delivery of Outputs)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do-nothing (no further DFID contribution)
£15 million grant for converter station only
£25 million grant for converter station only
£25 million grant + £6 million TA for CSPs (selected option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The £25 million grant + £6 million TA option was chosen because it: (1) plugs the critical financing gap for the converter station (avoiding 6-month delays), (2) ensures local community buy-in through CSPs (mitigating security risks), (3) aligns with DFID’s comparative advantage in community development, and (4) provides the highest economic returns (NPV > £11.5 million, BCR > 2). The WBG’s established delivery platform and DFID’s ability to influence through co-financing were also key factors.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (avoiding delays, securing local support)
partner capacity (WBG’s track record in regional projects)
equity (targeted support for women and poor communities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in converter station procurement due to Tajikistan’s reluctance to assume liability without full funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s £25 million grant provides reassurance to Tajik authorities to proceed, with a condition that the remaining gap must be filled before disbursement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Wavering political commitment from partner countries if implementation is delayed
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s timely contribution helps maintain momentum, particularly for Pakistan’s election-linked energy goals.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: EBRD or other donors failing to meet their commitments, leaving residual gaps
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: WBG has a robust plan to fill the gap by 2016/17, and DFID’s MoU includes conditions for disbursement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Light-touch WBG incentives for community engagement (per MAR 2011 findings)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s £6 million TA explicitly targets CSPs and RAPs, with criteria to ensure activities meet local needs and include women’s voices.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 is recommended as having the highest likely NPV and BCR. [...] The returns are summarised in table 1 and in detail in Annex 5. [...] The economic appraisal clearly indicates that all considered options are economically feasible as they all have positive net present values (NPVs) and benefit-cost ratios (BCRs)." (D0003514.odt, Economic Appraisal Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile, conflict-affected context (FCAS) limits partner selection to multilateral institutions like WBG, which have the political neutrality, regional trust, and risk management capacity to operate across all four countries. Local Implementing Agencies are used for day-to-day delivery, but ultimate oversight rests with WBG due to weak national institutions and security risks.
q27_constraints_detail: Complex regional politics require a neutral multilateral lead (WBG).
Security risks (sabotage, inaccessible terrain) necessitate WBG’s risk management frameworks.
Weak institutions in Tajikistan/Kyrgyzstan make direct bilateral funding unviable.
Need for harmonized procurement across four countries favors a multilateral platform.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for large-scale, cross-border infrastructure (1300 MW transmission) determines the multilateral delivery structure, while the requirement for local community buy-in (to mitigate security risks) shapes the embedded TA component. The mix of hard infrastructure and soft community support necessitates a hybrid funding instrument (grant + TA).
q28_linkages: Regional electricity trade goal → multilateral delivery (WBG) for cross-border coordination.
Local community risks → embedded TA (CSPs/RAPs) for buy-in.
Financing gaps in Tajikistan → grant instrument to avoid sovereign debt risks.
Time-sensitive political momentum → rapid disbursement via WBG’s existing platforms.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between efficiency (rapid infrastructure delivery) and equity (ensuring poor communities benefit). While the transmission line itself may not directly serve local populations, the £6 million TA for CSPs/RAPs is designed to "minimise negative impacts on women and others socially vulnerable groups" and provide targeted livelihood support. The trade-off is managed by separating core infrastructure (efficient WBG delivery) from community benefits (flexible TA).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Infrastructure must be delivered quickly to meet Pakistan’s election timeline, but CSPs ensure local communities are not left behind.
Expertise vs. ownership: WBG leads for technical/financial expertise, but TA includes community-led decision-making for local ownership.
Cost vs. reach: While WBG’s overhead (2-5%) adds cost, it enables harmonized delivery across four fragile countries.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context increases oversight intensity, with milestone-based reviews, independent contract supervision (Owner’s Engineer), and a Procurement Committee for joint decisions. Security risks also necessitate embedded community engagement (CSPs) to mitigate local opposition.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The weak capacity of national institutions (e.g., Tajikistan’s fiscal constraints) shapes the WBG’s dominant role in fund management and procurement, while TA components are designed to strengthen local Implementing Agencies (e.g., Barki Tajik) and communities over time.
intersections.quote: "A conflict sensitive approach will be key to mitigate against these risks. In particular, significant care will need to be given to gaining the support of local communities. Through the provision of technical assistance (TA), DFID will work with the WBG to ensure local communities can directly benefit from the project through better livelihoods and access to services—thus encouraging strong local support for CASA-1000." (D0003514.odt, Geopolitical and security risks)

key_programme_risks: Delays in converter station procurement (6+ months) due to financing gaps, increasing costs and political risks.
Security threats (sabotage, theft) to transmission lines in hostile terrain, with difficult repairs.
Unequal benefit distribution creating local tensions, especially in Afghanistan where communities cannot draw electricity from the line.
Winter electricity crises in Tajikistan/Kyrgyzstan sparking public opposition to summer exports.
Geopolitical tensions (e.g., upstream/downstream water disputes) disrupting regional cooperation.
Wavering political commitment if implementation slows, particularly in Pakistan (election-linked energy promises).
EBRD or other donors failing to meet co-financing pledges, leaving residual gaps.
WBG’s light-touch incentives for community engagement (per MAR 2011) undermining CSP effectiveness.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID’s £25 million grant provides reassurance to Tajik authorities to proceed, with a condition that the remaining gap (£40 million) must be filled before disbursement. WBG has a robust plan to secure additional funding by 2016/17.
Conflict-sensitive TA for CSPs to secure local community buy-in. Owner’s Engineer provides independent oversight of construction quality and security.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Local opposition due to perceived inequities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: £6 million TA for CSPs/RAPs targets 670 poor communities, with explicit gender inclusion (e.g., female-headed household protections) and community-led activity selection.
Revenue from summer exports will help finance winter fuel imports. WBG/ADB are exploring links to year-round energy flows from Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan.
DFID will leverage UK diplomatic ties to facilitate dialogue and build consensus. The IGC and Procurement Committee provide structured inter-governmental forums.
DFID’s contribution is timed to catalyze other donors. WBG is considering reallocating IDA funds or diverting resources from other projects if needed.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: WBG’s weak incentives for community engagement
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID’s TA explicitly focuses on CSPs/RAPs, with criteria to ensure activities meet local needs and include vulnerable groups. Lessons from Nepal/AITF inform the design.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-sensitive approaches are critical in FCAS contexts—CSPs are designed to mitigate local opposition by ensuring tangible benefits for communities along the transmission corridor.
In fragile states, multilateral platforms (e.g., WBG’s MDTF) reduce fiduciary risks and transaction costs compared to bilateral delivery.
Political momentum is fleeting—DFID’s timely funding helps lock in commitments (e.g., Pakistan’s election-linked energy needs).
Regional projects in FCAS require structured inter-governmental bodies (e.g., IGC) to navigate complex politics and sustain cooperation.
Security risks in inaccessible terrain necessitate independent oversight (Owner’s Engineer) and contingency planning (20% budget buffer).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s South Asia Regional Trade and Integration Programme (SARTIP) and the WBG-managed Afghanistan Reconstruction Trust Fund (ARTF) informed the design. SARTIP demonstrated the value of flexible TA to unlock regional projects, while ARTF’s procurement processes (100+ packages) showed the effectiveness of WBG’s MDTF model in FCAS environments. The Nepal road project highlighted the importance of embedding gender and poverty reduction measures in infrastructure programmes.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The inclusion of £6 million TA for CSPs/RAPs was added to address lessons from WBG’s MAR 2011, which noted weak community engagement in infrastructure projects. The conditionality on filling the financing gap before DFID disbursement was introduced based on Tajikistan’s fiscal risks. The Procurement Committee structure was adapted from the IGC model to streamline cross-border contract awards.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID’s Multilateral Aid Review (MAR) update undertaken in 2013 re-confirmed that, overall, the WBG is one of the most effective multilateral institutions that DFID funds. It highlighted in particular that the International Development Association (IDA), which finances development projects in the world’s poorest countries, represented good value for money." (D0003514.odt, Delivery of Outputs)

co_funding_partners.partner: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The project has a total cost of $1.17 billion (~£900 million), with DFID’s £31 million (3.4%) catalyzing co-financing from multilaterals (WBG, EIB) and bilaterals (US). The £25 million grant helps unlock the remaining $221 million gap, with WBG confident of filling it by 2016/17. The TA component leverages WBG’s existing platforms (e.g., ARTF for Afghanistan CSPs).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £25 million (81%) is capital expenditure (converter station construction), while £6 million (19%) is revenue expenditure (technical assistance for CSPs/RAPs).
financial_details.quote: "The budget summarised in the table above is based on: Investment co-financing: £25 million to help plug part of the project’s $221 million current financing gap [...] Technical assistance: £6 million to fund community benefits activities." (D0003514.odt, Financial Details section)

metadata.programme_name: Commercial Agriculture for Smallholders and Agribusiness Programme (CASA)
metadata.duration_text: Start Date: 01 July 2017, End Date: 31 March 2024
metadata.quote: The programme will intervene in a small number of countries to support early-stage agribusinesses to prepare for and secure investment and to bring more, poorer smallholders into agribusiness supply chains. (D0003204.odt, Project Summary)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: Start Date: 01 July 2017, End Date: 31 June 2023; New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2024 (50583591.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CASA aims to increase economic opportunities for smallholder farmers by demonstrating the commercial viability of agribusinesses with significant smallholder supply chains and attracting more investment into the sector. It combines implementation research (testing interventions), financing mechanisms (channeling funds), and capacity building (strengthening agribusinesses and smallholders).
what_objectives.q1_source: CASA will increase economic opportunities for smallholder farmers by demonstrating the commercial viability of businesses with significant smallholder supply chains and by attracting more investment into the sector. (D0003204.odt, Project Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Support 24 businesses to prepare for and access early-stage investment of approximately £20 million
Support 12 projects to bring smallholders into commercial markets
Enable 12 reforms to regulations, laws, or practices benefiting smallholders and agribusinesses
Support up to 20 larger agribusinesses to increase their smallholder impact, benefiting at least 60,000 farmers
Benefit 76,000 smallholders through country-level interventions
Synthesize knowledge from interventions and research to influence investors, donors, and governments
Engage with senior representatives from governments, donors, and investors to influence actions and investments in agriculture
what_objectives.summary: CASA combines direct interventions to link smallholders with markets, support agribusiness investment, and improve enabling environments, alongside learning activities to shape global debates on smallholder agriculture.
what_objectives.quote: The programme will intervene in a small number of countries to support early-stage agribusinesses to prepare for and secure investment and to bring more, poorer smallholders into agribusiness supply chains. (D0003204.odt, Project Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with significant smallholder farming challenges, including fragile or conflict-affected states, and targets men at risk of returning to conflict. The risk is categorized as moderate-major due to the complexity of agricultural transformation and political economy issues.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate-Major (D0003204.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak land rights, unstable regulatory environments, lack of market information, and climate variability limit smallholder access to markets and investment. Political economy issues and fragile institutions in target countries increase delivery risks.
where_context.quote: Barriers limiting farmer access to value chains include: Insufficient surplus due to low productivity from poor inputs; Lack of infrastructure, including storage, and transport links to markets; Weak land rights and unstable regulatory environment; Lack of market information; Inability to meet required quality standards; and Monopoly power of local traders. (D0003204.odt, Improving Smallholder Access to Markets)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Senior Commercial Agriculture Adviser in DFID's Growth and Resilience Department (GRD) plays the SRO role, supported by a team in GRD. Decision-making power rests with DFID, with local partners implementing activities.
q10_capacity_building_details: Supporting 24 businesses to prepare for and access investment
Supporting 12 projects to bring smallholders into commercial markets
Enabling 12 reforms to regulations, laws, or practices
Providing technical assistance to agribusinesses to increase smallholder impact
Developing tools for local communities to engage with agribusiness investments

partner_organizations.name: CDC (UK organisation that supports building businesses through Development Capital)
partner_organizations.role: Investment partner

partner_organizations.name: AgDevCo (Africa Agriculture Development Company)
partner_organizations.role: Investment vehicle

partner_organizations.name: Local agribusinesses and smallholder organizations (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partners

partner_organizations.name: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS)
partner_organizations.role: Cross-HMG collaboration

who_partners.quote: The Senior Commercial Agriculture adviser in GRD will play the SRO role and will be supported by an experienced team in GRD. (D0003204.odt, Do the SRO and team have the capability and resources to deliver this programme?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants for early-stage agribusinesses, technical assistance for larger agribusinesses, and learning activities. It also leverages DFID's development capital investments through vehicles like CDC and AgDevCo.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID manages the programme through its Growth and Resilience Department (GRD), with a Senior Commercial Agriculture Adviser as SRO. Implementation involves a mix of direct support to businesses, technical assistance providers, and local partners, coordinated by DFID.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: A restricted two-stage tender process was adopted due to higher-than-expected market interest during early engagement events. The process was extended to accommodate SME bidders and align with new Cabinet Office requirements.
how_mechanism.quote: The decision to adopt a two-stage procurement process in response to the higher-than-expected interest from the market during the September 2017 Early Market Engagement Event; The decision to extend the bidding deadline over the summer holiday period and a subsequent decision to further extend the bidding period in order to enable smaller, SME bidders to submit proposals. (50583591.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Senior Commercial Agriculture Adviser in GRD acts as SRO, supported by a programme manager and team in GRD. Regular field visits and collaboration with the SRO are mentioned for monitoring performance.
how_governance.quote: A Commercial Agriculture Adviser and a programme manager in GRD will manage the programme and will closely monitor programme performance in collaboration with the SRO, including through regular field visits. (D0003204.odt, Do the SRO and team have the capability and resources to deliver this programme?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Flexibility exists during the analysis phase to adjust country-level interventions based on sector analyses. Throughout the programme, interventions will be adjusted based on experience and learning component findings.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a rolling annual programme of research and flexible learning component. Country-level interventions will be adjusted based on experience and findings from the learning component.
how_flexibility.quote: Throughout the programme the country-level interventions will be adjusted based on experience and the findings of the learning component. (D0003204.odt, Is there sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in the context?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (consortium/agribusinesses) → Smallholders/beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will intervene in a small number of countries to support early-stage agribusinesses to prepare for and secure investment... (D0003204.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct investment through DFIs like CDC
Challenge funds (e.g., Africa Enterprise Challenge Fund)
Market systems programmes
Combined approaches (e.g., FoodTrade programme)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The programme was designed to address gaps in current DFID commercial agriculture programming by: 1) Starting with a smallholder commercialisation lens in sector analysis; 2) Integrating direct interventions at both smallholder and agribusiness levels; 3) Targeting fragile/conflict-affected states and climate-vulnerable areas to demonstrate commercial potential.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited existence of locally owned agribusinesses ready for investment
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted support to reduce risks and increase company readiness through business incubators, accelerators, and technical assistance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial sensitivity inhibiting transparency and evidence sharing
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Develop standardised data collection and sharing mechanisms to demonstrate contribution to Global Goals while respecting commercial confidentiality.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Power imbalances in contract farming exposing farmers to exploitation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ensure contract arrangements are based on acceptable returns for farmers and buyers, with third-party oversight to promote trust.

why_rationale.quote: The programme will complement existing commercial agriculture programmes in the following ways: ... Intervening in a range of environments, including conflict affected states and areas vulnerable to climate change, to showcase the commercial potential for investment in these areas. (D0003204.odt, Rationale for DFID intervention and fit with existing programming)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme targets fragile/conflict-affected states and areas vulnerable to climate change, which limits partner selection to organizations with experience in high-risk environments and capacity to manage political economy challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict-affected states require partners with conflict sensitivity expertise
Climate vulnerability demands partners with climate-smart agriculture experience
Weak institutions necessitate partners capable of navigating regulatory and governance challenges
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to simultaneously support smallholders and agribusinesses requires a mixed delivery structure combining direct grants, technical assistance, and learning components. The focus on fragile states and climate vulnerability necessitates flexible, adaptive management.
q28_linkages: Smallholder commercialisation lens → Direct interventions at both farmer and business levels
Focus on fragile states → Need for conflict-sensitive, adaptive delivery mechanisms
Learning component → Requires embedded flexibility to adjust priorities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between including poorer, marginalized smallholders and ensuring commercial viability. There is a trade-off between reaching the poorest farmers (equity) and achieving scale/efficiency in value chain interventions.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusion of poorer smallholders vs. commercial viability of agribusiness models
Flexibility to adjust interventions vs. need for standardized approaches to demonstrate impact
Local ownership vs. Northern expertise in managing complex agribusiness investments
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate-major risk profile results in intensive oversight, including regular field visits, milestone-based monitoring, and a dedicated SRO team in DFID's GRD department.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme design, with technical assistance and business support aimed at increasing the readiness of local agribusinesses and smallholder organizations to engage in commercial value chains. This shapes partner roles to include both implementation and capacity development.
intersections.quote: The programme will intervene in a range of environments, including conflict affected states and areas vulnerable to climate change, to showcase the commercial potential for investment in these areas. (D0003204.odt, Rationale for DFID intervention)

key_programme_risks: Limited number of investible agribusinesses in target countries
Commercial sensitivity inhibiting transparency and learning
Power imbalances in value chains leading to farmer exploitation
Climate change exacerbating risks for smallholders and agribusinesses
Weak enabling environments (regulatory, infrastructure) limiting investment
Political economy issues creating barriers to reform
Lack of standardized data on agribusiness investments and impacts

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Provide targeted support through incubators/accelerators to increase company readiness (e.g., business planning, governance standards).
Develop standardized data collection frameworks that balance transparency needs with commercial confidentiality.
Promote third-party oversight and legally binding contracts with fair return guarantees for farmers.
Integrate climate-smart approaches and resilience-building into all interventions.
Include regulatory reform and infrastructure development as explicit programme components.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile states, agribusiness investments require enhanced community engagement to ensure stability and local buy-in.
Conflict sensitivity must be integrated into value chain analyses and business selection processes.
Local capacity to negotiate and enforce contracts is critical in post-conflict environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID commercial agriculture programmes were found to focus too narrowly on individual businesses rather than systemic value chain development. This programme adopts a more holistic, smallholder-focused approach to address this gap.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates: 1) A smallholder commercialisation lens in sector analysis; 2) Simultaneous interventions at farmer and business levels; 3) Explicit targeting of fragile/conflict-affected states; 4) Flexible learning component to adjust priorities based on evidence.
risks_lessons.quote: Current commercial agriculture programmes, however, tend to be focused at the business level... They generally do not take a systemic, value chain wide approach... There is a need for more programming which directly targets smallholders and seeks to bring more, poorer farmers into commercial value chains. (D0003204.odt, Rationale for DFID intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to attract £20 million in early-stage investment for supported businesses and influence larger investments by DFIs like CDC (£280 million in commercial agriculture in 2014).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both capital investments (through DFIs) and revenue expenditures (grants, technical assistance, learning activities).
financial_details.quote: Supporting 24 businesses to prepare for and access early stage investment of approximately £20 million – these businesses represent future investment opportunities for larger investors such as CDC; Supporting 12 projects to bring smallholders into commercial markets... (D0003204.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: UK Caribbean Infrastructure Fund (UKCIF)

quote.text: The overall objective of the UK Caribbean Infrastructure Fund (UKCIF) is to provide critical infrastructure to set the foundations for growth and prosperity, reducing poverty, promoting gender equality and inclusion, and increasing resilience to climate change.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: 2016–2020, extended to 2024 in 2017

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The UKCIF is a grant financing mechanism designed to fund critical economic infrastructure projects in Caribbean countries. It channels funds through the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB) to support infrastructure development that promotes growth, reduces poverty, and increases climate resilience. The programme does not generate new knowledge or directly deliver services, but rather provides the financial resources for infrastructure projects.

q1_source.text: The programme’s main activity is to provide economic infrastructure grants which will lay the foundations for growth and prosperity, create jobs and opportunities, reduce poverty, increase resilience to climate change, generate social benefits and promote gender equality and inclusion, including for people with disabilities.

q3_expected_outputs.output: major infrastructure projects delivered in each focus country (roads, bridges, renewable energy, water, sea defences, ports, sanitation/wastewater management)
q3_expected_outputs.target: at least two major projects per country

q3_expected_outputs.output: projects with at least 12% economic return on investment
q3_expected_outputs.target: all projects

q3_expected_outputs.output: climate-resilient infrastructure designed to withstand extreme weather events
q3_expected_outputs.target: all projects

q3_expected_outputs.output: jobs created and livelihoods improved
q3_expected_outputs.target: indirect outcome

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased regional and international trade opportunities (Montserrat port project)
q3_expected_outputs.target: direct result for Montserrat

q3_expected_outputs.output: reduced dependence on UK ODA for Montserrat
q3_expected_outputs.target: long-term outcome

q3_expected_outputs.output: enhanced capacity in governments for infrastructure management
q3_expected_outputs.target: indirect outcome

what_objectives.summary: The UKCIF is a strategic, long-term financing mechanism that funds critical infrastructure projects in the Caribbean to promote economic growth, reduce poverty, and increase climate resilience. It operates through grants managed by the Caribbean Development Bank, with a focus on delivering high-impact, climate-resilient infrastructure that meets specific economic return criteria.

quote.text: The UK Caribbean Infrastructure Partnership Fund will build physical infrastructure that will make a tangible difference for the communities in DFID focus countries in the Caribbean. This will include roads, bridges, renewable energy, ports, water, and sea defences.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The Caribbean region faces significant challenges including high debt levels, vulnerability to natural disasters, and weak fiscal capacity. The UKCIF programme has a 'major' risk rating due to constraints in government capacity, time/cost overruns, and the impact of natural disasters, which are frequent and severe in the region.

q5_source.text: The risk rating for the UKCIF programme at approval was ‘major’. Key risks include constraints in government capacity to oversee project processes including procurement and contracting; time and cost over-runs; and impact of natural disasters.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The infrastructure gap in the Caribbean is estimated at £3.5bn, hampering economic growth and increasing vulnerability to natural disasters. High debt levels (e.g., Jamaica at 140% debt-to-GDP ratio) limit fiscal space for infrastructure investment. Weak public financial management and limited capacity for project implementation slow down delivery. Climate risks, such as hurricanes and volcanic eruptions (e.g., Montserrat), further exacerbate these challenges, requiring resilient infrastructure designs that increase costs and complexity.

quote.text: The Caribbean is one of the most highly indebted regions of the world. The build-up of debt can be traced to the cost of dealing with natural disasters, poor fiscal management, loss making enterprises and weak growth. A debt to GDP ratio of 60% is widely used as an upper limit benchmark for sustainable debt levels - all DFID Caribbean focus countries have rates above that benchmark.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (via FCDO) and the CDB share decision-making power through a Steering Committee and embedded FCDO staff within the CDB. The CDB manages day-to-day implementation using its own systems, while FCDO retains oversight and approval authority for key decisions, including project selection and financial risks. The Government of Montserrat holds the contract with private sector contractors for the Little Bay Port project, with CDB providing oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for project management and maintenance
support for infrastructure programme management training
enhanced project management capacity in Government of Montserrat (GoM)
strengthening of CDB’s oversight and assurance processes

partner_organizations.name: Caribbean Development Bank (CDB)
partner_organizations.role: implementation partner, fund manager, and oversight body

partner_organizations.name: Government of Montserrat (GoM)
partner_organizations.role: contract holder for Little Bay Port project, local implementation

partner_organizations.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
partner_organizations.role: co-financer for Montserrat Port project (approx. £7.1m)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (formerly DFID) embedded team
partner_organizations.role: day-to-day oversight, programme management, and technical support within CDB

partner_organizations.name: Private sector contractors
partner_organizations.role: construction and delivery of infrastructure projects

quote.text: The Caribbean Development Bank was selected as the implementation partner for the UKCIF on the basis of its expertise in delivering climate-resilient infrastructure in the Caribbean. The UKCIF Reconstruction Window will work through the existing mechanisms for the UKCIF established with the CDB and under the same conditions.
quote.source: 35344167.odt, What is the approach to implementation? section

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UKCIF uses a combination of Promissory Notes and reimbursement mechanisms. Promissory Notes provide upfront assurance of funds (60% of grant value) to the CDB before grant agreements are signed with recipient countries. The remaining funds are disbursed on a reimbursement basis after the Promissory Notes are exhausted. For the Montserrat Port project, additional funds include a contingency held by FCDO to manage financial risks.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The CDB acts as the fund manager and implementer, using its own systems and procedures to select and deliver infrastructure projects. FCDO provides oversight through a Steering Committee, embedded staff within the CDB, and approval processes for key decisions. The Government of Montserrat manages the Little Bay Port project contract directly with private sector contractors, with CDB oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The CDB was selected based on its regional expertise, existing relationships with Caribbean governments, and capacity to deliver climate-resilient infrastructure. The direct award to CDB was justified by the need for quick delivery, existing pipelines of projects, and the CDB’s role as the region’s development institution, which would maximize visibility and impact for the UK.

quote.text: CDB was selected as the implementation partner for the UKCIF on the basis of its expertise in delivering climate-resilient infrastructure in the Caribbean. The UKCIF Reconstruction Window will work through the existing mechanisms for the UKCIF established with the CDB and under the same conditions.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The UKCIF Steering Committee (SC) includes senior FCDO and CDB personnel and meets quarterly to provide strategic oversight for the programme and individual projects. Projects are governed at an individual level through CDB’s supervisory oversight, rules, and procedures, with a 4-person FCDO team embedded at CDB providing day-to-day oversight. Enhanced governance arrangements are in place for the Montserrat Port project to ensure closer FCDO oversight due to the unique role of the UK government in the project.

quote.text: Senior FCDO and CDB persons oversee the UKCIF programme, including the Montserrat Little Bay Port Project, through the UKCIF Steering Committee (SC). The SC meets quarterly and provides strategic steer for the programme as well as individual projects. Projects are governed at an individual level through CDB’s supervisory oversight, CDB’s rules, policies and procedures, and a 4-person FCDO team embedded at CDB providing day-to-day oversight.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the UKCIF can be reallocated between projects, but specific conditions apply. For example, the £28 million allocated for Dominica and Barbuda reconstruction had to be approved by 30 June 2019 or risked reallocation. The Montserrat Port project includes a contingency fund held by FCDO to manage financial risks, indicating some flexibility in fund use but within controlled parameters.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in response to natural disasters or emerging needs, such as the Reconstruction Window created after Hurricanes Irma and Maria. However, changes require approval from FCDO and the Steering Committee. The Montserrat Port project’s scope was reduced to a "technical minimum" to manage costs, showing adaptive management in practice.

quote.text: Projects in Dominica and Barbuda to be funded through the £28 million replenishment of the Reconstruction Window must be approved by 30 June 2019 or the funds will be reallocated through the UKCIF.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Caribbean Development Bank (CDB) → Government of Montserrat (GoM)/Private Sector Contractors

quote.text: The financing mechanism for the grant funding elements of the Reconstruction Window will be Promissory Notes. All other UKCIF funding, including CDB management fees, will be disbursed on a reimbursement basis.

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rejected due to lack of affordability and visibility)
Ring-fenced grant contribution to the CDB (selected option)
New DFID-managed bilateral infrastructure initiative (rejected due to lack of experience and higher risks)
Working through the World Bank (rejected due to lower visibility and higher management costs)
Creation of a Caribbean window in existing DFID global infrastructure initiatives (rejected due to lack of regional experience and time constraints)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The CDB option was chosen because it offered the best combination of speed, visibility, and value for money. The CDB’s existing systems, regional expertise, and relationships with Caribbean governments allowed for quick implementation (projects could start within 12-18 months). The option also provided strong UK visibility through branding (e.g., "UK Caribbean Infrastructure Partnership Fund") and minimized operating costs by leveraging CDB’s infrastructure. The direct award to CDB was seen as a vote of confidence in the region and aligned with the UK’s goal of reinvigorating its relationship with the Caribbean.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government capacity constraints post-disaster
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UKCIF will mitigate these risks by considering the viability of any investments through the Reconstruction Window in light of institutional constraints and ability to boost capacity, either through the fund itself or other channels.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Land tenure sensitivity in Barbuda
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds will only be utilised for public infrastructure projects and UKCIF’s standard approach to social inclusion will be followed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks (fraud, corruption)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fund management systems and processes have been designed specifically to minimise fiduciary risks, including independent audits and CDB’s compliance policies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery delays due to weak project management capacity in GoM
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Increasing support to GoM’s project management team to enhance capacity and capability, and strengthening CDB and FCDO oversight.

quote.text: Option 2, "a ring-fenced grant contribution to the CDB", is best able to deliver against the design criteria and has the best prospect of delivering the programme’s outputs. Being able to utilise the systems and approaches of the CDB, including its safeguards, also offers the best prospects of delivering the indirect results related to transparency, anti-corruption and good governance that this business case can be used to promote.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Caribbean’s high debt levels, weak institutional capacity, and vulnerability to natural disasters limit the pool of potential partners. The CDB was selected because it is the region’s development institution with existing relationships and systems, making it the most feasible partner despite risks. Local governments (e.g., GoM) lack capacity to manage large infrastructure projects independently, necessitating CDB’s oversight and FCDO’s embedded support.
q27_constraints_detail: High debt levels restrict countries’ ability to take on loans, making grants essential (constrains financial partners).
Limited local capacity for project management requires reliance on CDB and FCDO oversight (constrains implementing partners).
Frequent natural disasters necessitate flexible, resilient designs and rapid response mechanisms (constrains technical partners).
Small island size and lack of economies of scale limit private sector engagement (constrains PPP options).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to deliver climate-resilient infrastructure quickly and at scale determined the choice of CDB as the implementation partner. The CDB’s existing project pipelines and regional expertise allowed for faster delivery than a new bilateral initiative. The financing mechanism (Promissory Notes + reimbursement) was designed to balance speed (upfront assurance) with accountability (reimbursement for remaining funds). The Reconstruction Window’s flexible criteria (e.g., waiving the 12% economic return requirement) were introduced to enable rapid post-disaster response, aligning the ‘how’ with the ‘what’ of disaster recovery.
q28_linkages: Climate resilience objectives → CDB’s regional expertise in resilient infrastructure → direct award to CDB.
Need for visibility and UK profile → ring-fenced fund within CDB with UK branding.
Post-disaster reconstruction needs → flexible Reconstruction Window with simplified criteria.
Capacity constraints in GoM → embedded FCDO team and CDB oversight for Montserrat Port project.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., inclusive growth, gender equality, support to smaller islands like Montserrat) with efficiency (e.g., using CDB’s existing systems to minimize costs). For example, the Montserrat Port project was justified despite not meeting the 12% economic return threshold because of its critical role in reducing ODA dependence and improving livelihoods. The Reconstruction Window’s waiver of the economic return requirement for post-disaster projects prioritizes equity (rapid recovery) over strict efficiency metrics.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Equity: Inclusion of Montserrat (small population, high costs) vs. Efficiency: Lower economic returns compared to larger countries.
Equity: Gender and social inclusion requirements vs. Efficiency: Additional costs for disaggregated data and targeted outreach.
Equity: Flexible criteria for Reconstruction Window vs. Efficiency: Higher risk of lower returns on investment.
Equity: Local capacity building vs. Efficiency: Slower implementation due to training needs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight, including quarterly Steering Committee meetings, embedded FCDO staff, and enhanced governance for high-risk projects like the Montserrat Port. The risk of cost overruns (e.g., due to unforeseen seabed conditions) led to the creation of a FCDO-held contingency fund, increasing management intensity but reducing financial exposure.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The limited capacity of Caribbean governments (e.g., GoM) shapes the roles of CDB and FCDO. CDB provides technical oversight and project management support, while FCDO embeds staff within CDB to build capacity and ensure compliance. For Montserrat, additional funds were allocated to strengthen GoM’s project management office, directly addressing capacity gaps.

quote.text: The programme has developed a comprehensive risk register and risks are monitored continuously with a formal review every month. Fund management systems and process have been designed specifically to minimise fiduciary risks, including the risk of fraud and corruption, are residual risks are proactively monitored and mitigated.

key_programme_risks.risk: Constraints in government capacity to oversee projects (e.g., procurement, contracting).
Time and cost overruns due to complex infrastructure projects.
Impact of natural disasters disrupting implementation.
Land tenure sensitivity in Barbuda affecting project viability.
Fiduciary risks (fraud, corruption) in fund management.
Delivery delays in Montserrat due to limited GoM capacity.
Cost increases during implementation (e.g., seabed conditions, currency fluctuations).
Reputational and political risks around the Montserrat Port project.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded FCDO team within CDB to provide day-to-day support; technical assistance for project management and maintenance.
Comprehensive risk register with monthly reviews; contingency funds for high-risk projects.
Reconstruction Window with flexible criteria; climate-resilient design standards.
Funds restricted to public infrastructure; adherence to UKCIF social inclusion standards.
CDB compliance policies; independent audits; reimbursement-based disbursements.
Additional funds to strengthen GoM’s project management office; increased CDB and FCDO oversight.
FCDO-held contingency fund; rigorous project contingency planning.
Close collaboration between FCDO’s Americas and SIDS Directorate and Overseas Territories Directorate (OTD).

fcas_specific_lessons: Post-disaster needs assessments (PDNAs) are critical for identifying reconstruction priorities but must be balanced with rapid response needs.
Flexible funding criteria (e.g., waiving economic return requirements) are essential for post-disaster recovery but require robust oversight to manage risks.
Embedded advisory teams (e.g., FCDO staff in CDB) are effective for building local capacity while maintaining donor oversight in high-risk environments.
Contingency funds held by the donor (FCDO) can mitigate financial risks in volatile contexts but require clear governance to avoid misuse.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 Annual Review highlighted the need for improved monitoring of climate resilience aspects and more strategic sustainability planning, including maintenance and operations. The mid-term review recommended stronger linkages between infrastructure projects and wider economic strategies to maximize development impacts. Lessons from the Montserrat Port project emphasized the importance of realistic cost estimates and capacity assessments before project approval.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Introduction of the Reconstruction Window to respond to Hurricanes Irma and Maria, with simplified criteria for post-disaster projects.
Enhanced governance arrangements for the Montserrat Port project, including a FCDO-held contingency fund and strengthened oversight.
Increased focus on climate resilience monitoring and sustainability planning in response to the 2021 mid-term review.
Additional funds allocated to bolster GoM’s project management capacity for the Montserrat Port project.

quote.text: A mid-term review, completed in April 2021, gave seven recommendations to help the programme improve performance and course-correct, including highlighting opportunities to improve how we monitor climate resilience aspects of projects and advising the UKCIF to be more strategic in its approach to sustainability, including through maintenance and operations planning.
quote.source: D0003229.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case section

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Montserrat Little Bay Port project leveraged approximately £7.1m from the European Investment Bank, supplementing the UKCIF grant of £14.4m (later increased to £26.5m with the cost extension). This represents a co-funding ratio of roughly 1:2 (EIB:UKCIF).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The UKCIF budget is primarily capital expenditure (infrastructure grants), with a small portion allocated to revenue expenses such as CDB management fees (4.43%), technical assistance, monitoring and evaluation, and FCDO programme-funded staff costs. For example, in the £19.8m cost extension for Montserrat, £12.1m is for infrastructure grants (capital), while £1.1m is for delivery capacity strengthening (revenue).

quote.text: The original budget for the UKCIF is £300,000,000. This cost extension will provide an additional £30 million, increasing the total amount of funding for the programme to £330,000,000. [...] Management fees for the CDB will be the same as for the main UKCIF funds and are set at 3.75% of the grant funding.
