metadata.programme_name: Tackling Serious and Organised Corruption (TSOC)
metadata.quote: The project purpose is to increase the likelihood and severity of sanctions for serious and organised corruption and related crimes in Malawi. (D0004216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: 28 July 2016 – 30 June 2026 (D0004216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening law enforcement agencies), implementation research (testing asset recovery approaches), and service delivery (direct support to investigations/prosecutions). It aims to increase sanctions for corruption through technical assistance, policy reform, and civil society engagement.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The project purpose is to increase the likelihood and severity of sanctions for serious and organised corruption and related crimes in Malawi." (D0004216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) AND "DFID will provide up to £6.9m over four years... to fund activities designed to increase the likelihood and severity of sanction for serious and organised corruption and related crime in Malawi." (5631652.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Establishment of a fully functional Asset Forfeiture Unit within the FIA (34274797.odt, Expected Results)
Enhanced Anti-Corruption Bureau research capabilities to better understand corruption risks (34274797.odt, Expected Results)
Established Private Sector Integrity pacts with Law Enforcement Agencies (34274797.odt, Expected Results)
Increased capacity by law enforcement agencies to understand and address asset forfeiture (34274797.odt, Expected Results)
13 convictions totaling 53 years custodial sentences from Cashgate investigations (5631652.odt, Impact and outcome)
£1.5m of stolen assets identified for recovery (5631652.odt, Impact and outcome)
Well researched and reported investigative stories on anti-corruption issues (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)
A coalition of civil society, private sector, and government actors championing a level playing field (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)
Strategic awareness of court procedures through judicial monitoring (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)
Innovative ways to identify procurement 'red flags' through information 'hackathons' (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)
A working asset forfeiture system (D0004216.odt, Expected Results)
Non-Conviction Based Forfeiture model for illicitly obtained assets (D0004216.odt, Expected Results)
what_objectives.summary: TSOC aims to reduce corruption in Malawi by strengthening law enforcement capacity, improving asset recovery systems, and increasing civil society oversight, with measurable outputs including convictions, asset recovery, and institutional reforms.
what_objectives.quote: "Through its support DFID will: Strengthen Malawi’s legal and regulatory framework... Increase the technical capacity and inter-agency coordination of Malawi’s law enforcement agencies... Increase cooperation at the international level... Increase the role of non-state actors" (5631652.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Malawi faces systemic corruption with 74% of citizens believing politicians are corrupt (Transparency International 2016), and the programme targets politically-connected elites. The OSJA rates the intervention as 'amber' due to risks of incarceration in overcrowded prisons or politically motivated cases.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall residual risk rating for the programme is ‘major’." (5631652.odt, Key risks) AND "The OSJA rates the intervention as ‘amber’" (5631652.odt, Overseas security and justice assessment)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political interference undermines law enforcement independence (e.g., budgets set by Ministry of Finance, appointments by President). Limited technical capacity in agencies (e.g., no experience with digital evidence or asset recovery). Weak civil society and media limit accountability. High illicit financial flows (£576m/year) distort markets.
where_context.quote: "Serious and organised corruption and related crime is often perpetrated by powerful, politically-connected individuals, and efforts to increase the likelihood and severity of sanction are often met with opposition by those with an interest in maintaining the status quo." (5631652.odt, Key risks) AND "Malawi’s law enforcement agencies have very limited experience or awareness of the use of publicly available databases... the analysis of electronic and financial data... or the use of an asset recovery regime." (5631652.odt, Causes of serious and organised corruption)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains approval authority for all major expenditures (e.g., contracts >£25k) and strategic direction, with ICAR (Swiss-based) managing technical delivery. Malawian agencies (ACB, FIA, DPP) receive embedded support but no direct budget control.
q10_capacity_building_details: embedded technical experts in ACB, DPP, FIA (5631652.odt, Delivery options)
mentoring for senior managers (5631652.odt, ICAR proposal)
training on asset recovery, financial intelligence, and investigative techniques (D0004216.odt, Expected Results)
support to civil society for investigative journalism and judicial monitoring (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)
institutional strengthening (e.g., Asset Forfeiture Unit, Financial Crimes Court) (D0004216.odt, Expected Results)

partner_organizations.name: International Centre for Asset Recovery (ICAR)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider (embedded experts, training, policy advice)

partner_organizations.name: Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiary (investigations, prevention, asset recovery)

partner_organizations.name: Financial Intelligence Authority (FIA)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary (asset forfeiture, financial intelligence)

partner_organizations.name: Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary (prosecutions, legal reform)

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (£1.17m for civil society component)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partners (investigative journalism, advocacy, monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: Private Sector (e.g., media groups)
partner_organizations.role: Partners for integrity pacts and procurement monitoring

who_partners.quote: "ICAR have been working with Malawi’s law enforcement agencies since 2013. Their staff have built strong relationships with local managers..." (5631652.odt, Delivery options) AND "The MACSS component will be implemented through a commercial contract... with a supplier selected via the IMDP framework." (D0003938.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses (1) an **accountable grant** to ICAR for technical assistance (£4.7m originally, later adjusted), and (2) **commercial contracts** for civil society components (e.g., £1.67m MACSS contract). The grant covers embedded experts and casework support, while contracts fund time-bound CSO activities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme with two parallel components: (1) ICAR (via accountable grant) for law enforcement support, and (2) a commercially contracted supplier (via IMDP framework) for civil society work. A Steering Committee (FCDO, USAID, CSOs, ICAR) oversees coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (ICAR was direct award based on prior work; MACSS supplier selected via IMDP framework)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ICAR was selected for its "international centre of excellence" status and existing relationships with Malawian agencies (since 2013). The MACSS contractor was procured via the IMDP framework to ensure compliance and leverage FCDO’s pre-approved suppliers.
how_mechanism.quote: "ICAR are recognised as an international centre of excellence in international corruption and asset recovery... Their staff have built strong relationships with local managers." (5631652.odt, Delivery options) AND "The procurement for [MACSS] is underway under the IMDP framework through PCD." (D0003938.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes FCDO, USAID, ICAR, law enforcement agencies (ACB, FIA, DPP), and civil society organizations. It meets quarterly to review progress and adjust activities. FCDO holds monthly delivery meetings and conducts spot checks.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO will continue holding monthly delivery plan meetings; facilitating the quarterly Steering Committee Meetings with ICAR, the LEAs and Civil Society... FCDO will conduct spot checks and monitoring visits to project sites." (D0004216.odt, Approach to implementation) AND "ICAR will be required to seek prior approval from the SRO for any spending (contracts or grants) with a value greater than £25,000." (5631652.odt, VfM assessment)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between ICAR and MACSS components with FCDO approval, as seen in the 2023 extension where £500k was shifted from ICAR to MACSS. However, major changes require formal addendums (e.g., D0003938.odt, D0004216.odt).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The Opportunity Fund (later MACSS) was designed to respond to emerging needs, and extensions were approved to adapt to election timelines (2025) and shifting political risks. ICAR’s focus shifted from technical support to asset recovery policy based on learning.
how_flexibility.quote: "The Opportunity Fund would be used to support activities and initiatives which contribute to the programme’s objectives as opportunities and needs arise." (5631652.odt, Option B) AND "Extending TSOC... by one year and three months to 30 June 2026 will allow our anti-corruption work to cover the 2025 election and the new administration’s crucial first few months in office." (D0004216.odt, Objective of extension)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) ICAR (accountable grant) OR (2) Commercial Supplier (contract) → Malawian agencies/CSOs. No sub-grantees beyond these two primary partners.
how_efficiency.quote: "ICAR will be required to seek prior approval from the SRO for any spending (contracts or grants) with a value greater than £25,000... DFID will undertake regular (at least twice-yearly) spot-checks of a risk-based sample of procurements." (5631652.odt, VfM assessment) AND "The MACSS component will be implemented through a commercial contract valued at £1,667,342." (D0003938.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (rely on other donors/regional programmes)
Option A: Contract out management to a commercial service provider
Option B: Provide accountable grant to ICAR + manage in-house Opportunity Fund (CHOSEN)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option B was selected for (1) **cost efficiency** (ICAR’s not-for-profit status vs. commercial fees), (2) **continuity** (ICAR’s existing relationships since 2013), (3) **expertise** (ICAR’s specialized asset recovery knowledge), (4) **speed** (immediate implementation vs. 6-month procurement for Option A), and (5) **control** (FCDO retains oversight of Opportunity Fund).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of ICAR’s institutional knowledge if switching to a commercial provider (Option A)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Retained ICAR via accountable grant to preserve relationships and technical memory.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management burden on FCDO staff (Option B)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Established Steering Committee and monthly delivery meetings to distribute oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in law enforcement agencies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Shifted ICAR’s focus to non-conviction-based asset forfeiture (less politically sensitive) and used civil society (MACSS) to publicly expose corruption.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak civil society capacity in Malawi
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Included capacity-building for CSOs in MACSS contract and provided £500k from FCDO budget to supplement USAID funds.

why_rationale.quote: "On balance, while contracting out management of the programme to a commercial service provider would place fewer resource demands on DFID Malawi staff... providing an accountable grant to ICAR and managing an in-house Opportunity Fund is assessed to be preferable because costs will be kept to a minimum; ICAR will be able to build on the knowledge and relationships they have established; the best experts and organisations will be used to deliver the work; the programme will be able to begin implementation immediately; and DFID will have more control over how programme funds are spent." (5631652.odt, Delivery options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Malawi’s weak institutional capacity and political interference limit partner selection to organizations with (1) **existing trust** (e.g., ICAR’s long-standing relationships), (2) **technical expertise** (e.g., ICAR’s asset recovery specialization), and (3) **political neutrality** (e.g., avoiding local NGOs perceived as opposition-aligned). The high-risk context requires partners who can navigate elite resistance.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited local capacity forces reliance on international experts (ICAR).
Political sensitivity excludes some Malawian CSOs/NGO partners.
Weak public financial management prevents direct budget support to government.
Transnational nature of corruption requires partners with international networks (e.g., ICAR’s links to NCA).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **legal and technical expertise** (e.g., asset forfeiture, financial intelligence) drove the choice of ICAR (a specialized center) over multilateral options (e.g., UNODC, which lacks Malawi presence). The **political sensitivity** of targeting elites required a **flexible, adaptive structure** (Opportunity Fund → MACSS) to respond to election cycles and emerging cases.
q28_linkages: Technical objectives (e.g., asset recovery) → ICAR’s embedded experts model.
Political risks (e.g., elite pushback) → Civil society component (MACSS) for public pressure.
Transnational corruption → ICAR’s international networks (e.g., NCA collaboration).
Election timelines → Programme extension to cover 2025 transition.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) **efficiency** (using ICAR’s existing expertise to avoid delays) with (2) **equity** (including Malawian CSOs despite weak capacity). Trade-offs include:
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: ICAR’s direct award (fast) vs. competitive tender (slower but potentially more inclusive).
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led technical assistance (ICAR) vs. Southern-led implementation (Malawian agencies).
Cost vs. reach: Limited civil society budget (£1.67m) despite high corruption levels.
Risk vs. ambition: Focus on "high-value public procurements" (D0004216.odt) despite political risks.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk rating (5631652.odt) justifies **intensive oversight** (quarterly Steering Committee, monthly delivery meetings, spot checks) and **adaptive management** (e.g., shifting to non-conviction-based forfeiture to reduce political exposure).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak Malawian institutional capacity led to (1) **embedded experts** (ICAR staff in ACB/FIA), (2) **capacity-building as a core objective** (training, mentoring), and (3) **gradual transition** (e.g., moving from ICAR-led investigations to Malawian-led asset recovery systems).
intersections.quote: "Malawi’s law enforcement agencies have very limited experience or awareness of the use of publicly available databases... the analysis of electronic and financial data... or the use of an asset recovery regime. These technical shortcomings are compounded by inter-agency coordination failures." (5631652.odt, Causes of corruption) AND "The MACSS component... will regularly coordinate with other relevant programmes to ensure activities are complementary, non-duplicative, and that MACSS is able to exploit opportunities that emerge across a range of anti-corruption programmes." (D0003938.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks: Political interference in law enforcement (e.g., budgets/appointments controlled by President).
Elite resistance to sanctions (74% of Malawians believe politicians are corrupt).
Weak civil society capacity to hold government accountable.
Transnational corruption requiring international cooperation (Malawi’s limited MLA experience).
Election-related instability (2025 vote increasing grand corruption risks).
Overcrowded prisons and potential human rights concerns (OSJA ‘amber’ rating).
Media reliance on repeating public information vs. investigative journalism.
Risk of programme being perceived as politically motivated.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Shift to non-conviction-based asset forfeiture (less reliant on trials) and public exposure via civil society (MACSS). Use FCDO’s political influence to pressure elites.
Include capacity-building in MACSS contract and provide direct support (e.g., £500k FCDO funds).
Leverage ICAR’s international networks (e.g., NCA, FATF) and strengthen Malawi’s MLA processes.
Extend programme to cover 2025 transition and post-election period.
Fund investigative journalism training and ‘hackathons’ to identify procurement red flags.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, **embedded technical experts** (ICAR) are more effective than standalone training due to weak institutional memory.
**Flexible funding** (Opportunity Fund → MACSS) is critical to adapt to political shocks (e.g., elections, Cashgate-like scandals).
**Public pressure** (via civil society/media) is essential to counter elite capture of reforms.
**Non-conviction-based approaches** (asset forfeiture) reduce reliance on fragile judicial systems.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Cashgate scandal (2013) demonstrated that (1) **public financial management reforms alone are insufficient** without enforcement, (2) **technical assistance must be long-term** (ICAR’s support since 2013 led to 13 convictions), and (3) **political economy constraints** require adaptive strategies (e.g., shifting from convictions to asset recovery).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. Added civil society component (MACSS) after initial focus on law enforcement proved insufficient to sustain pressure. 2. Extended programme to align with election cycle (2025). 3. Shifted ICAR’s focus from casework to **system-wide asset recovery policy** to reduce political exposure. 4. Increased coordination with FATF and international partners based on lessons from Cashgate’s transnational links.
risks_lessons.quote: "A recent visit to Malawi by the National Crime Agency – funded through the UK Action Against Corruption (UKACT) programme – was only made possible because of DFID Malawi’s ongoing support to the Cashgate investigations through ICAR." (5631652.odt, Whether to intervene) AND "The additional resources will contribute to the existing theory of change." (D0003938.odt, Key changes) AND "Allow our anti-corruption work to cover the 2025 election and the new administration’s crucial first few months in office." (D0004216.odt, Objective of extension)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: USAID contributed £1.17m to the civil society component (MACSS), enabling a 2-year implementation period and expanded activities (e.g., investigative journalism, judicial monitoring).
financial_details.quote: "The new programme budget will be £14,037,804.51... The additional USAID support will contribute to the Malawi Anti-Corruption Civil Society Support (MACSS) new component." (D0003938.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) AND "The projected breakdown of spend is as follows... ICAR total: £1,150,000 (FY24/25), £1,150,000 (FY25/26); MACSS total: £750,000 (FY24/25), £1,000,000 (FY25/26)." (D0004216.odt, Additional support)

metadata.programme_name: Humanitarian Emergency Response Operations and Stabilisation Programme (HEROS)
metadata.quote: "The HEROS programme provides humanitarian emergency response operations management and stabilisation support to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to respond to the full range of global humanitarian and stabilisation challenges." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Current project start and end dates: 01 November 2017 – 31 October 2024" (D0005475.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "New project end date (if applicable): 31 October 2025" (D0005475.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: HEROS is designed to provide rapid, at-scale humanitarian emergency response operations and stabilisation support to FCDO. It enables the UK government to respond to global humanitarian disasters, protracted crises, and stabilisation challenges in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS). The programme focuses on saving lives, alleviating suffering, and maintaining human dignity during and after crises, while also supporting stabilisation efforts to reduce violence and prepare for long-term recovery.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The purpose of this project is to provide humanitarian emergency response operations management and stabilisation support to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO). It enables the FCDO to respond rapidly, at scale, to global humanitarian disasters and support work on protracted crises, chronic emergencies and humanitarian reform." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: UK able to provide an effective and timely response to at least six new crises each year, including at least one large response and ongoing support to protracted crisis management
FCDO’s ability to provide a bespoke and flexible response to rapid onset disasters and protracted and chronic crises is increased
Robust humanitarian supply chain and operational capability improves FCDO’s ability to prepare for and respond to the full range of humanitarian crises
FCDO has proportionate and scalable operational capacity to effectively contribute towards achieving National Security Objectives to address conflict and instability overseas
Support to National Security Council (NSC) to address conflict and instability overseas
Provision of humanitarian and stabilisation services and technical expertise to enable FCDO to respond to the full range of global humanitarian and stabilisation challenges
Over 100 humanitarian responses supported and work in 150 countries, including through over 1,500 civilian expert deployments
what_objectives.summary: HEROS is a responsive humanitarian and stabilisation service delivery programme that provides rapid, scalable support to FCDO for global crises, including natural disasters, conflicts, and protracted emergencies. It aims to save lives, alleviate suffering, and contribute to stabilisation efforts in fragile and conflict-affected states.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will provide humanitarian emergency response operations management and stabilisation support to DFID and the SU. It will enable DFID to respond rapidly, at scale, to global humanitarian disasters and support work on protracted crises, chronic emergencies and humanitarian reform." (21664033.odt, Intervention summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), which are characterized by high levels of instability, conflict, and humanitarian need. These environments pose significant risks due to complex emergencies, weak institutions, and security challenges.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme will provide humanitarian emergency response operations management and stabilisation support to DFID and the SU. It will enable DFID to respond rapidly, at scale, to global humanitarian disasters and support work on protracted crises, chronic emergencies and humanitarian reform. It will provide SU with a flexible model to support the Government’s (HMG) conflict, stabilisation and security work in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)." (21664033.odt, Intervention summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates in environments where humanitarian space is limited, governments and warring parties may not respect humanitarian principles, and International Humanitarian Law is often disregarded. This creates challenges for effective response and requires complex, demanding strategies. Additionally, the increasing frequency of natural disasters, urbanisation, and climate change exacerbates risks and complicates delivery.
where_context.quote: "A lack of humanitarian space with governments and warring parties not respecting basic humanitarian principles and International Humanitarian Law is a major and growing risk in many contexts." (21664033.odt, Key risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by FCDO and delivered through a commercial contract with Palladium International, a UK-based organization. Decision-making power rests with FCDO and the contracted service provider, with no explicit mention of Southern partners having significant decision-making roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: targeted training for Home Civil Servants (HCS) in DFID to better understand emergency response and humanitarian skills
building crisis response skills within DFID through provision of targeted training and exercises, including to a cadre of Senior Civil Servants
support to embed Home Civil Servants (HCS) into future programme arrangements

partner_organizations.role: programme management (within FCDO)

who_partners.quote: "The programme is jointly managed by the Humanitarian Response Group (HRG) which sits within the Humanitarian, Migration and Food Security Directorate (HMFD) and the Office for Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation (OCSM). It is primarily delivered through a commercial contract with Palladium International who have established the UK Humanitarian and Stabilisation Operations Team (HSOT)." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is delivered through a commercial contract with Palladium International, which was awarded through a competitive tendering process. This contract establishes the UK Humanitarian and Stabilisation Operations Team (HSOT) to provide the required services.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by FCDO (through HRG and OCSM) and implemented by Palladium International via the HSOT. The contract defines the scope, deliverables, and governance arrangements, with FCDO retaining overall control and oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The contract was awarded through a competitive tendering process to ensure value for money and the selection of a capable service provider. Palladium International was chosen based on its ability to deliver the required capabilities under a single contract.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme is primarily delivered through a commercial contract with Palladium International who have established the UK Humanitarian and Stabilisation Operations Team (HSOT)." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.quote: "HEROS is a high value FCDO Gold Contract which has consistently scored ‘A’ at annual review and represents value for money delivering a range of capabilities under a single contract." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed to be scalable, allowing for adjustments in capacity and resources based on demand and the nature of crises. However, significant reallocation likely requires FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with the ability to scale up or down based on the evolving global context and FCDO priorities. This includes horizon scanning and operational planning to ensure the programme remains relevant and effective.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will provide a wider range of skills and partnerships to ensure a bespoke response depending on the nature of emergency. Arrangements under this programme will need to evolve in line with global context and DFID’s priorities." (21664033.odt, Main programme activities)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Palladium International (HSOT)
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme is primarily delivered through a commercial contract with Palladium International who have established the UK Humanitarian and Stabilisation Operations Team (HSOT)." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

q24_alternatives_considered: alternative modes of delivery for FCDO’s future requirements (as part of the Delivery Model Assessment by the Cabinet Office)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The current delivery model (commercial contract with Palladium International) was chosen for its ability to provide a flexible, scalable, and integrated response capability under a single contract. It has consistently demonstrated value for money, scoring 'A' in annual reviews, and is critical for enabling effective and timely responses to global emergencies. The model allows FCDO to harness a wide range of capabilities and expertise rapidly, which is essential for responding to complex and unpredictable crises.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential loss of capability during transition to a successor programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The extension ensures no break in service while FCDO procures a successor programme, allowing for a smooth transition and responsible closure of the current programme.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial risks of extending the contract beyond necessary limits
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The extension is limited to 12 months to balance flexibility with commercial risks.

why_rationale.quote: "HEROS is a high value FCDO Gold Contract which has consistently scored ‘A’ at annual review and represents value for money delivering a range of capabilities under a single contract." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), which require specialized expertise and partners capable of working in high-risk environments. This limits the pool of potential partners to those with experience in complex emergencies, security management, and rapid response capabilities.
q27_constraints_detail: need for partners with experience in FCAS and high-risk environments
requirement for rapid deployment and surge capacity
need for security and logistics expertise in austere conditions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid, scalable, and flexible response capabilities determines the delivery structure. The programme’s objectives—such as responding to at least six new crises annually and providing bespoke support—require a single, integrated contract with a provider that can manage deployments, logistics, and technical expertise globally. This necessitates a commercial contract with a specialized organization like Palladium International.
q28_linkages: rapid response needs → single implementer with global reach
scalability requirements → flexible contract with surge capacity
complex emergencies → integrated civilian-military expertise
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme prioritizes efficiency and speed in crisis response, which may limit opportunities for more inclusive or locally led partnerships. The focus on rapid deployment and specialized expertise can create tensions with efforts to build local capacity or ensure Southern ownership, though capacity building for FCDO staff is embedded in the programme.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion (rapid response may limit local partner involvement)
expertise vs. ownership (Northern-led expertise may overshadow local capacity)
flexibility vs. predictability (adaptive management requires trade-offs in planning)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk operating environments (FCAS) necessitate intensive oversight and robust management structures to ensure duty of care, security, and effective response. This includes evidence-based risk assessments, security advice, and management of deployments in complex conditions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme, particularly for FCDO staff, to enhance their ability to respond to crises. This includes targeted training, exercises, and embedding Home Civil Servants in programme arrangements to improve crisis response skills.
intersections.quote: "The programme will help manage and improve DFID systems, including through: timely and effective early warning and alert mechanisms to prompt quick decision making; provision of expertise to help teams plan for crisis in normal business planning; and help to manage resources more flexibly, for example through supporting deployment of DFID HCS staff in response to emergencies." (21664033.odt, Main programme activities)

key_programme_risks: External events and unanticipated global emergencies that DFID and SU may not have fully prepared for
Lack of humanitarian space and non-compliance with humanitarian principles by governments and warring parties
Complex and demanding response strategies required due to increasing humanitarian needs and conflicts
Potential loss of capability during transition to a successor programme
Commercial risks associated with contract extensions

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: External events and unanticipated global emergencies
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme includes horizon scanning, operational planning, and flexible capacity to respond to a wide range of emergencies. It also maintains standing and standby capacity to ensure rapid response.
The programme works in coordination with HMG structures and international partners (UN, Red Cross, NGOs) to navigate complex environments and ensure effective response.
The 12-month extension ensures no break in service while FCDO procures a successor programme, allowing for a smooth transition and responsible closure.
The extension is limited to 12 months to balance flexibility with commercial risks, and additional programme management resources have been secured to mitigate procurement delays.

fcas_specific_lessons: The importance of strong Whitehall and DFID partnerships ahead of crises to enable effective working and surge support (lessons from Nepal, Ebola, Iraq, and Syria)
The need for early warning mechanisms that prompt early action on a ‘no regrets’ basis (lessons from Ebola, Haiyan, Horn of Africa)
The importance of flexible capacity to manage direct delivery, including logistics and scalable procurement (lessons from Ebola and Hagupit)
The need for greater cross-Whitehall integration of crisis response, including increased engagement on delivering the NSC strategy
The importance of starting small-scale projects and adopting a phased approach in complex, rapidly-changing conflict environments (lessons from Syria, Ukraine)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Ebola response highlighted the need for greater surge capacity, early warning mechanisms, and direct delivery capabilities. The Syria crisis demonstrated the need for greater flexibility in working with diverse partners in protracted conflicts. These lessons have informed the design of HEROS, including its focus on scalability, adaptability, and integrated civilian-military expertise.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme has been designed to double DFID’s response capacity, improve surge capabilities, and embed Home Civil Servants in programme arrangements. It also includes greater emphasis on horizon scanning, operational planning, and adaptive management to respond to lessons from past crises.
risks_lessons.quote: "Learning from recent experience, DFID and where necessary SU crisis response capabilities will be increased, enabling HMG to respond to emergencies even more rapidly, coherently and comprehensively." (21664033.odt, Rationale for UK support and expected change)

co_funding_partners.partner: FCDO (Office for Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation)

financial_details.quote: "The original business case was approved for up to £81.35m over 5 years (£60m HRG, £21.35m OCSM). A first business case addendum was approved for a time-only extension of almost two years from the end of December 2022 to the end of October 2024. This second business case addendum allows a further 12 months of implementation to 31 October 2025. It further provides an additional £18.6m taking the total support under the business case to £99.95m." (D0005475.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Rehabilitation and Extension of Bo – Kenema Electricity Distribution System
metadata.quote: "This project will rehabilitate the electricity distribution system for Sierra Leone’s second and third largest towns, Bo and Kenema." (4552508.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: December 2016", "End Date: December 2020" (4552508.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines infrastructure rehabilitation (service delivery) with institutional strengthening (capacity building) and market integration (financing mechanism). It upgrades physical electricity distribution systems while building EDSA's operational capacity and connecting to the West Africa Power Pool.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will rehabilitate and upgrade an existing 33kV connection between Bo and Kenema; rehabilitate the associated distribution networks and sub-stations in each town; purchase pre-paid meters... and provide technical assistance to support the implementation of the project, and improve the capability of the state owned Electricity Distribution and Supply Authority (EDSA)." (4552508.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 70km of upgraded 33kV high-voltage line between Bo and Kenema
Rehabilitation of distribution networks in Bo, Kenema and surrounding areas
Connection of 37,000 additional households to the grid
Installation of pre-payment meters for commercial viability
Training and management support for EDSA staff
Improved electricity access for 316,000 people in 48 months
Potential 40MW additional capacity from West Africa Power Pool by 2019
Reduction of system losses from 40% to 20%
Increase in EDSA's revenue collection from 88% to 90%
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform electricity access in Sierra Leone's second and third largest cities through physical infrastructure upgrades, institutional capacity building, and regional power integration, directly benefiting 316,000 people and creating conditions for economic growth.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected Outcome of the programme will be that 316,000 people in Bo and Kenema and in the surrounding villages will benefit directly from improved access to electricity over the next 48 months." (4552508.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sierra Leone is classified as FCAS due to its recent civil war (1991-2002), Ebola outbreak (2013-2016), and ranking 181/188 on the 2015 Human Development Index. The document explicitly states "Despite improvement following the end of the Sierra Leone conflict (1991-2002), Sierra Leone has some of the poorest developmental indicators in the world."
where_context.q5_source: "Despite improvement following the end of the Sierra Leone conflict (1991-2002), Sierra Leone has some of the poorest developmental indicators in the world. Sierra Leone ranked 181st out of 188 countries in the United National Human Development Index 2015 data." (4552508.odt, Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The civil war destroyed physical infrastructure, the Ebola outbreak disrupted development, and current electricity access is only 10% nationally with 40% technical losses in the Bo-Kenema system. Weak institutional capacity at EDSA and EWRC limits tariff management and operational efficiency. Seasonal hydropower fluctuations create unreliable supply, forcing reliance on expensive diesel generation (0.35 USD/kWh).
where_context.quote: "Sierra Leone’s physical infrastructure, particularly electricity, water, and sanitation, was badly damaged during the 1991–2001 civil war... The Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak in 2013 proved a major setback... Electricity access in Sierra Leone is among the lowest in Africa, at less than 15% against an average rate of 40% in 2013." (4552508.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The AfDB (multilateral) leads implementation and financial management, while the Government of Sierra Leone (GoSL) through EDSA manages day-to-day operations. Key decisions require AfDB no-objection, but EDSA retains operational control with technical assistance from both AfDB and DFID.
q10_capacity_building_details: training in modern engineering techniques for EDSA staff
improvements to EDSA's financial systems
development of management information packages
cost of service study and tariff reform support
commercial skills development for customer acquisition
technical assistance for design/tender documents
support to revamp joint EDSA-EGTC training center

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: lead implementation agency and co-financier (£10.5m)

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Development (DFID)
partner_organizations.role: co-financier (£31.5m) and technical oversight

partner_organizations.name: Government of Sierra Leone (GoSL) - Ministry of Energy
partner_organizations.role: executing agency

partner_organizations.name: Electricity Distribution and Supply Authority (EDSA)
partner_organizations.role: implementing agency and operational manager

partner_organizations.name: Electricity Generation and Transmission Company (EGTC)
partner_organizations.role: technical partner for transmission components

partner_organizations.name: West Africa Power Pool (WAPP)
partner_organizations.role: regional power integration partner

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: previous funder of EDSA reforms and metering systems

partner_organizations.name: WS Atkins (consultancy)
partner_organizations.role: feasibility study and design

who_partners.quote: "The AfDB will be the lead implementation agency for this project and DFID will co-fund it through a standard administrative agreement with the AfDB... The Ministry of Energy will be the project’s executing agency, with day to day project management by EDSA as the implementing agency." (4552508.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID and AfDB enter a standard administrative agreement (technical cooperation framework) to co-finance the project, with AfDB managing implementation. Funds flow through AfDB's established procurement and financial systems, with DFID providing oversight through quarterly reports and joint supervision missions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: AfDB leads implementation with EDSA as the operational arm, supported by a Steering Committee (MoE, MoFED, EDSA, EGTC). DFID participates in oversight through joint supervision missions and quarterly financial reports. The Project Implementation Unit (PIU) within EDSA handles day-to-day management with technical assistance from AfDB and DFID.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: direct award (AfDB selected based on existing relationship)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AfDB was selected due to its existing experience implementing power projects in Sierra Leone (including Bumbuna I and CLSG), established procurement systems, and regional expertise. The document states: "AfDB already has experience of implementing a number of power sector projects in Sierra Leone, including the £60 million Bumbuna I hydroelectric project, and is a principal stakeholder in the CLSG regional interconnection project."
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID and the AfDB will enter into a standard technical cooperation framework arrangement which will govern the allocation of each organisation’s resources to the project budget... AfDB will be the lead implementation agency for this project." (4552508.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee is chaired by the Ministry of Energy and includes the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development, EDSA Director General, and EGTC Director General. It provides strategic oversight through coordinated monitoring of major milestones. All procurement decisions require AfDB no-objection.
how_governance.quote: "A Steering Committee (SC) will provide strategic oversight through coordinated monitoring and evaluation of major milestones. The SC will be under the Chairmanship of the Ministry of Energy and will consist of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development, the Director General of EDSA and the Director General of EGTC... The AfDB will conduct a minimum of two procurement supervision missions a year to undertake an ex-post review of the Borrower’s procurement actions." (4552508.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Any changes to the procurement plan must be submitted to AfDB for no-objection. The document states: "The procurement plan will be updated as required to reflect any changes in the project scope. Any changes will be submitted to the Bank for its no objection."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The technical assistance component can be tailored to EDSA's emerging needs, but core infrastructure designs are fixed based on feasibility studies. The document notes: "The technical assistance package will however be tailored to suit the emerging needs of EDSA." while also stating "No significant changes to the system design are expected."
how_flexibility.quote: "The technical assistance package will however be tailored to suit the emerging needs of EDSA... No significant changes to the system design are expected." (4552508.odt, Intervention Summary and Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → AfDB (lead implementer) → EDSA (operational manager) → local contractors/sub-grantees
how_efficiency.quote: "90% of funds will be spent on works and 10% on services... The AfDB have allowed for a physical contingency of 10% and a price contingency of 15%... DFID’s funds will be front loaded to optimise expenditure within the Presidential Recovery Priorities funding commitment period." (4552508.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Single-circuit 66kV overhead line (rejected due to higher cost and lower resilience)
33kV offline new route parallel to Bo-Kenema highway (rejected due to resettlement impacts)
33kV underground cable (rejected due to switchgear issues and higher capital cost)
Rehabilitating existing Bo/Goma generation plants (rejected as least cost-effective)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The double-circuit 33kV overhead line was selected because: 1) It uses existing right-of-way (minimizing environmental/social impacts); 2) It allows future uprating to 66kV; 3) It's 60% cheaper than 66kV single-circuit; 4) It aligns with the CLSG regional interconnection timeline; and 5) AfDB's established procurement systems mitigate fiduciary risks in Sierra Leone's weak institutional context.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays due to EDSA's limited capacity with AfDB procedures
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Recruitment of an experienced procurement specialist to EDSA team and AfDB's prior review of all procurement actions

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Construction delays in the 33kV line rebuild affecting Kenema's power supply
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Temporary 3.2MW generation for Kenema during the 6-month dry season construction period

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: EDSA's financial deterioration from tariff misalignment
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-payment meters to improve revenue collection and planned 25% tariff increase before 2020

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delay in CLSG interconnection reducing economic returns
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with temporary generation and regional political commitment to CLSG timeline

why_rationale.quote: "Taking power from the West Africa power pool is the best option for Bo, Kenema and surrounding areas, even recognising the risk of delays in completion of the CLSG project. The other option - rehabilitating the existing power generation plants at Bo and Goma - would be the least cost effective option... A 33kV double circuit OHL is a more resilient design in case of fault in one circuit; and A 66kV single circuit is estimated to be 60% more expensive." (4552508.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Sierra Leone's FCAS context and weak institutional capacity constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) Experience in fragile states; 2) Established procurement systems to mitigate corruption risks; 3) Regional expertise in West African power pools. This excludes local contractors for major works ("The AfDB has reviewed the capacity of the local construction industry and found it to be inadequate for delivering large contracts") and requires multilateral leadership.
q27_constraints_detail: Local construction industry lacks capacity for large contracts
EDSA lacks experience with AfDB procurement procedures
Weak regulatory environment requires AfDB's financial controls
High corruption risk necessitates international oversight
Post-Ebola recovery priorities demand rapid, reliable implementation
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (infrastructure + capacity building + regional integration) require a multilateral structure: 1) Physical upgrades need AfDB's procurement expertise; 2) EDSA's institutional weaknesses demand embedded technical assistance; 3) Regional power integration requires WAPP coordination. The document links the need for "tried and tested technology appropriate for the country context" with AfDB's role in procurement and supervision.
q28_linkages: Regional integration goal → AfDB leadership (as CLSG stakeholder)
EDSA capacity gaps → Technical assistance component and procurement specialist recruitment
FCAS risks → Multilateral financial controls and intensive oversight
Pre-payment meters → Commercial viability objective
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: 1) Speed (using existing RoW despite minor resettlement) vs inclusion (22 houses/153 PAPs affected); 2) Affordability (25% tariff increase) vs access (lifeline tariffs for low-income consumers); 3) Local ownership (EDSA implementation) vs risk mitigation (AfDB procurement controls). The document notes "there is likely to be a concentration of low income consumers benefiting from a lifeline tariff" while requiring tariff reforms for financial sustainability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Existing RoW used to minimize delays despite 22 houses/20 trees lost
25% tariff increase required for viability but with lifeline provisions
International contractors used for reliability despite higher costs
Pre-payment meters improve revenue but may exclude poorest households
intersections.risk_affects_management: The medium risk rating and FCAS context justify intensive oversight: quarterly AfDB supervision missions, embedded procurement specialist, and joint DFID-AfDB reviews. The document states this is "within DFID Sierra Leone’s high risk appetite" but requires "periodic financial management and internal control assessments."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: EDSA's limited capacity leads to: 1) AfDB managing all major procurements; 2) Technical assistance as a core component; 3) Steering Committee oversight; 4) Recruitment of a procurement specialist. The WB's existing management contract with EDSA is noted as critical for sustainability.
intersections.quote: "EDSA is a relatively weak utility and currently lacks capacity to operate as a commercial entity... The AfDB has concluded that the GoSL’s national procurement procedures and regulations are too unreliable for use in this project. The project will therefore adopt the AfDB’s Bank Procurement Policy and Methodology... An experienced procurement specialist with extensive experience of the Bank’s procurement policy will therefore be recruited to the EDSA team for this project." (4552508.odt, Commercial Case and Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Delay in CLSG interconnection (reduces EIRR from 20.4% to 11.8%)
Failure to align tariffs with EDSA's cost structure
Procurement delays due to EDSA's limited capacity
Construction interruptions during wet season
Lower-than-expected household connections (37,000 target)
Social resistance to resettlement (153 PAPs affected)
EDSA's financial deterioration without tariff adjustments
Dependence on temporary generation during construction
Potential HIV/AIDS/STI spread among construction workers
Climate risks (lightning storms, temperature fluctuations)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Temporary generation and phased implementation
Pre-payment meters and planned 25% tariff increase by 2020
Recruitment of procurement specialist and AfDB prior reviews
70-week timeline accounting for seasonal interruptions
Resettlement Action Plan and community sensitization
Worker sensitization, condom distribution, and awareness campaigns
Lightning arresters, vegetation clearance, and steel poles

fcas_specific_lessons: Use of multilateral procurement systems to mitigate corruption risks
Embedded technical assistance to address institutional weaknesses
Front-loaded funding to align with recovery priorities
Regional integration (WAPP) to overcome local generation constraints
Pre-payment meters to improve revenue collection in weak regulatory environments
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons incorporated from AfDB's Bumbuna I project and WB's Sierra Leone Infrastructure Development Fund, including: 1) Involvement of local councils and traditional leaders; 2) Technical support for tender documentation; 3) Management contracts for utilities; 4) Pre-payment metering systems. The document states: "Lessons from previous AfDB projects have been incorporated into the design of the Bo-Kenema rehabilitation project."
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Adoption of AfDB procurement procedures instead of GoSL's unreliable systems; 2) Inclusion of temporary generation based on Bumbuna I delays; 3) Expanded technical assistance component; 4) Ring-main 11kV networks instead of radial systems for reliability.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from previous AfDB projects have been incorporated into the design of the Bo-Kenema rehabilitation project, including the involvement of elected local councils, traditional leaders and communities in project preparation, and providing technical support to the implementing agency in the preparation of design and tender documentation and in following the AfDB’s disbursement procedures... The AfDB has concluded that the GoSL’s national procurement procedures and regulations are too unreliable for use in this project." (4552508.odt, Commercial Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The project leverages £10.5m from AfDB's ADF-13 allocation and connects to the £300m+ CLSG regional interconnection (WB/AfDB/EU funded), which will provide 40MW additional capacity to Sierra Leone by 2019. The document states: "The Côte d'Ivoire – Liberia - Sierra Leone - Guinea (CLSG) electricity networks interconnection project involves the construction of a 1,357-km-long double circuit high voltage (225 kV) line... The World Bank (WB), African Development Bank (AfDB) and the European Union (EU) are financing this project."
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: 100% of DFID's funds classified as capital expenditure (CDEL) and International Climate Finance (ICF). The project focuses on infrastructure rehabilitation with 90% of funds spent on works (capital) and 10% on services.
financial_details.quote: "Total project cost is £43 million, to be co-financed by the African Development Bank (AfDB) and the Government of Sierra Leone... DFID will provide £31.5 million... 90% of funds will be spent on works and 10% on services. 85% will be spent in foreign currency... 100% of DFID’s funds will be classified as capital expenditure (CDEL) and as International Climate Finance (ICF)." (4552508.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Partnerships for Development
metadata.quote: "The Partnerships for Development (P4D) programme will strengthen selected institutions in developing countries by facilitating and improving peer-to-peer development partnerships between those institutions and their counterpart UK institutions, thereby furthering Sustainable Development Goal 16." (42738310.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 1 October 2016 until 31 March 2021" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2023" (42738310.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **capacity building** through peer-to-peer partnerships to strengthen institutions in developing countries, while also generating **evidence** on the effectiveness of this aid modality and promoting **policy influence** by establishing the UK as a centre of excellence in peer-to-peer partnerships. It includes elements of **implementation research** by testing and scaling partnership approaches.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Partnerships for Development (P4D) programme will strengthen selected institutions in developing countries by facilitating and improving peer-to-peer development partnerships..." and "P4D will develop the evidence base around peer-to-peer partnerships, publishing documents on evidence, what works, and best practice." (42738310.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION and later sections)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased number of peer-to-peer partnerships across new sectors, institutions, and countries (contributing to UK diplomatic, development, and security objectives)
Enhanced effectiveness of peer-to-peer partnerships in achieving development impact
Improved coordination across different peer-to-peer partnerships and with other DFID/HMG programmes
Strengthened evidence base for peer-to-peer partnerships (identifying what works and best practice)
Strengthened institutions in partner countries supported by the programme
Promotion of peer-to-peer partnerships as an aid modality (raising awareness in donor community and establishing UK as a centre of excellence)
Community of Practice for UK and developing country institutions engaged in peer-to-peer partnerships
Wrap-around support (scoping, brokering, training, MEL) for selected partnerships
Conferences, workshops, and learning products to share knowledge on peer-to-peer partnerships
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to scale up and improve peer-to-peer partnerships between UK and developing country institutions, generating evidence on their effectiveness while strengthening institutions and promoting this approach as a viable aid modality. It combines direct capacity-building with research and policy influence objectives.
what_objectives.quote: "P4D has the following high-level objectives: Increase the number of peer-to-peer partnerships...; Enhance the effectiveness...; Improve coordination...; Build the evidence base...; Strengthen institutions...; Promote peer-to-peer partnerships as an aid modality..." (42738310.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a variety of contexts including fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), but the overall risk was revised from 'high' to 'moderate' due to accumulated experience and evidence from early partnerships. The programme has a high appetite for external context risk and explicitly supports partnerships in FCAS, recognizing political economy vulnerabilities.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall programme risk as set out in the original Business Case was high... Through the programme’s management of early partnerships... the overall net risk for this programme has been revised from high to moderate." and "P4D has a high appetite for external context risk and will support partnerships in fragile and conflict-affected states..." (42738310.odt, Risk section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy factors and institutional weaknesses in partner countries affect the sustainability and impact of partnerships. The programme explicitly notes that "the effectiveness of peer-to-peer partnerships are vulnerable to changes in ministers and senior officials on the developing country side." Data limitations are addressed through the programme's focus on building an evidence base where little systematic research exists.
where_context.quote: "The effectiveness of peer-to-peer partnerships are vulnerable to changes in ministers and senior officials on the developing country side." and "The research and literature on the benefits of peer-to-peer partnerships in a development context remains limited..." (42738310.odt, Risk and Evidence sections)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: DFID Governance, Open Societies and Anti-Corruption department (GOSAC)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by DFID GOSAC (UK) with strategic decisions taken by HMG civil servants. While partnerships are demand-driven from developing countries, the selection of which partnerships to fund/support is determined by UK institutions based on criteria set by DFID. The Partnership Platform (managed by Government Partnerships International, a UK cross-government unit) provides wrap-around support and brokering services.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., in geological data management, anti-corruption techniques)
mentorship (e.g., embedded advisers like NCA Anti-Corruption Mentors)
institutional strengthening (e.g., improving policy drafting, legislative processes, management systems)
peer learning (through Community of Practice and conferences)
political economy analysis coaching (Thinking and Working Politically)

partner_organizations.name: Government Partnerships International (GPI)
partner_organizations.role: Manages the Partnership Platform (community of practice, wrap-around support, MEL, communications, programme assurance)

partner_organizations.name: DFID Governance, Open Societies and Anti-Corruption department (GOSAC)
partner_organizations.role: Overarching leadership, strategic decision-making, governance, payments approval, policy links across HMG

partner_organizations.name: External Deployments Supplier (TBD via procurement)
partner_organizations.role: Deployments, logistics, and other operational support (e.g., duty of care, security)

partner_organizations.name: UK Partnership Institutions (e.g., National Crime Agency, British Geological Survey, Oxford Policy Fellowship)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver peer-to-peer partnerships with developing country counterparts (funded or supported by P4D)

partner_organizations.name: Developing country counterpart institutions
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of peer-to-peer support and co-designers of partnership activities

partner_organizations.name: DFID country offices and FCO posts
partner_organizations.role: Involved in decisions about partnerships in their respective countries

who_partners.quote: "DFID GOSAC will provide overarching leadership and management of P4D... GPI will manage the Partnership Platform... DFID GOSAC will engage an external Deployments Supplier to deliver support for deployments, logistics and other services..." and "The peer-to-peer partnerships themselves will be delivered by UK partnership institutions." (42738310.odt, INFORMATION section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** and **Accountable Grant Agreements** with UK Partnership Institutions for funded partnerships (Tier 1). A **contract** will be established with the external Deployments Supplier via OJEU procurement. **Budget transfers** are used between DFID and Government Partnerships International (GPI) for managing the Partnership Platform.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a **Partnership Platform** managed by GPI, which coordinates all activities (Community of Practice, wrap-around support, MEL, communications). DFID GOSAC retains strategic oversight and governance. An external Deployments Supplier handles logistics. UK institutions deliver partnerships directly with developing country counterparts, with varying levels of support from the Platform.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Government Partnerships International (GPI) was selected based on ministerial direction to use civil servants for substantive functions and GPI's existing track record in supporting peer-to-peer partnerships (e.g., through the Strengthening Civil Service Partnerships programme). The external Deployments Supplier will be selected via OJEU procurement.
how_mechanism.quote: "This Addendum reflects the changed delivery modality, with the programme managed... through a hybrid delivery model, using Government Partnerships International (GPI) to manage the Partnership Platform..." and "DFID GOSAC will engage an external Deployments Supplier... following a procurement process, complying with the Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU)." (42738310.odt, INFORMATION section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **Partnerships for Development Programme Board** oversees the programme, providing strategic guidance and ensuring alignment with HMG objectives. The Board's Terms of Reference are annexed to the Delivery Approach Paper. DFID GOSAC manages the Partnership Platform via an MoU with GPI, with regular reviews and financial/performance reporting.
how_governance.quote: "A Partnerships for Development Programme Board will be formed to oversee and provide strategic guidance to the programme..." and "DFID GOSAC will manage the Partnership Platform as other programmes, with an annual review, regular meetings and financial and performance reporting against the agreed objectives." (42738310.odt, INFORMATION section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between partnerships based on demand and performance, but this is constrained by the programme's capacity (e.g., Partnership Platform staffing limits). The programme uses a flexible model to "meet demand and apply lessons learned," but major shifts require approval from DFID GOSAC.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an **adaptive management** approach, with a 6-month inception period to revise the Theory of Change and logframe. The Partnership Platform continuously identifies lessons and feeds them back to the Community of Practice. Sectoral and geographic priorities can be adjusted based on demand and evidence, but changes are overseen by the Programme Board and DFID GOSAC.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will pilot various partnership approaches and use a flexible and iterative delivery model to meet demand and apply lessons learned." and "The MERL function of the Partnership Platform will continually identify lessons from P4D and feed these back... By taking a responsive and learning-focused approach to MEL, P4D will further develop the evidence base for peer-to-peer partnerships." (42738310.odt, INFORMATION section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (GOSAC) → Government Partnerships International (Partnership Platform) → UK Partnership Institutions/Deployments Supplier → Developing country counterparts
how_efficiency.quote: "Payments to UK Partnership Institutions will be made in arrears on a quarterly basis on receipt of valid invoices and financial reports." and "The Partnership Platform was launched in Q3 2018/19 with an estimated expenditure of £504,166... increasing to an annual expenditure of £1,994,709 by FY2022/23." (42738310.odt, Financial Structure and Partnership Platform sections)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (existing partnerships continue organically)
Within HMG (new DFID team or expand existing units like GPI)
External (procure an external organization to manage the initiative)
Hybrid (combination of internal and external delivery)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **hybrid model** was chosen to comply with **ministerial direction** for civil servants to deliver substantive functions while outsourcing deployments/logistics for flexibility. This approach balances **cross-government coordination** (via GPI's civil service status) with **operational efficiency** (via external supplier for logistics). It leverages GPI's existing expertise in peer-to-peer partnerships and aligns with the UK's strategic priorities (e.g., Global Britain agenda).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity in programme management due to separation of deployments/logistics (external supplier) from other functions (GPI)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust programme management and coordination mechanisms between GPI and the Deployments Supplier, with DFID GOSAC oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delay in deployments/logistics function availability due to OJEU procurement process
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early Market Engagement and proportionate procurement design to expedite selection.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential misalignment between UK supply and developing country demand
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnership Criteria (e.g., evidence of demand, alignment with strategic objectives) and wrap-around support to ensure quality.

why_rationale.quote: "The hybrid model will outsource deployments and logistics to the market, thus reducing burden on civil service... The combination of HMG staff access across government and external management of deployment and logistics could be powerful in enabling rapid expansion of partnerships programming." and "This Addendum changes the hybrid option, basing it largely within HMG, with only the deployments and logistics function outsourced..." (42738310.odt, Value for Money and Appraisal sections)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope (any ODA-eligible country) and focus on fragile/conflict-affected states (FCAS) require partners with **adaptive capacity** and **political economy expertise**. This limits partner selection to institutions like GPI (with cross-government experience) and UK public sector bodies (e.g., NCA, BGS) that can navigate complex contexts. The need for **duty of care** in high-risk environments also shapes the choice of Deployments Supplier.
q27_constraints_detail: Political economy vulnerabilities in FCAS require partners skilled in Thinking and Working Politically (e.g., GPI’s coaching role).
Security risks in conflict-affected countries necessitate robust deployments/logistics support (hence external supplier).
Weak institutions in partner countries demand long-term, embedded partnerships (e.g., 3-year NCA Anti-Corruption Mentor deployments).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **peer-to-peer capacity-building objective** drives the **platform-based delivery structure** (Partnership Platform + Deployments Supplier) to facilitate brokering, wrap-around support, and learning. The need to **generate evidence** on peer-to-peer effectiveness requires a **centralized MEL function** (managed by GPI). The **global, multi-sectoral scope** necessitates a **hybrid model** (HMG-led for strategy, external for logistics) to balance coherence with flexibility.
q28_linkages: Evidence-generation goal → Centralized MEL function within Partnership Platform.
Capacity-building focus → Wrap-around support (scoping, training, MEL) for partnerships.
Global/FCAS context → Hybrid delivery (GPI for adaptive management, external supplier for deployments).
Scaling partnerships → Community of Practice and conferences to share lessons.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between **inclusive partnerships** (open Community of Practice) and **focused delivery** (limited funded/supported partnerships due to capacity constraints). It also balances **UK strategic priorities** (e.g., Global Britain agenda) with **partner country demand**, using criteria to select partnerships that align with both.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scale-up is constrained by Partnership Platform’s capacity (8 funded + 14 supported partnerships max).
Expertise vs. ownership: UK institutions lead partnerships, but demand-driven selection and co-design mitigate this.
Cost vs. reach: Budget limits require prioritization (e.g., £15m pipeline contingent on Spending Review).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (with high appetite for external context risk) leads to **intensive oversight** (Programme Board, quarterly reviews) and **adaptive management** (flexible Theory of Change, iterative MEL). FCAS contexts require **embedded safeguarding** (e.g., enhanced due diligence for non-public sector partners).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building core objective** shapes partner roles: UK institutions receive **wrap-around support** (e.g., MEL training) to improve partnership quality, while developing country counterparts gain **institutional strengthening** (e.g., legislative drafting, data management systems). GPI’s role includes **coaching on political economy analysis** to build adaptive capacity.
intersections.quote: "The programme will pilot various partnership approaches and use a flexible and iterative delivery model to meet demand and apply lessons learned." and "P4D has a high appetite for external context risk and will support partnerships in fragile and conflict-affected states... The Partnership Platform will coach those involved in peer-to-peer partnerships in political economy analysis and Thinking and Working Politically." (42738310.odt, INFORMATION and Risk sections)

key_programme_risks: Delays in procurement of Deployments Supplier (affecting timely deployments).
Mismatch between UK expertise supply and developing country demand.
Political changes in partner countries disrupting partnerships.
Reputational risk from poorly designed or low-impact partnerships.
Fiduciary risks (e.g., fraud) in delivery chain.
Overstretch of Partnership Platform capacity (limited to ~8 funded partnerships).
Complexity in coordinating hybrid delivery model (GPI + external supplier).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Early Market Engagement and proportionate procurement process designed with DFID’s Procurement and Commercial Department.
Partnership Criteria (e.g., evidence of demand, conflict sensitivity) and demand-scoping before commitments.
Political economy analysis, Thinking and Working Politically coaching, and flexible partnership designs.
Robust MEL, communications strategy, and safeguarding protocols (e.g., enhanced due diligence).
Adherence to Smart Rules, delivery chain mapping, quarterly fraud/safeguarding reporting, and active risk management by Partnership Platform.
Prioritization via Partnership Criteria and iterative model to adjust staffing/resources.
Clear MoU between DFID and GPI, Standard Operating Procedures for payments, and joint governance (Programme Board).

fcas_specific_lessons: Peer-to-peer partnerships in FCAS require **long-term, embedded support** (e.g., 3-year NCA mentors in Nigeria/Kenya).
**Political economy analysis** is critical for sustainability (e.g., GPI’s work in Ghana/Ethiopia).
**Flexible, adaptive programming** is essential to respond to changing contexts (e.g., election cycles).
**Trust-building** through embedded advisers mitigates institutional weaknesses (e.g., BGS in Sierra Leone).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Early partnerships (e.g., Oxford Policy Fellowship, British Geological Survey) demonstrated that **peer-to-peer models** can achieve institutional reform where traditional technical assistance fails, by focusing on **relationships, local context, and softer skills** (e.g., leadership, change management). The **Strengthening Civil Service Partnerships programme** (managed by GPI) provided evidence that **wrap-around support** (scoping, MEL, brokering) improves partnership quality. Lessons included the need for **high-level commitment, clarity of roles, and long-term flexibility**.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expanded from sector-specific (anti-corruption, extractives) to **any development sector** based on demand and the Secretary of State’s Great Partnership Agenda.
Broadened geographic scope from **DFID priority countries** to **any ODA-eligible country** to align with Global Britain/Prosperity agendas.
Shifted from **external management agent** to **hybrid model** (GPI-led Platform + external logistics) per ministerial direction.
Added **Community of Practice** and **conferences/workshops** to strengthen evidence-sharing and learning.
Incorporated **political economy coaching** (Thinking and Working Politically) into wrap-around support.
Developed **Partnership Criteria** (e.g., demand evidence, conflict sensitivity) to prioritize partnerships.
risks_lessons.quote: "The evidence base for the peer-to-peer partnerships is still developing, and a central objective for the Partnerships for Development (P4D) programme is to strengthen the evidence base for this alternative aid modality." and "The GPImodel, using peer-to-peer partnerships to promote institutional reform, was developed in response to the inconsistent evidence for the success of technical assistance to progress institutional reform." (42738310.odt, Evidence section)

financial_details.quote: "The total support the UK will provide through the Partnerships for Development programme remains £35,000,000." and "The budget for P4D until the end of the current Spending Round is £20 million. The balance of £15 million will become pipeline budget, pending the outcome of the next Spending Review." (42738310.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION and Financial Structure sections)

metadata.programme_name: Jordan Compact Economic Opportunities Programme (JCEOP)
metadata.quote: "To deliver the transformative agenda set out in the Jordan Compact by: i) turning the refugee crisis into a development opportunity; ii) rebuilding Jordanian host communities; and iii) supporting Jordan’s macroeconomic framework." (5519561.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 22 July 2016-31 December 2018 (previously extended to 31 March 2022)" and "New project end date (if applicable): 30 June 2025" (52784557.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (leveraging concessional finance through multilateral banks), service delivery (infrastructure projects like wastewater treatment), and policy influence (supporting Jordan's economic reforms). It aims to create jobs, improve infrastructure, and support macroeconomic stability in Jordan while addressing the Syrian refugee crisis.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will be extended to March 2022 to (i) align with the Government of Jordan’s (GoJ) new Economic Growth Plan 2018-2022, and (ii) include two years for implementation of projects financed during FY2019/20."
