(33295258.odt, INFORMATION) and "The extension will improve the economic resilience of Jordan. The UK will provide a grant to the GCFF enabling the World Bank to provide additional concessional financing incentivising critical economic reforms and implementing projects while creating fiscal space for their implementation." (52784557.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 200,000 labour days created during construction of wastewater treatment facility (31615354.odt, Expected Results)
100,000m³/day increase in treated wastewater capacity (31615354.odt, Expected Results)
4.4 million people (including 500,000 Syrian refugees) benefiting from enhanced wastewater flows (31615354.odt, Expected Results)
Leverage of €150-200mn public-private partnership for wastewater project (31615354.odt, Expected Results)
Over 120,000 work permits issued to Syrian refugees (52784557.odt, Evidence of performance to date)
175 companies placed on fast-track customs approval process (52784557.odt, Evidence of performance to date)
3 million people benefiting from expanded landfill and waste management (52784557.odt, Evidence of performance to date)
178,000 poor Jordanians receiving support from National Aid Fund (52784557.odt, Evidence of performance to date)
30,000 Syrians and Jordanians benefitting from on-the-job training (5519561.odt, Expected Results)
3,600 additional tonnes of waste managed daily in Amman (5519561.odt, Expected Results)
10,000 households benefitting from increased wastewater flows (5519561.odt, Expected Results)
what_objectives.summary: JCEOP aims to transform Jordan's refugee crisis into economic opportunities through job creation, infrastructure development, and macroeconomic support, while leveraging significant concessional finance from multilateral partners.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will be extended to March 2022 to (i) align with the Government of Jordan’s (GoJ) new Economic Growth Plan 2018-2022, and (ii) include two years for implementation of projects financed during FY2019/20." (33295258.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Jordan faces significant economic instability due to hosting 640,000+ Syrian refugees (5519561.odt), with unemployment at 18.2% (31615354.odt) and public debt at 94% of GDP (52784557.odt). The programme documents repeatedly highlight risks to stability from economic pressures and regional conflicts.
where_context.q5_source: "Risks to Jordan’s economic stability are growing. Unemployment has increased, hitting a 25-year high of 18.2%." (31615354.odt, Strategic case) and "Jordan’s growth potential appears to be shrinking as necessary austerity targets are driving cuts in government capital investment." (52784557.odt, Strategic case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The refugee crisis has strained Jordan's infrastructure (water, waste management) and public services, while political sensitivities around refugee employment create implementation challenges. Economic reforms face domestic opposition, and frequent government turnover delays progress (5519561.odt, Strategic Case).
where_context.quote: "The political economy of the Jordan Compact offers a huge opportunity for success, although there are some recognised issues which will require close attention... Frequent turnover of government also likely delayed implementation of the reform program and weakened ownership of some of the reforms." (5519561.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank (GCFF) and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank and EBRD (both Northern-led multilateral institutions) make final decisions on project selection and implementation, though projects are prioritized by the Government of Jordan. The UK (DFID/FCDO) retains oversight through steering committees and annual approvals.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to Government of Jordan for reform implementation (52784557.odt)
skills training for Syrian refugees (e.g., Abdali Mall training centre via EBRD) (52784557.odt)
support to Project Management Unit for Compact implementation (5519561.odt)
analytical projects to inform policy (31615354.odt)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Global Concessional Financing Facility - GCFF)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner for economic reforms and concessional financing

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for infrastructure projects and private sector support

partner_organizations.name: Government of Jordan (GoJ)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary and co-implementer (prioritizes projects and implements reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation (MOPIC)
partner_organizations.role: Coordinates Compact implementation via Project Management Unit

partner_organizations.name: Water Authority of Jordan (WAJ)
partner_organizations.role: Implements wastewater infrastructure projects

partner_organizations.name: EU
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer for infrastructure projects (e.g., As Samra wastewater)

who_partners.quote: "EBRD has demonstrated an unparalleled ability to originate and sign infrastructure projects in Jordan. Their well-staffed country office has been critical in this regard." (31615354.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The World Bank are the GoJ lead partner on economic reforms, helping to deliver a more diversified and resilient economy by prioritising reforms, supporting implementation, and coordinating with donors." (52784557.odt, Commercial case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses grants to EBRD and GCFF (World Bank), which then leverage concessional loans and private sector financing. The initial phase included a £80m loan to World Bank's P4R (later converted to grant equivalent). Funds are channeled through multilateral mechanisms with UK oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank and EBRD manage project implementation with oversight from DFID Jordan. A Project Management Unit (PMU) under Jordan's MOPIC coordinates Compact activities. Annual budgets require UK Secretary of State approval, and a steering committee (with UK representation) guides GCFF allocations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank and EBRD were selected based on their established presence in Jordan, technical capacity, and ability to leverage significant additional financing. The 2016 Multilateral Aid Review rated both as 'very good' for delivery against UK objectives (52784557.odt).
how_mechanism.quote: "The World Bank-managed GCFF provides a unique platform to coordinate donor grants to leverage concessional finance from the multilateral development banks. All projects are prioritised by beneficiary governments, facilitating GoJ ownership." (31615354.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "DFID considered there to be a small window to lock-in this support prior to the conference and that conditional offers of UK support would be critical in convincing both Bank’s management." (5519561.odt, Appraising options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GCFF Steering Committee (with UK representation) approves project pipelines. For EBRD projects, DFID Jordan collaborates with EBRD's country office. The Jordan Compact PMU (under MOPIC) coordinates cross-government implementation with donor oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The JCEOP risk register will be updated following approval of the programme extension and upon approval of each annual budget." (31615354.odt, Risks) and "DFID sit on the GCFF Steering Committee and closely steer projects in country through engagement with the World Bank country team." (52784557.odt, Risks)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated annually between EBRD and GCFF projects based on emerging priorities, but require Secretary of State approval. The £1mn analytical fund allows responsive technical assistance (31615354.odt).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Projects are selected annually to align with Jordan's Economic Growth Plan and emerging needs. The programme reserves £1mn for time-bound analysis to inform adjustments (31615354.odt).
how_flexibility.quote: "EBRD and GCFF projects will be selected on an annual basis. This means the UK can select those projects which represent best the value for money, as projects are developed during JCEOP’s lifecycle." (31615354.odt, Project selection) and "We have identified several analytical projects which would support implementation of EBRD and GCFF investments... Under the JCEOP extension we will reserve up to £1mn for timebound, bespoke analysis and technical assistance." (31615354.odt, Complementary analysis)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank/EBRD (multilateral partners) → Government of Jordan/implementing agencies (e.g., WAJ for wastewater projects)
how_efficiency.quote: "An annual (financial year) budget detailing the split of funds between EBRD and GCFF investment projects will be submitted to the UK International Development Secretary for information by the end of the preceding calendar year." (31615354.odt, Project selection) and "The P4R will disburse funds based on disbursement linked indicators (DLIs) which are aligned to The Compact and are under the government’s control." (5519561.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Own DFID programme using other in-country partners (5519561.odt, Option 2)
Traditional humanitarian support (5519561.odt, Option 3)
Direct financing to EIB (non-concessional, separate business case) (5519561.odt, Non-appraisable options)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The multilateral approach was selected for its ability to leverage significant additional financing (£3-4 for every £1 of UK funding), align with Jordan's national priorities, and provide rapid, flexible responses to emerging needs. The World Bank and EBRD's established presence in Jordan and strong performance ratings (MAR 2016) were decisive factors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of control over specific project selection (GCFF funds are earmarked to Jordan but not to specific projects)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK sits on GCFF Steering Committee and engages with World Bank country team to influence priorities (52784557.odt)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in Jordanian reform implementation affecting disbursement-linked indicators
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual budget approvals and milestone-based payments maintain pressure for reforms (31615354.odt)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays in infrastructure projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: EBRD's well-staffed Jordan office and established relationships with WAJ mitigate implementation risks (31615354.odt)

why_rationale.quote: "The case for implementing through multilateral development banks remains unchanged, and is enhanced by the UK’s new bilateral labour market and investment/trade projects beginning in 2017." (31615354.odt, Appraisal case) and "A quantitative economic appraisal was not included in the original business case, although a Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model was run on the P4R Component of JCEOP. This stated that the overall net benefits from the proposed reforms... if enacted are likely to boost the country’s real income by US$2.2 billion, giving a benefit cost ratio of around 7.5." (52784557.odt, Appraisal case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Jordan's status as a middle-income country with high debt (94% of GDP) and limited fiscal space constrained partner selection to multilaterals capable of providing concessional finance. The political sensitivity of refugee employment required partners with strong government relationships (e.g., World Bank's role as GoJ's lead on economic reforms).
q27_constraints_detail: limited fiscal space for GoJ to borrow (52784557.odt)
political sensitivity of refugee employment (5519561.odt)
need for rapid disbursement to maintain reform momentum (31615354.odt)
requirement for leverage to maximize UK funding impact (all documents)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to create jobs quickly (200,000+ labour days) and improve infrastructure (wastewater for 4.4m people) required partners with existing project pipelines (EBRD) and government trust (World Bank). The macroeconomic stabilization objective necessitated concessional financing mechanisms that multilaterals uniquely provide.
q28_linkages: job creation targets → selection of EBRD for labour-intensive infrastructure projects (31615354.odt)
macroeconomic support → use of GCFF for concessional loans tied to reforms (52784557.odt)
need for government ownership → alignment with Jordan's Economic Growth Plan 2018-2022 (all addendums)
flexibility requirement → annual project selection process (31615354.odt)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging £3-4 per £1 UK funding) with equity considerations (targeting women, refugees, and poor Jordanians). Trade-offs include: (1) Faster disbursement through multilaterals vs. potential loss of control over specific project selection; (2) Focus on large-scale infrastructure (e.g., As Samra wastewater) that benefits broad populations vs. targeted support for vulnerable groups; (3) Use of existing MDB systems (efficient) vs. building local institutional capacity (equity).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of multilateral disbursement vs. local ownership (52784557.odt)
broad infrastructure benefits vs. targeted gender/women's employment outcomes (31615354.odt)
leverage efficiency (£3-4 per £1) vs. earmarking for specific vulnerable groups (52784557.odt)
use of Northern MDB expertise vs. Southern institutional strengthening (all documents)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context (refugee crisis, economic instability) justifies intensive oversight through annual budget approvals, steering committee representation, and milestone-based payments. The political sensitivity of reforms increases management intensity (e.g., weekly meetings with Minister Fakhoury during early implementation).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local capacity for large-scale infrastructure and economic reforms necessitated the use of multilaterals (EBRD, World Bank) as primary implementers. However, the programme includes embedded capacity building through the PMU and technical assistance to GoJ to gradually strengthen local systems.
intersections.quote: "The UK’s aid programme in Jordan is relatively modest compared to US and EU budgets. JCEOP will build on UK comparative advantages... Flexibility – the UK’s growing economic portfolio has been praised for its flexibility, an attribute which will be maintained in the programme extension." (31615354.odt, Principles) and "The nature of the GCFF funding instrument is that we can only earmark to the Jordan window – we cannot specify specific projects where we want our funds to be used. To mitigate this risk, DFID sit on the GCFF Steering Committee and closely steer projects in country through engagement with the World Bank country team." (52784557.odt, Risks)

key_programme_risks: GoJ failure to implement reforms due to domestic opposition (all documents)
Slow disbursement of international pledges undermining Compact credibility (5519561.odt)
Refugee returns or secondary migration affecting labour market targets (5519561.odt)
Macroeconomic instability (rising debt, inflation) derailing growth plans (52784557.odt)
Procurement delays in infrastructure projects (31615354.odt)
Reduced political appetite for reform post-elections (52784557.odt)
Gender equality outcomes not being adequately monitored (31615354.odt)
IMF reform fatigue affecting Compact implementation (52784557.odt)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Disbursement-linked indicators (DLIs) and annual budget approvals maintain pressure (31615354.odt)
EBRD's established Jordan office and WAJ relationships accelerate implementation (31615354.odt)
High-level Ministerial Committee and weekly donor coordination (5519561.odt)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GCFF funds not targeting UK priorities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK representation on GCFF Steering Committee and World Bank engagement (52784557.odt)
Explicit gender targets in reform matrix (e.g., female workforce participation +5%) and monitoring (52784557.odt)
Concessional financing creates fiscal space for reforms (52784557.odt)

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible financing mechanisms are critical in FCAS contexts where government priorities shift rapidly (31615354.odt)
Donor coordination platforms reduce transaction costs for fragile governments (52784557.odt)
Linking disbursements to reform milestones (not just inputs) improves accountability in weak institutional environments (all documents)
Combining humanitarian and development objectives requires adaptive management structures (5519561.odt)
Political economy analysis is essential to anticipate reform resistance (5519561.odt, Strategic Case)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The initial JCEOP phase demonstrated that: (1) Leveraging MDB resources creates significant multiplier effects (£400m mobilized from £110m UK funding); (2) Disbursement-linked indicators effectively incentivize reforms; (3) Infrastructure projects with clear job creation metrics (e.g., 200,000 labour days) build political support; (4) Annual project selection allows adaptation to changing needs (31615354.odt, Evidence of performance to date).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Subsequent addendums incorporated: (1) Extended duration to 2025 for project completion; (2) Increased focus on gender outcomes in reform targets; (3) Added technical assistance component (£1m) to support implementation; (4) Strengthened donor coordination mechanisms post-London Initiative; (5) Expanded leverage targets from £3-4 per £1 UK funding (52784557.odt).
risks_lessons.quote: "JCEOP’s first annual review found that the programme was performing effectively, and a recent DFID Internal Audit Department (IAD) report commended the programme’s management." (31615354.odt, Evidence of performance to date) and "The nature of the GCFF funding instrument is that we can only earmark to the Jordan window – we cannot specify specific projects where we want our funds to be used. To mitigate this risk, DFID sit on the GCFF Steering Committee and closely steer projects in country through engagement with the World Bank country team." (52784557.odt, Risks)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Each £1 of UK funding leverages approximately £3-4 in concessional finance through GCFF. The programme has mobilized over £400m in MDB projects from the initial £110m UK commitment (31615354.odt). The As Samra wastewater project alone leveraged a €150-200mn PPP with UK's £12mn contribution (31615354.odt).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on capital investments (infrastructure) with revenue components for technical assistance and programme management. For example, the As Samra wastewater expansion is capital-intensive, while the £1m analytical fund supports revenue activities (31615354.odt).
financial_details.quote: "An additional £1 of funding through this programme is expected to leverage approximately £3-4 concessional finance." (52784557.odt, Expected Results) and "To date, JCEOP has leveraged multilateral development bank projects worth £400mn." (31615354.odt, Evidence of performance to date)

metadata.programme_name: Uganda: Building Resilience and an Effective Emergency Refugee Response (BRAER)
metadata.quote: "BRAER will drive excellence in humanitarian response in Uganda. It will bring together relief and resilience activities with stronger safeguards, drive value for money and diversify our delivery chain." (43745249.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The programme will start in June 2018 and will initially focus on meeting lifesaving needs and strengthening safeguards and aid management systems. [...] The programme will deliver a core set of activities to the value of £165m over 5 years." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: BRAER combines **service delivery** (lifesaving humanitarian support, food/water/sanitation), **implementation research** (piloting self-reliance models, cash transfers), **capacity building** (strengthening Ugandan systems and safeguards), and **policy influence** (UN reform, Grand Bargain commitments). The programme tests innovative approaches while delivering direct aid.
what_objectives.q1_source: "BRAER will drive excellence in humanitarian response in Uganda. It will bring together relief and resilience activities with stronger safeguards, drive value for money and diversify our delivery chain. [...] The programme will innovate and expand with programming designed to challenge and improve the approach to supporting refugees and host communities." (43745249.odt, Programme Summary & Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 1,000,000+ beneficiaries reached in first year (humanitarian projects)
30% of refugee response directly benefits host communities (GoU policy requirement)
Scaled-up cash transfers (aligned with Grand Bargain commitment to double cash-based programming by 2025)
Strengthened safeguards: Third Party Monitors in all settlements, UN Inter-agency Action Plan on Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA)
Piloted self-reliance models (e.g., market-based approaches, private sector engagement)
Improved transparency: online portal (ugandarefugees.org), digital beneficiary feedback systems
Contribution to UK’s International Climate Finance targets
0.2% of DFID’s Single Departmental Plan targets for nutrition and water/sanitation
Reduction in food ration cuts through efficient resource use
Long-term planning integrated into emergency response (e.g., low-cost infrastructure, settlement site planning)
what_objectives.summary: BRAER aims to transform Uganda’s refugee response by blending emergency relief with long-term resilience-building, while addressing systemic issues like fraud, gender-based violence, and aid dependency. It serves as a pilot for global humanitarian reform (Grand Bargain, CRRF) and tests innovative approaches to self-reliance.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver UK Humanitarian Reform Policy including: upholding humanitarian norms and principles; delivering best of British response to rapid onset disasters; managing risk better to reduce fraud and increase the safety of refugees; supporting new approaches to protracted crises; and reforming the international system." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Uganda hosts 1.4M+ refugees from conflicts in South Sudan, DRC, and Burundi, with regional instability threatening further influxes. The programme explicitly notes "high" risk due to fraud/corruption, safeguarding failures, and potential destabilization from refugee pressures. The document highlights Uganda’s role in a "troubled region" with ongoing conflicts in neighboring countries.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" and "The programme risk is rated as 'high' which is within DFID Uganda’s risk appetite. The key risks are fraud and corruption (F&C), safeguarding issues, continued regional instability that could result in further mass refugee influxes, and insufficient funding for the overall refugee response." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary & Risk Section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: 1) **Security/Conflict**: Regional instability (South Sudan, DRC) drives unpredictable refugee influxes, straining resources. 2) **Weak Institutions**: Uganda’s progressive refugee policy is stretched by rapid scale-up, leading to "accountability and transparency issues" and fiduciary risks (e.g., fraud in food distribution). 3) **Infrastructure**: Remote settlements lack basic services (e.g., water coverage at 16.8L/person/day vs. SPHERE standard of 20L). 4) **Climate**: Rain-fed agriculture vulnerability exacerbates food insecurity. 5) **Data**: Outdated census data excludes recent refugees, distorting budget allocations. 6) **Political Economy**: Corruption allegations (e.g., bribery for services) and cultural norms (e.g., child marriage as a coping strategy) undermine protection efforts.
where_context.quote: "Uganda’s influence and relative stability in the region makes it a priority country for the UK. President Museveni plays a key role in regional stability. [...] The massive influx of refugees is creating a humanitarian legacy and a long-term development challenge with the majority of the refugee population likely to remain for more than a decade." (43745249.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with the Government of Uganda (GoU), with DFID providing technical leadership and funding while GoU leads policy implementation (e.g., Settlement Transformation Agenda). UN agencies and NGOs deliver services under joint agreements (e.g., Joint Plan of Action on Transparency). Decision-making is shared through structures like the CRRF Secretariat (where DFID funds a position) and the humanitarian donor group (co-chaired by DFID).
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening Ugandan district governments’ leadership in refugee response (e.g., through SUGAR programme)
Training for Third Party Monitors to oversee aid distribution
Support for Refugee Welfare Councils and local administrative structures
Financial inclusion programmes for refugees/host communities (via FSDU)
Institutional safeguarding reforms (e.g., UN Inter-agency Action Plan on SEA)
Technical assistance to GoU on anti-corruption and fiduciary risk management

partner_organizations.name: Government of Uganda (Office of the Prime Minister, Ministry of Finance)
partner_organizations.role: Policy leadership, settlement administration, co-design of Joint Plan of Action

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of goods/services in settlements, safeguarding, registration systems

partner_organizations.name: WFP
partner_organizations.role: Food assistance, cash transfers, market-based programming

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Child protection, nutrition, education

partner_organizations.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
partner_organizations.role: Protection activities, GBV response

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (IDA 18 Protracted Crisis Window)
partner_organizations.role: Potential $250-300M funding for northern Uganda, aligned with BRAER objectives

partner_organizations.name: GiveDirectly
partner_organizations.role: Pilot testing lump-sum cash transfers

partner_organizations.name: Financial Sector Deepening Uganda (FSDU)
partner_organizations.role: Scaling cash transfers, financial inclusion

partner_organizations.name: Local District Governments (Refugee Hosting Districts)
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery, long-term planning for host communities

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (agribusinesses, energy/water providers)
partner_organizations.role: Market-based approaches, livelihood opportunities

partner_organizations.name: USAID, EU, Comic Relief, IKEA Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Co-funding, joint initiatives (e.g., vulnerability study, cash programming)

who_partners.quote: "DFID Uganda has adopted a cross-office approach to addressing the protracted refugee crisis ensuring that this programme will work alongside programmes on governance, health, education and private sector development. [...] The programme is in line with Government of Uganda’s and the UN led Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary & Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **block funding** for core activities (£165M over 5 years) combined with an **Integrated Risk Facility** (£45M) for emergency scale-up. Funds are channeled through **performance-based agreements** with UN agencies (linked to UK’s core UN contributions) and **direct grants** to Ugandan government systems (e.g., district budgets). Cash transfers are delivered via **partnership agreements** with financial service providers (e.g., FSDU).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID Uganda acts as the convenor, with implementation shared across UN agencies, Ugandan government entities, and NGOs. The **CRRF Secretariat** (with a DFID-funded position) coordinates multi-stakeholder alignment. A **Joint Plan of Action** (agreed with GoU) governs transparency/accountability, while **technical working groups** (e.g., Cash Transfers Group) drive sectoral collaboration. The programme allows for dynamic partner entry (e.g., private sector in Phase 2).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **existing roles in Uganda’s refugee response** (e.g., UNHCR’s mandate, GoU’s policy leadership) and **alignment with UK priorities** (e.g., Grand Bargain, CRRF). The document emphasizes leveraging **established systems** (e.g., UN clusters, GoU’s Settlement Transformation Agenda) to ensure rapid scale-up and reform influence.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID is an influential partner in the humanitarian sector in Uganda and has been leading from the front in delivering smart, efficient and cost-effective humanitarian assistance. [...] BRAER will be a critical vehicle in enabling the UK to continue using its technical capability and commitment to leverage positive change." (43745249.odt, Leadership Section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: 1) **CRRF Secretariat**: DFID funds a position to coordinate international/GoU alignment. 2) **Humanitarian Donor Partner Group**: Co-chaired by DFID, includes traditional/non-traditional donors. 3) **Joint Plan of Action Oversight**: Monthly reviews with GoU/UN on transparency safeguards. 4) **Technical Working Groups**: E.g., Cash Transfers Group, Protection Cluster. 5) **Third Party Monitors**: Independent oversight of aid distribution in settlements.
how_governance.quote: "A review point is incorporated before Phase 2. Phase 2 would expand the programme to engage with the private sector, undertake research to drive innovation and influence, and pursue the strengthening of nutrition and education services. [...] The £210m budget [...] will allow for a rapid and flexible scale up from a core budget of £165m." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "DFID Ugandais providing regular updates to ministers on the progress that is being made against this Joint Plan of Action." (43745249.odt, Accountability Section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes: 1) **£45M Integrated Risk Facility** for emergency scale-up (approved by Director for East/Central Africa). 2) **Phase-gated design**: Decisions at Dec 2018 and Oct 2019 to adjust scope (e.g., private sector engagement in Phase 2). 3) **Re-prioritization clause**: DFID can shift funds across its portfolio or bid for central reserves if needs change.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: 1) **Research-driven adjustments**: Phase 2 expands based on "new evidence collected" from pilots (e.g., self-reliance models). 2) **Context-responsive**: Triggers for scaling up include deteriorating emergency indicators or new refugee influxes. 3) **Learning loops**: Monitoring tools (e.g., digital feedback systems) inform real-time adaptations. 4) **Policy windows**: Alignment with CRRF/Global Refugee Compact allows for strategic pivots.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will deliver a core set of activities to the value of £165m over 5 years. The expansion in scope of the programme will be triggered at key review points: December 2018 [...] October 2019 [...]. The £210m budget for the programme will allow for a rapid and flexible scale up from a core budget of £165m." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UN/GoU/NGOs) → End Beneficiaries. *Note*: Some activities (e.g., cash transfers) may involve a 3rd layer (financial service providers), but the core structure is bilateral.
how_efficiency.quote: "VfM metrics including unit costs have been strengthened and a VfM framework with monitoring tools developed." (43745249.odt, Quality Assurance) AND "The programme will innovate and expand with programming designed to challenge and improve the approach to supporting refugees and host communities." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Annual short-term funding (rejected due to inefficiency in protracted crises)
Pure humanitarian response (rejected; BRAER integrates development/humanitarian)
Traditional in-kind aid (rejected in favor of cash transfers for efficiency)
Centralized UN-led delivery (supplemented with direct GoU/local government channels)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed **open partnership** model was selected to: 1) **Leverage Uganda’s progressive refugee policy** (e.g., freedom of movement, host community integration) while addressing its implementation gaps (e.g., corruption, weak local systems). 2) **Pilot Grand Bargain reforms** (cash transfers, local actor engagement) in a stable FCAS context. 3) **Balance speed and inclusion**: Direct awards to UN/GoU enable rapid scale-up, while phased flexibility allows for learning/adaptation. 4) **Mitigate fiduciary risks** via Third Party Monitors and joint accountability mechanisms. 5) **Maximize UK influence** by co-leading CRRF and donor coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud/corruption in open partnership structure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Third Party Monitors in all settlements; UN-operated food distribution linked to biometric registration; Joint Plan of Action with GoU on transparency.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination overhead in multi-stakeholder model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: CRRF Secretariat (DFID-funded position); technical working groups (e.g., Cash Transfers Group); digital information-sharing (ugandarefugees.org).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner capacity gaps (e.g., district governments, private sector)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded capacity building (e.g., SUGAR programme for local governments); phased private sector engagement (piloted in Phase 2).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor fatigue/underfunding due to shared burden
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s 5% burden share commitment; advocacy to leverage additional funds (e.g., World Bank IDA window); Solidarity Summit co-hosted with UNSG.

why_rationale.quote: "Lessons Learnt from DFID’s Protracted Crisis Response in Uganda: Annual, short-term funding fails to address chronic problems [...] Multi-year protracted crisis funding will be more smart, effective and cost-efficient. [...] Stronger risk management assurance and safeguard systems are required to challenge, change and improve the aid management systems." (43745249.odt, Lessons Learnt) AND "The programme will contribute to the delivery of the 2016 World Humanitarian Summit commitments, including the Grand Bargain, in delivering greater efficiency and transparency." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: 1) **FCAS context limits partner pool**: Only organizations with existing Uganda presence (e.g., UNHCR, WFP) and risk tolerance (e.g., fraud investigations) could deliver. 2) **GoU policy framework**: Partners must align with Uganda’s Settlement Transformation Agenda (e.g., 30% host community benefit rule). 3) **Remote settlements**: Requires partners with logistical capacity (e.g., WFP for last-mile food delivery). 4) **Safeguarding crises**: Mandates partners with robust PSEA systems (e.g., UNICEF for GBV response).
q27_constraints_detail: Fraud allegations in 2018 restricted partner selection to organizations undergoing vetting (e.g., UN agencies with Joint Plan of Action compliance).
GoU’s progressive refugee policy requires partners to integrate host communities, limiting pure humanitarian actors.
Weak district capacity necessitates partners with institutional strengthening expertise (e.g., SUGAR programme).
Cash transfer scale-up depends on financial sector partners (e.g., FSDU) with refugee-inclusive models.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: 1) **Self-reliance objective → Open partnership**: Testing market-based approaches (e.g., GiveDirectly pilots) required private sector and NGO agility. 2) **UN reform goal → Multilateral structure**: Grand Bargain commitments necessitated UN agency engagement (e.g., performance-linked funding). 3) **Safeguarding needs → Embedded oversight**: Allegations of SEA/child marriage led to Third Party Monitors and UN Inter-agency PSEA Plan. 4) **Resilience focus → GoU leadership**: Long-term planning required district government capacity building (e.g., hydrological studies for settlements).
q28_linkages: Cash transfer scaling (WHAT) → Financial sector partnerships (HOW) via FSDU.
Fraud risks (WHERE) → Third Party Monitors (HOW) in all settlements.
Host community integration (WHAT) → 30% benefit rule (HOW) in GoU agreements.
Grand Bargain commitments (WHAT) → UN performance frameworks (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: 1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: Direct awards to UN/GoU enabled rapid scale-up but risked sidelining local NGOs. Mitigation: Phased private sector/NGO engagement in Phase 2. 2) **Cost vs. Reach**: Cash transfers (cheaper) replaced in-kind aid, but required financial inclusion programmes (FSDU) to ensure equity. 3) **Northern Expertise vs. Southern Ownership**: UN agencies led safeguarding reforms, but GoU co-chairs CRRF Secretariat to balance influence.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: UN’s existing systems enabled quick disbursement, but transparency risks required Third Party Monitors (adding cost).
Equity: Host community benefits (30% rule) increased costs but reduced conflict risks.
Flexibility: Integrated Risk Facility allowed emergency response but required complex approvals (Director-level).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘high’ risk rating** (fraud, regional instability) led to: 1) **Intensive oversight**: Monthly Joint Plan of Action reviews, Third Party Monitors. 2) **Phased flexibility**: Core £165M budget with contingent £45M for emergencies. 3) **Embedded safeguards**: UN Inter-agency PSEA Plan and GBV referral system upgrades.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: 1) **District Governments**: Limited capacity → DFID’s SUGAR programme provides training on anti-corruption and refugee response planning. 2) **UN Agencies**: Safeguarding failures → PSEA Action Plan with victim support mechanisms. 3) **Private Sector**: Lack of refugee-inclusive models → FSDU pilots financial inclusion tools.
intersections.quote: "The programme will increase transparency and accountability of support to refugees and deliver greater efficiency in the use of limited humanitarian resources. [...] DFID together with WFP, UNHCR, USAID and EU are leading a response to these allegations [fraud/corruption] which is structured around a Joint Plan of Action agreed with the Government of Uganda in February 2018." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "Strengthen District Governments can provide leadership in the response – DFID’s programme of support in Karamoja [...] has demonstrated the benefits of working with District Governments to build their leadership in the response." (43745249.odt, Lessons Learnt)

key_programme_risks: Fraud and corruption in aid distribution (e.g., food theft, bribery for services)
Safeguarding failures (SEA, child/early forced marriage, GBV)
Regional instability causing further mass refugee influxes (South Sudan, DRC)
Insufficient funding for refugee response undermining resilience efforts
Weak fiduciary risk management in GoU/UN systems
Climate shocks exacerbating food insecurity in refugee-hosting districts
Donor fatigue leading to underfunded appeals
Cultural norms (e.g., child marriage) undermining protection programmes
Overstretched Ugandan infrastructure (water, health, education) in hosting districts
Tensions between refugees and host communities over resources

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Third Party Monitors in all settlements; biometric registration for food distribution; Joint Plan of Action with GoU on transparency.
UN Inter-agency PSEA Plan; GBV referral system upgrades; investigations into allegations; victim support mechanisms.
Integrated Risk Facility (£45M) for emergency scale-up; political engagement on South Sudan/DRC conflicts.
UK’s 5% burden share commitment; advocacy via Solidarity Summit; leveraging World Bank IDA window.
SUGAR programme for anti-corruption; capacity building for district governments.
Hydrological studies for settlement planning; market-based approaches to reduce aid dependency.

fcas_specific_lessons: Multi-year funding is critical in FCAS to address chronic problems (vs. annual cycles).
Prepositioning goods and dedicated site planners reduce costs in unpredictable influx scenarios.
Local integration policies (e.g., Uganda’s 30% host community rule) mitigate conflict risks but require strong M&E.
Cash transfers in FCAS can stimulate local economies (e.g., $1 transfer → $2+ local income) but need financial inclusion safeguards.
Third Party Monitors are essential in high-fraud environments but add operational complexity.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Short-term funding inefficiency**: "Annual, short-term funding fails to address chronic problems and is not effective in achieving food security and economic independence." 2) **Market displacement**: "Provision of free supplies to refugees over a prolonged period has undermined business opportunities." 3) **Local leadership**: "Strengthen District Governments can provide leadership in the response." 4) **Flexibility needs**: "Programme flexibility is essential to deal with unpredictable refugee influxes." 5) **Cash effectiveness**: "Cash instead of food works. Every $1 given to a refugee through cash-based transfers increases total income in and around the settlement by $2 or more."
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Multi-year structure**: Shift from annual to 5-year funding to improve administrative efficiency. 2) **Cash focus**: Increased allocation to cash transfers (vs. in-kind) based on WFP/UC evidence. 3) **Private sector pilots**: Phase 2 includes private sector engagement (e.g., agribusiness in NUTEC) to address market displacement. 4) **Embedded safeguards**: Third Party Monitors added after 2018 fraud allegations. 5) **Host community integration**: 30% benefit rule enforced via GoU agreements and district planning support.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons Learnt from DFID’s Protracted Crisis Response in Uganda: [...] Multi-year protracted crisis funding will be more smart, effective and cost-efficient and will produce greater administrative efficiency, better use of staff time, more value for money through planned procurement, and scope for more ambitious monitoring and learning." (43745249.odt, Lessons Learnt) AND "Accountability and Transparency in the Response – In January 2018 a series of allegations regarding fraud and corruption in the refugee response were reported by UN delivery partners. [...] DFID together with WFP, UNHCR, USAID and EU are leading a response to these allegations." (43745249.odt, Accountability Section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: 1) **World Bank IDA Window**: Expected $250-300M for northern Uganda (aligned with BRAER). 2) **Solidarity Summit (2017)**: Raised $350M for refugee response. 3) **Cash programming**: DFID’s leadership encouraged other donors (e.g., USAID, EU) to scale up cash transfers. 4) **Private sector**: Pilots with GiveDirectly/Comic Relief leveraged match funding.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Core budget (£165M) focuses on **revenue** (service delivery, cash transfers, capacity building), while **capital** investments (e.g., low-cost infrastructure, hydrological studies) are embedded within resilience activities. The £45M Integrated Risk Facility can fund either depending on emergency needs.
financial_details.quote: "The programme will deliver a core set of activities to the value of £165m over 5 years. The expansion in scope of the programme will be triggered at key review points [...] The £210m budget for the programme will allow for a rapid and flexible scale up from a core budget of £165m." (43745249.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "DFID is engaging with the World Bank to provide support to maximise the effectiveness of resources from the new IDA 18 protracted crisis window. The World Bank could allocate up to US$600m through its new IDA 18 protracted crisis window for northern Uganda." (43745249.odt, Working with Others)

metadata.programme_name: UK Aid Match II
metadata.primary_sector: international development (financing civil society projects and public engagement)

quote.text: Support the achievement of the Global Goals for Sustainable Development through financing civil society projects and engaging the UK public in international development

metadata.duration_source: Start Date: 1 September 2016; End Date: 31 December 2023

what_objectives.q1_explanation: UK Aid Match II is a financing mechanism that combines direct funding of civil society projects in developing countries with public engagement activities in the UK. It aims to both deliver development outcomes through CSO projects and increase UK public engagement with international development issues.
what_objectives.q1_source: UK Aid Match II will finance high-quality civil society projects in developing countries and provide opportunities for the UK public to engage with international development issues and have a say in how UK aid spent.
q3_expected_outputs: 59+ grants awarded to civil society projects (current programme baseline)
£168.32 million in matched funding for development projects
3.6+ million public donations (current programme baseline)
2+ billion opportunities to view messaging about appeals (current programme baseline)
Increased public engagement in international development (behavioral and informational)
Projects contributing to 1-17 Sustainable Development Goals
Enhanced gender equality and women's empowerment in project design
Improved evidence base on what works in civil society programming
what_objectives.summary: The programme combines financing high-quality civil society projects in developing countries with mechanisms to engage the UK public in international development, aiming to achieve both development impact and increased public support for aid.

quote.text: UK Aid Match II will double the funding for UK Aid Match over this Parliament and increase the scope and reach of the programme by providing new ways to match public giving and diversify the organisations that are accessing matched funding. This aims to contribute to achieving the United Nations' Global Goals for Sustainable Development and building a wider and more diverse constituency of the UK public who are informationally and behaviourally engaged in international development and having a say in how UK aid is spent.

countries_regions: Countries ranked in the bottom 50 of the Human Development Index
Fragile and conflict-affected states as assessed by DFID's Bilateral Aid Review
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states which inherently carry higher risks, but the overall programme risk rating is assessed as moderate, suggesting managed risk through mitigation strategies.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
q6_contextual_constraints: limited capacity of smaller/less experienced downstream partners
data limitations (lack of socio-economic data on donors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Fragile contexts require additional due diligence and monitoring. Limited capacity of downstream partners increases fraud risks. Lack of donor data makes it difficult to measure which public segments are being reached.

quote.text: Countries ranked in the bottom 50 of the Human Development Index and fragile and conflict-affected states

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID retains approval authority for all funding decisions and project selections. Southern CSOs implement projects but must meet DFID's criteria and reporting requirements.
q10_capacity_building_details: support for transformative innovation and new collaborations
capacity-building for Southern CSOs
gender skills and competences among grantee staff
improved sex disaggregation of baseline data
building capacity of small organisations to apply for funds

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Project implementation in developing countries

partner_organizations.name: Comic Relief
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partner for public engagement campaigns (Red Nose Day, Sport Relief)

partner_organizations.name: Fund Manager (to be selected)
partner_organizations.role: Day-to-day management of the challenge fund, including application assessment and monitoring

partner_organizations.name: Schools and fundraising platforms
partner_organizations.role: New channels for public engagement and fundraising

partner_organizations.name: Communications partners (e.g., Bauer radio group)
partner_organizations.role: Publicity and outreach for appeals

quote.text: UK Aid Match II will form a major component of DFID's suite of central civil society funding instruments, which also includes UK Aid Direct (which supports small and medium sized CSOs), UK Aid Connect (which will encourage collaboration within the sector) and UK Aid Volunteers (which provides opportunities for volunteering).

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a challenge fund model where DFID matches public donations to approved CSO appeals. It combines grants for project implementation with contractual arrangements for fund management and evaluation services.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A fund manager will be contracted to handle day-to-day operations including application assessments, due diligence, monitoring, and reporting. DFID retains strategic oversight and approval authority.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The fund manager will be selected through competitive tender to ensure quality and value for money. CSO projects are selected based on their contribution to Global Goals, value for money, and track record.

quote.text: The contract will be awarded through a thorough competitive tender process. Bids will be evaluated against criteria for the necessary quality of performance required.

The fund manager will monitor project performance and risk through annual narrative and financial reporting from grantees. Projects which perform poorly will be subject to remedial work and/or cancellation.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Annual proposals for the year's package of match funding approaches will be submitted to Ministers for approval, allowing for adjustments based on evidence and learning.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme will build in opportunities for learning and adaptation over its course. Each year's package of approaches will be reviewed based on research, evidence, value for money, and results.

quote.text: Each year, a proposal for the year ahead's package of match funding approaches will be submitted to Ministers for approval. This will include assessment of research, evidence and learning, value for money and results.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager → CSO Implementers (with some CSOs having downstream partners adding a 4th layer in some cases)

quote.text: The fund manager will monitor project performance and risk through annual narrative and financial reporting from grantees.

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: 'Do nothing' - Allow UK Aid Match to end with no further funding
Option 2: 'Business as usual with some modifications' - Extend current model with uplifted funding
Option 3: 'UK Aid Match II' - New modular, flexible design with diverse approaches (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was chosen for its balanced portfolio approach that builds on current successes while allowing for innovation and adaptation. It provides greater flexibility to respond to new contexts and opportunities while maintaining robust value for money controls.
q25_decision_factors: flexibility to adapt to new contexts
ability to diversify organisations accessing funding

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Approved projects do not deliver value for money, development and/or other outcomes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust assessment by fund manager; annual monitoring; remedial work or cancellation for poor performers

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraudulent use of DFID funds, particularly with smaller/less experienced downstream partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence assessments; reporting mechanisms for fraud; annual external audits; rights for DFID to access records

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Underperformance of the fund manager
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Competitive tender process; detailed delivery plan; regular dialogue; KPIs and performance management

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient evidence to demonstrate theory of change assumption that UK Aid Match appeals increase public engagement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced data collection; external evaluation; learning opportunities built into programme

quote.text: Option 3 'UK Aid Match II' is the preferred option. This is based on a cost benefit analysis of each option.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on fragile and conflict-affected states limits partner selection to organisations with proven capacity to operate in challenging environments, requiring additional due diligence and risk management measures.
q27_constraints_detail: Only CSOs with track records in fragile states can qualify
Smaller organisations often lack capacity to meet requirements
Additional monitoring required for downstream partners in high-risk areas
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of development impact and public engagement require a mixed delivery structure: challenge funds for CSO projects combined with strategic partnerships (like Comic Relief) and new engagement channels (schools, platforms) to reach diverse audiences.
q28_linkages: Public engagement objective → requires diverse communications partners and channels
Development impact objective → requires robust CSO selection and monitoring
Leave No One Behind commitment → shapes gender and inclusion requirements for projects
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between reaching smaller organisations (equity) and maintaining rigorous standards (efficiency), noting that previous attempts to reserve funds for small organisations failed due to quality issues.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Competitive processes may exclude smaller organisations
Expertise vs ownership: Northern fund manager ensures quality but limits Southern decision-making
Cost vs reach: Comprehensive monitoring adds overhead but reduces fraud risks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk rating and operation in fragile states result in intensive oversight requirements including annual audits, due diligence for all partners, and performance management of the fund manager.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded to enable Southern CSOs to meet programme requirements, with specific support for small organisations to access funds and for all grantees to improve gender analysis and reporting.

quote.text: UK Aid Match II will expand opportunities for small organisations to access funding by working through fundraising platforms and by building the capacity of small organisations to apply for and manage UK Aid Match II funds successfully.

key_programme_risks: Approved projects not delivering value for money or outcomes
Fraudulent use of funds by downstream partners
Underperformance of fund manager
Insufficient evidence for public engagement theory of change
Failure to reach diverse UK public audiences
Projects not meeting Leave No One Behind commitments
Commercial partners not delivering on publicity commitments

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Approved projects do not deliver value for money, development and/or other outcomes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Fund manager carries out robust assessment; annual monitoring; remedial work or cancellation for poor performers; due diligence on track records

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fraudulent use of DFID funds, particularly when funding is managed by smaller/less experienced downstream partners
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Reporting mechanism for fraud; due diligence assessments; annual external audits; rights to access records; immediate reporting requirements
Competitive tender process; detailed delivery plan; regular dialogue; KPIs; performance management; escalation path

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient evidence to demonstrate the theory of change assumption that UK Aid Match appeals increase the breadth of UK public aware of DFID activities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Enhanced data collection; external evaluation; learning opportunities built into programme design

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Projects not meeting Leave No One Behind commitments
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Minimum standards for gender analysis; requirements to disaggregate data; focus on marginalized groups in project design

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for additional due diligence when working in fragile states
Importance of monitoring downstream partners in high-risk environments
Value of flexible approaches to adapt to changing contexts in FCAS
Challenges of reaching marginalized groups in conflict-affected areas
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The current UK Aid Match programme showed that: 1) Match funding can exceed expectations (most appeals raised more than estimated); 2) Smaller organisations struggle to meet quality standards; 3) Public engagement is hard to measure without enhanced data collection; 4) Coordination between programme and communications teams improves appeal quality; 5) First-time match funding has greatest impact on new donors.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: UK Aid Match II will: 1) Expand opportunities for small organisations through capacity building; 2) Include new engagement channels (schools, platforms); 3) Build in enhanced data collection and evaluation; 4) Allow annual adaptation of approaches; 5) Strengthen gender and inclusion requirements; 6) Partner strategically with Comic Relief for greater reach.

quote.text: UK Aid Match II will build on the momentum and success of UK Aid Match and Comic Relief match funding... Each year, a proposal for the year ahead's package of match funding approaches will be submitted to Ministers for approval. This will include assessment of research, evidence and learning, value for money and results.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: For every £1 of UK aid, at least £1 is raised from the UK public through matched donations (1:1 match ratio). The current programme leveraged £120 million in public donations matched by DFID.

quote.text: UK Aid Match II: Challenge fund, school fundraising, fundraising platforms, humanitarian appeals and programme evaluation - £116.32 million; UK Aid Match II: Comic Relief - £52 million

metadata.programme_name: International Growth Centre (IGC) Phase 3
metadata.quote: "The goal of the International Growth Centre (IGC) is to promote global prosperity by providing world class, context specific economic advice and analysis to influence policies that generate sustained higher rates of economic growth in developing countries." (50304890.odt, Title section)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 03/01/2019\nEnd Date: 30/12/2026" (50304890.odt, Programme details)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The IGC primarily focuses on **policy influence** by providing context-specific economic advice to governments, while also engaging in **evidence generation** through research and **capacity building** by strengthening economic governance institutions. Its core activity is influencing policy decisions to drive economic growth in developing countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The goal of the International Growth Centre (IGC) is to promote global prosperity by providing world class, context specific economic advice and analysis to influence policies that generate sustained higher rates of economic growth in developing countries." (50304890.odt, Title section)
q3_expected_outputs: 1,000 credible growth policies changed and implemented in developing countries (target)
160+ instances of demonstrable policy impact per year (baseline from Phase 2)
Policy briefs, research outputs, and synopsis papers (e.g., inflation forecasting models for Bank of Tanzania)
Training programmes (e.g., Female Promotion Toolkit in Bangladesh)
Support to economic governance functions (e.g., tax reform in Punjab, Pakistan)
Engagement in 15 countries with a population reach of ~1 billion (40% in poverty)
what_objectives.summary: The IGC delivers policy-influencing research and technical assistance to remove barriers to economic growth in low- and middle-income countries, with a focus on trade, productivity, infrastructure, energy, and governance. It aims to transition to financial sustainability while deepening impact in fragile states.
what_objectives.quote: "The IGC will deliver better growth policies in developing countries contributing towards sustainable, stable and inclusive economic growth by spurring economic transformation." (50304890.odt, Intervention Summary)

countries_regions: Specific countries: Ethiopia, Pakistan, Tanzania, Afghanistan, South Sudan, Bangladesh, India (Bihar/Central), Uganda, Sierra Leone, Jordan, Lebanon, Somaliland
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) like Afghanistan, South Sudan, and Somaliland, where political instability, weak institutions, and violence pose significant delivery risks. The document explicitly states a 'major' risk rating due to these contextual challenges.
where_context.q5_source: "Risk rating:\nMajor" (50304890.odt, Programme details) and "The programme is classed as having a ‘major’ risk profile, which is acceptable given the context and long term nature of the economic growth challenge." (50304890.odt, Risk section)
q6_contextual_constraints: energy blackouts (e.g., reducing growth by 2.1%/year in Africa)
data limitations (e.g., lack of comprehensive evidence on growth barriers)
regulatory barriers (e.g., tied advice from Multilateral Development Banks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and conflict undermine policy implementation (e.g., South Sudan’s exchange rate reform was critical to avert a foreign exchange crisis). Energy blackouts directly reduce GDP growth, while academic-driven research agendas sometimes misalign with policymaker priorities, limiting impact.
where_context.quote: "Weak institutions and low levels of investment are the root causes of why poor countries stay poor." (50304890.odt, Strategic Case) and "Energy blackouts reduce growth rates in Africa by an average of 2.1% per year." (50304890.odt, Key changes section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: London School of Economics (LSE) and University of Oxford
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is led by the LSE/Oxford consortium, with input from country offices and policymakers. The Governance Committee (DFID-led until additional funders join) approves key programme changes, and research commissioning boards are predominantly academic with "sporadic" country programme attendance (Phase 1-2). Phase 3 aims to increase country programme and Responsive Policy Unit representation on these boards.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., inflation forecasting for Bank of Tanzania staff)
mentorship (e.g., Female Promotion Toolkit in Bangladesh’s garment sector)
co-authorship (local researchers included in IGC network)
institutional strengthening (e.g., supporting Ethiopia’s Investment Commission reform)
research grants (via Responsive Policy Unit collaborations with local bodies)

partner_organizations.name: London School of Economics (LSE)
partner_organizations.role: Lead research and policy advice (co-management with Oxford)

partner_organizations.name: University of Oxford
partner_organizations.role: Lead research and policy advice (co-management with LSE)

partner_organizations.name: IGC Country Offices
partner_organizations.role: In-country engagement with policymakers, research prioritization

partner_organizations.name: Responsive Policy Unit (RPU)
partner_organizations.role: Short-term policy analysis and local capacity building (new in Phase 3)

partner_organizations.name: DFID (now FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Primary funder (40% by Phase 3 end), governance oversight

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (e.g., $4.2m for India work)

partner_organizations.name: Rockefeller Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (e.g., $900k for Sierra Leone)

partner_organizations.name: Partner Country Governments
partner_organizations.role: Demand-driven requests for advice (e.g., Punjab Tax Authority, Ethiopian Investment Agency)

who_partners.quote: "The IGC’s extensive network of country offices has been critical to building relationships with policy makers to deliver a large number of significant policy shifts." (50304890.odt, What is the added value section) and "The Governance Committee will approve all decisions to change the IGC country footprint, change research focus and other key programme management issues." (50304890.odt, Key changes section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID (FCDO) awards a time-bound contract to a supplier (initially LSE/Oxford, now open competition) to deliver the IGC programme. The contract includes phased funding reductions to incentivize financial sustainability, with DFID’s share dropping from 100% to 40% over 7 years. Payments are milestone-based, tied to policy impact delivery.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by a consortium led by LSE/Oxford (or a new supplier post-competition), with DFID oversight. Country offices report to the central team, and a Responsive Policy Unit (RPU) operates flexibly. A Governance Committee (DFID-led until co-funders join) approves major decisions. Research commissioning involves both academics and country teams, with Phase 3 adding RPU representation to reduce academic capture.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition was chosen to (1) comply with DFID procurement rules, (2) mitigate reputational/legal risks of sole-sourcing, (3) attract suppliers with stronger fund-raising and FCAS engagement capabilities, and (4) improve value for money by testing the market. The original LSE/Oxford contract had no extension clauses.
how_mechanism.quote: "Option 3: Competitively tender phase 3 of the IGC but with an augmented delivery model to maximise the probability of delivering more impact." (50304890.odt, Options section) and "Legal advice was clear that this option [sole-source] represents significant commercial, legal and reputational risk to DFID." (50304890.odt, Options section)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: The Governance Committee (initially DFID-led) approves country footprint changes and research focus. Research commissioning boards include academics, country programmes, and the Responsive Policy Unit (Phase 3). DFID retains approval rights for major shifts until financial sustainability is achieved.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Governance Committee includes DFID and external experts (until co-funders join). It approves key decisions like country footprint changes, research themes, and budget allocations. Country strategy notes drive engagement priorities, and commissioning boards balance academic and policy relevance.
how_governance.quote: "The Governance Committee will approve all decisions to change the IGC country footprint, change research focus and other key programme management issues. Until additional funders are on board, decision making lies with DFID drawing on the advice of external experts." (50304890.odt, Key changes section) and "DFID will begin to wind down funding by 10% per year after year 1... By the end of year 4 we will have an independent review of IGC performance in phase 3 with a recommendation on optimal country footprint." (50304890.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Budget lines are transferable across countries to meet priority needs, but requires Governance Committee approval for major shifts. The Responsive Policy Unit allows flexible engagement outside core country programmes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The Responsive Policy Unit (RPU) enables rapid response to policymaker requests, feeding into longer-term research commissioning. Country strategies are updated annually, and the RPU can surge into countries post-elections or crises. However, major research theme changes require Governance Committee approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "Budget lines will continue to be transferable across countries to meet priority needs and respond to performance of different components." (50304890.odt, Flexibility section) and "The Responsive Policy Unit can then feed policymaker priorities into research commissioning ensuring IGC research focus remains on the right policy challenges." (50304890.odt, Key changes section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Supplier Consortium (LSE/Oxford or new bidder) → Country Offices/Responsive Policy Unit → Local Researchers/Policymakers
how_efficiency.quote: "The majority of the funding (up to £33m) will be spent on the IGC’s country related activities... Up to £12m will be spent on central research." (50304890.odt, Funds section) and "DFID funding will continue to fall by 10% per year until the end of phase 3 in line with the schedule below." (50304890.odt, Appraisal Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Continue sole-sourcing to LSE/Oxford (discarded due to legal/commercial risks)
Option 2: Competitive tender for ‘business as usual’ (discarded for lacking lessons from Phase 1-2)
Option 3: Competitive tender with augmented model (chosen for higher impact potential)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected to (1) address **academic capture** by integrating the Responsive Policy Unit (RPU) and country programmes into research commissioning, (2) improve **financial sustainability** via phased DFID withdrawal and co-funding incentives, (3) enhance **FCAS engagement** through flexible RPU deployments, and (4) align with DFID’s **2017 Economic Development Strategy** priorities (trade, infrastructure, energy, governance). The open competition also mitigated reputational risks and tested market alternatives.
q25_decision_factors: past experience (Phase 1-2 lessons on academic capture)
partner capacity (need for stronger fund-raising and FCAS skills)
equity (focus on fragile states where other funders are unlikely to engage)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to attract 60% non-DFID funding by Phase 3 end
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased 10% annual DFID funding reductions; supplier must demonstrate fund-raising capacity in procurement; 18-month exit plan if viability not achieved.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Academic capture (research misaligned with policymaker needs)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Responsive Policy Unit (RPU) integrates policymaker demands into research commissioning; country programmes and RPU represented on all commissioning boards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of policymaker trust during country programme exits
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: RPU maintains relationships post-exit; phased withdrawals with 18-month transition support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FCAS operational challenges (security, weak institutions)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated FCAS focus in Phase 3; RPU designed for rapid, flexible engagements; due diligence for local partners.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (RPU reduces low-impact country programme costs)
equity (60% of Phase 3 DFID funds to fragile/low-income countries)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 was considered feasible for the following reasons:... These enhancements will ensure the IGC is far more policy focused and better able to respond to global development priorities to enhance its impact." (50304890.odt, Options section) and "By the end of phase 3 we aim to leave a financially sustainable and independent IGC that DFID influences, but which attracts a minimum of 60% of its total funding from other sources." (50304890.odt, Financial sustainability section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts limit partner selection to organizations with (1) **security-cleared local presence**, (2) **rapid-response capabilities** (e.g., RPU), and (3) **credibility with fragile state governments**. The document notes that multilateral agencies often lack trust in FCAS due to perceived geopolitical agendas, necessitating the IGC’s independent academic network.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks (e.g., South Sudan, Afghanistan) require partners with in-country networks
Weak institutions demand partners who can build trust quickly (e.g., RPU’s short-term engagements)
Conflict settings need flexible, demand-led models (e.g., RPU vs. fixed country offices)
Donor fatigue in FCAS limits co-funding options, increasing DFID’s burden share
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **policy-relevant, demand-driven research** (WHAT) shapes the delivery structure (HOW) by: (1) requiring **country offices** for long-term engagement, (2) adding a **Responsive Policy Unit** for short-term requests, and (3) embedding policymakers in **research commissioning boards** to counter academic capture. The shift to financial sustainability also drives the **phased funding model** and **open competition** to attract co-funders.
q28_linkages: Policy influence objective → Country offices + RPU for trusted engagement
FCAS focus → Flexible RPU deployments (vs. fixed country programmes)
Financial sustainability → Open competition + phased DFID withdrawal
Academic rigor → Peer-reviewed central research + country-driven priorities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: (1) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership** (e.g., academic-led commissioning boards with ‘sporadic’ country input in Phases 1-2), (2) **long-term research vs. short-term policy needs** (addressed by RPU in Phase 3), and (3) **cost efficiency vs. FCAS inclusion** (DFID retains 60% funding for fragile states where others won’t engage).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: RPU enables rapid response but risks sidelining long-term capacity building
Expertise vs. ownership: Academic-led research ensures rigor but may misalign with policymaker priorities (mitigated by RPU/country programme representation on boards)
Cost vs. reach: Phasing out low-impact country programmes improves VfM but reduces geographic coverage (offset by RPU)
Equity vs. sustainability: DFID’s 60% focus on fragile states limits co-funding potential (accepted as necessary for SDG alignment)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk profile (FCAS, political instability) drives **intensive oversight** via milestone-based funding, Governance Committee approvals for country footprint changes, and annual independent reviews. DFID retains control until financial viability is proven (Year 4 review).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the model: (1) **Country offices** strengthen policymaker relationships, (2) **RPU** builds local research/advocacy capacity, and (3) **commissioning boards** now include country/RPU reps to shift power from academics to practitioners. Phase 3 explicitly aims to reduce ‘academic capture’ by formalizing these roles.
intersections.quote: "The only programme closures to date have been forced by DFID (withdrawing support for the India programme) and by deteriorating security situations in Liberia and South Sudan." (50304890.odt, Lessons Learned) and "The Responsive Policy Unit provides the IGC with a way of engaging flexibly and changing the IGC country footprint in a parsimonious way... It also provides the IGC with a function that is potentially more likely to be able to charge fees for advice and analysis." (50304890.odt, Key changes section)

key_programme_risks: Failure to achieve 60% non-DFID funding by Phase 3 end (financial viability risk)
Academic capture (research misaligned with policymaker needs)
Policymaker trust erosion during country programme exits
FCAS operational challenges (security, weak institutions)
Over-reliance on DFID for fragile states (co-funding gaps)
Low impact in some country programmes (e.g., Bangladesh, Uganda in Phase 2)
Reputational risk if IGC is seen as a UK tool post-Brexit

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased 10% annual DFID funding reductions; supplier must demonstrate fund-raising capacity in procurement; 18-month exit plan if targets unmet.
Responsive Policy Unit (RPU) integrates policymaker demands; country programmes and RPU represented on all commissioning boards.
Dedicated FCAS focus in Phase 3; RPU designed for rapid, flexible engagements; due diligence for local partners.
Close underperforming programmes (e.g., India, Liberia); redirect resources to high-impact countries/RPU.
RPU maintains relationships post-exit; phased withdrawals with transition support.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible, demand-led models (e.g., RPU) work better than fixed country programmes in FCAS
Quick wins are critical for state legitimacy (e.g., exchange rate reform in South Sudan)
Local researcher inclusion builds trust but requires balancing with academic rigor
Security constraints limit long-term presence; surge capacity (RPU) is essential
Donor coordination is harder in FCAS; IGC’s independence is an asset
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1-2 lessons included: (1) **Academic capture** led to low-impact research (4-5 country programmes consistently underperformed); (2) **Fixed country offices** were inflexible for FCAS; (3) **Funding tied to DFID** limited sustainability; (4) **Commissioning boards** were academic-dominated, reducing policy relevance. Phase 3 addresses these via RPU, open competition, and governance reforms.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 3 changes include: (1) **Responsive Policy Unit** (RPU) for demand-led flexibility; (2) **Phased DFID withdrawal** to force co-funding; (3) **Country programme consolidation** (fewer, deeper engagements); (4) **Governance Committee** with country/RPU representation; (5) **FCAS focus** with dedicated resources.
