risks_lessons.quote: "In 2014 the IGC was put on a Programme Improvement Plan due to this poor performance in ensuring research commissioned by country programmes had a line of sight to policy priorities in country." (50304890.odt, Lessons Learned) and "The Responsive Policy Unit will have dedicated staff who can deploy to respond to policy maker requests and can surge into IGC country programmes to respond to increases in demand." (50304890.odt, Key changes section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Phase 2 attracted over $5 million (~£3.8m) in non-DFID funding. Phase 3 targets 60% non-DFID funding by end (minimum 30% by Year 4 review).
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £57.4 million" (50304890.odt, Programme details) and "During phase 2 the IGC has attracted over $5 million (£3.8million) in non-DFID funding. This includes $900,000 from the Rockefeller Foundation for work in Sierra Leone and $4.2 million from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation to continue working in India." (50304890.odt, Financial sustainability section)

metadata.programme_name: Invest Africa
metadata.quote: The business case sets out the need for up to £100 million investment in Invest Africa from 2017 to 2021. (24923374.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source:
Start Date: 1 April 2017
End Date: 31 March 2027 (24923374.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Invest Africa aims to increase Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in African manufacturing sectors to drive economic transformation, create jobs, and reduce poverty. It combines capacity building (strengthening government institutions), policy influence (improving investment climates), and financing mechanisms (crowding in additional FDI).
what_objectives.q1_source: Invest Africa aims to address the barriers to significantly increase Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in manufacturing sectors in Africa in order to help drive the creation of more, better and inclusive jobs in key focus countries. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: At least £400 million to £1 billion of additional FDI into African manufacturing sectors
10-20 new FDI deals over the life of the programme
Improved capacity of governments to attract and retain FDI
Enhanced political commitment to economic transformation through FDI
Coordination with relevant programmes and partners (e.g., World Bank, African Development Bank)
what_objectives.summary: Invest Africa is a strategic, long-term programme designed to catalyze FDI in African manufacturing, creating jobs and driving economic transformation through a mix of investor engagement, technical assistance, and policy dialogue.
what_objectives.quote: The programme is likely to result in significant (at least £400 million but potentially over £1 billion) additional FDI into African manufacturing sectors which will kick-start industrialisation in Africa. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a high-risk environment due to political, economic, and institutional fragility in many African countries, coupled with the complexity of engaging both governments and private sector actors.
where_context.q5_source:
Overall programmerisk rating:
High (24923374.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints such as weak investment promotion agencies, poor transport/energy infrastructure, and regulatory barriers limit FDI inflows and require targeted interventions to improve the investment climate.
where_context.quote: Addressing these requires political commitment, improvements in state capacity, improvements to transport and energy infrastructure, investing in the quality of key investment agencies, reforming regulations and policies... (24923374.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID leads the programme design, funding, and strategic direction, with African governments and local partners playing implementation roles under DFID's oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to governments (e.g., investment promotion agencies, special economic zones)
skills development for local workforce
support to local content units and trade facilitation

partner_organizations.name: China-Africa Development Fund
partner_organizations.role: catalyzing Chinese FDI for manufacturing and agro-processing

partner_organizations.name: China Council for Promotion of Investment and Trade
partner_organizations.role: linking Chinese investors with African opportunities

partner_organizations.name: International Trade Centre
partner_organizations.role: supporting trade linkages and investment promotion

partner_organizations.name: African governments (Kenya, Ethiopia, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: implementing reforms and attracting FDI

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: coordination and complementary programming

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank
partner_organizations.role: coordination and complementary programming

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Trade (DIT)
partner_organizations.role: promoting UK-Africa business partnerships

partner_organizations.name: China-Britain Business Council
partner_organizations.role: facilitating UK-China-Africa investment links

who_partners.quote: Invest Africa will bring together technical expertise, trade links, buyers and market specific information needed to generate investment deals, whilst improving the capacity of Governments to keep attracting FDI that benefits the host country. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for technical assistance), partnerships (e.g., with China-Africa Development Fund), and coordination mechanisms (e.g., with World Bank) to deliver its objectives. DFID provides core funding while leveraging additional resources from partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Invest Africa operates as a multi-country platform with DFID as the lead funder and coordinator, working through embedded technical experts, government partnerships, and private sector engagement. It integrates political dialogue, investor matching, and technical assistance under a unified programme framework.
how_mechanism.quote: It will be structured as a multi-country programme, with specialist expertise working across countries liaising closely with country offices for government and investor interface. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme involves coordination with DFID country offices, multilateral partners (World Bank, AfDB), and government agencies, suggesting a steering committee-like structure for oversight and alignment.
how_governance.quote: Invest Africa will provide coordination and coherence and complementarity with relevant programmes (other DFID programmes, including CDC and TMEA) and key partners, including the World Bank and African Development Bank. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be tailored to country needs, with technical assistance and investor engagement components adjusted based on progress and opportunities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes learning and sharing lessons, suggesting adaptive management where priorities can be refined based on emerging evidence and country-specific constraints.
how_flexibility.quote: The exact support provided will be tailored to country needs and will vary across countries... (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., technical assistance providers/government agencies) → End Beneficiaries (investors, local firms, workers).
how_efficiency.quote: The business case sets out the need for up to £100 million investment in Invest Africa from 2017 to 2021. (24923374.odt, Summary Sheet)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UK has a comparative advantage in providing politically savvy technical assistance, donor coordination, and leadership in FDI promotion. As the largest investor in Sub-Saharan Africa (30% of FDI stock), the UK is uniquely positioned to drive progress, especially given the time-bound opportunity to capture manufacturing capacity relocating from Asia.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Programme activities do not influence the investment decisions of MNEs, resulting in lower than predicted increases in FDI flows to Africa.
Failure of the supplier to deliver the desired outcome, given the innovative and complex nature of engaging both government and private sector.
Reputational risk to DFID by linking with MNEs who subsequently withdraw or are linked to poor business practices (e.g., exploitative labour, environmental pollution).

why_rationale.quote: The UK has a strong comparative advantage in terms of providing support through politically savvy technical assistance, political engagement, donor coordination and leadership in this area. (24923374.odt, Intervention Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country focus in Africa—characterised by weak institutions, infrastructure gaps, and political economy challenges—requires partners with deep local expertise and government relationships, limiting the pool of capable implementers to those with existing regional presence (e.g., DFID country offices, multilateral banks).
q27_constraints_detail: weak investment promotion agencies
political economy barriers
infrastructure deficits (transport/energy)
regulatory complexity
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to attract FDI through both investor engagement (private sector) and government capacity building (public sector) necessitates a mixed delivery structure combining technical assistance, political dialogue, and coordination platforms.
q28_linkages: Investor engagement (Component A) requires private sector expertise → delivered via partnerships with MNEs and trade bodies.
Technical assistance (Component C) requires embedded government support → delivered via local advisors and multilateral agencies.
Coordination (Component D) requires a platform approach → delivered via DFID-led steering with partners like World Bank.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme balances the efficiency of leveraging UK/FDI expertise (e.g., Chinese investors, UK retailers) with equity goals like local job creation and women’s economic empowerment, requiring trade-offs in partner selection (e.g., prioritizing investors with high job-creation potential over purely commercial actors).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed (rapid FDI attraction) vs inclusion (ensuring local benefits)
Northern expertise (UK/Chinese investors) vs Southern ownership (African government leadership)
cost (high-value FDI deals) vs reach (broad-based job creation)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (political, reputational, delivery) drives intensive oversight, with milestone-based reviews and embedded DFID coordination to mitigate risks of supplier failure or MNE misconduct.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with technical assistance designed to strengthen government agencies (e.g., investment promotion) and local firms, enabling them to take on greater roles in FDI attraction over time.
intersections.quote: The UK can add significant value in the current donor and broader international landscape of actors tackling these issues... DFID’s comparative advantage as a politically astute, well respected player and source of technical assistance presents an excellent opportunity to fill this gap. (24923374.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Failure to influence MNE investment decisions, leading to lower FDI flows.
Supplier failure due to programme complexity (government + private sector engagement).
Reputational risk from association with MNEs involved in poor labour/environmental practices.
Political instability or policy reversals in focus countries.
Climate and environmental risks affecting manufacturing sectors (e.g., water scarcity for agro-processing).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to influence MNE investment decisions
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible technical assistance and political engagement to address binding constraints (Component B/C).
DFID’s oversight and milestone-based management to ensure delivery quality.
Due diligence and monitoring of MNE practices, with climate-smart FDI criteria.
Country-specific scoping and adaptive programming to respond to changes.
Integration of climate resilience into technical assistance (e.g., energy-efficient plants, renewable energy sourcing).

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from DFID’s existing work (e.g., TMEA) highlight the need to tackle specific constraints to FDI to unblock manufacturing investment.
Political will and capacity in focus countries are on the right trajectory but require sustained support to overcome barriers.
Agglomeration and demonstration effects are weak in Africa, requiring targeted interventions to create industrial clusters.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous diagnostics (e.g., IGC, ODI, World Bank) show that manufacturing FDI in Africa is stagnant (12% of GDP, 6% of jobs) due to low productivity and binding constraints like infrastructure and skills. Invest Africa builds on these lessons by combining investor engagement with technical assistance to address these gaps.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates a partnership with the China-Africa Development Fund (PIGA) based on lessons from the 2015 UK-China State Visit, leveraging Chinese FDI interest in manufacturing. It also emphasizes climate-smart FDI, reflecting UK leadership on climate change.
risks_lessons.quote: Detailed analytical work shows that opportunities are already emerging... but addressing these requires political commitment, improvements in state capacity, improvements to transport and energy infrastructure... (24923374.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to catalyze at least £400 million to £1 billion in additional FDI, representing a leverage ratio of 4:1 to 10:1.
financial_details.quote: The business case sets out the need for up to £100 million investment in Invest Africa from 2017 to 2021. The programme is likely to result in significant (at least £400 million but potentially over £1 billion) additional FDI into African manufacturing sectors. (24923374.odt, Summary Sheet/Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Centre for Disaster Protection
metadata.quote: "The programme supports developing countries and the humanitarian and development community to strengthen their pre-disaster planning and financial arrangements so they can better manage crisis and disaster risks, thereby reducing the impact on people and helping to safeguard economic development." (D0006784.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Sept 2017 – Sept 2024" (61887576.odt) and "New project end date (if applicable): Sept 2029" (D0006784.odt)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills), policy influence (informing policy decisions), and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions) to improve disaster risk finance (DRF) systems. It provides technical assistance, analytics, and training to governments and humanitarian agencies, while also generating evidence and advocating for policy reforms to scale up pre-arranged financing mechanisms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme supports developing countries and the humanitarian and development community to strengthen their pre-disaster planning and financial arrangements so they can better manage crisis and disaster risks, thereby reducing the impact on people and helping to safeguard economic development." (D0006784.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 150 million people covered collectively through sovereign instruments
12 instruments/funding mechanisms adopted under risk financing strategies
8 countries with disaster, climate, and crisis risks included in budgetary planning and reporting
10 million people with greater financial protection due to market-based instruments
6 new DRF policies/laws/regulations adopted by governments
At least 12 countries benefit from improved data and awareness of disaster risks
At least 6 countries with strengthened pre-disaster planning and disaster risk financing strategies
At least 6 countries with improved enabling environment for local inclusive insurance market development
At least 3 countries in the process of implementing sovereign risk financing strategies
Improved systems for monitoring the effectiveness of disaster risk financing
Independent quality assurance process drives up standards of DRF across the international system
Technical assistance and capacity building underpin a step-change in the use and impact of DRF
Evidence and experimentation enable the Centre to learn and share what works and how
Advocacy and influencing to reform the international development and humanitarian system
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform how disasters are financed by embedding pre-arranged risk financing tools into government systems, strengthening local insurance markets, and generating evidence to influence global policy. It combines technical assistance, research, and advocacy to reduce disaster impacts and build financial resilience.
what_objectives.quote: "The Centre for Disaster Protection programme (the Centre programme) is the UK’s flagship Disaster Risk Finance (DRF) technical assistance programme. The programme has two main components, the directly implemented Centre for Disaster Protection (known as the Centre) and the World Bank Disaster Protection Programme (DPP)." (D0006784.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in disaster-prone regions with significant climate and economic risks, but the overall programme risk rating is classified as moderate. The programme includes work in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) like the Sahel, but the risk of funds being misappropriated for terrorist purposes is assessed as very low.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (18080341.odt, Summary Sheet) and "While the Centre may work with some Fragile and Conflict Affected States (FCAS), the risk of funds being misappropriated for terrorist purposes is assessed to be very low given the nature of the programme." (18080341.odt, Compliance with Relevant Legislation)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and political economy barriers limit the adoption of risk financing tools, while weak institutions and data limitations hinder effective implementation. Climate risks exacerbate the need for pre-arranged financing but also complicate delivery in vulnerable regions.
where_context.quote: "Barriers to risk finance – role of donor interventions: Sovereign risk finance: the use of sovereign risk finance products has been low to date... There are a number of issues here: Capacity: Low awareness of risk and risk financing approaches and lack of institutional capacity within government to design and implement risk financing approaches... Data: Lack of data to assess risks and design risk finance and delivery systems." (18080341.odt, Barriers to risk finance)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Centre for Disaster Protection (directly implemented) and World Bank (Disaster Protection Programme)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Centre is based in London and led by UK-based staff, with decision-making power concentrated in the UK. While the programme works with Southern partners, the governance and strategic direction are primarily driven by the Centre's leadership and FCDO oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
technical assistance
institutional strengthening
fellowship and internship programmes

partner_organizations.role: Current Managing Agent (from 2021)

who_partners.quote: "The programme will draw upon many partnerships across the development, humanitarian and finance communities... The programme will enable government-to-government knowledge sharing, including: A DFID senior advisor hosted within the Centre will ensure that it draws upon HMG capabilities links into the wider DFID portfolio on resilience, social protection and early warning systems." (18080341.odt, Partnerships and the role of the private sector)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for the Centre) and a Single Donor Trust Fund (for the World Bank DPP). The Centre operates under a managed contract with a Managing Agent, while the DPP is funded through a dedicated World Bank trust fund, now part of the Risk Finance Umbrella Trust Fund (RFUTF).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates as a platform with two main components: the directly implemented Centre for Disaster Protection (managed by a contract with DAI Global UK Limited) and the World Bank’s Disaster Protection Programme (DPP), which operates as a hub within the World Bank’s Crisis and Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance Program (CDRFI). Both components are co-located in London and work in complement.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its established expertise in disaster risk finance and existing relationships with Ministries of Finance. The Managing Agent for the Centre was procured through a competitive process, but the transition from OPM to DAI Global was managed as a direct award due to the need for continuity and the Centre’s high-profile UK branding.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme has two main components: (1) a directly implemented Centre team... and (2) a World Bank Disaster Protection Programme (DPP) or hub (that is part of the World Bank’s wider Crisis and Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance Program (CDRFI))." (61887576.odt, Programme Summary) and "A new Administrative Agent contract will be procured as the existing contract cannot be extended." (61887576.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Centre established a governing board in September 2021, comprising independent experts and representatives from FCDO and the Centre Director. The Board, along with its Finance and Risk Committee and People Committee, provides oversight, challenge, and strategic guidance. The DPP operates under the World Bank’s Risk Finance Umbrella Trust Fund (RFUTF) governance, with FCDO as part of the Partnership Council.
how_governance.quote: "The Centre is led by a Director and leadership team and is supported by a Managing Agent. The Centre also established a governing board in September 2021, that comprises independent experts as well as one representative from FCDO and the Centre Director. The Board, along with its active Finance and Risk Committee and People Committee, provides challenge, oversight and strategic guidance in support of the Centre’s mission and in line with its values of impartiality, quality, creativity, and empowerment." (D0006784.odt, Centre for Disaster Protection) and "The FCDO is now part of the Partnership Council of the RFUTF and have greater visibility of programmes funded by other donors." (D0006784.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, as demonstrated by the reallocation of premium financing funds to the Centre’s budget when the Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF) was established. The programme’s structure allows for adjustments based on demand and emerging needs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme’s Theory of Change and strategy are refreshed periodically to align with evolving global priorities (e.g., COVID-19, climate resilient debt clauses). The Centre’s work plans are designed to be adaptive, responding to country demand and policy opportunities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme’s Theory of Change (ToC) is being refreshed to align it to the Centre’s new five-year strategy, work plan and monitoring and evaluation framework." (61887576.odt, Changes to the Original Business Case) and "The Centre’s learning, including evaluation, beneficiary feedback and tracking, will seek to understand what works best, how and why." (18080341.odt, Gender Equality)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Managing Agent (DAI Global) → Centre Team / World Bank DPP. The World Bank DPP operates directly under the Bank’s trust fund mechanisms, while the Centre is managed through a contract with DAI Global.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme budget is currently £33.4m Sept 2017–Sept 2021, of which £30.4m is from the Prosperity Fund and £3m from the Commonwealth Summit 2018-2020 Fund. A costed extension of £62.1m over 3 years would take the total budget to £95.5." (61887576.odt, Additional Support) and "The programme has scored an A: meeting expectations in its first two annual reviews." (61887576.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Establishing the Centre as a standalone legal entity (special purpose vehicle)
Continuing with the existing Managing Agent structure
Transitioning to an Arm’s Length Body
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The current modality was chosen to maintain UK branding and control while allowing flexibility to scale up operations. The decision to continue with a Managing Agent contract (rather than transitioning to a standalone entity) was based on legal and commercial advice, which indicated that the Centre would need to be an Arm’s Length Body until it had sustainable revenue streams. The platform approach (Centre + World Bank DPP) was selected to leverage the UK’s expertise in risk analytics and finance while providing a neutral, global hub for disaster risk finance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of independence or perceived neutrality if the Centre becomes too closely associated with commercial interests
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Centre’s governance structure and values (impartiality, quality, challenge) are designed to maintain independence. The Board includes independent experts to provide oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single Managing Agent could limit innovation or create a monopoly
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The contract includes provisions for competition and performance reviews. The Centre’s strategy emphasizes diversity of funding and partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between the Centre and World Bank DPP
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Co-location in London and joint work planning. The DPP is now part of the World Bank’s Risk Finance Umbrella Trust Fund, which improves alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of the Centre post-FCDO funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Centre is developing a sustainable business model, including diversified funding sources and chargeable services.

why_rationale.quote: "The programme will not provide insurance. It addresses the missing pieces – strengthening pre-disaster planning, building capacity and informed, sustained demand, as well as ensuring risk finance delivers for the poorest people." (18080341.odt, Strategic Decisions) and "The Centre’s presence in London will allow it to draw upon the UK’s world-renowned expertise in risk analytics, finance, insurance and risk management but it will also act as global hub, bringing together partners from across the development, humanitarian and financial communities." (18080341.odt, Programme Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s global scope and focus on disaster-prone regions (including FCAS) require partners with specialized expertise in risk finance, climate resilience, and humanitarian response. This limits partner selection to organizations with proven track records in these areas, such as the World Bank, ARC, and CCRIF. The need for neutral, high-quality advice further constrains the pool of eligible partners to those perceived as impartial and technically credible.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with expertise in sovereign risk finance and insurance markets
Requirement for neutral, impartial advice to maintain trust with governments
Operational challenges in FCAS (e.g., Sahel) limit the types of organizations that can effectively engage
Regulatory and data barriers in target countries require partners with local knowledge and relationships
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—such as providing neutral advice, building local capacity, and influencing global policy—determine the delivery structure. The need for a ‘global hub’ that can convene diverse stakeholders (governments, insurers, humanitarian agencies) led to the creation of a physical Centre in London. The combination of technical assistance, research, and advocacy requires a mixed delivery model (Centre + World Bank DPP) to leverage complementary strengths.
q28_linkages: Need for impartial advice → Establishment of an independent Centre with a governing board
Focus on sovereign risk finance → Partnership with the World Bank for its expertise and government relationships
Goal of influencing global policy → Co-location in London to access UK’s financial and insurance expertise
Capacity building objectives → Embedded training and fellowship programmes within the Centre’s structure
Demand for rapid, reliable finance → Development of pre-arranged financing instruments and quality assurance processes
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between ensuring equitable access to disaster finance (e.g., for the poorest and most vulnerable) and the efficiency of market-based solutions. For example, sovereign risk finance is designed to protect the very poorest through social protection systems, while market insurance targets populations above the poverty line to prevent them from falling back into poverty. The Centre’s work on gender equality and inclusive insurance markets also reflects efforts to balance efficiency with equity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Sovereign risk finance vs. market insurance: "Whereas sovereign risk finance can assist the very poorest in society through funding social protection systems, market insurance is best targeted at populations above the poverty line, to help stop them falling back into poverty when disaster strikes." (18080341.odt, Development of inclusive local insurance markets)
Speed vs. inclusion: The programme emphasizes rapid finance but also requires inclusive planning processes to ensure benefits reach the poorest.
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: The Centre is UK-based but works to build local capacity and ensure country ownership of risk finance strategies.
Cost vs. reach: Premium financing is used to make insurance affordable for the poorest countries, balancing cost-effectiveness with broader coverage.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s moderate risk profile (with elements of FCAS work) has led to a governance structure that combines FCDO oversight with independent expertise. The Board’s Finance and Risk Committee provides additional scrutiny, while the Managing Agent model allows for flexible adjustments in response to emerging risks (e.g., COVID-19, climate shocks).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping the roles of partners like the World Bank (technical assistance) and the Centre (training and knowledge transfer). The programme’s focus on institutional strengthening—such as supporting Ministries of Finance and insurance regulators—directly influences how partners are engaged and what responsibilities they assume.
intersections.quote: "The Centre’s work is structured around three goals... Goal 3: Impactful communications and global policy engagement... The Centre has substantially strengthened its external profile and influence, with a strong track record of directly influencing policy and achieving high-profile media coverage on key policy priorities." (D0006784.odt, Major Achievements) and "The programme must also work to build capability and ensure that finance is plumbed into the right systems so that when disasters strike, the right assistance gets to the right people quickly and effectively, saving lives and cutting the costs of disasters." (18080341.odt, Strategic Decisions)

key_programme_risks: Low demand for risk finance products due to affordability and political incentives
Limited institutional capacity in target countries to design and implement risk finance strategies
Lack of trust in financial products among governments and communities
Insufficient data to assess risks and design effective instruments
Risk of funds being misappropriated in FCAS (assessed as very low but monitored)
Over-reliance on ex-post humanitarian financing creating disincentives for pre-disaster planning
Sustainability of the Centre post-FCDO funding
Coordinating effectively between the Centre and World Bank DPP
Ensuring risk finance benefits reach the poorest and most vulnerable
Balancing the need for rapid response with inclusive, participatory processes

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low demand for risk finance products
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Premium financing to reduce upfront costs; technical assistance to build awareness and capacity; advocacy to shift political incentives toward pre-disaster planning.
Embedded training and capacity-building programmes; long-term engagements with Ministries of Finance and disaster management agencies; partnerships with regional risk pools (e.g., ARC, CCRIF).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of trust in financial products
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Neutral, impartial advice from the Centre; transparency in decision-making; piloting and demonstrating the benefits of risk finance through case studies (e.g., ARC payouts in Senegal).
Investment in global public goods (data, models, analytics); partnerships with organizations like the Met Office and World Bank for risk modeling; support for national data collection systems.
Development of a sustainable business model with diversified funding sources; exploration of chargeable services; transition planning to potential independence.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Coordinating between Centre and World Bank DPP
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Co-location in London; joint work planning; integration into the World Bank’s Risk Finance Umbrella Trust Fund for better alignment.
Focus on shock-responsive social protection systems; gender and inclusion strategies; monitoring and evaluation frameworks to track equity outcomes.

fcas_specific_lessons: Engagement with fragile states requires tailored approaches, such as embedding DRF in adaptive social protection systems (e.g., Sahel project).
Political economy barriers in FCAS can be addressed through long-term relationships and demonstrating tangible benefits (e.g., ARC payouts).
In FCAS, stakeholder engagement throughout all project phases is critical for success.
Flexible, adaptive management is essential to respond to evolving crises in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme has learned that technical expertise is crucial for securing approval of complex DRF solutions (e.g., World Bank Board approval for HoADRIVE). Stakeholder involvement from project generation to implementation improves outcomes. Embedding DRF in government policies and programmes helps maintain commitment and continuity. The presence of a dedicated WB team in London has been key to attracting specialized staff and delivering niche expertise efficiently.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme extended its timeline and budget to respond to growing demand and policy opportunities (e.g., COP26, Global Shield). The Theory of Change was refreshed to better articulate incremental changes and intermediate outcomes. The Centre’s mission statement was updated to focus on constructive, descriptive language. The ‘empowerment’ value was replaced with ‘challenge’ to reflect the Centre’s role in asserting constructive critique to governments and international actors. The governance structure was formalized with a Board and committees to provide stronger oversight.
risks_lessons.quote: "During Phase 1, the DPP worked across 13 lending operations to implement financial solutions to increase the financial resilience of vulnerable countries and people against disaster risks... Learning on risk pools—During Phase 1, the DPPhas built a good relationship with African Risk Capacity (ARC) Group and found opportunities for broader WB teams to engage with ARC." (D0006784.odt, Lessons Learned) and "The Centre’s learning, including evaluation, beneficiary feedback and tracking, will seek to understand what works best, how and why." (18080341.odt, Gender Equality)

co_funding_partners.partner: German Government (for Global Shield Technical Assistance Group)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has mobilized significant co-financing through partnerships. For example, the World Bank’s Disaster Protection Programme (DPP) has supported operations with a total mobilization of US$2.1 billion of IDA funds, of which US$634 million was related to Disaster Risk Financing (DRF), complemented by US$67 million from the UK-supported Global Risk Financing Facility (GS-FF). The Centre’s work has also influenced other donors, such as the US and France, to commit to climate-resilient debt clauses.
financial_details.quote: "The programme budget is currently £33.4m Sept 2017–Sept 2021, of which £30.4m is from the Prosperity Fund and £3m from the Commonwealth Summit 2018-2020 Fund. A costed extension of £62.1m over 3 years would take the total budget to £95.5." (61887576.odt, Additional Support) and "During Phase 1, the DPP worked across 13 lending operations to implement financial solutions to increase the financial resilience of vulnerable countries and people against disaster risks. These operations had a total mobilization of US$2.1 billion of IDA, of which US$634 million was related to Disaster Risk Financing (DRF)." (D0006784.odt, Key Results)

metadata.programme_name: Financial Sector Deepening Africa (FSDAfrica) and FSDAfrica Investments (FSDAi)

quote.text: "Financial Sector Deepening Africa (FSDAfrica) is an FCDO funded not for profit organisation, set up to build financial markets and institutions across sub-Saharan Africa (SSA)."

metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 1 March 2017 – 31 March 2030", "New project end date (if applicable): 31 December 2030" (D0007217.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: FSDAfrica combines financing mechanisms (channeling funds, market shaping), capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills), and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions) to deepen Africa's financial markets. It operates through technical assistance, grants, investments, and research to improve financial sector development, with a focus on green finance, digital innovation, and capital markets.
what_objectives.q1_source: "FSDAfrica addresses the underlying, structural causes of poverty by improving the way financial market systems function. It aims to make financial services more accessible and to expand provision of investment capital to projects and sectors that benefit the poor." (62211076.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 23 million people and small businesses with improved access to basic services (health, housing, energy)
40,000 jobs created, supported, or protected
£375 million of capital mobilised (OECD methodology) and over £2 billion catalysed from public and private sectors
100% Paris-aligned investments, channeling approximately £145 million UK ICF by 2030
175 new policies/regulations and launch over 120 new financial products
6 million individuals and small businesses protected against environmental and financial shocks
50% of investments qualified as having a positive impact on women or women-led MSMEs

what_objectives.summary: FSDAfrica aims to transform Africa's financial markets by mobilizing capital, improving access to financial services, and fostering inclusive economic growth. It focuses on green finance, digital innovation, and strengthening capital markets, with explicit targets for job creation, climate finance, and gender inclusion.

quote.text: "FSDAfrica’s future strategy will deliver on three core priorities, aimed at creating investment growth and delivering continued support for a sustainable and resilient recovery from the ongoing economic impacts of COVID-19 across Africa: Strengthened Capital Markets in African Regional Financial Centres; Helping Africa Finance a Greener Future; UK Leadership in promoting Financial Innovation and FinTech in Africa."

countries_regions: West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a mix of stable and fragile contexts across Sub-Saharan Africa, with explicit risk management strategies for financial sector volatility, regulatory challenges, and climate vulnerabilities. The risk rating has consistently been assessed as 'moderate' in annual reviews.
where_context.q5_source: "Programme risk is assessed as moderate." (5723842.odt, Summary Sheet); "Latest (November 2023) Annual Review featuring an overall output score A; risk rating ‘moderate’" (D0007217.odt, INFORMATION)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers prevent institutional investors from diversifying into new asset classes (e.g., private debt). Weak infrastructure and limited interoperability in payment systems hinder financial inclusion. Climate risks exacerbate economic instability, while macroeconomic volatility affects investment returns. Political economy factors shape market interactions, often favoring incumbents over innovative solutions.

quote.text: "Regulation often prevents institutional investors from investing in new asset classes, such as private debt... There are still significant capacity constraints across financial markets, in both the public and private sphere; further challenged by macro-economic and currency volatility."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FSDAfrica, as a Kenyan-registered entity, holds primary decision-making authority over strategy and operations, with FCDO maintaining oversight through board representation and shareholder rights. The network model empowers local FSD entities (e.g., FSD Kenya, FSD Uganda) to adapt programming to country-specific contexts, while FSDAfrica coordinates regional priorities.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to regulators and governments
training for financial institutions (e.g., capital markets training in Ethiopia)
support for financial innovation (e.g., green bonds, digital finance)
gender-specific capacity building (e.g., Women’s World Banking partnership)
institutional strengthening (e.g., establishing stock exchanges, bond markets)
