quote.text: "FSDAfrica operates by providing: Technical assistance and capacity building to African governments and regulators; Grants and/or returnable grants to develop new financial products and services; Early-stage, risk-bearing investment capital to financial firms and projects to address market failures and crowd in third party investment; Research and knowledge-sharing activities... FSDAfrica is the largest member of the FSD Network, a collection of nine FSD programmes across sub-Saharan Africa."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FSDAfrica uses a combination of grants (for technical assistance and research), returnable grants, concessional debt, and equity investments (via FSDAi). Funding flows through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and FSDAfrica, with FSDAi operating as a separate legal entity issuing shares for capital drawdowns. Fiscal CDEL is deployed as convertible grants, while non-fiscal CDEL (FT) is used for risk-bearing investments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FSDAfrica acts as a regional platform coordinating the FSD Network, with country-level FSDs operating as autonomous special purpose vehicles (SPVs). FSDAi functions as a dedicated investment arm, while FSDAfrica’s three pillars (Capital Markets, Risk and Resilience, Digital Economy) align technical assistance with investment priorities. Governance is shared through overlapping boards and committees (e.g., Investment Committee with BII representation).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (FSDAfrica was established by FCDO as a dedicated vehicle)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: FSDAfrica was created as a specialized SPV to leverage FCDO’s long-standing leadership in financial sector development. The network model (country FSDs) was chosen for its proven flexibility, responsiveness, and lower overhead costs compared to contracted-out models (Bester, 2014 review). FSDAi’s establishment addressed the need for a dedicated risk-taking investor to complement BII’s offerings.

quote.text: "FSDAfrica was created in 2012 and has operated as an independent legal entity since 2015... A 2015 review confirmed the efficacy of the FSD SPV model... The effectiveness of the SPV model [was] found to be better – with greater flexibility, responsiveness and long-term orientation."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: FSDAfrica is governed by a Board with four committees: Investment Committee, Development Committee, Finance/Audit/Risk Committee, and Nominations/Remuneration Committee. FCDO sits on all committees and holds a board position, enabling direct oversight. FSDAi shares governance structures with FSDAfrica, including a joint Investment Committee with BII representation. Country FSDs have localized governance approved by FCDO, with UK Post advisers participating in oversight.

quote.text: "DFID will continue to have strong oversight of FSDAfrica and the country level FSDs. Strategic and operational oversight... is provided through well-qualified Boards... DFID sits on both the FSDAfrica Board and all Board Committees. DFID can therefore influence the decisions made by FSDAfrica management and the FSDAfrica Board as appropriate."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between FSDAfrica’s pillars (Capital Markets, Risk/Resilience, Digital Economy) and geographic priorities, but major shifts require FCDO approval. The split between fiscal and non-fiscal CDEL remains flexible during deployment to maintain risk appetite. Runway funding for country FSDs is contingent on securing co-funding.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: FSDAfrica’s strategy is reviewed annually, with adjustments made to respond to emerging priorities (e.g., green finance pivot, COVID-19 response). The 2025–2030 strategy refresh incorporates lessons from external reviews and shifting donor landscapes. FSDAi’s ‘test, accelerate, mobilise’ approach explicitly builds in iterative learning.

quote.text: "FSDAfrica’s future strategy will deliver on three core priorities... This represents a re-focus of FSDAfrica’s work in light of streamlined budgets... The theory of change will be updated by October 16th 2021, in line with the new strategy, to capture the increased ambition on priority activities."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → FSDAfrica/FSDAi → (end recipients: financial institutions, regulators, or local FSDs). FSDAi operates as a separate entity but shares governance with FSDAfrica.

quote.text: "Portfolio management costs will represent 2-3% p.a. of the investment capital allocation... FSDAi’s operating cost framework... includes a commitment to keep costs up to 1.7% of Total Portfolio."
quote.source: D0007217.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?

q24_alternatives_considered: contracted-out model (service provider delivering FSD programmes over a fixed period)
consolidation of country FSD funding under FSDAfrica (partially implemented)
fully commercial financing model for FSDAi (rejected to preserve additionality)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The SPV model was selected for its proven flexibility, lower overhead costs, and long-term orientation compared to contracted-out approaches (Bester, 2014). FSDAfrica’s regional platform structure enables economies of scale in administration, evaluation, and lesson-sharing across country programmes. FSDAi’s dedicated investment arm addresses a market gap by assuming higher risks than DFIs or private investors, with a mandate to test innovative financial instruments that crowd in commercial capital.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (lower overheads, shared services)
risk mitigation (FCDO oversight through governance roles)
flexibility (adaptive strategy and reallocation between pillars)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on FCDO funding reduces financial sustainability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FSDAfrica is diversifying funding sources (e.g., Gates Foundation, UK Posts) and exploring service-provider models. FSDAi’s fundraising efforts target co-investors (e.g., Schroders, ACP) to leverage FCDO’s capital increase.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex governance across multiple SPVs (FSDAfrica + country FSDs + FSDAi) may create coordination challenges.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Shared committees (e.g., Investment Committee with BII), regular FSD Platform Steering Group meetings, and centralized M&E systems (e.g., data management centre for the FSD Network).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High-risk investments (e.g., FSDAi’s early-stage ventures) may fail, affecting development outcomes.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Portfolio diversification, fiscal CDEL for highest-risk transactions, and explicit failure tolerance in the investment strategy (e.g., "many will fail but some will greatly exceed expectations").

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Withdrawal from country FSDs may disrupt local financial sector development.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Runway funding (£6.6m) to bridge gaps while securing co-funding; prioritizing regions where UK Posts can backstop activities (e.g., Ghana, Ethiopia).

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (systemic market changes, e.g., green bond programmes)
equity (gender-lensed investing, focus on fragile states)

quote.text: "The effectiveness of the SPV model [was] found to be better – with greater flexibility, responsiveness and long-term orientation. It was also found to be more efficient with lower average overhead costs... This new model for shared planning and delivery... will balance cross-continent and regional programming with ‘bottom-up’ in-country financial system development priorities."
quote.source: 53760423.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension and what will it achieve?

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating environment limits partner selection to entities with deep local expertise and regulatory navigation skills. For example, FSDAfrica’s focus on fragile states (e.g., Sudan, DRC) requires partners like Acre Export Fund, which can underwrite risk in high-perception markets. Regulatory barriers in countries like Nigeria (where pension funds are restricted to government securities) necessitate partnerships with local regulators and institutions (e.g., National Bank of Ethiopia for capital markets reform).
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory environments (e.g., Nigeria’s pension fund restrictions) shape investee selection.
Fragility in FCAS (e.g., Sudan, DRC) demands partners with conflict-sensitive approaches.
Currency volatility (e.g., Ethiopia, Zimbabwe) influences local vs. international partner roles.
Limited institutional capacity in nascent markets (e.g., WAEMU) requires hands-on technical assistance providers.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of systemic financial market transformation drives the platform/network structure, enabling coordination across capital markets, digital innovation, and resilience pillars. The need for early-stage risk capital led to FSDAi’s creation as a separate entity, while the focus on green finance shaped the Green Finance Transaction Accelerator (GFTA) facility. Country-specific priorities (e.g., Ethiopia’s stock exchange) determine the mix of technical assistance and investment tools deployed.
q28_linkages: Systemic change goals → Network model (FSDAfrica + country FSDs + FSDAi).
Green finance pivot → GFTA facility and 80% ICF-aligned portfolio.
Digital innovation focus → FinTech sandbox support and CaVex investment.
FCAS inclusion → Acre Export Fund partnership and refugee financing programmes.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., centralized M&E, shared services) with equity (e.g., 50% women-targeted investments, FCAS inclusion). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher transaction costs for small-ticket investments in fragile states vs. scalability; (2) Patient capital for women-led MSMEs (e.g., Nyala Venture) vs. commercial return expectations; (3) Local currency financing (e.g., ALCBF) to reduce FX risk vs. liquidity constraints.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid deployment in regional financial centres (e.g., Kenya, Nigeria) vs. slower, tailored approaches in FCAS (e.g., Sudan).
Expertise vs. ownership: UK technical assistance (e.g., capital markets training) vs. local institutional leadership.
Cost vs. reach: High-touch support for early-stage ventures (e.g., Lendable) vs. scalable digital platforms (e.g., MFSAfrica).
Risk vs. additionality: Fiscal CDEL for high-risk transactions vs. financial sustainability goals.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives intensive oversight (e.g., FCDO representation on all FSDAfrica board committees, quarterly reporting for GFTA). High-risk components (e.g., FSDAi’s direct investments) receive additional scrutiny through subordinated structures and fiscal CDEL allocation. Fragile contexts (e.g., Sudan, DRC) trigger embedded advisory support and tailored exit strategies.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) FSDAfrica’s technical assistance pillars (Capital Markets, Digital Economy) inform FSDAi’s investment pipeline (e.g., CaVex, EABX transitions from grants to equity); (2) Country FSDs’ regulatory work enables local market entry (e.g., Ethiopia’s capital markets regulator); (3) Gender-specific training (e.g., Women’s World Banking) shapes investee selection criteria (e.g., Nyala Venture’s women-led focus).

quote.text: "FSDAi’s approach is now clearly focused on testing, accelerating and mobilising capital for financial solutions that help to deliver on Africa’s growth ambitions... FSDAi will continue to deploy risk bearing capital into relevant market-shaping transactions, using its flexibility and active investor role to engage in—and at times co-create—innovative financial instruments and structures that address the bottlenecks in finance and capital markets."

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic volatility affecting investment returns and local currency stability.
Regulatory barriers limiting institutional investor participation in new asset classes (e.g., private debt).
Climate risks exacerbating fragility in target countries (e.g., droughts in Ethiopia, floods in Nigeria).
Overlap or gaps between FSDAfrica’s regional work and country FSD priorities.
Dependence on FCDO funding reducing long-term sustainability (mitigated via co-investor outreach).
High failure rate in early-stage investments (e.g., FSDAi portfolio expectations).
Reputational risk from country FSD closures (e.g., Nigeria, Sierra Leone).
Limited bankable projects for climate finance at scale.
De-risking by international banks affecting remittance flows in FCAS.
Digital divide excluding vulnerable populations from FinTech solutions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Local currency financing instruments (e.g., ALCBF) and hedging solutions to reduce FX exposure. Diversification across regions and sectors.
Technical assistance to reform policies (e.g., Ethiopia’s capital markets regulator). Advocacy for enabling environments via FSD Network collaboration.
Green Finance Transaction Accelerator (GFTA) to originate resilient transactions. Integration of climate adaptation metrics in investment criteria.
Bi-annual FSD Platform Steering Group meetings and shared M&E systems. Runway funding contingent on alignment with FSDAfrica’s priorities.
Diversification strategy targeting co-investors (e.g., Gates Foundation, Schroders). Service-provider models for sustainable revenue streams.
Portfolio approach with explicit failure tolerance. Fiscal CDEL for highest-risk transactions. Learning agenda to capture lessons from failures.
Responsible withdrawal process with runway funding (£6.6m). Transparent communication and handover to UK Posts where feasible.
GFTA facility to develop investable asset classes. Blended finance structures to de-risk transactions (e.g., nature-based solutions guarantees).
Partnerships with local financial institutions (e.g., Acre Export Fund). Advocacy for proportional AML/CFT regulations in FCAS.
Targeted interventions for excluded groups (e.g., refugee financing in Rwanda/Uganda). Gender-lensed digital solutions (e.g., Nyala Venture).

fcas_specific_lessons: Mobile money alone cannot serve the poorest in FCAS at scale; complementary solutions (e.g., cash transfers, agent networks) are needed.
Remittance costs remain prohibitively high in FCAS (e.g., 8.1% UK-Africa vs. 3.9% UK-India) due to de-risking; requires blended guarantees (e.g., Acre Export Fund).
Displaced populations (20 million in SSA) need tailored financial products; digital identity solutions can unlock access (e.g., Rwanda refugee programmes).
FCAS regulatory environments demand proportional AML/CFT approaches to avoid excluding vulnerable groups.
Local currency financing in FCAS (e.g., Sudan, DRC) reduces balance sheet fragility but requires liquidity backstops (e.g., FSDAi’s guarantees).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2014 Bester review demonstrated that the FSD SPV model outperformed contracted-out approaches in flexibility, responsiveness, and cost-efficiency. FSDAfrica’s 2017–2020 phase showed that combining technical assistance (e.g., green bond programmes) with catalytic investments (e.g., ALCBF) achieves systemic impact. The 2022 Agora Global review highlighted FSDAi’s additionality in early-stage, high-risk investments where DFIs and private investors hesitate. Lessons from COVID-19 (e.g., liquidity support to FIs) informed the 2025–2030 strategy’s emphasis on resilience and de-risking instruments.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from pure financial inclusion to sustainable financial sector development (e.g., green finance, capital markets depth).
Creation of FSDAi to address the gap in early-stage risk capital, complementing BII’s offerings.
Green Finance Transaction Accelerator (GFTA) added to originate investable climate transactions.
Explicit 80% ICF alignment target for FSDAi’s portfolio, up from previous phases.
Gender-lensed investing integrated into all transactions (e.g., 2X Challenge indicators).
Marquee transaction facilities introduced to mobilise larger pools of capital (e.g., £5–15m funds).
Runway funding mechanism formalized for responsible country FSD exits.
Digital Economy pillar added to address FinTech and data protection challenges.

quote.text: "FSDAi’s performance is most strongly evidenced through its midterm review (Agora Global 2022), which provided a comprehensive evaluation of FSDAi from inception. The review assessed FSDAi's results, organisational structure, investment strategies, and impact on market transformation. It found FSDAi to be playing a ‘unique and necessary role’ through targeting a section of the market not served by the domestic private sector or DFIs... [It] has provided direct assurance to other investors leading to co-investment from the private sector that would not otherwise have been invested."

co_funding_partners.partner: Schroders, ACP, The Cairns Group (potential co-investors)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: FSDAi has mobilised and catalysed £4.9 billion from public and private investors to date, with a target to mobilise £375m directly and catalyse over £2bn by 2030. ALCBF alone mobilised $2.4bn for local currency bonds, while Frontclear catalysed £1.9bn for money markets. The leverage ratio for FSDAi’s portfolio is described as ‘unusually large compared to the DFI sector’ (Agora Global 2022).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme combines revenue funding (RDEL: £342m) for technical assistance and grants with capital funding (non-fiscal CDEL: £230m) for investments. Fiscal CDEL (£49m) supports high-risk transactions. FSDAi’s portfolio is structured as 20% revenue-generating investments and 80% catalytic/patient capital.

quote.text: "FCDO funding will underpin deployment of FSDAi’s 2025-2030 strategy. Funding will be broken down based on the pipeline of transactions approved... Upto £150 million of non-Fiscal CDEL (FT)... Upto £49 million of Fiscal CDEL... The current projected pipeline relies on FCDO’s capital increase."
quote.source: D0007217.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?

metadata.programme_name: Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning (GOAL)
metadata.duration_text: Base budget of £130 million up to maximum of £190m
metadata.quote: The Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning (GOAL) programme will support the Governments of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) to improve education outcomes in their least developed districts for girls and the most marginalised. (D0003096.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GOAL combines implementation research (testing/scaling interventions like Teaching at the Right Level), capacity building (strengthening provincial education systems), and service delivery (direct support to enroll 250,000 marginalized children). The programme focuses on improving both access to education and learning outcomes for girls and marginalized groups in Pakistan's least developed districts.
what_objectives.q1_source: GOAL will support; Improvements in learning outcomes for 16.9 million children (7.8 million girls) by strengthening the provincial education systems to improve the quality of teaching and become more resilient post Covid. [...] GOAL will also improve learning outcomes for at least 16.9 million children [...] by strengthening the provincial education systems to improve the quality and equity of education, particularly the quality of teaching, and becoming more resilient post Covid. (D0003096.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: ~250,000 marginalised children, mainly girls and religious minorities, to enrol and stay in school
~150,000 girls to read by age 10
Improved learning outcomes for at least 16.9 million children (7.8 million girls) through strengthened provincial education systems
Reduced barriers (e.g., cultural barriers, safeguarding issues, discrimination) and schooling costs for girls and marginalised children
Improved teacher knowledge and skills, particularly for Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL)
Improved planning and management at school, district, and provincial levels
Strengthened provincial education data systems
Pilot interventions to improve inclusion within schools, with evidence generation on what works
what_objectives.summary: GOAL aims to create inclusive provincial education systems delivering quality education by directly increasing access for marginalized children (especially girls and religious minorities) while simultaneously strengthening teaching quality, learning outcomes, and system resilience in Punjab and KP's least developed districts.
what_objectives.quote: The Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning (GOAL) programme will support the Governments of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) to improve education outcomes in their least developed districts for girls and the most marginalised. [...] GOAL will directly support ~250,000 marginalised children, mainly girls and religious minorities, to enrol and stay in school and support an additional ~150,000 girls to read by age 10. (D0003096.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan is classified as FCAS due to ongoing conflict (especially in the Newly Merged Districts bordering Afghanistan), high vulnerability to natural disasters (ranked 8th globally for disaster risk), and systemic challenges like weak institutions, gender inequality, and terrorism threats. The Taliban's return in Afghanistan exacerbates instability in border regions.
where_context.q5_source: All provinces in Pakistan remain affected by violent conflict to some degree. [...] The return to power of the Taliban in Afghanistan may impact on the newly merged districts in KP. (D0003096.odt, Conflict and fragility section) || Pakistan ranked 8th on the list of 10 countries most vulnerable to natural disasters with more than 130 million people at risk in 2020. (D0003096.odt, Climate and Environment section)
q6_contextual_constraints: security (conflict in NMDs, Taliban spillover, school attacks)
weak institutions (limited government capacity, corruption, weak child protection systems)
political economy (gender norms restricting girls' mobility, minority discrimination)
infrastructure (poor school facilities, limited digital access)
data limitations (lack of reliable education data, weak M&E systems)
regulatory (restrictive social norms, censorship of textbooks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks (e.g., school attacks in KP) and cultural barriers (e.g., girls' mobility restrictions) directly limit programme reach in conservative areas. Weak institutions slow reform adoption, while climate disasters disrupt service delivery. Data gaps hinder evidence-based planning, and regulatory constraints (e.g., textbook censorship) affect curriculum development.
where_context.quote: The situation in Afghanistan since the return to power of the Taliban in August 2021 will affect the Newly Merged Districts in Pakistan that border Afghanistan. [...] Schools in KP have been frequently attacked by militant groups. (D0003096.odt, Conflict and fragility section) || Girls are significantly less likely to be in school. [...] Two thirds of the Out of School Children in KP are girls. The gender gap in Punjab enrolment widens at the post-primary level. (D0003096.odt, Gender Disparity section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Governments of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The provincial governments (Punjab and KP) lead decision-making on education reforms, with FCDO providing technical assistance and funding. The programme embeds interventions within provincial systems, ensuring local ownership.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening provincial education systems (planning, management, data systems)
teacher training (TaRL, inclusive education)
institutional strengthening (Special Education Departments, monitoring units)
policy development support (Education Sector Plans)
safeguarding system strengthening (child protection mechanisms)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Punjab
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer (system strengthening, policy adoption)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer (system strengthening, policy adoption)

partner_organizations.name: Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs)
partner_organizations.role: service delivery (enrolment drives, community schools)

partner_organizations.name: UN agencies
partner_organizations.role: service delivery support

partner_organizations.name: Delivery partner (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance provider (subject to FCDO due diligence)

partner_organizations.name: Independent Monitoring Unit (IMU) in KP
partner_organizations.role: data collection and progress monitoring

partner_organizations.name: British High Commission (BHC) Islamabad
partner_organizations.role: political engagement, advocacy, programme oversight

who_partners.quote: GOAL will be well embedded in, and adapted to, the school systems in KP and Punjab, and work for system-wide adoption. [...] GOAL will also work towards multiplying the effects of other country or centrally managed education and health programmes in Pakistan. (D0003096.odt, Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning Programme section) || The UK has been one of the key donors supporting education in Punjab and KP, alongside the World Bank. (D0003096.odt, Rationale for UK Spending section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of technical assistance (to governments) and service delivery grants (via NGOs/UN) to achieve system strengthening and direct enrolment targets. Block funding was used in predecessor programmes (PESP/KESP), but GOAL shifts toward targeted technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO provides funding and oversight, while provincial governments lead implementation with support from a delivery partner (for technical assistance) and NGOs/UN (for service delivery). The programme coordinates with other FCDO initiatives (e.g., DARE, GEC) and multilateral efforts (World Bank, GPE).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The provincial governments (Punjab and KP) are direct partners due to existing relationships and prior programme success (PESP/KESP). The delivery partner for technical assistance is subject to FCDO's due diligence but not selected via open competition.
how_mechanism.quote: GOAL is a successor programme to the KP Education Sector Programme (KESP) and the Punjab Education Sector (PESP). Both were large scale budget support programmes [...] GOAL will focus primarily on providing technical assistance to improve learning outcomes and inclusion within schools. (D0003096.odt, Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning Programme section) || A programme focused on systems strengthening (which would primarily be delivered through technical assistance) would have reduced transaction cost for FCDO. (D0003096.odt, Option Two: Systems Strengthening section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will be overseen through regular engagement with provincial governments and FCDO's monthly/bilateral meetings with the Economic Affairs Division. An Annual Review will assess Partnership Principles compliance.
how_governance.quote: The GOAL team will join FCDO’s monthly and bilateral meetings with the Economic Affairs Division. An annual update on Partnership Principles, and how it impacts the programme will be provided in the Annual Review. (D0003096.odt, Partnership Principles section) || The programme will be managed through a combination of technical assistance and service delivery, with embedded advisors likely playing a role in oversight.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can likely be reallocated between components (e.g., shifting between technical assistance and service delivery) with approval, given the programme's adaptive approach to emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19, Afghanistan crisis).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to respond to dynamic risks (e.g., pandemic disruptions, Taliban spillover) and incorporates lessons from prior programmes (e.g., PESP/KESP). Adjustments require FCDO approval but are anticipated given the volatile context.
how_flexibility.quote: The challenging and dynamic context of Pakistan, especially with the COVID-19 pandemic and upcoming elections in 2023 present both opportunities and risks. [...] This presents an opportunity to support the government to build resilient education systems that can cope with pandemics. (D0003096.odt, Opportunities and Risks section) || GOAL will adopt a gendered lens and focus on poor girls and marginalised children by targeting poor districts [...] Other groups that are not the focus but will be covered through reforms include children with disabilities. (D0003096.odt, Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning Programme section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partner (technical assistance) → Provincial Governments (Punjab/KP) → Schools/NGOs (service delivery). The delivery partner acts as an intermediary for system strengthening, while NGOs/UN implement direct services.
how_efficiency.quote: A programme focused on systems strengthening (which would primarily be delivered through technical assistance) would have reduced transaction cost for FCDO. (D0003096.odt, Option Two: Systems Strengthening section) || GOAL will work through a delivery partner subject to FCDO’s due diligence processes. (D0003096.odt, How does this Programme deliver FCDO’s Strategic Portfolio section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do Nothing
Systems Strengthening with a Primary Focus on Improving Learning Outcomes
Systems Strengthening and Improving Access of Marginalised Children through Service Delivery
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed approach (systems strengthening + service delivery) was selected to balance sustainability (through institutional reforms) with immediate impact (direct enrolment support). This aligns with FCDO's shift toward technical assistance while addressing the urgent need to reach marginalized groups (girls, minorities) in Pakistan's least developed districts. The modality leverages existing government partnerships and builds on lessons from PESP/KESP.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (combining cost-effective system reforms with targeted service delivery)
risk mitigation (government ownership reduces sustainability risks)
past experience (success of PESP/KESP in increasing enrolment/attendance)
partner capacity (provincial governments have demonstrated commitment)
equity (direct focus on girls and minorities aligns with SDG targets)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government absorption capacity: Provincial systems may struggle to adopt reforms at scale, limiting sustainability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with embedded technical assistance and capacity building for provincial staff. (D0003096.odt, Option Two: Systems Strengthening section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges: Fragmentation between technical assistance (delivery partner) and service delivery (NGOs/UN) could create inefficiencies.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of roles with joint planning mechanisms and FCDO oversight. (D0003096.odt, How does this Programme deliver FCDO’s Strategic Portfolio section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference: Changes in provincial leadership (e.g., 2023 elections) could disrupt reform continuity.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: High-level political engagement and alignment with provincial Education Sector Plans to ensure cross-party buy-in. (D0003096.odt, Rationale for UK Spending section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding gaps: Weak child protection systems in schools increase risks of abuse/exploitation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strengthening provincial safeguarding systems (e.g., hotlines, teacher training) and leveraging existing BHC mechanisms. (D0003096.odt, Safeguarding section)

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (reduced transaction costs via technical assistance)
sustainability (system strengthening over direct service delivery)
why_rationale.quote: Option Two: Systems Strengthening with a Primary Focus on Improving Learning Outcomes [...] This option is also in line with the new Strategic Framework for ODA that proposes a focus on building the governments’ own capability to deliver growth and development. (D0003096.odt, Strategic options appraisal) || The preferred option combines systems strengthening with targeted service delivery to reach marginalised children, reflecting lessons from PESP/KESP and the need for both immediate impact and long-term sustainability.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context (conflict in NMDs, gender norms, weak institutions) limits partner selection to entities with local legitimacy and security clearance. Provincial governments are prioritized as implementers due to their mandate in conservative areas, while international NGOs/UN are used for service delivery in high-risk zones.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in NMDs restrict partner mobility, favoring local government-led delivery.
Gender norms require female teachers/NGO workers for girls' education, limiting partner options.
Weak institutional capacity necessitates technical assistance providers with prior experience in Pakistan.
Political sensitivity (e.g., textbook censorship) requires partners aligned with government priorities.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of system strengthening (long-term) and direct enrolment (immediate) necessitate a mixed delivery structure: technical assistance for institutional reforms + NGO/UN service delivery for marginalized groups. The focus on girls/minorities requires embedded safeguarding and gender expertise in all partners.
q28_linkages: Implementation research (TaRL, inclusion pilots) → requires delivery partners with R&D capacity.
Capacity building (teacher training) → necessitates provincial government ownership.
Service delivery (enrolment drives) → demands NGO/UN presence in remote districts.
Policy influence (Education Sector Plans) → needs high-level government engagement.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting girls/minorities in poor districts) with efficiency (system-wide reforms). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher per-child costs for marginalized groups vs. scale; (2) Local partner capacity limitations vs. speed of delivery; (3) Adaptive management for inclusion vs. standardized approaches for efficiency.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct service delivery for marginalized children is slower but necessary for equity.
Expertise vs. ownership: International technical assistance providers offer skills but reduce local control.
Cost vs. reach: Targeting the poorest districts (e.g., South Punjab, NMDs) increases per-beneficiary costs.
Flexibility vs. accountability: Adaptive management for crises (COVID-19, Afghanistan) requires robust oversight.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (conflict, disasters) increases oversight intensity, with embedded advisors and milestone-based payments to mitigate risks of disruption or fund misuse. Safeguarding risks necessitate additional layers of partner vetting and monitoring.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with provincial governments taking on increasing ownership as their systems strengthen. Early phases rely more on technical assistance, while later stages transition to government-led implementation. NGOs/UN focus on service delivery where government capacity is lowest (e.g., NMDs).
intersections.quote: The challenging and dynamic context of Pakistan, especially with the COVID-19 pandemic and upcoming elections in 2023 present both opportunities and risks. [...] This is an opportunity for GOAL to push for reforms. (D0003096.odt, Opportunities and Risks section) || GOAL will focus on reducing barriers (e.g., cultural barriers that reduce mobility of girls, safeguarding issues, discrimination of children of minority faith) and schooling costs for girls and marginalised children. (D0003096.odt, Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning Programme section)

key_programme_risks: Political instability (e.g., 2023 elections disrupting reforms)
Security threats (Taliban spillover, school attacks in KP)
COVID-19 learning losses (1.5 years of lost learning per prior research)
Safeguarding failures (child abuse, exploitation in schools)
Climate disasters (floods/droughts disrupting education)
Government absorption capacity (slow reform adoption)
Gender backlash (community resistance to girls' education)
Economic crisis (reduced household ability to pay schooling costs)
Refugee inflows (strain on KP's education system from Afghanistan)
Data gaps (weak M&E limiting adaptive management)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Align with provincial Education Sector Plans to ensure cross-party continuity; maintain high-level engagement with Chief Ministers.
Work through government channels in high-risk areas; leverage existing BHC safeguarding mechanisms.
Prioritize accelerated learning programmes (e.g., TaRL) and resilient system-building (remote learning capacity).
Strengthen provincial child protection systems (hotlines, teacher training) and partner due diligence.
Integrate climate education into curriculum and support disaster-resilient school infrastructure.
Phase reforms with embedded technical assistance and capacity building for provincial staff.
Community engagement strategies and female teacher recruitment in conservative areas.
Expand stipend/voucher programmes and cost-sharing with households.
Coordinate with UN agencies and include refugee children in enrolment targets.
Strengthen provincial data systems (e.g., KP's Independent Monitoring Unit) and third-party validations.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-sensitive education: Schools in KP have been targeted by militants; GOAL incorporates safeguarding and community trust-building.
Local ownership: Prior programmes (PESP/KESP) showed sustainability requires provincial government leadership.
Adaptive delivery: COVID-19 and Afghanistan crisis demonstrate need for flexible funding and rapid reallocation.
Gender in FCAS: Girls in NMDs face compounded barriers; tailored interventions (e.g., community schools) are critical.
Resilience focus: Learning from Pakistan's disaster vulnerability, GOAL integrates climate education and system shock preparedness.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: PESP/KESP demonstrated that sector budget support can achieve scale (e.g., 2.6 million children enrolled via Punjab Education Foundation) but requires complementary technical assistance for quality improvements. Lessons include: (1) Teacher attendance incentives work (Punjab increased from 85% to 95%); (2) Provincial ownership is key (KP's IMU is now government-funded); (3) Marginalized groups need targeted approaches (e.g., stipends for girls); (4) Data-driven decision-making improves outcomes (e.g., monthly education data in KP).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: GOAL shifts from pure sector budget support (PESP/KESP) to a mixed model with technical assistance + targeted service delivery, based on lessons that system strengthening alone cannot reach the most marginalized. The programme also incorporates: (1) Explicit focus on religious minorities and children with disabilities; (2) Stronger safeguarding systems; (3) Climate resilience components; (4) Adaptive management for crises.
risks_lessons.quote: UK support to education in Punjab and KP has delivered significant gains; supporting Government of Pakistan to ensure these are consolidated and sustained post COVID-19 is critical. (D0003096.odt, Rationale for UK Spending section) || The foundation of a sound education system have been laid. However, challenges remain, increased by the pandemic. [...] GOAL will complete this unfinished agenda and leverage the UK’s investments in the sector. (D0003096.odt, Rationale for UK Spending section) || Option One (Do Nothing): FCDO has invested almost £800 million over the last decade [...] With the new Strategic Framework for ODA, and Pakistan’s status as a lower middle-income country, we are transitioning out of service delivery and sector budget support. (D0003096.odt, Option One: Do Nothing section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK's 12% contribution to IDA-19 and 20% contribution to GPE influences how multilateral funds (e.g., World Bank's $1.5 billion in Pakistan) are allocated to education. GOAL aligns with these funds to amplify impact.
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: Base budget of £130 million up to maximum of £190m. (D0003096.odt, Programme summary) || The UK contributed 12% of the latest round of International Development Association (IDA-19) [...] and with World Bank commitments in Pakistan worth $1.5 billion [...] this means the UK has a significant stake in how World Bank funds are used to improve education. (D0003096.odt, Rationale for UK Spending section)

metadata.programme_name: Shule Bora (Quality School)
metadata.quote: "Shule Bora (\"Quality School\" in Swahili) is a flagship, 6-year education programme..." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Shule Bora (\"Quality School\" in Swahili) is a flagship, 6-year education programme..." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Shule Bora combines two main approaches: (1) a Payment by Results (PbR) financing mechanism to incentivize national education reforms in Tanzania, and (2) testing, adapting, and delivering innovative approaches to improve education quality, inclusion, and safety at scale. The programme aims to improve learning outcomes, transition rates for girls, access for children with disabilities, and reduce violence in schools.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will work with the Government of Tanzania on achieving these outcomes through a payment-by-results mechanism. The programme will also provide technical assistance to support the government to achieve these results, as well as to test innovative approaches to deliver programme outcomes." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved learning outcomes for all children
q3_expected_outputs.target: Measured by improvements in average literacy and numeracy scores

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased transition rates to secondary school for girls
q3_expected_outputs.target: Measured by percentage of girls transitioning to secondary school

q3_expected_outputs.output: Prevention of physical and sexual violence in and around schools
q3_expected_outputs.target: Measured by indicators refined during programme implementation

q3_expected_outputs.output: Children with disabilities access quality education
q3_expected_outputs.target: Measured by percentage of children with disabilities accessing school at the right age

q3_expected_outputs.output: Technical assistance to the Government of Tanzania
q3_expected_outputs.target: Support to achieve results and test innovative approaches

q3_expected_outputs.output: Regional testing and scaling of innovative approaches
q3_expected_outputs.target: Delivered in 9 of Tanzania’s 26 regions

what_objectives.summary: Shule Bora is a mixed programme that combines national-level policy reform incentives with regional-level innovation testing to improve education quality, inclusion, and safety in Tanzania.
what_objectives.quote: "Shule Bora (\"Quality School\" in Swahili) is a flagship, 6-year education programme, which aims to improve learning outcomes for all children, to keep girls in school through the transition to secondary, to ensure that children with disabilities access and learn in school, and to reduce violence in schools." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as moderate risk due to contextual and fiduciary risks, including political risks on commitment to reforms, especially on equal access for girls to education. DFID Tanzania has zero tolerance for fraud and corruption.
where_context.q5_source: "This programme is a moderate risk for DFID Tanzania, and it is within the office’s overall portfolio risk appetite." (59817081.odt, Risk Section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The education system in Tanzania is under enormous pressure due to rapid population growth, high pupil-teacher ratios (1:129 in pre-primary), teacher absenteeism (43%), and limited resources. Schools are ill-equipped to support children with disabilities, and there is a lack of accurate data on disability rates. Climate resilience is a consideration for new school construction.
where_context.quote: "The average Pupil Teacher Ratio (PTR) for primary school has grown from 44 to 54 in only 2 years, while the PTR for pre-primary school has now reached 1:129. Twenty-one percent of primary schools in Tanzania now have a PTR over 75, with the number of teachers not increasing since 2016." (59817081.odt, Current State of the Education Sector in Tanzania)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed to work closely with and through the Government of Tanzania, ensuring their ownership of education reforms. Technical assistance and capacity building are provided to support the government in achieving results.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to Government ministries
teacher training (pre-service and in-service)
community engagement and accountability
use of technology for teaching and learning
effective use of data

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner and recipient of PbR financing

partner_organizations.name: Contracted Managing Agent (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver regional testing, adapting, and delivering at scale component; provide technical assistance to Government ministries

partner_organizations.name: DFID Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: Funder and programme oversight

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Complementary secondary education programme

partner_organizations.name: Global Partnership for Education (GPE)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary funding and coordination

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Coordination on preschool work and violence prevention

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Disability-Inclusive Education in Africa Programme Trust Fund

who_partners.quote: "Bringing these two approaches together will embed innovation much more firmly in government systems and policy, which is essential for impact and sustainability. Shule Bora will also be ground-breaking because it will be the first time that work on reducing violence and targeting children with disabilities and the critical bottleneck of girls’ transition to secondary school has been taken forward with government buy-in, through an approach that combines testing innovation with financial aid Payment by Results." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Payment by Results (PbR) mechanism for national-level reforms, where DFID disburses funds only if the Government achieves pre-agreed results. It also includes direct contracting for regional-level innovation testing and technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme combines a national-level PbR mechanism managed through a Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of Tanzania, and a regional-level component delivered by a contracted Managing Agent. The Managing Agent will also provide technical assistance to Government ministries.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will work with the Government of Tanzania on achieving these outcomes through a payment-by-results mechanism... The regional testing, adapting and delivering at scale component will be delivered directly by a contracted Managing Agent, who will also provide technical assistance to relevant Government ministries." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The PbR component is managed through a MoU with the Government of Tanzania. The regional component is delivered by a contracted Managing Agent, with technical assistance provided to Government ministries.
how_governance.quote: "DFID will only disburse money if the Government achieves pre-agreed key results indicators... This will be managed through a Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of Tanzania." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is adaptive and allows for modifications based on learning and evaluation activities. Adjustments can be made at the midline point of the programme.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, allowing for modifications based on learning and evaluation activities, particularly around large-scale piloting of activities on girls’ education, disability, and school safety.
how_flexibility.quote: "This is an adaptive programme, which will allow for modifications based on learning and evaluation activities of large scale piloting of activities on girls’ education, disability and school safety. This creates additional opportunity to make programme adjustments at the midline point of the programme." (59817081.odt, Flexibility Section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contracted Managing Agent → Government of Tanzania (for regional component); FCDO → Government of Tanzania (for PbR component)
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID will only disburse money if the Government achieves pre-agreed key results indicators..." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuation of existing programmes (EPforR and EQUIP-T) without scaling up
Focus only on national-level reforms without regional innovation testing
Focus only on regional innovation without national-level incentives
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed approach was chosen to embed innovation firmly in government systems and policy, ensuring sustainability and impact. The PbR mechanism incentivizes national reforms, while regional innovation testing allows for scalable solutions tailored to local contexts. This approach also aligns with the Government of Tanzania’s commitment to education quality and inclusion.
q25_decision_factors: past experience (building on successful EPforR and EQUIP-T programmes)
partner capacity (Government of Tanzania’s commitment and ownership)
equity (focus on girls, children with disabilities, and violence prevention)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government commitment to key reforms, especially on equal access for girls to education
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close monitoring of political risks and regular engagement with the Government of Tanzania.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks (fraud and corruption)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Zero tolerance for fraud and corruption, with robust financial management systems, including biannual reviews and quarterly meetings with the Government on fiduciary issues.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capacity challenges within the Government and implementing partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated technical assistance and capacity building to the Government, and an adaptive programme design that allows for learning and adjustments.

why_rationale.quote: "Bringing these two approaches together will embed innovation much more firmly in government systems and policy, which is essential for impact and sustainability." (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The context in Tanzania, including weak institutions, data limitations, and high pupil-teacher ratios, necessitates a strong partnership with the Government of Tanzania, which has the mandate and reach to implement national reforms. The regional innovation testing is limited to 9 out of 26 regions due to resource constraints and the need for manageable scaling.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited Government capacity to implement reforms at scale without external support
High pupil-teacher ratios and teacher absenteeism require innovative approaches to improve teaching quality
Lack of accurate data on children with disabilities limits targeted interventions
Political and social norms affect girls’ education and require context-sensitive approaches
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives to improve learning outcomes, inclusion, and safety require a mixed delivery structure. National-level PbR incentivizes systemic reforms, while regional innovation testing allows for context-specific solutions that can be scaled up if successful. The focus on girls, children with disabilities, and violence prevention necessitates community engagement and technical assistance to build local capacity.
q28_linkages: PbR mechanism (HOW) is linked to national reform objectives (WHAT) to ensure Government accountability for results.
Regional innovation testing (HOW) is linked to the need for scalable, context-specific solutions (WHAT) to improve learning and inclusion.
Technical assistance (HOW) supports the Government’s capacity to achieve both national reforms and regional innovations (WHAT).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between rapid delivery and inclusive partnerships, particularly in addressing the needs of girls and children with disabilities. While the PbR mechanism ensures efficiency and accountability, the regional innovation testing and technical assistance components prioritize equity by targeting marginalized groups and building local capacity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: The PbR mechanism incentivizes quick results, while regional innovation testing and disability inclusion require time and context-specific adaptations.
Expertise vs. ownership: External technical assistance is needed to build Government capacity, but the programme aims to ensure Government ownership for sustainability.
Cost vs. reach: The programme focuses on 9 regions for innovation testing to balance cost efficiency with the potential for scalable impact.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile, including political and fiduciary risks, necessitates intensive oversight through regular financial reviews, quarterly meetings, and embedded technical assistance to mitigate risks and ensure accountability.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with technical assistance and training provided to Government ministries, teachers, and communities. This shapes partner roles by empowering local institutions to lead reforms and innovation testing, ensuring sustainability and ownership.
intersections.quote: "Working closely with and through Government to ensure their ownership of education reforms is a key part of the sustainability strategy for the programme, alongside dedicated technical assistance and capacity building to the Government." (59817081.odt, Coherence Section)

key_programme_risks: Government commitment to key reforms, especially on equal access for girls to education
Fiduciary risks, including fraud and corruption
Capacity challenges within the Government and implementing partners
Contextual risks, such as political economy and weak institutions
Data limitations, particularly around disability and learning outcomes
Sustainability of reforms beyond the programme timeline

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Close monitoring of political risks, regular engagement with the Government, and alignment with national education strategies (e.g., Five-Year Development Plan and Education Sector Development Plan).
Zero tolerance for fraud and corruption, robust financial management systems, biannual financial reviews, and quarterly meetings with the Government on fiduciary issues.
Dedicated technical assistance and capacity building to the Government, adaptive programme design, and learning from previous programmes (EPforR and EQUIP-T).
Improved data collection and management systems, including the use of technology and alignment with Government priorities (e.g., Education Management Information Systems).
Embedding innovation in Government systems and policies, ensuring Government ownership, and aligning with long-term national strategies.

fcas_specific_lessons: The importance of Government ownership and alignment with national strategies to ensure sustainability in fragile contexts.
The need for adaptive programme design to respond to changing political and contextual risks.
The value of combining national-level incentives (PbR) with regional innovation testing to balance efficiency and equity.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from EPforR and EQUIP-T highlight the effectiveness of PbR in incentivizing Government reforms, the importance of technical assistance for capacity building, and the need for adaptive management to respond to contextual challenges. EPforR’s embedded approach in Government systems has strengthened planning, monitoring, and resource allocation, while EQUIP-T’s regional focus has demonstrated the impact of teacher training and community engagement on learning outcomes.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Shule Bora builds on the successes of EPforR and EQUIP-T by combining national PbR with regional innovation testing. The programme incorporates lessons on the need for adaptive management, Government ownership, and targeted interventions for girls and children with disabilities. The design also includes explicit safeguarding measures and a focus on violence prevention, which were identified as gaps in previous programmes.
risks_lessons.quote: "EPforR has sharply increased the GoT focus on results, strengthening planning, monitoring, and catalysing reforms to make the system more efficient... EQUIP-T... found a clear, positive impact on math and reading assessments, as well as improvements in teaching quality in a setting where without the intervention would have been a stall or decline in learning." (59817081.odt, Textbox: Achievements of DFID Tanzania bilateral programmes)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme is expected to leverage additional funding from the Government of Tanzania and other development partners, such as the World Bank and GPE, which are already investing in complementary education programmes in Tanzania.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £215m" (59817081.odt, Programme Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Developing and delivering agricultural technologies and knowledge to reduce poverty and hunger, and support adaptation to climate change

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Summary Information
quote.section: Original project start and end dates: September 2016–August 2020; New project end date: March 2022; Total budget: £35m + £18m extension

metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: September 2016–August 2020; New project end date: March 2022 (D0004392.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (e.g., pest-resistant crops, biopesticides), implementation research (scaling push-pull technology, Plantwise clinics), capacity building (training plant doctors, institutional strengthening), and service delivery (direct farmer outreach through clinics). The core focus is on delivering practical solutions to smallholder farmers while building systems for sustainable adoption.
what_objectives.q1_source: The UK will invest up to £35 million in international agricultural research over four years (2016-2020) to support three International Agricultural Research Centres [...] This new support will develop further the performance-related funding component implemented successfully in the previous programme. The intended outcome of the programme as a whole is: New technologies, products and knowledge, which reduce poverty and enhance food and nutrition security in the face of climate change, adopted at scale. (5455281.odt, Intervention Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 75,000 farm households in Tanzania, Kenya, and Nigeria adopting improved amaranth varieties (D-1)
100,000 smallholder households in Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Tajikistan adopting improved mungbean varieties (D-2)
60,000 smallholder households in Tanzania, Ghana, and Bangladesh adopting improved tomato varieties and IPM strategies (D-3)
Plantwise cumulative reach of 35 million farmers by 2022 (D-4)
10 million households with increased food security through invasive species control (D-6)
300,000 smallholder farmers adopting drought-resilient push-pull systems (D-9)
2 new biopesticides commercialized for vegetable pest management (D-7)
Novel tick treatment formulations registered in 4 countries (D-8)
5,000 farmers adopting improved tomato/chili/amaranth varieties in Ghana/Nigeria (D-10)
25,000 farmers adopting improved mungbean in Kenya/Tanzania/Uganda (D-11)
Development of coordinated approach for vegetable/cash crop pest control (new workstream)
Piloting climate-smart biopesticides for transboundary pests (new workstream)
Global Burden of Plant Pests and Disease (GBPPD) assessment framework (new workstream)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to develop and scale climate-resilient agricultural technologies (crop varieties, biopesticides, IPM systems) while strengthening plant health systems (Plantwise clinics, invasive species control) and commercial pathways (private sector partnerships). The extension focuses on deeper coordination between centres and piloting integrated approaches to pest/disease management.

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Expected Results
quote.section: The expected results of this cost extension are: Firstly, continuation and expansion of existing programmes [...] Secondly, engagement with the three Centres and emerging thinking within DFID [...] to support the development of new workstreams.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in stable and conflict-affected countries (e.g., Sierra Leone, Burkina Faso) but focuses on agricultural research with proven partners. The original business case rated risk as 'minor' due to portfolio diversification and strong partner track records, though invasive species and climate change add complexity. The addendum highlights emerging transboundary pests (e.g., Fall Armyworm) as new risks.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Minor [...] First, due to the size and diversity of the programme, funding a range of research initiatives across the Centres, risk is spread across programmes. (5455281.odt, Summary Sheet) AND The first two factors [climate change and trade] also increase the risk to the UK from the emergence and spread of transboundary pests and diseases. (D0004392.odt, Project Purpose)
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (droughts, floods, pests spreading due to climate change)
weak biosecurity systems (increased trade moving pests to new regions)
data limitations (lack of accurate plant disease impact data)
gender gaps (women's limited access to resources/inputs)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate change expands pest distributions (e.g., Fall Armyworm) and increases crop loss risks, while weak biosecurity accelerates invasive species spread. Regulatory hurdles delay biopesticide commercialization (e.g., tick treatments awaiting Kenyan registration). Market failures limit farmer access to inputs, and gender gaps reduce adoption rates among women farmers. Data gaps on plant disease burdens hinder prioritization.

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Project Purpose
quote.section: climate change, environmental degradation, population growth and resource scarcity will place increasing demands on global agriculture [...] weak biosecurity risk moving pests to new regions [...] habitat change linked to agriculture intensification is increasing the significance of existing pests and diseases.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: DFID Research and Evidence Division (Agriculture Team)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID sets strategic priorities, performance metrics, and funding allocations through annual reviews. Centres (two Africa-based, one UK-based) implement research but must align with DFID's theory of change and institutional development requirements. Southern partners (e.g., national agricultural services) deliver last-mile services (e.g., Plantwise clinics) under Centre guidance.

gender mainstreaming across Centre staff/projects
impact evaluation capacity building
private sector partnership development (e.g., seed companies)
