quote.name: 5455281.odt, Intervention Summary
quote.section: DFID will continue to build on these relationships with other donors during this programme and increase accountability for results. [...] The relationship with other donors allowed DFID to strengthen accountability, and technical and governance oversight of the Centres to an extent DFID would not be able to manage alone.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core funding is provided through Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with each Centre, combining: 1) multi-year block grants for predictable planning, and 2) annual performance-related payments (up to 20% of total) tied to pre-agreed metrics. The addendum extends this model with additional £18m under the same MOU framework.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID's Agriculture Team acts as the fund manager, with a Livelihoods Adviser as Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and Deputy Programme Manager (DPM) support. Each Centre operates independently but reports annually to DFID, with performance reviews determining discretionary payments. The addendum introduces stronger coordination between Centres for new workstreams (e.g., integrated pest management).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The three Centres (CABI, icipe, WorldVeg) were selected based on their "demonstrated evidence of excellent research quality with development impact and value for money for DFID during an earlier programme of funding (2011–2015)". The addendum notes their "strong track record of delivery against agreed objectives" and strategic alignment with DFID priorities.

quote.name: 5455281.odt, Intervention Summary
quote.section: The UK will invest up to £35 million [...] to support three International Agricultural Research Centres (the Centres) that have demonstrated evidence of excellent research quality with development impact and value for money for DFID during an earlier programme of funding.

quote.name: 5455281.odt, Performance Management Funding Mechanism
quote.section: The PMFM will adhere to the set of principles [...] Performance-related payment: to high performing Centres. Funding to comprise of a core contribution plus a discretionary Performance payment allocated to those Centres that achieve a set of pre-defined metrics, agreed annually.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research activities within a Centre's portfolio, but require DFID approval for major shifts. The addendum introduces new coordinated workstreams (e.g., vegetable cash crop pest control), suggesting some cross-Centre flexibility.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Annual performance reviews allow for resetting targets and adjusting priorities based on emerging challenges (e.g., Fall Armyworm outbreaks). The addendum explicitly adds new workstreams (GBPPD, climate-smart biopesticides) in response to evolving DFID priorities.

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Approach to Implementation
quote.section: annual resetting of performance criteria and changes to the timing of the performance award enabling improved planning.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → International Research Centres (CABI/icipe/WorldVeg) → National partners (e.g., agricultural services, private seed companies) → Farmers

quote.name: 5455281.odt, Management Case
quote.section: Funding to comprise of a core contribution plus a discretionary Performance payment allocated to those Centres that achieve a set of pre-defined metrics, agreed annually.

q24_alternatives_considered: CGIAR system-wide funding (rejected due to need for targeted DFID priorities)
Bilateral research partnerships (not mentioned as considered)
Direct implementation by DFID (rejected due to lack of technical capacity)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen to: 1) **Leverage proven partners**: The three Centres had demonstrated "excellent research quality with development impact and value for money" during 2011–2015 funding. 2) **Balance flexibility and accountability**: Multi-year core funding enables strategic planning, while performance-related payments (up to 20%) incentivize results. 3) **Align with DFID priorities**: The Centres' focus on climate-resilient crops, pest/disease control, and private sector partnerships directly supports DFID's Economic Development Strategy and UK Aid Strategy objectives. 4) **Avoid CGIAR limitations**: The Centres complement CGIAR by targeting "orphan crops" (e.g., amaranth, mungbean) and integrating commercialization pathways.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (proven 43% average ROI on agricultural research)
partner capacity (Centres' existing networks in Africa/Asia)
equity (gender mainstreaming and Southern farmer focus)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a few partners may limit innovation diversity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual performance reviews and discretionary payments incentivize continuous improvement; new workstreams (e.g., GBPPD) introduce fresh priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Performance-related funding could create perverse incentives (e.g., focusing on easily measurable outputs)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Refined PMFM with "fewer milestones and lighter reporting" (5455281.odt) and qualitative assessments of research quality/gender integration.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination overhead between Centres may reduce efficiency
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Addendum introduces explicit joint workstreams (e.g., vegetable cash crop pest control) with shared metrics to streamline collaboration.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (performance payments tie funds to results)
effectiveness (focus on scaling proven technologies like push-pull)

quote.name: 5455281.odt, Why is UK support required?
quote.section: The PMFM provided the Centres with a clear focus on the agreed outputs and outcomes. It has also been effective in facilitating the delivery of high quality research, the agreed results, and value for money [...] All the Centres received the performance-related payment at least once between 2012 and 2016, demonstrating buy-in and performance improvement.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on **Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia** (high-pest-pressure regions) necessitated partners with: 1) **Local presence**: icipe (Kenya-based) and WorldVeg’s Africa teams were critical for push-pull technology scaling and vegetable breeding. 2) **Climate expertise**: All Centres had to demonstrate adaptive research capabilities for drought/flood-resistant crops. 3) **Regulatory navigation**: Partners like CABI were chosen for their experience with biosecurity systems (e.g., Fall Armyworm response). 4) **Gender integration**: High female smallholder participation (e.g., 62% of push-pull adopters) required Centres with gender-responsive track records.
q27_constraints_detail: Geographic focus on Africa/Asia excluded Centres without regional offices
Climate adaptation requirements favored Centres with breeding programs for stress-tolerant crops
Invasive species threats (e.g., Fall Armyworm) prioritized partners with rapid-response capacities (e.g., CABI’s Plantwise)
Gender gaps in agriculture mandated partners with gender-mainstreaming experience
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **technology scaling objectives** (e.g., reaching 35M farmers via Plantwise) required: 1) **Decentralized delivery**: Plantwise’s clinic network (34 countries) needed a **network structure** with national agricultural services as sub-partners. 2) **Private sector integration**: Mungbean/tomato commercialization demanded **open partnerships** with seed companies, shaping the mixed funding instrument (core + performance-based). 3) **Adaptive research**: Climate-smart crop breeding (e.g., drought-resistant push-pull) necessitated **flexible milestones** to adjust to emerging pests (e.g., Tuta absoluta). 4) **Coordination needs**: Cross-cutting pests (e.g., striga) led to the addendum’s **joint workstreams**, moving from siloed Centre activities to integrated approaches.
q28_linkages: Scaling targets (e.g., 300,000 push-pull adopters) → Network delivery structure with national partners
Commercialization goals → Private sector engagement → Mixed funding (core + performance payments)
Climate adaptation needs → Flexible annual reviews to adjust priorities
Cross-cutting pests → Coordinated workstreams in addendum
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Performance payments incentivize rapid scaling (e.g., Plantwise’s 35M target) but risk sidelining marginalized farmers; mitigation includes gender-disaggregated adoption targets (e.g., 62% female-headed households for push-pull). 2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK-based CABI leads Plantwise, but local plant doctors (trained via capacity building) ensure context relevance. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Plantwise’s clinic model (£3 ROI per £1 invested) prioritizes efficiency, while biopesticide registration (e.g., Kenyan tick treatments) accepts higher costs for long-term sustainability. 4) **Research depth vs. scaling**: The addendum’s new workstreams (e.g., GBPPD) deepen evidence but reduce funds for direct delivery, reflecting a shift toward **systems strengthening** over immediate outputs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Performance payments may favor easily measurable crops (e.g., mungbean) over nutritious but complex crops (e.g., amaranth)
UK-based CABI’s leadership vs. Africa-based icipe/WorldVeg’s implementation roles
Plantwise’s rapid scaling (35M target) vs. time-intensive biopesticide registration processes
New workstreams (e.g., GBPPD) reduce direct delivery funds but aim for long-term policy impact
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (spread across Centres/crops) enables **milestone-based oversight** rather than intensive management. However, emerging transboundary pests (e.g., Fall Armyworm) triggered **higher coordination demands** in the addendum, adding joint workstreams and annual priority resets. Climate risks (droughts, floods) are mitigated through **adaptive research requirements** in the PMFM, allowing shifts in breeding targets (e.g., heat-tolerant mungbean).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building directly shapes partner roles: 1) **Plantwise clinics**: Trained plant doctors (local agricultural staff) become the **primary service deliverers**, reducing Centre burden. 2) **Gender mainstreaming**: Centres must now report on gender-disaggregated adoption (e.g., push-pull’s 62% female-headed households), influencing target-setting. 3) **Private sector partnerships**: WorldVeg’s work with seed companies (e.g., mungbean varieties) shifts its role from **researcher** to **market facilitator**. 4) **Impact evaluation**: Strengthened M&E systems (e.g., Plantwise’s £3 ROI analysis) enable Centres to take on **advocacy roles** with national governments.

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Approach to Implementation
quote.section: Gender has been a focus of DFID’s support to the Centres over the past three years, and each Centre has responded to this focus by improving how they consider gender in recruitment processes and taking specific steps to increase the recruitment of women [...] The underlying theory of change for the programme has not changed and evidence from reporting and regular engagement with the Centres demonstrates that not only are they delivering against agreed objectives but are responding to emerging DFID priorities.

key_programme_risks: Emergence of new transboundary pests (e.g., Fall Armyworm) outpacing control measures
Climate change reducing effectiveness of existing crop varieties (e.g., maize yield declines)
Regulatory delays in biopesticide/tick treatment registration (e.g., Kenyan approvals)
Over-reliance on performance metrics distorting research priorities toward "easy wins"
Sustainability of Plantwise clinics post-DFID funding (£3 ROI but unclear exit strategy)
Gender gaps limiting adoption among female farmers despite targeting (e.g., 62% push-pull adoption by women)
Private sector partnerships failing to reach remote smallholders (e.g., seed company focus on commercial farmers)
Data limitations on plant disease burdens hindering prioritization (GBPPD workstream addresses this)
Conflict in target regions (e.g., Burkina Faso) disrupting field activities
Supply chain failures (e.g., erratic input availability) reducing technology adoption
Resistance development in pests (e.g., Tuta absoluta to pesticides) requiring adaptive R&D

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: CABI’s invasive species program develops rapid-response tools (e.g., awareness campaigns) and leverages Plantwise networks for early detection. Addendum introduces coordinated workstreams for emerging pests.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Climate change impacts on crop yields
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Performance metrics include climate-smart traits (e.g., drought-resistant push-pull systems). Annual reviews allow reprioritization (e.g., heat-tolerant mungbean).
icipe works with national agencies (e.g., Kenya) to streamline registration; addendum supports piloting in multiple countries to diversify risk.
Refined PMFM with "fewer milestones and lighter reporting" (5455281.odt) and qualitative assessments of gender/impact.
New workstream tests private-sector-led models (D-5) and builds local capacity for biological control (D-6).
Centres must report gender-disaggregated data; push-pull targets 62% female-headed households. Capacity building focuses on women’s access to inputs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Private sector exclusion of remote farmers
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: WorldVeg’s new partnerships with African seed companies (addendum) aim to build demand-responsive breeding pipelines.
Addendum funds GBPPD workstream to create priority-setting evidence base.
Portfolio diversification across 34 countries; Centres have experience in FCAS (e.g., icipe in East Africa).
Push-pull’s input-light design (companion crops) reduces dependency; Plantwise clinics provide localized advice.
Integrated pest management (IPM) strategies (e.g., biopesticides + cultural practices) and adaptive breeding (e.g., Tuta absoluta-resistant tomatoes).

fcas_specific_lessons: In conflict-affected regions (e.g., Sierra Leone, Burkina Faso), **local partner networks** (e.g., Plantwise clinics) are critical for continuity during disruptions. Lessons from icipe’s push-pull scaling in post-conflict East Africa (120,000+ households) informed the addendum’s focus on **resilient delivery chains**.
Biosecurity weaknesses in FCAS accelerate invasive species spread (e.g., Fall Armyworm); CABI’s work with national services to strengthen **early warning systems** was prioritized.

Gender inequalities are exacerbated in FCAS; the programme’s **gender-mainstreaming requirements** (e.g., 62% female adoption targets) were strengthened based on lessons from icipe’s work in fragile contexts.

In FCAS, **private sector engagement** (e.g., seed companies) requires deeper due diligence; WorldVeg’s addendum workstream includes **capacity building for local partners** to manage supply chain risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Performance funding works**: The 2011–2015 PMFM "delivered high quality research and value for money" (5455281.odt), with all Centres earning performance payments at least once. 2) **Predictable core funding is critical**: Centres welcomed multi-year grants but requested clearer metrics to reduce uncertainty around performance payments. 3) **Gender integration requires incentives**: Initial gender mainstreaming was uneven; explicit PMFM criteria (e.g., gender-disaggregated adoption data) improved compliance. 4) **Scaling needs private sector**: Push-pull’s 120,000-household reach (2011–2015) was limited by seed availability; the addendum prioritizes **private sector partnerships** (e.g., mungbean seed companies). 5) **Light-touch oversight suffices for high-capacity partners**: Annual reviews were deemed effective, with transaction costs reduced by streamlining reporting.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Streamlined PMFM**: Reduced milestones and lighter reporting (5455281.odt) to cut transaction costs. 2) **Stronger coordination**: Addendum introduces **joint workstreams** (e.g., vegetable cash crop pest control) to address siloed delivery. 3) **Deeper commercialization focus**: New targets for private sector models (D-5) and seed company partnerships (WorldVeg workstream). 4) **Explicit climate adaptation**: Drought-resilient push-pull systems (D-9) and heat-tolerant crops (e.g., mungbean) added. 5) **Impact measurement**: GBPPD workstream addresses data gaps that hindered prior prioritization.

quote.name: 5455281.odt, Evaluation of DFID’s funding
quote.section: The PMFM provided the Centres with a clear focus on the agreed outputs and outcomes. It has also been effective in facilitating the delivery of high quality research [...] There is a need to return to the original intention of fewer milestones and lighter reporting [...] These refinements will allow for more effective results-based incentives, budget predictability and thus improve value for money.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages: 1) **Private sector investments** in seed systems (e.g., mungbean varieties commercialized by African companies). 2) **National government contributions** to Plantwise clinics (e.g., clinic data used for national pest monitoring). 3) **Other donor alignment**: DFID’s coordination with CGIAR and bilateral donors (e.g., USAID) amplifies reach (e.g., Plantwise’s 35M target).

quote.name: D0004392.odt, Summary Information
quote.section: Original project budget: £35 million; Cost extension value: £18 million; New project end date: March 2022.

metadata.programme_name: Directorate for a Research and Innovation Hub on Technology for Education (EdTech Hub)
metadata.quote: "The EdTech Hub is an opportunity to build the UK brand in innovation and digital technology to enable us to drive transformative change in education." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 17th June 2019–16th June 2027" (61065939.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research on EdTech interventions), implementation research (testing and scaling interventions), and policy influence (providing strategic advice to governments and donors). It also includes direct deployment support for EdTech interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The project will catalyse a significant global shift in the approach to EdTech in development with large scale learning impact across the DFID priority countries." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: gold standard research on what works in delivering EdTech at scale
early-stage innovations support through 'sandboxes' for testing new technologies
deployment support for EdTech interventions to governments and DFID programmes
global leadership through strategic advice, standards, and research outputs
direct support for early-stage innovation (e.g., onebillion intervention scaling)
publication of research findings and evidence products
quarterly dashboards and synthesis reports
support to DFID interventions via a 'call-down' service
establishment of a global community of practice
what_objectives.summary: The EdTech Hub aims to transform education through digital technology by generating rigorous evidence, supporting innovation, and deploying effective EdTech solutions at scale across DFID priority countries.
what_objectives.quote: "Research on interventions going to scale. There is a lack of reliable research around EdTech, especially its effectiveness at scale. In order to produce global shifts in this area, the programme will produce gold standard research on what works in delivering EdTech at scale." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)

countries_regions: Malawi (specific mention for sandbox and onebillion intervention)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in DFID priority countries, which include fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS). The original business case explicitly rated the programme as 'high' risk.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: High" (54104789.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited capacity in education systems)
data limitations (lack of rigorous evidence on EdTech impact)
gender inequities (digital access gaps for women and girls)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Infrastructure limitations (e.g., 3.6 billion people lack electricity access) affect the feasibility of digital interventions. Weak institutional capacity in target countries requires significant support for research uptake and implementation. Gender disparities in digital access (e.g., women 14% less likely to own mobile phones) necessitate equity-focused design.
where_context.quote: "3.6 billion people have no or partial access to electricity and over half the world’s population have internet access (World Development Report 2016)." (54104789.odt, Annex A)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Not explicitly named in the provided documents (consortium includes UK-based organizations)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The hub is led by a consortium with UK-based organizations (e.g., onebillion) and includes DFID-funded posts for oversight. Southern partners (e.g., in-country research teams) are implemented through competitive procurement but decision-making remains with the Northern-led consortium and DFID.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for in-country researchers (through regional/country research teams)
mentorship via DFID-funded programme posts (e.g., A2 Education Adviser)
institutional strengthening through research uptake support
co-authorship and knowledge sharing via global community of practice

partner_organizations.name: onebillion
partner_organizations.role: implementation of scaled EdTech intervention (maths and reading software)
partner_organizations.location: UK (operating in Malawi and East Africa)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: partnership for deployment support and in-kind contributions

partner_organizations.name: Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and strategic partner

partner_organizations.name: Regional/Country Research Teams (3 teams)
partner_organizations.role: conduct at-scale research on EdTech interventions

partner_organizations.name: Rapid Response Research Teams (RRRTs)
partner_organizations.role: initial identification of promising EdTech initiatives

partner_organizations.name: DFID Education Advisers (programme-funded posts)
partner_organizations.role: oversight, research uptake, and linkage with DFID country offices

who_partners.quote: "The programme will procure an excellent consortium of organisations to run the programme." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct contracts (for the consortium and research teams), accountable grants (e.g., £3 million to onebillion), and programme-funded posts (DFID advisers embedded in the hub). The hub itself operates as a secretariat with a mix of core funding and project-specific allocations.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The EdTech Hub operates as a global platform with a central secretariat (UK-based) managing multiple strands: at-scale research, innovation sandbox, and deployment support. It coordinates with DFID, World Bank, and in-country teams through a multi-stakeholder governance model.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition was chosen to ensure the highest quality bids and drive innovation. The process includes multi-stage procurement for regional/country research teams and innovation partners, with DFID retaining oversight through an Executive Steering Committee.
how_mechanism.quote: "Through open competition we are likely to secure the best programme management as well as attract several international figureheads to provide strategic and intellectual leadership." (54104789.odt, Option 3)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The hub is governed by an Executive Steering Committee with DFID, World Bank, and consortium representatives. Sub-awards for research teams and innovations are allocated through open competitive processes, with DFID approval required for major decisions.
how_governance.quote: "The hub would engage directly with donors and governments as well as businesses... DFID would have a larger role in selection through the Executive Steering Committee." (54104789.odt, Option 3)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research strands (e.g., at-scale research vs. innovation) with DFID approval. The £16 million extension explicitly allows flexibility to "fund the implementation of EdTech interventions as per SCSs and Ministerial steer."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an iterative approach, with research priorities adjusted based on emerging evidence (e.g., innovation sandbox outcomes). The £1.8 million "other grants" component is explicitly designed for iterative definition as the hub progresses.
how_flexibility.quote: "An additional £16m is requested to specifically fund the implementation of EdTech interventions and help take them to scale using the evidence generated by the hub. This will be spread over the life of the programme... The additional funding will stay within the goals and objectives of the hub programme but will help to accelerate the programme’s impact and reach." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → EdTech Hub Consortium (secretariat) → Regional/Country Research Teams/Innovation Partners → End Implementers (e.g., onebillion, governments)
how_efficiency.quote: "The budget for all teams includes travel (including international travel to the UK/REAL, Cambridge), as well as enumerators and field costs." (61065939.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do Nothing (counterfactual)
Option 2: Co-fund existing research (non-DFID led) through partnerships (e.g., IDRC)
Option 3: DFID-funded global multi-disciplinary EdTech Research Hub (DFID-led) through open competition
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (DFID-led hub) was selected for its ability to drive quality through competition, ensure DFID control over priorities, and create a multi-disciplinary platform. It was deemed superior for generating a global shift in EdTech evidence and practice, with greater flexibility to adapt to emerging needs.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (competition drives down costs and improves quality)
risk mitigation (DFID retains oversight through governance structures)
partner capacity (open competition attracts top global experts)
equity (explicit focus on marginalized groups, including girls and children with disabilities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity in establishing the hub and managing senior influencers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful procurement process and explicit expectations for DFID’s role; publicizing opportunities widely to attract leading thinkers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Difficulty in recruiting high-level global experts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging DFID’s reputation and cross-HMG networks (e.g., EdtechUK, No.10 Digital Task Force).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Administrative burden on DFID for hub management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated programme-funded posts (e.g., A2 Education Adviser) to oversee coordination and research uptake.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (targeted support for marginalized groups and gender-inclusive design)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 allows for the ‘hub’ to move around and be virtual – it could be convened in differing countries over the 8 years so as to draw in a wider pool of experts and researchers... Overall our assessment is that Option 3 is a significantly stronger proposal as it provides a better opportunity to deliver on the needs and challenges set out in the strategic case as it invites the market to compete for tender, helping to drive up the suitability and quality of bids and drive down the cost." (54104789.odt, Comparison of Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope and focus on DFID priority countries (including FCAS) constrain partner selection to organizations with proven capacity to operate in challenging environments. Infrastructure limitations (e.g., electricity, connectivity) require partners with adaptive technical solutions.
q27_constraints_detail: infrastructure constraints favor partners with off-grid or low-bandwidth EdTech solutions
FCAS contexts require partners with conflict-sensitive approaches and local trust
gender inequities necessitate partners with inclusive design expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rigorous, scalable evidence (WHAT) determines the platform-based delivery structure (HOW), which integrates research, innovation, and deployment strands. The focus on policy influence requires a governance model with DFID and multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank) to ensure credibility.
q28_linkages: evidence generation → platform structure (hub + research teams) to synthesize global learning
implementation research → deployment support strand to test and scale interventions
policy influence → steering committee with DFID/World Bank to guide strategic direction
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between rapid scaling (efficiency) and inclusive design (equity). For example, the onebillion intervention targets marginalized children (e.g., refugees, girls, children with disabilities) but requires additional funding to reduce costs to $1/child/year for scalability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: iterative innovation sandbox balances quick testing with equity considerations
expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led consortium ensures rigor but embeds Southern researchers for context relevance
cost vs. reach: accountable grants for onebillion prioritize learning gains over per-unit cost reductions
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (FCAS, weak institutions) necessitates intensive oversight, including embedded DFID advisers and milestone-based payments to mitigate implementation risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the hub’s design, with Southern researchers integrated into regional teams and DFID-funded posts (e.g., Country Link Adviser) to ensure knowledge transfer and local ownership.
intersections.quote: "The poorest and most marginalised are the least likely to get quality education... EdTech has a huge potential to level the playing field if we ensure interventions effectively reach and raise the learning outcomes of the most vulnerable and hard-to-reach." (54104789.odt, Gender Equality Act Compliance)

key_programme_risks: Failure to generate robust evidence on EdTech impact at scale
Limited research uptake by governments and donors
Inability to attract high-quality partners for innovation and research
Equity gaps in EdTech access (e.g., girls, children with disabilities)
Infrastructure barriers (electricity, connectivity) limiting intervention reach
Political or institutional resistance to EdTech adoption in target countries
Coordination challenges among multi-stakeholder consortium
Reputational risk if interventions fail to deliver learning outcomes

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-method research design (RCTs + qualitative studies) with DFID oversight; quarterly synthesis reports to ensure learning.
Embedded DFID advisers (e.g., Country Link Adviser) and targeted dissemination strategies (e.g., policy briefs, dashboards).
Explicit gender and disability targets in research design; partnerships with inclusive EdTech providers (e.g., onebillion).
Focus on adaptive technologies (e.g., offline-capable software) and partnerships with energy innovators (e.g., BBOXX).
Clear governance structures (Steering Committee) and milestone-based management.

fcas_specific_lessons: Prioritize interventions with low connectivity requirements (e.g., offline digital content).
Embed conflict sensitivity in EdTech design to avoid exacerbating tensions.
Leverage existing DFID country programmes (e.g., Girls Education Challenge) for rapid deployment.
Use rapid response teams (RRRTs) to assess feasibility in fragile contexts before scaling.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID EdTech programmes (e.g., in Tanzania) demonstrated the need for rigorous impact evaluation and adaptive management. The Girls Education Challenge highlighted the potential of technology to reach marginalized girls but also the risks of digital exclusion.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The £16 million extension was added post-procurement to address gaps in implementation funding, reflecting lessons on the need to pair research with deployment support. The innovation sandbox model was introduced to test interventions before scaling, based on past failures of one-size-fits-all approaches.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID has again pledged to help 11m children gain a decent education between 2015 and 2020... Millionsof children are still not learning basic skills; EdTech is increasingly seen as a solution to address this global learning crisis." (54104789.odt, Intervention Summary)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages in-kind support from the World Bank and attracts co-funding from multilateral partners (e.g., Gates Foundation). The hub’s evidence base is expected to catalyze additional investments from USAID, Norway, and private sector actors.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes both capital expenditures (e.g., EdTech hardware/software for interventions) and revenue expenditures (e.g., research costs, salaries, travel). The £10 million for implementation funding is explicitly for scaling interventions (capital), while research and hub operations are revenue.
financial_details.quote: "An additional £16m is requested to specifically fund the implementation of EdTech interventions and help take them to scale using the evidence generated by the hub." (61065939.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: Public Financial Management Multi Donor Trust Fund – Phase II
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to establish and support an effective Public Financial Management system that facilitates the delivery of better public services to improve the lives of the people of Nepal." (11750739.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: July 2017 - January 2026" and "New project end date (if applicable): January 2028" (D0004272.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening PFM institutions and systems), financing mechanism (channeling funds through a World Bank-managed Multi Donor Trust Fund), and implementation research (testing and scaling PFM reforms). It focuses on improving Nepal's public financial management systems to enhance service delivery and accountability.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme aims to establish and support an effective Public Financial Management system that facilitates the delivery of better public services to improve the lives of the people of Nepal. The programme will be delivered through a World Bank managed Multi Donor Trust Fund." (11750739.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened efficiency and results orientation of the budget cycle at national and sub-national level (e.g., capital budget execution rate reaches 50% at the end of the second trimester and 90% at the end of the year)
Increased professional capacity of key PFM stakeholders (e.g., 30 staff per year over 5 years receive internationally accredited diploma in PFM)
Enhanced accountability in PFM systems (e.g., strengthened OAG capacity to deliver on its mandate in compliance with ISSAI)
Improved financial and investment management practices (e.g., operationalisation of the Project Bank and quality assurance of the sixteenth Plan)
Strengthened inter-governmental fiscal transfer mechanisms (e.g., support to the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission)
Greater transparency and accountability of GoN finances (e.g., support GoN participation in the Open Government Partnership)
what_objectives.summary: The programme supports Nepal's PFM reforms through a World Bank-managed trust fund, focusing on budget efficiency, capacity building, and accountability to improve public service delivery and fiscal management.
what_objectives.quote: "The overall impact of the programme will be ‘an effective Public Financial Management system that facilitates the delivery of better public services to improve the lives of the people of Nepal.’" (11750739.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal's PFM systems remain weak with fiduciary risks due to systemic weaknesses such as poor coordination, weak capacity, and limited accountability. However, the programme is assessed as 'Minor risk' by DFID, indicating a moderate risk profile.
where_context.q5_source: "Despite some improvements in recent years, Nepal’s systems of PFM remain weak at all levels. Fiduciary risks remain due to systemic weaknesses such as poor intra-governmental coordination; weak technical and administrative capacity; weak accountability and oversight functions." (11750739.odt, Strategic Case) and "This programme is assessed to be Minor risk." (11750739.odt, Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The challenging intra-governmental context, weak technical capacity, and political patronage constrain PFM reforms. The recent constitutional restructuring and creation of new government tiers add complexity and risk to the implementation of PFM systems.
where_context.quote: "Coordination between the actors in Nepal’s fiscal architecture is limited, constrained by unclear organisational power, remits and political patronage; non-compatible systems (IT, HR, approvals etc); and limited data for decision-making." (11750739.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led) manages the trust fund and oversees implementation, with the Government of Nepal (Southern) as the primary beneficiary and implementer of reforms. Decision-making is shared through a joint WB-DP Technical Coordination Committee and Project Coordination Committee (PCC).
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., internationally accredited diploma in PFM for 30 staff per year)
institutional strengthening (e.g., capacity building for PEFA Secretariat, OAG, and other PFM stakeholders)
mentorship (e.g., support to strengthen accounting, reporting, and audit practices)

partner_organizations.role: Primary Beneficiary and Implementer

who_partners.quote: "The MDTF is administered by the WB according to WB policies and procedures. The WB has demonstrated its capacity to manage the programme in the first phase of funding (2010-2015)." (11750739.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of a World Bank-managed Multi Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) and bilateral contracts for technical assistance. The MDTF pools funds from multiple donors, while the bilateral component provides flexible technical support.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The MDTF is managed by the World Bank with oversight from a joint WB-DP Technical Coordination Committee and a Project Coordination Committee (PCC). The bilateral technical assistance is delivered through contracts with specialist suppliers.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected based on its established role as the MDTF manager and its technical expertise in PFM reforms. The bilateral technical assistance is procured through FCDO's EACD frameworks.
how_mechanism.quote: "The MDTF is administered by the WB according to WB policies and procedures." (11750739.odt, Commercial Case) and "The strategic PFM support and fiduciary risk management (£1.3m) will be delivered through contracts procured through EACD frameworks." (D0004272.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The MDTF is governed by a Project Coordination Committee (PCC) and a joint WB-DP Technical Coordination Committee. The PCC approves projects and updates work plans every six months.
how_governance.quote: "Projects will be approved by a Project Coordination Committee (PCC), enabling regular (six-monthly) updating and adjustment as required." (11750739.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated based on mid-term evaluations and emerging needs, but this requires approval from the PCC and alignment with GoN priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments based on mid-term evaluations, funding needs, and changes in the political/economic context. The MDTF strategy is designed to respond to emerging priorities, such as fiscal federalism.
how_flexibility.quote: "The results of the mid-term evaluation, combined with funding needs of the MDTF, calculation made on pipeline projects, current trust fund balance and expected DP contributions will determine additional contribution of DFID of up to £1.5 million to the MDTF." (11750739.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (MDTF Manager) → Government of Nepal (Implementer)
how_efficiency.quote: "At present centrally agreed rates, DFID is expecting to incur estimated cost of approximately 7.4% in combined management/administration costs." (11750739.odt, Commercial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Delivery through a contracted service provider
Delivery through GoN-managed Financial Aid
Do nothing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The MDTF was chosen because it is a trusted, established mechanism with a proven track record in Nepal. It aligns with GoN's preference for a 'single-window' approach to reduce transaction costs and improve coordination. The World Bank's technical expertise and robust management systems also provide strong value for money and risk mitigation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Centrally agreed WB management fees (7.4%) reduce the direct funding available for programme activities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The fees are justified by the WB's technical expertise and robust management systems, which reduce fiduciary risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited direct DFID control over programme management due to WB's administrative arrangements.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID works within established WB programme management practices and has influenced improvements, such as the recruitment of a full-time, in-country Programme Manager.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Heavy time investment required for DFID SRO to coordinate with multiple DPs under the MDTF.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The WB's in-country Programme Manager has improved coordination and reduced the burden on DFID.

why_rationale.quote: "The MDTF is a trusted and established mechanism with a proven track record of delivering core PFM reforms at the central level... The MDTF – drawing on UK contributions – has supported the rollout of the TSA system that has increased government control of expenditure and improved budget information for planning and fiscal management purposes." (11750739.odt, Commercial Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The weak and unstable governance context in Nepal limits the ability of GoN to manage funds directly, making a multilateral approach (via World Bank) necessary. The political economy and weak institutions also constrain the selection of local partners for direct implementation.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak technical and administrative capacity in GoN limits direct management of funds.
Political patronage and unclear organizational power constrain coordination and reform implementation.
High fiduciary risks in GoN systems necessitate external management (e.g., World Bank).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for large-scale, systemic PFM reforms requires a multilateral platform (MDTF) to coordinate multiple donors and align with GoN's long-term strategy. The complexity of reforms also necessitates technical expertise (World Bank) and flexible funding mechanisms (bilateral contracts).
q28_linkages: Systemic PFM reforms require a coordinated, multi-donor approach (MDTF).
Technical complexity necessitates World Bank's expertise and management.
Need for flexibility in responding to political/economic changes drives the use of bilateral contracts for technical assistance.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme balances the efficiency of a Northern-led multilateral mechanism (World Bank) with efforts to build Southern ownership (GoN implementation and capacity building). The trade-off is between the speed and expertise of the World Bank and the long-term sustainability of GoN-led reforms.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: World Bank's expertise enables rapid implementation but may limit GoN's direct control.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical leadership vs. Southern institutional strengthening.
Cost vs. reach: Management fees (7.4%) reduce direct funding but provide robust oversight and risk mitigation.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (weak institutions, political economy) necessitates intensive oversight through the MDTF's governance structure (PCC, Technical Coordination Committee) and milestone-based reporting.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with GoN staff trained to take on greater roles in PFM systems over time. The World Bank's initial leadership is expected to transition to stronger GoN ownership as capacity improves.
intersections.quote: "The MDTF has been instrumental in terms of improving the alignment and coordination of donor support for PFM reforms in Nepal... The MDTF’s credibility, influencing and convening power." (11750739.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Weak intra-governmental coordination and political patronage may hinder reform implementation.
Limited technical capacity in GoN could slow progress or reduce sustainability of reforms.
High staff turnover in GoN may disrupt continuity and institutional memory.
Fragmentation of PFM systems across government tiers (federal, provincial, local) could undermine coherence.
Political interference may disrupt budget processes and fiscal discipline.
Changes in GoN's fiscal federalism strategy may require programme adjustments.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: MDTF's joint coordination committees (PCC, Technical Coordination Committee) and World Bank's convening power help align stakeholders.
Capacity building is a core programme objective, with training and institutional strengthening embedded in all activities.
Long-term institutional support (e.g., PEFA Secretariat, OAG) and embedded technical assistance aim to build sustainable capacity.
MDTF's focus on harmonization and alignment across government tiers, with flexibility to adapt to federalism reforms.
World Bank's robust management systems and milestone-based oversight reduce risks of disruption.
Programme design includes flexibility to revisit support areas as GoN's plans evolve (e.g., separate fiscal federalism component).

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts like Nepal, donor coordination is critical to avoid fragmentation and reduce transaction costs for government.
Technical assistance must be long-term and adaptive to build capacity in weak institutional environments.
Flexibility in programme design is essential to respond to political and structural changes (e.g., federalism).
Embedded advisors and joint committees help mitigate risks of political interference and weak accountability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The first phase of the MDTF (2010-2015) demonstrated that despite challenges, technical reforms (e.g., Treasury Single Account, audit modernization) can be successfully delivered with strong government ownership and donor coordination. The Programme Completion Review highlighted the MDTF's role in improving alignment and reducing fragmentation among donors.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The second phase includes greater flexibility to respond to emerging needs (e.g., federalism), more focus on sub-national levels, and embedded fiduciary risk management across the portfolio. The addendum also integrates bilateral technical assistance to address gaps identified in the 2021 PFM Portfolio Review.
risks_lessons.quote: "The MDTF has been instrumental in terms of improving the alignment and coordination of donor support for PFM reforms in Nepal... The Review noted that the MDTF has played an important part in the achievements reflected in the second PEFA assessment." (11750739.odt, Strategic Case) and "An independent PFM review of the BEK portfolio pointed out that BEK programmes have a siloed approach to fiduciary risk management and BEK therefore misses opportunities for system strengthening." (D0004272.odt, INFORMATION)

co_funding_partners.partner: Australian Department for Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The MDTF pools resources from multiple donors, reducing transaction costs for GoN and improving coordination. The World Bank's management also leverages its technical expertise and global best practices.
financial_details.quote: "The total budget for PFM MDTF II is £3,220,000. This will be increased by £1,300,000 to a new total of £4,520,000." (D0004272.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "At present centrally agreed rates, DFID is expecting to incur estimated cost of approximately 7.4% in combined management/administration costs." (11750739.odt, Commercial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Transparency and Accountability to Improve Economic Development and Service Delivery (TRACTION)
metadata.quote: "The programme will invest up to £16.8m (£13.8m +£3m) over six years (2018-23) to improve the accountability and responsiveness of local and national government in Malawi, for tangible economic and service delivery outcomes for the poorest people." (31838223.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 22/05/2018 – 30/09/2024" and "New project end date: 31 December 2025" (D0003939.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: TRACTION combines implementation research (testing accountability interventions), capacity building (strengthening civil society and government institutions), and service delivery (improving public goods provision). It uses a politically-informed, adaptive approach to address governance constraints that hinder economic growth and service delivery in Malawi.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will invest up to £16.8m... to improve the accountability and responsiveness of local and national government in Malawi... It will take a problem-focused, politically-informed, adaptive approach with potential to deliver some of the transformative changes needed on critical issues that hold back Malawi’s development." (31838223.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: More money allocated and released to implement goods/services prioritized by citizens (output)
Evidence that regulations are being implemented to improve management of public services and market chains (output)
Evidence that citizen groups are engaging with state actors to resolve issues and monitor progress (output)
Evidence that elected representatives are seeking support from electorate for delivery of public goods (output)
1.5 million people directly benefiting from issues-based projects in the short-term (intermediary outcome)
Improved access to services and economic development opportunities for Malawians (impact)
Support to 100+ NGOs through Tilitonse Foundation (discontinued in later phase)
Training of 1,500+ political party agents and election observers (2019 elections)
Civic education reaching 1 million+ Malawians (2019 elections)
Strengthened capacity of Malawi Electoral Commission, Malawi Police Service, and Centre for Multi-party Democracy (2025 elections)
Establishment of Early Warning System (EWS) and Situation Room for conflict mitigation (2025 elections)
Support to inclusion of women, youth, PWDs, and people living with albinism in electoral processes (2025 elections)
what_objectives.summary: TRACTION aims to improve government accountability and responsiveness in Malawi through a politically-smart, issues-based approach that combines electoral support, civil society strengthening, and targeted interventions to address governance blockages affecting service delivery and economic development.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver the following high level objectives: The outcome of the programme will be that there is ‘Improved accountability and responsiveness in the management of public goods and services’." (31838223.odt, What will the project deliver?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Malawi is politically stable with peaceful transitions but faces governance challenges including patronage, weak institutions, and threats to civic space. The programme carries a 'moderate' risk rating as it operates in a context where civil society is fragmented and government occasionally restricts civic space.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (31838223.odt, Summary Sheet) and "Civil society is fragmented and there are signs of the Government attempting to further restrict civic space through a new NGO policy and amendment to the NGO Act." (31838223.odt, Strategic Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Patronage networks undermine merit-based service delivery, weak institutions limit policy implementation, and civic space restrictions hinder civil society's ability to hold government accountable. Climate vulnerability and high poverty exacerbate governance challenges by increasing pressure on resources and services.
where_context.quote: "Much of Malawi’s dysfunction has its roots in how the country is governed... Political parties act as vehicles for the election of their leaders rather than offering something closer to a collective national good... favouritism in procurement, access to goods and services... often serve patronage goals." (31838223.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority through steering committees and approval processes, though implementation involves significant Southern partner roles. For example, UNDP manages the Elections Basket Fund but must report to a Steering Committee co-chaired by the Malawi Minister of Finance.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for election observers and political party agents
technical assistance to Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC)
support to Centre for Multi-party Democracy (CMD) on oversight and gender mainstreaming
capacity building for civil society organizations through Tilitonse Foundation (discontinued)
political economy analysis training for CSOs
media and advocacy training
support to Malawi Police Service on election security and human rights
youth and women engagement programmes

who_partners.quote: "DFID has signed a Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID to deliver a £2.2m programme... USAID is responsible for management of the delivery partner." (49510810.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "UNDP will lead the delivery of the project... UNDP will be responsible for management of downstream partners such as the Malawi Electoral Commission and the Centre for Multiparty Democracy." (D0003939.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: (1) Delegated Cooperation Agreements with USAID for election support, (2) Contribution Arrangements with UNDP for the Elections Basket Fund, (3) Accountable Grants to Tilitonse Foundation (discontinued), and (4) commercial contracts with Palladium for the Issue-Based Accountability Project. This allows pooling of donor resources while maintaining FCDO oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through multiple layers: (1) FCDO provides funding to UNDP (Elections Basket Fund) and USAID (MEIP) as primary implementers; (2) UNDP and USAID then manage downstream partners like MEC, CMD, and CSOs; (3) Steering Committees (co-chaired by Malawi government and UNDP) provide strategic oversight. For IBAP, Palladium acts as a commercial supplier under direct FCDO contract.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: open competition for IBAP (Palladium selected through commercial tender); direct award for UNDP/USAID (existing partnerships)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNDP and USAID were selected based on existing multi-donor frameworks and their established roles in Malawi's electoral processes. Palladium was selected through a commercial tender process for IBAP to ensure a problem-driven, adaptive approach. The Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID leverages their existing CEPPS consortium.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID is in the process of procuring a commercial supplier to deliver a £10.8m problem-driven programme [IBAP]." (49510810.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "DFID has signed a Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID to deliver a £2.2m programme... USAID is responsible for management of the delivery partner." (49510810.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: For the Elections Basket Fund: (1) Technical Committee (monthly) with representatives from all contributing partners, MEC, CMD, and MPS oversees implementation and risk management; (2) Steering Committee (quarterly), co-chaired by Malawi Minister of Finance and UNDP Resident Representative, provides strategic oversight. For MEIP: a joint Project Management Board with FCDO and USAID representatives reviews progress. IBAP is managed directly by Palladium under FCDO contract.
how_governance.quote: "The Steering Committee (SC) is responsible for the oversight and strategic leadership of the Project and will comprise of all Heads of Missions, and chaired by the Minister of Finance, whilst the UNDP Resident Representative will co-chair... The Steering Committee shall convene on a quarterly basis." (D0003939.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "FCDO will conduct spot check and monitoring visits to project sites... An indicator tracking table will be developed to ensure that the project progressively achieves key results." (49510810.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the Elections Basket Fund can be reallocated across activities based on Technical Committee recommendations, but FCDO contributions are not earmarked for specific outputs. IBAP has flexibility to scale issues-based projects up or down based on progress, but requires FCDO approval for major changes. The 2020 reduction in Tilitonse Foundation support demonstrates ability to reallocate funds between components.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses real-time monitoring to identify successful interventions for scaling and underperforming ones for closure. IBAP's adaptive management allows shifting resources to issues showing greatest momentum. Mid-term reviews (e.g., IBAP in 2022) inform adjustments. However, major changes (e.g., component discontinuation) require Ministerial approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The issues-based component of the programme has been designed to be adaptable, with activities scaled up or down or closed depending on progress." (31838223.odt, Does the programme have sufficient flexibility?) and "The Mid-term Review... made a number of significant recommendations including shortening the issue selection and implementation process. Palladium (the contractor) will take this forward and implement more IBPs within the extension period." (D0003939.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNDP/USAID/Palladium (primary implementers) → MEC/CMD/CSOs (downstream partners). For IBAP: FCDO → Palladium → sub-grantees/state actors.
how_efficiency.quote: "UNDP will develop annual work-plans and budgets that will be reviewed by a technical committee before being approved by a steering committee." (49510810.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The Mid-term Review... found the programme to be meeting expectations and made recommendations including shortening the issue selection and implementation process." (D0003939.odt, IBAP)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (Option 1)
Building on the best to date: Elections, social accountability, and improved support to civil society (Option 2)
Doing things differently: A more politically informed approach to improve economic development and service delivery, complemented by successful elements from Option 2 (Option 3 - CHOSEN)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its adaptive, politically-informed approach that addresses Malawi's governance constraints more effectively than traditional accountability programmes. It combines electoral support (credibility), issues-based interventions (tangible results), and civil society strengthening (sustainability) while allowing flexibility to respond to context changes. The mixed modality leverages UNDP/USAID's existing platforms for efficiency and risk management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on UNDP/USAID platforms may limit FCDO's direct control over implementation details.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO participates in Steering/Technical Committees and conducts independent monitoring visits. Contribution Arrangements include clauses for strategic influence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented civil society in Malawi could undermine collective action in issues-based projects.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IBAP uses facilitators with deep political economy knowledge to build coalitions. Capacity building for CSOs is embedded (though Tilitonse support was reduced).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in elections could compromise credibility of results.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-donor Basket Fund and independent observation (e.g., Parallel Vote Tabulation) enhance transparency. Conflict mitigation mechanisms are strengthened.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Adaptive management in IBAP may lead to mission creep or lack of focus.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear issue selection criteria based on political economy analysis. Mid-term reviews and FCDO approval for major changes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Discontinuation of Tilitonse Foundation support reduces civil society engagement.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IBAP will prioritize issues with strong civil society involvement. Remaining funds focus on marginalized groups through other components.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3: Doing things differently... represents a significant change in DFID’s approach to tackling the underlying constraints to development in Malawi. It will be both explicitly more political in approach, and more integrated with the rest of the DFID portfolio." (31838223.odt, Appraisal Case) and "The programme approach – i.e. supporting coalitions of interest around tangible issues people care about... is more sustainable than traditional accountability programmes." (31838223.odt, Is the programme coherent with wider international community?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Malawi's political economy constraints (patronage, weak institutions, restricted civic space) limit partner selection to organizations with: (1) existing government relationships (e.g., UNDP, CMD), (2) ability to navigate elite networks (e.g., Palladium's political economy experts), and (3) donor protection (e.g., USAID's CEPPS consortium). Local CSOs are engaged but require capacity building due to fragmentation and repression risks.
q27_constraints_detail: Government restrictions on NGO activities limit direct funding to local CSOs, necessitating intermediaries like Tilitonse Foundation (later discontinued).
Patronage networks require partners with political savvy (e.g., Palladium's 'reform coalitions' approach).
Weak MEC capacity necessitates UNDP's technical support role rather than direct funding.
Security risks during elections require trusted implementers like USAID/CEPPS for observation and conflict mitigation.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for (1) **politically-informed, adaptive interventions** drives the mixed delivery structure (UNDP for elections, Palladium for issues-based work, USAID for civic engagement). (2) **Sustainability goals** explain the focus on Malawian institutions (MEC, CMD) and local CSOs. (3) **Risk mitigation** underpins the use of multi-donor platforms (Basket Fund) and delegated agreements (USAID).
q28_linkages: Issues-based approach (WHAT) → Requires flexible, politically-astute implementers (HOW: Palladium's adaptive management).
Election credibility focus (WHAT) → Necessitates neutral, experienced election support partners (HOW: UNDP/USAID).
Civil society strengthening (WHAT) → Shapes use of grant mechanisms (HOW: Tilitonse Foundation, later IBAP sub-grants).
Decentralization context (WHERE) → Informs local-level budget tracking and social accountability tools (HOW: district-focused IBAP projects).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: (1) **Inclusion vs. Speed**: Discontinuing Tilitonse Foundation (equity loss) to focus IBAP on high-impact issues (efficiency gain). (2) **Local Ownership vs. Expertise**: Using Palladium (Northern expertise) to build coalitions with Malawian reformers. (3) **Cost vs. Reach**: Pooling funds through UNDP (economies of scale) while accepting less direct control over implementation.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Reduced civil society grants (equity) to fund more targeted IBAP issues (efficiency).
Northern-led adaptive management (Palladium) to navigate political economy constraints, with capacity building for local actors.
Multi-donor Basket Fund (cost-effective) but with complex governance layers.
Focus on 'winnable' issues (short-term results) vs. broader systemic change (long-term equity).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives intensive oversight (quarterly Steering Committees, independent monitoring) and preference for established partners (UNDP/USAID) over direct funding to Malawian institutions. Election-related components have additional conflict mitigation layers (e.g., Early Warning Systems).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) MEC/CMD receive technical assistance to improve election delivery; (2) CSOs get training in political economy analysis to engage effectively; (3) Palladium's role includes facilitating coalitions where local capacity is insufficient. The shift from Tilitonse grants to IBAP reflects a move from standalone capacity building to embedded support.
intersections.quote: "The programme should recognise that it is easier to build coalitions of interest groups around material and more specific issues that people have a stake in, rather than broad-brushed approaches to improving accountability... By focusing on issues that matter to a sufficient number of empowered individuals and groups... it is possible to deliver transformative change." (31838223.odt, The way forward) and "Supporting the foundation would deliver important results in terms of improving civil society capacity, protecting civil space at a time it is being threatened, ensuring we leave no-one behind by supporting marginalised groups..." (31838223.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Political interference in elections compromising credibility.
Civil society fragmentation limiting collective action.
Patronage networks undermining merit-based service delivery.
Capacity constraints in MEC/CMD affecting implementation.
Restrictions on civic space reducing programme reach.
Adaptive management leading to mission creep in IBAP.
Discontinuation of Tilitonse support reducing social accountability focus.
COVID-19 delays affecting IBAP implementation.
Cybersecurity threats to election results transmission.
Violence against women and marginalized groups during elections.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-donor Basket Fund, independent election observation (including Parallel Vote Tabulation), and strengthened Electoral Dispute Resolution Mechanism.
IBAP's coalition-building approach and targeted support to women/youth/PWD groups. Use of intermediaries like CMD for dialogue.
Issues-based projects focusing on tangible public goods (e.g., water, agriculture) to shift incentives. Media campaigns to highlight delivery over handouts.
UNDP technical assistance, Training of Trainers (TOT) programmes, and institutional strengthening (e.g., MEC legal unit, CMD Board Charter).
Advocacy through international partners (UNDP, USAID) and conflict mitigation mechanisms. Early Warning Systems for repression risks.
Clear issue selection criteria, mid-term reviews, and FCDO approval for major changes. Focus on 'result momentum' in IBAP.
Reallocating funds to IBAP issues with strong civil society engagement. Prioritizing marginalized groups in remaining components.
12-month extension for IBAP (to July 2025) and focus on less resource-intensive issues.
UNDP support to MEC for internal cybersecurity policies and secure Results Transmission System.
MPS training on human rights and crowd control, community policing initiatives, and CSO-led early warning systems.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS-like contexts (e.g., Malawi's patronage systems), traditional accountability programmes fail without political economy analysis and adaptive management.
Multi-donor platforms (e.g., Basket Fund) reduce individual donor risk exposure while pooling expertise.
Election support must combine technical assistance (MEC capacity) with conflict mitigation (MPS training, CSO observation).
Civil society support requires protection mechanisms (e.g., legal units, fact-checking systems) when civic space is threatened.
Decentralization creates opportunities for local accountability but risks replicating patronage at district level without safeguards.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID programmes in Malawi (Tilitonse, Kalondolondo) showed that: (1) **Coalitions** (CSOs + government + private sector) achieve more sustainable results than standalone projects; (2) **Media engagement** (especially radio) amplifies accountability gains; (3) **Capacity building alone is insufficient** without addressing incentive structures; (4) **Election credibility** requires both technical support (MEC) and civic education to shift voter expectations from patronage to performance; (5) **Local issue focus** (e.g., water, agriculture) generates more traction than broad governance reforms.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations include: (1) Shifting from Tilitonse grants to issues-based projects (IBAP) for greater impact; (2) Adding cybersecurity and Early Warning Systems to election support after 2019 disputes; (3) Incorporating State House advisory support in IBAP based on political economy insights; (4) Extending IBAP timeline to recover from COVID-19 delays; (5) Strengthening MPS role in election security after 2019 violence; (6) Discontinuing Tilitonse to focus on higher-momentum issues.
risks_lessons.quote: "Coalitions for change: Where civil society organisations worked together in thematic areas... or where they worked in collaboration with government representatives... better results were achieved." (31838223.odt, Learning from previous DFID Malawi programming) and "The 2014 elections showed a shift towards more issues-based politics... While this is very unlikely to displace entirely traditional voting patterns by 2019, there is a basis to build on." (31838223.odt, Credible elections) and "The Mid-term Review... made a number of significant recommendations including shortening the issue selection and implementation process." (D0003939.odt, IBAP)

co_funding_partners.partner: EU, Irish Aid, Royal Norwegian Embassy (for Tilitonse Foundation)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Elections Basket Fund pools FCDO contributions (£2.5m for 2019; £2.6m for 2025) with other donors, increasing collective impact. The Tilitonse Foundation (discontinued) leveraged £9.25m from EU/Irish Aid/Norway against FCDO's planned £2.1m (24% of total).
financial_details.quote: "The EU, Irish Aid and the Royal Norwegian Embassy have committed £9.25 million to the foundation for the first five years of its operations... DFID’s contribution is estimated to be 24% of the overall commitment to the foundation." (31838223.odt, Appraisal Case) and "UK will provide an additional support of £2m to the UNDP Managed Elections Basket Fund. With this additional support, the total UK contribution to the Fund will be £2.5m." (49510810.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: J-PAL Governance, Crime and Conflict Initiative (GCCI)
metadata.quote: "The J-PAL Governance, Crime and Conflict Initiative (J-PAL GCCI) will help to address the operational evidence gap in tackling bad governance, conflict, and crime in DFID priority countries." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 01/04/2017", "End Date: 31/03/2022" (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through Randomised Control Trials (RCTs) to test interventions in governance, crime, and conflict. It also includes **policy influence** by engaging with policymakers to ensure uptake of research findings, and **capacity building** through training and researcher-policymaker matchmaking events.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The J-PAL Governance, Crime and Conflict Initiative (J-PAL GCCI) will help to address the operational evidence gap in tackling bad governance, conflict, and crime in DFID priority countries. It will deliver a new set of high quality Randomised Control Trials (RCTs) that test the effectiveness of practical interventions in governance, crime, and conflict; and engage with policy makers, including in HMG, to facilitate the uptake and impact of this new research." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet)
q3_expected_outputs: 23 new RCTs (9 in Governance, 5 in Conflict, 5 in Crime, 4 exploratory)
Policy engagement products (strategies, workshops, policy briefs)
Capacity building: J-PAL Executive Education courses, researcher-policymaker matchmaking events in LICs/MICs
Evidence synthesis papers (Governance White Paper, Conflict/Crime evidence reviews)
Research dissemination workshops to engage policymakers
what_objectives.summary: The programme generates rigorous evidence through RCTs to identify 'what works' in governance, crime, and conflict interventions, while building capacity among policymakers and researchers to use this evidence. It directly informs HMG and DFID programming to improve value for money and impact.
what_objectives.quote: "RCTs are the most rigorous way of establishing the impact of specific development interventions. The research will help identify ‘what works’ to inform HMG policy and programmes." (8260583.odt, Intervention Summary)

countries_regions: Middle East, South Asia, Africa (strategic regions for UK)
Latin America (for global evidence base, though not DFID priority)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS) where research is inherently high-risk due to security, political instability, and weak institutions. However, the overall programme risk is rated as **moderate** because risks are spread across a portfolio of grants, and J-PAL/IPA have established risk management strategies for challenging environments.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet) and "Risks (of opportunities for evaluating interventions not being available; field research being interrupted by conflict and violence) are greater in the new components on crime and conflict compared with the well tested governance initiative." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and conflict disrupt field research (e.g., "field research being interrupted by conflict and violence"). Weak institutions limit the availability of credible research partners and suitable interventions to evaluate. Data limitations in FCAS make rigorous evidence generation more challenging.
where_context.quote: "Risks (of opportunities for evaluating interventions not being available; field research being interrupted by conflict and violence) are greater in the new components on crime and conflict compared with the well tested governance initiative." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) at MIT
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: J-PAL (MIT) designs and manages grant competitions, selects research questions, and quality-assures delivery. Southern researchers participate as grantees, co-investigators, or through capacity-building activities, but decision-making power rests with J-PAL/IPA/CCL.
q10_capacity_building_details: J-PAL Executive Education courses for policymakers (including LIC/MIC officials)
Researcher-policymaker matchmaking events in LICs/MICs
Mentorship of early-career researchers (supervised by J-PAL Affiliates)
Co-authorship opportunities for Southern researchers in RCTs
Targeted engagement with UK academic sector to build RCT capability

partner_organizations.name: Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) at MIT
partner_organizations.role: Lead partner; manages Governance component, overall funds, and quality assurance

partner_organizations.name: Innovations for Poverty Action (IPA)
partner_organizations.role: Manages Conflict component; specializes in FCAS research
partner_organizations.location: North (USA, with country offices in LICs/MICs)

partner_organizations.name: University of Chicago Crime Lab (CCL)
partner_organizations.role: Manages Crime component; focuses on crime/violence RCTs

partner_organizations.name: Southern researchers (LICs/MICs)
partner_organizations.role: Grantees, co-investigators, participants in capacity-building

partner_organizations.name: DFID/HMG policy teams (CHASE, Stabilisation Unit, CSSF)
partner_organizations.role: Stakeholders; help identify interventions to evaluate and use evidence

who_partners.quote: "J-PAL (leading on governance); IPA (conflict) and Chicago (crime) will design and run grant competitions which fund RCTs on high priority policy questions... J-PAL will work with long-term partner ‘Innovations in Poverty Action’ (IPA) and a new partner – the University of Chicago Crime Lab (CCL)." (8260583.odt, Intervention Summary)
