how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides an **Accountable Grant** to J-PAL (MIT), which acts as the primary recipient and is responsible for distributing funds to IPA (Conflict) and CCL (Crime). J-PAL manages the grant competitions, quality assurance, and financial reporting. The instrument allows flexibility in research priorities while ensuring accountability through quarterly reports and audits.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: J-PAL acts as the **fund manager**, overseeing three specialized grant competitions (Governance, Conflict, Crime) run by J-PAL, IPA, and CCL respectively. Each component has its own peer review panels and boards. J-PAL consolidates financial/narrative reports from IPA/CCL and submits them to DFID.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: J-PAL was selected based on its **proven track record** in delivering high-quality RCTs, established granting processes, and strong policy engagement. An open competition was considered but rejected due to delays (12-18 months) and the likelihood that J-PAL would win anyway. Re-funding J-PAL was deemed the most efficient and lowest-risk option.
how_mechanism.quote: "Our preferred option is B: accept J-PAL’s proposal and enter negotiations with J-PAL to ensure maximal impact and value for money... J-PAL and IPA have a proven track record in running RCT granting competitions; supporting and quality assuring new RCTs and products." (8260583.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **DFID technical group** will provide formalized technical oversight. The group includes expertise from DFID’s Governance, Conflict and Social Development (GCSD) team, CHASE, Stabilisation Unit (SU), and CSSF. J-PAL will also engage with HMG policy teams to shape research priorities.
how_governance.quote: "Technical oversight will be formalized through establishing a DFID technical group." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet) and "DFID will disburse funds quarterly and in arrears, after receipt and approval of J-PAL’s quarterly invoice and report." (8260583.odt, Financial Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between the three components (Governance, Conflict, Crime) if one underperforms (e.g., slow granting or spend). DFID reserves the right to redirect funds to higher-performing components. Exploratory grants are used to test feasibility before committing to full RCTs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities are refined through **6-monthly grant competitions**, allowing adjustments based on emerging evidence gaps or HMG demands. The programme uses a **nested grant structure** (exploratory → pilot → full awards) to test and adapt research questions before scaling.
how_flexibility.quote: "We will move funds between the components if any struggle to find high quality proposals, or implementation is slow." (8260583.odt, Summary Sheet) and "J-PAL further improved vfm and risk management by developing a nested set of complementary grant types: Exploratory grants... Pilot grants... Full awards." (8260583.odt, Commercial Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → J-PAL (fund manager) → IPA/CCL (component leads) → end-researchers (grantees)
how_efficiency.quote: "J-PAL, IPA and CCL’s overhead costs are 11.6% overall (J-PAL 10%; IPA 15%; and CCL 10%)." (8260583.odt, Commercial Case) and "DFID will disburse funds quarterly and in arrears, after receipt and approval of J-PAL’s quarterly invoice and report." (8260583.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Run a new Research Programme Consortium (RPC) competition to select a contractor
Do Nothing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **Accountable Grant to J-PAL** was chosen because it offered the **best value for money** by leveraging J-PAL’s existing systems (grant competitions, quality assurance, policy engagement) and avoiding the **12-18 month delay** of an open competition. J-PAL’s track record in delivering high-quality RCTs and its ability to **front-load research** (starting trials early to ensure completion within 5 years) were decisive factors. The consortium structure (J-PAL + IPA + CCL) also provided **efficiency gains** and **coherence** across the three themes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: J-PAL’s independence could lead to misalignment with HMG priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID technical group provides oversight, and 6-monthly grant competitions allow for adjustments based on HMG input.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: CCL’s limited experience in LIC/MIC settings
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: J-PAL and IPA’s established presence in LICs/MICs mitigates risks through shared systems and local partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow spend or underperformance in one component
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds can be reallocated between components, and exploratory grants reduce the risk of wasted resources.

why_rationale.quote: "Our assessment is that negotiating a new Accountable Grant Agreement with JPAL/IPA/CCL offers DFID the best value for money by extending J-PAL’s proven approach... and avoiding the delays and high levels of risk that would be inevitable with i) running an open procurement for a new provider and ii) on contracting, and establishing a new granting process from scratch." (8260583.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with **proven experience in fragile settings** (e.g., IPA for conflict) and **established risk management systems**. Security risks and weak institutions in target countries require partners with local presence (e.g., J-PAL/IPA country offices) and ability to navigate complex environments.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with FCAS experience (rules out many Northern academia)
Local presence required for oversight in high-risk settings
Partners must comply with UK’s counter-terrorism financing rules
Research in conflict zones requires rapid, flexible funding mechanisms
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rigorous, policy-relevant RCTs** determines the **fund manager model** (J-PAL as intermediary) because: 1) RCTs require specialized methodological expertise (J-PAL’s Affiliate network); 2) Policy uptake demands trusted brokers (J-PAL’s Executive Education and HMG engagement); and 3) FCAS research needs flexible, rapid funding (6-monthly competitions).
q28_linkages: RCTs → need for specialized grant competitions → J-PAL’s established system
Policy influence → need for trusted intermediary → J-PAL’s HMG relationships
FCAS research → need for flexible funding → 6-monthly exploratory/pilot grants
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (using J-PAL’s existing Northern-led systems) with **equity** through: 1) Targeted capacity-building for Southern researchers (e.g., matchmaking events, Executive Education); 2) Incentives for J-PAL to engage UK/Southern academics; and 3) Requiring 75% of research to be in DFID partner countries (LICs/MICs). However, decision-making power remains Northern-led.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (re-funding J-PAL) vs. inclusion (open competition could engage new Southern partners)
Northern expertise (J-PAL’s RCT quality assurance) vs. Southern ownership (limited decision-making power for LIC/MIC researchers)
Global evidence base (some research in Latin America) vs. DFID priority focus (75% in partner countries)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (FCAS settings) leads to **quarterly oversight** and **nested grant structures** (exploratory → pilot → full awards) to mitigate implementation risks. Higher-risk components (Conflict/Crime) have greater flexibility for exploratory research in the first 2 years.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is **embedded** in the delivery structure: Southern researchers progress from grantees → co-investigators → potential Affiliates through J-PAL’s pathways. This shapes their roles from participants to leaders in future research.
intersections.quote: "As well as delivering high quality, operationally relevant new evidence, our support for J-PAL will also have a strong demonstration effect – pushing researchers to use the most rigorous methods to tackle the toughest development problems." (8260583.odt, Strategic Case) and "J-PAL has agreed to target greater attention on engaging with the UK academic sector to build interest and capability in the UK supplier market." (8260583.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Opportunities for evaluating interventions may not be available in target countries
Field research interrupted by conflict/violence (especially in Crime/Conflict components)
Slow spend or underperformance in one component (e.g., Crime RCTs may struggle to identify viable interventions)
CCL’s limited experience in LIC/MIC settings
Reputational risk if research compromises safety in conflict zones (e.g., UK branding issues)
Risk of terrorist financing in conflict-affected settings

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of exploratory grants to test feasibility; front-loading of trials; J-PAL/IPA’s established risk management for FCAS.
Funds can be reallocated to higher-performing components; ‘top-up’ grants for ongoing research to ensure early outputs.
Leverage J-PAL/IPA’s local presence and systems; start with exploratory research before committing to full RCTs.
Compliance with UK’s OSJA Guidance; due diligence checks by J-PAL/MIT; regular DFID reviews.

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for **rapid, flexible funding** to respond to crises (addressed via 6-monthly competitions and exploratory grants).
Importance of **local research partners** in FCAS (IPA’s country offices mitigate risks).
**Security protocols** for researchers (UK branding avoided in high-risk settings; duty of care standards enforced).
**Adaptive research designs** (e.g., adjusting interventions mid-trial if context changes).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the **J-PAL Governance Initiative (2010–2017)** include: 1) The value of **nested grants** (exploratory → pilot → full) to reduce wasted resources; 2) The need for **active incentivization** of grantees to deliver on time; 3) The importance of **policy engagement** (e.g., J-PAL’s Executive Education courses increased HMG uptake of evidence); and 4) **Cost negotiation** in grant competitions improves VFM (average RCT cost reduced from $400k ceiling to $225k).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **exploratory grants** to test feasibility before committing to full RCTs (learned from slow start-ups in GI).
**Front-loaded funding** to ensure trials complete within 5 years (addressed delays in earlier phases).
Stronger **gender analysis framework** (based on GI’s iterative improvements).
Increased **flexibility for Conflict/Crime components** (higher risk requires adaptive management).
Formalized **DFID technical oversight group** (response to need for closer alignment with HMG priorities).
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from the previous J-PAL grant were used to ensure that J-PAL skills, resources, incentives will ensure quality and timely delivery... J-PAL further improved vfm and risk management by developing a nested set of complementary grant types: Exploratory grants... Pilot grants... Full awards." (8260583.odt, Commercial Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: 65% of J-PAL Governance Initiative grantees leveraged co-funding from other sources, ranging from $40,000 to $1.3 million per project. The new GCCI is expected to continue this trend.
financial_details.quote: "J-PAL, IPA and CCL’s overhead costs are 11.6% overall (J-PAL 10%; IPA 15%; and CCL 10%)." (8260583.odt, Commercial Case) and "20 (65%) GI grantees have leveraged co-funding from other sources in amounts ranging from $40,000 to $1.3m." (8260583.odt, Commercial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Support to the Palestinian Authority to Build Stability, Deliver Services and Promote Reform in the Occupied Palestinian Territories ("Stability, Services and Reform Programme - SSRP")
metadata.quote: "To maintain stability and preserve the viability of the two state solution, by strengthening the Palestinian Authority’s capability and accountability." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "DFID will provide up to £138m over five years" (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financial aid (service delivery) with technical assistance (capacity building) to strengthen PA systems while maintaining stability. It directly funds education/health services while also reforming public administration, PFM, and revenue systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DFID will provide up to £138m over five years, as an integrated package of financial aid (FA) and technical assistance (TA) to the Palestinian Authority (PA) in order to: Maintain stability by preserving the viability of the two state solution; Strengthen the PA’s capability and accountability, in order to deliver basic services and improve fiscal stability." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Over 30,000 West Bank health and education public servants supported annually (20,000+ teachers, 2,900+ health workers)
Education for up to 25,200 young Palestinians (14,900 primary, 10,300 secondary) annually
Up to 3,700 child immunisations against communicable diseases annually
Up to 185,000 medical consultations annually
Improved policy/planning capability at centre-of-government
Strengthened public financial management (PFM) systems
Improved revenue policy/administration linked to business environment
Reduced recurrent budget deficit (fiscal stability)
Reduced fiduciary/corruption risk through PFM reforms
what_objectives.summary: The programme integrates financial aid for service delivery (education/health salaries) with technical assistance to reform PA core systems (PFM, revenue, public administration), aiming to preserve the two-state solution while improving fiscal stability and accountability.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact is that stability is maintained by preserving the viability of the two-state solution. At outcome level, expected results are: Increased effectiveness of service delivery (education and health outcomes); Improved PA fiscal stability (reduced recurrent budget deficit); Greater PA transparency and accountability (reduced fiduciary and corruption risk)." (19465976.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a fragile/conflict-affected context with severe political instability, occupation constraints, and high violence levels. The overall programme risk rating is "Severe".
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Severe" (19465976.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The context for state-building support to the PA has deteriorated significantly since 2011 and is characterised by increasing instability... violence has been at its highest levels since the Second Intifada." (19465976.odt, Political and Security Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Israeli occupation restrictions (500+ checkpoints, Area C access limitations) severely limit economic growth (GDP growth dropped from 8% to 2.7%), PA revenue collection (only 1.5% of building permits approved in Area C), and service delivery in Gaza/West Bank. Political split between Hamas/Fatah further fragments authority. High unemployment (42% in Gaza) and fiscal leakages (~$290m annually) exacerbate instability.
where_context.quote: "The Israeli occupation and the continuing geographical and political split between Hamas in Gaza and Fatah in the West Bank undermines the PA’s ability to effectively exercise legitimate authority across the OPTs... Various international reports (IMF, World Bank, UN) conclude that the fundamental constraints to economic growth are restrictions on access and movement due to the occupation." (19465976.odt, Political and Security Context/Economic and Fiscal Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID retains full decision-making authority over fund disbursement, policy dialogue, and technical assistance priorities. The PA implements reforms but must comply with DFID’s KPIs and counter-terrorism safeguards.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to strengthen PA core state systems (PFM, revenue administration, public administration)
institution-building at centre-of-government (policy, planning, communications)
support to social sector line ministries (education/health service delivery)
training for public servants (e.g., tax enforcement, budget execution)
mentorship via embedded advisors (e.g., World Bank expert support)

partner_organizations.name: Palestinian Authority (PA)
partner_organizations.role: Primary recipient of financial aid and technical assistance; implements reforms in PFM, revenue, and service delivery

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU PEGASE mechanism)
partner_organizations.role: Channel for DFID’s financial aid disbursement to PA; manages vetting of civil servant beneficiaries

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Palestinian Reform and Development Plan Trust Fund - PRDP-TF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer and technical advisor on PFM/wage bill reforms

partner_organizations.name: Georg Eckert Institute
partner_organizations.role: Independent research partner for textbook analysis (added via addendum)

partner_organizations.name: Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) Provider (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Independent evaluation of programme results

partner_organizations.name: Technical Assistance Providers (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of TA components (PFM, revenue, public administration reforms)

who_partners.quote: "DFID will provide TA to help strengthen PA core state systems and build PA capability and accountability. The TA will focus on (i) public administration reform... (ii) public financial management (PFM) reform... (iii) revenue reform..." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "DFID is the lead donor on Public Administration Reform (PAR), and co-chair of the PAR Sector Working Group." (19465976.odt, Donor Context)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Financial Aid (FA) is delivered via the EU PEGASE mechanism as non-budget support earmarked for education/health salaries, using a combination of "Managed Delivery" and "Results-based Aid" (disbursements linked to KPIs). Technical Assistance (TA) is provided through contracts/grants to implementers for system reforms. A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the PA governs compliance and safeguards.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID manages the programme directly, with financial aid channeled through EU PEGASE and TA delivered by selected providers (e.g., World Bank for PFM, Georg Eckert Institute for research). The PA implements reforms under DFID oversight, with annual ministerial sign-offs for FA disbursements.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct award for EU PEGASE; TA providers selected via unspecified process)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: EU PEGASE was chosen for its existing vetting mechanisms and alignment with donor harmonization. TA providers were selected based on technical expertise (e.g., World Bank for PFM, Georg Eckert Institute for textbook analysis).
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID will provide non-budget support financial aid to the PA through the European Union PEGASE mechanism... Disbursement will be linked to the achievement of key performance indicators (KPIs) on fiscal and public financial management (PFM) reform." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The original Business Case envisaged one delivery partner under the Monitoring and Evaluation component. As part of the programme’s risk management, it was assessed that there is a need for two additional research reports... These reports will be delivered by an additional delivery partner." (51843474.odt, Implementation Approach)

how_governance.quote: "Given the volatility of the political context, there will be an Annual Ministerial sign-off for disbursements of FA for the subsequent financial year, as well as a mid-way review point in 2018/19 where progress will be reviewed and adjustments made." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Robust, independent pre- and post-auditing of the CSP programme, including the UK’s contribution, to verify that funds have been used by the PA for payment of eligible beneficiaries only." (19465976.odt, Due Regard to Counter-terrorism)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for specific expenditures (education/health salaries) and require annual ministerial approval for disbursement. The addendum allows a £300k reallocation from M&E to a new research component, but this is an exception.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The mid-way review (2018/19) allows for adjustments based on progress. The addendum introduces new research components in response to emerging risks (e.g., textbook allegations), but these require explicit approval and budget shifts.
how_flexibility.quote: "There will be an Annual Ministerial sign-off for disbursements of FA for the subsequent financial year, as well as a mid-way review point in 2018/19 where progress will be reviewed and adjustments made." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Move £300k from component 300050-101 to the new component." (51843474.odt, Financial Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (EU PEGASE for FA; TA providers for reforms) → PA (end recipient). The addendum adds a third layer for research: FCDO → Georg Eckert Institute.
how_efficiency.quote: "Disbursement [of FA] will be linked to the achievement of key performance indicators (KPIs) on fiscal and public financial management (PFM) reform." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The proposed approach is in line with the objectives set out in DFID’s new framework for financial aid... combining type A (Managed Delivery) with type E (Results-based Aid)." (19465976.odt, DFID Financial Aid Framework)

q24_alternatives_considered: Counterfactual – ‘do nothing’ option (no FA or TA to PA)
A stand-alone TA programme with no financial aid component
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The integrated FA+TA model was selected to: (1) address the PA’s immediate financing gap (FA) while leveraging reforms (TA); (2) mitigate fiduciary risks by linking disbursements to KPIs; (3) build on DFID’s comparative advantage in PFM/revenue reforms; and (4) maintain donor harmonization via EU PEGASE. The mixed approach balances stability (FA) with long-term institutional strengthening (TA).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Diversion of funds to proscribed groups (terrorism risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: CT provisions in MoU, earmarking via EU PEGASE’s vetting process, and independent audits.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: PA non-compliance with reforms (fiduciary risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Results-based aid with KPIs, annual ministerial sign-offs, and mid-term review.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political volatility disrupting implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adaptive management via annual reviews and mid-term adjustments.

why_rationale.quote: "The proposed scale of FA will allow DFID to remain one of the most active donors in the OPTs... DFID has the technical capability to influence the manner in which FA is delivered to the PA, the policy dialogue that goes with it, and the aid effectiveness agenda." (19465976.odt, DFID’s Comparative Advantage) and "The new programme will provide an integrated package of FA and TA to support delivery of basic services, and leverage reform in priority areas." (19465976.odt, Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to entities with existing vetting mechanisms (e.g., EU PEGASE) and technical expertise in high-risk environments (e.g., World Bank for PFM). The Israeli-Palestinian conflict restricts direct engagement with Gaza-based actors, and counter-terrorism legislation excludes certain PA-affiliated entities.
q27_constraints_detail: Counter-terrorism legislation excludes partners without robust vetting (e.g., Hamas-affiliated entities).
Israeli restrictions limit engagement with Gaza-based institutions, forcing reliance on West Bank-centric partners.
Fiduciary risks require partners with strong audit capacities (e.g., EU PEGASE, World Bank).
Political sensitivity necessitates multilateral channels (e.g., EU, World Bank) over bilateral agreements.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of service delivery (FA) and systemic reform (TA) require a mixed modality: (1) FA is channeled through EU PEGASE for its vetting/safeguards; (2) TA is delivered via technical providers (e.g., World Bank for PFM) to ensure reform expertise; (3) Results-based aid links disbursements to KPIs to align FA with TA priorities.
q28_linkages: Service delivery goals (education/health) → FA earmarked for salaries via PEGASE.
PFM reform goals → TA contracts with World Bank/other experts.
Risk mitigation needs → Results-based aid with KPIs and independent audits.
Policy dialogue requirements → Annual ministerial reviews and MoU commitments.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (using existing multilateral channels like EU PEGASE) with equity (ensuring service delivery reaches marginalized groups). Trade-offs include: (1) Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid disbursement via PEGASE prioritizes stability over localized partner engagement. (2) Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: TA is led by international experts (e.g., World Bank) to ensure reform quality, but risks limiting PA ownership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (multilateral channels) vs. localization (limited direct PA control over funds).
Speed (pre-vetted PEGASE) vs. inclusivity (excludes Gaza-based actors due to risks).
Expertise (Northern TA providers) vs. ownership (PA implements but doesn’t lead reform design).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The "Severe" risk rating drives intensive oversight: annual ministerial sign-offs, independent audits, and embedded safeguards (e.g., CT clauses in MoU). High fiduciary risks necessitate results-based aid and earmarking.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: PA’s limited capacity in PFM/revenue systems justifies Northern-led TA (e.g., World Bank), while FA focuses on PA’s relative strength in service delivery (education/health). Capacity building is embedded in TA to transition ownership.
intersections.quote: "Given the volatility of the political context, there will be an Annual Ministerial sign-off for disbursements of FA... The programme will have strong safeguards to ensure compliance with Counter Terrorism (CT) legislation and manage risks." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "DFID is the lead donor on Public Administration Reform (PAR) and has been the largest provider of TA for PFM reform." (19465976.odt, Donor Context)

key_programme_risks: PA collapse due to fiscal crisis, triggering security deterioration and service delivery breakdown.
Diversion of UK aid to terrorism or proscribed groups (CT risk).
PA non-compliance with reform KPIs, undermining fiscal stability goals.
Political volatility (e.g., Israel-PA tensions, Hamas-Fatah split) disrupting implementation.
Fiduciary weaknesses in PA systems leading to corruption or mismanagement.
Reduced donor funding increasing PA’s financing gap (from $550m in 2016).
Israeli withholding of clearance revenues (70% of PA revenue) causing liquidity crises.
Social unrest due to salary delays or service cuts (e.g., teachers’ strikes).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Predictable FA flows via PEGASE to fund salaries; TA to strengthen revenue/PFM systems.
EU PEGASE vetting, CT clauses in MoU, independent audits, and exclusion of prisoners’ payments.
Results-based aid with KPIs; annual ministerial reviews; mid-term adjustments.
Adaptive management via annual reviews; engagement with Israeli/Palestinian decision-makers.
TA focused on PFM reforms (commitment control, reporting, audits); anti-corruption support via PACC.
DFID’s continued leadership to encourage burden-sharing; policy dialogue to improve aid effectiveness.
Advocacy via Office of the Quartet (OQ) to address fiscal leakages; TA on revenue reform.
Earmarking FA for education/health salaries to maintain public sector stability.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from DFID’s State-building Grant (SBG) showed that FA must be linked to measurable reforms to avoid dependency.
PFM reforms require sustained TA due to weak PA capacity (e.g., backlog in anti-corruption cases).
Results-based aid is critical in FCAS to incentivize reforms amid political instability.
Donor harmonization (e.g., via PEGASE) reduces transaction costs but limits flexibility.
Counter-terrorism safeguards must be embedded in FCAS programmes to comply with UK legislation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The ODI evaluation of DFID’s SBG/PGF (2015) found that FA helped stabilize the PA’s fiscal position and incentivized some reforms, but progress was uneven outside the Ministry of Finance’s direct control. The EU PEGASE evaluation (2015) highlighted the need for predictable aid to maintain PA functioning, but noted that earmarking can limit flexibility. These lessons informed the SSRP’s design: integrating FA/TA, strengthening KPIs, and adding adaptive management reviews.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addendum (51843474.odt) introduces textbook research in response to emerging risks (allegations of incitement), showing adaptive management. The shift from the SBG to SSRP included: (1) stronger KPIs; (2) explicit CT safeguards; (3) annual ministerial reviews; and (4) a mid-term adjustment mechanism.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons Learned from DFID Support to Governance Reforms in the OPTs [Box 1]: The ODI evaluation found that FA had helped to support the stability of the macro-economy and the PA’s fiscal stability in the short-term... but progress was mixed on reforms outside the MoF’s direct mandate." (19465976.odt, Box 1) and "The 2015 evaluation of the EU PEGASE instrument found that financial aid has contributed significantly to reducing the PA’s budget deficit... Without the CSP, the PA would not be able to pay salaries on a regular basis." (19465976.odt, Evidence on FA)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages multilateral mechanisms (EU PEGASE, World Bank PRDP-TF) to pool donor resources and reduce transaction costs. DFID’s £25m/year represents ~7% of traditional donor burden-sharing.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on recurrent expenditure (salaries, service delivery) with limited capital investment due to occupation constraints. Only 4.8% of PA expenditure was development-related in 2014.
financial_details.quote: "DFID will provide up to £138m over five years, as an integrated package of financial aid (FA) and technical assistance (TA)..." (19465976.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The proposed scale of FA will allow DFID to remain one of the most active donors in the OPTs. We estimate that an annual contribution of £25m would represent a burden share of approx. 7% within the traditional donor group." (19465976.odt, DFID’s Comparative Advantage)

metadata.programme_name: X(Cross)Border Conflict - Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT)
metadata.quote: The research programme will be framed by three questions: X-border conflict: What do we know about protracted conflict ‘hubs’ and the trans-national networks that facilitate flows of people, weapons and resources between them (‘spokes’)? Innovative responses: How should international conflict response systems adapt to meet the challenges of X-border conflict and the shifting international order? Violent Behaviour: What factors and narratives influence individual and group propensity to violent and peaceful behaviour in violent conflicts? (18779806.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source:
Start Date: 01/10/2017
End Date: 01/10/2024

what_objectives.q1_explanation: XCEPT is a research programme designed to generate high-quality evidence on protracted conflicts, X-border networks, and innovative conflict responses. It combines evidence generation with policy influence and capacity building, aiming to inform DFID and Whitehall policy while strengthening local research networks in conflict-affected areas.
what_objectives.q1_source: XCEPT will deliver high quality research on the world’s most protracted conflicts; Syria, Iraq, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Yemen, Libya and Afghanistan; on the X-border networks and narratives that connect them; and how UK and international conflict responses should innovate to tackle X-border challenges. [...] XCEPT will provide real-time data, expertise and public good research to inform DFID and Whitehall policy and operations. (18779806.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: real-time data on conflict dynamics
expertise and public good research to inform DFID/Whitehall policy
quarterly reports on changes in conflict-affected areas
empirically grounded research on violent/peaceful behaviour
longitudinal studies on trauma and recovery
local research capacity strengthened in 10+ countries
new quantitative and qualitative datasets on X-border flows
policy briefs and operational guidance for HMG
what_objectives.summary: XCEPT aims to improve understanding of cross-border conflict dynamics through rigorous research while building local research capacity and directly informing UK government policy and operations in fragile contexts.
what_objectives.quote: The research will inform HMG investments in fragile and conflict affected situations (FCAS), particularly through the Conflict, Security and Stability Fund (CSSF) [...] This will help HMG work more effectively to address long term drivers of conflict and develop new responses suited to X-border challenges. (18779806.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme focuses exclusively on fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCAS) with active armed conflicts, terrorist threats, and transnational criminal networks. The document explicitly states 'Overall programme risk rating: High' and notes these are 'hostile contexts'.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: High [...] This is a high risk programme delivered in hostile contexts. (18779806.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit researcher access to many areas, requiring reliance on local partners. Weak institutions and active conflicts create challenges for data collection and programme implementation. The document notes 'warring parties frequently hide their intentions, seek to distort or disrupt research findings, and impede access for international actors'.
where_context.quote: Warring parties frequently hide their intentions, seek to distort or disrupt research findings, and impede access for international actors to affected communities. This leads many practitioners to rely on remote management and monitoring arrangements. (18779806.odt, The Gap in the Research)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Research Programme Consortium (RPC) with Accountable Grant partners
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme combines a competitively tendered RPC contract (likely Northern-led) with an Accountable Grant to Southern research organizations (TAF, RVI, CMEC) that have decision-making authority over their regional research components. The AG partners 'will provide a regional infrastructure for the RPC consortium' suggesting collaborative governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: long-term investment in local research partners (5+ years)
training and mentorship for local researchers
support to meet international quality standards
development of sub-national research networks
peer review processes for local research
extension of research methods to new regions
catalytic effect on local research ecosystems

partner_organizations.name: Research Programme Consortium (RPC) - Lot 1
partner_organizations.role: lead research on X-border conflict and conflict response innovation

partner_organizations.name: Research Programme Consortium (RPC) - Lot 2
partner_organizations.role: specialist research on violent/peaceful behaviour

partner_organizations.name: The Asia Foundation (TAF)
partner_organizations.role: Accountable Grant lead, regional research in Asia

partner_organizations.name: Rift Valley Institute (RVI)
partner_organizations.role: Accountable Grant partner, regional research in Africa

partner_organizations.name: Carnegie Middle East Centre (CMEC)
partner_organizations.role: Accountable Grant partner, regional research in MENA

partner_organizations.name: Local research networks
partner_organizations.role: data collection and field research in 10+ countries

who_partners.quote: An AG will help guarantee access by researchers to difficult border areas, enable the research programme to start delivering operationally relevant research to HMG country teams within months of startup, and provide an important investment in the long-term research networks needed to work in the most challenging and dangerous conflict environments. (18779806.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses two parallel instruments: 1) A competitively tendered Research Programme Consortium (RPC) contract for the main research components, and 2) An Accountable Grant (AG) to three specialist Southern organizations (TAF, RVI, CMEC) to ensure immediate research delivery in hard-to-reach areas and build local capacity.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme combines a competitively selected RPC consortium (with potential for a Lot 1 lead partner to coordinate with Lot 2) with a parallel Accountable Grant to Southern partners. The AG partners will provide regional infrastructure for the RPC and support research uptake, suggesting a collaborative management approach across components.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: RPC: open competition; AG: direct award
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The RPC uses open competition to ensure quality and value for money for the main research components. The AG uses direct award to Southern partners (TAF/RVI/CMEC) based on their proven capability to operate in insecure areas and existing relationships with HMG, enabling immediate research delivery in hard-to-reach locations.
how_mechanism.quote: We propose that the RPC competition will have two 'Lots'. Lot 1 [...] will cover cross-border conflict, innovating conflict response, and overall research leadership and management. Lot 2 will deliver specialist research on violent and peaceful behaviour. [...] An AG will be agreed with Asia Foundation, working with the Rift Valley Institute (East Africa) and the Carnegie Middle East Centre. (18779806.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The document proposes establishing a 'Conflict Evidence Group' representing key HMG departments, which would prioritize research commissions. The AG partners will provide a regional infrastructure for the RPC consortium, suggesting coordinated governance between the contract and grant components.
how_governance.quote: This approach would enable DFID to disseminate conflict research more effectively across HMG, help shape National Security Council strategies, and support more effective ODA spending decisions and programming choices. (18779806.odt, The case for operationally relevant research)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes grants for 'emerging trends/geographies' to support adaptation. The AG component provides immediate flexibility to respond to new priorities, while the RPC contract likely has more structured reallocation processes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to adapt to changing conflict dynamics, with explicit mention of 'grants for research on 'emerging trends/geographies'' and capacity to adjust to new priorities. The 7-year timeframe allows for learning beyond usual programme cycles.
how_flexibility.quote: Research will help DFID/HMG adapt to conflicts and enable learning beyond usual programme cycles. Grants for research on 'emerging trends/geographies' will also support adaptation. (18779806.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → 1) RPC Consortium (contract) and 2) AG Partners (TAF/RVI/CMEC) → local research networks. The AG partners serve as both implementers and regional infrastructure for the RPC.
how_efficiency.quote: DFID will provide £25 million over 7 years for high quality research [...] The programme will combine a competitively tendered Research Programme Consortium (RPC) contract with an Accountable Grant (AG) with specialist organisations with local research networks. (18779806.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: single RPC contract without AG component
multiple separate research commissions
relying solely on existing research programmes (PSRP, SLRC, etc.)
expanded use of CSSF research funds
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed RPC+AG model was chosen to balance 1) competitive quality assurance for core research, 2) immediate delivery in hard-to-reach areas through trusted Southern partners, 3) long-term capacity building, and 4) flexibility to adapt to emerging conflict trends. The AG component enables rapid startup and access to insecure areas that Northern researchers cannot reach.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between RPC and AG components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: AG partners will provide regional infrastructure for RPC consortium to ensure coherence

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Security risks to researchers in conflict zones
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of local partners with established duty of care systems and reliance on AG organizations with proven access to insecure areas

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Data quality issues in fragile contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investment in local research capacity and use of technology-based methods complemented by traditional approaches

why_rationale.quote: We assess that access to these local services across the geography identified for the focus of this research is essential to the effective delivery of this programme and that this could not easily be replicated through other arrangements. (18779806.odt, Theme 4)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The extreme security risks and access limitations in the target FCAS countries constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) Physical presence in conflict zones, 2) Established local networks, 3) Proven duty of care systems, and 4) Language/cultural expertise. This explicitly limits the RPC competition to organizations capable of managing high-risk research and necessitates the AG component with Southern partners who can operate in areas inaccessible to Western researchers.
q27_constraints_detail: security risks prevent Western researchers from accessing many target areas
weak institutions create challenges for data collection and programme implementation
active conflicts require partners with conflict sensitivity expertise
border regions require partners with cross-border operational capacity
local language skills essential for quality research in contested areas
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both 1) rigorous comparative research across multiple conflict hubs and 2) hyper-local understanding of border dynamics determines the two-component structure: the RPC provides cross-cutting analysis while the AG enables sub-national, context-specific research. The X-border focus requires a networked approach that neither pure academic research nor traditional development programming could provide.
q28_linkages: X-border research objectives → require both regional comparators (RPC) and local expertise (AG)
Real-time policy relevance → necessitates embedded Southern partners for rapid response
Capacity building goals → shape the AG component's focus on local research networks
High-risk contexts → determine the need for specialized partners with conflict zone experience
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) The efficiency of using established Northern research institutions vs the equity imperative to build Southern research capacity, 2) The speed of Northern-led research vs the contextual relevance of Southern-led work, and 3) The cost-effectiveness of competitive tendering vs the transaction costs of managing complex partnerships in FCAS. The mixed model aims to balance these by combining competitive quality assurance with dedicated Southern capacity funding.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise vs Southern ownership in research design
competitive tendering efficiency vs capacity building investments
rapid policy relevance vs long-term local research development
centralized quality control vs decentralized contextual adaptation
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context drives intensive management requirements including: 1) Strong duty of care arrangements, 2) Ethical oversight for conflict zone research, 3) Financial controls for hostile environments, and 4) Continuous risk assessment. This increases management intensity beyond standard research programmes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The capacity building objective fundamentally shapes partner roles by: 1) Making Southern partners (TAF/RVI/CMEC) equal components rather than subcontractors, 2) Giving them responsibility for regional research infrastructure, 3) Tasking them with extending research methods to new areas, and 4) Positioning them as bridges between international research and local contexts.
intersections.quote: Previously DFID competitions for research in hard to reach, conflict-affected areas have demonstrated there is a limited supplier market of research organisations with suitable capability and operational systems in place. (18779806.odt, Theme 4)

key_programme_risks: Security risks to researchers and participants in conflict zones
Data quality and reliability issues in fragile contexts
Coordinating complex multi-component programme structure
Ensuring research uptake by policy makers under time pressure
Managing ethical challenges of conflict zone research
Political interference or distortion of research findings
Sustaining local research capacity beyond programme lifetime
Adapting to rapidly changing conflict dynamics
Balancing academic rigor with operational relevance
Avoiding unintended consequences from research activities

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of local partners with established duty of care systems and proven access to insecure areas; strong arrangements for management, financial systems, ethics and duty of care
Combination of technology-based methods with traditional approaches; investment in local research capacity; peer review processes
AG partners provide regional infrastructure for RPC consortium; joint workshops and learning sessions
Proposed Evidence and Uptake Unit with specialists tailoring research to HMG needs; Conflict Evidence Group to prioritize commissions
Robust ethical guidelines for conflict research; local partner oversight of sensitive fieldwork
Independent research design with academic oversight; transparent methodology
Long-term (7 year) investment in local research networks; catalytic funding approach

fcas_specific_lessons: Long-term investment in local research networks improves aid effectiveness in FCAS (citing SAVE 2017 and DFID Research Review 2016)
Borderlands and periphery areas are often misunderstood but critical to conflict dynamics (Goodhand 2012)
Remote management approaches have significant limitations in conflict zones (Campbell 2015)
Local narratives and peer networks significantly influence violent/peaceful behaviour (Maxwell 2002, Brown 1989)
State-centered approaches have failed to address sub-national conflict drivers (Woodward 2017)
Decentralization and local governance are emerging as critical for lasting peace in fragmented conflicts
Technology-based methods can complement but not replace local research in insecure environments (SAVE 2016)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID-funded research programmes (PSRP, SLRC, JSRP, SAVE) demonstrated that: 1) Longitudinal panel surveys are feasible and valuable in conflict zones, 2) Local research networks improve programme effectiveness, 3) Mixed methods approaches yield operationally relevant insights, 4) Conflict research can directly inform major international policy processes (e.g., World Bank WDR, UN Sustaining Peace agenda), and 5) Ethical challenges require specialized approaches in conflict settings.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The XCEPT design incorporates lessons by: 1) Including both competitive RPC and dedicated AG components to balance quality and access, 2) Extending successful methods (panel surveys, participatory approaches) from previous programmes, 3) Building on established local research networks rather than creating new ones, 4) Incorporating technology-based methods proven in earlier DFID studies, and 5) Structuring for both immediate policy relevance and long-term capacity building.
risks_lessons.quote: DFID funded research on access in volatile environments (SAVE, 2017) found that aid agencies that invested in long established local research networks and used locally generated evidence to inform programming, were better able to operate than those that did not. (18779806.odt, Theme 4)

financial_details.quote: Programme Value: £25,000,000 (18779806.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Building Resilience and Adapting to Climate Change in Malawi (BRACC)
metadata.quote: "The desired impact of the programme is to contribute to a reduction in extreme poverty and an end to the recurrent cycle of hunger and humanitarian assistance in Malawi." (D0003910.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original start date: 18/07/2018", "New project end date: 31/6/2026" (D0003910.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing resilience-building interventions), service delivery (direct support to households), capacity building (strengthening national systems), and policy influence (shaping Malawi's National Resilience Strategy). It also includes a financing mechanism (shock-responsive contingency funds) and evidence generation through robust MEL components.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will deliver four interlinked components to build the resilience of economic, ecological and social systems..." and "generate robust evidence about what works and what does not" (48353183.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 300,000 households increase agricultural production and achieve long-term food security (48353183.odt, Expected results)
300,000 vulnerable households have reduced exposure to drought and floods through sustainable natural resource management (48353183.odt, Expected results)
150,000 vulnerable people/year receiving predictable, coordinated assistance during lean seasons or after shocks (48353183.odt, Expected results)
6 vulnerable districts implement contingency planning and early warning systems (48353183.odt, Expected results)
Strengthened and more shock-sensitive national social protection system (48353183.odt, Expected results)
An additional 49,000 people (9,000 HH) receiving conditional cash transfers for asset creation post-Cyclone Idai (49890023.odt, Expected results)
An additional 66,000 people (12,000 HH) receiving core resilience-building packages (49890023.odt, Expected results)
Scaled-up alternative energy options and improved forest governance systems (49890023.odt, Natural Resource Management activities)
what_objectives.summary: BRACC aims to break Malawi's cycle of recurrent hunger by building household and systemic resilience to climate shocks through integrated livelihood support, social protection strengthening, natural resource management, and shock-responsive safety nets, while generating evidence on what works.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will provide targeted support in the most vulnerable districts to strengthen the resilience of poor and vulnerable households to shocks and reduce their annual dependence on humanitarian aid." (48353183.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Malawi faces chronic vulnerability to climate shocks (floods/droughts) and weak institutional capacity, but is not classified as FCAS. The programme's risk rating was assessed as 'moderate' within DFID's risk appetite for Malawi.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall risk rating: Moderate" (48353183.odt, Summary Sheet) and "Malawi is one of the most climate vulnerable countries in the world" (48353183.odt, Box 2)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (patrimonial politics, maize market distortions)
weak institutions (limited district capacity, siloed ministries)
infrastructure (limited access to markets, energy, transport)
data limitations (no national social register until recently)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy challenges distort maize markets and policy implementation. Weak district capacity hampers coordination of resilience programmes. Climate shocks (e.g., Cyclones Idai, Ana, Freddy) repeatedly disrupt livelihoods and require emergency responses that divert from long-term planning. Limited transport/infrastructure isolates rural communities, reducing their ability to diversify livelihoods.
where_context.quote: "Malawi’s political system is based on the supreme power of the president. Clientism, patronage politics, entrenched divisions based on tribal lines and manipulation of a largely-uneducated electorate are common... The mis-management of maize in the economy epitomises the failure of this brand of patrimonial politics." (48353183.odt, Political Economy Challenges)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority, with implementation delegated to UN/NGO consortia and technical partners. District-level actors have limited autonomy due to capacity constraints.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening District Civil Protection and Social Protection Committees (48353183.odt, Indicative Activities)
training for watershed management and public works (48353183.odt, MNSSP II pillars)
support to national social protection system design (48353183.odt, Component 1)
mentorship through embedded technical advisors (GIZ, IFPRI) (48353183.odt, Delivery mechanisms)

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Lead UN consortium for resilience activities (cash transfers, livelihoods support)

partner_organizations.name: Concern Worldwide
partner_organizations.role: Lead NGO consortium for community-level resilience building

partner_organizations.name: GIZ (German Development Agency)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support for district-level social protection systems

partner_organizations.name: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)
partner_organizations.role: Research and policy analysis for agricultural markets/social protection

partner_organizations.name: African Parks
partner_organizations.role: Illegal Wildlife Trade mitigation and community livelihoods near national parks

partner_organizations.name: USAID (via Delegated Cooperation Agreement)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financing for Modern Cooking for Healthy Forests programme

partner_organizations.name: Government of Malawi (Ministries of Agriculture, Social Welfare)
partner_organizations.role: Policy alignment and implementation (MNSSP II, National Resilience Strategy)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Multi-Donor Trust Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Platform for pooled social protection funding (post-2023)

who_partners.quote: "Delivery mechanisms included funding arrangements with two consortia: one comprising UN agencies led by WFP, and one comprising Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) led by Concern Worldwide; and two technical partners that delivered support on safety nets at district level (GIZ) and research to support reforms to agricultural markets and social safety nets (IFPRI)." (D0003910.odt, Background)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (to NGOs like Concern Worldwide), Standard Administrative Agreements (with UN agencies), Delegated Cooperation Agreements (with USAID), and direct contracts for technical partners (GIZ, IFPRI). The shock-response contingency operates as a flexible crisis modifier.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages two parallel consortia (UN and NGO) through separate funding agreements, with technical partners (GIZ, IFPRI) providing specialized support. Post-2023, funding will shift to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund for social protection, maintaining a coordinated but centralized structure.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships (e.g., WFP/Concern from prior DFID programmes like ECRP) and technical expertise. The UN and NGO consortia were pre-identified during programme design, with Irish Aid initially planned as a co-funder before withdrawing.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID and Irish Aid jointly launched a call for proposals... The budgets for the two selected proposals were larger than the approved budget available within the programme." (49890023.odt, Recovery and resilience activities)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The UN consortium is governed through a UN fund structure with FCDO as the sole donor, while the NGO consortium operates under an Accountable Grant with joint reporting requirements. Post-2023, the World Bank MDTF will include a coordination committee with donor representation.
how_governance.quote: "We will dedicate a similar staffing ratio to oversee FCDO funding through the MDTF as we did for PROSPER, and work with the World Bank and other MDTF members through the MDTF’s coordination committee to ensure effective decision-making." (D0003910.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, as seen with the £8.5m shift to Cyclone Idai recovery (2019) and £5m replenishment of the crisis modifier. However, structural changes (e.g., adding new partners) require formal addendums.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a £20m crisis modifier for shock responses (later increased to £25m) and has adjusted activities in response to Cyclones Idai (2019), Ana/Gombe (2022), and Freddy (2023). New natural resource management components were added post-approval via cost extensions.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme has a strong learning component. It is designed to be adaptive to emerging opportunities and risks, including expansion in response to major climate-related shocks." (48353183.odt, Is there sufficient flexibility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Consortium leads (WFP/Concern) → Implementing partners (NGOs, district actors) → Communities. Post-2023: FCDO → World Bank MDTF → Government systems → Districts.
how_efficiency.quote: "The UN Standard Administrative Agreement and the Accountable Grant with Concern will be amended to reflect the increased budget. Logframes and workplans will also be amended to reflect new activities." (49890023.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct bilateral funding to Government of Malawi (rejected due to weak capacity)
Pure humanitarian response (rejected as unsustainable)
Standalone research programme (rejected; evidence generation embedded instead)
Single-implementer model (rejected in favor of UN/NGO consortia for complementary strengths)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The consortium model was chosen to combine the UN's scale and government relationships with NGO agility and community reach, while technical partners (GIZ, IFPRI) addressed specific capacity gaps. The shock-responsive design aligns with DFID's Grand Bargain commitments to bridge humanitarian-development divides.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (leveraging existing UN/NGO platforms to reduce transaction costs)
risk-mitigation (diversifying across consortia to manage implementation risks)
experience (building on prior DFID programmes like ECRP and HPRP)
partner-capacity (UN for policy dialogue, NGOs for community engagement)
flexibility (crisis modifier and adaptive management for climate shocks)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating two parallel consortia (UN and NGO) with different cultures and systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Joint reporting frameworks, FCDO-led coordination meetings, and harmonized logframes (48353183.odt, Management Structure)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government absorption capacity for decentralized activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical advisors (GIZ) and district-level training (48353183.odt, Capacity Building)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in shock-responsive funding due to bureaucratic approvals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-agreed triggers for crisis modifier activation and delegated authority to country office (49890023.odt, Crisis Modifier)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other donor programmes (e.g., World Bank, EU)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sector working groups (Climate Change/Resilience and Social Protection) and alignment with MNSSP II (48353183.odt, Complementarity)

vfm_criteria_used: economy (pooling funds with EU/Germany/Ireland to reduce duplication)
efficiency (using existing consortia to minimize startup costs)
why_rationale.quote: "The programme builds on and complements other development partners’ work on resilience building... We will leverage other donors’ investments in social protection programmes, including the EU, Ireland, Germany and the World Bank." (48353183.odt, Linkages with other development partners)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Malawi's weak district capacity and patrimonial politics limit the role of local government as direct implementers, necessitating reliance on UN/NGO consortia. The high risk of climate shocks (e.g., Cyclone Freddy) requires partners with rapid-response capabilities, favoring established humanitarian actors like WFP.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited district capacity → reliance on international consortia for delivery
Patrimonial politics → need for depoliticized UN-led safety net systems
Frequent climate shocks → requirement for partners with emergency response experience
No national social register → necessity of technical partners (IFPRI) for targeting
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for integrated resilience packages (livelihoods + social protection + natural resource management) drove the consortium model, as no single partner had all required capacities. Shock-responsive requirements necessitated flexible funding instruments (crisis modifier) and rapid-disbursement partners (WFP).
q28_linkages: Multi-sectoral objectives → consortia with complementary expertise (UN for policy, NGOs for community)
Shock responsiveness → pre-positioned crisis modifier funds with WFP
Natural resource management → addition of USAID/African Parks as technical partners
Policy influence → embedded IFPRI researchers to link implementation to MNSSP II reforms
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (using consortia for scale) with equity (targeting ultra-poor households). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher transaction costs for managing two consortia vs. ensuring geographic coverage; (2) Speed of UN systems vs. NGO community engagement; (3) Centralized crisis modifier management vs. local flexibility.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Consortia management costs vs. ability to reach 300,000 households across 6+ districts
UN speed in cash transfers vs. NGO depth in livelihoods support
Centralized shock-response triggers vs. district-level adaptation needs
Standardized MEL systems vs. context-specific learning
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (climate vulnerability + weak institutions) justified intensive oversight (milestone-based reporting, embedded advisors) and adaptive management (crisis modifier, programme extensions). Cyclone responses (2019, 2022, 2023) triggered higher management intensity during emergencies.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited government capacity led to technical partners (GIZ, IFPRI) taking on training/mentorship roles, while consortium partners (WFP/Concern) delivered frontline services. The shift to the World Bank MDTF post-2023 reflects growing government capacity to absorb pooled funding.
intersections.quote: "Capacity and resource constraints at all levels of government has hampered efforts to transform the livelihoods of vulnerable households... Districts are overwhelmed by the number of projects being implemented by donors, and do not have the resources or capacity to monitor and coordinate activities." (48353183.odt, Capacity Constraints)

key_programme_risks: Recurrent climate shocks disrupting implementation (Cyclones Idai, Ana, Freddy)
Government capacity constraints at district level
Political interference in maize markets and social protection targeting
Coordinating parallel UN/NGO consortia with different systems
Sustainability of resilience gains without long-term economic growth
Overlap/duplication with other donor programmes (EU, World Bank)
Delays in shock-responsive funding disbursement
Limited private sector engagement in resilience-building

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Crisis modifier funds (£25m), pre-agreed triggers, and flexible activity adjustments (e.g., post-Idai recovery package)
Embedded technical advisors (GIZ), training for Civil Protection Committees, and simplified reporting tools
Harmonized logframes, joint workplans, and FCDO-led coordination meetings
Objective, transparent triggers for shock responses and third-party verification (IFPRI)
Linking to national systems (MNSSP II, NRS) and graduation pathways for beneficiaries

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from ECRP (2012-2018) included: (1) Value of integrated livelihoods packages over single interventions; (2) Importance of community consultation for ownership; (3) Need for longer-term natural resource management (5+ years); (4) Gaps in supporting ultra-poor labour-constrained households. HPRP (2016-2018) showed that productive assets only work when embedded in multi-year programmes.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added natural resource management component (£4m) to address ECRP's oversight
Expanded crisis modifier from £20m to £25m for greater shock responsiveness
Increased focus on ultra-poor and labour-constrained households
Shift to cash-based lean season support (replacing in-kind food aid)
Extended programme duration by 2.5 years (to 2026) for full implementation of delayed components
Transition to World Bank MDTF post-2023 to strengthen national systems
risks_lessons.quote: "Key lessons from ECRP that have helped inform this programme include: The value of targeting packages of local level livelihoods development activities... The importance of flexibility was a key part of ECRP’s success... However, programme impacts were limited by (i) the lack of focus on safety nets for ultra-poor labour-constrained households... and (iii) private sector engagement." (48353183.odt, Learning from DFID’s current resilience programming)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leveraged ~£100m in complementary investments from EU, Germany, and Ireland in social protection and resilience, with direct co-financing of £14m to programme components. Post-2023, the World Bank MDTF will pool additional donor resources.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both revenue expenditures (cash transfers, technical assistance) and capital investments (irrigation infrastructure, watershed rehabilitation, evacuation centres). Shock-response funds (£25m) are primarily revenue-based for flexible disbursement.
financial_details.quote: "UK funding is complemented by and builds on wider investments of some £100 million equivalent from the EU, Germany and Ireland in social protection and resilience. More specifically, these donors will directly provide about £14 million equivalent to different components of this programme." (48353183.odt, Programme Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Productivity for Prosperity (P4P)
metadata.quote: "Productivity for Prosperity (P4P) is a sustainable economic transformation programme designed to increase labour productivity and climate-resilience in Tanzania’s job-creating sectors." (D0003376.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01 March 2021", "AMP End Date: 31 December 2027" (D0003376.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: P4P combines implementation research (testing interventions to boost productivity), capacity building (strengthening firm capabilities and business environment), and financing mechanisms (facilitating investment flows). It aims to transform Tanzania’s economy through private sector development and policy reform.
what_objectives.q1_source: "P4P will achieve this through private sector development (investment facilitation, trade facilitation and building capabilities of firms) and business environment reform (supporting proportionate and predictable regulation)." (D0003376.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: increased labour productivity in agroprocessing and horticulture sectors
climate-resilient firms and supply chains
improved business environment (proportionate, predictable regulation)
increased investment flows (£230m Kilombero Sugar Factory example cited)
800,000 youth employment opportunities supported annually
pipeline of investible firms for commercial/concessional financiers
enhanced Tanzania-UK trade and investment links
what_objectives.summary: P4P is a 7-year economic transformation programme targeting Tanzania’s agroprocessing and horticulture sectors through firm-level support, investment facilitation, and business environment reforms to create jobs and climate resilience.
what_objectives.quote: "P4P will initially prioritise the agroprocessing and horticulture sectors, and will provide flexible support to bolster the UK’s current and future prosperity objectives." (D0003376.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Tanzania has maintained peace since independence but faces economic vulnerabilities (e.g., 49% poverty rate, climate shocks costing 1% GDP/year). The business environment remains challenging (Ease of Doing Business rank 141/190 in 2020).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003376.odt, Summary Sheet) and "Tanzania’s Ease of Doing Business rank was 141 out of 190 in 2020" (D0003376.odt, Context section)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (protectionist policies, mistrust of private sector)
data limitations (challenges in monitoring carbon credits)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory unpredictability deters investment (e.g., investor exits cited), while climate shocks (1% GDP/year cost) and deforestation (72.7% of GHG emissions) threaten long-term growth. Weak trade logistics limit horticulture export competitiveness.
where_context.quote: "Past challenges in the business environment have knocked investor confidence... high regulatory burden and unpredictable enforcement severely impacted the private sector" (D0003376.odt, Context section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight with implementation delegated to Tanzanian firms/institutions. Key decisions (e.g., sector prioritization, investment facilitation) are guided by FCDO’s prosperity objectives.
q10_capacity_building_details: management training for firms
technical assistance for climate resilience
supply chain linkage brokering
policy advocacy through local associations (e.g., TAHA)
investment readiness support

partner_organizations.name: CDC Group
partner_organizations.role: development finance institution (co-investor)

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Trade (DIT)
partner_organizations.role: trade and investment promotion

partner_organizations.name: Tanzania Horticulture Association (TAHA)
partner_organizations.role: sector advocacy and policy reform

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Finance and Planning (Tanzania)
partner_organizations.role: business environment reform partner

partner_organizations.name: CRDB Bank
partner_organizations.role: potential climate finance accredited institution

partner_organizations.name: Private sector firms (agroprocessing/horticulture)
partner_organizations.role: direct beneficiaries and implementers

who_partners.quote: "P4P will provide a single streamlined platform to support the UK’s economic and climate diplomacy in Tanzania, in partnership with CDC and the Department for International Trade." (D0003376.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument appears to be grants to firms and technical assistance providers, complemented by FCDO’s diplomatic leverage and partnership agreements with financial institutions (e.g., CDC). Investment facilitation suggests blended finance approaches.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as strategic lead with implementation decentralized to Tanzanian firms, investors, and government agencies. The programme coordinates with existing platforms (e.g., TAHA, SAGCOT) rather than creating new structures.
how_mechanism.quote: "P4P will establish a network of domestic, regional and international investors—both commercial and concessional... P4P will focus on Nairobi as a regional impact investing hub as well as CDC Group." (D0003376.odt, Pillar 2: Investment facilitation)

how_governance.quote: "P4P will not seek to reform entire institutions but instead provide targeted support to unblock specific issues where the interests of the Government of Tanzania, the UK and private sector align." (D0003376.odt, Pillar 3: Business environment reform)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Flexibility to shift between agroprocessing and horticulture sub-sectors, but constrained by pre-defined pillars (firm capabilities, investment, business environment).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Sectoral focus (initially agroprocessing/horticulture) can adapt based on market opportunities, but core pillars remain fixed. Climate resilience components may scale based on emerging shocks.
how_flexibility.quote: "P4P will initially prioritise the agroprocessing and horticulture sectors, and will provide flexible support to bolster the UK’s current and future prosperity objectives." (D0003376.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (firms/associations) → End beneficiaries (workers/farmers). No intermediary layer explicitly described.
how_efficiency.quote: "Programme value: £35,000,000" (D0003376.odt, Summary Sheet)

q24_alternatives_considered: direct firm subsidies (rejected due to unsustainability)
broad business environment reform (rejected due to political constraints)
sector-wide technical assistance (rejected for lack of scalability)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (firm-level support + investment facilitation + targeted reform) was selected to balance speed (direct firm interventions) with systemic change (policy influence). Lessons from past programmes showed that financial support alone is insufficient without technical assistance and market linkages.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (targeted reforms avoid political resistance)
partner capacity (building on TAHA/CDC existing platforms)
flexibility (adaptive to climate and market shocks)
equity (focus on youth employment and smallholder linkages)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on private sector uptake
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified firm pipeline and concessional finance options

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Policy reform delays
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted, politically feasible interventions (e.g., work permits, food safety labs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate finance accreditation bottlenecks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnering with pre-accredited institutions (e.g., CRDB, World Bank)

vfm_criteria_used: equity (youth and women inclusion in horticulture)
why_rationale.quote: "Lessons learnt will inform future prosperity work... financial support alone is insufficient to support firm growth and job creation. Technical assistance... is just as, if not more valuable." (D0003376.odt, Lessons learnt)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Tanzania’s regulatory environment and political economy limit partner selection to firms/associations with existing government trust (e.g., TAHA). Climate risks necessitate partners with adaptation expertise (e.g., agroprocessors with cold chain capacity).
q27_constraints_detail: business environment reforms require local advocates (e.g., TAHA) to navigate political sensitivities
climate finance partners must be pre-accredited (e.g., CRDB) due to slow government processes
horticulture focus driven by Tanzania’s comparative advantage and urban demand growth
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **both** firm-level productivity gains **and** systemic change (policy/investment) dictates the mixed delivery structure. Horticulture’s tradability and learning-intensive nature require cluster-based support (e.g., cold storage hubs) rather than isolated firm grants.
q28_linkages: tradable sectors (horticulture) → require investment facilitation (Pillar 2) and trade logistics reform (Pillar 3)
climate resilience → necessitates firm capabilities (Pillar 1) + carbon finance partnerships
youth employment → shapes focus on labour-intensive agroprocessing
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tension between supporting smallholder farmers (equity) and prioritizing high-growth firms (efficiency). Programme resolves this by targeting **medium-sized firms** that link informal smallholders to formal markets (e.g., Twiga Foods model).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion: direct exports (e.g., Africado) vs. domestic market focus for broader reach
expertise vs ownership: UK climate finance expertise vs. Tanzanian-led policy reforms
cost vs reach: high-touch firm support vs. scalable technical assistance
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., investment facilitation tracked against FDI targets) and embedded advisors for climate resilience components.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local management capacity (cited in Pillar 1) justifies technical assistance as a core objective, with Tanzanian associations (e.g., TAHA) leading policy advocacy to build sustainable ownership.
