intersections.quote: "While these activities [smallholder support] may have a meaningful impact... with Tanzania’s population expected to triple by 2060, direct support to smallholder farmers will not raise standards of living at the scale required... structural transformation is essential." (D0003376.odt, Economic transformation pathway)

key_programme_risks: private sector uptake failure (firms not adopting productivity innovations)
policy reform stalling (e.g., work permit or tax administration delays)
climate shocks disrupting supply chains (droughts/flooding)
carbon credit market volatility (permanence/additionality challenges)
youth employment targets not met (job quality vs. quantity trade-offs)
UK-Tanzania trade growth below expectations

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Combine grants with technical assistance and investor matchmaking (e.g., CDC network)
Focus on ‘low-hanging fruit’ (e.g., food safety labs) with clear private sector benefits
Build firm-level resilience (e.g., cold storage, drought-resistant crops) and diversify value chains
Partner with accredited institutions (e.g., World Bank’s Forest Carbon Partnership)

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid top-down business environment reforms; use local associations (e.g., TAHA) as intermediaries
Blended finance (grants + investment) critical in high-risk contexts to crowd in private capital
Climate adaptation must be embedded in productivity programmes (e.g., agroprocessing reduces post-harvest losses from droughts)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past FCDO programmes (e.g., Tanzania Agribusiness Window) showed that: 1) financial support alone fails without technical assistance; 2) exit strategies must be designed upfront to avoid ‘donor dependency’; 3) local political economy constraints require pragmatic, incremental reforms.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from smallholder-focused interventions to **medium-sized firms** acting as intermediaries; added explicit climate resilience components (absent in earlier agribusiness programmes); structured investment facilitation as a core pillar (previously ad-hoc).
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learnt will inform future prosperity work... technical assistance including for business management practices and brokering linkages with buyers and investors is just as, if not more valuable [than grants]." (D0003376.odt, Lessons learnt)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Expected to catalyse private investment (e.g., £230m Kilombero Sugar Factory cited as model) and climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund access).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Focus on revenue-generating activities (firm productivity, trade) with capital investments (e.g., cold storage) as enablers.
financial_details.quote: "P4P will establish a network of domestic, regional and international investors—both commercial and concessional... supporting progress towards increased productivity and greener, more inclusive growth." (D0003376.odt, Pillar 2: Investment facilitation)

metadata.programme_name: Modern Energy Cooking Services (MECS)
metadata.primary_sector: economic development / energy access / climate change

quote.text: MECS is the flagship FCDO research and innovation programme that accelerates the uptake of clean and modern energy cooking practices in Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and the Indo-Pacific.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: 07/10/2018 to 31/03/2026; New project end date: 31/12/2030

what_objectives.q1_explanation: MECS is a research and innovation programme that develops evidence, technologies, and business models to accelerate the transition to modern energy cooking services (e.g., electric/gas cooking) in low-income countries. It combines evidence generation, technology development, policy influence, and market-building activities to address the health, environmental, and gender impacts of biomass-based cooking.

q1_source.text: MECS develops and disseminates policy-focused research that informs and influences countries and key stakeholders to adopt principles around MECS into their own strategies and planning, it funds pilots and demonstrators of new clean cooking technologies and business models in developing countries, and it co-funds World Bank global tracking tools and key market building initiatives such as the Clean Cooking Fund.

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy-focused research products
people with improved clean energy/cooking access
leverage of private and public sector investment
q3_expected_outputs.target: £1 billion

q3_expected_outputs.output: countries actively implementing MECS-informed policies
Electric Pressure Cookers (EPCs) rolled out in Tanzania and Uganda
households benefiting from carbon payment pilot in Uganda
schools transitioning to clean cooking in Uganda

what_objectives.summary: MECS aims to accelerate the transition from biomass to modern energy cooking services (electric/gas) in low-income countries by generating evidence, developing technologies, influencing policy, and building markets. It targets 10 million people with improved access, leverages £1 billion in investment, and supports 12 countries to adopt MECS-informed policies by 2030.

quote.text: This cost-extension builds on the success of the MECS programme to date in advancing the clean cooking agenda globally. This extension will enable MECS to support 10 million people to transition to modern energy cooking and inform the adoption of electric cooking policies in 12 developing countries by 2030, while leveraging £1 billion in investment from the private and public sector towards this critical agenda.
quote.source: D0006716.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

countries_regions: Sub-Saharan Africa: Ghana, Ethiopia, Malawi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Nigeria, DRC
South Asia: Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Bhutan
Southeast Asia and Indo-Pacific: Indonesia, Cambodia, Fiji
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The overall risk level for MECS continues to be Moderate. The programme operates in diverse contexts, including fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS), but has robust risk management processes in place. The risk appetite statement notes that FCDO is 'receptive' to strategy and context risks but 'cautious' towards fiduciary, safeguarding, reputational, and people-related risks.

q5_source.text: The overall risk level for MECS continues to be Moderate and the risk appetite statement for the programme is as follows (this statement and the information below is adapted from the wider FCDO risk appetite for innovation programmes): FCDO’s risk appetite to invest in innovative clean energy research and development opportunities that have the potential to be scaled up is high. FCDO is receptive to strategy, context, policy, and programme delivery related risks. However, FCDO’s risk appetite in relation to fiduciary, safeguarding, reputational and people related risks, is cautious.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme notes challenges such as limited coordination around global tracking frameworks, poorly understood consumer behaviour, fragmented research efforts, and lack of affordable modern energy cooking services. In FCAS contexts, ESMAP tailors approaches for fragile settings, collaborates with local private sectors and UN agencies, and provides additional incentives via Results-Based Financing (RBF) facilities.

quote.text: ESMAP tailors approaches for FCV contexts, collaboration with local private sectors, nonprofits, and UN agencies, and additional incentives via the RBF Facility for FCV areas.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is led by Loughborough University (UK) and the World Bank (multilateral), with decision-making power primarily held by these Northern institutions. Southern partners (e.g., TaTEDO in Tanzania) are involved in implementation but not in strategic decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
research grants
institutional strengthening

quote.text: MECS is currently delivered via two Tier 1 implementing partners—Loughborough University and the World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP)—who in turn provide funding to a network to date of more than 200 innovators, academics, entrepreneurs, and civil society partners delivering research and innovation activities in 36 countries.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: MECS uses Accountable Grants for Loughborough University and CLASP, and a World Bank Administrative Agreement for ESMAP. Country demonstrators funded by FCDO Posts are channeled through these existing agreements, avoiding the need for new contracts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: MECS operates as a platform with three Tier 1 partners (Loughborough University, ESMAP, CLASP) managing distinct but complementary components. Each Tier 1 partner subcontracts to Tier 2 and Tier 3 partners. Country demonstrators are managed as separate components within the MECS platform, linked to FCDO country offices.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Loughborough University and ESMAP were selected based on their established track records in clean cooking research and policy influence. CLASP was promoted from Tier 2 to Tier 1 due to its expertise in appliance testing and venture building. Technology accelerators and challenge funds use competitive processes to select innovators.

quote.text: The programme will continue to be overseen by a G6 Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and managed by a G7 Programme Responsible Owner (PRO) and a SEO Senior Programme Manager, in the FCDO Climate, Environment, Energy and Water (CEEW) team, in the Research & Evidence Directorate (RED).
quote.source: D0006716.odt, What is the approach to implementation? > Management

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A MECS Advisory Group (MAG), chaired by Loughborough University and composed of clean cooking experts, provides specialist advice. The MAG works alongside the Ayrton Sector Engagement Group to steer the Modern Cooking Challenge. Country demonstrators are overseen by FCDO country offices in collaboration with RED.

quote.text: A MECS Advisory Group (MAG) chaired by the Loughborough University and made up of clean cooking experts, including some not involved in the implementation of MECS, will continue to share specialist experience and knowledge to benefit the programme. The MAG and Ayrton Sector Engagement Group will work together, helping to steer the direction of the Ayrton Fund Modern Cooking Challenge.
quote.source: D0006716.odt, What is the approach to implementation? > Deliver chain

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval. Unspent demonstrator budget headroom is converted to R&D in the final year. The programme is designed to respond to emerging opportunities and country demand.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach, with annual reviews informing adjustments. The Theory of Change and log frame are updated regularly to reflect new priorities. For example, the 2023 extension added new research priorities like carbon market data gathering and commercial eCooking.

quote.text: The programme is designed to be inherently flexible around different country contexts and market segments. The work on the drivers and pathways for countries to transition to modern energy cooking services will identify the barriers and opportunities for each context. It will learn from the recent and current status of the sector, and evidence possible ways forward.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Tier 1 partners (Loughborough/ESMAP/CLASP) → Tier 2 partners → Tier 3/end-implementers

quote.text: The budget under this output represents 7% of the total £35m R&D budget requested in this extension (including 7% by Loughborough University, 10% by ESMAP and 5% by CLASP), which is within an acceptable range and lower than the management and coordination costs in the current phase of MECS.
quote.source: D0006716.odt, 6. MECS Management and Ayrton Coordination

q24_alternatives_considered: do nothing beyond existing programming (counterfactual)
support a UK universities and innovators partnership led by Loughborough University
support delivery through a World Bank multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) such as ESMAP
utilize a Research Programme Consortium (RPC)
provide a window under existing UK research funds such as GCRF
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The current mixed modality (Loughborough + ESMAP + CLASP) was chosen for its ability to combine UK academic expertise, World Bank convening power, and venture-building capacity. This structure leverages existing partnerships, avoids duplication, and provides flexibility to respond to country demand. The 2023 extension added CLASP as a Tier 1 partner to fill gaps in appliance testing and market-building.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: fraud or financial mismanagement eroding funding resources
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence procedures in place; downstreampartner mapping and due diligence enforced for grantees and contractors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: a downstreampartner’s actions leading to a safeguarding incident
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence process includes substantial safeguarding checks; ESMAP tailors approaches for FCV contexts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: large currency fluctuations or changes in delivery costs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close collaboration with partners to monitor costs and currency risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: clean cooking being deprioritized politically or in funding allocations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MECS partners engage in high-level advocacy (e.g., High-Level Coalition of Leaders for Clean Cooking); Clean Cooking Fund links incentives with verified results.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: partners not delivering on time
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible delivery timelines; close monitoring of partner progress.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: dependence on private sector entering emerging markets
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified private sector engagement; Results-Based Financing to improve profitability.

quote.text: The strengths and key potential risks/mitigations of the approach proposed in this addendum, of MECS acting as a platform for delivery of innovative Demonstrators by Country Posts, is summarised below: [...] Avoids duplication of programme structures, annual reviews, etc, and offers good value for money, both to the FCDO and partners.
quote.source: D0003924.odt, What is the approach to implementation? > Strengths

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The geographic scope (multi-country, including FCAS) requires partners with global reach and adaptability. ESMAP’s role is critical for policy influence in fragile contexts, while Loughborough and CLASP provide technical and venture-building expertise. Local partners (e.g., TaTEDO) are essential for last-mile delivery but are constrained by weak institutions and market barriers in some regions.
q27_constraints_detail: regulatory barriers in some countries limit the adoption of modern energy cooking technologies
political economy factors (e.g., fuel subsidies) affect consumer uptake
weak institutions in FCAS require tailored approaches and additional incentives
market barriers (e.g., high upfront costs, limited supply chains) constrain private sector entry
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (research + implementation + policy + market-building) require a platform structure with complementary partners. Technology development and venture building are managed by Loughborough and CLASP, while ESMAP focuses on policy and global tracking. Country demonstrators are added as nested components to maintain flexibility.
q28_linkages: evidence generation (Loughborough) informs policy influence (ESMAP) and venture building (CLASP)
technology accelerators (competitive) feed into market-building activities (e.g., Clean Cooking Fund)
country demonstrators (FCDO Posts) test and scale R&D outputs
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (Loughborough, ESMAP) with Southern ownership (local partners, country offices). While efficiency is prioritized through existing agreements and competitive processes, equity is addressed via capacity building, gender-focused research, and inclusive partnership models (e.g., TaTEDO in Tanzania).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: competitive accelerators prioritize high-potential innovators, but gender and disability considerations are embedded in selection criteria
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: Loughborough and ESMAP lead strategically, but local partners (e.g., TaTEDO) implement context-specific solutions
cost vs. reach: leveraging ESMAP’s global platforms reduces transaction costs but may limit tailoring to hyper-local needs
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to quarterly oversight and embedded safeguarding measures. In FCAS, ESMAP tailors approaches and provides additional incentives via RBF. High-risk areas (e.g., fraud, safeguarding) are mitigated through due diligence and partner policies.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded across partners: Loughborough provides training and research grants, CLASP supports venture building, and ESMAP strengthens policy and planning tools. Southern partners (e.g., TaTEDO) receive institutional strengthening to improve delivery and ownership.

quote.text: The programme has been designed to be inherently flexible around different country contexts and market segments. The work on the drivers and pathways for countries to transition to modern energy cooking services will identify the barriers and opportunities for each context.

key_programme_risks: fraud or financial mismanagement
safeguarding incidents
currency fluctuations and delivery cost changes
deprioritization of clean cooking in policy/funding
partner delivery delays
private sector reluctance to enter emerging markets
failure to meet ambitious Clean Cooking Fund targets
programme mismanagement (reputational risk)
lack of local ownership in some contexts
unsustained multi-year funding

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Due diligence procedures; downstreampartner mapping and audits.
Due diligence includes safeguarding checks; ESMAP tailors FCV approaches.
Close monitoring with partners; flexible budget adjustments.
High-level advocacy (e.g., GeCCo, High-Level Coalition); RBF incentives.
Flexible timelines; regular progress reviews.
Diversified engagement; RBF to improve profitability.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: failure to meet Clean Cooking Fund targets
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ESMAP’s global coordination; capacity strengthening for country teams.
Adherence to World Bank/LU/CLASP quality assurance and financial oversight.
Country offices lead demonstrators; local partners (e.g., TaTEDO) embedded.
Clear agreements with partners/country offices; longer-term RED commitments.

fcas_specific_lessons: ESMAP tailors approaches for FCV contexts, including additional RBF incentives and collaboration with local private sectors/UN agencies.
Results-Based Financing (RBF) is used to mitigate risks in fragile settings by linking payments to verified outcomes.
Technical assistance and policy support are embedded in FCV engagements to strengthen local capacity.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Early phases demonstrated strong demand for MECS from policymakers (e.g., Tanzania, Uganda) and private sector (e.g., Bosch, Prestige). Challenge funds successfully crowded in innovators, and country demonstrators proved effective for scaling. The 2023 extension built on these lessons by expanding geographic scope, adding CLASP as a Tier 1 partner, and increasing flexibility for country-led demonstrators.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added CLASP as a Tier 1 partner to fill gaps in venture building and appliance testing (D0006716.odt).
Expanded research priorities to include carbon markets, commercial eCooking, and Pacific region activities (D0006716.odt).
Increased budget headroom for country demonstrators to £20m, allowing FCDO Posts to scale innovations without new agreements (D0003924.odt, D0006716.odt).
Extended programme duration to 2030 to align with SDG timeline and allow for longer-term impact (D0006716.odt).
Enhanced gender and disability inclusion frameworks based on early-phase feedback (D0006716.odt).

quote.text: The key changes have been prompted by an early and enthusiastic response to the MECS programme. [...] The scale up would allow MECS to make the most of the best of these opportunities, without getting spread too thinly.
quote.source: D0002851.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case

co_funding_partners.partner: FCDO Country Posts (Tanzania, Uganda, others TBD)
Private sector (via challenge funds, RBF, carbon finance)
National Institute for Health Research (NIHR, via University of Liverpool)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged £400 million in additional investment to date (14x the £28.15m spent by MECS), with a target of £1 billion by 2030. This includes co-financing from Multilateral Development Banks (e.g., AfDB’s 20% cleancooking pledge), private sector investments, and Results-Based Financing mechanisms.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Research is classified as capital expenditure, aligning with FCDO criteria for capital spend (D0002851.odt). The programme includes both R&D (capital) and demonstrator (revenue) components, with flexibility to reallocate between them.

quote.text: The programme has already leveraged £400 million of additional investment into clean energy and clean cooking technology research, innovation and scale-up from both private and public sources (14 times the funding spent by MECS to date).

metadata.programme_name: Sustainable Manufacturing and Environmental Pollution (SMEP)
metadata.quote: "The manufacturing processes currently being employed in most developing countries have a number of characteristics that render them unsustainable in the long term." (31255160.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "We are proposing an investment of £20 million over five years (2018-2023)." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The SMEP programme combines evidence generation (research on pollution impacts), technology development (cleaner production methods), policy influence (regulatory models), and implementation research (testing solutions in manufacturing contexts). It aims to reduce environmental pollution from manufacturing while improving economic productivity.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The SMEP programme will tackle the problem of pollution and environmental degradation generated by manufacturing processes in DFID priority countries across SSA and SA. More specifically, it will focus on preventing pollution from manufacturing sources being released in to the environment in the first place. It will do so by developing and testing the application of technology-based solutions and cleaner production methods aimed at reducing the levels of environmental pollution generated by targeted manufacturing activities, and by identifying the most suitable policy-based interventions and business models to enable change to happen." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: New scientific evidence on environmental/health impacts of manufacturing pollution
Technology-based solutions and supporting business models (10+ manufacturing areas across 6 countries)
Policy/regulatory models for adoption of technological solutions
Symbiotic production processes reducing environmental waste
Toolkits for policymakers and planners
5 million fewer people exposed to toxic pollution by 2030 (target)
500,000+ DALYs gained by 2030 (10% reduction in tanneries/product manufacturing)
15% improvement in worker productivity by 2030
what_objectives.summary: The programme integrates research, technology development, and policy work to create sustainable manufacturing solutions that reduce pollution while improving economic outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
what_objectives.quote: "The SMEP programme will also focus on generating evidence and practical solutions to address the problem of plastic ocean pollution, which was recently highlighted as a policy priority by the UK Prime Minister." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in developing countries with environmental degradation challenges but no active conflict zones. The overall risk was assessed as moderate during approval.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (31255160.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The overall risk level related to terrorist financing associated with the programme has been assessed as low." (31255160.odt, Terrorism and financing)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Outdated manufacturing infrastructure, weak pollution regulations, and political economy factors (where profits accrue to elites while costs are borne by marginalized groups) create barriers to adopting cleaner technologies. Data on chemical pollution impacts is limited in LMICs.
where_context.quote: "Environmental degradation and pollution are seen as ‘externalities’, which are not properly costed... the majority of the costs are borne by poor and politically disempowered people, who hold little or no influence in society, whereas the majority of profits are accrued by politically connected and economically wealthy classes." (31255160.odt, Strategic Case, Section 3)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID (UK) retains oversight and strategic direction, with UNCTAD (multilateral) providing technical support and political leverage. Research Consortia will be contracted through open competition managed by a Programme Management Agent (PMA) accountable to DFID.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
knowledge dissemination
policy toolkits for local governments
technical assistance to private sector

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner (technical assistance, political leverage, in-kind contributions)

partner_organizations.name: Programme Management Agent (PMA)
partner_organizations.role: day-to-day management, research commissioning, MEL, communications

partner_organizations.name: Research Consortia
partner_organizations.role: delivery of research activities and technology development
partner_organizations.location: mixed (international with local partners in SSA/SA)

partner_organizations.name: Private Sector Partners
partner_organizations.role: testing technology-based solutions in manufacturing operations
partner_organizations.location: SSA/SA (Ghana, Kenya, Zambia, Tanzania, Bangladesh, Pakistan)

partner_organizations.name: DFID Climate & Environment Department (CED)
partner_organizations.role: coordination for CHOGM 2018 messaging

partner_organizations.name: UK Mission to the UN (UKMIS Geneva)
partner_organizations.role: policy coordination with UNCTAD

who_partners.quote: "DFID will be contracting a Programme Management Agent (PMA) and will be working directly with players from across the manufacturing industry operating locally, nationally and internationally. DFID would directly supervise the PMA, who will be directly accountable to DFID." (31255160.odt, Appraisal Case, Option 4)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is a contract with a Programme Management Agent (PMA) for overall management, combined with competitive grants/contracts to Research Consortia for specific activities. UNCTAD provides in-kind contributions (£2M equivalent).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID contracts a PMA to manage research funding, sub-contracting, MEL, and communications. UNCTAD acts as a strategic partner for technical support and political leverage. Research Consortia deliver specific projects through open competition.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The PMA and Research Consortia will be selected through open competition to ensure transparency and value for money. UNCTAD was chosen for its technical expertise and ability to influence multinational corporations and governments.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID resources will be used to fund research and development (R&D) activities commissioned through open competition and managed by a competitively procured programme management agent." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The PMA will manage day-to-day operations under DFID supervision. UNCTAD provides strategic oversight. A modular structure allows termination of underperforming components without affecting the whole programme.
how_governance.quote: "The modular structure of the programme and its flexible management arrangement will ensure that, if any component of the programme is not successful, it can be terminated without significantly affecting the remaining elements." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary) and "We will also maintain a flexible and dynamic approach to identifying new thematic priorities and learning needs throughout the lifetime of the programme, as these emerge. This will include conducting yearly reviews and, if necessary, revisions of the logframe, as well as the Theory of Change." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The modular design allows funds to be reallocated between components. Unsuccessful components can be terminated without requiring approval for reallocation to other areas.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Yearly reviews will assess progress and may lead to revisions of the logframe and Theory of Change. New thematic priorities can be added as they emerge, subject to approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "We will also maintain a flexible and dynamic approach to identifying new thematic priorities and learning needs throughout the lifetime of the programme, as these emerge. This will include conducting yearly reviews and, if necessary, revisions of the logframe, as well as the Theory of Change." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Programme Management Agent (PMA) → Research Consortia/Private Sector Partners
how_efficiency.quote: "The SMEP programme will address the overarching principle and commitment towards achieving value for money and delivering efficiently by adopting a flexible structure that enables DFID to reduce overall administrative costs, streamline management and improve performance and delivery." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Would forfeit humanitarian/economic benefits and miss SDG targets.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Partner with UK Research Councils (BEIS/EPSRC)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: RCs lacked experience in LMIC engagement/policy influence and had UK-centric priorities. Delays in tendering processes.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: Contribute to existing international programme (UNIDO/ILO/World Bank)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: No existing programmes matched SMEP’s focus on prevention (vs. remediation). Limited DFID influence over strategic direction.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 4: Launch self-standing programme with PMA + UNCTAD (CHOSEN)
q24_alternatives_considered.selected_because: Allowed DFID control over scope, leveraged UNCTAD’s technical/political influence, and enabled flexible management.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 was selected for its balance of DFID control, UNCTAD’s technical/political leverage, and flexible management structure that could adapt to emerging priorities. It avoided the delays of RC partnerships and the limited influence of joining existing programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in PMA procurement could slow programme launch.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Competitive procurement process initiated early with clear timelines.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited LMIC stakeholder engagement by Research Consortia.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: PMA required to ensure local partner inclusion in consortia and capacity-building activities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector partners may prioritize profits over environmental goals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Business models and policy frameworks designed to align financial incentives with sustainability (e.g., productivity gains from cleaner processes).

why_rationale.quote: "Option 4: DFID launches a self-standing research programme, partnering with others, using an innovative structure and approach based on prior experience from existing programmes... This option would involve setting up a new international research programme that will deliver innovative solutions to improve the environmental footprint and health impacts of manufacturing in DCs." (31255160.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia—regions with weak regulatory environments and political economy challenges—required partners (UNCTAD, PMA) capable of navigating complex stakeholder landscapes and influencing multinational corporations and governments.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak pollution regulations in target countries limit enforcement of solutions.
Political economy imbalances (profits to elites, costs to marginalized groups) require partners with advocacy capacity.
Need for local private sector access to test technologies necessitated partnerships with firms operating in SSA/SA.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to develop *and test* technology-based solutions in real manufacturing settings (WHAT) required a delivery structure (HOW) that combined research expertise (Consortia) with private sector access (PMA partnerships) and policy influence (UNCTAD).
q28_linkages: Technology testing in factories → required private sector partnerships and flexible funding for pilot projects.
Policy influence goals → necessitated UNCTAD’s role for government/corporate engagement.
Prevention focus (vs. remediation) → shaped open competition for innovative solutions.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between rapid delivery and inclusive partnerships, particularly in ensuring Southern ownership while maintaining DFID’s strategic control. The modular design balances efficiency (terminating underperforming components) with equity (capacity-building embedded in all activities).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Open competition for Consortia risks excluding LMIC-led teams without targeted outreach.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern research expertise is prioritized for technical rigor, but capacity-building aims to shift ownership over time.
Cost vs. reach: Testing solutions in 6 countries (vs. broader regional work) balances depth of impact with budget constraints.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile led to a "milestone-based" oversight approach with yearly reviews, rather than intensive embedded monitoring. The modular structure allows for termination of high-risk components without disrupting the entire programme.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is embedded in the PMA’s role (training, toolkits) and UNCTAD’s technical assistance, ensuring Southern partners can eventually lead adoption of solutions. Research Consortia are required to include local partners.
intersections.quote: "The development of solutions which can improve the environmental and health impacts of manufacturing is highly needed, but severely underfunded... On the other hand, the cost of equipment is a larger proportion of operational costs [in LMICs], which makes the business case for large scale change more challenging." (31255160.odt, Strategic Case, Section 3)

key_programme_risks: Limited adoption of technological solutions by private sector due to upfront costs.
Political resistance to regulatory changes from influential industry groups.
Weak enforcement of environmental standards in target countries.
Delays in PMA procurement or Research Consortia selection.
Terrorism threats in one or more operating countries (assessed as low risk for financing).
Plastic pollution solutions may face resistance from informal recycling sectors.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Private sector resistance to cost of new technologies
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Develop business models showing productivity/efficiency gains (e.g., 15% worker productivity target). Partner with firms to pilot solutions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political economy barriers to policy change
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UNCTAD’s leverage with governments and multinational corporations; focus on ‘win-win’ solutions (e.g., job creation from symbiotic production).
Embed capacity-building for local regulators; use UNCTAD’s technical assistance to strengthen institutions.
Early initiation of competitive processes with clear timelines; modular design allows phased start of activities.
Screening of implementing partners; DFID programme team supervision to prevent fund diversion.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Pollution Management & Environmental Health (PMEH) programme (World Bank) highlighted the need to focus on *prevention* (SMEP) rather than remediation (PMEH). Experience with UK Research Councils showed their limited capacity for LMIC engagement and policy influence.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The modular structure and yearly review process were added to allow adaptive management, addressing rigidities seen in earlier programmes. Capacity-building was embedded (not standalone) to ensure sustainability.
risks_lessons.quote: "The SMEP programme will complement the work of the Pollution Management & Environmental Health (PMEH) programme... The PMEH programme is aimed at: i) reducing the levels of pollution that have already been released in the environment; ii) developing technical solutions to detect and monitor different types of pollution more effectively; and iii) cleaning-up contaminated sites... The SMEP programme will focus on preventing pollution from manufacturing from being released into the environment in the first place." (31255160.odt, Appraisal Case)

co_funding_partners.partner: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UNCTAD providing £2 million in-kind contributions (technical support, staff time, venues). Private sector partners contributing access to manufacturing operations/value chains.
financial_details.quote: "We are proposing an investment of £20 million over five years (2018-2023)... UNCTAD will provide £2 million in kind contributions towards the implementation of programme activities in the form of technical support and dedicated staff time, venues for high-level meetings and events and related resources." (31255160.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Climate-Compatible Growth (CCG)
metadata.quote: "Climate-Compatible Growth research programme (CCG) brings together a consortium of top UK and international researchers to deliver on key priorities set out in the International Development White Paper (IDWP)." (D0005256.odt, Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: January 2021 – March 2025", "New project end date (if applicable): March 2030" (D0005256.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CCG is a research and innovation platform that aims to accelerate the roll-out of improved infrastructure supporting low-carbon transitions and inclusive growth. It combines evidence generation (research), technology development (open-source tools), capacity building (training and partnerships), and policy influence (supporting national strategies and international commitments).
what_objectives.q1_source: "CCG is a research and innovation platform that aims to accelerate the roll-out of improved infrastructure that supports low-carbon transitions and inclusive growth." (D0005256.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
q3_expected_outputs: 400-500 working papers and policy briefs
200-280 peer-reviewed journal articles
Open-source energy and transport decarbonisation modelling tools (e.g., OSeMOSYS, CLEWs)
Training of 455+ people in face-to-face courses and 1,315+ in online courses
Establishment of 10-20 Masters courses in LMIC universities with 200+ scholarships per year by FY29/30
Support to 6-8 national partnerships and 10+ affiliate countries
Influence $5bn/year of MDB lending decisions on electrification and transport infrastructure
Development of 'Data-to-Deal' approach to mobilise green finance for infrastructure
New workstream on critical minerals for low-carbon transition
what_objectives.summary: CCG generates evidence and tools to support low-carbon infrastructure planning, builds capacity through partnerships, and influences policy and investment decisions in developing countries.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will seek to leverage direct impact by working initially with relevant International Development Association (IDA) programmes as prospective scaling candidates." (90000175.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with weak economic incentives, weak institutional environments, and politicised decision-making, but these are not classified as FCAS. The overall programme risk rating is explicitly stated as 'moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (90000175.odt, Risk section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak economic incentives, politicised decision-making (e.g., coal subsidies), and lack of regulatory frameworks hamper investment in climate-compatible infrastructure. COVID-19 has also reshaped energy/transport planning, creating both risks (e.g., cheap fossil fuels) and opportunities (e.g., green recovery packages).
where_context.quote: "The investment needed to achieve SDG targets and address growing emissions levels is hampered by weak economic incentives, weak institutional and regulatory environments, and politicised decision-making." (90000175.odt, Risk section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The core research consortium (UK universities) leads research design and delivery, while Southern partners contribute via flexible funds and capacity-building activities. Decision-making is anchored in the UK consortium, with Southern input structured through partnerships and advisory groups.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (face-to-face and online courses)
mentorship (Special Interest Groups, SIGs)
co-authorship (Southern researchers in SPF/FRF projects)
research grants (Southern Partners Fund, Flexible Research Fund)
institutional strengthening (Masters programmes, university curricula integration)
knowledge exchange ecosystems (government-researcher collaboration)
