who_partners.quote: "The majority of the work of the core research consortium is ‘programmed’ via seven long-term research strategies [...] Membership of the core consortium is reviewed annually to ensure it is best placed to deliver CCG’s priority research areas." (D0005256.odt, How section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an accountable grant to Loughborough University (primary mechanism) and direct funding partnerships with multilateral organizations (e.g., ADB). Flexible funds (Southern Partners Fund, Flexible Research Fund, Engagement Fund) allow responsive commissioning.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Loughborough University manages the programme on behalf of the core consortium (7 universities + 2 non-academic partners). The consortium delivers programmed research, while flexible funds support demand-led activities. International partnerships (e.g., ADB, IEA) are managed through direct agreements.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The core consortium was selected based on existing expertise in low-carbon energy/transport modelling. Flexible funds use open calls (e.g., Flexible Research Fund requires ≥40% to Southern researchers) to broaden participation.
how_mechanism.quote: "The majority of the work of the core research consortium is ‘programmed’ via seven long-term research strategies [...] A smaller component involves a direct funding partnership with the Asian Development Bank." (D0005256.odt, How section)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Flexible funds (FRF, SPF, Engagement Fund) are allocated via scored/prioritised requests from National/International Partners, reviewed by the CCG Partnerships Directorate and FCDO.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: CCG has an external Advisory Group (academics) and undergoes annual reviews by FCDO, including input from the Deputy Chief Scientific Adviser and Chief Economist. Research strategies are refreshed annually with external peer review.
how_governance.quote: "The programme has been reviewed internally at SCS level by the Deputy Chief Scientific Adviser as well as the Chief Economist, Heads of Professions for Climate & Environment and Infrastructure and FCDO Energy and Economics Senior Research Fellows." (90000175.odt, Oversight)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Flexible funds (20% of core budget) can be reallocated between research themes based on demand, but programmed research requires annual strategy reviews. Engagement Fund (new in FY24/25) will ring-fence resources for partner-driven research.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research strategies are refreshed annually, and flexible funds allow responsive commissioning. Major pivots (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine war) have been accommodated via FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The research strategies are subject to review by the FCDO, external expert peer reviewers and CCG’s external Advisory Group. They are refreshed on an annual basis [...] allowing the core programmed research to respond to evolving demands." (D0005256.odt, Programmed Research)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Loughborough University (consortium lead) → Southern partners/researchers
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme has three main features designed to closely integrate research and research uptake activities: a core research consortium; a partnership structure; and a flexible funding model." (D0005256.odt, How section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Contribution to multi-donor trust funds (rejected for lack of control/branding)
Bilateral technical assistance (not mentioned as considered)
Standalone research programme (rejected for lack of uptake focus)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The consortium model was chosen to combine (1) world-class UK academic expertise with (2) flexible, demand-led research uptake via partnerships. Direct funding to multilaterals (e.g., ADB) ensures alignment with country priorities, while flexible funds enable Southern ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Northern expertise limiting Southern ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible funds (SPF, FRF) require ≥40% allocation to Southern researchers; capacity-building is core to partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex consortium coordination slowing delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual strategy reviews, dedicated programme management team, and milestone-based oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexible funds being underutilised by Southern partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement Fund (FY24/25) will ring-fence resources for partner-driven research; SIGs co-create research agendas.

why_rationale.quote: "CCG’s offer is broad but at its core is a set of world-class, open-source energy and transport decarbonisation modelling tools, developed principally in UK institutions, coupled with tried-and-tested training programmes to support their uptake by developing country stakeholders." (D0005256.odt, Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Political economy and institutional weaknesses in target countries limit the ability to work with certain government agencies or utilities, requiring adaptive partnership strategies (e.g., focus on 'champion' ministries or academic institutions).
q27_constraints_detail: Weak regulatory environments → limits private sector engagement
Politicised decision-making → requires working with reform-minded 'champions'
Data limitations → necessitates co-creation of datasets with local partners
FCAS-like risks in some countries → affects in-country delivery models
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for integrated energy/transport systems analysis (WHAT) requires a consortium with multidisciplinary expertise (HOW), while the focus on research uptake demands embedded partnerships with Southern institutions.
q28_linkages: Open-source tools (WHAT) → require consortium with technical expertise (HOW)
Policy influence objective (WHAT) → necessitates partnerships with ministries/IFIs (HOW)
Capacity building (WHAT) → shapes flexible funds for Southern researchers (HOW)
Regional focus (WHERE) → determines selection of ADB/AfDB as partners (WHO)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) the efficiency of Northern-led research with (2) the equity goal of Southern ownership, using flexible funds and capacity-building to mitigate trade-offs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (Northern expertise) vs. inclusion (Southern ownership)
Cost (consortium management) vs. reach (multi-country partnerships)
Technical rigour (UK tools) vs. local relevance (co-created datasets)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'moderate' risk profile leads to milestone-based oversight and annual strategy reviews, while FCAS-like contexts in some countries require adaptive partnership models (e.g., working through academics rather than government).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building activities (e.g., SIGs, training) enable Southern partners to transition from recipients to co-creators of research, influencing their roles in the consortium.
intersections.quote: "CCG is built upon the principle that partner governments should develop ownership of national planning. This requires the development of national capacity within government and with non-governmental domestic institutions." (D0005256.odt, Capacity Building)

key_programme_risks: Politicised decision-making in partner countries distorting investment priorities (e.g., coal subsidies)
Weak institutional capacity limiting uptake of tools/evidence
COVID-19 disrupting energy/transport planning and recovery packages
Over-reliance on Northern expertise undermining Southern ownership
Complex consortium structure creating coordination challenges
Flexible funds being underutilised by Southern partners
Data limitations hindering modelling and scenario analysis
Climate risks (e.g., extreme weather) affecting infrastructure investments
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., China’s Belt and Road) influencing energy transitions
Regulatory lag failing to keep pace with technological change

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work with reform-minded ‘champions’ in government; use Political Economy Analysis to navigate constraints.
Embed capacity-building in partnerships (e.g., SIGs, training); co-create tools with local institutions.
Pivot research to analyse green recovery opportunities; engage with stimulus package designers.
Flexible funds (SPF, FRF) require ≥40% Southern allocation; capacity-building is a core objective.
Annual strategy reviews; dedicated programme management team; milestone-based oversight.
Co-create ‘starter data kits’ with local partners; build modelling capacity via training.
Integrate climate resilience into planning tools; support adaptive infrastructure designs.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS-like contexts, focus on academic institutions and civil society where government engagement is constrained.
Use Political Economy Analysis to identify ‘windows of opportunity’ for reform.
Prioritise flexible, demand-led research to adapt to rapidly changing contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Early phases showed that national partnerships take 2–3 years to mature; later phases emphasise patient, long-term engagement. The ‘Data-to-Deal’ approach emerged from learning that analytical capacity is a key barrier to mobilising climate finance.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added Engagement Fund (FY24/25) to better respond to partner demands.
Integrated Political Economy Analysis into country strategies.
Expanded ‘Data-to-Deal’ focus to link analysis directly to finance mobilisation.
Developed critical minerals workstream in response to geopolitical shifts (e.g., Ukraine war).
risks_lessons.quote: "CCG is early in its life. Past experience has demonstrated that national and international partnerships take time to reach their full potential [...] As relationships of trust are built, the technical capacity needed to facilitate uptake is developed and expanded." (D0005256.odt, Effectiveness)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £1.4m co-funding and £546k in-kind support mobilised in FY22/23; expected to increase with greater visibility of tools/training.
financial_details.quote: "During FY22/23, CCG’s International Partnerships and core research workstreams have reported over £1.4 million mobilised as co-funding as well as in-kind support to a value of £546,000." (D0005256.odt, Co-funding)

metadata.programme_name: Climate Adaptation and Resilience research framework programme (CLARE)
metadata.quote: "The Climate Adaptation and Resilience research framework programme (CLARE) will accelerate delivery of new and improved knowledge, data and tools focused on tackling real-world natural hazard, climate change adaptation and resilience problems facing the poor and vulnerable." (D0001123.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 01/04/2022 End Date: 31/03/2027" (D0001123.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CLARE is a research programme that generates new evidence (evidence generation) while also developing practical tools and technologies (technology development), strengthening local capacity (capacity building), and directly informing policy and programming (policy influence). It combines research with implementation support and service delivery to FCDO country offices.
what_objectives.q1_source: "CLARE will accelerate delivery of new and improved knowledge, data and tools focused on tackling real-world natural hazard, climate change adaptation and resilience problems... Combined with strengthening local capacity to do and use research and evidence, the Programme will drive better solutions and more effective investments in climate adaptation and resilience action and disaster risk management by HMG and other international and national development actors." (D0001123.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Actionable adaptation solutions to support the most vulnerable (at various scales)
Strengthened agency in the Global South to do and use research for equitable adaptation action
Strong cross-sectoral, diverse networks dedicated to equitable adaptation action
Enhanced capacity of research and development actors along whole value chain from research to action
Ground-breaking adaptation science and research for transformational change
Tested adaptation tools, technologies and data that work for decision makers and practitioners
Reach at least 5 million people within five years, working on issues affecting over one billion people at risk from climate impacts by 2030
what_objectives.summary: CLARE aims to generate actionable knowledge and tools for climate adaptation while strengthening local research capacity and directly supporting FCDO's climate programming through embedded services and technical assistance.
what_objectives.quote: "CLARE will drive better solutions and more effective investments in climate adaptation and resilience action and disaster risk management by HMG and other international and national development actors." (D0001123.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: Global (with focus on Africa and the Indo-Pacific)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in climate-vulnerable contexts with institutional and capacity constraints, but is not primarily focused on FCAS. The risk is categorized as moderate due to the complexity of multi-country operations and the need to coordinate across diverse partners.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0001123.odt, Programme summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and limited data on climate hazards/vulnerability in developing countries create barriers to effective adaptation. Regulatory and capacity gaps in using research for decision-making require targeted interventions. Climate risks themselves create urgency for the programme's work.
where_context.quote: "Significant advances have been made in recent years in the understanding of the climate system, climate risk and in the development of some climate services to support resilience and adaptation action... However, there are still substantial knowledge gaps that undermine our ability to meet the on-going and urgent solution-orientated evidence demands of decision-makers." (D0001123.odt, Context and need for intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes co-development with Southern partners, including through the Adaptation Research Alliance which requires strong Southern Hemisphere participation. Strategic partnerships with IDRC (Canada) and UKRI suggest shared decision-making, though FCDO retains overall oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
research grants
institutional strengthening
Chevening Scholarships expansion
fellowships for early-career researchers

partner_organizations.name: International Development Research Centre (IDRC)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner (co-funder and co-implementer)

partner_organizations.name: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner (co-funder and co-implementer)

partner_organizations.name: UK Met Office
partner_organizations.role: technical partner (climate science and services)

partner_organizations.name: Adaptation Research Alliance members (e.g., UNEP, WMO, IPCC, GCF, Future Earth)
partner_organizations.role: implementation partners and knowledge networks

partner_organizations.name: Southern research institutions (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: local research partners and capacity-building recipients

partner_organizations.name: FCDO country and regional offices
partner_organizations.role: end-users of research and technical assistance

who_partners.quote: "CLARE will deliver through two primary and proven strategic partnerships—with the International Development Research Centre (IDRC) of the Government of Canada, and with UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)." (D0001123.odt, Delivery Options)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants and contracts, with competitive commissioning for research components. The Adaptation Research Alliance secretariat (from the transition phase) was funded via an accountable grant to a hosting organization.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: CLARE operates as a research framework with multiple strategic partners (IDRC, UKRI) and an open consortium model for specific research projects. It includes a portfolio approach rather than separate programmes, allowing flexibility in commissioning. The Adaptation Research Alliance provides an overarching coordination mechanism.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme emphasizes competitive, demand-responsive research commissioning to ensure value for money and relevance. Past experience with UKRI and IDRC demonstrates the effectiveness of open calls for high-quality proposals.
how_mechanism.quote: "Using ‘smart’ competitive research commissioning to drive commercial advantage... The programme will use competitive processes to commission research, ensuring high quality and value for money." (D0001123.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: An Executive Board (EB) for CLARE is mentioned, suggesting high-level oversight. The Adaptation Research Alliance includes a secretariat and senior champions, with co-developed plans requiring member buy-in. FCDO retains ultimate approval authority.
how_governance.quote: "Governance and accountability systems will be established through the Accountable Grant or contractual arrangement used." (59949827.odt, Implementation Modality) AND "The Executive Board for the CLARE Programme (EB)" (D0001123.odt, Programme Governance)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The portfolio framework allows some reallocation between themes, but major changes require approval. The programme is designed to adapt to emerging priorities, with breakpoints for review.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes iterative learning and co-development with partners. Research priorities can be adjusted through competitive calls and stakeholder engagement, subject to FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The long-term, complex, non-linear, and emergent nature of climate impacts... requires that CLARE is designed to be flexible and responsive... The Programme has therefore been designed with flexibility in mind, including the possibility of expanding the scope of the above themes or if necessary, adding new ones as required." (D0001123.odt, Strategic Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Strategic Partners (IDRC/UKRI) → Research Consortia/Implementers. The Adaptation Research Alliance adds a coordination layer but operates separately.
how_efficiency.quote: "How the funds will be paid out and allocated: Funds will be disbursed based on agreed milestones and deliverables, with regular reporting and financial oversight." (D0001123.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: suite of separate programmes (rejected in favor of portfolio approach)
direct FCDO implementation (rejected due to lack of technical capacity)
sole reliance on multilateral mechanisms (rejected for lack of flexibility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The portfolio framework was selected for its flexibility, ability to realize synergies across themes, and improved value for money compared to separate programmes. Strategic partnerships with IDRC and UKRI leverage additional funds and expertise while maintaining FCDO oversight. The Adaptation Research Alliance provides a mechanism for global coordination and sustainability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating a large, diverse partnership may lead to delays or misalignment.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear governance structures (Executive Board, secretariat) and phased co-development of priorities with regular milestone reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Northern institutions for research leadership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit requirements for Southern Hemisphere participation in the Adaptation Research Alliance and capacity-building components.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexible funding may lead to mission creep.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular performance reviews and FCDO approval for major reallocations.

why_rationale.quote: "A single, portfolio-level partnership approach will improve synergies and collaboration among previously distinct programmes and delivery partners, facilitate the translation of research into action across multiple sectors, and increase effectiveness in the use and management of financial resources." (D0001123.odt, Assessment of Delivery Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on climate-vulnerable regions (Africa/Indo-Pacific) require partners with strong local presence and credibility. Weak institutional capacity in some target countries necessitates partnerships with organizations like IDRC and UKRI that have experience operating in these contexts.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing networks in Africa/Indo-Pacific
Requirement for organizations experienced in FCAS or high-risk environments
Local language and cultural knowledge for effective capacity building
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for action-oriented, user-centred research drives the open partnership model and competitive commissioning. The mix of evidence generation and implementation support requires both strategic partners (for coordination) and flexible funding mechanisms (for responsiveness).
q28_linkages: Action-oriented research → requires competitive calls and Southern partner engagement
Capacity building goals → necessitates embedded training and mentorship structures
Policy influence objective → drives need for FCDO oversight and country office engagement
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses balancing Northern expertise with Southern ownership, noting that "while UK institutions provide world-leading climate science, the Alliance must ensure strong Southern Hemisphere participation to address locally relevant needs." The portfolio approach aims to reconcile this by combining competitive quality assurance with targeted capacity building.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Competitive processes may favor established Northern institutions, mitigated by ring-fenced Southern capacity funds
Expertise vs. ownership: UK Met Office leadership balanced by co-development requirements in the Alliance
Cost vs. reach: Portfolio synergies improve efficiency while regional focus ensures relevance
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to milestone-based oversight with regular reporting, rather than light-touch management. FCAS contexts within the global scope require additional safeguards without full restrictive controls.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective that directly shapes partner roles—Southern institutions are positioned as both implementers (through competitive grants) and capacity recipients (via training/mentorship). The Chevening expansion and fellowships create pathways for Southern researchers to take leadership roles.
intersections.quote: "The Adaptation Research Alliance initiative is aimed to ensure that the research and action has the end-user in mind. The initiative will make considerable efforts to engage a broad range of stakeholders, including carefully considering gender and disability to ensure the outputs... are effectively communicated to all stakeholders." (59949827.odt, Gender Equality and Disability)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient buy-in from Southern Hemisphere partners
Misalignment between research outputs and country office needs
Delays in establishing the Adaptation Research Alliance
Overlap with other climate research initiatives
Capacity constraints in target countries limiting uptake
Political shifts affecting COP26 momentum
Data gaps undermining research quality
Climate risks outpacing adaptation solutions

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient buy-in from Southern Hemisphere partners
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased consultation process with senior champions; ring-fenced funds for Southern-led research; explicit Alliance participation requirements.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Misalignment between research and country needs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demand-responsive design with regular country office engagement; Climate Mainstreaming Facility for tailored support.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in establishing the Adaptation Research Alliance
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Rapid inception phase with high-profile champions; alignment with COP26 timeline as a forcing mechanism.
Embedded capacity building through fellowships, training, and institutional partnerships; focus on 'ecosystem-like' approaches.

fcas_specific_lessons: Adaptation research in fragile contexts must integrate conflict sensitivity (citing Peters et al. 2020 on climate-conflict links).
Local ownership is critical for sustainability in high-risk environments.
Flexible funding mechanisms are needed to respond to rapidly changing FCAS dynamics.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous programmes (FCFA, CARIAA, SHEAR) demonstrated the need for: 1) stronger research uptake mechanisms; 2) better integration of social and physical sciences; 3) more explicit focus on actionable outputs. CLARE adopts a portfolio approach and demand-responsive services to address these gaps.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from separate programmes to a unified portfolio framework; increased emphasis on transdisciplinary research; explicit capacity-building components; stronger links to FCDO country offices through services like the Climate Mainstreaming Facility.
risks_lessons.quote: "The extensive learning derived from these predecessor research programmes points to the need for adjustments and refinements in the way future projects are designed, commissioned and operated to ensure research programming is ‘fit for purpose’ in helping tackle the scale and urgency of the climate challenge." (D0001123.odt, Context and need for intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to catalyze additional funding through the Adaptation Research Alliance, with commitments from research and action funders. Exact leverage targets are not quantified but the Alliance concept note references increased funding as a core objective.
financial_details.quote: "CLARE represents a substantive commitment to the international Adaptation Research Alliance ambition to scale up investment and collaboration in action-orientated, user-centred research... This investment will lead the way for others to follow suit with similar commitments." (D0001123.odt, Rationale for UK/FCDO to invest)

metadata.programme_name: ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility (ACGF) - UK-ASEAN Green Recovery Accelerator Fund

quote.programme_name: The ACGF is an existing, multi-donor facility, which the UK would contribute to by establishing a new trust fund called the UK-ASEAN Green Recovery Accelerator Fund. (D0000978.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.duration: Start Date: August 2021; End Date: August 2026 (D0000978.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: Start Date: August 2021; End Date: August 2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling UK ODA funds through a trust fund) with implementation research (testing green infrastructure projects) and capacity building (technical assistance to improve project design). It aims to catalyze private and public investment in low-emissions, climate-resilient infrastructure across ASEAN countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme would result in new infrastructure in Southeast Asia that is greener than it would otherwise be – helping to reduce emissions, build resilience to climate change and protect biodiversity – while also reducing poverty and supporting a green, economic recovery to COVID-19. (D0000978.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 12-15 green infrastructure projects financed
reduced carbon emissions in infrastructure projects
increased climate resilience benefits of infrastructure
protected biodiversity
economic development and poverty reduction in ASEAN countries
strengthened UK-ASEAN government dialogue on green infrastructure growth and investment
increased UK investment in ASEAN green infrastructure projects
technical assistance for project preparation (rapid assessment studies, green impact assessments, legal work, etc.)
regulatory changes in ASEAN countries for green infrastructure
new investment models demonstrated and replicated

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to accelerate green infrastructure investment in ASEAN by providing concessional finance and technical assistance to make projects bankable, while strengthening UK-ASEAN cooperation on climate action.

quote.objectives: The programme will be delivered through a dedicated trust fund managed by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), where FCDO funds will be used to make infrastructure projects greener and more affordable. (D0000978.odt, Programme summary)
quote.approach: The programme will target both sovereign and private financing as appropriate for different types of infrastructure. (D0000978.odt, What is the narrative of the programme?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'Minor' risk in the document, but contextually, ASEAN countries face climate vulnerability, political risks, and weak policy environments for green infrastructure. Myanmar is explicitly excluded due to political instability.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Minor (D0000978.odt, Summary Sheet); Myanmar is not a country of operation until a democratic government is reinstalled. (D0000978.odt, Countries section)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (weak policy environments for renewable energy)
political economy (high perceived risks for private investors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The lack of bankable projects and weak policy environments hinder private investment in green infrastructure. Exchange rate volatility and political risks increase perceived risks for investors. The COVID-19 pandemic has further constrained public budgets, making concessional finance critical for project viability.

quote.constraints: The pipeline of commercially viable green investment opportunities is relatively limited. This can be due to high real or perceived risks, including political and regulatory risk, technology risk, and credit and capital market risk. (D0000978.odt, What are the barriers preventing investment in green infrastructure in ASEAN?)
quote.climate_risk: ADB estimates that the impact of climate change on the region could be as much as 11% of GDP by 2100 due to impacts on agriculture and tourism, health, ecosystems, labour productivity and because of catastrophic risks. (D0000978.odt, Context section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The ADB (a multilateral institution with significant Northern influence) manages the trust fund and project selection, though ASEAN governments prioritize projects. The UK provides governance oversight through the ACGF Partnership Group.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for project preparation (rapid assessment studies, green impact assessments)
legal work and regulatory support
training and skill-building for green finance champions
support for replicable financial structures and policy reforms
seconded UK expert to ADB to promote nature-based solutions and gender equality

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager and delivery agent for the trust fund; project origination and technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Infrastructure Fund (AIF)
partner_organizations.role: Oversees the ACGF as a dedicated window for green infrastructure; governed by ASEAN Finance Ministers

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funding provider and governance oversight through the ACGF Partnership Group

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia
partner_organizations.role: Project beneficiaries and co-financiers; prioritize national infrastructure projects

partner_organizations.name: Private investors (e.g., ADM Capital, BNP Paribas, OPIC)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-financiers for projects; targeted through investor events

partner_organizations.name: European Investment Bank (EIB), KfW (German development bank), Agence Française de Développement (AFD)
partner_organizations.role: Co-donors to the ACGF

quote.delivery_structure: The programme will be delivered through a dedicated trust fund managed by the Asian Development Bank (ADB). (D0000978.odt, Programme summary)
quote.capacity_building: Our technical assistance will help create regulatory changes in ASEAN countries and the new projects will demonstrate new investment models which can be replicated again. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.governance: Our position on the ACGF Partnership Group creates a new, and high level, mechanism for government to government dialogue on green investment. (D0000978.odt, Secondary benefits Theory of Change)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK contribution consists of (1) a grant-based trust fund (£100m capital + £10m technical assistance) managed by ADB, providing 0% interest loans/concessional finance to governments, and (2) technical assistance for project preparation. Funds are blended with ADB loans and private capital.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The ADB acts as the fund manager for the UK-ASEAN Green Recovery Accelerator Fund (a trust fund within the broader ACGF). ADB originates projects, manages technical assistance, and oversees financial flows, while the UK participates in governance through the ACGF Partnership Group.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The ADB was selected due to its existing role as manager of the ACGF and ASEAN Infrastructure Fund, its track record in green finance, and its ability to leverage public and private capital. The UK’s contribution builds on an established multilateral platform.

quote.instrument: FCDO grants would add to the amount of money available to be lent at very concessional rates – which in turn would increase the amount of public and private capital the ACGF would be able to attract (scaling). (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.selection: The Bank’s country offices and sector teams as well as ASEAN member nations will be the originator of projects. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.structure: We propose to establish a trust fund within the ADB that increases the number of very concessional loans being made to governments. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ACGF Partnership Group includes ASEAN Finance Ministers, ADB, and donor representatives (including the UK). This group oversees strategic direction and project approvals. The ADB manages day-to-day operations, while the UK has a seat at the governance table.

quote.governance: The major stakeholders are ASEAN Infrastructure Fund and its Board made up of ASEAN Finance Ministries. The Asian Development Bank is the Fund Manager for the ASEAN Infrastructure Fund and will be the delivery agent for our trust fund. (D0000978.odt, What are the stakeholder considerations?)
quote.oversight: The success of the facility will be dependent on originating a pipeline of quality projects. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects within the ACGF pipeline, but projects must meet strict green criteria (e.g., 90% climate finance, alignment with NDCs). Reallocation requires approval by the ACGF Partnership Group.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in technical assistance priorities (e.g., focusing on green recovery post-COVID) and project selection criteria, but changes require governance approval. The Theory of Change includes a review of screening criteria during implementation.

quote.reallocation: As the loans are repaid the money would then be recycled to finance other projects (12-15 in total). (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.adaptive: We will need to finalise the criteria for screening projects during the implementation of the programme. (D0000978.odt, Priority Green Projects)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ADB (fund manager) → end projects (governments/private sector). The ADB acts as both fund manager and implementer, reducing layers.

quote.layers: The ADB’s ability to source and develop clean infrastructure projects using the reach of its country and sector teams is one of the major advantages of delivering through this facility. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.payment: The technical assistance requirement is 10% of the capital being deployed, which reflects norms for blended finance programmes. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Multilateral climate funds (Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility)
MDB-led programmes (World Bank, ADB general lending)
Regional facilities (Southeast Asia Clean Energy Facility)
Development Finance Institutions (PIDG, CDC)
National green finance instruments (e.g., Malaysia’s Green Technology Financing Scheme)
Impact investors and commercial funds (e.g., Asia Climate Partners)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The ACGF was selected because it (1) is politically embedded in ASEAN (sovereign-backed and aligned with national priorities), (2) reaches projects not covered by other UK programming, (3) leverages ADB’s track record in green finance and project preparation, (4) allows the UK to influence a major regional climate fund, and (5) provides a mechanism to catalyze private sector investment through blended finance.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage ratio of 6:1 demonstrated by AIF)
risk mitigation (ADB’s strong safeguards and ESG standards)
partner capacity (ADB’s existing pipeline and technical expertise)
speed (building on an existing facility rather than creating a new one)
flexibility (ability to recycle funds and adjust priorities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on ADB’s project pipeline, which may not align with UK priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will second an expert to the ADB structuring unit to ensure alignment with ‘dark green’ priorities and monitor project selection.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited private sector leverage if projects remain sovereign-focused
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance will prioritize public-private partnerships and private sector mobilization; UK will use its governance role to push for higher private co-financing targets.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Displacement of private finance (crowding out)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK funds will only support projects that cannot proceed without concessional finance, with additionality checks for each project.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak monitoring of climate impacts (e.g., GHG reductions)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will strengthen ACGF reporting on greenhouse gas emissions and resource efficiency, with 15% of programme management costs allocated to M&E.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of ODA funds through blending)
efficiency (leverage of ADB’s existing systems and pipelines)
equity (targeting ODA-eligible countries and inclusive growth)

quote.alternatives: At a global level, multilateral climate funds (Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, Climate Investment Funds) provide grants and some concessional loans for climate-related infrastructure projects in individual Southeast Asia countries. (D0000978.odt, What options are available to the UK to support green infrastructure?)
quote.rationale: The ACGF occupies a specific niche with high potential to reduce CO2 emissions, increase climate resilience and drive clean growth. It is well politically embedded across the region, sovereign-backed and reaches projects which our other programming in the region does not. (D0000978.odt, The Strategic Case)
quote.vfm: The track record of AIF in mobilising public donor and national government capital ($3 billion to date at a leverage ratio of 6:1). (D0000978.odt, Evidence base for our intervention)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The regional focus on ASEAN (exclusive of Myanmar) and the need for sovereign backing limit partner selection to entities with existing ASEAN relationships (e.g., ADB, AIF). The political economy constraints (weak policy environments, high perceived risks) necessitate a multilateral fund manager with strong safeguards and technical capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Exclusion of Myanmar due to political instability
Need for sovereign-backed projects to mitigate private sector risks
ADB’s role as fund manager driven by its regional presence and technical expertise
Limited pool of private investors willing to engage in frontier markets (e.g., Cambodia, Laos)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (financing + capacity building + policy influence) require a multilateral fund manager (ADB) capable of blending finance, providing technical assistance, and engaging governments. The need for concessional finance to address the ‘viability gap’ in green projects shapes the use of a trust fund structure.
q28_linkages: Financing mechanism (trust fund) enables blending of UK ODA with ADB loans/private capital → addresses affordability barrier for governments.
Technical assistance component → builds pipeline of bankable projects to attract private investment.
Governance role (ACGF Partnership Group) → ensures UK influence over project selection and green ambition.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) the efficiency of leveraging ADB’s systems with (2) the equity goal of ensuring ODA-eligible countries (e.g., Cambodia, Laos) benefit. The use of a multilateral platform trades off some UK visibility for broader regional impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: ADB’s existing pipeline enables rapid deployment but may prioritize larger economies (Indonesia, Vietnam) over smaller ones (Laos, Cambodia).
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: UK technical assistance is embedded in ADB to ensure quality, but ADB/ASEAN governments retain project ownership.
Cost vs. reach: The 10% technical assistance budget ensures project quality but reduces funds available for direct financing.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk profile (e.g., political risks in ASEAN, weak policy environments) justifies milestone-based oversight and embedded UK expertise (seconded advisor) to monitor project quality. The recycling of funds mitigates financial risks by ensuring capital is reused.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The capacity building objectives (e.g., regulatory reforms, green finance training) shape partner roles by requiring ADB to deliver technical assistance and the UK to provide governance oversight. The seconded UK expert focuses on ‘dark green’ priorities (nature-based solutions, gender equality).

quote.constraints: ASEAN governments are meeting their infrastructure needs in several different, often overlapping ways – by engaging with China’s Belt and Road Initiative or Japan’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific, by working with the private sector to finance infrastructure and by working with multilaterals such as the ADB. (D0000978.odt, Context)
quote.tradeoffs: The UK’s participation in the programme could lead to UK expertise being used to help countries source, design, and appraise new projects... but commercial linkages are less certain. (D0000978.odt, Evidence base for our intervention)
quote.capacity: Our technical assistance will pay for... regulatory work... and communications to increase the demonstration effect. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient pipeline of bankable green projects in ASEAN
Limited private sector participation (crowding out risk)
Weak monitoring of climate/environmental impacts
Displacement of other public funds (additionality risk)
Political risks in ASEAN countries affecting project implementation
Exchange rate volatility increasing project costs
ADB’s sovereign focus limiting private sector leverage
UK secondary benefits (commercial opportunities) not materializing
Regulatory barriers in ASEAN countries delaying projects
Climate risks (e.g., extreme weather) affecting infrastructure resilience

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient pipeline of bankable green projects
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance will focus on project preparation (feasibility studies, financial structuring) and regulatory reforms to improve bankability. The UK will second an expert to ADB to accelerate pipeline development.
Prioritize projects with public-private partnerships; use UK governance role to push for higher private co-financing targets; organize investor roundtables (e.g., in London).
Strengthen ACGF reporting on GHG emissions and resource efficiency; allocate 15% of programme management costs to M&E; require climate impact assessments for all projects.
Conduct additionality checks for each project to ensure UK funds do not replace existing public/private finance.
Work through sovereign-backed ADB mechanisms; exclude Myanmar until democratic government is reinstalled; focus on countries with stable investment climates (e.g., Vietnam, Indonesia).
Align with DIT and Prosperity Fund programmes; promote UK expertise in green finance through knowledge products and investor events.

fcas_specific_lessons: Exclusion of Myanmar due to political instability (lesson from past engagements).
Need for concessional finance in lower-middle-income ASEAN countries (e.g., Cambodia, Laos) to address affordability gaps.
Importance of sovereign backing to mitigate political and regulatory risks in frontier markets.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The ASEAN Infrastructure Fund (AIF) has demonstrated a leverage ratio of 6:1 ($3 billion mobilized from $520 million AIF investment), but its focus has not been explicitly climate-aligned. The ACGF builds on this model with a dedicated green window. Lessons include the need for strong project pipelines and clear green criteria to avoid dilution of climate impacts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates (1) stricter green screening criteria (90% climate finance threshold for priority projects), (2) a focus on replicable financial structures, and (3) embedded gender and safeguarding standards based on ADB’s experience with other climate funds (e.g., UCCRTF).

quote.risks: The lack of ‘bankable’ projects (projects that lack strong revenues) in key sectors... is a major barrier. (D0000978.odt, What are the barriers preventing investment in green infrastructure in ASEAN?)
quote.mitigation: We will need to make sure that for every project our additional contribution does not crowd out either money that would have come from either a private source or a development finance institution and is additional. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)
quote.lessons: The track record of AIF in mobilising public donor and national government capital ($3 billion to date at a leverage ratio of 6:1). (D0000978.odt, Evidence base for our intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The ACGF aims to mobilize $1 billion in green infrastructure investment, with a target leverage ratio of 6:1 (based on AIF’s historical performance). Current commitments include $300m (ADB), €300m (KfW), €150m (EIB), and €150m (AFD).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £100m capital (concessional loans/grants) and £10m technical assistance (revenue for project preparation and capacity building).

quote.budget: Programme Value: Up to £110m (up to £100m in capital; up to £10m for technical assistance and programme funded experts). (D0000978.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.leverage: The track record of AIF in mobilising public donor and national government capital ($3 billion to date at a leverage ratio of 6:1). (D0000978.odt, Evidence base for our intervention)
quote.split: The technical assistance requirement is 10% of the capital being deployed, which reflects norms for blended finance programmes. (D0000978.odt, What will the programme do?)

metadata.programme_name: Revenue Mobilisation, Investment and Trade Programme (ReMIT)
metadata.quote: "ReMIT will support inclusive growth in Pakistan by creating the conditions for growth, undertake reforms and strengthen the institutions needed to raise tax revenues, increase investment and boost exports." (52009109.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 11 November 2019 - 30 September 2025" and "New project end date: 30 March 2028" (D0006326.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ReMIT provides technical assistance (TA) to support Pakistan's economic reforms, combining capacity building (strengthening institutions), policy influence (informing and supporting reforms), and implementation research (testing and scaling interventions). It focuses on tax revenue mobilization, investment climate improvement, trade facilitation, and macroeconomic policy coordination to achieve sustained economic growth.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ReMIT will support inclusive growth in Pakistan by creating the conditions for growth, undertake reforms and strengthen the institutions needed to raise tax revenues, increase investment and boost exports." (52009109.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Increase tax/GDP ratio from 13% to 18% by increasing the number of taxpayers (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary)
Move Pakistan towards being one of the top 50 countries to do business in (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary)
Increase goods exports by 35% to reduce Pakistan’s trade deficit (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary)
Modernize macroeconomic policy-making to avoid future financial crises (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary)
Increase in tax revenues of ~£1 billion (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
400% increase in response tax compliance through ‘nudge’ approaches (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
Release of £400 million through sales tax harmonization (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
Support to Prime Minister’s Strategic Reform Roadmap (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
Development of the first-ever Asaan Karobar (Business Made Easy) Act (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
Establishment of Climate Finance Facilitation Unit (CFFU) (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
First National State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) Policy approved (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
Post-flood damage assessment resulting in $50 million immediate support (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
what_objectives.summary: ReMIT aims to lock-in macroeconomic stability and lay the basis for higher, transformative, and less volatile growth in Pakistan through technical assistance in tax revenue mobilization, investment climate improvement, trade facilitation, and macroeconomic policy coordination.
what_objectives.quote: "ReMIT will achieve this with high quality, responsive and politically smart technical assistance provided through HMG and other implementing partners, helping Pakistan to unlock policy loans from international financial institutions." (52009109.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan's economy is characterized by volatile growth, weak institutions, and strong vested interests that resist reforms. The political economy works against macroeconomic stability, and the risk rating of the programme is 'major' due to the complex political economy of sustaining economic reforms.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk level of the programme is ‘major’ due to the complex political economy of sustaining economic reforms." (52009109.odt, Does the proposed level of risk to be taken fit with DFID’s risk appetite for this portfolio?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The political economy constraints, such as vested interests and weak institutions, hinder the implementation of structural reforms. Frequent changes in government disrupt reform continuity, and low tax revenue limits public investment. Regulatory inconsistencies across provinces create barriers for businesses, while corruption in tax administration undermines revenue mobilization efforts.
where_context.quote: "The political economy of economic management works against macroeconomic stability and closes down opportunity for structural reforms." (52009109.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO leads the programme design, oversight, and strategic direction, with Pakistani institutions (e.g., FBR, Ministry of Finance) implementing reforms under technical assistance and guidance from UK-based partners (e.g., HMRC, BEIS).
q10_capacity_building_details: mentoring expertise from HMRC to FBR (52009109.odt, How does the programme relate to other UK aid within the specific sector)
long-term advisers embedded in Pakistani institutions (52009109.odt, Theory of Change)
training large numbers of staff in new processes (52009109.odt, Theory of Change)
peer-to-peer mentoring model with BEIS (52009109.odt, How does the programme relate to other UK aid within the specific sector)
support to Prime Minister’s Strategic Reform Roadmap (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)
development of the Asaan Karobar Act (D0006326.odt, Achievement to date)

who_partners.quote: "ReMIT will utilise the expertise of private sector service providers, the World Bank, and other UK government departments (OGDs) including Her Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC)." (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: ReMIT uses a combination of grants (for technical assistance) and contracts (with commercial suppliers and OGDs). The programme also considers co-financing with the World Bank for specific components like the National Single Window (NSW).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a mix of commercial suppliers, World Bank trust funds, and OGDs (e.g., HMRC, BEIS). Each partner brings specific expertise, and DFID/FCDO coordinates the overall programme to ensure alignment with Pakistan’s reform agenda and IFI programmes.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme uses a mix of pre-existing relationships (e.g., HMRC’s long-standing support to FBR) and competitive frameworks for commercial suppliers to ensure high-quality, flexible technical assistance. The World Bank is selected for its niche analytical capabilities and alignment with IFI programmes.
how_mechanism.quote: "TA will be provided through a commercial supplier, World Bank trust fund, and OGDs and other partnerships." (52009109.odt, Option 3: Provide TA through several partners)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Programme Steering Committee (PSC) oversees ReMIT, with representation from DFID/FCDO, implementing partners, and Pakistani government counterparts. The PSC ensures coordination among partners and alignment with government priorities.
how_governance.quote: "DFID Pakistan is sufficiently resourced to provide technical oversight, programme management and coordination of different components to maximise overall impact." (52009109.odt, Does the Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) and team have the capability and resources to deliver this programme?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme has flexibility to rebalance across themes (tax, trade, investment, macroeconomic policy) and includes a mid-term review for course correction. However, significant reallocations require approval, especially for new components like the NSW.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach, with a mid-term review and annual reviews to adjust priorities based on traction and emerging opportunities. New activities (e.g., climate finance, post-flood recovery) can be integrated with approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexibility is embedded in programme design. There is flexibility to rebalance across the themes of tax, trade, investment and macroeconomic policy." (52009109.odt, Is there sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in the context?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (Commercial Supplier/World Bank/OGDs) → Pakistani Government Institutions
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will have a mid-term review, allowing course correction if specific activities don’t gain traction or deliver value for money (VFM)." (52009109.odt, Is there sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in the context?)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Limit engagement to routine dialogue with economic authorities, relying on IFIs for reform support. Risked lower quality, slower reforms, and reduced UK influence.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Provide financial aid to support economic reform efforts
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Results-based financial aid of £180m to incentivize reforms. Risked inconsistency with UK policy on budget support and high opportunity cost.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Provide TA through several partners (Preferred Option)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Technical assistance through commercial suppliers, World Bank, and OGDs to support institutional change and unlock IFI finance.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3 plus procurement of software development for National Single Window (NSW)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Add £15m for NSW software development to Option 3. Deferred pending further justification.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (Option 3: TA through several partners) was chosen because it aligns with government strategies, promotes systemic change, and is flexible to evolving needs. It leverages the strengths of different partners (commercial expertise, World Bank analytics, OGD specialization) while avoiding the risks of budget support. The model allows for adaptive management and risk diversification.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (leveraging HMRC, World Bank, BEIS expertise)
flexibility (adaptive to government priorities and IFI programmes)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination complexity due to multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong programme governance model to coordinate implementing partners and set clear roles (52009109.odt, Option 3).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political resistance to reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Politically smart TA with embedded long-term advisers to build ownership (52009109.odt, Theory of Change).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation delays due to government capacity constraints
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on change management and institutional strengthening (52009109.odt, Theory of Change).

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option at this time is Option 3. TA under Option 3 will help the government implement structural reforms alongside significant anticipated budget support from IFIs." (52009109.odt, Selection of preferred option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy and institutional weaknesses in Pakistan constrain partner selection to those with deep local expertise (e.g., HMRC’s long-standing relationship with FBR) and adaptive capacity (e.g., commercial suppliers able to navigate vested interests). Multilateral partners (World Bank) are included for their ability to operate in complex environments.
q27_constraints_detail: Vested interests resist reforms, limiting partner options to those with political savvy (e.g., DFID’s political economy expertise).
Weak institutional capacity requires partners with change management experience (e.g., long-term embedded advisers).
Provincial-federal tensions necessitate partners who can navigate sub-national politics (e.g., BEIS’s work with provincial investment units).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for systemic reforms (e.g., tax administration, trade facilitation) determines the mixed delivery structure, combining commercial suppliers for flexibility, World Bank for analytical rigor, and OGDs for specialized expertise (e.g., HMRC on taxation, BEIS on investment climate).
q28_linkages: Tax revenue mobilization requires embedded advisers (HMRC) and institutional strengthening → mixed delivery with long-term TA.
Trade facilitation needs coordination across agencies → World Bank’s trust fund for cross-cutting support.
Investment climate reforms require regulatory expertise → BEIS’s peer-to-peer mentoring.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., using commercial suppliers for speed) with equity (e.g., ensuring provincial inclusion in reforms). The extension phase prioritizes deeper embedding of reforms in government systems, even if it slows short-term delivery.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid reforms risk excluding provinces; the extension phase addresses this by expanding sub-national engagement.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern expertise (e.g., HMRC) accelerates reforms but requires careful management to build local ownership.
Cost vs. reach: Commercial suppliers offer flexibility but at higher cost than IFI-only support; justified by adaptive management needs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk profile drives intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, embedded advisers) and adaptive management (mid-term reviews, flexibility to reallocate funds).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: commercial suppliers focus on training and process redesign, while OGDs (e.g., HMRC) provide mentoring to build institutional leadership.
intersections.quote: "The number of delivery partners increases management risk. A strong programme governance model is needed to coordinate all implementing partners." (52009109.odt, Option 3: Provide TA through several partners)

key_programme_risks: Political resistance to reforms from vested interests (52009109.odt, Strategic Case)
Limited government capacity to implement structural reforms (52009109.odt, Strategic Case)
Frequent changes in government disrupting reform continuity (52009109.odt, Strategic Case)
Coordination challenges among multiple implementing partners (52009109.odt, Option 3)
Economic instability reducing incentives for long-term reforms (D0006326.odt, Risk Management)
Post-election political uncertainty affecting reform momentum (D0006326.odt, Risk Management)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded long-term advisers and politically smart TA to build ownership (52009109.odt, Theory of Change).
Focus on change management and institutional strengthening (52009109.odt, Theory of Change).
Strong programme governance model and regular steering committee meetings (52009109.odt, Option 3).
Extension to align with new government’s first 100 days and IMF programme (D0006326.odt, Risk Management).

fcas_specific_lessons: Front-load reforms during windows of political momentum (e.g., post-election or IMF programme initiation) (52009109.odt, Strategic Case).
Build institutions to lock in progress across election cycles (52009109.odt, Strategic Case).
Use adaptive management to respond to shocks (e.g., floods, economic crises) (D0006326.odt, Summary Information).
Leverage IFI coordination to sustain donor alignment (52009109.odt, Is the programme coherent with the wider international community?).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Stability and Growth Programme (S&G) highlighted the need for front-loaded reforms, strong government ownership, and deep structural changes to sustain growth. The current programme avoids budget support (used in S&G) in favor of flexible TA to address implementation gaps (52009109.odt, Strategic Case).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The no-cost extension was approved to address delays (procurement, ODA cuts) and deepen reform embedding, reflecting lessons on the need for sustained support during political transitions (D0006326.odt, Summary Information).
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons have been learnt by DFID and major donors such as the need for front-loaded reforms, strong government ownership and deep structural reforms to sustain higher levels of economic growth." (52009109.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: ReMIT’s TA helps unlock IFI policy loans (e.g., IMF, World Bank, ADB programmes) and supports Pakistan in accessing £1 billion in additional tax revenue annually. The programme also leverages UK government departments (HMRC, BEIS) for specialized expertise (52009109.odt, Intervention Summary).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily funds revenue expenditures (technical assistance, capacity building) with a potential capital component for the National Single Window (NSW) software (£15m deferred) (52009109.odt, Option 4).
financial_details.quote: "DFID will seek approval for a further £15m to procure software development only if it is clear that: 1) there is a role for DFID grant aid for this priority initiative..." (52009109.odt, Option 4)

metadata.programme_name: Support to TradeMark East Africa – Strategy 2 (STS2)
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to increase sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa by increasing East Africa’s trade with the region and the rest of the world." (24061876.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £229 million overall towards TMEA’s Strategy 2 over 6 years (July 2017 - June 2023)" (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing trade facilitation interventions), capacity building (strengthening trade institutions and private sector), and service delivery (direct support to infrastructure and systems). It aims to reduce trade barriers while building export capacity and promoting inclusive trade policies.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will (i) invest in improving the efficiency and capacity of transport, logistics and trade infrastructure at key port and border points; (ii) invest in systems to improve trading standards, reduce non-tariff barriers and enhance transparency in trade processes; (iii) improve the regulatory and policy environment for trade; and (iv) support private sector advocacy for trade competitiveness, the export capacity of East African businesses and the greater participation of women and small and growing businesses in trade." (24061876.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: poverty reduction

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce trade barriers and build export capacity in East Africa through infrastructure investments, policy reforms, and private sector support, with explicit targets for economic growth, poverty reduction, and inclusive trade participation.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver the following results. At an impact level: Increased sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa, by contributing to an additional 0.6% growth in East African gross domestic product (GDP) above trend; by helping to reduce the number of people living below the poverty line ($2/day) by 1.8 million; and by helping increase government revenue excluding grants by an additional $1.1 billion." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with political economy challenges and infrastructure deficits, but has strong regional integration momentum and donor alignment. The risk is managed through phased implementation and political economy analysis.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The largest risks will be those associated with procurement and with the political economy, and are well managed." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (alignment challenges among EAC states)
weak institutions (capacity gaps in standards bureaus, customs)
conflict (South Sudan instability affects border trade)
climate (not explicitly mentioned but logistics vulnerable to weather)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Poor infrastructure increases trade costs by up to 40% (e.g., Mombasa Port delays), regulatory barriers hinder food security and regional integration, and political economy factors slow reform implementation. Corruption at borders disproportionately affects small traders, particularly women.
where_context.quote: "Trade remains constrained by poor infrastructure which hampers access to markets, tariffs (which have not fallen uniformly across the East African Community) and non-tariff barriers (such as poorly designed and/or implemented standards or rules of origin)." (24061876.odt, Strategic Case) and "The busy Busia border crossing from Kenya to Uganda, where TMEA put in place a one stop border post, has reduced average crossing times by around 80%." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: TMEA (a regional African organization) leads implementation with oversight from DFID and a donor council. Decision-making involves EAC governments, private sector, and civil society, with DFID as the largest funder but not the primary implementer.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to ports/customs authorities
training for standards bureaus on SPS measures
gender sensitization for customs administrators
support to women trader cooperatives
private sector advocacy capacity building
institutional strengthening for EAC Secretariat
skills development for logistics hub operators
