partner_organizations.role: co-financing for Dar es Salaam Port ($345m) and border posts

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Netherlands, USA)
partner_organizations.role: co-funding for regional/country components

partner_organizations.name: British Standards Institute
partner_organizations.role: technical support on standards harmonization

partner_organizations.name: WTO Standards and Trade Development Facility (STDF)
partner_organizations.role: SPS measures alignment

who_partners.quote: "TMEA, initially set up by DFID, has attracted 7 other donors, has raised over £450 million (now the largest aid for trade facility globally) and works closely with governments, private sector and civil society in the EAC to reduce barriers to and costs of trade, and increase the region’s competitiveness." (24061876.odt, Strategic Case) and "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase. Each DFID office will assign an SRO to oversee their respective country/regional support, and the Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of core funding to TMEA (as a platform) and specific grants/contracts for infrastructure investments and technical assistance. DFID provides block funding to TMEA, which then allocates resources to country/regional components through a mix of direct implementation and sub-grants.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: TMEA acts as a regional platform with country offices, managed by a donor council (chaired by DFID Kenya). DFID provides strategic oversight through Senior Responsible Owners (SROs) in each country office, while TMEA coordinates implementation with EAC governments, private sector, and other donors. The structure allows for both centralized regional projects (e.g., standards harmonization) and country-specific interventions (e.g., port upgrades).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (TMEA was established by DFID and expanded with other donors)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TMEA was created by DFID in 2010 and has since attracted 7 other donors, demonstrating its effectiveness as a regional trade facilitation platform. The direct award reflects TMEA's proven track record in delivering Strategy 1 (2011-2017) and its established relationships with EAC governments and private sector.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID created TradeMark East Africa (TMEA) in 2010 to tackle these problems in East Africa. This programme is an extension of DFID support provided under TMEA’s Strategy 1 (2011-2017), recognising the progress it has already made and opportunities to build momentum." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The TMEA Council (comprising all donors, chaired by DFID Kenya) provides strategic oversight. Country-level National Oversight Committees (NOCs) and regional technical working groups (e.g., on standards, NTBs) guide implementation. DFID SROs in each country office monitor progress.
how_governance.quote: "The Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet) and "As the programme may spend beyond the current spending review period, progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets, which will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with DFID approval, particularly for newer elements like export capacity support. The mid-term review provides a formal mechanism for adjustments based on performance and context changes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a phased approach (e.g., logistics hubs pilot) and built-in flexibility for export capacity components. Adjustments require DFID approval, informed by mid-term reviews and political economy analysis.
how_flexibility.quote: "There is in-built flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context, particularly with regard to newer components on export capability support. The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet) and "progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets, which will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed and use any unspent budget beyond the spending review timeline." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TMEA (platform) → [implementing partners (governments/private sector/NGOs)]. The structure is streamlined with TMEA acting as the primary intermediary.
how_efficiency.quote: "The largest (£75 million) component of the programme (Kenya) was quality assured by the Quality Assurance Unit (QAU) in November 2016, receiving a “1” (the highest possible score)." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet) implies performance-based oversight, and "progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets" (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary) suggests milestone-based funding releases.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID’s trade competitiveness work through TMEA concludes; rely on non-trade DFID work and multilateral contributions.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Focus on 1-2 of the 3 Strategy 1 areas in depth
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Narrow focus to infrastructure OR standards/NTBs OR policy environment.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: Continue all Strategy 1 focus areas
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Maintain support for infrastructure, standards/NTBs, and policy environment.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 4: Expand beyond trade/logistics to broader business climate
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Add PPP policy, tax reform, land registration, and broader investment climate reforms.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 5: Strategy 1 focus areas + export capacity support (CHOSSEN OPTION)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Add private sector advocacy, women/SME inclusion, and export capability building.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 was selected because it builds on Strategy 1’s proven impact while addressing supply-side constraints (export capacity) and inclusion gaps (women/SMEs) that were identified as critical for sustainable trade growth. The phased approach to logistics hubs and adaptive management for export support mitigate risks while allowing for learning.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (Option 5 leverages existing TMEA structures and adds high-impact components)
risk mitigation (phased pilots for new elements like logistics hubs)
past experience (Strategy 1 demonstrated that combining infrastructure, standards, and policy reforms yields greater impact)
partner capacity (TMEA’s established regional presence and donor trust)
flexibility (built-in mid-term review and adaptive management)
equity (explicit focus on women and SMEs addresses inclusion gaps)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays in infrastructure projects (e.g., port upgrades)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with project preparation support (feasibility studies, master planning) and leverage of World Bank/ADB co-financing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy resistance to regional integration reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Politically aware technical assistance, alignment with EAC priorities, and private sector advocacy support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low private sector uptake of new systems (e.g., single window, OSBPs)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Behavior change campaigns, trader training, and incentives for formalization (e.g., reduced crossing times).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of donor-funded systems post-exit
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: TMEA’s sustainability strategy to reduce donor reliance via development capital instruments and EAC government co-financing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict in South Sudan affecting border trade interventions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Risk-assessed phased engagement, focus on stable border points (e.g., Nimule), and contingency planning.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging £300m+ in port investments via £7m DFID preparation support)
efficiency (reducing trade costs by 40% at Mombasa Port, 80% at Busia border)
effectiveness (0.6% GDP growth, 1.8m out of poverty, $1.1bn revenue increase)
equity (74% of informal cross-border traders are women; targeted inclusion measures)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 5: Do all of the previous focus areas from Strategy 1 as before and support export capacity... This option extends current support on trade competitiveness to include targeted supply-side interventions that seek to: expand private sector-led advocacy; promote greater inclusion of women and small businesses in trade... and build the export capability of the region’s private sector." (24061876.odt, Appraisal Case) and "The current intervention mix and approach have been significantly effective in reducing the constraints to trade in the EAC. Option 2 is thus not supported by strong evidence or lessons learnt and would unlikely maximise the effectiveness of DFID support as well as overall value for money." (24061876.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The EAC’s political economy and infrastructure deficits limit partner selection to organizations with strong regional credibility and government relationships. TMEA’s established presence and donor trust (7 other donors) make it uniquely positioned to navigate cross-border complexities (e.g., OSBPs requiring bilateral agreements) and leverage EAC Secretariat coordination.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for EAC Secretariat endorsement to ensure regional buy-in for standards harmonization
Port authorities (e.g., KPA) must be direct partners due to sovereign control over infrastructure
Private sector inclusion requires local chambers of commerce (e.g., EABC) for advocacy legitimacy
Women’s trade inclusion necessitates grassroots organizations (e.g., trader cooperatives) for outreach
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (infrastructure + policy + private sector) require a platform structure (TMEA) to coordinate diverse stakeholders. Logistics hubs (spatial clustering) and export capacity building demand flexible, phased pilots to test and adapt models before scaling, while standards harmonization needs centralized EAC-level coordination.
q28_linkages: Regional infrastructure projects (e.g., Mombasa Port) → require multilateral co-financing (World Bank/ADB) → delivered through TMEA’s convening role
Private sector advocacy → needs embedded capacity building (e.g., EABC training) → funded via TMEA’s technical assistance component
Women’s inclusion → necessitates gender-advisory roles within TMEA → integrated into all intervention designs via gender audits
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., reducing port clearance times from 11 to 3.8 days) with equity (e.g., small trader channels at borders, women’s sanitation facilities). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for inclusive designs (e.g., gender-sensitive customs training) and phased pilots (logistics hubs) that delay scale but ensure sustainability.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.example: One-stop border posts (OSBPs) could prioritize large traders for rapid throughput, but the programme adds small trader channels (slower clearance) to include informal women traders.
British Standards Institute provides technical SPS alignment support, but capacity is built within EAC National Standards Bureaux to ensure local ownership.
Electronic cargo tracking systems require upfront ICT investments but reduce long-term costs for small traders (e.g., Uganda’s system cut transit times from 8 to 3 days).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (political economy, procurement) drives milestone-based oversight (mid-term reviews, HMT approvals for unspent funds) and phased implementation (e.g., logistics hubs pilot). High-risk components (e.g., South Sudan borders) receive additional scrutiny.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: TMEA’s gender adviser ensures women’s inclusion is mainstreamed, EAC Secretariat’s strengthened standards committees lead regional harmonization, and port authorities (e.g., KPA) co-design efficiency reforms with TMEA technical assistance.
intersections.quote: "The nature of trade costs varies across geographical areas and income levels, and hence the effectiveness of trade facilitation interventions is likely to be determined by the degree and intensity of the factors that contribute to high trade costs." (24061876.odt, Box 1) and "TMEA has also initiated various specific interventions that target the benefits of trade benefit both men and women equally and specifically that women are included in trade for instance through support to informal cross-border trade (dominated by women) and through targeted capacity building and advocacy at the policy and regulatory level." (24061876.odt, Compliance with Gender Equality Act)

key_programme_risks: Procurement delays in infrastructure projects (e.g., port upgrades)
Political resistance to regional integration (e.g., NTB removal, standards harmonization)
Low private sector adoption of new systems (e.g., single window, OSBPs)
Sustainability of reforms post-DFID exit
Conflict in South Sudan disrupting border trade interventions
Gender disparities in trade benefits (e.g., women’s informal trade formalization)
Climate/vulnerability risks affecting logistics (not explicitly detailed but implied)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased project preparation (feasibility studies, master planning) and co-financing with World Bank/ADB to share risks.
Political economy analysis (PEA), private sector advocacy support, and alignment with EAC priorities.
Behavior change campaigns, trader training, and demonstrating cost savings (e.g., 50% clearance cost reduction for Uganda/Rwanda).
TMEA’s sustainability strategy to attract EAC government co-financing and development capital instruments.
Focus on stable border points (e.g., Nimule), risk-assessed engagement, and contingency planning.
Gender audits, women-specific interventions (e.g., sanitation at borders, trader cooperatives), and gender adviser role within TMEA.

fcas_specific_lessons: In South Sudan, work begins on border facilities immediately but with heightened risk assessments (e.g., Nimule border post).
Conflict-affected borders (e.g., Uganda/DRC) require integrated security and livelihoods approaches (e.g., Mpondwe-Kasindi World Bank project).
Informal cross-border trade (dominated by women) needs flexible formalization pathways to avoid exclusion.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
Strategy 1 (2011-2017) demonstrated that: 
1) Infrastructure improvements yield the highest trade volume increases, followed by customs efficiency and regulatory reforms.
2) Combining cost-reduction interventions (e.g., port upgrades) with supply-side support (e.g., export capacity) enhances impact.
3) Gender-specific constraints (e.g., harassment at borders) require targeted designs (e.g., women-only customs channels).
4) Regional harmonization (e.g., standards) must balance technical alignment with political feasibility.
5) Phased pilots (e.g., OSBPs) allow for iterative learning before scaling.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1) Added export capacity component (Option 5) to address supply-side gaps identified in Strategy 1.
2) Phased approach for logistics hubs to test spatial clustering models.
3) Strengthened gender mainstreaming (gender adviser, women-specific interventions).
4) Expanded SPS measures to address agricultural trade barriers.
5) Mid-term review embedded to enable adaptive management.
risks_lessons.quote:
"Box 1: Summary of lessons from TMEA Strategy 1
- Preferential market access carries less weight than cost/capacity factors in trade participation.
- Trade facilitation interventions improving infrastructure are most effective, followed by customs efficiency and regulatory reforms.
- Combining cost-reduction with export capacity interventions enhances impact.
- Context-specific evidence is critical; impact evaluations and case studies are needed.
- Trade liberalization can have short-term negative impacts on select groups, requiring pro-poor safeguards." (24061876.odt, Box 1) and "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (24061876.odt, Summary Sheet)

financial_details.leverage_achieved:
1) Mombasa Port: £7m DFID preparation support leveraged £300m+ in public/private funding.
2) Dar es Salaam Port: TMEA’s dialogue supported a $345m World Bank loan.
3) OSBPs: AfDB co-financing for Moyale border post.
4) Total TMEA facility: £450m+ raised from 7 donors (largest aid-for-trade facility globally).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Roughly 50% of resources support soft interventions (technical assistance, policy frameworks) and 50% support infrastructure-related constraints (public/private investments).
financial_details.quote:
"DFID funding will be used to promote sustainable and inclusive prosperity in East Africa through further reducing trade costs and barriers... Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions including technical assistance and development of regulatory/policy frameworks, systems and processes that support trade and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints to East Africa’s trade competitiveness." (24061876.odt, Intervention Summary) and

metadata.programme_name: PAMOJA – Kenya Integrated refugee and host community support programme
metadata.quote: "PAMOJA will promote social and economic integration between about 470,000 refugees and close to 50,000 people in host communities in Kenya by supporting the provision of basic humanitarian assistance and market led solutions." (48893306.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "PAMOJA will provide £84m over five years (2018 - 2023) to support refugees in camps and members of the surrounding host communities." (48893306.odt, PAMOJA: A different approach to protracted refugee situation)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PAMOJA combines service delivery (humanitarian assistance), policy influence (advocacy for refugee integration), and financing mechanisms (market-led solutions via IFC/AECF). It aims to transition from traditional aid to self-reliance while maintaining essential services.
what_objectives.q1_source: "PAMOJA will support two main objectives: i) maintain appropriate cost-effective humanitarian assistance to address immediate needs; and ii) promote lasting solutions for refugees and vulnerable host community members." (48893306.odt, PAMOJA: A different approach to protracted refugee situation)
q3_expected_outputs: A refugee policy environment that supports integration of refugees and members of the hosting communities
140,000 children under five years of age reached through nutrition-related interventions per year
37,000 malnourished children under five years of age and pregnant and lactating women treated for acute malnutrition each year
470,000 people (including 50,000 host community members) receive humanitarian assistance in and around the camps
Improved access to products and services, lower prices, and employment opportunities for host communities
Policy reforms supporting refugee self-reliance and economic integration
Market-led solutions for access to water, energy, and livelihoods via IFC/AECF partnerships
what_objectives.summary: PAMOJA integrates immediate humanitarian relief with long-term development goals, focusing on refugee-host community cohesion, self-reliance, and policy reform through a mix of UN agency service delivery and private sector engagement.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will support the provision of: i) cash transfers for food assistance; ii) health, nutrition, sanitation and protection services; and iii) livelihoods support for refugees in camps and members of the host communities." (48893306.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile counties (Turkana, Garissa, Wajir) with weak institutions, insecurity, and environmental strain from refugee camps, but has a structured risk management approach and government cooperation.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (48893306.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The presence of the refugee camps... exerts considerable strain on the environment and natural resources, resulting in latent and potential conflicts between host and refugees" (48893306.odt, Climate and environmental management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Restrictive refugee policies limit movement and economic participation; weak county systems require parallel service delivery; environmental degradation creates host-refugee tensions; and data gaps (e.g., duplicate nutrition beneficiaries) undermine targeting efficiency.
where_context.quote: "Kenya implements a refugee encampment policy where the majority of refugees are expected to live in one of two camp complexes (Kakuma and Dadaab)... movement of refugees out of the camps is restricted and access to employment or other economic engagement... is limited." (48893306.odt, Main issues facing refugees and host communities in Kenya)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UN agencies (Northern multilateral) retain control over fund allocation and strategic decisions, with Southern partners (NGOs, county governments) implementing services under UN contracts. The IFC/AECF private sector component introduces market-based decision-making but remains guided by UN/DFID priorities.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for county government staff to strengthen devolved service delivery (e.g., health, business licensing)
Support for refugee and host community entrepreneurs via IFC/AECF market-led solutions
Policy advocacy to reform Kenya’s Refugee Act and align county development plans with refugee inclusion
Technical assistance to UNHCR/WFP for improved targeting (e.g., nutrition beneficiary systems)

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR
partner_organizations.role: Lead coordinator for refugee services; implements protection, WASH, health, and livelihoods activities (via NGOs)

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Food assistance (cash/voucher programs like Bamba Chakula) and nutrition support

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Market-led solutions for refugee/host community access to water, energy, and livelihoods

partner_organizations.name: Africa Enterprise Challenge Fund (AECF)
partner_organizations.role: Private sector engagement to stimulate economic opportunities

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Child protection services (subcontracted via UNHCR)

partner_organizations.name: Turkana/Garissa/Wajir County Governments
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery integration (e.g., health, business licensing) and refugee inclusion in County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs)

partner_organizations.name: Local and International NGOs
partner_organizations.role: Downstream service providers for UNHCR/WFP in sectors like health, WASH, and protection
partner_organizations.location: mixed (local NGOs = South; international NGOs = North)

who_partners.quote: "The activities will be delivered through the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the World Food Programme (WFP), and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) in partnership with the Africa Enterprise Challenge Fund (AECF)." (48893306.odt, Programme Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core funding to UN agencies (UNHCR, WFP) for service delivery, combined with partnership agreements with IFC/AECF for market-based interventions. Includes a £12.5m Internal Risk Facility (IRF) for emergency response.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNHCR acts as the primary coordinator, with WFP and IFC/AECF managing sector-specific components. DFID retains oversight via annual reviews and policy engagement, while county governments and NGOs implement services under UN contracts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNHCR’s mandate as the global refugee coordinator in Kenya requires channelling funds through its pre-selected NGO partners (chosen via UNHCR’s biennial selection process). IFC/AECF were selected for their private sector expertise in market-led solutions.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNHCR have the global mandate for refugee protection. In Kenya, they have been given the mandate to coordinate provision of services to refugees. As such, DFID funding can only go to UNHCR and its partner UN agencies and NGOs... Only NGOs that have successfully gone through the selection process are eligible to receive funding through the UN agencies." (48893306.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DFID Kenya’s Humanitarian team leads policy engagement with GoK/UN, supported by a policy advocacy plan (Annex 1). A communication strategy involves DFID London and BHC Nairobi. No formal joint governance body is mentioned, but coordination occurs via the Informal Refugee Donor Working Group.
how_governance.quote: "A communication strategy will be developed in consultation with DFID’s communications team in London and the BHC Nairobi communications team... DFID Kenya has the skills, capacity and resources to deliver the programme." (48893306.odt, Summary Sheet) and "DFID Kenya will work with partners in the humanitarian system in Kenya and headquarters to implement reforms agreed in the Grand Bargain commitments." (48893306.odt, Delivering on UK Humanitarian Reform Priorities)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Budget allocations are provisional, with flexibility to move funds between sectors/years, but requires UNHCR/WFP approval. The £12.5m IRF allows emergency reallocation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adapt to refugee population fluctuations (e.g., South Sudan influx) and policy changes (e.g., CRRF opportunities), but major shifts require DFID approval. Research priorities can be adjusted via the IRF or East Africa Research Hub consultations.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme has been designed to adapt to changes in the operating context... Budget allocations across the life of the programme are provisional with the flexibility to move funds between and within years." (48893306.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The Internal Risk Facility (IRF) will respond to refugee related emergencies and other opportunities that might arise linked to delivery of the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework." (48893306.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNHCR/WFP/IFC → NGOs/county governments → end beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: "Delivering through UNICEF increases the programme management workload... an additional 7% administrative cost (relative to NGOs)." (48893306.odt, Option 2 – Funding UNICEF for Child Protection) and "WFP have realised cost savings of up to 11% in administrative and logistical costs of providing food assistance to refugees in the camps." (48893306.odt, Option 3 – Funding WFP for Food Assistance and Nutrition)

q24_alternatives_considered: Funding NGOs directly (rejected due to loss of UN consolidation economies of scale)
Funding UNICEF separately for child protection (rejected due to implementation delays and higher costs)
Direct government funding (rejected due to UK policy against budget support in Kenya)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UNHCR-led multilateral model was selected for its mandate legitimacy, existing coordination structures, and economies of scale in refugee operations, despite higher administrative costs. The IFC/AECF partnership was added to introduce market-based solutions missing in traditional aid.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (UN consolidation vs. NGO efficiency trade-off)
risk-mitigation (UNHCR’s global mandate reduces political risk)
flexibility (IRF and multi-year funding align with Grand Bargain)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN administrative costs (7% higher than NGOs) reduce direct service funding.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Cost savings from cash-based interventions (e.g., Bamba Chakula’s 11% efficiency gain) and economies of scale offset overheads.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delayed implementation due to UN bureaucracy (e.g., UNICEF child protection delays under SPARK).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s embedded Humanitarian Adviser (previously seconded to ECHO) and annual reviews monitor progress.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led UN control.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for county governments and policy advocacy for refugee inclusion in CIDPs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector (IFC/AECF) may prioritize profitability over refugee needs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s oversight of market-led solutions and alignment with CRRF’s self-reliance goals.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 1 – Funding NGOs directly... would be financially cheaper for DFID, but... the consolidation function played by UNHCR and the accruing benefit of economies of scale would be lost." (48893306.odt, Option 1 – Funding NGOs directly) and "PAMOJA will support activities with a long-term view of reinforcing household and community resilience aligned to the CRRF." (48893306.odt, Promoting lasting solutions for refugees and host communities)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Kenya’s encampment policy and weak county systems limit partner options to UN agencies (with global mandates) and pre-approved NGOs, excluding direct funding to government or unregistered local actors. Security risks in Turkana/Garissa/Wajir further restrict private sector engagement without UN/IFC intermediation.
q27_constraints_detail: Refugee Act 2006 restricts work permits and movement, requiring UN-led service delivery inside camps.
County government capacity gaps necessitate UN/NGO parallel systems despite devolution.
Security concerns (e.g., Dadaab closure threats) limit long-term private investment without multilateral guarantees.
Data limitations (e.g., duplicate nutrition beneficiaries) undermine local NGO accountability.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of immediate humanitarian relief and long-term self-reliance require a mixed delivery structure: UN agencies for service continuity and IFC/AECF for market integration. Policy advocacy (e.g., CRRF) necessitates multilateral legitimacy, while cash-based interventions demand flexible UN/NGO partnerships.
q28_linkages: Self-reliance goal → IFC/AECF private sector partnerships for livelihoods.
Policy reform objective → UNHCR’s coordination role with GoK.
Cost-effectiveness → WFP’s cash/voucher systems and UN consolidation.
Host-refugee integration → County government inclusion via CIDPs.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) UN overhead costs against NGO efficiency, (2) Northern-led decision-making against Southern capacity building, and (3) immediate aid delivery against long-term market development. For example, UNHCR’s 7% administrative cost is justified by its coordination role, while the IRF allows adaptive responses to equity gaps (e.g., South Sudan influx).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed-vs-inclusion: UNHCR’s pre-selected NGOs enable rapid deployment but may exclude local actors.
expertise-vs-ownership: IFC’s market solutions introduce private sector skills but risk sidelining community-led initiatives.
cost-vs-reach: Cash transfers (11% cheaper) expand coverage but require digital infrastructure lacking in remote areas.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (FCAS context) justifies intensive oversight (annual reviews, embedded advisers) and flexible tools (IRF), while the UN’s existing risk management frameworks reduce the need for additional DFID controls.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: County government capacity gaps relegate them to service recipients rather than decision-makers, while UNHCR’s mandate enables its lead role despite higher costs. Capacity building (e.g., CIDP inclusion) aims to gradually shift ownership Southward.
intersections.quote: "Contracting NGOs directly... does not represent the best value for money and is not a preferred option for delivery of basic services... Given DFID’s funding share in the different sectors, the consolidation function played by UNHCR and the accruing benefit of economies of scale would be lost." (48893306.odt, Option 1 – Funding NGOs directly) and "The shift from care and maintenance to self-reliance is expressed in the New York Declaration... harnessing the productive potential of refugees in Kenya could lead to economic gains." (48893306.odt, Promoting lasting solutions for refugees and host communities)

key_programme_risks: GoK policy shifts (e.g., Dadaab closure or Refugee Act reforms) disrupting service delivery.
Funding shortfalls from other donors increasing UK burden (historically only 27% of UNHCR’s 2017 budget was funded).
Fraud/corruption in camps exploiting refugee vulnerability (e.g., duplicate nutrition beneficiaries).
Environmental degradation from camp overuse sparking host-refugee conflicts.
Private sector (IFC/AECF) failing to reach ultra-poor refugees with market solutions.
County governments failing to allocate resources for refugee inclusion in CIDPs.
Somali repatriation fluctuations creating unpredictable caseloads.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID’s policy advocacy (e.g., Refugee Bill lobbying) and IRF contingency funding.
Multi-year PAMOJA commitment (£84m) and donor coordination via Informal Refugee Donor Working Group.
Strengthened UNHCR/WFP anti-corruption policies and refugee accountability forums.
World Bank DRDIP partnership for sustainable resource management.
IFC’s consumer market studies (e.g., Kakuma 2017/18) to tailor solutions.
DFID’s County Lead positions (e.g., Turkana) to influence CIDP inclusion.
Flexible targeting (e.g., vulnerability-based food assistance) and IRF.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Uganda’s progressive refugee model (equal host-refugee access) inform Kalobeyei’s integrated settlement design.
SPARK programme’s cash transfers (11% cheaper) prove effective in FCAS contexts, prompting PAMOJA’s expanded use.
County government engagement (e.g., Turkana’s LED approach) shows devolution can improve service equity despite fragility.
Dadaab closure threats highlight need for sustained donor lobbying to protect asylum space.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The SPARK programme (2016–2018) demonstrated that: (1) cash-based interventions improve value for money and social cohesion; (2) integrated host-refugee livelihoods reduce tensions; (3) vulnerability-based targeting (e.g., 4% self-reliant in Kakuma) can optimize aid; and (4) policy advocacy (e.g., CRRF adoption) requires long-term donor coordination.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expanded cash transfers (beyond SPARK’s 30% food voucher substitution).
Added IFC/AECF private sector component to address SPARK’s gap in market-based solutions.
Stronger county government engagement (e.g., CIDP inclusion) based on SPARK’s host community lessons.
IRF contingency fund to respond to emergencies (e.g., South Sudan influx) not covered under SPARK.
Policy advocacy plan (Annex 1) formalized based on SPARK’s ad-hoc lobbying.
risks_lessons.quote: "The main lessons from the most recent DFID supported programme – Support for the Protection and Assistance of Refugees in Kenya (£35m over 2016-2018) are that: Integrated support can promote peaceful co-existence... Value for Money can further be achieved through improved nutrition targeting... and vulnerability based targeting." (48893306.odt, Key DFID achievements so far in the Kenya refugee operation) and "PAMOJA will build on the progress made under the previous £35m Support for Protection and Assistance of Refugees in Kenya (SPARK) programme... with adaptations informed by experiences and lessons learnt." (48893306.odt, PAMOJA: A different approach to protracted refugee situation)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages World Bank’s $100m DRDIP loan for refugee-hosting areas and EU Trust Fund’s €65m for Kalobeyei/Somali repatriation, aligning with PAMOJA’s resilience goals. IFC/AECF partnerships mobilize private sector investments in refugee markets.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on revenue expenditure (humanitarian services, cash transfers) but includes capital elements via IFC/AECF’s market infrastructure investments (e.g., water/energy access) and World Bank DRDIP’s socio-economic infrastructure.
financial_details.quote: "The programme will provide £71.5m to UNHCR, WFP and IFC to support the provision of... services... up to £12.5m of contingency funding (Internal Risk Facility - IRF) may be sought during the life of the programme." (48893306.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Delivering through UNICEF increases the programme management workload... an additional 7% administrative cost (relative to NGOs)." (48893306.odt, Option 2 – Funding UNICEF for Child Protection)

metadata.programme_name: Sustainable Energy and Economic Development Programme (SEED)
metadata.quote: "SEED will provide £37.5 million over seven years to support provincial economic development and sustainable energy in Pakistan." (41216929.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 8 Oct 2018 – 7 October 2025" and "New project end date (if applicable): 07 October 2026" (D0006344.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SEED combines capacity building (strengthening provincial planning and investment management), financing mechanisms (leveraging private investment and climate finance), and implementation research (testing sustainable energy solutions). The programme aims to improve public investment efficiency while directly facilitating renewable energy adoption in industry.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SEED will provide £37.5 million over seven years to support provincial economic development and sustainable energy in Pakistan. It will support Pakistan's poorest province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, to plan and finance the infrastructure and investment it needs for growth, jobs and prosperity. The programme will also address Pakistan’s energy crisis by providing innovative financial solutions to industry for the adoption of sustainable energy practices." (41216929.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Provincial economic development plans and sector strategies (KP)
Institutional capacity for economic and urban planning in KP (systems/protocols for coordination, project design, selection, appraisal, implementation)
Leveraged funds from non-government sources for core infrastructure projects in KP (target: £400m+ of provincial annual development plan)
10 MWs in energy saved/generated nationally from renewable sources in industry (financed on commercial basis)
Increased share of renewable energy in national electricity fuel mix
Increased commercial bank-lending for renewable energy and efficiency purposes to industrial consumers nationwide
Higher public and private investment, and higher returns to public investment in economic sectors in KP
Support to 8 climate-focused project proposals for international climate finance (Green Climate Fund)
Establishment of Public Private Partnership (PPP) framework in KP (pipeline of $4bn identified)
Technical assistance for climate-resilient infrastructure appraisal process in KP
Monitoring and evaluation system for flood rehabilitation spending in Sindh (ME3F component)
what_objectives.summary: SEED aims to catalyze economic growth in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through improved public investment management and sustainable energy adoption, while responding to climate challenges and post-flood reconstruction needs. The programme combines technical assistance for planning capacity with direct financing mechanisms to demonstrate market viability for renewable energy solutions.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact of the programme is higher economic growth, productivity, and jobs nationally." (41216929.odt, Theory of Change)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a politically volatile environment with macroeconomic instability, but maintains a moderate risk rating due to mature risk management procedures and political economy analysis embedded in activity design. Pakistan faces significant climate risks (floods, heatwaves) and institutional capacity constraints at provincial level.
where_context.q5_source: "Programme’s overall risk rating is Medium. This is due to delivery risk and political context risks." (41216929.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The overall risk rating of the programme remains 'moderate', reflecting the challenging political and economic environment in which it operates" (D0006344.odt, Risk Management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political instability has delayed reforms and created uncertainty around fiscal policies. Weak provincial capacity limits implementation of economic plans, while climate shocks (2022 floods) have required programme reprioritization. Energy sector viability issues and low private investment constrain industrial growth. High official turnover affects sustainability of capacity building efforts.
where_context.quote: "Pakistan has been faced by a macroeconomic crisis... private sector investments have reached advanced stages but not yet been executed... political charged environment" (D0006344.odt, Achievement to date) and "Weaknesses in economic and urban development planning and an unreliable, unsustainable energy supply are two binding constraints to growth" (41216929.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains overall programme management and approval authority, with implementation delegated to international partners (World Bank, IFC) and local organizations (NRSP, GoKP departments). Southern partners have operational roles but strategic decisions remain with FCDO/UK institutions.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to KP Planning & Development Department for economic/urban planning
establishment of PPP frameworks and investment appraisal systems
training for commercial banks on renewable energy financing
support to Climate Resourcing Coordination Cell (CRCC) for climate finance access
behavioral insights unit ('Nudge Unit') for tax policy implementation
community monitoring capacity building for flood rehabilitation oversight

partner_organizations.name: Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (GoKP)
partner_organizations.role: primary beneficiary and implementation partner (Planning & Development Department, Energy Department, KP Board of Investment & Trade)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: implementation partner for ME3F flood monitoring programme in Sindh (via Pak@100 Multi-Donor Trust Fund)

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance provider for renewable energy finance component

partner_organizations.name: National Rural Support Programme (NRSP)
partner_organizations.role: climate finance facilitation and project development for Green Climate Fund submissions

partner_organizations.name: Karandaaz Pakistan
partner_organizations.role: initial partner for renewable energy financing (later shifted to investment facilitation approach)

partner_organizations.name: Climate Resourcing Coordination Cell (CRCC)
partner_organizations.role: climate finance access coordination and project development

partner_organizations.name: KP Economic Zone Development & Management Company
partner_organizations.role: special economic zone development support

partner_organizations.name: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS)
partner_organizations.role: UK government partner for technical expertise sharing

partner_organizations.name: Infrastructure and Projects Authority (UK)
partner_organizations.role: UK government partner for PPP and infrastructure planning expertise

who_partners.quote: "DFID Pakistan is sufficiently resourced to provide technical oversight, programme management and coordination of different components" (41216929.odt, SRO section) and "The programme will work with UK government departments such as Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy" (41216929.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (for NRSP/CRCC), Administration Arrangements with multilateral partners (World Bank), and technical assistance contracts. The initial design included direct financing for renewable energy projects, which was later shifted to investment facilitation and technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme with multiple parallel partnerships: 1) Direct Accountable Grants to Pakistani organizations (NRSP), 2) Administration Arrangement with World Bank for Sindh activities, 3) Technical assistance contracts with IFC and other providers. Components are managed separately but coordinated through FCDO oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: World Bank was selected through existing multilateral frameworks (Pak@100 Trust Fund). NRSP was selected based on prior experience with climate finance facilitation. IFC was chosen for its specialized expertise in renewable energy finance. The addendum notes reprogramming of existing commitments rather than new competitive processes.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will work with UK government departments... and the Infrastructure and Projects Authority" (41216929.odt) and "SEED’s climate action intervention... will continue to be delivered through an AGA [with NRSP]" (D0006344.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.quote: "Implementation partners will develop communications strategies during the inception phase and will be required to work with the British High Commission communications team" (41216929.odt) and "Progress against milestones will be reported on a quarterly basis" (D0006344.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The addendum describes reprogramming of approved but unspent CDEL (£5m) and RDEL (£7.4m) funds to new activities (ME3F in Sindh, CRCC support, economic reform scoping). This required approval through the addendum process but demonstrates ability to shift funds between components based on emerging needs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme was designed with phased implementation and break-points to allow adjustments. The 2022 floods triggered a reprioritization toward monitoring reconstruction spending. The shift from direct RE financing to investment facilitation demonstrates adaptive management in response to market development.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexibility has been built in to programme design. The programme will be implemented in phases, allowing for decisions on scaling-up to be taken... Continuous evaluation of interventions and flexible contractual arrangements with clearly defined break-points will be employed." (41216929.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The proposed no cost extension... will facilitate the following proposals: increased geographical scope to monitor implementation of the flood's rehabilitation projects" (D0006344.odt, Summary Information)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (World Bank/NRSP/IFC) → End beneficiaries (GoKP departments, private sector, communities). The World Bank acts as intermediary for Sindh activities while NRSP/IFC work directly with Pakistani entities.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Administration Arrangement is agreed based on a robust results framework and value for money (VfM) criteria and progress against milestones will be reported on a quarterly basis." (D0006344.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rely on existing government initiatives)
Technical assistance only for planning and RE/EE adoption
Support to specific downstream projects/sectoral pilots
Combined approach with upstream TA and downstream interventions (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The combined approach was selected to address both systemic constraints (weak planning capacity) and immediate market failures (lack of renewable energy financing) simultaneously. The phased design allows testing of interventions before scaling, while the technical assistance component builds local capacity for sustainable impact. The addendum extends this logic to flood response monitoring and climate finance facilitation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited political ownership due to vested interests influencing policy choices
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proactive engagement with senior BHC leadership and working with middle-tier civil servants who have more stable tenures

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High turnover of officials affecting sustainability of capacity building
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on institutional systems and middle-tier officials rather than senior leaders

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Data access challenges for monitoring activities (PETS, engineering audits)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early engagement with MoPDSI and provincial P&D departments to secure data sharing commitments

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential reversal of policy priorities with government changes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continuous engagement with planning departments and development partners to maintain reform momentum

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks with local partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners follow robust procurement procedures assessed through due diligence exercises

why_rationale.quote: "Option 4: A combined approach that provides TA for improving upstream planning/capacity building with direct downstream interventions including uptake of clean energy (Preferred Option)... This approach will combine options two and three above, so as to improve and build planning capacity and capability, support provincial government with downstream investments" (41216929.odt, Appraising the Preferred Option) and "The recommended approach would: i) finish activities where the results can be achieved according to the original timeframes, ii) implement new activities in areas where required due to changes in Pakistan's economic context" (D0006344.odt, Summary Information)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile context in KP (conflict history, weak institutions, climate vulnerability) necessitated working with established local partners like NRSP who had existing government relationships and climate finance experience. The extension to Sindh required leveraging World Bank's existing trust fund mechanism due to the complex post-flood reconstruction environment.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak provincial capacity in KP limited direct implementation options, requiring technical assistance focus
Post-flood reconstruction complexity in Sindh necessitated multilateral partner (World Bank) with existing systems
Political instability required adaptive partnerships that could work with changing government priorities
Climate finance access barriers required specialized partners (NRSP) with GCF experience
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both systemic change (planning capacity) and immediate market demonstration (RE financing) led to the two-component structure. The flood response extension required a monitoring-focused approach (ME3F) rather than direct implementation due to the scale of reconstruction needs. Climate finance objectives determined the selection of NRSP with its GCF track record.
q28_linkages: Systemic planning constraints → Technical assistance component with embedded capacity building
Energy market failures → Financial instrument testing and investment facilitation approach
Flood reconstruction scale → Independent monitoring mechanism rather than direct implementation
Climate finance access barriers → Specialized partner selection (NRSP) with GCF experience
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses balancing rapid economic growth needs with inclusive development. The gender and social inclusion mainstreaming across all components (including data disaggregation in monitoring) adds implementation complexity but aligns with equity objectives. The shift from direct RE financing to investment facilitation reflects a tradeoff between immediate impact and market sustainability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Gender/disability integration in all planning processes adds time but ensures marginalized groups benefit
Expertise vs ownership: International partners (IFC, World Bank) provide technical expertise while local partners (NRSP, GoKP) ensure ownership
Immediate impact vs sustainability: Direct RE financing was shifted to investment facilitation for longer-term market development
Targeted vs broad interventions: PPP support focuses on high-impact transactions while planning TA aims for systemic change
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk rating drives quarterly milestone reporting and results-based administration arrangements. Political risks necessitate continuous engagement strategies and adaptive management approaches. Fiduciary risks with local partners require robust due diligence processes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak provincial capacity in KP determined the intensive technical assistance focus and embedded advisory roles. The capacity building for CRCC enabled them to take on climate finance facilitation roles. Middle-tier official engagement strategies were developed to mitigate high turnover risks.
intersections.quote: "Gender equality and social inclusion mainstreaming will be integrated across all SEED supported interventions ex-ante and built into all stages of the project cycle." (41216929.odt) and "The programme will work with UK government departments... to draw on UK expertise in smart cities, urban development, PPPs and integrated infrastructure investment planning" (41216929.odt) and "The programme will use the UK aid logo and offer ample branding and communications opportunities" (41216929.odt, Communications)

key_programme_risks: Political instability and uncertain reform ownership
Macroeconomic crisis affecting private sector investment
High turnover of government officials
Data access challenges for monitoring activities
Potential reversal of policy priorities with government changes
Limited absorption capacity at provincial level
Climate change-induced extreme weather events
Fiduciary risks with local implementation partners
Delays in international climate finance approval processes
Implementation risks with complex multi-stakeholder coordination

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proactive engagement with senior BHC leadership and focus on middle-tier civil servants with more stable tenures
Adaptive support to economic reform priorities of new governments post-elections

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High official turnover affecting capacity building
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Working with middle-tier officials and institutionalizing systems rather than individual capacity

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Data access challenges for ME3F activities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Early engagement with MoPDSI and provincial departments to secure data sharing commitments
Continuous engagement with planning departments and development partners
Embedded technical assistance and phased capacity building approach
Integration of climate resilience in planning processes and climate finance facilitation
Robust due diligence processes and partner procurement procedures
Extended support timeline for CRCC to navigate GCF processes (24-month lead time)
Results frameworks with clear milestones and quarterly reporting

fcas_specific_lessons: Adaptive management is critical in politically volatile environments - SEED remained effective by focusing on middle-tier officials during political transitions
Climate resilience must be integrated into all infrastructure planning given Pakistan's extreme weather vulnerability
Local ownership mechanisms (like Nudge Units) can reinforce reform sustainability despite political changes
Post-disaster contexts require independent monitoring mechanisms to ensure equitable resource allocation
Phased programming with break-points allows adjustment to emerging crises (e.g., floods, economic shocks)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: DFID Pakistan's experience with TA programmes in health and education showed that interventions must be both technically sound and politically informed. The SNG programme demonstrated that provincial-level engagement requires sustained relationship building. Lessons from housing finance and SEZ pilots showed that standalone projects without systemic support are unsustainable.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from direct RE financing to investment facilitation based on market development 2) Addition of ME3F component for flood response monitoring 3) Extended support to CRCC for climate finance based on GCF process learning 4) Focus on middle-tier officials to mitigate turnover risks 5) Integration of behavioral insights unit based on tax policy implementation experience
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme has achieved an impressive set of results and value for money despite significant challenges in the external environment" (D0006344.odt, Annex 1) and "Flexibility has been built into programme design... allowing for decisions on scaling-up to be taken at the appropriate level based on results achieved" (41216929.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The programme will work closely with multilateral partners in KP to pave the way for increased investments in economic and urban infrastructure" (41216929.odt, Coherence)

co_funding_partners.partner: World Bank (via Pak@100 Multi-Donor Trust Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: 1) £335 million of private investment reached advanced stages (6.8x leverage on RE/EE component) 2) $95 million potential international climate finance through GCF submissions 3) Fiscal space creation through pension reforms (£36m annual savings, £411m cumulative)
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily focuses on technical assistance (revenue) with some financing components for demonstration effects. The ME3F extension uses CDEL funds (£5m) while other activities use RDEL.
financial_details.quote: "The programme will help attract additional investments from multilateral and development capital institutions as well as from the private sector" (41216929.odt, Costs) and "The programme has cumulatively supported $335m of private investment to reach advanced stage... with estimated 10.2 MWs production capacity directly attributable to SEED programme" (D0006344.odt, Annex 1)

metadata.programme_name: Kenya Hunger Safety Net Programme Phase III (HSNP Phase III)
metadata.quote: "HSNP Phase 3 will reduce the vulnerability and improve the resilience of extremely poor households in northern Kenya." (48446033.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 04 April 2019 to 30 March 2024" and "New project end date: 31 March 2025" (D0003998.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: HSNP Phase 3 combines service delivery (cash transfers to vulnerable households), capacity building (strengthening GoK institutions), implementation research (testing graduation approaches), and policy influence (supporting coherent social protection sector). The programme delivers regular cash transfers to 100,000+ households while building government capacity for sustainable transition and testing new approaches like graduation models.
what_objectives.q1_source: "HSNP Phase 3 will achieve the following four outputs: Output 1: Delivery of quality, timely and scalable cash transfers to households; Output 2: Build GoK capacity for a sustainable programme transition; Output 3: Support establishing a coherent social protection sector; Output 4: Test a systems approach to graduation" (48446033.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 100,000+ households receiving regular cash transfers (600,000+ people)
15,500 beneficiary households building resilience through graduation models (7,500 in pilot counties and 8,000 in expansion counties)
8,000 households receiving NICHE package of nutrition-sensitive social protection services
100% of regular cash transfers financed by GoK in all 8 HSNP counties
Emergency payments made to 100% of households triggered in all 8 HSNP counties
Disaster Risk Financing strategy implemented by NDMA
Single registry and Management Information System (MIS) database for social protection programmes
Two transition monitoring reports prepared and 100% of recommendations adopted
133,800 households supported to cope with effects of climate change (ICF indicator)
what_objectives.summary: HSNP Phase 3 delivers regular cash transfers to over 100,000 vulnerable households in Kenya's arid regions while building Government of Kenya capacity to eventually take full ownership, testing graduation approaches to move people out of poverty, and supporting nutrition and disaster risk financing components.
what_objectives.quote: "HSNP Phase 3 will reduce the vulnerability and improve the resilience of extremely poor households in northern Kenya... With UK support, the Hunger Safety Net Programme (HSNP) has worked in Turkana, Marsabit, Mandera and Wajir counties since 2007, delivering targeted cash transfers to the poorest and most vulnerable populations. The third phase will transition HSNP to full Government of Kenya (GoK) ownership and financing." (48446033.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) which are FCAS-like contexts with extreme poverty (74-90% below poverty line), cyclical droughts, weak institutions, and security threats from al-Shabaab in Wajir and Mandera counties. The overall programme risk rating is 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (48446033.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The HSNP operates in two counties (Wajir, Mandera) where terrorist operations by al-Shabaab are an acute threat." (48446033.odt, Terrorism and financing)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit DFID/FCDO staff movement in Wajir and Mandera, requiring remote management. Weak institutional capacity at NDMA requires technical assistance. Climate risks (droughts/floods) disrupt implementation. Data limitations affect targeting and M&E. Political economy challenges include coordination between two line ministries and fiscal constraints. Infrastructure limitations in ASALs affect service delivery.
where_context.quote: "DFID's ability for direct oversight in these contexts is limited because of security restrictions for DFID staff to visit the area." (48446033.odt, Terrorism and financing) and "Reliance of the GoK's National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) on external, donor-funded technical assistance." (48446033.odt, Weaknesses)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: National Drought Management Authority (NDMA), Government of Kenya
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is transitioning to full GoK ownership by 2025, with NDMA leading implementation while FCDO provides technical assistance and funding. Key decisions (e.g., targeting, payment systems) are made jointly through structures like the Programme Steering Committee (PSC) with GoK chairmanship. The 2023 addendum shows GoK leading NICHE and EIP components with FCDO providing TA and funding.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to NDMA for leadership/management
training on disaster risk financing
mentorship for graduation models
institutional strengthening of social protection systems
support to county governments for data analysis
localisation agenda (funding to local partners)

partner_organizations.role: implementation of COVID-19 urban cash transfers (2020 addendum)

partner_organizations.role: local implementation and coordination
