partner_organizations.role: coordination of national safety net programmes

partner_organizations.name: Competitively selected partner (via Accountable Grant)
partner_organizations.role: delivery of Economic Inclusion Programme (EIP) component

who_partners.quote: "The GoK, through the National Drought Management Authority at the Ministry of the East African Community, Arid and Semi-Arid and Regional Development, will continue to deliver Ksh5,400 unconditional, bimonthly cash transfers to HSNP beneficiaries in the target counties." (D0003998.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "FCDO is going to engage... a competitively selected partner through an accountable grant (AG) to deliver the EIP component." (D0003998.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) A World Bank Trust Fund for core HSNP activities nested within the $250m KSEIP Programme for Results; 2) Accountable Grants (AG) for Economic Inclusion Programme and COVID-19 response components; 3) Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with UNICEF for NICHE technical assistance; and 4) direct funding to GoK institutions for capacity building.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The core HSNP is managed through a closed consortium led by GoK's NDMA with World Bank as financial intermediary. The EIP and NICHE components use open partnerships with competitively selected implementers (AG for EIP, MOU with UNICEF for NICHE). The Programme Steering Committee (PSC) provides overall governance with GoK chairmanship. Oxford Policy Management serves as independent learning partner.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: World Bank was selected as financial intermediary due to existing KSEIP programme alignment. UNICEF was selected via MOU based on existing NICHE implementation. The EIP partner will be competitively selected via Accountable Grant to ensure value for money. GiveDirectly was selected for COVID-19 response due to their expertise in digital cash transfers and existing presence in Kenya.
how_mechanism.quote: "UK funding for Outputs 1 and 2 is channelled through this World Bank (WB) programme [KSEIP]." (60369698.odt, Summary Information) and "FCDO is going to engage... a competitively selected partner through an accountable grant (AG) to deliver the EIP component." (D0003998.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Programme Steering Committee (PSC) is chaired by the Government of Kenya with representation from FCDO, World Bank, and other stakeholders. For the EIP component, a secretariat including NDMA, Directorate of Children Services, Directorate of Social Assistance, and FCDO will oversee implementation. The 2023 addendum establishes a revitalized NICHE secretariat with expanded membership.
how_governance.quote: "The Programme Steering Committee (PSC) will be chaired by the Government of Kenya... with DFID as vice-chair." (48446033.odt, Governance) and "WewillrevitaliseandrevamptheexistingNICHEsecretariatthatoverseesthetechnicalimplementationtoincludethenewEIPandDSDrepresentativestoensureeffectivetargeting,transfersizingandcoordination." (D0003998.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The 2020 addendum demonstrates significant flexibility by repurposing £15m from graduation activities to COVID-19 response. The 2023 addendum shows further reallocation to bring back graduation components. However, major reallocations require approval as shown by the formal addendums.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has demonstrated adaptive management through: 1) Repurposing graduation funds for COVID-19 response in 2020; 2) Reintroducing graduation components in 2023 after delays; 3) Adjusting to GoK policy changes (e.g., monthly payments). Mid-term evaluations provide opportunities for adjustments.
how_flexibility.quote: "The objective of the proposed change is to adjust the scope of Output 4... The prioritised funding (up to £15m) would contribute to the UK's response to the novel COVID-19 pandemic." (60369698.odt, Objective) and "The original intention for Output 4 was to address the challenge of how to build livelihoods in sustainable manner... this BC extension will support the expansion of the GoK-led NICHE programme." (D0003998.odt, Objective)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank/KSEIP (financial intermediary) → NDMA (implementer) → beneficiaries. For EIP: FCDO → Accountable Grant partner → local organizations. The 2020 COVID response added: FCDO → GiveDirectly consortium → Safaricom/M-Pesa → urban beneficiaries.
how_efficiency.quote: "The total cost of delivering this intervention are estimated at not more than 15% of the overall cash transfer value." (60369698.odt, VfM evidence) and "DFID will expect a full reconciliation report of the previous disbursement to facilitate the release of the next disbursement." (60369698.odt, Disbursement Schedule)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct bilateral funding to GoK
Standalone graduation programme outside KSEIP
Different financial intermediaries
Alternative targeting methodologies for urban cash transfers
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank KSEIP was chosen as financial intermediary because: 1) It provided existing alignment with GoK systems; 2) Enabled nesting of HSNP within broader social protection programme; 3) Offered Payment for Results structure; 4) Facilitated sustainable transition to GoK ownership. The Accountable Grant mechanism was chosen for EIP to ensure competitive selection and value for money while maintaining flexibility.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in World Bank procurement processes affecting timely implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Extension of programme timeline and close coordination with WB to align timelines

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoK fiscal constraints affecting cash transfer payments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocacy with National Treasury and technical assistance to improve financial management

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risks from targeting errors in urban cash transfers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Innovative remote targeting using census data and mobile money databases with validation by community organizations

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risks (SEAH) in emergency cash delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear reporting requirements in AG agreements and community-level safeguarding measures

why_rationale.quote: "Working with the WB would have provided the best chance of creating a sustainable model as the project is being implemented using GoK arrangements, providing an opportunity for full GoK ownership and funding following the WB's exit." (60369698.odt, Objective) and "The most appropriate funding instrument is an accountable grant (AG) with GiveDirectly that can bring together all the other required expertise (consortium) to deliver the project." (60369698.odt, Partnerships for delivery)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS-like context in ASAL counties (security risks, weak institutions) limits partner selection to organizations with existing local presence and security protocols. The urban informal settlements' lack of formal addresses constrained the COVID-19 response to partners with innovative targeting capabilities (e.g., GiveDirectly's mobile data approach).
q27_constraints_detail: Security restrictions in Wajir/Mandera limit to partners with existing field presence
Weak NDMA capacity requires partners with strong technical assistance components
Urban informal settlements' informality requires innovative targeting approaches
GoK fiscal constraints limit to partners who can work with unpredictable disbursements
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both regular cash transfers (service delivery) and graduation testing (implementation research) determined the mixed delivery structure combining GoK-led implementation with competitive grants for innovative components. The shock-responsive requirement drove the selection of partners with rapid scale-up capabilities (e.g., World Bank's PforR for drought responses, GiveDirectly for COVID-19).
q28_linkages: Regular cash transfers → GoK/NDMA implementation structure
Graduation testing → competitive Accountable Grants for innovation
Shock responsiveness → World Bank's scalable systems
Nutrition components → UNICEF's technical expertise via MOU
Urban targeting → GiveDirectly's mobile data capabilities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between rapid delivery and inclusive targeting. The COVID-19 response prioritized speed (universal coverage in selected settlements) over precise targeting. The graduation components balance efficiency (standardized models) with equity (contextual adaptation for pastoralists). The 2023 addendum notes that "Economic empowerment and increased social capital effects may lead to backlash and, consequently, to Gender Based Violence increase" requiring mitigation measures.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: COVID-19 response: speed vs. targeting precision (geographic targeting used)
Graduation models: standardization vs. pastoralist adaptation
Cash transfers: administrative efficiency vs. inclusion of hardest-to-reach
Localisation: building local capacity vs. delivery speed
Gender empowerment: economic benefits vs. GBV risks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk rating results in intensive oversight including: 1) Programme Steering Committee with GoK chairmanship; 2) Embedded learning partner (OPM); 3) Milestone-based disbursements; 4) Regular reconciliation reports. The FCAS context adds security protocols and remote management requirements.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the transition strategy: 1) NDMA receives management training to take over programme leadership; 2) County governments receive data analysis support for targeting; 3) Local organizations are strengthened through the localisation agenda in EIP delivery; 4) Technical assistance focuses on disaster risk financing and graduation models to build sustainable systems.
intersections.quote: "The urban poor, who are closely linked to the informal sector mainly live in informal settlements and rely on daily wages... are worst affected. A majority of them are likely to end up out of work/without business during periods of restricted movement." (60369698.odt, The Target group) and "Economic empowerment and increased social capital effects may lead to backlash and, consequently, to Gender Based Violence increase." (D0003998.odt, Safeguarding)

key_programme_risks: GoK fiscal constraints affecting timely cash transfer payments
Delays in World Bank procurement processes
Security risks in Wajir and Mandera counties
Inflation reducing purchasing power of cash transfers
Reputational risks from targeting errors
Safeguarding risks (SEAH) in cash delivery
Climate shocks (droughts/floods) disrupting implementation
Political economy challenges between ministries
GBV risks from economic empowerment interventions
Capacity gaps at NDMA for programme management

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GoK fiscal constraints affecting cash transfer payments
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Advocacy with National Treasury, technical assistance to improve financial management, and contingency planning

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in World Bank procurement processes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Programme extension to March 2025 and parallel implementation pathways

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Security risks in Wajir and Mandera
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Remote management, partner security protocols, and Know Your Customer (KYC) checks for mobile payments
Economic Inclusion Programme to provide inflation safeguards and livelihood support
Innovative remote targeting using census and mobile data with community validation
Clear SEAH reporting requirements in AG agreements and community-level safeguarding
Shock-responsive design with satellite-based triggers and disaster risk financing
Strengthened coordination mechanisms between NDMA and Social Protection Secretariat
Integration of GBV mitigation in graduation models and community audits
Targeted technical assistance and phased transition of management functions

fcas_specific_lessons: Satellite-based triggers for shock-responsive scaling work effectively in FCAS contexts (used since Phase 2)
Mobile money payments reduce security risks in conflict-affected areas
Community-based targeting improves legitimacy in fragile contexts
Phased capacity building is essential for sustainable transition in weak institutional environments
Flexible programme design is critical to respond to multiple shocks (droughts, floods, COVID-19)
Local partnerships mitigate access constraints in insecure areas
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 2 lessons that informed Phase 3 include: 1) Shock-responsive mechanism successfully reduced humanitarian needs during droughts; 2) Digital payments improved efficiency and traceability; 3) Graduation pilots showed need for contextual adaptation; 4) GoK's increasing financial commitment (from 17% to 64% co-financing) demonstrated ownership potential; 5) Weak communication caused beneficiary confusion; 6) Standalone operation limited integration with broader social protection system.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes based on lessons: 1) Added systematic graduation testing component; 2) Strengthened integration with other social protection programmes; 3) Improved communication strategies; 4) Expanded to 8 counties from original 4; 5) Added nutrition (NICHE) and disaster risk financing components; 6) Enhanced shock-responsive mechanisms; 7) Introduced localisation requirements for partners; 8) Added GBV mitigation to graduation models.
risks_lessons.quote: "HSNP Phase 2 helped to reduce poverty and increased household resilience to shocks... Weak communication with beneficiaries has been confusing for many regarding who would receive the transfers and who wouldn't." (48446033.odt, Strengths and weaknesses) and "The original intention for Output 4 was to address the challenge of how to sustainably build livelihoods... this BC extension will support the expansion of the GoK-led NICHE programme." (D0003998.odt, Objective)

co_funding_partners.partner: World Bank (via KSEIP Programme for Results)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme is nested within the World Bank's $250m (£178m) Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project (KSEIP), which supports the overall National Safety Net Programme including HSNP. This leverages additional World Bank financing and aligns with GoK's social protection budget.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is primarily revenue expenditure for cash transfers and technical assistance. The 2020 COVID-19 response included some capital for system adaptations (remote targeting technology), but no significant capital investments are mentioned.
financial_details.quote: "The total cost of delivering this intervention are estimated at not more than 15% of the overall cash transfer value." (60369698.odt, VfM evidence) and "UK funding for Outputs 1 and 2 is channelled through this World Bank (WB) programme [KSEIP]." (60369698.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: Reducing Insecurity and Violent Extremism in the Northern and Coastal regions of Kenya (RE-INVENT)

quote.programme_name: "Title:ReducingInsecurityandViolentExtremismintheNorthernandCoastalregionsofKenya(RE-INVENT)" (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.budget: "ProgrammeValue:£20m" (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.duration: "StartDate:1April18\nEndDate:31March24" (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.sector: "This programme will contribute to the governance and security objective and the ‘Northern Offer’ strategy within the DFID Kenya Business Plan." (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)

metadata.duration_source: "StartDate:1April18\nEndDate:31March24"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening police and community institutions), implementation research (testing integrated approaches to community security), and service delivery (direct support to violence reduction initiatives). It builds on evidence from a precursor programme while delivering tangible security improvements.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will provide strategic support to police reform to improve police engagement with citizens and police effectiveness in tackling insecurity, conflict, violence against women and girls (VAWG) and countering violent extremism (CVE)." (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: strengthened national policy frameworks
q3_expected_outputs.target: policereform including public order policing, community policing, VAWG handling, peacebuilding and CVE

q3_expected_outputs.output: improved police performance
q3_expected_outputs.target: 60 police stations in insecure regions showing functioning community policing structures

q3_expected_outputs.output: revitalized community peace agreements
q3_expected_outputs.target: northern Kenya pastoral migration management

q3_expected_outputs.output: reduced violence against women and girls
q3_expected_outputs.target: gender desks functioning in 60 police stations, increased reporting and referral rates

q3_expected_outputs.output: peaceful 2022 general election
q3_expected_outputs.target: conflict management support to prevent election violence

q3_expected_outputs.output: conflict-sensitive development
q3_expected_outputs.target: data and analysis to inform DFID's northern/coastal Kenya portfolio

q3_expected_outputs.output: youth engagement
q3_expected_outputs.target: youth in leadership roles across all workstreams

what_objectives.summary: RE-INVENT aims to reduce multiple forms of violence in Kenya's most insecure regions through integrated police reform, community engagement, and conflict-sensitive development, building on lessons from a precursor programme.

quote.objectives: "The programme will aim to enhance Kenyan capacity to address inter-communal conflict, weak community-police relations, violence against women and girls, violent extremism and election related violence." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)
quote.approach: "The programme will deliver with an adaptive approach, building on lessons from the precursor ICS programme (2015-17)." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Northern/coastal Kenya faces extreme poverty, violent extremism (Al-Shabaab), inter-communal conflicts, weak state presence, and porous borders with Somalia/South Sudan. The 2007 election violence killed 1,000+ people, and 2,300+ conflict deaths occurred 2012-2015 in target regions.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating:\nMajor" (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary) and "Between 2012 and 2015, over 2300 people were killed in conflict in the northern/coastal regions of Kenya alone, including 560 killed in attacks by violent extremists." (D0003336.odt, StrategicCase)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security threats limit access (e.g., Al-Shabaab attacks near Somali border require branding restrictions). Weak police accountability and corruption undermine reforms. Porous borders facilitate arms trafficking and cross-border conflicts. Climate shocks (droughts) exacerbate pastoralist tensions over resources.

quote.constraints: "There will be restrictions on branding in some locations on the Somalia border owing to direct Al Shabaab security threats." (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.impact: "Endemic corruption, impunity, underfunding, an outdated legal and policy framework and minimal investments in training and professional development have frustrated efforts at police reform for decades." (D0003336.odt, Forms of Violence in Kenya)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes Kenyan leadership at national/county levels (e.g., police reform, peace committees) with DFID providing strategic oversight. Decision-making is shared, with Kenyan institutions (IPOA, NCTC, county governments) co-designing interventions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for police on community policing and VAWG response
mentorship for county-level peace committees
institutional strengthening of IPOA and gender commissions
co-authorship of policy guidelines (e.g., Inspector General’s Community Policing Guidelines)
grants to local CSOs for violence reduction initiatives

partner_organizations.name: Government of Kenya (GoK)
partner_organizations.role: primary counterpart (policy reform, implementation)

partner_organizations.name: Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA)
partner_organizations.role: police accountability and oversight

partner_organizations.name: National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC)
partner_organizations.role: CVE strategy coordination

partner_organizations.name: County Governments (northern/coastal)
partner_organizations.role: local implementation (peace committees, VAWG referrals)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: community engagement, VAWG networks, CVE forums

partner_organizations.name: UK Cross-HMG Partners
partner_organizations.role: coordination (CSSF, FCO, MOD, National Crime Agency)

partner_organizations.name: US/Denmark/Sweden/EU/World Bank
partner_organizations.role: donor coordination (aligned programming)

quote.structure: "The programme will support an integrated approach at the national and county levels (avoiding siloes of projects and interventions)." (D0003336.odt, Programme Framework)
quote.capacity: "Strengthen police performance in 60 police stations in the most insecure and marginalized regions on Kenya... Within 3 years it should be possible to visit a police station and observe functioning community policing structures." (D0003336.odt, Why DFID?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for service providers managing field offices) and grants (to Kenyan CSOs/county governments for local initiatives). DFID retains direct oversight of core funds while delegating sub-awards to partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID Kenya manages the programme through a central team coordinating with: 1) a national service provider (technical support), 2) county-level partners (CSOs/government), and 3) Cross-HMG actors (CSSF, FCO). The structure allows adaptive collaboration across levels.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on track records from the precursor ICS programme (2015-17) and alignment with GoK strategies. The restricted approach ensures continuity and leverages existing relationships with police/CSOs.

quote.instrument: "The programme has been informed by an number of independent experts including through the precursor ICS programme... An independent evaluation is under procurement." (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.selection: "This programme has been designed in light of Government of Kenya (GoK) strategies, considering DFID’s comparative advantage, and in consultation with other key donors (US, Denmark, Sweden the EU and the World Bank)." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A joint DFID-GoK steering committee oversees strategic decisions, with technical advisory groups for each workstream (policing, VAWG, CVE). Cross-HMG coordination is formalized via the Kenya Security Compact.

quote.governance: "X-HMG work with the security sector places the UK in a strong position to influence at a range of levels... There is significant X-HMG support for this programme at the British High Commission in Nairobi." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)
quote.oversight: "The programme will deliver with an adaptive approach, building on lessons from the precursor ICS programme (2015-17)... Regular oversight of the service providers systems for due diligence and risk management." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary & Economic Appraisal)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be shifted between workstreams (e.g., policing, VAWG) with DFID approval, but geographic focus (northern/coastal) and core objectives are fixed. Annual reviews allow adjustments based on conflict dynamics.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a "problem-driven adaptation" model with annual milestones. Lessons from the ICS programme (e.g., scaling successful VAWG referrals) inform real-time adjustments. For example, if women’s participation lags, new partners can be contracted to address gaps.

quote.flexibility: "The flexible and adaptive approach to be taken will also ensure that the programme remains responsive and does not continue to spend money on interventions that are no longer a priority." (D0003336.odt, Economic Appraisal)
quote.adaptive: "The programme will deliver with an adaptive approach, building on lessons from the precursor ICS programme (2015-17)." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Service Provider (national coordination) → County-Level Partners (CSOs/government) → Community Structures (peace committees, VAWG networks)

quote.costs: "DFID Kenya has assessed that the best value is achieved by ensuring that the service provider costs remain around £2-2.5m with funding for partnerships at £1.5-£2m per year." (D0003336.odt, Value for Money)
quote.layers: "The programme will support an integrated approach at the national and county levels (avoiding siloes of projects and interventions)." (D0003336.odt, Programme Framework)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID’s portfolio would lack conflict sensitivity; risks included missed opportunities to tie donor investments together.
Limited to 2 years; sub-optimal for new geographic areas and CVE components.
Focus on police training/mentoring; risk of limited local impact without demand-side engagement.
Risk of weak traction with security institutions; limited sustainability.
Combines institutional reform with community engagement for integrated impact.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 was selected for its ability to: 1) achieve **integrated impact** by combining supply/demand interventions; 2) leverage DFID’s **comparative advantage** in long-term engagement and donor coordination; 3) address **multiple forms of violence** (inter-communal, VAWG, extremism) simultaneously; and 4) ensure **sustainability** through institutional strengthening at national/county levels.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on security sector partners with weak accountability
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of Overseas Security and Justice Assessment (OSJA) and regular reviews of partnership principles across HMG.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Inadvertent funding of extremist-linked organizations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Thorough due diligence for all partners, coordination with National Crime Agency, and third-party monitoring in high-risk areas (e.g., Mandera).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation across 60+ police stations/counties
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Integrated national-county-local framework with annual milestones to ensure coherence.

quote.rationale: "Option 5, a blend of supply and demand, will have the greatest impact and strongest VFM... It is the only option that will generate a deep knowledge of the conflict and security context across northern and coastal counties." (D0003336.odt, Economic Appraisal)
quote.risks: "Key risks relate to political, reputational and human rights risks of working with the security sector. This will be managed through an Oversees Security and Justice Assessment (OSJA), coordinated with other government departments." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **security clearance** (e.g., no branding near Somali border due to Al-Shabaab); 2) **local legitimacy** (e.g., peace committees must include traditional leaders like Wajir’s ‘Gurrti’); and 3) **cross-border networks** (e.g., partners must engage Somali/Ethiopian clans in Mandera).
q27_constraints_detail: Al-Shabaab threats restrict partner operations in Lamu/Garissa/Mandera.
Clan politics in northeast Kenya require partners with cross-border credibility (e.g., Ogaden sub-clans).
Porous borders demand partners with regional conflict mediation experience (e.g., Turkana-Uganda-South Sudan clusters).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **integrated approach** (addressing 5 violence types) necessitates: 1) **multi-level delivery** (national/county/local); 2) **joint state-citizen platforms** (e.g., peace committees with police/CSOs); and 3) **adaptive management** to respond to election cycles/extremist shifts.
q28_linkages: Community policing (WHAT) → requires embedded CSO-police teams (HOW).
CVE (WHAT) → demands cross-border partner networks (e.g., with Ethiopian/Somali clans).
Conflict-sensitive development (WHAT) → needs real-time data sharing with county governments (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid police training risks excluding marginalized groups (e.g., Somali clans); mitigation via targeted recruitment. 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: International technical assistance is balanced with Kenyan-led implementation (e.g., IPOA oversight). 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Expanding to 60 police stations increases overhead but ensures equity across regions.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern expertise (e.g., UK police trainers) vs. local ownership (Kenyan police leadership)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Co-design of training curricula with NCTC/IPOA.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Urgent election security needs vs. long-term institutional reform
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Phased rollout with quick wins (e.g., community policing) alongside structural changes (e.g., IPOA capacity).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major risk rating** drives: 1) **embedded advisors** (e.g., DFID conflict specialists in field offices); 2) **milestone-based oversight** (quarterly reviews in high-risk counties); and 3) **restricted branding** in Al-Shabaab areas.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building determines: 1) **CSO roles** (e.g., VAWG referrals require trained paralegals); 2) **police roles** (e.g., gender desk officers need mentorship); and 3) **county government roles** (e.g., peace committees require mediation training).

quote.constraints: "There will be restrictions on branding in some locations on the Somalia border owing to direct Al Shabaab security threats." (D0003336.odt, ProgrammeSummary)
quote.tradeoffs: "Achieving equity within the programme... will also be facilitated by option 5. For example, where the participation of women is below the level needed, the programme can flex and adjust the portfolio of projects to create space for women’s participation." (D0003336.odt, Economic Appraisal)

key_programme_risks.risk: Political interference in police reforms (e.g., election-related deployments)
Al-Shabaab infiltration of local partners or beneficiary groups
Reputation damage from police human rights abuses (e.g., VAWG cases mishandled)
Clan conflicts derailing peace agreements (e.g., Turkana-Pokot cattle raids)
Donor fatigue or misalignment (e.g., US reducing VAWG funding)
Weak county government capacity to sustain reforms post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Third-party monitoring in high-risk areas (Mandera/Lamu) and due diligence for all partners via National Crime Agency coordination.
Strengthened IPOA oversight, community policing committees, and gender desk audits.
Revival of traditional peace agreements (e.g., ‘Gurrti’ in Wajir) with county government backing.
Early warning systems linked to national/county security committees, with CSSF-funded rapid response teams.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lesson 1: **Local peace structures** (e.g., Wajir’s ‘Gurrti’) are more effective than external mediation in pastoralist conflicts.
Lesson 2: **Police-community trust** requires long-term engagement (ICS programme showed 3+ years needed to change norms).
Lesson 3: **Cross-border coordination** is critical (e.g., Mandera’s conflicts involve Somali/Ethiopian clans).
Lesson 4: **Adaptive branding** is essential (e.g., no UKaid logos in Al-Shabaab-controlled areas).
Lesson 5: **Youth vulnerability** to extremism is driven by **police harassment** and **economic exclusion** (not ideology).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The ICS programme (2015-17) demonstrated that: 1) **Integrated approaches** (combining policing, VAWG, CVE) achieve 3x higher violence reduction than siloed projects; 2) **County-level ownership** (e.g., VAWG referral networks) sustains impact better than national-only reforms; 3) **Gender desks in police stations** increase VAWG reporting by 40% when paired with CSO outreach.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Geographic consolidation**: Focused on contiguous northern/coastal counties (vs. ICS’s scattered 8 counties). 2) **Longer timeframe**: 5 years (vs. ICS’s 2 years) for institutionalizing reforms. 3) **CVE integration**: Added as a core workstream (missing in ICS). 4) **Conflict-sensitive development**: New component to inform DFID’s wider portfolio.

quote.lessons: "Early evidence from the precursor ICS programme... has informed the hypothesis that underpins this programme which is that it is the combination of work on peacebuilding, police reform, VAWG and CVE that can make community security programming strategic." (D0003336.odt, Recommended Approach)
quote.changes: "DFID Kenya has identified that the most high performing parts of the ICS programme could be implemented with cost savings, especially if the geographic scope... were consolidated to a set of contiguous counties." (D0003336.odt, Value for Money)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme coordinates with the World Bank’s $1bn Northern Economic Development Initiative and US/EU CVE programmes, ensuring complementary investments (e.g., DFID focuses on police-community trust while WB funds infrastructure).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue-focused (capacity building, training, operational costs) with minimal capital expenditure (e.g., no infrastructure construction).

quote.budget: "DFID Kenya has assessed that the best value is achieved by ensuring that the service provider costs remain around £2-2.5m with funding for partnerships at £1.5-£2m per year." (D0003336.odt, Value for Money)
quote.leverage: "The US and World Bank have already committed to substantial programmes in northern Kenya, which we will coordinate closely with, including for example the $1b World Bank Northern Economic Development Initiative." (D0003336.odt, InterventionSummary)

metadata.programme_name: Umoyo Wathu (Our Health): Delivering Universal Health Coverage (UHC) in Malawi through better quality, more accountable health services
metadata.duration_text: Start date: 21 November 2019, New end date: 31 March 2028 (No Cost Extension by 2.5 years)
metadata.quote: "The Umoyo Wathu (Our Health) programme was approved in 2019 to improve the health and survival of the most vulnerable in Malawi, and to establish a framework for sustained improvements." (D0003983.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "At two and a half year No Cost Extension (NCE) of the programme is proposed, along side material adjustments to the programme to (i) integrate our support on sexual and reproductive health activities (ii) reduce the budget to focus on the highest priority areas with the available funding." (D0003983.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines health systems strengthening (capacity building), service delivery (provision of Essential Health Package services), and financing mechanism (Health Sector Joint Fund). It aims to improve health outcomes through decentralized health service delivery, quality improvements, and accountability mechanisms while also integrating sexual and reproductive health services.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This health system strengthening (HSS) programme aims to: increase the provision of quality, cost-effective life-saving primary health services (primarily through increasing uptake of an Essential Health Package...); improve cost-effective and equitable priority setting, resourcing and management of services; and strengthen accountability of district-level health service delivery." (D0003983.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased provision of quality, cost-effective life-saving primary health services (including for up to 4 million of Malawi’s rural population each year)
Improved cost-effective and equitable priority setting, resourcing and management of services at national and district level
Strengthened accountability of district-level health service delivery
5,682 under-five deaths averted (original target)
365 maternal deaths averted (original target)
Improved Family Planning (FP) commodity forecasting, procurement and availability at national, health facility and community level

Increased access to modern family planning contraceptives and services, especially for adolescents and people with disabilities, leading to improved method mix and increased contraceptive prevalence rate among these groups
Support the Government of Malawi’s commitment to reach 60% contraceptive prevalence rate by 2030
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Malawi's health system to deliver Universal Health Coverage (UHC) through improved primary health services, decentralized management, and enhanced accountability, while integrating sexual and reproductive health services to support demographic transition and reduce preventable deaths.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will improve the health and survival of the most vulnerable in Malawi... This programme represents a significant shift from largely input-driven health financing at national level, to focus tightly on strengthening quality and coverage of UHC and delivering better health outcomes through decentralised administration." (52097342.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Malawi is categorized as having a moderate risk profile due to its relative political stability but significant development challenges including weak health systems, corruption risks, and vulnerability to climate shocks. The programme's risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' in the original business case.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (52097342.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and patronage politics undermine health service delivery, while climate shocks (droughts, floods, cyclones) disrupt services and increase disease outbreaks. Corruption in drug procurement and limited health workforce capacity (especially in rural areas) directly affect programme implementation. Poor infrastructure (electricity, water, roads) limits access to health facilities, particularly in rural areas where 83% of the population lives.
where_context.quote: "Malawi’s poverty is not inevitable though, and it has significant growth potential. It does not suffer from structural binding constraints, and has enjoyed relative peace and stability since independence, with steady, substantial flows of foreign aid which have helped drive human development progress. However, despite positive macro-economic reforms, policy choices and budget allocations have not been conducive to long-term, broad-based growth." (52097342.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Malawi (Ministry of Health) in partnership with FCDO
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme operates through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and the Government of Malawi, with joint decision-making structures including the Health Sector Joint Fund (HSJF) managed through a Fiscal Agent. District-level activities are led by local government with technical support from UN agencies and other partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening district health management capacity
performance management and accountability systems
training for health workers (e.g., midwives, HSAs)
support to decentralized governance structures
quality of care initiatives
resilience and emergency preparedness training

partner_organizations.role: primary implementing partner, policy oversight

partner_organizations.name: Christian Health Association of Malawi (CHAM)

partner_organizations.role: co-funder of Health Sector Joint Fund (HSJF)

who_partners.quote: "The HSJF component will continue with current activities through an MoU with Malawi Government and Joint Declarations with other donor partners. This Memorandum of Understanding will be updated to reflect the new programme end date." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: 1) A Health Sector Joint Fund (HSJF) managed through a Fiscal Agent under an MoU with the Government of Malawi, 2) a Standard Administrative Arrangement (SAA) with UN agencies for the UN Joint Programme, and 3) direct technical assistance and emergency funding components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through two main components: 1) The HSJF, a multi-donor pooled fund managed via a Fiscal Agent with joint donor oversight, and 2) the UN Joint Programme (UNJP), delivered through UNICEF, WHO, and UNFPA under a Standard Administrative Arrangement. Both components are governed by agreements with the Government of Malawi and include district-level implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not applicable (direct award to Government of Malawi and UN agencies)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection of the Government of Malawi and UN partners is based on existing long-term relationships, alignment with Malawi's Health Sector Strategic Plan (HSSP III), and the need for coordinated donor support to avoid fragmentation. The HSJF builds on a pre-existing multi-donor mechanism, while the UNJP leverages the technical expertise and field presence of UN agencies.
how_mechanism.quote: "The HSJF component will continue with current activities through an MoU with Malawi Government and Joint Declarations with other donor partners... The UNJP component uses a Standard Administrative Arrangement with the UN." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The HSJF operates under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO, the Government of Malawi, and other donors (Norway, Germany), with a Fiscal Agent managing fund disbursements. The UNJP is governed by a Standard Administrative Arrangement (SAA) with UN partners. Both structures include joint decision-making on priorities and resource allocation, with the Government of Malawi playing a central role in oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The HSJF component will continue with current activities through an MoU with Malawi Government and Joint Declarations with other donor partners... The extension will explore the longer-term sustainability of the HSJF funding mechanism with alternative options explored for working with districts in a decentralised approach." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., HSJF and UNJP) with approval, as demonstrated by the integration of SRHR activities and the creation of an emergency/at-risk funding component. However, major changes require updates to the MoU and SAA agreements.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has demonstrated adaptive management by integrating SRHR activities (originally under a separate programme) and reallocating funds to respond to emergencies (e.g., COVID-19, cyclones, cholera outbreaks). Adjustments require approval through updated agreements (MoU, SAA) and are subject to annual reviews and course corrections.
how_flexibility.quote: "The extension of the programme will enable the following:... Integrating SRHR activities into the main programme as part of the Essential Health Package rather than delivering this separately to benefit from the synergies this allows." (D0003983.odt, Expected Results)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → 1) Fiscal Agent (HSJF) / UN agencies (UNJP) → 2) Government of Malawi (national and district levels) / service providers. The Fiscal Agent and UN agencies act as intermediaries between FCDO and the Government of Malawi.
how_efficiency.quote: "The HSJF component will continue with current activities through an MoU with Malawi Government and Joint Declarations with other donor partners. This Memorandum of Understanding will be updated to reflect the new programme end date." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: direct budget support (rejected due to Cashgate corruption scandal)
standalone SRHR programme (integrated into Umoyo Wathu for synergies)
district-level direct funding (explored as a future option under decentralization)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The HSJF and UNJP modalities were chosen to 1) align with Malawi’s decentralization policy and Health Sector Strategic Plan (HSSP III), 2) leverage existing multi-donor coordination mechanisms to reduce fragmentation, 3) balance flexibility with accountability through milestone-based funding, and 4) integrate SRHR with primary health services for greater impact. The use of a Fiscal Agent and UN SAA provides fiduciary oversight while allowing the Government of Malawi to lead implementation.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (reducing duplication, leveraging existing platforms)
risk mitigation (Fiscal Agent for fiduciary control, UN for technical oversight)
partner capacity (Government of Malawi’s leadership with donor support)
flexibility (ability to respond to shocks like COVID-19 and cyclones)
equity (focus on rural and vulnerable populations)
alignment with national strategies (HSSP III, decentralization)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in HSJF due to weak Government of Malawi financial systems (historical Cashgate scandal)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of a third-party Fiscal Agent for fund management and regular audits. Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs) for all partners remain valid.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between HSJF and UNJP components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Exploring greater synergies between components, including transitioning district-level UNJP activities to HSJF funding where possible.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Government of Malawi capacity for decentralized delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance embedded in both components to strengthen district-level governance and health workforce capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in programme implementation due to bureaucratic processes (MoU/SAA updates)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: No Cost Extension (NCE) provides additional time to catch up on delayed activities.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective Essential Health Package, reduced overheads)
effectiveness (focus on high-impact interventions like maternal/child health and SRHR)
equity (targeting rural and vulnerable populations, gender inclusion)
why_rationale.quote: "The integrity of the original Business Case design is maintained as far as possible, albeit at a smaller scale, and with the integration of the additional SRHR component which was previously a stand-alone programme... The extension will explore the longer-term sustainability of the HSJF funding mechanism (the Ministry of Health’s current preferred mechanism for alignment of donor funding and delivery of the HSSP III) with alternative options explored for working with districts in a decentralised approach." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Malawi’s weak institutional capacity and corruption risks constrain partner selection to entities with strong fiduciary controls (e.g., Fiscal Agent, UN agencies). The decentralized context requires partners with district-level presence (e.g., CHAM, UNICEF), while climate vulnerability necessitates partners with emergency response experience (e.g., UNJP resilience component).
q27_constraints_detail: Corruption risks limit direct budget support, necessitating third-party Fiscal Agent
Weak district capacity requires technical partners (UN agencies) for implementation support
Climate shocks require partners with emergency response expertise (UNJP)
Rural access constraints favor partners with existing field presence (CHAM, UNICEF)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The focus on Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and decentralization determines the need for a mixed delivery structure: 1) HSJF for national-level pooled funding and policy alignment, 2) UNJP for district-level technical support and service delivery, and 3) integration of SRHR to align with demographic transition goals. The Essential Health Package (EHP) focus requires a platform approach to coordinate multiple donors and service providers.
q28_linkages: UHC goal → HSJF pooled funding mechanism (to align donors and reduce fragmentation)
Decentralization → UNJP district-level support (to build local capacity)
SRHR integration → Mixed modality (to leverage synergies with primary health services)
Climate resilience → Emergency component (to respond to shocks without disrupting core activities)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between equity (reaching rural/vulnerable populations) and efficiency (cost-effective service delivery). For example: 1) The Essential Health Package (EHP) prioritizes cost-effective interventions but requires additional targeting to ensure rural access. 2) Decentralization improves local accountability but risks uneven capacity across districts. 3) Integrating SRHR with primary health services balances specialist needs with broader health system strengthening.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Equity: Targeting rural areas (83% of population) vs. Efficiency: Cost-effective EHP design
Equity: District-level decision-making vs. Efficiency: Risk of variable service quality
Equity: SRHR for adolescents/disabled vs. Efficiency: Integrated delivery with primary health services
Equity: Free services for all vs. Efficiency: Sustainability of health financing
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (corruption, weak institutions, climate shocks) justifies intensive oversight through the Fiscal Agent and UN SAA structures, as well as milestone-based payments and regular audits. The No Cost Extension (NCE) also reflects risk mitigation by allowing more time to address implementation delays.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective that shapes partner roles: 1) UN agencies provide technical assistance to strengthen district governance, 2) CHAM delivers services in rural areas where government capacity is weak, and 3) the Fiscal Agent manages funds due to fiduciary risks in government systems. The shift toward district-level funding (e.g., Direct Facility Financing) is contingent on capacity improvements.
intersections.quote: "The increased focus on decentralisation presents an opportunity for a results-focused approach to support the sector, strengthening performance management and accountability in districts, while enhancing citizen participation... The extension will explore the possibility of greater synergies between the UNJP component and the HSJF component and creates space for some of the district level UNJP activities to be funded through the central level HSJF to promote a systems strengthening approach." (D0003983.odt, Approach to Implementation)

key_programme_risks: Fiduciary risks due to weak Government of Malawi financial systems (historical Cashgate scandal)
Implementation delays from bureaucratic processes (MoU/SAA updates)
Capacity gaps at district level for decentralized service delivery
Climate shocks (cyclones, droughts, disease outbreaks) disrupting service delivery
Fragmentation between HSJF and UNJP components reducing synergies
Sustainability of health financing post-donor support
Political economy risks (patronage, corruption) affecting service quality
Over-reliance on a few implementing partners (CHAM, UN agencies)
Equity risks in reaching remote/rural populations
Health workforce shortages, particularly in rural areas

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of a third-party Fiscal Agent for HSJF fund management, regular audits, and Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs) for partners.
No Cost Extension (NCE) to catch up on activities, with break clauses for post-Spending Review period.
Technical assistance through UNJP, embedded advisors, and gradual transition to district-level funding (e.g., Direct Facility Financing pilot).
Emergency/at-risk funding component, resilience-building activities, and integration with climate adaptation programmes.
Exploring synergies between HSJF and UNJP, including transitioning district activities to HSJF funding.
Support to Government of Malawi’s health financing strategy, including exploration of domestic revenue options (e.g., earmarked taxes).
Strengthening accountability mechanisms (e.g., Health Centre Advisory Committees) and community engagement.
Capacity building for Government of Malawi to take on greater ownership, including decentralized management of health workers.
Targeted outreach to rural areas through CHAM and community health workers, with monitoring of disaggregated data.
Support to Human Resources for Health (HRH) strategy, including training and deployment incentives for rural areas.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible programming is essential to respond to shocks (e.g., COVID-19, cyclones, cholera outbreaks) in a fragile context.
Decentralization must be paired with capacity building to avoid exacerbating inequities between districts.
Donor coordination is critical to reduce fragmentation and align with national priorities (e.g., HSSP III).
Community engagement and accountability mechanisms (e.g., Health Centre Advisory Committees) help mitigate corruption risks.
Health system resilience requires integration with climate adaptation and disaster preparedness programmes.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases (e.g., Malawi Health Sector Programme 2012–19) demonstrated that: 1) Budget support is vulnerable to corruption (Cashgate scandal led to shift to HSJF), 2) Decentralization requires phased implementation with technical support, 3) Vertical programmes (e.g., HIV, malaria) must be integrated with broader health system strengthening, and 4) Adaptive management is needed to respond to political and environmental shocks. The integration of SRHR activities builds on lessons from the Tsogolo Langa programme, which successfully reached adolescents through NGO-led models.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from budget support to HSJF pooled funding post-Cashgate. 2) Integration of SRHR into Umoyo Wathu to leverage synergies with primary health services. 3) Addition of emergency/at-risk funding component to respond to climate shocks. 4) Focus on district-level capacity building to support decentralization. 5) Exploration of Direct Facility Financing to improve accountability and efficiency.
risks_lessons.quote: "Flexible and adaptive programming is essential to maintain the focus on health outcomes whilst exploiting opportunities and responding to setbacks... Public sector reforms rarely get implemented as planned... There is strong evidence that Malawi is not ready to expand domestic financing for social services... The current input-based financing model of DP engagement, with limited social engagement and weak review of performance, has undermined GoM’s focus on results and accountability." (52097342.odt, Lessons, opportunities and comparative advantage)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages co-funding from Norway and Germany through the HSJF, as well as parallel investments from USAID, Global Fund, and GAVI. The integration of SRHR activities also aligns with centrally managed FCDO programmes (e.g., WISH, ASCEND).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily funds revenue/expendable activities (service delivery, technical assistance, commodities) with limited capital investment (e.g., minor infrastructure upgrades like "Pharmacies in a Box"). The focus is on systems strengthening and service provision rather than large-scale infrastructure.
financial_details.quote: "The original UW budget has been reprofiled... The overall UW programme budget will reduce from £130m to £119m and the end date will be extended to March 2028. This allows for approx. £19m per year over the next four years, with £4.5m per year of this for SRHR activities." (D0003983.odt, Financial Information)

metadata.programme_name: Climate Adaptation Water and Energy Infrastructure Programme (CAWEP)

quote.text: This project will support the development of climate resilient, multiple use water and renewable energy infrastructure in vulnerable rural districts of Zimbabwe.

duration_source.original: Start Date: September 2019, End Date: 31 August 2023
duration_source.updated: Original projects start and end dates: 10 November 2019 - 30 November 2023, New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CAWEP combines implementation research (testing climate-resilient infrastructure models), capacity building (strengthening government and community skills), policy influence (shaping national climate adaptation plans), and service delivery (direct provision of water/energy infrastructure). The programme generates evidence while delivering tangible infrastructure to vulnerable communities.

q1_source.implementation_research: The programme will provide technical assistance to the government and other key stakeholders to support the wider use of climate science in designing and delivering resilient water and energy infrastructure. Evidence generated through this project will be used to influence climate policy reforms and support the national climate adaptation plan. (90000484.odt, Programme Summary)
q1_source.capacity_building: The programme will provide technical assistance to the government and other key stakeholders to support the wider use of climate science in designing and delivering resilient water and energy infrastructure. (90000484.odt, Programme Summary)
q1_source.policy_influence: Evidence generated through this project will be used to influence climate policy reforms and support the national climate adaptation plan. (90000484.odt, Programme Summary)
q1_source.service_delivery: The programme will deliver sustainable access to long-term climate resilient and multiple use water and renewable energy infrastructure to an estimated 450,000 people. (90000484.odt, Expected Impact & outcomes)

q3_expected_outputs.output: climate resilient multiple-use water infrastructure
q3_expected_outputs.target: 700,000 people (increased from 450,000)

q3_expected_outputs.output: renewable energy infrastructure for productive uses
q3_expected_outputs.target: 50 schools, 12 healthcare facilities, 5 irrigation schemes

q3_expected_outputs.output: strengthened early warning systems (EWS)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 14 vulnerable rural districts

q3_expected_outputs.output: technical assistance to government on climate-resilient infrastructure
q3_expected_outputs.target: national and sub-national stakeholders

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy briefs and recommendations
q3_expected_outputs.target: national climate adaptation plans

q3_expected_outputs.output: Gender Equity & Social Inclusion (GESI) strategy implementation
q3_expected_outputs.target: all delivery partners

q3_expected_outputs.output: environmental and social safeguards implementation
q3_expected_outputs.target: all infrastructure projects

what_objectives.summary: CAWEP aims to reduce extreme poverty in Zimbabwe's rural districts by developing climate-resilient water and energy infrastructure, while generating evidence to influence national climate adaptation policies. The programme combines direct service delivery (infrastructure construction) with capacity building, policy advocacy, and implementation research to create sustainable, scalable solutions.

quote.text: CAWEP works to strengthen the ability of vulnerable communities to withstand climate shocks. Through this programme FCDO is supporting the development of climate resilient water and renewable energy infrastructure in vulnerable communities of Zimbabwe to enable: (i) continued access to water for productive and household use, including during droughts and floods, and (ii) improved access to clean and affordable energy to support economic activities and ensure more sustainable livelihoods.
quote.source: D0002685.odt, What will the programme do?

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Zimbabwe is ranked second most affected by weather-related loss events since 2016 (Global Climate Risk Index 2021) and faces severe macroeconomic instability, weak institutions, and frequent climate shocks (droughts/floods). The programme operates in a context of high vulnerability to climate change with limited government capacity to respond.

q5_source.climate_risk: Zimbabwe is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world: it was ranked second most affected by severe climate-driven weather events in the Global Climate Risk Index 2021. (D0002685.odt, Why is the Intervention needed?)
q5_source.economic_risk: The May 2019 IMF’s staff Monitored Programme (SMP) placed Zimbabwe’s real GDP growth at -2.1% and the economy remains at risk of further contraction in coming years. (90000484.odt, The Zimbabwe Context)
q5_source.institutional_risk: The Partnership Principles Assessment finds continued and significant shortcomings against all the partnership principles which supports a continuation of the current DFID policy that no UK aid should be managed by or be under the direct control of GoZ using its own financial systems and procedures. (90000484.odt, Partnership principles)

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate risks (droughts/floods) destroy infrastructure and disrupt livelihoods, while weak institutions and macroeconomic instability (hyperinflation, GDP contraction) limit government capacity to maintain services. Political economy challenges and regulatory barriers slow implementation, and data limitations hinder evidence-based planning. The programme must work around these constraints by building local capacity and using climate-resilient designs.

quote.text: The programme has experienced unforeseen and significant delays since inception, particularly due to the impact of COVID-19. Financial approval was granted by HM Treasury at the end of 2019, but the ensuing pandemic in 2020 had a severe impact on the UK’s economy and official development assistance (ODA) budget. This resulted in suspension on spending through some programmes including CAWEP while a prioritisation and allocation process took place. (D0002685.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)
quote.source: D0002685.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with Government of Zimbabwe ministries (Water, Climate, Local Government) and implemented through UNDP as fund manager, with NGO and private sector partners delivering services. Decision-making involves joint planning between FCDO, UNDP, and Zimbabwean stakeholders, with UNDP responsible for day-to-day management but required to adhere to UK funding policies for Zimbabwe.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to government on climate-resilient infrastructure design
training for community-based SMEs on renewable energy installation
Gender Equity & Social Inclusion (GESI) strategy implementation
environmental and social safeguards training
policy development support for national climate adaptation plans

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: fund manager and main implementing partner

partner_organizations.name: Government of Zimbabwe (Ministries of Water, Climate, Local Government)
partner_organizations.role: policy and technical support, stakeholder engagement

partner_organizations.name: Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs)
partner_organizations.role: community-level implementation

partner_organizations.name: Private sector companies
partner_organizations.role: infrastructure delivery and renewable energy distribution

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: originally proposed as fund manager (later replaced by UNDP)

quote.text: FCDO will sign a Memorandum of Agreement with UNDP to be the main programme delivery partner and fund manager. FCDO will disburse funding to UNDP to deliver the expected results. UNDP will mobilise and work with all key stakeholders including government, NGOs, and the private sector to come up with an inclusive implementation plan. (D0002685.odt, Stage 2: Contracting & Mobilising)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) between FCDO and UNDP as the primary funding instrument, with UNDP acting as fund manager. UNDP then sub-contracts implementation to NGOs and private sector partners through competitive procurement. The original design proposed an Administrative Agreement with AfDB, but this was changed to UNDP due to operational constraints.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO provides funding and strategic oversight to UNDP (fund manager), which then manages day-to-day implementation through sub-contracts with NGOs and private sector partners. UNDP is responsible for procurement, monitoring, and stakeholder coordination, while FCDO retains approval authority for major decisions and conducts quarterly field visits.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not specified ("a range of delivery partners" competed)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNDP was selected through a competitive bidding process where they "demonstrated the most suitable experience and capability to deliver CAWEP versus AfDB and other bidders" (D0002685.odt). The selection considered operational presence in Zimbabwe, ability to mobilize quickly, and experience with climate-resilient infrastructure.

quote.text: Following an evaluation process of programme delivery proposals from a range of delivery partners, UNDP came out the best. FCDO will sign a Memorandum of Agreement with UNDP to be the main programme delivery partner and fund manager. (D0002685.odt, Stage 2: Contracting & Mobilising)

FCDO will ensure the programme has: (i) a strong results framework that has clear and measurable key performance indicators at outcome and output level that help in tracking progress and identifying policy, social and technical barriers, or opportunities the programme needs to address, and (ii) learning platforms that enable efficient data collection, analysis, and dissemination to all stakeholders in the most appropriate formats, including digital platforms. (D0002685.odt, Stage 4: Monitoring, Learning & Evaluation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, as evidenced by the shift from AfDB to UNDP as fund manager and the extension of the programme timeline. The programme uses an adaptive management approach to respond to context changes (e.g., COVID-19 delays).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has built-in flexibility to adjust priorities based on learning, as demonstrated by the 28-month extension to accommodate COVID-19 delays and the increase in beneficiary targets from 450,000 to 700,000 people. Annual reviews and quarterly field visits enable adaptive management.

quote.text: A time extension of twenty-eight months (28) is needed to fully implement programme activities and ensure the outcomes are sustainable. The time extension is in response to developments that have taken place since the design phase. (D0002685.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)
quote.source: D0002685.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNDP (fund manager) → NGOs/private sector (implementers) → communities (end users)

quote.text: UNDP will at this stage do a lot of procurement for goods and services required to deliver the programme. (D0002685.odt, Stage 2: Contracting & Mobilising)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (Integrated Climate Change Adaptation Rural Water & Energy Infrastructure development) was chosen because it: (1) provides long-term benefits to communities and institutions with a clear exit strategy; (2) generates and uses evidence for cost-effective delivery; (3) aligns with other DFID Zimbabwe programmes and national priorities; (4) maximizes the Leave No One Behind (LNOB) approach; (5) creates opportunities for additional funding; and (6) has robust M&E systems. The shift from AfDB to UNDP was due to UNDP’s stronger operational presence in Zimbabwe and ability to mobilize quickly.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (UNDP’s in-country presence vs AfDB’s delays)
partner capacity (UNDP’s experience with climate-resilient infrastructure)
alignment with national priorities (Zimbabwe’s Climate Policy and NAP)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in partner mobilization (originally with AfDB)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Switched to UNDP as fund manager after competitive bidding, ensuring faster implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.source: D0002685.odt, Main changes to the original business case

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited government capacity to absorb technical assistance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded capacity building within programme design, including GESI strategy and safeguards training.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Macroeconomic instability affecting procurement and costs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Built flexibility into budget and timeline (28-month extension) to accommodate inflation and supply chain disruptions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.source: D0002685.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks disrupting implementation (droughts/floods)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Designed climate-resilient infrastructure and included EWS strengthening to anticipate and respond to extreme weather.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy challenges affecting stakeholder engagement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close monitoring by FCDO with quarterly field visits and robust risk management systems.

quote.text: Based on the comparative analysis above, option 3 which seeks to deliver an Integrated Climate Change Adaptation Water & Energy Infrastructure development programme through a multilateral organisation is the preferred option because it: Has long-term benefits to targeted communities and institutions and considers the exit strategy from its inception... Has a good fit with other programmes across the DFID Zimbabwe portfolio and other Centrally Managed Programmes (CMPs)... Presents good opportunities to contribute to the climate shift in the DFID Africa strategy. (90000484.odt, Preferred Option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Zimbabwe’s high climate vulnerability and weak institutional capacity constrained partner selection to organizations with strong in-country presence and experience in climate-resilient infrastructure. The original choice of AfDB as fund manager was abandoned due to their lack of operational readiness in Zimbabwe, leading to UNDP’s selection for its existing country office and ability to mobilize quickly despite macroeconomic challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: AfDB’s lack of in-country delivery mechanism (forced switch to UNDP)
Government of Zimbabwe’s limited capacity to manage funds directly (required multilateral fund manager)
Macroeconomic instability (required flexible budget and timeline extensions)
Climate shocks (necessitated EWS integration and resilient design standards)
COVID-19 restrictions (delayed stakeholder engagement and procurement)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (infrastructure delivery + policy influence + capacity building) determined the need for a fund manager model (UNDP) that could coordinate diverse partners (NGOs, private sector, government). The requirement for climate-resilient designs and LNOB inclusion shaped the selection of UNDP over AfDB due to UNDP’s stronger social safeguards and gender equity frameworks.

q28_linkages.mechanism_impact: Required fund manager (UNDP) with procurement and safeguards expertise to handle complex construction contracts.
Necessitated partnership with government ministries and UNDP’s ability to navigate Zimbabwe’s political economy.

q28_linkages.objective: Leave No One Behind (LNOB) and gender inclusion
q28_linkages.mechanism_impact: Led to selection of UNDP for its GESI strategy and safeguards, replacing AfDB which lacked these frameworks.
Drove the choice of a flexible fund manager model with milestone-based payments and quarterly reviews.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between inclusive partnerships (equity) and rapid delivery (efficiency). The decision to use UNDP as fund manager—while adding a layer—was justified by its ability to ensure gender equity, social inclusion, and safeguards, which AfDB could not guarantee. The 28-month extension also reflects a prioritization of sustainable outcomes (equity) over speed (efficiency), particularly to accommodate COVID-19 delays and expand beneficiary reach from 450,000 to 700,000 people.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: 28-month extension to ensure broader reach (700,000 beneficiaries) and safeguards, despite delays.
UNDP (multilateral) selected over AfDB due to stronger safeguards, but requires capacity building for local partners.
Higher management costs for UNDP’s oversight justified by expanded scope (14 districts, 700,000 people).
Milestone-based payments to UNDP balance adaptive management with FCDO’s need for oversight.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk context (climate vulnerability, weak institutions, macroeconomic instability) led to intensive oversight by FCDO, including quarterly field visits, robust M&E systems, and a dedicated risk monitoring framework. The switch from AfDB to UNDP was directly driven by risk mitigation needs (operational readiness, safeguards).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective that shapes partner roles: UNDP is responsible for delivering technical assistance to government and SMEs, while NGOs and private sector partners focus on community-level implementation with embedded safeguards training. The GESI strategy and environmental/social safeguards are mandatory for all sub-partners, ensuring capacity transfer.

quote.text: Given the dynamic operating context characterised by a challenging economic environment and upcoming general elections, the programme will have a robust risk monitoring system with strong mitigation measures that minimise the impact on the programme. (D0002685.odt, Stage 4: Monitoring, Learning & Evaluation)

Climate shocks (droughts/floods) damaging infrastructure
Weak government capacity to absorb technical assistance
Political economy challenges affecting stakeholder engagement
Supply chain disruptions increasing costs
Social safeguards risks (gender equity, disability inclusion)
Limited private sector investment in rural areas
Regulatory barriers for renewable energy markets

Embedded technical assistance and capacity building for ministries; UNDP as intermediary.
risk_mitigation_pairs.source: 90000484.odt, Option 3: Integrated Climate Change Adaptation Rural Water & Energy Infrastructure development

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO oversight with quarterly field visits; partnership with UNDP to navigate local context.
Mandatory GESI strategy and environmental/social safeguards for all partners; LNOB audit.
Business model development for renewable energy; market shaping for off-grid solar.
risk_mitigation_pairs.source: 90000484.odt, Option 3: Integrated Climate Change Adaptation Rural Water & Energy Infrastructure development

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid direct funding to government due to weak financial systems (Partnership Principles Assessment).
Use multilateral fund managers (e.g., UNDP) to navigate political economy constraints.
Build flexibility into timelines and budgets to accommodate shocks (COVID-19, climate events).
Prioritize climate-resilient designs to reduce humanitarian needs post-disaster.
Embed safeguards and GESI strategies to mitigate social risks in fragile contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s ZRBF and LFSP programmes highlighted the need for climate-proofed infrastructure to complement resilience-building efforts. The lack of climate-resilient water/energy infrastructure was identified as a gap in these earlier programmes, informing CAWEP’s design. Additionally, the failure of AfDB’s ZIMFUND mechanism (non-renewed mandate) led to the competitive selection of UNDP as a more reliable partner.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Switch from AfDB to UNDP as fund manager due to operational risks.
Extension of timeline (28 months) and increase in beneficiary targets (450,000 → 700,000) based on feasibility study findings.
Integration of EWS component to address climate shock preparedness gaps identified in earlier programmes.
Stronger emphasis on GESI and safeguards following lessons from ZRBF/LFSP on social inclusion.

quote.text: Internal and external reviews of these programmes [ZRBF, LFSP] have identified the lack of climate-proofed water and renewable energy infrastructure as the missing component to effectively enable poor communities adapt to climate change and variability. (90000484.odt, Need for DFID Intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to attract private sector investment in renewable energy and water infrastructure, though specific leverage amounts are not quantified. Policy influence is expected to mobilize additional funding for Zimbabwe’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily supports capital investments (infrastructure construction) with embedded revenue components for operation/maintenance (e.g., business models for renewable energy). Technical assistance and capacity building are revenue expenditures.
