metadata.programme_name: African Cities Research Programme
metadata.quote: "The UK will provide £32.75 million over 6 years to fund a novel approach to urban research in Africa." (33503044.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £32.75 million over 6 years to fund a novel approach to urban research in Africa." (33503044.odt, Intervention Overview)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through research to understand African cities as systems, but also includes **policy influence** by informing urban development strategies and **implementation research** through testing solutions to complex urban problems. It aims to integrate political economy analysis with urban systems research to tackle interrelated challenges in African cities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The African Cities research programme will fund a novel approach to urban research in Africa. This will integrate ‘political settlements’ approaches with the concept of ‘the city as a system’ to provide the conceptual framework for tackling integrated sets of complex, priority problems in a number of African cities." (33503044.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: High-quality, policy-relevant research evidence on African cities as systems
New, operationally relevant evidence on ‘what works’ (and what does not) in policies and programmes to tackle complex problems in African cities
Development of a ‘city as a system’ conceptual framework
Research uptake strategy to ensure findings are used by policymakers and city managers
Synthesis of research findings for the East Africa Research Hub (EARH)
Research conducted in 12 cities initially, narrowed down to 5-8 cities

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to generate evidence on how to tackle complex, interrelated urban problems in African cities by integrating political economy analysis with a ‘city as a system’ approach. It will test solutions and inform policies to improve economic development, service delivery, and poverty reduction in urban areas.
what_objectives.quote: "The outcome of the programme will be evidence on new approaches to tackling interrelated priority problems in African cities, in contrast to previous approaches, which focused on sector-specific problems, often without considering political constraints to their solution." (33503044.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as ‘moderate’ risk due to the spread of cities ranging from high fragility to stable contexts. The political economy and institutional challenges in African cities are acknowledged as complex but manageable within DFID’s risk tolerance.
where_context.q5_source: "Assessing the risk level of the programme is difficult, given that the countries that it will work in are not yet known. However, the programme should still fall within DFID tolerances, and is provisionally regarded as ‘moderate’ risk at programme level." (33503044.odt, Risk Rating)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme notes that African cities face ‘urbanisation without growth’ due to complex, interrelated problems such as inefficient land use, poor infrastructure, weak governance, and political resistance to reforms. These constraints require a multi-disciplinary approach that considers political settlements and systemic barriers.
where_context.quote: "Many problems constraining growth and development in any city are inter-linked, with a system of common political economy factors that undermine reform efforts." (33503044.odt, Intervention Overview)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes collaboration with Southern researchers and institutions, with Southern partners included in the Research Programme Consortium (RPC) and decision-making processes. The Internal Management Group (IMG) includes DFID teams but also expects Southern engagement in research design and uptake.

mentorship
co-authorship
research grants
institutional strengthening

who_partners.quote: "The programme has been designed to provide scope for the IMG to shape the evolution of the programme... Inclusion in the RPC of credible Southern partner organisations." (33503044.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will be delivered through a contract with a Research Programme Consortium (RPC), which will manage sub-contracts for city-specific research. The RPC will oversee research, synthesis, and uptake activities, with DFID retaining oversight and approval rights.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will be managed by a Research Programme Consortium (RPC) comprising multiple research teams (GCSD, ART, GRT, ERT, CEW). The RPC will oversee research in selected cities, with some work sub-contracted to other implementers. DFID’s Internal Management Group (IMG) will provide oversight, and a Programme Advisory Group (PAG) will offer expert advice.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme will use a competitive tender process to select the RPC and sub-contractors, ensuring intellectual leadership, project management capability, and alignment with the ‘city as a system’ approach. The selection will prioritize experience in multi-disciplinary research and political economy analysis.
how_mechanism.quote: "The supplier market is large enough for DFID’s ITT to result in the selection of an RPC with the range of skills identified in the Commercial Case below, capable of developing the theoretic framework, and able to oversee or directly manage work in several African cities simultaneously." (33503044.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will be governed by an **Internal Management Group (IMG)** comprising DFID teams and a **Programme Advisory Group (PAG)** with external experts. The IMG will oversee implementation, approve work plans, and ensure alignment with the programme’s vision, while the PAG will provide technical advice. The RPC will report to the IMG and manage sub-contracts.
how_governance.quote: "An Internal Management Group (IMG) of the five RED funding teams will oversee implementation and ensure it is implemented in line with the original vision... The programme has been designed to provide scope for the IMG to shape the evolution of the programme." (33503044.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between cities and research themes during the Inception and Foundation Phases, subject to DFID approval. The programme includes break points at 6 months and 1 year to adjust priorities if needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed with adaptive management features, including break points for review and adjustment. The RPC will refine the research framework based on early findings, and DFID will approve changes to city selection and research themes.
how_flexibility.quote: "Twocontractbreak-pointsifDFIDconcludesthattheprogrammeisbadlyoffcourse:attheendofthesix-monthinceptionperiod;andthefirstyearoffullimplementation(FoundationPhase)." (33503044.odt, Intervention Overview)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Research Programme Consortium (RPC) → Sub-contracted researchers (mini-consortia for city-specific work)
how_efficiency.quote: "All RPC research sub-contracts will include break clauses so that they can be terminated if delivery is off track." (33503044.odt, Intervention Overview)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: One Large RPC which does everything
q24_alternatives_considered.description: A single RPC managing all research themes and city-specific work.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: One RPC covering everything except research on country priority problems (Theme 3)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: RPC manages Themes 1, 2, and 4, with separate implementers for Theme 3.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: One RPC implementing some country research, with other implementers for separate city research
q24_alternatives_considered.description: RPC manages part of the research, with competitive grants for the rest.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The chosen approach (Option 3) was selected to balance **intellectual coherence** with **flexibility and competition**. It allows the RPC to develop the ‘city as a system’ framework while leveraging specialized expertise through competitive sub-contracts for city-specific research. This structure mitigates risks of overloading a single RPC and ensures quality through peer review and DFID oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Researchers may revert to sector-specific silos instead of multi-disciplinary work
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Break points and DFID oversight to ensure alignment with the ‘city as a system’ approach. The RPC will include political economy analysts and sector specialists to maintain coherence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Large budget and geographical spread may overwhelm management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sub-contracting city-specific work to specialized implementers and incorporating DFID oversight and milestone reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funds may be misappropriated or poorly managed by sub-contractors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence by the RPC on all partners, monthly financial monitoring, and accountability mechanisms for the lead supplier.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in FCAS or fragile contexts may disrupt delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close monitoring of political situations, flexibility to suspend activities, and reallocation of funds as needed.

why_rationale.quote: "The proposed approach... allows for a combination of intellectual leadership and world-class project management, while also drawing on the best available expertise for specific city research through a competitive process." (33503044.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme explicitly notes that the **political and operational challenges in FCAS and fragile cities** (e.g., security risks, weak institutions, government hostility) limit the pool of researchers and implementers who can work effectively in these contexts. Southern partners with local knowledge and networks are essential for navigating these constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in FCAS may limit international researchers’ access, requiring reliance on local partners.
Government hostility to political economy research may necessitate adaptive approaches (e.g., demonstrating benefits to officials).
Weak institutions in some cities may require capacity-building embedded in research delivery.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **multi-disciplinary, political economy-focused objectives** require a **consortium structure** with diverse expertise (e.g., political scientists, urban planners, sector specialists). The need to test solutions across multiple cities necessitates **sub-contracting to local implementers**, while the systemic approach demands **centralized oversight by the RPC** to maintain coherence.
q28_linkages: The ‘city as a system’ framework (WHAT) requires a **consortium with cross-sectoral expertise** (HOW).
Political economy analysis (WHAT) necessitates **local partner engagement** to navigate sensitive contexts (WHO).
Adaptive management (HOW) is needed to address **complex, interlinked urban problems** (WHAT).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme acknowledges tensions between **inclusive partnerships (equity)** and **rapid, high-quality delivery (efficiency)**. For example: 
- **Southern ownership vs. Northern expertise**: The RPC includes Southern partners, but decision-making is shared with DFID’s IMG, which is UK-based. 
- **Flexibility vs. coherence**: Sub-contracting city research ensures local relevance but risks fragmentation without strong RPC oversight. 
- **FCAS inclusion vs. delivery risks**: Working in high-risk cities (e.g., Mogadishu, Kinshasa) is prioritized for impact but requires adaptive management to mitigate disruptions.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Competitive sub-contracts may favor established (often Northern) institutions, but the programme mandates Southern partner inclusion.
Expertise vs. ownership: Political economy research requires local insights, but DFID retains approval rights over key decisions.
Cost vs. reach: Including fragile cities increases costs (e.g., security, logistics) but aligns with the programme’s equity goals.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate-to-high risk profile** (FCAS, political sensitivity) leads to **intensive oversight** (milestone reviews, break points, DFID approval for adjustments) and **adaptive management** (flexibility to suspend activities or reallocate funds).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the delivery structure: Southern researchers are included in the RPC, and research uptake activities aim to strengthen local institutions’ ability to use evidence. The programme design explicitly links **Southern partner roles** (e.g., co-authorship, local research leadership) to **long-term capacity outcomes**.
intersections.quote: "The programme has been designed so that researchers work with people involved in running cities and making policy... There is also scope to try out new approaches as part of the research." (33503044.odt, Intervention Overview)

key_programme_risks: Delays in funding or procurement cycles (operational risk).
Researchers reverting to sector-specific silos instead of multi-disciplinary work (delivery risk).
Ineffective management due to programme complexity (operational risk).
Funds misappropriated or poorly managed by sub-contractors (fiduciary risk).
Non-delivery or delays in FCAS due to conflict or instability (external risk).
Government hostility limiting political economy research (external/operational risk).
New evidence not translating into policy/practice changes (delivery risk).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adequate time built into procurement processes; regular liaison with DFID procurement and commercial advisors.
Break points and DFID oversight to check alignment with ‘city as a system’ approach; RPC includes political economy analysts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Management overload due to programme size
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Sub-contracting city work to specialized implementers; DFID oversight and milestone reviews.
Due diligence by RPC on partners; monthly financial monitoring; accountability mechanisms for lead supplier.
Monitor political situations; suspend activities if needed; reallocate funds or revise work plans.
Researchers develop adaptive approaches (e.g., demonstrating benefits to officials).
Invest in research uptake activities; RPC designs uptake strategy; engage stakeholders from inception.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, **flexibility to suspend or adapt activities** is critical due to unpredictable security/political contexts.
Local partners are essential for **navigating access and political sensitivity** in fragile cities.
**Small, rapid evidence reviews** can help ground research in FCAS where data is scarce.
Duty of care assessments and **forward planning with country offices** mitigate risks in high-threat areas.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
The programme builds on lessons from DFID’s **Urban ARK**, **East Africa Research Hub (EARH)**, and **Growth and Urbanisation in Low-Income Countries** programmes, which demonstrated the value of: 
- Multi-disciplinary research teams for urban challenges. 
- Political economy analysis integrated with technical research. 
- Competitive processes for selecting high-quality implementers. 
- Adaptive management in complex urban contexts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates **break points** (6-month inception, 1-year foundation phase) and **flexible city selection** based on early findings, reflecting lessons from earlier programmes about the need for adaptive management in urban research.
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme has been designed to provide scope for the IMG to shape the evolution of the programme... The ‘city as a system approach’ is new, but some researchers have experience of working across sectors and incorporating political economy elements into research." (33503044.odt, Management Case)

metadata.programme_name: SPRING – Strengthening Peace and Resilience in Nigeria
metadata.quote: SPRING is a 4.5-year, Plus a year for procurement. £38 million conflict and stability programme, that will work to reduce conflict and support Nigerian communities to better adapt to the effects of climate change. (D0006150.odt, Programmesummary)
metadata.duration_source: SPRING is a 4.5-year, Plus a year for procurement. £38 million conflict and stability programme

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SPRING combines implementation research (testing/scaling interventions) with capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills) and service delivery (direct provision of conflict prevention and climate resilience services). It focuses on reducing rural violence and increasing peace, security, justice, and climate resilience in Northern Nigeria.
what_objectives.q1_source: SPRING will increase the safety of 1.5 million, and climate resilience of 300,000, poor and vulnerable women and men in Nigeria by: (a) supporting coalitions and locally-led solutions to improve conflict prevention, reduction, security and justice and natural resource management in target areas; (b) catalysing structural change on critical barriers to peace; and (c) supporting partnerships for peace with like-minded international partners to multiply every £1 spent by FCDO. (D0006150.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: 1.5 million people benefit from reduced violence in their communities
300,000 people better adapt to the effects of climate change
Support to coalitions and locally-led solutions for conflict prevention and natural resource management
Catalysing structural change on critical barriers to peace
Supporting partnerships for peace with international partners
Development of peace architecture, early warning systems, and conflict management frameworks
Training and capacity building for local civil society and government institutions
Policy influence on security sector reform and climate-sensitive peacebuilding
what_objectives.summary: SPRING aims to reduce conflict and improve climate resilience in Northern Nigeria through a politically smart, adaptive approach that combines system strengthening with locally-led coalitions. It targets 1.5 million people for safety improvements and 300,000 for climate adaptation, while addressing governance, exclusionary politics, and climate change as root causes of instability.
what_objectives.quote: SPRING will increase the safety of 1.5 million, and climate resilience of 300,000, poor and vulnerable women and men in Nigeria by: (a) supporting coalitions and locally-led solutions to improve conflict prevention, reduction, security and justice and natural resource management in target areas; (b) catalysing structural change on critical barriers to peace; and (c) supporting partnerships for peace with like-minded international partners to multiply every £1 spent by FCDO. (D0006150.odt, Programmesummary)

countries_regions: Nigeria (North West and North Central regions)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nigeria is experiencing rapidly rising conflict and insecurity, particularly in the North West and North Central regions, with 88% of conflict deaths in 2021 occurring in climate-vulnerable rural areas. The programme operates in a context of weak institutions, ethno-religious violence, criminal gangs, and violent extremism, all exacerbated by climate change and demographic pressures.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major. (D0006150.odt, ProgrammePurpose) / Conflict and insecurity have been rising rapidly in Nigeria. 2021 experienced the most conflict and political violence ever recorded, with the greatest escalation seen in inter-communal, ethno-religious and criminal violence in rural areas. (D0006150.odt, ProgrammePurpose)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security threats limit physical access to conflict zones, weak institutions hinder service delivery, climate risks exacerbate resource competition, and political economy factors create resistance to reform. Data limitations and infrastructure gaps (e.g., destroyed schools/health facilities) further complicate implementation.
where_context.quote: The North West has seen the sharpest deterioration, and is now the most violent region in Nigeria, surpassing the North East. (D0006150.odt, ProblemStatement) / The vast majority of these fatalities—88%—took place in climate-vulnerable areas of the rural North. (D0006150.odt, SummarySheet)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes locally-led coalitions (Southern ownership) but is designed and overseen by FCDO (Northern leadership). Decision-making for local interventions rests with Nigerian coalitions, while strategic direction and funding control remain with FCDO.

mentorship for coalitions and local organizations

how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The supplier will be selected through a competitive procurement process to ensure expertise in adaptive management, political economy analysis, and conflict-sensitive programming. how_mechanism.quote: SPRiNG’s main programme delivery will be through a contracted supplier to enable the breadth of expertise and integrated, agile management needed to make it a success. (D0006150.odt, ManagementCase) / SPRiNG will solicit proposals from civil society groups and coalitions for pilot projects to address issues identified in target locations. (D0006150.odt, Projectselectionandimplementation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Sub-awards to coalitions/CSOs will be allocated through a participatory process guided by the Component 1 (Strategic Direction) team, with technical review by the contracted supplier and FCDO approval for larger grants.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will report to HMG’s integrated management structures in Nigeria, including the Delivery Board (oversight of ODA spending) and the Country and Strategy Board. A core MEL team will provide real-time analysis to inform adaptive management.
how_governance.quote: A core team will provide real-time and periodic context, conflict and political economy analysis to inform which issues the programme should work on and how, to learn what’s working and course-correct accordingly. (D0006150.odt, StrategicDirection) / SPRiNG will report regularly to HMG’s integrated management structures in Nigeria, including the Delivery Board. (D0006150.odt, UKAddedValue)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed with flexibility to reallocate funds between components and geographic areas in response to contextual changes or emerging priorities, subject to FCDO approval for major shifts. Up to 15-20% of the budget can be adjusted for rapid response initiatives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: SPRING uses an iterative, politically smart approach with continuous learning loops. Priorities can be adjusted based on real-time conflict analysis (Component 1), but major shifts require FCDO sign-off. The programme includes a ‘rapid response’ mechanism for emerging crises.
how_flexibility.quote: It has been designed with flexibility to support pilot and/or rapid response initiatives in other regions in response to HMG priorities and contextual changes. (D0006150.odt, Programmesummary) / SPRiNG will apply a four-step cyclical process to operationalise this approach, including participatory analysis and project selection based on adaptive criteria. (D0006150.odt, Defining‘how’SPRiNGwilloperate)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contracted Supplier → Local Coalitions/CSOs → Beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: The programme has been designed with flexibility to scale-up if additional budget is made available to FCDO Nigeria, and subject to performance and availability of funds. (D0006150.odt, FinancialCase) / An estimated £7.5m of the proposed £38m budget... will contribute to FCDO Nigeria’s ICF allocation. (D0006150.odt, FinancialCase)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (counterfactual)
Supply-side interventions (systems/structures strengthening only)
Demand-side interventions (locally-led coalitions only)
Hybrid approach (combining systems strengthening with coalitions)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid approach was selected because it balances long-term systemic change with immediate, locally-led conflict reduction. Past UK programmes in Nigeria showed that purely supply-side or demand-side approaches were less effective: supply-side interventions often failed to address political realities, while demand-side efforts lacked sustainability without systemic reforms. The hybrid model leverages FCDO’s political access and adaptive management strengths.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (cost-effectiveness of prevention vs. crisis response)
risk mitigation (balancing high-risk/high-reward initiatives with safer bets)
past experience (lessons from NSRP, J4A, and other UK programmes)
partner capacity (building on existing coalitions and government reforms)
flexibility (ability to respond to unpredictable political openings)
equity (targeting women, youth, and marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on contracted supplier may limit local ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded capacity building for coalitions and gradual transition of management roles to Nigerian partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political resistance to reform from elites benefiting from the status quo
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Issue-based coalitions that include influential actors (e.g., religious leaders, traders) to build broad consensus.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funding reallocation delays due to FCDO approval processes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-approved flexibility for up to 20% of budget for rapid response, with delegated authority to supplier for minor adjustments.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per beneficiary compared to crisis response)
efficiency (leveraging £1 to mobilize additional partner funds)
effectiveness (sustainable reduction in violence and climate resilience)
equity (targeting 30% of resources to gender equality and inclusion)
why_rationale.quote: Option 4: Hybrid approach, combining longer-term system strengthening with support to Nigerian-led, issue-based coalitions, engaging at multiple levels to maximise impact and balance risk. (D0006150.odt, Introductionandsummaryofoptions) / SPRiNG builds on the lessons learned from two decades of UK work on conflict, security, justice and governance in Nigeria. A key lesson has been that our interventions are more impactful when they are fundamentally informed by local politics. (D0006150.odt, SummarySheet)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with existing access to conflict zones, political savvy, and ability to navigate ethno-religious divisions. Security risks exclude international staff from certain areas, requiring reliance on local CSOs with deep community trust but variable capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict physical presence of international partners in North West Nigeria
Weak state institutions require partners with experience in informal governance structures
Ethno-religious tensions necessitate coalitions with cross-community credibility
Climate vulnerabilities demand partners with natural resource management expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for politically smart, adaptive interventions drives the hybrid delivery structure (combining systems strengthening with coalitions). The focus on climate resilience requires integrating ICF-eligible activities, while the goal of scaling successful pilots necessitates partnerships with multilateral actors (e.g., World Bank, UNDP).
q28_linkages: Issue-based coalitions (WHAT) require flexible grant mechanisms (HOW) to respond to local priorities
Climate adaptation goals (WHAT) shape partnerships with World Bank’s ACRESAL programme (HOW)
Security sector reform objectives (WHAT) necessitate engagement with Nigeria Governors’ Forum (WHO)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (30% budget for gender/inclusion, women-led organizations) with efficiency (leveraging World Bank funds, rapid response mechanisms). Tensions include: (1) time needed for inclusive coalition-building vs. urgency of conflict response, and (2) cost of deep local engagement vs. scale of impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Participatory analysis slows initial implementation but ensures locally owned solutions
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical assistance vs. Southern decision-making in coalitions
Cost vs. reach: Intensive support for 3 target states vs. lighter touch in additional regions
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (high risk) drives intensive oversight (embedded MEL team, real-time conflict analysis) and adaptive management (quarterly reviews, rapid response funds). Political risks necessitate close coordination with FCDO’s diplomatic channels.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme’s Theory of Change: local coalitions receive grants + technical assistance to gradually take on larger roles, while the contracted supplier’s capacity determines the depth of systems strengthening (e.g., security sector reform support).
intersections.quote: SPRiNG will take an explicitly political and problem-driven, iterative approach based on learning from more than two decades of UK work on conflict, security, justice and governance in Nigeria and elsewhere. (D0006150.odt, ProgrammePurpose) / Combining grant funds with technical assistance has proved a successful model in multiple FCDO Nigeria interventions. (D0006150.odt, Capacitybuildingandsystemstrengthening)

key_programme_risks: Escalation of violence in target regions, overwhelming programme capacity
Political resistance to reforms (e.g., security sector, natural resource management)
Elite capture of coalition funds or peace processes
Climate shocks (e.g., droughts, floods) exacerbating resource conflicts
Weak state capacity undermining sustainability of interventions
Security incidents limiting access to conflict zones
Donor coordination failures leading to duplication or gaps
Reputational risk to FCDO if violence persists despite interventions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Rapid response mechanism with pre-approved funds; close coordination with security actors and early warning systems.
Issue-based coalitions that include influential elites; adaptive programming to seize political openings.
Transparency tools for coalition funding; participatory monitoring by marginalized groups.
Climate-sensitive conflict analysis; partnerships with World Bank’s ACRESAL for resilience-building.
Parallel support to formal institutions (Component 3) and informal coalitions (Component 2).

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict prevention is 2–7x more cost-effective than crisis response (World Bank ‘Pathways for Peace’)
Locally led peacebuilding is more sustainable but requires long-term investment
Security and justice reforms must address informal power structures, not just formal institutions
Climate change acts as a ‘threat multiplier’ in conflict zones, requiring integrated solutions
Women’s inclusion in peace processes improves outcomes but faces cultural resistance
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past UK programmes (NSRP, J4A) showed that: (1) interventions must be politically informed to avoid harm, (2) linear theories of change fail in dynamic contexts, (3) capacity building without accountability can strengthen abusive systems, and (4) adaptive management requires real-time analysis.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme reduced its budget/duration from the Concept Note (£90m/7 years to £38m/5 years) based on lessons about the value of focused, flexible engagements. Climate themes were integrated more deeply in response to emerging evidence on climate-conflict links.
risks_lessons.quote: A 2019 HMG review of 20 years of UK support to S&J in Nigeria found that: ‘If you are not prepared to invest in understanding the politics, and thinking and working politically, don’t engage in the sector.’ (D0006150.odt, Option2) / SPRiNG builds on the lessons learned from two decades of UK work on conflict, security, justice and governance in Nigeria. (D0006150.odt, SummarySheet)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Every £1 spent by FCDO is expected to multiply impact through partnerships (e.g., World Bank’s $1.25 billion ACRESAL programme). The programme aims to catalyse structural change that attracts additional donor funding.
financial_details.quote: An estimated £7.5m of the proposed £38m budget... will contribute to FCDO Nigeria’s ICF allocation. (D0006150.odt, FinancialCase) / SPRiNG will seek to influence joint donor funds and campaigns on issues of shared international interest... such as peace infrastructure, conflict early warning and response, and climate security. (D0006150.odt, PartnershipsforPeace)

metadata.programme_name: Tax and Development: Equity, Efficiency and Accountable Governance
metadata.quote: "The International Centre for Tax and Development (ICTD) will help to address major operational evidence gaps on how to make tax systems more equitable, efficient and conducive to poverty reduction, stable economic growth, and better governance." (34665392.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £13.3 million over seven years to fund best-in-class research to help make tax systems more equitable, efficient, and conducive to promoting economic development and strengthening governance and accountability." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation through research with capacity building for tax systems in low-income countries, and policy influence to improve tax equity, efficiency, and governance. It also includes direct implementation research through partnerships with revenue authorities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ICTD will work closely with tax specialists and tax administrations in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia to i) deliver a high quality set of research findings, ii) build tax research capacity in low income countries, and iii) engage with policy makers, including HMG, and other stakeholders, to facilitate the uptake and impact of this new research." (34665392.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 76 working papers published to date (with more expected)
33,326 and 47,713 downloads for 2 ICTD briefs (2015 Addis Ababa F4D Conference)
15 bids included in original budget, 16 undertaken (extension phase)
Research preparation grants, full research grants, research dissemination grants
ICTD policy briefs, working papers, African Tax Administration research papers, knowledge synthesis papers, peer-reviewed journal articles, blogs, social media messages
Topic-specific meetings in Africa and South Asia
Fixed-term training attachments for African revenue administration staff
Research methods workshops in Africa and South Asia
Policy dissemination workshops in Africa and South Asia
£11 million raised in Uganda from HNWI tax research (cost: £45,500)
US$9m raised in Rwanda from tax compliance experiments (cost: £29,841)
Government Revenue Dataset (2,449 downloads by April 2018)
30% Southern authorship in publications, increasing year-on-year
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to generate rigorous evidence on equitable and efficient tax systems while building research capacity in low-income countries and influencing policy through engagement with stakeholders.
what_objectives.quote: "ICTD will design a research strategy, run grant competitions, further develop existing partnerships, and fund research to address the following high priority themes: National tax policy and administration; Sub-national and informal taxation; Tax capacity of civil society." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary)

countries_regions: Sub-Saharan Africa (85%): Côte d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Tanzania, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Benin, Cameroon, Liberia, Somaliland, Swaziland
South Asia (15%): Unspecified countries (incremental scale-up planned)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) like DRC and Sierra Leone, with political economy challenges and weak institutions, but has risk management strategies in place.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (34665392.odt, Summary Sheet) and "ICTD has clear risk management strategies for working in/on challenging environments (FCAS) and themes (e.g. conflict, corruption)." (34665392.odt, Appraisal Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: data limitations (lack of formal tax data in many countries)
conflict (FCAS settings with coercive/informal tax systems)
regional tensions (South Asia geo-political barriers to cooperation)
gender inequality (informal taxes disproportionately affecting women)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Vested interests and weak institutions limit reform uptake; FCAS contexts require politically smart approaches; South Asia's geo-political tensions hinder regional cooperation; gender biases in informal taxation create hidden economic burdens.
where_context.quote: "Strong vested interests are often resistant to reform, including from tax collectors that actively seek and take illicit rents, and from elites that should pay more tax, but use their influence to block change." (34665392.odt, Strategic Case) and "ICTD’s quantitative and qualitative field research in Sierra Leone and DRC has provided reliable statistics and detailed information on sub-national tax systems – and how these can work against good government." (34665392.odt, ICTD Highlights)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: International Centre for Tax and Development (ICTD) at Institute of Development Studies (IDS), University of Sussex
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ICTD (UK-based) designs the research strategy and runs grant competitions, but African revenue authorities and researchers co-define priorities and lead many projects. Southern partners increasingly define and lead research (30% Southern authorship).
q10_capacity_building_details: training (annual Research Methods Workshops, Taxation and Transparency courses)
mentorship (direct mentoring of African/South Asian stakeholders)
co-authorship (30% Southern authorship in publications)
research grants (competitive grants for Southern researchers)
institutional strengthening (e.g., Uganda Revenue Authority research department base)
fixed-term training attachments for revenue authority staff

partner_organizations.name: International Centre for Tax and Development (ICTD)
partner_organizations.role: Lead research network and grant manager

partner_organizations.name: Institute of Development Studies (IDS), University of Sussex
partner_organizations.role: Host institution for ICTD

partner_organizations.name: African Revenue Authorities (e.g., Uganda Revenue Authority, Rwanda Revenue Authority)
partner_organizations.role: Research partners, co-designers, and implementers

partner_organizations.name: Ministries of Finance (multiple African countries)
partner_organizations.role: Stakeholders defining research priorities

partner_organizations.name: International Budget Partnership (IBP)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for civil society tax capacity research

partner_organizations.name: African Tax Research Networks (Ethiopia, Nigeria)
partner_organizations.role: Local research hubs (partially funded by Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Policy engagement partner

partner_organizations.name: DFID Country Offices
partner_organizations.role: Research priority identification and uptake

partner_organizations.name: HMT (HM Treasury)
partner_organizations.role: Technical input and priority-setting

who_partners.quote: "ICTD’s approach is demand-driven and engages African stakeholders, including revenue authorities and ministries of finance, to conduct research and develop research capacity." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary) and "Southern authors make up 30% of overall publication authorship, with the proportion of Southern authors increasing year on year." (34665392.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID will sign an Accountable Grant with ICTD, which acts as a fund manager to disburse sub-grants through competitive calls. ICTD is responsible for all DFID funds, due diligence, and safeguards.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ICTD acts as the lead partner in a consortium, managing all components of the research programme, including sub-grants to global researchers, capacity building, and policy engagement. It operates within IDS (its host institution) for financial and administrative support.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ICTD was selected due to its proven track record, existing networks in Africa, and ability to deliver high-value research quickly. An open competition was deemed too slow (12+ months) and risky, as ICTD would likely win anyway, and new entrants lack its established systems.
how_mechanism.quote: "We propose to accept ICTD’s proposal, and negotiate an Accountable Grant agreement with ICTD as the lead partner in a consortium." (34665392.odt, Commercial Case) and "Our preferred option is B: ICTD’s proposal builds on the organisation’s high profile successes, and a proven VfM model which we have previously tested and found to be robust." (34665392.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Technical oversight will be formalized through a new DFID technical group. ICTD’s Advisory Group includes African tax professionals.
how_governance.quote: "ICTD will run regular granting rounds. This provides flexibility to respond to new priorities (thematic, geographic)." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary) and "Technical oversight will be formalized through a new DFID technical group." (34665392.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be moved between components if proposals are weak or implementation is slow, but requires DFID agreement.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Regular granting rounds allow response to new priorities, and ICTD can adjust geographic/thematic focus based on demand and emerging evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "We will move funds between the components if any struggle to find high quality proposals, or implementation is slow." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary) and "ICTD will run regular granting rounds. This provides flexibility to respond to new priorities (thematic, geographic)." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ICTD (fund manager) → end-researchers/sub-grantees
how_efficiency.quote: "Management costs will account for less than 15% of the proposed research programme." (34665392.odt, Commercial Case) and "For each timed stage of the contract, there will be specific performance milestones and deliverables, based on the agreed budget and work plan." (34665392.odt, Commercial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: New Research Programme Consortium (RPC) competition
Do Nothing option
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: ICTD was chosen for its proven track record in delivering high-quality, politically-informed tax research; existing networks with African revenue authorities; ability to scale up efficiently; and speed (avoiding 12+ month procurement delays). The Accountable Grant model leverages ICTD’s established systems for VfM.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (avoiding procurement delays and new-entrant risks)
partner-capacity (strong African networks and policy uptake)
flexibility (regular granting rounds for adaptive management)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited competition (re-funding ICTD may be perceived as uncompetitive).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ICTD will run open grant competitions to stimulate the wider research market.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: South Asia experience gap (ICTD has limited presence in South Asia).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Incremental scale-up with additional staff hiring and horizon scanning; leverage individual researchers’ existing contacts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner dependency (ICTD as single fund manager).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Established systems at IDS provide back-up support; diverse sub-grantee portfolio spreads risk.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (existing networks and systems reduce startup time)
effectiveness (proven policy uptake and revenue impacts)
why_rationale.quote: "Our assessment is that negotiating a new Accountable Grant Agreement with ICTD offers DFID the best value for money by extending ICTD’s proven approach [...] and avoiding the delays and high levels of risk that would be inevitable with i) running an open procurement for a new provider and ii) on contracting, and establishing a new granting process from scratch." (34665392.odt, Summary VFM statement)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS contexts in Sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone) require partners with conflict-sensitive approaches and existing trust with revenue authorities, limiting viable implementers to organizations like ICTD with established networks. South Asia’s geo-political tensions also constrain regional cooperation, necessitating incremental, country-specific engagement.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS settings demand politically smart, locally trusted partners.
South Asia’s regional tensions prevent multilateral tax agency networks (unlike Africa).
Informal/coercive tax systems in FCAS require embedded, context-specific research methods.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for politically-informed, demand-driven research (WHAT) necessitates a fund manager model (HOW) that can run flexible granting rounds and engage revenue authorities as co-designers. The focus on capacity building also requires a network structure to embed training and mentorship.
q28_linkages: Demand-driven research → Open grant competitions with revenue authority input.
Capacity building → Network structure with training attachments and workshops.
Policy influence → ICTD’s existing policy networks (World Bank, DFID, ministries).
FCAS/conflict research → Need for adaptive management and local partnerships.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern efficiency (ICTD’s UK-based management) with Southern equity (30% Southern authorship, African-led research hubs). The incremental South Asia scale-up also reflects a trade-off between rapid delivery (focusing on ICTD’s African strengths) and inclusive expansion (building new regional networks).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct award to ICTD enables quick start but limits competition.
Expertise vs. ownership: UK-led fund management ensures quality control but Southern partners co-lead research.
Cost vs. reach: Focus on Africa (85%) maximizes existing networks but limits South Asia coverage (15%).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (FCAS, political economy challenges) justifies milestone-based oversight and embedded risk management strategies, such as ICTD’s experience in conflict settings and DFID’s technical advisory group.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with Southern partners (e.g., Uganda Revenue Authority) increasingly leading research and defining priorities, shifting from recipients to co-implementers.
intersections.quote: "ICTD’s approach is demand-driven and engages African stakeholders, including revenue authorities and ministries of finance, to conduct research and develop research capacity." (34665392.odt, Narrative summary) and "Southern authors make up 30% of overall publication authorship, with the proportion of Southern authors increasing year on year." (34665392.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Limited proposals from revenue authorities (especially in South Asia).
Reticence from partners to collaborate (vested interests resisting reform).
Political economy barriers in FCAS (corruption, elite capture).
Data gaps in informal taxation systems.
Safety risks in conflict-affected areas (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone).
Perception of uncompetitive re-funding of ICTD.
Slow uptake of research by policy makers.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ICTD will run regular granting rounds and provide research preparation grants to stimulate demand.
Incremental scale-up with additional staff hiring and horizon scanning; leverage existing researcher contacts.
Politically-informed research approaches (e.g., ‘windows of opportunity’ analysis) and engagement with local stakeholders.
Field research (e.g., Sierra Leone, DRC) and open-source datasets (e.g., Government Revenue Dataset).
Compliance with UK’s OSJA Guidance and case-by-case HMG approval for conflict/crime research.
Open grant competitions to stimulate wider research market; ICTD’s strong VfM track record.
Embedded policy engagement (e.g., DFID/HMT input, African Advisory Group) and demand-driven research.

fcas_specific_lessons: Politically smart approaches are essential (e.g., Uganda’s HNWI unit navigating elite resistance).
Local revenue authorities must co-design research to ensure feasibility and uptake.
Informal taxation systems often entrench gender inequality and corruption (e.g., Sierra Leone/DRC findings).
Conflict settings require adaptive management and safety protocols (OSJA Guidance).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous ICTD phases demonstrated that: 1) Politically-informed research achieves higher uptake (e.g., Rwanda’s tax compliance experiments); 2) Local ownership improves sustainability (e.g., Uganda Revenue Authority’s HNWI unit); 3) Open data (e.g., Government Revenue Dataset) enables comparative analysis; 4) Capacity building must be embedded (e.g., training attachments for revenue staff).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expanded focus on sub-national and informal taxation (based on Sierra Leone/DRC research).
Incremental South Asia scale-up (learning from Africa’s network model).
Stronger gender analysis (addressing overlooked biases in informal taxation).
Formalized DFID technical oversight group (response to ICAI’s recommendations on evidence uptake).
risks_lessons.quote: "ICTD has clear risk management strategies for working in/on challenging environments (FCAS) and themes (e.g. conflict, corruption)." (34665392.odt, Appraisal Case) and "DFID’s previous programme experience on tax highlights that while there are a few standard reforms that most countries can benefit from, overcoming the specific political and technical barriers in any context [...] is greatly facilitated with tailored research and advice from expert researchers." (34665392.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation funds partially autonomous tax research networks in Ethiopia and Nigeria, complementing DFID’s investment.
financial_details.quote: "Management costs will account for less than 15% of the proposed research programme." (34665392.odt, Commercial Case) and "ICTD has submitted a proposal to DFID to fund a new research programme to further increase the equity and efficiency of tax systems in low income countries [...] The proposal expands ICTD’s proven model in sub-Saharan Africa, and extends this to new work in South Asia." (34665392.odt, ICTD’s Proposal)

metadata.programme_name: Tax and Economic Governance (TEG) Programme
metadata.quote: "TEG supports a more inclusive economic growth trajectory by strengthening revenue collection, public investment, debt management, and medium to long term fiscal planning." (D0006869.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: June 2018 - March 2024" and "New project end date (if applicable): June 2025" (D0006869.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The TEG programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions like the Revenue Authority and Ministry of Economy and Finance), policy influence (supporting national dialogue on natural resource revenue management), and implementation research (testing and scaling tax administration reforms). It also includes a financing mechanism through co-funding with other donors.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will: (i) support Mozambique’s ability to raise its own revenues efficiently and equitably; (ii) help support more stable economic management, particularly challenges caused by the debt crisis in public investment, debt and fiscal risks management; (iii) provide short term, diagnostic and monitoring support to respond to DFID programme implementation needs." (40109555.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Simplified and more robust processes to register and file taxes (automation of Revenue Authority procedures)
Strengthened Unit for Taxation of Extractive Industries (UTIE) to better administer extractive industries
Improved debt reporting to Parliament and debt management
Integrated legal and regulatory framework for Public Investment Management (PIM)
Development of guidelines for oversight of State-Owned Enterprise (SoE) sector investment projects
Tax audit risk analysis system and tax auditors performance management system
Comprehensive review of the tax system and Medium-Term Revenue Strategy
Tax database for evidence-based policy making
Increased revenue collection from extractive industries
Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) activities to improve voluntary compliance among marginalized groups
what_objectives.summary: The TEG programme aims to strengthen Mozambique's economic governance by improving revenue collection, public investment management, and debt/fiscal risk management, with a focus on preparing for future natural resource revenues. It combines technical assistance, policy dialogue, and institutional capacity building.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will build, at the core, a national dialogue process on inclusive growth and natural resource revenue management." (40109555.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique is classified as a fragile and conflict-affected state (FCAS) with high debt distress (112% of GDP), recent hidden debt scandals, and ongoing political instability including peace negotiations with opposition groups. The programme's overall risk rating is 'major'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (40109555.odt, Summary Sheet) and "IMF now classifies Mozambique as a country in debt distress." (40109555.odt, Strategic Case - Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy constraints include vested interests resisting reform and pressure to invest in politically beneficial infrastructure. Weak institutions limit absorptive capacity for reforms. Conflict risks (Renamo peace process) and climate shocks (droughts, cyclones) create macroeconomic instability. Data limitations affect evidence-based policy making, while regulatory gaps in public investment and debt management create fiscal risks.
where_context.quote: "Mozambique’s political economy is challenging. It is important to recognise that effort to reform may come up against vested interests." (40109555.odt, Mozambique’s political economy of institutional reform)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains overall programme management and strategic decision-making, with implementation delivered through Northern contractors (Cowater International) and multilateral partners (World Bank). Mozambican institutions (MEF, MRA) are beneficiaries and collaborators but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for tax auditors and Revenue Authority staff
mentorship and coaching for tax audit teams
institutional strengthening of MEF and MRA (e.g., creating tax policy teams, performance management systems)
development of tax databases and risk analysis systems
support for Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) integration

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: funding and programme management

partner_organizations.name: Cowater International
partner_organizations.role: implementation of Tax component (TEDI project)

partner_organizations.role: primary government counterpart and beneficiary

partner_organizations.role: primary government counterpart and beneficiary

partner_organizations.name: Swiss Government
partner_organizations.role: potential co-funder (signaled interest)

partner_organizations.name: HMRC (UK)
