partner_organizations.role: technical expertise provider (tax policy)

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be delivered over a period of six years through a partnership with the World Bank and a DFID-contracted managing agent." (40109555.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for the managing agent Cowater International) and contributions to a World Bank Trust Fund (for the GEDI component). The addendum also introduces co-funding agreements with Sweden and potentially Switzerland.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme has two parallel delivery structures: 1) A DFID-contracted managing agent (Cowater International) for the tax component (TEDI), and 2) a World Bank Trust Fund for the economic governance component (GEDI). FCDO directly manages a small monitoring and diagnostic component. The structures are coordinated but operate separately under their respective agreements.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected based on existing partnerships and their macroeconomic expertise, while Cowater International was chosen for its technical capacity in tax administration. The rationale emphasizes leveraging existing relationships and technical fit rather than competitive selection.
how_mechanism.quote: "After careful consideration and consultation with a wide range of stakeholders, we concluded that the best and most feasible option was option 4: A programme of support focusing on tax administration and policy deploying a directly funded Managing Agent and supporting economic management through direct interventions targeted at improved public investment and debt and fiscal risks management through a World Bank Trust Fund." (40109555.odt, Delivery options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes an HMG Influencing Strategy and requires coordination with the World Bank, IMF, and Mozambican government. While not explicitly named as a 'steering committee,' the documents describe regular policy dialogue and joint planning with government counterparts (MEF, MRA) and donors, which implies a governance structure for oversight.
how_governance.quote: "An HMG Influencing Strategy will set out and deliver this collaboration. Our public communications strategy will be targeted primarily at maximising this benefit." (40109555.odt, Communications Strategy) and "The programme will adopt a flexible and adaptive approach to its interventions, which will be defined by a process of 'Try, Learn, Iterate, and Adapt'. Interventions not delivering results will be scaled back or ended and a mid-term review will formalise this." (40109555.odt, Flexibility)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within components based on performance and emerging needs, but major shifts require approval. The programme includes a mid-term review to formalize adjustments, and underperforming interventions can be scaled back or ended.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an explicit 'Try, Learn, Iterate, and Adapt' approach. New opportunities can be pursued if they are technically feasible and politically supported. The Monitoring Component tracks progress and lessons to inform adjustments. The addendum also highlights scale-up opportunities based on emerging government priorities (e.g., VAT policy, Medium-Term Revenue Strategy).
how_flexibility.quote: "The Programme will invest in reforms that are technically sound and politically feasible. Activities will be justified on the basis of need, opportunity and motivation. It will adopt a flexible and adaptive approach to its interventions, which will be defined by a process of 'Try, Learn, Iterate, and Adapt'." (40109555.odt, Flexibility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (Cowater International / World Bank) → Government Counterparts (MEF/MRA). No sub-grantees are mentioned, so the layers are limited to FCDO and the two primary implementers.
how_efficiency.quote: "The TEDI project will continue to provide technical assistance and support procurement of key resources for government (equipment, software and logistical services) both managed by the implementing partner (Cowater International)." (D0006869.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Doing nothing (discounted due to loss of UK influence and worsening economic governance)
Focus on tax administration only (discounted for ignoring fiscal risks and macroeconomic challenges)
Focus on economic management only (discounted due to uncertainty in political/institutional reforms)
Support to a World Bank Trust Fund only (discounted because World Bank does not work on tax)
Support via a DFID-funded managing agent only (discounted due to lack of capacity for complex macro-fiscal reforms)
Support to existing Government-managed Common Funds (discounted due to high fiduciary risks)
Working with the IMF on tax (discounted as IMF only provides short-term, ad-hoc support)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (Managing Agent + World Bank Trust Fund) was chosen to: 1) leverage the World Bank’s macroeconomic expertise and donor coordination role for economic governance reforms; 2) use a specialized managing agent (Cowater) for technically complex tax administration work; 3) maintain FCDO’s policy influence and flexibility; 4) mitigate fiduciary risks by avoiding direct financial aid; and 5) align with the Government of Mozambique’s PFM Strategy and donor coordination platforms.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (combining World Bank’s economies of scale with specialized tax expertise)
risk mitigation (avoiding high-fiduciary-risk modalities like Common Funds)
partner capacity (World Bank’s macroeconomic leadership and Cowater’s tax technical skills)
flexibility (adaptive management to respond to political/economic changes)
speed (building on existing partnerships to accelerate implementation)
equity (supporting Mozambican institutions while retaining Northern oversight)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between the World Bank and Managing Agent components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular policy dialogue and joint planning with government counterparts, supported by FCDO’s oversight and the HMG Influencing Strategy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs of managing two parallel delivery structures
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Streamlined monitoring through a dedicated FCDO component and adaptive management to align activities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on Northern contractors may limit local ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building embedded in both components (e.g., training for MRA staff, creation of tax policy teams in MEF) and emphasis on government buy-in.

why_rationale.quote: "This combined Delivery Option provides the best opportunity to maximise returns to the wider PFM donor Government coordination, linked to PFM Strategy, capacity support from in-country DFID expertise." (40109555.odt, Delivery options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context and weak institutional capacity in Mozambique constrain partner selection to organizations with strong fiduciary controls and technical expertise. Political economy risks (vested interests, election cycles) limit the feasibility of working with local implementers alone, necessitating Northern/multilateral partners to manage risks and ensure reform sustainability.
q27_constraints_detail: High fiduciary risks preclude direct funding to government-managed Common Funds
Limited local capacity requires Northern technical assistance for complex reforms (e.g., tax audit systems, PIM frameworks)
Political economy constraints (e.g., resistance to reform, election cycles) favor partners with influence and adaptability (e.g., World Bank, Cowater)
Need for multilateral coordination to align with IMF/WB programmes and donor platforms
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (tax administration + economic governance) determine the dual delivery structure: 1) A specialized managing agent (Cowater) for hands-on tax reforms, and 2) a World Bank Trust Fund for macroeconomic/PFM reforms. The need for adaptive management (due to political/economic volatility) shapes the 'Try, Learn, Iterate' approach and embedded monitoring.
q28_linkages: Tax administration reforms (TEDI) require technical expertise → delivered via contract with Cowater
Economic governance reforms (GEDI) require macroeconomic coordination → delivered via World Bank Trust Fund
Need for policy influence and flexibility → retained FCDO oversight and adaptive management
Capacity building objectives → embedded in both components (e.g., training, institutional strengthening)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between Northern efficiency and local ownership. While Northern contractors (Cowater, World Bank) ensure technical quality and speed, the documents emphasize capacity building (e.g., training MRA staff, creating tax policy teams in MEF) to address equity concerns. The addendum also highlights GESI activities to ensure marginalized groups benefit from tax reforms.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern-led implementation (efficient but risks limited ownership) vs. capacity building for Mozambican institutions (slower but more sustainable)
Technical expertise from HMRC/HMT (high quality but Northern) vs. local adaptation needs
Speed of reforms (using experienced partners) vs. inclusive dialogue (national policy processes)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'major' risk rating and FCAS context justify intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, mid-term adjustments) and adaptive management. Political economy risks require flexible delivery to respond to election cycles or reform stalls.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited capacity in Mozambican institutions (e.g., MRA’s weak risk management, MEF’s under-resourced PIM Committee) shapes the focus on embedded technical assistance and institutional strengthening. Northern partners lead implementation but are tasked with transferring skills to local counterparts.
intersections.quote: "Mozambique’s political economy is challenging... Insisting on best practice technical reforms is unlikely to deliver maximum value for money in this context. It will be important that this programme undertakes regular political economy and risk analysis that is used to inform flexible and politically smart approaches to implementation." (40109555.odt, Mozambique’s political economy of institutional reform)

key_programme_risks: Political instability (elections, Renamo peace process) may stall reforms
Macroeconomic shocks (debt crisis, commodity prices, climate events) could derail fiscal plans
Weak institutional capacity (e.g., MRA’s tax collection, MEF’s PIM systems) limits reform absorption
Corruption and state capture risks in public investment and procurement
Donor coordination challenges (aligning with IMF/WB programmes and other donors)
Delayed gas revenues (Rovuma basin projects) may reduce incentives for fiscal discipline
High staff turnover in government counterparts disrupts continuity
Fiduciary risks in public financial management systems

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive programming to 'work with the grain' and avoid standstill during election periods. Emphasis on high-level engagement with MEF and Prime Minister’s office.
Embedded technical assistance (e.g., Resident Advisers), capacity building (training, mentorship), and iterative reform design to match local capabilities.
Focus on transparency tools (e.g., tax databases, debt reporting to Parliament) and alignment with anti-corruption programmes (e.g., TACID).
Flexible programme design to respond to shocks (e.g., COVID-19, climate events) and adaptive management through the Monitoring Component.
Active participation in PFM and Tax Working Groups, co-chairing Donor Coordination Platform with Norway, and leveraging World Bank’s convening role.
Strengthening medium-term fiscal planning and debt management to prepare for future resource flows, regardless of timing.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from the 2016 debt crisis highlight the need for transparent fiscal risk management and debt reporting.
Experience with hidden loans underscores the importance of strengthening state-owned enterprise (SoE) oversight and public investment appraisal.
Political economy analysis is critical to identify feasible reforms that align with local incentives (e.g., focusing on 'politically tenable' bottlenecks rather than best-practice solutions).
Donor suspension after the debt scandal demonstrated the value of maintaining technical engagement even when budget support is paused.
The peace process with Renamo shows the need to align economic reforms with decentralization and political settlement priorities.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID programmes (e.g., Economic Development Policy Grant, tax reforms) showed that: 1) Reforms are slow without political commitment and local capacity; 2) Donor coordination is essential to avoid duplication (e.g., tax donor working group); 3) Embedded advisers (e.g., Resident Adviser in MEF) improve delivery; 4) Common Funds are ineffective without strong local management; 5) Flexibility to adjust to context (e.g., shifting from e-taxation to tax audit support) is critical.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Replaced planned e-taxation support with tax audit focus based on government demand and new World Bank automation projects. 2) Added Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) activities to address equity gaps. 3) Extended programme duration (to June 2025) to accommodate delays from COVID-19 and staff changes. 4) Scaled up tax policy and VAT reform support in response to IMF programme priorities. 5) Reduced Monitoring & Diagnostic component budget based on low initial uptake.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID has experience in supporting tax reform and co-chaired the tax donor group until recently. The last programme consistently scored A’s in its 3 initial years and a B in the final year largely due to a period of financial difficulties... Key lessons underline the importance of donor coordination and targeted support as opposed to funding the whole Strategy." (40109555.odt, Past DFID Mozambique programming)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has mobilized £6 million from Sweden for the TEDI component, with potential additional co-funding from Switzerland. The co-financing reduces UK contributions by £2.5 million while increasing total programme resources to £20 million. This leverages donor coordination to reduce transaction costs for the Government of Mozambique.
financial_details.quote: "The UK will reduce its total financial contribution to TEG by £2.5 million with £6 million of additional funds provided by Sweden (to the TEDI component)... The total TEG budget will increase from £16.5 million to £20 million as a result of these changes." (D0006869.odt, Additional and total support)

metadata.programme_name: Sudan Free of Female Genital Mutilation Phase 2 (SFFGM2)
metadata.quote: "SFFGM2 will build on the progress made through the Sudan Free of Female Genital Cutting programme (SFFGC 2013-2018), and open space for wider programming on gender equality." (53733826.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 08/01/2019-31/12/2023" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31/03/2026" (D0005349.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of SRH services, GBV prevention/protection), capacity building (strengthening government/NGO systems), and implementation research (testing social norm change approaches). It also includes policy influence (supporting legal frameworks) and evidence generation (data collection on FGM/GBV trends).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme aims to reduce the prevalence of FGM and child marriage (CM) in Sudan; striving to achieve positive shifts in social and gender norms around FGM and child marriage as well as strengthened governmental and non-governmental systems to both prevent FGM and child marriage and effectively support those who have been affected by the practice." (D0005349.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 140 additional communities declaring abandonment of FGM (cumulative total: 2000 communities)
5,000+ religious/community leaders engaged in countering FGM/CM/GBV
50,000+ girls benefitting from GBV-related services (PEP kits, dignity kits, medical services)
10,000 girls accessing mental health/psychosocial support
70,000 citizens accessing sexual/reproductive health services
450+ community protection networks established/strengthened
1,400+ law enforcement/health personnel trained on Article 141/FGM clinical management
Refined CM policy and Children’s Bill prepared/tested with CSOs
Rapid assessments conducted on conflict’s impact on FGM/CM/GBV trends
Qualitative assessment of SFFGM2 intervention effects
what_objectives.summary: SFFGM2 aims to eliminate FGM and child marriage in Sudan through community-led social norm change, while expanding to address GBV and SRH needs exacerbated by conflict. It combines direct service delivery with systemic capacity building and policy advocacy.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme works across 5 output areas: 1) community engagement on combating harmful social norms; 2) civil society and grassroot engagement; 3) prevention, protection, and care services improvement; 4) law and policy to support abandonment efforts of harmful social norms; and 5) building data and evidence." (D0005349.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sudan is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) with active conflict since April 2023, leading to mass displacement, GBV surges, and collapsed healthcare systems. The programme risk was upgraded from 'Moderate' to 'Major' due to war.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk has increased from moderate to major due to significant contextual changes since the assessment under the original business case." (D0005349.odt, Risks) AND "The conflict has led to increased displacements, gender-based violence, healthcare gaps, and fragility." (D0005349.odt, Context change)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict disrupts access to target communities, forces activity relocation to 'safe pockets,' and requires adaptive workplans. Weak institutions limit policy enforcement (e.g., FGM criminalization). Data gaps hinder real-time monitoring of prevalence trends. Regulatory barriers include contradictory Sharia/statuary laws on women’s rights.
where_context.quote: "There are notable risks and concerns around the issue of access, staff safety, and assets loss; however, FCDO and partners are taking measures to mitigate these risks... cessation of business-as-usual activities in high conflict areas, shifting those to serve displaced communities in safer pockets." (D0005349.odt, Risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between FCDO (funding/strategic oversight), UN agencies (implementation), and Sudanese government/CSOs (local ownership). The Programme Management Unit (PMU) includes a DFID-funded advisor to ensure alignment with UK priorities while embedding local stakeholders.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for 1,400+ law enforcement/health personnel on FGM laws (Article 141) and GBV clinical management
Strengthening National Council for Child Welfare (NCCW) and state-level task forces
Supporting youth-led social movements for norm change
Building data collection/MEL capacity for real-time monitoring
Establishing community protection networks (450+) as post-conflict support bases

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementing partner (community engagement, social movements, policy support)

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA
partner_organizations.role: SRH/GBV service delivery, clinical management of FGM complications

partner_organizations.name: WHO
partner_organizations.role: Health system strengthening, training for midwives/health workers

partner_organizations.name: National Council for Child Welfare (NCCW)
partner_organizations.role: Government counterpart for coordination and national strategy implementation

partner_organizations.name: State-level government entities
partner_organizations.role: Local policy enforcement and service delivery (e.g., State Councils for Child Welfare)
partner_organizations.location: Sudan (Red Sea, Kassala, White Nile, Gedarif, Blue Nile)

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs/CSOs
partner_organizations.role: Grassroots mobilization, community dialogues, and survivor support

partner_organizations.name: Combatting Violence Against Women (CVAW) units
partner_organizations.role: GBV prevention/response at state level

who_partners.quote: "SFFGM2 will continue to work with the programme’s existing UN partners (UNICEF, UNFPA & WHO). Downstream partners remain mostly the same as the programme continues to work with state-level government entities, arm-length bodies, local NGOs, CSOs and grassroot organisations." (D0005349.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a mix of direct funding to UN agencies (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO) via Participating UN Organization (PUNO) agreements, with embedded FCDO oversight through a Programme Management Unit (PMU) and Steering Committee. Funds flow through UN systems (HACT framework) to downstream partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The core consortium includes UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO with FCDO as the donor. A PMU coordinates implementation, and a Steering Committee (FCDO + partners) provides strategic oversight. The structure is 'closed' as new partners require FCDO approval but allows flexibility to engage local actors.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Existing UN partners were selected based on their established presence in Sudan, technical expertise in FGM/GBV, and ability to operate in FCAS contexts. Local NGOs/CSOs are identified through UN-led processes with FCDO approval.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will work with the programme’s existing UN partners (UNICEF, UNFPA & WHO)... These partners have retained the ability to operate on the ground despite the many difficulties caused by the conflict." (D0005349.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes heads of FCDO Sudan and programme partners (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO). It owns the programme risk register and approves major adaptations. A Technical Committee meets bi-weekly for operational oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The programme risk register will be owned by the Steering Committee, which is made up of the heads of DFID Sudan and the programme partners... Bi-weekly technical committee meetings will be utilised to closely follow up on workplan progress." (53733826.odt, Isthereaclearcommunicationsstrategy) AND (D0005349.odt, Risks)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between outputs/geographies based on Steering Committee approval, with a break clause allowing full closure if context deteriorates. The 2023 addendum explicitly reprioritized funds toward GBV/SRH responses due to conflict.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach with: 1) Annual reviews to adjust scope/scale; 2) Real-time monitoring via PMU; 3) Rapid ToC assessments (e.g., post-conflict analysis in 2023); 4) Flexible workplans revised bi-weekly by partners.
how_flexibility.quote: "SFFGC is designed to be flexible and adaptive... The programme will continue with current partners... integrating additional delivery partners as appropriate... The programme will have a B1 Programme Manager, and oversight from a senior programme manager." (53733826.odt, Isthereaclearcommunicationsstrategy) AND "The cost and time-extension will allow for the protection of the returns of SFFGM2’s previous investments, whilst building new equities that can yield greater development returns as a new governance equilibrium develops in Sudan." (D0005349.odt, Value for Money)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN agencies (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO) → Local NGOs/CSOs/government entities
how_efficiency.quote: "The tentative financial breakdown under this addendum as follows: FY23/24-£4.6m; FY24/25-£3.6m; FY25/26-£3.061m... The above profile is adjustable, given the rapidly changing context." (D0005349.odt, Finance and Commercial)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UN consortium was chosen for its ability to: 1) Operate in FCAS contexts (retention of access despite conflict); 2) Leverage existing relationships with Sudanese government/CSOs; 3) Provide integrated service delivery (FGM/GBV/SRH); 4) Ensure continuity from Phase 1; and 5) Meet FCDO’s risk mitigation requirements via HACT frameworks.
q25_decision_factors: speed (existing partnerships allowed rapid conflict response)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in conflict context
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: HACT framework controls, deliver chain mapping, spot checks, and mandatory reporting of suspicions to FCDO.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner access limitations due to security
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Relocation of activities to ‘safe pockets,’ continuous security monitoring, and UN staff security measures.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government counterpart instability
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on subnational/state-level authorities and defacto implementation of national plans.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (UN’s economies of scale in procurement)
why_rationale.quote: "The implementing partners (UN agencies) for the programme are well known by FCDO with a sound reputation on other FCDO and like-minded partners funded programmes. Their financial controls under Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) framework provide strong assurances." (D0005349.odt, Terrorism and financing)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Conflict and FCAS context constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) Existing Sudan presence; 2) FCAS operational capacity; 3) Acceptable risk profiles (HACT-compliant). This excludes many local NGOs without UN affiliation and limits direct funding to government entities.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict partners to those with UN/FCDO-approved safety protocols
Regulatory barriers (e.g., banking restrictions) favor multilateral partners over local NGOs
Government instability requires reliance on UN intermediaries for policy engagement
Data limitations necessitate partners with strong MEL systems (e.g., UNICEF)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for integrated FGM/GBV/SRH service delivery determines the consortium structure (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO’s complementary mandates). Social norm change objectives require embedded community partners, while policy influence needs government engagement channels.
q28_linkages: Service delivery goals → UN agencies’ health/protection mandates
Social norm change → Local NGOs/CSOs for grassroots engagement
Policy influence → Government counterparts (NCCW, state task forces)
Conflict response → UN’s humanitarian coordination structures
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid conflict response prioritized UN partners over slower local NGO processes; 2) Expertise vs. ownership: Technical capacity of UN agencies vs. limited decision-making by Sudanese CSOs; 3) Cost vs. reach: High UN overheads balanced by their ability to operate at scale in insecure areas.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UN agencies enable rapid, large-scale delivery but reduce funds available to local partners
Embedded FCDO advisor ensures UK priorities but adds management layers
Focus on ‘safe pockets’ improves security but limits geographic coverage
intersections.risk_affects_management: The Major risk profile (due to conflict) drives intensive oversight: bi-weekly Technical Committee meetings, real-time workplan adjustments, and FCDO approval for fund reallocations. This contrasts with the original ‘Moderate’ risk phase (annual reviews).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Tasking UN agencies with training government/CSO counterparts; 2) Embedding MEL capacity in local structures; 3) Transitioning community networks into post-conflict service providers.
intersections.quote: "The programme will work with the programme’s existing UN partners (UNICEF, UNFPA & WHO). Downstream partners remain mostly the same as the programme continues to work with state-level government entities... These partners have retained the ability to operate on the ground despite the many difficulties caused by the conflict." (D0005349.odt, Approach to implementation) AND "The programme will prioritise identifying and addressing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) needs... ensuring timely, quality, multisectoral response and prevention services for survivors/persons at risk." (D0005349.odt, What are the expected results?)

key_programme_risks: Conflict-induced displacement disrupting community engagement
GBV/SRH service gaps due to healthcare collapse
Aid diversion in unstable areas
Policy enforcement weaknesses (e.g., FGM criminalization)
Partner access limitations in high-conflict states
Loss of pre-conflict gains in social norm change
Emergence of new harmful practices (e.g., increased child marriage)
Asset loss/theft in insecure locations

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Relocate activities to ‘safe pockets’ and IDP receiving locations; adapt workplans for mobile populations.
Prioritize PPC (prevention/protection/care) services; train midwives on GBV clinical management.
HACT financial controls, delivery chain mapping, mandatory suspicion reporting to FCDO.
Focus on state-level implementation of national laws (e.g., Article 141 training for judges).
Leverage UN security protocols and local CSO networks; use remote management where needed.
Conduct rapid assessments on conflict’s impact; reinforce community protection networks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Localization is critical for continuity: "The strong localization of SFFGM2 further mitigates risks in communities that are not directly conflict-affected." (D0005349.odt, Risks)

Flexible funding is essential: "The cost and time-extension will allow for the protection of the returns of SFFGM2’s previous investments, whilst building new equities." (D0005349.odt, Value for Money)

State-level engagement can substitute national government: "It continues to be both important and possible for SFFGM2’s implementing partners to maintain effective relationships with federal officials and State-level governments." (D0005349.odt, Approach to implementation)
GBV risks escalate in conflict: "Conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence is deeply entrenched in Darfur, South Kordofan and Blue Nile." (53733826.odt, Gender Based Violence)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 demonstrated that: 1) Community declarations of FGM abandonment require sustained engagement (800+ communities with active social activists); 2) Religious leaders (Saleema/Almawada Wa Alrahma messaging) are critical for norm change; 3) Legal frameworks alone are insufficient without enforcement capacity; 4) Youth-led movements accelerate change but need structural support.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2023 addendum adjusted the design to: 1) Expand GBV/SRH services in response to conflict-induced needs; 2) Shift from national to state-level policy engagement; 3) Add rapid assessment components to monitor conflict impacts; 4) Include MHPSS as a core output; 5) Develop a responsible exit strategy for post-conflict transition.
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme has adapted and evolved in the past five months despite security, physical, payments and personnel disruptions... The Participating United Nations Organizations (PUNOs), NGOs and approved state-level authorities... have been able to pivot into an updated workplan." (D0005349.odt, Value for Money) AND "The programme will prioritise identifying and addressing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) needs of children, adolescents and their caregivers affected by FGM/CM and other forms of GBV." (D0005349.odt, What are the expected results?)

financial_details.quote: "The total BC budget will be increased from £15m to £19.95m... The tentative financial breakdown under this addendum as follows: FY23/24-£4.6m; FY24/25-£3.6m; FY25/26-£3.061m." (D0005349.odt, Finance and Commercial)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Climate Resilient Systems for Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Services in Ethiopia (SCRS–WaSH)
metadata.quote: "The UK will provide up to £95 million over five years (2019–2024), to support sustainable access to climate resilient clean water and improved sanitation services and good hygiene practices." (90000044.odt, SummarySheet)
metadata.duration_source: "five years (2019–2024)" (90000044.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **service delivery** (direct provision of climate-resilient WaSH infrastructure), **capacity building** (strengthening systems for sustainable service delivery), **financing mechanism** (channeling funds through pooled accounts), and **implementation research** (piloting innovations like menstrual hygiene products and adaptive learning). It aims to improve access to climate-resilient WaSH services while building institutional capacity and testing sustainable financing models.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The proposed SCRS–WaSH programme will contribute to the GoE’s Climate Resilient (CR) WaSH provision to drought prone areas. The programme aims to realise this through a combination of targeted Financial Aid and Technical Assistance support." (90000044.odt, SummarySheet)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 1.2 million people provided with access to climate-resilient water and improved sanitation services
150 new large, medium, and small multi-village climate-resilient water supply schemes constructed
At least 110 multi-village water supply schemes rehabilitated
900 inclusive (women, girls, and disability-friendly) WaSH facilities for schools and health facilities constructed/rehabilitated
98,000 new household sanitation facilities built
Innovative products to support effective menstrual hygiene management introduced, piloted, and scaled up
Systems for effective Operation and Maintenance strengthened in 3-4 selected regions
Organised women and youth groups supported for spare part supply chain and service maintenance
A robust sustainable financing strategy for domestic resource mobilisation developed
Deep dive learning evaluations to inform adaptive management

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve access to climate-resilient WaSH services for 1.2 million people in drought-prone areas of Ethiopia while strengthening systems for sustainability, equity, and adaptive learning. It combines infrastructure delivery with institutional capacity building and innovative financing approaches.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact of this intervention will be to improve public health, education and nutrition through the provision of lasting, quality WaSH services for people in the targeted drought prone areas." (90000044.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in drought-prone and conflict-affected regions with weak institutional capacity, but mitigations (e.g., World Bank safeguards, pooled funding) reduce risks to 'moderate'. Frequent climatic shocks (droughts/floods) and humanitarian crises create implementation challenges.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme is classed as having a moderate risk profile, which is acceptable given the context." (90000044.odt, SummarySheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited O&M capacity, staff shortages)
political economy (regional disparities, emergency response demands)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate variability (droughts/floods) disrupts water availability and increases O&M costs. Weak institutional capacity (e.g., 39% non-functional boreholes post-2016 drought) undermines sustainability. Regional disparities (e.g., Afar/Somali delivered only 14% of OWNP activities vs. 70% in Tigray) require tailored support. Emergency responses divert resources from long-term planning.
where_context.quote: "The 2016 drought increased the proportion of non-functional boreholes by 17 percentage points, rising to 39%. The likelihood of these extreme events is expected to increase with climate change." (90000044.odt, Strategic Case, para 16)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Ethiopia (GoE) via One WaSH National Programme (OWNP)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The GoE leads programme design and implementation through OWNP, with DFID and multilateral partners (World Bank, AfDB, UNICEF) providing technical/financial support. Decision-making is shared via the Consolidated WaSH Account (CWA) steering committee, where GoE and donors co-approve allocations. DFID’s Technical Assistance includes embedded experts in GoE institutions (e.g., National WaSH Coordination Office).
q10_capacity_building_details: embedded experts in GoE institutions (e.g., NWCO, regional bureaus)
training for rural/urban utility staff on O&M, financial management, and climate resilience
mentorship for women/youth groups in spare parts supply chains
institutional strengthening of multi-village management units
secondment of experts to low-performing Developing Regional States (DRS)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ethiopia (GoE)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer via One WaSH National Programme (OWNP); manages pooled funds and coordinates delivery

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer (£300m); lead on fiduciary/safeguard oversight; supports all OWNP components

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer; focuses on urban WaSH and regional strategies

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer; leads OneWaSH Plus component (gender/inclusion, urban innovations)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Finland
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer; supports CR WaSH pillar

partner_organizations.name: British Geological Survey (BGS)
partner_organizations.role: Technical partner for groundwater mapping/resilience research

partner_organizations.name: UK Universities
partner_organizations.role: Research partners for climate resilience and WaSH innovations

partner_organizations.name: Partners for Water and Sanitation (PaWS)
partner_organizations.role: UK private water companies consortium for utility strengthening

partner_organizations.name: National WaSH Coordination Office (NWCO)
partner_organizations.role: GoE body managing programme coordination and capacity assessments

partner_organizations.name: Developing Regional States (DRS) - Afar, Somali, Benishangul-Gumuz, Gambella
partner_organizations.role: Target regions for tailored TA and embedded support

who_partners.quote: "DFID will work in partnership with the World Bank, the African Development Bank, UNICEF, and Government of Finland in providing this support, as well as other donors like South Korea and Denmark." (90000044.odt, A11. Working with partners)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **block funding** (£80m Financial Aid channeled through the GoE’s Consolidated WaSH Account, a pooled fund with ring-fenced allocations for climate-resilient WaSH) and **contracts** (£15m Technical Assistance paid to service providers upon deliverable completion via open procurement). The FA leverages GoE’s public financial management (PFM) system, while TA follows DFID’s standard procurement rules.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **Consolidated WaSH Account (CWA)** acts as a multi-donor platform where funds from DFID, World Bank, AfDB, and others are pooled. The GoE (via OWNP) manages day-to-day delivery, with a **steering committee** (including donors) overseeing allocations. Technical Assistance is managed separately by DFID with direct contracts to service providers. The World Bank leads fiduciary safeguards, while DFID embeds advisors in GoE institutions (e.g., NWCO).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GoE and existing OWNP partners (World Bank, AfDB, UNICEF) were **directly selected** due to their established roles in the sector and alignment with the pooled funding mechanism. For **Technical Assistance**, service providers are selected via **open procurement** based on deliverables. The rationale emphasizes leveraging existing systems (CWA) for efficiency and continuity, while TA providers are chosen competitively to ensure value for money.
how_mechanism.quote: "The Financial Aid component uses GoE’s PFM system... The TA component is managed by DFID, and paid to service providers upon receipt of agreed deliverables following a fair and open procurement process." (90000044.odt, SummarySheet and How Mechanism)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **National WaSH Steering Committee (NWSC)** oversees the Consolidated WaSH Account (CWA), with representation from GoE (lead), DFID, World Bank, AfDB, UNICEF, and other donors. Decisions on fund allocations (e.g., ring-fencing for CR WaSH) are made jointly. The World Bank acts as the **lead agency for fiduciary oversight**, while DFID embeds advisors in GoE institutions (e.g., NWCO) for technical guidance. Quarterly financial reports track disbursements to end beneficiaries.
how_governance.quote: "The World Bank, on behalf of contributing partners, has been the lead agency in providing oversight on fiduciary, social and environmental safeguards. This established practice will continue for this new Business Case." (90000044.odt, A11. Working with partners)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the **Financial Aid component** are largely ring-fenced for climate-resilient WaSH but allow reallocation between construction/rehabilitation based on need (e.g., drought responses). **Technical Assistance** has predefined focus areas (e.g., DRS support, financing strategy) but includes a **Deep Dive Learning Evaluation** to enable adaptive adjustments. Major reallocations require donor committee approval via the CWA steering structure.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme explicitly includes **adaptive management** through: 1) **Deep Dive Learning Evaluations** to gather real-time evidence on scheme functionality and inform mid-course corrections; 2) **embedded capacity building** to address emerging gaps (e.g., in DRS); and 3) **pilot innovations** (e.g., menstrual hygiene products) that can be scaled based on performance. DFID allocates management resources to ensure flexibility, particularly for the sustainable financing strategy component.
how_flexibility.quote: "One of the key areas of the TA is a series of deep dive learning evaluations for continued adaptive learning. This will give an opportunity to make timely adjustments based on established evidence." (90000044.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Consolidated WaSH Account (GoE/OWNP)** → Implementing partners (regional bureaus, utilities, NGOs). For Technical Assistance: FCDO → **TA service providers** (direct contracts).
how_efficiency.quote: "The TA component is... paid to service providers upon receipt of agreed deliverables following a fair and open procurement process." (90000044.odt, SummarySheet)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID would stop bilateral funding, relying on multilaterals (e.g., World Bank) and other donors (Finland, Denmark) to fill gaps. The Centrally Managed Programme (£15m) would continue, but SDP results would drop significantly, and OWNP’s financing gap would worsen.
q24_alternatives_considered.evidence: Medium (historical data on OWNP underfunding and humanitarian costs)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue unrestricted funding to OWNP without targeting climate resilience. This was rejected due to insufficient focus on drought-prone areas and sustainability risks.
q24_alternatives_considered.evidence: Not explicitly detailed, but implied in strategic shifts (para 36-43)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Fund standalone projects (e.g., direct NGO contracts). Rejected due to fragmentation risks and loss of coordination benefits from the pooled CWA mechanism.
q24_alternatives_considered.evidence: Implied in rationale for using OWNP platform (para 55, 14)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **targeted Financial Aid + Technical Assistance** model was selected because: 1) **Value for Money**: Leverages existing OWNP systems (CWA) to reduce transaction costs and align with GoE priorities; 2) **Risk Mitigation**: World Bank’s fiduciary oversight and pooled funding reduce financial/safeguard risks; 3) **Sustainability**: Combines infrastructure delivery (FA) with systemic strengthening (TA) to address O&M gaps; 4) **Flexibility**: Adaptive learning components allow adjustments based on climate/drought realities; 5) **Equity**: Ring-fenced funds for drought-prone areas and inclusion (women, disabilities) align with Leave No One Behind.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (World Bank safeguards, pooled funds)
equity (targeting drought-prone areas and marginalized groups)
alignment with GoE priorities (OWNP/CR WaSH pillar)
speed (using established systems for rapid deployment)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Ring-fencing funds within CWA may create tensions with other OWNP pillars (e.g., urban WaSH).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with World Bank/AfDB to ensure complementarity and joint planning via the steering committee.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoE’s PFM weaknesses (e.g., procurement delays, staff turnover) could delay implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: World Bank’s lead oversight role on fiduciary safeguards and DFID’s embedded advisors in NWCO to strengthen capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Technical Assistance may not reach all regions equally (e.g., remote DRS).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Tailored TA for DRS with embedded experts and capacity gap assessments to prioritize support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector engagement (e.g., menstrual hygiene products) may face market barriers.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot innovations with behaviour change campaigns and social marketing to test scalability.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (targeting drought-prone areas for maximum impact)
equity (inclusive design for women, disabilities, and marginalized regions)
why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option offers substantial contribution to SDP results (>300-500,000/year), better opportunities for DFID influence, and low fiduciary risks due to WB oversight. It aligns with Government plans and provides predictable results." (90000044.odt, Appraisal Case, para 55)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **drought-prone and conflict-affected context** (Afar, Somali, Benishangul-Gumuz) constrains partner selection by: 1) **Limiting local capacity**: Only GoE and established multilaterals (World Bank, UNICEF) have the operational presence to deliver in these regions; 2) **Requiring climate expertise**: Partners must demonstrate experience in resilient technologies (e.g., deep boreholes, multi-village systems); 3) **Security risks**: Restricts NGO/private sector engagement without GoE/multilateral backing; 4) **Institutional weaknesses**: Necessitates embedded TA (e.g., DFID advisors in NWCO) to fill gaps.
q27_constraints_detail: GoE’s limited capacity in DRS (e.g., Afar delivered only 14% of OWNP activities) → requires embedded TA
Frequent droughts → partners must have climate-resilient WaSH expertise (e.g., World Bank, BGS)
Conflict in Somali/Afar → restricts private sector/NGO access without multilateral support
Weak O&M systems → necessitates utility-focused partners (e.g., PaWS for UK water expertise)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (service delivery + systems strengthening + innovation) determine the **hybrid delivery structure**: 1) **Pooled FA** aligns with the **scale** needed for 1.2M people and GoE’s OWNP framework; 2) **Targeted TA** addresses **systemic gaps** (e.g., O&M, financing) that FA alone cannot solve; 3) **Embedded advisors** reflect the **capacity-building core objective**; 4) **Pilot innovations** (e.g., menstrual hygiene) require **flexible, adaptive management** structures (Deep Dive Evaluations).
q28_linkages: Large-scale infrastructure targets (150 schemes) → pooled FA via CWA for efficiency
Sustainability goals (O&M, financing strategy) → TA with embedded experts
Inclusion objectives (women/youth) → tailored TA for spare parts supply chains
Adaptive learning needs → Deep Dive Evaluations and flexible TA components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) **Ring-fencing for drought areas** reduces flexibility for other regions but ensures equity; 2) **Embedded TA in DRS** increases costs but addresses historic underperformance (e.g., Afar’s 14% delivery rate); 3) **Pilot innovations** (e.g., menstrual hygiene) require upfront investment but aim for long-term market sustainability; 4) **Pooled funding** balances donor coordination (efficiency) with GoE ownership (equity).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Targeting drought-prone areas slows rollout but prioritizes vulnerable groups (e.g., 900 disability-friendly facilities).
UK water utility expertise (PaWS) strengthens systems but requires GoE buy-in to avoid dependency.
Deep boreholes/multi-village systems cost more but serve 10,000–20,000 people per scheme, improving VFM.
Adaptive learning components add complexity but enable responses to climate shocks (e.g., 2016 drought).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (droughts, weak institutions) drives **intensive oversight**: 1) World Bank’s fiduciary role mitigates financial risks; 2) Quarterly financial reports and annual audits address PFM weaknesses; 3) Embedded advisors in NWCO compensate for GoE capacity gaps; 4) Deep Dive Evaluations provide real-time risk data for adaptive management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) **Embedding DFID advisors** in GoE institutions (NWCO) to strengthen systems; 2) **Seconding experts** to DRS to address regional disparities; 3) **Training women/youth groups** in O&M to create local ownership; 4) **Piloting private sector models** (e.g., menstrual hygiene) to build market capacity. Partners like PaWS and BGS are selected for their ability to transfer skills (e.g., utility management, groundwater mapping).
intersections.quote: "The TA focus areas include... secondment of expertise to low performing Developing Regional States (informed by capacity gap assessment); and... support [for] women and youth groups to engage and support the effective operation and maintenance systems." (90000044.odt, Component 2)

key_programme_risks: Climate shocks (droughts/floods) disrupting water availability and increasing O&M costs.
GoE’s weak PFM systems (procurement delays, staff turnover) causing implementation lags.
Private sector reluctance to invest in WaSH without revenue guarantees.
Regional disparities (e.g., Afar/Somali underperformance) undermining equity goals.
Sustainability risks post-programme if domestic financing strategies fail.
Conflict in Somali/Afar regions limiting access and stability.
Reverse incentive structures (private suppliers losing business when public systems improve).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Climate-resilient technologies (deep boreholes, multi-village systems) and catchment management to ensure year-round water availability.
World Bank’s fiduciary oversight, embedded DFID advisors in NWCO, and quarterly financial tracking.
Pilot innovations (e.g., menstrual hygiene products) with market-building support and behaviour change campaigns.
Tailored TA for DRS with embedded experts and capacity gap assessments.
Sustainable financing strategy focusing on domestic resource mobilisation and private capital.
Multilateral coordination (World Bank, UNICEF) and GoE-led implementation to ensure continuity.

fcas_specific_lessons: Drought responses must integrate **long-term resilience** (e.g., CR WaSH) to reduce humanitarian costs (e.g., 2016 water trucking cost 4x regular programme expenses).
In **conflict-affected regions** (Somali/Afar), embedded TA and multilateral partnerships are critical to maintain access.
**Decentralized O&M models** (e.g., women/youth spare parts groups) improve sustainability in fragile contexts by creating local ownership.
Pooled funding (CWA) reduces donor fragmentation but requires **strong safeguards** (e.g., World Bank oversight) in FCAS settings.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **OneWaSH Plus Programme**: Demonstrated that climate-resilient systems (e.g., Wolenchiti Town’s multi-village scheme) can eliminate water trucking and sustain services through droughts. 2) **BACCH-RW Programme**: Highlighted the need for groundwater mapping and catchment protection to ensure year-round water availability. 3) **ESAP Findings**: Showed that weak community ownership (e.g., defunct water management groups) leads to scheme failures; addressed via embedded capacity building in this programme. 4) **2016 Drought Response**: Revealed that non-functional boreholes increased by 17% during shocks, necessitating proactive O&M in this design.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Ring-fenced CR WaSH funds**: Added to ensure drought-prone areas are prioritized (learned from 2016 drought’s disparate impact). 2) **Embedded advisors in DRS**: Introduced to address historic underperformance (e.g., Afar’s 14% delivery rate). 3) **Deep Dive Evaluations**: Incorporated for adaptive learning after past schemes failed due to lack of real-time monitoring. 4) **Private sector pilots**: Added to test sustainable models (e.g., menstrual hygiene products) after previous livelihoods approaches (e.g., hand-sewn pads) proved unscalable. 5) **Sustainable financing strategy**: Developed to reduce aid dependency, informed by OWNP’s 44% funding gap.
risks_lessons.quote: "The 2016 drought increased the proportion of non-functional boreholes by 17 percentage points... This shows the need for greater attention to climate resilience to ensure permanence of WaSH services." (90000044.odt, Strategic Case, para 16)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages the **Consolidated WaSH Account (CWA)**, a multi-donor pooled fund where DFID’s £95m is combined with contributions from the World Bank (£300m), AfDB, UNICEF, and Finland. This structure mobilizes additional resources (e.g., World Bank’s urban sanitation programme) and aligns with GoE’s domestic funding (50% of CR WaSH costs). The sustainable financing strategy aims to unlock further domestic/private capital post-programme.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The **Financial Aid (£80m)** is primarily capital expenditure (construction/rehabilitation of WaSH infrastructure), while the **Technical Assistance (£15m)** covers revenue costs (capacity building, evaluations, pilot innovations). The FA component is divided into: Climate Resilient WaSH (77%), Institutional WaSH (13%), and Capacity Building/Programme Management (10%).
financial_details.quote: "Component 1 (£80m): Financial Aid to the Government of Ethiopia’s (GoE’s) OneWaSH National Programme (OWNP)... Component 2 (£15m): Technical Assistance to transform the sector." (90000044.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Teacher Effectiveness and Equitable Access for all Children (TEACH) Programme in Zimbabwe

quote.text: The TEACH programme will contribute to improvements in learning outcomes in Zimbabwe by building a stronger and more sustainable education system.

duration_source.text: Original business case dates were 31 July 2019 to 31st July 2024; No cost time extension approved in 2021 to 31 October 2025; Further costed extension approved 2023 to 31 March 2026; This addendum seeks approval for a no-cost time extension to 31st December 2026.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The TEACH programme combines service delivery (direct support to schools and teachers), capacity building (teacher training and system strengthening), policy influence (supporting education reforms), and implementation research (piloting innovations like solarisation and social-emotional learning). It aims to improve learning outcomes by addressing both immediate needs (school grants, teacher training) and systemic challenges (policy reforms, equity in access).

q1_source.text: The TEACH programme will contribute to improvements in learning outcomes in Zimbabwe by building a stronger and more sustainable education system. [...] The programme will focus on: i) catalysing policy change; and ii) leveraging in additional resources from multilaterals to ensure long-term sustainability. [...] TEACH will now focus on: [...] innovation through the expansion of the solarisation in schools pilot; [...] policy influence to significantly improve the quality, safety and impact of teaching and learning; [...] responsible transition by ensuring our support to out-of-school girls started in our Centrally Managed Programme (CMP) can be completed and moving SIGs from bilateral to multilateral support.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Schools supported through School Improvement Grants (SIGs)
q3_expected_outputs.target: At least 1,000 schools supported through SIGs annually

q3_expected_outputs.output: Solarisation of rural schools
q3_expected_outputs.target: Up to 350 poorest rural remote schools with improved access to clean energy through solarisation; Over 150,000 beneficiaries with improved access to clean energy in schools

q3_expected_outputs.output: Teacher Professional Development (TPD)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 5,300 school leaders trained on school leadership for learning; 82,612 teachers trained on improved pedagogy including sensitising on teaching children with disabilities (CWDs); Teachers with disabilities (TWDs) (3% of total teachers) trained

q3_expected_outputs.output: Education system strengthening
q3_expected_outputs.target: Supporting HR reform in revision of Teacher Management Information System (TMIS); Policy reform support in key areas on curriculum, assessment, inspection, early learning, ICT, and domestic financing; Mixed methods evaluation on the UK’s support to education in Zimbabwe from 2019 to 2025

q3_expected_outputs.output: Marginalised girls supported
q3_expected_outputs.target: 5,000 out-of-school girls (including 472 CWDs) supported to continue their education to the end of the cycle of both foundational literacy and numeracy up to grade 5 level, and with skills training

q3_expected_outputs.output: Social and Emotional Learning (SEL)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1,000 schools with over 100,000 young boys and girls learning to ‘Think Equal’

q3_expected_outputs.output: Examination pass rates
q3_expected_outputs.target: At grade 7 from 52.8% to 47%; At form 4 from 33% to 30%

q3_expected_outputs.output: Drop-out rates
q3_expected_outputs.target: Drop-out rate at the end of O levels (form 4) adjusted to 16% (from baseline 15.9% in 2018)

what_objectives.summary: The TEACH programme aims to improve learning outcomes in Zimbabwe by strengthening the education system through equitable access, teacher professional development, policy influence, and innovation. It combines direct service delivery (school grants, teacher training) with systemic reforms (policy support, capacity building) and pilot innovations (solarisation, social-emotional learning).

quote.text: The TEACH programme’s objective is to contribute to the delivery of the International Development Strategy, the Women and Girls’ Strategy and FCDO’s global education policy. It also delivers a key Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary priority – girls education. [...] The proposed changes set out in the attached business case addendum will enable us to deliver the strategic shift set out in the country plan, following a 60% reduction in ODA. TEACH will now focus on: i. catalysing policy change; and ii. leveraging in additional resources from multilaterals to ensure long term sustainability.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Zimbabwe is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to political instability, economic crisis, and episodes of violence. The country has experienced hyperinflation, civil unrest, and humanitarian shocks like Cyclone Idai, which have severely impacted the education system and wider development outcomes.

q5_source.text: Zimbabwe matters to the UK for a range of development and diplomatic priorities. [...] Zimbabwe is also experiencing another period of rising inflation and economic collapse. [...] The Zimbabwean economy remains extremely vulnerable with a growing fiscal and trade deficit, resulting in a long-standing liquidity crisis that severely affects the country’s ability to access foreign currency for vital imports. [...] Zimbabwe has seen several episodes of violence and instability as well as human rights violations in the last year. [...] The fast-track land reform programme, implemented mainly between 2000 and 2002, saw violence used to evict commercial land-owners and the 2008 election was marred by violence, including the targeting of some people working in the social sectors. More recently, the period following the 2018 elections saw security service personnel kill civilians and carry out a range of human rights violations and violence in January 2019 related to fuel price increases, which led to the shutting off of the internet.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political uncertainty and economic instability disrupt policy implementation and programme delivery. Weak institutions limit the government's capacity to manage education reforms effectively. Climate risks (droughts, cyclones) damage infrastructure and increase humanitarian needs, while data limitations hinder evidence-based decision-making. Hyperinflation and liquidity crises affect the affordability of school fees and operational costs, increasing drop-out rates and reducing teacher motivation.

quote.text: The Government of Zimbabwe have been involved in supporting the design this programme. Multiple consultations have been held with MoPSE, ZIMSEC, Civil society (AWET, Udaciza) through the umbrella organisation, ECOZI, implementing partners for education programmes (UNICEF, Plan International, CAMFED, World Vision), Disabled Persons organisations (FODPZ, Henrys (DPO), private sector ICT providers, and other Development partners (World Bank, EU, SDC, KfW) and are committed to play a significant role in implementing their part of their commitment to reduce poverty in Zimbabwe. [...] The challenge is to determine how best the policy could be finalised and implemented, especially in the current difficult macro-economic crisis and is a priority for education sector dialogue with the TEACH programme.
quote.source: D0002689.odt, Partnership Principles and School Financing Policy

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is led by FCDO (UK) with UNICEF as the primary implementing partner. Decision-making power rests with FCDO and UNICEF, with Southern partners (e.g., Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education, local NGOs) playing implementation roles but not leading strategic decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training of teachers and school leaders
mentorship through teacher professional development
institutional strengthening of education inspection and management systems
policy reform support (e.g., School Financing Policy, curriculum reforms)
community engagement to support marginalised groups (girls, children with disabilities)

quote.text: Implementation: With the approval of this addendum, the TEACH programme will be delivered through up to four delivery partners: UNICEF, Education Development Trust (EDT), Plan Zimbabwe and a new supplier for the solarisation in schools if not done through UNICEF. [...] UNICEF will deliver an ECD pilot through a new downstream partner (ThinkEqual) and agreed activities related to curriculum delivery, data improvement and safeguarding. [...] Plan Zimbabwe will be contracted through a new accountable grant to deliver support to out-of-school girls. [...] EDT – no change to the current contract, but delivery will be more digitalised to increase Value for Money (VfM).

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of funding instruments: Contribution Agreements with UNICEF (for SIGs, solarisation, and policy support), Accountable Grants with EDT (for TPD) and Plan Zimbabwe (for out-of-school girls), and direct contracts for specific components like the SEL pilot. This mixed approach allows for flexibility in addressing different programme needs while maintaining oversight through FCDO.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a combination of direct contracts, contribution agreements, and accountable grants with multiple partners. A steering committee oversees implementation, linking into the Education Coordination Group (chaired by the Minister of Primary and Secondary Education) and annual reviews. This structure allows for coordination among partners while maintaining FCDO’s strategic oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNICEF was selected based on its existing role in the Education Development Fund (EDF) and capacity to deliver at scale. EDT was chosen for its expertise in teacher professional development, while Plan Zimbabwe and ThinkEqual were added to address specific needs (out-of-school girls and SEL, respectively). The selection reflects a balance of existing relationships, technical expertise, and the need for specialised interventions.

quote.text: The TPD component of the TEACH programme, subject of this submission, will be delivered through a contract with Education Development Trust. It is a component of the TEACH programmes so will be supervised and work jointly with the implementers of the other components, including UNICEF. There is a steering committee that will hold quarterly meetings and will link into the six weekly Education coordination Group meetings to report on progress. [...] The solarisation in schools scale up will either be contracted through UNICEF or through a new implementing partner; whichever delivers the best value for money.
quote.source: D0003304.odt and D0007295.odt, Approach to Implementation

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The steering committee includes representatives from FCDO, UNICEF, EDT, Plan Zimbabwe, and other key partners. It meets quarterly and reports into the Education Coordination Group (chaired by the Minister of Primary and Secondary Education). Decisions on implementation are made jointly, with FCDO retaining overall oversight.

quote.text: The programme coordination and implementation structure is set out in figure 3. This option would require an additional steering committee to be set up for decision making on implementation. It would allow the teacher professional development issues to have more focus and remain more targeted. [...] For implementation and monitoring purposes, there is a TEACH/EDF steering committee that will hold quarterly meetings and will link into the six weekly Education coordination Group meetings to report on progress.
quote.source: D0002689.odt, Programme Coordination and D0007295.odt, Approach to Implementation

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, as demonstrated by the shift of £1.8m from other components to the solarisation pilot (Component 105) and the reclassification of £1.6m from C-DEL to R-DEL for teacher development. However, major reallocations require FCDO approval and are subject to annual review processes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has demonstrated adaptive management through multiple addendums adjusting priorities in response to COVID-19, economic crises, and policy changes. For example, the solarisation component was expanded, and SEL was added after initial delays. Adjustments are made through formal addendums and annual reviews, requiring FCDO approval.

quote.text: The design of this programme has built in options for adaption, depending on how the context deteriorates or improves. This is likely to happen over the course of the programme and the situation will be monitored regularly during implementation, including working with our delivery partners to develop robust mitigation measures against the worst-case scenarios. Adaptation is not limited to the political and economic context, but also takes into account how evidence generated in implementation of the programme can help test/learn and adapt different interventions to achieve the programme outcomes and impact.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UNICEF, EDT, Plan Zimbabwe) → Downstream Partners (e.g., ThinkEqual, AWET, CBM, Open University)

quote.text: The programme will be delivered through up to four delivery partners: UNICEF, Education Development Trust (EDT), Plan Zimbabwe and a new supplier for the solarisation in schools if not done through UNICEF. [...] UNICEF will deliver an ECD pilot through a new downstream partner (ThinkEqual) and agreed activities related to curriculum delivery, data improvement and safeguarding. [...] Plan Zimbabwe will be contracted through a new accountable grant to deliver support to out-of-school girls. They will receive £5.15m and will deliver through three downstream partners: Apostolic Women’s Empowerment Trust (AWET), Christian Blind Mission (CBM), and Open University in the UK.

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuing comprehensive support to education exclusively through the pooled Education Development Fund (EDF)
Focusing narrowly on only providing improved teacher education (rejected due to insufficient support for equitable access)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery model was chosen to balance value for money, risk mitigation, and the need for both immediate service delivery (SIGs, teacher training) and long-term systemic change (policy influence, capacity building). The use of multiple partners allows for specialisation (e.g., UNICEF for SIGs, EDT for TPD) while maintaining FCDO oversight. The structure also enables flexibility to adapt to shocks (e.g., COVID-19, economic crises) and leverage multilateral funding (e.g., GPE).
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (political and economic instability in Zimbabwe)
partner capacity (UNICEF’s existing role in EDF, EDT’s expertise in TPD)
flexibility (need to adapt to shocks like COVID-19 and economic crises)
equity (targeting marginalised groups like girls and children with disabilities)
speed (leveraging existing partnerships to accelerate delivery)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational risks due to political and economic instability in Zimbabwe (e.g., hyperinflation, civil unrest)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular monitoring and adaptive management through annual reviews; flexibility in fund reallocation; use of multilaterals (e.g., GPE) to ensure continuity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges among multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Steering committee and Education Coordination Group for oversight; clear division of roles (e.g., UNICEF for SIGs, EDT for TPD).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risks for marginalised groups (e.g., out-of-school girls, children with disabilities)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnerships with specialised NGOs (e.g., Plan Zimbabwe, CBM, AWET); embedded safeguarding policies and community engagement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in policy reforms (e.g., School Financing Policy, curriculum changes)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance and advocacy through UNICEF and FCDO; alignment with government priorities (e.g., ESSP 2021-2025).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Value for Money (VfM) erosion due to inflation and economic crisis
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular VfM reviews; shift to digital delivery where possible (e.g., EDT’s TPD); leveraging multilateral funds (e.g., GPE).

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (focus on measurable outcomes like pass rates, retention)
equity (targeting marginalised groups and poorest schools)

quote.text: The appraisal case sets out why the option of remaining in the EDF pooled fund is only one modality that was considered for the TEACH programme. The options in the appraisal case are based on evidence from both DFID’s chief economist on best buys in Education [...] and on the international evidence that formed the basis of DFID’s Education policy launched in February 2018, which includes the key finding that teachers are the core element to improve education quality and learning outcomes. [...] Specifically, the GPE approved additional funding for Zimbabwe for a total value of $23.9 million programme for Zimbabwe over 3 years, in 2018. This is to boost learning outcomes in basic education through continuous professional development of teachers, improved teacher supervision and management as well as strengthened evidence-based policy and strategic planning. [...] The objectives and interventions of both programmes have been aligned in order to maximise value for money and results, and to avoid duplication of activities.
quote.source: D0002689.odt, Feasible Options to Achieve the Outcomes

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Zimbabwe constrains partner selection by limiting the use of government systems for fund channelling (due to corruption risks) and requiring partners with strong safeguarding and adaptive capacities. This has led to the reliance on multilaterals (UNICEF) and specialised NGOs (Plan Zimbabwe, CBM) that can navigate political instability, economic volatility, and weak institutional environments.
q27_constraints_detail: Political instability and weak institutions limit direct funding to government; funds are channelled through UNICEF and NGOs.
Economic volatility (hyperinflation, liquidity crises) requires partners with financial management expertise and adaptive capacity.
Safeguarding risks for marginalised groups necessitate partners with strong community engagement and protection policies (e.g., Plan Zimbabwe for out-of-school girls).
Climate risks (droughts, cyclones) demand partners with experience in resilience-building and infrastructure support (e.g., solarisation).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (service delivery, capacity building, policy influence) determine its delivery structure. Direct service needs (SIGs, teacher training) are handled by UNICEF and EDT, while policy influence and innovation (solarisation, SEL) require flexible partnerships with specialised organisations (ThinkEqual, Plan Zimbabwe). The need for both immediate impact and systemic change drives the use of multiple, complementary partners.
q28_linkages: Service delivery objectives (SIGs, teacher training) → UNICEF and EDT as implementing partners with scale and technical expertise.
Policy influence objectives → Leveraging UNICEF’s government relationships and FCDO’s advocacy role.
Innovation objectives (solarisation, SEL) → Specialised partners (ThinkEqual, solarisation suppliers) with niche capabilities.
Equity objectives → NGOs (Plan Zimbabwe, CBM, AWET) with community trust and safeguarding experience.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting marginalised girls, children with disabilities, and poorest schools) with efficiency (leveraging multilaterals, digital delivery, and existing partnerships). For example, SIGs are targeted to the poorest schools despite higher transaction costs, and the solarisation pilot prioritises rural areas with lower connectivity. The shift from bilateral to multilateral funding (e.g., GPE) also reflects a trade-off between direct control and long-term sustainability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Targeting marginalised groups (girls, CWDs) increases transaction costs but aligns with equity goals.
Using multilaterals (GPE) reduces FCDO’s direct oversight but improves sustainability and leverage.
Digital delivery (e.g., EDT’s TPD) improves efficiency but may exclude groups with limited connectivity.
Policy influence requires long-term engagement, slowing short-term delivery but ensuring systemic impact.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context has led to intensive management structures (quarterly steering committee meetings, embedded safeguarding) and adaptive mechanisms (annual reviews, fund reallocation). Oversight is more hands-on than in stable contexts, with regular VfM and risk assessments to mitigate operational and fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include training (EDT for teachers), institutional strengthening (UNICEF for MoPSE), and community engagement (Plan Zimbabwe for girls’ education). Southern partners (e.g., MoPSE, local NGOs) are involved in implementation but rely on Northern/multilateral partners (FCDO, UNICEF) for strategic direction and technical support.

quote.text: The design of this programme has built in options for adaption, depending on how the context deteriorates or improves. [...] Adaptation is not limited to the political and economic context, but also takes into account how evidence generated in implementation of the programme can help test/learn and adapt different interventions to achieve the programme outcomes and impact. [...] The TEACH programme is designed to be GESI transformative. It has a particular focus on inclusion of girls, children with disabilities (CWDs) and children who are geographically marginalised. [...] The programme will ensure that project activities, benefits and suppliers do not in any way discriminate, harass or victimise based on gender, age, disability, ethnicity or religion.

key_programme_risks: Political uncertainty adversely affecting GoZ policy making and implementation (e.g., delays in School Financing Policy).
Deterioration in the economy and decline in donor funding, reducing resources for the education sector.
Cash/liquidity concerns disrupting programme implementation and increasing industrial action/civil unrest.
Parental engagement reducing as they fail to meet levies/fees without GoZ providing additional operational funding.
Lack of integration/complementarity among DFID-supported programmes (bilateral, centrally managed, multilateral).
Corruption, fraud, and misuse of funds.
Hyperinflation affecting teacher motivation and GoZ’s ability to meet financial commitments.
