Safeguarding risks for marginalised girls and children with disabilities.
Delays in solarisation pilot due to bureaucratic and certification issues.
Attrition of community facilitators in out-of-school girls’ programme.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular policy dialogue with MoPSE; alignment with government priorities (e.g., ESSP 2021-2025); technical assistance through UNICEF.
Flexible fund reallocation; leveraging multilateral funds (GPE); VfM reviews; digital delivery to reduce costs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Parental disengagement due to inability to pay fees
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted SIGs to poorest schools; advocacy for School Financing Policy to reduce fees for poorest families.
Steering committee and Education Coordination Group for oversight; alignment with GPE and other DFID programmes.
Funds channelled through UNICEF with strict accounting procedures; no direct funding to GoZ systems.
Intrinsic motivation through TPD; solarisation of teachers’ housing to improve living conditions.
Partnerships with NGOs (Plan Zimbabwe, CBM) with strong safeguarding policies; community engagement and sensitisation.
Time extension for certification; training for teachers and administrators; simplified maintenance models.
Capacity building through Open University; incentives and support for facilitators.

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid direct funding through government systems due to corruption risks; use multilaterals (UNICEF) as intermediaries.
Build flexibility into programme design to adapt to political and economic shocks (e.g., COVID-19, hyperinflation).
Prioritise safeguarding and community engagement when working with marginalised groups in fragile contexts.
Leverage multilateral partnerships (e.g., GPE) to ensure continuity and reduce bilateral risk exposure.
Use pilot programmes (e.g., solarisation, SEL) to test innovations in high-risk environments before scaling.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Education Development Fund (EDF) informed TEACH’s design, particularly the effectiveness of School Improvement Grants (SIGs) in keeping poorest schools functional. The EDF’s experience with teacher training and policy alignment also shaped TEACH’s focus on evidence-based approaches and adaptive management. The transition from EDF to TEACH was designed to build on these lessons while addressing gaps in equity and systemic reforms.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from School Improvement Grants (SIGs) to School Equity Grants (SEGs) to better target the poorest schools.
Expansion of solarisation pilot based on positive feedback from initial phase, despite bureaucratic delays.
Addition of Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) component to address violence in schools, informed by global evidence and government commitments.
Transition of girls’ education and SIGs to GPE for long-term sustainability, based on lessons from EDF and ZGSE.
Adjustment of pass rate and drop-out rate targets to reflect COVID-19 impacts, based on annual review data.

quote.text: The TEACH programme is in line with DFID’s new education policy. TEACH will focus on improving teaching. Effective teachers as the single most important factor in getting all children learning. To be effective, teachers need training that is targeted and school based, with their performance regularly monitored. This has to be done in the context of reforming the education system to support learning more effectively and needs to include teaching at the right level. [...] The appraisal case sets out why the option of remaining in the EDF pooled fund is only one modality that was considered for the TEACH programme. [...] The design of this programme has built in options for adaption, depending on how the context deteriorates or improves. [...] The TEACH programme is designed to be GESI transformative. It has a particular focus on inclusion of girls, children with disabilities (CWDs) and children who are geographically marginalised.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leveraged an additional £5.2m for the education sector in Zimbabwe through the GPE multiplier fund, which has a 3:1 matching ratio for new resources. This was enabled by the UK’s bilateral funding under TEACH.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) for components like solarisation (e.g., £2m in FY24/25 and FY25/26) and International Climate Finance (ICF), alongside revenue spending for activities like teacher training and SIGs.

quote.text: This addendum sets out the case for an additional £15,700,000 for the TEACH programme to be utilised by the end of March 2026. This will change the overall budget from the original of £39,840,000 to £55,540,000. The indicative allocation which will be utilised as follows: £8.1m in FY23/24; £9m in FY24/25 (of which £2m is CDEL and ICF); £9m in FY25/26 (of which £2m is CDEL and ICF). [...] There is one additional benefit to this £15.7m cost extension of TEACH. We are intending to use the window within GPE, called the multiplier fund, to leverage an additional £5.2m allocation for the education sector in Zimbabwe through GPE. This is possible because the multiplier fund has a 3:1 matching ratio for any new resources coming into the education sector.

metadata.programme_name: Support to TradeMark East Africa – Strategy 2 (STS2)
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to increase sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa by increasing East Africa’s trade with the region and the rest of the world." (24605596.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The programme will run for 6 years (July 2017 - June 2023)." (24605596.odt, Programme Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing trade facilitation interventions), capacity building (strengthening trade institutions and private sector skills), and service delivery (direct support to improve trade infrastructure and systems). It also includes policy influence through advocacy and regulatory reforms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will (i) invest in improving the efficiency and capacity of transport, logistics and trade infrastructure at key port and border points; (ii) invest in systems to improve trading standards, reduce non-tariff barriers and enhance transparency in trade processes; (iii) improve the regulatory and policy environment for trade; and (iv) support private sector advocacy for trade competitiveness, the export capacity of East African businesses and the greater participation of women and small and growing businesses in trade." (24605596.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased GDP growth
q3_expected_outputs.target: 0.6% additional GDP growth above trend

q3_expected_outputs.output: poverty reduction
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1.8 million fewer people living below $2/day

q3_expected_outputs.output: government revenue increase
q3_expected_outputs.target: $1.1 billion net additional revenue

q3_expected_outputs.output: total trade increase
q3_expected_outputs.target: $600 million net added total trade; 1.1% increase above trend

q3_expected_outputs.output: exports to rest of world
q3_expected_outputs.target: $200 million net added exports; 1.9% increase

q3_expected_outputs.output: intra-EAC exports
q3_expected_outputs.target: $100 million net added intra-EAC exports; 1.3% increase

q3_expected_outputs.output: time reduction for port clearance
q3_expected_outputs.target: from 11 days to 3.8 days at Mombasa Port

q3_expected_outputs.output: border crossing time reduction
q3_expected_outputs.target: 80% reduction at Busia border

q3_expected_outputs.output: harmonized standards
q3_expected_outputs.target: 80 most traded goods in EAC

q3_expected_outputs.output: women in trade participation
q3_expected_outputs.target: 74% of informal cross-border trade dominated by women

q3_expected_outputs.output: logistics hubs
q3_expected_outputs.target: up to seven pilot hubs (Kigali, Busia, Jinja, Gulu, Kampala, SAGCOT, Mombasa)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce trade barriers and enhance private sector competitiveness in East Africa through infrastructure improvements, regulatory reforms, and targeted support to women and SMEs, ultimately increasing trade volumes and economic growth.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme has two overall outcomes: Outcome 1: Reduced barriers to trade; Outcome 2: Enhanced private sector markets and increased export capability." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with political economy challenges and infrastructure constraints, but has strong government and donor alignment. The overall risk is assessed as moderate due to effective management of procurement and political risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (24605596.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The largest risks will be those associated with procurement and with the political economy, and are well managed." (24605596.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (mentioned in Green Port policy)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Poor infrastructure increases trade costs by up to 40%, regulatory barriers impede food security, and political economy challenges slow reform implementation. Conflict in South Sudan creates additional risks for border projects.
where_context.quote: "Trade remains constrained by poor infrastructure which hampers access to markets, tariffs (which have not fallen uniformly across the East African Community) and non-tariff barriers." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The nature of trade costs varies across geographical areas and income levels, and hence the effectiveness of trade facilitation interventions is likely to be determined by the degree and intensity of the factors that contribute to high trade costs." (24605596.odt, Box 1)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: TMEA (based in Kenya) leads implementation with oversight from DFID/FCDO. The TMEA Council (comprising all donors including UK) provides strategic direction, while individual country offices have assigned SROs. Decision-making is shared between Northern donors and Southern implementing partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to public and private sectors
training for customs officials and standards bureaus
support for women traders (skills, advocacy, certification)
institutional strengthening for EAC Secretariat and national agencies
gender mainstreaming across all interventions

partner_organizations.name: TradeMark East Africa (TMEA)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer

partner_organizations.name: East African Community (EAC) Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: regional coordination and policy reform

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Ports Authority (KPA)
partner_organizations.role: port infrastructure improvements

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA)
partner_organizations.role: customs modernization

partner_organizations.name: Uganda Revenue Authority
partner_organizations.role: electronic cargo tracking

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: Dar es Salaam port improvements

partner_organizations.name: Government of Rwanda
partner_organizations.role: Lake Kivu transport projects

partner_organizations.name: East Africa Business Council (EABC)
partner_organizations.role: private sector advocacy

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: co-financing (e.g., $345m for Dar Port)

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: co-financing (e.g., Moyale border post)

partner_organizations.name: DFID/FCDO
partner_organizations.role: funding and oversight

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Netherlands, USA)
partner_organizations.role: co-funding

who_partners.quote: "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase. Each DFID office will assign an SRO to oversee their respective country/regional support, and the Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (24605596.odt, Summary Sheet) and "TMEA has also outlined a sustainability strategy that provides a plan to reduce its reliance on donor funding by exploring development capital instruments as well as encouraging EAC governments and private sector to finance the reforms and infrastructure investment." (24605596.odt, Coherence with partners and exit strategy)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants for technical assistance and catalytic investments (e.g., project preparation, feasibility studies) alongside direct capital investments in infrastructure. The funding is channeled through TMEA as a fund manager, with DFID/FCDO providing core funding and oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: TMEA operates as a regional platform coordinating multiple country programmes and donors. It manages implementation through country offices (Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda) and a regional team, with strategic oversight from the TMEA Council (all donors) and DFID SROs. The structure allows for both centralized coordination and country-level adaptation.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (TMEA was established by DFID in 2010)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TMEA was created by DFID specifically to address trade barriers in East Africa and had already demonstrated effectiveness during Strategy 1 (2011-2017). The direct award reflects continuity, existing relationships with EAC governments, and the need for a coordinated regional approach.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID created TradeMark East Africa (TMEA) in 2010 to tackle these problems in East Africa. This programme is an extension of DFID support provided under TMEA’s Strategy 1 (2011-2017), recognising the progress it has already made and opportunities to build momentum." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase." (24605596.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The TMEA Council, comprising all donors (including DFID/FCDO) and chaired by the Head of DFID Kenya, provides strategic oversight. Country-level SROs manage day-to-day delivery, with technical advisory groups supporting specific components (e.g., standards, SPS).
how_governance.quote: "The Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (24605596.odt, Summary Sheet) and "To provide further assurance, the revised Business Case will be submitted to QAU in parallel with approval by Ministers, particularly to look at overall implementation coherence aspects." (24605596.odt, Quality assurance and capacity to deliver the programme)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, particularly for newer areas like export capacity support. The programme uses a phased approach (e.g., logistics hubs) to allow adjustments based on lessons learned.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a mid-term review to assess progress and reallocate resources. For example, the logistics hubs will be piloted sequentially, with learnings informing later phases. Export capacity support was added based on lessons from Strategy 1.
how_flexibility.quote: "There is in-built flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context, particularly with regard to newer components on export capability support. The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (24605596.odt, Flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context) and "As the programme may spend beyond the current spending review period, progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets, which will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TMEA (regional platform) → [country teams/implementing partners]. Some activities involve additional layers (e.g., TMEA → national standards bureaus → private sector)
how_efficiency.quote: "Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions including technical assistance and development of regulatory/policy frameworks, systems and processes that support trade and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints to East Africa’s trade competitiveness." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary) implies layered implementation, but exact % not stated.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID’s support ends; reliance on other donors/multilaterals. Risks losing momentum and reform commitment.
Narrow focus on infrastructure, customs, or policy reforms only. Risks reputational damage and reduced impact.
Maintain existing interventions without expansion. Misses opportunity to address export capacity gaps.
Broaden to PPP policy, business climate reforms, and investment climate. Risks diluting trade focus.
Combine Strategy 1 areas with new focus on private sector advocacy, women/SME inclusion, and export capability. Maximizes impact by addressing supply-side constraints.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 was selected because it builds on proven interventions from Strategy 1 while addressing critical gaps in export capacity and inclusion. The mixed approach (infrastructure + policy + private sector support) aligns with evidence that "complementing interventions that seek to reduce the cost of trade with those that seek to improve the local export capacity significantly enhances the impact of trade facilitation programmes." (Box 1, 24605596.odt). The phased implementation of logistics hubs and adaptive management structure allow for learning and risk mitigation.
q25_decision_factors: evidence (trade facilitation + export capacity = greater impact)
value for money (leveraging £300m+ in port investments)
risk mitigation (phased approach for new components)
equity (targeted support for women and SMEs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with milestone-based payments and QAU oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy resistance to reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Politically aware technical assistance and private sector advocacy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges across 6 countries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: TMEA’s regional platform structure and EAC Secretariat partnership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of donor-funded interventions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sustainability strategy to transition to EAC government/private sector financing.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 5: Do all of the previous focus areas from Strategy 1 (option 3) and support export capacity... This option extends current support on trade competitiveness to include targeted supply-side interventions that seek to: expand private sector-led advocacy; promote greater inclusion of women and small businesses in trade; and build the export capability of the region’s private sector... This option is supported by strong evidence and lessons learnt and would maximise the effectiveness of DFID support as well as overall value for money." (24605596.odt, Option 5) and "The current intervention mix and approach have been significantly effective in reducing the constraints to trade in the EAC." (24605596.odt, Option 2)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The regional scope and political economy context constrain partner selection to organizations with existing EAC relationships and multilateral credibility. For example: (1) TMEA’s regional platform structure is necessary to coordinate across 6 countries with varying regulatory environments; (2) Conflict in South Sudan limits partner options for the Nimule border project; (3) Weak institutions require capacity-building embedded in delivery (e.g., customs modernization with KRA).
q27_constraints_detail: need for regional convening power (rules out single-country partners)
political economy requires trusted intermediaries (TMEA’s donor council structure)
FCAS contexts (South Sudan) limit implementation partners
infrastructure gaps necessitate partners with technical + financial leverage (e.g., World Bank for Dar Port)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (infrastructure + policy + private sector) determine the platform-based delivery structure. For example: (1) Infrastructure investments require capital funding instruments and partnerships with ports authorities; (2) Policy reforms need embedded technical assistance with EAC Secretariat; (3) Private sector advocacy demands flexible, demand-driven support mechanisms. The phased logistics hubs reflect the need to test and adapt the ‘clusters’ approach.
q28_linkages: regional scope → platform structure (TMEA)
infrastructure goals → capital funding + technical assistance mix
policy objectives → embedded advisory roles with EAC
private sector focus → flexible grants/loans for SMEs
gender inclusion → targeted capacity building components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency through: (1) Targeted support for women traders (74% of informal cross-border trade) despite higher per-beneficiary costs; (2) Phased logistics hubs to ensure poverty reduction focus alongside economic growth; (3) Capacity building for SMEs to address market failures. The design acknowledges that "trade liberalisation can have short-term negative impacts on select groups... and interventions must incorporate mitigating measures."
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: slower rollout of logistics hubs to ensure women/SME participation
expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical assistance paired with Southern institutional strengthening
cost vs. reach: higher per-project costs for gender-sensitive border infrastructure (e.g., sanitation for women traders)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (procurement + political economy) drives milestone-based oversight and QAU reviews. FCAS contexts (e.g., South Sudan) trigger additional safeguards like phased implementation and contingency planning.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) TMEA’s technical assistance strengthens EAC Secretariat’s policy leadership; (2) Customs modernization includes training for KRA officials to sustain reforms; (3) Women’s trade programmes build local cooperatives’ advocacy capacity.
intersections.quote: "The ultimate impact on the poor and on women and men will largely depend on the type of sectors impacted and whom they employ and interventions must incorporate mitigating measures to avoid adverse effects." (24605596.odt, Strategic Case) and "TMEA has also initiated various specific interventions that target the benefits of trade benefit both men and women equally and specifically that women are included in trade for instance through support to informal cross-border trade (dominated by women)." (24605596.odt, Compliance with Gender Equality Act)

key_programme_risks: procurement delays (e.g., port infrastructure, Lake Kivu projects)
political resistance to regulatory reforms
coordination challenges across EAC member states
sustainability of interventions post-DFID funding
conflict disruption (e.g., South Sudan border projects)
climate risks affecting transport infrastructure
gender disparities in trade benefits

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: phased implementation, milestone-based payments, and QAU oversight
politically aware technical assistance and private sector advocacy
TMEA’s regional platform and EAC Secretariat partnership
transition plan to EAC government/private sector financing
contingency planning and phased rollout in FCAS areas
targeted women’s trade programmes and gender audits

fcas_specific_lessons: In South Sudan, "attention will be paid to the risks of working in South Sudan, but it is likely that work can begin on new border facilities immediately" (D0004419.odt, Annex A).
FCAS contexts require flexible timelines and localized partner networks (e.g., Nimule border project).
Conflict zones prioritize quick wins (e.g., border infrastructure) over complex reforms.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from TMEA Strategy 1 (2011-2017) include: (1) Infrastructure improvements are most effective for reducing trade costs; (2) Combining trade facilitation with export capacity support enhances impact; (3) Gender-specific interventions are needed to ensure equitable benefits; (4) Phased pilots allow for adaptive management. The Box 1 summary in 24605596.odt highlights that "preferential market access carries less weight than cost and capacity factors," validating the focus on supply-side constraints.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Strategy 2 incorporates: (1) Explicit export capacity component (new); (2) Phased logistics hubs (pilot approach); (3) Strengthened gender mainstreaming; (4) Adaptive management framework with mid-term review; (5) Expanded use of ICT for trade (building on Strategy 1’s electronic systems).
risks_lessons.quote: "Box 1: Summary of lessons from TMEA Strategy 1... Evidence is context specific, but unequivocal that trade facilitation interventions which improve infrastructure are the most effective in increasing trade volumes and reducing trade costs, followed by reforms that improve customs efficiency and then reforms improving the regulatory/business environment. It is also clear that complementing interventions that seek to reduce the cost of trade with those that seek to improve the local export capacity significantly enhances the impact of trade facilitation programmes." (24605596.odt, Box 1) and "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (24605596.odt, Flexibility to learn and adjust)

co_funding_partners.leverage: $345 million for Dar es Salaam Port

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged over £300 million in public and private funding for Mombasa Port and attracted a World Bank loan of $345 million for Dar es Salaam Port. TMEA’s total funding across donors exceeds £450 million, making it the largest aid-for-trade facility globally.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: "Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions including technical assistance and development of regulatory/policy frameworks... and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary)
financial_details.quote: "DFID funding will be used to promote sustainable and inclusive prosperity in East Africa through further reducing trade costs and barriers along the transport corridors from the coast, improving standards of East Africa goods, helping government meet its economic development commitments, and supporting the private sector/civil society to influence key stakeholders on the trade agenda." (24605596.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Table 1: TMEA Strategy 2 funding shows DFID’s £229m alongside other donors’ £90m, totaling £319m." (24605596.odt, Table 1)

metadata.programme_name: The United Kingdom Nigeria Infrastructure Advisory Facility (UKNIAF)
metadata.quote: "Enhanced management and planning of climate smart infrastructure development" (61400109.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Setup 15 May 2017 ... New end date: 12 April 2027" (61400109.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: UKNIAF provides technical assistance to improve infrastructure management in Nigeria, combining capacity building (strengthening institutions like FERMA, TCN, and NSIA), policy influence (supporting power sector reforms and climate-smart planning), and financing mechanisms (leveraging private capital through PPPs and blended finance). The programme aims to transform Nigeria's infrastructure systems to support inclusive growth, with a recent shift to prioritize climate-smart solutions and energy transition.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UKNIAF aims to deliver transformation in at least 3 of its 5 components, defined as: Successful completion of Nigeria's power sector reforms... A transformational improvement in way public money is spent on the Federal Road Network... Substantially improved processes for the wider capital budget... At least £3 billion of Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) will have reached financial close... UKNIAF will have improved the timeliness and quality of at least £500 million of Nigerian Government and multilateral reconstruction spending in Borno and Yobe." (5757822.odt, Expected Results) AND "The main changes are to put climate (including energy transition) at the heart of the infrastructure development in line with UK Government ambition (and increased Nigerian ambition), with UK International Climate Finance being a main source of funding." (61400109.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)
q3_expected_outputs: Successful completion of Nigeria's power sector reforms with a contract-based market operating sustainably (including reforming TCN)
Transformational improvement in Federal Road Network spending using a climate-smart Road Asset Management System (RAMS)
Substantially improved capital budget processes with climate and environmental impact assessments prioritized
£2 billion pipeline of climate-smart Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) reaching financial close
200,000 people with improved access to energy (ICF KPI 2) by 2024
Greenhouse gas emissions reduced by 1,396 CO2e tonnes per year (ICF KPI 6)
£35 million of public and private finance mobilized (ICF KPIs 11 and 12) by 2024
6 MW of energy installed (ICF KPI 7) by 2024
5 principal commercial investments in off-grid energy/clean cooking catalysed by 2022
what_objectives.summary: UKNIAF is a technical assistance facility that supports Nigeria's infrastructure development through systemic reforms, climate-smart planning, and private sector engagement. The programme shifted from broad infrastructure support to a focused climate and energy transition agenda, leveraging blended finance to catalyse private investment in off-grid energy and clean cooking solutions.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will therefore have International Climate Finance as the main element of its funding. The results indicators will include ICF indicators - in particular mobilisation of climate finance, institutional transformational change and GHG emissions." (61400109.odt, Implementation Approach)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nigeria faces significant security challenges, particularly in the North East where Boko Haram and Islamic State have created instability. The programme initially included a North East reconstruction component but removed it due to "unsuitable" security conditions. Corruption risks are also explicitly noted as "high" in the Nigerian context.
where_context.q5_source: "The 2015 Business case assumed continued stability in the North East and that NIAF could advise the Nigerian Government and donor around rebuilding infrastructure. In practice the situation in Borno and Yobe is unsuitable for this as Boko Haram and Islamic State have gained territory and made both States too unstable for large scale investments." (61400109.odt, Results) AND "Fraud and corruption risks are high in Nigeria, and need to be monitored carefully." (5757822.odt, Key Risks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints led to the removal of the North East component and shifted PPP focus to state-level projects. Regulatory and political economy challenges (e.g., resistance from sector ministries) have historically limited PPP adoption. Weak institutions require capacity building embedded in all components. Climate risks (e.g., floods, heat) now shape infrastructure planning requirements. Data limitations affect monitoring, particularly for off-grid energy and clean cooking sectors where baseline data is described as "nascent" or "limited."
where_context.quote: "The Federal government is supportive of off grid access and the Rural Electrification Agency is a well-managed institution... Nigeria’s minigrid regulations have been assessed as some of the best globally... The Solar Naija initiative... has made no disbursements to the projects which the donors have worked on due to the Central Bank having repayment concerns." (90000316.odt, Off-grid Energy) AND "The Nigerian Energy Sector... 79% of energy usage is residential - far higher than for similar countries... The Nigerian Energy Sector... Work by the African Development Bank... showed that road, rail and port infrastructure were all close to being the worst in Africa." (5757822.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Tetra Tech International (primary implementer) with InfraCredit (for CDEL component)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Tetra Tech (UK-based) manages day-to-day delivery with oversight from FCDO. Nigerian institutions (e.g., NSIA, FERMA, TCN) are key counterparts but do not lead implementation. The Technical Review Panel includes Nigerian experts, but final decisions rest with FCDO/Tetra Tech.
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (e.g., FERMA's use of RAMS, TCN reforms)
training (e.g., for Budget Office staff on capital budget processes)
mentorship (embedded advisors in NSIA and Ministry of Finance)
policy development support (e.g., PPP frameworks, climate-smart planning guidelines)

partner_organizations.name: Tetra Tech International
partner_organizations.role: primary technical assistance provider

partner_organizations.name: InfraCredit
partner_organizations.role: blended finance fund manager for CDEL component

partner_organizations.name: Nigerian Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA)
partner_organizations.role: key counterpart for PPPs and climate finance

partner_organizations.name: Federal Road Maintenance Agency (FERMA)
partner_organizations.role: counterpart for road sector reforms

partner_organizations.name: Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN)
partner_organizations.role: counterpart for power sector reforms

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Budget and National Planning
partner_organizations.role: counterpart for capital budget reforms

partner_organizations.name: Rural Electrification Agency (REA)
partner_organizations.role: counterpart for off-grid energy access

partner_organizations.name: Montrose (contract pending)
partner_organizations.role: monitoring and evaluation provider

partner_organizations.name: PIDG (Private Infrastructure Development Group)
partner_organizations.role: affiliate supporting InfraCredit's fund structure

who_partners.quote: "Tetra Tech International (previously named WYG) is implementing the main contract after winning the open competitive tender in 2019." (61400109.odt, Implementation Approach) AND "The preferred choice is the Infracredit supported fund for a range of reasons, including... Infracredit has strong governance structures, systems and processes (due diligence has been completed)..." (90000316.odt, Management Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for Tetra Tech's technical assistance) and blended finance (for the CDEL component via InfraCredit's fund). The RDEL component is managed through a performance-based contract with Tetra Tech, while the CDEL uses a first-loss facility to de-risk private investments in climate-smart infrastructure.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Tetra Tech manages the RDEL technical assistance component, while InfraCredit manages the CDEL blended finance fund. FCDO oversees both through separate agreements, with a programme-funded adviser facilitating coordination. The Technical Review Panel provides independent oversight of Tetra Tech's performance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Tetra Tech was selected through an open competitive tender in 2019. InfraCredit was chosen for the CDEL component due to its existing relationship with PIDG, local presence in Nigeria, and ability to leverage Nigerian pension funds—criteria that aligned with FCDO's value-for-money and additionality requirements.
how_mechanism.quote: "Tetra Tech International... is implementing the main contract after winning the open competitive tender in 2019." (61400109.odt, Implementation Approach) AND "The preferred choice is the Infracredit supported fund for a range of reasons, including... as Infracredit is a multilateral entity, this enables easier and effective management of development capital... Infracredit has strong governance structures..." (90000316.odt, Management Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Technical Review Panel (TRP) reviews Tetra Tech's performance every 6 months, assessing evidence against milestones. For the CDEL component, an Investment Policy binds the fund manager, and FCDO nominates a staff member to approve investments. The TRP includes independent experts who interview counterparts to validate results.
how_governance.quote: "The logframe is updated every 6 months based on recommendations from the programme's Technical Review Panel (TRP)... A self-assessment and evidence file is submitted to the TRP before each of its visits, and it then tests these in its interviews with counterparts." (5757822.odt, Results Expected) AND "The sidecar fund will need separate governance, most likely including a nominated staff FCDO staff member to agree each investment." (90000316.odt, Governance and Influence)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., shift from roads to PPPs) but require approval. The 2021 addendum notes pivots due to COVID-19 and ODA reductions, including removing the North East component and focusing CDEL on climate priorities. The logframe is updated every 6 months to reflect changes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a dynamic logframe updated every 6 months based on TRP recommendations. The CDEL component allows for recycling of capital if investments perform well. The 2021 addendum explicitly describes pivots in response to budget cuts (e.g., shifting from Federal to State-level PPPs) and COVID-19 (e.g., focusing on off-grid energy).
how_flexibility.quote: "The logframe is updated every 6 months based on recommendations from the programme's Technical Review Panel (TRP)..." (5757822.odt, Results Expected) AND "The programme will also seek to track some potential Greenhouse Gas emissions avoided through their work and people made more resilient to climate change..." (61400109.odt, Expected Results) AND "The plan is to deploy the CDEL alongside an InfraCredit supported low carbon fund... The duration of the programme will need to reflect this [recycling of capital]." (90000316.odt, Duration)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Tetra Tech/InfraCredit → Nigerian counterparts (e.g., NSIA, FERMA) → end beneficiaries (e.g., off-grid energy consumers)
how_efficiency.quote: "Tetra Tech’s payments link to performance under Economy and Effectiveness indicators." (61400109.odt, Value for Money Framework) AND "The payments for the fund are likely to be made from a custodian account to ensure smooth and rapid disbursement when needed for investments." (90000316.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: general budget support (rejected due to high fiduciary risk)
sector budget support (rejected due to high fiduciary risk)
project support through government PMU (rejected due to high fiduciary risk)
direct capital investments in specific infrastructure projects (rejected as inferior to technical assistance for leveraging larger volumes of Nigerian/private funds)
smaller technical assistance programme focused only on power sector (rejected due to synergies across components)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed technical assistance + blended finance model was chosen because: 1) Nigeria's middle-income status and private sector potential make leveraging (rather than substituting) local funds more cost-effective; 2) the flexibility of technical assistance allows adaptation to Nigeria's dynamic political and security context; 3) the reputation of previous NIAF phases provided influence with Nigerian counterparts; 4) blended finance addresses market failures in off-grid energy/clean cooking where commercial capital is reluctant to engage due to perceived risks.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging £80m TA to influence billions in Nigerian/private infrastructure spend)
risk mitigation (flexible TA adapts to political/security changes; blended finance de-risks private investments)
past experience (NIAF 1/2 success with Nigerian counterparts)
partner capacity (Tetra Tech's existing relationships; InfraCredit's local pension fund access)
flexibility (adaptive logframe and ability to pivot components)
equity (focus on pro-poor outcomes through climate-smart infrastructure)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Deterioration of traction with Nigerian Government counterparts as elections near (2023), reducing reform appetite
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pivot to state-level projects (e.g., PPPs in Kaduna, Kano) where governors have more stability. Focus on 'easier' entities like NSIA where traction remains strong.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient skilled FCDO resourcing to supervise the programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme-funded adviser (G6 Infrastructure Adviser) to provide technical expertise and liaison support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund is used quickly due to risks materializing (e.g., consumer repayment defaults in off-grid energy)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful investment selection and acceptance that early losses provide market learning. The 'bet' on first-loss capital may prove premature but generates valuable lessons.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in approvals (e.g., SEC for InfraCredit fund) causing spend deadline issues
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use COP26 as an incentive for management to accelerate approvals. Continuous pushing by FCDO to maintain momentum.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capital investment from third parties limited due to security/nervousness with Nigeria
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Target Nigerian investors (e.g., pension funds) who have local risk appetite. Spread investments across lower-risk states.

why_rationale.quote: "Assessment of expected benefits suggests that well targeted technical assistance will generate substantially higher returns than even a well chosen individual project. This [is] largely because the volume of capital investment the technical assistance can work with in Nigeria means that even a relatively small improvement in spend quality produces higher benefits than could be expected from a single fully funded project." (5757822.odt, Options Considered) AND "The money will be used to de-risk and leverage private sector investment in these higher risk parts of the off-grid energy sector... This will be done by deploying the money in a blended finance fund model." (90000316.odt, The Role of Finance)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Nigeria constrains partner selection by: 1) Limiting work in the North East due to Boko Haram/ISIS territory gains, forcing removal of that component; 2) Shifting PPP focus from Federal to State level due to election-related instability at the federal level; 3) Requiring partners with strong local presence (e.g., InfraCredit) to navigate regulatory and security challenges; 4) Prioritizing Nigerian pension/insurance funds as investors due to their local risk appetite.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in Borno/Yobe removed the North East component entirely
Federal election cycles reduce traction with federal ministries, shifting focus to state-level partners
Regulatory barriers (e.g., Central Bank delays) require partners with local expertise (e.g., InfraCredit)
Data limitations in off-grid sectors necessitate partners with existing local networks (e.g., REA)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The shift to climate-smart infrastructure objectives determined: 1) The creation of a separate CDEL component managed through InfraCredit's blended finance fund (rather than traditional TA); 2) The integration of ICF KPIs into the logframe (e.g., GHG emissions, energy access); 3) The focus on off-grid energy/clean cooking as sectors where market failures justified blended finance; 4) The need for local currency financing to match consumer revenue streams, shaping the fund structure.
q28_linkages: Climate objectives → Blended finance mechanism (CDEL via InfraCredit)
Off-grid energy focus → Local currency fund structure to avoid FX risk for consumers
State-level PPP emphasis → Selection of states with stable governors (e.g., Kaduna, Kano)
ICF KPIs → Addition of GHG tracking and energy access metrics to logframe
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: The shift from Federal to State-level PPPs sacrifices some national-scale impact for faster implementation where governors are more stable; 2) **Commercial Viability vs. Pro-Poor Focus**: The blended finance fund targets sectors (off-grid energy, clean cooking) where commercial lenders are reluctant, accepting higher subsidy needs for equity outcomes; 3) **Local Ownership vs. Expertise**: Nigerian institutions (e.g., FERMA) are counterparts but Tetra Tech (UK) leads delivery to ensure technical quality; 4) **Climate vs. Immediate Poverty Impact**: The pivot to climate-smart infrastructure delays some pro-poor spending (e.g., North East reconstruction) but aims for longer-term resilience benefits.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Federal vs. State focus: "PPP plans have shifted to State level projects where Governors have more stability" (61400109.odt) at the cost of national coordination
Blended finance subsidy: "Viability risks—minigrids still require some subsidy... The tariff is above 55c/KwH even with VAT and tariffs removed" (90000316.odt) to reach poorer consumers
Local vs. International leadership: "Tetra Tech manages day-to-day delivery with oversight from FCDO" (61400109.odt) despite capacity building for Nigerian institutions
Climate vs. poverty: Removal of North East component due to security (61400109.odt) despite humanitarian needs, reprioritizing climate spending
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context increases oversight intensity: 1) Quarterly reports and TRP reviews for TA component; 2) FCDO-nominated staff approval for each blended finance investment; 3) Shift from annual to milestone-based payments for Tetra Tech; 4) Embedded adviser role to manage government relations during election periods.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Embedding advisors in NSIA and Ministry of Finance to transfer skills; 2) Requiring Tetra Tech to include Nigerian experts in the Technical Review Panel; 3) Designing the blended finance fund to build local investor (pension/insurance funds) capacity in climate-smart infrastructure; 4) Prioritizing states (e.g., Kaduna) with existing capacity to absorb PPP technical assistance.
intersections.quote: "The Federal government is supportive of off grid access and the Rural Electrification Agency is a well-managed institution with whom the FCDO has good relations... The REA commercial viability assessment... ascertained that there are medium scale minigrid sites which can be viable—200kW with returns within 3 years so long as higher tariffs are charged." (90000316.odt, Off-grid Energy) AND "The programme will also seek to track some potential Greenhouse Gas emissions avoided through their work and people made more resilient to climate change..." (61400109.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks: Worsening security situation (especially in North East)
Reduced political commitment to reforms during election cycles
Failure to maintain strong partnerships with reformist counterparts (transition risk)
High fraud and corruption risks in Nigeria
Gas infrastructure attacks disrupting power sector reforms
Delays in World Bank/multilateral funding for reconstruction
Limited traction with Federal Government post-2020 ODA cuts
Consumer repayment risks in off-grid energy/clean cooking sectors
Policy reversals (e.g., tariff adjustments, PPP regulations)
Insufficient skilled FCDO staff to supervise complex blended finance
Fund deployment too rapid due to underestimated risks (e.g., minigrid viability)
Reputational damage from poorly performing investments

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Deterioration of security in North East
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Removed North East component entirely and focused on more stable states (e.g., Kaduna, Kano, Lagos).
Shifted PPP focus to state-level where governors have more stability. Targeted 'easier' entities like NSIA.
Embedded advisors in key institutions (e.g., NSIA, FERMA) and used performance-based payments for Tetra Tech.
Supported government efforts to estimate financial deficits and craft responses to maintain market liquidity.
Programme-funded G6 Infrastructure Adviser to support supervision and liaison.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Consumer repayment risks in off-grid sector
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Blended finance first-loss capital to absorb defaults. Focus on anchor commercial customers for minigrids.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in fund approvals (e.g., SEC for InfraCredit)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Used COP26 as incentive for accelerated approvals. Continuous FCDO pushing.
Technical support to regulators (e.g., NERC) to build evidence for cost-reflective tariffs.

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid direct implementation in conflict zones (North East component removed due to Boko Haram/ISIS territory gains)
State-level engagement can be more stable than federal during election periods
Local currency financing reduces FX risk for consumers in volatile economies
Blended finance required to de-risk sectors (off-grid energy) where commercial lenders are reluctant
Embedded advisors (e.g., in NSIA) build trust and navigate political economy challenges
Flexible logframes essential to adapt to security/political shocks (e.g., COVID-19, ODA cuts)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous NIAF phases demonstrated that: 1) Infrastructure reforms take decades and require sustained technical assistance; 2) Partial reforms (e.g., power privatization without tariff adjustments) can create financial black holes; 3) Nigerian counterparts value non-partisan, flexible support (e.g., quotes from NSIA CEO and Power Minister in 5757822.odt); 4) Road Asset Management Systems (RAMS) can objectively prioritize investments but require long-term institutionalization; 5) PPPs face resistance from sector ministries preferring public procurement.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Removed North East component due to worsened security (61400109.odt); 2) Shifted from Federal to State-level PPPs due to election-related traction loss (61400109.odt); 3) Added climate-smart focus and ICF KPIs post-2021 (61400109.odt); 4) Introduced blended finance CDEL component to address off-grid energy market failures (90000316.odt); 5) Combined capital budget and PPP components due to overlap (61400109.odt); 6) Reduced broader capacity building to focus on key institutions (e.g., TCN, FERMA) (61400109.odt).
risks_lessons.quote: "It may be that for a particular reform to deliver a sustained transformation 10 different difficult problems need to be solved. If 7 of the 10 have been dealt with, it may be that there will still be no transformational impact until the remaining 3 are dealt with... Until all the critical challenges are resolved there will always remain a risk that one or more binding constraint never gets dealt with." (5757822.odt, Strategic Case) AND "The 2015 Business case assumed continued stability in the North East... In practice the situation in Borno and Yobe is unsuitable for this as Boko Haram and Islamic State have gained territory and made both States too unstable for large scale investments." (61400109.odt, Results)

co_funding_partners.partner: BEIS (Business Energy and Industrial Strategy Department)
PIDG (Private Infrastructure Development Group) via InfraCredit
Nigerian pension/insurance funds (leveraged, not direct co-funding)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £10m CDEL aims to mobilize £35m in public/private finance (3.5x leverage) for off-grid energy/clean cooking. The RDEL component leverages Nigerian government and multilateral spending (e.g., influencing £500m+ reconstruction spend, though this target was later removed).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £80m RDEL (revenue for technical assistance) + £10m CDEL (capital for blended finance). The CDEL is structured as first-loss/concessional capital to de-risk private investments.
financial_details.quote: "The UK is intending to provide an additional £10m of CDEL which will bring the total of funding permitted by the Business case to £90m." (90000316.odt, Summary Information) AND "The £10m CDEL aims to catalyse £35m of public and private finance (ICF KPIs 11 and 12) by end of 2024." (90000316.odt, Expected Results) AND "Tetra Tech’s payments link to performance under Economy and Effectiveness indicators." (61400109.odt, Value for Money Framework)

metadata.programme_name: AXE-FILLES - Accès et Égalité pour l'Éducation des Filles

quote.text: This programme aims to increase girls' access to quality education in the central province of Kasai in DRC, which has the highest percentage of children out of primary school in the DRC, as well as being among the poorest regions in DRC.

duration_source.text:
Start Date: 01/04/2022
End Date: 31/08/2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct support to 60,000 marginalised girls' education), implementation research (testing approaches to improve access, retention, and quality), and policy influence (working with DRC government on education reforms). It builds evidence while delivering tangible education outcomes.

q1_source.text: This programme will help deliver the third campaign goal in the DRCCountryPlan: "DRC provides basic services to accelerate a demographic transition and sustainably reduce poverty" (SDGs 1,4,5,10). [...] Building on lessons from a one-year pilot on girls' education, this programme will improve: Access, Retention, Quality.

q3_expected_outputs.output: 60,000 children (at least 60% marginalised girls) supported to attend school
8,000 girls supported to recover education losses from COVID-19 through catch-up lessons
Improved education assessments and data quality for better decision-making
Scholarships to support girls remaining in secondary school
Better teacher training and recruitment of female teachers
Publication on girls' education in Kasai to advocate for better provincial strategies
Reduced unintended pregnancy and delayed early marriage (measured by 2023 DHS)
Increased participation in labour force (long-term impact)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform girls' education in Kasai province through direct service delivery (scholarships, catch-up lessons), system strengthening (teacher training, data improvement), and policy engagement to create sustainable change in one of DRC's poorest regions with the worst education indicators.

quote.text: By working in tandem with our Maternal and Child Health programme (SEMI), already approved by the Minister for Africa, we will improve DRC's human capital and accelerate the demographic transition, contributing to stability in this fragile, post-conflict province.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: DRC is classified as FCAS due to ongoing conflict, extreme poverty (9% of world's extreme poor), weak institutions, and recent UN peacekeeping drawdown. Kasai specifically faces high levels of gender-based violence, child marriage, and education system collapse with only 14% secondary school attendance.

q5_source.text: DRC is one of the most fragile and poorest countries globally: 9% of the world's extreme poor live in DRC, growing to a sixth by 2030 [...] Kasai, a province of 4.5 million people, has the lowest school attendance in the country (57%) [...] The prevalence of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV) is widespread: more than half of women (52%) have experienced physical violence since 15.
q5_source.source: D0004815.odt, CONTEXT and Kasai Province sections

q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (payroll fraud, 62 billion CF embezzled, unpaid teachers)
political economy (patronage, corruption in education sector)
data limitations (missing UIS data, poor learning assessments)
social norms (child marriage, GBV, gender discrimination)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit school attendance; weak institutions create payroll fraud and unpaid teachers; poor infrastructure (roads, electricity) hinders access to schools; social norms (child marriage at 10% by age 15) pull girls out of school; COVID-19 closed schools for 27M learners, increasing pregnancy rates. Data gaps make monitoring difficult, and corruption risks divert funds from intended beneficiaries.

quote.text: Decades of instability and inter-community violence have deprived millions of people of their fundamental right to education through school closures, collateral damage and military use of school buildings, fear of sending children to school together with teachers' fear of attending school due to targeted or threats of attacks and increased child marriage.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO/BEK retains strategic control and policy engagement leadership, with provincial education authorities and local NGOs implementing delivery. Decision-making on programme design and adjustments rests with UK government teams.
q10_capacity_building_details: teacher training (including female teacher recruitment)
parent and community engagement programmes
support to provincial education authorities for data management
gender unit development within Ministry of Education
SRHR education integration
safeguarding training for partners

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Primary, Secondary and Technical Education (MEPST)
partner_organizations.role: Government counterpart for policy alignment and national strategy implementation

partner_organizations.name: Kasai Provincial Education Authorities
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation of teacher training and school management

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Multilateral partner for education sector support (data, monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer for education governance reforms (£800m programme)

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Donor coordination through Technical and Financial Partners' Group (PTF)

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs (Save the Children, World Vision, Cordaid, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Community-level implementation (catch-up clubs, scholarships, GBV prevention)

partner_organizations.name: Faith-Based Organizations (FBOs)
partner_organizations.role: School management (80% of primary schools are conventionnées)

partner_organizations.name: School Parent Committees (COPAs)
partner_organizations.role: Community mobilization and accountability

quote.text: We will engage with the local Education Representative and the provincial Ministry of Education to ensure that the programme complements its regional strategies. [...] The UK is an active member and co-lead of the Financial and Technical Partners' Group (PTF) and regularly attends donor meetings, ensuring coordination and prioritisation amongst critical donors.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants to implementing partners (NGOs, provincial authorities) and technical assistance agreements with multilateral organizations (World Bank, UNICEF). Funds are channelled through vetted partners with FCDO-standard agreements, including due diligence assessments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO/BEK leads overall strategy and policy engagement, with implementation delegated to a mix of provincial education authorities, international NGOs, and multilateral partners. The structure allows for flexibility in partner selection based on local context (e.g., FBOs for school management, NGOs for community outreach).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected from a pre-approved list of vetted organizations with existing presence in Kasai (e.g., Save the Children, World Vision) and must comply with FCDO's due diligence requirements. The restricted approach mitigates risks in a high-corruption environment while leveraging local expertise.

quote.text: The programme will only be awarded to a known and vetted partner(s) approved by FCDO. Use of FCDO's standard agreement templates, Due Diligence Assessments, and ongoing risk management will ensure implementing partners understand and comply with their legal obligations.
quote.source: D0004815.odt, COMPLIANCE WITH UK LAW AND POLICY PRIORITIES section

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A steering committee with representation from FCDO, MEPST, provincial authorities, and key donors (World Bank, UNICEF) will oversee implementation. Decision-making involves joint reviews of progress against the Education Sector Strategy 2016-2025.

quote.text: Engaging at both the national and provincial levels will ensure that lessons learned through the programme shape national-level policies and reforms. [...] The UK plays an active role in setting these objectives with the Government of DRC.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., scholarships vs. teacher training) with FCDO approval, based on emerging needs identified through annual sector reviews. The mixed delivery structure allows shifts between school-based and community-based activities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an explicit adaptive management approach, with annual reviews to adjust priorities based on learning from the pilot phase and emerging data (e.g., COVID-19 recovery needs, shifts in child marriage rates).

quote.text: This programme will seek to build a better evidence base, implementing approaches that have been tested in the DRC context and have demonstrated success. This is a pragmatic approach, given the well-documented barriers to girls' education [...] Above all, understanding girls' and boys' differing needs, experiences, achievements, and outcomes in the education system are at the core of this programme analysis and design.
quote.source: D0004815.odt, WHY SHOULD THE UK ENGAGE? section

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (NGOs/provincial authorities) → Sub-grantees (schools/community groups). For multilateral components: FCDO → World Bank/UNICEF → Local execution.

quote.text: The programme will actively leverage multilateral efforts to which the UK is a key contributor (Global Partnership for Education, World Bank education sector support), ensuring that our interventions complement each other to advocate for key policy reforms.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: Scholarship programme focused on financial barriers
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Direct funding to schools/communities to cover costs (uniforms, transport, fees) for girls' education.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Non-formal education for out-of-school girls
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Targeted catch-up lessons and alternative education pathways for girls who dropped out or never attended.
Combines school-based quality improvements with community-targeted support for adolescent girls, including scholarships, teacher training, and SRHR education.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its ability to address multiple barriers simultaneously (financial, social, quality) while generating evidence on what works in FCAS contexts. The blended approach maximizes reach to marginalised girls (60% target) and leverages existing UK investments in health (SEMI programme) for synergistic impact.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (Option 3 scored highest in multi-criteria analysis with 9/10 for reaching marginalised girls)
risk-mitigation (diversified delivery reduces reliance on any single partner)
experience (builds on GEC and ACCELERE! lessons)
partner-capacity (uses vetted NGOs with local presence)
equity (explicit focus on intersecting vulnerabilities: poverty, disability, conflict)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on local partners with limited capacity in Kasai
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will provide technical assistance and embed safeguarding advisors to strengthen local systems. Only vetted partners with existing Kasai presence will be selected.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption in education payroll systems diverting funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds will bypass central government payrolls, using direct payments to provincial authorities and NGOs with robust financial controls. Regular audits and spot checks will be conducted.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Social backlash against girls' education in conservative communities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Community engagement strategies will involve religious leaders and male champions. Pilot tested approaches (e.g., girls-only clubs) will be scaled cautiously.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability post-programme without continued funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocacy for provincial education budget increases and integration of successful approaches into national Education Sector Strategy 2016-2025.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per girl reached compared to alternatives)
effectiveness (evidence from GEC on what works for girls' education)
equity (60% target for marginalised girls, disability inclusion)

quote.text: Option 3: Blending approaches that work with schools to improve access and learning outcomes for girls and boys, alongside targeted activities that specifically support adolescent girls transitioning from primary to secondary to ensure they continue with secondary education. [...] Score: 9 - The potential to reach marginalised adolescent girls is high. Delivery through a bespoke programme that can respond to multiple barriers in parallel with the flexibility to respond to the community’s needs will enable the programme to engage with more girls and their wider communities.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Kasai limits partner selection to organizations with existing security clearances, local trust, and experience navigating corruption risks. Faith-based organizations (FBOs) are essential due to their management of 80% of primary schools, despite potential conservative resistance to girls' education. Weak provincial capacity requires partners who can provide embedded technical assistance.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict partner mobility, favoring locally embedded NGOs over international staff
Corruption in education payrolls necessitates bypassing central government systems
Social norms require partners skilled in community engagement (e.g., working with religious leaders)
Limited NGO presence in Kasai reduces competition but increases reliance on fewer partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address intersecting barriers (financial, social, quality) requires a mixed delivery structure. School-based interventions (teacher training) are paired with community-level work (scholarships, GBV prevention) because: 1) Girls face different obstacles at home vs. school; 2) Evidence shows direct learning support (e.g., tutoring clubs) has larger effects than indirect financial aid alone; 3) Leveraging both formal and non-formal pathways maximizes reach in a context with 86% learning poverty.
q28_linkages: Multi-sectoral needs (education + health) → Joint delivery with SEMI programme
Multiple barriers (cost, safety, quality) → Blended scholarship + quality interventions
Weak systems → Capacity building embedded in implementation
Data gaps → Monitoring and evaluation designed to generate public goods
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are acknowledged between rapid delivery and inclusive reach. The programme prioritizes marginalised girls (60% target) despite higher costs per beneficiary, justifying this through long-term demographic dividend arguments. Trade-offs include: 1) Higher transaction costs for community-level work vs. school-based efficiency; 2) Slower scale-up to ensure safeguarding in GBV-prevalent areas; 3) Balancing direct service delivery with system-strengthening investments.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Community engagement slows implementation but is critical for sustainability
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern TAs provide quality assurance but risk undermining local capacity
Cost vs. reach: Targeting the most marginalised (e.g., girls with disabilities) increases per-capita costs
Flexibility vs. standardization: Adaptive management requires more intensive oversight
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context drives intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, embedded safeguarding advisors) and restricted partner selection (vetted organizations only). High safeguarding risks (GBV prevalence) necessitate additional layers of monitoring despite efficiency trade-offs.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited provincial capacity shifts more implementation to NGOs, while FCDO retains strategic control. Capacity building is embedded in roles (e.g., provincial authorities co-manage teacher training) to ensure skills transfer, but decision-making remains Northern-led.

quote.text: The complexity of challenges facing girls from different groups is as significant and careful understanding of the ethnic makeup of schools and/or the ethnic spread across selected intervention schools is essential. [...] Teacher wellbeing, conflict-sensitive education with teachers, child protection and safeguarding work is critical. Working with teachers and their community leaders was fundamental to supporting girls’ education.
quote.source: D0004815.odt, UK COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE ON GIRLS' EDUCATION section

key_programme_risks: Corruption in education sector (62 billion CF embezzled in payroll fraud)
Social resistance to girls' education (52% GBV prevalence, 10% child marriage by 15)
Weak provincial capacity (half of Kasai schools not on payroll)
COVID-19 learning losses (27M learners affected, spike in teenage pregnancies)
Sustainability post-funding (reliance on external donors for education financing)
Safeguarding risks (high GBV prevalence in schools)
Data gaps (missing UIS data, poor learning assessments)
Climate vulnerabilities (floods, droughts disrupting education)
Conflict recurrence (military use of schools, inter-community violence)
Disability exclusion (23% of children with functional difficulties out of school)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Bypass central government payrolls; use direct payments to vetted provincial authorities and NGOs with financial controls.
Engage religious leaders and male champions; pilot girls-only clubs; provide SRHR education to shift norms.
Embed technical advisors in provincial education offices; provide training on data management and financial oversight.
8,000 girls targeted for catch-up lessons; teacher training on accelerated learning; community catch-up clubs.
Advocate for increased provincial education budgets; integrate successful approaches into national Education Sector Strategy.
Zero-tolerance policies; whistleblowing mechanisms; regular spot checks; partner due diligence on child protection.
Commission annual sector reviews through UNESCO; improve school-level data collection on gender and disability.
School infrastructure improvements (e.g., flood-resistant buildings); climate-adaptive education planning.
Conflict-sensitive education approaches; community dialogue to prevent school militarization.
Mainstream disability inclusion in all activities; targeted support for girls with functional difficulties.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from ACCELERE! programme: Native-language instruction and interactive radio lessons improved resilience during conflicts/school closures.
Girls' Education Challenge (GEC) findings: Teacher wellbeing and community leader engagement were critical in conflict-affected areas.
Need for flexible funding to respond to sudden disruptions (e.g., COVID-19, conflict flare-ups).
Importance of embedding safeguarding in all activities due to high GBV prevalence.
Local power dynamics (e.g., ethnic makeup of schools) significantly affect enrolment and retention.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous UK programmes (ACCELERE!, GEC, REALISE) demonstrated that: 1) Direct learning support (tutoring clubs) has larger effects than financial aid alone; 2) Teacher training must address both pedagogical skills and gender biases; 3) Community engagement is essential for shifting social norms; 4) Hybrid approaches (girls-only and mixed clubs) can balance inclusion and effectiveness; 5) Data disaggregation by gender/age/disability is critical for equity.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: 1) Blended delivery model (school + community) based on GEC evidence; 2) Explicit focus on adolescent girls (not just primary) to address secondary school dropout; 3) Integration with health programme (SEMI) to tackle interconnected barriers (e.g., pregnancy, child marriage); 4) Adaptive management framework to respond to emerging risks (e.g., COVID-19 spikes); 5) Stronger safeguarding protocols based on DRC's high GBV prevalence.

quote.text: Through the Girls’ Education Challenge, we found that the complexity of challenges facing girls from different groups is as significant and careful understanding of the ethnic makeup of schools and/or the ethnic spread across selected intervention schools is essential. [...] Teacher wellbeing, conflict-sensitive education with teachers, child protection and safeguarding work is critical. Working with teachers and their community leaders was fundamental to supporting girls’ education.
quote.source: D0004815.odt, UK COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE ON GIRLS' EDUCATION section

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will leverage the UK's contributions to multilateral mechanisms (GPE, World Bank's $800m education programme) to advocate for gender-sensitive reforms and complementarity with UK bilateral funding.

quote.text: Programme Value: £35 Million [...] We will actively leverage multilateral efforts to which the UK is a key contributor (Global Partnership for Education, World Bank education sector support), ensuring that our interventions complement each other to advocate for key policy reforms to improve transparency, accountability, and management.
quote.source: D0004815.odt, Summary Sheet and WHY SHOULD THE UK ENGAGE? sections

metadata.programme_name: BUILDING THE EVIDENCE ON FORCED DISPLACEMENT – A MULTI-STAKEHOLDER PARTNERSHIP
metadata.quote: The evidence base on forced protracted displacement needs and interventions is significantly strengthened; Policies and investments on forced and protracted displacement are based on strong evidence, and as a result are better prioritized and targeted, leading to more effective and efficient programmes benefiting more people. (Document: 55822964.odt, SummarySheet)
metadata.duration_source: DFID will provide £10 million over four years (2016-2020) to the World Bank Group (WBG) Global Program on Forced Displacement (GPFD). (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) and **implementation research** (testing/scaling interventions) to improve policies and programmes for forced protracted displacement. It also includes elements of **policy influence** and **capacity building** through multi-stakeholder partnerships.
what_objectives.q1_source: The purpose is to assess the likely effectiveness, efficiency and impact of current and potential programmes on displacement, and generate new evidence to support the development of more effective policies and interventions for the displaced, hosting countries and communities. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Rigorous analytics and impact evaluations on forced displacement interventions
A shared platform for the collection and sharing of evidence across stakeholders (host governments, donors, civil society, private sector)
Pilots of innovative approaches (e.g., cash transfers, social protection systems, education interventions)
Impact evaluations of comparative outcomes in urban vs. camp settings
Policy recommendations for host governments and humanitarian actors
Synthesis of findings for global, regional, and country-level decision-makers
Leverage of additional funding from stakeholders for research and programmes (target: £8m+ from other donors)
Reduction in stunting among displaced and host communities (specific target not quantified)
Increased economic productivity among displaced and host communities (specific target not quantified)
Improved access to education for displaced children (specific target not quantified)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to generate robust evidence on what works in protracted displacement contexts, test innovative interventions, and influence global policy and practice through a multi-stakeholder partnership led by DFID, the World Bank, and UNHCR.
what_objectives.quote: The proposed partnership will support rigorous analytics and impact evaluations and make both findings, and the underpinning data, available to all. Eventually, the programme aims to develop a shared platform for the collection and sharing of evidence across host governments, donors, civil society, private sector, and other relevant stakeholders. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)** hosting displaced populations, with risks including political sensitivity, data limitations, and operational challenges in humanitarian contexts. However, the overall programme risk is rated as **moderate**, reflecting managed risks through partnerships with trusted actors (WBG, UNHCR).
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate. (Document: 55822964.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and conflict limit access to displaced populations, particularly in remote areas.
