Weak institutions in host countries (e.g., Chad) hinder service delivery. Data limitations (e.g., unreliable statistics on displacement) affect evidence quality. Political sensitivity slows policy adoption, and humanitarian funding cycles (short-term, annual) misalign with long-term displacement needs.
where_context.quote: Humanitarian contexts are challenging environments in which to conduct research, and project design will need to take account of these challenges in order to produce research outputs on time and on budget. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary); The make-up of the displaced population, in terms of education, skill levels and expectations, as well as their resources and local and regional connections (e.g. diaspora) are also significant in determining what kinds of livelihoods interventions might be successful. (Document: 55822964.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank Group (WBG) Global Program on Forced Displacement (GPFD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **multi-stakeholder partnership is initiated by DFID (UK), GPFD (World Bank), and UNHCR**, with ownership by host governments sought prior to analytical work. Decision-making power rests with Northern institutions (DFID, WBG, UNHCR), though host governments are consulted.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for host government officials on evidence-based policy-making
Knowledge-sharing platforms for humanitarian and development actors
Pilot interventions to test and scale innovative approaches (e.g., cash transfers, education models)
Technical support for data collection and analysis in host countries

partner_organizations.name: World Bank Group (WBG) Global Program on Forced Displacement (GPFD)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer; houses the programme within its Fragility, Conflict and Violence Cross-Cutting Solutions Area; conducts research and analytics
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (HQ in Washington D.C., operations global)

partner_organizations.name: UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
partner_organizations.role: Co-initiator; provides technical expertise on refugee policies and data; supports research uptake

partner_organizations.name: DFID (UK Department for International Development)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic lead; sets research priorities; oversees programme governance

partner_organizations.name: Host governments (e.g., Uganda, Jordan, Chad)
partner_organizations.role: Local ownership and policy adoption; data provision; pilot implementation

partner_organizations.name: Civil society and private sector (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Stakeholders in evidence-sharing platform; potential co-financiers

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Denmark, Switzerland, Norway, USAID, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financing and leverage (target: £8m+ from others)

who_partners.quote: The multi-stakeholder partnership will be initiated by DFID, the GPFD, and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), and will be open to other stakeholders. Ownership by relevant governments is critical to success, especially for host countries, and will be sought prior to any analytical work. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides **£10m over 4 years** to the WBG’s GPFD under a partnership agreement to establish a multi-stakeholder platform. Funds are managed by GPFD, with research priorities set jointly by DFID, WBG, and UNHCR. The agreement includes an **inception phase** (6 months) to finalize outputs and governance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured as an **open multi-stakeholder partnership** led by DFID, WBG, and UNHCR, with host governments and other donors invited to join. A **steering committee** (implied but not explicitly named) oversees research priorities, while WBG’s GPFD manages day-to-day delivery. Research is commissioned through competitive calls or direct awards to implementing partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: WBG GPFD was selected as the **trusted partner** due to its existing mandate on forced displacement, global reach, and capacity to manage multi-stakeholder research. UNHCR’s inclusion ensures alignment with refugee policies, while DFID’s leadership guarantees strategic oversight.
how_mechanism.quote: DFID will provide £10 million over four years (2016-2020) to the World Bank Group (WBG) Global Program on Forced Displacement (GPFD)... in order to establish a multi-stakeholder partnership to oversee a comprehensive programme of research activities. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **multi-stakeholder partnership** (DFID, WBG, UNHCR, host governments) oversees the programme. While not explicitly named as a 'steering committee,' the structure functions similarly, with joint decision-making on research priorities and uptake. WBG GPFD manages operational delivery, and DFID retains oversight.
how_governance.quote: The programme outputs and outcomes will be finalised and agreed between DFID and the GPFD during the proposed six-month Inception Phase. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary); Significant time and resources will be dedicated to ensuring that research outputs are widely disseminated, accessible and targeted to relevant policy and programme decision-makers. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research components **with approval** during the inception phase and based on emerging evidence. The programme allows for adjustments to country case studies and interventions based on feasibility and partner input.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted based on **new evidence or policy needs**, but changes require agreement between DFID and WBG GPFD. The inception phase explicitly includes finalizing outputs, suggesting built-in flexibility.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme outputs and outcomes will be finalised and agreed between DFID and the GPFD during the proposed six-month Inception Phase. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary); Research will focus on filling the critical gaps in current research, and answering the pressing questions on displacement, as outlined in the Strategic Case. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → WBG GPFD (implementer) → [sub-contracted researchers/NGOs for specific studies] (implied but not explicitly detailed).
how_efficiency.quote: We will finalise a detailed budget for the programme during the inception phase, as we finalise the selection of country case studies and interventions to research. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct funding to UNHCR or other humanitarian agencies (rejected due to WBG’s broader development mandate)
Bilateral research contracts with universities (rejected due to need for multi-stakeholder coordination)
Standalone DFID-managed research programme (rejected due to WBG’s existing GPFD platform)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **multi-stakeholder partnership model** was chosen to: (1) **leverage WBG’s global reach and analytical capacity**, (2) **ensure policy uptake** through UNHCR’s refugee expertise, (3) **pool resources** from multiple donors, and (4) **build host government ownership**. The WBG’s GPFD provided an existing platform, reducing startup costs and aligning with IDA18 priorities.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (WBG’s existing infrastructure reduces overhead)
risk mitigation (trusted partners with FCAS experience)
policy influence (direct link to World Humanitarian Summit and SDGs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Research fails to provide clear evidence on effective approaches
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on high-quality research methodologies and targeted uptake strategies (e.g., WBG as key partner for dissemination).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Research does not lead to policy/programme changes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embed research uptake activities and leverage multi-stakeholder partnerships for advocacy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Humanitarian contexts delay research delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Build contingency into timelines and work with trusted partners (WBG/UNHCR) experienced in FCAS.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Working in partnership creates coordination overhead
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use WBG’s existing GPFD platform to streamline governance and reduce transaction costs.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (inclusion of host governments and civil society in evidence-sharing)
why_rationale.quote: The risks of not undertaking this research far outweigh the risks of investment – there are large potential gains in terms of programme effectiveness and benefits to displaced people and the communities that host them over the longer term. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary); DFID is already a global leader in supporting high-quality, development research, and through the establishment of the HIEP has shown that quality, high-impact evidence can also be generated to inform humanitarian policies and responses. (Document: 55822964.odt, Why should DFID invest in evidence and innovation in this area?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with **operational experience in fragile states** (e.g., WBG, UNHCR). Host governments must be **willing to engage**, excluding high-risk or non-cooperative countries. Security constraints require partners with **local presence and trust** (e.g., UNHCR’s field offices).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict zones restrict access to displaced populations, favoring partners with existing field operations (e.g., UNHCR).
Political sensitivity in host countries (e.g., Chad) requires partners with diplomatic leverage (e.g., WBG).
Data limitations necessitate partners with strong analytical capacity (e.g., WBG’s GPFD).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for multi-country, multi-sector evidence** drives the **open partnership structure**, while the **focus on policy influence** requires inclusion of UNHCR and host governments. The **implementation research** component (pilots) necessitates flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., inception phase adjustments).
q28_linkages: Global scope → Multi-stakeholder partnership (to cover Sub-Saharan Africa and MENA).
Policy influence objective → Inclusion of UNHCR and host governments.
Pilot interventions → Need for adaptive management (6-month inception phase).
Data-sharing platform → Open partnership to include civil society and private sector.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **Northern expertise** (WBG/UNHCR leadership) with **Southern ownership** (host government consultation). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to WBG enable rapid startup but limit competitive selection. (2) **Cost vs. reach**: Leveraging WBG’s platform reduces overhead but may sideline local researchers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: WBG’s existing GPFD platform reduces startup time but centralizes decision-making.
Equity: Host governments are consulted but do not lead research design, risking misalignment with local priorities.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern institutions (WBG/UNHCR) drive research, while Southern partners (host governments) are primarily data providers.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** (FCAS context) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and a **6-month inception phase** to assess feasibility. High-risk areas (e.g., active conflict zones) are avoided in initial case studies.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in the partnership: Host governments receive training on evidence use, while WBG/UNHCR provide technical support. Southern partners (e.g., local NGOs) are engaged as sub-implementers for pilots but lack decision-making power.
intersections.quote: Ownership by relevant governments is critical to success, especially for host countries, and will be sought prior to any analytical work. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary); The risks of not undertaking this research far outweigh the risks of investment – there are large potential gains in terms of programme effectiveness and benefits to displaced people and the communities that host them over the longer term. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

key_programme_risks: Research fails to generate clear evidence on effective interventions.
Findings are not adopted by policymakers or practitioners.
Humanitarian contexts (conflict, insecurity) delay or disrupt research.
Partnership coordination creates overhead without added value.
Host governments resist evidence-based policy changes.
Data quality limitations undermine research credibility.
Pilot interventions fail to scale due to funding or political constraints.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Research fails to provide clear evidence
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use rigorous methodologies and target uptake through WBG/UNHCR networks.
Embed research uptake strategies and leverage high-profile events (e.g., World Humanitarian Summit).
Work with experienced partners (WBG/UNHCR) and build contingency into timelines.
Use WBG’s existing GPFD platform to streamline governance.
Seek ownership early and align research with national priorities.
Invest in data validation and triangulate sources.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, **local ownership is critical** but often lacks capacity; thus, partnerships must include technical support (e.g., WBG training).
**Flexible funding** is essential to adapt to changing contexts (e.g., new displacement crises).
**Political sensitivity** requires framing research as neutral/technical (e.g., WBG’s economic focus).
Leverage **existing platforms** (e.g., GPFD) to reduce startup risks in fragile states.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **HIEP programme** (DFID’s Humanitarian Innovation and Evidence Programme) demonstrated that: (1) **High-quality evidence can drive policy change** (e.g., Plumpy’Nut adoption). (2) **Research uptake requires active dissemination** (e.g., WBG’s role in this programme). (3) **Inception phases improve adaptability** (adopted here). (4) **Multi-stakeholder partnerships increase leverage** (target: £8m from other donors).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) A **6-month inception phase** (learned from HIEP’s adaptive management). (2) **Explicit research uptake strategies** (addressing HIEP’s lesson on dissemination gaps). (3) **Host government consultation** (responding to FCAS lessons on ownership). (4) **Milestone-based oversight** (to mitigate FCAS risks).
risks_lessons.quote: The HIEP is already having an impact on the use of evidence and innovation in the design, financing, planning and delivery of humanitarian policies, programmes and practices. (Document: 55822964.odt, Why should DFID invest in evidence and innovation in this area?); The risks of not undertaking this research far outweigh the risks of investment – there are large potential gains in terms of programme effectiveness and benefits to displaced people and the communities that host them over the longer term. (Document: 55822964.odt, Intervention Summary)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage £8m+ from other donors (e.g., Denmark, Switzerland, Norway, USAID) and in-kind contributions from UNHCR/UNICEF. Early HIEP investments helped mobilize £8m from Dutch Government, USAID, OCHA, and WFP.
financial_details.quote: Additional funding is leveraged from stakeholders for research and innovative programmes on protracted forced displacement. (Document: 55822964.odt, SummarySheet); We anticipate that this research will require minimum funding of £10m. (Document: 55822964.odt, Proposed focus of research on forced protracted displacement)

metadata.programme_name: Health Systems Research Initiative (2017-2023)
metadata.quote: "togenerate world class and cutting-edge research evidence to address keyquestions on strengthening and improving health systems that have direct relevance to decision makers and practitioners in low and middle income countries" (18711585.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "DFID will provide £8.5 million over five years from 2017/18 to 2022/23 to the joint ‘Health Systems Research Initiative’ (HSRI) programme" (18711585.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through research to strengthen health systems in LMICs, but also includes **capacity building** (e.g., grants for LMIC researchers) and **policy influence** (e.g., pathways to impact for decision-makers). The research directly informs **implementation** of health interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "to generate world class and cutting-edge research evidence to address key questions on strengthening and improving health systems..." and "The programme will encourage applications from researchers based in low and middle income countries, and all funded studies will have co-investigators from the country in which the research is taking place." (18711585.odt, Intervention Summary and Impact and Outcome)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 50 high-quality health systems research projects
q3_expected_outputs.target: at least 50

q3_expected_outputs.output: publications in peer-reviewed journals
policy briefs
pathways to impact documented
strengthened operational/implementation research capacity in LMICs
new knowledge on maternal/newborn health, malaria, TB, and mobile populations

what_objectives.summary: The programme funds interdisciplinary research to generate evidence on strengthening health systems in LMICs, with explicit pathways to influence policy and practice. It combines research grants with capacity-building for Southern institutions.
what_objectives.quote: "The headline results over the next five year phase of the programme will be to deliver at least 50 high quality health systems research projects to provide evidence about how to strengthen health systems..." (18711585.odt, Impact and Outcome)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as "moderate" risk, reflecting the complexity of health systems research in LMICs but mitigated by established partnerships and rigorous oversight.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (18711585.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The expected return of the programme is high and the overall residual risk is moderate." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The document highlights that health systems in LMICs face pressures from "interlocking social, political and economic influences" (e.g., fragile governance, natural disasters, evolving disease burdens) and notes a "scarcity of research into the health systems of conflict-affected fragile states." These constraints necessitate adaptive research approaches and partnerships with local institutions.
where_context.quote: "Developing countries have come under sustained pressure from interlocking social, political and economic influences; ranging from rapid globalisation, evolving disease burdens, natural disasters, fragile governments and governance systems; weak institutions and poor accountability." (18711585.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared through a **joint funders oversight committee** (including DFID, MRC, Wellcome, ESRC) and an **independent expert scientific panel** (coordinated by Wellcome). LMIC researchers are required as co-investigators, and the programme encourages LMIC-led bids.
q10_capacity_building_details: development grants for LMIC institutions (12-18 months)
co-investigator requirements for LMIC researchers
training through research collaboration
publicity to LMIC institutions about eligibility to lead bids
monitoring gender equity in research teams

partner_organizations.name: DFID (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funder and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Medical Research Council (MRC)
partner_organizations.role: grant administration, financial management, and peer review

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: coordinates independent expert scientific panel, financial eligibility checks

partner_organizations.name: Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder

partner_organizations.name: LMIC research institutions
partner_organizations.role: co-investigators, lead applicants (encouraged), implementation partners

who_partners.quote: "The MRC would continue to provide the grant management support with Wellcome running the independent expert scientific panel." and "all funded studies will have co-investigators from the country in which the research is taking place." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case and Impact and Outcome)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)** between DFID, MRC, Wellcome, and ESRC to pool funds. Research grants are awarded through **competitive calls** managed by MRC, with **reimbursement-based payments** to awardees. The MOU enables joint governance and leveraged funding.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **MRC administers grants** and financial systems, while **Wellcome manages the independent expert panel** for scientific review. DFID and other funders collaborate via a **Joint Funders Oversight Committee** for strategic decisions. The structure leverages existing MRC/Wellcome systems (e.g., peer review, financial due diligence) to minimize setup costs.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme uses **open competitive calls** to ensure high-quality, multidisciplinary proposals. The MRC/Wellcome’s reputation attracts top-tier applications, and the peer-review process (via the independent expert panel) guarantees rigor. DFID’s involvement ensures alignment with development priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: "The HSRI has established a transparent application process, utilising a well-managed and rigorous peer review process, using a high quality and diverse panel." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case) and "Routine investigator initiated application process supported by the online joint application submission process." (18711585.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Joint Funders Oversight Committee** (DFID, MRC, Wellcome, ESRC) meets quarterly to monitor progress and adapt to changes. The **independent expert scientific panel** (managed by Wellcome) reviews proposals. MRC handles financial reporting and grant management.
how_governance.quote: "DFID and the other funders will continue to meet quarterly to monitor progress and ensure the HSRI adapts to changes in need and context." and "Annual review meetings will be held between DFID, Wellcome, MRC and ESRC." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case and Financial Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be varied between activities during the funding period, subject to joint funder agreement. The MOU allows adjustments to align with changing priorities, but major shifts require consensus.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has evolved in response to learning from previous calls (e.g., new research areas identified by the expert panel). Quarterly meetings enable adaptive management, and the MOU includes a break clause for reassessment in 2020/21.
how_flexibility.quote: "DFID, Wellcome, ESRC and MRC staff will keep the funding position under review at regular meetings and if necessary funding can be varied between different activities and new activities may be established during the funding period." (18711585.odt, Financial Case) and "There will be a break clause at the end of financial year 2020/21 to reassess progress and priorities."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → MRC/Wellcome (joint management) → end-researchers (LMIC institutions/consortia).
how_efficiency.quote: "The cost of administering the scheme is less than 1% of our total contribution" (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case) and "Funds will be paid in arrears, at three or six monthly intervals, to the MRC." (18711585.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 0: DFID withdraws from HSRI ("do nothing")
q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID would fund health systems research only through existing Research Programme Consortia (RPCs), losing partnership benefits and reducing total funding pool.
Continue joint funding with MRC/Wellcome/ESRC, leveraging their systems and reputation to maximize quality and impact.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: DFID funds specific projects via competing organizations
q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID would procure organizations to manage health systems research, but this would incur higher setup costs and fragment oversight.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (renewing HSRI) was selected because it: 1) **leverages additional funding** (£28.5m total vs. £8.5m DFID alone), 2) **minimizes management costs** (<1% overhead), 3) **utilizes proven systems** (MRC/Wellcome’s rigorous peer review and grant management), 4) **shares risk** among partners, and 5) **enhances UK leadership** in health systems research. The joint branding and reputation attract high-quality proposals, and the structure allows adaptive management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of momentum if DFID withdraws (Option 0)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continued DFID funding ensures sustained partnership and leveraged investments from other funders.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High setup costs for new procurement (Option 2)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Avoiding procurement by renewing HSRI (Option 1) saves time and resources.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented oversight in Option 2
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: HSRI’s joint governance (Option 1) provides coherent monitoring and reduces duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputation risk if research quality declines
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MRC/Wellcome’s "gold standard" peer review and DFID’s oversight maintain high standards.

vfm_criteria_used: impact (addresses Global Goal 3 and DFID health targets)
additionality (fills gaps in health systems research funding)
quality (rigorous peer review and high competition for grants)
why_rationale.quote: "Given the costs and benefits and the associated risks outlined above, the judgement is that Option 1 (DFID continues to fund the HSRI) is the best value for money option because it: increases the overall pool of funding... represents the lowest management cost option... helps share the risk... improves funding decision processes... increases the visibility and the branding of the HSRI." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope (LMICs)** and **complex health systems challenges** (e.g., fragile states, weak institutions) necessitate partnerships with **UK research councils (MRC/ESRC)** for their technical expertise and **Wellcome** for global reputation, while requiring **LMIC co-investigators** to ensure contextual relevance. The document notes that "research into health systems of conflict-affected fragile states" is neglected, highlighting the need for specialized partners.
q27_constraints_detail: LMIC institutional capacity limits (requires MRC/Wellcome’s grant management support)
Conflict/fragility in some target countries (needs adaptive research approaches)
Data limitations in LMICs (requires robust M&E systems from partners)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for multidisciplinary, policy-relevant research** (WHAT) drives the **consortium structure** (HOW), as no single organization could provide the required breadth of expertise (health, social science, economics). The **global scope** and **complexity of health systems** necessitate a **joint funder model** to share risks and leverage diverse strengths (e.g., MRC’s grant management, Wellcome’s scientific panels).
q28_linkages: Multidisciplinary research → Requires consortium of funders with complementary expertise (MRC for biomedical, ESRC for social science, Wellcome for global health).
Policy influence objective → Needs independent expert panel (Wellcome) for credibility and joint branding for uptake.
LMIC focus → Mandates co-investigators from target countries and capacity-building components.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (e.g., LMIC-led bids, capacity building) with **efficiency** (e.g., leveraging MRC/Wellcome’s existing systems to minimize costs). For example: "The programme will encourage applications from researchers based in low and middle income countries," but also notes that "MRC grants are seen as the ‘gold standard’," which may favor Northern institutions in competitive calls. The **<1% management cost** reflects efficiency, while **development grants for LMICs** address equity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Open competition may disadvantage LMIC institutions, but development grants and co-investigator requirements mitigate this.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern funders (MRC/Wellcome) manage grants for efficiency, but LMIC researchers are embedded in governance.
Cost vs. reach: Joint funding pool (£28.5m) maximizes reach, but requires coordination overhead.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (complex LMIC contexts, high-risk research) justifies **quarterly oversight meetings** and a **joint funders committee** for adaptive management. The document states: "DFID and the other funders will continue to meet quarterly to monitor progress and ensure the HSRI adapts to changes in need and context."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building objective** (e.g., LMIC co-investigators, development grants) directly shapes partner roles: LMIC institutions are positioned as **active collaborators** (not just beneficiaries), with eligibility to lead bids and participate in governance. The MRC/Wellcome provide **backstopping** (grant management, peer review) to address LMIC capacity gaps.
intersections.quote: "Recognising that health systems are complex and multidimensional, multidisciplinary research is required that will generate evidence on how to strengthen and improve health systems... Partnering with the UK research councils and funders to invest in research into health systems strengthening will help to ensure that the funding opportunity reaches a broad range of expertise." (18711585.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Research may not achieve policy impact (high-risk, complex systems).
LMIC institutional capacity limits could hinder implementation.
Political instability in target countries may disrupt research.
Funding gaps if other partners reduce contributions.
Private sector unlikely to fill gaps (market failures in health systems research).
Fraud risk in LMIC financial management (mitigated by MRC’s due diligence).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low policy uptake of research findings
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pathways to impact are required in all proposals, with early engagement of policymakers. Quarterly reviews track progress.
Development grants (12-18 months) and co-investigator requirements build local capacity. MRC/Wellcome provide grant management support.
Flexible funding adjustments and break clause (2020/21). MRC’s internal audit includes overseas visits.
MOU locks in partner commitments (£28.5m total). DFID’s continued involvement incentivizes other funders.
MRC’s financial sanctions and due diligence (e.g., eligibility checks, audits). Wellcome advises on budgetary matters.

fcas_specific_lessons: Health systems in fragile states are under-researched; the programme prioritizes inclusive calls to address this gap.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., development grants) are critical for conflict-affected contexts.
Early engagement with LMIC policymakers increases uptake in unstable environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The first phase (2013–2016) demonstrated that: 1) **Joint funding attracts higher-quality proposals** (competition drives up standards), 2) **MRC/Wellcome’s systems are efficient** (<1% admin costs), 3) **LMIC co-investigators improve relevance** but require targeted outreach. The expert panel’s recommendations led to adjustments in research priorities (e.g., new focus areas).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **development grants** (12-18 months) to build LMIC capacity.
Strengthened **pathways to impact** requirements in proposals.
Increased **publicity to LMIC institutions** about eligibility to lead bids.
Adapted **research themes** based on panel feedback (e.g., focus on fragile states).
risks_lessons.quote: "Over the three research calls issued to date, the programme has evolved in response to learning identified by the independent expert scientific panel..." and "The HSRI has established a transparent application process, utilising a well-managed and rigorous peer review process, using a high quality and diverse panel." (18711585.odt, Appraisal Case and Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID’s £8.5m leverages £20m from other partners (total £28.5m), a 2.4:1 ratio. The partnership also leverages in-kind contributions (e.g., MRC/Wellcome’s grant management systems).
financial_details.quote: "The total funding for the programmes will be at least £28.5 million for five funding rounds... The current agreed contributions of each funder to the HSRI extension are: DFID (£8.5m), ESRC (£5m), Wellcome (£10m), MRC (£5m)." and "The cost of administering the scheme is less than 1% of our total contribution." (18711585.odt, Financial Case and Appraisal Case)

metadata.programme_name: Medical Research Council and Department for International Development Concordat (MRC-DFID Concordat)
metadata.quote: "DFID will provide funding to the UK Medical Research Council to produce a broad range of health research evidence that improves the health of the poorest people in low and lower middle income countries." (33150207.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 01 April 2018\nEnd Date: 31 March 2023" (33150207.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (health research), capacity building (African research leadership), and policy influence (evidence to inform health services). It funds biomedical and public health research while strengthening research capacity in LMICs, particularly Africa.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DFID will provide funding to the UK Medical Research Council to produce a broad range of health research evidence that improves the health of the poorest people in low and lower middle income countries. The Concordat will provide flexibility to respond to emerging global health challenges and will help build capacity for research, particularly in Africa." (33150207.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: High quality, peer-reviewed research that can change policy or practice (1457 publications from previous Concordat)
New evidence effectively communicated, shared and disseminated
Increased African research capacity and expertise (African Research Leadership scheme, 14 awards in 2017)
Effective partnership, management, governance and oversight of the Concordat
Policy influence (112 reports of policy influence from previous Concordat)
Research themes: prevention/control of infections (HIV, TB, malaria, NTDs), maternal/neonatal health, NCDs, public health
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds high-quality health research to generate evidence for improving health outcomes in LMICs, while building African research capacity and influencing global health policy.
what_objectives.quote: "The main outcomes will be the generation of new knowledge to help decision makers in the delivery of health services; and stronger leadership and partnerships including a new cadre of African scientists." (33150207.odt, Intervention Summary)

countries_regions: Low and lower middle income countries (LMICs) globally
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Research projects are inherently high-risk due to uncertainty of results, but the MRC's strong management history and potential for significant impact keep the overall risk moderate.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk is moderate. Research projects are always relatively high risk because of the uncertainty of results. The MRC has a long history of strong management of the Concordat with a wide range of successful research outcomes." (33150207.odt, Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Inequalities persist within/between countries, with worse health outcomes among the poorest. Many deaths are preventable but data often doesn't capture morbidity, creating additional burden. Women/girls are disproportionately affected by health system gaps.
where_context.quote: "Inequalities persist within and between countries, and both health and life expectancy amongst the poorest are worse almost everywhere. Many deaths are unnecessary, due to easily treatable or preventable conditions and often the data available do not measure morbidity, that is illness or disability, which create an even greater burden." (33150207.odt, Strategic Case - Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The MRC (UK-based) manages the Concordat and makes funding decisions, though African researchers participate in governance and African units (Gambia/Uganda) implement research. The African Research Leadership scheme provides some Southern decision-making in research design.
q10_capacity_building_details: African Research Leadership scheme (3-5 year awards to African researchers with UK mentors)
Support to MRC's African research units (Gambia and Uganda)
Training and mentorship through research partnerships
Institutional strengthening in Sub-Saharan Africa

partner_organizations.name: Medical Research Council (MRC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: MRC Unit The Gambia
partner_organizations.role: Research implementation and capacity building

partner_organizations.name: MRC/UVRI Uganda Research Unit
partner_organizations.role: Research implementation and capacity building

partner_organizations.name: African Research Leaders (individual grantees)
partner_organizations.role: Research leadership and implementation

partner_organizations.name: UK universities/research institutions
partner_organizations.role: Partners for African Research Leaders scheme

partner_organizations.name: Department of Health (DH)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Joint Global Health Trials

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Joint Global Health Trials

partner_organizations.name: Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)
partner_organizations.role: Partner in Joint Health Systems Research Initiative

who_partners.quote: "The Concordat with the MRC provides DFID an opportunity to support a strong portfolio of diverse, internationally competitive research... Partnership with DFID influences the breadth, nature and volume of research and capacity strengthening undertaken in the poorest countries that the MRC supports." (33150207.odt, Appraisal Case - Option 2)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The Concordat is a long-standing agreement (since 1993) between DFID and MRC to jointly fund health research. DFID provides block funding (£25m over 5 years) which MRC combines with its own resources to manage a portfolio of research grants through its existing systems.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The MRC manages the entire programme using its existing research management systems, with DFID providing oversight. No separate consortium or platform is created; funds flow through MRC's established grant-making processes.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The MRC is a "unique organisation" with a 20+ year track record of managing the Concordat successfully. Its global reputation, transparent systems, and alignment with DFID priorities make it the only viable partner for this modality.
how_mechanism.quote: "The MRC, as one of the UK Research councils, is a unique organisation with a long history of both supporting and carrying out high quality research and building research and technical capacity in health and medical research... An MRC-DFID Concordat has been in place since 1993." (33150207.odt, Appraisal Case - Option 2)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Concordat is overseen by MRC's existing governance structures, including its boards and peer review panels (which include LMIC scientists). DFID is represented in strategic discussions but does not manage day-to-day operations.
how_governance.quote: "The MRC has a long history of strong management of the Concordat... Working jointly, DFID and MRC have a greater critical mass than either working individually." (33150207.odt, Intervention Summary) \n\n "Researchfish, an online research impact reporting mechanism, has become more sophisticated and is able to provide a more comprehensive monitoring of results." (33150207.odt, Appraisal Case - External Evaluation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The Concordat allows funds to be shifted between research areas in response to emerging priorities or crises without needing to establish new mechanisms.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can respond rapidly to new global health challenges (e.g., Zika virus response in 2016) and adjust research themes as priorities evolve. Unrestricted funding enables adaptive management.
how_flexibility.quote: "The proposed aid modality (the Concordat) provides DFID and the MRC with flexibility in order to respond to crises or new priorities." (33150207.odt, Intervention Summary) \n\n "The Concordat has always been a key component of the DFID health research portfolio... It has underpinned the willingness and ability of the UK funders to jointly respond rapidly to emerging situations." (33150207.odt, Appraisal Case - Option 2)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → MRC → end-researchers (no additional intermediaries)
how_efficiency.quote: "The administration charge is very low at 1.6%. Most organisations charge much more for programme management as a proportion of total scheme funds." (33150207.odt, Economic Appraisal) \n\n "MRC utilises 1.6% of the total budget for all administration and management costs. This includes all costs for staff time, peer review, grant monitoring, etc." (33150207.odt, Economic Appraisal)

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" counterfactual (DFID would continue funding research through its own portfolio and other MRC partnerships, but lose the Concordat's flexibility and breadth)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The Concordat was chosen for its proven track record (20+ years), cost efficiency (1.6% overhead), flexibility to respond to emerging priorities, and ability to leverage MRC's global reputation and existing systems. It provides better value for money than alternatives by avoiding setup costs and utilizing MRC's mature grant management processes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk of withdrawing from a high-performing partnership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continuing the Concordat maintains DFID's influence and avoids losing leverage with MRC.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced opportunity for future health interventions if Concordat ends
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Renewing the Concordat ensures continuity in research pipelines and capacity building.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of leveraging opportunities with other UK government departments (e.g., BEIS, Department of Health)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Concordat serves as a foundation for broader HMG collaborations (e.g., Joint Global Health Trials).

why_rationale.quote: "Option 2. MRC-DFID Concordat... provides DFID with the efficiencies of a single, robust research management process... Over the past 20 years the focus of the Concordat has moved to more translational and applied research... It gives DFID a responsive funding mode that can respond to new and emerging issues fairly rapidly without the need to set up any new mechanisms." (33150207.odt, Appraisal Case) \n\n "The administration charge is very low at 1.6%... This results in savings and contributes to cost effectiveness." (33150207.odt, Economic Appraisal)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on LMICs (particularly Africa) requires partners with established presence in these regions. The MRC's African units (Gambia/Uganda) and African Research Leaders scheme address this by embedding research capacity locally.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing LMIC infrastructure (addressed by MRC's African units)
Requirement for local policy maker engagement (addressed by including LMIC scientists in governance)
Focus on African research leadership (addressed by African Research Leaders scheme)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both high-quality research and capacity building in LMICs requires a flexible, partnership-based approach. The Concordat's structure (MRC management with DFID oversight) enables this by combining MRC's research excellence with DFID's development priorities.
q28_linkages: Flexibility to respond to emerging health challenges → Concordat's adaptive management structure
Capacity building in Africa → Direct funding to African Research Leaders and MRC African units
Policy influence goals → MRC's global reputation and existing relationships with WHO/other policy bodies

intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's objectives—mobilizing private investment in climate-resilient infrastructure, operating in FCAS, and delivering systemic market transformation—determine its platform-based delivery structure. The need to provide end-to-end support (from early-stage de-risking to long-term financing) requires a diverse set of specialized facilities (e.g., InfraCos for project development, GuarantCo for local currency guarantees) working in an integrated but flexible manner.
q28_linkages: Objective: Climate action → How: Dedicated climate and nature strategy, with all investments screened for climate resilience (D0005292.odt, Climate and Nature Strategy)
Objective: Operate in FCAS → How: Facilities like InfraCo Africa and GuarantCo designed for high-risk environments, with technical assistance embedded (30423562.odt, Section 4)
Objective: Mobilize private finance → How: Blended finance model combining donor funds with private capital, with EAIF and GuarantCo playing key roles (D0005292.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

Objective: Market transformation → How: Demonstration effects and local capital market development (e.g., InfraCredit in Nigeria) to encourage replication by others (D0005292.odt, Capital market development)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between efficiency (speed, leverage) and equity (inclusivity, local ownership). For example, PIDG's use of viability gap funding (VGF) balances the need to make projects commercially viable (efficiency) with ensuring affordability for low-income users (equity). Similarly, the focus on local currency guarantees (e.g., through GuarantCo) reduces foreign exchange risks for end-users but requires complex structuring and technical assistance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion: Rapid mobilization of private finance must be balanced with ensuring projects benefit the poorest and most vulnerable (e.g., through VGF and gender lens investing).

expertise vs ownership: Northern-led technical expertise is critical for de-risking projects, but PIDG aims to build local capacity and ownership over time (e.g., through local guarantee companies like InfraCredit).
cost vs reach: Operating in FCAS and LICs increases costs (e.g., due to higher risks and technical assistance needs) but is necessary to reach the most underserved markets.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of PIDG's target markets (FCAS and LICs) necessitates intensive oversight and adaptive management. The PIDG Board and committees (e.g., Risk, Credit) play a central role in monitoring and mitigating risks, while the programme's structure allows for flexibility in reallocating funds and adjusting priorities as conditions change.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective that shapes partner roles across the programme. For example, PIDG Technical Assistance (TA) provides embedded advisors and feasibility funding to ensure projects are affordable and viable, while DevCo works with governments to strengthen PPP frameworks. The focus on local capital market development (e.g., through GuarantCo's guarantees) also builds the capacity of domestic financial institutions to finance infrastructure.

key_programme_risks: Market and political risks in frontier countries may delay or derail projects.

Regulatory and policy instability in target countries may create barriers to private investment.
Currency and inflation risks may affect the financial viability of projects.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Market and political risks in frontier countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: PIDG's risk management systems, technical assistance, and close engagement with governments and local partners help navigate challenges. The programme also diversifies its portfolio across geographies and sectors.

PIDG is working to diversify its funding base by attracting private sector investors (e.g., EAIF's capital raise) and exploring partnerships with DFIs and MDBs. The goal is to achieve financial sustainability by 2030.
The 2018 governance restructuring and the new 2023-2030 strategy include measures to strengthen group-level coordination, such as sector/industry teams and a more deliberate origination approach.

PIDG's adaptive strategy and flexible funding allow it to pivot in response to crises (e.g., COVID-19 response). The programme also focuses on building resilient infrastructure to withstand future shocks.

PIDG provides technical assistance to governments to improve enabling environments and works with local partners to navigate regulatory challenges. The programme also advocates for policy reforms through engagements with governments and multilateral institutions.

fcas_specific_lessons: Operating in FCAS requires deep local expertise and adaptive management to navigate political and security risks. PIDG's facilities (e.g., InfraCo Africa) are designed to take on early-stage risks that other investors avoid.

Blended finance and guarantees are critical tools for mobilizing private investment in high-risk environments. For example, GuarantCo's local currency guarantees have unlocked domestic capital in countries like Nigeria and Vietnam.
Technical assistance and capacity building must be embedded in project design to address weak institutions and limited local capacity. PIDG TA and DevCo play key roles in this area.

Demonstration effects are particularly important in FCAS, where successful projects can catalyze further investment. PIDG's track record in countries like Malawi and Nepal has helped attract follow-on private finance.

Partnerships with local governments and communities are essential for project sustainability in fragile contexts. PIDG's focus on inclusive stakeholder engagement helps build local ownership and resilience.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2019-2023 strategy period, which overlapped with COVID-19, demonstrated PIDG's ability to maintain delivery despite external shocks. Key lessons included the importance of adaptive management, the need for flexible funding to respond to crises, and the value of diversifying funding sources. The programme also learned that demonstration effects (e.g., first-of-a-kind projects in Vietnam and Malawi) can have outsized impacts on mobilizing private finance in frontier markets. The new 2023-2030 strategy builds on these lessons by elevating climate action, increasing focus on local capital markets, and aiming for greater financial sustainability.
design_changes_based_on_learning: The new strategy places climate action at the center of all investments, reflecting the urgent need to align infrastructure development with climate goals.
PIDG will increase its focus on local capital market development (e.g., through GuarantCo's guarantees) to reduce reliance on hard currency and mobilize domestic resources.
The programme will adopt a more targeted geographic approach, concentrating efforts in selected countries where PIDG has a strong track record and high impact potential.

PIDG will rebalance incentives for its project development companies (InfraCos) to focus more on impact and less on the number of deals, aiming for a mix of large strategic projects and scalable investments.
The strategy includes a stronger focus on urban infrastructure to address rapid urbanization trends in Africa and Asia.

metadata.programme_name: Global Security Rapid Analysis (GSRA)

quote.text: To produce research and analysis designed to inform conflict strategy, programming and policy, and address immediate needs and emerging priorities across FCDO.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: 8 February 2017 - 31 March 2022; New project end date: March 2025

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GSRA programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) and **policy influence** (informing policy decisions). It funds rapid research and analysis to address immediate needs in conflict and security, directly supporting FCDO's conflict strategy and policy priorities. The programme also includes elements of **implementation research** (testing innovative approaches) and **capacity building** (through sustained analytical partnerships).

q1_source.text: The objective of the cost extension is to continue funding rapid research and analysis on conflict and security. All outputs will be aligned with the Office of Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation (OCSM) priorities... The GSRA provides OCSM with an in-house resource through which to fund rapid research and analysis, allowing HMG and partners to address evidence gaps and gain contextual knowledge in priority and/or high risk geographies.

innovative research projects (e.g., machine learning/AI for conflict analysis)

what_objectives.summary: The GSRA programme funds rapid, policy-relevant research and analysis to inform FCDO's conflict prevention and security strategies. It combines short-term responsive research with longer-term strategic initiatives, focusing on filling evidence gaps and supporting innovative approaches to conflict analysis.

quote.text: The GSRA will support stronger evidence-based policy and decision making. The expected outcomes of the additional funding are: Greater uptake of high-quality evidence and research on security and stability in HMG's and other international donor's policy and programmes.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), where conflict and instability are key drivers of poverty and global insecurity. The documents explicitly state that by 2030, 80% of the world’s poorest people will live in FCAS, and that conflict is becoming more protracted and complex, with new forms of warfare (e.g., disinformation, illicit finance, cyber-attacks).

q5_source.text: Conflict and instability overseas are key drivers of poverty and global insecurity which affects UK interests. In recent years, the global incidence of armed conflict has been increasing, and these conflicts are becoming more protracted and complex. Insecure environments undermine development efforts. By 2030 it is estimated that 80% of the world’s poorest people will live in FCAS (OECD, 2018, State of Fragility Report).

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit field research and data collection in conflict zones. Weak institutions in FCAS reduce the reliability of local partners and data sources. Climate change exacerbates conflict risks, requiring adaptive research priorities. Data limitations (e.g., lack of real-time conflict monitoring) necessitate investments in external datasets like ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Events Database).

quote.text: The nature of warfare is also changing, with hostile states increasingly using disinformation, illicit finance and cyber-attacks to further their interests. Conflict therefore posts a clear threat to the UK, both at home and overseas. [...] The GSRA will support rapid geographic analysis which directly supports the creation of early warning capabilities as outlined in the SCF. This will include the procurement of conflict monitoring data, which is crucial for informing high quality analysis.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is centralized within FCDO's Office of Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation (OCSM). Southern partners (e.g., local researchers or NGOs) are engaged as suppliers or sub-contractors but do not hold governance roles. The programme explicitly states that partners are selected based on their ability to deliver high-quality research, not to build capacity.

lesson learning events to share best practices
support for innovative research methods (e.g., machine learning for conflict analysis)
