how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **contracts** (for direct procurement of research services), **accountable grants** (for NGO partners), and **Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs)** (for long-term partnerships). Short-term research is typically contracted, while longer-term strategic research may use grants or MOUs. The choice depends on the partner type and workstream.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by FCDO's Evidence & Analysis Team (EA) within OCSM. It operates through three workstreams: 1) Strategic Research (long-term, single supplier), 2) Rapid Geographic Analysis (multiple suppliers), and 3) Innovative Research (open calls). Each workstream has tailored delivery mechanisms, but all are overseen by FCDO.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: For **Strategic Research**, a tender process will select a single supplier (or consortium) for a multi-year agreement, ensuring in-depth exploration of key issues. For **Rapid Geographic Analysis**, suppliers may be selected through commercial contracts or non-commercial agreements, depending on demand. **Innovative Research** uses open calls to invite proposals from external suppliers, supported by FCDO leads. The approach balances competition (for quality) with flexibility (for responsiveness).

quote.text: The £500K Strategic Research workstream [...] will be managed through one multi-year agreement with a single supplier (individual partner or consortium), which will ensure an in-depth exploration of the key issues. Identifying a supplier will require a tender process to be initiated immediately after the extension period commences in April 2022. [...] The workstream will be led by the EA team, working in collaboration with FCDO’s geographic teams at Desk and Post to understand emerging priorities and requirements. It is expected that the work will be delivered through commercial and/or non-commercial suppliers, either through a single contractor or multiple contracts.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GSRA Steering Committee (chaired by the SRO) reviews progress, agrees on interventions, and tracks risks. It includes OCSM leadership, technical advisers, and may invite regional or cross-HMG representatives. Decisions on research proposals require unanimous approval by the Committee, with criteria including alignment with OCSM priorities, value for money, and dissemination plans.

quote.text: A Programme Steering Committee, which will be chaired by the SRO and include at a minimum the CSJ Group Head, CSJ Senior Conflict Adviser, and Programme Manager. The role of this committee will be to review progress against the overall programme logframe, agree on interventions to be funded through both short-term and long-term windows, and track any emerging risks to programme delivery. The committee will meet at least quarterly.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between workstreams (e.g., Strategic Research, Rapid Geographic Analysis, Innovative Research) but require Steering Committee approval. The programme is designed to respond to emerging priorities (e.g., Russia-Ukraine crisis), but major shifts would need justification and alignment with OCSM’s research strategy.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme explicitly emphasizes adaptability to emerging conflicts and policy needs. For example, the Rapid Geographic Analysis workstream is designed to be highly responsive to new or escalating conflicts, and the Innovative Research window allows for piloting new approaches. However, adjustments require Steering Committee approval to ensure alignment with strategic objectives.

quote.text: The GSRA will continue supporting innovative and catalytic research which can be scaled for broader use across HMG. [...] The workstream will be led by the EA team, working in collaboration with FCDO’s geographic teams at Desk and Post to understand emerging priorities and requirements.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (supplier/NGO/consortium) → [End researchers if sub-contracted]. The programme minimizes layers by using direct contracts or accountable grants, with FCDO managing partners directly.

quote.text: Performance-based contracting (including for accountable grants) will be used, using agreed milestones and agreed quality standards as the basis for releasing payments to partners.

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing: rely on existing funding options for research (e.g., K4D Helpdesk, RED conflict research, Evidence Into Action)
New programme focused only on short-term research activities
New programme combining short and long-term research activities (CHOSEN OPTION)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed short- and long-term research model was selected because it balances **flexibility** (rapid response to emerging conflicts) with **strategic depth** (multi-year research on key questions). This approach builds on lessons from DFID’s previous CHASE Policy Research Fund, which demonstrated that combining both types of research maximizes policy impact while reducing transaction costs. The current design also aligns with FCDO’s need for both immediate analysis (e.g., early warning) and longer-term evidence (e.g., conflict prevention strategies).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor performance by long-term research partners could undermine strategic workstream outputs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year agreements include review/break points to terminate underperforming partners. Due diligence and performance-based contracting are used to select and monitor suppliers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management burden from coordinating multiple short-term contracts and open calls.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme uses a dedicated Evidence & Analysis Team (EA) within OCSM to manage partnerships, with support from the Steering Committee for prioritization.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from funding research in high-risk FCAS contexts (e.g., contact with extremist groups).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence assessments for all partners, adherence to DFID Ethics Principles for Research, and clear contractual clauses on duty of care.

quote.text: Based on the analysis above, we conclude that option 3 (a new programme combining both short and long-term research activities) represents the best model to meet the need set out in the Strategic Case. Evidence supporting the choice of programme design is strong, given DFID’s extensive experience with a wide range of research partnerships. [...] This option combines the advantages of option 2 [short-term] with a number of further benefits: it enables DFID and other departments to form an ongoing relationship with high quality partners [...] and proportionately reduces programme management requirements.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS operating environment limits partner selection to organizations with proven capacity to work in high-risk, data-scarce contexts. For example, the programme prioritizes suppliers with existing conflict monitoring capabilities (e.g., ACLED) or expertise in political economy analysis (e.g., Chemonics). Local partners in FCAS are rarely directly engaged due to security and capacity constraints, leading to reliance on international NGOs or research consortia.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in FCAS exclude many local researchers from direct partnerships.
Data limitations require investment in external datasets (e.g., ACLED), favoring partners with global data access.
Weak institutions in FCAS reduce reliance on government partners, shifting focus to NGOs/think tanks.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, policy-relevant research** drives the use of flexible, short-term contracts and open calls (e.g., Innovative Research workstream). Conversely, the requirement for **strategic, multi-year evidence** (e.g., conflict prevention questions) necessitates long-term partnerships with consortia. The mix of instruments (contracts, grants, MOUs) directly reflects the dual objectives of responsiveness and depth.
q28_linkages: Short-term research → Open calls/contracts for agility.
Long-term research → Multi-year agreements for depth.
Innovative research → Competitive pilots to test scalability.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritizes **efficiency and speed** (e.g., using established international suppliers) over **local ownership**. While Southern partners are engaged as sub-contractors or data providers, decision-making remains Northern-led. The documents note that capacity building is embedded but not a core objective, reflecting a trade-off between rapid delivery and inclusive partnerships.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (e.g., PRP consortium) vs. Southern ownership (limited local leadership roles).
Speed (direct contracts) vs. inclusion (competitive processes may exclude smaller Southern organizations).
Cost efficiency (single suppliers for long-term research) vs. diversity (fewer local partners).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context increases oversight intensity (e.g., quarterly Steering Committee reviews, due diligence for all partners). Security risks also centralize management within FCDO/OCSM rather than delegating to local partners.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded but secondary to evidence generation. For example, sustained analytical partnerships aim to improve FCDO’s internal uptake of research, while innovative research pilots (e.g., machine learning) may build technical skills in partner organizations. However, the primary role of partners remains delivery, not capacity development.

quote.text: The programme will be managed by the Evidence & Analysis Team (EA) within the Office of Conflict, Security and Mediation (OCSM). Gender mainstreaming will remain a requirement for all projects. [...] The £500K Strategic Research workstream will focus on two/three research questions aligned to OCSM’s research strategy, and underpinned by the objectives and shifts identified in the SCF related to conflict prevention. The emphasis will be on bridging the gap between theory and practice, providing FCDO advisors and other practitioners with the 'how'.

key_programme_risks: Programme fails to deliver quality research outputs (Major/Possible).
Research findings not translating into practice due to poor dissemination (Major/Possible).
Reputational risk from funding activities that inadvertently cause harm (Major/Unlikely).
Security risk to implementers working in fragile states (Moderate/Possible).
Programme does not achieve value for money (Moderate/Possible).
Financial risk and fraud (Moderate/Major/Possible).
Poor performance by long-term research partners (High impact if realized).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Programme fails to deliver quality research outputs.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Only high-quality experts and organizations will be commissioned. Performance-based contracting with milestones and break clauses.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Research findings not translating into practice.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dissemination plans agreed upfront with departments; Steering Committee ensures alignment with policy needs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk including DFID funding being used for harmful purposes.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Due diligence assessments for all partners; DFID Ethics Principles for Research shared with implementers.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Security risk to implementers in fragile states.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Contracts specify that duty of care is the supplier’s responsibility; partners must comply with DFID security protocols.
Due diligence for all partners (including downstream); quarterly financial reporting; annual audits.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict prevention is more cost-effective than response ($5–70 billion saved annually globally).
Early warning systems require real-time data (e.g., ACLED) and rapid analysis capabilities.
Innovative methods (e.g., machine learning for conflict forecasting) can improve responsiveness but require piloting.
Local context expertise is critical but must be balanced with security constraints.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on DFID’s CHASE Policy Research Fund (PRF), which demonstrated that combining short-term flexibility with long-term partnerships maximizes policy impact. Lessons included: 1) Short-term research must align with immediate policy windows; 2) Long-term partnerships reduce transaction costs; 3) Dissemination within government is as critical as research quality. The 2021 Annual Review noted that more attention to internal FCDO dissemination improved uptake.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Extended programme duration (3 years instead of 1) to allow for longer-term research and reduce the limitations of short project cycles.
Added a **Strategic Research** workstream to focus on 2–3 key questions aligned with the cross-HMG Strategic Framework for Conflict (SCF).
Increased emphasis on **innovative research** (e.g., AI/machine learning) based on successful pilots.
Stronger internal dissemination processes (e.g., SRO-led engagement) to address prior gaps in FCDO uptake.

quote.text: The programme has performed well to date: scoring an A in 2018, an A+ in 2019, 2020, and an A in 2021. The programme consistently meets all log-frame targets, but in the last AR it was noted that more attention should be paid to dissemination within FCDO. This has been addressed in 2021–2022 through the SRO taking a more hand-on approach to dissemination. The intention to streamline the research we produce around key evidence questions is intended to further improve take-up and impact within the organisation.
quote.source: D0003595.odt, KEY CHANGES TO THE ORIGINAL BUSINESS CASE

quote.text: The £5.52 million will be spent over three financial years (2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25) until the closure of the GSRA programme at the end of March 2025. This will provide £1.84 million of funding per year. This will enable the GSRA to fund the following: Strategic Research (£500k), Rapid Geographic Analysis (£940k), Innovative Research (£400k).

metadata.programme_name: Supporting Inclusive Growth in Somalia (SIGS)
metadata.quote: The SIGS programme (£38m, 2020–2027) will be the UK’s flagship economic development programme in Somalia. (Document: 57397679.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The SIGS programme (£38m, 2020–2027) will be the UK’s flagship economic development programme in Somalia.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SIGS combines implementation research (testing interventions in high-value sectors), financing mechanisms (leveraging investment and improving financial sector access), and capacity building (strengthening SMEs, financial institutions, and policy actors). It also includes evidence generation to inform policy and practice.
what_objectives.q1_source: SIGS will deliver activities to: Develop/diversify businesses in 3-4 high-value sectors; Stimulate investment through developing the financial sector and related policy/regulatory capacity; Develop the evidence base on inclusive, sustainable, economic development in Somalia. (Document: 57397679.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Leverage up to £60m in investment (financing mechanism)
Deliver over £30 million in increased incomes (implementation research)
Create/retain up to 20,000 jobs, including for women and youth (service delivery/capacity building)
Improved SME access to knowledge, skills, technology, and networks (capacity building)
Improved linkages to domestic and international markets (implementation research)
Improved public goods in target sectors (policy influence)
Increased availability of appropriate finance and financing options (financing mechanism)
Increased evidence on sustainable private sector development in Somalia (evidence generation)
what_objectives.summary: SIGS aims to stimulate inclusive economic growth in Somalia by addressing systemic constraints through a mix of financing, capacity building, and evidence generation, with a focus on high-value sectors, financial sector development, and policy reform.
what_objectives.quote: Impact: Stimulate inclusive growth that reduces poverty, vulnerability and the drivers of instability. Outcome: Support inclusive growth in higher value more sustainable activities/sectors. (Document: 57397679.odt, Theory of Change)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Somalia is one of the world’s poorest and most fragile states, with persistent humanitarian crises, extreme vulnerability to climate change, weak institutions, and active conflict (Al-Shabaab control over 12 districts). The programme is rated 'Major' risk by DFID.
where_context.q5_source: Somalia is one of the world’s poorest and most fragile states and one of the most challenging operating environments in which DFID works. [...] Almost 70% live below the international ($1.90 a day) poverty line, [...] nearly one in seven of Somalia’s 14.7m people are internally displaced as a result of conflict and humanitarian crises. (Document: 57397679.odt, Department Country Development Diagnostic)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (low tax-to-GDP ratio, limited state legitimacy)
data limitations (no statistically representative poverty estimates, limited enterprise data)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit physical access to certain regions, forcing reliance on local partners. Weak institutions and corruption require intensive oversight (e.g., Third Party Monitoring). Climate shocks disrupt agricultural/livestock sectors, requiring adaptive programming. Data gaps hinder evidence-based targeting, necessitating rapid surveys and proxy metrics.
where_context.quote: Al-Shabaab controls and administers 12 districts within the country [...] illicit markets and informal economies dominate. [...] The effects of climate change pose a significant risk to the economy, government revenue and security. (Document: 57397679.odt, Context: Overview of poverty, the economy and additional Covid-19 impacts)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight and approval authority, with implementing partners (likely Northern-led firms) managing day-to-day delivery. Southern partners (Somali institutions, MSMEs) are beneficiaries and sub-grantees with limited decision-making power.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to Central Bank of Somalia and financial institutions (via World Bank/IFC programmes)
business development services for MSMEs (e.g., skills training, market linkages)
policy/regulatory capacity building for ministries (e.g., AML/CFT, financial inclusion)
climate resilience training for sectors like agriculture
gender and social inclusion (GESI) mainstreaming across activities

partner_organizations.name: World Bank Group
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and implementer (Multi-Partner Fund, SCORE, SCALEDUP, SICRP, FIDEP programmes)

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: financial sector development, investment climate reforms

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (GEEL programme, de-risking instruments)

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (ILED programme, investment vehicles)

partner_organizations.name: UNDP/UNIDO
partner_organizations.role: youth entrepreneurship, SME support, ministry technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: Central Bank of Somalia
partner_organizations.role: beneficiary (capacity building, regulatory reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Somali MSMEs
partner_organizations.role: direct beneficiaries (financing, training, market access)

partner_organizations.name: Somali Ministry of Commerce/Finance
partner_organizations.role: policy/regulatory reform beneficiaries

who_partners.quote: It will partner and leverage the resources of others, notably the World Bank and USAID. [...] SIGS provides both an immediate response to the economic effects of Covid-19 and a systemic (micro, meso, macro) response to the constraints outlined. (Document: 57397679.odt, Programme summary and UK’s comparative advantage)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument appears to be **contracts** (for implementing partners) combined with **grants** (for financial sector interventions and MSME support). The programme also leverages **blended finance** through partnerships with DFIs (e.g., IFC) and multilateral trust funds (e.g., World Bank’s Multi-Partner Fund).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as the funder and strategic overseer, with a lead implementing partner (likely a Northern firm) managing a consortium of sub-contractors and local partners. The structure includes coordination with multilateral programmes (World Bank, IFC) and alignment with Somali government priorities, but no direct funding to government systems.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The FCAS context and need for rapid Covid-19 response likely justified a restricted competition to select partners with proven experience in Somalia (e.g., prior work on PIMS or SERS programmes). The document emphasizes the UK’s "track record of delivering flexible and adaptive economic development programmes in fragile states."
how_mechanism.quote: As a flexible and adaptive programme, SIGS is designed to respond to budget and other changes; continuing to develop and build on past gains. (Document: 57397679.odt, Key UK supported programmes)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Sub-awards to MSMEs and financial institutions are likely allocated through a joint process involving the implementing partner, FCDO, and multilateral actors (e.g., World Bank’s apex fund for MSMEs). The document notes SIGS will "partner and leverage the resources of others," suggesting collaborative decision-making.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly detailed, the programme’s coordination with the World Bank, IFC, and Somali government (e.g., Economic Development Pillar Working Group) implies a steering committee-like structure. The UK chairs this Working Group, indicating a leadership role in governance.
how_governance.quote: Risk mitigation and management processes established by DFID Somalia under our Enhanced Risk Management Strategy will be used, including comprehensive Third Party Monitoring (currently delivered for all DFID Somalia programmes by an independent contractor). (Document: 57397679.odt, Counter Terrorist financing)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed as "flexible and adaptive" to respond to Covid-19 and other shocks. A 10% financial buffer is built into Activity 1 (agriculture sectors) to address climate extremes, and targets may be iterated during implementation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: SIGS emphasizes adaptive management with milestone-based reviews (e.g., annual reviews) to adjust priorities. The programme’s Theory of Change allows for iteration in intermediate outcomes (e.g., sector selection, financing options) based on context changes.
how_flexibility.quote: SIGS will be a flexible and adaptive programme and indicators and targets may iterate during the life of the programme. [...] Based on this approach, activities 1 and 2 are eligible to be classified as ICF. (Document: 57397679.odt, Climate and Environment)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (consortium lead) → Sub-contractors/Local Partners (e.g., Somali financial institutions, MSMEs). Multilateral partners (World Bank, IFC) operate in parallel but are coordinated through the programme.
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will deliver Value for Money. For example, on effectiveness, sector development work will generate a return on investment of approximately £9 for each £1 spent. (Document: 57397679.odt, Results)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct budget support to Somali government (rejected due to corruption/weak PFM)
Standalone sector-specific projects (rejected for lack of systemic impact)
Pure humanitarian aid (rejected as not addressing root causes of fragility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **flexible, adaptive consortium model** was chosen to: 1) **Mitigate FCAS risks** (e.g., corruption, conflict) through intensive oversight and Third Party Monitoring; 2) **Leverage UK comparative advantage** in financial sector reform and debt relief advocacy; 3) **Build on past successes** (e.g., PIMS programme’s £13.1m private investment mobilized); 4) **Respond to Covid-19** with rapid, systemic interventions; 5) **Align with Somali government priorities** (e.g., National Development Plan) while avoiding direct funding to weak institutions.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (high ROI projected: £9 return per £1 spent in sector development)
risk-mitigation (Third Party Monitoring, restricted partner selection)
experience (UK’s track record in Somalia, e.g., PIMS, SERS)
partner-capacity (World Bank/IFC’s existing programmes in Somalia)
equity (focus on women, youth, IDPs, and marginalized clans)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Elite capture: Dominant clans/businesses may divert funds or block reforms to maintain status quo.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted support to MSMEs and marginalized groups; conflict-sensitive analysis; public-private dialogue mechanisms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption in financial flows: Risk of funds being siphoned via informal channels or Al-Shabaab taxation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Comprehensive due diligence on partners; Third Party Monitoring; AML/CFT compliance support to Central Bank.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation delays due to weak state capacity: Slow regulatory reforms or policy uptake.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Parallel tracks for immediate Covid-19 response (e.g., remittance support) and long-term systemic work (e.g., apex fund for MSMEs).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks disrupting activities: Droughts/floods may derail agricultural/livestock interventions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: 10% financial buffer for climate adaptation; focus on climate-resilient sectors; contingency planning linked to seasonal forecasts.

why_rationale.quote: The UK has the expertise and experience to deliver, with a track record of leadership in economic development in Somalia and strong long-standing relationships with the Somali Government and strategic partners such as the IFC, World Bank, the EU, and US. [...] Our partnership with others like the US provides a stronger approach in our influencing work. (Document: 57397679.odt, UK’s comparative advantage)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **Proven FCAS experience** (e.g., prior work in Somalia); 2) **Robust risk management systems** (e.g., AML/CFT compliance for financial sector partners); 3) **Local legitimacy** (e.g., clan networks or government relationships to navigate political economy). Small/local firms are excluded as direct implementers due to weak capacity and corruption risks, though they may be sub-grantees.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks exclude international partners without local presence/protection.
Regulatory gaps (e.g., no microfinance laws) require partners with policy influence capacity.
Clan politics necessitate partners with conflict-sensitive approaches.
Data limitations favor partners with existing Somali networks for rapid surveys.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objective** (financing + capacity building + evidence) requires a **multi-layered structure**: 1) **Financial sector reforms** → Partnered with World Bank/IFC (multilateral leverage); 2) **MSME support** → Local implementing partners with business development expertise; 3) **Policy influence** → Embedded in Somali government working groups (e.g., Economic Development Pillar). The need for **adaptive management** (Covid-19/climate) drives the choice of a flexible consortium over rigid grants.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (e.g., enterprise surveys) → Informs sector selection for financing.
Financial sector strengthening → Enables MSME access to credit (linking macro/meso/micro).
Climate resilience focus → Shapes partner selection (e.g., agri-tech firms for drought-resistant crops).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid Covid-19 response risks sidelining marginalized groups (e.g., nomads, IDPs) without targeted outreach. Mitigation: Disaggregated indicators by gender/social inclusion. 2) **Elite capture vs. scalability**: Supporting large conglomerates (e.g., telecoms) for quick wins may entrench inequality. Mitigation: Parallel MSME/diaspora-focused tracks. 3) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK-led design ensures technical rigor but limits Somali institutional leadership. Mitigation: Capacity building for Somali ministries and apex fund governance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Leveraging World Bank/IFC for quick regulatory reforms vs. Equity: Ensuring minority clans benefit.
Cost: High oversight (Third Party Monitoring) vs. Reach: Expanding to rural areas with limited infrastructure.
Expertise: Northern firms lead financial sector work vs. Ownership: Somali Central Bank’s limited decision-making role.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight**: 1) Third Party Monitoring for all activities; 2) Milestone-based payments (not upfront); 3) Restricted partner selection (no open competition). The **high flexibility** in fund reallocation is balanced by **rigorous due diligence** on sub-grantees.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) **Implementing partners** must embed GESI and conflict-sensitivity training; 2) **Financial institutions** (e.g., Gargaara) receive TA to improve MSME lending; 3) **Somali ministries** are supported to lead public-private dialogue, gradually taking over regulatory functions.
intersections.quote: The success of large Somali firms has complex consequences for stability in Somalia. Highly influential business networks that have a commercial interest in maintaining a level of ‘stable instability’—with strong influence over political elites. (Document: 57397679.odt, Specific characteristics of the Somali private sector)

key_programme_risks: Political economy risks: Elite capture by dominant clans/businesses resisting inclusive reforms.
Security risks: Al-Shabaab disruption of activities or taxation of beneficiaries.
Financial risks: Diversion of remittance/financing flows to illicit actors.
Climate risks: Droughts/floods derailing agricultural/livestock interventions.
Implementation risks: Weak Somali institutional capacity delaying reforms.
Reputational risks: UK associated with corruption or ineffective aid in fragile context.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Target 30% of funds to women/youth-led MSMEs; conflict-sensitive analysis; public-private dialogue platforms.
Avoid direct implementation in contested areas; use local partners with clan legitimacy; digital/remote delivery where possible.
Third Party Monitoring; AML/CFT compliance support to Central Bank; payment-by-results for partners.
10% financial buffer; focus on climate-resilient sectors (e.g., fisheries over livestock); seasonal forecasting.
Parallel tracks: immediate Covid-19 support (e.g., remittances) + long-term institutional strengthening (e.g., apex fund).

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible programmes with **short-term milestones** outperform rigid designs in FCAS (lesson from PIMS).
**Clan-sensitive approaches** are critical: "Significant social, political and economic exclusion occurs for Bantu Jareer and the Yobir, Gabooye and Tumaal communities."
**Blended finance** (e.g., IFC guarantees) can de-risk private sector engagement where commercial banks fear instability.

**Conflict-sensitive business support** must address both economic and political drivers: "Large firms with greater fixed assets develop productive relationships with conflict actors to protect their assets."
**Mobile money** (73% penetration) is a more effective channel than formal banking in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: From **PIMS (2014–2019)**: 1) **Extended timeframes** are needed for FCAS (PIMS took 5 years to show impact); 2) **Sector coordination** is critical (e.g., linking livestock, fisheries, and financial sectors); 3) **Climate buffers** must be built into budgets (PIMS used a buffer for the 2016/17 drought); 4) **Women’s economic empowerment** can backfire without safeguards (e.g., increased GBV risk with income gains). From **SERS (2017–2020)**: Multilateral partnerships (e.g., World Bank MPF) accelerate policy reforms but require intensive UK coordination.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Added 10% climate buffer** to Activity 1 (learned from PIMS drought response). 2) **Stronger GESI focus**: All indicators disaggregated by gender/social inclusion; standalone GESI analysis in inception. 3) **Conflict-sensitivity mandatory**: Lessons from PIMS on elite capture led to explicit political economy analysis requirements. 4) **Adaptive management framework**: Formal milestone reviews to adjust priorities (response to Covid-19 lessons).
risks_lessons.quote: Lessons learned: The need for flexible and adaptive programmes in FCAS that couple long-term goals with short-term milestones and flexible contracts. [...] Building in extended timeframes for all programme elements from design to completion. (Document: 57397679.odt, Lessons learned)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Up to £60m in investment leveraged; £30m in increased incomes generated.
financial_details.quote: Headline results will include leveraging up to £60m in investment; over £30 million in increased incomes, and up to 20,000 new/retained jobs. [...] The programme will deliver Value for Money. For example, on effectiveness, sector development work will generate a return on investment of approximately £9 for each £1 spent. (Document: 57397679.odt, Results)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Public Financial Management in Tanzania
metadata.quote: "This programme will support the Government of Tanzania to make better fiscal policies, improve allocation of financial resources and spend them efficiently and effectively." (24053414.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £20m over five years to the Government of Tanzania and to other organisations working in Tanzania through this intervention." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening PFM systems and institutions), policy influence (supporting fiscal/tax policy reforms), and service delivery (improving budget execution for better public services). It also includes a financing mechanism (multi-donor basket fund) and implementation research (piloting local government reforms).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This intervention seeks to address these challenges by strengthening policy-making and public financial management in Tanzania complementing other work happening across HMG to improve the business environment." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved fiscal and tax policies contributing to revenue mobilisation (target: 16.5% of GDP by FY 21/22, up from 15.7% baseline)
Enhanced public capital spending (target: 8.5% of GDP by FY 21/22, up from 7.5% baseline)
Improved budget execution (target: ≤10% deviation from approved budget by FY 21/22, down from 15% baseline)
Reduced arrears (target: <1% of GDP by FY 21/22, down from 2% baseline)
Strengthened financial accountability (target: 90% unqualified audit opinions by FY 21/22, up from 86%/81% baseline)
Procurement compliance improved (target: 80% by FY 21/22, up from 74%/69% baseline)
PFM systems rolled out to all 26 regions and 188 LGAs (up from 10 regions/67 LGAs)
Scholarship scheme for 5 MoFP staff (3 women) in first year
Policy advocacy through local think-tanks
Flexible fund for business environment initiatives

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Tanzania's public financial management by improving fiscal policies, budget execution, and financial accountability while scaling up local government reforms and supporting a conducive business environment.
what_objectives.quote: "This will help support Tanzania to (a) Improve fiscal and tax policies that contribute to revenue mobilisation and policy certainty (b) Enhance public spending in economic and social sectors (c) Improve budget execution and (d) Strengthen financial accountability." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is explicitly rated as HIGH risk due to political and economic transition challenges, including centralization of power, policy uncertainty affecting investors, and institutional weaknesses despite strong political commitment to reforms.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: High" (24053414.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The programme is assessed as HIGH risk, and is within DFID’s risk appetite." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The weakening business environment (due to radical contract reviews and new economic policies on natural resources) poses risks for private investment and growth. Increasing centralization of power risks undermining local governments, while limited private sector engagement on policy issues affects dialogue. Policy uncertainty and aggressive tax collection have lowered growth projections from >7% to ~6.6-6.7%.
where_context.quote: "Challenges: At the same time, radical measures being taken to review contractual arrangements with the private sector pose significant risks for the investment climate. [...] The aggressive approach to tax collection and the prevailing policy uncertainty is affecting business sentiment." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with the Government of Tanzania, with DFID as the lead donor and chair of the PFM Development Partners Group. Decision-making involves joint steering committees (e.g., Joint Steering Committee of PFMRP V) and strategic dialogue mechanisms between GoT and donors.
q10_capacity_building_details: long-term technical assistance to MoFP and TRA
scholarship scheme for MoFP staff via British Council
training for local government PFM reforms
policy advocacy support through local think-tanks
HMRC support to TRA for IT security, ethics, and transparency

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania (Ministry of Finance & Planning, TRA, PO-RALG)
partner_organizations.role: primary beneficiary and co-implementer

partner_organizations.name: DFID
partner_organizations.role: lead donor and programme manager

partner_organizations.name: HMRC
