who_partners.quote: "DFID, as Chair of the PFM donor group, led a group of seven bilateral basket fund donors on PFMRP IV. It also acts as the co-chair of the Joint Steering Committee of the PFM reform programme." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses (1) a multi-donor basket fund for financial aid to PFMRP V (£11m), (2) technical assistance contracts for MoFP/TRA support (£6m), and (3) a flexible fund for HMG initiatives (£3m). The basket fund pools DFID's contribution with other donors (Norway, Denmark, Finland) under government leadership.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID chairs the PFM Development Partners Group and co-chairs the Joint Steering Committee with the Government of Tanzania. The programme involves multiple stakeholders (donors, government, HMRC, British Council, think-tanks) with coordinated but distinct roles. Technical assistance is managed through separate contracts, while the flexible fund allows adaptive support.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct engagement with GoT and pre-selected partners like HMRC/British Council)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Government of Tanzania is the primary partner due to its ownership of PFMRP V, while HMRC and British Council are selected for their specialized expertise in tax administration and scholarships, respectively. Think-tanks are chosen based on local reputation.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID, as Chair of the PFM donor group, led a group of seven bilateral basket fund donors on PFMRP IV. [...] The programme will provide opportunities for building partnerships with UK institutions like HMT and HMRC." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary and Strategic Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Joint Steering Committee of PFMRP V, co-chaired by DFID and the Government of Tanzania, oversees the basket fund. The PFM Development Partners Group (chaired by DFID) coordinates donor engagement. Technical assistance and flexible fund initiatives are managed through separate agreements with specific oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through reviews done every six months, where decisions will be taken to scale activities up or down based on performance and need." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary) and "DFID, as Chair of the PFM donor group, led a group of seven bilateral basket fund donors on PFMRP IV. It also acts as the co-chair of the Joint Steering Committee of the PFM reform programme." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on six-monthly reviews, but major shifts require approval. The flexible fund (£3m) is explicitly designed for adaptive use.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes six-monthly reviews to adjust activities based on performance and context changes. The flexible fund allows responsive support to emerging priorities in business environment improvements.
how_flexibility.quote: "This programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through reviews done every six months, where decisions will be taken to scale activities up or down based on performance and need." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (GoT, HMRC, British Council, think-tanks) → End beneficiaries (no further sub-grantees mentioned).
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme is intended to be flexible to adapt to changes in context through reviews done every six months [...]" (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary) implies milestone-based disbursements.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID invests no additional funding; PFM reforms continue at lower level without UK support.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: PFM Reforms including support on Tax Administration
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Comprehensive support for both PFM and tax reforms, but risks tolerance for non-performance by TRA.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: PFM Reforms not including support on Tax Administration (preferred)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focuses on PFM while maintaining engagement with TRA through technical assistance only.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (PFM reforms without tax administration funding) was chosen to (1) align with GoT’s PFMRP V priorities, (2) scale up local government support, (3) minimize risk of failure due to TRA’s poor performance, and (4) maintain flexibility to reconsider tax support if TRA improves. It balances strategic alignment with risk mitigation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited leverage over Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA) due to excluding financial support for tax administration reforms.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continue technical assistance through HMRC to maintain engagement and monitor TRA performance for potential future support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges in multi-donor basket fund (PFMRP V).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s role as chair of the PFM Development Partners Group and co-chair of the Joint Steering Committee ensures strong oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Policy uncertainty and centralization affecting local government reforms.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Scale up support to all 26 regions to strengthen downstream PFM and use strategic dialogue mechanisms with GoT.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3: PFM Reforms not including support on Tax Administration. This is the preferred option. [...] It aligns well with the government’s PFM Reform Programme V; enables DFID to scale up its support to all Regions/Local governments; minimises risk of failure on tax administration, while keeping open the option of future support." (24053414.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political and institutional context in Tanzania constrains partner selection by necessitating strong government ownership (e.g., PFMRP V must be GoT-led) and limiting direct engagement with the private sector due to policy uncertainty. The centralization of power also requires working through presidential directives and MoFP leadership.
q27_constraints_detail: Government ownership requirement (PFMRP V must be GoT-led)
Limited private sector engagement due to policy uncertainty
Need to align with presidential priorities and MoFP leadership
Donor coordination required through existing platforms (PFM Development Partners Group)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for multi-level PFM reforms (central + local government) determines the mixed delivery structure (basket fund for national reforms + scaled-up technical assistance for local governments). The inclusion of business environment improvements requires a flexible fund to respond to emerging priorities.
q28_linkages: Scaling to 26 regions/LGAs → requires technical assistance component alongside basket funding
Business environment focus → necessitates flexible fund for adaptive initiatives
Policy advocacy needs → leads to engagement with local think-tanks
TRA’s poor performance → shifts from financial support to technical assistance only
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses balancing efficiency (e.g., rapid scaling of local government reforms) with equity (e.g., ensuring women’s participation in scholarships and capacity building). There is also a trade-off between technical improvements (easier to achieve) and structural changes (requiring long-term engagement).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed of scaling (all 26 regions) vs. depth of institutional change
Technical assistance (short-term gains) vs. structural reforms (long-term impact)
Women’s inclusion in scholarships (3/5 in first year) vs. broader gender mainstreaming
Efficiency of basket funding vs. flexibility needs for business environment initiatives
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (political/economic transition) leads to intensive oversight through six-monthly reviews, joint steering committees, and adaptive management via the flexible fund. Embedded advisors (e.g., HMRC for TRA) are used where institutional risks are highest.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The limited capacity at local government level (despite fiscal devolution) justifies the scaled-up technical assistance component, while MoFP’s stronger capacity allows for more direct financial support via the basket fund. Think-tanks are engaged to fill evidence gaps for policy advocacy.
intersections.quote: "The limited support to 10 regions (67 local governments) under the existing programme yielded significant improvements and provides a strong rationale for scaling up." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case) and "Strengthening engagement with other stakeholders [e.g., think-tanks] [...] could possibly lead to better policy advocacy outcomes." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Fiscal policy used as a political tool, undermining budget credibility
Increasing centralization weakening local governments
Policy uncertainty and aggressive tax enforcement deteriorating business environment
Limited private sector engagement on policy issues
Institutional weaknesses and political appointments affecting reform implementation
TRA’s poor performance in tax administration reforms
Donor coordination challenges in multi-donor basket fund
Potential backsliding in democratic space and public discourse

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-stakeholder engagement and policy advocacy through think-tanks to broaden ownership.
Scale up PFM support to all 26 regions/LGAs to strengthen downstream capacity.
Flexible fund for responsive initiatives and strategic dialogue with GoT on investor concerns.
Shift from financial to technical support (HMRC) and monitor for future reconsideration.
DFID’s leadership in PFM Development Partners Group and Joint Steering Committee.
Long-term technical assistance and embedded advisors (e.g., HMRC for TRA).

fcas_specific_lessons: Strong political leadership can drive reforms but also introduce volatility (e.g., Magufuli’s "Bulldozer" to "Builder" phase transition).
Fiscal consolidation must be balanced with private sector confidence to avoid growth slowdowns.
Local government capacity lags behind fiscal devolution, requiring targeted support.
Donor harmonization is critical in high-risk contexts to avoid fragmentation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous PFM phases (I-IV) showed that: (1) Technical improvements (e.g., IFMIS, audit compliance) are achievable but structural issues (e.g., fiscal policy politicization) persist; (2) Local government pilots (10 regions) demonstrated scalability potential; (3) TRA’s tax administration reforms faced delays and weak accountability, necessitating a shift in approach; (4) Multi-stakeholder engagement was underutilized and needs strengthening.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Scaling up local government support from 10 to 26 regions based on pilot success.
Replacing financial support to TRA with technical assistance due to poor performance.
Introducing a flexible fund to respond to emerging business environment priorities.
Strengthening policy advocacy through local think-tanks to address earlier gaps in stakeholder engagement.
Enhanced monitoring via six-monthly reviews (vs. annual in previous phases).
risks_lessons.quote: "We will need to: Use a multi-pronged approach for influencing policy outcomes through multi-stakeholder engagement and policy advocacy; Better align our support to reforms which have strong political and administrative commitment; Scale up the positive achievements of downstream PFM reforms at local government level for translating these improvements into better service delivery." (24053414.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £20m DFID contribution leverages a total £45m multi-donor basket fund for PFMRP V, with co-funding from Norway, Denmark, and Finland. The programme also complements World Bank, IMF, and EU initiatives in PFM.
financial_details.quote: "Our support will be part of £45m that will be contributed by several donors and the government." (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Financial Aid (£11.0m) to the Government of Tanzania for supporting implementation of the PFM Reform Programme Phase V [...] Technical Support (£6.00m) [...] research and policy advocacy through local reputed think-tanks and for implementing scholarship scheme for MoFP staff through British Council (£3.0m)" (24053414.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Supporting the International Monetary Fund (SIMF)
metadata.quote: SIMF will fund at least 6 IMF thematic funds offering targeted support on PFM and DRM. (38775785.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: Supporting the International Monetary Fund (SIMF) is a £21.7m, 2.5-year programme (38775785.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SIMF delivers specialist IMF capacity development on public financial management (PFM) and domestic revenue mobilisation (DRM) through technical assistance, policy advice, and capacity building. It aims to increase DFID's influence over IMF's tax and PFM support programmes while testing a unified management mechanism for multiple funds.
what_objectives.q1_source: Deliver specialist IMF capacity development on public financial management and domestic revenue mobilisation, increase DFID’s influence over the IMF’s tax and public financial management capacity development support programmes. (38775785.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Technical assistance to 6+ IMF thematic funds on PFM and DRM
Support to 10+ developing countries via Fiscal Transparency Evaluations
Capacity development for finance ministries, central banks, revenue authorities
13% average annual revenue growth in Rwanda Revenue Authority (case example)
Increased tax-to-GDP ratios in supported countries (e.g., 14.9% to 16.2% in RMTF countries)
Development of global public goods like TADAT diagnostic tool
Improved coordination with World Bank/OECD via Platform for Collaboration on Tax (PCT)
what_objectives.summary: SIMF combines financing, capacity building, and policy influence to strengthen developing countries' tax systems and public financial management through IMF's technical expertise.
what_objectives.quote: SIMF will fund at least 6 IMF Thematic Funds (TFs) which provide targeted support on PFM and DRM to key macroeconomic policy institutions. (38775785.odt, What will the programme deliver)

countries_regions: Anglophone West Africa (Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia)
East Africa (Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda)
Southern Africa (Mozambique, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe)
Fragile states (Afghanistan, South Sudan, Central African Republic, etc.)
Global (via TADAT tool and RMTF regional projects)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated 'Minor' risk overall but operates extensively in fragile states where IMF capacity development faces challenges. The Independent Evaluation Office notes IMF cannot meet all demand for CD in fragile states due to resource constraints.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Minor (38775785.odt, Summary Sheet); The IMF is not able to provide enough resources to meet demand for capacity development in fragile states (38775785.odt, Why are UK funds needed)
q6_contextual_constraints: limited domestic revenue (5-20% GDP in most DFID countries)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Low domestic revenue (5-20% GDP vs 25-45% in high-income countries) limits public service delivery. Weak PFM systems create risks of corruption and inefficient spending. Fragile states receive only 17% of IMF CD despite higher needs. Political economy factors often override technical solutions in tax/PFM reforms.
where_context.quote: Domestic revenue levels remain low, and systems and processes to promote more efficient and effective expenditure are often weak. (38775785.odt, Context and need)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID and IMF jointly set strategic priorities through annual dialogues, but IMF implements all technical assistance. Southern partners (country institutions) receive capacity building but have no formal governance role in fund management.
q10_capacity_building_details: hands-on training for government staff via AFRITACs
diagnostic tools (TADAT, Fiscal Transparency Evaluations)
mentoring and peer learning
institutional strengthening of revenue authorities
policy advice and reform implementation support
development of model legislation and toolkits

partner_organizations.name: IMF Institute for Capacity Development (ICD)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer of all technical assistance and capacity building

partner_organizations.name: AFRITAC East (Tanzania)
partner_organizations.role: regional technical assistance center for East Africa

partner_organizations.name: AFRITAC South (Mauritius)
partner_organizations.role: regional technical assistance center for Southern Africa

partner_organizations.name: AFRITAC West 2 (Ghana)
partner_organizations.role: regional technical assistance center for Anglophone West Africa

partner_organizations.name: Revenue Mobilisation Trust Fund (RMTF)
partner_organizations.role: global fund for DRM capacity development

partner_organizations.name: DFID Public Finance and Tax Department (PFTD)
partner_organizations.role: programme management and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: HM Treasury
partner_organizations.role: policy coordination via HMG-IMF Strategic Dialogue

who_partners.quote: SIMF will be managed within the existing Strategic Partnership between DFID and the IMF Institute of Capacity Development (ICD). (38775785.odt, How will SIMF be managed)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is block funding to IMF thematic funds (£19.3m new + £2.4m repurposed from FAST programme). Operates as a partnership agreement under DFID-IMF Strategic Partnership with annual performance reviews.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Unified DFID programme managing 7 IMF thematic funds through annual strategic dialogues between DFID and IMF ICD. Existing AFRITACs and RMTF have their own governance (Steering Committees) where DFID participates. New Fragile States Facility will be designed in Year 1.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IMF is the "world's largest, best resourced and most influential source of policy and technical advice on economic management" (38775785.odt, Intervention Summary). Existing strategic partnership and IMF's mandated role in macroeconomic stability justify sole-source selection.
how_mechanism.quote: The IMF is the world’s largest, best resourced and most influential source of policy and technical advice on economic management. (38775785.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each thematic fund (AFRITACs, RMTF, FSF) has its own Steering Committee with donor representation. DFID participates in all relevant committees. Annual DFID-IMF Strategic Partnership dialogues complement fund-level governance. IMF ICD acts as conduit to implementing departments.
how_governance.quote: The Strategic Partnership discussions complement the six-monthly HMG-IMF Strategic Dialogue... These annual discussions will be a key element in management of SIMF. (38775785.odt, How will SIMF be managed)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Annual review cycle allows adding/removing funds between components based on performance, but requires Steering Committee approval for thematic funds. DFID can unilaterally debar countries but this requires donor consensus at fund level.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Geographic and thematic focus can be adjusted through Steering Committees (e.g., RMTF, FSF) and strategic dialogues. DFID aims to align with UK priorities but cannot earmark funds unilaterally due to IMF rules.
how_flexibility.quote: SIMF is a flexible programme. The annual cycle includes reporting, review and allocation phases allowing funding to be added, taken away and moved between its components. (38775785.odt, Does the programme fit with DFID’s strategic architecture)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IMF ICD → (1) AFRITAC regional centers or (2) IMF HQ departments. No additional sub-grantees mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: Management structures for SIMF will be underpinned by the existing strategic partnership between DFID and the IMF Institute of Capacity Development. (38775785.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral country-level programmes (rejected due to lack of IMF's global expertise)
Separate management of each IMF fund (rejected due to higher transaction costs)
Relying solely on IMF internal resources (rejected due to insufficient coverage of LICs/fragile states)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The IMF's unparalleled technical expertise in PFM/DRM and existing DFID-IMF strategic partnership made it the optimal vehicle. Unifying 7 funds under one programme reduces administrative costs (from 7 annual reviews to 1) while increasing UK influence over IMF priorities. Thematic funds allow targeting of DFID priority countries/regions (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa, fragile states) where other donors are underfunding needs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IMF's internal resource allocation may prioritize systemic stability over LIC needs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID's strategic partnership and Steering Committee participation ensures LIC/fragile state focus

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Other donors' priorities may conflict with DFID's geographic targeting
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual dialogues and burden-sharing limits (max 16% DFID contribution to most funds)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragile states may lack capacity to absorb technical assistance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Design of Fragile States Facility with tailored approaches and DFID input on eligibility criteria

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy constraints may limit reform implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on countries with demonstrated political commitment; MTRS initiative for holistic reform planning

why_rationale.quote: Unifying funding into a single programme... will increase the UK’s leverage and influence on shaping the IMF’s engagement on DRM and PFM... and reduce DFID administrative costs. (38775785.odt, How will SIMF be managed)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Fragile states' limited absorption capacity and political instability constrain partner selection to organizations with existing regional presence (IMF AFRITACs) and ability to navigate complex environments. DFID cannot work with partners lacking field offices in high-priority FCAS regions.
q27_constraints_detail: IMF's AFRITACs selected for their regional embeddedness (e.g., AFRITAC East in Tanzania covers 6 DFID priority countries)
RMTF's 49% Sub-Saharan Africa focus aligns with DFID's geographic priorities
Fragile States Facility design must accommodate weak institutional environments
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both upstream diagnostics (TADAT, Fiscal Transparency Evaluations) and downstream implementation support (AFRITACs) requires a mixed structure combining global funds with regional centers. Political economy focus necessitates IMF's country-level advisors rather than HQ-only delivery.
q28_linkages: Global public goods (TADAT tool) enable standardized diagnostics across countries
Regional centers (AFRITACs) provide localized implementation support
Steering Committees allow donor coordination on geographic/thematic targeting
Annual dialogues link strategic priorities to operational delivery
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) efficiency gains from unified management with (2) equity needs of fragile states. While consolidating funds reduces transaction costs, the 16% burden-sharing cap ensures DFID's withdrawal wouldn't collapse activities in partner countries. The Fragile States Facility design process reflects tension between targeted support and inclusive access.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Unified management (efficiency) vs. fund-specific Steering Committees (inclusivity)
IMF's technical expertise (quality) vs. local ownership (sustainability)
Global tools (scalability) vs. country-specific adaptations (relevance)
DFID's strategic influence (control) vs. multilateral decision-making (legitimacy)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Minor' risk rating enables light-touch oversight for most components, but fragile states receive intensive monitoring through specialized facilities (e.g., proposed FSF) and higher DFID engagement in Steering Committees.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Southern partners' limited capacity leads to IMF-led implementation with embedded advisors (AFRITACs), while DFID focuses on strategic influence and quality assurance. Capacity building is core to all components but decision-making remains Northern-led.
intersections.quote: DFID will work to align support towards UK country and thematic priorities... The 2.5-year duration will allow DFID to test whether management of multiple funds through a single mechanism is effective. (38775785.odt, Intervention Summary)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient political commitment in partner countries to implement reforms
IMF's internal priorities overriding LIC/fragile state needs
Conflict between DFID's geographic priorities and other donors' preferences
Limited absorption capacity in fragile states
Sustainability of reforms post-DFID funding
Coordination gaps between IMF and other development agencies (WB, OECD)
Over-reliance on technical solutions without addressing political economy constraints

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on countries with demonstrated reform commitment; use MTRS framework for government-led planning
Annual DFID-IMF strategic dialogues and Steering Committee participation
Burden-sharing caps (16%) and coordinated donor engagement via Platform for Collaboration on Tax
Tailored Fragile States Facility design with DFID input on eligibility criteria
Integration with Medium Term Revenue Strategies and country-owned reform plans
Participation in Platform for Collaboration on Tax and joint monitoring with WB/OECD

fcas_specific_lessons: Fragile states received only 17% of IMF CD in 2016 despite higher needs (IEO 2018)
Local political economy factors are primary determinants of reform success (World Bank 2014)
Embedded regional advisors (AFRITACs) outperform HQ-based support in FCAS
Flexible, long-term engagement required (DFID Rwanda Revenue Authority case)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: DFID's 2008 review found PFM reform evaluations were rare and relied on observational data. Successful cases like Rwanda Revenue Authority (revenue growth from £68m to £1.1bn) required sustained engagement (1998-2017) and political commitment. Technical assistance must be paired with political economy analysis.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: SIMF consolidates previously separate DFID-IMF funds into a unified programme to improve coherence. Added explicit focus on political economy factors in reform design. Increased coordination mechanisms (Steering Committees, annual dialogues) based on past fragmentation issues.
risks_lessons.quote: Existing evidence is clear that domestic political factors are as important to the success of reforms as the quality of technical support provided. (38775785.odt, Theory of Change)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID's £21.7m leverages £100m+ in total thematic fund resources (estimated from 16% burden-sharing cap). The programme also leverages IMF's existing technical capacity and regional infrastructure (AFRITACs).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: All revenue expenditure (capacity development and technical assistance); no capital investments mentioned.
financial_details.quote: DFID’s burden share is not above 16%, so UK withdrawal / non-entry would lead to a reduction rather than a discontinuation of activity. (38775785.odt, Is the programme coherent with the wider international community)

metadata.programme_name: FCDO Investment in the UN Development System to Achieve Agenda 2030
metadata.primary_sector: multi-sector (governance, health, education, gender equality, climate, humanitarian)
metadata.quote: "The UN Development System plays an important role in responding to global challenges and supporting countries to deliver the Sustainable Development Goals. Through this programme we provide core funding to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), UN Women and the UN Resident Coordinators system." (90000033.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 20/11/2017–31/08/2021" and "New project end date (if applicable): 30/09/2022" (90000033.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to UN agencies (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women) to sustain their operational and normative functions while driving reform. It combines financing mechanisms (core funding), capacity building (strengthening UN systems), and service delivery (direct programme implementation). The payment-by-results component incentivizes organizational effectiveness and collaboration.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UK support is important to sustain UN development system operational and normative delivery, whilst driving further reform to ensure these organisations are individually and collectively fit to respond to the challenges of the 21st century." (16010493.odt, Narrative summary) AND "Core funding enables agencies to function effectively and: run their overseas platform, including in fragile states; provide strong central and oversight functions such as evaluation and audit; maintain a long-term team of permanent policy staff to support agencies normative/standard setting functions; support their delivery across the breadth of their strategic priorities." (90000033.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Reach nearly 244 million children with services to prevent stunting and other forms of malnutrition (2020 results)
Support 48 million out-of-school children (49% of them girls) with access to education (2020 results)
Support 118 countries strengthen their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) as part of the Paris Agreement (2020 results)
Extend legal aid to more than 50,000 women in 20 countries (2020 results)
Avert 160,000 maternal deaths through the supply of contraceptives (2018-2020)
Support 350,630 girls and women with access to services to prevent or address the impact of female genital mutilation (2018-2020)
Ensure 3 million people, 43 percent of them women, across 27 crisis-affected countries got a job or improved their livelihoods (2020 results)
Support 82 countries to top up or expand social assistance programmes, with a focus on the poorest and newly vulnerable groups (2020 results)
Help 1.1 million Yemeni people to get access to clean water and 250,000 to basic sanitation (2020 results)
Support 34 countries on preventing violent extremism and over one third of all countries on tackling hate speech (2020 results)
Assist 1.9 million safe births in 42 humanitarian-affected countries (2020 results)
Help more than 6,700 government entities across 82 countries to keep working during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020 results)
Improved organisational effectiveness of UN agencies (output area 1)
UN Development System supports more coherent UN approach to peace and security (output area 2)
UN entities aligned to Agenda 2030 priorities (output area 3)
Improved UN agency coordination at country level (output area 4)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the UN development system's capacity to deliver Agenda 2030 through predictable core funding to four UN agencies, while incentivizing reform through payment-by-results mechanisms. It focuses on improving organizational effectiveness, coordination, and alignment with global priorities like gender equality, climate action, and conflict prevention.
what_objectives.quote: "The objective of this programme is to ensure that the UN system is fit for purpose to support implementation of the 2030 Agenda, ensuring delivery of priorities as outlined in the Department’s Single Departmental Plan strategic objectives, and underpinned by the UK Aid Strategy and UK National Security Strategy of: strengthening global peace, security and governance; strengthening resilience and response to crises; promoting global prosperity; tackling extreme poverty and helping the world’s most vulnerable." (16010493.odt, Expected impact and outcome of the programme)

countries_regions: global (170+ countries through UN agency networks)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states through UN agencies, but the overall risk rating is medium as per the original business case. The UN's global reach includes high-risk environments, but the funding mechanism (core funding to established UN agencies) mitigates direct implementation risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Medium" (16010493.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "In particular, the UN is able to operate in fragile and conflict affected states, where other actors cannot reach." (90000033.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The UN operates in fragile states where other actors cannot reach, requiring flexible core funding to maintain presence. Data limitations (e.g., 80% of gender equality SDG indicators lack data) constrain monitoring. Political economy challenges affect reform implementation across 193 member states.
where_context.quote: "The UN is the pre-eminent international actor on peace and security, and works across the full range of peace and security, humanitarian and development roles. The UN system has recognised the need to improve coordination and coherence among its development, humanitarian and peacebuilding work to ensure their objectives are mutually reinforcing." (16010493.odt, Addressing conflict and fragility) AND "Currently, many countries lack reliable data and comparability across countries remains a challenge, especially when it comes to aggregating data at regional and global levels: the UN estimates that 80% of the indicators for gender equality across the SDGs are lacking data." (16010493.odt, Gender Equality section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations Development System (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women, UN Development Coordination Office)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making occurs through UN agency Executive Boards where the UK (as a major donor) has influence but shares power with 192 other member states. The UN agencies themselves (multilateral) implement programmes globally, with country offices led by international and local staff.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening UN agency coordination at country level
improving organisational effectiveness (e.g., transparency, accountability)
supporting gender mainstreaming across UN entities
building government statistical capacity for gender data (via UN Women’s Flagship Programme)
encouraging adoption of the UN System-Wide Action Plan for Gender Equality
training and technical support for UN staff on reform priorities

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (core funding recipient)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (core funding recipient)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (core funding recipient)

partner_organizations.name: UN Women
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (core funding recipient) and coordinator for gender data flagship programme

partner_organizations.name: UN Development Coordination Office (Resident Coordinator system)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (core funding recipient for coordination functions)

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funder and strategic oversight (via Executive Board participation)

who_partners.quote: "FCDO has long established relationships with these partners, has designated institutional leads who manage the day-to-day relationship, and participates actively in their governance structures. This includes participating in the Executive Boards of the agencies that take place three times a year and provide oversight of a range of policy, programming and corporate issues." (90000033.odt, What is the approach to implementation?) AND "The programme will seek to incentivise the system to be fit to deliver the new global gender goal and demonstrate commitment to Leave No-one Behind. This includes ensuring that gender is effectively mainstreamed throughout the UN system including through implementation of the UN System Wide Action Plan for Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment (SWAP)." (16010493.odt, Gender Equality section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme provides multi-year, unearmarked core funding to UN agencies, which allows them to allocate resources flexibly according to their mandates and strategic priorities. A portion (30%) is tied to performance-based results (PbR) to incentivize reform and collaboration.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Funding is channeled through the UN’s existing governance structures (Executive Boards) with FCDO participating in oversight. A dedicated FCDO team (UN Development System Core Funding Team) manages the programme, supported by institutional leads for each agency and UK Mission staff in New York. A six-weekly programme board provides coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (direct award to pre-selected UN agencies)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UN agencies were selected based on the 2016 Multilateral Development Review (MDR), which assessed their criticality to UK priorities and organisational effectiveness. The MDR concluded these four agencies (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women) were best placed to deliver on Agenda 2030 and UK strategic objectives.
how_mechanism.quote: "The MDR has been thorough and robust in reviewing the 38 agencies or funds currently supported in terms of the criticality of their role the contribution to UK objectives. We have concluded that the current group of agencies are appropriate for the role they currently play and their potential contribution in future." (16010493.odt, Comprehensively review and/or change the agencies funded?) AND "The UK is currently the second highest donor to UN Operational Activities for Development after the United States. In ‘15/’16 DFID provided £865 million in non-core and £181 million in core, making the ratio of earmarked to core 5:1." (16010493.odt, The critical role of core funding)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Oversight occurs through the Executive Boards of each UN agency (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women), where FCDO participates as a member. These boards meet three times a year to review strategy, results, financial performance, and audits. FCDO complements this with bilateral strategic dialogues at senior management levels and regular technical engagement.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO has long established relationships with these partners, has designated institutional leads who manage the day-to-day relationship, and participates actively in their governance structures. This includes participating in the Executive Boards of the agencies that take place three times a year and provide oversight of a range of policy, programming and corporate issues, including strategy, results, financial performance, evaluation and audit." (90000033.odt, What is the approach to implementation?) AND "We will undertake an Annual Review of progress in the autumn and a Project Completion Review at the end of the programme." (90000033.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The single business case approach allows some flexibility between agencies over the programme duration to incentivize collaboration. However, the Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with each agency set baseline allocations, and reallocation requires agreement through governance structures.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive approach for the payment-by-results component, with 30% of core funding in 2019-2020 held back if results are not achieved. Indicators can be adjusted through annual reviews and strategic dialogues with agency leaders. The 2021 extension also reflects adaptation to COVID-19 and UK ODA reductions.
how_flexibility.quote: "The MoU will leave some scope for future flexibility. The introduction of performance based funding is new, and to mitigate risks, we propose to pursue an adaptive approach here." (16010493.odt, Does the programme have sufficient flexibility?) AND "The extension will build on the results achieved to date, supporting agencies to deliver against the final year of their current Strategic Plans, and we will further use the results framework for this programme to drive outputs related to UK priorities around UN reform, Leave No one Behind and safeguarding." (90000033.odt, What are the expected results?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN Agencies (UNDP/UNICEF/UNFPA/UN Women) → [country-level implementation]. The UN agencies act as both fund recipients and implementers, with no additional sub-grantee layers mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: "The total cost of the extension is £52.8m. This will take the total value of the programme to £582.3m." (90000033.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?) AND "A six-weekly programme board provides co-ordination and oversight, supported by weekly co-ordination meetings." (90000033.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Stop or reduce core funding
Reduce core funding in favor of earmarked funding
Comprehensively review and/or change the agencies funded (e.g., add new UN entities or replace existing ones)
Increase core funding beyond current levels
Continue core funding at static levels with payment-by-results (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (core funding with 30% payment-by-results) was chosen because: 1) Core funding is critical for sustaining UN agencies' normative and operational functions (e.g., maintaining country offices in fragile states, central oversight functions); 2) The UK’s influence in UN governance is tied to its core contributions; 3) Payment-by-results incentivizes reform without undermining predictability; 4) The Multilateral Development Review (MDR) confirmed these agencies’ alignment with UK priorities; 5) Reducing core funding would signal lost confidence and risk copycat cuts by other donors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of influence if core funding is reduced
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain core funding levels to retain Executive Board seats and negotiating power, while using payment-by-results to drive reform.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of UN system due to earmarked funding trends
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocate for increased core funding globally and use UK’s Board positions to push for system-wide coherence (e.g., Quadrennial Comprehensive Policy Review implementation).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Agencies may prioritize PbR targets over broader mandates
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limit PbR to 30% of core funding and focus indicators on systemic issues (e.g., collaboration, transparency) rather than narrow outputs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Signaling effect of UK funding reductions on other donors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Communicate reforms and results achieved through UK funding to maintain donor confidence (e.g., via UNGA announcements).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN resistance to collaboration (e.g., Delivering as One approach)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use Executive Board negotiations and the Secretary-General’s reform mandate to push for country-level coordination, supported by PbR incentives.

why_rationale.quote: "We have concluded that reducing core funding significantly will undermine DFID objectives, threatening the ability of the agency to deliver, or send a signal to other donors that we have lost faith in an organisation, causing a copy-cat effect." (16010493.odt, Reduce core) AND "The proposed programme will allow DFID to continue to influence the work of the UN to drive reform, improve impact and achieve value for money for the UK taxpayer." (16010493.odt, UK Influence) AND "Payment by results will be introduced. It will focus on the impact and effectiveness of both the individual agencies and the system as a whole. Indicators will focus on collaboration, as well as thematic issues such as health, gender, nutrition, and disability." (16010493.odt, Shifting the UK’s approach)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The UN’s universal membership and mandate require working with established multilateral agencies (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women) that have global reach, including in fragile states where other partners cannot operate. The need for normative functions (e.g., standard-setting) and coordination roles (e.g., Resident Coordinator system) limits partner selection to these core UN entities.
q27_constraints_detail: UN agencies’ global mandates require multilateral partners with existing country platforms
Fragile/conflict contexts necessitate partners with security and logistical capacity (e.g., UNICEF’s rapid crisis response)
Normative functions (e.g., gender equality standards) require UN Women’s convening role
Payment-by-results requires agencies with existing results frameworks and Board oversight
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to sustain UN agencies’ normative and operational functions (e.g., maintaining country offices, central audit teams) requires core funding rather than project-specific grants. The goal of driving systemic reform (e.g., collaboration, transparency) shapes the use of payment-by-results tied to collective indicators. The global scope necessitates a multilateral delivery structure with FCDO influence exercised through Executive Boards.
q28_linkages: Core funding instrument → sustains normative functions (e.g., UN Women’s gender standards)
Payment-by-results → incentivizes collaboration (e.g., shared indicators for UNDP/UNICEF/UNFPA/UN Women)
Multilateral structure → enables global reach (e.g., 170+ countries via UNICEF/UNDP)
Executive Board oversight → aligns with UK policy priorities (e.g., Agenda 2030, Leave No One Behind)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., core funding’s economies of scale) with equity (e.g., targeting fragile states, gender inclusion). For example: 1) Core funding is less earmarked (efficiency) but includes PbR to ensure focus on vulnerable groups (equity); 2) UN agencies’ global platforms enable rapid response (efficiency) but require sustained funding to maintain presence in high-risk areas (equity); 3) The 30% PbR component adds transaction costs (efficiency trade-off) but drives reforms that benefit marginalized groups (equity).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Core funding (efficient) vs. PbR conditions (equity-focused indicators)
Global UN platforms (scale) vs. need for country-level adaptation (local ownership)
Influence via Executive Boards (UK priorities) vs. multilateral decision-making (shared power)
Predictable funding (agency planning) vs. adaptive management (responding to crises like COVID-19)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (operating in fragile states, reform resistance) justifies intensive oversight (e.g., annual reviews, Executive Board participation) and adaptive tools (e.g., PbR, strategic dialogues). The extension phase added flexibility to respond to COVID-19 and ODA reductions, reflecting higher uncertainty.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme’s design: 1) Core funding supports UN agencies’ central functions (e.g., audit, evaluation teams); 2) PbR indicators include organisational effectiveness targets (e.g., transparency, collaboration); 3) The gender data flagship programme explicitly builds statistical capacity in 12 ‘pathfinder countries’ via UN Women.
intersections.quote: "The UN’s universal membership gives it a unique legitimacy amongst multilateral organisations to lead the response to these global challenges and to support countries to deliver on global agreements such as Agenda 2030 for Sustainable Development." (16010493.odt, What the UN offers) AND "Payment by results will be introduced. It will focus on the impact and effectiveness of both the individual agencies and the system as a whole. Indicators will focus on collaboration, as well as thematic issues such as health, gender, nutrition, and disability." (16010493.odt, Shifting the UK’s approach) AND "Core funding enables agencies to function effectively and: run their overseas platform, including in fragile states; provide strong central and oversight functions such as evaluation and audit; maintain a long-term team of permanent policy staff to support agencies normative/standard setting functions." (90000033.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

key_programme_risks: Slow pace of UN reform due to member state resistance
Reduction in UK ODA budget affecting core funding levels
Fragmentation of UN system despite reform efforts
Agencies prioritizing PbR targets over broader mandates
Loss of UK influence if core funding is perceived as declining
COVID-19 disrupting programme delivery and results
Resident Coordinator system not fully adopted at country level
Gender data gaps persisting despite flagship programme
Donor fatigue leading to reduced core funding globally
UN agencies’ operational roles expanding beyond comparative advantage

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use UK’s Executive Board seats and the Secretary-General’s reform mandate to push for QCPR implementation; tie 30% of core funding to PbR indicators on collaboration and transparency.
Extend programme by 13 months to maintain continuity while designing a successor programme; prioritize core functions (e.g., Resident Coordinators, gender data).
Advocate for Delivering as One approach in Executive Boards; use PbR to reward inter-agency collaboration.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Agencies prioritizing PbR targets over broader mandates
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Limit PbR to 30% of core funding; focus indicators on systemic issues (e.g., Leave No One Behind) rather than narrow outputs.
Maintain core funding levels to retain Executive Board seats; use high-profile announcements (e.g., UNGA) to signal commitment.
Allow agencies to pivot core funding to crisis response (e.g., UNICEF’s COVID-19 water/sanitation programmes); adjust PbR indicators for 2021 extension.
Direct core funding to the UN Development Coordination Office; use PbR to incentivize country-level coordination.
Fund UN Women’s Flagship Programme (Making Every Woman and Girl Count) to build statistical capacity in 12 pathfinder countries.
Leverage UK’s influence to advocate for increased core funding from other donors; demonstrate results (e.g., 160,000 maternal deaths averted).
Use strategic dialogues to push agencies to focus on comparative advantages; encourage other donors to fund operational activities.

fcas_specific_lessons: Core funding is essential for UN agencies to maintain presence in fragile states (e.g., Yemen, where 1.1 million people gained water access).
Payment-by-results must account for FCAS volatility (e.g., adjust indicators during conflicts or pandemics).
UN’s convening role is critical in FCAS for coordination among humanitarian/development/peacebuilding actors.
Gender and disability inclusion require explicit targets in FCAS contexts (e.g., 50,000 women receiving legal aid in 20 countries).
Resident Coordinators need dedicated funding to lead in FCAS (e.g., £1.8m allocated in extension).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2016 Multilateral Development Review (MDR) found that UN agencies were making progress on organisational effectiveness but needed to accelerate reform. The single business case approach (replacing four individual cases) improved coherence and allowed DFID to emphasize common objectives across agencies. Past reductions in core funding (e.g., to UN-Habitat in 2011) led to copycat cuts by other donors, signaling the importance of sustained UK support.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Introduced payment-by-results (30% of core funding) to drive reform, based on MDR findings. 2) Added a £2m learning/monitoring budget to evaluate PbR effectiveness. 3) Extended programme by 13 months to adapt to ODA reductions and COVID-19. 4) Included explicit targets for Leave No One Behind and safeguarding in the results framework. 5) Funded the Resident Coordinator system directly to strengthen coordination.
risks_lessons.quote: "Past experience demonstrates that the UK withdrawing its core funding from the UN development system could also have signalling effects, being seen to represent a loss of confidence, which could affect the behaviour of other donors and contribute to long-term trends of declining core funding. For example, when the UK cut core funding to UN-HABITAT following the Multilateral Aid Review in 2011, they reported that several other donors similarly cut their core funding." (16010493.odt, Stop or reduce core funding) AND "The extension will build on the results achieved to date, supporting agencies to deliver against the final year of their current Strategic Plans, and we will further use the results framework for this programme to drive outputs related to UK priorities around UN reform, Leave No one Behind and safeguarding." (90000033.odt, What are the expected results?) AND "We have worked closely with the UN agencies and other donors on ambitious indicators in priority areas [for PbR]." (16010493.odt, Core funding with PbR introduced for all agencies)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UN Women Flagship Programme (Making Every Woman and Girl Count) attracted $10m from Australia, Ireland, and USAID over two years, with an expected $10m from the Gates Foundation. The programme’s total cost is $61.5m, with the UK contributing £10m (20.3%).
financial_details.quote: "The total cost of the extension is £52.8m. This will take the total value of the programme to £582.3m." (90000033.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?) AND "A UK contribution of £10,000,000 ($12,522,500 at current exchange rates) is deemed proportional coming in at 20.3% of the overall programme cost. The programme has already attracted support from Australia, Ireland and USAID to the tune of $10m over the next two years. We also expect the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation to confirm support approximating $10m." (16010493.odt, Introduce earmarked funding amounting to £10m) AND "As in prior years, our core funding contributions to UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF and UN Women will include a performance-based component. Thirty percent of core funding will be subject to achievement of specific, pre-agreed results targets (‘payment by results’)." (90000033.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Disability Inclusive Development (DID) Programme
metadata.quote: "This programme will address the lack of attention and prioritisation to support, and include, people with disabilities in the world’s poorest countries. Importantly, it will deliver tangible outcomes to improve the lives of people with disabilities (to deliver jobs, education, healthcare and reduce stigma and discrimination for children/young people and people of working age) and generate a significant evidence base on ‘what works’ to deliver results." (45466853.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 5/12/17–31/12/2026" (D0003680.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (through rigorous research and impact evaluations), implementation research (testing and scaling disability-inclusive interventions), and capacity building (strengthening disability-inclusive research institutions and practitioners). It directly delivers interventions while also producing global public goods through research outputs.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will predominantly be delivered through one contractor, who will manage a consortium of organisations including civil society, academic and research institutions, and Disabled Persons’ Organisations (DPOs). The ‘best-in-class’ research will be commissioned separately by RED, as well as a separate independent evaluation tendered through the evaluation framework." (45466853.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 11 small-scale and 9 large-scale interventions addressing education, health, stigma reduction, and livelihoods
3.25 million people with disabilities reached directly/indirectly (with extension)
15 million people without disabilities reached (with extension)
13 impact evaluations (including 5-8 RCTs) producing global public goods
70+ peer-reviewed journal articles and evidence products
Disability Evidence Portal with systematic reviews and policy briefs
Capacity building for 20+ Southern researchers with disabilities (PhDs, post-docs)
Institutional strengthening of 5+ LMIC research centers
Integration of disability-inclusive approaches into mainstream FCDO programmes (e.g., Shule Bora in Tanzania, Lafiya in Nigeria)
Development of disability-inclusive research tools (e.g., WASH checklist, MICS data analysis frameworks)
what_objectives.summary: The programme tests innovative disability-inclusive interventions at scale while generating rigorous evidence through RCTs and process evaluations, with a strong focus on building Southern research capacity and influencing global policy through dissemination of findings.
what_objectives.quote: "DID is a unique global programme, bringing together an adaptive approach to trialling novel interventions in disability inclusive development and scaling those that show promise, aligned with impact evaluations. Together these approaches produce robust evidence of what does and does not work in this neglected area of supporting people with disabilities in low- and middle-income country (LMIC) contexts." (D0003680.odt, Programme Purpose)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in contexts with weak institutional capacity for disability inclusion, limited disability-disaggregated data, and significant stigma/discrimination against people with disabilities. Many target countries (e.g., Nigeria, Uganda) have fragile health/education systems and face challenges like conflict (Nigeria) or extreme poverty (Bangladesh).
where_context.q5_source: "This programme is judged to be high risk due to the high level of innovation and also the critical importance of influencing others to catalyse change." (45466853.odt, Risk Rating) AND "People with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries are poorer than their non-disabled peers in terms of access to education, healthcare, employment, income, justice, social support and civic involvement." (45466853.odt, Contextual Challenges)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited capacity in DPOs and government ministries)
data limitations (lack of disability-disaggregated data, poor data collection methods)
climate risks (emerging focus on climate change impacts on people with disabilities)
regulatory (lack of policy implementation for CRPD)
political economy (low prioritization of disability in national budgets)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Data limitations force reliance on small-scale studies and hinder comparability across contexts. Weak institutions require capacity-building investments that slow implementation. Stigma/discrimination necessitates additional advocacy components in interventions. Conflict settings (e.g., Nigeria) require adaptive humanitarian approaches that increase complexity and cost.
where_context.quote: "A lack of rigorous and comparable data and the invisibility of people with disabilities often leads to an under-estimation of disability prevalence. This masks the scale of the challenge and makes it difficult to determine if people with disabilities are benefitting or being excluded from development and humanitarian assistance." (45466853.odt, Data Challenges) AND "People with disabilities often face stigma and discrimination and many people living with disabilities do not have voice, choice, or control over their lives." (45466853.odt, Barriers to Inclusion)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO (via two contracts: DIDIF and PENDA)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by UK-based contractors (Sightsavers for DIDIF, LSHTM for PENDA) with decision-making power, but includes structured Southern leadership in research (e.g., LMIC-led evaluations, Southern PhD candidates) and implementation (e.g., BRAC in Bangladesh, local DPOs). The Executive Steering Committee includes Southern representatives (IDA, LMIC academics).
q10_capacity_building_details: PhD scholarships for researchers with disabilities in LMICs (3+ candidates)
post-doctoral support for Southern researchers
training in disability-inclusive research methods for 500+ researchers/activists
institutional strengthening of 5+ LMIC universities/research centers
mentorship for DPOs in research design and advocacy
development of Southern-led evaluation teams (e.g., Bangladesh, Uganda)
co-authorship on 70+ peer-reviewed publications with Southern researchers
technical support to mainstream disability inclusion in FCDO programmes

who_partners.quote: "DID is delivered under two contracts: a) the Disability Inclusive Development–Inclusive Futures (DIDIF) contract [...] to implement a set of smaller-scale innovative interventions and scaling up interventions that have already been proven at small-scale to produce evidence about how effective they are; b) the Programme for Evidence to inform Disability Action (PENDA) contract [...] to carry out high quality research and evaluations (including randomised controlled trials) of interventions." (D0003680.odt, Programme Structure) AND "PENDA funds people with disabilities to undertake PhDs on disability-inclusion, trains researchers and representative organisations in disability-inclusive research methods and supports research centres at universities." (D0003156.odt, PENDA Activities)

how_mechanism.q12_funding_instrument: contract (two separate contracts: DIDIF for implementation, PENDA for research)
how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO uses two time-bound contracts with fixed budgets and deliverables. DIDIF focuses on intervention delivery with milestone-based payments, while PENDA focuses on research outputs (RCTs, systematic reviews) with approvals required for major changes. Both contracts include no-cost extensions for COVID-19 delays.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DIDIF is managed by Sightsavers leading a fixed consortium of NGOs, DPOs, and local partners. PENDA is managed by LSHTM with sub-contracts to Southern research institutions for specific evaluations. An Executive Steering Committee (FCDO, LSHTM, Sightsavers, IDA) oversees both contracts.
how_mechanism.q14_partner_selection_method: restricted competition (framework agreement for DIDIF; direct award to LSHTM for PENDA based on prior relationship)
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not specified for DIDIF; PENDA appears to be direct award to LSHTM
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: DIDIF partners were selected through a framework agreement to ensure rapid deployment of disability expertise. PENDA was awarded to LSHTM due to their existing capacity in disability research and impact evaluation experience, with Southern partners added through sub-contracts.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will predominantly be delivered through one contractor, who will manage a consortium of organisations including civil society, academic and research institutions, and Disabled Persons’ Organisations (DPOs)." (45466853.odt, Delivery Structure) AND "The ‘best-in-class’ research will be commissioned separately by RED, as well as a separate independent evaluation tendered through the evaluation framework." (45466853.odt, Research Component) AND "DID’s Executive Steering Committee (ESC) comprises members from FCDO (Deputy Directors from EdGE and RED, and SRO and PRO for both DIDIF and PENDA contracts); Sightsavers programme directors; lead academics from LSHTM; IDA; and a representative from a UK-based DPO for external challenge." (D0003680.odt, Governance)

how_governance.q15_day_to_day_manager: shared management (implementing partners with FCDO oversight)
how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation: joint committee (ESC approval for major sub-awards, with partner-led operational decisions)
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ESC includes FCDO (EdGE/RED), Sightsavers, LSHTM, IDA, and a UK DPO representative. It meets quarterly to review progress, approve major changes (e.g., new evaluations), and resolve cross-contract issues. Technical advisory groups support specific workstreams (e.g., research methods).
how_governance.quote: "DID’s ESC [...] agreed to reduce the number of evaluations commissioned out from four to two. The remaining two evaluations are being led by LSHTM in collaboration with southern-based research institutes. The ESC agreed that, in a change to BC original plans, equal or more value could be gained across the sector through proactively building the capacity in disability inclusive research in targeted southern-based research institutes by working in partnership to undertake impact evaluations." (D0003680.odt, Governance) AND "Both contracts have been performing as expected [...] All logframe milestones have been achieved (or very narrowly missed) despite complications from budget cuts over recent years, late notifications of budgets, and redirecting programme activities to focus on COVID-19 during 2020 and 2021." (D0003156.odt, Performance)

how_flexibility.q19_fund_reallocation: moderate (requires ESC approval for major shifts)
how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be moved between DIDIF/PENDA components with ESC approval, particularly to respond to emerging evidence (e.g., shifting from small-scale to large-scale interventions). COVID-19 pivots required addenda but were approved.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach with: 1) Annual theory-of-change reviews; 2) ESC approval for major changes (e.g., reducing commissioned evaluations from 10 to 8 to fund capacity building); 3) COVID-19 pivots (e.g., adding qualitative research on pandemic impacts); 4) Evidence-based shifts (e.g., scaling successful poverty graduation models from Uganda to Bangladesh).
how_flexibility.quote: "Innovation is central to this programme which focuses on learning how best to learn from disability inclusive development. Furthermore, the programme will be designed with flexibility to move funds between the components to respond to emerging evidence, learning, risks and new priorities, if there is any difficulty in finding high quality proposals, or if implementation is slow." (45466853.odt, Flexibility) AND "The ESC will guide the best implementation modality for the additional evaluations." (D0003680.odt, Adaptive Management)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contractors (Sightsavers/LSHTM) → Sub-partners (LMIC NGOs/researchers/DPOs)
how_efficiency.quote: "The budget for the whole programme will rise to £39.9 million [...] Just under £30 million is for the DIDIF contract. The remaining £9.9 million is for the PENDA contract, up from the original £7 million." (D0003156.odt, Budget) AND "The DIDIF contract is for six years – i.e., it already includes the additional two years this addendum is requesting." (D0003156.odt, Contract Duration)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct FCDO implementation (rejected due to lack of disability expertise)
Multilateral funding (rejected due to limited disability focus in UN agencies)
Pure research programme (rejected as it wouldn’t deliver tangible outcomes)
Pure implementation programme (rejected as it wouldn’t generate evidence)
Single-contractor model (rejected in favor of separate implementation/research contracts for specialization)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The dual-contract model was chosen to: 1) Combine FCDO’s need for both evidence generation and tangible outcomes; 2) Leverage Sightsavers’ implementation expertise and LSHTM’s research capacity; 3) Enable adaptive management through separate but coordinated contracts; 4) Ensure Southern ownership via structured partnerships with LMIC institutions; 5) Mitigate risk by separating innovative (DIDIF) and evaluative (PENDA) functions.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (combining implementation and research in one programme)
risk mitigation (separate contracts for delivery vs. evaluation)
partner capacity (Sightsavers’ disability inclusion experience; LSHTM’s RCT expertise)
past experience (building on DFID’s Disability Catalyst Programme)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating two separate contracts (DIDIF/PENDA) could create misalignment between implementation and research timelines
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Joint ESC governance and regular coordination meetings between contractors

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Northern contractors (Sightsavers/LSHTM) could limit Southern ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structured capacity-building requirements (PhDs, LMIC-led evaluations) and ESC inclusion of Southern representatives

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: RCTs may not capture context-specific nuances in disability inclusion
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Complementary qualitative research and process evaluations led by Southern partners

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fixed consortium limits ability to add new partners with emerging expertise
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sub-contracting mechanisms for specialized evaluations (e.g., Bangladesh Institute for Governance and Development)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management costs from dual-contractor model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Shared ESC and joint dissemination activities to reduce duplication

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing frameworks to reduce procurement costs)
why_rationale.quote: "This programme will be delivered through one contractor, who will manage a consortium of organisations including civil society, academic and research institutions, and Disabled Persons’ Organisations (DPOs). The ‘best-in-class’ research will be commissioned separately by RED, as well as a separate independent evaluation tendered through the evaluation framework." (45466853.odt, Delivery Structure) AND "The collaboration between DIDIF as an intervention-delivery project and PENDA as an evaluation has been successful [...] This learning will be captured and used to help design a subsequent programme and shared across FCDO to inform similar collaborations." (D0003680.odt, Lessons Learned)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and high-risk contexts (e.g., Nigeria’s conflict settings, Bangladesh’s extreme poverty) required partners with: 1) Experience in FCAS (e.g., BRAC in Bangladesh); 2) Local legitimacy (e.g., DPOs for community access); 3) Adaptive capacity (e.g., BBC Media Action for conflict-sensitive communications). The need for disability-specific expertise excluded many mainstream development contractors.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Nigeria required partners with humanitarian experience (e.g., BBC Media Action for accessible messaging)
Extreme poverty in Bangladesh/Uganda necessitated partners with graduation programme expertise (e.g., BRAC)
Weak data systems required partners with mixed-methods research capacity (e.g., LSHTM + LMIC universities)
Stigma/discrimination required DPO-led advocacy components in all interventions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to generate both implementation outcomes (e.g., 3.25M people reached) and rigorous evidence (e.g., 13 evaluations) drove the dual-contract structure. The focus on scaling successful interventions required flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., shifting from small to large-scale projects). The emphasis on Southern ownership shaped the capacity-building components (e.g., PhD programmes, LMIC-led evaluations).
q28_linkages: RCT requirements → Need for specialized research contractor (PENDA/LSHTM)
Scaling goals → Need for implementation contractor with consortium management experience (DIDIF/Sightsavers)
Southern ownership goals → Structured sub-contracts to LMIC institutions
Adaptive management needs → Separate contracts with ESC coordination
Policy influence objectives → Integrated dissemination components in both contracts
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) Northern contractors (Sightsavers/LSHTM) enable rapid start but require structured Southern capacity building to address equity; 2) RCTs provide rigorous evidence but are costly, reducing funds for direct implementation; 3) Fixed consortium ensures coherence but limits ability to add new Southern partners; 4) Global scope increases reach but requires additional coordination layers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Framework agreements allowed quick start but initially had limited Southern partners (mitigated by later capacity-building investments)
Rigor vs. relevance: RCTs ensure evidence quality but may miss context-specific nuances (mitigated by qualitative components)
Scale vs. depth: Large-scale interventions reach more beneficiaries but with less intensity (addressed via targeted components like assistive devices)
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: UK contractors lead but with structured Southern co-leadership (e.g., LMIC evaluation teams)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (innovation + influencing) led to: 1) Quarterly ESC reviews instead of annual; 2) Milestone-based payments rather than upfront funding; 3) Mandatory capacity-building components to mitigate partner risks; 4) Separate contracts to isolate implementation and research risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shaped: 1) PENDA’s focus on Southern PhD candidates and LMIC-led evaluations; 2) DIDIF’s inclusion of DPOs in consortium governance; 3) The shift from 10 to 8 commissioned evaluations to fund Southern capacity building; 4) Development of disability-inclusive research tools (e.g., WASH checklist) as global public goods.
intersections.quote: "The programme will predominantly be delivered through one contractor, who will manage a consortium of organisations including civil society, academic and research institutions, and Disabled Persons’ Organisations (DPOs)." (45466853.odt, Delivery Structure) AND "PENDA funds people with disabilities to undertake PhDs on disability-inclusion, trains researchers and representative organisations in disability-inclusive research methods and supports research centres at universities." (D0003156.odt, Capacity Building) AND "The ESC agreed that, in a change to BC original plans, equal or more value could be gained across the sector through proactively building the capacity in disability inclusive research in targeted southern-based research institutes by working in partnership to undertake impact evaluations." (D0003680.odt, Adaptive Management)

key_programme_risks: Implementation delays due to COVID-19 (mitigated by no-cost extensions)
Budget cuts reducing intervention scale (addressed via prioritization of large-scale projects)
Weak disability data limiting evaluation quality (mitigated by MICS analysis workstreams)
Partner capacity gaps in LMICs (addressed via structured training and PhD programmes)
Political risks in target countries (e.g., Nigeria’s conflict; mitigated by adaptive interventions)
High cost of RCTs reducing funds for implementation (balanced by shifting to LMIC-led evaluations)
Coordinating dual contracts (mitigated by joint ESC and dissemination plans)
Sustainability of interventions post-programme (addressed via government integration in Tanzania/Nigeria)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: No-cost extensions for both contracts; pivot to COVID-19 response work (e.g., inclusive hygiene programmes); remote data collection methods
Prioritized large-scale interventions with highest evidence potential; reduced number of commissioned evaluations to fund capacity building
PhD programmes for researchers with disabilities; LMIC-led evaluation teams; institutional partnerships with African/Asian universities

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Weak government systems in target countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Integration with mainstream FCDO programmes (e.g., Shule Bora in Tanzania) to leverage existing platforms

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High cost of RCTs limiting implementation funds
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Shifted from 10 to 8 evaluations; increased focus on process evaluations and secondary data analysis (e.g., MICS)
Community sensitization components in all projects; DPO-led advocacy; behaviour change communications (e.g., BBC Media Action radio plays)

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict settings (Nigeria) required adaptive humanitarian approaches (e.g., radio-based behaviour change campaigns)
Extreme poverty contexts (Bangladesh/Uganda) necessitated integrated graduation models combining cash transfers, skills training, and social protection
Weak institutional environments required capacity-building investments to be embedded in all interventions
Data scarcity in FCAS led to innovative methods (e.g., participatory livelihoods mapping in Uganda)
Local DPOs were essential for accessing marginalized groups in high-risk areas
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s Disability Catalyst Programme (2015-2018) included: 1) The need for structured DPO involvement in governance; 2) The value of small grants for local innovation; 3) Challenges of scaling without rigorous evidence (addressed via PENDA’s evaluation component). The 2016 Bilateral Development Review’s emphasis on disability data gaps directly shaped DID’s focus on the Washington Group questions and MICS analysis.
