risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added COVID-19 response components (2020) including inclusive hygiene programmes and qualitative research on pandemic impacts; 2) Reduced commissioned evaluations from 10 to 8 to fund Southern capacity building (2021); 3) Shifted from Northern-led to LMIC-led evaluations for better value and ownership (2022); 4) Expanded focus on women/girls with disabilities based on early gendered findings; 5) Added climate change and social protection research streams based on emerging evidence gaps.
risks_lessons.quote: "Learning from the early parts of the PENDA programme are being used to improve further work. For example, two of the impact evaluations have been contracted out and led by universities in LMICs. LSHTM has noted that these offer poorer VfM owing to the level of support LSHTM has had to provide. In contrast, though, other capacity-building work (e.g., the PhD programme, development of institutional capacity and commissioning of evidence notes for the Disability Evidence Portal) provides better VfM growing disability inclusive research capacity in LMICs." (D0003156.odt, Lessons Learned) AND "The success of the Uttarakhand Cluster: a case study of organisational change towards disability inclusive development [showed] that outcomes may not be apparent until after a programme ends." (45466853.odt, Evidence Gaps)

co_funding_partners.partner: Stellenbosch University (Disability Evidence Portal match funding)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: PENDA leveraged over £3.4 million in additional investment for disability-inclusive research programmes through match funding and partnerships (e.g., Disability Evidence Portal at Stellenbosch University).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Primarily revenue (implementation costs, research activities, capacity building) with minor capital investments in tools/portals (e.g., Disability Evidence Portal development).
financial_details.quote: "The budget for the whole programme will rise to £39.9 million [...] Just under £30 million is for the DIDIF contract. The remaining £9.9 million is for the PENDA contract, up from the original £7 million." (D0003156.odt, Budget) AND "PENDA has leveraged over £3.4m in investment into DID research programmes." (D0003156.odt, Leverage) AND "Original budget: £37,065,000; Cost extension value: £9,600,000; New budget: £46,665,000 (though later revised to £45.6m)." (D0003680.odt, Budget Extension)

metadata.programme_name: Education Research in Conflict and Protracted Crisis (ERICC)
metadata.quote: "The overall goal of ERICC is to address critical evidence gaps, providing rigorous research to inform policy and practice in conflict and protracted crisis around the world." (D0006795.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: Start: 05/11/2018, End: 30/09/2024. A Business Case addendum in 2019 extended the programme end date to 30/09/2026. New project end date (if applicable): 30/06/2028." (D0006795.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ERICC is primarily an evidence generation programme focused on "what works" in education in conflict and protracted crises, but it also includes significant capacity building (through fellowships and institutional strengthening), policy influence (through evidence dissemination and uptake), and implementation research (through operational support to FCDO country offices).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The overall goal of ERICC is to address critical evidence gaps, providing rigorous research to inform policy and practice in conflict and protracted crisis around the world. [...] Strengthening knowledges systems and research capacity in the Global South through a targeted and innovative fellowship and institutional strengthening component." (D0006795.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Rigorous research on effective approaches to education provision in conflict and protracted crises (global and country level)
Operational in-country support through a helpdesk for technical assistance to FCDO education advisors in 10 countries
Evidence dissemination and uptake through multi-media communications and events for global audiences
Strengthened knowledge systems and research capacity in Bangladesh, Iraq, and Lebanon (through fellowships and institutional strengthening)
Direct benefit to at least 500,000 children in focal countries (Northern Nigeria, South Sudan, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Iraq, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon)
Indirect benefit to 230 million children living in conflict-affected contexts globally
Strengthened education programming in at least six FCDO countries
Improved effectiveness of multilateral programming (e.g., Education Cannot Wait)
Creation of research environments and cultures in education research that outlast the programme
what_objectives.summary: ERICC aims to generate rigorous evidence on effective education interventions in conflict and protracted crises, strengthen research capacity in the Global South, and ensure evidence uptake by policymakers and practitioners. It combines research, operational support, dissemination, and capacity building to improve education outcomes for children affected by crises.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme aims to: Organise, synthesise and advance the evidence base on what works to improve the holistic learning of children and strengthen the coherence of education systems in conflict and protracted crisis contexts; Strengthen education programming through research insights in at least six FCDO countries; Deliver insights that contribute to improving the effectiveness of multilateral programming; Better enable EiEPC practitioners and decision makers to access and use evidence; Sustainably strengthen knowledge systems in Bangladesh, Iraq and Lebanon." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries affected by conflict, protracted crises, and fragility, with high levels of displacement, weak institutions, and volatile security situations. These contexts are explicitly described as "fragile and conflict-affected states" with significant risks to delivery, including safety, security, and challenges of conducting research.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme will contribute to the Foreign Secretary’s following key priorities: Address fragility, prevent and resolve conflict, by strengthening research on how to deliver quality education in conflict-affected contexts." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION) AND "Key risks include safety, security and challenges of conducting research in conflict and crisis contexts." (D0006260.odt, Risks and opportunities)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and conflict limit access to research sites, require extensive risk mitigation, and may disrupt implementation. Weak institutions and political economy challenges affect the ability to engage with local governments and ensure research uptake. Data limitations (e.g., lack of baseline data, fragmented evidence) hinder the ability to measure impact and design interventions. Climate risks (e.g., shocks resulting from climate change) add complexity to education system resilience.
where_context.quote: "Key risks include safety, security and challenges of conducting research in conflict and crisis contexts as well as ensuring a delivery model that catalyses strong in-country stakeholder buy-in, delivers high quality evidence and ensures uptake of research findings." (D0006260.odt, Risks and opportunities) AND "The body of evidence on education in emergencies and protracted crisis (EiEPC) is fragmented, with major knowledge gaps about how children learn and develop in these contexts." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: International Rescue Committee (RPC lead for Components 1 & 2)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Research Programme Consortium (RPC) is led by Northern institutions (e.g., International Rescue Committee, University College London), with Southern partners (e.g., research institutions in Bangladesh, Iraq, Lebanon) playing implementation roles. Decision-making power rests with the RPC and FCDO, though Southern partners are involved in co-construction of research agendas.
q10_capacity_building_details: targeted fellowship programme
institutional strengthening of research institutions in Bangladesh, Iraq, and Lebanon
building capacity to manage research grants
strengthening research design, publication, and policy engagement skills
creating lasting research partnerships between UK and Global South

partner_organizations.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead for Research Programme Consortium (RPC); Components 1 (Research) and 2 (Operational Support)

partner_organizations.name: University College London (UCL)
partner_organizations.role: Academic partner for RPC (replaced NYU in 2024)

partner_organizations.name: Inter-agency Network for Education in Emergencies (INEE)
partner_organizations.role: Component 3: Evidence Dissemination and Uptake

partner_organizations.name: British Academy
partner_organizations.role: Component 4: Knowledge Systems Strengthening (fellowships and institutional strengthening in Bangladesh, Iraq, Lebanon)

partner_organizations.name: Research institutions in Bangladesh, Iraq, and Lebanon
partner_organizations.role: Local partners for capacity building and research

partner_organizations.name: Education Cannot Wait (ECW)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partner for evidence uptake and multilateral programming

partner_organizations.name: FCDO country offices
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries of operational support and research insights

who_partners.quote: "Component 4 – Knowledge Systems Strengthening (British Academy). Strengthening knowledge systems and research capacity in the Global South through a targeted and innovative fellowship and institutional strengthening of research institutions in Bangladesh, Iraq, and Lebanon." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The RPC will be responsible for developing a conceptual framework and research, dissemination and uptake strategy that clarifies the expectations of the country research." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 1)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: ERICC uses a commercial contract for Components 1 and 2 (RPC-led research and operational support) and accountable grant agreements for Components 3 and 4 (evidence dissemination and knowledge systems strengthening). The contract with the RPC is performance-based, while grants to INEE and the British Academy are results-focused.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured around four components, each led by a specific partner: 1) RPC (IRC/UCL) for research, 2) RPC for operational support, 3) INEE for dissemination, and 4) British Academy for capacity building. The RPC acts as the central implementer for research and operational activities, with FCDO maintaining oversight through regular reporting and annual reviews.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The RPC was selected through a competitive tender process to ensure value for money and access to world-class expertise. The British Academy and INEE were chosen as strategic partners due to their complementary strengths in capacity building and global networks, respectively.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID will commercially procure an RPC with the in-house expertise to fulfil all programme functions." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 1) AND "The programme is delivered as outlined above; through a commercial contract for Components 1 and 2, and Accountable Grant agreements for Components 3 and 4." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The RPC is guided by an Advisory Board, and a Funders Group coordinates between DFID, AHRC, ESRC, and the British Academy. A joint Advisory Board provides strategic advice across the programme. FCDO maintains oversight through regular engagement, reporting, and annual reviews.
how_governance.quote: "The RPC will be responsible for developing a conceptual framework and research, dissemination and uptake strategy [...] It will be critical to balance adherence to programme priorities with a certain level of flexibility that ensures academic independence and control over research design." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 1) AND "FCDO maintains oversight of the programme through regular engagement, reporting and the Annual Review process." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within components, but major shifts (e.g., between components or countries) require FCDO approval. The programme has built-in flexibility to respond to emerging crises or evidence gaps, as seen in the addition of Bangladesh and Iraq as focal countries.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted based on emerging evidence or country needs, but changes require approval from the Advisory Board and FCDO. The programme is designed to be demand-driven, with breakpoints to guide funding shifts. For example, the research agenda was expanded to include climate shocks and refugee education in response to new challenges.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme is designed to respond flexibly to the demand for learning from country offices. This learning will be fed directly back into programming. We will make sure there are break points to guide the level of funding." (D0006260.odt, Isthere sufficient flexibility) AND "The programme is now fully procured and fully staffed. The ERICC FCDO programme team have advanced preparations for the commercial contract extension for timely continuation of activities under components one and two." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → RPC/INEE/British Academy → Local research institutions (for Components 1, 3, 4). For Component 2 (operational support), the RPC works directly with FCDO country offices.
how_efficiency.quote: "The RPC will be responsible for [...] managing a technical responsive resource for demand-led technical assistance to education programmes; establishing an external Review Panel for operational support to the three countries/regions." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 1) AND "The programme is delivered as outlined above; through a commercial contract for Components 1 and 2, and Accountable Grant agreements for Components 3 and 4." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

q24_alternatives_considered: Expansion of existing DFID research programmes (discounted due to lack of scope to cover the breadth of functions)
Core funding to a multilateral partner or network (discounted as no single partner had the capacity to lead the agenda)
Collaboration with a bilateral donor (discounted as it would not provide the necessary control or alignment with DFID priorities)
Establishing a five-year research programme through a Research Programme Consortium (RPC) only (Option 1)
Establishing a five-year research programme through an RPC + partnering with UK Research Councils (preferred Option 2)
Do nothing (counterfactual)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (RPC + strategic partnerships) was chosen to combine the RPC’s operational and research expertise with the British Academy’s strength in capacity building and INEE’s global networks for dissemination. This approach maximizes value for money by leveraging co-funding (e.g., £2M savings through British Academy co-funding), ensures academic rigor, and enables flexible response to country demands while maintaining FCDO oversight.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (e.g., co-funding, competitive tender for RPC)
risk mitigation (e.g., diversified partners, phased implementation)
partner capacity (e.g., RPC’s in-house expertise, British Academy’s track record in capacity building)
equity (e.g., Southern institutional strengthening, co-construction of research agendas)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: RPC unable to fulfil all programme functions to a high standard (e.g., lack of multidisciplinary expertise in-house)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early market engagement and competitive procurement to ensure quality; flexibility to commission additional expertise as needed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited capacity to influence governments on sensitive policy issues
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with FCDO centrally and in-country to lead on influencing; RPC to work closely with local institutions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in FCDO procurement processes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active management of procurement timeline; no-cost extensions considered if delays occur (as happened in 2020-2021).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited supplier base for knowledge systems strengthening
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnering with the British Academy to leverage their expertise and networks in the Global South.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safety and security challenges in conflict contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Extensive risk assessments for each country; phased approach to implementation; lessons from past DFID research in Syria applied.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (e.g., RPC’s in-house expertise to avoid costly commissioning)
effectiveness (e.g., academic independence balanced with programme priorities)
equity (e.g., capacity building in Global South, inclusive research agendas)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 2: Establishing a five year research programme by 1) commercially procuring a Research Programme Consortium and 2) partnering with the British Academy, the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) and the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) – preferred option [...] This option entails a direct cost saving for DFID of £2 million, through a co-funding of the knowledge systems strengthening component with the British Academy." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 2) AND "The RPC model ensures in-house expertise to conduct a majority of the primary research, which means that lengthy and costly commissioning processes are avoided to a great extent." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 1)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS contexts limit partner selection to organizations with proven experience in conflict-affected areas, strong risk management capacities, and existing networks in focal countries. For example, the RPC lead (IRC) was chosen for its operational expertise in emergencies, while the British Academy was selected for its ability to navigate academic partnerships in fragile states like Iraq and Lebanon.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks require partners with robust safety protocols and insurance (e.g., IRC’s experience in Syria, South Sudan)
Weak institutions necessitate partners with capacity-building expertise (e.g., British Academy’s fellowship model)
Data limitations demand partners skilled in innovative research methods (e.g., RPC’s adaptive research designs)
Political sensitivity requires partners with diplomatic experience (e.g., FCDO’s role in government engagement)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both rigorous evidence generation and real-time operational support shaped the mixed delivery structure: the RPC combines academic and operational expertise to ensure research is both high-quality and policy-relevant, while the British Academy and INEE address capacity building and dissemination. The multi-component design reflects the programme’s dual goals of generating global public goods (e.g., comparative research) and country-specific solutions (e.g., helpdesk support).
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (WHAT) → RPC’s in-house research teams (HOW) to ensure academic independence while aligning with FCDO priorities
Operational support (WHAT) → RPC’s helpdesk function (HOW) to provide demand-led technical assistance to country offices
Capacity building (WHAT) → British Academy’s fellowships (HOW) to strengthen Southern research institutions as sustainable partners
Dissemination (WHAT) → INEE’s global networks (HOW) to maximize uptake of evidence by practitioners
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (e.g., RPC led by IRC/UCL) with Southern ownership (e.g., co-construction of research agendas, fellowships for Global South academics). Trade-offs include: 1) Speed vs. inclusion: Competitive tender for the RPC ensured rapid mobilization but limited Southern leadership in initial design. 2) Cost vs. reach: Investing in institutional strengthening (Component 4) reduces funds available for direct research but ensures long-term capacity. 3) Academic rigor vs. policy relevance: The RPC’s dual role (research + operational support) aims to bridge this gap but risks diluting depth in either area.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern-led RPC (efficiency) vs. Southern co-construction (equity): Mitigated by Advisory Board representation and capacity-building components
Competitive procurement (speed) vs. inclusive partnerships (local ownership): Addressed through phased onboarding of Southern partners
Global research standards (rigor) vs. context-specific methods (relevance): Balanced via RPC’s adaptive frameworks and country-level engagement
Short-term outputs (e.g., reports) vs. long-term capacity (e.g., fellowships): Budget allocated to both, with 24% (£6M) for knowledge systems strengthening
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context drives intensive oversight (e.g., milestone-based reporting, embedded FCDO advisors) and adaptive management (e.g., breakpoints for funding reallocation). For example, delays due to ODA pauses in 2020-2021 triggered a no-cost extension and phased implementation to mitigate risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Positioning Southern institutions as co-producers of research (e.g., through British Academy fellowships), 2) Embedding knowledge systems strengthening as a core component (not an add-on), and 3) Requiring RPC to include Global South academics in leadership roles. This ensures Southern partners transition from beneficiaries to equal collaborators over time.
intersections.quote: "The programme will work with external partners to ensure a coherent approach. We will work with Education Cannot Wait to strengthen their capacity for research and evidence-based programming and we will work closely with the Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies (INEE), to capitalise upon their broad network of stakeholders." (D0006260.odt, Research approach) AND "Strengthen knowledge systems and research capacity in the Global South through a targeted and innovative fellowship and institutional strengthening component, in order to build new partnerships and ensure sustained capacity for research in this important area." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

key_programme_risks: Safety and security risks in conflict zones (e.g., Syria, South Sudan)
Limited supplier base for knowledge systems strengthening
Delays in procurement and implementation (e.g., ODA pauses in 2020-2021)
RPC’s ability to fulfil all programme functions (e.g., balancing research and operational support)
Ensuring research uptake by policymakers in fragile contexts
Political sensitivity of education research in conflict-affected areas
Data limitations and fragmented evidence base
Retention of academic partners (e.g., NYU’s exit in 2023)
Coordinating across multiple components and partners
Adapting to evolving crises (e.g., climate shocks, new displacements)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Extensive risk assessments for each country; phased implementation; lessons from past DFID research in Syria; insurance and security protocols for RPC staff.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited supplier base for knowledge systems strengthening
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Partnering with the British Academy to leverage their expertise and GCRF co-funding; targeted fellowships to build Southern capacity.
No-cost extensions (e.g., 2019 addendum); active management of procurement timeline; phased onboarding of partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: RPC unable to fulfil all functions
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Competitive tender to ensure quality; flexibility to commission additional expertise; Advisory Board oversight.
Embedded dissemination component (INEE); co-construction of research agendas with country offices; annual conferences and policy forums.
Close engagement with FCDO centrally and in-country; RPC to work with local governments and institutions.
Rigorous evidence synthesis and adaptive research methods; investment in data collection and monitoring systems.
Contract amendments to onboard new partners (e.g., UCL in 2024); diversified consortium to reduce dependency on single institutions.
Joint Advisory Board for strategic alignment; RPC as convening force for cross-component activities.
Demand-driven research design; breakpoints for funding reallocation; flexible global research agenda.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from DFID’s past research in Syria demonstrated that research in conflict is "both possible and necessary," with risk mitigation strategies such as remote data collection and local partnerships.
The need for phased implementation in FCAS contexts to manage security risks and build trust with local stakeholders.
The importance of co-constructing research agendas with Southern partners to ensure relevance and ownership, as seen in the British Academy’s fellowship model.
The value of embedding capacity building within research programmes to address systemic gaps in FCAS contexts (e.g., lack of local research institutions).
The necessity of flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., helpdesk for operational support) to respond to rapid-onset crises or shifting priorities in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Inception Phase (2017) highlighted the need for: 1) Rigorous evidence reviews to identify gaps, 2) Mapping of research institutions in focal countries, 3) Ethical guidance for data collection in crisis contexts, and 4) Strong in-country engagement. These lessons shaped the RPC’s research strategy and the British Academy’s capacity-building approach. Additionally, delays in the initial phase (2018-2020) due to staffing gaps and market engagement challenges led to improved procurement planning in later stages.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Addition of Bangladesh and Iraq as focal countries in response to emerging crises (e.g., Rohingya displacement, climate shocks). 2) Expansion of research themes to include refugee education and climate resilience based on new evidence gaps. 3) Adjustment of the RPC’s structure to include UCL as a replacement for NYU, ensuring continuity of academic leadership. 4) Phased implementation of Component 4 (capacity building) to align with partner readiness and ODA constraints. 5) Enhanced flexibility in the helpdesk function (Component 2) to provide rapid response to country office demands.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learnt from recent DFID funded research in Syria demonstrate that while challenging, research in difficult contexts is both possible and necessary, and there are ways of mitigating risks." (D0006260.odt, Risks and opportunities) AND "The programme has faced delivery delays due to two main reasons: The ODA funding restrictions in 2020 and 2021 [...] resulted in delivery delays. As a result, all partners across all four components did not become fully operational until 2024." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

co_funding_partners.partner: British Academy (via Global Challenges Research Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leveraged £2M in co-funding from the British Academy (via GCRF) for the knowledge systems strengthening component, reducing DFID’s direct costs. Additional in-kind contributions and human resources were provided by AHRC and ESRC, though exact amounts are not specified.
financial_details.quote: "This option entails a direct cost saving for DFID of £2 million, through a co-funding of the knowledge systems strengthening component with the British Academy." (D0006260.odt, OPTION 2) AND "The programme will remain within the original Business Case value of £26.5m, and within the allocated amount for each component." (D0006795.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Scaling up Family Planning in Tanzania
metadata.quote: "Scaling up Family Planning in Tanzania is a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health (SRHR) programme that works in partnership with the Government of Tanzania to scale up access to family planning, comprehensive post-abortion care, management of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and integrated HIV counselling and testing across 22 regions in Tanzania." (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 14/10/2017–31/12/2024" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31/12/2026" (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines direct service delivery (family planning, post-abortion care, GBV support) with health system strengthening, policy engagement, and capacity building. It aims to scale up access to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services while building government capacity for sustainable impact.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Scaling up Family Planning in Tanzania is a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health (SRHR) programme that works in partnership with the Government of Tanzania to scale up access to family planning, comprehensive post-abortion care, management of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and integrated HIV counselling and testing across 22 regions in Tanzania. To ensure no one is left behind, the programme prioritises access to young people and adolescents to reduce teenage pregnancy and prevent unwanted pregnancies." (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Provision of quality and voluntary family planning services to 900,000 additional users by 2026
Generation of approximately 4.8 million couple years of protection (CYPs)
Averting 1,783 maternal deaths, over 2 million unwanted pregnancies, and over 500,000 unsafe abortions
Training of healthcare providers and strengthening of the supply chain
Reaching young people (15-19) to reduce teenage pregnancy and increase schooling completion
Providing services for people with disabilities using innovative approaches
Comprehensive post-abortion care (CPAC) services to women with incomplete abortions or miscarriages
Integrated service delivery for women exposed to sexual violence
Strengthening government capacity through embedded nurses and mentorship
Procurement of family planning commodities to address stock-outs
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to scale up comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services in Tanzania, focusing on marginalized groups (youth, people with disabilities, refugees) while strengthening health systems and government capacity for sustainable impact.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver the following additional results: Provision of quality and voluntary family planning services to 900,000 additional users. This will generate approximately 4.8 million couple years of protection; averting 1,783 maternal deaths, more than 2 million unwanted pregnancies, and more than 500,000 unsafe abortions." (D0005054.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a challenging political environment with occasional opposition to family planning, but Tanzania is generally stable without significant conflict. The risk is categorized as moderate due to operational challenges rather than fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (20372373.odt, Summary Sheet) and "In the first year of service delivery operations (2019), the previous government publicly opposed family planning and banned all community-based outreaches." (D0005054.odt, Expected Results)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political opposition led to bans on community outreach in 2019, COVID-19 disrupted operations in 2020-2021, and budget cuts in 2022-2023 limited scale. Weak supply chains cause commodity stock-outs, and conservative social norms create resistance to family planning services.
where_context.quote: "In the first year of service delivery operations (2019), the previous government publicly opposed family planning and banned all community-based outreaches. Covid-19 brought further disruption in 2020 and 2021, after which budget cuts in 2022 and 2023 limited the scale at which partners could operate." (D0005054.odt, Expected Results)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is implemented through a mix of international NGOs (Marie Stopes International, EngenderHealth) and local partners (CCBRT), with decision-making shared between FCDO, the Government of Tanzania, and implementing partners. The Government of Tanzania co-leads policy and system strengthening, while NGOs deliver services.
q10_capacity_building_details: training of government healthcare workers
mentorship of district health management teams
strengthening supply chain systems
embedded nurses to build public sector capacity
policy engagement with the Government of Tanzania

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA
partner_organizations.role: procures family planning commodities; coordinates with government; builds capacity

partner_organizations.name: Marie Stopes International (MSI)
partner_organizations.role: direct service provision via roving medical teams and embedded nurses; reaches refugees with IRC

partner_organizations.name: EngenderHealth
partner_organizations.role: delivers comprehensive family planning through community outreach, routine services, and post-partum family planning (PPFP); leads consortium with Pathfinder International, DKT International, and CCBRT

partner_organizations.name: Pathfinder International
partner_organizations.role: consortium member under EngenderHealth

partner_organizations.name: DKT International
partner_organizations.role: consortium member under EngenderHealth

partner_organizations.name: Comprehensive Community Based Rehabilitation in Tanzania (CCBRT)
partner_organizations.role: local consortium member focusing on disability-inclusive services

partner_organizations.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
partner_organizations.role: partners with MSI to reach refugees

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania (Ministry of Health)
partner_organizations.role: policy engagement, co-financing, health system strengthening

who_partners.quote: "The programme is implemented by UNFPA, EngenderHealth and Marie Stopes International (MSI). EngenderHealth and MSI are both working to reach more clients with comprehensive SRHR services. UNFPA procures family planning commodities on behalf of the Government of Tanzania." (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for MSI and EngenderHealth) and a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with UNFPA for commodity procurement. The contracts include provisions for extensions (up to 50%) and are performance-based.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme and contracts two primary implementers (MSI and EngenderHealth) through competitive tender. UNFPA operates under a separate MOU for commodity procurement. The implementers work directly with the Government of Tanzania and sub-partners (e.g., IRC, CCBRT) under their contracts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: MSI and EngenderHealth were selected through a competitive tender in 2019, with provisions for extensions included in their contracts. The selection was based on their capacity to deliver comprehensive SRHR services, innovate for marginalized groups, and work with government systems.
how_mechanism.quote: "EngenderHealth and Marie Stopes International were awarded contracts in 2019 through a competitive tender process and provision for an extension of up to 50% was included in their contracts." (D0005054.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: MSI and EngenderHealth manage their own sub-partners (e.g., IRC, CCBRT) under their contracts with FCDO. FCDO does not directly oversee sub-awards.
how_governance.quote: "The programme has scored A in the last three annual reviews." (D0005054.odt, Expected Results) and "Aspart of the contract extension, partners will be asked to present a revised proposal and work plan. Activities will be reassessed for sustainability, effectiveness and value-for money." (D0005054.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within the same contractor's scope (e.g., MSI or EngenderHealth can shift resources between service delivery models), but major changes require FCDO approval. The £2m contingency for commodity procurement is explicitly flexible.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities (e.g., revising refugee camp work or youth outreach models) based on learning, but changes must be approved by FCDO during annual reviews or work plan revisions.
how_flexibility.quote: "Activities that have not proven their impact or are too expensive for government to replicate going forwards, or that no longer provide strategic fit for the UK, will not be continued." (D0005054.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "We will consider a limited procurement of commodities where this is critical to enable continued provision of services, while working with the Tanzanian Government and other partners to strengthen the supply chain." (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contractors (MSI/EngenderHealth) → End users (with embedded government providers). UNFPA operates as a parallel layer for commodities.
how_efficiency.quote: "Cost per CYP is £2 compared to £4.8 five years ago." (D0005054.odt, Value for Money) and "Aspart of the contract extension, partners will be asked to present a revised proposal and work plan." (D0005054.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Delivery through UNFPA (multilateral MOU)
Competitive tender for delivery of services (contract)
Working directly with Government of Tanzania as earmarked sector budget support (financial aid)
Using centrally managed WISH programme funds
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed model (contracts for service delivery + MOU with UNFPA for commodities) was chosen for: (1) **Value for Money**: Competitive tender ensures cost-effectiveness and local adaptability; (2) **Risk Mitigation**: UNFPA’s global procurement advantage and government relationships reduce commodity risks; (3) **Flexibility**: Bilateral contracts allow rapid adaptation (e.g., innovations for youth/disabilities) compared to multilateral or budget support; (4) **Partner Capacity**: MSI and EngenderHealth have proven track records in Tanzania and can deliver at scale; (5) **Government Ownership**: Working through public facilities and embedded nurses builds sustainability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government opposition to family planning (e.g., 2019 outreach ban)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified delivery models (e.g., facility-based services, embedded nurses) and advocacy with progressive government officials.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commodity stock-outs due to supply chain weaknesses
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UNFPA’s pooled procurement and £2m contingency fund for emergency purchases, coupled with supply chain strengthening.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner capacity gaps in innovative areas (e.g., disability inclusion)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Consortium model (EngenderHealth + CCBRT) and piloting approaches before scale-up.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in service delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with Ministry of Health and alignment with national policies to ensure legitimacy.

why_rationale.quote: "By DFID Tanzania scaling up through the bilateral programme, this would mean that the resources from WISH can be used elsewhere, such as places where it is not possible to have a country led programme that includes post abortion care, or in the Sahel where there is limited DFID presence and needs are significant." (20372373.odt, Appraisal Case) and "PREFERRED OPTION: DFID PROCUREMENT TO A CONTRACTED PARTNER/S WORKING WITH PUBLIC AND PRIVATE PROVIDERS" (20372373.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The conservative political and social context in Tanzania limits partner selection to organizations with: (1) **Local legitimacy** (e.g., UNFPA’s government relationships); (2) **Experience navigating resistance** (e.g., MSI’s work with refugees and Catholic populations); (3) **Ability to work with public systems** (e.g., embedded nurses model). International NGOs are preferred over local CSOs due to capacity gaps in managing large-scale, sensitive SRHR programmes.
q27_constraints_detail: Government opposition to community outreach (2019 ban)
Conservative social norms around family planning and abortion
Weak local CSO capacity for SRHR service delivery
Refugee camp restrictions (faith-based resistance, food ration incentives for large families)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **direct service delivery to marginalized groups** (youth, disabilities, refugees) drives the consortium structure (MSI + EngenderHealth) and embedded models (nurses in public facilities). **Commodity procurement challenges** necessitate UNFPA’s role due to their global pooled purchasing power. **Government capacity gaps** require hands-on training and mentorship, shaping the embedded nurse and supply chain strengthening components.
q28_linkages: Direct service delivery → Consortium of implementers with specialized roles (MSI for outreach, EngenderHealth for PPFP)
Marginalized groups (youth/disabilities) → Innovative sub-models (school linkages, CCBRT partnership)
Commodity risks → UNFPA MOU for procurement + contingency fund
Sustainability goals → Embedded nurses and government training
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Higher costs for youth services** (£5.74-£11.48 per CYP vs. £2 average) justified by equity goals; (2) **Refugee camp work** is resource-intensive but aligns with "leave no one behind" commitments; (3) **Embedded nurses** reduce short-term efficiency (higher per-unit costs) but build long-term government capacity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: cost-vs-reach: Youth services cost 2-5x more per CYP but are prioritized for equity
speed-vs-inclusion: Refugee camp work is slower due to operational challenges but critical for humanitarian goals
expertise-vs-ownership: International NGOs lead delivery while building local capacity
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (political opposition, stock-outs) drives **intensive oversight**: annual reviews, revised work plans, and contingency funds. High risks in commodity supply chains lead to UNFPA’s procurement role and parallel government capacity-building.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited government capacity shapes the **embedded nurse model** (MSI/EngenderHealth staff co-deliver services while training public providers) and **supply chain strengthening** (rather than direct budget support). Partner roles explicitly include mentorship to transition responsibilities to government over time.
intersections.quote: "The programme will deliberately include work with youth to reduce teenage pregnancy and prevent unwanted pregnancies. In addition, this programme will provide services for people with disabilities, through understanding their needs and find cost effective and innovative solutions." (20372373.odt, Intervention Summary) and "MSI’s model involves the direct provision of services via roving medical teams (including surgeons), complemented by embedded nurses in public health facilities. Embedded nurses deliver services directly while building the capacity of government providers." (D0005054.odt, Summary Information)

key_programme_risks: Government opposition to family planning (e.g., 2019 outreach ban)
Commodity stock-outs due to supply chain weaknesses
Political instability or leadership changes affecting priorities
High teenage pregnancy rates (27% of 15-19 year olds)
Gender-based violence (40% of women experience physical violence)
Refugee camp operational challenges (faith-based resistance, high birth rates)
Funding gaps from other donors (e.g., US uncertainty)
Weak government procurement capacity for commodities
COVID-19 or other health emergencies disrupting service delivery

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversify delivery models (facility-based, embedded nurses) and engage progressive officials. Align with national policies (e.g., Costed Implementation Plan).
UNFPA’s pooled procurement, £2m contingency fund, and supply chain strengthening with government.
Targeted youth services (school linkages, innovative outreach) and advocacy for comprehensive sexuality education.
Integrated services for survivors, training for health workers, and partnerships with GBV programmes.
Partner with IRC and Tanzanian Red Cross; adapt models to faith-based contexts (e.g., focus on maternal health).
Advocate for increased government financing and coordinate with other donors (e.g., UNFPA, Gates Foundation).

fcas_specific_lessons: Despite Tanzania’s stable context, **political opposition to SRHR** can emerge suddenly (e.g., 2019 ban), requiring adaptive delivery models.
In **refugee camps**, faith-based resistance and incentive structures (e.g., food rations tied to family size) necessitate tailored approaches beyond standard outreach.
**Embedded capacity building** (e.g., nurses in public facilities) is critical in contexts with weak institutions to ensure sustainability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2011-2018 Family Planning Outreach Programme demonstrated that: (1) **Outreach models** are effective for rural areas but not sustainable long-term; (2) **Government ownership** requires hands-on training and supply chain support; (3) **Youth services** are costlier but essential for equity. The current programme builds on these by adding urban focus, disability inclusion, and stronger health system integration.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Based on lessons, the programme: (1) Expanded to **urban areas** (where fertility rates are rising); (2) Added **disability-inclusive services** (previously neglected); (3) Strengthened **supply chain components** (beyond the 2011-2018 buffer stock model); (4) Included **refugee camps** (not covered in prior phases); (5) **Embedded nurses** to transition from outreach to system strengthening.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID has been running a Family Planning Outreach Programme since 2011. This programme has scaled up the delivery of family planning services in rural and hard to reach parts of Tanzania... The programme is on track to meet these results and will close in 2018. Family planning outreach services funded by donors is a stop-gap approach... At present, using outreach mobile teams is the most cost-effective and feasible mechanism to ensure service coverage. However, one of the objectives of the new programme is to complement outreach with more sustainable health systems strengthening work." (20372373.odt, Strategic Case) and "During the proposed extension period, the programme will continue its focus on targeted interventions that reduce unmet need for family planning, teenage pregnancy rates, and maternal morbidity and mortality. We will however adopt some inputs to reflect evidence from the implementation and operating environment." (D0005054.odt, Theory of Change)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other donors (e.g., Gates Foundation, KfW, DANIDA)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme advocates for increased government financing (e.g., budget for family planning commodities rose from £1.7m to £4.8m in 2017) and coordinates with other donors to fill the £24m financing gap for 2024.
financial_details.quote: "The proposed £12m addition to the programme will lift our total support from £53.1 million to £65.1m for the period 2017-2026." (D0005054.odt, Additional Support) and "The Government of Tanzania has made public commitments to scale up family planning. In May 2017, the Government of Tanzania’s budget showed an increase in allocation for family planning commodities from 5 to 14 billion shillings (£1.7 million to £4.8 million)." (20372373.odt, Strategic Case)

metadata.programme_name: Partnership for Learning for All in Nigeria (PLANE)
metadata.quote: "A flagship basic education programme to enable more inclusive and effective state and non-state systems to deliver foundational skills to all children" (58726273.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "This business case proposes a multi-window basic education programme, over the next eight years to improve foundational skills (reading, writing and mathematics)." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PLANE combines implementation research (testing/scaling interventions like Hausa early grade reading), capacity building (strengthening state and non-state education systems), service delivery (direct support to 1.5 million children), and policy influence (working at federal level to shape education reforms). The programme uses evidence-based approaches to improve foundational skills while addressing systemic constraints.
what_objectives.q1_source: "PLANE balances evidence-based classroom and child-level interventions with interventions that are higher risk/higher return system-level changes. It is aligned to wider donor support and seeks to influence additional reform through others." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 1.5 million children in Kano, Kaduna, Jigawa (KKJ) directly supported to improve teaching and learning
600,000 children in Borno and Yobe (BY) enabled to continue schooling through Education in Emergencies support
Potential reach of up to 8 million children nationally through systemic improvements
Improved state systems for teacher management, procurement, and public financial management
Enhanced non-state school regulation and performance to deliver foundational skills
Strengthened use of evidence and communication for citizen engagement
Community support to marginalised children's participation and learning
Proportion of P4 & P6 students meeting minimum standards for early grade reading (targets to be agreed at inception)
Increase in primary completion rates (targets to be agreed at inception)
what_objectives.summary: PLANE aims to transform Nigeria's basic education system by improving foundational skills (reading, writing, mathematics) for marginalised children through a mixed portfolio of classroom interventions, system reforms, and community engagement, while working across state, non-state, and federal levels to create sustainable change.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will enable a more inclusive and effective basic education system, through three windows and a DFID managed component: [...] Window One: Getting the Foundations right - a systems approach. [...] Window Two: Education in Emergencies. [...] Window Three: Community support to learning." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nigeria faces a protracted crisis in the North East due to the Boko Haram insurgency (now in its 9th year), with over 35,000 lives lost and 1.7 million displaced. The programme operates in conflict-affected Borno and Yobe states where 71% of primary-age girls are out of school and infrastructure has been destroyed. The overall programme risk rating is assessed as 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: "Nigeria has a protracted crisis in the North East, and conflict in other parts of the country. The Boko Hararam insurgency, now in its 9th year, has led to the loss of over 35,000 lives and displacement of 1.7 million people in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa." (58726273.odt, Context section) && "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (58726273.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: security (Boko Haram insurgency, violence against women/girls)
infrastructure (destroyed schools, lack of safe water in 54% of Jigawa primary schools)
weak institutions (unclear accountability, corruption in procurement, low budget execution)
conflict (protracted crises in North East, farmer-herder conflicts)
political economy (oil revenue dependence, patronage systems)
data limitations (weak monitoring systems, lack of SEND data)
regulatory (overlapping institutional mandates, non-alignment of Social Investment Programmes with Ministry of Education)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit access to conflict zones and require Third Party Monitoring for compliance. Weak institutions create challenges in budget execution (e.g., Kano's 58% execution rate) and procurement transparency. Political economy issues affect teacher deployment and resource allocation, while data limitations hinder evidence-based planning for marginalised groups like children with disabilities.
where_context.quote: "The Boko Hararam insurgency [...] has led to the loss of over 35,000 lives and displacement of 1.7 million people in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa. [...] Infrastructure has been destroyed and commerce, agricultural production and livelihoods have been significantly affected." (58726273.odt, Context) && "Budget execution from 2010-15 was 95% (Jigawa), 58% (Kano) and 83% (Kaduna)." (58726273.odt, Financial Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID Nigeria Office (UK government) retains overall programme management and decision-making authority, with implementing partners (including Southern organizations) delivering components under contracts/grants. The Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) is a DFID Education Adviser supported by a predominantly UK-based team.
q10_capacity_building_details: teacher training and coaching (65,000+ teachers trained in previous programmes)
support to state systems for teacher workforce reforms
improvement of procurement and public financial management
community engagement through school-based management committees (SBMCs)
institutional strengthening of non-state school regulation
evidence generation and use (monitoring systems, Delivery Approach pilot)

partner_organizations.name: Consortium (Window 1 - Getting the Foundations Right)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance to support schools and improve systems (teacher training, governance, data use)

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Bilateral agreement for Education in Emergencies (Window 2) in Borno and Yobe

partner_organizations.name: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs)
partner_organizations.role: Accountable grant for community support to learning (Window 3) and Education in Emergencies (Window 2)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Multilateral agreement for programme-funded adviser, third-party monitoring, and research (DFID-managed component)

partner_organizations.name: State Governments (Kano, Kaduna, Jigawa, Borno, Yobe)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partners for system reforms and service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Federal Ministry of Education and agencies (UBEC, SUBEBs)
partner_organizations.role: Policy influence and federal-level coordination

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be managed from the DFID Nigeria office (at the BHC in Nigeria), drawing on support from financial, programme management, commercial, social development, economic, political, regional, conflict and humanitarian expertise." (58726273.odt, SRO section) && "Window One: [...] delivered through a contracted consortium." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: PLANE uses a combination of instruments: (1) OJEU contract + bridging grant for Window 1 (systems approach), (2) Delegated Cooperation Agreement (DCA) with USAID for Window 2 (Education in Emergencies), (3) Accountable Grants for Window 3 (community support) and part of Window 2, and (4) multilateral agreements with the World Bank for monitoring and research. This allows tailored approaches for different components while maintaining DFID oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Window 1 is delivered through a contracted consortium (closed group of pre-selected partners), while Windows 2 and 3 use delegated agreements (USAID) and accountable grants (NGOs) respectively. The DFID-managed component involves multilateral partnerships (World Bank). Day-to-day management sits with implementing partners under DFID Nigeria Office oversight, with annual work plans and quarterly milestones.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Window 1 uses an OJEU (open competition) contract for the consortium to ensure value for money and technical quality. USAID was selected for Window 2 via a Delegated Cooperation Agreement due to their existing presence and expertise in conflict zones. NGOs for Window 3 and other components were chosen through accountable grants, likely based on track record in community engagement and inclusion. The mix balances competition (for technical components) with strategic partnerships (for conflict and community work).
how_mechanism.quote: "Window One: [...] delivered through a contracted consortium." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary) && "Window Two: [...] a bilateral agreement with USAID or/and non-governmental organisations." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary) && "Window Three: [...] an accountable grant to a partnership of non-governmental organisations." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary) && "OJEU contract + Bridging grant" (58726273.odt, Table 1)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly named, the programme describes mutual expectations with supported states (e.g., political leadership, domestic financing) and regular monitoring through annual work plans, quarterly milestones, and a breakpoint review in Year 5. The DFID Nigeria Office oversees implementation with support from technical advisers (e.g., Education, Governance, Evaluation).
how_governance.quote: "The programme will learn, and adjust, in line with results from monitoring and evaluation. [...] A breakpoint is proposed in year five (2023/24), allowing evidence generated by the mid-point of the programme in year four (2022/23) to trigger the option to exit if required." (58726273.odt, Flexibility) && "There is flexibility to adjust activities in line with state-specific priorities and changes in context, through the annual work plans and quarterly milestones." (58726273.odt, Flexibility)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between activities within windows based on annual work plans and quarterly milestones, with a breakpoint in Year 5 (2023/24) allowing for potential reallocation or exit based on mid-term evidence. However, major shifts between windows (e.g., from systems reform to emergencies) would likely require approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an adaptive management approach with: (1) annual work plans and quarterly milestones to adjust activities, (2) a breakpoint in Year 5 to reassess based on evidence, and (3) flexibility to respond to state-specific priorities. Implementing partners are expected to use evidence to propose and adjust activities, particularly for higher-risk interventions.
how_flexibility.quote: "There is flexibility to adjust activities in line with state-specific priorities and changes in context, through the annual work plans and quarterly milestones. A breakpoint is proposed in year five (2023/24), allowing evidence generated by the mid-point of the programme in year four (2022/23) to trigger the option to exit if required." (58726273.odt, Flexibility) && "A flexible approach, with a focus on understanding and monitoring the results chain, and adapting to emerging information, will be sought from implementing partners." (58726273.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO Nigeria Office → Implementing Partners (consortium/USAID/NGOs). Sub-grantees (e.g., local NGOs or schools) may add a third layer in some components but are not explicitly detailed.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will be managed from the DFID Nigeria office [...] drawing on support from financial, programme management, commercial, social development, economic, political, regional, conflict and humanitarian expertise." (58726273.odt, SRO section) && "Annual work plans and quarterly milestones" (58726273.odt, Flexibility)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct bilateral funding to Nigerian government (rejected due to corruption risks and weak systems)
Purely technical assistance without systemic reforms (rejected as unsustainable)
Focus only on state systems without non-state actors (rejected given the 33% enrolment in non-state schools)
Single-window approach (rejected in favor of a portfolio to balance risk/return)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was chosen to: (1) **Balance risk/return**: Combining lower-risk classroom interventions (e.g., Hausa reading) with higher-risk system reforms (e.g., teacher management) to achieve both immediate results and long-term sustainability. (2) **Address scale vs. depth**: Using a portfolio approach to reach up to 8 million children nationally while targeting 1.5 million directly. (3) **Leverage partnerships**: Aligning with USAID (for conflict zones), World Bank (for monitoring), and NGOs (for community work) to pool expertise and reduce duplication. (4) **Adapt to context**: The three-window structure allows tailored responses to diverse challenges (e.g., conflict in North East vs. systemic weaknesses in North West). (5) **Build on evidence**: Prior DFID programmes (e.g., ESSPIN, GEP3) demonstrated that mixed approaches yield better outcomes than single-input interventions.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (portfolio approach maximizes cost-effectiveness by blending interventions)
risk-mitigation (diversifying across windows reduces exposure to any single failure)
experience (lessons from ESSPIN, GEP3, TDP showed mixed modalities work best)
partner-capacity (leveraging USAID’s conflict expertise and World Bank’s monitoring)
flexibility (adaptive management allows adjustments based on evidence)
equity (targeting marginalised groups through community and emergency windows)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination complexity in multi-window structure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of windows with dedicated implementing partners (consortium for systems, USAID for emergencies, NGOs for community) and DFID oversight through annual plans/milestones.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation risks in conflict zones (Borno/Yobe)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID (experienced in FCAS) and Third Party Monitoring to ensure compliance with safeguarding and risk strategies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of system reforms given weak institutions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on political economy (e.g., Delivery Approach pilot) and embedding reforms in state plans (e.g., Kaduna’s education sector operational plans).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication with other donors (e.g., World Bank BESDA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit alignment with World Bank/GPE programmes and DFID’s role as GPE Coordinating Agency to harmonize priorities.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective instruments like accountable grants for NGOs)
efficiency (milestone-based payments and Third Party Monitoring)
effectiveness (evidence-based interventions like Teaching at the Right Level)
equity (targeted support for girls, children with disabilities, and conflict-affected areas)
why_rationale.quote: "PLANE balances evidence-based classroom and child-level interventions with interventions that are higher risk/higher return system-level changes. [...] Such a mixed modality programme is necessary given the large need and (relatively) small financial resources in this programme." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary) && "The programme’s support for basic education services to crisis-affected areas is in line with the UK National Security Council’s resolutions and with HMG’s North-East Nigeria strategy." (58726273.odt, Alignment with DFID Strategy)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in North East Nigeria (Borno/Yobe) constrains partner selection to organizations with: (1) **Security clearance and experience** (e.g., USAID for Education in Emergencies), (2) **local legitimacy** (NGOs with community trust for Window 3), and (3) **Third Party Monitoring capacity** to ensure compliance in high-risk areas. In contrast, the North West (KKJ) allows for more diverse partners (e.g., consortium for systems reform).
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks limit partners in Borno/Yobe to those with FCAS experience (e.g., USAID).
Weak state capacity in KKJ requires technical consortiums for system strengthening.
Corruption risks necessitate Third Party Monitoring and milestone-based payments.
Cultural norms (e.g., early marriage) shape community partner selection for gender inclusion work.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (classroom interventions + system reforms + community engagement) determine the **multi-window structure**: (1) **Technical complexity** of systems reform → closed consortium for Window 1, (2) **FCAS context** in North East → delegated agreement with USAID for Window 2, (3) **Community focus** → accountable grants to NGOs for Window 3. The need for **adaptive management** drives the milestone/breakpoint approach.
q28_linkages: System-level goals (e.g., teacher management reforms) → require consortium with governance expertise (Window 1).
Conflict-sensitive education → necessitates USAID’s FCAS experience (Window 2).
Inclusion of marginalised groups → demands community-based NGOs (Window 3).
Evidence generation → embedded in all windows via monitoring and Delivery Approach pilot.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid scaling of Hausa reading (efficient) vs. tailored support for children with disabilities (equity). (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led consortium for technical quality (efficiency) vs. Southern partner decision-making (equity). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Higher-cost system reforms (e.g., teacher training) vs. lower-cost community interventions (e.g., SBMCs). The programme addresses this through a **portfolio approach**, balancing core equity targets (e.g., 600,000 conflict-affected children) with efficiency mechanisms (e.g., milestone payments).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Higher transaction costs for Third Party Monitoring in FCAS areas (equity) vs. efficiency gains from delegated agreements.
Northern technical leadership in consortium (efficiency) vs. Southern implementation through state governments (equity).
Focused interventions for girls/disabled children (equity) vs. broad systemic reforms (scale).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major risk rating** (due to FCAS and weak systems) drives **intensive oversight**: (1) Quarterly milestones and annual work plans, (2) Third Party Monitoring for compliance, (3) Breakpoint review in Year 5, and (4) embedded safeguarding processes. High-risk areas (North East) receive more frequent monitoring than moderate-risk components (e.g., KKJ systems reform).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles: (1) **Consortium** (Window 1) must include local partners for sustainability and is tasked with institutional strengthening (e.g., teacher training systems). (2) **NGOs** (Window 3) are selected based on community engagement capacity and receive grants to build local ownership. (3) **State governments** are treated as implementation partners with increasing responsibility over time (e.g., co-financing teacher training).
intersections.quote: "The programme will enable a more inclusive and effective basic education system, through three windows and a DFID managed component: Window One: Getting the Foundations right [...] Window Two: Education in Emergencies [...] Window Three: Community support to learning." (58726273.odt, Intervention Summary) && "There is flexibility to adjust activities in line with state-specific priorities and changes in context, through the annual work plans and quarterly milestones." (58726273.odt, Flexibility)

key_programme_risks: Insecurity in North East disrupting implementation (Boko Haram insurgency).
Weak state capacity leading to poor budget execution or reform ownership.
Corruption in procurement and financial management (e.g., textbook distribution).
Low teacher competency persisting despite training (content knowledge gaps).
Harmful socio-cultural norms limiting girls’ and disabled children’s participation.
Coordinating across three windows and multiple partners creating inefficiencies.
Sustainability of reforms post-PLANE due to political economy constraints.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID (FCAS experience) and Third Party Monitoring for compliance.
Delivery Approach pilot to galvanise political attention and embed reforms in state plans.
Milestone-based payments, Third Party Monitoring, and tracking expenditure indicators.
Focused early grade reading interventions with coaching and materials (e.g., Hausa language support).
Community engagement (Window 3) and partnerships with traditional/religious leaders.
Clear window division, annual work plans, and DFID oversight through quarterly milestones.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict zones require **flexible, adaptive programming** (e.g., Teaching at the Right Level for non-formal contexts).
**Local legitimacy** is critical—partners must have existing community trust (e.g., NGOs in Borno/Yobe).
**Third Party Monitoring** is essential for safeguarding and compliance in high-risk areas.
Education in Emergencies must link to **system recovery** (e.g., supporting state capacity post-conflict).
**Security protocols** must be integrated into all activities (e.g., UKAid branding restrictions).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from ESSPIN, GEP3, and TDP include: (1) **Teacher training alone is insufficient**—must combine with materials, coaching, and system reforms. (2) **Mother-tongue instruction works** (e.g., Hausa reading improvements). (3) **Community engagement drives inclusion** (e.g., SBMCs mobilised £4.8m for schools). (4) **Non-state schools can outperform public schools** with similar resources. (5) **Political leadership is necessary but not sufficient**—must pair with capacity building. These lessons shaped PLANE’s mixed modality and focus on foundational skills.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from broad "learning outcomes" to **focused foundational skills** (reading/writing/numeracy) based on evidence that children couldn’t access the curriculum without basics.
Adoption of **Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL)** for remediation, informed by global evidence and local pilots.
**Portfolio approach** blending lower-risk (e.g., Hausa reading) and higher-risk (e.g., teacher management reforms) interventions.
**Delivery Approach pilot** to address political economy bottlenecks, drawn from DFID’s governance programme (PERL).
Greater emphasis on **disability inclusion** (e.g., testing approaches for children with SEND) based on recent research.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from ESSPIN, EDOREN, DEEPEN [...] have informed the design of PLANE. Some of those lessons include: [...] State (and local government) teacher development systems are necessary to provide the structure for training and ongoing coaching of teachers." (58726273.odt, Lessons Learned) && "PLANE will: Adopt a more focused approach to children learning the basic foundational skills of reading and writing (in local language), and numeracy." (58726273.odt, Pivots in Approach)

co_funding_partners.partner: State Governments (Kano, Kaduna, Jigawa, Borno, Yobe)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: PLANE aims to leverage additional resources through: (1) **GPE coordination**: DFID is the Coordinating Agency for Nigeria’s next $100m GPE grant, aligning PLANE with GPE priorities. (2) **State co-financing**: Previous programmes (e.g., ESSPIN) saw states contribute £21.9m to scale models. (3) **World Bank BESDA**: Alignment with the $611m results-based financing programme to drive complementary investments. (4) **Community mobilisation**: Earlier programmes mobilised £4.8m from communities for school improvements.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £170m" (58726273.odt, Summary Sheet) && "DFID has accepted the invitation of the Federal Government to be the Coordinating Agency for this grant [GPE], giving an opportunity to contribute strongly to project design." (58726273.odt, Working with Partners) && "N6 billion (£21.9m) was spent by state governments across the 6 states to scale up ESSPIN’s school improvement model." (58726273.odt, Box 2: Achievements)

metadata.programme_name: UK-India Green Growth Equity Fund (GGEF)
metadata.duration_text: The total life of the Fund is expected to be 12 years, although in line with market norms there is flexibility to extend by up to 2 years if appropriate.
metadata.quote: "Investment into a joint UK-India Fund (GGEF) promoted as a part of India’s National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), along with complementary technical assistance, to catalyse private investments into Indian infrastructure projects." (29091038.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The total life of the Fund is expected to be 12 years, although in line with market norms there is flexibility to extend by up to 2 years if appropriate." (29091038.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes a joint UK-India equity fund (GGEF) under India’s National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) to catalyse private investments into Indian green infrastructure projects. It combines Development Capital Investment (£120m) with Technical Assistance (£10m) to address market failures, reduce risks for private investors, and demonstrate the commercial viability of green infrastructure investments in India.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Investment into a joint UK-India Fund (GGEF) promoted as a part of India’s National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), along with complementary technical assistance, to catalyse private investments into Indian infrastructure projects." (29091038.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Establishment of the UK-India Green Growth Equity Fund (GGEF) under NIIF
Attraction of private capital (up to £500m) alongside UK/India anchor investments (£240m)
q3_expected_outputs.target: £700m total equity (after Fund Manager fees)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Investment in green infrastructure projects (renewable energy, clean transportation, water/waste management)
Creation of ~100,000 jobs (UK’s pro rata share: 16,000 jobs)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 100,000 jobs overall

q3_expected_outputs.output: Access to clean energy for ~580,000 households (UK’s pro rata share: 94,000 households)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 580,000 households

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy/regulatory improvements via Technical Assistance Facility (TAF)
Mobilization of ~£2bn private debt at project level (1:3 equity-to-debt ratio)
q3_expected_outputs.target: £2bn debt

q3_expected_outputs.output: Reduction in GHG emissions through renewable energy substitution

what_objectives.summary: The GGEF is a 12-year equity fund designed to catalyse private investment in Indian green infrastructure by demonstrating commercial viability, reducing perceived risks, and leveraging £700m in equity (including £240m from UK/India governments) to mobilize £2bn in project-level debt. It combines Development Capital (£120m) with Technical Assistance (£10m) to address market failures, improve the investment pipeline, and generate development impacts (jobs, clean energy access, emissions reduction) while delivering secondary benefits for UK investors and firms.
what_objectives.quote: "The Fund will deliver development impact by investing in infrastructure sectors that contribute to inclusive growth whilst applying high environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. It is estimated that the projects will benefit some 580,000 households access clean energy and create around 100,000 jobs overall." (29091038.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: India is perceived as a high-risk country for infrastructure investments due to policy/regulatory uncertainties, coordination failures, and historical challenges with stalled projects. The programme’s residual risks include financial risk (currency fluctuations, Fund performance), failure to attract private capital, and reputational risks (ESG impacts, corruption).
where_context.q5_source: "The risk rating is ‘Major’ post mitigation. It is a high risk intervention with the potential for high returns." (29091038.odt, Risk Appetite) && "India continues to be perceived as a high risk country for infrastructure investments." (29091038.odt, Theory of Change)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and policy barriers (e.g., land rights, off-take agreements) stall projects; weak institutions and coordination failures between government/private actors deter investment; high cost of capital and lack of long-term financing (only 3% from pension/insurance funds) limit project viability; currency risk (Indian Rupee depreciation) threatens returns. Historical stalled projects (2007–2013) and non-performing loans in the banking sector have reduced investor appetite.
where_context.quote: "Poor coordination between developers, investors and government agencies is an obstacle to the identification and preparation of projects." (29091038.odt, Rationale for Public Intervention) && "The Indian banking sector is facing deteriorating asset quality and increasing non-performing loans." (29091038.odt, Financing Public Infrastructure)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Fund is jointly governed by the UK and Indian governments via a Task Force and Advisory Committee, with day-to-day management delegated to a commercial Fund Manager. Both governments provide equal anchor investments (£120m each) and share oversight of the investment strategy and TA deployment.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) to build deal pipeline and address policy/regulatory barriers
Support for project structuring and feasibility assessments
Strengthening ESG standards and safeguards
Knowledge transfer via Fund Manager’s expertise
Policy reform engagement with GoI and state governments

partner_organizations.name: Government of India (GoI)
partner_organizations.role: Co-anchor investor (£120m), joint governance via Task Force/Advisory Committee, policy/regulatory support

partner_organizations.name: UK Government (HMG)
partner_organizations.role: Co-anchor investor (£120m Prosperity Fund + £10m DFID TA), joint governance, oversight via DFID India
