quote.text: DFID will: [...] Provide bespoke technical assistance to innovation in priority regions to provide sustained engagement to strengthen scale, such as: by supporting business model development for scale and sustainability; partnership brokering; signposting to sources of further investment; documenting and sharing evidence and lessons; and providing training and support to DFID staff on humanitarian innovation (£6 million).

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for thematic innovation funds), core funding (for system-strengthening components like GAHI and the Humanitarian Innovation Hub), and innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., venture capital, prizes) for scaling. Funds are channelled through DFID’s Research and Evidence Division (RED) and managed via thematic windows and technical assistance facilities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates as a platform with multiple components: 1) Thematic innovation funds (managed by partners like Elrha), 2) System-strengthening strands (GAHI, Humanitarian Innovation Hub), and 3) a Technical Assistance Facility. DFID/RED oversees the platform, while implementation is decentralized across global partners. Thematic funds are open to competitive proposals, while system components are directly managed or co-funded.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Thematic innovation funds (e.g., disability inclusion, WASH, UAVs) use open competitive calls to ensure the best ideas are selected. System-strengthening partners (e.g., GAHI, Humanitarian Innovation Hub) were chosen based on existing track records and alignment with DFID’s strategic priorities (e.g., GAHI’s multi-donor coordination role).

quote.text: Over 600 applications were received following the first call for applications [for Creating Hope in Conflict], and sifting is currently underway. [...] This programme will initially fund priority innovation thematic components, including: A new fund on disability inclusion innovation (£5 million); New support to tackle and scale evidence-based innovation on sexual and gender-based violence in emergencies (£2 million); Further support to innovation in water, sanitation and public health in emergencies and protracted crises (£3 million)...

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A Programme Steering Committee includes DFID staff from CHASE, EPIC, RED, and other teams. The committee oversees thematic funds, technical assistance, and system-strengthening components. Thematic funds (e.g., disability inclusion) are managed by partners like Elrha, with DFID retaining oversight. The Humanitarian Innovation Hub and GAHI have separate governance structures but report into DFID’s coordination mechanisms.

quote.text: The programme has been fully reviewed by a Steering Group made up of DFID staff from CHASE, EPIC, RED and other relevant teams working on humanitarian innovation. The programme has been quality assured by the RED Deputy Director and approved by the Chief Scientific Advisor. [...] The SRO for this programme has substantial experience, and is part of an experienced team managing a portfolio of humanitarian research and innovation projects. The SRO will sit on the Programme Steering Committee...

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between thematic components with Ministerial approval, and a portion of the budget is set aside to scope new emerging areas. However, core system-strengthening funds (e.g., GAHI, Technical Assistance Facility) are earmarked.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with mechanisms to "fail fast" and reallocate resources to promising innovations. New thematic areas can be added based on emerging priorities, subject to approval. Lesson-learning is embedded, with requirements to document and share evidence across components.

quote.text: Innovation programmes need to be flexible and adaptive by nature. This programme has been designed to allow for flexibility within the thematic components. Funding has been set aside to scope new areas of work as they emerge, so that additional priority thematic components can be added to the Business Case in future if required (subject to Ministerial approval).
quote.source: 58564882.odt, Flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context and future commitments

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Intermediate partners (e.g., Elrha, GAHI, Technical Assistance Facility) → Implementing organizations (local NGOs, private sector, humanitarian agencies) → End beneficiaries (affected populations).

quote.text: The programme will be structured as follows: [...] 3. Significant investment in scaling humanitarian innovation through innovative financing mechanisms and leveraging private sector partnerships for social impact.

q24_alternatives_considered: Fully open calls for proposals (rejected in favor of thematic focus)
Reliance on grant funding only (rejected in favor of mixed financing mechanisms including venture capital)
Short-term innovation projects (rejected in favor of 5-year programme for scaling)
Decentralized coordination (rejected in favor of centralized platforms like GAHI and the Humanitarian Innovation Hub)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed platform model was chosen to balance flexibility with strategic focus. Thematic funds ensure coherence in priority areas (e.g., disability inclusion, WASH), while system-strengthening components (GAHI, Technical Assistance Facility) address cross-cutting challenges like coordination and scaling. Innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., venture capital) were included to overcome the reliance on short-term grants. The 5-year duration allows for testing, scaling, and course correction, aligning with DFID’s Humanitarian Reform Policy and Grand Bargain commitments.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (value for money through pooled resources and scaling)
experience (building on DFID’s track record with HIF and GAHI)
partner-capacity (leveraging existing platforms like Elrha and WFP)
speed (competitive calls for rapid idea generation)
flexibility (adaptive management to respond to emerging crises)
equity (focus on under-served groups like persons with disabilities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of innovation efforts due to dispersed small-scale projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Centralized coordination via GAHI and the Humanitarian Innovation Hub to share portfolios and align scaling efforts. Thematic funds consolidate activity in priority sectors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of sustainability for scaled innovations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical Assistance Facility provides business model development and partnership brokering. Innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., venture capital) attract private sector investment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Northern expertise in innovation design
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for Southern partners (e.g., training, evidence synthesis) and inclusion of local actors in testing/coordination (e.g., UAV applications in Papua New Guinea).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow uptake of innovations by humanitarian agencies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical support and evidence-sharing mechanisms (e.g., lessons from mVAM’s scale-up). Longer-term funding (5 years) allows for iterative testing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory barriers to technologies like UAVs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Support for multi-agency coordination (e.g., WFP’s UNIT process) and policy influencing through GAHI.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (thematic focus targets high-impact areas like SGBV and WASH)
equity (explicit funding for under-served groups, e.g., disability inclusion)

quote.text: This Business Case is therefore proposing to address the problems identified above as follows: [...] Problem 1: Limited coherence and coordination in the international humanitarian system → Solution: Support to GAHI and Humanitarian Innovation Hub. [...] Problem 3: Limited number of examples of innovations reaching scale → Solution: Invest in new Humanitarian Innovation Window through the Global Innovation Fund to focus on scale and sustainability; use innovative funding mechanisms such as venture capital. [...] Problem 4: Lack of thematic focus in innovation portfolios → Solution: Fund work against four priority thematic areas.
quote.source: 58564882.odt, How should humanitarian innovation funding be invested?

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with proven experience in insecure environments (e.g., WFP for UAVs in conflict zones, Elrha for SGBV in displacement camps). Local partners are often excluded from design roles due to capacity constraints, though the programme aims to address this via the Technical Assistance Facility. Regulatory barriers (e.g., drone restrictions) further restrict who can implement certain innovations.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks exclude partners without field presence in conflict zones (e.g., Syria, Yemen).
Regulatory barriers (e.g., UAV laws) limit private sector engagement in some countries.
Weak institutions in FCAS reduce the pool of capable Southern implementers.
Political constraints (e.g., aid diversion) favor multilateral partners (e.g., UN agencies) over local NGOs.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **scaling** (WHAT) drives the choice of a **platform model** (HOW), with centralized coordination (GAHI) and financing mechanisms (e.g., venture capital) to overcome fragmentation. The focus on **under-served groups** (e.g., disability inclusion) necessitates **embedded technical assistance** to build local capacity. The **FCAS context** (WHERE) requires **flexible, milestone-based oversight** to adapt to crises.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Platform model with GAHI coordination + venture capital financing
Dedicated fund + Technical Assistance Facility for capacity building
Multi-agency coordination (WFP’s UNIT process) + regulatory support
Evidence-based fund + partnership with IRC/George Washington University

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., disability inclusion fund) with efficiency (e.g., competitive calls for rapid idea generation). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Open competitions may favor established Northern organizations, mitigated by capacity-building for Southern partners. 2) **Cost vs. reach**: Scaling innovations (e.g., UAVs) requires upfront investment, justified by long-term efficiency gains. 3) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Technical Assistance Facility provides Northern expertise but includes training for local innovators.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Open competitive calls accelerate innovation but risk excluding less-resourced Southern partners; mitigated by capacity-building components.
Investing in scaling (e.g., £12M for Global Innovation Fund) prioritizes long-term impact over short-term cost savings.
Northern-led technical assistance ensures quality but is balanced by training and support for Southern innovators.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** (FCAS context, innovation uncertainty) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and **embedded technical support**. High-risk components (e.g., UAV testing in conflict zones) receive intensive coordination (e.g., WFP’s UNIT process), while lower-risk areas (e.g., WASH innovations) use lighter-touch management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) **Technical Assistance Facility** providing training to Southern innovators, enabling them to lead implementation; 2) **GAHI** brokering partnerships to strengthen local institutions; 3) **Thematic funds** requiring Southern co-design (e.g., disability inclusion in LMICs). Northern partners (e.g., Elrha) focus on coordination and evidence synthesis, while Southern partners test and scale innovations.

quote.text: The programme has been designed to allow for flexibility within the thematic components. Funding has been set aside to scope new areas of work as they emerge [...] Lesson learning and sharing is an essential principle of this programme, where individual thematic strands will be required to gather, document and share evidence of impact, what works and what doesn’t. [...] The technical assistance facility will have oversight of the level, timing and type of support required across the portfolios of programmes, and play a brokering and facilitation role.
quote.source: 58564882.odt, Flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context and future commitments

key_programme_risks: Innovations failing to scale due to lack of sustainability models (mitigated by Technical Assistance Facility and venture capital).
Duplication of efforts across humanitarian actors (mitigated by GAHI coordination).
Regulatory barriers to technologies like UAVs (mitigated by WFP’s UNIT process and policy influencing).
Limited Southern partner capacity to lead innovation (mitigated by embedded training and support).
Humanitarian access constraints in FCAS (mitigated by local partnership models).
Over-reliance on short-term grant funding (mitigated by mixed financing mechanisms).
Lack of evidence on what works in humanitarian innovation (mitigated by rigorous evaluation requirements).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Centralized coordination via GAHI and the Humanitarian Innovation Hub to align portfolios and share lessons. Thematic funds consolidate activity in priority sectors (e.g., WASH, disability inclusion).
£12M investment in scaling via the Global Innovation Fund, combined with Technical Assistance Facility support for business models and partnerships.
Support for WFP’s UNIT process to harmonize regulations and advocate for humanitarian exemptions.
Capacity-building embedded in all components (e.g., training for DFID staff and local innovators; partnership brokering).
Mandatory evaluation and lesson-sharing across thematic strands, with synthesis by the Technical Assistance Facility.
Partnerships with agencies experienced in insecure environments (e.g., WFP, IRC) and adaptive management to reallocate funds as crises evolve.

fcas_specific_lessons: Local businesses are critical for last-mile delivery but require sustained engagement to define viable business models (learned from 2015 University of Brighton report).
Innovations must be designed for rapid deployment in insecure environments (e.g., UAVs for mapping in conflict zones).
Social barriers (e.g., gender norms, disability exclusion) require explicit mitigation strategies (e.g., SGBV gap analysis, accessible latrine designs).
Multi-year funding is essential for protracted crises (aligned with Grand Bargain commitments).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID programmes (e.g., Humanitarian Innovation Fund) demonstrated that: 1) Thematic focus (e.g., WASH portfolio) yields more coherent results than open calls. 2) Early-stage innovations require sustained support to reach scale (e.g., mVAM’s 5-year journey from pilot to 28 countries). 3) Private sector engagement is underutilized but critical for sustainability (e.g., Google.org’s investment in mVAM). 4) Local innovators are often excluded from design processes, limiting ownership.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from open calls to **thematic funds** (e.g., disability inclusion, SGBV) based on evidence of greater impact. 2) Addition of a **Technical Assistance Facility** to address the lack of scaling support in earlier programmes. 3) Longer duration (5 years) to allow for iterative testing and scaling. 4) Explicit focus on **equity** (e.g., disability inclusion fund) to correct under-representation in past portfolios. 5) Integration of **private sector partnerships** (e.g., venture capital) to improve sustainability.

quote.text: A recent review of DFID’s humanitarian innovation portfolio [...] found that the global humanitarian innovation system needs consolidation, with stronger partnerships between donors and other actors. [...] It also found that there are significant advantages to pooling resources and attention around a focused functional challenge area to build a critical mass of activity and knowledge on what works, rather than by funding fully open calls for proposals. [...] Most investment in humanitarian innovation has to date gone into the earlier stages of innovation [...] with little investment in wider scaling work.
quote.source: 58564882.odt, How should humanitarian innovation funding be invested?

co_funding_partners.partner: Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage private sector partnerships (e.g., venture capital, corporate foundations like Google.org) and multi-donor platforms (e.g., GAHI) to mobilize additional funding for scaling. Past examples (e.g., mVAM) attracted follow-on investment from Google.org and USAID after DFID’s initial support.

quote.text: This new programme will initially fund priority innovation thematic components, including: A new fund on disability inclusion innovation (£5 million); New support to tackle and scale evidence-based innovation on sexual and gender-based violence in emergencies (£2 million); Further support to innovation in water, sanitation and public health in emergencies and protracted crises (£3 million); Strengthening efficiencies through increasing access to cash and in financial services, including work on digital identity (£1 million); New support to testing and coordination of further applications of UAVs in humanitarian contexts for mapping and last mile delivery (£1.7 million); A new fund for logistics and supply chain innovation (£1 million); Further support to innovation in disaster emergency preparedness and resilience in high risk regions (£6 million). In addition to funding priority innovation themes, this Business Case will also make significant investment available to strengthen the international humanitarian innovation system [...] (£12 million for scaling; £6 million for technical assistance; £900,000 each for GAHI and Humanitarian Innovation Hub).

metadata.programme_name: Building an Evidence Base on Humanitarian Protection of People Affected by Conflict (BEPAC)
metadata.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Summary Sheet")
metadata.duration_source: "Building an Evidence Base on Humanitarian Protection of People Affected by Conflict (BEPAC), will improve our understanding of the risks people affected by conflict face, and what can be done to avoid/reduce and mitigate against them. [...] Start Date: 01/01/2019, End Date: 31/03/2024"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) about humanitarian protection in conflict settings, but also includes **capacity building** (investing in local/international measurement capabilities) and **policy influence** (informing UK advocacy and programming). It tests interventions (implementation research) and channels funds through partnerships (financing mechanism).
what_objectives.q1_source: "Through studying the effectiveness of interventions that seek to improve the protection of persons affected by conflict, and improving our understanding of what factors increase or decrease rights violations, **evidence will be generated to inform more effective programming and policy**. [...] Improved evidence on the impact of protection interventions **including investing in local and international capacity to measure and assess protection outcomes**"
q3_expected_outputs: 18 case studies (12 DFID-funded, 6 GCRF-funded)
3 synthesis reports (one per theme)
15 evaluations of protection outcomes (3 per topic, 5 topics)
5 meta-evaluations (one per theme)
5 synthesis reports on existing evidence (for component 2)
5 guidance notes summarizing methodologies (for component 2)
Standardized data collection on attacks on healthcare (component 1)
Methodological innovations for assessing impacts of attacks on healthcare
Uptake activities (policy briefs, workshops, advocacy)
Capacity building for 10 Southern researchers (6 DFID/4 GCRF)
Improved understanding of gender dimensions in protection risks
Disaggregated data by sex where possible
Specialist reports on gender and disability inclusion
what_objectives.summary: BEPAC aims to generate rigorous evidence on what improves humanitarian protection in conflict zones, while building local/international capacity to measure outcomes and informing UK policy/advocacy (e.g., UNSCR 2286 compliance). It combines research, evaluation, and capacity strengthening across three components: healthcare attacks, protection interventions, and thematic research.
what_objectives.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Intervention Summary", "Strategic Case")

countries_regions: Middle East & North Africa: Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Occupied Palestinian Territories, Libya
Africa: Sudan, South Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Somalia, Nigeria, Chad, Sahel region
Refugee-hosting countries: Lebanon, Jordan, Turkey, Bangladesh, Kenya
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **Fragile and Conflict-Affected States (FCAS)** with active conflicts, high displacement, and systematic IHL violations. The World Bank predicts 46% of the world’s poor will live in FCAS by 2030, and the UN describes Syria/Yemen/Gaza as "protection crises."
where_context.q5_source: "The number of conflicts worldwide has increased since 2010 and the World Bank (WB) predicts that by 2030 46% of the worlds’ poor will live in Fragile and Conflict Affected States (FCAS). [...] The UN has described the situations in Syria, Yemen and Gaza as first and foremost **protection crises** and in these contexts civilians are increasingly subjected to the worst effects of conflict."
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit researcher access and require passive consent from warring parties; ethical challenges (e.g., informed consent, confidentiality) are heightened; humanitarian access is often denied; and publishing sensitive data can compromise neutrality. Research in active war zones faces logistical barriers (visas, safety) and methodological challenges (counterfactuals, attribution).
where_context.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Strategic Case: Evidence Gaps")

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Department for International Development (DFID) / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/UKRI design research calls and oversee implementation; Southern partners (e.g., local researchers, NGOs) participate in delivery but decision-making rests with Northern institutions (e.g., AHRC, consortium leads). Co-financing with GCRF includes capacity-building for Southern researchers, but core governance remains Northern-led.
q10_capacity_building_details: methodology training for Southern researchers
substantive peer mentoring
local research institute partnerships
capacity-building add-on funding (£1m total, split DFID/GCRF)
inclusion of practitioners in research to improve uptake

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Component 1: **Accountable Grant** to NGO/academic consortium; Component 2: **procurement route TBD** (grant or contract via market engagement); Component 3: **Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)** with AHRC, co-funded by GCRF. The mix allows flexibility for different research needs (e.g., rapid response vs. long-term studies).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Component 1: **Closed consortium** (HDRG) managed by a lead organization; Component 2: **Consortium** of practitioners/academics led by a prime implementer; Component 3: **Fund manager model** (AHRC manages competitive calls for research proposals). DFID retains oversight via advisory groups and co-financing agreements.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Component 1: direct award to HDRG consortium; Component 2: restricted competition (minimum 3 eligible orgs for Accountable Grant) or open tender; Component 3: open competitive calls for research proposals
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Component 1 uses a **direct award** to a pre-identified consortium with proven expertise (e.g., WHO, ICRC, top universities). Component 2’s method depends on **market engagement** to identify capable orgs. Component 3 uses **open competitive calls** to ensure quality and relevance, with AHRC managing peer review.
how_mechanism.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Delivery", "Appraisal Case")

how_governance.q17_governance_details: An **advisory group** with cross-cutting thematic policy leads (e.g., DFID’s Safeguarding Unit) provides oversight. For Component 3, AHRC/DFID/GCRF **jointly design research calls** and workshops. Component 2’s consortium lead ensures co-development of methodologies with practitioners.
how_governance.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Delivery", "Strategic Case: Governance")

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The business case includes a **provision to extend successful components by 50% of time/budget** (subject to approvals), allowing reallocation to emerging priorities. Co-financing (e.g., GCRF) adds flexibility, but core component budgets are fixed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research themes can be adjusted via **extension provisions** (e.g., incorporating safeguarding if prioritized at the 2018 Safeguarding Conference). Component 3’s competitive calls allow responsiveness to new evidence gaps, but major shifts require DFID approval.
how_flexibility.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Delivery", "Appraisal Case: Flexibility")

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Intermediary (AHRC/consortium lead)** → **Implementers (researchers/practitioners)** → **End beneficiaries (conflict-affected populations)**. Component 3 adds a layer (AHRC manages calls).
how_efficiency.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Delivery", "Financial Details")

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do Nothing" (rejected: would leave evidence gaps and impede UK commitments)
Option A: Three separate components (selected)
Option B: Single component delivering all themes (rejected: less flexible)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option A (three components) was selected for **flexibility**, **specialization**, and **risk management**: (1) **Component 1** leverages an existing consortium (HDRG) with proven expertise on healthcare attacks; (2) **Component 2** allows tailored procurement for impact evaluations; (3) **Component 3** uses AHRC’s competitive calls to ensure high-quality, policy-relevant research. The mixed modality balances **speed** (direct awards where expertise exists) with **rigor** (competitive processes for new areas).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Attribution challenges in protection research (difficulty proving intervention impact in complex conflicts)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investment in **alternative methodologies** (e.g., quasi-experimental designs) and capacity-building for local measurement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safety/sensitivity of research in conflict zones (risk to researchers/participants)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: **Safeguarding protocols** (informed consent, confidentiality, local partnerships) and **DFID Duty of Care** standards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Access restrictions limiting data collection
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Passive consent from warring parties; **remote management** where needed; practitioner partnerships for operational access.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Neutrality concerns if research criticizes conflict actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Balancing advocacy with **operational pragmatism**; DFID/FCO coordination to mitigate diplomatic risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low Southern partner capacity in rigorous research methods
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: **Capacity-building add-ons** (£1m fund) for methodology training and mentorship.

why_rationale.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Appraisal Case", "Strategic Case: Why DFID Should Fund")

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with: (1) **proven access** to conflict zones (e.g., ICRC, MSF); (2) **ethical safeguarding expertise** (e.g., LSHTM’s Health in Humanitarian Crises Centre); (3) **local networks** (required for Component 3 bids). Northern academics/practitioners dominate due to **security risks** and **methodological complexity**, but Southern partners are included via capacity-building.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks exclude less-experienced organizations
Ethical challenges require specialized safeguarding protocols
Access dependencies favor established humanitarian actors
Data limitations necessitate partnerships with local researchers
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rigorous evidence** (e.g., RCTs, mixed methods) shapes the **consortium-based delivery** (Components 1–2) and **competitive calls** (Component 3). **Policy relevance** drives the AHRC/DFID/GCRF collaboration, while **operational constraints** (e.g., access, safety) justify the mixed funding instruments (grants, contracts, MOUs).
q28_linkages: Rigorous evidence needs → Consortium model (Component 1–2) + competitive calls (Component 3)
Policy influence goal → AHRC/DFID/GCRF co-design of research themes
FCAS risks → Direct awards to proven actors (e.g., HDRG) + safeguarding protocols
Capacity-building objective → Embedded training/mentorship in Component 3
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **Northern efficiency** (e.g., AHRC’s management, pre-existing consortia) with **Southern equity** (e.g., capacity-building add-ons, local researcher inclusion). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to Northern consortia accelerate delivery but risk sidelining Southern voices; mitigated via capacity-building. (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led methodologies ensure rigor but may limit local adaptation; addressed through interdisciplinary teams.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern-led consortia (Component 1–2) prioritize speed/expertise over Southern ownership
Capacity-building add-ons (Component 3) address equity but add cost/complexity
Competitive calls (Component 3) ensure quality but may disadvantage less-resourced Southern applicants
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** (FCAS context) justifies **milestone-based oversight**, **advisory group governance**, and **DFID’s embedded safeguarding standards**. High-risk components (e.g., field research) receive **intensive monitoring** (e.g., ethical reviews, security protocols).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is **embedded in delivery**: Southern researchers gain skills via **Component 3’s add-ons**, while practitioners (e.g., IOM, ICRC) co-develop methodologies in Component 2. This shifts Southern partners from **beneficiaries** to **co-implementers** over time.
intersections.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Strategic Case: Delivery", "Intersections")

key_programme_risks: Ethical/safety risks to researchers and participants in conflict zones
Attribution challenges in measuring protection outcomes
Access restrictions limiting data collection
Neutrality risks if research criticizes conflict actors
Low capacity for rigorous research in Southern institutions
Political sensitivity of protection data (e.g., IHL violations)
Coordinating diverse partners (academics, practitioners, donors)
Sustaining uptake of research findings post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Safeguarding protocols (informed consent, confidentiality, local partnerships); DFID Duty of Care standards; passive consent from warring parties.
Investment in alternative methodologies (quasi-experimental designs); capacity-building for local measurement.
Remote management where needed; practitioner partnerships for operational access; flexible research designs.
Balancing advocacy with operational pragmatism; DFID/FCO coordination to mitigate diplomatic risks.
£1m capacity-building fund for methodology training/mentorship; local research institute partnerships.
Anonymization protocols; selective publishing to avoid compromising humanitarian access.
Advisory group governance; joint workshops (AHRC/DFID/GCRF); clear MOUs.
Co-financing models (e.g., GCRF); practitioner engagement in research design; policy briefs/advocacy.

fcas_specific_lessons: Remote management is often necessary but limits data quality; mitigate via local partnerships.
Informed consent processes must account for stigma/targeting risks (ICRC standards).
Publishing sensitive data requires balancing transparency with operational security.
Flexible funding (e.g., extensions) is critical to adapt to evolving conflicts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior DFID-funded reviews (e.g., *What Works in Protection*, 2013) found **limited impact assessments** and **methodological gaps** in protection research. Lessons applied here include: (1) **Investing in methodologies** (e.g., quasi-experimental designs); (2) **Practitioner-academic collaboration** to improve uptake; (3) **Capacity-building** to address Southern research gaps.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) **Extension provisions** (50% time/budget) to capitalize on learning; (2) **Southern researcher add-ons** (£1m) to address equity gaps; (3) **Thematic focus on local protection mechanisms** (lesson from prior top-down approaches).
risks_lessons.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Strategic Case: Evidence Gaps", "Risks & Lessons")

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **mobilize additional donor co-financing** for Component 1 (under negotiation) and **leverage GCRF’s 40% co-funding** (£6m) for Component 3, increasing total resources beyond DFID’s £20m.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Not explicitly mentioned; budget primarily supports **revenue expenditures** (research, evaluations, capacity-building) with potential **capital investments** in methodologies/datasets (e.g., standardized attack-on-healthcare data).
financial_details.quote: ("45907015.odt", "Delivery", "Financial Details")

metadata.programme_name: Africa Food Trade and Resilience Programme
metadata.quote: "The programme will stimulate an increase in regional food trade in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), contributing to satisfying a growing food demand and to addressing food shortages through regional food production, processing and trade, and generating more rural jobs, climate resilience and income for farmers." (41799948.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: September 2018" and "That you approve a no-cost time extension to the Business Case end date from 31 August 2023 to 31 March 2025" (D0004421.odt, Request to approve)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines policy influence (improving predictability of government interventions), implementation research (testing market facilitation approaches), capacity building (supporting companies to integrate smallholder farmers), and service delivery (direct support to farmers). It aims to stimulate regional food trade while building resilience to climate shocks.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will: (i) work with companies that source, process, and trade food in the region, to maximise investment, coordination and benefits to smallholder farmers and (ii) contribute to improve the transparency and predictability of government policies to unlock regional food trade." (41799948.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Up to date market and political economy analysis of regional food trade flows (70 markets)
More predictable, private sector friendly and climate friendly government interventions (policy reforms in selected countries)
Improved coordination and investment in regional food value chains (120 companies supported)
More resilient smallholder farmers accessing better services (1.8 million farming families directly benefiting)
Income increase by 30% for 1.8 million farming families (4.5 million individuals directly attributable to DFID funding)
De-risk and stimulate at least £100 million in private sector investment
Public-private dialogues initiated on policy issues affecting cross-border trade
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to increase regional food trade in Sub-Saharan Africa by addressing two key constraints: lack of coordinated investments in regional food value chains and unpredictability of government policies, while building climate resilience and economic opportunities for smallholder farmers.
what_objectives.quote: "By 2023, we expect the programme will increase income by 30% for 1.8 million farming families and over 8 million people will directly benefit, with 4.5 million of those directly attributable to funding in this business case." (41799948.odt, Narrative summary)

countries_regions: Sahel (Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Niger, Mauritania)
West Africa (Cote d'Ivoire, Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea Conakry)
East Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan, DRC, Eritrea)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in conflict-affected regions (Sahel) and faces risks from political interference in food markets, climate shocks, and fragile governance structures. The overall programme risk rating is "Major" primarily due to political risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" and "The programme takes a flexible, politically savvy and market led approach. We will prioritize countries where opportunity for policy reform exist, working in coalition with influential African and international partners." (41799948.odt, Strategic Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (droughts, floods, climate change impacts on agriculture)
weak institutions (lack of transparent policy processes)
data limitations (scarce evidence on food stock availability)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Government interventions (price subsidies, trade restrictions) create market distortions and deter private investment. Climate shocks disrupt production and trade flows. Political instability in the Sahel affects programme delivery and policy reform prospects.
where_context.quote: "Faced with high level of poverty and food insecurity, most African Governments’ default position has been that a country needs to be food self-sufficient... Typical tools used by Governments include intervening directly in the market through price subsidies, establishing physical food reserves... and imposing trade restrictions on specific crops." (41799948.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-led by African institutions (AGRA, IDH's Nairobi office) with strategic input from Northern partners (BMGF, DFID). Decision-making on policy reforms and company engagements involves both Northern and Southern actors, with AGRA leading the policy component and IDH/SIP leading the private sector engagement.
q10_capacity_building_details: mentorship of local service providers by SIP team
technical support to companies to improve business models
training on gendered market mapping
public-private dialogue facilitation
benchmarking and data-driven advice for companies

partner_organizations.name: Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)
partner_organizations.role: Policy component delivery (market analysis, political economy analysis, policy influencing)
partner_organizations.location: LMIC (Africa-based NGO with expanding country presence)

partner_organizations.name: IDH Sustainable Trade Initiative
partner_organizations.role: Incubator of Smallholder Innovation Platform (SIP); private sector engagement and benchmarking

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (expansion of SIP and policy work)

partner_organizations.name: Rockefeller Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partner for policy reforms

partner_organizations.name: World Bank/IFAD
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partners for policy reforms

partner_organizations.name: Local service providers (competitively sourced)
partner_organizations.role: Market facilitators connecting farmers to regional companies (50 additional cases)

partner_organizations.name: Commercial companies (70 markets)
partner_organizations.role: Anchor buyers and service providers to smallholder farmers

who_partners.quote: "We will deliver the policy component through Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)... We will work with private companies to address the constraints preventing businesses from sourcing more from local farmers... The programme will co-fund with BMGF the expansion of the Smallholder Innovation Platform (SIP), incubated by IDH Sustainable Trade Initiative." (41799948.odt, Programme approach)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses Accountable Grant Agreements with implementing partners (AGRA, IDH) and co-funding arrangements with BMGF. Funds are allocated through competitive sourcing of local service providers and direct support to companies via the SIP platform.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a coalition of partners with distinct roles: AGRA leads policy work, IDH/SIP leads private sector engagement, and local providers deliver market facilitation. DFID provides oversight and strategic direction while partners implement activities autonomously within agreed frameworks.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not specified (competitive sourcing for local service providers)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AGRA and IDH were selected based on their established track records in African agriculture and private sector engagement, respectively. Local service providers are competitively sourced to ensure quality and alignment with programme goals, mentored by the SIP team.
how_mechanism.quote: "Through AGRA and IDH, we will competitively source local service providers for similar work, mentored by the SIP team." and "We will deliver the policy component through Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)... leveraging co-funding by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation." (41799948.odt, Programme approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by DFID's Pan-Africa Department with a Senior Responsible Officer (SRO). Implementing partners (AGRA, IDH) manage day-to-day delivery, with competitive allocation of sub-awards to local providers. The 2022 extension request mentions formal approval processes through DFID's governance channels.
how_governance.quote: "Following approval, the changes will be communicated to implementing partners. The implementing partners will submit revised work plans and financial forecasts detailing how the remaining resources will be used to deliver existing work and any reallocations required to adapt." (D0004421.odt, Next steps) and "Management structure" section in 41799948.odt

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated yearly based on market and political economy analysis, with flexibility to respond to emerging priorities. The 2022 extension allows reallocation to adapt to COVID-19 and Ukraine crisis impacts, but requires formal approval for significant changes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme design allows for annual adjustments based on performance and context changes. The 2022 extension explicitly notes pivoting to address food value chain disruptions from COVID-19 and the Ukraine-Russia crisis, with new activities remaining within the original scope and budget.
how_flexibility.quote: "Funds will be allocated yearly informed by market and political economy analysis and regional performance, with scope to flex for emerging priorities." (41799948.odt, Management Case) and "Delivery of some new activities... have been made possible by pivoting the programme to deal with disruptions in food value chains because of the COVID-19 pandemic and the Ukraine-Russia crisis." (D0004421.odt, Advice)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (AGRA/IDH) → Local Service Providers/Companies
how_efficiency.quote: "The implementing partners will submit revised work plans and financial forecasts detailing how the remaining resources will be used." (D0004421.odt, Next steps) implies milestone-based payments.

q24_alternatives_considered: Achieving objectives through existing trade programs (Trade Mark East Africa) - discarded due to limited geographic coverage and lack of agri-food expertise
Supporting regional market development through Regional Economic Communities - discarded due to complexity of overlapping memberships and lack of flexibility
Working through investment programs (CDC, AgDevCo) - discarded due to lack of expertise in addressing policy barriers
Focusing exclusively on staple foods - discarded due to diet diversification trends and risk mitigation needs
Exclusively addressing policy/regulatory environment - discarded as policy reform alone is high-risk without private sector engagement
Exclusively stimulating investment through market facilitation - discarded as policy risks would remain unaddressed
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was chosen to balance policy influence with private sector engagement, leveraging AGRA's policy expertise and IDH's private sector networks. This approach mitigates risks by combining top-down policy reforms with bottom-up market facilitation, while allowing flexibility to adapt to political and market opportunities across regions.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (combining policy and market interventions for greater impact)
risk-mitigation (dual approach reduces reliance on single strategy)
experience (builds on lessons from FTESA, WAFM, and VUNA programmes)
partner-capacity (AGRA and IDH have proven track records)
flexibility (annual allocations allow responsiveness to context changes)
equity (gender and smallholder focus ensures inclusive benefits)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coalition coordination complexity (managing multiple partners with distinct roles)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of labor (AGRA for policy, IDH for private sector) and mentorship of local providers by SIP team

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Policy reversal risks (governments may revert to protectionist measures)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on achievable micro-reforms with private sector buy-in and public-private dialogues

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector engagement variability (companies may not adopt inclusive business models)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SIP's benchmarking and co-funding incentives, plus technical support to improve profitability for both companies and farmers

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (leveraging £100M private investment per £35M public funding)
equity (gender-disaggregated targets and women's economic empowerment focus)
why_rationale.quote: "The combination of the two options [policy + private sector] also provides an opportunity to reach out to wider market... A conducive policy environment will facilitate growth in productivity, increased regional food trade and sustainability of business models." (41799948.odt, Feasible Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's regional focus across FCAS and non-FCAS contexts requires partners with political savvy and local presence. Conflict in the Sahel limits engagement to areas with reform opportunities, while the need for climate resilience shapes partner selection toward organizations with environmental expertise (e.g., AGRA's climate-smart agriculture focus).
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS contexts (Sahel) require partners with conflict sensitivity and local trust (AGRA's country presence)
Climate risks necessitate partners with adaptation expertise (IDH's focus on resilient value chains)
Policy volatility demands partners skilled in political economy analysis (AGRA's policy unit)
Market thinness requires partners able to work with smallholder aggregators (SIP's company benchmarking)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of policy reform and private sector engagement necessitate a two-pronged structure: AGRA (policy) + IDH/SIP (private sector). The need for regional coordination requires a platform approach (SIP database) rather than siloed country programs, while the focus on smallholder inclusion shapes the use of competitive local providers mentored by SIP.
q28_linkages: Policy objectives → AGRA's leadership role and public-private dialogue focus
Private sector objectives → IDH/SIP's company benchmarking and technical support
Regional scope → Multi-partner coalition with sub-regional hubs
Climate goals → Integration of climate considerations in both policy and business models
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging existing platforms like SIP) with equity (gendered market mapping, women's empowerment targets). The choice to work through African-led partners (AGRA) prioritizes local ownership over potentially faster Northern-led delivery, while competitive sourcing of local providers aims to combine cost-effectiveness with inclusivity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Competitive local provider selection slows implementation but ensures quality and alignment
Expertise vs ownership: Northern funders (BMGF) provide resources while African partners (AGRA) lead delivery
Cost vs reach: SIP's benchmarking platform enables scale but requires upfront investment
Policy focus vs market needs: Balancing achievable micro-reforms with transformative systemic change
intersections.risk_affects_management: The "Major" risk rating (due to political interference) leads to intensive oversight through annual reviews, milestone-based payments, and DFID's direct approval requirements for extensions or significant adaptations. FCAS contexts in the Sahel trigger enhanced due diligence for partners.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: AGRA's policy capacity enables its leadership on government engagement, while IDH's private sector expertise shapes its role in company benchmarking. The programme invests in mentoring local providers to build their capacity to replicate SIP's model, explicitly linking capacity building to partner roles.
intersections.quote: "The programme takes a flexible, politically savvy and market led approach. We will prioritize countries where opportunity for policy reform exist, working in coalition with influential African and international partners." (41799948.odt, Programme approach) and "Through AGRA and IDH, we will competitively source local service providers for similar work, mentored by the SIP team." (41799948.odt, Programme approach)

key_programme_risks: Political interference in food markets (risk rating: Major)
Policy reversal or lack of reform implementation
Climate shocks disrupting production and trade flows
Private sector disengagement due to market risks
Coalition coordination challenges among multiple partners
Data scarcity on food stocks and cross-border trade
Conflict in Sahel affecting programme delivery
Gender inequalities limiting women's benefits
COVID-19/Ukraine crisis exacerbating food insecurity

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Building coalitions with influential partners, political economy analysis, focusing on achievable reforms where political will exists
Private sector engagement to create constituencies for reform; public-private dialogues
Promotion of climate-smart agriculture and resilient value chains; 70% of funding counts toward UK International Climate Finance
Co-funding and technical support through SIP; demonstrating profitability of inclusive business models
Enhanced due diligence for partners; focusing on stable areas within countries
Programme extension and pivot to address food value chain disruptions

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for flexible, politically savvy approaches in FCAS contexts
Importance of local partnerships with established country presence (AGRA)
Enhanced due diligence requirements for conflict-affected areas
Focus on resilience-building to mitigate climate and conflict shocks
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from FTESA, WAFM, and VUNA programmes showed that: (1) Public-private dialogues achieve policy micro-reforms; (2) Company engagements work best when linked to commercial anchor buyers; (3) Regional approaches require flexibility to navigate political economy complexities; (4) Climate-smart interventions reduce long-term humanitarian needs.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) Annual fund allocation flexibility; (2) Competitive sourcing of local providers with SIP mentorship; (3) Gendered market mapping as a core component; (4) Explicit climate finance targeting (70% of funds); (5) Adaptive management to respond to crises (COVID-19, Ukraine war).
risks_lessons.quote: "Previous DFID funded work on which this intervention builds have proved that public-private sector dialogue and other forms of private-sector-led advocacy... can lead to the establishment of private sector-friendly reforms and achieve enhanced regional food trade." (41799948.odt, Strategic Case) and "The current situation of the Africa food crisis and response required, presents a sufficiently compelling case for extending the programme." (D0004421.odt, Request to approve)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to de-risk and stimulate at least £100 million in private sector investment (nearly 3:1 leverage ratio).
financial_details.quote: "DFID funding will de-risk and stimulate at least £100 million in private sector investment aimed at enhancing smallholder farmers’ productivity and resilience." (41799948.odt, Narrative summary) and "There is no additional funding required. The extension is to allow us to deliver the support expected in the existing Accountable Grant Agreements." (D0004421.odt, Advice)

metadata.programme_name: UK Support for Health in Nigeria
metadata.quote: "DFID Nigeria’s flagship health programme aims to i) Encourage Government of Nigeria to increase resources invested in health; ii) Improve effectiveness and efficiency of public and private basic health services and iii) Reduce total fertility rate in Nigeria" (57156661.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "This business case will be DFID Nigeria’s flagship health programme, which proposes to invest £235 million over eight years" (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of basic health services), capacity building (strengthening health systems and private sector engagement), and financing mechanism (supporting the Basic Health Care Provision Fund). It aims to save lives, reduce suffering, and improve economic prospects through health system strengthening and demographic interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This business case will be DFID Nigeria’s flagship health programme, which proposes to invest £235 million over eight years in order to save lives, reduce suffering and improve economic prospects for the poorest and most vulnerable in Nigeria through: [...] Improving effectiveness and efficiency of public and private basic health services (through innovative financing mechanisms, strengthening health system and working with private sector to deliver affordable health services for the poorest populations)" (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 4,250 maternal deaths averted
50,741 under-five deaths averted
£128 per disability-adjusted life-year averted
Over 20% of programme (over £50 million) on targeted family planning interventions
Strengthening health systems to deliver range of health interventions including family planning and malaria
Support to Basic Health Care Provision Fund (innovative financing mechanism)
Improved coverage of maternal and child health services in target states (Borno, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Yobe)
Reduction in total fertility rate through social norms change and family planning services
what_objectives.summary: The programme is a strategic, long-term health intervention combining direct service delivery, health system strengthening, and demographic management to address Nigeria's severe health challenges, particularly in maternal/child mortality and high fertility rates.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will contribute to DFID’s Strategic Objective 2 (through delivery of basic health services to crisis affected populations); Strategic Objective 3 (through impact on human capital in Nigeria); and Strategic Objective 4 (through our theory of change)." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a fragile context with significant security risks (Boko Haram insurgency in Northeast), weak institutions, and corruption, but is assessed as moderate risk due to DFID's long experience in the region and mitigation strategies.
where_context.q5_source: "This is a moderate risk programme, although with major risks in a number of areas, including challenges of delivering programmes in Northern Nigeria." (57156661.odt, A10: Risk)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (corruption, poor public financial management)
political economy (low government health spending, weak accountability)
infrastructure (poor health facility coverage in rural areas)
data limitations (weak health management information systems)
climate risks (not explicitly detailed but implied in population growth pressures)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict limits access to Northeast regions; corruption undermines fund utilization; weak institutions reduce service delivery effectiveness; low government spending creates dependency on donor funds; poor data systems hinder monitoring.
where_context.quote: "The conflict in northeast Nigeria has become a protracted crisis [...] continued insecurity and lack of access in many parts of the northeast of Nigeria, (particularly Borno) makes it an environment that is very challenging for delivering interventions." (57156661.odt, A9: Conflict, Fragility and Crises)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Nigeria (Federal Ministry of Health and State Primary Health Care Development Agencies)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with Government of Nigeria at federal and state levels, with DFID providing funding and technical support but decision-making shared through joint mechanisms like the Basic Health Care Provision Fund. State governments have autonomy in implementation within national frameworks.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening State Primary Health Care Development Agencies (SPHCDAs)
Training health workers (especially female) through Women for Health programme
Supporting Ward Development Committees for community accountability
Building private sector capacity to deliver affordable services
Institutional strengthening for health financing (e.g., Basic Health Care Provision Fund)
Technical assistance for health management information systems

partner_organizations.name: Government of Nigeria (Federal Ministry of Health)
partner_organizations.role: Policy-making, coordination, and regulation of health sector; co-financing through Basic Health Care Provision Fund

partner_organizations.name: State Governments (Borno, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Yobe)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of primary health care services; budget allocation and release

partner_organizations.name: National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA)
partner_organizations.role: Development of national primary health care policy; oversight of state-level implementation

partner_organizations.name: State Primary Health Care Development Agencies (SPHCDAs)
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation of primary health care services

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer of Basic Health Care Provision Fund; technical support for health financing

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer of health programmes; alignment in Kaduna and Kano states

partner_organizations.name: Private sector providers (patent medicine vendors, faith-based facilities, private clinics)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of health services, especially in rural areas

partner_organizations.name: Ward Development Committees
partner_organizations.role: Community advocacy and accountability

partner_organizations.name: DFID Nigeria office
partner_organizations.role: Funding, technical assistance, and programme oversight

who_partners.quote: "The programme will work across DFID Nigeria office (and HMG in Nigeria), including drawing on support from financial, programme management, statistical, commercial, social development, governance, economic, political, regional, conflict and humanitarian expertise." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct funding to government mechanisms (e.g., Basic Health Care Provision Fund), grants to implementing partners, and technical assistance. The Basic Health Care Provision Fund is a pooled financing mechanism co-funded by Government of Nigeria, World Bank, and Gates Foundation, with DFID providing advocacy and technical support.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a decentralized structure involving federal, state, and local government agencies, with coordination mechanisms like the Basic Health Care Provision Fund. DFID provides oversight and technical support but implementation is led by Nigerian institutions with private sector engagement.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme is coherent with the wider international community, including support the Basic Health Care Provision Fund which is a new, unique mechanism that has been established by the Government of Nigeria for financing basic health services." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Basic Health Care Provision Fund operates with a governance structure involving Government of Nigeria, World Bank, and other funders. DFID participates in coordination meetings with partners like Gates Foundation and state governments (e.g., MOU in Kaduna).
how_governance.quote: "There will be flexibility built into the programme, including annual adjustments to work plans with review-points/break-clauses, which will be informed through ‘real time’ learning delivered by independent monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Contingency mechanisms enable response to new priorities or crises; geographic priorities can be adjusted if states under-invest in health. Annual work plan adjustments are informed by real-time MEL.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes break-point reviews (e.g., after 3 years) and annual adjustments based on MEL findings. Geographic and thematic priorities can be shifted based on performance and context changes.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme has significant flexibility to adjust to changes in the context. This includes contingency mechanisms to enable response to new priorities or crises and enabling delivery of services to crisis affected populations as required." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Government of Nigeria (federal/state agencies) → Service providers (public/private). Some technical assistance may add a third layer for specific components.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will be managed by a Senior Health Adviser (SRO) supported by a team within DFID Nigeria, with implementation led by Nigerian government agencies." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Standalone family planning programme (rejected in favor of integrated health approach)
Direct service delivery without system strengthening (rejected due to sustainability concerns)
Pure advocacy without financing support (rejected as insufficient to drive change)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was chosen to: 1) Align with Government of Nigeria’s priorities and existing mechanisms (e.g., Basic Health Care Provision Fund); 2) Ensure sustainability by building local capacity and systems; 3) Address both immediate service gaps and long-term systemic issues; 4) Leverage DFID’s experience in Northern Nigeria and existing partnerships (e.g., Gates Foundation).
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (using existing government structures to reduce fiduciary risks)
experience (DFID’s long history in target states)
partner-capacity (building on strengths of Nigerian institutions)
equity (focus on poorest states and vulnerable groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government of Nigeria’s low health budget releases undermine co-financing commitments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocacy and technical support to improve budget execution; contingency funds for gaps

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption in health sector diverts programme funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Third-party monitoring; community accountability mechanisms; performance-based financing

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict in Northeast limits access to beneficiaries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Conflict-sensitive programming; partnerships with local NGOs; flexible delivery modalities

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak state capacity delays implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical assistance; gradual scaling based on absorption capacity

vfm_criteria_used: equity (focus on poorest and most vulnerable)
why_rationale.quote: "The entire theory of change of this business case is a major step as part of a sustainable exit strategy, encouraging Government of Nigeria to budget for health, and supporting public and private health services to be delivered effectively and efficiently." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile context in Northeast Nigeria (Borno, Yobe) limits partner selection to organizations with conflict experience and local trust (e.g., local NGOs over international actors). Weak state capacity in target regions requires partners with embedded technical assistance capabilities. Security risks necessitate partnerships with community-based organizations for access.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Northeast restricts international partners’ operations
Low institutional capacity in target states requires partners with strong TA components
Corruption risks demand partners with robust fiduciary controls
Cultural norms (e.g., gender roles) shape partner selection for family planning components
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both immediate service delivery (e.g., maternal health) and long-term system change (e.g., health financing) requires a mixed delivery structure combining direct implementation with government-led mechanisms. The focus on private sector engagement necessitates market-shaping instruments like the Basic Health Care Provision Fund.
q28_linkages: Service delivery objectives → need for state-level implementation partners
System strengthening goals → use of pooled funds (BHCPF) and technical assistance
Family planning targets → partnerships with private providers (e.g., patent medicine vendors)
Conflict sensitivity → local NGO partnerships in Northeast
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) Rapid scaling of services vs. inclusive governance (e.g., balancing speed with community accountability mechanisms); 2) Northern technical expertise vs. Southern ownership (e.g., DFID advisors supporting but not leading implementation); 3) Cost-effective delivery vs. reach to hardest-to-access areas (e.g., higher costs in conflict zones).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: "The programme will maintain a conflict sensitive approach and will be aware of the risks of doing harm, particularly in the conflict affected parts of the country" (57156661.odt, A9: Conflict)

Expertise vs. ownership: "The SRO is a Senior Health Adviser, who will be supported by Human Development Team Leader, 2 Health Advisers [...] The programme will work across DFID Nigeria office" (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)
Cost vs. reach: "There will be flexibility to adjust geographic priorities if State Governments are not sufficiently investing in health" (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate-high risk profile (conflict, corruption) drives intensive oversight mechanisms: real-time MEL, annual adjustments, and break-point reviews. Insecure areas require embedded advisors for implementation support.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: states with stronger capacity (e.g., Kaduna) take leadership in implementation, while weaker states receive more direct TA. Private sector partners are engaged based on their ability to reach underserved populations (e.g., patent medicine vendors in rural areas).
intersections.quote: "The programme will draw from the experience and lessons of engaging with traditional institutions and structures, facilitating engagement between government and citizens, and inclusion of vulnerable groups in health sector governance processes." (57156661.odt, A3: Health System Building Blocks)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient Government of Nigeria investment in health (financial/human resources)
Weak political leadership undermining reforms
Oil price downturns reducing government health spending
Conflict/insecurity in Northeast limiting access
High fiduciary risks (fraud/corruption in health sector)
State-level budget execution failures
Private sector quality variations affecting service delivery
Demographic pressures outpacing health system capacity
Social norms limiting family planning uptake
Weak health information systems hindering monitoring

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Advocacy for Abuja Declaration targets; support to Basic Health Care Provision Fund; performance-based financing
Conflict-sensitive programming; local NGO partnerships; flexible delivery modalities
Third-party monitoring; community accountability (Ward Development Committees); transparent financing mechanisms
Embedded technical assistance; gradual scaling; capacity building for SPHCDAs
Standards enforcement; training for patent medicine vendors; quality assurance mechanisms
Community engagement; male involvement strategies; integration with other health services

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for conflict-sensitive approaches in Northeast (e.g., "do no harm" principles)
Importance of local partnerships for access in insecure areas
Flexible funding mechanisms to respond to crises (e.g., contingency funds)
Community accountability critical where state institutions are weak
Real-time MEL essential in volatile contexts
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID programmes (e.g., MNCH2, PATHS2) demonstrated that: 1) Integrating family planning with other services improves uptake; 2) Drug revolving funds can sustain commodity supply; 3) State-level advocacy drives budget increases (e.g., Kaduna’s health budget rose to 12%); 4) Private sector already delivers majority of child health services in North (56-70% for malaria/diarrhea treatment).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme builds on lessons by: 1) Focusing on DFID’s priority states with worst indicators; 2) Using innovative financing (BHCPF) to address sustainability; 3) Strengthening private sector engagement based on its dominant role in service delivery; 4) Incorporating real-time MEL for adaptive management.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID has supported a range of health programmes over the past 20 years [...] The key lessons learnt from the recent health programmes are summarised in Annex 8 and the key results summarised in Annex 9." (57156661.odt, A7: DFID’s Past Investments)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, a pooled mechanism with Government of Nigeria (£123m in 2018), World Bank, and Gates Foundation contributions, creating a unified funding approach for basic health services.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme supports both capital investments (e.g., facility renovations) and revenue expenditures (e.g., commodity procurement, health worker salaries), with a focus on systemic changes like health financing mechanisms.
financial_details.quote: "The Basic Health Care Provision Fund is the only mechanism that enables a unified funding approach to funding health [...] and is receiving funding from Government of Nigeria, World Bank and Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, with potential support from other funders in the coming years." (57156661.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Support to TradeMark East Africa – Strategy 2 (STS2)
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to increase sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa by increasing East Africa’s trade with the region and the rest of the world." (25513241.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide £229 million overall towards TMEA’s Strategy 2 over 6 years (July 2017 - June 2023)" (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing/scaling trade facilitation interventions), capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills for trade), and financing mechanisms (channeling funds to leverage private/public investments). It focuses on reducing trade barriers while building export capacity and inclusive trade systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will (i) invest in improving the efficiency and capacity of transport, logistics and trade infrastructure at key port and border points; (ii) invest in systems to improve trading standards, reduce non-tariff barriers and enhance transparency in trade processes; (iii) improve the regulatory and policy environment for trade; and (iv) support private sector advocacy for trade competitiveness, the export capacity of East African businesses and the greater participation of women and small and growing businesses in trade." (25513241.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: reduced trade barriers
q3_expected_outputs.target: 0.6% additional GDP growth; 1.8 million fewer people living below $2/day; $1.1 billion additional government revenue

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased trade volumes
q3_expected_outputs.target: $600m net added total trade; 1.1% increase above trend; $200m net added exports to RoW (1.9% increase); $100m net added intra-EAC exports (1.3% increase)

q3_expected_outputs.output: improved infrastructure
q3_expected_outputs.target: Mombasa Port clearance time reduced from 11 to 3.8 days; Busia border crossing times reduced by 80%

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy/regulatory reforms
q3_expected_outputs.target: harmonization of 80+ trading standards; implementation of EAC Elimination of NTBs law

q3_expected_outputs.output: private sector capacity
q3_expected_outputs.target: 7 logistics hubs piloted; increased women/SME participation in trade

q3_expected_outputs.output: systems/platforms
q3_expected_outputs.target: electronic cargo tracking; single window trade systems; trade community information portals

what_objectives.summary: STS2 aims to transform East Africa’s trade competitiveness through infrastructure investments, regulatory reforms, and private sector capacity building, with explicit targets for economic growth, poverty reduction, and inclusive trade expansion.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver the following results. At an impact level: Increased sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa, by contributing to an additional 0.6% growth in East African GDP above trend; by helping to reduce the number of people living below the poverty line ($2/day) by 1.8 million; and by helping increase government revenue excluding grants by an additional $1.1 billion." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with political economy challenges (e.g., Tanzania’s restrictive environment) and procurement risks, but these are deemed manageable. The overall risk rating is explicitly stated as "moderate."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The largest risks will be those associated with procurement and with the political economy, and are well managed." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Poor infrastructure (e.g., Mombasa Port delays adding 40% to goods costs), regulatory barriers (e.g., NTBs for staples), and political economy issues (e.g., resistance to reforms in Tanzania) directly hinder trade flows. Corruption at borders and weak institutions (e.g., customs agencies) increase transaction costs and reduce private sector competitiveness.
where_context.quote: "Trade remains constrained by poor infrastructure which hampers access to markets, tariffs (which have not fallen uniformly across the EAC) and non-tariff barriers (such as poorly designed and/or implemented standards or rules of origin)." (25513241.odt, Strategic Case) and "The poor performance of logistics means that EAC states remain largely excluded from global value chains." (25513241.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: TMEA (a regional platform with EAC governments, private sector, and donors) makes strategic decisions jointly. DFID provides funding and oversight but does not unilaterally direct implementation. The TMEA Council (comprising all donors) is chaired by DFID Kenya, indicating shared governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to public/private sectors
gender mainstreaming (e.g., gender audits, adviser hiring)
private sector advocacy training
institutional strengthening (e.g., customs agencies, standards bureaus)
skills development for exporters/women traders
policy/regulatory reform support

partner_organizations.name: TradeMark East Africa (TMEA)
partner_organizations.role: implementing platform; coordinates all interventions

partner_organizations.name: DFID (UK Government)
partner_organizations.role: primary funder; strategic oversight via TMEA Council

partner_organizations.name: East African Community (EAC) Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: policy/regulatory reform partner; regional integration

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan
partner_organizations.role: public sector reform; infrastructure co-funding

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (e.g., East Africa Business Council, exporters)
partner_organizations.role: advocacy; trade capacity building

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral donors (World Bank, AfDB, USAID, DANIDA, etc.)
