partner_organizations.role: co-funding; complementary programmes

partner_organizations.name: Civil society (e.g., women trader associations)
partner_organizations.role: inclusive trade advocacy; grassroots engagement

who_partners.quote: "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase. Each DFID office will assign an SRO to oversee their respective country/regional support, and the Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet) and "TMEA, initially set up by DFID, has attracted 7 other donors, has raised over £450 million (now the largest aid for trade facility globally) and works closely with governments, private sector and civil society in the EAC." (25513241.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides core funding to TMEA via a partnership agreement, which is then allocated through a mix of grants (for technical assistance), capital investments (for infrastructure), and leveraged financing (public/private co-funding). The instrument combines block funding for TMEA’s operational costs with earmarked funds for specific interventions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: TMEA operates as a regional platform with a centralized secretariat and country offices. DFID and other donors provide funding to TMEA, which then manages sub-awards to governments, private sector, and civil society partners. A TMEA Council (chaired by DFID Kenya) oversees strategic decisions, while day-to-day delivery is led by TMEA’s technical teams.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (TMEA was established by DFID and expanded to include other donors)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TMEA was created by DFID in 2010 and has since attracted 7 additional donors. Its proven track record (e.g., £450m raised, measurable trade improvements) and existing governance structures (e.g., donor council) made it the logical vehicle for continued support. The 2016 QAU assessment scored TMEA’s Kenya component as ‘1’ (highest possible), validating its capacity.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID created TradeMark East Africa (TMEA) in 2010 to tackle these problems in East Africa. This programme is an extension of DFID support provided under TMEA’s Strategy 1 (2011-2017), recognising the progress it has already made and opportunities to build momentum." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The largest (£75 million) component of the programme (Kenya) was quality assured by the Quality Assurance Unit (QAU) in November 2016, receiving a ‘1’ (the highest possible score)." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The TMEA Council (comprising all donors, chaired by DFID Kenya) oversees strategic decisions. Technical Advisory Groups (e.g., for standards harmonization) and National Oversight Committees (e.g., for NTB monitoring) provide operational governance. DFID retains approval rights for major budget reallocations beyond the spending review period.
how_governance.quote: "The Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet) and "To provide further assurance, the revised Business Case will be submitted to QAU in parallel with approval by Ministers, particularly to look at overall implementation coherence aspects." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with DFID approval, particularly for newer areas like export capacity support. A mid-term review is required to unlock unspent budgets beyond the initial spending review period, incentivizing evidence-based adjustments.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme adopts a phased approach (e.g., logistics hubs) to incorporate lessons learned. Adjustments require DFID approval, with flexibility built into newer components (e.g., export capability support) to respond to emerging evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "There is in-built flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context, particularly with regard to newer components on export capability support. The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (25513241.odt, Summary Sheet) and "As the programme may spend beyond the current spending review period, progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets, which will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TMEA (platform) → [governments/private sector/civil society implementers]. No additional intermediary layers are explicitly described.
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID funding will be used to promote sustainable and inclusive prosperity in East Africa through further reducing trade costs and barriers..." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary) implies direct funding to TMEA, which then disburses to partners. Payment structures are tied to "proposed work-plans and budgets" (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary).

q24_alternatives_considered.description: DFID’s trade support ends; reliance on other donors/multilaterals. Risks losing momentum on reforms (e.g., OSBPs) and impairs UK Aid Strategy delivery.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Focus on 1-2 of 3 Strategy 1 areas
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Narrow focus to infrastructure OR standards/NTBs OR policy reforms. Reputational risk of withdrawing from key areas; evidence shows all three are needed for impact.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: Continue all Strategy 1 focus areas
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Maintain support for infrastructure, standards/NTBs, and policy reforms. Builds on proven success but misses opportunities to address export capacity gaps.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 4: Expand beyond trade/logistics to broader business climate
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Add PPP policy, tax reform, land registration, etc. High risk of mission creep; TMEA’s comparative advantage is trade facilitation.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 5: Strategy 1 areas + export capacity support (CHOSSEN)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Adds private sector advocacy, women/SME inclusion, and export capability building to core trade facilitation work. Aligns with evidence that supply-side constraints limit trade impact.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 was selected because: (1) **Evidence**: Trade facilitation impact is maximized when complemented by export capacity building (e.g., logistics hubs pilot). (2) **Value for Money**: Leverages TMEA’s existing platform and donor base to address new constraints without creating parallel structures. (3) **Risk Mitigation**: Phased implementation (e.g., hubs) allows learning; TMEA’s track record (QAU score of 1) reduces delivery risk. (4) **Strategic Fit**: Aligns with UK Aid Strategy’s focus on trade as an engine for poverty reduction and DFID’s goal of responsible exit from aid by building local capabilities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays in infrastructure projects (e.g., Mombasa Port)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased investments with project preparation support (e.g., feasibility studies) and leveraging World Bank/AfDB co-funding to share risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political resistance to reforms (e.g., Tanzania’s restrictive environment)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Politically aware technical assistance; alignment with EAC integration priorities to build regional peer pressure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overstretch from expanding into export capacity (new for TMEA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot approach for logistics hubs; mid-term review to assess progress before scaling.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination challenges with 7+ partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: TMEA Council (chaired by DFID) ensures alignment; joint monitoring frameworks.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 5: Do all of the previous focus areas from Strategy 1 as before and support export capacity... This option extends current support on trade competitiveness to include targeted supply-side interventions that seek to: expand private sector-led advocacy; promote greater inclusion of women and small businesses in trade... and build the export capability of the region’s private sector." (25513241.odt, Appraisal Case) and "The current intervention mix and approach have been significantly effective in reducing the constraints to trade in the EAC. Option 2 is thus not supported by strong evidence or lessons learnt and would unlikely maximise the effectiveness of DFID support as well as overall value for money." (25513241.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The EAC’s political economy limits partner selection to organizations with regional legitimacy and government buy-in. For example: (1) **Tanzania’s restrictions** require working through the EAC Secretariat to avoid bilateral tensions. (2) **South Sudan’s fragility** restricts direct implementation to border infrastructure (e.g., Nimule) with minimal in-country presence. (3) **Private sector fragmentation** necessitates platforms like the East Africa Business Council for advocacy.
q27_constraints_detail: Tanzania’s political resistance to reforms → reliance on EAC Secretariat for regional peer pressure
South Sudan’s conflict → limited to border projects with Uganda/Kenya
Weak customs institutions → need for embedded technical assistance (e.g., KRA modernization)
Informal cross-border trade dominance → requires civil society partners for women trader inclusion
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **integrated trade facilitation** (combining infrastructure, standards, and policy) drives the platform-based delivery structure (TMEA). For example: (1) **Infrastructure investments** (e.g., Mombasa Port) require capital funding instruments and public-private partnerships, shaping the mixed financing modality. (2) **Regulatory reforms** (e.g., NTB elimination) need multi-stakeholder governance, leading to the TMEA Council model. (3) **Export capacity building** demands flexible, phased pilots (e.g., logistics hubs), influencing the adaptive management approach.
q28_linkages: Multi-sectoral objectives (trade + export capacity) → platform structure (TMEA) to coordinate diverse partners
Need for leverage (e.g., World Bank co-funding) → mixed funding instruments (grants + capital investments)
Political economy risks → joint governance (donor council) to share accountability
Inclusive trade goals → embedded capacity building (e.g., gender advisers) in all components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (e.g., focusing on high-impact corridors like Mombasa-Dar) with **equity** (e.g., including landlocked countries like Burundi/South Sudan and women traders). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Phased logistics hubs delay full rollout but ensure poor/women benefit. (2) **Cost vs. reach**: Electronic systems (e.g., single window) reduce long-term costs but require upfront investment in digital literacy for SMEs. (3) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern technical assistance (e.g., for customs modernization) is paired with Southern-led advocacy (e.g., EABC) to build local capacity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: High-impact corridors (e.g., Northern Corridor) vs. marginalized areas (e.g., South Sudan borders)
Upfront costs for electronic trade systems vs. long-term savings and SME accessibility
Donor-driven reforms (e.g., standards harmonization) vs. local private sector priorities
Rapid infrastructure delivery vs. time needed for inclusive consultation (e.g., women traders)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (procurement/political economy) leads to **milestone-based oversight** with embedded advisors for high-risk components (e.g., Tanzania ports). For example, the World Bank’s $345m Dar Port loan is complemented by TMEA’s project management support to mitigate implementation risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: (1) **Governments** receive technical assistance to lead reforms (e.g., KRA customs modernization). (2) **Private sector** gains advocacy skills to influence policy (e.g., EABC). (3) **Civil society** (e.g., women trader groups) is empowered to participate in trade systems design. This shifts partners from passive recipients to active co-implementers, e.g., NTB monitoring committees include private sector reps.
intersections.quote: "The nature of trade costs varies across geographical areas and income levels, and hence the effectiveness of trade facilitation interventions is likely to be determined by the degree and intensity of the factors that contribute to high trade costs." (25513241.odt, Box 1) and "TMEA has also initiated various specific interventions that target the benefits of trade benefit both men and women equally and specifically that women are included in trade for instance through support to informal cross-border trade (dominated by women)." (25513241.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Procurement delays in infrastructure projects (e.g., Mombasa/Dar ports)
Political resistance to reforms (e.g., Tanzania’s restrictions on private sector engagement)
Sustainability of donor-funded systems post-exit (e.g., electronic trade platforms)
Corruption at borders undermining efficiency gains (e.g., OSBPs)
Private sector capacity gaps limiting export growth (e.g., SMEs’ ability to meet standards)
Regional integration tensions (e.g., non-uniform tariff reductions across EAC)
Climate/conflict disruptions to trade corridors (e.g., South Sudan instability)
Gender inequality in trade benefits (e.g., women’s limited access to formal export channels)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased project preparation (e.g., feasibility studies for Dar Port); leveraging World Bank/AfDB co-funding to accelerate implementation.
EAC Secretariat-led regional peer pressure; technically neutral framing of reforms (e.g., SPS alignment as ‘trade facilitation’).
TMEA’s sustainability strategy to reduce donor reliance via development capital instruments and EAC government co-funding.
Electronic systems (e.g., cargo tracking) to reduce human discretion; gender-sensitive safeguards (e.g., safe reporting channels for women traders).
Logistics hubs pilot with embedded training; partnerships with business associations (e.g., EABC).
EAC Common Market Protocol implementation support; transport observatories for transparent NTB monitoring.
Focus on resilient infrastructure (e.g., Nimule border post upgrades); contingency planning for South Sudan.
Targeted interventions (e.g., women trader cooperatives); gender audits of all TMEA activities.

fcas_specific_lessons: In South Sudan, limit engagement to border infrastructure (e.g., Nimule) with minimal in-country presence due to conflict risks.
For Burundi, focus on regional integration benefits (e.g., Rusizi border with Rwanda) to circumvent political isolation.
Use EAC frameworks to depoliticize reforms in fragile states (e.g., framing NTB reduction as ‘regional compliance’).
Prioritize quick-win infrastructure (e.g., OSBPs) in FCAS contexts to build trust before tackling deeper reforms.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
1. **Infrastructure first**: "Evidence is context specific, but unequivocal that trade facilitation interventions which improve infrastructure are the most effective in increasing trade volumes and reducing trade costs." (25513241.odt, Box 1)
2. **Complementarity matters**: "Complementing interventions that seek to reduce the cost of trade with those that seek to improve the local export capacity significantly enhances the impact of trade facilitation programmes."
3. **Phased learning**: "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes."
4. **Gender integration**: Lessons from TMEA Strategy 1 showed that women’s informal cross-border trade (74% of CBT) was initially overlooked; STS2 embeds gender audits and targeted support.
5. **Donor coordination**: The expansion from DFID-only to 7+ donors required formal governance (TMEA Council) to align priorities.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Added export capacity component**: Response to evidence that supply-side constraints (e.g., SME productivity) limited the impact of trade facilitation alone.
2. **Phased logistics hubs**: Replaces Strategy 1’s corridor-only approach with spatial clustering to intensify impact.
3. **Gender mainstreaming**: Hiring a gender adviser and requiring gender appraisals in all Project Appraisal Reports (PARs).
4. **SPS programme**: New focus on sanitary/phytosanitary standards to address agricultural export barriers identified in Strategy 1.
5. **Mid-term review gate**: Introduced to ensure evidence-based adjustments before committing funds beyond the spending review period.
risks_lessons.quote:
"Box 1: Summary of lessons from TMEA Strategy 1
- Preferential market access carries less weight than cost/capacity factors in trade participation.
- Trade facilitation + export capacity interventions have greater impact than either alone.
- Infrastructure improvements are most effective, followed by customs efficiency and regulatory reforms.
- Need for more evidence on trade-poverty linkages, especially gender-differentiated impacts.
- Short-term negative impacts of liberalization require pro-poor safeguards." (25513241.odt, Box 1)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: TMEA’s Strategy 1 leveraged over £7m in public/private funding for Mombasa Port, with expectations to attract £300m+ when fully implemented. The Dar es Salaam Port improvements secured a World Bank loan of $345m (£264m).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Roughly 50% of resources support ‘soft’ interventions (technical assistance, regulatory frameworks) and 50% address infrastructure constraints (public/private investments).
financial_details.quote: "DFID proposes to invest £229m (including £42m previously approved for TMEA S2 and £187m in additional funding) over 6 years... Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions... and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Table 1: TMEA Strategy 2 funding shows DFID’s £187m alongside £58m from other donors, totaling £319m." (25513241.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Pioneer Outcomes Funds
metadata.quote: "The programme will address barriers to using innovative pay-for-success instruments effectively and drive better public services for delivering the Sustainable Development Goals." (D0003473.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 2019", "End Date: 2026" (D0003473.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (Outcomes Funds), capacity building (Centre of Excellence, technical assistance), and implementation research (testing pay-for-success models) to drive better public services for SDGs. It focuses on scaling innovative financial instruments while generating evidence on their effectiveness.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will address barriers to using innovative pay-for-success instruments effectively and drive better public services for delivering the Sustainable Development Goals. The programme will do so by launching: Pioneer Outcomes Funds... Market Acceleration Platform... Centre of Excellence..." (D0003473.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Pioneer Outcomes Funds in education, poverty graduation, sanitation (funding pay-for-success contracts)
Market Acceleration Platform (pipeline of future deals, structuring new instruments)
Centre of Excellence (evidence generation, capacity strengthening in governments)
Better value for money in commissioning public services
Transition from aid to domestic commissioning of public services
Better results for more poor people (quantitative targets not specified)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform public service delivery through pay-for-success instruments, combining direct financing (Outcomes Funds), market development (Platform), and knowledge generation (Centre of Excellence) to achieve SDG outcomes.
what_objectives.quote: "As a result, the programme will drive better value for money in commissioning public services, facilitate transition from aid, and deliver better results for more poor people." (D0003473.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'Major' risk, reflecting complex partnerships with impact investors, fragile contexts, and innovative financial instruments that require careful design to avoid misappropriation or inefficiency.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003473.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited commissioning expertise in governments)
political economy (short-term focus of governments, siloed budgets)
market barriers (lack of coordination among commissioners, high transaction costs)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and institutional constraints limit the ability of governments to adopt pay-for-success models, while data limitations and high transaction costs reduce efficiency. Political economy factors create resistance to long-term, outcomes-focused commissioning.
where_context.quote: "Lack of commissioning and design expertise in-house to launch quality projects... Uncertainty over how best to scale instruments to lower costs and improve efficiency... high costs involved in establishing partnerships between providers, investors and commissioners" (D0003473.odt, Challenge–Barriers to growth in developing-country contexts)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO retains primary decision-making authority over fund design, partner selection, and strategic direction, with domestic governments and other partners contributing to implementation and co-funding. Southern partners (governments, service providers) have operational roles but limited influence over programme-level decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to domestic governments (commissioning expertise)
training for service providers (performance management, outcome measurement)
investor education (opportunities in impact bonds, investment approaches)
Centre of Excellence (evidence synthesis, policy guidance)
intermediary support (legal structures, deal coordination)

partner_organizations.name: Domestic governments (e.g., Ghana Ministry of Education, Rwanda Ministry of Health)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and implementer (outcomes-based commissioning, policy alignment)

partner_organizations.name: Impact investors (e.g., social investment funds, philanthropic investors)
partner_organizations.role: financier (upfront capital for service delivery, risk-sharing)

partner_organizations.name: Service providers (NGOs, social enterprises, private sector)
partner_organizations.role: service delivery (education, sanitation, poverty graduation)

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral organizations (e.g., World Bank)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and technical partner (e.g., Ghana Accountability for Learning Outcomes Project)

partner_organizations.name: Academic institutions (e.g., Government Outcomes Lab, University of Oxford)
partner_organizations.role: research and evidence generation (evaluation, lessons learned)

partner_organizations.name: Intermediaries (e.g., Social Finance, outcome fund managers)
partner_organizations.role: deal structuring, legal frameworks, investor-provider matching

who_partners.quote: "The success of the programme will rely on DFID’s ability to build effective market links and partnerships with actors relevant to this market. These include: Domestic governments in developing countries... Other donors and multilaterals... Investors... Service providers... Academic institutions... Intermediaries" (D0003473.odt, Summary: How a new DFID programme will make a difference)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **Outcomes Funds** (pooling donor/government resources to pay for verified results) and **technical assistance grants** (for capacity building). Outcomes Funds operate as pay-for-success contracts where investors provide upfront capital and are repaid only upon delivery of agreed outcomes, verified by independent evaluators.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a **central platform** (Market Acceleration Platform) that coordinates multiple Outcomes Funds, each focused on specific SDG areas (e.g., education, poverty). Funds are managed by intermediaries (e.g., fund managers) with oversight from DFID and partner governments. The Centre of Excellence provides cross-cutting support (evidence, capacity building).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners (governments, investors, providers) are selected based on **alignment with programme objectives**, **capacity to deliver outcomes**, and **willingness to co-fund**. Early scoping identified governments with existing interest in pay-for-success models (e.g., Ghana, Rwanda), while investors and providers were engaged through the Impact Bonds Working Group and prior DFID pilots.
how_mechanism.quote: "The design of first Outcomes Funds... included an early assessment of government appetite to test impact bonds... The table below outlines findings [e.g., Ghana: 'Strong interest from Ministry of Education to harness non-state capacity']" (D0003473.odt, Country focus) && "The programme will drive better value for money... through addressing the barriers to using pay-for-success instruments effectively... The programme will adapt its approach to work with both: Donors looking to grow efficiency... Government commissioners transitioning from aid" (D0003473.odt, Summary: How a new DFID programme will make a difference)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each Outcomes Fund has a **Technical Design Taskforce** (e.g., for Poverty Alleviation Outcomes Fund in Rwanda/Kenya) comprising government representatives, DFID, and other donors. The Market Acceleration Platform and Centre of Excellence are overseen by DFID with input from academic partners (e.g., Government Outcomes Lab).
how_governance.quote: "First country to implement performance-based financing nationwide... Government part of the Technical Design Taskforce of the Fund" (D0003473.odt, Country focus) && "The programme will seek to tailor its approach to each country according to the current status of public sector capability and funding capacity" (D0003473.odt, Country focus)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between Outcomes Funds (e.g., education to health) with DFID approval, but individual fund designs (outcomes, metrics) require upfront agreement with governments/investors, limiting flexibility.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses **adaptive management** to tailor approaches by country (e.g., outcomes funding in low-income contexts vs. investment guarantees in middle-income). Adjustments require DFID sign-off and alignment with government priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will seek to tailor its approach to each country according to the current status of public sector capability and funding capacity... identify opportunities for growth" (D0003473.odt, Country focus) && "Tomaximise impact, we therefore propose that in implementation, the programme incorporates:... Geographictailoring, especially in testing investment mechanisms to accelerate domestic outcomes funding" (D0003473.odt, Option appraisal conclusions)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Outcomes Fund managers** (intermediaries) → **Service providers** (end implementers). Some funds may add a 4th layer (e.g., sub-contracted evaluators).
how_efficiency.quote: "Impact Bonds are pay-for-success partnerships that pull in private investors to share in the financing risk of delivering development results. They enable government and donors to only pay when results are delivered for beneficiaries" (D0003473.odt, Context and evidence)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (continue existing pilot only)
Option 2: ‘Do nothing yet’ (wait for more evidence)
Option 3: Capacity building only (no outcomes funding)
Option 4: Single Outcomes Fund (focus on one SDG area)
Option 5: Multiple Outcomes Funds (portfolio approach) **[PREFERRED]
Option 6: Direct investment/guarantees (DFID as investor)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 (multiple Outcomes Funds) was selected because it **diversifies risk** across sectors/geographies, **engages a broader range of partners**, and **generates comparative evidence** on what works. It balances scale (through pooled funding) with flexibility (tailored fund designs) while leveraging DFID’s experience in pay-for-success models.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (diversified portfolio reduces risk of underperformance in one sector)
experience (builds on UK Outcomes Funds like Life Chances Fund)
equity (targets marginalized groups through focused funds e.g., women’s economic empowerment)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs for fund design/launch
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use common contracting structures across funds (e.g., shared evaluation frameworks) and leverage existing platforms (e.g., Impact Bonds Working Group).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited government capacity to commission outcomes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embed technical assistance (Centre of Excellence) and require government co-funding (e.g., 15% in Ghana) to build ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Investor reluctance in fragile contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use guarantees or blended finance to de-risk investments; prioritize countries with existing government interest (e.g., Rwanda’s Imihigo performance contracts).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Misalignment between donor/investor priorities and government needs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early scoping with governments (e.g., Technical Design Taskforces) and flexible fund designs to accommodate local priorities.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (comparing value for money across providers)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 5 is the preferred option as it is best aligned with the objective... to deliver sustained SDG outcomes... through pay-for-success interventions... However, appraisal and evidence also show that a number of other options could be strong on selected critical success factors... the programme incorporates: Focus on building evidence and capacity... Tailoring outcomes funding strategies to SDG areas... Geographictailoring" (D0003473.odt, Option appraisal conclusions)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Contextual constraints (weak institutions, regulatory barriers) limit partner selection to governments/investors with **existing capacity** (e.g., Rwanda’s performance-based financing experience) or **donor support** (e.g., World Bank co-funding in Ghana). Fragile contexts exclude some investors/providers due to compliance risks.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory constraints (e.g., procurement rules) exclude providers without legal frameworks for outcomes-based contracts.
Institutional weakness (e.g., lack of commissioning expertise) limits government participation to those with prior PbR experience (e.g., Rwanda, Kenya).
FCAS risks (e.g., terrorism financing) reduce investor appetite, requiring guarantees or blended finance.
Data limitations (e.g., outcome verification challenges) favor partners with robust M&E systems.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **financing mechanism objective** (pay-for-success) drives the **platform structure** (Outcomes Funds) to pool risk and scale efficiently, while the **capacity-building objective** necessitates embedded technical assistance (Centre of Excellence). The need for **comparative evidence** shapes the multi-fund approach (Option 5).
q28_linkages: Pay-for-success financing → Outcomes Funds (to aggregate demand and reduce transaction costs).
Capacity building → Centre of Excellence (to address lack of commissioning expertise).
Evidence generation → Portfolio of funds (to compare effectiveness across sectors).
Risk mitigation → Geographic tailoring (e.g., guarantees in middle-income countries).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: **speed vs. inclusion** (faster scaling through Outcomes Funds may exclude smaller providers), **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership** (UK-led design risks limited local adaptation), and **cost vs. reach** (high transaction costs for fund setup may reduce resources for direct service delivery).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (pooled funds) vs. Equity (smaller providers may lack capacity to compete).
Expertise (Northern intermediaries manage funds) vs. Ownership (Southern governments have limited decision-making power).
Speed (rapid fund launch) vs. Adaptation (less flexibility for local context adjustments).
Risk mitigation (guarantees for investors) vs. Cost (higher overheads reduce direct spending).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight** (milestone-based reporting, Technical Design Taskforces) and **adaptive management** (tailored approaches by country risk profile, e.g., guarantees in FCAS).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: governments with stronger commissioning capacity (e.g., Rwanda) co-design funds, while those with weaker systems (e.g., Bangladesh) receive more technical assistance. Investors with prior impact bond experience are prioritized for complex funds.
intersections.quote: "The programme will adapt its approach to work with both: Donors looking to grow efficiency... Government commissioners transitioning from aid... The success of the programme will rely on DFID’s ability to build effective market links and partnerships with actors relevant to this market" (D0003473.odt, Summary) && "At the same time, the programme will work through relatively complex partnerships, including impact investors, and must consider the risk of increased compliance reducing investor appetite in fragile contexts" (D0003473.odt, Countering the Financing of Terrorism)

key_programme_risks: Limited government capacity to design/commission outcomes-based contracts (especially in LMICs).
High transaction costs for fund setup and deal structuring.
Investor reluctance in fragile/conflict-affected states (FCAS) due to compliance risks.
Misalignment between donor priorities and government needs (e.g., SDG focus vs. local politics).
Difficulty in measuring/verifying outcomes cost-effectively (risk of gaming or fraud).
Over-reliance on Northern intermediaries reducing Southern ownership.
Market saturation if too many funds compete for limited investor/provider capacity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Centre of Excellence provides technical assistance; require government co-funding (e.g., 15% in Ghana) to build ownership.
Use common contracting structures across funds; leverage existing platforms (e.g., Impact Bonds Working Group).
Use guarantees/blended finance; prioritize countries with existing government interest (e.g., Rwanda’s performance contracts).
Early scoping via Technical Design Taskforces; flexible fund designs to accommodate local priorities.
Invest in robust M&E systems; use independent evaluators (e.g., academic partners).
Embed Southern partners in governance (e.g., government Taskforces); capacity building for local intermediaries.

fcas_specific_lessons: Use **guarantees or blended finance** to de-risk investments in fragile contexts.
Leverage **existing government systems** (e.g., Rwanda’s Imihigo contracts) to reduce compliance burdens.
Prioritize **sectors with clear outcome metrics** (e.g., education enrollment) over complex areas (e.g., governance reform).
Partner with **multilaterals** (e.g., World Bank) to share risk in high-risk environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s **Development Impact Bonds Pilot** (2017) and UK **Outcomes Funds** (e.g., Life Chances Fund) highlight: 1) Need for **upfront government buy-in** (co-funding improves sustainability); 2) **High design costs** for first projects (subsequent deals can reuse structures); 3) **Investor education** is critical (many impact investors lack experience in developing countries); 4) **Flexible outcome metrics** allow adaptation to local context.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Changes from pilot phase include: 1) **Portfolio approach** (multiple funds instead of single-sector focus) to diversify risk; 2) **Geographic tailoring** (e.g., guarantees for middle-income countries); 3) **Stronger government co-funding requirements** (e.g., 15% in Ghana); 4) **Embedded capacity building** (Centre of Excellence) to address design expertise gaps.
risks_lessons.quote: "Whilst the small size and high cost of first projects is understandable... there is growing recognition among commissioners, service providers and investors that to drive public service transformation, these instruments need to be further developed and used at an appropriate scale to drive efficiency" (D0003473.odt, Challenge–Barriers to growth) && "The programme will also contribute to UK Aid Strategy commitments in promoting sustainable economic reforms, including public sector reform... Any approach to growing capacity in commissioning impact bonds... will need to consider differences in existing commissioning capacity" (D0003473.odt, Opportunity–Transforming domestic public service commissioning)

co_funding_partners.partner: World Bank (Ghana Accountability for Learning Outcomes Project)
Other donors/multilaterals (e.g., in Education Outcomes Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **crowd in private investment** through pay-for-success models, with an expected multiplier effect from government co-funding (e.g., Ghana’s 15% contribution) and investor capital. Exact leverage ratios are not specified but are modeled on UK Outcomes Funds (e.g., Life Chances Fund leveraged £80m for £60m in outcomes payments).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily supports **revenue expenditures** (technical assistance, fund management, evaluations) with some **capital investments** in outcome verification systems and provider capacity building. No explicit split is provided.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £168m" (D0003473.odt, Summary Sheet) && "First country to implement performance-based financing nationwide... Government part of the Technical Design Taskforce of the Fund" (D0003473.odt, Country focus) && "The programme will seek to tailor its approach to each country according to the current status of public sector capability and funding capacity" (D0003473.odt, Country focus)

metadata.programme_name: Tax Systems Transformation Programme (TSTP) / Tax Transformation Programme (TTP)
metadata.quote: "TSTP will be a 5 year £35m technical assistance (TA) programme" (45010791.odt, Programme Summary) and "The TTP was originally envisaged as a £35 million programme to support a GOE policy priority... With this extension the programme will only spend 53% of the originally envisaged £35 million" (D0005147.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "5 year £35m technical assistance (TA) programme" (45010791.odt, Programme Summary) and "This twenty-four month no-cost extension (NCE) to the TTP (extending it until 31 March 2026)" (D0005147.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening Ethiopian tax institutions), implementation research (testing tax system reforms), and service delivery (direct technical assistance to improve tax administration). It aims to transform Ethiopia's tax systems to increase domestic revenue mobilization while improving fairness and reducing compliance costs for businesses.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The proposed Tax Systems Transformation Programme (TSTP) will be a 5 year £35m technical assistance (TA) programme... The programme is expected to deliver: additional annual tax revenues of at least 8.9b ETB (£295 million) by programme end; reduced tax compliance costs; and improved certainty and fairness for private sector business and investors." (45010791.odt, Intervention Summary) and "To transform Ethiopia’s tax systems so that the Ethiopian Government can fund more services for its population from its own revenues and become less dependent on aid." (D0005147.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Additional annual tax revenues of at least 8.9 billion ETB (£295 million) by programme end
Reduced tax compliance costs for businesses
Improved certainty and fairness in the tax system for private sector and investors
Stability of core IT system (SIGTAS) maintained
Business process transformations implemented to improve operational efficiency
Support to domestic resource mobilization during macroeconomic adjustment
Donor coordination function established to avoid duplication and align strategies
Legal drafting support for tax policy changes
Data recovery plans developed for tax databases
Regular revenue collection reports produced for fiscal budget execution
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform Ethiopia's tax system through technical assistance, capacity building, and policy support to increase domestic revenue mobilization while improving the business environment and reducing poverty.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme is expected to deliver: additional annual tax revenues of at least 8.9b ETB (£295 million) by programme end; reduced tax compliance costs; and improved certainty and fairness for private sector business and investors." (45010791.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Ensuring the stability of the core IT system (SIGTAS)... Providing the IT support to new business processes that reduce compliance costs... Providing a donor coordination function to the MOR" (D0005147.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia is described as being on the 'arc of instability' with recent shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic and Tigray War. The programme operates in a fragile economic context with high fiscal deficits, macroeconomic imbalances, and potential political instability risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Ethiopia is considered a stable country on the 'arc of instability' that cuts through Africa... A slowdown in growth, and potential political instability and violence as a consequence, combined with the presence of established migratory routes, could dramatically increase flows of refugees and economic migrants towards Europe." (45010791.odt, Strategic Case) and "Ethiopia’s macroeconomy and fiscal position is in a fragile state and reform priorities are subject to alteration. New pressures will emerge if the authorities reach a Staff Level Agreement with the IMF on a new programme." (D0005147.odt, Expected Results)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The multiple shocks (pandemic, Tigray War) have disrupted programme delivery, caused budget cuts, and led to adviser departures. Economic challenges including high inflation and foreign exchange shortages have made revenue collection more difficult and increased pressure on businesses. The fragile IT system (SIGTAS) was at risk of collapse, which would have catastrophic impacts on state revenue collection.
where_context.quote: "The programme has faced a rapidly changing and challenging operating environment. Large shocks, including the covid-19 pandemic and Tigray War, caused frequent shifts in GOE priorities... Covid restrictions in March 2020 caused all international advisers to leave the country... The Tax Delivery Unit in the Office of the Prime Minister closed early in the programme..." (D0005147.odt, Background) and "The WBand IMF recognise the UK as having prevented the collapse of [SIGTAS] system." (D0005147.odt, Key Achievements)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO maintains overall programme control and decision-making authority, with Ethiopian institutions (Ministry of Revenue, Ministry of Finance) implementing specific components under FCDO guidance. The programme is designed to build Ethiopian capacity but ultimate strategic decisions remain with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: Embedded advisers in Tax Transformation Office (TTO)
Training on tax audit, data management, customer service
Organizational change management support
Legal drafting training for tax policy unit
IT systems capacity building
Knowledge transfer through joint working
Skills development in research capacity

partner_organizations.name: Cowater Sogema International Inc.
partner_organizations.role: Main implementing partner (programme delivery)

partner_organizations.name: IPE Global Limited
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring and Evaluation supplier

partner_organizations.name: Ethiopian Ministry of Revenue (MoR)
partner_organizations.role: Primary government counterpart (hosts TTO, implements reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Ethiopian Ministry of Finance (MoF)
partner_organizations.role: Policy counterpart (tax policy development)

partner_organizations.name: HMRC (Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider (peer-to-peer support)

partner_organizations.name: Prime Minister's Office (Ethiopia)
partner_organizations.role: High-level oversight and political leadership

partner_organizations.name: Ethiopian Investment Advisory Facility (EIAF)
partner_organizations.role: Previous programme that established initial delivery units

who_partners.quote: "The TTP is implemented via seven embedded advisers in the Tax Transformation Office (TTO) now located in the Ministry of Revenue... A legal adviser is embedded in the tax policy unit of the Ministry of Finance." (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The programme is designed to build capacity within Ethiopian institutions while maintaining FCDO oversight." (implied throughout both documents)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses competitive contracts with implementing partners (Cowater Sogema won through open tender) to deliver technical assistance. Funds are disbursed against deliverables rather than upfront grants.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Cowater Sogema serves as the main implementing partner managing embedded advisers within Ethiopian government institutions (Ministry of Revenue and Ministry of Finance). The structure combines external management with in-country embedded technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The business case emphasizes the need for high-quality technical expertise and adaptive capacity, suggesting competitive selection was used to identify the most capable partner to work in Ethiopia's challenging environment.
how_mechanism.quote: "Cowater Sogema (hereafter referred to as 'Cowater') are the main implementing partner for the Tax Systems Transformation Programme. Cowater won a competitive tender to be contracted to implement the programme." (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "This appraisal case therefore outlines two options... Option 2: Scaled up UK support to tax reform through accelerated delivery" (45010791.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_structure: FCDO oversight with embedded advisory model
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme uses embedded advisers within Ethiopian ministries (MoR and MoF) with direct reporting lines to both the host institutions and the implementing partner (Cowater). FCDO maintains overall programme oversight through regular reviews and the implementing partner's management structure.
how_governance.quote: "Cowater are recruiting a new programme director... Cowater have committed to provide a programme manager in Ethiopia, to handle much of the bureaucracy and support the new stream of work around donor coordination" (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The M&E supplier, IPE, will be moved from a drawdown to a deliverables approach, focused on providing detailed annual reports that will inform FCDO annual reviews and PCRs." (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme has demonstrated flexibility in reallocating funds between components in response to changing priorities and shocks (e.g., COVID-19, Tigray War), though major reallocations likely require FCDO approval. The no-cost extension itself represents significant adaptation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme was designed with explicit flexibility to respond to changing government priorities and external shocks. The no-cost extension allows for pivoting to new areas like donor coordination and supporting macroeconomic adjustment. Annual reviews and detailed M&E reports inform adaptive management.
how_flexibility.quote: "TTP was designed to be flexible and adaptive in order to fully support dynamic reforms and has coped well with these changes... Immediately, the no-cost extension will allow us to: initiate discussions on contracts with the two above-named programme partners, enabling us to agree timely amendments; and allow us provide continued assistance to a key priority of the GOE" (D0005147.odt, Changes to Business Case) and "Delivery unit operations are flexible by design, responding quickly to data and context." (45010791.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Cowater Sogema (implementing partner) → Embedded advisers in Ethiopian ministries
how_efficiency.quote: "The M&E supplier, IPE, will be moved from a drawdown to a deliverables approach, focused on providing detailed annual reports" (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "Cowater have committed to provide a programme manager in Ethiopia" (D0005147.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: UK support through traditional bilateral technical assistance (instead of accelerated delivery)
Continue UK support at current levels (~£3.4 million per annum)
UK support through multilateral channels
UK support to regional tax authorities
UK support to tax administration only
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The accelerated delivery approach with embedded technical assistance was chosen because: 1) It leverages strong political commitment from the Prime Minister; 2) Previous traditional technical assistance had limited impact; 3) The delivery unit model had proven effective in other contexts; 4) Ethiopia's tax challenges require transformational rather than incremental change; 5) The approach allows for rapid response to changing priorities.
q25_decision_factors: past experience (limited success with traditional TA)
partner capacity (need for high-level political buy-in)
flexibility (ability to adapt to changing context)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on political commitment from Ethiopian leadership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: High-level engagement with Prime Minister and regular performance reviews to maintain commitment

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High sunk costs in establishing delivery units (TTO and PMDU)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased implementation with proof of concept before full scaling

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capacity constraints within Ethiopian institutions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded advisers and intensive capacity building components

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential leadership changes disrupting programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Building broad institutional buy-in beyond individual leaders

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating with multiple donors in tax space
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK playing convening role and establishing donor coordination function

why_rationale.quote: "The current climate is now more conducive to tax reform, positive developments include... the Prime Minister's public commitment to tax transformation... The sustainability of Ethiopia's debt is a pressing issue... Domestic Revenue Mobilisation has become a critical priority for GoE." (45010791.odt, Feasibility and Sustainability) and "In the design of TSTP we considered several other options including... Each option was assessed according to the following criteria: political feasibility; technical appropriateness; GoE institutional capacity. None of the above options were considered sufficient for the transformational change required." (45010791.odt, Discarded Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile context in Ethiopia (FCAS status, recent conflicts, economic shocks) constrained partner selection to organizations with: 1) Proven ability to operate in challenging environments; 2) Existing relationships with Ethiopian government; 3) Capacity to manage security risks; 4) Flexibility to adapt to rapidly changing priorities. This led to selection of Cowater Sogema with its experience in Ethiopia and ability to manage embedded advisers.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing in-country presence due to security risks
Requirement for flexibility to handle frequent priority shifts from GOE
Need for partners who can work effectively with Ethiopian government institutions
Capacity to manage IT systems stabilization (critical due to SIGTAS fragility)
Ability to navigate complex political economy of tax reform
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The transformational objectives (system-wide tax reform rather than incremental changes) determined the need for: 1) An embedded delivery model (TTO within ERCA/MoR); 2) High-intensity technical assistance; 3) Direct engagement with political leadership (PM Delivery Unit); 4) Flexible funding mechanisms to respond to changing needs; 5) Combination of international expertise with local capacity building.
q28_linkages: Need for transformational change → Required embedded delivery units rather than traditional TA
Political economy challenges → Needed high-level PM engagement mechanism
IT system fragility → Required specialized technical support component
Capacity constraints → Necessitated intensive capacity building approach
Multiple donor involvement → Created need for coordination function
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The documents explicitly discuss tensions between: 1) Speed of reform vs. inclusive stakeholder engagement; 2) International expertise vs. local ownership; 3) Short-term revenue targets vs. long-term system sustainability; 4) Need for rapid results vs. capacity building requirements. The accelerated delivery approach was chosen to balance these, with embedded advisers meant to transfer skills while driving rapid changes.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: "Delivery units... focus on a limited number of key outcome-focused priorities" potentially at expense of broader stakeholder consultation
Expertise vs ownership: "HMRC support will continue for at least 3 years after programme end" shows reliance on Northern expertise while aiming for local capacity
Short-term vs long-term: Revenue targets must be met quickly but "long term investment in IT systems and organisational change" is needed for sustainability
Centralization vs localization: TTO embedded in central institutions but needs to work with regional tax authorities
Donor coordination vs autonomy: UK plays convening role but must balance with GOE ownership of reforms
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context led to intensive management approach with: 1) Embedded advisers for real-time monitoring; 2) Regular performance reviews with PM; 3) Flexible funding to respond to shocks; 4) Multiple layers of oversight (FCDO, implementing partner, Ethiopian ministries); 5) Detailed M&E systems to track progress in volatile environment.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The significant capacity building needs in Ethiopian institutions shaped the delivery structure by: 1) Requiring embedded advisers rather than remote support; 2) Making capacity development a core programme component; 3) Structuring knowledge transfer through joint working; 4) Including legal drafting and IT support as specific workstreams; 5) Designing exit strategy around gradual handover of delivery units to GOE.
intersections.quote: "The programme has faced a rapidly changing and challenging operating environment. Large shocks... caused frequent shifts in GOE priorities... Cowater Sogema... has displayed considerable adaptability to this shifting environment." (D0005147.odt, Background) and "Delivery unit operations are flexible by design, responding quickly to data and context... They focus on a limited number of key outcome-focused priorities." (45010791.odt, Delivery Units section)

key_programme_risks: Loss of political commitment from Ethiopian leadership
Failure to achieve revenue targets leading to increased debt burden
Collapse of critical IT systems (SIGTAS)
Inability to coordinate effectively with other donors
Economic shocks (inflation, foreign exchange shortages) undermining reform efforts
Capacity constraints in Ethiopian institutions limiting reform implementation
Security risks disrupting programme delivery
Changes in GOE leadership disrupting programme continuity
Revenue collection pressures leading to unfair burden on businesses/poor
Failure to balance short-term revenue needs with long-term system strengthening

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular high-level engagement with Prime Minister and monthly performance reviews
Dedicated IT support team and system stabilization efforts
Establishment of formal donor coordination function within MoR
Flexible programme design allowing pivot to macroeconomic adjustment support
Intensive embedded capacity building and knowledge transfer
Focus on reducing compliance costs and improving fairness alongside revenue increases
Building broad institutional buy-in and multiple champions within GOE

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for extreme flexibility in programme design to handle frequent shocks
Importance of stabilizing core systems (like SIGTAS) as foundation for other reforms
Value of embedded advisers who can continue working during crises
Critical role of high-level political engagement in fragile contexts
Necessity of balancing short-term stabilization with long-term capacity building
Importance of donor coordination to avoid duplication in complex environments
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID tax programmes in Ethiopia (like TAUT) had limited impact because: 1) Lack of strategic focus in leadership; 2) Inadequate coordination among donors; 3) Insufficient political buy-in; 4) Limited capacity building components; 5) Failure to address systemic IT weaknesses. The current programme was designed to address these through the delivery unit model and intensive technical assistance.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes based on lessons included: 1) Establishment of dedicated delivery units (TTO and PMDU); 2) Embedded adviser model instead of remote TA; 3) Focus on IT system stabilization as foundation; 4) Inclusion of donor coordination function; 5) Flexible funding mechanisms to handle shocks; 6) More intensive M&E systems; 7) Explicit capacity building components in all workstreams.
risks_lessons.quote: "Over the last two decades, DFID and other donors have engaged in tax reform with mixed success. The step change required to meet ambitious GoE targets has not been achieved... We have drawn the following lessons: Political buy-in and leadership: Leadership in ERCA has lacked strategic focus... Size and coordination: The overall size of financial support to tax reform remains inadequate. Despite interest from several donors, progress to date remains insufficient and uncoordinated." (45010791.odt, How TSTP will use lessons) and "The programme has faced a rapidly changing and challenging operating environment... The programme is now much smaller than originally planned... Despite this disruption TTP has had some key achievements" (D0005147.odt, Background)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage additional donor support through its coordination function, with potential for other donors to use the existing contract vehicle. The World Bank and IMF are developing complementary programmes on Domestic Resource Mobilisation.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses primarily on revenue/operational expenditures (technical assistance, capacity building) with some capital components related to IT system stabilization and upgrades.
financial_details.quote: "The TTP was originally envisaged as a £35 million programme to support a GOE policy priority... With this extension the programme will only spend 53% of the originally envisaged £35 million" (D0005147.odt, Summary Information) and "There will be three components and two sub-components to this work: Component 1: Accelerated Delivery (£31.5m), Component 2: Peer-to-peer support from HMRC (£1.98m), Component 3: Strategic Tax Transformation Support Fund (£1.5m)" (45010791.odt, Option 2 details)

metadata.programme_name: Rohingya Response and National Resilience Programme (RRNRP)
metadata.duration_text: April 2021 - March 2025 (intended four-year programme, though HM Treasury rules limit commitment to March 2024)
metadata.quote: "The RRNRP will help Bangladesh manage a protracted refugee crisis, while a political solution is sought to allow voluntary, safe and dignified repatriation to Myanmar." (60403949.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: April 2021", "End Date: March 2025", "HMTrules mean FCDO cannot commit spend beyond March 2024 but the intention is for a four-year programme." (60403949.odt, ProgrammeCode section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The RRNRP is a humanitarian programme delivering direct services (food, water, sanitation, education, protection) to Rohingya refugees and vulnerable host communities in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. It combines emergency relief with longer-term resilience-building for both refugees and disaster-prone populations nationally.
what_objectives.q1_source: "It will deliver food; clean water; sanitation; improved schooling, protection (especially for survivors of gender-based violence); forest rehabilitation; and livelihood opportunities." (60403949.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Reduced domestic and gender-based violence in camps (quantitative target not specified)
Basic food requirements for up to 100,000 refugees provided each year
Primary healthcare through 24-hour clinics and health posts (coverage not quantified)
Access to quality education for up to 40,000 refugee children and adolescents
Improved durable shelter for up to 50,000 refugee households
Clean water and sanitation for over 250,000 refugees and host community members
Cooking gas needs of 200,000 people provided annually to reduce deforestation
Reforestation and maintenance of 1,500 hectares of land in host communities
Stabilization of 400 hectares of vulnerable land in camps
Over 200,000 people affected by disasters receive immediate humanitarian assistance annually
Economic opportunities created for Rohingya and Bangladeshis in Cox's Bazar (specific numbers not provided)
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance to 890,000 Rohingya refugees and 490,000 vulnerable host community members while building Bangladesh's national resilience to climate-related disasters. It combines emergency relief with longer-term development interventions across protection, health, education, WASH, and environmental rehabilitation.
what_objectives.quote: "The RRNRP will help Bangladesh manage a protracted refugee crisis, while a political solution is sought to allow voluntary, safe and dignified repatriation to Myanmar... It will deliver food; clean water; sanitation; improved schooling, protection... forest rehabilitation; and livelihood opportunities." (60403949.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Bangladesh hosts the world's largest and most densely populated refugee camp (Cox's Bazar) with 890,000 Rohingya refugees alongside extreme poverty (58% of population), climate vulnerability (ranked 22/191 on INFORM Global Risk Index), and protracted conflict in neighboring Myanmar that prevents refugee returns. The region faces cyclones, flooding, trafficking, and growing local conflicts.
where_context.q5_source: "Bangladesh is currently hosting the largest and most densely populated refugee camp in the world... The refugee crisis is becoming protracted, as Rakhine... is riven with conflict." and "Bangladesh is ranked 22 out of 191 countries under the INFORM Global Risk Index 2019 and therefore at high risk of humanitarian crisis and disasters." (60403949.odt, sections 6 and 23)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: GoB restrictions on refugee movement, livelihoods, and education create dependency and desperation. Limited access to justice (only 4% would report crimes to police) and formal institutions. Cyclones and monsoons destroy camp infrastructure annually. COVID-19 lockdowns eliminated already-limited income opportunities. Host community resentment grows due to environmental degradation and economic competition. Bhasan Char relocations proceed without UN technical assessments, raising protection concerns.
where_context.quote: "GoB’s approach to the refugee crisis is driven by its determination that the Rohingya cannot be a permanent burden to Bangladesh... GoB’s policy towards the Rohingya, including camp fencing, shutting down internet access, curbing civil society in the camps, blocks on humanitarian assistance, and limitations on livelihoods and education have resulted in increased despondency, violence and criminality." (60403949.odt, section 15)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG) hosted by IOM and UNHCR
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by FCDO with implementation led by UN agencies (IOM, UNHCR, WFP, UNICEF) and international NGOs. Local partners (Bangladesh Red Crescent, national NGOs) play service delivery roles but decision-making rests with FCDO and UN coordination structures.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for Rohingya community health workers (1,500+ engaged, 75% women)
Skills development for host communities through BRAC's ultra-poor graduation programmes
Support to Bangladesh Forest Department for tree nursery training
Justice sector capacity building (studies on access to formal/informal mechanisms like Shalish)
Community engagement initiatives to build trust between refugees and humanitarian agencies

partner_organizations.name: IOM (International Organization for Migration)
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead of Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG); camp coordination and protection services

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR (UN Refugee Agency)
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead of ISCG; refugee protection and shelter management

partner_organizations.name: WFP (World Food Programme)
partner_organizations.role: Food security and cash-for-work programmes

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Education, child protection, and WASH services

partner_organizations.name: WHO
partner_organizations.role: Health and COVID-19 response coordination

partner_organizations.name: FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization)
partner_organizations.role: Agricultural livelihoods support

partner_organizations.name: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS)
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation partner for humanitarian services

partner_organizations.name: BRAC
partner_organizations.role: Livelihoods and ultra-poor graduation programmes for host communities

partner_organizations.name: Action Contre la Faim (ACF)
partner_organizations.role: Nutrition and food security interventions

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs (3 consortia + individual grants)
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery in sectors like protection, WASH, and education

partner_organizations.name: Government of Bangladesh (GoB)
partner_organizations.role: Policy oversight and camp management (Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commission)

partner_organizations.name: Bangladesh Forest Department
partner_organizations.role: Environmental rehabilitation and reforestation

who_partners.quote: "Hosted by IOM and UNHCR, ISCG coordinates the overall Rohingya refugee crisis response and delivery of the Joint Response Plan... We will reinforce coordination and the role of the Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG)." (60403949.odt, section 32)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (AG) to UN agencies and NGOs, with some funds managed through UNOPS as a fund management agency. The final structure blends bilateral agreements with pooled funding mechanisms for specific components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the programme through a hybrid model: (1) Direct bilateral agreements with 6 UN agencies (WFP, UNHCR, UNICEF, IOM, WHO, UNFPA) and selected NGOs, and (2) a fund management component via UNOPS for smaller grants. A third-party Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) unit provides oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The shift from multiple NGO consortia to specific NGO partnerships (including calls for proposals) aims to "enhance access to justice and engaging civil society" while consolidating service quality. UN agencies were selected based on their mandated roles in the Joint Response Plan and existing coordination structures.
how_mechanism.quote: "This would streamline the delivery chain and set of activities and shift towards more strategic, multi-year agreements... Compared to Option 1, the number of agencies supported would be reduced from 14 partners to 6 UN agencies and a small number of NGO grants." (60403949.odt, section 55)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG), co-chaired by IOM and UNHCR, serves as the primary governance body for the Rohingya response. FCDO participates in this structure alongside other donors, UN agencies, and the Government of Bangladesh. Strategic decisions are reviewed every six months by FCDO Directors, Heads of Mission, and Development Directors.
how_governance.quote: "Progress is reviewed every six months by Directors, Heads of Mission and Development Directors... We will reinforce coordination and the role of the Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG)." (60403949.odt, sections 7 and 32)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The multi-year funding structure allows some reallocation between sectors (e.g., shifting from food to protection if needs change), but requires FCDO approval. The pooled fund option (for £45-50m/year) includes a contingency mechanism for disaster response.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes "increased flexibility to address disasters and other crises in Cox’s Bazar and nationally" (section 29) and allows for operational research to investigate bottlenecks. However, major shifts require FCDO sign-off due to annual spending reviews in the first two years.
how_flexibility.quote: "A multi-year response with predictable funding will provide the impetus for multi-year planning... Increased flexibility to address disasters and other crises in Cox’s Bazar and nationally." (60403949.odt, section 29)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager (UNOPS) → Implementing Partners (UN agencies/NGOs) → [Sub-grantees if applicable]. The document notes: "FCDO funds flow through multiple partners in the delivery chain, and NPACs or profits are charged at each level."
how_efficiency.quote: "It is estimated that NPACs will consume up to £10m in Option 2... These estimates only include NPACs charged by UNOPS and the first tier of implementing partners." (60403949.odt, section 61) and "FCDO funds flow through multiple partners in the delivery chain." (section 61)

q24_alternatives_considered: Delivery Option 1: Short-term, multi-sector support to diverse partners via fund manager (status quo)
Delivery Option 2: Multi-year support to streamlined sectors/partners managed bilaterally (CHOSEN)
Delivery Option 3: Multi-year funding through a pooled fund (OCHA-style)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (bilateral multi-year agreements) was selected for its balance of predictability, cost efficiency, and strategic coherence. It reduces transaction costs compared to Option 1 (14 partners → 6 UN agencies + NGOs) while avoiding the dilution of UK influence and high start-up costs of Option 3 (pooled fund). The choice aligns with lessons from the SHPR programme, which scored 'A' in annual reviews despite a complex environment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dilution of UK leverage in a pooled fund (Option 3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Retained bilateral management (Option 2) to maintain strategic control over priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs with multiple partners (Option 1)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Streamlined to 6 UN agencies and reduced NGO consortia in Option 2.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Annual JRP focus reducing multi-year benefits (all options)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO’s multi-year commitment (intended 4 years) despite HM Treasury’s annual spending rules.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoB restrictions on livelihoods/education limiting impact
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocacy and piloting of Myanmar curriculum to build trust for future policy changes.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 2... would streamline the delivery chain and set of activities and shift towards more strategic, multi-year agreements, whilst maintaining flexibility to address shocks and shifts in policy... Compared to Option 1, the number of agencies supported would be reduced from 14 partners to 6 UN agencies and a small number of NGO grants." (60403949.odt, sections 55-56)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Cox’s Bazar limits partner selection to organizations with existing security clearances and experience in high-risk environments. GoB restrictions on refugee livelihoods and education exclude partners without government approval (e.g., no direct funding to Rohingya-led organizations). The need for rapid disaster response favors UN agencies with pre-positioned staff over local NGOs.
q27_constraints_detail: GoB’s camp fencing and internet restrictions require partners with physical access and government relationships
Climate risks (cyclones/flooding) necessitate partners with disaster response capacity (e.g., WFP, UNHCR)
Limited formal justice systems favor partners experienced in informal mechanisms (e.g., Shalish mediation)
Host community tensions require partners with conflict sensitivity expertise (e.g., BRAC)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The multi-sectoral objectives (protection, health, education, WASH, environment) require a mixed delivery structure: UN agencies lead sectoral coordination (ISCG), while NGOs provide localized services. The need for both emergency relief and long-term resilience justifies combining bilateral agreements (for predictability) with flexible contingency funds (for disasters).
q28_linkages: Protection objectives → IOM/UNHCR leadership via ISCG coordination structure
Environmental rehabilitation → Bangladesh Forest Department partnerships for local ownership
Livelihoods constraints → BRAC’s ultra-poor graduation model adapted for host communities
Disaster resilience → WFP/UNICEF’s pre-positioned stocks and early warning systems
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid disaster response favors UN agencies over local partners; (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led technical assistance (e.g., WASH Master Plan) vs. community co-design; (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Cash-for-work programmes are blocked by GoB despite being more efficient than in-kind aid.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: UNOPS fund management adds 3% overhead but reduces FCDO transaction costs
Equity: Rohingya participation in camp governance is limited by GoB security concerns
Trade-off: "The high use of short-term contracts... has cost and quality implications" (section 54) but provides flexibility
Trade-off: Environmental rehabilitation (Objective 3) competes with immediate food needs (Objective 1) for budget
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (protracted crisis + climate shocks) justifies intensive oversight: six-monthly Director-level reviews, embedded PSEA safeguarding, and contingency funds. "Given the vulnerability of Bangladesh to disasters, we will maintain support to anticipate and respond rapidly to disasters." (section 38)
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: (1) UN agencies (IOM/UNHCR) train Rohingya community workers; (2) BRAC’s skills programmes target host communities; (3) Bangladesh Forest Department receives technical support for reforestation. The shift from NGO consortia to specific partnerships (section 56) aims to build localized capacity while maintaining service quality.
intersections.quote: "The complexity of arrangements hampers co-ordination between the different strands... and delivery of a cohesive overall programme strategy." (section 54) and "We will work with the Bangladesh Forest Department to support tree nurseries through training and planting." (section 37)

key_programme_risks: Protracted refugee crisis with no near-term repatriation solutions (Myanmar conflict)
GoB policy restrictions on livelihoods/education increasing refugee desperation
Climate disasters (cyclones/flooding) destroying camp infrastructure
Host community resentment leading to violence or reduced cooperation
Trafficking and drug smuggling networks exploiting vulnerable populations
Bhasan Char relocations proceeding without UN technical assessments
Reduced international donor funding due to COVID-19 global priorities
Limited access to justice for GBV survivors and crime victims
Environmental degradation (deforestation, water scarcity) fueling conflicts
Rohingya youth radicalization due to lack of education/livelihoods

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pilot skill training aligned with Myanmar curriculum to demonstrate benefits for future repatriation (section 34). Advocacy for policy changes through ISCG.
Pre-positioned emergency stocks, stabilized slopes, and early warning systems (section 32). Reforestation to reduce cyclone/wind damage (section 37).
Economic opportunities for locals (e.g., BRAC programmes) and Cox’s Bazar District Development Plan (section 36).
