PSEA network, GBV case management, and Murad Code principles (section 32). Cash-for-work to reduce vulnerability (section 33).
FCDO representations to GoB for UN assessments; RRNRP will not support Bhasan Char until conditions meet international standards (section 22).
Multi-year FCDO commitment to provide predictability; co-hosted donor conferences (section 13).
Study on formal/informal justice mechanisms (Shalish); support to community policing (section 32).

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from SHPR (2016-2021): Multi-year funding improves staff retention and service quality despite FCAS challenges (section 26).
Localization constraints: "The complexity of arrangements hampers coordination" (section 54) → Streamlined to 6 UN agencies in RRNRP.
Cash programming blocked by GoB: "This is currently blocked, apart from a few cases" (section 32) → Workarounds via foster family support.
Protection mainstreaming: PSEA network established after sexual exploitation cases in earlier phases (section 48).
Climate adaptation: Cyclone Amphan (2020) showed early warning systems reduce fatalities (22 deaths vs. 3,000 in 2007) (section 25).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The SHPR programme (2016-2021) scored ‘A’ in annual reviews despite FCAS challenges, demonstrating that predictable funding and UN coordination can deliver results. Key lessons: (1) Multi-year agreements reduce staff turnover; (2) Localized service delivery improves trust; (3) Contingency funds are critical for disaster response. The IDC (2020) recognized the UK’s "substantial contribution" but noted camp conditions remain dire without political solutions in Myanmar.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: RRNRP shifts from SHPR by: (1) Reducing partners from 14 to 6 UN agencies + NGOs for coherence; (2) Adding multi-year funding for predictability; (3) Embedding climate resilience (Objective 4) after Cyclone Amphan; (4) Prioritizing Rohingya voices in camp governance (section 32); (5) Expanding LPG distribution to 200,000 people after deforestation studies showed 80% reduction in fuelwood demand (section 37).
risks_lessons.quote: "The current Strengthening Humanitarian Preparedness and Response (SHPR) Programme... has scored ‘A’ in the last three Annual Reviews despite a challenging operating environment... We will build on significant results and lessons from the previous programme." (60403949.odt, section 26) and "The improvement in resilience is evident by the reduced number of fatalities [in Cyclone Amphan]." (section 25)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages the UN’s Joint Response Plan (JRP), which has mobilized $950m in 2021 from multiple donors. Additional $452m has been mobilized by bilateral donors for host communities since 2017, plus $100m from Asian Development Bank and $590m from World Bank for broader support.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Not explicitly mentioned. Budget covers both operational costs (e.g., food, health services) and capital investments (e.g., durable shelters, reforestation).
financial_details.quote: "It is estimated that NPACs will consume up to £10m in Option 2... These estimates only include NPACs charged by UNOPS and the first tier of implementing partners." (60403949.odt, section 61) and "The top five donors... account for 68% of total funding [to JRP]." (section 41)

metadata.programme_name: Land Facility (LF)

quote.text: The Land Facility (LF) will enable the UK to make a significant contribution to improved land governance and more secure land and property rights across Africa and South East Asia.

metadata.duration_source: The LF will initially run for 7 years and work in up to 10 countries depending on size and needs. (58850441.odt, What the programme will deliver)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Land Facility (LF) combines capacity building (strengthening land administration systems), policy influence (promoting responsible land investment frameworks), and implementation research (testing and scaling land governance interventions). It aims to build government capacity for land reform while facilitating responsible investment and improving tenure security.
what_objectives.q1_source: The LF will work with governments, businesses and communities to build efficient, fair and transparent land administration systems and land investment frameworks. (58850441.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: strategic land reform ‘roadmaps’ developed
technical assistance for land registration pilots
legal reforms supported
central land administration systems developed
legal advice to companies investing in land
community legal empowerment for land negotiations
global monitoring of SDG land indicators strengthened
political support for sustained land reform mobilized
business case for long-term national financing for land governance developed

what_objectives.summary: The LF aims to strengthen land governance systems in up to 10 African countries by building government capacity for land reform, promoting responsible investment frameworks, and improving tenure security for vulnerable groups including women and rural youth.

quote.text: The aim of the LF is to build the basic capacity and systems and mobilise the necessary political support so (a) governments implement and resource sustained land reform, including land tenure regularisation, and (b) land transactions for investment are governed efficiently, fairly and transparently.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile states and faces delivery risks due to political economy constraints, weak institutions, and complex land governance reforms. The risk rating is 'major' due to the difficulty of influencing reforms in multiple countries with varying political contexts.
where_context.q5_source: LF has a risk rating of major, which fits within GRD’s risk appetite. This rating is due to the delivery risk of implementing multiple levels of intervention in a range of countries, including fragile states, and the difficulty and complexity of influencing reforms and change in behaviour in governments, donors and businesses. (58850441.odt, IstheproposedlevelofrisktobetakenfitwithDFID’sriskappetiteforthisportfolio?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak land governance systems, overlapping statutory and customary legal frameworks, and political resistance to reform create barriers to land registration and investment. Climate pressures (drought, desertification) exacerbate land disputes, while fragile contexts increase instability risks. Limited government capacity and donor coordination further constrain effective implementation.

quote.text: Key blockers to establishing effective land governance in Africa have been identified as lack of central administrative and technical capacity, opaque and inefficient land investment systems and lack of political will to drive reform.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Narrative summary of why UK support needed

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID retains overall programme management and strategic decision-making, with technical assistance provided by UK-based Her Majesty’s Land Registry (HMLR) and a lead supplier. Southern partners (governments, communities) are recipients of capacity-building and technical support but have limited decision-making authority over programme design.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for land agencies and ministries
technical assistance for land registration systems
legal empowerment for communities (especially women)
institutional strengthening of central land administration
development of land reform roadmaps

partner_organizations.name: DFID (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funding and programme management

partner_organizations.name: Her Majesty’s Land Registry (HMLR)
partner_organizations.role: technical advisory (global level) and technical assistance (country level)

partner_organizations.name: Lead Supplier (to be contracted)
partner_organizations.role: implementation of Land Reform Facility and Responsible Land Investment Facility

partner_organizations.name: Decision Support Unit (DSU)
partner_organizations.role: independent monitoring, evaluation, and challenge function

partner_organizations.name: Focus country governments (e.g., Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe)
partner_organizations.role: recipients of capacity-building and reform support

partner_organizations.name: Investment Promotion Agencies (IPAs)
partner_organizations.role: support for responsible land investment

partner_organizations.name: Communities and businesses
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries of legal empowerment and investment support

partner_organizations.name: Global Donor Working Group on Land
partner_organizations.role: coordination with other donors

partner_organizations.name: Network of Excellence on Land Governance in Africa (NELGA)
partner_organizations.role: potential collaboration for capacity-building

quote.text: The intervention will be delivered by DFID through a jointly managed programme in partnership with HMLand Registry; it will deliver through one lead supplier and a separate Decision Support Unit.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Narrative summary of why UK support needed

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID will contract a lead supplier and a Decision Support Unit (DSU) to deliver the programme. The lead supplier will implement the two main components (Land Reform Facility and Responsible Land Investment Facility), while the DSU provides independent oversight. Funds are disbursed based on delivery against agreed milestones.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID manages the programme jointly with HMLR, with a lead supplier delivering core components and a separate DSU for independent monitoring. The structure includes a central contract management team within DFID’s Growth and Resilience Department (GRD), with country-level engagement through DFID country offices and HMG posts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The business case implies a competitive process for selecting the lead supplier, though the exact method is not detailed. The rationale is to ensure value for money and access to specialized technical expertise in land governance and investment frameworks.

quote.text: DFID will contract a Decision Support Unit that will provide DFID and supplier/partners with independent advice. [...] The programme will be led by a B1 Programme Manager (staff-time 80%) and B2 (staff-time 50%) in the Agriculture and Land Team.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will be jointly managed by DFID and HMLR, with oversight from a Decision Support Unit (DSU) providing independent advice. The DSU will monitor results, conduct process evaluations, and challenge delivery partners. Country-level engagement will involve DFID country offices and HMG posts.

quote.text: To support this, DFID will contract a Decision Support Unit that will provide DFID and supplier/partners with independent advice. [...] The design includes a series of measures to manage the political economy risks inherent in a multi-country, land governance reform programme.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed to dial country engagement up or down or pull out altogether depending on progress. Funds can be reallocated between components and countries based on emerging opportunities and political context.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The LF uses an adaptive management approach to test interventions with short feedback loops, allowing for rapid scaling or termination of activities. The programme can adjust priorities based on political economy analysis and real-time learning, with the DSU providing independent challenge and verification.

quote.text: LF is designed as an adaptive programme to respond quickly to opportunities; test interventions with short feedback loops so they can be quickly scaled out or stopped; and dial country engagement up or down or pull out altogether depending on progress.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Isthere sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in the context?

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Supplier → Sub-contractors/DSU; FCDO → HMLR (advisory role).

quote.text: The programme will be led by a B1 Programme Manager (staff-time 80%) and B2 (staff-time 50%) in the Agriculture and Land Team. Two programme-funded A2 advisers will be recruited and seconded to Lead Suppliers.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Dothe SRO and team have the capability and resources to deliver this programme?

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" (counterfactual)
Bilateral approach with light support from the centre (status quo)
Delivering through multilaterals (e.g., World Bank, FAO, UN Habitat)
Jointly-managed, adaptive, centrally contracted programme with multiple components (D.1 - recommended)
Jointly-managed, adaptive, centrally contracted programme with a single component (D.2)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The D.1 option (jointly-managed, adaptive programme with multiple components) was chosen because it overcomes capacity constraints in country offices, provides flexibility to respond to political contexts, and allows for specialized technical delivery while maintaining DFID oversight. It balances risk management with adaptive programming, which is critical for land governance reforms in fragile contexts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single lead supplier (D.2 risk) could create transaction-heavy and inefficient downstream management.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: D.1 uses multiple components with separate contracts (lead supplier + DSU) to avoid concentration of risk and improve accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing multiple contracts (D.1 risk) could increase administrative burden.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The DSU provides independent oversight to streamline coordination and verify results, reducing DFID’s direct management load.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy risks in fragile states may undermine reform efforts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adaptive management and short feedback loops allow for rapid adjustments; the programme focuses on building political will alongside technical capacity.

quote.text: Based on our experience with LEGEND and other, similar programmes also suggest such approaches severely constrain flexibility and adaptability down the delivery chain. [...] The proposed approach under the LF involves a significant reduction in the number of components and central transactions compared to LEGEND, which has had 12 components over its lifetime. LF will involve only two main delivery components with two supporting components.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Why was the D.2 approach rejected?

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political and institutional fragility in focus countries (e.g., clan-based power structures in Mogadishu, race-based land tensions in South Africa) limits the pool of capable local partners and requires reliance on international technical expertise. Weak government capacity necessitates DFID-led programme management with embedded advisory roles (e.g., HMLR).
q27_constraints_detail: Fragile states require international expertise due to limited local capacity.
Political sensitivity of land reform limits engagement with certain local actors (e.g., elites resisting reform).
Donor coordination gaps necessitate DFID’s central role in convening partners.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for adaptive, politically smart interventions (e.g., influencing reform processes, building political will) requires a flexible, centrally managed structure (D.1) rather than rigid bilateral or multilateral channels. The mix of technical assistance (e.g., land registration) and political engagement (e.g., reform roadmaps) necessitates a consortium model with specialized partners.
q28_linkages: Political economy focus → requires adaptive management and independent challenge (DSU).
Multi-country scope → needs centralized coordination to avoid duplication.
Capacity-building objectives → embedded technical assistance from HMLR and lead supplier.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery and inclusive partnerships, particularly in gender equity. For example, securing women’s land rights requires targeted interventions (e.g., legal reforms, community empowerment) that may slow progress but are critical for long-term impact. The choice of a Northern-led structure (DFID/HMLR) is justified by the need for technical expertise but risks limiting Southern ownership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid land registration may exclude vulnerable groups (e.g., women, youth) without targeted support.
Expertise vs. ownership: Reliance on UK-based HMLR ensures technical quality but reduces local decision-making.
Cost vs. reach: Adaptive programming increases overhead but improves responsiveness in fragile contexts.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk profile (due to fragile states and political complexity) justifies intensive oversight through the DSU and milestone-based payments. High flexibility in fund reallocation is paired with strict verification to mitigate fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: HMLR provides technical training, the lead supplier delivers hands-on assistance to governments, and the DSU ensures skills transfer is monitored. Southern partners (e.g., land agencies) are positioned as recipients of capacity-building rather than co-designers.

quote.text: Promoting and unblocking land reform requires tackling the political economy of land, which cannot be addressed solely with technical solutions and is highly context-specific. [...] The TWP approach [...] provides a good framework. The approach must be grounded in robust political economy analysis that encompasses political, economic, social and cultural factors in a given context.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Tackling the Political Economy of land

key_programme_risks: Delivery risk in fragile states with weak institutions.
Political resistance to land reform from elites or vested interests.
Coordinating multiple donors and government agencies in focus countries.
Ensuring gender equity in land rights amid customary practices.
Sustaining reforms post-programme without long-term national financing.
Managing complex contracts with lead supplier and DSU.
Balancing adaptive programming with fiduciary safeguards.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive management with short feedback loops; DSU provides independent oversight.
Political economy analysis to identify entry points; build coalitions with reform-minded actors.
DFID’s leadership in the Global Donor Working Group on Land; align with VGGT processes.
Targeted legal reforms and community empowerment (e.g., Namati’s approach).
Develop business cases for national financing; build government capacity for long-term management.
Reduce components compared to LEGEND; clear division of roles between lead supplier and DSU.

fcas_specific_lessons: Land disputes are a key driver of conflict in FCAS; reforms must address underlying power structures (e.g., clan-based systems in Mogadishu).
In fragile contexts, technical solutions (e.g., land registration) must be paired with political engagement to avoid backlash.
Flexible funding is critical to respond to rapidly changing contexts (e.g., post-conflict windows of opportunity).
Donor coordination is essential to avoid undermining local legitimacy (e.g., aligning with national reform agendas).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s LEGEND programme highlight that technical assistance alone is insufficient without addressing political economy constraints. Successful land tenure regularisation (e.g., in Rwanda) required sustained political buy-in, donor coordination, and complementary investments in land financial markets. The LF design reduces the number of components (from 12 in LEGEND to 2 main components) to improve focus and flexibility.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The LF incorporates: 1) A Decision Support Unit for independent oversight (addressing LEGEND’s monitoring gaps); 2) adaptive management to respond to political contexts; 3) stronger focus on urban land governance (a gap in previous programmes); 4) explicit gender equity targets; 5) reduced contractual complexity compared to LEGEND.

quote.text: DFID’s major Land Tenure Regularisation (LTR) programmes in Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania and Mozambique have distributed over 14 million land rights documents and helped over 12 million women improve their land rights. [...] The most successful cases [...] were characterised by substantial work which built central administrative capacity, stimulated the land financial market, improved donor coordination and stimulated political will around land reform.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, DFID has successfully implemented extensive land tenure regularisation programmes

quote.text: DFID will provide £55 million to the Land Facility (LF) Programme over 7 years from 2020 to 2027.
quote.source: 58850441.odt, Narrative summary of why UK support needed

metadata.programme_name: Kenya Catalytic Jobs Fund

quote.programme_name: "Kenya Catalytic Jobs Fund" (48638757.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
quote.budget: "The UK will spend £5m over 4 years" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.duration: "August 2018 – August 2022" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.sector: "jobs, youth, and building a more modern strategic development partnership" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "The UK will spend £5m over 4 years to test innovations that have the potential for large-scale job creation... Start Date: August 2018; End Date: August 2022" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing/scaling job-creation innovations) with a financing mechanism (flexible challenge fund) and capacity building (technical assistance to selected firms). It aims to generate evidence on what works in youth employment while directly creating jobs through market-led solutions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The UK will spend £5m over 4 years to test innovations that have the potential for large-scale job creation... The programme will focus particularly on youth and through a flexible fund provide a mix of technical assistance and grant support." (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 10-15 grants awarded to entrepreneurs/SGBs/firms (40577885.odt, Theory of Change)
Increased employment opportunities for young people in Kenya (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Expanded innovative solutions and disruptive technologies within formal and informal sectors (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Increased private sector investment in solutions and small businesses (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Improved enterprise performance in selected sectors (via productivity gains, investment and/or growth) (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Independent learning studies to determine effect of grants on small business growth (40577885.odt, Theory of Change)
what_objectives.summary: The programme tests market-led innovations to create productive employment for vulnerable youth (especially women, disabled, and ASAL residents) through a £5m challenge fund combining grants and technical assistance, while generating evidence on effective job-creation strategies.

quote.objective: "test innovations that have the potential for large-scale job creation, unlocking barriers in key productive sectors and generating employment for those that are most vulnerable" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.approach: "The programme will focus particularly on youth and through a flexible fund provide a mix of technical assistance and grant support" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.outputs: "Anticipated 10-15 grants (including funding TA as appropriate) awarded to entrepreneurs/SGBs/firms" (40577885.odt, Theory of Change)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in Kenya's mixed formal/informal economy with structural barriers to youth employment (e.g., weak TVET systems, gender disparities, ASAL vulnerabilities) but without active conflict. DFID Kenya has a 'medium to high appetite for contextual/operational risks' and 'low appetite for fiduciary/reputational risks'.
where_context.q5_source: "Programme risk rating: Moderate" (40577885.odt, Summary Sheet) and "DFID Kenya has a medium to high appetite for contextual, operational and delivery risks; and a low appetite for fiduciary and reputational risks" (40577885.odt, Management Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (cumbersome business regulations, especially firm entry/exit)
weak institutions (limited TVET quality, weak labour market information systems)
political economy (gender disparities in credit access, disability exclusion)
data limitations (weak evidence base on informal sector productivity)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory barriers (e.g., firm registration costs) and infrastructure gaps (e.g., electricity) limit private sector growth and job creation. Weak TVET systems reduce youth employability, while gender/ASAL disparities exclude marginalized groups from formal opportunities. Data gaps on informal sector productivity complicate evidence-based interventions.

quote.constraints: "Barriers in Kenya include lack of access to affordable finance and business support, cumbersome or obstructive business regulations (particularly around firm entry/exit into markets)... and poor quality infrastructure and utilities (especially lack of access to electricity)" (40577885.odt, Evidence for Intervention)
quote.data_gaps: "There is little evidence with regards to the informal sector... closing this productivity gap would greatly enhance the quality of Kenya’s informal jobs" (40577885.odt, Evidence for Intervention)
quote.gender_asal: "Youth—particularly women, the poor/disabled and those living in conflict-affected areas—are at a significant disadvantage... Women-run businesses face greater difficulties accessing credit" (40577885.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP) includes HMG Kenya and local stakeholders (e.g., CDC, county governments), while the not-for-profit fund manager (e.g., Mercy Corps, Balloon Ventures) implements calls for proposals and grant management. DFID retains oversight but delegates operational decisions to the fund manager and SAP.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to grantees (e.g., business development services, productivity tools)
mentorship through fund manager support
linkages to investors/incubators for scaling
gender-disaggregated monitoring to inform inclusive practices

partner_organizations.role: funder and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP)
partner_organizations.role: determining scope/criteria for calls, selecting applicants, bringing investor networks

partner_organizations.name: Independent monitoring and learning partner
partner_organizations.role: assessing success/failure of innovations, disseminating lessons

partner_organizations.name: CDC Group
partner_organizations.role: potential investor for scaling successful innovations

partner_organizations.name: County governments (e.g., Mombasa, ASAL regions)
partner_organizations.role: policy dialogue, local implementation support

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (anchor investors, incubators, impact investors)

quote.structure: "DFID will hire a flexible fund manager to issue calls for proposals, sift applications and manage contracts/reporting with successful applicants. An expert Selection and Advisory Panel will be established and chaired by DFID" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.sap_composition: "The Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP) for this programme will include representatives from HMG Kenya (not just DFID) as well as from CDC and/or its investee funds" (40577885.odt, Management Case)
quote.capacity_building: "Funds will be disbursed to selected proposals to risk-share and test business models that can create economic opportunities for the poor... Proposals may request funding for tailored technical assistance as part of their proposals" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)
quote.nfp_switch: "this addendum changes the commercial route... to an accountable grant arrangement with a not-for-profit service provider" (48638757.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an accountable grant with a not-for-profit fund manager (replacing the originally planned commercial contract) to disburse sub-grants and technical assistance. This instrument allows for payment-by-results milestones and includes a break clause for underperformance. The fund manager subcontracts grantees through competitive calls for proposals.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID contracts a single not-for-profit fund manager (e.g., Mercy Corps) to operate the challenge fund. The fund manager issues calls for proposals, selects grantees via a Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP), disburses grants/TA, and reports to DFID. An independent monitoring partner evaluates outcomes. The SAP includes HMG and local stakeholders to guide strategic decisions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The fund manager was selected through a "rigorous and independent competitive process" (48638757.odt) to ensure technical capacity and value for money. The switch from private sector to not-for-profit was based on market engagement showing NGO capacity to deliver flexible funds with lower setup costs and faster procurement (3 vs 7 months).

quote.instrument: "The accountable grant with the fund manager will be based on a system that incorporates a payment by results approach for particular milestones" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)
quote.structure: "The fund manager will be responsible for subcontracting grantees with innovations/solutions that have the potential for large-scale job creation" (48638757.odt, Approach to Implementation)
quote.selection: "Bids will be expected both from organisations that are purely not-for-profit as well as not-for-profit arms of profit-making entities. The selected fund manager... will be responsible for subcontracting grantees" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)
quote.rationale: "Many local and international NGOs implementing jobs programmes implies lower programme set-up costs and potential value for money through competitive tendering" (48638757.odt, Annex 1)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP) is chaired by DFID and includes HMG Kenya representatives, CDC, and local stakeholders. The SAP determines the scope/criteria for calls for proposals and selects applicants, while the fund manager executes operational decisions. DFID retains oversight through quarterly performance reviews and a break clause in the accountable grant.

quote.day_to_day: "The selected fund manager will be responsible for subcontracting grantees with innovations/solutions" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)
quote.sub_awards: "The fund manager will... issue calls for proposals, sift applications, and manage grants" (40577885.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.sap_role: "The Selection and Advisory Panel (SAP)... will determine the scope and criteria for Calls for Proposals and select applicants" (40577885.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.oversight: "The accountable grant arrangement will also incorporate a break clause that will define at what point(s) DFID will determine (dis)continuation of the arrangement based on the fund manager’s performance... quarterly performance reviews" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between thematic areas (agriculture/manufacturing/informal sector) and grant sizes based on learning, but requires DFID approval for major shifts. The programme uses staggered calls for proposals over 2 years to allow adaptation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs "experimentation, flexibility and on-the-go learning" with a focus on generating and disseminating evidence. The fund manager can adjust selection criteria and support types (e.g., grants vs TA) based on lessons, but strategic priorities (e.g., youth focus) remain fixed. Independent monitoring partners assess what works/doesn’t work to inform adjustments.

quote.reallocation: "The programme will not prescribe one-size-fits-all technical assistance... grants sizes, type of support provided... can respond to lessons being learnt and emerging priorities" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)
quote.adaptive: "A rigorous monitoring and lesson-learning process will form a core part of the programme... The calls for proposals are envisaged to end within the first 2 years... with monitoring and learning to extend into the last 2 years" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)
quote.constraints: "Although anew fund has start-up costs, the management costs are anticipated to be limited to 12% and monitoring and learning to 3% of fund value" (40577885.odt, Value for Money)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Not-for-profit fund manager (e.g., Mercy Corps) → Grantees (entrepreneurs/SGBs/firms)

quote.management_costs: "the management costs are anticipated to be limited to 12% and monitoring and learning to 3% of fund value" (40577885.odt, Value for Money)
quote.layers: "The fund manager will be responsible for subcontracting grantees" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)
quote.payment: "The accountable grant... incorporates a payment by results approach for particular milestones" (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (rejected due to misalignment with UK Africa Strategy and low VFM)
Option 2: Follow-on to Kuza programme (rejected due to limited scale and low cost-per-job)
Option 3: Fund World Bank Youth Employment Project (rejected due to limited influence over design and high risk of delays)
Option 4: Establish new flexible fund (selected for strategic fit, additionality, and flexibility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The not-for-profit fund manager approach (via accountable grant) was chosen over the original private sector contract due to: (1) **faster procurement** (3 vs 7 months), (2) **lower setup costs** (existing NGO capacity reduced overhead), (3) **greater flexibility** (AGs allow adaptations without contract renegotiation), and (4) **stronger local networks** (NGOs like Mercy Corps have deep roots in Kenya’s entrepreneurial ecosystem). The challenge fund model was selected for its ability to catalyze private investment, test innovations at scale, and generate evidence on job creation strategies.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (lower NGO overheads, competitive tendering)
partner capacity (NGOs’ experience with flexible funds in Kenya)
equity (NGOs’ focus on marginalized groups like women/ASAL youth)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor response to calls for proposals (market risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by strong response to interim mini-competition and fund manager’s outreach networks (e.g., Mercy Corps’ Google Impact Challenge experience).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund manager underperformance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Payment-by-results milestones, quarterly reviews, and break clause in accountable grant.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Value for money concerns with NGO overheads
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Non-Programme/Project-Attributable Cost (NPAC) scrutiny and competitive tendering.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure of selected innovations to scale
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Independent monitoring partner to assess and disseminate lessons; co-investment requirements for grantees.

quote.alternatives: "Option 4: Establish a flexible fund to support innovative market-led projects for youth employment (recommended option)... scores highest across the four criteria: strategic fit, additionality, risk, and value for money" (40577885.odt, Options)
quote.nfp_rationale: "Many local and international NGOs implementing jobs programmes implies lower programme set-up costs and potential value for money through competitive tendering... AGs provide more flexibility since they are not legally-binding like contracts" (48638757.odt, Annex 1)
quote.challenge_fund: "Challenge funds use competition to find the most innovative and cost-effective solution to accomplish development goals; enable donor money to partly leverage private capital... and reduce market distortions" (40577885.odt, Option 4)
quote.risks: "Poor performance [of fund manager] will be mitigated by adopting a payment by results approach and having regular interactions... For value for money, a rigorous and independent competitive process of selecting the fund manager will be adopted" (48638757.odt, Changing the Commercial Approach)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Kenya’s context limits partner selection to organizations with: (1) **local presence** (to navigate regulatory/infrastructure barriers like firm registration), (2) **informal sector expertise** (83% of workforce is informal), (3) **ASAL networks** (to reach marginalized youth), and (4) **gender-inclusive approaches** (given women’s credit access barriers). The switch to not-for-profit fund managers (e.g., Mercy Corps, Balloon Ventures) reflects their embeddedness in Kenya’s entrepreneurial ecosystem compared to international private sector firms.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory barriers (firm entry/exit) require partners with local compliance expertise
Informal sector dominance (83% of workforce) demands partners experienced in micro-enterprise support
ASAL vulnerabilities necessitate partners with rural/conflict-sensitive approaches
Gender disparities (e.g., credit access) favor partners with women-focused programmes
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **implementation research** objectives (testing job-creation innovations) determine its **fund manager structure** to: (1) enable competitive calls for proposals (to identify scalable solutions), (2) provide flexible grant/TA packages (to test different support models), and (3) include independent monitoring (to generate evidence). The **financing mechanism** (challenge fund) is tailored to catalyze private investment in high-potential sectors (agriculture/manufacturing/informal) identified through the diagnostic phase.
q28_linkages: Testing innovations → Requires open competitive calls (fund manager model)
Generating evidence → Needs independent monitoring (separate from fund manager)
Catalyzing private investment → SAP includes investors (CDC) to link grantees to scaling capital
Informal sector focus → Fund manager must support micro-enterprise clusters (e.g., aggregators)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency by: (1) **targeting marginalized groups** (women, disabled, ASAL youth) while requiring **co-investment** from grantees to ensure sustainability; (2) using **staggered calls** to allow learning but **fixed strategic priorities** (youth focus) to maintain coherence; and (3) selecting a **not-for-profit fund manager** (for local reach) with **payment-by-results** (for VFM). The trade-off between inclusive partnerships (e.g., ASAL focus) and rapid delivery is mitigated by leveraging existing NGO networks (e.g., Mercy Corps’ Google Impact Challenge experience).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusion (ASAL/women focus) vs speed (competitive calls may exclude remote applicants without support)
Local ownership (NGO fund manager) vs expertise (private sector’s investor networks)
Flexibility (adaptive learning) vs coherence (fixed youth employment strategic goal)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., potential failure of innovations, delays in OJEU procurement) drives **milestone-based oversight** (quarterly reviews, payment-by-results) and **diversified portfolio** (10-15 grants across sectors). High innovation risk is offset by independent monitoring to capture lessons from failures, while fiduciary risks are mitigated through NPAC controls and SAP investor representation.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: (1) **Fund manager** provides technical assistance to grantees (e.g., business development services); (2) **SAP** includes CDC to link grantees to investors for scaling; (3) **Monitoring partner** generates evidence to inform grantee improvements. The not-for-profit fund manager’s role was expanded (from interim to main) due to its capacity to deliver **tailored support** (e.g., Mercy Corps’ experience with Kenyan micro-businesses).

quote.context_partners: "There are several not-for-profit organisations that have capacity and experience in selecting and supporting enterprises in Kenya... Some have been contracted directly by development partners, while others have been sub-contracted by private sector contractors" (48638757.odt, Annex 2)
quote.objectives_structure: "The programme will select and pilot proposals that show potential to act as a catalyst for investment and/or productivity improvements in job creating sectors... A rigorous monitoring and lesson-learning process will form a core part of the programme" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)
quote.equity_efficiency: "The programme explicitly takes an equitable approach by focusing on ways to create new and/or better-quality jobs for those that are most disadvantaged... Success will also be measured by the authenticity of evidence generated on what works/does not work" (40577885.odt, Value for Money)
quote.risk_management: "Key risks include... potential failure of selected proposals... Mitigation measures include... establishing a high-quality SAP which will... bring with it a network of potential investors; and using independent monitoring and learning" (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
quote.capacity_roles: "Funds will be disbursed to selected proposals to risk-share and test business models... Proposals may request funding for tailored technical assistance as part of their proposals" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)

key_programme_risks: Failure of selected innovations to scale or create jobs (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
Delays in OJEU procurement for fund manager (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
High transaction/management time relative to budget size (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
Poor response to calls for proposals (48638757.odt, Changing the Commercial Approach)
Fund manager underperformance (48638757.odt, Changing the Commercial Approach)
Value for money concerns with NGO overheads (48638757.odt, Changing the Commercial Approach)
Weak evidence base on informal sector productivity (40577885.odt, Evidence for Intervention)
Gender and ASAL disparities limiting reach (40577885.odt, Strategic Case)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Independent monitoring to assess success/failure; co-investment requirements; SAP investor networks for scaling support (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
Interim fund manager (Mercy Corps) to kick-start implementation; regular updates to Head of Office (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
Limit management costs to 12% of fund value; NPAC scrutiny for NGO overheads (40577885.odt, Value for Money)
Leverage fund manager’s networks (e.g., Mercy Corps’ Google Impact Challenge experience); market engagement prior to calls (48638757.odt, Changing the Commercial Approach)
Payment-by-results milestones; quarterly performance reviews; break clause in accountable grant (48638757.odt, Accountable Grant contracting)
Independent monitoring to generate data; focus on productivity gains in informal clusters (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Gender-disaggregated monitoring; SAP includes local stakeholders; geographic focus guided by SUED programme (40577885.odt, Gender Equality)

fcas_specific_lessons: Youth unemployment in ASALs increases radicalization risks, requiring conflict-sensitive approaches (40577885.odt, Strategic Case)
Informal sector dominance (83% of workforce) demands non-traditional support models (e.g., aggregators, savings groups) (40577885.odt, Intended Programme Impact)
Women’s credit access barriers necessitate tailored financial products and investor linkages (40577885.odt, Strategic Case)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s Kuza programme (2014–2017) showed that: (1) **cost-per-job** (£1,780) was high for informal sector interventions; (2) **sustainability** required private sector linkages; and (3) **competitive calls** (vs direct implementation) improved VFM. The Financial Deepening Challenge Fund (FDCF) demonstrated that flexible funds can catalyze systemic change (e.g., M-PESA) but require rigorous monitoring to avoid perverse incentives (40577885.odt, Options).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The switch from a **private sector fund manager** (original plan) to a **not-for-profit fund manager** (addendum) was based on: (1) market engagement showing NGO capacity; (2) lower setup costs; (3) faster procurement (3 vs 7 months); and (4) greater flexibility in AGs vs contracts. The interim arrangement with Mercy Corps validated this approach (48638757.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION).

quote.risks: "Key risks include... (i) potential failure of selected proposals (both at testing and at scale)... (ii) the potential for delays in undertaking OJEU procurement for a fund manager; and (iii) relatively high transaction and management time needed to mobilise the programme" (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
quote.mitigations: "Mitigation measures include... using the fund manager to bear the burden of sifting applications and managing grant contracts... establishing a high-quality SAP which will... bring with it a network of potential investors; and using independent monitoring and learning" (40577885.odt, Risk Register)
quote.lessons: "Kuza... had an overall cost per job created at approximately £1,780... More of the same also presents relatively low value for money and additionality" (40577885.odt, Option 2)
quote.design_changes: "While writing the detailed Terms of Reference (ToR) for the interim arrangement... some of the assumptions made during programme design came under challenge... The new scores put the not-for-profit approach ahead of the private sector service provider approach" (48638757.odt, Annex 1)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to crowd in private sector investment (e.g., CDC, impact investors) and donor funding through: (1) co-investment requirements for grantees; (2) SAP investor networks; and (3) replication of successful models. M-PESA (supported by DFID’s FDCF) demonstrates potential leverage (40577885.odt, Option 4).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £5m" (40577885.odt, Summary Sheet) and "the management costs are anticipated to be limited to 12% and monitoring and learning to 3% of fund value" (40577885.odt, Value for Money)
quote.leverage: "Success criteria for interventions could include... the crowding-in of other donors or DFIs onto the fund... links to business support organisations (e.g. incubators and accelerators) established" (40577885.odt, Recommended Option)
quote.fdcf_example: "FDCF supported M-PESA in 2005 which has had far-reaching benefits for millions of poor Kenyans... created extensive linkages with the real economy that firms have been able to exploit" (40577885.odt, Option 4)

metadata.programme_name: Green Cities and Infrastructure Programme (GCIP)
metadata.quote: The International Development Strategy sets out the UK’s development ambitions on sustainable and inclusive economic development. British Investment Partnerships (BIP), underpins our economic support for developing countries, providing them with investment and technical assistance so that they can be greener, more productive and generate high quality jobs. (D0004565.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 13/02/20-31/06/25", "New project end date (if applicable): 31/12/25" (D0004565.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GCIP is a flexible facility that provides technical assistance to FCDO posts to expand infrastructure and cities programming, develop bankable projects, and unlock capital from British International Investment (BII) and the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG). It combines capacity building, policy influence, and financing mechanisms to accelerate inclusive and sustainable economic growth.
what_objectives.q1_source: "GCIP is a flexible facility for accelerating inclusive and sustainable economic growth in Africa and Asia. It is the core, flexible facility that will deliver many of the objectives of the UK Centre of Expertise (CoE) in Green Cities and Infrastructure. It will provide technical assistance to FCDO Posts, enabling the UK to expand our infrastructure and cities programming across a greater range of geographies and sectors, providing technical leadership on transport, energy, waste management and water." (D0004565.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Increase in the number of people with new and improved access to infrastructure services
Increase in the number of bankable infrastructure projects that unlock capital from BII and PIDG
Increase in the number of people supported to adapt to climate shocks and change
Increase in the number of people employed through construction of large-scale urban transport systems and roads
Increase in the volume of renewable energy installed (on-grid and off-grid)
what_objectives.summary: GCIP aims to scale up technical assistance for infrastructure planning and delivery in Asia and Africa, deepening the impact of UK's infrastructure programming as part of the British Investment Partnerships (BIP) offer. It focuses on developing bankable projects, mobilizing finance, and delivering climate-resilient infrastructure.
what_objectives.quote: "The results achieved through a scaling up of technical and MEL expertise across a greater range of countries will be reflected in improvements in our key programmatic indicators including: Increase in the number of people with new and improved access to infrastructure services; Increase in the number of bankable infrastructure projects that unlock capital from BII and PIDG; Increase in the number of people supported to adapt to climate shocks and change; Increase in the number of people employed through construction of large-scale urban transport systems and roads; Increase in the volume of renewable energy installed (on-grid and off-grid)." (D0004565.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in emerging economies and fragile states, where infrastructure is often scarce and in poor condition. The Commission on State Fragility highlighted that donors should support governments in fragile states to build core capacities, particularly in urban infrastructure and tax administration.
where_context.q5_source: "Essential infrastructure facilities in fragile states are often scarce and in a poor condition limiting public service provision. The Commission on State Fragility, Growth and Development highlighted that donors should seek to support governments in fragile states to build their core capacities particularly the provision of urban infrastructure and tax administration." (90000406.odt, Scope of the Centre’s Remit)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Poor infrastructure governance, lack of financeable projects, limited fiscal autonomy in cities, and inadequate urban planning hinder effective delivery. Climate risks such as flooding and droughts exacerbate these challenges, particularly in fragile states.
where_context.quote: "The five key areas, have been identified, which significantly impede sustainable infrastructure delivery and urban planning in the key countries where the programme will operate, and where the programme will have a particular focus. This includes two key barriers to effective infrastructure delivery: lack of prepared, financeable, infrastructure projects, and inadequate infrastructure governance and policy, and two key barriers to the delivery of well-functioning cities: limited fiscal autonomy and poor financial management in cities, and lack of effective urban planning and land use." (90000406.odt, Addressing the Key Constraints to Sustainable Infrastructure and City Development)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO leads the programme, with technical delivery and oversight managed by UK-based senior experts (G6/7) and country-based staff. The hub-and-spoke model ensures that UK experts retain decision-making power while deploying technical assistance to partner countries.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical support to FCDO posts
management of country-based advisers
strategic policy advice
monitoring and evaluation

partner_organizations.name: Infrastructure and Projects Authority (UK)
partner_organizations.role: technical partnership

partner_organizations.name: Connected Places Catapult (UK)
partner_organizations.role: technical partnership

partner_organizations.name: Crossrail International (UK)
partner_organizations.role: technical partnership

partner_organizations.name: Infrastructure Transparency Initiative (CoST)
partner_organizations.role: anti-corruption work

partner_organizations.name: Commercial supplier (to be contracted)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance delivery

who_partners.quote: "We have created a hub and spoke model. The hub is underpinned by a secretariat (Resilient Cities and Infrastructure Team in KCS) that will oversee the CoE strategy. The spokes (G6/7 senior experts) will be regional leads (SE Asia, South Asia, Africa), covering multiple countries/posts. This support to posts will be blended with technical assistance delivered by external experts procured through a TA facility." (D0004565.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for commercial suppliers) and partnerships (with UK government agencies and multilateral organizations). The commercial contract is for an initial two years with provisions for extensions, while partnerships leverage existing UK expertise and multilateral platforms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A hub-and-spoke model is used, with a central secretariat (Resilient Cities and Infrastructure Team) overseeing strategy and regional leads (G6/7 experts) managing country-based staff and technical delivery. External experts are procured through a technical assistance facility.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The commercial supplier is to be contracted imminently, suggesting a pre-existing framework or direct award process. Partnerships with UK agencies (e.g., Infrastructure and Projects Authority) are based on their recognized expertise and alignment with FCDO priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: "The commercial contract will be for an initial two years, with provisions for two extensions of three years each. Authority for spend under the extensions will be sought through a new business case in due course." (D0004565.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by the Resilient Cities and Infrastructure Team in FCDO, with regional leads (G6/7 experts) managing delivery. The Head of the Resilient Cities and Infrastructure team acts as the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) of the programme.
how_governance.quote: "A new Green Cities and Infrastructure Programme delivery structure will be created, reporting to one of the G6 senior experts. They will report to the Head of the Resilient Cities and Infrastructure team who oversees the CoE strategy and acts as the SRO of the Green Cities and Infrastructure programme." (D0004565.odt, Management and delivery)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated within the programme’s technical remit, with flexibility to respond to DFID’s and HMG’s needs. However, significant changes (e.g., extensions) require new business case approvals.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be demand-led and flexible, allowing adjustments in response to changing country needs and political environments. However, major shifts require approval through updated business cases.
how_flexibility.quote: "The Centre will be designed to be flexible – providing adaptable and demand-led support to meet DFID’s and HMG’s needs, with the ability to be flexible within its technical remit." (90000406.odt, Scope of the Centre’s Remit)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Commercial Supplier/Partnerships → Country-based staff/end beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: "The commercial contract will be for an initial two years, with provisions for two extensions of three years each. Authority for spend under the extensions will be sought through a new business case in due course." (D0004565.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing – no additional support beyond status quo
Provide funding to Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)
Additional advisers in country offices and specialists based in DFID’s central or regional departments
Building on existing DFID programmes/structures (e.g., PIDG, CIG)
Finance for advisers to use existing frameworks
Setup a facility to provide a call-down contract for DFID country offices, OGDs, and DFID central teams
A range of partnerships managed from DFID headquarters
Call-down facility and partnerships together
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (a combination of a technical assistance facility and partnership organizations) was chosen because it provides the agility to respond to different enabling environments across DFID geographies and addresses all identified constraints. It balances flexibility, UK branding, and the ability to scale up while maintaining alignment with DFID’s strategies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Management burden due to complex delivery structure (facility + partnerships)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear governance arrangements and regular coordination between facility and partnerships to ensure shared objectives and learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential misalignment with DFID strategies if partners are not flexible
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Transparent partner selection process and flexibility to change partnerships if needed.

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option based on the multi-criteria analysis is option nine: a combination of a technical assistance facility and partnership organisations. This combination would provide the basis for addressing all of the constraints identified in the strategic case through a range of interventions with the agility to respond to the particular nature and conditions associated with different enabling environments across DFID geographies." (90000406.odt, Summary of Preferred Option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s geographic scope (Asia and Africa, including fragile states) requires partners with expertise in emerging economies and FCAS. This limits partner selection to organizations capable of operating in high-risk, low-infrastructure environments and navigating political economy challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: need for expertise in fragile states
ability to work in high-risk environments
capacity to address urban infrastructure and climate resilience
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives (developing bankable projects, climate resilience, inclusive growth) require a mixed delivery structure (facility + partnerships) to provide both technical expertise and flexible, demand-led support. The hub-and-spoke model ensures that UK expertise is deployed where most needed, while partnerships expand the range of solutions available.
q28_linkages: technical assistance facility → supports design and scaling of new programmes
partnerships → expand range of solutions for urban/infrastructure challenges
hub-and-spoke model → ensures flexibility and responsiveness to country needs
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the need to balance efficiency (rapid delivery, UK expertise) with equity (inclusive partnerships, Southern ownership). For example, while the programme is Northern-led, it includes country-based staff and aims to build local capacity through embedded technical assistance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership (UK-led but with country-based staff)
speed of delivery vs. inclusive partnerships (facility allows rapid deployment but partnerships ensure local relevance)
cost efficiency vs. reach (hub-and-spoke model balances central oversight with local flexibility)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (including fragile states) necessitates a more intensive management structure, with embedded advisors (G6/7 experts) and milestone-based oversight to ensure accountability and adaptability.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme, with country-based staff and technical assistance designed to strengthen local institutions. This shapes partner roles, as local staff are integral to delivery and monitoring.
intersections.quote: "The Centrewillcontaintheskillsandexpertiserequiredtoworkinfragilestates.Essentialinfrastructurefacilitiesinfragilestatesareoftenscarceandinapoorconditionlimitingpublicserviceprovision.TheCommissiononStateFragility,GrowthandDevelopmenthighlightedthatdonorsshouldseektosupportgovernmentsinfragilestatestobuildtheircorecapacitiesparticularlytheprovisionofurbaninfrastructureandtaxadministration." (90000406.odt, Scope of the Centre’s Remit)

key_programme_risks: Inadequate infrastructure governance and policy in partner countries
Lack of prepared, financeable infrastructure projects
Limited fiscal autonomy and poor financial management in cities
Lack of effective urban planning and land use
Limited capacity to support clean growth in cities and infrastructure
Political and institutional barriers to municipal borrowing
Climate risks (flooding, droughts) threatening infrastructure resilience
Management burden of complex delivery structure (facility + partnerships)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Provide technical assistance to improve transparency, project preparation, and governance frameworks.
Develop a pipeline of bankable projects through the technical assistance facility and partnerships.
Support cities in developing municipal finance mechanisms (e.g., land value capture, property taxes).
Embed climate and adaptation advice in all programme activities and align with countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
Use a hub-and-spoke model with clear governance and regular coordination to streamline oversight.

fcas_specific_lessons: Donors have systematically underplayed the importance of investments in urban infrastructure in fragile situations (Commission on State Fragility).
Support to Somalia on urban interventions has used DFID’s Building Stability Framework to respond to different levels of fragility and conflict.
In fragile states, hybrid forms of security emerge where states are too weak to tackle organized private violence, requiring tailored approaches to urban service provision.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on the successful Infrastructure and Cities for Economic Development (ICED) programme, which delivered £337m of new DFID and OGD programmes and strengthened urban/infrastructure programming in over 20 countries. Lessons include the need for flexible, demand-led support and strong political economy awareness.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The GCIP design incorporates a hub-and-spoke model and embedded MEL expertise, based on lessons from ICED and other DFID programmes (e.g., Cities and Infrastructure for Growth). The addition of in-house delivery roles (G6/7 experts) was introduced to improve coordination and results monitoring.
risks_lessons.quote: "The ICED programme included an ICED Facility, which by June 2019 had designed £337m of new DFID and other government department (OGD) programmes, with £270m now either in procurement or delivery. The Facility has also delivered direct impacts in over twenty countries, where it has strengthened DFID and OGD programmes." (90000406.odt, Fit with DFID’s Comparative Advantage)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to unlock capital from BII, PIDG, and UKEF for bankable infrastructure projects, contributing to the UK’s goal of mobilizing up to £8bn per year by 2025 for development and climate objectives.
financial_details.quote: "Under BIP, the UK has committed to mobilising up to £8bn a year by 2025 that contribute to our development and climate policy objectives, a goal that will bridge the infrastructure finance gap and meet the relevant Sustainable Development Goals." (D0004565.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Humanitarian Grand Challenge: Creating Hope in Conflict (CHIC)

quote.programme_name: "Humanitarian Grand Challenge: Creating Hope in Conflict (CHIC)" (Document: 48455259.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.duration: "Start Date: March 2018", "End Date: March 2023" (Document: 48455259.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.sector: "To support innovation to solve humanitarian access challenges and reach populations affected by humanitarian crises with life-saving and life-improving humanitarian assistance" (Document: 48455259.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: March 2018", "End Date: March 2023"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is a financing mechanism that funds implementation research and technology development to address humanitarian access challenges. It focuses on identifying and scaling innovative solutions (tools, products, and approaches) to improve humanitarian assistance delivery in conflict-affected areas, with a strong emphasis on private sector engagement and scaling successful innovations.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Humanitarian Grand Challenge is a major new, multi-partner innovation challenge fund. It will leverage private sector engagement to help transform the way humanitarian assistance is provided to vulnerable people in hard-to-reach, conflict-affected areas." (Document: 48455259.odt, Intervention Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 15 seed grants (up to £200,000 each) for promising innovations
2 scaling grants (up to £600,000 each) for innovations ready to transition to scale
Increased capacity among partners and beneficiaries to use innovative products or services
Increased awareness of innovative products/services among partners and beneficiaries
Greater ability by innovators to attract investment/funding (especially from the private sector)
Successful innovations tested and ready to scale
Partnerships brokered between humanitarian organisations, local communities, and the private sector
A wider innovation community built to support humanitarian innovations

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to fund and scale innovative solutions to improve humanitarian access in conflict-affected areas, focusing on water/sanitation, energy, life-saving information, and health. It combines financing, technical assistance, and partnership brokering to enable sustainable and scalable innovations.

quote.objectives: "Through this initiative we expect to identify and scale a series of innovative solutions that apply new insights, resources, technologies or approaches and to increase survival or improve lives of the most vulnerable people in the hardest-to-reach areas of need in humanitarian crises." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section B: Expected Results)
quote.outputs: "Around 15 seed grants (up to £200,000) to develop and test promising innovations, and around 2 scaling grants or other forms of finance (up to £600k) to support innovations that can prove their concept works to reach scale" (Document: 48455259.odt, Section B: Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in conflict-affected and fragile states, where humanitarian access is severely constrained by violence, insecurity, and physical/social barriers. The overall programme risk rating is 'moderate,' but the operating environment is high-risk due to conflict and humanitarian crises.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 48455259.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The humanitarian system is under unprecedented strain. Crises are increasing in frequency and magnitude and, in many countries, violence and insecurity continue to cause massive internal and cross-border displacement." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section A: Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks (e.g., threats to humanitarian workers, blockades) and damaged infrastructure (e.g., disrupted water/sanitation systems) limit access to affected populations. Political constraints and aid diversion further complicate delivery. Local agencies lack resources to manufacture goods or deliver assistance in besieged areas, and only 0.2% of humanitarian funding goes to local actors.

quote.constraints: "International aid agencies face huge challenges in delivering humanitarian aid in complex emergencies, due to damaged infrastructure, aid diversion, corruption, and threats of violence, as well as political constraints on access." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section A: Context)
quote.local_actors: "Local agencies are typically better placed to reach beneficiaries in insecure settings, but often lack specialised skills, technical capacity, or resources to manufacture goods, or cannot deliver goods to besieged communities despite their proximity due to violence or aid blockages." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section A: Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Grand Challenges Canada (based in Canada) manages the fund and selects innovators, with DFID and USAID providing oversight via a steering committee. Local actors (Southern partners) are innovators/implementers but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to innovators
advice on business models
innovation support (e.g., business model development, scaling strategies)
partnership brokering with private sector/humanitarian agencies

partner_organizations.name: Grand Challenges Canada (GCC)
partner_organizations.role: fund manager and administrator of the Humanitarian Grand Challenge

partner_organizations.name: USAID Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (matched DFID’s £5.5 million contribution)

partner_organizations.name: DFID (UK Government)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and steering committee member

partner_organizations.name: Innovators (private sector, non-profits, local communities)
partner_organizations.role: recipients of seed/scaling grants; developers/implementers of innovations

partner_organizations.name: Humanitarian agencies (e.g., ICRC, ODI)
partner_organizations.role: steering committee members; potential partners for innovators

partner_organizations.name: Private sector organizations
partner_organizations.role: potential partners for innovators; co-funders for scaling

quote.delivery_structure: "The Grand Challenges model is a partner-driven, open innovation approach to drive attention and resources to solving global problems by sourcing and accelerating high-potential solutions through open competition." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section D: Options Appraisal - Option 1)
quote.capacity_building: "Technical assistance provided to support innovators in testing innovations and working to scale" and "Partnerships brokered between humanitarian organisations, local communities and private sector to develop, test and implement innovations" (Document: 48455259.odt, Section B: Expected Results)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses competitive grants (seed and scaling) to fund innovators. Seed grants (up to £200k) support proof-of-concept testing, while scaling grants (up to £600k) support innovations ready for implementation at scale. Grants are awarded through open competition managed by Grand Challenges Canada.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Grand Challenges Canada (GCC) acts as the fund manager, administering grants and providing technical assistance. A steering committee (including DFID, USAID, ICRC, ODI) oversees the programme. Innovators apply competitively, and GCC brokers partnerships between humanitarian agencies, local communities, and the private sector.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The open competition model is used to source high-potential solutions globally, ensuring transparency and attracting diverse innovators (private sector, non-profits, local actors). GCC’s experience with similar challenges (e.g., Saving Lives at Birth) demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach.

quote.funding_instrument: "The programme will use two forms of grant awards: Seed funds: up to CAD$250,000 each [...] Transition to scale funding: up to CAD$1 million each to support the refinement, testing and implementation of innovative solutions that have already achieved ‘proof of concept’." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section D: Options Appraisal - Option 1)
quote.management_structure: "Grand Challenges Canada (GCC) will administer the fund, with DFID and USAID as key funders and steering committee members. Innovators will be competitively selected to receive funds and technical innovation support." (Document: 48455259.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The steering committee includes DFID, USAID, ICRC, ODI, and other humanitarian experts. It provides oversight and strategic direction but does not manage day-to-day operations (handled by GCC).

quote.governance: "DFID will sit on the Steering Committee, and the SRO will identify suitable people to take part in review and screening of proposals" (Document: 48455259.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.sub_awards: "Innovators (via Grand Challenges Canada), who could be from the private sector or non-profit organisations, will be competitively selected to receive funds and technical innovation support." (Document: 48455259.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between seed and scaling grants based on the pipeline of successful projects, but this requires approval. The exact number of scaling grants depends on the performance of seed projects.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in focus areas (e.g., water/sanitation, energy, health) based on emerging needs, but major changes would require steering committee approval. The open competition model inherently allows for adaptive responses to new challenges.

quote.reallocation: "The exact number of transition to scale grants will depend upon the pipeline of successful early stage/seed projects." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section B: Expected Results)
quote.adaptive_management: "The Grand Challenge will be launched in early 2018 (see options appraisal for further details), with funding for both early stage (up to 250,000 Canadian dollars) and transition to scale (up to $1m Canadian dollars) grants." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section C: The Grand Challenge)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Grand Challenges Canada (fund manager) → Innovators (end-implementers).

quote.management_costs: "In the first three years of the programme direct operational costs are on average around 10% of the total budget." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section D: Options Appraisal - Option 1)
quote.layers: "Grand Challenges Canada (GCC) will administer the fund [...] Innovators will be competitively selected to receive funds and technical innovation support." (Document: 48455259.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Fund the Humanitarian Grand Challenge (preferred option)
Set up an externally managed new innovations fund
Set up a funding window within an existing programme (e.g., Humanitarian Innovation Fund)
Do nothing (rely on existing programmes)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (Humanitarian Grand Challenge) was chosen because it maximizes potential to scale innovations, leverages private sector engagement, aligns with DFID’s humanitarian innovation commitments, and offers strong value for money. The existing platform (GCC) reduces setup costs and time, while the multi-donor approach (DFID + USAID) enhances coherence and crowding-in of additional funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of the humanitarian innovation ecosystem if DFID set up a competing fund (Options 2/3).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Chose Option 1 to avoid duplication and leverage GCC’s existing platform.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited private sector engagement in existing programmes (e.g., HIF).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Option 1 explicitly encourages private sector partnerships and business model development.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational risks in conflict-affected areas (e.g., security, aid diversion).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GCC has strong due diligence processes and DFID’s risk appetite allows for moderate-risk programmes in FCAS.

quote.rationale: "Option 1 – to fund the Humanitarian Grand Challenge through Grand Challenges Canada, is the preferred option. This option is therefore recommended for funding, as it best meets the above criteria and demonstrates the greatest potential to: Identify transformational approaches to humanitarian access challenges; Engage the private sector in developing and sustaining innovative solutions; Strengthen the international humanitarian innovation system; Deliver on DFID and UK priorities, and; Present good value for money for the UK taxpayer." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section D: Options Appraisal)
quote.vfm: "The MCDA allocated a score against 5 objective criteria across each of the options including: 1. Maximising potential to scale innovations; 2. Coherence with the wider international community; 3. Crowding in investment and commitment from the private sector; 4. Fit with UK commitments on humanitarian innovation; 5. Affordability and value for money for the taxpayer." (Document: 48455259.odt, Section D: Options Appraisal)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The conflict-affected and hard-to-reach contexts (WHERE) require partners with specialized skills in security, logistics, and local knowledge. This limits partner selection to organizations like GCC, which have experience managing innovation in FCAS and can broker partnerships with local actors/private sector despite access challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks limit the ability of international agencies to operate directly in besieged areas, necessitating local partnerships.
Weak infrastructure (e.g., disrupted water/sanitation systems) requires innovations that are adaptable to low-resource settings.
