It also mentions 'The support in FY23/24 is currently forecast at £1.825 million, consisting of £1.5 million from Trade for Development Department's (TfD) ODA allocation and £325,000 from British Investment Partnerships Department's (BIPD) ODA allocation.'

metadata.programme_name: Just Transitions for Water Security (JTWS)
metadata.duration_text: AMP Start Date: Jan 2023 (Design work) - AMP End Date: 30th Sept 2029

quote.text: "The Just Transitions for Water Security programme (JTWS) will support vulnerable people in developing countries to better adapt and build resilience to the impacts of climate change and nature loss through improved management and stewardship of water resources."

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: Jan 2023 (Design work) - AMP End Date: 30th Sept 2029" (D0006014.odt, Programme summary section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions for water governance), policy influence (integrating water security into national climate plans), implementation research (testing market-based approaches for water investment), and financing mechanisms (mobilizing private capital for water infrastructure). It focuses on systemic change through technical assistance rather than direct service delivery.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will address the governance and market failures outlined above to catalyse systemic changes that improve water security, building the climate resilience of communities and economies to water related shocks and stresses." (D0006014.odt, Challenges section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: National policies, plans, and institutional structures for climate-resilient water management
q3_expected_outputs.target: 5-10 countries with integrated water-climate strategies

q3_expected_outputs.output: Adoption of water security indices (e.g., Water InSecurity Experience Index - WISE)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Global community adoption (X number not specified)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Independent audits of supply chains against water stewardship standards
q3_expected_outputs.target: X audits in X supply chains (numbers TBD)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Additional finance mobilized for climate-resilient water management
q3_expected_outputs.target: Y GBP (amount TBD)

q3_expected_outputs.output: People with improved water security
q3_expected_outputs.target: 40 million vulnerable people (to be reviewed after Phase 1)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Technical Assistance (TA) outputs
q3_expected_outputs.target: Diagnostic tools, policy frameworks, and investment strategies developed

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform water governance systems in 5-10 lower-income countries by integrating climate resilience into national policies, strengthening institutional capacity, and mobilizing private investment through market-based incentives and technical assistance.

quote.text: "The programme will take to scale systems approaches that have been developed through catalytic UK ODA funding and key policy initiatives that aim to transform the governance of water security and create the market environments to mobilise large scale investments for water."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' in the document. This reflects the complex governance challenges and climate vulnerabilities in target countries, balanced by the programme's adaptive, country-led approach and focus on political economy analysis.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006014.odt, Programme summary section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions limit integrated water resource management (e.g., Rwanda's fragmented responsibilities across government). Climate risks exacerbate water scarcity (e.g., Pakistan's 2022 floods costing $15.2bn). Market failures disincentivize private investment (e.g., water sector responsible for 10% of global emissions but underpriced). Data limitations hinder evidence-based planning (e.g., lack of localized data for programme design).

quote.text: "Weak and fragmented governance is exacerbating the water crisis. Governments particularly in developing countries often lack capacity, tools, and finance to deliver the type of integrated water resource management that is needed to deliver water security in the context of a changing climate."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The document emphasizes country ownership and political will as selection criteria, but decision-making power within the consortium is not explicitly described. Technical Assistance (TA) is designed to build local capacity, suggesting a collaborative approach, but leadership roles are held by UK-based entities (e.g., FCDO, IIED).
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (e.g., Water Resources Boards)
training for government officials (e.g., climate-water risk integration into NAPs/NDCs)
stakeholder engagement mechanisms
Gender and Social Inclusion (GESI) mainstreaming
evidence-based strategic planning support

partner_organizations.name: IIED (International Institute for Environment and Development)
partner_organizations.role: Gender and Social Inclusion (GESI) workstream lead; MEL support

partner_organizations.name: AGWA (Alliance for Global Water Adaptation)
partner_organizations.role: Water Tracker diagnostic tool; technical assistance on climate-water integration

partner_organizations.name: Fair Water Footprint (FWF) Initiative
partner_organizations.role: Water stewardship standards and supply chain audits

partner_organizations.name: Resilient Water Accelerator
partner_organizations.role: Mobilizing investment for climate-resilient water infrastructure

partner_organizations.name: World Resources Institute (WRI)
partner_organizations.role: Evidence generation on water investment barriers

partner_organizations.name: Local government institutions
partner_organizations.role: Policy implementation and institutional reform (e.g., Water Resources Boards)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector partners
partner_organizations.role: Supply chain water stewardship (e.g., Nature’s Pride, SIFAV, UK food/drink companies)

quote.text: "TA is intended to build and facilitate lasting capacity and processes for country-based stakeholders to develop locally relevant evidence analysis, stakeholder engagement mechanisms and strategic planning."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme primarily uses Technical Assistance (TA) contracts for governance and policy work, combined with grants for catalytic initiatives (e.g., £75k to AGWA for KPI development). It also leverages existing platforms (e.g., Water Tracker, Fair Water Footprint) and aims to mobilize private finance through blended mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is delivered through a pre-selected consortium of partners (e.g., IIED, AGWA) with specialized roles, coordinated by FCDO. The structure includes three workstreams (Policy, Stewardship, Investment) managed collaboratively, with adaptive programming cycles (Evidence → Analysis → Engagement → Action).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on prior engagement during the Design and Build phase (e.g., AGWA, Fair Water Footprint) and their technical expertise in water governance, climate adaptation, and private sector engagement. The document highlights their proven track records in delivering similar initiatives (e.g., Water Tracker in 12 countries).

quote.text: "The proposed approach to delivery is through Technical Assistance (TA), rather than direct financial investment in water-related infrastructure. This is based on the assessment that TA can support improvements in governance that are essential to address the current water stewardship and market failures."

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Sub-awards for country-level activities are allocated through a collaborative process involving FCDO, the consortium lead, and local stakeholders, based on diagnostic results (e.g., Water Tracker assessments) and political economy analyses.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes a governance structure with a Steering Committee comprising FCDO representatives, consortium leads (e.g., IIED for GESI), and country government focal points. Decision-making is guided by adaptive management cycles and MEL frameworks.

quote.source: D0006014.odt, Monitoring Evaluation and Learning section
quote.text: "Monitoring Evaluation and Learning (MEL) will be embedded throughout the programme, with a focus on adaptive management. The programme will use an iterative learning cycle (Evidence → Analysis → Engagement → Action) to adjust strategies based on real-time data."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between workstreams (Policy, Stewardship, Investment) with FCDO approval, based on Phase 1 (18-24 months) evidence reviews. The programme’s adaptive management approach allows for adjustments to country focus and intervention design.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an explicit adaptive programming cycle: 1) Evidence building, 2) Analysis, 3) Engagement, 4) Action. Priorities are adjusted during Phase 1 based on diagnostic results (e.g., Water Tracker data) and stakeholder feedback, with FCDO sign-off required for major shifts.

quote.source: D0006014.odt, Phasing and Scale Up section
quote.text: "The target number [of beneficiaries] will be reviewed at the end of Phase 1 (18-24 months) based on evidence of what works and likely impact."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Consortium Lead (e.g., IIED/AGWA) → Local Implementing Partners (government institutions/private sector)

quote.text: "Programme Value: £39.1m" and "The proposed approach to delivery is through Technical Assistance (TA)... using a range of tools, instruments and platforms."

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct infrastructure investment (rejected due to governance failures)
Standalone research programmes (rejected for lack of systemic impact)
Bilateral country programmes (rejected for limited scalability)
Multilateral trust funds (complemented but not replaced due to need for country ownership)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The Technical Assistance (TA) consortium model was selected to address root causes of water insecurity—governance failures and market barriers—rather than symptoms. This approach leverages UK strengths in policy influence, private sector engagement, and adaptive learning, while aligning with the UK’s International Climate Finance (ICF) focus on transformational change. The direct award to pre-vetted partners (e.g., AGWA, IIED) ensures continuity from the Design phase and reduces transaction costs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on TA may limit direct infrastructure impact in water-scarce contexts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Complementary focus on mobilizing private investment (e.g., $1trn identified by WRI) and linking TA to tangible policy reforms (e.g., NDC integration).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented governance in target countries may hinder TA uptake.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Political economy analyses and cross-sectoral stakeholder engagement (e.g., Rwanda’s Water Resources Board model).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector engagement may prioritize commercial interests over equity.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GESI workstream (led by IIED) and stewardship standards (e.g., Fair Water Footprint) to ensure inclusive benefits.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing platforms like Water Tracker)

quote.source: D0006014.odt, Assessment criteria for the Appraisal Case section
quote.text: "The choice of technical assistance as an impact pathway is the direct result of learning from the previous, UK funded Water Security Programme (2012-2019)... TA can support improvements in governance that are essential to address the current water stewardship and market failures."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Contextual constraints (e.g., weak institutions, climate risks) directly shape partner selection. Countries must demonstrate political will, ODA eligibility, and vulnerability to water insecurity (e.g., Malawi’s flood/drought history). Supply chain connections (e.g., UK food companies’ external water footprints) also influence partner choices (e.g., Fair Water Footprint’s focus on Tanzania/Kenya/Ethiopia).
q27_constraints_detail: ODA eligibility limits country selection to LMICs.
Political will is a prerequisite (e.g., Rwanda’s Water Resources Board reform).
Climate vulnerability prioritizes countries like Bangladesh and Malawi.
Supply chain linkages target producer countries (e.g., Ethiopia for UK food imports).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s systemic objectives (governance + market + investment transformation) require a consortium structure with specialized workstreams (Policy, Stewardship, Investment). TA is chosen over direct delivery to address root causes (e.g., market failures in water pricing) rather than symptoms (e.g., building dams). Adaptive management cycles reflect the need for iterative learning in complex, climate-vulnerable contexts.
q28_linkages: Governance failures → Need for TA-focused consortium with policy expertise (e.g., AGWA for NDC integration).
Market barriers → Requirement for private sector engagement workstream (e.g., Fair Water Footprint).
Climate uncertainty → Adaptive programming cycles (Evidence → Action).
Scalability goals → Tiered country engagement (Tier 1 vs. Tier 2).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are noted between rapid scaling (efficiency) and inclusive governance (equity). For example: 1) The target of 40m beneficiaries may be revised downward if equity considerations (e.g., gender inclusion via IIED’s GESI workstream) slow implementation. 2) Private sector engagement risks prioritizing commercial water users over marginalized groups, mitigated by stewardship standards and MEL frameworks.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Phase 1 (18-24 months) allows for adaptive learning but delays full-scale rollout.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern partners (e.g., IIED) provide technical leadership while emphasizing country-led processes.
Cost vs. reach: TA model is cost-effective but requires complementary private investment to achieve infrastructure impacts.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Moderate’ risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., Phase 1 reviews) and adaptive management structures. High climate vulnerability in target countries necessitates real-time MEL adjustments, while governance fragility (e.g., fragmented institutions) requires embedded TA support.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: 1) Local governments lead policy implementation (e.g., Water Resources Boards) with TA support. 2) Private sector partners (e.g., Nature’s Pride) co-develop stewardship standards. 3) IIED’s GESI workstream ensures inclusion is embedded in all roles.

quote.text: "Our approach to engagement with countries... will be centred on political will, country ownership, addressing vulnerability and scope for scalability, with a strong emphasis on inclusion."

key_programme_risks: Governance fragmentation in target countries may limit policy uptake (e.g., cross-ministerial coordination gaps).
Climate shocks (floods/droughts) could disrupt implementation (e.g., Pakistan’s 2022 floods).
Private sector resistance to water pricing reforms (e.g., Costa Rica’s 4-year tariff negotiations).
Underinvestment in water infrastructure due to market failures (e.g., only 1% of climate finance for basic water services).
Data limitations may hinder evidence-based planning (e.g., lack of localized climate-water risk data).
Equity risks in benefit distribution (e.g., women/girls excluded from water access despite policy reforms).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Political economy analyses and cross-sectoral task forces (e.g., Rwanda’s Prime Minister-led Water Resources Board).
Adaptive programming cycles and climate-resilient infrastructure standards (e.g., AGWA’s Water Tracker).
Incentive structures (e.g., Payments for Ecosystem Services in Costa Rica) and stewardship standards (Fair Water Footprint).
Blended finance models and guarantees (e.g., World Bank’s Water Global Practice partnership).
Diagnostic tools (Water Tracker) and localized evidence-building in Phase 1.
GESI workstream (IIED) with targeted indicators and inclusive stakeholder engagement.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Pakistan’s 2022 floods ($15.2bn economic cost) highlight the need for shock-responsive programming.
Malawi’s experience with 16 floods/2 droughts since 2010 informs the focus on sub-national resilience.
India’s groundwater crisis (60% of aquifers critical by 2032) underscores the urgency of integrated water-energy-agriculture planning.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The UK’s Water Security Programme (2012-2019) initially claimed 23m direct beneficiaries but was reclassified as indirect after ICF indicator reviews, leading JTWS to adopt a ‘contribution’ (not ‘attribution’) approach to results. Lessons included: 1) TA is more effective than infrastructure for systemic change; 2) Country ownership is critical for sustainability; 3) Adaptive management must be explicit.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from direct beneficiary counting to systemic indicators (e.g., water security indices). 2) Embedded MEL and adaptive cycles (Phase 1 review). 3) Stronger focus on private sector leverage (e.g., $1trn WRI-identified capital). 4) Explicit GESI integration (IIED workstream).

quote.source: D0006014.odt, Risks and our approach to risk management section
quote.text: "The Programme Completion Report [for the 2012-2019 programme] recorded 23 million direct beneficiaries but this was reclassified as indirect beneficiaries after a review of the criteria for ICF indicators... This programme will take a ‘contribution’ approach to results."

co_funding_partners.partner: Private sector (e.g., Nature’s Pride, WRAP Water Roadmap)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize private capital for water infrastructure, with WRI estimating $1 trillion ready to invest if barriers are addressed. Initial leverage targets include Y GBP (amount TBD) in additional finance for climate-resilient water management.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on revenue expenditure (Technical Assistance, capacity building) with the goal of catalyzing capital investment (e.g., private sector finance for infrastructure) through systemic changes.

quote.text: "Programme Value: £39.1m" and "The World Resources Institute estimates that there is about $1 trillion of investment capital ready to invest in water if the barriers to started in 2 countries (WRI, 2020)."

metadata.programme_name: UK Action to support Developing Countries Fighting Corruption (UKACT)

quote.text: UKACT will reduce incentives for corrupt individuals in developing countries to use the UK to launder money; or for UK business and UK nationals or their agents to bribe in developing countries.

duration_source.text: Start Date: April 2020; End Date: March 2025

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening UK law enforcement's ability to tackle corruption linked to developing countries), implementation research (testing and scaling anti-corruption interventions), and service delivery (directly investigating and prosecuting corruption cases). It focuses on recovering stolen assets and prosecuting bribery involving UK entities in developing countries.

q1_source.text: This programme is focused on interventions in the UK to address impunity for corruption affecting developing countries and will provide support to law enforcement action between 2020 and 2025, to continue and scale-up existing work.
