what_objectives.summary: UKACT aims to reduce impunity for corruption affecting developing countries by strengthening UK law enforcement's capacity to investigate and prosecute money laundering and bribery cases linked to developing countries, recover stolen assets, and deter corrupt practices through a mix of enforcement, intelligence, and international coordination.

quote.text: The desired programme impact is that the culture of impunity for corruption is reduced in developing countries by the UK taking action to recover and return assets stolen from developing countries; and to pursuing companies and nationals who bribe in developing countries.
quote.source: 54291270.odt, Evidence, Assumptions and Theory of Change

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated as 'moderate risk' due to the complexity of cross-border corruption cases, the need to coordinate with multiple law enforcement agencies, and the political sensitivity of targeting high-profile individuals. However, the UK's stable legal and institutional environment mitigates some risks.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

q6_constraints_impact.weak_institutions: Developing countries often lack specialist expertise to investigate complex economic crimes, and their law enforcement systems may be corruptible or lack capacity. This necessitates UK-based investigations (e.g., "In many cases, the stolen funds are laundered in another country, often the UK.").
q6_constraints_impact.political_economy: Corrupt elites in developing countries may use political influence to avoid prosecution domestically, requiring international action (e.g., "their law enforcement systems are often weak and corruptible").
q6_constraints_impact.regulatory: The UK's financial and legal systems are exploited to launder corrupt funds, requiring complex cross-border legal coordination (e.g., "The proceeds of this corruption may then be used... to fund political parties or elections; or be sent to foreign bank accounts, trusts and other financial ‘vehicles’").
q6_constraints_impact.conflict: Some target countries are affected by conflict, where corruption exacerbates instability and domestic action is limited (e.g., "Some of the cases investigated under this programme are in states affected by conflict").
q6_constraints_impact.data_limitations: Digital forensics and intelligence gathering are resource-intensive due to the evolving nature of technology and the need for highly trained personnel (e.g., "this work is time-consuming, expensive and requires highly trained personnel").

quote.text: Developing countries face two principal challenges in this area. First, they often lack the specialist expertise required to investigate complex economic crimes... Second, their law enforcement systems are often weak and corruptible.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The NCA (UK-based) leads operational decisions, including case selection and investigation priorities, with DFID providing funding and strategic oversight. Developing country partners are primarily sources of referrals or recipients of capacity-building support (e.g., "The ICU has a wider remit to pursue cases relating to developing countries and has the flexibility to pursue new investigations where evidence emerges. However... ICU is operationally independent of DFID").

q10_capacity_building_details.activity: Mentoring law enforcement agencies from developing countries on grand corruption cases
Facilitating intelligence sharing on grand corruption between NCA and developing countries
Coordinating international initiatives (e.g., International Centre on Asset Recovery, World Bank Stolen Asset Recovery Centre)
Engaging with UK businesses to tackle bribery and corruption in developing countries
Training and workshops for UK private sector on AML and bribery risks

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (NCA)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer; hosts the International Corruption Unit (ICU) and Bribery, Corruption and Intelligence Unit (BCIU); conducts investigations and intelligence work

partner_organizations.name: Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)
partner_organizations.role: Prosecutes cases developed by ICU; handles asset recovery via the Proceeds of Crime Unit (POCU)

partner_organizations.name: UK Central Authority (UKCA) in the Home Office
partner_organizations.role: Processes mutual legal assistance requests; supports developing countries to use international/UK systems

partner_organizations.name: Serious Fraud Office (SFO)
partner_organizations.role: Receives referrals for complex cases; complements ICU work

partner_organizations.name: Metropolitan Police Service (MPS)
partner_organizations.role: Legacy cases; previously focused on money laundering

partner_organizations.name: City of London Police (COLP)
partner_organizations.role: Legacy cases; previously focused on overseas bribery

partner_organizations.name: Developing country law enforcement agencies
partner_organizations.role: Sources of referrals, intelligence, and mutual legal assistance requests; recipients of capacity-building

partner_organizations.name: International Anti-Corruption Coordination Centre (IACCC)
partner_organizations.role: Coordinates cross-border cases (e.g., Nigeria-UAE); complements ICU work

partner_organizations.name: National Economic Crime Centre (NECC)
partner_organizations.role: New HMG hub for economic crime; expected to synergize with ICU

partner_organizations.name: Africa International Liaison Network (ILOs)
partner_organizations.role: Provides intelligence and operational support in Africa; funded by DFID

quote.text: The main delivery partner is the International Corruption Unit (ICU) at the National Crime Agency (NCA), with some support being given to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and the UK Central Authority (UKCA) in the Home Office.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides block funding to the NCA, CPS, and UKCA to support dedicated teams (ICU, BCIU, POCU) working on corruption cases linked to developing countries. Funds are ring-fenced for ODA-eligible cases and managed through annual agreements with break clauses for flexibility.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is implemented through three UK government partners (NCA, CPS, UKCA), each managing distinct but coordinated functions: investigations (ICU), prosecutions (CPS), and mutual legal assistance (UKCA). DFID’s Governance, Open Societies and Anti-Corruption (GOSAC) team oversees the programme.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The NCA, CPS, and UKCA were selected due to their statutory roles in UK law enforcement and existing expertise in economic crime. The ICU was established in 2015 by merging two DFID-funded police teams (MPS and COLP), consolidating a long-standing relationship (since 2006).

quote.text: This programme will be implemented by two HMG partners with whom DFID has an established relationship on delivery of UKACT – CPS and NCA. DFID has tested mechanisms for effective delivery and achieving value for money.
quote.source: 54291270.odt, Value for Money of the Preferred Option

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DFID (now FCDO) provides strategic oversight and funding but does not interfere in operational decisions, which are led by the NCA/ICU. Annual reviews and a mid-term review (2023) are planned, with break clauses to adjust commitments based on performance.

quote.text: Funding agreements with partners will include break clauses to allow DFID to scale up or down commitments to respond to context and performance, especially following a mid-term review of the programme in 2023.
quote.source: 54291270.odt, Isthere sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust...

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., ICU, BCIU, CPS) with DFID approval, using break clauses in funding agreements. However, operational independence of law enforcement limits DFID’s control over case selection.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities based on emerging evidence (e.g., new intelligence on suspicious transactions) or changes in context (e.g., new government priorities in Pakistan). The mid-term review (2023) will assess performance and context to inform adjustments.

quote.text: The ICU has a wider remit to pursue cases relating to developing countries and has the flexibility to pursue new investigations where evidence emerges. However... ICU is operationally independent of DFID and within its remit, decides which cases to pursue based on the viability of the evidence.
quote.source: 54291270.odt, Isthere sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust...

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → NCA/CPS/UKCA (implementers). No sub-grantees are mentioned; all delivery is through HMG partners.

quote.text: Funding agreements with partners will include break clauses to allow DFID to scale up or down commitments...
quote.source: 54291270.odt, Isthere sufficient flexibility to learn and adjust...

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: Continue support at current level (£5m/year) with minor consolidation
Option 2 (Preferred): Increase support to £8.1m/year to deliver wider outputs

q24_alternatives_considered.reason: Would end the UK’s capability to recover stolen assets and tackle UK bribery in developing countries.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Cost recovery from asset recovery cases
q24_alternatives_considered.reason: Would counter the objective of returning maximum assets to developing countries and is unpredictable.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Funding from other HMG departments (e.g., Home Office, FCO)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason: Unlikely to be available in the next 2-3 years; existing funds are allocated to the National Economic Crime Centre (NECC).

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Cross-HMG funds (e.g., Prosperity Fund, Conflict Stabilisation and Security Fund)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason: No decision yet on extension beyond 2021; unclear if aligned with programme needs.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 was chosen because it enables a significant scale-up of investigations (5 additional cases/year), intelligence packages (30% increase), and asset recovery (extra £50m/year), while maintaining the programme’s track record of high impact. The 2018 Evaluation showed that increased enforcement volume and high-profile cases have a deterrent effect on corrupt individuals and companies. The option also aligns with HMG’s strategic priorities (UK Anti-Corruption Strategy, Illicit Financial Flows Strategy) and leverages synergies with new initiatives like the NECC and IACCC.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (historical return of £114 restrained per £1 spent)
risk mitigation (operational independence of ICU ensures integrity)
past experience (programme operational since 2006 with consistent results)
partner capacity (NCA/ICU has demonstrated expertise in complex cases)
speed (Option 2 allows faster response to emerging opportunities, e.g., Pakistan’s new government priorities)
flexibility (break clauses and mid-term review enable adjustments)
equity (focus on poorest and most fragile developing countries)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Competition for skilled investigators: The NCA may struggle to recruit sufficient staff for the ICU due to competition with other HMG economic crime initiatives (e.g., NECC).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased scale-up and flexibility in team structure (e.g., adding staff to existing teams rather than creating new teams).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational independence vs. DFID objectives: ICU’s autonomy in case selection may lead to misalignment with DFID’s poverty reduction focus.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ring-fencing funds for ODA-eligible cases and regular performance reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Unpredictable income from asset recovery: Cost recovery is not viable due to unpredictability and conflict with programme objectives.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Reliance on DFID block funding with break clauses for flexibility.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other HMG initiatives: Potential duplication or gaps in coordination with NECC, IACCC, and IFFS.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of labor (e.g., UKACT focuses on UK-locus cases; IFFS on non-UK cases) and leveraging NECC for coordination.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per case and asset recovered)
effectiveness (deterrence effect on corrupt actors and recovery of assets)
equity (focus on poorest and most fragile countries)

quote.text: Option Two is the preferred option. It gives the teams under UKACT the additional resources they need to increase the volume of criminal and civil cases against corrupt individuals and companies. The demonstration effect of both volume and high impact cases, was shown in the 2018 Evaluation to have a deterrent effect on corrupt individuals and companies using the UK to launder money from developing countries.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on developing countries—many of which are fragile, conflict-affected, or have weak institutions—constrains partner selection to UK-based law enforcement agencies (NCA, CPS, UKCA) with the expertise and legal authority to handle complex cross-border cases. Developing country partners are limited to providing referrals, intelligence, or mutual legal assistance due to their lack of capacity to investigate grand corruption domestically (e.g., "Developing countries... often lack the specialist expertise required to investigate complex economic crimes").
q27_constraints_detail: Weak institutions in developing countries necessitate UK-led investigations.
Political sensitivity of targeting elites in developing countries requires operational independence (e.g., ICU’s autonomy).
Legal and financial systems in the UK (e.g., UWOs, Criminal Finances Act 2017) shape the delivery structure around UK agencies.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—recovering stolen assets, prosecuting bribery, and deterring corruption—require a delivery structure centered on UK law enforcement (NCA/ICU) due to: (1) the need for legal authority to investigate and prosecute cross-border cases; (2) the complexity of digital forensics and intelligence work; and (3) the requirement for mutual legal assistance to coordinate with developing countries. The mixed approach (investigations + intelligence + prosecutions) is reflected in the partnership with NCA (ICU/BCIU), CPS (POCU), and UKCA.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Dedicated ICU teams + CPS POCU + UWO specialists (CRT) to freeze and confiscate assets.
ICU investigations → CPS prosecutions → UKCA mutual legal assistance.
BCIU intelligence packages → ICU cases → outreach to UK businesses.
ICU engagement with IACCC, NECC, and developing country agencies.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritizes equity (focusing on poorest and most fragile countries) over efficiency in some areas: (1) Ring-fencing funds for ODA-eligible cases may reduce the volume of cases handled compared to a purely efficiency-driven approach; (2) Cost recovery from asset recovery is avoided to maximize returns to developing countries, despite potential to offset programme costs; (3) The operational independence of ICU may lead to cases that are not the most cost-effective but are high-impact for deterrence.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Focus on poorest countries (e.g., Nigeria, Pakistan) may limit the number of cases pursued compared to higher-income countries with stronger evidence.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Maximizing asset returns vs. cost recovery
q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: The programme prioritizes returning assets to developing countries over recovering costs, which could have funded additional cases.
Operational independence of ICU ensures integrity but may slow alignment with DFID’s strategic priorities (e.g., poverty reduction).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., complexity of cases, political sensitivity) justifies annual reviews and a mid-term review, rather than lighter-touch oversight. The need to coordinate with multiple HMG and international partners (e.g., NECC, IACCC) also increases management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme (e.g., mentoring developing country agencies, intelligence sharing) but is secondary to the core objective of UK-based enforcement. Southern partners’ roles are constrained by their limited capacity, leading to a Northern-led structure where UK agencies drive investigations and prosecutions.

quote.text: Without DFID funding and intervention, it is unlikely that cases from poorer, developing countries would secure adequate attention in the UK.

key_programme_risks: Insufficient staffing for ICU due to competition with other HMG economic crime initiatives (e.g., NECC).
Delays in cases due to complexity of cross-border investigations and mutual legal assistance.
Political interference or lack of cooperation from developing countries targeting elites.
Unpredictable asset recovery income, limiting cost recovery options.
Overlap or gaps with other HMG initiatives (e.g., IFFS, NECC).
Changes in UK or developing country political priorities affecting cooperation.
Legal challenges in prosecuting cases with evidence from fragile states.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased scale-up of teams (Option 2) and flexibility in team structure (e.g., adding staff to existing teams).
Increased digital forensics support and dedicated UKCA resources for mutual legal assistance.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of cooperation from developing countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Capacity-building for developing country agencies and strategic intelligence to identify high-risk jurisdictions.
Reliance on DFID block funding with break clauses; no cost recovery from asset recovery.
Clear division of labor (e.g., UKACT for UK-locus cases; IFFS for non-UK cases) and coordination via NECC.
Focus on cases with strong UK nexus and viable evidence; operational independence of ICU to prioritize viable cases.

fcas_specific_lessons: Cases from fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) require additional time and resources due to weak institutions and political instability (e.g., "In many cases, the stolen funds are laundered in another country, often the UK").
Mutual legal assistance is critical but challenging in FCAS due to limited capacity (e.g., UKCA support for preparing requests).
High-profile cases (e.g., James Ibori in Nigeria) demonstrate the deterrent effect of targeting grand corruption in FCAS, but require robust UK-led investigations.
Intelligence-sharing with FCAS partners must account for political risks (e.g., corruption within law enforcement).

lessons_from_previous.summary: The 2018 Evaluation highlighted the programme’s success in deterring corrupt PEPs (e.g., Nigerian elites) and UK companies from bribery, as well as its role in establishing the UK as a leader in anti-corruption enforcement. Key lessons include: (1) The importance of dedicated funding for developing country cases, which would otherwise be deprioritized; (2) The value of combining investigations, prosecutions, and asset recovery; (3) The need for flexibility to pursue emerging cases (e.g., suspicious activity reports).

examples.evidence: Without DFID support, corruption cases from developing countries—particularly the poorest and most fragile—are unlikely to be prioritized by UK law enforcement.
The UKACT programme has made the UK less attractive to corrupt PEPs as a place to launder money (e.g., Nigerian case study).
The merger of MPS and COLP teams into ICU in 2015 improved coordination and case volume.

examples.lesson: Flexibility to adapt to new tools
examples.evidence: The 2017 Criminal Finances Act (UWOs) created new opportunities for asset recovery, requiring programme adaptation.

design_changes_based_on_learning: Expansion of ICU teams (Option 2) to handle increased case referrals, particularly from fragile states (e.g., Pakistan).
Addition of a dedicated UWO team to exploit new civil recovery tools for grand corruption cases.
Enhanced digital forensics support to address the evolving complexity of financial crime.
Increased resources for mutual legal assistance (UKCA) to improve coordination with developing countries.
Stronger focus on intelligence-sharing (BCIU) to identify high-risk jurisdictions and sectors.

quote.text: The 2018 independent Evaluation of the programme and its case study of Nigeria, indicate that the UKACT programme has made the UK less attractive to corrupt politically exposed persons (PEPs), as a place to launder money.

co_funding_partners.role: Funds 10 of 50 ICU posts (20%) and provides infrastructure/overheads.
Partial funding for mutual legal assistance functions.

co_funding_partners.partner: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) - Prosperity Fund/Conflict Stabilisation and Security Fund
co_funding_partners.role: Potential future co-funding, but uncertain post-2021.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has leveraged additional HMG resources (e.g., NECC) and international coordination (e.g., IACCC) but does not report specific external funding mobilized. Historically, it has achieved a high return on investment (£114 restrained per £1 spent).

capital_vs_revenue_split.description: The budget is primarily revenue (salaries, operational costs) with minimal capital expenditure. Non-pay costs (e.g., travel, IT) are included but not separately reported as capital.
examples: £13.46m for NCA non-pay costs (e.g., digital forensics, travel).

quote.text: Option Two enables us to be flexible as to how and when that scale up happens... The size of the scale-up will depend on the NCA’s ability to recruit sufficient staff for the ICU, at a time when there is greater competition with the government scaling up the response to economic crime more widely.

metadata.programme_name: Invest Salone: Private Sector Development, Trade and Job Creation in Sierra Leone
metadata.quote: "Invest Salone is DFID Sierra Leone’s flagship private sector development programme. By catalysing investment in export sectors – agriculture, tourism, fisheries and manufacturing – Invest Salone will help Sierra Leone to realise the benefits of international trade, raising the incomes of 370,000 people by 2025." (39216545.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start: November 2018", "End: December 2025" (90000879.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Invest Salone combines financing mechanisms (matching firms with investors), market systems development (overcoming market failures), and business environment reform (policy influence) to catalyze private sector growth in Sierra Leone. The programme aims to create 370,000 jobs by 2025 through increased private investment in non-extractive tradable sectors.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Invest Salone is DFID Sierra Leone’s flagship private sector development programme. By catalysing investment in export sectors – agriculture, tourism, fisheries and manufacturing – Invest Salone will help Sierra Leone to realise the benefits of international trade, raising the incomes of 370,000 people by 2025." (39216545.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 370,000 people with higher incomes or new jobs by 2025
Firms better able to trade, compete, and grow due to a fairer business environment and more efficient market systems
Increased labour value and productivity
Increased market linkages
Increased firm productivity and diversification
Regulatory and institutional strengthening
Increased government accountability
Poor people integrated into formal markets
Increased global competitiveness
Reduced cost of trading and doing business
what_objectives.summary: Invest Salone aims to transform Sierra Leone's private sector by addressing binding constraints to growth, including a risky business environment and small domestic market, through a combination of business environment reform and market systems development.
what_objectives.quote: "Invest Salone’s impact statement is: 370,000 people will have higher incomes or new jobs due to increased private investment in Sierra Leone’s non-extractive tradable sector." (39216545.odt, Impacts and outcome that we expect to achieve)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sierra Leone is categorized as having a moderate risk profile due to its fragile state, weak institutions, and challenging business environment, but with potential for growth given recent political changes and natural resources.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (39216545.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The risky business environment (ranked 160/190 in Doing Business) and weak institutions deter investment and limit firm growth. Poor infrastructure (90% lack electricity, 50% of roads impassable in rainy season) and a severe skills deficit (57% illiteracy) further constrain private sector development.
where_context.quote: "Sierra Leone’s business environment is defined by weak institutions that are vulnerable to capture by entrenched interests... This results in high business risk, deterring new investment and preventing diversified, job creating growth." (39216545.odt, Risky business environment)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO retains oversight and approval authority over all interventions, with a UK-based Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) managing the programme. The supplier (likely a Northern-led consortium) implements interventions with local partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to firms
support to government institutions (e.g., EPA reform)
training for private sector actors
institutional strengthening (e.g., business associations)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Sierra Leone (Ministries and Agencies)
partner_organizations.role: implementation partner (e.g., Ministry for Trade, Port Authority, Environmental Protection Agency)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector firms (domestic and international)
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries and partners (e.g., cocoa traders, rice processors, supermarkets)

partner_organizations.name: Investors (CDC, AgDevCo, IFC, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: co-financiers and investment partners

partner_organizations.name: Associations (e.g., artisanal fishers, cocoa cooperatives)
partner_organizations.role: local partners for market integration

partner_organizations.name: Supplier (lead contractor, likely a consortium)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer of programme activities

partner_organizations.name: Trade and Relationships Adviser (DFID-funded post)
partner_organizations.role: embedded advisor to facilitate UK objectives and investment linkages

who_partners.quote: "Invest Salone will be implemented by a service provider under a competitively tendered contract... The supplier’s responsibilities will include implementing the programme’s strategy, managing the intervention portfolio, designing new interventions, coordinating downstream partners and managing the programme’s risks." (39216545.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Invest Salone will be delivered through a competitively tendered contract with a lead supplier (likely a consortium), managed by DFID/FCDO. The contract includes payment-by-results mechanisms and break-points for flexibility and accountability.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A lead supplier (contractor) manages the programme under DFID/FCDO oversight, with flexibility to sub-contract specialists and partner with local firms, government agencies, and investors. The supplier is accountable for results and must adhere to DFID’s policies on subsidies and safeguarding.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: An Early Market Engagement (EME) workshop was held to attract diverse bidders, including large generalists and smaller specialists. The supplier must demonstrate expertise in fragile contexts, adaptive programming, and value for money.
how_mechanism.quote: "Invest Salone will be implemented by a service provider under a competitively tendered contract... An Early Market Engagement (EME) workshop held in April 2018 attracted 30 participants in London and Sierra Leone." (39216545.odt, Appraisal Case and Commercial Case)

how_governance.quote: "The supplier will provide DFID with monthly dashboards detailing the progress of the intervention portfolio and flagging any risks. The supplier will also draft an annual report with detailed results verified by the M&E function, which will inform DFID’s annual reviews... DFID will monitor intervention progress via (at least) fortnightly SRO meetings, (at least) quarterly field visits and published annual reviews." (39216545.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Flexibility is built into the programme design, with a six-month inception phase to design interventions and adaptive management to respond to new opportunities. However, reallocation requires DFID approval for new interventions and is guided by a governance framework.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses adaptive management to "fail fast" where necessary and scale up successful interventions. Political economy analysis and results monitoring inform adjustments, with flexibility underpinned by robust governance and risk management.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexibility will be informed by ongoing political economy analysis and robust results monitoring. This flexibility will also allow Invest Salone to quickly and effectively respond to future UK priorities... Interventions will quickly respond to new information, scaling up where we have success and ‘failing fast’ where necessary." (39216545.odt, Intervention Summary and Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Supplier (lead contractor) → Sub-contractors/Partners (firms, government, investors)
how_efficiency.quote: "Expenses and overheads: £3.1m (10%)" (39216545.odt, Financial Case); "Payment by Results. To ensure the supplier is incentivised to deliver value for money throughout the programme, a payment by results mechanism will be agreed in the contract." (39216545.odt, Commercial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (Option 1)
Support self-employed entrepreneurs through a livelihoods approach (Option 2)
Overcome market failures through a market systems development approach (Option 3)
Business environment reform through support to government (Option 4)
Combined market systems development and business environment reform (Option 5, preferred)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 (combined approach) was chosen because it fully addresses the strategic case needs by tackling both market failures and the business environment, aligning with UK objectives (Africa Strategy, Economic Development Strategy), and leveraging lessons from past programmes. The combined approach is expected to deliver higher impact (370,000 jobs) and better value for money (£2+ return per £1 spent).
q25_decision_factors: lessons from past programmes (e.g., SOBA Project Completion Review)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier may lack flexibility to adapt to Sierra Leone’s complex political economy, leading to ineffective interventions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adaptive programming with ongoing political economy analysis, robust results monitoring, and governance mechanisms (e.g., break-points, payment by results).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption and patronage could undermine reforms and market development.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Comprehensive due diligence, supply chain mapping, and safeguarding procedures to manage fiduciary and reputational risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap or conflict with government priorities could limit impact.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with the new government (post-2018 elections) and alignment with their economic diversification agenda.

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option is Option 5... This option fully addresses the needs in the strategic case. By tackling market failures, this option will incentivise firms to invest in job-creating growth. By reducing the cost of doing business, these firms will be more competitive in global markets, enabling them to trade and attract international investment." (39216545.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile context of Sierra Leone (weak institutions, corruption, and limited capacity) constrains partner selection to organizations with proven experience in similar environments. Local partners must be vetted for fiduciary risks, and international suppliers must demonstrate adaptive programming skills.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak institutions require suppliers with strong government engagement capabilities.
Corruption risks necessitate robust due diligence and safeguarding procedures.
Limited local capacity means technical assistance and capacity building are embedded in the programme.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address both market failures (e.g., poor linkages, low productivity) and the business environment (e.g., regulatory barriers, corruption) determines the mixed delivery structure (combining market systems development and business environment reform). The complexity of the objectives requires a lead supplier with diverse expertise and flexibility to manage multiple interventions.
q28_linkages: Market systems development (e.g., linking farmers to buyers) requires private sector engagement → necessitates a supplier with commercial acumen.
Business environment reform (e.g., EPA, port reforms) requires government collaboration → necessitates a supplier with political economy expertise.
Flexibility to adapt to context → requires an adaptive management structure with embedded M&E.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., gender and disability inclusion, support to informal firms) with efficiency (e.g., focusing on tradable sectors with high growth potential). For example, interventions must demonstrate systemic impact (not just individual firm benefits) but are also required to collect disaggregated data to ensure no harm to marginalized groups.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid job creation targets (370,000 by 2025) may conflict with deep inclusion of women and disabled individuals.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led suppliers provide technical expertise, but local ownership is fostered through capacity building and government engagement.
Cost vs. reach: Payment-by-results incentivizes efficiency but may limit risk-taking in fragile markets.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (FCAS context) justifies intensive oversight (e.g., monthly dashboards, quarterly field visits) and adaptive management to mitigate political and fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme to strengthen local partners (e.g., government institutions, private firms) and enable them to take on greater roles over time, reducing dependency on Northern expertise.
intersections.quote: "We will use DFID’s comparative advantage in political economy analysis and adaptive programming to deliver a flexible portfolio that evolves as the context changes and new opportunities arise." (39216545.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Political instability or changes in government priorities could disrupt reforms.
Corruption and patronage may undermine business environment improvements.
Weak institutions could limit the enforcement of reforms.
Market failures (e.g., coordination failures, information gaps) may persist despite interventions.
Limited skills and infrastructure could constrain private sector growth.
Reputational risks from partnering with firms or government agencies with poor safeguarding.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political instability or changes in government priorities.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Align with government’s economic diversification agenda and leverage the post-election window of opportunity for reform. Use adaptive programming to respond to political changes.
Comprehensive due diligence, supply chain mapping, and safeguarding procedures. Focus on reforms with political will (e.g., new EPA Chairman).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Weak institutions limiting enforcement of reforms.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Target institutions with demonstrated capacity and political will. Provide technical assistance to strengthen implementation.
Use a spectrum of tools (e.g., brokering linkages, technical assistance) and adaptive management to address emerging constraints.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited skills and infrastructure constraining growth.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Leverage complementary DFID programmes addressing skills (e.g., World Bank Skills Development Fund) and infrastructure (e.g., energy, roads).
Comprehensive due diligence on all partners, including assessments of financial systems, ownership structures, and links to Politically Exposed People.

fcas_specific_lessons: Interventions must adapt to complex political economy dynamics; rigid programmes fail in FCAS contexts (e.g., Sierra Leone).
Flexible, adaptive programming is critical to respond to shocks (e.g., Ebola, political transitions).
Local ownership and capacity building are essential to sustain reforms in fragile institutions.
Payment-by-results can incentivize efficiency but must be balanced with risk-sharing in unstable environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s previous private sector programme (SOBA) highlighted that: (1) transformational results take time in thin markets, and (2) combining market development with business environment interventions yields better results. Invest Salone builds on this by integrating both approaches and allowing flexibility to adapt.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme includes a six-month inception phase to design interventions based on live context analysis, unlike the previous programme. It also embeds adaptive management and political economy analysis to respond to lessons about the need for flexibility in Sierra Leone.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID Sierra Leone’s previous private sector development programme performed well... The two key lessons learnt were that: (1) transformational results take time given Sierra Leone’s extremely thin markets and (2) results are best achieved when market development interventions are combined with business environment interventions." (39216545.odt, Rationale for intervention)

co_funding_partners.partner: Private sector investors (e.g., CDC, AgDevCo, IFC)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to crowd in private sector investment through mechanisms like the Flexible Facility (matching grants/guarantees) and Prosper Salone (risk-sharing with impact investors). For example, a Prosper grant leveraged £400,000 for an organic cocoa business to upgrade machinery.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme initially used only Resource DEL (RDEL), but the addendum recognizes £10m (33%) as Capital DEL (CDEL) for activities supporting capital asset creation (e.g., grants for machinery, green finance).
financial_details.quote: "The total budget of the Business Case is not increasing, FCDO expects roughly £10m of the existing programme budget to be spend on CDEL going forward... This is needed as the Business Case’s Financial Case is only stipulating use of RDEL, although the programme is undertaking activities that have created capital assets." (90000879.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: UK Trade Partnerships (UKTP) Programme
metadata.quote: The purpose of the programme is to maximise the benefits of preferential UK market access, which directly contributes towards fulfilling the UK’s development cooperation commitments in EPAs. UKTP supports this purpose by focusing on the international trade environment and export promotion in each country. (D0007216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: 01.04.2018 to 31.03.2024; New project end date: 31.03.2026 (D0007216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The UKTP programme combines capacity building (strengthening SMEs' export capabilities), service delivery (direct technical assistance to firms), and implementation research (testing new approaches for trade promotion). It focuses on increasing trade with developing countries through preferential trading arrangements, aiming for economic growth and job creation.
what_objectives.q1_source: The purpose of the programme is to maximise the benefits of preferential UK market access, which directly contributes towards fulfilling the UK’s development cooperation commitments in EPAs. UKTP supports this purpose by focusing on the international trade environment and export promotion in each country. (D0007216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 14,046 jobs created, maintained, or improved (including 9,126 for women employees)
£64 million ($80 million) worth of exports by SMEs directly supported
4,414 business contacts established for 137 beneficiary enterprises
931 MSMEs supported with advisory services (338 women business enterprises)
458 MSMEs improved business practices and operational performance (170 women-led)
Support to further establish buyer trust in SMEs to help realise business deals in the UK
Enable SMEs to obtain additional certifications tailored to UK buyers
Facilitate institutional reforms in Cambodia, Sri Lanka, and the Pacific
what_objectives.summary: UKTP aims to increase trade with developing countries through preferential trading arrangements, focusing on export promotion and capacity building for SMEs to achieve economic growth and job creation.
what_objectives.quote: The purpose of the programme is to maximise the benefits of preferential UK market access, which directly contributes towards fulfilling the UK’s development cooperation commitments in EPAs. UKTP supports this purpose by focusing on the international trade environment and export promotion in each country. (D0007216.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

countries_regions: Africa: Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Ethiopia, DRC, Egypt, Senegal, Zambia, Mozambique
South Asia: India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a diverse set of developing countries with varying levels of institutional capacity and market access challenges, but no explicit high-risk or FCAS context is mentioned.
where_context.q5_source: Risk is assessed as moderate. This is consistent with DFID’s risk appetite. (D0007141.odt, Overall programme risk rating)
q6_contextual_constraints: limited ability to meet quality standards
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints such as weak institutions, regulatory barriers, and logistical challenges limit the ability of firms to export effectively. For example, the inability to meet quality standards and administrative hurdles reduce the competitiveness of SMEs in UK/EU markets.
where_context.quote: The inability to use this information reflects: a lack of export diversification in many partner countries; low volumes of production; lack of supply chain integration and linkages with UK/EU firms; inability of firms to meet quality standards; as well as the limited ability of firms to comply with the administrative processes associated with exporting using EPA preferences. (D0007141.odt, The inability to use this information reflects)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by FCDO (UK) with technical assistance delivered by ITC (multilateral), indicating Northern-led decision-making with Southern implementation support.
q10_capacity_building_details: tailored training and coaching
improving product quality, marketing, branding, and packaging
support to make links with potential buyers
EPA and DCTS awareness-raising
trade data updates
embedding ITC Market Access Tools (MAT)
digital transformation for business support organizations (BSOs)

partner_organizations.name: International Trade Centre (ITC)
partner_organizations.role: main delivery partner, technical assistance provider

partner_organizations.name: SheTrades Commonwealth
partner_organizations.role: gender mainstreaming and women's empowerment support

partner_organizations.name: Trade and Investment Advocacy Fund (TAF2+)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance for EPA rollover

partner_organizations.name: CARICOM Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: regional support for Caribbean EPA implementation

partner_organizations.name: UK Processing and Packaging Machinery Association
partner_organizations.role: trade show participation for packaging solutions

who_partners.quote: The International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint body of the UN and the WTO, as a provider of technical assistance in both programmes, continually draws lessons from SheTrades for UKTP’s approach to making sure that women as well as men in developing countries benefit from better opportunities. (D0007216.odt, approach to implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of ODA funding from FCDO and potential non-ODA funding for non-eligible objectives. Funds are allocated through agreed work plans and revised log frames.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is delivered through the International Trade Centre (ITC) as the main implementer, with technical support from other partners like SheTrades Commonwealth and TAF2+ for specific components.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ITC was selected based on its proven expertise in trade-related technical assistance and existing partnerships with DFID/FCDO. The rationale emphasizes ITC's experience in delivering similar programmes and its ability to leverage networks across multiple countries.
how_mechanism.quote: The International Trade Centre (ITC) is a UN and WTO agency mandated to work with both the public and private sectors and is very experienced in delivering trade-related technical assistance, including in key DFID priority countries. (D0007141.odt, Components 2 and 3 – International Trade Centre)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by DFID/FCDO with support from technical advisers and country offices. A steering group includes DIT staff for coordination, and country-level decisions are made in collaboration with local stakeholders.
how_governance.quote: DFID’s Trade for Development team manages a number of aid for trade programmes and has the appropriate resources to manage this programme. TFD’s A2 Private Sector Development Adviser will be the programme’s SRO, supported by a programme manager and a range of advisers. (D0007141.odt, DoestheSROandteamhavethecapabilityandresourcestodeliverthisprogramme?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, as evidenced by the extension and inclusion of DCTS countries, but specific processes are not detailed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has an adaptive approach, allowing adjustments based on learning and context changes, such as the inclusion of DCTS countries and testing new approaches for the Trade Centre of Expertise (COE) model.
how_flexibility.quote: The extension to the UKTP programme and inclusion of the DCTS countries will be delivered through agreed work plans. The log frame will be revised to include the additional countries and trade facilitation ambitions. (D0007216.odt, approach to implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ITC (implementer) → SMEs/beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: The overall value of the programme will change from £20 million to £29 million. (D0007216.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1 – Do nothing
Option 2 – EPA Implementation (technical assistance only)
Option 3 – EPA implementation with communications
Option 4 – EPA implementation with communications and export promotion (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (Option 4) was chosen because it addresses the full range of needs: ensuring continuity in trade agreements, improving awareness of EPA preferences, and directly increasing export flows through pilot export promotion projects. This option provides the best value for money by combining technical assistance, communications, and hands-on export support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential to undermine other EPA countries not in the pilot
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will monitor and assess impacts to determine if wider rollout is warranted, ensuring benefits are balanced across regions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited sustainability of benefits without long-term institutional support
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on digital transformation and capacity building for Business Support Organizations (BSOs) to ensure lasting impact.

why_rationale.quote: The preferred option is Option 4. (D0007141.odt, Option 4 – EPA implementation with communications and export promotion)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The geographic scope (multi-country, diverse developing contexts) requires a partner like ITC with global reach and experience in navigating varied institutional and market environments. Local constraints such as weak institutions and regulatory barriers necessitate adaptable partners capable of tailored technical assistance.
q27_constraints_detail: diverse institutional capacities across countries
regulatory and logistical barriers to trade
need for partners with multi-country experience
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's focus on export promotion and capacity building for SMEs requires a delivery structure that combines technical expertise (ITC) with local market knowledge (country offices, BSOs). The need for both broad reach (multi-country) and deep impact (SME-level support) shapes the mixed delivery structure.
q28_linkages: export promotion objectives → need for ITC's technical assistance and trade fair organization
capacity building for SMEs → requirement for embedded training and advisory services
geographic expansion → necessity for a partner with multi-country operational capability
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses balancing efficiency (rapid delivery through ITC's existing networks) with equity (ensuring women-led businesses and smaller SMEs benefit). For example, SheTrades Commonwealth integration addresses gender equity, while ITC's efficiency ensures broad reach.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of delivery (ITC's experience) vs. inclusive reach (support for women-led SMEs)
cost efficiency (centralized technical assistance) vs. localized impact (country-specific adaptations)
Northern expertise (ITC, FCDO) vs. Southern ownership (capacity building for BSOs)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to a milestone-based oversight approach, with regular monitoring to address challenges like weak institutions and market access barriers. Adaptive management is emphasized to respond to context changes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: ITC provides technical training, SheTrades focuses on gender mainstreaming, and TAF2+ supports institutional strengthening for EPA implementation. This ensures partners contribute to both immediate delivery and long-term sustainability.
intersections.quote: The programme will continue to work with sector organisations and beneficiaries in target countries to encourage them to adopt business practices that yield trade benefits. (D0007216.odt, approach to implementation)

key_programme_risks: Discontinuity in trade agreements post-Brexit
Limited private sector awareness of EPA preferences
Inability of firms to meet quality standards for UK/EU markets
Weak institutions in partner countries
Logistical and supply chain constraints
Potential to undermine non-pilot EPA countries
Sustainability of benefits post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance for EPA rollover and communications campaigns to ensure continuity.
Targeted communications and export promotion activities to increase understanding of EPA preferences.
Capacity building on product quality, packaging, and certification requirements.
Support for Business Support Organizations (BSOs) and digital transformation to strengthen institutional capacity.
Trade fair participation and linkage with UK suppliers for packaging and equipment solutions.
Monitoring and potential wider rollout based on pilot success.
Focus on self-sustaining platforms and institutional reforms.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Learning from SheTrades Commonwealth highlighted the need for gender-inclusive support systems. Experience showed that awareness-raising alone (Output 1) is insufficient without market linkages (Output 5). Digital transformation was adopted for BSOs based on their varying capabilities.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Inclusion of DCTS countries in FY23/24, greater focus on market linkages (Output 5) over just awareness-raising, adoption of digital transformation for BSOs, and integration of SheTrades lessons for gender mainstreaming.
risks_lessons.quote: Experience has shown that output 1 was not sufficient to deliver additional trade unless market linkages are established under output 5. (D0007216.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme attracts additional geographically earmarked ODA allocations from Posts in priority countries, e.g., at least £1 million from SEAPD.
financial_details.quote: The overall value of the programme will change from £20 million to £29 million. The support from Trade for Development Department’s (TfD) FY24/25 ODA allocation is estimated to be approximately £6 million. (D0007216.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: What Works to Prevent Violence: Impact at Scale
metadata.quote: The What Works to Prevent Violence: Impact at Scale Programme (‘WhatWorksII’) is the first global effort to systematically design, implement and rigorously evaluate the scale-up of proven violence prevention approaches. (D0004264.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: 13/02/2019 to 31/08/2027; New project end date (if applicable): 31 August 2029 (D0004264.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research to identify what works in preventing violence), implementation research (testing and scaling up proven interventions), capacity building (strengthening skills and knowledge among grantees and governments), and policy influence (using evidence to drive global action). It is a comprehensive effort to translate research into large-scale programmes and strategies.
what_objectives.q1_source: Systematically design, implement and rigorously evaluate a range of approaches to scaling up violence prevention efforts, translating proof-of-concept evidence into robust, large-scale programmes and strategies; [...] Strengthen long-term capability and capacity to deliver cutting-edge, evidence-based violence prevention interventions across the programme’s grantees, FCDO, and developing country governments; [...] Use evidence to influence a more effective, scaled-up global response to end VAWG. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: A measurable reduction in violence in development and humanitarian contexts in which the programme operates, including for the most marginalised groups

An expanded global knowledge and evidence base on what works to prevent violence across development and humanitarian contexts, including for the most marginalised groups, and the most cost-effective approaches
A more effective, scaled-up global response to VAWG and VAC through the use of evidence to develop effective new and strengthened prevention strategies

Two research grants in LMICs to expand research on how Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV) affects women with disabilities, indigenous women; lesbian, bisexual, queer, and transgender women
Support for locally-led and LGBTQI+-led organizations to design and implement new GBV prevention approaches (innovation grants)
Production of evidence syntheses, policy briefs, practice briefs, and practical tools/guidance for practitioners on mental health and VAWG
Technical advice and capacity support to strengthen knowledge and skills for evidence-based VAWG prevention among programme grantees and FCDO
An Ending Violence Against Women and Children Helpdesk for FCDO and HMG to deliver demand-driven, bespoke advice and build capacity
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to systematically scale up proven violence prevention approaches while generating new evidence, building capacity, and influencing global policy. It focuses on translating research into large-scale programmes across sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East/North Africa, including conflict and humanitarian settings.
what_objectives.quote: The What Works to Prevent Violence: Impact at Scale Programme (‘WhatWorksII’) is the first global effort to systematically design, implement and rigorously evaluate the scale-up of proven violence prevention approaches. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in conflict and humanitarian settings, which inherently carry higher risks. However, the risk is assessed as moderate due to the programme's adaptive nature, robust systems, and technical assistance available to partners, particularly in conflict-affected contexts.
where_context.q5_source: Risk is assessed as moderate, reflecting the programme’s ambition and scale, the innovative nature of interventions, and the challenges of working with marginalised groups and in conflict-affected contexts. (D0003788.odt, Section 1: Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and humanitarian settings pose significant challenges for implementation, including security risks, weak institutional capacity, and limited data availability. These constraints affect the ability to deliver interventions consistently and to monitor and evaluate outcomes effectively.
where_context.quote: VAWG can dramatically increase in scale and severity in conflict and crisis. (D0003788.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is led by the IRC (international) in partnership with Southern-based organizations such as Raising Voices (regional women’s fund) and Breakthrough (Indian-based women’s rights organization). Decision-making involves both Northern and Southern partners, with technical advice and capacity support provided to strengthen Southern partners' skills and knowledge.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical advice and capacity support to strengthen knowledge and skills for evidence-based VAWG prevention among programme grantees and FCDO
capacity development to strengthen grantees’ knowledge and skills for evidence-based GBV prevention (innovation grants)
building the long-term capacity of other actors, including developing country governments

partner_organizations.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
partner_organizations.role: Consortium lead, overall programme management

partner_organizations.name: CARE International
partner_organizations.role: Consortium partner

partner_organizations.name: Raising Voices
partner_organizations.role: Regional women’s fund with grant-making experience

partner_organizations.name: Breakthrough
partner_organizations.role: Women’s rights organization

partner_organizations.name: Social Development Direct
partner_organizations.role: Previous provider of VAWG Helpdesk

partner_organizations.name: George Washington University (Global Women’s Institute)
partner_organizations.role: Research and Evaluation Consortium lead

partner_organizations.name: Sexual Violence Research Initiative (SVRI)
partner_organizations.role: Resource partner for research on TFGBV

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Co-financing partner

who_partners.quote: A £45.5m Consortium managed by FCDO’s Gender and Equalities Department (G&E) and led by the International Rescue Committee (IRC), in partnership with CARE International, Raising Voices, Breakthrough and Social Development Direct. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for the consortium and research components) and a Delegated Cooperation Agreement (a type of MOU) with USAID for co-financing. The agreement allows USAID to contribute funds that are managed through FCDO’s existing contracts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through three main contracts: a £45.5m consortium led by IRC for implementation, a £14.9m research consortium led by George Washington University, and a £1m independent evaluation. USAID funds are integrated into these contracts via a Delegated Cooperation Agreement.
how_mechanism.quote: The Programme will deliver this through three contracts: A £45.5m Consortium managed by FCDO’s Gender and Equalities Department (G&E) and led by the International Rescue Committee (IRC)... A £14.9m Research and Evaluation Consortium managed by FCDO’s Research and Evidence Division (RED)... A £1m G&E-managed Independent Evaluation. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: USAID participates in reviewing SVRI's Request for Proposal documentation and approving selected grantees for TFGBV research grants, indicating a joint decision-making process for sub-awards.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes annual meetings with all partners, quarterly management meetings with FCDO and lead suppliers, and national advisory boards in countries where USAID-funded grants are implemented. USAID also participates in these structures to facilitate learning and capacity development.
how_governance.quote: USAID will participate in key WhatWorksII meetings including the annual meeting of the programme, which brings together all programme partners including grantees, Independent Advisory Board, and quarterly management meetings with FCDO and the lead suppliers. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme has some flexibility to respond to emerging opportunities, with £7.5m of scale-up funds reserved for this purpose. However, reallocation between major components (e.g., research vs. implementation) likely requires approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is described as adaptive, using piloting, monitoring, and action research to refine interventions. Two cycles of innovation programming provide flexibility to respond to emerging opportunities, and additional grants may be made available depending on future-year funding.
how_flexibility.quote: This is an adaptive programme that will use piloting, monitoring, and action research to refine interventions to maximise impact and value. (D0003788.odt, Section 1: Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Consortium lead (IRC) → sub-grantees (e.g., Raising Voices, Breakthrough, local organizations). For research: FCDO → George Washington University → SVRI/other research partners.
how_efficiency.quote: Crown Agents Bank provides management, payment and reporting services to partner donors in relation to ‘Third Party Monies’. (D0004264.odt, INFORMATION)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The consortium model was chosen to leverage the complementary strengths of multiple organizations with specialized expertise in VAWG prevention, research, and capacity building. The inclusion of Southern partners (e.g., Raising Voices, Breakthrough) ensures local ownership and context-specific adaptation, while Northern partners (e.g., IRC, George Washington University) provide global technical leadership and research rigor. The Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID enables co-financing and shared learning without increasing UK funds.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging existing contracts and co-financing)
risk mitigation (robust systems and technical support for partners in high-risk contexts)
partner capacity (combining global expertise with local knowledge)
flexibility (adaptive programming to respond to emerging evidence)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing a multi-partner consortium across diverse contexts (e.g., conflict settings, multiple regions)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust management structures, including quarterly reviews, technical support for partners, and adaptive programming to refine interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between research and implementation components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Integrated governance structures (e.g., annual meetings, joint advisory boards) and clear division of roles between the G&E-managed consortium (implementation) and RED-managed consortium (research).

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (streamlined management through Crown Agents Bank for third-party funds)
equity (inclusive partnerships and focus on marginalized groups)
why_rationale.quote: The purpose of this Business Case Addendum is to formally recognise the partnership with USAID and enable additional future financial support from other donors. (D0003701.odt, INFORMATION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on conflict and humanitarian settings (WHERE) necessitates partnerships with organizations experienced in these contexts (WHO), such as the IRC and Raising Voices. Local partners are critical for navigating security risks, weak institutions, and cultural complexities in these environments.
q27_constraints_detail: conflict and humanitarian settings require partners with specialized expertise in security and adaptive programming
weak institutional capacity in target regions demands technical support and capacity building for local partners
data limitations in high-risk areas affect the choice of research partners (e.g., George Washington University for rigorous evaluations)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (WHAT)—combining research, implementation, and capacity building—require a consortium structure (HOW) to integrate diverse expertise. The need for both global evidence generation and local adaptation drives the equal partnership between Northern and Southern organizations.
q28_linkages: Scaling up interventions (WHAT) → Consortium model with implementation and research components (HOW)
Focus on marginalized groups (WHAT) → Inclusive partnerships with Southern-led organizations (WHO)
Adaptive learning (WHAT) → Flexible funding and quarterly reviews (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (inclusive partnerships, focus on marginalized groups) with efficiency (leveraging existing contracts, co-financing). For example, the Delegated Cooperation Agreement with USAID enables additional funding without increasing UK costs, while the consortium includes Southern partners to ensure local ownership despite higher coordination complexity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to established partners (e.g., IRC) enable rapid start-up, while competitive calls for innovation grants ensure diverse voices are included
expertise vs. ownership: Northern partners (e.g., George Washington University) lead research for rigor, while Southern partners (e.g., Raising Voices) drive implementation for contextual relevance
cost vs. reach: Reserving £7.5m for flexible responses allows adaptation but reduces upfront allocable funds
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (due to conflict settings and innovative interventions) justifies intensive oversight, including quarterly management meetings, embedded technical support, and adaptive programming to mitigate risks in real time.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include mentorship, co-authorship, and institutional strengthening. Southern partners like Raising Voices and Breakthrough are positioned as both implementers and capacity builders, receiving support to scale their own interventions.
intersections.quote: The programme is designed to accelerate progress towards Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets to end all forms of violence against women and girls (SDG5.2) and children (SDG16.2). (D0003788.odt, Intervention Summary)

key_programme_risks: Challenges of scaling up interventions from small pilots to large programmes while maintaining effectiveness
Limited capacity and political will in target countries to use evidence for policy and programming
High prevalence and severity of VAWG in conflict and humanitarian settings, complicating intervention delivery
Coordination risks in a multi-partner consortium with diverse geographic and thematic foci
Data limitations in conflict-affected areas, affecting monitoring and evaluation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Piloting, monitoring, and action research to refine interventions; reserving £7.5m for flexible responses to emerging opportunities.
Technical advice and capacity support embedded in the consortium; focus on strengthening long-term capability among grantees and governments.
Partnerships with experienced organizations (e.g., IRC); adaptive programming and quarterly reviews to adjust to context changes.
Clear division of roles between implementation (G&E consortium) and research (RED consortium); joint governance structures (e.g., annual meetings, advisory boards).

fcas_specific_lessons: VAWG escalates in conflict and persists post-conflict, requiring long-term, adaptive interventions.
Local ownership and context-specific adaptations are critical for sustainability in fragile settings.
Technical support and capacity building must be prioritized for partners operating in high-risk environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The predecessor programme (What Works I) demonstrated that VAWG is preventable through rigorously evaluated pilots, achieving ~50% reductions in violence. However, it also highlighted the need for better evidence on scaling up and mainstreaming interventions into larger programmes. The Independent Commission for Aid Impact (ICAI) recommended that DFID scale up efforts by integrating VAWG into programming across sectors, which is addressed in What Works II through mainstreaming and flexible funding.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Inclusion of a £7.5m flexible fund to respond to emerging opportunities, addressing ICAI’s recommendation for adaptive scaling.
Stronger focus on conflict and humanitarian settings, building on evidence that VAWG increases in these contexts.
Explicit integration of capacity building as a core objective, responding to the need for long-term local ownership.
risks_lessons.quote: ICAI’s follow-up report in 2018 reiterated that ‘at country level there has not been any scaling up or significant mainstreaming of VAWG initiatives.’ (D0003788.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: USAID contributed up to $8m (£6.2m equivalent at 2022 exchange rates), with $3m already transferred. The programme is also designed to attract additional co-financing from other donors, expanding its reach and impact without additional UK funds.
financial_details.quote: USAID and FCDO have drawn up and signed a Delegated Cooperation Agreement (a specific type of Memorandum of Understanding) to confirm acceptance of funding and programme arrangements. (D0003701.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: Support to the International Security Sector Advisory Team (ISSAT)
metadata.quote: "Security and Justice' refers to values and goals (freedom, fairness, personal safety) and the institutions established to deliver them (defence forces, police, courts) to ensure fairness, rights, protection and freedom from fear and violence at all levels. (Document: 51871720.odt, SummarySheet)
metadata.duration_source: "DFID will support the International Security Sector Advisory Team (ISSAT), a foundation that supports the international community in their efforts to improve security and justice (S&J), with up to £2.1m of funding over six years. [...] bringing the total business case value to £2.6m over six years." (Document: 51871720.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme aims to strengthen international donor coordination and capability in security and justice (S&J) reform through ISSAT, while also providing direct advisory support, knowledge development, and technical assistance to DFID and HMG. It combines capacity building, policy influence, and implementation research to improve S&J interventions in fragile states.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DFID will support the International Security Sector Advisory Team (ISSAT), a foundation that supports the international community in their efforts to improve security and justice (S&J), with up to £2.1m of funding over six years. ISSAT will provide operational support that will both reinforce the international community’s security and justice reform capability, and provide a programme scoping, design, monitoring and evaluation capability that will be made available to DFID and other HMG departments." (Document: 51871720.odt, SummarySheet)
q3_expected_outputs: Advisory field support for HMG S&J activities (tools and guidance for bilaterals/multilaterals)
Knowledge and professional development for HMG (technical advice, training, MEL capacity)
Improved coordination between donors and multilaterals (joint assessments, policy alignment)
Public goods: SSR tools, training modules, and practitioner guidance available to the donor community
Support to DFID’s S&J uplift (scoping, design, M&E for new programmes)
Gender-sensitive S&J interventions (e.g., Gender+Security Sector Reform Toolkit refresh)
what_objectives.summary: The programme leverages ISSAT’s multilateral platform to enhance DFID/HMG’s S&J programming through three pillars: 1) tailored advisory support for HMG, 2) knowledge/learning products for the international community, and 3) donor coordination to improve coherence and standards in fragile contexts. It directly addresses UK national security priorities by tackling drivers of terrorism and organised crime through stabilized governance institutions.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will accelerate DFID’s re-entry into S&J programming and place DFID and HMG in a central influencing position among donors and multilaterals, promoting coherence and excellence." (Document: 51871720.odt, SummarySheet)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly targets fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where S&J failures drive terrorism and organised crime. These contexts are characterized by weak governance, corrupt security forces, and violent extremism, requiring adaptive, conflict-sensitive approaches.
where_context.q5_source: "Instability, conflict and state failure overseas pose a serious risk to the stability and economic development of poor countries and an indirect risk to the UK. Violations by weak and abusive security forces and perceptions of injustice from a state seen as corrupt and illegitimate are among the reasons why people join violent extremist groups." (Document: 51871720.odt, Strategic Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and conflict limit the ability to implement direct reforms, requiring work with non-state providers and adaptive programming. Political sensitivities around security sector reform (SSR) constrain donor coordination, while data gaps in FCAS hinder evidence-based decision-making. ISSAT’s neutral branding and multilateral backing help navigate these constraints.
where_context.quote: "Working on S&J is however complex and at times challenging. The sector can present risks, though the potential rewards in terms of peace and stability can also be high. It is a broad and complex area involving intricated delivery chains, institutions with divergent mandates as well as political sensitivities." (Document: 51871720.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ISSAT’s Governing Board (comprising 16 bilateral donors, including the UK, and multilateral actors like the EU/AU) sets strategic priorities, with the UK holding a seat on the Core Group. While Southern partners (e.g., African Union) are represented, decision-making power rests with Northern donors and multilaterals.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for HMG/DFID staff (e.g., S&J courses, shadowing ISSAT missions)
mentorship through advisory field support and peer-to-peer learning
institutional strengthening of multilateral partners (e.g., AU, UNDP, World Bank)
knowledge products (tools, guidelines, e-learning modules for practitioners)
MEL capacity development for global programmes (e.g., UNDP Rule of Law)

partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer; provides advisory support, donor coordination, and knowledge development

partner_organizations.name: Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance (DCAF)
partner_organizations.role: Parent organization overseeing ISSAT; manages pooled trust fund

partner_organizations.name: African Union (AU)
partner_organizations.role: Multilateral partner; collaborates on regional SSR frameworks (e.g., African Security Sector Forum)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partner; joint work on Rule of Law programmes and MEL systems

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Collaborator on public finance and security sector reform

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU)
partner_organizations.role: Multilateral partner; joint SSR policy frameworks and donor mapping

partner_organizations.name: Stabilisation Unit (UK)
partner_organizations.role: HMG technical partner; complements ISSAT with UK-specific S&J expertise

partner_organizations.name: Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder and Governing Board member

partner_organizations.name: German Federal Foreign Office
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder and Governing Board member

who_partners.quote: "ISSAT is at the centre of donor co-ordination efforts in the S&J sector, and the UK Government previously had a central position in ISSAT as a founding member, and through membership of the ISSAT Governing Board Core Group." (Document: 51871720.odt, The case for UK investment via ISSAT)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The primary instrument is a **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)** with DCAF (ISSAT’s parent) for core contributions to a **multi-donor pooled trust fund** (£2.1m over 6 years).
