Additionally, a **separate technical assistance facility** (£500k over 5 years) is established for HMG-specific needs outside ISSAT’s scope, using a direct award mechanism.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ISSAT operates as a **pooled trust fund** under DCAF, with a Governing Board (16 bilateral/multilateral members) setting priorities. DFID sits on the **Core Group**, influencing strategic direction and budget allocation. Day-to-day delivery is managed by ISSAT’s secretariat, with DFID’s SRO overseeing HMG’s engagement.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ISSAT was selected as the **sole provider** due to its unique mandate as a donor coordination platform for S&J, established track record with DFID (A+ rated in previous reviews), and existing multilateral governance structure. The business case states no competition was held because ISSAT’s role is "uniquely placed to influence the way that other donors and multilateral organisations work on S&J."
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID has concluded that the International Security Sector Advisory Team (ISSAT) is best placed to deliver the intended outputs and manage the risks. DFID will not conduct a commercial procurement or request for services under this Business Case." (Document: 51871720.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: ISSAT is governed by a **Governing Board** (16 members, including DFID) and a **Core Group** (DFID is a member), which approves budgets and strategic priorities. The Board meets biannually, with DFID influencing decisions through its seat. Pillar 1 funds (DFID-specific tasks) are allocated via a workplan agreed between DFID’s SRO and ISSAT, while Pillars 2–3 (multilateral/knowledge) are decided collectively by the Board.
how_governance.quote: "As a Pooled Trust Fund donor, DFID will be a Member of the Board and its Core Group, which gives DFID the opportunity to influence ISSAT’s budget decisions and strategic priorities." (Document: 51871720.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be switched **from Pillar 1 (DFID-specific) to Pillars 2–3 (multilateral/knowledge)** if unused, but not vice versa. This allows ISSAT to respond to emerging multilateral demands while protecting DFID’s core priorities. Reallocation requires Core Group approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes **annual reviews** to adjust priorities based on DFID’s evolving S&J portfolio and external context (e.g., new conflict dynamics). ISSAT’s 4-year strategy (developed with DFID input) provides a framework for adaptive management, with milestones reviewed every 6 months. Major shifts require Governing Board approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "Funds can be switched from Pillar 1 to Pillar 2 & 3 (but not vice versa), for example, where there is greater demand for work in one area or unused funds under Pillar 1." (Document: 51871720.odt, Commercial Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ISSAT (implementer) → [consultants/subcontractors for specific tasks]. No further sub-awards to Southern partners are mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID will pay 8% overheads which will include funding for a corporate level crisis management capacity and a dedicated security officer and other overheads such as the annual audit, office rent (in an office that is co-shared with other organisations) and human resources." (Document: 51871720.odt, Approach to Value for Money)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Rely on existing HMG capabilities (e.g., Stabilisation Unit)
Option 2: Purchase technical advice for DFID only (no donor coordination)
Option 3: Purchase technical advice + donor-influencing capability + multilateral access (CHOSEN)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (ISSAT) was selected for its **unparalleled donor coordination mandate**, **cost efficiency** (pooled funding, low overheads), and **strategic influence** over multilaterals. The business case highlights ISSAT’s proven track record (A+ in DFID’s 2016 review), existing relationships with 16 donors, and ability to amplify HMG’s S&J priorities globally. Alternatives (e.g., Stabilisation Unit) lacked multilateral reach or required costly new procurement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced HMG control over pooled funds (Pillars 2–3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s seat on the Core Group ensures influence over strategic priorities and budget allocation. Annual reviews and milestone tracking maintain accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with Stabilisation Unit (SU) mandates
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of labor: ISSAT focuses on **multilateral coordination and global tools**, while SU provides **UK-specific technical support**. Joint workplans prevent duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited justice expertise (ISSAT’s strength is security sector reform)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Complementary partnerships (e.g., UNDP for rule of law) and targeted Pillar 1 tasks address gaps. DFID can use the £500k technical assistance facility for justice-specific needs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor fatigue or shifting priorities reducing ISSAT’s relevance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s Core Group membership and 4-year strategy development ensure alignment with evolving S&J agendas (e.g., counter-terrorism, organised crime).

why_rationale.quote: "Although Option 3 represents the higher immediate cost it presents the best value for money (VfM) overall. The simplicity of one provider covering DFID’s needs frees staff time to work on policy direction and on more complex or sensitive tasks in support of Country Offices." (Document: 51871720.odt, Summary Value for Money Statement)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with **neutral multilateral branding** (e.g., ISSAT) and proven experience in conflict-sensitive S&J reform. Direct bilateral implementers or Northern-led contractors would face political resistance in fragile states, while Southern partners often lack the **donor coordination mandate** required for this programme.
q27_constraints_detail: Political sensitivities around SSR require a **multilateral platform** (not a single country or NGO)
Weak institutions in FCAS necessitate partners with **adaptive, non-state engagement** experience
Conflict dynamics demand **neutral actors** to facilitate donor coordination
Limited Southern partner capacity for **global knowledge products** (e.g., tools/guidance)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for donor coordination** (a core objective) dictates the **multilateral platform structure** (ISSAT). The **global public goods** output (tools, training) requires a **neutral, established hub** rather than a bilateral or NGO-led approach. The **uplift in DFID’s S&J portfolio** necessitates **flexible, on-demand support** (Pillar 1), which ISSAT’s pooled fund model provides.
q28_linkages: Global coordination objective → Multilateral governance structure (ISSAT Board)
Adaptive programming needs → Pooled fund with reallocation flexibility
Public goods focus → Neutral branding and open-access knowledge products
HMG influence requirement → Core Group seat and Pillar 1 earmarking
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly balances **Northern efficiency** (pooled funding, low overheads) with **Southern equity** (e.g., AU partnership, gender-sensitive tools). Trade-offs include: 
- **Speed vs. inclusion**: ISSAT’s existing platform enables rapid scale-up but limits direct Southern ownership of governance.
- **Expertise vs. localization**: Northern-led technical assistance (e.g., surge capacity) is prioritized for immediate impact, with long-term capacity building embedded via training/mentorship.
- **Cost vs. reach**: The 8% overhead supports multilateral coordination but reduces funds available for direct Southern implementation.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Pooled funding (efficient) vs. earmarked Southern budgets (equitable)
Northern-led knowledge products (scalable) vs. context-specific Southern tools (localized)
Multilateral decision-making (inclusive) vs. HMG strategic influence (directed)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** increases oversight intensity (e.g., **milestone-based reviews**, Core Group approvals for reallocation) and justifies the **multilateral structure** (shared risk pooling). High political sensitivities in S&J reform require **neutral intermediaries** (ISSAT) to manage donor coordination, reducing bilateral exposure.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 
- **ISSAT** provides **training/mentorship** to HMG staff (e.g., shadowing missions) and multilaterals (e.g., AU SSR rollout).
- **Southern partners** (e.g., AU) are engaged as **implementers of regional frameworks** (e.g., African Security Sector Forum) but rely on ISSAT/DFID for **technical backstopping**. 
- **DFID’s SRO** ensures Southern priorities (e.g., gender, customary justice) are integrated into ISSAT’s global tools.
intersections.quote: "Working on S&J is however complex and at times challenging. The sector can present risks, though the potential rewards in terms of peace and stability can also be high. [...] Strategic and operational level coordination with other donors will be essential to DFID’s success in S&J." (Document: 51871720.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Donor fatigue or shifting priorities reducing commitment to S&J/ISSAT
Overlap or confusion with Stabilisation Unit’s mandate
Limited justice sector expertise within ISSAT (security-focused)
Political resistance to SSR in FCAS contexts
Failure to influence multilateral S&J standards as intended
Underutilization of Pillar 1 funds (DFID-specific tasks)
Reputational risk if ISSAT-associated programmes underperform
Currency/fluctuation risks affecting pooled fund value

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DFID’s Core Group role ensures ISSAT’s strategy aligns with evolving donor priorities (e.g., counter-terrorism). Annual reviews adjust to new contexts.
Clear division: ISSAT handles **multilateral coordination/global tools**; SU focuses on **UK-specific technical support**. Joint workplans prevent duplication.
Complementary partnerships (e.g., UNDP for rule of law) and targeted Pillar 1 tasks. £500k technical assistance facility can fund justice-specific inputs.
ISSAT’s **neutral branding** and **conflict-sensitive approaches** (e.g., customary justice guidance) reduce backlash. DFID’s SRO ensures adaptive programming.
DFID’s Governing Board seat and **strategic partnerships** (e.g., with UNDP, World Bank) embed HMG priorities in multilateral S&J frameworks.
Flexible reallocation to Pillars 2–3 if unused. Annual demand assessments with Country Offices.
ISSAT’s **strong track record** (A+ in 2016 review) and **transparency** (IATI reporting, audited accounts) mitigate risks. Break clause allows DFID to exit if underperformance.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-sensitive programming is critical: ISSAT’s tools (e.g., on customary justice, risk management) reflect lessons from FCAS like the Gambia and DRC.
Donor coordination in FCAS must be **neutral and adaptive**: ISSAT’s multilateral model was designed to overcome political blocks to bilateral SSR support.
Local ownership requires **long-term engagement**: Previous DFID programmes showed that rushed S&J reforms in FCAS often fail; ISSAT’s 4-year strategy aligns with this lesson.
Gender and inclusion must be **mainstreamed**: FCAS contexts exacerbate inequalities; the Gender+SSR Toolkit refresh addresses this.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
DFID’s 2013–2015 funding to ISSAT (£750k) achieved an **A+ rating** for over-delivering on indicators. Key lessons included: 
- **Pooled funds improve coherence** but require active donor engagement (hence DFID’s Core Group role).
- **Multilateral backing** (e.g., AU, UN) is essential for legitimacy in FCAS.
- **Flexible pillars** allow adaptation to emerging priorities (e.g., shifting from post-conflict SSR to counter-terrorism).
- **Knowledge products** (e.g., SSR tools) have higher uptake when co-developed with multilaterals.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Pillar flexibility**: Added ability to reallocate funds from Pillar 1 to Pillars 2–3 based on demand (learned from underused earmarked funds in 2013–2015).
2. **Strategic partnerships**: Formalized collaborations with UNDP/World Bank to address justice sector gaps identified in previous reviews.
3. **Gender mainstreaming**: Explicit focus on Gender+SSR Toolkit refresh, responding to critiques of male-dominated SSR approaches.
4. **Adaptive management**: Introduced **6-month milestone reviews** (previously annual) for faster course correction.
5. **Southern engagement**: Expanded AU partnership to operationalize regional SSR frameworks (e.g., African Security Sector Forum).
risks_lessons.quote: "Previous DFID financial support has enabled us to buy into ISSAT’s strong relationships and access to other multilaterals and bilateral donors. [...] ISSAT have contributed to an increase in the effectiveness and coherence of the international community’s support to security and justice services for poor people in fragile states." (Document: 51871720.odt, The case for UK investment via ISSAT)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: ISSAT’s pooled fund model leverages contributions from **8+ bilateral donors** and multilaterals (e.g., EU, AU), amplifying DFID’s £2.1m investment. For example, joint donor assessments (Pillar 2) reduce duplication across HMG/EU/World Bank programmes. The **public goods** (tools, training) benefit all 62 DCAF member states.
financial_details.quote: "DFID will pay 8% overheads which will include funding for a corporate level crisis management capacity and a dedicated security officer and other overheads such as the annual audit, office rent (in an office that is co-shared with other organisations) and human resources." (Document: 51871720.odt, Approach to Value for Money)

metadata.programme_name: Strategic Impact Evaluation and Learning (SIEL) Programme

quote.programme_name: "The Strategic Impact Evaluation and Learning (SIEL) Programme" (D0005273.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £13m" (D0005273.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.duration: "AMP Start Date: June 2023", "AMP End Date: March 2030" (D0005273.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.sector: "Country/Region or Sector: Economics and Evaluation" (D0005273.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: June 2023", "AMP End Date: March 2030"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The SIEL programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** through rigorous impact evaluations (RCTs and quasi-experimental methods) to assess FCDO interventions. It also includes **capacity building** within FCDO to commission, manage, and interpret evaluations, and aims for **policy influence** by generating actionable knowledge to inform decision-making. The programme supports **implementation research** by testing and scaling interventions adaptively.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Strategic Impact Evaluation and Learning (SIEL) programme will support FCDO to use Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental methods and other techniques as appropriate to rigorously assess the impact of FCDO’s interventions. It will fund evaluations with high potential to generate actionable knowledge. SIEL will follow up where previous studies have measured impact to assess long term sustainability, and raise capacity in FCDO to commission, manage and interpret impact evaluation evidence." (D0005273.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Impact evaluation studies (RCTs/quasi-experimental)
Follow-up studies to assess long-term impact
Capacity-building workshops for FCDO staff
Evidence and Learning Plans for interventions
Policy briefs and working papers
Peer-reviewed journal publications
Stakeholder engagement and evidence use plans
Adaptive learning tools (e.g., nimble RCTs)

what_objectives.summary: SIEL aims to generate rigorous evidence on FCDO interventions through impact evaluations, build FCDO’s capacity to use this evidence, and influence policy and programme design globally. It focuses on strategic priorities like climate change, women and girls, and humanitarian aid, while testing adaptive management approaches.

quote.objectives: "SIEL will: Generate evidence on what is (or is not) working to inform policy and programme decision-making through robust impact evaluations; Assess the impact of interventions after programme completion and in the longer term; Build capacity in FCDO to commission, manage, interpret, and identify opportunities for future rigorous impact evaluation." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.approach: "In the context of a limited Official Development Assistance (ODA) budget, FCDO spend needs to be more strategic than ever, supporting policies and interventions with the highest impact and VfM." (D0005273.odt, Strategic Overview)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated as "moderate" risk, reflecting operational challenges in fragile contexts (e.g., conflict-affected areas) but with mitigations like due diligence and coordination with FCDO posts. The risk of terrorist financing is assessed as low due to robust safeguards.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0005273.odt, Summary Sheet); "Our assessment is that the risk of programme resources being used to fund terrorism is low." (D0005273.odt, Mandatory Assurances)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks in fragile contexts require coordination with FCDO posts to align with risk appetite. Data limitations (e.g., recontacting beneficiaries for follow-up studies) and weak institutions may affect evaluation feasibility. Conflict-affected areas necessitate robust financial management and ethical safeguards.

quote.constraints: "When activities involve conducting research in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, the SIEL provider will be required to co-ordinate with FCDO Posts to align with FCDO risk appetite and agree a practical approach to ensuring robust financial management throughout the supply chain." (D0005273.odt, Mandatory Assurances)
quote.data_risks: "Criteria are likely to include... likelihood of success in recontacting intervention beneficiaries and respondents." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO Evaluation Unit (UK-based) leads decision-making on evaluation selection, design, and strategic priorities. Southern partners (e.g., local researchers) are engaged as sub-contractors or collaborators, with limited decision-making authority over core programme directions.
q10_capacity_building_details: Workshops for FCDO advisory cadres on impact evaluation
Hands-on support for programme teams to design evaluations
Mentorship on data analysis and interpretation
Training for Senior Civil Servants to foster evaluative culture
Engagement with local enumerators/researchers for data collection

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Evaluation Unit
partner_organizations.role: Lead manager and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: SIEL Implementing Partner (TBD - e.g., academic consortium)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of impact evaluations, capacity building, and research dissemination

partner_organizations.name: Local research institutions/enumerators
partner_organizations.role: Data collection, fieldwork, and contextual expertise

partner_organizations.name: Research and Evidence Directorate (RED)
partner_organizations.role: Collaboration on evidence gaps and strategic priorities

partner_organizations.name: Development Impact Evaluation (DIME) Department (World Bank)
partner_organizations.role: Past partner (Fund for Impact Evaluation); potential technical advisor

quote.structure: "SIEL will be implemented through a partner who will centralise delivery of the programme." (D0005273.odt, SIEL Delivery Options)
quote.capacity_building: "SIEL will build capacity in FCDO through a dedicated technical support component for FCDO staff. This could include: Engagement with FCDO’s advisory cadres... Workshops and engagement with policy advisors..." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.southern_role: "SIEL will... incentivise opportunities for equitable partnerships at local level, where research takes place whilst ensuring beneficiaries and most marginalised groups are engaged through every step of the research process." (D0005273.odt, Mandatory Assurances)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will primarily use an **accountable grant or MOU** for the implementing partner (depending on whether the partner is multilateral or not-for-profit). Sub-awards for specific evaluations may use **contracts** or **grants** to research institutions. Non-ODA activities (e.g., diplomatic influencing) will use separate funding streams.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A single implementing partner (or consortium) will centralise delivery, with FCDO’s Evaluation Unit providing oversight. The partner must have in-house impact evaluation expertise but may sub-contract specific studies. A Steering Committee (FCDO + partner) will select evaluations based on strategic alignment.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: A **Call for Proposals** will be used instead of open competition because: 1) The technical skills required are extensive and limited to a small number of organisations (academic/multilateral/non-profit); 2) Some potential partners cannot enter fully competitive tendering; 3) Direct award was considered but rejected to ensure value for money among eligible candidates.

quote.instrument: "Depending on whether the chosen partner is a multilateral organisation or a not-for-profit or academic organisation, either an MOU or an accountable grant will then be drawn up." (D0005273.odt, SIEL Procurement Route)
quote.selection: "We consider a direct award but given that we believe more than one organisation can deliver the model of SIEL set out in this appraisal case the best option will be to carry out a Call for Proposals whereby identified candidates have the opportunity to answer a questionnaire setting out how they would deliver SIEL." (D0005273.odt, SIEL Procurement Route)
quote.structure: "Option 2 – Partnership with an organisation with recognised impact evaluation leadership expertise... The implementing partner will be expected to have capacity to directly deliver impact evaluations through their own resources but could also form a consortium and/or contract out some of the work." (D0005273.odt, SIEL Delivery Options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **SIEL Steering Committee** will include representatives from FCDO’s Economics and Evaluation Directorate, Research and Evidence Directorate, and the implementing partner. It will select evaluations based on criteria like strategic relevance, evidence gaps, and feasibility. The Evaluation Quality Assurance Service (EQUALS) may provide independent QA.

quote.manager: "The implementing partner will be responsible for ensuring each IE study receives ethical approval and that research protocols and design are adhered to." (D0005273.odt, Option 2)
quote.sub_awards: "Projectswill then be selected by a team of reviewers from Economics and Evaluation Directorate, Research and Evidence Directorate and the implementing partner... Criteria are likely to include... strategic relevance, meaningful contribution to the evidence base, relevance to upcoming policy decision making, feasibility and an assessment of additionality." (D0005273.odt, Engagement and influencing)
quote.governance: "The SIEL Steering Committee will then choose which evaluations to finance based on their strategic relevance, potential to fill an evidence gap, relevance to upcoming policy decision-making, feasibility, and additionality." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.oversight: "The programme will monitor understanding and use of evidence generated on at least a yearly basis (at minimum) and conduct evaluative activities to understand bottlenecks to evidence use if needed." (D0005273.odt, Theory of Change)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between thematic windows or studies if approved by the Steering Committee, but core budget lines (e.g., capacity building vs. evaluations) are likely fixed. Follow-up studies may require co-financing to leverage funds.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive: 1) **Phased thematic windows** allow response to shifting priorities; 2) **Nimble RCTs** enable mid-course corrections; 3) **Steering Committee** can adjust evaluation selection criteria. However, long-term IEs (5-year studies) have limited flexibility to avoid compromising rigour.

quote.reallocation: "A diversified portfolio including long-term IEs, nimble experiments and follow-up evaluation studies must be built to minimise the risk that the IE portfolio will become obsolete after just 1 or 2 years." (D0005273.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.adaptive: "SIEL will support rigorous and evidence-based adaptive programme support. This could include ex-ante data collection for diagnostic purposes, lab-in-the-field experiments for proof of concept ahead of the programme initiation, and nimble adaptive trials testing the best delivery options before scaling-up." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.approvals: "The goal of the SIEL Steering Committee and this process is to maximise the Value for Money of knowledge generated through the programme." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → SIEL Implementing Partner (consortium lead) → [Data collection providers (if sub-contracted)]. Under Option 2, most evaluations are delivered directly by the partner, reducing layers compared to Option 3 (which would add a third tier for sub-contracted studies).

quote.layers: "With two or more tiers of suppliers, overheads are likely to be higher under Option 3... In Option 2 we would only have two tiers of suppliers much of the time: the SIEL main implementing partner and the data collection providers on the ground." (D0005273.odt, Choosing the Best Value for Money Option)
quote.payments: "Funds will then be disbursed by the SIEL implementing partner to the research institution(s) that they contract to implement the chosen FCDO evaluations." (D0005273.odt, Option 3)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Impact evaluations commissioned ad-hoc by programme teams with existing budgets/expertise. Follow-up studies rare. Rejected because it fails to address strategic evidence gaps or smaller programmes.
SIEL partner acts as a fund manager, contracting out all evaluations to third parties. Considered but rejected due to higher overheads, fragmented learning, and slower implementation.
Hybrid approach using Option 2 for core delivery and Option 3 for follow-up studies. Rejected due to added complexity and procurement costs.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (partnership with a lead organisation) was chosen because it: 1) **Maximises adaptive learning** by centralising delivery with a partner that can iterate approaches across studies; 2) **Reduces overheads** compared to Option 3’s multi-tiered contracting; 3) **Accelerates implementation** by leveraging the partner’s in-house expertise; 4) **Strengthens capacity building** through direct collaboration with FCDO; 5) **Aligns with past success** (e.g., Fund for Impact Evaluation with World Bank’s DIME).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single partner’s expertise
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partner may form a consortium or sub-contract to fill gaps; FCDO retains oversight via Steering Committee.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slower response to new priorities under centralised model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased thematic windows and nimble RCTs allow adaptability; annual portfolio reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership in decision-making
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Stakeholder engagement plans and equitable partnerships at local level (though core decisions remain with FCDO/partner).

quote.why_chosen: "Option 2, a close partnership with an implementing organisation, is the best option provided that a suitable partner or consortium can be found, because it has greater potential for adaptive learning, high quality capacity building, and getting impact evaluations running rapidly with low overhead costs." (D0005273.odt, Choosing the Best Value for Money Option)
quote.risks: "A necessary criterion for an evaluation to be selected will be senior (SCS) buy-in and commitment of staff on the programming/intervention side to manage their side of the evaluation." (D0005273.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.vfm: "The conclusion is that Option 2... is the best option... because it has greater potential for adaptive learning, high quality capacity building, and getting impact evaluations running rapidly with low overhead costs." (D0005273.odt, Multi-Criteria Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope and FCAS contexts** constrain partner selection by: 1) Requiring partners with **proven experience in fragile settings** (e.g., security protocols, ethical safeguards); 2) Limiting data collection to organisations with **local networks** (e.g., recontacting beneficiaries for follow-ups); 3) Necessitating **FCDO coordination** for conflict-affected areas, which favours partners with existing relationships (e.g., multilateral organisations).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for ethical approvals in high-risk contexts
Local data collection capacity for follow-up studies
Alignment with FCDO’s risk appetite in FCAS
Language/cultural barriers for stakeholder engagement
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for adaptive learning and long-term evidence** determines the delivery structure by: 1) Requiring a **centralised partner** (Option 2) to synthesise lessons across studies; 2) Embedding **real-time monitoring** (e.g., nimble RCTs) in the management model; 3) Prioritising **in-house expertise** to enable rapid design adjustments. The **capacity-building objective** shapes the partner’s role to include hands-on collaboration with FCDO teams.

q28_linkages.how_affected: → Requires follow-up studies → Needs partner with access to original IE data → Favours Option 2’s centralised model over Option 3’s fragmented contracting.
→ Demands embedded research teams → Leads to co-production of Evidence and Learning Plans → Shapes partner selection toward organisations with field presence.
→ Requires hands-on training → Partner must have technical advisors → Excludes pure fund-manager models (Option 3).

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly acknowledges tensions between: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: "Option 2 offers faster implementation but may limit Southern ownership"; 2) **Expertise vs. local relevance**: "Northern-led partners provide rigour but require mitigation for equitable engagement"; 3) **Cost vs. reach**: "Centralised data tools (Option 2) reduce overheads but may sideline local providers."

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: The lead partner (likely UK-based) ensures methodological rigour but risks marginalising local researchers in decision-making. Mitigation: "SIEL will incentivise equitable partnerships at local level."
Option 2’s centralised model accelerates delivery but limits opportunities for diverse suppliers (cf. Option 3’s competitive contracting).
Common survey tools (Option 2) improve efficiency but may overlook local data needs. Mitigation: "Adaptations for specific operating contexts."

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (including FCAS operations) increases management intensity by: 1) Requiring **dual oversight** (partner + FCDO posts) for conflict-affected studies; 2) Mandating **real-time monitoring** of financial flows; 3) Adding **ethical safeguards** layers (e.g., UKCDR guidelines). This justifies Option 2’s centralised partner over Option 3’s lighter-touch fund manager.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Requiring **embedded technical advisors** (not just sub-contractors); 2) Prioritising partners with **training experience** (e.g., past work with FCDO cadres); 3) Including **stakeholder engagement plans** as deliverables to ensure local uptake.

quote.where_who: "When activities involve conducting research in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, the SIEL provider will be required to co-ordinate with FCDO Posts to align with FCDO risk appetite..." (D0005273.odt, Mandatory Assurances)
quote.what_how: "SIEL will support rigorous and evidence-based adaptive programme support... nimble adaptive trials testing the best delivery options before scaling-up." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.equity_efficiency: "Option 2... has greater potential for adaptive learning, high quality capacity building... but may limit diversity of suppliers compared to Option 3." (D0005273.odt, Multi-Criteria Analysis)
quote.risk_management: "Our assessment is that the risk of programme resources being used to fund terrorism is low. When activities involve... fragile and conflict-affected contexts, the SIEL provider will be required to co-ordinate with FCDO Posts to align with FCDO risk appetite." (D0005273.odt, Mandatory Assurances)

key_programme_risks: Limited senior leadership bandwidth for evidence engagement
Shifting FCDO priorities rendering long-term IEs obsolete
Low demand from programme teams for impact evaluations
Failure to recontact beneficiaries for follow-up studies
Overlap/duplication with other FCDO evaluation initiatives
Ethical breaches in data collection (especially FCAS)
Partner’s lack of thematic/geographic expertise for specific studies
Delays in contracting research teams missing programme windows

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Require SCS buy-in as a selection criterion; incorporate capacity-building for Senior Civil Servants.
Phase thematic windows; diversify portfolio (long-term IEs + nimble experiments).
Proactive outreach via Heads of Profession; highlight VfM benefits of IEs.
Prioritise studies with high-quality original IE designs; involve original evaluators in follow-ups.
Adhere to UKCDR safeguarding guidelines; require ethical approvals for all studies.
Allow consortium formation or sub-contracting; use EQUALS for QA.

fcas_specific_lessons: Coordinate with FCDO Posts to align with risk appetite in conflict zones.
Use local enumerators with security training for data collection.
Prioritise digital/remote data tools (e.g., geo-satellite) to reduce field risks.
Build contingency time/budget for FCAS-related delays.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Fund for Impact Evaluation**: Workshops successfully matched demand/supply for IEs; adaptive trials (e.g., Senegal HIV campaign) improved VfM. 2) **CEDIL Programme**: Combining experimental methods with qualitative analysis (e.g., structural models) deepened understanding of "why" interventions work. 3) **DIME’s Trial and Adopt**: Embedded learning functions improved delivery efficiency.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Phased thematic windows** (vs. upfront selection) to adapt to shifting priorities. 2) **Nimble RCTs** added to test delivery options mid-programme. 3) **Stakeholder engagement plans** made mandatory (learned from Fund for Impact Evaluation’s low uptake). 4) **Follow-up studies** prioritised (addressing gap from past programmes).

quote.risks: "A challenge faced by many programmes... is that they have a lot of traction at the onset but with rapidly shifting priorities and high turn-over of staff they often end up being off-focus after just few years." (D0005273.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.mitigations: "SIEL to incorporate some flexibility to respond to changes in strategic direction to keep portfolio of IEs in line with current priorities." (D0005273.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.lessons: "The Fund for Impact Evaluation programme provides many examples of how to support fast learning in adaptive programming using RCTs to maximise VfM... In Senegal the programme used an RCT to test two different campaign delivery strategies to support HIV prevention." (D0005273.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.design_changes: "SIEL will trial innovative methods where appropriate... nimble adaptive trials testing the best delivery options before scaling-up." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Co-financing for follow-up studies is encouraged: "Where possible we will seek interested partners to co-finance these follow up studies to leverage our funding and increase the potential take-up of their findings."
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Primarily capital budget (as R&D activity) from ODA, with non-ODA funds for non-eligible activities (e.g., diplomatic influencing).

quote.budget: "The funding to deliver the SIEL programme is £13m over seven years. Since impact evaluations are an R&D activity, this will principally be capital budget, from Official Development Assistance." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.leverage: "Where possible we will seek interested partners to co-finance these follow up studies to leverage our funding and increase the potential take-up of their findings." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)
quote.oda_split: "Non-ODA budget will be included for evaluation of influencing or other activities that do not classify as ODA eligible spend." (D0005273.odt, What will SIEL do?)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Impact Investing Markets for Agriculture (SIIMA)
metadata.quote: "Agriculture accounts for more than half of total employment in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, but many smallholder farmers remain trapped in poverty" (40384354.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 1 April 2019\nEnd Date: 30 March 2024" (40384354.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SIIMA combines financing mechanisms (investment in businesses), evidence generation (research on technology uptake and impact measurement), and capacity building (supporting businesses to scale). It aims to catalyze private sector investment in agricultural technologies while generating robust evidence on what works.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SIIMA will address this problem by building a pipeline of high-impact businesses that can deliver technologies to farmers at scale, and developing tools for impact measurement, to mobilise additional capital into the sector." (40384354.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Financial and technical support to 15 businesses with potential to reach scale
Creation of over 200,000 jobs in the agriculture sector
Catalyzing £110m of additional financing
8-10 peer-reviewed high-quality publications
50 public-facing knowledge and learning outputs (blogs, videos, panels, workshops)
Innovations in impact measurement using frontier technologies (Big Data, machine learning, blockchain)
Improved lives for at least 1 million people
what_objectives.summary: SIIMA aims to transform agricultural productivity and climate resilience for smallholder farmers by combining investment in innovative businesses with research on technology adoption and impact measurement tools.
what_objectives.quote: "By 2024 the programme will deliver: improved lives for at least 1 million people, by directly investing in 15 businesses with potential to scale, creating over 200,000 jobs, catalysing £110m of additional financing, and generating innovations and robust tools to measure and communicate development impacts on the poor." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in regions with market and climate risks but has mitigation strategies through portfolio diversification and adaptive programming. Fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) are included but not the primary focus.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (40384354.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The programme will directly invest in 15 businesses with potential to scale, including expansion into riskier, harder-to-reach markets (including fragile and conflict-affected states)." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and market barriers limit access to finance and technology adoption. Climate risks increase vulnerability of smallholder farmers. Weak institutions and data limitations constrain impact measurement and investment flows.
where_context.quote: "New technologies such as solar irrigation, cold storage, and mechanisation of production... can boost productivity, create jobs, help manage risks and income volatility, and reduce food waste. Getting these technologies into the hands of poor farmers is essential for delivering the SDGs, yet remains an intractable development challenge." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: DFID (now FCDO) in partnership with Shell Foundation and Acumen
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between DFID (UK) and implementing partners (Shell Foundation and Acumen, with operations in LMICs). Shell Foundation and Acumen have Board seats in investee companies and provide strategic advice, indicating shared governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical support to businesses
mentorship through Board participation
training on impact measurement
research partnerships with local institutions (e.g., Busara Centre for Behavioural Economics)

partner_organizations.name: Shell Foundation
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and implementer (CASEE component)
partner_organizations.location: UK (headquarters) with operations in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia

partner_organizations.name: Acumen
partner_organizations.role: implementer (ARAF and Lean Data components)
partner_organizations.location: US/UK (headquarters) with operations in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia

partner_organizations.name: Busara Centre for Behavioural Economics
partner_organizations.role: research partner (behavioural studies)

partner_organizations.name: DFID (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funder and programme manager

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be delivered by three components... Partnership with the Shell Foundation... linked to the Acumen Resilient Agriculture Fund (ARAF)... A Lean Data Development Platform, to innovate with the aim of improving how DFID and others measure and communicate development impact of our investments." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses grants for research and technical assistance (e.g., £2m for Lean Data and climate-smart research) and matched funding for investments (e.g., £15m from DFID matched by Shell Foundation for CASEE). Equity or equity-like instruments are used for ARAF investments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID manages the overall programme with close collaboration between Shell Foundation and Acumen, each leading specific components. The structure allows for adaptive programming and synergy across components (e.g., CASEE, ARAF, Lean Data).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Shell Foundation and Acumen were selected based on their strong track records in impact investing and existing partnerships with DFID (e.g., Transforming Energy Access programme).
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will work with the leading impact investors Shell Foundation and Acumen to support early- and growth-stage organisations delivering solutions for farmers, and generate cutting-edge innovations in impact measurement." (40384354.odt, Strategic Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes Board participation by Shell Foundation and Acumen in investee companies, with DFID overseeing overall programme management. Technical advisory support is provided through partnerships (e.g., Busara Centre).
how_governance.quote: "SF’s model of providing grant funding with intensive management support through Board participation has a track record of successfully bringing in additional sources of private finance." (40384354.odt, Component 1) and "The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID to (1) shape the outputs (2) defer/cancel payments if quality is lacking, and (3) accelerate activities in response to opportunities." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities based on performance and opportunities, but major changes require DFID approval. The programme uses adaptive management principles.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed with "flexible and adaptive programming" to respond to emerging evidence or opportunities, such as synergies with other programmes or policy objectives.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID to... accelerate activities in response to opportunities, e.g. synergies with other programmes or UK policy objectives." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (Shell Foundation/Acumen) → Investee Companies/Research Teams
how_efficiency.quote: "CASEE will provide financial and technical support to 15 innovative agricultural technology businesses... conditional on achievement of milestones (product development, finance raised)." (40384354.odt, Component 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: Integrated investment and research programme (chosen option)
Extending the research scope of the DFID Impact Programme
Standalone research programme
Challenge Fund
Do nothing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The integrated approach was selected to combine direct investment in businesses with research and impact measurement, maximizing value for money (VfM) and learning. It allows DFID to test interventions while generating evidence to inform future investments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of supporting businesses that fail (inherent in early-stage investments)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by a diversified portfolio including both incubation and early-stage growth businesses, and by working with experienced partners (Shell Foundation, Acumen).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Distortion of markets through grant finance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Assessed as low risk due to focus on market-based solutions and patient capital.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 1: Integrated research and investment programme... The approach would enable DFID to (1) directly (through its investments) support smallholder farmers to access new technologies; (2) allow operationally relevant research findings and tools to be tested and validated with specific investments, and (3) maximise value from its investments by accessing timely data on investment portfolios for research." (40384354.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, including fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), requires partners with experience in high-risk environments. Shell Foundation and Acumen were selected for their track records in these regions and ability to manage risks (e.g., climate, market barriers).
q27_constraints_detail: need for partners with FCAS experience
requirement for adaptive programming due to climate and market volatility
local institutional capacity limitations
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (investment + research + impact measurement) necessitate a hybrid delivery structure. Investment components (CASEE, ARAF) require equity-like instruments and Board-level engagement, while research (Lean Data) needs flexible, technology-driven partnerships.
q28_linkages: Investment in businesses (CASEE/ARAF) generates data for research (Lean Data).
Research informs adaptive management of investments.
Impact measurement tools (Lean Data) are tested on investee companies.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (rapid scaling of technologies) with equity (reaching the poorest and women-led businesses). For example, it includes a "gender lens investing" approach and targets the "last mile" while using market-based mechanisms to ensure financial viability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion: patient capital for businesses to reach poorest farmers
expertise vs ownership: Northern partners (Shell, Acumen) lead but include local institutions (e.g., Busara Centre)
cost vs reach: Lean Data reduces measurement costs to enable broader impact tracking
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to milestone-based oversight and adaptive management, with flexibility to defer or cancel payments if quality is lacking. High-risk activities (e.g., FCAS expansion) are balanced by experienced partners.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme, with Shell Foundation and Acumen providing technical assistance and Board-level support to investee companies. This shapes partner roles to include mentorship and strategic advice.
intersections.quote: "The programme will take a ‘gender lens investing’ approach which aims to maximise investment impact by (1) taking an evidence-based approach to gender in investing... and (2) building capacity of women-led businesses through active investment and support." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID to... defer/cancel payments if quality is lacking." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

key_programme_risks: Business failure in early-stage investments
Low technology uptake by farmers
Market distortion from grant finance
Inability to reach the poorest or women-led businesses
Data quality and reliability in impact measurement
Climate and political risks in FCAS regions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversified portfolio across 15 businesses and stages (incubation to growth).
Behavioural research and technical assistance to address barriers (e.g., access to finance, information).
Focus on market-based solutions and patient capital; risk assessed as low.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Inability to reach the poorest or women-led businesses
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Gender lens investing approach and inclusivity ratios in impact measurement.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Data quality and reliability in impact measurement
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of frontier technologies (blockchain, machine learning) and third-party audits (e.g., Impact Matters).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Climate and political risks in FCAS regions
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive programming and partnerships with experienced organizations (Shell Foundation, Acumen).

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for patient capital and technical support to expand into FCAS regions.
Importance of local partnerships to navigate regulatory and security challenges.
Flexibility to adjust activities based on context (e.g., defer payments if quality is lacking).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s existing partnerships with Shell Foundation (e.g., TIME programme) and Acumen (Lean Data) informed the design. For example, the TIME programme achieved an A+ rating in its Annual Review and mobilized 5x additional capital, demonstrating the effectiveness of patient incubation and Board-level engagement.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme builds on successful elements from previous phases, such as Shell Foundation’s Board participation model and Acumen’s Lean Data approach, while adding new components (e.g., climate-smart research, blockchain for impact measurement).
risks_lessons.quote: "The TIME partnership has performed strongly and was awarded an A+ at a recent DFID Annual Review. It has delivered 17 new business models and 16 new business applications and delivered fully on the research, learning and publication programme, with 20 studies completed in 2017." (40384354.odt, Component 1) and "The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID to... accelerate activities in response to opportunities." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

co_funding_partners.partner: Green Climate Fund (via Acumen Resilient Agriculture Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to catalyze £110m of additional financing through its investments. The CASEE component (£30m total, with £15m from DFID) is expected to mobilize 5x additional capital, based on past performance of similar DFID-Shell Foundation partnerships.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both capital investments (equity/equity-like instruments for ARAF) and revenue funding (grants for research and technical assistance in CASEE and Lean Data components).
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £19,500,000" (40384354.odt, Summary Sheet) and "DFID will provide £15m over 5 years, match-funded by the Shell Foundation (SF), to establish the Catalysing Agriculture by Scaling Energy Ecosystems (CASEE) partnership." (40384354.odt, Component 1) and "The programme will mobilise £110m of additional financing." (40384354.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Private Enterprise Programme Zambia Phase II (PEPZ2)
metadata.quote: "The Private Enterprise Programme Zambia II (PEPZ2) programme will aim to systematically transform the finance and investment environment for SMEs in Zambia, helping companies to take promising business ideas to scale and become the engine of job creation in the economy." (D0004043.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 7 April 2020 for 7 years" (D0004043.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PEPZ2 is a financing mechanism that channels funds to SMEs while also building their capacity to utilize finance effectively. It combines direct investment (through Prospero Ltd) with policy support and learning components. The programme aims to transform Zambia's SME investment climate by attracting new investors, improving business capabilities, and addressing policy bottlenecks.
what_objectives.q1_source: "PEPZ2 will aim to systematically transform the finance and investment environment for SMEs in Zambia, helping companies to take promising business ideas to scale and become the engine of job creation in the economy." (D0004043.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Development of a more vibrant SME investment climate, with at least 5 new SME finance vehicles entering the Zambian market
At least 1,000 SMEs supported by the programme demonstrating growth and formalisation (measured by increased annual earnings before tax)
At least 30,000 jobs created, including at least 50% for women (and other groups such as people with disabilities)
Leverage of at least £100 million of private finance, with at least 10% from domestic Zambian sources
Scaled-up Zambian SMEs improving nutritional outcomes and climate resilience of populations accessing their goods/services
Research and evidence generated by the programme used to inform adaptive programming and influence other private sector programmes
Improved access to sustainable power for SMEs (through CIG support)
Enhanced trade facilitation through Nakonde border post upgrades (through TMA support)
what_objectives.summary: PEPZ2 combines financing mechanisms with capacity building and policy reform to create jobs through SME growth in Zambia, while addressing key constraints like access to finance, business capabilities, and the doing business environment.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will create jobs at scale, including for women, disabled people, and rural communities with high levels of poverty. SMEs supported by the programme will help to improve nutrition outcomes and improve climate resilience of smallholder farmers." (57554322.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Zambia is described as a stable democracy with macroeconomic management challenges and debt sustainability concerns, but not classified as FCAS. The programme identifies risks related to economic vulnerability, inequality, and institutional weaknesses that could affect SME growth.
where_context.q5_source: "Zambia is a stable democracy with a relatively good record on macroeconomic management (though this is currently in question with recent debt sustainability concerns)." (57554322.odt, A.2 Need for the programme)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and administrative barriers (e.g., slow e-government adoption, complex trade tariffs) make it difficult for SMEs to grow. Infrastructure deficits (e.g., unreliable power, poor border facilities) hinder trade and productivity. Climate risks (e.g., droughts) affect agricultural SMEs, while limited data (e.g., outdated enterprise surveys) constrain evidence-based decision-making.
where_context.quote: "The Global Competitiveness Report 2018 ranked Zambia at 118 out of 140 economies on competitiveness. The report highlights weaknesses in legal frameworks, slow adoption to e-government services, and poor connectivity." (57554322.odt, A.2 Need for the programme)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Prospero Ltd (Special Purpose Vehicle in Zambia)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Prospero Ltd board includes representatives from DFID-Zambia, CDC (UK), and the Zambian private sector, indicating shared decision-making. Operational delivery is led by local partners (Prospero, CIG, TMA) with FCDO oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to SMEs to utilize finance effectively
mentorship and strategic support for entrepreneurs
sector-specific policy and regulatory reforms
gender-inclusive investment practices
climate resilience training for agricultural SMEs

partner_organizations.name: Prospero Ltd
partner_organizations.role: Special Purpose Vehicle for SME investments and market development

partner_organizations.name: Cowater International (CIG Zambia)
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support for energy sector planning and infrastructure

partner_organizations.name: TradeMark Africa (TMA)
partner_organizations.role: Trade facilitation and border infrastructure upgrades (Nakonde border post)
partner_organizations.location: Zambia (LMIC, with regional HQ in Kenya)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Zambia
partner_organizations.role: Funding, oversight, and strategic direction

partner_organizations.name: CDC Group
partner_organizations.role: Co-investor and board representation in Prospero Ltd

partner_organizations.name: Policy Learning and Support (PLS) Adviser (to be recruited)
partner_organizations.role: Policy analysis and learning coordination

who_partners.quote: "Prospero has emerged as an important vehicle to support the achievement of the commitments under the UK-Zambia Green Growth Compact and FCDO’s business plan outcome on green and resilient economic development." (D0004043.odt, Summary Information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: PEPZ2 uses a combination of: 1) **Accountable Grant** to Prospero Ltd (a Zambian-registered SPV) for SME investments; 2) **Contracts** with CIG and TMA for technical assistance; and 3) **Direct FCDO funding** for the PLS adviser. Prospero recycles returns from investments to reinvest in new SMEs, creating a revolving fund.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Prospero Ltd acts as the central investment platform, with CIG and TMA as specialized technical partners. FCDO provides oversight through annual reviews and a unified logframe. The PLS adviser coordinates learning across components. Decision-making is shared between FCDO, Prospero’s board (with UK/Zambian representation), and technical partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: CIG and TMA were selected as existing FCDO suppliers with proven track records in Zambia. Prospero Ltd was established under PEPZ1 and continued for its demonstrated success. The PLS adviser will be recruited through open competition (ORB process).
how_mechanism.quote: "Both suppliers have successful track records of delivering FCDO programmes in Zambia and other countries. The incorporation of them into FCDO Zambia’s PEPZ2 programme builds on their existing FCDO business cases and extends their current programme activities in Zambia." (D0004043.odt, Information on additional suppliers)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Prospero Ltd is governed by a board with representatives from FCDO-Zambia, CDC, and the Zambian private sector. CIG and TMA report to FCDO Zambia under separate contracts but align with PEPZ2’s unified logframe. Annual reviews assess performance against shared indicators.
how_governance.quote: "The Annual Review will report on targets from the previous logframes as well as, where appropriate, targets from the revised consolidated logframe." (D0004043.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within Prospero Ltd can be reallocated between SME investments based on performance, but major shifts (e.g., adding new sectors) require FCDO approval. The addition of CIG and TMA reflects adaptive expansion to address emerging priorities (energy, trade).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses annual strategic planning to adjust sector focus (e.g., potential expansion into manufacturing/IT) and reallocate funds based on learning. New partners (CIG, TMA) were added mid-programme to address energy and trade barriers identified as critical for SME growth.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will focus on high potential growth sectors—initially the focus will be on agriculture, tourism, and supply chain services for the mining sector but there will be scope to expand into other high-potential sectors such as manufacturing, technology services." (57554322.odt, A.1 Programme purpose)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → [Prospero Ltd/CIG/TMA] → SMEs. The PLS adviser sits within FCDO Zambia, reducing layers for learning components.
how_efficiency.quote: "Prospero has so far received UK£4.4 million (US$6 million) from DFID since its incorporation. This has enabled Prospero to disburse US$5.5 million to Kukula Seed Fund, which has leveraged another US$9.7 million." (57554322.odt, Box 2: Recycling funds in Prospero)

q24_alternatives_considered: Micro-credit schemes (rejected: unlikely to drive SME growth at scale)
Direct support to formal banking sector (rejected: covered by FSDZ programme)
Angel investment funds (not ruled out but require rigorous appraisal)
Development Impact Bonds (considered but need thorough monitoring)
Sector-focused business environment reforms (selected: tailored to Zambian context)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was chosen to: 1) **Leverage existing platforms** (Prospero Ltd’s success in PEPZ1); 2) **Address multiple constraints** (finance, capacity, policy) simultaneously; 3) **Recycle funds** for sustainability (Prospero’s revolving model); 4) **Adapt to emerging needs** (adding CIG/TMA for energy/trade); and 5) **Balance efficiency and inclusion** (combining direct investments with technical assistance).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other programmes (e.g., FSDZ)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of labor (e.g., PEPZ2 focuses on SMEs needing £50k–£2m; FSDZ on formal banking sector) and joint coordination mechanisms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of Prospero Ltd post-programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Design as a revolving fund with recycled returns; board includes Zambian private sector for local ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Unified logframe and annual reviews to align activities; FCDO oversight for coherence.

why_rationale.quote: "The appraisal recommends that in order to achieve objectives 1 and 2, the PEPZ2 programme takes forward a portfolio of other activity options—ranging from business linkages, incubators, accelerators, direct investments, and investment promotion—with an emphasis on how they are collectively implemented to deliver change." (57554322.odt, B.4 VFM statement)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Zambia’s weak financial infrastructure (e.g., limited equity markets, high lending rates) necessitated the creation of Prospero Ltd as a local SPV to channel funds. Political economy constraints (e.g., slow regulatory reforms) led to focusing on sector-specific policy work (e.g., tourism, mining supply chains) rather than economy-wide changes.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited local investment vehicles → Prospero Ltd established as SPV
High due diligence costs for banks → Technical assistance embedded in programme
Border inefficiencies → TMA selected for trade facilitation
Energy deficits → CIG added for power sector support
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to **combine financing with capacity building** drove the mixed modality (Prospero for investments + technical partners for support). The goal of **scaling SMEs** required a revolving fund (Prospero) to recycle returns. **Policy bottlenecks** necessitated sector-specific partners (CIG for energy, TMA for trade).
q28_linkages: Financing objective (Objective 1) → Prospero Ltd as investment platform
Capacity building (Objective 2) → Embedded TA in Prospero and CIG/TMA
Policy reforms (Objective 3) → Sector-specific partners (CIG, TMA) linked to FCDO compact
Learning (Objective 4) → PLS adviser to synthesize across components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **speed** (using existing partners like CIG/TMA) with **inclusion** (50% women-owned SMEs target, disability analysis). **Efficiency** (Prospero’s revolving fund) is paired with **equity** (gender/disability safeguards in investments). The addition of CIG/TMA reflects a trade-off between **focus** (original SME finance mandate) and **broader impact** (addressing energy/trade barriers).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to CIG/TMA for rapid energy/trade fixes vs. competitive processes for equity
Expertise vs. ownership: UK-backed Prospero board vs. Zambian private sector representation
Focus vs. adaptation: Original sector focus (agriculture/tourism/mining) vs. adding energy/trade components
intersections.risk_affects_management: Zambia’s **moderate risk profile** (debt concerns, institutional weaknesses) led to **milestone-based oversight** (annual reviews) and **shared governance** (Prospero board with UK/Zambian reps) to mitigate fiscal and political risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local fund management capacity → Prospero Ltd designed as a **capacity-building vehicle** (training SMEs to use finance) while also **recycling funds** for sustainability. CIG/TMA added to fill gaps in **energy/trade expertise** lacking in original design.
intersections.quote: "The programme will aim to build a sustainable and vibrant investment environment for the SME sector, attracting new investors to the Zambian market; and helping firms to effectively access and utilise that finance." (57554322.odt, A.5 Intended impact)

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic instability (debt, inflation) affecting SME growth
Limited domestic capital mobilization despite programme targets
Political barriers to policy reforms (e.g., trade tariffs, licensing)
Climate shocks (droughts) disrupting agricultural SMEs
Overlap with other donors (e.g., World Bank, FSDZ)
Sustainability of Prospero Ltd post-FCDO funding
Gender/disability inclusion targets not met in male-dominated sectors (e.g., mining)
Border infrastructure delays (Nakonde upgrades)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversify SME sectors (beyond mining-dependent supply chains); focus on climate-resilient agriculture.
Prospero’s revolving fund design; partnerships with Zambian private sector (e.g., board representation).
Sector-specific reforms (e.g., tourism strategy) linked to FCDO-Zambia compact; political economy analysis.
Support off-grid energy SMEs; climate resilience training for farmers.
Coordination with FSDZ (banking sector) and World Bank (trade); unified logframe.
Recycled returns; board includes CDC and Zambian private sector for continuity.
50% women-owned SME target; gender analysis in start-up phase; TA for female entrepreneurs.
Phased upgrades (scanner first); World Bank co-funding for Nakonde OSBP.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: PEPZ1 demonstrated that SMEs need **‘more than just capital’** (e.g., TA for business plans) and that **venture capital can work in Zambia** (Kukula Seed Fund success). Challenges included **high due diligence costs** for banks and **low implementation rates** without mentorship. The **Impact Capital Africa** model (£40m SME opportunities) showed potential for scaling.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added **technical assistance** as core component (not just finance); 2) Expanded to **energy/trade** based on SME constraints; 3) **Unified logframe** for CIG/TMA to align with PEPZ2 outcomes; 4) **Gender/disability safeguards** embedded in investment criteria.
risks_lessons.quote: "PEPZ1 has demonstrated the potential for the UK support to private sector growth in Zambia... The programme has done some work on the ‘doing business’ environment, but not to the scale envisioned under PEPZ2." (57554322.odt, A.1 Programme purpose)

co_funding_partners.partner: Zambian private sector (via Prospero Ltd returns)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Target: £100 million private finance (10% from Zambian sources). PEPZ1 leveraged £16m; Prospero has already leveraged $9.7m alongside $5.5m DFID funds.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The addendum highlights increased focus on **capital spend** (e.g., Nakonde border infrastructure, energy planning) from FY24/25, alongside Prospero’s revolving fund for SME investments.
financial_details.quote: "Additional funding is expected to enable Prospero to expand its investment in SMEs and open the opportunity for the PEPZ2 programme to also address two key enabling environment barriers for SMEs: 1) access to sustainable power; 2) access to markets through international trade." (D0004043.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

metadata.programme_name: The Kenya Devolution Support Programme II
metadata.quote: The Kenya Devolution Support Programme II aims to strengthen the effectiveness of Kenya’s devolution process, specifically to improve development results by strengthening effective, open and accountable County Governments that improve service delivery and reduce poverty. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source:
Start Date: Jan 20
End Date: March 2025 (60043274.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening county governments), implementation research (testing digital approaches), and service delivery (improving public services). It also includes evidence generation and policy influence components.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will provide technical assistance to national and county government and also support civil society to build accountability. Citizens in target counties will benefit from improved service delivery by county government. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Intergovernmental relations support devolution
County governments effectively manage public finances, staff performance and county planning
Government and citizens collaborate effectively to address key problems in service delivery and poverty reduction
Evidence generation, learning and digital approaches improve county government delivery
The UK development portfolio is better aligned with county government priorities
County Capacity Assessment (CCA) Index scores increased from 33% in 15/16 to 64% in 17/18 (historical output)
Number of disclaimed county audits reduced from 22 to 5 from 16/17 to 17/18 (historical output)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Kenya's devolution process by improving county government effectiveness, service delivery, and poverty reduction through technical assistance, capacity building, and digital innovation.
what_objectives.quote: The programme will contribute to SDG16: Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a context with corruption risks, political disputes between county executives and legislatures, and occasional corruption scandals, but is not classified as high-risk or FCAS.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate (60043274.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political disputes between county executives and legislatures have caused delays in budget approvals. Corruption scandals and adverse audit reports affect some counties. Climate-related disasters (droughts/floods) create fiscal liabilities. Historical marginalization of regions like northern Kenya creates service delivery inequities.
where_context.quote: In a number of counties there have been political disputes between the county executive and legislature which have caused delays in budget approvals and expenditure. (60043274.odt, DFID’s support to Devolution in Kenya to date)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: UK FCDO (with World Bank, UNDP, and County Governments)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between UK FCDO (funding/strategic oversight), implementing partners (World Bank/UNDP), and county governments (local execution). The programme explicitly aims to strengthen county government ownership.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to national and county governments
support to civil society for accountability
training for county fiscal units modelled after the Parliamentary Budget Office
digital capacity building (e.g., SMS platforms, GIS laboratories)
performance management systems
gender audits of county budgets
disability audits for inclusive planning

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (Kenya Accountable Devolution Programme)

partner_organizations.name: UNDP
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (Devolution Support Programme)

partner_organizations.name: Council of Governors (Kenya)
partner_organizations.role: local coordination and peer learning (Maarifa Centre)

partner_organizations.name: County Governments (47 counties)
partner_organizations.role: primary beneficiaries and local implementers

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (e.g., Africa Centre for Open Governance)
partner_organizations.role: accountability and oversight

partner_organizations.name: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics
partner_organizations.role: data generation (e.g., Gross County Product)

partner_organizations.name: University of Nairobi (Institute for Development Studies)
partner_organizations.role: research and capacity assessments (County Capacity Assessment Index)

who_partners.quote: The programme will provide technical assistance to national and county government and also support civil society to build accountability. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (to implementing partners like World Bank/UNDP) and technical assistance contracts (e.g., for embedded advisors). It also includes direct support to county governments through capacity-building interventions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a multi-partner arrangement with FCDO as the funder, World Bank/UNDP as implementing partners, and county governments as local executors. It includes a Devolution Donor Working Group for coordination among donors (EU, Sweden, Denmark, etc.).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct continuation of KDSP I)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme builds on the previous Kenya Devolution Support Programme (KDSP I, 2015-19), which was implemented by the same partners (World Bank, UNDP). The rationale emphasizes continuity and leveraging existing relationships.
how_mechanism.quote: The £23.5m Kenya Devolution Support Programme (KDSP) will close in December 2019. It was implemented through three pre-existing devolution programmes: [...] DFID Kenya invested in innovation and efficiency by including a component on learning and coordination. (60043274.odt, DFID’s support to Devolution in Kenya to date)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DFID chairs the Devolution Donor Working Group, which includes donors (EU, Sweden, Denmark, etc.) and government stakeholders. The group uses a joint implementation matrix tracked monthly to coordinate interventions.
how_governance.quote: DFID currently chairs the devolution donor working group and convenes meetings amongst the devolution donors [...] The donors have a joint implementation matrix which they track monthly to ensure that the interventions are coordinated. (60043274.odt, DFID’s support to Devolution in Kenya to date)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between counties based on performance (e.g., scaling up in Makueni due to high performance, scaling down in Nairobi due to political disputes).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a break clause requiring additional approval for funding from March 2024. Political economy analysis and regular reviews inform adjustments.
how_flexibility.quote: This business case includes a break clause which will be replicated in all partner agreements. Funding from March 2024 will require additional approval in 2023. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (World Bank/UNDP) → County Governments/Civil Society
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will provide technical assistance to national and county government and also support civil society to build accountability. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: The counter-factual (do not fund, engage politically only)
Option 2: Technical assistance (expert advisors)
Option 3: Direct financial aid (transfers to government)
Option 4: Strengthening civil society
Option 5: Support priority service delivery sectors (e.g., health)
Option 6: Combination of the above (CHOSEN OPTION)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: A combined approach (Option 6) was selected to maximize impact by addressing multiple barriers simultaneously: weak intergovernmental relations, poor public financial management, limited citizen engagement, and evidence gaps. The rationale emphasizes the need for technical assistance, civil society support, and digital innovation to achieve sustainable devolution.
