q25_decision_factors: past experience (building on KDSP I lessons)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political contestation within counties (e.g., 2022 elections) may disrupt implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust political economy analysis, close monitoring via programme-funded posts, and regular review of county partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption scandals in target counties could damage HMG reputation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Scaling support based on performance (e.g., reducing support to Nairobi due to disputes) and public calls for accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented donor activity at sub-national level may reduce coherence.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s leadership in the Devolution Donor Working Group and joint implementation matrix for coordination.

why_rationale.quote: A combined set of interventions is required to have a maximum development impact. (60043274.odt, Programme summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy context (e.g., disputes between county executives and legislatures, corruption risks) limits partner selection to counties demonstrating commitment to open government and poverty reduction. Marginalized regions (e.g., northern arid lands) require tailored support due to capacity gaps.
q27_constraints_detail: Political disputes in counties (e.g., Nairobi) lead to reduced support
Corruption scandals exclude certain counties from partnership
Historical marginalization of arid lands requires targeted interventions
Urban-rural divides affect service delivery priorities
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both technical assistance (e.g., PFM strengthening) and civil society engagement (for accountability) requires a mixed delivery structure with multiple partners. Digital approaches (e.g., SMS platforms) necessitate partnerships with county governments and tech providers.
q28_linkages: Capacity building (WHAT) → Requires embedded advisors and local partners (HOW)
Evidence generation (WHAT) → Needs research institutions (e.g., University of Nairobi) and digital tools (HOW)
Service delivery improvements (WHAT) → Demands direct county government engagement (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting marginalized counties like Mandera, Wajir) with efficiency (scaling successful models like Makueni’s digital systems). Tensions include: (1) Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scaling of digital tools may exclude counties with low capacity; (2) Northern expertise vs. ownership: Technical assistance from World Bank/UNDP must align with local priorities.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: "Counties had very different levels of development at the outset of devolution [...] some will need far greater levels of assistance than others."

Expertise vs. ownership: "The UK is considered by the Government of Kenya as an important partner in the governance sector [...] Investing in subnational governance is essential for Kenya to build the systems to sustainably raise revenue."
Cost vs. reach: "The deployment of a limited number of programme-funded staff will further strengthen the depth of UK partnership with county governments."
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (political disputes, corruption) justifies intensive oversight via the Devolution Donor Working Group, monthly tracking of interventions, and adaptive management (e.g., break clause for 2024 funding).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with partners like the Council of Governors (Maarifa Centre) and University of Nairobi (CCA Index) playing key roles in knowledge sharing and performance monitoring. County governments with higher capacity (e.g., Makueni) receive scaled-up support.
intersections.quote: In recognition of the significance of devolution, DFID Kenya has developed a sub-national strategy which this programme will resource [...] to improve the coherence and relevance of the full DFID aid portfolio at the sub-national level. (60043274.odt, DFID’s sub-national strategy)

key_programme_risks: Political disputes between county executives and legislatures delaying budgets
Corruption scandals in target counties (reputational risk for HMG)
Variable progress across counties due to differing capacities
Public dissatisfaction in counties where minority groups feel excluded
Climate-related disasters (droughts/floods) disrupting service delivery
Fragmented donor activity at sub-national level
Potential constitutional review process politicizing devolution
Terrorism financing risks in operational areas

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Scale support based on performance (e.g., reduced support to Nairobi, increased to Makueni). Use political economy analysis to inform targeting.
Public calls for governors implicated in scandals to step aside. Support Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) and Auditor General.
Conduct County Capacity Assessments (CCA) to tailor support. Focus on peer learning via Regional Economic Blocks.
Integrate climate change adaptation into county planning. Support County Climate Change Funds.
Lead the Devolution Donor Working Group to coordinate interventions via a joint implementation matrix.
Apply due diligence frameworks to all partners. Include terrorism legislation references in agreements. Use third-party monitoring in high-risk areas.

fcas_specific_lessons: Devolution can address historic grievances (e.g., secessionist movements in coast/northeast) but requires conflict-sensitive approaches.
Intra-county tensions (e.g., non-local teachers threatened in Mandera) need localized conflict mitigation strategies.
Climate shocks (droughts/floods) must be integrated into fiscal planning to reduce long-term liabilities (2.4% of GDP annually).
Marginalized groups (women, youth, disabilities) require targeted inclusion to prevent exacerbating inequalities.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: KDSP I (2015-19) demonstrated that: (1) Capacity building (e.g., PFM improvements) leads to measurable gains (e.g., unqualified audits in 2 counties); (2) Digital tools (e.g., SMS platforms in Meru) improve service delivery but require scaling; (3) Political economy analysis is critical for targeting (e.g., scaling down in Nairobi due to disputes); (4) Regional Economic Blocks (e.g., Lake Region) enhance coordination.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Increased emphasis on measurable service delivery results (e.g., health outcomes) based on KDSP I’s mixed health sector impacts.
Stronger focus on digital approaches (aligned with Kenya’s Digital Economic Blueprint 2019) due to success of pilot projects (e.g., GIS lab in Makueni).
Enhanced inclusion agenda (youth, women, disabilities) based on gaps identified in KDSP I.
Adaptive management mechanisms (e.g., break clause for 2024 funding) added to respond to political risks.
Deeper integration with DFID’s sub-national strategy to improve portfolio coherence.
risks_lessons.quote: The KDSP Annual Review recommended that the new DFID devolution programme should: Increase emphasis on achieving measurable improvements in priority sector-specific service delivery results [...] Develop further the UK’s role in championing the inclusion agenda. (60043274.odt, The KDSP Annual Review recommended)

co_funding_partners.partner: World Bank (via Kenya Accountable Devolution Programme)
EU, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, US (via Devolution Donor Working Group)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages multi-donor coordination through the Devolution Donor Working Group, which includes EU, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and US. Previous phases (KDSP I) mobilized £28m+ from multiple donors.
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: £38.5m (60043274.odt, SummarySheet)

metadata.programme_name: Innovative Methods and Metrics for Agriculture and Nutrition Actions (IMMANA) Phase 2
metadata.quote: Tackling global challenges of malnutrition in the face of growing climate change and environmental constraints requires robust evidence to underpin investments in agriculture and food systems. (49121134.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: Start Date: 01.07.2019; End Date: 31.07.2024. (49121134.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: IMMANA Phase 2 aims to generate high-quality evidence linking agriculture, nutrition, and health to underpin effective policy and programme investments. It combines evidence generation (research), technology development (metrics and tools), capacity building (training researchers), and policy influence (synthesis and uptake of data).
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will create a step change in the generation of high quality evidence linking agriculture, nutrition and health, to underpin effective policy and programmes. (49121134.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 16 IMMANA competitive research grants to develop new and validate existing innovative methods and metrics
24 IMMANA Fellows equipped to develop or apply innovative methods and metrics
24 Fellowship reports, each with at least one methodologically oriented article publishable in an internationally peer-reviewed journal
At least 20 peer-reviewed research articles and research uptake products suite
5 annual Academy weeks with 350-400 participants primarily from the global south
At least 5 synthesis products on tools, methods, metrics published in high-impact journals
A global research network (ANH Academy) with over 1,500 members
A synthesis centre to enable better use of existing data for decision-making
what_objectives.summary: IMMANA Phase 2 builds on Phase 1's achievements to validate and scale new methods and metrics, strengthen research capacity, and foster a global network for knowledge sharing and policy uptake in agriculture, nutrition, and health.
what_objectives.quote: The first phase of IMMANA has delivered new methods and metrics, and built a global community of practice (>1,500 members) to share evidence and build capacity. (49121134.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as moderate risk, based on an independent review of Phase 1 which showed it to be well-managed and effective.
where_context.q5_source: The level of risk is assessed as moderate. (49121134.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The lack of reliable tools to evaluate policy and programme impacts, assess trade-offs, and measure cost-effectiveness constrains effective interventions. Climate change and resource scarcity add to the challenges of meeting food and nutrition needs.
where_context.quote: Effective, evidence-based interventions are constrained by a lack of reliable tools to evaluate policy and programme impacts, assess trade-offs and cost-effectiveness. (49121134.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The lead institution (LSHTM) and Tufts University (USA) manage the programme, with significant involvement from Southern partners through fellowships and the ANH Academy network.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (Learning Labs, webinars, online courses)
mentorship (Fellowships with 24 emerging leaders)
research grants (competitive grants for Southern researchers)
institutional strengthening (ANH Academy network)

partner_organizations.name: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
partner_organizations.role: Lead institution, programme management, ANH Academy

partner_organizations.name: Tufts University
partner_organizations.role: Core partner, leads IMMANA Fellowship component

partner_organizations.name: SOAS University of London
partner_organizations.role: Strengthened role in IMMANA 2.0

partner_organizations.name: CGIAR Agriculture for Nutrition and Health (A4NH)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder, technical support, Academy sponsorship

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder (subject to approval)

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: Steering committee member, potential co-funder

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-funder

who_partners.quote: LSHTM is the IMMANA Phase 1 grant-holder. Both the EMTR and successive DFID Annual Reviews have shown that it has a successful track record in adapting its systems to ensure a high-quality programme. (49121134.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an Accountable Grant for the core funding, with additional co-funding from other donors (e.g., BMGF, CGIAR). Competitive grants are awarded to researchers through open calls.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by LSHTM and Tufts University, with a Steering Committee involving multiple donors. The ANH Academy operates as a global network for knowledge sharing and capacity building.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The decision to continue with the existing partners (LSHTM and Tufts) was based on their strong performance in Phase 1, as evidenced by the External Mid-Term Review, and to avoid high transaction costs of procuring a new supplier.
how_mechanism.quote: Under this option, DFID would negotiate the design of a new phase of support to the current IMMANA programme, with the existing providers. (49121134.odt, Why the modality was chosen)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee involves a wider set of research funders and meets at least 3 times a year to approve competitive grants and advise on direction.
how_governance.quote: A Steering Committee involving a wider set of research funders would meet at least 3 times a year to approve competitive grants, and advise on direction. (49121134.odt, Option 2: Invest in a new phase of support)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID and the Steering Committee to shape outputs, defer/cancel payments if quality is lacking, and accelerate activities in response to opportunities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments based on emerging priorities, as evidenced by the shift from subsistence agriculture to complex food systems thinking.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme will be managed using principles of flexible and adaptive programming, with flexibility for DFID and members of the Steering committee to (1) shape the outputs (2) defer/cancel payments if quality is lacking, and (3) accelerate activities in response to opportunities. (49121134.odt, Summary Sheet)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → LSHTM/Tufts Consortium → Sub-grantees (researchers, fellows)
how_efficiency.quote: The cost of managing grants within IMMANA is broadly comparable with the costs levied through other programmes (10-20%). (49121134.odt, Option 2: Strength of evidence)

q24_alternatives_considered: Procure a new Research Fund Manager to develop and manage a new competitive grants programme
Invest in a new phase of support to the existing programme, drawing in additional funders
Discontinue dedicated investment in this area beyond the current project; continue with some metrics investments via CGIAR A4NH programme

It also includes elements of **capacity building** through collaboration with developing country partners.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This research programme will enable us to better understand which economic activities in developing countries generate the highest productivity gains and whether resources are allocated efficiently towards these most productive activities... help developing countries determine what paths of economic development will best facilitate economic growth and sustained development." what_objectives.summary: STEG aims to generate new evidence on productivity and structural change in low-income countries (LICs) to inform policies and interventions that facilitate sustained economic growth and poverty reduction. The programme combines research, policy engagement, and capacity-building activities to achieve its objectives.

quote.text: "The objective of the Structural Change and Economic Growth Programme (STEG) is to better understand how governments and development partners can facilitate the process of structural change and improved productivity, growth and poverty reduction in Africa." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)

countries_regions: Low-Income Countries (LICs) with high population growth rates
Global (not limited to Africa; includes success stories from other regions)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as "minor/moderate" risk, with funds likely to go to established research institutions with robust systems for managing delivery, finance, and risk. The Research Programme Consortium (RPC) will be required to develop risk management frameworks, particularly for low-capacity and FCAS contexts.
where_context.q5_source: "Risk is assessed as minor/moderate. Funds are likely to go to established research institutions with robust systems for managing delivery, finance and risk." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)
q6_contextual_constraints: heterogeneity in productivity across firms and sectors
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The lack of detailed data on productivity and structural change in LICs limits the ability to design effective interventions. Weak institutions and political economy factors may hinder the implementation of policies that facilitate structural change. Rapid technological changes (e.g., automation) may alter traditional development pathways, requiring adaptive research and policy responses.

quote.text: "Recent evidence highlights the large dispersion of productivity in developing countries within each of the traditional sectors of agriculture, manufacturing and services, across firms, plants and farms... This calls for new approaches that document where productivity gains are highest, and that go beyond the study of allocation between the three traditional sectors." (Document: 35715594.odt, Programme Summary)

While the document emphasizes collaboration with developing country partners (e.g., Advisory Group with country representatives), it does not explicitly state who holds decision-making power. The RPC lead will likely be a Northern institution, but Southern partners will be involved in research design and implementation.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will be delivered through a **competitively tendered contract** for a Research Programme Consortium (RPC). The RPC will manage the research funds and sub-contract research activities as needed. This approach ensures accountability and alignment with DFID’s operational priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The RPC will act as a **closed consortium** with a lead organization responsible for managing sub-contracts and ensuring coherence across research streams. The consortium will include multiple partners (likely a mix of universities, think tanks, and research institutions) but will operate under a single contract with DFID. An Advisory Group (AG) with DFID and developing country representatives will provide oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: An **open competitive tender** was chosen to ensure high-quality research at a competitive price. This method also allows DFID to select a consortium with the best combination of technical expertise, policy influence, and experience in LICs. The tender process will include criteria such as the ability to engage with policymakers, link to DFID’s country work, and demonstrate value for money.

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: The RPC will manage sub-awards, though the document suggests that **60% or more of research funds may be subject to open competition** (Option 2 considered). This would allow the RPC to issue competitive calls for specific research projects, ensuring continued quality and value for money.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: An **Advisory Group (AG)** will include DFID policy and country staff, as well as developing country representatives. The AG will provide input into the research programme and help translate findings into policy and practice. The RPC will also be required to link with existing DFID-funded research programmes (e.g., IGC, PEDL).
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: The RPC contract will include **regular reviews** to allow for course correction. The programme steering group (including country representatives) will provide ongoing input. This structure balances flexibility with accountability, ensuring alignment with DFID’s priorities.

quote.text: "The RPC contract will be structured to ensure regular review in order to allow course correction. It is anticipated that the project steering group will include country representation who will input into the research programme." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components **with approval**, as the RPC contract will include mechanisms for regular review and course correction. The steering group (with country representation) will provide input on adjustments, but major shifts will likely require DFID approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be **adaptive**, with regular reviews and an Advisory Group to ensure research remains relevant. While the overarching objectives (productivity, structural change, growth) are fixed, specific research questions and country foci can be adjusted based on emerging evidence and context changes. The 9-month inception phase will allow for fine-tuning of the research agenda.

quote.text: "The RPC contract will be structured to ensure regular review in order to allow course correction... This management structure will allow for work-streams and funds to be shifted should the context require." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Research Programme Consortium (RPC) → end researchers (including sub-contracts). The RPC acts as an intermediary, managing sub-awards and ensuring coherence.

quote.text: "The RPC contract will be structured to ensure regular review in order to allow course correction." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Single new contract for RPC (all research delivered through RPC)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: A closed consortium with no open competition for sub-awards. Risk of limited innovation and potential capture of funds by RPC members.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Single new contract for RPC with 60%+ funds subject to open competition
q24_alternatives_considered.description: RPC manages core research but issues competitive calls for 60%+ of funds. Balances coherence with innovation and value for money.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Partner with multilateral institution (e.g., World Bank or UNU-WIDER)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Faster procurement but less control over research agenda and linkages with DFID country offices.
Not explicitly detailed but implied as a potential hybrid approach.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **RPC with 60%+ open competition (Option 2)** was preferred because it balances **coherence** (single consortium) with **innovation and value for money** (competitive calls). This model leverages DFID’s past experience with RPCs (e.g., EDI, PEDL) and ensures continued competition, which drives quality and efficiency. The structure also allows for flexibility in research priorities and strong linkages with DFID’s country work.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (competitive calls drive efficiency)
risk mitigation (established RPC model with regular reviews)
past experience (success of similar RPCs like EDI and PEDL)
policy relevance (strong links to DFID country offices)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capture of funds by RPC members (limited competition post-award)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Requiring 60%+ of funds to be subject to open competition throughout the programme life.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of coherence with open competition
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong RPC management and regular reviews to ensure alignment with programme objectives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in procurement (competitive tender process)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structured procurement timeline with clear milestones; inception phase to refine research agenda.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership in RPC-led model
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advisory Group with developing country representatives; requirement for RPC to undertake research in LICs.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (open calls for 60%+ of funds to drive VfM)
effectiveness (policy-relevant research with strong uptake mechanisms)
equity (inclusion of Southern partners via Advisory Group and country focus)

quote.text: "Option 2: A single new contract for a Research Programme Consortium (RPC) selected through competitive tender – BUT with 60% or more of research funds subject to open competition... The major and significant benefit over option 1 is that some of the funds will be subject to continued competition throughout the programme’s life." (Document: 35715594.odt, Assessment of the supplier market)
quote.source: Document: 35715594.odt, Assessment of the supplier market

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope with a focus on LICs (especially Sub-Saharan Africa)** constrains partner selection to organizations with: (1) **experience in fragile and low-capacity contexts**, (2) **ability to work across diverse economic structures**, and (3) **links to DFID priority countries**. The need for **policy-relevant research** further limits partners to those with strong ties to governments and multilateral institutions in LICs.
q27_constraints_detail: requirement for experience in LICs/FCAS contexts
need for multi-country research capacity
policy engagement skills for uptake in DFID priority countries
ability to manage data limitations in LICs
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for cross-country comparative research** (to understand diverse structural change pathways) determines the **consortium delivery structure**, as no single institution could cover all required contexts. The **policy influence objective** drives the inclusion of an Advisory Group with country representatives. The **adaptive nature of the research** (responding to new data/technological changes) requires a flexible RPC structure with regular reviews.
q28_linkages: multi-country scope → consortium model (no single org could cover all contexts)
policy influence goal → Advisory Group with country reps
adaptive research needs → RPC with regular reviews and open competition
focus on LICs → requirement for RPC to include Southern partners
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly acknowledges tensions between: (1) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership** (mitigated via Advisory Group and country-focused research), and (2) **coherence vs. competition** (addressed by RPC structure with 60% open calls). The **9-month inception phase** also reflects a trade-off between speed and inclusive agenda-setting.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Advisory Group with developing country reps; research in LICs
60% of funds via open calls; RPC manages integration
9-month inception to refine agenda with stakeholders

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (minor/moderate) leads to **milestone-based oversight** with regular reviews. The RPC must develop **risk management frameworks**, especially for work in **low-capacity and FCAS contexts**. This increases management intensity compared to a low-risk programme but is balanced by the use of established research institutions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in the programme, with Southern partners playing key roles in: (1) **Advisory Group** (strategic input), (2) **country-level research** (data collection/analysis), and (3) **policy uptake** (translating findings into local interventions). The RPC is expected to include **gender specialists** and ensure disaggregated data, further shaping partner roles.

quote.text: "We will ask bidders to show how they will ensure the research is undertaken in developing countries with different economic characteristics, is highly policy relevant and linked to DFID’s country work... We anticipate having DFID policy and country staff as well as developing country representatives sitting on an Advisory Group (AG) for the project." (Document: 35715594.odt, Intervention Summary)

key_programme_risks.risk: Limited understanding of productivity and structural change in LICs
key_programme_risks.description: Existing evidence is fragmented, and traditional sectoral analyses (agriculture/manufacturing/services) may not capture current dynamics.

key_programme_risks.risk: Automation and AI altering development pathways
key_programme_risks.description: Technological changes (e.g., robotics in manufacturing) may render traditional industrialization paths obsolete for LICs.

key_programme_risks.risk: Erratic growth episodes in LICs
key_programme_risks.description: Many LICs experience boom-bust cycles rather than sustained growth, complicating policy design.

key_programme_risks.risk: Capture of research agenda by RPC
key_programme_risks.description: Without competition, RPC members may dominate the research priorities, limiting innovation.

key_programme_risks.risk: Weak policy uptake in partner countries
key_programme_risks.description: Even with strong evidence, political economy factors may hinder the adoption of recommended policies.

key_programme_risks.risk: Data limitations in LICs
key_programme_risks.description: Lack of detailed productivity data may constrain the quality of research outputs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-country research with diverse economic contexts; use of new micro and macro data.
Explicit research questions on technology and future productivity pathways.
Focus on understanding political economy drivers of growth (e.g., "Deals and Development" framework).
60%+ of funds via open competition; Advisory Group with external stakeholders.
Pro-active engagement with policymakers from research design stage; targeted communication strategies.
Collaboration with local institutions for data collection; methodological innovations.

fcas_specific_lessons: Risk management frameworks must be tailored for **low-capacity and FCAS contexts** (e.g., robust financial controls, compliance checks).
Research in fragile states requires **additional oversight** (e.g., HMG OSJA Guidance for security/justice-related work).
While fragility is a cross-cutting issue, STEG will **not focus specifically on highly fragile economies**, as these require dedicated programmes.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **PEDL, EDI, and IGC** highlight the value of: (1) **open competitive calls** for driving quality and VfM, (2) **Advisory Groups** for policy relevance, and (3) **regular reviews** for adaptive management. The **RAND review (2016)** of DFID-funded research confirmed that open calls improve both research quality and cost-effectiveness.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Inclusion of **60% open competition** (learned from PEDL/EDI).
Stronger **Advisory Group** with country reps (based on IGC experience).
Explicit **gender mainstreaming** (from GLM-LIC lessons).
**9-month inception phase** to refine agenda (addressing past issues with rigid research plans).

quote.text: "Experience with other DFID programmes (such as the Private Enterprise Development in LICs (PEDL) and Economic Development and Institutions (EDI)) has shown that this approach helps research programmes to continue to benefit from competition driving costs, efficiency and VfM." (Document: 35715594.odt, Assessment of the supplier market)
quote.source: Document: 35715594.odt, Assessment of the supplier market

quote.text: "Programme Value: £12m" (Document: 35715594.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Supporting Economic Empowerment and Development in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (SEED OPTs)
metadata.duration_text: Start Date: 02 November 2018, End Date: March 2028
metadata.quote: "The Support Economic Empowerment and Development in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPTs) programme provides economic development assistance to address binding constraints to sustainable growth and job creation in the OPTs." (D0007021.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 02 November 2018, End Date: March 2028" (D0007021.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (institutional strengthening), policy influence (engagement with PA and Israel), implementation research (testing approaches for economic inclusion), and service delivery (infrastructure investment in water/electricity). It also includes financing mechanisms through the Liquidity Support Facility.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will focus on policy engagement; capacity building and infrastructure investment in the following four sectors, which constitute the most binding constraints to economic growth: Access, movement and trade; Clean water and sanitation; Electricity; Customs revenue collection and management." (36210494.odt, Focus of UK Support and Desired Impact) AND "The additional funding will be used to establish a Liquidity Support Facility to promote private sector investment and help the sector become financially sustainable." (52339643.odt, Expected Results)
q3_expected_outputs: 1,000 full-time equivalent jobs (with minimum 390 in Gaza and 200 for women)
£5 million increase in directly attributable annual business sales (including £1.53m for Gaza-based SMEs)
£609k saved annually for 50 companies receiving solar panel support (equivalent to 38,000 kg of CO2 per company)
Basic water and energy services resumed in project areas in Gaza
PA’s water and energy institutions’ capacities improved including development of reconstruction plans
Water and energy infrastructure developed in support to stabilise the West Bank economy
Analytical work on the resumption of basic services in Gaza developed
Key asks developed to coordinate international efforts to lobby for resumption of basic services in Gaza
Reduction in the average cost of electricity supplied to Gaza and West Bank
Reduction in the average grid carbon intensity in the West Bank and Gaza
Increases in water supplied for domestic/agricultural use
Reductions in non-revenue water (water losses)
Increases in the value of shipments between the West Bank and Israel using the Door-to-Door programme
Reductions in fiscal leakages as a result improved implementation of the Paris Protocol
Formal allocation of specific spectrum bands for 4G and 5G in the OPTs
Improved coordination and cooperation between Israeli and Palestinian security forces in the West Bank
what_objectives.summary: SEED OPTs aims to address binding constraints to sustainable economic growth in the OPTs through a combination of infrastructure investment, institutional capacity building, policy engagement, and private sector support, with a focus on water, electricity, trade, and customs. The programme explicitly targets marginalized groups (women, youth, disabled) and adapts to the volatile political context, including recent conflicts.
what_objectives.quote: "The desired impact of the UK economic development programme is to contribute to the viability of a two-state solution by supporting inclusive economic growth." (36210494.odt, Focus of UK Support and Desired Impact) AND "The objectives of this time and cost extension are therefore to: Maintain economic stability in the West Bank, Support early economic recovery of Gaza when the situation allows, and Provide strategic technical assistance to the new Prime Minister." (D0007021.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

countries_regions: Occupied Palestinian Territories (West Bank and Gaza)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a fragile and conflict-affected setting (FCAS) with major risks due to ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict, political instability, and recent escalations (October 2023 Hamas attacks). The risk rating is explicitly stated as 'major' with high volatility.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme is assessed as a major risk because of the extremely challenging political context - but has the potential to deliver extremely high returns." (36210494.odt, Overall programme risk rating) AND "The current programme continues to operate in a complex and volatile environment. Some of the previously identified risks in the original Business Case have materialised and new, significant risks have been identified due to the Gaza conflict and new interventions proposed." (D0007021.odt, Risk Overview)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Israeli-imposed restrictions on movement/access/trade (e.g., Gaza blockade, Area C controls) cripple economic activity. Weak PA institutions and fiscal crises (e.g., clearance revenue withholding) limit service delivery. Energy/water shortages (e.g., 4-8 hours/day electricity in Gaza) disrupt businesses and households. Political divisions (Fatah-Hamas) hinder Gaza investments. Recent conflict (Oct 2023) destroyed 60% of Gaza’s infrastructure, requiring reconstruction. Climate vulnerabilities (e.g., water scarcity, reliance on diesel generators) exacerbate economic fragility.
where_context.quote: "The fundamental barrier to a stronger economy is the political conflict between the Government of Israel and both the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the de facto authorities in Gaza; and between the PA and the de facto authorities in Gaza." (36210494.odt, Context and the need for a DFID intervention) AND "The war in Gaza and security deterioration in the West Bank have significantly worsened the fundamental challenges facing the OPTs." (D0007021.odt, Context and economic situation)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority, with implementation delegated to multilateral partners (World Bank, OQ) and a UK-based service provider (Cowater). Palestinian institutions (PA, PENRA) have operational roles but limited strategic control due to political constraints.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to PA ministries (Finance, National Economy, Industry)
embedded advisors in Prime Minister’s Office and Delivery Unit
training for Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority (PENRA)
support to Palestinian Electricity Transmission Company (PETL) and DISCOs
gender-inclusive training for women-led businesses
institutional reforms for water/electricity utilities

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of water/energy infrastructure projects (PID MDTF, ASPIRE programme) and Liquidity Support Facility

partner_organizations.name: Office of the Quartet (OQ)
partner_organizations.role: Policy coordination between PA and Israel; sectoral dialogue (water, energy, trade, customs)

partner_organizations.name: Cowater International (Tasdeer programme)
partner_organizations.role: Trade facilitation, customs support, private sector grants, and technical assistance to PA ministries

partner_organizations.name: Palestinian Authority (PA) institutions
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary and operational partner (e.g., PENRA, Ministry of Finance, PETL, CMWU)

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Trade finance and energy efficiency investments (initial phase, later replaced by World Bank)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF/UNDP
partner_organizations.role: Emergency water/energy service delivery in Gaza (via World Bank trust funds)

who_partners.quote: "DFID support to the OQ will be focused on... Energy, Water, Movement and Trade, Rule of Law." (36210494.odt, The Office of the Quartet) AND "The programme will be delivered by the World Bank (WB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), a contracted service provider and the Office of the Quartet (OQ)." (36210494.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "The addendum will increase Tasdeer’s budget by £15m and amend its end date from September 2025 to March 2028." (D0007021.odt, Our Response)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of: 1) **Core funding** for the Office of the Quartet (shifted from earmarked to core in D0001028.odt), 2) **Trust funds** managed by the World Bank (PID MDTF, ASPIRE), and 3) **Contract** with Cowater for the Tasdeer programme. The Liquidity Support Facility operates as a revolving fund within ASPIRE.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees three parallel components: 1) World Bank trust funds (water/energy), 2) OQ policy coordination, and 3) Cowater-led Tasdeer programme (trade/customs). Each component has distinct governance but reports to FCDO’s Economic Development and Institutions Team in Jerusalem.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: World Bank and OQ were selected due to their existing mandates and track records in OPTs. Cowater was awarded via a **commercial contract** (D0007021.odt: "FCDO has an operating commercial contract with Cowater International"). The shift to core funding for OQ (D0001028.odt) aimed to reduce management costs and improve efficiency.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will be delivered by the World Bank (WB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), a contracted service provider and the Office of the Quartet (OQ)." (36210494.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "The payment modality for UK support will change from earmarked funding to core funding." (D0001028.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "FCDO has an operating commercial contract with Cowater International to deliver the Tasdeer programme." (D0007021.odt, Risk and Safeguarding)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The World Bank’s ASPIRE programme includes a **Project Management Unit (PMU)** with PA institutions (PENRA, PETL) and donor oversight. The Liquidity Support Facility has a **sunset clause** and **5-year reviews** with DFID/World Bank participation. OQ’s governance was strengthened in 2021 with a **single log frame** and central office monitoring (D0001028.odt).
how_governance.quote: "The disbursement of funding into the Liquidity Support Facility is conditioned on the ability of the Ministry of Finance (MOF), PENRA, and PETL to establish the facility within a pre-defined period... There will also be a review of the facility’s effectiveness and use every five years." (52339643.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "The OQ has also strengthened its central office operation to implement a new system to monitor progress and evaluate impact." (D0001028.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "The business case will continue to be managed by the BCGJ Jerusalem’s Economic Development and Institutions Team." (D0007021.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be shifted between components (e.g., water/energy/trade) with FCDO approval, as demonstrated by the £20m reallocation to ASPIRE in 2019 (52339643.odt) and the £32m extension in 2024 (D0007021.odt). The Liquidity Support Facility allows adaptive use based on private sector demand.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme explicitly designs for volatility: 1) **Breakout period** in FY2025 to adjust budgets post-UK spending review (D0007021.odt), 2) **Contingent funding** (£3m IRF) for Gaza recovery, 3) **Scalable interventions** (e.g., solar PV pilots → potential SPV), 4) **Context-driven shifts** between West Bank/Gaza based on security.
how_flexibility.quote: "A flexible and adaptive approach will be utilised to deliver the programme’s objectives. This will include the ability to move funding between these modalities to reflect performance and opportunities as they arise whilst maintaining within the overall budget ceiling." (36210494.odt, The Preferred Option) AND "The addendum will include a breakout period at the start of FY2025 in any agreements. This will enable funding modifications (including increased or decreased budgets) following the UK’s spending review." (D0007021.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (World Bank/OQ/Cowater) → End Beneficiaries (PA institutions, businesses, households). No explicit sub-grantee layer documented.
how_efficiency.quote: "The disbursement of funding into the Liquidity Support Facility is conditioned on the ability of the Ministry of Finance (MOF), PENRA, and PETL to establish the facility within a pre-defined period." (52339643.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "The programme will be managed by the BCGJ Jerusalem’s Economic Development and Institutions Team." (D0007021.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do-Nothing: Inaction would fail to address post-conflict needs (D0007021.odt).
New Business Case: Would create delivery gaps during design phase (D0007021.odt).
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The extension was selected to: 1) **Leverage existing partnerships** (World Bank/OQ/Cowater) with proven delivery in OPTs, 2) **Respond rapidly** to post-October 2023 crisis without design delays, 3) **Maintain flexibility** for Gaza recovery timing, 4) **Capitalize on PA reform momentum** under new government (2024), and 5) **Achieve economies of scale** by building on £59m existing investment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in Gaza due to Hamas presence and weak PA governance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Zero-tolerance policy with due diligence (vetting beneficiaries, delivery chain mapping, zero-tax invoices). Funds channeled via World Bank trust funds with PA agencies under stringent safeguards (52339643.odt, D0007021.odt).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political blockages (e.g., Israel-PA dialogue collapse, Hamas-Fatah divisions)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: OQ’s convening role and FCDO’s diplomatic leverage to broker technical agreements (e.g., electricity PPAs). Adaptive funding shifts between West Bank/Gaza (D0007021.odt).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector reluctance to invest in energy sector
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Liquidity Support Facility provides payment guarantees to de-risk investments. Pilot solar projects demonstrate viability (52339643.odt).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: PA fiscal collapse limiting co-financing
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance to Ministry of Finance and Prime Minister’s Office to improve revenue collection (e.g., electronic VAT clearance). Direct support to critical utilities (PETL, CMWU) (D0007021.odt).

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option is Option 2 [scaled-up mixed modality]... because it delivers the right combination of political and strategic engagement, institutional capacity building, infrastructure development and firm level support given available resources." (36210494.odt, The Preferred Option) AND "The addendum will allow the programme to provide further support to the three main project components... with indicative annual allocations by component." (D0007021.odt, Our Response) AND "The proposed additional funding is expected to further contribute to the gender equality as part of the programme’s overarching objectives." (52339643.odt, Gender Equality)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context restricts partner selection to entities with: 1) **Multilateral legitimacy** (World Bank/OQ can engage Israel/PA), 2) **Conflict-sensitive safeguards** (e.g., World Bank’s PA agency channels in Gaza), 3) **FCDO’s diplomatic cover** (OQ’s role in Israel-PA dialogue). Local Palestinian institutions lack direct access to funds due to Hamas risks and weak fiscal systems.
q27_constraints_detail: Israeli restrictions on Gaza access limit on-the-ground implementers
Hamas’ presence requires multilateral intermediaries (World Bank trust funds)
PA’s weak capacity necessitates embedded technical assistance (Cowater advisors)
Donor coordination gaps demand OQ’s convening role
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (infrastructure + policy + private sector) require a **multi-instrument structure**: 1) **Trust funds** for capital-intensive water/energy projects (World Bank), 2) **Core funding** for political coordination (OQ), 3) **Contracts** for agile private sector support (Cowater). The **adaptive management** design reflects the need to toggle between West Bank stabilisation and Gaza recovery based on conflict dynamics.
q28_linkages: Policy influence objectives → OQ’s convening role and FCDO diplomatic leverage
Infrastructure goals → World Bank’s trust funds and technical assistance
Private sector focus → Cowater’s grant mechanisms and Tasdeer programme
Gender inclusion → Cross-cutting requirements across all components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid Gaza recovery risks sidelining marginalized groups (e.g., disabled, female-headed households), mitigated by targeted solar/PV pilots (52339643.odt). 2) **Northern expertise vs. local ownership**: Cowater’s UK-based management ensures efficiency but limits PA decision-making; mitigated by embedded advisors in PMO (D0007021.odt). 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Liquidity Facility’s private sector focus may exclude informal businesses; addressed via grants for micro-enterprises.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Urgent energy/water needs vs. long-term institutional reform
Multilateral safeguards (World Bank) vs. PA ownership
West Bank stabilisation vs. Gaza recovery priorities
Technical assistance costs vs. scalable impact
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **major/FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight**: 1) World Bank’s 5-year reviews for Liquidity Facility, 2) OQ’s strengthened monitoring systems (D0001028.odt), 3) FCDO’s embedded Economic Development Team in Jerusalem, 4) Quarterly risk reassessments post-October 2023 (D0007021.odt).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **central to partner roles**: 1) **PA institutions** (PENRA, PETL) receive technical assistance to qualify for Liquidity Facility access, 2) **Cowater** embeds advisors in ministries to co-develop reforms, 3) **OQ** brokers Israel-PA dialogues to unlock sectoral changes (e.g., customs revenue transfers).
intersections.quote: "The fundamental barrier to a stronger economy is the political conflict between the Government of Israel and both the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the de facto authorities in Gaza... This reduces incentives for Israel to support growth in the OPTs as a whole, and for the PA to invest in Gaza." (36210494.odt, Context and the need for a DFID intervention) AND "The OQ plays a unique role in the OPTs by bringing together Palestinian and Israeli officials and politicians to agree on actions to promote economic development and ease restrictions of the occupation." (36210494.odt, The Office of the Quartet) AND "The addendum will increase Tasdeer’s budget by £15m and amend its end date from September 2025 to March 2028... to support economic stabilisation in the West Bank and recovery in Gaza." (D0007021.odt, Our Response)

key_programme_risks: Israeli-Palestinian political stalemate blocking sectoral agreements (e.g., water purchases, customs transfers)
PA fiscal collapse limiting co-financing for infrastructure
Hamas diversion of aid in Gaza (mitigated via World Bank trust funds)
Private sector reluctance to invest in energy sector without guarantees
Climate vulnerabilities (e.g., water scarcity, diesel pollution) exacerbating economic shocks
Gender backsliding due to conflict (e.g., 61% of women report increased domestic violence during energy crises - 52339643.odt)
Donor fatigue reducing parallel funding for reconstruction
PA institutional fragmentation (e.g., Fatah-Hamas divide) hindering Gaza interventions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: World Bank trust funds with PA agencies; vetting of beneficiaries; zero-tax invoices; delivery chain mapping (D0007021.odt).
Technical assistance to Ministry of Finance for revenue collection (e.g., electronic VAT); Liquidity Facility to reduce energy sector arrears (52339643.odt).
OQ’s convening role for civil measures; adaptive funding shifts to West Bank if Gaza access blocked (D0007021.odt).
Liquidity Support Facility guarantees; solar PV pilots to demonstrate viability; grants for MSMEs (D0007021.odt).
Solar energy investments; efficient irrigation systems; integration of climate resilience in reconstruction plans (D0007021.odt).
Targeted support for female-headed households in solar programmes; gender-disaggregated monitoring (52339643.odt).

fcas_specific_lessons: **Donor coordination is critical**: OQ’s role in aligning international efforts post-2023 conflict (D0007021.odt).
**Flexible instruments work**: Liquidity Facility and IRF allow rapid response to spikes in need (52339643.odt).
**Local ownership requires embedded support**: Cowater advisors in PA ministries improve reform uptake (D0007021.odt).
**Conflict pauses require bridge funding**: £20m ASPIRE extension (2019) and £32m addendum (2024) maintained continuity (D0007021.odt).
**Safeguards must adapt**: Enhanced due diligence for Gaza post-October 2023 (D0007021.odt).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Paris Protocol reforms**: DFID’s earlier leadership on customs revenue transfers achieved partial success (e.g., GoI transferred $300m to clear arrears - 36210494.odt). 2) **Energy sector**: Pilot solar projects under ESPIP demonstrated scalability (52339643.odt). 3) **Trade facilitation**: PMDP’s 1% Initiative (IT outsourcing) showed potential but required sustained support (36210494.odt). 4) **Gender inclusion**: Women’s employment pilots (e.g., industrial zones) needed tailored designs for Palestinian context (36210494.odt).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Shift to core funding** for OQ to reduce management costs (D0001028.odt). 2) **Added Liquidity Support Facility** to de-risk private sector investments (52339643.odt). 3) **Expanded solar focus** based on ESPIP pilots (52339643.odt). 4) **Embedded advisors** in Prime Minister’s Office to capitalise on 2024 reform window (D0007021.odt). 5) **Breakout clause** in FY2025 to align with UK spending review (D0007021.odt).
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learned from previous World Bank energy programmes in the OPTs are being applied in the design of ASPIRE." (52339643.odt, Gender Equality) AND "The programme is explicitly designed to be adaptive to changes in the volatile political environment." (36210494.odt, Does the proposed level of risk fit with DFID’s risk appetite?) AND "The addendum will include a breakout period at the start of FY2025 in any agreements. This will enable funding modifications following the UK’s spending review." (D0007021.odt, Our Response)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Liquidity Support Facility aims to leverage **3x private sector investments** (£15.5m public → £46.5m private) for renewable energy. World Bank’s ASPIRE co-financed with Kuwait/France (total $137.4m programme; DFID contributes £9m).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Capital-intensive: Majority of funds (~60-70%) allocated to infrastructure (e.g., Gaza Desalination Plant, electricity connection upgrades) and Liquidity Facility. Revenue supports technical assistance (~30-40%) (e.g., Cowater’s Tasdeer programme, OQ core funding).
financial_details.quote: "DFID proposes funding up to £9m [of World Bank’s ESPIP], which has a total cost of US$35 million." (36210494.odt, World Bank’s Electricity Sector Performance Improvement Project) AND "The additional £20 million will increase our financial commitment to the World Bank energy programme to £29 million." (52339643.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?) AND "The addendum will increase Tasdeer’s budget by £15m and amend its end date from September 2025 to March 2028." (D0007021.odt, Our Response)

metadata.programme_name: Developing science and technology solutions to the global food security and climate crisis with CGIAR
metadata.primary_sector: economic development (agriculture, climate resilience, food security)
metadata.quote: "The CGIAR programme will support coherent and effective international action to address the multiple and interconnected threats facing the global food system purpose through targeted research and innovation funding." (D0004136.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original Project start and end dates: 1 October 2023 – 1 October 2025" and "New project end date (if applicable): 1 October 2026" (D0004136.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research to create new knowledge) and **technology development** (developing climate-resilient crop varieties, sustainable agricultural practices). It also includes **policy influence** (supporting evidence-based policy development) and **capacity building** (training, partnerships with Southern institutions). The programme leverages CGIAR's global research platform to deliver science and innovation for food security, climate resilience, and biodiversity protection.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The overarching objective of the CGIAR programme is to support coherent and effective international action to address the multiple and interconnected threats facing the global food system purpose through targeted research and innovation funding." (D0004136.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to deliver science and technology solutions to global food security and climate challenges through CGIAR, focusing on climate-resilient crops, sustainable agriculture, gender equality, and biodiversity conservation. It combines research, innovation, and policy influence to achieve large-scale impact in Africa and Asia.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will: Support the delivery of the IDS through high impact R&D programmes that it would be impossible to deliver using UK funding alone, reaching millions of people in Africa and Asia and delivering improved outcomes for women and girls." (D0004136.odt, Summary Information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in regions with climate vulnerability, food insecurity, and political fragility, but the overall risk rating is classified as moderate. The food system is under stress from climate change, conflict, and economic shocks, which exacerbates food insecurity and malnutrition.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004135.odt, Business Case Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (fragile states, limited fiscal headroom)
weak institutions (limited access to resources for women and youth)
data limitations (need for better evidence on gender and food systems)
market volatility (fertilizer and food price spikes)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate risks reduce agricultural productivity and increase food insecurity, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Political fragility and weak institutions limit the ability of governments to absorb shocks (e.g., food price volatility) and implement policies. Conflict exacerbates food insecurity, while data gaps hinder evidence-based decision-making.
where_context.quote: "High and volatile food prices are a risk multiplier in politically fragile states, particularly those heavily dependent on imports and with limited fiscal headroom to absorb rapid changes in food prices." (D0004135.odt, Food insecurity section)

Decision-making is collaborative, with the UK influencing priorities through its seat on the System Council and designated funding allocations.

research grants (funding for Southern-led innovation)

who_partners.quote: "CGIAR plays a key commissioning and directing role in global agricultural research, providing a focus for global research efforts aimed at developing and deploying evidence and technology to address the long-term strategic challenges facing the food system." (D0004135.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO funding is channeled through the **CGIAR Fund**, a Financial Intermediary Fund held by the World Bank. Funds are designated to specific CGIAR Research Initiatives based on alignment with UK priorities. This allows pooled funding with other donors while maintaining UK influence over resource allocation.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: CGIAR operates as an integrated innovation platform with a **portfolio of research initiatives** managed through a stage-gate system. FCDO designates funds to specific initiatives, which are implemented by CGIAR centers in collaboration with national and international partners. The UK-CGIAR Science Collaboration Centre acts as a bridge between UK science and CGIAR’s global network.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: CGIAR was selected based on its **unmatched track record** in agricultural research (50+ years), global reach, and alignment with UK priorities. The partnership leverages CGIAR’s existing infrastructure, scientific expertise, and partnerships to deliver impact at scale. The UK has historically funded CGIAR (5-10% of its budget) and uses its influence to shape reforms and priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO will continue to utilise Designated Window 1 funding along with other major CGIAR funders. CGIAR Designated Window 1 is pooled but can be allocated (designated) to specific initiatives." (D0004136.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Funds are released to CGIAR initiatives based on decisions by the **System Council**, which includes UK representation. The UK designates funds to specific initiatives, and CGIAR centers retain responsibility for implementation.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **System Council** is the highest governing body of CGIAR, with the UK as a member. It oversees strategic direction and resource allocation. The UK representative currently chairs the **Strategic Impact, Monitoring and Evaluation Committee**, influencing priorities and ensuring alignment with UK goals.
how_governance.quote: "The UK funding commitment set out here would be just sufficient to maintain the UK’s membership of the System Council, the influential highest governing body of the CGIAR, through which we are able to influence other funders' priorities, and shape CGIAR strategy and delivery." (D0004136.odt, Diplomatic objectives)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between CGIAR initiatives if they are fully funded, based on FCDO priorities. The **designated funding** model allows flexibility within the overall portfolio but requires alignment with CGIAR’s strategic goals.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted through the **CGIAR 2030 Research and Innovation Strategy**, which allows for reprioritization based on emerging risks (e.g., climate shocks, conflicts). The UK uses its influence on the System Council to steer investments toward high-impact areas.
how_flexibility.quote: "Where those initiatives are fully funded, money will be reallocated to other research initiatives prioritised by FCDO." (D0004136.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → CGIAR (platform) → CGIAR Research Initiatives (implementation). The UK-CGIAR Science Collaboration Centre adds a coordination layer but streamlines partnerships.
how_efficiency.quote: "FCDO funding will be channelled to the research and innovation portfolio where, along with funding from other international partners, it will contribute to the delivery of cutting-edge technology and evidence-based solutions." (D0004136.odt, The programme)

q24_alternatives_considered: bilateral research programmes (rejected due to limited scale and higher transaction costs)
direct funding to national research systems (rejected due to fragmented capacity and lower global coordination)
private sector partnerships (limited by market failures in public goods research)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: CGIAR was chosen for its **global reach, scientific excellence, and ability to deliver impact at scale** through pooled funding and international partnerships. The platform model reduces transaction costs, leverages existing infrastructure, and aligns with UK priorities on climate, food security, and open science. The UK’s historical influence in CGIAR ensures strategic alignment and value for money.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (£10 return for every £1 invested)
risk mitigation (moderate risk rating, stable governance)
past experience (50+ years of CGIAR impact)
partner capacity (global network of 13 research centers)
equity (focus on women, youth, and marginalized crops)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: coordination complexity in a multi-partner platform
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK uses its System Council seat and designated funding to align priorities and streamline decision-making.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: dependency on CGIAR’s reform success
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK is actively driving CGIAR’s institutional reforms to improve efficiency and impact.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: funding volatility from other donors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s stable, multi-year funding (£100m over 3 years) provides predictability.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (proven track record in delivering climate and food security impacts)
equity (focus on women, smallholders, and marginalized regions)
why_rationale.quote: "The CGIAR has a major offer to make in meeting future demand for food and halting and reversing land expansion and environmental damage through sustainable productivity growth." (D0004136.odt, Background)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **geographic focus on Africa and South Asia** (high climate vulnerability, weak institutions) necessitates partnerships with **local research systems (NARS)** and **international centers (CGIAR)** to bridge capacity gaps. Conflict and fragility in regions like the Sahel require adaptive, resilient research approaches.
q27_constraints_detail: climate vulnerability limits local research capacity (requires CGIAR’s global expertise)
political fragility necessitates multilateral platforms (e.g., CGIAR) for neutral coordination
market failures in LMICs justify public funding for global goods (e.g., genebanks)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for large-scale, cross-border solutions** (e.g., climate-resilient crops, genebanks) determines the **platform delivery model** (CGIAR). The complexity of food systems research requires **integrated initiatives** (e.g., Genetic Innovation, Resilient Agri-Food Systems) managed through a **stage-gate system** to ensure coherence.
q28_linkages: global challenges (climate, biodiversity) → platform delivery (CGIAR)
need for policy influence → governance via System Council
Southern ownership → partnerships with NARS and local institutions
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (pooled funding, CGIAR’s economies of scale) with **equity** (targeting women, smallholders, and underutilized crops). For example:

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid delivery of climate-resilient crops (e.g., wheat, rice) is prioritized, but the **Vision for Adapted Crops and Soils (VACS)** programme explicitly targets **marginalized crops** (millet, sorghum) to ensure inclusivity.
UK science (e.g., gene editing, climate modeling) is leveraged, but **local breeding programmes** (e.g., in Ethiopia, India) lead adaptation and scaling.
Genebank conservation (high cost) is justified by its **global public good** value (e.g., 800,000 crop accessions shared openly).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (climate shocks, political fragility) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and **adaptive management** (e.g., reprioritization via System Council). High-risk regions (e.g., conflict zones) receive targeted support through resilient crop varieties and policy advice.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in the delivery structure: the **UK-CGIAR Science Collaboration Centre** strengthens Southern partners’ roles in **co-designing research**, while CGIAR’s training programmes (60,915 people in 2022) build local expertise for long-term ownership.
intersections.quote: "Ensuring equitable access to technologies that reduce women’s burden and increase their productivity is essential, improving household nutrition and incomes." (D0004135.odt, Tackling Inequality in the Food System)

key_programme_risks: climate shocks disrupting agricultural productivity (e.g., droughts, floods)
political instability in target regions limiting policy uptake
volatility in fertilizer/food prices affecting smallholder incomes
gender inequalities restricting women’s access to resources
biodiversity loss undermining long-term food security
slow adoption of new crop varieties by farmers
dependency on CGIAR’s institutional reforms for efficiency gains

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Development of **climate-smart crops** (e.g., drought-tolerant maize, flood-tolerant rice) and **early warning systems** for food security risks.
Engagement with **national governments** (e.g., Kenya, Vietnam) to embed research in policy and **multilateral platforms** (CGIAR) to ensure continuity.
Support for **input-efficient farming practices** (e.g., reduced fertilizer use) and **market stabilization policies** (e.g., genebank conservation).
Targeted **women-focused interventions** (e.g., labor-saving technologies, access to credit) and **gender-responsive breeding programmes**.
**Sustainable intensification** (e.g., agroecology, land-sparing techniques) and **genebank conservation** (800,000 crop accessions).
**Farmer participatory breeding** and **local extension services** to ensure varieties meet smallholder needs (e.g., 63% maize adoption in Ethiopia).
UK leadership in **System Council** to drive efficiency and **designated funding** to high-impact initiatives.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan, Yemen), **resilient crop varieties** (e.g., sorghum, millet) are prioritized over high-input systems.
**Local partnerships** (e.g., with NARS) are critical for last-mile delivery in conflict zones.
**Flexible funding** (e.g., reallocation between initiatives) allows rapid response to emerging crises (e.g., Pakistan floods).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past CGIAR programmes (e.g., Green Revolution) demonstrated that **long-term R&D investments** (e.g., wheat breeding) yield high returns (£73-£101 per £1 invested) but require **adaptive scaling** to local contexts. Lessons include:
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **individual center projects** to **integrated portfolios** (e.g., Genetic Innovation, Resilient Agri-Food Systems) for greater coherence.
Stronger focus on **underutilized crops** (e.g., millet, pigeon pea) through **VACS programme**, addressing gaps in previous staple-crop dominance.
**UK-CGIAR Science Collaboration Centre** added to accelerate translation of UK science (e.g., gene editing) into global solutions.
risks_lessons.quote: "The CGIAR has a strong track record in delivering tangible climate and development impacts in countries which are a priority for FCDO." (D0004136.odt, Background)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages **£3.5bn/year in additional R&D investments** (from other donors and private sector) by 2030, as modeled in the FCDO-commissioned study on sustainable agriculture intensification. CGIAR’s pooled funding model attracts co-investment from allies (e.g., US, Germany) and multilateral partners.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The **£5m for Crop Trust Endowment Fund** is capital investment (long-term genebank conservation), while the remaining **£105m** supports revenue expenditures (R&D, training, partnerships).
financial_details.quote: "This Costed Addendum to the CGIAR business case is for an additional £45m to the CGIAR BC taking it to a total of £110m." (D0004136.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: Low Carbon Development Initiative: Phase 2 (LCDI 2)
metadata.quote: "The LCDI2 programme aims to support (i) mainstreaming of LCDI into the RPJMN, with delivery of RPJMN targets, which are currently focussed on the medium ambition scenario (though on forestry / land-use the targets for the medium and high scenarios are the same) and (ii) raising ambition to realise the ‘high’ and ‘plus’ LCDI scenarios" (90000769.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "LCDI 2 is a four-year programme which will be focused on working hand-in-hand with a globally significant country on implementing the highest levels of ambition contained in the LDCI Report as part of National Development Plan and Indonesia Vision 2045." (90000769.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The LCDI 2 programme combines policy influence (mainstreaming low carbon development into national/provincial plans), capacity building (training provincial governments on MRV and modelling), and implementation research (piloting innovative policies through the Innovation Fund). It aims to institutionalize Indonesia's Low Carbon Development Initiative while testing scalable solutions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The LCDI2 programme will aim to mainstream low carbon development, both at national level and with key provinces." and "LCDI2 will establish a competitive fund that will be used to support the GoI to test new and scalable ideas, policies, innovations, and technologies in key sectors" (90000769.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Provincial governments developing and agreeing provincial yearly low carbon development plans (RPRKD) and 5-year strategic plans (RPJMD)
Integration of low carbon development commitments into Indonesia's 20-year (2025-2045) national plan
Significant improvements to Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) of emissions
Concrete policy decisions on carbon taxation, carbon markets, and complementary policy measures
Protection of 41.1m ha of forest including 15m ha of peatland
500k ha of degraded land restored to secondary forest status each year (2021-24)
Scaling up renewable energy share from 8% (2015) to 23% by 2030
Reduction in total GHG emissions from 2.14 GtCO2e (2017) to 1.49 GtCO2e by 2030
what_objectives.summary: LCDI 2 aims to institutionalize Indonesia's low carbon development pathway by embedding it into national/provincial planning systems, while piloting innovative solutions to achieve higher ambition scenarios. It combines technical assistance, capacity building, and political engagement to deliver measurable emissions reductions alongside economic growth.
what_objectives.quote: "The LCDI2 programme provides a unique opportunity to work hand in hand with a high emitting G20 country to decarbonise its economy." (90000769.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'. While Indonesia faces challenges like deforestation and political economy constraints, the programme operates in a stable partnership with the Government of Indonesia (GoI) and has established trust through previous phases.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (90000769.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy constraints include vested interests resisting low-carbon transitions (e.g., "Mainstreaming and implementing LCDI will face competing interests from politically influential actors"). Weak institutions are evident in the need to strengthen BAPPENAS's LCDI Secretariat. Conflict risks arise from competition over natural resources, requiring conflict sensitivity analysis. Climate risks include forest fires exacerbating GHG emissions and COVID-19 vulnerabilities. Data limitations are addressed through support for integrated MRV systems.
where_context.quote: "Mainstreaming and implementing LCDI will face competing interests from politically influential actors." and "Conflict sensitivity analysis will be routinely conducted as part of the programme design and implementation" (90000769.odt, Workstream 3 and Risk sections)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: British Embassy Jakarta (BEJ) and BAPPENAS (Indonesia's Ministry of Planning and Development)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with BAPPENAS, with decision-making shared between BEJ (providing technical/funding support) and GoI institutions (leading implementation). The hybrid delivery model ensures Indonesian ownership while leveraging UK expertise.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV)
system dynamic modelling for emissions projections
strengthening BAPPENAS's LCDI Secretariat
bespoke capacity building for provincial governments
knowledge sharing on low carbon policy tools

partner_organizations.role: Lead government partner; co-designer and implementer of LCDI 2

partner_organizations.role: Programme management, technical assistance, and donor coordination

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Engagement in political advocacy and community-level implementation
