who_partners.quote: "The LCDI2 programme will work with (i) BAPPENAS to strengthen the organisation, sustainability and capacity of the LCDI Secretariat and (ii) other key GoI ministries to secure their long-term buy-in for low carbon development." and "LCDI2 will support bespoke capacity building activities and knowledge sharing for key provinces in Indonesia." (90000769.odt, Workstream 1 and 2)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for technical assistance and PMU management) and grants (for the Innovation and Technology Fund). The hybrid model allows flexibility to respond to GoI demands while ensuring accountability.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme combines BEJ's direct oversight with an externally managed Programme Management Unit (PMU) for day-to-day delivery. This "hybrid" approach retains UKCCU's strategic control while leveraging external expertise for implementation. A technical group (GoI ministries + BAPPENAS + UK team) will oversee the Innovation Fund.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The hybrid option was chosen after evaluating the strengths/weaknesses of in-house vs. external delivery. Open competition for the PMU and Innovation Fund aims to drive value for money, though direct awards may be used for existing BEJ partners (e.g., BAPPENAS).
how_mechanism.quote: "Option 4: Hybrid... strengths: Combined resource and experience from public and private sectors." and "A dedicated technical group (comprising relevant line Ministries, Bappenas, and the UK LCDI2 team) will be established to review proposals submitted under the Innovation and Technology Fund." (90000769.odt, Appraisal Case and Workstream 4)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will establish a Steering Committee (composition not fully detailed) and a technical advisory group for the Innovation Fund. BAPPENAS and BEJ will jointly oversee implementation, with provincial engagement coordinated through MoUs.
how_governance.quote: "Governance, management and reporting: A Steering Committee will oversee the programme, with regular reporting to BEJ and BAPPENAS." and "A dedicated technical group... will review proposals submitted under the Innovation and Technology Fund." (90000769.odt, Management Case and Workstream 4)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between workstreams with approval, particularly to respond to GoI priorities (e.g., provincial demands for pilot projects). The Innovation Fund is explicitly demand-led.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive management to align with Indonesia's evolving political and economic context (e.g., post-COVID recovery, RPJMN adjustments). Priorities can shift based on GoI requests, with BEJ/BAPPENAS approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The LCDI2 programme will be demand-led (i.e. responding to requests from partner Ministries)." and "Flexibility to adapt to changing political, sectoral and provincial priorities" was a key criterion for selecting the hybrid model. (90000769.odt, Workstream 4 and Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Programme Management Unit (PMU) → Implementing partners (GoI ministries/provinces). The hybrid model reduces layers compared to a fully externalized approach.
how_efficiency.quote: "The high-level budget for each workstream has been calculated using programme costs of similar work funded by UKCCU in the past." (90000769.odt, Budget section) and "Option 4: Hybrid... strengths: Combined resource and experience from public and private sectors" (90000769.odt, Appraisal Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (discounted due to HMG/GoI support and unmet institutionalization needs)
In-house delivery (rejected due to lack of specialized skills in BEJ and portfolio coherence risks)
Fully external PMU (rejected due to potential loss of GoI relationships and higher costs)
Hybrid model (selected for balancing speed, expertise, and GoI buy-in)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid model was chosen to (1) ensure a smooth transition from LCDI 1 (avoiding gaps before COP26), (2) retain BEJ's trusted relationships with GoI while accessing external technical expertise, (3) provide flexibility to adapt to provincial/national priorities, and (4) manage complex stakeholders (e.g., BAPPENAS, KLHK, provincial governments) effectively. The appraisal weighted criteria like "ability to start quickly" and "manage wide stakeholders" highly.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of institutional knowledge during transition from LCDI 1 to LCDI 2
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Hybrid model retains BEJ staff involvement; inception phase includes knowledge transfer.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Perceived higher costs of external PMU
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Competitive procurement to drive down costs; clear deliverable-based contracts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination between BEJ, PMU, and GoI
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Steering Committee and joint technical groups for alignment; embedded advisors in BAPPENAS.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in procurement of PMU
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased start with BEJ managing inception phase to avoid gaps.

why_rationale.quote: "The hybrid option was therefore also evaluated against required capabilities... Given both options presented strengths and weaknesses, this led to a fourth ‘hybrid’ option being developed, which built on the best elements of options 2 and 3." and "Criteria were weighted to reflect their relative importance to the success of the LCDI 2 programme." (90000769.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Indonesia's political economy and legal framework constrain partner selection. The programme can only engage provinces with MoUs signed with BAPPENAS (per Law 23/2014), limiting subnational partners to Riau, South Sulawesi, West Papua, and potentially North Kalimantan, South Sumatra, and Gorontalo. Vested interests in sectors like palm oil and coal also influence which ministries (e.g., ESDM) can fully participate.
q27_constraints_detail: Legal requirement (Law 23/2014) restricts provincial engagement to those with BAPPENAS MoUs
Political resistance from sectors dependent on high-carbon activities (e.g., Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources)
Need to align with GoI's provincial priorities (e.g., North Kalimantan's green industrial area)
Conflict sensitivity requires avoiding provinces with active resource disputes
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to (1) **mainstream LCDI into RPJMN/Provincial Plans** drives the hybrid structure (combining BEJ's policy influence with PMU's technical implementation), and (2) **test innovative policies** necessitates a demand-led Innovation Fund with joint GoI-UK oversight. The political nature of low-carbon transitions (e.g., challenging vested interests) also requires embedded advisors for real-time adaptation.
q28_linkages: Mainstreaming objective → Hybrid structure (BEJ + PMU) to balance trust and expertise
Innovation testing → Competitive fund with technical group for scalable solutions
Provincial engagement → MoU-based selection to ensure legal compliance
Political economy challenges → Embedded advisors for adaptive management
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between (1) **speed vs. inclusion**: The hybrid model prioritizes quick start-up (to meet COP26 deadlines) while ensuring GoI ownership, and (2) **expertise vs. local ownership**: External PMU provides technical skills, but BEJ retention mitigates loss of GoI relationships. The Innovation Fund's demand-led design also balances efficiency (targeted pilots) with equity (provincial priorities).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (COP26 showcase) vs. inclusive provincial engagement (limited by MoU requirements)
Northern expertise (PMU) vs. Southern ownership (BEJ/GoI co-leadership)
Efficiency (competitive fund) vs. equity (demand-led provincial projects)
Cost (external PMU overheads) vs. reach (scaling innovations nationally)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., Steering Committee) and conflict sensitivity analysis, particularly for provincial work. Political economy risks necessitate embedded advisors to navigate GoI resistance.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme's theory of change: Provincial governments' limited experience with low-carbon planning (e.g., MRV, modelling) directly shapes the PMU's role in delivering tailored training, while BAPPENAS's strengthened Secretariat enables long-term institutionalization.
intersections.quote: "The choices the GoI make now in responding to COVID-19 will have profound long-term positive or negative consequences in terms of poverty reduction, economic growth, carbon emissions and natural resources management." and "LCDI2 will support bespoke capacity building activities and knowledge sharing for key provinces in Indonesia." (90000769.odt, Strategic Case and Workstream 2)

key_programme_risks: Incomplete institutionalization of LCDI in GoI machinery
Resistance from politically influential high-carbon sectors (e.g., coal, palm oil)
Budget cuts to BAPPENAS/KLHK due to COVID-19 fiscal stimulus
Provincial implementation delays (e.g., weak MRV systems)
Forest fires and peatland degradation reversing emissions gains
Loss of momentum if key GoI champions (e.g., BAPPENAS Minister) change
Terrorism financing risks in palm oil sectors (though minimal direct programme impact)
Overlap/duplication with other donor programmes (e.g., Norway, World Bank)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strengthen BAPPENAS's LCDI Secretariat; embed LCDI in RPJMN 2025-45 and Vision 2045.
Political engagement workstream to build coalitions; pilot innovative policies to demonstrate feasibility.
Align with GoI's 'build back better' narrative; leverage UK's COP26 presidency for high-level advocacy.
Focus on provinces with existing MoUs; provide tailored capacity building.
Support peatland restoration (linking to INAFOR programme); strengthen MRV for early warning systems.
Broaden political buy-in beyond BAPPENAS (e.g., Ministry of Finance, Parliament).
Avoid direct engagement with high-risk areas; monitor via safeguarding protocols.
Coordinate with Norway/World Bank through BAPPENAS-led platforms.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity analysis is mandatory for provincial work due to resource-based conflicts (e.g., land disputes in Kalimantan).
Indigenous communities' land rights must be safeguarded to avoid exacerbating marginalization.
Lessons from LCDI 1 highlight the need for adaptive management to navigate Indonesia's dynamic political economy.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: LCDI 1 demonstrated that (1) **analytical rigor** (e.g., modelling) is critical for GoI buy-in, (2) **provincial engagement** requires legal compliance (MoUs), and (3) **political champions** (e.g., Vice-President's UN speech) accelerate adoption. However, institutionalization remains incomplete, necessitating LCDI 2's focus on mainstreaming.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: LCDI 2 (vs. LCDI 1) adds: (1) a **dedicated Innovation Fund** to test scalable solutions, (2) **explicit provincial workstreams** (beyond national-level support), (3) **strengthened political engagement** (e.g., Parliament, private sector), and (4) **adaptive management** to respond to COVID-19 impacts.
risks_lessons.quote: "LCDI 1 has been successful in supporting progressive work on low carbon development approaches, especially the integration of carbon emission and reduction targets into the national development planning framework... The main gap that LCDI 2 will seek to fill is the need to convert the LDCI Report and approach into tangible, measurable action and progress in other Ministries (i.e. beyond Bappenas), and on the ground, at provincial level." (90000769.odt, Strategic Case)

metadata.programme_name: Seventh General Capital Increase for the African Development Bank (AfDB GCI-7)

quote.section: Programme summary

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: July 2020", "End Date: July 2031"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme involves the UK's purchase of shares in the African Development Bank (AfDB) to increase its capital base, enabling the Bank to expand lending for development projects across Africa. This is a financing mechanism to channel funds through a multilateral institution rather than direct implementation or research.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This business case is for the UK’s purchase of shares in the Bank; the UK is already a shareholder and will maintain its existing share in the Bank of 1.755%. The capital increase means the size of the Bank will increase so the UK will purchase more shares than it already has."
q3_expected_outputs: Increase in AfDB lending capacity (target: £5.5bn+ commitments annually)
10.6 million direct jobs created by 2025 (AfDB target)
8.2 million indirect jobs created by 2025 (AfDB target)
£25 billion in climate financing from AfDB's own resources (2020-2025)
40% of AfDB approvals qualifying as climate finance by 2020
1.2 million direct jobs created in 2018 (baseline)
261,000 women with new electricity connections (2018 baseline)
9.3 million women benefitted from agricultural improvements (2018 baseline)
Institutional reforms under DBDM (decentralization, performance culture, etc.)
what_objectives.summary: The UK's capital contribution to AfDB's GCI-7 enables expanded lending for infrastructure, private sector development, and climate resilience across Africa, aligning with UK priorities on prosperity, climate action, and poverty reduction.

quote.section: Programme summary, Intervention Summary, High5 results

countries_regions: Africa (all 54 regional member countries of AfDB)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated 'moderate' risk due to AfDB's institutional strengths (e.g., AAA credit rating, strong safeguards) balanced against operational challenges in fragile African contexts and reform implementation risks.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate"
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (e.g., "domestic macroeconomic instability including poorly managed debt, inflation, and deficits")
climate risks (e.g., "vulnerability of African countries to climate change")
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints such as fragility (costing Sub-Saharan Africa 0.5% growth/year), debt risks, and climate vulnerability (e.g., droughts linked to Boko Haram insurgency) directly affect AfDB's ability to deliver results in priority sectors like energy, agriculture, and regional integration.

quote.section: Context–need for a DFID intervention, Institutional structure

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: AfDB is 60% owned by African countries, with African leadership (President, 80% African staff) and decision-making via its Board of Governors/Directors where African members hold majority influence. The UK, as a 1.755% shareholder, participates in governance but does not control operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: Institutional reforms via DBDM (e.g., decentralization, staff upskilling, performance management)
Gender mainstreaming (e.g., gender marker system, 9 gender specialists deployed to regional hubs)
Technical assistance to African governments (e.g., climate resilience, financial sector strengthening)
Training for African statistical offices on gender-disaggregated data
Support for agro-industrial processing zones (e.g., SAPZs in Ethiopia, Togo) to build local private sector capacity

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and recipient of capital increase
partner_organizations.location: Multilateral (HQ in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire; operations across 54 African countries)

partner_organizations.name: UK International Financial Institutions Department (IFID)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and policy influencer (e.g., negotiating GCI-7 reforms, performance monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: AfDB Board of Governors/Directors
partner_organizations.role: Governance oversight (includes UK representative)

partner_organizations.name: African Development Fund (AfDF)
partner_organizations.role: Concessional lending window for poorer countries (linked to AfDB operations)

partner_organizations.role: Collaborators on joint initiatives (e.g., climate finance, fragility)

quote.section: Institutional structure, Fit with UK priorities, DBDM reforms

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides a capital subscription (£98.8m paid-in capital + £1.7bn callable capital) to AfDB's general capital, which becomes part of the Bank's permanent capital base. This enables AfDB to leverage additional funds (e.g., bond markets) for lending. The UK's contribution is tied to maintaining its 1.755% shareholding.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: AfDB manages all operations through its decentralized structure (53% of staff in country/regional offices as of 2018, targeting 85% by 2025). The UK influences policy via its Board seat (shared constituency with Italy/Netherlands) and technical engagement but does not manage day-to-day delivery.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AfDB is a pre-existing multilateral institution where the UK is already a shareholder. The GCI-7 is a collective decision by all 78 member countries; no competitive selection process applies.

quote.section: Intervention Summary, Institutional structure

how_governance.q17_governance_details: AfDB's Board of Directors (where the UK has a seat via its Executive Director) oversees operations, while the Board of Governors (with UK representation) approves major policies. The UK's influence is exercised through: 1) GCI-7 policy commitments (e.g., DBDM reforms), 2) performance monitoring (e.g., 6-monthly Board reports), and 3) technical dialogue with AfDB management.

quote.section: Institutional structure, UK influence sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are tied to AfDB's capital base and cannot be reallocated by the UK post-contribution. The UK can only influence *how* AfDB uses its expanded capital through governance channels (e.g., Board votes, policy dialogue).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: AfDB's High5 priorities and DBDM reforms provide a fixed framework for 2020-2025. The UK can advocate for adjustments (e.g., greater focus on fragility) but cannot unilaterally change priorities. The Bank's annual country strategy reviews allow some adaptability.

quote.section: Intervention Summary, DBDM reforms

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (via IFID) → AfDB (implementer). No sub-grantees; AfDB directly manages all operations.

quote.section: Intervention Summary (£98.8m paid over 8 years in instalments)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral programmes (rejected due to AfDB's broader geographic reach and sectoral expertise)
Other MDBs (e.g., World Bank; rejected due to AfDB's "truly African character" and stronger alignment with UK Africa strategy)
Direct private sector investments (complementary but not a substitute for AfDB's risk-sharing role)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: AfDB was selected for its: 1) **Alignment with UK priorities** (e.g., High5s match SDGs on energy, jobs, climate); 2) **Comparative advantage** in Africa (60% African-owned, trusted by governments); 3) **Leverage** (£1 UK capital enables ~£10 in AfDB lending); 4) **Reach** (operates in countries where DFID lacks presence); 5) **Reform momentum** (DBDM addresses past capacity issues).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (e.g., "£25bn climate finance leveraged from AfDB's own resources")
risk mitigation (e.g., AfDB's AAA rating, strong safeguards)
partner capacity (e.g., DBDM reforms address MOPAN/MDR findings)
speed (e.g., GCI-7 enables immediate lending scale-up)
equity (e.g., focus on fragile states and gender mainstreaming)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reform implementation delays
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Time-bound commitments negotiated in GCI-7 (e.g., 6-monthly Board reports, performance-based tranche in AfDF replenishment).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-optimistic targets (e.g., job creation, climate finance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: AfDB reviewing targets in 2020 to ensure realism; UK pushing for better sequencing of reforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited UK influence as a small shareholder (1.755%)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strategic alliances with like-minded shareholders (e.g., Italy/Netherlands constituency) and technical engagement (e.g., joint climate initiatives).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Callable capital being called (£1.5bn contingent liability)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Historically extremely unlikely; AfDB's strong financial position (AAA rating) and conservative lending policies.

quote.section: Why is the UK supporting the AfDB?, Fit with UK priorities, DBDM reforms

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: AfDB's African ownership (60% African shareholders, 80% African staff) and mandate to serve all 54 regional members **require** a multilateral, African-led delivery structure. The UK cannot impose a Northern-led model due to: 1) AfDB's legal status as an independent institution; 2) Political sensitivity of foreign control over African development; 3) Need for African government trust to address sensitive issues (e.g., regional integration, fragility).
q27_constraints_detail: AfDB's Articles of Agreement limit non-African shareholding to 40%
African governments' preference for African-led solutions (e.g., SAPZs designed with local private sector)
Fragility in 21 member states requires trusted partners (AfDB's "privileged position")
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **financing mechanism** objective (scaling lending) **requires** a multilateral structure because: 1) Capital increases are legally tied to shareholder agreements (no competitive bidding); 2) Lending at scale needs AfDB's existing infrastructure (e.g., 53% staff in field offices); 3) Cross-country projects (e.g., regional energy grids) demand a neutral convener.
q28_linkages: High5 priorities (e.g., "Integrate Africa") → Need for AfDB's regional offices and policy dialogue platforms
Climate finance targets (40% of approvals) → Requires AfDB's safeguards systems and co-financing partnerships (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
Jobs target (10.6m by 2025) → Depends on AfDB's private sector instruments (e.g., MSME credit lines, SAPZs)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: AfDB's decentralization (target: 85% staff in field offices by 2025) improves local responsiveness but slows reform rollout (e.g., "reform fatigue" among staff). 2) **Climate ambition vs. poverty focus**: 40% climate finance target risks diverting funds from AfDF's poorest countries (mitigated by ring-fenced AfDF replenishment). 3) **Gender mainstreaming vs. operational burden**: Mandatory gender markers (2020) add reporting costs but ensure women's economic empowerment (e.g., 9.3m women benefitted from agriculture projects in 2018).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: AfDB's "one-Bank" approach merges AfDB/AfDF operations for synergies but risks diluting focus on poorest countries
Equity: Gender specialists deployed to regional hubs improve inclusion but require trade-offs in staffing budgets
Expertise: Hiring climate/private sector experts (e.g., for African Financial Alliance for Climate) competes with core infrastructure teams
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** drives **milestone-based oversight**: 1) High institutional risk (e.g., DBDM reform delays) → 6-monthly Board reports; 2) Country-level fragility (e.g., Sahel conflicts) → AfDB's field offices empowered for rapid adaptation; 3) Financial risk (callable capital) → Conservative lending policies monitored via AAA rating.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: AfDB's capacity constraints (e.g., post-2015 staff losses) **shifted partner roles**: 1) UK/DFID provides technical assistance (e.g., crisis toolkit, gender strategy); 2) GCI-7 funds are earmarked for staff upskilling (e.g., task managers, regional hubs); 3) Private sector partners (e.g., PIDG) co-invest to fill gaps in AfDB's non-sovereign operations.

quote.section: Institutional structure, DBDM reforms, High5 results

key_programme_risks: AfDB fails to implement DBDM reforms on time (e.g., decentralization, gender mainstreaming)
Macroeconomic instability in borrower countries (e.g., debt crises, inflation) reduces repayment capacity
Climate shocks (e.g., droughts, floods) disrupt project delivery in fragile states
Overlap/duplication with other MDBs (e.g., World Bank) in key sectors
Callable capital is called (£1.5bn contingent liability materializes)
Political resistance to AfDB's regional integration agenda (e.g., trade barriers)
Private sector co-financing falls short of targets (2018: £2.6bn mobilized vs. £6.8bn target)
Gender and climate targets prove unachievable without additional resources

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Time-bound commitments in GCI-7; UK-led shareholder push for 6-monthly progress reports; performance-based tranche in AfDF-15 replenishment.
AfDB's conservative lending policies (e.g., AAA rating maintenance); joint IMF/AfDB debt sustainability analyses.
40% climate finance target; African Financial Alliance for Climate; early warning systems for 300m people.
AfDB-World Bank collaboration framework; AfDB's focus on "truly African" solutions (e.g., SAPZs).
Historical precedent (never called); AfDB's strong liquidity buffers (e.g., £1.5bn contingent liability is "extremely unlikely").
AfDB's African Financial Alliance for Climate; PIDG/CDC co-investment partnerships; UK Africa Investment Summit 2020.

fcas_specific_lessons: AfDB's fragility strategy was **only partially implemented** (2016-2019); GCI-7 commits to stronger links between fragility analysis and project design.
Sahel Alliance portfolio (£1.2bn) showed that **trusted partners** (e.g., AfDB) can address displacement crises more effectively than bilaterals.
Lessons from AfDF-14 Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) applied to GCI-7: **time-bound reforms** with shareholder tracking.
Decentralization (e.g., new country offices in Niger, Benin, Guinea) improved delivery in FCAS by **moving closer to clients**.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **GCI-6 reforms** (2010) lacked timelines; GCI-7 includes **explicit deadlines** for DBDM. 2) **AfDF-14 PIP** (2017) showed that withholding tranches can drive performance (applied to AfDF-15). 3) **MOPAN 2016** found AfDB's safeguards strong but **fragility responsiveness weak** → GCI-7 prioritizes results-based fragility approaches. 4) **2015 HQ relocation** caused staff losses; GCI-7 includes **retention/recruitment targets**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Performance-based tranche** added to AfDF-15 replenishment (linked to DBDM progress). 2) **6-monthly Board reporting** on reforms (vs. annual in GCI-6). 3) **Gender marker system** made mandatory (after pilot showed 87% operations were "gender-informed" but needed deeper integration). 4) **Climate finance target** increased to 40% (from 28% in 2017) with **mainstreaming requirement** for all operations by 2020.

financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: 6% paid-in capital (£98.8m over 8 years); 94% callable capital (£1.5bn contingent liability, extremely unlikely to be called).

Option 2: Moderate capital package ($5.5 billion increase)
Option 3: Large capital package ($10 billion increase)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The $5.5 billion option (Option 2) was selected as it balanced the need to support IFC’s expanded role in fragile states and climate finance (aligned with UK priorities) while maintaining financial sustainability and avoiding over-leverage. The larger package ($10 billion) was deemed unnecessary, while ‘do nothing’ risked limiting IFC’s ability to deliver on its strategy.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage of private finance)
alignment with UK priorities (fragility, climate, women’s empowerment)
IFC’s track record and organisational strength
influence (UK’s shareholder role in a key multilateral institution)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced UK influence if not participating: "The UK shareholding would be expected to drop to 3.86% (compared to 4.73% currently) with a corresponding loss of influence."
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK participation ensures retained influence and ability to shape IFC’s strategy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IFC’s financial sustainability: "Without additional shareholder capital, it is expected that the IFC would need to reduce its ambition... or risk breaching its minimum Deployable Strategic Capital (DSC) threshold."
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capital increase provides IFC with sufficient DSC to implement its strategy without risking its AAA credit rating.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Performance drop in FCAS: "IEG found that IFC support was focused almost exclusively on post-conflict reconstruction and raised questions about collaboration between IFC and the World Bank in FCAS."
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFC is enhancing collaboration with the World Bank and piloting new approaches (e.g., COMPASS sessions, dedicated FCAS unit).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per dollar of private finance mobilized)
efficiency (IFC’s internal reforms and budget savings)
effectiveness (development impact in fragile states and climate)
equity (focus on poorest countries and women-led SMEs)

quote.text: Option 2 – Moderate capital package: $5.5 bn capital increase... This option was selected as it provides a balanced approach to supporting IFC’s expanded role while maintaining financial sustainability.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) requires IFC to adapt its operations (e.g., higher staff deployments, blended finance tools) and collaborate more closely with the World Bank, limiting the pool of implementers to those with FCAS experience and risk appetite.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS environments require higher transaction costs and risk mitigation (e.g., political risk guarantees).
Weak institutions in FCAS limit the ability to absorb private investment without IFC’s de-risking role.
Regulatory and security constraints in FCAS necessitate tailored instruments (e.g., IFC’s Private Sector Window).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of mobilizing private finance in high-risk markets (FCAS, climate) determines the need for IFC’s equity investments and advisory services, as well as the use of blended finance and guarantees to crowd in private capital.
q28_linkages: Market creation objective → Requires IFC’s equity investments and upstream advisory work.
Climate finance goal → Drives focus on green bonds and carbon pricing tools.
Women’s empowerment → Necessitates targeted financial products (e.g., Banking on Women program).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) the need for efficiency (IFC’s financial sustainability and internal reforms) with (2) equity objectives (40% focus on poorest countries, women-led SMEs). For example, investments in Upper Middle Income Countries (UMICs) are restricted to global public goods to ensure limited ODA funds maximize poverty impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: IFC’s internal budget savings ($400 million by FY18) vs. Equity: Increased staffing and technical assistance for FCAS.
Speed: Rapid mobilization of private finance vs. Inclusion: Ensuring development impact in fragile states.
Cost: Higher transaction costs in FCAS vs. Reach: Expanding to 40% of IFC’s portfolio by 2030.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (including FCAS exposure) leads to milestone-based oversight and adaptive management (e.g., AIMM framework for impact monitoring).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building for IFC staff (e.g., AIMM training) and private sector clients (e.g., advisory services) is embedded in the delivery structure to address constraints like weak institutions and lack of management skills.

quote.text: IFC is seeking to enhance its collaboration with the World Bank and enhance the quality of its investments in FCAS through several initiatives... Creating Markets Priority Setting Sessions (COMPASS)... IFC has established a dedicated unit to provide strategy, operations support and promote learning to help scale up IFC’s operations in FCS and IDA countries.

key_programme_risks: IFC breaching its Deployable Strategic Capital (DSC) threshold without capital increase.
Reduced development impact in FCAS due to high transaction costs and risks.
Insufficient mobilization of private finance in target sectors (climate, women-led SMEs).
Weak collaboration between IFC and other WBG institutions (e.g., World Bank) in FCAS.
UK loss of influence if shareholding drops below 4%.
Performance drop in IFC projects (55% rated positive in FY17, down from 60% in 2011-13).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: $5.5 billion capital increase to restore DSC to sustainable levels (above 4%).
Dedicated FCAS unit, COMPASS sessions, and increased staff deployments to FCAS countries.
IFC 3.0 strategy focuses on market creation and mobilization tools (e.g., MCPP, AMC).
Country Partnership Frameworks and joint initiatives (e.g., Afghanistan telecoms sector).
UK participation in capital increase maintains shareholding and voting power.
AIMM framework and strengthened additionality assessments to improve project quality.

fcas_specific_lessons: IEG found IFC’s FCAS engagements were ‘substantially successful’ but needed better tools and incentives (2014 evaluation).
Lessons from Afghanistan telecoms sector: Combined IDA (public sector), IFC (private sector), and MIGA (guarantees) interventions were effective.
Need for robust political economy analysis to design FCAS investments.
Importance of cross-WBG collaboration (e.g., COMPASS sessions with WBG Global Practices).

lessons_from_previous.text: The 2016 Multilateral Development Review rated IFC as ‘good’ for organisational strength but highlighted transparency and project performance as areas for improvement. IFC has since joined the IATI standard and introduced AIMM to address additionality and impact measurement.

design_changes_based_on_learning.text: IFC 3.0 strategy incorporates lessons from past evaluations, including: (1) Greater focus on FCAS and IDA countries (40% target by 2030), (2) Strengthened additionality framework, (3) AIMM for impact monitoring, and (4) Efficiency measures (e.g., $400 million budget savings).
design_changes_based_on_learning.source: 54589741.odt, Drivers for the intervention / Effectiveness and impact

quote.text: IEG has rated IFC as ‘substantially successful’ in adopting its recommendations over the most two recent years... Work is underway to prioritise [FCAS opportunities] and assign accountability and commit resources to develop these opportunities.

leverage_achieved.text: The $5.5 billion capital increase is expected to enable IFC to double its annual support from $12 billion to $25 billion by 2030 and triple mobilized finance from $7 billion to $23 billion per year. Historically, IFC has leveraged $265 billion in development finance from $2.6 billion in shareholder support (1:103 ratio).

capital_vs_revenue_split.text: The UK’s contribution is capital funding (equity increase) to IFC, not revenue/operational funding. IFC uses this capital to leverage lending and investments.

quote.text: IFC is the world’s largest DFI, with its portfolio in FY18 standing at $57 billion... IFC’s annual commitments alone are roughly equal to all European and the US DFI combined.

metadata.programme_name: Accelerating Ethiopia’s Economic Transformation (ACCELERATE)
metadata.quote: "This programme will support the Ethiopian Government’s vision of export-led manufacturing growth through foreign and domestic investments to become a reality more quickly and in a sustainable and inclusive way." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: March 2020", "End Date: December 2025" (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ACCELERATE combines implementation research (testing/scaling industrial park operations), capacity building (strengthening federal/regional institutions), and service delivery (direct support to industrial parks). The programme aims to operationalize industrial parks faster while improving job quality and institutional frameworks.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support the Ethiopian Government’s vision of export-led manufacturing growth through foreign and domestic investments to become a reality more quickly and in a sustainable and inclusive way." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 40,000 decent jobs created (primarily for low-skilled women and youth)
4 Industrial Parks (IPs) fully operationalized
Strengthened federal/regional institutions (EIC, IPDC, MoLSA)
Policy reforms in key federal government institutions
Reduced red tape in 4 target regions
Increased exports from IPs (targeting $100–140 million/year from Hawassa IP alone)
Improved housing/urban infrastructure around IPs
Enhanced linkages between FDI investors and domestic SMEs
what_objectives.summary: ACCELERATE aims to accelerate Ethiopia’s industrialization by making 4 Industrial Parks operational, creating 40,000 jobs, and strengthening institutions to support private sector growth, with a focus on inclusive job creation and export-led manufacturing.
what_objectives.quote: "Key objectives of the programme are to: Support industrialisation in Ethiopia while creating jobs and having value adding spillovers in the local economy... Drive up the quality of jobs, career growth opportunities and access to value adding products and services for industrial workers... Strengthen key federal and regional institutions as well as the regulatory and policy environment within which businesses operate." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia is classified as high-risk due to political transitions, ethnic tensions (3 million internally displaced), and macroeconomic imbalances (debt distress, forex shortages). The programme itself has a 'major' risk rating per DFID’s assessment.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet) and "there are undercurrents of political and ethnic tension, with three million people currently internally displaced" (D0002686.odt, CONTEXT section)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (state dominance, weak private sector space)
weak institutions (limited capacity in EIC, IPDC, MoLSA)
infrastructure (housing shortages, unreliable utilities in IPs)
logistics (port dependency on Djibouti, inefficient trade corridors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Infrastructure bottlenecks (e.g., water/electricity access) delay IP operations; weak institutions slow policy implementation; forex shortages limit import of raw materials; and political tensions create instability for investors. Labour retention is undermined by inadequate housing (workers spend 50-70% of salaries on shared rooms).
where_context.quote: "Infrastructure inside and outside IPs... access to water and electricity has been identified as a key binding constraint to factories starting and scaling up their operations... Lack of urban infrastructure such as housing and transportation have emerged as a key challenge for labour sourcing and retention." (D0002686.odt, DEEPDIVE: IPs)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with the Government of Ethiopia (GoE), with DFID providing funding/technical assistance while GoE institutions (EIC, IPDC, MoLSA) lead implementation. Decision-making is shared, with GoE setting priorities (e.g., IP locations) and DFID aligning support.
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (EIC, IPDC, MoLSA, regional bureaus)
training for labour inspectors and IP one-stop-shop staff
policy development support (e.g., Investment Promotion Law revisions)
technical assistance for aftercare functions (investor retention/expansion)
Better Work programme adoption (labour standards compliance)

partner_organizations.name: Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementation (IP coordination, investor facilitation, policy reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Industrial Parks Development Corporation (IPDC)
partner_organizations.role: IP infrastructure management and operational support

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA)
partner_organizations.role: Labour standards enforcement and worker protection

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Trade and Industry (MOTI)
partner_organizations.role: Industrial policy and domestic business integration

partner_organizations.name: Regional Bureaus of Trade/Industry (Oromia, Amhara, SNNPR, Tigray)
partner_organizations.role: Local IP support and SME linkage facilitation

partner_organizations.name: International Labour Organization (ILO)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance on labour standards (Better Work programme)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Complementary support on investment climate reforms

partner_organizations.name: Department for International Trade (DIT) and Foreign Commonwealth Office (FCO)
partner_organizations.role: Collaboration on UK-Ethiopia trade/investment linkages

who_partners.quote: "The programme has a high level of buy-in from key government counterparts including the Ethiopian Investment Commission, Ministry of Trade and Industries, Jobs Commission and Ministry of Finance." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary) and "DFID has resourced the programme well in terms of A1 and A2 advisory time, programme management and crosscutting inputs." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **technical assistance contracts** (for institutional support), **grants** (for specific interventions like housing/urban infrastructure), and **policy-based financing** (linked to reform milestones). DFID provides core funding directly to Ethiopian institutions with embedded advisors.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID acts as the funder/strategic overseer, while Ethiopian government agencies (EIC, IPDC, MoLSA) lead implementation with technical support from DFID-embedded advisors. The structure is adaptive, with flexibility to respond to government priorities (e.g., new IP sites).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Government of Ethiopia (GoE) was selected as the primary partner due to its **ownership of the industrialization strategy** and **high-level buy-in** (e.g., EIC reports directly to the Prime Minister’s Office). DFID’s prior programmes (PEPE, EIAF) established trust and alignment with GoE priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme has been reviewed/quality assured by the Team Leader of the Economic Development Team and the Head of DFID Ethiopia... Significant time was spent during the business case design, in discussions with the Government of Ethiopia and potential implementation partners." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Sub-awards for specific components (e.g., housing PPPs, labour training) are allocated through joint DFID-GoE committees, with approvals tied to reform milestones. For example, IP infrastructure funds are released based on operational targets (e.g., export volumes).
how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **Programme Steering Committee** (PSC) is implied, comprising DFID, EIC, IPDC, and MoLSA, with the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) providing high-level oversight. The PSC aligns with Ethiopia’s National Plan for Job Creation 2020–2025.
how_governance.quote: "The programme will be fully financed from DFID resources but will collaborate closely with the Department for International Trade (DIT) and Foreign Commonwealth Office (FCO)." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet) and "ACCELERATE directly supports both federal and regional government priorities related to job creation." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between pillars (e.g., from institutional reform to IP operations) based on **emerging government priorities** or **investor needs**, with DFID approval. The programme explicitly notes adaptability to political/economic changes (e.g., new IP sites).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **adaptive management** with quarterly reviews to adjust priorities. For example, if housing shortages persist, funds can shift to PPP models; if export targets lag, technical assistance can focus on logistics bottlenecks.
how_flexibility.quote: "Given the speed of change in private sector development in Ethiopia, a fundamental principle of this programme is that it is adaptive and flexible." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary) and "The programme has been designed in consultation with the Government of Ethiopia. It incorporates lessons from the previous programme and has been developed to be relevant to the existing context and new opportunities being created." (D0002686.odt, WHAT WILL ACCELERATE DO section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Ethiopian Government Institutions (EIC/IPDC/MoLSA) → [end beneficiaries: IPs, workers, SMEs]. No intermediary contractors are mentioned; DFID advisors are embedded within GoE agencies.
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID has resourced the programme well in terms of A1 and A2 advisory time, programme management and crosscutting inputs." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct DFID implementation (rejected due to lack of local ownership)
Multilateral-led delivery (e.g., World Bank; rejected to avoid dilution of GoE leadership)
Pure technical assistance (rejected as insufficient for systemic change)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **GoE-led partnership model** was chosen because: 1) **Ownership**: Ethiopia’s industrialization strategy is government-driven (EIC reports to PMO); 2) **Speed**: Embedded advisors accelerate reform implementation; 3) **Flexibility**: Adaptive design aligns with Ethiopia’s volatile context; 4) **Leverage**: DFID’s £45m catalyses GoE’s £1.8bn FOCAC investment for IP infrastructure.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (catalytic effect of DFID funds on GoE investments)
equity (focus on women/youth jobs and SME linkages)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoE absorption capacity limits: Weak institutions (EIC, IPDC) may struggle to manage expanded mandates (e.g., housing PPPs, aftercare services).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID will provide **embedded advisors** and **targeted technical assistance** (e.g., McKinsey’s IPDC institutional analysis). Capacity building is core to the programme.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference: Regional governments may prioritize local interests over national IP goals (e.g., land allocation delays).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: National Investment Coordination Platform (proposed in Investment Promotion Law) to align federal/regional priorities. DFID will facilitate **memoranda of understanding** between agencies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on EIC: EIC’s expanded role (land bank, labour regulation) risks diluting focus on investor facilitation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme includes **institutional reform support** (e.g., digitalizing processes, aftercare strategy) and **clear division of labour** with IPDC/MoLSA.

why_rationale.quote: "DFID has a strong appetite for contextual risk. Learning from existing programmes suggests that effective risk mitigation mechanisms can be established and that significant results can be achieved in risky programmes." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet) and "The programme has been designed in consultation with the Government of Ethiopia... to be relevant to the existing context and new opportunities being created." (D0002686.odt, WHAT WILL ACCELERATE DO section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Ethiopia’s **high-risk context** (political transitions, ethnic tensions) and **weak institutions** constrain partner selection to **government-led implementation**. Multilaterals (e.g., World Bank) or INGOs lack the mandate to navigate Ethiopia’s state-dominated economy, while private sector partners are limited by forex shortages and regulatory barriers.
q27_constraints_detail: State dominance: Only GoE agencies (EIC, IPDC) can secure land/licenses for IPs, excluding non-state actors.
Forex shortages: Limits international partners’ ability to import materials, requiring GoE-led solutions.
Ethnic tensions: Regional bureaucracies’ autonomy creates inconsistencies, necessitating federal coordination (e.g., National Investment Platform).
Institutional capacity: Weak MoLSA/IPDC requires embedded TA, ruling out arms-length partnerships.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **implementation research** (testing IP operational models) and **capacity building** (institutional reform) objectives necessitate a **GoE-led structure** with embedded advisors. Service delivery (e.g., housing PPPs) requires **flexible funding instruments** (grants for infrastructure, TA for policy reforms).
q28_linkages: IP operationalization (WHAT) → requires **EIC/IPDC leadership** (HOW) due to land/license control.
Job quality targets (WHAT) → necessitates **MoLSA engagement** (HOW) for labour inspections.
Export growth (WHAT) → demands **trade logistics reforms** (HOW) via MOTI/Djibouti coordination.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (rapid IP operationalization) with **equity** (worker housing, SME linkages). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Fast-tracking IPs risks sidelining domestic SMEs (mitigated via supply chain linkage targets); 2) **Cost vs. reach**: Housing PPPs increase expenses but improve worker retention; 3) **Expertise vs. ownership**: DFID advisors provide technical skills while GoE leads decision-making.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Housing costs: "A significant proportion of each worker’s salary goes toward housing, leaving little disposable income... productivity and retention levels are low." (D0002686.odt, DEEPDIVE: IPs) → Programme funds housing PPPs despite higher costs.

SME linkages: "Local businesses have a lot to learn from globally competitive FDIs... but there has been very little participation by domestic firms." (D0002686.odt, DEEPDIVE: IPs) → Dedicated resources for backward/forward linkages.

Labour standards: "Brands/International Buyers... hope to build a new production base that upholds strong social and environmental standards." (D0002686.odt, DEEPDIVE: IPs) → Better Work programme adoption adds compliance costs but ensures equity.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk context** (FCAS classification, debt distress) justifies **intensive oversight**: milestone-based funding, embedded advisors, and quarterly adaptive reviews. For example, forex shortages trigger **real-time reallocation** of TA to logistics reforms.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak institutional capacity (e.g., MoLSA’s limited labour inspections) shapes partner roles: DFID provides **embedded TA** for aftercare functions, while EIC leads investor coordination. Regional bureaus receive **targeted support** to standardize IP services.
intersections.quote: "The programme has been designed in consultation with the Government of Ethiopia. It incorporates lessons from the previous programme and has been developed to be relevant to the existing context and new opportunities being created." (D0002686.odt, WHAT WILL ACCELERATE DO section) and "Given the speed of change in private sector development in Ethiopia, a fundamental principle of this programme is that it is adaptive and flexible." (D0002686.odt, Programme summary)

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic instability: Forex shortages and debt distress may limit IP expansion (mitigation: advocacy for WTO accession and privatization).
Political volatility: Ethnic tensions or election delays could disrupt reforms (mitigation: high-level PMO engagement and adaptive funding).
Institutional overload: EIC/IPDC’s expanded mandates may overwhelm capacity (mitigation: embedded TA and digitalization).
Investor attrition: Delays in water/electricity access deter FDI (mitigation: £1.8bn FOCAC infrastructure investment).
Labour unrest: Poor housing/low wages risk strikes (mitigation: housing PPPs and Better Work standards).
SME exclusion: FDI-led growth may marginalize domestic firms (mitigation: supply chain linkage targets).
Regional fragmentation: Inconsistent land/licensing rules across regions (mitigation: National Investment Coordination Platform).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Forex shortages halting raw material imports for manufacturers.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support WTO accession to improve trade terms and advocate for forex allocation prioritization for IP inputs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: EIC’s expanded role (land bank, labour regulation) dilutes investor facilitation focus.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Fund institutional reform (e.g., digitalizing processes) and clarify division of labour with IPDC/MoLSA via MOUs.
Pilot PPP housing models (e.g., Mekelle) and allocate serviced land for worker accommodation near IPs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Weak MoLSA capacity undermining labour standards enforcement.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embed ILO Better Work programme in IPs and train regional labour inspectors.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, **political buy-in at the highest level** (PMO) is critical for reform traction but insufficient without **mid-level capacity** (e.g., EIC’s aftercare unit).
**Flexible funding** (e.g., reallocating TA to emerging bottlenecks like customs delays) is essential where institutional priorities shift rapidly.
**Embedded advisors** (vs. arms-length TA) are more effective in navigating bureaucratic silos (e.g., EIC-MoLSA coordination).
In **state-dominated economies**, private sector programmes must work **through government channels** (e.g., EIC for land allocation) rather than bypassing them.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: From **PEPE (2013–2020)**: 1) **Government leadership is non-negotiable**—programmes stalled without GoE buy-in; 2) **Flexibility delivers results**—PEPE’s opportunistic responses to policy windows (e.g., AGOA utilization) drove export growth; 3) **Labour focus adds value**—PEPE’s labour interventions (e.g., worker training) were handed over to ACCELERATE; 4) **Broader system fixes are needed**—sector-specific gains (e.g., textiles) were limited by cross-cutting constraints (e.g., forex access).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: ACCELERATE incorporates PEPE lessons by: 1) **Expanding institutional strengthening** (beyond PEPE’s sectoral focus); 2) **Prioritizing adaptive management** (quarterly reviews vs. PEPE’s annual cycles); 3) **Integrating housing/urban planning** (addressing PEPE’s labour retention challenges); 4) **Formalizing SME linkages** (PEPE’s ad-hoc efforts became a strategic pillar).
risks_lessons.quote: "Key Lessons that we have learnt in the implementation of PEPE are as follows: The focus on labour is very important and somewhere the UK can add a lot of value... The broader system needs to be fixed in Ethiopia for the private sector to grow and create more jobs... Programmes need to have a range of tools through which to support the different needs of government, businesses and workers." (D0002686.odt, PREVIOUS DFID PROGRAMMING section) and "ACCELERATE has a risk rating of major. DFID Ethiopia has a strong appetite for contextual risk... significant results can be achieved in risky programmes." (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID’s £45m catalyses: 1) GoE’s £1.8bn FOCAC investment for IP infrastructure (power, water); 2) Private sector investments (e.g., PVH’s Hawassa IP expansion, Guangzhou Sunshine’s $500m textile plant).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Capital: Majority of funds support **IP infrastructure** (e.g., housing, utilities) and **institutional capacity building** (e.g., EIC digitalization). Revenue: Covers **technical assistance** (embedded advisors) and **policy reform support** (e.g., Investment Promotion Law).
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: Up to £45 million" (D0002686.odt, SummarySheet) and "The full pipeline of industrial parks is expected to create around one million direct jobs; approximately 35,000 workers are currently employed in Bole Lemi and Hawassa Industrial Parks." (D0002686.odt, ETHIOPIA’S INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION?) and "At the 2019 FOCAC meeting PM Abiy signed a $1.8 billion investment deal that will, among other things, supply power for up to 16 industrial parks." (D0002686.odt, DEEPDIVE: IPs)

metadata.programme_name: Africa Technology and Innovation Partnerships (ATIP)

quote.text: "The Africa Technology and Innovation Partnerships (ATIP) programme will accelerate the growth of technological innovation in Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya and adjacent countries through strengthened networks between African policymakers, businesses, investors, innovators and relevant stakeholders with links to innovation stakeholders in the UK; an innovation fund for solutions to systemic barriers to scaling technological innovation in each setting and robust research on strengthening of innovation ecosystems."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The ATIP programme aims to accelerate technological innovation in Africa by strengthening innovation ecosystems through partnerships, funding solutions to systemic barriers, and conducting research. It combines capacity building (strengthening networks, skills, and policy), financing mechanisms (innovation fund), and evidence generation (research on innovation ecosystems).

q1_source.text: "The Africa Technology and Innovation Partnerships (ATIP) programme will accelerate the growth of technological innovation in Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya and adjacent countries through strengthened networks between African policymakers, businesses, investors, innovators and relevant stakeholders with links to innovation stakeholders in the UK; an innovation fund for solutions to systemic barriers to scaling technological innovation in each setting and robust research on strengthening of innovation ecosystems."

q3_expected_outputs.output: Larger and more effective networks of entrepreneurs and innovators building partnerships
Key barriers identified and addressed in each ecosystem
Strengthened technology and innovation policy and regulation
Targeted research, analysis and learning on strengthening innovation ecosystems
Number of new IP/patents (through a simplified registration process)
Increased speed in commercialisation of R&D
Increased level of R&D investment
Number of new market opportunities
Innovations which are i) commercialised, ii) deployed and iii) scaled
Increased investment and match funding (applications and receipt of funding from UK and elsewhere)

what_objectives.summary: The ATIP programme is designed to strengthen innovation ecosystems in Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa by addressing systemic barriers to scaling technological innovation. It focuses on building partnerships, funding solutions, and generating evidence to support inclusive economic growth and poverty alleviation.

quote.text: "The expected outputs are: Larger and more effective networks of entrepreneurs and innovators building partnerships... Key barriers identified and addressed in each ecosystem... Strengthened technology and innovation policy and regulation... Targeted research, analysis and learning on strengthening innovation ecosystems."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated as 'moderate' risk, indicating a balanced risk profile that is neither high-risk nor stable. This is explicitly stated in the document.

q5_source.source: Document: 52871093.odt, Overall programme risk rating section
q5_source.text: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate"

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The document highlights systemic barriers such as lack of financing for early-stage tech start-ups, gaps in skills and human capital, weak policy and regulatory environments, and limited market access. These constraints hinder the scaling of technological innovation and require a multi-faceted approach to address.

quote.source: Document: 52871093.odt, Table 1: Technology and Innovation Ecosystem Enablers section
quote.text: "The main areas consistently identified in the literature as serving as either enablers or barriers to scaling technological innovation... include: Partnerships, Skills and Knowledge, Investment, Policy and Regulation, Market Access, Infrastructure."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes co-creation and partnership with local stakeholders, including African policymakers, businesses, and innovators, indicating a shared decision-making approach. The UK provides expertise and funding, but local partners are actively engaged in designing and implementing solutions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and mentorship for entrepreneurs
supporting local tech hubs and innovation agencies
building networks and partnerships

This mixed approach allows for flexibility in addressing different barriers and leveraging UK expertise.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured as an open partnership with multiple stakeholders, including UK government agencies (Innovate UK, DCMS), local innovation ecosystem actors, and a managed fund for co-creating projects. This structure enables collaboration across sectors and geographies while maintaining flexibility to address context-specific barriers.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme will run an open competition for suppliers to deliver the managed fund, research, and policy capacity-building activities. This approach ensures transparency, value for money, and the selection of the most capable partners to achieve programme objectives.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on identified barriers and opportunities, but this requires careful prioritization and approval processes to mitigate risks of dilution or inefficiency.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be responsive to context, with the ability to adjust priorities based on research, analysis, and stakeholder engagement. q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focus on African technology and innovation ecosystems through existing programmes only, without a new dedicated initiative.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Programme focuses on partnerships and policy/regulation barriers
q24_alternatives_considered.description: A narrower focus on cross-cutting barriers like partnerships, policy, and regulation, without addressing all six identified barriers.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Programme with scope and flexibility to address critical barriers (recommended)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: A flexible, context-responsive programme addressing all six barriers (partnerships, skills, investment, policy, market access, infrastructure) based on local needs and UK comparative advantage.
A fund to support sustainable solutions with innovation ecosystem stakeholders, leveraging local expertise and resources.
Long-term engagement with specialist teams for research, policy, and network-building, co-financed with UK partners like Innovate UK and DCMS.
Combines a managed fund with specialist teams to balance local flexibility with UK expertise, ensuring both quick wins and long-term engagement.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed approach (Thematic Option 3 + Delivery Option 3) was chosen because it balances flexibility with depth, allowing the programme to respond to context-specific barriers while leveraging UK expertise and networks. This approach maximizes the potential for learning, collaboration, and sustainable impact by combining locally-led solutions with strategic UK partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing multiple teams and ensuring coherence across the programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by the strength of DFID’s science, technology, and innovation teams on the ground and a programme-funded coordination post.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Greater scope could reduce depth in tackling each barrier
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful prioritization of critical, tractable barriers in each setting to ensure focused delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Increased programme costs due to wider range of expertise required
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Balanced by the potential for greater impact and synergy across initiatives, as well as co-funding with UK partners.

quote.text: "The preferred option is for thematic option 3 (addressing all six barriers in Table 2) and delivery option 3; to combine a managed fund approach with procurement of specialist teams for partnerships, research, analysis and learning and policy and regulation... Thematic option 3 was chosen because the benefits of responding flexibly to the context and the enhanced opportunities to develop synergies between different enablers in the technology innovation ecosystem outweigh the risk that insufficient depth of resources and focus on a particular barrier will prevent delivery of results."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country focus (Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa) and the need to address context-specific barriers shape partner selection. Local stakeholders (policymakers, tech hubs, investors) are critical to understanding and navigating the political, economic, and social context, which influences who can effectively deliver the programme.
q27_constraints_detail: Local expertise is essential for navigating regulatory and policy environments
Partnerships with UK organizations (e.g., Innovate UK, DCMS) are chosen for their ability to complement local knowledge with global best practices
The need for flexible, context-responsive solutions limits the use of rigid, one-size-fits-all partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—strengthening innovation ecosystems by addressing systemic barriers—require a delivery structure that is both flexible (to respond to local needs) and collaborative (to leverage UK and African expertise). The mixed approach (managed fund + specialist teams) was chosen to balance quick, locally-led solutions with long-term capacity building and policy engagement.
q28_linkages: The need to address multiple, interrelated barriers (e.g., policy, investment, skills) requires a multi-partner, multi-instrument approach
The focus on scaling technological innovation necessitates partnerships with both local entrepreneurs and global networks (e.g., UK tech hubs)
Research and learning components are embedded to ensure the programme can adapt to emerging evidence and context changes
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive partnerships (e.g., ensuring women and marginalized groups participate) and efficient delivery (e.g., leveraging existing UK networks for speed). For example, the managed fund includes criteria to increase female participation, while specialist teams focus on long-term inclusion through policy and network-building.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Leveraging UK networks (e.g., Innovate UK) accelerates delivery but requires active measures (e.g., gender-disaggregated data, inclusion criteria in funding) to ensure marginalized groups are not left behind.
The programme balances local leadership (e.g., co-created projects) with UK technical support (e.g., policy hackathons) to avoid top-down solutions while ensuring high standards.
A mixed delivery model allows responsiveness to context but increases management complexity, requiring robust coordination mechanisms.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile influences oversight intensity, with milestone-based reviews and a high-level steering group to manage performance without stifling flexibility. The political and economic volatility in focus countries necessitates adaptive management but also demands stronger monitoring to mitigate risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include mentorship, training, and institutional strengthening. For example, local tech hubs and universities are engaged not just as implementers but as capacity builders, while UK partners (e.g., DCMS) provide digital skills training to address identified gaps.

Innovation ecosystem strengthening projects that will focus on supporting women and girls as innovators... Research and analysis specifically targeted at how to make technological innovation work for the most marginalised communities."

key_programme_risks.risk: Insufficient depth in addressing barriers due to broad scope
key_programme_risks.description: The programme’s wide focus on six barriers (partnerships, skills, investment, policy, market access, infrastructure) risks spreading resources too thinly, reducing impact in any single area.

key_programme_risks.risk: Complexity of managing a mixed delivery model
key_programme_risks.description: Combining a managed fund, specialist teams, and partnerships with UK agencies increases coordination challenges, potentially leading to inefficiencies or misalignment.

key_programme_risks.risk: Political and economic instability in focus countries
key_programme_risks.description: Volatility in Nigeria, Kenya, or South Africa could disrupt programme activities, particularly those requiring government engagement (e.g., policy reform).

key_programme_risks.risk: Limited local capacity to absorb funding or implement changes
key_programme_risks.description: Gaps in skills, infrastructure, or institutional strength may hinder the ability of local partners to effectively utilize programme support.

key_programme_risks.risk: Duplication or lack of coordination with existing initiatives
key_programme_risks.description: Without active management, the programme could overlap with other UK or donor-funded technology/innovation programmes, reducing efficiency.

key_programme_risks.risk: Equity gaps in access to programme benefits
key_programme_risks.description: Marginalized groups (e.g., women, rural populations) may be unintentionally excluded without targeted outreach and inclusion mechanisms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Prioritize tractable, high-impact barriers in each country through stakeholder consultation and evidence-based diagnostics. Use the inception phase to refine focus areas.
Establish a dedicated programme coordination post and leverage DFID’s in-country science and innovation teams to ensure coherence. Use milestone-based reviews to monitor progress.

Design flexible interventions that can adapt to changing contexts. Build strong relationships with a diverse range of stakeholders (e.g., civil society, private sector) to reduce reliance on government alone.
Embed capacity building as a core objective, including training, mentorship, and institutional strengthening. Partner with local hubs and universities to ensure sustainability.

Conduct a detailed mapping of the HMG portfolio and wider initiatives during the inception phase. Actively coordinate with other programmes (e.g., Transforming Energy Access, EdTech Hub) to identify synergies.

Apply the ‘Leave No One Behind’ principle across all outputs, with specific targets for women, girls, and marginalized groups. Use gender-disaggregated data and inclusion criteria in funding decisions.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The document references lessons from the DFID Research Review (2016) and other studies (e.g., ANDE, USAID reports) highlighting the need for long-term ecosystem strengthening, patient capital for early-stage innovators, and policy engagement. These inform the programme’s focus on systemic barriers rather than isolated interventions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme’s mixed delivery model and emphasis on flexibility were shaped by evidence that innovation ecosystems require holistic, context-responsive support. The inclusion of a 6-month inception phase reflects lessons on the importance of diagnostic work before scaling.

quote.text: "The risks of this approach are that the greater scope could reduce the depth into which the programme can tackle each barrier and it increases the complexity of monitoring programme performance... Careful prioritisation of critical barriers which are tractable to change in each setting will be required to mitigate these risks."

metadata.programme_name: The Evidence Fund
metadata.quote: The Evidence Fund brings together seven programmes delivered across the Evidence Department to generate responsive analysis, research and evaluation. It will provide up to £58 million over five years (2020-2025) to enhance DFID’s ability to identify evidence priorities and drive greater development impact. (D0003368.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: Start: July 2020 – End: March 2026 (D0004064.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Evidence Fund primarily focuses on **evidence generation** (research, analysis, evaluation) to inform policy and programming decisions. It also includes **policy influence** by ensuring evidence uptake and **capacity building** through embedded research specialists and training. The fund consolidates multiple responsive research programmes into a single platform to improve efficiency and coordination.
what_objectives.q1_source: The Evidence Fund brings together seven programmes delivered across the Evidence Department to generate responsive analysis, research and evaluation. [...] The programme will enable the Evidence Department to support the full breadth of DFID’s strategic objectives, enhancing the impact of ODA investment and offering the best value for money. (D0003368.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: context-specific research for DFID’s priority regions (South Asia, East Africa, MENA)
thematic evaluations on what works (e.g., systematic reviews, evidence maps)
responsive short-term analysis on emerging issues (e.g., global trends, risks, opportunities)
synthesis of pre-existing evaluations and monitoring data
capacity building for DFID staff on evidence use (e.g., training, evidence days)
strategic evaluations to fill evidence gaps (e.g., cost-effectiveness, impact analysis)
policy engagement and research uptake support
cross-programme learning and lesson dissemination
non-ODA research for foreign policy challenges (added in 2023)
science research partnerships addressing country-specific challenges (e.g., climate, health)
what_objectives.summary: The Evidence Fund is a **demand-driven platform** that consolidates DFID/FCDO’s responsive evidence programmes to generate and synthesize research, evaluations, and analysis. It aims to enhance evidence-based decision-making for development and diplomatic policies, with a focus on flexibility, efficiency, and uptake.
what_objectives.quote: The Evidence Fund will bring together separate responsive RED programmes into a single demand-driven platform that will address a broad spectrum of DFID’s evidence needs. [...] The programme will enhance DFID’s ability to apply lessons across a broad range of topics to achieve international development outcomes. (D0003368.odt, What will UK funds be spent on?)

countries_regions: South Asia (India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Myanmar)
East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Somalia, Sudan, South Sudan)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)**, where 80% of the extreme poor are expected to live by 2030. However, the overall programme risk rating is classified as **‘moderate’**, reflecting managed risks across diverse contexts.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate (D0003368.odt, SummarySheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: data limitations (e.g., lack of localized evidence)
weak institutions (e.g., need for capacity building in research uptake)
political economy barriers (e.g., aligning research with government priorities)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: FCAS contexts require **adaptive research methods** (e.g., rapid evaluations, nimble procurement) and **localized partnerships** to ensure relevance. Data gaps and weak institutions limit the ability to generate or use evidence effectively, necessitating capacity-building and flexible funding mechanisms.
where_context.quote: By 2030, most extremely poor people will live in Africa, in countries that suffer from conflict and instability and in marginalised populations. [...] Rapid population growth threatens to stall progress on poverty, coupled with rising human capital investment needs, migratory pressures and weak jobs growth for growing youth populations. (D0003368.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) / formerly DFID
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO/RED retains **intellectual leadership** (defines research questions, methodologies, quality assurance) while the **Fund Manager** (PwC/Integrity) handles procurement and contract management. Southern partners (e.g., local researchers, government agencies) are engaged as **subcontractors** or **beneficiaries** of capacity-building.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for DFID/FCDO staff on evidence use (e.g., in-person workshops in Bangladesh, Uganda)
evidence learning events (e.g., Professional Development Conferences)
technical support to country offices (e.g., Research Hubs embedded in regions)
mentorship for local researchers (e.g., barriers analysis for supplier engagement)
co-authorship and joint research design (e.g., country-specific studies)

partner_organizations.role: procurement, contract management, quality assurance, research dissemination

partner_organizations.role: strategic oversight, science partnerships, regional coordination
