partner_organizations.role: facilitation of science partnerships (e.g., Southeast Asia pilot)

who_partners.quote: A lead Fund Manager will perform a range of functions on behalf of DFID (including procurement, contract management, support quality assurance/peer review and dissemination) to reduce duplication, management costs and free up the capacity of Research Specialists to maximise policy engagement and research uptake. (D0003368.odt, What will UK funds be spent on?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **competitive contracts** for the Fund Manager and research commissions, alongside **grants** for specific studies. The Fund Manager operates under a **framework agreement** with FCDO, while sub-awards to researchers are issued via **competitive calls for proposals** or **direct commissions** (for rapid analysis).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO’s **Evidence Department** provides strategic oversight via an **Evidence Fund Board**. The **Fund Manager (PwC/Integrity)** handles procurement, contract management, and dissemination, while **DFID/FCDO Research Specialists** retain intellectual leadership (defining research questions, quality assurance). Regional **Research Hubs** (e.g., SARH, EARH) engage with country offices to shape demand.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Fund Manager was selected via **OJEU competition** to ensure cost-efficiency and expertise in managing multiple research streams. Research suppliers are chosen through **competitive calls** to access global expertise, with flexibility for **direct awards** under £118k for rapid needs (e.g., SARH’s 17 demand-responsive studies in 2019).
how_mechanism.quote: The Fund Manager role will be procured through an OJEU competition. [...] The majority of the individual research studies will be commissioned through competitive calls for proposals from research organisations with contracts as the main funding arrangement. (D0003368.odt, Who will implement the support we provide?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Evidence Fund Board** provides strategic direction, while **Technical Steering Panels** (ad-hoc groups of DFID advisors, Heads of Profession, and RED teams) oversee quality assurance. The **Fund Manager** organizes external peer reviews, and **DFID country offices** co-design research with regional hubs.
how_governance.quote: The overall business case will be coordinated and managed by the Evidence Department. The Evidence Fund Board will provide strategic direction and oversight of the activity under this business case. [...] A lead adviser from the Evidence Department team will lead coordination between DFID stakeholders and external partners. (D0003368.odt, Who will implement the support we provide?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated **between regions** (e.g., underspend in one hub used for emerging priorities like West/South Africa) but require **approval** for major shifts. The **Fund Manager** has discretion for rapid-response studies under £118k.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities are **demand-driven** and adjusted annually via the **Evidence Fund Board**. The programme includes a **flexible mechanism** for urgent requests (e.g., disease outbreaks, climate emergencies) and **adaptive management** for emerging themes (e.g., Covid-19, Sargassum).
how_flexibility.quote: The programme will be inherently flexible to support RED’s evolving strategic priorities [...] and will provide flexible funding options to respond to high impact and quality proposals in new regions. (D0003368.odt, What will UK funds be spent on?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Fund Manager (PwC/Integrity)** → **Research Suppliers (subcontractors)** → End Researchers
how_efficiency.quote: Fund Manager Component Total Value: £48.7m (£43.4m without management fee) (D0003368.odt, Diagram 2)

q24_alternatives_considered: maintaining separate funding mechanisms (rejected due to inefficiencies)
full insourcing of procurement (rejected due to staff capacity constraints)
outsourcing all research management (rejected to retain DFID’s intellectual leadership)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **Fund Manager model** was chosen to **reduce duplication** (e.g., separate procurement teams), **free up DFID staff time** for policy engagement, and **improve coordination** across evidence streams. It balances **flexibility** (rapid response to country needs) with **rigor** (quality assurance, peer review). The platform structure enables **cross-programme learning** and **strategic prioritization** via the Evidence Fund Board.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (reducing management costs by 10.9%)
partner capacity (access to global expertise via competitive calls)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in Fund Manager procurement could stall research delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Year 1 funds were delivered through existing frameworks while the tender was run.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Northern contractors may limit Southern ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regional hubs (e.g., SARH, EARH) embedded in LMICs to shape demand; local supplier engagement strategies (e.g., market analysis, inclusive feedback to bidders).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High demand may exceed capacity, leading to unmet requests.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritization framework managed by the Evidence Fund Board; flexible funding for underspend reallocation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Non-ODA funding uncertainty (annual approvals).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capped at £500k for FY23/24; allocation across RED platforms for flexibility.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (reduced duplication, staff time freed for policy engagement)
effectiveness (evidence uptake metrics, e.g., policy influence in Kenya, India)
equity (regional hubs ensure localized research priorities)
why_rationale.quote: By both rationalising and contracting out procurement functions, the Evidence Fund will enable more efficient commissioning of world-leading research and evaluation, without removing DFID research leads from the content and findings from the research. (D0003368.odt, What needs to change?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts and **localized evidence gaps** constrain partner selection to those with **regional expertise** and **rapid-response capabilities**. For example, MENA’s fragile settings require partners familiar with conflict-sensitive research methods, while South Asia’s climate challenges demand suppliers with environmental science expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS contexts limit pool of eligible suppliers (e.g., security clearance requirements).
Data scarcity in LMICs necessitates partners with **primary data collection** capacity.
Language/cultural barriers favor local/regional researchers (e.g., SARH’s supplier market study).
Regulatory environments (e.g., procurement rules) shape subcontracting approaches.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **demand-responsive nature** of the programme (e.g., urgent policy questions, emerging crises) determines the **flexible, multi-layered structure**: a **Fund Manager** for rapid procurement, **regional hubs** for localized engagement, and **competitive calls** for global expertise. The need for **cross-programme learning** drives the platform model (vs. siloed programmes).
q28_linkages: Need for **real-time decision support** → Fund Manager’s rapid-analysis mechanism (4–8 week turnaround).
Focus on **policy uptake** → Embedded Research Specialists and Technical Steering Panels.
**Global public goods** (e.g., systematic reviews) → Open competitive calls for suppliers.
**Localized evidence** (e.g., Kenya elections) → Regional hubs with country-office links.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between **Northern efficiency** (e.g., Fund Manager’s centralized procurement) and **Southern ownership** (e.g., limited local supplier engagement in EARH). Mitigations include **regional hubs** (to embed local priorities) and **supplier market analyses** (to reduce barriers for LMIC researchers).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: **Rapid-response studies** (4–8 weeks) may bypass local partners; mitigated by hubs’ outreach.
Expertise vs. ownership: **Global contractors** ensure rigor but may sideline LMIC researchers; mitigated by co-design with country offices.
Cost vs. reach: **Competitive calls** maximize VfM but favor established institutions; mitigated by capacity-building for local suppliers.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (FCAS, data gaps) justifies **milestone-based oversight** (e.g., Technical Steering Panels) and **adaptive management** (e.g., reallocating underspend to emerging regions). High-risk contexts (e.g., Somalia) trigger additional safeguards (e.g., third-party monitoring).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: (1) **Embedding Research Specialists** in hubs to co-design research with country offices; (2) **Training DFID staff** to improve evidence demand/uptake; (3) **Supplier development** (e.g., EARH’s study on local research market barriers).
intersections.quote: Flexibility to respond to rapid requests for evidence for urgent business needs. [...] The Evidence Fund will include a flexible mechanism to procure studies within a short turnaround time using existing well-established procurement mechanisms. (D0003368.odt, What needs to change?)

key_programme_risks: Delays in recruitment of project-funded roles (mitigation: pre-approved recruitment processes).
Underutilization of non-ODA funding (mitigation: flexible allocation across RED platforms).
Limited engagement of local suppliers (mitigation: market analysis, inclusive feedback to bidders).
High demand outstripping capacity (mitigation: prioritization framework, Evidence Fund Board oversight).
Non-ODA budget uncertainty (mitigation: capped annual allocations, redeployment options).
Overlap with other FCDO research programmes (mitigation: coordination via Global Science Department).
Quality assurance gaps in rapid-response studies (mitigation: Technical Steering Panels, peer review).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Year 1 delivery through existing frameworks (e.g., EARH’s EARF).
SARH/EARH to conduct supplier market studies and develop inclusion strategies.
Pre-allocated £500k for FY23/24; option to redeploy staff to ODA work if needed.
Evidence Fund Board prioritizes requests; underspend reallocated to high-demand regions.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Rapid evaluations** (e.g., nimble evaluations in conflict zones) are critical for FCAS; the programme includes a **£12m thematic evaluation component** to address this gap.
**Localized research hubs** (e.g., EARH) improve relevance and uptake in fragile settings by embedding staff with country offices.
**Third-party monitoring** is used in high-risk contexts (e.g., Somalia) to ensure data quality.
**Flexible funding** (e.g., under £118k direct awards) enables responses to crises (e.g., Covid-19 in Kenya).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **EARH’s SCOR programme** (A++ in Annual Reviews) and **SARH’s SACRF** demonstrated that: (1) **Fund Manager models** reduce DFID staff burden; (2) **Embedded hubs** increase policy uptake; (3) **Cross-programme learning** maximizes VfM. These informed the Evidence Fund’s design, including the **learning function** within the Fund Manager.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Consolidated **seven separate programmes** into one platform to reduce duplication.
Added **non-ODA component** (2023) to address diplomatic research needs, piloted successfully in FY22/23.
Expanded **science partnerships** (e.g., Covid-19 seroprevalence studies) based on demand from HMG Posts.
Increased **flexible funding** for emerging regions (e.g., West/South Africa) using underspend.
Strengthened **supplier diversity** requirements (e.g., EARH’s local market study).
risks_lessons.quote: The challenges the Evidence Fund will address: [...] (i) multiple delivery channels; (ii) inflexibility to respond to rapid requests; (iii) inefficient and duplicated procurement; (iv) complex strategic oversight at the Divisional level; and (v) barriers to maximising the collective impact and learning of research and evaluation. (D0003368.odt, What needs to change?)

metadata.programme_name: St Helena: Economic Development Investment Programme

quote.text: Supporting economic development in St Helena through enhanced dialogue on policy reforms, infrastructure development and through harnessing private investment opportunities.

duration_source.text: The economic development investment programme is a 6 year programme broken down into a 3 year committed investment of £15m over for three years to 2021/22, a breakpoint consisting of a review and decision point in June 2021/22, followed by an indicative 3 year investment contingent upon the outcome of the breakpoint review. Given that there are a number of elements of the programme that are due to be finalised in the next 6-9 months, followed by a programme review, only a 3 year commitment makes sense at this juncture for approval purposes.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines infrastructure development (service delivery), policy reforms (capacity building), and private sector mobilization (financing mechanism) to support St Helena's economic self-sufficiency. It aims to leverage previous UK investments (e.g., the airport) while addressing systemic barriers to growth through a mix of capital projects, technical assistance, and institutional reforms.

q1_source.text: The programme will help support policy & institutional reforms, implement strategic infrastructure development and leverage private sector investment opportunities on the island. This support is vital to underpin the economic gains expected from the airport, the expected submarine cable investment, and the other benefits expected from private sector investment in renewable energy, and in tourism and other sectors.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Infrastructure fit for current needs, resilient against natural disasters, and supporting future economic growth
Increased revenues from tourism and niche sectors
Adequate public utilities addressing needs of aging, disabled, and vulnerable groups
Economic reforms in land development, immigration, labour markets, and taxation
Jobs created (e.g., construction jobs)
£5m mobilisation of private sector funds for infrastructure investment
Improved SHG project management and procurement capabilities
Delivery of an asset management system to prevent deterioration of public infrastructure

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform St Helena’s economy by combining strategic infrastructure investments with policy reforms and private sector mobilization, building on recent developments like the airport and planned submarine cable connectivity.

quote.text: The programme aims to support St Helena on a steady path to growing self-sufficiency, through increased tourism and economic development, driven by a growing private sector, by ensuring that the basic infrastructure needs of St Helenians are met.
quote.source: 48790896.odt, Impact and Outcome that we expect to achieve

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as moderate risk due to St Helena’s remote location, limited institutional capacity, and dependency on UK aid, but with low conflict/terrorism risks and a stable political environment under UK governance.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The island’s remoteness and small scale create high unit costs and limit access to materials/labour, while weak institutional capacity hampers planning and reform implementation. Infrastructure maintenance has historically followed a 'build-neglect-rebuild' cycle due to budget pressures.

quote.text: St Helena is a remote small island state with limited capacity to support self-sustaining economic growth. Its economic development remains highly constrained by barriers like scale and high unit costs, insufficient resources (physical, human, business and financial), and relatively low capacity to plan and manage change effectively.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO retains strategic oversight and approval authority (e.g., breakpoint review, compact negotiations), while St Helena Government (SHG) implements projects with technical assistance. Key decisions (e.g., project approvals, reform milestones) require joint agreement via the High-Level Panel.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for policy/institutional reforms
project management and procurement training
support for public-private partnerships
asset management systems

partner_organizations.name: St Helena Government (SHG)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer; accountable for financial contributions and project delivery

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO/DFID)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic overseer; provides technical assistance and governance oversight

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder via European Development Fund (EDF11) for infrastructure projects

partner_organizations.name: Private Sector (local and international)
partner_organizations.role: Investment mobilization and public-private partnerships (e.g., tourism, renewable energy)

partner_organizations.name: Technical Assistance Contractors
partner_organizations.role: Short-term specialized support for project design, reform implementation, and monitoring

quote.text: The programme will be primarily implemented by SHG, who will be fully accountable and responsible for the management of the financial contributions of DFID. [...] The SRO for this programme will be the Senior Economic Adviser within the OTD Team, supported by Infrastructure & Private Sector Advisers, and will draw on the support of DFID staff on island and from within the Overseas Territories’ department and beyond, as necessary.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **block funding** (£15m committed for 3 years, with a breakpoint review for the next £15m) and **technical assistance contracts** for capacity building. Funds are channeled as non-budgetary financial aid to SHG’s capital programme, with ring-fenced allocations for specific projects.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Strategic oversight is provided by a **High-Level Panel (HLP)** (joint DFID-SHG), while day-to-day management involves a **Capital Programme Review Group** and a **Project Management Unit (PMU)** within SHG. DFID retains control over major procurements (>£2m) and technical assistance contracts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: SHG is the sole implementer due to its status as the local government, while technical assistance contractors are selected based on specialized needs (e.g., project design, reform support). No competitive process is described for partners beyond SHG’s mandatory role.

quote.text: The programme will be primarily implemented by SHG, who will be fully accountable and responsible for the management of the financial contributions of DFID. [...] For major procurements (greater than £2m), DFID will consider undertaking these through DFID Procurement and Commercial Department as per DFID procurement rules.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **High-Level Panel (HLP)** includes the Governor, DFID/FCO representatives, SHG’s Financial Secretary, and Chief Executive for Economic Development. It oversees reform progress, infrastructure deliverables, and investment decisions. A **Capital Programme Review Group** and **Project Management Unit (PMU)** handle operational management.

quote.text: The HLP will have oversight of the overall pace of reforms, their progress and their outcome; oversight of the actual programme infrastructure deliverables; and decisions regarding next investments. [...] The programme will have specific related review milestones to be agreed between SHG and DFID which will operate throughout the lifetime of the project.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects within the capital programme, subject to joint DFID-SHG agreement and alignment with the compact’s strategic objectives. The breakpoint review (2021/22) allows for adjustments based on performance.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a **breakpoint review** (2021/22) to assess progress and adjust the second £15m tranche. Annual reviews and milestone tracking enable adaptive management, with reforms and projects reprioritized as needed via the HLP.

quote.text: The programme’s governance structure is designed to be agile and adaptive to changes in context, taking into account ongoing lessons learned, emerging reform requirements, emerging infrastructure priorities, and changing management arrangements as required.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO/DFID → St Helena Government (SHG) [→ sub-contractors for technical assistance]. SHG manages day-to-day delivery, with DFID overseeing major procurements and strategic direction.

quote.text: Funds will be provided to SHG from DFID’s OTD capital resources and will be made available to departments through SHG’s capital budget management mechanisms. [...] For major procurements (greater than £2m), DFID will consider undertaking these through DFID Procurement and Commercial Department as per DFID procurement rules.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No additional capital support; SHG would rely on its limited resources and EU EDF11 funds, leading to infrastructure deterioration and delayed economic growth.
£30m over 6 years with a breakpoint review, combining economic and social infrastructure investments under a compact framework.
£8–9m over 3 years for backlog social investments, with limited economic development focus and no reform incentives.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 was selected for its **strategic alignment** with St Helena’s long-term vision (e.g., doubling tourism, private sector growth), **higher value for money** (leveraging previous investments like the airport), and **reform incentives** tied to the compact. The 6-year horizon and breakpoint review balance ambition with adaptability.
q25_decision_factors: alignment with St Helena’s 10-Year Plan and SEDP
need for policy reforms to underpin infrastructure investments
risk mitigation via phased funding (breakpoint review)
speed of economic impact (quick wins + long-term growth)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low SHG capacity to manage complex procurements and projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID oversight for procurements >£2m; technical assistance for project management; phased funding with milestone reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited local competition for contracts, risking poor VFM
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Grouping projects to attract international bidders; open competitive tendering where feasible; DFID procurement rules for major contracts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays due to slow SHG decision-making or reform implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: High-Level Panel to monitor reform milestones; breakpoint review contingent on progress; adaptive management via annual reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Leakage of funds via imports (materials/labour)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritize local sourcing where possible; monitor macroeconomic effects to minimize leakages.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (achieving economic growth and reform targets)
equity (addressing needs of disabled, aging, and vulnerable groups)

quote.text: The preferred option is Option 1 because it is most consistent with the future direction of the HMG relationship with St Helena and with lagging regions. [...] Under Option 1 Economic Development Investment Programme—a programme of investments was developed on the back of the emerging vision described in the strategic case. The £30m investment programme is prefaced on the importance of medium-term commitments and a mutual accountability framework of a compact to arrive at the £30m, 6-year commitment (2019/20-2024/25).

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: St Helena’s remoteness and small market size limit the pool of qualified local partners, necessitating reliance on SHG as the sole implementer with DFID-provided technical assistance. The lack of competition among local contractors (due to limited private sector capacity) requires DFID to manage major procurements directly to ensure VFM.
q27_constraints_detail: No multilateral or regional funds available (e.g., St Helena is ineligible for UK-Caribbean Infrastructure Partnership or Pacific Regional Infrastructure Facility)
Limited local contractor base (historically exacerbated by airport construction absorbing skilled labour)
High import costs for materials/labour due to remoteness
SHG’s weak procurement and project management capacity
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **mixed objectives** (infrastructure + reforms + private sector mobilization) require a **hybrid delivery structure**: SHG implements projects (due to local accountability), while DFID manages strategic oversight and technical assistance (to address capacity gaps). The need for **policy reforms** (e.g., immigration, land use) necessitates joint governance via the compact.
q28_linkages: Infrastructure goals → SHG implementation with DFID oversight (to ensure technical standards)
Policy reform goals → High-Level Panel (joint DFID-SHG) to monitor progress
Private sector mobilization → Technical assistance to design PPPs and investment frameworks
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (e.g., grouping projects to attract international bidders) with **equity** (e.g., ring-fencing funds for disability-accessible infrastructure and social housing). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Quick wins are prioritized to build confidence, but must still meet disability/gender standards; (2) **Local ownership vs. expertise**: SHG leads delivery, but DFID retains control over major procurements to mitigate VFM risks.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Projects must maximize local employment (e.g., construction jobs) but may require international contractors for specialized tasks (e.g., rockfall protection), increasing costs.
Ambitious reforms (e.g., immigration, taxation) are critical for economic growth but may face local resistance; the compact includes milestones to balance urgency with political buy-in.
Early projects (e.g., rockfall protection) are prioritized for visible impact, but must align with the 10-Year Plan’s strategic goals (e.g., tourism growth).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (due to weak institutions and remoteness) justifies **intensive oversight** via the High-Level Panel, milestone reviews, and DFID’s role in major procurements. Adaptive management (e.g., breakpoint review) mitigates uncertainties in SHG’s capacity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: SHG’s limited capacity dictates the need for **embedded technical assistance** (e.g., project management support) and DFID’s direct management of high-value procurements. Capacity building is a **core objective**, with reforms and training designed to gradually shift responsibilities to SHG.

quote.text: The programme’s governance structure is designed to be agile and adaptive to changes in context, taking into account ongoing lessons learned, emerging reform requirements, emerging infrastructure priorities, and changing management arrangements as required. [...] There is also a long history to DFID support to capital investment in St Helena, through which we have built up a strong understanding of the operating environment. The programme is very high on St. Helena’s political and economic development agenda and programme management capabilities on the island will be augmented by mobilising short-term specialised resources under a technical assistance contract.

key_programme_risks.risk: SHG’s limited capacity to deliver complex infrastructure projects on time/budget
Low competition among local contractors, leading to poor VFM
Delays in policy reforms (e.g., immigration, land use) stalling private sector investment
Leakage of economic benefits via imports (e.g., materials, labour)
Natural disasters (e.g., rockfalls) damaging new infrastructure
Insufficient tourism growth to justify airport/port investments
Public resistance to reforms (e.g., taxation, land development)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: SHG’s limited capacity to deliver complex infrastructure projects
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance for project management; DFID oversight for procurements >£2m; phased funding with milestone reviews.
Group projects to attract international bidders; open competitive tendering; DFID procurement rules for major contracts.
Compact with clear milestones; High-Level Panel to monitor progress; breakpoint review contingent on reform implementation.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Leakage of economic benefits via imports
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Prioritize local sourcing; monitor macroeconomic effects; design projects to maximize local employment (e.g., construction jobs).
Invest in resilient design (e.g., rockfall protection); include maintenance budgets in project planning.
Quick wins to boost visitor economy (e.g., accommodation infrastructure); align investments with SEDP’s tourism targets.
Citizen engagement via surveys and feedback loops; phased reform rollout with communication campaigns.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID capital programmes in St Helena highlighted needs for: (1) **stronger project management** (e.g., delays due to low SHG capacity); (2) **procurement reforms** (e.g., limited local competition); (3) **maintenance planning** (to avoid ‘build-neglect-rebuild’ cycles). The current programme addresses these via technical assistance, DFID procurement oversight, and asset management systems.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) A **breakpoint review** (lesson: need for adaptive management); (2) **ring-fenced funds for social infrastructure** (lesson: balance economic and social needs); (3) **explicit disability/gender inclusion criteria** (lesson: past projects lacked equitable access).

quote.text: The most recent project completion review offers lessons for future development of programmes namely on management and procurement options. PCRs demonstrate some gains to job creation in the construction sector, consumption spending, and improvements to capital asset base to the island. KPIs of this type of a programme highlight more infrastructure focused indicators. [...] The programme’s governance structure is designed to be agile and adaptive to changes in context, taking into account ongoing lessons learned, emerging reform requirements, emerging infrastructure priorities, and changing management arrangements as required.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage £5m in private sector funds for infrastructure investment, alongside mobilizing additional resources through public-private partnerships (PPPs).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is **capital-focused**, with funds allocated to SHG’s capital programme for infrastructure projects. A small proportion (~£300k) is earmarked for technical assistance, monitoring, and evaluation.

quote.text: The UK Government will provide up to £30m, £15m committed for the next 3 years (2019/20-2021/22), followed by a breakpoint review to unlock the remaining £15m indicatively planned for the following three years (2021/22-2024/25). [...] A small proportion of this (up to £300k) would be set aside for independent evaluation, annual reviews and independent verification of programme quality.

metadata.programme_name: Unlocking Digital Impact for Development
metadata.quote: "This programme aims to support the international development community to more efficiently and effectively harness digital technologies to improve the lives of the poor, transform economies and societies, and accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)." (53314291.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The programme budget is £18.5 million between 2019/20-2023/24." (53314291.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (digital products/tools), capacity building (training/skills-building), policy influence (data-driven policy-making tools), and implementation research (trialling/institutionalising good practices). It also includes a financing mechanism component through strategic partnerships.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will identify, trial and institutionalise good practice and common standards for digital development work. It will deliver the following outputs: i) sustainable and reusable digital products which create new or improved services; ii) replicable business and partnership models which increase the use of digital products and data; iii) data-driven policy-making tools and products which inform and advance digital transformation in developing countries; and iv) training offerings and skills-building tools which improve investments in digital technologies." (53314291.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: sustainable and reusable digital products (tools/platforms/services)
replicable business and partnership models for digital/data services
data-driven policy-making tools/products
training offerings and skills-building tools
identification and institutionalisation of good practices/standards

what_objectives.summary: The programme seeks to systematically address four key barriers to digital development (fragmentation, business models, policy guidance, and capability gaps) through a mix of product development, capacity strengthening, policy tools, and strategic coordination.
what_objectives.quote: "This programme aims to address each of these barriers, working with DIAL and other strategic partners." (53314291.odt, Barriers to harnessing the potential of digital technology for development)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk in the business case, with no specific focus on FCAS contexts though it acknowledges operating in countries with digital capability gaps and fragmented ecosystems.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (53314291.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Fragmented investments at country level lead to duplicative digital initiatives lacking scale/sustainability. Limited evidence-based policy guidance and inadequate business models hinder uptake of digital services. Digital capability gaps among donors/governments reduce effective decision-making. MNO data access is constrained by privacy/regulatory concerns.
where_context.quote: "Significant barriers stand in the way of realising the full potential of digital technologies for development purposes. In particular, fragmented investments in technologies at the country-level have resulted in a proliferation of duplicative, immature digital initiatives that lack scale and sustainability." (53314291.odt, Barriers to harnessing the potential of digital technology for development)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DIAL's Board (comprising Northern donors like DFID, BMGF, USAID, Sida) sets strategic direction, with DFID having a Board seat. Operational decisions are made by DIAL's CEO (UNF employee) reporting to the Board. Southern partners (e.g., country governments) are beneficiaries/implementers but lack governance roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: training offerings
skills-building tools
donor capability building (US/Europe)
in-country practitioner training (e.g., Principles for Digital Development workshops)

partner_organizations.name: Digital Impact Alliance (DIAL)
partner_organizations.role: Primary delivery vehicle (£15m allocation)

partner_organizations.name: UN Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Host/fiduciary agent for DIAL

partner_organizations.name: Pathways for Prosperity Commission
partner_organizations.role: Policy research/advice pillar (£3m allocation)
partner_organizations.location: UK (hosted by Oxford University’s Blavatnik School of Government)

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: DIAL Founding Partner/funder

partner_organizations.name: Swedish International Development Agency (Sida)
partner_organizations.role: DIAL Founding Partner/funder

partner_organizations.name: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)
partner_organizations.role: DIAL Founding Partner/funder

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Malawi/Tanzania/Sierra Leone/Mozambique
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partners (country-level operations)

who_partners.quote: "DIAL’s neutral, cross-sectoral and adaptive approach positions the organisation to bring different stakeholders together to advance the implementation and use of more efficient, easy to use and cost-effective digital solutions." (53314291.odt, DIAL section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) an Accountable Grant to UN Foundation for DIAL (£15m); 2) a mix of Accountable Grants, Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), and contracts for the policy pillar (£3m); and 3) a separate budget for learning/evaluation (£0.5m).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DIAL operates as a multi-donor platform hosted by UN Foundation, with an independent Board (including DFID) overseeing strategy. The policy pillar involves additional partnerships (e.g., Pathways for Prosperity) managed through flexible funding agreements. DFID retains influence via Board representation and strategic partnerships.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: DIAL was selected due to its alignment with DFID’s Digital Strategy, existing multi-donor structure, proven track record, and DFID’s prior engagement (including Board membership). The Pathways for Prosperity Commission was chosen for its policy expertise and alignment with DFID’s goals.
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID has already experienced through our initial engagement, DIAL’s set of structural and governance processes will allow DFID significant influence at Board level, as well as facilitate extensive engagement between staff at working level, ensuring that DFID can shape both strategy and delivery." (53314291.odt, Appraisal of programme delivery options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DIAL is governed by an 11-member Board comprising donors (DFID, BMGF, USAID, Sida), private sector, and NGO leaders. The Board approves annual goals/work plans by consensus and reviews progress quarterly. DFID has a Board seat and influences DIAL 2.0 strategy.
how_governance.quote: "The DIAL Board approves the annual goals, the annual work plan and budget. DIAL reports on progress toward these targets three times a year and uses agile management and learning strategies to monitor successes, failures and adaptive programming." (53314291.odt, DIAL’s management structure)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the £3m policy pillar can be flexibly allocated to new partnerships as opportunities arise, but the £15m DIAL allocation is tied to Board-approved work plans. Reallocation requires Board consensus.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: DIAL uses "agile management and learning strategies" to respond to the "ever-changing ecosystem," with quarterly progress reviews enabling adaptive programming. The policy pillar explicitly allows for new partnerships to be added based on emerging opportunities.
how_flexibility.quote: "DIAL reports on progress toward these targets three times a year and uses agile management and learning strategies to monitor successes, failures and adaptive programming to respond to the ever changing ecosystem." (53314291.odt, DIAL’s management structure)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → DIAL (UN Foundation) → [sub-grantees/implementers in-country]. The policy pillar adds a parallel layer: FCDO → Pathways for Prosperity/other partners.
how_efficiency.quote: "DIAL reports on progress toward these targets three times a year," implying milestone-based accountability. (53314291.odt, DIAL’s management structure)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue current DFID digital support without scaling up (£0 additional cost).
Outsource to an external consultancy to design/deliver outputs (£18.5m).
Establish partnerships with DIAL (£15m) and complementary organizations (£3m).

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The strategic partnership option (3) was chosen for its: 1) **alignment** with DIAL’s existing focus on the four digital barriers; 2) **value for money** (shared operational costs via multi-donor platform); 3) **influence** (DFID Board seat and ability to shape DIAL 2.0); 4) **flexibility** (policy pillar allows adaptive partnerships); 5) **track record** (DIAL’s proven delivery across all four outputs).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from limited control
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s Board seat and influence over DIAL 2.0 strategy mitigate detachment risks. Quarterly reporting and agile management ensure accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Management burden of multiple partnerships
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging existing platforms (DIAL/UNF) reduces setup costs compared to a new initiative. DFID’s prior engagement with DIAL streamlines coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reliance on DIAL’s stakeholder relationships
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DIAL’s neutral convener role and cross-sectoral networks (built over 5 years) provide a strong foundation. DFID can supplement with additional partnerships (e.g., Pathways for Prosperity).

why_rationale.quote: "According to the qualitative appraisal and the value for money analysis, option 3 is the favoured approach. [...] By financing DIAL, whose strategic framework is structured around the four barriers to harnessing technology for development, DFID will directly deliver on the four outputs of this programme." (53314291.odt, Summary VfM statement for the Preferred Option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and need to operate in countries with weak digital ecosystems (e.g., Malawi, Sierra Leone) require partners with: 1) **neutral convening power** (DIAL’s cross-sectoral role); 2) **existing country presence** (DIAL’s operations in 4 DFID priority countries); 3) **adaptive capacity** (agile management for fast-changing contexts). Southern-led delivery was deemed impractical due to limited local institutional capacity (e.g., only 4% of NGOs use MNO data effectively).
q27_constraints_detail: Fragmented country-level digital investments → Need for a coordinator like DIAL to avoid duplication.
Limited Southern institutional capacity → Northern partners (DIAL/UNF) lead governance/strategy.
Regulatory barriers to MNO data → Requires partners with private-sector relationships (DIAL’s MNO engagement).
Rapidly evolving tech landscape → Demands adaptive partners (DIAL’s agile management).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **four outputs** (products, business models, policy tools, training) directly shaped the **multi-partner platform structure**: 1) **DIAL** was selected for its cross-cutting work on all four outputs; 2) The **policy pillar** was separated to allow flexible partnerships (e.g., Pathways for Prosperity) where DIAL lacks comparative advantage; 3) **Training/capacity building** necessitated a mix of global (DIAL) and local (in-country) partners.

q28_linkages.mechanism: DIAL’s Open Source Centre and turnkey models → Platform structure enables sharing/scaling.
Separate £3m pillar → Flexible partnerships with policy experts (e.g., Pathways for Prosperity).
DIAL’s global training (e.g., Principles for Digital Development workshops) + local implementation support.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly acknowledges tensions between: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: DIAL’s Northern-led governance enables rapid scaling but risks limited Southern ownership (mitigated by country-level operations in 4 African nations). 2) **Expertise vs. local relevance**: Northern partners (DIAL/UNF) provide technical expertise, while Southern partners (e.g., Malawi/Tanzania governments) ensure contextual adaptation. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Multi-donor platform (DIAL) reduces overheads but requires trade-offs in tailor-made country solutions.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern governance (DIAL Board) vs. Southern implementation
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Board sets strategy; country teams adapt delivery (e.g., DIAL’s work in Malawi/Tanzania).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Standardized digital products vs. local customization
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: DIAL’s ‘turnkey models’ balance replication with country-specific testing (e.g., Malawi pilots).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Flexible policy pillar (£3m) vs. core DIAL focus (£15m)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Separate funding streams allow agility in policy work while maintaining DIAL’s scale.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** drives **quarterly oversight** (DIAL Board reviews) and **agile management** (adaptive programming). Fragmentation risks in-country justify DIAL’s convening role, while reputational risks from multi-donor reliance are mitigated by DFID’s Board seat.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building objective** (Output 4) directly informs partner roles: 1) **DIAL** leads global training (e.g., Principles for Digital Development); 2) **Pathways for Prosperity** focuses on policy capacity (e.g., Digital Economy Kits); 3) **Southern partners** (e.g., Malawi government) co-implement to build local skills. The £3m policy pillar explicitly targets ‘improved digital transformation’ via capacity tools.
intersections.quote: "DIAL’s neutral, cross-sectoral and adaptive approach positions the organisation to bring different stakeholders together to advance the implementation and use of more efficient, easy to use and cost-effective digital solutions. [...] The programme will also establish a small number of strategic partnerships to support the delivery of the programme’s outputs, with a particular focus on the third output regarding policy-making tools and products." (53314291.odt, DIAL section and Appraisal of programme delivery options)

key_programme_risks.risk: Fragmentation of digital investments at country level
Inadequate business/partnership models limiting digital uptake
Lack of evidence-based policy guidance for digital transformation
Digital capability gaps among donors/governments/implementers
Reputational risk from multi-donor reliance (DIAL Board decisions)
Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led governance

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DIAL’s whole-of-government frameworks (e.g., IndEA in India) and donor coordination mechanisms.
DIAL’s ‘turnkey’ pricing/operational models and MNO engagement strategies.
£3m policy pillar with Pathways for Prosperity to develop actionable tools (e.g., Digital Roadmap).
Training/skills-building tools (Output 4) and embedded capacity support (e.g., in-country workshops).
DFID Board seat, quarterly reviews, and agile adaptive management.
Country-level operations (e.g., Malawi/Tanzania) and local partner engagement in implementation.

fcas_specific_lessons: While not FCAS-focused, the programme notes that digital tools (e.g., mobile cash) can improve humanitarian responses (e.g., Ebola crisis payments to 60,000 workers). Lessons emphasize **interoperability** and **real-time data** for fragile contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: DIAL’s Phase 1 (2015–2020) demonstrated the need for: 1) **donor coordination** to avoid duplication; 2) **adaptive programming** for fast-changing tech; 3) **country-level testing** (e.g., Malawi/Tanzania pilots). The Pathways for Prosperity Commission’s Digital Roadmap provided a model for actionable policy tools.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: DIAL 2.0 (2020–2025) will expand country operations and refine its **turnkey models** based on Phase 1 lessons. The programme’s **policy pillar** was added to address gaps in Phase 1’s policy support.
risks_lessons.quote: "DIAL’s 2018 Baseline Ecosystem Study found ‘75% of funder respondents indicated that their organizations prefer funding solutions that build on or scale existing solutions. However, key informants across stakeholder groups noted that digital solutions are generally not scaled or sustained to the desired extent.’ This insight shaped DIAL 2.0’s focus on replicable models and sustainability." (53314291.odt, Barrier 1: Systemic fragmentation)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DIAL is a multi-donor platform with existing contributions from BMGF, Sida, and USAID (total £45m over 5 years). DFID’s £15m leverages these funds and UN Foundation’s back-office support, reducing operational costs.
financial_details.quote: "Collectively the Founding Partners [BMGF, Sida, USAID] have committed £45 million towards DIAL over the past five years. [...] DFID will provide £15 million to DIAL over the 5-year period." (53314291.odt, DIAL section)

metadata.programme_name: Water Resources Accountability in Pakistan (WRAP)

quote.programme_name: "Water Resources Accountability in Pakistan (WRAP)" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.total_budget: "The UK will provide an additional GBP15 million to broaden the geographic scope... Original project budget: GBP15 million" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.duration: "Original project start and end dates: July 2021–July 2026", "New project end date: 31/07/2028" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.primary_sector: "WRAP will ‘strengthen the governance of water at national and provincial levels, supporting adaptation to climate change and improving environmental sustainability’" (D0004193.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: July 2021–July 2026", "New project end date: 31/07/2028" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: WRAP combines capacity building (strengthening water institutions), implementation research (testing nature-based solutions), and policy influence (integrating climate-resilient water management into national strategies). It also includes a financing mechanism (Catalytic Fund) to scale innovations.
what_objectives.q1_source: "WRAP will ‘strengthen the governance of water at national and provincial levels, supporting adaptation to climate change and improving environmental sustainability’... Nature-Based Solutions (NbS) demonstrates how restoring the health of water systems... Catalytic Fund to demonstrate and upscale new innovative solutions" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 250,000 additional people supported to adapt to climate change (ICF KPI1)
Hectares of land under sustainable land management practices (ICF KPI17)
Water distribution and use more evidence-based in at least two provinces
80,000 direct beneficiaries of NbS interventions (2022 results)
2,500 hectares of land under sustainable practices (2022 results)
Institutional buy-in for data-driven water allocation in Punjab
KP Water Act (2020) operationalized

what_objectives.summary: WRAP aims to transform Pakistan’s water governance through institutional strengthening, nature-based solutions, and innovative financing, directly addressing climate resilience and economic productivity challenges.

quote.objectives: "WRAP programme aims to ‘strengthen the governance of water at national and provincial levels, supporting adaptation to climate change and improving environmental sustainability’" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.outputs: "It is expected that this cost and time extension will support around 250,000 additional people to better adapt to the effects of climate change (ICF KPI1)... Hectares of land that have received sustainable land management practices... Water distribution and use is more evidence-based and government institutions are better organised to manage water resources at least across two provinces" (D0005617.odt, Expected Results)
quote.approach: "The UK aims to support Pakistan’s water management through flexible and adaptive technical assistance as part of a broader climate portfolio" (D0004193.odt, A.4)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan is recognized as the fifth most climate-vulnerable country globally, with water governance deeply political and contested. The programme operates in a context of institutional fragmentation, inter-provincial tensions, and climate-induced water stress.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0004193.odt, SummarySheet), "Pakistan is already recognised as the fifth most climate vulnerable country in the world" (D0004193.odt, A.1), "The programme faces an overall residual risk rating of ‘Major’" (D0005617.odt, Risk Management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Inter-provincial water sharing is highly politicized, with accusations of withholding water and lack of trusted data. Weak institutional capacity hampers implementation of reforms, while climate change exacerbates water scarcity and flood risks. Limited technical expertise in nature-based solutions slows adoption.

quote.constraints: "Decisions about water management are deeply political and water is a consistent driver of regional and national conflicts in Pakistan... The institutional structure, particularly at the provincial and district levels, lacks the capacity to implement improved regulatory frameworks" (D0004193.odt, A.1/A.2)
quote.climate_impact: "Climate change is one of the biggest long-term threats to Pakistan’s water security... one-third of the current glacial cover in the Himalayan region could be gone by 2100" (D0004193.odt, A.1)
quote.data_issues: "Reliable water data is not yet sufficiently embedded in Pakistani water governance institutions" (D0004193.odt, B.2)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is managed by FCDO Pakistan with implementing partners in Pakistan, but decision-making power distribution between UK and Pakistani entities is not explicitly detailed.
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (Water Commissions, Regulatory Authorities)
training for water data management
technical assistance for nature-based solutions
pilot demonstrations for scaling
policy development support

partner_organizations.name: Punjab Water Resource Commission
partner_organizations.role: implementation of Punjab Water Act

partner_organizations.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Irrigation Department
partner_organizations.role: operationalizing KP Water Act (2020)

partner_organizations.name: Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) local authorities
partner_organizations.role: NbS interventions for flood resilience

partner_organizations.name: Catalytic Fund grantees (CSOs, entrepreneurs)
partner_organizations.role: piloting innovative water solutions

quote.structure: "The programme extension will continue to follow the management arrangements set out in the original WRAP business case... individual agreements with all delivery partners are agreed based on robust results frameworks" (D0005617.odt, Approach to Implementation)
quote.capacity_building: "Provide technical support to improve the capacity of water institutions at federal and provincial levels... demonstrate how restoring the health of water systems and applying nature-based solutions could help communities adapt to climate change" (D0004193.odt, Programme summary)
quote.partners: "The Water Governance component will be expanded from Punjab to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) to operationalise the KP Water Act (2020); NbS interventions will be expanded to communities across Punjab, KP and GB" (D0005617.odt, Key Objectives)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of technical assistance agreements for governance/NbS components and a competitive Catalytic Fund for innovative solutions. The fund operates through grants to CSOs, entrepreneurs, and businesses.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme with multiple implementing partners (provincial institutions, CSOs, private sector) under separate agreements. The Catalytic Fund adds a competitive element for innovative proposals.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Existing partners (e.g., Punjab/KP institutions) were selected based on prior engagement and political buy-in. Catalytic Fund grantees will be selected competitively based on innovation and scalability potential.

quote.instruments: "The individual agreements with all delivery partners are agreed based on robust results frameworks... The Catalytic Fund component... will provide research and analysis... as well as grants implemented under the Fund" (D0005617.odt, Approach to Implementation)
quote.selection: "The UK has a comparative advantage it can use to support Pakistan to manage its water resources... FCDO in Pakistan has the expertise, proven track record and strong political relationships required to deliver governance and system strengthening reforms" (D0004193.odt, A.1)

quote.management: "The BHC Islamabad Team along with all implementing partners will ensure alignment of all programme interventions... All arrangements will be renegotiated for any additional funding" (D0005617.odt, Approach to Implementation)
quote.oversight: "FCDO will have the option to invoke a break clause at regular quarterly progress assessment points... Progression beyond the break clause points will be subject to satisfactory performance" (D0005617.odt, Additional Support)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., expanding NbS or Catalytic Fund) but require FCDO approval and are tied to performance reviews.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses quarterly assessments and annual reviews to adjust priorities. The Catalytic Fund explicitly supports adaptive learning, and the extension allows for geographic/ thematic expansion based on emerging needs.

quote.flexibility: "Due consideration is given to flexibility within the programme design to meet emerging challenges... regular assessments including political economy analysis will continue throughout the programme’s lifecycle" (D0004193.odt, A.5)
quote.adaptive: "The extension will enable us to reset the level of programme ambition, strengthen programme impact and enable more vulnerable communities... to better adapt to the effects of climate change" (D0005617.odt, Objective of Extension)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (provincial institutions/CSOs) → End Beneficiaries (no explicit sub-grantee layer mentioned beyond Catalytic Fund grantees)

quote.budget: "Original project budget: GBP15 million", "The UK will provide an additional GBP15 million" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.layers: "The individual agreements with all delivery partners are agreed based on robust results frameworks... self-reported data is validated by the BHC Islamabad Team" (D0005617.odt, Approach to Implementation)
quote.payments: "Quarterly targets against relevant logical frameworks are agreed... to assess the programme delivery against agreed costed work plans" (D0005617.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Limit engagement to routine dialogue; Pakistan would continue infrastructure-focused approaches with 4% GDP loss from poor water management.
Focus on governance reforms without NbS or Catalytic Fund; limited to institutional capacity building.
Combines governance strengthening, nature-based demonstrations, and innovative financing for scalable solutions.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was selected to address Pakistan’s interconnected challenges: weak institutions (governance component), climate vulnerability (NbS), and need for innovation (Catalytic Fund). The UK’s political influence and prior experience in Pakistan positioned it to deliver transformational impact ahead of COP26.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political sensitivity of water reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on less sensitive entry points (e.g., water use efficiency within provinces) and leverage senior local champions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited civil society engagement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Expand district pilots and Catalytic Fund to include CSOs/entrepreneurs, ensuring broader stakeholder involvement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow uptake of nature-based solutions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demonstrate co-benefits through pilots and integrate NbS into provincial development plans.

quote.alternatives: "Option 1: Do Nothing... Option 2: Technical assistance to build GoP’s capacity... Option 3: Option 2 plus further technical assistance to provide GoP access to innovative and scalable models... Based on this analysis, option 3 scores 12/16 compared to 6/16 for option 2 and is the preferred option" (D0004193.odt, B.4)
quote.rationale: "The UK aims to support Pakistan’s water management through flexible and adaptive technical assistance... This is needed to support Pakistan in meeting the water management challenges that are burdening its economy with further debt for large-scale infrastructure" (D0004193.odt, A.4)
quote.vfm: "WRAP will continue to represent good VfM for the UK as it will contribute to a more prosperous Pakistan which has improved resilience to adapt to changing climate... The BHC Islamabad Team continue to believe that the expected benefits of this extension in Pakistan’s evolving context offer a sound return on investment" (D0005617.odt, Value for Money)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy of water in Pakistan limits partner selection to entities with provincial/federal government buy-in. Inter-provincial tensions and vestigial interests require partners who can navigate sensitive reform areas (e.g., water sharing) without exacerbating conflicts.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing government relationships (e.g., Punjab Irrigation Department)
Exclusion of actors perceived as biased in inter-provincial disputes
Prioritization of local champions to mitigate political risks
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (governance reform + NbS + innovation) necessitate a hybrid delivery structure: technical assistance for institutional strengthening, competitive funding for innovation, and adaptive management to respond to political/economic changes.
q28_linkages: Governance reforms require embedded support → consortium structure with provincial partners
NbS demonstrations need flexible pilots → Catalytic Fund mechanism
Scaling innovations demands private sector engagement → open partnership model
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (rapid scaling of NbS through Catalytic Fund) with equity (targeting marginalized communities in KP/GB). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for inclusive partnerships vs. faster delivery through government-only channels.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Competitive Catalytic Fund may exclude smaller CSOs without capacity-building support.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical assistance risks undermining local institutional leadership if not carefully managed.
Cost vs. reach: Expanding to remote areas (GB/KP) increases logistical costs but aligns with equity goals.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk profile drives intensive oversight (quarterly reviews, break clauses) and adaptive management (political economy analyses). High sensitivity around water reforms requires embedded advisors to navigate provincial tensions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is core to partner roles: provincial institutions lead governance reforms with FCDO support, while CSOs/entrepreneurs (via Catalytic Fund) pilot innovations. Technical assistance gradually transitions to local ownership (e.g., Punjab Water Commission).

quote.context_partners: "The UK in Pakistan has already supported the Government of Punjab at federal and sub-national levels with relevant technical assistance programmes and is therefore well-positioned to support political reforms" (D0004193.odt, A.4)
quote.objectives_structure: "Option 3... works with all tiers of government (federal, provincial and district) and harnesses the interconnectivity between them to make progress on water sector reform and nature-based solutions" (D0004193.odt, B.2)
quote.equity_efficiency: "The cost extension will also facilitate greater access to remote and marginalised communities at risk to climate change... while ensuring greater cross-component integration" (D0005617.odt, Key Objectives)
quote.risk_management: "The programme faces an overall residual risk rating of ‘Major’... WRAP continues to focus on initial entry points with less sensitivities, building on the UK Pakistan Network’s existing relationships" (D0005617.odt, Risk Management)

key_programme_risks.risk: Political resistance to water reforms
Institutional capacity gaps in implementing NbS
Climate-induced disasters disrupting interventions
Limited civil society engagement in remote areas
Shrinking operating space for implementing partners
Fund diversion or mismanagement

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on less sensitive entry points (e.g., intra-provincial efficiency) and leverage senior champions. Use evidence from pilots to build consensus.
Embed technical assistance within provincial institutions (e.g., Punjab Water Commission) and provide hands-on training through demonstrations.
Integrate disaster risk reduction into NbS designs (e.g., flood-resistant wetlands) and maintain flexible budgets for adaptive responses.
Expand Catalytic Fund to include grassroots organizations and provide capacity-building support for proposal development.
Strengthen partnerships with government-aligned entities and use diplomatic channels to advocate for NGO access.
Quarterly due diligence assessments, milestone-based payments, and FCDO validation of self-reported data.

fcas_specific_lessons: Prioritize conflict-sensitive approaches in water governance to avoid exacerbating inter-provincial tensions (e.g., neutral data-sharing platforms).
Use NbS to build trust between communities and government by demonstrating tangible co-benefits (e.g., flood protection + livelihoods).
Leverage existing government structures (e.g., Irrigation Departments) as entry points to navigate political complexities.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The South Asia Water Governance Programme (2015–18) demonstrated that: (1) Data-as-a-Service (DaaS) models can build trust in water sharing; (2) Provincial replication of reforms (e.g., Punjab’s Water Act) is feasible with tailored support; (3) Civil society engagement requires sustained capacity-building.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The extension expands NbS to KP/GB based on successful Punjab pilots, adds a Catalytic Fund to address innovation gaps identified in the original design, and integrates independent monitoring to improve lesson-learning.

quote.risks: "The programme faces an overall residual risk rating of ‘Major’. The main risks relate to strategy, context, and programme delivery... Political economy plays a strong role in decisions about water" (D0005617.odt, Risk Management)
quote.mitigations: "WRAP continues to focus on initial entry points with less sensitivities, building on the UK Pakistan Network’s existing relationships... The programme will also continue to maintain a level of flexibility within the design to adapt to unforeseen scenarios" (D0005617.odt, Risk Management)
quote.lessons: "Stakeholders more open to the idea of establishing an independent water auditor... Parties agreed to share data readings publicly via daily SMS messages" (D0004193.odt, Table 2: SAWGP results)
quote.design_changes: "The extension will enable us to reset the level of programme ambition, strengthen programme impact and enable more vulnerable communities... to better adapt to the effects of climate change" (D0005617.odt, Objective of Extension)

quote.budget: "Original project budget: GBP15 million", "The UK will provide an additional GBP15 million" (D0005617.odt, Summary Information)
quote.allocation: "The UK will provide an additional GBP15 million to broaden the geographic scope of the water governance and NbS components, as well as the thematic scope for the Catalytic Fund" (D0005617.odt, Additional Support)

metadata.programme_name: T-WASHII: Transforming Access to WASH and Nutrition Services in Mozambique
metadata.primary_sector: WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) and Nutrition
metadata.quote: "The programme will deliver sustainable, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and nutrition services for up to 4.6 million poor people." (90000499.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 1 September 2019\nEnd Date: 30 September 2026" (90000499.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of WASH and nutrition services), capacity building (strengthening government systems at sub-national levels), and financing mechanism (performance-based funding to incentivize sustainable service delivery). It also includes policy influence through technical assistance and coordination with government and partners.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will deliver sustainable, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and nutrition services for up to 4.6 million poor people. [...] A performance-based approach will drive improvements in the sustainability, efficiency and equity of government and private sector service delivery at the sub-national level." (90000499.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved hygiene, sanitation, and nutrition practices
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2,133,000 people (revised to 900,000 in addendum)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved knowledge of hygiene, sanitation, and nutrition through mass communication campaigns
q3_expected_outputs.target: 4,605,000 people (revised to 1,980,000 in addendum)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased climate-resilient and appropriate drinking water, sanitation, and nutrition services
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1,282,000 people (revised to 800,000 in addendum)

q3_expected_outputs.output: People with improved climate resilience due to ICF WASH investments

q3_expected_outputs.output: People gaining access to safe water through emergency water supply interventions
q3_expected_outputs.target: 94,000 people (addendum only)
