q3_expected_outputs.target: Districts and provinces with low coverage, high rates of diarrhoeal disease and malnutrition

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened systems for decentralised service delivery
q3_expected_outputs.target: Government institutions at provincial and district levels

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve sustainable access to WASH and nutrition services for over 2 million people in Mozambique, with a focus on women, girls, and children, while strengthening government systems for long-term service delivery. It uses a performance-based funding approach to incentivize equity, sustainability, and climate resilience in service provision.
what_objectives.quote: "The overall objective of the programme is to improve sustainable and inclusive access to water, sanitation and hygiene services and improved nutrition and hygiene behaviours at the sub-national level for over 2 million people, in particular women, young girls, and children." (D0005796.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique is described as fragile due to political instability, conflict risks, economic crises, and vulnerability to climate shocks. The programme explicitly mentions the country's exposure to cyclones, floods, droughts, and violent extremism, which affect service delivery and stability.
where_context.q5_source: "Mozambique is at a critical juncture. [...] Vulnerability is increasing due to the frequency and severity of climate shocks. [...] Mozambique is at a critical time of its political and security setting. There are unknowns with regards to upcoming elections, decentralisation plays a key role in the consolidation of the peace accords, and challenges from organised crime and violent extremism if unaddressed are a threat to longer term prosperity." (90000499.odt, Strategic Case / Conflict and Fragility)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (single-party dominance, lack of accountability, pervasive corruption)
weak institutions (low civil service capacity, poor public financial management)
data limitations (weak monitoring and information systems)
infrastructure (low coverage of basic WASH services, poor maintenance)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The constraints limit the government's ability to deliver basic services, exacerbate inequalities between regions, and increase vulnerability to climate shocks. Weak institutions and corruption reduce the effectiveness of public spending, while political instability and conflict disrupt programme implementation. Poor infrastructure and data systems hinder monitoring and service sustainability.
where_context.quote: "The vicious cycle of dominance of a single party, lack of accountability, pervasive corruption, and weak institutions creates a negative incentive structure that dampens both private investment and public sector performance." (90000499.odt, BusinessCase)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains oversight and approval authority, with implementation managed through UK-contracted partners (fund manager, capacity building agent). Government of Mozambique (GoM) has operational roles but limited financial control due to fiduciary risks.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and coaching for government staff at district, provincial, and national levels
support for multi-sectoral planning and budgeting (e.g., nutrition-sensitive district plans)
strengthening monitoring and information systems (e.g., WASH information management system)
social behaviour change communication (SBCC) for hygiene and nutrition
private sector capacity building (e.g., contractors for water systems, sanitation marketing)
community-based organisation support (e.g., water management committees)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Mozambique (GoM)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner (PRONASAR programme, decentralised service delivery)

partner_organizations.name: DNAAS (National Directorate of Water Supply and Sanitation)
partner_organizations.role: Key government counterpart for WASH service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Capacity Building Agent (CBA)
partner_organizations.role: Provides technical assistance and capacity building to government institutions (contract managed by FCDO)

partner_organizations.name: SNV (Netherlands Development Organisation)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner (mentioned in addendum as a key partner for technical assistance)

partner_organizations.name: Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP)
partner_organizations.role: Verifies results and progress against performance-based funding (contracted by FCDO)

partner_organizations.name: Joint Fund Partners (Austria, Switzerland, UNICEF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers of the PRONASAR Joint Fund

partner_organizations.name: WASHand Climate Change Adviser (programme-funded role)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support to DNAAS and SNV, policy influencing, and coordination (FCDO-employed, based in Mozambique)

partner_organizations.name: Services Delivery Adviser (programme-funded role)
partner_organizations.role: Gathers lessons-learned, supports institutional capacity building and policy dialogue

who_partners.quote: "DFID will fund the government’s national rural WASH programme through a Joint Fund mechanism that currently includes funds from the Government of Mozambique, Austria, Switzerland and UNICEF. DFID funds will be channelled through a DFID contracted fund manager in order to reduce fiduciary risks." (90000499.odt, Component 1)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **Joint Fund mechanism** (pooling donor funds for PRONASAR) with performance-based funding (PBF) to incentivize results. FCDO channels funds through a **contracted fund manager** to mitigate fiduciary risks. Additional components include **contracts** for capacity building and independent monitoring, and **programme-funded adviser roles** (direct FCDO employment).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO contracts a fund manager to oversee the PRONASAR Joint Fund, reducing fiduciary risks. A Capacity Building Agent (CBA) delivers technical assistance, while an Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP) verifies results. Programme-funded advisers (FCDO staff) provide strategic guidance and coordination. The structure aligns with government systems but avoids direct budget support.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Joint Fund partners (Austria, Switzerland, UNICEF) were selected based on existing collaboration and alignment with PRONASAR. The fund manager and CBA were likely chosen through restricted competition or framework agreements (not explicitly stated), while programme-funded roles are FCDO appointments. The addendum justifies in-house delivery for the WASH and Climate Change Adviser to "maintain credibility and political capital."
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID funds will be channelled through a DFID contracted fund manager in order to reduce fiduciary risks. A performance-based funding mechanism will apply to the entire Joint Fund partner, and for at least 20% of the total value of the fund." (90000499.odt, Component 1) \n\n "The new programme-funded WASH and Climate Change country-based adviser will be paid from savings available [...] in the ‘Policy Dialogue and lesson learning’ component [...] to ‘influence and drive change in government multi-sector services delivery’." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: The PRONASAR Joint Fund uses a performance-based framework where payments are triggered by verified results. The Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP) assesses progress, and decisions are made collectively by Joint Fund partners (GoM, FCDO, Austria, Switzerland, UNICEF).
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Joint Fund operates with a governance arrangement that includes the Government of Mozambique and donor partners (FCDO, Austria, Switzerland, UNICEF). The addendum mentions high-level coordination meetings and the role of the SRO (Senior Responsible Officer) in oversight. However, explicit composition or decision-making processes are not detailed.
how_governance.quote: "An independent monitoring agent will be procured by DFID, for the benefit of the Joint Fund in order to verify the robustness of government reporting systems and whether results in the field are being achieved. This will inform DFID and PRONASAR Joint Fund partners in making payment decisions to the PRONASAR." (90000499.odt, Component 3) \n\n "The postholder [WASH and Climate Change Adviser] will not be seconded to an external organization and will work from the British High Commission offices [...] will provide technical support and strategic guidance for policy influencing, as well as coordination with Government and key partners at central and decentralised levels." (D0005796.odt, APPROACH TO IMPLEMENTATION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within components (e.g., PRONASAR Joint Fund, Capacity Building) appear earmarked, but the programme can adjust activities based on performance and learning. The addendum demonstrates flexibility by reallocating savings to fund the new adviser role.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses performance-based funding, which allows adjustments based on results. The Policy, Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning component (£2.2m) supports adaptive management by generating evidence to reorient implementation. The addendum explicitly notes the need for agility in responding to results-based payments.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will use a performance-based approach [...] to improve the sustainability, efficiency and equity of government and private sector service delivery at the sub-national level." (90000499.odt, Programme summary) \n\n "This option [adding an insourced adviser] will enhance the programme's agility in responding to the start of results-based payments and the final years of the programme, aimed at achieving the identified outcomes." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager/CBA/IMP → Government/Private Sector/Community Implementers
how_efficiency.quote: "A performance-based funding mechanism will apply to the entire Joint Fund partner, and for at least 20% of the total value of the fund. This will be designed in the mobilisation stage." (90000499.odt, Component 1) \n\n "The new insourced role will be paid from savings available (up to £120,000) in the ‘Policy Dialogue and lesson learning’ component." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Stop support to WASH and Nutrition (counterfactual)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Discontinuing engagement would undermine progress in service delivery and policy influence, particularly in rural WASH and nutrition.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Improved and scaled-up WASH programme only (without integrating nutrition)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focus solely on expanding the successful WASH model without nutrition components, allocating £56.5m to WASH, £10.5m to capacity building, and smaller amounts to verification and policy.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Integrating pilot nutrition-sensitive activities within an improved and scaled-up WASH programme (CHOSEN OPTION)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Combines WASH and nutrition to address interconnected challenges, leveraging multi-sectoral approaches and existing political momentum (e.g., ESANIII strategy).
Rejected as it would inhibit the programme’s ability to respond agilely to results-based payments.
Rejected due to administrative burden and time constraints.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The integrated WASH-nutrition approach was selected to address the **interlinked causes of stunting and diarrhoeal disease**, align with government priorities (e.g., ESANIII, PRONASAR), and leverage donor coordination. The performance-based funding model was chosen to **incentivize sustainability and equity**, while the fund manager structure mitigates fiduciary risks. The addendum’s insourced adviser role was added to **enhance agility during results-based payments** and ensure a responsible UK exit strategy.
q25_decision_factors: effectiveness (addressing root causes of malnutrition and WASH deficits)
equity (focus on women, girls, and marginalized groups)
efficiency (leveraging existing platforms like PRONASAR and Joint Fund)
risk mitigation (fiduciary risks addressed via fund manager)
partner capacity (building on GoM and donor commitments)
policy influence (aligning with decentralisation and multi-sectoral strategies)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risk due to GoM’s weak financial systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of a DFID-contracted fund manager to channel funds and reduce diversion risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political risks from decentralisation process
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme supports decentralisation capacity building and aligns with government systems to adapt to changes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented coordination among donors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s leadership in donor coordination (e.g., Nutrition Partners Forum, WASH sector donor group) and Joint Fund mechanism.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited government absorption capacity for funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for sub-national institutions and performance-based incentives to improve delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict or natural disasters disrupting implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Climate-resilient infrastructure and contingency planning (e.g., emergency water supply component).

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (performance-based funding to maximize results per pound)
equity (targeting women, girls, and poorest populations)
why_rationale.quote: "In order to deliver across those priority areas, three important shifts are being made: 1) rationalising the portfolio by reducing the number of programmes; 2) streamlining and integrating the portfolio by making linkages between sectors and a stronger geographical focus; 3) leverage full ODA and UK offer by making full use of UK expertise to leverage resources, influence others and maximise the outcomes our HMG footprint offers." (90000499.odt, BusinessCase) \n\n "This option [insourced adviser] will enhance the programme's agility in responding to the start of results-based payments and the final years of the programme, aimed at achieving the identified outcomes. It offers the best value for money, requiring fewer resources and no changes to existing delivery mechanisms." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with strong risk management capacities and local presence. Fiduciary risks preclude direct budget support to GoM, necessitating a fund manager. Climate vulnerability and conflict risks require partners with resilience expertise (e.g., SNV for climate-smart WASH). Decentralisation constraints demand partners who can work at sub-national levels (e.g., CBA for district-level capacity building).
q27_constraints_detail: fiduciary risks → fund manager required (not direct GoM funding)
climate vulnerability → need for partners with climate-resilient WASH experience
decentralisation challenges → partners must support sub-national institutions
conflict risks → partners need adaptive, context-aware approaches
weak government capacity → reliance on technical assistance providers (e.g., CBA, SNV)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **integrated WASH-nutrition objective** requires a **multi-sectoral delivery structure** (Joint Fund + CBA) to coordinate across health, agriculture, and WASH sectors. The **performance-based funding** approach is chosen to align with the goal of **sustainable, equitable service delivery**, while **capacity building** is embedded to address systemic weaknesses in GoM institutions. The **geographical focus** on high-need provinces shapes partner roles (e.g., targeting Zambezia and Nampula).
q28_linkages: integrated objectives → multi-sectoral Joint Fund structure
sustainability goals → performance-based funding mechanism
systems strengthening → embedded capacity building (CBA)
climate resilience → climate-smart infrastructure and adviser role
equity focus → gender and disability inclusion in all components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting women, girls, and disabled populations) with **efficiency** (performance-based payments to maximize outcomes). Trade-offs include: 
1. **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid scaling of WASH services is tempered by requirements for gender-sensitive and disability-inclusive designs. 
2. **Cost vs. reach**: Climate-resilient infrastructure increases upfront costs but reduces long-term vulnerability. 
3. **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK-funded advisers provide technical leadership, while capacity building aims to transition ownership to GoM.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: gender and disability inclusion → higher design costs but greater equity
climate-resilient infrastructure → higher initial investment for long-term sustainability
performance-based funding → administrative complexity but better results
UK advisers → ensures quality but risks limiting local ownership
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk FCAS context** justifies **intensive oversight** (e.g., independent monitoring partner, embedded advisers) and **flexible adaptive management** (e.g., reallocating funds for advisers in the addendum). Decentralisation risks lead to **strengthened sub-national capacity building**, while fiduciary risks necessitate **third-party fund management**.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building is a **core objective**, shaping partner roles as follows: 
- **CBA** focuses on institutional strengthening (e.g., multi-sectoral planning, SBCC). 
- **GoM** gradually takes on more responsibility as capacity improves (e.g., results-based payments). 
- **Private sector** is engaged for service delivery (e.g., sanitation marketing) as local capacity grows. 
- **Advisers** provide tailored support where government systems are weakest (e.g., policy dialogue, climate resilience).
intersections.quote:
"The lack of sanitation costs USD 125 million per year to the Mozambican economy (WSP 2012). In addition, the lack of WASH services contributes to time poverty, taking women away from productive tasks and keeping children, especially girls, away from school. [...] The programme goes beyond addressing the needs of women and girls to address some of the root causes of gender inequalities by working with both men and women through social behaviour change communication." (90000499.odt, Gender Equality) 

 "The programme will use a performance-based approach [...] to improve the sustainability, efficiency and equity of government and private sector service delivery at the sub-national level." (90000499.odt, Programme summary) 

 "The new insourced role will provide technical support and strategic guidance for policy influencing, as well as coordination with Government and key partners at central and decentralised levels." (D0005796.odt, APPROACH TO IMPLEMENTATION)

key_programme_risks: Fiduciary risks due to GoM’s weak financial systems
Political instability and election uncertainties
Conflict and violent extremism disrupting implementation
Climate shocks (floods, droughts, cyclones) damaging infrastructure
Limited government capacity to absorb funds at sub-national levels
Fragmented coordination among donors and sectors
Sustainability of services post-programme (e.g., handpump maintenance)
Social norms slowing behaviour change (e.g., open defecation, nutrition practices)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of a DFID-contracted fund manager to channel funds and independent verification of results.
Alignment with government priorities (e.g., PRONASAR, ESANIII) and decentralisation support.
Climate-resilient infrastructure design and emergency response components.
Capacity building for sub-national institutions and performance-based incentives.
DFID’s leadership in donor coordination (e.g., Nutrition Partners Forum) and Joint Fund mechanism.
Private sector engagement (e.g., sanitation marketing) and community-based operation models.
Intensive, gender-sensitive social behaviour change communication (SBCC).

fcas_specific_lessons: Decentralisation requires **gradual capacity building** to avoid overwhelming local institutions.
Performance-based funding must be **adaptive to context** (e.g., adjusting indicators for conflict-affected areas).
**Donor coordination** is critical in FCAS to avoid duplication and leverage resources.
**Climate resilience** must be integrated into all infrastructure to withstand shocks.
**Political economy analysis** is needed to navigate patronage risks in service allocation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
The **T-WASH I programme** demonstrated that: 
1. **Performance-based funding + capacity building** improves service delivery at district levels. 
2. **Multi-sectoral planning** at sub-national levels increases complementarity (e.g., WASH-nutrition linkages). 
3. **Private sector participation** (e.g., in water system management) enhances sustainability. 
4. **Gender and disability inclusion** requires explicit targeting (e.g., MHM-friendly school toilets). 
5. **Independent monitoring** strengthens accountability and data quality.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Expanded performance-based funding** in the Joint Fund (from T-WASH I’s pilot). 
2. **Stronger focus on climate resilience** (e.g., adviser role added in addendum). 
3. **Deeper integration of nutrition** (building on SBCC and agriculture lessons). 
4. **Enhanced sub-national capacity building** (e.g., district-level planning support). 
5. **Adaptive management** (e.g., reallocating funds for advisers in addendum).
risks_lessons.quote:
"An independent mid-term review assessed DFID’s current support to PRONASAR as effective in unlocking specific bottlenecks for services delivery at the decentralised level, by linking collaborative, flexible and adaptive capacity building with performance-based funding. The success of the model for strengthening WASH systems has already shaped the second phase of the PRONASAR programme and influenced donors to maintain and increase their funding to the PRONASAR, leveraging additional funds." (90000499.odt, Strategic Case) 

 "The current programme has a strong track-record of delivery, evidenced by annual reviews and the independent mid-term review. It has improved the effectiveness of procurement processes at the district and provincial levels and their ability to deliver more services." (90000499.odt, Strategic Case) 

 "The key change to the original Business Case is to add an additional programme funded role that will work closely with the SRO until the end of the programme in September 2026." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Joint Fund mechanism is designed to attract additional donor funding. The current T-WASH programme influenced donors to maintain/increase funding to PRONASAR, with one large bilateral donor considering contributions. The performance-based approach is expected to incentivize further investments.

component_allocation.component: Independent Monitoring of PRONASAR Joint Fund

financial_details.quote: "Component 1: PRONASAR Joint Fund (up to £47.2m). [...] Component 2: Capacity Building and Nutrition Fund (up to £19.7m). [...] Component 3: Independent monitoring of PRONASAR Joint fund (£0.9m). [...] Component 4: Policy, monitoring, evaluation and learning (up to £2.2m)." (90000499.odt, Components 1-4) \n\n "The new programme-funded WASH and Climate Change country-based adviser will be paid from savings available (up to £120,000) in the ‘Policy Dialogue and lesson learning’ component." (D0005796.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: ATscale – the Global Partnership for Assistive Technology

quote.programme_name: "ATscale – the Global Partnership for Assistive Technology" (Document: 52876804.odt, Title section)
quote.budget: "DFID will contribute twenty million pounds" (Document: 52876804.odt, Programmesummary section)
quote.duration: "Through this 4-year programme" (Document: 52876804.odt, Programmesummary section)
quote.sector: "Country/Region or Sector: Global – Disability, AT" (Document: 52876804.odt, Metadata section)

metadata.duration_source: "Through this 4-year programme, DFID will contribute twenty million pounds" (Document: 52876804.odt, Programmesummary section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ATscale aims to catalyse access to Assistive Technology (AT) for 500 million people by 2030 through a combination of market shaping, policy reform, investment mobilisation, and systems strengthening. It applies successful approaches from health commodity markets (like vaccines) to AT, while also creating an enabling environment through advocacy, policy influence, and capacity building.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ATscale, the Global Partnership for Assistive Technology (AT), aims to catalyse access to AT for an additional 500 million people by 2030. ATscale will bring to AT the market shaping approaches that have been successfully used over the last decade to cut prices and increase access to life-saving health commodities such as vaccines. This will be complemented by creating an enabling environment through increasing political will, policy reform, investment, and systems strengthening." (Document: 52876804.odt, Programmesummary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 500 million people reached with life-changing AT by 2030
Development of a global advocacy plan and participation in international forums
Global investment case for AT to increase donor and government funding
Support for WHO Global Report on effective access to AT (GReAT report)
Market shaping investments in 5 priority AT products
Establishment of ATscale’s organisational setup, governance structure, and communications
Translation of product narratives into investable plans

what_objectives.summary: ATscale is a global partnership designed to transform access to Assistive Technology (AT) by combining market shaping interventions with systemic changes in policy, investment, and service delivery. The programme aims to reach 500 million people by 2030 through a twin-track approach: shaping AT markets to overcome supply/demand barriers and building an enabling environment at global, regional, and country levels.

quote.objectives: "Together, this twin-track approach will address many of the barriers to access to AT described above and will help ATscale reach the ambitious goal to catalyse action to ensure that 500 million more people globally are reached with life-changing AT by 2030." (Document: 52876804.odt, Long-term Outcomes and Impacts section)
quote.outputs: "Initial outputs will be more precisely defined as part of this process, but could include: Developing a global advocacy plan..., Developing a global investment case..., Attracting additional donors..., Supporting the WHO Global Report..., Using learning from the AT2030 programme..., Supporting CHAI to create the AT2030-funded product narratives..., Translating product narratives..., Scoping and possibly initiating high-priority cross-cutting AT initiatives..., Establishing ATscale’s organisational setup..., Establishing ATscale’s longer-term governance structure..., Establishing communication guidelines..." (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as "moderate" risk, reflecting the complexity of addressing global AT market failures and the need for coordination across multiple stakeholders and sectors. The risks are mitigated by DFID's experience in market shaping and the partnership's structured approach.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 52876804.odt, Metadata section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The constraints affect delivery by creating barriers to demand (e.g., lack of awareness, stigma), supply (e.g., limited manufacturing, high prices), and service delivery (e.g., poorly trained personnel, weak procurement). These challenges are exacerbated in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where 80% of people with disabilities live and where systems are often under-resourced or disorganised.

quote.constraints: "Despite millions of people escaping poverty over the last 20 years, the global situation and well-being of the majority of people with disabilities has not improved, especially in low- and middle-income countries.... There is largely a cyclical relationship between disability and poverty.... Disability disproportionately affects the most marginalised in society—women, older people and the poorest." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Need for Assistive Technology section)
quote.market_failures: "The barriers to access to AT are complex, multi-faceted challenges, driven by a number of supply and demand failures for both the AT product and the associated services.... Demand is often significantly curtailed as potential users and even service providers are unaware of the need for and the existence or importance of appropriate AT products and how to access them." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Barriers to Access to Assistive Technology section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: ATscale Forming Committee (transitioning to permanent structure)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The ATscale Forming Committee includes representatives from Northern donors (e.g., DFID, USAID, Norad), Southern governments (e.g., Government of Kenya), multilateral agencies (e.g., WHO, UNICEF), and Disabled People’s Organisations (DPOs). Decision-making is shared across these stakeholders, with a mandate to "coordinate stakeholders, mobilise resources, measure and evaluate progress, identify and consider potential interventions and investments."
q10_capacity_building_details: training for service providers on AT prescription and use
strengthening AT delivery systems at global/regional/country levels
supporting policy reform and institutional capacity
mobilising investment and political will

partner_organizations.role: Lead donor and strategic partner

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF

partner_organizations.role: Southern government representative and co-host of Global Disability Summit

partner_organizations.role: Southern representative and advocate

quote.structure: "DFID has had a leading role in the development of the partnership through the ATscale Forming Committee (FC), which was set up with the mandate to oversee ATscale’s development. It currently consists of: China Disabled Persons’ Federation, Clinton Health Access Initiative, Global Disability Innovation Hub, Government of Kenya, International Disability Alliance, Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, Office of the UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for Financing the Health Millennium Development Goals and for Malaria, UK Department for International Development, UNICEF, United States Agency for International Development, and the World Health Organization." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)
quote.decision_power: "The Forming Committee advises on strategy, coordinates stakeholders, mobilises resources, measures and evaluates progress, identifies and considers potential interventions and investments, and will shepherd ATscale to its permanent structure in partnership with the ATscale director." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)
quote.capacity_building: "Building an enabling environment involves combining an advocacy approach to build political will, mobilise investment, and reform policy, with a system strengthening approach to improve AT provision systems and service delivery at global, regional, and country levels." (Document: 52876804.odt, What is our strategic approach to increasing access to AT? section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: ATscale operates as a global partnership with a shared governance structure (Forming Committee) and pooled resources from multiple donors. DFID’s £20 million contribution is part of a broader funding mechanism that supports coordinated interventions across market shaping, policy reform, and service delivery.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ATscale is structured as an open partnership with a Forming Committee overseeing strategy and investments. The partnership will transition to a permanent governance structure, including a secretariat and operational support. Decision-making is shared among Northern/Southern partners, multilateral agencies, and DPOs.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Forming Committee was established through direct engagement with key stakeholders (donors, governments, DPOs, and technical partners) identified during the scoping phase. The rationale emphasises the need for a broad coalition to address the multi-faceted barriers to AT access, leveraging DFID’s leadership in disability inclusion and market shaping.

quote.instrument: "DFID has had a leading role in the development of the partnership through the ATscale Forming Committee (FC), which was set up with the mandate to oversee ATscale’s development.... The Forming Committee advises on strategy, coordinates stakeholders, mobilises resources, measures and evaluates progress, identifies and considers potential interventions and investments." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)
quote.selection: "Overall, this scoping and consultation process provided validation that the proposed approach had the potential to create a significant and catalytic change in access to AT. These discussions led to a widening coalition of partners with interests in establishing a formal partnership that could identify, fund and deliver targeted market-shaping interventions as part of a cohesive approach to addressing barriers to AT access." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ATscale Forming Committee acts as a steering committee with representatives from donors, governments, DPOs, and technical partners. It oversees strategy, resource mobilisation, and intervention selection. The committee will transition to a permanent governance structure, including a secretariat for operational support.

quote.governance: "The Forming Committee advises on strategy, coordinates stakeholders, mobilises resources, measures and evaluates progress, identifies and considers potential interventions and investments, and will shepherd ATscale to its permanent structure in partnership with the ATscale director." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)
quote.oversight: "These outputs should result in the initial outcome of having a strong partnership, well-placed to catalyse change for increased access to AT." (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., market shaping vs. enabling environment) as part of the partnership’s adaptive approach, but this requires approval from the Forming Committee and alignment with the strategic objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasises learning and adaptation, particularly through the AT2030 programme and WHO GReAT report. Priorities can be adjusted based on new data and stakeholder engagement, but changes are overseen by the Forming Committee.

quote.flexibility: "ATscale will actively engage with new data as it becomes available and will adapt programmes and initiatives accordingly. It may also consider providing additional support to strengthen data systems as a cross-cutting intervention in the future and will coordinate with other programmes accordingly." (Document: 52876804.odt, Data and Evidence section)
quote.adaptation: "Initial outputs will be more precisely defined as part of this process, but could include:... Using learning from the AT2030 programme to increase understanding of the AT landscape at the country level to inform future ATscale engagement." (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ATscale Forming Committee/Secretariat → Implementing Partners (e.g., CHAI, WHO, UNICEF). The structure is designed to minimise layers by using a platform model with shared governance.

quote.layers: "Establishing ATscale’s organisational setup with a host, including operational support, and a secretariat" (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)
quote.payment: Implied by milestone-based oversight: "These outputs should result in the initial outcome of having a strong partnership, well-placed to catalyse change for increased access to AT." (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)

q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Reputational risk for DFID in reneging on Global Disability Summit commitments; no catalytic impact.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Pooling resources to buy commodities at volume (e.g., Gavi model)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Insufficient global donor resources (~$50 billion needed to reach 500 million people by 2030).
Unlikely to achieve significant impact without additional investment and political will.
Would not overcome supply/demand market failures in AT markets.
Would not address systemic gaps in policy, investment, and service delivery.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Ecosystem approach (combining enabling environment + market shaping)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_selected: Addressed both market failures and systemic barriers; aligned with evidence from health sector.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The "ecosystem approach" (Option 6) was selected because it combines market shaping (to tackle supply/demand barriers) with systemic changes (policy, investment, service delivery) to create a mutually reinforcing strategy. This approach is evidence-based, drawing on lessons from health commodity markets (e.g., vaccines, bed nets) and aligns with DFID’s strengths in market shaping and disability inclusion. The partnership model leverages a broad coalition of stakeholders to ensure sustainability and global reach.
q25_decision_factors: alignment with DFID’s Disability Inclusion Strategy

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination across diverse stakeholders (donors, governments, DPOs, technical partners) may slow decision-making.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structured governance through the Forming Committee and clear mandates for each partner; transition to a permanent governance structure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited data on AT markets and needs may hinder targeted interventions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active engagement with new data (e.g., WHO GReAT report, AT2030 programme) and adaptive management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market shaping in AT may not replicate success from health commodities due to unique barriers (e.g., stigma, fragmented demand).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Twin-track approach addressing both market failures and enabling environment; learning from AT2030 and other DFID programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of ATscale beyond DFID’s initial £20 million investment.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mobilising additional donors and innovative funding sources; building political will for long-term country-level investment.

quote.rationale: "Option 6 – an ‘Ecosystem’ approach (options 4 and 5)... is considered viable and will be considered further.... Investment in both the enabling environment and carefully targeted market interventions has potential to meet the ambitious access targets set out in the strategic case. Previous evidence from the health sector demonstrates that a twin-track approach can drive step-change and systematically address supply and demand barriers." (Document: 52876804.odt, Assessment of viable strategic approach options section)
quote.risks: "Though other DFID programmes work in this area, this approach does not directly target the social stigma which surrounds AT. Stigma has the ability to limit demand and still lead to under-consumption." (Document: 52876804.odt, Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis table)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope of the programme requires a diverse partnership (Northern/Southern, multilateral, DPOs) to address context-specific barriers (e.g., stigma in LMICs, weak institutions, data gaps). Southern partners (e.g., Government of Kenya, China Disabled Persons’ Federation) are critical for legitimacy and local ownership, while Northern partners (e.g., DFID, USAID) provide technical expertise and funding.
q27_constraints_detail: Stigma and discrimination in LMICs necessitate inclusion of DPOs and Southern governments in design/delivery.
Weak institutions in LMICs require capacity building embedded in the partnership.
Data limitations demand adaptive approaches and reliance on WHO/UNICEF for global data.
Market fragmentation requires a platform model to coordinate stakeholders.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The twin-track objective (market shaping + enabling environment) necessitates a platform structure with shared governance. Market shaping requires technical partners (e.g., CHAI for product narratives), while systemic changes need policy actors (e.g., WHO, governments) and DPOs for advocacy. The global scale and complexity of AT markets demand a flexible, multi-stakeholder approach rather than a single-implementer model.
q28_linkages: Market shaping (WHAT) → Requires technical partners like CHAI and GDI Hub (HOW).
Policy reform (WHAT) → Needs WHO and government partners in governance (HOW).
Global reach (WHAT) → Platform model with regional/country engagement (HOW).
Stigma reduction (WHAT) → DPOs embedded in decision-making (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., reaching the "poorest of the poor," women with disabilities) with efficiency (e.g., market shaping to reduce costs). Trade-offs include: (1) Inclusive partnership structures (e.g., DPOs, Southern governments) may slow decision-making but ensure relevance; (2) Adaptive management adds complexity but addresses context-specific barriers; (3) Twin-track approach requires more resources but is necessary for sustainability.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Broad stakeholder engagement (e.g., DPOs, LMIC governments) ensures equity but may reduce agility.
Technical partners (e.g., CHAI) provide efficiency, while Southern partners (e.g., Kenya, China DPOs) ensure legitimacy.
Market shaping reduces unit costs, but enabling environment investments (e.g., policy reform) are needed for sustainability.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., market failures, stigma, weak institutions) justifies milestone-based oversight and a structured governance model (Forming Committee). High complexity requires adaptive management but also demands clear accountability mechanisms.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the partnership (e.g., training for service providers, strengthening LMIC systems) and shapes roles: Southern partners lead context-specific delivery, while Northern/multilateral partners provide technical/financial support. DPOs are central to advocacy and monitoring.

quote.where_who: "Disability disproportionately affects the most marginalised in society—women, older people and the poorest.... The ATscale Forming Committee includes... Government of Kenya, China Disabled Persons’ Federation, International Disability Alliance." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Need for Assistive Technology and The Formation of ATscale sections)
quote.what_how: "Taking a twin-track approach would be mutually reinforcing, developing the environment to increase access whilst executing interventions to overcome market failures in AT markets." (Document: 52876804.odt, What is our strategic approach to increasing access to AT? section)
quote.equity_efficiency: "ATscale was launched at the Global Disability Summit as a demonstration of the UK’s leadership ambition in disability.... AT is a cross-cutting priority for DFID’s Disability Inclusion Strategy and vision to Leave No One Behind." (Document: 52876804.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending? section)

key_programme_risks: Limited global prioritisation of AT and disability inclusion historically.
Complex market failures on both supply (e.g., high prices, low production) and demand (e.g., stigma, lack of awareness) sides.
Weak data systems for AT needs and outcomes, hindering targeting and monitoring.
Fragmented service delivery and procurement practices in LMICs.
Sustainability of ATscale beyond initial DFID funding.
Stigma and discrimination reducing demand for AT, especially among women and marginalised groups.
Policy and regulatory gaps in many countries, with 50% lacking AT-related legislation (2005 survey).
Limited manufacturing supply and competition, leading to high prices and low volumes.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited data on AT markets and needs.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Active engagement with WHO GReAT report, AT2030 programme, and new research; adaptive management based on emerging evidence.
Inclusion of DPOs in governance and advocacy; focus on social acceptability in product design and delivery.
System strengthening at global/regional/country levels; coordination with existing programmes (e.g., AT2030).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High costs and limited supply of AT products.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Market shaping interventions (e.g., volume guarantees, competition) to reduce prices and increase supply.
Advocacy and investment case development to mobilise country-level resources.
Mobilising additional donors (e.g., USAID, Norad) and innovative funding sources; building country ownership.

lessons_from_previous: Market shaping tools from health commodities (e.g., vaccines, bed nets) can be adapted to AT but require tailored analysis for AT’s unique barriers (e.g., stigma, fragmented demand).
Twin-track approaches (enabling environment + market interventions) have driven step-change in health sectors and are likely effective for AT.
Partnership models with shared governance (e.g., Gavi, Global Fund) are critical for scaling access to global public goods.
Embedding capacity building (e.g., training, policy reform) ensures sustainability and local ownership.
Data gaps in disability/AT sectors require proactive efforts to build evidence (e.g., WHO GReAT report).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Inclusion of DPOs and Southern governments in the Forming Committee to address equity and legitimacy.
Twin-track approach (market shaping + enabling environment) adopted based on health sector evidence.
Adaptive management framework to respond to new data and context-specific barriers.
Focus on 5 priority AT products (e.g., wheelchairs, hearing aids) based on scoping research.

quote.risks: "The barriers to access to AT are complex, multi-faceted challenges, driven by a number of supply and demand failures for both the AT product and the associated services.... Demand is often significantly curtailed as potential users and even service providers are unaware of the need for and the existence or importance of appropriate AT products and how to access them." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Barriers to Access to Assistive Technology section)
quote.lessons: "Lessons learnt from previous market shaping interventions (such as DFID investments in CHAI and Unitaid) have demonstrated that successful market shaping interventions need to be developed using robust analysis tailored to specific markets.... Using this approach will identify a set of integrated cross-product interventions to address barriers along the AT value chain." (Document: 52876804.odt, What is our strategic approach to increasing access to AT? section)
quote.design_changes: "DFID complemented this work with engagement with DPOs, technical inputs from Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) and also commissioned a scoping study from the Global Disability Innovation (GDI) Hub.... It also became clear that in order to influence the complex systems for access to and provision of AT, and to make sustained impact, a broad set of stakeholders across sectors would be needed to invest in and coordinate a multi-faceted, systematic approach." (Document: 52876804.odt, The Formation of ATscale section)

co_funding_partners.partner: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
Other ATscale members (e.g., WHO, UNICEF, Government of Kenya)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilise additional donors and innovative funding sources beyond DFID’s £20 million, though specific leverage targets are not quantified in the document.

quote.leverage: "Attracting additional donors and partners to ATscale" (Document: 52876804.odt, Initial outputs section)

metadata.programme_name: Tackling global plant and animal health risks which threaten global food systems and health – in partnership with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
metadata.quote: The programme’s impact will be two-fold. First, it will contribute directly to securing global food supplies in the face of pest and disease threats, climate change and the increasing scarcity of natural resources. Secondly, the programme will improve the agricultural productivity of smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, thereby reducing poverty at the household and community level, and contributing to economic growth at the national level. (51484745.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source:
Start Date: September 2019
End Date: September 2023 (51484745.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (e.g., disease-resistant crop varieties, surveillance systems), evidence generation (e.g., rigorous studies on agricultural productivity), and capacity building (e.g., strengthening African research institutions). It aims to address plant and animal health threats to global food systems while improving smallholder farmer productivity.
what_objectives.q1_source: This proposed programme builds on a successful agricultural research and technology development partnership between DFID’s Agriculture Research team and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF). With BMGF, DFID will co-fund a portfolio of agricultural technology investments to protect global food systems from the risks posed by plant and animal health problems. These investments will deliver improved crop varieties with resistance to pests, diseases and changing climatic conditions; coordinated surveillance and control mechanisms to tackle plant health threats in sub-Saharan Africa; improved monitoring and response mechanisms for significant animal health diseases; and rigorous evidence enabling more effective agricultural policy-making, programming and pest and disease management in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. (51484745.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: A systematic approach to plant pest and disease control in sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., surveillance and coordinating initiative)
New agricultural tools and technologies adopted by smallholder farmers (e.g., disease-resistant crop varieties, livestock drugs)
Enabling environment for agricultural innovation (e.g., national research capacity, evidence-based policies)
15-30 randomised control trials and 10-30 diagnostic data studies (J-PAL ATAI)
9 genomics/metagenomics-based technologies for tropical dairy cattle (CTLGH)
10 genomics/metagenomics-based technologies for tropical poultry (CTLGH)
50%+ yield increase in staple crops through photosynthetic efficiency (RIPE)
10,000+ smallholder farmers adopting NextGen cassava varieties
National bovine TB control programmes in Ethiopia and India
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to secure global food supplies and improve smallholder productivity by developing technologies (e.g., disease-resistant crops, surveillance systems), generating evidence (e.g., RCTs on technology adoption), and building capacity (e.g., African research institutions) to address plant and animal health threats exacerbated by climate change.
what_objectives.quote: The programme’s impact will be two-fold. First, it will contribute directly to securing global food supplies in the face of pest and disease threats, climate change and the increasing scarcity of natural resources. Secondly, the programme will improve the agricultural productivity of smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, thereby reducing poverty at the household and community level, and contributing to economic growth at the national level. (51484745.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme targets transboundary bio-security threats in regions vulnerable to climate change and weak bio-security, but the overall risk rating is classified as 'Minor' in the document. The focus is on systemic risks (e.g., pest/disease spread) rather than FCAS-level instability.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Minor (51484745.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (e.g., lack of border controls for bio-security in sub-Saharan Africa)
climate risks (e.g., climate change increasing pest/disease spread)
data limitations (e.g., dearth of early-warning systems for plant health)
regulatory (e.g., lack of harmonized phytosanitary systems)
infrastructure (e.g., limited access to agro-chemicals in rural areas)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and lack of surveillance systems in sub-Saharan Africa hinder rapid response to pest/disease outbreaks, while climate change exacerbates transboundary threats. Smallholder farmers lack access to affordable solutions (e.g., agro-chemicals) and advisory services, trapping them in cycles of low productivity.
where_context.quote: National agricultural research institutions in sub-Saharan Africa are ill-equipped to manage the increasing frequency and severity of pest and disease outbreaks. Donors have tended to fund project-based responses to particular outbreaks, often focusing on single diseases, single crops, and within one or a small number of countries. (51484745.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: BMGF manages the portfolio of grants and day-to-day delivery, with DFID providing strategic oversight through a seconded staff member. Decision-making authority rests primarily with BMGF, though DFID influences priorities via annual partnership meetings.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., surveillance and advisory services integration in Ethiopia/Kenya)
institutional strengthening (e.g., African Plant Health Initiative)
research grants (e.g., co-funded projects with national agricultural systems)
evidence uptake (e.g., engagement with policymakers on RCT findings)

who_partners.quote: BMGF will directly manage the projects, and DFID will work with BMGF to provide strategic oversight. Building on the success of the current programme-funded DFID secondment to BMGF, this arrangement will be extended under this programme. (51484745.odt, Outputs, outcomes and impact)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme operates under the DFID-BMGF Research Collaboration Framework (2016–2026), which formalizes co-funding arrangements. BMGF manages grants on DFID’s behalf without charging a management fee, enabling joint oversight and leveraged funding.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: BMGF acts as the fund manager, administering all projects and sub-awards. DFID provides strategic oversight via a seconded staff member (80% time) and annual partnership meetings. Projects are selected jointly but managed by BMGF.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Projects are co-funded based on alignment with DFID/BMGF priorities and technical peer review. The partnership leverages BMGF’s existing grant management systems and DFID’s strategic goals, with 90% of the budget pre-earmarked for 9 projects and 10% reserved for emerging opportunities.
how_mechanism.quote: DFID will co-fund a portfolio of 9 or more projects with BMGF to deliver these output areas. 90% of the Business Case budget has been earmarked to co-fund, subject to peer review and technical approval by the BMGF and DFID teams, the 9 co-investments tabulated below. (51484745.odt, Outputs, outcomes and impact)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The DFID-BMGF Research Collaboration Framework (2016) governs the partnership. A DFID staff member is seconded to BMGF for strategic coordination, and annual partnership meetings guide funding allocations. Technical approval for projects involves joint DFID/BMGF peer review.
how_governance.quote: Building on the success of the current programme-funded DFID secondment to BMGF, this arrangement will be extended under this programme. One DFID staff member will be seconded to BMGF for at least 80% of their time, to support implementation of DFID’s partnership with BMGF in agriculture. (51484745.odt, Outputs, outcomes and impact)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: 90% of the budget is pre-allocated to 9 projects, but 10% is reserved for emerging opportunities identified through annual strategic meetings. Reallocation between pre-approved projects is not explicitly mentioned.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The 10% flexible fund allows for adjustments based on annual reviews. New priorities can be added via DFID/BMGF partnership meetings, but core projects require technical approval.
how_flexibility.quote: The remaining 10% of funding is set aside to enable DFID and BMGF to co-fund emerging opportunities over the programme lifespan, to be identified through DFID and BMGF’s annual strategic partnership meetings. (51484745.odt, Outputs, outcomes and impact)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BMGF (fund manager) → Implementing partners (e.g., national research institutions, J-PAL, CGIAR)
how_efficiency.quote: This partnership with BMGF reflects high value for money for DFID. BMGF manages the portfolio of grants on behalf of both donors, without charging any management fee to DFID. (51484745.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF)

q24_alternatives_considered: Co-investment with BMGF (chosen option)
Direct DFID management of grants (rejected due to lack of capacity for small grants)
Multilateral funding (not explicitly detailed)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The BMGF partnership was selected for its value for money (0% management fee), leveraged funding (BMGF’s larger budget), technical expertise (e.g., in genomic research), and ability to operate in regions where DFID lacks presence (e.g., Sahel). The model also allows DFID to influence priorities while benefiting from BMGF’s grant management systems.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (no management fee, leverage of BMGF funds)
partner-capacity (BMGF’s technical expertise in agricultural R&D)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on BMGF’s priorities, potentially misaligning with DFID’s strategic goals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual partnership meetings and DFID’s seconded staff ensure alignment. DFID retains approval rights for co-funded projects.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited direct control over sub-awards, given BMGF’s management role.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Joint technical peer review for project selection and DFID’s oversight via secondment.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (prior success in delivering impacts, e.g., $50M annual benefit from wheat rust resistance in Ethiopia)
equity (gender-sensitive research and Southern institution engagement)
why_rationale.quote: By partnering with BMGF, DFID is able to co-fund a set of relatively small (<£5m) research grants with potential for significant impact which DFID could not manage as a sole funder. (51484745.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia—regions with weak agricultural research institutions and transboundary pest/disease threats—necessitates partnerships with organizations like BMGF and CGIAR that have existing regional networks and technical capacity. Local institutions lack the resources to manage large-scale surveillance or R&D independently.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak national research capacity in sub-Saharan Africa requires external expertise (e.g., BMGF/CGIAR).
Transboundary nature of pests/diseases demands regional coordination (e.g., WAVE initiative across 10 countries).
Climate vulnerability in target regions prioritizes partners with adaptive agricultural technologies (e.g., RIPE for drought-resistant crops).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both rapid technological solutions (e.g., disease-resistant crops) and systemic changes (e.g., surveillance platforms) drives the mixed delivery structure: BMGF manages high-risk R&D (e.g., photosynthetic efficiency), while DFID ensures policy relevance (e.g., via J-PAL RCTs) and regional uptake (e.g., African Plant Health Initiative).
q28_linkages: Technology development (e.g., NextGen Cassava) → requires CGIAR’s global breeding networks → delivered via BMGF’s grant management.
Evidence generation (e.g., J-PAL RCTs) → needs local policy engagement → facilitated by DFID’s government relationships in Africa/Asia.
Capacity building (e.g., surveillance systems) → depends on national institution buy-in → addressed through co-funded projects with governments (e.g., Ethiopia/Kenya pilots).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging BMGF’s systems for speed) with equity (e.g., gender-sensitive crop breeding, Southern researcher inclusion). For example, NextGen Cassava integrates gender preferences into variety selection, while the 10% flexible fund allows responsive adjustments to local needs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: BMGF’s existing networks enable rapid deployment but risk sidelining local institutions. Mitigated via capacity-building components (e.g., African Plant Health Initiative).
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led R&D (e.g., CTLGH in Edinburgh) is paired with Southern adoption strategies (e.g., national bovine TB programmes in Ethiopia/India).
Cost vs. reach: Co-funding with BMGF reduces overheads but limits DFID’s direct control over sub-awards.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Minor’ risk rating enables a lighter-touch oversight model (e.g., milestone-based reviews) compared to high-risk FCAS programmes. However, transboundary bio-security threats require coordinated management, hence the focus on BMGF’s regional platforms (e.g., WAVE for cassava viruses).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak Southern institutional capacity (e.g., lack of surveillance systems) justifies BMGF’s lead role in R&D, while DFID’s funding ensures local policy alignment (e.g., via secondment and annual reviews). Capacity-building outputs (e.g., trained researchers, data-sharing arrangements) are designed to transition ownership to Southern partners over time.
intersections.quote: National agricultural research institutions in sub-Saharan Africa are ill-equipped to manage the increasing frequency and severity of pest and disease outbreaks. [...] A ‘systems’ approach is required to enable organisations with plant disease responsibilities in sub-Saharan Africa to deploy preventative (and not just reactive) responses. (51484745.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Emergence of new, more virulent pests/diseases outpacing technological solutions.
Limited adoption of new technologies by smallholder farmers due to market or institutional barriers.
Weak national capacity in sub-Saharan Africa to sustain surveillance systems post-programme.
Climate change accelerating pest/disease spread beyond projected models.
Political instability in target regions disrupting implementation (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone).
Over-reliance on BMGF’s priorities potentially misaligning with DFID’s strategic goals.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: 10% flexible fund for emerging threats; annual reviews to adjust priorities.
RCTs (J-PAL ATAI) to identify barriers; gender-sensitive design (e.g., NextGen Cassava).
Pilot phase in Ethiopia/Kenya to test scalability; engagement with national governments (e.g., WAVE’s phytosanitary strengthening).
Investments in climate-resilient crops (e.g., RIPE, ENSA) and adaptive breeding programmes.
Regional approaches (e.g., WAVE across 10 countries) to distribute risk; BMGF’s experience in fragile contexts.

fcas_specific_lessons: Regional coordination (e.g., WAVE’s 10-country approach) is critical in FCAS-prone areas to pool resources and share data.
Local government engagement (e.g., cassava viral disease response plans) increases buy-in and sustainability.
Flexible funding (10% reserve) allows rapid response to crises (e.g., new disease outbreaks).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior DFID/BMGF collaborations (2010–2020) demonstrated the value of co-funding for leverage (e.g., $50M annual benefit from wheat rust resistance in Ethiopia) but also highlighted the need for systemic approaches beyond single-crop/disease projects. The shift to a ‘plant health systems’ model addresses this gap.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift 1: From single-disease projects to a ‘systems’ approach (e.g., African Plant Health Initiative).
Shift 2: Increased focus on commercialization pathways for technologies (e.g., bovine TB skin test).
Shift 3: Expanded evidence generation on multi-layered constraints (e.g., J-PAL RCTs on adoption barriers).
Added 10% flexible fund to address emerging priorities, based on past rigid allocation challenges.
risks_lessons.quote: However, new and more virulent varieties of pests and diseases are constantly evolving, and climate change is hastening that process of evolution. This programme responds to the urgent need for more ambitious, larger scale investments in sustainable mechanisms to track and facilitate rapid response to agricultural pests and diseases. (51484745.odt, Programme summary)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: In the prior phase (2016–2020), DFID’s £34.5M leveraged ~USD $145M from BMGF (a 4:1 ratio). This programme continues the model, with BMGF managing grants and contributing additional funds beyond DFID’s £38M.
financial_details.quote: This partnership with BMGF reflects high value for money for DFID. BMGF manages the portfolio of grants on behalf of both donors, without charging any management fee to DFID. (51484745.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF)

metadata.programme_name: International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD): Core Contribution to Twelfth Replenishment (2022–24)

quote.text: "To support IFAD in delivering results and impact through programmes that enable poor rural people to improve their food and nutrition security, increase incomes, and strengthen resilience, including to the effects of climate change."

duration_source.text: "Core Contribution to Twelfth Replenishment (2022–24)" and "Programme Value: £36.96 million (over three-year period from 2022-24)"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme channels core funding to IFAD, a multilateral institution, to support its Twelfth Replenishment (2022–24). IFAD uses these funds to provide loans and grants to governments for rural development programmes targeting poverty reduction, food security, and climate resilience. The UK's contribution leverages additional financing and supports IFAD's institutional reforms to improve efficiency and impact.

q1_source.text: "Core Contribution to Twelfth Replenishment (2022–24)" and "Funding will also support institutional reforms as IFAD continues to strengthen its financial architecture in line with its AA+ credit rating, and its country presence, programme delivery, and risk management to deliver IFAD12 commitments to improve results and their sustainability."

q3_expected_outputs.output: 127 million people supported by IFAD projects
increase income of 68 million people
increase production for 51 million people
improve market access of 55 million people
strengthen resilience of 28 million people (including climate change)
improve nutrition of 11 million people
1.9 million hectares of land under climate-resilient management
3.25 million people trained in production practices/technologies
19,000 km of roads constructed/rehabilitated/upgraded
22.5 million people accessing financial services
900,000 rural enterprises accessing business development services
3.1 million people trained in income-generating activities/business management
6 million people provided with targeted nutrition support

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce rural poverty and hunger (SDGs 1 and 2) by financing IFAD's core operations, which provide loans and grants to developing countries for agricultural and rural development. It focuses on climate resilience, women's empowerment, and institutional strengthening, with 100% of core funding allocated to the poorest countries and 40% dedicated to climate work.

quote.source: D0006568.odt, IFAD12: Recovery. Rebuilding. Resilience. section
quote.text: "IFAD12 will allocate 100 percent (up from 90 percent) of core funding to the poorest countries, supporting countries as their economies evolve to transition from grants to loans on highly concessional to ordinary terms. 40 percent of core funding will be dedicated to climate work. 50 percent of funding will be invested in Africa. At least 25 percent of funding will target fragile and conflict-affected countries to reach those most at risk of being left behind."

countries_regions: Global (with 50% focus on Africa, particularly Sub-Saharan Africa)
Fragile and conflict-affected countries (25% of funding)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected contexts (25% of funding), where food insecurity and poverty are acute. However, IFAD's institutional strength (AA+ credit rating) and focus on long-term resilience mitigate some risks. The document explicitly states: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate."

q5_source.text: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate."

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate change and conflict exacerbate food insecurity and poverty, particularly in Africa and fragile states. Weak institutions in target countries limit implementation capacity, while economic shocks (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine war) increase vulnerability. For example, "80 percent of the world’s extremely poor people live in rural areas," and "fragile situations disproportionately affect the most vulnerable people and communities."

quote.text: "With an estimated 80 percent of the world’s extremely poor people living in fragile situations by 2030, IFAD will enhance its focus on addressing the drivers of fragility. Fragile situations disproportionately affect the most vulnerable people and communities, including women and girls, and persons with disabilities, and are a major driver of migration and humanitarian crises."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: IFAD's governance includes 177 member states (both Northern donors and Southern recipients), with decisions made collectively through the Governing Council and Executive Board. The UK is one of 36 Executive Board members, indicating shared decision-making power.

support for climate adaptation (2.63 million people in 2019)
business development services for microenterprises (163,637 in 2019)
gender-transformative projects (35% of new projects)
youth employment focus (60% of new projects)
institutional reforms (e.g., financial architecture, risk management)

quote.text: "IFAD is a specialised UN Agency and an International Finance Institution (IFI) that works exclusively in rural areas where 80 percent of the world’s poorest people live, focusing on SDGs 1 and 2 to end extreme poverty and hunger. IFAD priorities are closely aligned with UK objectives as it targets the poorest and most vulnerable to leave no-one behind, including women, young people, indigenous groups, and people with disability."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides a core contribution (£36.96 million) to IFAD's Twelfth Replenishment (2022–24), which is pooled with other donors' funds. IFAD uses these resources to provide loans and grants to developing countries, leveraging additional co-financing and borrowing (e.g., bonds) to scale impact. The UK's contribution is disbursed via Promissory Notes deposited with the Bank of England.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IFAD manages the programme through its decentralized country offices (45% of staff in regional hubs) and headquarters in Rome. The UK engages via the Executive Board (oversight) and Audit Committee (risk management), but day-to-day delivery is led by IFAD in partnership with recipient governments and local communities.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IFAD is a pre-existing multilateral partner with a mandate aligned to UK priorities. The UK's contribution is part of a replenishment process negotiated among 177 member states, not a competitive selection.

quote.text: "Based on IFAD’s priorities that are closely aligned with UK objectives, including focus on the poorest and most vulnerable, climate change, women’s economic empowerment, delivering results and impact, as well as leveraging ODA to increase investment, Ministers decided to support IFAD12 with a contribution of £36.96 million over the three-year period."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: IFAD's Governing Council (177 member states) sets strategic direction, while the Executive Board (36 members, including the UK) oversees implementation. The UK also participates in the Audit Committee to strengthen financial oversight. Decisions on sub-awards (loans/grants to countries) are made by IFAD's management in consultation with recipient governments.

quote.text: "FCDO will continue to push IFAD for greater efficiency and collaboration, both through working together with other Member States in governing bodies, and through its bilateral interactions with IFAD. FCDO will continue to strengthen engagement in the Executive Board and other governing bodies, particularly the Audit Committee where the UK will seek to continue its membership, using the opportunity to support the strengthening of IFAD’s internal audit and investigations, risk management, implementation of improvements to commercial and procurement capability."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: IFAD can reallocate funds across countries/programmes within the replenishment framework (e.g., 50% to Africa, 25% to fragile states), but core funding must remain focused on the poorest countries. Major shifts require Executive Board approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: IFAD's "proximity" principle (decentralized staff) and adaptive management approach allow adjustments to country programmes based on emerging needs (e.g., climate shocks, conflicts). However, strategic shifts (e.g., reallocating >10% of funds) require Governing Council/Executive Board approval.

quote.source: D0006568.odt, Translating the inputs into outputs, outcomes and impact section
quote.text: "A more adaptive approach to management will also further facilitate the ability to learn, respond and adapt. [...] IFAD will also embed new core indicators on citizens’ engagement in country strategies and project designs, and ensure that national grievance redress mechanisms [...] are reported on as part of the stakeholder feedback framework."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IFAD (multilateral fund manager) → Recipient governments/local communities (implementers).

quote.source: D0006568.odt, How funds will be disbursed section
quote.text: "Payment will be made through Promissory Notes (PNs) deposited with the Bank of England within the IFAD12 period from 2022-24 to be drawn down in line with an agreed schedule."

q24_alternatives_considered: increased bilateral support (per UK International Development Strategy)
balancing engagement across multilateral system
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: IFAD's mandate aligns closely with UK priorities (rural poverty, climate resilience, women's empowerment) and offers a proven financing mechanism to leverage additional resources (1:6 ratio). The UK's influence via the Executive Board and Audit Committee allows it to shape reforms while benefiting from IFAD's technical expertise in rural development.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (IFAD's AA+ credit rating and financial reforms)
partner capacity (IFAD's 45 years of experience in rural development)
equity (100% of core funding to poorest countries, 50% to Africa)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Project-level inefficiency in fragile contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFAD will develop an "efficiency action plan" for IFAD12, including timelier implementation support, increased local presence, and technical assistance to governments. Project risk matrices will be used to monitor delivery risks (financial management, procurement, safeguards).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud/corruption in high-risk environments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFAD's Office of Audit and Oversight (AUO/IS) investigates allegations and applies sanctions (debarment, criminal referral). The UK, via the Audit Committee, pushes for stronger internal controls and transparency (e.g., public Operations Dashboard).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low co-financing from recipient governments due to economic shocks (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine war)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFAD will diversify funding sources (e.g., bonds, private sector partnerships) and use its AA+ credit rating to borrow additional resources. The Rural Poor Stimulus Facility provides flexible recovery support.

quote.text: "Based on IFAD’s priorities that are closely aligned with UK objectives, including focus on the poorest and most vulnerable, climate change, women’s economic empowerment, delivering results and impact, as well as leveraging ODA to increase investment, Ministers decided to support IFAD12 with a contribution of £36.96 million over the three-year period."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: IFAD's focus on rural areas (80% of extreme poor) and fragile states (25% of funding) requires partners with deep local presence and adaptability. The document notes: "Fragile situations disproportionately affect the most vulnerable people and communities, including women and girls," necessitating partners like IFAD with experience in these contexts. The UK cannot deliver directly in many of these areas due to security/access constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: 80% of extreme poor live in rural areas (limits urban-focused partners)
25% of funding targets fragile/conflict-affected states (requires conflict-sensitive partners)
Climate vulnerability demands partners with adaptation expertise (e.g., ASAP+ programme)
Weak institutions in LMICs necessitate capacity-building embedded in delivery
