intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to reach rural poor (SDGs 1 and 2) and build climate resilience (SDG 13) drives IFAD's decentralized structure (45% staff in regional hubs) and adaptive management approach. For example, the 40% climate funding target requires integrating climate finance into all projects, shaping how IFAD engages with partners like the Green Climate Fund.
q28_linkages: Rural focus → Decentralized country offices (proximity principle)
Climate goals → Partnerships with climate finance vehicles (GCF, GEF)
Fragility targets → Enhanced safeguards and grievance mechanisms
Leverage objective → Core funding structure to catalyze co-financing
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly acknowledges tensions between efficiency and equity, noting: "Going the last mile is costly, and given IFAD’s target groups, some compromise on project-level efficiency is inevitable." Trade-offs include:

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Reaching remote rural communities (e.g., 8,645 km of roads in 2019) slows implementation but ensures equity.
51% of beneficiaries are women, requiring gender-transformative designs that may increase costs.
IFAD's global safeguards must adapt to local contexts (e.g., land rights, indigenous groups), adding complexity.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The "moderate" risk rating and focus on fragile states (25% of funding) justify intensive oversight via the Executive Board/Audit Committee. For example, IFAD's enhanced risk management includes: "An integrated project risk matrix will be elaborated in IFAD12 for all new and ongoing projects to identify, assess, mitigate, manage and monitor risks to programme delivery."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: IFAD trains local staff (e.g., 2.6 million in 2019) and strengthens rural institutions to improve project ownership. The document states: "IFAD will increase focus on ensuring timelier implementation support, increasing local presence and technical support, and exploring how to support government capacity more directly."

quote.source: D0006568.odt, How weaknesses and knowledge gaps will be addressed section
quote.text: "Project-level efficiency has been highlighted as a recurrent weakness [...] In order to expand impact for rural poor people, IFAD will place special emphasis on project-level efficiency in IFAD12."

key_programme_risks: Global food insecurity worsening due to climate change, COVID-19, and Ukraine war
Low co-financing from recipient governments (economic shocks)
Fraud/corruption in high-risk environments
Project inefficiencies in fragile contexts (e.g., staff turnover, weak financial management)
Climate-related disruptions to agricultural production
Gender-based violence and exploitation in crisis settings

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IFAD's Rural Poor Stimulus Facility provides flexible recovery support. The 40% climate funding target and ASAP+ programme build resilience to shocks.
Diversify funding sources (e.g., bonds, private sector) using IFAD's AA+ credit rating. Strengthen domestic resource mobilization via policy dialogue.
Zero-tolerance policy enforced by AUO/IS (80 cases investigated in 2021). Sanctions include debarment and criminal referral. UK pushes for stronger controls via the Audit Committee.
Efficiency action plan for IFAD12, including timelier support, local technical assistance, and robust procurement plans. Project risk matrices monitor delivery risks.
40% of core funding dedicated to climate work; ASAP+ programme targets small-scale producers. Partnerships with GCF/GEF leverage additional climate finance.
Gender-transformative projects (35% of new investments) and safeguards aligned with UN policies. Grievance mechanisms strengthened for vulnerable groups.

fcas_specific_lessons: Fragile states require tailored interventions: "Interventions will be tailored to the specific conditions in fragile and conflict-afflicted countries and regions."

Enhanced engagement in Sahel/Horn of Africa: "Initiatives for enhanced engagement in the Sahel and Horn of Africa will be developed, with a view to increasing resources and strengthening collaboration with partners."
Protecting livelihoods in crises: "IFAD plays a particular role in fragile situations, complementing relief efforts with a focus on longer-term recovery and resilience of rural populations."
Local capacity gaps: "High staff turnover, inadequate local capacity, weak disbursement, poor financial management and procurement issues" are recurrent challenges in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: IFAD10 impact assessments showed strong results but below-target efficiency. Lessons include:
design_changes_based_on_learning: Efficiency action plan for IFAD12 to address recurrent project-level weaknesses (e.g., procurement delays, monitoring gaps).
Stronger focus on adaptive management: "A more adaptive approach to management will also further facilitate the ability to learn, respond and adapt."
Enhanced safeguards: "IFAD will review the steps needed to ensure an adequate focus on safeguards, including through a review of its capacity in this area."
Decentralization: Increase staff in regional hubs from 32% to 45% to improve proximity to beneficiaries.

quote.source: D0006568.odt, How weaknesses and knowledge gaps will be addressed section
quote.text: "Analysis of problem projects has demonstrated that project performance is linked to several challenges, including high staff turnover, inadequate local capacity, weak disbursement, poor financial management and procurement issues. IFAD12 will increase focus on ensuring timelier implementation support, increasing local presence and technical support, and exploring how to support government capacity more directly."

co_funding_partners.partner: Climate finance vehicles (GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: For IFAD12, US$1 of member state core contribution translates into US$6 of investment on the ground (including co-financing). The total programme of work is estimated at US$9.275 billion (including US$3.8 billion PoLG and US$5.475 billion co-financing).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Funds come from FCDO's capital budget and are counted as ODA. IFAD uses core contributions for both grants (to poorest countries) and loans (concessional/ordinary terms).

quote.text: "For IFAD12, despite pressure on co-financing from recipient governments due to COVID-19, it is estimated that US$1 of member state core contribution will translate into US$6 of investment on the ground. The ratio of contributions to PoLG at IFAD is similar to the World Bank’s IDA, which is recognised as providing good value for money."

metadata.programme_name: Funding for polio eradication 2020-2024

quote.text: This Business Case proposes providing £400 million over the next four years to polio eradication (2020-2024).

metadata.duration_source: This Business Case proposes providing £400 million over the next four years to polio eradication (2020-2024).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing (channeling £400m to GPEI), service delivery (vaccinating 450m children annually), and capacity building (strengthening health systems for broader disease surveillance). It aims to eradicate polio while ensuring transition of GPEI infrastructure into national health systems post-eradication.
what_objectives.q1_source: UK investment in GPEI over this 2020 to 2024 period will: Support GPEI to reach over 450 million children every year with polio vaccines... GPEI estimates that it contributes to saving 650,000 children from life-long paralysis every year... Contribute up to $32 billion in savings to global health systems... Support more than 20 million staff and volunteers worldwide deliver polio vaccination and broader health services to communities.
q3_expected_outputs: 450 million children vaccinated annually ("Support GPEI to reach over 450 million children every year with polio vaccines")
650,000 children saved from paralysis yearly ("GPEI estimates that it contributes to saving 650,000 children from life-long paralysis every year")
$32 billion savings to global health systems ("Contribute up to $32 billion in savings to global health systems")
20 million staff/volunteers delivering vaccines and health services ("Support more than 20 million staff and volunteers worldwide deliver polio vaccination and broader health services")
Transition of polio infrastructure into national health systems ("ensuring countries can transition effectively away from dedicated GPEI funding")
Containment of vaccine-derived poliovirus outbreaks within 120 days ("Ensuring GPEI continue to contain outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio within 120 days")
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) to deliver polio vaccines to 450m children annually, prevent 650,000 paralyses yearly, and transition polio infrastructure into national health systems post-eradication. It combines eradication financing, service delivery, and health system strengthening.

quote.text: This Business Case proposes providing £400 million over the next four years to polio eradication (2020-2024). It is a continuation of the UK’s 25-year investment in a successful programme which has already reduced global circulation of the poliovirus by over 99%. UK support will help eradicate the virus from the three remaining endemic countries, stop the spread of outbreaks and prepare for the eventual transition of countries away from reliance on funding from the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) once the virus is eradicated.

countries_regions: Nigeria (endemic, expected to be declared polio-free in 2020)
70+ countries with GPEI presence (disease surveillance/technical assistance)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The three remaining endemic countries (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria) are all FCAS contexts. Afghanistan has 2m children inaccessible due to anti-government control, while Pakistan faces vaccine resistance and misinformation. The programme is rated 'Major' risk overall.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major... In Afghanistan, nearly 2 million children are not being vaccinated due to inaccessibility in areas controlled by anti-government elements... In Pakistan... challenges include populations resistant to vaccinations, partly due to spread of misinformation...
q6_contextual_constraints: security ("inaccessibility in areas controlled by anti-government elements")
infrastructure ("weak health systems in poorest countries")
political economy ("lack of political consensus in Pakistan")
conflict ("Afghanistan: areas controlled by anti-government elements")
misinformation ("populations resistant to vaccinations, partly due to spread of misinformation")
data limitations ("poorer surveillance due to Covid-19")
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints in Afghanistan/Pakistan prevent vaccination of ~2m children. Misinformation fuels vaccine resistance in Pakistan. Covid-19 has paused campaigns, risking immunity gaps. Weak health systems in endemic countries limit transition readiness.

quote.text: In Afghanistan, nearly 2 million children are not being vaccinated due to inaccessibility in areas controlled by anti-government elements... In Pakistan... challenges include populations resistant to vaccinations, partly due to spread of misinformation... The current pause in immunisation campaigns due to Covid-19 is expected to lead to an upsurge in cases...
quote.source: D0001078.odt, Wild poliovirus / Covid-19 pandemic sections

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: GPEI's Polio Oversight Board (POB) and WHO Executive Board (194 Member States) make strategic decisions. The UK holds influential seats (Strategy Committee, Finance and Accountability Committee) but decision-making rests with multilateral governance bodies dominated by Northern donors/institutions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training ("20 million staff and volunteers deliver polio vaccination and broader health services")
institutional strengthening ("polio infrastructure supports wider disease surveillance and health systems")
transition planning ("ensuring countries can transition effectively away from dedicated GPEI funding")

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; leads certification, transition planning, and country-level implementation

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; procures vaccines and supports social mobilization

partner_organizations.name: Rotary International
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; funds advocacy and surveillance

partner_organizations.name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; provides technical expertise

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; major funder and strategic advisor

partner_organizations.name: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
partner_organizations.role: Core partner; funds IPV procurement and market shaping

partner_organizations.name: National governments (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation and transition planning

quote.text: GPEI is a public-private partnership led by national governments with six core partners—WHO, Rotary International, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF), and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance... The UK has been a major contributor, providing £1.3 billion since 1995 and is the second largest state donor.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, The Global Polio Eradication Initiative section

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides unearmarked core funding to GPEI (via WHO), allowing flexible allocation across eradication and transition activities. This is described as critical for "effective budget management and ability to promptly respond to changing needs."
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: GPEI operates through a partnership of six core agencies (WHO, UNICEF, etc.) governed by the Polio Oversight Board (POB). The UK participates in key governance bodies (Strategy Committee, Finance and Accountability Committee) but does not manage implementation directly.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (direct award to existing multilateral partnership)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GPEI is the "only partnership with the required scale to coordinate global eradication responses." Past DFID reviews concluded GPEI offered the strongest value for money compared to bilateral channels.

quote.text: UK funding for polio to date has placed no programme specifications, a characteristic that GPEI regularly note as being critical to effective budget management and ability to promptly respond to changing needs... It is a high performing partnership that has achieved many notable successes... It would not be possible to recreate the same level of reach through bilateral programmes alone.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, UK Leadership / Why was THIS modality chosen sections

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Polio Oversight Board (POB) oversees GPEI, with sub-committees including the Strategy Committee (where the UK represents all donors) and Finance and Accountability Committee (where the UK holds the only donor seat). Decisions require endorsement by the WHO Executive Board (194 Member States).

quote.text: The UK has a strong presence on GPEI governance bodies, representing all donors on the Strategy Committee, holding the only donor seat on the Finance and Accountability Committee and actively participating in Polio Oversight Board meetings... The Polio Oversight Board (POB), the main governing body of GPEI, approved the redeployment of staff and assets to support the [Covid-19] response.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, UK Leadership / Covid-19 pandemic sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The UK's £400m commitment includes a flexible £50m tranche that can be allocated to either GPEI (eradication) or WHO (transition) based on "programmatic needs throughout the strategic period." This responds to epidemiological changes (e.g., Covid-19 pauses, cVDPV outbreaks).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: GPEI's strategy is updated annually to respond to challenges like cVDPV outbreaks or Covid-19. The UK's flexible £50m allows reallocation between eradication and transition. The programme uses "evidence-based" adjustments (e.g., nOPV rollout timing).

quote.text: Part of this funding could also be used to provide technical assistance to GPEI and/or WHO through a secondment. In either scenario, we would continue to influence WHO on polio transition... If WPV cases come under control... more UK funds could be channelled to WHO for transition. If epidemiological challenges remain... more UK funds could be channelled to GPEI for eradication.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GPEI (multilateral partnership) → Implementing agencies (WHO/UNICEF/etc.) → Country-level delivery. No explicit sub-grantee layer mentioned.

quote.text: GPEI has scored an ‘A’ or above in every annual review performed to date. It is a high performing partnership... UK funding for polio to date has placed no programme specifications, a characteristic that GPEI regularly note as being critical to effective budget management.

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to endemic countries (rejected: "It would not be possible to recreate the same level of reach through bilateral programmes alone")
Reduced UK burden share below 10% (rejected: "would send a signal to other donors of reduced UK support")
Flat £300m contribution (Option 1; rejected: "would likely limit GPEI’s ability to meet health objectives")
£400m with fixed £50m for WHO transition (Option 2; rejected: "not the most appropriate decision at this point" due to Covid-19 delays)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 (£400m with flexible £50m) was selected for its balance of increased burden share (11.4–12.9%), adaptive flexibility, and influence. The multilateral GPEI model was chosen over bilateral channels due to its proven scale, value for money ("scored ‘A’ or above in every annual review"), and ability to coordinate global eradication.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation ("only partnership with the required scale")
experience ("25-year investment in a successful programme")
partner-capacity ("GPEI has specific skills, expertise and capacity")
flexibility ("flexible use of £50m to best meet needs")
equity ("leaving no one behind"; "reach the hardest to reach populations")

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor fatigue / reduced confidence if UK reduces contribution
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK increased burden share to 11.4–12.9% to "retain the UK as a global leader in polio" and incentivize other donors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Earmarking by other donors creating budget imbalances
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK provides unearmarked core funding to "give GPEI the flexibility and surety they need for longer-term planning."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Transition cliff-edge if polio funds withdraw abruptly
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible £50m for WHO transition activities; UK advocacy for "smooth transition" planning via WHO Core Voluntary Contribution.

vfm_criteria_used: economy ("lower cost than the alternative of permanent control")
efficiency ("high performing partnership"; "scored ‘A’ or above in annual reviews")
effectiveness ("reduced global circulation of poliovirus by over 99%")
equity ("fits well with DFID’s commitment to ‘leave no one behind’")

quote.text: Option four is the best fit with UK objectives and is our preferred option... Increasing the UK’s burden share and overall financial contribution, as well as maintaining some level of flexibility over the funds, will give the greatest level of influence for the UK... This option scored the highest overall, largely in terms of most flexibly meeting programmatic needs in a highly uncertain context.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS contexts in Afghanistan/Pakistan constrain partner selection to organizations with security access and community trust (e.g., WHO/UNICEF’s female vaccinator networks). GPEI’s multilateral structure is necessary because "it would not be possible to recreate the same level of reach through bilateral programmes alone" in these high-risk areas.
q27_constraints_detail: Security access ("nearly 2 million children are not being vaccinated due to inaccessibility in Afghanistan")
Community trust ("female vaccinators can enter households and interact with female caregivers")
Conflict sensitivity ("areas controlled by anti-government elements")
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for global coordination ("only partnership with the required scale") and adaptive response ("changing epidemiology of polioviruses") determines the multilateral, flexible funding structure. Eradication goals require GPEI’s technical expertise, while transition objectives necessitate WHO’s health system role—hence the split funding in Option 4.
q28_linkages: Global scale → multilateral structure ("GPEI is the only partnership with the required scale to coordinate global eradication responses")
Epidemiological uncertainty → flexible funding ("flexible use of £50m to best meet needs based on context")
Transition needs → WHO’s role ("part of the polio funding envelope could be used by WHO to progress this work")
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses balancing (1) rapid eradication (efficiency) with (2) inclusive transition (equity). For example: "If WPV cases come under control... more UK funds could be channelled to WHO for transition [equity]. If epidemiological challenges remain... more UK funds could be channelled to GPEI for eradication [efficiency]."
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion ("rapid response to outbreaks" vs "ensuring no child is left behind")
Expertise vs ownership ("GPEI’s technical leadership" vs "national governments taking on transition responsibilities")
Cost vs reach ("lower cost than permanent control" vs "reaching the hardest to access children")
intersections.risk_affects_management: The "Major" risk rating drives intensive oversight: the UK holds seats on GPEI’s Strategy Committee and Finance and Accountability Committee, with quarterly donor updates. Covid-19 added urgency to adaptive management (e.g., pausing campaigns, reallocating funds).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: GPEI’s capacity building (e.g., training 20m staff/volunteers) enables Southern partners to take on transition roles. The UK’s influence via WHO Core Funding ensures "countries do not face a cliff edge when polio funding ceases," linking capacity investments to sustainable roles.

quote.text: The last mile of eradication is extremely difficult. The remaining areas in which polio continues to be transmitted are extremely challenging to work in... GPEI’s Strategy is the right approach to achieving eradication. However... we should not now commit to a ‘deadline for eradication’... The UK has been a leading advocate on the importance of ensuring a smooth transition away from polio funds whilst retaining key infrastructure and capacity.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, Wild poliovirus / UK Leadership sections

key_programme_risks: Resurgence of 200,000+ polio cases annually if eradication fails ("modelling suggests... global resurgence of over 200,000 cases within 10 years")
Transition cliff-edge ("sudden discontinuation of employment would disrupt immunisation programmes")
Vaccine-derived outbreaks ("increase in cVDPV cases from 71 (2018) to 354 (2019)")
Covid-19 disruptions ("pause in immunisation campaigns... likely to lead to an upsurge in cases")
Donor fatigue ("globaleconomicinstability" may reduce funding)
Political resistance in Pakistan/Afghanistan ("populations resistant to vaccinations")

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain eradication funding; introduce nOPV to reduce cVDPV risk.
Flexible £50m for WHO transition; advocate for gradual withdrawal of GPEI support.
GPEI’s dedicated cVDPV strategy; roll out nOPV2 via WHO Emergency Use Listing.
Repurpose polio infrastructure for Covid-19 response; plan catch-up campaigns.
UK increased burden share to 11.4–12.9% to "retain the UK as a global leader."
Gender-sensitive strategies (female vaccinators); community mobilization via UNICEF.

fcas_specific_lessons: Female vaccinators are critical in conservative contexts ("areas where only female vaccinators can enter households").
Conflict-sensitive delivery is essential ("inaccessibility in areas controlled by anti-government elements").
Community trust outweighs top-down approaches ("caregivers are critical decision-makers in allowing vaccination").
Polio infrastructure doubles for emergency response ("played a significant role in preventing Ebola in Nigeria and Yellow Fever in DRC").
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID reviews (2015) found GPEI offered stronger value for money than bilateral channels. The 2013–2019 strategy successfully eradicated two of three poliovirus strains (types 2 and 3), proving the multilateral model’s effectiveness. However, "previous commitments to achieve eradication by certain dates have suffered from optimism bias," leading to no fixed deadlines in the current strategy.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. **Flexible funding**: Added £50m adaptable tranche in Option 4 to respond to Covid-19/cVDPV uncertainties. 2. **Transition focus**: Explicit £50m for WHO transition (Options 2–3) based on lessons from Nigeria’s 2016 polio-free certification delays. 3. **No deadlines**: Removed fixed eradication timelines after past "optimism bias." 4. **Gender integration**: Formalized GPEI Gender Equality Strategy (2019–2023) based on data showing female vaccinators improve coverage.

quote.text: The last mile of eradication is extremely difficult... Previous commitments to achieve eradication by certain dates have suffered from optimism bias... The UK has been a leading advocate on the importance of ensuring a smooth transition away from polio funds whilst retaining key infrastructure and capacity... GPEI has introduced several measures over the years to strengthen the programme’s economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, Wild poliovirus / UK Leadership / Lessons from previous phases sections

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s £400m commitment (11.4–12.9% burden share) leveraged additional donor pledges at the 2019 UAE pledging event, closing a $670m gap in GPEI’s $4.2bn budget. The UK’s early announcement "had an important leveraging effect on other state donors."
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes: (1) Revenue: routine vaccination campaigns, surveillance, and outbreak response; (2) Capital: one-time OPV stockpile costs for post-certification. No explicit split provided.

quote.text: The total cost of financing the strategy is $5.1 billion. This figure includes just under $1 billion of non-GPEI components; $814 million for Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine (IPV) procurement... and a one-time cost of OPV stockpiles to be used post-certification... The UK’s burden share... is 11.4–12.9%... This option scored the highest overall, largely in terms of most flexibly meeting programmatic needs in a highly uncertain context.
quote.source: D0001078.odt, Financial Resource Requirements / Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis sections

metadata.programme_name: Commonwealth Veterans Cash Transfer Programme
metadata.quote: "FCDO is supporting a cash transfer programme designed to provide sustained nutrition for older people living in absolute poverty in up to 28 ODA eligible countries which are members of the Commonwealth." (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 01/02/2019–31/03/2024" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31/03/2027" (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers direct cash transfers to approximately 7,500 elderly Commonwealth veterans and surviving spouses living in absolute poverty across 28 ODA-eligible countries. The transfers enable beneficiaries to afford sustained nutrition, lifting them out of extreme poverty and providing dignity in their final years.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The key outcome is that approximately 7,500 vulnerable older people will receive cash transfers to be able to afford sustained nutrition, which will strengthen resilience and lift them out of absolute poverty." (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 3,353 elderly and vulnerable veterans and widows lifted out of fast starvation diet during the extension period (2024-2027)
Cash transfers equivalent to the cost of two meals a day delivered every six months to eligible beneficiaries
Support provided across 23 Commonwealth countries through Tier 2 partners
Reduction of beneficiaries living in absolute poverty from 7,000+ to ~2,434 by 2027
what_objectives.summary: The programme provides sustained nutrition through cash transfers to elderly Commonwealth veterans and widows living in absolute poverty, with a focus on dignity and poverty alleviation.
what_objectives.quote: "The beneficiaries, living in some of the world’s poorest countries, are Commonwealth veterans and surviving spouses of veterans who served in the British Armed Forces prior to their countries gaining independence." (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

countries_regions: 28 ODA-eligible Commonwealth countries (exact countries not listed but includes Kenya, India, and 21 others)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates across multiple countries with varying stability, but the overall risk rating is moderate due to RCEL's experience and established networks. Some countries may be FCAS (Fragile and Conflict-Affected States), but the programme has mitigation strategies in place.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk rating for the programme is ‘moderate’, reflecting the scale and size of the programme and its ambition." (45149253.odt, Strategic Case) and "The political situation in all implementing countries is closely monitored by component leads with regular updates provided to DFID." (45149253.odt, Risk Description)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Delivery challenges include working in FCAS environments where political instability may delay outputs, limited banking infrastructure in some countries requiring cash distributions, and difficulties in verifying beneficiary eligibility in regions with poor record-keeping. The programme adapts by using electronic transfers where possible and vetted volunteers for cash distribution.
where_context.quote: "Non-delivery/ delay of outputs or elements of the programme due to difficulties working in FCAS" (45149253.odt, Risk Description) and "Where this is not possible, the delivery partner uses a network of volunteers to distribute the cash directly to beneficiaries." (45149253.odt, Phase Two – Delivery)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: RCEL (UK-based) manages the programme centrally, including fund distribution, risk management, and oversight of Tier 2 partners (local organizations in Commonwealth countries). Decision-making authority rests with RCEL, with DFID/FCDO providing oversight and approval for major changes.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical support and capacity building for RCEL to meet FCDO standards (e.g., financial management, due diligence)
training for Tier 2 partners on financial management and fraud detection
mentorship through Defence Attachés for in-country oversight

partner_organizations.name: Royal Commonwealth Ex-Services League (RCEL)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and programme manager

partner_organizations.name: Tier 2 delivery partners (e.g., Royal British Legion Kenya, Defence Forces Comrades Association, regional ex-services associations in India)
partner_organizations.role: Local distribution of cash transfers, beneficiary assessment, and reporting

partner_organizations.name: UK Ministry of Defence (MOD) Defence Attachés
partner_organizations.role: Oversight and monitoring in delivery countries

partner_organizations.name: UK-based veterans charities (e.g., The Royal British Legion, Army Benevolent Fund, Soldiers Charity)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funding (£3.7m over 5 years)

who_partners.quote: "RCEL is the only NGO globally which provides Commonwealth veterans with targeted cash transfer support." (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "RCEL will manage the delivery of the programme and will be required to resource it with sufficient programme management, social development, research and monitoring expertise." (45149253.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID/FCDO provides an accountable grant to RCEL, which then distributes funds to Tier 2 partners for cash transfer delivery. The grant includes conditions for due diligence, reporting, and value-for-money assessments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: RCEL acts as the sole programme manager, with DFID/FCDO oversight. RCEL sub-contracts delivery to Tier 2 partners in each country, who handle local distribution. Defence Attachés provide additional monitoring in some countries.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: RCEL was selected without competition because it is the only organization globally that specializes in supporting Commonwealth veterans with cash transfers. It has a pre-established network, unique expertise in beneficiary eligibility, and existing relationships with Tier 2 partners.
how_mechanism.quote: "RCEL has been selected to be the delivery partner without competition because they provide the following commercial benefits: RCEL is the only NGO globally which provides Commonwealth veterans with targeted cash transfer support." (45149253.odt, Commercial Case) and "By default, government grants should be competed. By exception, a grant may be awarded without competition... awarding a grant to an organisation that is the only provider of the service." (45149253.odt, Delivery Mechanisms)

how_governance.quote: "RCEL will manage the delivery of the programme... DFID will be required to proportionately resource the oversight of the relationship between DFID and RCEL." (45149253.odt, Intervention Summary) and "RCEL will provide DFID with quarterly spending reports. The SRO will scrutinize the reports to ensure RCEL are conducting the appropriate effective financial management." (45149253.odt, Financial Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted annually based on beneficiary numbers and country-specific needs, but major reallocations require DFID/FCDO approval. The programme design allows for flexibility in response to political risks or changes in beneficiary demographics (e.g., shift from veterans to widows).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes annual assessments of beneficiary numbers and can adapt to changes in political/conflict risks. Adjustments to transfer values (e.g., reducing calorie targets from 2,400 to 2,000 for elderly beneficiaries) were made based on learning.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme design will allow for annual assessments of beneficiary numbers and will build in sufficient flexibility to allow DFID to adjust the funding levels accordingly." (45149253.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The original target of 2,400 calories has been reduced which has allowed scope for the programme to adapt to the increase in beneficiary numbers and rising global inflation." (D0003841.odt, ADDENDUM)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → RCEL (Tier 1) → Tier 2 delivery partners → beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: "DFID will pay the grant on a quarterly basis prior to the financial year commencing." (45149253.odt, Financial Case) and "RCEL to the implementing organisations: RCEL’s distribution of the funding will vary with the downstream delivery partner. With most of cases this will be through a quarterly grant." (45149253.odt, Phase Two – Delivery)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: DFID partners with RCEL to reach all known eligible veterans (34 countries, £11.8m)
Option 2: DFID partners with RCEL but only supports lowest-income countries (9 countries, £4.9m)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (later extended) was chosen because it provided the highest poverty reduction impact (supporting all 7,000+ eligible beneficiaries) and aligned with DFID’s strategic objectives of reducing extreme poverty and supporting vulnerable groups. RCEL’s unique expertise, existing networks, and ability to leverage co-funding from UK veterans’ charities made it the most value-for-money option despite higher delivery risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Downstream delivery partners’ deliberate diversion of funds or mismanagement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: RCEL is held accountable for financial management of sub-contracted funds and must conduct due diligence on all Tier 2 partners. Monthly financial reports and capacity-building are required.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Non-delivery due to difficulties in FCAS environments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Political situations are monitored closely, with contingency plans to suspend activities or reallocate funds. Country offices provide additional assurance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from other veteran groups demanding support
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular liaison with MOD and a joint communications plan to clarify the unique historical obligations to pre-independence veterans.

why_rationale.quote: "This option would see the programme delivered across 34 countries... By supporting an increase in RCEL’s operational capacity, this would address a lead risk associated with the programme." (45149253.odt, Option 1 Analysis) and "RCEL is the only NGO globally which provides Commonwealth veterans with targeted cash transfer support... There is no other NGO that specifically focusses on these beneficiaries." (45149253.odt, Commercial Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country, FCAS-inclusive scope requires a partner like RCEL with pre-existing global networks and experience navigating diverse political and operational environments. Local Tier 2 partners must be vetted for capacity to handle cash distributions in challenging contexts (e.g., limited banking infrastructure).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with reach across 28+ countries, including FCAS
Requirement for local knowledge to verify beneficiary eligibility in regions with poor records
Dependence on volunteers or government-affiliated organizations in countries with weak institutions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of providing dignified, flexible support to elderly beneficiaries necessitates a cash-transfer mechanism (vs. in-kind aid) and a decentralized delivery structure. The need to reach remote, hard-to-verify individuals requires Tier 2 partners with local trust and networks.
q28_linkages: Cash transfers chosen over food aid to respect beneficiary dignity and accommodate dietary needs (e.g., "older people have more specific nutritional requirements")
Network of Tier 2 partners enables last-mile delivery in areas without banking (e.g., "volunteers distribute cash directly")
Quarterly disbursements balance efficiency with the need for frequent monitoring in high-risk contexts
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (supporting all eligible veterans/widows regardless of country income level) with efficiency (e.g., reducing calorie targets to stretch funds further). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for reaching remote beneficiaries vs. the ethical imperative to leave no one behind.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusion of middle-income countries (e.g., India) to ensure no eligible veteran is excluded, despite higher per-beneficiary costs
Use of volunteers for cash distribution increases assurance but raises costs vs. electronic transfers
Adaptive management (e.g., reducing calorie targets) prioritizes reaching more beneficiaries over strict nutritional standards
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile and FCAS contexts justify quarterly oversight, embedded safeguards (e.g., fingerprint verification), and Defence Attaché involvement, increasing management intensity but reducing fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: RCEL’s initial lack of institutional capacity led to FCDO-funded technical support, shaping its role as a stronger programme manager. Tier 2 partners’ varying capacities determine whether funds are disbursed quarterly or monthly.
intersections.quote: "The programme design will allow for annual assessments of beneficiary numbers and will build in sufficient flexibility to allow DFID to adjust the funding levels accordingly." (45149253.odt, Intervention Summary) and "RCEL has downstream delivery partners in 34 ODA eligible countries, the relationship varies with each country but as a general rule RCEL will transfer the capital on a quarterly basis to each delivery partner." (45149253.odt, Delivery Mechanisms)

key_programme_risks: Downstream delivery partners’ diversion of funds or mismanagement
Non-delivery due to FCAS instability
Reputational risk from other veteran groups demanding support
Fraud in cash distribution chains
Beneficiary numbers declining slower than forecast (actuarial risk)
Currency fluctuations affecting transfer values
Lack of safeguarding policies in Tier 2 partners

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Downstream delivery partners’ deliberate diversion of funds
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: RCEL conducts due diligence on all partners, requires monthly financial reports, and builds capacity for financial management. DFID reserves the right to cease funding to partners with unmanageable risks.
Political situations are monitored by DFID country offices, with contingency plans to suspend activities or reallocate funds. Defence Attachés provide additional oversight.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk from other veteran groups
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Joint communications plan with MOD to clarify the historical context of pre-independence veterans’ unique eligibility.
Use of electronic transfers where possible, fingerprint verification for cash distributions, and whistleblowing policies.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Beneficiary numbers declining slower than forecast
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Programme extension and additional funding secured to cover the increased need. Actuarial forecasts now incorporate nutrition-related longevity.
Exchange rates and food prices are monitored, with fund releases adjusted to maintain transfer values.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS environments, local partner vetting and Defence Attaché involvement are critical for assurance.
Flexible fund disbursement (quarterly/monthly) adapts to partners’ capacity in unstable contexts.
Electronic transfers reduce risks but may not be feasible in all FCAS; cash distributions require robust verification (e.g., fingerprints).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The original actuarial forecasts underestimated beneficiary longevity due to improved nutrition, leading to a funding shortfall. Lesson: Combine actuarial data with field research on beneficiary numbers. The programme also learned that technology for GPS-tagged photos was not cost-effective at current scale.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Extended programme duration from 5 to 8 years to account for slower-than-expected beneficiary attrition.
Reduced calorie target from 2,400 to 2,000 for elderly beneficiaries to stretch funds further.
Increased focus on widow inclusion as their proportion of beneficiaries grew (forecast to reach 61% by 2024).
Formalized MOD Defence Attachés’ oversight role in more countries.
risks_lessons.quote: "The original assumptions of beneficiary numbers did not hold up against implementation experience. The increased number of widows not previously identified in research has added pressure to the programme." (D0003841.odt, ADDENDUM) and "A lesson for the programme is that actuarial forecasts alone were not strong enough to form a baseline for the programme, and research into beneficiary numbers should have been included." (D0003841.odt, ADDENDUM)

co_funding_partners.partner: UK-based veterans charities (e.g., The Royal British Legion, Army Benevolent Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages £3.7m from UK veterans’ charities, reducing the required FCDO contribution. RCEL’s existing relationships with these charities were a key factor in the value-for-money case.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget covers both operational costs (e.g., RCEL’s programme management, due diligence) and direct cash transfers to beneficiaries. No explicit capital/revenue split is provided.
financial_details.quote: "The UK will provide additional funding of £5,990,172 bringing the total value of the programme to £18,326,370, exclusive of FCDO staff costs." (D0003841.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "Further funding of £3.7m will be provided direct to RCEL by UK-based veterans charities." (45149253.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Digital Identity as an Enabler for Development – Identification for Development

quote.programme_name: "Digital Identity as an Enabler for Development – Identification for Development" (Document: 54076057.odt, Title section)
quote.duration: "This programme will finance ID4D to: [...] between 2019/2020-2023/24" (Document: 54076057.odt, Programme summary section)
quote.sector: "This programme will support the implementation of trusted, secure and inclusive digital identification and civil registration systems in developing countries" (Document: 54076057.odt, Programme summary section)

metadata.duration_source: "This programme will finance ID4D to: [...] between 2019/2020-2023/24"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research on digital ID systems), capacity building (technical assistance to governments), policy influence (global platforms and convening), and implementation research (piloting and scaling digital ID systems). It also includes a financing mechanism by channeling funds through the World Bank’s ID4D initiative.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support governments to implement trusted, secure and inclusive digital Identification (ID) and civil registration systems, informed by international evidence and experience, by providing GB£15 million to the World Bank Group’s ‘Identification for Development (ID4D)’ initiative between 2019/2020-2023/24. [...] This programme will finance ID4D to: i) produce evidence-based guidance on the preferred approaches for digital ID and illustrate the development value of these systems; ii) establish and support global platforms, convening and peer-to-peer exchange to share lessons and experiences of what works and why; and iii) provide technical assistance to over 30 governments and regional institutions to support countries to roll-out digital ID and civil registration systems."

q3_expected_outputs.output: evidence-based guidance on digital ID approaches
global platforms for peer-to-peer exchange
technical assistance to 30+ governments/regional institutions
independent evaluation of ID4D programme
increase in number of people with trusted digital ID
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative_target: 75 million people (25% of ID4D’s 300 million target)

q3_expected_outputs.output: reduction in gender divide in ID access
Practitioner’s Guide for designing inclusive ID systems
Global ID4D Dataset updates
Principles on Identification for Sustainable Development (endorsed by 25+ organizations)
Modular Open Source Identity Platform (MOSIP) adoption

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to scale up trusted digital identification systems globally by financing the World Bank’s ID4D initiative, combining research, technical assistance, and global advocacy to improve access to services and rights for 1 billion people currently without legal identity.

quote.objectives: "The overall objective of this programme is for people to have improved access to public and private services and resources, facilitated through gaining an official proof of identity, and that these services are provided with greater efficiency and inclusivity." (Document: 54076057.odt, What will this programme deliver section)
quote.outputs: "The programme will deliver the following outputs: [...] i) Implement robust, applied and ambitious thought-leadership and analytics work; ii) Establish and support global platforms, convening and peer-to-peer exchange; iii) Provide technical assistance to over 30 governments and regional institutions." (Document: 54076057.odt, What will this programme deliver section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate risk' in the business case, reflecting challenges in implementing digital ID systems across diverse contexts (including FCAS) but with mitigations through the World Bank’s established systems and DFID’s oversight.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 54076057.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak civil registration systems, lack of technical capacity, gender barriers (15% gap in ID ownership for women in LICs), and conflict/fragility (e.g., displaced populations) limit the ability to implement inclusive digital ID systems. Regulatory and data protection challenges also constrain cross-border interoperability.

quote.risk: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 54076057.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.constraints: "Women, and members of other vulnerable populations (including non-nationals, internally displaced persons, people living in rural and remote areas), are the most likely to struggle to prove their identity. [...] The countries with the greatest gender gaps in ID coverage also tend to be those with the most significant barriers and score poorly on other indicators of gender equality and empowerment." (Document: 54076057.odt, What is the need for a DFID intervention? section)
quote.fcas: "ID plays a critical role in delivering humanitarian assistance, but the unique considerations for conflict-affected populations and how ID systems could be better used to respond to forced displacement and natural disasters is not well understood." (Document: 54076057.odt, Conflict and fragility section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank Group’s Identification for Development (ID4D) initiative
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led multilateral) sets the strategic direction for ID4D, with DFID as a major donor influencing priorities but requiring consensus among all Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) contributors. Southern governments receive technical assistance but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to 30+ governments
peer-to-peer learning platforms
diagnostic tools (e.g., ID4D Guidelines for Diagnostics)
training on data protection and inclusion
support for regional institutions (e.g., ECOWAS)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank Group (ID4D initiative)
partner_organizations.role: lead implementer (thought leadership, global convening, technical assistance)

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (MDTF contributor)

partner_organizations.name: Omidyar Network
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (MDTF contributor)

partner_organizations.name: Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (MDTF contributor)

partner_organizations.name: 30+ national governments (e.g., Afghanistan, Nigeria, Philippines)
partner_organizations.role: recipients of technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: ECOWAS Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: regional partner

partner_organizations.name: UN’s Partnership on Legal Identity for All (POLIA)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner (interoperability)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: partner (child-focused ID systems)

quote.structure: "This option involves a partnership with the WBG’s ID4D initiative. [...] ID4D has become a powerful voice for building inclusive and trusted ID and civil registration systems in service of development." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)
quote.capacity_building: "Providing technical assistance to countries and regional organisations, in collaboration with other development partners and donors, in three stages: assessment and roadmap; design and upstream advisory services and implementation advice." (Document: 54076057.odt, What will this programme deliver section)
quote.decision_power: "By joining a multi-donor trust fund DFID have less influence over the strategic direction of the WBG initiative, than it would have under option 2, because agreement between all donors of the MTDF will be required." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID contributes £15.25 million to the World Bank’s ID4D Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF), a pooled financing mechanism where funds are managed by the WBG but earmarked for specific outputs (thought leadership, convening, technical assistance). The MDTF allows co-financing with other donors (e.g., Gates Foundation, Australia).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank’s ID4D initiative manages delivery through its existing global platform, with DFID as a major contributor to the MDTF. ID4D operates across WBG practices (digital development, social protection, governance) and coordinates with 30+ country offices. A 17% management fee covers WBG personnel/operational costs.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The WBG’s ID4D was selected due to its established track record (35+ countries supported), global convening power, and alignment with DFID’s digital strategy. Setting up a new initiative (Option 2) was deemed higher-risk and less efficient than leveraging ID4D’s existing platform.

quote.instrument: "A Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) was established in November 2016 to finance the work of ID4D with contributions from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Omidyar Network and Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade." (Document: 54076057.odt, Theory of Change section)
quote.selection: "This option is the preferred delivery mechanism because of the strong performance of ID4D and the WBG to date and because it offers greater scope to influence digital ID thinking and practice, as well as leverage additional resources to advance the agenda." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ID4D Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) is governed by a steering committee with representation from all contributing donors (DFID, Gates Foundation, Omidyar Network, Australia). Decisions require consensus among donors, with the WBG providing secretariat support. DFID’s influence is proportional to its financial contribution.

quote.governance: "By joining a multi-donor trust fund DFID have less influence over the strategic direction of the WBG initiative, than it would have under option 2, because agreement between all donors of the MTDF will be required." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)
quote.oversight: "The WBG has a standard MDTF 17% management fee for WBG executed funds which covers personnel costs (staff and consultants)." (Document: 54076057.odt, Value for Money appraisal section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to three pillars (thought leadership, convening, technical assistance) with fixed budgets (£3.75m, £3.75m, £7.5m respectively). Reallocation between pillars requires MDTF donor approval, but flexibility exists within pillars for adaptive management (e.g., shifting technical assistance between countries).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in country focus or technical assistance priorities based on emerging needs, but changes require consensus among MDTF donors. The WBG’s existing systems enable rapid reallocation of resources (e.g., responding to new country requests for diagnostics).

quote.flexibility: "Output 1 (thought-leadership & analytics): GB£3.75m; Output 2 (global platforms & convening): GB£3.75m; Output 3 (country & regional action): GB£7.5m." (Document: 54076057.odt, Table 1: Four E Value for Money Framework)
quote.adaptive: "Building on the ID4D Diagnostics, the WBG responds to requests from countries for technical assistance, which includes a range of activities to support the design of identification systems using global good practice." (Document: 54076057.odt, Theory of Change section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank ID4D (MDTF) → Country governments/regional institutions (no additional sub-grantees mentioned).

quote.costs: "The WBG has a standard MDTF 17% management fee for WBG executed funds which covers personnel costs (staff and consultants)." (Document: 54076057.odt, Value for Money appraisal section)
quote.layers: "ID4D is providing technical assistance to support to over 35 governments and a regional institution [...] and the WBG has ring-fenced nearly US$1 billion to finance the implementation of ID and civil registration systems." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)
quote.payment: "The programme will deliver the following outputs: [...] Providing technical assistance to over 30 governments and regional institutions in collaboration with other development partners and donors, in three stages: assessment and roadmap; design and upstream advisory services and implementation advice." (Document: 54076057.odt, What will this programme deliver section)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: Continue to voice support for digital ID without additional financial partnerships
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Status quo with no new funding; DFID would advocate for digital ID but not provide programmatic support.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Contract out delivery to a commercial firm
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Procure a consultancy to deliver research, convening, and technical assistance, tailored to DFID’s priorities.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: Strategic partnership with WBG’s ID4D initiative (selected)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Leverage ID4D’s existing platform, global reach, and $1 billion WBG ring-fenced funds for co-financing.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its value for money (leveraging WBG’s $1 billion and existing donor partnerships), lower delivery risk (ID4D’s proven track record in 35+ countries), and greater influence (global convening power and alignment with DFID’s digital strategy). The WBG’s multilateral structure also mitigates country-specific risks (e.g., FCAS) and ensures adherence to international standards.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (proven WBG performance, shared donor oversight)
partner capacity (ID4D’s global reputation and country reach)
equity (focus on vulnerable groups, gender inclusion)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced DFID influence over strategic direction (consensus-based MDTF governance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s status as a major financial contributor and strong international reputation positions it to shape the agenda.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential misalignment with UK values (e.g., privacy, openness) in WBG-led systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID’s input promotes pro-development, pro-poor approaches and advocates for open, private, and secure systems.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Operational delays in multi-donor coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: WBG’s established MDTF processes and existing country engagements streamline implementation.

quote.rationale: "Option 3 is preferred because it allows DFID to capitalise on successful work already underway in coordination with other donors. Alongside the inputs DFID will directly finance, this investment will leverage the US$1 billion ring-fenced by the WBG to finance the implementation of ID and civil registration systems, which are very expensive for countries and a key constraint to providing universal identification." (Document: 54076057.odt, Preferred option section)
quote.vfm: "The VFM assessments support the recommendation in the qualitative options appraisal, which identifies option 3 [...] as the preferred delivery mechanism to deliver this programme." (Document: 54076057.odt, Value for Money appraisal section)
quote.risks: "By joining a multi-donor trust fund DFID have less influence over the strategic direction of the WBG initiative, than it would have under option 2, because agreement between all donors of the MTDF will be required. However, DFID will be one of the main financial contributors to ID4D and has a strong international reputation, so it is well positioned to shape the agenda." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on low-income/FCAS countries (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia) require a multilateral partner with existing country offices and trust from governments. Local capacity constraints (e.g., weak civil registration systems) necessitate a partner like WBG that can provide long-term technical assistance and leverage co-financing (e.g., $1 billion WBG ring-fenced funds).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for in-country presence (35+ governments already engaged by ID4D)
FCAS contexts require multilateral credibility (WBG’s risk mitigation systems)
Gender barriers demand embedded capacity building (e.g., ID4D’s focus on women’s inclusion)
Regulatory fragmentation needs global convening power (ID4D’s Principles on Identification)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (research + implementation + advocacy) require a delivery structure that combines global thought leadership (Pillar I), peer learning (Pillar II), and country-level technical assistance (Pillar III). The WBG’s ID4D was selected because its three-pillar model directly mirrors these needs, while a commercial firm (Option 2) or ad-hoc support (Option 1) could not provide all three.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (Pillar I) informs technical assistance (Pillar III) via diagnostic tools (e.g., ID4D Guidelines).
Global convening (Pillar II) amplifies country-level impact by sharing lessons (e.g., Principles on Identification).
Technical assistance (Pillar III) requires a multilateral partner to navigate sovereign government relationships.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., targeting 75 million people, reducing gender gaps) with efficiency (leveraging WBG’s $1 billion to lower per-person costs). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid scale-up risks excluding vulnerable groups (e.g., displaced persons), mitigated by ID4D’s focus on ‘good ID’ principles; (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: WBG-led design ensures technical rigor but limits local control, addressed through peer-to-peer learning.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Option 3 achieves lower per-person cost (£25,000 per 100,000 people) by leveraging WBG funds, but requires accepting WBG’s 17% management fee.
ID4D’s Principles on Identification ensure interoperability but may limit country-specific customization.
DFID gains global influence through WBG but cedes some control to MDTF consensus-based governance.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., annual MDTF reviews) and justifies the multilateral structure, which spreads risk across donors. FCAS contexts (e.g., Somalia, DRC) require WBG’s existing safeguards and conflict-sensitive approaches.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: (1) WBG provides technical assistance to strengthen government systems; (2) Southern governments (e.g., Nigeria, Philippines) co-design implementations with WBG advisors; (3) Regional bodies (e.g., ECOWAS) facilitate cross-country learning.

quote.context_who: "Many of [the countries implementing digital ID] are low-income, in need of more detailed guidance, in-depth and longer-term technical assistance to ensure that their digital ID systems are designed and implemented in a way that fully harnesses their benefits for development." (Document: 54076057.odt, Why should the UK address this need? section)
quote.what_how: "ID4D focuses on three mutually reinforcing pillars of work: Pillar I: Thought Leadership & Analytics; Pillar II: Global Platforms & Convening; Pillar III: Country & Regional Action. These pillars are aligned with the three outputs for this programme." (Document: 54076057.odt, Theory of Change section)
quote.tradeoffs: "Under this scenario, it is unlikely that the achievement of the target in outcome 3 [...] could be attributed to DFID’s on-going action. [...] Option 3: [...] it will cost the UK taxpayer GB£25,000 to provide 100,000 people with a trusted, secure and inclusive digital ID." (Document: 54076057.odt, Value for Money appraisal section)
quote.risk_management: "The widespread coverage and utilisation of digital technologies across the world has created a significant new opportunity to address this challenge and provide trusted, secure and inclusive identification systems at considerable speed and scale." (Document: 54076057.odt, What is the need for a DFID intervention? section)

key_programme_risks: Sub-optimal digital ID systems implemented by countries without adequate guidance (risk of exclusion, privacy breaches).
Gender gaps in ID access persisting due to social/legal barriers.
Fragmentation of ID systems across sectors (e.g., humanitarian vs. government systems).
Data protection and privacy risks in digital ID rollouts (e.g., biometric data misuse).
Political resistance or lack of government ownership in recipient countries.
Limited interoperability between national/regional ID systems (e.g., for migrants).
Over-reliance on technology without addressing underlying institutional weaknesses.
Donor coordination challenges in the multi-donor MDTF structure.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ID4D’s technical assistance and diagnostic tools (e.g., Guidelines for ID4D Diagnostics) ensure systems are designed for inclusion and sustainability. Peer-to-peer learning shares best practices.
Targeted research on gender barriers and technical assistance focused on countries with the largest gaps (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa).
Principles on Identification for Sustainable Development promote interoperability. ID4D’s global convening harmonizes approaches.
WBG’s safeguards and ID4D’s focus on ‘good ID’ principles (e.g., user control, transparency). Mission Billion Challenge incentivizes privacy-enhancing innovations.
Country-led diagnostics and roadmaps (e.g., Nigeria’s co-financed programme with France/EIB). Long-term technical assistance builds local capacity.
Research on ID models for refugees/displaced persons and piloting in conflict-affected contexts (e.g., Somalia, DRC).

fcas_specific_lessons: ID systems in FCAS must prioritize interoperability with humanitarian actors and address unique data protection needs for displaced populations.
Conflict-sensitive design is critical (e.g., avoiding exclusion of non-nationals or marginalized groups).
Regional bodies (e.g., ECOWAS) can facilitate cross-border recognition of IDs for migrants.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The WBG’s ID4D initiative has demonstrated that: (1) **Diagnostic tools** (e.g., ID4D Guidelines) are essential for country engagement; (2) **Multi-stakeholder endorsement** (e.g., Principles on Identification) accelerates adoption; (3) **Open-source solutions** (e.g., MOSIP) reduce vendor lock-in; (4) **Co-financing** (e.g., Nigeria’s programme with France/EIB) leverages additional resources.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates lessons from ID4D’s 2014–2018 work, including: (1) Expanding the Global ID4D Dataset to track progress toward SDG 16.9; (2) Launching the Mission Billion Challenge to address persistent issues like privacy; (3) Strengthening focus on gender and vulnerable groups in technical assistance.

quote.risks: "Without heightened international intervention, there is a real risk that countries implement sub-optimal digital ID systems, that fail to incorporate lessons from experience and are not designed to maximise the benefits for development." (Document: 54076057.odt, What is the need for a DFID intervention? section)
quote.mitigations: "ID4D has developed or supported a number of tools that make it easier for countries to design and implement inclusive and trusted ID systems, including: [...] Modular Open Source Identity Platform (MOSIP) [...] to provide countries with an open source option for their core ID software." (Document: 54076057.odt, Theory of Change section)
quote.fcas: "ID plays a critical role in delivering humanitarian assistance, but the unique considerations for conflict-affected populations and how ID systems could be better used to respond to forced displacement and natural disasters is not well understood." (Document: 54076057.odt, Conflict and fragility section)
quote.lessons: "ID4D has become a powerful voice for building inclusive and trusted ID and civil registration systems in service of development. The deep and cross-cutting knowledge base developed over the past few years is now being applied to support the implementation of these systems across the globe." (Document: 54076057.odt, Option 3 section)

co_funding_partners.partner: Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

financial_details.leverage_achieved: DFID’s £15.25 million leverages the WBG’s ring-fenced US$1 billion for ID/civil registration systems (e.g., co-financing in Nigeria with France and the European Investment Bank). The MDTF structure also attracts additional donors (e.g., Gates Foundation).

quote.budget: "GB£15.25 million to finance the three pillars of ID4D: Output 1 (thought-leadership & analytics): GB£3.75m; Output 2 (global platforms & convening): GB£3.75m; Output 3 (country & regional action): GB£7.5m; Independent Evaluation: GB£250,000." (Document: 54076057.odt, Table 1: Four E Value for Money Framework)
quote.leverage: "The WBG has, to date, committed approximately US$1 billion for ID and civil registration projects over the next five years. By financing the WBG ID4D initiative the UK government will support governments to leverage these funds." (Document: 54076057.odt, Why should the UK address this need? section)
quote.overhead: "The WBG has a standard MDTF 17% management fee for WBG executed funds which covers personnel costs (staff and consultants)." (Document: 54076057.odt, Value for Money appraisal section)

metadata.programme_name: Progressing Action on Resilient Systems for Nutrition through Innovation and Partnership (PARSNIP) / Child Wasting and Innovation Programme (CWIP)
metadata.quote: "The programme aims to contribute to ending the preventable deaths of children by 2030 by strengthening the resilience of services to treat and prevent child wasting in the face of climate change." (D0004554.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2030" (D0004554.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (Child Nutrition Fund), implementation research (testing prevention/treatment approaches), evidence generation (modelling COVID-19 impacts, operational research), and policy influence (UN coordination, global guidelines). It directly delivers services through UNICEF while also shaping global policy and financing systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The extension will build and expand on the successes and lessons learned over the first three years of the CWIP programme around improving the sustainability of financing for wasting through the Child Nutrition Fund and strengthening the global evidence base for better prevention of wasting." (D0004554.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 132,000+ children and pregnant/breastfeeding women reached through CNF (conservative estimate)
Joint UN strategy/policy for wasting prevention
UN prevention "toolkit" of evidence-based interventions
Robust monitoring framework for prevention impact
500,000 cartons of RUTF procured through Match Fund (already achieved)
Mathematical models of COVID-19/malnutrition interactions (55541884.odt)
Operational research on COVID-19 patient outcomes (55541884.odt)
Updated WHO global guidelines for wasting prevention/treatment
Integration of wasting treatment into primary health systems in 23 GAP countries
Reduction in child deaths associated with undernutrition (modelled)
12% reduction in preventable child deaths attributable to wasting (theoretical target)
what_objectives.summary: The programme combines a financing mechanism (Child Nutrition Fund matching domestic investments 1:1) with UN coordination to generate evidence on wasting prevention, while directly supporting treatment service delivery through UNICEF's global RUTF procurement and country-level health system integration.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme aims to contribute to ending the preventable deaths of children by 2030 by strengthening the resilience of services to treat and prevent child wasting in the face of climate change... This will be achieved by: Integrating treatment for child wasting into health systems as part of Universal Health Coverage; Optimising treatment services to reduce cost, improve coverage and enable services to scale up to deal with climate shocks and other crises effectively; Generating evidence of how government services can more effectively prevent child wasting." (D0004554.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in 23 countries classified as fragile/conflict-affected (e.g., Afghanistan, DRC, South Sudan, Yemen) with high malnutrition burdens. Climate shocks and conflict drive recurrent nutrition crises, requiring shock-responsive service delivery models.
where_context.q5_source: "The geographical focus of the programme are the 23 Global Action Plan (GAP) frontrunner countries... where child wasting remains persistently high and climate change is increasing risks... including Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cambodia, DRC, Ethiopia, Haiti, Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Timor Leste, and Yemen." (D0004554.odt, INFORMATION)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints increase travel costs and limit access in conflict zones (e.g., Yemen, South Sudan). Weak health systems require 'shock-responsive' service models to handle caseload spikes during crises. Climate shocks disrupt food production and increase wasting prevalence. Data limitations hamper evidence generation in fragile states.
where_context.quote: "The nature of this programme will mean that global/regional staff posts will be more likely to need to travel to contexts where security considerations and poor infrastructure result in higher travel costs." (58006857.odt, Overview of costs) AND "Acute climate shocks, disruptions to the quality and quantity of food production, and an increase in climate-related disease outbreaks are already driving more frequent spikes in wasting across Africa and parts of South Asia." (58006857.odt, Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UNICEF (multilateral) and FCDO jointly set strategic direction, with UNICEF managing day-to-day implementation. Country-level adaptation occurs through UNICEF Country Offices, but core decisions (e.g., CNF governance, research priorities) are driven by Northern donors/FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for government health workers on wasting treatment integration
Technical support to ministries for RUTF procurement planning
Joint UNICEF-WHO coordination to build country-level policy capacity
Performance-based financing to incentivize domestic resource allocation
Operational research partnerships with LMIC academic institutions

partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer (financing mechanisms, service delivery, research coordination)
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (HQ in New York, operations in 23 LMICs)

partner_organizations.role: Joint development of global guidelines for wasting prevention/treatment

partner_organizations.role: Collaboration on prevention toolkit and food security linkages

partner_organizations.role: Mathematical modelling support (55541884.odt)

partner_organizations.role: Co-financing (via Child Nutrition Fund), policy adoption, service delivery
