partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Child Nutrition Fund

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Child Nutrition Fund

partner_organizations.name: Academic partners (sub-Saharan Africa)
partner_organizations.role: Operational research on COVID-19/malnutrition (55541884.odt)

who_partners.quote: "UNICEF will work with experts in mathematical modelling (including from Johns Hopkins University and Imperial College London)... UNICEF is developing an approach to undertaking operational research so that they can capture data on patients with COVID-19 with and without malnutrition in developing countries to enable analysis of outcomes. They are in discussion with academic and operational partners in sub-Saharan Africa on this." (55541884.odt, Modelling the impact of COVID-19 / Operational research)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) **Framework Agreements** with UNICEF for core components (8% recovery cost); 2) **Trust Funds** for the Child Nutrition Fund (0% recovery) and Match Fund (5% handling fee); 3) **Direct contributions** to the VII Nutrition Window (special purpose account with revolving funds).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNICEF’s Nutrition Section (HQ) oversees global coordination, with Regional Nutrition Advisors supporting country adaptation. The Child Nutrition Fund is managed by UNICEF Supply Division, while research components involve joint UN agency collaboration. FCDO provides strategic oversight through quarterly reviews.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNICEF’s unique role as the largest global RUTF procurer (80% market share) and its existing infrastructure for pre-positioning/stockpiles justified direct award. The extension builds on prior FCDO-UNICEF frameworks, with no evidence of competitive processes.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNICEF currently procures 80% of the RUTF distributed globally – including more than 90% of the supply financed by FCDO... At this stage no other actor has a proven and viable proposition that would compete with the role UNICEF plays." (58006857.odt, UNICEF-led approach to smooth procurement of RUTF) AND "Disbursement of the upper limit of PARSNIP funding will be based on evidence that UNICEF is driving forward progress on child wasting in a way that is transparent, collaborative, prioritises government leadership, maximises value for money and is supportive of innovation." (55541884.odt, INFORMATION)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: 1) **FCDO Nutrition Policy Team** (A1 Senior Nutrition Adviser as SRO) with cross-FCDO advisory group; 2) **UNICEF Nutrition Section** (HQ) with Emergency Nutrition Unit for implementation; 3) **Joint UN agency coordination** for prevention research (UNICEF/WFP/WHO). Child Nutrition Fund governance includes pre-agreed disbursement principles verified by UNICEF Country Offices.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO will monitor UNICEF’s performance through: Holding quarterly joint meetings; Reviewing progress and financial reports; Undertaking annual reviews of progress against agreed milestones, including payment-linked milestones." (58006857.odt, Monitoring, reporting and accounting for funds) AND "A virtual cross-FCDO advisory group will be established to provide strategic oversight and to ensure linkages are made between this programme and other initiatives." (58006857.odt, Management arrangements for implementing the programme)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adapted across years/components but require FCDO approval. The 2023 extension includes 25% at-risk budget annually to accommodate uncertainty. Reallocation between CNF and Joint UN components is possible with justification.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities (e.g., COVID-19 modelling) were added via addendum (55541884.odt). Prevention research focus can shift based on UN agency consensus. CNF disbursements adjust to country demand, but core guidelines require FCDO sign-off for major changes.
how_flexibility.quote: "In order to adapt to budget uncertainty there will be 25% at-risk built into the budget every year." (D0004554.odt, INFORMATION) AND "The suggested funding allocation split has significant flexibility within it to allow for changes both across components and years depending on factors such as FCDO spending review outcomes (for outer years) and partners’ ability to spend." (D0004554.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNICEF (HQ/Supply Division) → [Country Offices/academic partners]. No additional sub-grantee layers documented.
how_efficiency.quote: "Funding for this component will be linked to key performance indicators enabling increased financing to be allocated if UNICEF meets expected targets." (58006857.odt, Monitoring, reporting and accounting for funds) AND "The VII Nutrition Window would sit within the existing VII trust fund which would avoid costs associated with establishing an entirely new mechanism." (58006857.odt, VfM assessment)

q24_alternatives_considered: A2: Investing in research (£20m for evidence generation only)
A3: Focus on bilateral programmes and multilateral engagement (business-as-usual)
Alternative RUTF procurement mechanisms (e.g., non-UNICEF managers)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: UNICEF’s unmatched global RUTF procurement infrastructure (80% market share), existing VII trust fund mechanisms, and proven ability to leverage domestic co-financing (e.g., Match Fund’s 1:1 model) justified the multilateral approach. The mixed model (financing + research + implementation) was selected to address both immediate treatment gaps and long-term prevention evidence needs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of effective UNICEF coordination with broader nutrition community (moderate risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly joint meetings and cross-FCDO advisory group to monitor collaboration. Performance-linked financing tied to transparency and inclusivity metrics.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UNICEF perceived as controlling RUTF market non-transparently (moderate risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Independent oversight of VII Nutrition Window by UNICEF Comptroller. Public release of modelling outputs and peer-reviewed publications.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government defaults on CNF repayment obligations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Legally binding MOUs with Ministries of Finance. Suspension from fund access for non-repayment, with debit to VII’s guarantee fund as last resort.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High travel costs in fragile contexts eroding budget
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage UNICEF’s existing security/logistics capacity. Pre-agreed travel policies with central oversight.

why_rationale.quote: "UNICEF has already attracted additional donor support for its implementation plan to improve approaches for child wasting and will continue to advocate for more support... This should help to further strengthen the value for money of the investment through this programme." (58006857.odt, Overview of costs) AND "The VII Nutrition Window, the pre-positioned supplies and the Nutrition Match Fund are projected to triple the spending power of FCDO’s support, stretching the £10 million allocated into £32.6 million worth of RUTF procurement over five years." (58006857.odt, B. Improving financing for treatment of child wasting)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan, Yemen) limit partner options to organizations with existing security/logistics infrastructure (e.g., UNICEF). Local academic partners in sub-Saharan Africa were selected for operational research due to proximity to COVID-19/malnutrition cases, but Northern institutions (Johns Hopkins, Imperial College) lead modelling due to technical capacity gaps in LMICs.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in FCAS countries restrict field research to partners with UNICEF’s logistics support
Weak government capacity in GAP countries necessitates UNICEF-led financing mechanisms (e.g., CNF) to bypass bureaucratic delays
Climate shocks require partners with global supply chain expertise (e.g., UNICEF’s pre-positioning hubs)
Data limitations in fragile states limit evidence generation to partners with existing country presence
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **both** immediate treatment scale-up (via UNICEF’s RUTF procurement) **and** long-term prevention evidence (via UN collaboration) drove the mixed multilateral structure. Financing mechanisms (CNF) were designed to incentivize domestic ownership, while research components require academic partnerships for credibility.
q28_linkages: Global guidelines development (WHO) → requires UNICEF-WHO collaboration structure
Domestic financing gaps (GAP countries) → necessitates CNF’s 1:1 match model
COVID-19 urgency (55541884.odt) → justified direct awards to UNICEF for rapid modelling
Climate resilience focus → requires UNICEF’s shock-responsive service models
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: 1) **Efficiency**: UNICEF’s centralized procurement achieves economies of scale (£1 → £3.26 leverage), but risks crowding out local suppliers; 2) **Equity**: CNF’s 1:1 match incentivizes domestic ownership, but requires governments to front-load financing, excluding poorer states. Northern-led modelling (Johns Hopkins) ensures rigour but limits LMIC research leadership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (direct UNICEF awards) vs. inclusion (limited local competitor involvement in procurement)
Northern expertise (modelling by Imperial College) vs. Southern ownership (LMIC academics relegated to data collection)
Cost efficiency (UNICEF’s 80% RUTF market share) vs. market diversity (risk of monopolistic practices)
Flexibility (25% at-risk budget) vs. predictability (challenges for government planning)
intersections.risk_affects_management: High FCAS risk profile (e.g., Yemen, South Sudan) justified intensive oversight (quarterly reviews, embedded FCDO advisors). Fragile contexts require adaptive management (e.g., 25% at-risk budget) but complicate milestone tracking.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: UNICEF’s existing Supply Division capacity enabled its role as CNF fund manager, while weak government capacity in GAP countries limited their role to co-financing (via Match Fund) rather than direct implementation.
intersections.quote: "The nature of this programme will mean that global/regional staff posts will be more likely to need to travel to contexts where security considerations and poor infrastructure result in higher travel costs." (58006857.odt, Overview of costs) AND "UNICEF’s work through this Option will be underpinned by a strong emphasis on learning to improve evidence and understanding of the drivers of wasting and the strategies that can be deployed to prevent and treat child wasting as cost-effectively as possible." (58006857.odt, Investment in learning and evidence)

key_programme_risks: Lack of effective linkages with UHC agenda (moderate risk)
Government disinterest in adopting new wasting approaches (minor risk)
Failure of aligned programmes to reduce wasting (moderate risk)
Poor UNICEF coordination with broader nutrition community (moderate risk)
UNICEF perceived as controlling RUTF market non-transparently (moderate risk)
Generation of clear evidence base limited by poor-quality evaluations (moderate-to-major risk)
High travel costs in fragile contexts eroding budget (moderate risk)
Currency fluctuations increasing RUTF input costs (milk powder prices)
Government defaults on CNF repayment obligations
Climate shocks overwhelming shock-responsive service capacity

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of government leadership for nutrition
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: CNF’s legally binding MOUs with Ministries of Finance and performance-based financing. Technical support to integrate wasting into GFF investment cases.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNICEF’s RUTF market dominance perceived as non-transparent
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Independent Comptroller oversight of VII Nutrition Window. Public release of procurement data and modelling outputs.
Joint UN strategy development with shared indicators. Quarterly cross-agency reviews led by FCDO.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High travel costs in FCAS countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Leverage UNICEF’s existing security/logistics infrastructure. Pre-agreed travel policies with central monitoring.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Currency/exchange rate volatility increasing RUTF costs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: VII Nutrition Window’s revolving fund buffers price shocks. Contracting models to hedge raw material costs.

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-positioned RUTF stockpiles achieve 160% savings-to-investment ratio in crisis response (vs. air freight)
Performance-based financing works better than humanitarian grants in fragile states (e.g., Match Fund’s A+ rating)
UNICEF’s existing country offices are critical for rapid scale-up in insecure contexts (e.g., Somalia, Yemen)
Domestic co-financing (e.g., Pakistan, Afghanistan) is possible even in FCAS with incentivized models
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Match Fund’s success (500,000 RUTF cartons procured vs. 73,000 target) demonstrated that: 1) Domestic governments will co-finance when incentives are clear; 2) Revolving funds (VII Window) triple spending power; 3) Pre-positioning saves costs and lives in crises. The COVID-19 addendum (55541884.odt) showed that rapid modelling partnerships (Johns Hopkins) could inform real-time programme adaptations.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Expanded CNF from Match Fund based on demand; 2) Added 25% at-risk budget to handle FCAS volatility; 3) Shifted from humanitarian-focused RUTF procurement to health-system integration; 4) Prioritized joint UN agency collaboration for prevention evidence.
risks_lessons.quote: "The success of the match fund has highlighted a clear demand from domestic governments for support to invest on child wasting and has prompted the expansion of the fund to include other new and innovative financing mechanisms... The UK is currently the only bilateral donor to the CNF and have been instrumental in the design of the new fund including its governance structure." (D0004554.odt, Objective 1) AND "Pre-positioned RUTF will bring concrete savings, but it will have limited impact on ensuring more governments pay for RUTF themselves... UNICEF plans to establish a Nutrition Match Fund to complement the VII Nutrition Window with the objective of incentivising domestic resource allocation." (58006857.odt, B. Improving financing for treatment of child wasting)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £10m VII Nutrition Window + Match Fund is projected to mobilize £32.6m in RUTF procurement over 5 years (3.26x leverage). CNF’s £16m UK contribution will be matched 1:1 by domestic governments, doubling reach to ~264,000 beneficiaries.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: 100% revenue (no capital expenditure). All spend counts against Resource Departmental Expenditure Limit (RDEL).
financial_details.quote: "The VII Nutrition Window, the pre-positioned supplies and the Nutrition Match Fund are projected to triple the spending power of FCDO’s support, stretching the £10 million allocated into £32.6 million worth of RUTF procurement over five years." (58006857.odt, B. Improving financing for treatment of child wasting) AND "The £16m contribution to CNF is expected to reach at least 132,000... This will in turn be matched by an equal contribution from domestic government budgets for a doubling of these results." (D0004554.odt, What are the expected results?)

metadata.programme_name: Global Risk Financing Facility (GRiF)
metadata.quote: The Global Risk Financing Facility (GRiF) helps to save lives and build resilience to shocks (such as droughts, hurricanes and floods, as well as Covid-19) by enabling quicker, more effective and predictable responses. (62108744.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: August 2019–December 2027" (S30075130.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GRiF is primarily a financing mechanism that channels funds to support disaster risk financing (DRF) instruments like insurance and contingent credit. It also includes capacity building through technical assistance and knowledge-sharing to promote best practices. The programme aims to enable earlier and more effective disaster response and recovery, thereby saving lives and reducing the impact of shocks like droughts, hurricanes, and floods.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Global Risk Financing Facility (GRiF) helps to save lives and build resilience to shocks (such as droughts, hurricanes and floods, as well as Covid-19) by enabling quicker, more effective and predictable responses. It does this by providing grant finance through the World Bank and the African Development Bank (AfDB) to support governments to develop and use disaster risk financing (DRF) instruments, such as insurance, that will payout rapidly after disasters." (62108744.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: £967m of risk finance cover for 133m people (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
1.2m people received cash transfers in 2020 as part of GRiF-funded social protection programmes (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
£4.5m through ADRiFi will support 5 African countries to access drought and tropical cyclone insurance in 2021, covering approximately 1,935,000 people (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
Support for public asset protection and advice on continuity planning for critical services after disasters (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)
New and improved options for crisis risk financing instruments and greater knowledge, evidence and learning on best practice (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
Greater use of risk financing approaches within the multilateral system (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
An additional up to £39m in total risk finance (the cumulative value of the insurance policies that can be supported), protecting 4.8m people (S30075130.odt, New results)
what_objectives.summary: GRiF is a financing mechanism that provides grants to support disaster risk financing instruments, enabling quicker and more effective responses to shocks. It combines premium subsidies, technical assistance, and capacity building to help countries access insurance and other financial tools for disaster preparedness and recovery.
what_objectives.quote: "The Global Risk Financing Facility (GRiF) helps to save lives and build resilience to shocks (such as droughts, hurricanes and floods, as well as Covid-19) by enabling quicker, more effective and predictable responses." (62108744.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme focuses on innovative projects and 'learning by doing,' which introduces a high level of inherent risk. However, most activities are delivered within risk appetite, and fiduciary, operational, safeguarding, and reputational risks are moderate or minor due to robust project management and safeguard frameworks in the World Bank and AfDB.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk rating for the GRIF programme is major. It focuses on innovative projects and ‘learning by doing’ so there is a high level of inherent risk within the programme, although most GRiF activities are being delivered comfortably within risk appetite." (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The economic impact of Covid-19 has significantly affected government budgets globally, making it harder for countries to afford insurance premiums. In fragile and conflict-affected states, governments may be unable or unwilling to manage disaster responses, requiring support through humanitarian agencies.
where_context.quote: "The economic impact of Covid-19 and the global economic downturn precipitated by the pandemic has significantly impacted on Government budgets globally, so whilst countries might be willing to pay the full costs of insurance, they might be unable to do so." (62108744.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case including the theory of change or new evidence from ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: GRiF uses a multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) administered by the World Bank and AfDB, which provides grants to co-finance risk finance components alongside larger programmes. It also includes accountable grant agreements with civil society organizations like Start Network.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through trust fund administrative agreements with the World Bank and AfDB, and an accountable grant agreement with Start Network. The FCDO’s Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) oversees high-level governance through the GRIF Steering Committee.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank and AfDB were selected due to their existing systems and capabilities to achieve GRiF’s objectives. The selection was based on their ability to manage multi-donor trust funds and deliver disaster risk financing instruments effectively.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme is implemented through the World Bank as this is currently it is the only multilateral with the systems and capabilities in place to achieving the GRIF’s project and wider objectives." (60478697.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GRIF Steering Committee includes the FCDO’s Senior Responsible Owner (Rachel Turner, IFD Director) for high-level oversight. The Centre for Disaster Protection offers independent quality assurance and advice.
how_governance.quote: "Rachel Turner, IFD Director, sits on the GRIF Steering Committee for high level oversight. The Centre for Disaster Protection also offers independent quality assurance and advice." (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated based on need and strategic fit, as decided by the programme’s Senior Responsible Owner (SRO).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities based on emerging needs, such as the shift towards premium subsidies and public asset protection in response to country demands.
how_flexibility.quote: "GRIF allocations are (and will continue to be) made on the basis of need and strategic fit. This ensures that support reaches the most vulnerable in a range of countries, for work in a range of sectors in order to be able to deliver development impact and demonstration effects, as well as learn." (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank/AfDB → implementing partners (e.g., Start Network, UN agencies)
how_efficiency.quote: "The GRIF programme would continue to be delivered as it is now, supporting work through the World Bank (trust fund administrative agreement), AfDB (trust fund administrative agreement) and civil society (Start Network accountable grant agreement)." (S30075130.odt, Implementation)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank and AfDB were chosen due to their existing systems, capabilities, and experience in managing multi-donor trust funds and delivering disaster risk financing instruments. The programme leverages their global reach and technical expertise to achieve GRiF’s objectives effectively.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependency on subsidies that cannot be sustained long-term
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will work closely with private sector and other partners to develop self-sustaining initiatives, making it clear that there is no ongoing obligation on UK support.

why_rationale.quote: "The programme is implemented through the World Bank as this is currently it is the only multilateral with the systems and capabilities in place to achieving the GRIF’s project and wider objectives." (60478697.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on climate-vulnerable countries require partners with the capacity to operate in diverse and often high-risk environments. This limits partner selection to multilateral institutions like the World Bank and AfDB, which have the necessary systems and safeguards in place.
q27_constraints_detail: need for multilateral partners with global reach
requirement for robust safeguards in high-risk environments
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to provide rapid, scalable disaster risk financing determines the use of multilateral trust funds and partnerships with institutions that can manage large-scale financial instruments and technical assistance.
q28_linkages: financing mechanism requires multilateral trust funds for scalability
technical assistance embedded within larger World Bank/AfDB programmes for efficiency
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme balances the need for rapid, efficient delivery through multilateral partners with efforts to ensure equity, such as targeting women and girls in contingency plans and supporting locally-led actions through Start Network.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion (rapid payouts through multilateral vs. local ownership)
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership (World Bank/AfDB leadership vs. country-led risk management)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The major risk profile leads to intensive oversight through annual reviews and a steering committee with FCDO representation to ensure accountability and risk management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded within the programme to strengthen local systems for disaster response and recovery, ensuring that Southern partners can eventually take on more responsibility for risk management.
intersections.quote: "The programme is implemented through the World Bank as this is currently it is the only multilateral with the systems and capabilities in place to achieving the GRIF’s project and wider objectives." (60478697.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Dependency on subsidies that cannot be sustained long-term (S30075130.odt, Risk)

Economic downturn making it harder for countries to afford insurance premiums (62108744.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case including the theory of change or new evidence from ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work?)
Delivery and influence risk due to UK budget pressure (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)
Sustainability/exit risk as countries may struggle to take on DRF costs post-GRiF (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work closely with private sector and other partners to develop self-sustaining initiatives, making it clear that there is no ongoing obligation on UK support.
Provide longer periods of support for countries unable to afford premiums, with IMF and World Bank helping to identify criteria for such countries.
Robust project management and safeguard frameworks in the World Bank and AfDB to manage fiduciary, operational, and reputational risks.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), governments may be unable or unwilling to manage disaster responses, requiring support through humanitarian agencies like the UN and NGOs. (62108744.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The original Business Case correctly identified market failures that have hampered uptake of DRF by climate-vulnerable countries. The rationale for addressing demand failures through subsidised technical assistance and premium finance has been validated by ongoing monitoring and evaluation. (62108744.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case including the theory of change or new evidence from ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work?)
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme has shifted focus towards premium subsidies to enable countries to access insurance through regional risk pools, responding to clear demands from vulnerable countries. It has also expanded support to include public asset protection and continuity planning for critical services. (62108744.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)
risks_lessons.quote: "The original Business Case correctly identified the market failures that have hampered uptake of DRF by climate vulnerable countries, and the rationale for addressing those demand failures through subsidised technical assistance (for project development) and premium finance (to help bring down costs in the early years of new programmes)." (62108744.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case including the theory of change or new evidence from ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £65.5m of UK aid matched by a similar amount of German funding has leveraged larger programme resources of $775m ($400m in low-income countries). (62108744.odt, What are the expected results?)
financial_details.quote:
"The UK will provide an additional up to £60m for the GRIF programme, bringing the total budget up to £150m." (62108744.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)
"The proposed £15m extension will enable FCDO to maintain momentum towards greater use of PAF... The changes proposed here will enable spend to be made against the programme’s confirmed resource budget of £12m for FY25/26." (S30075130.odt, Changes proposed)

metadata.programme_name: Securing global wheat crops for food and nutritional security – in partnership with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)

quote.programme_name: "Title: Securing global wheat crops for food and nutritional security – in partnership with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)" (Document: 51484648.odt, Title section)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: Up to £16 million" (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme Value section)
quote.duration: "Start Date: September 2019; End Date: 1 October 2025" (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme Code section)
quote.sector: "This programme will contribute directly to achievement of the UK Aid Strategy: ... Promoting global prosperity: By increasing wheat yields and productivity, this programme will contribute to improved incomes for smallholder farmers who rely on wheat production for their livelihoods." (Document: 51484648.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending section)

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: September 2019; End Date: 1 October 2025"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (new wheat varieties), evidence generation (research on climate resilience and disease resistance), and capacity building (strengthening surveillance networks and national research systems). It aims to address both food security and nutritional deficiencies through biofortification.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will deliver on three interlinked objectives: Enable increased wheat production, by developing higher-yielding wheat varieties which are more resilient to climate change and disease; Enable more effective response to wheat disease outbreaks by strengthening a global surveillance network to track emerging diseases; Spearhead a new initiative to enhance the zinc content (and by extension, iron) of all new wheat varieties." (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 60-80 new wheat varieties with improved traits (disease resistance, climate resilience, higher yields)
20 zinc-enriched wheat varieties released
q3_expected_outputs.target: by 2025 across Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, India, and Ethiopia

q3_expected_outputs.output: Precision Phenotyping Platforms established
q3_expected_outputs.target: in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Bangladesh

q3_expected_outputs.output: Enterprise Breeding System operational
q3_expected_outputs.target: shared database for CGIAR-CIMMYT and national partners

q3_expected_outputs.output: Global wheat disease surveillance system strengthened
q3_expected_outputs.target: real-time monitoring of wheat rust and other diseases

q3_expected_outputs.output: Zinc content in wheat increased to provide up to 50% of daily zinc requirement
q3_expected_outputs.target: for consumers in South Asia and East Africa

q3_expected_outputs.output: Genetic gain rate for wheat yield accelerated
q3_expected_outputs.target: from 0.7% to 1.5% annually

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform global wheat production by developing climate-resilient, disease-resistant, and nutrient-rich wheat varieties while strengthening surveillance systems and research capacity in developing countries.
what_objectives.quote: "This programme will deliver on three interlinked objectives: Enable increased wheat production...; Enable more effective response to wheat disease outbreaks...; Spearhead a new initiative to enhance the zinc content..." (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme summary section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with climate vulnerability and weak agricultural systems but is not classified as high-risk or FCAS. The document explicitly states: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor." (Document: 51484648.odt, Overall programme risk rating section)
q6_contextual_constraints: market limitations (small-scale stone mills for flour in Pakistan)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate change reduces wheat yields and exacerbates disease outbreaks, while weak national research systems limit capacity to respond. Small-scale milling infrastructure in countries like Pakistan constrains fortification strategies, necessitating biofortification as a more feasible approach.

quote.climate: "Climate change... has already reduced global wheat production by approximately 5% relative to a counterfactual scenario with no climate change... increased climate variability, temperature and rainfall changes are likely to place increasing stress on all crop and farming systems, including wheat." (Document: 51484648.odt, Problem statement section)
quote.institutions: "Significant capacity has been built within the national agricultural research systems in key wheat-growing countries... However, wheat diseases are a constant threat to wheat production: they are notoriously difficult to control, as they are constantly evolving and they spread very easily." (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme summary section)
quote.market: "In countries where large mills dominate the flour market, fortification strategies can be successful. However, in countries like Pakistan – where the majority of wheat flour is produced in small-scale stone mills – it is not feasible for fortification to reach widespread coverage." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 3 section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: CGIAR-CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF), a Northern institution, manages the programme directly, with CGIAR-CIMMYT (multilateral) as the primary implementer. National agricultural research systems in Southern countries participate as sub-partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for national agricultural research systems (e.g., rust race analysis in Ethiopia and Kenya)
technology transfer (e.g., Precision Phenotyping Platforms)
institutional strengthening (e.g., Enterprise Breeding System for national partners)
skills development (e.g., disease surveillance and breeding techniques)

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: lead funder and programme manager

partner_organizations.name: CGIAR-CIMMYT
partner_organizations.role: primary implementing partner (wheat research and breeding)

partner_organizations.name: National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS) in Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, India, Ethiopia, Kenya
partner_organizations.role: local implementation, variety testing, and surveillance

partner_organizations.name: John Innes Centre (UK)
partner_organizations.role: collaborator on rust surveillance technology

quote.structure: "This programme will accelerate the rate of wheat breeding within the CGIAR and national agricultural institutes in Africa and South Asia... BMGF will directly manage the co-funded initiative, and DFID will second a staff member to BMGF for 80% of their time." (Document: 51484648.odt, How this programme will operate section)
quote.capacity: "Significant capacity has been built within the national agricultural research systems in key wheat-growing countries. For example, through skills and technology transfer, research laboratories in Ethiopia and Kenya are better equipped to identify wheat diseases as they emerge, and to breed wheat varieties resistant to disease strains and tolerant of local climatic conditions." (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme summary section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme operates under the DFID-BMGF Research Collaboration Framework (2016–2026), with co-funding from both donors. BMGF manages the funds directly, and DFID seconds a staff member to oversee the partnership.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: BMGF manages the programme directly, with CGIAR-CIMMYT as the primary implementer. National research systems and the John Innes Centre are sub-partners. DFID provides strategic oversight through a seconded staff member.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: CGIAR-CIMMYT is the global leader in wheat research, with a proven track record in delivering high-impact varieties. The DFID-BMGF Collaboration Framework formalizes this long-standing partnership.

quote.instrument: "This programme falls under the operating procedures for co-funding linked to the DFID-BMGF Research Collaboration Framework, which was signed by DFID’s Permanent Secretary and BMGF’s CEO in 2016 and which formalised the two donors’ shared intention to continue to collaborate closely in agricultural research." (Document: 51484648.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF section)
quote.selection: "To achieve this programme’s intended scale of impact in wheat research, there is no alternative to investment in the CGIAR-CIMMYT, as the most important wheat breeding entity globally." (Document: 51484648.odt, Option 1 analysis section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The DFID-BMGF Collaboration Framework governs the partnership, with BMGF managing day-to-day operations. A DFID-secondee provides oversight, and annual reviews are conducted.

quote.management: "BMGF will manage the programme on behalf of both donors... DFID will work with BMGF to provide strategic oversight. As part of RED’s broader agricultural partnership with BMGF, one DFID staff member will be seconded to BMGF for at least 80% of their time." (Document: 51484648.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF section)
quote.oversight: "This programme’s impact on gender equality will be monitored during the Annual Review process." (Document: 51484648.odt, Compliance with the International Development (Gender Equality) Act 2014 section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can likely be reallocated between components (e.g., disease surveillance vs. breeding) with BMGF approval, but the document does not specify explicit flexibility mechanisms.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to respond to emerging diseases and climate changes, but adjustments would require agreement between DFID and BMGF.

quote.flexibility: No explicit statement on fund reallocation, but the programme’s focus on "emerging diseases" and "climate variability" implies adaptive capacity. "This programme will accelerate the rate of wheat breeding within the CGIAR and national agricultural institutes in Africa and South Asia, allowing wheat breeding to keep pace with emerging diseases and climate change." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 1 section)
quote.adaptive: "Wheat pathogens continue to evolve rapidly, and new virulent races are moving between regions with increasing frequency. Given this proliferation of emerging threats, sustained global surveillance and monitoring efforts that are linked to wheat breeding for disease resistance and disease management efforts are increasingly important." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 2 section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BMGF (manager) → CGIAR-CIMMYT (implementer) → National Agricultural Research Systems (sub-partners)

quote.management_costs: "BMGF will not charge DFID any overhead or management fee for their work in directly managing the programme." (Document: 51484648.odt, Option 1 analysis section)
quote.layers: "BMGF will manage the programme on behalf of both donors... CGIAR-CIMMYT will deliver the outputs, with support from national agricultural research systems in target countries." (Document: 51484648.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF section)
quote.payment: No explicit payment structure described, but milestone-based delivery is implied by output targets (e.g., "By 2025, this programme will: Develop and release 60-80 wheat varieties...").

q24_alternatives_considered: Co-investment with BMGF in CGIAR-CIMMYT (chosen option)
Direct investment by DFID in CGIAR-CIMMYT (without BMGF co-funding)
Alternative programming by DFID (not investing in CGIAR-CIMMYT), procuring a Research Fund Manager
Discontinue stand-alone investment in wheat research
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The co-investment with BMGF in CGIAR-CIMMYT was selected for its unparalleled global reach, proven impact (benefit-cost ratio of 73:1–103:1), and ability to leverage BMGF’s technical expertise and DFID’s geographical focus on South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. The partnership maximizes synergies, reduces transaction costs, and aligns with DFID’s strategic priorities.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (BMGF’s management reduces DFID’s operational burden)
partner capacity (CGIAR-CIMMYT’s global leadership in wheat research)
speed (accelerated breeding to meet climate/disease challenges)
equity (targeting smallholder farmers in low-income countries)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on CGIAR-CIMMYT as a single implementer
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified partnerships with national research systems and the John Innes Centre to spread risk and build local capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: BMGF’s management priorities may not fully align with DFID’s development goals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID secondee embedded in BMGF to ensure strategic oversight and alignment with UK Aid Strategy.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (no management fees charged by BMGF)
effectiveness (proven CGIAR impact with benefit-cost ratios of 73:1–103:1)
equity (focus on smallholder farmers and low-income consumers)

quote.alternatives: "Four options were considered when determining the best way to deliver the objectives... Option 1: Co-investment with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in the CGIAR-CIMMYT to deliver the programme’s objectives (chosen)." (Document: 51484648.odt, What are the feasible options section)
quote.rationale: "By investing in this ambitious programme of research at CGIAR-CIMMYT, DFID will accelerate the pace of global wheat improvement and spearhead an initiative to improve the nutritional content of all wheat germplasm used by CGIAR and by wheat breeding programmes around the world... BMGF will not charge DFID any overhead or management fee for their work in directly managing the programme." (Document: 51484648.odt, Option 1 analysis section)
quote.vfm: "The DFID Best Buys assessment... identified the development of improved crop varieties as a ‘Mega Buy’, representing the best value for money for DFID in terms of benefit:cost ratios and long-term impact." (Document: 51484648.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope (Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia) and the need for localized disease surveillance and breeding necessitate partnerships with national agricultural research systems (NARS) in target countries. CGIAR-CIMMYT’s global reach is essential to coordinate across regions, while BMGF’s management ensures alignment with donor priorities.
q27_constraints_detail: Climate variability requires localized breeding (e.g., heat-tolerant varieties for South Asia vs. drought-resistant for Ethiopia)
Disease surveillance networks must include national labs (e.g., Ambo in Ethiopia, Njoro in Kenya) to enable real-time responses
Smallholder farmer preferences (e.g., zinc content in wheat) shape variety development, requiring NARS engagement
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—rapid wheat breeding, disease surveillance, and biofortification—require a centralized but adaptive structure. CGIAR-CIMMYT’s global breeding pipeline is paired with national research systems for localization, while BMGF’s management ensures efficiency and donor alignment.
q28_linkages: Global breeding (CGIAR-CIMMYT) + local adaptation (NARS) = accelerated variety release
Surveillance data (national labs) + CGIAR analytics = real-time disease response
BMGF management + DFID oversight = balanced donor control
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging CGIAR’s global pipeline and BMGF’s management) with equity (targeting smallholder farmers and low-income consumers). For example, biofortification is prioritized over commercial fortification in Pakistan due to the dominance of small-scale mills, despite higher costs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid breeding (efficiency) is paired with national research system engagement (inclusion) to ensure varieties meet local needs.
CGIAR-CIMMYT (Northern-led) leads breeding, but NARS (Southern) are embedded in surveillance and testing to build ownership.
Biofortification (higher upfront R&D cost) is chosen over fortification (lower cost but limited rural coverage) to reach smallholders.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s moderate risk profile (e.g., climate threats, disease evolution) justifies intensive oversight through BMGF’s management and DFID’s embedded advisor, ensuring adaptive responses without excessive bureaucracy.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building for NARS (e.g., rust race analysis labs in Ethiopia/Kenya) enables them to take on surveillance and testing roles, reducing reliance on CGIAR-CIMMYT over time.

quote.where_who: "This programme will accelerate the rate of wheat breeding within the CGIAR and national agricultural institutes in Africa and South Asia... Establish Precision Phenotyping Platforms with high throughput capacity in the national agricultural research systems of Kenya (for wheat stem rust), Ethiopia (for wheat stem rust) and Bangladesh (for wheat blast disease)." (Document: 51484648.odt, Outputs section)
quote.what_how: "To protect and enhance the world’s wheat production, there is a need for much more rapid development (breeding) of wheat varieties which are higher-yielding, resistant to emerging diseases, and able to tolerate increasing climate variability... This programme responds to that need: it will accelerate the rate of wheat breeding within the CGIAR and national agricultural institutes." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 1 section)
quote.equity_efficiency: "Biofortification is a particularly effective nutritional intervention in rural areas where dietary diversity is limited and where it is challenging to reach adequate coverage through supplementation programmes or commercial fortification strategies... In countries where large mills dominate the flour market, fortification strategies can be successful. However, in countries like Pakistan – where the majority of wheat flour is produced in small-scale stone mills – it is not feasible for fortification to reach widespread coverage." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 3 section)

key_programme_risks: Evolving wheat diseases (e.g., new rust strains) outpacing breeding efforts
Climate change reducing wheat yields faster than varieties can adapt
Weak national research systems limiting surveillance and adoption
Smallholder farmer risk aversion slowing uptake of new varieties
Market failures (e.g., lack of incentives for biofortified wheat in commercial chains)
Political instability in target countries disrupting implementation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strengthened global surveillance network with real-time data sharing and rapid breeding response mechanisms (e.g., Enterprise Breeding System).
Accelerated breeding for climate resilience (target: 1.5% annual yield gain) and Precision Phenotyping Platforms to test varieties under stress conditions.
Capacity building for NARS (e.g., rust labs in Ethiopia/Kenya) and embedded training in surveillance and breeding.
Ensuring biofortified varieties match or exceed yields of traditional varieties and integrating farmer preferences in breeding (e.g., gender-sensitive variety selection).
Mainstreaming zinc biofortification in all CGIAR wheat germplasm to ensure long-term adoption, regardless of commercial incentives.

fcas_specific_lessons: Early detection systems (e.g., wheat rust surveillance in Ethiopia) are critical in fragile contexts where crop failures can trigger food crises.
Local institutional capacity (e.g., national rust labs) reduces dependency on external actors in conflict-prone regions.
Biofortification is more resilient than fortification in FCAS contexts where supply chains are unreliable.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID-BMGF co-funding (2011–2016) demonstrated that: (1) CGIAR-CIMMYT’s breeding pipeline delivers high returns (73:1–103:1 benefit-cost ratio); (2) global surveillance networks (e.g., rust tracking) enable preemptive action; and (3) biofortification is cost-effective in rural areas (e.g., zinc wheat in Mexico/India).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: This programme builds on prior lessons by: (1) expanding surveillance to include fusarium head blight and Septoria; (2) integrating gender-sensitive breeding (e.g., NextGen Cassava model); and (3) mainstreaming zinc biofortification in all CGIAR wheat germplasm (not just targeted varieties).

quote.risks: "Wheat diseases are a constant threat to wheat production: they are notoriously difficult to control, as they are constantly evolving and they spread very easily... Climate change... has already reduced global wheat production by approximately 5% relative to a counterfactual scenario with no climate change." (Document: 51484648.odt, Problem statement section)
quote.mitigations: "This programme will: Establish Precision Phenotyping Platforms...; Strengthen the global wheat disease surveillance system...; Develop and release 20 zinc-enriched wheat varieties..." (Document: 51484648.odt, Outputs section)
quote.lessons: "With previous DFID and BMGF co-funding: 169 disease-resistant wheat varieties have been developed and adopted in 11 ‘at-risk’ wheat-growing countries... A global surveillance network has been created, enabling near real-time monitoring of significant diseases of wheat." (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme summary section)
quote.design_changes: "This programme will build on DFID’s previous investments in biofortification, to ‘mainstream’ zinc biofortification in wheat breeding at the CGIAR... Drawing on lessons from the approach adopted by NextGen Cassava, CGIAR-CIMMYT will use improved breeding decision-making tools to ensure that all wheat varieties developed through this programme will meet the needs and preferences of both women and men." (Document: 51484648.odt, Objective 3 and Compliance with Gender Equality Act sections)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: BMGF’s co-funding leverages DFID’s £16 million, with historical BMGF contributions at ~3:1 ratio (e.g., £34 million DFID leveraged ~£102 million BMGF in 2011–2016 phase).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: Up to £16 million" (Document: 51484648.odt, Programme Value section)
quote.leverage: "A co-funding partnership was established, spanning the period 2011-2016, with DFID funding of £34 million leveraging BMGF funding of approximately three times this value." (Document: 51484648.odt, Background to existing partnership with BMGF section)
quote.overhead: "BMGF will not charge DFID any overhead or management fee for their work in directly managing the programme." (Document: 51484648.odt, Option 1 analysis section)

metadata.programme_name: Reversing Environmental Degradation in Africa and Asia (REDAA)
metadata.duration_text: five years (with an initial £10m, two-year break clause)

quote.name: 60046808.odt, Programme summary section
quote.text: "This programme focuses on addressing the challenge of environmental degradation in Africa and Asia..."

metadata.duration_source: "Programme activities will involve developing new nature-based solutions (NBS) and using emerging technologies to enhance the conservation and restoration of natural landscapes and ecosystems, protect wildlife and improve the lives of the poorest and most vulnerable communities." (60046808.odt, Programme summary section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The REDAA programme combines evidence generation (research on ecosystem functions), technology development (nature-based solutions and tools), capacity building (training and institutional strengthening), and implementation research (testing and scaling interventions). It aims to reverse environmental degradation in Africa and Asia by developing innovative approaches to managing natural environments, supporting livelihoods, and protecting wildlife.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme focuses on addressing the challenge of environmental degradation in Africa and Asia—seeking to improve the condition of natural landscapes in ways that enable people and nature to thrive together. REDAA will expand the technical knowledge and evidence base for environmental restoration and sustainable natural resources management in Africa and Asia; and develop innovative solutions that address serious environmental challenges and support the design and implementation of sustainable livelihoods strategies for local communities." (60046808.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: New scientific evidence and results on ecosystem functions
Innovative technical solutions and landscape management regimes
Tools and applications for environmental management strategies
Real-time, actionable information for interventions
Effective governance systems and financing mechanisms

what_objectives.summary: REDAA aims to reverse environmental degradation in Africa and Asia through research, innovation, and capacity building, focusing on ecosystem restoration, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable livelihoods.

quote.name: 60046808.odt, What are the intended Impact, Outcomes & Outputs?
quote.text: "The expected Impact from this programme is that: ‘Improved management of ecosystems and natural resources in target countries leads to a reduction in biodiversity loss rates, loss of forested areas, CO2 emissions from deforestation, land use change and mismanaged agricultural land.’"

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in regions with significant environmental degradation, climate vulnerability, and potential conflict risks, but is not classified as high-risk or FCAS.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (60046808.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks in fragile areas may affect researcher safety, while climate risks exacerbate environmental degradation. Weak institutions limit local capacity, and data limitations hinder evidence-based decision-making.

quote.text: "This programme might fund research activities in fragile and conflict affected areas, therefore safeguarding risks may be present..."

how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID will oversee a Scientific Coordination Unit (SCU) and a Programme Management Agent (PMA), which will manage research consortia and sub-awards. The SCU focuses on technical quality, while the PMA handles financial and administrative tasks.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: DFID will supervise the SCU and PMA, which are directly accountable to DFID. The SCU and PMA will manage sub-awards and research activities, with DFID retaining oversight.

quote.name: 60046808.odt, Option 4: DFID launches a self-standing research and innovation programme

how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a demand-led component to respond to emerging priorities, with adjustments requiring DFID approval.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on fragile and conflict-affected areas (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa) requires careful partner selection to ensure safety and effective delivery, limiting options to organizations with experience in high-risk environments.

need for local institutional capacity

intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for innovative, context-specific solutions (e.g., nature-based approaches) requires a flexible, adaptive delivery structure with multiple partners (SCU, PMA, research consortia) to integrate scientific, technical, and local expertise.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation → requires scientific coordination (SCU) and local research partners.
Technology development → requires PMA to manage emerging tech (e.g., satellite data, AI).
Capacity building → requires embedded technical assistance and institutional strengthening.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (e.g., NERC, UKSA) with Southern ownership (e.g., local universities, government agencies) to ensure both technical rigor and context relevance, though decision-making remains Northern-led.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership (DFID retains oversight, but local partners implement).
Speed (flexible reallocation) vs. inclusion (competitive calls for sub-awards).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., fragile areas, safeguarding) necessitates milestone-based oversight and embedded safeguarding measures, increasing management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with Southern partners (e.g., government agencies, universities) receiving technical assistance to strengthen their roles in implementation and decision-making.

metadata.programme_name: Sierra Leone Secondary Education Improvement Programme (Phase 2) – SSEIP2
metadata.quote: "SSEIP2 will improve access to quality education, learning, safety and health outcomes for 1.6 million children (including 800,000 adolescent girls and children with disabilities)." (D0003774.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01/10/2022; AMP End Date: 30/10/2027" (D0003774.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SSEIP2 combines **service delivery** (direct provision of education access and quality improvements) with **capacity building** (strengthening government systems and community engagement) and **policy influence** (supporting reform of education policies). The programme focuses on implementing interventions while simultaneously building institutional capacity and shaping national education policies.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SSEIP2 will improve access to quality education, learning, safety and health outcomes for 1.6 million children... through: Support to policy and planning reform... Strengthening government systems... Engagement with communities..." (D0003774.odt, Programme summary)

Doubling of enrolment of children with disabilities in secondary school

Reduction in adolescent childbearing rates

what_objectives.summary: SSEIP2 aims to transform secondary education in Sierra Leone by combining direct service delivery (enrolment, learning outcomes, safety) with systemic reforms (policy, governance, community engagement) to ensure 1.6 million children—especially girls and children with disabilities—access quality education, while building resilient institutions capable of sustaining progress.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will contribute to education Key Performance Indicators by halving the number of adolescent out-of-school girls and improving learning conditions for 1.6 million girls and boys." (D0003774.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sierra Leone is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to its recent emergence from conflict (post-2002), extreme poverty (life expectancy of 55 years, highest maternal mortality globally), weak institutions, and vulnerability to climate shocks and disease outbreaks (Ebola, COVID-19). The country ranks 165th/174 on the UN Human Capital Index (HCI=0.35).
where_context.q5_source: "Sierra Leone has successfully emerged from conflict and is relatively stable... but remains extremely poor... the third most vulnerable country to climate change... Government institutions, systems and capacities are developing but still extremely weak." (D0003774.odt, Country and Sector Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions limit policy implementation (e.g., Radical Inclusion Policy lacks costed plans); climate risks disrupt education (flooding, school closures); data gaps hinder monitoring (e.g., no sex-disaggregated data on children with disabilities); corruption affects financial management (teacher payroll, textbook procurement); and harmful social norms (early marriage, GBV) reduce girls’ enrolment. The 2023 elections may disrupt programme delivery or instrumentalize UK support.
where_context.quote: "Government institutions, systems and capacities are developing but still extremely weak... Sierra Leone remains vulnerable to health and climate change shocks... Repressive societal norms remain prevalent regarding gender and disability." (D0003774.odt, Country and Sector Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO (UK) in partnership with Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education (MBSSE, Sierra Leone)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between FCDO and MBSSE, with technical support provided by UK-based advisors (e.g., Education Partnership Group) but policy ownership and implementation led by MBSSE. The programme emphasizes local leadership, e.g., School Quality Assurance Officers (SQAOs) are government employees, and District Inclusion Officers (DIOs) are embedded in MBSSE.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for 160 School Quality Assurance Officers (SQAOs) in monitoring and inclusive education
Mentorship for headteachers on school leadership and Radical Inclusion Policy implementation
Technical assistance for MBSSE/TSC on teacher workforce planning and policy development
Community engagement training for Boards of Governors and local leaders
Support for MBSSE to develop EMIS (Education Management Information Systems) and disability-inclusive data tools
Capacity building for social workers and health professionals on assistive devices and GBV response
