who_partners.quote: "A trusting relationship between FCDO and MBSSE... has existed for years and endured a previous change in government... This programme will build on the experiences and achievements of its predecessor [SSEIP1], which was by far the largest ongoing intervention in the secondary education subsector for the past six and a half years." (D0003774.odt, Rationale for UK investment)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a blend of **accountable grants** (e.g., to EPG for technical assistance), **contracts** (e.g., previous SSEIP1 contract with Mott MacDonald), and **direct support to government systems** (e.g., SQAOs salaries, policy development). This builds on SSEIP1’s approach, which combined "a blend of funding instruments... including accountable grants and contracts."
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as the primary funder and strategic lead, with implementation shared across MBSSE (policy/operations), EPG (technical assistance), and local partners (community engagement). The structure is **non-exclusive**, with coordination mechanisms (e.g., Operations, Policy and Planning Executive Committee) to align with other donors (World Bank, UNICEF) and government priorities.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct award to MBSSE/EPG based on existing relationships)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme builds on long-standing partnerships with MBSSE and EPG, which have "a trusting relationship" and demonstrated capacity (e.g., EPG’s role in developing the Radical Inclusion Policy). The direct award reduces transaction costs and leverages existing systems, though new partners (e.g., for community engagement) may be selected competitively.
how_mechanism.quote: "Our current education programme has contributed to a 46% increase in the number of girls and disabled children in secondary school... The UK is uniquely placed to support the reform-minded government, and leverage funding and coordination amongst like-minded donors." (D0003774.odt, Rationale for UK investment)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Operations, Policy and Planning Executive Committee**, chaired by MBSSE with FCDO participation, oversees progress. This committee reviews priorities quarterly and ensures alignment with the Education Sector Plan (ESP) 2022–25. Sub-awards (e.g., for community interventions) are allocated through joint decision-making between FCDO, MBSSE, and technical partners.
how_governance.quote: "Progress is frequently reviewed through the Operations, Policy and Planning Executive Committee, chaired by the MBSSE with FCDO... Significant effort is invested to ensure coordination with other Ministries including Health and Sanitation, Social Welfare and Gender and Child Affairs." (D0003774.odt, Pillar 1: Policy and Planning)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme preserves flexibility to scale up interventions where evidence of impact emerges, but reallocation requires approval through the Executive Committee. The budget is not fully contracted at the start, allowing adjustments based on quarterly reviews.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Priorities are reviewed quarterly to respond to emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19 catch-up programmes) or political changes (e.g., 2023 elections). The programme uses an **adaptive management** approach, with a greater focus on policy development in early years and implementation support later.
how_flexibility.quote: "The full available budget will not be contracted at the start of the project—preserving some flexibility for the scaling up of interventions and innovations for which evidence of impact increases during the life of the programme." (D0003774.odt, Pillar 2: System Strengthening)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (MBSSE/EPG) → End Beneficiaries (schools/communities). Sub-awards (e.g., to NGOs for community work) add a third layer in some cases.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will combine central and in-country managed programmes... ensuring this programme is coordinated closely with these initiatives." (D0003774.odt, Box 1: Multilateral programmes)

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" option (rejected due to risk of reversing gains for girls and children with disabilities)
Focus on early childhood education (rejected in favor of secondary education due to UK’s comparative advantage)
Pure service delivery without systemic reform (rejected as unsustainable)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (direct service delivery + capacity building + policy influence) was selected because: 1) **Past experience**: SSEIP1’s blended approach (grants/contracts) successfully increased enrolment and exam passes; 2) **Government ownership**: MBSSE’s reform appetite and existing trust with FCDO enable joint delivery; 3) **Risk mitigation**: Embedding support within government systems (e.g., SQAOs) reduces sustainability risks post-2027; 4) **Value for money**: Leveraging multilateral partnerships (World Bank, UNICEF) avoids duplication; 5) **FCAS adaptability**: Flexible technical assistance allows responses to shocks (e.g., COVID-19, elections).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political instrumentalization: UK support may be used for electioneering ahead of 2023 polls.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with MBSSE to ensure alignment with sector plans (not political cycles); flexible design to adapt to potential government changes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government absorption capacity: Weak MBSSE systems (e.g., SQAOs stretched with 70+ schools each) may limit delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted technical assistance to build MBSSE capacity (e.g., EMIS training, policy implementation guidelines); phased rollout of interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner coordination: Overlap with World Bank/GPE on EMIS or teacher training could create inefficiencies.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit division of labor (e.g., FCDO focuses on secondary education; World Bank on primary); joint planning through the Executive Committee.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability: Gains may not be maintained post-2027 due to weak domestic financing.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on institutionalizing reforms (e.g., Radical Inclusion Policy guidelines, SQAO systems) and advocating for increased education budget (from 22% to 24% of public expenditure).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding: High GBV risks in schools (e.g., transactional sex for grades) may undermine programme goals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Zero-tolerance policies; strengthened School Safety Committees; training for teachers/SQAOs on GBV case management.

why_rationale.quote: "The ‘do nothing’ option was rejected... because it will not be possible for GoSL to sustain previous gains for adolescent girls and children with disabilities in secondary schools without further support... The decision to focus our efforts at secondary level... was agreed at concept note stage, having established a comparative advantage in support to secondary education." (D0003774.odt, Feasible Intervention Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with **local trust and adaptability**. For example: 1) **Weak institutions** necessitate partners like EPG (embedded in MBSSE) to bridge capacity gaps; 2) **GBV risks** require NGOs with safeguarding expertise (e.g., Concern Worldwide); 3) **Rural access challenges** prioritize partners with community networks (e.g., local NGOs for home visits). Multilateral partners (World Bank, UNICEF) are essential for leverage but require careful coordination to avoid overlap.
q27_constraints_detail: MBSSE’s weak capacity → reliance on embedded technical assistance (EPG)
High GBV prevalence → need for partners with safeguarding track records
Rural infrastructure gaps → partners must have local presence (e.g., District Inclusion Officers)
Election risks → partners must be politically neutral but adaptive
Data limitations → partners need monitoring expertise (e.g., Tangerine software for SQAOs)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (service delivery + systemic reform) drive the **hybrid delivery structure**: 1) **Policy influence** requires embedded advisors (EPG in MBSSE); 2) **Community engagement** needs localized partners (NGOs in 7 target districts); 3) **Sustainability** demands government ownership (SQAOs, DIOs as civil servants). The **adaptive management** approach (quarterly reviews) reflects the need to balance **fixed targets** (e.g., 160,000 girls enrolled) with **flexible responses** (e.g., COVID-19 catch-up).
q28_linkages: Policy objectives (Radical Inclusion) → embedded technical assistance (EPG)
Service delivery targets (enrolment) → direct support to schools (SQAOs, DIOs)
Community barriers (GBV, early marriage) → localized NGO partnerships
System strengthening (EMIS) → coordination with World Bank
Shock resilience (climate/health) → flexible funding for distance learning
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid enrolment gains (e.g., FQSE policy) risked overwhelming schools, requiring subsequent quality interventions (e.g., CPD for teachers); 2) **Cost vs. reach**: Targeting rural girls (e.g., home visits) is resource-intensive but critical for equity; 3) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK advisors (EPG) provide technical skills, but decision-making rests with MBSSE to ensure legitimacy. The programme prioritizes equity (e.g., doubling disability enrolment) over pure efficiency.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Urban vs. rural allocation: Higher costs per student in rural areas (e.g., assistive devices, safe spaces)
Short-term enrolment vs. long-term quality: FQSE boosted access but strained teacher capacity, requiring CPD investments
Direct delivery vs. capacity building: SQAOs (government employees) replace project-paid SSOs for sustainability, despite initial capability gaps
Multilateral alignment vs. programme autonomy: Coordination with World Bank adds layers but reduces duplication
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight**: 1) Quarterly Executive Committee reviews (not annual) due to political/election risks; 2) Embedded advisors (EPG) to mitigate absorption capacity risks; 3) Flexible funding to adapt to shocks (e.g., COVID-19 school closures). The **moderate risk rating** justifies this intensity, balancing accountability with government ownership.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) MBSSE leads policy but receives TA for implementation (e.g., Radical Inclusion guidelines); 2) SQAOs (government staff) replace project-hired SSOs, requiring training; 3) Communities (Boards of Governors) are empowered to hold schools accountable, shifting from passive recipients to active participants. Partners like EPG transition from direct delivery (SSEIP1) to **capacity-building roles** (SSEIP2).
intersections.quote: "Working through GoSL systems may present delivery bottlenecks... Some activities (e.g., work with SQAOs, CSE, and PFM) will require careful partner coordination... The programme will also help design and implement a MBSSE/TSC capacity building plan in policy development to reduce external dependency." (D0003774.odt, Pillar 2: System Strengthening)

key_programme_risks: Reversal of gains for girls/children with disabilities without continued support
Political disruption due to 2023 elections (instrumentalization or delivery delays)
Weak MBSSE capacity to absorb/implement reforms (e.g., SQAOs stretched)
High GBV prevalence undermining school safety and retention
Climate shocks (flooding, disease outbreaks) disrupting education
Corruption in financial systems (e.g., teacher payroll, textbook procurement)
Data gaps hindering monitoring (e.g., disability-disaggregated data)
Sustainability risks post-2027 due to low domestic financing
Coordinating with multiple donors (World Bank, UNICEF) creating inefficiencies
Social norms (early marriage, FGM) persisting despite interventions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Align programme messaging with sector-wide priorities (not political cycles); maintain flexibility to adapt to election-related disruptions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: MBSSE absorption capacity limits (e.g., SQAOs managing 70+ schools)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phase rollout of interventions; provide targeted TA to SQAOs (e.g., Tangerine software, monitoring tools).
Strengthen School Safety Committees; zero-tolerance policies; train teachers/SQAOs on case management.
Develop shock-responsive plans (e.g., distance learning protocols); integrate resilience into policy reforms.
Support PFM reforms (e.g., teacher payroll transparency); advocate for increased domestic education budget.
Strengthen EMIS with World Bank; pilot sex-disaggregated disability tracking.
Institutionalize reforms (e.g., SQAOs as civil servants); phase out project-paid roles (e.g., SSOs → SQAOs).
Explicit division of labor (FCDO on secondary, World Bank on primary); joint planning via Executive Committee.

fcas_specific_lessons: Embed technical advisors within government (e.g., EPG in MBSSE) to navigate weak institutions.
Use adaptive management (quarterly reviews) to respond to political/election risks.
Prioritize resilience-building (e.g., shock-responsive policies) given climate/health vulnerabilities.
Leverage community structures (e.g., Boards of Governors) to compensate for weak state reach in rural areas.
Combine direct service delivery (e.g., enrolment drives) with systemic reforms (e.g., Radical Inclusion Policy) to balance immediate impact and sustainability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: SSEIP1 lessons applied to SSEIP2: 1) **Sustainability**: Transition from project-paid SSOs to government SQAOs; 2) **Policy influence**: EPG’s role in developing Radical Inclusion Policy demonstrated the value of embedded TA; 3) **Community engagement**: Home visits (from GEC projects) proved effective for retaining vulnerable girls; 4) **Data use**: Tangerine software for monitoring improved teacher coaching; 5) **Flexibility**: SSEIP1’s adaptive response to Ebola/COVID-19 informed SSEIP2’s shock-responsive design.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Shift from SSOs to SQAOs**: SSEIP1’s School Support Officers (project-hired) are replaced by government SQAOs for sustainability; 2) **Stronger focus on non-formal education**: Lessons from EAGER/GATE projects expanded NFE components; 3) **Explicit GBV mitigation**: SSEIP1’s Reducing Violence in Schools (RVS) Guide scaled up with School Safety Committees; 4) **Disability inclusion**: SSEIP2 doubles down on assistive devices and data tracking, addressing SSEIP1’s gaps; 5) **Adaptive funding**: SSEIP2 preserves unallocated budget for scaling innovations, unlike SSEIP1’s fixed contracts.
risks_lessons.quote: "The current programme (SSEIP1) has consistently scored ‘A’ in its annual reviews... Deliver was supported by deployment of 200 School Support Officers (SSOs)... This is a more sustainable approach, but the transition will need continued technical support." (D0003774.odt, Rationale for UK investment)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages multilateral investments, e.g., World Bank’s FREE Project ($86m, including $2m FCDO contribution) and GPE ($17.2m). FCDO’s influence as a major IDA contributor is used to shape these programmes (e.g., aligning FREE’s teacher management reforms with SSEIP2).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Not explicitly stated, but budget covers both **capital** (e.g., assistive devices, school infrastructure adaptations) and **revenue** (e.g., SQAO salaries, CPD training, policy TA).
financial_details.quote: "The UK will work closely with others and seek to positively influence them... We are the only partner investing across a range of financial instruments, supporting the education sector in Sierra Leone through: core multilateral investments (e.g., to IDA), sector-specific multilateral arrangements (e.g., GPE), and centrally-managed bilateral programmes." (D0003774.odt, Box 1: Multilateral programmes)

metadata.programme_name: "Unlocking children’s potential to thrive: Research into taking early childhood development (ECD) interventions to scale" (THRIVE–ECD Research at scale)
metadata.duration_text: First phase up to £20.5m over 5 years; second phase up to £10m over 3 years
metadata.quote: The programme focuses on early childhood development (ECD) interventions, which are critical for educational attainment and human capital development. (90000824.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: As per the approval of the Concept Note for this programme, DFID Ministers will need to approve the £10m/3-year extension based on the level of demonstrable impact over the first 5 years of the programme. (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is primarily focused on **implementation research** to generate rigorous evidence on how to scale quality ECD interventions, while also aiming for **policy influence** by supporting governments and DFID programmes to improve ECD delivery. It includes elements of **capacity building** through technical assistance and **evidence generation** for global public goods.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will respond to demand by generating rigorous evidence on implementing quality ECD interventions in five LMICs... It will support at least four DFID bilateral ECD programmes through research to drive real-time improvements... (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: rigorous body of evidence on ‘what works’ to strengthen systems of ECD service delivery at scale
improved efficiency of DFID’s ECD programming in four countries
increased government engagement in ECD policies and programming
a strong network of ECD stakeholders and community of practice to share learning
direct impact on education and health outcomes for children aged 0-8
q3_expected_outputs.target: over one million children (collectively, through DFID bilateral programmes)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to generate evidence on scaling quality ECD interventions while directly improving DFID’s ECD programmes and influencing government policies. It combines research, implementation support, and capacity building to achieve sustainable impact.
what_objectives.quote: The ultimate intended direct impact of this ECD research programme will be improved education... and health... for children aged 0-8, achieved through a better understanding of how to implement effective ECD interventions at scale. (90000824.odt, Intended outcomes and impact)

countries_regions: four DFID priority countries (Rwanda, Tanzania, Nigeria, and one unspecified)
one Pacific Island country (selected by New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme includes one fragile and conflict-affected state (FCAS) among the five countries, but the overall programme risk rating is classified as 'moderate.' This suggests a balanced approach to risk management across diverse contexts.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate (90000824.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: lack of systematic regulation or monitoring of service providers
political economy challenges (multi-agency, multi-sectoral coordination without a lead Ministry for ECD)
data limitations (fragmented measurement tools for child development)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: These constraints affect the ability to deliver quality, multi-sectoral ECD services at scale, particularly in low-resource settings. For example, weak health systems limit coverage and coordination with other sectors like education or WASH, while the lack of standard measurement tools complicates evidence generation and programme adaptation.
where_context.quote: There are unique complicating factors with regard to ECD... we don’t yet know enough about how to combine and deliver different sectoral interventions... or how to best engage the wide variety of potential service providers... or how to navigate the political economy of a multi-agency, multi-sectoral system when there is no lead Ministry for ECD. (90000824.odt, Evidence Base)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: DFID (now FCDO) Research and Evidence Division (RED)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The document does not explicitly state decision-making power dynamics, but DFID (UK) leads the programme design, funding, and oversight, with implementation research embedded in LMICs. Southern partners (e.g., World Bank Early Years Fellows, national governments) play roles in evidence uptake and policy impact, but the extent of their decision-making authority is not detailed.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to DFID bilateral programmes
support for World Bank ‘Early Years Fellows’ as national champions
demand-led technical advice to governments
training and coordination for in-country research teams

partner_organizations.name: DFID (FCDO) Research and Evidence Division (RED)
partner_organizations.role: lead funder and programme designer

partner_organizations.name: World Bank Early Years Fellows
partner_organizations.role: national champions for evidence uptake and policy impact

partner_organizations.name: New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder for Pacific Island country component

partner_organizations.name: DFID country offices (Rwanda, Tanzania, Nigeria, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: implementation support and programme alignment

partner_organizations.name: In-country research teams (multisectoral and interdisciplinary)
partner_organizations.role: conduct mixed-methods implementation research

partner_organizations.name: British Academy (BA) and World Bank Early Learning Partnership (WBELP)
partner_organizations.role: prior research programmes informing this initiative

who_partners.quote: This programme will build implementation research directly onto DFID’s bilaterally funded ECD programming... It will leverage World Bank ‘Early Years Fellows’ as national champions to support evidence uptake and policy impact. (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **grants** (for research teams) and **contracts** (for implementation support to DFID bilateral programmes). The funding is structured to align with DFID’s existing ECD programming, ensuring research is demand-led and integrated with policy and practice.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates as a **platform** for implementation research, convening multiple stakeholders (researchers, donors, DFID country offices, governments) to generate and disseminate evidence. It includes embedded technical assistance (e.g., World Bank Fellows) and real-time feedback loops to adapt interventions.
how_mechanism.quote: The programme offers space for innovation... and will encourage synergies with DFID’s EdTech programme... It will leverage World Bank ‘Early Years Fellows’ as national champions... (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions the use of **World Bank Early Years Fellows** as national champions and **DFID advisers** to coordinate evidence uptake. While no formal governance body (e.g., steering committee) is explicitly described, the involvement of multiple stakeholders (DFID RED, country offices, research teams, World Bank) suggests a **technical advisory group** model for oversight and alignment.
how_governance.quote: DFID Ministers will need to approve the £10m/3-year extension based on the level of demonstrable impact over the first 5 years of the programme. (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can likely be reallocated between research components to respond to emerging evidence or contextual needs, but this requires alignment with DFID’s bilateral programmes and approval for major changes (e.g., the Phase 2 extension).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be **adaptive**, with implementation research providing real-time feedback for programme iteration. However, significant adjustments (e.g., shifting research priorities) would require DFID approval, as seen in the Phase 2 extension process.
how_flexibility.quote: Rigorous implementation research... will provide robust recommendations for improvements for DFID’s programme efficiency—enabling programmes to improve the delivery of ECD services for children. (90000824.odt, Intended outcomes and impact)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (RED) → In-country research teams/World Bank Fellows → End beneficiaries (children, parents, service providers). The programme embeds research within DFID’s existing bilateral programmes, reducing layers but adding complexity in coordination.
how_efficiency.quote: Full 5-year research programme implementation to start from date of successful procurement, likely to be late 2020/early 2021. (90000824.odt, Summary Sheet)

q24_alternatives_considered: Standalone research grants (rejected due to lack of alignment with DFID programming)
Pure technical assistance (rejected due to limited evidence generation)
Multilateral pooling (not mentioned as a serious alternative, likely due to DFID’s bilateral focus)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **mixed model** (implementation research + embedded technical assistance) was chosen to: 1) **generate rigorous evidence** on scaling ECD while 2) **directly improving DFID’s bilateral programmes** in real time. This approach balances **efficiency** (leveraging existing programmes) with **effectiveness** (adaptive, context-specific research).
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (moderate risk rating with embedded oversight)
partner capacity (World Bank Fellows, in-country researchers)
equity (focus on marginalised children and fragile contexts)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating multi-sectoral research across diverse country contexts may lead to fragmentation or misalignment.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical assistance (World Bank Fellows) and demand-led research design to ensure local relevance and policy uptake.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap or duplication with other ECD initiatives (e.g., World Bank, UNICEF).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close liaison with ECD networks (e.g., ECDAN, Moving Minds Alliance) and explicit focus on DFID’s bilateral programmes to avoid redundancy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited capacity of Southern partners to lead research or decision-making.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building through technical assistance and co-production of evidence with national champions (e.g., World Bank Fellows).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing DFID programmes to reduce costs)
efficiency (real-time feedback loops to improve programme delivery)
effectiveness (rigorous evidence generation for global public goods)
equity (targeting marginalised children and fragile states)
why_rationale.quote: This programme will respond to demand by generating rigorous evidence on implementing quality ECD interventions... It will support at least four DFID bilateral ECD programmes through research to drive real-time improvements... (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **multi-country, low-resource context** limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) experience in **fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)**, 2) ability to navigate **weak institutional environments**, and 3) capacity to work across **health, education, and social protection sectors**. This excludes many Northern academia-led consortia without LMIC embeddedness.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with **in-country presence** (e.g., World Bank Fellows) due to weak institutions.
Requirement for **multi-sectoral expertise** (health, nutrition, education, social protection).
Focus on **LMIC-led implementation** to ensure contextual relevance and policy uptake.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **implementation research objective** (testing how to scale ECD interventions) necessitates: 1) **embedded delivery** within DFID’s bilateral programmes for real-time learning, 2) **flexible funding** to adapt to emerging evidence, and 3) **multi-stakeholder governance** (DFID, World Bank, national governments) to align research with policy.
q28_linkages: **Real-time feedback loops** (research → programme adaptation) require close collaboration between researchers and implementers.
**Global public goods** (evidence generation) demand rigorous, standardized methods across countries.
**Policy influence** (government engagement) needs national champions (e.g., World Bank Fellows) and demand-led technical assistance.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **rapid scaling** (efficiency) vs. **inclusive reach** (equity for marginalised children), and 2) **Northern expertise** (e.g., DFID RED) vs. **Southern ownership** (e.g., national champions). Mitigations include adaptive management and targeted ‘deep dives’ into contextual barriers.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid scaling of interventions may exclude hard-to-reach groups (e.g., rural girls in Nigeria). The programme addresses this via ‘deep dive’ studies on marginalised families and adaptive delivery mechanisms.
Northern-led research design (DFID RED) risks limited LMIC ownership. Mitigated by embedding World Bank Fellows as national champions and co-producing evidence with local stakeholders.
Delivering high-quality, multi-sectoral ECD is resource-intensive. The programme focuses on ‘minimal optimum packages’ of interventions to balance affordability and impact.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (including one FCAS) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and embedded advisors (World Bank Fellows) to navigate political economy challenges and weak institutions. Higher risk contexts would likely require more intensive management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: World Bank Fellows act as **national champions** for evidence uptake, while in-country research teams **co-produce knowledge** with DFID. This ensures Southern partners move beyond implementation to **decision-making** (e.g., adapting interventions).
intersections.quote: It is anticipated that the specific implementation challenges will vary between countries, but there will be overall lessons to be learnt about the delivery of multisectoral ECD... in low-resource contexts which face similar challenges. (90000824.odt, Programme summary)

key_programme_risks: Limited evidence on how to combine multi-sectoral ECD interventions at scale in LMICs.
Weak health and education systems in target countries may hinder service delivery and coordination.
Political economy challenges (e.g., no lead Ministry for ECD) could fragment implementation.
Fragmented measurement tools for child development complicate evidence generation.
Risk of low uptake of research findings by governments or DFID programmes.
Capacity constraints in Southern partners to lead research or adapt interventions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited evidence on scaling multi-sectoral ECD
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Implementation research embedded in DFID programmes to test adaptive, context-specific models.
Leverage World Bank Early Years Fellows as national champions and provide technical assistance.
Use mixed-methods research and align with global frameworks (e.g., Nurturing Care Framework).
Demand-led research design, real-time feedback loops, and policy engagement strategies.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts, **multi-agency coordination** is critical but challenging due to weak governance. The programme will test models for navigating this (e.g., via World Bank Fellows).
**Adaptive management** is essential in FCAS to respond to shifting priorities or security constraints.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior DFID-funded research (e.g., British Academy and World Bank Early Learning Partnership) identified critical evidence gaps in **implementation at scale**, particularly around **multi-sectoral coordination** and **cost-effective delivery**. This programme builds on these lessons by focusing on **real-time adaptation** and **minimal optimum packages** of interventions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates **‘deep dive’ studies** into contextual barriers (e.g., for marginalised families) and **behavioural science analyses** to improve messaging—direct responses to past challenges in reaching vulnerable groups.
risks_lessons.quote: Recent literature reviews and DFID-led expert consultation has confirmed an evidence gap in how to provide quality ECD services at scale... (90000824.odt, Evidence Base)

co_funding_partners.partner: New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to catalyse complementary UK investment into ECD research through UK Research Councils (e.g., ESRC, MRC) and may attract additional donor funding by demonstrating impact in the first phase.
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: First phase up to £20.5m over 5 years; second phase up to £10m over 3 years. (90000824.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Mozambique Agricultural Jobs and Climate-Resilient Investment Programme (MAJI)
metadata.duration_text: The initial phase is for £18.5 million. Additional funding up to £40 million is subject to availability of resources and Ministerial approval.
metadata.quote: "This programme aims to improve incomes, create better/more jobs for women and men in Mozambique and support their resilience to climate shocks." (D0003507.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The initial phase is for £18.5 million. Additional funding up to £40 million is subject to availability of resources and Ministerial approval." (D0003507.odt, ProgrammeValue)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (catalytic investment, grants), implementation research (testing climate-smart agriculture models), and policy influence (research and advocacy for enabling environments). It aims to transform agricultural value chains while building climate resilience and creating jobs, particularly for women.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme aims to improve incomes, create better/more jobs for women and men in Mozambique and support their resilience to climate shocks. Proposed interventions will address key constraints to private sector participation in selected areas of agriculture, promote greater climate resilience and stimulate sectoral growth and transformation of Mozambique’s economy." (D0003507.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 500,000 young people estimated to join the labour force annually (target group for job creation)
Increased availability of finance and catalytic investments for farmers and agri-SMEs
Policy reforms to improve enabling environment for climate-smart agriculture
150 million emerging commercial smallholders targeted for market access (potential £1.8 billion rural income increase)
Climate-smart agricultural practices adopted in cassava, maize, soybean, and poultry value chains
Reduction in post-harvest losses (currently 30% of agricultural produce wasted)
Increased private sector investment in green finance, agri-tech, and agro-related machinery
Strengthened government institutions for climate-smart market linkages
Development of climate risk management strategies and contingency plans
Creation of a pipeline of investable agri-businesses for UK BII, IFC, and other investors
what_objectives.summary: MAJI is a mixed-modality programme that combines financing (£18.5m initial phase), technical assistance, and policy advocacy to transform Mozambique's agricultural sector through climate-resilient value chains, with explicit targets for job creation (especially for women) and private sector engagement.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will: (a) increase the availability of finance and catalytic investments to allow farmers and agri-SMEs to operate at scale and become more resilient to climate shocks; (b) Policy, influencing, and research to help improve the enabling environment for investment and encourage a shift to climate-smart agriculture practices." (D0003507.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique is classified as FCAS due to active conflict in Cabo Delgado (5,000+ deaths since 2017), high poverty (67% live on <$1.90/day), recurrent climate shocks (cyclones/floods), and institutional fragility. The programme explicitly targets conflict-affected areas and notes "very high vulnerability of Mozambique’s agriculture sector to the impacts of climate change."
where_context.q5_source: "Mozambique remains one of the poorest countries in the World... Recurring natural disasters like cyclones and floods have aggravated high poverty levels and inequality... Mozambique has also been negatively affected by... growing conflict in the northern provinces deteriorating poverty situation... These challenges have contributed to slow economic growth and have made it difficult for the country to lift its population out of poverty." (D0003507.odt, Context section) AND "Agriculture provides an economic opportunity in Cabo Delgado, the province currently most affected by conflict... High poverty levels and unemployment are the key drivers of the insurgency in Northern Mozambique, resulting in the deaths of approximately 5,000 people since 2017." (D0003507.odt, Conflict section)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (low firm capabilities, weak management practices)
political economy (corruption risks, land governance issues)
data limitations (lack of market information for smallholders)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit operations in Northern provinces; climate risks reduce agricultural productivity (20-40% yield losses projected); weak institutions hinder policy implementation; financial constraints (20%+ interest rates) block SME growth; and poor infrastructure increases transaction costs for smallholders. The programme must navigate these while avoiding exacerbation of gender inequalities or child labour risks.
where_context.quote: "The agriculture sector suffers from multiple constraints, including access to finance and high vulnerability to climate variability and shocks... Weak management practices of Mozambican firms mean a lack of efficient production mechanisms, limited modern technologies, ineffective talent development, and insufficient planning and targeting." (D0003507.odt, Context section) AND "High-cost capital and low appetite from financial institutions to lend to agriculture inhibit the growth of these value chains impacting smallholder farmers." (D0003507.odt, Financial Constraints section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains approval authority for all major components (Components 1-3), with implementing partners (e.g., AgDevCo, World Bank) executing delivery under FCDO oversight. Southern partners (e.g., Government of Mozambique) are consulted but do not have decision-making power over fund allocation or strategic direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to agri-SMEs for climate-smart practices
policy dialogue support for Government of Mozambique
training for smallholder farmers on value chain integration
institutional strengthening for agricultural risk management
gender-responsive policy reform support

partner_organizations.role: Implementation partner for investment pipeline and technical cooperation (Component 1 and 3)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Food System 2030 Trust Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Administrative agreement for policy/influencing component (Component 2)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Mozambique
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary and policy counterpart (no implementation role)
