partner_organizations.role: Potential co-investor for de-risked agri-SMEs

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-investor for larger-scale agribusinesses

partner_organizations.name: Local agri-SMEs and producer organizations
partner_organizations.role: Direct beneficiaries/implementers of climate-smart practices

who_partners.quote: "The UK has considerable expertise in value chain development, skills development, land governance for inclusive growth, policy-oriented research, financial services, climate-smart investments, agri-tech, and nutrition-sensitive agriculture." (D0003507.odt, Rationale) AND "Component 1 – Accountable Grant to a Third-Party Organisation (AgDevCo)... Component 2 – Administrative Agreement with World Bank under Food System 2030 Trust Fund." (D0003507.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses (1) **accountable grants** to AgDevCo for investment pipeline development, (2) an **administrative agreement** with the World Bank for policy/research, and (3) **technical cooperation** for direct support to agri-SMEs. Grants are combined with catalytic investments to de-risk private sector engagement, while policy components use trust fund mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages three distinct components through separate agreements: (1) AgDevCo (grant), (2) World Bank (administrative agreement), and (3) technical cooperation (likely competitive contracts). Each component has predefined roles, with FCDO retaining oversight. The structure is **not open to additional partners** post-award.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AgDevCo and World Bank were selected based on **prior experience** with FCDO in Mozambique (e.g., AgDevCo’s pilot projects demonstrating market gaps) and **alignment with UK strategic priorities**. The document states: "The UK has long-standing experience on what is required to develop the private sector in Mozambique... These lessons have informed the programme design."
how_mechanism.quote: "Component 1 – Accountable Grant to a Third-Party Organisation... Component 2 – Administrative Agreement with World Bank under Food System 2030 Trust Fund... Component 3 – Technical Cooperation." (D0003507.odt, Commercial Case) AND "Two initiatives with AgDevCo supporting existing agribusinesses to revamp their smallholder farmers’ supply chain were piloted. These pilots demonstrated a market gap in financing... Therefore, these pilots demonstrated that donors’ grants could support additional high-risk equity capital by other private investors." (D0003507.odt, Strategic Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme establishes a **Programme Governance Arrangement** (E.1) with distinct oversight for each component: (1) Investment/Finance, (2) Policy/Influencing/Research, and (3) Technical Cooperation. FCDO retains approval authority for sub-awards, and a **joint monitoring framework** is implied through the MEL system (E.2).
how_governance.quote: "E.1 Programme Governance Arrangement: The programme will have a governance structure that includes distinct oversight for each of the three components... E.1.1 Component 1. Investment and Finance; E.1.2 Component 2. Policy, Influencing and Research; E.1.3 Component 3. Technical cooperation." (D0003507.odt, Management Case) AND "The programme will use two sets of instruments to facilitate and de-risk the agribusinesses investment allowing them to grow and access other sources of capital, including Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)." (D0003507.odt, How interventions will work)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for specific components (finance, policy, technical cooperation) with limited flexibility between them. Reallocation would require FCDO approval, as components are tied to distinct agreements (e.g., World Bank trust fund vs. AgDevCo grant).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes **adaptive management** clauses to respond to climate shocks or market changes, but adjustments require FCDO sign-off. Pilot projects demonstrated the need for adaptability: "The pilots are also demonstrating the need to be adaptive to the economic context."
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will also identify opportunities and engage development capital investment vehicles like BII and IFC to invest patient capital or use blended finance to attract private investors by helping to de-risk the initial investment." (D0003507.odt, Finance Component) AND "A comprehensive political economy analysis will be integral to the programme design and implementation... The programme implementation approach and selection of partners should be instrumental, especially the degree to which the implementer is seen as independent (non-partisan), transparent, and credible by all stakeholders." (D0003507.odt, Strategic Approach)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (AgDevCo/World Bank) → Agri-SMEs/Smallholder Farmers. For technical cooperation, an additional layer may exist (FCDO → intermediary → local service providers → farmers).
how_efficiency.quote: "Component 1 – Accountable Grant to a Third-Party Organisation... Component 2 – Administrative Agreement with World Bank... Component 3 – Technical Cooperation." (D0003507.odt, Commercial Case) AND "The programme will provide a catalytic fund to support agribusinesses... enabling these agribusinesses to test, innovate, and expand their agriculture processing." (D0003507.odt, Finance Component)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Targeted interventions to build investment pipeline and link smallholders to existing agribusinesses (CHOSEN)
Option B: Broader MSME support to increase capital across crops/value chains (REJECTED)
Direct lending to farmers (rejected due to high risk)
Pure policy advocacy (rejected as insufficient without financing)
Standalone climate adaptation programmes (rejected for lack of market linkage)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option A was selected for its **transformative potential**, **climate integration**, and **alignment with UK strengths** in de-risking private investment. The multi-criteria analysis scored it higher on economic impact (8/10), climate-smart criteria (8/10), and sustainability (8/10). The rationale emphasizes leveraging UK credibility in blended finance and the need to address the "missing middle" ($0.1m–$2m) gap in agri-SME financing.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (Option A scored 7.85 vs. 5.85 for Option B)
risk-mitigation (pipeline approach reduces risk of market distortion)
experience (UK’s prior success with AgDevCo pilots)
equity (explicit focus on women/youth in value chains)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market distortion from catalytic grants
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on de-risking (not substituting) private capital; require commercial viability plans from agri-SMEs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on AgDevCo/World Bank limiting local ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embed gender/political economy analyses; include Government of Mozambique in steering committees.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks disrupting value chains
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mandate climate-smart practices in financing packages; build contingency plans into business models.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exclusion of marginalized groups (e.g., women, disabled)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Disaggregated monitoring by gender/disability; targeted outreach in Cabo Delgado/Niassa.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low absorption capacity of local agri-SMEs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Combine grants with technical assistance; phase investments based on readiness.

why_rationale.quote: "Option A – build pipeline and support mid-level... Criteria and weight: 1. Likely economic impact (20%): 8(1.6) – hybrid model more likely to produce greater impact on economic transformation... 2. Climate smart (20%): 8(1.6) – climate considerations integral to investment decisions... 3. Impact on inclusion (20%): 7(1.4) – benefits smallholders in targeted regions... 4. Gap analysis (15%): 9(1.35) – underserved segment... 5. Sustainable, market-driven (15%): 8(1.2) – draws in wider funding sources." (D0003507.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "The chosen option under the finance component is Option A... Under this component, the programme will develop and support the growth of several commercial ventures between farmers and agribusinesses by providing matching grants, investment, and technical assistance." (D0003507.odt, Finance Component)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** (conflict in Cabo Delgado, climate vulnerability) limits partner selection to organizations with (1) **security clearance** (e.g., AgDevCo’s existing Mozambique operations), (2) **climate adaptation expertise** (World Bank’s Food System 2030 Trust Fund), and (3) **risk appetite** for early-stage agri-SMEs. Local NGOs or government agencies cannot lead due to capacity/credibility gaps, forcing reliance on international intermediaries.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Northern provinces excludes partners without security protocols
Climate risks require partners with adaptation track records (e.g., World Bank)
Weak local financial sector necessitates UK-led de-risking mechanisms
Gender inequalities demand partners with explicit inclusion strategies
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **financing mechanism objective** (catalytic investments) dictates a **closed consortium structure** (AgDevCo/World Bank) to manage fiduciary risks, while the **policy influence objective** enables a **trust fund model** (World Bank) for credibility. The need for **climate-smart value chains** requires embedded technical assistance, shaping the **three-component design** (finance + policy + technical cooperation).
q28_linkages: Financing goals → Direct awards to AgDevCo for pipeline development
Policy goals → Administrative agreement with World Bank for trust fund
Climate resilience → Mandatory climate-smart practices in all components
Gender equity → Disaggregated MEL framework across all partners
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are noted between (1) **speed** (direct awards to AgDevCo/World Bank accelerate delivery) vs. **inclusion** (limited local partner roles), and (2) **expertise** (Northern-led climate-smart models) vs. **ownership** (Southern institutions’ limited decision power). The programme mitigates this via **gender-responsive design** and **political economy analyses** but acknowledges trade-offs in the business case.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to AgDevCo/World Bank prioritize efficiency over local capacity-building
Expertise vs. ownership: UK-designed climate-smart models may limit Mozambican institutional learning
Cost vs. reach: High transaction costs for smallholder inclusion (e.g., technical assistance) reduce funds available for scaling
Risk vs. innovation: De-risking requirements may exclude highest-risk/highest-reward agri-SMEs
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS/moderate-risk profile** drives **milestone-based oversight** (not light-touch) and **embedded safeguards** (e.g., climate risk assessments for all investments). Conflict in Cabo Delgado requires **additional due diligence** for partners operating in Northern regions, increasing management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local capacity (e.g., "Mozambican firms’ weak management practices") justifies **Northern-led technical assistance** and **restricted sub-award authority**. However, capacity building is embedded via **policy dialogue support** for Government of Mozambique and **training for agri-SMEs** to gradually shift roles.
intersections.quote: "A comprehensive political economy analysis will be integral to the programme design and implementation. Understanding the appetite, incentives, and driving forces behind investments in agriculture... is key to identifying a viable value chain that can create jobs and increase farmers’ incomes." (D0003507.odt, Strategic Approach) AND "The programme implementation approach and selection of partners should be instrumental, especially the degree to which the implementer is seen as independent (non-partisan), transparent, and credible by all stakeholders." (D0003507.odt, Strategic Approach)

key_programme_risks: Climate shocks disrupting agricultural productivity (20-40% yield losses projected)
Conflict in Cabo Delgado limiting programme reach and increasing security costs
Market distortion from catalytic grants crowding out private investment
Low absorption capacity of local agri-SMEs for climate-smart technologies
Gender backlash from male household members resisting women’s economic empowerment
Child labour risks in intensified agricultural value chains
Policy resistance from vested interests in traditional agriculture
Currency fluctuations affecting investment returns
High interest rates (15-20%) limiting SME participation
Weak contract enforcement increasing risks for smallholders in outgrower schemes

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Mandate climate-smart practices in financing; build contingency plans into business models; focus on drought-resistant crops.
Partner with organizations having security protocols; target neighbouring provinces (Niassa/Nampula) for spillover benefits; disaggregate results by conflict status.
Require commercial viability plans; phase out grants as private capital enters; monitor for crowding-out effects.
Conduct gender analyses; involve male community members in training; monitor intra-household resource allocation.
Include child labour safeguards in contracts; monitor supply chains; partner with labour rights NGOs.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-sensitive programming is critical: "Careful consideration will be given to how smallholders in Cabo Delgado... can be supported to promote agriculture and job creation in the conflict-affected areas."
Adaptive management for shocks: Pilots demonstrated need to "be adaptive to the economic context" in FCAS settings.
Local legitimacy matters: Partners must be "seen as independent, transparent, and credible by all stakeholders" to operate in fragile areas.
Leverage existing platforms: Use multilateral programmes (e.g., World Bank’s Sustainable Rural Economy Programme) to share risks in high-conflict zones.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior UK programmes (e.g., AgDevCo pilots, BRILHO off-grid renewables) demonstrated that: (1) **blended finance** can de-risk early-stage agri-SMEs; (2) **technical assistance** must accompany grants to ensure adoption of climate-smart practices; (3) **policy dialogue** is needed alongside financing to address structural constraints (e.g., high interest rates); and (4) **gender-disaggregated data** is essential to track equity impacts. The business case cites these as justification for the three-component design.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) **mandatory climate risk assessments** (learned from prior yield losses); (2) **political economy analyses** (to avoid elite capture); (3) **disability-inclusive monitoring** (from FCDO PSED requirements); and (4) **conflict-sensitive value chain selection** (e.g., avoiding maize due to climate vulnerability).
risks_lessons.quote: "Two initiatives with AgDevCo supporting existing agribusinesses to revamp their smallholder farmers’ supply chain were piloted. These pilots demonstrated a market gap in financing... Currently, the financial sector offers only commercial private capital at a higher cost, suitable for more mature businesses... Most commercial agriculture ventures with high potential for smallholders are either in an incipient or early growth stage." (D0003507.odt, Strategic Case) AND "The programme will focus on promoting more climate-resilient agriculture while managing climate risks... Every investment will be accompanied by a review of the specific climate and biodiversity risks." (D0003507.odt, Climate Approach)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize private capital through de-risking mechanisms. For every £1 of UK funding, the target is to leverage £3-£5 in private investment (implied by the £1.8 billion potential income uplift from 10% of 150 million smallholders). Specific leverage ratios are not quantified but are a core objective: "The programme will also identify opportunities and engage development capital investment vehicles like BII and IFC to invest patient capital or use blended finance to attract private investors."
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme blends **catalytic capital** (grants for de-risking) with **revenue-generating investments** (agri-SME growth). Components include: (1) **grants** for technical assistance, (2) **matching grants** for agri-SMEs, and (3) **patient capital** to attract FDI. The split is not quantified but emphasizes shifting from grants to commercial finance over time.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: The initial phase is for £18.5 million. Additional funding up to £40 million is subject to availability of resources and Ministerial approval." (D0003507.odt, ProgrammeValue) AND "The programme will provide a catalytic fund to support agribusinesses... enabling these agribusinesses to test, innovate, and expand their agriculture processing, and also increase the number of smallholders participating in the supply chain." (D0003507.odt, Finance Component) AND "Based on a minimum £120 income uplift per year... if 10% of the estimated 150 million emerging commercial smallholders were to access formal markets, the increase in rural incomes is estimated to exceed £1.8 billion." (D0003507.odt, Economic Appraisal)

metadata.programme_name: Disability Inclusion Capacity Building programme
metadata.quote: "Programme Value: £25m over four years" (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)
metadata.duration_source: "Programme Value: £25m over four years" (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **capacity building** for Disabled People’s Organisations (DPOs) to advocate for disability rights and inclusion, while also incorporating **financing mechanisms** (direct funding to DPOs) and **policy influence** (advocacy for legislative changes). It aims to strengthen the disability rights movement globally, ensuring representation and accountability.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support the development and growth of an organised, capable, diverse, representative and accountable global disability rights movement... Through the provision of direct funding to DPOs to support core functions and technical advice and training at national, regional and global levels, the programme will build the organisational capacity, knowledge and skills of DPOs around the world." (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved capability, experience, and skills of people with disabilities and their representative groups at all levels
Enhanced leadership and voice of people with disabilities (including underrepresented groups) in decision-making and international fora
Reform and adaptation of the disability rights movement to include a more diverse range of DPOs and underrepresented groups (e.g., women and girls, psychosocial/intellectual disabilities, youth)
Improved government accountability to support implementation and delivery of UNCRPD and Global Disability Summit (GDS) commitments
Improved collaboration and partnerships between the UN, governments, and DPOs
Technical advice and training provided to people with disabilities and their representative organisations
Funding provided to support core functions of DPOs, including marginalised and underrepresented groups
Support to analyse and advocate for changes needed in national policies, legislation, and programmes to address discrimination
Accountability mechanisms and coalitions built, particularly at local and national levels

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to build the capacity of DPOs globally to advocate for disability rights, ensure inclusion in policy-making, and hold governments accountable for commitments under the UNCRPD and SDGs. It focuses on strengthening the disability rights movement, improving diversity and representation, and fostering collaboration between DPOs, governments, and the UN.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact of the programme is ‘People with disabilities across the life course are engaged, empowered and able to enjoy rights on an equal basis with others, contributing to poverty reduction, improved outcomes and wellbeing and delivery of the sustainable development goals, and implementation of the UNCRPD.’" (57281837.odt, Theory of Change section)

countries_regions: Approximately 15-20 countries around the world (aligned with DFID priority countries)
Countries include Malawi, Uganda, Rwanda, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Indonesia, Pacific Islands (based on DRF’s existing footprint)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a mix of stable and fragile contexts, with DPOs often working in environments of closing civic space and limited government engagement. The overall programme risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate.'
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (57281837.odt, Summary Sheet section)
q6_contextual_constraints: lack of coordination among disability movements
stigma and discrimination against people with disabilities
financial management and safeguarding gaps in DPOs
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: DPOs often lack capacity in financial management, governance, and advocacy, which limits their ability to operate effectively and engage with governments. Closing civic space and accessibility barriers further hinder participation, while stigma and discrimination exacerbate exclusion. These constraints require long-term support to build organisational resilience and inclusivity.
where_context.quote: "DPOs are often emerging organisations, with little experience of advocacy and lacking management, financial and governance skills... They are often working in a context of closing civic space and a reduction of opportunities to engage." (57281837.odt, Accountable governance and the role of DPOs section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed to be led by people with disabilities through their representative organisations (DPOs), with support from Northern and multilateral partners. Decision-making is shared, with DPOs at the forefront of advocacy and accountability efforts, while partners like IDA, DRF, and UNPRPD provide technical and financial support.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on disability rights, leadership, financial management, and governance
technical advice on advocacy, policy analysis, and legal frameworks
core funding for DPO operations (e.g., financial management, safeguarding)
peer-to-peer learning and mentorship
support for underrepresented groups (e.g., women, youth, psychosocial disabilities)
institutional strengthening of DPOs to engage with governments and UN agencies

partner_organizations.name: Disability Rights Fund (DRF)
partner_organizations.role: Grant-making organisation providing direct funding to DPOs for advocacy and CRPD implementation

partner_organizations.name: International Disability Alliance (IDA)
partner_organizations.role: Global advocacy and capacity-building for DPOs, including technical support and coordination

partner_organizations.name: UN Partnership for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNPRPD)
partner_organizations.role: Supporting UN agencies to embed disability inclusion in programming and policy, with a focus on CRPD implementation

partner_organizations.name: Global Support Facility (GSF) (delivered by Sightsavers and IDA)
partner_organizations.role: New fund to support DPOs in additional countries, focusing on capacity building and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Disabled People’s Organisations (DPOs)
partner_organizations.role: Local, national, and regional organisations leading advocacy, policy influence, and accountability efforts

who_partners.quote: "This programme will fund the three existing delivery partners of the 2017-2020 Disability Catalyst Programme: (i) the Disability Rights Fund; (ii) the International Disability Alliance (IDA); and (iii) UN Partnership for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It will also fund a new fourth initiative: (iv) the Global Support Facility (GSF) delivered by Sightsavers and IDA." (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **core funding** (for DPO operational costs), **grants** (for advocacy and capacity-building projects), and **partnership agreements** (with DRF, IDA, UNPRPD, and GSF). Funds are channelled through these partners to DPOs, with a focus on participatory grant-making and technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a **fund manager model**, where DFID provides funding to four key partners (DRF, IDA, UNPRPD, GSF), who then disburse grants and technical support to DPOs. Each partner has distinct roles: DRF focuses on grant-making, IDA on global advocacy, UNPRPD on UN system engagement, and GSF on expanding reach to new countries.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The partners (DRF, IDA, UNPRPD) were selected based on their **track record** in delivering the 2017-2020 Disability Catalyst Programme, which scored highly in annual reviews. The GSF was added as a new initiative to expand support to DPOs in additional countries. The selection prioritised organisations with proven expertise in disability rights and capacity building.
how_mechanism.quote: "The existing Disability Catalyst Programme delivery partners have had a good track record for delivering and scoring well under the annual review process... This programme will fund the three existing delivery partners... and a new fourth initiative: the Global Support Facility (GSF)." (57281837.odt, Programme summary and Introduction sections)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A ‘keystakeholder group’ (KSG) for Global Disability Summit (GDS) accountability was established to oversee commitments and progress. The programme also aligns with the UN Disability Inclusion Strategy (UNDIS), which includes DPOs in decision-making processes. However, explicit governance structures (e.g., board composition) are not detailed beyond these collaborative mechanisms.
how_governance.quote: "A concept set of objectives and proposed work plan for the GDS Partnership... was designed in partnership with a set of stakeholders in a ‘keystakeholder group’ (KSG) for GDS18 accountability." (57281837.odt, Objective 3 section) && "The last Annual Review of the programme scored an A." (57281837.odt, Introduction section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, particularly to address emerging needs or context-specific barriers. The programme emphasises adaptive management to respond to evolving challenges faced by DPOs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to evolve based on lessons learned and changing contexts. For example, support will adapt to the specific needs of underrepresented groups (e.g., women, youth, psychosocial disabilities) and emerging advocacy priorities. The Theory of Change will be updated during the inception phase to reflect new evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "Over time this support will also need to evolve as the issues facing DPOs around the world changes... Lessons learnt would also be fed into DFID’s wider efforts to build the capacity of grassroots civil society." (57281837.odt, Objective 1 section) && "The ToC will be updated based on evidence from DID and other studies used to help to inform the selection of interventions for this programme." (57281837.odt, Theory of Change section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partners (DRF/IDA/UNPRPD/GSF) → DPOs (end recipients)
how_efficiency.quote: "Programme Value: £25m over four years" (57281837.odt, Summary Sheet section) && "This programme will fund the three existing delivery partners... and a new fourth initiative: the Global Support Facility (GSF)." (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **fund manager model** was chosen to leverage the **proven track record** of existing partners (DRF, IDA, UNPRPD) in delivering disability rights programmes, while adding the GSF to expand reach. This approach ensures **efficiency** (by building on existing systems), **effectiveness** (through partners with deep expertise), and **equity** (by prioritising underrepresented groups). The model also aligns with DFID’s Disability Inclusion Strategy, which emphasises empowering DPOs as rights-holders.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (building on successful existing programmes)
risk mitigation (partners with strong governance and accountability mechanisms)
partner capacity (DRF, IDA, UNPRPD have demonstrated results in annual reviews)
flexibility (adaptive management to respond to DPO needs)
equity (focus on marginalised groups within the disability movement)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of efforts due to disjointed disability movements at national/regional levels
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will invest in coordination mechanisms (e.g., peer learning, horizontal/vertical links between DPOs) and align with global frameworks like the UNCRPD and UNDIS to ensure coherence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited capacity of DPOs to absorb funds or manage safeguarding/financial risks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Core funding will include support for financial management, governance, and safeguarding training. Fiscal sponsors and peer-to-peer mentorship will be used to build capacity, particularly for nascent organisations.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exclusion of underrepresented groups (e.g., women, psychosocial disabilities) within DPOs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted funding rounds and earmarked funds (e.g., 15% for women’s groups) will ensure inclusion. Deliberate strategies will be used to reach marginalised groups, such as partnerships with parents’ groups and youth-led movements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Closing civic space limiting DPOs’ ability to engage with governments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will support DPOs to navigate political barriers through advocacy training, legal analysis, and strategic engagement with power-holders (e.g., using CRPD Concluding Observations for legitimacy).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing partners to reduce setup costs)
effectiveness (focus on tangible outcomes like policy changes and DPO capacity)
equity (prioritising underrepresented groups and marginalised voices)
why_rationale.quote: "Supporting advocacy and capacity building of DPOs is an effective intervention for disability inclusive development... DFID can build on this evidence and its previous investments, by supporting the disability inclusion movement to diversify and flourish." (57281837.odt, DFID’s track record on disability rights section) && "The existing Disability Catalyst Programme delivery partners have had a good track record for delivering and scoring well under the annual review process." (57281837.odt, Introduction section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **operating context** (e.g., closing civic space, weak institutions, accessibility barriers) directly limits **partner selection** and delivery. For example, DPOs in fragile states may lack the capacity to manage funds or engage with governments, requiring intermediaries like DRF or GSF to provide additional support. The programme prioritises partners with experience navigating these constraints (e.g., IDA’s global advocacy role, UNPRPD’s work with UN country teams).
q27_constraints_detail: closing civic space restricts DPOs’ ability to operate independently
weak financial/governance capacity in DPOs necessitates intermediary support
accessibility barriers (e.g., sign language, venue accessibility) exclude certain groups from participation
political economy barriers (e.g., lack of government will) require strategic advocacy partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The **objectives** (capacity building, policy influence, accountability) shape the **delivery structure** by requiring a **multi-layered approach**: 
1. **Core funding** for DPO operations (addressing capacity gaps).
2. **Technical partners** (DRF, IDA, UNPRPD) to provide training and advocacy support.
3. **Global/regional coordination** (e.g., GDS Partnership) to align with international frameworks like the UNCRPD.
4. **Targeted funds** for underrepresented groups to ensure diversity.
The mixed delivery structure (fund manager + direct grants) was chosen to balance **flexibility** (adapting to local contexts) with **accountability** (aligning with global standards).
q28_linkages: Capacity-building objectives → Need for embedded training/mentorship → Selection of partners like IDA and GSF with technical expertise
Policy influence goals → Requirement for advocacy support → DRF’s grant-making model for local DPOs
Accountability focus → Need for coordination mechanisms → GDS Partnership and UNDIS alignment
Diversity goals → Targeted funding rounds → Earmarked funds for women, youth, and psychosocial disabilities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly acknowledges tensions between **equity** (inclusive, diverse representation) and **efficiency** (rapid delivery through established partners). For example:
- **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct funding to larger DPOs might be faster, but the programme earmarks funds for underrepresented groups (e.g., 15% for women’s groups) to ensure equity.
- **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: While partners like IDA (global) and UNPRPD (multilateral) provide technical support, the programme centres DPOs as leaders in advocacy and decision-making.
- **Cost vs. reach**: Supporting nascent DPOs requires higher investment in capacity building, but this is justified by the long-term goal of sustainable, locally led movements.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of delivery (using existing partners) vs. time needed to build capacity in nascent DPOs
cost of targeted funds for marginalised groups vs. broader reach with limited resources
reliance on Northern/multilateral partners for technical support vs. ensuring Southern-led advocacy
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., fragile contexts, closing civic space) justifies **intensive oversight** in some areas (e.g., financial management training for DPOs) while allowing **flexibility** in others (e.g., adaptive advocacy strategies). For example, annual reviews and embedded safeguarding support mitigate risks associated with DPOs’ limited capacity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity-building objectives directly shape partner roles:
- **DRF** focuses on **grant-making** to build DPOs’ financial and advocacy skills.
- **IDA** provides **technical training** (e.g., CRPD implementation, leadership).
- **UNPRPD** strengthens **UN system engagement** to hold governments accountable.
- **GSF** expands reach to **new countries** with tailored support.
Partners are selected based on their ability to address specific capacity gaps (e.g., safeguarding, gender inclusion, policy analysis).
intersections.quote: "DPOs are often emerging organisations, with little experience of advocacy and lacking management, financial and governance skills... They are often working in a context of closing civic space and a reduction of opportunities to engage." (57281837.odt, Accountable governance section) && "The programme will build the organisational capacity, knowledge and skills of DPOs around the world... Support should also be built in to make sure DPOs can develop and enact robust safeguarding policies." (57281837.odt, Objective 1 section)

key_programme_risks: Limited capacity of DPOs to absorb funds or manage operations (e.g., financial safeguarding)
Exclusion of underrepresented groups (e.g., women, psychosocial disabilities) within DPOs
Fragmentation and lack of coordination in the global disability movement
Closing civic space restricting DPOs’ ability to engage with governments
Political resistance to disability-inclusive policies at national/regional levels
Sustainability of DPOs post-programme without long-term funding
Accessibility barriers (e.g., communication, venues) limiting participation

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited capacity of DPOs to absorb funds or manage operations
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Core funding will include support for financial management, governance training, and safeguarding. Fiscal sponsors and peer-to-peer mentorship will be used to build capacity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Exclusion of underrepresented groups within DPOs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted funding rounds (e.g., 15% for women’s groups) and deliberate outreach to marginalised groups (e.g., youth, psychosocial disabilities).
Invest in coordination mechanisms (e.g., peer learning, GDS Partnership) and align with global frameworks (UNDIS, CRPD).
Support DPOs to navigate political barriers through advocacy training, legal analysis, and strategic engagement with power-holders.
Use international frameworks (CRPD, SDGs) to legitimise advocacy efforts and hold governments accountable through mechanisms like the GDS Partnership.
Build long-term capacity (e.g., financial management, leadership transitions) and foster links with umbrella organisations for ongoing support.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts, DPOs require **additional safeguarding and financial management support** to mitigate risks of mismanagement or exploitation.
Closing civic space necessitates **flexible advocacy strategies**, such as leveraging international commitments (e.g., CRPD Concluding Observations) to legitimise local demands.
Partnerships with **parents’ groups and youth-led movements** can strengthen advocacy in contexts where formal DPOs are weak or excluded.
**Peer-to-peer learning** is critical in FCAS to share context-specific strategies for engaging with governments or navigating political barriers.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
Lessons from the **2017-2020 Disability Catalyst Programme** highlight the effectiveness of:
1. **Core funding** for DPO operations (e.g., financial management, governance) to ensure sustainability.
2. **Targeted support** for underrepresented groups (e.g., women, youth) to improve diversity and inclusion.
3. **Technical training** on advocacy, CRPD implementation, and policy analysis to strengthen DPOs’ influence.
4. **Coordination mechanisms** (e.g., regional networks, peer learning) to reduce fragmentation in the disability movement.
5. **Adaptive management** to respond to evolving contexts (e.g., political changes, emerging priorities).

The programme builds on these lessons by expanding support to **15-20 countries** (up from 8-10) and adding the **Global Support Facility (GSF)** to reach new regions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
Based on lessons from the Disability Catalyst Programme, the new programme includes:
- **Explicit safeguarding requirements** for DPOs (e.g., policies on sexual exploitation and abuse).
- **Earmarked funds** for underrepresented groups (e.g., 15% for women’s groups).
- **Stronger accountability mechanisms** (e.g., GDS Partnership to track commitments).
- **Expanded geographic reach** (GSF to support DPOs in additional countries).
- **Longer-term core funding** to address sustainability gaps identified in previous phases.
risks_lessons.quote: "Many valuable lessons have been learnt from the 2017-2020 Disability Catalyst Programme which will be built into this new programme... Capacity building for DPOs cannot focus solely on the development of advocacy skills to build and grow an effective disability movement." (57281837.odt, Addressing the lack of capacity in DPOs section) && "The last Annual Review of the programme scored an A." (57281837.odt, Introduction section)

co_funding_partners.partner: UN Partnership for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNPRPD)
Global Support Facility (GSF) (delivered by Sightsavers and IDA)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme builds on the **Disability Catalyst Programme (2017-2020)**, which leveraged DFID’s £11.9m investment to support over 300 organisations through DRF. The new programme expands this model to include the GSF and increase geographic reach.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £25m over four years" (57281837.odt, Summary Sheet section) && "This programme will fund the three existing delivery partners of the 2017-2020 Disability Catalyst Programme: (i) the Disability Rights Fund; (ii) the International Disability Alliance (IDA); and (iii) UN Partnership for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It will also fund a new fourth initiative: (iv) the Global Support Facility (GSF)." (57281837.odt, Programme summary section)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Research Institutions in Africa (SRIA)
metadata.quote: "SRIA will strengthen the research systems in DFID partner countries so that both local and donor research investment achieves economic and social impact." (51695038.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "SRIA will invest £20m over 5 years to support the development of thriving research systems in seven DFID partner countries in East and West Africa." (51695038.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SRIA primarily focuses on **capacity building** (strengthening research institutions and systems) with significant elements of **policy influence** (aligning research with national development priorities) and **financing mechanism** (coordinating UK ODA research spend). The programme aims to create systemic change in research ecosystems rather than just generating new evidence or delivering services.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme purpose is unchanged from the original business case. SRIA will strengthen the research systems in DFID partner countries so that both local and donor research investment achieves economic and social impact. It will do this by strengthening the institutions that regulate and shape research in country to ensure that research investment is aligned with national development priorities." (51683326.odt, INFORMATION)

q3_expected_outputs.output: high-quality research aligned with national development priorities
strengthened research sector foundations (recruitment/retention policies, grant management, research communication)
improved UK-partner country research partnerships (more equitable, coherent with national strategies)
national research strategies developed/implemented
q3_expected_outputs.target: 7 countries (Kenya, Ghana, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Nigeria, Tanzania)

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased capacity of research councils/agencies to align funding with national agendas
training/mentoring networks for researchers and administrators
gender equity policies implemented in research institutions
coherence of £4.7bn UK ODA research spend with local priorities

what_objectives.summary: SRIA aims to transform research systems in 7 African countries by strengthening institutional capacity, improving research alignment with development needs, and ensuring UK research investments create sustainable impact rather than extractive outputs.
what_objectives.quote: "The intended impact of SRIA is a thriving national research system which contributes to social and economic development in the countries where the programme operates." (51695038.odt, Impact and Outcomes)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in stable but institutionally weak environments where research systems face governance and capacity challenges. Political economy factors (e.g., elite capture, donor distortions) are explicitly noted as risks, but no active conflict is mentioned.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (51695038.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak research management systems, lack of national funding strategies, and poor IT infrastructure ('last mile internet access') limit collaboration and grant absorption. Donor practices (e.g., preferential funding of elite institutions) distort local priorities. Gender barriers reduce women's participation in research careers.
where_context.quote: "Organisational infrastructure also requires attention. DFID’s work in this area has highlighted the challenges of ‘last mile internet access’ whereby institutions may have access to global research literature via subscriptions to international journals coupled with strong research faculty but these are undermined by weak IT infrastructure and internet access." (51695038.odt, Barriers to Building Effective National Research Systems)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/RED designs the programme and selects the managing agent, which then commissions projects. Southern partners implement activities but have limited strategic decision-making power. The 'strategic fund' allows some Southern-led initiatives if they meet DFID criteria.
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (grant management, research communication)
training/mentoring for researchers and administrators
gender equity policies and implementation support
negotiation/leadership skills for Southern partners
networks linking universities, business, and civil society

partner_organizations.role: implement country/regional projects, manage £12.3m+ of programme funds

partner_organizations.name: Strategic Fund Partners (established non-profits)
partner_organizations.role: deliver emerging initiatives, engagement analysis, learning (up to £6m)

partner_organizations.role: liaise between UK/HMG and African research leaders, align ODA spend

partner_organizations.name: East Africa Research Hub (DFID)
partner_organizations.role: provide regional expertise, support implementation

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: potential co-funder, alignment on research standards

partner_organizations.role: alignment of portfolios, joint initiatives
