who_partners.quote: "The programme will be focussed on countries where there is existing research capacity and where there is considerable UK ODA research activity... SRIA will work strategically with the leads of these programmes to ensure we harness the complementarity and limit any risks of duplication." (51695038.odt, Current UK ODA Investment in Research)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is a **contract** with a managing agent (competitive procurement) for £12.3m+. Additional funds (up to £6m) will use **accountable grants** or **MOUs** for the strategic fund, and **programme-funded posts** (employment contracts) for the coherence unit.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID/RED oversees a **managing agent** (contract) that commissions country/regional projects. A separate **strategic fund** (grants/MOUs) supports emerging initiatives, and a **coherence unit** (2 posts) aligns UK ODA spend. Projects are designed collaboratively by DFID and the managing agent but implemented by local/regional partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition for the managing agent to ensure innovation and value for money. The strategic fund uses restricted competition (established partners only) for speed and reliability. Programme posts are directly recruited by DFID.
how_mechanism.quote: "Our preferred option is Option 1: A programme procured competitively and managed by a third party managing agent." (51695038.odt, Options for Delivery of the Strengthening Building Blocks Component)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Strategic Coherence of ODA Research (SCOR) Board** provides high-level oversight across UK ODA research. DFID will also embed staff in Research Councils UK (RCUK) for coordination. Country-level governance involves DFID offices and regional hubs.
how_governance.quote: "The Strategic Coherence of ODA Research (SCOR) Board has been established to provide a high-level mechanism across all significant Government ODA-funded science and research (including the Wellcome Trust) to ensure the UK has comprehensive offer on research for development, including a coherent approach to ODA compliance." (51695038.odt, Coherence Workstream)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Unused resources from staff programming or the strategic fund can be reallocated to managing agent projects, but core component budgets (e.g., £12.3m for managing agent) appear fixed. Reallocation requires DFID approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes flexibility to respond to political/economic changes and learning, but adjustments require DFID sign-off. The engagement phase (first 6 months) allows for course correction before implementation.
how_flexibility.quote: "The importance of flexible and adaptive programming is emphasised throughout the Business Case... Unused resources allocated to staff programming or the strategic fund may be used to support further projects identified by the managing agent." (51683326.odt, INFORMATION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Managing Agent → Local Implementers (or Strategic Fund Partners). For coherence workstream: FCDO → Programme Posts → Regional Stakeholders.
how_efficiency.quote: "Use of management agent puts DFID staff one step removed from programme delivery. Managing agent adds costs (typically 10-13%) to overall programme spend." (51695038.odt, Options for Delivery)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Competitive open call managed internally by DFID
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Staff time required to administer SRIA would draw resources from other RED demands.
DFID partner countries would not realize full benefits of research investments; UK soft power and development impact would be reduced.
Poor value for money compared to fixed-term posts and lack of authority to engage senior leaders.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: FLD posts in East Africa Research Hub
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Poor VFM due to expensive operating environment; limited FLD resources in RED.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **managing agent model** was selected for its balance of **flexibility** (allowing diverse interventions across 7 countries), **innovation** (open competition taps wider market than traditional UK research providers), and **efficiency** (freeing DFID staff for other priorities). The **strategic fund** enables rapid support for emerging initiatives, while **programme posts** ensure coherence with UK ODA spend. This structure addresses the need for both **systemic change** (institutional strengthening) and **political alignment** (coherence with national priorities).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Managing agent adds 10-13% overhead costs, reducing funds for direct delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Competitive procurement to ensure cost-effectiveness; clear performance management against DFID smart guides.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: DFID staff are "one step removed" from delivery, potentially reducing oversight.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Milestone-based oversight, SCOR Board governance, and embedded coherence unit to maintain alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Strategic fund partners may lack capacity to manage DFID funds.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Restrict eligibility to established non-profits with track records; use accountable grants with performance clauses.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coherence workstream posts may be co-opted by host organization priorities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear terms of reference linked to regional development needs; no more than 20% time for host organization tasks.

why_rationale.quote: "Our preferred option is Option 1: A programme procured competitively and managed by a third party managing agent... This approach would allow us to tap into a wider market than existing UK research providers." (51695038.odt, Options for Delivery)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **multi-country scope** and **moderate-risk contexts** limit partner selection to organizations with: (1) **regional presence** (managing agent must operate across 7 countries), (2) **track records in FCAS-adjacent environments** (though no active conflict, institutional weakness requires experienced partners), and (3) **ability to navigate political economy challenges** (e.g., elite capture, donor distortions). Local NGOs/SMEs can bid for country-specific lots but must meet DFID due diligence standards.
q27_constraints_detail: Multi-country operations require partners with regional networks (limits small local NGOs).
Weak institutional capacity in some countries necessitates established intermediaries.
Donor coordination gaps (e.g., lack of national research strategies) demand partners skilled in stakeholder alignment.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **systemic change objective** (strengthening entire research ecosystems) necessitates a **multi-layered structure**: (1) **Managing agent** for scalable, standardized interventions (e.g., grant management training), (2) **Strategic fund** for context-specific, emergent needs (e.g., gender equity policies), and (3) **Coherence unit** to align UK ODA spend with local priorities. The **political economy focus** (e.g., engaging ministries, research councils) requires embedded posts rather than arm’s-length grants.
q28_linkages: Systemic outcomes → Fund manager model (managing agent can coordinate across institutions).
Flexibility needs → Strategic fund for responsive, non-competitive support.
UK ODA coherence → Dedicated posts to bridge HMG and African stakeholders.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Strategic fund restricts eligibility to established partners for rapid disbursement, potentially excluding innovative local actors. (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: Managing agent model risks Northern-led implementation, mitigated by requiring Southern participation in projects and local market engagement. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Programme posts offer deep engagement but are expensive; managing agent adds overhead but enables scale.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Established partners prioritized for strategic fund (speed) vs. open competition (inclusion).
Managing agent efficiency (standardized delivery) vs. local ownership (context-specific adaptation).
Programme posts (high touch) vs. grants (lower cost but less control).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (institutional weakness, political economy challenges) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and **embedded coherence posts** rather than light-touch management. DFID retains approval authority for fund reallocations and priority adjustments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives (e.g., grant management, gender equity) directly shape partner roles: (1) **Managing agent** must demonstrate capacity to strengthen institutional systems (not just deliver research). (2) **Strategic fund partners** are selected based on track records in equity-focused interventions (e.g., women’s participation). (3) **Coherence posts** require skills in negotiating with both HMG and African leaders.
intersections.quote: "The programme will be focussed on countries where there is existing research capacity and where there is considerable UK ODA research activity... The key and most persistent weakness is the lack of national research funding strategies and varying capacity to formulate and drive research agendas." (51695038.odt, Research and Innovation in Africa)

key_programme_risks: Elite capture: Donor practices may reinforce inequalities by funding elite institutions.
Extractive partnerships: Northern institutions may dominate research benefits.
Sustainability: Systemic changes require long-term commitment beyond 5 years.
Political shifts: Changes in government priorities could disrupt alignment.
Coordination gaps: UK ODA research may remain misaligned with local needs without active management.
Gender barriers: Structural challenges limit women’s participation in research careers.
IT infrastructure: ‘Last mile’ internet access undermines collaboration and data sharing.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Target consortia of institutions (not just top universities) and require equitable participation policies.
Support Research Fairness Initiative; require Southern co-leadership in projects.
Focus on embedding changes in existing institutions (e.g., research councils) with domestic buy-in.
Engage senior leaders during inception phase; flexible programme design to adapt to changes.
Dedicated coherence unit and SCOR Board to align UK ODA spend with local priorities.
Require gender equity policies in all projects; monitor participation statistics.
Support bandwidth management and connectivity improvements on campus networks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid FCAS contexts where instability undermines systemic interventions (SRIA explicitly excludes fragile states).
In moderate-risk environments, focus on countries with existing capacity and political intent (e.g., Kenya’s 0.79% GDP R&D investment).
Use regional hubs (e.g., East Africa Research Hub) to navigate political economy challenges.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID programmes (e.g., DRUSSA, PERI) showed that: (1) Training individuals without institutional support fails to create systemic change. (2) Donor coordination is critical to avoid duplication (e.g., alignment with Wellcome Trust, SIDA). (3) Collective negotiation (e.g., library consortia saving £79m across 17 countries) achieves greater impact than isolated interventions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: SRIA’s design reflects lessons by: (1) **Focusing on institutions** (not just individuals), (2) **Prioritizing coherence** (dedicated workstream and posts), (3) **Using flexible funding** (strategic fund for emergent needs), and (4) **Embedding gender equity** as a core requirement.
risks_lessons.quote: "SRIA will go beyond providing excellent training to individuals as our experience has shown that this is not enough if those individuals are located in dysfunctional institutions and systems." (51695038.odt, How SRIA Will Support Research Systems)

co_funding_partners.partner: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (via CARI)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: SRIA aims to improve the impact of £4.7bn UK ODA research spend (GCRF, Ross Fund, Newton Fund, DFID commitments) by aligning it with local priorities. No explicit leverage targets are stated.
financial_details.quote: "The total cost of the programme is £20m... SRIA will spend £18m to strengthen the building blocks of research systems in seven DFID priority countries over 5 years... and £2m to deliver the coherence workstream." (51695038.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: DueDiligenceHub
metadata.duration_text: July 2019 to March 2023 (original); extended to 30 June 2025 (revised)

quote.programme_name: "The programme would establish a new Due Diligence Hub to reform DFID’s approach to due diligence" (D0005709.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.duration_original: "Start Date: July 2019; End Date: March 2023" (D0005709.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.sector: "Duediligence is one of the core tools in DFID’s overall risk management framework" (D0005709.odt, main text)

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: July 2019; End Date: March 2023" (D0005709.odt) and "Extended to 30/06/2025" (D0006823.odt)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes a Due Diligence Hub to improve the quality, use, and efficiency of due diligence processes across DFID/FCDO. It focuses on strengthening internal capabilities (both first-line programme teams and second-line central functions) to better assess and manage risks associated with delivery partners, while reducing duplication of effort.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme would establish a new Due Diligence Hub to reform DFID’s approach to due diligence, improving: the quality of due diligence assessments; programme teams’ insight into their partners’ capacity and capability to deliver, and their follow through on due diligence findings as part of programme delivery and risk management; and the efficiency of the due diligence process by reducing duplication of effort." (D0005709.odt, SummarySheet)
q3_expected_outputs: Improved quality of due diligence assessments (technical rigour and development insight)
Increased use of due diligence assessments to inform programme risk management
Improved process efficiency in delivery of due diligence (reduced duplication of effort)
A coherent approach to due diligence across grants, MoUs, and contracts
Stronger capability and capacity within first-line programme teams and second-line central functions
More effective and efficient outsourcing of due diligence
More effective knowledge management and growth of internal skills
6 central due diligence assessments of NGOs per year (under mixed model)
100 due diligence assessments on contracts per year (under mixed model)
High-quality external partner risk assessments (HQAs, CAAs, integrity checks) delivered via third-party providers
what_objectives.summary: The Due Diligence Hub aims to reform DFID/FCDO's due diligence processes by improving assessment quality, enhancing risk management, and increasing efficiency through centralized support, training, and reduced duplication. It combines internal capacity-building with selective outsourcing to address gaps in expertise.

quote.objectives: "To achieve value for money for the taxpayer, we add a third objective: Objective 3: Increase the efficiency of the due diligence process by reducing duplication of effort." (D0005709.odt, main text)
quote.outputs: "The main outcomes of the intervention would be improved quality of due diligence assessments, increased use of due diligence assessments to inform programme risk management and improved process efficiency in the delivery of due diligence." (D0005709.odt, main text)
quote.addendum_outputs: "The programme budget is used to fund partner risk assessments using a third-party provider, to fill gaps in expertise and capacity for conducting a range of partner risk assessments including HQAs, CAAs, strategic high risk DDAs and organisational integrity checks." (D0006823.odt, Detailed information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme itself is classified as 'moderate' risk, but it operates in contexts where DFID/FCDO increasingly works in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), which elevates the importance of robust due diligence. The hub aims to mitigate risks of aid diversion and terrorist financing by improving financial management assessments and follow-through.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0005709.odt, SummarySheet) and "As DFID increasingly operates in fragile and conflict affected states, our approach to programme delivery and risk management grows more sophisticated, and public expectations of our capacity to hold partners accountable grows, so does our reliance on robust due diligence assessments." (D0005709.odt, main text)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates in contexts where DFID/FCDO works in fragile and conflict-affected states, requiring sophisticated risk management. Weak institutional capacity of partners and limited data availability (e.g., financial records, safeguarding policies) necessitate robust due diligence to prevent aid diversion and ensure accountability. The hub addresses these constraints by centralizing expertise and improving knowledge-sharing.

quote.fcas: "As DFID increasingly operates in fragile and conflict affected states, our approach to programme delivery and risk management grows more sophisticated, and public expectations of our capacity to hold partners accountable grows, so does our reliance on robust due diligence assessments." (D0005709.odt, main text)
quote.constraints: "Duediligence is one of the core tools in DFID’s overall risk management framework, helping to identify and manage risks that could threaten the effective use of funds, and one of the most highly relied upon programme controls for obtaining assurance." (D0005709.odt, main text)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making power rests with FCDO/BDD (UK-based), which designs the due diligence framework, manages the central hub, and oversees outsourced assessments. Programme teams (global) retain ownership of partner-specific assessments but operate under centralized guidance and quality assurance.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (blended learning packages for programme managers)
mentorship (duediligence partners support programme teams through assessments)
institutional-strengthening (centralized knowledge management, quality assurance processes)
technical assistance (outsourced expertise for high-risk assessments)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Better Delivery Department (BDD)
partner_organizations.role: Lead institution; policy and framework development; central hub management; quality assurance

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Procurement and Commercial Department (PCD)
partner_organizations.role: Due diligence for commercial contracts; supplier code of conduct; collaboration on framework refresh

partner_organizations.name: Third-party provider (via X-HMG contract managed by DESNZ)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of high-quality external partner risk assessments (HQAs, CAAs, integrity checks)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Programme Teams (global)
partner_organizations.role: First-line due diligence assessments for grants/MoUs; implementation of hub guidance

partner_organizations.name: Internal Audit Department (IAD)
partner_organizations.role: Assurance reviews of due diligence processes

partner_organizations.name: Safeguarding Unit (SGU)
partner_organizations.role: Input on enhanced safeguarding due diligence

quote.structure: "The hub would be a medium-sized central unit which brings together BDD and PCD resource." (D0005709.odt, Option 3)
quote.capacity_building: "A comprehensive due diligence blended learning (online plus face-to-face) package is developed as part of the new BDD training offer to reach our programme network." (D0005709.odt, Table 2)
quote.addendum_partners: "The programme budget is used to fund partner risk assessments using a third-party provider, to fill gaps in expertise and capacity for conducting a range of partner risk assessments including HQAs, CAAs, strategic high risk DDAs and organisational integrity checks." (D0006823.odt, Detailed information)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of internal FCDO funding (TOC and programme funds) for the central hub and a **commercial framework agreement** (X-HMG contract managed by DESNZ) for outsourcing high-risk partner assessments. Programme teams retain discretionary funds for localized due diligence needs, but the hub centralizes strategic assessments and quality assurance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Due Diligence Hub operates as a **centralized platform** within FCDO, integrating resources from BDD and PCD. It provides shared services (training, quality assurance, knowledge management) to programme teams globally while managing outsourced assessments via a commercial framework. The hub acts as a virtual team during inception, transitioning to a unified management structure in delivery phase.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The third-party provider was selected via a **cross-HMG framework agreement** (Lot 21 of the International Multi-Disciplinary Programme, managed by DESNZ) to ensure pre-vetted suppliers with verified technical skills. This approach reduces procurement lead times (from 6–9 months to 1–2 weeks) and guarantees quality through pre-agreed rates and DFID-approved suppliers.

quote.instrument: "The call-downs for the Due Diligence Hub can access the new International Multi-Disciplinary Programme (IMDP) framework under lot 21 statistics and data." (D0005709.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.structure: "The hub would be a medium-sized central unit which brings together BDD and PCD resource... working towards an integrated operating model over the longer run." (D0005709.odt, Option 3)
quote.selection: "Option a. [IMDP framework] is the preferred option, as this provides access to a set of DFID approved suppliers." (D0005709.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.addendum_selection: "The existing provider was commissioned through a X-HMG contract managed by DESNZ." (D0006823.odt, Detailed information)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Governance is provided by: 1) **FCDO’s corporate structure** (Audit and Risk Assurance Committee; Investment Committee via Programme Cycle Committee); 2) **SRO oversight** (BDD Head of Risk as Senior Responsible Owner); and 3) **matrix management** during inception (dotted-line relationships between BDD/PCD staff). The hub reports into the Centre for Delivery (CfD) post-merger.

quote.management: "During the inception phase, the Due Diligence Hub would be made up of BDD and PCD staff working in alignment as part of a virtual team, reporting in through departmental line management chains, but with dotted line objective management relationships which cross departmental boundaries." (D0005709.odt, Delivery Phase)
quote.governance: "DFID’s corporate governance structure would provide governance oversight, notably: The Audit and Risk Assurance Committee... and The Investment Committee." (D0005709.odt, Governance)
quote.oversight: "During the inception phase, we will report against process indicators, focusing on: Design of the refreshed framework; Development and sign-off of a final resourcing model; Development of role profiles; and Achievement of commercial milestones to establishing a central contract." (D0005709.odt, Monitoring)
quote.addendum_governance: "The existing SRO and PRO based within CfD will continue to manage the programme." (D0006823.odt, Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between hub components (e.g., training vs. outsourcing) with approval, but the commercial framework budget is ring-fenced. The 2023 addendum notes no new work will be commissioned during the extension period, focusing only on completing already-contracted assessments.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The hub is designed to adapt to demand fluctuations via the **commercial framework** (call-down contracts for external support) and **phased implementation**. However, major changes (e.g., new assessments during the extension period) require explicit approval, as seen in the 2023 addendum restricting new commissions.

quote.reallocation: "The hub will hold the budget for the call-down contracts and manage the commissioning." (D0005709.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.adaptive: "The use of draw down the contract to provide additional resources to deliver DDAs will help mitigate this risk [of bottlenecks]." (D0005709.odt, Efficiency)
quote.addendum_flexibility: "Nonew work will be commissioned during the extension period." (D0006823.odt, Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (BDD/PCD) → **Due Diligence Hub** (central unit + outsourced providers) → **Programme Teams** (global). The hub consolidates what was previously fragmented (individual teams procuring due diligence independently).

quote.budget: "We estimate the total costs of these additional investments at £3,181,831 over a 3.75 year period." (D0005709.odt, Financial Case)
quote.layers: "The hub would be a medium-sized central unit which brings together BDD and PCD resource... supporting programme teams across the network." (D0005709.odt, Option 3)
quote.payment: "The call-downs will therefore be much less burdensome and will significantly reduce the overall lead times from a typical procurement processes of 6-9 months down to possibly 1-2 weeks to agree a terms of reference and issue a contract." (D0005709.odt, Theory of Change)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Strengthen our decentralised delivery model (empowered accountability with minimal central uplift)
Option 2: Centralise and outsource delivery of due diligence (full outsourcing to consultants)
Option 3: Establish a mixed model (central hub + programme team partnership + outsourcing for high-risk gaps) - **CHOSEN**
Do nothing (discounted due to risk of false assurance)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **mixed model (Option 3)** was selected for its balance of **effectiveness** (improved quality via central expertise + programme team insight), **efficiency** (reduced duplication through shared framework and knowledge management), and **equity** (retaining programme team ownership while addressing capability gaps). It avoids the high costs of full outsourcing (Option 2) and the uneven quality risks of pure decentralization (Option 1).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partners under the commercial framework may not invest sufficient effort or lack understanding of FCDO’s operating environment, leading to poor-quality due diligence.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Effective commercial and contract management throughout the programme cycle, including quality assurance processes and pre-vetted suppliers via the IMDP framework.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The partnership model with programme teams may prove challenging to implement, failing to deliver anticipated quality improvements or creating delivery bottlenecks.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Recruitment of due diligence partners with technical capabilities and soft skills; building continuous improvement into delivery; internal communications to sustain buy-in; and a phased 25% quality assurance process.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Departments may reduce programme teams’ capacity to lead due diligence, making the partnership model unworkable.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Effective communications, process design, and input to strategic workforce planning to ensure programme teams retain ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to identify the right technology/knowledge management solution, weakening efficiency gains.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engage technology specialists to support decision-making and test solutions prior to roll-out (e.g., State of Flux and Maplecroft systems).

quote.alternatives: "We have appraised each option using the ‘4Es’ framework (Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness, Equity)." (D0005709.odt, Appraisal)
quote.why_chosen: "Option 3 (mixed model) stands out as the best value for money option, outperforming option 1 on effectiveness, efficiency and equity." (D0005709.odt, Summary Value for Money)
quote.risks: "Effective commercial and contract management through out the programme cycle." (D0005709.odt, Table 7: Risks and Mitigations)
quote.vfm: "The additional input costs of option 3 (mixed model) are higher, this is justified by the return: substantial gap between the two options in terms of effectiveness... greater reduction in duplication of effort." (D0005709.odt, Summary Value for Money)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s **global scope** and focus on **fragile/conflict-affected states** constrain partner selection by requiring suppliers with **verified technical skills in high-risk contexts** (e.g., safeguarding, financial integrity). This led to the use of a **pre-approved HMG framework** (IMDP) to ensure quality and reduce procurement delays.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for suppliers with experience in FCAS (fragile and conflict-affected states)
Requirement for pre-vetted providers to meet DFID/FCDO’s safeguarding and fiduciary standards
Limited pool of partners capable of delivering high-risk assessments (e.g., HQAs, integrity checks) at scale
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for both technical rigour and contextual insight** in due diligence assessments shaped the **mixed delivery model**. Centralized expertise (hub + outsourced providers) addresses technical gaps, while programme team involvement ensures assessments reflect local partner contexts. The **phased quality assurance** (25% under mixed model vs. 10% under decentralized) directly responds to the objective of improving assessment quality.
q28_linkages: Objective 1 (improve quality) → Mixed model with central QA and outsourced expertise for high-risk assessments
Objective 2 (programme team insight) → Retained programme team leadership with hub support
Objective 3 (reduce duplication) → Centralized knowledge management (State of Flux) and shared commercial framework
FCAS context → Framework agreement to ensure supplier capability in high-risk settings
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between **centralization (efficiency)** and **programme team ownership (equity/insight)**. The mixed model was chosen to balance these: centralizing **repetitive/high-risk assessments** (e.g., NGO HQAs) for efficiency while keeping programme teams engaged in **partner-specific assessments** for contextual insight. The 2023 addendum reinforces this by restricting new commissions to avoid over-centralization.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Centralization vs. local ownership: Hub manages 6 NGO HQAs/year centrally, but programme teams lead local assessments
Outsourcing vs. internal capacity: External providers fill technical gaps, but hub invests in training programme teams
Standardization vs. flexibility: Shared framework reduces duplication but allows tailored assessments via call-down contracts
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** and FCAS operating context justify **milestone-based oversight** (e.g., inception phase process indicators, annual reviews) and **matrix governance** (BDD/PCD collaboration). High-risk areas (e.g., safeguarding, financial integrity) receive intensified scrutiny via centralized assessments and 25% QA coverage.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives (training, mentorship) shape partner roles by: 1) **Empowering programme teams** to lead assessments with hub support (e.g., duediligence partners embedded in first-line); 2) **Upskilling via blended learning** to reduce reliance on outsourcing; and 3) **Quality assurance feedback loops** to iteratively improve team capabilities.

quote.context_who: "Option a. [IMDP framework] is the preferred option, as this provides access to a set of DFID approved suppliers." (D0005709.odt, Theory of Change) and "The existing provider was commissioned through a X-HMG contract managed by DESNZ." (D0006823.odt, Detailed information)
quote.what_how: "The mixed model would improve quality by incorporating internal due diligence partners into the first line, who would work in partnership with programme teams to deliver due diligence assessments." (D0005709.odt, Option 3)

quote.capacity_roles: "Duediligence partners would manage a central contract, allowing programme teams access to deliver due diligence assessments in high-risk settings and access specialist technical advice." (D0005709.odt, Option 3)

key_programme_risks: Spending Review negotiations may not deliver additional resources, requiring redesign (external context)
Commercial framework partners may deliver poor-quality due diligence (delivery risk)
Partnership model with programme teams may fail to improve quality or create bottlenecks (operational risk)
Inability to secure staff with the right capabilities (operational risk)
Departments may reduce programme teams’ capacity, undermining the model (operational risk)
Staff motivation may decline due to changing roles (operational risk)
Failure to identify the right technology for knowledge management (operational risk)
Hub may insufficiently prioritize safeguarding or fiduciary risks (safeguarding/fiduciary risk)
Hub may fail to meet partner/programme team expectations on timelines (reputational risk)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Spending Review negotiations fail to deliver resources
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Effective engagement with FPD colleagues to ensure hub is considered in Spending Review negotiations.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Commercial framework partners deliver poor-quality work
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Effective commercial and contract management; pre-vetted suppliers via IMDP framework; quality assurance processes.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Partnership model proves challenging or creates bottlenecks
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Recruit due diligence partners with technical and soft skills; build continuous improvement into delivery; internal comms for buy-in; 25% QA coverage.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Unable to secure staff with right capabilities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Robust recruitment process with outreach; clear role profiles; effective leadership change management.
Effective comms, process design, and input to strategic workforce planning.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Staff motivation affected by role changes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Effective leadership change management and line management.
Engage technology specialists for decision-making and pre-rollout testing.
Ensure safeguarding is reflected in framework refresh; engage Safeguarding Unit (SGU).
Ensure fiduciary risk is reflected in framework refresh; engage Financial Control Department (FCD).
Effective project management; change management; internal/partner comms; continuous improvement.

fcas_specific_lessons: Centralized assessments (e.g., NGO HQAs) are critical in FCAS to ensure consistent standards where local capacity is weak.
Outsourced expertise must be **pre-vetted** for FCAS contexts to avoid delays (e.g., via IMDP framework).
Knowledge management systems (e.g., State of Flux) must accommodate **fragmented data** from high-risk partners.
Safeguarding due diligence requires **specialized providers** given heightened risks in FCAS (e.g., sexual exploitation, terrorist financing).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous decentralized due diligence processes suffered from **uneven quality**, **duplication of effort**, and **limited follow-through** on risks. The hub was designed to address these by centralizing quality assurance (25% coverage), reducing duplication via shared frameworks, and embedding learning loops (e.g., QA feedback to training).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **Option 1 (decentralized)** to **Option 3 (mixed model)** to address quality inconsistencies.
Introduction of **central NGO HQ assessments** to provide a baseline for local teams.
Use of **commercial framework (IMDP)** to reduce procurement delays (from 6–9 months to 1–2 weeks).
Phased implementation with **inception period** to test resourcing and governance before full rollout.
2023 addendum **restricted new commissions** during extension to focus on completing high-quality assessments.

metadata.programme_name: Project Soteria: stopping perpetrators of sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment from working in the aid sector
metadata.quote: "Project Soteria" is a joint initiative between the UK Department for International Development (DFID), the International Criminal Police Organization INTERPOL and the UK’s ACRO Criminal Records Office to support organisations in the aid sector to stop perpetrators of sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH) from working in the aid sector via more and better criminal records checks on staff. (47927966.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 25/6/2019–30/4/2021" and "New project end date (if applicable): April 2025" (D0000809.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Project Soteria combines **capacity building** (strengthening criminal records systems and law enforcement capabilities), **technology development** (piloting an online platform for background checks), **implementation research** (testing and scaling the platform and investigative support), and **service delivery** (direct operational support for SEAH investigations). The core goal is to prevent perpetrators of SEAH from working in the aid sector by improving vetting and information-sharing mechanisms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Project Soteria aims to stop perpetrators of sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH) from working in the aid sector. DFID will fund INTERPOL and ACRO to carry out more and better criminal records checks on staff." (47927966.odt, Narrative summary) AND "The project will now move from an inception phase to its implementation phase... Capacity Building for Law Enforcement; Information Sharing and Notices; Criminal Analysis and Investigative Support; AssistancetotheAidSector; Threat Identification Scheme (TIS) Pilot; Digital Solutions." (D0000809.odt, Describe any key changes)
q3_expected_outputs: Online platform for criminal records checks (pilot → scale)
Two regional hubs (Africa and Asia) with 7-9 specialists supporting national criminal bureaus
INTERPOL Green and Purple Notices to disseminate intelligence on SEAH offenders
Centralized criminal analysis to identify patterns of SEAH in the aid sector
Threat Identification Scheme (TIS) pilot for selected aid organizations
Global Knowledge Hub platform for non-operational data sharing
Training and capacity building for law enforcement on SEAH prevention
Operational support for SEAH investigations in high-priority countries
Feasibility study on legal/technical aspects of the platform (completed in Phase 1)
what_objectives.summary: Project Soteria is a **multi-component initiative** to deter and detect SEAH perpetrators in the aid sector through **criminal records checks, law enforcement capacity building, and global information-sharing**. It combines **technological innovation** (online platform), **institutional strengthening** (regional hubs, training), and **direct investigative support** to create a systemic barrier against abusers.
what_objectives.quote: "The project has three main components: 1) An online platform to strengthen background checks on staff; 2) Capacity building of national crime agencies via two regional hubs; 3) Analytical and Operational support for investigations on SEAH." (47927966.odt, Programme Summary) AND "Soteria aims to enhance the capacity of law enforcement to use more effectively criminal record keeping to manage sex offenders as well as increase their awareness on the issue of sexual abuse in the context of aid work." (D0000809.odt, Describe any key changes)

countries_regions: Two regional hubs: Africa and Asia (specific countries not named)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **fragile environments** where aid workers interact with vulnerable populations, and targets **criminal SEAH**, which involves sensitive law enforcement cooperation across jurisdictions with varying legal frameworks. The risk of harm to survivors and data protection challenges are explicitly flagged.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (47927966.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Aid organisations employ highly mobile international staff to work in fragile environments, delivering development and humanitarian assistance to some of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable people." (47927966.odt, Programme Summary) AND "A full risk assessment will be undertaken in the first quarter of the programme... risks related to survivor participation, risk of doing further harm to the survivor, the protection of personal and police data." (47927966.odt, Management Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (willingness of member countries to participate)
weak institutions (capacity of national criminal bureaus in high-risk countries)
data limitations (scalability of criminal records systems)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory and legal constraints may **delay or block** the sharing of criminal records data across borders, while weak institutional capacity in target countries could **limit the effectiveness of training and system upgrades**. Political resistance from member states could **undermine the global platform’s adoption**.
where_context.quote: "INTERPOL will examine national data protection limitations and rules, existing national certification schemes, and the scalability of the project." (47927966.odt, Management Case) AND "Feasibility study suggests that Interpol’s member countries will not support the platform" (listed as a major risk). (47927966.odt, Risk Matrix)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with **DFID (UK)/INTERPOL (global)**. While the project includes capacity building for Southern law enforcement, the **governance (Advisory Board), funding control, and strategic direction** are held by Northern entities (DFID, ACRO, Home Office). Southern partners (national criminal bureaus) provide input but do not lead.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for national criminal bureaus on criminal records management
Support to strengthen information-sharing capabilities via INTERPOL tools
Awareness-raising on SEAH in aid sector contexts
Pilot of Threat Identification Scheme (TIS) with selected aid organizations
Technical assistance to apply INTERPOL’s databases and notices (e.g., Green/Purple Notices)

partner_organizations.name: INTERPOL
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer; provides global law enforcement coordination, regional hubs, investigative support, and platform development

partner_organizations.name: ACRO Criminal Records Office (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Technical partner; contributes expertise on criminal records checks (e.g., International Child Protection Certificate) and policy alignment with UK disclosure laws

partner_organizations.name: UK Home Office
partner_organizations.role: Policy and technical support; ensures alignment with UK sexual offences legislation and law enforcement priorities

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Advisory role; provides operational advice on criminal investigations and data-sharing

partner_organizations.name: National Central Bureaus (NCBs) of INTERPOL member countries (Africa/Asia)
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation; receive capacity building and share criminal records data

partner_organizations.name: Selected aid sector organizations (pilot phase)
partner_organizations.role: Test Threat Identification Scheme (TIS) and provide feedback on platform usability

partner_organizations.name: Survivors of SEAH and women’s rights organizations
partner_organizations.role: Advisory group members; inform project design to mitigate harm and retraumatization

who_partners.quote: "INTERPOL will assign a project manager and a project assistant to oversee the delivery of the programme, who will supervise, manage and coordinate between Interpol’s units, National Central Bureaus, Regional Bureaus, National Police Units, NGOs, Criminal Intelligence officers, and other actors." (47927966.odt, Management Case) AND "The programme will be overseen by a Project Advisory Board which will include INTERPOL, ACRO and DFID." (47927966.odt, Management Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: A **Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)** was established with INTERPOL, bypassing open competition due to INTERPOL’s **unique global mandate and existing infrastructure**. The MOU outlines roles, accountability, and governance, with DFID providing block funding for agreed activities. This instrument was chosen for **speed and alignment with INTERPOL’s operational model**.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by a **closed partnership** between DFID, INTERPOL, and ACRO, with **no open calls for additional partners**. INTERPOL acts as the primary implementer, while DFID retains oversight via a **Project Advisory Board** and regular reporting. The Home Office and NCA provide technical input but are not formal consortium members.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: INTERPOL was selected via **direct award** due to its **uniqueness**: no other organization has the **global reach (194 member countries), existing criminal databases (I-24/7 system), and law enforcement coordination mandate** required. Replicating its capabilities was deemed **cost-prohibitive and time-consuming**. The decision was endorsed by the UK Home Office.
how_mechanism.quote: "Given this, we do not propose to put out an open tender to market for the delivery of this project, but will establish an MOU with INTERPOL, in line with commercial advice from DFID’s Procurement and Commercial Department." (47927966.odt, Commercial Case) AND "It would be difficult if not impossible to replicate the scale and competencies of INTERPOL." (47927966.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Project Advisory Board** includes **INTERPOL, ACRO, and DFID**, meeting **twice yearly** to review progress. INTERPOL also convenes **two working groups**: 1) Aid sector organizations + survivors (focus: safeguarding); 2) National Central Bureaus (focus: legal/technical challenges). Decisions are made jointly, with DFID retaining **final approval authority** for major changes.
how_governance.quote: "The programme will be overseen by a Project Advisory Board which will include INTERPOL, ACRO and DFID. The Board will meet twice a year to review progress, with ad hoc engagement on risk management as needed." (47927966.odt, Management Case) AND "Monthly INTERPOL internal project boards, the bi-weekly FCDO Project management meetings and the quarterly advisory board." (D0000809.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be **reallocated between components** (e.g., platform development vs. capacity building) **with Project Board approval**, but major shifts require **DFID sign-off**. The adaptive approach allows adjustments based on feasibility study findings.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an **"adaptive approach"**: operational strands (e.g., regional hubs) run **in parallel with feasibility work**, allowing real-time adjustments. If the platform proves unviable, the **entire programme may be reconsidered**. The **Theory of Change** was revised post-inception phase to reflect learning.
how_flexibility.quote: "This will be an adaptive project and our agreement with INTERPOL will allow for sufficient flexibility to adjust its course as required." (47927966.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "Decisions about the shape or focus of the initiative will be taken by the Project Board... based on the evidence generated by the operational and feasibility components." (47927966.odt, Intervention Summary) AND "A Theory of Change for the implementation phase has also been developed and agreed with FCDO." (D0000809.odt, Describe any key changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → INTERPOL (implementer) → **National Central Bureaus/aid organizations** (end users). No additional intermediaries are involved.
how_efficiency.quote: "Quarterly financial and information reports will be submitted by INTERPOL to DFID to be reviewed by the programme manager." (47927966.odt, Financial Case) AND "DFID funding will allow INTERPOL rapidly to set up and pilot a new approach... Without this funding there would be significant delays." (47927966.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rejected: high long-term costs of inaction)
Individual bilateral interventions (rejected: inefficient, high transaction costs, poor scalability)
Working through INTERPOL (selected: unique global reach, low start-up costs, existing infrastructure)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: INTERPOL was chosen for its **unparalleled global mandate** (194 member countries), **existing criminal databases** (I-24/7 system), and **low start-up costs** (no need to build new infrastructure). The **speed of implementation** and **potential for scalability** were critical, given the urgent need to address SEAH. The **value-for-money** case was strongest due to INTERPOL’s ability to leverage existing systems (e.g., Notices, Command Centre) and avoid duplication.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (cost-efficiency of using INTERPOL’s existing systems)
partner-capacity (INTERPOL’s unique competencies in cross-border law enforcement)
speed (rapid deployment vs. years to build alternatives)
flexibility (adaptive design to respond to feasibility findings)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of political will from INTERPOL member countries to engage with the platform
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: INTERPOL and DFID will **monitor political will** and engage key stakeholders (e.g., NGOs, donor countries). A working group with National Central Bureaus will address country-specific concerns.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Feasibility study finds the online platform is not achievable or requires significant redesign
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adopt an **adaptive approach**: run operational strands (e.g., regional hubs) in parallel with feasibility work, or **reconsider programme viability** if insurmountable barriers are identified.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow disbursement of funds undermines programme delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain **constructive financial oversight** through standard monitoring/evaluation procedures and quarterly reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in hiring specialist staff
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: INTERPOL will **proactively seek specialists internally and externally** to avoid bottlenecks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Project activities retraumatize survivors or do further harm
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: INTERPOL will establish a **working group with survivors and women’s rights organizations** to design safeguards and mitigate risks.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (low start-up costs by leveraging INTERPOL’s existing systems)
efficiency (improved information-sharing reduces duplication of efforts)
effectiveness (expected increase in arrests/convictions and deterrence of SEAH perpetrators)
equity (focus on protecting vulnerable groups, especially women/girls with disabilities)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 3: The preferred option is therefore to work through INTERPOL which we assess is the only organisation with the global reach and relationships required to deliver this project... Because it already has the structures and mechanisms in place to deliver this programme, the start-up costs are low and it can deliver results early on." (47927966.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "This option represents the best value for money and most efficient way to deliver the desired outcome." (47927966.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global, high-risk context** (fragile environments, varying legal frameworks) **limits partner selection to organizations with pre-existing cross-border mandates**. INTERPOL was the **only viable lead** due to its **universal membership (194 countries)** and **secure data-sharing protocols**, which are essential for operating in jurisdictions with weak institutions or political resistance.
q27_constraints_detail: Legal barriers (data protection laws vary by country, requiring INTERPOL’s expertise to navigate)
Institutional weakness (national criminal bureaus in high-risk countries lack capacity, necessitating INTERPOL’s training role)
Political sensitivity (SEAH investigations require neutral, multilateral coordination to avoid backlash)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for global criminal records checks** (WHAT) **dictated a centralized, multilateral delivery structure** (HOW). The **three components** (platform, capacity building, investigations) required: 1) **INTERPOL’s databases** for the platform; 2) **regional hubs** for localized training; 3) **law enforcement coordination** for investigations. This **rules out decentralized or bilateral models**.
q28_linkages: Online platform (global reach) → INTERPOL’s I-24/7 system (existing infrastructure)
Capacity building (localized) → Regional hubs in Africa/Asia (INTERPOL’s NCBs)
Investigative support (cross-border) → INTERPOL’s Notices and Command Centre (global coordination)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme **prioritizes efficiency** (rapid global rollout via INTERPOL) **over deep localization**, which could have involved more Southern-led institutions but at the cost of **speed and scalability**. The **trade-off** is acknowledged in the **survivor participation safeguards** and **working groups with NCBs**, but **decision-making remains Northern-led**.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion (INTERPOL’s existing systems enable quick launch but limit Southern ownership)
Global reach vs. context-specific adaptation (platform design may not fully align with all national legal systems)
Cost vs. equity (sole-source award to INTERPOL maximizes VfM but reduces opportunities for local partners)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk profile** (Major rating) **justifies intensive oversight**: quarterly Advisory Board meetings, monthly INTERPOL internal reviews, and bi-weekly FCDO check-ins. The **adaptive management** approach (e.g., parallel feasibility/operational work) is a direct response to **legal/technical uncertainties** in the operating context.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building objective** (core to the programme) **defines partner roles**: INTERPOL leads **training and system upgrades** for NCBs, while aid organizations are **limited to pilot testing** (TIS) due to their **lack of law enforcement mandate**. Survivors inform **safeguarding design** but do not manage implementation.
intersections.quote: "Because it already has the structures and mechanisms in place to deliver this programme, the start-up costs are low and it can deliver results early on." (47927966.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "INTERPOL will examine national data protection limitations and rules, existing national certification schemes, and the scalability of the project." (47927966.odt, Management Case) AND "The programme will seek to ensure thorough participation in the design and inception phase from survivors and/or women’s rights organisations to mitigate this risk." (47927966.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Lack of political will from INTERPOL member countries to engage
Feasibility study finds the online platform unachievable
Funds mismanaged or slow to disburse
Delays in hiring specialist staff
Project activities retraumatize survivors
Legal/technical barriers to cross-border data-sharing
National criminal bureaus lack capacity to implement upgrades
Covid-19 pandemic disruptions (realized risk, addressed via no-cost extension)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of political will to engage
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: INTERPOL/DFID to monitor and engage key stakeholders; working group with National Central Bureaus.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Feasibility study suggests platform is unachievable
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive approach: run operational strands in parallel or reconsider programme viability.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Funds mismanaged or slow to disburse
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Constructive financial oversight via quarterly reports and Project Board reviews.
INTERPOL to proactively seek specialists internally/externally.
Working group with survivors/women’s rights organizations to inform design.
No-cost extension to April 2025 to recover lost time.

fcas_specific_lessons: Overseas Security and Justice Assessments (OSJAs) required to avoid human rights violations in fragile contexts.
Need for **adaptive management** to respond to evolving risks (e.g., political instability, data protection laws).
**Survivor participation** critical to mitigate harm in high-risk environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **inception phase** revealed the need for: 1) **stronger cross-sector collaboration** (aid sector + law enforcement); 2) **digital solutions** (Global Knowledge Hub) to share non-operational data; 3) **expanded use of INTERPOL Notices** for border management. These were incorporated into the **implementation phase design**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **new activities** in implementation phase: Threat Identification Scheme (TIS) pilot, digital knowledge-sharing platform, and expanded criminal analysis. **Theory of Change revised** to reflect these adjustments.
risks_lessons.quote: "A full risk assessment will be undertaken in the first quarter of the programme... risks related to survivor participation, risk of doing further harm to the survivor, the protection of personal and police data." (47927966.odt, Management Case) AND "The overall objectives of the project and the originally envisaged outputs have remained the same, however the programme has identified a number of additional activities which will support delivery of its overall objectives." (D0000809.odt, Describe any key changes) AND "Project delivery was impacted by the Covid-19 pandemic. The purpose of the no-cost extension is to provide additional time for the project to deliver its objectives." (D0000809.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **attract additional donor funding** post-pilot to expand the platform, but no external funds have been secured yet. INTERPOL’s existing budget (~€124m/year) supports core infrastructure used by the project.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily covers **revenue expenditures** (staff salaries, training, platform operation) with minimal **capital costs** (e.g., IT upgrades for regional hubs). No explicit split is provided.
financial_details.quote: "DFID funding will allow INTERPOL rapidly to set up and pilot a new approach... We are proposing an initial one year MoU with funding of up to £1.8m and further funding beyond that will depend on the findings of the feasibility study." (47927966.odt, Financial Case) AND "As the world’s largest international police organization... INTERPOL had an annual budget of approximately €124 million, most of which was provided through annual contributions by its membership." (47927966.odt, Commercial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Ghana Revenue Programme (GRP)
metadata.quote: "Through partnerships with UK fiscal and law enforcement agencies and the procurement of global expertise, GRP will deliver skills, knowledge-sharing and new partnerships to support the Government of Ghana (GoG) to secure catalytic and systemic revenue reforms." (90000424.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Programme Value £3m to £4.6m over 5 years." (90000424.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GRP combines capacity building (strengthening Ghana Revenue Authority and tax systems), policy influence (supporting tax policy reforms), and implementation research (testing revenue mobilization approaches). It aims to increase Ghana's tax-to-GDP ratio from 12.2% to 16% by 2025 through systemic reforms, while also addressing corruption and improving fiscal accountability.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Through partnerships with UK fiscal and law enforcement agencies and the procurement of global expertise, GRP will deliver skills, knowledge-sharing and new partnerships to support the Government of Ghana (GoG) to secure catalytic and systemic revenue reforms." (90000424.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Increase tax-to-GDP ratio from 12.2% to 16% by 2025 (additional £1.8bn in domestic revenues)
£135m annual revenue increase directly attributable to programme
£50m additional oil and gas revenue
Organisational reform of Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA)
Improved tax policy to close tax gaps
Reduced non-compliance in under-taxed areas (High Net Worth Individuals, e-commerce, customs)
Strengthened oil and gas policy framework
Enhanced data analytics for evidence-based policy
Stronger fiscal contract between citizens and state
Increased capacity to investigate and prosecute financial crimes
what_objectives.summary: The GRP aims to transform Ghana's revenue systems through technical assistance, policy reform, and institutional strengthening to enable sustainable domestic resource mobilization and reduce aid dependency.
what_objectives.quote: "GRP will deliver skills, knowledge-sharing and new partnerships to support the Government of Ghana (GoG) to secure catalytic and systemic revenue reforms... helping move Ghana onto a more sustainable path of domestic revenue mobilisation and support Ghana's post-COVID recovery." (90000424.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ghana faces macroeconomic instability and high debt distress risk (classified by IMF as 'high risk of debt distress'), but has stable governance structures and a committed reform agenda. The programme's own risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (90000424.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The IMF has classified Ghana as being at high risk of debt distress" (90000424.odt, A1: Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political interference in tax systems, widespread tax exemptions (6% of GDP), low compliance levels (53% for small taxpayers), and organisational challenges within GRA (e.g., 60% of staff in low-revenue areas) directly hinder revenue collection. Corruption within GRA (noted in Afrobarometer reports) and volatile oil prices add complexity.
where_context.quote: "The main factors underpinning insufficient and ineffective revenue collection in Ghana are:... Political interference in the tax system and corruption within the GRA... Weaknesses in management of oil contracts often resulting in non-payment of dues by oil companies; Low taxpayer compliance levels..." (90000424.odt, A1: Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight and funding control, with Ghanaian institutions (GRA, Ministry of Finance) implementing reforms. Decision-making is shared operationally but ultimately guided by FCDO's programme framework.
q10_capacity_building_details: Embedded HMRC advisers in GRA
Training for GRA staff on tax compliance and investigations
Support for organisational restructuring of GRA
Mentorship for High Net Worth Unit and Petroleum Unit
Technical assistance to Ministry of Finance's Tax Policy Unit
Civil society engagement for fiscal accountability

partner_organizations.name: Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner for revenue reforms

partner_organizations.name: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC)
