who_partners.quote: The political, strategic and diplomatic skills of ex-FCO combined with the technical and programme management expertise of ex-DFID is a strong combination. The complementary knowledge and skills that the two Departments bring together will help achieve the objectives of this programme. (90000345.odt, Management Case); Harnessing the political diplomacy skills of the climate attaché network and other colleagues will help overcome political obstacles and respond opportunistically to favourable political economy conditions in order to obtain stronger political commitment to tackling climate change. (90000345.odt, Management Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for components like WCIS and CAFI), contracts (for technical assistance), and partnerships (e.g., with World Bank for TWM). Block funding is allocated to thematic areas, with flexibility to reallocate based on emerging priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees the programme with a combination of direct implementation (e.g., through UK Met Office), closed consortia (e.g., World Bank for TWM), and open partnerships (e.g., regional bodies like AU and CAFI). An Analysis and Evidence hub tracks implementation and lessons.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on track records of delivery (e.g., CAFI, SRMI, WCIS) and alignment with UK strategic priorities. The World Bank was chosen for TWM due to its experience in transboundary water governance, while UK Met Office was selected for its technical expertise in climate services. Early components focus on scaling existing successful initiatives.
how_mechanism.quote: ARCAN brings together a range of otherwise separate interventions into one flexible and adaptive approach with a common aim. This approach will enable the consolidation of partnerships and sharing of knowledge to maximise impact. It will initially focus on existing initiatives where there is a track record of delivery and opportunity for early impact at scale, namely: Central Africa Forest Initiative (CAFI); Sustainable Renewables Risk Mitigation Initiative (SRMI); Weather and Climate Information Services (WCIS). (90000345.odt, Programme summary); The programme is 100% International Climate Finance (ICF), represents a central pillar of Africa Directorate’s ICF ambition towards 2025/6 and will contribute to spend commitments on nature and biodiversity. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The governance structure includes FCDO oversight with representatives from Posts (country offices) sitting on the ARCAN governance body. The World Bank and other partners (e.g., UK Met Office) have defined roles in component delivery, with joint decision-making for cross-cutting activities (e.g., WCIS-TWM integration).
how_governance.quote: Representative of Posts sitting on FCDO ARCAN governance structure, and, where appropriate, governance structures for ARCAN projects. (90000345.odt, Management Case); An Analysis and Evidence for Delivery and Impact component will track programme implementation in relation to initial VfM indicators and test the theory of change. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on emerging priorities, but this requires approval through the governance structure (e.g., spending review outcomes). The programme is designed to scale investments up or down as needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an adaptive management approach, with an Analysis and Evidence hub to test the theory of change and adjust priorities. New components and partners can be phased in post-Spending Review, and cross-component work (e.g., WCIS-TWM integration) is encouraged.
how_flexibility.quote: This flexible programme can scale investments up or down based on emerging priorities and affordability. An initial budget of £100m has been approved pending Spending Review outcomes. (90000345.odt, Programme summary); Other components and partners, and cross-component working will be phased following the next Spending Review. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (e.g., World Bank, UK Met Office) → End beneficiaries (e.g., national governments, communities). No explicit sub-grantee layer is described beyond the primary implementers.
how_efficiency.quote: The programme’s design means that it is well-positioned to deliver the refreshed cross-HMG Africa Strategy including strategic objectives of a cleaner, greener planet, resilient and productive economies, reducing security threats and human development. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral programming (rejected due to limited scale and cross-border coordination)
Centralised FCDO delivery (rejected due to lack of technical expertise in all areas)
Pure research programmes (rejected due to need for implementation at scale)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery modality was chosen to maximise impact by leveraging UK technical and diplomatic expertise while working at a regional scale. The flexible, adaptive approach allows for consolidation of partnerships (e.g., CAFI, SRMI, WCIS) and knowledge sharing across sectors. The regional focus addresses transboundary challenges (e.g., water, forests) that cannot be solved by single-country interventions. The structure also aligns with UK strategic priorities (e.g., COP26, ICF commitments) and allows for scaling successful initiatives.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging existing successful initiatives like CAFI and WCIS)
risk mitigation (flexibility to adjust to emerging priorities and political economy constraints)
past experience (building on FCDO’s regional programmes like WISER and CRIDF)
partner capacity (utilising World Bank for TWM, UK Met Office for climate services)
speed (phased approach with early focus on proven components)
flexibility (ability to scale up/down and reallocate funds)
equity (focus on marginalised groups and gender inclusion)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination complexity due to multiple partners and components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Analysis and Evidence hub to track implementation and lessons; joint governance structures with Post representatives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy barriers in FCAS (e.g., vested interests, weak governance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of UK diplomatic skills and climate attachés to navigate political obstacles; conflict sensitivity analysis for all interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led structure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Inclusion of African regional bodies (e.g., AU, Lake Chad Basin Commission) in delivery; capacity building for national governments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexibility leading to mission creep or lack of focus
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased approach with initial focus on proven components; governance oversight for fund reallocation.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing initiatives to reduce startup costs)
efficiency (regional approach to capture economies of scale)
effectiveness (focus on high-impact sectors like energy, water, forests)
equity (targeting poorest and most vulnerable, including women and girls)
why_rationale.quote: The programme’s design means that it is well-positioned to deliver the refreshed cross-HMG Africa Strategy including strategic objectives of a cleaner, greener planet, resilient and productive economies, reducing security threats and human development. (90000345.odt, Programme summary); ARCAN brings together a range of otherwise separate interventions into one flexible and adaptive approach with a common aim. This approach will enable the consolidation of partnerships and sharing of knowledge to maximise impact. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk, multi-country context limits partner selection to organisations with proven regional experience (e.g., World Bank for TWM, CAFI for forests) and strong fiduciary controls. FCAS constraints (e.g., conflict in DRC, South Sudan) require partners with conflict sensitivity expertise and diplomatic backing (e.g., UK Met Office for climate services). Weak institutional capacity in many countries necessitates Northern technical leadership (e.g., FCDO, UK advisors).
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS risks require partners with conflict sensitivity experience (e.g., World Bank, UK Met Office).
Transboundary challenges (e.g., water, forests) necessitate regional/multilateral partners (e.g., AU, Lake Chad Basin Commission).
Weak national institutions limit direct funding to Southern governments, requiring intermediaries (e.g., World Bank).
Political economy constraints favour partners with diplomatic leverage (e.g., FCDO climate attachés).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (adaptation, mitigation, energy transition) require a multi-component structure with specialised partners for each theme (e.g., World Bank for water, SRMI for energy). The regional scope demands a platform-like approach to coordinate transboundary actions (e.g., WCIS-TWM integration). The need for flexibility and scaling dictates a phased, adaptive management model with an evidence hub to test and adjust priorities.
q28_linkages: Transboundary water management (TWM) requires multilateral partners (World Bank) due to cross-border nature of rivers.
Energy transition (SRMI) needs private sector engagement (PIDG) to de-risk investments and influence national grids.
Climate services (WCIS) demand technical expertise (UK Met Office) for data-intensive early warning systems.
Forest protection (CAFI) relies on regional bodies (e.g., Congo Basin Commission) for cross-country coordination.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive partnerships and rapid delivery. For example: (1) Northern-led management ensures efficiency and fiduciary control but risks limiting Southern ownership; (2) Phased scaling of components balances speed (early wins) with equity (gradual inclusion of more countries); (3) Conflict sensitivity measures add complexity but are critical for FCAS contexts; (4) Gender and social inclusion requirements (e.g., GESI analysis) are mandated but may slow implementation.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (e.g., UK Met Office) vs. Southern ownership (e.g., national meteorological agencies).
Speed (scaling proven initiatives like CAFI) vs. inclusion (phasing in new countries/partners).
Efficiency (centralised FCDO oversight) vs. responsiveness (adaptive management at country level).
Cost (high transaction costs for multi-partner coordination) vs. reach (regional scale for transboundary issues).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk rating drives intensive oversight, including milestone-based tracking, embedded FCDO advisors, and joint governance structures. FCAS contexts require additional conflict sensitivity analysis and political economy assessments, increasing management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: (1) Southern partners (e.g., national governments) are primarily implementers with technical support from Northern institutions; (2) Regional bodies (e.g., AU, Lake Chad Basin Commission) receive institutional strengthening; (3) UK advisors provide embedded mentorship to build long-term skills.
intersections.quote: The barriers to action are complex and multi-faceted, they cannot be solved by solely technical solutions. (90000345.odt, Barriers to action); The programme will provide regional and national support, recognising the cross-border nature of sustainable natural resources management, particularly for water and forests, as well as the opportunities for greater efficiency such as increasing trade in hydropower. (90000345.odt, Programme design)

key_programme_risks: Political economy barriers in FCAS (e.g., vested interests blocking climate action).
Weak institutional capacity limiting absorption of funds and technical assistance.
Climate shocks disrupting implementation (e.g., droughts, floods).
Conflict or instability in priority countries (e.g., DRC, South Sudan).
Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led structure.
Coordination challenges across multiple components and partners.
Data limitations affecting early warning systems and M&E.
Gender and social exclusion risks (e.g., women/girls disproportionately affected by climate shocks).
Environmental crime (e.g., illegal wildlife trade, charcoal smuggling) fuelling conflict.
Risk of mal-adaptation (e.g., interventions worsening inequality or resource conflicts).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of UK diplomatic skills and climate attachés to navigate obstacles; conflict sensitivity analysis for all interventions.
Capacity building embedded in all components; technical assistance for national governments.
Adaptive management approach; early warning systems (WCIS) to anticipate shocks.
Conflict sensitivity embedded in programme design; alignment with peacebuilding efforts (e.g., transboundary water cooperation).
Inclusion of African regional bodies in governance; capacity building for national partners.
Analysis and Evidence hub to track implementation; joint governance structures.
Investment in climate information systems (WCIS); partnerships with UK Met Office for technical support.
GESI analysis mandatory for all interventions; targeted inclusion of women/girls and marginalised groups.
Support to legal frameworks for natural resource management; collaboration with INTERPOL on illegal trade.
Ex-ante impact assessments; monitoring for unintended consequences (e.g., resource conflicts).

fcas_specific_lessons: Transboundary water cooperation is more likely than violent conflict and can build peace (Bohmelt et al 2014; Herbert 2019).
Natural resource management can be a tool for peacebuilding if governance structures are inclusive (Mosello et al 2019).
Conflict sensitivity must be embedded in all interventions, particularly for water, forests, and land (90000345.odt, Security and stability).
In FCAS, technical solutions must be paired with political economy analysis to address vested interests (90000345.odt, Barriers to action).
Early warning systems (e.g., WCIS) are critical for shock-responsive programming in fragile contexts (90000345.odt, Forecast-based and early action).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from previous FCDO regional programmes (e.g., WISER, CRIDF, CONGOs) highlight the benefits of regional approaches for transboundary issues (e.g., water, forests). Key takeaways include: (1) Regional programmes can capture efficiencies of scale and address spillover effects (e.g., Congo Basin forests affecting Horn of Africa rainfall); (2) Cross-border collaboration is essential for managing shared resources (e.g., Nile Basin, Lake Chad); (3) Political economy analysis is critical for navigating regional dynamics (e.g., Nile water negotiations); (4) Local ownership is enhanced by embedding capacity building in regional bodies (e.g., Lake Chad Basin Commission).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates lessons by: (1) Phasing new components post-Spending Review to ensure flexibility; (2) Including an Analysis and Evidence hub to test and adapt the theory of change; (3) Mandating conflict sensitivity analysis for all interventions; (4) Strengthening links between climate data and decision-making (e.g., WCIS-TWM integration); (5) Embedding gender and social inclusion (GESI) in all components.
risks_lessons.quote: Existing and recent Pan-Africa Department (PD) programmes, including Climate Resilient Infrastructure Development Facility (CRIDF), Co-operation in International Waters (CIWA), Improving Livelihoods and Land Use in Congo Basin Forests (CONGOs), Regional Vulnerability Assessment and Analysis (RVAA) and Weather and Climate Information Services for Africa (WISER) have all demonstrated the benefit of working regionally. (90000345.odt, Rationale for regional approach); The evidence on the causal pathway between climate change and conflict is limited, however there is evidence that many fragile and conflict affected states are also amongst those most vulnerable to climate change and environmental degradation. (90000345.odt, Security and stability)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to influence billions in government, private, and multilateral investments (e.g., through SRMI’s support for renewable energy grid integration). Specific leverage targets include: (1) SRMI influencing billions in energy investments; (2) WCIS contributing to REAP’s target of 1 billion people with improved resilience; (3) CAFI protecting 10 million ha of forest (a globally significant carbon sink).
financial_details.quote: ARCAN is 100% International Climate Finance (ICF), represents a central pillar of Africa Directorate’s ICF ambition towards 2025/6 and will contribute to spend commitments on nature and biodiversity. (90000345.odt, Programme summary); The programme’s design means that it is well-positioned to deliver the refreshed cross-HMG Africa Strategy including strategic objectives of a cleaner, greener planet, resilient and productive economies, reducing security threats and human development. (90000345.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: The Gateway for Growth (the Gateway)

quote.duration: "The Gateway is a £50 million 5-year programme" (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Gateway is a coordinated service platform that combines financing mechanism (channeling funds to businesses), service delivery (direct support to businesses), and capacity building (enhancing HMG's trade/investment offer). It aims to increase trade and investment benefiting poor women and men in developing countries by improving access to UK Government support.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Gateway is a X-HMG (DFID, DIT, FCO, BEIS) initiative which seek to increase the volume and type of trade and investment that benefits poor women and men in developing countries... by establishing a coordinated, improved single entry point service for businesses" (D0002842.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased utilisation of existing HMG "offer to business" instruments
% increase and £ value of trade (imports/exports with Africa) resulting from Gateway
% increase and £ value of FDI (with Africa) resulting from Gateway
# of jobs directly created in-country as a result of deals facilitated through the Gateway
% improvement in productivity among in-country businesses with trade/investment contracts resulting from Gateway support
development of a digital platform integrated with DIT GREAT architecture
establishment of a UK-based core team (10+ staff)
creation of a Flexible Fund for responsive support

what_objectives.summary: The Gateway aims to accelerate poverty reduction through increased pro-development trade and investment by providing a single entry point for businesses to access HMG's fragmented support offer, while temporarily filling gaps in under-resourced services.

quote.objectives: "The primary purpose of the Gateway is to support businesses (developing country, UK and other international) to contribute towards poverty reduction, through increasing the volume and type of trade and investment that generates positive benefits for poor women and men." (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)
quote.approach: "The Gateway builds on DFID’s Economic Development Strategy and ‘building markets’ strategic direction approach, supporting sustainable inclusive economic growth." (D0002842.odt, Rationale section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: High" and operates in developing markets with challenging business environments including weak institutions, corruption risks, and political instability.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: High" (D0002842.odt, metadata table)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Businesses cite high costs of doing business, sector-specific investment climate barriers, limited data on viable opportunities, and legal systems that require navigating context-specific rules. Women face additional barriers from laws and social norms preventing workforce entry or business ownership.

quote.scope: "The Gateway will adopt a regional approach, starting in Africa (including North Africa in line with the Africa Uplift), and then, subject to meeting expansion criteria, pivot to frontier Asia in year 2/3." (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)
quote.constraints: "Businesses regularly cite the high costs of doing business; general and sector specific investment climate barriers; and limited data to inform them about viable investment opportunities in new markets as key barriers to their greater engagement in developing markets." (D0002842.odt, Need for DFID Intervention section)

quote.structure: "The Gateway will be a single-entry point for those wanting to trade and invest in developing markets, linking into all relevant HMG services operating in these markets" (D0002842.odt, The problem this work will address section)
quote.partners: "The Gateway for Growth (‘the Gateway’) is a X-HMG (DFID, DIT, FCO, BEIS) initiative" (D0002842.odt, Title section)
quote.capacity: "The Gateway will... provide flexible and responsive new and enhanced services to businesses... and the HMG network (Posts and UK) to facilitate more trade and investment" (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)
quote.decision_power: "The Gateway core team will... be mandated to read across HMG’s offer to business in developing markets to provide joined-up support to businesses and HMG stakeholders." (D0002842.odt, How? section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of ODA grants (£45m) and non-ODA funds (£5m from other government departments) to deliver a platform service. The Flexible Fund operates as a pot of funding for responsive activities, while core services are delivered through contracts (externally procured staff) and civil servant roles.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Gateway operates as an "umbrella service offer" with three components: 1) a digital platform integrated with DIT’s GREAT architecture; 2) a UK-based core team (civil servants + externally procured staff); and 3) a Flexible Fund for demand-driven activities. It links to but does not house individual HMG financial instruments.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme is a cross-HMG initiative with mandated partners (DFID, DIT, FCO, BEIS). Externally procured staff for the core team are selected based on private sector expertise and understanding of developing markets, but no competition process is described.

quote.instrument: "The Gateway is a £50 million 5-year programme (£45m ODA; £5m non-ODA)... The initiative will secure 10% of the programme funds (£5 million of non-ODA) from other government departments" (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary and Financial sections)
quote.structure: "The Gateway will support the entire suite of existing services across HMG to be better understood and utilised... via a digital offer, a UK-based core team, and a Flexible Fund." (D0002842.odt, How? section)
quote.selection: "The Gateway X-HMG design team are carefully working out the appropriate balance... The team will be a mix of civil servants and staff recruited from the private sector and will possess a deep understanding of the private sector, HMG structures and the complexities of operating in developing markets." (D0002842.odt, How? section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A set of principles will govern activities, including development impact and additionality criteria. The Flexible Fund will have prioritization criteria finalized during inception, suggesting a structured decision-making process. Cross-HMG collaboration is mandated by the "Fusion Doctrine."

quote.manager: "The Gateway core team will... be mandated to read across HMG’s offer to business in developing markets to provide joined-up support" (D0002842.odt, How? section)
quote.sub_awards: "A detailed set of Gateway ‘criteria for support’ will be finalised during inception... Annex N (on the Gateway Flexible Fund) sets out more detail on how flexible support... will be prioritised." (D0002842.odt, How will Gateway prioritise the support it gives? section)
quote.governance: "The ‘Fusion Doctrine’ encourages HMG to make the most of all available levers to deliver shared objectives—the Gateway maximises HMG’s trade and development offer by drawing on expertise and the comparative advantage of DIT, DFID, FCO and BEIS" (D0002842.odt, Rationale section)
quote.oversight: "The Gateway will establish a code of conduct for service firms and strong principles to ensure that services are compliant with the International Development Act... Much of the activity of the Gateway will be signposting to other ODA funded services that are anyway developmentally focused." (D0002842.odt, How will Gateway prioritise the support it gives? section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The Flexible Fund is designed to "fill in for HMG services that are still under development or inadequately resourced" and will evolve frequent requests into core services. The Gateway will step back as HMG fills gaps through other services, indicating dynamic reallocation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme will "constantly adapt, providing surge support when gaps exist and stepping back as HMG fills gaps." Criteria for support and prioritization will be finalized during inception, allowing adjustments based on emerging needs and HMG capacity building.

quote.reallocation: "This flexible adaptive function is critical to its success as a service, and the adjustment of activities as new capabilities across HMG are built will be carefully monitored to appraise programme performance." (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)
quote.adaptive: "The Gateway will... be able to address temporary gaps in existing HMG services that are still under development, or inadequately resourced... This flexible adaptive function is critical to its success as a service" (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)
quote.criteria: "A detailed set of Gateway ‘criteria for support’ will be finalised during inception... The Gateway will only provide support where there is a clear potential for developmental impact and where the service offered by the Gateway is additional to what already exists within Government and in the private sector." (D0002842.odt, How will Gateway prioritise the support it gives? section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (via DFID/GRD) → Gateway Core Team (implementing partner, including externally procured staff) → [end businesses]. The Flexible Fund adds a sub-layer for specific activities but operates under the Core Team.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £50 million over 5 years" (D0002842.odt, metadata table)
quote.layers: "Second via the Core UK-based team—this team will: Be a mix of civil servants and staff recruited from the private sector... Third via a Flexible Fund" (D0002842.odt, How? section)
quote.payments: "The Gateway is a £50 million 5-year programme... The Flexible Fund (FF)—a pot of flexible funding managed by the Gateway Core team for activities that cannot be carried out by the core team" (D0002842.odt, Intervention Summary section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuing with the fragmented, uncoordinated HMG offer to business
Relying solely on private sector intermediaries (e.g., Chambers of Commerce)
Expanding individual HMG instruments without a coordinating platform
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The Gateway was chosen to address market failures in information provision and coordination gaps across HMG’s fragmented trade/investment support offer. It leverages the "Fusion Doctrine" to maximize cross-HMG collaboration, fills temporary gaps in under-resourced services, and provides a demand-driven response to business needs while ensuring development impact. The platform model was selected for its ability to signpost existing services, provide flexible support, and adapt as HMG builds permanent capacity.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (avoiding duplication, leveraging existing instruments)
risk mitigation (addressing information gaps and perceived risks in developing markets)
partner capacity (building on HMG’s comparative advantage and private sector expertise)
flexibility (adaptive management to fill gaps and step back as HMG services mature)
equity (targeting poor women and men, inclusive growth)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication with existing HMG services
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear criteria for additionality and development impact; regular monitoring to adjust as HMG fills gaps. "The Gateway will only provide support where... the service offered is additional to what already exists within Government and in the private sector."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with private sector service providers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on underserved segments (e.g., SMEs, high-development-impact sectors) and complementarity. "HMG can provide additionality by... improving signposting to them and filling gaps."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of coordinating across HMG departments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Core team mandated to "read across HMG’s offer" with deep understanding of structures; digital platform for transparency. "The team will... possess a deep understanding of... HMG structures."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability as HMG services evolve
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible Fund designed to step back as permanent HMG services are established. "The Gateway will... step back as these gaps are filled."

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing HMG instruments, avoiding duplication)
efficiency (digital platform for scalability, core team with mixed skills)
equity (prioritizing poor women and men, inclusive growth)

quote.alternatives: "HMG has developed a suite of ODA and non-ODA ‘offer to business instruments’... However, businesses... report this offer is complex, difficult to navigate and insufficient." (D0002842.odt, The problem this work will address section)
quote.rationale: "The Gateway maximises HMG’s trade and development offer by drawing on expertise and the comparative advantage of DIT, DFID, FCO and BEIS to deliver development benefits... This join up should make the offer greater than the sum of its parts." (D0002842.odt, How does this work fit with DFID’s strategic objectives? section)
quote.risks: "The Gateway will only provide support where there is a clear potential for developmental impact and where the service offered by the Gateway is additional to what already exists within Government and in the private sector." (D0002842.odt, How will Gateway prioritise the support it gives? section)
quote.vfm: "The Gateway will... focus effort where the potential impact on economic growth is high and avoid or mitigate any adverse distributional or displacement impacts on the poor." (D0002842.odt, How will Gateway prioritise the support it gives? section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The challenging business environments in Africa/Asia (weak institutions, corruption, information gaps) limit the ability of private sector intermediaries to provide comprehensive support, necessitating HMG’s coordinated platform. Local Chambers of Commerce lack capacity in many markets, and cultural/legal barriers (e.g., for women) require government-backed solutions to build trust.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited in-country presence of private sector providers (e.g., Chambers of Commerce only in largest markets)
High costs and risks discourage private sector from serving SMEs or frontier markets
Legal and regulatory complexity requires government-to-government influence
Gender-specific barriers (laws/social norms) need targeted support beyond commercial offerings
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to increase *pro-development* trade/investment (not just any trade) shapes the platform’s design: 1) **Signposting** addresses information failures; 2) **Flexible Fund** fills gaps in under-resourced HMG services; 3) **Core team** provides joined-up support across departments; 4) **Development impact criteria** guide all activities. The focus on poor women/men requires embedded equity considerations in service design.
q28_linkages: Information failures → Digital platform + HMG network signposting
Fragmented HMG offer → Core team with cross-departmental mandate
Gaps in services → Flexible Fund for temporary support
Equity goals → Targeted outreach to women/SMEs and inclusive design
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging existing HMG instruments, digital scalability) with equity (targeting poor women/men, high-impact sectors). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid coordination vs. ensuring marginalized groups benefit; 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: UK-based core team vs. local delivery partners; 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Affordable services for SMEs vs. resource-intensive support.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: The digital platform enables quick scalability but requires additional efforts (e.g., language support, gender-targeted content) to ensure marginalized groups can access services. "Site availability in English, French and Portuguese" addresses some barriers.

The UK-based core team (with private sector expertise) ensures high-quality support but risks limited local ownership. Mitigation includes regional integration plans and Flexible Fund support for local partners.

Providing deep support to high-impact sectors/firms may limit breadth, while light-touch signposting risks insufficient impact. The Flexible Fund balances this by offering both surge support and scalable digital tools.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (operating in developing markets with weak institutions) drives intensive oversight: 1) **Development impact criteria** for all activities; 2) **Code of conduct** for businesses; 3) **Adaptive management** to respond to emerging risks; 4) **Cross-HMG coordination** to mitigate political/regulatory barriers.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: 1) **HMG network** receives analytical support to improve policy coherence; 2) **Businesses** get guidance on responsible standards and market navigation; 3) **Core team** includes private sector staff to bridge government-business gaps, with knowledge transfer as a key function.

key_programme_risks.risk: Insufficient demand from businesses due to lack of awareness or trust in the Gateway
Duplication or overlap with existing HMG or private sector services
Failure to demonstrate additionality or development impact
Political or regulatory barriers in target countries limiting trade/investment
High transaction costs for businesses (especially SMEs) to access services
Reputational risk from supporting businesses with poor labour/environmental standards
Sustainability challenges as HMG services evolve and Gateway steps back
Digital platform fails to reach marginalized groups (e.g., women, rural businesses)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proactive outreach through HMG network (Posts), targeted marketing, and integration with DIT’s GREAT platform. "The Gateway should become a clear entry point... supported by a Gateway digital team."
Strict additionality and development impact criteria; regular mapping of HMG offer. "The Gateway will only provide support where... the service offered is additional to what already exists."

Robust MEL framework with disaggregated targets (gender, sector, country); focus on high-impact sectors. "The Gateway will establish a code of conduct... and strong principles to ensure compliance with the International Development Act."

Leverage FCO’s diplomatic network and DIT’s trade expertise; adaptive Flexible Fund to respond to emerging barriers. "The Gateway puts the ‘fusion doctrine’ into practice—practically joining up HMG’s work on trade and investment."
Flexible Fund to provide surge support; digital tools to reduce costs; targeted outreach to SMEs. "The Gateway will... provide flexible and responsive services to businesses... including SMEs."
Code of conduct for all supported firms; alignment with IFC/CDC Performance Standards. "Supporting firms that are committed to develop responsible business standards beyond core minimum standards."
Phased step-back as HMG services mature; knowledge transfer to permanent HMG functions. "The Gateway will... step back as these gaps are filled."
Multilingual site (English, French, Portuguese); gender-inclusive design; Flexible Fund for targeted support. "Site availability in English, French and Portuguese."

fcas_specific_lessons: Information gaps and misperceptions disproportionately deter businesses from entering FCAS/frontier markets. The Gateway addresses this through curated market information and risk-mitigation support.
Weak local institutions increase transaction costs; the programme mitigates this by leveraging HMG’s government-to-government influence (e.g., FCO political teams).
Corruption and integrity risks require robust compliance mechanisms. The Gateway enforces a Supply Partner Code of Conduct and zero-tolerance for bribery/fraud.
Gender-specific legal and social norms in FCAS necessitate targeted support. The programme includes gender analysis in all activities and Flexible Fund guidance for women-owned businesses.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from DFID’s RATE programme highlighted market failures in understanding ‘bottom of the pyramid’ consumers. The Gateway incorporates this by: 1) Prioritizing firms that serve poor markets; 2) Including willingness-to-pay analysis in sector targeting; 3) Supporting technology transfer for affordable products.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added explicit gender equality aims (aligned with UK Gender Equality Act) based on evidence that trade/investment can disproportionately benefit men without targeted design.
Included a Supply Partner Code of Conduct (updated 2018) to address corruption and integrity risks identified in previous programmes.
Designed the Flexible Fund to temporarily fill gaps (a lesson from siloed ‘Aid for Trade’ strategies in comparator countries).
Integrated digital and in-person support (e.g., trade fairs) based on evidence that bundled services are more effective than isolated assistance.

metadata.programme_name: UK-India Global Innovation Partnership programme (GIP)
metadata.quote: "GIP will foster, transfer and scale up innovations from India (including ones developed with UK enterprises) to African, Asian and Indian Ocean countries. GIP will prioritise innovations in climate-smart growth sectors for shared prosperity and a greener planet." (D0003591.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 23.02.2022 and 30.06.2036" (D0003350.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GIP is a financing mechanism that supports the transfer and scaling of Indian innovations to developing countries, with a focus on climate-smart growth. It combines investment, grants, and technical assistance to foster South-South innovation transfer, open markets, and create opportunities for businesses and investors, including those from the UK.
what_objectives.q1_source: "GIP will foster, transfer and scale up innovations from India (including ones developed with UK enterprises) to African, Asian and Indian Ocean countries. GIP will prioritise innovations in climate-smart growth sectors for shared prosperity and a greener planet. It will strengthen South-South transfer of innovation, open markets and provide opportunities for businesses and investors, including those from the UK." (D0003591.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Scale up Indian innovations in African, Asian, and Indian Ocean countries
Strengthen South-South transfer of innovation
Open markets for UK innovators and investors
Create opportunities for businesses and investors
Build capacity and evidence through technical assistance
Generate investment, trade, science, and partnership opportunities for UK and Indian institutions
50% of GIP’s budget will score as ICF (International Climate Finance), contributing to the UK’s international climate commitments
Expected to benefit partner countries and generate secondary benefits for the UK
what_objectives.summary: GIP aims to transfer and scale Indian innovations to developing countries, focusing on climate-smart sectors, while fostering South-South cooperation and creating economic opportunities for UK and Indian businesses.
what_objectives.quote: "GIP will foster, transfer and scale up innovations from India (including ones developed with UK enterprises) to African, Asian and Indian Ocean countries. GIP will prioritise innovations in climate-smart growth sectors for shared prosperity and a greener planet." (D0003591.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: Africa (Ethiopia, Tanzania, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Mozambique, Zambia, Ghana, Nigeria)
South Asia/Indian Ocean region (Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Afghanistan, Indian Ocean islands)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with significant poverty, weak health systems, and vulnerability to climate change. Many target countries are in Sub-Saharan Africa, which is described as having extreme poverty rates above 60% in some cases, weak infrastructure, and high inequality.
where_context.q5_source: "Extreme poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa declined from around 60% in the early 90s to nearly 40% today. Population growth, however, means that an estimated 63m more people live in extreme poverty in Africa today than in 1990... In 12 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, the extreme poverty rate is still above 60%; in four cases it is above 80%." (D0003591.odt, Poverty and inequality in Africa and South Asia)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak health systems, poor infrastructure (e.g., lack of access to basic water and electricity), regulatory barriers, and climate vulnerability (e.g., droughts, floods) are explicitly mentioned as challenges that affect the ability to deliver innovations and achieve development impact.
where_context.quote: "SSA has the weakest health system globally with the ratio of health professionals to population being as low as 1 doctor per 5,000 people and capability for intensive care is limited. Only half of the healthcare facilities in the region have access to basic water... 60% lack access to reliable electricity." (D0003591.odt, COVID-19 and its effect on SSA health systems)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-funded and co-designed by the UK (FCDO) and India (MEA), with joint decision-making and implementation. The Government of India is described as an "equal partner" in the programme.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to build capacity and evidence
support to innovators and adopters to overcome barriers to transfer
training and skill development for local partners

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Development Capital Investment (DCI), grants, and technical assistance. The DCI component was increased by moving the entire Development Capital Grant (DCG) budget to DCI, simplifying the investment strategy.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will engage a commercial supplier through a contract for the Grant component and Technical Assistance (TA), preferably a single supplier for both. The UK and India will jointly oversee the programme as equal partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: An open procurement process will be followed to achieve better value for money, strengthen oversight, and ensure consistent delivery for a programme of this size and complexity.
how_mechanism.quote: "Engage a commercial supplier through a contract for the Grant component, instead of an Institutional Partner through an MoU as originally proposed in the Business Case (BC). In procurement we will also seek a single supplier for Grants and TA." (D0003350.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is managed jointly by the UK (FCDO) and India (MEA) through a Joint Programme Team (JPT).
how_governance.quote: "The UK and India will co-fund equally the total budget of £75m... The Joint Programme Team (JPT) comprising FCDO and MEA will oversee implementation." (D0003591.odt, Programme summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds were reallocated from Development Capital Grants (DCG) to Development Capital Investment (DCI) to simplify the programme and improve value for money. However, no further reallocation flexibility is explicitly mentioned.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be flexible to respond to emerging crises (e.g., COVID-19) and repurpose resources as needed. This is part of the 'adaptive programming' approach noted in the original Business Case.
how_flexibility.quote: "Most importantly with the learning from the current COVID-19 situation, GIP will remain a flexible programme which can repurpose and focus its resources and sectors to respond to emerging crisis situations on ground." (D0003591.odt, The proposed new intervention)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Commercial Supplier (Delivery Partner) → Indian Enterprises/Not-for-profits → End Beneficiaries in Africa/South Asia
how_efficiency.quote: "An open procurement process will be followed for selecting a delivery partner for Grants and preferably a single supplier will be selected for management of TA and Grants." (D0003350.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Institutional Partner through an MoU (original proposal)
Separate suppliers for Grants and Technical Assistance (TA)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The current modality (commercial supplier via contract) was chosen to achieve better value for money, strengthen oversight, avoid advance payments, and ensure consistent delivery for a complex programme. The shift from DCG to DCI was based on feasibility, market feedback, and mutual agreement with the Government of India to reduce complexity and delivery risk.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing multiple funding instruments (grants, investments, TA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Consolidated DCG into DCI to simplify the investment strategy and reduce delivery risk.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of suitable funding options for SMEs to expand innovations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical Assistance (TA) to build capacity and help innovators access financing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory and market barriers in target countries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: TA to provide market intelligence and support adaptation of business models.

why_rationale.quote: "The proposed changes are based on learning and feedback gathered from market research and discussions with potential partners through the two EME exercises, alongside close coordination with the Government of India as our equal partner in the programme." (D0003350.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating environment in target countries (e.g., weak institutions, regulatory barriers, and climate risks) limits the types of partners that can effectively deliver innovations. For example, SMEs and local enterprises often lack access to formal credit and require TA to navigate regulatory and market challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Lack of access to formal credit for SMEs in target countries
Regulatory barriers (trade, tax, duties) in destination countries
Underdeveloped financial markets and high interest rates
Poor infrastructure (e.g., lack of reliable electricity, water access)
Climate vulnerability affecting agricultural and health innovations
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to transfer and scale climate-smart innovations across multiple countries requires a mixed funding approach (grants, investments, TA) and a flexible, adaptive management structure. The focus on South-South cooperation and commercial viability shapes the use of open procurement for delivery partners.
q28_linkages: Mixed funding instruments (DCI, grants, TA) are used to address different stages of innovation scaling (early-stage vs. mid/growth-stage).
Open procurement for delivery partners ensures flexibility to select the best-suited organizations for grants and TA management.
Technical Assistance is embedded to support innovators in adapting to local contexts and overcoming market barriers.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between reaching the poorest communities (equity) and ensuring commercial viability (efficiency). For example, innovations must be both inclusive (e.g., affordable for low-income groups) and scalable (e.g., financially viable for enterprises).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Balancing the need for low-cost, inclusive innovations with the requirement for financial sustainability and scalability.
Ensuring that technical assistance and grants reach small enterprises while maintaining oversight and value for money.
Adapting innovations to local contexts (e.g., regulatory, cultural) without increasing costs prohibitively.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of target countries (e.g., weak institutions, climate vulnerability) necessitates intensive oversight, embedded TA, and adaptive management to mitigate delivery risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building (e.g., TA, training) is embedded to enable Southern partners (Indian enterprises, African/Asian adopters) to overcome barriers such as lack of market intelligence, regulatory knowledge, and access to finance.
intersections.quote: "The high interdependency of poor on vulnerable resources and limited capacities to adapt to disasters (like COVID-19) increases the need for flexible, adaptive programming and technical support to ensure innovations can be effectively transferred and scaled." (D0003591.odt, Challenges-South-South transfer)

key_programme_risks: Lack of access to suitable funding options for SMEs in target countries
Regulatory and trade barriers in destination countries
Weak infrastructure (e.g., electricity, water) limiting innovation adoption
Climate vulnerability affecting agricultural and health innovations
Limited capacity of local institutions to support scaling of innovations
High cost of market intelligence for SMEs
Reluctance of investors to provide high-risk capital for untested markets
Political and economic instability in target countries (e.g., FCAS contexts)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of suitable funding options for SMEs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Provide Development Capital Investment (DCI) and Technical Assistance (TA) to de-risk investments and build enterprise capacity.
Use TA to provide market intelligence and support enterprises in navigating regulatory requirements.
Focus on innovations that are climate-resilient and adaptable to low-infrastructure settings (e.g., off-grid energy, water solutions).
Embed capacity-building components (e.g., training, mentorship) and partner with local organizations to strengthen ecosystems.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High cost of market intelligence for SMEs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Provide TA to gather and disseminate market intelligence, reducing the burden on individual enterprises.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Investor reluctance to fund high-risk markets
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use blended finance (grants + investments) to de-risk early-stage innovations and attract private capital.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, innovations must be adaptable to volatile environments (e.g., conflict, disasters) and focus on building resilience.
Local partnerships are critical for navigating political and security risks in fragile states.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., grants, TA) are essential to respond to sudden shocks (e.g., COVID-19, climate disasters).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The pilot programme (Global INVENT) demonstrated that: 1) Grants can mobilize expertise and validate innovations for scaling; 2) Technical Assistance is critical for overcoming barriers to transfer; 3) Flexibility in sector focus (e.g., disability, COVID-care) allows for demand-led approaches; 4) Market-based innovations with commercial viability are more sustainable.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shifted from Development Capital Grants (DCG) to Development Capital Investment (DCI) to simplify the programme and improve value for money.
Replaced Institutional Partner (MoU) with a commercial supplier (contract) for better oversight and consistency.
Embedded Technical Assistance (TA) as a core component to support innovators and adopters.
Designed the programme to be flexible and adaptive to emerging crises (e.g., COVID-19).
risks_lessons.quote: "The pilot Global Invent Programme demonstrated strong potential for countries in the two regions to benefit from India’s inclusive innovations... The evaluation of the pilot highlighted potential for bigger sustained impact and secondary benefits to the UK." (D0003591.odt, The Pilot Global Invent Programme)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme is designed to attract private capital by de-risking innovations through grants and technical assistance. The pilot programme showed a two-fold return on investment, with £2.8m of investment generating £5.4m in benefits.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £50m for investment (£35m Development Capital Investment, £15m originally Development Capital Grants now merged into DCI), £25m for other capital (likely grants and TA), £15m for Technical Assistance.
financial_details.quote: "£50m investment (£35m Development Capital Investment and £15m Development Capital Grants) and £10m grant assistance will back enterprises and not-for-profits to introduce and scale up Indian innovations in other countries. £15m technical assistance will build capacity and evidence and deepen investment impact." (D0003350.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

metadata.programme_name: AT2030 – Life Changing Assistive Technology for All (Africa Scale-Up)

quote.text: "AT2030: Africa will triple the impact and reach of AT2030, DFID’s flagship ‘what works’ programme for AT, by doubling the investment with a focus on DFID priority African countries."

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 16 July, 2019", "End Date: Nolaterthan1.10.2024"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: AT2030: Africa combines evidence generation (research on AT effectiveness), technology development (30 new disruptive AT products), capacity building (training, innovation hubs), policy influence (WHO World Report on AT), implementation research (piloting country capacity assessments), and service delivery (reaching 9 million people with AT). The programme tests and scales interventions while building markets and health systems for sustainable AT provision.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will deliver against commitments in the RED Business Plan to increase investments in technologies, their delivery and take up to generate new opportunities for evidence and development returns. These investments prioritise testing products and services, building evidence and ensuring they can be scaled."
q3_expected_outputs: 30 new disruptive technologies with life-changing potential
4 innovative service delivery models developed and tested
Up to 50 new start-ups supported
9 million people reached through core programme (6m additional)
6 million people reached through Paralympics stigma reduction
Country Capacity Assessments (CCAs) in 10 DFID priority countries
2 national trials of AT provision models
Inclusive Design case studies and built environment improvements
Support to WHO’s first World Report on Assistive Technology
£1m open call for AT research
East African AT Innovation Ecosystem (InnovateNow) strengthened
Paralympic sport programmes in Malawi and Ethiopia
what_objectives.summary: AT2030: Africa scales DFID’s flagship assistive technology programme by doubling investment to £19.8m, focusing on African countries to reach 15 million people through AT interventions, market shaping, and stigma reduction via Paralympic engagement. The programme combines research, innovation, and system strengthening to create sustainable AT ecosystems.

quote.text: "The scale-up will triple the impact of AT2030... by doubling the investment with a focus on DFID priority countries in Africa... enabling the programme to reach 9 million people by improving access to life-changing AT..."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in developing countries with weak AT markets and health systems, requiring significant investment to overcome the 'valley of death' for entrepreneurs. Political and institutional constraints are noted in the need for country capacity assessments and policy advice.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate"
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions ("Country Governments... need advice and practical case studies")
market failures ("valley of death for AT entrepreneurs")
stigma ("tackle stigma and discrimination across Africa")
data limitations ("need to bring forward as much evidence as possible")
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The weak AT markets and health systems in target countries create a 'valley of death' that requires sustained investment ("Innovation in the AT space is harder than initially anticipated"). Physical infrastructure barriers ("inaccessibility of the Built Environment") limit AT usability, while stigma prevents uptake. Regulatory gaps and lack of standards hinder market development.

quote.text: "Innovation in the AT space is harder than initially anticipated. The ‘Valley of Death’ (VOD) is longer and deeper for AT... requiring much more investment before sustainability is reached."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The GDI Hub (UK-based) leads the consortium and manages all sub-awards, with Southern partners (e.g., AMREF, University of Nairobi) implementing specific components under contracts. Decision-making rests with the GDI Hub Advisory Board (chaired by Lord Chris Holmes) and DFID’s oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for community health workers (AMREF’s LEAP platform)
business support curriculum for start-ups (InnovateNow)
inclusive design training for built environment professionals
research capacity through open calls and WHO collaboration
country capacity assessments (CCAs) with local teams

partner_organizations.name: Global Disability Innovation (GDI) Hub
partner_organizations.role: Consortium lead and programme manager

partner_organizations.name: University College London (UCL)
partner_organizations.role: Research, data/evidence, innovation hubs

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: World Report on AT, CCAs, standards

partner_organizations.name: Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI)
partner_organizations.role: Country implementation, CCAs

partner_organizations.name: AMREF Health Africa
partner_organizations.role: Innovation accelerator (LEAP platform), East Africa delivery

partner_organizations.role: Paralympic engagement, TV coverage, school programmes

partner_organizations.name: Royal College of Art (RCA)
partner_organizations.role: Inclusive design, built environment

partner_organizations.role: Innovation challenge fund, start-up support

partner_organizations.role: Innovation Hub India, product development

partner_organizations.role: Innovation Hub India

partner_organizations.role: Local innovation programme delivery

partner_organizations.name: Strathmore University
partner_organizations.role: Local innovation programme delivery

partner_organizations.name: 'In-country' partners (TBC)
partner_organizations.role: CCA implementation, national trials

quote.text: "GDI Hub lead the consortium for AT2030... The programme extension will enable the whole AT2030 programme to reach a total of 9 million people through improving access to life-changing AT."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is delivered through an Accountable Grant from DFID to the GDI Hub, which then sub-contracts to consortium partners. The grant includes quarterly disbursements with payment-by-results for outputs, and requires 100% match funding from partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The GDI Hub manages a fixed consortium of pre-selected partners (expanded for Africa scale-up) with defined roles. New partners are added via direct sub-contracts under the existing Accountable Grant terms, with DFID approval. The structure includes an Advisory Board for strategic oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The existing consortium was already delivering successfully, with £3.6m match funding secured. Creating a new consortium would lose momentum and require additional setup costs without guaranteed match funding. The business case explicitly rejects alternative options to change the consortium.

quote.text: "Creating consortia is a risk, and the current one is functioning and delivering well. The momentum gained over the past year in creating the current consortium would fail to be leveraged if this option were taken... It would also cost additional funds to establish a new consortium, and there is no guarantee the 100% matched funding would be maintained."

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: The GDI Hub allocates funds to sub-partners via competitive calls (e.g., Innovation Investment Fund) or direct contracts (e.g., CCAs). New partners are selected by GDI Hub under the existing Accountable Grant terms, with DFID approval for major changes.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The AT2030 Advisory Board (chaired by Lord Chris Holmes) provides strategic oversight, technical advice, and risk mitigation support. It includes external advisors and meets quarterly to review progress. DFID participates as a member, with ultimate approval authority resting with the Minister.

quote.text: "GDI Hub will submit a quarterly payment request to DFID that will provide a narrative of programme activity completed in the previous quarter and planned for the following quarter... AT2030 Advisory Board meetings occur quarterly and will be expanded to review both AT2030 and AT2030: Africa activities."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with DFID approval, as shown by the adaptive responses to early learning (e.g., adding Sport and Inclusive Design themes). However, major changes require contract amendments and Ministerial sign-off.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a ‘fail-fast’ approach, continuously reassessing interventions based on validation of results. New themes (Sport, Inclusive Design) were added based on early learning, and the Theory of Change was refined. Adjustments require DFID approval but are encouraged to maximize impact.

quote.text: "A ‘fail-fast’, adaptive programme, AT2030+AT2030: Africa will respond to ongoing validation of results and continuously reassess interventions, adapting to maximise impact... The concept of AT2030: Africa has been informed by these insights and was designed to respond to these needs."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GDI Hub (consortium lead) → Delivery Partners (e.g., AMREF, UCL) → Sub-grantees (e.g., start-ups, local NGOs)

quote.text: "Payment will be made via bank transfer within the agreed number of days in the contract (30 days for most partners)... Partners will submit quarterly payment requests by the date agreed in contract; these will include a short narrative report (linked to their log frame) and a succinct financial report detailing spend in the previous quarter."

q24_alternatives_considered: Deliver through ATscale (rejected: not yet operational, different focus)
Stop using GDI Hub consortium (rejected: would lose momentum and match funding)
Extend AT2030 with GDI Hub (selected: maximizes existing investment)
Continue AT2030 at original level (rejected: would miss multiplier effect)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The GDI Hub-led consortium was selected because it (1) leverages existing momentum and £3.6m match funding, (2) provides 100% cost efficiency through matched resources, (3) reduces unit costs from £3.33 to £2.20 per person reached, and (4) allows rapid scaling while maintaining DFID oversight. The ‘Option 3’ analysis showed it offered the best value for money (£1.63 per additional unit vs £3.33 original).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (reduced unit cost, 100% match funding)
partner capacity (proven track record with £3.6m leverage)
speed (avoids delays in establishing new structures)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Consortium dependency: Reliance on GDI Hub’s management capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly reviews, Advisory Board oversight, and DFID’s payment-by-results structure

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Match funding shortfall: Private sector may not meet 100% commitment
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified funding sources (NGOs, governments, academia) and leverage of existing partnerships (e.g., Paralympics, WHO)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination: Managing expanded consortium across multiple countries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear log frames, joint Advisory Board, and standardized reporting (quarterly payment requests)

quote.text: "Option 3: Extend AT2030 to include AT2030: Africa, led by GDI Hub consortium... This option provides a sensible and realistic investment in Assistive Technology innovation. Overall for a £9.8m investment, the programme will generate over £9.8m in matched funding over the lifetime of the programme. This option offers the best value for money and high levels of efficiency and effectiveness."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The African context (weak AT markets, stigma, and infrastructure barriers) necessitates partners with local delivery capacity (e.g., AMREF for East Africa, University of Nairobi) and global standards expertise (WHO). The ‘valley of death’ for entrepreneurs requires incubators like InnovateNow, while built environment constraints demand RCA’s design expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: Market failures → Need for innovation hubs (InnovateNow, IIT Delhi)
Stigma → Requires Paralympic partners (IPC, Loughborough)
Weak health systems → CCAs and WHO collaboration
Inaccessible infrastructure → RCA and LUL for inclusive design
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (research + implementation + market shaping) require a consortium structure to integrate expertise: UCL/WHO for evidence, AMREF/BGV for innovation, and IPC for stigma reduction. The need for rapid testing of interventions (e.g., CCAs) drives the closed consortium model with quarterly oversight.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (WHO/UCL) → Informing CCAs and national trials
Technology development (BGV/AMREF) → Linked to Innovation Investment Fund
Stigma reduction (Paralympics) → Requires media partnerships (IPC)
Inclusive design → Needs RCA/LUL’s built environment expertise
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging existing consortium, 100% match funding) with equity (disability inclusion marker ‘principal’, gender focus). Trade-offs include: (1) Northern-led management for speed vs. Southern implementation for relevance, and (2) standardized CCAs vs. country-specific adaptations.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to existing consortium accelerate delivery but limit new Southern partners
Cost vs. reach: Paralympic media programmes (6m indirect reach) are cost-effective but less targeted than direct AT provision
Expertise vs. ownership: UK-based GDI Hub ensures technical quality but local partners (AMREF) deliver contextually
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk profile drives quarterly oversight (vs. annual) and payment-by-results structures. FCAS-like constraints (weak systems) necessitate DFID’s approval for sub-awards and adaptive management clauses.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: AMREF runs accelerators, University of Nairobi reduces travel costs by hosting innovation programmes, and CCAs include local team training. Southern partners’ capacity determines their delivery scope (e.g., AMREF’s LEAP platform enables rural innovator inclusion).

quote.text: "Innovation in the AT space is harder than initially anticipated... particularly in East Africa, India, and South Asia AT2030 is demonstrating a strong and growing interest for sustained investment in AT once ‘product-market fit’ is established. This requires partners like AMREF and BGV to bridge the Valley of Death."

key_programme_risks: Market failure: AT entrepreneurs face a prolonged ‘valley of death’ (mitigation: Innovation Investment Fund, BGV support)
Stigma: Cultural barriers limit AT uptake (mitigation: Paralympic engagement, school programmes)
Weak health systems: Countries lack capacity for AT provision (mitigation: CCAs, WHO standards)
Sustainability: Donor dependency risks post-programme collapse (mitigation: 100% match funding, local innovation hubs)
Coordination: Complex multi-partner delivery (mitigation: quarterly Advisory Board, standardized log frames)
Built environment: Physical barriers limit AT usability (mitigation: inclusive design case studies, RCA partnership)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient evidence for WHO World Report on AT
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Dedicated £1m research call and UCL/WHO collaboration to fill gaps

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low start-up survival rates in East Africa
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: InnovateNow ecosystem with AMREF’s LEAP platform and BGV’s ‘tech for good’ expertise
Pilot case studies and London 2012 legacy principles to demonstrate cost-effectiveness

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Paralympic engagement fails to shift attitudes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-channel approach (TV + schools + athlete role models) with Loughborough University’s expertise

fcas_specific_lessons: Country Capacity Assessments (CCAs) were added to address weak institutional capacity in FCAS-like settings
Rapid Implementation Fund allows flexible responses to country-specific constraints
Local innovation hubs (e.g., InnovateNow) reduce dependency on Northern expertise
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Early AT2030 learning showed: (1) Stigma and built environment are critical barriers, leading to new Sport and Inclusive Design themes; (2) Innovation requires more investment than anticipated, prompting the Innovation Investment Fund; (3) Country engagement needs formalized tools (CCAs). The London 2012 Paralympics legacy provided a model for stigma reduction.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added Sport Against Stigma theme based on London 2012 lessons
Included Inclusive Design component due to built environment barriers
Expanded Innovation Investment Fund to address the ‘valley of death’
Formalized CCAs and Rapid Implementation Fund for country-level action
Increased focus on East Africa (InnovateNow) where market gaps are deepest

quote.text: "The learning from AT2030 tells us that there is a critical link between the product narratives... and the need for a more formal country-specific scoping process to pilot-test the ability to generate sustainable provision... AT2030: Africa will therefore focus on developing a set of formal ‘CCA’ tools, which will result in country-level action plans and pilots backed by rapid investment."

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £9.8m DFID investment is 100% match-funded (£9.8m), bringing total programme funding to £19.8m. Additional leverage includes: (1) Indian Government funds via Innovation Hub India, (2) Royal Academy of Engineering Africa Prize alignment, and (3) Paralympic movement resources for stigma reduction.

activity_budget_allocation.activity: Innovation Investment Fund (start-ups, Valley of Death)
Data and Evidence (WHO Report, research calls)

quote.text: "DFID’s funding will be 100% matched by private sector investment, other research monies, partner match and business growth... Already AT2030 has exceeded expectations, matching £3.6m in less than one year (just under two-times DFID’s spend (£1.75m) in the same period)."

metadata.programme_name: UK voluntary contributions to the OECD Development Assistance Committee in 2023 and 2024

quote.programme_name: "UK voluntary contributions to the OECD Development Assistance Committee in 2023 and 2024." (D0004969.odt, Summary Information)
quote.sector: "The DAC is a key forum of ‘like-minded’ donors for setting international development norms and standards, monitoring and measuring development finance flows" (D0004916.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.duration_source: "New project end date (if applicable): 01/04/2023-31/03/2025" (D0004969.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **policy influence** by ensuring the DAC remains a credible forum for setting development standards and norms. It also includes **financing mechanism** elements by channeling UK voluntary contributions to support the DAC's core work, and **capacity building** through technical and policy expertise provided by the DAC Secretariat.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UK voluntary contributions (VCs) to the OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) will help ensure that the DAC remains a credible and effective forum for setting and promoting standards for effective development cooperation and that development assistance has the greatest impact for those most in need." (D0004916.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Mobilising and aligning finance for the 2030 Agenda
Making development co-operation more effective, impactful, and inclusive including through better partnerships and innovation
Preventing and addressing fragility and crises
Tackling poverty and inequalities, achieving gender equality, and enabling inclusive governance in order to leave no one behind
Promoting Climate Objectives and Sustainable Management and Use of Natural Capital
DAC Core Business: ensuring the DAC retains and buttresses its key role in the international development finance system as the guardian of Official Development Assistance (ODA)

Financing for Development: providing analysis and support for the global community on how to use ODA to mobilise non-concessional public and private finance at scale to deliver the SDGs and Paris Agreement
Climate and development: implementing the DAC’s Climate Declaration, recognising the nature of the challenges facing LDCs and SIDS and increasing finance for adaptation
Accelerating progress on gender equality: rolling out the DAC’s updated guidance on gender equality and empowerment of women and girls

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the OECD DAC's role as the guardian of ODA standards and a forum for peer learning, while supporting UK priorities in climate, gender equality, and poverty reduction. It provides unearmarked voluntary contributions to fund technical expertise and policy analysis within the DAC Secretariat.

quote.objective: "The DAC’s long-term objective and mandate is to ‘promote development co-operation and other relevant policies so as to contribute to implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, through sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, poverty eradication, improvement of living standards in developing countries, and to a future in which no country will depend on aid.’" (D0004916.odt, Impact and Outcome)
quote.outputs: "The DAC PWB 2023-24 focuses on the following five outputs: Mobilising and aligning finance for the 2030 Agenda; Making development co-operation more effective, impactful, and inclusive including through better partnerships and innovation; Preventing and addressing fragility and crises; Tackling poverty and inequalities, achieving gender equality, and enabling inclusive governance in order to leave no one behind; Promoting Climate Objectives and Sustainable Management and Use of Natural Capital." (D0004916.odt, Outputs)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk due to the DAC's established role as a multilateral forum with robust financial controls and a track record of delivery. The risk is mitigated by the OECD's internal mechanisms and the UK's ongoing engagement.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004916.odt, Overall programme risk rating)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (need for consensus among 31 like-minded donors)
regulatory (OECD Financial Regulations and compliance requirements)
data limitations (challenges in tracking and validating ODA flows)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The need for consensus among DAC members can slow decision-making and limit the UK's ability to unilaterally influence priorities. Regulatory compliance adds administrative layers, while data limitations affect the accuracy of ODA reporting and analysis.

quote.risk: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004916.odt, Overall programme risk rating)
quote.constraints: "Decisions are based on consensus. The DAC Chair oversees the work of the Committee and as a neutral Chair, represents the views of all its members." (D0004916.odt, Theory of change)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The DAC Secretariat (based in Paris, OECD HQ) manages the programme, with decision-making power resting with the DAC Chair and member consensus. The UK, as a major donor, has influence but no unilateral control.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical and policy expertise provided by DAC Secretariat staff
peer learning and knowledge sharing among DAC members
implementation of DAC guidance on gender equality, climate, and development finance

partner_organizations.name: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and technical/policy expert

partner_organizations.name: UK Delegation to the OECD (UKDEL)
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring and engagement with DAC Secretariat

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Development Partnerships & Multilateral Effectiveness Department
partner_organizations.role: Programme oversight and strategic direction
