quote.structure: "The DAC is a key forum of 31 like-minded donors for setting international development policy and standards, monitoring and measuring financial flows, as well as for exchanging best practice and peer learning." (D0004916.odt, Context)
quote.capacity: "The DAC’s added value and comparative advantage is the technical and policy analysis the Secretariat offers to support members." (D0004916.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides unearmarked voluntary contributions (VCs) to the DAC Secretariat through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This allows flexible allocation of funds to core DAC activities while maintaining UK influence over priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The DAC Secretariat (DCD) manages day-to-day delivery under the oversight of the DAC Chair and member consensus. The UK Delegation to the OECD (UKDEL) monitors implementation and engages with the Secretariat, while FCDO provides strategic direction.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The OECD DAC is the unique global guardian of ODA standards, with no alternative forum capable of replicating its mandate. The UK's long-standing membership and prior positive experience with unearmarked VCs justify direct funding.

quote.instrument: "The FCDO will provide a total of £735,000 in unearmarked voluntary contributions (VC) to support delivery of the DAC’s PWB 2023-24. The terms of the agreement are set out in a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)." (D0004916.odt, Value for Money)
quote.selection: "There is no alternative to the DAC and its subsidiary bodies. The DAC remains an authoritative forum for donors to improve practices and policies and act as the guardian of the ODA system." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The DAC operates by consensus among its 31 members, with the DAC Chair overseeing work and representing all members. The UK engages through the UK Delegation to the OECD (UKDEL) and participates in DAC meetings and networks.

quote.governance: "The DAC Chair oversees the work of the Committee and as a neutral Chair, represents the views of all its members." (D0004916.odt, Theory of change)
quote.oversight: "The DAC Secretariat produces regular Committee Progress Reports on the implementation of the PWB during the biennium. Two progress reports are published for each year of the PWB." (D0004916.odt, Monitoring, reporting and accounting for funds)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Unearmarked VCs provide flexibility for the DAC Secretariat to allocate funds across core workstreams, but the UK monitors usage through Progress Reports and bilateral engagement to ensure alignment with priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The DAC's Programme of Work and Budget (PWB) is agreed by members every two years, with progress reviewed annually. The UK can influence adjustments through engagement with the DAC Chair and Secretariat, but changes require member consensus.

quote.flexibility: "Unearmarked funding also gives the UK influence and a strong voice in the DAC, including on PWB priority setting and budget management." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)
quote.adjustment: "The DAC’s Programme of Work and Budget (PWB) is agreed by members and delivered by the DCD. Priority outputs for the UK are set out in the PWB 2023-24." (D0004916.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → OECD DAC Secretariat (DCD) → (no further sub-awards; funds used for in-house technical/policy experts)

quote.budget: "The FCDO will provide a total of £735,000 in unearmarked voluntary contributions (VC) to support delivery of the DAC’s PWB 2023-24." (D0004916.odt, Value for Money)
quote.costs: "There is also an overhead charge of 6.3% (with a 1% discount for VCs exceeding 500k EUR) which covers indirect administrative services." (D0004916.odt, Financial and fraud risk)
quote.layers: "The vast proportion of this component will be used to fund the employment of technical and policy experts working on the programmed activities." (D0004916.odt, Financial and fraud risk)
quote.payments: "The UK VC of £735,000 will be paid annually: £316,216 in December 2023 and £418,784 in December 2024." (D0004916.odt, Financial and fraud risk)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Provides flexibility to the DAC Secretariat and maintains UK influence over priorities.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Approving the VC as earmarked (not recommended)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Would limit DAC flexibility and undermine Secretariat efforts to improve effectiveness.
Would limit UK influence, damage reputation, and reduce ability to shape global development policies.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The unearmarked VC option was chosen because it: (1) aligns with the UK's strategic priorities for the DAC; (2) provides maximum flexibility to the Secretariat to deliver the PWB; (3) reduces transaction costs; and (4) maintains the UK's influence in priority-setting. The DAC's track record of scoring 'A' (met expectations) in programme reviews further justified this approach.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (reputational risks of not funding)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The DAC does not receive enough Voluntary Contributions (VCs) to deliver fully on its 2023/24 PWB.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UK continues to provide full unearmarked VCs and encourages other donors to do the same, while contributing to discussions on sustainable fundraising strategies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The UK’s funding goes towards PWB output areas that do not fall under the UK’s priorities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close engagement with the DCD/Director in budget discussions and sending letters to outline UK priorities. Monitoring via Committee Progress Reports.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: DAC is detached from and has limited influence beyond traditional donors.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Support for the DAC’s global relations strategy and encouragement of better coordination across OECD committees. Successful outreach activities (e.g., Global Meeting of Development Co-operation Providers).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Transition in DAC Chair leadership and DCD Director slows delivery and impacts cohesion.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK engagement with OECD senior leadership, the DAC Chair’s office, and members to ensure momentum on core work and smooth leadership transitions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: DAC members are unsupportive of UK priorities (e.g., SIDS access to finance).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close engagement with the DAC Chair’s office, DCD, and members to identify consensus areas and build coalitions.

quote.alternatives: "Option 1: Approve the VC as unearmarked and revisit earmarked as a potential option in the future (recommended). The VC helps ensure that the DAC delivers on its priorities under core outputs and that the UK’s voice remains influential in this forum." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)
quote.rationale: "Unearmarked funding is recommended as it not only reduces programme management transaction costs but gives maximum flexibility to the secretariat in the implementation of the PBW." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)
quote.risks: "Risk: The DAC does not receive enough Voluntary Contributions (VCs) to deliver fully on its 2023/24 PWB. Mitigation: UK continues to provide full unearmarked VCs as proposed and encourages other donors to make their VCs unearmarked too." (D0004916.odt, Summary of key risks and mitigation measures)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global, multilateral context of the DAC constrains partner selection to the OECD DAC Secretariat, as it is the sole authoritative forum for setting ODA standards. The need for consensus among 31 members limits the UK's ability to unilaterally direct funds or priorities.
q27_constraints_detail: No alternative to DAC for ODA standard-setting ("there is no alternative to the DAC and its subsidiary bodies")
Consensus-based decision-making ("Decisions are based on consensus")
Limited influence beyond traditional donors ("DAC is detached from and has limited influence and visibility beyond traditional donors")
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's objectives—such as influencing global development standards, promoting gender equality, and addressing climate change—require a multilateral delivery structure (the DAC) due to its unique mandate as the guardian of ODA. The need for technical expertise and peer learning among donors necessitates a centralized Secretariat (DCD) with flexible, unearmarked funding.
q28_linkages: Policy influence objectives → Multilateral forum (DAC) as the only credible standard-setter
Flexibility needs (adapting to global challenges) → Unearmarked VCs for Secretariat discretion
Technical expertise requirements → Funding for in-house DAC policy/technical experts
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The choice of unearmarked VCs balances efficiency (reduced transaction costs, flexible allocation) with equity (ensuring burden-sharing among G7 donors and supporting global public goods like ODA standards). However, it risks misalignment with UK-specific priorities if funds are allocated to lower-priority areas.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (unearmarked VCs reduce management costs) vs. Equity (ensuring UK priorities are reflected)
Flexibility (Secretariat discretion) vs. Accountability (UK influence over fund use)
Global public goods (DAC standards) vs. National interests (UK-specific development objectives)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., reputational risks, budget pressures) justifies milestone-based oversight through Progress Reports and bilateral engagement with the Secretariat, rather than intensive day-to-day management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The DAC Secretariat's technical expertise and role as a knowledge hub enable it to act as the primary implementer, while the UK's capacity-building objectives (e.g., gender equality, climate) are embedded in the DAC's workstreams and guided by UK engagement.

quote.constraints: "There is no alternative to the DAC and its subsidiary bodies. The DAC remains an authoritative forum for donors to improve practices and policies and act as the guardian of the ODA system." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)
quote.linkages: "The DAC’s added value and comparative advantage is the technical and policy analysis the Secretariat offers to support members." (D0004916.odt, Programme summary)
quote.tradeoffs: "Unearmarked funding is recommended as it not only reduces programme management transaction costs but gives maximum flexibility to the secretariat in the implementation of the PBW." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient Voluntary Contributions (VCs) to deliver the DAC’s 2023/24 Programme of Work and Budget (PWB).
UK funding allocated to non-priority PWB outputs while other members earmark funds for their priorities.
DAC’s limited influence and visibility beyond traditional donors.
Leadership transitions (DAC Chair and DCD Director) disrupting delivery and member cohesion.
Lack of DAC member support for UK priorities (e.g., SIDS access to finance).
Reputational risks to the UK if it ceases or reduces VC funding.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK provides full unearmarked VCs and encourages other donors to contribute unearmarked funds. Engages in discussions on sustainable fundraising strategies.
Monitoring via Committee Progress Reports; bilateral engagement with DCD/Director; letters to outline UK priorities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: DAC’s limited influence beyond traditional donors
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support for DAC’s global relations strategy; encouragement of cross-OECD coordination; outreach activities (e.g., Global Meeting of Development Co-operation Providers).
UK engagement with OECD senior leadership, DAC Chair’s office, and members to maintain momentum.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of support for UK priorities (e.g., SIDS)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Close engagement with DAC Chair’s office, DCD, and members to build coalitions and identify consensus areas.
Continued provision of VCs to maintain UK influence and reputation as a committed DAC member.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The DAC programme scored ‘A’ (met expectations) in the 2019/20 and 2021/22 annual reviews, demonstrating effective delivery of core outputs. However, the 2021/22 review noted the need for more evidence of progress on humanitarian and climate priorities, as well as higher member engagement with DAC Reference Groups on Ending SEAH and Gender Equality.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2023-24 programme continues the use of unearmarked VCs based on past success, but includes stronger monitoring of fund allocation via Progress Reports and bilateral engagement to address previous risks of misalignment with UK priorities.

quote.risks: "Risk: The DAC does not receive enough Voluntary Contributions (VCs) to deliver fully on its 2023/24 PWB. Mitigation: UK continues to provide full unearmarked VCs as proposed and encourages other donors to make their VCs unearmarked too." (D0004916.odt, Summary of key risks and mitigation measures)
quote.lessons: "The programme scored an ‘A’ (met expectations) during the annual review process in the most recent bienniums (2019/20 and 2021/22)." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)
quote.design_changes: "We will ensure UK unearmarked VCs for 2023-2024 are being used by the DCD for priority UK outputs by monitoring the DCD’s Committee Progress Reports [...] and by strengthening engagement between UK Del Paris and the DCD." (D0004916.odt, Programme options)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other DAC member countries (e.g., Sweden, Switzerland, Ireland)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s £735k VC leverages the DAC’s broader budget of ~£35m (40.4m EUR) for 2023-24, enabling influence over global ODA standards and policies. The DAC’s work also supports the mobilisation of non-concessional finance for the SDGs and Paris Agreement.

quote.budget: "The FCDO will provide a total of £735,000 in unearmarked voluntary contributions (VC) to support delivery of the DAC’s PWB 2023-24." (D0004916.odt, Value for Money)
quote.leverage: "The DAC agreed a budget of 41.1m EUR for the 2023-24 biennium [...] The resulting budget envelope will be 40.4m EUR instead of 41.1m EUR." (D0004916.odt, Value for Money)
quote.overhead: "There is also an overhead charge of 6.3% (with a 1% discount for VCs exceeding 500k EUR) which covers indirect administrative services." (D0004916.odt, Financial and fraud risk)

metadata.programme_name: Support to Social Protection Programme 2 (SSPP2)
metadata.quote: The programme will leverage additional donor and government resources of about £70m per year. Ultimately, SSPP2 will support the creation of a sustainable, nationally owned system to redistribute revenues from gas that Mozambique is expected to start earning in the next decade. (90000651.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source:
Start Date: March 2020
End Date: March 2025 (90000651.odt, Contents)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SSPP2 combines service delivery (direct cash transfers to vulnerable households), capacity building (strengthening Mozambique's social protection systems), and policy influence (developing shock-responsive social protection mechanisms). It aims to create a sustainable, nationally owned system to redistribute gas revenues while addressing immediate poverty and vulnerability through cash transfers.
what_objectives.q1_source: SSPP2 will help poor and vulnerable people meet their basic needs and cope better with crises through social protection. [...] It will develop government capacity to respond to crises quickly and effectively through the national social protection system. (90000651.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 60,000 vulnerable households per year receiving cash transfers (300,000 people)
PSSB programme reaching over 450,000 direct beneficiaries by 2025
INAS database and information management system fully operational
75% of cash transfer programme beneficiaries paid via outsourced/digital payment providers
Shock-responsive social protection system with agreed protocols between INGC and INAS
Evidence on use of social protection for resilience building generated and used to inform policy
£70m per year leveraged from additional donor and government resources
what_objectives.summary: SSPP2 aims to create a bigger, better, and more shock-responsive social protection system in Mozambique by 2030, combining direct service delivery with systemic strengthening and policy development.
what_objectives.quote: The UK vision for social protection and cash transfers in Mozambique is that by 2030, the social protection system will be bigger (with increased coverage and transfer values), better (more effective, efficient and equitable) and more shock responsive. (90000651.odt, Strategic Case)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique faces multiple fragility factors including conflict (resumed conflict between political parties), climate vulnerability (frequent cyclones/droughts), weak institutions, and high poverty rates (69% below $1.90). The document explicitly mentions it as a fragile context with 'deepening grievances and increasing risks of conflict'.
where_context.q5_source: Mozambique remains one of the poorest countries in the world (7th poorest; 69% below $1.90). [...] deepening grievances and increasing risks of conflict. (90000651.odt, Business Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak public institutions and limited administrative capacity hamper programme expansion (only 20% of poor households currently covered). Climate shocks (cyclones/droughts) disrupt service delivery and increase vulnerability. Political instability and corruption risk misallocation of funds. Data limitations affect targeting accuracy.
where_context.quote: The expansion of social protection coverage as envisaged in Mozambique's five year national development plans has been hampered by the impact of the macroeconomic crisis and the limited administrative and technical capacity within Government. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led multilateral) manages the MDTF and technical assistance, with DFID (UK) providing strategic oversight and policy influence. Mozambican institutions (INAS/MGCAS) implement programmes but have limited decision-making power over fund allocation or design changes.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening INAS's Management Information System (e-INAS)
digitizing payment processes and financial management systems
training on shock-responsive social protection protocols
technical assistance for disaster risk financing
institutional strengthening of INAS/MGCAS

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: MDTF manager (funding and technical assistance)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Mozambique (INAS/MGCAS)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (programme delivery)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations agencies
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance and emergency response

partner_organizations.name: Government of Sweden
partner_organizations.role: co-funder

partner_organizations.name: Government of the Netherlands
partner_organizations.role: co-funder

partner_organizations.name: WFP
partner_organizations.role: emergency cash transfer delivery

who_partners.quote: DFID has been active in shaping the sector, as the lead donor and has played a convening role to bring all the actors together. [...] The UK has been active in shaping the sector, as the lead donor. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) managed by the World Bank, combining: 1) a Recipient-Executed Trust Fund (RETF) for direct cash transfers to the government, and 2) a Bank-Executed Trust Fund (BETF) for technical assistance. An Emergency Response Fund (ERF) is also included for crisis situations, managed via pre-arranged UN agreements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank manages the MDTF with two sub-components (RETF for programme funding, BETF for TA). DFID oversees the overall programme and manages separate agreements for the Emergency Response Fund (with UN agencies) and MEL activities. A joint secretariat coordinates donors.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected based on its existing capacity in social protection, established relationship with DFID, and ability to manage multi-donor funds. The choice reflects DFID's strategic partnership approach and the need for rapid mobilization in a fragile context.
how_mechanism.quote: The new social protection sector architecture has a UN joint programme for technical assistance [...] and a World Bank MDTF to manage funding to programmes and operational technical assistance. The UK has been active in shaping the sector, as the lead donor. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The MDTF includes a secretariat to improve coordination between donors and the Government of Mozambique. DFID has a programme-funded adviser embedded in the BETF to manage political economy risks. Decision-making involves the World Bank, DFID, and Mozambican institutions (INAS/MGCAS).
how_governance.quote: The BETF technical assistance will also support the creation of policies and processes needed for a shock responsive social protection system. [...] The programme funded adviser and the secretariat together will boost DFID's capacity to engage with Government. (90000651.odt, Component 1)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the MDTF can be reallocated between social protection programmes (PSSB/PASP/PASD) with donor agreement, but the Emergency Response Fund (ERF) is ring-fenced and requires separate activation. Major reallocations would need DFID approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a MEL component to generate learning and inform course corrections. Shock-responsive protocols are designed to be adaptive, but structural changes (e.g., adding new programme components) would require DFID approval.
how_flexibility.quote: This component will contribute to output 4 and to the effectiveness of outputs 1, 2 and 3. [...] generate programme level learning and evidence that can be used to support programme decisions and course correction. (90000651.odt, Component 3)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (MDTF manager) → INAS (implementer) → beneficiaries. For emergency response: FCDO → UN agencies → beneficiaries.
how_efficiency.quote: The MDTF will provide funds to the Government National Institute of Social Action (INAS) to fund social protection programmes. (90000651.odt, Component 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (let current programmes end)
Invest in a larger, more effective shock-responsive social protection system (without ERF)
Invest in shock-responsive system + include Emergency Response Fund (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (shock-responsive system + ERF) was chosen because: 1) Mozambique's high climate and conflict risks require both long-term systemic strengthening AND immediate crisis response capacity; 2) The ERF allows rapid response while the shock-responsive system is being developed (expected to take until 2025); 3) The World Bank's MDTF structure reduces complexity for DFID by consolidating funding streams; 4) The model builds on DFID's successful pilot of hybrid cash transfers during the 2016 El Niño drought.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in developing shock-responsive capacity may leave gaps in emergency coverage
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Inclusion of the pre-approved Emergency Response Fund (ERF) to bridge the gap until 2025

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: World Bank's limited expertise in emergency response could slow adaptation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID's embedded adviser in the BETF and partnership with UN agencies for emergency delivery

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between multiple donors (UK, Sweden, Netherlands, World Bank)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MDTF secretariat and joint programme design to align incentives

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in Mozambican systems (following hidden loans scandal)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Bank-Executed Trust Fund for TA to strengthen financial management, with DFID oversight

why_rationale.quote: Option 3 will be the same as Option 2, but will include a pre-approved emergency response fund (ERF) for use in case of crisis. [...] The advantages of having a pre-approved ERF are that it allows a faster response in a crisis, removing the requirement to draft and seek approval for a new business case. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Mozambique's FCAS context (weak institutions, conflict risk, climate vulnerability) limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) existing in-country presence (e.g., World Bank, UN agencies); 2) capacity to manage fiduciary risks (excluding direct budget support); 3) ability to operate in Portuguese. Local NGOs are not mentioned as partners due to capacity constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited Mozambican institutional capacity requires reliance on multilateral partners
Conflict and corruption risks necessitate Bank-Executed Trust Fund for TA
Climate shocks demand partners with rapid response experience (e.g., WFP for emergencies)
Language/regulatory barriers favor established international organizations
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both immediate service delivery (cash transfers) and long-term systemic change (shock-responsive systems) drives the mixed modality: 1) MDTF for scalable funding; 2) BETF for technical capacity building; 3) ERF for crisis flexibility. The hybrid approach reflects the dual objectives of poverty alleviation and institutional strengthening.
q28_linkages: Cash transfer delivery (WHAT) → requires World Bank's MDTF (HOW) for financial scale
Shock-responsive systems (WHAT) → necessitates BETF for TA and UN partnerships (HOW) for emergency expertise
Government ownership (WHAT) → shapes joint secretariat governance (HOW) for coordination
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) Speed vs. inclusion: The ERF allows rapid response but bypasses local systems; 2) Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: World Bank-led TA strengthens systems but limits Mozambican control; 3) Cost vs. reach: Digital payments improve efficiency but may exclude remote populations without infrastructure.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: World Bank's MDTF reduces transaction costs but centralizes control
Equity: Direct cash transfers target women (63% beneficiaries) but risk excluding men from economic opportunities
Speed: ERF enables quick crisis response but may undermine long-term systemic resilience
Ownership: Mozambican institutions implement programmes but depend on Northern donors for design/funding
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (high risk of corruption, conflict, climate shocks) justifies intensive oversight: embedded DFID adviser in BETF, annual audits of MDTF spend, and pre-approved ERF protocols to ensure rapid but accountable crisis response.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited Mozambican capacity leads to: 1) INAS focusing on implementation (not design); 2) World Bank/UN handling technical assistance; 3) DFID retaining strategic oversight. Capacity building (e-INAS, financial systems) aims to gradually shift roles toward local ownership.
intersections.quote: The Government of Mozambique (GoM) has demonstrated an unusually high level of commitment and support [but] significant challenges remain in the social protection system. Programme coverage as a proportion of those eligible remains low. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic instability disrupting programme funding
Political conflict derailing decentralization/peace processes
Climate shocks overwhelming system capacity
Corruption or mismanagement of funds (following hidden loans scandal)
Low administrative capacity limiting programme expansion
Gender inequalities persisting despite women-targeted transfers
Digital payment systems excluding remote populations
Donor coordination challenges in multi-partner MDTF

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversified funding through MDTF with multiple donors (UK, Sweden, Netherlands, World Bank)
ERF for immediate response + long-term shock-responsive system development
Bank-Executed Trust Fund for TA, annual MDTF audits, DFID embedded adviser
Technical assistance to strengthen INAS systems (e-INAS, digital payments)
Sex-disaggregated data, high female beneficiary targeting (63%), linkage with DFID's Gender-Responsive Social Protection programme
Gradual rollout with parallel manual systems during transition

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from 2016 El Niño drought: Need for slow-onset crisis preparedness (not just rapid-onset)
Post-hidden loans scandal: Avoid direct budget support; use Bank-Executed funds for TA
Cyclone Idai (2019): Importance of pre-positioned emergency agreements with UN agencies
Decentralization challenges: Align social protection with local governance structures
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous SSPP phase (2008-2016) showed that: 1) Direct financial aid to INAS increased coverage 4x (from 70 to 310 Meticais transfers) but required parallel system strengthening; 2) Community-based targeting had high inclusion errors; 3) Manual payments were inefficient and prone to delays. Current design addresses these through digital systems and shock-responsive protocols.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added ERF component based on El Niño drought delays; 2) Included shock-responsive protocols following Cyclone Idai; 3) Expanded MEL component to address previous monitoring gaps; 4) Digital payment systems to improve on manual process inefficiencies.
risks_lessons.quote: The El Niño drought of 2016 highlighted weaknesses in the current DRM system to enable timely interventions reaching larger numbers of people facing drought. [...] SSPP2 addresses this challenge by building a government-owned shock responsive social protection system. (90000651.odt, Appraisal Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will leverage additional donor and government resources of about £70m per year (total £350m over 5 years). The MDTF pools funds from multiple donors to create a larger programme with transformational potential.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily supports revenue expenditures (cash transfers, TA, programme management) with limited capital investment (IT systems like e-INAS).
financial_details.quote: SSPP2 will fund GoM cash transfer programmes to tackle chronic poverty and vulnerability through the RETF. The BETF will provide technical assistance to continue support to social protection systems. [...] This component will deliver most of all four outputs. (90000651.odt, Component 1)

metadata.programme_name: Propcom+ – Supporting economic development in conflict and climate affected regions in Nigeria
metadata.quote: "Propcom+ is an eight-year £95 million International Climate Finance (ICF) programme. The programme aims to support inclusive and resilient growth by promoting a transformation of Nigeria’s rural economy." (D0003546.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "May 2022 – April 2030" (D0005028.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Propcom+ combines implementation research (testing/scaling climate-smart interventions), financing mechanisms (grants to private sector), and capacity building (technical assistance to agribusinesses). It focuses on market development to improve productivity, resilience, and emissions reduction in Nigeria's rural economy.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Propcom+ will increase the incomes and climate resilience of 3.79 million poor and vulnerable men and women in Nigeria by: (a) scaling-up Proven climate-smart business models and markets; (b) developing and Piloting new business models that improve productivity, enhance resilience to climate change, and reduce emissions, and (c) supporting enabling Policies for an improved enabling environment for sustainable land and agricultural systems." (D0003546.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 3,790,000 people supported with improved income (£132 average net attributable income change per year)
3,790,000 people supported with improved resilience to climate change (ICF KPI4)
4,120,000 people supported to adapt to the effects of climate change (ICF KPI1)
£204,440,000 private finance mobilised (climate and non-climate)
Scaling proven climate-smart interventions (e.g., livestock vaccines, biofortified crops, climate-smart crop varieties)
Piloting new business models (e.g., aggregation, irrigation schemes, land governance)
Enabling policies for sustainable food and land-use systems
what_objectives.summary: Propcom+ aims to transform Nigeria's rural economy through climate-smart agriculture, focusing on scaling proven interventions, piloting new business models, and enabling policies to improve productivity, resilience, and emissions reduction.
what_objectives.quote: "Propcom+ will increase the incomes and climate resilience of 3.79 million poor and vulnerable men and women in Nigeria by: (a) scaling-up Proven climate-smart business models and markets; (b) developing and Piloting new business models that improve productivity, enhance resilience to climate change, and reduce emissions, and (c) supporting enabling Policies for an improved enabling environment for sustainable land and agricultural systems." (D0003546.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nigeria is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to ongoing insurgency in the northeast, farmer-herder conflicts, climate vulnerability, and weak governance. The programme explicitly addresses these challenges as drivers of instability.
where_context.q5_source: "Nigeria’s potential to unlock its economic opportunities are constrained by instability, conflict, poverty, inequality, weak governance, and exclusion across the country." (D0003546.odt, Problem C) AND "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003546.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: infrastructure (poor rural infrastructure, high transport costs)
political economy (corruption, weak public sector capacity)
weak institutions (limited state capacity for service delivery)
conflict (protracted crises in Northeast and Northwest)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit access to conflict-affected areas; weak infrastructure increases costs; regulatory gaps hinder market development; climate shocks disrupt agricultural productivity. These constraints require adaptive programming and partnerships with private sector actors who can operate in challenging environments.
where_context.quote: "Fragility, conflict, and insecurity afflict many parts of the country, including insurgency in the north-east and natural resource-based conflicts, layered with violent criminality, in the north-west." (D0003546.odt, Problem C) AND "Nigeria is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to the impacts of climate change and natural hazards." (D0003546.odt, Problem B)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority, with implementation delegated to a contracted service provider (likely UK-based). Nigerian private sector and state governments are engaged as partners but do not lead governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to agribusinesses (e.g., climate-smart investment identification, business model design)
training and mentoring for private sector entities
linkage creation between private sector and rural poor (B2C and B2B)
policy advocacy support to state governments

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner (co-design of climate-smart models, alignment with ACReSAL programme)

partner_organizations.name: State Governments (e.g., Kaduna, Jigawa, Borno, Edo)
partner_organizations.role: policy and enabling environment support (e.g., vaccine distribution, land governance)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector agribusinesses (SMEs, veterinary pharmaceutical manufacturers, financial institutions)
partner_organizations.role: direct implementation of climate-smart interventions (e.g., vaccine production, renewable energy deployment)

partner_organizations.name: Key Political Partners Group (KPPG: UK, US, EU, World Bank, UN)
partner_organizations.role: coordination platform for high-level engagement with Nigerian government

partner_organizations.name: Contracted Service Provider (TBD)
partner_organizations.role: primary programme implementation (technical assistance, grant management, MERL)

who_partners.quote: "Propcom+’s main programme delivery will be through a contracted service provider and will have a strong emphasis on adaptive and flexible management." (D0003546.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "A central priority will be collaborating and coordinating with others through strategic partnerships, leveraging strengths of other UK initiatives, Development Partners, and Federal and State government." (D0003546.odt, Strategic Partnerships)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **grants** (for private sector de-risking and innovation) and **technical assistance** (for capacity building). The grants include both **Resource-DEL (R-DEL)** for operational costs and **Capital-DEL (C-DEL)** for capital assets (e.g., manufacturing equipment, renewable energy infrastructure).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A contracted service provider (single entity) manages day-to-day delivery, with FCDO oversight. The provider delivers technical assistance, manages grants, and operates a MERL unit. Strategic partnerships (e.g., World Bank, state governments) supplement implementation but are not part of a formal consortium.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme will use a **Request for Proposals (RfP)** process for selecting SMEs and market partners in FY24/25, ensuring competitive selection aligned with FCDO’s principles on private sector subsidies. Direct awards may be used for quasi-governmental institutions.
how_mechanism.quote: "It is anticipated that SMEs will make up most of the market partners in FY24/25 through a Request for Proposals against eligible market sectors, with some direct award to quasi-governmental institutions." (D0005028.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "Propcom+ will operate within the FCDO’s principles on subsidies to the private sector." (D0005028.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.quote: "Propcom+’s main programme delivery will be through a contracted service provider." (D0003546.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "The programme’s iterative approach to implementation will help manage behaviour change risk, testing programme and intervention Theory of Change, to guide investment decisions." (D0003546.odt, MERL Approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between the "3Ps" (P1: Scaling Up, P2: Building Markets, P3: Enabling Policies) based on performance, but requires approval. A **Performance Fund** (£30m) is earmarked for scaling high-performing activities from Year 4, subject to mid-term evaluation and ministerial approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an **adaptive management** approach, with a MERL unit testing interventions in real-time to inform scaling, adaptation, or termination. A mid-term independent evaluation will guide adjustments, including allocation of the Performance Fund.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme’s iterative approach to implementation will help manage behaviour change risk, testing programme and intervention Theory of Change, to guide investment decisions." (D0003546.odt, MERL Approach) AND "The Performance Fund will act as a programme safeguard, managing delivery, financial and commercial risk, with the allocation subject to affordability, programme performance, value for money, and recommendations from the mid-term independent evaluation." (D0003546.odt, Performance Fund)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contracted Service Provider → Private Sector/SMEs (no additional intermediary layers explicitly described).
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will include an independent evaluation on effectiveness and value for money of programme interventions and overall approach." (D0003546.odt, Management Case) AND "Propcom+’s main programme delivery will be through a contracted service provider." (D0003546.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct implementation by FCDO (rejected due to lack of private sector expertise)
Pure grant-making without technical assistance (rejected due to need for capacity building)
Multilateral-led delivery (rejected to maintain UK leadership and flexibility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **contracted service provider model** was chosen for its ability to: (1) leverage private sector expertise in market development, (2) provide flexibility to adapt to Nigeria’s dynamic context, (3) combine grants and technical assistance for systemic change, and (4) align with FCDO’s principles on private sector subsidies. The inclusion of **C-DEL** was added post-inception to address capital constraints exacerbated by Nigeria’s 2023 economic shocks (fuel subsidy removal, naira devaluation).
q25_decision_factors: vfm (value for money through competitive grants and performance-based scaling)
risk-mitigation (diversified portfolio across SMEs, FIs, and impact investors)
experience (building on Propcom Mai-Karfi’s success with private sector-led growth)
partner-capacity (targeting SMEs and progressive state governments)
flexibility (adaptive management to respond to climate/conflict shocks)
equity (50% women beneficiaries, focus on Northern Nigeria)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Grant dependency among SMEs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structuring financing to minimise subsidies and require private sector co-investment; focusing on systemic change.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market distortion from subsidies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adhering to FCDO’s principles on private sector subsidies, ensuring additionality and leveraging patient capital.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak state government capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focusing on progressive states with demonstrated commitment; providing technical assistance for policy reforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Currency and inflation risks (post-2023 shocks)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Using C-DEL for capital assets to offset high upfront costs; deploying grants early to support ongoing R-DEL technical assistance.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (50% women beneficiaries, focus on climate-vulnerable regions)
why_rationale.quote: "Propcom+ will operate within the FCDO’s principles on subsidies to the private sector, as well as additional principles that are in line with the UK’s net zero commitment. This includes ensuring there is a clear development rationale to overcome market failures or equity goals, that the funding drives outcomes that are additional to what private sector partners might have committed to otherwise, and that interventions create sustainable, systemic change that avoid market distortions." (D0005028.odt, Approach to Implementation) AND "The original Propcom+ Business Case recommended opportunities to catalyse and/or facilitate programme interventions using C-DEL would be explored during programme inception, aligned to FCDO’s commitment to make further use of investment and capital instruments." (D0005028.odt, The Case for C-DEL)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nigeria’s **FCAS context** (conflict, weak governance, climate vulnerability) limits partner selection to: (1) **private sector actors** capable of operating in high-risk areas, (2) **progressive state governments** with sufficient capacity, and (3) **multilateral partners** (e.g., World Bank) for leverage. Traditional NGOs or federal agencies are deprioritised due to corruption risks and bureaucratic inefficiencies.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Northeast/Northwest restricts direct implementation to private sector partners with local networks.
Weak federal institutions necessitate focus on state-level and private sector engagement.
Climate shocks (flooding, desertification) require partners with adaptive capacity and resilience expertise.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need to scale climate-smart interventions** (WHAT) drives the **market facilitator model** (HOW), which combines grants (for de-risking) and technical assistance (for capacity building). The **focus on systemic change** (policy, markets, proven models) requires a **flexible, adaptive structure** rather than rigid project implementation.
q28_linkages: Scaling proven interventions (P1) → Requires **grants + TA** to private sector for adoption.
Piloting new models (P2) → Needs **competitive calls** to identify innovative SMEs.
Enabling policies (P3) → Demands **state government partnerships** for reform ownership.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions between **speed/efficiency** (working with established private sector players) and **equity/inclusion** (reaching women, conflict-affected populations). The programme mitigates this by: (1) setting a **50% women beneficiary target**, (2) focusing on **Northern Nigeria** despite higher costs, and (3) using **performance-based grants** to incentivise inclusive models.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Leveraging existing private sector networks for rapid scaling vs. Equity: Ensuring 50% women beneficiaries in male-dominated sectors (e.g., livestock).
Speed: Direct grants to SMEs vs. Inclusion: Requiring gender-sensitive business models as a condition.
Cost: Higher overheads in conflict zones vs. Reach: Prioritising Northeast/Northwest despite challenges.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** (high residual risk) drives **intensive oversight** (milestone-based reporting, mid-term evaluation) and **adaptive management** (MERL unit testing interventions in real-time). The **Performance Fund** acts as a safeguard to reallocate resources based on emerging risks/opportunities.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in the delivery structure: (1) **Technical assistance** to SMEs ensures they can absorb grants effectively, (2) **Policy engagement** with state governments builds their ability to sustain reforms, and (3) **Gender-sensitive TA** addresses cultural barriers to women’s economic empowerment.
intersections.quote: "FCDO assesses the risk of including C-DEL funding within the grant facility as moderate. By exploring three distinct types of partners there will be opportunities to diversify the portfolio, mitigate risks, and reduce management and oversight costs." (D0005028.odt, Risks) AND "A central priority will be collaborating and coordinating with others through strategic partnerships, leveraging strengths of other UK initiatives, Development Partners, and Federal and State government." (D0003546.odt, Strategic Partnerships)

key_programme_risks: Private sector grant dependency (mitigated by structuring financing to minimise subsidies).
Market distortion from interventions (addressed via additionality checks and leverage requirements).
State government capacity gaps (mitigated by focusing on progressive states and providing TA).
Climate shocks disrupting agricultural productivity (managed through adaptive programming and resilience-focused interventions).
Conflict limiting access to target regions (mitigated by private sector partnerships with local networks).
Currency/inflation risks (offset by C-DEL for capital assets and early grant deployment).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Financing structured to require private sector co-investment; focus on systemic change to avoid long-term reliance.
Adherence to FCDO’s subsidy principles; ensuring outcomes are additional to private sector commitments.
Targeting progressive states (e.g., Kaduna, Edo) with demonstrated commitment; providing technical assistance for policy reforms.
Piloting climate-smart technologies (e.g., drought-resistant seeds, solar pumps) and embedding resilience in all interventions.
Partnering with private sector entities already operating in high-risk areas; adaptive implementation approaches.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Propcom Mai-Karfi: "Very few market constraints are a result of a simple oversight or missing market component. In many cases there are numerous factors affecting the lack of market activity." (D0003546.odt, Risks & Lessons)
Need for **adaptive management** in FCAS: Iterative testing of interventions with real-time MERL feedback.
Importance of **private sector leadership** in fragile contexts where government capacity is limited.
**Policy engagement** must be tailored to state-level actors given federal weaknesses.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Propcom Mai-Karfi (predecessor programme) demonstrated that: (1) **Private sector-led models** can achieve scale even in conflict-affected areas, (2) **Market constraints are complex** and require multi-faceted solutions, and (3) **Gender inclusion** requires going beyond women-specific interventions to address structural barriers (e.g., cultural norms in livestock sectors).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations in Propcom+ design: (1) **Explicit 50% women beneficiary target** (up from 34.6% in Mai-Karfi), (2) **Stronger focus on climate resilience** (integrated into all interventions), (3) **C-DEL addition** to address capital constraints post-2023 economic shocks, (4) **Performance Fund** for adaptive scaling of high-impact activities.
risks_lessons.quote: "Propcom Mai-Karfi’s 2018 evaluation highlighted that ‘very few market constraints are as a result of a simple oversight or missing market component. In many cases there are numerous factors affecting the lack of market activity.’" (D0003546.odt, Risks & Lessons) AND "The programme will also include an independent evaluation on effectiveness and value for money of programme interventions and overall approach." (D0003546.odt, Management Case)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £204.44 million in private finance mobilised (climate and non-climate) by 2029/30
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £85 million Resource-DEL (operational/revenue) and £10 million Capital-DEL (capital assets, e.g., manufacturing equipment, renewable energy infrastructure).
financial_details.quote: "TotalsupportwillremainaspertheoriginalBusinessCaseat£95million,with£85millionofR-DELand£10millionofC-DEL." (D0005028.odt, Summary Information) AND "Private finance Mobilised – climate (ICF KPI12) and non-climate: £33,340,000 (by 2025/26) → £204,440,000 (by 2029/30)." (D0003546.odt, Key Results)

metadata.programme_name: TradeConnect

quote.programme_name: "TradeConnect" (D0001016.odt, Programme summary)
quote.budget: "£20 million" (D0001016.odt, Programme Value)
quote.duration: "01/04/2021-31/03/2026" (D0001018.odt, Original project start and end dates)
quote.sector: "DFID’s Economic Development Strategy focuses on trade as an engine for poverty reduction" (D0001016.odt, Department CDD/Portfolio/Business Plan Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 01/04/2021-31/03/2026" (D0001018.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: TradeConnect aims to unlock sustainable economic development by increasing the capacity of developing country exporters to tackle barriers to international trade and take advantage of the UK’s post-Brexit preferential trade arrangements. It combines service delivery (providing market information, connecting buyers/sellers, coaching firms), capacity building (strengthening business support institutions), and implementation research (testing interventions to improve export readiness).
what_objectives.q1_source: "TradeConnect aims to unlock sustainable economic development by increasing the capacity of developing country exporters to tackle barriers to international trade and take full advantage of the UK’s post-Brexit preferential trade arrangements by: Providing market information and guidance to demystify the export process; Connecting buyers and suppliers to increase business linkages; Increasing awareness of how to use preferential trading arrangements; Coaching firms to become ‘export-ready’ and strengthening business support institutions." (D0001016.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Firms in targeted developing countries have increased knowledge of international markets, including the UK (output)
Firms in targeted developing countries have increased awareness of preferential market access and how to use this access (output)
Increased business connections between suppliers in developing countries and international buyers (output)
More export-ready firms with improved business processes and capability to trade internationally (output)
Increase in quality jobs in supported firms (outcome)
Increased exporter revenue in targeted developing countries (outcome)
Increased imports in sectors the UK does not specialise in (secondary outcome)
Increased consumer choice and reliability at lower prices (secondary outcome)
UK businesses have better awareness and understanding of developing markets (secondary output)
UK businesses are able to source from a greater pool of suitable and reliable suppliers in developing markets (secondary output)
UK businesses are able to identify and establish relationships with new suppliers in developing markets (secondary output)
what_objectives.summary: TradeConnect is a strategic programme designed to increase developing country exports to the UK by addressing information gaps, building business linkages, and strengthening export capacity, while delivering secondary benefits to UK businesses and consumers.

quote.objectives: "The objective of the TradeConnect programme is to increase developing country exports as a means of supporting jobs, increasing incomes and reducing poverty." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.outputs: "The expected primary outputs are: Firms in targeted developing countries have increased knowledge of international markets, including the UK; Firms in targeted developing countries have increased awareness of preferential market access and how to use this access; Increased business connections between suppliers in developing countries and international buyers; More export-ready firms with improved business processes and capability to trade internationally." (D0001016.odt, Theory of Change)

countries_regions: A country from the MENAD region
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting a balanced assessment of operational challenges in developing countries without extreme fragility or conflict. The risk is considered manageable through standard due diligence and safeguarding measures.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0001016.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: information barriers (lack of market knowledge, regulatory complexity)
financial constraints (limited access to trade finance, high interest rates)
trust and credibility gaps (difficulty establishing business relationships)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Information barriers create uncertainty about export profitability, leading firms to underinvest in entering new markets. Regulatory complexity and financial constraints disproportionately affect SMEs, while trust gaps prevent the formation of reliable supply chains. Infrastructure limitations and political economy factors (like underutilization of preference schemes) further hinder trade growth.

quote.constraints: "Firms hoping to enter into new markets face significant information constraints creating uncertainty about the profitability of moving towards export markets... The cost of collecting technical information on tariff barriers, customs procedures and regulatory requirements in foreign markets can be prohibitively high... Inability to build overseas business relationships... Shortage of working capital and trade finance to finance exports." (D0001016.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.risk: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0001016.odt, Summary Sheet)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed and overseen by DFID/FCDO (UK), with implementation likely delegated to Northern-based contractors or consortia. Decision-making authority rests with DFID, though local Business Support Organisations (BSOs) in target countries may play operational roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: coaching firms to become ‘export-ready’
strengthening business support institutions (BSOs)
executive coaching and advisory support
support with national and sector branding
technical training on product lines and compliance

partner_organizations.name: DFID/FCDO
partner_organizations.role: funding and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Business Support Organisations (BSOs) in target countries
partner_organizations.role: local implementation support (potential partners)

partner_organizations.name: UK Trade Partnerships Programme
partner_organizations.role: complementary programming on EPAs

partner_organizations.name: SheTrades Commonwealth
partner_organizations.role: gender-focused trade support (alignment planned)

partner_organizations.name: UK importers and developing country exporters
partner_organizations.role: primary beneficiaries

quote.structure: "The programme will focus primarily on ‘last mile’ export and ‘first mile’ import support for those exporters closest to meeting demand in export markets... Where feasible the programme will also consider opportunities to work with local Business Support Organisations (BSOs)." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.capacity: "Coaching firms to become ‘export-ready’ and strengthening business support institutions." (D0001016.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is funded through a £20m DFID (FCDO) allocation, likely structured as a mix of grants and contracts. The addendum (D0001018.odt) confirms the budget remains unchanged but extends the timeline, suggesting a contract-based implementation with potential for sub-grants to local partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will be managed by a single implementing partner or a tightly coordinated consortium, with DFID/FCDO retaining oversight. The structure emphasizes flexibility to adjust resources between components (information provision, matchmaking, capacity building) based on learning.

quote.funding: "The UK will provide £20m over 5 years" (D0001018.odt, Summary Information)
quote.structure: "Resources [will be] flexed between [components] as required." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A steering group will meet every six months to oversee progress, with quarterly reports and annual DFID reviews. The addendum (D0001018.odt) specifies this structure, including a mid-term review linked to a break clause.

quote.governance: "Progress will be monitored through quarterly reports and meetings with the implementing partner and through six monthly meetings of the steering group. DFID annual review processes will be implemented." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)
quote.oversight: "DFID will commission an end of project review now in 2026. The programme will require an in-depth mid-term review, assessing impact, scale and the need for any corrective measures, linked to a break clause if objectives are not being met." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Resources can be flexed between programme components (information provision, matchmaking, capacity building) based on performance and learning. The addendum emphasizes adaptive management to respond to evidence gathered during inception and implementation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a mid-term review to assess impact and scale, with a break clause if objectives are not met. This suggests structured flexibility to adjust priorities, though major changes would require DFID approval.

quote.flexibility: "Resources flexed between them as required." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)
quote.adaptive: "The programme will require an in-depth mid-term review, assessing impact, scale and the need for any corrective measures, linked to a break clause if objectives are not being met." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (potential consortium) → Local BSOs/beneficiaries (if sub-awards are used). The structure is streamlined to avoid excessive layers, with direct oversight by FCDO.

quote.budget: "The UK will provide £20m over 5 years" (D0001018.odt, Summary Information)
quote.layers: "The platform will remain firmly plugged into international best practice in this area which will be incorporated where possible." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)
quote.payments: Implied by milestone-based monitoring: "Progress will be monitored against the theory of change and logframe" (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (baseline scenario)
Information provision only (Option 2)
Information provision + matchmaking (Option 3)
Information provision + matchmaking + capacity building (Option 4, preferred)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 (information + matchmaking + capacity building) was selected because it addresses the broadest range of barriers to trade (information gaps, trust deficits, and firm-level constraints) and aligns with evidence from similar programmes (e.g., CBI Netherlands, USAID East Africa Trade Hub). The mixed approach allows for testing multiple interventions while maintaining flexibility to adjust based on learning.
q25_decision_factors: evidence (lessons from CBI, USAID, and scoping studies)
value for money (potential for high returns on investment)
risk mitigation (diversified interventions reduce failure risk)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overly complex scope for a pilot phase
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limiting initial focus to ‘last-mile’ export support and a select few countries to manage complexity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low utilisation of services by target firms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Tailored outreach and awareness-raising, especially for SMEs, and partnerships with local BSOs to ensure relevance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to build trust between buyers and sellers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structured matchmaking with pre-screened participants and follow-up support to cement relationships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient demand from UK importers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging DFID’s existing relationships with UK businesses and aligning with the Gateway for Growth platform.

quote.alternatives: "Option 4 is the preferred option... this option offers greater reach and potential to reduce the barriers to trade to developing country exports." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.rationale: "Given that this programme will be initially piloted, this option creates a broader package of ‘last-mile’ support to developing country exporters that will allow for testing of their effectiveness." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.risks: "Giventhe gaps in the evidence base, it is important to test the programme approach... The programme will be initially piloted in a select few low- and middle-income countries." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope and moderate-risk contexts (e.g., Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan) constrain partner selection to organizations with regional expertise and the ability to navigate diverse regulatory and business environments. Local BSOs are prioritized where feasible, but political and economic constraints (e.g., in FCAS-adjacent regions) limit the pool of viable partners.
q27_constraints_detail: need for regional expertise (multi-country scope)
regulatory diversity (different trade rules across countries)
political stability requirements (moderate risk profile)
logistical challenges (infrastructure gaps in some countries)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (information provision, matchmaking, capacity building) necessitate a flexible, multi-component delivery structure. The need to test different interventions (per the pilot rationale) drives the choice of a single implementer/consortium with the ability to manage diverse activities and adapt based on learning.
q28_linkages: information gaps → need for digital platforms and helpdesks (structured under one implementer)
trust deficits → requirement for matchmaking services (integrated into delivery)
firm-level constraints → demand for capacity-building support (embedded in implementation)
pilot phase → adaptive management structure (flexible resource allocation)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly acknowledges trade-offs between inclusive reach (supporting SMEs and women-owned businesses) and efficiency (focusing on ‘export-ready’ firms for quicker results). For example, targeting smaller firms requires more hands-on support (less efficient) but aligns with equity goals, while the preference for ‘last-mile’ support balances immediacy with long-term capacity building.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: SME focus vs. scalability (smaller firms need more support but generate fewer exports)
women-owned businesses vs. speed (gender-inclusive approaches may slow initial uptake)
local BSO partnerships vs. consistency (tailored support improves relevance but complicates standardization)
pilot flexibility vs. cost (adaptive management increases overhead but improves effectiveness)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile justifies intensive oversight (quarterly reports, six-monthly steering group meetings, and a mid-term review). This reflects the need to closely monitor a pilot programme operating across multiple countries with diverse constraints.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The core objective of capacity building (e.g., coaching firms, strengthening BSOs) directly shapes partner roles, with local institutions (BSOs) positioned as key operational partners to ensure sustainability. However, their limited capacity in some contexts necessitates Northern-led management and technical support.

quote.context_who: "The potential countries partaking in the pilot will be chosen from the list below but can be added to if there is a strong justification, including through ‘buy-in’ from other DFID country offices and programmes or HMG departments." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.what_how: "The programme will focus primarily on ‘last mile’ export and ‘first mile’ import support for those exporters closest to meeting demand in export markets... The respective weight of information provision, matchmaking and capacity building will be adjusted based on further evidence gathered at inception and lessons from implementation." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.equity: "TradeConnect will provide capacity-building support to women-owned exporting firms and strengthen BSOs to support their women-owned SME clients to be more competitive and internationalise." (D0001016.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.risk_management: "Progress will be monitored through quarterly reports and meetings with the implementing partner and through six monthly meetings of the steering group." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

key_programme_risks: Low utilisation of UK’s post-Brexit preferential trade arrangements by developing countries
Failure to generate sufficient demand from UK importers for developing country products
Inability to overcome trust and credibility gaps between buyers and sellers
Limited capacity of local BSOs to sustain support after programme ends
Regulatory divergence post-Brexit creating new barriers
Overly ambitious scope for a pilot phase leading to diluted impact
Political or economic instability in target countries disrupting trade flows
Insufficient working capital or trade finance for exporters

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low utilisation of preferential trade arrangements
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted awareness-raising and simplified guidance on rules of origin/preferences, coupled with matchmaking to demonstrate tangible benefits.
Leverage DFID’s existing relationships with UK businesses and align with the Gateway for Growth platform to promote opportunities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Trust gaps between buyers and sellers
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Structured matchmaking with pre-screened participants, follow-up support, and use of intermediaries to broker relationships.
Selective partnerships with BSOs where capacity exists, complemented by direct firm-level support where needed.
Close coordination with DIT’s UK Trade Helpdesk and Standards Platform to ensure up-to-date information.
Focus on a select few countries and sectors initially, with clear criteria for expansion.
Country selection based on stability and export potential, with contingency plans for shifts in context.
Linkages to financial institutions and advisory support on available finance products (though direct finance support is out of scope).

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from similar programmes (e.g., CBI Netherlands, USAID East Africa Trade Hub) highlight the importance of tailored matchmaking, hands-on capacity building, and combining information provision with active brokerage. The scoping study also emphasized the need for sector-specific support and addressing non-tariff barriers like standards compliance.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates flexibility to adjust the balance between information provision, matchmaking, and capacity building based on inception-phase evidence. The mid-term review and break clause (added in D0001018.odt) reflect lessons on the need for adaptive management in pilot programmes.

quote.risks: "Not intervening in this space presents a number of risks for the UK including: Lower impact and utilisation for the UK’s post-Brexit preferential trade arrangements and agreements with developing countries, thereby lessening the UK’s ability to promote sustainable development through trade." (D0001016.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.mitigations: "To ensure this, DFID and its delivery partners will be required to: (a) identify our partners (including robust due diligence) and ensure they are aware of their responsibilities in relation to the legislation; (b) keep appropriate records; (c) establish internal procedures and controls to mitigate risks..." (D0001016.odt, Compliance)
quote.lessons: "Option 4 builds on option 3 and adds a flexible fund that aims to build the capacity of firms to be ‘export-ready’... Evidence from the stakeholder engagement suggests that they require more hands-on support to link with partners and direct capacity building to become ‘export-ready’." (D0001016.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.design_changes: "The programme will require an in-depth mid-term review, assessing impact, scale and the need for any corrective measures, linked to a break clause if objectives are not being met." (D0001018.odt, Approach to implementation)

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £20 million" (D0001016.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The UK will provide £20m over 5 years" (D0001018.odt, Summary Information)
quote.breakdown: No explicit breakdown provided in either document.

metadata.programme_name: Enabling Predictable, Quick and Effective Responses to Humanitarian Crises
metadata.quote: "The programme’s three key objectives are achieved through UK funding to the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF), the British Red Cross (BRC) and the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), in order to provide timely humanitarian assistance, utilise early action initiatives, and enable effective country-level responses in humanitarian contexts." (D0003882.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 17 July 2020 – 30 September 2024" and "New project end date (if applicable): 30 September 2026" (D0003882.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily functions as a **financing mechanism** to channel funds through CERF and DREF for rapid humanitarian response. It also includes **implementation research** components (testing early action approaches) and **capacity building** (improving country-level response quality). The focus is on saving lives through timely assistance while generating evidence on effective early action models.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will: Provide time-critical life-saving humanitarian assistance through the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) that can rapidly release finance to tackle imminent, worsening or underfunded crises; Test new approaches to scale up a system-wide approach to ‘Early Action’ to save more lives and deliver better value for money; Support higher quality and more effective country-level responses to urgent needs." (50223479.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: Time-critical life-saving humanitarian assistance delivered through CERF (global reach)
Early action approaches tested and scaled (e.g., forecast-based financing in Somalia, Yemen, Malawi)
Improved country-level response quality (e.g., joint needs assessments, accountability to affected populations)
£30m Internal Risk Facility for surge capacity during spikes in need
Payment by Results (PbR) mechanism to incentivize UN agency collaboration (10% of CERF funding)
Discontinuation of Performance & Effectiveness component (except £1.5m for IPC food security assessments)
Two-year no-cost extension to 2026 to accommodate Ukraine war pressures
what_objectives.summary: The programme channels UK aid through CERF and DREF to enable rapid, needs-based humanitarian responses while piloting early action models (e.g., forecast-based financing) and improving system coordination. It balances immediate life-saving goals with longer-term reforms to shift the humanitarian system toward anticipatory action.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme’s three key objectives are achieved through UK funding to the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF)... to provide timely humanitarian assistance, utilise early action initiatives, and enable effective country-level responses in humanitarian contexts." (D0003882.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where "conflict, displacement, climate change, disasters, and poverty have combined to generate unprecedented levels of humanitarian need." The 2019 Global Humanitarian Overview predicted 132 million people affected by crises, with protracted conflicts and climate shocks driving recurrent emergencies. The risk rating is explicitly stated as "Moderate" in the original business case, but the context describes extreme fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (50223479.odt, SummarySheet) and "Conflict, displacement, climate change, disasters, and poverty have combined to generate unprecedented levels of humanitarian need and greater instability." (50223479.odt, Today’s humanitarian challenges)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Protracted conflicts and climate change create unpredictable spikes in need (e.g., Ukraine war, Cyclone Idai), while political economy incentives in the UN system prioritize agency autonomy over coordination. Underfunding (44% gap in 2018) forces trade-offs in response quality. Data limitations hinder early action triggers, and weak local institutions limit absorption capacity for rapid disbursements.
where_context.quote: "The current trajectory of humanitarian need will continue in the foreseeable future. However, the supply of available funds to meet this challenge has not grown in proportion... funding gap of $11.01 billion (44%) in 2018." (50223479.odt, Today’s humanitarian challenges)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with the UN’s Emergency Relief Coordinator (ERC) and CERF Advisory Group (CAG), which includes donor representatives (e.g., UK’s Beverley Warmington). While funds reach local actors (e.g., National Red Cross Societies via DREF), strategic priorities and allocation rules are set by Northern-led multilateral bodies. The programme’s PbR framework further reinforces Northern oversight of UN agency performance.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to CERF for early action pilots (e.g., Somalia, Yemen, Malawi)
Support to Red Cross Movement for forecast-based financing systems
Joint needs assessment (JNA) training and accountability mechanisms
£1.5m for Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) to improve data quality

partner_organizations.name: Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF)
partner_organizations.role: Primary funding channel for rapid humanitarian response; tests early action models

partner_organizations.name: Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary fund for small/medium disasters; pilots forecast-based action

partner_organizations.name: British Red Cross (BRC)
partner_organizations.role: Originally funded for early action initiatives (discontinued in 2022 addendum)

partner_organizations.name: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)
partner_organizations.role: Food security assessments triggering CERF/DREF responses (£1.5m allocation)

partner_organizations.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
partner_organizations.role: Manages CERF; implements early action pilots with DFID/FCDO technical support

partner_organizations.name: International Federation of Red Cross (IFRC)
partner_organizations.role: Oversees DREF; scales anticipatory approaches in Red Cross Movement

partner_organizations.name: Centre for Disaster Protection
partner_organizations.role: Provides technical assistance for early action monitoring/evaluation (e.g., Somalia/Yemen pilots)

who_partners.quote: "The CERF is also increasingly focusing on how to address under-funding of certain sectors within crises, drawing much-needed focus to issues such as gender-based violence, education, disability and protection."
