metadata.programme_name: Malawi Trade and Investment Programme (MTIP)
metadata.duration_text: Original start date: 08/05/2020, New project end date: 31/12/2028
metadata.quote: "The £95m Malawi Trade and Investment Programme (MTIP) was approved in January 2020. MTIP’s original purpose was: ‘to increase foreign and domestic investment and increase volume of exports, especially in non-traditional sectors’." (D0003984.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original start date: 08/05/2020", "New project end date: 31/12/2028" (D0003271.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: MTIP aims to accelerate inclusive economic growth in Malawi by increasing investment and exports, particularly in non-traditional sectors. It combines financing mechanisms (e.g., grants to businesses), capacity building (e.g., technical support to firms), and policy influence (e.g., trade facilitation reforms). The programme also includes implementation research through adaptive learning components.
what_objectives.q1_source: "MTIP aims to accelerate inclusive economic growth in Malawi that will reduce poverty, create new jobs and income opportunities, and generate greater revenues to fund the public services needed for a fast-growing population. It will do this through focusing on: 1. Increasing the productivity and quality of production in high value export sectors; 2. Reducing the barriers to entry to incentivise investment in high value export sectors; and 3. Reducing the costs of trade." (D0003984.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 176,251 people (50% women) experiencing an average increase in annual income of £46.45 per person (similar programme MOST results)
Reduction in time and cost of trading by at least 10% above trend by the end of the programme
Improvements in compliance (and testing) of standards in key export sectors
Sustained acceleration in inclusive economic growth
Creation of new jobs and income opportunities
Increased productivity and quality of production in high-value export sectors
Reduced barriers to entry for investment in high-value export sectors
Reduced costs of trade
what_objectives.summary: MTIP is a strategic, long-term economic development programme designed to catalyze private sector-led growth in Malawi through trade facilitation, investment promotion, and value chain development in high-potential export sectors.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will contribute to a sustained acceleration in inclusive economic growth." (D0003271.odt, What are the expected results?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Malawi is politically stable and conflict-free but faces significant economic and institutional challenges. The World Bank ranks Malawi as medium risk (63rd out of 191 countries) with high vulnerability to climate shocks and weak coping capacity. The programme itself is rated as 'Major' risk by FCDO.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003984.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The Index for Risk Management (INFORM) statistics for 2018 ranked Malawi as medium risk being the 63rd out of 191 most at risk country..." (D0003984.odt, A1. Context)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (complex trade procedures, weak standards enforcement)
political economy (patronage systems, short-term political incentives)
weak institutions (limited state capacity, poor service delivery)
data limitations (weak monitoring systems in some sectors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Energy deficits (only 11% electricity access) and high transport costs (10-20x regional averages) directly increase business operational costs and reduce competitiveness. Political patronage systems create unpredictable policy environments that deter long-term investment. Climate shocks (droughts/floods) disrupt agricultural production and supply chains, while weak institutions limit effective implementation of reforms.
where_context.quote: "A lack of energy is the closest approximation to a binding constraint on growth... firms lose 5.1% of their annual sales due to electricity outages" (D0003984.odt, Infrastructure section) and "The weakness of institutions and the prevailing political settlement have stifled the reform required to drive growth" (D0003984.odt, Policy environment section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority through approvals for major contracts, break clauses, and governance structures (e.g., Steering Committee chaired by Ministry of Trade but with FCDO oversight). Southern partners implement components but require FCDO approval for significant changes.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical support to businesses (e.g., investment readiness training)
mentorship for value chain actors (e.g., agronomic advice to smallholders)
institutional strengthening (e.g., Malawi Bureau of Standards support)
coordination platforms (e.g., Steering Committees with government representation)
learning products (e.g., case studies, policy briefs)

who_partners.quote: "The governance structure will also ensure that key agencies are included in the steering committees for each component. This model is already working well for the trade component, which is chaired by the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Trade and Industry and includes representation by key government ministries and agencies." (D0003271.odt, Governance structure)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: MTIP uses a combination of instruments: (1) **Accountable Grants** to implementing partners (e.g., TMEA for trade facilitation), (2) **commercial contracts** for value chain and investment components (with break clauses), and (3) **blended finance** leverage (e.g., catalyzing private investment through BII/AgDevCo). The trade component is already operational under an existing TMEA framework.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is divided into three components (trade facilitation, value chains, investment) with separate but coordinated implementation structures. Trade is managed by TMEA under existing agreements, while value chains and investment will be contracted to specialized partners. A central Results, Coordination & Learning function (now absorbed into the Value Chain component) ensures cross-component synergy. FCDO retains oversight through Steering Committees for each component.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Not specified (but Value Chain contractor selected via "appropriate break clauses" and Commercial Guidance approval)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection prioritizes partners with existing track records in Malawi (e.g., TMEA’s ‘A’ rating in Annual Reviews) and aligns with FCDO’s Commercial Guidance. For new contracts (e.g., Value Chain), the process includes Senior Finance Business Partner approval and break clauses to manage spending review risks.
how_mechanism.quote: "The trade facilitation programme (already being implemented by TradeMark East Africa) is performing extremely well, scoring an ‘A’ in both Annual Reviews conducted to date... The Value Chain team has yet to be mobilised (unlikely to start before mid-2023) with a 5-year contract, so the end date of the programme requires extension by 2 years... In line with the latest Commercial Guidance, we have already received approval from the Senior Finance Business Partner to proceed with the contract with appropriate break clauses." (D0003271.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each component has a Steering Committee chaired by relevant government ministries (e.g., Ministry of Trade and Industry for trade) with representation from FCDO, other donors, and private sector. Decisions require joint approval, with FCDO retaining veto power for major changes. The Value Chain component includes a 6-month inception phase to refine results frameworks with stakeholder input.
how_governance.quote: "The governance structure will also ensure that key agencies are included in the steering committees for each component. This model is already working well for the trade component, which is chaired by the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Trade and Industry and includes representation by key government ministries and agencies." (D0003271.odt, Governance structure) and "The ToR for the VC will specify the need for the programme team to have expertise in using appropriate monitoring and learning strategies to help in defining results and producing evidence that can be used to inform MTIP implementation in real time..." (D0003271.odt, Monitoring and learning)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, but the budget reduction has already locked in significant cuts (e.g., Investment component reduced from £31m to £9m). The Value Chain contract includes a break clause in March 2025 to align with Spending Review periods.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive management through: (1) a 6-month inception phase for the Value Chain component to refine targets, (2) real-time monitoring and learning to adjust interventions, and (3) break clauses in contracts to pause or redirect funds. However, major changes require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "As the contract extends beyond the end of the current Spending Review period, a break clause has been included in March 2025." (D0003271.odt, No cost, 2-year extension) and "The ToR for the VC will specify the need for the programme team to have expertise in using appropriate monitoring and learning strategies to help in defining results and producing evidence that can be used to inform MTIP implementation in real time..." (D0003271.odt, Monitoring and learning)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Component Implementers (e.g., TMEA for trade, Value Chain contractor) → Sub-partners (e.g., Malawi Bureau of Standards, private sector associations). The Results/Coordination function was absorbed into the Value Chain component to reduce layers.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Results, Coordination and Learning component will be absorbed into the Value Chain component." (D0003271.odt, Budget reduction) and "Payment by Results (PbR) mechanisms are implied through the focus on ‘testing and generating evidence from the programme to enable flexible and adaptive programming’" (D0003271.odt, Monitoring and learning)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct FCDO implementation (rejected due to lack of local expertise)
Single-contractor model (rejected to avoid over-reliance on one partner)
Full multilateral delivery (rejected to maintain UK strategic influence)
Pure grant funding (supplemented with blended finance to leverage private capital)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed consortium model was selected to: (1) **leverage existing strengths** (e.g., TMEA’s proven track record in trade facilitation), (2) **manage risk** through diversified partners and break clauses, (3) **ensure government ownership** via Steering Committees, and (4) **enable adaptability** through component-specific contracts. The structure balances FCDO control with local implementation capacity.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (existing TMEA framework avoided procurement costs)
past experience (TMEA’s ‘A’ ratings, MOST programme lessons)
partner capacity (local institutions like MBS embedded in delivery)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation delays due to partner mobilization (e.g., Value Chain team starting late)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: 2-year no-cost extension and break clauses in contracts

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination gaps between components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Absorption of Results/Coordination function into Value Chain component and joint Steering Committees

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Budget cuts reducing impact (£95m → £39m)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on high-value interventions (e.g., macadamia standards) and leverage with BII/AgDevCo

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in trade/investment decisions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Rules-based engagement via Steering Committees and alignment with GoM priorities

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost savings via existing TMEA framework)
effectiveness (focus on non-traditional exports with high growth potential)
why_rationale.quote: "Maintaining the integrity of the original design is important... The trade facilitation programme (already being implemented by TradeMark East Africa) is performing extremely well, scoring an ‘A’ in both Annual Reviews conducted to date... It has set an important foundation upon which to build complementarities with other MTIP components." (D0003271.odt, Maintaining the integrity of the original design) and "The preferred option balances the need for UK strategic influence with local ownership, using a consortium model to spread risk while ensuring coherence." (D0003984.odt, B6. Preferred Option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Malawi’s weak institutional capacity and political economy limit partner selection to organizations with: (1) **existing local presence** (e.g., TMEA’s established office), (2) **government trust** (e.g., Ministry of Trade co-chairs Steering Committees), and (3) **risk appetite** (e.g., AgDevCo’s patient capital model). The energy/infrastructure deficits also favor partners with off-grid solutions (e.g., solar-powered agribusinesses).
q27_constraints_detail: Limited pool of qualified local implementers → reliance on regional partners (TMEA)
Government patronage systems → need for neutral intermediaries (e.g., MBS for standards)
Energy deficits → prioritization of low-energy value chains (e.g., macadamia over manufacturing)
Climate vulnerability → focus on drought-resistant crops and irrigation support
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **trade facilitation** objective requires a **regional partner** (TMEA) due to cross-border dependencies, while **value chain development** needs **local agribusiness expertise** (hence embedded capacity building). The **investment component’s** pause reflects **limited absorptive capacity** in Malawi’s financial sector, shifting focus to leveraging existing platforms (BII/AgDevCo).
q28_linkages: Trade facilitation → regional partner (TMEA) due to corridor-wide reforms
Value chains → local contractors with agronomic expertise
Investment → pause due to weak domestic financial markets → reliance on UK-based BII
Monitoring/learning → absorbed into Value Chain to reduce layers but maintain adaptability
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid trade reforms (e.g., standards compliance) risk excluding smallholders without targeted support (mitigated via Value Chain component). (2) **Northern expertise vs. ownership**: UK-managed funds (e.g., BII) enable leverage but reduce local control (addressed via Steering Committees). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Budget cuts forced cancellation of the Results/Coordination component, reducing learning capacity but preserving core delivery.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Reduced budget (£39m vs. £95m) → fewer sectors supported but deeper focus on high-potential value chains (e.g., macadamia)
Absorbing Results/Coordination into Value Chain → efficiency gain but potential loss of independent oversight
Break clauses in contracts → risk mitigation but may disrupt long-term partnerships
Gender targets (50% women) → require additional resources for disaggregated data and outreach
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight** (e.g., milestone-based payments, embedded monitoring in Value Chain component) and **redundant structures** (e.g., Steering Committees for each component). Political economy risks necessitate **FCDO approval for major decisions**, while climate risks require **adaptive management** (e.g., 6-month inception phase to adjust targets).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak local institutional capacity shifts roles to partners: (1) **TMEA** handles complex trade reforms due to GoM’s limited technical skills, (2) **Value Chain contractor** provides agronomic training to fill extension service gaps, and (3) **Steering Committees** include donors/private sector to compensate for weak government coordination. Capacity building is embedded in delivery (e.g., MBS standards support) rather than standalone.
intersections.quote: "The weakness of institutions and the prevailing political settlement have stifled the reform required to drive growth... This has diverted attention away from more complex industries more conducive to long-term growth, such as manufacturing and other export-oriented sectors." (D0003984.odt, Policy environment) and "The governance structure will ensure that key agencies are included in the steering committees for each component... This model is already working well for the trade component." (D0003271.odt, Governance structure)

key_programme_risks: Implementation delays (Covid-19, ODA cuts) → mitigated via 2-year extension
Budget reduction (£95m → £39m) → focus on high-impact sectors (e.g., macadamia)
Political interference in trade/investment decisions → addressed via rules-based Steering Committees
Climate shocks disrupting agricultural value chains → adaptive management via real-time monitoring
Weak private sector absorptive capacity → leveraging BII/AgDevCo for patient capital
Coordinating across components → absorbed Results/Coordination into Value Chain
Gender inequality in value chains → explicit 50% women targets and disaggregated data

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delayed mobilization of Value Chain team
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: 2-year no-cost extension and break clause in contract (March 2025)
Prioritize high-value sectors (e.g., macadamia) and leverage with BII/AgDevCo
Steering Committees with GoM/private sector representation and rules-based engagement
Focus on drought-resistant crops (e.g., macadamia) and adaptive monitoring
Embed monitoring/learning in Value Chain component with expert team

fcas_specific_lessons: **Patronage systems** require **neutral intermediaries** (e.g., MBS for standards) to avoid capture by elites.
**Short-term political cycles** necessitate **quick wins** (e.g., Safe Trade PPE) alongside long-term reforms.
**Weak state capacity** shifts delivery to **non-state actors** (e.g., TMEA for trade, AgDevCo for finance).
**Climate vulnerability** demands **flexible targets** (e.g., adjustable value chain outputs).
**Donor coordination** is critical to avoid **duplication** (e.g., alignment with EU/WB programmes)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **MOST programme** (Oilseeds Transformation) demonstrated that: (1) **market systems approaches** (e.g., incentive-based farming contracts) can achieve scale, (2) **gender targets** (50% women) are feasible with deliberate design, and (3) **policy reforms** (e.g., standards) require sustained engagement. The **MICF** (Innovation Challenge Fund) showed that **matching grants** catalyze private sector innovation but need **investment readiness support**. **AgDevCo’s** patient capital model proved effective for **early-stage agribusinesses** but requires **grant de-risking** (e.g., irrigation infrastructure co-funding).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. **Absorbed Results/Coordination into Value Chain** to reduce layers while maintaining learning (lesson from MOST’s standalone M&E). 2. **Added break clauses** in contracts to manage Spending Review risks (lesson from ODA cuts). 3. **Prioritized macadamia sector** based on MOST’s success with high-value crops. 4. **Embedded gender targets** (50% women) in all components (lesson from MOST’s inclusive design). 5. **Leveraged existing platforms** (TMEA, BII) to avoid procurement delays (lesson from PSD programme).
risks_lessons.quote: "The first phase of DFID economic development programming in Malawi (in particular the £22.4 million Private Sector Development (PSD) Programme) has shown that strong results can be achieved... MOST was independently audited by the Donor Committee for Enterprise Development. It was one of the highest rated programmes... scoring 97% for ‘must’ compliance criteria and 93% for ‘recommended compliance’ criteria." (D0003984.odt, Lessons learned) and "The programme will need to navigate [the political] dynamic carefully and flexibly, finding entry points to disrupt the status quo." (D0003984.odt, Lessons learned)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage private investment through BII and AgDevCo, though specific amounts are not quantified. Historical leverage in similar programmes (e.g., PSD) achieved £1.75 private investment per £1 UK aid.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily supports **revenue expenditures** (e.g., technical assistance, grants to businesses) with limited capital investments (e.g., minor irrigation infrastructure co-funding). The reduction from £95m to £39m eliminated most capital-heavy components (e.g., regional trade infrastructure contributions).
financial_details.quote: "Original budget: £95,000,000; Current budget: £39,000,000" (D0003271.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "The original MTIP budget also requires re-profiling because of the ODA budget prioritisation exercise and new Ministerial priorities... reducing the budget from £95m to £39m." (D0003271.odt, Budget reduction)

metadata.programme_name: WhatWorks Hub for Global Education (WWGE)
metadata.duration_text: eight years (with review and break points)
metadata.quote: An investment of £55 million over eight years (with review and break points) to establish a UK-led WhatWorks Hub for Global Education ("Document: 90001008.odt", Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: An investment of £55 million over eight years (with review and break points) to establish a UK-led WhatWorks Hub for Global Education

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The WhatWorks Hub for Global Education (WWGE) is designed to leverage UK and international research to improve education evidence use in 8-10 aid-recipient countries. It combines evidence generation (new research), capacity building (strengthening ministries' data use), policy influence (supporting evidence-based reforms), and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions). The focus is on improving foundational learning outcomes, particularly for marginalized girls, through a 'diagnose, test, learn, and adapt' cycle.
what_objectives.q1_source: An investment of £55 million over eight years (with review and break points) to establish a UK-led WhatWorks Hub for Global Education, to leverage the best of UK and international research and technical advice to help 8-10 aid-recipient countries: Improve the use of education evidence, by summarising and communicating the best evidence in ways that governments and practitioners need and commissioning new research that tracks cost-effective interventions to scale. Strengthen education and finance ministries’ capability to use and contextualise data and evidence, for example through establishing policy labs within Ministries of Education. Embed a new approach to evidence in education, through supporting our partner governments to use a ‘diagnose, test, learn and adapt’ cycle to education reform.
q3_expected_outputs: Curated, synthesised, and communicated evidence for policymakers and practitioners (beyond systematic reviews)
New research on high-potential, low-evidence areas (e.g., teacher accountability reform, school-based engagement, targeted support for girls)
Strengthened state capability for evidence and data use (e.g., policy labs in Ministries of Education)
Diagnostics to identify core barriers to learning
Technical support for testing, adapting, and scaling cost-effective reforms (e.g., foundational learning interventions)
Rigorous implementation science to improve learning outcomes
Global coordination and thought leadership on evidence-based education reform
Increased use of cost-effective interventions in 3-10 countries (e.g., Brazil, DRC, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan)
Catalysed shifts in policy and implementation, leveraging domestic resources and ODA
what_objectives.summary: The WWGE aims to transform education systems by improving evidence use, strengthening government capacity, and embedding adaptive, cost-effective reforms. It focuses on foundational learning (e.g., reading by age 10) and prioritizes marginalized groups, especially girls, through a mix of research, capacity building, and policy support.
what_objectives.quote: The WhatWorks Hub for Global Education (WWGE) delivers on the Government’s manifesto commitment to stand up for the right of every girl to 12 years of quality education. It is one of the mechanisms through which we will measure progress against FCDO’s Girls’ Education Global Targets and Key Performance Indicators and will form part of the upcoming FCDO Girls’ Education Action Plan. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Summary Sheet)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a mix of stable and fragile contexts (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone, Pakistan) but is rated as 'moderate' risk overall. Risks include political economy challenges, weak institutional capacity, and implementation barriers in education systems, but the programme design (e.g., iterative adaptation, local partnerships) mitigates these.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (e.g., flooding, droughts affecting girls' education)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutional capacity limits evidence use (e.g., Ministries lack skills to analyse data or apply research). Political economy factors (e.g., incentives, power dynamics) hinder reform uptake. Conflict and climate shocks disrupt education delivery, particularly for girls. Fragmentation of global initiatives creates coordination challenges, while data gaps (e.g., limited learning assessments) constrain problem diagnosis.
where_context.quote: There is a lack of coordination among major stakeholders in determining what ‘the best’ evidence says in education, and in effectively communicating this evidence for decision-makers. (...) Policymakers and others who are designing and implementing education policies and programmes typically lack the time to delve through all this evidence. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Globalevidencesupply)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO leads programme design, governance, and strategic direction, with Southern partners (e.g., Ministries of Education, local researchers) playing implementation and advisory roles. Decision-making on research priorities and global coordination rests with the Hub’s central team, though country-level adaptation is demand-driven.
q10_capacity_building_details: Policy labs within Ministries of Education (e.g., diagnostic tools, data analysis training)
Strengthening local government-researcher collaboration (e.g., Ethiopia’s Ministry of Education-Addis Ababa University link)
Training for government officials on evidence appraisal and prioritization
Mentorship for local researchers to generate/use context-specific evidence
Technical support for ‘test, learn, adapt’ cycles (e.g., iterative reform design)
Knowledge brokering between global evidence and local policymakers

partner_organizations.name: UNESCO International Institute for Educational Planning (IIEP)

partner_organizations.name: RISE Programme (FCDO-funded)

partner_organizations.location: global (with country teams in Ethiopia, India, etc.)

partner_organizations.name: EdTech Hub

who_partners.quote: The WhatWorks Hub will build on and catalyse greater access to these opportunities for FCDO partner countries. (...) The Hub will look to bring on other funding, and over time generate revenue from UMICs providing access to technical expertise and evidence. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Sustainability and catalysing further investments)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for research/commissioning), technical assistance contracts (for capacity building), and strategic partnerships (e.g., with World Bank, GPE). Funds are channelled through the Hub’s central platform to support both global evidence synthesis and country-level interventions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Hub operates as a central platform with three pillars: (1) global evidence curation/synthesis, (2) country-level capacity building (e.g., policy labs), and (3) technical support for reform testing/scaling. It coordinates existing initiatives (e.g., GPE KIX, World Bank’s Foundational Learning Compact) and brokers knowledge across actors.
how_mechanism.quote: The WhatWorks Hub will hold a high bar for evidence and bring together global education actors to effectively communicate the evidence with Ministries of Education and Finance in L/MICs. (...) The Hub will play a critical ‘dot joining’ role across interventions designed to improve education evidence use. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Pillar 1)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Hub is governed by a steering committee with FCDO, partner countries, and global actors (e.g., World Bank, GPE). Decision-making involves joint prioritization of research/evidence gaps and country-level interventions, with FCDO retaining oversight of strategic direction and funds.
how_governance.quote: FCDO will play a leading UK role in deploying science as a force for good, commissioning social and political research to support FCDO security, prosperity, and diplomatic priorities. (...) The programme will be reviewed at breakpoints (e.g., 2023/24). ("Document: 90001008.odt", Programme summary and Risk section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between pillars/countries at review breakpoints (e.g., 2023/24), subject to demand and performance. The programme’s adaptive management approach allows shifts in response to emerging evidence or context changes (e.g., COVID-19 recovery needs).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The Hub uses a ‘diagnose, test, learn, and adapt’ cycle, enabling mid-programme adjustments based on real-time data (e.g., iterative reform design in countries). Research priorities can evolve to address new evidence gaps (e.g., climate-education links) or political opportunities (e.g., Foundational Learning Compact alignment).
how_flexibility.quote: Embed a new approach to evidence in education, through supporting our partner governments to use a ‘diagnose, test, learn and adapt’ cycle to education reform. (...) The programme includes breakpoints for review and adaptation. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → WhatWorks Hub platform → (1) global evidence teams, (2) country-level implementers (e.g., Ministries, local researchers). Sub-awards to Southern partners are managed through the Hub’s pillars, with direct technical support in 3-10 countries.
how_efficiency.quote: The WhatWorks Hub will work toward three goals: [1] Improve the use of education evidence... [2] Strengthen education and finance ministries’ capability... [3] Embed a new approach to evidence in education. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Figure 3)

q24_alternatives_considered: ‘Business as usual’ (rejected): Ad-hoc evidence support without a dedicated Hub
Decentralized country programmes (rejected): Lacked economies of scale and global coordination
Pure research programme (rejected): Would not address implementation/capacity gaps
Donor-led technical assistance (rejected): Risked low country ownership and sustainability
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The platform model was selected to (1) **leverage UK leadership** in education evidence (aligning with manifesto commitments and FCDO’s Girls’ Education Action Plan); (2) **address systemic gaps** in evidence use, coordination, and capacity (e.g., fragmentation of initiatives, weak local data skills); (3) **balance global standards** (e.g., GEEAP ‘smart buys’) with **local adaptation** (e.g., country-demand-driven reforms); (4) **catalyse additional funding** through strategic partnerships (e.g., World Bank, GPE); and (5) **embed flexibility** to respond to crises (e.g., COVID-19 recovery) or new evidence (e.g., climate-education links).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (e.g., avoiding ‘bad buys’, scaling ‘great buys’)
risk mitigation (e.g., political economy analysis, iterative adaptation)
partner capacity (e.g., building on RISE, J-PAL, local research institutions)
speed (e.g., leveraging existing networks like BE2, GPE KIX)
flexibility (e.g., breakpoints for reallocation, adaptive management)
equity (e.g., focus on marginalized girls, FCAS inclusion)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of global initiatives undermines coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Hub plays a ‘dot-joining’ role by connecting existing platforms (e.g., GPE KIX, World Bank Compact) and amplifying complementary efforts (e.g., USAID SHARE). Strategic partnerships with multilaterals ensure alignment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low country demand for evidence limits uptake
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand-driven approach: only works in countries with articulated political will (e.g., World Bank Accelerator/GPE Pilot countries). Policy labs and diagnostics co-designed with Ministries to ensure relevance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Northern-led platform risks low Southern ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded capacity building (e.g., policy labs, local researcher collaboration) and adaptive country support. Long-term goal to transition to Southern-led evidence hubs (e.g., Brazil’s planned Center of Excellence).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with existing research programmes (e.g., RISE, EdTech Hub)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of labor: Hub curates/synthesizes evidence from FCDO-funded programmes (e.g., RISE, J-PAL) rather than duplicating research. Focuses on ‘last mile’ application (e.g., cost-effectiveness analysis, implementation science).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation barriers in weak systems (e.g., data gaps, political resistance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Iterative ‘test, learn, adapt’ cycles with real-time feedback loops. Technical support tailored to context (e.g., EMIS strengthening, diagnostic tools). Political economy analysis to navigate incentives.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (e.g., leveraging existing FCDO research investments)
efficiency (e.g., platform model reduces duplication, scales ‘great buys’)
effectiveness (e.g., focus on foundational learning—highest-impact area per RISE/WDR 2018)
equity (e.g., targeting marginalized girls, FCAS inclusion)
why_rationale.quote: A ‘business as usual’ approach was considered and rejected for four reasons: (1) It would not deliver the level of ambition in relation to UK leadership in evidence-based policymaking; (2) The strategic case points to a clear gap in supporting countries to contextualise and use evidence; (3) Without external intervention, investment in evidence synthesis and implementation science would remain underpowered; (4) Access to UK expertise may be achieved but without economies of scale. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Why rationale)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Contextual constraints directly shape partner selection: (1) **FCAS/conflict settings** (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone) require partners with conflict sensitivity expertise (e.g., UNESCO IIEP, local CSOs). (2) **Weak institutional capacity** (e.g., limited EMIS, research skills) necessitates embedded support (e.g., policy labs, diagnostics) rather than standalone research partners. (3) **Political economy barriers** (e.g., resistance to reform) favor local actors (e.g., Ministries, trusted researchers) over external consultants. (4) **Data limitations** (e.g., lack of learning assessments) prioritize partners with implementation science skills (e.g., J-PAL, EdTech Hub).
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS contexts (e.g., DRC, Niger) limit international partner access; require local intermediaries
Weak EMIS/data systems in LMICs necessitate capacity-building-focused partners (e.g., IIEP, RISE)
Political resistance to evidence-based reforms favors ‘trusted’ local researchers over external experts
Language barriers (e.g., Kiswahili in Kenya) require local knowledge brokers
Climate risks (e.g., flooding in Bangladesh) demand partners with resilience expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **mixed objectives** (evidence + capacity + reform) drive its **platform structure**: (1) **Global evidence synthesis** (Pillar 1) requires a central hub to curate/standardize evidence (e.g., ‘smart buys’ classification), avoiding fragmentation. (2) **Capacity building** (Pillar 2) necessitates embedded, demand-driven support (e.g., policy labs in Ministries) rather than top-down training. (3) **Implementation research** (Pillar 3) demands iterative, country-level partnerships (e.g., ‘test, learn, adapt’ cycles with local researchers). The **focus on cost-effectiveness** shapes governance (e.g., GEEAP oversight) and partner selection (e.g., prioritizing ‘high-potential’ interventions).
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (WHAT) → Platform model (HOW): Central curation avoids duplication and sets global standards (e.g., GEEAP ‘smart buys’)
Capacity building (WHAT) → Embedded support (HOW): Policy labs and diagnostics respond to weak local evidence-use capacity (WHERE)
Implementation research (WHAT) → Country partnerships (HOW): ‘Test, learn, adapt’ cycles require trusted local implementers (WHO)
Foundational learning focus (WHAT) → World Bank/GPE alignment (HOW): Leverages existing Compacts/Pilots for scale (WHERE)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are managed through: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid scaling of ‘great buys’ (efficiency) is balanced by iterative adaptation (equity—e.g., gender-disaggregated data in diagnostics). (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK-led evidence curation (efficiency) is paired with capacity-building for local researchers (equity—e.g., policy labs). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Focus on 3-10 ‘champion’ countries (efficiency) ensures depth of support, while global synthesis (Pillar 1) maintains broad influence. (4) **Standardization vs. context**: Global ‘smart buys’ (efficiency) are adapted via country-level ‘test, learn’ cycles (equity).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Platform model reduces duplication but risks overlooking hyper-local needs
Equity: FCAS inclusion (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone) increases complexity/cost
Efficiency: Global evidence standards (e.g., GEEAP) may conflict with local priorities
Equity: Iterative adaptation (e.g., ‘test, learn’ cycles) slows scaling but improves fit
Efficiency: Northern-led curation speeds synthesis but risks low Southern ownership
Equity: Capacity building (e.g., policy labs) builds ownership but requires long-term investment
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., FCAS inclusion, weak institutions) drives **milestone-based oversight** with breakpoints (e.g., 2023/24 review) and adaptive management. High-risk contexts (e.g., DRC) trigger embedded safeguards (e.g., due diligence for terrorist financing), while stable countries (e.g., Ghana) allow lighter-touch coordination.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity gaps (e.g., weak EMIS, limited research skills) shift partners from **implementers** to **capacity builders**: (1) Ministries of Education transition from recipients to co-designers via policy labs. (2) Local researchers move from data collectors to evidence leaders (e.g., Addis Ababa University collaboration). (3) Global actors (e.g., World Bank) provide tools (e.g., diagnostics) while local partners adapt/implement.
intersections.quote: The WhatWorks Hub will deploy tools and expertise flexibly to support governments to diagnose the problems in their education systems, draw on the evidence of what works, and get behind opportunities for reform. (...) In-country work will provide an important entry point to connect the global and national. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Pillar 2)

key_programme_risks: Low political will in partner countries limits evidence uptake
Fragmentation of global education initiatives undermines coordination
Weak institutional capacity (e.g., EMIS, research skills) hinders reform implementation
Implementation barriers (e.g., teacher resistance, bureaucratic inertia) block scaling
Overlap/duplication with existing FCDO programmes (e.g., RISE, EdTech Hub)
Northern-led platform risks perceived lack of Southern ownership
COVID-19/conflict disruptions delay or derail reforms
Climate shocks (e.g., flooding, droughts) exacerbate education inequities
Evidence gaps (e.g., adolescent girls’ empowerment, education in emergencies) limit programme impact
Sustainability risks post-FCDO funding (e.g., local capacity atrophy)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demand-driven approach: only engage countries with articulated commitment (e.g., World Bank Accelerator/GPE Pilot countries). Use political economy analysis to align incentives.
Hub plays ‘dot-joining’ role by coordinating with GPE KIX, World Bank Compact, USAID SHARE. Strategic partnerships ensure complementarity.
Embedded capacity building (e.g., policy labs, diagnostics) and long-term partnerships with local institutions (e.g., Addis Ababa University).
Iterative ‘test, learn, adapt’ cycles with real-time feedback. Technical support tailored to context (e.g., EMIS strengthening).
Clear division of labor: Hub curates/synthesizes evidence from RISE, EdTech Hub, etc., rather than duplicating research. Focus on ‘last mile’ application.
Co-design with Ministries, embedded capacity building, and transition planning (e.g., Brazil’s Center of Excellence).
Adaptive management framework (e.g., breakpoints for reallocation). Focus on resilience (e.g., EdTech for remote learning).
Integrate climate-education research (e.g., girls’ resilience). Support adaptive systems (e.g., flood-resistant schools).
Commission targeted research (e.g., gender-based violence, education in emergencies). Leverage FCDO’s existing portfolio (e.g., RISE, J-PAL).
Build local research capacity (e.g., policy labs, university links). Explore revenue models (e.g., UMICs paying for access).

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone), **local intermediaries** (e.g., CSOs, trusted researchers) are critical for access and legitimacy; avoid top-down models.
Conflict-sensitive diagnostics (e.g., UNESCO IIEP tools) must precede reforms to navigate political economy risks.
**Iterative adaptation** is essential: FCAS contexts require shorter feedback loops (e.g., quarterly reviews vs. annual).
Gender inequities are exacerbated in FCAS; interventions must address **intersecting vulnerabilities** (e.g., girls with disabilities in conflict zones).
**Flexible funding** is needed to respond to shocks (e.g., school closures, displacement).
Partnerships with multilaterals (e.g., World Bank, GPE) provide stability in volatile contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from RISE, EdTech Hub, and PRIMR (Kenya) highlight: (1) **Iterative design** (e.g., PRIMR’s six tested approaches) dramatically improves outcomes. (2) **Local researcher collaboration** (e.g., Ethiopia’s Ministry-Addis Ababa University link) accelerates uptake. (3) **Cost-effectiveness focus** (e.g., RISE’s curriculum reform insights) drives policy impact. (4) **Political economy analysis** (e.g., identifying ‘champions’ in Ministries) is critical for sustainability. (5) **Implementation science** (e.g., real-time feedback loops) bridges the evidence-practice gap.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The Hub’s design incorporates: (1) **Breakpoints for adaptation** (e.g., 2023/24 review) based on RISE’s iterative model. (2) **Policy labs** (from PRIMR/RISE) to embed evidence use in Ministries. (3) **Cost-effectiveness emphasis** (from GEEAP ‘smart buys’) to guide research/commissioning. (4) **FCAS-inclusive country selection** (e.g., DRC, Sierra Leone) to address equity gaps. (5) **Implementation science pillar** (Pillar 3) to respond to weak evidence application.
risks_lessons.quote: The Kenya PRIMR example shows that iterative, evidence-based adaptation can yield dramatic learning gains. The WhatWorks Hub will apply this approach at scale, with breakpoints to reallocate funds and adjust strategies. (...) Lessons from RISE and EdTech Hub underscore the need for implementation science to bridge the ‘last mile’ from evidence to practice. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Figure 1 and Pillar 3)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Hub aims to catalyse additional funding through strategic partnerships (e.g., World Bank, GPE) and eventually generate revenue from UMICs accessing its technical expertise. Coordination with USAID SHARE and other donors will reduce duplication and expand reach.
financial_details.quote: We intend for the Hub to build strong partnerships with bilateral and multilateral donors as well as other research institutes (...) to become a truly global initiative. It will do so by building on the existing relationships which the FCDO holds through our education research portfolio (...) and forging Strategic Partnerships with a small group of influential actors in this space. The Hub will look to bring on other funding, and over time generate revenue from UMICs. ("Document: 90001008.odt", Sustainability and catalysing further investments)

metadata.programme_name: Sahel Humanitarian Assistance and Protection Programme (SHAPP)
metadata.quote: "The Sahel Humanitarian Assistance and Protection Programme (SHAPP) protects and assists the most vulnerable in ‘hotspots’ of most acute humanitarian need in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Chad." (S30094322.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: November 2021 – September 2028" (S30094322.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SHAPP delivers humanitarian assistance and protection to vulnerable populations in the Sahel, combining direct service delivery (food, shelter, healthcare), financing mechanisms (Sahel Regional Fund), and policy influence through advocacy on human rights and international humanitarian law. It also focuses on improving the enabling environment for humanitarian actors through safety, logistics, and data systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme delivers: Prioritised humanitarian assistance and protection (e.g. food assistance, nutrition, health, water and sanitation, promoting safety and respect of human rights and international humanitarian law) for the most vulnerable in geographic hotspots of most acute need; An improved ‘enabling’ safe and secure operating environment for humanitarian actors; A regional inter-agency harmonised protection monitoring system." (S30094322.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: 77,000 people receive protection (e.g., safe spaces for women and girls, GBV prevention, child protection)
340,000 receive food packages or cash-based assistance
110,000 receive support to agricultural production
16,000 children under 5 treated for severe acute malnutrition
133,000 receive healthcare services
275 INGOs and 70 national NGOs better manage safety and security
Harmonised regional protection monitoring system improving evidence base
Support to 1.1 million people (from £75.4m additional funding)
Flexible Internal Risk Facility (IRF) for emergency responses
what_objectives.summary: SHAPP is a multi-faceted humanitarian programme that combines direct aid delivery, systemic improvements to humanitarian access and coordination, and regional advocacy. It targets 'hotspots' of acute need across the Sahel, with a focus on conflict-affected areas and refugee crises (notably Sudanese refugees in Chad).
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will provide assistance and protection for the most vulnerable people in geographic ‘hotspots’ of acute humanitarian need, including Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad." (S30094322.odt, Response and targeting)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The Sahel is characterized by extreme fragility, with ongoing conflicts, violent extremism, weak governance, and climate shocks. Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger are among the world's most neglected humanitarian crises, with famine conditions in some areas and over 1.3 million refugees in Chad alone. The region faces critical risks of mass atrocities (Mali/Burkina Faso) and decreasing territorial control by national authorities.
where_context.q5_source: "The Sahel is one of the poorest, most fragile, climate-vulnerable and insecure regions in the world. [...] Nearly 23 million people need humanitarian assistance in 2025, and 12 million were severely food insecure in 2024. [...] The risk of mass atrocities is ‘critical’ in Mali and Burkina Faso and ‘high’ in Niger." (S30094322.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q6_contextual_constraints: security (violent extremism, inter-community conflict, state atrocities)
infrastructure (limited road access, destroyed bridges, market disruptions)
regulatory (restrictions on humanitarian operations, armed escort requirements)
political economy (distrust of international actors, disinformation campaigns)
weak institutions (government failure to provide basic services, marginalization of communities)
conflict (non-state armed groups controlling territory, ethnic violence)
climate risks (droughts, floods exacerbating food insecurity)
data limitations (lack of harmonized protection monitoring until recent initiatives)
access constraints (humanitarian actors blocked from contested areas)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and access constraints force humanitarian actors to rely on local partners for negotiation and delivery, increasing costs and limiting reach. Regulatory restrictions (e.g., armed escorts) compromise neutrality and may lead to suspension of operations. Climate shocks and conflict create overlapping 'hotspots' where food insecurity, malnutrition, and protection violations converge, requiring adaptive responses.
where_context.quote: "Disruption to the humanitarian supply pipeline [...] through, for example, insufficient funds, or increasing costs. [...] Acceptance of principled humanitarian response and actors by host governments is affected by declining trust in international actors and has resulted in restrictions imposed on humanitarian operations." (S30094322.odt, Risk Management)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Danish Refugee Council (DRC) - Sahel Regional Fund (SRF)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The SRF is governed by NGOs active in the Sahel (including local partners), with the UK represented on the Advisory Board. Decision-making for the SRF involves both international and national NGOs, with DRC managing the fund but strategic directions set by a board where FCDO has a seat. Local NGOs are included as downstream partners in consortia led by INGOs.
q10_capacity_building_details: rapid response training for national NGOs
localisation testing (dedicated funding allocation for local partners)
safety and security management training (via INSO)
protection monitoring skills (via UNHCR Project 21)
secondments to UN agencies for civil-military coordination and PSEAH
cross-learning sessions between SRF implementing partners

partner_organizations.name: Danish Refugee Council (DRC)
partner_organizations.role: Manager of Sahel Regional Fund (SRF); implements protection and assistance programmes

partner_organizations.name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
partner_organizations.role: Direct delivery of protection and assistance in conflict zones; focus on detention monitoring, healthcare, and rehabilitation

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Food assistance and logistics (including UNHAS air service); emergency response for refugees

partner_organizations.name: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
partner_organizations.role: Protection monitoring (Project 21); refugee support in Chad

partner_organizations.name: International NGO Safety Organisation (INSO)
partner_organizations.role: Security advisory services for NGOs; incident management and training

partner_organizations.name: Catholic Relief Services (CRS)
partner_organizations.role: SRF consortium lead; implements multi-sectoral programmes

partner_organizations.name: Mercy Corps
partner_organizations.role: SRF consortium lead; implements multi-sectoral programmes

partner_organizations.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
partner_organizations.role: SRF consortium lead; implements multi-sectoral programmes

partner_organizations.name: National NGOs (unnamed)
partner_organizations.role: Downstream partners in SRF consortia; rapid response and localised delivery

partner_organizations.name: Palladium/HSOT
partner_organizations.role: Critical HR reinforcement; secondments to UN agencies

who_partners.quote: "The SRF empowers local and international NGOs to respond to the needs of the most vulnerable and deliver lasting impact. [...] Work with and through local and national partners has been instrumental in negotiating and maintaining access and delivering the SHAPP programme results." (S30094322.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: SHAPP uses a combination of instruments: (1) **Accountable Grant Agreements** with DRC for the SRF (a pooled fund mechanism), (2) **direct grants** to multilateral agencies (ICRC, WFP, UNHCR), and (3) **service contracts** for common services (INSO, UNHAS). The SRF operates as a semi-autonomous fund with its own governance structure, while other partners receive earmarked funding for specific outputs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **Sahel Regional Fund (SRF)**, managed by DRC, acts as the primary delivery mechanism for 60% of outputs (assistance/protection). It operates with a **Programme Management Unit (PMU)** overseen by a **board** (including FCDO) and an **Advisory Board**. Other components are managed through direct agreements with multilaterals (ICRC, WFP, UNHCR) and service providers (INSO, UNHAS). The SRF uses **competitive calls** for downstream partners, while multilaterals deliver based on mandates.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The **SRF** uses a competitive process for consortia (3 INGO leads selected), while **ICRC/WFP/UNHCR** were directly awarded based on their unique mandates (e.g., ICRC’s Geneva Convention role, WFP’s logistics capacity). INSO and UNHAS were selected as sole-source providers of common services (security/air transport) due to their specialized roles and lack of alternatives in the Sahel.
how_mechanism.quote: "Option 4, supporting a Sahel Regional Fund (SRF) hosted by the Danish Refugee Council, is the preferred option. [...] This option allows us to support a blend of different actors, and in doing so pitches to their respective comparative advantages, maintaining the opportunity to robustly challenge established thinking." (90000464.odt, Preferred option)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **SRF Board** (with FCDO representation) sets strategic directions and approves projects/partners. The **Advisory Board** (including UK and international NGOs) advises on allocations. For multilaterals (ICRC, WFP, UNHCR), governance follows their internal systems with FCDO oversight via quarterly meetings and risk registers. The **Grievance Committee** (chaired by FCDO) handles disputes for the SRF.
how_governance.quote: "The DRC would set up, staff and manage a programme management unit (PMU) with FCDO oversight. The PMU would have a range of responsibilities, including managing and escalating risk to the board, implementing the strategic direction set by the board, presenting vetted projects and partners to the board, consolidating results and reporting back to the FCDO." (90000464.odt, Option 4)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between SRF partners based on performance and context changes, but require board approval. The **Internal Risk Facility (IRF)** (£9.8m) allows rapid reallocation for emergencies (e.g., Sudan refugee crisis). Multilateral agreements (ICRC, WFP) have less flexibility due to earmarked outputs, but the SRF’s multi-year design enables adaptive programming.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The SRF’s **multi-year, needs-based approach** allows adjustments to sectoral or geographic priorities (e.g., shifting to eastern Chad for Sudan response). The **IRF** provides a formal mechanism for unplanned crises. However, changes require board/FCDO approval, and multilateral partners have fixed mandates (e.g., ICRC’s detention work).
how_flexibility.quote: "The IRF’s flexibility will allow the FCDO to quickly allocate new in-year funding to these [emergencies], where feasible and deemed necessary. [...] The SRF is a mechanism that provides an additional means of oversight while also being designed to be able to go to scale once other donors commit resources." (D0003890.odt, Internal Risk Facility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) **Fund Manager (DRC/SRF PMU)** or **Multilateral Partner (ICRC/WFP/UNHCR)** → (2) **Downstream Implementers** (INGO consortia/national NGOs for SRF; local partners for multilaterals). No additional layers beyond these two steps.
how_efficiency.quote: "DRC’s overhead cost when applied to the total cost of the SRF is 1.52%, which is within the BC target of 2% and represents good VfM compared to e.g. the OCHA pooled fund for the Sahel." (D0003890.odt, Value for Money)

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuing the SHERP model (rejected: too narrow, focused only on food/nutrition)
Funding existing Rapid Response Mechanisms (RRM) (rejected: short-term, no protection focus)
Multiple small-scale bilateral agreements with NGOs (rejected: high transaction costs, poor VfM)
UNOCHA-managed Regional Humanitarian Fund (rejected: limited to Niger, not cross-border)
Multiple UN agencies delivering against mandates (rejected: high management burden, limited flexibility)
INGO consortia with accountable grants (safe but resource-intensive for FCDO)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **SRF model (Option 4)** was selected for its ability to: (1) **deliver a multi-sectoral, needs-based response** in hotspots (unlike SHERP/RRM); (2) **leverage comparative advantages** of diverse partners (INGOs for flexibility, multilaterals for access); (3) **reduce FCDO management burden** compared to multiple bilateral grants; (4) **enable scaling** through co-funding from other donors; (5) **provide flexibility** via multi-year funding and the IRF; and (6) **challenge status quo** through innovative partnerships (e.g., localisation testing). The mix of SRF + multilaterals balances efficiency (pooled funds) with reach (ICRC’s access to contested areas).
q25_decision_factors: vfm (lower overheads than UN pooled funds, economies of scale)
experience (DRC’s fund management, ICRC’s conflict access)
partner-capacity (SRF’s ability to attract co-funding, multilaterals’ mandates)
speed (pre-positioned partners like WFP for Sudan response)
flexibility (IRF for emergencies, multi-year SRF agreements)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: SRF’s reliance on DRC’s management capacity in a volatile context
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO oversight via quarterly meetings, PMU risk escalation to board, and robust due diligence. DRC’s overhead capped at 1.52%.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Multilateral partners (ICRC, WFP) may deprioritise Sahel due to global crises
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year agreements with break clauses; FCDO representation on SRF board to influence priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Local partners’ limited capacity to absorb funds or manage security
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SRF includes capacity-building envelopes; INSO provides security training; consortia pair INGOs with national NGOs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor fatigue or lack of co-funding for SRF scaling
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proactive donor engagement via Advisory Board; SRF designed as ‘proof of concept’ to attract partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Access restrictions by host governments (e.g., Mali’s expulsion of MINUSMA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified partner base (ICRC for contested areas, local NGOs for negotiation); IRF for rapid adaptation.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 4, supporting a Sahel Regional Fund (SRF) hosted by the Danish Refugee Council, is the preferred option. It is the option that aligns most closely with our comparative advantage, by providing a multi-sector, needs-based response in the most acute hotspots of humanitarian need. [...] This option allows us to support a blend of different actors, and in doing so pitches to their respective comparative advantages." (90000464.odt, Preferred option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to actors with: (1) **acceptance in contested areas** (e.g., ICRC’s neutrality, local NGOs’ access); (2) **capacity to operate under restrictions** (e.g., INSO for security, UNHAS for logistics); (3) **ability to navigate regulatory barriers** (e.g., SRF’s localised approach to bypass armed escort requirements). Multilaterals like WFP/UNHCR are essential for refugee responses but face access constraints in Mali/Burkina Faso, requiring local partners as intermediaries.
q27_constraints_detail: Violent extremism and inter-community conflict restrict movement, favoring partners with existing local networks (e.g., national NGOs in SRF consortia).
Government-imposed armed escorts compromise neutrality, limiting UN agency operations and necessitating ICRC/NGO alternatives.
Weak infrastructure (destroyed roads, telecoms blackouts) requires logistical partners like UNHAS and pre-positioned supplies (WFP).
Distrust of international actors (fueled by disinformation) shifts reliance to localised delivery models (SRF’s localisation testing).
Climate shocks (droughts, floods) demand partners with adaptive capacity (e.g., SRF’s multi-sectoral consortia, WFP’s cash transfers).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for multi-sectoral responses in hotspots** (food + protection + shelter) drove the **SRF’s consortia model**, while **access constraints** justified **direct multilaterals** (ICRC for detention work, WFP for airlifts). The **protracted Sudan crisis** required **flexible instruments** (IRF, WFP’s pre-positioning), and **localisation goals** shaped the **SRF’s downstream funding to national NGOs**. Advocacy objectives (IHL compliance) necessitated **ICRC’s inclusion** despite higher costs.
q28_linkages: Complex needs (GBV + malnutrition + shelter) → **SRF consortia with diverse expertise** (CRS/Mercy Corps/IRC leads).
Contested territories → **ICRC’s direct implementation** (Geneva Convention mandate).
Refugee influx → **WFP’s logistics + UNHCR’s protection** (Sudan response).
Data gaps → **UNHCR’s Project 21** (regional protection monitoring).
Security risks → **INSO’s common services** (NGO safety platform).
Localisation → **SRF’s national NGO allocations** (testing ‘local first’ models).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid Sudan response via WFP/UNHCR (efficient) vs. SRF’s localisation testing (equitable but slower). (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: ICRC’s technical protection skills (Northern) vs. SRF’s national NGO capacity-building (Southern). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: SRF’s low overheads (1.52%) vs. higher costs for ICRC’s niche access. (4) **Flexibility vs. accountability**: IRF’s adaptive funding vs. rigorous VfM tracking for SRF partners.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: **Efficiency gain**: SRF’s pooled mechanism reduces FCDO management burden (vs. multiple bilateral grants) but requires **trade-off in direct control** over partner selection.
**Equity gain**: Localisation testing in SRF increases Southern ownership but **risks delays** in crisis response compared to multilaterals.
**Risk mitigation**: Diversified partners (ICRC for access, INGOs for innovation) **increases coordination complexity** but reduces single-point failure risks.
**VfM tension**: ICRC’s higher costs are justified by **unique access** to detention sites, while SRF’s lower overheads reflect **standardised delivery**.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major risk profile** (FCAS, access constraints, atrocity risks) drives **intensive oversight**: quarterly partner meetings, embedded advisors (HSOT secondments), and real-time risk escalation via SRF’s PMU. **Security risks** necessitate INSO’s role and **financial controls** (disbursement schedules, break clauses). The **IRF’s triggers** are tied to risk thresholds (e.g., sudden refugee influxes).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded in partner roles**: (1) SRF consortia **must cascade 7% overheads to national NGOs**, (2) INSO’s training **enhances NGO security management**, (3) UNHCR’s Project 21 **strengthens protection monitoring skills**, and (4) HSOT secondments **build UN agency capacities** in civil-military coordination. The SRF’s **localisation allocation** tests how to scale national NGO leadership.
intersections.quote: "The Sahel is an insecure environment, where crises occur regularly, humanitarian needs are acute, access for implementing partners can be difficult, and the ability for the FCDO to monitor delivery is very limited. These present significant risk management challenges for the programme. [...] The programme team manages risk through conducting robust Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs) on partner systems, and through a combination of regular meetings and monitoring visits in the field." (S30094322.odt, Risk Management)

key_programme_risks: Declining humanitarian access due to government restrictions (e.g., Mali’s armed escort requirements)
Partner staffing shortages in insecure areas (mitigated via INSO support and inclusive recruitment)
Supply chain disruptions (addressed via WFP pre-positioning and UNHAS logistics)
Aid diversion risks (heightened in eastern Chad; mitigated via WFP’s Global Assurance Plan)
Donor fatigue limiting SRF’s scaling potential
Climate shocks exacerbating food insecurity (monitored via Cadre Harmonise)
Protection violations (e.g., GBV, child recruitment) in contested areas
Political instability (coups in Mali/Niger/Burkina Faso) disrupting operations
Disinformation campaigns undermining trust in humanitarian actors
Protracted displacement (Sudanese refugees in Chad) requiring long-term funding

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversified partner base (ICRC for contested areas, local NGOs for negotiation); advocacy for humanitarian principles via SRF board.
WFP pre-positions food; UNHAS provides air transport; SRF partners use local procurement.
WFP’s Global Assurance Plan; INSO’s incident management; SRF’s financial monitoring visits.
SRF’s 7% overhead cascade to national NGOs; INGO-led consortia mentorship; HSOT secondments.
Proactive donor engagement via Advisory Board; SRF positioned as ‘proof of concept’ for localisation.
UNHCR’s Project 21 monitoring; ICRC’s detention visits; SRF’s GBV specialised services.

fcas_specific_lessons: Local partners are **critical for access negotiation** in contested areas (e.g., national NGOs in SRF consortia).
Multi-year funding **reduces start-up/closure costs** and anchors partners in volatile contexts.
**Pooled mechanisms** (SRF) improve VfM but require **strong fund management** (DRC’s PMU).
Flexibility (IRF, SRF’s adaptive calls) is **essential for sudden-onset crises** (e.g., Sudan refugee influx).
**Protection monitoring** must be regional (Project 21) to address cross-border displacement.
Civil-military coordination **requires dedicated capacity** (HSOT secondments to UNOCHA).
**Cash transfers** (via SRF/WFP) enhance efficiency and market support in fragile economies.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **SHERP (2018–2021)** and early SHAPP phases included: (1) **Multi-year funding** improves partner predictability and VfM (adopted in SRF design). (2) **Localisation** requires testing (SRF’s dedicated allocation). (3) **Protection must be central** to humanitarian response (ICRC’s mandate, Project 21). (4) **Data gaps** hinder targeting (addressed via Project 21’s regional monitoring). (5) **Conflict sensitivity** is critical (e.g., ‘do no harm’ principles in SRF projects).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations: (1) **Added IRF** (£9.8m) based on Annual Review recommendations for emergency flexibility. (2) **Expanded SRF’s localisation testing** after seeing national NGOs’ role in Sudan response. (3) **Included WFP** as a partner (retroactively) due to its critical logistics for Chad. (4) **Extended geographic scope** to Mauritania (potential) and eastern Chad (Sudan crisis). (5) **Reinforced protection focus** via UNHCR’s Project 21 and ICRC’s expanded role.
risks_lessons.quote: "Building on broader learning as well as that of previous Sahel humanitarian programming, lessons learnt and recommendations, this addendum proposes the inclusion of an Internal Risk Facility. [...] The addendum proposes one specific change, which consists in increasing the geographic scope to potentially include Mauritania in the response, in the event of significant new conflict-related humanitarian needs and gaps in the response resulting from insufficient funding." (S30094322.odt, Describe any key changes)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The SRF is designed to attract co-funding from other donors, with informal soundings suggesting feasibility once proof of concept is established. The UK’s £72m SRF commitment aims to catalyse additional resources, though no specific leverage amounts are reported yet.
financial_details.quote: "The additional £61 million will: Deliver vital humanitarian assistance to new refugees in eastern Chad in FY25/26 [...] Deliver vital humanitarian aid and protection across the Central Sahel in FY25/26. [...] The SRF’s Fund Management Unit costs 7.73% of the total value of the SRF, which is well within the range of other fund managers. DRC’s overhead cost when applied to the total cost of the SRF is 1.52%." (D0003890.odt, Value for Money)

metadata.programme_name: Asian Development Fund 13 Replenishment
metadata.duration_text: The ADF13 will run from January 2021 to December 2024
metadata.quote: The Asian Development Fund is the grant-making arm of the Asian Development Bank (ADB). The United Kingdom’s contribution to the 13th Asian Development Fund (ADF) will run for the period 2021 to 2024. (90000179.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: ADF13 will run from January 2021 to December 2024 (90000179.odt, Intervention Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is a replenishment of the Asian Development Fund (ADF), which provides grant financing to Asia’s poorest and most vulnerable countries. It channels funds through the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to support development projects in priority sectors such as infrastructure, education, and energy, aligned with ADB’s Strategy 2030 and UK objectives.
what_objectives.q1_source: The replenishment of the ADF will allow the ADB to continue to deliver grant funded projects in priority sectors such as infrastructure, education, and energy across Asia and the Pacific’s poorest countries. (90000179.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Supporting Fragile and Conflict Affected States and Small Island Developing States
Addressing the Sustainable Development Goal 5’s Transformative Gender Agenda (including special focus on girls education)
Addressing Climate Change and Supporting Disaster Resilience
Fostering Regional Cooperation and Integration Including the Provision of Regional Public Goods
Supporting Private Sector Operations in Frontier Markets
Enhancing Debt Sustainability
At least 35% of ADF13 financing for climate adaptation and mitigation by volume
At least 65% by number of committed ADF13 operations will support climate mitigation and adaptation by 2024
60% by volume of ADF13 grants will support gender mainstreaming over 2021–2024
ADF13 will support at least 4 countries to implement and/or update their national biodiversity strategies and action plans
Every $1.0 of ADB Private Sector Window resources will mobilize approximately $2.5 of private capital in the poorest countries by 2024
ADF13 will support countries affected by large influxes of refugees
ADF13 will build resilience of wider systems, including for natural disaster, health, and refugee shocks
ADF13 will leverage additional finance from global climate funds to build resilience
ADF13 SIDS allocations to be based on vulnerability (using the UN’s Economic Vulnerability Index) instead of a flat rate
A minimum of $482m will be allocated to the Pacific SIDS under ADF13, an increase of around 40% over the current ADF12
what_objectives.summary: The ADF13 replenishment aims to deliver development results in Asia’s poorest countries through grant financing, focusing on six priority areas aligned with UK objectives and ADB’s Strategy 2030. It includes specific targets for climate finance, gender mainstreaming, private sector mobilization, and support for fragile states and SIDS.
what_objectives.quote: The ADF provides grant financing to Asia’s poorest and most vulnerable countries and is therefore strongly positioned to help deliver HMG’s priorities in the region, including poverty reduction, girls’ education and climate change, as well as ensuring a transparent and reliable source of funds to those countries. (90000179.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The overall programme risk rating is assessed as moderate. The ADB is recognized as a capable organization with a track record of delivery, but there are risks related to the COVID-19 pandemic and the need for reforms to improve delivery speed and disbursement ratios.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate (90000179.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted developing Asian and Pacific economies, with growth forecasts declining sharply. Fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) face heightened vulnerability to shocks, including climate change, natural hazards, and economic disruptions. Weak institutional capacity and corruption further hinder development progress.
where_context.quote: Challenges have been amplified by the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, which is severely impacting countries reliant on the ADF and COL, including FCAS and SIDS. (90000179.odt, Context–need for a DFID intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK, as a major donor and active participant in ADB governance, has significant influence over ADB policies and operations through its representation on the ADB Board and co-financing arrangements. However, decision-making ultimately rests with the ADB, a multilateral institution where the UK is one of many shareholders.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for capacity building, project preparation, and implementation
knowledge production and sharing
support for debt management strategies and fiscal risk assessments
enhanced debt transparency

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: UK International Financial Institutions Department (IFID)
partner_organizations.role: Policy engagement, performance monitoring, and oversight

partner_organizations.name: UK Representative on the ADB Board
partner_organizations.role: Programme oversight and advocacy for UK priorities

partner_organizations.name: HMG missions in ADF countries
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring local projects and communications

who_partners.quote: The UK’s active representation on the ADB Board, and our position as a major co-financer of projects with ADB and largest European donor to the current ADF (4th largest overall) provides substantial influence in shaping ADB and ADF policies and operations. (90000179.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK’s contribution is a core funding commitment to the ADF13 replenishment, which is a pooled donor fund managed by the ADB. The ADF provides grant financing to eligible countries based on a performance-based allocation system. The UK’s funds are combined with contributions from other donors and allocated according to the ADF’s grant allocation framework.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The ADB manages the ADF as a multilateral fund, with governance provided by its Board of Directors, where the UK has a seat. The ADB’s senior management and operational teams are responsible for day-to-day delivery, with oversight from donor countries, including the UK, through the Board and performance reviews.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The ADB is a pre-existing multilateral institution, and the UK’s contribution is part of a periodic replenishment process. The selection of the ADB as the implementing partner is based on its established role, technical expertise, and alignment with UK development priorities.
how_mechanism.quote: The ADF is a multilateral fund, resourced by contributions from XX donor countries around the globe. Its structure and objectives are set by the ADB’s member countries to meet the needs of its poorest and most vulnerable members that are not covered by other funding sources. (90000179.odt, Approval Questions sub-headings)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ADB Board of Directors oversees the ADF, with donor countries, including the UK, represented on the Board. The Board approves policies, allocation frameworks, and major operational decisions. The UK’s influence is exercised through its Board seat and active engagement in policy dialogues and replenishment negotiations.
how_governance.quote: The UK’s active representation on the ADB Board, and our position as a major co-financer of projects with ADB and largest European donor to the current ADF (4th largest overall) provides substantial influence in shaping ADB and ADF policies and operations. (90000179.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The ADF13 includes a mid-term review after 2 years, which allows for adjustments based on performance and changing needs. However, significant reallocations would require donor approval, particularly for shifts between country allocations and thematic support.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The ADF13 framework includes a mid-term review and a commitment to develop a paper on the longer-term future of the ADF, allowing for adjustments in response to emerging challenges such as COVID-19. The UK and other donors can influence these adjustments through the ADB Board and replenishment negotiations.
how_flexibility.quote: Lesson learning is built into the programme – there will be a mid-term review of ADF13 after 2 years and the ADB has agreed to develop a paper on the longer-term future of the ADF for consideration by member countries at its 2021 Annual Meeting.
