who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (via BEK and FCDO) retains primary decision-making authority, with Nepal Police and government as implementing partners. The programme is designed by UK experts and leverages UK policing expertise (e.g., HMICFRS, College of Policing).
q10_capacity_building_details: training of police and justice actors on GBV response and gender-sensitive policing
technical advice to ministries and police organisations
support to assemblies and civil society for monitoring security services
institutional strengthening of provincial police forces and judicial committees

partner_organizations.name: Nepal Police
partner_organizations.role: primary implementing partner for policing reforms

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Home Affairs (Nepal)
partner_organizations.role: federal-level counterpart for police governance

partner_organizations.name: Provincial Ministries (e.g., Interior, Social Development)
partner_organizations.role: provincial-level partners for police devolution and GBV response

partner_organizations.name: Municipal Judicial Committees
partner_organizations.role: local justice providers for GBV and civil disputes

partner_organizations.name: Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of the Constabulary and Fire Services (HMICFRS)
partner_organizations.role: UK technical partner for police oversight and standards

partner_organizations.name: College of Policing (CoP)
partner_organizations.role: UK technical partner for training and professional standards

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: community engagement and monitoring

who_partners.quote: "The UK has a significant comparative advantage. A long history of engagement and a well-performing IPSSJ Phase One [...] has positioned the UK as a partner of choice on policing for the Nepal Government and police, and as an innovator on GBV work." (D0002741.odt, The UK’s comparative advantage)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for CSOs and local partners) and technical assistance contracts (for UK policing experts). The flexible fund allows for adaptive support across security and justice themes as opportunities arise.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by BEK/FCDO with a core team of UK technical advisors (e.g., from HMICFRS, CoP) and Nepal-based implementing partners (e.g., Nepal Police, provincial governments). The structure is hierarchical, with FCDO overseeing delivery through contracted partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme builds on Phase 1 of IPSSJ, which had a strong track record (five consecutive "A" scores for performance). The UK’s long-standing relationship with Nepal Police and government positioned it as the "partner of choice," making direct awards to existing partners logical for continuity and trust.
how_mechanism.quote: "IPSSJ has achieved five consecutive ‘A’ scores for programme performance since 2016. [...] Our engagement has delivered real change in how Nepal Police relate to citizens and has matured from focusing on training and capacity building to supporting organisational reform." (D0002741.odt, The UK’s comparative advantage)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme involves inter-ministerial consultations and cross-HMG workshops, suggesting a steering committee with federal/provincial government, police, and civil society representation. BEK/FCDO retains oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The design process began in September 2019. It has involved several visits to each focus province, three cross-HMG workshops, inter-ministerial consultations with federal government, and extensive consultative sessions with civil society, community groups, and GBV, security and policing experts." (D0002741.odt, The government welcomes BEK engagement)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, particularly to respond to emerging opportunities or risks (e.g., political changes, COVID-19). The programme has a flexible fund to support work across themes as needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The theory of change and logframe are described as ‘living documents’ that will be updated as required. Regular MEL reviews will assess progress and contextual changes, allowing for adjustments. Contracts with implementing partners are designed to be flexible.
how_flexibility.quote: "Being able to respond to opportunities in real time as they present themselves will be important to maintaining buy-in and momentum. [...] The theory of change and logframe for the programme will be ‘living documents’ and updated as required." (D0002741.odt, Be flexible and adapt)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., Palladium or similar) → Nepal Police/Provincial Governments → Municipal Judicial Committees/CSOs
how_efficiency.quote: "IPSSJ2 will be 22% smaller in size than IPSSJ while taking a more ambitious approach. IPSSJ2 will focus more on using UK technical expertise to influence outcomes." (D0002741.odt, Programme modalities)

q24_alternatives_considered: Smaller, less ambitious ‘train and equip’ projects (e.g., US approach)
Short-term or single-issue programmes (e.g., UNFPA/UN Women GBV projects)
Direct bilateral support without multi-level engagement
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The integrated, long-term approach was selected because: 1) Nepal’s federalism transition requires sustained support across federal/provincial/local levels; 2) GBV and policing are interconnected and require a holistic response; 3) The UK’s comparative advantage lies in its long-term trust with Nepal Police and proven track record in Phase 1; 4) A flexible, adaptive programme is needed to navigate Nepal’s dynamic political context.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in police devolution could derail reforms or create inter-governmental tensions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Balanced investment across federal/provincial/municipal levels and politically aware engagement to avoid exacerbating conflicts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overstretch of UK technical expertise given the programme’s ambition.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage existing partnerships (e.g., HMICFRS, CoP) and focus on strategic influence rather than direct implementation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Backlash from shifting harmful social norms around GBV.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with men and boys to reflect on gender norms and use mass communications to catalyse change gradually.

why_rationale.quote: "IPSSJ2 will be the primary vehicle for delivering British Embassy Kathmandu’s (BEK) Country Plan Campaign Goal Outcome 2.4: ‘By 2023, UK support develops more representative and accountable security and justice institutions that respect human rights, tackle GBV, and address exclusionary practices and impunity that fuel grievances.’" (D0002741.odt, How does this Programme deliver FCDO’s strategic portfolio?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s federalism transition and political fragility limit partner selection to actors with existing trust and legitimacy. The contested nature of police devolution requires partners who can navigate inter-governmental tensions (e.g., Nepal Police, provincial governments). GBV’s sensitivity necessitates partners with proven safeguarding expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: Federal-provincial tensions require neutral intermediaries (e.g., BEK) to broker collaboration.
GBV work demands partners with cultural understanding and safeguarding capacity (e.g., local CSOs).
Police reform requires partners acceptable to both political leaders and rank-and-file officers (e.g., UK’s long-standing relationship with Nepal Police).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual focus on policing reform and GBV prevention requires an integrated delivery structure (single programme with cross-cutting teams) to avoid silos. The need for multi-level engagement (federal/provincial/local) shapes the consortium model, combining UK technical expertise with local implementation.
q28_linkages: Policing + GBV integration → Closed consortium with shared oversight to align objectives.
Federalism support → Multi-layered governance structure (steering committee with federal/provincial reps).
Social norm change → Embedded advisors (UK experts) working with local CSOs for contextual adaptation.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., targeting marginalized groups like Dalit women) with efficiency (e.g., focusing on 10% of palikas in 4 provinces for scalable impact). There is tension between the ambition to devolve policing (a political priority) and the risk of diverting resources from other sectors like health/education.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid police devolution risks excluding marginalized groups if not carefully managed (mitigated by gender quotas and targeted training).
Expertise vs. ownership: UK technical leadership ensures quality but risks limiting Nepali ownership (mitigated by capacity building for provincial/municipal actors).
Cost vs. reach: Focus on 4 provinces balances depth of impact with geographic coverage.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (political instability, contested federalism) necessitates intensive oversight (e.g., regular MEL reviews, adaptive management) and a flexible fund to respond to crises (e.g., COVID-19, political changes).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak capacity in provincial/municipal institutions shapes the programme’s focus on institutional strengthening (e.g., training for judicial committees, support to provincial police forces). UK partners (e.g., HMICFRS) provide technical backstopping where local capacity is lacking.
intersections.quote: "A politically-aware approach is needed because working on policing and GBV is at the heart of power relations in a society [...] and in Nepal also at the centre of contestation over federalism." (D0002741.odt, Work politically)

key_programme_risks: Failure to deliver police devolution (constitutional commitment) risks reigniting conflict.
Political interference in police or judicial committees undermines legitimacy.
Backlash against GBV norm-shifting efforts from conservative groups.
Overstretch of provincial/municipal capacity to absorb devolved policing responsibilities.
GBV survivors facing revictimization due to weak safeguarding in justice systems.
COVID-19 or other crises diverting government attention from reforms.
UK technical expertise being perceived as neo-colonial or out of touch with local realities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support balanced engagement across federal/provincial/municipal levels; use UK’s convening power to broker agreements.
Politically aware engagement; align with government priorities while fostering local agency.
Work with men/boys on gender norms; use mass communications to shift norms gradually.
Targeted training for provincial police and judicial committees; embed UK advisors.
Strong safeguarding protocols for implementing partners; spot-checks on compliance.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, sustained engagement over multiple programme cycles is critical for institutional change (cited from ICAI review).
‘Going with the grain’ of local power structures is essential to avoid exacerbating conflicts (e.g., balancing federal/provincial interests).
Flexibility to adapt to political shocks (e.g., parliament dissolution) is necessary for maintaining momentum.
Community engagement (e.g., community scorecards) builds trust in fragile settings.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 of IPSSJ demonstrated that: 1) Multi-year programming is needed for institutional change; 2) Combining policing reform with GBV work creates synergies (e.g., increased reporting of GBV where police are more responsive); 3) UK’s long-term engagement built trust with Nepal Police; 4) Pilot approaches (e.g., community scorecards) can be scaled up if integrated into local systems.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: IPSSJ2 is more ambitious than Phase 1, shifting from capacity building to governance reform (e.g., supporting police devolution). It incorporates lessons on adaptive management (e.g., ‘living’ theory of change) and deeper political economy analysis to navigate Nepal’s contested federalism.
risks_lessons.quote: "[DFID] is most effective where it sustained its engagement within institutions or policy issues over several programme cycles. This allowed DFID to build up relationships of trust with national counterparts and to generate cumulative results over time." (D0002741.odt, Policing)

financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £35m (over seven years)" (D0002741.odt, BUSINESS CASE SUMMARY SHEET)

metadata.programme_name: Democratic Resilience Platform

quote.text: The Democratic Resilience Platform provides a cohesive and effective offer to posts on democratic governance.

duration_source.text: Original programme start and end dates: 20/12/2022 - 31/03/2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Democratic Resilience Platform (DRP) is designed to provide technical assistance, capacity building, and policy support to FCDO posts globally to strengthen democratic governance. It operates through a Centre of Expertise (CoE) that delivers tailored support, training, and tools to posts, while also consolidating funding for strategic, cohesive prioritization of democratic governance programming. The platform aims to reverse democratic declines and shape the international system by enhancing the UK's leadership on open societies.

q1_source.text: The Democratic Resilience Platform is part of the FCDO’s Open Societies Directorate programme reform strategy to provide a more cohesive and effective offer to posts on democratic governance. At the forefront of this effort, the Platform will launch a Centre of Expertise (DemGov CoE) to equip Posts to deliver more effectively across Open Societies objectives and to respond to democratic crises and openings through agile, call-down Technical Assistance.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Bespoke technical advice, analysis, and programmatic support on democratic governance issues delivered to ODA-eligible posts throughout FCDO
Bespoke evidence and learning derived from CoE post-specific enquiries synthesised to support cross-FCDO learning
At least eight thematic policy guidance and tools for posts
Supported posts are in a stronger position to engage and act on democratic governance issues in-country
Support to journalists in distress, including women journalists, by providing practical and legal support
Enabling independent media to publish content in the public interest
Promotion of open and accountable use of emerging digital technologies with democratic safeguards
Strategic political economy analysis support provided to posts
CoE has completed enquiries in 11 Posts and currently has live enquiries with around 20 Posts
Delivered three network-wide products with a further four anticipated by the end of 2023/24
Support to over half of ODA eligible Posts to date
Rollout of two diagnostic tools (Women’s Political Empowerment toolkit and the Democratic Governance Diagnostic) to increasing numbers of Posts
Provide psychosocial and mental health support (MHPSS) to journalists and media professionals in Gaza
Provide reporting equipment to maintain media activity in Gaza
Explore measures to combat misinformation, disinformation, and hate speech in Gaza
Organize and facilitate recreational activities for journalists in Gaza

what_objectives.summary: The Democratic Resilience Platform aims to reverse democratic declines and shape the international system by providing technical assistance, capacity building, and policy support to FCDO posts globally. It consolidates funding for strategic, cohesive prioritization of democratic governance programming and enhances the UK's leadership on open societies.

quote.text: The purpose is to provide significant support to reverse democratic declines and shape and influence the international system.

Political economy constraints and weak institutions in many target countries affect the ability to deliver democratic governance support effectively. The programme must navigate these challenges while ensuring that support reaches intended beneficiaries.
