quote.text: The Democratic Governance CoE has seen a high level of demand from Posts since its launch in 2023. Over half of ODA eligible Posts have been supported to date and it is on track to become an authoritative source of expertise across dem gov issues within the FCDO and to strengthen systems and knowledge-sharing between the centre and Posts.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a mix of funding instruments, including accountable grants (AG) to partners like OGP and UNESCO, and direct management of the Centre of Expertise (CoE) through a combination of in-sourced FCDO staff and external experts sourced through WFD. This allows for flexible and responsive support tailored to the needs of FCDO posts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Democratic Resilience Platform operates as a platform that consolidates multiple funding streams and partners under a single programme. The Centre of Expertise (CoE) is managed through a mix of in-sourced FCDO experts and external partners (WFD), with a Steering Committee overseeing strategic decisions. Partners like UNESCO and OGP deliver specific components through accountable grants, while the CoE provides direct technical assistance to FCDO posts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners like UNESCO and WFD were selected based on their established track records and alignment with FCDO priorities. The selection process considered credibility, impact, and value-added of strategic, centrally-managed grants. For example, OGP was chosen for its global platform role and ability to support digital governance reforms, while WFD was selected for its expertise in democratic governance and existing relationship with FCDO.

quote.text: OGP is mentioned in the Business Case (e.g., Para 98 of the Strategic Case) as an example of Module III and IV activity where we may look to fund new partners. Paras 20-22 of the Commercial Case set out the criteria we used to evaluate their proposal for AG arrangements. Our evaluation looked at the principles set out in the Business Case, as well as previous Project Completion Reviews and the DFID-funded independent evaluation.
quote.source: D0004914.odt, What is the approach to implementation?

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee has the power to reallocate funds from low-performing components to higher-performing ones to achieve greater value for money (VFM) and impact. It also oversees strategic decisions and ensures alignment with FCDO priorities.

quote.text: The Steering Committee (see the Management Case) will have the power to reallocate funds from low performing components to higher performing ones to achieve greater VFM and impact.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The Steering Committee can reallocate funds between components to maximize impact and value for money. This flexibility is a key feature of the platform model, allowing resources to be shifted based on performance and emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with the Steering Committee overseeing adjustments to priorities and funding allocations. The Centre of Expertise (CoE) is demand-led, responding to enquiries from FCDO posts and tailoring support based on context and needs. The programme also incorporates monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) to inform adaptive management.

quote.text: A Platform model with flexible funding can be used to manage risk, increase VFM and enhance impact. The Steering Committee will have the power to reallocate funds from low performing components to higher performing ones to achieve greater VFM and impact.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partners (WFD, UNESCO, OGP, etc.) → End beneficiaries (FCDO Posts, journalists, media organizations)

quote.text: The Platform will be delivered through a mixture of UK-based in-sourced G6 senior experts and external experts and will recruit up to four G6 experts into in-sourced roles in 23/24 with one additional role planned (five in total) for a subsequent (generation II) stage of the CoE in 24/25.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1 – Stop existing democratic governance CMPs
q24_alternatives_considered.description: This would result in savings of roughly £2.75 million in the first year but was not recommended as it would be counterintuitive given the prominence of the Open Societies agenda in the Integrated Review and International Development Strategy.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2 – Continue to fund delivery of individual democracy partners through CMPs
q24_alternatives_considered.description: This represented business as usual with no Centre of Expertise and would cost £2.75 million in year one. It was not recommended as it missed the opportunity to create a CoE to support Posts and bring greater policy coherence across the OSHRD Directorate.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3 – Recommended: Develop a new Democratic Resilience Platform that brings together support to partners and hosts a Centre of Expertise offering technical assistance to Posts
q24_alternatives_considered.description: This option was chosen as it would be most effective for achieving the objectives outlined in the Strategic Case and ultimately supporting the high-level outcomes of the Integrated Review, the OSHR Strategy, and the Foreign Secretary’s priorities.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The Democratic Resilience Platform (Option 3) was chosen because it offers greater policy coordination, procurement efficiency, management flexibility, and impact compared to the alternatives. The platform model allows for economies of scale, better overall coordination within the portfolio, and more focused resources and activities on outcomes. The Centre of Expertise (CoE) provides responsive and tailored support to Posts, which was identified as a critical need. The platform also aligns with the UK’s strategic priorities to reverse democratic declines and shape the international system, as outlined in the Integrated Review and International Development Strategy.
q25_decision_factors: ability to consolidate and streamline programming

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Demand for CoE services may be below or exceed expectations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The CoE team has robust processes to assess and prioritize demands across the network while managing resources to deliver a quality service.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Recruitment may fail to attract and retain staff with the key skills needed to deliver
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Recruitment is merit-based, and successful applicants are supported throughout their tenure with continuous professional learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery in conflict-affected zones like Gaza increases risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UNESCO has put in place sufficient mitigations to ensure funding is delivered to intended beneficiaries.

quote.text: Option 3 would be most effective for achieving the objectives outlined in the Strategic Case and, ultimately, supporting the high-level outcomes of the IR, the OSHR Strategy and the FS’s priorities.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and operation in conflict-affected zones like Gaza constrain partner selection to those with proven capacity to deliver in high-risk environments. Partners must demonstrate compliance with UK legislation, including anti-bribery and counter-terrorism financing laws, and have robust safeguarding and due diligence processes.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict and security risks in Gaza limit partners to those with local networks and experience in conflict zones
Regulatory and compliance requirements (e.g., Terrorism Act) restrict partner selection to those meeting UK standards
Need for partners with global reach and credibility to support the UK’s leadership on open societies
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to provide responsive, tailored support to FCDO posts determines the platform structure, which combines in-sourced experts and external partners to offer flexible and demand-led technical assistance. The consolidation of multiple funding streams under one platform is designed to improve coordination, reduce duplication, and enhance the UK’s strategic influence on democratic governance.
q28_linkages: Demand for tailored, rapid support from Posts → Platform structure with in-sourced and external experts
Need for policy coherence and strategic alignment → Consolidation of funding under a single platform with a Steering Committee
Requirement for adaptive management → Flexible funding and governance structure with reallocation powers
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the balance between in-sourced and outsourced expertise to maximize cost-effectiveness while ensuring high-quality, tailored support. In-sourced experts are more cost-effective and better understand FCDO Posts’ needs, but external partners provide specialized expertise not available in-house. The mix is designed to offer the best of both, though the documents do not deeply explore tensions between Northern leadership and Southern ownership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Cost-effectiveness of in-sourced experts (£94k/year) vs. higher cost of external consultants (£174k/year)
Trust and understanding of FCDO needs with in-sourced staff vs. specialized expertise from external partners
Flexibility of external partners to scale up/down vs. institutional knowledge retained with in-sourced roles
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of the programme influences the oversight intensity, with quarterly programme boards and annual reviews to monitor progress and adapt as needed. Higher risks in specific components (e.g., Gaza) lead to more intensive oversight and mitigation measures by partners like UNESCO.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with the CoE designed to upskill FCDO Posts and harmonize approaches to democratic governance. The diagnostic tools and network-wide guidance developed by the CoE aim to strengthen the capacity of Posts to engage effectively on democratic issues, while partnerships with organizations like OGP and WFD provide specialized support and learning opportunities.

quote.text: In-sourced experts are more likely to understand the specific requirements of FCDO Posts and partners, leading to better outcomes (effectiveness). This is especially important when working on politically sensitive areas and to help build the trust of Post.

key_programme_risks: Demand for CoE services may be below or exceed expectations, affecting resource allocation and delivery
Recruitment challenges may limit the ability to attract and retain staff with the necessary skills
Delivery risks in conflict-affected zones like Gaza may impact the effectiveness of support to journalists
Political and security risks in target countries may constrain programme activities and outcomes
Changes in UK government priorities post-2025 may affect the programme’s continuity and focus

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Demand for CoE services may be below or exceed expectations
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The CoE team has robust processes to assess and prioritize demands across the network while managing resources to deliver a quality service.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Recruitment may fail to attract and retain staff with the key skills needed to deliver
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Recruitment is merit-based, and successful applicants are supported throughout their tenure with continuous professional learning.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delivery in conflict-affected zones like Gaza increases risk
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UNESCO has put in place sufficient mitigations to ensure funding is delivered to intended beneficiaries.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political and security risks in target countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme’s adaptive management approach and flexible funding allow for adjustments based on emerging risks and opportunities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Changes in UK government priorities post-2025
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme end-date (March 2026) allows for a review in 2025 to align with new government priorities if needed.

fcas_specific_lessons: Operating in conflict-affected zones requires partners with local networks, experience, and robust safeguarding measures
Flexible and adaptive programming is essential to respond to rapidly changing contexts and emerging needs
Close coordination with in-country and international partners enhances the effectiveness and safety of interventions
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from previous FCDO democratic governance initiatives, such as the need for a Centre of Expertise to provide tailored, responsive support to Posts. The consolidation of multiple funding streams under one platform aims to improve coordination, reduce duplication, and enhance strategic focus, addressing gaps identified in earlier programming.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme has evolved based on learning from its inception phase, including the expansion of in-sourced roles in the CoE to better meet demand and improve knowledge-sharing. The adoption of diagnostic tools and network-wide guidance reflects lessons on the need for structured, scalable support to Posts. The trial of technical assistance to support Posts’ work with partners is another adaptation based on emerging needs and feedback.

quote.text: The use of in-sourced roles has amplified and deepened the CoE’s offer to Posts. In-house technical experts understand the specific requirements of FCDO Posts and can build their trust. In particular, the CoE team has found that in-house experts are able to talk to Posts on more sensitive issues to unlock how to support them best and to make that support more tailored (than we could do with only outsourced experts).
Original programme budget: £16.475m

metadata.programme_name: 20th Replenishment of the International Development Association (IDA20)

quote.text: The World Bank’s (‘Bank’) International Development Association (IDA) is the largest provider of grants, low or zero interest rate loans, and technical advice to the Governments of 74 of the poorest countries to support poverty reduction and shared prosperity.

metadata.duration_source: Upto £1,531 million (fiscal CDEL) - between December 2022 and June 2025.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: IDA20 is a replenishment mechanism that channels funds from donors to 74 of the poorest countries, combining donor contributions with market borrowing to provide grants, low-interest loans, and technical advice. The programme aims to support poverty reduction, shared prosperity, and a green, resilient, inclusive recovery from COVID-19.
what_objectives.q1_source: The World Bank’s (‘Bank’) International Development Association (IDA) is the largest provider of grants, low or zero interest rate loans, and technical advice to the Governments of 74 of the poorest countries to support poverty reduction and shared prosperity. IDA has been ranked among the top three aid agencies for the quality of its support to countries... IDA20 will allow IDA to sustain elevated funding levels over the next three years to support IDA countries to respond to the ongoing pandemic crisis, reduce economic scarring and achieve a green, resilient, and inclusive recovery.
q3_expected_outputs: 90-105 million people with enhanced access to transportation services
35-50 million people with improved electricity services
105-200 million children with immunisations
140-150 million women and children supported with basic nutrition services
10 GW of renewable energy generation
Support for at least 15 countries to increase childcare access
Support for 10 countries to integrate gender into fiscal policies
Commitment to close learning gaps and improve learning outcomes in 20 IDA countries
35% of IDA20 financing to tackle climate change
Support for all IDA countries with vaccine roll-out, testing, and treatments
Increase of up to 20% in expected financing for fragile countries
what_objectives.summary: IDA20 is a financing mechanism that leverages donor contributions to provide grants, loans, and technical assistance to 74 of the world's poorest countries. It aims to support a green, resilient, and inclusive recovery from COVID-19 while addressing key UK priorities such as climate change, girls' education, women's economic empowerment, and crisis preparedness.

quote.text: IDA20 will allow IDA to sustain elevated funding levels over the next three years to support IDA countries to respond to the ongoing pandemic crisis, reduce economic scarring and achieve a green, resilient, and inclusive recovery.

countries_regions: 74 of the poorest countries eligible for IDA support
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: IDA operates in fragile, conflict, and violence (FCV)-affected countries, with 20 million people in these states living in extreme poverty. The programme explicitly targets FCV-affected countries with dedicated financing windows and increased support.
where_context.q5_source: IDA is one of the largest development actors in Fragility Violence and Conflict-affected countries. Since 2017, the Bank has significantly increased financing and staffing to FCV-affected states... By 2030, two thirds of the poorest people are expected to live in FCV affected states.
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The COVID-19 crisis has set back development in IDA countries, with per capita income expected to be 18% below pre-pandemic projections by 2022. Climate change and conflict further exacerbate poverty and instability, while weak institutions and high debt levels limit countries' ability to respond effectively.

quote.text: The COVID-19 crisis has had significant health, social and economic impact on IDA countries that have further set back their development and compounded existing inequalities... More women than men lost their jobs and more women-owned, than men-owned, Micro-, Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (MSMEs) have been forced to close... Climate change poses further risks with the Bank estimating that more than 100 million people living in IDA countries will be pushed into extreme poverty by 2030.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank, governed by its Board of Executive Directors (representing shareholder countries including the UK, US, Japan, China, Germany, and France), makes ultimate decisions on IDA's operations and policies. The UK, as a leading donor, has significant influence but does not control day-to-day operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: support for at least 15 countries to increase childcare access
support for 10 countries to integrate gender into fiscal policies
support for 20 countries to address learning gaps in girls' education
support for 50 countries to develop or update Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) for climate action
support for 17 countries to develop digital infrastructure
training and institutional strengthening in FCV-affected countries
support for disability-inclusive development through mainstreaming in Bank activities

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (IDA)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Private sector support arm of the World Bank Group

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA)
partner_organizations.role: Provides political risk guarantees to private sector investors

partner_organizations.name: Governments of 74 IDA-eligible countries
partner_organizations.role: Recipient governments implementing country programmes

partner_organizations.name: G7 and like-minded donor countries
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers and strategic partners

quote.text: IDA works as one of five institutions of the World Bank Group (WBG)... The WBG is governed by its shareholders (currently 189 member countries) who are represented by a Board of Governors... The five largest IBRD shareholders each appoint a single Executive Director, while other member countries elect Executive Directors who represent their constituencies.
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Box 1 – the World Bank Group

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK's contribution to IDA20 is provided as core funding to the World Bank's IDA, which combines donor contributions with market borrowing and loan repayments to finance development projects. This allows IDA to leverage each £1 of donor funding into more than £3 of total financing for poor countries.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IDA operates as part of the World Bank Group, governed by its Board of Executive Directors. The UK contributes funds to IDA's central pool, which are then allocated to 74 eligible countries based on performance-based criteria, dedicated windows for fragile states, and special themes like climate change and gender.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank/IDA is a long-standing multilateral partner with a proven track record. The UK's contribution is part of a regular replenishment process involving all shareholder countries, not a competitive selection.

quote.text: IDA is replenished by donors every three years... The UK has been a leading donor to IDA since its establishment in 1960 and its largest donor since 2007.

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: IDA allocates funds to countries through three mechanisms: 1) Core country allocations based on performance, 2) Dedicated financing for fragile states and special windows, and 3) Arrears clearance. The UK, as a donor, influences these allocations through negotiations but does not directly control sub-awards.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The World Bank Group is governed by its Board of Governors (typically Ministers of Finance or Development) and a Board of Executive Directors. The UK is represented on the Board of Executive Directors, which oversees IDA's operations and allocations. The IDA Deputies (representatives from donor countries) also play a key role in replenishment negotiations.

quote.text: The WBG is governed by its shareholders (currently 189 member countries) who are represented by a Board of Governors... who are the ultimate decision-makers. The Governors delegate specific duties to 25 Executive Directors... IDA allocates support to IDA countries through three mechanisms: Core country allocations... Dedicated financing... and Arrears clearance.
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Box 1 and Role of IDA sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: IDA's financial model allows for some reallocation between countries based on performance and emerging needs, particularly through the Crisis Response Window and FCV Envelope. However, core allocations are largely predetermined by performance-based formulas.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The IDA20 replenishment includes commitments to adjust priorities in response to emerging challenges (e.g., COVID-19, climate change), but these require donor approval during negotiations. The UK has influenced the inclusion of new priorities like climate alignment and gender equality through the replenishment process.

quote.text: IDA’s financial model has allowed it to frontload financing to respond to the pandemic crisis... IDA20 will see the size of IDA’s dedicated financing window for crisis response in its Crisis Response Window increased to $3.3bn... The UK has worked with like-minded partners through the IDA20 discussions to secure the following commitments in relation to UK priorities...
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Crisis preparedness and Rationale for UK Aid spending sections

how_efficiency.q21_management_costs_details: The World Bank's total operating costs are approximately 1% of its total portfolio ($2.7 billion operating costs on a $260 billion portfolio in FY20). IDA's administrative expenditure is self-financed from returns on its investments and constrained by a 'budget anchor' that limits spending to loan revenue.
how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (IDA) → Recipient country governments. The UK contributes funds to IDA, which then disburses to country governments based on agreed allocations.
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: The UK's contribution is provided upfront as part of the replenishment, but IDA's disbursements to countries are tied to performance and specific financing instruments (e.g., Investment Project Financing, Development Policy Financing).

quote.text: In FY20 the Bank’s total portfolio was estimated at $260 billion with operating costs of $2.7 billion or around 1% of the Bank’s total portfolio... IDA has a commitment to maintain its administrative expenditure within its loan revenue (known as IDA’s ‘budget anchor’).
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Economy section under Value for Money

q24_alternatives_considered: Provide further bilateral guarantees to Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)
Increase UK support to regional development banks (African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: IDA was chosen because it is the only part of the international financial system that supports low-income countries while being able to borrow from capital markets to supplement donor contributions. It provides unmatched scale (74 countries, $30+ billion/year), leverage (each £1 of UK support generates >£3 in total financing), and alignment with UK priorities (climate, gender, education, fragility). The UK's influence as a leading donor also allows it to shape IDA's strategic direction.
q25_decision_factors: scale and reach (74 countries, multiple sectors)
alignment with UK priorities (climate, gender, education, fragility)
UK influence (as a leading donor and shareholder)
proven effectiveness (ranked top 3 in aid quality)
financial sustainability (IDA's AAA credit rating and balance sheet optimization)
speed and flexibility (ability to frontload financing for crises like COVID-19)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced UK contribution could lead other donors to reconsider their pledges, shrinking the overall replenishment size.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UK's significant contribution maintains its role as a leading donor, encouraging others to follow suit and preserving IDA's financial model.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IDA's AAA credit rating (which reflects donor support) could be downgraded if major donors reduce contributions, increasing borrowing costs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: A continued significant UK pledge supports IDA's creditworthiness, ensuring it can continue to borrow affordably from markets.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Without UK influence, IDA's strategic priorities might shift away from UK interests (e.g., climate, gender, fragility).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintaining a leading donor position allows the UK to shape IDA20 commitments and future replenishment negotiations.

quote.text: The UK has been a leading donor to IDA since its establishment in 1960 and its largest donor since 2007. There are two main drivers for prioritising a significant UK contribution: 1) Value for money and impact... IDA is the only part of the International Financial system which supports Low Income Countries that is currently able to borrow from capital markets to supplement donor contributions... 2) UK influence over the WBG and wider international system... A continued significant UK contribution would support the UK’s ability to continue to influence the World Bank Group.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's global scope and focus on the 74 poorest countries, many of which are FCV-affected, necessitates a multilateral delivery structure. The World Bank/IDA is one of the few institutions with the capacity, risk appetite, and existing country presence to operate effectively in such high-risk environments. Bilateral or smaller regional banks lack the scale and specialized instruments (e.g., Crisis Response Window, FCV Envelope) required.
q27_constraints_detail: High risk of debt distress in many IDA countries limits the use of non-concessional financing, requiring IDA's grant and low-interest loan instruments.
Fragility and conflict in target countries demand specialized windows (e.g., FCV Envelope, Crisis Response Window) that only a multilateral like IDA can manage.
Weak institutions in recipient countries necessitate IDA's technical assistance and policy dialogue, which are embedded in its financing instruments.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's objectives—such as leveraging donor funds, supporting fragile states, and addressing global challenges like climate change—require a multilateral mechanism with significant financial engineering capacity. IDA's ability to combine donor contributions with market borrowing (achieving >3x leverage) and its existing infrastructure (e.g., country offices, sectoral expertise) make it uniquely suited to deliver on these ambitions at scale.
q28_linkages: The need for leverage and scale (WHAT) → Multilateral delivery through IDA (HOW).
Focus on fragile and conflict-affected states (WHERE) → Requires IDA's specialized FCV Envelope and crisis instruments (HOW).
Climate and gender priorities (WHAT) → IDA's thematic windows and cross-cutting commitments (HOW).
Global reach (WHERE) → IDA's existing presence in 74 countries and sectoral breadth (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document highlights tensions between maximizing financial leverage (efficiency) and ensuring funds reach the poorest and most fragile countries (equity). For example, IDA's financial model achieves high multiples of donor contributions (£1:£3+) by borrowing from capital markets, but this requires maintaining a strong credit rating, which in turn depends on consistent donor support. The FCV Envelope and Crisis Response Window represent equity-focused instruments that slightly reduce overall leverage but ensure funds flow to the most vulnerable contexts.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Leverage vs. concessionality: Higher grant elements for fragile states reduce IDA's overall financial multiples but align with equity goals.
Scale vs. tailoring: IDA's standardized instruments enable rapid disbursement at scale but may limit country-specific customization.
Donor influence vs. recipient ownership: The UK's significant contribution buys influence over IDA priorities but risks being perceived as donor-driven rather than country-owned.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile of IDA countries (FCV, debt distress, climate vulnerability) necessitates intensive oversight mechanisms such as the Crisis Response Window, FCV Envelope, and performance-based allocations. These instruments require robust monitoring and frequent adjustments, increasing management intensity compared to lower-risk programmes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme embeds capacity building within its core delivery structure. For example, IDA's support for country platforms in fragile states (WHERE) is directly tied to its role in providing technical assistance and institutional strengthening (WHO). The Bank's Country Private Sector Diagnostics and Risk and Resilience Assessments inform how capacity-building activities are targeted and delivered.

quote.text: IDA is one of the largest development actors in Fragility Violence and Conflict-affected countries... The Bank has launched Risk and Resilience Assessments to assess the drivers of conflict and fragility and feed these into its country diagnostics and strategies... IDA’s financial model has allowed it to frontload financing to respond to the pandemic crisis... The UK has worked with like-minded partners through the IDA20 discussions to secure commitments in relation to UK priorities, including... support for country platforms in the poorest and most fragile countries.
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Fragility, Conflict and Violence and Rationale for UK Aid spending sections

key_programme_risks: Economic scarring in IDA countries from COVID-19 could lead to long-term development setbacks.
Climate change may push over 100 million people in IDA countries into extreme poverty by 2030.
Increased fragility and conflict could reverse poverty reduction gains, with two-thirds of the poorest expected to live in FCV-affected states by 2030.
Debt distress in many IDA countries limits their ability to access affordable financing.
Reduced donor contributions could shrink IDA's overall replenishment size, limiting its impact.
A downgrade in IDA's credit rating (due to lower donor support) could increase borrowing costs and reduce leverage.
Insufficient crisis preparedness could leave countries vulnerable to future shocks (e.g., pandemics, natural disasters).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reduction in IDA financing levels due to lower donor contributions.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK's significant contribution (£1.531 billion) helps sustain elevated funding levels and encourages other donors to maintain their pledges.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited financing for fragile and conflict-affected states.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IDA20 increases the FCV Envelope to $8.5-9.0 billion and introduces new allocations for prevention, resilience, and post-conflict recovery.
IDA20 commits 35% of financing to climate action, aligns all operations with the Paris Agreement by 2023, and supports at least 50 countries in developing NDCs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Slow vaccine rollout and weak health systems in IDA countries.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IDA has made $10 billion available for vaccine rollout, testing, and treatments, with further support expected under IDA20.
IDA20 frontloads financing to support recovery, with a focus on green, resilient, and inclusive growth to reduce long-term impacts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High operating costs in FCV-affected countries.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IDA's financial model accounts for higher FCV costs (86% uplift) and includes dedicated windows to ensure sustained engagement in these contexts.

fcas_specific_lessons: Increased financing and staffing for FCV-affected states since 2017, with IDA19 providing $19 billion in support.
Introduction of the FCV Envelope in IDA19, which is expanded in IDA20 to include Prevention and Resilience Allocations, Remaining Engaged during Conflict Allocations, and Turn Around Allocations.
Development of Risk and Resilience Assessments to better understand and address drivers of conflict and fragility.
Recognition that two-thirds of the poorest people will live in FCV-affected states by 2030, necessitating specialized instruments and sustained engagement.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: IDA19 demonstrated the effectiveness of frontloading financing in response to crises (e.g., COVID-19), leading to IDA20 being brought forward by a year to maintain elevated funding levels. The introduction of the FCV Envelope and Crisis Response Window in IDA19 proved critical for addressing fragility and are thus expanded in IDA20. Lessons on gender and climate integration from IDA19 have been retained and strengthened in IDA20, with new commitments on childcare, fiscal policies, and Paris Agreement alignment.
design_changes_based_on_learning: IDA20 was brought forward by a year (from 2022 to 2021) to avoid a drop in financing levels after IDA19's frontloaded support.
The FCV Envelope was increased from $7.5 billion in IDA19 to $8.5-9.0 billion in IDA20, with new allocations for conflict prevention and resilience.
Climate finance commitments were increased from 26% in IDA19 to 35% in IDA20, with a stronger focus on adaptation and Paris Agreement alignment.
New commitments on gender were added, including support for childcare access and gender-responsive fiscal policies, building on IDA19's gender strategy.
The Crisis Response Window was expanded to $3.3 billion, with higher limits for early response financing and contingent instruments like Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Options (CAT-DDOs).

quote.text: In response to the significant financing needs among IDA countries resulting from the COVID-19 crisis, donors agreed to frontload IDA19 resources... As the overall commitment authority of IDA19 was capped at $82 billion over three years... donors agreed to move the next replenishment, IDA’s 20th (IDA20), forward a year to permit sustained elevated financing levels... IDA19 further increased IDA’s ambition with almost $19 billion of support for FCV-affected countries... IDA20 will build on, and further enhance, IDA’s support for reducing gender inequality... IDA20 is expected to support implementation of the Bank’s 2021-25 Climate Change Action Plan, including its commitment to... align all its new support to Governments with the Paris Agreement by end-FY23.
quote.source: D0003947.odt, Need for IDA replenishment and Climate Change sections

co_funding_partners.partner: World Bank (via market borrowing and IBRD transfers)
co_funding_partners.leverage_description: Each £1 of donor support to IDA20 is expected to support more than £3 of additional financing through market borrowing and loan repayments.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: IDA20 is expected to provide $90-95 billion in total financing, with donor contributions of $25-29 billion (a multiple of ~3.3x). The UK's contribution of £1.531 billion thus supports approximately £4.5-5 billion in total IDA financing.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: IDA's financial model combines donor contributions (revenue) with market borrowing and loan repayments (capital-like instruments) to maximize leverage. The Deployable Strategic Capital ratio ensures financial sustainability by balancing equity, loan loss reserves, and risk-weighted credit exposures.

quote.text: IDA combines donor contributions with market borrowing, loan repayments, and transfers from the Bank’s arm for lending to middle-income countries... to deliver more than £3.37 for each £1 provided by donors... In FY20 the Bank’s total portfolio was estimated at $260 billion with operating costs of $2.7 billion or around 1% of the Bank’s total portfolio... The UK’s contribution would be expected to support IDA20 financing of $90-95bn... IDA planst to manage the use of this equity over time through the gradual reduction of its Deployable Strategic Capital ratio to zero by FY34.
quote.source: D0003947.odt, How UK support will be used and Economy sections

metadata.programme_name: UK-South Africa Partnership to Harness an inclusive Demographic Dividend in Africa
metadata.quote: "The purpose of this programme is to partner with South Africa to support African countries to design, fund implement and monitor National Frameworks that capture the economic benefits of a younger population." (D0007064.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: November 2021–October 2024 [Amended to March 2025 in March 2024] New programme end date (if applicable): 30 October 2025" (D0007064.odt, Detailed information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (channeling funds through the GBV-F Fund), capacity building (training, peer exchanges, and technical assistance), policy influence (supporting South Africa's leadership in regional demographic dividend frameworks), and service delivery (direct support to community-based organizations tackling GBV). It aims to strengthen demographic data systems, promote gender equality, and address gender-based violence through a mix of research, advocacy, and direct interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme has had two previous business case amendments: a cost extension in August 2022, following a successful first year performance of the Fund, evidence of lack of resources available for the sector and delays to establishment of the GBVF Council. A second amendment enabling a cost and time extension was approved in March 2024. This second amendment was to provide additional support to CBOs working in Mpumalanga province, in support of the ‘Just’ objectives of our Just Energy Transition Partnership." (D0007064.odt, Changes)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened national data systems and capacity to use disaggregated demographic and socio-economic data to tackle poverty and inequality
Collaboration within and between countries to build capacity and Community of Practice for the application of a demographic and gender lens
Strengthened coordination on Generation Equality Forum to accelerate the implementation of the Global Acceleration Plan
Accelerating economic justice and rights thereby improving resilience of women and girls
Tackling the scourge of GBV-F – including support to South Africa’s National Strategic Plan on GBV and Femicide
Support to 26 Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) across the country working to implement the National Strategic Plan on GBV-F
Refurbishment of two Thuthuzela Care Centres (TCCs) in KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape

Reach an estimated additional 129,482 individuals over a six-month period, of which 80,526 will be women and girls, 1,878 will be individuals living with a disability, and 2,100 will be individuals in the LGBT+ community
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to harness South Africa's experience and influence to support African countries in designing and implementing national frameworks for demographic dividends, with a strong focus on gender equality, women's empowerment, and tackling gender-based violence. It combines policy advocacy, capacity building, and direct service delivery through partnerships with UN agencies and local organizations.
what_objectives.quote: "The purpose of this programme is to partner with South Africa to support African countries to design, fund implement and monitor National Frameworks that capture the economic benefits of a younger population." (D0007064.odt, Programme Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a context with high levels of gender-based violence and economic inequality, but South Africa is not classified as a fragile or conflict-affected state. The overall programme risk rating is assessed as moderate.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (90000521.odt, Rationale)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: High levels of GBV and femicide create significant challenges for service delivery and community engagement. Political and institutional delays (e.g., establishment of the GBVF Council) affect programme planning and continuity. Limited resources and capacity in some regions constrain the ability to scale interventions effectively.
where_context.quote: "South Africa’s high rates of gender-based violence have been acknowledged by President Cyril Ramaphosa as a national crisis." (90000521.odt, Rationale)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Gender-Based Violence and Femicide Response Fund (GBV-F Fund)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The GBV-F Fund, a South African entity, leads the implementation and decision-making for the GBV component, with strategic guidance from a board that includes South African government representatives and civil society. The UK provides funding and technical support but does not direct operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and capacity building support to existing grant partners
capacity building for Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) and grassroots organisations
organisational development support for CBOs
safeguarding training for downstreampartners

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA South Africa
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for demographic data and analysis component

partner_organizations.name: UN Women
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for Generation Equality Forum commitments and GBV support

partner_organizations.name: Gender-Based Violence and Femicide Response Fund (GBV-F Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner for GBV interventions, including grants to CBOs and TCC refurbishment

partner_organizations.name: Department of Social Development (DSD) - National Population Unit
partner_organizations.role: Convenes advisory committee and provides strategic direction

partner_organizations.name: Department of Women, Youth and People with Disabilities (DWYPwD)
partner_organizations.role: Leads multi-sectoral response to promote gender equality and women’s empowerment

partner_organizations.name: Soul City Institute
partner_organizations.role: Grant management partner supporting CBOs in four provinces

partner_organizations.name: National Prosecuting Authority (NPA)
partner_organizations.role: Manages refurbishment of Thuthuzela Care Centres

who_partners.quote: "The Fund is a largely private sector led initiative which was originally set up as a temporary entity to support implementation of the National Strategic Plan on Gender Based Violence and Femicide (NSP), launched by the President in 2020, until the establishment of the National Council on GBVF." (D0004780.odt, Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with UN agencies (UNFPA and UN Women) and an Accountable Grant Agreement with the GBV-F Fund. Funds are pooled with other donors in the GBV-F Fund, which then disburses grants to CBOs and manages refurbishment projects.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The GBV-F Fund acts as a fund manager, disbursing grants to downstream partners (CBOs) and managing specific initiatives like TCC refurbishment. The UK's Human Development Team in the British High Commission (BHC) South Africa oversees the programme and maintains regular engagement with the Fund and other partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships and alignment with programme objectives. UNFPA and UN Women were chosen for their technical expertise and established programmes in South Africa, while the GBV-F Fund was selected as the primary mechanism for implementing South Africa’s National Strategic Plan on GBV and Femicide.
how_mechanism.quote: "We considered procuring a contractor to manage the programme but discarded that option for the following reasons: Using a private sector company would be more costly than working through the 3 proposed partners with overheads and management costs assessed to range between 10-15%." (90000521.odt, Contracting)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: The GBV-F Fund's Disbursement Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Committee recommends funding rounds to the main board for approval. The UK is involved in monitoring but does not directly approve sub-awards.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GBV-F Fund is governed by a board that includes representatives from the private sector, philanthropic foundations, and potentially government entities. The board delegates approval for funding initiatives to the Disbursement Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Committee, which recommends to the main board. The UK participates in advisory roles but does not have voting power.
how_governance.quote: "The Board had final approval for all funding initiatives delegated through the board committees. Approvals for funding rounds are completed by the Disbursement Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Committee who recommend to the main board for approval." (D0004780.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with agreement from partners, as demonstrated by the multiple cost extensions and shifts in budget allocations (e.g., increased support to the GBV-F Fund). However, significant changes require approval from the UK and alignment with programme objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has demonstrated adaptive management through multiple amendments to respond to emerging needs, such as increased GBV during COVID-19 and the Just Energy Transition priorities in Mpumalanga. Adjustments require approval from the UK and alignment with the overall theory of change.
how_flexibility.quote: "The funding arrangements are flexible enough to accommodate variances to forecast spend within and between different components if needed." (90000521.odt, Budget and Cost Drivers)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GBV-F Fund (implementing partner) → Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) and Thuthuzela Care Centres (end beneficiaries)
how_efficiency.quote: "Management costs will be kept below 10% and are expected to reduce to 5% as a result of pro-bono support pledged by 11 companies." (90000521.odt, Contracting)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rely on other actors working on demographic dividend in Africa)
Rely on existing UK investment to engage South Africa (e.g., Women’s Integrated Sexual Health programme, What Works to Prevent Violence Against Women)
Design a bespoke programme (chosen option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The bespoke programme was selected to leverage South Africa’s unique expertise and regional influence systematically, rather than through ad-hoc engagements. It allows the UK to deploy financial, diplomatic, and technical resources strategically to strengthen the UK-South Africa partnership and support South Africa’s role in the region through South-South and trilateral cooperation. This approach complements existing UK-funded initiatives by bringing South Africa’s expertise into regional or bilateral opportunities in a coordinated manner.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of the GBV-F Fund due to over-reliance on UK funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Fund is working to diversify its donor base, including pursuing funding from private sector organizations and international philanthropic foundations. The UK facilitates private sector roundtables and raises the Fund’s profile to attract additional partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk if safeguarding issues are not adequately addressed
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced Safeguarding Due Diligence Assessment by BHC South Africa and regular monitoring of safeguarding practices by the Fund, including training for downstream partners.

why_rationale.quote: "By channelling resources through the UN and GBV Fund in South Africa, the UK will be able to enhance and influence existing efforts. By supporting a combination of South Africa’s policy and operational activities and practical action on the ground, the UK will be able to engage strategically in policy discussions and also have a direct impact on people affected by GBV." (90000521.odt, Option 3: Bespoke development diplomacy programme)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high levels of gender-based violence and institutional delays in South Africa necessitate partnerships with local organizations that have deep community roots and trust, such as the GBV-F Fund and CBOs. The political and social context also requires alignment with South African government priorities, limiting the pool of potential partners to those already engaged in the National Strategic Plan on GBV and Femicide.
q27_constraints_detail: high GBV rates require trusted local partners
delays in establishing the GBVF Council extend reliance on the GBV-F Fund
need for alignment with South African government priorities limits partner options
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s focus on tackling GBV and promoting gender equality requires a delivery structure that can reach grassroots organizations and survivors directly. This necessitates a fund manager model (GBV-F Fund) to disburse small grants to CBOs and manage localized interventions like TCC refurbishments, rather than a centralized or top-down approach.
q28_linkages: Direct service delivery to GBV survivors → requires local CBOs and TCCs as partners
Policy influence at regional level → requires partnership with South African government and UN agencies
Capacity building for CBOs → requires embedded support through partners like Soul City Institute
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., reaching marginalized groups like people with disabilities and LGBT+ individuals) with efficiency (e.g., using the GBV-F Fund as a single fund manager to reduce administrative overhead). The focus on Mpumalanga province, while strategic for the Just Energy Transition, also reflects a trade-off between targeted impact and broader geographic coverage.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: targeted support in Mpumalanga vs. national coverage
inclusive reach (disability, LGBT+) vs. administrative complexity
local ownership (CBO-led interventions) vs. speed of delivery
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of the programme (e.g., safeguarding, financial risks) has led to quarterly oversight and embedded safeguarding measures, rather than a light-touch approach. The UK’s significant financial contribution (initially 40% of the GBV-F Fund’s budget) also increases the intensity of monitoring to ensure accountability.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with partners like Soul City Institute explicitly tasked with providing organisational development support to CBOs. This shapes the roles of implementing partners, who must balance service delivery with strengthening the capacity of local organisations to sustain interventions beyond the programme lifetime.
intersections.quote: "The Fund is working to enable an accessible ecosystem of support services for victims of GBV within the province given there is currently only one shelter in Mpumalanga." (D0004780.odt, Objective of the cost extension)

key_programme_risks: Safeguarding and reputational risk if issues are not integrated or followed through (Moderate likelihood, High impact)
Misappropriation of funds or fraud (Moderate likelihood, High impact)
Delays in delivery and spend due to domestic political priorities (Moderate likelihood, Moderate impact)
Sustainability of the GBV-F Fund due to over-reliance on UK funding (Moderate likelihood, High impact)
Uncoordinated response among stakeholders (Moderate likelihood, Moderate impact)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Enhanced Safeguarding Due Diligence Assessment by BHC South Africa; regular safeguarding training for downstream partners.
Due diligence assessments on UNFPA, UN Women, and GBV-F Fund; partners to provide BHC financial and audit reports; no funds spent through government.
Programme team to work closely with partners to ensure a credible pipeline of activities; dedicate sufficient advisory and management resources.
Fund is diversifying its donor base, including pursuing private sector and philanthropic funding; UK facilitates roundtables and advocacy to attract new partners.
Regular coordination meetings among partners (DSD, UNFPA, UN Women, GBV-F Fund, BHC) and alignment with national strategies like the NSP on GBV-F.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme built on South Africa’s existing experience in demographic analysis and GBV response, as well as lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, which highlighted the need for robust data systems and adaptive programming. The success of the GBV-F Fund in its first year (scoring A+ in FCDO Annual Review) demonstrated the effectiveness of pooling resources and leveraging local expertise.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme was extended and refocused to address emerging needs, such as the impact of the Just Energy Transition on GBV in Mpumalanga and the delayed establishment of the GBVF Council. Additional funding was allocated to support CBOs in crisis and refurbish TCCs, based on monitoring data and partner feedback.
risks_lessons.quote: "The Fund has a strong track record in delivery, with this component scoring an A+ in the last FCDO Annual Review." (D0004780.odt, Implementation)

co_funding_partners.partner: Private sector organizations (e.g., FirstRand Foundation, Absa)
International philanthropic foundations (e.g., Gates Foundation, Ford Foundation)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The GBV-F Fund has developed a pipeline of funding for 2024 from major donors, including private sector and philanthropic foundations, to reduce reliance on UK funding. Pro-bono services (e.g., Deloitte for audit, ENS for legal services) also reduce overhead costs.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both revenue spending (grants to CBOs, operational costs) and capital spending (refurbishment of Thuthuzela Care Centres).
financial_details.quote: "The UK is the only bilateral Government donor and currently comprises 36% of overall support, with the remaining support being from private sector organisations and international philanthropic foundations." (D0004780.odt, Approach to Implementation)

metadata.programme_name: Effective Governance for Economic Development (EGED) in Central Asia
metadata.quote: The programme will provide £25m over five years to improve economic policy performance in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan by embedding evidence-informed processes into government reform planning and implementation. (Document: 59933417.odt, Intervention Summary)
metadata.duration_source: The programme will provide £25m over five years to improve economic policy performance in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan by embedding evidence-informed processes into government reform planning and implementation.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: EGED aims to improve the effectiveness, accountability, and transparency of economic policy delivery in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan through two pillars: 1) supporting evidence-informed design and delivery of economic policies, and 2) strengthening civil society to hold governments accountable. The programme combines capacity building, policy influence, and implementation research.
what_objectives.q1_source: EGED will improve the effectiveness, accountability and transparency of economic policy delivery on selected reform priorities in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan through two pillars: Supporting effective, evidence informed design and delivery of economic policies. [...] Strengthening civil society to hold the governments of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to account on the specific issues selected under pillar one, through improved use of data. (Document: 59933417.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened evidence and coordination processes, practices, and capabilities within government (Pillar 1)
Improved performance on selected economic development/reform policies (Pillar 1)
Enhanced capacity of civil society to hold government to account (Pillar 2)
Increased public sector revenue generated as a result of better planning and monitoring
Improved evidence use in policymaking
Improved quality of engagement between government and civil society
Support for up to 15 economic reforms (selected during inception and implementation)
Digitalised monitoring system for the tourism sector in Tajikistan
Citizen-led data dashboards scrutinising reform progress in Uzbekistan
what_objectives.summary: EGED is a strategic, long-term programme designed to embed evidence-informed policy processes in Central Asian governments and strengthen civil society's role in holding governments accountable for economic reforms. It focuses on improving governance for economic development by addressing both supply-side (government capacity) and demand-side (civil society engagement) constraints.
what_objectives.quote: EGED will deliver two pillars: Supporting more effective, evidence-informed design and delivery of economic policies. [...] Strengthening civil society (including media, non-governmental organisations, think tanks, business associations, and others) to hold the governments of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to account on the specific issues selected under pillar one, through improved use of data and evidence. (Document: 59933417.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is 'major,' reflecting political economy constraints such as corruption, patronage, and weak rule of law in all three countries. The region is described as fragile, with significant risks for stability and prosperity, including external influences and economic reversals.
where_context.q5_source: The programme’s overall level of risk is major, which is within DFID Central Asia’s risk appetite. (Document: 59933417.odt, Risk section)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited capacity, high staff turnover, poor coordination)
data limitations (poor data quality, limited analytical skills)
regulatory (ineffective policy implementation, lack of transparency)
civil society constraints (weak platforms, limited independence, shrinking space)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy constraints and weak institutions hinder effective policy implementation and civil society engagement. For example, in Tajikistan, high staff turnover and patronage-based recruitment limit policy coordination, while in Uzbekistan, rapid reforms are constrained by capacity gaps and coordination challenges. Civil society in all three countries faces restrictions, with limited space for independent voices and weak platforms for engagement.
where_context.quote: Political economy constraints (vested interests, patronage, corruption) and limited capacity of government and civil society. [...] In Tajikistan, capacity and political economy constraints hinder more inclusive and sustainable economic development. [...] In Uzbekistan, major implementation, coordination and prioritisation challenges risk reversals in the mid-term. (Document: 59933417.odt, Why? Overall context and problem analysis)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: DFID/FCDO retains decision-making authority, with implementing partners (including multilateral and international NGOs) delivering activities under contractual agreements. Local civil society and government actors are engaged as beneficiaries and collaborators but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and mentoring for government and civil society
embedded advisory resources at the centre of government
support for evidence uptake and coordination mechanisms
institutional strengthening for civil society platforms

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Implement activities with the centre of government and line ministries (Pillar 1)

partner_organizations.name: International NGO or multilateral (TBD)
partner_organizations.role: Civil society capacity building (Pillar 2)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector supplier
partner_organizations.role: Cross-country learning, coordination, and logistics

partner_organizations.name: Government Partnerships International (GPI)
partner_organizations.role: Embed HMG expertise on evidence-based policymaking at the centre of government

who_partners.quote: The programme will be delivered by three different suppliers, including the World Bank who will implement activities with the centre of government and line ministries, an international non-governmental organisation or multilateral responsible for civil society capacity building, and a private sector supplier supporting cross-country learning, coordination and logistics. (Document: 59933417.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID will contract multiple suppliers (World Bank, INGO/multilateral, and private sector) to deliver distinct components of the programme. Funds will be managed by these suppliers, with payments likely tied to milestones or deliverables.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will be delivered through a structured consortium of three cross-country partners: one for Pillar 1 (government support), one for Pillar 2 (civil society), and a third for logistics/coordination. This model ensures coherence across countries while allowing flexibility for country-specific adaptation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection was based on a rigorous appraisal of three delivery models, with Option 3 (cross-country partners) chosen for its balance of context specificity, cost efficiency, effectiveness, and flexibility. Partners were selected based on their regional presence, expertise, and ability to deliver tailored activities in each country.
how_mechanism.quote: Option 3. EGED is delivered through cross-country partners (preferred). [...] This option would allow DFID to have the expertise and context specificity required as it would work only with partners with a presence and expertise on the ground in each of the countries. (Document: 59933417.odt, Appraisal case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A steering committee will ensure expertise from relevant stakeholders continuously feeds into delivery. The committee will include DFID representatives and likely partners, focusing on oversight and strategic direction.
how_governance.quote: A steering committee will ensure expertise from relevant stakeholders will continuously feed into delivery. (Document: 59933417.odt, SRO and team capability)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between countries in case of limited tractability in one country or changes in UK priorities. The issue-based approach also allows for flexibility within countries to respond to emerging needs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme will select up to 6 reform issues during inception and up to 9 during implementation, based on emerging evidence and analysis. This allows for continuous adaptation to political and contextual changes.
how_flexibility.quote: EGED will deliver improved performance on 15 selected economic policy issues, however, these are not defined upfront but will be selected during inception (up to 6 reform issues) and throughout implementation (up to 9 reform issues) based on emerging evidence and analysis, allowing for continuous adaptation. (Document: 59933417.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (Pillar 1, Pillar 2, and logistics/coordination). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned, suggesting a two-layer structure.
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will be delivered by three different suppliers, including the World Bank [...] and a private sector supplier supporting cross-country learning, coordination and logistics. (Document: 59933417.odt, Intervention Summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: EGED delivered by one fund manager (not recommended due to limited context specificity and high costs)
Option 2: EGED delivered through country-specific implementing partners (not recommended due to high management burden and limited cross-country learning)
Option 3: EGED delivered through cross-country partners (preferred for its balance of expertise, cost efficiency, and flexibility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its ability to balance context specificity, cost efficiency, effectiveness, and flexibility. It allows DFID to work with partners experienced in all three countries, reducing management burden while fostering cross-country learning and coherence. The model also mitigates risks by enabling fund reallocation and adaptive issue selection.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (flexibility to reallocate funds and adapt to political changes)
flexibility (adaptive issue selection and cross-country learning)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited coherence between Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 partners in each country
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Requirements for cross-pillar coordination will be incorporated into contractual agreements, and capacity building will support constructive engagement between government and civil society.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management burden for DFID if partners do not work effectively together
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The third-party logistics/coordination partner will streamline corporate and compliance requirements and facilitate learning across countries.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (low administrative burden and overhead costs)
efficiency (effective use of staff time and resources)
effectiveness (coherence, political economy analysis, and learning)
flexibility (adaptability to political shifts and emerging needs)
why_rationale.quote: Option 3. EGED is delivered through cross-country partners (preferred). [...] This option would allow DFID to have the expertise and context specificity required as it would work only with partners with a presence and expertise on the ground in each of the countries. [...] This option would allow relocation of funds between countries in case of political shifts in any of the three or change of UK priorities. (Document: 59933417.odt, Appraisal case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy and institutional constraints in Central Asia limit the pool of potential partners. For example, weak civil society platforms and government-controlled NGOs in Uzbekistan require partners with specific expertise in navigating state-dominated spaces. Similarly, patronage and corruption in all three countries necessitate partners skilled in politically smart, adaptive approaches.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited independent civil society in Uzbekistan (mostly government-owned NGOs)
High staff turnover and patronage in Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan
Need for partners experienced in evidence-informed policymaking (a niche area in the region)
Requirements for cross-country presence and regional expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's focus on evidence-informed policymaking and civil society accountability requires a delivery structure that can integrate government and civil society actors around specific policy issues. This necessitates cross-country partners with expertise in both pillars, as well as a mechanism for coordination and learning across countries.
q28_linkages: Issue-based approach (WHAT) → Requires partners operating in all three countries (HOW) to ensure coherence and learning
Focus on embedding tools/processes (WHAT) → Needs long-term, embedded advisory support (HOW) for sustainability
Civil society engagement (WHAT) → Requires partners with experience in constructive government-CSO platforms (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between inclusive partnerships and efficient delivery. For example, while Option 2 (country-specific partners) would allow for highly tailored approaches, it was rejected due to the high management burden and limited cross-country learning. Option 3 balances these trade-offs by using cross-country partners with regional expertise, reducing administrative costs while maintaining context specificity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid delivery (e.g., through a single fund manager) would limit local ownership and adaptability
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern partners bring technical expertise but may reduce Southern decision-making power
Cost vs. reach: Fewer partners (Option 3) reduce overheads but require careful selection to ensure regional coverage
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'major' risk profile of the programme drives the need for intensive oversight, including a steering committee and milestone-based management. The adaptive, issue-based approach also reflects the high-risk context, allowing for quick adjustments if political will shifts or reforms stall.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include embedded advisory support for governments and targeted training for civil society. For example, the World Bank's role in Pillar 1 includes building government capacity to use evidence, while Pillar 2 partners focus on strengthening civil society's ability to engage with government.
intersections.quote: The programme’s overall level of risk is major, which is within DFID Central Asia’s risk appetite. [...] EGED’s delivery model is underpinned by flexibility and adaptability within and across countries. [...] The issue-based approach will help ensure that successful interventions can be scaled up while entry points that prove less effective will be closed down swiftly. (Document: 59933417.odt, Risk and Flexibility sections)

key_programme_risks: Limited political will for economic reforms post-2020, risking reversals
Weak coordination between government institutions and civil society
High staff turnover in line ministries (e.g., up to 40% in Tajikistan)
Shrinking space for civil society, particularly in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan
Risk of funds being diverted due to corruption or patronage networks
Limited capacity of civil society to effectively use data for advocacy
Potential resistance from vested interests (e.g., business elites) to reforms
Uncertainty about the sustainability of reforms beyond the programme lifetime

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Issue-based approach allows for adaptive selection of reform priorities based on emerging political opportunities. The programme will focus on less politicised entry points (e.g., data and evidence use).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Weak coordination between government and civil society
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Cross-pillar coordination requirements in partner contracts and capacity building for constructive engagement. Existing platforms (e.g., Open Government Partnership in Kyrgyzstan) will be leveraged.
Embedded advisory resources and longer-term capacity building for 'islands of effectiveness' at the centre of government.
Focus on government-funded or semi-independent platforms (e.g., GONGOs in Uzbekistan) and digital tools for oversight where traditional engagement is restricted.
Funds managed by contracted suppliers with milestone-based payments and arrears mechanisms to reduce diversion risks.
Targeted capacity building for civil society on data use, advocacy, and engagement with government, including mentorship and training.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from DFID's Public Sector Reform programme in Kyrgyzstan highlight the need for politically smart, adaptive approaches that align with elite incentives.
Experience from Tajikistan's PFM project shows that opening state budgets to the public only strengthens accountability when civil society has integrated platforms for feedback.
The programme builds on the 'islands of effectiveness' approach, focusing on embedding reforms in parts of government where there is buy-in (e.g., centre of government in Uzbekistan).
Digital tools are emphasised as a way to navigate restrictions on traditional civil society engagement, particularly in Uzbekistan.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous governance programmes in Central Asia (e.g., Kyrgyz Public Sector Reform, Tajik Public Financial Management) had limited success due to a focus on formal/legal changes without addressing underlying political economy constraints. EGED adopts a problem-driven, iterative approach (PDIA) to avoid these pitfalls, focusing on pragmatic entry points like data use that are less politicised.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates flexibility to select reform issues during inception and implementation, based on emerging evidence. This adaptive approach was included to respond to lessons about the unpredictability of reform traction in FCAS contexts. The cross-country partner model was also chosen to facilitate learning across contexts, addressing past issues with isolated country programmes.
risks_lessons.quote: Traditional good governance approaches to address corruption and poor policymaking have had limited success in Central Asia due to political economy constraints [...] EGED will embed ongoing, context-specific political economy analysis and a focus on pragmatic entry points in all three countries. [...] The programme is underpinned by focusing on ensuring the governments’ response to citizen needs is both transparent and inclusive. (Document: 59933417.odt, How? Evidence, lessons learnt and principles for EGED)

financial_details.quote: Programme Value: £25m (Document: 59933417.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: Syria Independent Monitoring 2 (SIM2)

quote.programme_name: "Syria Independent Monitoring 2" (52126037.odt, Title section)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £16,180,000" (52126037.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.duration: "Start Date: 01/03/2020", "End Date: 28/02/2025" (52126037.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.sector: "humanitarian" (context: Syria crisis, 11.1 million in need, 52126037.odt, A: Context and need for intervention)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides independent third-party monitoring of DFID-funded projects in Syria to verify results and ensure accountability. It combines verification (service delivery oversight) with lesson learning (implementation research) to improve programme quality. The focus is on both operational oversight (accountability) and generating evidence for strategic improvements (evidence generation).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The purpose of this project is to provide independent third-party monitoring of DFID-funded projects in Syria and to verify results reported by implementing partners." quote.objectives: "The purpose of this project is to provide independent third-party monitoring of DFID-funded projects in Syria and to verify results reported by implementing partners... helping us to drive up the quality of projects and contributing to greater accountability." (52126037.odt, Programme summary)
