where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Syria is classified as a fragile and conflict-affected state (FCAS) with "fractured governance structures and ongoing conflict," ranked 178/180 on Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index. DFID’s overall risk is rated as "severe" due to context, fiduciary risks, and complex delivery chains.
where_context.q5_source: "Syria is a fragile country with fractured governance structures and ongoing conflict. It is rated as highly corrupt and ranked 178 of 180 countries in Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index." AND "Overall programme risk rating: Severe" (52126037.odt, F: Risk, Conflict and Fragility)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks prevent DFID in-country presence, requiring remote management. Conflict and access restrictions limit direct oversight, creating reliance on down-stream partners. Corruption and weak institutions increase fiduciary risks (e.g., aid diversion). Counter-terrorism legislation adds compliance burdens. Data limitations hinder verification, necessitating independent monitoring.

quote.constraints: "Due to security risks and lack of access, DFID has no presence in Syria and our staff are unable to directly monitor projects... Consequently, there is limited reliable independent information about the projects we fund." (52126037.odt, A: Context and need for intervention)
quote.impact: "DFID has no presence in Syria and our staff are unable to directly monitor projects. Our staff manage projects remotely from the UK and Lebanon and rely on partner reporting... However, most of these implementing partners also manage their projects remotely, relying on their own ‘downstream partners’ to keep oversight of projects." (52126037.odt, A: Context and need for intervention)

technical support to implementing partners on M&E systems via assessments and recommendations

quote.structure: "One supplier (with use of downstream suppliers if required)." (52126037.odt, Option D description)

AND "SIM2 will assess the extent to which DFID’s implementing partners deliver an inclusive humanitarian response... and are Accountable to Affected Populations (AAP)." (52126037.odt, Activity descriptions)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID will award a commercial contract to a single supplier via the IMPERFA framework (fees-and-expenses model). Payments are tied to deliverables (e.g., timely, high-quality reports) with KPIs and break clauses. The contract covers all monitoring activities, including field visits, assessments, and potential M&E platform development.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: DFID Syria team manages the contract directly with one prime supplier, who may subcontract specialized tasks (e.g., field monitors, technical assessments). The supplier reports to DFID’s M&E team, with no consortium or platform structures.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: 3:1 (3 pre-vetted suppliers on IMPERFA MENA lot)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The IMPERFA framework was chosen to avoid gaps in monitoring coverage (current contract expires March 2020) and to leverage pre-vetted suppliers with regional experience. A mini-competition among framework suppliers ensures compliance with EU procurement rules while accelerating the selection process (12 weeks vs. 12-18 months for open tender).

quote.instrument: "The IMPERFA framework is the selected route to market for all monitoring and evaluation contracts for DFID... The cost model in the framework is a fees and expenses model." (52126037.odt, RoutetoMarket)
quote.selection: "The IMPERFA framework is the selected route to market to provide us with independent monitoring for phase one of the programme... It is DFID’s preferred route to market for independent monitoring services." AND "A robust terms of reference (ToR) is being drafted, in readiness for approval of the business case. Given the value of the contract, the process will take the form of a mini-competition between suppliers listed on the framework." (52126037.odt, RoutetoMarket)

quote.management: "DFID Syria will have a holistic oversight of how effective delivery of aid is... Field reports will be used to inform programming decisions in the future." (52126037.odt, Option D advantages)
quote.oversight: "The commercial structure of the contract... will be structured to ensure payment and performance is managed on the basis of deliverables received (e.g. timeliness and quality reports) through robust Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)." AND "Outputs will be tracked through the log frame to ensure quality and quantity of reports are being received as expected." (52126037.odt, RoutetoMarket)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activity types (e.g., more field visits vs. contextual analysis) with DFID approval, but the contract’s fees-and-expenses model limits flexibility compared to output-based contracts. Break clauses allow adjustments if supplier performance is inadequate.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a phased approach (Option D for Years 1-2, Option E for Years 3-5) to allow adjustments based on portfolio evolution. Annual reviews and quarterly KPI assessments enable adaptive management, though major changes (e.g., adding an M&E platform) require re-tendering.

quote.flexibility: "Appropriate break or cancellation clauses will be included in the contract terms to ensure that the team have adequate flexibility to adapt or make changes as required." (52126037.odt, RoutetoMarket)
quote.adaptive: "As we don’t yet know what the future DFID Syria portfolio will look like... it is too early to determine if an M&E system for reporting (Option E) is actually required... For these reasons, we recommend that we pursue Option D in the first two to three years... and Option E in years three to five." (52126037.odt, Evaluation of Options)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Prime Supplier (IMPERFA contractor) → Field Monitors/Subcontractors (no additional layers to end beneficiaries)

quote.layers: "One supplier (with use of downstream suppliers if required)." (52126037.odt, Option D description)
quote.payment: "The commercial structure of the contract... will be structured to ensure payment and performance is managed on the basis of deliverables received (e.g. timeliness and quality reports)." (52126037.odt, RoutetoMarket)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No independent monitoring; rely solely on partner reporting.
Focus solely on verifying aid delivery (e.g., call centres, satellite imagery) without learning components.
Field visits combining verification and lesson learning, but without higher-level analyses.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: D: Accountability + lesson learning + improved programming (selected)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Field visits, lessons learned summaries, operational/contextual analyses, M&E/AAP assessments.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: E: Option D + interactive M&E platform
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Adds a digital platform for real-time monitoring (deferred to Years 3-5).
Payments-by-results (PbR) with full verification + strategic evaluation.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option D was selected for its balance of accountability (verification), strategic learning (lessons/analyses), and programme improvement (AAP/inclusion assessments) at a cost (£3.3M/year) deemed proportional to DFID Syria’s portfolio (1.8% of budget). It addresses ICAI’s 2018 recommendation for higher verification standards while mitigating risks in a high-fragility context. The phased approach (D → E) allows adaptation as the portfolio evolves.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (1.8% of budget vs. 2% industry standard for M&E)
risk mitigation (FCAS context requires intensive oversight)
past experience (current monitoring contract improved portfolio quality)
partner capacity (pre-vetted IMPERFA suppliers reduce procurement risks)
speed (12-week mini-competition vs. 12-18 months for open tender)
equity (inclusion/AAP assessments align with Public Sector Equality Duty)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier technical capabilities may not meet DFID’s inclusion/AAP assessment requirements.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit ToR requirements and mini-competition evaluation (60% technical, 40% commercial). Prime suppliers directed to engage sub-contractors (including incumbent) if gaps exist.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fees-and-expenses model may incentivize delays (suppliers paid for work performed, not outputs).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust KPIs for timeliness/quality, quarterly performance reviews, and break clauses.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Syria’s unique context may challenge framework suppliers accustomed to other MENA countries.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Incumbent supplier available as sub-contractor; supplier liaison with framework Lot sub-contractors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential monitoring gap during transition (current contract ends March 2020).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased approach with IMPERFA’s 12-week timeline; contingency for interim supplier if needed.

quote.why_chosen: "Option D (Accountability, lesson learning and improved programming) and Option E (Option D + Interactive M&E system for reporting) are the options that will give DFID greater assurance of projects in Syria and best value for money... Option D provides... a more holistic perspective on Syria." (52126037.odt, Evaluation of Options)
quote.vfm: "Overall, the project represents good value for money because it provides DFID Syria with the assurance that the projects we fund are being undertaken (including to a sufficient quality) reducing risks related to the implementation of projects in an operating environment where DFID staff are unable to pursue their own checks." (52126037.odt, Value for Money)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Syria’s FCAS context severely limits partner selection: (1) Security risks prevent in-country presence, requiring remote management and reliance on local field monitors; (2) Corruption and weak institutions necessitate pre-vetted suppliers (IMPERFA framework) to mitigate fiduciary risks; (3) Counter-terrorism legislation restricts partner types (e.g., UN/NGOs with compliance systems). Only organizations with existing regional networks and risk management protocols (e.g., IMPERFA suppliers) are viable.
q27_constraints_detail: No DFID in-country staff → reliance on third-party monitors
High corruption (178/180 CPI) → pre-vetted suppliers mandatory
Ongoing conflict → field monitors must have Syrian access/language skills
Sanctions/CTF laws → partners must comply with UK legislation
Data limitations → need for primary data collection via field visits
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **both verification (accountability) and strategic learning (quality improvement)** drives the mixed delivery structure: (1) **Field visits** address the lack of ‘eyes on the ground’ (WHAT: verification need → HOW: local monitors); (2) **Lessons learned summaries** respond to ICAI’s call for portfolio-level insights (WHAT: evidence generation → HOW: centralized analysis); (3) **AAP/Inclusion assessments** reflect DFID’s equity goals (WHAT: inclusive programming → HOW: specialized assessments). The phased approach (D → E) mirrors the uncertainty in Syria’s future portfolio (WHAT: adaptive needs → HOW: flexible contracting).

q28_linkages.objective: Verify aid delivery in high-risk FCAS
q28_linkages.mechanism: Field monitoring visits by local contractors (not DFID staff)
Quarterly visits + cross-cutting lessons learned summaries
Mandatory AAP/Inclusion assessments in all visits
Phased contracting (D → E) with break clauses

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions are discussed between: (1) **Inclusion vs. Speed**: AAP/inclusion assessments (equity) require more time/resources than verification-only visits (efficiency), but are deemed critical for PSED compliance; (2) **Local ownership vs. Risk mitigation**: While Syrian field monitors enable access, DFID retains all decision-making (Northern-led) to ensure accountability; (3) **Cost vs. Reach**: Interactive M&E platforms (Option E) could improve efficiency but reduce funds for field visits (direct oversight). The business case justifies these trade-offs by prioritizing equity (PSED) and risk management (FCAS) over pure cost efficiency.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Inclusion assessments increase visit complexity (3-day visits with beneficiary/non-beneficiary interviews) vs. faster verification methods (e.g., call centres).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Prioritized inclusion to meet PSED obligations, accepting higher costs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern-led management (DFID control) vs. Southern implementation (local monitors).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Hybrid model: DFID designs/oversees; locals execute fieldwork.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Fees-and-expenses model (IMPERFA) may cost more than output-based contracts but reduces procurement delays.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Accepted higher costs for speed and pre-vetted suppliers.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘severe’ risk rating** (FCAS + corruption) directly shapes the **intensive oversight** model: (1) **No in-country presence** → requires embedded field monitors with real-time reporting; (2) **High fiduciary risks** → mandates quarterly visits (vs. annual) and financial spot checks; (3) **Aid diversion risks** → adds verification layers (beneficiary interviews, document checks). The management intensity (KPIs, break clauses) is explicitly tied to risk mitigation.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded but **asymmetric**: (1) **Field monitors** receive training on inclusion/AAP standards to improve data collection (capacity input → better outputs); (2) **Implementing partners** get M&E assessments/recommendations but no decision-making role (capacity for compliance, not leadership); (3) **DFID staff** use monitoring findings to ‘inform decisions’ (capacity to adapt), while partners ‘implement recommendations’ (capacity to execute).

(52126037.odt, A: Context and RoutetoMarket)

We will require the independent monitoring supplier... to have the technical expertise to conduct robust inclusion assessments." (52126037.odt, D: Gender Equality and Disability Inclusion)

DFID’s overall risk in Syria is severe due to the context, fiduciary risks in a corruption prone country, and due to the complex technical nature of programming." (52126037.odt, F: Risk, Conflict and Fragility)

(52126037.odt, Activity descriptions)

key_programme_risks: Aid diversion or misuse in corrupt/conflict environment (FCAS risk).
Inability to verify partner reporting due to access restrictions.
Supplier failure to meet technical standards (especially inclusion/AAP).
Monitoring gaps during contract transitions (March 2020 expiry).
Resistance from implementing partners to independent oversight.
Over-reliance on downstream partners with unknown capacities.
Data quality issues from field monitors in high-pressure environments.
Equity trade-offs (e.g., excluding hard-to-reach groups due to security).
Cost overruns with fees-and-expenses model vs. output-based contracts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Quarterly field visits with beneficiary interviews, document verification, and financial spot checks. Supplier must assess and report on diversion risks.
Explicit ToR requirements; mini-competition evaluates technical capacity (60% weight). Incumbent supplier available as sub-contractor.
Phased approach with IMPERFA’s 12-week timeline; contingency for interim supplier if needed.
DFID retains control over visit scheduling and report dissemination. KPIs include partner satisfaction rates.
Training on inclusion standards; cross-checking with multiple sources (beneficiaries, non-beneficiaries, documents).
Mandatory sampling of non-beneficiaries and acute-need groups; interviews without downstream partners present.

fcas_specific_lessons: Independent monitoring is critical in FCAS where **‘no in-country presence’** exists (Syria lesson since 2016).
**Downstream partner risks** require direct verification (not just prime partner reporting).
**Corruption contexts** necessitate financial spot checks and beneficiary confirmation.
**Conflict dynamics** demand flexible visit planning (adjust locations/sectors based on access).
**Inclusion is harder in FCAS**—explicit barriers assessment (physical, institutional, attitudinal) is needed.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2016–2020 monitoring contract demonstrated that: (1) **Verification improves quality**: "Independent monitoring reports... have allowed DFID to evaluate performance... and challenge partners where evidence suggests improvements." (2) **Lessons drive change**: Findings were used to stop underperforming activities. (3) **FCAS adaptations are needed**: Shifted to 3-day learning+verification visits in 2018 per ICAI recommendations. (4) **Inclusion gaps exist**: Current contract lacked robust inclusion/AAP assessments, prompting SIM2’s expanded scope.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: (1) Added **inclusion/AAP assessments** as core activities (addressing 2016–2020 limitations). (2) Increased visit frequency to **quarterly** (from ICAI’s recommendation). (3) Expanded **non-beneficiary interviews** to assess equity. (4) Phased approach (D → E) to allow **adaptive management** as portfolio evolves. (5) **Explicit barriers assessment** (beyond physical access) for disability/gender inclusion.

quote.risks: "DFID’s overall risk in Syria is severe due to the context, fiduciary risks in a corruption prone country, and due to the complex technical nature of programming that includes long delivery chains and lack of access to the ground for both DFID and most of our implementing partners." (52126037.odt, F: Risk, Conflict and Fragility)
quote.lessons: "The current model has adapted to changing needs of the context in Syria and DFID users... Lessons learned are used as an opportunity to improve project delivery and this has had an obvious impact on the overall quality of our portfolio." (52126037.odt, Appraisal of Current Independent Monitoring Contract)

metadata.programme_name: Nepal in Business (NIB)
metadata.quote: The primary goal of Nepal in Business (NIB) is to unlock economic prosperity by generating growth, expanding businesses, and addressing income poverty in Nepal. (D0004649.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: FY2023/24", "End Date: FY2030/31" (D0004649.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: NIB combines financing mechanisms (providing returnable capital to SMEs) with capacity building (strengthening SME management and productivity) and policy influence (partnering with government to improve the business environment). It also includes elements of service delivery through technical assistance and market shaping.
what_objectives.q1_source: "NIB will provide financing and support to strengthen companies’ management, operations, productivity, and competitiveness, to enable them to grow and create jobs." and "It will partner with government to create a more conducive business environment in Nepal, delivering the reforms that matter to improve the ease of business and crowd-in private finance." (D0004649.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Support and finance 40,000+ microenterprises (based on predecessor A2F programme)
Create 600+ direct and indirect jobs (based on predecessor A2F programme)
Improve economic empowerment for women and disadvantaged groups
Generate a pipeline of projects for British International Investment (BII) to invest in
Support SMEs across Nepal, including in disadvantaged regions
Promote inclusive business models prioritizing jobs for women and disadvantaged groups
Scale green business practices in renewable energy and other sectors
Strengthen the SME financing ecosystem by filling gaps in concessional funding
Improve the ease of doing business through policy reforms
what_objectives.summary: NIB aims to unlock economic prosperity in Nepal by financing and strengthening SMEs, improving the business environment, and promoting inclusive, green growth through a mix of financing, capacity building, and policy reform.
what_objectives.quote: "NIB will help Nepal to crowd in private finance to grow a secure, open, and thriving economy. NIB complements and will support British Investment Partnerships, generating a pipeline of projects for BII to invest in." (D0004649.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal faces political instability (nine changes in prime ministers in the last decade), weak institutions, and vulnerability to climate change. The programme is rated as 'Major' risk, indicating significant challenges to delivery.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0004649.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet) and "Political instability is consistently identified as the most binding constraint to private sector investment in Nepal... Nepal has had nine changes in prime ministers in the last decade." (D0004649.odt, Political and Institutional Appraisal)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (frequent government changes, elite domination)
infrastructure (unreliable energy, poor roads, limited all-weather access)
climate risks (vulnerability to climate change, energy supply disruptions)
data limitations (lack of updated economic data in some sectors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political instability and weak institutions create policy uncertainty and delay reforms. Poor infrastructure increases business costs (e.g., 28% higher shipping costs than regional peers). Regulatory barriers limit FDI and private sector growth. Social norms and anti-competitive practices exclude women and disadvantaged groups from economic opportunities.
where_context.quote: "Nepal’s ease of ‘doing business’ score improved from 110 to 94 out of 190 countries in the World Bank Index for 2020, however, substantial institutional weaknesses remain. Business registration practices and the Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) regime have not kept up with global good practice." (D0004649.odt, Political and Institutional Appraisal)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO/British Embassy Kathmandu (BEK) designs and oversees the programme, with Nepali partners (government, SMEs, financial institutions) implementing components under FCDO guidance. Decision-making power rests with FCDO, though local governments (e.g., provincial Chief Minister’s Employment Funds) are consulted.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to SMEs (management, productivity, competitiveness)
policy support to Government of Nepal (GoN) for business environment reforms
training for women and disadvantaged groups (skills, financial access)
institutional strengthening of financial intermediaries (e.g., banks, private equity firms)
support for green business practices (e.g., renewable energy adoption)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: NIB uses a combination of returnable capital (concessional loans/equity for SMEs), grants for technical assistance, and challenge funds (co-investment with private sector). This evolves FCDO’s prior grant-based approach to a more commercial model, filling gaps between pure grants and fully commercial BII investments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO/BEK oversees the programme, with a fund manager (or similar entity) likely allocating financing to SMEs and partners. Implementation involves direct partnerships with Nepali government agencies, financial institutions, and SMEs, with technical assistance provided by contractors or intermediaries.
how_mechanism.quote: "NIB will provide financing and support to strengthen companies’ management, operations, productivity, and competitiveness... It will evolve BEK’s current approach to supporting SMEs by taking a more commercial approach to support market building. This will provide returnable capital, rather than non-returnable capital (grants) to SMEs." (D0004649.odt, Programme summary and Collaborating with Partners)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions collaboration with multiple stakeholders (FCDO, BEK, GoN, provincial governments, BII) and alignment with other BEK programmes, suggesting a steering committee or similar structure for oversight. However, explicit governance details are not provided.
how_governance.quote: "NIB will work with other BEK programmes... to ensure capacity building and policy influencing activities are coherent." (D0004649.odt, Collaborating with Partners) and "Monitoring" and "Evaluation" sections imply structured oversight, but no explicit governance body is named.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with a focus on emerging growth corridors and sectors. However, reallocation likely requires approval given the structured focus on SMEs, green business, and women’s economic empowerment.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes flexible and adaptive management, with a results framework that allows for adjustments based on learning. Priorities can shift within the broad objectives (e.g., sectoral focus, geographic corridors) but likely require FCDO/BEK approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexible and Adaptive Management: NIB will adopt a flexible and adaptive management approach, allowing for adjustments based on emerging evidence, learning, and changes in the context." (D0004649.odt, Flexible and Adaptive Management)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager/Intermediary (e.g., financial institutions, technical assistance providers) → SMEs/End Beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: "Disbursement, Reporting and Assurance Mechanisms" section implies structured payments tied to milestones, but exact details are not specified. (D0004649.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuation of grant-based technical assistance (prior UK Aid approach)
Pure commercial financing (e.g., BII-only investments)
Focused sectoral programmes (e.g., standalone renewable energy or tourism projects)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: NIB’s mixed model (returnable capital + technical assistance) was chosen to: 1) Fill a gap in the SME financing ecosystem (between grants and commercial investments); 2) Support Nepal’s transition to middle-income status by fostering a sustainable private sector; 3) Leverage UK expertise (BII, FCDO) while building local capacity; 4) Address structural constraints (e.g., access to finance, firm capabilities) through integrated support.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (combining financing with capacity building for greater impact)
risk mitigation (gradual shift from grants to returnable capital)
partner capacity (building on prior UK programmes like A2F and NMDP)
speed (accelerating private sector growth to meet Nepal’s 2030 goals)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market distortion: Concessional financing may crowd out private sector lenders or create dependency.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeting gaps in the ecosystem (e.g., smaller investments than BII, more concessional than commercial lenders) and focusing on demonstration effects to attract private capital.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference: Frequent government changes may disrupt policy reforms or partnerships.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engaging across federal, provincial, and local governments to build broad support; aligning with GoN’s long-term goals (e.g., upper-middle-income status by 2030).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation capacity: Weak institutional capacity in Nepal may limit absorption of funds or technical assistance.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded capacity building (e.g., training for SMEs, policy support to GoN) and phased disbursements tied to milestones.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Equity trade-offs: Focus on commercial viability may exclude the poorest or most remote SMEs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit targeting of women, disadvantaged groups, and lagging regions (e.g., Karnali, Madhesh, Lumbini); blending financing with grants for inclusion.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (streamlined delivery through fund manager model)
effectiveness (measurable job creation, productivity gains, policy reforms)
equity (inclusive focus on women and disadvantaged groups)
why_rationale.quote: "NIB fills a gap in the SME financing ‘ecosystem’ where other donors, international financial institutions (IFI) and private sector actors do not finance... NIB will fund smaller investments than existing private sector funds and BII; the level of concessionality (NIB will be more concessional than private sector financing and most IFIs, but more commercial than most development programmes)." (D0004649.odt, Collaborating with Partners)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s political instability and weak institutions limit the pool of capable local partners, necessitating FCDO/BEK’s lead role in programme design and oversight. The reliance on remittances and informal sector dominance also constrain the types of SMEs that can absorb financing (e.g., lack of collateral, formal registration).
q27_constraints_detail: Political instability → limits long-term partnerships with government agencies
Weak financial institutions → requires intermediaries for fund disbursement
Social norms → restricts women’s participation, requiring targeted outreach
Infrastructure gaps → affects sectoral focus (e.g., renewable energy in rural areas)
Regulatory barriers → necessitates policy reform component
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to combine financing with capacity building (due to low firm capabilities) drives the mixed delivery structure (fund manager + technical assistance). The focus on green business and women’s empowerment requires embedded partners (e.g., NREP for energy, gender-focused intermediaries).
q28_linkages: Financing SMEs → requires fund manager structure to allocate returnable capital
Capacity building → necessitates technical assistance providers (embedded or standalone)
Policy influence → demands government partnerships (MoICS, provincial governments)
Inclusion goals → shapes partner selection (e.g., women-led intermediaries)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances commercial viability (efficiency) with inclusion (equity) by: 1) Targeting women and disadvantaged groups, which may reduce speed but aligns with equity goals; 2) Using returnable capital (more efficient than grants) while providing concessional terms (equitable access); 3) Focusing on lagging regions (e.g., Karnali), which may yield lower immediate returns but supports long-term stability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Targeting disadvantaged groups slows disbursement but aligns with equity
Cost vs. reach: Concessional financing increases budget needs but expands access
Expertise vs. ownership: UK-led design ensures technical rigor but limits local decision-making
Risk vs. innovation: Supporting early-stage SMEs carries higher risk but drives transformation
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight (milestone-based disbursements, adaptive management) and necessitates flexible structures (e.g., ability to reallocate funds across sectors/regions). Political risks require broad stakeholder engagement (federal/provincial/local).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Low firm capabilities in Nepal justify the programme’s dual focus on financing and technical assistance. Weak institutional capacity leads to embedded support for government partners (e.g., policy reform guidance).
intersections.quote: "Nepal’s political settlement and the nature of its private sector mean that the state is not well placed to lead a transformation... NIB will address some of these constraints in targeted sectors to support the growth of SMEs." (D0004649.odt, What is the Problem?) and "NIB will adopt a flexible and adaptive management approach, allowing for adjustments based on emerging evidence, learning, and changes in the context." (D0004649.odt, Flexible and Adaptive Management)

key_programme_risks: Political instability disrupting policy reforms or partnerships
Low absorption capacity among SMEs or government partners
Market distortion from concessional financing
Climate change exacerbating infrastructure vulnerabilities
Social norms limiting women’s participation
Economic shocks (e.g., remittance declines, Covid-19-like disruptions)
Implementation delays due to bureaucratic hurdles
Equity trade-offs (e.g., urban bias in financing)
Dependence on remittances limiting domestic productivity growth
Anti-competitive practices (cartels) stifling SME growth

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Engage across federal, provincial, and local governments; align with GoN’s long-term goals (e.g., 2030 upper-middle-income target).
Combine financing with technical assistance (management, productivity support).
Target gaps in financing ecosystem (smaller/t riskier investments than BII).
Prioritize renewable energy and climate-resilient infrastructure.
Explicit targets for women-led SMEs and gender-inclusive financing mechanisms.
Flexible fund reallocation and adaptive management.
Phased disbursements tied to milestones; embedded advisors.

fcas_specific_lessons: Political economy analysis is critical to navigate elite capture and anti-competitive practices.
Blended finance (grants + returnable capital) can mitigate risks in fragile contexts.
Decentralized implementation (e.g., provincial partnerships) builds resilience against national-level instability.
Gender and social inclusion require explicit targeting due to deep-rooted norms.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The predecessor AccesstoFinance Programme (A2F) demonstrated that: 1) Combining financing with capacity building yields higher job creation; 2) Partnerships with business accelerators and private equity firms can scale impact; 3) Women-led SMEs require tailored financial products (e.g., collateral-free loans). NMDP showed that sector-specific policy reforms (e.g., tourism strategy) need sustained government engagement.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: NIB shifts from A2F’s grant-based model to returnable capital, reflecting Nepal’s graduation from LDC status. It also expands geographic focus to lagging provinces (Karnali, Madhesh) and prioritizes green business, aligning with GoN’s net-zero commitments.
risks_lessons.quote: "NIB builds on successful UK programming in Nepal. The AccesstoFinance Programme (A2F) provided financial access to over 40,000 microenterprises, supported the growth of 40 SMEs, and created over 600 direct and indirect jobs... BEK established relationships with businesses and financial institutions through A2F that will benefit NIB." (D0004649.odt, Rationale for Intervention) and "NIB will align with BEK’s focus on Karnali, Madhesh and Lumbini Provinces... prioritisation of the corridors will be based on more detailed analysis on those that have high potential in the priority sectors." (D0004649.odt, Collaborating with Partners)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: NIB aims to crowd in private finance and generate a pipeline for BII investments, though specific leverage targets are not quantified.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme uses a mix of returnable capital (concessional loans/equity) and revenue expenditure (technical assistance grants), but exact splits are not specified.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £36.2 Million" (D0004649.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet) and "NIB will evolve BEK’s current approach to supporting SMEs by taking a more commercial approach to support market building. This will provide returnable capital, rather than non-returnable capital (grants) to SMEs." (D0004649.odt, Collaborating with Partners)

metadata.programme_name: African Union Conflict and Governance Support Programme (AUCG)
metadata.quote: The programme will provide technical assistance to the African Union (AU) to strengthen its role in elections and governance, conflict early warning and analysis, conflict prevention and conflict early response, including mediation. (D0002887.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 1 October 2022" and "AMP End Date: 31 March 2025" (D0002887.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The AUCG programme combines capacity building (strengthening AU's conflict prevention and governance capabilities), policy influence (supporting AU's normative frameworks), and service delivery (technical assistance for elections, mediation, and early warning systems). It aims to make the AU more effective in addressing peace and security challenges across Africa.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will provide technical assistance to the African Union (AU) to strengthen its role in elections and governance, conflict early warning and analysis, conflict prevention and conflict early response, including mediation." (D0002887.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened AU capacity in conflict early warning and analysis (e.g., improved early warning systems)
Enhanced AU mediation and dialogue capabilities (e.g., support to FemWise and mediation missions)
Improved electoral observation missions (e.g., technical assistance to AU EOMs, training for female observers)
Development of AU frameworks on climate security and human rights (e.g., gender-sensitive climate fragility assessment methodology)
Increased AU ability to set standards and drive country-led responses (e.g., normative frameworks on women’s participation in peace processes)
Systems strengthening between AUC and Regional Economic Communities (RECs)
what_objectives.summary: AUCG aims to build the AU’s institutional capacity to prevent and manage conflicts, promote good governance, and address emerging threats like climate security, while ensuring inclusive participation in political processes. It focuses on upstream prevention rather than costly peacekeeping interventions.
what_objectives.quote: "AUCG will focus on two core areas, which will help build institutional capacity, cement normative frameworks and deliver more systematic implementation across the continent: Building AU capacity to manage peace and security across the continent... and exploring new areas where the AU has the potential to set standards and drive country-led responses." (D0002887.odt, What will UK support provide?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a politically complex environment with institutional weaknesses in the AU, including limited absorption capacity and competing Member State interests. However, the AU is a committed peace and security actor with growing momentum under reform-minded leadership.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0002887.odt, Summary Sheet) and "the AU is hampered by institutional weaknesses, through staffing, funding, capability gaps and Member State interests." (D0002887.odt, A Changing Union)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (Member State interests limit AU’s mandate)
weak institutions (limited AU Commission staffing and funding)
conflict (ongoing crises in Sahel, Sudan, Ethiopia, etc.)
climate risks (climate security nexus with peace and stability)
data limitations (challenges in early warning systems interoperability)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Member State interests and institutional weaknesses constrain the AU’s ability to implement decisions at country/regional levels. Limited staffing (only ~3,000 officials in AUC, 70% on short-term contracts) and reliance on donor funding (80% of programme budget) affect absorption capacity. Conflict and climate vulnerabilities exacerbate fragility, requiring adaptive responses.
where_context.quote: "the AU is only as strong as its Member States allow it to be, and is only able to act on the issues that Member States permit it to." (D0002887.odt, A Changing Union)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-designed with the AU’s Department of Political Affairs, Peace and Security (DPAPS), with the UK providing technical assistance and funding while the AU retains policy ownership. Decision-making is shared, with the AU Commissioner for DPAPS (Bankole Adeoye) setting priorities and the UK aligning support through diplomatic engagement.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., workshops for AU election observers, climate security methodology)
mentorship (e.g., secondees embedded in DPAPS for early warning and mediation)
institutional strengthening (e.g., support to AU’s Human Rights and Governance Division, FemWise network)
technical assistance (e.g., development of gender-sensitive climate fragility tools)

partner_organizations.name: African Union Commission (AUC) - Department of Political Affairs, Peace and Security (DPAPS)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiary and co-implementer; leads on conflict prevention, mediation, and governance

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Trust Fund for Human Rights)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for early warning systems and climate security work

partner_organizations.name: Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)
partner_organizations.role: Potential partner for human rights technical assistance via MoU

partner_organizations.name: FemWise (Network of African Women in Conflict Prevention and Mediation)
partner_organizations.role: AU-affiliated network for deploying women mediators and election observers

partner_organizations.name: International IDEA
partner_organizations.role: Partner for electoral observation and governance support (mentioned in AUSP lessons)

partner_organizations.name: NORCAP (for AUCG predecessor AUSP)
partner_organizations.role: Deployed embedded experts for capacity gaps (model for AUCG’s deployment mechanism)

partner_organizations.name: UK Office to the AU (Addis Ababa)
partner_organizations.role: Diplomatic representation and programme coordination (e.g., AU Development Counsellor)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Africa Directorate (London HQ)
partner_organizations.role: Programme management, strategic oversight, and technical backstopping

partner_organizations.name: Regional Economic Communities (RECs)
partner_organizations.role: Collaboration on early warning systems interoperability and conflict prevention

who_partners.quote: "AUCG will... provide a secondment into DPAPS to ensure that early warning is being used by AU Directors and Commissioner Bankole... [and] provide technical support to the Mediation and Dialogue Division in DPAPS." (D0002887.odt, What will UK support provide?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **accountable grants** (for NGOs), **administrative arrangements** (e.g., with World Bank Trust Fund), **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** (e.g., with OHCHR and AUC’s Peace and Security Joint Funding Arrangement), and **direct funding** to the AU’s pooled fund. This hybrid approach balances UK control over priority areas with AU ownership and flexibility.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by a core FCDO team (HQ and Addis Ababa) with technical oversight from multiple departments (e.g., OCSM, Open Societies Directorate). Implementing partners (World Bank, NGOs, AU divisions) deliver specific components, coordinated by FCDO. The AU’s DPAPS acts as a central hub for alignment, with regular engagement between UK diplomats and AU leadership (e.g., Commissioner Bankole).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on **proven track records with the AUC**, **AU buy-in**, **sustainability of support**, and **gender commitment**. The restricted approach prioritizes organizations already embedded with the AU (e.g., World Bank, FemWise) to ensure rapid implementation and alignment with AU priorities, reducing transaction costs.
how_mechanism.quote: "We expect to be approached by partners that have an existing relationship with the AUC and be presented proposals by them... Implementing partners with a proven track-record of successful working with the AUC." (D0002887.odt, Grant Funding Options)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Flexible funding windows and adjustments to partner grants require SRO approval, with proposals jointly developed by the programme team and AUC. For the Peace and Security JFA, disbursements are governed by a rolling one-year MoU with the AUC, subject to due diligence.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO)** (G6 Conflict/Governance Adviser) oversees governance, with quarterly reporting cycles and annual activity workplans approved by FCDO. The World Bank Trust Fund includes a **Steering Committee** with FCDO representation, while the AU’s Peace and Security JFA has an **all-partner MoU** (renegotiated in 2023). The UK Office to the AU provides diplomatic coordination.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: Quarterly reports from partners, monthly financial reconciliations, and annual narrative/audit reports for the JFA. The World Bank Trust Fund provides cross-fund reporting annually and project-specific updates quarterly. High-risk areas (e.g., direct AUC funding) undergo additional due diligence and fraud risk assessments.
how_governance.quote: "Annual activity workplans and budgets will be approved by the SRO through the programme’s governance structures. A quarterly reporting cycle will be adopted with partners through their respective MOUs or grant agreements." (D0002887.odt, Expenditure Monitoring, Reporting and Accounting)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with **SRO approval**, particularly through the flexible funding window in years 2–3. However, sector input codes (e.g., conflict, governance, women and girls) must be adhered to, and major shifts require alignment with AU priorities and due diligence.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a **flexible funding window** (subject to available finance) to respond to emerging AU/UK priorities (e.g., mediation missions after coups). Adjustments require SRO sign-off and are guided by the AU’s evolving needs, as demonstrated in the predecessor AUSP’s adaptive response to Covid-19.
how_flexibility.quote: "AUCG will retain the ability to contribute a small amount of money to the Peace and Security JFA on an annual basis... This will be a means of empowering the AU to make its own decisions around funding." (D0002887.odt, Implementing the Preferred Option) and "The programme also includes a flexible funding window for years two and three." (D0002887.odt, Financial Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (e.g., World Bank, NGOs) → AU Divisions (e.g., DPAPS). For the JFA, it is FCDO → AUC (direct).
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: NGOs are paid **quarterly in arrears**; the World Bank is paid **against need** (not in advance); the Peace and Security JFA follows a **rolling one-year MoU** with disbursements planned to match the UK financial year.
how_efficiency.quote: "We will distribute funds to all NGOs quarterly in arrears. The World Bank will not be paid in advance of need." (D0002887.odt, Flow of Funds)

q24_alternatives_considered: No further programme support after AUSP ends (September 2022)
Limited and narrow support to election observation and crisis response
Increased support for AU momentum on early warning/conflict prevention + modest support for new areas (e.g., climate security)
Exclusive support to the AU’s Peace and Security Joint Funding Arrangement (pooled fund)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **third option** (core support + flexible funding) was selected because it: (1) **aligns with AU momentum** under Commissioner Bankole’s reform agenda; (2) **balances UK priorities** (conflict prevention, governance, climate) with AU ownership; (3) **retains flexibility** to adapt to emerging crises; and (4) **complements existing UK investments** (e.g., AMISOM/ATMIS stipends). The pooled fund option (JFA) was deemed too limiting for UK alignment, while the "do nothing" option risked losing diplomatic credibility.
q25_decision_factors: risk-mitigation (spread across multiple partners and instruments)
experience (builds on AUSP’s agile, responsive model)
flexibility (adaptive to AU’s dynamic political economy)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on short-term consultants/substitution for AU capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritize partners with **sustainability plans** and **AU buy-in**; monitor to ensure technical assistance builds institutional (not just individual) capacity. Example: Embedded secondees in DPAPS to transfer skills.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: AU absorption capacity limits (only ~3,000 AUC staff, 70% on short-term contracts)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use **third-party off-budget support** (e.g., NGOs, World Bank) to circumvent budget ceilings and flex quickly. Commissioner Bankole acknowledged this utility despite preferring direct funding.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political contingencies (Member States restricting AU’s mandate)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Combine technical support with **senior UK diplomatic engagement** (e.g., Ministerial-level interactions with Commissioner Bankole) to influence political will.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud/fiduciary risks in complex environments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Conduct **fraud risk assessments**, regular field visits, and financial process reviews. For the JFA, require **independent audits** and limit direct AUC funding to ~20% of the budget.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exchange rate fluctuations (GBP-denominated grants)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with suppliers to **modify deliverables or seek VFM savings** to offset long-term GBP variations.

vfm_details.economy: Compare unit costs of technical assistance (e.g., consultancy rates) and training across partners; use Pan Africa Dept’s TPM contract for cost recommendations.
vfm_details.efficiency: Track speed of grant issuance, disbursement forecasting, and financial variance monitoring. Avoid duplication across the portfolio.
vfm_details.effectiveness: Use **contribution analysis** to assess outcomes (e.g., improved AU capacity in early warning, elections). Assign **OECD-DAC Gender Equality Marker (GEM) principal objective** scores across the logframe.
vfm_details.equity: Ensure gender-disaggregated data, inclusive procurement, and compliance with the Gender Equality Act. Consult Senior Social Development Adviser on proposals.

why_rationale.quote: "We used a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to support decision-making... [Option III] covers a range of activity, while retaining the ability to pivot and adapt funding where necessary." (D0002887.odt, Options for Support) and "Promoting Britain and our values, by building strategic partnerships with multilateral organisations, including the AU, is a key part of the Foreign Secretary’s vision." (D0002887.odt, Summary Sheet)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The AU’s **political economy** (Member State interests, institutional weaknesses) and **absorption capacity** (limited staff, donor dependence) constrain partner selection to organizations with **existing AUC relationships** and **proven track records**. For example:
q27_constraints_detail: Member State restrictions on AU mandate → Partners must navigate AU’s principle of subsidiarity (e.g., RECs’ role in conflict prevention).

Limited AUC staffing (70% on short-term contracts) → Preference for partners who can **embed experts** (e.g., secondees to DPAPS) or provide **off-budget support** (e.g., NGOs circumventing budget ceilings).
FCAS contexts (Sahel, Sudan, Ethiopia) → Requires partners with **rapid-response capabilities** (e.g., FemWise for mediation deployments).
Climate-fragility nexus → Need for partners with **cross-sectoral expertise** (e.g., World Bank for climate security early warning).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **upstream focus** on conflict prevention and governance (vs. downstream peacekeeping) shapes the **mixed delivery structure**:
q28_linkages: Need for **technical depth** (e.g., early warning systems) → Hybrid of **embedded secondees** (for AU ownership) and **third-party NGOs** (for flexibility).
AU’s **normative role** (e.g., gender, climate standards) → Partnerships with **AU-affiliated networks** (e.g., FemWise) and **multilaterals** (e.g., OHCHR for human rights).
Requirement for **adaptive funding** (e.g., coups, elections) → **Flexible funding window** and **JFA contributions** to respond to crises.
Diplomatic objectives (UK-AU strategic partnership) → **Senior political engagement** (e.g., Ministerial interactions with Commissioner Bankole) alongside technical support.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Yes, explicitly discussed in the context of **gender mainstreaming vs. rapid delivery** and **AU ownership vs. donor control**:
q29_tradeoffs_detail: **Speed vs. inclusion**: The programme prioritizes **existing partners** (e.g., World Bank, FemWise) for quick implementation, but this risks excluding newer Southern-led organizations. Mitigation: Flexible funding window can onboard new partners in later years.

**Expertise vs. ownership**: While the AU prefers **direct funding**, the programme uses **third-party NGOs** to bypass absorption constraints, which may reduce AU institutionalization of skills. Mitigation: Secondees and capacity-building targets (e.g., training for female election observers).

**Cost vs. reach**: Pooled funding (JFA) offers **AU-led prioritization** but limits UK alignment; restricted competitions **reduce transaction costs** but may miss innovative Southern partners. Mitigation: Balance JFA contributions (20% of budget) with targeted grants.

**Gender equity vs. technical focus**: Assigning **GEM principal objective scores** across all components adds reporting burdens but ensures gender is not siloed. Mitigation: Dedicated gender advisors in the programme team.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (institutional weaknesses, FCAS contexts) drives **quarterly oversight**, **embedded advisors** (e.g., secondees in DPAPS), and **fraud risk assessments**. High-risk areas (e.g., direct AUC funding) receive **additional due diligence** and **milestone-based disbursements**.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles through: (1) **Secondees** to DPAPS for skills transfer; (2) **Training components** in all grants (e.g., election observers, climate security); (3) **AU-led needs assessments** to define technical assistance; (4) **REC collaboration** to strengthen regional systems (e.g., early warning interoperability).
intersections.quote: "The AU is only as strong as its Member States allow it to be... [and] the programme must ensure that the medium- and longer-term direction is not one where the AUC is overly reliant on short-term consultants." (D0002887.odt, Sustainability) and "AUCG’s approach will be to vigorously mainstream gender considerations through design and delivery... assigning OECD-DAC Gender Equality Marker principal objective values." (D0002887.odt, Women & Girls)

key_programme_risks: AU Member States restricting mandate implementation (e.g., non-interference principles).
Limited AUC absorption capacity (staffing, funding gaps) delaying programme delivery.
Political instability in focus countries (e.g., Sahel, Sudan) disrupting activities.
Over-reliance on short-term consultants substituting for institutional capacity.
Fraud/fiduciary risks in complex, high-corruption environments.
Exchange rate fluctuations affecting GBP-denominated budgets.
AU’s slow reform progress undermining sustainability of interventions.
Competing donor priorities (e.g., Russia/China influence) diverting AU attention.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Combine technical support with **UK diplomatic engagement** (e.g., Ministerial-level advocacy with Commissioner Bankole) to build political will. Use **REC collaboration** to navigate subsidiarity.
Channel ~80% of funds through **third-party partners** (e.g., World Bank, NGOs) to bypass budget ceilings. Prioritize **embedded secondees** for skills transfer.
Retain **flexible funding window** (years 2–3) to pivot to emerging crises (e.g., unconstitutional changes of government). Use **rapid-response partners** like FemWise.
Require partners to demonstrate **sustainability plans** and **AU buy-in**. Monitor **institutionalization of tools** (e.g., climate security methodologies into AU systems).
Conduct **fraud risk assessments**, **regular field visits**, and **independent audits** (e.g., for JFA). Limit direct AUC funding to ~20% of budget.
Negotiate **GBP-denominated contracts** with suppliers to manage risk. Adjust deliverables or seek **VFM savings** if GBP weakens.
Align with **Commissioner Bankole’s 1-year plan** and **AU’s Green Recovery Action Plan**. Use **contribution analysis** to track incremental progress.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from AUSP: **Flexible funding** was critical for adapting to Covid-19 and emerging conflicts. AUCG retains this via the **flexible window** and **JFA contributions**.

In FCAS contexts (e.g., Sahel, Sudan), **preventive diplomacy** (e.g., AU missions on unconstitutional changes of government) is more cost-effective than reactive interventions. AUCG prioritizes **early warning and mediation**.
**REC collaboration** is essential for legitimacy and local ownership in fragile states (e.g., G5 Sahel, IGAD). AUCG supports **systems strengthening** between AUC and RECs.
In **post-coup transitions** (e.g., Chad, Sudan), AU’s **normative frameworks** (e.g., ACDEG on elections) provide leverage for diplomatic pressure. AUCG supports their implementation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **AUSP (2018–2022)** demonstrated that: (1) **Flexible, adaptive programming** (e.g., repurposing budgets for Covid-19) is critical in dynamic contexts; (2) **Embedded experts** (e.g., NORCAP secondees) effectively bridge capacity gaps; (3) **Third-party off-budget support** can circumvent AU absorption limits while building trust; (4) **Senior political engagement** (e.g., with Commissioner Bankole) amplifies technical assistance. AUCG incorporates these lessons via its **flexible funding window**, **secondee mechanism**, and **diplomatic-TA linkage**.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **flexible funding window** (years 2–3) to replicate AUSP’s agility.
Included **deployment mechanism for embedded experts** (modeled on AUSP’s NORCAP trial).
Strengthened **gender mainstreaming** (GEM scores) after AUSP’s standalone gender components showed limited sustainability.
Expanded **climate security focus** based on AU’s growing prioritization (e.g., PSC communiqués on climate-peace nexus).
Increased **coordination with RECs** to address AUSP’s lesson on subsidiarity challenges.
Adopted **contribution analysis** for outcome reporting to better capture AU’s complex political economy.
risks_lessons.quote: "A key management lesson from the one-year cost extension of AUSP (2021–2022) was the difficulty of getting activities up-and-running quickly given AUC reform, the complex and highly political nature of the programme, and continental delivery during Covid-19." (D0002887.odt, Financial Case) and "The AUSP has scored an A across all three of its annual reviews conducted up until now." (D0002887.odt, Fusing Development and Diplomacy)

co_funding_partners.partner: African Union Peace and Security Joint Funding Arrangement (JFA)
World Bank Trust Fund for Human Rights

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **catalyze additional donor contributions** to the AU’s Peace and Security JFA by demonstrating UK commitment. The JFA is a pooled fund with multiple partners, and UK contributions (£500k in 2021 via CSSF) have historically leveraged further investments. The flexible funding window may also attract co-funding for high-priority AU initiatives.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: All funding is **revenue (RDEL)**; no capital (CDEL) expenditure is included.
financial_details.quote: "The budget profile is shown in figure three below and is in line with indicative 2022–2025 spending review allocations totaling 7.37m... The Ministerially agreed concept note stated that 7.5m was ‘the minimum level of programmatic engagement which we assess will maintain credibility with AU partners.’" (D0002887.odt, Programme budget and forecast) and "All funding will be ODA-eligible. This funding will come from programme resources (RDEL). There is no capital funding (CDEL) in this programme." (D0002887.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: UK-Jamaica Violence Prevention Partnership (VPP)
metadata.quote: "The programme will support the Government of Jamaica (GOJ) to develop and deliver more effective responses to address the underlying risk factors that promote excessive violence levels and to strengthen protective factors for youth-at-risk." (D0003978.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The total budget is estimated at £15.0M over six (6) years and the programme aims to deliver the following:" (D0003978.odt, What will the programme deliver?)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening state systems for violence prevention), implementation research (piloting a multi-sectoral approach in seven communities), and service delivery (direct interventions in schools and communities). It aims to create systemic change by addressing root causes of violence while testing scalable models.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will support the Government of Jamaica (GOJ) to develop and deliver more effective responses to address the underlying risk factors that promote excessive violence levels and to strengthen protective factors for youth-at-risk. It will pilot a multi-sectoral and integrated approach [...] in seven volatile communities, using their low performing schools as entry points." (D0003978.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened national capabilities to assess drivers of crime and violence (data architecture)
Enhanced data collection, management, and cross-government sharing (1 integrated database at PIOJ)
Improved capability of 3+ key ministries/agencies to deliver holistic prevention services (coordinated platform)
7 volatile communities receiving integrated interventions (psychosocial support, case management, literacy, parenting)
14+ low-performing schools used as entry points for community interventions
Increased capacity of 10+ civil society groups for advocacy and service delivery
Reduction in victimization levels in targeted communities (tracked via indicators)
Improved educational outcomes in intervention schools (monitored)
Scalable violence prevention model for national adoption (policy framework)
what_objectives.summary: The VPP aims to transform Jamaica's approach to violence prevention by strengthening state leadership, piloting integrated community interventions, and building civil society capacity, with all activities aligned to the national Citizen Security Plan.
what_objectives.quote: "Achieving a sustained (and sustainable) reduction in violence and creating the conditions for security and development in the worst-affected communities will take time. However, our intervention seeks to support GoJ’s efforts to lead the systemic changes required to achieve sustainable reductions in violence over time." (D0003978.odt, What will the programme deliver?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a high-violence context (49.4 homicides/100,000 in 2021) with weak institutions and governance challenges, but the document explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" based on FCDO's risk appetite and mitigation strategies.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0003978.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit field operations in volatile communities; weak public sector coordination hampers multi-agency delivery; political instability threatens sustained commitment; fragmented data systems impede evidence-based planning; and hurricane risks may disrupt implementation. For example: "The public sector remains siloed across Departments, unable or willing to deliver a coordinated effort" and "storage of much of the data is paper based."
where_context.quote: "The programme carries major gross risks as it seeks to challenge and change political norms, behaviours and ways of working which have been instilled in the public sector over decades." (D0003978.odt, Risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is explicitly positioned as a "bilateral UK-Jamaica partnership" with shared leadership. While FCDO provides funding and technical expertise, the GoJ leads implementation through its Citizen Security Plan framework, with joint decision-making on strategic directions (e.g., selection of intervention communities and monitoring frameworks).
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to strengthen data architecture (PIOJ, Citizen Security Secretariat)
Training for ministries/agencies on coordinated service delivery (MoEY, MoHW, MNS)
Mentorship for civil society on advocacy and service delivery
Institutional strengthening of National Commission on Violence Prevention
Embedded advisors to support policy reform and M&E systems

partner_organizations.name: Government of Jamaica (GoJ)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner; leads national coordination and service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ)
partner_organizations.role: Data repository and policy analysis hub

partner_organizations.role: Community engagement, advocacy, and local service delivery

partner_organizations.role: Parallel interventions in community policing and youth programmes
