partner_organizations.role: co-funder (Civic Space component)

partner_organizations.name: Tanzania Media Fund (TMF)
partner_organizations.role: potential downstream partner (media capacity building)

partner_organizations.name: Foundation for Civil Society (FCS)
partner_organizations.role: potential downstream partner (CSO support)

partner_organizations.name: Legal Services Facility (LSF)
partner_organizations.role: potential downstream partner (legal/rights support)

partner_organizations.name: Twaweza Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: potential downstream partner (civic engagement)

partner_organizations.name: Accountability in Tanzania (AcT)
partner_organizations.role: predecessor programme (lessons inform Wajibika)

partner_organizations.name: KPMG (or similar commercial supplier)
partner_organizations.role: likely implementer (contract delivery)

quote.text: "The Swiss Development Corporation has expressed strong interest in co-funding the Civic Space component of Wajibika." and "Delivery of GIF (Component Three of Wajibika) is currently being trialled under an existing FCDO Tanzania programme called Strengthening Public Financial Management (SPFM)... using a combination of an accountable grant with an NGO consortium and a call-down contract via the FCDO Expert Advice Call-down Service (EACDS)."
quote.source: D0003899.odt, Delivery structure and Commercial Case

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use a **competitively procured contract** (for core delivery) combined with **accountable grants** (for catalytic funding to CSOs/media) and a **Governance Innovation Fund (GIF)** for flexible, demand-driven interventions. The contract will manage most activities, while grants will support smaller, adaptive initiatives.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A single commercial supplier (selected via competitive tender) will manage day-to-day delivery, with FCDO retaining oversight. The supplier will sub-contract or provide grants to local CSOs, media, and other actors. The Governance Innovation Fund (GIF) will operate as a separate, flexible mechanism for targeted interventions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition was chosen to ensure value for money, technical expertise, and accountability. The market assessment indicated strong capability among commercial suppliers (e.g., KPMG’s past delivery of AcT2) and NGO consortia, but contracts were preferred for their stronger risk management and accountability mechanisms.

quote.text: "Delivering all three components through a contract is a more viable option for Wajibika. Competitive contracting will bring in genuine expertise, enable the delivery arrangement to embrace more flexibility and will provide FCDO with opportunity to have more directive engagement with the Supplier." and "Option A: Delivery through a Contract, competitively procured (a single open commercial tender or draw-down framework contract issued to private sector)."

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: The commercial supplier will manage sub-awards to CSOs/media, with FCDO setting strategic priorities. The Governance Innovation Fund (GIF) will use a mix of accountable grants and call-down contracts for technical assistance.

quote.text: "During implementation, level of management input from FCDO reduces and involves milestones tracking and performance payment." and "The inherent risks in delivering governance programmes in Tanzania will require close management by the commercial supplier to ensure that the programme remains within the FCDO’s risk appetite."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, particularly through the Governance Innovation Fund (GIF), which is designed for adaptive, demand-driven interventions. The programme emphasizes "politically smart" adjustments to respond to emerging opportunities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an **adaptive management approach**, allowing partners to adjust strategies based on political economy analysis and emerging opportunities. The GIF and catalytic grants are explicitly designed to test and scale innovative solutions.

quote.text: "Wajibika as a flexible and adaptive programme... This approach is necessary because the civil and political rights environment in Tanzania continues to change in ways that are hard to predict in advance." and "Wajibika’s adaptive programming will help to test and generate more evidence on the extent to which both media and civil society... are able to demonstrate greater credibility, accountability, capability and strategic intent."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Commercial Supplier (contract holder) → Downstream Partners (CSOs/media/public institutions)

quote.text: "During implementation, level of management input from FCDO reduces and involves milestones tracking and performance payment."

q24_alternatives_considered: Delivery through a Contract (competitively procured)
Hybrid delivery model (BHC coordination + NGO suppliers)
In-house delivery (BHC-managed)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **competitive contract** option was selected for its stronger accountability, risk management, and ability to deliver high-quality technical expertise. While more expensive upfront, it offered better value for money through performance-based payments, reduced fraud risks, and alignment with FCDO’s strategic goals. The hybrid and in-house options were dismissed due to higher management burdens and lack of internal capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High upfront costs and longer mobilization time for competitive contracting
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by using an early accountable grant to respond to immediate opportunities (e.g., pre-local elections in 2024) while the contract is finalized.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial suppliers may struggle with local staff retention, affecting delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Performance payments and robust ToRs will incentivize suppliers to invest in local talent and adaptive management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of information hoarding by suppliers (principal-agent problem)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful ToR design to align incentives with FCDO goals and require transparency.

quote.text: "Competitive contracting will bring in genuine expertise, enable the delivery arrangement to embrace more flexibility and will provide FCDO with opportunity to have more directive engagement with the Supplier... While this potentially entails higher input cost drivers and longer mobilization timelines, these are outweighed by the greater confidence that this route will deliver a range of high-quality potential partners, and strong accountability to FCDO during implementation."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Tanzania’s restrictive civic space and complex regulatory environment limit partner selection to legally registered organizations that comply with government frameworks (e.g., NGO Act, Media Services Act). This excludes unregistered grassroots groups or those critical of the government, reducing the pool of potential partners.
q27_constraints_detail: Only legally registered CSOs/media can receive funds (excludes informal groups)
NGO laws and media regulations create high compliance costs, favoring established organizations
Political sensitivity requires partners to avoid controversial issues (e.g., party politics, elections)
Government preference for 'safe' partners may limit diversity of voices
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s focus on **adaptive, politically smart interventions** requires a flexible, contract-based delivery structure to navigate Tanzania’s unpredictable civic space. The need for rapid response (e.g., pre-election opportunities) and multi-stakeholder coalitions (CSOs, media, government) shapes the choice of a commercial supplier with grant-making capacity.
q28_linkages: Adaptive programming → Contract with performance incentives (to allow flexibility)
Coalition-building → Supplier must manage networks across CSOs, media, and government
Catalytic funding → Mixed instruments (contract + grants) to test innovations
Political economy focus → Need for supplier with local expertise and risk management
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (using a single commercial supplier for accountability) with **equity** (ensuring women, marginalized groups, and local CSOs benefit). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Competitive contracting prioritizes quick mobilization but may sideline smaller, less formal organizations. (2) **Northern expertise vs. local ownership**: UK-based suppliers lead delivery, while Tanzanian CSOs are downstream partners with limited decision-making power.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Open competition favors established suppliers (e.g., KPMG) over local NGOs, potentially excluding grassroots groups.
Northern contractors provide technical capacity but may limit Southern leadership in programme design.
Strict contract terms reduce fraud risks but may constrain adaptive responses to local needs.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk context** (repressed civic space, political volatility) increases oversight intensity, with milestone-based tracking and performance payments to mitigate delivery risks. FCDO retains closer control than in lower-risk environments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a **core objective**, with partners (CSOs/media) expected to gradually take on more influential roles in policy dialogue. The programme designs interventions to strengthen their ability to engage government (e.g., evidence generation, coalition-building).

quote.text: "The current administration under President Samia is actively reaching out to stakeholders in a way that did not occur under the 5th phase government... CSOs could bring evidence and potential solutions to the 6th phase government’s priorities via meaningful, structured dialogue." and "Wajibika will support linkages between women political leaders and activists and support state–citizen engagement mechanisms that are not gender-blind."
quote.source: D0003899.odt, Strategic Case and Gender considerations

key_programme_risks.risk: Political backsliding (reversal of democratic gains under President Samia)
Regulatory crackdowns on CSOs/media (e.g., NGO deregistration, media suspensions)
Limited CSO capacity to engage government effectively (weak analytical skills, coordination)
Commercial supplier failure to retain local staff or adapt to political changes
Fraud or mismanagement of funds (given complex grant chains)
Harassment/intimidation of programme partners by security agents
Low women’s participation in political processes despite programme efforts

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Adaptive programming to seize windows of opportunity (e.g., pre-election periods) and flexible funds (GIF) to respond to changes.
Due diligence to ensure partners comply with Tanzanian laws; legal support for CSOs facing restrictions.
Embedded capacity building (training, mentorship) and coalition support to strengthen advocacy skills.
Performance payments tied to local hiring and adaptive management; early market engagement to attract capable suppliers.
Milestone-based payments, audits, and FCDO oversight of sub-awards.
Safeguarding protocols, annual reviews, and routine monitoring of partner safety.
Targeted support for women-led organizations and gender-inclusive dialogue mechanisms.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from AcT2: **Political will is a prerequisite** for civic space improvements; sustained engagement with government on its priorities builds legitimacy.
Lessons from AcT2: **Coalitions amplify impact**—CSOs working together can open policy spaces that remain closed to individual organizations.
Lessons from AcT2: **Mechanics of dialogue matter**—framing issues in non-confrontational terms (e.g., avoiding media spotlight during sensitive negotiations) preserves government relationships.
Lessons from AcT2: **Not all Parliamentarians understand policy processes**—CSOs must invest time in building their capacity to influence change.
Lessons from Magufuli era: **Rapid regulatory changes can disrupt delivery**—programmes must build flexibility to adapt to new laws (e.g., NGO Act amendments).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Accountability in Tanzania (AcT2) programme** (2016–2022) informed Wajibika’s design, particularly: (1) The need for **flexible, long-term funding** to allow partners to adapt to political shocks. (2) The importance of **working ‘from inside’ on government priorities** to gain traction. (3) The value of **coalitions** (e.g., CSO-media-faith groups) to amplify advocacy. (4) The **limited sustainability** of gains under authoritarian regimes (e.g., Magufuli’s crackdowns reversed progress).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **thematic sectors** (AcT2) to **open societies focus** (Wajibika) to address root causes of civic space restrictions.
Inclusion of a **Governance Innovation Fund (GIF)** for adaptive, demand-driven interventions (learned from AcT2’s rigid structure).
Greater emphasis on **women’s political participation** and gender-inclusive mechanisms (response to AcT2’s limited progress on gender).
Stronger **risk management** in contract design (e.g., performance payments, brake clauses) to address past fraud risks.
Explicit **safeguarding measures** (e.g., harassment monitoring) added after AcT2 partners faced intimidation.

quote.text: "Lessons from the six years of funding AcT2 programme confirm that CSOs’ internal capacities remain weak, attributed largely to the Magufuli authoritarian era which damaged a lot of gains from AcT and other programmes... Thus we concluded that a future programme must address issues of resource management, monitoring, learning and evaluation and the ability to work in issue-based coalitions if it is to empower CSOs to be more effective." and "AcT2 partners have learned that in order to influence the government, working ‘from inside’ on issues that are of priority to the government is crucial."

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Swiss Development Corporation’s co-funding increases the programme’s strategic and financial value, though the exact amount is not specified.

quote.text: "Programme Value: £15m" and "The Swiss Development Corporation has expressed strong interest in co-funding the Civic Space component of Wajibika."
quote.source: D0003899.odt, Programme summary and Commercial Case

metadata.programme_name: Resilient Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Emergency Preparedness Programme (RWEPP)
metadata.primary_sector: WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) / Humanitarian Preparedness / Climate Resilience
metadata.quote: "The RWEPP aims to increase inclusive access to sustainable and resilient Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, and strengthen the resilience of communities to deal with climate-induced disasters." (61401356.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: July 2021; AMP End Date: June 2026" (61401356.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: RWEPP combines **service delivery** (direct provision of WASH infrastructure), **capacity building** (strengthening local government and community systems), **implementation research** (testing approaches for sustainability and resilience), and **policy influence** (supporting government WASH and disaster risk reduction plans). The programme also includes **emergency response** components (e.g., COVID-19 support) and **private sector engagement** for market-based solutions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will finance: staff; WASH infrastructure, capacity building on emergency preparedness and WASH system strengthening of government." (61401356.odt, Programme summary) AND "RWEPP will increase access to sustainable and resilient Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, and strengthen the resilience and preparedness of communities to disasters." (61401356.odt, Overview of the programme)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 14 Palikas prepare and implement WASH and Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Sectoral Plans
Public institutions (14 schools and 6 Healthcare Facilities) equipped with functional WASH facilities
Water schemes built
Households served with basic water services (150,000 people)
Households with improved sanitation and hygiene practices
People with improved knowledge and skills on disaster resilience
Strengthened private sector capacity to meet demand for WASH and emergency products/services
Immediate COVID-19 response support (WASH, PPE, testing capacity)

what_objectives.summary: RWEPP is a **multi-component programme** that delivers WASH infrastructure, strengthens local government systems for sustainability, builds community resilience to climate disasters, and integrates emergency response (e.g., COVID-19). It explicitly targets marginalized groups (women, Dalits, people with disabilities) and aligns with Nepal’s federalism transition and SDG commitments.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will increase access to sustainable and resilient Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, and strengthen the resilience and preparedness of communities to disasters. This will be achieved primarily through delivery of sustainable WASH services and strengthening capacity and systems at the local government and community levels." (61401356.odt, Overview of the programme)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal is **highly vulnerable to climate change** (ranked 4th globally), faces **frequent natural disasters** (earthquakes, floods, landslides), and has **weak subnational institutional capacity** post-federalism transition. The 2015 earthquake and COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated fragility, with 60% of the population vulnerable to shocks. Political instability and civil unrest risks persist due to low public confidence in new local governments (palikas).
where_context.q5_source: "Nepal is highly vulnerable to climate-related, natural and man-made crises... ranked fourth, in terms of vulnerability to climate change (Global Climate Index 2019)." AND "60% of the population is highly vulnerable to natural hazards, health and economic shocks." AND "This transition also brings risk: the palikas currently lack the requisite sectoral capacities and systems to effectively deliver their mandates in key areas... may undermine public confidence in the palikas’ credibility and competency, with associated risks of political instability and civil unrest." (61401356.odt, Context and overview of needs)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (palikas lack capacity for WASH/DRR mandates)
political economy (federalism transition, low public trust in local governments)
regulatory (policy gaps between WASH and disaster risk reduction)
infrastructure (75% of households use unsafe water sources; 50% of water schemes damaged in 2015 earthquake)
data limitations (only 255/753 palikas have WASH plans; lack of real-time monitoring systems)
social norms (patriarchal barriers to women’s participation in WASH decision-making)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak palika capacity delays WASH service delivery and disaster response, while climate shocks destroy infrastructure (e.g., 50% of water schemes damaged in 2015 earthquake). Gender norms limit women’s roles in WASH governance, and federalism transition has created coordination gaps between federal/provincial/local levels. Lack of data systems (e.g., nWASH database not fully operational) hampers planning.
where_context.quote: "The palikas currently lack the requisite sectoral capacities and systems to effectively deliver their mandates in key areas... their financial management, planning, and budgeting systems may not guarantee that resources are utilised in the most equitable, accountable, or efficient manner." AND "During the 2015 earthquake... nearly 50% of the country’s water supply systems were damaged." (61401356.odt, Context and overview of needs)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **Gurkha Welfare Trust (GWT, Nepal-based)** leads implementation with technical oversight from the **British Embassy Kathmandu (BEK, UK)**. Decision-making is shared: GWT designs and delivers activities, while BEK provides strategic direction and quality assurance. Palikas (local governments) co-develop plans and co-finance infrastructure, ensuring Southern ownership.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for palikas on WASH/DRR planning, monitoring, and regulation
Technical assistance to Water Sanitation User Committees (WSUCs) and School Management Committees (SMCs)
Support for private sector (artisans, businesses) to produce WASH/emergency products
Gender and social inclusion (GESI) training for local committees (50% women representation mandated)
Disaster resilience simulations and rapid response team training for communities
Performance monitoring systems for palikas

partner_organizations.name: Gurkha Welfare Trust (GWT)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer (delivery of WASH infrastructure, capacity building, emergency response)

partner_organizations.name: British Embassy Kathmandu (BEK) / FCDO
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic oversight; technical guidance on alignment with UK/Nepal priorities

partner_organizations.name: Palikas (local governments)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financing partners; co-development of WASH/DRR plans; service delivery

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Water Supply (MoWS) and Department of Water Supply and Sewerage (DWSS)
partner_organizations.role: Policy alignment and technical guidance at federal level

partner_organizations.name: National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)
partner_organizations.role: DRR policy coordination and strategic action plan implementation

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (local businesses, artisans)
partner_organizations.role: Production and retail of WASH/emergency products; service maintenance

partner_organizations.name: School Management Committees (SMCs) and Health Facility Operation and Maintenance Committees (HFOMCs)
partner_organizations.role: Local-level WASH facility management and behaviour change promotion

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be implemented by GWT, which will ensure continuity of the UK government’s 32 years partnership with GWT... GWT will support the strengthening of palikas’ capacities for enabling and sustaining WASH services for all their citizens." AND "RWEPP will provide technical assistance to federal and provincial ministries and institutions such as the Ministry of Water Supply (MoWS), Department of Water Supply and Sewerage (DWSS) and National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)." (61401356.odt, Overview of the programme and Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is delivered through a **long-standing partnership agreement** between FCDO (via British Embassy Kathmandu) and GWT, building on 32 years of collaboration. Funds are channelled to GWT as the primary implementer, with co-financing from palikas (local governments) for infrastructure. The instrument allows flexibility for emergency response (e.g., COVID-19) and adaptive management.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: GWT is the **sole implementer** but works in **close collaboration with palikas (local governments)**, federal/provincial ministries, and community committees (WSUCs, SMCs). Palikas co-finance and co-implement activities, while GWT provides technical leadership. BEK/FCDO oversees strategic alignment and quality assurance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GWT was selected due to its **32-year proven track record** in WASH delivery in Nepal, existing partnership with BEK, and unique role linking UK-Nepal defence ties (Gurkha veterans’ welfare). The direct award ensures continuity of a historically successful collaboration and leverages GWT’s deep local expertise in remote areas.
how_mechanism.quote: "The partnership between GWT and the BEK has been successful and has strategic value for both... GWT has a proven track record of high-quality WASH delivery, good project management, financial management and responsiveness to BEK." AND "This programme is well aligned with the new UK Government Strategic Framework for ODA spending and the key pillars of the UK’s Indo-Pacific Tilt engagement." (61401356.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Sub-awards to palikas and private sector are allocated through **joint planning** between GWT and local governments, based on prioritized needs in WASH/DRR sectoral plans. Palikas co-finance infrastructure, and GWT provides technical oversight.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **Project Advisory Committee (PAC)** is explicitly mentioned, comprising representatives from BEK, GWT, and government stakeholders (MoWS, NDRRMA). The PAC oversees strategic direction, risk management, and adaptive learning. Palikas are engaged in decision-making through sectoral planning processes.
how_governance.quote: "Programme governance and management: The programme will be governed by a Project Advisory Committee (PAC) comprising of representatives from BEK, GWT and other key stakeholders." AND "The programme will be designed to be adaptive, particularly to adapt to the emerging context and learning around working with, and potentially implementing through, palikas." (61401356.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., WASH infrastructure vs. emergency response) with **PAC approval**, as demonstrated by the immediate shift to COVID-19 support in 2021. However, major changes require BEK endorsement.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **adaptive management** to respond to emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19, climate shocks). Learning from monitoring and community feedback loops informs adjustments, with a focus on "reaching the hardest to reach." The PAC reviews progress quarterly to approve pivots.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will be designed to be adaptive, particularly to adapt to the emerging context and learning around working with, and potentially implementing through, palikas." AND "The programme will ensure effective ongoing monitoring, reflection, and feedback loops to inform programme adaptation." (61401356.odt, Management Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GWT (implementer) → [Palikas/private sector as co-delivery partners]. No additional sub-grantee layers are explicitly documented.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will finance: staff; WASH infrastructure, capacity building on emergency preparedness and WASH system strengthening of government." (61401356.odt, Programme summary) [Implied milestone-based disbursements for infrastructure/capacity building outputs.]

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing – end UK engagement in WASH sector and partnership with GWT
Engage in the WASH sector through another mechanism (unspecified)
Continue with the same approach – RWSP Phase 6
Continue with a revised approach – RWEPP (selected option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: RWEPP was selected for its **strategic alignment with UK/Nepal priorities**, **proven partner capacity (GWT)**, and **adaptive design** to address emerging challenges (climate change, COVID-19, federalism). The revised approach integrates **disaster resilience**, **private sector engagement**, and **gender/social inclusion**—lessons from RWSP-V and ICAI reviews. Direct award to GWT ensures **continuity of a 32-year partnership** with high delivery quality and **cost-efficiency** (leveraging existing systems).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (GWT’s proven track record and low overheads)
risk mitigation (GWT’s experience in remote/FCAS contexts)
partner capacity (GWT’s technical expertise and local trust)
equity (targeting marginalized groups and gender inclusion)
strategic alignment (UK’s Indo-Pacific Tilt and Nepal’s federalism transition)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on GWT may limit local ownership by palikas.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Co-financing and joint planning with palikas; capacity building for local governments to take over WASH/DRR mandates.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Palikas’ weak capacity could delay implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded technical assistance from GWT; performance monitoring systems; incentive mechanisms for palikas.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks or disasters could disrupt activities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Built-in emergency response funds; resilient infrastructure designs; community preparedness training.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political instability during federalism transition may affect coordination.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with all three tiers of government (federal/provincial/local); alignment with national DRR strategies.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging GWT’s existing infrastructure and partnerships)
efficiency (streamlined delivery through single implementer with local co-financing)
effectiveness (evidence-based outputs from RWSP-V, e.g., 95% of GWT-built schemes survived 2015 earthquake)
equity (targeted inclusion of women, Dalits, and people with disabilities)
why_rationale.quote: "The partnership between GWT and the BEK has been successful and has strategic value for both... GWT has a proven track record of high-quality WASH delivery, good project management, financial management and responsiveness to BEK." AND "RWEPP has been designed within the context of the new UK Country Plan in Nepal, which includes five strategic objectives: Open Societies; Stability and Security; Trade and Prosperity; Climate and Resilience; Girls’ Education and the Rights of Women and Girls." (61401356.odt, Appraisal Case and Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s **federalism transition** and **palikas’ weak capacity** constrain partner selection to organizations like GWT, which have **existing local trust and technical expertise**. The **high disaster risk** (earthquakes, floods) necessitates partners with proven resilience experience (e.g., GWT’s 95% scheme survival rate in 2015). **Patriarchal norms** limit women-led organizations’ roles, addressed through mandatory 50% women representation in committees.
q27_constraints_detail: Palikas lack capacity to manage complex WASH/DRR programmes independently → requires technical partners like GWT.
Remote geography and climate vulnerability → needs partners with experience in resilient infrastructure.
Gender exclusion in WASH governance → mandates partners committed to GESI mainstreaming.
Federalism transition → requires partners who can navigate multi-tiered government coordination.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (service delivery + systems strengthening + emergency response) necessitate a **hybrid delivery structure**: GWT leads implementation (for efficiency), while palikas co-deliver (for ownership). **Disaster resilience goals** require embedded private sector and community roles (e.g., rapid response teams). **Gender/social inclusion targets** shape partner selection (e.g., women-led committees, disability-accessible designs).
q28_linkages: Service delivery outputs (400 water schemes) → require GWT’s engineering capacity + palika co-financing.
Systems strengthening (palika plans) → necessitates joint BEK/GWT/ government governance (PAC).
Emergency response flexibility → enabled by GWT’s direct award and adaptive management.
Private sector engagement → requires GWT’s market-shaping role (training artisans, setting standards).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions between **rapid delivery** (using GWT’s existing systems) and **local ownership** (building palika capacity). The programme mitigates this by: (1) **co-financing requirements** for palikas, (2) **mandated GESI representation** in committees, and (3) **gradual handover** of WASH/DRR functions to local governments. **Cost vs. reach** is addressed by targeting the "hardest to reach" (remote, marginalized) despite higher per-capita costs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: GWT’s direct implementation ensures efficiency, but risks sidelining palikas → mitigated via joint planning and capacity building.
Northern technical oversight (BEK/GWT) balances local decision-making (palikas) to ensure quality without undermining sovereignty.
Targeting remote/marginalized groups increases per-capita costs but aligns with equity goals (e.g., 50% women in committees).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk context** (disasters, weak institutions) justifies **intensive oversight** (quarterly PAC reviews, embedded advisors) and **adaptive management** (flexible funds for emergencies). Palikas’ capacity gaps require **hands-on GWT support**, while climate risks mandate **resilience-focused monitoring**.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: GWT trains palikas to eventually take over WASH/DRR mandates; private sector partners are upskilled to meet quality standards; and community committees (WSUCs) are mentored for inclusive governance. This ensures **sustainable exit** for GWT.
intersections.quote: "The palikas currently lack the requisite sectoral capacities and systems to effectively deliver their mandates... this transition also brings risk... may undermine public confidence in the palikas’ credibility." AND "RWEPP will support the strengthening of palikas’ capacities for enabling and sustaining WASH services for all their citizens." (61401356.odt, Context and Management Case)

key_programme_risks: Palikas’ weak capacity delays WASH/DRR plan implementation.
Climate-induced disasters damage infrastructure (e.g., 50% of water schemes damaged in 2015 earthquake).
Political instability during federalism transition disrupts coordination.
Gender and social exclusion limits participation of women/Dalits/people with disabilities.
Private sector may lack capacity to meet WASH product demand.
COVID-19 or other epidemics overwhelm health systems.
Over-reliance on GWT limits local ownership.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded technical assistance from GWT; performance monitoring systems; incentive mechanisms for palikas to adhere to plans.
Resilient infrastructure designs; community emergency preparedness training; flexible funds for rapid response.
Engagement with all three tiers of government; alignment with national DRR strategies; adaptive management.
Mandatory 50% women representation in committees; targeted outreach to Dalits/people with disabilities; GESI-trained staff.
Training and marketing support for local businesses; quality standards enforcement by palikas.
Immediate WASH/PPE support; integration of infection prevention in healthcare facilities; behaviour change campaigns.
Gradual handover of functions to palikas; co-financing requirements; cross-learning platforms.

fcas_specific_lessons: Post-2015 earthquake: **Community-led rescue** was most effective → RWEPP prioritizes local rapid response teams.
2017 floods: **Prepared communities** (e.g., Kailali) had fewer casualties → RWEPP scales up simulations and stockpiling.
Federalism transition: **Palikas need handholding** → GWT provides embedded advisors during transition.
GESI in disasters: **Women and people with disabilities** face higher risks → RWEPP mandates inclusive planning.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: From **RWSP-V (2017 Mid-Term Review)**: (1) **Geographical clustering** improves value for money; (2) **Balancing cost-efficiency with equity** is critical (reaching remote groups is harder but necessary); (3) **Aligning with palikas** early avoids delays. From **ICAI WASH Review (2016)**: Systematic focus on **sustainability** (e.g., post-construction support for WSUCs) is essential.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: RWEPP incorporates: (1) **Stronger palika engagement** (co-planning, co-financing); (2) **Explicit disaster resilience** (climate-sensitive designs, emergency funds); (3) **Private sector component** (lesson from RWSP’s limited market engagement); (4) **Adaptive management** (response to ICAI’s call for flexibility).
risks_lessons.quote: "A key learning from the 2015 earthquake was that the overwhelming majority of those rescued were done so by their own community, highlighting the critical role of emergency preparedness and response capacity in communities." AND "The RWSP-V Mid-Term Review in 2017 highlighted the growing importance for WASH services progressively aligning and collaborating with the palikas." (61401356.odt, Evidence and Learning sections)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Co-financing from palikas for WASH infrastructure; potential mobilization of private sector investments in WASH products/services.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Capital expenditure includes WASH infrastructure (400 water schemes, school/health facility upgrades); revenue covers capacity building, behaviour change campaigns, and emergency response.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £19.7 million" (61401356.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "The programme will co-fund together with palika, the rehabilitation, expansion, and construction of water supply schemes." (61401356.odt, WASH Infrastructure section)

metadata.programme_name: Climate Smart Jobs (CSJ)
metadata.duration_text: Start date: 27 September 2021, End Date: 31 December 2027
metadata.quote: "Climate Smart Jobs (CSJ) spearheads The British High Commission Kampala’s campaign goal to create jobs and UK partnerships that support inclusive economic growth: supporting large-scale job creation for the growing youth population, positioning the UK as a partner of choice for trade and investment and pushing more ambitious climate action." (D0006357.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project’s start and end dates: Start date: 27 September 2021, End Date: 31 December 2027" (D0006357.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (providing loans, technical support, and investment capital), implementation research (testing and scaling climate-smart agriculture interventions), and capacity building (training agribusinesses and communities). It aims to create jobs, increase incomes, and build climate resilience through market systems development, financial services, and sustainable land management.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Climate Smart Jobs will: Grow climate smart agribusinesses to create jobs: providing loans and technical support directly to businesses to enable them to expand into large commercial operations able to access mainstream finance, be more resilient to climate change and increase incomes for over 300,000 households." (90000130.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 300,000 households with increased incomes
145,000 individuals supported to increase climate resilience (from NUTEC baseline)
1.8 million tons of CO2 stored over 10 years through sustainable land management
£94 million (revised to £80 million in addendum) of benefit from climate services
£60 million return on investment from removing trade/investment barriers
2000 hectares of new agroforestry absorbing ~670,000 tons of CO2e
225,000 jobs supported through SME financing (estimated)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Uganda’s shallow financial sector and climate vulnerability limit partner options to those with existing risk mitigation tools (e.g., Aceli’s credit guarantees, AgDevCo’s patient capital). Political economy constraints (e.g., incumbent agribusinesses) require partners with local networks and diplomatic skills.
q27_constraints_detail: High interest rates (28.8%) restrict SME access to finance → necessitates partners like Aceli Africa with risk-sharing mechanisms.
Climate risks (droughts, erratic rainfall) → requires partners with climate adaptation expertise (e.g., AgDevCo’s technical assistance).
Weak data on climate/land use → limits partners to those with existing monitoring systems.
Gender disparities → partners must have gender-inclusive approaches (e.g., NUTEC’s women-focused interventions).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **climate-smart job creation** drives the mixed delivery structure: (1) **Market development** requires flexible, locally embedded partners (e.g., Palladium’s village agent model), (2) **SME financing** needs specialized financial intermediaries (Aceli Africa), and (3) **long-term investment** demands patient capital providers (AgDevCo). The trade/investment component adds a diplomatic layer (in-house role for BIPs coordination).
q28_linkages: Climate adaptation goals → require partners with technical assistance capacity (e.g., AgDevCo’s agroforestry support).
Job creation targets → necessitate financial intermediaries (Aceli Africa) to leverage private capital.
Trade/investment barriers → justify the in-house role (addendum) for FDI facilitation.
Gender equity → embedded in all components (e.g., Aceli’s incentives for women-led businesses).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritizes **gender equity** (e.g., women’s productivity, land access) and **youth employment** even if it reduces overall job numbers: "This programme will focus on delivering jobs for women, even if that means it delivers slightly fewer jobs overall." Efficiency (e.g., cost per job) is balanced with equity through targeted components (e.g., women’s access to finance, climate-resilient crops for smallholders).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid job creation could exclude women/marginalized groups → mitigated by gender-targeted incentives.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern partners (e.g., AgDevCo) provide climate expertise, but local ownership is fostered via Ugandan Agribusiness Alliance engagement.
Cost vs. reach: High transaction costs for SME loans (28.8% interest) → addressed via Aceli’s first-loss guarantees to reduce lender risk.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (climate shocks, financial sector weaknesses) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and adaptive management. For example, drought risks require flexible fund reallocation between components, while shallow banking sector necessitates intensive technical assistance to financial institutions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: (1) **Aceli Africa** provides business development services to SMEs, (2) **AgDevCo** offers "business incubation" (e.g., board participation, marketing strategies), and (3) the **in-house role** (addendum) strengthens FCDO’s private sector engagement capacity.
intersections.quote: "While this impact metric will take account of other outcomes achieved, it is also important to mention that during the programme’s time it has already supported ~150,000 individuals with increased access to climate information and markets... This programme will focus on delivering jobs for women, even if that means it delivers slightly fewer jobs overall." (90000130.odt, Component 1: Market Development) && "The objective of the change is to agree to the use of programme funds to pay for programme funded staff... This role is an integral part of delivering the programme’s theory of change, programme outputs and outcomes." (D0006357.odt, Summary Information)

key_programme_risks: Shallow pipeline for long-term investments in Northern Uganda (mitigation: geographic flexibility).
Climate shocks (droughts, floods) disrupting agricultural productivity (mitigation: climate-smart crops, insurance).
High interest rates (28.8%) limiting SME access to finance (mitigation: Aceli’s credit incentives).
Gender disparities in land ownership/productivity (mitigation: women-targeted technical assistance).
Low private sector interest in climate public goods (mitigation: competitive Uganda Innovation Climate Fund).
Political economy barriers (incumbent firms, land disputes) (mitigation: stakeholder engagement via Ugandan Agribusiness Alliance).
COVID-19 reversals in poverty reduction (mitigation: agriculture as coping mechanism).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited bankable agribusinesses in Northern Uganda
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Allow AgDevCo to invest nationally if regional pipeline is weak; provide technical assistance to improve investment readiness.
Promote drought-resistant crops, agroforestry, and climate information systems (e.g., early warning).
Aceli Africa’s portfolio first-loss coverage and origination incentives to compensate for higher operating costs.
Targeted technical assistance for women (e.g., financial literacy, land rights training) and higher Aceli incentives for women-led businesses.

fcas_specific_lessons: Agriculture acts as a coping mechanism during crises (e.g., COVID-19 saw 10% increase in agricultural employment).
Climate resilience must be integrated into all components to protect development gains (e.g., NUTEC’s climate risk assessments).
Flexible geographic focus is needed to balance regional equity with pipeline viability (lesson from NUTEC’s Northern Uganda restrictions).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: NUTEC (2014–2021) demonstrated that: (1) **Cost per beneficiary declined from £44.63 to £12.80** through economies of scale, (2) **Capital leverage ratios improved from 2–3X to 9.5X** as financial sector matured, (3) **Climate-smart practices (e.g., Quality Declared Seeds) increased resilience**, and (4) **Geographic restrictions limited impact** for long-term investments.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **Component 4 (climate-smart land management)** to address NUTEC’s gap in public goods (e.g., biodiversity, carbon markets).
Introduced **Component 5 (trade/investment technical assistance)** to build on NUTEC’s market development successes.
Expanded **geographic flexibility** beyond Northern Uganda to avoid pipeline bottlenecks.
Added **in-house Programme Funded Role** (addendum) to improve coordination with British Investment Partnerships (BIPs).
Incorporated **Uganda Innovation Climate Fund** to pilot high-risk, high-reward climate ideas.
risks_lessons.quote: "NUTEC has already raised incomes for 680,000 individuals, supported 145,000 individuals in increase their climate resilience and mobilised over £60m in additional investment into the sector... The success of this programme has made a compelling case to continue with the three main components (market systems development, financial services to SMEs and long-term investment finance). However, several design lessons have been learnt from this programme experience." (90000130.odt, Summary Options Appraisal) && "The objective of the change is to agree to the use of programme funds to pay for programme funded staff... This role is an integral part of delivering the programme’s theory of change, programme outputs and outcomes." (D0006357.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **capacity building** (strengthening Southern CSOs' organizational resilience and sustainability) with a **financing mechanism** (providing core and restricted funding through a fund structure) and **implementation research** (testing interventions to generate evidence on effective civil society strengthening approaches). It also includes **policy influence** objectives by aiming to shift power dynamics in aid and demonstrate alternative narratives about development effectiveness to the UK public.

q1_source.financing_mechanism: "The programme will be comprised of two core elements: 1) Strengthening African Civil Society Fund; 2) Community Resourcing Match Fund [...] The Match Fund will provide training for CSOs in alternative forms of local income generation and will match the resulting revenue that they generate to incentivise income diversification and financial sustainability." (Document: 55428258.odt, Attached summary section)
q1_source.implementation_research: "The programme will generate learning on the efficacy of different interventions designed to advance organisational capacity and resilience which will be influential in programme design within DFID, other funders and amongst CSOs themselves." (Document: 55428258.odt, Programme objectives section)
q1_source.policy_influence: "This programme will enable Comic Relief and DFID to communicate a positive narrative to the UK public about how aid works. what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen African civil society by providing long-term core funding, capacity development, and incentives for financial sustainability, while generating evidence on effective interventions. It focuses on shifting power to Southern CSOs, testing innovative funding models, and communicating progressive narratives about aid to the UK public.

quote.objectives: "The intended impact of Strengthening African Civil Society is that civil society in Ghana, Zambia and Malawia are more resilient, independent and effective in delivering the priorities of local people in the areas of early childhood development, mental health, gender justice and safe and secure shelter." (Document: 55428258.odt, Intended outcomes section)
quote.outputs: "The intended outcomes are: Measurable improvement in the capacity and capability of at least 60 recipient organisations in three countries [...] CSOs diversify income and raise new income locally are measurably more financially sustainable [...] CSOs are more responsive to local priorities and better able to deliver social accountability [...]" (Document: 55428258.odt, Intended outcomes section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'. The document notes that civic space is "narrowed" in Ghana and "obstructed" in Zambia/Malawi, but these countries were selected as relatively stable contexts where CSOs can operate without threat of violence. The programme aims to test interventions in countries at different stages of aid transition (Ghana moving toward aid exit, Zambia on the path, Malawi still aid-dependent).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (Document: 55428258.odt, Programme details section) and "Civic freedom in Ghana is rated by Civicus Monitor as ‘Narrowed’ and in Zambia and Malawi as ‘Obstructed’." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (legal environment for CSOs and philanthropy)
political economy (narrowing civic space in Zambia/Malawi)
aid transition (Ghana reducing donor footprint, Zambia/Malawi at different stages)
financial sustainability (CSOs face challenges with unpredictable funding flows)
capacity gaps (need for organisational development support)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory environments affect CSOs' ability to generate local income and operate freely. Political restrictions in Zambia/Malawi limit civic space, while Ghana's 'Beyond Aid' agenda creates pressure to demonstrate sustainability. The programme design (e.g., match funding for local income generation) directly responds to these constraints by testing models that could work in transitioning contexts.

quote.constraints: "The general operating environment for CSOs: Consideration was given to whether the legal and regulatory environment was conducive to the strengthening of civil society and the growth of local income streams and charitable/philanthropic giving in particular." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)
quote.civic_space: "Civic space: [...] The programme seeks to understand to what extent building civil society capacity and sustainability can help to protect civil society from these threats in different contexts such as Ghana, where civic space is relatively unchallenged and Zambia and Malawi where space is increasingly restricted." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)
quote.aid_transition: "Transition from aid: The programme aims to test the efficacy of interventions at strengthening the financial sustainability, independence and resilience of civil society in different contexts. By focusing in three countries at different positions in the journey from ‘aid dependency’ to ‘aid exit’ [...] Ghana—where some donors are already reducing their footprint—will offer learning that will inform our strategy in Zambia (on the path towards aid exit) and Malawi (still in aid dependency)." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme explicitly shifts power to Southern CSOs by: 1) Putting grantmaking decisions in the hands of local people; 2) Prioritising locally-led CSOs for funding; 3) Designing interventions based on priorities identified by CSOs themselves. While Comic Relief (UK) manages the fund, the Theory of Change emphasises shifting both funding and decision-making power to the Global South.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **fund structure** with two components: 1) **Strengthening African Civil Society Fund** (core/restricted grants + capacity development); 2) **Community Resourcing Match Fund** (training + matched funding for locally generated income). how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Comic Relief serves as the fund manager, responsible for day-to-day operations, grantmaking, and monitoring. A **Programme Advisory Panel (PAP)** provides oversight, and DFID retains strategic oversight through its Inclusive Societies Department. The structure is designed to devolve decision-making to local CSOs while maintaining accountability to both DFID and Comic Relief.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme emphasises **inclusive grantmaking** with principles to ensure accessibility to a wide variety of CSOs. Selection will be based on locally identified priorities and capacity needs, with explicit efforts to reach marginalised groups (e.g., women-led organisations). The design phase included consultations with country offices to ensure alignment with local contexts.
