q24_alternatives_considered: Annual UKAid Match programmes (status quo)
Direct funding to Southern CSOs without intermediary
Short-term projectised grants (3-year model)
Northern-led capacity building programmes
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **long-term partnership with Comic Relief** was chosen to: 1) **Shift power** to Southern CSOs by putting grantmaking in local hands; 2) **Generate evidence** on effective civil society strengthening (addressing a gap identified by ICAI); 3) **Leverage Comic Relief’s unique public engagement** to communicate progressive aid narratives; 4) **Test financial sustainability models** (e.g., match funding) for CSOs in transitioning countries; 5) **Reduce management complexity** by consolidating five annual appeals into one programme. The fund manager model balances local ownership with DFID’s accountability requirements.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (long-term efficiency vs annual programme costs)
partner capacity (Comic Relief’s track record with UK public and Southern CSOs)
equity (explicit focus on shifting power to marginalised groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Comic Relief as single fund manager
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme Advisory Panel (PAP) with Southern representation; DFID oversight through ISD’s strategic board.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Local income generation may fail in restrictive civic spaces (Zambia/Malawi)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot match funding in Ghana first (more enabling environment), then adapt for other countries; provide training and technical support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Short-term political changes could disrupt CSO operations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Long-term core funding (5+ years) to build organisational resilience; focus on financial sustainability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Power imbalances persist despite ‘shifting power’ rhetoric
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit principles for inclusive design; local decision-making on grant allocation; feminist analysis of power dynamics.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (consolidating five appeals into one programme reduces transaction costs)
efficiency (Comic Relief’s existing systems for grant management)
effectiveness (long-term core funding + capacity building for sustainable impact)
equity (prioritising women-led, disability-inclusive, and marginalised CSOs)

quote.alternatives: "In the past, we have co-designed a new programme for each annual matched Comic Relief appeal. Though these programmes have been successful, this has created a complex and strategic programme portfolio. While we will continue to do annual matched public appeals with Comic Relief [...] this new long-term programme will ensure that each appeal contributes to a single programme to ensure efficiency in management, consistency in strategy and value for money." (Document: 55428258.odt, Strategic Case section)
quote.rationale: "A longer-term partnership agreement with Comic Relief will offer the opportunity for deeper strategic alignment, more effective programme interventions and increased value for money. [...] The grant conditions of UKAid Match are designed around successful grantees delivering a project which has been agreed before an appeal is made whereas Comic Relief—itself a grantmaker—needs the flexibility to adapt programmes around CSO delivery partners who bid to Comic Relief to deliver programmes post-appeal." (Document: 55428258.odt, Strategic Case section)
quote.risks: "The programme will begin to address the negative consequences that short-term, projectized donor funding can have on the ability of Southern-based CSOs to stay true to their missions and respond to the priorities of local people." (Document: 55428258.odt, Rationale section)
quote.vfm: "This programme will enable Comic Relief and DFID to communicate a progressive narrative to the UK public about how aid is empowering local people to pursue their own priorities and to stand up for their rights." (Document: 55428258.odt, Rationale section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **regulatory and civic space constraints** in Zambia/Malawi limit the types of CSOs that can operate freely, excluding more advocacy-focused organisations. The **aid transition context** in Ghana/Zambia means some international donors are exiting, requiring CSOs to demonstrate financial sustainability to remain viable. These factors shaped the selection of **locally embedded CSOs** with existing community trust and the inclusion of **financial resilience components** (e.g., match funding).
q27_constraints_detail: Zambia/Malawi’s ‘obstructed’ civic space limits CSO advocacy roles, favouring service-delivery organisations
Ghana’s ‘Beyond Aid’ agenda pressures CSOs to reduce donor dependency, influencing the focus on income diversification
Legal environments affect philanthropic giving, shaping the match fund’s design
Security considerations (no high-risk contexts) exclude conflict-affected areas
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **capacity-building objectives** (organisational resilience, local income generation) require a **fund manager model** (Comic Relief) to provide flexible support while maintaining accountability. The **power-shifting goal** necessitates devolved grantmaking but retains Comic Relief as intermediary to manage UK public funds. The **evidence-generation aim** drives the 10-year timeline and learning components, while the **public narrative objective** leverages Comic Relief’s media reach.
q28_linkages: Need for **long-term core funding** → 10-year programme duration and 5-year minimum grants
Focus on **local income generation** → Creation of Match Fund with training components
**Shift the Power** principle → Grantmaking decisions by local panels
**Public engagement** goal → Partnership with Comic Relief for media campaigns
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **Inclusive grantmaking** (reaching small, marginalised CSOs) vs **transaction costs** (managing many small grants); 2) **Local ownership** (CSO-led priorities) vs **donor accountability** (DFID/Comic Relief reporting requirements); 3) **Flexible capacity building** vs **standardised M&E**. Mitigations include tiered funding (core/restricted), feminist power analysis, and a Programme Advisory Panel to balance these trade-offs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusive design (e.g., small CSOs) increases management complexity but aligns with equity goals
Long-term core funding improves sustainability but reduces short-term measurable outputs
Local income generation (Match Fund) may favour urban CSOs with existing networks, risking exclusion of rural groups
Power-shifting to Southern CSOs requires trusting local decision-making, which may conflict with DFID’s risk aversion
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** and **narrowing civic space** in Zambia/Malawi lead to **milestone-based oversight** (quarterly reporting) and a **phased approach** (testing match funding in Ghana first). The Programme Advisory Panel provides additional scrutiny in higher-risk contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity gaps in Southern CSOs** (identified through country visits) shape the **fund manager’s role** (Comic Relief provides facilitation/training) and the **grant structure** (core funding + capacity development). The focus on **financial sustainability** leads to the Match Fund’s design, while **weak local philanthropy ecosystems** necessitate training components.

quote.context_constrains_who: "Civic space: Over the last decade political rights and civil liberties have come under increasing pressure [...] The programme seeks to understand to what extent building civil society capacity and sustainability can help to protect civil society from these threats in different contexts such as Ghana, where civic space is relatively unchallenged and Zambia and Malawi where space is increasingly restricted." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)
quote.objectives_shape_how: "The programme will be comprised of two core elements: Strengthening African Civil Society Fund [...] Community Resourcing Match Fund [...] The Fund will provide a mix of core and restricted funding as well as quality facilitation to support CSOs in identifying and addressing key capacity and capability barriers." (Document: 55428258.odt, Attached summary section)
quote.equity_efficiency: "ANNEX 1: Options for ensuring the grantmaking process is inclusive" (Document: 55428258.odt, Annex title) and "DFID and Comic Relief have agreed a set of principles for design to ensure that the programme will [...] be inclusive—including in its design phase—and informed by people from the contexts the programme will work in." (Document: 55428258.odt, Design principles section)
quote.risk_management: "The programme will begin to address the negative consequences that short-term, projectized donor funding can have on the ability of Southern-based CSOs to stay true to their missions and respond to the priorities of local people." (Document: 55428258.odt, Rationale section)

key_programme_risks: Comic Relief’s over-reliance as single fund manager may create bottlenecks
Local income generation fails in restricted civic spaces (Zambia/Malawi)
Political changes disrupt CSO operations or civic space
Power imbalances persist despite ‘Shift the Power’ principles
Short-term donor pressures conflict with long-term capacity building
Match funding incentivises income generation over mission alignment
Learning and adaptation mechanisms prove too slow for dynamic contexts
Public narrative backlash if CSO failures are highlighted

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Programme Advisory Panel (PAP) with Southern representation; DFID’s strategic oversight board.
Pilot in Ghana first; provide training and technical support; adapt model based on learning.
Long-term core funding (5+ years); focus on financial sustainability; diversified CSO portfolio.
Explicit principles for inclusive design; local grantmaking panels; feminist power analysis.
10-year programme horizon; consolidated appeals reduce annual reporting burdens.
Core funding alongside match funding; capacity support to align income generation with mission.
Sustained learning investment; quarterly reviews; flexibility to extend post-2025.
Comic Relief’s media expertise; focus on success stories and progressive framing.

fcas_specific_lessons: In obstructed civic spaces (Zambia/Malawi), financial sustainability interventions must be carefully adapted to avoid government backlash
Core funding is critical in FCAS-like contexts to enable CSOs to respond to sudden political changes
Local income generation requires context-specific models (e.g., urban vs rural strategies)
Power-shifting mechanisms must account for elite capture in restricted civic spaces
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous DFID-Comic Relief programmes (e.g., UKAid Match) were successful but created **complex portfolios** due to annual redesigns. The **short-term projectised funding** undermined CSO resilience, and **Northern intermediaries** often diluted local ownership. The Civil Society Partnership Review (2016) highlighted the need for **longer-term support** and **direct funding to Southern CSOs**, while ICAI (2019) recommended **strategic focus on localisation**. These lessons shaped the 10-year duration, core funding emphasis, and power-shifting design.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Consolidated five annual appeals** into one programme to reduce management complexity; 2) **Added core funding** (not just project grants) to address CSO starvation cycle; 3) **Included match funding** to test financial sustainability models; 4) **Explicit power-shifting principles** (e.g., local grantmaking panels); 5) **Longer minimum grant duration** (5 years) for organisational resilience.

quote.previous_lessons: "The negative consequences that short-term, projectized donor funding can have on the ability of Southern-based CSOs to stay true to their missions and respond to the priorities of local people." (Document: 55428258.odt, Rationale section)
quote.design_changes: "In the past, we have co-designed a new programme for each annual matched Comic Relief appeal. Though these programmes have been successful, this has created a complex and strategic programme portfolio. [...] this new long-term programme will ensure that each appeal contributes to a single programme to ensure efficiency in management, consistency in strategy and value for money." (Document: 55428258.odt, Strategic Case section)
quote.fcas_lessons: "Civic space: [...] The programme seeks to understand to what extent building civil society capacity and sustainability can help to protect civil society from these threats in different contexts such as Ghana, where civic space is relatively unchallenged and Zambia and Malawi where space is increasingly restricted." (Document: 55428258.odt, Country selection section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages Comic Relief’s annual matched appeals (e.g., Red Nose Day, Sport Relief), which have historically raised over £60m per appeal from the UK public. The £30m DFID contribution is matched by £30m from Comic Relief, effectively doubling the impact of public donations. Additionally, the match funding component aims to catalyse local philanthropy in Ghana/Zambia/Malawi.

quote.co_funding: "The programme will provide £60 million in funding (£30 million from DFID plus £40k in design costs, and £30m from Comic Relief) over 10 years." (Document: 55428258.odt, Attached summary section)
quote.leverage: "Bypartnering with Comic Relief and the British public through five annual televised matched appeals, Shifting the Power will invest up to £60m (up to £30 from DFID) in building the capacity and sustainability of locally-led civil society organisations." (Document: 55428258.odt, Programme summary section)
quote.match_funding: "The Match Fund will provide training for CSOs in alternative forms of local income generation and will match the resulting revenue that they generate to incentivise income diversification and financial sustainability." (Document: 55428258.odt, Attached summary section)

metadata.programme_name: Combatting International Illicit Finance: Accelerating the 2030 Agenda
metadata.quote: The programme will run from "01/04/2024" to "31/03/2029" (D0005384.odt, SummarySheet)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01/04/2024" and "AMP End Date: 31/03/2029" (D0005384.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **evidence generation** (through the International Centre of Expertise on Illicit Finance for research/analysis), **capacity building** (expanding a network of UK IF experts globally), and **policy influence** (supporting reforms in partner jurisdictions). It aims to strengthen international systems to combat illicit finance (IF) by providing technical expertise, political engagement, and strategic analysis to FCDO posts and partners.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Enhancing the UK’s capability to combat illicit finance (IF) through: a new International Centre of Expertise on Illicit Finance (ICE) to improve our international understanding, preparedness, and response to IF threats... and a strengthened network of UK experts in key jurisdictions and multilateral bodies to build our partners’ resilience to IF and tackle shared challenges." (D0005384.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: Horizon scanning reports on future IF risks/vulnerabilities (disseminated via briefs/alerts)
Specialist research/analysis on IF systems (2–4 month action-oriented studies)
Flexible advisory support to FCDO posts (9-month deployments, phone calls, or dedicated in-country support)
Monitoring/evaluation of ‘what works’ in IF resilience (evidence base for global learning)
Expanded network of 10+ additional IF experts in ODA/non-ODA jurisdictions (from current 4 to 14 total)
Secondments to multilateral bodies (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies, World Bank)
IF Resilience Fund for catalytic, one-off interventions (e.g., regional programming pilots)
Public-facing knowledge library (ICE products published on .gov or custom system)
Training/mentorship for FCDO staff and partner governments (embedded in Country Action Plans)
Policy reforms in partner jurisdictions (e.g., FATF compliance, anti-corruption measures)
what_objectives.summary: The programme establishes a **central hub (ICE)** for IF expertise and expands a **global network of UK IF leads** to strengthen political will, technical capacity, and systemic resilience against illicit financial flows. It bridges gaps between law enforcement, development, and diplomatic efforts while generating actionable evidence to inform HMG and international partners.
what_objectives.quote: "ICE will enhance the FCDO country network and policy teams’ ability to deliver impact by providing... specialist action-oriented research and analysis into IF systems... flexible advisory support to develop technically sound and politically feasible IF responses... and monitoring, evaluation, and lesson learning on ‘what works’ to enhance resilience to IF." (D0005384.odt, Component 1)

countries_regions: Current IF leads in: Nigeria, Somalia, Kenya, Mauritius (G7 IF leads)
SOCnet IF leads in: US, UAE, Singapore, Switzerland, Russian neighbourhood, China, Australia, Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories
Planned expansion to 10 additional jurisdictions (ODA/non-ODA), including:
- Emerging financial centres (e.g., Africa, Middle East)
- Source countries for predicate crimes (e.g., grand corruption, organised crime)
- Multilateral organisations (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies, World Bank, African Union)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as **moderate risk** due to the inherently political and opaque nature of illicit finance, which involves navigating complex transnational networks, kleptocratic elites, and vulnerable jurisdictions. However, the risk is mitigated by FCDO’s existing experience and the phased, adaptive approach.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0005384.odt, SummarySheet) and "IF is a continuously evolving, inherently opaque and intrinsically political problem. Criminals and kleptocrats benefit from vulnerabilities across a wide range of jurisdictions and the international system is only as strong as its weakest link." (D0005384.odt, Context and need for FCDO intervention)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (e.g., kleptocratic regimes, lack of political will)
weak institutions (e.g., financial sector vulnerabilities, corporate transparency gaps)
regulatory (e.g., varying AML/CFT standards across jurisdictions)
data limitations (e.g., opaque shell companies, secretive financial flows)
conflict (e.g., IF funding terrorism or aggression, as seen in Russia-Ukraine)
climate risks (e.g., illegal natural resource extraction linked to IF)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints such as **weak institutions** and **political economy challenges** limit the effectiveness of reforms in partner countries, while **data limitations** hinder tracking and analysis of IF flows. **Conflict zones** increase the risk of aid diversion, and **regulatory fragmentation** complicates cross-border coordination. The programme addresses these by focusing on systemic resilience and political engagement.
where_context.quote: "Experiences in regions like Africa and the Middle East demonstrate challenges for the FCDO country network, especially those without an IF expert, in engaging with complex transnational webs of shell companies, financial crime and political deals." (D0005384.odt, Context and need for FCDO intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **FCDO (UK)** retains full decision-making authority over programme design, partner selection, and strategic direction. While Southern partners (e.g., host governments, multilateral bodies) are engaged in implementation, the **ICE core team and network leads are FCDO project-funded staff**, and external experts are contracted under FCDO frameworks. Southern partners influence priorities through consultation but do not co-lead.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for FCDO country teams on IF analysis and response
Mentorship for host government officials (e.g., FATF compliance, financial sector reforms)
Secondments to multilateral bodies (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies) to build institutional knowledge
Technical assistance to partner jurisdictions (e.g., Kenya’s Financial Action Task Force recommendations)
Knowledge-sharing through ICE’s library and public-facing products
IF Resilience Fund for catalytic interventions (e.g., regional programming pilots)

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (NCA)
partner_organizations.role: Operational response to IF threats (complementary to ICE’s strategic focus)

partner_organizations.name: HM Treasury (HMT) Technical Assistance Unit
partner_organizations.role: Support to countries on FATF standards (parallel to ICE’s political/economic focus)

partner_organizations.name: National Economic Crime Centre (NECC)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of ICE secondee; leads UK’s domestic IF response

partner_organizations.name: SOCnet (Overseas Serious and Organised Crime Policy Network)
partner_organizations.role: Existing network of IF advisers (8 posts) covering non-Africa jurisdictions; to be integrated with ex-DFID IF leads

partner_organizations.name: FATF-Style Regional Bodies (FSRBs)
partner_organizations.role: Potential secondment hosts for UK IF experts; disseminate AML/CFT standards

partner_organizations.name: World Bank / African Union / IMF
partner_organizations.role: Target for UK IF expert secondments; recipients of ICE-generated evidence

partner_organizations.name: Host governments (e.g., Kenya, Nigeria, Somalia, Mauritius)
partner_organizations.role: Implementers of Country Action Plans; recipients of technical advice

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (financial institutions, law firms)
partner_organizations.role: Contributors to ICE’s external expertise network (e.g., cryptocurrency, asset recovery)

partner_organizations.name: Think tanks, academia, NGOs
partner_organizations.role: Providers of specialist research/analysis for ICE products

partner_organizations.name: Civilian Stabilisation Group (CSG)
partner_organizations.role: Roster for deployable IF experts (short-term contracts)

who_partners.quote: "ICE’s design reflects a substantive process... to provide a hub for knowledge, evidence, learning, and expert partnerships from academia, civil society, and the private sector to tackle IF." (D0005384.odt, Component 1) and "The FCDO plays a leading role in the UK’s efforts to combat IF... through bilateral partnerships and relationships with civil society, the private sector, other donors or international actors." (D0005384.odt, Context and need for FCDO intervention)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **combination of project-funded FCDO staff roles (core ICE team and network leads), commercial contracts (for external expertise), and grants (for multilateral/NGO partnerships)**. Funding flows through FCDO’s internal systems, with procurement via framework agreements or low-value contracts. The **IF Resilience Fund** operates as a flexible grant mechanism for catalytic interventions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **FCDO’s Illicit Finance and Anti-Corruption Department (IFAC)** manages the programme directly, with ICE operating as an internal FCDO capability. The **core ICE team (9–15 FCDO staff)** coordinates all delivery, including external partnerships. There is no consortium or multilateral structure; instead, FCDO contracts specialists and secondments as needed.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: External experts are selected via **pre-approved FCDO framework agreements** to ensure rapid, compliant procurement while maintaining value for money. For niche IF themes (e.g., cryptocurrency), **direct awards or single-source contracts** may be used if justified. The **Civilian Stabilisation Group roster** provides vetted deployable experts for short-term needs.
how_mechanism.quote: "Procurement through FCDO Framework Agreements (FA)... Using the frameworks reduces procurement timescale but still offers a competitive process to ensure we’re continuing to drive VFM." (D0005384.odt, Delivery Instruments) and "ICE will use existing FCDO systems to set up an evidence library and helpdesk to triage FCDO posts and teams’ requests." (D0005384.odt, ICE Library)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Economic Crime Delivery Board (ECDB)**, chaired at Director-General level, oversees strategic decisions. The **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO, Brendan McGillen)** manages day-to-day delivery, with gateways for transitioning between ambition levels. **Annual reviews** and **monitoring/evaluation** feed into FCDO’s risk registers and programme adjustments.
how_governance.quote: "The SRO will ensure that a focus is placed on risk management throughout the life of the programme and that the programme remains within FCDO risk appetite... Risk will be identified, assessed, treated, and monitored along all stages of delivery." (D0005384.odt, Risk) and "The programme will hold a risk register that will allow stakeholders easy access to programme risks and enable regular monthly monitoring and review." (D0005384.odt, Risk)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated **between ICE functions and network expansion** based on demand (tracked via ICE’s enquiries system) and performance reviews. However, **major shifts (e.g., adding new jurisdictions)** require SRO approval and alignment with the International Illicit Finance Strategy. The **IF Resilience Fund** allows for one-off catalytic interventions without long-term commitments.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a **phased approach (low → medium → high ambition)** with **annual stocktakes** to adjust priorities. **ICE’s monitoring/evaluation plan** feeds into real-time learning, and the **SRO can approve transitions between ambition levels** based on evidence. The **IF Resilience Fund** enables responsive, innovative piloting (e.g., regional programming).
how_flexibility.quote: "A recommendation: An approach which aims for the programme to scale through and up the levels of ambition over time depending on service performance and demand... Evaluation of the programme may also lead to hybrid recommendations e.g., that the programme scales up ambition on one function such as the network following review, while maintaining service levels for another." (D0005384.odt, Recommendation) and "ICE’s monitoring, evaluation, and lesson learning on ‘what works’ to enhance resilience to IF across the international system." (D0005384.odt, Component 1)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **ICE core team/external experts** (no additional intermediary layers; direct contracting via frameworks or secondments). For multilateral partnerships, an extra layer may exist (FCDO → multilateral → in-country implementation), but this is not the primary model.
how_efficiency.quote: "ICE will operate using a blended delivery model... It will achieve flexibility and value for money (VfM) through a core team of specialist staff alongside partnerships with public and private sector bodies, academia, and civil society." (D0005384.odt, Component 1) and "The actual cost associated with IF lead expansion in the programme’s first year will be small due to no expenditure during the recruitment period (which takes approximately 10 months)." (D0005384.odt, Overview of levels of ambition)

q24_alternatives_considered: No new programme (counterfactual): Rely on existing NCA/HMT capabilities and limited FCDO IF leads
Low ambition: Minimal ICE team (9 staff) + 5 IF leads; limited geographic coverage
Medium ambition: Expanded ICE (12 staff) + 7 IF leads; broader but still selective coverage
High ambition: Full ICE (15 staff + secondments) + 10 IF leads; global coverage including multilaterals
Outsourced ICE: External provider (rejected due to higher costs and lower institutional control)
Standalone ICE: Independent entity (rejected due to setup costs and coordination risks)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen:
The **phased, FCDO-led model** was chosen for: 
1. **Value for Money**: Internal FCDO staff reduce mark-ups (20% savings vs. outsourcing).
2. **Flexibility**: Blended delivery allows adaptive scaling based on demand/learning.
3. **Coordination**: Direct FCDO management ensures alignment with HMG’s Economic Crime Plan and International Illicit Finance Strategy.
4. **Risk Mitigation**: Phased ambition levels allow testing before full scale-up.
5. **Political Access**: FCDO’s diplomatic network enables influence in priority jurisdictions.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (cost savings from in-house staff vs. outsourcing)
experience (builds on existing FCDO IF networks since 2019)
speed (framework agreements enable rapid expert deployment)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on external experts if ICE core team lacks capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased recruitment of core staff (9 → 15) to build in-house expertise before scaling external partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between SOCnet and ex-DFID IF networks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: JEGS process to harmonize grading and formal integration plan by 2024.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow recruitment delays early delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Staggered hiring aligned with ambition levels; use of CSG roster for interim support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Diminishing returns from network expansion beyond 10 posts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Gateway evaluations to assess coverage vs. cost; cap at 10 additional posts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led design
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Country Action Plans co-developed with host governments; secondments to multilaterals (e.g., African Union).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost savings from in-house vs. outsourced delivery)
efficiency (blended model optimizes core staff + external expertise)
effectiveness (phased scaling ensures impact before full investment)
equity (targets developing countries disproportionately affected by IF)
why_rationale.quote: "Hosting ICE within FCDO (rather than establishing an independent capability) from the outset and recruiting civil servants to expand the network will substantially reduce the costs of initial set-up... This is consistent with the broader vision for FCDO’s model for Centres of Expertise." (D0005384.odt, Assessment of efficiency and effectiveness) and "The recommended approach is phased build-up through the levels of ambition until Level 3 (high ambition) which will ultimately deliver the most efficiency, effectiveness, and economy." (D0005384.odt, Recommendation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who:
The **global, transnational nature of IF** constrains partner selection by requiring: 
1. **Jurisdictional access**: Partners must operate in high-risk financial hubs (e.g., Crown Dependencies, UAE) or source countries (e.g., Africa), limiting options to entities with existing networks.
2. **Political sensitivity**: Engagement in kleptocratic regimes (e.g., Russian neighbourhood) requires trusted, discreet partners (e.g., FCDO diplomats or multilaterals like FATF).
3. **Technical capacity**: Southern partners often lack IF expertise, necessitating Northern-led support (e.g., ICE advisory, secondments).
4. **Regulatory alignment**: Partners must comply with FATF standards, excluding non-cooperative jurisdictions.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for **security-cleared experts** (limits pool to FCDO/vetted contractors)
**FATF compliance** requirements restrict partner eligibility
**Kleptocratic regimes** in source countries require diplomatic channels (e.g., FCDO posts)
**Emerging financial centres** (e.g., Africa) lack local expertise, necessitating external deployment
**Multilateral engagement** (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies) prioritized for systemic influence
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The **strategic, political, and systemic focus** of the programme determines its delivery structure by: 
1. **Complexity of IF**: Requires a **centralized hub (ICE)** to synthesize global expertise and a **decentralized network** to engage locally.
2. **Political economy challenges**: Demands **embedded FCDO staff** (not outsourced providers) to navigate sensitive reforms.
3. **Need for agility**: Uses **framework agreements** for rapid expert deployment and an **IF Resilience Fund** for catalytic interventions.
4. **Knowledge gaps**: Combines **in-house research** (ICE) with **external partnerships** (academia, private sector) to cover technical depth.
q28_linkages: **Evidence generation (WHAT)** → **Centralized hub (HOW)**: ICE’s research/analysis function requires a core FCDO team to ensure HMG alignment.
**Capacity building (WHAT)** → **Network expansion (HOW)**: Scaling IF leads from 4 to 14 mirrors the need for geographic coverage to address transnational IF flows.
**Policy influence (WHAT)** → **Diplomatic channels (HOW)**: FCDO’s country posts and multilaterals (e.g., FATF) are leveraged to drive reforms.
**Flexibility needs (WHAT)** → **Phased scaling (HOW)**: Ambition levels adjust based on demand, linking adaptive management to real-time learning.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
Explicit trade-offs include: 
1. **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: The programme prioritizes **UK-led expertise (ICE core team, SOCnet)** for efficiency but risks limited local ownership. Mitigation includes secondments to multilaterals (e.g., African Union) and co-developed Country Action Plans.
2. **Speed vs. inclusion**: **Framework agreements** enable rapid expert deployment but may exclude Southern institutions lacking pre-approval. The IF Resilience Fund allows some responsive Southern-led pilots.
3. **Global coverage vs. depth**: Expanding to **10+ jurisdictions** risks spreading resources thinly; the phased approach balances breadth (transit/hub countries) with depth (source countries).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: **UK staffing (efficiency)** vs. **local capacity (equity)**: Core ICE team is FCDO-project-funded, with Southern partners as implementers.
**Framework contracts (speed)** vs. **open competition (inclusion)**: Pre-approved suppliers ensure VFM but limit Southern firm participation.
**Global hub (coordination)** vs. **regional adaptation (relevance)**: ICE’s centralized research may overlook context-specific needs; regional pilots (e.g., Africa) address this.
**High-ambition scaling (impact)** vs. **cost control (economy)**: Level 3 ambition (£10.84m/year) risks diminishing returns; gateways assess VFM.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (political opacity, kleptocratic actors) drives **intensive oversight**: monthly risk reviews, SRO approval for ambition transitions, and embedded M&E. High-risk jurisdictions (e.g., conflict zones) use **CSG roster experts** for short-term, controlled engagements.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 
- **Host governments** receive training/mentorship to implement Country Action Plans.
- **Multilateral secondments** (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies) build institutional knowledge.
- **IF Resilience Fund** pilots enable Southern partners to test innovative approaches, feeding into global learning.
intersections.quote: "The programme will set risk appetite for each of the seven risk categories... Risk will be identified, assessed, treated, and monitored along all stages of delivery, and risk that exceeds category risk appetite will be escalated appropriately." (D0005384.odt, Risk) and "Recognising the success of FCDO’s initial investment in building a small overseas network, the White Paper commits the FCDO to ‘deploy an expanded network of IF experts’ at post." (D0005384.odt, Component 2)

key_programme_risks: Insufficient political will in partner jurisdictions to enact IF reforms
Displacement of IF to new jurisdictions as existing hubs strengthen controls
Over-reliance on external experts if ICE core team lacks capacity
Fragmentation between SOCnet and ex-DFID IF networks
Slow recruitment delays early delivery (10-month lead time)
Aid diversion in high-risk/conflict contexts
Diminishing returns from network expansion beyond 10 posts
Limited Southern ownership due to Northern-led design
Emerging threats (e.g., crypto, new transit hubs) outpacing programme adaptation
Reputational risk if UK’s financial centre status is undermined by IF scandals

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient political will in partner jurisdictions
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ICE’s political economy analysis informs targeted engagement; IF Resilience Fund supports catalytic reforms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Displacement of IF to new jurisdictions
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: 'Follow the money' approach with expanded network coverage; regional programming pilots.
Phased recruitment of core ICE team (9 → 15) to build in-house capacity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fragmentation between SOCnet and ex-DFID networks
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: JEGS process for grading harmonization; formal integration plan by 2024.
Staggered hiring; use of CSG roster for interim support.
Enhanced due diligence; quarterly risk reviews; PrOF Rule 18 compliance.
Cap at 10 additional posts; gateway evaluations to assess coverage.
Secondments to multilaterals (e.g., African Union); co-developed Country Action Plans.
ICE’s horizon scanning; adaptive management via annual reviews.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk to UK financial centre
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Alignment with Economic Crime Plan 2; NECC secondee for domestic-international linkage.

fcas_specific_lessons: In **Africa and the Middle East**, weak institutions and political deals complicate IF engagement; response: **long-term, patient approach** with local political economy analysis.
**Conflict zones** (e.g., Somalia) require **short-term, flexible experts** (CSG roster) due to security risks.
**Kleptocratic regimes** necessitate **diplomatic channels** (FCDO posts) over direct technical assistance.
**Emerging financial centres** (e.g., Mauritius) need **preemptive support** to avoid becoming IF hubs.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
1. **TIFIG programme (2020–21)**: Pilots showed that **small core teams risk over-reliance on externals**; ICE’s design now includes scaled core staff.
2. **SOCnet transfer to FCDO (2022)**: Highlighted **governance fragmentation**; current programme formalizes integration.
3. **DFID’s initial IF network (2019)**: Proved **long-term deployments** more effective than short-term missions; informed 10+ post expansion.
4. **UK-UAE Partnership on IF**: Demonstrated **bilateral technical support** can catalyse large-scale cases (e.g., money laundering prosecutions).
5. **CSSF Combatting Illicit Economies Programme**: Regional programming **strengthened cross-border responses**; informed IF Resilience Fund’s regional pilot.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Phased ambition levels** (low → high) added to **test demand before scaling** (learned from TIFIG pilots).
2. **JEGS process for grading harmonization** to address **morale/retention risks** in SOCnet vs. ex-DFID networks.
3. **IF Resilience Fund** created to **enable rapid, catalytic interventions** (lesson from CSSF’s regional approach).
4. **Secondments to multilaterals** (e.g., FATF-Style Regional Bodies) added to **leverage systemic influence** (from DFID network limitations).
5. **Blended delivery model** (core staff + external experts) balances **in-house control with specialist depth** (from TIFIG’s outsourcing challenges).
risks_lessons.quote: "Multiple Annual Reviews of the TIFIG programme have found that a modest, flexible resource for IF leads to draw on where rapid programme funding is required to build relationships or catalyse progress to tackle IF considerably increases the effectiveness and impact of IF leads." (D0005384.odt, Component 2) and "Learning from HMG’s Conflict, Stability and Security Fund (CSSF) Combatting Illicit Economies Programme... suggests that regional programming... would strengthen the network’s impact." (D0005384.odt, Component 2)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages **£4m/year (2022/23–2025/26) from JFU** for SOCnet IF leads, reducing ODA requirements. It also **catalyses multilateral funding** (e.g., IMF Anti-Money Laundering Trust Fund) by providing political/economic analysis to inform technical assistance.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget is **primarily revenue** (staff salaries, contracts, grants) with minimal capital expenditure (e.g., potential custom knowledge management system in later phases).
financial_details.quote: "A provision for up to 10 additional, programme-funded posts in ODA and non-ODA eligible jurisdictions is proposed... Non-ODA programme budget is set aside in this business case to cover the costs of the existing SOCnet IF network should this be necessary beyond 2025/26." (D0005384.odt, Component 2) and "When SOCnet was transferred to FCDO... a transfer of funds to the amount of £4 million per year from Joint Funds Unit (JFU) to the FCDO was agreed." (D0005384.odt, Component 2)

metadata.programme_name: Nigeria Governance and Climate Programme (NGCP)

quote.text: NGCP is a 4-year £38.8m programme supporting more accountable and inclusive institutions to respond to Nigeria’s interrelated governance and climate change challenges.

duration_source.text: The NGCP is a 4-year, £38.8 million programme designed to support more accountable and inclusive institutions to respond to Nigeria’s interrelated governance and climate change challenges. This includes 6 months for inception.
duration_source.source: D0006126.odt, Programme summary and Financial Case

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The NGCP combines capacity building (strengthening institutions), policy influence (mainstreaming climate action in government systems), and implementation research (testing politically-informed coalitions). It focuses on governance reforms to address climate change through institutional change and citizen empowerment.

q1_source.text: The NGCP will build on learning and successes of 20 years of governance programming in Nigeria... It will take an explicitly political approach, addressing climate change as a political and governance issue... It will facilitate new coalitions, bringing together reformers, civil society, the private sector, and those impacted by poor governance and/or climate change... combined with targeted, politically informed assistance to strengthen government systems and targeted, politically informed support to citizen empowerment and accountability.
q1_source.source: D0006126.odt, Programme purpose and Approach sections

q3_expected_outputs: Institutional and legal reform processes that support more inclusive power structures and climate change response
Coalitions of citizens (NGOs, civil society, private sector, legislatures) influencing government to resolve climate/governance problems and hold government accountable
Increased state government income from Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) and better preparedness to access climate finance
Strengthened state planning, budgeting, and policies for better response to climate risks and impacts, including through social protection
Strengthened elections delivery and credibility
30% of resources driven towards gender equality and inclusion
what_objectives.summary: The NGCP aims to create more accountable and inclusive institutions in Nigeria that can effectively respond to governance and climate change challenges by combining systems strengthening, coalition-building, and citizen empowerment with a strong political economy focus.

quote.text: The NGCP is designed to support more accountable and inclusive institutions to respond to Nigeria’s interrelated governance, population, and climate change challenges... A major focus of the programme is climate adaptation and resilience, recognising the linkages between governance challenges and an effective response to climate change.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Programme summary and Programme purpose

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nigeria faces multiple acute development and climate challenges, with high levels of poverty (86 million living on <$1.90/day), conflict (third largest number of conflict deaths globally), and climate vulnerability (floods, droughts, desertification). The political settlement is elitist, reinforcing social exclusion and inhibiting effective climate response.

q5_source.text: Nigeria faces multiple and acute development and climate challenges... Nigeria now has the third largest number of conflict deaths globally... The political settlement is underpinned by five interlinked governance constraints... These strategies have until recent years maintained stability, holding an ethnically diverse country together and allowing for a relatively peaceful transition between elite groups. Externaldrivers and shocks today place this system under stress... Growing tensions, manifesting as conflict and instability in all parts of the country are now proving harder to contain.
q5_source.source: D0006126.odt, Context and need for FCDO intervention

q6_contextual_constraints: security (conflict and instability in North-East and North-West)
political economy (elitist power structures, weak social contract)
weak institutions (under-resourced state ministries, poor climate finance implementation)
conflict (high fertility areas with rapid population growth and climate vulnerability)
data limitations (limited climate data collection at state level)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The elitist political settlement and weak institutions make it difficult to implement climate adaptation measures. Conflict in the North-East and North-West exacerbates vulnerability, while limited state capacity (e.g., single Climate Desk Officers without resources) hinders effective planning and budgeting for climate resilience. Rapid population growth and climate shocks further strain services and governance systems.

quote.text: Governance in Nigeria is elitist, reinforcing social exclusion and inhibiting the provision of basic services... State Ministries of Environment are typically under-resourced... Climate data collection at federal and state level is limited and not used to drive policy or planning... The social contract is breaking down as the population grows and the impacts of climate change are being felt by the poorest and most vulnerable in society.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Context and need for FCDO intervention

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed to be locally led, with Nigerian facilitators and state governments driving issue selection and coalition-building. FCDO provides strategic oversight and technical support, but local ownership is central to sustainability. Decision-making on issues and interventions is guided by political economy analysis and local context, with 30% of the budget earmarked for gender equality and inclusion.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to state governments (e.g., climate-sensitive public financial management, social protection systems)
peer learning between states (e.g., knowledge sharing on fiscal reforms)
citizen empowerment (e.g., training for civil society to engage in budget tracking and advocacy)
support to electoral institutions (e.g., INEC for election credibility and voter mobilization)
research and learning integration (e.g., continuous political economy analysis to inform adaptive programming)

partner_organizations.name: State Governments (Kano, Kaduna, Jigawa, Yobe, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiaries and co-implementers of governance and climate reforms

partner_organizations.name: Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for strengthening election delivery and credibility

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (e.g., Civil Society Situation Room, #NotTooYoungToRun)
partner_organizations.role: Coalition partners for citizen accountability and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Private Sector
partner_organizations.role: Member of issue-based coalitions for climate and governance reforms

partner_organizations.name: USAID (potential partner for Component 3 on elections)
partner_organizations.role: Possible MoU or Accountable Grant for electoral support (VFM and coordination)

partner_organizations.name: Contracted Service Provider/Consortium
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of Components 1, 2, 4, and 5 (issue-based coalitions, governance capability, research, and strategic opportunities)

partner_organizations.name: Nigeria Governors’ Forum / DAWN Commission / South-East Governors Forum
partner_organizations.role: Platforms for light-touch technical assistance (Tier 2 engagement)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (SFTAS programme)
partner_organizations.role: Leverage partner for governance reforms and climate finance

quote.text: Local ownership is at the heart of the programme, as this is proven to deliver results and ensures sustainability of impact... The programme will deploy expert Nigerian facilitators with deep understanding of the context and political economy... FCDO Nigeria may seek an MoU with USAID or Accountable Grant for Component 3 (elections)... The NGCP will be implemented in 3 states in Nigeria, with targeted strategic engagement at Federal or regional level.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Approach to implementation and Delivery sections

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a commercial contract for Components 1, 2, 4, and 5 (issue-based coalitions, governance capability, research, and strategic opportunities), while Component 3 (elections) may be delivered via an MoU with USAID or an Accountable Grant. This hybrid approach allows flexibility to leverage existing partnerships (e.g., USAID’s governance programmes) while maintaining control over core components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Components 1, 2, 4, and 5 will be managed by a contracted service provider or consortium under a commercial agreement with FCDO. Component 3 (elections) may involve a separate partnership with USAID. FCDO retains oversight through its programme management team (1.6% of budget), with embedded learning and adaptive management across all components.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The use of a commercial contract for most components suggests a competitive procurement process to select the service provider/consortium. For Component 3, an MoU with USAID is preferred for value for money (VFM), coordination, and leverage, given USAID’s existing governance programmes in Nigeria (e.g., State2State).

quote.text: Delivery of the NGCP will be through two routes: Components 1, 2, 4 and 5 - a contracted service provider or consortium. Component 3 - FCDO will consider an MoU with USAID or Accountable Grant or combination of both. We believe this offers the best VFM, coordination with other international partners and leverage for FCDO.

NGCP will report regularly to HMG’s integrated management structures in Nigeria, including the Delivery Board, which provides in-depth controls and oversight of ODA spending... The programme will integrate learning across all elements... Specialist staff will design and implement a crosscutting learning strategy that will enable NGCP to learn what is working, adapt as necessary, and support other FCDO programmes.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Management Case and Learning approach

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme is designed to be flexible and adaptive, with resourcing adjusted based on political opportunities and intervention success. Up to 20% of the issue-based coalitions budget can be notionally reserved for federal interventions if linked to tangible opportunities. The Strategic Opportunities Fund (1% of budget) allows rapid response to emerging needs (e.g., climate disasters).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes a ‘thinking and working politically’ approach, with continuous learning integrated across all components. The Theory of Change assumes that institutional changes require flexible, politically informed adaptations. Specialist staff will monitor progress and enable adjustments based on real-time evidence.

quote.text: The component structure has been designed to be flexible and adaptive so that resourcing can be adjusted depending on political opportunities and the success of the interventions... The NGCP will take a flexible and adaptive way to take advantage of political opportunities as they arise, allowing scale up or scale back of activities... Learning will inform implementation and support flexible and adaptive programming.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Component structure and Learning approach

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Contracted Service Provider/Consortium (Components 1,2,4,5) and FCDO → USAID (Component 3, if MoU route is selected).

quote.text: Programme Management (1.6% of budget) - not shown on diagram below - is an internal FCDO programme fund covering costs to manage the programme... Delivery of the NGCP will be through two routes: Components 1, 2, 4 and 5 - a contracted service provider or consortium. Component 3 - FCDO will consider an MoU with USAID or Accountable Grant...
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Financial Case and Delivery section

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (counterfactual - no additional FCDO support)
Capacity building and systems strengthening (focused on State Ministries of Budget, Planning, Social Protection, Elections, and Climate Change)
Climate and governance-focused issue-based coalitions (bringing stakeholders together to tackle specific problems)
Holistic, political economy approach (combining coalition support with targeted systems strengthening and accountability interventions)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The holistic, political economy approach was selected because it addresses the root causes of Nigeria’s governance and climate challenges—elitist power structures and weak accountability—through a combination of coalition-building, systems strengthening, and citizen empowerment. This approach is evidence-based (20 years of FCDO governance programming in Nigeria) and aligns with the UK’s Integrated Review priorities on democratic governance and climate resilience. The mixed delivery structure (contract + potential USAID partnership) balances control with leverage, while adaptive management ensures responsiveness to Nigeria’s dynamic political context.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging USAID’s existing programmes for elections support)
risk mitigation (flexible design to adapt to political opportunities and shocks)
past experience (building on 20 years of FCDO governance work in Nigeria)
partner capacity (using expert Nigerian facilitators and trusted state relationships)
flexibility (adaptive programming to respond to emerging needs, e.g., climate disasters)
equity (30% of budget for gender equality and inclusion, focus on marginalized regions)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Procurement delays (as experienced by other FCDO Nigeria programmes) may truncate implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: A 17-month cost extension (instead of 12 months) was requested to align with the original Business Case timeline and allow for a 4-year commercial contract with the supplier.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coalition-building in an elitist political context may face resistance from entrenched interests.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme uses politically savvy Nigerian facilitators and a ‘thinking and working politically’ approach to identify feasible reform opportunities and build broad stakeholder alliances.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: State-level implementation may be hindered by weak institutional capacity (e.g., under-resourced Ministries of Environment).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted technical assistance and peer learning (e.g., through the Nigeria Governors’ Forum) will strengthen state systems, while federal engagement is limited to strategic opportunities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate finance accountability risks due to Nigeria’s poor track record (e.g., green bond project failures).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will sensitize state governments to climate finance opportunities while embedding transparency and citizen oversight mechanisms.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing platforms like USAID’s State2State programme)
effectiveness (evidence-based approach with 20 years of FCDO learning)
equity (30% budget for gender/inclusion, focus on North-West/North-East regions)

quote.text: The Appraisal Case sets out three realistic options... for how FCDO can influence institutional, financial, policy, and legal reform to ensure that governance in Nigeria is more accountable and inclusive and better positioned to deal with the impacts of climate change on poor people... The NGCP will build on learning and successes of 20 years of governance programming in Nigeria... The programme is designed to be flexible and adaptive... The NGCP combines a deliberate focus on issue-based working with targeted technical assistance to government and support to citizen empowerment, all underpinned by thinking and working politically and flexible and adaptive approaches.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Appraisal Case and Approach sections

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Nigeria—particularly conflict in the North-East/North-West and elitist power structures—limits partner selection to organizations with deep local trust and political savvy. State governments in these regions are prioritized due to their high climate vulnerability and poverty, but their weak institutional capacity requires targeted technical assistance. The need for rapid adaptation to climate shocks (e.g., floods) also shapes the choice of flexible partners like USAID for elections support.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict and insecurity in North-East/North-West restrict operations to trusted local partners (e.g., state governments with existing FCDO relationships).
Elitist political economy necessitates politically astute facilitators (e.g., Nigerian experts) to navigate power dynamics.
Weak state institutions require partners with capacity-building expertise (e.g., World Bank SFTAS for fiscal reforms).
Climate vulnerability demands partners able to respond quickly to disasters (e.g., Strategic Opportunities Fund for sudden-onset events).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s focus on politically informed coalitions and adaptive governance reforms drives the mixed delivery structure: a commercial contract for flexible, issue-based work (Components 1, 2, 4, 5) and a potential USAID partnership for elections (Component 3). The need for local ownership and learning requires embedded Nigerian facilitators, while the risk of procurement delays justifies the 17-month extension.
q28_linkages: Issue-based coalitions (Component 1) require a contracted provider with expertise in convening diverse stakeholders, linked to the adaptive management approach.
Governance capability strengthening (Component 2) aligns with the use of technical assistance partners (e.g., World Bank SFTAS) to leverage existing platforms.
Elections support (Component 3) is delivered via USAID to capitalize on their ongoing governance programmes and ensure VFM.
Research and learning (Component 4) is integrated across all components to enable real-time adaptations, requiring a provider with MEL expertise.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (30% budget for gender/inclusion, focus on marginalized regions) with efficiency (leveraging USAID partnerships, 1.6% management costs). Trade-offs include: (1) prioritizing high-vulnerability states (North-West/North-East) over easier-to-reach areas, and (2) investing in long-term institutional change (e.g., social protection systems) despite slower results than direct service delivery.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Adaptive programming allows rapid response to political opportunities but requires continuous stakeholder engagement to ensure marginalized groups (e.g., women, youth) are included.
Expertise vs. ownership: While Nigerian facilitators lead implementation, FCDO retains oversight to balance local leadership with UK priorities (e.g., ICF eligibility).
Cost vs. reach: The 17-month extension increases costs but is necessary to achieve meaningful governance reforms in a complex context.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS risk profile (conflict, weak institutions) drives intensive oversight through FCDO’s Delivery Board and milestone-based reporting. Embedded learning and adaptive management are critical to mitigate risks of political resistance or implementation delays.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with partners selected based on their ability to strengthen state systems (e.g., IGR reforms) and citizen accountability (e.g., budget tracking). The role of Nigerian facilitators is central to ensuring interventions are politically feasible and locally owned.

quote.text: The NGCP will operate largely at the State and Local Government level because Nigeria’s federal structure grants substantial authority to State Governments... States in the North-West and North-East regions of Nigeria suffer the greatest levels of poverty and climate vulnerability... The programme will deploy expert Nigerian facilitators with deep understanding of the context and political economy... The NGCP will build on learning and successes of 20 years of governance programming in Nigeria, taking a ‘thinking and working politically’ approach... The component structure has been designed to be flexible and adaptive so that resourcing can be adjusted depending on political opportunities.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Geographic engagement, Approach, and Component structure sections

key_programme_risks: Procurement delays truncating implementation (mitigated by 17-month extension).
Elitist power structures resisting reforms (mitigated by politically informed coalitions and Nigerian facilitators).
Weak state capacity hindering climate adaptation (mitigated by technical assistance and peer learning).
Climate finance accountability risks (mitigated by transparency mechanisms and citizen oversight).
Conflict and insecurity in target regions (mitigated by trusted local partnerships and adaptive programming).
Low citizen awareness of climate change links to livelihoods (mitigated by advocacy and social protection integration).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Procurement delays (as seen in other FCDO Nigeria programmes) may shorten the effective implementation period.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Requested a 17-month (instead of 12-month) extension to align with the original Business Case and allow for a 4-year commercial contract.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political resistance to governance reforms from elite groups.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of ‘thinking and working politically’ approaches, issue-based coalitions that unite diverse stakeholders, and Nigerian facilitators with deep contextual knowledge.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: State Ministries of Environment lack resources and authority to implement climate plans.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted technical assistance to mainstream climate action in state budgets and planning cycles, combined with citizen engagement to demand accountability.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor track record of climate finance implementation in Nigeria (e.g., green bond failures).
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Sensitize state governments to climate finance opportunities while embedding transparency and tracking mechanisms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Conflict and insecurity in North-East/North-West may disrupt programme activities.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on states with existing FCDO relationships (e.g., Kaduna, Kano, Jigawa) and adaptive programming to respond to shocks.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low citizen awareness of climate change impacts on livelihoods (e.g., flooding, droughts).
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Integrate climate adaptation with social protection and service delivery issues that resonate with citizens, using coalitions to raise awareness.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts like Nigeria, governance reforms must address elite power structures directly rather than bypassing them (lesson from 20 years of FCDO programming).
Conflict-affected regions require adaptive, politically informed interventions that build on existing trust (e.g., FCDO’s long-term engagement in Kaduna, Kano).
Climate vulnerability is exacerbated by weak institutions, so interventions must combine technical support (e.g., IGR reforms) with accountability mechanisms (e.g., citizen budget tracking).
Elections in FCAS contexts need both institutional strengthening (e.g., INEC) and citizen mobilization (e.g., PVT exercises) to enhance credibility.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous FCDO programmes in Nigeria (e.g., PERL, LEAP) demonstrated that: (1) interventions are more impactful when informed by local politics and power dynamics; (2) durable governance changes occur where there is strong citizen engagement; (3) peer learning between states accelerates reforms; and (4) flexible, adaptive programming is essential in dynamic contexts. The NGCP builds on these lessons by embedding political economy analysis, citizen accountability, and adaptive management.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The NGCP’s design reflects lessons from prior programmes through: (1) a flexible component structure to adjust resourcing based on opportunities; (2) explicit focus on gender and inclusion (30% of budget); (3) integration of learning across all components rather than siloed MEL; (4) use of Nigerian facilitators for political savvy; and (5) a Strategic Opportunities Fund (1% of budget) for rapid response to emerging needs (e.g., climate disasters).

quote.text: A key lesson has been that our interventions are more impactful when they are fundamentally informed by local politics... Evidence shows that the most durable changes to core governance processes occurred where there was strong citizen engagement... The NGCP will take a ‘thinking and working politically’ approach, facilitating coalitions which unite diverse actors... The programme will work in a flexible and adaptive way to take advantage of political opportunities as they arise... The NGCP will build on learning and successes of 20 years of governance programming in Nigeria.
quote.source: D0006126.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending and Approach sections

co_funding_partners.partner: Potential development partners (e.g., via Key Political Partners Group and Nigeria Development Partners Group)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: FCDO Nigeria aims to mobilize up to £10 million in additional funding from other donors, which would offset UK ODA allocations for scaling successful approaches. The programme will also leverage existing platforms like the World Bank’s SFTAS (which has unlocked $750m in grant funding for state-level reforms) and USAID’s State2State programme.

quote.text: The projected budget is £38.8m over 4 years... Programme Management (1.6% of budget)... FCDO Nigeria may seek a Phase 2 costed extension... to bring the total programme up to £67m... It will be subject to demand and need; affordability; programme and supplier performance; value for money; and recommendations from the mid-term independent evaluation. FCDO Nigeria will seek to bring other donors on board with the programme objectives through our strategic engagement and advocacy... to mobilise additional funding contributions of up to £10 million.

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Africa’s Science Granting Councils (SGCI2)

quote.programme_name: "Strengthening Africa’s Science Granting Councils (SGCI2)" (D0006963.odt, Title)
quote.duration: "Programme start and end date: August 2021–Mar 2025" (D0006963.odt, Part1–ForMAG&HMT)
quote.primary_sector: "Science, technology and innovation" (90000723.odt, Country/Region or Sector)

metadata.duration_source: "Programme start and end date: August 2021–Mar 2025" (D0006963.odt, Part1–ForMAG&HMT)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SGCI2 is a multi-faceted programme that combines capacity building of Science Granting Councils (SGCs) in Africa, financing mechanisms for research competitions, policy influence through evidence generation, and strategic partnerships to strengthen national research systems. It aims to improve research management, private sector engagement, gender inclusivity, and UK-Africa science diplomacy.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SGCI2 will build on the UK’s already strong investment in science to improve the capabilities of Africa’s national Science Granting Councils (SGCs)... SGCI2 will support the production of research to address local challenges and build economies... SGCI2 will also allow the UK to engage with Africa as we develop a new framework for international science partnerships..." (90000723.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: More efficient research competitions among the SGCs
Strengthened funding bodies or new ST&I funding bodies in West Africa
Increased use of data and evidence in policy and decision-making among SGCs
Improved private sector engagement and commercialization of research results
Greater integration of gender equality and inclusivity among SGCs
Increased communication, uptake of knowledge outputs and collaboration between SGCs
Support for 17 national SGCs in sub-Saharan Africa
Leverage of £11.7 million co-funding from Sida, NRF, DFG, and IDRC
UK/Africa Science Partnership fund promoting research collaboration (£1.34 million)
what_objectives.summary: SGCI2 aims to strengthen Africa’s national Science Granting Councils to improve research management, foster private sector engagement, promote gender inclusivity, and enhance UK-Africa science partnerships for sustainable economic growth and addressing local challenges.

quote.objectives: "SGCI2 will build on the UK’s already strong investment in science to improve the capabilities of Africa’s national Science Granting Councils (SGCs)... SGCI2 will support the production of research to address local challenges and build economies through the creation of commercially viable products and services in Africa." (90000723.odt, Programmesummary)
quote.outputs: "Outputs measured under this SGCI2 are listed below...: More efficient research competitions among the SGCs; Strengthened funding bodies or new ST&I funding bodies in West Africa; Increased use of data and evidence in policy and decision-making among SGCs..." (90000723.odt, Outputs measured under this SGCI2)

Limited private sector engagement due to lack of policy frameworks and enabling structures for knowledge transfer between public and private sectors. Data limitations affect evidence-based policy making.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is led by IDRC (Canada) with technical leadership from NRF (South Africa) and FCDO involvement through regional RED hubs. Decision-making is shared across partners, with IDRC managing the overall programme and FCDO providing oversight through regional hubs.

mentorship programmes
research grants for collaborative competitions
institutional strengthening of SGCs
gender equality and inclusivity mainstreaming
policy framework development for private sector engagement

quote.delivery_structure: "SGCI2 is a multi-donor partnership programme led by Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC) and FCDO that leverages additional funding from IDRC, Swedish International Development Co-operation Agency (Sida), South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF), and the German Research Foundation (DFG)..." (90000723.odt, Delivery method)
quote.lead_institution: "The overall programme will be led by IDRC, who have extensive experience in research capacity development in Africa in partnership with the regional RED hubs." (90000723.odt, Option 2 Appraisal)
quote.capacity_building: "Strengthening the ability of 17 of Africa’s Science Granting Councils to manage research competitions and promote collaborative research... Support establishment of new and stronger Councils in West Africa... Promoting Gender Equality and Inclusivity through explicit work to improve gender balance in the research systems in Africa..." (90000723.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme operates as a multi-donor partnership with a joint funding pool managed by IDRC. FCDO contributes £9.94 million (later revised to £11.24 million) alongside co-funding from Sida, NRF, and DFG. Funds are allocated through collaborative agreements rather than traditional grants or contracts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IDRC manages the overall programme with technical leadership from NRF and oversight from FCDO’s regional RED hubs. The structure includes multiple partners with defined roles, open procurement for technical agencies, and coordination through a joint governance framework.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (direct award to IDRC based on existing partnership)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection of IDRC as lead partner is based on their extensive experience in research capacity development in Africa and successful management of SGCI Phase 1. The partnership approach leverages existing relationships and co-funding commitments from other donors.

quote.funding_instrument: "This partnership programme would be jointly funded with IDRC, NRF, Sida and DFG... IDRC manages the overall programme..." (90000723.odt, Option 2 Appraisal)
quote.management_structure: "IDRC manages the overall programme, with a variety of third-party organisations to ensure delivery happens at an internationally recognised standard, whilst also ensuring FCDO has oversight of the programme." (90000723.odt, Delivery method)
quote.partner_selection: "This option takes a pragmatic approach to work with other funding partners to support research systems development. In this case FCDO would leverage existing partnerships through a jointly funded programme with Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC)..." (90000723.odt, Option 2: The Partnership Approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is governed by an Executive Committee (likely the steering committee) that includes representation from FCDO’s RED hubs to ensure oversight and coordination. The committee may consider inviting additional countries and manages the overall programme direction.

quote.day_to_day: "IDRC manages the overall programme..." (90000723.odt, Delivery method)
quote.sub_award: "The SGCI Executive Committee may consider inviting additional countries." (90000723.odt, Support establishment of new and stronger Councils in West Africa)
quote.governance: "The RED Regional Research and Innovation Hubs will be present in the governance structures of the programme to ensure read across." (90000723.odt, Option 2 Appraisal)
quote.oversight: "A strong learning and evaluation component was included in SGCI1 and will be continued in SGCI2 which will help mitigate this risk." (90000723.odt, Option 2: The Partnership Approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated across distinct but synergistic workstreams with some flexibility to respond to emerging priorities, particularly in areas like COVID-19 research. Reallocation likely requires approval from the governance structure.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a learning and evaluation component to monitor progress and adapt to changing needs. Adjustments to research priorities can be made in response to national priorities (e.g., COVID-19) but require coordination among partners.
