how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IDRC (lead partner) → Technical agencies/contractors → National Science Granting Councils (end implementers)

quote.layers: "IDRC manages the overall programme, with a variety of third-party organisations to ensure delivery happens at an internationally recognised standard... FCDO’s involvement will be led by the RED research and innovation Hubs based in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa..." (90000723.odt, Delivery method)
quote.payment: "The programme will be informed by and build on previous SGCI programming and consultations with national SGCs." (90000723.odt, Option 2 Appraisal) [implies milestone-based disbursements]

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Counterfactual – "do nothing more" (minimal coordination, no new funding)
Option 2: Partnership Approach (preferred) – multi-donor consortium led by IDRC
Option 3: Delivery through Direct Commissioning – FCDO-designed programmes with implementing partners
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The partnership approach (Option 2) was chosen for its ability to leverage £11 million in additional co-funding, build on successful Phase 1 outcomes, and provide a coordinated donor approach. It maximizes effectiveness by combining FCDO’s strategic priorities with IDRC’s technical expertise and regional presence, while mitigating risks through shared governance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of coherence in a multi-donor partnership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong learning and evaluation component continued from SGCI1; FCDO RED hubs embedded in governance structures for oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of coordinating multiple funders and partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IDRC’s experience in managing multi-donor programmes; clear division of roles among partners.

quote.alternatives: "Option 1: The counterfactual - ‘do nothing more’... Option 2: The Partnership Approach (preferred option)... Option 3: Delivery through Direct Commissioning..." (90000723.odt, Options appraisal)
quote.why_chosen: "This option takes a pragmatic approach to work with other funding partners to support research systems development... This approach would maximise the effectiveness of Councils to strengthen national ST&I systems... and continue to position the UK as a science partner of choice for Africa..." (90000723.odt, Option 2: The Partnership Approach)
quote.risks: "The risk: of this approach is loss of coherence of the overall programme. A strong learning and evaluation component was included in SGCI1 and will be continued in SGCI2 which will help mitigate this risk." (90000723.odt, Option 2: The Partnership Approach)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope in sub-Saharan Africa, including fragile states (e.g., Ethiopia, Nigeria), requires partners with regional experience and the ability to navigate diverse political and institutional contexts. This constrains partner selection to organizations like IDRC and NRF, which have established presence and trust in the region.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with experience in fragile contexts (e.g., Ethiopia, Nigeria, Uganda)
Requirement for multilingual capacity (English, French, Portuguese)
Limited pool of organizations with pan-African reach and credibility
Dependence on existing donor relationships (e.g., Sida, DFG) for co-funding
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives to strengthen research systems and promote UK-Africa partnerships necessitate a consortium structure. Capacity building for SGCs requires embedded technical support (hence IDRC/NRF leadership), while the need for UK diplomatic influence requires FCDO’s direct involvement through regional hubs.
q28_linkages: Research system strengthening → requires long-term partnerships → consortium model chosen
Need for private sector engagement → requires policy frameworks → technical agencies contracted for support
UK science diplomacy goals → requires FCDO oversight → RED hubs embedded in governance
Gender inclusivity → requires tailored support → standalone workstream with dedicated budget
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (leveraging IDRC’s existing systems) with equity (ensuring Southern leadership through NRF and SGCs). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for multi-donor coordination vs. greater legitimacy and ownership by African partners.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (direct commissioning would be faster) vs. inclusivity (partnership approach ensures African ownership)
Cost (consortium management is resource-intensive) vs. reach (multi-country scope maximizes impact)
Northern expertise (IDRC’s management) vs. Southern leadership (NRF’s technical role and SGC implementation)
Flexibility (adaptive management) vs. accountability (milestone-based oversight)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (including fragile states) increases oversight intensity, with FCDO RED hubs playing an active role in governance and milestone-based reviews to ensure accountability. This is more intensive than a low-risk programme would require.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: IDRC/NRF provide technical leadership and training, while SGCs are both beneficiaries and implementers. The ‘learning by doing’ approach (e.g., research competitions) embeds capacity development into delivery.

Low private sector engagement in target countries

Gender inequality in research systems

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Loss of coherence in multi-donor partnership
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strong learning and evaluation component; FCDO RED hubs in governance structures.
Dedicated workstream to develop IP policies and commercialization strategies; collaboration with national innovation agencies.
Build evidence base for R&D impact to incentivize government funding; monitor GERD as % of GDP.
No special adaptations planned; standard FCDO procedures for fragile states applied.
Gender Equality and Inclusivity Mainstreaming Framework with annual targets; studies on women’s role in research.

fcas_specific_lessons: No significant FCAS-specific adaptations were required, as the programme focuses on institutional strengthening rather than direct service delivery.
Standard FCDO procedures for fragile states (e.g., Ethiopia, Nigeria) are sufficient for this programme’s scope.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: SGCI Phase 1 demonstrated the value of South-South collaborations (e.g., joint research calls on manufacturing and food processing) and the importance of ‘learning by doing’ for SGCs. The COVID-19 Rapid Grant Fund showed the ability to rapidly mobilize multi-donor funding for context-specific research. Lessons included the need for sustained gender mainstreaming and stronger private sector linkages.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expanded gender and inclusion workstream based on SGCI1 recommendations.
Added dedicated support for West African SGCs (Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone) to address regional gaps.
Increased focus on commercialization and IP policies to strengthen private sector engagement.
Stronger monitoring of national R&D investments (GERD as % of GDP).

Supporting Ghana’s Ministry of Environment... in the establishment of the Ghana Innovation and Research Commercialisation Centre (GIRC)..." quote.design_changes: "Building on these accomplishments and learnings from SGCI1, a second 4-year phase of the SGCI (SGCI2; 2021-2024) will extend engagement with Councils... and institutionalise the ongoing work with the Councils..." (90000723.odt, Building on these accomplishments)

quote.co_funding: "This partnership programme will be jointly funded with IDRC, South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF is the most established Science Granting Councils in sub-Saharan Africa), German Research Foundation (DFG) and Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) (leveraging a total of £11,738,623 co-funding...)." what_objectives.q1_explanation: EQUALS2 is primarily a **service delivery** programme providing independent quality assurance and technical advice for evaluations, while also having **capacity building** elements to improve FCDO's in-house evaluation skills. It supports **evidence generation** by ensuring high-quality evaluations that inform policy decisions, and indirectly contributes to **policy influence** through robust evidence.
what_objectives.q1_source: "EQUALS2 will improve evaluation quality and relevance across the FCDO and other government departments spending ODA. It will continue a highly demanded service that delivers independent quality assurance of evaluation products and provides a range of specialist evaluation and monitoring technical advice." (D0001083.odt, Programmesummary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Quality assurance of evaluation products (e.g., Terms of Reference, inception reports, final reports)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 94% of quality assurance requests met within 10-day deadline (historical performance)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Technical advice on evaluation design and methodologies
Evaluation Insights reports synthesizing learning across thematic areas
Training and capacity-building events for FCDO staff
Improved management information on evaluations across HMG

what_objectives.summary: EQUALS2 delivers independent quality assurance and technical advice to ensure FCDO's evaluations are high-quality, ethical, and useful for decision-making. It also builds internal capacity and synthesizes learning across the ODA portfolio.

quote.objectives: "EQUALS2 will play a key role in providing independent and unbiased scrutiny of the evaluation system to ensure high quality, value for money and ethical soundness." (D0001083.odt, Programmesummary)
quote.outputs: "The three core services of: 1) Short-term technical advice; 2) Quality assurance of evaluation and monitoring products; 3) Evaluation Insights to assess portfolio quality and synthesize learning." (D0001083.odt, Core Services)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as 'Minor' risk in the business case, with no mention of FCAS or high-risk contexts. It operates globally but focuses on evaluation quality assurance, which is a low-risk administrative/technical support function.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor" (D0001083.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Data confidentiality and ethical compliance are critical constraints, requiring strict protocols for handling sensitive programme data. Regulatory constraints include ensuring independence of quality assurance to avoid conflicts of interest.

quote.constraints: "Data confidentiality issues will require experts to sign confidentiality agreements. Protocols will be put in place to ensure that sensitive information is sufficiently protected and destroyed when the work is completed." (D0001083.odt, RiskAssessment)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The lead supplier (UK-based) will manage the consortium, allocate expertise, and liaise with FCDO. Southern partners may be subcontractors but have no decision-making power over the programme's strategic direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for FCDO staff on evaluation methodologies
learning events between panel members and FCDO evaluation advisors
knowledge-sharing on monitoring and evaluation best practices
synthesis of evaluation insights to inform FCDO guidance

partner_organizations.name: Lead Supplier (TBD through competitive tender)
partner_organizations.role: contract management, brokerage of evaluation expertise, quality assurance, technical advice

partner_organizations.name: Subcontracted evaluation consultants (panel members)
partner_organizations.role: provide thematic/methodological expertise for quality assurance and technical advice

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Evaluation Unit
partner_organizations.role: oversight, programme management, learning synthesis

partner_organizations.name: Other Government Departments (OGDs) spending ODA
partner_organizations.role: users of the service (e.g., Home Office, Department of Health and Social Care)

quote.structure: "The supplier would work with FCDO on identifying expertise that could respond to FCDO and OGD demands. It would then allocate that expertise as demands came in from spending units." (D0001083.odt, AppraisalOptions)
quote.capacity: "The new programme will place a greater emphasis on boosting in-house capacity. Those working on EQUALS2 will gain important insights on how FCDO and its suppliers could improve." (D0001083.odt, Building in-house expertise)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO will award a single contract to a lead supplier through open competition. The supplier will manage a panel of evaluation consultants and provide services on a 'pay-as-you-go' basis for technical advice, quality assurance, and Evaluation Insights. Payments are milestone-based and tied to deliverables.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The lead supplier manages a pre-qualified panel of consultants and subcontracts expertise as needed. FCDO's Evaluation Unit oversees the contract, monitors performance, and ensures learning is fed back into the organization. A programme-funded post may act as a bridge between FCDO and the supplier.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition was chosen to ensure value for money, access to a broad range of expertise, and independence of quality assurance. The Early Market Engagement event confirmed sufficient market interest (30+ suppliers, including 32% new to FCDO).

quote.instrument: "FCDO will run an open and fair competitive process and best practice procurement procedure." (D0001083.odt, DeliveryChainMappingandRisk)
quote.structure: "The contractor would work with FCDO on identifying expertise that could respond to FCDO and OGD demands. It would then allocate that expertise as demands came in from spending units." (D0001083.odt, AppraisalOptions)
quote.selection: "An Early Market Engagement event was undertaken in February 2020 to test the market to inform the development of this business case. The EME was well attended by approximately 30 suppliers." (D0001083.odt, StructureoftheContractwiththeSupplier)

quote.management: "The programme manager will be responsible for managing supplier relationships and contract management alongside the SRO." (D0001083.odt, ManagementStructure)
quote.oversight: "Contract and supplier performance management will be undertaken using existing established mechanisms in FCDO. This is set out in more detail in the management case and will include quarterly discussions and reports." (D0001083.odt, StructureoftheContractwiththeSupplier)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between technical advice, quality assurance, and Evaluation Insights based on demand, but major changes require FCDO approval. The contract may be extended by up to 2 years if demand is lower than expected.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is demand-driven, allowing FCDO teams to request support as needs arise. However, significant shifts in priorities (e.g., new thematic areas) would require contract amendments or FCDO approval. The supplier can add panel members if new expertise is needed.

quote.reallocation: "The programme will flex according to FCDO’s need. Key reasons for a higher budget compared to previous programmes include: the new department will mean the service must serve a bigger department with more diverse needs." (D0001083.odt, Affordabilityandfundingsources)
quote.adaptive: "The service will be demand-driven, with programme teams requesting support, and it will therefore directly respond to the needs of FCDO and other ODA-delivering HMG staff." (D0001083.odt, Core Services)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Supplier (consortium) → Panel Members (individual consultants/organizations)

quote.budget: "Total: £4,700,000" (D0001083.odt, ResourcesRequired)
quote.management_costs: "Management costs assumed to be 8% of total contract value with supplier." (D0001083.odt, ResourcesRequired)
quote.payment: "Payments will only be made in arrears on agreed deliverables." (D0001083.odt, Monitoring, reporting and accounting for funds)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: FCDO contracts directly with evaluation experts using a framework agreement
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: Risk of bias in quality assurance, high management burden, and inability to respond to emerging needs.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Do not renew; manage service through in-house capacity
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: Insufficient internal expertise, inability to meet OGD demand, and lack of independence in quality assurance.
Contract limits reached; new programme needed to align with post-merger FCDO priorities.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The outsourced consortium model was chosen to: 1) ensure independence of quality assurance; 2) provide timely access to a broad range of expertise; 3) offer better value for money by using short-term experts rather than retaining all skills in-house; 4) allow flexibility to respond to diverse and evolving demands across FCDO and OGDs; and 5) reduce administrative burden on FCDO staff.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict of interest if suppliers conducting evaluations also provide quality assurance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Legal entity supplying EQUALS2 and core helpdesk staff cannot participate in evaluations reviewed by EQUALS. Controls will be put in place to separate technical advice and quality assurance roles for panel members.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor supplier performance or lack of expertise
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Detailed ToRs, performance incentives (e.g., output-based payments), and regular monitoring. Supplier must demonstrate access to a broad panel of experts during tender.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management fees or cost overruns
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Caps on consultancy days per product, competitive tender process, and quarterly budget reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low demand from OGDs leading to underutilization
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Contract can be extended by up to 2 years if demand is lower than expected, allowing budget to be utilized over a longer period.

quote.rationale: "Preferred Option – This option is most likely to enable the delivery of a range of outputs that will be of sufficient quality to achieve the desired outcome, for example: High quality technical expertise can be accessed quickly depending on demands; Quality assurance will be independent of FCDO." (D0001083.odt, AppraisalOptions)
quote.risks: "There is a risk of conflict of interest if suppliers conducting evaluations also conduct quality assurance reviews, thereby essentially rating their own work." (D0001083.odt, ConflictsofInterest)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and need for rapid, flexible support constrain the delivery structure to a UK-based lead supplier with a broad panel of experts. The programme cannot rely on Southern-led consortia due to the need for immediate access to diverse methodological/thematic expertise and FCDO’s preference for UK-based contractual oversight.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for rapid turnaround (e.g., 10-day deadline for 94% of quality assurance requests)
Requirement for independence and unbiased quality assurance
Diverse and evolving demands across FCDO and OGDs
Ethical and data confidentiality standards
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **independent, high-quality, and flexible** evaluation support determines the consortium structure: 1) **Independence** requires arm’s-length quality assurance (hence outsourced model); 2) **Breadth of expertise** necessitates a panel of consultants rather than a single organization; 3) **Demand-driven nature** requires a responsive 'pay-as-you-go' system; 4) **Capacity building** embeds learning mechanisms (e.g., Evaluation Insights, training).

q28_linkages.mechanism: Outsourced consortium with strict conflict-of-interest controls
Panel of pre-qualified consultants managed by lead supplier
Embedded learning events and Evaluation Insights reports
Open competition to select supplier with broad expertise

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritizes **efficiency and expertise** over **Southern ownership**: 1) **Northern-led consortium** ensures rapid, high-quality support but limits Southern decision-making; 2) **UK-based contractual management** reduces administrative risks but may exclude Southern institutions from leadership; 3) **Short-term consultancy model** maximizes flexibility but limits long-term capacity building in LMICs. The trade-off is justified by the need for credibility and responsiveness in quality assurance.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid turnaround (10-day deadlines) favors Northern experts with immediate availability over potentially slower Southern partners.
UK-based lead supplier ensures methodological rigor but limits Southern control over evaluation standards.
Demand-driven, short-term consultancy maximizes efficiency but offers limited long-term institutional strengthening in LMICs.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **low-risk profile** (rated 'Minor') enables a **light-touch oversight** approach (milestone-based rather than intensive). However, risks around conflict of interest and supplier performance necessitate **specific controls** (e.g., separation of roles, performance incentives).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Requiring the lead supplier to include **training and learning events** in their deliverables; 2) Embedding a **programme-funded post** to bridge FCDO and supplier learning; 3) Using **Evaluation Insights** to synthesize lessons for FCDO guidance. Southern partners may participate as panel members but are not positioned as capacity-builders.

quote.where_who: "The supplier would work with FCDO on identifying expertise that could respond to FCDO and OGD demands. It would then allocate that expertise as demands came in from spending units." (D0001083.odt, AppraisalOptions)
quote.what_how: "The new programme will place a greater emphasis on boosting in-house capacity... EQUALS2 will prioritise unlocking these insights and utilising them across HMG." (D0001083.odt, Building in-house expertise)
quote.equity: "The lead organisation for this contract would need to include senior professionals in evaluation types and approaches and offer high quality expertise in evaluation methods or sectors that link to FCDO and OGD’s forthcoming demands for evaluation." (D0001083.odt, StructureoftheContractwiththeSupplier)

key_programme_risks.risk: Conflict of interest in quality assurance (suppliers reviewing their own work)
Poor supplier performance or lack of expertise
Low demand from OGDs leading to underutilization of budget
Delays in turnaround times for quality assurance/technical advice
Insufficient data management or confidentiality breaches
Failure to improve FCDO’s in-house evaluation capacity

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Legal entity supplying EQUALS2 and core helpdesk staff excluded from evaluations they review. Panel members providing technical advice cannot conduct quality assurance for the same evaluation. Supplier must demonstrate watertight controls in bid.
Performance incentives (e.g., output-based payments, blind client feedback), quarterly reviews, and option to remove underperforming panel members.
Contract can be extended by up to 2 years to utilize budget over a longer period if demand is low.
Caps on consultancy days per product (e.g., 4 days for baseline report QA), with SRO approval required for exceptions.
Confidentiality agreements for experts, protocols for data protection/destruction, and FCDO information security guidance shared with supplier.
Programme-funded post to bridge FCDO and supplier, regular learning events, and Evaluation Insights reports to synthesize lessons.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **High demand for services**: EQUALS (2016–2020) handled 834 quality assurance requests, with 80% of users reporting improved evaluation quality. 2) **Need for flexibility**: Previous programme adapted to support new priorities (e.g., influencing activities, Delivery Frameworks). 3) **Importance of independence**: SEQAS (2012–2016) and EQUALS embedded quality assurance as mandatory in DFID’s Evaluation Policy. 4) **Efficiency of outsourced model**: Current programme met 94% of requests within 10 days, demonstrating the value of a brokerage approach.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Expanded scope**: EQUALS2 will support non-ODA areas and new FCDO priorities (e.g., influencing, Delivery Frameworks). 2) **Greater focus on learning**: New Evaluation Insights component to synthesize lessons and identify evidence gaps. 3) **Enhanced capacity building**: Programme-funded post to improve knowledge transfer between supplier and FCDO. 4) **Stronger ethical oversight**: Ethics expertise included in panel and quality criteria, building on DFID’s ethical guidance.

quote.lessons: "During the first four years of EQUALS (2016–2020), the service supported a total of 834 quality assurance requests... 80% of users responding to the EQUALS 2020 survey agreed that EQUALS has improved the overall quality of their evaluation products." (D0001083.odt, Importance of renewing EQUALS for OGDs)
quote.changes: "The new programme will place a greater emphasis on boosting in-house capacity... EQUALS2 will prioritise unlocking these insights and utilising them across HMG." (D0001083.odt, Building in-house expertise)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Potential 20% increase in contract budget for OGD usage (up to £940,000 additional funding if fully utilized).

quote.budget: "This value represents the value of the FCDO contribution. There is the possibility of a 20% increase of the Contract budget for OGD usage of the service." (D0001083.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.breakdown: "Management costs assumed to be 8% of total contract value with supplier." (D0001083.odt, ResourcesRequired)
quote.leverage: "There is the possibility of a 20% increase of the Contract budget for OGD usage of the service." (D0001083.odt, SummarySheet)

metadata.programme_name: Conflict Prevention and Peacebuilding Programme (C3P)
metadata.quote: "Programmesummary(100wordsmaximum): There have been alarming increases in instability across the world since 2010. In response, and with UK support, the multilateral system has put an increased emphasis on more effective conflict prevention interventions." (61484103.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: March 2021", "AMP End Date: March 2024" (61484103.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The C3P programme combines financing mechanisms (supporting the UN Peacebuilding Fund and Joint Programme), capacity building (through Peace and Development Advisers and secondees), and policy influence (shaping UN reform and conflict prevention strategies). It aims to leverage multilateral systems to address conflict drivers and reduce threats to UK national security.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The C3P programme fits extremely well with HMG and international priorities: ... The programme contributes to National security Council (NSC) objectives for a stronger Rules-Based International System (RBIS), our Global Britain commitment to work to deliver the SDGs by increasing our conflict prevention work with the UN..." (61484103.odt, Strategic Fit)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased support to the UN’s dedicated Peacebuilding Fund (up to £69m over four years)
Enhanced UN Peace and Development Adviser (PDA) network (up to £10.7m over 4 years)
Additional UK secondments to key multilaterals (up to £0.6m over 3 years)
Support to the UN Humanitarian-Development-Peacebuilding and Partnership Facility (HDPP-F) (£500,000 in 2022/23)
Continuation of the Peace Responsiveness Facility (PRF) (£500,000 in 2022/23)
More conflict prevention and peacebuilding activity across 40+ countries
Improved multilateral coordination and delivery
Progress in delivering the UN Secretary General’s Sustaining Peace reform agenda
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the multilateral system's capacity to prevent conflict and build peace by providing financial support, technical expertise, and policy influence through the UN Peacebuilding Fund, Peace and Development Advisers, and strategic secondments.
what_objectives.quote: "By leveraging sustainable and effective finance for peacebuilding, through the provision of technical capacity, policy support and contributions to multilateral funds, this programme will contribute to the following anticipated outcome: a multilateral system that more effectively addresses the underlying causes of conflict and fragility." (61484103.odt, Impact and Outcomes)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where 60% of conflicts that ended in the early 2000s relapsed into violence within five years. The UN estimates over 70 million people are displaced by conflict, and by 2030, 80% of the world’s poor will live in fragile and conflict-affected states.
where_context.q5_source: "60% of conflicts that ended in the early 2000s have relapsed into violence within five years... By 2030, 80% of the world’s poor will live in fragile and conflict affected states." (61484103.odt, Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and weak institutions limit the ability to operate effectively in conflict zones. Climate risks exacerbate instability, and data limitations make monitoring and evaluation challenging. The COVID-19 pandemic has further strained already fragile systems, increasing gender-based violence and stalling peace processes.
where_context.quote: "The COVID-19 crisis will likely exacerbate these issues: we are already seeing increased gender-based violence, stalled peace processes and authoritarian responses... Increased food insecurity will exacerbate instability, at the same time as traditional conflict resolution mechanisms are weakened by the socio-economic impact of the virus." (61484103.odt, Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations (UN Peacebuilding Fund and UNDP-DPPA Joint Programme)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) provides funding and strategic direction, while UN agencies implement programmes. Decision-making power lies primarily with Northern institutions (FCDO, UN HQ) though local UN country teams and PDAs have operational autonomy.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (Peace and Development Advisers provide conflict analysis and prevention support)
mentorship (PDAs support UN country teams in conflict-sensitive programming)
institutional strengthening (support to UN reform and peacebuilding architecture)

partner_organizations.name: UN Peacebuilding Fund (PBF)
partner_organizations.role: Primary financing mechanism for peacebuilding and conflict prevention programming

partner_organizations.name: UNDP-DPPA Joint Programme on Building National Capacities for Conflict Prevention
partner_organizations.role: Deploys Peace and Development Advisers (PDAs) to UN country teams

partner_organizations.name: UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA)
partner_organizations.role: Manages PDAs and supports conflict prevention strategies

partner_organizations.name: UN Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: Supports peacebuilding and development programming

partner_organizations.name: Peacebuilding Support Office (PBSO)
partner_organizations.role: Oversees strategic direction of PBF and provides expert advice

partner_organizations.name: Interpeace (Peace Responsiveness Facility)
partner_organizations.role: Builds UN agencies’ capacity to design conflict-sensitive peacebuilding interventions

partner_organizations.name: UN-World Bank Humanitarian Development Peacebuilding Partnership (HDPP)
partner_organizations.role: Facilitates UN-World Bank partnerships in crisis-affected settings

who_partners.quote: "The Joint Programme, operating since 2004, manages the deployment of over 50 UN PDAs across 50 countries... PDAs operate as part conflict advisors, part political counsellors, giving critical support to UNRCs and country teams." (61484103.odt, Component 2)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses multi-year, un-earmarked core funding through UN framework agreements for the PBF and Joint Programme. Secondments are managed through HMG-UN Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs), while the HDPP and PRF components use specific project agreements (MoU for HDPP, Accountable Grant for Interpeace).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through existing UN systems (PBF, UNDP-DPPA Joint Programme) with FCDO oversight. The PBF and Joint Programme have their own management teams responsible for planning and expenditure tracking, while FCDO provides strategic direction and performance monitoring.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UN Peacebuilding Fund and UNDP-DPPA Joint Programme are established multilateral mechanisms with a proven track record. The UK has historically supported these entities, and their alignment with UK priorities (e.g., conflict prevention, UN reform) makes them natural partners.
how_mechanism.quote: "The proposed funding mechanism for the PBF and Joint Programme elements of the C3P programme would be multi-year, un-earmarked core funding through UN framework agreements." (61484103.odt, Financial Details)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The PBF has a 'Group of Friends' that brings together all donors for information sharing and feedback. The Joint Programme is overseen by UNDP and DPPA, with FCDO providing strategic oversight. The C3P programme is managed by the Office for Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation (OCSM) within FCDO.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO will hold at least one meeting with both partners each quarter, with financial forecasts and the updated C3P Risk Register reviewed every month." (D0002740.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated through multi-year agreements but can be adjusted based on performance reviews. The PBF’s flexible, catalytic funding allows for responsive programming in dynamic conflict contexts.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments based on emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19 response) and performance reviews. The PBF’s 2020-24 Strategy includes new focus areas (e.g., gender, youth empowerment) that reflect evolving priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: "The PBF has moved fast to set out its immediate COVID-19 related offer to UN country teams... focusing on crisis management and communications." (61484103.odt, Component 1)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN (PBF/UNDP-DPPA/Interpeace) → end beneficiaries (no further sub-grantees mentioned)
how_efficiency.quote: "FCDO will sign an MoU with HDPP, and an Accountable Grant with Interpeace; prior to payments, both partners will provide written performance reports... FCDO intends to pay both partners in two equal installments." (D0002740.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Ending FCDO’s multilateral peacebuilding work and taking a more ‘reactive’ approach to national security
Investing bilaterally in conflict prevention and peacebuilding
Providing multilateral peacebuilding funding (chosen option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The multilateral approach was chosen because it leverages the UN’s global reach, expertise, and legitimacy, which bilateral approaches cannot match. It also aligns with the UK’s commitment to multilateralism, UN reform, and the Rules-Based International System (RBIS), while providing a force multiplier effect for UK funding.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (multilateral funding acts as a force multiplier)
risk-mitigation (UN’s local legitimacy and expertise reduce operational risks)
experience (UK has a history of successful engagement with the PBF and Joint Programme)
partner-capacity (UN’s ability to operate at scale in fragile contexts)
flexibility (PBF’s catalytic funding allows for responsive programming)
equity (multilateral approach ensures broader geographic and thematic coverage)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN prevention and peacebuilding engagement fails to adequately reduce or mitigate the scale of global conflict.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will continue to advocate for UN reform and provide strategic direction through secondees and policy engagement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Geo-political tensions and shifts pose an increased challenge to the UN, undermining the effectiveness of prevention efforts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will work with like-minded partners to build coalitions and support the UN Secretary General’s Sustaining Peace agenda.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient progress on UN reform required for effective peacebuilding.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will use its influence as a major donor to push for reforms and ensure the PBF and Joint Programme align with the 2020 Peacebuilding Architecture Review.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of funds through multilateral mechanisms)
efficiency (leveraging UN’s existing systems and expertise)
effectiveness (proven track record of PBF and Joint Programme)
why_rationale.quote: "The UK strengthens the conflict prevention capacity of the multilateral system and reduces the impact of conflict and instability on the UK’s security. Our investments in multilateral conflict prevention act as a force multiplier, as the UN reaches areas and tackles issues the UK cannot." (61484103.odt, Option 3)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme operates in high-risk, fragile, and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where security constraints and weak institutions limit the ability of bilateral actors to operate effectively. This necessitates reliance on multilateral partners like the UN, which have the local legitimacy, expertise, and reach to work in these environments.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in FCAS limit bilateral operations, making multilateral partnerships essential.
Weak institutions in target countries require capacity-building support from UN agencies.
Conflict dynamics necessitate flexible, adaptive programming that multilaterals are better positioned to deliver.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—strengthening multilateral conflict prevention and peacebuilding—require a delivery structure that leverages the UN’s global footprint and expertise. The financing mechanism (un-earmarked core funding) and management structure (multilateral with FCDO oversight) are designed to maximize flexibility, coordination, and impact across diverse conflict contexts.
q28_linkages: The need for global reach and legitimacy → multilateral delivery structure (UN PBF and Joint Programme).
The focus on conflict prevention and peacebuilding → reliance on UN’s conflict-sensitive programming and PDAs.
The requirement for adaptive, responsive funding → PBF’s catalytic and flexible financing model.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between the efficiency of multilateral delivery (leveraging UN systems for scale and reach) and the equity of ensuring locally tailored, inclusive approaches. The use of PDAs and the PBF’s focus on local ownership and gender equality aim to balance these priorities.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Multilateral funding allows for rapid, large-scale deployment but may reduce local ownership.
Equity: PDAs and conflict-sensitive programming ensure local context is considered, though this may slow decision-making.
Speed vs. inclusion: The PBF’s flexible funding enables quick responses to crises but requires robust oversight to ensure inclusivity.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context necessitates intensive oversight, including quarterly meetings, performance reviews, and a detailed risk register. The programme’s management intensity (e.g., embedded advisors, milestone-based payments) reflects the need to mitigate risks in fragile environments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme through PDAs and secondees, who provide technical expertise and strategic direction to UN country teams. This strengthens the ability of local and multilateral partners to design and implement effective peacebuilding interventions.
intersections.quote: "The Joint Programme has substantially exceeded all targets set at the outcome level... The Programme contributes to bridging the peace and development parts of the UN system at both Headquarters and at the country-level." (61484103.odt, Component 2)

key_programme_risks: UN prevention and peacebuilding efforts may fail to reduce global conflict adequately.
Geo-political tensions could undermine UN reform and prevention efforts.
Insufficient progress on UN reform may limit the effectiveness of peacebuilding interventions.
Reduced donor contributions (e.g., due to COVID-19) could constrain PBF’s ability to meet demand.
Short-term nature of PBF projects may limit sustainability and long-term impact.
Coordination challenges between UN agencies could reduce programme coherence.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UN prevention and peacebuilding engagement fails to reduce conflict adequately.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK will provide strategic direction through secondees, policy engagement, and advocacy for UN reform.
UK will build coalitions with like-minded partners to support the UNSG’s Sustaining Peace agenda.
UK will use its influence as a top donor to push for incremental, achievable reforms and play the ‘long game.’

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reduced donor contributions due to COVID-19.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK will engage with the Peacebuilding Support Office (PBSO) to understand shifting demands and respond to funding gaps.
PBF’s 2020-24 Strategy includes a greater focus on sustainability and long-term prevention.
PDAs and secondees will ensure cross-UN conflict-sensitive analysis and coherence.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict relapse is high in FCAS, requiring sustained, long-term engagement.
Local ownership and context-specific programming are critical for effectiveness in fragile states.
Flexible, catalytic funding (e.g., PBF) is essential for responding to dynamic conflict environments.
Gender and youth inclusion must be central to peacebuilding in FCAS to address root causes of conflict.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past evaluations of the PBF and Joint Programme highlight their effectiveness in delivering conflict prevention and peacebuilding. The PBF has been scored A+ in DFID annual reviews, with feedback from recipient governments (e.g., Chad, Sri Lanka) praising its contributions to peace and stability. The Joint Programme has exceeded targets and bridged peace and development efforts within the UN system.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The C3P programme builds on lessons from previous phases, including the need for: longer-term investments in prevention, stronger coordination between UN agencies, enhanced gender and youth focus, and adaptive programming to respond to crises like COVID-19. The addition of HDPP and PRF components reflects learning around the importance of UN-World Bank collaboration and organizational capacity for peace responsiveness.
risks_lessons.quote: "DFID annual reviews have consistently scored both the PBF and Joint Programme at A/A+... The PBF delivers a growing portfolio with a lean headquarters staff... The Joint Programme has substantially exceeded all targets set at the outcome level." (61484103.odt, Evidence of Previous Performance)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s contributions leverage additional funding from other donors (e.g., Germany, Sweden) and catalyze UN-World Bank collaboration through initiatives like the HDPP. The PBF’s 2020-24 Strategy aims to secure $1.5 billion in funding over five years, with UK support helping to mobilize this broader investment.
financial_details.quote: "The PBF’s new 2020-24 Strategy... sets out its ambitious target of securing $1.5bn in funding over five years... The UK confirms its clear support for the RBIS and multilateral conflict prevention work." (61484103.odt, Component 1)

metadata.programme_name: Education Quality Improvement Programme – Bangladesh (EQUIP-B)

quote.text: The Concept Note was approved on 23 October 2019 providing up to £25 million over six years. This Business Case proposes a reduction, due to the recent cuts in UK ODA, to provide up to £16 million over six years through technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB).

duration_source.text: This Business Case proposes a reduction, due to the recent cuts in UK ODA, to provide up to £16 million over six years through technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: EQUIP-B combines capacity building (strengthening education systems), policy influence (evidence-based reforms), and implementation research (testing interventions like blended learning and teacher training). It focuses on improving learning outcomes, especially for girls, through technical assistance to the Government of Bangladesh.

q1_source.text: The programme will: Support interventions to improve low learning outcomes by, for example, introducing pre-service teacher training and strengthening in-service teacher training... Strengthen the education system’s efficiency and effectiveness by improving national examinations and student learning assessments... Support interventions to enable adolescent girls to stay in secondary school...

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved reading and basic grade-level learning competencies of students in primary and secondary education
q3_expected_outputs.target: 4 million girls to improve their reading by age 10

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased number of girls accessing and completing secondary education
q3_expected_outputs.target: Contribute to 40 million more girls in school globally by 2025

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased use of data and evidence to influence reforms and policy decisions of GoB
Improved national examinations and student learning assessments
Development of a policy framework and pilot of a pre-service teachers’ education programme
Increased access and retention of girls in school
Institutionalised academic supervision and mentoring of teachers
Piloted blended learning approaches (in-person and distance teaching)

what_objectives.summary: EQUIP-B aims to improve education quality in Bangladesh by addressing systemic barriers to learning, particularly for girls, through technical assistance that strengthens teacher training, curriculum development, data systems, and policy reforms. It combines evidence generation, capacity building, and implementation of targeted interventions.

quote.text: The programme will offer the best of UK and international research and expertise to help drive up education outcomes for girls and boys. This TA will focus on areas where the UK has experience and expertise such as girls’ education, teacher training, learning assessments, technology-based education, data systems, and education research.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Bangladesh faces political economy challenges, corruption risks, and systemic inefficiencies in education governance, but is not classified as FCAS. The programme notes "Major" risk rating, indicating significant but manageable risks.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Major

q6_constraints_impact.political economy: Reforms to improve education quality are less politically tractable than access expansion. Teacher unions resist accountability measures, and political settlements prioritize system expansion over quality (ESID Working Paper No. 86).
q6_constraints_impact.weak institutions: The education system is highly centralized, leading to weak local initiative, transparency, and accountability. BANBEIS lacks capacity to integrate education data for planning (Section: Strategic Case).
q6_constraints_impact.corruption: Corruption affects teacher recruitment, promotions, and infrastructure, with 42.9% of households reporting bribery for education services (TIB 2017).
q6_constraints_impact.data limitations: Lack of a unified EMIS system hampers evidence-based decision-making and real-time monitoring.
q6_constraints_impact.climate risks: Climate shocks disrupt education continuity, requiring resilient systems to support children’s learning.
q6_constraints_impact.COVID-19 impact: School closures exacerbated learning poverty, with only 25% of students accessing remote learning, disproportionately affecting girls and poor households.
q6_constraints_impact.centralized bureaucracy: Mid-fiscal year budget revisions and slow approval processes delay programme implementation.

quote.text: The highly centralised system stifles local initiative and contributes to weak management, transparency, and accountability. The teachers’ unions are organised and a powerful political lobby, and they resist reforms they judge would negatively affect their status or terms and conditions... Political hegemony of the elites and politicians plays a significant role in making the institutions corrupt and inefficient.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) sets strategic priorities and approves TA plans, while multilateral partners (World Bank, UNICEF) and a Commercial Managing Agent (CMA) implement activities. Local stakeholders (GoB ministries) are consulted but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: pre-service and in-service teacher training
gender-responsive curriculum and textbook development
data management systems (EMIS)
academic supervision and mentoring of teachers
policy framework development for inclusive education
piloting blended learning models
community engagement for girls’ retention

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider (reading programmes, examinations, teacher preparedness, digital monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider (data management, gender mainstreaming, community engagement)

partner_organizations.name: Commercial Managing Agent (CMA)
partner_organizations.role: Flexible, demand-driven TA for emerging needs (e.g., pre-service teacher training, blended learning pilots)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Bangladesh (MoPME and MoE)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiary and implementing partner (policy adoption, system reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Community-level innovation and advocacy (girls’ retention models)

quote.text: Option 2: Technical assistance (TA) through multilaterals and commercial managing agent (up to £16 million)... This option will provide up to £16 million over six years as TA to the GoB and will be delivered through multilaterals and a commercial managing agent. The TA will focus on improving education quality through improving learning outcomes, system strengthening, and increasing girls’ retention in school.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants to multilaterals (World Bank, UNICEF) and a competitive contract for a Commercial Managing Agent (CMA). Funds are channeled as technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh, with no direct financial aid.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured as a tripartite delivery model: (1) World Bank and UNICEF for policy-aligned TA, (2) a CMA for flexible, demand-driven support, and (3) an independent evaluation. The UK (FCDO) oversees coordination but does not directly implement.

q14_competition_ratio.CMA: open competition ("competitively selected commercial managing agent")

q14_selection_rationale.World Bank/UNICEF: Leverages existing relationships, technical expertise, and credibility with GoB to ensure rapid uptake of TA.
q14_selection_rationale.CMA: Provides flexibility to respond to emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19) and brings global/UK expertise without bureaucratic delays.

quote.text: This option will be delivered through a tripartite delivery model including two multilaterals (WB and UNICEF) and a competitively selected commercial managing agent (CMA). While all three implementing bodies of EQUIP-B are appropriate for delivering the programme, they have specific strengths in terms of policy influence, technical expertise, credibility and relationship with the government, and global and in-country networks.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will establish a governance structure to manage TA partner performance and risks, including a Programme Coordination Committee (PCC) with GoB ministries (MoPME, MoE) and donors. The UK will be part of the joint government-donor consortium for buy-in.

quote.text: The UK will be a member of the joint government-donor consortium, through which buy-in from the government and other donors will be secured early on. We will also set up a governance structure to manage the performance of TA partners and risks throughout the programme period.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between the three components (WB, UNICEF, CMA) with approval, based on emerging needs (e.g., COVID-19 response). The CMA component is explicitly designed for flexible, demand-driven support.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a political economy analysis during inception to adjust TA demands. The CMA allows rapid response to unanticipated needs, while WB/UNICEF components require prior agreement for changes.

quote.text: The CMA component will provide TA to both the education ministries via a flexible fund that is demand driven and responsive to GoB needs... The use of a CMA will enable the UK to engage with GoB and respond at pace to offer flexible TA.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilaterals (WB/UNICEF) or CMA → GoB ministries (no sub-grantees mentioned).

quote.text: The procurement process for the CMA, open to a broad set of stakeholders, would create competition between institutions, potentially lowering the costs and minimising overhead and management costs.

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing
TA through multilaterals only (WB/UNICEF)
Direct delivery by British High Commission staff
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed model (multilaterals + CMA) was selected to balance (1) **policy influence** (leveraging WB/UNICEF’s credibility with GoB), (2) **flexibility** (CMA’s ability to respond to emerging needs like COVID-19), (3) **value for money** (competitive CMA procurement), and (4) **risk mitigation** (multilaterals’ existing relationships reduce implementation delays). The UK’s reduced ODA budget also required a cost-efficient structure.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (competitive CMA, leveraging GPE funds)
partner capacity (WB/UNICEF’s technical expertise + CMA’s agility)
speed (multilaterals can mobilize quickly for urgent reforms)
equity (focus on girls’ education and marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Misalignment with GoB’s emerging priorities (e.g., shift to technical/vocational education).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Joint planning with MoPME/MoE to set TA parameters and accountability mechanisms upfront.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow bureaucratic approvals from GoB delaying delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s membership in the joint government-donor consortium to secure early buy-in and establish a governance structure for performance management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low-quality consultants engaged due to political pressure from GoB.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will set criteria and collaborate with partners in selecting consultants for specific TA.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Multilaterals’ internal bureaucracy limiting responsiveness (e.g., during COVID-19).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: CMA component provides agility to respond to unplanned needs, complementing multilaterals’ structured support.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (competitive CMA procurement, leveraging existing multilateral funds)
effectiveness (focus on evidence-based interventions like teacher training and reading programmes)
equity (targeted support for girls and marginalized children)

quote.text: This option will strengthen coherence across initiatives beyond EQUIP-B, provide an opportunity to influence both the multilaterals and CMA to work together to deliver efficiently and effectively, and strengthen coordination and cooperation with government... It allows UK the flexibility to respond to government needs at pace and with quality by using the most appropriate and relevant platform.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The centralized and politicized education system in Bangladesh limits partner selection to entities with (1) **existing GoB relationships** (e.g., WB/UNICEF’s long-term credibility) and (2) **flexibility to navigate bureaucratic delays** (hence the CMA). Local NGOs are excluded due to systemic corruption risks and weak institutional capacity for nationwide reforms.
q27_constraints_detail: Teacher unions’ political influence requires partners with negotiation experience (WB/UNICEF).
GoB’s slow approval processes necessitate partners who can mobilize quickly (CMA).
Corruption risks preclude direct funding to local entities without multilaterals’ oversight.
COVID-19 disruptions demand partners with adaptive capacity (CMA’s flexible fund).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **mixed objectives** (system strengthening + girls’ retention + learning outcomes) require a **hybrid delivery structure**: (1) **Multilaterals** for policy-level reforms (e.g., examinations, data systems), (2) **CMA** for innovative pilots (e.g., blended learning), and (3) **embedded governance** to align political incentives. The need for both **scalable solutions** (WB/UNICEF) and **local adaptation** (CMA) shapes the tripartite model.

q28_linkages.mechanism: WB’s technical expertise in assessments + CMA’s pilots for pre-service teacher education.
UNICEF’s community engagement models + CMA’s flexible funding for localized interventions.
WB/UNICEF’s policy influence + UK’s governance oversight via joint consortium.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting marginalized girls) with **efficiency** (leveraging multilaterals’ scale). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: CMA enables rapid response but may bypass slower, inclusive GoB processes. (2) **Global expertise vs. local ownership**: WB/UNICEF bring technical rigor but risk limited local adaptation without CMA’s flexibility. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Competitive CMA procurement reduces overhead but requires careful partner selection to avoid low-quality consultants.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: CMA’s agility accelerates delivery but may sideline GoB’s bureaucratic inclusion mechanisms (e.g., teacher union consultations).
WB/UNICEF’s standardized approaches ensure quality but may conflict with GoB’s political priorities without adaptive management.
Competitive CMA selection reduces costs but risks underinvesting in harder-to-reach groups (e.g., children with disabilities).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight**: milestone-based governance, embedded political economy analysis, and a joint consortium to mitigate GoB’s bureaucratic delays and corruption risks. High corruption risks (42.9% households report bribery) justify multilaterals’ role as fiscal intermediaries.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: (1) WB/UNICEF strengthen **system-level capacity** (e.g., EMIS, examinations), (2) CMA builds **localized implementation capacity** (e.g., teacher mentoring pilots), and (3) GoB’s **absorptive capacity** determines the pace of TA absorption (e.g., mid-year budget revisions).

quote.text: Working at the national, local, school and community levels will be essential to improve system efficiency... The management and use of authentic data are critical in decision making... A new culture of evidence in education is needed to shift education systems towards the learning gains required.

key_programme_risks: UK’s TA support may not align with GoB’s emerging priorities (e.g., technical/vocational education).
Evidence from research/piloting may not influence sector reforms due to political resistance.
Delays in GoB’s bureaucratic approval processes (e.g., mid-year budget revisions).
Low accountability and weak bureaucratic incentives for learning reforms.
Engagement of low-quality consultants due to political pressure from GoB.
COVID-19 exacerbating learning poverty and dropout rates, especially for girls.
Corruption in teacher recruitment/promotions undermining merit-based reforms.
Stipend mistargeting excluding eligible girls from financial support.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Joint planning with MoPME/MoE to set TA parameters and accountability mechanisms.
Detailed sectoral political economy analysis post-approval to identify reform pathways.
UK’s membership in joint government-donor consortium to secure early buy-in; governance structure for performance management.
Monitor political economy dynamics regularly; adaptive TA to respond to context/needs.
UK sets selection criteria and collaborates with partners on consultant recruitment.
CMA’s flexible fund for low-tech remote learning tools; pilots for blended education models.
Leverage multilaterals’ (WB/UNICEF) anti-corruption safeguards and transparent procurement.
Advocate with donors/CSOs to harmonize targeting; use data systems to improve eligibility verification.

lessons_from_previous.lesson: Demand-led, flexible TA programmes aligning with country priorities are critical for effectiveness in complex political environments (lessons from Ethiopia, Nepal, Ghana).
lessons_from_previous.application: EQUIP-B’s design incorporates flexible CMA funding and political economy analysis to navigate Bangladesh’s education sector politics.

design_changes_based_on_learning.change: Reduction from £25m to £16m due to UK ODA cuts, with shifted focus to high-impact TA areas (e.g., teacher training, girls’ retention).
design_changes_based_on_learning.rationale: Prioritizes areas with UK expertise and GoB demand, filling gaps left by other donors (WB/UNICEF funding shortages).

quote.text: The TA programmes in Ethiopia, Nepal and Ghana provide good examples of how best TA support can be used for influence over domestic spend. Lessons learnt from these programmes suggest that demand-led, and flexible TA programmes aligning with a country’s development strategies and priorities is a key determinant of effectiveness in responding to complex political environment and execution challenges. The EQUIP-B programme is designed based on these lessons learnt and our earlier experience of TA support to the primary education sector programme and in the health sector programme.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: EQUIP-B will leverage and multiply the effectiveness of UK contributions made through the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), for which both WB and UNICEF are managing agents in Bangladesh. The programme fills critical TA gaps in PEDP4 and SEDP, enhancing the impact of other donors’ financial aid.

quote.text: The UK will jointly work with the WB and UNICEF to ensure that EQUIP-B and GPE support areas are aligned and can build on one another’s policy advocacy and influencing... Our relatively small TA, with the right tools in place, will influence and enhance the effectiveness of a larger investment from GoB and other donors.

metadata.programme_name: Emergency Deployment Teams Programme (EDT2)
metadata.quote: The Emergency Deployments Team2 (EDT2) programme enables the UK to offer assistance to countries in need of emergency medical assistance and international search and rescue. (D0003487.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The programme will have a budget of £25m over five years. (D0003487.odt, Summary of the proposed programme)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: EDT2 combines service delivery (rapid emergency response), capacity building (training and mentoring for local responders), and policy influence (shaping international standards). It maintains deployable medical and search-and-rescue teams while building partnerships for knowledge exchange and capacity strengthening in priority countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: The EDT2 programme will build on this legacy as part of FCDO’s humanitarian rapid response toolkit. [...] It will do this by responding to countries affected by major disasters and supporting and complementing local emergency responders. [...] Through EDT2, the UK will help implement and strengthen international emergency response standards and coordination. (D0003487.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)
q3_expected_outputs: Rapid, coordinated medical and search-and-rescue capabilities deployed to disaster-affected countries (output: "Countries are supported by rapid, coordinated and appropriate medical and search and rescue capabilities")
Lives saved, suffering alleviated, and dignity maintained for disaster-affected people (impact: "Lives are saved, suffering is alleviated and dignity is maintained")
Strengthened capacity of first responders in partnered countries (output: "First responders in partnered countries have greater knowledge and capacity to provide coordinated and timely response")
Enhanced UK domestic resilience through skills/expertise of NHS and Fire and Rescue Service personnel (secondary outcome: "building stronger resilience at home")
Generation of evidence to improve international emergency deployment systems (output: "Evidence is generated to improve the international emergency deployment system")
Development of new flexible response teams (e.g., flood rescue, wildfire response) (activity: "UKISAR: to include new formalised capabilities e.g. flood and water rescue")
Decommissioning of UKEMT Field Hospital (design change: "No longer include a dedicated UK Field Hospital asset")
Partnership projects with 2–3 priority countries for capacity building (activity: "partnership programme of capacity building and knowledge exchange")
Knowledge exchange and joint exercises with national response teams (activity: "Joint training and exercising with national ISAR and EMT teams")
Technical assistance to develop emergency preparedness plans (activity: "Provision of targeted technical assistance to national response actors")
Mentoring for national EMT/ISAR teams to achieve accreditation (activity: "Mentoring to national EMT or ISAR to achieve ‘national accreditation’ levels")
what_objectives.summary: EDT2 is a humanitarian response programme that deploys UK medical and search-and-rescue teams to global disasters while simultaneously building local capacity in priority countries. It replaces EDT1 with an expanded, flexible model that addresses climate-related disasters and strengthens international coordination standards.
what_objectives.quote: The EDT2 programme will build on this legacy as part of FCDO’s humanitarian rapid response toolkit. It delivers on the Integrated Review’s strategic priority to prepare for and respond to humanitarian crises and continues to demonstrate that the UK is a principled humanitarian donor. (D0003487.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in disaster-prone contexts with variable stability, but the overall risk rating is assessed as moderate. Each deployment carries context-specific risks (e.g., conflict, extreme weather) that are managed case-by-case.
where_context.q5_source: The overall programme risk rating: Moderate. (D0003487.odt, Summary of the proposed programme)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate-related disasters (e.g., floods, wildfires) require new response capabilities, while conflict and weak institutions in priority countries may limit partnership effectiveness. Post-disaster infrastructure damage can hinder deployment speed and coordination.
where_context.quote: Much of the difference is explained by a rise in climate-related disasters including extreme weather events [...] It is in those countries with high vulnerability and low resilience that rapid onset emergencies are likely to have the most impact. (D0003487.odt, Overall context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains oversight and approval authority, with Southern partners (e.g., national response teams) receiving capacity-building support but no explicit decision-making role in programme design or deployment decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for local first responders
mentorship for national EMT/ISAR teams
knowledge exchange with UK teams
technical assistance for emergency preparedness plans
joint exercises with national teams

partner_organizations.name: UK International Search and Rescue (UKISAR)
partner_organizations.role: Deployable search-and-rescue teams (heavy/medium/light configurations)

partner_organizations.name: UK Emergency Medical Team (UKEMT)
partner_organizations.role: Deployable medical personnel (specialised care teams, outbreak response)

partner_organizations.name: National Health Service (NHS)
partner_organizations.role: Source of medical personnel for UKEMT; domestic resilience beneficiary

partner_organizations.name: Fire and Rescue Service (FRS)
partner_organizations.role: Source of search-and-rescue personnel for UKISAR; domestic resilience beneficiary

partner_organizations.name: United Nations INSARAG
partner_organizations.role: Global coordination network for urban search and rescue; sets accreditation standards

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO) EMT Initiative
partner_organizations.role: Global coordination for emergency medical teams; sets Blue Book standards

partner_organizations.name: Priority country national response teams
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of capacity-building partnerships (e.g., training, mentoring)

partner_organizations.name: Lead Partner (UKEMT)
partner_organizations.role: Single entity managing UKEMT capabilities (to be selected via competition)

partner_organizations.name: Lead Partner (UKISAR)
partner_organizations.role: Single entity managing UKISAR capabilities (to be selected via competition)

who_partners.quote: EDT2 will have a single lead partner for each of the UKISAR and UKEMT components. This will allow each component to be more effective and efficient. (D0003487.odt, What does this mean for the EDT2 programme?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses grant arrangements with lead partners for roster management, deployments, and capacity-building, alongside commercial contracts for specific services (e.g., equipment caches). Contingency funds are earmarked for small-scale responses.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees two closed consortia (one for UKISAR, one for UKEMT), each led by a single partner responsible for delivery. Two FCDO-funded Implementation Roles provide technical coordination. Partnership activities are developed in consultation with FCDO country offices.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The shift to single lead partners for UKISAR/UKEMT aims to improve efficiency and accountability, addressing lessons from EDT1 where fragmented governance created duplication and blurred accountability.
how_mechanism.quote: Deliver of the UKEMT under EDT1 was through three accountable grant partners and one commercial arrangement [...] Having a lead partner with oversight of all aspects of the UKEMT would ensure much clearer structures for delivery and accountability. (D0003487.odt, EDT1 lessons)

how_governance.quote: FCDO will work with partners to establish each deployment risk [...] Wider risks and mitigation measures are detailed in the Management Case and Risk Register. (D0003487.odt, Risk)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Contingency funds are earmarked for small-scale deployments, and partnership activities can be scaled based on annual reviews. However, major reallocations (e.g., between UKISAR/UKEMT components) require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes annual reviews to adjust capabilities (e.g., new specialised teams) and partnership focus based on emerging needs (e.g., climate-related disasters). Learning from deployments feeds into real-time adjustments.
how_flexibility.quote: Building in flexibility on how much we want to scale up capability and partnership building will manage resource and overstretch. (D0003487.odt, What does this mean for the EDT2 programme?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Partner (UKEMT/UKISAR) → End responders (no sub-grantees mentioned)
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will have a budget of £25m over five years. (D0003487.odt, Summary of the proposed programme)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Maintain basic deployable UKISAR/UKEMT capabilities only (no new teams/partnerships)
Option 2: Expand UKISAR/UKEMT specialised capabilities (e.g., flood rescue, outbreak teams) without partnerships
Option 3 (preferred): Expand capabilities + add partnership projects for capacity building
Do-nothing scenario (rejected as it would eliminate UK rapid response capability)
Splitting UKEMT/UKISAR into separate programmes (rejected due to inefficiencies)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected because it (1) aligns with the Integrated Review’s priority to improve humanitarian preparedness, (2) addresses UN strategic shifts toward localisation and flexible response, (3) maximises value for money by redirecting savings from decommissioning the Field Hospital to higher-impact activities, and (4) mitigates reputational risks by demonstrating UK leadership in adapting to climate-related disasters.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery risk that partnership activities may not align with country strategies or institutional needs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by programme-funded advisors working with FCDO country desks to ensure alignment with national priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk that UK is seen as deprioritising EMT/ISAR due to Field Hospital decommissioning
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Addressed by expanding specialised teams and partnerships to demonstrate continued leadership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of overstretch from adding new capabilities/partnerships
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Managed via flexible budget allocation and phased rollout of partnership projects.

why_rationale.quote: This option represents a higher-level ambition to deliver against the IR strategic objective for humanitarian preparedness and response, and will demonstrate that the UK remains a global leader on humanitarian response as well as adapting and responding to wider contextual and UN shifts. (D0003487.odt, Appraisal summary: Option 3)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The increasing frequency of climate-related disasters (WHERE) necessitates partnerships with countries vulnerable to these risks, limiting partner selection to those with aligned national strategies and institutional capacity to absorb training/mentoring.
q27_constraints_detail: Climate vulnerability (prioritises countries at risk of floods/wildfires)
National accreditation requirements (limits partnerships to countries pursuing INSARAG/WHO standards)
FCDO country office alignment (partnerships must complement existing programmes)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid deployment (WHAT) drives the closed consortium structure (HOW) with single lead partners to streamline accountability, while the localisation objective (WHAT) requires embedded capacity-building components (HOW) via partnerships.
q28_linkages: Rapid response requirement → Single lead partners for efficiency
Localisation agenda → Partnership projects with national teams
Flexible capabilities (e.g., flood rescue) → Adaptive management structure
UN accreditation standards → Need for centralised quality control via lead partners
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances (1) the efficiency of Northern-led deployments (speed, standards) with (2) equity goals of localisation (capacity building for Southern partners). Trade-offs include:
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: UK teams deploy rapidly, but partnerships require time to build local capacity.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern expertise ensures high standards, but risks undermining Southern leadership in responses.
Cost vs. reach: Specialised teams (e.g., rehabilitation) are costly but fill critical gaps; partnerships expand reach but require investment.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., deployment-specific risk assessments) rather than intensive day-to-day management, with flexibility built in for adaptive responses to disasters.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives elevate Southern partners from passive recipients (in EDT1) to active collaborators in joint exercises and knowledge exchange, though decision-making remains Northern-led.
intersections.quote: Strengthening emergency resilience in prioritised vulnerable countries through partnerships and capacity building with local and regional responders is the best way to prevent suffering and loss of life in the immediate aftermath of disasters. (D0003487.odt, Theory of Change)

key_programme_risks: Delivery risk: UKISAR/UKEMT capabilities may not be deployed if host governments decline offers of assistance (evidenced by Haiti/Beirut stand-downs in EDT1).
Reputational risk: Perception of UK deprioritising humanitarian response due to Field Hospital decommissioning.
Operational risk: Lack of dedicated UKISAR equipment cache may delay deployments (addressed in EDT2 design).
Partnership risk: Capacity-building may not align with national strategies or institutional capacities in priority countries.
Competition risk: Proliferation of other EMT/ISAR teams may reduce UK deployment opportunities.
Climate risk: Increasing climate-related disasters require new capabilities (e.g., flood response) that may stretch resources.
Safeguarding risk: Ensuring protection of vulnerable groups during deployments/partnerships.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited deployments of large capabilities (e.g., UKEMT Field Hospital never used in EDT1)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: EDT2 shifts to smaller, flexible teams and redirects savings to higher-impact activities (e.g., specialised care teams, partnerships).
