Expertise vs. ownership: UK-based organizations have technical skills but limit Southern leadership
Cost vs. reach: UN channels add overhead but enable access in restricted contexts
Gender equity vs. Taliban compliance: Female deminer teams are effective but face legal barriers in Afghanistan
intersections.risk_affects_management: High-risk FCAS contexts (e.g., Yemen, Somalia) require intensive oversight (quarterly conflict sensitivity reviews), while stable countries (e.g., Cambodia) allow lighter-touch management. The business case links risk profiles to specific oversight mechanisms (e.g., enhanced due diligence in Lebanon for Hezbollah risks).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives directly shape partner roles: national authorities are given progressively greater responsibility for coordination as their capacities improve (measured via the capacity development framework). Local NGOs are prioritized for sub-contracts only after demonstrating conflict sensitivity skills.

quote.context_who: "In Sudan... access for international demining organisations is extremely limited, making delivery through the UN (which can procure local demining organisations where necessary) the only viable option." (D0003708.odt, Ability to deliver the full geographic scope)
quote.what_how: "To promote long-term sustainability, we will invest in building the capacity of national authorities to enable them to manage mine action work effectively." (D0003708.odt, Programme Activities)
quote.tradeoffs: "The GMAP2 formative evaluation recommended that HMG encourage implementing partners to adopt more consistent approaches to conflict sensitivity... We will develop a mine action conflict sensitivity framework." (D0003708.odt, Conflict sensitivity)

key_programme_risks: Elite capture of cleared land for political/military use
Diversion of funds to terrorist organizations (e.g., Hezbollah in Lebanon)
Safeguarding incidents in remote demining teams
Reduced access due to conflict escalation (e.g., Ukraine, Yemen)
Gender equity backsliding (e.g., Taliban restrictions in Afghanistan)
Overemphasis on outputs (m² cleared) at expense of outcomes (land use)
Donor fatigue leading to funding gaps
National authority instability disrupting coordination

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Conflict sensitivity framework requiring political economy analysis before clearance; embassy engagement to lobby for equitable land allocation.
Enhanced due diligence and supply chain mapping (e.g., Lebanon Hezbollah checks); compliance with UK counter-terrorism finance policy.
Enhanced due diligence assessments; FCDO safeguarding unit oversight; mandatory reporting systems.
Flexible delivery channels (UN for high-risk areas); contingency planning for rapid scale-up (e.g., Ukraine).
Negotiations for female employment exemptions in Afghanistan; gender-disaggregated M&E; all-female teams where permissible.
Shift to outcome-focused indicators (e.g., land use tracking); supplier payments tied to development impacts, not just clearance.

fcas_specific_lessons: In Somalia, sub-clan representation in hiring reduces conflict risks
In Sri Lanka, ethnically diverse teams support peacebuilding
In Afghanistan, female risk education teams require Taliban exemptions
In Yemen, UN channels are essential for access but add delays
In Ukraine, rapid demining must align with recovery priorities to avoid aid fragmentation
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: GMAP2 lessons included: (1) Need for more outcome-focused M&E (not just m² cleared); (2) Conflict sensitivity gaps required a dedicated framework; (3) National capacity-building was insufficiently problem-driven; (4) Procurement perceptions of favouritism needed addressing; (5) Longer timeframes improve value for money by reducing mobilization costs.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Extended GMAP3 timeframe to 3 years (from GMAP2’s shorter pilot phase)
Added outcome indicators (e.g., land use, behaviour change) alongside output targets
Developed conflict sensitivity framework with practical tools for partners
Increased competition in procurement process
Prioritized problem-driven capacity-building (e.g., political lobbying for reforms)
Added dedicated research component to build evidence on mine action’s development impacts

quote.risks: "Mine action can itself affect conflict dynamics... there is a risk that mine action could be used as a political tool... or even as a conflict tool." (D0003708.odt, Conflict sensitivity)
quote.lessons: "Building on the GMAP2 evaluation and Annual Reviews, for GMAP3 we have prioritised... standardised and outcome-focused monitoring and evaluation... more problem-driven national capacity development." (D0003708.odt, What will be different about GMAP3?)
quote.changes: "GMAP2 had a shorter initial timeframe in order to test whether the significant scale-up... could be delivered effectively. Given GMAP2’s success, we are confident in setting a longer timeframe for GMAP3." (D0003708.odt, Programme timeframe)

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £48.63M over 3 years... The Afghanistan Directorate will be providing up to £5.5m over 2 years for demining operations in Afghanistan." (D0003708.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.allocation: "Table 4: country selection" shows indicative allocations (e.g., Ukraine: £4.3m in 2024/25; Afghanistan: £3m in 2024/25). (D0003708.odt, Options for country focus)

metadata.programme_name: Access to Medicine Index and Antimicrobial Resistance Benchmark (2021-25)

quote.programme_name: "AccesstoMedicineIndexandAntimicrobialResistanceBenchmark(2021-25)" (90000349.odt, Title)
quote.duration: "1st October 2021 - 30th September 2026" (D0006908.odt, New programme end date)
quote.sector: "Global Health Directorate" (90000349.odt, Country/Region or Sector)

metadata.duration_source: "New programme end date (if applicable): 30th September 2026" (D0006908.odt)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme aims to increase access to medicines and essential health products for people in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by influencing pharmaceutical industry practices. It combines evidence generation (rankings and research), policy influence (stimulating competition and sharing best practices), and financing mechanism (funding the Access to Medicine Foundation).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme aims to increase access to medicines and essential health products for people in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and to increase efforts by the pharmaceutical industry to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by funding the Access to Medicine (ATM) Foundation." (90000349.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Two iterations of the Access to Medicine Index (biennial)
AMR Benchmark reports (e.g., 2023 report)
Patient Reach Report (2024)
Research on access to generics, diagnostics, and medical oxygen
Engagement with stakeholders (governments, academics, investors)
Methodology reviews for the ATM Index
Thematic studies on AMR and access challenges
what_objectives.summary: The programme focuses on improving access to medicines in LMICs and tackling AMR by leveraging the ATM Foundation’s rankings and research to incentivize pharmaceutical companies to adopt better practices. It combines research, advocacy, and stakeholder engagement to drive systemic change.

quote.objectives: "This programme aims to improve access to medicine in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and to increase efforts by the pharmaceutical industry to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by funding the Access to Medicine Foundation (ATMF)." (D0006908.odt, Programme summary)
quote.outputs: "ATMF have completed two cycles of the Access to Medicine Index (published biennially), including review and publication of the Index methodology in the intervening year." (D0006908.odt, Implementation)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates globally with minimal risks from natural hazards or unstable environments. The risk rating is classified as 'minor' due to the stable operating context and trusted implementing partner (ATM Foundation).
where_context.q5_source: "The programme presents a low risk of safeguarding issues as it will not operate with children or other vulnerable individuals and we will ensure that the implementing partner develops and implements an effective safeguarding policy." (90000349.odt, Wider assurances) AND "The overall programme risk rating: Minor" (90000349.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: limited R&D focus on LMIC-relevant diseases
political economy factors (e.g., pharmaceutical industry priorities)
data limitations (e.g., tracking access in LMICs)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak health systems and substandard medicines hinder delivery of medicines to those in need, while industry priorities often neglect LMIC-relevant diseases due to perceived low returns on investment. Data gaps make it difficult to track progress in access.

quote.constraints: "Timely access to necessary and appropriate medicines can be hindered or prevented through various avenues. The barriers most frequently cited is the price of medicines, which can often be too high for LMICs and poor populations to afford. [...] Other factors preventing access to medicines arise from weak national health systems, which can hinder the delivery of medicines to those that need them." (90000349.odt, Barriers to accessing medicines)
quote.risk: "The overall programme risk rating: Minor" (90000349.odt, Summary Sheet)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The ATM Foundation (based in Amsterdam, Netherlands) holds decision-making authority for programme delivery, with FCDO providing oversight and funding. No explicit Southern-led decision-making is mentioned.
q10_capacity_building_details: sharing best practices with pharmaceutical companies
engaging stakeholders (including LMIC governments) to drive progress
identifying and advocating for inclusive business models
applying a gender lens to research (e.g., focusing on women/girls' access needs)

partner_organizations.name: Access to Medicine Foundation (ATMF)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (research, rankings, stakeholder engagement)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: funder and oversight

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (24% of ATMF budget)

partner_organizations.name: Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (23% of ATMF budget)

partner_organizations.name: Dutch Ministry of Health
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (7% of ATMF budget)

partner_organizations.name: AXA Investment Managers
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (4% of ATMF budget)

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (4% of ATMF budget)

partner_organizations.name: Evaluation delivery partner (TBD)
partner_organizations.role: independent evaluation (procured competitively by ATMF)

quote.structure: "This programme will be delivered by a single implementing partner, the ATM Foundation, which FCDO has worked with over a number of years and has proved to be an effective and trusted organisation." (90000349.odt, Governance and management arrangements)
quote.capacity: "The ATM Foundation works to stimulate competition between the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies by publishing rankings and research on how companies are responding to access to medicine and AMR-related challenges, identifying and sharing best practices within the industry." (D0006908.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_funding_instrument: core funding via Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO provides core funding to the ATM Foundation through an MoU, allowing flexibility for the ATMF to allocate resources according to its strategic plan. This avoids earmarking and reduces administrative burden.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The ATM Foundation is the sole implementer, with FCDO delegating day-to-day decisions to ATMF while retaining oversight. No downstream partners are involved, simplifying management.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The ATM Foundation is uniquely positioned due to its technical expertise, reputation, and track record (e.g., A+ in Programme Completion Review). No viable alternatives exist for this specific role.

quote.instrument: "The FCDO will award the ATM Foundation an MoU for core funding up to a total of £4 million." (90000349.odt, Financial Case) AND "We propose a single source tender through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the ATM Foundation, a not-for-profit foundation." (90000349.odt, Management Case)
quote.selection: "We are confident that a full competitive tender process would not yield further bids to easily deliver this programme. The risks of a commercial challenge are minimal because there are no other organisations working in this unique manner." (90000349.odt, Management Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The ATM Foundation is accountable to its Supervisory Board (which includes donor representatives) and to FCDO through reporting requirements. FCDO attends Supervisory Board meetings annually to ensure alignment with donor priorities.

quote.governance: "The ATM Foundation is also accountable to its other donors. The FCDO will attend the ATM Foundation Supervisory Board meetings at least annually with other donors to ensure alignment of views and prevent the programme skewing its focus to any specific donor priorities." (90000349.odt, Governance and management arrangements)
quote.oversight: "The FCDO will monitor programme performance and progress through quarterly programme meetings with the ATM Foundation, receiving six-monthly reporting from the ATM Foundation, which will include a progress update, financial report, asset register, and risk register." (90000349.odt, Governance and management arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated within the ATM Foundation’s strategic plan, but major changes require FCDO approval (e.g., expanding into new areas like diagnostics). Tranches are released based on milestone completion.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The ATM Foundation can adjust research priorities (e.g., expanding into generics or medical oxygen) with FCDO agreement, as evidenced by the 2024 evaluation recommendations. The programme is designed to be adaptive to emerging global health priorities (e.g., COVID-19, AMR).

quote.flexibility: "Core funding from the FCDO would enable the ATM Foundation to help fill this gap and offer the greatest return on investment for the FCDO." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "The extension will support ATMF’s work on the 10th edition of the Access to Medicine Index, which will be published in Autumn 2026. It will also provide continuity of funding and support ATMF’s retention of staff and expertise." (D0006908.odt, Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ATM Foundation (no downstream partners)

quote.budget: "The original business case approved a budget of £4 million over 4 years [...] This costed extension increases the proposed budget by £1 million, to a revised total of £5 million." (D0006908.odt, Budget)
quote.layers: "This programme will be delivered by a single implementing partner, the ATM Foundation, which FCDO has worked with over a number of years [...] there will be no downstream implementing partners." (90000349.odt, Governance and management arrangements)
quote.payments: "Payments will be released upon receipt by the FCDO of six-monthly progress and finance reports from the ATM Foundation, detailing how previously disbursed funds have been spent." (90000349.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (no FCDO investment)
Provide earmarked funding to ATM Foundation for specific products (ATM Index/AMR Benchmark only)
Provide core funding to ATM Foundation to implement its five-year strategic plan (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Core funding was chosen to maximize flexibility, value for money, and alignment with ATMF’s strategic expansion into new areas (e.g., generics, diagnostics). The ATMF’s unique role, proven track record (A+ in PCR), and ability to leverage donor funds efficiently justified sole-source selection. Earmarked funding was rejected due to higher administrative costs and limited scope.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (trusted partner with strong controls)
speed (direct award avoids lengthy tender processes)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: ATM Foundation’s capacity to expand into new areas (e.g., diagnostics, generics) without compromising quality.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ATMF will recruit additional staff with relevant expertise and phase expansion carefully. FCDO will monitor progress through milestone reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single implementer (ATMF) could disrupt delivery if donor funding shifts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ATMF has diversified its donor base (6 donors) and maintains reserve funds. FCDO is the largest contributor (37%), providing stability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited competition in partner selection could reduce VfM or innovation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ATMF’s unique role and strong independent evaluations (e.g., 90% of stakeholders agreed on its significant contribution) justify sole-source selection. Regular evaluations ensure accountability.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of inputs, e.g., staff remuneration)
effectiveness (proven impact on pharmaceutical industry practices)
equity (focus on LMIC access and gender-inclusive approaches)

quote.alternatives: "Option 1 – Do nothing [...] Option 2 - Provide core funding to the ATM Foundation to implement its five-year strategic plan [...] Option 3 - Support the ATM Foundation to deliver further iterations of its ATM Index and the AMR influencing programme." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.rationale: "The preferred option is Option 2: Provide core funding to the ATM Foundation to implement its five-year strategic plan. [...] Core funding from the FCDO would enable the ATM Foundation to fill this gap and offer the greatest return on investment for the FCDO." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.risks: "The overall risk rating for this option is moderate with the main risks relating to the ATM Foundation’s capacity and capability to deliver should it expand its scope into new areas." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on pharmaceutical industry practices necessitate a partner with strong international reputation and existing relationships (e.g., ATMF’s networks with companies, governments, and investors). LMIC-specific constraints (e.g., weak health systems) are addressed indirectly through ATMF’s advocacy for inclusive business models.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for a neutral, trusted intermediary to engage pharmaceutical companies globally
Requirements for technical expertise in AMR and access metrics
Limited pool of organizations with ATMF’s unique focus on cross-industry transparency
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives (influencing pharmaceutical companies and generating global public goods) require a centralized, independent implementer (ATMF) with credibility to publish rankings and engage stakeholders. The lack of downstream partners reflects the need for consistency in methodology and messaging.
q28_linkages: Global public goods (rankings/research) → Single implementer (ATMF) to ensure standardization
Industry influence → Direct funding to ATMF to maintain independence
Adaptive priorities (e.g., COVID-19, AMR) → Core funding for flexibility
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme prioritizes efficiency (single implementer, core funding) over direct Southern ownership, but includes equity considerations (e.g., gender lens in research, focus on LMIC access). The trade-off is mitigated by ATMF’s engagement with LMIC stakeholders and global health organizations.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (direct award to ATMF) vs. inclusion (no competitive tender)
Northern expertise (ATMF’s technical capacity) vs. Southern ownership (limited LMIC-led decision-making)
Global reach (pharmaceutical industry focus) vs. localized adaptation (no country-specific implementers)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘minor’ risk profile enables light-touch oversight (milestone-based reporting) while still ensuring accountability. High-risk areas (e.g., financial controls) are mitigated by ATMF’s robust systems (e.g., audits, conflict-of-interest policies).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: ATMF’s capacity to engage pharmaceutical companies and produce high-quality research shapes its central role. FCDO’s capacity constraints (e.g., workload) are addressed by delegating day-to-day management to ATMF while retaining strategic oversight.

quote.where_who: "The UK is in a strong position to ensure the success of this programme due to our effective relationships with UK-based pharmaceutical companies and investors, our membership on the boards of various global health institutions and our position as a global leader on AMR." (90000349.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
quote.what_how: "The ATM Foundation has a unique and valued role in the access ecosystem, providing trusted and transparent data on industry performance from an independent standpoint." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.equity: "The programme will also contribute towards the government’s manifesto commitment to end the preventable deaths of mothers, newborns and children by building consensus on expected pharmaceutical industry contributions." (90000349.odt, Alignment with UK priorities)

key_programme_risks: Pharmaceutical industry distraction (e.g., COVID-19 reducing engagement with ATMF)
ATMF’s capacity to expand into new areas (e.g., diagnostics, generics) without diluting impact
Donor funding shifts affecting ATMF’s financial stability
Limited attribution of ATMF’s influence on access/AMR outcomes (due to wider systemic factors)
Environmental impact of stakeholder travel (mitigated by virtual engagement)
Potential safeguarding issues for ATMF staff (addressed by policies)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ATMF streamlined data collection to reduce burden on companies and expanded its engagement team.
ATMF will recruit additional staff and phase new projects carefully, with FCDO monitoring.
ATMF diversified its donor base (6 donors) and maintains reserve funds.
ATMF tracks tracer medicines and uses qualitative data to demonstrate influence. Independent evaluations (e.g., 2024) provide external validation.
ATMF’s travel policy prioritizes virtual meetings and low-carbon transport. Carbon offsets are calculated quarterly.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2016–21 programme exceeded targets (A+ in PCR) and demonstrated ATMF’s ability to influence industry practices (e.g., voluntary licensing, access plans). Lessons included the need for adaptive management (e.g., responding to COVID-19) and the value of core funding for flexibility. The 2024 evaluation confirmed ATMF’s continued effectiveness, supporting the extension.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Expansion into new areas (generics, diagnostics, medical oxygen) based on stakeholder demand and evaluation recommendations.
Increased focus on gender equity (e.g., sex-disaggregated data in ATM Index).
Streamlined data collection to reduce industry burden (lesson from COVID-19).
Enhanced stakeholder engagement in LMICs (response to 2024 Annual Review).

quote.risks: "The main Strategy and Context risks associated with this programme relate to potential changes in the operating environment, such as the pharmaceutical industry, that may reduce the impact the ATM Foundation may have." (90000349.odt, Risk appetite statement)
quote.lessons: "The previous programme delivered two iterations of the ATM Index and the first AMR Benchmark and supported the ATM Foundation to substantially increase its engagement and influence with the pharmaceutical industry and other stakeholders." (90000349.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "In a 2024 independent evaluation, 90% of key informants agreed that the ATMF have made a significant contribution to improving access to medicines in LMICs." (D0006908.odt, Programme summary)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The ATM Foundation’s donor base expanded from 5 to 6 donors during the programme, increasing financial robustness. The FCDO’s £5m contribution (37% of ATMF’s total funds) leverages co-funding from other donors, amplifying impact.

quote.co_funding: "The FCDO will be one of six donors funding the ATM Foundation and will contribute the largest share (37%) to its total funds." (90000349.odt, Financial Case)
quote.breakdown: "Management and operations: 8%" (90000349.odt, Financial Case) AND "The ATM Foundation has strong financial controls in place to monitor budgets and spend." (90000349.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Increasing Global Aid Transparency

quote.programme_name: "Title: Increasing Global Aid Transparency" (D0003164.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £801K" (D0003164.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.duration: "The first version of the concept note was drafted and approved with a draft budget of £800,000 over five years in 2020." (D0003164.odt, Financial Details)
quote.sector: "This programme is central to the FCDO’s delivery of its aid transparency objectives." (D0003164.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: The first version of the concept note was drafted and approved with a draft budget of £800,000 over five years in 2020. However, the previous programme was extended due to the impact of COVID-19 and the merger pressures, resulting in a need to refresh and update the original concept note before finalising the new business case. The revised concept note continues with the proposal of up to £800,000.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme aims to improve global and UK aid transparency by supporting the International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI), funding assessments like the Aid Transparency Index, and enhancing data quality and use. It combines capacity building (training partners on IATI standards), policy influence (pushing for global transparency standards), and financing mechanisms (membership fees to IATI).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support improvements in global and UK aid transparency and data publication, including data quality and impact, with the aim of increasing the effectiveness of global aid as developing countries, donors, civil society and academics will be better able to explore, scrutinise, use and apply quality aid data." (D0003164.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Membership fees to IATI (2023–2027)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 53.2% of funding (£426K)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Follow-up to the 2020 UK Aid Transparency Review
q3_expected_outputs.target: Assessment in 2025 (25% of funding, £200K)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Contribution to Publish What You Fund’s Global Aid Transparency Index (2026)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 12.5% of funding (£100K, with £50K contingency)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved tools/training for supplier partner transparency and research on IATI data impact
q3_expected_outputs.target: 9.4% of funding (£75K)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Publication of IATI’s strategic plan outputs (data quality, training, assessments)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Annual outputs aligned with IATI’s strategy

q3_expected_outputs.output: Assessment of UK Government Departments’ aid transparency
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2025, covering ODA-spending departments

what_objectives.summary: The programme focuses on strengthening global aid transparency through financial support to IATI, independent transparency assessments, and capacity-building for partners to publish high-quality aid data. It directly addresses ICAI recommendations and aligns with the UK’s Open Government Partnership commitments.

quote.objective: "This programme will provide membership fees to support the International Aid Transparency Initiative standard (IATI)’s work on aid data quality and use, fund a follow-up to the 2020 UK Aid Transparency review assessing the transparency of UK government departments spending aid, contribute to Publish What You Fund’s Global Aid Transparency Index assessment in 2026, fund research on the impact and uptake of IATI data, review the UK’s investment in IATI to date, and improve supplier partner transparency." (D0003164.odt, Programme Summary)
quote.approach: "The programme is central to delivering Ministers’ stated ambition for the FCDO to be a global leader in aid transparency." (D0003164.odt, Rationale)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme faces operational risks due to IATI’s governance changes and funding uncertainties for the Aid Transparency Index. The UK’s reputation on aid transparency has declined, requiring mitigation. Political and institutional changes (e.g., FCDO merger, pandemic) have impacted delivery capacity.
where_context.q5_source: "The risk for the programme overall is moderate. [...] The global Aid Transparency Index is an established publication backed by evidence of real change in donor behaviour, but funding issues mean that future Indices are at risk." (D0003164.odt, Risk Register)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: IATI’s governance transition and potential fee increases create financial uncertainty. The UK’s reduced engagement during the pandemic and FCDO merger weakened its influence. Data variability among publishers limits usability, and smaller UK government departments struggle with transparency standards. Safeguarding risks arise from inadvertent sharing of sensitive data in conflict contexts (e.g., Afghanistan, Ukraine).

quote.risk: "The pandemic and the merger of FCO and DFID impacted on staff and systems, and continues to have an impact on FCDO’s delivery. This, alongside political changes in the UK, has impacted on perceived commitment to aid transparency." (D0003164.odt, Risk Register)
quote.constraints: "There is significant variability in the data in IATI between donors because the standard is relatively flexible to take into account different accounting approaches by different types of organisation." (D0003164.odt, Theory of Change)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) holds decision-making power through its IATI membership vote and funding influence, while IATI’s secretariat (currently a UN consortium) manages operational delivery. Southern partners (e.g., developing country governments) are beneficiaries of the data but have limited direct influence over IATI’s governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for FCDO staff on IATI standards (via International Academy modules)
Training for UK partners (e.g., CSOs) on IATI publication requirements
Support for developing countries to use IATI data (via IATI’s data use work)
Research on data uptake to inform future capacity-building needs

partner_organizations.name: International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer of global aid transparency standards; receives membership fees (53.2% of budget)

partner_organizations.name: Publish What You Fund (PWYF)
partner_organizations.role: Conducts Global Aid Transparency Index assessments (12.5% of budget for 2026 Index)

partner_organizations.name: UK Government Departments (ODA-spending)
partner_organizations.role: Subject of transparency assessments (25% of budget for 2025 review)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO’s supplier partners (e.g., CSOs, contractors)
partner_organizations.role: Required to publish aid data to IATI; potential recipients of training (9.4% of budget)

partner_organizations.name: Development Initiatives (DI)
partner_organizations.role: Current IATI secretariat member (transitioning); provides technical support

quote.structure: "The programme is central to delivering Ministers’ stated ambition for the FCDO to be a global leader in aid transparency. Ministers have been clear in their view that the FCDO’s development objectives are only achievable when working efficiently with other aid actors." (D0003164.odt, Rationale)
quote.capacity: "FCDO should consider how to ensure partners have the information they need to publish the information the FCDO requests them to publish. Ideas include online training modules, and/or online drop-in clinics for implementing partners of UK (FCDO to start with) ODA programmes." (D0003164.odt, Partner Training)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **membership fees** (for IATI), **grants** (for PWYF’s Aid Transparency Index), and **contracts** (for the 2025 UK transparency assessment). IATI funding is provided via direct payments to the secretariat, while PWYF and assessment work may use MOUs or commercial agreements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages relationships with IATI (as a member), PWYF (via contributions), and UK government departments (via assessments). Day-to-day delivery is decentralized: IATI manages its strategic plan, PWYF runs the Index independently, and FCDO oversees internal/partner training. A Grade 7 FCDO role focuses on external engagement.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IATI and PWYF were selected due to their **unique global roles** in aid transparency (no alternatives exist for IATI’s standard or PWYF’s Index). The 2025 UK assessment will likely use PWYF again for **methodological consistency**, though alternatives (consultants/internal) were considered. Partner training providers are undecided pending a needs assessment.

quote.instrument: "Funding will be provided through MOUs, rather than contracts." (D0003164.odt, Value for Money)
quote.selection: "IATI is the only global organisation that provides an aid standard of this kind and the UK is a member." (D0003164.odt, Global Transparency)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: IATI is governed by a **Governing Board** and **Members’ Assembly**, where the UK has a vote as a paid member. FCDO engages via working groups and the Assembly. PWYF operates independently but reports progress to FCDO. Internal FCDO governance includes monthly programme meetings and risk reviews.

quote.governance: "IATI is currently made up of a consortium of three organisations—UNDP, UNOPs and Development Initiatives—though this consortium is due to change, bringing with it elements of risk in terms of future financial management." (D0003164.odt, Audit Information)
quote.oversight: "Programme meetings will be held monthly where risks are checked and updated as needed." (D0003164.odt, Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between lower-priority interventions (e.g., training/research) if underspends occur in core areas (IATI fees, UK assessment). Contingency budgets (e.g., £50K for PWYF’s 2026 Index) allow flexibility, but IATI fees are fixed commitments.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities (Intervention 5) will be finalized in FY24/25 based on emerging evidence. Training approaches (Intervention 4) will adapt based on a needs assessment in Year 1. The programme can respond to IATI’s governance changes but requires FCDO approval for major shifts.

quote.reallocation: "Any underspend will be re-directed to areas of the business case which are lower priorities, and unlikely to otherwise be fully funded." (D0003164.odt, Financial Details)
quote.adaptive: "Exploration of research options will be pursued in FY23/24 but will not be commissioned until FY24/25 onwards." (D0003164.odt, Research and Analysis)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → [IATI/PWYF/Assessment Provider] → (no further sub-grantees; end users are governments/citizens).

quote.layers: "The management of the largest single part of the finances of the programme was historically relatively straightforward, being a membership payment to the International Aid Transparency Initiative." (D0003164.odt, Management)
quote.payment: "IATI fees are $85K USD per year, the cost in Table Three is based on the exchange rate at time of writing." (D0003164.odt, Financial Details)

alternatives: Not renewing IATI membership (rejected due to loss of influence)
Reducing engagement (rejected due to UK’s leadership ambitions)
Internal assessment (rejected due to legitimacy concerns)
Consultants (rejected due to higher costs and methodological inconsistency)
FCDO-delivered training (not feasible until systems are finalized)
Funding IATI to develop UK-specific modules (preferred for scalability)
Internal FCDO research (lower cost but less global consistency)
Collaborative research with IATI (preferred for alignment)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen:
The modality was chosen for **value for money**, **global influence**, and **alignment with UK priorities**:
- **IATI membership** is the only way to retain voting rights and shape global standards.
- **PWYF’s Index** is the sole independent assessment of donor transparency, with proven impact on behavior.
- **Direct UK assessments** ensure accountability to Parliament and ICAI recommendations.
- **Embedded training** addresses ICAI/Foreign Affairs Committee critiques of FCDO’s capacity gaps.
- **Flexible research** allows adaptation to emerging evidence on data use.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (e.g., IATI’s global reach vs. cost)
risk mitigation (e.g., securing UK’s reputation post-merger)
past experience (e.g., evidence that PWYF’s Index improves transparency)
partner capacity (e.g., IATI’s role as the sole global standard-setter)
flexibility (e.g., contingency funds for PWYF’s 2026 Index)
equity (e.g., supporting developing countries’ data use)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IATI governance transition disrupts delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will engage actively in the new secretariat’s setup and monitor financial management via audits and Members’ Assembly updates.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: PWYF fails to secure funding for 2026 Index
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: £50K contingency allocated; FCDO will advocate with other donors to share costs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UK government departments resist transparency assessments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use PWYF’s established methodology (from 2020) to ensure legitimacy and Open Government Partnership commitments as leverage.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partners (e.g., CSOs) lack capacity to publish IATI data
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Needs assessment in Year 1 to design targeted training (e.g., drop-in clinics, modules).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (e.g., minimizing costs for IATI membership)
effectiveness (e.g., focusing on areas with proven impact like the Aid Transparency Index)
equity (e.g., ensuring developing countries can use the data)

quote.rationale: "Being a member provides the UK with a vote and influence through payment of fees (currently $85K USD per annum), though this may change under the new secretariat. [...] Failing to pay our IATI fees would hugely degrade the UK’s ability to influence decision making on global aid transparency practice." (D0003164.odt, Intervention 1)
quote.vfm: "Value for money and cost effectiveness of contributing membership fees to IATI and supporting transparency as a contribution to a global good, as well as the sustainability of investment, was considered during the previous programme." (D0003164.odt, Intervention 1)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope** and **multilateral nature of IATI** limit partner selection to organizations with existing global mandates (e.g., IATI, PWYF). The UK’s **reputational risks** post-merger/pandemic necessitate working with established partners (e.g., PWYF for legitimacy). **Data variability** among publishers constrains who can effectively use the training (e.g., smaller CSOs struggle more).
q27_constraints_detail: No Southern-led alternatives to IATI/PWYF exist for global standards/assessments.
UK government departments’ varying capacities require tailored assessments (e.g., PWYF’s methodology may not fit smaller spenders).
Conflict contexts (e.g., Afghanistan, Ukraine) limit data publication, affecting partner roles in sensitive areas.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for global standards** (IATI) and **independent scrutiny** (PWYF Index) dictates a **multilateral, arms-length delivery structure**. The **focus on data use** (not just publication) requires embedded training and research components. **ICAI’s recommendations** drive the inclusion of UK-specific assessments and partner capacity-building.
q28_linkages: Global transparency goals → IATI membership and PWYF Index funding (multilateral mechanisms).
UK accountability needs → Direct assessments of government departments (national focus).
Capacity gaps (ICAI/Foreign Affairs Committee findings) → Embedded training for FCDO/partners.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme prioritizes **global efficiency** (e.g., funding IATI as a single standard-setter) over **local equity** (e.g., limited direct funding to Southern institutions). **Northern expertise** (IATI/PWYF) is leveraged for speed, but **Southern data use** is a secondary objective (addressed via IATI’s data use work).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Using PWYF’s existing methodology ensures rapid UK assessments but may disadvantage smaller departments.
IATI’s Northern-led secretariat ensures technical quality but limits Southern governance influence.
Contingency funds for PWYF’s 2026 Index prioritize global coverage over deeper country-level support.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., IATI governance changes, PWYF funding gaps) justifies **milestone-based oversight** (monthly FCDO meetings) and **contingency budgets**. Higher risks (e.g., reputational damage) drive proactive engagement (e.g., FCDO’s Grade 7 role for external advocacy).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **need to build FCDO/partner capacity** (per ICAI) shapes the inclusion of training components and research on data use. IATI’s **data use work** targets developing countries, while FCDO training focuses on **UK partners first** (due to resource constraints).

quote.constraints: "There is no alternative global institution of this nature focused on providing collective in-year data of expenditure across the whole ODA system." (D0003164.odt, Intervention 1)
quote.tradeoffs: "The UK’s current reputation on transparency has suffered during the pandemic and following the merger, most notably in FCDO failing to reach ‘Very Good’ in ATI24 (FCDO’s first ATI assessment)." (D0003164.odt, Risk Register)
quote.capacity: "Ensuring our own staff in country are fully aware of the information available from IATI will reduce duplication of donor work and support work on country aid effectiveness." (D0003164.odt, Partner Training)

key_programme_risks.risk: IATI governance transition disrupts operations (Major)
PWYF fails to secure 2026 Index funding (Moderate)
UK government departments resist transparency improvements (Moderate)
Exchange rate fluctuations increase IATI fee costs (Moderate)
Data publication puts individuals at risk in conflict zones (e.g., Afghanistan, Ukraine) (Moderate)
FCDO staff vacancies delay partner training (Moderate)
Smaller CSOs lack resources to publish IATI data (Moderate)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will engage actively in the new secretariat’s setup, monitor via Members’ Assembly, and use contingency funds for fee changes.
Allocated £50K contingency; FCDO will advocate with other donors (e.g., Netherlands) to share costs.
Use Open Government Partnership commitments and PWYF’s methodology to ensure legitimacy.
Budgeted £82K/year for IATI fees (vs. $85K) with flexibility to adjust other spend if costs rise.
FCDO uses FOI/GDPR frameworks to decide publication; works with donors on responsible data-sharing protocols.
Two technical vacancies included in Strategic Workforce Planning; interim support from existing team.
Needs assessment in Year 1 to design targeted training (e.g., drop-in clinics).

fcas_specific_lessons: Sensitive data in conflict contexts (e.g., Afghanistan, Ukraine) requires **adaptive publication protocols** (e.g., temporary removal of data).
Developing countries’ **limited data use** highlights need for IATI’s simplified tools and FCDO’s focus on capacity-building.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
The **2016–2022 programme** showed that:
- IATI data quality improved but remained underutilized by developing countries.
- The Aid Transparency Index **drove donor behavior change** (Honig & Weaver, 2019), but funding gaps threatened its continuity.
- **UK transparency improved** but smaller departments lagged due to methodological rigidity.
- **Training needs** were unmet post-BOND’s withdrawal, requiring new approaches (e.g., online modules).
- **Data use** (not just publication) is critical for impact but requires local support (Keijzer, 2016).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **contingency funds** for PWYF’s 2026 Index (addressing past funding vulnerabilities).
Included **partner training needs assessment** (Year 1) to replace ad-hoc BOND support.
Expanded **research on data use** (Intervention 5) to address limited evidence on impact.
Increased **FCDO engagement in IATI governance** (Grade 7 role) to reverse post-merger disengagement.
Adapted **UK assessment methodology** to accommodate smaller departments (lesson from 2020 review).

quote.risks: "The risk for the programme overall is moderate. [...] The global Aid Transparency Index is an established publication backed by evidence of real change in donor behaviour, but funding issues mean that future Indices are at risk." (D0003164.odt, Risk Register)
quote.lessons: "The annual reviews and Programme Completion Report indicated that there was clear evidence that the Aid Transparency Index was improving global donor aid transparency, that more publishers than ever were publishing to the International Aid Transparency Initiative, and that the data in IATI was beginning to be useful and used. However, [...] IATI data quality had improved but there was still a significant way to go for the data to be fully useful to users." (D0003164.odt, Rationale)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages **IATI’s global publisher network** (1,300+ organizations) and **PWYF’s donor relationships** to mobilize co-funding for the 2026 Index. IATI’s 2024 Index is fully funded by IATI itself, reducing FCDO’s burden.

quote.leverage: "IATI have, however, confirmed they will not provide funding for future assessments. The cost of each assessment is $300,000 per year for two years. [...] FCDO aid transparency colleagues are engaging with PWYF and other supportive donors to reduce reliance on the UK for 2026 (and beyond)." (D0003164.odt, Intervention 2)

metadata.programme_name: Transformative Economic Policy Programme (TEPP)
metadata.quote: "The Transformative Economic Policy Programme (TEPP) is FCDO’s main economic policy programme in Bangladesh. TEPP aims to improve the effectiveness of economic policy through three complementary actions: Generate policy-relevant data, research, and analysis; Support local think-tanks to develop expertise, produce high-quality analysis and advocate for policy action; Provide targeted technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) in key areas for economic policy." (D0006370.odt, INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 1st June 2021 to 30th June 2023 (extended to 31st March 2024 after COVID delays) [...] 1st cost extension for an additional £10m over 4 years (till FY 27/28) [...] Cost extension value (if applicable): £3m (Total value: £16.54m)" (D0006370.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: TEPP combines policy influence (informing economic policy decisions), capacity building (strengthening government and think-tank expertise), and evidence generation (producing policy-relevant data and research). The programme aims to improve economic policy effectiveness through technical assistance, research, and advocacy, with a focus on COVID-19 recovery, green growth, and LDC graduation.
what_objectives.q1_source: "TEPP aims to improve the effectiveness of economic policy through three complementary actions: Generate policy-relevant data, research, and analysis; Support local think-tanks to develop expertise, produce high-quality analysis and advocate for policy action; Provide targeted technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) in key areas for economic policy." (D0006370.odt, INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Establishment of Research and Analysis Units (RAUs) within government departments (e.g., BIDA, Commerce Ministry)
Support to 3-4 local think-tanks (e.g., Policy Research Institute, Centre for Policy Dialogue) to develop expertise and advocate for policy action
Development of economic data tools (e.g., Purchasing Managers’ Index, retail sales index)
Technical assistance to the central bank on banking stability and monetary policy reforms
Flexible, need-based technical assistance to respond to economic shocks (e.g., banking crisis, IMF programme)
Policy analysis and advice on LDC graduation, investment climate, and trade reforms
Data disaggregated by gender, age, and disability to inform inclusive policy-making
Public policy debates and media engagement to build demand for reforms
what_objectives.summary: TEPP is a strategic, long-term programme designed to strengthen Bangladesh’s economic policy-making through a mix of technical assistance, research, and advocacy. It focuses on building government capacity, supporting think-tanks, and generating data to inform inclusive, green, and resilient economic recovery and reform.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will scale up existing projects to support the Bangladesh government strengthen trade policy capability and implement trade policy and investment climate reforms. The interim government has much greater ambitions for reforms than the previous administration and has requested UK support." (D0006370.odt, INFORMATION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Bangladesh is experiencing significant macroeconomic turbulence, a banking crisis, and political instability following a public uprising in July-August 2024. The economy is at high risk of financial instability, and the interim government faces pressures to implement urgent reforms while navigating a volatile political environment.
where_context.q5_source: "Bangladesh is currently in the midst of a critical juncture in its political and development trajectory. The economy has been experiencing significant macroeconomic turbulences since 2023 and is at high risk of a banking crisis. A mass public uprising in July-August 2024 led to a change in government resulting in an interim government taking over." (D0006370.odt, INFORMATION)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The political economy constraints, including vested interest groups and weak institutional capacity, have historically blocked major reforms. Data limitations hinder evidence-based policy-making, while economic volatility (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine war, banking crisis) creates urgency but also instability. The interim government’s reform agenda provides a window of opportunity but is constrained by time and political uncertainty.
where_context.quote: "Major reforms were not feasible over the last decade due to the government’s unwillingness to acknowledge economic problems and take effective action. Reform initiatives were also blocked by strong vested interest groups that gained from the status quo." (D0006370.odt, INFORMATION)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is shared between FCDO (funding and strategic oversight) and local partners (implementation and technical delivery). Local think-tanks and government agencies (e.g., BIDA, Bangladesh Bank) have significant roles in shaping priorities and delivering outputs, while FCDO retains approval authority for major decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: Embedded technical experts in government ministries (e.g., Research and Analysis Units in BIDA)
Training and mentorship for think-tanks (e.g., Policy Research Institute, Centre for Policy Dialogue)
Institutional strengthening of government agencies (e.g., Bangladesh Bank, Commerce Ministry)
Development of long-term expertise in economic data analysis and policy advocacy
Support for civil society engagement in policy debates

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for technical assistance to government (e.g., Research and Analysis Units, trade policy reforms)

partner_organizations.name: Policy Research Institute (PRI)
partner_organizations.role: Local think-tank specializing in macroeconomic policy analysis and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD)
partner_organizations.role: Local think-tank focusing on domestic resource mobilization and environmental policy

partner_organizations.name: BRAC Institute for Governance and Development (BIGD)
partner_organizations.role: Local think-tank coordinating policy research and advocacy (e.g., tax reform, LDC graduation)

partner_organizations.name: RAPID
partner_organizations.role: Local think-tank working on tax system reforms

partner_organizations.name: Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI)
partner_organizations.role: Private sector partner for economic data generation (e.g., Purchasing Managers’ Index)

partner_organizations.name: Singapore Institute of Purchasing and Materials Management (SIPMM)
partner_organizations.role: Technical partner for developing economic data tools (e.g., PMI)

partner_organizations.name: Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA)
partner_organizations.role: Government partner hosting a Research and Analysis Unit for policy support

partner_organizations.name: Bangladesh Bank (Central Bank)
partner_organizations.role: Government partner receiving technical assistance on banking stability and monetary policy reforms

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Commerce
partner_organizations.role: Government partner for trade policy and investment climate reforms

partner_organizations.name: International Growth Centre (IGC)
partner_organizations.role: Former research partner (phased out due to low traction with government)

partner_organizations.name: Commercial consulting firm (unnamed)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider for banking stability (procured via tender)

who_partners.quote: "The programme will increase the funding to UNDP to scale up its technical assistance by amending the existing cooperation agreement. [...] The programme will work closely with UNDP and GoB to select the exact policy issues which the programme will support and the type of assistance to be provided (e.g., embedded policy experts, written advice)." (D0006370.odt, Components and Delivery Partners)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: TEPP uses a combination of instruments: (1) **Contribution Agreements** with UNDP for technical assistance; (2) **grants** to local think-tanks and research institutes; (3) **commercial contracts** for specialized technical assistance (e.g., banking crisis response); and (4) **flexible funds** managed directly by FCDO for agile responses. The programme also explores pooled funding with other development partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: TEPP is organized around four components, each with distinct delivery partners and management arrangements. FCDO’s Prosperity and Economic Growth Team provides overarching coordination, while UNDP, think-tanks, and commercial suppliers deliver specific components. The programme includes a flexible fund managed directly by FCDO to respond to emerging priorities (e.g., banking crisis).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNDP was selected for its existing trust and embedded relationships with the Bangladesh government, while think-tanks were chosen based on their local expertise and policy influence. Commercial suppliers (e.g., for banking stability) are procured via tender to ensure specialized technical skills. The shift from IGC to local think-tanks reflects lessons on government traction and demand for policy-relevant (vs. academic) research.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNDP will be the implementing partner for delivering technical assistance on economic policy. UNDP works very closely with the government on policy making and has staff embedded within various ministries, including the Planning Commission and the Cabinet Division. This is a significant advantage, which exceeds the benefits of delivering the programme through the international financial institutions." (61196925.odt, Delivery options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Senior Economic Advisor (SRO)** and **Programme Manager (PRO)** from FCDO’s Prosperity and Economic Growth Team oversee strategic and operational decisions. The **Country Board** and **Programme Assurance Committee (PAC)** provide guidance on strategic and programme management issues. For the flexible fund, the **SRO and PEG Team Leader** make all funding decisions, while UNDP and think-tanks manage their respective components under FCDO oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The SRO will escalate issues of strategic importance, and significant risks, as appropriate to the Deputy Development Director, Development Director, and High Commissioner. The Country Board and Programme Assurance Committee (PAC) provide guidance and advice on strategic and programme management issues respectively." (D0006370.odt, Programme Team)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on traction and emerging priorities (e.g., shifting from academic research to data tools), but major changes require FCDO approval. The flexible fund (£1m) is explicitly designed for agile responses to crises (e.g., banking stability) and is replenished as needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: TEPP uses rapid economic and political economy analysis to adjust priorities. The programme dropped academic research due to low government traction and added data tools and flexible TA based on demand. New issues (e.g., banking crisis) can be incorporated if they align with strategic objectives, while underperforming areas are phased out.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will include a flexible component for technical assistance. [...] This would allow TEPP to respond to such opportunities. We will agree on a distinct set of policy priorities in the first 1-2 months after approval of the addendum, which will enable us to continually identify key entry points and opportunities for the use of this fund." (D0003523.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) UNDP/think-tanks/commercial suppliers → (2) End users (government ministries, central bank, private sector). The flexible fund is managed directly by FCDO with no intermediary.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will increase the funding to UNDP to scale up its technical assistance by amending the existing cooperation agreement. [...] The programme will shortly enter into a funding agreement with a fourth think-tank that specialises in macroeconomic policy." (D0006370.odt, Components and Delivery Partners)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct implementation by FCDO staff (rejected due to lack of technical capacity and potential government sensitivity)
Commercial supplier-led delivery (rejected due to high costs, low traction, and slow mobilization)
World Bank partnership (rejected due to muted government interest and limited added value)
Multilateral-led research (rejected due to concerns over quality and cost)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery model (UNDP for TA, think-tanks for advocacy, flexible FCDO-managed funds) was chosen for: (1) **Speed**: UNDP’s embedded relationships allowed quick mobilization; (2) **Traction**: Local think-tanks have trusted government access; (3) **Flexibility**: Direct FCDO management of agile funds enables rapid crisis response; (4) **Value for Money**: Think-tanks cost less than commercial suppliers; (5) **Risk Mitigation**: UNDP’s credibility reduces political risks compared to FCDO-led delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low government demand for academic research
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Shifted focus from IGC-led academic research to think-tank advocacy and data tools with higher policy traction.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in commercial supplier procurement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Used UNDP’s existing agreements and flexible FCDO funds for urgent needs (e.g., banking crisis).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Think-tank capacity limitations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Provided targeted TA to strengthen expertise (e.g., Expert Policy Centres) and pooled funding with other donors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government sensitivity to foreign advice
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Used UNDP as intermediary and embedded local experts in ministries to build trust.

why_rationale.quote: "We assessed that it would be much more effective to provide technical assistance, research and policy influencing through two partners: a multilateral organisation to deliver technical assistance and an academic institution that will manage a portfolio of research and grants to think-tanks to undertake policy influencing. [...] UNDP works very closely with the government on policy making and has staff embedded within various ministries, including the Planning Commission and the Cabinet Division. This is a significant advantage." (61196925.odt, Delivery options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy context in Bangladesh constrains partner selection by: (1) **Government sensitivity**: Ruling out direct FCDO implementation or commercial suppliers without local intermediaries (e.g., UNDP); (2) **Vested interests**: Requiring partners with trusted relationships (e.g., think-tanks with long-standing government ties); (3) **Data limitations**: Prioritizing partners who can generate timely data (e.g., MCCI for economic indicators); (4) **Reform windows**: Needing agile partners (e.g., flexible FCDO funds) to capitalize on crises like the banking sector collapse.
q27_constraints_detail: Government reluctance to work with foreign entities without local intermediaries
Need for partners with pre-existing trust and embedded relationships (e.g., UNDP, think-tanks)
Limited civic space under previous government (now improved with interim government)
Urgent demand for crisis response (e.g., banking stability) requiring rapid-procurement partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives determine its delivery structure through: (1) **Policy influence goals**: Requiring embedded TA (via UNDP) and think-tank advocacy to navigate political economy barriers; (2) **Capacity building**: Using local think-tanks and RAUs to ensure sustainability; (3) **Crisis responsiveness**: Flexible FCDO-managed funds for unpredictable needs (e.g., banking crisis); (4) **Data gaps**: Partnering with MCCI/SIPMM to create economic indicators absent in Bangladesh.
q28_linkages: Embedded TA (UNDP) → Addresses government’s weak policy capacity and need for trusted advisors
Think-tank advocacy → Builds public demand for reforms and bridges government-civil society gaps
Flexible funds → Enables rapid response to emerging crises (e.g., banking sector collapse)
Data tools (MCCI) → Fills critical evidence gaps for both government and private sector decision-making
Shift from academic research (IGC) to policy-relevant analysis → Aligns with government’s low demand for rigorous research
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Local ownership vs. speed**: Using local think-tanks (slower but more sustainable) over commercial suppliers (faster but less embedded); (2) **Inclusive partnerships vs. traction**: Prioritizing think-tanks with government access over broader civil society engagement; (3) **Rigorous research vs. policy relevance**: Dropping academic research (IGC) in favor of actionable data tools and advocacy.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Local think-tanks (higher traction) vs. international researchers (higher technical capacity)
Flexible FCDO funds (rapid response) vs. multilateral processes (slower but more legitimate)
Targeted TA to champions of change (efficient) vs. broad capacity building (more equitable)
Data tools for policymakers (immediate utility) vs. long-term research (deeper evidence)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk context (banking crisis, political instability) justifies **intensive oversight** (e.g., quarterly reviews, embedded FCDO advisors) and **adaptive management** (e.g., flexible funds, rapid reallocation). The interim government’s reform agenda increases risk appetite but also demands closer monitoring to ensure traction.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) Think-tanks receive grants + TA to develop expertise (e.g., Expert Policy Centres); (2) Government agencies (e.g., BIDA) host RAUs with embedded economists; (3) UNDP’s role includes institutional strengthening; (4) Flexible funds are used to ‘top up’ capacity where gaps emerge (e.g., central bank monetary policy team).
intersections.quote: "The programme will provide targeted technical assistance (TA) to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) in key areas for economic policy. This includes establishing policy analysis units within government departments to build long-term capability. [...] The programme will also explore opportunities to continue working with a2i on digitalisation more broadly, including on the digital economy and digital public services." (D0003523.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

key_programme_risks: Political instability and uncertainty about the interim government’s tenure
Low government demand for academic research (leading to pivot to data tools)
Vested interest groups blocking reforms (e.g., banking sector, tax changes)
Capacity gaps in think-tanks and government agencies
Economic volatility (e.g., banking crisis, inflation) disrupting reform plans
Delays in commercial supplier procurement for urgent needs
Staffing gaps in FCDO’s Prosperity and Economic Growth Team
Risk of banking crisis escalating and requiring costly interventions
Potential backsliding on reforms if elected government replaces interim administration

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political instability and reform appetite changes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on consensus areas (e.g., banking stability, LDC graduation) likely to sustain across governments; use diplomatic channels to encourage continuity.
Shifted funding to think-tank advocacy and user-friendly data tools (e.g., PMI, retail sales index).
Targeted TA to reform champions (e.g., Finance Ministry, Bangladesh Bank) and flexible funds to capitalize on windows of opportunity.
Embedded experts (e.g., RAUs in BIDA) and institutional strengthening support (e.g., UNDP-led TA).
Flexible fund for rapid response (e.g., banking stability TA) and contingency planning with central bank.
Pre-qualified suppliers for urgent needs and direct FCDO management of flexible funds.
Programme Management Advisor support and clear escalation paths to High Commissioner.

fcas_specific_lessons: Crisis contexts (e.g., banking collapse, political transition) create urgency but also opportunities for reform; flexibility and rapid-response funds are critical.
Local intermediaries (e.g., UNDP, think-tanks) are essential for traction in sensitive political environments.
Embedded TA (e.g., RAUs) builds trust and sustainability compared to external advice.
Data limitations in FCAS require investments in basic economic indicators (e.g., PMI) to inform decision-making.
Political transitions (e.g., interim government) can open reform windows but demand adaptive programming and risk management.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases showed that: (1) Academic research had low government traction, leading to a pivot toward policy-relevant data tools; (2) Think-tanks needed targeted TA to strengthen advocacy capacity; (3) Embedded units (e.g., RAU in BIDA) were more effective than standalone advice; (4) Flexible funds enabled responses to unanticipated crises (e.g., banking sector support). The shift from IGC to local think-tanks reflected lessons on government demand for actionable (vs. academic) analysis.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes include: (1) **Phasing out IGC-led research** in favor of think-tank advocacy and data tools; (2) **Adding a flexible fund** for agile responses to crises; (3) **Scaling up RAUs** (e.g., BIDA, Commerce Ministry) based on early success; (4) **Focusing on economic indicators** (e.g., PMI) to address data gaps; (5) **Direct FCDO management** of high-priority components (e.g., banking stability) to ensure speed and alignment with UK interests.
risks_lessons.quote: "The experience over the last two years of implementation suggests that the original theory of change remains broadly valid. There is strong demand for timely and reliable economic data and analysis for use in policy making. [...] However, our assessment is that the absence of an economics cadre in the civil service hinders the use of such research. [...] Therefore, while the overall theory of change remains valid, under this extension TEPP will pivot more towards providing policy makers and economic decision-makers with reliable data and user-friendly data tools and move away from funding academic research as a means for informing policy makers." (D0003523.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case including the theory of change or new evidence from ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work?)

metadata.programme_name: Investing in Nature, Forests and Land Use (Inafolu)

quote.programme_name: "The Inafolu programme will support increased investment in Indonesia’s natural capital assets through two complementary approaches." (S30110610.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "The programme is designed for a programme of 4 years, for a value of up to £38.8m" (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)

metadata.duration_source: "The programme is designed for a programme of 4 years, for a value of up to £38.8m (this includes up to £500k already budgeted to support programme design, of which £280k has been utilised)." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Inafolu programme combines financing mechanisms (channeling funds for natural capital projects), implementation research (testing and scaling interventions like peatland restoration), and capacity building (strengthening governance and policy implementation). It aims to increase investment in Indonesia’s natural capital while improving the enabling environment for sustainable land use.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Inafolu programme will support increased investment in Indonesia’s natural capital assets through two complementary approaches. The first approach is to increase investment in the sector, including by identifying and prioritising a pipeline of natural capital projects... The second approach is to strengthen the enabling environment for investment through a variety of measures that disincentivise the erosion of natural capital." (S30110610.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: A pipeline of natural capital projects prioritised for investment (e.g., peatland restoration, mangrove conservation)
Direct investment in high-priority natural capital projects (e.g., "rewetting, revegetation and revitalisation of degraded peatlands")
Strengthened implementation of FoLU policies (e.g., social forestry, spatial planning, ecological fiscal transfers)
Enhanced capacity of subnational governments and communities to manage natural capital (e.g., "capacity building to better link national and subnational delivery")
Leveraged additional public and private finance for FoLU sector (e.g., "mobilise and target public and private finance")
Support for Indonesia’s FoLU Net Sink 2030 targets (e.g., "achieve its ambitious 2030 Forest and other Land Use (FoLU) sector emissions reductions targets")
Improved monitoring and evaluation frameworks (e.g., "independent MEL hub provides an opportunity to build learning on policy and investment")
what_objectives.summary: Inafolu aims to accelerate Indonesia’s transition to a low-carbon, nature-positive economy by mobilising finance for natural capital projects and strengthening governance systems. It directly addresses the country’s FoLU emissions reduction targets while supporting livelihoods and biodiversity conservation.

quote.objectives: "The programme aims to: (i) support the Government of Indonesia to achieve its ambitious 2030 Forest and other Land Use (FoLU) sector emissions reductions targets; (ii) protect and restore ecosystems in one of the most biodiverse countries on earth; and (iii) support communities reliant on Indonesia’s forest resources." (S30110610.odt, Programme summary)
quote.approach: "The programme is designed to enable rapid, agile and adaptive mobilisation to kickstart this commitment [£350m over 10 years]." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme’s risk rating is explicitly stated as "moderate" in the document. Indonesia faces challenges like deforestation, weak policy enforcement, and political transitions (e.g., 2024 elections), but the Government of Indonesia (GoI) has demonstrated commitment to FoLU reforms, providing a stable foundation for collaboration.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (S30110610.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (e.g., "loopholes in policies" like moratoria on primary forest clearance)
political economy (e.g., "political conditions may limit engagement across all areas simultaneously")
weak institutions (e.g., "patchy enforcement" of environmental laws, "insufficient financial structuring and institutional planning")
climate risks (e.g., peat fires, deforestation driven by agricultural expansion)
data limitations (e.g., discrepancies between GoI and Global Forest Watch deforestation figures)
corruption (e.g., "work with the KPK [Anti-Corruption Commission] to review concession licenses")
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory loopholes and weak enforcement undermine policy effectiveness (e.g., fines for deforestation are issued but often unpaid). Political transitions (2024 elections) may disrupt continuity, while institutional gaps at subnational levels limit the flow of finance to local projects. Climate risks like peat fires directly threaten natural capital assets, requiring adaptive programme responses.

quote.constraints: "Government actions to reduce deforestation have aligned with several external factors... But the GoI can legitimately attribute reductions in deforestation to its policy intervention... [However,] there are loopholes in these policies, and enforcement is patchy, especially against private companies holding concessions." (S30110610.odt, A Supportive National Context)
quote.political_risk: "The programme will work as political conditions allow – engagement across all areas immediately and simultaneously may not be possible and require careful political handling." (S30110610.odt, Theory of Change)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes GoI ownership and leadership, with FCDO providing catalytic funding and technical support. Decision-making on project prioritization and policy implementation rests with Indonesian authorities (e.g., Ministry of Environment and Forestry, BAPPENAS), while the UK shapes programme design and investment strategies.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening subnational government systems for ecological fiscal transfers
Supporting the Indonesian Environment Fund (IEF) to channel climate finance
Building technical capacity for peatland and mangrove restoration
Enhancing community engagement in social forestry schemes (e.g., Hutan Adat)
Training for law enforcement and oversight bodies (e.g., KPK, CSOs)
Developing bankable project proposals for green finance (e.g., green bonds, carbon markets)
