quote.ownership: "The Inafolu Programme will raise investment in the FoLU sector in Indonesia, based on the principle of GoI ownership and leadership." (S30110610.odt, What Will the Programme Do?)
quote.capacity_building: "The programme will support development of specific bankable project proposals, targeting technical capacity and community engagement." (S30110610.odt, Private Finance)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for capacity building and policy support) and direct investments (Capital Expenditure/CDEL for ecosystem restoration). Funds will flow through the Indonesian Environment Fund (IEF) and other GoI mechanisms, with FCDO providing both core funding and co-financing for leveraged projects.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will operate through a flexible partnership model, with FCDO as the primary funder, the GoI as the strategic lead, and an implementing partner (or consortium) managing day-to-day delivery. The MEL Hub will provide independent oversight. Subnational governments, CSOs, and private sector actors will be engaged as sub-partners for specific projects.

quote.funding: "The programme will use a large proportion of Capital Expenditure (CDEL), in order to create natural assets, primarily through ecosystem restoration activities." (S30110610.odt, Part 1b: Investment in natural capital projects)
quote.structure: "The two parts of the programme will aim to tie together. During the inception phase of part 1, and throughout the delivery phase, the implementing partner of part 1 will be requested to provide evidence of enabling environment challenges encountered as part of its project preparation work." (S30110610.odt, Part 2: Strengthening implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: While not explicitly detailed, the programme implies a steering committee-like structure with the GoI, FCDO, and implementing partners coordinating priorities. The MEL Hub will provide independent oversight, and subnational allocations will align with GoI’s FoLU Net Sink 2030 Operational Plan.

quote.governance: "An independent MEL hub provides an opportunity to build learning on policy and investment in the FoLU sector. The hub will... evaluate the effectiveness of the programme to support GoI policies... in partnership with the GoI." (S30110610.odt, Monitoring Evaluation and Learning)
quote.oversight: "The programme design provides a flexible framework for the programme to prioritise according to political conditions." (S30110610.odt, Theory of Change)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., Part 1a pipeline design to Part 1b direct investments) based on emerging priorities, but this requires alignment with GoI’s FoLU Net Sink 2030 plan and MEL Hub evidence. The programme’s adaptive framework allows for reprioritization as political conditions evolve.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an adaptive management approach, with the MEL Hub feeding real-time evidence into decision-making. Adjustments to project pipelines or policy support will be made in consultation with the GoI, particularly post-2024 elections.

quote.flexibility: "The programme will work as political conditions allow – engagement across all areas immediately and simultaneously may not be possible and require careful political handling. The programme design provides a flexible framework for the programme to prioritise according to political conditions." (S30110610.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.adaptive: "After an initial phase of delivery (2-3 years), the FCDO will be well-placed to determine progress of the programme, assessing this in line with Indonesia’s FoLU 2030 climate targets. At this point, a decision can be made on how best to continue programmatic work." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner → Subnational Governments/CSOs/Private Sector (for project delivery). The IEF may act as an additional layer for financial flows.

quote.layers: "The programme will support the development of systems that will channel the investment needed to deliver the plan; provide direct investment in areas prioritised under the plan... strengthening underlying governance through the development, enforcement and implementation of policies." (S30110610.odt, Supporting 2030 Net Sink-Finance and Investment)
quote.payments: "Implementing partners will be tasked with seeking wider financing for projects in order to raise impact." (S30110610.odt, Part 1b: Investment in natural capital projects)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed financing and capacity-building modality was selected to address Indonesia’s dual needs: (1) **urgent investment gaps** in natural capital (e.g., £13.9bn financing gap for FoLU Net Sink 2030) and (2) **systemic barriers** to sustainable land use (e.g., weak policy enforcement, subnational capacity gaps). The programme’s design leverages the UK’s strengths in catalytic funding and the GoI’s policy ownership, while its adaptive framework mitigates political and implementation risks.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (value for money through leveraging private/public co-financing)
risk-mitigation (flexible framework to adapt to political transitions and enforcement challenges)
experience (builds on 20 years of UK-Indonesia FoLU collaboration, e.g., SVLK timber regulation)
partner-capacity (GoI’s demonstrated commitment via FoLU Net Sink 2030 Operational Plan)
speed (rapid mobilisation to kickstart UK’s £350m 10-year pledge)
flexibility (adaptive management to respond to MEL Hub evidence and political conditions)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Misalignment with GoI priorities post-2024 elections
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible framework and close coordination with BAPPENAS/MoEF to ensure continuity; MEL Hub to track political risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak subnational capacity to absorb funds or implement policies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted capacity building for ecological fiscal transfers and social forestry schemes; technical assistance to provinces/districts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector reluctance to invest in nature-based solutions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Develop bankable project pipelines (e.g., carbon market linkages, green bonds) and demonstrate leverage potential.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Enforcement gaps in concession landscapes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Support KPK and CSOs in monitoring; align with Omnibus Law implementation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap or duplication with other donor programmes (e.g., World Bank, Norway)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Coordinate via IEF and FoLU Net Sink 2030 Operational Plan; focus on complementary niches (e.g., spatial planning in new Papua provinces).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging £38.8m to mobilise additional public/private finance)
efficiency (streamlined delivery through IEF and existing GoI systems)
effectiveness (alignment with FoLU Net Sink 2030 targets and Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration)
equity (focus on IPLCs, women’s groups, and poor forest-dependent communities)

quote.rationale: "The Inafolu programme is designed to enable rapid, agile and adaptive mobilisation to kickstart this commitment [£350m over 10 years]... It aims to provide tangible action and boost investment as the GoI looks to the international community to support delivery of its FoLU 2030 goals." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)
quote.risks: "The programme will work as political conditions allow – engagement across all areas immediately and simultaneously may not be possible and require careful political handling." (S30110610.odt, Theory of Change)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Indonesia’s **decentralized governance structure** and **political economy** constrain partner selection: (1) Subnational capacity gaps require partners with local expertise (e.g., CSOs for community engagement). (2) The GoI’s insistence on ownership limits the role of international implementers to technical support. (3) Regulatory complexities (e.g., concession licenses) necessitate collaboration with anti-corruption bodies like KPK.
q27_constraints_detail: Subnational capacity gaps → Need for partners with provincial/district-level experience (e.g., spatial planning in new Papua provinces).
GoI ownership → Limits Northern-led implementation; requires Southern institutions (IEF, BRGM) as primary channels.
Corruption risks → Mandates involvement of oversight bodies (KPK, CSOs) in concession reviews.
Political transitions (2024 elections) → Requires partners with adaptive management experience.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **dual objectives** (financing + governance) shape its **two-part structure**: (1) **Part 1 (investment)** requires a fund manager-like approach (e.g., pipeline development, direct investments) to mobilise capital. (2) **Part 2 (policy implementation)** demands embedded technical assistance (e.g., spatial planning support, social forestry training) to address systemic barriers. The MEL Hub bridges both by feeding evidence from investment challenges into policy adjustments.
q28_linkages: Financing goals → Need for a **project pipeline** (Part 1a) → Requires partners with financial structuring expertise (e.g., IEF, private sector).
Governance goals → Need for **policy implementation support** (Part 2) → Requires partners embedded in MoEF/BAPPENAS.
Leverage targets → Need for **co-financing mechanisms** → Requires coordination with multilateral donors (World Bank, Norway).
Adaptive management → Need for **real-time MEL** → Requires independent hub with GoI/FCDO access.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (e.g., social forestry for IPLCs, women’s groups) with **efficiency** (e.g., leveraging IEF for rapid finance deployment). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct investments (Part 1b) may prioritise high-leverage projects over smaller community-led initiatives. (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern technical assistance (e.g., carbon market development) risks sidelining local knowledge without deliberate capacity-building (e.g., Hutan Adat schemes).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: "The programme is designed to enable rapid, agile and adaptive mobilisation" (efficiency) but must align with "supporting communities reliant on Indonesia’s forest resources" (equity).

Expertise vs. ownership: "Lack of information about and experience in peatland management, carbon trading... are barriers to engagement" (need for Northern expertise) vs. "Social Forestry schemes enable communities to apply for different types of rights to tenure" (local ownership).
Cost vs. reach: Direct investments in peatland/mangrove restoration (high cost) compete with broader spatial planning support (wider reach).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** drives a **milestone-based oversight** approach: (1) Political risks (e.g., elections) necessitate adaptive management via the MEL Hub. (2) Enforcement gaps require intensive monitoring of subnational partners. (3) Financial risks (e.g., private sector reluctance) demand rigorous due diligence for direct investments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives **define partner roles**: (1) **GoI ministries** (MoEF, BAPPENAS) lead policy implementation but receive technical support for subnational delivery. (2) **CSOs** are critical for community engagement where government capacity is weak. (3) **Private sector** partners are targeted for bankable projects but require capacity-building in carbon markets and sustainable practices.

quote.context_who: "Indonesia’s political cycle, with a national election in 2024... The programme design provides a flexible framework for the programme to prioritise according to political conditions." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)
quote.what_how: "The two parts of the programme will aim to tie together. During the inception phase of part 1, and throughout the delivery phase, the implementing partner of part 1 will be requested to provide evidence of enabling environment challenges encountered as part of its project preparation work. This evidence will feed into the prioritisation of grant-making under Part 2." (S30110610.odt, Part 2: Strengthening implementation)
quote.equity_efficiency: "Social Forestry schemes help to reconcile [economic] needs with an environmentally sustainable development pathway... Opportunities for Inafolu include: (i) expanding the livelihood dimensions of the scheme (ii) targeted support for women’s groups." (S30110610.odt, Social Forestry)

key_programme_risks: Political transition risks (2024 elections disrupting continuity)
Subnational capacity gaps limiting project absorption
Private sector disengagement from nature-based investments
Weak enforcement of FoLU policies (e.g., concession violations)
Overlap with other donor programmes (e.g., World Bank, Norway)
Climate risks (peat fires, extreme weather affecting restoration)
Data discrepancies between GoI and independent sources (e.g., deforestation rates)
Corruption in land-use permitting and carbon markets
Community resistance to spatial planning changes
Macroeconomic shocks (e.g., palm oil price volatility affecting deforestation drivers)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible programme framework; close coordination with incoming administration via BAPPENAS/MoEF; MEL Hub to track political risks.
Targeted technical assistance for ecological fiscal transfers and social forestry; partner with CSOs for community engagement.
Develop bankable project pipelines (e.g., carbon market linkages); demonstrate co-financing opportunities.
Support KPK and CSOs in monitoring; align with Omnibus Law implementation and concession license reviews.
Coordinate via IEF and FoLU Net Sink 2030 Operational Plan; focus on complementary niches (e.g., new Papua provinces).
Integrate fire prevention into peatland restoration; support BRGM’s early warning systems.
Use MEL Hub to reconcile GoI and independent data; strengthen GoI’s monitoring systems.
Partner with KPK for oversight; transparent project selection via IEF.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from UK’s prior FoLU work in Indonesia (e.g., SVLK timber regulation) highlight the need for **long-term engagement** to build trust and institutional capacity.
Experience with peatland fires (2015) underscores the importance of **community-based fire prevention** alongside restoration.
Previous concession license reviews (e.g., West Papua) show that **multi-stakeholder oversight** (KPK + CSOs) improves enforcement.
Spatial planning in Papua demonstrates that **locally led processes** reduce conflict and improve compliance.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The UK’s 20-year partnership with Indonesia on FoLU provides critical lessons: (1) **Alignment with GoI priorities** (e.g., FoLU Net Sink 2030) ensures sustainability. (2) **Subnational engagement** is essential for addressing deforestation drivers. (3) **Results-based payments** (e.g., Norway’s model) can incentivise emissions reductions but require robust MRV systems. (4) **Adaptive management** is key to navigating political and economic shocks (e.g., palm oil price fluctuations).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates lessons by: (1) **Prioritising GoI ownership** (e.g., channelling funds via IEF). (2) **Focusing on subnational delivery** (e.g., ecological fiscal transfers to districts). (3) **Integrating MEL from inception** to enable real-time adjustments. (4) **Targeting leverage** (e.g., carbon markets, green bonds) based on evidence of financing gaps.

quote.lessons: "The UK has a 20-year partnership of working with Indonesia on FoLU... A key achievement has been the successful development of Indonesia’s own regulation for legal timber (SVLK), becoming the first country to export to the EU market under the FLEGT regulation, which the UK was instrumental in supporting." (S30110610.odt, Context for UK Intervention)
quote.adaptations: "The programme is designed to enable rapid, agile and adaptive mobilisation... After an initial phase of delivery (2-3 years), the FCDO will be well-placed to determine progress of the programme, assessing this in line with Indonesia’s FoLU 2030 climate targets." (S30110610.odt, Summary of Intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage additional finance from: (1) **International donors** (e.g., Norway’s $56m payment to IEF). (2) **Private sector** (e.g., carbon markets, green bonds). (3) **Indonesian state budgets** (e.g., ecological fiscal transfers). The FoLU Net Sink 2030 Operational Plan identifies a £13.9bn financing gap, of which Inafolu’s £38.8m is a catalytic contribution.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme will use a **large proportion of Capital Expenditure (CDEL)** for ecosystem restoration (e.g., peatland rewetting, mangrove replanting) and **Revenue Expenditure (RDEL)** for capacity building, policy support, and MEL activities. Part 1a (pipeline design) is likely RDEL, while Part 1b (direct investments) and Part 2 (policy implementation) will include both.

quote.leverage: "The programme will also seek to prioritise projects which leverage further investment in natural capital. Additional financing may be leveraged from other donors, Indonesian state budgets, and private investors." (S30110610.odt, Part 1b: Investment in natural capital projects)
quote.capital: "This part of the programme will use a large proportion of Capital Expenditure (CDEL), in order to create natural assets, primarily through ecosystem restoration activities." (S30110610.odt, Part 1b: Investment in natural capital projects)
