partner_organizations.role: co-funder for data collection in Ethiopia, India, Peru

partner_organizations.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (historical)

partner_organizations.name: Children’s Investment Fund Foundation (CIFF)
partner_organizations.role: co-funder (historical)

who_partners.quote: "The University of Oxford lead coordination, quality assure the data, and produce global communications products while the country-based organisations conduct the survey, ensure high quality data and lead local policy impact work." (52784570.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DFID provides an **Accountable Grant** to the University of Oxford, which sub-contracts country teams. The grant covers core data collection and research costs, with co-funding required for Round 7.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Oxford acts as the hub, sub-contracting four country teams (spokes) under a fixed management model. A Steering Committee and Advisory Board oversee direction.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Oxford has led Young Lives since 2005, with proven capacity to manage the hub-and-spokes model and deliver high-quality longitudinal data.
how_mechanism.quote: "We will sign an Accountable Grant with the University of Oxford, who have led the Young Lives study since 2005." (52784570.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee meets bi-annually and includes the Programme Director, Country Directors, DFID representatives, other funders, and thematic experts. An Advisory Board of academics/practitioners provides oversight.
how_governance.quote: "A Steering Committee will also be established to oversight the direction of the programme. It will meet bi-annually and include the Programme Director, the Country Directors, representatives from DFID and other funders as well as thematic experts." (52784570.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between components (e.g., data collection vs. communications) as additional funders join, but core DFID funding is fixed for Rounds 6–7.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The logframe can be expanded to include new funders’ priorities, but DFID’s core focus (education/labour/gender) remains fixed unless approved changes occur.
how_flexibility.quote: "As additional funders come on board to cover these costs, we will expand the log frame so that it is one reporting framework for all funders." (52784570.odt, What are the key changes to the original business case?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → University of Oxford (hub) → Country Teams (spokes).
how_efficiency.quote: "Annual budgets are agreed with partners based on work plans, and partner budgets, work plans and quarterly financial reports are scrutinised by YL team and payment is made in arrears." (53923995.odt, What are the key risks to the success of the programme?)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hub-and-spokes model was chosen for its **proven track record** in delivering high-quality longitudinal data, **efficiency** in coordinating multi-country research, and **alignment with DFID’s strategic priorities** (youth employment, education, gender). Oxford’s central role ensures quality assurance and global policy influence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to secure 50% co-funding for Round 7
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Breakpoint clause to stop DFID funding in late 2022 if matching funds are not met.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial mismanagement by country teams
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Oxford’s financial regulations and quarterly scrutiny of budgets/reports.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Disengagement of DFID country offices
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly updates via Microsoft Teams and inclusion in working groups.

why_rationale.quote: "The objective of this additional investment is to provide robust evidence to inform DFID policy and programming on youth, as we aim to support productivity and employability in the face of growing demographic, education system and labour market challenges." (52784570.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope requires a **centralized hub (Oxford)** to manage cross-country comparability, limiting the ability to use purely Southern-led institutions due to coordination complexity.
q27_constraints_detail: need for standardized data collection across diverse contexts
political changes (e.g., Andhra Pradesh bifurcation) disrupting local partnerships
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **longitudinal, mixed-methods design** requires a hub-and-spokes structure to ensure data quality and comparability, while **policy influence objectives** necessitate Oxford’s central role in global communications.
q28_linkages: longitudinal data → need for centralized quality assurance (Oxford)
policy influence → Oxford’s global communications capacity
multi-country scope → sub-contracting model for local implementation
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The **Northern-led hub** ensures efficiency and quality but limits Southern ownership; **co-funding requirements** for Round 7 balance DFID’s budget constraints with sustainability goals.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (Oxford) vs. Southern ownership (country teams)
cost control (DFID’s 50% funding cap) vs. programme continuity (risk of Round 7 cancellation)
intersections.risk_affects_management: Moderate risk profile (e.g., financial, political) leads to **quarterly oversight** and **breakpoint clauses** rather than light-touch management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building for country teams is **embedded** in the model, with training and co-authorship ensuring they can lead local policy work while Oxford retains quality control.
intersections.quote: "The University of Oxford lead coordination, quality assure the data, and produce global communications products while the country-based organisations conduct the survey, ensure high quality data and lead local policy impact work." (52784570.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Failure to secure 50% co-funding for Round 7 (2024)
Financial mismanagement by country teams
Disengagement of DFID country offices
Political disruptions (e.g., Andhra Pradesh bifurcation)
Data quality issues in longitudinal tracking

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to secure 50% co-funding for Round 7
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Breakpoint clause to halt DFID funding in late 2022 if matching funds are unmet.
Oxford’s financial regulations, annual budgets, and quarterly scrutiny.
Quarterly updates and inclusion in Young Lives working group.
Flexible logframe adjustments and adaptive management.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2019 evaluation confirmed the **hub-and-spokes model’s effectiveness** but highlighted the need for **stronger country team engagement** and **co-funding diversification**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added a **breakpoint clause** for Round 7 funding and **expanded the logframe** to accommodate new funders’ priorities.
risks_lessons.quote: "The Inception Phase report of the evaluation of Young Lives, commissioned in 2018 by DFID, confirmed that the University of Oxford play the critical central role in a ‘hub and spokes’ model." (52784570.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Young Lives raised £7m from partners (2009–2017) and requires 50% co-funding for Round 7 (2024).
financial_details.quote: "DFID will provide £9.4 million over six years for an additional two rounds of data collection and analysis." (52784570.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Societal and Economic Resilience in Jordan (SSERJ)
metadata.primary_sector: social protection / humanitarian assistance / economic development
metadata.quote: "The UK’s £65m intervention over five years will support Government of Jordan (GoJ) to build an inclusive and sustainable safety net system." (D0003134.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: April 2022–April 2027" (D0003411.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SSERJ combines **implementation research** (piloting cash transfer schemes and social insurance expansions), **capacity building** (strengthening GoJ systems and technical assistance), **policy influence** (evidence generation to inform GoJ decisions on refugee inclusion and economic reforms), and **service delivery** (direct cash transfers to vulnerable refugees and Jordanians). The programme tests innovative social protection models while delivering immediate humanitarian support.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will use catalytic financial support to demonstrate that investments in non-contributory social assistance alongside technical assistance can facilitate a shift of individuals into the formal, contributory, sector." (D0003134.odt, UK’S INTERVENTION) AND "The additional £30m to SSERJ will largely be utilised from April 2024... £26m will be allocated as unearmarked humanitarian cash assistance to vulnerable refugees through UNHCR and WFP." (D0003411.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Expanded contributory social insurance schemes (e.g., formalizing informal jobs)
Expansion of tax-financed social assistance schemes (e.g., Takaful programme reaching 185,000 households by 2021 → sustained growth)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 185,000 households (baseline from 2021, ongoing expansion)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Cash transfers to vulnerable refugees
q3_expected_outputs.target: 70,000 individuals/year (2024-2026)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy papers/research on refugee economic inclusion
q3_expected_outputs.target: At least one paper/seminar every 6 months

q3_expected_outputs.output: Alignment of humanitarian and national social protection systems (e.g., joint vulnerability assessments)
Technical assistance reports on shock-responsive systems
Management Information System (MIS) and Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) for NAF
Pilots for economic inclusion of refugees (e.g., ICT/green economy sectors)

what_objectives.summary: SSERJ aims to **strengthen Jordan’s social safety net system** by expanding coverage, improving targeting, and integrating humanitarian and national systems, while **protecting vulnerable groups** (refugees, women, disabled, elderly) from economic shocks. The programme combines **financial support** (cash transfers, co-financing), **technical assistance** (systems strengthening, research), and **policy dialogue** to shift Jordan toward a sustainable, inclusive social contract.
what_objectives.quote: "The impact of the programme will be: ‘Strengthened societal and economic resilience in Jordan and stability maintained in Jordan.’ The outcome will be: ‘A sustainable, inclusive and efficient Jordanian social safety net system protecting the most vulnerable from economic impacts and shocks and a strengthened social contract.’" (D0003134.odt, UK’S INTERVENTION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Jordan is classified as **fragile** due to protracted refugee crises (1.3M Syrians, 30% non-citizens), economic instability (23.9% unemployment, 85% debt-to-GDP), and climate vulnerability (water scarcity, heat stress). The document explicitly notes risks of instability from austerity measures, subsidy removals, and high youth unemployment (48%).
where_context.q5_source: "Jordan is on the frontline of multiple crises including the protracted crisis and conflict in Syria and the COVID-19 pandemic... Areduction in exports, increases in government deficit and rising debts have depressed growth." (D0003134.odt, CONTEXT) AND "Jordan is significantly impacted by climate change and is amongst the most water stressed countries in the world." (D0003411.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited NAF/SSC capacity, weak tax administration)
data limitations (restricted access to Household Income and Expenditure Survey)
regulatory (exclusion of non-Jordanians from NAF permanent programmes)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints **limit system integration** (e.g., NAF legally excludes refugees), **delay reforms** (e.g., electricity tariff protests), and **complicate targeting** (e.g., 33% of population experience transient poverty). Weak tax collection (67% from regressive sales tax) restricts fiscal space for social protection. Climate shocks exacerbate water/energy pressures, increasing conflict risks.
where_context.quote: "The withdrawal of subsidies in bread combined with the intention to raise income tax in 2018 sparked the set of demonstrations that brought down the Mulki premiership." (D0003134.odt, CONTEXT) AND "NAF regulations excluding non-Jordanians for the permanent programme remain in place... This is driven by a valid concern of GoJ that if refugees migrated into the National Social Protection systems, humanitarian donor funding may cease." (D0003134.odt, Social Protection in Jordan)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making is **shared** between FCDO/GoJ for strategic direction (e.g., NSPS alignment) and **delegated** to implementing partners (UNHCR, WFP, NAF, SSC) for operational delivery. GoJ leads policy ownership (e.g., refugee inclusion thresholds), while FCDO provides catalytic funding and technical oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to NAF/SSC on targeting systems (e.g., National Unified Registry)
Training for GoJ on shock-responsive social protection
Support to UNHCR/WFP for economic inclusion research
Establishment of Project Management Unit (PMU) within NAF
Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) for beneficiaries
Pilot design for refugee integration into SSC

partner_organizations.name: Government of Jordan (GoJ) - Ministry of Social Development (MoSD)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiary and co-implementer; leads National Social Protection Strategy (NSPS) and policy decisions

partner_organizations.name: National Aid Fund (NAF)
partner_organizations.role: Implements tax-financed cash transfers (e.g., Takaful programme); manages National Unified Registry (NUR)

partner_organizations.name: Social Security Corporation (SSC)
partner_organizations.role: Expands contributory social insurance coverage; includes refugees since 2018

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR
partner_organizations.role: Delivers humanitarian cash assistance to refugees; supports economic inclusion research

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Provides multi-purpose cash transfers; leads skills mapping for refugee economic inclusion

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Co-financer (e.g., $350m concessionary loan for COVID-19 response); technical advisor

partner_organizations.name: USAID, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, Denmark, Spain
partner_organizations.role: Co-donors via Joint Financing Agreement (JFA) for NAF programmes

partner_organizations.name: International Labour Organization (ILO)
partner_organizations.role: Supports SSC expansion and labour market formalization

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Members of NSPS Steering Committee; implement Government commitments

who_partners.quote: "The NSPSSteering Committee, chaired by the Minister of Social Development, includes representatives from government ministries and agencies as well as Civil Society Organisations." (D0003134.odt, Social Protection in Jordan) AND "UNHCR and WFP are the principal providers of humanitarian cash assistance in Jordan... They have been working closely with national social protection agencies in Jordan—particularly the National Aid Fund (NAF)." (D0003411.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: 1) **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)**: Unrestricted funding to UNHCR/WFP for cash transfers, allowing flexibility to target most vulnerable refugees. 2) **Joint Financing Agreement (JFA)**: Pooled donor funds (FCDO + 6 other donors) for NAF programmes, reducing transaction costs. 3) **Direct grants**: Technical assistance to GoJ agencies (e.g., SSC, MoSD) via FCDO-managed contracts.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as **convenor/funder** but delegates implementation to **GoJ agencies (NAF, SSC)** for national systems and **UNHCR/WFP** for refugee support. A **light-touch coordination mechanism** (MoUs, JFA) enables adaptive management, with FCDO retaining oversight via quarterly reviews and a mid-term evaluation. Technical assistance is delivered through **embedded advisors** (e.g., economists in MoSD).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **existing relationships** (e.g., UNHCR/WFP’s decade-long refugee response in Jordan), **technical expertise** (e.g., NAF’s role in national cash transfers), and **policy alignment** (GoJ’s NSPS priorities). The JFA was established by FCDO to streamline multi-donor coordination.
how_mechanism.quote: "The Joint Financing Arrangement (JFA), which the UK was instrumental in establishing, is effective for multiple donors to transfer funds efficiently... It has substantially improved coordination among donors and with GoJ." (D0003134.odt, UK Support to Date) AND "FCDO would prepare and then agree a separate Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with each organisation [UNHCR/WFP]. The MoU would set out the arrangements and the broad purpose for which the UK funding would be used, but as with our previous support it would be unearmarked." (D0003411.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: 1) **NSPS Steering Committee**: Chaired by MoSD, includes GoJ ministries, CSOs, and donors (FCDO participates). Sets strategic direction for social protection reforms. 2) **SSERJ Programme Team**: FCDO-led with GoJ counterparts, oversees technical assistance and adaptive management. 3) **Joint Financing Agreement (JFA) Board**: Multi-donor forum for NAF programme oversight.
how_governance.quote: "The NSPSSteering Committee, chaired by the Minister of Social Development, includes representatives from government ministries and agencies as well as Civil Society Organisations." (D0003134.odt, Social Protection in Jordan) AND "The programme will be overseen by a revised governance structure including a Steering Committee with representation from GoJ, FCDO and other key stakeholders." (D0003134.odt, Programme Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the **£30m addendum** can be reallocated between cash transfers and economic inclusion activities based on **emerging needs** (e.g., new shocks) but require FCDO approval. The **JFA mechanism** allows GoJ/NAF to adjust caseloads (e.g., during COVID-19). Core SSERJ budget (£65m) has **pre-defined phases**: Years 1-2 focus on proof-of-concept; Years 3-5 depend on mid-term review.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: 1) **Mid-term review (2025)**: Decides Year 3-5 financial support based on GoJ co-financing commitment and pilot results. 2) **Shock responsiveness**: UNHCR/WFP MoUs include clauses for rapid reallocation during crises (e.g., climate shocks). 3) **Technical assistance**: Priorities adjusted via **quarterly dialogues** with GoJ (e.g., new sectors for refugee inclusion).
how_flexibility.quote: "The midterm review will act as a decision point when pilot/s will be selected. Key considerations will include: GoJ’s responsiveness and willingness to co-finance pilot schemes... long term sustainability and VfM for the UK." (D0003134.odt, UK’S INTERVENTION) AND "In the event of a new or expanded humanitarian crisis impacting Jordan, we would use the arrangements agreed under this addendum with UNHCR and WFP... to provide additional humanitarian assistance if funding was available." (D0003411.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Implementing Partners** (UNHCR/WFP/GoJ agencies). Sub-grantees (e.g., CSOs) are managed by partners, not directly by FCDO.
how_efficiency.quote: "The MoUs would include provision for both organisations [UNHCR/WFP] to bid for the £4m allocated under this addendum for work supporting economic inclusion." (D0003411.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Separate humanitarian cash programme for refugees (rejected in favour of integration into SSERJ)
Direct budget support to GoJ (not chosen due to fiscal sustainability concerns)
Standalone refugee economic inclusion programme (integrated into SSERJ for coherence)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: 1) **Policy coherence**: Aligns humanitarian cash with GoJ’s NSPS, avoiding parallel systems. 2) **Value for Money (VfM)**: Leverages existing UNHCR/WFP platforms (e.g., mobile money) and JFA’s low transaction costs. 3) **Sustainability**: Catalytic funding (e.g., £30m addendum) incentivizes GoJ co-financing. 4) **Flexibility**: MoUs allow rapid response to shocks (e.g., climate crises). 5) **Influence**: FCDO’s convening power (e.g., London Jordan Conference 2019) enhances donor coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risks (e.g., unethical targeting by partners)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence assessments; mandatory partner safeguarding policies; grievance mechanisms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks (misuse of funds by partners)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Compliance checks for terrorism financing; simple delivery chains; small individual transfer sizes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Technical risks (GoJ ignores evidence on refugee inclusion)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand-driven research; policy-relevant framing; donor coordination via JFA.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political risks (GoJ resistance to refugee integration)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased alignment (e.g., SSC pilots before NAF); focus on sectors with labour shortages.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (low transaction costs for cash transfers)
why_rationale.quote: "Bringing humanitarian cash assistance, economic inclusion and social protection under the same programme will provide better policy coherence and VfM than doing them separately." (D0003411.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?) AND "The Joint Financing Arrangement (JFA)... has substantially improved and facilitated coordination and collaboration among donors and with GoJ, minimising duplication of reporting requirements." (D0003134.odt, Lessons learnt from UK support to date)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: 1) **Legal constraints**: NAF’s exclusion of non-Jordanians limits partner roles (e.g., UNHCR cannot channel funds through NAF). 2) **Fiscal constraints**: GoJ’s low social spending (0.67% GDP) requires donor catalytic funding, restricting local CSO leadership. 3) **Political constraints**: Refugee inclusion is sensitive; only SSC (not NAF) can pilot integration, shaping UNHCR/WFP’s scope.
q27_constraints_detail: NAF regulations exclude non-Jordanians from permanent programmes
GoJ spends only 0.67% GDP on social assistance (vs 3% benchmark)
Public opposition to refugee economic inclusion (e.g., labour market competition)
Weak tax administration limits fiscal space for co-financing
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: 1) **Pilot testing** (WHAT) → **Adaptive management** (HOW): Need for proof-of-concept (e.g., SSC refugee inclusion) requires flexible MoUs with UNHCR/WFP. 2) **Policy influence** (WHAT) → **GoJ-led governance** (HOW): NSPS Steering Committee ensures GoJ ownership of reforms. 3) **Humanitarian-development nexus** (WHAT) → **Joint platforms** (HOW): JFA and UNHCR/WFP MoUs bridge parallel systems.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation (research on refugee inclusion) → Embedded advisors in MoSD
Cash transfer delivery → UNHCR/WFP’s existing mobile money platforms
System alignment → JFA’s multi-donor coordination for NAF
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid cash transfers (via UNHCR) risk bypassing GoJ systems, but MoUs require alignment discussions. 2) **Cost vs. reach**: Targeting „extreme vulnerability“ (22% of refugee caseload) balances VfM with equity. 3) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: FCDO technical assistance supports GoJ-led NSPS, but donor priorities (e.g., refugee inclusion) may conflict with GoJ’s fiscal constraints.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UNHCR/WFP’s efficiency in cash delivery vs. GoJ’s slow system reforms
Donor push for refugee inclusion vs. GoJ’s fiscal burden concerns
Short-term cash needs vs. long-term system strengthening
intersections.risk_affects_management: High FCAS risks (instability, refugee tensions) → **Intensive oversight** of cash transfers (quarterly reviews) but **light-touch** for technical assistance (adaptive to GoJ priorities).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: 1) **NAF’s weak MIS** → FCDO funds PMU and digital systems. 2) **SSC’s limited refugee coverage** → Pilots focus on sectors with existing labour demand (e.g., tourism). 3) **GoJ’s low analytical capacity** → Embedded economists for cost-benefit analysis.
intersections.quote: "The NAF, through donor support, has invested in changes to its overall targeting system... For Jordanians engaged in the informal sector, the NUR applies an algorithm to estimate imputed income and determine eligibility." (D0003134.odt, Social Protection in Jordan) AND "The use of this money [£4m] will be agreed in consultation with UNHCR, WFP and GoJ but is likely to include: capacity support for research and analysis within UNHCR and WFP and GoJ agencies." (D0003411.odt, Promoting economic inclusion of refugees)

key_programme_risks: GoJ reduces co-financing for social protection post-pilot
Public backlash against refugee economic inclusion
Climate shocks exacerbate water/energy crises
NAF/SSC systems fail to absorb increased caseloads
Donor fatigue reduces humanitarian funding for refugees
Gender-based violence increases with economic stress
Tax reforms stall due to political resistance
Parallel humanitarian/development systems persist

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Mid-term review assesses GoJ commitment; phased exit strategy.
Target sectors with labour shortages; cost-benefit analysis to demonstrate economic gains.
Shock-responsive design in NAF systems; UNHCR/WFP flexibility clauses.
Technical assistance to NAF/SSC; gradual caseload increases.
Demonstrate VfM via JFA; advocate for refugee self-reliance.

fcas_specific_lessons: Protracted crises require **dual-track** approaches: immediate cash + long-term system strengthening.
Refugee inclusion must be **phased** (e.g., SSC before NAF) to manage political risks.
**Cash-plus** models (cash + economic inclusion) reduce dependency and tensions.
Donor coordination (e.g., JFA) prevents **aid fragmentation** in FCAS contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **JFA success**: Improved donor coordination and reduced GoJ reporting burden. 2) **COVID-19 response**: SSC’s rapid adaptation (e.g., reduced contribution rates) demonstrated shock-responsive potential. 3) **Targeting improvements**: NAF’s shift to means-testing reduced leakage but excluded some vulnerable groups (e.g., elderly). 4) **Refugee labour pilots**: Compact’s work permit waivers increased formal employment but faced sectoral limits.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Addendum integration**: Merged humanitarian cash into SSERJ to avoid parallel systems. 2) **Economic inclusion focus**: Added £4m for refugee labour research based on Compact lessons. 3) **Adaptive management**: Mid-term review replaces rigid annual planning. 4) **GESI mainstreaming**: Dedicated funds for disability/inclusion analysis after 2018 gender audit.
risks_lessons.quote: "The Joint Financing Arrangement (JFA)... has substantially improved and facilitated coordination and collaboration among donors and with GoJ, minimising duplication of reporting requirements." (D0003134.odt, Lessons learnt from UK support to date) AND "The SSC had a very strong response to COVID-19... Approximately 1 million participants benefited from their emergency response to the COVID-19 crisis." (D0003134.odt, COVID-19 Social Protection Response)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The JFA pooled £65m (FCDO) + £100m+ from other donors, enabling NAF to scale Takaful programme. UNHCR/WFP’s existing platforms (e.g., mobile money) reduce FCDO’s delivery costs.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue-focused: 90%+ of budget supports cash transfers, technical assistance, and operational costs. Minimal capital expenditure (e.g., NAF MIS upgrades).
financial_details.quote: "Other donors who plan to support the GoJ implement the different pillars of the NSPS in the medium–longer term include: Netherlands, Switzerland, EU, Norway, USAID (tbd), Germany (tbd)." (D0003134.odt, Social Protection in Jordan) AND "The additional £30m to SSERJ will largely be utilised from April 2024... £26m will be allocated as unearmarked humanitarian cash assistance to vulnerable refugees through UNHCR and WFP." (D0003411.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Pitcairn Financial Aid 2023-2025

quote.programme_name: "Pitcairn Financial Aid 2023-2025" (D0005527.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.budget: "£9,040,000 original + £550,000 (1st addendum) + £680,000 (2nd addendum) = £10,270,000" (D0005373.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
quote.sector: "to work with OTs to strengthen good governance arrangements, public financial management and economic planning" (D0005527.odt, A1)

metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 01/04/2023 to 31/03/2025" (D0005373.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides financial aid to bridge the gap between Pitcairn's domestic revenues and necessary expenditure, ensuring essential public services (health, education, shipping) are maintained. It operates as a direct budget support mechanism to meet the UK's obligation to provide 'reasonable assistance needs' to Pitcairn, a non-self-governing territory with no prospect of economic self-sufficiency.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Pitcairn Financial Aid programme aims to assist the Government of the Pitcairn Islands (GPI) bridge the gap between their domestic revenues and necessary expenditure. Through transfers to GPI’s recurrent budget, this programme will enable GPI to provide essential services to the people of Pitcairn." (D0005527.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Sustained budget management, in line with best practice
Public service provision maintained, including off-island professionals for key positions (safeguarding support)
Regular, safe, and reliable sea access to Pitcairn
Provision of four expatriate professionals (Social Worker, Doctor, Police Officer, Teacher when required) for child safeguarding and basic services
Shipping subsidy covering annual operational costs of the supply ship (£3.02m forecast for 23/24)
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers direct financial aid to Pitcairn Islands to maintain essential public services and meet the UK's treaty obligations, with a focus on shipping access, healthcare, and child safeguarding in a context where economic self-sufficiency is impossible.

quote.objective: "The UK’s vision for its OTs as vibrant and flourishing territories... HMG recognises that the prospect of economic self-sufficiency for Pitcairn will never be possible... Without UK financial aid, the government would be unable to provide most essential public services" (D0005373.odt, INFORMATION)
quote.outputs: "1. Sustained budget management, in line with best practice; 2. Public Service Provision maintained... 3. Regular, safe, and reliable sea access to Pitcairn" (D0005373.odt, Whataretheexpectedresults?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a stable but highly constrained environment with extreme remoteness, small population (43 inhabitants), and complete dependency on external funding. A 2020 Fiduciary Risk Assessment classified corruption risk as 'Low to Moderate' with credible PFM reforms.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall assessment of fiduciary risk is Low to Moderate... The assessment of corruption risk is Low and unchanged" (D0005527.odt, D5)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (population of 43 with 26 in paid employment; 12 FTE government roles)
regulatory (maritime laws for international waters complicate shipping contracts)
political economy (no tax base; 90-95% budget from UK aid)
climate risks (remote location vulnerable to supply chain disruptions)
data limitations (no formal income declaration system)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Shipping costs (67% of budget) and expatriate professional salaries consume most funds, leaving minimal flexibility. The island's remoteness requires all essential goods to be imported, with fuel price volatility directly impacting operational costs. The ageing population (58% over 50) and lack of children on-island create long-term sustainability challenges for service delivery.

quote.constraints: "Access on and off the island: Access and shipping costs have risen in recent years and represent the majority of Financial Aid spending... The lack of access is an obstacle to the socio-economic development of the island" (D0005527.odt, A4(iii))
quote.impact: "The cost of the shipping service... will always dominate in such a remote location... The high fixed costs of financial aid skew the level of support provided per capita" (D0005527.odt, B3)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains full oversight and approval authority. The Pitcairn Island Office (PIO, based in Auckland) manages logistics but all financial calls require Governor's countersignature. Local government (Pitcairn Island Council) has advisory input only.
q10_capacity_building_details: Provision of four expatriate professionals (Social Worker, Doctor, Police Officer, Teacher) to maintain critical services and safeguarding
Annual financial aid reviews with PIO to improve budget management
Technical assistance for public sector reform (2023 review planned)
Training for local government posts through transparent competition overseen by Governor's Office

partner_organizations.name: Pitcairn Island Office (PIO)
partner_organizations.role: Financial controller; manages off-island logistics, procurement, and banking; produces monthly financial reports

partner_organizations.name: Government of Pitcairn Islands (GPI)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of budget support; delivers public services on-island with 12.5 FTE local staff

partner_organizations.name: New Zealand Police Force
partner_organizations.role: Seconds police officer for community policing and child safeguarding

partner_organizations.name: External Auditors (Auckland-based)
partner_organizations.role: Annual audit of GPI accounts to NZ/international standards

partner_organizations.name: Shipping Contractor (Silver Supporter vessel)
partner_organizations.role: Provides 23 passenger voyages/year + 4 freight runs between NZ and Pitcairn

quote.structure: "The proposed funding mechanism for support to Pitcairn continues to be Non-Budget Support Financial Aid (Financial Aid)... a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and the Governor of Pitcairn is used" (D0005373.odt, Whatistheapproachtoimplementation?)
quote.decision_power: "Approved recurrent expenditure will be monitored... The Administrator conducts monthly reviews... PIO produces monthly progress reports... FCDO provides feedback as necessary" (D0005527.odt, D6)
quote.capacity_building: "Provision of four expatriate professionals funded from financial aid: a Social Worker (Family and Community Adviser-FCA), Teacher, Doctor and a Police Officer... each of whom have specific roles to ensure continued child safeguarding" (D0005527.odt, A4(i))

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Financial aid is provided through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and the Governor of Pitcairn. Funds are disbursed quarterly in advance to the Pitcairn Island Office (PIO) upon receipt of call-down requests countersigned by the Governor’s Office. This is classified as Non-Budget Support Financial Aid under FCDO's PrOF Rules.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO channels funds directly to the Pitcairn Island Office (PIO), which acts as the financial controller and logistics manager. PIO reports monthly to FCDO and produces quarterly estimates. The Administrator on Pitcairn oversees 12.5 FTE local staff delivering services, with all key decisions requiring FCDO/Governor approval.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UK has a legal obligation to meet Pitcairn's 'reasonable assistance needs' under UN Charter provisions for Non-Self-Governing Territories. PIO and expatriate posts are selected through transparent processes overseen by the Governor's Office, but the overall funding mechanism is non-competitive due to the UK's treaty responsibilities.

quote.instrument: "The proposed funding mechanism for support to Pitcairn continues to be Non-Budget Support Financial Aid (Financial Aid). In line with FCDO’s PrOF Rules, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and the Governor of Pitcairn is used" (D0005373.odt, Whatistheapproachtoimplementation?)
quote.selection: "Government posts being funded through Financial Aid are open to fair and transparent competition with oversight of the process being provided by the Governor’s Office and the Administrator on island" (D0005527.odt, C2)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: No formal steering committee or board is mentioned. Oversight is conducted through: 1) Monthly expenditure reviews by PIO; 2) Quarterly estimates submitted to FCDO; 3) Annual external audits (NZ standards); 4) Governor's Office countersignature for all fund requests. The Deputy Director of Inhabited Territories acts as Senior Responsible Owner (SRO).

quote.day_to_day: "Daily management of the intervention will be undertaken by PIO with inputs on progress being received from the relevant Divisional Manager and the Pitcairn Island Council... The Administrator has management oversight of all divisional managers" (D0005527.odt, E1)
quote.oversight: "PIO produces monthly progress reports, comparing actual expenditure against the budget... An annual external audit, including an island visit is carried out according to NZ and international standards... The PIO is located within the office of the Deputy Governor" (D0005527.odt, D6)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Re-profiling of the budget is permitted within the year by PIO, but requires FCDO agreement. Exchange rate fluctuations between GBP and NZD are monitored, and any savings must be discussed with FCDO for utilization or return.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme follows a fixed results framework focused on sustaining basic services. While annual reviews monitor performance, the core objectives (shipping, safeguarding, public services) cannot be adjusted without a formal addendum process (as seen in D0005373.odt for the £680k extension).

quote.reallocation: "There may be in-year re-profiling of the budget and this will be done by PIO on agreement from FCDO" (D0005527.odt, D1)
quote.adjustment: "The Delivery Plan, Risk Register, Logframe and Delivery Chain will be updated as necessary throughout the year" (D0005527.odt, E6) [but core priorities remain fixed]

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Pitcairn Island Office (PIO) → Government of Pitcairn Islands (GPI). PIO acts as both financial controller and logistics manager, with GPI delivering services on-island.

quote.management_costs: "The cost of PIO represents 16% of the financial aid costs" (D0005527.odt, B4)
quote.layers: "PIO... is responsible for all off-island logistics... The Administrator has management oversight of all divisional managers" (D0005527.odt, C4/E1)
quote.payments: "Funds will be paid quarterly in advance to PIO on receipt of call-down requests for funds against the MOU, countersigned by the Governor’s Office" (D0005527.odt, C1)

q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: FCDO is already closely involved in shipping management; no evidence of benefits from separation

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Take direct control of Pitcairn’s budget (projectised approach)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Would require substantially increased UK administrative resources; HMG would hold all political/reputational risk without adequate local control; unlikely to deliver value for money

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Devolve financial control to Pitcairn Island Office (PIO)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: HMG would still hold majority of political/reputational risk

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Devolve control to Pitcairn Island Council
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Too high fiduciary/operational risk for FCDO, especially as most costs (shipping/off-island professionals) are managed off-island

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Financial Aid was selected as the only acceptable option because it provides the correct balance between direct engagement with PIO/Council and HMG oversight to ensure value for money and manage fiduciary risk. This aligns with the approach used for the other three aided Overseas Territories and meets the UK's legal obligation to provide 'reasonable assistance needs' under the UN Charter.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (Financial Aid is the most efficient method for meeting Pitcairn’s needs despite high shipping costs)
risk mitigation (HMG retains oversight while PIO manages logistics)
past experience (consistent with approach used for other aided OTs since 2004)
equity (ensures fair distribution of benefits across the small population)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: No major incidents impacting government expenditure (e.g., exchange rate fluctuations)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monthly monitoring of NZD/GBP rates; savings discussed with FCDO for utilization/return

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: No incidents in safeguarding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-agency approach with four expatriate professionals; bi-annual independent reviews

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: No more than one emergency medivac/year or routine referral cost overruns
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Budget line for medical expenses with FCDO oversight

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Ability to attract/retain suitably qualified professionals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Recruitment from NZ/Australia markets with regional experience; competitive salaries

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Stability in fuel prices
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust international procurement for shipping contract; fuel costs built into annual budget

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Vessels able to land in poor weather
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Contractual requirements for vessel specifications; maritime law compliance

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (70 government roles delivered by 12.5 FTE)
effectiveness (multi-agency safeguarding approach with independent reviews)
equity (salaries paid at hourly rate regardless of gender; social protection policy)

quote.alternatives: "Option 5 - Provide Financial Aid (preferred option): The provision of financial aid is the only acceptable option as it provides the correct balance between direct engagement with PIO and Council as well as HMG oversight" (D0005527.odt, B1)
quote.rationale: "Financial Aid continues to represent the best Value for Money (VfM) option, providing the most efficient method for meeting Pitcairn’s reasonable needs" (D0005527.odt, B3)
quote.risks: "Assumptions: No major incidents which impact on government expenditure... No incidents in safeguarding... No more than one emergency medivac per year... Ability to attract and retain suitably qualified professionals" (D0005527.odt, Assumptions)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The extreme remoteness and small population (43 inhabitants) constrain partner selection to entities with existing regional presence. Shipping services must comply with international maritime laws for voyages through international waters, limiting contractors to those with specialised vessels. Expatriate professionals must be recruited from NZ/Australia due to proximity and reduced mobilisation costs.
q27_constraints_detail: Geographic isolation requires partners with Pacific region operational capacity
Maritime regulations limit shipping contractors to those with internationally compliant vessels
Small population (43) makes local institutional strengthening impractical; reliance on expatriates
No tax base or formal economy restricts revenue-generating partners to tourism-related entities
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of maintaining essential public services (health, education, shipping) in a non-self-sufficient territory necessitates a direct budget support mechanism. The need for stringent child safeguarding (legacy of abuse) requires embedded expatriate professionals with FCDO oversight. Shipping costs (67% of budget) demand intensive procurement management via PIO.
q28_linkages: Direct budget support → enables rapid disbursement for fixed costs (shipping, salaries)
Expatriate professionals → address safeguarding obligations while building minimal local capacity
PIO logistics management → mitigates risks of remote location (fuel procurement, vessel compliance)
Quarterly FCDO reviews → balance flexibility with accountability for public funds
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritises equity (equal hourly wages, social protection policy) over pure cost efficiency. The high per-capita spend (£105,000/year) is justified by the UK's legal obligations and the fixed costs of maintaining basic services for a tiny population. Safeguarding measures (four expatriates) are maintained despite no children currently on-island to ensure readiness for potential returnees.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: High per-capita costs (£105k) vs. legal obligation to provide 'reasonable assistance'
Expatriate salaries (NZ/AU market rates) vs. local employment opportunities (12.5 FTE)
Shipping subsidy (67% of budget) vs. economic development potential from tourism
Safeguarding infrastructure (maintained without children present) vs. immediate cost savings
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (Low-Moderate fiduciary risk but high operational vulnerability due to remoteness) justifies intensive oversight: monthly PIO reports, quarterly FCDO reviews, and annual audits. The shipping contract—representing 67% of costs—receives specialised legal/maritime expertise during procurement.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local capacity (population 43; 12.5 FTE government) necessitates PIO's dual role as financial controller and logistics manager. Expatriate professionals fill all technical roles (doctor, police, social work) with training focused on safeguarding rather than broad institutional strengthening.

quote.constraints: "The remoteness of Pitcairn, ageing population and increasing global shipping costs will continue to put pressure on the Pitcairn budget... The cost of the shipping service... will always dominate in such a remote location" (D0005373.odt, Whatistheobjectiveofthecostextensionorotherchanges?)
quote.linkages: "Financial Aid continues to represent the best Value for Money (VfM) option... The cost of PIO represents 16% of the financial aid costs... The workforce carries out 70 GPI roles on a part-time basis (12.5 FTE)" (D0005527.odt, B3/B4)
quote.tradeoffs: "The high fixed costs of financial aid skew the level of support provided per capita... The per capita spend for the financial aid settlement increases to £105,000" (D0005527.odt, B5)
quote.risk_management: "A Fiduciary Risk Assessment... concluded that the overall assessment of fiduciary risk is Low to Moderate... The shipping service is one of Pitcairn’s biggest risks... international maritime regulations apply" (D0005527.odt, D5/C5)

key_programme_risks: Exchange rate fluctuations between GBP and NZD affecting purchasing power
Failure to attract/retain expatriate professionals (doctor, police, social worker)
Shipping contract disputes or vessel reliability issues (67% of budget)
Medical emergencies requiring off-island evacuation (cost volatility)
Safeguarding incidents given legacy of child abuse
Fuel price volatility impacting shipping operational costs
Population decline (current 43; 58% over 50) threatening service sustainability
Tourism revenue shortfalls (post-COVID recovery uncertainty)
Supply chain disruptions for essential goods (90%+ imported)
Constitutional/legal challenges to UK oversight arrangements

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Monthly monitoring by PIO; savings returned to FCDO or reallocated with agreement
Regional recruitment (NZ/Australia) with competitive salaries; FCDO oversight of hiring
Specialist maritime legal advice; contractual penalties for non-performance; 12-month extension option
Dedicated budget line; NZ hospital agreements; medivac protocols
Four expatriate professionals; bi-annual independent reviews; multi-agency approach
Fuel costs built into shipping contract; international procurement standards
Tourism promotion; immigration incentives; public sector reform to improve efficiency
Increased shipping voyages (23/year); homestay promotion; cruise ship engagement
Stockpiling essential goods; diversified suppliers; long-boat operational redundancy

fcas_specific_lessons: In small island contexts, fixed costs (shipping) dominate budgets regardless of population size—scaling support requires different metrics than per-capita spending
Expatriate professionals are essential for specialised roles (health, policing) but require cultural integration support to avoid turnover
Direct budget support works where local institutions lack capacity for project management (Pitcairn’s 12.5 FTE government)
Safeguarding frameworks must be maintained even when vulnerable groups (children) are temporarily absent to ensure readiness
Maritime contracts in remote locations need international legal expertise due to cross-jurisdictional voyages
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2020 Child Safeguarding Review noted a "significant shift in attitudes" among islanders toward cooperating with HMG on protection measures, but warned against complacency. Previous shipping contracts highlighted the need for vessel reliability over cost savings, leading to the current service’s 23 annual voyages (up from 12). The 2016 Fiduciary Risk Assessment’s ‘Low to Moderate’ corruption rating was reaffirmed in 2020, validating the light-touch financial controls.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Increased shipping voyages from 12 to 23/year based on tourism demand (2019 contract); 2) Added social protection policy (2022) to address individual vulnerabilities; 3) Expanded safeguarding framework to include family/community adviser role; 4) Public sector reform planned for 2023 to improve efficiency with ageing workforce.

quote.risks: "The main causes for [budget challenges] are rising costs in key budget areas which dominate spending... namely in shipping, medical and legal expenses" (D0005373.odt, Whatistheobjectiveofthecostextensionorotherchanges?)
quote.lessons: "The Review states that in recent years... there has been a significant shift in the attitudes of members of the Pitcairn community from denying and justifying child abuse... to a fresh approach of cooperating and collaborating with HMG" (D0005527.odt, A4(i))
quote.design_changes: "A review was undertaken... to consider the best approach for an evidence-based social protection system... Agreement was reached in 2022 to implement a proportionate policy" (D0005527.odt, A27)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Tourism revenue (projected £435,357 in 23/24 from homestays, cruise ships, and online sales) offsets ~4% of financial aid. Internet domain registrations (“.pn”) generate ~NZ$80,000 annually due to cultural media references (The Hunger Games).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: 100% revenue expenditure (no capital expenditure allocated in 23/24-24/25 budgets). All funds cover operational costs (salaries, shipping, utilities, technical cooperation).

quote.budget: "Original project budget: £9,040,000... Cost extension value: £550,000 (1st addendum) + £680,000 (2nd addendum) = £10,270,000" (D0005373.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
quote.revenue: "Expected Revenues (2023/24): £435,357... Other income (i.e. rent from government buildings, telephone and electricity charges)" (D0005527.odt, A24)
quote.overhead: "The cost of PIO represents 16% of the financial aid costs" (D0005527.odt, B4)

metadata.programme_name: Bangladesh Collaborative, Accountable and Peaceful Politics (B-CAPP) Programme

quote.programme_name: "Bangladesh Collaborative, Accountable and Peaceful Politics (B-CAPP) Programme" (D0004195.odt, Title)
quote.budget: "With a proposed budget of up to £27m it will be the UK’s main intervention in supporting a more open and inclusive political system in Bangladesh." (D0004195.odt, Programmesummary)
quote.duration: "AMP Start Date: 01/06/2022", "AMP End Date: 31/05/2027" (D0004195.odt, Metadata section)
quote.sector: "The intended impact of the cross-HMG Country Plan for Bangladesh is: Effective and integrated delivery of UK security, prosperity, development, humanitarian and climate objectives, supporting a more open, democratic and inclusive Bangladesh" (D0004195.odt, SummarySheet)

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01/06/2022", "AMP End Date: 31/05/2027"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The B-CAPP programme combines **capacity building** (strengthening civil society, media, and political parties), **implementation research** (testing coalitions and mediation approaches), and **service delivery** (direct support for peace-building and accountability mechanisms). It aims to foster collaboration, accountability, and peaceful conflict resolution in Bangladesh’s political system.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will protect civic space, foster political collaboration, reduce corruption, and mitigate tensions that lead to violence." (D0004195.odt, Programmesummary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Mobilised civil society and media coalitions to advocate for policy solutions
Citizen groups equipped with tools to monitor public service delivery
Improved decision-making within political parties, with increased women and youth leadership
Strengthened community mediation to prevent violence
q3_expected_outputs.target: Peace Facilitator Groups (PFGs) in 46 upazilas (potentially expanded to 65)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Digital platform for real-time corruption data collection
q3_expected_outputs.target: Network of Active Citizen Groups (ACGs) across 38 districts and 7 sub-districts

q3_expected_outputs.output: Training and mentorship for 1,000+ women and youth political leaders
National platform of pro-peace religious leaders
Policy influence through advocacy linking local issues to national planning

what_objectives.summary: B-CAPP aims to transform Bangladesh’s political landscape by strengthening accountability (citizen-state), collaboration (cross-party and civil society), and peace (mediation and conflict prevention). It combines grassroots mobilisation with national-level advocacy, using adaptive, issue-based coalitions to drive systemic change.

quote.objectives: "The B-CAPP programme will strengthen accountability between citizens and the state in Bangladesh, improve local collaboration and inclusion of political parties, and mitigate tensions that lead to violent conflict." (D0004195.odt, Programme summary)
quote.outcomes: "The impact this programme seeks to contribute to is: More collaborative and peaceful politics in Bangladesh, and greater accountability of the state to its citizens." (D0004195.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Bangladesh exhibits **fragile governance indicators**: shrinking civic space (Freedom House: ‘partly free’), endemic corruption (147/180 on CPI), political violence (1500+ DSA cases filed in 2020–21), and institutional weakness (tax-to-GDP ratio <9%). The 2021 World Bank graduation from LDC status masks persistent instability, with risks of election-related violence and communal tensions (e.g., 2021 Hindu-Muslim riots).
where_context.q5_source: "Bangladesh has enjoyed three decades of sustained economic growth [...] However, further development success as a Lower Middle-Income Country is threatened by poor governance and weak institutions." and "The inherent risks in delivering governance programmes in Bangladesh will require close management by the FCDO to ensure that the programme remains within the BHC’s risk appetite." (D0004195.odt, Context and Risk sections)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (tax collection stagnation, anti-corruption failures)
conflict (election violence, communal riots, jihadist threats)
regulatory (restrictions on civil society and media)
climate risks (vulnerability to shocks, RMG sector instability)
data limitations (lack of real-time corruption monitoring)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints **directly shape delivery**: (1) Polarisation limits cross-party collaboration, requiring neutral convening spaces; (2) Weak institutions necessitate informal accountability mechanisms (e.g., citizen coalitions); (3) Security risks demand adaptive, low-profile interventions (e.g., localised mediation); (4) Data gaps drive the need for digital platforms (ACGs). The programme’s **local-first approach** (e.g., upazila-level PFGs) mitigates national-level blockages.

quote.constraints: "A winner-takes-all approach to governing in Bangladesh has increased polarisation between the two main political parties [...] Centrally-driven efforts are failing to address Bangladesh’s systemic corruption." (D0004195.odt, Collaboration/Accountability sections)
quote.impact: "Local-level collaboration will be supported by research, evidence-gathering, and advocacy at the national level, linking grassroots issues with central policymaking to encourage responsiveness and accountability." (D0004195.odt, Programme summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Southern partners (CSOs) lead implementation with FCDO strategic oversight. Decision-making is decentralised to local coalitions (e.g., ACGs, PFGs) and Bangladesh-based CSOs (TIB, TAF), while FCDO retains approval authority for high-level adjustments via the Strategic Fund.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for 1,000+ women/youth political leaders (fellowships, mentorship)
Skills development for Active Citizen Groups (ACGs) in data collection/advocacy
Mediation training for Peace Facilitator Groups (PFGs)
Institutional strengthening of political parties (inclusive policies, cross-party dialogue)
Digital platform capacity for Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB)
Peer-to-peer learning networks for journalists and local officials

partner_organizations.name: Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead on corruption monitoring (digital platform, ACGs)

partner_organizations.name: The Asia Foundation (TAF)
partner_organizations.role: Political party engagement and youth/women leadership training

partner_organizations.name: Democracy International (DI)
partner_organizations.role: Civil society coalition-building and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: The Hunger Project (THP)
partner_organizations.role: Community mobilisation and local governance strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Peace Facilitator Groups (PFGs)
partner_organizations.role: Local mediation and conflict prevention (46+ upazilas)

partner_organizations.name: Active Citizen Groups (ACGs)
partner_organizations.role: Grassroots corruption monitoring and service delivery oversight

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funding, strategic oversight, and diplomatic leverage

quote.structure: "Option 3: Agreements with CSOs [...] This option would build on the foundation of existing BHC programmes that are ending, through Accountable Grant agreements with a network of CSOs." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)
quote.capacity: "The programme will build the capability of a network of thousands of volunteer Active Citizen Groups (ACGs) across 38 districts and seven sub-districts to utilise this analysis in local advocacy." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument: **Accountable Grants (AGs)** to CSOs (TIB, TAF, DI, THP) for core delivery, complemented by a **Strategic Fund** (flexible, FCDO-managed) for emergent opportunities. Grants are issue-based (e.g., health, land, corruption) with participatory design.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as **funding hub**, with CSOs as **direct implementers** (no intermediary layer). A **coordination component** (led by one CSO partner) ensures alignment across workstreams, while the **Strategic Fund** allows FCDO to respond to risks/opportunities. Local coalitions (ACGs, PFGs) operate autonomously but report into CSO partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Selected based on **legacy relationships** (existing BHC programmes like SPP2, TRIP) and **contextual expertise**. CSOs (TIB, TAF) have pre-established trust with government/civil society, enabling rapid mobilisation. The document states: "This option could be the fastest to mobilise as these partners already have teams in the field."

quote.instrument: "Option 3: Agreements with CSOs [...] This option would build on the foundation of existing BHC programmes that are ending, through Accountable Grant agreements with a network of CSOs." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)
quote.structure: "To build coherence across the different workstreams, a specific component will be created to drive cross-cutting learning and collaboration for B-CAPP. This programme component will provide coordinated reporting, identify opportunities for implementing partners to work together, and ensure learning is being captured and disseminated." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)
quote.selection: "This option could be the fastest to mobilise as these partners already have teams in the field mobilised to deliver programme objectives." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **coordination component** (led by a CSO partner) acts as a de facto steering body, with FCDO oversight. The structure includes: (1) **shared results framework** (aligned ToC); (2) **quarterly learning exchanges**; (3) **FCDO approval** for Strategic Fund allocations. No formal board is mentioned, but the BHC’s **Programme Responsible Owner (PRO)** and **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO)** provide high-level oversight.

quote.governance: "The programme’s governance arrangements will facilitate dialogue and learning exchange across the different partners, and partners will be incentivised to capture and embed lessons through reporting and funding conditions." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)
quote.oversight: "A unified ToC and results framework will be designed to ensure shared ownership for the delivery of outputs and outcomes, and alignment of reporting timeframes and templates." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core component budgets are fixed, but the **Strategic Fund** (size undisclosed) allows reallocation for emergent needs (e.g., election violence, COVID-19 responses). Reallocation requires FCDO approval and alignment with ToC pathways. Criteria include "scale of expected impact" and "demonstration of VfM."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **participatory Political Economy Analysis** to reprioritise issues (e.g., health, land, education) based on local needs. Adjustments are permitted if they: (1) align with ToC pathways; (2) respond to political shifts (e.g., elections); (3) leverage new opportunities (e.g., donor coordination). The document notes: "Flexibility and adaptiveness have allowed programmes to respond more effectively in a dynamic operating environment."

quote.flexibility: "A small Strategic Fund will be created under the B-CAPP programme to enable the BHC to respond to emerging opportunities and challenges. This fund will give the Mission flexibility to resource short-term assignments [...] Criteria is likely to include considerations such as alignment with change pathways and objectives set out in the Theory of Change." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)
quote.adaptive: "The programme will conduct participatory Political Economy Analysis to identify issues that have the greatest impact on the lives of Bangladesh’s poorest and most marginalised citizens, and where there is likely to be the greatest political buy-in." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → CSO partners (TIB, TAF, DI, THP) → **no further sub-grantee layer** (ACGs/PFGs are volunteer networks, not sub-contracted).

quote.layers: "This programme component will provide coordinated reporting, identify opportunities for implementing partners to work together, and ensure learning is being captured and disseminated." (D0004195.odt, What we will do) [Implies direct FCDO-CSO relationship]
quote.payment: "The supplier of services under this component will also commission and oversee a full impact evaluation, and will track value for money." (D0004195.odt, What we will do) [Suggests output-based payments]

q24_alternatives_considered.drawbacks: Lack of mandate for political engagement; limited flexibility; high overheads (8–12%); coherence risks across issues.
Lengthy procurement (unlikely to mobilise before 2023); high management fees; less visibility over downstream partners.
Coherence risks across multiple partners; capacity gaps in adaptive management.

q24_alternatives_considered.reason: Risks to stability and UK influence ahead of 2023/24 elections outweigh cost savings.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: CSO modality was selected for: (1) **speed** (existing partners already mobilised); (2) **contextual expertise** (deep local knowledge and political relationships); (3) **cost efficiency** (lower overheads at 6–8% vs. 8–12% for multilaterals); (4) **flexibility** (Strategic Fund enables rapid response); and (5) **risk management** (direct FCDO oversight of partners). The document states: "Building on the legacy expertise and relationships, CSOs could mobilise quickly and ensure low-cost delivery."
q25_decision_factors: value for money (low overheads, volunteer networks)
partner capacity (proven track record in Bangladesh)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coherence risks across multiple CSO partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Unified ToC/results framework; coordination component led by one CSO; quarterly learning exchanges.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Capacity gaps in adaptive management among CSOs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will "explore bringing in new partners and experts with wider international experience to encourage more innovative practice."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication of activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust FCDO management approach with "full coordination between implementing partners."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from partner actions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs) for all partners; compliance with PrOF Rule 19 (mandatory reporting of fraud/abuse).

quote.rationale: "Based on this assessment of delivery options against the criteria, the third option (working through CSOs) is the preferred approach." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)
quote.risks: "The FCDO would need to ensure implementing partners cooperate and coordinate, and low-capacity local partners [are] upskilled." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Contextual constraints **directly limit partner selection**: (1) **Polarisation** requires neutral convenors (CSOs like TIB/TAF with cross-party trust); (2) **Security risks** (DSA, extrajudicial killings) exclude international actors without local cover; (3) **Weak institutions** necessitate partners with informal influence (e.g., ACGs using personal networks); (4) **Corruption** demands partners with existing anti-graft credibility (e.g., TIB’s CPI role). The document notes: "Informal relationships and processes can be more powerful in driving accountability than formal institutions."
q27_constraints_detail: Polarisation → Need for neutral, trusted intermediaries (CSOs over multilaterals)
Security risks → Local implementation (no high-profile international staff)
Weak institutions → Reliance on informal networks (ACGs, PFGs)
Corruption → Partners must have anti-corruption mandates (TIB’s CPI role)
Election timing → Partners must be apolitical yet influential (e.g., religious leaders’ platform)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: Objectives **shape delivery structure** through: (1) **Issue-based coalitions** (health, land, education) → Decentralised CSO networks; (2) **Peace-building needs** → Localised PFGs with partisan balance; (3) **Accountability goals** → Digital platforms (ACGs) for real-time data; (4) **Youth/women inclusion** → Fellowship programmes embedded in political parties. The document links **collaboration outcomes** to open partnership structures: "Local-level collaboration will be supported by [...] advocacy at the national level, linking grassroots issues with central policymaking."
q28_linkages: Issue-based coalitions → CSO-led, adaptive workstreams
Peace-building → Local PFGs with mediation training
Anti-corruption → TIB’s digital platform + ACG networks
Political inclusion → Party fellowships for women/youth
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to CSOs enable rapid mobilisation but risk excluding newer actors; (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: International CSOs (TAF, DI) provide technical skills but Southern partners (TIB, THP) lead implementation; (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Volunteer ACGs reduce costs but require capacity-building investments. The document acknowledges: "While the World Bank works on corruption, the more sensitive political engagement falls outside its mandate" (justifying CSO selection over multilaterals).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Direct awards to legacy CSOs accelerate delivery but limit competitive opportunities for new partners.
International CSOs (TAF, DI) provide governance expertise, while local CSOs (TIB, THP) ensure contextual legitimacy.
Volunteer ACGs reduce overheads but require training/mentorship to ensure data quality.
Strategic Fund allows adaptability but risks fragmentation without strong coordination.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS context** drives **intensive oversight**: (1) **High political risks** (elections, DSA) → Milestone-based reporting; (2) **Corruption risks** → PrOF Rule 19 compliance checks; (3) **Violence risks** → Embedded safeguarding in PFGs. The document states: "The inherent risks in delivering governance programmes in Bangladesh will require close management by the FCDO."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building **defines partner roles**: (1) **TIB** leads corruption monitoring due to its CPI expertise; (2) **TAF/DI** focus on political party engagement leveraging past SPP2 experience; (3) **THP** handles grassroots mobilisation via existing local networks. The programme’s **coordination component** explicitly aims to "upskill" partners in adaptive management.

quote.constraints: "In Bangladesh, the Strengthening Political Participation in Bangladesh (SPP) programme [...] has tested a variety of approaches in the local context. However, a range of other UK programmes globally offer important lessons [...] Informal relationships and processes can be more powerful in driving accountability than formal institutions." (D0004195.odt, Progress and lessons learned)
quote.tradeoffs: "While the World Bank works on corruption, the more sensitive political engagement falls outside its mandate [...] CSOs could mobilise quickly and ensure low-cost delivery." (D0004195.odt, Delivery Options)
quote.capacity: "The programme will build the capability of a network of thousands of volunteer Active Citizen Groups (ACGs) [...] and provide a convening space for civil society and government representatives." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)

key_programme_risks: Shrinking civic space (DSA restrictions, extrajudicial killings)
Political polarisation undermining cross-party collaboration
Corruption in service delivery (e.g., COVID-19 PPE scandals)
Election-related violence (2023/24 polls)
Communal violence (Hindu-Muslim tensions, Chittagong Hill Tracts)
Capacity gaps in CSO adaptive management
Overlap/duplication among implementing partners
Reputational risk from partner misconduct (PrOF Rule 19)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Convening informal coalitions (ACGs) and leveraging diplomatic channels to protect activists.
Neutral issue-based coalitions (health, education) and cross-party youth/women fellowships.
Real-time digital monitoring (TIB platform) and citizen grievance redressal mechanisms.
PFGs trained in mediation; Codes of Conduct for parties; Strategic Fund for rapid response.
National platform of religious leaders for rapid condemnation of hate speech.
Coordination component for upskilling; international experts for innovative practices.
Unified ToC/results framework; FCDO-led quarterly coordination.
Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs); PrOF Rule 19 reporting requirements.

fcas_specific_lessons: Informal networks (e.g., ACGs) are more effective than formal institutions in FCAS contexts.
Issue-based coalitions (health, land) build trust where partisan engagement fails.
Local mediation (PFGs) prevents escalation of tensions better than centralised interventions.
Digital tools (TIB platform) enable real-time monitoring where traditional oversight is weak.
Flexible funds (Strategic Fund) are critical for responding to sudden crises (e.g., elections, COVID-19).

lessons_from_previous.SPP programme: Issue-based approaches (e.g., health advocacy) successfully influenced local decision-makers mid-pandemic.
lessons_from_previous.TRIP programme: Informal relationships drove accountability more effectively than formal institutions.
lessons_from_previous.PROKAS programme: Multi-stakeholder coalitions (e.g., on labour rights) built trust and institutional strength.
lessons_from_previous.EPRP programme: Localised mediation reduced communal violence in targeted upazilas.
lessons_from_previous.COVID-19 response: Civil society advocacy triggered Anti-Corruption Commission investigations into PPE scandals.

design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **centralised anti-corruption enforcement** (failed prosecutions) to **localised monitoring** (ACGs + digital platform).
Replacement of **high-profile international actors** with **embedded CSOs** to navigate DSA risks.
Integration of **peace-building** (PFGs) into political party engagement (previously separate workstreams).
Addition of **Strategic Fund** to address lessons on flexibility needs during crises (e.g., COVID-19).
Expansion of **gender-focused components** (e.g., women peace-builders) based on SPP2’s gender gap findings.

quote.risks: "The inherent risks in delivering governance programmes in Bangladesh will require close management by the FCDO to ensure that the programme remains within the BHC’s risk appetite." (D0004195.odt, Risk section)
quote.lessons: "Issue-based approaches that engage with practical problems that matter to citizens have been more effective. These interventions build multi-stakeholder coalitions with a common interest in finding solutions to these problems." (D0004195.odt, Progress and lessons learned)
quote.design: "The programme will complement existing research-based advocacy and civic engagement on corruption with a new digital platform for collecting and sharing data led by an expanded network of local volunteer groups." (D0004195.odt, What we will do)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Co-funding from USAID/Sweden/Switzerland for complementary programmes (e.g., party strengthening, anti-corruption). The document notes: "The BHC will closely coordinate with other donors to take a coherent approach by effectively combining both programmatic and diplomatic levers."

quote.budget: "With a proposed budget of up to £27m it will be the UK’s main intervention in supporting a more open and inclusive political system in Bangladesh." (D0004195.odt, Programmesummary)
