metadata.programme_name: Yemen Food Security Safety Net Programme
metadata.quote: This programme will provide cash transfers to up to 1.5 million of Yemen’s most food insecure households. It will be FCDO Yemen’s flagship programme and the backbone of our humanitarian response. It will spend up to £250 million over 5 years, replacing 3 existing programmes which last year spent in the region of £120 million per year. (D0001246.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: It will spend up to £250 million over 5 years (D0001246.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct cash transfers to 1.5 million food-insecure households) with implementation research (testing coordinated cash interventions) and capacity building (strengthening national social protection systems). It aims to address immediate famine risk while building long-term resilience through coordinated humanitarian and development approaches.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will provide cash transfers to up to 1.5 million of Yemen’s most food insecure households... It will continue provision of life-saving cash assistance to those most in need (including women), build resilience to reduce famine risk in the future, and ensure a more efficient, effective and sustainable response to the high on-going needs of this protracted crisis. (D0001246.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 1.5 million food-insecure households receiving cash transfers annually
Reduced famine risk through regular, predictable cash transfers
More efficient humanitarian response through coordination of cash programmes
Strengthened national social protection systems (long-term vision)
Improved resilience of vulnerable communities to future shocks
Harmonized cash transfer values and eligibility criteria across actors
Common beneficiary identification and targeting approaches
Establishment of a centralised social protection database (2021)
Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) systems strengthened
Technical facility to support adaptive management
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers immediate humanitarian relief through cash transfers while strategically building a coordinated, sustainable response to Yemen's protracted food insecurity crisis. It combines service delivery with system strengthening and adaptive learning.
what_objectives.quote: The Food Security Safety Net programme will deliver cash assistance to up to 1.5 million of the most severely food insecure households in Yemen on an annual basis, immediately alleviating critical humanitarian need amongst conflict-affected people. This will: Reduce the risk of famine... Incentivise reform of cash-based responses to food insecurity in Yemen... to build a holistic and coherent response that includes humanitarian and development actors along with national social protection institutions (D0001246.odt, What FCDO will do)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Yemen is experiencing the world's worst humanitarian crisis after over six years of continuous conflict since 2015, with 66% of the population (20.7 million people) needing humanitarian assistance. The conflict has caused state fragmentation, economic collapse (50% contraction since 2015), and institutional breakdown.
where_context.q5_source: After more than six years of continuous conflict since early 2015, the humanitarian crisis in Yemen remains the worst in the world... Today, 20.7 million people, 66% of the population, need humanitarian assistance... The conflict continues to inflict civilian casualties and cause extensive damage to public and private infrastructure. (D0001246.odt, CONTEXT: The worst humanitarian crisis in the world)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict restricts access to 16.5 million people in hard-to-reach areas (up from 5 million two years ago). Bureaucratic obstacles are the most pervasive constraint for aid delivery. The economy has shrunk by half since 2015 with 90% currency depreciation since 2017, making food unaffordable. Only half of health facilities are operational due to conflict damage. Remittances (17% of GDP) have dropped up to 80% in some communities due to COVID-19 restrictions. State fragmentation means two competing authorities (GoY and De Facto) with no central social protection ministry.
where_context.quote: Access remains highly restricted by parties to the conflict leaving 16.5 million people in hard to reach areas... bureaucratic obstacles presenting the most pervasive constraint for the safe, sustained and principled delivery of assistance and protection services. (D0001246.odt, CONTEXT: The worst humanitarian crisis in the world)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO Yemen (with World Bank, UN agencies, and NGO consortium)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO and international partners (World Bank, UN agencies) hold primary decision-making authority. Southern partners (SFD, national NGOs) implement programmes under international oversight due to limited government capacity and conflict constraints.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to strengthen national social protection systems
support to SFD for improved targeting and monitoring
training on harmonized cash transfer mechanisms
institutional strengthening of Yemen's Social Fund for Development (SFD)
development of common beneficiary identification systems
support for Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) systems

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: implementation of large-scale cash and food assistance programmes; biometric registration systems

partner_organizations.name: Yemen Social Fund for Development (SFD)
partner_organizations.role: national social protection institution delivering Cash for Work and cash-based safety nets; community-led development

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: implementation of Emergency Cash Transfer Programme (ECTP) in partnership with World Bank; child-focused interventions

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: funding and technical support for Emergency Cash Transfer Programme (ECTP); social protection system strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Cash Consortium of Yemen (CCY) - 13 INGOs and 12 national NGOs
partner_organizations.role: delivery of cash programming including Rapid Response Mechanism; beneficiary targeting and verification

partner_organizations.name: Food Security and Agriculture Cluster (FSAC)
partner_organizations.role: coordination of food security response across UN agencies and NGOs

partner_organizations.name: Yemen's Social Welfare Fund (SWF)
partner_organizations.role: historical national social protection mechanism (currently non-functional due to conflict)

partner_organizations.name: Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group
partner_organizations.role: coordination platform for donors (co-led by FCDO, ECHO, and World Bank)

who_partners.quote: The UK will use its solid understanding of cash programming in Yemen and strong relationships with the key cash actors to help build a more effective and efficient response to food insecurity... Through its bilateral funding and relations, the UK has played a key role in promoting cash programming and supported continuous improvement of standards and quality. (D0001246.odt, FCDO comparative advantage)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme consolidates three existing FCDO-funded programmes (WFP, YeSP, MHRP) into a single flagship initiative. Funding flows through a combination of direct grants to multilateral agencies (WFP, World Bank/UNICEF), block funding to national institutions (SFD), and consortium agreements with NGOs (Cash Consortium of Yemen).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a coordinated platform approach with FCDO as the strategic funder, multilateral agencies (WFP, World Bank, UNICEF) as primary implementers, and national institutions (SFD) and NGOs as delivery partners. Coordination occurs through existing clusters (FSAC) and donor working groups (Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme builds on long-standing FCDO partnerships with WFP (since 2010), SFD (since 2004), and the World Bank/UNICEF ECTP (since 2018). Partners were selected based on existing track records in Yemen's cash programming and their roles in the humanitarian architecture.
how_mechanism.quote: This programme will bring together humanitarian and social protection interventions currently funded under three FCDO programmes and build on learning to date... WFP, YeSP (delivered by SFD and UNICEF/World Bank ECTP), and MHRP (delivered by a consortium of NGOs). (D0001246.odt, FCDO response to date)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group (co-led by FCDO, ECHO, and World Bank) provides strategic oversight. Operational coordination occurs through the Food Security and Agriculture Cluster (FSAC) for humanitarian response and the Yemen Cash and Markets Working Group (CMWG) for technical harmonization. FCDO maintains ultimate approval authority for major adaptations.
how_governance.quote: The UK was instrumental in establishing the Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group in 2020, which we currently co-lead with ECHO and the World Bank. A common vision and work plans set in 2020 will guide collective donor efforts from 2021... Greater coordination between aid actors will require reform and incentives. Donors have a key role to play in shifting incentives for reform towards a collective vision. (D0001246.odt, FCDO comparative advantage)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between cash components (e.g., adjusting transfer values or modalities) with FCDO approval, particularly to respond to currency depreciation or new shocks. The programme includes a technical facility to support adaptive management.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme will adopt a flexible approach to adjust modalities (e.g., shifting from cash to vouchers/food in-kind if markets fail) and respond to emerging evidence. A technical facility will help FCDO identify when context changes or evidence warrants adaptations. The balance between life-saving and resilience-building can be revisited annually based on context.
how_flexibility.quote: This programme will adopt a flexible approach to ensure that the modality can be adapted to the context... and can respond to emerging evidence on what works to support longer-term impact... The first year will allocate greater proportion to saving lives while still investing in reducing future famine risk. For following years, the balance will be revisited based on the context. (D0001246.odt, WHAT FCDO WILL DO)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral agencies/NGO consortia (WFP, World Bank/UNICEF, CCY) → National partners (SFD, local NGOs) → Beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: FCDO manages these programmes remotely as its teams are not able to be based in Yemen and uses Third Party Monitoring to assess progress and quality, understand impact and extract learning across programmes. (D0001246.odt, YeSP)

q24_alternatives_considered: Continuing fragmented cash programmes (rejected due to inefficiencies and duplication)
Direct government-led social protection (rejected due to current state fragmentation and lack of capacity)
Pure humanitarian response without development linkage (rejected as unsustainable for protracted crisis)
In-kind food assistance instead of cash (rejected due to market functionality and affordability being the core issue)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The consolidated cash platform was chosen to: 1) Address duplication and inefficiencies in the current fragmented response (estimated 30% overlap in beneficiary lists); 2) Leverage Yemen's functional markets (88% of food is imported and markets operate, but people lack purchasing power); 3) Build on existing FCDO partnerships with proven implementers (WFP, SFD, World Bank); 4) Create pathways for eventual transition to nationally-owned systems while maintaining humanitarian principles in a conflict context; 5) Enable adaptive management through coordinated structures (Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (reducing duplication and improving efficiency)
risk mitigation (using established partners in high-risk FCAS context)
past experience (building on FCDO's decade-long engagement with partners)
partner capacity (leveraging multilateral agencies' existing systems)
flexibility (need for adaptive response in protracted crisis)
equity (targeting most vulnerable including women and IDPs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication of efforts across humanitarian and social protection programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Harmonization through the Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group, interoperable beneficiary lists, and common targeting approaches. Establishment of a centralised social protection database in 2021.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient cash transfer values due to currency depreciation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO-funded 'top-ups' to transfer values (implemented in 2020/2021) and flexible adjustment mechanisms based on market monitoring.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in conflict context
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Biometric registration systems for cash programmes (being rolled out by WFP) and strengthened safeguarding measures.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of government capacity to eventually take over social protection
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Gradual strengthening of national institutions like SFD through technical assistance and parallel humanitarian systems that can transition to national ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented accountability mechanisms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investment in common Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) systems and beneficiary feedback mechanisms across all cash programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Competition between aid actors hindering coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Donor-led incentives through the Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group and alignment with global initiatives like the UN Common Cash Statement.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (consolidating three programmes to reduce overhead)
efficiency (harmonized transfer values and eligibility criteria)
effectiveness (evidence that cash transfers improve food security outcomes)
equity (targeting most vulnerable groups including women and IDPs)
why_rationale.quote: Poorly coordinated humanitarian and social protection programmes risk leaving people behind... The result is a fragmented landscape of programmes that risks leaving people excluded or not necessarily receiving the type of assistance that is cheaper and works best for their situation... A well-funded humanitarian response in 2019 helped reverse the risk of famine identified in late 2018. Food insecurity has once again soared after a year of limited funding... Coordination is a first step towards a nationally owned and financed response to food insecurity. (D0001246.odt, NEED FOR INTERVENTION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context severely limits partner selection: 1) Security risks prevent FCDO from having in-country teams, requiring remote management through multilateral partners; 2) State fragmentation means no central government ministry can lead social protection, necessitating parallel humanitarian systems; 3) Conflict restrictions in north-west Yemen limit access to 16.5 million people, requiring partners with existing field presence (WFP, NGOs); 4) Bureaucratic obstacles from both GoY and De Facto authorities create operational constraints that only established actors can navigate.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks prevent FCDO in-country presence → reliance on multilateral partners
State fragmentation → no central social protection authority → need for parallel systems
Conflict access restrictions → 16.5M people in hard-to-reach areas → requirement for partners with existing field networks
Currency collapse (90% depreciation since 2017) → need for partners with financial systems to adjust transfer values
Bureaucratic obstacles from competing authorities → only established actors can operate
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to deliver both immediate life-saving assistance AND build long-term resilience determines the mixed delivery structure: 1) Service delivery (cash transfers) requires scale and speed → use of established humanitarian actors (WFP, NGOs); 2) System strengthening requires government engagement → partnership with national institutions (SFD) despite their limited capacity; 3) Coordination requirements to avoid duplication → platform approach with donor working groups; 4) Adaptive management needs → technical facility for real-time adjustments.
q28_linkages: Immediate cash needs → WFP and NGO consortium for rapid delivery
Long-term system building → SFD and World Bank for institutional strengthening
Coordination requirements → Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group platform
Adaptive management → technical facility for evidence-based adjustments
Accountability needs → common AAP systems across all partners
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) Speed vs inclusion: 'Holding to humanitarian principles, including neutrality, can limit engagement with government actors especially in a conflict-affected context where parties to the conflict can be compounding humanitarian need' (equity concern) vs need for rapid delivery; 2) Northern expertise vs Southern ownership: International partners (WFP, World Bank) lead implementation due to capacity constraints, while aiming to build national systems; 3) Cost vs reach: 'Social protection transfers are kept low to keep the scheme affordable for the state in the future' (efficiency) vs need for adequate transfer values to address depth of need (equity); 4) Harmonization vs context-specific needs: Common transfer values improve efficiency but may not match varying local costs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: humanitarian neutrality vs government engagement for sustainability
international implementation capacity vs national ownership
low transfer values for sustainability vs adequate amounts for impact
standardized approaches vs context-specific adaptations
rapid delivery vs inclusive beneficiary identification
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Severe' risk rating (FCAS context) drives intensive oversight: 1) Remote management with third-party monitoring due to security risks; 2) Biometric systems and safeguarding measures due to diversion risks; 3) Technical facility for adaptive management due to volatile context; 4) Donor working group for coordination due to fragmented authority.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited national capacity shapes the partner roles: 1) International actors (WFP, World Bank) lead implementation due to SFD's constrained capacity; 2) FCDO provides technical assistance to SFD for targeting and monitoring; 3) NGO consortium handles beneficiary verification that SFD cannot; 4) Long-term vision includes gradual transition as national capacity builds.
intersections.quote: In a context where the state has limited capacity and motivations which can affect neutrality and impartiality, humanitarian policies and efforts have been largely driven by international donors and implementing agencies. However, this should not prevent humanitarians delivering assistance in ways that can support the re-establishment of government participation and the building of a stronger national system in the future. (D0001246.odt, FCDO LEARNING AND RESPONSE TO DATE)

key_programme_risks: Famine risk affecting 47,000 people in 2021 with 16.2 million severely food insecure
Currency depreciation (90% since 2017) making food unaffordable despite functional markets
Fragmented cash programmes with estimated 30% beneficiary overlap
State fragmentation with competing GoY and De Facto authorities
Access restrictions affecting 16.5 million people in hard-to-reach areas
Insufficient funding levels (45% of HRP funded in 2021 vs 87% in 2019)
Weak accountability mechanisms and beneficiary feedback systems
Gender inequalities with Yemen ranked worst place for women globally
Protection risks including child marriage, GBV, and armed group recruitment
Climate change increasing frequency of natural disasters
COVID-19 impact on remittances (dropped up to 80% in some communities)
Limited government capacity to eventually take over social protection systems

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Famine risk due to food insecurity
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular, predictable cash transfers to 1.5 million most food-insecure households to reduce reliance on negative coping strategies
FCDO-funded 'top-ups' to transfer values and flexible adjustment mechanisms
Consolidation into single programme with harmonized transfer values and eligibility criteria through Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group
Parallel humanitarian systems with gradual strengthening of national institutions (SFD) through technical assistance
Use of established partners (WFP, NGOs) with existing field presence and negotiation access
Advocacy for increased funding and more efficient use of resources through coordination
Investment in common Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) systems and beneficiary feedback mechanisms
Targeted support to female-headed households and integration of protection services with cash programming
Flexible programme design that can adapt to new shocks and technical facility for real-time adjustments
Long-term technical assistance to SFD and phased approach to national ownership

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, parallel humanitarian systems are necessary when government capacity is limited, but should be designed to eventually transition to national ownership
Biometric systems and third-party monitoring are essential for managing diversion risks in conflict settings
Donor coordination platforms (like the Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group) are critical for aligning incentives in fragmented authority contexts
Flexible funding mechanisms are required to respond to currency volatility and sudden shocks
Local implementation partners (NGOs, SFD) are essential for reaching conflict-affected areas where international actors have limited access
Social protection systems in FCAS require different sequencing - first build coordination, then national capacity, then transition
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases showed that: 1) Short-term humanitarian financing alone is ineffective for protracted crises; 2) Cash transfers are more effective than in-kind assistance when markets function (82-90% of transfers spent on food); 3) Common beneficiary lists reduce duplication but require interoperable systems; 4) Technical assistance to national institutions (SFD) can improve targeting but takes time; 5) Donor coordination can drive reform but requires sustained incentives; 6) Predictable multi-year funding is more effective than annual cycles for building resilience.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The new programme design incorporates: 1) Consolidation of three separate programmes to reduce duplication; 2) Technical facility for adaptive management based on real-time learning; 3) Stronger focus on Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) systems; 4) Explicit pathway for eventual transition to national systems; 5) Flexible balance between life-saving and resilience-building that can be adjusted annually; 6) Common monitoring frameworks across partners to enable comparison of impact.
risks_lessons.quote: Throughout their lifespan, the WFP, YeSP and MHRP programmes have delivered well on their objectives and on UK priorities as shown by Annual Review ratings and audit results. Where improvements were needed, those were captured in Annual Reviews and acted upon, leading subsequently to better results. This programme will continue building on our learning to date on our key partners and their cash interventions. (D0001246.odt, FCDO response to date)

co_funding_partners.partner: EU/ECHO (co-lead of Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage additional funding through the Cash and Social Protection Donor Working Group's collective vision and by demonstrating the efficiency of coordinated cash programming to other donors (including Gulf donors).
financial_details.quote: This programme will provide cash transfers to up to 1.5 million of Yemen's most food insecure households. It will be FCDO Yemen's flagship programme and the backbone of our humanitarian response. It will spend up to £250 million over 5 years, replacing 3 existing programmes which last year spent in the region of £120 million per year. (D0001246.odt, Programme summary)

q1_source.text: This programme will seek to boost short-term economic stabilisation and encourage economic de-escalation to combat drivers of food insecurity. Weak policy capacity and economic warfare have pushed food prices to record highs. The lack of international coordination and fragmented institutions (with separate authorities in North and South) complicates delivery. Data limitations and security risks further constrain operations.

While the MDTF aims to eventually include Northern authorities, current engagement is limited to Southern institutions due to political constraints.

institutional strengthening for economic policy implementation

quote.text: Direct technical assistance to key government institutions. Building on the Yemen CSSF pilots (which conclude in March 2022), this will initially focus on strengthening the capacity of key central government agencies (the Ministry of Finance and Executive Bureau for Acceleration of Aid Absorption and Support for Policy Reforms in the Prime Minister’s Office) and the Central Bank of Yemen.
quote.source: D0001182.odt, WHAT IS THE PROPOSED APPROACH?

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants for technical assistance (e.g., to CBY and MoF), contributions to the World Bank's Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF), and a flexible fund for catalytic activities. The MDTF operates as a pooled funding mechanism with fixed World Bank management fees (12% for Bank-executed activities).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured around four components: 1) direct technical assistance to Yemeni institutions, 2) economic data/evidence generation, 3) the World Bank MDTF (as a convening and financing platform), and 4) a flexible fund for adaptive programming. The MDTF is designed to eventually transition to government execution when conditions allow.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships and pilot successes under the CSSF programme. The World Bank was chosen for its convening power and technical expertise, while Yemeni institutions were pre-identified as key reform agents. The rationale emphasizes continuity and leveraging proven partnerships.

quote.text: Building on the Yemen CSSF pilots (which conclude in March 2022), this will initially focus on strengthening the capacity of key central government agencies [...] and the Central Bank of Yemen. [...] The UK’s investment through AFFY and the initial focus of the MDTF [...] will be on Transition and Program Enablers, which will be Bank-Executed only.
quote.source: D0001182.odt, WHAT IS THE PROPOSED APPROACH?

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: The MDTF governance structure includes World Bank oversight with donor input. Sub-awards under the flexible fund would likely require FCDO approval, while MDTF activities follow World Bank procedures. The Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) of the Quad Ambassadors provides additional coordination.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The MDTF governance is structured to balance the equities of both the Government of Yemen and de facto authorities, with decision-making roles for both parties once political progress allows. The World Bank Board approves major decisions, and the UK (as seed funder) has significant influence. The Quad Ambassadors’ Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) serves as a coordination forum.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: Oversight includes regular (quarterly) risk reviews, programme-level risk registers updated every three months, and escalation of severe risks to the MENA-level register. The FCDO Yemen Country Board oversees the portfolio, with embedded conflict advisors supporting adaptive management.

quote.text: The FCDO programme team will take a dynamic and action-orientated approach to risk management, with regular monitoring of risks and progress made in mitigating them. [...] Current and emerging risks, including safeguarding and fraud risks, will be discussed with partners at least every three months, in line with updating the portfolio level risk register.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, particularly through the flexible fund (20% of budget). The MDTF allows for scaling up activities as the political context improves, but major shifts (e.g., from Bank-executed to recipient-executed) require World Bank Board approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed with explicit flexibility to respond to shifts in the political and economic context. The flexible fund enables rapid piloting of catalytic activities (e.g., economic de-escalation measures), and the MDTF can adapt its focus as conditions evolve. Learning from CSSF pilots (e.g., seizing unplanned opportunities for peace process engagement) is embedded in the design.

quote.text: The programme spend will be complemented by our efforts on coordination and influencing. [...] The flexible fund to support catalytic or pilot activities. This is the key element that allows our programme to be adaptive and responsive to the context. [...] This is particularly important for supporting the peace process, where there is a need to capitalise on pivotal moments when political interests align.
quote.source: D0001182.odt, WHAT IS THE PROPOSED APPROACH?

how_efficiency.q21_management_costs_details: For Bank-executed activities under the MDTF, a 12% indirect rate applies. Recipient-executed activities have lower management fees (2-5%).
how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (MDTF) → Yemeni institutions (e.g., CBY, MoF). For direct technical assistance: FCDO → implementing partners (e.g., ACAPS, IGC) → Yemeni institutions.

quote.text: For Bank executed activities, an indirect rate of 12% is applied (applies to new TFs established after 1 January 2021). The indirect cost of recipient-executed activities will be lower (from 2-5%, depending on the size of the grant).

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (counterfactual)
Option 2: Fund interventions to support economic reform, but without support for a new World Bank MDTF
Option 3: Fund interventions to support economic reforms, including through cautious support for a new World Bank MDTF, with flexible funding (CHOSEN OPTION)
Option 4: Channel all available funding into the MDTF
Direct financial aid to the Government of Yemen (discounted due to high fiduciary risk)
Supporting the IFC Trade Finance Facility (discounted as IFC launched its own facility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected because it balances immediate economic stabilization with long-term recovery planning, leverages the World Bank’s convening power to coordinate international support, and retains flexibility to adapt to Yemen’s volatile context. The MDTF provides a scalable platform for future recovery funding, while the flexible fund allows for responsive programming (e.g., seizing peace process opportunities). This approach mitigates risks of aid fragmentation and builds on successful CSSF pilots.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging World Bank’s economies of scale and existing partnerships)
risk mitigation (MDTF reduces fiduciary risks compared to direct bilateral aid)
past experience (building on CSSF pilot successes)
partner capacity (World Bank’s technical expertise and Yemeni institutions’ reform potential)
flexibility (adaptive design for shifting political/economic dynamics)
equity (MDTF designed to eventually include Northern authorities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MDTF may fail to materialize if other donors do not contribute, undermining coordination efforts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s seed funding and diplomatic lobbying to attract additional donors; reputational risk to World Bank if MDTF fails.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited absorptive capacity of Yemeni institutions may delay reforms.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased technical assistance with embedded advisors; focus on preserving existing capacity (e.g., Executive Bureau).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political fragmentation (North-South divide) limits whole-of-Yemen impact.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MDTF governance designed to eventually include de facto authorities; flexible fund for cross-line initiatives (e.g., currency unification).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Economic warfare or conflict escalation could derail progress.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adaptive management to repurpose funds (e.g., shift to private sector support if institutional engagement becomes impossible).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on World Bank may reduce Yemeni ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MDTF designed to transition to government execution; capacity building for Yemeni institutions to lead reforms.

quote.text: Option 3 will aim to reserve a flexible fund (just under 20% of the overall programme budget) for catalytic or pilot activities that respond to emerging opportunities and political will. [...] The MDTF component provides a flexible vehicle that allows for scale up across a wide range of different areas. [...] This option minimises risk that the international community is unprepared and uncoordinated in supporting economic recovery by establishing a scalable funding vehicle.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to entities capable of operating in Yemen’s fragmented and high-risk environment. Direct engagement with Northern (Houthi-controlled) authorities is currently impossible due to political constraints, restricting partnerships to Southern institutions and multilateral actors (e.g., World Bank). Security risks and data limitations further narrow the pool of viable implementers.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict fragmentation (North-South divide) forces initial focus on Southern institutions.
Political sensitivities prevent direct engagement with de facto authorities in the North.
Weak institutional capacity requires partners with technical expertise (e.g., World Bank, USAID).
Security risks limit on-the-ground presence, favoring remote or multilateral delivery models.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both immediate economic stabilization (e.g., exchange rate management) and long-term recovery (e.g., MDTF for reconstruction) drives the mixed delivery structure. Technical assistance requires embedded partnerships with Yemeni institutions, while the MDTF provides a scalable platform for future recovery. The flexible fund addresses the uncertainty of Yemen’s context, allowing adaptive responses to emerging opportunities (e.g., peace process windows).
q28_linkages: Capacity building (WHAT) → Direct technical assistance to CBY/MoF (HOW).
Coordinated donor support (WHAT) → MDTF as a financing platform (HOW).
Adaptive programming (WHAT) → Flexible fund for catalytic activities (HOW).
Whole-of-Yemen impact (WHAT) → MDTF governance designed for eventual Northern inclusion (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly acknowledges trade-offs between rapid stabilization (focusing on Southern institutions) and inclusive recovery (eventual Northern engagement). The MDTF’s design attempts to balance efficiency (pooled donor funds, World Bank management) with equity (governance structure for future Northern participation). The flexible fund allows for testing inclusive approaches (e.g., cross-line economic measures) without compromising core delivery.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Initial focus on Southern institutions for quick wins, with plans to expand North later.
Expertise vs. ownership: World Bank-led MDTF provides technical rigor but risks reducing Yemeni leadership.
Cost vs. reach: Direct technical assistance is resource-intensive but necessary for institutional preservation.
Risk vs. impact: Flexible fund allows high-risk/high-reward pilots (e.g., peace process support) alongside safer MDTF investments.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight (quarterly reviews, embedded conflict advisors) and adaptive structures (flexible fund, MDTF scalability). The volatile context requires dynamic risk management, with severe risks escalated to regional (MENA) level. Oversight intensity is higher for direct bilateral components (e.g., CBY support) than for MDTF activities.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with partner roles designed to strengthen Yemeni institutions’ ability to lead reforms. For example, the Executive Bureau’s capacity determines its role as a reform interface, while the CBY’s technical gaps shape the scope of embedded advisors. The MDTF’s transition to government execution is contingent on institutional progress.

quote.text: Yemeni ownership will be key. [...] The intention is an ‘MDTF first’ approach, which will help ensure greater efficiency across the programme. We will retain flexibility however to continue with some direct technical assistance to key institutions, where there is a case for retaining the relationship at a bilateral level, for example because of political sensitivities or the strength of the UK relationship.
quote.source: D0001182.odt, WHAT IS THE PROPOSED APPROACH?

key_programme_risks: Political collapse of the Government of Yemen due to economic instability, undermining peace efforts.
Escalation of conflict or economic warfare derailing reform progress.
Failure to attract additional donors to the MDTF, limiting its scalability.
Inability to unify North-South economic policies, perpetuating fragmentation.
Global food/fuel price shocks (e.g., Ukraine war) exacerbating Yemen’s affordability crisis.
Weak absorptive capacity of Yemeni institutions delaying reforms.
Backlash from de facto authorities in response to Southern stabilization efforts.
Humanitarian access restrictions due to economic or security deteriorations.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Government collapse due to economic pressures.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance to improve fiscal management and donor coordination to unlock external finance (e.g., Gulf support).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: MDTF fails to attract other donors.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK seed funding and diplomatic lobbying; World Bank’s reputational stake in MDTF success.
Flexible fund to repurpose activities (e.g., shift to private sector support); adaptive management framework.
MDTF governance designed for eventual Northern inclusion; flexible fund for cross-line initiatives (e.g., currency measures).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Global price shocks worsen food insecurity.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on structural drivers of instability (e.g., exchange rate volatility) to build resilience to external shocks.
Phased capacity building with embedded advisors; focus on preserving existing reform champions (e.g., Executive Bureau).

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, economic stabilization must be paired with political engagement to address root causes of conflict (e.g., economic warfare in Yemen).
Flexible, adaptive programming is essential to seize unpredictable windows of opportunity (e.g., CSSF’s rapid response to peace process moments).
Pooled funding mechanisms (e.g., MDTF) can mitigate donor fragmentation but require careful governance to balance efficiency and inclusivity.
Local ownership is critical but must be nurtured gradually in fragmented contexts (e.g., initial focus on Southern institutions with plans to expand).
Economic data and analysis are vital for evidence-based policymaking in information-scarce environments (e.g., YETI platform).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The CSSF Economic Stabilisation Programme (2019–2022) demonstrated the value of flexibility in Yemen’s context, allowing rapid responses to emerging opportunities (e.g., peace process consultations). It also highlighted the need for sustained capacity building, as short-term pilots had limited impact on institutional resilience. The success of the foreign exchange auction (supported by US/UK technical assistance) showed that targeted reforms can stabilize the currency and improve food affordability, but require continuous political backing.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The AFFY design incorporates longer programme durations (3 years vs. CSSF’s short-term pilots) to allow for deeper institutional engagement. The flexible fund (20% of budget) was added to replicate CSSF’s adaptive successes. The MDTF was introduced to address donor coordination gaps identified in earlier phases, while the ‘MDTF first’ approach aims to improve efficiency over direct bilateral programming.

quote.text: The CSSF has demonstrated the value of flexibility in economic programming in Yemen, allowing us to drive change quickly and test proof of concept before scaling up initiatives. [...] Without a twin-track political and programmatic approach, the programme will fail. [...] A programme without such flexibility would not be fit-for-purpose in this context; it would also be irresponsible and offer poor value for money.
quote.source: D0001182.odt, WHAT IS THE PROPOSED APPROACH? and Risk sections

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The MDTF is designed to leverage additional donor contributions, with the UK’s £10m seed funding expected to attract further international support. The programme aims to ‘pave the way for large-scale recovery and reconstruction funding’ post-settlement, though specific leverage targets are not quantified.

The programme will increase protection for women and children through preventing and responding to gender-based violence, assisting and protecting people in conflict, and influencing respect for International Humanitarian Law." what_objectives.summary: The programme combines direct service delivery (healthcare, nutrition, WASH, protection) with system strengthening to address Yemen's humanitarian crisis, focusing on women and children as the most vulnerable groups. It aims to reduce excess mortality while building resilience against future shocks.

quote.objectives: "The programme will seek to deliver against two outcomes: 1. Reduce preventable disease and death in women and children; 2. Increase protection for women and children." (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.rationale: "The Yemen Women and Children Programme will implement two key objectives in the International Development Strategy: ‘step up our life-saving humanitarian work’ and ‘provide women and girls with the freedom they need to succeed.’" (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Yemen is in its 8th year of conflict with 70% of the population living in Houthi-controlled areas, 23.4 million people needing humanitarian assistance, and active frontlines in 45 districts. The health system is on the brink of collapse with only 49% of facilities fully functional.
where_context.q5_source: "Now in its 8th year of conflict since early 2015, Yemen’s previous developmental gains have been eroded and the country currently ranks 179 out of 189 countries in the Human Development Index... 2022 is predicted to be Yemen’s worst year since the start of the conflict with 23.4 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, 77% of whom are women and children." (D0005481.odt, Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Active conflict restricts service delivery and monitoring; bureaucratic requirements from both Northern and Southern authorities create access barriers; 70% of health facilities lack sustainable water sources; only 35 safe spaces and 7 shelters exist for GBV survivors across 21 governorates; Mahram requirements limit women's mobility and programme implementation.

quote.conflict: "The operating environment for the humanitarian response in Yemen is extremely challenging. In addition to active conflict which challenges service delivery, substantial bureaucratic requirements and restrictions imposed by various authorities in both North and South impeded data collection and assessment of needs, delivery and monitoring." (D0005481.odt, Context)
quote.infrastructure: "The availability of WASH services at healthcare facilities is essential for the provision of quality care... 70% of health facilities in Yemen do not have sustainable water sources... 61% of health facilities do not have adequate sanitation facilities." (D0005481.odt, Problem A2)
quote.regulatory: "It is therefore extremely challenging for humanitarian agencies to gain approval from authorities, particularly in the North, to conduct 'protection' programmes... Responding to GBV in Yemen is further restricted by an increasing requirement since 2017 in some locations, for female members of staff to be accompanied by a male guardian (Mahram)." (D0005481.odt, Problem B3)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with FCDO and UN agencies (Northern institutions), with Southern partners (local NGOs) implementing under their guidance. The document emphasizes 'international support for the capacities of these partners is critical' (D0005481.odt, Problem B4).

strengthening referral pathways for GBV survivors

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct funding to UN agencies (UNICEF, WHO) and block funding for NGO consortia. Previous FCDO programmes in Yemen (e.g., MHRP) used NGO consortia for multi-sectoral responses, suggesting a similar approach here.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the programme through a closed group of pre-selected partners (UNICEF, WHO, MoPHP, and NGOs) with regular coordination meetings. The Yemen Country Board and Development Director provide oversight, and technical alignment is ensured through donor coordination groups.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNICEF and WHO are the established multilateral partners for health/nutrition in Yemen, with existing systems for service delivery. how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Yemen Country Board (including HMA and Development Director) approves the programme, with technical oversight from FCDO's health/nutrition team. quote.governance: "Approved by Yemen HMA, Yemen Development Director and Yemen Country Board" (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet)

Donors also convene the Senior Officials Meeting roughly every 6 months to bring together donors, UN and NGOs at a senior level on Yemen issues, and the monthly Technical Monitoring Group to agree common approaches on issues of humanitarian access." (D0005481.odt, International Response)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between health/nutrition/WASH components with FCDO approval, as evidenced by the shift toward integrated programming. However, protection funding faces stricter controls due to sensitivity.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive management to respond to changing frontlines and emerging needs (e.g., famine risk, disease outbreaks). Adjustments require FCDO approval, particularly for protection activities.

quote.flexibility: "This programme will address the factors that directly lead to excess mortality among women and children, focusing on malnutrition, disease and childbirth and is complemented by the Food Security and Safety Net Programme... The alignment of the two programmes alongside the ability of the UK to have multi-year agreements with partners will ensure maximum value for money will be achieved across the two programmes." (D0005481.odt, Strategic Fit)
quote.adaptive: "Theremay also be increased demand for services if access to populations is improved. There will be a need to continue monitoring of International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law, and new protection needs amongst the 4.3 million displaced and the potential for further conflict and resulting protection needs if populations start to return home." (D0005481.odt, Context)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNICEF/WHO (implementing partners) → Local NGOs/MoPHP (service providers)

quote.layers: "Primary Healthcare in Yemen is provided by the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MoPHP) with support from UNICEF... NGOs also support the provision of primary healthcare through MoPHP clinics and mobile teams." (D0005481.odt, International Response)
quote.payment: "FCDO worked with other donors and agencies to produce a harmonised incentive scale [for health workers] which has resulted in lower incentive payments, but which are still higher than regular salaries." (D0005481.odt, FCDO Response to Date)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to MoPHP (rejected due to weak institutional capacity)
Expanded NGO consortia (limited by bureaucratic restrictions in North Yemen)
Direct cash transfers (complements but doesn't replace service delivery)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UNICEF/WHO-led consortium model was selected for its existing infrastructure in Yemen, ability to navigate access constraints, and alignment with FCDO's strategic priorities (famine prevention, GBV response). The document highlights that 'international support for the capacities of [local] partners is critical' (D0005481.odt, Problem B4), justifying the multilateral approach despite its Northern-led structure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Bureaucratic restrictions from Northern authorities limiting protection programming
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sustained engagement with authorities and use of 'health entry points' to integrate protection services (e.g., GBV screening in health facilities).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Mahram requirements hindering women's access to services
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Community engagement strategies and male guardian accompaniment for female staff.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication of services due to fragmented donor coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monthly Technical Monitoring Group and Senior Officials Meetings to align approaches.

quote.rationale: "The alignment of the two programmes [Yemen Women and Children Programme + Food Security Programme] alongside the ability of the UK to have multi-year agreements with partners will ensure maximum value for money will be achieved across the two programmes." (D0005481.odt, Strategic Fit)
quote.risks: "Responding to GBV in Yemen is further restricted by an increasing requirement since 2017 in some locations, for female members of staff to be accompanied by a male guardian (Mahram)... Agencies have reported that these restrictions are becoming tighter across the country." (D0005481.odt, Problem B3)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with existing access agreements (primarily UNICEF/WHO) and restricts local NGOs' roles due to bureaucratic requirements (e.g., Mahram rules, protection programming approvals). Conflict dynamics also prioritize Northern-led multilateral actors over Southern institutions.
q27_constraints_detail: Mahram requirements exclude unaccompanied female staff from implementation
Northern authorities' restrictions on 'protection' programming limit local NGO roles
Active frontlines in 45 districts reduce the pool of viable Southern partners
Only 49% of health facilities are fully functional, constraining service delivery locations
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for integrated health-nutrition-protection services (WHAT) drives the consortium structure (HOW), as no single partner could deliver all components. The focus on GBV response requires embedding protection specialists within health teams, shaping the mixed delivery structure.
q28_linkages: Integrated programming (health + nutrition + WASH) → Consortium of UNICEF (health), WHO (tertiary care), and NGOs (community outreach)
GBV protection needs → Embedded protection advisors in health facilities despite access restrictions
Famine prevention goal → Alignment with Food Security Programme and multi-year partner agreements
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between rapid delivery (efficiency) and inclusive targeting (equity), particularly for marginalized groups like Muhamasheen, IDPs, and people with disabilities. For example: 'targeting in the Yemen operation has proven challenging... large inclusion and exclusion errors mean the most vulnerable may be overlooked' (D0005481.odt, Problem A6).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Rapid scaling risks missing marginalized groups (e.g., only 4.8% of people with disabilities are reached)
Northern expertise vs Southern ownership: UNICEF/WHO leadership ensures delivery but limits local decision-making
Cost vs reach: Integrated services increase per-beneficiary costs but improve outcomes for complex cases (e.g., malnourished children with GBV trauma)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Severe' risk rating (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet) justifies intensive oversight (monthly monitoring groups, Senior Officials Meetings) and restrictive sub-award processes (FCDO approval required).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building for local partners is embedded but focused on implementation (e.g., training health workers) rather than strategic decision-making, which remains with FCDO/UN agencies. The document states: 'international support for the capacities of these partners is critical' (D0005481.odt, Problem B4).

quote.equity: "The Inter-agency Humanitarian Evaluation found that targeting in the Yemen operation has proven challenging... in the absence of careful, well implemented targeting, there is a danger that large inclusion and exclusion errors mean the most vulnerable may be overlooked." (D0005481.odt, Problem A6)
quote.capacity: "The Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation also identified the potential of national organizations to implement protection services, including sensitizing the authorities. However, it noted that international support for the capacities of these partners is critical." (D0005481.odt, Problem B4)

key_programme_risks: Collapse of Yemen's health system (only 49% of facilities functional)
Famine risk for 161,000 people already in famine-like conditions
GBV underreporting due to stigma and Mahram restrictions
Protection programming approval delays from Northern authorities
Duplication of services without proper coordination
Exclusion of marginalized groups (Muhamasheen, IDPs, people with disabilities)
Funding gaps (only ~50% of $4.3bn 2022 appeal expected to be met)
Ukraine war exacerbating food/fuel price inflation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Direct support to MoPHP for salaries/medical supplies; UNICEF/WHO technical assistance; mobile health teams for hard-to-reach areas.
Integration with Food Security Programme; multi-year funding agreements; targeted nutrition interventions for 2.2M children and 1.3M pregnant women.
Safe spaces in health facilities; male guardian accompaniment for female staff; community engagement strategies.
Use of 'health entry points' to deliver protection services; sustained authority engagement; embedding protection advisors in health teams.
Targeted outreach to Muhamasheen communities; disability-inclusive service design; data disaggregation by gender/age/disability.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from 2017-2021 MHRP programme: Cash transfers effective but need complementing with services; incentive payments require harmonization to avoid distortion.
2020 famine aversion experience: Multi-sectoral integration (health + nutrition + WASH) critical for sustainability.
GBV programming adaptations: Health facility-based services more acceptable to authorities than standalone safe spaces.
Local partner lessons: National NGOs can deliver protection services but require 'critical international support' (D0005481.odt, Problem B4).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2017-2021 Multi-sectoral Humanitarian Response Programme (MHRP) demonstrated that: 1) Cash transfers alone are insufficient without service integration; 2) Health worker incentives must be aligned with salaries to avoid market distortion; 3) Community consultation procedures need strengthening to improve targeting. The Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation (2022) highlighted that 'further strengthening of health information systems would improve the availability of data on illnesses and deaths' (D0005481.odt, Problem A7).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from standalone to integrated health-nutrition-protection services; 2) Embedding GBV screening in primary healthcare; 3) Linking WASH funding to health facilities with highest morbidity; 4) Multi-year agreements with partners for stability; 5) Strengthened community feedback loops.

quote.lessons: "The MHRP provided cash transfers to 1 million people in hard-to-reach areas of Yemen and treated 55,000 children under 5 years and 24,000 pregnant or breastfeeding women for malnourishment... Annual reviews have highlighted the need for further integration of services including mental health and psycho-social support." (D0005481.odt, FCDO Response to Date)
quote.adaptations: "FCDO is now requiring UNICEF to adopt a more integrated approach in areas of high need. This includes linking a large part of FCDO WASH funding to supported health facilities where the greatest reduction in morbidity and mortality can be achieved." (D0005481.odt, Problem A5)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aligns with the UK's Food Security and Safety Net Programme, together comprising 'up to 90% of UK spend in Yemen' (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet). This coordination is expected to mobilize additional resources from Gulf donors.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £160 million" (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.leverage: "Alongside the UK’s Food Security and Safety Net Programme, which aims to ensure that Yemenis have enough food to eat and increased resilience, these two programmes together will provide up to 90% of UK spend in Yemen." (D0005481.odt, SummarySheet)

metadata.programme_name: Saving Lives in Sierra Leone Phase 3
metadata.quote: This programme will support the delivery of quality health services at national level through essential commodities procurement for the Free Healthcare Initiative; ensuring the functionality of Special Care Baby Units, saving the lives of premature, low birth weight and sick newborns; as well as supporting health service provision within six districts in Sierra Leone (including a focus on quality of care and workforce capability). (D0005245.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source:
AMP Start Date: September 2023
AMPEnd Date: March 2028

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of health services, including neonatal care and essential medicines) with health systems strengthening (capacity building, policy reform, and workforce training). It also includes elements of implementation research (testing and scaling interventions like Special Care Baby Units) and financing mechanisms (co-financing of free healthcare commodities).
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will support the delivery of quality health services at national level through essential commodities procurement for the Free Healthcare Initiative; ensuring the functionality of Special Care Baby Units, saving the lives of premature, low birth weight and sick newborns; as well as supporting health service provision within six districts in Sierra Leone (including a focus on quality of care and workforce capability). (D0005245.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Fewer preventable deaths among women, adolescent girls, and children in Sierra Leone (impact-level)
Universal Health Coverage improved in Sierra Leone (outcome-level)
Maternal mortality ratio reduced in target districts (quantitative target not specified)
Neonatal mortality rates reduced in target districts (quantitative target not specified)
Child (under-five) mortality rates reduced in target districts (quantitative target not specified)
Adolescent birth rates reduced (quantitative target not specified)
17,000 babies safely discharged from Special Care Baby Units (SCBUs) between 2017 and 2022 (historical achievement)
3,500+ babies discharged from SCBUs annually (2021-22 data)
85%+ survival rate in SCBUs (2022 data)
Support to 147 water and sanitation facilities in health centres (historical achievement)
Training and mentorship for 1,284 newly qualified midwives (2022 data)
Demand creation and delivery of family planning services for over 152,000 adolescents and young people (2022 data)
Strengthened maternal death surveillance and response systems
Capacity building of District Health Management Teams (DHMTs)
Community partnerships to empower demand for quality health services
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce preventable maternal, neonatal, and child deaths in Sierra Leone by strengthening health systems at district and national levels, while sustaining critical nationwide interventions like Special Care Baby Units (SCBUs) and free healthcare commodities. It builds on past gains from Phases 1-2 of Saving Lives, focusing on quality of care, workforce capacity, and community engagement.
what_objectives.quote: The intended programme impact is: Fewer preventable deaths among women, adolescent girls and children in Sierra Leone. In order to achieve this, the intended programme outcome will be: Universal Health Coverage improved in Sierra Leone. (D0005245.odt, Proposed Programme Impact and Outcome)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sierra Leone is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to its history of civil war (1991-2002), Ebola crisis (2014-2015), weak government institutions, and ongoing risks of civil unrest during elections. The country also faces high poverty ($494 GDP per capita), limited health infrastructure, and vulnerability to climate-related health events.
where_context.q5_source: Sierra Leone has moved on from civil war (1991-2002) and an Ebola crisis (2014-2015) and is relatively stable, although its population (estimated at 8.4 for 2021) is still very poor ($494 per head per year, the third lowest in the world). (D0005245.odt, Country context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak government capacity hampers policy implementation and donor coordination (e.g., MoHS has limited ability to manage multiple partners). Poor infrastructure (e.g., only 11% of the population has access to clean water meeting SDG6 standards) and unreliable electricity affect service delivery. Climate change increases health risks (e.g., 25% more climate-related health events in Africa 2011-2021). Data quality issues hinder planning, and security risks (e.g., civil unrest during elections) may disrupt operations. The narrow tax base limits GoSL’s ability to sustain health services amid growing demand.
where_context.quote: Democracy is maturing but the functioning of government is weak (Economist Intelligence Unit World Democracy Index 2021), and civil unrest can flare up during election periods. (D0005245.odt, Country context); Weaknesses in policy and planning for delivering universal health coverage (UHC): despite the development of progressive policies, inadequate capacity exists for policy development and planning at national level, operational planning at district level and weak translation of policy into implementation at all levels. (D0005245.odt, Lessons from the UK’s past engagement)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains primary decision-making authority, with implementing partners (a mix of Northern NGOs and UN agencies) delivering services under FCDO oversight. While Southern partners (e.g., MoHS, DHMTs) are involved in implementation, strategic decisions and funding control remain with FCDO and Northern-led consortia.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and mentorship for health workers (e.g., 1,284 midwives trained in 2022)
workforce planning and continuous professional development (CPD)
support to District Health Management Teams (DHMTs) for leadership and planning
community health worker engagement and empowerment
institutional strengthening of MoHS and national systems (e.g., National Medical Supplies Agency)
supervision and quality improvement mechanisms (e.g., maternal death surveillance)

who_partners.quote: The programme will be implemented through two consortia of specialised implementing partners, the NGO-led UNITE consortium and a United Nations (UN) consortium. (D0005245.odt, Current bilateral UK support); The UK will continue to lean into sector governance structures to coordinate efforts, working with the MoHS and the Office of the Vice President. (D0005245.odt, Wider donor support and coordination)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (to consortia) and co-financing agreements (with GoSL for free healthcare commodities). Funds are channelled through implementing partners (NGO and UN consortia) for service delivery, with FCDO retaining oversight. The mechanism includes conditional co-financing for drugs and supplies, requiring GoSL contributions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is delivered through two pre-selected consortia: 1) the UNITE consortium (NGO-led) and 2) the UN consortium (UNFPA, UNICEF, WHO). FCDO manages the overall programme, with consortia responsible for day-to-day implementation in assigned districts. The structure is closed (no open competition for new partners) but includes coordination mechanisms with GoSL and other donors (e.g., World Bank, USAID).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct award to existing consortia)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The consortia were selected based on their track record under Phases 1-2 of Saving Lives (2016-2023) and their alignment with MoHS priorities. The direct award reflects the need for continuity, existing relationships with GoSL, and the urgency of sustaining gains in maternal and child health.
how_mechanism.quote: The Saving Lives programme is delivered through two consortia of specialised implementing partners, the NGO-led UNITE consortium and a United Nations (UN) consortium. (D0005245.odt, Current bilateral UK support); The UK has taken steps to coordinate to align future health sector support with other donors including USAID and World Bank. (D0005245.odt, Wider donor support and coordination)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by a Health Development Partners group (main forum for coordinating donors) and aligns with MoHS governance structures established after the 2022 Health Summit. FCDO leads coordination with the Office of the Vice President and MoHS, while consortia manage operational decisions. Annual reviews and technical advisory mechanisms are implied but not explicitly detailed.
how_governance.quote: The UK will continue to lean into sector governance structures to coordinate efforts, working with the MoHS and the Office of the Vice President and taking a leading role in the Health Development Partners group (the main forum for coordinating international donors and health partners). (D0005245.odt, Wider donor support and coordination); Counterterrorist financing: the proposed programme will comply with all relevant UK legislation... All suppliers will be vetted through a full due diligence assessment. (D0005245.odt, Required Assurances)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., districts, interventions) with FCDO approval, particularly to address emerging priorities or gaps. Flexibility is built in to respond to health emergencies (e.g., disease outbreaks) and adapt to donor coordination needs, but requires justification and alignment with MoHS plans.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with adjustments allowed based on district-specific needs, emerging data (e.g., maternal mortality estimates), and lessons from implementation. Changes require FCDO approval and consultation with MoHS. Adaptive management is explicitly mentioned as a response to the dynamic context (e.g., political changes, new health threats).
how_flexibility.quote: The programme is designed to be flexible and adaptive. Adaptation can be necessary for three broad reasons: firstly, the programme will be most effective if it is able to respond with interventions tailored to the specific priority needs of the districts, hospitals and health facilities supported. (D0005245.odt, What the programme might look like); As for previous UK support, the programme will include flexibility to respond to health emergencies if necessary. (D0005245.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Consortia (UNITE/UN) → District Health Management Teams (DHMTs)/health facilities. Some activities may involve additional sub-grantees (e.g., community organizations), but the core structure has 3 layers.
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will be implemented through two strands... These will both be implemented at national level and cover the whole country. (D0005245.odt, What the programme might look like); Programme Value: up to £35 million (D0005245.odt, Programme summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: "Do nothing" (rejected due to risk of reversing past gains)
Successor RMNCAH programme with nation-wide remit (rejected as poor value for money given new donor funding)
Focus on national-level health systems strengthening only (rejected as insufficient to sustain district-level gains)
Option 1: District-level support only (6 districts)
Option 2: District-level support + nationwide interventions (SCBUs, free healthcare commodities) - **PREFERRED**
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (district support + nationwide interventions) was selected because it: 1) aligns with both UK and GoSL priorities (e.g., ending preventable deaths, UHC); 2) maximizes equity by covering critical nationwide gaps (e.g., SCBUs, drugs) not funded by other donors; 3) ensures sustainability by phasing in GoSL leadership; 4) leverages UK’s comparative advantage in health systems and EPD; 5) allows flexibility to adapt to donor coordination (e.g., with World Bank/USAID); and 6) balances efficiency (focused districts) with impact (nationwide interventions). The mixed approach mitigates risks of reversal in maternal/child health gains while building long-term capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on consortia may weaken GoSL ownership and sustainability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased transition plans to handover responsibility to GoSL/DHMTs, with capacity-building embedded in all components. Co-financing requirements for free healthcare commodities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating multiple donors (UK, World Bank, USAID) in different districts may create fragmentation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active UK leadership in the Health Development Partners group; harmonized data systems; joint planning with MoHS to avoid duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexibility in fund reallocation could lead to misalignment with MoHS priorities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: All adaptations require MoHS consultation and FCDO approval, with decisions based on district-level needs assessments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Direct awards to consortia may limit competition and innovation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging lessons from Phases 1-2 and piloting innovative approaches (e.g., SCBU model reviews) within the consortium structure.

why_rationale.quote: Option Two is therefore recommended. As Table 1 above shows, both options will deliver on country business plan commitments, align with UK policy, and promote greater equity in access... Option Two scores more highly on sustainability by ensuring a phased transition plan for high impact UK investments with clear targets to ensure a sustainable long-term handover to GoSL and/or other partners. (D0005245.odt, Option Selection); The UK’s comparative advantage across the options and the combined option gives the best scope to realise these benefits. (D0005245.odt, Option Selection)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context and weak GoSL capacity constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) proven experience in fragile settings (e.g., IRC, UNICEF); 2) ability to navigate complex donor coordination (e.g., World Bank/USAID); 3) existing relationships with MoHS/DHMTs; and 4) capacity to manage security/political risks (e.g., election-related unrest). Local partners (e.g., DHMTs) are included but limited to implementation roles due to capacity gaps in leadership and financial management.
q27_constraints_detail: GoSL’s weak capacity for donor coordination limits open competition for new partners.
Security risks (e.g., election violence) favor experienced international NGOs/UN agencies.
Infrastructure gaps (e.g., electricity, water) require partners with logistics expertise (e.g., Crown Agents).
Data limitations necessitate partners with strong M&E systems (e.g., WHO, UNICEF).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (service delivery + systems strengthening) determine a dual consortia structure: 1) **UNITE (NGO-led)** for adaptive, community-focused delivery in districts; 2) **UN consortium** for standardized, technical support (e.g., SCBUs, drugs). The need for nationwide interventions (e.g., free healthcare commodities) requires a centralised mechanism (FCDO-GoSL co-financing), while district flexibility is enabled through consortia with local presence.
q28_linkages: Service delivery goals (e.g., SCBUs) → require clinical expertise → UN consortium (WHO/UNICEF).
Systems strengthening (e.g., DHMT capacity) → requires embedded mentorship → UNITE consortium (IRC, CUAMM).
Nationwide equity (e.g., drug access) → needs GoSL buy-in → FCDO-GoSL co-financing agreement.
Community engagement → local trust → NGO partners (e.g., Restless Development).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., nationwide drug procurement, SCBUs) with efficiency (e.g., focusing on 6 districts). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to consortia enable rapid scale-up but limit opportunities for local organizations. 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led consortia ensure technical quality but may reduce GoSL leadership. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Nationwide interventions (e.g., free drugs) are costly but critical for equity, while district focus improves cost-efficiency.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Northern expertise (e.g., RCPCH training) vs. Southern ownership (GoSL/DHMTs).
Rapid delivery (consortia) vs. inclusive partnerships (limited local CSO roles).
High-impact districts (6) vs. nationwide coverage (risk of exclusion).
Flexibility (adaptive management) vs. standardization (donor coordination needs).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (high risk) drives **intensive oversight**: annual reviews, embedded safeguarding officers, and strict compliance with UK legislation (e.g., Terrorism Act 2000). Political/election risks necessitate real-time adaptation (e.g., pivoting funds during unrest), while weak GoSL capacity requires FCDO-led coordination.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: 1) **Consortia** focus on training (e.g., midwives, DHMTs) and mentorship to transition responsibilities to GoSL. 2) **MoHS/DHMTs** are positioned as co-implementers with increasing leadership over time. 3) **Community structures** are empowered to demand accountability, shifting from passive recipients to active partners.
intersections.quote: The UK’s long engagement in the sector has identified specific lessons... Compared to many other settings in which FCDO works, longer-term and higher intensity support has been shown to be required to sustain gains. (D0005245.odt, Lessons from the UK’s past engagement); The programme will seek to enhance access to services for marginalised groups including people with disabilities... This includes increased and effective representation of people with disabilities in health governance at community and district levels. (D0005245.odt, Disability considerations)

key_programme_risks: Reversal of gains in maternal/child health if UK funding ceases (e.g., SCBUs, free drugs).
GoSL’s limited financial capacity to sustain health services post-handover.
Weak MoHS coordination leading to donor fragmentation (e.g., World Bank/USAID misalignment).
Political instability (e.g., election violence) disrupting service delivery.
Climate-related health events (e.g., cholera outbreaks) straining systems.
Supply chain failures for drugs/equipment (e.g., last-mile distribution gaps).
High staff turnover in health workforce (e.g., only 10% of specialist posts filled).
Safeguarding risks (e.g., exploitation of vulnerable groups in health facilities).
Data quality issues hindering evidence-based planning.
Equity gaps (e.g., rural/urban disparities in access to clean water, sanitation).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reversal of gains if UK funding ceases
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased transition plans for SCBUs/drugs with GoSL co-financing commitments; exploring co-funding from other donors.
Capacity-building for MoHS in resource mobilisation; advocacy for increased health budget (target: 15% per Abuja Declaration).
UK-led coordination through Health Development Partners group; harmonized data systems with World Bank/USAID.
Flexible funding to respond to emergencies; safeguarding plans for election periods.
Integration of climate-smart policies in MoHS plans; solarisation of hospitals (via ‘Powering Hospitals in Sierra Leone’ programme).
Support to National Medical Supplies Agency (NMSA); community monitoring of drug stocks.
Mentorship programmes; improved workforce planning (e.g., HRH Strategy 2017-2021).
Zero-tolerance policies; dedicated Safeguarding Officers in consortia; codes of conduct for health workers.
Strengthening DHMT data collection/use; digital tools for real-time monitoring.
