Targeted interventions for rural/poor communities; disability-inclusive service design.

fcas_specific_lessons: Longer-term, high-intensity support is required to sustain gains in FCAS contexts (vs. standard 5-year programmes).
Donor coordination must be actively managed by external partners (e.g., UK) due to weak GoSL capacity.
Flexibility to respond to emergencies (e.g., Ebola, COVID-19) is critical but requires pre-agreed triggers.
Community engagement is essential for demand creation in low-trust environments.
Phased handovers (vs. rapid exits) are necessary to avoid collapse of services post-donor withdrawal.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from Saving Lives Phases 1-2 (2016-2023) include: 1) **Sustainability**: Direct service delivery without systems strengthening leads to reliance on donors. 2) **Coordination**: Bilateral alignment with MoHS is more effective than siloed donor efforts. 3) **Flexibility**: Rapid reallocation of funds during COVID-19/Ebola saved lives. 4) **Quality vs. access**: High coverage of services does not guarantee quality (e.g., maternal death surveillance gaps). 5) **Local capacity**: DHMTs need embedded support, not just training. 6) **Equity**: Rural-urban disparities persist despite national programmes (e.g., 50% rural access to clean water vs. 78% urban).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 3 adaptations include: 1) **Geographic focus**: Reduced from 16 to 6 districts to deepen impact and align with World Bank/USAID. 2) **Systems strengthening**: Shift from direct delivery to capacity-building (e.g., DHMT leadership). 3) **Nationwide critical interventions**: Retained SCBUs/free drugs to prevent reversal of gains. 4) **Co-financing**: Introduced GoSL contributions for drugs to improve sustainability. 5) **Adaptive management**: Formalised flexibility for emergencies and learning. 6) **Disability inclusion**: Explicit marker and targeted interventions (vs. ad-hoc in Phases 1-2).
risks_lessons.quote: Compared to many other settings in which FCDO works, longer-term and higher intensity support has been shown to be required to sustain gains. Although it is clear how far health indicators have improved as a result of long-term FCDO investments, a rapid handover to GoSL, by their own admission, runs the risk of derailing progress. (D0005245.odt, Lessons from the UK’s past engagement); Weaknesses in policy and planning for delivering UHC... inadequate capacity exists for policy development and planning at national level, operational planning at district level and weak translation of policy into implementation at all levels. (D0005245.odt, Lessons from the UK’s past engagement)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages co-financing from GoSL (for free healthcare commodities) and aligns with new donor funds: World Bank ($60m for 5 districts), USAID (redesigned programme), and Global Fund ($126m for 2021-2024). This replaces partial UK funding reductions post-2021, maintaining net international support near pre-2021 levels.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes both revenue (e.g., salaries, drugs, training) and limited capital expenditures (e.g., WASH facilities in health centres, solarisation of hospitals via linked programmes). Most funds are for recurrent costs (service delivery, workforce support).
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: up to £35 million (D0005245.odt, Programme summary); The World Bank has recently launched a new $60 million maternal and child health programme supporting five districts... USAID are redesigning a programme with similar priorities and scope, also supporting five districts. (D0005245.odt, Wider donor support and coordination); Support from other donors and options for co-financing will also be explored with the aim of a tapered reduction in UK expenditure. (D0005245.odt, Option 2)

metadata.programme_name: Pioneering a Holistic approach to Energy and Nature-based Options in MENA for Long-term stability – PHENOMENAL
metadata.quote: "A 5 year International Climate Finance programme up to £60m. It will deliver green growth through building back better in EBRD Partner Countries (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Jordan, Lebanon and OPTS)." (D0000872.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "A 5 year International Climate Finance programme up to £60m." (D0000872.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PHENOMENAL is a climate finance programme that combines financing mechanisms (mobilizing private sector climate finance), implementation research (testing nature-based solutions for water security), capacity building (strengthening regional institutions), and policy influence (supporting regulatory reforms). It aims to address both mitigation (low-carbon transition) and adaptation (climate resilience) challenges in the MENA region.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This is MENA’s flagship climate programme. It will prioritise action in 3 key areas mobilising climate finance to support transition and build back better, water security and improved weather and climate information." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1. Context and need for FCDO intervention)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Mobilized private sector finance for adaptation and mitigation
q3_expected_outputs.target: Leveraged private finance (specific target not quantified)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) for water security tested and scaled
q3_expected_outputs.target: 4 projects demonstrating NBS in Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and OPTs

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved weather and climate information services
q3_expected_outputs.target: Enhanced forecasting capability and early warning systems (regional coverage)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened water governance and efficiency
q3_expected_outputs.target: Water accounting and natural capital accounts developed

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy and regulatory reforms for climate action
q3_expected_outputs.target: Support to National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)

q3_expected_outputs.output: People supported to adapt to climate change
q3_expected_outputs.target: Aligned with ICF KPI1: Number of people supported to better adapt (quantitative target not specified)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Reduced per capita emissions
q3_expected_outputs.target: Aligned with ICF KPI7: Level of installed capacity of clean energy (MW) (quantitative target not specified)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased access to clean energy
q3_expected_outputs.target: Aligned with ICF KPI2: Number of people with improved access (quantitative target not specified)

what_objectives.summary: PHENOMENAL is a £60m, 5-year programme designed to catalyze climate-smart development in MENA through three components: (1) Green Finance (mitigation), (2) Regional Water Management (adaptation via Nature-Based Solutions), and (3) Weather and Climate Information Services (adaptation). It combines financing, technical assistance, and policy reform to build resilience and drive low-carbon growth.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver on the UK’s number one international priority of tackling climate change and biodiversity loss, as set out in the Integrated Review (IR), and also delivers against the ‘Enduring Resilience’ and ‘Prosperity’ pillars of the new MENA 2030 Strategy." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1. Context and need for FCDO intervention)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The MENA region is classified as 'Major' risk due to its exposure to climate vulnerabilities (e.g., water scarcity, extreme heat), political instability, and conflict-affected states (e.g., Lebanon, OPTs). Climate change acts as a threat multiplier, exacerbating existing tensions and fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0000872.odt, Summary Sheet) and "In a region which is already marked by security and stability issues, climate change is likely to act as a threat multiplier and to exacerbate underlying tensions which political systems are unlikely to be able or in some cases willing to respond to effectively." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1.1 Vulnerabilities to Climate Change)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and political economy barriers (e.g., rentier states reliant on fossil fuels) hinder climate action. Data limitations and lack of adaptive capacity constrain evidence-based decision-making. Conflict and water scarcity exacerbate regional tensions, while regulatory frameworks disadvantage renewable energy. For example, energy subsidies and lack of independent regulators create market distortions, and water governance issues are compounded by transboundary disputes.
where_context.quote: "The political economy of MENA states creates a specific set of constraints to improving climate action. Described as ‘rentier states’, the MENA economies rely on significant external rent that is often controlled by the government... This political economy creates barriers to change whereby the institutions with power to enact reform lies with those most set to benefit from continuing the status quo." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1.5 Political and Policy environment) and "Lack of reliable, contextualized, and accessible data and information hinders countries’ ability to design and implement effective climate mitigation and adaptation policies." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1.5 Political and Policy environment)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight and approval authority, while implementation is delegated to multilateral partners (EBRD, IWMI, UK Met Office). Southern partners (e.g., national governments, regional bodies) are engaged as beneficiaries and co-implementers but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for water managers and technicians
institutional strengthening of national meteorological agencies
multi-stakeholder platforms for knowledge exchange
technical assistance for policy/regulatory reform
gender and inclusion mainstreaming

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer for Green Finance component (Component A); mobilizes private sector finance and provides technical assistance
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (HQ in London, regional offices in MENA)

partner_organizations.name: International Water Management Institute (IWMI)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer for Regional Water Management component (Component B); focuses on Nature-Based Solutions and transboundary water governance

partner_organizations.name: UK Met Office
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer for Weather and Climate Information Services component (Component C); expands WISER programme to MENA

partner_organizations.name: National governments (Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, OPTs)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and co-implementers; engage in policy reform and project delivery

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Engaged in multi-stakeholder platforms and knowledge exchange

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (including SMEs and financial institutions)
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of green finance and partners in low-carbon transitions

who_partners.quote: "FCDO have proactively worked with EBRD to highlight and direct interventions to adaptation and nature spaces, and have earmarked our funds towards a 60:40 split between adaptation and resilience." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component A) and "The project will focus activities in Egypt, Jordan, OPTs and Lebanon but also engage at a regional and global level in relation to knowledge sharing." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component B)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: (1) **Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)** with EBRD for Green Finance, (2) **Accountable Grant** to IWMI for Regional Water Management, and (3) **MOU** with UK Met Office for Weather and Climate Information Services. These instruments allow FCDO to earmark funds for specific activities while leveraging partners' existing platforms and co-financing.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as the funder and strategic overseer, while implementation is delegated to three multilateral/technical partners (EBRD, IWMI, UK Met Office). Each component has its own governance (e.g., EBRD’s HIPCA framework, IWMI’s multi-stakeholder platforms) but reports to FCDO’s Steering Committee. The structure centralizes FCDO’s management while decentralizing delivery to specialized partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships, regional presence, and technical expertise. EBRD, IWMI, and UK Met Office are established actors in MENA with proven track records in climate finance, water management, and weather services, respectively. The business case emphasizes building on "known partners in the region" to minimize risk and leverage co-financing.
how_mechanism.quote: "We have received a proposal from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to stimulate private sector activity in the climate space..." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component A) and "We have worked with the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), to refine a proposal... This proposal builds on the existing work of IWMI and International Union for Conservation for Nature (IUCN) in the region." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component B)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Steering Committee** is chaired by FCDO and includes representatives from EBRD, IWMI, UK Met Office, and potentially other donors. It oversees strategic direction, risk management, and performance review. Component-level governance (e.g., EBRD’s HIPCA, IWMI’s platforms) operates under this umbrella.
how_governance.quote: "The Steering Committee... will meet twice a year to review progress against the programme’s log frame and Theory of Change, and to provide strategic guidance." (D0000872.odt, Management Case, 12. The Steering Committee) and "Each component has its own MEL framework, aligned with the overall programme ToC, with annual reviews and a mid-term evaluation." (D0000872.odt, 15. Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked by component (A/B/C) but can be adjusted within components based on pipeline demand (e.g., EBRD’s flexible delivery across sectors). Reallocation between components requires FCDO approval, as each has distinct partners and objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an **inception phase** (6 months for Component B) to refine activities based on stakeholder input. Adjustments to priorities (e.g., scaling successful pilots) are permitted but subject to Steering Committee approval. The EBRD’s GET model allows for adaptive financing based on market opportunities.
how_flexibility.quote: "EBRD will be providing a pipeline for investment to ensure finance is not in advance of need." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component A) and "This 6 months scoping phase is included to establish multi-stakeholder platforms, capitalize on earlier studies, identify and select... options for NBSW/AWM to be further tested at priority sites, and refine the Result Framework." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component B)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (EBRD/IWMI/UK Met Office) → End Beneficiaries (e.g., private sector, governments, CSOs). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned beyond the three core partners.
how_efficiency.quote: "Funds will be disbursed based on delivery of agreed milestones, as outlined in the MOUs and grant agreements." (D0000872.odt, Financial Case, 10.2 How will funds be paid out?) and "The programme will have a centralized management structure, with FCDO overseeing three components delivered by EBRD, IWMI, and UK Met Office." (D0000872.odt, Management Case, 11. FCDO Management Team)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: FCDO would integrate climate considerations into bilateral programmes without a dedicated regional initiative. Pros: No additional cost. Cons: Limited ambition, no leadership on COP26 outcomes, and inability to address transboundary issues.

Focused intervention on climate finance, water, and weather with established partners (EBRD, IWMI, UK Met Office). Pros: Catalytic impact, leverages existing relationships, and simple delivery. Cons: Medium ambition; limited coverage of FCAS states and non-ODA countries.

High-ambition platform with multiple components (e.g., challenge funds, technical assistance). Pros: Flexibility, comprehensive coverage, and transformational potential. Cons: Complex management, higher risk, and requires new networks in MENA.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (Streamlined Programme) was selected for its **balance of ambition and feasibility**. It leverages **proven partners** (EBRD, IWMI, UK Met Office) with existing regional footprints, minimizing start-up risks while allowing for catalytic impact. The modality aligns with FCDO’s need for **speed** (immediate disbursement possible) and **value for money** (co-financing from partners). The business case emphasizes that a platform approach (Option 3) would require "new networks for delivery" in MENA, where FCDO’s climate programming is currently limited.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited visibility of UK funding in multi-donor trust funds (e.g., EBRD’s HIPCA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will negotiate earmarked funds and branding opportunities to ensure UK contributions are recognizable. Example: 60:40 split for adaptation/resilience in EBRD component.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on multilateral partners may reduce FCDO’s direct influence
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Steering Committee chaired by FCDO with biannual reviews to guide strategic decisions. Embedded gender/inclusion requirements in partner agreements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Component silos limiting cross-learning
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Centralized MEL framework and annual reviews to synthesize lessons across Green Finance, Water, and Weather components.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 2: Streamlined Programme (Recommended)... Pros: A streamlined programme targeting intervention at specific activities which have catalytic impact; Building on past lessons as delivered through known partners in the region; limited human resource capacity needed and already in place; a simple delivery mechanism and reduced programme management burden." (D0000872.odt, 6.0 Appraisal of Options) and "The UK’s contribution to multilateral funds (e.g., ICF) and platforms coordinated by HMG... will help steer and progress priority reforms which will also impact investment." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component A)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **political economy of MENA** (rentier states, weak institutions) and **conflict/fragility** (e.g., Lebanon, OPTs) constrain partner selection to organizations with: (1) **existing regional presence** (e.g., EBRD’s local currency lending, IWMI’s offices in Cairo/Amman), (2) **multilateral status** (to navigate sovereignty sensitivities), and (3) **technical expertise in high-risk environments**. Southern partners (e.g., national governments) are engaged as co-implementers but cannot lead due to capacity gaps and political barriers.
q27_constraints_detail: EBRD selected for its ability to operate in FCAS contexts (e.g., Lebanon) and provide local currency finance, addressing regulatory risks.
IWMI’s existing offices in MENA mitigate security/operational risks for water projects in conflict-affected areas.
UK Met Office’s global reputation enables engagement with national meteorological agencies despite data-sharing sensitivities.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (financing + implementation research + policy influence) necessitate a **multi-partner structure**: (1) **EBRD** for private sector finance (mitigation), (2) **IWMI** for Nature-Based Solutions (adaptation), and (3) **UK Met Office** for climate services (adaptation). The **transboundary nature** of water/weather issues requires regional platforms (e.g., multi-stakeholder dialogues), while the **need for policy reform** embeds technical assistance in all components.
q28_linkages: Green Finance (Component A) uses EBRD’s **GET business model** (combining finance + policy dialogue + TA) to address both mitigation (renewables) and adaptation (resilience investments).
Regional Water Management (Component B) links **NBS pilots** (local) to **regional knowledge-sharing** (transboundary) via IWMI’s platforms.
Weather Services (Component C) integrates **data generation** (technical) with **policy reform** (e.g., early warning systems) to bridge science and decision-making.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (using established partners for speed) with **equity** (gender/inclusion requirements). Trade-offs include: (1) **Northern-led management** (FCDO/EBRD) vs. **Southern ownership** (limited to co-implementation), and (2) **standardized MEL frameworks** (for comparability) vs. **context-specific adaptation** (e.g., FCAS tailoring). The business case acknowledges that "climate scepticism" in MENA requires **localized engagement** but opts for multilateral partners to ensure delivery at scale.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Direct awards to EBRD/IWMI enable rapid disbursement but limit opportunities for local CSOs to lead. Mitigation: Gender/inclusion clauses in partner agreements and CSO engagement in Component B’s multi-stakeholder platforms.

Northern partners (EBRD, UK Met Office) provide technical expertise, but decision-making remains centralized. Mitigation: Capacity-building for Southern institutions (e.g., national met agencies) and inception phases to co-design activities.

Regional approach (vs. bilateral) reduces per-country costs but may dilute impact in FCAS states. Mitigation: Prioritization of Egypt, Jordan, OPTs for water/weather components, with lessons scaled regionally.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight** (biannual Steering Committee reviews, embedded gender/inclusion requirements) and **adaptive management** (inception phases, flexible pipelines). For example, EBRD’s **GET model** allows reallocation within the 60:40 adaptation/mitigation split based on market opportunities, while IWMI’s **6-month scoping phase** refines activities in response to local constraints.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: (1) **Embedding TA** in all components (e.g., EBRD’s policy dialogue, IWMI’s institutional strengthening), (2) **Requiring gender/inclusion plans** from partners to address low adaptive capacity in MENA, and (3) **Linking pilots to upscaling** (e.g., NBS demonstrations → investment proposals) to build local ownership. Southern partners (e.g., national met agencies) are positioned as **co-implementers** with increasing responsibility over time.
intersections.quote: "The political economy of MENA states creates a specific set of constraints to improving climate action... This political economy creates barriers to change whereby the institutions with power to enact reform lies with those most set to benefit from continuing the status quo." (D0000872.odt, Strategic Case, 1.5) and "At minimum, the programme will be fully compliant with the 2014 Gender Equality Act but seeks to go beyond minimum compliance in a number of the components to achieve women’s economic and political empowerment and/or transformational change." (D0000872.odt, 4.2 Cross-cutting Issues, Gender)

key_programme_risks: Low adaptive capacity in MENA institutions and populations, limiting ability to respond to climate interventions.
Political economy barriers (e.g., fossil fuel subsidies, rentier states) resisting low-carbon transitions.
Conflict and fragility (e.g., Lebanon, OPTs) disrupting implementation.
Data limitations hindering evidence-based decision-making.
Limited visibility of UK funding in multi-donor platforms (e.g., EBRD’s HIPCA).
Risk of mal-adaptation (e.g., stranded assets from misaligned investments).
Regulatory frameworks disadvantage renewable energy and cross-border cooperation.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded capacity-building in all components (e.g., training for water managers, gender/inclusion mainstreaming). Example: IWMI’s inception phase includes stakeholder platforms to co-design solutions.
Policy dialogue and technical assistance to reform subsidies/regulations (e.g., EBRD’s HIPCA includes enabling environment support). Leverage UK’s diplomatic influence via Steering Committee.
Prioritize stable countries (Egypt, Jordan) for core activities while using multilateral partners (EBRD, IWMI) with FCAS experience for limited engagement in Lebanon/OPTs.
Component C (Weather Services) focuses on improving data generation and forecasting capability, with UK Met Office’s expertise.
Negotiate earmarked funds and branding in EBRD’s HIPCA. Highlight UK’s role in Steering Committee and annual reviews.
Climate risk integration in decision-making (e.g., WISER’s early warning systems) and FCDO oversight of investment pipelines.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts (e.g., Lebanon, OPTs), **flexible, small-scale pilots** (e.g., NBS demonstrations) are prioritized over large infrastructure to mitigate disruption risks.
Multi-stakeholder platforms (Component B) are used to **build trust** among conflicting parties in transboundary water management.
Partners with **existing FCAS experience** (e.g., EBRD’s local offices, IWMI’s Levant work) are preferred to navigate sovereignty sensitivities.
**Inception phases** (e.g., 6-month scoping for Component B) allow for conflict-sensitive adjustments before full implementation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from WISER in East Africa (scored A+ in 2020) highlight the importance of **user-led co-production** of climate services, which is replicated in Component C. The Africa Regional Climate and Nature (ARCAN) programme demonstrated the value of **regional knowledge-sharing**, informing PHENOMENAL’s cross-country approach. Past EBRD projects in MENA showed that **blending finance with technical assistance** (e.g., GET model) accelerates private sector engagement.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **gender/inclusion requirements** beyond minimum compliance, informed by critiques of past programmes’ limited transformational impact.
Included **6-month inception phase** for Component B to avoid top-down design, based on lessons from ARCAN.
Expanded **WISER’s value chain approach** (data → decision-making) to MENA, replicating its success in East Africa.
Earmarked **60:40 adaptation/mitigation split** in EBRD component to address underfunding of adaptation, a gap identified in ODI (2012) analysis.
risks_lessons.quote: "The WISER programme has been successful in delivery in East Africa (2020 Annual Review scoring A+). PHENOMENAL will provide financial support to expand geographic coverage to MENA..." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component C) and "The programme will build on lessons from other regional climate programmes and from bilateral programmes in FCDO and beyond." (D0000872.odt, 3.2 FCDO/UK expertise and work to date)

co_funding_partners.partner: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
Other donors (via IWMI and WISER platforms)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage private sector finance through EBRD’s HIPCA (e.g., de-risking investments in renewables, water efficiency) and mobilize additional donor co-financing via IWMI/WISER platforms. Specific leverage targets are not quantified but aligned with ICF KPI12 (Volume of private finance mobilised).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme combines **capital investments** (e.g., renewable energy projects via EBRD, NBS infrastructure via IWMI) with **revenue spending** (e.g., technical assistance, capacity-building, policy dialogue). No explicit split is provided.
financial_details.quote: "UK funds will be targeted towards mobilising private sector money for adaptation and nature including demonstrating proof of concept and bringing pilots to scale..." (D0000872.odt, 4.0 Main Programming Activities, Component A) and "The programme will have a centralized management structure, with FCDO overseeing three components delivered by EBRD, IWMI, and UK Met Office." (D0000872.odt, Management Case, 11. FCDO Management Team)

metadata.programme_name: Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience (SIDAR)
metadata.quote: "The programme will provide £40m over five years for capacity support that enables SIDS to draw down climate and wider concessional funding from other sources, deliver programmes and improve policy frameworks." (90000404.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 2/11/2021 to 31/10/2026" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31/03/2028" (D0005363.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening SIDS institutions to access and deliver climate finance), financing mechanism (channeling funds through regional partners), and policy influence (pressing for multilateral system reforms). It focuses on enabling SIDS to better utilize existing climate finance resources while advocating for system changes.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will provide £40m over five years for capacity support that enables SIDS to draw down climate and wider concessional funding from other sources, deliver programmes and improve policy frameworks." and "The second direction of support will focus on the suppliers of climate and concessional finance – those bodies with which SIDS must work in order to deliver mitigation, adaptation and resilience." (90000404.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Increased SIDS access to climate finance (target: higher disbursement rates against approved allocations)
Improved SIDS delivery of climate adaptation/resilience programmes (target: reduced failure rates)
Simplified multilateral systems tailored to SIDS capacity (target: streamlined approval processes)
Strengthened regional technical support networks (e.g., Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre, Pacific Community)
Enhanced UK bilateral offer through small projects fund for posts (target: 38 states and 20 territories)
Scaled-up initiatives through £14.5m extension (e.g., GEF SCCF SIDS Window, SPREP core funding, Pacific Resilience Facility)
Development of innovative finance tools (e.g., Climate Resilient Debt Clauses, debt swaps)
Fintech solutions for SIDS financial inclusion (e.g., Fintech Challenge Fund in Pacific)
Capacity Development Focal Points deployed to broker system changes
what_objectives.summary: SIDAR aims to bridge the gap between SIDS' low capacity and the complex demands of climate finance systems through direct capacity support (Component 1), technical advisory roles (Component 2), and multilateral reform advocacy (Component 3). The £54.5m programme (original £40m + £14.5m extension) targets improved absorption of climate funds, successful programme delivery, and systemic changes in how providers engage with vulnerable states.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected overall impact of the programme will be that SIDS have more resilient development pathways, better adapted to climate change, and will benefit from resilient green/blue economic growth embracing nature-based solutions." (90000404.odt, Impact and Outcome)

countries_regions: Atlantic, Indian Ocean, South China Sea (AIS)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: SIDS face existential climate threats (e.g., Kiribati/Tuvalu at risk of disappearance) and economic vulnerability (e.g., 225% GDP loss from hurricanes in Dominica), but the programme itself is categorized as moderate risk due to established multilateral partnerships and FCDO oversight systems.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (90000404.odt, SummarySheet) and "SIDS are on the frontline of climate change and are ranked by the OECD as the most vulnerable developing states" (90000404.odt, Context)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (low absorption capacity, small government units)
climate risks (existential threats from rising sea levels, storms)
data limitations (SIDS are often 'data-light' due to capacity constraints)
regulatory (complex eligibility criteria for global funds)
political economy (high debt levels, undiversified economies)
security (vulnerability to economic shocks and natural disasters)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Low capacity acts as a 'brake' on climate mitigation/adaptation, with only 50% of GCF-approved SIDS grants disbursed and high programme failure rates. Small government units (e.g., Montserrat's public sector employs ~50% of working-age population) become rapidly overloaded, while complex funder systems (e.g., GCF's 31 preparation facility projects, only 4 in SIDS) create barriers to access. Climate shocks (e.g., COVID-19, hurricanes) exacerbate systemic fragility.
where_context.quote: "The low capacity of SIDS, particularly in relation to planning and delivery, acts as a brake on mitigation, adaptation and resilience, and reduces the quality and value for money of existing ICF investments." and "SIDS have allocations for large volumes of ring-fenced climate and concessional funding... but only half of approved SIDS grants have been disbursed." (90000404.odt, Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains central oversight and approval authority, with Southern partners (e.g., SPREP, PFTAC) implementing regionally. Decision-making on scaling/expansion requires central SIDSHub approval, and Capacity Development Focal Points report through FCDO systems.
q10_capacity_building_details: direct technical support (e.g., GCF application navigation)
training (e.g., procurement, project management)
mentorship (Capacity Development Focal Points)
institutional strengthening (e.g., SPREP, Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre)
peer-to-peer learning (island-to-island support)
shared services (pooled programmes across SIDS)
capacity supplementation (providing staff to 'do the work' for SIDS)

partner_organizations.name: Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP)
partner_organizations.role: Regional implementation (environmental management, climate adaptation)

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Financial Technical Assistance Centre (PFTAC)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support (macroeconomic stability, financial management)

partner_organizations.name: Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs)
partner_organizations.role: Climate finance access and project delivery

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Community (SPC)
partner_organizations.role: Regional technical support (e.g., nature-based solutions)

partner_organizations.name: Commonwealth Secretariat (Climate Finance Access Hub)
partner_organizations.role: Access/approval support for climate finance

partner_organizations.name: Global Environment Facility (GEF) - Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF)
partner_organizations.role: Financing mechanism (SIDS Window A for adaptation)

partner_organizations.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
partner_organizations.role: Host of PFTAC; macroeconomic advisory

partner_organizations.name: UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)
partner_organizations.role: Potential Fintech Challenge Fund partner

partner_organizations.name: The Nature Conservancy
partner_organizations.role: Innovative finance (e.g., Debt Swaps, Climate Resilient Debt Clauses)

partner_organizations.name: CARTAC (Caribbean Regional Technical Assistance Centre)
partner_organizations.role: Public financial management and resilience planning

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Islands Forum
partner_organizations.role: Regional coordination and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: UK Delegations to Multilateral Bodies
partner_organizations.role: Advocacy for SIDS-tailored systems at GCF/WB/IMF

who_partners.quote: "The programme will work through specialist bodies able to target capacity constraints... including the Commonwealth Secretariat (climate finance access hub), the Pacific CROP Council of Regional Organisation of the Pacific... and the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs)." and "A second component will focus on directly addressing specific problems within SIDS through direct provision of expertise to work with partners in the form of programme funded expert advisory roles." (90000404.odt, Our Approach)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of core funding (e.g., £3m to SPREP, £1.5m to PFTAC), competitive grants (e.g., Fintech Challenge Fund), and partnership agreements (e.g., GEF SCCF SIDS Window). The original £40m was structured as a multi-component programme with direct capacity support contracts, while the £14.5m extension adds targeted initiatives through existing multilateral mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO's SIDSHub centrally manages the programme with regional delivery boards (Caribbean, Pacific, AIS/OTs). Component 1 uses a Direct Capacity Support Consortium (DCSC) of ~8 regional implementers (2 per region), while Components 2-3 involve embedded Capacity Development Focal Points and multilateral engagement. Oversight is maintained through a monitoring partner and FCDO's regional posts.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were pre-selected based on proven track records in SIDS capacity building (e.g., CARTAC, 5Cs, SPREP) and existing FCDO relationships. The inception phase engaged with these organizations to form a consortium, prioritizing those with "specialist skills and capacity building footprints" in target regions.
how_mechanism.quote: "This engagement process will identify an initial Direct Capacity Support Consortium (the DCSC consortium) with a proven track record of working directly with SIDS counterparts on capacity development." and "The programme will work through specialist bodies able to target capacity constraints... these specialist agencies can work with SIDS to achieve higher levels of approvals." (90000404.odt, Our Approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Regional delivery boards (Caribbean, Pacific, AIS/OTs) provide oversight, with final decisions routed through the central SIDSHub. A monitoring and evidencing partner reports independently to FCDO. The addendum notes that "the Programme and Policy Teams within the SIDSHub use the FCDO Network and international organisations to identify suitable initiatives to fund."
how_governance.quote: "Regional delivery boards will therefore be encouraged to streamline programming through 1-2 partners and any expansion beyond these numbers would need to be agreed with the central SIDSHub." and "The approach to implementation will remain the same as the previous two years, where the Programme and Policy Teams within the SIDSHub use the FCDO Network... to identify suitable initiatives to fund." (90000404.odt/D0005363.odt, Our Approach/Addendum)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between regions/components with SIDSHub approval, but expansion beyond 2 implementers per region requires central agreement. The addendum's scale-up maintains the original structure while adding new initiatives (e.g., PRF, Fintech).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes iterative approaches, with an inception phase to test activities before scaling. Capacity Development Focal Points can adjust support based on local needs, but major shifts require FCDO sign-off. The 2024 addendum introduces new priorities (e.g., innovative finance) while retaining core components.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme is centred on responding to evidence of what works, and on addressing the core underlying problems that constrain adaptation and resilience... interventions also need to have the flexibility to vary approaches." and "The additional funding will allow the scaling up of existing initiatives as well as funding new initiatives." (90000404.odt/D0005363.odt, Principles/Addendum)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Regional Implementers (e.g., SPREP, 5Cs) → SIDS government counterparts. For multilateral components (e.g., GEF SCCF), an additional layer exists: FCDO → GEF → Regional Partner → SIDS.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme will work through specialist bodies able to target capacity constraints... These agencies... will work with SIDS to achieve higher levels of approvals." and "The approach to implementation... [uses] Due Diligence Assessment... before agreeing the funding arrangement (including reporting requirements)." (90000404.odt/D0005363.odt, Our Approach/Addendum)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: A climate finance fund delivering adaptation projects directly (similar to Australian/NZ model), with capacity building as a secondary element. Rejected due to limited scalability and duplication risks.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Flex and adapt existing FCDO portfolio (Option 3)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Repurpose current Caribbean/Pacific programmes to address capacity issues. Rejected due to dilution of focus and lack of multilateral reform leverage.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Rely on existing regional approaches (Option 3 variant)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Depend on multilateral actors to fill gaps. Rejected due to insufficient coverage of vulnerable SIDS and slow progress.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (new multi-component capacity programme) was selected for its ability to address the capacity gap from both supply (multilateral reform) and demand (SIDS capability) sides simultaneously. The mixed structure allows for direct support through regional specialists while leveraging FCDO's influence on global funds. The consortium model balances tailoring to SIDS' small-scale needs with the efficiency of centralized oversight.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging £11.6bn UK climate finance commitment)
risk mitigation (moderate risk rating with established partners)
past experience (building on DFID/FCDO SIDS engagements)
partner capacity (using proven regional organizations like SPREP, 5Cs)
equity (targeting 38 states/20 territories with highest vulnerability)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs in SIDS environments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limit to 2 implementers per region; use regional hubs (e.g., Suva, Bridgetown) to reduce travel/logistics costs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overload on small government units
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity supplementation (providing staff to 'do the work') and shared services (e.g., pooled procurement).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination weaknesses
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity Development Focal Points to act as local advocates and brokers between SIDS and funders.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited scalability of small-scale approaches
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Test-review-scale-share cycle; expand only those activities with proven impact (e.g., Commonwealth Climate Finance Access Hub).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Multilateral resistance to reform
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage UK's board seats (GCF, WB) and aggregate evidence from Component 3 to press for changes.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (balancing small-scale tailoring with centralized oversight)
effectiveness (focusing on back-office constraints like procurement, not just front-line delivery)
equity (prioritizing most vulnerable SIDS by climate/economic indicators)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 2 (new capacity programme) is our preferred option... The three components... play a mutually supportive role in closing the SIDS capacity gap from both sides – increasing available capacity, while also reducing the demands which are currently beyond SIDS capabilities." and "The programme is centred on responding to evidence of what works... interventions also need to have the flexibility to vary approaches." (90000404.odt, Feasible Options/Principles)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The small size and remoteness of SIDS limit partner selection to organizations with existing regional footprints (e.g., SPREP, 5Cs) or multilateral reach (e.g., Commonwealth Secretariat). High transport costs and weak institutions necessitate partners who can provide embedded support (e.g., Capacity Development Focal Points) rather than fly-in/fly-out consultants. The programme explicitly avoids global firms without SIDS experience, prioritizing "practitioner-to-practitioner support" from similar low-population contexts.
q27_constraints_detail: Geographical remoteness → Requires partners with regional hubs (e.g., PFTAC in Pacific)
Small government units → Need for capacity supplementation (direct staff provision)
Complex funder systems → Partners must specialize in navigating GCF/GEF procedures
Data limitations → Partners must tolerate 'data-light' environments (e.g., Belize's comment on data-heavy processes)
High vulnerability to shocks → Requires flexible, rapid-response partners (e.g., post-disaster support)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address both approvals (Component 1) and delivery (Component 2) while reforming systems (Component 3) drives the mixed consortium/platform structure. Direct capacity support requires regional specialists (e.g., CARTAC for Caribbean PFM), while multilateral advocacy leverages FCDO's board seats. The 'test-review-scale-share' approach reflects the evidence that SIDS programming must be iterative due to unpredictable shocks (e.g., hurricanes, COVID-19).
q28_linkages: Back-office constraints (e.g., procurement delays) → Need for embedded technical roles (Capacity Development Focal Points)
Low disbursement rates → Requires absorption-focused partners (e.g., PFTAC for financial management)
Multilateral complexity → Necessitates advocacy components (Component 3) alongside direct support
Peer-to-peer learning effectiveness → Shapes consortium design to include island-to-island networks
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly accepts higher transaction costs to ensure inclusion of the most vulnerable SIDS (e.g., Atlantic/Oceanic territories). Tensions include: (1) Small-scale tailoring vs. economies of scale: limiting to 2 implementers per region balances reach and oversight; (2) Capacity supplementation (doing work for SIDS) vs. sustainability: justified as "unavoidable" in SIDS contexts but paired with institutional strengthening; (3) Northern expertise (FCDO oversight) vs. Southern ownership: mitigated by regional partner leadership (e.g., SPREP, 5Cs).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Prioritizing 38 states/20 territories with highest vulnerability indicators slows implementation but aligns with equity goals.
Capacity Development Focal Points (often Northern-funded) work within Southern institutions to balance technical skills with local leadership.
Higher per-SIDS costs accepted to serve remote territories (e.g., UK Overseas Territories) not covered by other donors.
Regional delivery boards can adapt approaches, but expansions require central SIDSHub approval to manage risk.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives milestone-based oversight and the use of a monitoring partner for independent verification. High vulnerability to shocks (e.g., hurricanes) necessitates embedded advisors (Capacity Development Focal Points) rather than light-touch management. FCDO's direct management of multilateral engagement (Component 3) reflects the higher risk of reform resistance.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Partners are selected based on their ability to address specific capacity gaps: (1) Regional technical agencies (e.g., 5Cs) handle access/approval constraints; (2) Financial management specialists (e.g., PFTAC) target absorption issues; (3) Shared-service providers (e.g., Commonwealth Hub) reduce back-office loads. The programme's structure mirrors the evidence that SIDS require "supplementing capacity" (direct staff support) alongside traditional training.
intersections.quote: "The structural challenges faced by SIDS... make it difficult to manage shocks... small states systems make it difficult to manage shocks, and the narrow economic base... impacts on available sources of revenue." and "The programme will address the capacity challenges of SIDS from two directions... [including] direct capacity building through regional technical providers." (90000404.odt, Context/Our Approach)

key_programme_risks: Low absorption capacity in SIDS (e.g., only 50% of GCF grants disbursed)
High programme failure rates (worse than conflict-affected states per ADB)
Multilateral resistance to tailored systems (e.g., GCF's complex procedures)
Overload on small government units (e.g., Montserrat's public sector employs ~50% of working-age population)
Donor coordination weaknesses (56% of SIDS report needing stronger statistical capacity)
Climate shocks disrupting implementation (e.g., hurricanes, COVID-19)
Limited scalability of small-scale approaches in fragmented island contexts
Risk of capacity supplementation creating dependency (vs. sustainable systems)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Direct capacity supplementation (e.g., project management units) and back-office support (e.g., procurement, financial management).
Test-review-scale-share approach; only expand activities with proven success (e.g., Commonwealth Climate Finance Access Hub).
Leverage UK board seats (GCF, WB) and aggregate evidence from Component 3 to press for reforms.
Limit to 2 implementers per region; use shared services (e.g., pooled procurement across SIDS).
Capacity Development Focal Points to broker action and advocate for simplified systems.
Flexible, iterative design with rapid-response capacity (e.g., post-disaster support).
Pair direct support with institutional strengthening (e.g., SPREP core funding).

fcas_specific_lessons: SIDS are 73% more vulnerable than income-level peers (OECD Economic Vulnerability Index)
Even upper-middle-income SIDS face high fragility; income growth does not reduce vulnerability
Small states require capacity supplementation (direct staff support) as a bridge, not just training
Peer-to-peer learning (island-to-island) is more effective than traditional North-South technical assistance
Vertical funds and separate project units can weaken institutional capacity (ADB/World Bank lessons)
SIDS transitioning between support levels (e.g., graduation from LDC status) are vulnerable to SDG regression (OECD Cabo Verde pilot)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID/FCDO engagements showed that: (1) Fragmented support without lesson-sharing limits impact; (2) Small grants to regional bodies (e.g., 5Cs) had high leverage but lacked scale; (3) Multilateral 'readiness' programmes (e.g., GCF) often failed to address back-office constraints; (4) Direct capacity supplementation, though controversial, was necessary in SIDS contexts (Justine Davila 2019 review). The Commonwealth Climate Finance Access Hub's success (mobilizing $39.9m with £0.5m UK funding) informed the scaling approach.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations include: (1) Adding Capacity Development Focal Points to address coordination gaps identified in OECD/GCF evaluations; (2) Explicit focus on back-office systems (e.g., procurement, PFM) based on 2020 GCF portfolio review findings; (3) Regional consortium model to avoid duplication of Australian/NZ trust funds; (4) Embedded monitoring partner to track capacity metrics (e.g., World Bank Governance Indicators); (5) £14.5m extension targeting innovative finance (e.g., CRDCs) and fintech to address access barriers highlighted in 2020 UN financing assessment.
risks_lessons.quote: "A 2020 evaluation of the Green Climate Fund’s SIDS portfolio found that despite high nominal allocations... actual disbursements are low and programmes performance poor." and "The programme will... leverage the UK’s overall position within the governance of these bodies [multilaterals]... to secure simplified systems and tailored approaches." (90000404.odt, Context/Our Approach) and "The additional funding will allow the scaling up of existing initiatives as well as funding new initiatives... based on ongoing monitoring, evaluation or learning work." (D0005363.odt, Addendum)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £8m GEF SCCF contribution is expected to catalyze up to $650m in climate adaptation projects (based on Commonwealth Hub's 1:130 leverage ratio). SPREP and PFTAC funding will co-mobilize Australian/NZ resources. The Pacific Resilience Facility aims to bridge the gap for £5-20m projects underserved by GCF/MDBs.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The extension includes both revenue (e.g., SPREP/PFTAC core funding) and capital-like instruments (e.g., Pacific Resilience Facility for mid-size climate projects).
financial_details.quote: "Original project budget: £40m" and "Cost extension value: £14.5m" with allocations including "GEF SCCF, SIDS Window - £8m", "SPREP - £3m", "PFTAC - £1.5m". (D0005363.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION) and "The UK’s funding, along with existing funding from like-minded donors (Australia and New Zealand) will improve SPREP’s capacity and capability to deliver its mandate." (D0005363.odt, Expected Results)

metadata.programme_name: Sudan Economic Impact and Reform (SEIR) Programme

quote.text: The purpose of the programme was to join with the international community in supporting Sudan’s transition to democracy via a programme that contributed to economic stabilisation of the country.

duration_source.text: An additional no-cost extension of 3 years is required now (taking the end date to December 2028).
duration_source.source: D0004219.odt, Rationale for business case extension

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The SEIR programme combines financing mechanism (channeling £80m to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund) with service delivery (providing cash transfers to mitigate economic shocks from reforms). It also includes capacity building elements through technical assistance to Sudan's government.

q1_source.text: Our SEIR programme will help mitigate the impact of these reforms on ordinary people while helping close the fiscal gap identified by the SMP and maintaining public confidence in the CLTG’s approach. To achieve this, this business case proposes that £80m be contributed to a World Bank (WB) Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF), alongside contributions from other donors.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Cash transfers to 25.9 million people (4.6 million families) for 6 months
q3_expected_outputs.target: 25.9 million people (4.6 million families)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Support to close Sudan’s $5.4bn fiscal gap
q3_expected_outputs.target: $5.4bn fiscal gap closure

q3_expected_outputs.output: Help Sudan reach HIPC Decision Point by June 2021
q3_expected_outputs.target: HIPC Decision Point by June 2021

q3_expected_outputs.output: Unconditional cash transfers of $9/month for two years to 2.6 million people (SRSNP phase)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2.6 million people

q3_expected_outputs.output: Community Development Fund (CDF) for local initiatives and SMEs
q3_expected_outputs.target: CDF establishment

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved access to basic services (health, education, WASH) in targeted areas
q3_expected_outputs.target: 500,000 beneficiaries estimated for phase 2

what_objectives.summary: The SEIR programme aims to stabilize Sudan's economy through economic reforms while mitigating the impact on vulnerable populations via cash transfers, and building resilience through community-focused interventions.

quote.text: The SEIR programme is part of a coordinated international effort to raise sufficient funds to support vital economic reforms being implemented by Sudan’s civilian-led transitional government (CLTG), while mitigating the economic shock of reforms for ordinary people, including ending unaffordable fuel subsidies.
quote.source: D0002872.odt, Title: SUDAN–SUDAN ECONOMIC IMPACT AND REFORM (SEIR) PROGRAMME

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sudan is classified as a 'highly vulnerable/strategic interest' country with deep economic crisis, ongoing conflicts, and a recent military coup (October 2021). The country faces inflation over 167%, currency depreciation, and 9.8 million people requiring humanitarian aid.

q5_source.text: Sudan’s transition remains precarious. The country risks economic collapse after decades of kleptocracy and mismanagement. Inflation is over 167% and the currency has depreciated over 100% this year. Ordinary people are less able to afford basics and the number of people requiring humanitarian aid has increased by 78% since 2018 to 9.8 million people (21% of the population).

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The military coup in October 2021 paused all programmes operating through the Government of Sudan (GoS), leaving $438m in unspent donor funds. Conflict and insecurity limit access to rural areas, and the economic crisis exacerbates food insecurity and humanitarian needs. The lack of reliable economic data (e.g., no household survey since 2012) complicates targeting and implementation.

quote.text: In October 2021, a military coup took place. The WB triggered its OP7.30 policy for engagement with de facto authorities and paused all programmes that operated through the GoS leaving $443m unspent donor funds and $354m unspent WB funds at the time of the coup. HIPC progress and the IMF programme stalled.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (a Northern-led multilateral) manages the Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) and oversees implementation, with decision-making power resting with the WB and donor group led by the UK. Local partners (e.g., WFP, UNICEF) implement but do not control fund allocation or strategic direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to Government of Sudan (GoS) on economic reforms and social protection
Strengthening community development committees (CDCs) and local NGOs for service delivery
Training for local staff on cash transfer systems and digital payments
Support for SMEs in agricultural value chains

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (WB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead multilateral partner; manages the Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) and oversees programme implementation

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for cash/food transfers (Phases 1 and 2); delivers transfers to 1.9 million people

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for Phase 2 (basic services component); selected for delivery capacity

partner_organizations.name: Government of Sudan (GoS)
partner_organizations.role: Original programme owner (pre-coup); intended to resume control post-transition

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs and Community-Based Organisations (CBOs)
partner_organizations.role: Sub-contracted for service delivery and community engagement; empowered to select local priorities

partner_organizations.name: Community Development Committees (CDCs)
partner_organizations.role: Local groups empowered to prioritise basic services and resilience projects

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Lead donor; provides £80m and sets strategic direction for the Trust Fund

partner_organizations.name: EU, Germany, France, Sweden
partner_organizations.role: Co-donors to the Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF)

quote.text: WB will contract third parties to deliver the programme because it cannot work with the de facto GoS. WB has reviewed the entities working in the humanitarian and resilience sectors in Sudan and assessed that UNICEF is best placed to deliver component 1 and WFP to deliver component 2.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK contributes £80m to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF), which pools donor resources for the Sudan Family Support Programme (SFSP). The MDTF provides fiduciary oversight and disburses funds to implementing partners (e.g., WFP, UNICEF) via contracts. Post-coup, funds were repurposed through direct awards to multilateral agencies.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank manages the MDTF and oversees implementation through contracted partners (WFP, UNICEF). The UK leads donor coordination and strategic direction, while local NGOs and CDCs deliver services on the ground. Post-coup, the WB directly contracts UN agencies to bypass the de facto government.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank reviewed entities working in Sudan and selected UNICEF and WFP based on implementation capacity, local footprint, and experience. The selection prioritised agencies that could deliver quickly in a high-risk environment and transfer capacity to local partners.

quote.text: WB has reviewed the entities working in the humanitarian and resilience sectors in Sudan and assessed that UNICEF is best placed to deliver component 1 and WFP to deliver component 2. The agencies will be required to sub-contract NGOs (with a strong focus on Sudanese NGOs), community-based organisations (CBOs) and a Sudanese financial intermediary to deliver the programme.

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: The World Bank allocates funds to UNICEF/WFP via contracts, which then sub-contract local NGOs/CBOs. The WB retains oversight over sub-contracting, capacity building, and performance evaluation.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The UK leads a donor group that sets strategic direction for the Trust Fund. The World Bank manages day-to-day operations and reports to donors annually. Post-coup, the WB established a flat hierarchy with direct lines to sub-contracted NGOs to ensure compliance with standards.

quote.text: WB will have oversight over the sub-contracting of the entities, the capacity building done with them, performance evaluation, and will ensure strict compliance with WB standards. WB has established selection criteria to ensure that sub-contractors have the capacity to deliver and are working in Sudan.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds were repurposed post-coup from cash transfers to emergency food aid (Phase 1) and then to resilience-building (Phase 2/3). However, reallocation requires donor approval and WB Board sign-off, particularly for major shifts like the Community Development Fund (CDF).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme adapted to the coup by repurposing funds from economic stabilisation to humanitarian/resilience goals. Phase 2 (SRSNP) adjusted targeting to focus on IDPs and host communities, and Phase 3 will scale successful elements based on learning. However, changes require WB/donor agreement.

quote.text: The original business case anticipated a short-term cash transfer programme to support economic stabilisation during a period of economic reform... The repurposed programme will continue to provide cash transfers, but to a more targeted population and for a longer period of time to build resilience and reduce those classified as in need on the IPC scale.
quote.source: D0002874.odt, Key changes to the original business case

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (MDTF manager) → UNICEF/WFP (implementers) → Local NGOs/CBOs (sub-contractors).

quote.text: We anticipate three disbursements: £40m in Q3 2020/21; £20m in Q4 2020/21 and £20m in Q1 2021/22... Payment will be made on a no-regrets basis and not in advance of need.
quote.source: D0002872.odt, Table One – Disbursement Schedule and Milestones

q24_alternatives_considered.option: UK contribution to SFSP via World Food Programme (WFP) ‘wheat swap’
q24_alternatives_considered.description: WFP would sell imported wheat to the GoS at a discounted exchange rate, freeing up foreign exchange for cash transfers. This was assessed as less scalable and lacking the technical assistance provided by the WB MDTF.
Rejected due to Sudan’s debt arrears and inability to access IFI finance, as well as high fiduciary risks.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank MDTF was selected because it (1) pools donor funds for scale, (2) provides fiduciary oversight to mitigate corruption risks, (3) enables rapid disbursement to support IMF reforms, and (4) leverages WB’s technical expertise in social protection. The UK’s leadership in the donor group also helped mobilise additional funding (e.g., WB’s $400m Pre-Arrears Clearance Grants).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (pooling funds for scale)
partner capacity (WB’s technical expertise in cash transfers)
speed (urgent need to support IMF reforms)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary and fraud risks due to weak GoS systems and large-scale cash transfers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: WB MDTF provides fiduciary controls, third-party monitoring, and electronic systems to track disbursements. Capacity building for GoS and local partners is embedded.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation delays due to complex registration and payment systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased rollout starting with states having existing capacity (Khartoum, Red Sea). Use of mobile payments and existing social protection databases (NCR).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Social tensions from exclusion of non-beneficiaries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strategic communications campaign (via FCDO’s SSGP programme) to explain limited duration and targeting criteria. Community-based targeting groups involved in beneficiary selection.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market distortions from cash injections in fragile areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeting areas with functioning food markets; monitoring by WB and WFP to adjust transfer values quarterly based on inflation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Post-coup pause in programme delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Repurposing funds to WFP for emergency food/cash transfers, with flexibility to revert to original objectives if civilian government is restored.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (pooling funds to reduce transaction costs)
efficiency (leveraging WB’s existing systems for rapid scale-up)
effectiveness (targeting 25.9m people to mitigate reform shocks)

quote.text: Option 1 – A UK contribution to the Sudan Family Support Programme (SFSP) via the World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (STARS) – is the preferred option... Pooled support will help deliver cash transfers at scale and providing SEIR funds via STARS will help mobilise support from other donors, both delivering enhanced value for money.
quote.source: D0002872.odt, Table Two - Multi-Criteria Analysis of SEIR Options

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Sudan constrained partner selection to multilaterals (WB, WFP, UNICEF) due to: (1) GoS’s inclusion on the US State Sponsor of Terrorism list, which prevented direct US funding; (2) the military coup, which required bypassing de facto authorities; and (3) weak local institutional capacity, necessitating reliance on international agencies for fiduciary oversight and delivery.
q27_constraints_detail: US SST list limits direct funding to GoS, favouring multilaterals
Post-coup WB policy (OP7.30) pauses GoS-led programmes, requiring repurposing via UN agencies
Limited local NGO capacity necessitates sub-contracting under UNICEF/WFP
Conflict and insecurity restrict operations to 5 ‘safe’ states in Phase 2
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid, large-scale cash transfers to mitigate economic shocks (WHAT) determined the choice of a multilateral fund manager (WB MDTF) and implementing partners with existing systems (WFP/UNICEF). The shift from economic stabilisation to resilience-building post-coup (WHAT) led to a more localised, community-driven delivery structure (HOW) via CDCs and NGOs.
q28_linkages: Large-scale cash transfers (WHAT) → WB MDTF for fiduciary oversight and pooling (HOW)
Urgent timeline (WHAT) → Pre-existing WFP systems for rapid rollout (HOW)
Post-coup humanitarian focus (WHAT) → Shift to UNICEF/WFP implementation (HOW)
Resilience-building (WHAT) → Empowerment of CDCs and local NGOs (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between rapid delivery (efficiency) and inclusive targeting (equity). For example: (1) Phased rollout prioritised states with existing capacity (efficiency) but risked excluding needy areas; (2) Community-based targeting (equity) slowed implementation compared to centralised approaches; (3) Post-coup, the shift to WFP (efficiency) reduced local ownership but ensured continuity.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Initial SFSP rollout targeted 4 states with existing capacity (80% coverage) for speed, delaying expansion to other high-need areas.
WB/WFP-led implementation ensured scale but limited GoS/local NGO control, especially post-coup.
Uniform cash transfer values ($5/month) simplified delivery but did not account for local price variations until quarterly inflation adjustments were introduced.
Reliance on WB/UNICEF for fiduciary oversight (Northern) constrained opportunities to build GoS systems (Southern) until post-transition.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context led to intensive oversight (e.g., WB’s direct contracts with NGOs, embedded safeguarding advisors, and quarterly inflation adjustments). The coup triggered a shift from light-touch (pre-coup GoS implementation) to intensive management (WB-led repurposing with flat hierarchies).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme’s adaptive design: (1) Pre-coup, technical assistance to GoS aimed to transition ownership of the cash transfer system; (2) Post-coup, CDCs and local NGOs are empowered to prioritise services, with UNICEF/WFP providing capacity support; (3) The Community Development Fund (CDF) is designed to eventually transfer to GoS, contingent on restored civilian rule and demonstrated capacity.

quote.text: The WB will contract third parties to deliver the programme because it cannot work with the de facto GoS... The intention is that the programme is locally delivered as soon as possible and should include local government when the context allows.

key_programme_risks.risk: Economic collapse if reforms fail
key_programme_risks.description: Failure to implement IMF reforms could lead to state collapse, increased humanitarian need, and regional instability.

key_programme_risks.risk: Social unrest from subsidy removal
key_programme_risks.description: Fuel subsidy reforms are politically contentious and risk public backlash, as seen in 2013 civil unrest.

key_programme_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in cash transfers
key_programme_risks.description: Large-scale transfers in a weak institutional environment risk fraud, leakage, and misuse.

key_programme_risks.risk: Implementation delays
key_programme_risks.description: Complex registration and payment systems in remote areas could slow rollout.

key_programme_risks.risk: Market distortions
key_programme_risks.description: Cash injections could inflate local prices or attract predatory violence in conflict zones.

key_programme_risks.risk: Exclusion errors
key_programme_risks.description: Targeting may miss vulnerable groups or create tensions between beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries.

key_programme_risks.risk: Political instability
key_programme_risks.description: Coup and ongoing conflict disrupt programme delivery and HIPC progress.

key_programme_risks.risk: Low digital literacy
key_programme_risks.description: Limits uptake of mobile money transfers, especially in rural areas.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: WB MDTF provides fiduciary controls, third-party monitoring, and electronic confirmation systems. Capacity building for GoS and local partners is embedded.
Phased rollout starting with states having existing capacity (Khartoum, Red Sea). Use of mobile payments and existing social protection databases (NCR).
Strategic communications campaign (via FCDO’s SSGP programme) to explain limited duration and targeting criteria. Community-based targeting groups involved in beneficiary selection.
Targeting areas with functioning food markets; monitoring by WB and WFP to adjust transfer values quarterly based on inflation.
Repurposing funds to WFP for emergency food/cash transfers, with flexibility to revert to original objectives if civilian government is restored.
Phase 2 (SRSNP) includes technical assistance to improve digital literacy and network access in rural areas.

fcas_specific_lessons.lesson: Flexible design is critical in FCAS
fcas_specific_lessons.detail: The ability to repurpose funds post-coup (from economic stabilisation to humanitarian aid) ensured continuity. The original MDTF structure allowed rapid reallocation to WFP.

fcas_specific_lessons.lesson: Local ownership must be balanced with fiduciary controls
fcas_specific_lessons.detail: Empowering CDCs to prioritise services (Phase 2) improved relevance but required intensive WB oversight to mitigate corruption risks.
Phase 2 design explicitly avoids areas of active conflict and includes safeguards to prevent programme resources from fuelling tensions (e.g., balancing host/IDP benefits).
Linking subsidy reforms to past structural adjustment failures (1980s) required tailored messaging to maintain public trust in the CLTG.

fcas_specific_lessons.lesson: Parallel systems are needed for continuity
fcas_specific_lessons.detail: Post-coup, the shift from GoS to UNICEF/WFP implementation required pre-existing relationships and rapid contract adjustments.

from_phase1.lesson: Community-based targeting groups need stricter guidance
from_phase1.detail: Phase 1 grievances over beneficiary selection led to clearer WB rules for Phase 2, including third-party monitoring.

from_phase1.lesson: Mobile money uptake requires infrastructure support
from_phase1.detail: Only 6% enrolment in Phase 1 (vs 10% target) due to digital literacy and network issues; Phase 2 includes technical assistance for rural areas.

from_phase1.lesson: Food transfers are needed where markets fail
from_phase1.detail: Phase 1 shifted to food aid in areas without functioning markets, informing Phase 2’s dual cash/food approach.

from_similar_programmes.detail: MENA region case studies showed that cash transfers (e.g., Egypt, Jordan) improved public acceptance of fuel subsidy cuts.
Lessons from Indonesia and India highlighted the importance of piloting and gradual scale-up to manage shocks.

from_similar_programmes.lesson: Cash transfers can build social cohesion
from_similar_programmes.detail: Evidence from Brazil and the Philippines demonstrated that transfers strengthen government legitimacy if paired with communications.

design_changes_based_on_learning.change: Shift from GoS to UNICEF/WFP implementation post-coup
design_changes_based_on_learning.detail: Enabled continuity despite WB’s OP7.30 policy pause on de facto authorities.

design_changes_based_on_learning.change: Introduction of Community Development Committees (CDCs) in Phase 2
design_changes_based_on_learning.detail: Empowers local prioritisation of services, addressing Phase 1 grievances over top-down targeting.
Phase 2 provides food aid in market-failed areas, based on Phase 1’s adaptive shifts.

design_changes_based_on_learning.change: Longer-term resilience focus (2 years vs 6 months)
design_changes_based_on_learning.detail: Extends support duration to build self-reliance, informed by Phase 1’s short-term limitations.
Tests community asset-building (e.g., water conservation) to reduce humanitarian dependency, adding to unconditional transfers.
Phase 2 includes measures to avoid exacerbating host/IDP tensions, e.g., balanced beneficiary selection.

quote.text: The performance of WFP was assessed by WB as moderately satisfactory. Rollout is proceeding faster than planned but WB guidance on forming community-based targeting groups was not strictly followed and some grievances have arisen over who is and is not a beneficiary. These lessons are being fed into the design of phase 2 and 3 of repurposing.

co_funding_partners.note: Pre-Arrears Clearance Grants (PACG) for SFSP
Donor pledges to SFSP (total $497.5m)

leverage_achieved.description: The UK’s £80m contribution leveraged $400m from the World Bank (PACG) and $497.5m from other donors, totaling $897.5m for the SFSP. The UK’s leadership helped mobilise non-traditional donors (e.g., Germany, France).

quote.text: Current donor pledges and PACGs, including the UK’s pledge of £80m ($100m), should provide sufficient funds for phase 1 and phase 2 of the SFSP providing sufficient funds to stand up the IMF SMP and work towards achieving a HIPC DP in the first half of 2021.

metadata.programme_name: FCDO Centre for Research Commissioning and Coherence of Results, Influence and Identity for FCDO R&D Outputs

quote.text: FCDO will invest up to £25 million over the five-year period to create a new research Commissioning Centre (CC), as the first milestone towards establishing a virtual UK national research centre for development and diplomacy for FCDO.

duration_source.text: FCDO will invest up to £25 million over the five-year period to create a new research Commissioning Centre (CC)...

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes a Commissioning Centre (CC) to streamline FCDO's research commissioning processes, improve efficiency, and enhance the visibility and impact of FCDO-funded research. It combines evidence generation (research), capacity building (strengthening research systems), policy influence (driving evidence into FCDO programming), and a financing mechanism (outsourcing administrative tasks).

q1_source.text: The CC will be implemented through a new operating model based on a strategic partnership between FCDO and the UK academic sector. This will bring FCDO’s approach to commissioning research in line with other research funding government departments and wider UK R&D industry, building on FCDO’s experience and lessons learned from the existing sector-level research models. This will lead to more efficient, faster and nimble processes for sourcing FCDO mission-driven research, responsive to organisational priorities and needs.

q3_expected_outputs: A new centralised research commissioning process aligned with UKRI/NIHR standards
A centralised FCDO R&D platform for results collation and impact communication
A new FCDO R&D brand identity to promote research outputs
Increased visibility of FCDO research outputs (targeting 500 million people in LMICs benefiting from FCDO R&D)
More efficient use of in-house research expertise (shifting from transactional to strategic engagement)
