Flexible technical hub to support high-quality research design
Post-grant funding to maximise impact and support Southern partners with Open Access costs
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform FCDO's research commissioning through a hybrid partnership model, improving efficiency, coherence, and impact while maintaining FCDO's strategic control over research priorities. It seeks to create a 'virtual UK national research centre for development and diplomacy' by outsourcing administrative tasks to a Commissioning Centre while retaining intellectual leadership in-house.

quote.text: The CC will be available to access by any team in RED, and potentially more widely in FCDO seeking to commission new research calls - ODA or non-ODA. The CC will also support Research Department in building FCDO’s research excellence by establishing the specialist functions for i) strategic engagement and uptake; ii) flexible technical hub to support teams with the design of high-quality research calls; and iii) post-grant funding to maximise impact and support Southern-based partners with Open Access costs.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, How this investment will be used to respond to the above challenges?

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as 'moderate' risk overall, with risks managed through regular reviews and a risk register. The context involves complex research environments but no explicit FCAS or high-risk settings are highlighted as primary constraints.

q5_source.text: Considering the current risks and mitigation strategies identified in Annex 5, the programme is classified overall as ‘Moderate’ risk.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Current FCDO research commissioning is described as 'complex' and 'out of step' with UK government standards, creating inefficiencies. Limited visibility of research outputs (43% of non-peer-reviewed outputs unpublished) and weak systems for tracking impact constrain evidence-based decision making. Open access policies require updates to improve data workflows and compliance monitoring.

quote.text: Currently, about 20–30% of RED research budget is delivered through commercial procurement. In contrast, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) funded by the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS), or National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) funded by the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) have been using a two-stage competitive research process (involving peer review and expert panel discussion) to award funding... Although the FCDO direct procurement process is well designed and appropriate for procuring non-research requirements, its complexity puts FCDO out of step with the rest of the research industry standards, making our funding less attractive and accessible, especially for smaller institutions.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, Need to address issues with the current operational model

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains intellectual leadership and strategic control over research priorities, while the Commissioning Centre (likely UK-based academic consortium) manages administrative and operational tasks. Southern partners are supported through post-grant funding but decision-making remains with FCDO/UK partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: post-grant funding to support Southern partners with Open Access costs
incentivising equitable partnerships at local level
engaging beneficiaries and marginalised groups through research process
maintaining 30% target for SME funding (including Southern institutions)

partner_organizations.name: UK academic sector (consortium partner)
partner_organizations.role: Commissioning Centre (CC) lead - managing research calls, peer review, grant administration, and impact communication

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Research & Evidence Directorate (RED)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic oversight, defining research questions, quality assurance, and driving evidence into policy

partner_organizations.name: Southern research institutions
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of research grants and capacity-building support (e.g., Open Access funding)

partner_organizations.name: Existing FCDO thematic platforms (e.g., Climate Compatible Growth, What Works to Prevent Violence)
partner_organizations.role: Alignment with new FCDO R&D brand and communication platform

quote.text: Through a hybrid delivery model FCDO will control the scope of calls and quality of results to ensure full alignment with the mission-driven needs of FCDO. FCDO have a number of successful examples of this type of approach based on a partnership with academia in different sectors... This model will build on the existing capacity and resources offered by a potential partner/consortium, avoiding creating a parallel system and infrastructure whilst reducing a number of research projects directly procured and managed by FCDO.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a hybrid model: (1) A **partnership agreement** between FCDO and a UK academic consortium to establish the Commissioning Centre (CC), and (2) **grants** for downstream research projects commissioned through the CC. The CC itself is funded via FCDO’s capital budget, while research calls (ODA/non-ODA) are disbursed as grants to implementers.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **Commissioning Centre (CC)** acts as an intermediary platform between FCDO and researchers. FCDO retains strategic control (defining research questions, quality assurance) while the CC manages operational tasks (call design, peer review, grant administration, impact tracking). The structure mirrors the NIHR model, with a central hub coordinating multiple research calls.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The hybrid partnership model was chosen to leverage existing academic capacity and avoid creating parallel systems. The selection process for the CC lead will likely follow open competition (as per UKRI/NIHR standards), though the document does not specify the ratio. The rationale emphasizes aligning with industry standards and maximizing value for money by outsourcing administrative tasks while retaining FCDO’s strategic role.

quote.text: As the final option, we have considered forming a mutually-benefiting partnership (with an external like-minded organisation or a consortium of organisations, to create a blend of in-house and outsourced delivery that will optimise RED’s resources and lead to the increased research outcomes. The advantages of the partnership will come from (i) drawing on existing knowledge, expertise, networks; and infrastructure; (ii) sharing values and vision; and (iii) strategic alignment to create opportunities for collaboration and added value.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The governance includes: (1) **FCDO RED** setting strategic priorities and quality-assuring ToRs; (2) **CC Lead** managing operational delivery (calls, peer review, grants); (3) **Joint FCDO/CC panels** for proposal selection; and (4) **Strategy Board** for oversight. The model explicitly references NIHR’s governance structure, suggesting a technical advisory group and regular progress reviews.

quote.text: FCDO will retain intellectual leadership, strategic engagement across FCDO teams and control over quality and technical aspects of commissioning such as defining questions and research approaches. This will release FCDO’s vital internal research capacity to focus on strategic engagement, driving evidence into practice and shaping research priorities... The CC will manage the commissioning process: call for proposals; answering questions; review panels to assess applications; and providing feedback to applicants.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, How this investment will be used to respond to the above challenges?

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research calls within the CC’s portfolio, but major shifts require FCDO approval. The model is designed for scalability (ODA/non-ODA calls) and adaptive management, with a ‘steady pipeline of projects’ to ensure responsiveness to FCDO priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted through the CC’s flexible technical hub, which supports rapid design of new calls. However, strategic shifts (e.g., major thematic changes) require FCDO sign-off. The model emphasizes ‘nimble processes’ responsive to organisational needs, with annual reviews to test assumptions.

quote.text: A more coordinated and centralised approach to our research portfolio (including ODA and non-ODA investments), in place of many individually managed research calls... will drive key learning and findings from rigorous FCDO research in a coherent manner... Implementation of both ODA and non-ODA investments will maximise opportunities to meet wider RED, FCDO and UK objectives—domestically and internationally.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, What improvements will be delivered by the CC?

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Commissioning Centre (CC) → End researchers/implementers. The CC acts as a single intermediary layer, reducing bureaucracy compared to current multi-contract models.

quote.text: The CC will move to a scale and sustain phase funded via a standard menu of charges... The initial pipeline of projects will be used during a proof of concept phase to test and develop a new approach to commissioning research.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, How this investment will be used to respond to the above challenges?

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Develop a new commissioning model for all FCDO RED-funded research
q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: High risk; would dismantle existing high-impact partnerships and disrupt delivery.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Build a new in-house Commissioning Centre from scratch
q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: Inflexible, costly (requires significant staffing increases), and misaligned with public sector trends toward outsourcing.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Outsource CC as an independent autonomous research body
q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: Loses FCDO control over mission-driven priorities and brand influence; risks contracting out a strategic UK government agenda.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Outsource CC as a commercial Fund Manager
q24_alternatives_considered.rejection_reason: Lacks academic expertise; would require subcontracting, increasing costs and reducing alignment with FCDO’s technical needs.

q24_alternatives_considered.rationale: Balances FCDO control with academic expertise; builds on existing capacity (e.g., NIHR model); avoids parallel systems; and enables scalable, flexible research commissioning.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid partnership model was selected to: (1) **align with UK government R&D standards** (UKRI/NIHR processes), (2) **leverage existing academic infrastructure** (avoiding duplication), (3) **retain FCDO strategic control** over research priorities, (4) **improve efficiency** by outsourcing administrative tasks, and (5) **enhance flexibility** to respond to changing FCDO needs. The model addresses bureaucratic inefficiencies in current procurement while maintaining mission-driven research.
q25_decision_factors: past experience (successful academic partnerships like Covid Collective)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependency on external partner for research calls
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO retains intellectual leadership and quality assurance; annual reviews to test partnership effectiveness.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of direct control over operational details
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear separation of roles: FCDO sets strategic parameters, CC manages administration; regular progress reporting.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential misalignment with FCDO’s evolving priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible technical hub and adaptive management processes to adjust research questions; steady pipeline of projects.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (improved research quality and policy impact)
equity (30% SME target, Southern partner support)

quote.text: Through a hybrid delivery model FCDO will control the scope of calls and quality of results to ensure full alignment with the mission-driven needs of FCDO... This model will build on the existing capacity and resources offered by a potential partner/consortium, avoiding creating a parallel system and infrastructure whilst reducing a number of research projects directly procured and managed by FCDO... Delivering research through a strategic partnership will also enable FCDO to build new brand over a longer period of time, in a flexible and sustainable way.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope** and **moderate-risk context** constrain partner selection to organizations with: (1) **UKRI/NIHR-aligned processes** (to meet FCDO’s need for industry-standard commissioning), (2) **existing academic infrastructure** (to avoid building parallel systems), and (3) **capacity for Open Access compliance** (addressing data visibility constraints). The requirement for **rapid, flexible research** (post-COVID recovery) favors partners with proven agile grant management (e.g., Covid Collective).
q27_constraints_detail: Need for UKRI/NIHR-aligned partners (to address bureaucratic inefficiencies)
Open Access policy gaps limit Southern partner eligibility unless supported by CC
Global scope requires partners with multi-regional networks (e.g., existing FCDO thematic platforms)
Moderate risk profile permits hybrid models but excludes high-risk FCAS specialists
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (evidence generation + policy influence + capacity building) determine the **hybrid delivery structure**: (1) **Policy influence** requires FCDO’s retained strategic control; (2) **Efficiency needs** drive outsourcing of administrative tasks to the CC; (3) **Capacity building** embeds Southern partner support (Open Access funding) into the CC’s role; (4) **Flexibility for ODA/non-ODA** necessitates a scalable platform model.

q28_linkages.how: Two-stage competitive calls (peer review + expert panels) via CC, mirroring UKRI/NIHR

q28_linkages.objective: Policy influence (driving evidence into FCDO programming)
q28_linkages.how: FCDO retains intellectual leadership; CC includes strategic engagement functions
Post-grant Open Access funding and 30% SME target embedded in CC operations
Outsourcing administrative tasks to CC reduces FCDO transactional workload

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid commissioning (post-COVID) risks sidelining smaller/Southern institutions without targeted support (mitigated by 30% SME target and Open Access funding). (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led CC ensures UKRI standards but requires proactive measures (equitable partnership principles, Southern engagement strategies) to avoid marginalizing LMIC researchers. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Centralised platform improves efficiency but may limit tailored support for niche research areas (addressed via flexible technical hub).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Speed of commissioning (efficient processes) vs. Southern inclusion
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: 30% SME funding target and post-grant Open Access support for Southern partners

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: UKRI-aligned expertise (Northern partners) vs. LMIC ownership
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Equitable partnership principles and beneficiary engagement requirements in CC operations

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Standardised processes (cost-efficient) vs. tailored research support
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Flexible technical hub to adapt to diverse research needs

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** enables **milestone-based oversight** (not intensive) with annual reviews, while still requiring robust due diligence (e.g., counter-terrorist financing checks for fragile contexts). The hybrid model balances risk by retaining FCDO control over strategic decisions while outsourcing operational risks to the CC.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: (1) **Embedding Southern support** into the CC’s core functions (Open Access funding, equitable partnerships); (2) **Requiring 30% SME allocation**, ensuring Southern institutions are direct beneficiaries; (3) **Incentivising local engagement** through CC’s dissemination strategies. However, decision-making remains Northern-led, reflecting a **‘capacity-building within constraints’** approach.

quote.text: The CC will incentivise opportunities for equitable partnerships at local level, where research takes place whilst ensuring beneficiaries and most marginalised groups are engaged through every step of the research process... RED’s current level of directly contracted funding to Small and Medium Enterprises for research projects is 30% and the CC will be expected at minimum to maintain this target for the CC portfolio.

key_programme_risks: Dependency on CC partner for operational delivery
Loss of direct FCDO control over research administration
Insufficient demand from FCDO teams to sustain CC
Ineffective proposal selection or funding disbursement
Failure of due diligence model (e.g., safeguarding, counter-terrorism)
Limited capacity to drive lessons learned and research uptake
Weak central guidance on research standards
Data accessibility constraints (Open Access policy gaps)
Structural inequalities in global research (Southern citation gaps)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO retains intellectual leadership; annual reviews to test partnership effectiveness; clear separation of strategic vs. operational roles.
Proof-of-concept phase with initial project pipeline; strategic communication to secure buy-in.
CC conducts checks per FCDO standards; regular risk reporting to FCDO.
CC includes strategic uptake functions; FCDO drives internal capacity-building for evidence use.
CC supports Southern partners with Open Access costs; incremental improvements to data workflows.

fcas_specific_lessons: When operating in fragile contexts, CC must coordinate with FCDO Posts to align with risk appetite and ensure robust financial management (e.g., counter-terrorist financing checks).
Research in FCAS requires adaptive management (e.g., flexible technical hub) to respond to changing security/political conditions.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **Covid Collective** demonstrated the effectiveness of grant mechanisms for rapid, Southern-inclusive research calls. **DFID-ESRC Joint Fund** showed that project-based capacity building alone cannot compensate for structural inequalities in global research (e.g., Southern citation gaps). **NIHR model** provided a template for balancing centralised commissioning with thematic flexibility.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Adopted **two-stage competitive process** (like UKRI/NIHR) to replace complex procurement, improving accessibility for smaller institutions.
Embedded **post-grant Open Access funding** to address DFID’s historical gaps in non-peer-reviewed output visibility.
Included **30% SME funding target** (matching RED’s current level) to mitigate exclusion of Southern/LMIC partners.
Added **flexible technical hub** to support ‘right-sized’ projects, addressing critiques of oversized contracts in RED’s portfolio.
Centralised **impact communication platform** to collate dispersed research outputs (lesson from ICAI’s critique of DFID’s learning systems).

quote.text: The evidence from the FCDO-funded Development and Economic Growth Research Programme completion report... demonstrated that FCDO has limited capacity to support researchers with strategic communications of their research findings or track the extent to which the programme’s research is making a difference to policy and practice... Therefore, in order to deliver outcomes more quickly and accelerate development progress, FCDO will need to reduce its bureaucracy to drive innovation and increase responsiveness to changes in the context.
quote.source: D0003696.odt, Need to support post-Covid recovery

capital_vs_revenue_split.text: Of the £25m total, £20m is earmarked for new research calls (including up to £3m for non-ODA), suggesting ~80% direct delivery costs. The remaining £5m likely covers CC setup/management (20%).

quote.text: Programme Value: £25m, of which £20m to be disbursed for new research calls, including up to £3m on non-ODA.

metadata.programme_name: Hygiene and Behaviour Change Coalition for COVID-19 Control (HBCC)
metadata.quote: "The HBCC brings together DFID funding, Unilever’s unique developing country commercial expertise and market presence, LSHTM’s world leading technical/academic expertise, and a range of capable NGOs and UN organisations to promote hygiene behaviour change, focusing on vulnerable populations in low and middle income countries." (58198409.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: April 2020–March 2022 (includes extension from December 2021–March 2022)" and "New project end date (if applicable): March 2023" (90000810.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The HBCC is a public-private partnership that combines service delivery (direct provision of hygiene products and handwashing stations), implementation research (testing and scaling behaviour change interventions), and capacity building (training staff and strengthening local systems). It also includes evidence generation through the Hygiene Hub and research on urban WASH.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The HBCC brings together DFID funding, Unilever’s unique developing country commercial expertise and market presence, LSHTM’s world leading technical/academic expertise, and a range of capable NGOs and UN organisations to promote hygiene behaviour change..." and "The programme will also be providing soap, handwashing stations, surface cleaner (i.e. bleach), and other appropriate hygiene supplies." (58198409.odt, Programme summary and "Theory of change")
q3_expected_outputs: 1.2 billion people reached with hygiene behaviour change communication (Phase 1)
150 million people reached with social and behaviour change messages (extension phase)
20+ million hygiene products donated (soap, hand sanitiser, surface cleaner)
Handwashing stations and surface cleaners provided to healthcare facilities and schools
Staff trained to deliver COVID-19 preventive measures
Hygiene Hub established as a global resource (234 technical enquiries answered, 176,721 website views)
Research outputs on urban WASH and vaccine hesitancy
COVID-19 response integrated into national hygiene and behaviour change communication plans
Legacy for future pandemic preparedness and sustainable public health promotion
what_objectives.summary: The HBCC aims to reduce COVID-19 transmission in LMICs through mass hygiene behaviour change campaigns, direct provision of hygiene products, and research to inform policy. It combines Unilever's commercial reach, LSHTM's technical expertise, and NGO/UN implementation capacity to deliver both immediate pandemic response and long-term system strengthening.
what_objectives.quote: "The intended impact of this programme is to reduce the spread of COVID-19, by reducing the infection rate, and, therefore, the burden of cases and deaths around the globe... the intended outcomes for the programme are increased practice of frequent and correct handwashing, as well as increased number of healthcare facilities complying with infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols." (58198409.odt, Theory of change)

countries_regions: Specific focus countries: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Somalia, Uganda, Yemen, Mozambique, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Zimbabwe, India, Indonesia, Philippines, South Africa, Vietnam (extension phase)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The original business case explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (58198409.odt). The extension focuses on fragile contexts (e.g., Afghanistan, Somalia, Yemen) and pandemic hotspots, but no updated risk rating is provided.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (58198409.odt, Summary Sheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: high population density (urban slums, refugee camps)
limited access to handwashing facilities (3 billion people globally lack access)
language barriers (requirement for translation into multiple languages/dialects)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and limited infrastructure (e.g., 43% of healthcare facilities lack hygiene facilities) directly hinder service delivery. Conflict zones require specialized partners with humanitarian access. High density and mobility in urban/informal settlements increase transmission risks, demanding tailored messaging. Language diversity necessitates extensive translation efforts, delaying rollout.
where_context.quote: "The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) estimates that 3 billion people (2 out of 5 worldwide) lack access to functioning handwashing facilities with the soap and water necessary to practice safe hand hygiene... Additionally, estimates suggest that 43% of healthcare facilities and 36% of schools lack hygiene facilities" (58198409.odt, Hygiene practices in low- and middle-income countries)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Unilever (UK-based) leads day-to-day programme management, partner selection, and budget disbursement through Crown Agents. FCDO retains oversight via the Management Team and approval rights for major decisions. Southern partners (NGOs/UN) implement activities but have limited strategic decision-making authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for staff to deliver COVID-19 preventive measures
technical support to HBCC partners via LSHTM’s Hygiene Hub (234 enquiries answered)
knowledge transfer to local partners and governments
research capacity building through COVID Action Co-Labs
behavioural science training for sustainable hygiene promotion

partner_organizations.role: Programme secretariat, in-kind contributor (products/media/expertise), day-to-day management

partner_organizations.name: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
partner_organizations.role: Technical adviser, Hygiene Hub management, research/evidence generation

partner_organizations.role: Fund manager (disbursements to third parties)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partner (coordination of WASH in schools/healthcare facilities, emergency response)

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partner (refugee contexts)

partner_organizations.name: NGOs (e.g., BRAC, Behavioural Insights Team)
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation of behaviour change interventions

partner_organizations.name: Results for Development (R4D) / Frontier Tech Hub
partner_organizations.role: COVID Action Co-Labs (oxygen/vaccine data innovation)

partner_organizations.role: Policy integration and coordination

who_partners.quote: "Unilever will be responsible for the financial and progress reporting for the Programme, as well as creating the budgets for approval by Unilever and DFID... The Management Team will include Unilever (3+ reps), DFID (2+ reps), LSHTM (1 rep)." (58198409.odt, Governance and management arrangements)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The core instrument is a **collaboration agreement** between FCDO and Unilever, supplemented by: (1) **accountable grants** to LSHTM and R4D; (2) **MoUs** with UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF); and (3) **sub-contracts** to NGOs via Unilever. Crown Agents Bank acts as the financial intermediary, holding and disbursing funds to third parties.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Unilever acts as the **secretariat**, managing day-to-day operations, partner contracts, and budget disbursements (via Crown Agents). A **Management Team** (Unilever, FCDO, LSHTM) provides strategic oversight. Implementing partners (NGOs/UN) deliver activities on the ground. LSHTM and COVID Action provide technical/research support. The structure is **open** to additional donors but centrally coordinated.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Phase 1: restricted competition (existing DFID/Unilever partners); Phase 2: open call to UK WASH NGO network
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Phase 1 prioritized **speed** by leveraging existing relationships with proven partners (e.g., UNICEF, NGOs with WASH experience). Phase 2 used an **open call** to address gaps (geographic/thematic) identified in Phase 1. Selection criteria included: in-country presence, cost-effectiveness, ability to reach vulnerable groups, and evidence-based theories of change.
how_mechanism.quote: "Phase 1–Given the urgency of response required, Phase 1 entailed mobilising existing DFID/Unilever relationships to elicit proposals from implementing partners with the known capacity and credibility to respond to such pandemics in LMICs at speed and scale... Phase 2–Following the completion of the contracting process for Phase 1, Phase 2 comprised an open-call to the UK WASH NGO network." (90000810.odt, Disbursement arrangements)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Management Team** (3+ Unilever reps, 2+ FCDO reps, 1 LSHTM rep) provides oversight, approves budgets, and ensures portfolio balance. Unilever leads operational decisions (e.g., contractor selection, milestone approvals) but requires FCDO sign-off for major expenditures. Technical advisory support is provided by LSHTM and COVID Action.
how_governance.quote: "The objective of the programme’s governing body (Management Team) is to: Provide overall oversight of the programme, including budget, spend and portfolio; Ensure the portfolio of projects is well balanced (i.e., needs, geography); Ensure project selection guidelines are followed and funded projects meet agreed criteria." (58198409.odt, Governance and management arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between **geographic areas** and **thematic focuses** (e.g., shifting from mass media to community-based interventions) with Management Team approval. The extension phase explicitly reprioritized countries based on Omicron transmission risks. However, major structural changes (e.g., adding new partners) require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **real-time adaptive management**: (1) LSHTM’s Hygiene Hub provides **ongoing epidemiological updates** to adjust messaging; (2) **formative research** informs campaign iterations (e.g., emotional appeals, trusted messengers); (3) **quarterly reviews** allow pivoting based on performance data; (4) COVID Action Co-Labs test innovations (e.g., oxygen delivery models) iteratively. The extension phase explicitly builds on lessons from Phase 1 to refine targeting and channels.
how_flexibility.quote: "Formativeresearch, active learning and adaptive programming allowed partners to adapt behaviour change communication to the evolving epidemiological contexts, tailor messages to evolving norms and behaviours as the pandemic progressed, and to the specific needs of marginalised and vulnerable groups and people with disability." (90000810.odt, Monitoring and evaluation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Unilever (secretariat) + Crown Agents (fund manager) → Implementing Partners (NGOs/UN) → [End beneficiaries]. LSHTM and COVID Action provide parallel technical support.
how_efficiency.quote: "Once a milestone has been achieved by a third party they will invoice Crown Agents for payment. Unilever and DFID will authorize Crown Agents to make payment." (58198409.odt, Financial risk management)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (counterfactual)
Option 2: Supplementary funding to UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF, UNHCR, WHO)
Option 3: Hybrid approach (channelling funds via existing programmes like TRANSFORM)
Option 4: The Hygiene and Behaviour Change Coalition (HBCC) (selected)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The HBCC was selected for its **unparalleled speed, scale, and value for money**, leveraging: (1) **existing partnerships** (Unilever/DFID’s TRANSFORM programme reduced startup time); (2) **private sector match** (£50m in-kind from Unilever, doubling FCDO’s £50m); (3) **global reach** (Unilever’s commercial networks + NGO/UN presence in 37 countries); (4) **adaptive design** (LSHTM’s real-time technical guidance); and (5) **risk mitigation** (Crown Agents as fiduciary intermediary). The platform model allowed rapid disbursement while maintaining FCDO oversight.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (£0.05 per person reached in Phase 1)
partner capacity (Unilever’s behaviour change expertise + LSHTM’s technical rigor)
risk mitigation (Crown Agents as trusted intermediary)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from partnership with a multinational corporation (Unilever)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Collaboration agreement ensures no DFID funds pass to Unilever; Crown Agents manages disbursements; clauses highlight compliance with Terrorism Act 2000.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risk with rapid disbursements to new partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds held by Crown Agents; robust due diligence on all suppliers; zero-tolerance approach to fraud with annual audits.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication of efforts across mass media/digital channels
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Unilever’s media help desk coordinates campaigns to avoid overlap; HBCC-branded umbrella campaign ensures consistency.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on Unilever’s systems for programme management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: DFID programme manager embedded in Management Team; quarterly reviews and annual audits.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (behaviour change linked to reduced transmission)
equity (targeting vulnerable groups, e.g., refugees, people with disabilities)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 4: The Hygiene and Behaviour Change Coalition (HBCC) was quickly identified as the preferred response... This option takes DFID’s existing strategic partnership with Unilever and Unilever’s existing handwashing programmes as a blueprint for a new programme, specific to the COVID-19 response efforts... The partnership prioritises speed, scale and effectiveness of response." (58198409.odt, Summary of available options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **fragile contexts** (e.g., Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan) and **high-density urban settings** (e.g., informal settlements in Nairobi) necessitated partners with **specialized humanitarian access** and **local trust**. For example: (1) UNHCR was essential for refugee camps; (2) NGOs with existing community relationships (e.g., BRAC in Bangladesh) were prioritized; (3) Language barriers required partners with multilingual capacity (Unilever’s translation of assets into new dialects).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict zones excluded partners without humanitarian experience
Urban slums required partners with community-based approaches (not just mass media)
Limited infrastructure (e.g., no handwashing facilities) demanded partners who could provide physical supplies (e.g., UNICEF for WASH in schools)
Rapidly evolving variants (e.g., Omicron) required partners with adaptive capacity (e.g., LSHTM’s Hygiene Hub for real-time updates)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rapid, large-scale behaviour change** shaped the **platform structure**: (1) **Mass reach** required Unilever’s commercial media networks; (2) **Local adaptation** necessitated open calls to NGOs; (3) **Technical rigor** embedded LSHTM as an advisor; (4) **Supply chain gaps** (e.g., soap shortages) led to Unilever’s product donations. The **mixed funding instruments** (collaboration agreement + grants) reflected the blend of service delivery (UNICEF contracts) and research (LSHTM grants).
q28_linkages: Behaviour change objectives → Unilever’s media expertise + NGO community engagement
Urgency → Pre-existing partner relationships (TRANSFORM programme)
Vulnerable groups → Direct contracts with specialized NGOs (e.g., for refugees)
Research needs → Accountable grants to LSHTM/COVID Action
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions included: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Phase 1 used restricted competition (existing partners) for rapid rollout, risking exclusion of local actors; Phase 2 added open calls to address this. (2) **Scale vs. depth**: Mass media reached billions cheaply (£0.05/person) but required targeted interpersonal communication for marginalized groups (e.g., people with disabilities), increasing costs. (3) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: Unilever’s global campaigns ensured consistency but limited local adaptation until Phase 2’s open call.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Restricted competition (Phase 1) sacrificed some local ownership for speed
Mass media (efficient) vs. community-based (equitable) channels created budget tradeoffs
Unilever’s centralized management (efficient) vs. local NGO flexibility (adaptive)
Standardized messaging (scalable) vs. tailored content for vulnerable groups (inclusive)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (original) and **fragile contexts** (extension) led to **intensive oversight**: (1) Crown Agents as intermediary; (2) quarterly Management Team reviews; (3) embedded FCDO programme manager; (4) annual audits. High-risk countries (e.g., Yemen) triggered additional due diligence for partners.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building was **embedded** in partner roles: (1) NGOs received **technical support** from LSHTM’s Hygiene Hub (e.g., 234 enquiries answered); (2) Local staff were **trained** to deliver interventions (Output 4); (3) COVID Action Co-Labs included **research grants** to Southern institutions; (4) UNICEF’s role expanded to **coordinate WASH in schools/healthcare facilities**, strengthening systemic capacity.
intersections.quote: "The first wave of humanitarian COVID-19 response, the HBCC was rapidly established and is already delivering results in 29 countries... Marginalised groups can be the most difficult to reach with effective behaviour change messaging and may also be the most vulnerable to COVID-19 due to dense living situations, limited access to handwashing facilities, and comorbidities." (58198409.odt, Rationale and Theory of Change)

key_programme_risks: Reputational risk from corporate partnership (Unilever)
Fiduciary risk with rapid disbursements
Duplication of efforts across partners
Over-reliance on Unilever’s systems
Campaign fatigue (waning adherence to hygiene practices)
Supply chain disruptions (soap/sanitizer shortages)
Evolving epidemiological context (new variants like Omicron)
Limited reach in conflict zones (access constraints)
Language barriers in multilingual contexts
Sustainability of behaviour change post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Collaboration agreement ensures no DFID funds pass to Unilever; Crown Agents manages disbursements; compliance clauses included.
Funds held by Crown Agents; due diligence on all suppliers; zero-tolerance fraud policy with annual audits.
Unilever’s media help desk coordinates campaigns; HBCC-branded umbrella ensures consistency.
Adaptive management using formative research; emotional/norm-based messaging; trusted community messengers.
Unilever’s global logistics network; pre-positioned stockpiles; local procurement where possible.
LSHTM Hygiene Hub provides real-time technical updates; rapid-burst campaigns for new waves.
Partnerships with UNHCR and NGOs with humanitarian access (e.g., in Syria, Yemen).

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-existing relationships with UN agencies (UNICEF, UNHCR) were critical for rapid deployment in fragile states
Local NGOs with community trust outperformed international actors in conflict zones
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., via Crown Agents) enabled pivoting when access changed
Behaviour change messaging in FCAS required simpler, more visual formats (low literacy)
Supply chains in FCAS needed redundancy (e.g., multiple local distributors)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 lessons informed the extension: (1) **Mass media alone insufficient** → added community-based interventions; (2) **One-size-fits-all messaging failed** → tailored content for vulnerable groups; (3) **Local partners needed more support** → expanded LSHTM’s technical assistance; (4) **Digital divide limited reach** → balanced digital with radio/TV; (5) **Short-term behaviour change unsustainable** → extension focused on systemic capacity (e.g., WASH in schools).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Extension phase adjustments: (1) **Narrowed geographic focus** (12 countries vs. original 37) for depth; (2) **Added vaccine hesitancy** to behaviour change scope; (3) **Strengthened research component** (COVID Action Co-Labs); (4) **Prioritized healthcare facilities/schools** for WASH; (5) **Increased local partner capacity building** via Hygiene Hub.
risks_lessons.quote: "The HBCC programmes scored A++ in its 2021 Annual Review. Recent findings of the LSHTM’s led process evaluation highlighted that combining Unilever’s behaviour change and programme management expertise, with science and evidence-based programming led to strong behaviour change approaches... Delivering high quality mass media and digital hygiene and behaviour change campaigns at scale enhanced understanding of how media and digital innovation can reach people at scale." (90000810.odt, Monitoring and evaluation)

co_funding_partners.partner: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (for Hygiene Hub)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Unilever provided at least £50m in-kind (products, media, expertise), matching FCDO’s £50m cash in Phase 1. The extension phase continues to leverage Unilever’s media/expertise and scales COVID Action’s oxygen/vaccine innovations with industry partners (e.g., Philips).
financial_details.quote: "With additional support, this HBCC extension aims to reach 150 million people with social and behaviour change messages... This £30m extension is split with £20m from the COVID-19/Vaccines allocation managed by Global Health and Covid19 Directorate (GH/C-19), and £10m from Research and Evidence Department." (90000810.odt, Summary Information and Components)

metadata.programme_name: Ethiopia–Human Rights and Peacebuilding Programme (HARP)
metadata.quote: "The Human Rights and Peacebuilding Programme (HARP) was set up in 2021, to contribute to a reduction of violent conflict and help enable the conditions for peaceful political transition in Ethiopia by addressing three of the main dimensions of Ethiopia’s instability: political tensions, inter-communal violence, and human rights violations." (S30119165.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: 01 Jan 2021–31 March 2027" and "HARP is seeking a no-cost time extension from 31 March 2027 to 31 December 2027" (S30119165.odt, Programme summary and Programme amendments)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: HARP combines implementation research (testing/scaling peacebuilding interventions), capacity building (strengthening institutions like the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission), policy influence (informing UK diplomatic and programmatic activities), and service delivery (direct support to GBV survivors and peacebuilding processes). The programme generates evidence through its Conflict Research Facility while simultaneously delivering concrete interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "HARP will provide a platform for doing so [responding to instability] through four interlocking areas of activity delivering a blend of tried-and-tested long-term peacebuilding efforts, and new pilot interventions that will support HMG’s efforts to respond to the urgency of the current situation as well as lay foundations for future work" (D0000847.odt, Overview) and "The four programme components will be adapted to reflect these priorities and the changes in the context...: 1) Reduce violence and support peace processes... 2) Improve accountability for human rights and support transitional justice processes... 3) Promote women peace and security (WPS)... 4) Strengthen conflict related policy and programming" (D0004228.odt, What is the objective of the extension?)
q3_expected_outputs: 45,000 combatants demobilized under Pretoria Agreement implementation (by July 2025)
Increased numbers and quality of political or civic attempts to address violence in Ethiopia (e.g., sustained talks between government and OLA)
25% of EHRC recommendations adopted by public authorities by 2024 (from 10% baseline)
24 annual EHRC statements on human rights concerns published without political restrictions
65% of women and girls in supported areas reporting access to GBV response services (from 20% baseline)
45% of women and girls in WLiE groups actively participating in decision-making spaces (from 10% baseline)
Monthly conflict trends reports and responsive analysis directly informing BE Addis policy positions
Establishment of Ethiopian Women Researchers’ Network (EWNET) as national platform
Support to National Electoral Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) for inclusive elections process
Creation of CSO coalitions for voter education and election observation
Facilitation of inter-political party dialogue platforms
what_objectives.summary: HARP aims to reduce violent conflict and enable peaceful political transition in Ethiopia through a blended approach combining peacebuilding implementation, human rights accountability, GBV response services, and conflict-sensitive research to inform policy. The programme directly supports peace processes (including Pretoria Agreement implementation), strengthens national institutions like EHRC, provides services to GBV survivors, and generates actionable conflict analysis for diplomatic use.
what_objectives.quote: "The Human Rights and Peacebuilding (HARP) programme will support the UK’s strategic response to conflict in Ethiopia... [through] four interlocking areas of activity: 1) Building Peace... 2) Human Rights and Accountability... 3) Addressing GBV... 4) Conflict Research Facility" (D0000847.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia is classified as FCAS due to ongoing armed conflict (Tigray war, Oromia-Amhara violence), extreme human rights abuses documented by international investigations, proliferation of armed militias, and risks of state fragmentation. The 2022 Joint Assessment of Conflict and Stability (JACS) identifies lack of inclusive political settlement, weakening central control, and nationalist mobilizations as primary conflict drivers.
where_context.q5_source: "Ethiopia is witnessing its worst levels of instability for years. The civil war, centred in the northern region of Tigray, has displaced millions, killed thousands... Moreover, it is threatening the integrity of the country as ethnic tensions are markedly increasing" (D0000847.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending) and "The JACS concludes that a new elite bargain is needed to rebalance power between the centre and the regions, and to agree a new allocation of resources and benefits between (and within) the regions" (D0004228.odt, Context analysis)
q6_contextual_constraints: security (ongoing armed conflict in multiple regions)
political economy (contested federalism and elite power struggles)
weak institutions (EHRC lacks capacity for independent investigations)
conflict (active violence in Oromia, Amhara, and border disputes)
climate risks (land degradation in Somali region peacebuilding)
regulatory (potential CSO law changes restricting civic space)
data limitations (patchy information due to telecom blackouts)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit access to conflict zones (e.g., Tigray access 'highly constrained'), political economy tensions create volatile implementation environments where 'both sides try to bolster their positions', weak institutions require capacity building before they can fulfill mandates, and regulatory risks may block CSO funding for election-related activities. Data limitations from telecom blackouts and access restrictions create evidence gaps for monitoring.
where_context.quote: "Telecommunication blackouts and access constraints mean that information is patchy" (D0000847.odt, Background) and "Potential changes in law and policy restricting CSO funding and activities may present a strategic risk to HARP’s ability to contribute to inclusive elections" (S30119165.odt, Civic Space Constraint Risk)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO Ethiopia (BE Addis) with multiple implementing partners
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes co-design and co-leadership with Southern partners, with local organizations determining 'what to deliver and how' (e.g., Women’s Association of Tigray co-leading GBV work, EHRC co-chairing steering committees). Decision-making is shared through structures like the Peace Research Facility’s strategic sharing with local working groups and the programme’s explicit commitment to localization.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to EHRC for investigations
training for EHRC commissioners on mandate areas
peer-to-peer exchanges with other National Human Rights Institutions
support to Somali Regional State’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission
capacity building for women’s organizations to engage in peace processes
mentorship for local researchers through the Peace Research Facility
institutional strengthening of NEBE for election management

partner_organizations.name: Danish Institute for Human Rights (DIHR)

who_partners.quote: "During the first phase, each component was co-designed and/or co-led by local organizations and local actors were funded through consortium leads. Emphasis was placed on ensuring these organisations had voice in determining what to deliver and how, drawing on their local expertise" (D0004228.odt, Localization commitment) and "Women’s Association of Tigray work in partnership with CARE on GBV and DIHR co-chair the funding steering committee with Ethiopian Human Right Commission (EHRC)" (D0004228.odt, Partner examples)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants (for CSOs and local partners), Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with multilateral agencies like UNDP, and direct contracts (e.g., with Rift Valley Institute for the Peace Research Facility). The accountable grants allow flexibility for local adaptation while MoUs enable pooled funding for large-scale components like DDR.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: HARP operates through a hub-and-spoke model where FCDO (BE Addis) provides central oversight while multiple implementing partners (Conciliation Resources, DIHR, CARE, RVI) manage distinct components with significant autonomy. The structure includes direct contracting for research/analysis (RVI), accountable grants for implementation (local CSOs), and MoUs for multilateral channels (UNDP). Partners are expected to collaborate through mechanisms like the Peace Research Facility’s knowledge-sharing platforms.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (direct awards to existing partners with proven track records)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships and comparative advantage: Conciliation Resources for their legacy peacebuilding work in Somali Region, DIHR for their human rights institution expertise, CARE for GBV response capacity, and RVI for conflict analysis. The addendum notes that "each component was co-designed and/or co-led by local organizations" during Phase 1, suggesting continuity with proven partners for Phase 2.
how_mechanism.quote: "All contracting modalities will be accountable grant or MoU" (D0004228.odt, Implementation approach) and "RVI will be contracted directly, proactively made available as a resource to other HARP projects and relevant FCDO and partner projects" (D0004228.odt, Component 4 details)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by a Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and Programme Responsible Owner (PRO) from FCDO, with a Deputy Programme Manager and conflict advisors providing technical support. A Programme Advisory Team includes governance experts, and component-specific steering committees (e.g., DIHR-EHRC committee for human rights work) manage implementation. The Peace Research Facility serves as a cross-cutting coordination hub.
how_governance.quote: "The programme is managed under the oversight of a Senior Responsible Owner (SRO), who provides technical guidance, and a Programme Responsible Owner (PRO), who ensures effective implementation... A Deputy Programme Manager supports overall programme oversight" (S30119165.odt, Programme management) and "Suppliers will report quarterly on spending and progress against milestones" (S30119165.odt, Results & Monitoring)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme explicitly states that "it may be necessary to adjust the relative scale of each component and adjust our approach to implementation" in response to evolving conflict dynamics. Annual breakpoints are built into grant agreements to enable budget flexibility, and the 2024 amendment demonstrates reallocation from transitional justice to election support.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: HARP uses iterative political and conflict analysis to guide adjustments, with the Peace Research Facility providing real-time data to inform shifts. The 2024 amendment shows adaptive management in practice: reallocating £2.7m from stalled transitional justice work to election-related activities based on updated context analysis. Components are designed to "retain the flexibility to respond to changing dynamics" (D0004228.odt).
how_flexibility.quote: "Given the fluid operating environment in Ethiopia and the need to respond to evolving conflict dynamics and adapt programming appropriately, it may be necessary to adjust the relative scale of each component" (D0004228.odt, Budget flexibility) and "Funds beyond the spending round are subject to approval and annual breakpoints will be incorporated into each grant agreement/MoU to enable budget flexibility" (D0004228.odt, Implementation approach)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (Conciliation Resources, DIHR, CARE, RVI) → Local sub-partners (e.g., Women’s Association of Tigray, local CSOs). The structure is intentionally flat with direct relationships between FCDO and primary implementers, who then sub-contract to local organizations.
how_efficiency.quote: "Suppliers will report quarterly on spending and progress against milestones" (S30119165.odt, Results & Monitoring) and "Partners are expected to begin spending and delivery quickly since this is an extension of an existing programme" (D0004228.odt, Implementation approach)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (no additional UK engagement)
Geographically focussed, multi-sectoral response (concentrating all resources in one region like Tigray or Somali)
Sector-specific reform (focusing solely on human rights or peacebuilding)
Blended approach (multi-sectoral, multi-geographic) – CHOSEN OPTION
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The blended approach was selected because it (1) maximizes UK comparative advantage by building on legacy work (e.g., Somali Region peacebuilding) while responding to new crises (Tigray war), (2) enables flexibility to adapt to Ethiopia’s fluid conflict dynamics, (3) allows catalytic influence across multiple stability drivers, and (4) provides a platform to reinforce HMG’s diplomatic efforts. The appraisal matrix shows it scored highest on capacity to deliver against HMG priorities (4/5), likelihood of sustained impact (4/5), and ability to flex to changing context (5/5).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (blended approach scored 4.25/5 in weighted appraisal)
risk mitigation (diversified geographic/sectoral focus reduces exposure to single-point failures)
past experience (builds on successful Somali Region work)
partner capacity (leverages existing relationships with Conciliation Resources, DIHR, etc.)
flexibility needs (critical for Ethiopia’s volatile context)
equity considerations (explicit focus on women, youth, and marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Civic Space Constraint Risk: Potential CSO law changes could block funding for election-related activities, undermining HARP’s ability to support inclusive elections and conflict reduction.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will reassess support to elections to ensure alignment with strategic objectives, coordinate with UNDP/EU/Germany to leverage joint efforts, and focus on NEBE functions still viable under restrictions (e.g., public outreach, complaints mechanisms).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Electoral Legitimacy and Trust Risk: Non-transparent NEBE decisions on staggered elections or party registration could fuel perceptions of bias and instability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Higher-level diplomatic engagement and closer NEBE monitoring through UNDP’s SEEDS2 Project Management Board and EWG co-chair roles to ensure careful handling of decisions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Programme Delivery Delays Due to National Elections: Election preparations may distract stakeholders and create operational restrictions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: No-cost time extension to 31 Dec 2027 accommodates potential 12-month staggered elections; prioritization of critical deliverables ahead of election periods; adjusted implementation timelines.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict and Security: Ongoing violence in Amhara/Oromia or renewed Tigray conflict could disrupt elections or programme activities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Support to NEBE for conflict-sensitive electoral planning (e.g., preparedness for conflict-affected areas, staggered elections); diplomatic engagement on security/access coordination.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (reallocating funds from stalled transitional justice to higher-priority elections work)
efficiency (leveraging existing partner relationships to reduce startup costs)
effectiveness (blended approach targets multiple conflict drivers simultaneously)
equity (explicit focus on women’s participation, marginalized groups, and inclusive processes)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 4 - Blended approach: This option takes the best of Options 2 and 3... It allows for engagement across a wider spectrum of stability and human rights priorities... Allows for flexibility to respond to the context as needed... Makes best use of UK resources and comparative advantage" (D0000847.odt, Options Appraisal) and "This analysis reinforces the narrative provided for Option 4 above: that a blended approach to tackling the issues of concern is the approach that will offer the best value for money" (D0000847.odt, Summary of preferred option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Ethiopia directly shapes partner selection by (1) requiring organizations with proven conflict-sensitive experience (e.g., Conciliation Resources’ Somali Region work), (2) limiting international partners’ access to conflict zones (necessitating local co-leads like Women’s Association of Tigray), and (3) creating regulatory risks that favor established relationships over new entrants. For example, potential CSO law changes make it "strategically risky" to onboard new civil society partners without existing trust relationships.
q27_constraints_detail: Security access limitations favor partners with existing local networks (e.g., CARE’s Tigray presence)
Political sensitivity requires partners experienced in navigation elite bargains (e.g., Conciliation Resources’ work with ONLF transition)
Regulatory risks (CSO laws) privilege established organizations over new entrants
Conflict dynamics demand partners with adaptive capacity (e.g., RVI’s real-time analysis)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives to (1) support peace processes, (2) strengthen human rights accountability, (3) address GBV, and (4) generate conflict analysis directly determine the mixed delivery structure: accountable grants for local implementation (peacebuilding/GBV), MoUs for multilateral channels (DDR via UNDP), direct contracts for research (RVI’s Conflict Research Facility), and embedded advisory roles for governance support (e.g., NEBE election planning).
q28_linkages: Peace process support → requires flexible grants for local mediators (Conciliation Resources) + multilateral channels for DDR (UNDP)
Human rights accountability → necessitates institutional strengthening (DIHR-EHRC partnership) + international monitoring (OHCHR)
GBV response → demands community-level partners (Women’s Association of Tigray) with technical backstopping (CARE)
Conflict analysis → needs independent research capacity (RVI) with diplomatic uptake mechanisms
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly grapples with tensions between (1) rapid delivery needs (e.g., Pretoria Agreement implementation) and inclusive processes (e.g., ensuring women’s participation in peace talks), (2) Northern expertise (DIHR’s human rights technical support) and Southern ownership (EHRC co-chairing steering committees), and (3) cost efficiency (leveraging existing partners) versus reach (expanding to new conflict hotspots like Amhara). The 2024 amendment’s reallocation from transitional justice to elections work reflects a strategic trade-off favoring immediate conflict prevention over long-term accountability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: "Promoting the meaningful participation of women in shaping [peace processes]... giving them a better chance of success" (D0004228.odt) requires additional time/resources but is deemed critical for sustainability
Expertise vs ownership: International partners (DIHR, RVI) provide technical capacity while local actors (EHRC, women’s groups) lead implementation
Cost vs reach: Expanding to Oromia/Amhara increases budget needs but addresses evolving conflict loci
Flexibility vs accountability: Adaptive management enables context responsiveness but complicates results measurement
intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s ‘Major’ risk rating (FCAS context, election volatility) drives intensive oversight mechanisms: quarterly supplier reporting, embedded governance advisors, and real-time conflict analysis through the Peace Research Facility. The management structure includes a dedicated conflict advisor and Deputy Programme Manager to handle the complex risk environment, with annual breakpoints in grants to enable rapid reallocation.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: EHRC moves from recipient to co-chair of steering committees as its investigative capacity strengthens; local women’s organizations transition from service delivery to shaping national WPS agendas; and NEBE’s role expands from election management to conflict-sensitive planning with HARP support. The programme’s theory of change assumes that "strengthened systems... promote accountability in support of long-term peace" (D0004228.odt, Outcome 2).
intersections.quote: "The UK’s main comparative advantage in Ethiopia in the fields of peacebuilding and human rights are fourfold:... Legacy peacebuilding work in Somali Regional State... HMG’s role as a long-term actor to Ethiopia and able to act as a critical friend; Convening power" (D0000847.odt, UK Comparative Advantage) and "During the first phase, each component was co-designed and/or co-led by local organizations and local actors were funded through consortium leads" (D0004228.odt, Localization commitment)

key_programme_risks: Conflict escalation disrupting peace processes (e.g., Amhara-Oromia violence or Tigray agreement collapse)
Human rights abuses continuing despite transitional justice efforts (documented in Oromia/Amhara)
Shrinking civic space limiting CSO ability to monitor elections or advocate (regulatory risks)
Electoral disputes triggering new violence (historical precedent from 2020 postponement)
Programme delivery delays due to election-related distractions (stakeholder attention shifts)
EHRC’s limited capacity to investigate abuses without political interference
GBV service gaps persisting in rural/conflict areas despite programme support
Donor coordination challenges in crowded peacebuilding/human rights space

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Conflict and Security (Major): Ongoing violence in Amhara/Oromia or renewed Tigray conflict could disrupt elections/programme activities.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support NEBE in conflict-sensitive electoral planning (staggered elections, conflict-area preparedness); diplomatic engagement on security/access coordination.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Electoral Legitimacy and Trust Risk (Major): Non-transparent NEBE decisions could fuel instability.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Higher-level diplomatic engagement and NEBE monitoring through UNDP’s SEEDS2 Board and EWG co-chair roles.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Civic Space Constraint Risk (Severe): CSO law changes may block election-related funding.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Reassess election support to align with strategic objectives; coordinate with EU/Germany to work around restrictions; focus on viable NEBE functions (public outreach, complaints mechanisms).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Programme Delivery Delays (Moderate): Elections may distract stakeholders.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: No-cost time extension to Dec 2027; prioritize critical deliverables pre-elections; adjust timelines.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: EHRC Capacity Limits: EHRC may fail to implement recommendations due to political/technical constraints.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: DIHR-led training and peer exchanges with other NHRIs; multi-donor pool fund for sustained capacity building.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GBV Service Gaps: Rural/conflict-area survivors may remain unreached.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Expand Women Leading in Emergencies (WLiE) groups to Oromia/Amhara; community-level awareness campaigns.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Transitional Justice Stalls: Political resistance may block accountability processes.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Reallocate funds to election support (2024 amendment); engage with national dialogue processes.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity must be applied across all activities (JACS 2024 warning that even basic services can exacerbate tensions)
Local peacebuilding processes require long-term commitment (Somali Region’s 9-year UK support cited as model)
Women’s meaningful participation in peace processes improves sustainability (WPS integration across all components)
Real-time analysis is critical in fluid contexts (Peace Research Facility’s monthly trend reports)
Staggered elections may be necessary in conflict-affected areas (NEBE planning support)
Human rights monitoring must be independent (OHCHR-led networks in hotspots)
DDR programmes need parallel reintegration support (lesson from Tigray combatant demobilization)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 lessons (2022-23 review) highlighted: (1) Shrinking civic space requires alternative delivery approaches for human rights monitoring, (2) Barriers to women’s participation in peace processes remain significant despite programme efforts, (3) Conflict sensitivity and real-time analysis are valuable for UK engagement, and (4) Flexibility is essential in Ethiopia’s volatile context. The Somali Region experience demonstrated that "long-term, problem-focused approaches" with political acumen can reduce violence (D0000847.odt, Box 1).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2024 amendment reflects lessons by: (1) Adding election support to mitigate conflict risks around 2026 votes, (2) Reallocating £2.7m from stalled transitional justice to higher-priority election work, (3) Expanding WPS focus to Oromia/Amhara based on evolving GBV patterns, (4) Strengthening the Peace Research Facility’s role in providing actionable analysis, and (5) Extending the programme timeline to December 2027 to accommodate potential election delays.
risks_lessons.quote: "Through this programme, the British Embassy should explore extending and/or expanding current areas of support and look for opportunities to support mechanisms that further support peace processes and peaceful political transitions" (D0004228.odt, Phase One Learning) and "The disagreement in 2020 over the one-year postponement of national elections was a proximate cause to the outbreak of the two year war in Tigray and northern Ethiopia" (S30119165.odt, Evidence for election focus)

co_funding_partners.partner: UNDP (National Demobilisation and Reintegration Programme pool fund)
Danish Institute for Human Rights (DIHR-managed multi-donor fund for EHRC)
EU and Germany (parallel election support programmes)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages UNDP’s SEEDS2 multi-donor pool for DDR funding and coordinates with EU/German election support to maximize joint impact. The EHRC capacity building is part of a DIHR-managed multi-donor fund, though specific leverage figures are not quantified.
financial_details.quote: "The total budget for the costed extension will amount to £36.5m up to 31/03/27, bringing the total UK funding provided under this business case to £41m" (D0004228.odt, Budget) and "FCDO plans to disburse £7m/year under component 1 by joining a pooled fund administered by UNDP for the National Demobilisation and Reintegration Programme (NDRP)" (D0004228.odt, Implementation approach)

metadata.programme_name: Building Health System Resilience to End Preventable Deaths in Ethiopia (EPD-E)

quote.programme_name: "Building Health System Resilience to End Preventable Deaths in Ethiopia (EPD-E)" (D0003183.odt, Title)
quote.budget: "£100m over 5 years (April 2023–April 2028)" (D0003183.odt, Programme Value)
quote.sector: "Health Sector, Ethiopia" (D0003183.odt, Country/Region or Sector)

metadata.duration_source: "£100m over 5 years (April 2023–April 2028)" (D0003183.odt, Programme Value)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **service delivery** (direct provision of RMNCH interventions), **financing mechanism** (pooled funding to government), **capacity building** (technical assistance for health system strengthening), and **implementation research** (testing adaptive approaches in fragile contexts). It aims to protect health gains while building long-term system resilience.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will help Ethiopia protect and consolidate health gains to date through: A strategic focus on the most off-track reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH) indicators to end the avoidable deaths of mothers and babies; Concerted efforts to build the longer-term capability of the Ethiopian health system to work towards universal health coverage (UHC)." (D0003183.odt, Programme summary)

Under-five mortality reduced from 59 to 44 per 1,000 live births
Universal Health Coverage (UHC) index increased from 65.5 to 68
Health Security Index (HSI) increased from 0.63 to 0.78
Improved quality of maternal and newborn health services (e.g., skilled birth attendance, antenatal care)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Not quantified

q3_expected_outputs.output: Reduced regional inequalities in RMNCH service coverage
q3_expected_outputs.target: Implementation of National Health Equity Strategy

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened health system capabilities (planning, financial management, disease surveillance)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Not quantified

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased domestic health financing (from 8% to 15% of national budget)
Family planning coverage expanded (modern contraceptive prevalence rate)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 20-25% of Financial Aid allocated to family planning

q3_expected_outputs.output: Pandemic preparedness and response mechanisms strengthened
q3_expected_outputs.target: Not quantified

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to **end preventable maternal, newborn, and child deaths** in Ethiopia by strengthening health system resilience, addressing regional inequalities, and improving RMNCH service quality. It combines **direct financing** (for essential drugs/commodities), **technical assistance** (for system capacity), and **adaptive management** to respond to Ethiopia’s fragile context (conflict, climate shocks, COVID-19).

quote.objectives: "This programme will help Ethiopia protect and consolidate health gains to date through: A strategic focus on the most off-track reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH) indicators to end the avoidable deaths of mothers and babies; Concerted efforts to build the longer-term capability of the Ethiopian health system to work towards universal health coverage (UHC)." (D0003183.odt, Programme summary)
quote.targets: "The UK will support Ethiopia achieve its own ambitious Health Sector Plan 2025 targets including: Maternal mortality rate (MMR) reduced from 401 to 279; Under five mortality reduced from 59 to 44 per 1000 live births; Universal Health Coverage index increased from 65.5 to 68." (D0003183.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia is classified as **FCAS (Fragile and Conflict-Affected State)** due to protracted conflicts (Tigray, Benishangul-Gumuz, Oromia), climate-induced shocks (droughts, flooding), high inflation, and residual COVID-19 impacts. The document explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" but describes a **high-risk operating environment** with "unpredictable context" and "significant stresses on basic service systems."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0003183.odt, Overall programme risk rating) **AND** "Ethiopia is currently experiencing a series of crises, further compounding its existing challenges. These include climate-induced shocks including flooding and severe drought, protracted conflict in multiple parts of the country leading to high inflation, and the continued impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–Current Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflicts have **destroyed health infrastructure** (48 hospitals, 545 health centres damaged), **displaced health workers**, and **limited access** in Tigray/Afar/Somali regions. Climate shocks (droughts, flooding) exacerbate **food insecurity** and **disease outbreaks** (malaria, cholera). Weak public financial management (PFMs) and **fiduciary risks** (procurement, accounting) complicate direct funding to government. High inflation reduces the **real-value of cash transfers** and programme budgets.

quote.conflict: "It is estimated that a total of 48 hospitals, 545 health centres and 3,106 health posts have been affected by the conflict. In Tigray, UNHCR report a lack of medicine, medical assistance and medical supplies caused by damage to facilities and lack of supplies/and humanitarian access." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–Current Context)
quote.climate: "Climate-induced shocks are increasing in frequency and severity. Ethiopia has experienced an unprecedented number of failed rainy seasons in recent years... 7.5m people need emergency nutrition and there were record admissions to health facilities for severe acute malnutrition in quarter one of 2022/23." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–Current Context)
quote.fiduciary: "Remaining areas of major fiduciary risk are procurement, accounting and internal controls, fiscal transparency, public investment and asset management, implementation of audit recommendations and in-year budget reallocations." (D0003183.odt, Risk mitigation)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **Ethiopian government (FMoH)** leads programme design, implementation, and budget allocation through the **SDG Pooled Fund (SDG-PF)**, with donors (including UK) providing financing and technical assistance. Decision-making is **joint** for results-based triggers but ultimately aligned with GoE’s Health Sector Transformation Plan (HSTP-II).
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for health sector administrative staff (e.g., public financial management, planning)
Technical assistance to Regional Health Bureaus (RHB) for equity-focused service delivery
Support for MoH to improve evidence-based planning and donor coordination
Mentorship on health system resilience (e.g., pandemic preparedness, climate adaptation)
Institutional strengthening for absorptive capacity (to secure higher budget allocations)

partner_organizations.name: Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH), Ethiopia
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager (via SDG-PF)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Intermediary for Performance-for-Results (P4R) financing

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Manager of Health Pooled Fund (HPF) under MoH oversight

partner_organizations.name: Regional Health Bureaus (RHBs)
partner_organizations.role: Sub-national service delivery and equity implementation

partner_organizations.name: UK Public Health Security Agency (UKPHSA)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance for pandemic preparedness

partner_organizations.name: UN/NGO consortium (e.g., UNHCR, WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Emergency service delivery in conflict-affected areas (e.g., Tigray)

partner_organizations.name: Ethiopia Crisis to Resilience (EC2R) programme
partner_organizations.role: Parallel humanitarian mechanism for non-government-controlled areas

quote.lead_role: "The general objective of the HPF was conceived to contribute to the achievement of the overall health sector performance by supporting its implementation process through flexible, time-sensitive, and less cumbersome funding mechanisms, in line with the Harmonization Action Plan and the International Health Partnership (IHP+) principles." (D0003183.odt, Background–What is the Health Pooled Fund)
quote.capacity_building: "Technical assistance will be conflict-sensitive and target multiple areas. Our TA (at the national and sub-national level...), will complement service delivery financing by supporting efforts to: Improve the quality of maternal and new-born health services...; Tackle stubborn geographical inequalities in health service coverage...; Build stronger decision-making, delivery and public financial management capabilities." (D0003183.odt, How will this investment respond to the problem?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **non-budgetary Financial Aid** channeled through the **SDG Pooled Fund (SDG-PF)**, a **Programme-for-Results (P4R) modality** with results-based triggers. Funds are disbursed to the **Ethiopian Ministry of Health (MoH)** based on achievement of **fiduciary and performance milestones** (e.g., skilled birth attendance rates, vaccination coverage). The UK also contributes to the **World Bank’s HLNP P4R** and may use **UN/NGO intermediaries** in conflict zones.
