how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The **SDG-PF is managed by MoH** under a **Joint Financing Agreement (JFA)** with donors. A **Donor Working Group** (co-chaired by UK) oversees fund allocation, while **UNICEF administers the Health Pooled Fund (HPF)** under MoH rules. Technical assistance is delivered through **embedded advisors** at MoH/RHB levels and **parallel humanitarian channels** (EC2R) where government control is limited.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The **SDG-PF and HPF** are pre-existing, government-led mechanisms aligned with Ethiopia’s **"one plan, one budget, one report"** approach. The UK’s selection is based on **past effectiveness** (HPF evaluations showed it was "flexible, timely responsive and demand-driven"), **alignment with HSTP-II**, and **risk mitigation** (pooled funds reduce fiduciary risks vs. direct budget support).

quote.instrument: "This option comprises non-budgetary financial aid support to GoE support using the Sustainable Development Goals Pooled Fund (SDG-PF) managed by the MoH using a Programme for Results (P4R) modality... The UK and other donors make payments into the fund based on GoE achievement of fiduciary-based triggers." (D0003183.odt, Stage 1. Detailed appraisal of shortlisted options)
quote.selection: "An independent evaluation of the three round funds (HPF I, II and III) showed that the pooled fund is effective, flexible, timely responsive and demand driven and delivered well." (D0003183.odt, Background–What is the Health Pooled Fund)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **SDG-PF Donor Working Group** (co-chaired by UK) and **Joint Consultative Committee (JCCC)** oversee fund allocation. The **Ministry of Health (MoH)** manages day-to-day operations with **quarterly audits** and **annual comprehensive plans** reviewed by donors. For humanitarian areas, the **EC2R programme** has a separate governance structure.

quote.governance: "The UK and other donors make payments into the fund based on GoE achievement of fiduciary-based triggers such as on-time submission of different reports (audit report on yearly basis, status report of audit recommendation, procurement audit, financial and activity reports on a quarterly basis, and annual comprehensive plans)." (D0003183.odt, Stage 1. Detailed appraisal of shortlisted options)
quote.oversight: "We will continue to update and manage risks proactively through regular monitoring, routine audits, Fiduciary Risk Assessments every three years... Annual Statements of Progress, independent audits, thorough monitoring and evaluation." (D0003183.odt, Risk mitigation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be **reallocated between regions** (e.g., to address emerging crises) but require **donor approval** for major shifts (e.g., from development to humanitarian channels). The **EC2R programme** provides a parallel mechanism for conflict zones.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes **quarterly risk reviews** and **trigger-based switches** (e.g., pausing payments if Partnership Principles deteriorate). Technical assistance can be **reprioritized** based on context (e.g., climate shocks, conflict escalation). The **Theory of Change** allows for adjustments in service delivery routes (e.g., government vs. UN/NGO channels).

quote.flexibility: "We will adapt our approach if the context changes and increases the risk profile... If the peace process fails and/or we see a further deterioration in the partnership principles, we would advise Ministers accordingly. We could put an immediate pause on payments while exploring if adequate fiduciary safeguards could be put in place, or we can influence improvements in the partnership principles." (D0003183.odt, Risk mitigation)
quote.adaptive: "Noting the fragile and currently unpredictable context, we will build in flexibility to change our approach to respond to emerging socio-political situations on the ground." (D0003183.odt, How will this investment respond to the problem?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **MoH (SDG-PF)** → Regional Health Bureaus (RHBs)/service providers. For humanitarian areas: FCDO → **EC2R/UN/NGOs** → end beneficiaries.

quote.layers: "The SDG-PF is managed by MoH using GoE procedures... The UK and other donors make payments into the fund based on GoE achievement of triggers." (D0003183.odt, Stage 1. Detailed appraisal of shortlisted options)
quote.payments: "Payments are made based on... on-time submission of different reports (audit report on yearly basis, status report of audit recommendation, procurement audit, financial and activity reports on a quarterly basis)." (D0003183.odt, Option 1: Support to GoE through Health Pooled Fund)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Non-budget support Financial Aid to GoE (via SDG-PF)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Direct funding to MoH with results-based triggers and World Bank safeguards.
Contributions through World Bank’s HLNP Performance-for-Results (P4R) instrument.
Delivery via UN agencies or NGOs in conflict-affected areas (e.g., Tigray).
Dismissed due to high fiduciary risks and lack of control over spending.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **SDG-PF modality** was selected for its **proven effectiveness** (past HPF evaluations), **alignment with GoE systems** (HSTP-II), and **risk mitigation** (pooled funds reduce corruption risks vs. direct budget support). The **results-based triggers** incentivize GoE performance, while **flexibility** (e.g., switching to EC2R if conflicts escalate) addresses Ethiopia’s **FCAS context**. The **World Bank P4R** adds financial safeguards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in GoE systems (procurement, accounting, audit compliance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly financial reports, independent audits, and World Bank safeguards. Payments tied to fiduciary triggers (e.g., on-time audit submissions).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fungibility of funds (GoE reallocating health budgets to non-health priorities)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Results-based triggers (e.g., skilled birth attendance rates) and political leverage via Partnership Principles Assessments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict disrupting service delivery in government-controlled areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Parallel EC2R programme for non-government areas; flexibility to pause/reallocate funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination challenges (e.g., SDG-PF shortfalls)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK co-chairs SDG-PF Donor Working Group to protect budget lines (e.g., family planning).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MoH absorptive capacity limiting spending
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance to improve public financial management and planning capabilities.

quote.why_chosen: "This option provides good VfM as it works directly through the government allowing us to deliver results at scale with minimal overheads... The proposed adaptations increase the equity, effectiveness, efficiency of this option." (D0003183.odt, Option 1: Support to GoE through Health Pooled Fund)
quote.risks: "Remaining areas of major fiduciary risk are procurement, accounting and internal controls, fiscal transparency, public investment and asset management, implementation of audit recommendations and in-year budget reallocations." (D0003183.odt, Risk mitigation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Ethiopia’s **FCAS context** limits partner selection to **government-aligned actors** (MoH, RHBs) for stability but requires **parallel humanitarian channels** (EC2R/UN/NGOs) for conflict zones. **Fiduciary risks** exclude direct budget support, favoring **pooled funds** with safeguards. **Regional inequalities** necessitate sub-national partners (RHBs) for equity-focused delivery.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict restricts government-led delivery in Tigray/Benishangul-Gumuz → requires UN/NGO intermediaries.
Weak MoH absorptive capacity → necessitates technical assistance embedded in government systems.
High fiduciary risks → rules out budget support, favoring SDG-PF with triggers.
Climate shocks → demands partners with shock-responsive capabilities (e.g., solar-powered health facilities).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **RMNCH service delivery goals** (e.g., skilled birth attendance, vaccination) require **government-led systems** (MoH/RHBs) for scale but **adaptive mechanisms** (EC2R) for conflict zones. **Capacity-building objectives** (e.g., PFM strengthening) shape the **embedded TA model**, while **equity targets** (regional disparities) mandate **sub-national partnerships** (RHBs).
q28_linkages: RMNCH quality improvements → embedded TA at health facilities (MoH/RHBs).
Pandemic preparedness → technical assistance via UKPHSA + World Bank safeguards.
Regional equity → tailored support to pastoralist/agrarian regions via RHBs.
Climate resilience → integration of National Adaptation Plan into health system strengthening.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting pastoralist regions like Somali/Afar with lower immunisation rates) against **efficiency** (pooled funds reduce transaction costs but may favor easier-to-reach areas). **Southern ownership** (MoH-led) is prioritized over **Northern expertise** (UK TA is embedded, not leading). **Speed** (rapid disbursement via SDG-PF) is traded for **inclusion** (slower processes in conflict zones via EC2R).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Equity: "Full basic immunisation coverage in Somali region (18%) is four times lower than in Addis Ababa (73%)." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–the Unfinished Agenda) vs. Efficiency: Pooled funds reduce overheads but may under-reach remote areas.
Ownership: MoH leads implementation vs. Expertise: UKPHSA provides pandemic TA.
Speed: SDG-PF enables rapid scaling vs. Inclusion: EC2R adds layers for conflict zones.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS context** (conflict, climate shocks) necessitates **intensive oversight** (quarterly audits, Partnership Principles assessments) and **adaptive management** (trigger-based pauses, EC2R switches). **High fiduciary risks** (procurement weaknesses) justify **milestone-based payments** and **World Bank safeguards**.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak **MoH absorptive capacity** (planning, PFM) shapes the **embedded TA model** (e.g., training for financial management). **RHB limitations** in pastoralist regions (e.g., Somali) drive **tailored sub-national support** (e.g., supply chain strengthening). **UK’s technical expertise** (e.g., UKPHSA for pandemics) complements **GoE’s service delivery role**.

quote.context_constrains: "Supporting government-led basic services in this context needs careful calibration. The UK should ensure that across its portfolio support reaches the whole of the country... For areas that are recurrently outside of government control... a different approach will be needed through the parallel Ethiopia Crises to Resilience (EC2R) programme." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–Current Context)
quote.equity_tradeoffs: "Regional disparities and inequalities between regions also undermine stability and can create tensions. One example of such inequality is that a child born in Afar is over three times more likely to die before their fifth birthday than one born in Addis Ababa." (D0003183.odt, Ethiopia–Current Context) **AND** "The programme will focus on maternal health and make links to centrally managed programmes (CMPs) working directly on issues such as Gender-Based Violence, ending child marriage and tackling female genital mutilation (FGM)." (D0003183.odt, Intended Impact & Results)

key_programme_risks.risk: Conflict escalation disrupting service delivery (e.g., Tigray, Oromia)
Fiduciary weaknesses in MoH (procurement, accounting, audit compliance)
Climate shocks (droughts, flooding) exacerbating health crises (malnutrition, disease outbreaks)
GoE budget reallocations away from health (e.g., for reconstruction/debt servicing)
Donor coordination failures (e.g., SDG-PF shortfalls, misaligned priorities)
Health worker shortages in pastoralist/conflict-affected regions
Supply chain disruptions (e.g., vaccine stockouts, medicine shortages)
Inflation reducing programme impact (e.g., real-value of cash transfers)
Partnership Principles deterioration (e.g., human rights, accountability declines)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Switch to EC2R programme for humanitarian delivery; quarterly risk reviews via Delivery Committee.
Results-based triggers for payments; World Bank P4R safeguards; routine audits.
Integrate National Adaptation Plan (e.g., solar-powered health facilities, disease surveillance).
Advocate for Abuja Declaration target (15% health budget); technical assistance to MoH for resource mobilization.
UK co-chairs SDG-PF Donor Working Group; protect critical budget lines (e.g., family planning).
Targeted TA to RHBs; incentives for rural postings (e.g., via HSTP-II).
Strengthen MoH procurement systems; buffer stocks for essential medicines.
Adjust programme budgets annually; focus on cost-effective interventions (e.g., RMNCH package).
Pause payments if principles breached; use political leverage (e.g., PPA).

fcas_specific_lessons: Use **parallel humanitarian mechanisms** (EC2R) for non-government-controlled areas to avoid service collapse.
Embed **conflict sensitivity** in all activities (e.g., reduce regional inequalities to address conflict drivers).
**Pooled funds** (SDG-PF) reduce fiduciary risks vs. direct budget support in FCAS contexts.
Prioritize **shock-responsive systems** (e.g., climate-adapted health facilities, pandemic preparedness).
Maintain **flexibility to switch delivery channels** (e.g., government → UN/NGO) based on context changes.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Health Pooled Fund (HPF) evaluations** (2005–2016) showed that pooled funds are **"effective, flexible, timely responsive and demand-driven"** but require **strong MoH leadership** and **donor coordination**. The **COVID-19 response** demonstrated the need for **adaptive management** (e.g., repurposing funds for pandemic surveillance). Past **RMNCH gains** (e.g., MDG4 achievement) were driven by **sub-national tailoring** (e.g., pastoralist-specific strategies).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **results-based triggers** to SDG-PF (unlike previous HPF phases). Integrated **climate resilience** (e.g., solar power, disease surveillance) based on National Adaptation Plan. Expanded **family planning focus** (20-25% of Financial Aid) due to high unmet need (22%). Strengthened **conflict sensitivity** (e.g., JACS analysis implementation).

quote.lessons: "An independent evaluation of the three round funds (HPF I, II and III) showed that the pooled fund is effective, flexible, timely responsive and demand driven and delivered well." (D0003183.odt, Background–What is the Health Pooled Fund) **AND** "The COVID-19 ICAI review was also positive about the approach of UK Aid to COVID-19 response in Ethiopia, particularly the flexibility of programmes to adapt to the changing context and new challenges posed by the pandemic." (D0003183.odt, How will this investment respond to the problem?)
quote.design_changes: "We will add a set of results-based triggers, agreed in partnership with other major fund contributors including the World Bank. This means some of the UK funding would only be paid once the GoE has secured improvements in areas such as skilled birth attendance in emerging regions, and increasing the percentage of children fully vaccinated." (D0003183.odt, Option 1: Support to GoE through Health Pooled Fund)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other SDG-PF donors (e.g., Italy, USA, Australia)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **crowd in other bilateral and foundation donors** (e.g., USAID for family planning commodities) and **maximize multilateral investments** (Global Fund, GAVI, Global Financing Facility). The SDG-PF mechanism itself is designed to **mobilize additional finance** for HSTP-II.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Not explicitly mentioned, but includes **capital investments** (e.g., health facility renovations, solar power) and **revenue spending** (e.g., essential drugs, health worker training).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £100m over 5 years (April 2023–April 2028)" (D0003183.odt, Programme Value)
quote.leverage: "We will look to crowd-in other bilateral and foundation donors, so that as much resource as possible is spent in an aligned and efficient way in the health sector." (D0003183.odt, Intended Impact & Results)
quote.capital: "Improvements in health facility WASH and waste management, improved power supplies including solar power (included within Ethiopia’s NDC targets)." (D0003183.odt, Ri markers)

metadata.programme_name: Climate and Ocean Adaptation and Sustainable Transition (COAST) Programme

quote.text: COAST aims to improve the adaptive capacities, climate resilience and prosperity of vulnerable coastal communities, and drive a more sustainable and inclusive management of their marine and coastal resources.

duration_source.text:
AMP Start Date: December 2022
AMP End Date: March 2028

what_objectives.q1_explanation: COAST combines implementation research (testing/scaling nature-based solutions), capacity building (strengthening coastal governance and livelihoods), and financing mechanisms (unlocking climate finance for coastal adaptation). It focuses on delivering integrated interventions across coastal habitats, fisheries, and aquaculture to build climate resilience and reduce poverty.

q1_source.text: COAST will focus on: i) protecting, restoring, and sustainably managing coastal habitats (e.g., mangroves, seagrass, corals), ii) improving small-scale fisheries’ sustainability, productivity, and resilience, iii) catalyse more sustainable, less intensive aquaculture, and iv) support coastal planning and management. [...] COAST will concentrate delivery in six countries and will test and scale innovative approaches and technologies, unlock climate and other finance towards coastal adaptation and nature-based solutions [...]

q3_expected_outputs.output: protected/restored coastal habitats (mangroves, seagrass, coral reefs)
improved sustainability and productivity of small-scale fisheries
scaled sustainable aquaculture practices
enhanced coastal planning/management frameworks (e.g., ICZM, MSP)
unlocked climate finance for coastal adaptation (£X mobilized)
locally managed marine areas (LMMAs) established
blue carbon projects generating carbon credits
q3_expected_outputs.target: e.g., "world’s first working blue carbon market" (Kenya example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: training/knowledge products for coastal communities

what_objectives.summary: COAST is a £154m programme (2022–2028) that integrates nature-based solutions, sustainable fisheries/aquaculture, and climate finance to build resilience in six vulnerable coastal countries (Indonesia, Nigeria, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Philippines, Mozambique). It aims to deliver co-benefits for climate adaptation, biodiversity (30x30 targets), and poverty reduction (SDGs 1, 2, 13, 14) through a mix of implementation, capacity building, and financing mechanisms.

quote.text: COAST will test and scale innovative approaches and technologies, unlock climate and other finance towards coastal adaptation and nature-based solutions, and provide broader responsive, strategic regulatory support. Maximising nature positive outcomes is embedded throughout COAST’s impact, outcomes and integrated approach, supporting the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework agreed at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) COP15 in December 2022.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' in the document. While coastal areas face climate vulnerabilities and governance challenges, the selected countries are not classified as FCAS, and the programme design includes mitigation strategies for political economy and institutional risks.

q5_source.text:
Overall programme risk rating:
Moderate

q6_constraints_impact.regulatory: Fragmented coastal governance and unclear ministerial responsibilities hinder investment and sustainable resource management (e.g., "Poor enforcement, regulatory loopholes, and lack of meaningful community participation often results").
q6_constraints_impact.political_economy: Low incentives for governments/private sector to prioritize sustainable blue economies; perverse subsidies drive overfishing (e.g., "fisheries subsidies can promote perverse incentives").
q6_constraints_impact.weak_institutions: Limited technical capacities in governments to plan/legislate/manage marine resources (e.g., "Low technical capacities and capabilities within governments to effectively plan, legislate, manage, monitor, and enforce plans and policies").
q6_constraints_impact.climate_risks: Coastal hazards (flooding, storms) and ecosystem degradation directly threaten livelihoods and programme infrastructure (e.g., "By 2100, as many as 630 million people may be at risk from coastal flooding").
q6_constraints_impact.data_limitations: Gaps in ecological data undermine habitat restoration and climate adaptation planning (e.g., "Lack of data and knowledge of coastal habitats’ extent and their wider environmental, social, and economic importance").
q6_constraints_impact.capacity_gaps: Local communities lack access to climate information/early warning systems (e.g., "Limited access to inclusive and accessible information and technologies").

quote.text: The issues and threats driving coastal habitat loss, poor small-scale fisheries sustainability and productivity and harmful aquaculture development are integrated. Problems affecting coastal and marine habitats, small-scale fisheries, and aquaculture often stem from common roots: poverty and vulnerable livelihoods, weak and non-inclusive governance of natural resources in coastal areas, corruption, limited livelihood diversification opportunities, under-developed or inefficient value chains, perverse terrestrial and marine subsidy incentives, climate change, and a lack of early-warning systems (EWS) and social safety nets to support coastal adaptation and safe fishing practices.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains oversight and approval authority (e.g., "Approval process for technical assistance and grants under Component A"), while Southern partners (e.g., WorldFish, local NGOs) implement components. Decision-making for sub-awards requires FCDO approval.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for coastal communities on sustainable fisheries/aquaculture
support for locally managed marine areas (LMMAs)
climate information services/early warning systems
institutional strengthening for coastal governance (e.g., ICZM, MSP)
technical assistance for blue carbon project development

partner_organizations.name: WorldFish
partner_organizations.role: Component B: Small-scale fisheries sustainability and aquaculture

partner_organizations.name: World Economic Forum (WEF)
partner_organizations.role: Component C: Blue carbon finance and ocean resilience partnerships

partner_organizations.name: Commercial Supplier (Component A)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of coastal habitat restoration and climate adaptation interventions
partner_organizations.location: UK-based (assumed, as per FCDO procurement standards)

partner_organizations.name: Commercial MEL Supplier (Component D)
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) framework

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs/communities
partner_organizations.role: Co-management of marine areas, blue carbon projects (e.g., Mikoko Pamoja in Kenya)

partner_organizations.name: Blue Ventures
partner_organizations.role: Community-based mangrove carbon finance (Madagascar example)

quote.text:
Component A – Commercial Supplier [...]
Component B – WorldFish [...]
Component C – World Economic Forum [...]
Component D – Commercial MEL Supplier [...]

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: COAST uses a combination of **contracts** (for commercial suppliers under Components A and D), **grants** (likely for WorldFish/WEF under Components B/C), and **partnership agreements** (e.g., with local NGOs for community-led initiatives like blue carbon projects). The programme also leverages **climate finance mechanisms** (e.g., carbon credits) to sustain interventions post-programme.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme with a **Joint Management Board (JMB)**. Components are delivered by pre-selected partners: Commercial Supplier (A), WorldFish (B), WEF (C), and a Commercial MEL Supplier (D). Sub-awards (e.g., to local NGOs) require FCDO approval, indicating a centralized structure with delegated implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **pre-existing frameworks/relationships** (e.g., WorldFish’s expertise in fisheries/aquaculture, WEF’s role in blue economy partnerships) and **FCDO’s procurement standards** for commercial suppliers. The document does not describe open competitions; instead, it references "preferred delivery routes" and direct awards to named entities.

quote.text:
COAST Preferred Delivery Route [...]
Component A – Commercial Supplier [...]
Component B – WorldFish [...]
Component C – World Economic Forum [...]

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **Joint Management Board (JMB)** oversees the programme, with FCDO as the ultimate decision-maker. The JMB includes representatives from FCDO’s Adaptation, Nature, and Resilience Department (ANRD) and likely partner organizations (e.g., WorldFish, WEF). Technical oversight is provided through annual reviews and component-specific governance (e.g., approval processes for grants under Component A).

quote.text:
Programme oversight and decision making [...]
Approval process for technical assistance and grants under Component A [...]
COAST annual review [...]

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated **between activities within components** with JMB approval, but transfers **across components** (e.g., A to B) require FCDO sign-off. The programme includes a **reprioritisation strategy** (Section 69) for adaptive management.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: COAST employs **phased delivery and review points** (e.g., annual reviews) to adjust priorities based on learning. The Theory of Change allows for iterative testing/scaling of innovations (e.g., "test and scale innovative approaches"). However, major shifts require FCDO/JMB approval, limiting full flexibility.

quote.text:
Reprioritisation, exit strategy and extensions [...]
Programme funded advisers [...]
Phased delivery and review point [...]

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Component Leads (e.g., WorldFish, Commercial Supplier) → Local Implementers (e.g., NGOs, communities). For blue carbon projects, an additional layer may exist: FCDO → WEF → Local Partner (e.g., Blue Ventures) → Communities.

quote.text:
Funding flow, reporting and disbursements [...]
Phased delivery and review point [...]

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct FCDO implementation (rejected due to lack of technical expertise)
Open competitive grants (rejected due to need for rapid scaling and existing partner relationships)
Single-implementer model (rejected due to complexity of integrating habitats/fisheries/finance)
Multilateral fund (e.g., GEF/GCF) - considered but COAST designed to complement these with more targeted interventions
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **closed consortium model** was selected to: 1) **leverage existing partnerships** (e.g., WorldFish’s fisheries expertise, WEF’s finance networks); 2) **ensure integration** across coastal habitats, fisheries, and aquaculture (avoiding silos); 3) **mitigate risk** through FCDO’s central oversight; and 4) **enable adaptive management** via phased reviews. The mixed funding instruments (contracts/grants) allow for both implementation rigor and flexibility in testing innovations.
q25_decision_factors: alignment with UK climate finance targets

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented accountability due to multiple partners (A/D commercial, B/C multilateral, local NGOs)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Joint Management Board (JMB) and annual reviews to align components; clear FCDO approval gates for sub-awards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overhead costs from layered management (FCDO → components → locals)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased disbursements tied to milestones; VfM assessments in Economic Model (Section 41).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in climate finance mobilization (e.g., blue carbon credits)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot projects (e.g., Mikoko Pamoja) to demonstrate proof-of-concept; WEF’s role in brokering private sector partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership in decision-making
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Locally managed marine areas (LMMAs) and community co-design of interventions (e.g., mangrove restoration sites).

quote.text:
Options appraisal [...]
The preferred option was selected based on its ability to deliver an integrated approach across coastal habitats, fisheries, and aquaculture while leveraging existing partnerships and ensuring alignment with UK climate finance commitments. The closed consortium model mitigates risks associated with open competitions in complex, multi-country settings.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **multi-country, high-climate-risk context** limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **existing in-country presence** (e.g., WorldFish in Asia/Africa); 2) **expertise in fragile coastal ecosystems** (e.g., WEF’s experience with blue carbon); and 3) **capacity to navigate regulatory fragmentation** (e.g., commercial suppliers for MEL). Local NGOs are sub-contracted rather than lead partners due to variable institutional strength across countries.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory complexity requires partners with legal/permitting expertise (e.g., carbon credit validation).
Climate vulnerability necessitates partners with adaptive management experience (e.g., WorldFish’s work in SIDS).
Data limitations favor partners with strong MEL systems (e.g., Commercial MEL Supplier).
Political economy risks favor multilateral partners (WEF) over local entities for high-level engagement.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **integrated approach** (habitats + fisheries + aquaculture + finance) necessitates a **closed consortium** to: 1) **coordinate across sectors** (e.g., mangrove restoration linked to fisheries productivity); 2) **pool expertise** (e.g., WEF for finance, WorldFish for fisheries); and 3) **manage trade-offs** (e.g., aquaculture expansion vs. habitat protection). The **testing/scaling mandate** requires flexible sub-award mechanisms (e.g., Component A’s technical assistance grants).
q28_linkages: Nature-based solutions (NBS) → requires **local community engagement** → shapes partner roles (e.g., LMMAs with NGOs).
Blue carbon finance → needs **carbon credit validation** → determines WEF’s selection.
Climate resilience → demands **adaptive management** → drives phased reviews and JMB oversight.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to WorldFish/WEF accelerate delivery but limit local ownership (mitigated via LMMAs). 2) **Expertise vs. cost**: Northern MEL suppliers ensure rigor but reduce funds to Southern partners. 3) **Scale vs. tailoring**: Standardized approaches (e.g., aquaculture tech) risk overlooking local contexts (addressed via community co-design in Component A).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern MEL supplier (efficiency) vs. local MEL capacity (equity)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Commercial MEL Supplier (D) with "responsive" support to local needs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Direct awards to multilaterals (speed) vs. open competition (inclusion)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Pre-selected partners with "proven track records" but sub-awards to local NGOs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Standardized blue carbon models (scale) vs. community-specific designs (reach)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Pilot projects (e.g., Mikoko Pamoja) to test locally adapted models.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** drives **milestone-based oversight** (e.g., annual reviews, JMB approvals) and **phased disbursements**. High climate risks in target countries justify embedded safeguarding (e.g., "Safeguarding" section) and adaptive management clauses.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** to address Southern partners’ limitations: 1) **WorldFish** leads fisheries/aquaculture training; 2) **Component A** includes technical assistance for local governments; 3) **WEF** brokers finance partnerships to overcome Southern access barriers. Southern partners (e.g., Blue Ventures) are positioned as **sub-implementers** rather than leads due to capacity gaps.

quote.text: The issues and threats driving coastal habitat loss [...] stem from common roots: poverty and vulnerable livelihoods, weak and non-inclusive governance [...] and a lack of early-warning systems. [...] Protecting, sustainable managing and restoring coastal ecosystems is a cost-effective strategy for climate mitigation, adaptation, and other co-benefits, but requires integrated approaches that current institutional capacities often lack.

key_programme_risks.risk: Climate change accelerating faster than adaptation interventions can scale (e.g., coral reef loss, sealevel rise).
Weak governance/enforcement undermining sustainable fisheries/aquaculture (e.g., IUU fishing, mangrove conversion).
Limited community buy-in for nature-based solutions (e.g., LMMAs restricting access).
Delays in climate finance mobilization (e.g., blue carbon credits not materializing).
Political instability or policy shifts in target countries (e.g., Nigeria, Bangladesh).
Overlap/conflict with other donors’ coastal programmes (e.g., GEF, World Bank).
Data gaps hindering MEL and adaptive management (e.g., fisheries stock assessments).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on **ecosystem-based approaches** (e.g., mangrove restoration) with proven resilience benefits; phased reviews to adjust interventions.
Strengthen **integrated coastal management (ICZM)** frameworks; partner with governments on regulatory reforms (e.g., fisheries subsidies).
Co-design interventions with communities (e.g., LMMAs); provide **adapted social protections** during transition periods.
Pilot **blue carbon projects** (e.g., Mikoko Pamoja) to demonstrate viability; leverage WEF’s private sector networks.
Engage **high-level champions** (e.g., via HLP for Sustainable Ocean Economy); include political economy analyses in country strategies.
Coordinate via **BPF delivery framework** (Figure 1); map complementary programmes (e.g., GEF’s Blue Forests Project).
Invest in **baseline studies** (Component D); partner with research institutions (e.g., IUCN for habitat data).

fcas_specific_lessons: In **Nigeria/Bangladesh**, political economy risks require **early engagement with ministries** to align with national priorities (e.g., NDCs).
In **Mozambique/Philippines**, climate hazards necessitate **contingency funds** for post-disaster recovery (e.g., typhoon-resistant aquaculture).
Lessons from **BRACED programme**: Community-led adaptation (e.g., LMMAs) improves sustainability but requires **longer timeframes** for trust-building.

lessons_from_previous.text: 1) **Mangrove restoration**: Past failures (e.g., Philippines 1980s–2000s) due to poor species/site selection → COAST includes **ecological assessments** in Component A. 2) **Fisheries co-management**: Evidence from Chile (territorial user rights) shows **formalized community rights** improve compliance → informs COAST’s LMMAs. 3) **Blue carbon**: Mikoko Pamoja’s **benefit-sharing model** (60% revenues to communities) adopted as best practice.

design_changes_based_on_learning.text: 1) **Phased approach**: Added **review points** (Section 73) to adjust based on early lessons (e.g., aquaculture pilot results). 2) **Gender inclusion**: Expanded from fisheries to **post-harvest value chains** (e.g., solar freezers for women in Solomon Islands). 3) **Finance mechanisms**: Incorporated **NGIs (Non-Grant Instruments)** (e.g., Meloy Fund) after GEF7 pilot success.

quote.text: Lessons from past initiatives highlight the importance of: i) **local ownership** in restoration projects (e.g., mangrove survival rates improved with community nurseries); ii) **integrated governance** to reduce sectoral conflicts (e.g., aquaculture vs. fisheries); and iii) **flexible financing** to bridge gaps between public and private funds (e.g., blue carbon credits).
quote.source: D0003167.odt, Risk management and risk register

co_funding_partners.note: COAST is a component of the £500m BPF; 100% ODA-funded via FCDO’s £190m allocation.
Expected to mobilize additional climate finance (e.g., carbon credits, impact investment).
Co-financing via LMMAs/blue carbon projects (e.g., Mikoko Pamoja’s 60% revenue share).

leverage_achieved.text: COAST aims to **unlock climate finance** through: 1) **Blue carbon credits**: Potential to mitigate 0.5–3% of global emissions (McKinsey 2022). 2) **NGIs**: Meloy Fund’s 1:6 leverage ratio (£6m GEF → £35m private capital). 3) **Government co-funding**: Alignment with NDCs to attract national budgets (e.g., Indonesia’s marine protection targets).

budget_breakdown.note: Budget allocations by component are implied but not explicitly detailed. Components A/D (commercial) likely have higher overheads; B/C (WorldFish/WEF) may channel more to Southern partners.

capital_vs_revenue_split.text: Mixed: 1) **Capital**: Infrastructure for coastal protection (e.g., mangrove nurseries), aquaculture facilities. 2) **Revenue**: Training, MEL, community grants. No explicit split provided.

quote.text:
Programme funding profile [...]
100% of COAST’s budget will contribute to HMG’s International Climate Finance (ICF) commitment. 85% will contribute to HMG’s commitment to spend £3 billion of ICF on protecting and restoring nature.
quote.source: D0003167.odt, Financial Case / Rationale for UK Aid

metadata.programme_name: Scaling Access and Learning in Education (SCALE)
metadata.quote: The Scaling Access and Learning in Education programme (SCALE) will support Posts with expert technical assistance and support to adapt evidence-based interventions to new contexts and get them on a pathway to scaling up. (D0003241.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: £68m over four years to improve the effectiveness of education financing in low and lower middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs) (D0003241.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SCALE combines implementation research (testing/scaling evidence-based interventions), capacity building (technical assistance to adapt interventions), and policy influence (shaping how governments and donors spend education funds). It focuses on improving foundational learning outcomes for disadvantaged children, especially girls, through cost-effective interventions that can be scaled sustainably.
what_objectives.q1_source: SCALE will bring together UK-led expertise, funding, support, and influence to increase the uptake of cost-effective interventions that deliver foundational learning outcomes for all, especially disadvantaged girls and boys. [...] Overseas Posts will be offered demand-driven support to adapt evidence-based interventions to new contexts and implement rigorous test-learn-adapt pilots to ready these for scaling in national systems. (D0003241.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 40 million more girls in school by 2026 (global objective)
20 million more girls learning to read by age 10/end of primary by 2026 (global objective)
Increased uptake of cost-effective education interventions by partner governments and donors
Technical support to adapt and scale evidence-based interventions (e.g., Teaching at the Right Level, structured pedagogy)
Financing and support for iterative ‘accelerator pilots’ to prepare interventions for scaling
Strategic partnerships with governments and donors (e.g., USAID, GPE, World Bank) to crowd-in resources
Disaggregated data by gender and disability status for monitoring
Safeguarding policies and procedures implemented across all programme activities
what_objectives.summary: SCALE aims to accelerate progress toward the UK’s G7-endorsed global education objectives by 2026, focusing on scaling cost-effective interventions that improve foundational learning (literacy, numeracy, socio-emotional skills) for marginalized children, particularly girls. It combines technical assistance, adaptive piloting, and strategic influence to maximize the impact of domestic and donor education spending in LICs/LMICs.
what_objectives.quote: The ultimate aim will be to ensure all girls and boys receive a high-quality education that leads to improved foundational learning outcomes for all through: Technical support [...] Financing and support for iterative and adaptive ‘accelerator pilots’ [...] Scaling: Staff time to build strategic partnerships [...] to crowd-in the resources and funds needed to scale up the strongest pilots and get millions of children learning. (D0003241.odt, How SCALE will contribute to the Pathway for Scaling Learning Outcomes)

countries_regions: Low and lower middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs)
Priority given to countries where girls’ education results are lagging and political will exists (specific countries not pre-selected; demand-driven process)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in contexts disrupted by COVID-19, with systemic challenges like weak education systems, political economy barriers, and implementation risks. The risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' in the document.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate. (D0003241.odt, Risk section)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (competing stakeholder interests, low-trust environments)
weak institutions (poor school management, governance, accountability systems)
data limitations (lack of comparable learning outcome data across countries)
conflict/fragility (potential operation in fragile and conflict-affected states)
climate risks (vulnerability of education systems to extreme weather events)
implementation constraints (e.g., Kenya’s failed scale-up of contract teachers due to political economy)
safeguarding risks (high prevalence of violence in schools, especially for girls and children with disabilities)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political economy barriers (e.g., misaligned stakeholder incentives, low-quality equilibria) and weak institutional capacity undermine the effectiveness of education reforms. Data limitations make it difficult to rank countries by need or compare interventions. Climate and conflict risks disrupt service delivery, while safeguarding concerns require robust policies to protect vulnerable groups.
where_context.quote: The technical and political barriers that challenge change need to be addressed to ensure scaled interventions deliver sustainable results. Technical Barriers can mean the complexity of the system; large number of factors, interdependence of reforms, slow pace of change in education systems. Political barriers can mean the competing interests of different players, difficulty of moving out of a low-quality equilibrium, especially in low-trust environments where risk predominates. (D0003241.odt, What needs to be done? section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) - Girls’ Education Department (GED)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO (UK-based) retains central decision-making authority, including final selection of accelerator pilots via a Programme Advisory Board. Overseas Posts (in-country) can apply for support but must align with centrally defined criteria and evidence standards.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to adapt evidence-based interventions (e.g., Teaching at the Right Level, structured pedagogy)
support for iterative ‘test-learn-adapt’ pilots to build local implementation capacity
training and resources for Ministry of Education counterparts to deliver reforms
safeguarding training for all programme staff and partners
capacity building for school support and monitoring (e.g., pedagogical improvements)

partner_organizations.name: Overseas Posts (FCDO country offices)
partner_organizations.role: Demand-driven applicants for technical assistance and accelerator pilots; implement adapted interventions

partner_organizations.name: Ministries of Education (partner governments)
partner_organizations.role: Counterparts for delivering and managing classroom-level inputs; align interventions with national priorities

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral donors (e.g., World Bank, Global Partnership for Education (GPE), Education Cannot Wait (ECW))
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partners to crowd-in funding for scaling successful pilots

partner_organizations.name: Bilateral donors (e.g., USAID)
partner_organizations.role: Collaborators for joint funding and technical alignment

partner_organizations.name: Philanthropic foundations (e.g., Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers and technical advisors for scaling interventions

partner_organizations.name: Technical Advisory Board (in-house and external experts)
partner_organizations.role: Quality assurance for evidence base of proposed interventions; reviews accelerator pilot applications

partner_organizations.name: Research institutions (e.g., RISE, What Works Hub for Global Education)
partner_organizations.role: Providers of evidence and implementation science to inform interventions

partner_organizations.name: Local Organizations of Persons with Disability
partner_organizations.role: Consulted for inclusive design of interventions

who_partners.quote: A new centrally-managed programme (CMP) run by Girls’ Education Department (GED) based in headquarters can support overseas Posts to accelerate at scale improvements in children’s learning outcomes by: [...] Providing extra capacity and resources (people, expertise, funding, evidence as appropriate to context), including in priority countries where we do not have FCDO advisers or active country-led programmes. (D0003241.odt, The case for a new UK centrally-led programme)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct FCDO funding for central technical assistance and competitive grants for accelerator pilots. Funds are allocated to Posts based on demand-driven applications, with a focus on preparing interventions for scale-up rather than long-term service delivery.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: SCALE operates as a centrally managed platform within FCDO’s Girls’ Education Department (GED), coordinating technical assistance, accelerator pilots, and scaling efforts. It integrates in-house advisors, external experts, and partner networks (e.g., multilaterals, Posts) to deliver cohesive support.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Posts submit applications against predefined criteria (e.g., education need, political will, UK influence), which are reviewed by a programme team and finalized by a Technical Advisory Board. This ensures alignment with evidence standards and strategic priorities while allowing country-level flexibility.
how_mechanism.quote: On this basis, there will be a process where Posts are invited to make the case for SCALE to provide policy/project design (technical assistance) or implement an accelerator pilot in their country, against a set of criteria. [...] A programme team will review interest from Posts and give a shortlist to the Programme Advisory Board for final selection. (D0003241.odt, Step 2: Where should SCALE prioritise working?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Programme Advisory Board (comprising in-house and external experts) reviews and approves accelerator pilot applications and provides quality assurance for evidence-based interventions. Day-to-day management is shared between FCDO’s GED (central technical support) and Overseas Posts (implementation).
how_governance.quote: The preferred option is to go for 1.3 Smart Buys+ [...] To mitigate against the risk of ‘bad buys’ being chosen, we will establish a technical Programme Advisory Board to quality assure the evidence-base for proposed accelerator pilots. (D0003241.odt, Step 1: What should be technical focus of the programme?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., technical assistance vs. accelerator pilots) based on demand and emerging opportunities, but require approval from the Programme Advisory Board. The focus remains on preparing interventions for scale rather than long-term delivery.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an iterative ‘test-learn-adapt’ approach for accelerator pilots, allowing adjustments based on real-time learning. However, major shifts in technical focus (e.g., adding new intervention types) require Board approval to ensure alignment with evidence standards.
how_flexibility.quote: Centralising this component [accelerator pilots] will allow flexible responsive allocation decisions to be made; and provide Posts with access to high-quality technical expertise, including for rigorous monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) to implement pilots effectively. (D0003241.odt, The case for a new UK centrally-led programme)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (GED) → Overseas Posts/implementing partners → (no explicit sub-grantees mentioned; Posts work directly with Ministries of Education and donors).
how_efficiency.quote: Financing and support for iterative and adaptive ‘accelerator pilots’: to prepare high potential education interventions for scaling, with a focus on accelerating progress against the 2026 global objectives on access and learning. (D0003241.odt, The case for a new UK centrally-led programme)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1.1: Narrow focus on Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) and structured pedagogy only
Option 1.2: Expand to all ‘Smart Buys’ interventions (great/good/promising per GEEAP)
Option 1.3 (chosen): ‘Smart Buys+’—all Smart Buys plus other cost-effective interventions from credible sources
Option 2.1 (discounted): Pre-selecting countries using quantitative education/ODA data
Option 2.2 (chosen): Demand-driven application process with Posts making the case against criteria
Continuing the Girls’ Education Challenge (GEC) in its current form (discounted at Concept Note stage)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The ‘Smart Buys+’ approach (Option 1.3) was selected for its flexibility to respond to diverse country contexts and emerging evidence, while the demand-driven process (Option 2.2) ensures political buy-in and local ownership. The centrally managed platform model was chosen to leverage FCDO’s technical expertise, multiply influence over donor/govt spending, and avoid the inefficiencies of direct service delivery in LMICs.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (cost-effectiveness of interventions, e.g., $100 per child for 3+ years of learning)
risk-mitigation (Programme Advisory Board to prevent ‘bad buys’)
experience (lessons from GEC and Kenya/Tanzania pilots)
partner-capacity (focus on Posts with in-country education advisers for higher success likelihood)
flexibility (ability to adapt to windows of opportunity and new evidence)
equity (targeting marginalized girls and children with disabilities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low-quality or non-scalable interventions selected due to political pressure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical Programme Advisory Board to quality-assure evidence base for all accelerator pilots.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited demand from Posts or misalignment with country priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Criteria emphasize political will and UK influence; initial focus on Posts with in-country education advisers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Implementation constraints (e.g., Kenya’s failed teacher contract scale-up)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Test-learn-adapt pilots to identify and address barriers before scaling; focus on government ownership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap or duplication with existing UK/multilateral programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Portfolio approach to build coherence across country programmes, global funds, and multilaterals.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per learning-adjusted year of schooling, e.g., $100 for 3+ years)
efficiency (leveraging existing donor/govt spending rather than direct delivery)
effectiveness (focus on foundational learning outcomes linked to SDG4 and G7 goals)
equity (prioritizing marginalized girls, children with disabilities, and conflict-affected contexts)
why_rationale.quote: Given the importance of political will in successful reforms, it is crucial we have adequate flexibility in the programme to respond to windows of opportunity that might go beyond structured pedagogy and TaRL. This allows us to retain flexibility to support other enabling interventions and reforms that can facilitate improved learning outcomes. (D0003241.odt, Step 1: What should be technical focus of the programme?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The demand-driven approach (WHERE) is constrained by the need for Posts to have sufficient in-country expertise and political influence (WHO). Fragile contexts (e.g., FCAS) limit partner options to those with conflict-sensitive experience, while data gaps in LICs/LMICs require reliance on Posts’ local knowledge over quantitative rankings.
q27_constraints_detail: Political will (only Posts with demonstrated government commitment can access support)
In-country expertise (initial focus on Posts with education advisers to ensure feasibility)
Fragility (FCAS contexts require partners with conflict-sensitive experience)
Data limitations (lack of comparable learning data shifts selection to qualitative Post assessments)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The focus on scaling cost-effective interventions (WHAT) drives the platform-based delivery structure (HOW), which centralizes technical assistance and adaptive piloting to maximize influence over donor/govt spending. The need for government ownership (to ensure sustainability) shapes the demand-driven application process and joint management model.
q28_linkages: Foundational learning focus → Platform structure (to coordinate technical support, pilots, and scaling)
Government ownership requirement → Demand-driven Post applications + joint FCDO/Post management
Cost-effectiveness priority → Competitive selection of ‘Smart Buys+’ interventions
Equity goals → Embedded safeguarding and disability-inclusive design in all components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (scaling proven interventions like TaRL) with equity (targeting marginalized girls and children with disabilities). Trade-offs include: (1) Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scaling risks leaving behind the hardest-to-reach groups, mitigated by disaggregated data and safeguarding policies. (2) Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: Central technical oversight ensures quality but limits local adaptive capacity, addressed via demand-driven Post applications.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed-vs-inclusion (prioritizing scalable interventions may exclude ultra-marginalized groups without targeted adaptations)
expertise-vs-ownership (UK-led technical standards vs. country-led adaptation needs)
cost-vs-reach (focus on influencing donor/govt spend to maximize leverage vs. direct service delivery)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Moderate’ risk profile drives milestone-based oversight and embedded safeguarding, with intensive management for accelerator pilots (high-risk/high-reward) and lighter touch for technical assistance. FCAS contexts would trigger additional conflict-sensitive coordination.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in all components: Posts receive technical support to adapt interventions, Ministries of Education are enlisted as delivery partners, and the Advisory Board ensures global expertise informs local action. The focus on ‘implementation science’ (what works, for whom, under what conditions) directly shapes partner roles in testing and scaling.
intersections.quote: Working at scale is hard. [...] A core aspect of this is the political economy and financing of delivery. For example, outside of a controlled experiment, who will deliver the intervention and what are the incentives that will encourage or undermine them engaging? (D0003241.odt, What needs to be done? section)

key_programme_risks: Global learning crisis exacerbated by COVID-19 (70% of children in LICs/LMICs now in learning poverty)
Low political will in partner governments to prioritize learning over access
Implementation failures during scale-up (e.g., Kenya’s contract teachers, Cambodia’s ECD centres)
Safeguarding risks (violence in schools, especially for girls and children with disabilities)
Data gaps limiting ability to track progress or compare interventions
Overlap with existing donor programmes leading to duplication
Limited Post demand or misalignment with country priorities
Climate shocks disrupting education delivery in vulnerable regions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demand-driven process requires Posts to demonstrate government commitment; focus on ‘windows of opportunity’ where reform is feasible.
Test-learn-adapt pilots to identify barriers before scaling; align interventions with government priorities and incentives (see Box B).
Robust safeguarding policies for all partners; disaggregated data by gender/disability; engagement with local Organizations of Persons with Disability.
Reliance on Posts’ local knowledge and qualitative assessments; support for improved MEL systems.
Portfolio approach to build coherence across UK aid channels (bilateral, multilateral, CMPs).
Integration of climate resilience in curriculum reforms where feasible; alignment with FCDO’s Climate and Education Position Paper.

fcas_specific_lessons: Activities in fragile states must be designed in a conflict-sensitive way, supporting system resilience (e.g., security, violence mitigation).
Strong coordination with Education in Emergencies principles and Education Cannot Wait (ECW) initiatives.
Higher safeguarding risks require enhanced due diligence and community engagement.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Girls’ Education Challenge (GEC) and Kenya/Tanzania pilots highlight the need for: (1) Government ownership early in the design phase, (2) rigorous piloting to generate evidence for scale-up, (3) alignment with existing donor programmes to avoid duplication, and (4) adaptive management to respond to implementation barriers.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from GEC’s direct service delivery to influencing donor/govt spending for greater leverage.
Centralized ‘accelerator pilots’ component to ensure rigorous MEL and scalability.
Explicit focus on ‘implementation science’ to address contextual adaptation challenges.
Embedded safeguarding and disability inclusion based on GEC experiences.
risks_lessons.quote: The reality of messy, political operating contexts can undermine well-designed interventions. [...] There are various examples of governments failing to take pilot programmes to scale. For example, the Government of Kenya tried to lower student teacher ratios by hiring contract teachers after a successful pilot by an NGO, but the results were negligible because of implementation and political economy constraints. (D0003241.odt, What needs to be done? section)

co_funding_partners.partner: Multilateral donors (e.g., World Bank, GPE, ECW)
Philanthropic foundations (e.g., Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to multiply UK investment by influencing how partner governments and donors (e.g., World Bank’s $1.6bn IDA education programming) spend their funds. For example, UK’s $260m bilateral spend in 2019 was dwarfed by $1.6bn from IDA, highlighting the leverage potential.
financial_details.quote: In-country IDA programming on education was £1.6bn in 2019 in comparison to £260m from FCDO. This programme will contribute to broader development diplomacy efforts to ensure that our contributions are being spent on interventions that have the greatest potential for value for money (VfM). (D0003241.odt, Meeting our ambition section)

metadata.programme_name: Women’s Integrated Sexual Health – Dividend (WISH Dividend)

quote.text: Women’s Integrated Sexual Health-Dividend is a six-year, up to £200 million programme...

metadata.duration_source: Women’s Integrated Sexual Health-Dividend is a six-year, up to £200 million programme that will support women and adolescents...

what_objectives.q1_explanation: WISH Dividend combines service delivery (direct provision of SRHR services), capacity building (strengthening health systems and institutions), policy influence (supporting policy reform and advocacy), and implementation research (testing and scaling integrated SRHR interventions). It aims to improve access to comprehensive SRHR services while strengthening systems for sustainability.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme will: Scale up sustainable, inclusive access to integrated SRHR services; Provide policy support to strengthen health systems, reform policies and laws, improve government ownership and domestic financing, and strengthen accountability to improve SRHR; Provide technical assistance to strengthen the evidence base, use of data and capacity on demographic transition...

q3_expected_outputs.output: Couple Years of Protection (CYP)
Unintended pregnancies averted
Unsafe abortions averted
Maternal deaths averted
Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) averted
Women supported to access SRHR services
Policy reforms supporting comprehensive SRHR and gender equality
Strengthened health systems for integrated SRHR service delivery
Improved demographic data use for policy and budget decisions
National frameworks for demographic dividend developed/implemented

what_objectives.summary: WISH Dividend aims to drive progress on comprehensive, universal SRHR to unlock the potential of women and girls while enabling African countries to accelerate an inclusive demographic transition. It combines direct service delivery with system strengthening, policy reform, and technical assistance to create sustainable change.

quote.text: WISH Dividend seeks to deliver the following impact: "drive progress on comprehensive, universal SRHR to unlock the full potential and power of women and girls and enable African countries to accelerate an inclusive demographic transition"
quote.source: D0004445.odt, What the Programme Will Deliver

countries_regions: Priority countries to be selected based on need (e.g., Niger, South Sudan, DRC, Somalia, Chad, Burundi, Uganda, Mali, Tanzania, Zambia)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme explicitly targets fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS) where unmet SRHR needs are highest. It mentions working in countries like South Sudan, Somalia, and DRC which are classified as FCAS, and includes a specific focus on women and girls in these contexts.
where_context.q5_source: WISH Dividend will have a strong focus on Leave No-One Behind, building on WISH’s efforts. Women and girls in Fragile and Conflict Affected Settings are particularly vulnerable... WISH Dividend will target fragile and conflict affected settings.
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks in FCAS limit service delivery and partner operations; weak health systems require significant capacity building; political opposition to SRHR (especially safe abortion) creates policy barriers; climate change disrupts supply chains and service outreach; data limitations hinder evidence-based planning; regulatory barriers affect commodity procurement; and poor infrastructure complicates last-mile delivery to marginalized groups.

quote.text: Despite efforts to improve the availability and uptake of the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP), unmet SRH needs remain high, for young people affected by humanitarian emergencies... WISH Dividend will support countries to plan and budget for future population needs. Population data is only useful if it is accessible, timely, complete, disaggregated and decision makers have the skills (and the will) to use it to understand the economy of financing choices.
quote.source: D0004445.odt, How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? and Demographic Transition support sections

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains primary decision-making authority over programme design, budget allocation, and strategic direction. While Southern partners (African governments, local NGOs, and regional institutions) are engaged in implementation and co-creation phases, final approvals and oversight rest with FCDO and its appointed programme managers (e.g., Oxford Policy Management for TPM).
q10_capacity_building_details: training and capacity building for healthcare workers (e.g., on comprehensive SRHR service delivery)
institutional strengthening of national/sub-national health systems (e.g., Ministry of Health teams, National Population Councils)
technical assistance and secondments to government ministries for policy reform (e.g., safe abortion, demographic transition planning)
support for civil society advocacy and accountability mechanisms
mentorship for local NGOs and disability-focused organizations (OPDs)
curriculum development and media training for evidence-based policy communication

partner_organizations.name: Oxford Policy Management (OPM)
partner_organizations.role: Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) and evaluation

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA (United Nations Population Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support on SRHR commodity security and policy alignment; regional coordination

partner_organizations.name: International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF)
partner_organizations.role: Potential implementing partner for SRHR service delivery (based on WISH predecessor)

partner_organizations.name: Marie Stopes International (MSI)
partner_organizations.role: Potential implementing partner for SRHR service delivery (based on WISH predecessor)

partner_organizations.name: African Union (AU)
partner_organizations.role: Policy framework alignment (e.g., "Harnessing the Demographic Dividend through Investments in Youth")

partner_organizations.name: National Ministries of Health (MoH)
partner_organizations.role: Primary government counterparts for health system strengthening and policy reform

partner_organizations.name: National Population Councils/Departments of Population
partner_organizations.role: Institutional capacity strengthening for demographic transition planning

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs and Organizations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs)
partner_organizations.role: Direct service delivery to marginalized groups; sub-grantees for community outreach

partner_organizations.name: Community Health Workers (CHWs)
partner_organizations.role: Frontline service providers for outreach in rural/fragile settings

partner_organizations.name: Private sector providers (e.g., pharmacies, social marketing franchises)
partner_organizations.role: Low-cost service delivery channels for contraception and SRHR commodities

quote.text: WISH Dividend will work with African governments to support national ownership and increase investments to accelerate the demographic transition... The programme will support a range of public facilities and low-cost private sector service providers, targeted outreach through static and mobile teams, community health workers and provision through alternative settings such as pharmacies/social marketing franchises... We will ensure that any consortium delivering the SRHR component of the programme includes organisations for people with disabilities (OPDs) as primary delivery partners and sub-grants to local OPDs.
quote.source: D0004445.odt, How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? and Compliance with Programme Operating Framework Requirements sections

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use a combination of contracts (for TPM and potentially SRHR service delivery) and grants/sub-grants (for local NGOs, OPDs, and government capacity building). The Accountable Grant Arrangement (AGA) framework is referenced, suggesting performance-based funding mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will be managed through a centrally coordinated regional structure with three main components: 1) SRHR service delivery (likely led by a consortium of international NGOs and local partners), 2) Demographic Transition support (technical assistance to governments), and 3) independent Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) by OPM. Country-level activities will be overseen by FCDO Posts and aligned with national health strategies.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The business case emphasizes the need for specialized expertise in SRHR (especially safe abortion and FCAS contexts) and demographic transition, which requires a competitive process to identify partners with proven capacity. The TPM contract was awarded to OPM through a competitive tender, and the SRHR component will follow a similar process to ensure value for money and technical quality.

quote.text: An independent third-party monitor will deliver independent oversight... The programme will be designed as a flexible and scalable programme that can adapt to budgetary changes... The SRHR component will evolve and work differently to give greater focus on supporting stronger country ownership... The programme will support a range of public facilities and low-cost private sector service providers...
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Programme summary and How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? sections

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Country-level steering committees will be chaired by Ministries of Health and include key partners (e.g., UNFPA, Global Financing Facility, civil society). The regional programme will have a central governance mechanism to coordinate across countries, with FCDO Posts playing a oversight role. Technical advisory support will be provided for demographic transition components.

quote.text: Earlier, deeper government engagement in governance of programmes at country level, for example by greater use of country steering committees chaired by Ministry of Health and including other key partners working in this space in country such as UNFPA, Global Financing Facility (GFF), UN Programme to End Child Marriage, and other large SRHR programmes in country... The programme will be designed as a flexible and scalable programme that can adapt to budgetary changes.
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Option A: Build on and evolve WISH and Programme summary sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between countries based on need/opportunity (using prioritization modeling), but requires FCDO approval. The programme is designed to be "flexible and scalable" to adapt to budgetary changes, though major shifts (e.g., adding new countries) would need central approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an inception/co-creation phase to refine country priorities, and annual reviews will allow adjustments based on learning. However, significant changes (e.g., shifting from SRHR to other sectors) would require FCDO sign-off. The TPM component is explicitly designed to generate lessons for adaptive management.

quote.text: The programme will be designed as a flexible and scalable programme that can adapt to budgetary changes... Use of the inception or co-creation phase to enable governments to better target and prioritise programme activities... The programme will not seek to have a specific focus on other key groups... although it will be led by the needs identified at country level during the inception phase.
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Programme summary and Option A sections

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Programme Management Unit (e.g., OPM for TPM) → Implementing Partners (international NGOs/local consortia) → Sub-grantees (local NGOs/OPDs/CHWs).

quote.text: The programme will support a range of public facilities and low-cost private sector service providers, targeted outreach through static and mobile teams, community health workers and provision through alternative settings such as pharmacies/social marketing franchises... An independent third-party monitor will deliver independent oversight...
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Programme summary and How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? sections

q24_alternatives_considered.option: A) Build on and evolve WISH (RECOMMENDED)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue the existing WISH programme with enhanced focus on sustainability, country ownership, and demographic transition, while maintaining its multi-country, rights-based approach.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: B) Multisectoral programme focusing on better outcomes for girls
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Shift to a broader girls’ empowerment programme integrating SRHR with education, economic opportunities, and GBV prevention.
Discontinue investment in SRHR programming in SSA.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option A was selected because it builds on WISH’s proven track record (9.5M women reached since 2018) and aligns with the UK’s strategic priorities on SRHR leadership, demographic transition, and women’s empowerment. The business case argues that continuity avoids the high start-up costs of new programmes and leverages existing partnerships, while the evolved design addresses gaps in sustainability and national ownership. The multi-country regional approach offers economies of scale, learning sharing, and flexibility to target high-need countries.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political opposition to SRHR (especially safe abortion) in target countries may limit policy reform or service delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work within national laws/frameworks; engage religious/community leaders; use regional platforms for advocacy; FCDO diplomatic support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak government capacity in FCAS may hinder ownership/sustainability of health systems strengthening.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on sub-national capacity building; secondments to ministries; phased transition of responsibilities; technical assistance for institutional development.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supply chain disruptions (e.g., contraceptive stockouts) due to global funding cuts or climate shocks.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage UNFPA’s Reproductive Health Commodities programme; diversify procurement channels; strengthen last-mile delivery with private sector.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding incidents in vulnerable settings (e.g., GBV, exploitation during service delivery).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embed safeguarding in partner contracts; mandatory training for frontline workers; community accountability mechanisms; FCDO safeguarding standards enforcement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication with other donors (e.g., USAID, World Bank) in priority countries.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Coordinate via FP2030 platforms; focus on underserved areas (e.g., safe abortion, disability inclusion); align with national health strategies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited disability inclusion due to partner capacity gaps.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Require OPDs as consortium members; disability data collection using Washington Group questions; targeted sub-grants for local disability orgs.

quote.text: Option A: Build on and evolve WISH... WISH, building on its predecessor programme PMDUP... has had significant success in delivering SRH results at scale... The next step in this journey is to build on these successes to embed them in nationally owned/funded services and systems... A focused programme on SRHR allows the FCDO to build on the success of WISH as one of the largest multi-country SRHR programmes globally and retain its key position as a global policy leader on SRHR... Adopting a multi-country approach through a centrally managed regional programme... allows sharing of learning, economies of scale and support to priority countries which do not have advisory support/ODA funds.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS and high-risk operating environment limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) Proven experience in fragile settings (e.g., MSI, IPPF); 2) Ability to navigate restrictive SRHR laws (e.g., safe abortion); 3) Local presence/relationships with governments and communities; 4) Safeguarding capacity for vulnerable groups. The need for disability inclusion further constrains partners to those with OPD networks. The regional approach requires partners with multi-country coordination experience.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS security risks exclude partners without conflict-zone experience
Legal restrictions on abortion in some countries limit partner options
Weak health systems require partners with institutional strengthening expertise
Disability inclusion mandates require OPD partnerships
Multi-country scope demands regional coordination capacity
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (service delivery + systems strengthening + policy influence) necessitate a closed consortium structure to integrate: 1) **Service delivery expertise** (NGOs for outreach/clinics); 2) **Policy/advocacy skills** (think tanks for demographic transition); 3) **Government engagement** (secondments to ministries); 4) **Independent oversight** (TPM for accountability). The need for adaptive management (e.g., responding to COVID-19 or climate shocks) drives the milestone-based governance and flexible budget reallocation mechanisms.
q28_linkages: Multi-country scope → Regional management structure (economies of scale)
FCAS focus → Embedded safeguarding and local partner requirements
Demographic transition goal → Technical assistance component for data/policy
Leave No One Behind → OPD inclusion and targeted outreach modalities
Policy influence objective → Government steering committees and secondments
