intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **Reaching marginalized groups** (e.g., PWD, adolescents in FCAS) vs. **achieving scale efficiently** (e.g., prioritizing high-population countries); 2) **Local ownership** (transitioning to government-led systems) vs. **rapid results** (NGO-led delivery in weak systems); 3) **Comprehensive SRHR** (including sensitive services like safe abortion) vs. **political feasibility** (working within national laws). The regional approach and flexible design are presented as solutions to balance these trade-offs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Inclusion of people with disabilities (PWD) increases costs (e.g., accessible clinics, OPD partnerships) but aligns with equity goals.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Mandated OPD inclusion in consortia; targeted sub-grants for local disability orgs.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Safe abortion services are high-impact but politically sensitive, risking programme disruption.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Delivered through specialized NGOs with regional advocacy support; framed within comprehensive SRHR.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Government ownership (slow, capacity-constrained) vs. NGO delivery (faster but less sustainable).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Phased transition plan with secondments and sub-national capacity building.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Multi-country flexibility (adaptive) vs. transaction costs of coordination.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Centralized TPM and regional learning platforms to reduce duplication.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk/FCAS context drives **intensive oversight** (e.g., embedded TPM, quarterly reviews in fragile settings) and **restricted partner selection** (only organizations with FCAS experience). Safeguarding risks necessitate additional layers of accountability (e.g., community feedback mechanisms). Political risks require FCDO diplomatic engagement at country level.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: 1) **International NGOs** (e.g., MSI, IPPF) provide technical training for service delivery; 2) **Local NGOs/OPDs** receive mentorship for advocacy and outreach; 3) **Government partners** get secondments for policy reform; 4) **TPM (OPM)** builds M&E capacity across implementers. The shift from vertical service delivery (WISH) to system strengthening (WISH Dividend) requires partners to take on **coaching roles** alongside direct implementation.

quote.text: A regional approach to SRHR brings additional benefits... it balances risk across different countries, allowing resources to be shifted to where they are most needed and where prospects for impact are greatest... The programme will not seek to have a specific focus on other key groups such as people living with HIV/AIDS, LGBT+ or sex workers, although it will be led by the needs identified at country level during the inception phase... WISH Dividend will focus on strengthening the evidence base, data systems and capacity of African stakeholders to use population data to inform policy and budget decisions...
quote.source: D0004445.odt, How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? and What the Programme Will Deliver sections

key_programme_risks: Sustained political will for SRHR/population policies may wane, disrupting reforms (e.g., safe abortion, family planning budgets).
Reductions in global/domestic SRHR funding could cause contraceptive stockouts, affecting service delivery.
Reputational risks due to sensitive nature of SRHR (e.g., abortion, adolescent services) in conservative contexts.
Safeguarding incidents in high-risk settings (e.g., GBV, exploitation during outreach).
Weak government capacity in FCAS may delay transition to national ownership.
Climate change and COVID-19 aftershocks may disrupt supply chains and service access.
Overlap with other donors (e.g., USAID, Global Fund) could lead to duplication or gaps.
Limited progress on demographic transition if fertility declines lag behind mortality improvements.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Engage religious/community leaders; align with national laws; use regional platforms for advocacy; FCDO diplomatic support at country level.
Leverage UNFPA’s commodity security programmes; diversify procurement; strengthen last-mile delivery with private sector partners.
Mandatory safeguarding training for all partners; community accountability mechanisms; FCDO safeguarding standards enforcement; incident reporting systems.
Phase transition to national ownership; provide secondments to ministries; focus on sub-national capacity building; technical assistance for institutional development.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risks from sensitive SRHR components
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work within national legal frameworks; develop robust communication strategies with FCDO comms teams; frame services as part of comprehensive health rights.
Build climate resilience into supply chains; use mobile/outreach teams for last-mile delivery; integrate SRHR into humanitarian response plans.
Coordinate via FP2030 and Global Financing Facility platforms; focus on underserved areas (e.g., safe abortion, disability inclusion); align with national health strategies.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, **Minimum Initial Service Packages (MISP)** for SRHR are often neglected in humanitarian responses; WISH Dividend will prioritize these through dedicated outreach teams.
Conflict settings require **localized partnerships** (e.g., with women’s groups, CHWs) to navigate access constraints; the programme will build on WISH’s experience in South Sudan/Somalia.
In fragile states, **government ownership is slower**—phased capacity building and secondments are critical (lesson from WISH).
**Safeguarding risks are higher** in FCAS; the programme will expand WISH’s referral pathways for GBV and exploit community feedback mechanisms.
FCAS **data systems are weaker**; the programme will invest in sub-national data collection (e.g., poverty hotspot mapping) to target interventions.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: WISH (2018–2023) demonstrated that: 1) **Multi-country programmes** achieve economies of scale but require strong regional coordination; 2) **Policy engagement** is most effective when paired with service delivery (e.g., using data to advocate for reforms); 3) **Localization** works best with phased capacity building (e.g., transitioning supervision to government teams); 4) **Safe abortion services** can be integrated into broader SRHR with careful advocacy; 5) **Disability inclusion** requires dedicated partners (OPDs) and data systems (Washington Group questions). WISH Dividend will address gaps in sustainability (e.g., domestic financing) and deepen work on social norms.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **vertical service delivery** (WISH) to **health systems strengthening** (WISH Dividend), with focus on integrating SRHR into primary care.
Added **demographic transition component** to address lagging fertility declines in SSA, building on FCDO’s existing advisory work.
Stronger emphasis on **national ownership** through earlier government engagement (e.g., co-creation phases, steering committees).
Expanded **Leave No One Behind** approach with explicit targets for PWD, adolescents, and FCAS populations.
**Flexible budget allocation** between countries based on need/opportunity (lesson from WISH’s rigid country assignments).
Enhanced **safeguarding measures** (e.g., mandatory partner assessments, community accountability) in response to incidents in WISH.
**Regional learning platforms** to replace HQ-led knowledge sharing, improving South-South exchange.

quote.text: There has been significant learning from WISH on what works... The next step in this journey is to build on these successes to embed them in nationally owned/funded services and systems... WISH Dividend will build on the lessons and successes of these programmes as priorities evolve... The programme will have a strong focus on Leave No One Behind... WISH Dividend will seek to offer continuity of support to countries previously supported under WISH where needed and feasible within resources...
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Options Appraisal and How will WISH Dividend meet these needs? sections

quote.text: The programme is estimated to support 10.4m women to access SRHR services, avert 9.5m unintended pregnancies, 3.4m unsafe abortions and 30,600 maternal deaths. It will be designed as a flexible and scalable programme that can adapt to budgetary changes... The programme will spend up to £200 million between 2023 and 2029...
quote.source: D0004445.odt, Programme summary and Expected Results sections

metadata.programme_name: African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Support Programme
metadata.quote: This programme will support the successful negotiation and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). It will contribute to the reduction of barriers to trade across the continent, increase economic integration and improve the trading environment for both UK and African business. (90000778.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: This BC proposes a budget of up to £35.12m over 4.5 years (i.e. c. £8.5m annually from 2022-23 and £1.04m during 2021-22). (90000778.odt, Scale–Ambition and Budget)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening African institutions), policy influence (supporting AfCFTA negotiations), and implementation research (testing trade facilitation measures). It also includes research components to understand impacts on poverty, gender, and climate.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will support the successful negotiation and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)... The programme will support faster and more complete implementation of the AfCFTA, working at both continental and national levels. (90000778.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Technically capable African institutions coordinate well and use strong policy knowledge to enable an effective and inclusive AfCFTA (outcome)
An effectively negotiated and implemented AfCFTA reduces barriers to trade, drives inclusive and green economic growth and reduces poverty (impact)
Support to continental trade policy via policy documents, training sessions, and a digital information hub
Support to national trade policy via policy documents, discussions, and training
Support to continental trade facilitation via policy documents and training
Support to national trade facilitation via ICT systems and capacity building
Trade policy research on gender, green recovery, industrialisation, and poverty impacts
30 million people lifted from extreme poverty and 68 million from moderate poverty (World Bank estimate)
29% increase in total African exports by 2035 (World Bank estimate)
81% increase in intra-African exports by 2035 (World Bank estimate)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to accelerate AfCFTA implementation through technical assistance, capacity building, and research to reduce trade barriers, promote inclusive growth, and lift millions out of poverty.
what_objectives.quote: Fully implementing the AfCFTA could lift an additional 30 million people from extreme poverty and 68 million people from moderate poverty. (90000778.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: Targeted countries likely including South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The document explicitly states 'Overall programme risk rating: Major' and discusses political economy challenges, weak institutions, and fragmented regional governance across Africa.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major (90000778.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: High trade costs, bureaucratic delays (66% longer and 72% more expensive than East Asia), poor logistics infrastructure, protectionist tendencies, and lack of coordination between RECs create significant barriers to intra-African trade. COVID-19 has exacerbated these challenges by disrupting supply chains and increasing health-related trade restrictions.
where_context.quote: The World Bank’s ‘Trading Across Borders’ dataset shows that bureaucracy and border delays make trading across borders in Africa significantly more challenging than in any other region: it takes 66% longer and is 72% more expensive in sub-Saharan Africa compared to the average for East Asia and the Pacific. (90000778.odt, Why is trade so constrained?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority through governance structures and approval processes, while African institutions (AfCFTA Secretariat, AUC, RECs) provide technical input and implementation support. The programme explicitly aims to build African institutional capacity to eventually reduce reliance on external support.
q10_capacity_building_details: embedded advisors in AfCFTA Secretariat
training for trade officials
institutional strengthening of RECs and member states
development of trade facilitation guidelines
ICT systems for trade (e.g., single windows)
policy research fellowships
gender-focused capacity building
climate mainstreaming training

partner_organizations.name: Overseas Development Institute (ODI)
partner_organizations.role: Primary delivery partner (technical assistance, research, embedded advisors)

partner_organizations.name: TradeMark East Africa (TMEA)
partner_organizations.role: Trade facilitation implementation (ICT systems, customs support)

partner_organizations.name: AfCFTA Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: Continental coordination and monitoring

partner_organizations.name: African Union Commission (AUC)
partner_organizations.role: Political oversight and regional integration

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) - African Trade Policy Centre (ATPC)
partner_organizations.role: Policy research and advisory support

partner_organizations.name: Targeted African governments (e.g., South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana)
partner_organizations.role: National implementation and policy reform

partner_organizations.name: Regional Economic Communities (RECs: COMESA, ECOWAS, EAC, SADC)
partner_organizations.role: Sub-regional implementation and coordination

who_partners.quote: The preferred option would work with our existing implementing partner, ODI, to maximise the benefits of building on the relationships and expertise already established through the AUSP. It would also bring in additional expertise in trade facilitation through TMEA. (90000778.odt, Preferred Option–How)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses accountable grants for ODI and a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) annex for TMEA, combining direct funding with partnership agreements to leverage existing relationships and expertise.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the programme through a consortium of two primary partners (ODI and TMEA) with predefined roles. ODI leads on policy and research, while TMEA focuses on trade facilitation implementation. Governance includes advisory boards at continental and national levels.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection builds on existing successful relationships established through the African Union Support Programme (AUSP) and TradeMark East Africa (TMEA), which have demonstrated effectiveness in supporting AfCFTA negotiations and trade facilitation. This avoids procurement delays and leverages institutional knowledge.
how_mechanism.quote: The preferred option would work with our existing implementing partner, ODI, to maximise the benefits of building on the relationships and expertise already established through the AUSP. (90000778.odt, Preferred Option–How)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme includes continental and national advisory boards composed of FCDO, partner representatives, and African stakeholders. These boards provide strategic oversight and approve major decisions, with FCDO retaining final approval authority. Political support is integrated through HMG colleagues in Addis Ababa, Accra, and selected countries.
how_governance.quote: The political analysis will enable flexibility and adaptability across the programme, building the programme’s confidence to learn lessons and to stop doing things if not successful or not gaining the necessary political traction. A pipeline of activities will be developed to enable the programme to adapt quickly. (90000778.odt, Preferred option-What)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme uses a portfolio approach that allows reallocation between components (e.g., shifting focus from stalled negotiation areas to faster-moving themes like digital trade or investment). Funds can be redirected based on political economy analysis and progress reviews.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes regular political economy analysis to identify emerging opportunities or blockages. Activities can be dropped or expanded based on traction, with advisory boards providing real-time feedback. For example, if services liberalisation talks stall, resources can shift to e-commerce or investment protocols.
how_flexibility.quote: A successful programme will have a mechanism to regularly review opportunities and reallocate resources as appropriate... Some themes will move faster than others... An additional complication is the need to build coalitions of member states who are willing to push for more ambitious action on a specific topic. (90000778.odt, Appraisal Criteria)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Primary partners (ODI/TMEA) → End beneficiaries (AfCFTA Secretariat, AUC, member states, businesses). The structure avoids additional intermediaries by working directly with established partners.
how_efficiency.quote: The use of ODI and TMEA as delivery partners will promote efficiency, as they are in any case heavily engaged with this agenda, and so FCDO will not have to cover the full cost of their overhead and management time. (90000778.odt, Value for money will be designed)

q24_alternatives_considered: Support only continental processes (no direct member state engagement)
Support only member states (no continental-level work)
Drawdown facility only (rapid response mechanism without sustained support)
Support research on cross-cutting themes (no implementation focus)
Provide funding to other development partners (e.g., World Bank, EU)
Procure new delivery partner (open competition)
Provide financial aid directly to AfCFTA Secretariat
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed approach (continental + national + research + drawdown) was selected to address coordination gaps identified in previous programmes, leverage existing partner expertise (ODI/TMEA), and ensure flexibility to adapt to the AfCFTA’s evolving political economy. Direct awards to existing partners were chosen for speed, institutional knowledge, and proven track records in African trade support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a small number of partners (ODI/TMEA) could limit innovation or local ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme includes advisory boards with African representation and regular political economy analysis to ensure responsiveness to local needs. Capacity building for African institutions is a core objective to reduce long-term dependency.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Direct awards without competition may reduce value for money or introduce perceptions of bias.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners were selected based on demonstrated success in prior phases (e.g., AUSP’s independent evaluation praised ODI’s flexibility and influence). The mixed consortium structure (ODI + TMEA) introduces complementary expertise.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex governance with multiple advisory boards could slow decision-making.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear decision-rights are assigned to FCDO, with boards focused on strategic oversight rather than operational details. The portfolio approach allows for rapid reallocation if bottlenecks emerge.

why_rationale.quote: The overall preferred option is to support all four activities, while working with existing partners. This option is now explored in detail... A significant advantage of this approach will be to overcome coordination problems that can sometimes beset trade agreements, by actively supporting coalitions of member states where they wish to push for more ambitious and liberalising outcomes. (90000778.odt, Preferred option-What)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The pan-African scope and political fragmentation across 55 AU member states require partners with deep regional experience (e.g., ODI/ATPC) and the ability to navigate complex RECs. Weak institutional capacity in some member states limits the pool of potential local implementers, necessitating a mix of continental (Secretariat/AUC) and national engagement.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing relationships across multiple RECs (COMESA, ECOWAS, etc.)
Language barriers require multilingual teams (AU has 4 official languages)
Political economy varies significantly between countries (e.g., Nigeria’s protectionist tendencies vs. Kenya’s liberalisation)
Secretariat’s limited financial management capacity precludes direct funding
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for simultaneous continental (negotiation support) and national (implementation) engagement drives the consortium structure (ODI for policy + TMEA for facilitation). The mixed objective of policy influence and capacity building requires embedded advisors (for real-time influence) alongside standalone research (for evidence generation).
q28_linkages: Policy influence objectives → Require embedded advisors in Secretariat/AUC
Implementation research → Requires TMEA’s trade facilitation expertise
Capacity building core objective → Shapes partner selection (ODI’s training experience)
Flexibility needs → Dictate portfolio approach and adaptive management
Gender/climate cross-cutting themes → Require ATPC’s thematic expertise
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery (using Northern partners like ODI) and local ownership (building African institutional capacity). For example, embedded advisors provide immediate technical support but require parallel capacity building to ensure sustainability. The drawdown facility balances efficiency (rapid response) with equity (supporting non-focus countries).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to ODI/TMEA accelerate delivery but risk sidelining local firms
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led technical assistance vs. Southern-led implementation
Cost vs. reach: Limited budget (£35.12m) must cover 55 countries, requiring prioritisation
Flexibility vs. accountability: Adaptive management needs robust oversight to prevent mission creep
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, political economy analysis) and governance structures (advisory boards). High fragmentation across RECs necessitates coordination mechanisms like the digital implementation monitoring hub.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak capacity in some member states shifts more responsibility to continental bodies (Secretariat/AUC), while stronger countries (e.g., South Africa, Kenya) receive direct support. Capacity building is embedded in all components (e.g., training for Secretariat staff, ICT systems for customs agencies).
intersections.quote: Political economy can be a challenge to effective implementation of regional trade agreements in Africa... It is essential for any trade programming to carefully evaluate the political economy. (90000778.odt, Building on the UK’s track record)

key_programme_risks: Lack of political commitment from member states derailing implementation
Protectionist backlash against liberalisation
Weak institutional capacity in RECs/Secretariat slowing progress
Coordinating 55 diverse countries with varying priorities
COVID-19 disrupting trade flows and negotiations
Informal traders (mostly women) being disadvantaged by formalisation
Climate shocks affecting trade corridors
Donor coordination challenges leading to duplication
Sustainability of reforms post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded advisors in Secretariat/AUC to maintain momentum; targeted support to influential countries (e.g., Nigeria, South Africa); regular political economy analysis.
Focus on ‘win-win’ areas like trade facilitation (e.g., customs reform) that reduce costs without threatening domestic industries; build coalitions of progressive member states.
Capacity building as a core objective (training, ICT systems, institutional twinning); gradual transfer of responsibilities to African institutions.
Portfolio approach to focus on willing countries; digital monitoring hub to track progress; RECs as intermediaries.
Flexible funding to address emerging barriers (e.g., health-related NTBs); research on pandemic-resilient trade policies.
Gender-focused research and policy design; simplified trading regimes for small businesses; consultation with women’s trade associations.
Climate mainstreaming across all activities; support for green recovery policies; resilient infrastructure design.

fcas_specific_lessons: Past RECs (e.g., Tripartite Agreement) stalled due to protectionist blocages—AfCFTA must avoid ‘least common denominator’ outcomes
Fragmented regional governance requires continental-level coordination (hence Secretariat support)
Political economy analysis is critical in FCAS contexts to identify reform champions and veto players
Trade facilitation (e.g., single windows) reduces rent-seeking opportunities that fuel conflict
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The AUSP evaluation highlighted the effectiveness of embedded advisors and flexible, demand-driven support. Key lessons included: (1) Regional dynamics are critical—programmes must work across multiple countries; (2) National-level implementation is essential for regional agreements to take effect; (3) Private sector engagement is vital for translating policy into practice; (4) Trade agreements must be paired with facilitation to deliver real-world benefits; (5) Unintended consequences (e.g., job losses in protected sectors) require mitigation strategies.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The new programme expands AUSP’s scope to include national implementation (previously continental-only), adds a drawdown facility for responsiveness, and integrates climate/gender analysis (absent in earlier phases). The consortium structure (ODI + TMEA) addresses the need for both policy and practical trade facilitation expertise identified in lessons learned.
risks_lessons.quote: Regional dynamics are key, and any trade programming must be able to work effectively in multiple countries and with regional bodies... While regional governance is important, trade policy and trade facilitation can only be practically implemented through action at national level. (90000778.odt, Building on the UK’s track record)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme expects to leverage additional donor coordination through the UK-chaired donor group and by aligning with World Bank/GIZ activities, though no specific co-funding amounts are stated.
financial_details.quote: A budget of up to £35.12m over 4.5 years (i.e. c. £8.5m annually from 2022-23 and £1.04m during 2021-22)... Continental level: About £1.5m per annum is needed to fund three experts at the Secretariat... Countries would be more demanding of budgets, with £1.65m allocated to each country. (90000778.odt, Scale–Ambition and Budget)

metadata.programme_name: Building Peace and Stability in Iraq (BPSI)
metadata.quote: The Building Peace and Stability in Iraq (BPSI) programme will use ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ components of rehabilitation to address barriers to return and reintegration in Daesh-affected communities in north and west Iraq including underlying socio-political grievances at the root of displacements. (D0001021.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: A 5-year approach will enable us to effect transformative policy change on complex issues, advocate for a coherent international response and bolster Government ownership including the proposed roadmap for reintegration in north and west Iraq. (D0001021.odt, Problem Statement)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The BPSI programme combines implementation research (testing interventions for return and reintegration), capacity building (strengthening local institutions and civil society), policy influence (advocating for legal and coordination reforms), and service delivery (providing hard infrastructure and soft rehabilitation services). It aims to address both immediate barriers to return and long-term drivers of instability in Iraq.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme will: Address barriers to return, reintegration and reconciliation of Iraqis still displaced including perceived Da’esh-affiliated families. [...] Evaluate impact and generate evidence to inform engagement, targeted advocacy and enhance institutional memory. (D0001021.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Barriers to return and reintegration of 1.2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) addressed
Access to justice for local communities and reintegration of juveniles in disenfranchised areas supported
Donor influence and Government commitment to reconstruction and reconciliation maximized
Evidence generated to inform engagement, targeted advocacy, and institutional memory
Social cohesion and political settlement in Daesh-affected governorates (Ninewa, Anbar, Salah al-Din, Diyala, Kirkuk) enhanced
Women’s rights and access to justice improved, particularly for women-headed households
Localisation of durable solutions increased through empowerment of Iraqi civil society and government ownership
Policy influence at national and governorate levels on legal systems, coordination, and Al Hol returns
Institutional memory developed through research and comparative analysis with other conflict zones
what_objectives.summary: BPSI aims to create durable solutions for Daesh-related displacement in Iraq by combining grassroots rehabilitation (both hard infrastructure and soft social/legal interventions) with national-level advocacy to influence government policy and international coordination. The programme focuses on the most conflict-affected governorates while promoting women’s inclusion and local ownership.
what_objectives.quote: The intended Outcome of the programme is: Daesh-related displacement is addressed by ensuring that barriers to returns and reintegration are tackled, and the displaced are rehabilitated and returned to Daesh affected governorates. This should contribute to the Impact: the social, political, and institutional capacity for reintegration of returnees and IDPs are enhanced in the Daesh affected governorates. (D0001021.odt, The Proposed Approach)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Iraq remains in a fragile post-conflict state with ongoing tensions between Sunni and Shi’a communities, weak government institutions, active Daesh insurgency tactics, and 1.2 million IDPs facing barriers to return. The programme explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Major" and operates in areas with security restrictions where HMG staff cannot travel.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major (D0001021.odt, Summary Sheet) [...] Conflict will persist, whether in overt or covert form, until northern and western Iraq become stable, peaceful, and prosperous. (D0001021.odt, Building Peace and Stability) [...] HMG staff are at much higher risk than those of UN agencies and NGOs. (D0001021.odt, The Programme)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit HMG staff travel to conflict-affected areas, requiring third-party monitoring. Weak institutions and political fragmentation (e.g., delayed government formation post-2021 elections) hinder coordination. Infrastructure destruction (30,000+ houses damaged) and legal system inconsistencies (tribal vs. formal law) create barriers to return. Language barriers (meetings in English) and lack of localised planning reduce inclusion of Iraqi NGOs. Data limitations on displacement dynamics complicate targeting.
where_context.quote: HMG staff are at much higher risk than those of UN agencies and NGOs. (D0001021.odt, The Programme) [...] The Government has many often competing priorities spreading human and financial resources thinly. (D0001021.odt, Localisation) [...] National NGOs complain that they are not properly included in planning and implementation. This is partly because of funding shortages. There is also an issue of language. Iraqi NGOs point out that most meetings are held in English and most documents are written in English. (D0001021.odt, Localisation)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme uses a blended approach where IOM (multilateral) leads on hard infrastructure and national advocacy, while a consortium of Iraqi NGOs (Southern) drives soft rehabilitation and grassroots implementation. Decision-making is shared: IOM and NGOs jointly identify project areas and priorities, with IOM handling national-level influencing and the consortium manager (an INGO) ensuring compliance. Local NGOs have significant input in community-level decisions, while IOM provides technical and coordination leadership.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for national NGOs on programme management and safeguarding
mentorship through consortium management by an international NGO
institutional strengthening of Iraqi civil society for sustainability
advocacy capacity building for NGOs to influence policy
legal system training to rationalize formal/tribal/informal laws
coordination skills for local NGOs to engage with UN/government systems

partner_organizations.role: UN implementing partner (hard infrastructure, advocacy, coordination)

partner_organizations.name: Consortium of ~5 national NGOs (names TBD via competitive bidding)
partner_organizations.role: Soft rehabilitation (legal work, community engagement, social cohesion)

partner_organizations.name: International NGO (consortium manager)
partner_organizations.role: Management of national NGO consortium, compliance, capacity building

partner_organizations.name: NGO Coordination Committee for Iraq (NCCI)
partner_organizations.role: Advocacy partner to strengthen influencing capacity

partner_organizations.name: Third-party monitoring organization
partner_organizations.role: Independent verification of results and safeguarding checks

partner_organizations.name: Social researchers/academics
partner_organizations.role: Evidence generation and comparative analysis

partner_organizations.name: Government of Iraq (GoI) ministries
partner_organizations.role: Policy target and implementation partner (e.g., Ministry of Migration)

partner_organizations.name: Local government and civil society in target districts
partner_organizations.role: Direct implementation partners for grassroots action

who_partners.quote: FCDO would partner with implementing partner UN agency directly. However, given the risks of working directly with National NGO’s identified under Option 3, FCDO would contract an international NGO to act as Consortium Manager to ensure compliance with FCDO requirements and international standards of programme, financial and risk management. (D0001021.odt, Option 4) [...] The NGO consortium will work in conjunction with IOM. Collectively, they will identify project areas, recommend policies, and shape the nature of programme activities. (D0001021.odt, The Programme)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of direct contracts (with IOM and the consortium manager INGO) and sub-grants (to national NGOs via competitive bidding). IOM receives block funding for hard infrastructure, while the consortium manager distributes funds to local NGOs for soft rehabilitation. This blended approach allows FCDO to leverage UN technical capacity while ensuring local ownership.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO contracts IOM directly for hard infrastructure and an international NGO as consortium manager for soft rehabilitation. The consortium manager oversees ~5 national NGOs selected via competitive bidding. IOM and the NGO consortium coordinate jointly at the community level, with IOM leading national advocacy. A third-party organization handles monitoring due to security constraints.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Early Market Engagement followed by a call for proposals (ratio not specified)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition ensures selection of national NGOs with demonstrated experience in BPSI’s priority areas (legal and social cohesion) and deep local knowledge. The two-stage process (Early Market Engagement + call for proposals) balances inclusivity with quality assurance, while the consortium manager mitigates risks of working directly with local NGOs (e.g., political affiliations, capacity gaps).
how_mechanism.quote: Through a competitive bidding process, approximately five national NGOs and an international NGO will be recruited as implementers of BPSI’s soft project elements. There will be an Early Market Engagement and thereafter a call for proposal to kickstart the selection process. (D0001021.odt, The Programme) [...] FCDO would contract an international NGO entity to manage the consortium. This organisation would help FCDO with due diligence, compliance, and accounting. (D0001021.odt, Option 3)

how_governance.quote: The NGO consortium will work in conjunction with IOM. Collectively, they will identify project areas, recommend policies, and shape the nature of programme activities [...] Their decisions will align with the overarching objectives of BPSI and Iraq’s Country Business Plan. (D0001021.odt, The Programme) [...] Monitoring will be an important part of the programme [...] We will use third-party monitoring to address this issue, contracting a specialist organisation with reach and trust in target communities. (D0001021.odt, The Programme)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be shifted between hard and soft components based on community needs, but requires joint decision-making by IOM and the NGO consortium. The blended approach allows flexibility in resource allocation across geographic locations and intervention types, though major reallocations would likely need FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme incorporates regular monitoring and locally driven policy design to adjust to volatile conditions. Flexibility is explicitly noted as integral due to Iraq’s instability, with provisions to reallocate funds or change locations based on results and learning. The Theory of Change assumes adaptive management to respond to deteriorating security or emerging needs.
how_flexibility.quote: Flexibility is integral. Iraq is highly volatile, and interventions and locations may change over the course of the programme depending on results and learning. (D0001021.odt, The Programme) [...] If conflict intensity were to increase [...] flexibility should be incorporated so that, should the situation deteriorate, funds can be reallocated to humanitarian operations. (D0001021.odt, Theory of Change)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) IOM (hard infrastructure) and (2) International NGO consortium manager → (3) National NGOs (soft rehabilitation)
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will be compliant with the International Development Act (2002), Public Sector Equality Duty as incorporated in the Gender Equality Act, 2010. (D0001021.odt, Assurance) [...] Monitoring will be an important part of the programme [...] We will use third-party monitoring to address this issue. (D0001021.odt, The Programme)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (no programme)
Option 2: Multilateral approach (delivery through UN agencies only)
Option 3: Localised approach (delivery through national NGOs only)
Option 4: Blended approach (delivery through both multilateral and national organisations) - PREFERRED
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The blended approach (Option 4) was selected because it combines the technical capacity and influence of UN agencies (IOM) with the local knowledge and sustainability of national NGOs, while mitigating the weaknesses of each. The UN provides hard infrastructure expertise and government access, while NGOs offer grassroots legitimacy and cost-efficiency. This structure maximizes value for money, flexibility, and leverage for policy influence—critical for addressing Iraq’s complex displacement challenges.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: National NGOs may be associated with criminal or terrorist organizations (political affiliations).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Thorough due diligence, third-party AML/CTF risk management, and triangulation of information from diverse sources. Consortium manager (international NGO) will oversee compliance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN agencies’ top-down approach may lack local ownership and sustainability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pairing IOM with national NGOs ensures local embedding and transition planning. Advocacy focuses on government leadership to avoid parallel systems.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs from UN sub-contracting fees (typically 7%).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Blended approach reduces reliance on UN for soft components, using cost-effective national NGOs where possible.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak administrative controls in national NGOs.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: International NGO consortium manager provides financial/programme oversight and capacity building.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government unwillingness to assume responsibility for reconstruction.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will supplement programme work with collaboration with like-minded donors and soft conditionality to incentivize government ownership.

why_rationale.quote: Neither Option 2 nor Option 3 provides everything that is needed. The strengths and weaknesses of NGOs and the UN are complementary: where the UN is strong, the NGOs are weak, and vice versa. By joining these options, FCDO would get the best of both worlds: the resources and influence of the UN system combined with the local knowledge of Iraqi civil society while maximising sustainability, VFM and leverage. (D0001021.odt, Conclusion of options’ analysis) [...] Criteria assessed: Technical capacity, Local knowledge, Sustainability, Influence, Cost-effective, Equitable, Administration and control, Flexibility. (D0001021.odt, The Strategic Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Iraq constrains partner selection by: (1) limiting international staff access to conflict zones (requiring local NGOs for grassroots work), (2) necessitating security-vetted partners due to Daesh risks, (3) demanding Arabic/Kurdish language skills for community engagement, and (4) requiring partners with existing trust in Sunni-majority areas where government presence is weak. The volatile security environment also mandates third-party monitoring, as FCDO staff cannot travel to most target areas.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks prevent FCDO/HMG staff from operating directly in target areas, requiring local partners with existing access.
Political fragmentation (Sunni-Shi’a tensions, militia influence) necessitates partners with neutral credibility.
Legal system complexities (tribal vs. formal law) demand partners with specialized knowledge.
Language barriers (English-dominated UN meetings) exclude non-international actors without translation support.
Weak government capacity in Daesh-affected governorates requires partners who can navigate bureaucratic gaps.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (hard/soft rehabilitation + policy influence) determine the blended delivery structure: (1) Hard infrastructure requires UN technical capacity (IOM), (2) Soft rehabilitation demands local NGOs’ community trust, and (3) Policy influence needs IOM’s government access paired with NGOs’ grassroots evidence. The need for both rapid service delivery (UN) and sustainable local ownership (NGOs) shapes the consortium model.
q28_linkages: Hard infrastructure goals → UN/IOM implementation (technical expertise for roads, housing, clinics).
Soft rehabilitation goals → National NGO consortium (social cohesion, legal aid, community dialogue).
Policy influence goals → IOM (national advocacy) + NCCI (civil society amplification).
Localisation goals → Consortium manager (capacity building for NGOs) + direct NGO funding.
Evidence generation goals → Third-party monitoring (independent verification) + academic researchers.
Flexibility needs → Blended structure allows shifts between hard/soft components based on context.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between: (1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: UN agencies offer faster delivery but risk excluding local NGOs (only 31% of HRP partners are national), while direct NGO funding requires lengthy due diligence. (2) **Expertise vs. Ownership**: International actors (IOM/INGO manager) provide technical capacity but reduce local control; the consortium model aims to balance this. (3) **Cost vs. Reach**: National NGOs are cost-effective but lack economies of scale for hard infrastructure, necessitating UN involvement despite higher overheads.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: UN agencies provide rapid, large-scale service delivery but create parallel systems that undermine government ownership (e.g., FFS co-funding stipulations ignored).
National NGOs offer sustainable, context-specific solutions but require significant capacity building and risk management (e.g., political affiliations).
Direct NGO funding reduces transaction costs (no UN sub-contracting fees) but increases FCDO management burden for compliance and safeguarding.
Localisation improves equity but slows implementation due to language barriers (English-dominated coordination) and weak NGO administrative systems.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight mechanisms: (1) third-party monitoring replaces FCDO field visits, (2) consortium manager adds a compliance layer for NGOs, (3) milestone-based payments mitigate fraud in high-corruption environments, and (4) adaptive management structures allow reallocation if conflict escalates. The FCAS context also necessitates embedded safeguarding controls (e.g., enhanced due diligence for CTF risks).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) National NGOs receive training on programme management and safeguarding to meet FCDO standards, (2) IOM’s role includes mentoring NGOs on advocacy to amplify local voices in policy dialogues, (3) The consortium manager’s capacity-building mandate ensures NGOs can eventually transition to direct government partnerships, and (4) Legal system training for NGOs enables them to bridge formal/tribal/informal justice gaps.
intersections.quote: The UN systems are typically macro and top-down, failing to incorporate the ‘hyper-localised’ approach required for Durable Solutions. (D0001021.odt, Localisation) [...] National NGOs have extremely strong local knowledge, as they live within the communities that they assist. (D0001021.odt, Option 3) [...] The UN is expensive, as they have high staff and overhead costs when compared with other options. (D0001021.odt, Option 2) [...] FCDO would contract an international NGO to act as Consortium Manager to ensure compliance with FCDO requirements and international standards. (D0001021.odt, Option 4)

key_programme_risks: Government inability/unwillingness to assume responsibility for reconstruction (mitigation: donor collaboration and soft conditionality).
National NGOs’ potential affiliation with criminal/terrorist groups (mitigation: due diligence, third-party AML/CTF checks).
Daesh resurgence or conflict escalation (mitigation: adaptive management, humanitarian reallocation provisions).
Lack of social acceptance for returnees (mitigation: holistic reintegration programmes targeting both returnees and host communities).
Weak coordination between UN, government, and NGOs (mitigation: IOM-led coordination with NCCI support).
Insufficient localised planning in UN-led frameworks (mitigation: NGO consortium input into project design).
Economic instability (e.g., unemployment, youth bulge) fueling extremism (mitigation: livelihoods support integrated into rehabilitation).
Legal system inconsistencies blocking property/ID access (mitigation: advocacy for unified legal processes).
FCDO’s small budget (~£25m) being too thinly spread (mitigation: leveraging influence to mobilize partner financing).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Government loses appetite for addressing social/political rehabilitation.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will supplement programme work with collaboration with like-minded donors and officials to incentivize government ownership, including through soft conditionality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: National NGOs are front organizations for political parties/militias.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Thorough due diligence, third-party AML/CTF risk management, and triangulation of information from diverse sources. Consortium manager oversees compliance.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Conflict intensifies, making community dialogue unsafe.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexibility built into programme to reallocate funds to humanitarian operations if needed. Adaptive management structures allow shifts in intervention types.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UN-led Durable Solutions framework ignores local complexities.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: NGO consortium provides hyper-local input into project design; Area-Based Coordination mechanisms include national NGOs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Women and girls face discrimination in legal/property rights.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Explicit focus on women’s access to justice; gender equality marker (‘Significant’); women-headed households prioritized in legal aid.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of trust in justice system deters returns.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support for ‘locally rooted restorative justice mechanisms’ (Mercy Corps) and advocacy to rationalize formal/tribal/informal laws.

fcas_specific_lessons: Localisation is critical but requires mitigating risks of elite capture (e.g., NGOs as militia fronts).
Top-down UN frameworks must be adapted to ‘hyper-local’ contexts to avoid exclusion.
Legal pluralism (tribal/formal/informal laws) demands tailored interventions—one-size-fits-all approaches fail.
Post-conflict rehabilitation must address both physical (housing, services) and social (trust, stigma) barriers simultaneously.
Women’s disenfranchisement in conflict zones requires targeted legal and economic empowerment to prevent marginalization.
Transitioning from humanitarian aid to durable solutions requires phased government capacity building to avoid gaps.
Coordinating humanitarian, stabilisation, and development actors in FCAS contexts needs aligned systems to prevent duplication.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous stabilisation efforts in Iraq (e.g., FFS, REFAATO) focused on reconstruction but failed to address political grievances or local ownership, leading to unsustainable parallel systems. The UK’s prior humanitarian spending (£278m) created dependency without durable solutions. Lessons learned include: (1) Local NGOs must be embedded in design, not just implementation, (2) Legal barriers (e.g., property rights) are often overlooked in infrastructure projects, and (3) Coordination gaps between UN and government undermine transitions. BPSI’s blended approach and focus on ‘soft’ elements (e.g., social cohesion) directly respond to these failures.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) **Consortium model** (vs. direct NGO funding) to mitigate capacity/risks, (2) **Third-party monitoring** (due to FCDO access constraints), (3) **Explicit gender focus** (after recognizing women-headed households’ vulnerabilities), (4) **Flexible reallocation** (learning from rigid humanitarian programmes), and (5) **Policy influencing component** (to address past failures in government engagement). The ‘hard/soft’ rehabilitation split reflects lessons that physical reconstruction alone is insufficient without social trust-building.
risks_lessons.quote: The UN systems are typically macro and top-down, failing to incorporate the ‘hyper-localised’ approach required for Durable Solutions. (D0001021.odt, Localisation) [...] The Government has many often competing priorities spreading human and financial resources thinly. (D0001021.odt, Localisation) [...] Experiences show that [UN programmes] substitute for Government capacity or create parallel systems. (D0001021.odt, Option 2) [...] The programme’s innovative approach and focus on evidence generation increases the importance of effective monitoring. (D0001021.odt, The Programme)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage its £25m investment to influence larger UN/GoI budgets (e.g., FFS, REFAATO) and mobilize partner financing through advocacy. Specific leverage targets are not quantified but focus on policy changes (e.g., government funding for durable solutions) and donor coordination.
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: Up to £25m over 5 years. (D0001021.odt, Summary Sheet) [...] The programme is designed to leverage a proportionally small investment in conflict prevention to deliver wider systemic impact. (D0001021.odt, Assurance) [...] FCDO’s contribution to [UN agencies] would represent a small proportion of their overall budgets. (D0001021.odt, Option 2)

metadata.programme_name: Better Regional Migration Management (BRMM)

quote.text: The Better Regional Migration Management (BRMM) Programme aims to harness the benefits of regular migration in line with the Global Compact on Migration (GCM) and Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 10.7 (to facilitate orderly, safe and responsible migration and mobility of people).

duration_source.text:
Start Date: 2021/22
End Date: 2024/25

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The BRMM programme combines implementation research (testing regular migration pathways), capacity building (strengthening migration management systems), and evidence generation (evaluating impacts of migration policies). It aims to improve regional migration governance while simultaneously evaluating a new healthcare worker migration pathway to the UK.

q1_source.text: The programme will provide funding for better regional migration management, initially in East Africa. It will make intraregional migration more productive by strengthening the use of data in labour market information systems and policy; improving labour migration governance and skills recognition and protecting labour migrants from exploitation and abuse. It will simultaneously build the evidence base on the benefits of well managed regular migration through an impact evaluation of the new regular pathway for healthcare workers into the UK/NHS from Ghana.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved labour migration statistics for evidence-based policy making in selected countries in East Africa
Returnees and potential migrants in East Africa have access to integrated employment services
Enhanced inclusive and dignified employment of migrant workers through ethical recruitment
Improved evidence base on impact of regular migration pathways on migrants and their countries of origin
Two evaluations: rapid performance evaluation of regional migration management component and impact evaluation of healthcare worker pathway

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to transform migration into a productive force by improving data systems, skills recognition, and protection mechanisms while generating evidence on what works in migration management.

quote.text: The programme aims to test assumptions that underpin the links between poverty reduction and migration. It will support different but complimentary approaches to maximising the benefits of regular migration, initially in East Africa and along new pathways to the UK.
quote.source: D0001076.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in East Africa where migration governance is complex and fragmented, with significant challenges including weak institutions, conflict risks, and high informality in labour markets. The overall risk rating is classified as 'major'.

q5_source.text: The overall risk rating for BRMM is major and risk will be closely monitored and managed throughout the programme lifecycle. This is an ambitious programme in a new area for the FCDO, engaging delivery partners to work alongside national governments and marginalised communities in East Africa.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak migration governance systems, lack of reliable data, and high informality in labour markets create significant barriers to effective policy implementation. Conflict and climate vulnerabilities further complicate delivery in the region.

quote.text: At present in East Africa, labour migration governance is complex, fragmented and lacks a reliable evidence base. Two different Regional Economic Communities have competence on migration with overlapping membership. [...] Implementation of the free movement of labour in the EAC remains contentious.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains overall decision-making authority, with multilateral organizations (IOM, ILO) implementing activities in East Africa. Southern partners (national governments) are engaged through these multilaterals but do not have direct decision-making power over programme design or budget allocation.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for national/regional actors on data collection and labour market information systems
support for skills recognition and qualification portability
building capacity for ethical recruitment practices
strengthening social protection portability mechanisms

partner_organizations.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
partner_organizations.role: implementation (data systems, protection, regional coordination)
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (with regional offices in East Africa)

partner_organizations.name: International Labour Organization (ILO)
partner_organizations.role: implementation (skills recognition, labour governance)
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (with regional offices in East Africa)

partner_organizations.name: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC)
partner_organizations.role: collaborator (healthcare worker pathway to UK)

partner_organizations.name: East African Community (EAC) and IGAD member states
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries/engaged governments

partner_organizations.name: UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund (potential)
partner_organizations.role: possible GCM implementation funding mechanism

quote.text: The programme is ambitious and innovative for the FCDO: working with another government department (Department for Health and Social Care); taking a ‘whole of route’ approach and addressing multiple dimensions of migration (management, evidence & protection).
quote.source: D0001076.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants to multilateral organizations (IOM, ILO) and direct collaboration with UK government departments (DHSC). Funding flows through FCDO to implementing partners with specific deliverables and milestones.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FCDO manages the overall programme with IOM and ILO as primary implementers. A Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) oversees delivery, with regular coordination between FCDO's Migration Department and the implementing partners. The structure is hierarchical with defined roles for each partner.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their existing mandates and expertise in migration governance (IOM, ILO) and their ability to operate effectively in East Africa. The collaboration with DHSC stems from a specific UK government priority (healthcare worker recruitment).

quote.text: The programme is complementary to ongoing migration work across FCDO and HMG including: productive migration programming in South Asia; the UK issued Call to Action on remittances; the EU Trust Fund for addressing the root causes of irregular migration in Africa which the UK retains an interest in post EU exit; and the Conflict, Stability and Security Fund (CSSF).

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by a Senior Responsible Owner (Victoria Hermon) within FCDO's Migration Department, with monthly risk reviews and escalation protocols. While not explicitly called a 'steering committee,' the structure includes regular coordination between FCDO, IOM, ILO, and DHSC with defined decision-making authority resting with FCDO.

quote.text: The SRO will have overall responsibility for risk management and will work with the PRO to ensure that programme risk remains within Migration Department’s risk appetite. Programme risks will be discussed on a monthly basis and any risks that fall outside our risk appetite will be escalated.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (regional management, evaluations, GCM implementation) but require approval through the Spending Review process and ministerial sign-off. The programme has built in contingency for different funding scenarios (high/medium/low).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an adaptive management approach where lessons from Year 1 will inform activities in subsequent years. Adjustments require approval through FCDO's governance processes, particularly around the Spending Review outcomes.

quote.text: The programme’s continuation beyond year one is dependent on the outcome of the Spending Review, for which the team has considered and prepared for three different outcomes: High, Medium, and Low funding scenarios. [...] Ministers will have a further opportunity to make decisions on the programme at this point.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (IOM/ILO) → [National/regional actors in East Africa]. The DHSC collaboration adds a parallel UK-focused component.

quote.text: Activities delivered during this period will lay the groundwork for future years. The scale & scope of the programme in future years will depend on the outcome of the Spending Review.

q24_alternatives_considered: Remittances (encouraging diaspora to buy bonds for productive investment)
Circular migration to the Gulf from SSA (facilitating movement through bilateral agreements/training/fair recruitment)
Circular migration to the UK (fixed-period work with return)
Skills partnerships (training in occupations with UK shortages)
Data improvements (working with countries to enhance migration data systems)
Policies towards refugees (work/school opportunities in host countries)
Brain drain research (understanding net effects of skilled migration)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The regional migration management approach was selected because it: (1) aligns with FCDO's strategic priorities on economic development and migration governance; (2) addresses multiple dimensions of migration (data, skills, protection) simultaneously; (3) leverages existing multilateral partnerships (IOM, ILO) with proven capacity in East Africa; (4) allows for testing assumptions about migration's development impacts through embedded evaluations; and (5) complements other HMG priorities like the Illegal Migration Strategy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political risk of working with national governments in East Africa with varying commitments to migration reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement through multilateral organizations (IOM/ILO) to navigate political sensitivities and build on existing regional frameworks (EAC, IGAD).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination between multiple partners (FCDO, DHSC, IOM, ILO) with different mandates
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear division of roles with FCDO retaining overall oversight, monthly risk reviews, and defined escalation protocols.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Tight timelines for Year 1 delivery given the August 2021 start date
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on laying groundwork in Year 1 with flexibility to adjust future activities based on Spending Review outcomes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: COVID-19 impacts on migration patterns and programme delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners (like IOM) have demonstrated ability to adapt activities during the pandemic, and programme design incorporates monitoring of COVID-19 effects.

quote.text: On the basis of this scoring the team elected to move forward with remittances, facilitating circular movement towards the Gulf from SSA and better regional migration management, including a data component. [...] We therefore concluded that we did not have enough information and evidence on which to make choices [on remittances]. We decided instead to look at making use of the M4D programme to fill these knowledge gaps, potentially to inform future work. Design continued on the other two components - circular migration and regional migration management (including work on data).

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The East African context - with its complex migration governance, weak data systems, and high informality - necessitates working through multilateral partners (IOM, ILO) rather than direct engagement with national governments. The presence of Regional Economic Communities (EAC, IGAD) with overlapping mandates also shapes partner selection to ensure alignment with existing regional frameworks.
q27_constraints_detail: Fragmented migration governance requires multilateral intermediaries
Weak national data systems necessitate capacity building through international organizations
High informality in labour markets limits direct engagement with private sector actors
Conflict sensitivities in some countries (e.g., South Sudan, Somalia) restrict operational modalities
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's mixed objectives (implementation + research) require a structure that can both deliver concrete governance improvements (through IOM/ILO) and generate rigorous evidence (through embedded evaluations). The need to test assumptions about migration's development impacts drives the inclusion of impact evaluations as a core component rather than an add-on.
q28_linkages: Multi-dimensional objectives (data + skills + protection) → require consortium of specialized partners (IOM for data/protection, ILO for skills)
Implementation research focus → necessitates embedded evaluation components with academic rigor
Regional scope → demands partners with existing East Africa presence and relationships (IOM/ILO)
Policy influence goal → requires alignment with GCM/SDG frameworks that multilaterals are positioned to deliver
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive migration policies and efficient delivery. For example: (1) The need to protect vulnerable migrants (equity) versus the challenge of working in high-informality contexts where formal protections are weak (efficiency); (2) The ambition to create 'triple win' migration outcomes (for origin countries, destination countries, and migrants) versus the practical difficulties of measuring and achieving balanced benefits; (3) The inclusion of gender and disability considerations in a programme where these are not the primary focus.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Protection goals vs. practical challenges in informal labour markets
Inclusive migration policies vs. speed of implementation in complex regional contexts
Gender/disability inclusion vs. primary focus on economic migration outcomes
Balanced 'triple win' objectives vs. measurable short-term results
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'major' risk rating drives intensive oversight structures, including monthly risk reviews, defined escalation protocols, and the SRO's direct responsibility for risk management. The complex operating environment in East Africa justifies this high-intensity management approach despite potential efficiency trade-offs.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The capacity building objectives directly shape partner roles: IOM and ILO are selected not just for implementation but for their ability to strengthen national/regional systems (e.g., labour market information systems, skills recognition frameworks). The programme design embeds capacity development within core delivery rather than as a separate component.

quote.text: The programme is ambitious and innovative for the FCDO: working with another government department (Department for Health and Social Care); taking a ‘whole of route’ approach and addressing multiple dimensions of migration (management, evidence & protection). It adds value to, rather than replicates, what an individual Post or bilateral programme could achieve.
quote.source: D0001076.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending

key_programme_risks: Political risks in engaging with national governments with uneven commitment to migration reforms
Complex coordination between FCDO, DHSC, IOM, and ILO with different priorities
COVID-19 impacts on migration patterns and programme delivery
Tight Year 1 timelines with August 2021 start date
Data limitations hindering evidence-based policy development
Protection gaps for migrants in informal labour markets
Potential reputational risks if migration pathways are perceived as extractive
Spending Review uncertainty affecting multi-year planning

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Engagement through multilateral partners (IOM/ILO) and alignment with existing regional frameworks (EAC, IGAD).
Clear role division with FCDO oversight, monthly risk reviews, and defined escalation protocols.
Adaptive programme design with partners experienced in pandemic response (e.g., IOM's SSSII adaptation).
Focus on groundwork activities in Year 1 with flexibility for future adjustments.
Capacity building for national data systems as a core programme component.
Explicit focus on ethical recruitment and social protection portability in programme design.
Impact evaluation of healthcare worker pathway to demonstrate 'triple win' outcomes.
Scenario planning for high/medium/low funding outcomes with adaptive management approach.

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for flexible programming in conflict-affected contexts (e.g., South Sudan, Somalia components)
Importance of multilateral partners in FCAS environments where direct government engagement is challenging
Value of regional approaches (EAC/IGAD) to navigate national-level fragilities
Lessons from SSSII programme on adapting to crisis conditions (e.g., COVID-19 response)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from the Safety, Support and Solutions (SSS) programmes, particularly around adaptive management in crisis contexts and the importance of gender-responsive approaches in migration programming. The experience with IOM during SSSII demonstrated the value of partners who can quickly adapt to changing circumstances (e.g., COVID-19).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) Explicit gender and disability inclusion components based on SSSII lessons; (2) Adaptive management structures informed by COVID-19 experiences; (3) Stronger focus on data systems and evidence generation to address identified gaps from previous programmes; (4) Regional approach (East Africa) selected based on analysis of where FCDO could add most value given existing programming in South Asia.

quote.text: The pandemic has exposed the significant policy gaps in current migration systems to deliver fair and equitable benefits for migrant workers and their families, as well as their countries of origin and destination. These changes and impacts have been carefully factored into programme design and will be monitored throughout. One of the proposed partners, IOM, were a key implementing partner for SSSII, and proved able to adapt their activities quickly and appropriately to the changing circumstances caused by Covid-19.

co_funding_partners.partner: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage additional funding through potential contributions to the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund for GCM implementation in outer years, building on the current Migration for Development (M4D) programme.

quote.text: Programme Value: £35,000,000.00 total [...] In the event of a ‘high’ scenario, it is anticipated that the majority of the uplift will be allocated towards the regional migration management component, allowing IOM and ILO to continue and scale up their activities across East Africa. [...] Approximately £7.5 million per year will be allocated towards this component. Spend on monitoring, evaluation and learning will also increase to £1 million per year and the remaining £1.5 million will be allocated towards the new component incorporating the continuation of the M4D programme for GCM implementation.

metadata.programme_name: Jordan Protection Programme (JPP): Support for Vulnerable Refugees and Jordanians
metadata.quote: This programme will provide protection services to an expected 45,000 vulnerable refugees and members of their host communities in Jordan. Services will include case management for children at risk of exploitation and child labour, mental health services for survivors of gender-based violence or those suffering from trauma. (Document: 90000343.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: AMP Start Date: 15/10/2021; AMP End Date: 31/03/2025

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers **direct protection services** (case management, mental health support) while simultaneously **strengthening national protection systems** through technical assistance and capacity building. It combines **service delivery** with **systems strengthening** to transition from humanitarian to development approaches.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will provide protection services to an expected 45,000 vulnerable refugees and members of their host communities in Jordan. [...] Through technical support, the programme will also strengthen national protection services to be more sustainable and promote the inclusion of vulnerable refugees in national systems. (Document: 90000343.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 45,000 direct beneficiaries reached with protection services (child protection, SGBV, mental health)
Increased capacity of national protection systems (e.g., Ministry of Social Development, Family Protection Department)
Improved well-being of vulnerable people (measured via % reporting improved mental/physical health and social interactions)
Pilot integration of refugee protection services into government systems (inception phase)
Strengthened evidence base for transitioning from humanitarian to development approaches
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to enhance resilience among vulnerable refugees and Jordanians by delivering specialized protection services (child protection, SGBV, mental health) while building the capacity of national systems to sustain these services long-term. It explicitly links humanitarian response with development objectives through systems strengthening and advocacy for refugee inclusion in national services.
what_objectives.quote: The intended impact of the programme is that vulnerable refugees and Jordanians (including women, girls and PwDs) have an enhanced resilience against the impact of shocks and life-cycle vulnerabilities. [...] The intended outcome is increased capacity and quality of protection systems that are more sustainable and the improved well-being of vulnerable people. (Document: 90000343.odt, Intended Outcome and Impact)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Jordan is categorized as 'moderate risk' within FCDO's risk appetite (set at 'receptive'). The context involves protracted refugee hosting (8% of population are refugees), economic fragility, and political sensitivity around refugee inclusion in national systems, but the operating environment is stable enough for programme delivery.
where_context.q5_source: The overall risk rating for the programme is cautious which is within the overall risk appetite for Jordan (set at receptive). (Document: 90000343.odt, Risk section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: 1) **Political economy**: Government hesitancy to include refugees in national systems due to financial constraints and limited capacity. 2) **Weak institutions**: Poor coordination between ministries and lack of accountability in protection service delivery at community levels. 3) **Regulatory**: Restrictions on refugee employment and movement limit economic opportunities. 4) **Conflict**: Protracted Syrian crisis with no near-term resolution, exacerbating vulnerabilities. 5) **Data limitations**: Gaps in legal documentation (e.g., 39% of Syrian children lack birth certificates) hinder access to services.
where_context.quote: While efforts have been made to standardise and improve statutory protection services through the establishment of National Standard Operating Procedures (SoPs) for case management, implementation remains weak at the community level. Poor internal coordination between ministries and lack of overall accountability and monitoring exacerbate the problem. (Document: 90000343.odt, Need for the Intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The lead partner (either a UN agency or INGO consortium) will manage day-to-day delivery, with downstreampartners primarily being **national NGOs** responsible for service delivery. Decision-making is decentralized to local actors, with technical support from international partners. The programme explicitly requires 30% of beneficiaries to be Jordanians, ensuring local ownership.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical training for national service providers (e.g., case management, mental health)
Strengthening government systems (e.g., early detection of disabilities, referral pathways)
Building local NGO capacity to take over service delivery (including conflict-sensitive approaches)
Advocacy for refugee inclusion in national social protection systems
Pilot testing service delivery through government systems

partner_organizations.name: Potential INGO Consortium (3 identified)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer (if selected)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Potential lead implementer (if selected)

partner_organizations.name: National NGOs (downstream partners)
