partner_organizations.role: Service delivery (case management, counselling, referrals)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Social Development (GoJ)
partner_organizations.role: Technical counterpart for systems strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Family Protection Department (GoJ)
partner_organizations.role: Government partner for child protection and SGBV response

who_partners.quote: We will select an NGO consortium for implementation, with a single lead organisation to maximise efficiency. [...] Many of the downstream activities will be carried out by national NGOs. (Document: 90000343.odt, Partnership Principles and Delivery Structure)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use either a **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)** for UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF) or an **Accountable Grant Arrangement (AGA)** for INGO consortia. Both instruments include clauses for flexibility, crisis response, and technical assistance to government systems. The MoU/AGA will outline reporting, monitoring, and risk management responsibilities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A single lead organization (UN agency or INGO) will manage the programme, sub-contracting to downstream partners (primarily national NGOs). The lead is responsible for all financial reporting, M&E, and risk management, with FCDO oversight. The structure is designed to streamline coordination and reduce management burdens compared to the previous multi-partner model.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection process began with an open call for concept notes through the Protection Working Group, generating 14 submissions. These were scored against alignment with UK priorities, technical strength, and value for money. The top 4 (3 INGO consortia + 1 UN agency) were invited to submit full proposals. This approach balanced **innovation** (new partners could apply) with **continuity** (previous partners could bid), while ensuring alignment with the UK’s localisation and transition objectives.
how_mechanism.quote: Following Ministerial approval of the Concept Note which outlined our approach, under guidance from our Commercial Adviser, we launched a call for concept notes through the Protection Working Group (PWG). [...] 14 concept notes were scored and assessed as a panel based on their theory of change, technical strengths, value for money, and alignment with our strategy. [...] We have selected 3 INGO consortia and one UN agency to develop full proposals. (Document: 90000343.odt, Why this modality chosen)

how_governance.quote: BEA’s role will be to oversee the implementation of the programme as well as conduct regular quarterly meetings and field visits. [...] The selected partner will be responsible for delivering these services and for selecting and managing downstream partners. (Document: 90000343.odt, Management and Financial Cases)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities **with FCDO approval**, particularly to respond to emerging protection needs (e.g., COVID-19, new refugee inflows). The £4m crisis modifier facility allows rapid response to unexpected crises, but its use requires justification and approval by the Development Director.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an **inception phase** (1 year) to assess technical assistance needs and pilot government system integration. Adjustments to priorities (e.g., shifting focus between child protection, SGBV, or systems strengthening) require FCDO approval but are encouraged to respond to evidence or context changes. The crisis modifier facility enables adaptive management for shocks.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme will retain the flexibility to adapt and respond to beneficiary feedback and internal monitoring. [...] Should the context change to an extent where what is outlined and agreed with the partner cannot be delivered, we will request an amendment to the Business Case if relevant. (Document: 90000343.odt, Flexibility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Partner (UN/INGO) → National NGOs (downstream implementers). The structure reduces layers compared to the previous model (which had 3+ partners under separate AGAs).
how_efficiency.quote: Funds will be disbursed to the selected partner quarterly in arrears after thorough scrutiny of the financial report. [...] Should the partner request payments in advance, we will ensure there is an adequate VfM argument and evidence of need. (Document: 90000343.odt, Financial Management)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Deliver a wide range of protection services through existing mechanisms (multiple partners, separate AGAs)
Option 2: Deliver specific/discreet protection services to the most vulnerable (narrower scope, e.g., only child protection)
Option 3: Provide financial support for protection services + technical assistance to build sustainable systems (preferred option)
Option 4: Counter-factual 'do nothing' approach (redirect funds to cash assistance only)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected because it: 1) **Aligns with UK priorities** of localisation and transitioning from humanitarian to development approaches; 2) **Maximizes value for money** by combining service delivery with systems strengthening (economies of scale); 3) **Address composite vulnerabilities** holistically (unlike Option 2); 4) **Reduces long-term reliance on humanitarian aid** by building government capacity; 5) **Leverages lessons from the previous programme**, where systems strengthening proved effective but required deeper government engagement.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (economies of scale in Option 3 vs. narrower scope in Option 2)
alignment with UK priorities (localisation, transition, streamlining services)
sustainability (Option 3 builds government capacity vs. standalone services in Options 1/2)
risk mitigation (Option 4 risks losing progress; Option 1’s multi-partner model was complex to manage)
equity (Option 3 reaches both refugees and Jordanians, avoiding community tensions)
flexibility (Option 3’s crisis modifier allows adaptive response)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Difficulties in transitioning protection services to government systems
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close alignment with the Protection Taskforce (including MoSD) and UK’s social protection programming. Use of an influencing/diplomacy strategy tied to Jordan’s interest in a new Refugee Compact.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: COVID-19 restrictions disrupting service delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners must demonstrate remote delivery mechanisms (e.g., tele-counselling, digital referrals) and adaptive programming. Lessons from 2020 COVID-19 response will be applied.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding incidents (harm to beneficiaries/staff)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced due diligence assessments of partners, mandatory safeguarding policies/training, and FCDO oversight of downstream partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funds diverted for unintended purposes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Thorough due diligence, spot-checks, and partner accountability systems. Clear MoU/AGA clauses on financial reporting and fraud prevention.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (streamlined delivery vs. previous multi-partner model)
effectiveness (evidence from prior programme on systems strengthening impact)
equity (inclusion of Jordanians, PwDs, and remote areas)
why_rationale.quote: Option 3 [...] is an expansion of option 1, where it enables the programme to deliver a wide range of protection services, accompanied with technical assistance and support to strengthen national systems. This approach would be effective in contributing to the programme’s intended impact as well as to the planned outcome of building sustainable services. (Document: 90000343.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **Established presence in Jordan** (due to regulatory and security constraints); 2) **Experience navigating government systems** (critical for systems strengthening); 3) **Capacity to work in refugee camps and urban areas** (geographical reach requirement); 4) **Ability to manage safeguarding risks** in a high-vulnerability setting. New entrants without local roots were excluded early in the process.
q27_constraints_detail: Government restrictions on refugee employment/movement require partners with legal expertise.
Weak institutional capacity means partners must have **existing relationships with MoSD/FPD** to influence systems.
Security risks in informal tented settlements limit partners to those with **local staff networks**.
Cultural norms around GBV/child protection necessitate partners with **contextualized approaches** (e.g., Sharia court engagement for child marriage).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objective** (service delivery + systems strengthening) requires a **consortium structure** to: 1) **Combine specialized expertise** (e.g., child protection, SGBV, disability inclusion) under one lead; 2) **Balance humanitarian speed** (direct service delivery) with **development sustainability** (government capacity building); 3) **Manage risk** by diversifying across multiple downstream partners while centralizing accountability.
q28_linkages: Need for **holistic protection services** → Consortium model to integrate child protection, SGBV, and mental health under one programme.
Goal of **systems strengthening** → Requires lead partner with **government relationships** (e.g., MoSD, FPD) to co-design interventions.
**Localisation priority** → Downstream partners must be **national NGOs** with community trust, shaping the two-tier structure.
**Transition objective** → Technical assistance component necessitates **embedded advisors** within government ministries.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs discussed include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Option 2 (narrower services) would be faster but exclude composite vulnerabilities; Option 3’s broader scope risks slower start-up but better equity. 2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: International partners provide technical support, but **national NGOs lead delivery** to ensure cultural appropriateness and sustainability. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Direct service delivery (Options 1/2) is cheaper per beneficiary but **Option 3’s systems focus** yields longer-term efficiency gains by reducing parallel humanitarian systems.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency loss from **consortium coordination** (vs. single partner) mitigated by streamlined management compared to the previous multi-AGA model.
**Higher upfront costs** for systems strengthening justified by reduced long-term humanitarian spending.
**Geographical trade-offs**: Urban focus (east Amman, northern governorates) balances reach with feasibility, excluding some remote areas.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (FCAS context) drives **quarterly oversight** (vs. annual in stable settings) and **enhanced due diligence** (e.g., safeguarding audits, financial spot-checks). The crisis modifier facility (£4m) reflects the **volatile environment**, requiring adaptive management structures.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) **Lead partner** must demonstrate ability to **train national NGOs** in case management and safeguarding; 2) **Downstream partners** are selected based on potential to **take over services** post-programme; 3) **Government counterparts** (MoSD, FPD) co-design interventions to ensure **institutional ownership** of strengthened systems.
intersections.quote: The programme’s design reflects this approach [humanitarian-development nexus] by combining direct service delivery with technical assistance to government. [...] Many of the downstream activities will be carried out by national NGOs. The potential partners will be responsible for raising local NGO capacity to a level that allows for handover. (Document: 90000343.odt, Delivery Structure and Capacity Building)

key_programme_risks: Government resistance to refugee inclusion in national systems (political risk)
COVID-19 or other shocks disrupting service delivery (operational risk)
Safeguarding incidents undermining trust (reputational/protection risk)
Fund diversion or fraud (fiduciary risk)
Parallel humanitarian systems persisting due to weak government capacity (sustainability risk)
Community tensions from unequal service access (social cohesion risk)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Difficulties transitioning services to government systems
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Align with Protection Taskforce (MoSD + key actors) and UK’s social protection programme. Use diplomacy tied to Jordan Compact negotiations.
Require partners to demonstrate remote service delivery models (e.g., tele-mental health, digital referrals).
Enhanced due diligence, mandatory partner safeguarding policies, and FCDO monitoring of downstream partners.
Due diligence assessments, spot-checks, and MoU/AGA clauses on financial reporting.
Pilot government-led service delivery during inception phase; advocate for refugee inclusion in national frameworks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from the **previous UK protection programme (2018–2021)**: Early government engagement and **local NGO capacity building** were critical for sustainability, but COVID-19 disrupted handover plans.
**Protracted crisis context** requires blending humanitarian and development funding to avoid service gaps (e.g., cash assistance alone cannot address protection needs).
In FCAS settings, **flexible funding** (e.g., crisis modifier) is essential to respond to shocks like COVID-19 or sudden policy changes.
**Localisation** must be **gradual**—direct funding to government is not feasible yet, but technical assistance can build trust.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Project Completion Review (PCR) of the previous programme (2018–2021) scored A+ and highlighted: 1) **Sustainability requires early government engagement** (e.g., training on disability detection); 2) **Local volunteers** are key for reaching vulnerable families; 3) **Transition programming** must be **context-adaptive**—COVID-19 showed the need for flexible timelines. These lessons shaped the **inception phase** and **technical assistance focus** in the new programme.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Single lead partner** (vs. multiple AGAs) to reduce management complexity; 2) **Explicit systems strengthening component** (missing in prior programme); 3) **Crisis modifier facility** added based on COVID-19 experience; 4) **Stronger safeguarding requirements** for downstream partners; 5) **Pilot government integration** during inception phase to test feasibility.
risks_lessons.quote: The PCR highlighted the main lessons learned which related to the sustainability of service delivery in a protracted crisis situation where early and clear engagement with local service providers and relevant government ministries helped build their capacity and improve overall systems to deliver services both to refugees and Jordanians. (Document: 90000343.odt, Lessons from Previous Programme)

financial_details.quote: The total proposed budget for the programme is up to £15m, with a core budget of £11m to be distributed over four financial years. [...] Upto £4 million has been included as a crisis modifier facility. (Document: 90000343.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Empowerment and Development for Girls Education (EDGE)
metadata.quote: "The programme will deliver 36,100 more girls in school and 33,300 girls with increased literacy attainment during the grant period alone." (90000395.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: June 2021 to August 2025" (D0004786.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The EDGE programme combines **service delivery** (building schools, expanding access to secondary education) with **implementation research** (testing an innovative school management model) and **policy influence** (development diplomacy to integrate reforms into government systems). It aims to demonstrate a cost-effective, scalable model for secondary education while directly improving learning outcomes for marginalized girls.
what_objectives.q1_source: "EDGE will deliver 36,100 more girls in school and 33,300 girls with increased literacy attainment... It will spend up to £7 million over four years to address challenges facing disadvantaged girls... The programme will also have a development diplomacy component to integrate effective reforms into government systems." (90000395.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 36,100 more girls in school (direct service delivery)
33,300 girls with increased literacy attainment
70,000 children (half girls) reaching minimum learning standards in numeracy and literacy
Construction of 3 new schools and 6 school expansions (climate-resilient infrastructure)
School management and teaching improvement plans in targeted districts
Policy reforms to strengthen accountability and financial management in the education sector
Evidence generation on cost-effective school models (for replication nationwide)

what_objectives.summary: EDGE aims to expand access to quality secondary education for marginalized girls in Zambia through direct school construction, innovative management models, and policy influence. It combines service delivery with research to create a scalable, cost-effective approach that can be adopted by the Zambian government.
what_objectives.quote: "The expected impact is increased access to secondary schooling for adolescents in underserved areas, improved quality of secondary education in targeted schools and a sustainable model of secondary education that can be replicated nationwide." (D0004786.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as "moderate risk" due to dependencies on government financing, economic instability, climate shocks, and COVID-19 impacts. Mitigations include backup strategies for school operations without government funding and robust procurement processes.
where_context.q5_source: "This programme is assessed overall as moderate risk... Sustainability & Financing Risk: The delivery context is highly dependent on government financing... Mitigation: Partners to have a backup strategy where the school network could operate without government financing." (90000395.odt, Risk Category table)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Economic instability (debt crisis, inflation) limits government spending on education. Weak institutional capacity in the Ministry of General Education (MoGE) affects absorption of technical assistance. Climate risks (droughts, floods) threaten school infrastructure and attendance. High prevalence of gender-based violence requires safeguarding measures. Limited data on learning outcomes hampers evidence-based planning.
where_context.quote: "Zambia’s fiscal situation has been extremely constrained in the past few years, partly due to heavy debt servicing obligations... The kwacha lost almost half its value in 2020... The previous government failed to agree a deal for an IMF debt relief package." (90000395.odt, Context and need for an intervention) && "A lack of official mechanisms for data collection in Zambia on issues of safeguarding limits the capacity of policymakers and schools to take action to protect students." (90000395.odt, Safeguarding section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: PEAS (UK-based) leads the programme design and implementation, with Zambian staff (PEAS Zambia) delivering operations. The Ministry of General Education (MoGE) is a key government partner but does not hold primary decision-making authority. The FCDO Education Advisor (UK-funded) provides technical oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: Capacity building and training for PEAS Zambia team by UK-based technical teams
Annual Education Specialist programme placing UK educators in Zambia for knowledge transfer
Training for Zambian school staff on teaching quality and school management
Mentorship through virtual meetings with UK educators
Institutional strengthening of MoGE via development diplomacy and policy influencing

partner_organizations.name: Promoting Equality in African Schools (PEAS)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner (school construction, management, and teaching improvements)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of General Education (MoGE), Government of Zambia
partner_organizations.role: Government counterpart (policy alignment, PPP agreements, school inspections)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Education Advisor (short-term)
partner_organizations.role: Technical oversight, government relations, and programme influencing

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: Previous technical assistance provider (ZESSTA programme); limited role in EDGE

partner_organizations.name: Education Partnerships Group (EPG)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for school inspection processes (linked to Ark, a UK charity)

who_partners.quote: "The programme will partner with PEAS (Promoting Equality in African Schools) to support the scale-up of their proven school network. PEAS brings together best practice from the UK education sector with Zambian education experts... UK-based technical teams provide high-quality technical assistance to the PEAS Zambia team." (90000395.odt, Why PEAS and why UK spend on this now?) && "The in-house education advisory role is also essential for the delivery of the programme due to... increased political will and commitment resulting in good policy environment." (D0004786.odt, Describe any key changes)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **accountable grants** for PEAS and a **supplier contract** for the FCDO Education Advisor. Funds are disbursed against approved activities with milestone-based payments and financial oversight (audits, spot checks).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: PEAS is the sole implementing partner for school construction and management, with FCDO providing oversight through an embedded Education Advisor. The Ministry of General Education (MoGE) is involved in policy alignment but not day-to-day management.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: PEAS was selected due to its proven track record in Zambia/Uganda, existing PPP agreement with MoGE, and alignment with UK education expertise. The selection leverages prior UK investments in PEAS and its cost-effective school model.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will build on the Zambian presence of a UK-based social enterprise called Promoting Equality in African Schools (PEAS) who have an award-winning school development model... PEAS and the Ministry of General Education (MoGE) have established an innovative cost-sharing mechanism." (90000395.odt, What needs to happen?) && "The in-house education advisory role is also essential for the delivery of the programme due to increased financing towards the EDGE Programme which requires advisory & technical expertise." (D0004786.odt, Describe any key changes)

how_governance.quote: "FCDO standard clauses on terrorism, fraud and money laundering will be included in negotiated contracts... Rigorous financial management including audits, that assess policies and procedures will be carried out by FCDO staff." (90000395.odt, Summary assessment on terrorism and financing) && "A detailed mid-term review will be conducted to review progress and course correct if necessary." (90000395.odt, Key risks to the success of the programme)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., school expansions vs. new schools) with FCDO approval, as evidenced by the £5m cost extension for additional schools. However, major shifts require justification and alignment with programme objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a mid-term review for course correction and an embedded Education Advisor to respond to political opportunities (e.g., new government priorities). The addendum reflects adaptive management by adding schools in new provinces based on demand.
how_flexibility.quote: "A detailed mid-term review will be conducted to review progress and course correct if necessary." (90000395.odt, Key risks) && "The objective of this addendum is to increase the value of the Business Case by £5,000,000, and this additional funding will be used to scale up FCDO’s support to access to secondary schooling... by building a number of model schools." (D0004786.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → PEAS (implementing partner). The Education Advisor is embedded within FCDO but works closely with PEAS and MoGE, acting as a bridge rather than an additional layer.
how_efficiency.quote: "Funds disbursed against approved activities only; and spot checks." (90000395.odt, Fiduciary Risk) && "The in-house education advisory role... will be more externally focused to develop closer relationships with government counterparts." (D0004786.odt, Describe any key changes)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No new bilateral education programme; rely on existing GPE/GEC contributions. Risked missing UK targets for girls' education and reputational damage.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Extending the Keeping Girls in School (KGS) National Programme
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Expand bursaries for secondary school girls in districts not covered by current programmes. Limited to demand-side support (fees) without addressing supply-side issues (school quality, infrastructure).

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Strengthening secondary school learning through policy influencing
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focus on technical assistance and global evidence to influence MoGE policies. Risked low traction without Zambia-specific proof of concept.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Catalytic investments in education innovation and systems strengthening, with evidence-based development diplomacy (CHOSEN OPTION)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Direct investment in PEAS’s proven model, combined with policy influence and scaling through government systems. Addresses both supply (schools) and demand (access/quality) while generating evidence for replication.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The selected modality was chosen for its **value for money** (PEAS’s cost-effective school model), **scalability** (potential for government adoption), **alignment with UK expertise** (leveraging UK education systems), and **balanced approach** (combining service delivery with policy influence). It addresses both immediate gaps (school access) and systemic challenges (government capacity) while mitigating risks through PEAS’s existing PPP with MoGE.
q25_decision_factors: policy influence opportunities (new government’s education priorities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability & Financing Risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: PEAS and partners will develop a backup strategy to operate schools without government financing. The PPP model includes income-generating activities to reduce dependency on public funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery Risk (local capacity constraints)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust procurement and partner selection processes. PEAS’s existing presence in Zambia and UK technical support mitigate capacity gaps.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Construction Quality Risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adherence to Zambian government guidelines and best practices, with oversight by an infrastructure advisor. PEAS will pilot sustainable construction methods and meet climate-resilient standards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication and overcomplication
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Coordination through the Education Cooperating Partners Group (ECPG) and an embedded Education Advisor to align with other donors (USAID, World Bank, GPE).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary Risk (financial mismanagement)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence of partners, realistic budget forecasts, milestone-based disbursements, and FCDO spot checks.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 4: Catalytic investments in education innovation and systems strengthening... is the preferred option as it directly addresses the supply-side constraints... while also providing a proof of concept for alternative investment models... It aligns with the UK’s comparative advantage in education and the opportunity to influence the new government’s priorities." (90000395.odt, What is the feasible option) && "The programme will showcase an effective investment and school management approach to GRZ and demonstrate how secondary school coverage can be expanded at a significantly lower cost than current delivery." (90000395.odt, Intervention Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Zambian context constrains partner selection to organizations with **existing PPP agreements with MoGE** (e.g., PEAS) and **capacity to operate in remote, climate-vulnerable areas**. Weak institutional capacity in MoGE limits the feasibility of direct government implementation, necessitating a Northern-led partner (PEAS) with local embedded teams. Economic instability and debt constraints reduce the pool of potential co-financiers, increasing reliance on UK aid.
q27_constraints_detail: MoGE’s weak public financial management requires a partner (PEAS) with proven fiduciary systems.
Climate risks (droughts, floods) necessitate partners with experience in climate-resilient infrastructure (PEAS’s sustainable construction pilots).
Limited government budget for education restricts co-funding options, favoring partners with income-generating models (PEAS’s PPP).
High prevalence of gender-based violence requires partners with strong safeguarding policies (PEAS’s child protection tools).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The **mixed objectives** (service delivery + policy influence + research) determine the **hybrid delivery structure**: 
1. **Direct implementation** by PEAS for school construction/management (service delivery).
2. **Embedded FCDO Advisor** for policy influencing and government relations.
3. **Milestone-based funding** to balance flexibility with accountability (research/evidence generation).
The need for **scalable evidence** drives the choice of a single implementer (PEAS) with a proven model, while **policy influence goals** necessitate close FCDO oversight via the Advisor.
q28_linkages: Service delivery (schools) → requires a partner with construction/management capacity (PEAS).
Policy influence → requires FCDO’s embedded Advisor to navigate MoGE’s political economy.
Evidence generation → requires a partner with existing data systems (PEAS’s monitoring tools) and FCDO’s oversight for credibility.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between **cost efficiency** and **equity**:
- **Efficiency**: PEAS’s model reduces per-school costs by simplifying designs and using PPPs, but this risks excluding areas where government co-financing is unavailable.
- **Equity**: Targeting marginalized girls (disabilities, rural areas) increases costs but aligns with UK’s gender equality priorities. The mid-term review balances these by assessing whether cost savings compromise access for the most vulnerable.
- **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK technical support (e.g., Education Specialists) improves quality but limits local decision-making; mitigated by PEAS’s Zambian operational team.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Cost vs. reach: Lower-cost school designs may limit amenities (e.g., boarding facilities) needed for remote girls.
Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scaling risks overlooking girls with disabilities; mitigated by targeted recruitment.
UK standards vs. local adaptation: UK-inspired pedagogy (e.g., OFSTED tools) may not fully align with Zambian teacher capacities; addressed via contextualized training.
intersections.risk_affects_management:
The **moderate risk profile** (economic instability, climate shocks) drives **intensive oversight**:
- Embedded FCDO Advisor to monitor political/economic shifts.
- Milestone-based payments to mitigate fiduciary risks.
- Mid-term review to adjust to new risks (e.g., COVID-19 school closures).
- Backup strategies for school operations if government financing falters.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building is **core to partner roles**:
- **PEAS**: Receives UK technical assistance (e.g., Education Specialists) to strengthen Zambian team’s management/teaching skills, enabling eventual handover to MoGE.
- **MoGE**: Limited capacity leads to a **non-implementing role** (policy alignment, inspections) rather than direct delivery.
- **FCDO Advisor**: Fills gaps in MoGE’s strategic planning, ensuring UK expertise shapes system-wide reforms.
intersections.quote: "The programme will partner with PEAS... to support the scale-up of their proven school network. PEAS brings together best practice from the UK education sector with Zambian education experts... UK-based technical teams provide high-quality technical assistance to the PEAS Zambia team." (90000395.odt, Why PEAS) && "The in-house education advisory role is also essential for the delivery of the programme due to increased political will and commitment resulting in good policy environment." (D0004786.odt, Describe any key changes) && "There is a risk that rather than complementing existing development partner efforts... the programme duplicates, complicates or over-burdens an already weak system. This risk should be able to be managed through effective design, consultation, and ongoing coordination." (90000395.odt, Duplication and overcomplication risk)

key_programme_risks: Sustainability & Financing Risk: Dependency on government per-pupil payments, threatened by economic instability (debt crisis, inflation).
Delivery Risk: Local capacity constraints in MoGE and PEAS’s reliance on Zambian systems.
Construction Quality Risk: Schools may not meet national standards, requiring further investment.
Duplication/Overcomplication: Risk of overlapping with USAID/World Bank efforts in a weak system.
Fiduciary Risk: Potential mismanagement of funds by PEAS or downstream partners.
Safeguarding Risks: High prevalence of gender-based violence in Zambian schools.
Climate Risks: Droughts/floods may disrupt school operations or damage infrastructure.
Political Risk: Changes in government priorities could reduce support for education reforms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: PEAS to develop backup strategies for operating schools without government financing; income-generating activities included in PPP model.
Robust procurement and partner selection; UK technical teams to support PEAS Zambia.
Adherence to Zambian government guidelines; infrastructure advisor oversight; piloting sustainable construction methods.
Coordination through Education Cooperating Partners Group (ECPG); Education Advisor to align with other donors.
Due diligence of partners; milestone-based disbursements; FCDO spot checks and audits.
Enhanced due diligence assessments; zero-tolerance policies; training for staff/beneficiaries on child protection and whistleblowing.
Schools designed to climate-sensitive and disaster-resilient standards; climate appraisal integrated into planning.
Development diplomacy component to align with government priorities; flexible programme design to adapt to policy shifts.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS-like contexts (economic instability, weak institutions), **PPP models** can improve service delivery but require backup plans for government financing gaps.
Embedded advisors (FCDO Education Advisor) are critical to navigate **political economy constraints** and avoid donor duplication.
**Climate-resilient infrastructure** is non-negotiable in shock-prone environments (droughts, floods).
Safeguarding requires **localized mechanisms** (e.g., trust-building for reporting gender-based violence) beyond standard policies.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
Lessons from **ZESSTA (2015–2018)**:
- Technical Assistance (TA) facilities require **stable, supportive institutional leadership** from both funders and ministries to be effective.
- **Long-term embedded advisors** (vs. short-term consultants) better understand political economy and can influence change.
- **Alignment with government systems** is critical but challenging; ZESSTA’s limited success led to deprioritization of bilateral education programmes until EDGE.

Lessons from **Girls’ Education Challenge (GEC)**:
- **Pathways for girls** into education/employment must be strengthened post-school (e.g., linkages to Chevening scholarships).
- **Community engagement** is essential to address demand-side barriers (e.g., early marriage, pregnancy).

Lessons from **PEAS in Uganda/Zambia**:
- **Cost-sharing PPPs** can deliver quality education at ~1/3 of government expenditure per school.
- **UK-Zambia knowledge transfer** (e.g., Education Specialists) improves teaching quality but requires contextual adaptation.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Addendum (2022)**: Added £5m to scale up school construction in **Southern and Eastern Provinces**, responding to demand and political opportunities under the new government.
2. **Embedded FCDO Advisor**: Replaced the British Council’s external advisory role due to limited impact (evidenced in 2023 Annual Review).
3. **Climate-resilient designs**: Integrated lessons from PEAS’s Uganda experience to pilot sustainable construction methods.
4. **Safeguarding enhancements**: Strengthened child protection measures based on UNICEF/Coram findings on school-related gender-based violence.
risks_lessons.quote: "From 2015-2018 DFID supported a bilateral Technical Assistance (TA) Education Programme, The Zambia Education Sector Support Technical Assistance (ZESSTA) Facility... Following fraud in the education sector and a lack of clear opportunity and commitment from the Government, bilateral education programming was deprioritised by FCDO Zambia." (90000395.odt, Option 3) && "The in-house education advisory role is also essential for the delivery of the programme due to... the gap will be closed by the programme-funded education advisor in-house role which will be more externally focused to develop closer relationships with government counterparts." (D0004786.odt, Describe any key changes) && "PEAS has a Public Private Partnership (PPP) agreement with MoGE and have been assessed by MoGE as providing good quality infrastructure at a reduced cost whilst also achieving higher educational outcomes." (90000395.odt, Insufficient, inequitable and inefficient education financing)

co_funding_partners.partner: Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to leverage **government co-financing** through the PPP model, where GRZ provides per-pupil payments to PEAS-managed schools. The addendum notes increased political will under the new government, which may unlock additional domestic or World Bank/IMF funding for education.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes **capital expenditures** (school construction/expansions: ~£5m added in 2022) and **revenue expenditures** (teacher training, school management, FCDO Advisor salary). The addendum focuses additional funds on capital (new schools) but maintains revenue support for operations.
financial_details.quote: "An increase to the business case value from £7,000,000 to £12,000,000 was approved by Ministers in July 2022... This additional funding will be used to scale up FCDO’s support to access to secondary schooling... by building a number of model schools." (D0004786.odt, What is the additional and total support) && "The programme will spend up to £7 million over four years to address challenges facing disadvantaged girls... It will build three new schools, four school expansions and system strengthening via school management and teaching improvement plans." (90000395.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: Climate Investment Fund for Pakistan (CIFPAK)
metadata.duration_text: seven-year programme will be entirely ODA-eligible and entirely International Climate Finance-eligible. The programme includes a break clause and review at the end of the current Spending Review (March 2025). [...] The programme will also complete a mid-term review in March 2028 to assess progress and potential scope for budget upscaling or reduction dependent on the achieved results.
metadata.quote: "CIFPAK will mobilise private climate finance to support Pakistan’s green growth and climate resilience ambitions." (D0006507.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Under this Business Case, BHC Islamabad is seeking approval for a flagship new climate finance programme to spend up to £108 million from April 2024 to April 2031. This seven-year programme will be entirely ODA-eligible and entirely International Climate Finance-eligible." (D0006507.odt, What approval is sought?)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CIFPAK is a blended finance facility designed to mobilize private climate finance at scale in Pakistan. It uses concessional capital to de-risk investments and crowd-in private sector funding for climate adaptation and mitigation projects. The programme combines grant capital, technical assistance, and financial instruments to address Pakistan's US$348 billion climate financing gap.
what_objectives.q1_source: "CIFPAK will mobilise private climate finance to support Pakistan’s green growth and climate resilience ambitions. Currently the 8th most climate vulnerable country in the world, the World Bank estimates that Pakistan will require US$348 billion of investment to become climate resilient and make the transition to a low-carbon economy by 2030. CIFPAK aims to crowd in private climate finance using a blended finance approach (public/private, concessional/non-concessional), supported by targeted technical assistance." (D0006507.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Mobilise 2.0x DFI capital and 3.0x private capital (5.0x total leverage)
Support over 100,000 low-carbon climate-resilient jobs
Support over 250,000 direct and indirect beneficiaries to enhance climate resilience and livelihoods
Support generation of over 200MW of clean energy
Save nearly $500 million of Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves
Develop Pakistan’s first private sector green bond issuance
Provide first-loss capital for climate-resilient agriculture fund
Introduce pay-at-harvest crop insurance and disaster microinsurance products
Conduct feasibility study for first green hydrogen plant in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
what_objectives.summary: CIFPAK is a £108m blended finance programme that uses UK aid to catalyze private sector investment in Pakistan's climate resilience and green growth. It combines risk capital, technical assistance, and market development to address the country's massive climate financing gap while supporting the UK's economic and trade partnership goals.
what_objectives.quote: "CIFPAK aims to directly mobilise 5.0x capital (2.0x DFI and 3.0x private sector), and support over 100,000 low carbon climate resilient jobs through its blended climate investments, as well as supporting over 250,000 direct and indirect beneficiaries to enhance their climate resilience and livelihoods." (D0006507.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan faces macroeconomic instability, climate vulnerability (ranked 8th most vulnerable), and security risks particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The programme risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' in the document despite these challenges.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006507.odt, Programme summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa may deter investors; macroeconomic instability affects capital market access; weak banking sector limits climate finance intermediation; shallow capital markets constrain green bond issuance; insurance penetration remains critically low at 1-2% of properties; political turbulence may reduce commitment to green growth.
where_context.quote: "Worsening of the security situation in Pakistan, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa could place staff and partners at risk. Uncertain environment for facilitating investment - deterring DFI and private financiers from investing in Pakistan, and businesses from investing in new projects." (D0006507.odt, What are the main risks?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO maintains overall programme control with implementation through Northern-based DFIs (BII, IFC) and technical assistance providers. Pakistani institutions (e.g., capital market authorities) receive support but have limited decision-making power over fund allocation.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to Pakistan Capital Market Authorities for green bond development
advisory support to strengthen investees' operational efficiency and ESG compliance
demand-led technical assistance to address policy and regulatory gaps
support for developing ESG standards in private sector

partner_organizations.name: British International Investment (BII)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Blended Finance Facility and Project Preparation Facility (Components 1 & 2)

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Green Capital Markets Development (Component 3) and potential delivery of Components 1 & 2

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Centres of Expertise
partner_organizations.role: Demand-led Technical Assistance (Component 4)

partner_organizations.name: GEMFA framework supplier
partner_organizations.role: Evaluations and Learning (Component 5)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Pakistan (various ministries)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary and policy counterpart

partner_organizations.name: Pakistan Capital Market Authorities
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of technical assistance for green bond development

partner_organizations.name: Private sector entities (banks, insurance companies, project developers)
partner_organizations.role: Ultimate recipients of blended finance and technical support

who_partners.quote: "Components 1 and 2 will be delivered by a development finance institution: British International Investment (BII) or the International Finance Corporation (IFC)" (D0006507.odt, What will CIFPAK do and how will it deliver?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of: 1) Blended finance facility (concessional capital + private investment); 2) Technical assistance grants; 3) Project preparation grants; and 4) Potential guarantee mechanisms. The blended finance approach combines FCDO's concessional 'fiscal C-DEL' with commercial pools to catalyze private sector investment.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees the programme with implementation delegated to specialized partners: BII/IFC manage the investment components (Components 1-3), FCDO Centres of Expertise deliver technical assistance (Component 4), and a GEMFA supplier handles MEL (Component 5). Each component has distinct delivery partners with separate accountability to FCDO.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection leverages existing FCDO relationships with British International Investment (BII) and International Finance Corporation (IFC), which have specialized capabilities in blended finance and capital market development. The document states these were chosen based on their "world-leading financial expertise" and alignment with the British Investment Partnerships toolkit.
how_mechanism.quote: "Components 1 and 2 will be delivered by a development finance institution: British International Investment (BII) or the International Finance Corporation (IFC)" [...] "Component 3 will be delivered by the International Finance Corporation (IFC)" (D0006507.odt, What will CIFPAK do and how will it deliver?)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Investment decisions for the blended finance facility will be made jointly between FCDO and the DFI partner (BII/IFC) based on agreed development impact criteria. The document specifies that deals must meet an 'Enhanced Development Impact' hurdle modeled on BII's framework.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions periodic reviews with break clauses (March 2025, March 2026) and a mid-term review (March 2028) that require submission to the 2PUS and Ministers, implying a high-level governance structure. The Blended Finance Facility will have specific governance arrangements between FCDO and the DFI partner.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: The programme includes mandatory reviews at fixed intervals (2025, 2026, 2028) with break clauses, plus ongoing monitoring against the Enhanced Development Impact framework. The technical assistance components will use demand-led approaches with embedded advisors.
how_governance.quote: "The programme includes a break clause and review at the end of the current Spending Review (March 2025). [...] The programme will also complete a mid-term review in March 2028 to assess progress and potential scope for budget upscaling or reduction dependent on the achieved results." (D0006507.odt, What approval is sought?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme has built-in break clauses allowing for budget adjustments at predetermined review points (2025, 2026, 2028). The mid-term review explicitly allows for "potential scope for budget upscaling or reduction dependent on the achieved results." However, reallocation between components appears constrained by the fixed partnerships with different DFIs.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities through the periodic reviews (2025, 2026, 2028) which require Ministerial approval. The demand-led Technical Assistance facility (Component 4) is explicitly designed to be flexible in responding to emerging policy gaps. The blended finance facility can also adapt to new investment opportunities that meet the development impact criteria.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will also complete a mid-term review in March 2028 to assess progress and potential scope for budget upscaling or reduction dependent on the achieved results. Recommendations of this 2028 review will then be submitted to the 2PUS and Ministers before FY2028/29." (D0006507.odt, What approval is sought?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → DFI partners (BII/IFC) → Pakistani private sector entities/beneficiaries. For technical assistance: FCDO → Centres of Expertise/FCDO advisors → Government of Pakistan institutions.
how_efficiency.quote: "The programme includes a break clause and review at the end of the current Spending Review (March 2025)." (D0006507.odt, What approval is sought?) implies milestone-based funding releases.

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct grant funding to Government of Pakistan
Pure technical assistance programme without blended finance
Multilateral climate fund contributions (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
Bilateral climate projects with individual private sector partners
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The blended finance approach was selected because: 1) Pakistan's climate financing gap (US$348 billion) cannot be addressed by public funds alone; 2) The private sector in Pakistan is risk-averse and requires de-risking to invest in climate projects; 3) UK has comparative advantage through its financial sector expertise (City of London) and existing DFI relationships (BII); 4) The model aligns with both UK's International Development Strategy and Integrated Review 2023 priorities for private-sector-led growth; 5) It allows for leverage (5x capital mobilization target) and market transformation beyond direct UK aid spending.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (blended finance reduces private sector risk exposure)
partner capacity (utilizing BII/IFC's existing climate finance expertise)
speed (building on existing BIP toolkit relationships)
equity (explicit focus on gender and marginalized groups through 2X criteria)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Macroeconomic shocks could impair blended finance returns and deter private investors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Senior BHC engagement to reinforce macroeconomic stability; portfolio diversification; no expectation of reflows from Fiscal C-DEL investments

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa may limit project implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: BHC Overseas Security Managers monitor risks; contingency plans for high-risk locations; strict adherence to security protocols

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government of Pakistan political turbulence reduces commitment to green growth
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ongoing policy influencing through other FCDO programmes (e.g., REMIT); maintaining relationships with local counterparts

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Shallow capital markets limit green bond issuance potential
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance to develop ESG standards; co-funding for initial issuances; specialist de-risking tools

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Blended finance facility may crowd out other climate investments if not properly structured
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Application of Enhanced Development Impact hurdle; sector-specific risk limits; alignment with DFI Principles on blended concessional finance

why_rationale.quote: "Delivering low-carbon climate resilient infrastructure and investment through British Investment Partnerships (BIP) is central to both the UK’s Integrated Review 2023 and UK International Development Strategy. The UK is well placed to leverage the BIP Toolkit through CIFPAK [...] to build climate resilience and reduce Pakistan’s GHG emission trajectory." (D0006507.odt, Why should the UK intervene?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Pakistan's moderate risk profile and specific constraints (security risks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, macroeconomic instability, shallow capital markets) directly shape partner selection: 1) Security risks limit field presence to established DFIs with existing Pakistan operations; 2) Macroeconomic volatility necessitates partners with strong risk management capabilities (hence BII/IFC selection); 3) Weak local capital markets require international expertise for green bond development; 4) Political economy constraints favor multilateral partners (IFC) over direct government engagement.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa require partners with existing in-country security protocols
Macroeconomic instability necessitates DFIs with strong balance sheets and risk management
Shallow capital markets limit local partner options for green finance instruments
Regulatory environment favors international DFIs familiar with Pakistan's business climate
Political economy constraints make multilateral partners preferable to bilateral government engagement
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The financing mechanism objective (mobilizing 5x private capital) determines: 1) The blended finance structure (combining concessional and commercial capital); 2) The need for specialized DFI partners with balance sheets to absorb risk; 3) The technical assistance components to develop bankable projects; 4) The periodic review structure to demonstrate leverage to UK ministers; 5) The focus on capital market development to create sustainable financing channels beyond the programme lifetime.
q28_linkages: Leverage target (5x) → requires blended finance structure with risk-absorbing DFIs
Adaptation focus → necessitates project preparation facility for underdeveloped pipeline
Gender inclusion (2X) → shapes partner selection criteria and monitoring requirements
Capital market development → determines need for IFC's specialized expertise
Macroeconomic risks → drives periodic review structure with break clauses
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses several equity-efficiency tradeoffs: 1) Gender inclusion (2X criteria) is prioritized despite potentially reducing the pool of eligible investments; 2) Climate adaptation focus (which has fewer bankable projects) is maintained alongside mitigation for equity reasons; 3) Technical assistance to local institutions is included despite higher transaction costs than pure financial intermediation; 4) The blended finance facility accepts lower financial returns to achieve development impact in frontier sectors.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Gender lens investing (2X) may reduce financial returns but is required for equity
Adaptation projects (higher risk) are included alongside mitigation for balanced impact
Local capacity building increases costs but is necessary for sustainable markets
Concessionality in blended finance reduces leverage ratios but enables frontier investments
Periodic reviews add management burden but ensure accountability to UK taxpayers
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives intensive oversight through: 1) Mandatory break clauses at 2025/2026; 2) Mid-term review in 2028 with Ministerial approval; 3) Enhanced Development Impact hurdles for all investments; 4) Portfolio diversification requirements; 5) Embedded security management for high-risk regions. The oversight intensity is explicitly calibrated to the identified macroeconomic and security risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Requiring DFIs to provide post-investment advisory support to strengthen ESG compliance; 2) Including a standalone technical assistance component for policy/regulatory gaps; 3) Mandating gender inclusion (2X) criteria that require partners to develop specific expertise; 4) Tasking IFC with capital market development to build local institutional capacity; 5) Using demand-led approaches to ensure technical assistance responds to actual partner needs.
intersections.quote: "The use of the facility will need to demonstrate that it addresses high risk associated with high uncertainty, first mover disadvantage, or high structural costs." (D0006507.odt, What is the expected development impact) shows how the 'what' (frontier climate investments) determines the 'how' (blended finance structure with risk absorption).

key_programme_risks: Macroeconomic shocks impairing investment pipeline and financial returns
Deteriorating security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa affecting implementation
Reduced government commitment to green growth due to political turbulence
Inability to develop bankable adaptation projects (current pipeline is mitigation-skewed)
Capital market closure due to credit rating downgrades and high interest rates
Low insurance penetration limiting disaster risk financing instruments
Currency volatility affecting foreign exchange savings targets
Gender inclusion targets not being met in male-dominated sectors
First-loss capital being exhausted without sufficient private sector follow-on
Regulatory inconsistencies deterring private climate investors

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Senior BHC and HMG engagement to reinforce macroeconomic stability; REMIT programme supporting reforms; no expectation of reflows from Fiscal C-DEL; portfolio diversification
BHC Overseas Security Managers monitoring; movement restrictions and protocols; regular risk monitoring; security training; contingency plans for high-risk locations
Maintaining relationships with local counterparts; ongoing policy influencing through REMIT; coordination with other donors
Dedicated Project Preparation Facility; aggregation of smaller projects; focus on developing bankable adaptation projects
Technical assistance to develop ESG standards; co-funding for initial green bond issuances; specialist de-risking tools
2X criteria for all investments; explicit focus on women's resilience in project design; monitoring of gender-disaggregated impacts
Concessional currency risk solutions for international investors; focus on local currency capital market development

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for embedded security management in conflict-affected regions (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa)
Importance of flexible technical assistance to adapt to changing political priorities
Value of multilateral partners (IFC) in FCAS contexts for risk sharing
Necessity of periodic break clauses to manage macroeconomic volatility
Critical role of demand-led approaches in fragile policy environments
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The document references lessons from: 1) Existing FCDO programmes in Pakistan (SEED, REMIT) that demonstrated the need for project preparation support; 2) Global blended finance facilities showing the importance of flexible instruments for risk mitigation; 3) BII's enhanced development impact framework for measuring transformational change; 4) IFC's AIIM impact framework for inclusion criteria; 5) Previous climate funds highlighting the need to address the mismatch between investor risk perception and actual project risks.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design adaptations include: 1) Explicit adaptation focus (not just mitigation) based on Pakistan's vulnerability; 2) Dedicated project preparation facility to address pipeline weaknesses; 3) Gender lens (2X) integrated throughout based on flood impact assessments; 4) Capital market development component added to create sustainable financing channels; 5) Periodic review structure with break clauses to manage macroeconomic risks; 6) Demand-led technical assistance based on partner feedback from earlier programmes.
risks_lessons.quote: "Elections and political turbulence lead to reduced federal and provincial political commitment to green Pakistan's economy, increase climate resilience and support green growth." (D0006507.odt, What are the main risks?) shows the FCAS-specific political risks being addressed through the programme design.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize 5.0x capital against the £108m UK investment (2.0x from DFIs and 3.0x from private sector), targeting £540m in total climate finance. This includes both direct mobilization through the blended finance facility and indirect mobilization through market development effects.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme uses Fiscal C-DEL (capital expenditure) for the blended finance components, with resource spending (R-DEL) likely used for technical assistance and programme management. The document specifies that "there is no expectation of reflows from Fiscal C-DEL investments."
financial_details.quote: "CIFPAK aims to directly mobilise 5.0x capital (2.0x DFI and 3.0x private sector), and support over 100,000 low carbon climate resilient jobs through its blended climate investments." (D0006507.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: FCDO Kenya: Kenya Anti-Corruption Programme

quote.text: This £3 million programme will seek to build the evidence base and develop innovative and practical interventions to address corruption in Kenya. Over a 3-year period, it will aim to sustain momentum on combatting corruption through the 2022 election cycle and to increase citizen confidence through the delivery of priority results.

metadata.duration_source: Over a 3-year period

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (building evidence base on corruption), capacity building (strengthening institutions), policy influence (supporting legislative reforms), and implementation research (piloting interventions). It aims to address systemic corruption through both prevention and accountability mechanisms.
what_objectives.q1_source: This £3 million programme will seek to build the evidence base and develop innovative and practical interventions to address corruption in Kenya. [...] The programme will aim to achieve four outputs: 1) Improved evidence, data and analysis of corruption and innovation in programming; 2) Strengthened efforts to prevent corruption in the public and private sectors; 3) Strengthened institutions deliver criminal justice and accountability; 4) Strengthened regional institutions and cooperation to counter illicit financial flows.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved evidence, data and analysis of corruption and innovation in programming

what_objectives.summary: The programme is a mixed-objective initiative designed to combat corruption in Kenya through evidence generation, institutional strengthening, and accountability mechanisms. It focuses on both prevention (public/private sectors) and enforcement (criminal justice) while leveraging regional cooperation to counter illicit financial flows.

quote.text: The programme will aim to achieve four outputs: 1) Improved evidence, data and analysis of corruption and innovation in programming; 2) Strengthened efforts to prevent corruption in the public and private sectors, and delivery of the Kenya government’s anti-corruption commitments; 3) Strengthened institutions deliver criminal justice and accountability through effective prosecutions and asset recovery; 4) Strengthened regional institutions and cooperation to counter illicit financial flows.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Corruption in Kenya is described as "complex, systemic, and pervasive," with weak institutions and political economy challenges. However, the programme risk rating is explicitly stated as "Moderate," reflecting a balance between endemic corruption and the existence of reform efforts and international partnerships.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions (e.g., Auditor General’s inability to determine government net worth due to poor record-keeping) and political economy factors (e.g., patronage networks, election-related corruption) undermine accountability. Regulatory loopholes (e.g., in campaign finance, beneficial ownership) enable corruption. Climate risks and illicit financial flows (e.g., trade misinvoicing costing ~$900m/year) divert resources from development goals. The 2022 election cycle increases political competition and risks rolling back reforms.

quote.text: Corruption in Kenya is complex, systemic, and pervasive. Illicit finance, tax evasion and fraud in public procurement are widespread. [...] Weak and inadequate maintenance of accounting records across several Ministries made it difficult to determine the net worth of the Government of Kenya as a whole. [...] The Auditor’s estimates suggest that Kenya could be losing GBP 7.7 billion (1 Trillion Ksh) a year. [...] There is intense political competition ahead of the 2022 election. [...] Poor financial governance in East Africa enables the financing of terrorism, diverts revenue away from achieving development goals, drives crime and conflict and enables corrupt elites to entrench their power.
quote.source: 90000487.odt, Context and strategic fit with UK objectives

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO Kenya retains strategic oversight and decision-making authority, with implementation delivered through a mix of UK-procured technical assistance, grants to local/regional CSOs, and partnerships with Kenyan institutions (e.g., EACC, ODPP). Southern partners (e.g., TI-Kenya, KEMSA) play operational roles but are not described as having equal decision-making power.
