Infrastructure project delays (e.g., road design changes from erosion data)
Financial mismanagement (weak PFM systems, irregular audits)
Harbour failure (loss of access if EDF replacement funding gaps)
Limited local uptake of training (small population, resistance to change)
Reputational damage to UK if obligations under UN Charter are unmet
Storm/geological events disrupting infrastructure or records

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use **specialized UK recruitment agencies**; involve island officials in selection; budget for relocation allowances.
Phase spending (e.g., roads in 2023/4, harbour in 2024/5); incorporate erosion data into designs.
**Chief Finance Officer TC** embedded in Treasury; quarterly accounts to FCDO; Annual Audited Statements.
Allocate **£1.5m in 2024/5** to replace EDF funds; prioritize annual maintenance in MoU.
Schedule **partner training** during off-island trips; monitor via TC reviews.
Work with external partners to **assess geological risks**; build resilience into infrastructure designs.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Small island fragility**: Previous storms caused **lost financial records**, prompting regularization efforts.
**TC dependency**: Past programmes showed **limited reduction in TC needs** due to population size; current design accepts long-term reliance.
**Procurement limitations**: "Very small number of suppliers" → MoU includes FCDO procurement support.
**Auditing challenges**: 9-month delay for Annual Audited Statements due to remoteness → now mitigated via quarterly reviews.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
**Knowledge transfer is challenging**: Past TC programmes struggled to pass on expertise due to the tiny community. **Mitigation**: Added Chief Operating Officer to monitor training; regular TC reviews.

**Infrastructure declines rapidly**: Previous ad-hoc repairs led to higher long-term costs. **Mitigation**: Shift to **planned maintenance regimes** and capital upgrades (e.g., roads).

**Administrator capacity is a bottleneck**: Overloaded in past projects. **Mitigation**: New **Chief Operating Officer role** to share workload.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Added Chief Operating Officer** to address Administrator overload.
2. **Increased capital budget** for proactive infrastructure upgrades (vs. reactive repairs).
3. **Formalized knowledge transfer** in MoU (e.g., TC training logs).
4. **Phased harbour funding** to avoid EDF withdrawal gaps.
5. **Gender-inclusive training** (partners trained alongside TCs).

quote.source: D0005568.odt, Overview and Lessons Learnt sections
quote.text: "Our approach will build on lessons learnt from previous programmes. In particular, throughout the programme particular efforts will be focussed on ensuring that TCs on island pass on as much of their expertise as possible to those present. [...] The Administrator capacity has been an issue throughout the current and previous projects. We will address this through the addition of the Chief Operating Officer Role."

capital_vs_revenue_split.description: £2m for **Technical Cooperation (TC) support** (revenue/RDEL); £3.8m for **essential capital works** (CDEL). Capital focuses on roads (£1m in 2023/4, £1.5m in 2024/5) and harbour maintenance.

quote.source: D0005568.odt, Programme Value and Financial Year sections
quote.text: "Programme Value: £5,800,000 over 2 years (£2m RDEL, £3,800,000 CDEL)" and "2023/4 (confirmed): £1,000,000 (RDEL), £1,500,000 (CDEL); 2024/5 (estimated): £1,000,000 (RDEL), £2,300,000 (CDEL)."

metadata.programme_name: Data for Foundational Learning (Data4FL)

quote.text: £27m over four years to track the numbers of children in school and learning globally, and to support the better generation and use of national data on learning, to address the global learning crisis.

duration_source.text: £27m over four years to track the numbers of children in school and learning globally

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (improving global measurement of learning), technology development (new assessment tools), capacity building (supporting national governments to use data), and policy influence (tracking SDG4 progress). It focuses on addressing the global learning crisis by improving data systems and ensuring learning outcomes are measured and acted upon.

q1_source.text: In partnership with global specialists, Data4FL will draw on a new package of global public goods, education standards, and assessment tools; to significantly improve the global measurement of learning and bolster the efforts of national governments and education partners committed to driving progress on children’s learning outcomes. [...] This programme will enable better information on the numbers of children in school and learning, including girls, which will strengthen the tracking and the effective policies and interventions needed to make progress on SDG4.1.1, countries’ own national benchmarks, World Bank’s learning poverty reduction, and the G7 endorsed Global Objectives on access and learning.
q1_source.source: D0003277.odt, Programme summary and Expected impact and outcomes

q3_expected_outputs.output: More developing partner countries report internationally on comparable and disaggregated data on learning, including in Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises (EiEPC)
More state capability to regularly use disaggregated learning data so more governments and teachers implement and monitor interventions to improve foundational learning for all in priority countries
Global public goods: new package of education standards and assessment tools for measuring learning
Support to national governments to generate cost-effective data on learning in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs)
Improved tracking of SDG4.1.1 (proportion of children achieving minimum proficiency in reading and mathematics)
Reduction in learning poverty (children unable to read a simple text by age 10) by 2030
q3_expected_outputs.target: Reduce global share of children unable to read by age 10 by half by 2030

q3_expected_outputs.output: Disaggregated data by gender, disability, and other characteristics to identify marginalized groups

what_objectives.summary: Data4FL aims to improve the global measurement of learning outcomes and support national governments in using data to address the learning crisis, with a focus on foundational skills like literacy and numeracy. It aligns with SDG4 and the UK’s G7 commitments on girls’ education and learning poverty reduction.

quote.text: The Data for Foundational Learning programme will deliver the following high-level objectives. IMPACT: Contribute to progress against SDG4.1.1 and learning poverty reduction in LICs and MICs. [...] OUTCOME 1: More developing partner countries report internationally on comparable and disaggregated data on learning, including in EiEPC. OUTCOME 2: More state capability to regularly use disaggregated learning data so more governments and teachers implement and monitor interventions to improve foundational learning for all in priority countries.

countries_regions: Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises (EiEPC) contexts globally
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a wide range of contexts globally, including fragile and conflict-affected states (EiEPC), which introduces complexity. However, the overall risk rating is classified as 'Minor' in the document, suggesting managed risks with mitigation strategies in place.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Minor

q6_constraints_impact.weak_institutions: Educations systems in LICs and MICs lack capability to generate or use learning data effectively. For example, teachers are often not trained to use assessments, and ministries struggle to share data across departments.
q6_constraints_impact.conflict: In EiEPC contexts, there is limited systematic data on student numbers or learning outcomes, making it difficult to track progress or target support. Example: "More effort is needed to identify and understand the challenges faced by out of school children globally, so they can be effectively supported to access education and to learn."
q6_constraints_impact.climate_risks: Climate change disrupts education provision, increasing the need for data on how schools protect children from climate impacts. Example: "Education provision in LICs and LMICs is vulnerable to the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events."
q6_constraints_impact.data_limitations: 78 countries have not reported SDG learning indicators in the last seven years, and only 17/48 sub-Saharan African countries have recent high-quality assessments. Example: "Most governments and education partners struggle to rigorously demonstrate the impact of their education programming on children’s learning outcomes at scale in LICs and MICs."
q6_constraints_impact.political_economy: Political ambition often doesn’t match investment in learning data due to short-term incentives (e.g., focusing on access over quality). Example: "Improving learning is hard to do, less easily visible to the community, and takes time to achieve."
q6_constraints_impact.language_barriers: 37% of students in LICs and MICs are not taught in a language they understand, affecting assessment validity. Example: "An estimated 37% of students in LICs and MICs are not even taught in a language they understand."

quote.text: The situation is significantly worse in contexts of emergency and/or protracted crisis (EiEPC), where there is already limited systematic and timely data to show the numbers of students and where they are, let alone if they are learning or not. [...] In many contexts, political ambition does not match the level of investment and expertise needed to introduce or reform learning data generation.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) and Global Education Monitoring Report (GEMR)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is designed and overseen by FCDO (UK), with implementation support from multilateral partners (UIS, GEMR) and global specialists. Southern partners (e.g., PAL Network, national governments) adapt and use tools but do not lead decision-making on global standards or funding allocations.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for teachers and officials on using learning assessments
Support to national governments to generate and use disaggregated data
Technical assistance to align assessments with global proficiency frameworks
Strengthening education data systems in EiEPC contexts
Building demand for learning data among citizens (e.g., through PAL Network)

partner_organizations.name: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS)
partner_organizations.role: Global tracking of SDG4 indicators; development of Global Proficiency Framework and assessment tools

partner_organizations.name: UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report (GEMR)
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring progress on SDG4; national benchmarking support

partner_organizations.name: People’s Action for Learning (PAL) Network
partner_organizations.role: Citizen-led assessments; bottom-up data generation in 15 countries
partner_organizations.location: Southern-led (South-South partnership across Africa, Asia, Latin America)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank, UNICEF, USAID, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Partners in the Learning Data Compact and Accelerator Programme; co-funding and technical support

partner_organizations.name: National governments in priority countries (e.g., Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, Sierra Leone)
partner_organizations.role: Adopt and implement learning assessments; use data for policy reforms

partner_organizations.name: Education Cannot Wait (ECW)
partner_organizations.role: Support in EiEPC contexts; coordination with humanitarian actors

quote.text: UK aid, in close partnership with leading partners, will get behind national governments efforts to improve learning, by providing options for solutions and targeted specialist expertise. [...] The programme will fit into a wider package of global support to address the learning crisis. Working with partners, this programme will be part of a major shift by the UK and its global partners to improve the measurement of learning levels, and then signpost to the necessary interventions and support needed to take action and see progress.
quote.source: D0003277.odt, What will the programme do?

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of core funding to multilateral partners (UIS, GEMR) and targeted grants/contracts for specific components (e.g., PAL Network, national government support). The exact instruments for each component are not detailed, but the structure suggests a blend of block funding (for global public goods) and project-specific agreements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through existing multilateral platforms (UIS, GEMR) for global tracking, with additional partnerships (e.g., PAL Network, Accelerator Programme) for country-level implementation. FCDO provides oversight and strategic direction, while technical delivery is delegated to specialized agencies.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners like UIS and GEMR were selected based on their global mandates for SDG4 monitoring and existing relationships with FCDO (e.g., through the BESTA programme). The PAL Network and Accelerator Programme countries were chosen for their demonstrated commitment to learning data reforms.

quote.text: We propose to implement Component 1 through continued funding to UNESCO’s Institute for Statistics (UIS) and UNESCO’s Global Education Monitoring Report (GEMR). [...] The programme will proactively build political demand for better learning data and help with market shaping, including in fragile contexts, in addition to the supply of technical support.
quote.source: D0003277.odt, Component 1 and Programme delivery sections

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Sub-awards (e.g., to national governments or CSOs) are likely allocated through joint decision-making between FCDO and multilateral partners (e.g., UIS, World Bank), based on country demand and alignment with global objectives. Example: The Accelerator Programme targets countries demonstrating political commitment to learning reforms.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Learning Data Compact and Accelerator Programme include coordinated governance among UNESCO, UNICEF, World Bank, and donors (including FCDO). For example: "National governments and education partners will be supported to draw flexibly on an available menu of evidenced-based methodologies, tools, and solutions."

quote.text: The approved Concept Note proposed three priority activities to deliver the outcomes and contribute to the impact set out in the strategic case: Track children’s learning outcomes at global level; Improve national government reporting of children’s learning outcomes; Ensure learning data is used to inform policies, plans and interventions.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can likely be reallocated between components (e.g., global tracking vs. country support) with FCDO approval, as the programme is designed to respond to demand (e.g., from Accelerator Programme countries). However, core funding to multilaterals (UIS/GEMR) may have less flexibility.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive management to respond to emerging needs, such as new crises (e.g., climate impacts) or country demand for specific tools. Example: "The programme will proactively build political demand for better learning data and help with market shaping, including in fragile contexts."

quote.text: The programme will fit into a wider package of global support to address the learning crisis. Working with partners, this programme will be part of a major shift by the UK and its global partners to improve the measurement of learning levels, and then signpost to the necessary interventions and support needed to take action and see progress.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral partners (UIS/GEMR/PAL) → National governments/CSOs. The structure is relatively streamlined, with multilaterals acting as intermediaries for global public goods and country-level support.

quote.text: The programme will build on previous investments to continue to improve the tracking and generation of learning data globally. For example, through support to UNESCO’s Institute of Statistics, Global Education Monitoring Report, and the PAL network.

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Focused support to a smaller set of countries with deep technical assistance
Option B: Global public goods development without targeted country implementation
Option A+B (preferred): Mixed approach combining global tools (Component 1) with country-level support (Component 2)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed approach (A+B) was chosen to maximize reach (global tools) while ensuring uptake and adaptation at the country level. This balances efficiency (scaling proven tools) with effectiveness (tailored support where political will exists). The rationale emphasizes the need for both supply (tools/data) and demand (country ownership) to drive systemic change.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging existing investments in BESTA)
risk mitigation (diversifying across global and country levels)
partner capacity (building on UIS/GEMR’s mandates and PAL Network’s reach)
flexibility (responding to country demand and crises)
equity (ensuring marginalized groups are included via disaggregated data)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented uptake of global tools by countries due to varying capacities or political priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted support to Accelerator Programme countries and demand-driven technical assistance to ensure tools are adapted and used. Example: "Countries will be supported to learn from others what is now possible in relation to generating effective learning assessments."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low ownership of data by national governments, leading to rejection of findings
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedding data generation in national systems (e.g., via SDG4 benchmarking) and building political demand through citizen-led assessments (PAL Network). Example: "Data must be rigorous, transparent, and owned from the beginning by the decision-makers, i.e., national governments, officials, headteachers and teachers."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other donor initiatives (e.g., World Bank’s Accelerator Programme, Learning Data Compact)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Coordinating through existing platforms (e.g., GAML, UIS repository) and aligning with global commitments (e.g., Commitment to Action on Foundational Learning). Example: "The programme will fit into a wider package of global support to address the learning crisis."

vfm_criteria_used: economy (building on existing investments in BESTA)
efficiency (scaling cost-effective tools like the Global Proficiency Framework)
effectiveness (focusing on foundational learning as a high-impact area)
equity (prioritizing disaggregated data to reach marginalized groups)

quote.text: The preferred option is the latter; a mixed approach of Option A and Option B. This complementary approach will enable maximum reach globally, while also leveraging bespoke targeted UK support to improve learning data globally. [...] Determining how to improve national reporting must go in hand in hand with how to strengthen the use of learning data by national governments, school leaders, and teachers.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s global scope and focus on fragile contexts (EiEPC) limit partner selection to organizations with multilateral mandates (e.g., UIS, UNICEF) or proven reach in LMICs (e.g., PAL Network). Local CSOs or governments in high-risk areas may only be engaged through intermediaries like Education Cannot Wait (ECW).
q27_constraints_detail: Fragile contexts require partners with humanitarian expertise (e.g., ECW)
Data limitations necessitate partners with technical capacity (e.g., UIS for SDG4 tracking)
Political economy constraints favor multilaterals over direct government funding
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **comparable global data** (WHAT) drives the use of multilaterals (UIS/GEMR) for standard-setting, while the goal of **country-owned reforms** (WHAT) requires flexible partnerships (e.g., Accelerator Programme, PAL Network). The mix of global public goods and tailored support reflects the dual objectives of scalability and contextual relevance.
q28_linkages: Global measurement goals → Multilateral management (UIS/GEMR)
Country-level action → Demand-driven partnerships (Accelerator/PAL)
Equity focus → Disaggregated data tools and Southern-led networks (PAL)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (scaling global tools) with equity (targeting marginalized groups). For example, while the Global Proficiency Framework ensures comparability, the PAL Network’s citizen-led assessments include out-of-school children often missed by top-down systems. The trade-off is managed by layering global standards with localized adaptations.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid global tracking (via UIS) may miss nuanced local needs, addressed by slower but inclusive citizen-led data (PAL).
Global tools (developed by UIS/World Bank) are adapted by Southern partners (e.g., PAL Network, national governments) to ensure relevance.
Investing in high-quality assessments (costly) is justified by the need to reach 70% of children in learning poverty (high impact).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (including FCAS contexts) leads to milestone-based oversight with embedded safeguards (e.g., safeguarding policies for vulnerable groups). Example: "Strong central and post-based co-ordination efforts will be made to align and adhere to Education in Emergencies principles."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with partners selected based on their ability to strengthen national systems. For example, UIS provides technical training on the Global Proficiency Framework, while PAL Network builds citizen demand for data. Southern partners (e.g., national governments) are positioned as adaptors/implementers rather than decision-makers on global standards.

quote.text: The programme will proactively build political demand for better learning data and help with market shaping, including in fragile contexts, in addition to the supply of technical support. [...] Countries will be supported to learn from others what is now possible in relation to generating effective learning assessments and select and adapt the most cost-effective option for themselves.
quote.source: D0003277.odt, Intersections of context, objectives, and delivery

key_programme_risks: Low political prioritization of learning data over access (e.g., school buildings)
Fragmented or infrequent learning assessments limiting comparability
Weak national capacity to use disaggregated data for decision-making
Data rejection by governments due to perceived poor quality or lack of ownership
Overlap or duplication with other donor initiatives (e.g., World Bank’s Accelerator Programme)
Climate and conflict disruptions in EiEPC contexts affecting data collection
Limited demand for learning data from teachers/parents due to lack of awareness

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low political prioritization of learning data
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Build demand through citizen-led assessments (PAL Network) and link data to visible outcomes (e.g., SDG4 benchmarks). Example: "The PAL Network explicitly builds awareness and demand amongst citizens for better data on learning in the longer term."

Promote the Global Proficiency Framework and policy-linking methods to harmonize national and international data. Example: "‘Policy linking’ enables countries that do not engage in regional and international assessments to link their national assessment to the Global Proficiency Framework."

Provide targeted technical assistance (e.g., through Accelerator Programme) and embed data use in teacher training. Example: "Alleducation stakeholders, including teachers, need support to understand their roles and how to use simple learning assessments effectively."
Ensure data is co-generated with national stakeholders and transparent. Example: "Data must be rigorous, transparent, and owned from the beginning by the decision-makers."

Coordinate through existing platforms (e.g., GAML, Learning Data Compact) and align with global commitments. Example: "The programme will fit into a wider package of global support to address the learning crisis."

Work with EiEPC specialists (e.g., ECW) and design conflict-sensitive data systems. Example: "Where support takes place in EiEPC contexts, this will be designed in a conflict-sensitive way, supporting the strengthening of education systems where possible."

fcas_specific_lessons: In EiEPC contexts, data systems must prioritize tracking out-of-school children and mobile populations. Lesson: "More effort is needed to identify and understand the challenges faced by out of school children globally."

Partnerships with humanitarian actors (e.g., ECW) are critical for reaching conflict-affected areas. Lesson: "Strong central and post-based co-ordination efforts will be made to align and adhere to Education in Emergencies principles."
Data tools must be simple and low-tech to function in low-infrastructure settings. Lesson: "Learning assessments need to be simple and low stakes, to increase their effectiveness and reduce costs."

lessons_from_previous.text: The programme builds on the BESTA programme’s successes, including: (1) The Global Proficiency Framework’s ability to link national and international assessments; (2) The effectiveness of citizen-led assessments (PAL Network) in mobilizing community demand for data; (3) The need for political engagement to drive data use, as seen in SDG4 benchmarking. Example: "This new programme will build on the progress made by BESTA."
lessons_from_previous.source: D0003277.odt, Box 1: UK support to improve education data

design_changes_based_on_learning.text: Key adaptations include: (1) Shifting from access-focused data to learning outcomes data post-COVID; (2) Prioritizing foundational learning (literacy/numeracy) over broader education metrics; (3) Embedding equity considerations (e.g., disaggregation by disability/gender) based on lessons from SDG4 monitoring. Example: "The UK has supported improvements in the coverage, depth and quality of education data globally [...] Most recently this has been through the ‘Better Education Statistics and Action to improve learning’ (BESTA) programme."
design_changes_based_on_learning.source: D0003277.odt, Lessons from BESTA and programme design

quote.text: The programme will learn from the Girls’ Education Challenge projects to understand how to ensure data reform is sensitive to the needs of the most marginalised. [...] Currently, where there are learning assessments, they are very fragmented and infrequent, especially in LICs and MICs, where the effects of the learning crisis are most severely felt.

leverage_achieved.text: The programme leverages co-funding from the Learning Data Compact (UNESCO/UNICEF/World Bank) and the Accelerator Programme (World Bank/BMGF/USAID). FCDO’s support to UIS/GEMR has also catalyzed additional funding, e.g., BMGF’s support for the GEMR spotlight report on Sub-Saharan Africa.
leverage_achieved.source: D0003277.odt, Box 1 and Global Coalition sections

quote.text: £27m over four years to track the numbers of children in school and learning globally, and to support the better generation and use of national data on learning, to address the global learning crisis.

metadata.programme_name: Green Growth Nepal (GGN)
metadata.quote: "GGN will increase green, resilient, and inclusive growth by expanding investment in green industries and services, improving climate-resilient infrastructure, and strengthening sustainable economic policy and facilitating economic opportunities across Nepal." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: FY2023/24; AMP End Date: FY2030/31" (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GGN combines capacity building (strengthening government institutions for green growth), policy influence (supporting economic policy reforms), implementation research (testing green finance instruments), and financing mechanisms (leveraging private climate finance). The programme aims to drive green economic transformation in Nepal by addressing constraints in investment, infrastructure, and financial sectors.
what_objectives.q1_source: "GGN will support the Government of Nepal (GoN) to: Strengthen sustainable economic policy and improve Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) to drive green growth. Support city governments to attract and implement climate-resilient investment projects. Underpin Nepal’s green growth by deepening the financial sector and mobilising private climate finance." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Green growth strategies and investment promoted (£17.8m)
targets: MoICS, MoF, and provincial governments to introduce and deliver greener economic strategies
GoN to introduce improved FDI and investment legislation/procedures
Three provincial governments with higher capacity to plan, budget, and implement economic infrastructure

q3_expected_outputs.output: Investment Board Nepal (IBN) strengthened as FDI and PPP fast-track agency (£11.3m)
targets: Increased volume and quality of investment (>£500m) committed to large-scale projects, especially in green sectors
Financial and human resource sustainability of IBN to deliver functions set in Nepal’s legislation
Social and environmental safeguards enforced through the project lifecycle

q3_expected_outputs.output: Climate-resilient infrastructure investment enabled in cities (£8.9m)
targets: Improved approach to economic investment strategy, planning, and delivery of capital budgets by sub-national governments
Catalytic climate-resilient investments leveraged at subnational level (£100m)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Financial sector deepening (£9m)
targets: Mechanisms for Nepali institutions to access more green and international capital (e.g., green taxonomy, sovereign credit rating)
Green financial vehicles and instruments mobilized for projects

q3_expected_outputs.output: Feasibility studies and adaptive management (£1.46m)
targets: Evidence generation for delivery partner and FCDO management team
Independent assessments against outputs and outcomes set in the log-frame

what_objectives.summary: GGN aims to catalyze Nepal’s transition to a green, resilient, and inclusive economy by 2030 through a combination of policy reforms, institutional strengthening, and private sector engagement. The programme focuses on leveraging UK expertise in infrastructure, cities, and finance to address Nepal’s constraints in green growth, including inadequate FDI, weak financial sectors, and insufficient climate-resilient infrastructure.
what_objectives.quote: "GGN will leverage expertise and resources from British Investment Partnerships (BIPs). It will work with PIDG and BII to directly support investment project development and finance; test the BSIP model to support Nepal government institutions to improve infrastructure project pipelines; and draw down from the following UK Centres of Expertise—Green Cities and Infrastructure, Green Inclusive Growth and Financial Services." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal is categorized as "Major" risk in the document, indicating significant challenges but not FCAS-level fragility. The country faces governance weaknesses, climate vulnerability, and economic constraints but has a stable political transition post-conflict.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak government effectiveness (WGI score of 15.87 vs. South Asian average of 38.22) hampers policy implementation. Complex FDI regulations, underdeveloped financial markets, and inadequate climate-resilient infrastructure limit private investment. Climate vulnerability (1.5-2% GDP loss annually from extreme events) exacerbates economic risks. Rapid urbanization without planning reduces liveability and increases pollution-related health burdens.
where_context.quote: "Nepal ranks well below the South Asian average on government effectiveness [...] Governmenteffectiveness captures perceptions of the quality of public services, the quality of the civil service and the degree of its independence from political pressures, the quality of policy formulation and implementation." (D0003513.odt, Section A: Strategic Case, p. 15)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) / British Embassy Kathmandu (BEK)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO/BEK) designs the programme, selects partners, and oversees delivery, with Nepali institutions (e.g., IBN, MoF, provincial governments) implementing components under UK technical assistance. Decision-making authority rests with FCDO, though local governments are engaged in project prioritization.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to federal/provincial governments on economic/industrial strategy
institutional strengthening of Investment Board Nepal (IBN)
training for city governments on climate-resilient infrastructure planning
support to Central Bank/Ministry of Finance for green finance instruments
mentorship for local governments on debt management and private sector engagement

partner_organizations.name: Government of Nepal (GoN) - Ministry of Finance (MoF)
partner_organizations.role: policy reform and fiscal management for green growth

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies (MOICS)
partner_organizations.role: industrial strategy and FDI policy development

partner_organizations.name: Investment Board Nepal (IBN)
partner_organizations.role: FDI and PPP project facilitation; institutional strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Provincial and Local Governments
partner_organizations.role: urban infrastructure planning and climate-resilient investment

partner_organizations.name: British International Investment (BII)
partner_organizations.role: private sector investment in green growth sectors

partner_organizations.name: Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG)
partner_organizations.role: climate-resilient infrastructure project support

partner_organizations.name: UK Centres of Expertise (Green Cities/Infrastructure, Green Inclusive Growth, Financial Services)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance and advisory services

partner_organizations.name: Private sector actors (e.g., commercial banks, infrastructure developers)
partner_organizations.role: co-investment in green projects

who_partners.quote: "GGN will work with PIDG and BII to directly support investment project development and finance; test the BSIP model to support Nepal government institutions to improve infrastructure project pipelines [...] GGN will change the model of support to IBN to create an institutional setup that can be backed by government, multilaterals and other donors in the long-term." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet and Section E: Management Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **contracts** (for technical assistance providers), **grants** (for feasibility studies and research), and **partnership agreements** (with BIPs like BII/PIDG). Funds are disbursed through FCDO to implementing partners, with milestone-based payments for delivery components.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO/BEK manages the programme through a **Programme Responsible Owner (PRO)** and **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO)**, with technical components delivered by pre-selected partners (e.g., IBN, BII, UK Centres of Expertise). The structure includes embedded advisors for adaptive management but limits open competition for core delivery roles.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct awards to IBN, BII, and UK Centres of Expertise)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **existing UK-Nepal relationships** (e.g., IBN’s prior UK support), **specialized expertise** (BII/PIDG for private investment), and **alignment with FCDO’s strategic priorities** (e.g., British Investment Partnerships). The document emphasizes leveraging proven partnerships rather than open competition.
how_mechanism.quote: "The UK has supported the IBN to establish itself as the lead FDI and PPP agency [...] GGN will change the model of support to IBN to create an institutional setup that can be backed by government, multilaterals and other donors in the long-term." (D0003513.odt, Section A: Strategic Case, p. 16)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **joint governance structure** is implied, with FCDO/BEK overseeing strategic direction and Nepali institutions (IBN, MoF) managing operational delivery. The **Programme Responsible Owner (PRO)** and **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO)** within FCDO provide oversight, while technical advisory groups (e.g., UK Centres of Expertise) support adaptive management. No explicit steering committee composition is detailed, but the document references "programme governance and oversight" roles.
how_governance.quote: "FCDO’s Programme Governance and Oversight: The PRO and SRO will ensure alignment with FCDO’s strategic objectives and adapt to emerging priorities. Monitoring will include monthly and quarterly reporting against log-frame indicators." (D0003513.odt, Section E: Management Case, p. 38)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components **with FCDO approval**, based on adaptive management reviews. A feasibility study (£1.46m) is explicitly set aside for testing and adjusting urban investment strategies.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes **quarterly reviews** and **independent assessments** to adjust priorities. For example, the urban component will commission a feasibility study to "determine whether and how UK interventions can have green, climate-resilient impact" before scaling investments. The UK Centres of Expertise provide real-time advice to "inform adaptive management and scale-up/down decisions."
how_flexibility.quote: "A budget line of £1.46m will set aside money for the management team to commission a Feasibility Study for the Cities Component [...] Provide advice on where to scale up, down or close existing activities and when to start new workstreams." (D0003513.odt, Section D: Financial Case, p. 34)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (e.g., IBN, BII, UK Centres of Expertise) → Sub-national Governments/Private Sector
how_efficiency.quote: "Profiling and Sequencing of the Payments: Payments will be tied to delivery milestones as set out in the log-frame and contract agreements." (D0003513.odt, Section D: Financial Case, p. 35)

q24_alternatives_considered: Multilateral-led delivery (rejected due to lack of focus on institution-building for FDI/infrastructure)
Purely public-sector financing (rejected due to need for private climate finance)
Open competition for all components (limited to avoid fragmentation)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **closed consortium model** was chosen to: 1) **leverage existing UK-Nepal partnerships** (e.g., IBN’s prior UK support), 2) **ensure alignment with British Investment Partnerships (BIPs)**, 3) **mitigate risks** in Nepal’s weak institutional environment, and 4) **enable adaptive management** through embedded UK expertise. The document emphasizes that "the UK has a strong track record" in Nepal and that GGN builds on prior programmes (e.g., Accelerating Investment in Infrastructure in Nepal).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leveraging proven partners like IBN/BII)
risk mitigation (avoiding open competition in fragile governance context)
partner capacity (UK Centres of Expertise provide specialized skills)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on IBN’s capacity, which remains weak despite UK support
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GGN will provide technical/operational support to IBN and pilot BIP engagement (e.g., BSIP) to diversify project pipelines.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited competition may reduce innovation in delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Feasibility studies and UK Centres of Expertise will introduce external validation and adaptive learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between federal/provincial/local governments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GGN will support intergovernmental coordination frameworks and align with PLGSP (Provincial/Local Government Support Programme).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing partnerships to reduce transaction costs)
effectiveness (focus on catalytic investments, e.g., £500m+ leveraged)
equity (targeting disadvantaged groups in urban planning and financial access)
why_rationale.quote: "The UK has a strong track record supporting economic policy reform, financial sector development and more recently urban development in Nepal [...] GGN builds on that success, whilst pivoting our support towards green growth pathways." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s **weak government effectiveness** (WGI score: 15.87) and **complex FDI regulations** limit partner selection to institutions with prior UK support (e.g., IBN). The **underdeveloped financial sector** necessitates reliance on UK Centres of Expertise for green finance instruments. **Climate vulnerability** (1.5-2% GDP loss annually) requires partners with resilience-focused technical skills (e.g., PIDG for infrastructure).
q27_constraints_detail: Government effectiveness scores limit trust in local implementers
Lack of sovereign credit rating restricts financial partners to those with UK backing
High urbanization rates (cities producing 40% of GDP) demand partners with urban planning expertise
FDI restrictions (e.g., sectoral caps) require partners like IBN with legislative mandates
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for catalytic private investment** (£500m+ target) drives the choice of BII/PIDG as financial partners. **Climate-resilient infrastructure gaps** justify the closed consortium with UK Centres of Expertise. **Federalism challenges** (e.g., provincial/local coordination) shape the embedded advisory model for subnational governments.
q28_linkages: Output 1 (green growth strategies) → Direct TA to MoF/MOICS → Closed consortium with UK policy experts
Output 2 (IBN strengthening) → Direct awards to IBN → Mitigates FDI regulatory risks
Output 3 (urban investment) → Feasibility study first → Adaptive management for untested contexts
Output 4 (financial deepening) → Sovereign credit rating support → Addresses lack of investor confidence
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between **speed** (direct awards to IBN/BII) and **local ownership** (limited competitive selection of Nepali partners). It also highlights trade-offs in **urban focus** (cities produce 40% of GDP but risk excluding rural poor) vs. **inclusive growth** (targeting disadvantaged groups in project safeguards).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Direct awards to UK-backed partners (efficiency) vs. open competition (equity)
Urban infrastructure investments (economic growth) vs. rural poverty reduction (inclusion)
Embedded UK advisors (technical quality) vs. local capacity development (sustainability)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** justifies intensive oversight (quarterly reviews, embedded advisors) and adaptive management (feasibility studies, UK Centres of Expertise input). Fragile institutions (e.g., IBN’s financial sustainability) require **hands-on FCDO involvement** in day-to-day delivery.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: IBN receives operational support to become self-sustaining; provincial governments get TA for economic planning; and city clusters are trained on climate-resilient project pipelines. The UK’s role shifts from direct delivery to **‘backstopping’** as local capacity improves.
intersections.quote: "GGN will work with PIDG and BII to directly support investment project development and finance [...] The UK has supported the IBN to establish itself as the lead FDI and PPP agency [...] GGN will change the model of support to IBN to create an institutional setup that can be backed by government, multilaterals and other donors in the long-term." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet and Section A: Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: IBN’s limited capacity to manage increased FDI/PPP pipelines
Low absorption of climate finance due to weak safeguards
Political instability disrupting federal/provincial coordination
Private sector reluctance to invest in untested green instruments
Urban projects failing to reach disadvantaged groups
Overlap with multilateral programmes (e.g., World Bank/ADB) causing fragmentation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: GGN will provide operational/technical support and pilot BIP engagement (e.g., BSIP) to diversify funding sources.
TA to Central Bank/Ministry of Finance for green taxonomy and sovereign credit rating; partnership with UK Centres of Expertise.
GGN will support intergovernmental coordination frameworks and align with PLGSP.
Pilot green bonds and hedging instruments; use BII/PIDG to de-risk investments.
Embed GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) safeguards in project design; target women-led SMEs in green sectors.

fcas_specific_lessons: Nepal’s **graduation from LDC status (2026)** will reduce concessional financing, requiring GGN to focus on **blended finance** and **private sector mobilization**.
Lessons from **AIIN programme**: Institutional strengthening must pair technical assistance with legislative reforms (e.g., IBN’s PPP Act 2019).
**Post-conflict federalism** (since 2017) demands flexible TA to provincial governments, as their capacities vary widely.
**Climate vulnerability** (1.5-2% GDP loss annually) necessitates embedding resilience in all infrastructure investments, not just climate-specific projects.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Accelerating Investment in Infrastructure in Nepal (AIIN) programme** (UK-funded) leveraged **$2bn in investment** but faced challenges in **sustainability** (e.g., IBN’s reliance on UK support) and **coordination** (federal-provincial overlaps). GGN adopts a more **adaptive model**, testing new instruments (e.g., BSIP) and focusing on **institutionalizing reforms** (e.g., IBN’s financial independence).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Shift from financial stability to deepening** (e.g., green bonds instead of cybersecurity support). 2) **Narrower urban focus** (prioritizing growth corridors over broad planning). 3) **Pilot phases** (e.g., urban feasibility study before scaling). 4) **BIP integration** (e.g., PIDG/BII for project pipelines).
risks_lessons.quote: "The UK has a strong track record supporting economic policy reform, large-scale FDI, financial sector development and more recently urban development in Nepal. The seven-year UK funded Accelerating Investment in Infrastructure in Nepal programme leveraged more than $2bn in investment. GGN builds on that success, whilst pivoting our support towards green growth pathways." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: GGN aims to leverage **£500m+ in private/international investment** for green sectors and **£100m in climate-resilient urban projects**. The programme expects to catalyze **blended finance** through BIPs (e.g., PIDG, BII) and **green bonds**.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes **capital expenditures** (e.g., infrastructure project TA) and **revenue expenditures** (e.g., institutional strengthening, feasibility studies), but no explicit split is provided.
financial_details.quote: "GGN will leverage expertise and resources from British Investment Partnerships (BIPs) [...] It will work with PIDG and BII to directly support investment project development and finance." (D0003513.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Fighting Corruption Globally (FCG)

quote.text: The programme will address transnational grand corruption by supporting efforts to put in place the tools and capabilities to prevent corrupt actors from stealing and moving significant financial resources around the world, and to hold them to account when transnational corruption does occur.

duration_source.text: The FCDO is committing up to £31 million ODA to resource the FCG programme over five years, 2023/24-2027/28

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening law enforcement and civil society), policy influence (shaping international norms on beneficial ownership transparency), and implementation research (testing asset recovery mechanisms). It also includes evidence generation through research on corruption trends and enablers.

q1_source.text: The programme will do this by: Enabling governments, civil society, the private sector and law enforcement to use high-quality beneficial ownership data to prevent or identify cases of grand corruption; Improving the effectiveness of international law enforcement to increase the volume of recovered assets; Equipping the FCDO’s networks and other actors with evidence and learning for effective policy and programming on anti-corruption.

q3_expected_outputs.output: 19 countries making progress on beneficial ownership transparency (BENOT) registers
Greatervolumeofassetsfrozen,recoveredandreturned
GreatervolumesofqualityBENOTinformationgloballyusedtopreventcorruptionandrespondtograndcorruption
Moreevidenceusedtoinformactionagainstcorruption
Tailored technical assistance to at least 4 ODA-eligible countries per year (including Ukraine)
Coordinating technical assistance delivery and facilitating peer learning between 15 countries in Africa under the UK/AfDB-led Africa Beneficial Ownership Network
New and targeted evidence of the impact of BENOT reforms coupled with concrete guidance for countries on implementing challenging aspects of the reforms
Better data standards for BENOT and three new tools to enable use of BO data in sectoral or thematic policy areas
International Anti-Corruption Coordination Centre (IACCC) to support case development in referral countries (e.g., Angola, Zambia, Seychelles, Moldova)
International Centre for Asset Recovery (ICAR) to provide technical assistance to anti-corruption bodies in ODA-eligible countries
U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre to provide FCDO staff access to anti-corruption research, tailored advice, and online training courses
Research on enablers of grand corruption by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP)

what_objectives.summary: The FCG programme aims to combat transnational grand corruption by improving beneficial ownership transparency, enhancing asset recovery capacities, and generating evidence to inform anti-corruption policies. It supports governments, civil society, and law enforcement to prevent and respond to corruption, with a focus on closing international loopholes that enable corrupt actors to hide and move illicit wealth.

quote.text: The programme will address transnational grand corruption by supporting efforts to put in place the tools and capabilities to prevent corrupt actors from stealing and moving significant financial resources around the world, and to hold them to account when transnational corruption does occur.

countries_regions: Africa (15 countries under Africa Beneficial Ownership Network)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is assessed as moderate, with top risks including delays in UK domestic reforms, political changes in partner countries, and ODA budget reductions. These risks could undermine delivery and UK leadership on fighting corruption internationally.

q5_source.text: Overall, the risk rating for this programme (at business case stage) is moderate. Top three risks are: Delays in implementing UK domestic reforms (including through the Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories) to address corruption undermine our ability to encourage and persuade other countries to enact reforms; Changes in political circumstances in delivery partners’ focus countries reduce or compromise opportunities for progress or reform; Further reductions in ODA limit funds available to project partners, undermining delivery and impact, and UK leadership on fighting corruption internationally.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and political economy constraints in partner countries can hinder the implementation of beneficial ownership reforms and asset recovery efforts. Conflict and regulatory gaps enable corrupt actors to exploit financial systems, while data limitations affect the ability to trace and recover stolen assets.

quote.text: Developing countries frequently lack the robust law enforcement systems needed to pursue and recover stolen assets. This can delay the progress of investigations and at worst, result in failed prosecutions and the inability to reclaim stolen assets.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains central oversight and decision-making authority, with implementing partners (both Northern and Southern) delivering specific components under FCDO direction. Southern partners are involved in implementation but strategic decisions remain with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to governments on beneficial ownership transparency
training for law enforcement on asset recovery
peer learning networks (e.g., Africa Beneficial Ownership Network)
knowledge sharing through U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre

partner_organizations.name: Open Ownership
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance on beneficial ownership transparency (BENOT) and global register management

partner_organizations.name: International Centre for Asset Recovery (ICAR)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance to anti-corruption bodies in ODA-eligible countries for complex investigations and prosecutions

partner_organizations.name: International Anti-Corruption Coordination Centre (IACCC)
partner_organizations.role: Intelligence support and case development for grand corruption investigations

partner_organizations.name: U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre
partner_organizations.role: Research, helpdesk, training, and policy forums for FCDO and partners

partner_organizations.name: Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP)
partner_organizations.role: Research on enablers of grand corruption and cross-case analysis

partner_organizations.name: Africa Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Secretariat for Africa Beneficial Ownership Network (peer learning and technical assistance)

partner_organizations.name: IMF Anti-Money Laundering/Countering Terrorism Financing Thematic Fund
partner_organizations.role: Integration of BENOT into public procurement transparency

partner_organizations.name: National Crime Agency (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Host for IACCC and domestic law enforcement collaboration

partner_organizations.name: Crown Prosecution Service (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Investigation and prosecution of transnational corruption cases

quote.text: The FCDO will work with other UK Government departments to ensure FCG is an effective delivery mechanism for the priorities in the UK Anti-corruption Strategy and to encourage other departments to deliver complementary international and country actions... This will over time continue assisting in mitigating the risks of corrupt actors channelling stolen assets through financial centres and company structures beyond the reach of current norms.
quote.source: D0005460.odt, Section A.Strategic Case (Theory of Change)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), Accountable Grants, and limited low-value contracts for evidence and innovation work. This allows flexibility to support diverse partners while maintaining oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FCDO centrally manages the programme with a core team overseeing multiple implementing partners (Open Ownership, ICAR, IACCC, U4, etc.). Partners operate semi-autonomously but align with FCDO’s strategic priorities, with regular coordination through forums and reviews.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their established track records in anti-corruption work, technical expertise, and alignment with FCDO’s strategic objectives. The business case highlights past successful collaborations (e.g., GACP, IACT) as justification for direct awards.

quote.text: The proposed funding modalities will be: (i) Memorandum of Understanding, (ii) Accountable Grant, (iii) limited but appropriate low value contracts for the evidence and innovation work. We have good evidence from the recently ended International Action Against Corruption programme of the importance of working with partner organisations that have the technical and commercial capacity to deliver sustainable and high-quality interventions which represent good value for money.

The FCDO will gain assurance on this through due diligence, annual reports, audits, and spot checks. FCG will practice robust due diligence, monitoring, and auditing of partner accounts, to ensure compliance with the Terrorism Acts 2000 and 2006. Progress against performance will be monitored quarterly and for multilaterals at six months, through the UK engagement on steering committees, donor meetings and bilateral dialogue.
quote.source: D005460.odt, Sections D.Financial Case and A.Strategic Case

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects based on performance reviews (e.g., after the second annual review in FY 2024/25), but this requires FCDO approval and is contingent on results and UK fiscal conditions.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a mid-term assessment and allows for adjustments based on emerging evidence (e.g., new dynamics in grand corruption or illicit finance). However, major shifts require FCDO approval and alignment with strategic priorities.

quote.text: All funding commitments will contain an exit strategy which makes continued funding contingent on delivery of results, adequate reporting and the UK’s fiscal situation. FCG will provide a flexible resource to enable IFAC (and HMG partners) to commission short-term evidence and knowledge work to help officials develop appropriate policy responses to core challenges on corruption and illicit finance.
quote.source: D0005460.odt, Sections D.Financial Case and A.Strategic Case

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (e.g., Open Ownership, ICAR). No explicit mention of sub-grantees beyond the primary partners, suggesting a relatively flat structure.

quote.text: Payments will be made at regular intervals by bank transfer based on partners’ formal requests and in accordance with the respective signed MoU or accountable grant. The payment process will be managed through the FCDO’s HERA system... They year-by-year profile for FCG will be agreed in advance with partners following internal sign-off.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No central FCDO resources allocated; rely on existing HMG funding (e.g., CSSF, HMT Technical Assistance Unit). Risks unaddressed gaps in BENOT, asset recovery, and evidence generation.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Support a broad number of anti-corruption initiatives via FCG (multi-component programme)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Similar to past programmes (GACP, IACT) with multiple components. Carries higher delivery risk and management burden without guaranteed synergies.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Fund a small number of initiatives addressing critical gaps (preferred option)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focuses on high-impact areas (BENOT, asset recovery, evidence) with proven partners, complementing other donors and avoiding duplication.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Provide support through existing multi-donor initiatives (e.g., StAR)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Leverages other donors’ funds but limits FCDO control over priorities and resource allocation.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Bilateral programme support through FCG (direct FCDO management)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Maximizes FCDO control and flexibility but increases administrative burden.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (funding a small number of initiatives addressing critical gaps) was chosen for its balance of focus, value for money, and alignment with FCDO’s strategic priorities. It avoids the high management burden of a multi-component programme while targeting areas where the UK can have outsized impact (BENOT, asset recovery, enablers research). The approach leverages proven partners with strong track records and allows for adaptive management in a rapidly evolving geopolitical context.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (focused portfolio reduces delivery risk)
partner capacity (proven deliverers like ICAR, Open Ownership)
flexibility (ability to respond to emerging issues like Russia/Ukraine)
complementarity (avoids duplication with other UK/HMG initiatives)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in UK domestic reforms (e.g., Crown Dependencies/Overseas Territories) undermine credibility to advocate for reforms globally.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monitor UK reform progress and adjust diplomatic messaging; maintain momentum through international leadership (e.g., G7, FATF).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political changes in partner countries reduce opportunities for progress.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversify country engagements and focus on resilient partners (e.g., Zambia’s multi-agency approach). Use adaptive management to shift resources as needed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Further ODA reductions limit funds and undermine UK leadership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritize high-impact areas (e.g., BENOT, asset recovery) and leverage multilateral platforms (e.g., AfDB, IMF) to stretch resources. Advocate for ODA protection for anti-corruption work.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner underperformance or fraud.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust due diligence, quarterly financial checks, and break clauses in funding agreements. Annual audits and spot checks for high-risk partners.

quote.text: Option 3 is the preferred option. The significant reductions in the ODA budget, combined with the changing geopolitical context, mean that FCDO needs to focus on those policy areas that have the potential to make the most difference, where there are effective delivery partners to support, and where there are funding gaps... This approach will enable FCDO and its partners to complement others, address the biggest harms from corruption and boost efforts to close loopholes in the international financial system that make transnational corruption possible.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and transnational nature of corruption require partners with specialized expertise (e.g., Open Ownership for BENOT, ICAR for asset recovery) that may not exist in all partner countries. Weak institutions in some regions limit the pool of Southern partners capable of leading complex investigations or reforms, necessitating Northern technical support.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited Southern expertise in beneficial ownership transparency requires Northern partners (e.g., Open Ownership).
Legal and regulatory gaps in partner countries necessitate international organizations (e.g., StAR, IMF) for technical assistance.
Conflict-affected contexts (e.g., Ukraine) require flexible, adaptive partners like OCCRP for investigative work.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for cross-border coordination (e.g., asset recovery across jurisdictions) dictates a centrally managed, multi-partner structure. Beneficial ownership transparency requires a global register (Open Ownership) and standardized data tools, while asset recovery demands specialized law enforcement collaboration (IACCC, ICAR).
q28_linkages: Transnational corruption → Requires multi-country partners (e.g., IACCC for cross-border cases).
BENOT reforms → Needs global data standards (Open Ownership) and peer learning (AfDB Network).
Asset recovery → Demands legal expertise (ICAR) and intelligence sharing (IACCC).
Enablers research → Requires investigative journalism networks (OCCRP).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme prioritizes efficiency (e.g., leveraging existing partners like U4 for research) over deep equity investments (e.g., limited direct funding to Southern CSOs). Northern-led technical assistance (e.g., ICAR, Open Ownership) ensures rapid delivery but may limit Southern ownership in design phases.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to proven partners (e.g., ICAR) accelerate delivery but reduce opportunities for new Southern actors.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern organizations lead on complex areas (e.g., BENOT standards) while Southern partners implement locally.
Cost vs. reach: Centralized tools (e.g., global BENOT register) maximize impact but may not address country-specific equity needs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., political instability in partner countries, ODA uncertainty) justifies milestone-based oversight and quarterly reviews, with more intensive monitoring for high-risk components (e.g., asset recovery in conflict zones).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in technical assistance (e.g., ICAR training for Zambian investigators) but stops short of full institutional ownership, reflecting a focus on immediate results over long-term Southern leadership.

quote.text: The cross-border nature of corruption means having a centrally managed programme which can learn and adapt to real-time events and provide an oversight function is crucial... The programme will tap into our Illicit Finance expertise across the FCDO network to inform our work throughout the FCG programme’s lifecycle.

key_programme_risks: Delays in UK domestic reforms (e.g., Crown Dependencies) undermine global advocacy.
Political changes in partner countries (e.g., elections, coups) disrupt reforms.
ODA reductions limit programme scope and UK leadership.
Partner underperformance or fraud (e.g., mismanagement of funds).
Low adoption of BENOT registers in priority countries.
Legal barriers to asset recovery in host jurisdictions.
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., Russia/Ukraine) divert attention from anti-corruption efforts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Monitor reform progress; maintain international leadership through G7/FATF engagement.
Diversify country portfolio; focus on resilient institutions (e.g., Zambia’s multi-agency approach).
Prioritize high-impact areas; leverage multilateral platforms (e.g., AfDB, IMF).
Robust due diligence; quarterly reviews; break clauses in funding agreements.
Targeted technical assistance; peer learning networks (e.g., Africa BENOT Network).
Strengthen international cooperation (e.g., IACCC); focus on jurisdictions with existing MLATs.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-affected states (e.g., Ukraine) require flexible, adaptive support mechanisms (e.g., OCCRP for investigative journalism).
Weak institutions in FCAS demand embedded capacity building (e.g., ICAR’s work with Zambian Anti-Corruption Commission).
Sanctions and illicit finance risks in FCAS necessitate closer monitoring (e.g., quarterly financial checks).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past programmes (GACP, IACT) demonstrated that multi-component approaches carry high management burdens without guaranteed synergies. Direct funding to specialized partners (e.g., ICAR for asset recovery) yields higher impact than scattered small grants. Beneficial ownership transparency requires sustained advocacy (e.g., UK’s leadership in G7) and technical support for implementation.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: FCG streamlines the number of partners compared to GACP/IACT, focuses on proven deliverers, and embeds adaptive management (e.g., mid-term assessments). It also prioritizes areas with clear UK comparative advantage (e.g., BENOT, sanctions-related asset recovery).

quote.text: Lessons from both IACT and GACP show that multi-component programmes carry higher delivery risk (not all partners are effective), require a substantially higher programme management burden, and without substantial central direction, do not necessarily add up to more than the sum of their parts... FCG will provide a flexible resource to enable IFAC (and HMG partners) to commission short-term evidence and knowledge work to help officials develop appropriate policy responses to core challenges on corruption and illicit finance.
quote.source: D0005460.odt, Sections B.Appraisal Case and A.Strategic Case

co_funding_partners.partner: IMF Anti-Money Laundering/Countering Terrorism Financing Thematic Fund

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s 12% contribution to U4’s core budget (£3.6m over 3 years) leverages a disproportionate share of services (23% of helpdesk queries in 2022). IACCC’s £1.53m in secondees from member countries supplements FCDO’s core funding. Multilateral platforms (e.g., AfDB, IMF) stretch resources through co-funded networks.

quote.text: The FCDO is committing up to £31 million ODA to resource the FCG programme over five years, 2023/24-2027/28... The UK was one of U4’s four founders—now with eight partners paying an equal membership fee into a core basket fund. This maximises the VfM of each partner’s investment, buying far wider ranging, and deeper, outputs than any partner could secure from a sole funded project with the same budget.
quote.source: D0005460.odt, Sections D.Financial Case and B.Appraisal Case

metadata.programme_name: Global Environment Facility – Eighth Replenishment (GEF8)
metadata.quote: "The GEF funds projects and programmes in developing countries to protect and restore biodiversity, tackle climate change, protect international waters, halt and reverse land degradation and address chemical pollution." (D0003092.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 1 July 2022; AMP End Date: 30 June 2026" (D0003092.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GEF is a multilateral financing mechanism that channels funds to developing countries to address global environmental challenges. It serves as the official financing mechanism for five major international environmental agreements (UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD, Stockholm and Minamata Conventions). The UK's contribution is core funding to be pooled with other donors and deployed against GEF's mandate.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The GEF funds projects and programmes in developing countries to protect and restore biodiversity, tackle climate change, protect international waters, halt and reverse land degradation and address chemical pollution. It is the official financing mechanism for the major international environmental agreements and has a strong track record delivering this assistance effectively. This business case is for the UK's core funding to the next replenishment of the GEF." (D0003092.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 97 million metric tonnes CO2e of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions avoided or reduced
7.9 million hectares of terrestrial protected areas created or under improved management
10.2 million hectares of landscapes under improved practices (excluding protected areas)
5.2 million hectares of marine areas protected or under improved management
110 thousand metric tonnes of globally over-exploited fisheries moved to more sustainable levels
3.7 million hectares of marine habitat under improved practices (excluding protected areas)
15.7 thousand metric tonnes of toxic chemicals of global concern (e.g., mercury, persistent organic pollutants) reduced, disposed, or phased out
164.4 million direct beneficiaries (106 million women) from GEF investments
what_objectives.summary: The GEF8 replenishment aims to generate global environmental benefits through system transformations by supporting climate change mitigation/adaptation, biodiversity protection, sustainable land/sea management, and chemical/waste management in developing countries.
what_objectives.quote: "Impact statement: To generate global environmental benefits through system transformations so that we have a healthy, productive, and resilient environment underpinning the well-being of human societies." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The overall programme risk rating is assessed as minor, with fiduciary and safeguarding risks managed through GEF's policies and accredited agencies. The GEF has strong track record with 80% of projects achieving expected outcomes.
where_context.q5_source: "Given the good track record of the GEF, and our assessment of their processes and policies, the risks of this programme are considered minor and within FCDO's risk appetite." (D0003092.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Overall risk was assessed as minor for the enhanced Sexual Exploitation and Abuse approved in February 2020." (D0003092.odt, Management Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Environmental interventions in fragile states require special consideration as 1/3 of GEF's portfolio is in conflict-affected countries. The GEF currently lacks a formal policy for fragile/conflict-affected contexts, though it is developing guidance. Climate risks and land degradation directly affect food/water security and economic stability in target countries.
where_context.quote: "As of 2020 one third of GEF's portfolio, amounting to $4bn, was invested in countries affected by armed conflict... While individual projects and some GEF IAs have started to account for fragile and conflict-affected contexts in their design, implementation and monitoring and evaluation the GEF does not currently have a definition, policy, or procedures for designing and implementing projects in fragile and conflict affected states." (D0003092.odt, Risk section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The GEF Council has balanced representation from developed and developing countries, with the UK holding its own seat. Decision-making is shared between Northern donors and Southern recipients through the Council's governance structure.
q10_capacity_building_details: policy and legislative reform assistance
technical support for integrated programming
training in sustainable practices (e.g., agriculture, fisheries)
institutional strengthening for environmental management
gender mainstreaming support

partner_organizations.name: Global Environment Facility Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: coordination and programme management

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Trustee (fiduciary management)

partner_organizations.name: 18 Accredited Agencies (including UNDP, UNEP, FAO, regional development banks, international NGOs)
partner_organizations.role: project implementation

partner_organizations.name: GEF Council
partner_organizations.role: governance and approval of projects/programmes

partner_organizations.name: Scientific and Technical Advisory Panel (STAP)
partner_organizations.role: technical guidance and programme evaluation

partner_organizations.name: Independent Evaluation Office (IEO)
partner_organizations.role: independent performance evaluation

who_partners.quote: "GEF projects and programmes are developed and delivered through 18 accredited agencies. These agencies are the multilateral development banks, UN agencies, and international NGOs who work with developing countries to design and implement programmes." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "The GEF is governed by a balanced board of developed and developing country representatives (GEF Council)." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK's contribution is core funding to the GEF Trust Fund, which is pooled with other donors' contributions and allocated according to GEF's mandate and replenishment priorities. Funds are disbursed to accredited agencies for project implementation.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The GEF operates through a Secretariat (programme management), Council (governance), STAP (technical advice), and IEO (evaluation). Implementation is decentralized through 18 accredited agencies that design and deliver projects in developing countries.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Agencies must meet GEF's Minimum Fiduciary Standards and are accredited based on their capacity to deliver environmental programmes. The World Bank serves as Trustee, ensuring financial integrity.
how_mechanism.quote: "GEF projects and programmes are developed and delivered through 18 accredited agencies... The World Bank acts as Trustee, meaning the GEF is implemented using the Bank's fiduciary standards and controls." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "GEF's Minimum Fiduciary Standards... requires GEF agencies to demonstrate that they have in place the necessary policies, procedures, systems, and capabilities to systematically screen individuals and/or entities." (D0003092.odt, Management Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GEF Council is the governing body with balanced representation from developed and developing countries. It approves projects/programmes and sets strategic direction. The UK has its own seat on the Council.
how_governance.quote: "The GEF governing body, the GEF Council, approves the projects and programmes... The UK has its own seat on the Council." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "GEF also provides 6-monthly reports on performance against indicators." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated through the System for Transparent Allocation of Resources (STAR), which uses a formula based on environmental assets, GDP, and past performance. Reallocation between focal areas requires Council approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The GEF's programming is adjusted during replenishment negotiations (every 4 years) to reflect new priorities. Mid-term adjustments require Council approval, though integrated programmes allow some flexibility to address emerging challenges.
how_flexibility.quote: "The GEF system for allocating resources to eligible countries, known as the System for Transparent Allocation of Resources (STAR), uses a formula based on the global value of environmental assets in that country, the GDP of the country and the success in delivery results through GEF projects."
