(D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "GEF policies, programmes and priorities are effectively evaluated, discussed, and updated as part of the replenishment process." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GEF Secretariat/Council → Accredited Agencies → Local Implementers (governments/NGOs/communities)
how_efficiency.quote: "GEF projects and programmes are developed and delivered through 18 accredited agencies... The GEF governing body, the GEF Council, approves the projects and programmes." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "GEF also provides 6-monthly reports on performance against indicators." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: do-nothing (zero contribution to GEF8)
bilateral programming in climate/environment sectors
funding other multilateral mechanisms (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The GEF was chosen for its unique mandate as the financial mechanism for five major environmental conventions, its global reach (143 countries), strong track record (80% project success rate), and ability to leverage co-financing (£1.82bn mobilized per £1 UK contribution in GEF7). The multilateral structure allows the UK to influence global environmental policy while sharing risks/costs with other donors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of UK influence in GEF governance if contribution is reduced
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain a contribution level commensurate with the UK's strategic priorities (e.g., 10-12.5% burden share) to retain Council seat and shaping power.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication with other climate funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Push for GEF to focus on underfunded areas (e.g., nature-based solutions, chemicals/waste) and integrated programming to ensure complementarity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited additionality in co-financing (some private sector funds may have materialized without GEF)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Advocate for higher co-financing ratios and improved monitoring of additionality through GEF's evaluation systems.

why_rationale.quote: "The arguments presented in the Appraisal Case show that withdrawal from the GEF could have implications on the UK's ambitions on climate and environment, and practically limit the UK's ability to influence significant funding and the nature agenda over the next four years... The GEF received a score of 'Good' (second highest possible) in the 2016 multilateral review, and 80% of their programmes are rated satisfactory." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "The UK has been effective in shaping and influencing the GEF's strategic direction... Our priority of improving VfM and better managing synergies and trade-offs has meant that the UK has pushed the GEF to pilot and scale up integrated programmatic approaches." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The GEF's global mandate (143 countries) requires accredited agencies with wide geographic coverage and multilingual capacity. Conflict-affected contexts (1/3 of portfolio) necessitate partners with strong safeguarding and risk management systems, limiting the pool to established MDBs/UN agencies.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for agencies with fiduciary standards compliant with World Bank requirements
Capacity to operate in fragile states (e.g., security protocols, conflict sensitivity)
Ability to mobilize co-financing in middle-income countries
Expertise in integrated programming across climate/biodiversity/land/water sectors
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The GEF's financing mechanism role (core objective) requires a multilateral structure to pool funds, ensure donor coordination, and align with five environmental conventions. The need for integrated programming (tackling interlinked drivers of environmental degradation) shapes the use of 18 accredited agencies to deliver cross-sectoral projects.
q28_linkages: Global mandate → Multilateral delivery structure with accredited agencies
Convention alignment → GEF Council governance with balanced North-South representation
Integrated programming → Use of multiple agencies to deliver cross-cutting projects
Co-financing targets → Partnerships with MDBs/private sector to leverage additional funds
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between (1) the need for rapid, large-scale environmental action and (2) inclusive country ownership. For example, the STAR allocation formula balances equity (prioritizing poor/vulnerable countries) with efficiency (rewarding past performance). The UK pushes for higher co-financing from middle-income countries to maximize leverage, while advocating for increased support to LDCs/SIDS.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: "Countries have programmed most of their allocated GEF7 resources, with LDCs and SIDS reaching 92% and 77% of their allocations respectively" (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case) - suggesting efficiency gains but potential equity gaps.
Expertise vs. ownership: Use of Northern-based MDBs/UN agencies for implementation vs. Southern-led project design (e.g., community-based mangrove restoration in Kenya/Madagascar).

Cost vs. reach: "The GEF uses relatively small funds (<0.5% of global spend on nature) strategically to create a multiplier effect" (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) - prioritizing global impact over localized depth.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The minor risk rating enables light-touch oversight for most projects, but conflict-affected contexts (1/3 of portfolio) require enhanced due diligence. The UK monitors these through annual reviews and safeguarding reports.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in project design (e.g., training for sustainable agriculture in Kenya) and shapes partner roles: accredited agencies must demonstrate ability to deliver both technical assistance and institutional strengthening. The GEF's gender policy requires agencies to include capacity-building measures in gender action plans.
intersections.quote: "The GEF's niche and comparative advantage lies in supporting pilots that demonstrate positive benefits and establishing conditions for scaling-up... The GEF has made substantial improvements in integrated programming, expanding the role of lead agency to act as a regional co-ordination hub to ensure coherence of projects with the programme level goals." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "Although not consistently applied, GEF has an explicit focus on establishing conditions for positive environmental benefits which attracts support from other actors to provide funding for full-scale up." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: Reduced UK influence in global environmental governance if contribution is cut
Overlap with other climate funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund) without clear division of labor
Limited additionality in some co-financing (private sector funds may have materialized without GEF)
Durability of project outcomes (62% sustainability rate, below World Bank's 65%)
Gender mainstreaming gaps (only 30% of stakeholder consultations include gender perspective)
Fragile/conflict-affected contexts (1/3 of portfolio lacks formal GEF policy/guidance)
Potential safeguarding risks in high-risk countries (mitigated by GEF's prohibited practices policy)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain 10-12.5% burden share to retain Council seat and policy-shaping role. The UK's GEF7 contribution (10.07%) secured the 3rd-largest donor position.
Advocate for GEF to focus on underfunded areas (nature-based solutions, chemicals/waste, international waters) and integrated programming. Push for clearer complementarity in GEF8 strategy.
Support GEF's efforts to improve monitoring of additionality (e.g., STAP's scrutiny of co-financing claims). Set higher co-financing targets for middle-income countries.
Strengthen GEF's post-project monitoring and evaluation. The UK will push for improved sustainability planning in GEF8, including exit strategies and local ownership.
Monitor implementation of GEF's gender policy closely. Include gender indicators in logical framework and advocate for adequate budget to support gender mainstreaming in GEF8.
Support GEF Secretariat's commitment to develop guidance for fragile states. Include conflict-sensitivity in project design and track progress through annual reviews.

fcas_specific_lessons: Develop formal GEF policy/guidance for fragile and conflict-affected states (currently absent).
Use project review process to identify conflict/fragility risks and provide feedback to agencies.
Build learning into GEF's knowledge management systems to share lessons across conflict-affected portfolios.
Ensure safeguarding and AML/CFT policies are rigorously applied in high-risk contexts (e.g., GEF's Prohibited Practices Policy).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: GEF7 demonstrated strong performance (80% projects achieved outcomes, 'A' rating in annual reviews) but identified areas for improvement: (1) durability of outcomes (62% sustainability rate), (2) gender mainstreaming (only 57% of projects used gender analysis), (3) additionality of co-financing. Integrated programming (18% of GEF7 funds) showed promise in tackling interlinked environmental drivers but needs more systematic application.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Increased focus on integrated programming in GEF8 (from 3 pilot programmes in GEF6 to 5 in GEF7, with 18% of funds).
Stronger emphasis on nature-based solutions and biodiversity mainstreaming (aligned with post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework).
Enhanced private sector engagement strategy to improve co-financing additionality.
New non-grant instruments (e.g., equity investments) to test innovative finance models (e.g., Meloy Fund for sustainable fisheries).
Improved monitoring of gender outcomes and safeguarding risks.
risks_lessons.quote: "GEF7 was performing well with annual reviews consistently giving an output score of 'A' for the programme overall... Although durability of projects remains a challenge, this has improved over time with 62% of all projects found to have durable outcomes... GEF has made substantial improvements in integrated programming, expanding the role of lead agency to act as a regional co-ordination hub." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "The UK welcomes the IEO report and recognises the GEF secretariat's commitments and will keep track of progress against these commitments by including relevant output indicators in the log frame." (D0003092.odt, Risk section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: GEF7: £1 UK contribution mobilized £1.82bn in additional public/private co-financing (nearly 10:1 leverage). GEF8 targets higher co-financing ratios, particularly in middle-income countries.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The GEF provides grant financing (capital) for projects/programmes, with a focus on catalytic investments to leverage additional revenue streams (e.g., private sector co-financing, domestic budgets).
financial_details.quote: "The UK invested £250m into the current replenishment (GEF7), which meant approx. 10% of the USD$4.1bn total. Of this, 60% of programmes under GEF7 have clear climate benefits and so £150m of our contribution is scored as international climate finance... Several of the major donors have indicated that for this replenishment they will increase their contribution compared to GEF7, most notably the US." (D0003092.odt, Strategic Case) AND "USD$2.7bn of GEF7 funds has leveraged a further USD$22.6bn of public and private funding." (D0003092.odt, Appraisal Case)

metadata.programme_name: Zambia Democratic Governance Programme (ZDGP)
metadata.quote: "The UK is providing £7,000,000 to strengthen democracy and governance in Zambia." (D0007026.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: 20/10/2020 - 31/03/2024 (extended to 31/05/2026 in Jan 25)" (D0007026.odt, Detailed information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions), policy influence (evidence-based decision making), and implementation research (testing approaches to democratic governance). It supports both state institutions and civil society to improve democratic processes, with a focus on elections, anti-corruption, and civic engagement.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme aims to bring stakeholders together to address key challenges or opportunities that we foresee in the lead up to the 2026 elections. These include the need to strengthen key democratic institutions, the closing of civic space, combating corruption and the move towards decentralisation." (D0007026.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 101 radio programmes delivered (including nationwide coverage with weekly audience of over 5 million)
Over 200 people trained on democracy and governance (focus on women, girls, and people with disabilities)
Support to recover assets valued at £41,000,000 through anti-corruption efforts
Major policy reform in agriculture sector saving $80,000,000 and removing 200,000 fraudulent beneficiaries
Voter registration observation and up to two by-election observations
Long-term pre-election observation and political polling for 2026 elections
Advocacy on civic space issues including reform of Public Order Act and Cyber Security Bills
Support to reform three pieces of agricultural legislation (Food Reserves Act, Agriculture Marketing Act, Agricultural Credits Act)
what_objectives.summary: The programme supports democratic governance in Zambia through capacity building, policy reform, and civic engagement, with a focus on elections, anti-corruption, and decentralization. It aims to strengthen institutions, promote transparency, and enable evidence-based decision making.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme has performed well over its lifetime, scoring an ‘A’ (met expectation) in all three of its Annual Reviews." (D0007026.odt, Detailed information)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Zambia is described as having a "moderate" risk profile with concerns about shrinking civic space, political polarization, and potential electoral violence. However, it is not classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS).
where_context.q5_source: "The health of Zambia’s democracy matters for UK core interests; poverty reduction, long-term security and prosperity, and building an alliance based on common interests. Those interests are under threat due to declining trust in the elections process and closing democratic space." (90000596.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The political environment is highly competitive and polarized, with restrictions on opposition activities and media freedom. Economic hardship and ethnic/regional divisions exacerbate tensions, affecting the credibility of elections and democratic processes.
where_context.quote: "Political competition is stiff, and tension is high. The economic hardships and the growing popularity of the main opposition party has left the ruling party feeling vulnerable. Current Zambian Government behaviours point towards an increasingly uneven electoral playing field." (90000596.odt, Summary Sheet)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme involves both Northern and Southern partners in decision-making, with Diakonia (international) managing the overall programme but working closely with local CSOs, media organizations, and government institutions in Zambia.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for CSOs and media organizations
technical assistance to government institutions (e.g., Anti-Corruption Commission)
support for inclusive participation of marginalized groups (women, youth, PLWDs)
embedded advisors for long-term capacity building

partner_organizations.name: Diakonia
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementing partner (manages Deepening Democracy Facility and sub-grants)

partner_organizations.name: BBC Media Action
partner_organizations.role: Media support and training (radio programmes, media literacy)

partner_organizations.name: Zambia Federation for Disability Organisations (ZAFOD)
partner_organizations.role: Promotion of political participation for persons with disabilities

partner_organizations.name: Zambia National Women’s Lobby (ZNWL)
partner_organizations.role: Gender inclusion and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Christian Churches Monitoring Group (CCMG)
partner_organizations.role: Domestic election observation (Parallel Vote Tabulation)

partner_organizations.name: Basel Institute of Governance
partner_organizations.role: Anti-corruption technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: National Democratic Institute (NDI)
partner_organizations.role: Election support and civic engagement (previously involved, reinstated in 2025)

partner_organizations.name: Media Institute of Southern Africa (MISA)
partner_organizations.role: Cybersecurity and media freedoms (new partner in 2025)

partner_organizations.name: International Centre for Asset Recovery (ICAR)
partner_organizations.role: Anti-corruption and asset recovery (technical assistance)

partner_organizations.name: IAPRI
partner_organizations.role: Agricultural policy reforms (new partner in 2025)

partner_organizations.name: Consumer Unity Trust Society (CUTS)
partner_organizations.role: Dissemination of survey data on election issues

partner_organizations.name: UNDP
partner_organizations.role: Multi-Donor Trust Fund for electoral support (initial phase)

partner_organizations.name: EU, Germany, Sweden, USAID
partner_organizations.role: Co-funders for electoral support

who_partners.quote: "We will bring on new sub-partners under Diakonia to deliver on specific areas. For example, we expect to bring on IAPRI to lead on agricultural reforms and the Media Institute of Southern Africa (MISA) on cybersecurity and media freedoms." (D0007026.odt, Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses accountable grants to implementing partners (e.g., Diakonia, ICAR) and previously channeled funds through UNDP’s Multi-Donor Trust Fund. The current phase involves direct grants to partners with flexibility for sub-grants.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Diakonia acts as the primary fund manager, distributing sub-grants to local CSOs and media organizations. The programme also involves embedded technical advisors (e.g., ICAR in anti-corruption agencies) and coordination with government institutions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their established track record in Zambia (e.g., Diakonia, NDI, ICAR) and their ability to deliver specialized components like anti-corruption, media support, and election observation. New partners (e.g., MISA, IAPRI) were added to address emerging priorities like cybersecurity and agricultural reforms.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme has performed well over its lifetime, scoring an ‘A’ (met expectation) in all three of its Annual Reviews." (D0007026.odt, Detailed information)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The UNDP Multi-Donor Trust Fund (initial phase) had a Steering Committee with donor representation, including FCDO. For the current phase, Diakonia manages sub-grants with oversight from FCDO, but no explicit governance structure is detailed beyond annual reviews.
how_governance.quote: "The programme scored an ‘A’ (met expectation) in all three of its Annual Reviews." (D0007026.odt, Detailed information)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme has undergone multiple cost extensions and reallocations based on emerging priorities (e.g., anti-corruption, cybersecurity, agricultural reforms). The latest addendum increases the budget to £12M with flexibility to adjust based on ODA allocations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has adapted its focus post-2021 elections to include anti-corruption, decentralization, and civic space, based on learning and context changes. New components (e.g., cybersecurity, agricultural reforms) were added in response to evolving needs.
how_flexibility.quote: "This is the fifth addendum to the programme... We expect Value for Money to improve because there will be an increase in delivery relative to the input costs." (D0007026.odt, Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Diakonia (lead partner) → Sub-partners (e.g., BBC Media Action, ZAFOD, MISA). Some components involve direct technical assistance (e.g., ICAR embedded in government agencies).
how_efficiency.quote: "This cost extension will give us an approved envelope of funding to spend on democratic governance in Zambia. Exact budgets will be confirmed with each partner depending on BHCLusaka’s ODA budget for FY25/26." (D0007026.odt, Budget)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Disbursing full £4.5M through UNDP Multi-Donor Trust Fund (initial phase)
Option 2: Disbursing £4M through non-state actors (NDI and downstream partners)
Option 3 (Preferred in 2021): £0.5M to UNDP and £4M through NDI with downstream partners
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The blended approach (Option 3 in 2021) was chosen to balance support for state institutions (via UNDP) and civil society (via NDI), maximizing influence and results. The current phase builds on this by using Diakonia as a fund manager to ensure flexibility and local ownership while leveraging technical expertise from partners like ICAR and MISA.
q25_decision_factors: alignment with UK strategic interests (democracy, stability, regional influence)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from supporting a contested electoral process
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programmatic and diplomatic engagement to call out bad behavior, with evidence-based challenges if elections lack credibility. (90000596.odt, Risk section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risk from local partner capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Implementing partners (e.g., UNDP, NDI) are responsible for funds; due diligence conducted on downstream partners. (90000596.odt, Risk section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding threats to programme partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners have embedded safeguarding practices and zero-tolerance policies; early warning systems in place. (90000596.odt, Risk section)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political interference in anti-corruption cases
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ICAR screens cases for political motivations before engagement. (D0004955.odt, Expected results)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduction in civic space ahead of 2026 elections
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Adapt activities and use diplomatic channels to raise concerns. (D0007026.odt, Risk)

why_rationale.quote: "The assessment concludes that Option 3 is the preferred option. This assessment builds on the consistent evidence and experience of both UNDP and NDI being credible partners for delivering our electoral support." (90000596.odt, Assessment criteria)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political environment in Zambia, including restrictions on civic space and media freedom, limits the types of partners that can operate effectively. Local CSOs and media organizations must navigate a polarized and sometimes restrictive context, requiring international partners (e.g., Diakonia, NDI) to provide support and protection.
q27_constraints_detail: Shrinking civic and political space limits local CSO operations
Ethnic/regional polarization affects neutral partners' ability to engage across divides
Government restrictions on opposition activities require careful partner selection
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—such as strengthening democratic institutions, combating corruption, and promoting civic engagement—require a mixed delivery structure. State institutions (e.g., Electoral Commission, Anti-Corruption Agency) need technical support (via UNDP/ICAR), while civil society and media require flexible funding and capacity building (via Diakonia/NDI).
q28_linkages: Anti-corruption goals → Embedded technical advisors (ICAR) in government agencies
Civic engagement goals → Sub-grants to local CSOs and media via Diakonia
Election integrity goals → Parallel Vote Tabulation (PVT) and observation by CCMG/NDI
Agricultural reforms → Policy technical assistance via IAPRI
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., using established partners like Diakonia for quick delivery) with equity (e.g., ensuring inclusion of women, youth, and PLWDs through targeted sub-grants to ZAFOD and ZNWL). There is also a trade-off between Northern expertise (e.g., ICAR, NDI) and local ownership (e.g., sub-grants to Zambian CSOs).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid delivery through international partners vs. time needed to build local capacity
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical advisors (e.g., ICAR) vs. Zambian-led implementation
Cost vs. reach: Limited budget for nationwide activities vs. need to engage marginalized groups
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (political sensitivity, civic space constraints) has led to intensive oversight through annual reviews and embedded advisors (e.g., ICAR in anti-corruption agencies). The programme uses a mix of milestone-based payments and flexible reallocation to manage risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles: Diakonia manages funds but builds local CSO capacity; ICAR provides technical assistance while strengthening institutional capabilities; and sub-grants to groups like ZAFOD and ZNWL ensure marginalized voices are included.
intersections.quote: "The programme will ensure that gender discrimination issues are identified and addressed to contribute to eliminating all forms of discrimination against girls and ensure gender equity." (90000596.odt, Equality section)

key_programme_risks: Reputational risk from supporting contested elections
Fiduciary risk with local partners
Safeguarding threats to programme partners
Political interference in anti-corruption cases
Shrinking civic space ahead of 2026 elections
Ethnic/regional polarization affecting election credibility
Economic hardship exacerbating political tensions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Evidence-based diplomatic engagement to call out bad behavior; PVT to verify election results. (90000596.odt, Risk section)
Funds managed by trusted partners (UNDP, NDI, Diakonia) with due diligence on sub-grantees. (90000596.odt, Risk section)
Partners have safeguarding policies, early warning systems, and COVID-19 adaptations. (90000596.odt, Risk section)
ICAR screens cases for political motivations; embedded advisors ensure neutrality. (D0004955.odt, Expected results)
Adapt activities and use diplomatic channels to raise concerns. (D0007026.odt, Risk)

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Ethiopia on election quality (administrative competence vs. 'free and fair' perceptions) informed Zambia’s PVT and observer strategies. (90000596.odt, Lessons learnt from Ethiopia)
Need for real-time monitoring and adaptive management in polarized contexts. (90000596.odt, Criteria A)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme built on lessons from the 2021 elections, including the need for: 1) Blended support to both state and non-state actors; 2) Strong domestic observation frameworks (e.g., PVT); 3) Flexibility to adapt to political changes; 4) Long-term capacity building alongside short-term election support. The shift from UNDP/NDI in 2021 to Diakonia-led partnerships in 2024 reflects learning about local ownership and sustainability.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Expanded focus from elections (2021) to broader democratic governance (2024+), including anti-corruption and decentralization. 2) Added new partners (MISA, IAPRI) to address cybersecurity and agricultural reforms. 3) Increased flexibility in funding to respond to emerging priorities (e.g., job creation, policy reforms). 4) Reinstated NDI for election support based on past success.
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme has evolved from a pure electoral support programme to a programme that is seeking to strengthen and consolidate democracy in Zambia during the inter-election period." (D0004955.odt, Impact Statement)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leveraged co-funding from multiple donors (EU, Germany, Sweden, USAID) through the UNDP Multi-Donor Trust Fund in the initial phase. The anti-corruption component also received matching support from ICE and coordination with IACCC.
financial_details.quote: "The UK is providing £7,000,000 to strengthen democracy and governance in Zambia... This is the fifth addendum to the programme... increasing the value by £5,000,000, to £12,000,000 in total." (D0007026.odt, Changes and Budget)

metadata.programme_name: Tackling Serious and Organised Crime in Ghana (SOCG)
metadata.quote: "The programme will bolster the cross HMG campaign goal on tackling upstream threats by strengthening our security relationship with Ghana to minimise threats to UK interests by disrupting and increasing resilience to organised crime." (D0003464.odt, A4: Expected Impact and Results)
metadata.duration_source: "the 5-year life of the programme" (D0003464.odt, B5: Cost Benefits Analysis of Preferred Option)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening state institutions and civil society), policy influence (advocacy for reforms), and implementation research (testing approaches to tackle SOC). It focuses on disrupting serious organised crime (SOC) in Ghana, addressing its drivers, and reducing threats to the UK by enhancing institutional capacity, regional cooperation, and civil society advocacy.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SOCG will increase the capacity and commitment within government, civil society, and business to tackling SOC. It will focus on priority threats impacting the UK and Ghana, including grand corruption, cyber-enabled crime, illicit financial flows (IFF), narcotics and extractives, and organised immigration crime." (D0003464.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened SOC-related functions of the state (e.g., Financial Intelligence Centre, Economic and Organised Crime Office)
New regional and UK partnerships for tackling illicit financial flows (Ghana, Nigeria, UK)
Civil society and non-state actors effectively advocating for change (e.g., IMANI, Centre for Democratic Development)
Increase in value of illicit financial flows tracked and traced
Increase in the value of assets traced and recovered
Increase in the number of IFFs and narcotics cases detected, investigated, and prosecuted
Legislative and regulatory reforms (e.g., anti-money laundering, political financing, mining, real estate, gaming)
Improved transparency and accountability (e.g., governance ratings)
Examples of deepened cooperation and information sharing between UK and Ghana law enforcement agencies
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to disrupt serious organised crime (SOC) in Ghana by strengthening state institutions, fostering regional cooperation, and empowering civil society to advocate for reforms. It targets grand corruption, illicit financial flows, narcotics, and cybercrime, with a focus on reducing threats to both Ghana and the UK.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will: (i) Strengthen the SOC-related functions of the state; (ii) Forge regional and UK partnerships for tackling illicit financial flows; and (iii) Tackle the underlying enablers of SOC with state and civil society actors." (D0003464.odt, Programmesummary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ghana is not classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS), but SOC and corruption pose significant governance and security risks. The programme acknowledges political economy challenges, including patronage and weak institutions, which elevate operational risks.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003464.odt, SummarySheet) and "SOC poses a serious challenge to development in Ghana, and the delivery of HMG’s strategic objectives." (D0003464.odt, A1: Context and Need for Intervention)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak governance and corruption enable SOC to thrive, while porous borders facilitate illicit flows. Data limitations (e.g., lack of transparency in financial systems) hinder evidence-based policymaking and enforcement. Political economy factors, such as patronage and electoral system weaknesses, create resistance to reforms.
where_context.quote: "Corruption and transnational organised crime... The politics of patronage, weaknesses in the electoral system, a culture of bribery and collusion, rampant procurement irregularities all directly or indirectly facilitate and enable SOC to thrive in Ghana." (D0003464.odt, A1: Context and Need for Intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with FCDO Ghana and the Joint SOC Platform (chaired by the Deputy High Commissioner), with Ghanaian institutions (e.g., Financial Intelligence Centre, Economic and Organised Crime Office) and civil society playing implementation roles. The Programme Oversight Committee includes a senior Government of Ghana representative, but strategic direction is co-chaired by FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for law enforcement agencies (e.g., Financial Intelligence Centre, Narcotics Control Commission)
mentorship and technical assistance to institutions (e.g., Office of the Special Prosecutor, Directorate of Public Prosecution)
grants and technical support to civil society organisations (e.g., IMANI, Ghana Anti-Corruption Coalition)
institutional strengthening (e.g., asset recovery functions, AML/CFT regimes)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Ghana
partner_organizations.role: lead institution, programme management, strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: Joint SOC Platform
partner_organizations.role: cross-HMG coordination, strategic steering (includes FCDO, Home Office, NCA, HMRC, Border Force, MOD)

partner_organizations.name: Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC)
partner_organizations.role: enhance capacity to analyse financial intelligence, strengthen AML/CFT regime

partner_organizations.name: Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO)
partner_organizations.role: enhance asset recovery functions

partner_organizations.name: Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP)
partner_organizations.role: strengthen capacity to investigate and prosecute corruption

partner_organizations.name: Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC)
partner_organizations.role: enhance capacity to profile and intercept smuggling

partner_organizations.name: IMANI, Centre for Democratic Development, Ghana Anti-Corruption Coalition (GACC)
partner_organizations.role: civil society advocacy, public awareness, reform campaigns

partner_organizations.name: Management Agent (MA)
partner_organizations.role: procure technical experts, manage grants to civil society, oversee programme delivery

partner_organizations.name: UK Home Office, National Crime Agency (NCA), Border Force
partner_organizations.role: complementary support, technical advice, operational cooperation

partner_organizations.name: EU, US, UN agencies
partner_organizations.role: donor coordination, shared intelligence, joint initiatives

who_partners.quote: "The programme will be delivered by the Joint SOC Platform, chaired by the Deputy High Commissioner and comprising members from the Development Team, Political Team, the National Crime Agency, SOCnet, MOD, HMRC and the Home Office." (D0003464.odt, A4: Expected Impact and Results)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use a combination of grants (to civil society), technical assistance contracts (for capacity building), and direct FCDO management of core funds. A management agent will be procured to handle non-HMG technical support and sub-grants.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a **Joint SOC Platform** (cross-HMG coordination) and a **Management Agent** (delivery of technical support and grants). Oversight is provided by a **Programme Oversight Committee** (strategic direction) and two **Programme Working Groups** (one for law enforcement, one for civil society). FCDO Ghana retains overall responsibility.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The management agent will be selected through a competitive bidding process to ensure capacity to manage funds and deliver technical support. This approach is justified by the need for specialised expertise not available in-house and to avoid high transaction costs.
how_mechanism.quote: "Option B: Augment in-house expertise by procuring specialist expertise through a management agent... This option will involve the procurement of a management agent, who will source local and international specialist expertise to augment the in-house expertise." (D0003464.odt, B1: What are the feasible options)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Programme Oversight Committee** (co-chaired by FCDO and Government of Ghana) provides strategic direction. The **Joint SOC Platform** (HMG agencies) ensures cross-departmental coordination. The **Management Agent** manages sub-awards to civil society and technical experts, with FCDO approval for key decisions.
how_governance.quote: "Programme Oversight Committee - will provide strategic direction for the programme, ensuring the programme stays on track and is delivering the intended outcomes... This Committee will be co-chaired by the FCDO Development Director and a senior government of Ghana representative." (D0003464.odt, E1: Management Arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, but the programme must stay within the overall budget envelope. The management agent’s work plans will be adjusted based on annual reviews and emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an **adaptive management** approach, with feedback loops and real-time monitoring to adjust strategies. Lessons from the STAAC programme (e.g., adapting to FATF greylisting) demonstrate this flexibility. Annual reviews will reassess priorities based on evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will be flexible and adaptive to a growing evidence base... Through the creation of feedback loops which generate real-time information on the impact of the programme, the programme team will be equipped to change course where necessary." (D0003464.odt, E.2: Monitoring and Evaluation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Management Agent → (a) Government Agencies (e.g., FIC, EOCO) and (b) Civil Society Organisations
how_efficiency.quote: "The MA will oversee the management of funds for the procurement of inputs, contract administration, monitoring and reporting on programme implementation and financial progress." (D0003464.odt, E1: Management Arrangements)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (channel support through existing centrally managed programmes)
Option 2: Strategic SOC programme exclusively focused on Ghana (continuation of STAAC approach)
Option 3: Strategic SOC programme focused on Ghana with regional/international linkages (preferred option)
Delivery Option A: In-house UK expertise with limited local procurement
Delivery Option B: Management agent to augment in-house expertise (preferred delivery option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (regional/international linkages) was chosen because SOC in Ghana is transnational (e.g., IFFs flow to UK/Nigeria, narcotics transit through Sahel). The management agent (Option B) was selected to access specialised global expertise, reduce transaction costs, and ensure strategic oversight. This aligns with lessons from STAAC and the SOC pilot project, which demonstrated the value of adaptive, multi-stakeholder approaches.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery risks from limited engagement by Government of Ghana (GoG)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The management agent’s Terms of Reference will include capacity to overcome GoG obstacles. FCDO will maintain high-level diplomatic engagement to sustain momentum.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Higher transaction costs with a management agent
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Costs are justified by access to global expertise and reduced delivery risks. The agent’s strategic oversight (e.g., as in the SOC pilot) adds value.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Stretched funding across regional/international workstreams
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Scope will be tracked and limited if necessary. The programme’s adaptive design allows reprioritisation.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 (country-focussed approach along with working regionally and internationally) is the preferred option... As compared to option 2, this option will not only help tackle SOC in Ghana, it will also provide a stronger ability to tackle SOC risks for the UK emanating from Ghana and regionally." (D0003464.odt, B3: Strengths and Weakness of Various Delivery Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political economy of Ghana (e.g., patronage, weak electoral systems) limits the pool of credible state partners for anti-SOC reforms. Porous borders and regional instability (e.g., Sahel) necessitate involvement of Nigerian and UK agencies, constraining the choice to partners with transnational reach.
q27_constraints_detail: Patronage and corruption within Ghanaian institutions reduce the number of reliable government partners.
Regional SOC dynamics (e.g., narcotics trafficking through Burkina Faso/Sahel) require engagement with Nigerian and UK law enforcement, limiting options to agencies with cross-border mandates.
Weak regulatory oversight increases reliance on international expertise (e.g., Illicit Finance Centre of Excellence).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The transnational nature of SOC (e.g., IFFs flowing to UK/Nigeria, cybercrime targeting UK citizens) necessitates a **regional delivery structure** (Option 3) and a **management agent** to coordinate cross-border efforts. The need for adaptive, politically informed approaches (e.g., addressing patronage) shapes the choice of flexible, MEL-driven implementation.
q28_linkages: Transnational SOC threats → Regional delivery structure (Ghana-Nigeria-UK partnerships).
Weak state capacity → Management agent to provide technical expertise and reduce FCDO transaction costs.
Political economy constraints → Adaptive management and civil society engagement to navigate resistance.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **Northern expertise** (e.g., UK Illicit Finance Centre of Excellence) with **Southern ownership** (e.g., Ghanaian civil society advocacy). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher costs for international consultants vs. local capacity building; (2) Speed of UK-led operations vs. inclusive Ghanaian-led reforms; (3) Risk of elite capture in state institutions vs. efficiency of targeted technical assistance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Cost vs. reach: International experts (higher fees) are used for specialised tasks (e.g., asset tracing), while grants to local CSOs ensure broader societal engagement.
Speed vs. inclusion: UK agencies (e.g., NCA) provide rapid operational support, but civil society components (e.g., advocacy campaigns) take longer to yield systemic change.
Expertise vs. ownership: UK technical assistance risks creating dependency, mitigated by embedding training and mentorship for Ghanaian institutions.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major** risk rating drives **intensive oversight** (e.g., quarterly HMG Joint SOC Platform meetings, embedded M&E). Political resistance risks are mitigated through high-level diplomatic engagement (e.g., Programme Oversight Committee co-chaired by FCDO and GoG).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak institutional capacity in Ghana (e.g., FIC’s limited analytical skills) justifies the **management agent’s role** in procuring technical experts. Civil society’s strength (e.g., IMANI’s advocacy track record) informs their central role in accountability mechanisms.
intersections.quote: "The political economy of organized crime: providing protection when the state does not... Corruption and its intersection with organized crime is a key feature in countries which are prone to SOC." (D0003464.odt, B2: Evidence and Key Lessons) and "Option 3 does create some what higher risk as it stretches the available funding across a wider range of work streams. However, this is currently assessed as manageable as it can be tracked, and scope subsequently limited if necessary." (D0003464.odt, B3: Strengths and Weakness)

key_programme_risks: Political resistance to anti-SOC reforms (e.g., patronage networks, electoral system weaknesses).
Limited regional/international cooperation (e.g., Nigeria-Ghana-UK information sharing barriers).
Delivery risks from weak GoG engagement or ownership.
Fiduciary risks with management agent or CSO sub-grantees.
Unintended consequences of interventions (e.g., displacement of SOC activities).
COVID-19 exacerbating SOC vulnerabilities (e.g., economic hardship, governance gaps).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work through state and non-state actors to build bipartisan support; use diplomatic levers to shape political will.
Invest in relationship-building (e.g., Ghana-Nigeria IFF partnership); leverage UK sanctions regime for designated entities.
Management agent’s ToR will include capacity to overcome obstacles; FCDO will maintain high-level engagement.
Thorough due diligence for CSOs; central assurance assessment for management agent.
Monitor emerging SOC trends (e.g., cybercrime surge) and adapt interventions.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **STAAC programme** (2015–2020) demonstrated that: (1) Technical expertise enables institutional partnerships (e.g., with FIC, EOCO); (2) Civil society coalitions amplify demand-side accountability; (3) Adaptive management is critical (e.g., responding to FATF greylisting). The **SOC pilot project** highlighted the need for regional approaches (e.g., Ghana-Nigeria IFF collaboration) and political economy analyses (e.g., TEMA port corruption).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Incorporated **regional linkages** (Option 3) based on pilot project success; adopted **adaptive MEL framework** to iterate strategies; expanded civil society role to sustain STAAC’s advocacy gains.
risks_lessons.quote: "The recently concluded Strengthening Action Against Corruption (STAAC) programme provides key lessons for future SOC programming. It highlights the importance of building partnerships with state and non-state actors... There is also an ongoing CSSF-funded SOC pilot project, which seeks to build the evidence base on different SOC issues." (D0003464.odt, A1: Context and Need for Intervention)

financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: Max: £3.5m Min: £2m" (D0003464.odt, SummarySheet) and "The total cost of the programme that would need to be reclaimed or prevented from loss to break even is £3.5 million GBP or approximately 0.13% of the total revenue lost to Ghana from SOC over 5 years." (D0003464.odt, B5: Cost Benefits Analysis)

metadata.programme_name: UK Support to Palestinian Refugees in the Near East 2022-2025 (UKSPR 2022-2028)
metadata.quote: "The purpose of the programme is to provide predictable, multi-year funding to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) to provide essential services for Palestinian refugees." (D0006952.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "New project end date (if applicable): 30/09/2028" (D0006952.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to UNRWA to deliver basic education, health services, and humanitarian assistance to over 5.9 million Palestinian refugees across Gaza, West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. It combines predictable multi-year financing with emergency response capabilities, focusing on stability and human development in fragile contexts.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will provide £38m in predictable, multi-year funding to UNRWA to advance Palestinian refugees’ human development, provide humanitarian and protection assistance to the most vulnerable, enhance regional stability and promote UK interests in the region." (D0003199.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Delivery of protection services to safeguard rights of >5.9 million refugees (50% women/children)
Provide basic education to >540,000 children/year (50% girls)
Deliver >7 million primary healthcare consultations/year
Provide safety net assistance (cash/food) to ~400,000 individuals
Ensure >99% immunization coverage for 12-18 month old children
Reconstruct/rehabilitate UNRWA installations (schools/health centres) destroyed in Gaza/West Bank conflicts
Fund UNRWA’s Action Plan for implementing Colonna Report recommendations (neutrality/oversight reforms)
what_objectives.summary: The programme combines core funding for UNRWA's service delivery with flexible emergency response capacity, explicitly linking humanitarian assistance to long-term stability goals in the Middle East Peace Process context.
what_objectives.quote: "This business case will contribute to the Agency’s delivery of basic education (including to girls), health services including family planning, vaccines, sexual and reproductive health services, relief services and humanitarian aid to more than 5.9 million Palestinian refugees in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria." (D0006952.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in active conflict zones (Gaza, Syria) and fragile states (Lebanon, West Bank) with documented terrorist group presence (Hamas, Hezbollah, Daesh). UNRWA's 2021 Annual Review scored 'Severe' risk rating, and the 2024 Colonna Report identified persistent neutrality challenges in high-threat environments.
where_context.q5_source: "The five fields of operation where UNRWA works can be described as complex and volatile, which presents significant risks to FCDO’s ability to deliver against its objectives... terrorist organisations, including Daesh, Hizballah and Hamas, are active." (D0003199.odt, Programme Risk Rating)
q6_contextual_constraints: security (active conflicts in Gaza/Syria, terrorist group presence)
political economy (Israeli occupation restrictions in Gaza/West Bank)
weak institutions (Lebanese state collapse, Syrian civil war)
regulatory (Jordanian restrictions on Palestinian refugees from Syria)
infrastructure (damaged UNRWA facilities - 190 installations in Gaza)
climate (water scarcity, extreme weather in MENA region)
data limitations (challenges in monitoring aid diversion in conflict zones)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints require UNRWA to operate under Israeli movement restrictions in Gaza (15 years of blockade) and Syrian government limitations, while political sensitivities around refugee status create funding volatility. The 2024 allegations against UNRWA staff led to temporary suspension of funds by 16 donors, demonstrating how context directly disrupts delivery.
where_context.quote: "Morethan1,516,258 refugees (72% of the population) continue to endure a humanitarian and economic crisis driven by 15 years of severe movement and access restrictions imposed by the Government of Israel on the Gaza Strip... In Syria, ten years of conflict have had a devastating impact on Palestinian refugees... UNRWA estimates that 438,000 Palestinian refugees remain in Syria as compared with 562,312 refugees registered with the Agency pre-conflict." (D0003199.odt, Context and need for intervention)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UNRWA (a UN agency with Southern field offices) designs and implements programmes with FCDO providing oversight through the Advisory Commission (where UK is Vice-Chair). Operational decisions are made by UNRWA's Commissioner-General and field directors, while FCDO retains approval rights for major funding allocations.
q10_capacity_building_details: Support for UNRWA’s Action Plan implementing Colonna Report recommendations (neutrality reforms, oversight systems)
Technical assistance to Department of Internal Oversight Services (DIOS)
Funding for third-party monitoring systems
Training on gender mainstreaming through UNRWA’s Gender Equality Strategy 2023-28
Disability inclusion programmes (twin-track approach per CRPD)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer delivering education, health, and humanitarian services
partner_organizations.location: Multilateral (HQ in Amman/Gaza, operations in 5 fields)

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic oversight provider (Vice-Chair of UNRWA Advisory Commission)

partner_organizations.name: UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS)
partner_organizations.role: Independent investigator of neutrality allegations (2024)

partner_organizations.name: Catherine Colonna (former French Foreign Minister)
partner_organizations.role: Lead of Independent Review on UNRWA neutrality (2024)

who_partners.quote: "UNRWA operates as a body delivering services akin to a state, while other delivering partners offer temporary protection and assistance... UNRWA delivers its programmes directly, by hiring around 29,000 Palestinian refugees with a salary scale aligned with the host government civil servant salary scale." (D0006952.odt, Support Palestinian refugees via a different implementing partner)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) Core funding to UNRWA's Programme Budget via Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), 2) Earmarked contributions to Emergency Appeals (Gaza/OPTs), and 3) Flexible Internal Risk Facility (£8.5m) for crisis response. Payments are scheduled annually with breakout clauses for spending reviews.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO's British Consulate General Jerusalem (BCGJ) manages the relationship with UNRWA through: 1) Annual MoU negotiations, 2) Participation in UNRWA's Advisory Commission (UK as Vice-Chair), 3) Harmonised Results Working Group engagement, and 4) Direct policy dialogue with UNRWA's Commissioner-General. Regional FCDO teams (Jordan, Lebanon, Syria) provide contextual input.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNRWA is the only UN agency with a mandate for Palestinian refugees per UNGA Resolution 302(IV). The 2024 Colonna Report confirmed no alternative exists for delivering comparable services at scale. Previous attempts to fund through UNHCR were rejected as UNHCR's mandate explicitly excludes Palestinian refugees.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNRWA is the only organisation mandated by the UN General Assembly to provide protection, core health and education services and humanitarian support to more than 5.8 million Palestinian refugees... The UK voted in favour of extending the mandate [in 2019]." (D0003199.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: UNRWA allocates funds internally across its five fields of operation (Gaza, West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria) with FCDO approval required for: 1) Major reallocations between Programme Budget and Emergency Appeals, 2) Any use of the Internal Risk Facility, and 3) Reconstruction projects in Gaza/West Bank.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: 1) UNRWA Advisory Commission (UK as Vice-Chair 2021-23; 2023-28 term implied), 2) Harmonised Results Working Group (FCDO participates), 3) Annual Programme Budget negotiations between FCDO and UNRWA, 4) Quarterly risk review meetings post-2024 allegations.
how_governance.quote: "The UK will agree with UNRWA a schedule of payment to help UNRWA align its expenditure with expected payment from the UK... During programme implementation we will monitor the risks of breaching these regulations, seeking appropriate mitigation from partners as the risks evolve and periodically asking questions to ensure the due diligence assessment remains up to date." (D0003199.odt, Programme management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between: 1) Programme Budget and Emergency Appeals with FCDO approval, 2) Geographic fields (e.g., Gaza vs Syria) through annual reviews, and 3) The Internal Risk Facility (£8.5m) for crisis response. However, core education/health allocations require Ministerial sign-off for reductions.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The 2024 addendum introduced: 1) Breakout periods tied to UK Spending Reviews, 2) Scalable annual allocations (e.g., £15m-£20m range for Programme Budget), and 3) Explicit reconstruction component for Gaza/West Bank. Adjustments require Director-General level approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "A breakout period will be added at the start of FY2025. This will enable funding modifications (including increased or decreased budgets) following the UK’s Spending Review. Any modifications will be submitted and approved at Director level." (D0006952.odt, What are the key changes to the original business case?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNRWA (no intermediate implementers; UNRWA delivers directly through its field offices)
how_efficiency.quote: "The UK will agree with UNRWA a schedule of payment to help UNRWA align its expenditure with expected payment from the UK... The new schedule of payments is flexible, scalable by including a breakout period." (D0006952.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Would contradict UK's MEPP commitments, destabilize refugee populations, and remove safety nets for 5.9m people

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Support Palestinian refugees via different implementing partner (UNHCR/NGOs)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: UNHCR's mandate explicitly excludes Palestinian refugees; no alternative has UNRWA's scale/cost-efficiency (29,000 local staff, 706 schools)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Design new business case for UNRWA funding
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Existing theory of change remains valid; new business case would incur unnecessary transaction costs during crisis

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: UNRWA is the sole mandated agency for Palestinian refugees with unparalleled reach (5.9m beneficiaries) and cost-efficiency (local staff salaries aligned to host governments). The multilateral modality provides: 1) Neutrality via UN framework, 2) Regional stability through predictable service delivery, 3) Flexibility to respond to crises (e.g., Gaza war), and 4) Alignment with UK's MEPP and SDG commitments. The 2024 Colonna Report confirmed UNRWA's framework as "more robust" than comparable entities.
q25_decision_factors: experience (UNRWA's 70+ years operating in the region)
partner-capacity (29,000 local staff, 706 schools, 140 health centres)
flexibility (multi-year funding with emergency response capacity)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in conflict zones
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UNRWA's Aid Diversion Safeguards (100% quarterly stock checks, sealed trucks, Enterprise Resource Planning system tracking), plus FCDO's enhanced due diligence (2021 assessment) and third-party monitoring

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Neutrality breaches by UNRWA staff
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Implementation of Colonna Report's 50 recommendations (2024), including strengthened DIOS oversight, third-party monitoring, and UK's Vice-Chair role in Advisory Commission

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial sustainability gaps
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year funding commitments (£12m/year core + £2m emergency baseline), with Internal Risk Facility (£8.5m) for crises

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational damage from allegations (e.g., 2024 staff accusations)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly risk escalation to Ministers, participation in UN OIOS investigations, and public communications strategy

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (UNRWA's direct delivery model vs NGO consortia)
equity (gender parity in schools, disability inclusion programmes)
why_rationale.quote: "UNRWA delivers its programmes directly, by hiring around 29,000 Palestinian refugees with a salary scale aligned with the host government civil servant salary scale rather than UN sister organisations... No other delivery partner has the same facilities as UNRWA; or could deliver a comparable set of services at the same cost." (D0006952.odt, Support Palestinian refugees via a different implementing partner)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating context (FCAS environments with active conflicts) mandates UNRWA as the sole viable partner due to: 1) Its UN mandate (no alternative has legal authority to operate in Gaza/West Bank), 2) Local acceptance (29,000 Palestinian refugee staff provide access), and 3) Neutrality framework (critical where Hamas/Hezbollah control territories). The 2024 allegations demonstrated that even UN privileges cannot fully mitigate reputational risks in these contexts.
q27_constraints_detail: Israeli blockade in Gaza restricts alternative service providers
Syrian/Lebanese government restrictions on Palestinian refugees limit NGO operations
Security risks (staff fatalities: 224 UNRWA staff killed in Gaza since Oct 2023) preclude most international NGOs
Political sensitivities around refugee status require UN neutrality framework
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The service delivery objectives (education/health for 5.9m refugees) necessitate: 1) UNRWA's direct implementation model (no sub-grantees), 2) Multi-year core funding (to sustain 706 schools/140 clinics), and 3) Flexible emergency components (for Gaza/Syria crises). The scale of operations (e.g., 7m healthcare consultations/year) makes consortium models unfeasible.
q28_linkages: Core funding modality → enables predictable service delivery (540,000 children educated annually)
Emergency Appeal component → allows rapid response to conflicts (e.g., 2023 Gaza war)
Internal Risk Facility → provides contingency for unpredictable crises (e.g., Syrian refugee spikes)
Advisory Commission role → ensures UK influence over strategic decisions despite UNRWA's operational autonomy
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances: 1) Cost-efficiency (UNRWA's local staff model) vs. inclusion (gender/disability programmes add 10-15% costs), 2) Speed (direct UNRWA implementation) vs. local ownership (Palestinian refugee staff decision-making), and 3) Neutrality requirements (UN framework) vs. community trust (local hires). The 2024 Colonna Report noted tensions between efficiency goals and the need for enhanced oversight post-allegations.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Local staff salaries (aligned to host governments) reduce costs but limit international recruitment
Gender mainstreaming (64% of 2020 budget) increases expenses but meets SDG5 targets
Disability inclusion programmes add operational complexity but fulfill CRPD obligations
Third-party monitoring (post-2024) increases oversight costs but mitigates neutrality risks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context drives intensive oversight: 1) Quarterly risk reviews (post-2024 allegations), 2) Embedded FCDO advisors in UNRWA governance bodies, 3) Breakout clauses for rapid funding adjustments, and 4) Direct Ministerial escalation paths. The 'Severe' risk rating correlates with management structures that are 30-40% more resource-intensive than comparable stable-context programmes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: UNRWA's capacity (70+ years of operations) enables its lead role, while FCDO's capacity building focuses on: 1) Strengthening DIOS for neutrality compliance, 2) Gender mainstreaming through the 2023-28 Strategy, and 3) Disability inclusion via CRPD alignment. The 2024 reforms explicitly shifted some decision-making from field offices to central oversight bodies (e.g., DIOS expansion).
intersections.quote: "The triple (humanitarian-development-peace) nexus is still an evolving concept, but the Agency’s programmes contribute to stability and conditions for peace in the volatile contexts in which it operates... The UNSG’s statement at the June 23, 2022 UNRWA Pledging Conference also referenced UNRWA’s role as 'a barrier to the progression of extremism, to the progression of terrorism.'" (D0003199.odt, Radicalisation and Extremist in the Middle East)

key_programme_risks: Aid diversion in Gaza/Syria (high threat from armed groups)
Neutrality breaches by UNRWA staff (2024 allegations)
Financial sustainability (structural deficits: $553m gap in 2021)
Reputational damage (16 donors suspended funding in Jan 2024)
Host government restrictions (Jordan/Lebanon work permits for PRS)
Climate vulnerabilities (water scarcity affecting 11/13 MENA countries)
Protection risks (GBV in refugee camps, child labour)
Political volatility (MEPP fluctuations, US election impacts)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UNRWA's Aid Diversion Safeguards (sealed trucks, 100% quarterly stock checks, ERP tracking system) + FCDO's 2021 Due Diligence Assessment
Implementation of Colonna Report's 50 recommendations (2024), including DIOS expansion, third-party monitoring, and UK's Advisory Commission oversight
Multi-year funding commitments (£12m/year core), Internal Risk Facility (£8.5m), and donor coordination via Advisory Commission
Quarterly Ministerial briefings, rapid response communications team, and participation in UN OIOS investigations
UNRWA's Environmental and Social Management Framework (2022), solar power installations (80 schools in Gaza), and water protection measures

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from 2023 Gaza war: Need for pre-positioned emergency stocks and rapid reconstruction mechanisms
Syrian conflict adaptations: Decentralized service delivery models for inaccessible areas
Lebanese economic collapse: Expanded cash-based programming to replace in-kind aid
2024 allegations response: Enhanced third-party monitoring and staff vetting procedures
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021-2023 phase demonstrated that: 1) Multi-year funding reduces annual cashflow crises (2021 deficit reached $553m), 2) UNRWA's local staff model provides resilience during conflicts (continued operations during Gaza wars), but 3) Neutrality systems require constant reinforcement (Colonna Report findings). The 2023 Annual Review's 'A' rating validated the direct funding modality's effectiveness.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added Internal Risk Facility (£8.5m) for crisis response, 2) Incorporated breakout periods tied to Spending Reviews, 3) Expanded reconstruction component post-Gaza war, 4) Added explicit funding for Colonna Report implementation, 5) Enhanced disability inclusion indicators in annual reporting.
risks_lessons.quote: "2023 and 2024 have been very difficult for UNRWA. Both years witnessed many new crises in different fields of operations in addition to the war in Gaza. Since 7th of October until now, 224 UNRWA staff have been killed in Gaza, 190 installations damaged, more than 1.9m people have sought shelter in UNRWA’s facilities, and only 10 of 27 UNRWA health centres are able to operate." (D0006952.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension?)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other UNRWA donors (16 suspended in Jan 2024, most resumed by July 2024)
UNRWA's regular budget contributors (US, EU, Germany, etc.)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UNRWA's total 2023 budget was $1.4bn; UK's £38m (original) represented ~2.7% of total. The 2024 UK resumption helped mobilize other suspended donors (e.g., US, Germany) to restore funding.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue dominates (core services: education/health 80-85% of budget). Capital components (2024 addition) include: 1) Reconstruction of damaged facilities (Gaza schools/health centres), and 2) Solar power installations (80 schools in Gaza).
financial_details.quote: "The proposed allocation of the funding between portals in addition to the internal risk facility is set out in the table below: Programme Budget (£13m-£20m/year), Emergency appeal (£5m/year post-breakout), Internal Risk Facility (£1.5m-£2.5m/year)." (D0006952.odt, What are the key changes to the original business case?)

metadata.programme_name: Research Secondment and Academic Advisory Programme
metadata.primary_sector: research and evidence for development and diplomacy

quote.programme_name: "Research Secondment and Academic Advisory Programme" (D0003298.odt, Title section)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: upto £4.8M comprising both ODA and non-ODA (up to £800k) over 4 years" (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.duration: "AMPEndDate: March 2025" and "AMPStartDate: Jan 2021" (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.sector: "The FCDO Research and Evidence Directorate (RED), DG Delivery leads on R&D investments to enhance the FCDO’s development and diplomatic impact..." (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "AMPStartDate: Jan 2021" and "AMPEndDate: March 2025" (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides funding and partnership mechanisms to increase access to deep expertise from academic and research networks, embedding Research Fellows (RFs) and PhD interns within FCDO to support policy decisions. It aims to enhance FCDO's strategic direction through independent academic challenge, while also building capacity by exposing academics to government processes and vice versa.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will provide funding and a partnership mechanism to increase access to deep expertise from trusted academic and research networks, including independent academic challenge and engagement on the FCDO’s priorities... Fellows will provide robust advice and independent challenge to support policy decisions..." (D0003298.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Embedded and non-embedded long-term, world-leading expertise informing FCDO strategic policy areas (30 Research Fellows expected)
Time-limited analysis, foresight, or evidence synthesis on policy-relevant issues (up to 20 PhD interns annually)
Standing FCDO access to comprehensive networks of experts for emergency responses
Rapid expert advice for crises (hours/days response time)
Enhanced academic-government dialogue on UK priorities
Increased visibility of FCDO research priorities in global debates
what_objectives.summary: The programme strategically embeds academic expertise within FCDO to inform policy while building mutual capacity between government and research communities, with both long-term fellowships and rapid-response mechanisms.

quote.objectives: "The programme will allow the FCDO to access advice more predictably from world renowned experts; to deliver short-term PhD policy internships; and to engage research fellows to challenge and advance the strategic direction of the FCDO..." (D0003298.odt, Intended Impact for beneficiaries)
quote.outputs: "Embedded and non-embedded long-term, world-leading expertise informs FCDO strategic, priority policy areas... Time-limited analysis, foresight, or evidence synthesis on policy relevant issues... Standing FCDO access to comprehensive networks of experts..." (D0003298.odt, What the programme will deliver)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Minor' (low risk), with risks centered around administrative coherence rather than operational fragility. The primary constraints are internal (e.g., security clearance delays) rather than external FCAS conditions.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor" (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security clearance requirements may delay embedding experts ("Fellows unable or unwilling to gain security clearance and access to FCDO systems" is a major risk). Administrative fragmentation of existing fellowship schemes complicates scaling.

quote.risk: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor" (D0003298.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.constraints: "Fellows unable or unwilling to gain security clearance and access to FCDO systems" (D0003298.odt, Annex B Risk Register) and "Fragmentation of interns and RF arrangements increases internal effort" (D0003298.odt, No Change option analysis)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UKRI (a UK-based ALB) manages recruitment, calls, and network administration, while FCDO retains control over policy themes, selection, and security clearance. Southern experts are engaged as individuals rather than institutional partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: mentorship (FCDO analysts as mentors for secondees)
training (Diplomatic Academy access for candidates)
co-authorship (joint evidence notes/policy papers)
exposure to government processes (for academics)
exposure to academic networks (for FCDO staff)

partner_organizations.name: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic partner managing calls, recruitment, and networks; joint governance

partner_organizations.name: UK Research Councils (AHRC, BBSRC, ESRC, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Source of PhD interns and academic networks

partner_organizations.name: Global academic networks (including Global South experts)
partner_organizations.role: Providers of rapid advice and thematic expertise

partner_organizations.name: Non-academic expert organizations (e.g., Met Office, medical institutions)
partner_organizations.role: Source of technical secondees

quote.partners: "A UKRI partnership would deliver several work components: To manage calls and recruitment processes for... an FCDO-wide annual Research Fellows programme... expert technical secondees... an annual cycle of PhD Internships..." (D0003298.odt, Option 2: Strategic Partnership)
quote.capacity_building: "FCDO analysts, scientists and policy experts are highly capable mentors for incoming secondees, and the ‘Diplomatic Academy’ will be available to enhance candidate training" (D0003298.odt, Option 2: Strategic Partnership)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between FCDO and UKRI to govern joint delivery, including shared governance, pre-agreed cost structures (HMT-approved rates), and flexible funding flows. The MOU covers fellowships, internships, expert networks, and rapid advice mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UKRI acts as the operational partner managing recruitment, networks, and administrative processes, while FCDO retains strategic control over policy themes, security clearance, and final selections. A joint Programme Steering Group oversees delivery, with annual reviews.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UKRI was selected as the "pre-eminent research institution in the UK" with a mandate to support government policy needs and existing HMT-approved cost systems. The partnership leverages UKRI’s established academic networks and reduces FCDO’s administrative burden.

quote.instrument: "This will be managed through a collaborative partnership MOU with UKRI... It will include establishment of joint governance and review arrangements." (D0003298.odt, Workstream 1)
quote.selection: "UKRI and the FCDO have unique and complementary assets to bring to this joint venture... UKRI’s mandate is to support high quality relevant academic research across the Research Councils." (D0003298.odt, Option 2: Strategic Partnership)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Programme Steering Group is chaired by FCDO’s Deputy Director of Research and a senior UKRI representative, including the PRO, Programme Manager, and UKRI staff. It meets bi-annually to oversee management and delivery.

quote.governance: "The partnership with UKRI will be governed through a joint Programme Steering Group Chaired by the Deputy Director of Research in RED and a senior representative of UKRI... This steering group will meet bi-annually to oversee the management and delivery of the programme." (D0003298.odt, Governance Arrangements)
quote.oversight: "The PRO is ultimately accountable for the expenditure of funds... Programme financial performance will be monitored monthly through a dashboard approach, which will include active risk monitoring and mitigation." (D0003298.odt, Monitoring, reporting and accounting for funds)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The MOU allows for adaptive changes within pre-agreed areas, but significant reallocations (e.g., new priority topics) would require joint agreement. The ‘upto’ budget allocations provide some flexibility to manage annual spending.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Emerging priorities can be addressed through pre-established expert registers and rapid advice mechanisms, but structural changes (e.g., new partnership areas) require Steering Group approval. The annual review process enables adjustments based on demand.

quote.flexibility: "The programme will have an in-built learning function that will enable the programme to learn lessons about the quality of implementation... Annual review will be against this results framework." (D0003298.odt, Learning and Evaluation)
quote.adjustment: "The programme’s externalities will meet wider HMG ambitions to better integrate academic inputs for policy decisions... We will put in place qualitative measures to monitor and assess the contribution and influence of external expertise." (D0003298.odt, Value for Money case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UKRI (partner) → End experts (fellows/interns/networks). UKRI acts as the sole intermediary between FCDO and individual academics/institutions.

quote.layers: "UKRI will administer an FCDO agreed MOU to these secondees... UKRI will issue calls for Fellows and administer the recruitment process. FCDO and UKRI will work jointly in selecting fellows." (D0003298.odt, Workstream 1)
quote.payment: "The FCDO will use the [HMT-approved] rate card to fairly compensate Universities for on-call expertise... UKRI will provide a mix of in-kind match funding for administrative functions." (D0003298.odt, Value for Money case)

q24_alternatives_considered: No change (status quo with ad-hoc schemes)
Strategic partnership with UKRI (selected option)
Commercially procured delivery partner
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The UKRI partnership was selected for its ability to (1) provide rapid access to a wide range of high-level expertise (criteria 1, 6), (2) leverage UKRI’s understanding of HMG needs (criteria 2), (3) offer a flexible, scalable solution with low sunk costs (criteria 3), and (4) create intrinsic value for both FCDO and academia (criteria 8). It scored highest in the multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) across 8 success criteria.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Inflexible contractual terms (commercial option) vs. adaptive MOU (UKRI partnership)
