q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UKRI partnership allows for easier process changes and shared funding, reducing FCDO’s administrative burden.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Higher costs for commercial partner (20%+ overheads) vs. HMT-approved rates with UKRI
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UKRI’s pre-agreed cost structures maximize VFM for HMG funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial partner may lack academic-policy linkage incentives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UKRI has a mandate to support government policy needs and existing HMG relationships.

quote.rationale: "Option 2 is the recommended route for this programme approach... [It] scores highest across criteria including rapid access to expertise, flexibility, global convening power, and intrinsic value creation." (D0003298.odt, Summary Multi-criteria decision analysis)
quote.risks: "A commercial arrangement carries risk of additional costs and less flexibility... FCDO would bear full programming and administration costs and would not benefit from UKRI funding earmarked to provide academics with government experience." (D0003298.odt, Option 3: Commercially procured delivery partner)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Security clearance requirements (WHERE) limit the pool of eligible experts (WHO), particularly for rapid responses. The need for pre-vetted networks constrains partner selection to those willing/able to undergo clearance.
q27_constraints_detail: Security clearance delays (risk: "Fellows unable or unwilling to gain security clearance")
Limited to experts from institutions with existing HMG relationships (e.g., UKRI-affiliated universities)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, policy-relevant expertise** (WHAT) drives the choice of a **UKRI partnership** (HOW) due to its pre-existing academic networks and HMT-approved systems. The mix of **long-term fellowships** and **emergency advice** requires a flexible mechanism (MOU) rather than rigid contracts.
q28_linkages: Policy-relevant outputs → UKRI’s academic networks (pre-established)
Emergency response needs → Pre-agreed expert registers (rapid convening)
Capacity-building goals → Joint governance and mentorship structures
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **inclusive access** (global expert networks, diversity tracking) with **delivery speed** (pre-vetted registers, UKRI’s search function). Trade-offs include: (1) **Northern-led management** (UKRI) vs. **global expert inclusion**, and (2) **rapid response needs** vs. **equitable partner selection**.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Pre-established networks enable rapid responses but may exclude non-traditional experts.
Expertise vs. ownership: UKRI’s administrative role ensures efficiency but centralizes control in a Northern institution.
Cost vs. reach: HMT-approved rates optimize VFM but may limit funding for Southern partners’ overheads.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **low-risk profile** enables **light-touch oversight** (bi-annual Steering Group meetings) and **flexible funding** (MOU-based). Higher risk contexts would likely require more intensive governance (e.g., embedded advisors).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives (exposing academics to government) shape UKRI’s role as a **broker** (managing internships/fellowships) and FCDO’s role as a **mentor** (Diplomatic Academy access, policy team integration).

quote.intersections: "Maintaining high quality and wide but adaptive capability for science or diplomacy policy advice requires rapid access to... experts who can work flexibly with government on priority policy needs... UKRI’s mandate is to anticipate and effectively deploy resources to serve government policy needs." (D0003298.odt, Option 2: Strategic Partnership)
quote.tradeoffs: "The programme will give the FCDO’s research priorities greater visibility within global science and political debates... We are therefore conscious that our aim is to improve UK international policy and its implementation rather than to build academic disciplinary domains for their own sake." (D0003298.odt, Intended Impact for beneficiaries)

key_programme_risks: Inability to reach agreement with UKRI on liabilities (Policy & Programme Delivery - Moderate)
Fellows’ advice not taken up by FCDO users (Public Service Delivery - Moderate)
Fellows unable/unwilling to gain security clearance (Public Service Delivery - Major)
Fluctuating FCDO demand outpaces programme response (Strategy & Context - Moderate)
Weak governance across fragmented fellowship mechanisms (Policy & Programme Delivery - Moderate)
Unrealistic timelines for fellows (Public Service Delivery - Moderate)
Internal demand outstrips budget (Policy & Programme Delivery - Major)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Unable to reach agreement with UKRI
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Leverage solid track record of joint delivery; discussions underway on risk-sharing.
Mentoring and stakeholder engagement to ensure policy relevance; high-quality engagement processes.
Long lead times for fellowships and pre-registration; close work with FCDO Security/IT.
Forward planning with expert registers; maintain good relations with UKRI for wider networks.
Centralized governance arrangements in FCDO; annual Steering Committee reviews.
Prioritization framework within FCDO; ‘upto’ budget allocations for flexibility.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: COVID-19 demonstrated the need for **pre-established links** between researchers and policymakers. Existing medical networks were effective, but other emergency science areas (e.g., conflict, climate) lacked government integration. This informed the programme’s focus on **thematic registers** and **rapid-response mechanisms**.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme consolidates fragmented legacy schemes (e.g., DFID Research Fellows) into a **coherent, FCDO-wide offer** with joint governance. Transition funding ensures continuity while new UKRI partnerships are established.

quote.risks: "Annex B: Risk Register" (D0003298.odt, full table of risks/mitigations)
quote.lessons: "COVID demonstrated that science responses for emergencies need to pre-establish links across networks of researchers and policymakers... science for other emergencies is not well linked with government or policy priorities." (D0003298.odt, No Change option analysis)
quote.design: "This programme will harmonise secondment arrangements for current Senior Research Fellows, ensure that their Terms of Reference support the delivery of outcomes of this programme... and enable a transition to the next fellowship arrangements." (D0003298.odt, Workstream 3)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UKRI provides in-kind match funding for administrative functions and leverages HMT-approved cost structures to maximize VFM. The partnership also unlocks access to Research Council-funded PhD interns (e.g., 3-month extensions to bursaries).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is revenue-funded (CDEL) for operational costs, including fellowships, internships, and network management. No capital expenditure is mentioned.

quote.budget: "This programme will spend up to £4.8M over 3 years... The indicative allocation of funds...: Partnership with UKRI (up to £3M), Programme Management (up to £250k), Transition arrangements (up to £1.5M)." (D0003298.odt, Overview of costs)
quote.leverage: "Intern’s living costs are paid by their research council through a 3-month extension of their PhD bursary... UKRI will provide a mix of in-kind match funding for administrative functions." (D0003298.odt, Workstream 1)

metadata.programme_name: UK Support to Global Partnership for Education (GPE) 2021-2026
metadata.quote: A UK contribution of up to £430 million to support the operations of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) in up to 90 countries over five years (2021-2026). (D0003273.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: A UK contribution of up to £430 million to support the operations of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) in up to 90 countries over five years (2021-2026).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme channels UK funding through the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to support basic education in low- and middle-income countries. It aims to address the global learning crisis, particularly for girls, by leveraging GPE's multilateral platform to expand access to primary and secondary education and improve learning outcomes.
what_objectives.q1_source: This will allow GPE to expand its programming for primary and secondary education, addressing the global learning crisis, including the setbacks posed by COVID-19 (C-19), particularly to girls. (D0003273.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 40 million more girls in school by 2026
20 million more girls reading by age 10 by 2026
Support to 1.1 billion school-aged girls and boys in GPE partner countries
Leverage $48.3 billion in additional funding for education (including $29.6 billion from domestic spend and $15.7 billion in savings)
Improved foundational learning outcomes in 90 eligible countries
what_objectives.summary: The programme leverages GPE's multilateral platform to expand access to quality education and improve learning outcomes, with a focus on girls in low- and middle-income countries. It aims to contribute to the UK's Global Objectives of getting 40 million more girls in school and 20 million more girls reading by age 10 by 2026.
what_objectives.quote: The programme will help GPE deliver funding to transform education in countries that are home to 1.1 billion school-aged girls and boys. GPE estimates that its support, alongside other education spend, will help partner countries get 40 million more girls into school and support 17 million more girls to read in Lower Income Countries (LICs, 70%) and Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMICs, 30%) over its five-year strategic plan. (D0003273.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: 90 eligible low- and middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs)
Including 16 countries where FCDO has bilateral education programmes
Specific examples: Kenya, Tajikistan, El Salvador, Uganda
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where half of GPE partner countries are fragile or conflict-affected. However, the overall programme risk rating is assessed as moderate and within FCDO's risk appetite.
where_context.q5_source: The risk rating of the programme is moderate and within FCDO’s risk appetite. (D0003273.odt, Risk section) || Halfof GPE partner countries are fragile or conflict-affected. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: learning poverty (70% of children in LICs and MICs unable to read by age 10)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and fragility disrupt education systems, climate change exacerbates vulnerabilities (e.g., flooding destroys schools), and data limitations hinder evidence-based planning. Learning poverty and weak institutions reduce the effectiveness of reforms.
where_context.quote: Halfof GPE partner countries are fragile or conflict-affected. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || Climate change and associated environmental degradation are already having a major detrimental impact on education, and this is set to worsen exponentially during the GPE 2025’s strategic period. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: GPE's governance includes high-level representatives from developing country governments, donors, multilateral organisations, civil society, the private sector, and philanthropic foundations. The UK sits on GPE’s Board alongside these constituencies, ensuring a balanced decision-making structure.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to partner governments (e.g., through the new Centre of Expertise for Education)
Support for evidence-based reforms (e.g., Data for Foundational Learning Programme)
Training and institutional strengthening via Local Education Groups (LEGs)
Pilot programmes to test and scale interventions (e.g., Girls’ Education Multiplier Programme)

partner_organizations.name: Global Partnership for Education (GPE)
partner_organizations.role: Lead multilateral organisation implementing education reforms

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Grant Agent for ~80% of GPE funds, alongside UNICEF

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Grant Agent for ~80% of GPE funds, alongside World Bank

partner_organizations.name: Local Education Groups (LEGs)
partner_organizations.role: Country-level coordination platforms led by partner governments

partner_organizations.name: UK FCDO Girls’ Education Department (GED)
partner_organizations.role: Strategic oversight, policy influence, and technical support

partner_organizations.name: Education Cannot Wait (ECW)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary fund for education in emergencies (coordination priority)

who_partners.quote: GPE’s partnership approach is replicated at country level, driving coordination and collaboration around key priorities. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || The UK sits on GPE’s Board alongside high-level representatives from GPE’s key constituencies, including developing country governments, donors, multilateral organisations, civil society, the private sector, and philanthropic foundations. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides core funding to GPE as part of its $5 billion replenishment target. This funding is disbursed through GPE’s multilateral mechanisms, including grants to partner countries, leveraging additional domestic and donor resources. The UK’s contribution is tied to GPE’s results framework and conditional on reforms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: GPE operates as a multilateral partnership with a Secretariat, Board, and country-level Local Education Groups (LEGs). The UK influences GPE through its Board seat, policy engagement, and technical support at global and country levels. Grant Agents (World Bank/UNICEF) manage ~80% of funds.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GPE is the only multilateral organisation entirely dedicated to basic education, with a proven track record in expanding access and improving learning outcomes. The UK’s long-standing partnership and influence within GPE justify direct funding.
how_mechanism.quote: The UK is a founding member of GPE and long-standing donor. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || GPE is the only multilateral entirely dedicated to basic education, including foundational learning. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Funds are allocated through GPE’s country-level Partnership Compacts, which prioritise reforms agreed with partner governments. The UK influences these allocations via its role in Local Education Groups (LEGs) and as a Coordinating Agent in 18 countries.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: GPE’s Board includes representatives from developing country governments, donors (including the UK), multilateral organisations, civil society, and philanthropic foundations. The UK has a permanent seat and influences strategic decisions. Technical oversight is provided by the Performance, Impact and Learning Committee (PILC).
how_governance.quote: The UK sits on GPE’s Board alongside high-level representatives from GPE’s key constituencies. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || The UK has a permanent seat on GPE’s Board. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || FCDO has a seat on the Performance, Impact and Learning Committee (PILC). (D0003273.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: GPE’s new Operating Model allows adaptive programming and redeployment of funds across the portfolio, with 40% of each grant conditional on reform achievement. However, reallocation requires approval through GPE’s governance structures.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The new Operating Model includes adaptive programming to course-correct based on evidence. Priorities can be adjusted through the Partnership Compact process, which requires approval from GPE’s Board and technical advisory panels (e.g., ITAP).
how_flexibility.quote: The new operating model focuses on [...] iii) adaptive programming, providing impetus and opportunity to course-correct. (D0003273.odt, Box 3) || Conditional funding is attached to achievement of these reforms (40% of each grant). (D0003273.odt, Box 3)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GPE Secretariat/Grant Agents (World Bank/UNICEF) → Partner Country Governments. The UK also influences through Local Education Groups (LEGs) at country level.
how_efficiency.quote: GPE’s funds leverage further resources. [...] Based on GPE’s $5bn fundraising target, it expects approximately $3bn to be leveraged by 2026. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || The UK is the only donor with an independent results framework for GPE. This provides additional incentive for GPE to deliver FCDO priorities, or risk losing funding. (D0003273.odt, Management Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to individual countries (rejected due to limited reach and influence)
Funding other multilateral organisations (e.g., World Bank, UNICEF) - rejected due to GPE’s stronger pro-poor focus and alignment with UK priorities
Direct implementation by FCDO (not feasible due to scale and lack of in-country presence in many GPE partner countries)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: GPE was chosen for its unique role as the only multilateral dedicated to basic education, its strong pro-poor focus (70% of funds to LICs), and its ability to leverage $48.3 billion in additional funding. The UK’s influence within GPE’s governance and the alignment with the UK’s Global Objectives for girls’ education justified the direct award.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (GPE’s robust risk management framework)
partner capacity (GPE’s track record in system reform)
flexibility (adaptive programming in new Operating Model)
equity (focus on marginalised girls and fragile states)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Influence dilution due to declining bilateral ODA
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fund additional staff capacity at country level and provide technical support through the Centre of Expertise for Education.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Grant Agents (World Bank/UNICEF) not aligning with GPE priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Established a Coalition on Learning with Grant Agents to drive coordination on foundational learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GPE’s new Operating Model not delivering expected efficiencies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful monitoring of reform progress and conditional funding tied to results.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per additional year of learning: $118 in LICs)
effectiveness (33.5 million children achieving minimum proficiency)
equity (70% of funds to LICs, focus on girls and marginalised groups)
why_rationale.quote: GPE’s multiplier effect offers good potential to mobilise new sector funding for GPE Partnership Compacts and grants designed at the country level. (D0003273.odt, Box 2) || The UK is the only donor with an independent results framework for GPE. (D0003273.odt, Management Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country scope (90 LICs/LMICs) and focus on fragile states constrain partner selection to organisations with global reach and FCAS experience. This excludes smaller, local NGOs and limits direct partnerships to multilateral Grant Agents (World Bank/UNICEF) and GPE’s country-level structures (LEGs).
q27_constraints_detail: Fragility in half of GPE partner countries requires partners with conflict-sensitive expertise (e.g., World Bank, UNICEF).
Limited FCDO bilateral presence in many GPE countries necessitates reliance on GPE’s footprint.
Data limitations in LICs/LMICs require partners with strong M&E systems (e.g., GPE Secretariat).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The objective of improving foundational learning for 33.5 million children determines the need for a multilateral platform (GPE) with: 1) scale (90 countries), 2) technical capacity (e.g., ITAP for evidence-based reforms), and 3) leverage ($48.3 billion mobilised). The focus on system reform requires a structure that can influence domestic spending (70% of education finance).
q28_linkages: Global Objectives (40M girls in school) → Multilateral delivery (GPE’s 90-country footprint).
Foundational learning focus → Need for technical advisory panels (ITAP) and data programmes.
Leverage requirement ($48.3B) → Conditional funding tied to domestic reforms.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (70% funds to LICs, focus on girls with disabilities) with efficiency (leverage ratio of 1:9.7). Trade-offs include: 1) Speed vs inclusion: Rapid disbursement through Grant Agents may bypass local CSOs. 2) Northern expertise vs Southern ownership: UK’s Board seat ensures influence but may limit partner country autonomy in some cases.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: "GPE’s initial response to C-19 was powerful in scale and speed, mobilising $500 million" (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) vs need for local CSO engagement.
Expertise vs ownership: UK’s "outsized influence" (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) vs GPE’s country-led Partnership Compacts.
Cost vs reach: Focus on "pro-poor" funding (70% LICs) limits resources for middle-income countries.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (including FCAS contexts) justifies milestone-based oversight and conditional funding. For example, 40% of grants are tied to reform achievement, and the UK’s Board seat allows intensive monitoring of fragile states.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, shaping partner roles through: 1) Technical assistance (e.g., Centre of Expertise for Education), 2) Data programmes (e.g., Data for Foundational Learning), and 3) Local Education Groups (LEGs) where FCDO provides "targeted investment" to enhance influence.
intersections.quote: GPE’s geographic footprint complements the UK’s bilateral education portfolio. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || The UK’s support to GPE will be critical to delivering all three pillars of the [Girls’ Education] Action Plan. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: GPE fails to raise sufficient funds ($5bn target)
Partner countries do not implement agreed reforms (40% of grants conditional)
Learning data remains insufficient in half of GPE countries
Climate shocks disrupt education systems (e.g., flooding, droughts)
Coordinating Agent role diluted due to declining bilateral ODA
Safeguarding incidents (sexual exploitation, abuse, harassment)
Grant Agents (World Bank/UNICEF) misalign with GPE priorities

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK’s historic role in co-hosting the 2021 Global Education Summit (raised $4bn) and ongoing donor coordination.
40% of grants conditional on reform achievement; Independent Technical Advisory Panel (ITAP) assesses reform readiness.
New Data for Foundational Learning Programme and participation in the Learning Data Compact.
GPE’s Climate Smart Education Framework and UK’s Climate and Education Position Paper.
Fund additional staff capacity at country level and technical support through the Centre of Expertise.
GPE’s 2021 Policy on Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment (SEAH) and risk assessments for all programmes.
Coalition on Learning with World Bank/UNICEF to drive coordination on foundational learning.

fcas_specific_lessons: Protective measures in GPE’s Operating Model to prevent FCAS contexts from being disproportionately affected.
Accelerated Financing mechanism for fragile states to ensure funding is not diverted from system strengthening.
Lessons from COVID-19 response (e.g., $500m for remote learning) applied to climate resilience.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past GPE programmes demonstrated that: 1) Conditional funding drives reform (e.g., 65% increase in girls’ enrolment in primary school), 2) UK’s influence is tied to ODA levels (mitigated by funding Coordinating Agents), and 3) Technical engagement (e.g., What Works Hub) improves programme quality.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The new Operating Model incorporates lessons from MOPA (2018) and the Effective Partnership Review, including: 1) Decentralised mutual accountability, 2) Differentiated approach for FCAS, 3) Reduced transaction costs, and 4) Evidence-based prioritisation (ITAP).
risks_lessons.quote: The UK has a long policy and operating model reform history with GPE. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || GPE’s new Strategy and Operating Model present a key opportunity to cement reform progress to date. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other GPE donors (e.g., France, Germany, EU)
Domestic governments in GPE partner countries

financial_details.leverage_achieved: GPE’s $5bn target is expected to leverage $48.3bn in additional funding, including: $29.6bn from domestic spend, $15.7bn in savings from efficiencies, and $3bn through GPE’s multiplier funding mechanism.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The majority of funds are revenue (non-capital) expenditures, focused on system reforms, teacher training, and learning materials. Infrastructure (capital) is a smaller component of GPE grants.
financial_details.quote: Based on GPE’s $5bn fundraising target, it expects approximately $3bn to be leveraged by 2026. [...] In total, GPE expects that $5bn will leverage a further $48.3bn. (D0003273.odt, Strategic Case) || A large proportion of education budgets are spent on recurrent activities, such as teacher salaries, which leave little discretionary funding available for quality reforms. (D0003273.odt, Appraisal Case)

metadata.programme_name: Technical Assistance Facility for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure in Small Island Developing States (SIDS)
metadata.primary_sector: climate adaptation / disaster resilience / infrastructure development

quote.programme_name: "The technical assistance facility will support SIDS to implement climate and disaster resilient infrastructure, reducing economic and social losses due to disasters and slow onset climate impacts." (D0002638.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "The facility aims to secure a total $50-60m of funding from multiple donors over an 8 year lifetime, with the capacity to adjust according to demand and opportunity." (D0002638.odt, Programme summary)
quote.budget: "The proposed UK contribution to the facility is £7.3m (US$10m) over eight years (2021–2029)" (D0002638.odt, Financial details)

metadata.duration_source: "The facility aims to secure a total $50-60m of funding from multiple donors over an 8 year lifetime, with the capacity to adjust according to demand and opportunity."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **capacity building** (institutional strengthening for SIDS), **financing mechanism** (Multi-Donor Trust Fund to channel funds), **implementation research** (demand-led research on resilient infrastructure), and **policy influence** (upstream engagement to shape regulations). It is demand-driven and focuses on systemic resilience in SIDS infrastructure.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The technical assistance facility will support SIDS to implement climate and disaster resilient infrastructure, reducing economic and social losses due to disasters and slow onset climate impacts. The facility will support partners through institutional capacity building, demand-led research and evidence generation, and the convening of partnerships for cooperation and the sharing of best-practices." (D0002638.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved resilience of SIDS infrastructure to climate change and disaster risks
Strengthened knowledge and partnerships for integrating resilience in SIDS infrastructure
Gender equality and disability inclusion promoted through resilient SIDS infrastructure

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen:
Option 1a (direct financial support via MDTF, managed by BHC New Delhi) was selected because it: 
1. **Leverages existing UK-India partnership** (CDRI co-chairmanship) and BHC’s strong relationship with CDRI. 
2. **Reduces perceived risk for other donors**, encouraging co-funding (e.g., Australia’s $10m AUD commitment). 
3. **Aligns with UK’s Indo-Pacific strategy** and COP26 climate adaptation goals. 
4. **Provides flexibility** for demand-driven SIDS support while maintaining UK oversight via BHC. 
5. **Avoids high management burden** of in-kind support (Option 2) or reputational risk of non-contribution (Option 3).

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who:
The **geographic dispersion and small size of SIDS** constrain partner selection by: 
1. Limiting local implementing partners due to **low technical capacity** (e.g., "lack of domestic technical capacity and institutional frameworks"). 
2. Requiring **multilateral platforms** (like CDRI) to pool expertise and reduce diseconomies of scale. 
3. Necessitating **regional bodies** (e.g., CARICOM, Pacific Islands Forum) for coordination. 
4. Making **direct bilateral aid ineffective** due to high transaction costs for small projects.
q27_constraints_detail: limited local technical expertise in SIDS
high transaction costs for small-scale projects
need for regional coordination to overcome isolation
donor eligibility criteria exclude some SIDS
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The **need for systemic resilience** (not just project-level fixes) determines the **platform-based delivery structure**: 
1. **Demand-led technical assistance** requires a flexible, SIDS-responsive mechanism (hence MDTF + CDRI). 
2. **Policy influence objectives** necessitate upstream engagement with governments (hence CDRI’s regulatory diplomacy role). 
3. **Capacity building as a core objective** shapes the peer-to-peer knowledge exchange model. 
4. **Financing mobilization goals** require a trusted multilateral fund manager (MDTF).
q28_linkages: systemic resilience goal → platform structure (CDRI + MDTF)
SIDS capacity gaps → embedded technical assistance and peer networks
policy influence → upstream engagement with CDRI’s regulatory tools (e.g., ORN31 updates)
financing needs → MDTF to pool donor funds and reduce SIDS transaction costs
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
Explicit trade-offs discussed: 
1. **Speed vs. inclusion**: The facility prioritizes **SIDS-led demand** over rapid disbursement, accepting slower implementation for greater ownership. 
2. **Expertise vs. local ownership**: Northern technical expertise (e.g., UK’s ORN31 standards) is balanced with **SIDS co-design** and peer learning. 
3. **Cost vs. reach**: Pooling funds via MDTF adds a layer (reducing efficiency) but enables **smaller SIDS to access finance** (equity). 
4. **Scaling vs. customization**: Standardized tools (e.g., HDM-4) are adapted for SIDS contexts to avoid one-size-fits-all solutions.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: slower disbursement for SIDS ownership
Northern standards (e.g., ORN31) adapted for local contexts
MDTF overhead enables access for capacity-constrained SIDS
regional peer networks reduce reliance on external experts
intersections.risk_affects_management:
The **moderate risk profile** (institutional constraints, disaster vulnerability) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and adaptive management. For example: 
- **High disaster risk** → flexible reallocation of funds post-crisis. 
- **Limited SIDS capacity** → embedded technical assistance and inception phase mapping. 
- **Donor coordination risks** → UK’s early commitment to signal credibility.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 
1. **SIDS as co-designers**: Representation in governance bodies and demand-driven prioritization. 
2. **CDRI as convener**: Facilitates peer-to-peer knowledge exchange to address skill gaps. 
3. **UK/India as technical backstops**: Provide upstream policy tools (e.g., ORN31 updates) and downstream project support. 
4. **Regional bodies as implementers**: Leverage existing networks (e.g., CARICOM) to reduce transaction costs.

fcas_specific_lessons: SIDS’ **existential climate threats** require **long-term, adaptive support** (not short-term projects).
**Peer-to-peer models** work better than traditional capacity building in small states (DFID, 2019).
**High disaster risk** necessitates upstream policy engagement (e.g., integrating resilience into standards).
**Donor coordination failures** in SIDS often stem from **complex eligibility criteria** (OECD, 2018).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
1. **Traditional capacity building in SIDS has limited impact** (DFID, 2019): Peer-to-peer knowledge exchange is more sustainable. 
2. **SIDS struggle to access concessional finance** (OECD, 2018; UN-OHRLLS, 2020): Simplified, demand-driven mechanisms (like the MDTF) are critical. 
3. **Infrastructure losses in SIDS exceed GDP** (World Bank, 2017): Resilient design standards (e.g., ORN31 updates) must be locally adapted. 
4. **Women and disabled groups are disproportionately affected** (UN Women, World Bank): Inclusive capacity building is explicitly integrated.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Demand-driven model**: Shift from donor-led to SIDS-prioritized interventions. 
2. **Peer networks**: Replaced standalone training with regional knowledge exchange. 
3. **Regulatory focus**: Added upstream engagement (e.g., ORN31 updates) to address systemic gaps. 
4. **Inception phase**: Added to map SIDS-specific bottlenecks before scaling.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The NGP aims to strengthen institutional mechanisms for whole-of-government coordination between federal and provincial levels in Pakistan. It focuses on improving the capacity of key institutions (CCI, NFC, PMO, Planning Commission) to address coordination deficits and enhance service delivery, particularly during crises.

This means providing technical support to the Prime Minister’s Office to focus political leadership on prioritised policy areas; ensuring decisions are evidence-based and are supported by effective monitoring frameworks and feedback loops." what_objectives.summary: NGP is a governance reform programme designed to improve federal-provincial coordination in Pakistan by strengthening key institutions (CCI, NFC, PMO) and enabling evidence-based decision-making. It complements existing UK aid programmes by addressing systemic coordination barriers that undermine service delivery and crisis response.

q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ensure NGP support builds rather than displaces government capability; institutionalize reforms post-completion.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political fragmentation undermining coordination
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on constitutionally mandated bodies (CCI, NFC) with cross-party legitimacy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited donor complementarity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Steering Committee to identify synergies with other BHC programmes (e.g., SNG-II, REMIT).

quote.rationale: "Option 2 provides the best opportunity to achieve greatest results with given cost... It would work to address key policy areas including climate change, revenue mobilisation, demography, and gender." (D0004395.odt, Assessment of options)
quote.risks: "There is a sustainability risk, as with all TA programmes, that government becomes reliant on external capacity and does not meaningfully build its own." (D0004395.odt, Option 2 weaknesses)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Pakistan’s federal-provincial tensions and weak institutional capacity limit partner selection to entities with existing government trust (e.g., UNDP, World Bank). Local political economy requires engagement with constitutionally mandated bodies (CCI, NFC) rather than new structures.
q27_constraints_detail: federal-provincial distrust (requires neutral intermediaries like UNDP)
weak public administration (limits direct implementation by new actors)
climate/economic crises (demand rapid, flexible responses from trusted partners)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for whole-of-government coordination (WHAT) necessitates a mixed delivery structure (HOW) combining direct TA to institutions (CCI, NFC) with multilateral partnerships (UNDP/World Bank) for credibility and technical depth.

q28_linkages.mechanism: direct TA + UNDP Contribution Arrangement for neutral facilitation
flexible PIF managed via implementer with FCDO oversight
embedded support to committees via TA providers

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (FCDO/UNDP technical support) with Southern ownership (Pakistani institutions leading reforms). Trade-offs include:

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Direct TA to PMO/CCI enables rapid reforms but risks bypassing provincial input; mitigated via Steering Committee representation.
UNDP/World Bank provide global best practices, but capacity-building ensures Pakistani institutions drive implementation.
Focus on federal institutions (CCI, NFC) maximizes systemic impact but requires complementary sub-national programmes (e.g., SNG-II).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (political fragmentation, weak institutions) justifies milestone-based oversight and a mid-term review to adjust strategies. Embedded advisors in PMO/CCI enable real-time risk management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: (1) positioning UNDP/World Bank as TA providers (not decision-makers), and (2) designing the PIF to pilot innovations led by Pakistani ministries.

quote.context_who: "The UK has developed strong working relationships with counterparts in federal and provincial governments... BHC has already supported Federal and Provincial governments in Pakistan with relevant TA programmes." (D0004395.odt, Proposed Intervention)
quote.what_how: "The proposed intervention is mostly geared towards addressing ‘how’ the institutions of governance work rather than ‘what’ they are working on... This means providing technical support to the Prime Minister’s Office to focus political leadership on prioritised policy areas." (D0004395.odt, Programme summary)
quote.tradeoffs: "The programme will provide support in select areas with a view to incentivise change and accelerate progress of public sector reforms implemented by the Government of Pakistan." (D0004395.odt, Programme summary)

key_programme_risks.risk: Sustainability: Government reliance on external TA without building internal capacity.
Political fragmentation: Federal-provincial tensions undermining coordination reforms.
Limited complementarity: Overlap/gaps with other donor programmes (e.g., World Bank PFM reforms).
Climate/economic shocks: New crises diverting government attention from reforms.
Implementation delays: Bureaucratic inertia in adopting reforms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Design activities to institutionalize reforms (e.g., NFC secretariat capacity) and phase out TA gradually. Use PIF to pilot Pakistani-led innovations.
Focus on constitutionally mandated bodies (CCI, NFC) with cross-party representation. Engage provincial governments via Steering Committee.
Steering Committee to map synergies with BHC programmes (e.g., SNG-II, REMIT) and donor initiatives (World Bank PFM).
Integrate strategic foresight into PMO/Planning Commission processes to anticipate crises. Flexible PIF to respond to emerging needs.
Milestone-based payments and embedded advisors in key institutions (PMO, CCI).

fcas_specific_lessons: Leverage existing constitutional bodies (CCI, NFC) rather than creating parallel structures, as seen with the short-lived NCOC (COVID-19 response).
Combine technical assistance with political economy analysis to navigate federal-provincial tensions (lesson from SNG-I/II).
Use crises as entry points for reform (e.g., post-flood recovery to strengthen NFC resource allocation).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Sub-National Governance Programme (SNG-I/II) demonstrated that: (1) Flexible, high-quality TA aligned with political consensus yields results; (2) Technical solutions must be backed by bureaucratic and political ownership; (3) Reforms can survive political transitions if institutionalized in neutral bodies (e.g., CCI).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added Policy Innovation Fund (PIF) to test adaptive approaches (lesson from SNG-II’s rigid structure).
Explicit focus on strategic foresight to address gaps in crisis anticipation (lesson from COVID-19/floods).
Stronger linkages to sub-national programmes (e.g., SNG-II) to ensure federal-provincial coherence.

quote.lessons: "Lessons from previous and existing governance support: (a) A model that works: The SNG programme (I and II) provides a tested model of engagement... (b) Good mapping of the stress points... (c) Good understanding of the critical junctions between policies, resource allocation, and sectoral implementation." (D0004395.odt, Lessons from previous and existing governance support)
quote.risks: "There is a sustainability risk, as with all TA programmes, that government becomes reliant on external capacity and does not meaningfully build its own." (D0004395.odt, Option 2 weaknesses)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will leverage World Bank financing for NFC reforms and UNDP’s implementation capacity, but no explicit co-funding amounts are stated.

metadata.programme_name: Investing in the humanitarian capability of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)

quote.text: The cost extension will enable the FCDO to support the ICRC to deliver life-saving assistance to people affected by armed conflicts and to continue to deliver on the objectives set out in the project’s purpose.

duration_source.text: New project end date (if applicable): 30/06/25

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to the ICRC to deliver humanitarian protection and assistance in conflict zones, while also strengthening the ICRC’s institutional capacity, oversight, and assurance frameworks. It combines service delivery (direct humanitarian assistance) with capacity building (strengthening ICRC’s operational and organizational effectiveness) and policy influence (promoting International Humanitarian Law).

q1_source.text: This project provides core support to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The project will: Protect people and reduce instability in armed conflict through promoting and disseminating International Humanitarian Law; Enhance humanitarian access and armed groups’ adherence to humanitarian principles; Prioritise the most vulnerable people in need and deliver humanitarian protection and assistance in situations of armed conflict; Implement policy priorities to enhance the ICRC’s operational humanitarian response in conflict settings; Support and incentivise the ICRC to strengthen core oversight and assurance frameworks to manage safeguarding and fraud risks.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Engaging more consistently with parties to armed conflict
Increased engagement with States and Non-State Armed Groups on International Humanitarian Law
Improved capacity in the prevention of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment (SEAH), and risk management
Preventing disappearances and increasing positive case resolution for people separated from their loved ones
Adapting programming to systematically prevent environmental degradation and enhance environmental responsibilities and policies
Increased value for money through reduced operational costs
Strengthening the ICRC’s capacity to achieve sustainable, impactful humanitarian outcomes
Strengthening the Central Agency and transforming it for the future
Diversity and inclusion initiatives
Digital transformation and data management
Partnerships within and beyond the humanitarian sector
Implementation of the ICRC’s new Resource Mobilisation Strategy 2020-2030
Investment in the institution’s global shared services

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the ICRC’s ability to deliver humanitarian protection and assistance in conflict zones while improving its institutional capacity, accountability, and adherence to International Humanitarian Law. It focuses on operational effectiveness, organizational accountability, and strategic priorities such as climate change, digital transformation, and safeguarding.

quote.text: The cost extension will enable the FCDO to support the ICRC to deliver life-saving assistance to people affected by armed conflicts and to continue to deliver on the objectives set out in the project’s purpose.

countries_regions: global (all conflict-affected countries where ICRC operates)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The ICRC operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) with high levels of instability, violence, and humanitarian need. The programme’s overall risk rating is 'Severe' due to the challenging operational contexts, including armed conflicts, corruption, and weak institutional environments.

q5_source.text: The overall level of risk for this programme is rated as 'Severe'. The ICRC works in inherently high-risk environments, delivering protection and assistance activities of armed conflicts. These are often situations with high levels of corruption and lower levels of development.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The ICRC operates in environments with active armed conflicts, high corruption, and weak governance, which limit access, increase risks to staff, and complicate the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Climate change and environmental degradation further exacerbate vulnerabilities, while data limitations (e.g., disaggregation challenges) affect monitoring and reporting.

quote.text: The ICRC works in inherently high-risk environments, delivering protection and assistance activities of armed conflicts. These are often situations with high levels of corruption and lower levels of development. The FCDO expects that its partner has a strong control framework, that it actively addresses weaknesses identified and manages risks effectively. However, there are some concerns that the ICRC has underinvested in these.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The ICRC, as a multilateral organization headquartered in Geneva (Switzerland), retains full decision-making authority over programme design, implementation, and resource allocation. The FCDO provides core funding but does not directly manage operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: strengthening core oversight and assurance frameworks
risk management and fraud prevention training
safeguarding and SEAH prevention
digital transformation and data management
inclusive programming (gender, disability, age)
environmental sustainability and climate change adaptation

partner_organizations.name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
partner_organizations.role: sole implementer and recipient of core funding

quote.text: The ICRC is a strongly performing organisation with a legal mandate and comparative advantage in its ability to deliver in challenging humanitarian contexts, particularly in armed conflict and other situations of violence. It has a clear mission to protect the life and dignity of victims and provide them with protections services and humanitarian assistance.
quote.source: D0002723.odt, The Case for Providing Support Through the ICRC

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme provides unearmarked core funding to the ICRC, with 30% of the budget linked to Payment by Results (PbR) indicators. This allows the ICRC flexibility to allocate resources based on need while incentivizing performance against agreed milestones. The core funding supports institutional strengthening and operational agility in conflict settings.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The ICRC is the sole implementer of the programme, with FCDO providing oversight through quarterly programme management meetings and annual reviews. The ICRC reports progress against KPIs and PbR indicators, with additional scrutiny through the Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The ICRC was selected due to its unique mandate under the Geneva Conventions, unparalleled access to conflict zones, and long-standing relationship with the UK (dating back to 1863). Its role as the guardian of International Humanitarian Law and its ability to engage with all parties to conflicts (including non-state armed groups) makes it a strategic partner for the UK’s humanitarian and diplomatic objectives.

quote.text: The ICRC has a unique legitimacy to engage all parties to conflicts and has unparalleled access to vulnerable groups in conflict situations. The ICRC is frequently the only agency operating at scale in many conflicts. Its unique role engaging with all arms-bearers, including the growing number of Non-State Armed Groups, is coupled to its direct delivery of a comprehensive range of integrated humanitarian assistance and protection programmes.
quote.source: D0002723.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The FCDO monitors progress through quarterly meetings with the ICRC’s Red Cross Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) and reviews against the Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan. There is no formal steering committee or board; oversight is conducted through regular reporting and performance reviews.

quote.text: Overall programme implementation will be monitored by the Red Cross SRO through quarterly meetings. In addition to the programme reporting, we have been clear to the ICRC that performance against the Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan remains a critical part of our continued funding and we will monitor implementation of this quarterly.
quote.source: D0002725.odt, What is the approach to implementation?

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are unearmarked, allowing the ICRC to allocate resources based on evolving needs in conflict zones. However, 30% of the budget is tied to PbR indicators, which limits flexibility for those components. Reallocation between PbR and core components requires FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in response to changing conflict dynamics or humanitarian needs, but significant changes (e.g., shifts in PbR targets) require FCDO agreement. The ICRC’s annual planning process (Planning for Results) incorporates lessons learned and evolving priorities.

quote.text: The extension will see a continuation of the same activities, KPIs, milestones and targets from one year results framework for an additional three years. This longer time period was the initial intention of the Business Case and four-year targets were developed with the ICRC from the start.
quote.source: D0002725.odt, Describe any key changes to the original business case

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ICRC (direct funding with no intermediaries).

quote.text: FCDO funding arrangements, core support under this programme will be comprised of 70% unearmarked funding and 30% funding linked to performance indicators, known as Payment by Results (PbR).
quote.source: D0002725.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The core funding modality was chosen due to the ICRC’s unique mandate, operational agility, and proven track record in conflict zones. Unearmarked funding allows the ICRC to respond rapidly to emerging crises and maintain a presence in underfunded or forgotten conflicts. The inclusion of PbR (30%) incentivizes performance while preserving flexibility. The long-term partnership (since 1863) and the ICRC’s role as a pillar of the international humanitarian system further justify this approach.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (flexibility and rapid response in crises)
risk-mitigation (ICRC’s unparalleled access and acceptance in conflict zones)
partner-capacity (ICRC’s institutional strength and global reach)
flexibility (ability to adapt to evolving conflicts)
equity (focus on most vulnerable and hard-to-reach populations)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud and corruption
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strengthening the ICRC’s Ethics, Risk and Compliance Office (ERCO) and implementing the Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan. Regular audits and FCDO oversight of risk management frameworks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding (SEAH)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investing in integrity training, feedback mechanisms, and accountability systems. Monitoring progress against KPIs on SEAH prevention and response.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk (e.g., failure to deliver in high-profile conflicts)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly reviews and PbR indicators to ensure performance. Close coordination with ICRC on high-risk operations.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Underinvestment in risk management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Directing a portion of core funding to strengthen oversight and assurance frameworks, including the Global Compliance Office (ERCO) and field-level risk management units.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (high implementation rate of 92% over 5 years)
equity (focus on most vulnerable and hard-to-reach populations)

quote.text: Providing core funding to the ICRC supports the institutional strengthening, oversight and assurance of this founding pillar of the modern International Humanitarian System. Core funding enables the ICRC to be agile, to engage in all conflict situations and to respond appropriately based on the level of need.
quote.source: D0002723.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The ICRC is the only viable partner for this programme due to its unique mandate under the Geneva Conventions, which grants it unparalleled access to conflict zones and acceptance by all parties (including non-state armed groups). No other organization has the legal authority, operational presence, or neutrality to deliver humanitarian protection and assistance at this scale in active conflicts.
q27_constraints_detail: Legal mandate (only the ICRC has the Geneva Conventions mandate to engage all conflict parties)
Operational access (ICRC’s acceptance in high-risk environments where other agencies cannot operate)
Neutrality and impartiality (critical for engaging with non-state armed groups and governments alike)
Long-term presence (ICRC’s average 36-year presence in its top 10 operations enables trust-building)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—delivering humanitarian protection in active conflicts, promoting IHL, and strengthening institutional capacity—require a single, agile implementer with global reach and legal authority. The ICRC’s integrated approach (combining protection, assistance, and prevention under one mandate) necessitates direct core funding rather than a fragmented, multi-partner structure. The need for rapid response and adaptability in conflicts further justifies unearmarked funding with PbR incentives.
q28_linkages: Global mandate → Single implementer (ICRC’s unique role requires direct funding)
Conflict agility → Core funding (unearmarked funds enable rapid reallocation)
Institutional strengthening → Embedded capacity building (PbR tied to organizational KPIs)
IHL promotion → Direct engagement with states/armed groups (ICRC’s neutrality enables dialogue)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (direct funding to a high-performing multilateral) with equity (ensuring assistance reaches the most vulnerable in conflicts). Trade-offs include: 1) Speed vs. inclusion: The ICRC’s rapid response in crises is prioritized, but efforts are made to improve inclusive programming (e.g., gender, disability, age disaggregation). 2) Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: While the ICRC is Northern-led, it invests in local staff (e.g., 42% women in managerial roles globally) and National Society partnerships. 3) Cost vs. reach: Core funding enables presence in underfunded conflicts, but overheads are scrutinized via PbR and assurance frameworks.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion (rapid response prioritized, but inclusive programming is a KPI)
Expertise vs. ownership (ICRC’s global systems balanced with local staff development)
Flexibility vs. accountability (unearmarked funds with 30% PbR to ensure performance)
Risk vs. reach (operating in high-risk FCAS to assist the most vulnerable)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Severe’ risk profile (due to FCAS contexts) drives intensive oversight: quarterly reviews, PbR indicators, and a dedicated focus on strengthening the ICRC’s risk management frameworks (e.g., ERCO office, fraud prevention, SEAH safeguards). The FCDO’s oversight intensity (e.g., Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan) is directly proportional to the operational risks in conflict zones.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the ICRC’s role as the sole implementer. For example: 1) Risk management units are being expanded in field operations; 2) SEAH prevention training is mandatory for all staff; 3) Digital transformation and data systems are being upgraded to improve monitoring in high-risk environments. These investments enable the ICRC to fulfill its mandate more effectively in complex conflicts.

quote.text: The ICRC works in inherently high-risk environments, delivering protection and assistance activities of armed conflicts. These are often situations with high levels of corruption and lower levels of development. The FCDO expects that its partner has a strong control framework, that it actively addresses weaknesses identified and manages risks effectively.

key_programme_risks: Fraud and corruption in high-risk environments
Safeguarding failures (SEAH)
Reputational damage from failures in high-profile conflicts
Underfunded operations due to donor fatigue
Access restrictions in escalating conflicts
Climate change exacerbating humanitarian needs
Data limitations affecting monitoring (e.g., disability disaggregation)
Underinvestment in risk management and assurance frameworks
Political changes disrupting operations
Scaled-up conflicts overwhelming capacity

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strengthening the Ethics, Risk and Compliance Office (ERCO); implementing the Internal Control Framework and Assurance Strategy; regular audits and FCDO oversight.
Mandatory integrity training for 95% of staff; expanding feedback mechanisms for affected populations; victim-centered reporting channels; monitoring via PbR KPIs.
Quarterly performance reviews; PbR linked to high-profile operations; close coordination with ICRC on media and stakeholder engagement.
Core funding enables presence in forgotten crises; PbR incentivizes efficient resource allocation.
ICRC’s neutrality and dialogue with armed groups; adaptive programming based on conflict dynamics.
Integrating environmental safeguards into operations; KPIs on climate adaptation and greenhouse gas reduction.
Investing in digital transformation and data management systems; Wilton Park dialogue on responsible data sharing.
Directing core funds to strengthen ERCO and field risk units; Central Assurance Assessment Action Plan.

fcas_specific_lessons: The ICRC’s long-term presence (average 36 years in top operations) is critical for trust-building and rapid scaling in conflicts.
Flexible core funding is essential for responding to unpredictable crises (e.g., Nagorno-Karabakh, Burkina Faso).
Local staff and National Society partnerships enhance acceptance and last-mile delivery.
PbR must be balanced with flexibility to avoid disincentivizing work in high-risk, low-visibility crises.
Safeguarding and fraud risks are heightened in FCAS; proactive measures (e.g., ERCO, integrity training) are necessary.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The previous Joint Business Case (2017–2021) demonstrated that core funding enables the ICRC to: 1) Maintain presence in protracted conflicts; 2) Scale rapidly in new crises; 3) Focus on underfunded operations with unique added value (e.g., tracing missing persons, forensic identification). The ICRC’s high implementation rate (92% over 5 years) and ‘A’ rating in the Project Completion Report justified continued investment. Lessons included the need for stronger risk management (leading to the ERCO’s establishment) and deeper focus on inclusive programming (e.g., gender, disability).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Introduction of PbR (30%) to incentivize performance while preserving flexibility; 2) Expanded focus on safeguarding (SEAH) and fraud prevention via KPIs; 3) Strengthened risk management frameworks (ERCO, field risk units); 4) Greater emphasis on climate change and environmental sustainability in programming; 5) Enhanced reporting on inclusive programming (gender, disability, age).

quote.text: The ICRC scored an ‘A’ in the recently approved PCR of the previous Joint Business Case, during which time the risk associated with supporting the ICRC rose from ‘Major’ to ‘Severe’. This reflected the very challenging operational contexts of ICRC operations, which have been exacerbated by the direct and indirect impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic which have increased needs and risks even further in many countries.
quote.source: D0002723.odt, What does this Programme Build on?

quote.text: The cost extension would be £144m, comprised of core funds for ICRC covering a multi-year period from 2022–2024, which includes a 30% PbR funding contingent on making sufficient performance against the PbR indicators.
quote.source: D0002725.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO’s six-person Forest and Sustainable Land Use Investment team provides overall strategic policy direction, technical expertise, and programme management oversight. Decision-making is centralized in the UK, with delivery outsourced to service providers and grants to non-profit partners.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to smallholder farmers (Component 2)
business incubation and market development (Components 1 & 3)
policy support and convening (Component 4)
independent monitoring and evaluation (Component 5)

partner_organizations.name: Service Provider Contracts (2)
partner_organizations.role: Programme delivery (business incubation, smallholder support, Congo Basin market development)

partner_organizations.name: Strategic non-profit partners (accountable grants)
partner_organizations.role: Direct partnership for policy initiatives and collective action platforms

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Embassy Network
partner_organizations.role: Diplomatic engagement and in-country coordination

partner_organizations.name: International Forest Unit (IFU, joint FCDO-DESNZ)
partner_organizations.role: Cross-Whitehall policy coordination

quote.structure: "The programme will be delivered through two service provider contracts (using existing frameworks where practical) and a limited number of accountable grants to strategic non-profit partners." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.lead: "The FCDO’s Energy, Climate and Environment Division (ECED) co-hosts the joint FCDO-DESNZ International Forest Unit (IFU), providing a solid coordination mechanism to draw together cross-Whitehall policy expertise and Ministerial interests." (D0003948.odt, Management Case)
quote.capacity: "Component 2: Enhanced support for smallholder farmers (£45.5m): This reflects evidence and strong demand from partner country governments to mobilise increased support for smallholder farmers." (D0003948.odt, Programme design)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of service provider contracts (for business incubation, smallholder support, and market development) and accountable grants to non-profit partners (for policy engagement and collective action). This builds on the Phase 1 model, which successfully leveraged £1bn in private investment through similar instruments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FCDO’s Forest and Sustainable Land Use Investment team (6 staff) provides strategic oversight, while delivery is outsourced to two service providers and a limited number of non-profit partners. The International Forest Unit (IFU) coordinates cross-Whitehall policy alignment, and embassies support in-country engagement.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme builds on Phase 1’s proven model, using existing frameworks to select service providers. This approach leverages prior experience and reduces transaction costs, while accountable grants enable direct partnerships with non-profits for policy work.

quote.instrument: "The commercial strategy to deliver these results will emphasise outsourcing of programme delivery wherever possible. Building on the proven model for IFSLU1, the programme will be delivered through two service provider contracts (using existing frameworks where practical) and a limited number of accountable grants to strategic non-profit partners." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.structure: "With the IFU, the FCDO’s six-person strong Forest and Sustainable Land Use Investment team will provide overall strategic policy direction, technical expertise, and programme management oversight of IFSLU2." (D0003948.odt, Management Case)
quote.selection: "Building on the proven model for IFSLU1, the programme will be delivered through two service provider contracts (using existing frameworks where practical)." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)

quote.manager: "The FCDO’s six-person strong Forest and Sustainable Land Use Investment team will provide overall strategic policy direction, technical expertise, and programme management oversight of IFSLU2." (D0003948.odt, Management Case)
quote.sub_awards: "The programme will be delivered through two service provider contracts (using existing frameworks where practical) and a limited number of accountable grants to strategic non-profit partners, some of which will be directly managed to enable the UK to enter into direct partnership with other donors." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.oversight: "Monitoring during programme implementation will be used to understand and adapt to the fluid and uncertain operating environment." (D0003948.odt, Risk management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to five components, but the programme is designed to adapt to emerging evidence and context changes. The initial £195m (2023-28) is structured as the first tranche of a £500m 10-year commitment, with flexibility to adjust based on evaluations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive delivery with key decision points and monitoring to respond to the "fluid and uncertain operating environment." Lessons from Phase 1 (e.g., smallholder focus, Congo Basin adjustments) are explicitly integrated into Phase 2 design.

quote.reallocation: "The current five-year £195m commitment has been designed and calibrated to form the first tranche of the envisaged ten-year programme but will achieve a robust set of results within the first five years, even if the subsequent funding is not approved." (D0003948.odt, Financial Case)
quote.adaptive: "Keydelivery phases, timeframes and decision points in adaptive delivery" (D0003948.odt, Management Case)
quote.learning: "Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) will support learning, inform management decisions and programme strategy and delivery and strengthen evidence." (D0003948.odt, Management Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) Service providers/non-profit partners → (2) End beneficiaries (smallholders, businesses, communities). The structure is streamlined compared to Phase 1, with a focus on outsourcing to reduce layers.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £500m, (2023-33)" (D0003948.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.layers: "The programme will be delivered through two service provider contracts and a limited number of accountable grants to strategic non-profit partners." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.payment: "Award and mobilisation of contract and non-contract agreements" (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case, Section C)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Direct FCDO management with in-house delivery teams (rejected due to lack of scalability and private sector engagement)
Option B: Single large contractor (rejected due to risk of monopolistic practices and limited flexibility)
Option C: Preferred option - Mixed model with service providers + accountable grants (chosen for scalability, private sector leverage, and adaptive capacity)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed model was selected to balance scalability (via service providers), private sector engagement (critical for mobilizing £2bn in investment), and adaptive flexibility (via grants for policy work). It builds on Phase 1’s success (£1bn leveraged, 1:10 ratio) while addressing gaps (smallholder inclusion, Congo Basin capacity).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (proven 1:10 leverage ratio in Phase 1)
partner capacity (service providers with forest/agriculture expertise)
equity (targeted support for smallholders and Congo Basin)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on private sector partners may dilute development impact in favor of commercial interests.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Accountable grants to non-profits for policy and inclusion work; clear additionality criteria for Upper Middle-Income Countries.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conflict or political instability in target regions (e.g., Congo Basin) could disrupt delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Conflict-sensitive approaches, regional strategies, and minimal dependency on state-led reforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market volatility (e.g., commodity prices, climate shocks) may affect private sector engagement.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified portfolio across regions/commodities; adaptive management to respond to shocks.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (scaling proven Phase 1 models with 320%+ target overachievement)
equity (targeted components for smallholders and Congo Basin)

quote.alternatives: "Option A: Direct FCDO management... Option B: Single large contractor... Option C: Preferred option - Mixed model with service providers + grants" (D0003948.odt, Annex E: Delivery options appraisal)
quote.rationale: "The programme will provide the key focus, building on a strong UK comparative advantage established through a successful first phase of the programme, and scaling-up this support to help secure the COP26 legacy." (D0003948.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
quote.vfm: "Based on conservative modelling we have projected a strong benefit-cost ratio and a low donor cost per tonne (£6/tCO2e), offering good value for money compared to the wider ICF portfolio." (D0003948.odt, Executive Summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Congo Basin’s weak private sector and fragile governance limit the use of Phase 1’s business incubation model, requiring a new Component 3 focused on building enabling conditions. Conflict risks in regions like DRC necessitate conflict-sensitive partners with regional expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: Congo Basin: Underdeveloped markets require capacity-building partners instead of direct incubation (Component 3).
Smallholders: Need for scalable, efficient delivery models to reach millions of farmers (Component 2).
FCAS contexts: Partners must have conflict-sensitive experience and regional networks.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to mobilize £2bn in private investment drives the use of service providers with commercial expertise (Component 1), while policy influence objectives require direct grants to non-profits (Component 4). Smallholder inclusion (Component 2) necessitates partnerships with organizations experienced in agricultural extension.
q28_linkages: Private investment goal → Service provider contracts for business incubation (Component 1).
Smallholder focus → Grants to partners with agricultural extension capacity (Component 2).
Congo Basin challenges → Specialized capacity-building component (Component 3).
Policy influence → Direct grants to non-profits for convening (Component 4).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (scaling via service providers) with equity (targeted smallholder/Congo Basin components). Trade-offs include higher transaction costs for inclusive delivery (e.g., smallholder partnerships) vs. the speed of private sector-led models.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Service providers enable rapid scaling, but smallholder components require slower, relationship-based delivery.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led technical assistance vs. local partner capacity-building in the Congo Basin.
Cost vs. reach: Higher costs for conflict-sensitive approaches in FCAS regions vs. lower-cost operations in stable countries.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Moderate’ risk rating drives milestone-based oversight and adaptive management structures, with intensive monitoring in FCAS contexts (e.g., Congo Basin) and lighter-touch oversight in stable regions (e.g., Southeast Asia).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak private sector capacity in the Congo Basin shifts the role of partners from direct incubation (Phase 1) to capacity-building (Phase 2, Component 3). Smallholder components require partners with agricultural extension experience, shaping grant allocations.

quote.where_who: "The Phase 1 approach focused on business incubation did not get sufficient uptake in the Congo Basin, due to underlying weaknesses in the private sector. This component will address this lesson through a strengthened focus on interventions to build the enabling conditions." (D0003948.odt, Component 3)
quote.what_how: "Component 1: technical assistance facility and business incubation (£101.5m) ... Component 2: support for smallholder farmers (£45.5m) ... Component 3: Business and market development in ‘thin’ markets (of the Congo Basin) (£31.5m)." (D0003948.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.tradeoffs: "Engaging the private sector and mobilising private investment will be key to meeting the scale of these challenges. The programme will provide the key focus, building on a strong UK comparative advantage... and scaling-up this support to help secure the COP26 legacy." (D0003948.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
quote.risk_management: "In the fragile contexts where some programme components operate, there is a risk that conflict could affect programme delivery. Conflict-sensitive approaches to design and delivery will be deployed." (D0003948.odt, Risk management)

key_programme_risks: Geopolitical challenges diluting climate/nature ambition.
Commodity market volatility affecting private sector engagement.
Conflict disrupting delivery in FCAS regions (e.g., Congo Basin).
Climate shocks (fires, droughts) accelerating deforestation.
Weak land governance undermining interventions.
Smallholder adoption of sustainable practices at scale.
Private sector prioritizing profits over development impacts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Ministerial and official-level engagement to maintain climate ambition; narrative focused on short-term opportunities with long-term benefits.
Diversified portfolio across regions/commodities; adaptive management to respond to shocks.
Conflict-sensitive approaches; regional strategies; minimal dependency on state-led reforms.
Focus on resilience-building (e.g., fire management, drought-resistant crops); adaptive monitoring.
Support for securing community land rights; multi-stakeholder dialogues.
Strategic partnerships with agricultural extension organizations; incentives for sustainable practices.
Clear additionality criteria; accountable grants for policy/inclusion work.

fcas_specific_lessons: Use regional approaches to mitigate conflict risks (e.g., Congo Basin).
Avoid over-reliance on state-led reforms in fragile contexts.
Build private sector capacity as a prerequisite for business incubation (lesson from Phase 1 failure in Congo Basin).
Integrate political economy and conflict analysis into programme design.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 (2015-23) demonstrated the effectiveness of business incubation (£1bn leveraged, 1:10 ratio) but identified gaps in smallholder inclusion and Congo Basin engagement. Key lessons: (1) Smallholders require targeted support to participate in sustainable transitions; (2) Underdeveloped markets (e.g., Congo Basin) need capacity-building before incubation; (3) Policy engagement is critical to scaling impact.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 2 adds two new components: (1) Enhanced support for smallholder farmers (£45.5m); (2) Business and market development in the Congo Basin (£31.5m). These address Phase 1’s gaps by focusing on inclusion and capacity-building in underdeveloped markets.

quote.risks: "Based on the outlook at this point in the programme cycle, there is a risk that government and corporate ambition on climate and nature will be diluted by geopolitical challenges, food and commodity market volatility." (D0003948.odt, Risk management)
quote.mitigations: "This risk will be mitigated by Ministerial and official-level engagement to maintain climate ambition; and a programme narrative and action focused on opportunities to take beneficial short-term measures which set a course towards addressing long-term challenges." (D0003948.odt, Risk management)
quote.lessons: "Phase 1 has exceeded expectations in all three of its outcome areas: leveraging £1bn of additional finance (485% of its target), bringing over 4m hectares of land under sustainable management (336% of its target) and reaching over 250,000 people (320% of its target)." (D0003948.odt, Background)
quote.design_changes: "Phase 2 will include two new components, helping smallholder farmers in the transition to sustainable land use; and developing private sector capacity to support sustainable economic development in underdeveloped markets, such as the Congo Basin." (D0003948.odt, Introduction)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize £2bn in private investment (a 1:4 leverage ratio on the £500m ODA), building on Phase 1’s 1:10 ratio (£140m ODA leveraged £1bn private investment).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £500m, (2023-33)" (D0003948.odt, SummarySheet)
quote.leverage: "These interventions are expected to mobilise an estimated £2bn in private investment." (D0003948.odt, Executive Summary)
quote.phase1: "Investments in Forests and Sustainable Land Use Phase 1 (IFSLU1, £140m 2015-2023) has to date mobilised over £1bn of private investment (at a leverage ratio of 1:10)." (D0003948.odt, Introduction)
