metadata.programme_name: UK core contribution to United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) 2021-2026

quote.text: This programme is to fund the UK’s assessed core contribution to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) for the next 5 years (2021-2026).

metadata.duration_source: This programme is to fund the UK’s assessed core contribution to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) for the next 5 years (2021-2026).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme funds the UK’s assessed core contribution to the UNCCD, which is a legally binding international agreement focused on combating desertification and land degradation. The contribution supports the Secretariat’s core functions, including advocacy, policy development, and evidence-building, rather than direct implementation or research.
what_objectives.q1_source: The UK core contribution will be used to support the Secretariat with its key function to service the Sessions of the COP and subsidiary bodies in a manner that enables well-founded decision-making and successful action in advancing the implementation of the UNCCD. This will include advocacy, support for the development of policy frameworks and evidence building.
q3_expected_outputs: The proportion of global land that is degraded is at most 20% and reducing

Global ODA flows are on average £500m per annum for projects focused on land degradation (marked principal for the desertification/land degradation marker) and £4,000m per annum for projects that deliver land degradation co-benefits (marked significant)
At least 82% of performance indicators for gender equality are met or exceeded
110 countries have set Land Degradation Neutrality targets
16 UNCCD supported projects have secured funding from international funds and are being implemented
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to support the UNCCD Secretariat’s core functions to combat desertification and land degradation, aligning with the UK’s international priorities on climate change and biodiversity. It focuses on advocacy, policy frameworks, and evidence-building to achieve Land Degradation Neutrality by 2030.

quote.text: The UNCCD is the sole legally binding international agreement on combatting desertification and land degradation. The UK is one of 197 Parties to the Convention, committed to working together towards the long-term goal of a future that avoids, minimizes, and reverses desertification/land degradation and mitigates the effects of drought.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a global context with risks related to the UNCCD’s ability to deliver on its mandate, but these risks are mitigated by the UN’s strong reporting systems and the shared responsibility among 197 Parties. The overall risk rating is classified as 'minor' in the document.
where_context.q5_source: The overall programme risk rating: Minor.
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The UNCCD operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (e.g., Sahel), where projects may fail due to challenging environments. Land degradation is exacerbated by climate change, and data limitations affect monitoring and evaluation.

quote.text: UNCCD supports and partners with implementing bodies that operate in challenging contexts, including fragile, conflict-affected states (e.g., the Great Green Wall Initiative in the Sahel). In these areas where projects can fail and safeguarding and fiduciary risks are high and therefore projects carry a higher reputational risk.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) Secretariat
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UNCCD Secretariat, based in Bonn, Germany, manages the programme, with decision-making power resting with the Conference of the Parties (COP), where all 197 Member States (including the UK) have voting rights. The UK, as a donor, influences priorities but does not directly control implementation.
q10_capacity_building_details: support for the development of policy frameworks
evidence-building
gender-responsive policies and guidelines
training and tools for gender considerations in land degradation neutrality projects

partner_organizations.name: UNCCD Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and manager of core functions (advocacy, policy, evidence-building)

partner_organizations.name: Global Mechanism (GM)
partner_organizations.role: Subsidiary body assisting countries in mobilizing financial resources for UNCCD implementation

partner_organizations.name: IUCN and UN Women
partner_organizations.role: Partners assisting countries in designing gender-responsive land degradation neutrality projects

quote.text: The Secretariat’s key function is to support Parties, the sessions of the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies. This includes several tasks ranging from the preparation of documents to making the logistical arrangements. It aims to do this in a manner that enables well-founded decision-making and successful action in advancing the implementation of the UNCCD.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides an assessed core contribution to the UNCCD, which is a mandatory payment based on the UN scale of assessment. This funding supports the Secretariat’s operational costs, including staffing, advocacy, and policy development, rather than specific projects.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The UNCCD Secretariat manages the programme, with oversight from the Conference of the Parties (COP), which meets biennially to set policy, strategy, and budget. The UK engages with the Secretariat through the FCDO’s Climate & Environment Directorate.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UNCCD is the sole legally binding international agreement on desertification and land degradation. As a Party to the Convention, the UK is obligated to pay its assessed contribution to maintain membership and influence.

quote.text: As a Party to the Convention, the UK is expected to pay its annual assessed contribution. Late or non-payment would leave the UK in arrears.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the supreme governing body of the UNCCD, meeting every two years to set policy, strategy, and budget. The Secretariat supports the COP and its subsidiary bodies, including the Global Mechanism and the Evaluation Office.

quote.text: The UNCCD’s supreme governing body is the COP, which meets every two years. This meeting covers policy, strategy for the organisation and sets the overall budget level. In addition, it authorises any new areas of work.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to the UNCCD’s core budget, which is determined biennially by the COP. The UK can scrutinize the budget but has limited ability to reallocate funds unilaterally.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The UK can influence UNCCD priorities through its engagement in the COP and by advocating for specific issues (e.g., gender equality, climate-biodiversity linkages). However, major shifts require consensus among all 197 Parties.

quote.text: The UK will ensure that the UNCCD Secretariat continues to focus on achieving the results in the strategic framework and modulating them according to their resources.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNCCD Secretariat (no further sub-awards mentioned)

quote.text: The UK is invoiced by the Secretariat in November with a request for payment by 1 January for that calendar year. Cash payments covered by this business case span the period 2022-2026.

q24_alternatives_considered: Decide not to pay the assessed contribution (Option 1)
Continue to pay the annual assessed core contributions for the next 5 years (Option 2)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (continuing to pay) was chosen to maintain the UK’s membership in the UNCCD, avoid reputational damage, and leverage the Convention as a key entry point for tackling land degradation, climate change, and biodiversity loss. The UNCCD is uniquely positioned to address these issues globally, and non-payment would undermine the UK’s leadership on international environmental initiatives, including COP26 commitments.
q25_decision_factors: strategic alignment with UK priorities (climate, biodiversity, COP26)
partner capacity (UNCCD’s role as a global convenor)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UNCCD is insufficiently ambitious or unrealistic in its contribution to halting and reversing land degradation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UK will ensure the UNCCD Secretariat focuses on achieving results in the strategic framework and strengthens links with UNFCCC and CBD.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UNCCD staff and financial resources are insufficient to run the Secretariat effectively
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UK will scrutinize budgets to ensure adequate resources are provided.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks associated with procurement leads
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The UNCCD presents independently audited financial accounts to the COP every 2 years, and the UK will ensure standards and processes are upheld.

quote.text: Option 2 would mean that the UK continues to pay its annual assessed core contributions to the UNCCD. This option is the only option that allows the UK, as one of the 197 Parties, to work collectively with others, to drive the global agenda on land degradation and desertification, with the UNCCD proving to be an effective entry point to tackling this issue as well as the contribution of land to climate change and biodiversity.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope of the UNCCD (operating in 197 countries, including fragile states) necessitates a multilateral delivery structure, as no single country or organization could effectively address land degradation at this scale. The UNCCD’s mandate and membership base constrain partner selection to its Secretariat and subsidiary bodies.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for a legally binding global agreement to address land degradation
Operational challenges in fragile and conflict-affected states (e.g., Sahel)
Requirement for consensus among 197 Parties for major decisions
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objective to combat desertification and land degradation globally requires a multilateral mechanism (UNCCD) with a centralized Secretariat. The need for policy influence, advocacy, and evidence-building (rather than direct implementation) shapes the choice of core funding to the Secretariat.
q28_linkages: Global mandate → multilateral delivery structure
Policy influence objective → core funding for Secretariat
Need for coordination among 197 Parties → centralized governance (COP)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document highlights tensions between the need for inclusive global participation (equity) and the efficiency of a centralized Secretariat. For example, the UNCCD’s Gender Action Plan and efforts to support vulnerable countries (e.g., through the Great Green Wall) are balanced against the administrative efficiency of channeling funds through a single multilateral body.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusive global membership (197 Parties) vs. decision-making efficiency
Support for vulnerable countries (e.g., Sahel) vs. administrative overhead of a multilateral Secretariat
Gender equality targets vs. limited resources for monitoring and implementation
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., reputational risks in fragile states) justifies annual reviews and light-touch oversight, with escalation to FCDO leadership only if risks exceed appetite. The shared risk among 197 Parties reduces the need for intensive UK-specific management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The UNCCD’s capacity-building efforts (e.g., gender-responsive policies, support for Land Degradation Neutrality targets) shape the roles of Southern partners, who are expected to participate in planning and decision-making but rely on the Secretariat for technical and financial support.

quote.text: The UNCCD commits all partners to account for gender-responsive policies, ensuring full participation of both men and women in planning and decision-making. The UNCCD also has a Gender Action Plan and a series of guidelines and tools with gender considerations embedded.

key_programme_risks: UNCCD is insufficiently ambitious or unrealistic in halting and reversing land degradation
UNCCD staff and financial resources are insufficient to run the Secretariat effectively
Fiduciary risks associated with procurement leads
UNCCD-supported projects fail in challenging contexts (e.g., fragile states)
Reputational risk to the UK if UNCCD underperforms or if the UK falls into arrears

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNCCD is insufficiently ambitious or unrealistic in halting and reversing land degradation
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK will ensure the Secretariat focuses on the strategic framework and strengthens links with UNFCCC and CBD. The UK will advocate for a higher profile for land degradation issues.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNCCD staff and financial resources are insufficient to run the Secretariat effectively
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK will scrutinize budgets to ensure adequate resources and push for cost savings where possible.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fiduciary risks associated with procurement leads
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UNCCD presents independently audited financial accounts to the COP every 2 years. The UK will ensure UN standards and processes are upheld.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNCCD-supported projects fail in challenging contexts
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK will ensure the UNCCD maintains up-to-date risk, safeguarding, and mitigation processes, including partner due diligence.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk to the UK if UNCCD underperforms or if the UK falls into arrears
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK will continue to pay its assessed contributions to maintain membership and influence. The shared risk among 197 Parties reduces individual reputational exposure.

fcas_specific_lessons: Projects in fragile states (e.g., Sahel) require robust safeguarding and fiduciary controls due to higher risks of failure.
The UNCCD’s Great Green Wall Initiative highlights the need for adaptive management in conflict-affected areas.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Programme Completion Report for 2012-2020 noted that the UNCCD was largely successful but recommended more quantitative targets to assess progress. The UNCCD has improved gender equality performance (from 47% to 82% on UN-SWAP indicators) but needs to sustain this progress.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The UK will push for clearer quantitative targets in the UNCCD’s strategic framework and monitor gender equality performance more closely.

quote.text: Annual review programme scores for 2012-2020 were A and we would expect this to continue for the next five years. A key recommendation from the Programme Completion Report for this period was clear that more quantitative targets were needed to better assess progress.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UNCCD contributes to mobilizing substantial resources for land degradation projects, including the Great Green Wall Initiative and the Land Degradation Neutrality Fund. However, the UK’s core contribution does not directly leverage additional funds.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget supports revenue expenditures (staffing, advocacy, policy development) rather than capital investments.

quote.text: The UK contribution of £1,583,000 will cover five years of annual payments to the UNCCD covering financial years 2021/22-2025/26 to support the core functions of the UNCCD Secretariat and Subsidiary Bodies.

metadata.programme_name: Peace and Stability in Mozambique (PS) Programme
metadata.quote: "This programme will promote peace and stability through initiatives to prevent the spread of violent extremism and foster peacebuilding in Cabo Delgado and Northern Mozambique, and to consolidate the peace process in Central Mozambique." (D0004974.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Programme start and end date: 23/11/2021-31/03/2026" (D0005304.odt, Part1–ForMAG&HMT)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening community resilience, security/justice sector professionalism), policy influence (supporting peace process implementation), and service delivery (pilot initiatives for conflict management). It also includes implementation research through monitoring/evaluation frameworks.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will promote peace and stability through initiatives to prevent the spread of violent extremism and foster peacebuilding in Cabo Delgado and Northern Mozambique, and to consolidate the peace process in Central Mozambique. [...] We will pilot initiatives with strong monitoring, evaluation and learning frameworks – successful efforts will be scaled up through influencing programmes and public policies." (D0004974.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Empowerment and resilience of groups/communities at risk of violent radicalisation (Output 1)
Improved professionalism of security and justice sectors (Output 2)
Improved capacity for conflict management and coordination (Output 3)
Support for DDR of former RENAMO combatants (Output 4)
Technical support for Mozambique’s CVE/CTE strategy (new in addendum)
Country-based staff member in Cabo Delgado for on-the-ground insight (new in addendum)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to prevent violent extremism and consolidate peace in Mozambique through community resilience, security sector reform, and support to the Maputo Peace Accords implementation, with a focus on Northern and Central Mozambique.
what_objectives.quote: "The aim of this programme is to promote peace and stability in Mozambique through initiatives to prevent the spread of violent extremism and foster peacebuilding in Cabo Delgado and Northern Mozambique, and to consolidate the peace process in Central Mozambique." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM TO BUSINESS CASE)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique is described as one of the poorest, climate-vulnerable, and most fragile countries, with ongoing insurgency in Cabo Delgado, historical conflict in Central Mozambique, and weak state capacity. The programme's risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate' but the context clearly meets FCAS criteria.
where_context.q5_source: "Mozambique remains one of the poorest, climate-vulnerable and most fragile countries in the world – and conflict and violence have greatly undermined development efforts." (D0004974.odt, Section A) and "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004974.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The insurgency in Cabo Delgado has displaced nearly 1 million people, killed over 4,000, and disrupted LNG investments. Weak governance, historical marginalization, and climate vulnerability exacerbate tensions. Security constraints limit access to conflict zones, requiring adaptive delivery mechanisms.
where_context.quote: "Since this attack, violence in Cabo Delgado has escalated dramatically. [...] insurgents have carried out over 850 attacks across the province. [...] There are currently around 800,000 internally displaced people living in resettlement camps." (D0004974.odt, Section 1.3) and "The existing delivery components do not offer the degree of agility that is required to maximise support for Mozambique’s peace and stability objectives." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains approval authority for all new activities, with implementation partners (including Southern organizations) requiring sign-off from the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) or Development Director for expenditures. The addendum introduces more Southern-focused roles (e.g., country-based staff in Cabo Delgado) but decision-making remains with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for security/justice actors on human rights-compliant approaches
support to government-led conflict management mechanisms
technical advice for GoM on CVE/CTE strategy (via Deployable Civilian Experts)
mentorship through embedded country-based staff in Cabo Delgado

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation support for Peace Process Secretariat (Outcome 2)

partner_organizations.name: TAG (Technical Assistance Group) - commercial contractor
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Outcome 1 (preventing radicalisation, peacebuilding)

partner_organizations.name: Peace Process Secretariat (PPS)
partner_organizations.role: Operationalisation of Maputo Peace Accords activities

partner_organizations.name: Deployable Civilian Experts (DCE)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support to GoM on CVE/CTE strategy (new in addendum)

partner_organizations.name: Country-based staff (Cabo Delgado)
partner_organizations.role: On-the-ground insight and coordination (new in addendum)

who_partners.quote: "Outcome 2 – Memorandum of Understanding with United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS)" (D0004974.odt, Section C) and "It is proposed a total of up to £420k will be assigned to additional activity delivered by new delivery mechanisms [...] Deployable Civilian Expert support to GoM in development and implementation of their CVE/CTE strategy." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a contract with a commercial service provider (TAG) for Outcome 1, a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with UNOPS for Outcome 2, and the addendum introduces direct contracting (e.g., Deployable Civilian Experts) and potential accountable grants to NGOs/CSOs or framework drawdowns.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Originally structured as two parallel delivery routes (one per outcome), the addendum introduces a third, more flexible mechanism for tailored support. FCDO retains oversight, with approvals required for new activities. The structure combines commercial contracts, multilateral MOUs, and direct FCDO-managed interventions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TAG was selected via competitive tender (implied by 'contract with service provider' and commercial case), while UNOPS was chosen via MOU likely due to its existing role in the peace process. New mechanisms (e.g., DCE) are directly awarded by FCDO for agility. The addendum explicitly rejects developing a new business case due to "administrative burden and time."
how_mechanism.quote: "1. Outcome 1 – Contract with service provider" (D0004974.odt, Section C) and "Preferred Option: Expand delivery routes – this was the preferred option as this option will support greater agility in responding to the changing dynamics of the conflict (within an existing Business Case) enabling HMG to identify more fit for purpose delivery mechanisms to achieve the identified outcomes." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen by a Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and the FCDO Maputo Development Director, with new activities requiring their approval. The Peace Process Secretariat (PPS) and UNOPS have defined roles for Outcome 2, while TAG manages Outcome 1. The addendum introduces case-by-case sign-off for flexible mechanisms.
how_governance.quote: "Each submission will set out the VfM case for intervention, the rationale for proposed delivery mechanism and risk management approach." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM) and "The DCE will be overseen by the SRO of this programme and performance monitored through standard management procedures." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The addendum allows reallocation of up to £420k between outcomes/pillars with SRO approval, noting "there could be minor re-allocations between outcome pillars during implementation." The original structure was rigid (fixed contracts/MOUs), but the addendum introduces adaptive mechanisms.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The addendum explicitly broadens Outcome 2 to include Mozambique’s regional/global peacemaker role and introduces new delivery mechanisms (e.g., DCE, country-based staff) to respond to evolving needs. Adjustments require SRO/Director approval and VfM justification.
how_flexibility.quote: "This business case addendum proposes a change to outcome 2, broadening the outcome to respond to changing regional and global security dynamics." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM) and "Activity approved within this business case addendum includes Deployable Civilian Expert support to GoM in development and implementation of their CVE/CTE strategy." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (TAG/UNOPS/DCE). The addendum reduces layers for new mechanisms (e.g., direct DCE contracts).
how_efficiency.quote: "The full ToRs outline reports and products that will be delivered following each visit to Maputo." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM) and budget tables in D0005304.odt/D0005676.odt showing phased spend.

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing – rejected as "not feasible given the current restrictive nature of delivery of the current programme"
Develop new business case – rejected due to "administrative burden and time involved"
Expand delivery routes (preferred) – chosen for agility and responsiveness
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The expanded delivery routes were selected to "support greater agility in responding to the changing dynamics of the conflict" and to enable "more fit for purpose delivery mechanisms" without the time/cost of a new business case. The original rigid structure (fixed contracts/MOUs) was deemed insufficiently responsive.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Administrative burden of managing multiple delivery mechanisms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Modest additional administration for programme management team; case-by-case approvals with VfM justification.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential duplication or fragmentation with existing partners (TAG/UNOPS)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear segregation of roles (e.g., DCE for technical advice, country-based staff for coordination) and SRO oversight.

why_rationale.quote: "Preferred Option: Expand delivery routes – this was the preferred option as this option will support greater agility in responding to the changing dynamics of the conflict (within an existing Business Case) enabling HMG to identify more fit for purpose delivery mechanisms to achieve the identified outcomes." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Cabo Delgado (insurgency, displacement, weak governance) limits partner options to those with existing in-country presence (e.g., UNOPS) or specialized security clearance (e.g., DCE). Local capacity constraints necessitate Northern-led technical support (e.g., CVE/CTE strategy advice).
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict partner access to conflict zones, favoring multilateral/UN partners.
Weak local institutions require external technical assistance (e.g., DCE for GoM).
Political sensitivity of peace process limits partner selection to neutral actors (e.g., UNOPS).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both immediate stabilisation (e.g., community resilience pilots) and long-term peacebuilding (e.g., DDR support) requires a mixed delivery structure: commercial contracts for flexible pilots, MOUs for multilateral coordination, and direct FCDO mechanisms for adaptive technical support.
q28_linkages: Piloting (Output 1) → Commercial contract (TAG) for agility.
Peace process (Output 2) → UNOPS MOU for legitimacy/coordination.
Adaptive needs (addendum) → Direct FCDO mechanisms (DCE, country-based staff) for responsiveness.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (e.g., DCE, TAG) with Southern ownership (e.g., Peace Process Secretariat, country-based staff). The addendum introduces more Southern-focused roles but retains FCDO approval authority, reflecting a tension between local relevance and donor control.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct DCE contracts enable rapid technical support but bypass local partner selection.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led CVE/CTE advice (DCE) vs. Southern-led implementation (PPS).
Cost vs. reach: Commercial contracts (TAG) for efficiency vs. UNOPS MOU for broader coordination.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk rating and FCAS context justify intensive oversight (SRO approvals, milestone-based payments) and adaptive mechanisms (e.g., country-based staff for real-time insight).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak local capacity in Cabo Delgado necessitates embedded roles (country-based staff) and technical assistance (DCE), while stronger institutions in Central Mozambique (e.g., Peace Process Secretariat) enable more direct support.
intersections.quote: "The existing delivery components do not offer the degree of agility that is required to maximise support for Mozambique’s peace and stability objectives. Adding a third delivery mechanism which can be tailored will enable more impactful and sensitive support." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

key_programme_risks: Escalation of insurgency in Cabo Delgado disrupting implementation.
Delayed DDR process in Central Mozambique risking renewed conflict.
Weak coordination between military, humanitarian, and development actors.
Limited state capacity to absorb technical support (e.g., CVE/CTE strategy).
Potential overlap/duplication with other donor initiatives.
Security risks to personnel (e.g., country-based staff in Cabo Delgado).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible delivery mechanisms (e.g., reallocatable funds, country-based staff) and close coordination with military/humanitarian actors.
Direct support to Peace Process Secretariat and UNOPS for implementation oversight.
Participation in Development Coordination Platform (DCP) and International Community Crisis Taskforce (ICCT).
Deployable Civilian Experts for targeted technical assistance and mentorship.
Travel Risk Authorisation from Senior Risk Owners and adherence to FCDO amber-zone protocols.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Mozambique’s civil war highlight the need to address both local grievances and ideological drivers of conflict.
Historical marginalization of Northern regions requires decentralized, community-centered approaches.
Coordination between military, humanitarian, and development actors is critical in FCAS (triple nexus approach).
Flexible funding is essential to respond to evolving conflict dynamics (e.g., insurgency spread to Nampula/Niassa).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from the Rome Peace Accords (1992), which succeeded through dialogue and DDR but failed to address underlying inequalities, leading to Renamo’s resurgence. Current efforts emphasize inclusive political processes and socio-economic inclusion to avoid past mistakes.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addendum introduces adaptive delivery mechanisms (e.g., DCE, country-based staff) and broadens Outcome 2 to include regional peacemaker roles, reflecting lessons on the need for agility and broader conflict prevention.
risks_lessons.quote: "The historiography around the origins of the civil war is growing, but there remains much debate about the relative weight of internal and external factors. [...] The conflict did come to an end through dialogue and negotiation – with promises of a more inclusive political settlement." (D0004974.odt, Section 1.1) and "The existing delivery components do not offer the degree of agility that is required to maximise support for Mozambique’s peace and stability objectives." (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM)

financial_details.quote: "Original project budget: £5m" (D0005676.odt, ADDENDUM) and budget tables in D0005304.odt/D0005676.odt showing allocations by outcome/pillar: Outcome 1 (£3.98m), Outcome 2 (£0.6m), new mechanisms (£0.42m).

metadata.programme_name: Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience Programme (HARP)
metadata.quote: "HARP is FCDO’s Humanitarian and Resilience Programme in Nigeria. HARP reduces mortality and increases resilience for people with the most severe humanitarian needs by (i) addressing food insecurity and malnutrition and (ii) protecting vulnerable people from harm." (D0006690.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 01/10/2022-31/03/2025", "New project end date (if applicable): 30/09/2027" (D0006690.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: HARP is a humanitarian programme designed to deliver life-saving assistance (food security, nutrition, and protection) directly to vulnerable populations affected by conflict in Nigeria. It combines immediate humanitarian response with resilience-building activities to address severe needs in fragile contexts.
what_objectives.q1_source: "HARP reduces mortality and increases resilience for people with the most severe humanitarian needs by (i) addressing food insecurity and malnutrition and (ii) protecting vulnerable people from harm." (D0006690.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: 160,000 people receiving food assistance
500,000 children screened for acute malnutrition monthly
66,000 children admitted for severe acute malnutrition treatment
40,000 women and girls targeted/reached with GBV services
what_objectives.summary: HARP delivers life-saving humanitarian assistance (food, nutrition, protection) while building resilience in conflict-affected regions of Nigeria, with explicit targets for food assistance, malnutrition treatment, and GBV services.
what_objectives.quote: "Overall targets for this extension period are likely to be in line with the results demonstrated in the first two years of HARP, with indicative figures as follows: Number of people receiving food assistance: 160,000; Number of children screened for acute malnutrition monthly: 500,000; Number of children admitted for severe acute malnutrition treatment: 66,000; Number of women and girls targeted/reached with GBV services: 40,000" (D0006690.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa, Yobe) and North-West Nigeria (Zamfara, Sokoto, Katsina), regions characterized by violent conflict, displacement, and extreme humanitarian needs. The context includes active armed groups, severe food insecurity, and protection risks.
where_context.q5_source: "The complex interaction between displacement, rising food insecurity and violence across the North has resulted in rising humanitarian needs outside the Non-International Armed Conflict in the North-East." (D0006690.odt, Humanitarian Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit humanitarian access (e.g., 85% of Borno State is inaccessible due to armed groups), while weak state capacity and climate shocks (droughts, flooding) exacerbate food insecurity. Data limitations and infrastructure gaps (e.g., non-functional health facilities) hinder service delivery.
where_context.quote: "Activities of NSAGs. 85% of Borno State’s territory and much of eastern Yobe have been inaccessible to humanitarian agencies since September 2019, due to the presence of NSAGs, who openly target humanitarian workers and refuse them access into areas under their control." (D0001348.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO Nigeria retains strategic oversight and decision-making authority, while local NGOs and state governments are engaged as downstream partners for implementation. The programme emphasizes a 'localisation-first' approach but ultimate accountability lies with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for local NGOs
institutional strengthening of state government systems
mentorship through downstream partnerships
technical support for cash transfer programmes

partner_organizations.name: UN Agencies (WFP, UNICEF, UNOCHA, ICRC)
partner_organizations.role: implementation of food security, nutrition, protection, and rapid response activities

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs (INGOs)
partner_organizations.role: service delivery in food security, nutrition, and protection

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs (Nigeria-based)
partner_organizations.role: downstream implementation, particularly in North-West expansion

partner_organizations.name: State Governments (Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Zamfara, Sokoto, Katsina)
partner_organizations.role: coordination and integration of humanitarian services

who_partners.quote: "The major implementation decisions in the original HARP business case will stand, including the use of multi-year Memoranda of Understanding to engage UN agencies and ICRC and Accountable Grants to engage INGOs." (D0006690.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: HARP uses **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** for UN agencies and the Red Cross, and **Accountable Grants (AGs)** for INGOs. MoUs provide multi-year funding with flexibility, while AGs enable direct engagement with NGOs under FCDO terms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO Nigeria manages a portfolio of partners (UN, INGOs, local NGOs) through separate agreements (MoUs/AGs), with coordination mechanisms (e.g., Humanitarian Country Team) but no formal consortium. Partners operate semi-autonomously under FCDO’s strategic oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **existing performance** under previous programmes (e.g., NENTAD) and **comparative advantage** in humanitarian response. The addendum extends agreements with high-performing partners without re-competition.
how_mechanism.quote: "The major implementation decisions in the original HARP business case will stand, including the use of multi-year Memoranda of Understanding to engage UN agencies and ICRC and Accountable Grants to engage INGOs, with appropriate break clauses to take into account Spending Review timings. New agreements with existing partners will be managed from available allocations." (D0006690.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.quote: "FCDO will ensure that all selected partners (existing and new) have robust policies, procedures and monitoring systems to manage aid diversion risks and suspected cases." (D0001348.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between sectors (food security, nutrition, protection) and geographies (North-East to North-West) without business case amendments, provided thresholds are met. The programme retains 20% flexibility for North-West expansion.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: HARP includes **rapid response mechanisms** and **real-time monitoring** to adjust to emerging needs (e.g., climatic shocks, displacement spikes). Major shifts (e.g., regional spillover) require business case amendments.
how_flexibility.quote: "HARP can respond to the first three scenarios without a business case amendment... However, the last three may require a business case amendment due to the implications of a significant increase in the scale of humanitarian need." (D0001348.odt, Strategic Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UN/INGOs) → Local NGOs/State Governments (for North-West expansion)

q24_alternatives_considered: Focus on food security only (1 sector)
Integrated food security and nutrition (2 sectors)
Focus on all 12 humanitarian sectors
Standalone cross-cutting activities (AAP, cash, gender, localisation)
Mainstreamed cross-cutting activities
Implement through 1-2 UN/Red Cross MoUs
Implement through Nigeria Humanitarian Pooled Fund (NHF) alone
Directly fund local NGOs through Accountable Grants
Blended approach (MoU/AG with UN, INGOs, Red Cross)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **blended approach** (MoUs for UN/Red Cross + AGs for INGOs) was selected to **balance scale, flexibility, and oversight**. MoUs leverage UN’s operational reach, while AGs enable targeted engagement with INGOs and local actors. This aligns with FCDO’s **risk appetite** and **technical capacity** to manage multiple partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in high-risk environments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust due diligence assessments (DDAs) and compliance checks on partners to ensure adherence to Terrorism Act 2000 and Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overstretch of FCDO management capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritizing fewer strategic sectors (food security, nutrition, protection) and using multi-year agreements to reduce administrative burden.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited humanitarian access in insecure areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investing in real-time security monitoring, air transportation (UNHAS), and advocacy for negotiated access.

why_rationale.quote: "We have appraised three key areas (‘dimensions’) in order to reach a recommendation on what HARP focuses on and how HARP is delivered... Scores for each dimension range from (1) Very low, (2) Low, (3) Medium, (4) High, (5) Very high, accompanied by brief justifications. The highest scoring dimensions will best achieve HARP’s objectives." (D0001348.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with **proven security protocols, local acceptance, and operational presence in inaccessible areas**. For example, 85% of Borno State is controlled by armed groups, restricting partners to those with negotiated access (e.g., ICRC, UNHAS).
q27_constraints_detail: Armed group restrictions on humanitarian access (e.g., NSAG-controlled territories)
Government policies limiting IDP camp support (e.g., Borno State’s camp closure policy)
Security risks requiring air transportation (UNHAS) for staff movement
Weak state capacity necessitating reliance on international partners for service delivery
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rapid, large-scale service delivery** in a high-risk environment drives the **blended funding structure** (MoUs + AGs). Direct service sectors (food, nutrition, protection) require **UN/INGO scale**, while **localisation** and **flexibility** necessitate downstream partnerships with local NGOs.
q28_linkages: Service delivery objectives → MoUs with UN for scale and AGs with INGOs for targeted interventions
Resilience-building goals → Downstream partnerships with local NGOs/state governments
FCAS context → Emphasis on security-vetted partners and real-time monitoring
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between **inclusive partnerships** (localisation, gender equality) and **rapid delivery** (reliance on international actors). For example, while local NGOs are prioritized for North-West expansion, UN/INGOs remain central due to their **operational capacity** in high-risk areas.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: International partners enable rapid scale but may sideline local actors.
Expertise vs. ownership: UN/INGOs provide technical expertise, but local NGOs offer contextual knowledge.
Cost vs. reach: Cash transfers are cost-effective but require financial infrastructure lacking in some areas.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** (extreme insecurity, aid diversion risks) justifies **intensive oversight** (e.g., embedded TPM, real-time monitoring) and **restricted partner selection** (security-vetted organizations only).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building for local NGOs is **embedded** in downstream partnerships to enable their gradual takeover of service delivery, particularly in the North-West expansion. This includes training, mentorship, and institutional strengthening.
intersections.quote: "HARP’s focus on improving localisation will (i) strengthen humanitarian access by community-based organisations; (ii) increase the sustainability of interventions as local actors will remain in the area long-term; (iii) increase participation of and accountability to the locally affected population." (D0001348.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Inaccessibility due to armed group control (85% of Borno State)
Aid diversion in high-corruption environments
Secondary displacement from premature IDP camp closures
Food price volatility exacerbating malnutrition
Protection risks (GBV, explosive ordnance) in displacement settings
Limited state capacity to absorb humanitarian transitions
Donor fatigue and underfunding of humanitarian appeals

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Invest in UNHAS for air transportation, real-time security monitoring, and advocacy for negotiated access.
Conduct regular due diligence assessments (DDAs) and enforce compliance with anti-terrorism financing laws.
Monitor returns to ensure safety and service availability; advocate for phased, voluntary returns.
Scale up cash transfers and market monitoring to adjust assistance packages.
Fund GBV prevention programmes, risk education, and safe shelter provision.

fcas_specific_lessons: Humanitarian response must shift from ‘access-led’ to ‘needs-led’ to avoid excluding marginalized groups (e.g., people with disabilities, elderly).
Localisation reduces exclusion risks but requires investment in local NGO capacity.
Real-time data collection is critical for adaptive programming in dynamic conflicts.
Cash transfers can build resilience but require market assessments to avoid inflationary effects.
Coordinated advocacy with Nigerian government is needed to improve humanitarian access.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from NENTAD (2017–2022) include: (1) **Flexibility** is critical to respond to evolving crises; (2) **Localisation** improves sustainability but requires long-term support; (3) **Protection mainstreaming** must be explicit in all sectors; (4) **Cash transfers** are more effective than in-kind aid but need market support; (5) **Humanitarian access** requires both negotiation and technical solutions (e.g., air transport).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: HARP’s design incorporates: (1) **Rapid response mechanisms** for unanticipated shocks; (2) **Localisation targets** (e.g., 20% North-West expansion via local NGOs); (3) **Enhanced protection monitoring** (e.g., GBV, explosive ordnance); (4) **Climate-sensitive programming** (e.g., solar-powered water systems); (5) **Stronger referral networks** between sectors.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lesson 1: Humanitarian needs will continue for some time – so focus on building people’s resilience against current and future shocks and crises wherever possible... Lesson 4: HARP must be flexible and adaptable to keep pace with rapidly changing contexts in Nigeria’s North-East and other regions." (D0001348.odt, Lessons Learned)

financial_details.quote: "This Business Case addendum is a time and cost extension, proposing to continue the programme for two further years, providing up to an additional £41.9m. The new total value of the programme (2022–2027) will be £191.9m (RDEL only)." (D0006690.odt, Summary Information)

metadata.programme_name: Mozambique Humanitarian Response Programme (MHRP)
metadata.quote: "The Mozambique Humanitarian Response Programme (MHRP) was approved in 2022, to provide life saving assistance for those affected by conflict and by climate disasters." (D0004773.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: February 2022 – May 2025" and "New project end date (if applicable): May 2027" (D0004773.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The MHRP combines direct service delivery (emergency shelter, food security, protection) with system strengthening (coordination, preparedness, local capacity building). It aims to reduce suffering for conflict- and disaster-affected communities while improving the humanitarian response system's effectiveness.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The MHRP provides direct delivery of assistance to those in need and helps strengthen humanitarian systems for more effective response." (D0004773.odt, Summary Information)
q3_expected_outputs: 250,000 people reached with humanitarian assistance (direct and indirect)
100,000 people receiving emergency shelter following displacement/disaster
1,200 families receiving more resilient housing
30,000 people benefiting from mental health support
30,000 people receiving birth certificates, IDs, and legal assistance
10% of overall humanitarian caseload receiving emergency assistance through OCHA pooled fund
15 local organizations mentored through capacity building
400 households benefiting from housing upgrades
400 latrines constructed in IDP sites/host communities
At least 40,000 people receiving emergency shelter and non-food items annually
Support for vulnerability-based targeting covering all of Cabo Delgado
Strengthened anticipatory action for drought and cyclone-affected areas
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers life-saving humanitarian assistance while strengthening systems for better coordination, preparedness, and local response capacity. It balances direct service delivery with investments in the enabling environment.
what_objectives.quote: "The extension gives the UK a larger footprint in the humanitarian sector than it currently has, though our overall contribution will still only be the equivalent of 3.6% of overall needs. The uplift will also result in better links with conflict, diplomacy and other development outcomes for the BHC, through increasing life saving response that result in less people falling further into need, by working towards durable solutions, and supporting the localisation agenda." (D0004773.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique faces ongoing conflict in Cabo Delgado, climate disasters (cyclones, droughts), weak institutions, and high vulnerability to shocks. The programme operates in areas with active conflict, displacement, and limited humanitarian access.
where_context.q5_source: "Mozambique is the third most vulnerable country in Africa to disaster risks and the frequency and intensity of climate emergencies it faces are increasing due to the global climate crisis." (D0001506.odt, Double vulnerability from increasing climate events) and "The overall risk profile for the programme moves from moderate to high, due to the shift to more direct delivery in a complex operating environment with constrained access, ongoing population movements, and the reality of large-scale climate disasters." (D0004773.odt, Risk Profile)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit access to conflict zones; weak infrastructure hampers service delivery; regulatory hurdles delay programme implementation; political economy factors affect coordination; climate risks exacerbate vulnerability; data limitations hinder targeting. For example: "High levels of insecurity in parts of the north have led to those most in need of ten not being able to receive assistance for months at a time during 2021." (D0001506.odt, Humanitarian access constraints increase vulnerability)
where_context.quote: "Humanitarian access in Mozambique has been ranked as ‘High Constraints’ by ACAPS in the 2022 Humanitarian Access Overview. This is based on access of people to aid, and access of organizations to those in need, as well as physical and security constraints." (D0001506.odt, Humanitarian access constraints increase vulnerability)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority through the Country Board and Development Director approval processes, while implementing partners (UN agencies and INGOs) manage day-to-day delivery. Local organizations receive capacity building but have limited direct decision-making power in the current structure.
q10_capacity_building_details: mentoring for local organizations on humanitarian response
small-scale funding for local emergency response
support for local organizations to become eligible for OCHA pooled fund
PSEA training and safeguarding capacity building
support for localisation through funding and technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
partner_organizations.role: Shelter cluster lead, emergency shelter provision, camp management, local capacity building

partner_organizations.name: Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)
partner_organizations.role: Protection interventions, civic documentation, legal assistance

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Food security, vulnerability-based targeting, anticipatory action

partner_organizations.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
partner_organizations.role: Emergency pooled fund management, coordination support

partner_organizations.name: International NGO Safety Organization (INSO)
partner_organizations.role: Security analysis and training for humanitarian actors

partner_organizations.name: Local organizations (up to 20)
partner_organizations.role: Mentored for capacity building, potential emergency response implementers

who_partners.quote: "The UK will ensure that at least 40% of funding is directly for local organisations [through the Country-Based Pooled Fund]." (D0001506.odt, Localisation of humanitarian action) and "A multi-donor effort will see IOM setting up a mechanism to build the capacity of local actors, with close mentoring in all aspects of design, implementation, and monitoring of interventions." (D0004773.odt, New workstreams)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses Accountable Grants with UN agencies and INGOs (multi-year agreements), framework agreements for monitoring, and potential contributions to pooled funds (OCHA-managed). The Internal Risk Facility allows for rapid scale-up through shorter-term grants and MOUs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages a portfolio of agreements with multiple partners (IOM, NRC, WFP, OCHA, INSO) through Accountable Grants and framework agreements. Partners operate semi-autonomously within agreed results frameworks, with FCDO providing oversight through quarterly reviews and a dedicated programme team.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Existing partners were selected based on strong track records during the first two years of implementation (all received 'A' scores in Annual Reviews) and their established presence in Mozambique. New partners like OCHA were added for specific functions (pooled fund management) based on their global mandate and experience.
how_mechanism.quote: "Forthe cost extension, the approach is to continue with existing partners, given their strong track record and progress on achieving outcomes under the MHRP." (D0004773.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "OCHA will be the only new partner at this stage, due to the mandate on delivery the emergency pooled funds and based on experiences of their implementation in other contexts." (D0004773.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: For the local capacity building fund managed by IOM, sub-awards to local organizations will be decided through a mentoring process with set milestones. The OCHA pooled fund will use standard allocation processes defined by the Humanitarian Coordinator.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: Decision-making rests with the British High Commission's Country Board and Development Director. The programme team (Team Leader, Humanitarian Advisor, Programme Officer) provides day-to-day oversight but partners manage implementation. For the Internal Risk Facility, the Country Board approves usage (or Development Director for urgent cases).
how_governance.quote: "The team has established strong relations with all existing partners, through regular monitoring visits, quarterly meetings, and in decision-making forums." (D0004773.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "Decisions on use of IRF will be approved through the Country Board when time allows, or if urgent by the Development Director." (D0004773.odt, Internal Risk Facility)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The Internal Risk Facility (10% of total budget) allows rapid reallocation between components. Funds can be shifted between partners/activities based on emerging needs (e.g., new displacements, climate disasters) with Country Board approval. The programme is designed to adapt to "pendular" population movements and changing conflict dynamics.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach with: 1) Quarterly reviews to adjust priorities; 2) Internal Risk Facility for rapid response; 3) Flexibility to shift between direct delivery and system strengthening based on context; 4) Annual logframe updates with partners. Major shifts require Country Board approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "The time and cost extension will provide... flexibility of funding, allowing partners to scale up rapidly following a disaster or large-scale displacement, as well as ensuring preparedness activities in advance of disasters based on good practice." (D0004773.odt, Objective) and "The IRF allows for rapid scale up of different components based on new or deteriorating humanitarian and disasters... This allows the MHRP to pivot to meet new/emerging UK priorities." (D0004773.odt, Internal Risk Facility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (IOM/NRC/WFP/OCHA) → [for some activities] Local Organizations
how_efficiency.quote: "The team has established strong relations with all existing partners, through regular monitoring visits, quarterly meetings, and in decision-making forums. All existing partners have been assessed as having the expertise and the absorption capacity for the scale up of funding." (D0004773.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Multilateral delivery (all funding through UN agencies)
Larger number of INGOs bidding annually
Limited partnerships in set sectors
Commercial delivery through contracting modality
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed partnership model was chosen to balance: 1) **Value for Money**: Existing partners (IOM, NRC, WFP) had proven track records (Annual Review scores of 'A') and established systems; 2) **Flexibility**: Allows rapid scale-up through known entities while adding new partners (OCHA) for specific functions; 3) **Localisation**: Direct relationships with INGOs enable better capacity building of local actors than pure multilateral approaches; 4) **Risk Mitigation**: Existing partnerships reduce due diligence burdens in a high-risk environment; 5) **System Strengthening**: Combines direct delivery with investments in coordination (OCHA fund) and preparedness.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a small number of international partners may limit local ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building component for local organizations (£2.7m) and requirement that 40% of OCHA pooled fund goes to local actors

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination between multiple partners could reduce efficiency
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated programme team (Humanitarian Advisor, Programme Officer) for oversight and quarterly review meetings

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Direct delivery in conflict zones increases security and fraud risks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Third-party monitoring (£750k), PSEA safeguarding measures, and INSO security analysis support

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Pooled fund may not reach most vulnerable if UN coordination is weak
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK contribution (10%) comes with advocacy for prioritization of underfunded sectors and hard-to-reach areas

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 (Limited number of targeted grants) would mean response sectors would be more limited, but with the ability to scale up as needs expand. Specific partnerships would be defined based on UK priorities, and the smaller number of organizations would allow for more effective programme management and advisory input." (D0001506.odt, Options Appraisal) and "The cost extension will allow the British High Commission (BHC) to increase focus on the conflict-affected province of Cabo Delgado through more direct humanitarian assistance, and in line with the BHC Country Business Plan." (D0004773.odt, Objective)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) Established security protocols (e.g., INSO for security analysis); 2) Existing presence in Mozambique (to navigate regulatory hurdles); 3) Capacity to operate in conflict zones (e.g., IOM's shelter pipeline); 4) Ability to manage fraud/safeguarding risks in high-risk environments. Local organizations are included but require capacity building due to limited experience with large-scale humanitarian response.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict zones require partners with security expertise (e.g., INSO)
Regulatory delays favor partners already registered in Mozambique
Weak local capacity necessitates international partners for direct delivery
Climate risks require partners with prepositioning capabilities (e.g., IOM shelter pipeline)
Protection concerns limit partner options to those with robust PSEA systems
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (direct delivery + system strengthening) require a hybrid structure: 1) **Direct delivery** → Accountable Grants with operational partners (IOM, NRC, WFP); 2) **System strengthening** → OCHA pooled fund and capacity building components; 3) **Flexibility needs** → Internal Risk Facility for rapid response; 4) **Localisation goals** → Mentoring component and 40% local allocation in pooled fund.
q28_linkages: Direct service delivery (shelter, protection) → requires operational partners with logistics capacity (IOM, NRC)
System strengthening (coordination, preparedness) → requires UN leadership (OCHA, WFP)
Localisation objectives → requires capacity building mechanisms and local partner inclusion
Adaptive management needs → requires flexible instruments (IRF, multi-year grants)
Climate preparedness → requires partners with anticipatory action experience (WFP)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions discussed include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid response through international partners vs. slower local capacity building; 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern INGOs/UN agencies have delivery capacity but limit local leadership; 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Direct implementation by internationals is more expensive but enables faster scale-up in emergencies; 4) **Targeting precision vs. administrative burden**: Vulnerability-based targeting improves equity but requires more data collection.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: International partners enable rapid scale-up but may sideline local actors
Pooled funds improve coordination but add administrative layers
Vulnerability targeting improves equity but slows initial response
Capacity building takes time but is essential for sustainable response
Direct delivery in conflict zones increases costs but is necessary for access
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context increases management intensity through: 1) Quarterly (vs annual) reviews; 2) Third-party monitoring for inaccessible areas; 3) Embedded safeguarding advisors; 4) Strict financial controls (break clauses, MAG approvals); 5) IRF governance requiring Country Board approval. "The overall risk profile for the programme moves from moderate to high, due to the shift to more direct delivery in a complex operating environment with constrained access, ongoing population movements, and the reality of large-scale climate disasters." (D0004773.odt, Risk Profile)
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building determines partner roles in three ways: 1) **Local organizations** start as mentees but can become direct implementers for small-scale responses; 2) **International partners** (IOM, NRC) lead direct delivery while building local capacity; 3) **Progress milestones** (e.g., PSEA training completion) gatekeep access to funding. For example: "A multi-donor effort will see IOM setting up a mechanism to build the capacity of local actors, with close mentoring in all aspects of design, implementation, and monitoring of interventions... the capacity building will also result in more local organisation becoming eligible to be partners of the OCHA fund once set milestones have been reached." (D0004773.odt, New workstreams)
intersections.quote: "The current context in northern Mozambique, with changing access based on fighting and displacement, has highlighted the need for more investment in, and engagement with, local civil societies, who are able to operate more efficiently as first responders in a difficult operating environment." (D0001506.odt, Localisation of humanitarian action) and "The cost extension will allow the UK to have better assurance from third party monitoring of the changing context and of UK funding in areas that we cannot access directly." (D0004773.odt, Expected Results)

key_programme_risks: Continued conflict and insecurity in Cabo Delgado
Climate disasters (cyclones, droughts) exceeding response capacity
Weak humanitarian coordination limiting effectiveness
Fraud and safeguarding risks in high-risk operating environment
Local capacity constraints hindering localisation
Government restrictions on humanitarian access
Funding gaps leaving critical needs unmet
Protection risks for vulnerable groups (women, children, disabled)
Economic shocks (e.g., Ukraine war) increasing food prices
Political sensitivity around LNG investments affecting operations

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: INSO security analysis, flexible IRF funding, pendular movement planning
Prepositioned shelter stocks (15% earmarked for climate), anticipatory action with WFP, IRF reserve
OCHA pooled fund contribution, HCT engagement, UK seat on Good Humanitarian Donorship forum
Third-party monitoring, PSEA coordinator, enhanced due diligence, hotline systems
£2.7m local capacity building fund, mentoring, 40% pooled fund allocation to locals
Security analysis sharing, advocacy with government, remote management protocols
IRF for scale-up, advocacy for burden sharing, prioritization of underfunded sectors
PSEA networks, birth certification support, GBV specialized services, safeguarding advisors
Vulnerability-based targeting, market monitoring, flexible food security programming
Clear separation from LNG investments, principled humanitarian messaging, conflict sensitivity training

fcas_specific_lessons: Local actors are critical first responders but need capacity support to scale up
Prepositioning stocks is essential given unreliable supply chains in conflict zones
Vulnerability targeting must adapt to pendular population movements
Protection mainstreaming requires dedicated resources (e.g., PSEA coordinators)
Humanitarian access requires continuous negotiation with both state and non-state actors
Climate and conflict risks must be addressed simultaneously (e.g., shelter stocks for both)
Localisation requires long-term investment beyond single projects
Coordinated advocacy is needed to address government restrictions on aid
Flexible funding mechanisms (like IRF) are critical for FCAS contexts
Safeguarding systems must be context-adapted (e.g., community-based reporting)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The first two years showed that: 1) International partners could deliver at scale but local capacity building was insufficient; 2) Prepositioning was effective but stocks were depleted by multiple disasters; 3) Vulnerability targeting improved equity but required more data; 4) Coordination gaps persisted despite UN leadership; 5) Protection risks (especially GBV) were underestimated. The 2023 Annual Review recommended more direct delivery, better returns-area support, and improved monitoring.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Based on lessons, the cost extension: 1) Increased direct delivery components; 2) Added housing/land/property support for returns; 3) Expanded local capacity building fund; 4) Added dedicated monitoring component; 5) Increased prepositioning allocations; 6) Added anticipatory action for drought; 7) Strengthened PSEA safeguarding measures; 8) Included HLP interventions for durable solutions.
risks_lessons.quote: "The past two Annual Reviews have received scores of ‘A’, based on the output of the partners, strong delivery and the contribution to the enabling environment. The 2023 Annual Review recommended shift to more direct delivery, some shifting towards support in returns area, and better monitoring of outputs." (D0004773.odt, Approach to Implementation) and "The other area needing strengthening is wider coordination with government and its efforts to coordination around the PRCD (Cabo Delgado reconstruction Plan) and the wider reconstruction effort for the north." (D0001506.odt, Humanitarian Coordination and Leadership needs strengthening)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK's contribution to the OCHA pooled fund (£3.6m) is expected to leverage additional donor contributions (Germany, Ireland, and others committed). The local capacity building fund will be multi-donor with US and Ireland already expressing commitment. The programme's coordination role helps mobilize broader humanitarian funding.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both revenue spending (e.g., food assistance, protection services) and capital investments (e.g., prepositioned shelter stocks, latrine construction). Approximately 15% of the uplift (£3.3m) is classified as CDEL for strategic stockpiles and emergency supplies.
financial_details.quote: "The UK will ensure that at least 40% of funding is directly for local organisations [through the Country-Based Pooled Fund]." (D0001506.odt, Localisation of humanitarian action) and "Ofthe total uplift, around 15% will be CDEL, contributing to BHC’s overall CDEL allocation of £13.3m for 2024/25." (D0004773.odt, Finance) and "The UK, along with at least three other donors, has expressed interest in the establishment of the CBPF as means of contributing to priority gaps in the humanitarian sector, strengthening UN coordination and leadership, and supporting localised response." (D0001506.odt, Strengthened leadership and coordination)

metadata.programme_name: Indo-Pacific Humanitarian Mechanism (IPHM)
metadata.quote: "The Indo-Pacific Humanitarian Mechanism (IPHM) will strengthen the UK’s agility to prepare and deliver rapid assistance to the most vulnerable, crisis-affected populations in a region that is increasingly vulnerable to climate and other shocks." (D0006634.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The IPHM is a financing mechanism designed to channel funds rapidly for humanitarian response while also building regional preparedness partnerships. It combines a response component (rapid deployment of assistance) with a preparedness component (strengthening regional coordination and capabilities).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Indo-Pacific Humanitarian Mechanism (IPHM) will strengthen the UK’s agility to prepare and deliver rapid assistance to the most vulnerable, crisis-affected populations in a region that is increasingly vulnerable to climate and other shocks. It will do this by channelling funds to pre-agreed capabilities, arrangements and partners. It will also build regional and bilateral partnerships to enhance disaster preparedness and reinforce UK response through stronger coordination, grounding and influence in the region." (D0006634.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Rapid response to major shocks (e.g., over 1,000 fatalities and 100,000 affected people)
Immediate deployment of UK emergency medical and search and rescue teams
Funding for UN, Red Cross & Crescent Societies, and NGOs to provide humanitarian assistance (shelter, food, cash, WASH, health, protection)
Provision of core relief items (CRIs) such as family tents, shelter kits, hygiene kits, blankets, and solar lights
Support for smaller-scale disasters in vulnerable countries (e.g., Pacific)
Strengthened regional partnerships (e.g., with Partners in the Blue Pacific, ASEAN’s AHACentre)
Enhanced bilateral humanitarian partnerships (e.g., with India, Australia)
Mutual learning and capacity building in disaster risk finance, risk modelling, and forecasting
Training for national search and rescue or medical teams
Support for anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., in the Philippines, Fiji)
Reduced bureaucratic burden on posts by avoiding separate business cases for each crisis
what_objectives.summary: The IPHM aims to deliver rapid humanitarian response and build regional preparedness in the Indo-Pacific, focusing on climate and disaster resilience. It combines a financing mechanism for quick deployment of assistance with partnerships to strengthen regional coordination and capabilities.
what_objectives.quote: "The IPHM establishes the vehicle for channelling regional and central funds and accompanying protocols and arrangements for how and with whom a response could be made. Planning in advance would enable rapid response to major shocks (e.g. over 1,000 fatalities and 100,000 affected people)." (D0006634.odt, Objective 1: Deliver rapid response)

countries_regions: Pacific Island Countries (e.g., Kiribati, Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Fiji, Papua New Guinea)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The Indo-Pacific region faces compounding humanitarian risks from climate shocks (typhoons, cyclones, droughts, heat extremes), economic shocks, conflict (Myanmar, potential Taiwan/South China Sea tensions), and natural disasters (earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions). Five of the top ten countries most affected by weather extremes globally are in this region, and food insecurity is high. The document explicitly states the overall programme risk rating as "Major."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0006634.odt, Growing vulnerability to climate and other risks) AND "Climate and economic shocks, conflict, epidemics, earthquakes, volcanos, tsunamis and landslides are the main drivers of humanitarian risk in the Indo-Pacific. Some occur simultaneously, compounding impacts. The region includes five out of the ten top countries most affected by weather extremes globally..." (D0006634.odt, Growing vulnerability to climate and other risks)
q6_contextual_constraints: logistical challenges (e.g., remote islands in the Pacific)
limited local response capacity in some countries
variable government capacity to manage crises
displacement and protection issues (e.g., GBV, trafficking)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate risks and conflicts create compounding humanitarian needs, while logistical challenges (e.g., accessing remote Pacific islands) and variable government capacities affect the speed and effectiveness of response. Geopolitical competition (e.g., in the Pacific and South Asia) influences how humanitarian assistance is coordinated and perceived.
where_context.quote: "The region includes five out of the ten top countries most affected by weather extremes globally... There is increasing risk of drought... heat extremes... and deadly winters... The region contains major urban areas that are particularly vulnerable to earthquakes... It also has live conflicts (Myanmar), frozen conflicts (DPRK) and potential conflicts (Taiwan and the South China Sea)." (D0006634.odt, Growing vulnerability to climate and other risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains decision-making authority over fund allocation, response activation, and partner selection, with regional posts and partners playing implementation roles. The mechanism is designed to reinforce "the primacy of posts and regional teams in owning relationships, risk, preparedness and delivery," but central FCDO capacities (e.g., HMFD) provide support and oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: training national search and rescue or medical teams
disaster risk finance and risk modelling support
mutual learning on humanitarian and disaster risk finance
strengthening preparedness planning and measures
support for anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., in Fiji, Vanuatu, Solomon Islands)
enhancing regional partnerships (e.g., with ASEAN’s AHACentre, Partners in the Blue Pacific)

partner_organizations.name: UN Agencies (e.g., WFP, UNICEF, OCHA, IOM, UNFPA, UNHCR)
partner_organizations.role: Humanitarian response delivery (food, WASH, health, protection, shelter, logistics, coordination)

partner_organizations.name: Red Cross & Red Crescent Societies (IFRC, national societies)
partner_organizations.role: Disaster response, CRIs distribution, capacity building

partner_organizations.name: NGOs (local and international)
partner_organizations.role: Sector-specific response (e.g., shelter, protection, cash assistance), localisation

partner_organizations.name: Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)
partner_organizations.role: Reciprocal arrangement for CRIs deployment in the Pacific; joint humanitarian partnership

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance (AHA Centre)
partner_organizations.role: Regional coordination and preparedness

partner_organizations.name: Partners in the Blue Pacific (e.g., Pacific Community/SPC)
partner_organizations.role: Pacific humanitarian warehousing and CRI stockpiles

partner_organizations.name: UK Ministry of Defence (MOD)
partner_organizations.role: Logistics, medical teams, reconnaissance (in extremis)

partner_organizations.name: UK International Search and Rescue (UKISAR) and UK Emergency Medical Team (UKEMT)
partner_organizations.role: Rapid deployment for life-saving support

partner_organizations.name: Humanitarian-to-Humanitarian Network (H2H)
partner_organizations.role: Specialist services (e.g., mapping, data analysis)

partner_organizations.name: Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC)
partner_organizations.role: Public appeals and matched funding for NGO responses

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Catastrophe Risk Insurance Company (PCRIC)
partner_organizations.role: Disaster risk finance

partner_organizations.name: Governments in the Indo-Pacific (e.g., India, Pacific Island Countries)
partner_organizations.role: Bilateral humanitarian partnerships, joint exercises, and dialogue

who_partners.quote: "The mechanism has two objectives: 1) Deliver rapid response to the most vulnerable, crisis-affected populations in the Indo-Pacific by channelling funds to pre-agreed capabilities, arrangements and partners... 2) Build preparedness partnerships both regionally and bilaterally to enhance readiness and reinforce UK response through stronger coordination, grounding and influence in the region." (D0006634.odt, Objective 2: Build preparedness partnerships)
