how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The IPHM serves as a conduit for channelling both regional FCDO funds and central funds (e.g., from the Humanitarian Crisis Reserve) to pre-agreed partners for rapid response. It operates through pre-agreed protocols and partnerships, including reciprocal arrangements (e.g., with DFAT for CRIs) and direct funding to UN agencies, Red Cross, and NGOs. The mechanism does not hold a standing budget but enables rapid fund flows when activated.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The IPHM acts as a regional platform to coordinate and channel funds from FCDO (regional and central) to a range of pre-identified partners (UN, Red Cross, NGOs, UK deployable capabilities). It is managed by FCDO’s Indo-Pacific Regional Directorate (IPRD) in collaboration with the Humanitarian, Migration and Food Security Directorate (HMFD), with posts and regional teams leading relationships and delivery.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are pre-agreed based on their existing capacities, regional presence, and past performance. This avoids the inefficiency of developing new business cases for each crisis and ensures rapid deployment. The selection is informed by preparedness planning exercises and consultations with posts, OCHA, and other donors.
how_mechanism.quote: "The IPHM establishes the vehicle for channelling regional and central funds and accompanying protocols and arrangements for how and with whom a response could be made... Setting up the IPHM will avoid delays, offer more predictable and coordinated response, and reduce the burden on posts by not requiring separate programmes." (D0006634.odt, Objective 1: Deliver rapid response) AND "There are a range of delivery partners that could be drawn on for response to match the specific needs of each situation. This includes the UK’s own capabilities... as well as direct funding of UN agencies, Red Cross/Crescent societies and NGOs." (D0006634.odt, Deliverypartners and capacities)

how_governance.quote: "Posts in the region are keen to increase the UK’s response capability and reduce the bureaucratic burden by having a regional mechanism that can channel both regional and central funds to deliver at pace in times of need. This reinforces the principle of the primacy of posts and regional teams in owning relationships, risk, preparedness and delivery, with central humanitarian response capabilities playing a role to support, challenge and fill gaps in geographic capacities in the immediate 2-4 weeks of a response." (D0006634.odt, Indo-Pacific Humanitarian Mechanism) AND "For all this support, including a ‘no regrets’ response through HMFD using the HCR, funds will need to be channelled through a regional or country specific business case, in this case the IPHM." (D0006634.odt, Decision making criteria to determine whether to respond and with which funds)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between response and preparedness components, but this requires approval through FCDO’s existing processes (e.g., consultation between geographic directorates and the Director-General’s Office). The mechanism is designed to blend regional and central funds (e.g., HCR) as needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The IPHM allows for phased responses (e.g., initial ‘no regrets’ actions followed by scaled-up support) and can adapt to emerging needs based on real-time assessments. However, significant changes (e.g., sectoral shifts or new partners) would require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.quote: "UK responses could be made in phases. This could include, for example, an immediate ‘no regrets’ response and then a further uplift in support when a more comprehensive assessment has taken place... Depending on the level and source of funds, a submission to the geographic director, D-G or ministers will be made to seek approval for the response." (D0006634.odt, Decision making criteria to determine whether to respond and with which funds)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UN/Red Cross/NGOs/UK capabilities). The IPHM reduces layers by pre-agreeing partners and protocols, avoiding the need for separate business cases per crisis.
how_efficiency.quote: "The IPHM will reduce this burden but, most importantly, place the UK in a heightened level of readiness through pre-agreed protocols and partnerships that can trigger to respond rapidly to the rising number of major shocks." (D0006634.odt, Indo-Pacific Humanitarian Mechanism) AND "Programme Value: Up to £35m" (D0006634.odt, Summary Sheet)

q24_alternatives_considered: Maintaining the status quo (developing a new business case for each crisis)
Developing a mechanism solely for response (without a preparedness component)
Creating a response mechanism AND supporting regional preparedness (chosen option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed response-and-preparedness mechanism was selected to address inefficiencies in the status quo (e.g., bureaucratic delays, disincentives for small-scale responses) while reinforcing the UK’s bilateral response through stronger regional grounding and partnerships. The pre-agreed protocols and partners enable rapid deployment, and the preparedness component aligns with the Prime Minister’s priority to rebuild the UK’s reputation in international development through genuine partnerships with the Global South.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (reducing bureaucratic burden and delays)
risk mitigation (pre-agreed partners and protocols for rapid response)
speed (enabling timely assistance in critical windows)
partner capacity (leveraging existing regional and global humanitarian actors)
strategic alignment (supporting UK priorities in the Indo-Pacific)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in partner mobilization due to pre-agreed arrangements not covering all contexts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular updates to partner matrices and response plans, with contingency options for unanticipated needs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on central FCDO capacities (e.g., HMFD) for initial response, limiting regional ownership
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Design reinforces "primacy of posts and regional teams" in delivery, with central support limited to the first 2-4 weeks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funding shortages if regional budgets are exhausted before HCR approvals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Blending of regional and HCR funds through the IPHM, with phased response options.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited localisation if pre-agreed partners are predominantly international actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit focus on including local NGOs (e.g., through PIANGO in the Pacific) and women-led organisations, with due diligence streamlined for existing post partners.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (reducing transaction costs via pre-agreed protocols)
effectiveness (targeting critical gaps and most vulnerable populations)
equity (inclusion principles for marginalised groups, e.g., women, people with disabilities)
why_rationale.quote: "The status quo was rejected as it would be inefficient, a disincentive for responding to smaller scale crises and slower, as potential partners would not be pre-identified. The third option was recommended and approved as it includes both a response component, which would allow rapid response and reduce the burden on posts, and support preparedness, so reinforcing our bilateral response through a stronger grounding and network in the region." (D0006634.odt, Summary) AND "This will support the delivery of the Foreign Secretary’s and ministers’ priorities to ensure a rapid and agile UK and international humanitarian system... The preparedness component will reinforce the Prime Minister’s priority to rebuild Britain’s reputation on international development with a new approach based on genuine respect and partnership with the global South." (D0006634.odt, Strategic fit and rationale for UK intervention)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Indo-Pacific’s geographic diversity (e.g., remote Pacific islands, urban earthquake risks in South Asia) and variable government capacities constrain partner selection. For example, UKISAR deployment may not be feasible in the Pacific due to distances, so the mechanism relies on DFAT’s regional stockpiles and local partners. In conflict-affected areas (e.g., Myanmar), partner choices are limited to agencies with access (e.g., ICRC).
q27_constraints_detail: Logistical challenges in the Pacific favour local/regional partners (e.g., DFAT, SPC) over UK-deployed teams.
Conflict contexts (e.g., Myanmar) restrict partnerships to neutral actors (e.g., Red Cross).

Variable government response capacities require tailored partnerships (e.g., direct support in vulnerable Pacific islands vs. auxiliary roles in countries with strong systems like Australia or Japan).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid response (Objective 1) drives the pre-agreed protocols, partner matrices, and reciprocal arrangements (e.g., DFAT for CRIs), while the preparedness objective (Objective 2) shapes the focus on regional partnerships (e.g., AHA Centre, Partners in the Blue Pacific) and capacity building (e.g., anticipatory action frameworks).
q28_linkages: Rapid response needs → Pre-agreed partners and ‘no regrets’ checklists for immediate deployment.
Preparedness goals → Regional partnerships (e.g., ASEAN, Pacific Community) and mutual learning initiatives.
Inclusion principles → Requirements for partners to address marginalised groups (e.g., women, people with disabilities) in delivery.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses balancing rapid response (efficiency) with inclusive delivery (equity). For example, while pre-agreed partners enable speed, the mechanism includes principles to ensure assistance reaches marginalised groups (e.g., women, people with disabilities, ethnic minorities). The use of cash transfers is highlighted as both efficient (where markets function) and equitable (empowering beneficiaries to prioritise needs).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Pre-agreed partners enable rapid response but require explicit inclusion principles to avoid excluding vulnerable groups.
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership: UK deployable capabilities (e.g., UKISAR) are balanced with local/regional partnerships (e.g., DFAT CRIs, Pacific Community).
Cost vs. reach: Cash transfers are prioritised where markets function, but in-kind assistance (e.g., CRIs) is used in remote areas with limited markets.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The "Major" risk rating drives intensive oversight for initial responses (e.g., HMFD support in the first 2-4 weeks) and the need for pre-agreed protocols to mitigate delays. High climate and conflict risks justify the focus on anticipatory action and regional coordination.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building (e.g., training for national search and rescue teams, disaster risk finance) is embedded to strengthen local partners’ roles in response. For example, the Pacific Humanitarian Warehousing initiative aims to enhance Pacific governments’ ability to manage CRI stockpiles, shifting their role from recipients to managers.
intersections.quote: "The capacity to manage crises by countries in the region is variable... There is a third set of countries that are particularly vulnerable, such as in the Pacific, that regularly call for international assistance." (D0006634.odt, Growing vulnerability to climate and other risks) AND "In the design and delivery of assistance, close attention will be given to the approach taken by partners, making sure that it reflects the voices, needs, experiences, and aspirations of affected populations, in particular marginalised people including women and girls, and civil society, including women-led organisations." (D0006634.odt, Sectors and approaches)

key_programme_risks: Increasing frequency and intensity of climate shocks (e.g., cyclones, droughts, heat extremes) outpacing regional resilience efforts.
Geopolitical competition (e.g., in the Pacific, South China Sea) affecting humanitarian coordination.
Limited local response capacity in vulnerable countries (e.g., Pacific Island States) requiring sustained international support.
Protection risks (e.g., GBV, trafficking) escalating during disasters, particularly in displacement settings.
Delays in fund mobilization if regional budgets are exhausted before HCR approvals.
Over-reliance on a small number of pre-agreed partners limiting localisation and innovation.
Logistical constraints (e.g., accessing remote islands) hindering timely assistance.
Government restrictions on international assistance (e.g., Myanmar, DPRK).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in response due to bureaucratic processes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IPHM’s pre-agreed protocols and partners reduce the need for new business cases per crisis, enabling rapid activation. ‘No regrets’ checklists allow immediate life-saving actions (e.g., UKISAR deployment) before full assessments.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited local capacity in vulnerable countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Preparedness component funds regional partnerships (e.g., Partners in the Blue Pacific, AHA Centre) and capacity building (e.g., training for national response teams, anticipatory action frameworks).
Inclusion principles and safeguarding measures are embedded in partner agreements, with a focus on GBV prevention, child protection, and support for women-led organisations.
Support for disaster risk finance (e.g., PCRIC, Global Shield) and anticipatory action pilots (e.g., in Fiji, Philippines) to reduce acute impacts.
Engagement through neutral platforms (e.g., ASEAN’s AHA Centre) and bilateral dialogues (e.g., with India, Australia) to maintain humanitarian space.

fcas_specific_lessons: In conflict-affected areas (e.g., Myanmar), neutral actors (e.g., ICRC) are essential for access, but require robust safeguarding due to high protection risks.
In FCAS, anticipatory action and cash transfers can mitigate shocks without exacerbating tensions, but require context-specific design (e.g., avoiding exclusion of ethnic/religious groups).
Lessons from Myanmar and the Rohingya crisis highlight the need for flexible funding to address both rapid-onset disasters and protracted displacement.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past UK responses (e.g., Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines, Nepal earthquake, Cyclone Yagi in Vietnam) demonstrated the value of pre-positioned stockpiles (e.g., DFAT’s CRIs in Brisbane) and phased responses. The inefficiency of developing separate business cases for each crisis (e.g., Pacific cyclones) led to the IPHM’s design. The reciprocal arrangement with DFAT, piloted in 2023/24 (e.g., PNG landslide, Vanuatu cyclones), proved effective for rapid CRI deployment.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The IPHM integrates lessons by: 1) Pre-agreeing partners and protocols to avoid delays; 2) Including a preparedness component to address gaps in local capacity; 3) Embedding inclusion principles to mitigate protection risks; 4) Using phased responses (e.g., ‘no regrets’ actions followed by scaled-up support) to balance speed and adaptability.
risks_lessons.quote: "The concept note for this business case assessed different options for how the Indo-Pacific Region and its three Directorates could support preparedness and response... The status quo was rejected as it would be inefficient, a disincentive for responding to smaller scale crises and slower, as potential partners would not be pre-identified." (D0006634.odt, Summary) AND "There is a growing body of evidence on the value for money of early action and pre-agreed response options and arrangements... The IPHM will quickly respond to new crises across the region by reducing the need to develop a new business case and determine the appropriate partners for each humanitarian intervention." (D0006634.odt, Theory of change)

co_funding_partners.partner: Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)
Partners in the Blue Pacific (e.g., France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, US)
Global humanitarian funds (CERF, DREF, Start Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The IPHM leverages existing global funds (e.g., CERF, DREF) and regional mechanisms (e.g., DFAT’s CRI stockpiles, Pacific Catastrophe Risk Insurance Company) to amplify the UK’s response capacity. The reciprocal arrangement with DFAT allows shared use of warehouses and logistics, reducing duplication.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: Up to £35m" (D0006634.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "The UK has made a commitment to contribute up to £400,000 over two years [to the Pacific Humanitarian Warehousing initiative], which will be provided for the purchase of CRIs through the DFAT-UK reciprocal mechanism..." (D0006634.odt, Preparedness component)

metadata.programme_name: Essential Services for Maternal and Child Health programme in DRC [Services Essentiels de Santé Maternelle et Infantile en RDC (SEMI)]

quote.text: This programme will focus on improving health outcomes for 1.6 million women, girls and children and on ending preventable deaths in Kasai, one of the poorest provinces in DRC, with the highest maternal mortality rate in the country.

duration_source.text:
AMP Start Date: April 2022
AMPEnd Date: March 2025

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of maternal, child health, nutrition, and family planning services) with health systems strengthening (improving governance, health information systems, and community engagement). It also includes capacity building for health personnel and policy engagement with the Government of DRC.

q1_source.text:
It two-pronged approach, based on global and DRC evidence of what works, will:
i) Strengthen health systems and improve access to quality, effective and affordable health services by improving the skills of health personnel and increasing the use of health information for better decision-making.
ii) Deliver basic maternal, child health, nutrition and family planning services to meet immediate, often life saving needs in Kasai province.

q3_expected_outputs.output: 1.6 million women, girls, and children reached with improved health services
Reduction in maternal mortality rate in Kasai province
Reduction in under-five mortality rate in Kasai province
Increased access to family planning services (modern contraceptive prevalence rate)
Improved skills of health personnel (training and capacity building)
Strengthened health information systems (DHIS2) for better decision-making
Enhanced community engagement in health service design and delivery
Policy engagement with Government of DRC on Universal Health Coverage (UHC) strategy
Integration with girls’ education programmes for mutually reinforcing benefits

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce maternal and under-five mortality in Kasai province through a dual approach: (1) strengthening health systems (governance, health information, community engagement) and (2) delivering essential maternal, child health, nutrition, and family planning services. It aligns with DRC’s Universal Health Coverage strategy and complements UK’s broader development goals in education and governance.

quote.text: The intended impact of the health programme is to ‘reduce maternal and under-five mortality rates in Kasai province’. It aims to achieve this through a stronger public health system which delivers quality maternal, newborn and child health services.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: DRC is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) with ongoing insecurity, weak institutions, and high levels of poverty. Kasai province is recovering from violent conflict (2016-2018) that caused over 3,300 deaths and displaced 1.4 million people. The health system is underfunded, with chronic underdevelopment and limited government capacity.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Major [...] Key risks include: political and security risks including commitment to health sector reforms; delivery risks around the ability to procure, manage and distribute pharmaceutical supplies through a weak public health system; and fiduciary risks due to high levels of corruption and lack of accountability.

q6_constraints_impact.security: Ongoing insecurity in Kasai province affects service delivery and access to health facilities. The 2016-2018 conflict displaced 1.4 million people, and inter-ethnic tensions remain high.
q6_constraints_impact.infrastructure: Only 19% of the population has access to electricity, and 52% have access to clean water. Poor road conditions hinder drug supply and immunisation campaigns.
q6_constraints_impact.regulatory: Weak regulation of pharmaceuticals (42% of sampled drugs were counterfeit in 2017) and limited enforcement of health policies at facility level.
q6_constraints_impact.political economy: Low domestic financing for health (only $3.5 per capita in 2019) and weak public financial management. Budget execution rate was 57% in 2019, with 42% of health expenditure out-of-pocket.
q6_constraints_impact.weak institutions: Health system suffers from poor governance, lack of accountability, and weak health information systems (DHIS2 data quality is variable). Only 6 doctors/nurses/midwives per 10,000 population (vs WHO threshold of 23).
q6_constraints_impact.conflict: Kasai province is recovering from a 2016-2018 conflict with 3,300+ deaths and 1.4M displaced. Security remains fragile, with potential for small-scale violence.
q6_constraints_impact.climate risks: DRC is exposed to floods, droughts, and extreme temperatures, which exacerbate malaria, cholera, and malnutrition. Rising temperatures may expand malaria to higher altitudes.
q6_constraints_impact.data limitations: Poor civil registration (only 1 in 4 births registered) and weak disease surveillance systems lead to underreporting of mortality and outbreaks.

quote.text: Kasai province is still recovering from the impact of the devastating violent conflict that broke out in 2016 causing more than 3,300 deaths. At its peak, up to 1.4 million were internally displaced persons (IDPs) and more than 30,000 refugees sought shelter across the border in Angola. [...] Whilst the conflict has largely lessened, the security crisis is far from over and numerous challenges remain: insecurity is still rife and the potential for small-scale violent incidents remains high; inter-ethnic tensions remain high; and many of the fundamental problems that contributed to the conflict i.e. chronic underdevelopment, political power struggles, and localised conflicts, remain unresolved.
quote.source: D0002941.odt, Wider contextual factors affecting health outcomes

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of DRC (Ministry of Health and Kasai provincial authorities)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is implemented through DRC’s public health system, with decision-making shared between national/provincial government and local health authorities. UK/FCDO provides oversight and technical support but does not directly manage delivery.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for health personnel (skills improvement for maternal, child health, and family planning services)
Strengthening health information systems (DHIS2) for data-driven decision-making
Support to provincial health authorities for governance and public financial management reforms
Community engagement to improve demand for services and local accountability
Technical assistance for drug supply and management systems

partner_organizations.name: Government of DRC (Ministry of Health)
partner_organizations.role: Policy and strategic oversight; alignment with Universal Health Coverage strategy

partner_organizations.name: Kasai Provincial Health Authorities
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of services at provincial level; management of Regional Drug Distribution Centres (CDRs)

partner_organizations.name: Global Fund
partner_organizations.role: Procurement of bed nets and antimalarial commodities for Kasai province; support to health information systems

partner_organizations.name: GAVI
partner_organizations.role: Support for routine immunisation and cold chain systems

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Technical leadership and policy support for health systems strengthening

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Complementary nutrition programme in Kasai; performance-based financing for health facilities

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs/Health Facilities
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery at community and facility levels (e.g., maternal health, family planning)

partner_organizations.name: Groupe Inter-Bailleurs de Santé (GIBS)
partner_organizations.role: Donor coordination platform for health sector reforms

quote.text: This programme will work in tandem with our girls’ education programme and complement governance activities in the province of Kasai. [...] By joining up this programme with our girls’ education work, we will deliver mutually-reinforcing benefits to DRC’s human capital and accelerate the drivers of a demographic transition in a fragile, post-conflict context, contributing to stability.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants to implementing partners (for service delivery) and direct support to provincial health authorities (for systems strengthening). Funds for drugs/equipment are channeled through Regional Drug Distribution Centres (CDRs), with management costs paid to provincial authorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is implemented through a mix of provincial government structures (for health systems strengthening) and local/NGO partners (for service delivery). Coordination occurs via the GIBS donor platform and alignment with DRC’s Universal Health Coverage strategy. The World Bank, Global Fund, and GAVI provide complementary funding for specific components (e.g., nutrition, malaria, immunisation).

quote.text: Drugs and medical equipment funded by the programme will be procured by the programme implementing partner and will be channelled through the provincial authorities’ Regional Drug Distribution Centres (CDRs), who will be paid management costs. We also expect a small amount of funds to be allocated at the point of service delivery to health authorities and facilities to support some of their basic running costs and cover the cost of some health services for the poorest.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is overseen through the Groupe Inter-Bailleurs de Santé (GIBS), a donor coordination platform that includes the UK, World Bank, EU, US, and DRC government. Decisions on health sector reforms and resource allocation are made jointly. At provincial level, discussions are underway to establish GIBS-like structures for local coordination.

quote.text: Co-ordination of donor activities and definition of joint priorities is supported by a donor coordination platform for development partners, the Groupe Inter-Bailleurs de Santé (GIBS). The GIBS provides the opportunity to discuss key reforms with the Government, including the need to increase domestic financing. BEK works closely with the GIBS and directly with donors to inform programming, coordinate where possible, and ensure that there is no duplication of activities between donors.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components (e.g., health systems vs service delivery) with approval, particularly to address emerging needs like disease outbreaks or humanitarian crises. The programme is designed to respond to shocks (e.g., Ebola, COVID-19) while maintaining core objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes mechanisms to adjust priorities based on real-time data (e.g., DHIS2) and emerging health threats. Adaptive management is embedded to respond to fragility risks (e.g., conflict flare-ups in Kasai) and climate-related health risks (e.g., malaria outbreaks).

quote.text: The programme will strengthen the capacity to prepare and respond to climate-related health risks and strengthen systems to withstand future shocks. [...] The programme will integrate preparedness on potential disease impacts related to flood situations, extreme heat etc. within disease surveillance and response systems.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (NGOs/provincial authorities) → Health Facilities/Community Levels. The World Bank and Global Fund add additional layers for specific components (e.g., nutrition, malaria).

quote.text: PDSS’ financing for health facilities tends to be spent in the following way: 60% for staff salaries, 15% for running facilities (e.g. for fuel etc.), 5% buffer to meet additional needs and 20% for drugs.
quote.source: D0002941.odt, Engagement with Key Stakeholders (referencing World Bank’s PDSS programme, which is complementary)

q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Would lead to regression in health indicators, increased maternal/child mortality, and higher humanitarian costs. Kasai’s fragile context requires continued support to avoid destabilization.
DRC’s health challenges are systemic; a siloed approach would not address underlying health system weaknesses (e.g., governance, human resources, data systems).
Spreading resources thinly across DRC would dilute impact. Kasai was prioritized due to its extreme poverty, high maternal mortality, and post-conflict fragility.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Working through multilateral mechanisms only (e.g., Global Fund, WHO)
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_because: While multilateral partners are critical, bilateral support is needed to address gaps in governance, community engagement, and local systems strengthening that multilaterals cannot fully cover.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery model (direct service provision + systems strengthening) was chosen to: (1) address immediate lifesaving needs in Kasai while building long-term resilience; (2) leverage DRC’s existing health structures (e.g., CDRs, DHIS2) for sustainability; (3) align with DRC’s Universal Health Coverage strategy and donor coordination (GIBS); (4) mitigate risks of fragility by embedding flexibility for shocks (e.g., disease outbreaks, conflict); and (5) maximize value for money by combining UK bilateral funds with multilateral investments (e.g., Global Fund for malaria commodities, World Bank for nutrition).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (combining bilateral and multilateral funds)
partner capacity (working through provincial government and local NGOs)
speed (responding to urgent health needs in Kasai)
equity (targeting the poorest province with highest maternal mortality)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks due to weak public financial management in DRC (e.g., low budget execution rates, corruption).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds for drugs/equipment are channeled through Regional Drug Distribution Centres (CDRs) with management fees, avoiding direct cash transfers to central government. Enhanced due diligence and third-party monitoring (TPM) for financial flows.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery risks in a fragile context (e.g., insecurity in Kasai, drug stockouts, weak supply chains).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of multiple implementing partners to diversify risk; pre-positioning of essential drugs; and integration with World Bank/Global Fund supply chains. Contingency plans for conflict-related disruptions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination risks with multiple donors (e.g., duplication, misalignment with DRC priorities).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active participation in GIBS donor platform to harmonize priorities; joint planning with World Bank, EU, and US; and alignment with DRC’s National Health Development Plan (PNDS).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability risks post-programme (e.g., reliance on donor funding, weak government ownership).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for provincial health authorities; policy engagement to increase domestic health financing; and integration with DRC’s UHC strategy. Leveraging Global Financing Facility (GFF) for long-term funding.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of resources, e.g., leveraging multilateral procurement)
efficiency (streamlined delivery through existing systems like CDRs and DHIS2)
effectiveness (evidence-based interventions targeting Kasai’s highest-burden health issues)
equity (focusing on the poorest province with highest maternal/child mortality and unmet family planning needs)

quote.text: Investing in a ‘health system’ approach—strengthening the systems and supporting the delivery of a range of highly-evidence-based health interventions (best buys)—will have a multiplier effect and enable those vertical programmes to become more effective. There is evidence that systems interventions can reduce both illness and premature death [...] and evidence from previous DRC health programming indicated that this approach reduces communities’ and individuals’ vulnerability to shocks during humanitarian crises.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Kasai province limits partner selection to organizations with: (1) experience operating in fragile settings (e.g., conflict sensitivity, security protocols); (2) existing relationships with provincial authorities (to navigate weak governance); (3) capacity to manage supply chains in low-infrastructure areas (e.g., drug stockouts, poor roads); and (4) ability to work through local structures (e.g., CDRs, health zones) due to limited international NGO presence. The post-conflict environment also requires partners to integrate community engagement to build trust and address social norms (e.g., gender inequality, SGBV).
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in Kasai require partners with conflict-sensitive approaches and local networks.
Weak provincial capacity necessitates partners who can provide embedded technical assistance (e.g., for drug management, DHIS2).
Limited electricity/internet restricts digital health solutions, favoring partners with offline-capable systems.
High corruption risks demand partners with robust fiduciary controls and third-party monitoring.
Cultural barriers (e.g., gender norms) require partners with experience in community mobilization and SGBV response.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s dual objectives (service delivery + systems strengthening) shape a mixed delivery structure: (1) **Service delivery** requires local NGOs/health facilities for community reach, while (2) **systems strengthening** necessitates government partnership (e.g., provincial authorities for CDRs, DHIS2). The need for adaptive management (due to fragility) leads to milestone-based funding and joint governance (GIBS). The focus on equity (targeting Kasai’s poorest) drives decentralized implementation through provincial structures rather than central government.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Partnership with provincial health authorities to improve skilled birth attendance and emergency obstetric care, using CDRs for drug supply.
Technical assistance to provincial government for DHIS2 and public financial management, with GIBS oversight.
Community-based NGOs for demand generation, linked to provincial health facilities for service delivery.
Integration of flood/heat preparedness into disease surveillance systems, managed by provincial health teams.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency by: (1) **Targeting Kasai** (highest maternal mortality, poorest province) despite higher delivery costs in a fragile context; (2) **Using provincial systems** (e.g., CDRs) for sustainability, even though they are weaker than central structures; (3) **Combining vertical funds** (e.g., Global Fund for malaria) with horizontal systems strengthening to maximize reach without duplicating efforts; and (4) **Prioritizing women/girls** in design (e.g., SGBV response, family planning) despite cultural barriers that may slow uptake.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Rapid scale-up of services is constrained by the need to build trust in post-conflict Kasai, requiring slower community engagement processes.
Technical assistance from multilaterals (e.g., WHO, World Bank) is balanced with capacity building for provincial authorities to ensure local leadership.
Delivering services in remote areas of Kasai increases costs, but is justified by equity goals (targeting the poorest with highest unmet needs).
Adaptive management for shocks (e.g., Ebola outbreaks) requires flexible funds, but risks weaker fiduciary controls in a high-corruption environment.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **major risk rating** (FCAS context) drives **intensive oversight**: (1) Embedded advisors for provincial capacity building; (2) Quarterly reviews via GIBS; (3) Third-party monitoring for financial flows; and (4) Contingency plans for insecurity/disease outbreaks. The fragility of Kasai province necessitates closer management than in stable contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) **Provincial authorities** receive technical assistance for governance/PFM to take on greater management over time; (2) **Local NGOs** are trained in data collection (DHIS2) and community mobilization to improve service uptake; (3) **Health workers** receive clinical skills training to reduce reliance on external experts; and (4) **GIBS** builds coordination capacity among donors to align with DRC’s UHC strategy.

quote.text: The programme will work in tandem with our girls’ education programme and complement governance activities in the province of Kasai. [...] By joining up this programme with our girls’ education work, we will deliver mutually-reinforcing benefits to DRC’s human capital and accelerate the drivers of a demographic transition in a fragile, post-conflict context, contributing to stability.

key_programme_risks: Political and security risks (e.g., instability in Kasai, low government commitment to reforms).
Delivery risks (e.g., drug stockouts, weak supply chains, absenteeism of health workers).
Fiduciary risks (e.g., corruption, low budget execution rates, misallocation of funds).
Health system risks (e.g., poor data quality, weak governance, lack of accountability).
Climate and environmental risks (e.g., floods, disease outbreaks, poor WASH infrastructure).
Social and cultural risks (e.g., gender norms limiting family planning, SGBV).
Sustainability risks (e.g., reliance on donor funding, weak domestic resource mobilization).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political and security risks in Kasai
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work through provincial authorities and local NGOs with existing community trust; integrate conflict sensitivity into programme design; maintain flexibility to adapt to security changes.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Drug stockouts and supply chain weaknesses
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pre-position essential medicines; leverage Global Fund/World Bank procurement systems; strengthen CDRs with technical assistance; use third-party monitoring for distribution.
Channel funds through CDRs with management fees (not central government); use accountable grants with strict reporting; conduct enhanced due diligence on partners.
Invest in data quality training for provincial staff; integrate DHIS2 with Global Fund/GAVI systems; use real-time data for adaptive management.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Climate-related health risks (e.g., malaria outbreaks, floods)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strengthen disease surveillance systems; integrate climate resilience into WASH and infrastructure projects; pre-position supplies for emergencies.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low demand for family planning due to social norms
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Combine service delivery with community sensitization; engage religious leaders and men in dialogues; link with girls’ education programmes to shift norms.
Align with DRC’s UHC strategy; build provincial capacity for drug management/PFM; advocate for increased domestic health financing via GIBS.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts like Kasai, **local ownership is critical**—previous programmes (e.g., ASSP) showed that working through provincial structures (not central government) improves sustainability.
**Flexible funding** is essential to respond to shocks (e.g., Ebola, conflict displacement). The programme includes contingency mechanisms for rapid reallocation.
**Community engagement** reduces risks of service rejection. Lessons from ASSR highlight the need to involve local leaders (e.g., CODESA committees) in design.
**Third-party monitoring (TPM)** is necessary where government oversight is weak. Previous programmes faced fraud risks without independent verification.
**Donor coordination (GIBS)** prevents duplication and aligns with government priorities. In DRC, fragmented donor efforts have led to inefficiencies.

ASSP (2012-2019): Quality of care must be prioritized alongside access—high utilization rates did not always translate to better outcomes.
Community engagement is critical for service uptake, especially for family planning and nutrition.
Drug supply systems require technical assistance to reduce stockouts and expiry.
Complementary interventions (e.g., WASH, social protection) are needed to address broader determinants of health.
ASSR (2019-2020): Efficient drug supply management is a bottleneck—logistics challenges must be addressed early.
Provincial government capacity is limited; embedded support is needed for planning and resource allocation.
Malaria Control Programme (2013-2018): Involving schools in mass distribution campaigns (e.g., bed nets) improves reach.
Private sector engagement can improve availability of quality-assured commodities (e.g., QAACT for malaria).

design_changes_based_on_learning.alignment_with_government: Unlike ASSP (which had misaligned user fees), SEMI will adhere to DRC’s UHC strategy and provincial priorities to improve sustainability.
design_changes_based_on_learning.provincial_focus: Shift from multi-province (ASSP) to whole-of-province (Kasai) for deeper impact and easier coordination.
design_changes_based_on_learning.integration_with_education: Explicit linkage with girls’ education programmes to address social norms (e.g., adolescent pregnancy, SGBV) that previous health programmes could not tackle alone.
design_changes_based_on_learning.strengthened_monitoring: Enhanced TPM and DHIS2 integration to address fraud risks identified in ASSR.
design_changes_based_on_learning.climate_resilience: Added components for climate-adaptive WASH and disease surveillance, based on lessons from Ebola/COVID-19 disruptions.

quote.text: Lessons from previous health programming in the DRC highlight the importance of getting the basics right and delivering quality care. Essential healthcare will be provided in Kasai province alongside strengthening the quality of care. [...] Lessons from the impact evaluation for future programmes are: (i) improve quality of care, (ii) improve community engagement to increase uptake of service, (iii) support drug supply and management systems through technical assistance in order to reduce drug stockout and expiry; and (iv) the need for complementary interventions such as WASH, agriculture, social protection and (vi) address the broader determinants of health such as nutrition, education, poverty reduction.
quote.source: D0002941.odt, UK Support to the Health Sector

co_funding_partners.details: Provides ~$200m/year for DRC (malaria, TB, HIV). SEMI will use GF-procured bed nets and antimalarial commodities in Kasai.
£50m (2018-2023) for DRC’s reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child, and adolescent health. SEMI will align with GFF’s results-based financing (RBF) approach.
Supports routine immunisation in DRC (~$20m for 2021-2025). SEMI will integrate with GAVI’s cold chain and DHIS2 systems.
$1bn Nutrition Programme (2022-2032) in Kasai/Kasai Central. SEMI will complement with maternal/child health services.
Technical leadership for UHC and health security. SEMI will leverage WHO’s policy support and surveillance systems.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages ~$200m/year from the Global Fund, $50m from GFF, and $1bn from the World Bank for complementary activities in Kasai. By aligning with these partners, SEMI avoids duplication and extends its reach (e.g., using GF bed nets, WB nutrition support).

capital_vs_revenue_split.text: Funds are primarily revenue expenditure (service delivery, training, technical assistance). Limited capital expenditure is mentioned (e.g., WASH infrastructure, solar water pumps), but no explicit split is provided.
details: 60% of World Bank’s complementary PDSS funds go to staff salaries (revenue).
20% of PDSS funds are for drugs (revenue).
SEMI includes minor capital for climate-resilient WASH (e.g., solar pumps).
