metadata.programme_name: Democracy Deepening in Mozambique programme (DD)
metadata.quote: The Democracy Deepening programme takes a two-track approach. Initially, the focus will be on activities to promote more credible and inclusive elections, which should contribute to popular participation and the sustainability of the peace process. Over time, we will ramp up our work to support greater civic and policy engagement on national priorities, particularly of vulnerable groups, such as youth, women and girls, and on the promotion and protection of human rights and media freedom, all of which should lead to more inclusive development and help reduce poverty in the country. (D0005491.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: This is a 4,5 years’ programme cutting across two Spending Reviews/SRs. (D0005491.odt, Financial details section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening civil society and state institutions), policy influence (advocacy on human rights and governance), and service delivery (election monitoring and civic engagement). It aims to deepen democracy in Mozambique through both immediate electoral support and long-term civic engagement.
what_objectives.q1_source: The Democracy Deepening programme takes a two-track approach. Initially, the focus will be on activities to promote more credible and inclusive elections, which should contribute to popular participation and the sustainability of the peace process. Over time, we will ramp up our work to support greater civic and policy engagement on national priorities, particularly of vulnerable groups, such as youth, women and girls, and on the promotion and protection of human rights and media freedom, all of which should lead to more inclusive development and help reduce poverty in the country. (D0005491.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Municipal and general elections with greater participation, scrutiny, transparency, and accountability (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change)
A more enabling environment for civic engagement and policy dialogue (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change)
Stronger promotion and protection of human rights, including media freedoms (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change)
Electoral civic education and dispute resolution mechanisms (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change - Output goals)
Elections observation and monitoring (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change - Workstreams)
Facility for Technical Assistance (TA) + Innovation + Monitoring, Evaluation, Research, and Learning (MERL) (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change - Workstreams)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Mozambique's democracy through credible elections, civic engagement, and human rights protection, with a focus on vulnerable groups and long-term institutional resilience.
what_objectives.quote: The programme’s long-term impact should contribute to the: ‘(…) consolidation of democratic norms and behaviours of political contestation and civic participation in society’ (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mozambique's democracy faces challenges including election irregularities, human rights abuses, and political violence. The programme's overall risk is rated as 'major' due to the fragile political and security environment.
where_context.q5_source: Mozambique’s democratic journey began three decades ago, when the country introduced political and economic reforms; changed its constitution and introduced a bill of rights; and held its first multiparty elections in the early 1990s. Since then, the country’s democratic actors, from political parties to media and civil society, have been on a bumpy road – with progress and challenges. (D0005491.odt, Context section) && This programme overall risk is major, even after mitigation measures have been taken into account. (D0005491.odt, Risks section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Elections are marred by irregularities and opposition complaints; freedom of expression and assembly are curtailed; human rights abuses are frequent, especially outside the capital. Two pending bills (media law and NGO law) threaten to further restrict civic space. Political marginalization has driven cycles of violence, affecting programme delivery and partner safety.
where_context.quote: Elections are held regularly but turnout has been low and there have been frequent complaints of fraud; freedom of expression, media and assembly are often curtailed; there are frequent reports of human rights abuses, particularly outside of the country’s capital; the boundaries of the state and ruling party are porous and checks and balances often ineffective; and democratic actors face an uphill struggle to fully exercise their rights. (D0005491.odt, Context section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains decision-making authority over programme design, budget allocations, and strategic direction, while local partners implement activities. The programme explicitly states that 'No UK funding will be channelled directly through the Government of Mozambique or Mozambican state institutions.' (D0005491.odt, Partnership Principles)
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., election observers, human rights advocates)
technical assistance (e.g., to electoral authorities, judiciary, police)
institutional strengthening (e.g., civil society organizations, media)
grants (e.g., funding for local CSOs to facilitate civic engagement)
mentorship (e.g., support for vulnerable groups like youth, women, and LGBTQ+)

partner_organizations.name: National/local civil society organisations (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver elections monitoring/observation and civic/policy engagement and human rights work (three components)

partner_organizations.name: UN agencies (e.g., UNDP, OHCHR)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver elections work with government and state authorities (one component)

partner_organizations.name: Service providers/local organisations (procured locally or through FCDO frameworks)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver support facility (TA + Innovation + MERL) (one component)

who_partners.quote: Ofthe programme’s budget, around 70% (£3,6mln) will be delivered through accountable grants with national NGOs/CSOs; around 15% delivered through the UN; and around 15% through service providers. (D0005491.odt, Financial details section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants (for CSOs), Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs with UN agencies), and contracts (with service providers). This allows flexibility to engage different types of partners for different components (elections, civic engagement, human rights, and support facility).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is structured as a hybrid model with multiple implementing partners: CSOs for civic engagement, UN agencies for elections, and service providers for technical assistance. FCDO retains oversight but delegates day-to-day management to partners, with a 'Facility for Assistance, Innovation, Monitoring, Evaluation, Research, and Learning (MERL)' to coordinate adaptation and learning.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection method varies by component: UN agencies are chosen for their existing relationships with government (elections), local CSOs are selected for their grassroots reach (civic engagement), and service providers are procured for technical expertise (support facility). The document notes that an international procurement process for a service provider would take ~9 months, which is incompatible with urgent election timelines, hence the mixed approach.
how_mechanism.quote: Giventhe diversity of our proposed areas of work, and our gradual approach, the best delivery mechanism for the programme’s activities would include a combination of options A+B+C (option D): National/local civil society organisations will deliver on elections monitoring and observation, and most of the work on civic/policy engagement and human rights (three components). UN agencies will deliver on our elections work with government and state authorities (one component). Service providers/local organisations, procured locally or through our procurement frameworks, will deliver on our support facility (one component). (D0005491.odt, Delivery modalities section)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: All implementation agreements include provisions for unilateral budget/timeframe adjustments by FCDO based on resource allocations. Partners must submit forecasts and reports for FCDO review, and any sub-awards require FCDO approval.
how_governance.quote: BHCM programme officer will liaise monthly with partners’ finance manager to review programme spend and make any necessary adjustments to budgets and forecasts. (D0005491.odt, Financial management) && The agreements will stipulate measures in the event that poor performance, failure to deliver on expected results and failure to optimise value for money are detected. (D0005491.odt, Financial management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, especially if contextual changes or underperformance occur. The programme includes break clauses in contracts/MoUs/grants to allow adjustments. However, reallocation requires formal amendments and is not fully flexible.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptability: 'if the context changes, or if approaches are not working, there will be changes to areas of engagement and/or ways of working.' A 'Facility for Assistance, Innovation, MERL' is established to drive innovation and learning. However, changes require FCDO approval and may involve business case amendments for scope/timeframe extensions.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme’s outcome will not change; however, pathways towards this outcome can change throughout the lifetime of the programme – with new priorities, partners, ways of working, additional resources. (D0005491.odt, Flexibility section) && There is scope for scaling up programme resources and extending its timeframe, though this will need a business case amendment and ministerial approval. (D0005491.odt, Financial details section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (CSOs/UN/service providers) → End beneficiaries (no sub-grantees mentioned beyond direct partners).
how_efficiency.quote: Payment schedules will vary by component and be clearly set out in partner agreements. (D0005491.odt, Financial management) && Implementing partners will provide forecasts of expenditure alongside a detailed work plan to BHCM at the beginning of the project and at the start of each financial year. (D0005491.odt, Financial management)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing different – remain engaged at policy/political level without technical/financial support (counterfactual).
Option 2: Support elections only (assuming this is the most pressing issue).
Option 3: Support a combination of democratic processes (elections, civic engagement, human rights) – *preferred option*.
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (mixed approach) was chosen because it aligns with HMG priorities (inclusive governance, women/girls, climate, conflict), is supported by international evidence on 'what works' for democracy promotion, and offers a sustainable approach by addressing both immediate electoral needs and long-term civic engagement. The mixed delivery modality (Option D: CSOs + UN + service providers) was selected to balance timeliness (UN for elections), local ownership (CSOs), and innovation (service providers).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in procurement: International procurement for a service provider would take ~9 months, missing election timelines.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use existing UN relationships for elections work and local procurement frameworks for faster mobilization.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited impact on local capacity if relying solely on UN/international providers.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Allocate 70% of budget to national CSOs to strengthen local organizations.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges with multiple partners.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Establish a MERL facility to harmonize monitoring, evaluation, and learning across components.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of harassment/intimidation of programme partners by police or state actors.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proactive safeguarding measures and close monitoring of partner security.

why_rationale.quote: Option 3: Support a combination of democratic processes, with a focus on elections, civic engagement and human rights. (D0005491.odt, Appraisal case) && Giventhe diversity of our proposed areas of work, and our gradual approach, the best delivery mechanism for the programme’s activities would include a combination of options A+B+C (option D). (D0005491.odt, Delivery modalities section) && Altogether, these criteria provide a good framework for assessing the Value for Money/VfM of these delivery options. We will therefore assess these four options on economy, efficiency, equity, and effectiveness (cost-effectiveness). (D0005491.odt, VfM assessment)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Mozambique constrains partner selection by: 1) Limiting direct funding to government due to corruption/weak institutions; 2) Requiring partners with conflict sensitivity (e.g., election monitors must navigate political tensions); 3) Prioritizing local CSOs for grassroots reach but needing UN/service providers for technical credibility; 4) Security risks (e.g., harassment of partners) restricting who can operate safely.
q27_constraints_detail: No direct funding to government due to corruption risks (D0005491.odt, Partnership Principles).
Pending repressive laws (media/NGO bills) threaten civic space, limiting partner operations (D0005491.odt, Legal backlash section).
Election irregularities and opposition boycotts require neutral, credible partners (e.g., UN for electoral authorities) (D0005491.odt, Context section).
Security risks (e.g., police harassment) necessitate safeguarding measures for local partners (D0005491.odt, Safeguarding section).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s two-track approach (immediate elections + long-term civic engagement) directly shapes the delivery structure: 1) **Elections urgency** → UN agencies (existing government relationships) for rapid support; 2) **Civic engagement needs** → Local CSOs (grassroots trust) for sustainability; 3) **Innovation/learning** → Service providers (technical expertise) for adaptability. The MERL facility bridges these components to ensure coherence.
q28_linkages: Elections work requires **centralized, fast-moving partners** (UN) due to time sensitivity (D0005491.odt, Delivery modalities).
Civic engagement demands **decentralized, local partners** (CSOs) for legitimacy and reach (D0005491.odt, Civic engagement lessons).
Human rights protection needs **flexible, adaptive mechanisms** (service providers + MERL facility) to respond to legal/political changes (D0005491.odt, Human rights section).
Vulnerable groups (youth, women, LGBTQ+) require **tailored, inclusive partners** → embedded in all components (D0005491.odt, Gender/disability inclusion).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Urgent election support (UN) risks sidelining local CSOs, but 70% budget allocation to CSOs mitigates this. 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: International service providers bring innovation but may reduce local control; the MERL facility aims to balance this. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Decentralized work (provincial focus) increases costs but is critical for marginalized groups.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Elections: 'Providingsupport to both electoral authorities and civil society... can only work if delivered with time and in a decentralised fashion.' (D0005491.odt, Lessons from TASTE) → Trade-off between timely UN support and local CSO empowerment.

Civic engagement: 'Mozambique’s civil society... still need continuous financial and technical support to carry out their work.' (D0005491.odt, Lessons) → Efficiency of direct funding vs. sustainability of capacity building.

Human rights: 'Legal frameworks... often do not translate into meaningful changes... focus should move from legal change to implementation.' (D0005491.odt, Lessons) → Short-term advocacy vs. long-term behavioral change.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'major' risk profile (FCAS context) drives **intensive oversight**: monthly financial reviews, embedded safeguarding, and adaptive management structures (e.g., MERL facility). High risks of election fraud or partner harassment require real-time monitoring and flexible mitigation (e.g., reallocating funds if security deteriorates).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: 1) CSOs receive grants + technical assistance to **lead civic engagement**; 2) Electoral authorities/judiciary receive **targeted TA** to improve transparency; 3) Vulnerable groups (youth, women, LGBTQ+) are **prioritized in all components** through tailored strategies. The programme’s ‘localisation agenda’ explicitly links capacity strengths to partner selection (e.g., provincial CSOs for decentralized work).
intersections.quote: Our assistance will factor in the need for financial and technical support. Also, we will strive to work more through provincial/local organisations. (D0005491.odt, Lessons - Civic engagement) && The programme’s approach will focus on dialogue and partnerships between government and citizens, working with both state and non-state actors. (D0005491.odt, Lessons - Civic engagement) && DDimplementing partners will: a) Select, fund and provide capacity to local actors, particularly civil society organisations and public officials, to facilitate civic engagement in decision and policy-making. (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change - Activities)

key_programme_risks: Election irregularities and opposition boycotts undermining credibility (D0005491.odt, Context).
Pending repressive media/NGO laws curtailing civic space (D0005491.odt, Legal backlash).
Security risks (harassment/attacks on partners or beneficiaries) (D0005491.odt, Safeguarding).
Low citizen turnout and trust in democratic processes (D0005491.odt, Context).
Limited capacity of local CSOs to drive innovation without support (D0005491.odt, Lessons).
Coordinating multiple partners (UN, CSOs, service providers) without duplication (D0005491.odt, Delivery modalities).
Budget reductions due to FCDO spending reviews (D0005491.odt, Financial details).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support both electoral authorities (via UN) and civil society (via CSOs) to improve transparency/accountability, with a provincial focus. (D0005491.odt, Lessons from TASTE)
Advocacy through HMG diplomatic channels and support to local CSOs to monitor/oppose bills. (D0005491.odt, Legal backlash)
Safeguarding protocols, conflict-sensitive approaches, and flexible funding to adapt to threats. (D0005491.odt, Safeguarding)
Electoral civic education, dispute resolution mechanisms, and targeted outreach to marginalized groups. (D0005491.odt, Theory of Change)
70% budget to CSOs with embedded technical assistance and MERL support. (D0005491.odt, Financial details)
MERL facility to harmonize activities and regular donor coordination meetings. (D0005491.odt, Delivery modalities)
Break clauses in contracts/grants and provisions for unilateral adjustments. (D0005491.odt, Financial details)

fcas_specific_lessons: Decentralized approaches are critical in FCAS to reach marginalized areas and build local trust (D0005491.odt, Lessons - Civic engagement).
Conflict sensitivity must be embedded in all activities to avoid exacerbating tensions (e.g., election monitoring in contested regions) (D0005491.odt, Conflict-sensitive section).
Legal/political backsliding (e.g., media/NGO laws) requires proactive advocacy and rapid-response mechanisms (D0005491.odt, Legal backlash).
In FCAS, 'programmes need to develop specific strategies to deal with inequalities related to gender, disability and age' (D0005491.odt, Lessons from TASTE).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the **Transparency and Accountability for Inclusive Development (TACID, 2018–2024)** and **TASTE (2019–20)** programmes highlight: 1) Elections support must start **early** and be **decentralized**; 2) CSOs need **continuous financial/technical support**; 3) **Dialogue between government and citizens** increases responsiveness; 4) **Marginalized groups** (women, youth, disabled) require tailored strategies; 5) **Legal changes alone are insufficient**—focus on implementation and behavioral change. (D0005491.odt, Lessons section)
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Earlier engagement**: Despite resource constraints, the programme starts a year before general elections (vs. previous late mobilization). 2) **Provincial focus**: Explicit shift to decentralized work (e.g., provincial CSOs) based on TACID/TASTE lessons. 3) **MERL facility**: New structure to drive adaptive management and innovation, addressing past rigidity. 4) **Inclusion strategies**: Explicit budgets for vulnerable groups (youth, women, LGBTQ+) in all components. 5) **Flexible funding**: Break clauses and reallocation provisions to respond to context changes (e.g., budget cuts). (D0005491.odt, Lessons and Flexibility sections)
risks_lessons.quote: Drawn from business case for the Transparency and Accountability for Inclusive Development in Mozambique (TACID) programme (2018/2024), and the PCR of our last elections programme (TASTE, 2019/20). The DD programme will, to the extent possible, take these lessons and recommendations into account for greater impact. (D0005491.odt, Lessons section) && The programme’s approach will focus on dialogue and partnerships between government and citizens, working with both state and non-state actors. (D0005491.odt, Lessons - Civic engagement)

financial_details.quote: Ofthe programme’s budget, around 70% (£3,6mln) will be delivered through accountable grants with national NGOs/CSOs; around 15% delivered through the UN; and around 15% through service providers. (D0005491.odt, Financial details section) && The programme will be funded from FCDO Mozambique bilateral aid budget under RDEL. (D0005491.odt, Financial details section)

metadata.programme_name: Tanzania Humanitarian Assistance Programme (T-HAP)

quote.duration_quote: "T-HAP is a four-year programme" (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Overview)
quote.sector_quote: "The Tanzania Humanitarian Assistance Programme (T-HAP) aims to build conducive and supportive humanitarian systems that save lives and reduce suffering" (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "T-HAP is a four-year programme with three main objectives." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Overview)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: T-HAP combines service delivery (protection assistance, food security, WASH, education), policy influence (engaging with Government of Tanzania on refugee policies and disaster management), and capacity building (strengthening national disaster response systems). The programme aims to save lives, reduce suffering, and build resilience while advocating for adherence to international refugee law.
what_objectives.q1_source: "T-HAP aims to build conducive and supportive humanitarian systems that, save lives, and reduce suffering. As well as providing protection assistance, the programme aims to build capacity for disaster response nationally." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Stronger platforms for discussing humanitarian & emergency coordination with government and stakeholders
Protection services (child protection, GBV prevention, mental healthcare, registration)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 266,000 refugees and asylum seekers

q3_expected_outputs.output: Food security and nutrition support
WASH services (water supply, latrines, hygiene promotion)
Education access (teacher training, curriculum support)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 55% of refugee population are children (~117,384)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Livelihood activities (skills training, kitchen gardening, alternative cooking fuels)
Disaster management capacity building (national and regional levels)
Policy engagement outputs (research, advocacy, coordination on refugee policies)
Emergency response mechanisms (contingency funds, rapid response)

what_objectives.summary: T-HAP is a mixed-objective programme that delivers humanitarian assistance (protection, food, WASH, education) while simultaneously engaging in policy advocacy to improve Tanzania’s refugee response system and building national capacity for disaster management. The programme is designed to be adaptive, with a strong focus on protection and resilience-building for refugees and host communities.

quote.objectives_quote: "T-HAP has three main objectives: i) Improved enabling environment for humanitarian response, through enhanced policy engagement; ii) Sustain appropriate integrated and cost-effective humanitarian assistance to address immediate needs including on protection; iii) Improved resilience through livelihood and environment activities for refugees, and better disaster management capabilities at national and regional levels." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Overview)
quote.mixed_evidence_quote: "The programme will support a broader UK offer on humanitarian action in Tanzania, combining humanitarian assistance and policy engagement." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Rationale)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Tanzania is in the fragile Great Lakes Region, hosting over 240,000 refugees from DRC and Burundi, with ongoing conflicts in neighboring countries driving forced displacement. The document explicitly states the programme has a "Major" risk rating, and the region is described as volatile with political unrest, climate-induced disasters, and protracted refugee crises.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (Document: D0006587.odt, SummarySheet) && "The Great Lakes Region has been volatile for many years. Conflicts, political unrest, and climate induced disasters are prevalent in the region resulting in population flows across borders." (Document: D0006587.odt, Context Overview)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: 1) **Security/Conflict**: Ongoing conflicts in DRC and Burundi drive refugee influxes, straining Tanzania’s capacity. 2) **Regulatory/Political Economy**: Tanzania’s withdrawal from the CRRF (2018) introduced encampment policies restricting refugee mobility and livelihoods. The government views new asylum seekers as security threats. 3) **Weak Institutions**: The humanitarian system is underdeveloped, with coordination challenges between refugee response and disaster management. 4) **Climate Risks**: Deforestation and firewood shortages (90% dependency) expose women/girls to SGBV during collection. 5) **Data Limitations**: Lack of protection monitoring data for repatriated refugees limits evidence-based interventions.

quote.constraints_quote: "Tanzania’s withdrawal from the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework (CRRF) in January 2018 saw the introduction of restrictions on refugee movements, access to labour markets and integration opportunities." (Document: D0006587.odt, Policy Context) && "The lack of a holistic approach comprising refugee assistance, disaster relief, and public health emergency response has led to coordination challenges." (Document: D0006587.odt, Humanitarian System Overview)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO (UK) leads policy engagement and strategic decisions, with implementation delivered through a "small portfolio of partners" (likely international NGOs) who have technical expertise. Local partners (e.g., government ministries) are engaged but in advisory/coordination roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for refugee skills (e.g., baking, tailoring, financial literacy) to support repatriation/reintegration
Strengthening Government of Tanzania’s disaster management capabilities (e.g., policy reviews, coordination frameworks)
Supporting UNHCR and partners in protection systems (e.g., child protection, GBV prevention, registration)
Building accountability mechanisms for affected populations (AAP)
Environmental programming (e.g., alternative cooking fuels to reduce deforestation)

partner_organizations.name: UNHCR
partner_organizations.role: Co-lead on refugee protection, coordination, and service delivery (e.g., registration, camp management)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania (Ministry of Home Affairs, Prime Minister’s Office - Disaster Management Department)
partner_organizations.role: Policy engagement, operational access, and national disaster management coordination

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs (unnamed in document)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of humanitarian services (WASH, education, livelihoods, protection) in refugee camps

partner_organizations.name: Humanitarian Donor Group (HDG)
partner_organizations.role: Coordination platform for donors (UK chairs this group)

partner_organizations.name: Research hubs/think tanks (e.g., Regional Durable Solutions Secretariat - ReDSS, Mixed Migration Centre - MMC)
partner_organizations.role: Evidence generation for policy engagement and durable solutions

quote.structure_quote: "T-HAP will be delivered through a small portfolio of partners who have a long track record of working effectively in refugee camps, strong technical knowledge, experience of shaping policy and capacity to deliver at scale." (Document: D0006587.odt, Implementation Approach)
quote.north_south_quote: "The UK will maintain a leading role... taking a predictable, flexible, and multi-year funding approach, allowing partners to better plan." (Document: D0006587.odt, UK Role) && "FCDO will agree a set of policy influencing priorities [with UNHCR]." (Document: D0006587.odt, Policy Engagement)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **block funding** (multi-year, flexible allocations to partners) and **partnership agreements** (with UNHCR and NGOs for service delivery). The UK’s role as chair of the Humanitarian Donor Group (HDG) also implies a **coordination mechanism** for leveraging other donors’ funds.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO leads policy and strategic engagement, while implementation is decentralized to a portfolio of partners (UNHCR, NGOs, government ministries). The programme emphasizes **coordination platforms** (e.g., HDG, Inter-Sector Coordination Group) and **adaptive management** with annual reflections on policy engagement effectiveness.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on **track record in refugee camps**, **technical expertise**, and **capacity to deliver at scale**. The document states: "a small portfolio of partners who have a long track record of working effectively in refugee camps," suggesting pre-existing relationships rather than open competition.

quote.instrument_quote: "The UK’s provision of predictable, flexible, and multi-year funding... allowing partners to better plan." (Document: D0006587.odt, Financial Approach) && "T-HAP will be delivered through a small portfolio of partners... strong technical knowledge, experience of shaping policy." (Document: D0006587.odt, Implementation Approach)
quote.selection_quote: "Partners [selected] who have a long track record of working effectively in refugee camps, strong technical knowledge, experience of shaping policy and capacity to deliver at scale." (Document: D0006587.odt, Implementation Approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions **formal coordination mechanisms** with donors (e.g., Humanitarian Donor Group) and government (e.g., Ministry of Home Affairs). While not explicitly called a "steering committee," the document describes structured engagement with decision-makers (e.g., "establish formalise and strengthen coordination structures").

quote.governance_quote: "Establish (formalise) and strengthen coordination structures through which partners have access to the Government of Tanzania." (Document: D0006587.odt, Policy Engagement) && "The programme will be designed with break clauses in the policy engagement components, allowing for regular and annual reflections on what is effective." (Document: D0006587.odt, Adaptive Management)
quote.oversight_quote: "Break clauses in the policy engagement components, allowing for regular and annual reflections on what is effective." (Document: D0006587.odt, Adaptive Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components, but **policy engagement** has built-in break clauses for pausing ineffective activities. Emergency response funds are set aside for unpredictable crises (e.g., new refugee influxes, disasters).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes: 1) **Annual reflections** on policy engagement effectiveness; 2) **Contingency funds** for emergencies; 3) **Flexibility to respond to new crises** (e.g., lessons from COVID-19/Ebola responses). Partners must align with evolving government priorities and refugee needs.

quote.flexibility_quote: "T-HAP will invest in rapid response delivery mechanisms, so funds can be released in case of unpredicted additional crises." (Document: D0006587.odt, Lessons Learned) && "The programme will be designed with break clauses in the policy engagement components, allowing for... the ability to pause activities that are not yielding the desired results." (Document: D0006587.odt, Adaptive Management)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UNHCR/NGOs) → [No explicit sub-grantees mentioned]. The document describes a "small portfolio of partners" without further sub-award layers.

quote.layers_quote: "T-HAP will be delivered through a small portfolio of partners who have a long track record..." (Document: D0006587.odt, Implementation Approach)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen to: 1) **Leverage UK’s diplomatic role** (e.g., chairing Humanitarian Donor Group) for policy influence; 2) **Address funding gaps** in Tanzania’s underfunded refugee response (only 37% of UN appeal funded in 2023); 3) **Build on past UK programmes** (e.g., lessons from 2017–2021 £55.9m programme); 4) **Balance flexibility and accountability** through multi-year funding with adaptive management clauses; 5) **Strengthen coordination** in a fragmented humanitarian system.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented coordination among humanitarian actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Invest in strengthening UN-led and donor-led coordination systems (e.g., formalizing Humanitarian Donor Group structures).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government policy shifts limiting refugee rights (e.g., encampment, repatriation pressure)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sustained policy engagement with Ministry of Home Affairs and Prime Minister’s Office to advocate for incremental changes (e.g., livelihood opportunities, protection standards).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a small portfolio of partners creating bottlenecks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Select partners with "strong technical knowledge and capacity to deliver at scale" and build flexibility into partner agreements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced humanitarian funding globally affecting programme scope
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year funding approach to provide predictability; leverage UK’s donor coordination role to mobilize additional resources.

quote.rationale_quote: "The UK will maintain a leading role even though the financial burden share is reducing by taking a predictable, flexible, and multi-year funding approach, allowing partners to better plan, be more strategic and respond to changing needs." (Document: D0006587.odt, UK Role) && "Lessons from past programmes... showed building flexibility into the programme allowed BHC Tanzania to mobilise resources essential in responding to the Ebola Virus Outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic." (Document: D0006587.odt, Lessons Learned)
quote.risk_quote: "Coordination among refugee actors needs strengthening. T-HAP will therefore invest time and resources into supporting the UN-led, and donor-led coordination system to improve coordination." (Document: D0006587.odt, Lessons Learned)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: 1) **Encampment policies** limit partner selection to organizations with experience in camp-based delivery (e.g., UNHCR, NGOs with refugee camp access). 2) **Government restrictions on livelihoods** require partners to focus on repatriation-preparation skills (e.g., baking, tailoring) rather than local integration. 3) **Weak disaster management institutions** necessitate capacity-building components in partner roles (e.g., training for Disaster Management Department).
q27_constraints_detail: Encampment policies restrict refugee mobility, requiring partners to operate within camps (Nduta, Nyarugusu).
Government’s repatriation focus limits livelihood interventions to skills portable to Burundi/DRC.
Underdeveloped disaster management systems require partners to include capacity-building for national/regional actors.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: 1) **Protection objectives** drive the need for **embedded partners** (e.g., UNHCR for registration, child protection) with direct camp access. 2) **Policy influence goals** require **high-level engagement structures** (e.g., coordination with Ministry of Home Affairs, Humanitarian Donor Group). 3) **Resilience-building** (livelihoods, disaster management) necessitates **multi-sectoral partners** (e.g., NGOs for skills training, government for policy reforms).

q28_linkages.link: Protection services (e.g., GBV prevention) → Requires partners with **camp-based presence** (e.g., UNHCR, NGOs) and **community trust** (e.g., refugee-led committees).
q28_linkages.mechanism: Direct implementation by partners with technical expertise in protection.

q28_linkages.link: Policy engagement (e.g., advocating for refugee rights) → Requires **diplomatic leverage** (UK’s HDG chairmanship) and **government relationships** (Ministry of Home Affairs).
q28_linkages.mechanism: Formal coordination structures and high-level dialogues.

q28_linkages.link: Disaster management capacity building → Requires **institutional partnerships** (Prime Minister’s Office, local governments) and **technical training providers**.
q28_linkages.mechanism: Embedded advisors and joint planning with government departments.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: 1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: Rapid emergency response (e.g., new DRC refugee influx) may bypass slower community consultation processes. 2) **Expertise vs. Ownership**: Northern-led policy engagement (FCDO/UNHCR) risks overshadowing local government ownership of refugee responses. 3) **Cost vs. Reach**: Investing in **alternative cooking fuels** (to reduce SGBV) is costlier than traditional firewood but aligns with equity goals for women/girls.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Prioritizing **repatriation support** (e.g., skills for Burundian refugees) over **local integration** (limited by government policy).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.impact: Efficiency: Aligns with government priorities; Equity: Excludes long-term solutions for Congolese refugees.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Using **multi-year funding** for predictability vs. **annual prioritization** to adapt to changing needs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.impact: Efficiency: Reduces administrative burden; Equity: May miss emerging vulnerabilities.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: **Direct service delivery** (e.g., food aid) vs. **systems strengthening** (e.g., disaster management capacity).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.impact: Efficiency: Immediate lives saved; Equity: Long-term resilience for host communities.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major risk rating** (FCAS context) justifies **intensive oversight** (e.g., annual reflections on policy engagement, break clauses) and **flexible funding** (contingency for emergencies). The volatile regional context (DRC/Burundi conflicts) requires adaptive management to reallocate resources quickly.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles: 1) **UNHCR/NGOs** receive support for protection systems (e.g., GBV prevention, child protection); 2) **Government ministries** (Disaster Management Department) get technical training for emergency response; 3) **Refugee communities** participate in decision-making (AAP) to refine interventions.

quote.intersection_quote: "The lack of a holistic approach comprising refugee assistance, disaster relief, and public health emergency response has led to response and coordination challenges." (Document: D0006587.odt, Humanitarian System Overview) && "T-HAP will aim to deliver on key policy outcomes working with like-minded donors, Ministry of Home Affairs, Prime Minister’s Office, and Disaster Management Department." (Document: D0006587.odt, Policy Engagement)
quote.tradeoffs_quote: "The programme will support an estimated 266,000 refugees and asylum seekers... [while] the total refugee population will be influenced by on-going repatriation activities and new influx from DRC." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Scope) && "T-HAP will use vulnerability targeting to prioritise vulnerable households, and target women and girls." (Document: D0006587.odt, Protection Activities)

key_programme_risks: Government policy shifts further restricting refugee rights (e.g., forced repatriation, encampment).
Reduced global humanitarian funding limiting programme scope (only 37% of 2023 UN appeal funded).
Fragmented coordination among humanitarian actors leading to gaps/duplication.
Climate-induced disasters (floods, droughts) exacerbating refugee and host community vulnerabilities.
Protection risks (SGBV, child labor) increasing due to food ration cuts and firewood shortages.
Limited durable solutions for Congolese refugees (protracted displacement >20 years).
Weak disaster management capacity at national/local levels (lack of technical expertise).
Refugee repatriation pressures (e.g., Burundi) without adequate reintegration support.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Sustained policy engagement with Ministry of Home Affairs and Prime Minister’s Office; leverage UK’s diplomatic role as HDG chair.
Multi-year funding approach; coordinate with like-minded donors to mobilize additional resources.
Invest in strengthening UN-led and donor-led coordination systems (e.g., formalize HDG structures).
Build national disaster management capabilities; preposition shelter/NFI supplies for emergencies.
Alternative cooking fuels to reduce firewood collection; targeted livelihoods for women/girls.
Advocate for expanded resettlement opportunities (e.g., for Congolese refugees); skills training for repatriation.
Technical training for Disaster Management Department; establish contingency funds.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Lessons from DRC/Burundi conflicts**: Protracted displacement requires **long-term funding** and **flexible programming** (e.g., adaptive management clauses).
**Lessons from Tanzania’s CRRF withdrawal (2018)**: Policy engagement must balance **government priorities** (repatriation) with **protection principles** (non-refoulement).
**Lessons from COVID-19/Ukraine funding cuts**: **Multi-year funding** and **contingency mechanisms** are critical in FCAS contexts with volatile donor flows.
**Lessons from Uganda’s refugee model**: **Host community integration** (e.g., livelihoods, services) reduces tensions but requires government buy-in (currently limited in Tanzania).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Coordination gaps**: Past programmes showed weak coordination among refugee actors; T-HAP will invest in formalizing structures (e.g., HDG, ISCG). 2) **Policy shifts**: Tanzania’s withdrawal from CRRF (2018) highlighted need for **sustained policy engagement** to mitigate restrictive policies. 3) **Flexibility value**: Previous UK programme’s flexibility enabled rapid response to Ebola/COVID-19; T-HAP includes **contingency funds** and **break clauses**. 4) **Protection gains**: Investments in WASH and education infrastructure (e.g., schools, water networks) provided **comparative advantage** for low-cost, high-impact interventions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Added adaptive management**: Break clauses in policy engagement components to pause ineffective activities. 2) **Expanded disaster management focus**: Previous programmes were refugee-only; T-HAP now includes **national disaster capacity building**. 3) **Stronger coordination mechanisms**: Formalizing donor coordination (HDG) and government engagement (Ministry of Home Affairs). 4) **Targeted livelihoods**: Focus on **repatriation-aligned skills** (e.g., baking, tailoring) due to government restrictions on local integration.

quote.lessons_quote: "Lesson 1: Coordination among refugee actors needs strengthening. T-HAP will therefore invest time and resources into supporting the UN-led, and donor-led coordination system." (Document: D0006587.odt, Lessons Learned) && "Lesson 4: Programme flexibility allowed the country office to immediately respond to emergencies. T-HAP will invest in rapid response delivery mechanisms." (Document: D0006587.odt, Lessons Learned)
quote.design_changes_quote: "T-HAP will broaden its mandate beyond refugee response to include building national disaster management capabilities." (Document: D0006587.odt, Programme Adaptations) && "The programme will be designed with break clauses in the policy engagement components, allowing for regular and annual reflections on what is effective." (Document: D0006587.odt, Adaptive Management)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s role as **second-largest donor** (after the US) and **chair of the Humanitarian Donor Group** enables it to leverage other donors’ funding and shape collective priorities. The programme aims to contribute **6% of UNHCR’s 2024 operational budget** for Tanzania (£89.9m required).

quote.budget_quote: "Programme Value: £19,800,000" (Document: D0006587.odt, SummarySheet) && "An annual contribution of up to £6m for the first two years... equivalent to 6 percent of the total refugee response funding required." (Document: D0006587.odt, Financial Overview)
quote.leverage_quote: "The UK’s provision of predictable, flexible, and multi-year funding... allowing partners to better plan, be more strategic and respond to changing needs." (Document: D0006587.odt, UK Role) && "The UK maintained this position [as second-largest donor] through to 2021... This position will help the UK build relationships with like-minded donors." (Document: D0006587.odt, Donor Context)

metadata.programme_name: ODI Fellowship Scheme
metadata.quote: "The ODIFellowship Scheme recruits and deploys early-career economists and statisticians to partner governments in low and middle-income countries for two-year placements. These technical experts help build strategic economic partnerships creating stronger institutions by i) strengthening the internal systems of ministries ii) improving national and sub-national policies iii) strengthening networks and building coalitions." (D0002804.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original Project start and end dates: 1st April 2022-31st March 2025. Time extension agreed to January 2026." (D0006078.odt, Summary Information) and "New project end date (if applicable): December 2026" (D0006078.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The ODI Fellowship Scheme deploys early-career economists and statisticians to government ministries in low- and middle-income countries for two-year placements. The primary objective is to build institutional capacity by embedding fellows within host organizations to strengthen internal systems, improve policy-making, and foster networks. This approach focuses on long-term skill transfer and institutional strengthening rather than short-term technical assistance.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The ODIFellowship Scheme recruits and deploys early-careereconomists and statisticians to partner governments in low and middle-income countries for two-year placements. These technical experts help build strategic economic partnerships creating stronger institutions by i) strengthening the internal systems of ministries ii) improving national and sub-national policies iii) strengthening networks and building coalitions." (D0002804.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened internal systems of ministries (e.g., fiscal policy, budgeting, statistics)
Improved national and sub-national policies (e.g., macro-economic policy, government administration)
Strengthened networks and coalitions (e.g., between ministries, international donors, investors)
Training and mentoring of host country staff (e.g., formal and informal training on data management, economic analysis)
Co-production of policy design, research, and analysis (e.g., models, reports, policy papers)
Creation of a cadre of 'international civil servants' with deeper understanding of LMIC contexts (48 fellows in 2024 cohort)
Direct support to 14-16 FCDO priority countries (e.g., Pacific Island Countries, Africa, South Asia)
Contribution to climate resilience and economic recovery in vulnerable regions (e.g., Pacific Island Countries)
what_objectives.summary: The ODI Fellowship Scheme is a long-term capacity-building programme that embeds early-career economists and statisticians in government ministries to strengthen institutions, improve policies, and build networks. It combines technical support with skill transfer and institutional development, focusing on sustainable impact in priority countries.
what_objectives.quote: "Fellows will be embedded within host government institutions, often Ministries of Finance, Planning, Statistics, Health and Education. We will seek to align placements with FCDO’s sectoral objectives in climate and protecting nature; global health security and educating women and girls." (D0002804.odt, Alignment with Research & Evidence Department’s (RED) Business plan)

countries_regions: Pacific Island Countries (Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Tonga, Papua New Guinea, Samoa)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in low- and middle-income countries with varying degrees of fragility, including Pacific Island Countries vulnerable to climate change and economic shocks. While not explicitly classified as FCAS, the context includes weak institutions, high staff turnover, and structural economic challenges, which are mitigated through embedded support and close monitoring.
where_context.q5_source: "The Pacific is region is becoming less resilient and more vulnerable. Climate change is an existential threat for many Pacific Island Countries (PICs). COVID exacerbated structural economic weaknesses—notably heavy reliance on aid and tourism—and reversed development gains." (D0002805.odt, Objective of the cost extension) and "In low-and middle-income countries the civil service frequently operates in challenging environments where human and financial resources are constrained." (D0002804.odt, UK Expertise and the Skills Gap)
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (e.g., existential threat to Pacific Island Countries)
economic vulnerability (e.g., reliance on aid/tourism in Pacific)
political economy challenges (e.g., limited capacity to retain skilled staff)
language barriers (e.g., need for fellows fluent in local languages)
security risks (e.g., high-risk countries requiring third-party security providers)
data limitations (e.g., need for improved data management systems)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and high staff turnover in host countries limit the sustainability of capacity-building efforts, requiring fellows to focus on embedded, collaborative work and system strengthening. Climate and economic vulnerabilities in regions like the Pacific necessitate tailored support for resilience. Security and language constraints affect fellow placement and onboarding, while data limitations shape the technical focus of the programme.
where_context.quote: "In many low-and middle-income countries the national civil service operates in challenging environments where human and financial resources are constrained. In these circumstances governments often struggle to attract and retain high-quality civil servants across a variety of sectors." (D0002804.odt, UK Expertise and the Skills Gap)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ODI (UK-based) manages the programme, including fellow selection, placement, and performance monitoring, with input from FCDO country offices and host governments. Host institutions employ fellows but rely on ODI for technical and managerial support. Decision-making power rests primarily with ODI and FCDO, with limited autonomy for Southern partners beyond host ministry collaboration.
q10_capacity_building_details: embedded training (on-the-job skill transfer to host ministry staff)
mentorship (informal and formal support from fellows to colleagues)
co-production of work (joint development of policies, models, and systems)
institutional strengthening (e.g., setting up committees, HR systems, data management)
network building (linking host institutions with international donors and investors)
post-fellowship alumni engagement (leveraging ODI’s global network)

who_partners.quote: "ODI – the Overseas Development Institute – will arrange the placements, recruit and deploy the Fellows. They will follow their usual procedures for the Scheme, including safeguarding, gender equality and diversity." (D0002805.odt, Approach to implementation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is funded through an Accountable Grant to ODI, with quarterly reimbursements in arrears. This instrument allows FCDO to reimburse ODI for actual costs incurred, including fellow salaries, programme management, and overheads, while maintaining oversight through regular reporting and approvals.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ODI is the sole implementer, responsible for all aspects of delivery, including recruitment, placement, monitoring, and technical support. FCDO provides strategic oversight through a steering group and programme manager, while country offices and host ministries collaborate on placement selection and local engagement. The structure is centralized but includes decentralized elements like country focal points.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ODI was selected due to its long-standing relationship with FCDO (since 1963), specialized expertise in embedding fellows, existing networks in host countries, and proven track record of delivering the Fellowship Scheme. The direct award reflects ODI’s unique role as the sole provider of this type of embedded technical assistance.
how_mechanism.quote: "AfurtherAccountableGranttoODIisthepreferredoption.Weconsiderthisdeliverychoice(alongwithourCommercialBusinessPartner)thebestoptiontomeettheprogrammeoutcomesandimpactoutlinedintheToC." (D0002804.odt, Delivery choice) and "ODI has submitted a proposal for an extension to the current scheme. We have carefully considered the proposed costs noting that these represent the actual costs of the cost of FCDO funded fellows, direct programme management costs and the correct proportion of Non-Project Attributable Costs (NPAC)." (D0002804.odt, Delivery choice)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The governance structure includes: 1) A joint FCDO-ODI management group for day-to-day oversight, meeting monthly; 2) A strategic FCDO Steering Group that meets quarterly and at key stages (e.g., approval of placements and country strategies); 3) FCDO country offices (Economic and Statistics Advisers) engaged in selecting placements and producing country engagement plans. ODI also manages a ‘network of fellowship funders’ to coordinate with other donors.
how_governance.quote: "The FCDO SRO will take a strategic overview with the PRO managing day to day programme decisions along with the Programme Manager. The Programme Manager will convene regular management meetings with ODI (monthly) as well as a more strategic quarterly meeting of an FCDO Steering Group." (D0002804.odt, FCDO management) and "Regular quarterly reporting will be used to monitor if the programme is meeting its objectives as planned." (D0002804.odt, Log frame monitoring against disbursements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, as seen in the cost extensions for Pacific fellows and adjustments to country footprints. However, major changes (e.g., adding new thematic areas) require explicit approval and are deferred to future business cases.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities mid-stream with FCDO approval, as demonstrated by the expansion into the Pacific region and the focus on climate resilience. Country engagement plans and fellow objectives are agreed in advance but can be revised based on emerging needs, subject to steering committee oversight.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme is agile enough to be able to re-direct focus between cohorts of Fellows." (D0002804.odt, FCDO risk appetite statement) and "FCDO country offices hosting Fellows will be engaged with through specific country engagement plans." (D0002804.odt, Increasing impact)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ODI (implementer) → Host ministries (employer of fellows). ODI acts as both the fund manager and direct implementer, with no additional sub-grantees.
how_efficiency.quote: "Funding will be made through an Accountable Grant and will be paid quarterly in arrears (in line with standard FCDO AG procedures)." (D0002804.odt, Funding mechanism and frequency) and "The key costs are: Direct support for fellows; Direct costs of ODI supervision; ODI’s indirect delivery costs (Non-Project Attributable Costs)." (D0002804.odt, Delivery choice)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: No intervention (discontinuing FCDO funding, relying on other donors)
Option 2: Consultancy capacity development programme (short-term external consultants in 8-10 countries)
Option 3: Funding a more FCDO priorities-focused element of the ODI Fellowship Scheme (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The ODI Fellowship Scheme was chosen for its unique embedded approach, which builds long-term institutional capacity and aligns with FCDO’s strategic objectives (e.g., economic management for poverty reduction, soft power, and diplomatic influence). The scheme offers better value for money compared to consultancy models, leverages ODI’s existing networks and expertise, and allows for closer alignment with FCDO priority countries and sectors (e.g., climate, health, education). The direct award to ODI reflects its unmatched track record and the need for agility in responding to country contexts.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (lower cost per fellow vs. consultancies)
risk mitigation (embedded fellows reduce reputational and delivery risks)
partner capacity (ODI’s 60-year experience and host government relationships)
flexibility (ability to adapt to emerging country needs)
equity (focus on diverse recruitment and inclusive development impacts)
diplomatic impact (scheme’s role in UK soft power and influence)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fellows fail to deliver expected development and diplomatic impacts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear objectives agreed upfront for each fellowship, linked to HQ and Mission Campaign Goals, with stronger monitoring and supervision.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funding is not available for fellows to complete their two-year fellowships
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO provides funding by cohort, with cost extensions approved as needed (e.g., Pacific expansion).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fellows are involved in Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (SEAH)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-fellowship training, clear reporting lines, safeguarding standards in MoUs with hosts, and ongoing monitoring by ODI with immediate reporting to FCDO.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced FCDO funding weakens the ODI-FCDO relationship
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on a smaller number of more aligned fellowships to modernize the partnership and ensure coherence with FCDO objectives.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High staff turnover in host organizations limits sustainability
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on co-production of work, formal training, and system improvements that outlive fellow placements.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost per fellow compared to alternatives)
efficiency (streamlined management with small central team)
effectiveness (evidence of capacity building and policy impact)
equity (diverse recruitment and inclusive development outcomes)
why_rationale.quote: "This is the preferred option as it will deliver the long-term outcome and impact detailed in the ToC. It addresses weaknesses in evidence detailed in the ToC to mitigate risks to the programme success. It offers the best value for money in that this option recognises the benefits of the low cost of the existing model but, that with a little more investment the impact and sustainability of the programme could be much greater." (D0002804.odt, Recommendation) and "The total cost of an ODI fellow (expected cost £45,000-£70,000 per year per fellow) compares favourably with that for junior consultancy inputs (estimated at £88,000 per year plus travel, accommodation, technical/in country support and duty of care costs)." (D0002804.odt, Evaluation findings on value)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country scope and focus on low- and middle-income contexts constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) Existing networks in priority countries (e.g., ODI’s 60-year history); 2) Capacity to manage safeguarding and logistics in high-risk or remote settings (e.g., Pacific Island Countries); 3) Ability to navigate weak institutional environments (e.g., through embedded fellows rather than external consultants). The need for language skills and local knowledge further limits partners to those with in-country associates or ex-fellow networks.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for existing host government relationships (limits new partners)
Capacity to operate in fragile or remote contexts (e.g., Pacific Islands)
Requirement for language fluency and cultural understanding (favors ODI’s alumni network)
High staff turnover in host ministries (requires long-term embedded support)
Security risks in some countries (necessitates ODI’s global security department)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s capacity-building objectives (embedded, long-term skill transfer) determine the delivery structure: 1) **Embedded placements** require a single implementer (ODI) to manage recruitment, onboarding, and performance, rather than a consortium; 2) **Co-production of work** necessitates close collaboration with host ministries, shaping the governance structure (e.g., country engagement plans); 3) **Diverse technical needs** (economics, statistics, climate, health) drive the use of thematic support networks (e.g., University of York for health economics). The focus on sustainability and soft power also informs the intensive oversight model (e.g., quarterly steering groups).
q28_linkages: Embedded capacity building → Single implementer (ODI) with decentralized country focal points
Long-term skill transfer → Intensive oversight (quarterly reviews, performance monitoring)
Diverse technical areas → Thematic support networks (e.g., health, climate) integrated into ODI’s structure
Diplomatic and soft power goals → FCDO-led steering group and alignment with country business plans
Need for agility → Accountable Grant with moderate fund reallocation flexibility
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) **Diverse recruitment vs. speed**: Efforts to attract a more diverse pool of candidates (e.g., underrepresented groups) require wider dissemination and updated materials, which may slow recruitment; 2) **Inclusive development vs. cost**: Expanding to new regions (e.g., Pacific) or thematic areas (e.g., health) increases impact but requires additional funding and management resources; 3) **Local ownership vs. technical quality**: While fellows are embedded in host ministries, decision-making power remains with ODI/FCDO to ensure standards, limiting Southern-led autonomy.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Diverse recruitment (e.g., disability, socio-economic background) vs. reliance on established academic networks for high-quality candidates
Expansion to Pacific Island Countries (equity) vs. higher per-fellow costs and logistical challenges (efficiency)
Embedded, long-term placements (effectiveness) vs. higher management intensity and slower scalability (economy)
Host ministry employment of fellows (ownership) vs. ODI/FCDO control over selection and objectives (accountability)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s moderate risk profile (e.g., weak institutions, climate vulnerability in Pacific) drives intensive management structures: 1) **Quarterly oversight** and steering groups mitigate risks of misaligned placements; 2) **Country engagement plans** address contextual constraints (e.g., political economy, language barriers); 3) **Safeguarding officer and security protocols** respond to high-risk country placements; 4) **Break clauses** in funding agreements manage financial risks (e.g., Pacific extensions). The need for adaptability in fragile contexts also informs the use of country focal points for local troubleshooting.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) **Embedding fellows as employees** of host ministries to foster skill transfer and institutional ownership; 2) **Using ex-fellows as country focal points** to leverage local knowledge and networks; 3) **Including thematic experts** (e.g., University of York for health economics) to provide tailored technical support; 4) **Prioritizing co-production** in fellow-colleague relationships to ensure sustainable systems (e.g., data management, HR processes). The focus on mutual learning also informs ODI’s post-fellowship alumni engagement.
intersections.quote: "The beauty is that fellows are embedded. It is not Technical Assistance (TA), bringing in external experts. ODI people are embedded in the system and help the system to develop from inside it. It is different from a classic TA approach." (D0002804.odt, Option 2 Consultancy capacity development programme interventions) and "ODI will experiment working through nominated ‘country focal points’ in those countries where ODI has an established network of in-country associates." (D0002804.odt, Supporting effective placements through ‘country focal points’) and "ODI will be more deliberate and comprehensive in how it provides technical support and peer exchange across different specialisms." (D0002804.odt, Drawing from ODI research staff and networks to provide thematic expertise)

key_programme_risks: Fellows fail to deliver expected development and diplomatic impacts (mitigated by clear objectives and monitoring)
Funding gaps interrupt fellow placements (mitigated by cohort-based funding and cost extensions)
Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (SEAH) incidents (mitigated by training, reporting lines, and ODI safeguarding officer)
High staff turnover in host ministries limits sustainability (mitigated by co-production and system improvements)
Reputational risk to FCDO from reduced scheme funding (mitigated by focusing on aligned, high-impact placements)
Climate and economic shocks in Pacific region (mitigated by tailored support and flexibility in placements)
Weak onboarding processes in host organizations (mitigated by country focal points and engagement strategies)
Limited diversity in fellow recruitment (mitigated by updated promotional materials and wider dissemination)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fellows fail to deliver expected impacts
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Set clear, SMART objectives for each fellowship upfront, linked to FCDO campaign goals, with stronger monitoring and supervision.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Funding unavailable for fellows to complete placements
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO provides funding by cohort (e.g., £3m extension in 2024) and approves cost extensions as needed.
Pre-fellowship safeguarding training, clear reporting lines, standards in MoUs with hosts, and ongoing monitoring by ODI with immediate FCDO reporting.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High staff turnover in host ministries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on co-producing work with colleagues, formal training, and improving systems (e.g., HR, data management) to outlast placements.
Shift to fewer, more aligned fellowships in priority countries to modernize the partnership and ensure coherence with FCDO objectives.
Tailored support for resilience (e.g., fiscal policy, macroeconomic advice) and flexible funding extensions (e.g., £1.1m for Pacific fellows).
Country focal points support host ministries in strengthening onboarding and setting objectives for fellows.
Update promotional materials to encourage underrepresented groups, disseminate widely, and monitor diversity metrics.

fcas_specific_lessons: Embedded fellows are more effective than external consultants in fragile contexts, as they build trust and adapt to local systems (e.g., "The beauty is that fellows are embedded... help the system to develop from inside it.")
Co-production and iterative approaches work better than "best practice" transplants in weak institutional environments (cites Andrews et al. on state capability)
Long-term placements (2 years) allow time for colleagues to learn and systems to strengthen, unlike short-term TA
Country focal points (e.g., ex-fellows) help navigate political and leadership challenges in fragile states
Safeguarding and duty of care must be prioritized in high-risk FCAS contexts (e.g., evacuation plans, security monitoring)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 external evaluation highlighted: 1) **Need for clearer role definitions**: Ambiguity about whether fellows should fill skills gaps or focus on capacity building led to mismatched expectations; 2) **Importance of performance management**: Lack of structured support from ODI hindered fellow effectiveness; 3) **Sustainability challenges**: Limited systematic effort to measure long-term impact or promote sustainability beyond placements; 4) **Diversity gaps**: Underrepresentation in disability and socio-economic backgrounds due to unclear application guidance; 5) **Monitoring weaknesses**: Inconsistent debriefs and lessons-sharing across placements. These led to reforms in the 2022 proposal, including country focal points, revised recruitment, and stronger M&E.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes based on lessons include: 1) **Country focal points**: Introduced to improve placement support and troubleshooting; 2) **Revised recruitment**: Updated application forms to focus on skills (e.g., language, work experience) and wider dissemination to diverse candidates; 3) **Stronger performance management**: Dedicated lead for placements to provide guidance and monitor progress; 4) **Enhanced safeguarding**: New policies, buddy systems, and counselling services post-COVID; 5) **Thematic expansion**: Pilot support for climate and health specialists (though deferred to future cohorts); 6) **Extended timeframe**: 10-month extension to 2026 to accommodate delayed 2023 cohort; 7) **Pacific focus**: Added placements in Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, etc., due to climate vulnerability.
risks_lessons.quote: "The evaluation found that there was general agreement amongst Fellows and supervisors that working alongside each other in the co-production of policies and strategies strengthened the capacities of the staff around them. This was pointed out by many stakeholders to be in stark contrast to the alternative modality of short-term external consultants." (D0002804.odt, Option 2 Consultancy capacity development programme interventions) and "The recent external programme evaluation found that ‘the scheme is highly aligned with FCDO’s strategic objectives around economic management for poverty reduction and good statistics to inform good decision-making’. The scheme has a strong track record in supporting institution building and mutual learning. The evaluation further found that ‘Fellows mostly operate at high levels of government, and the large amount of goodwill they garner, is often a strong tool for soft power and key for diplomacy.’" (D0002804.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has mobilized co-funding from 11 partners, supporting 19 of the 48 fellows in the 2024 cohort (40%). This includes multilateral organizations (e.g., Global Fund, WHO), governments (e.g., Australia, Timor-Leste), and foundations (e.g., Gates). The Pacific expansion also leveraged coordination with Australia (DFAT) to maximize impact.
financial_details.quote: "The business case ceiling will be increased by an additional £1.1 million in addition to the £3 million approved in August 2024 to ensure uninterrupted funding of the ODI Fellowship Scheme in the Pacific while a new business case is written." (D0006078.odt, Objective of the cost extension) and "The key costs are: Direct support for fellows (compensation, health, insurance, travel); Direct costs of ODI supervision; ODI’s indirect delivery costs (Non-Project Attributable Costs)." (D0002804.odt, Delivery choice) and "FUNDER [TABLE]: FCDO main (29 fellows), FCDO Pacific (6), Office for National Statistics (1), Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (1), The Global Fund (3), WHO Guinea Bissau (1), Government of Timor-Leste (3), EdTech (1), Namibia Nature Foundation (1), DFAT (2)." (D0006078.odt, Funder table)

metadata.programme_name: Africa Humanitarian Response Fund II (AHRFII)
metadata.quote: "The programme will deliver quality humanitarian assistance in African contexts where the FCDO has no in-country humanitarian expertise or where a regional response is more efficient than a country-by-country approach." (D0003594.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: 10 August 2023 – 30 June 2027" (S30138115.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct humanitarian assistance), financing mechanism (channeling funds to partners), and capacity building (technical assistance and preparedness). It delivers life-saving assistance while also strengthening humanitarian systems and response capabilities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will deliver quality humanitarian assistance in African contexts... It will also provide technical assistance, operational support and preparedness drawing on UK expertise and scientific evidence." (D0003594.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 500,000 people receiving multi-sector humanitarian assistance across CAR, Cameroon and Eritrea in the first year (D0003594.odt, Table 4)
200,000+ people reached in regional Sudan crisis response (D0006248.odt, Expected results)
100,000 people potentially reached in extended CAR support (S30138115.odt, Results)
Technical assistance for system-wide Accountability to Affected Persons (AAP) projects (D0003594.odt, Technical assistance section)
Support for preparedness and early warning systems (D0003594.odt, Technical assistance section)
Multi-year funding for 3-4 protracted crises (CAR, Eritrea, Cameroon, Madagascar) (D0003594.odt, Protracted Crises Response)
Rapid response to sudden onset crises through Internal Risk Facility (IRF) (D0003594.odt, Sudden onset and emerging crises)
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers life-saving humanitarian assistance in African contexts where FCDO lacks in-country expertise, combining direct service delivery with system strengthening through technical assistance and preparedness support.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver quality humanitarian assistance in African contexts where the FCDO has no in-country humanitarian expertise or where a regional response is more efficient than a country-by-country approach." (D0003594.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in conflict-affected regions with severe humanitarian needs, including CAR where armed groups control territory and the government is virtually bankrupt. Multiple countries face instability, climate disasters, and economic shocks.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme will continue to have a severe rating because it accepts that a lot of activities carry a severe degree of residual risk. Many of the countries the programme operates in, including the Central African Republic are conflict affected." (S30138115.odt, Risk section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit partner operations in conflict zones like CAR and Cameroon. Weak institutions in countries like Eritrea make needs assessment difficult. Climate risks (droughts, floods) create unpredictable spikes in need. Data limitations in closed contexts like Eritrea hinder evidence-based planning. Political economy factors (e.g., Russia's involvement in CAR) complicate donor coordination.
where_context.quote: "Humanitarian access in the North-West South-West regions has been very challenging since the start of this crisis, with administrative impediments but also more worryingly aid workers and humanitarian beneficiaries attacked and even killed." (D0003594.odt, Cameroon section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains full decision-making authority over fund allocation, strategy, and partner selection. Southern partners implement according to FCDO-approved plans.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to improve humanitarian operations
support for system-wide Accountability to Affected Persons (AAP) projects
deployment of UN-embedded experts
monitoring and accountability mechanisms
preparedness and early action support
localisation through country-based pooled funds

partner_organizations.role: implementing partner

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner

partner_organizations.name: Stand-By Partnership arrangements
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance provider

partner_organizations.role: climate data/technical support

partner_organizations.name: African Union
partner_organizations.role: regional coordination
