partner_organizations.role: sub-implementers

who_partners.quote: "The programme will work through trusted partners with strong controls who have been assessed for their ability to manage risk, including losses, and on the mitigation measures they have in place." (S30138115.odt, Risk section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of multi-year grants for protracted crises, an Internal Risk Facility (IRF) for rapid response, and technical assistance agreements. The IRF operates as a contingent fund activated through a formal decision process.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO's Pan Africa Department manages the fund centrally, with technical input from Humanitarian Department. Implementing partners (UN agencies, NGOs) deliver services according to FCDO-approved strategies. The IRF component has a specific activation protocol involving multiple FCDO stakeholders.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on track record in-country, alignment with HRP priorities, and ability to operate in high-risk environments. In some contexts (e.g., CAR), only limited numbers of partners are willing/able to operate, making continuity of existing suppliers the best value for money.
how_mechanism.quote: "A track record of delivery in-country will be a consideration in partner selection; continuity of existing suppliers may therefore be considered the best value for money, particularly in CAR, Eritrea and Cameroon." (D0003594.odt, Programme delivery section)

how_governance.quote: "Approval for the intervention will be sought from the head of PD through a submission setting out: i) The humanitarian needs; ii) Justification for UK response; iii) The humanitarian implementation strategy..." (D0003594.odt, Guidelines for accessing the IRF)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between protracted crises and sudden onset responses with approval. The IRF allows rapid reallocation for emergencies, but has a £9.2m ceiling. Reprogramming requires formal submission and approval process.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes annual reviews and can adjust priorities based on evolving needs. Partners delivering protracted crises can flex activities to respond to sudden shocks (e.g., flooding) with agreement. New crises require activation through the IRF decision tree.
how_flexibility.quote: "Partners delivering against protracted crises will be able, with agreement, to flex their activities to respond to sudden onset emergencies, such as flooding, cyclones and other shocks." (D0003594.odt, Protracted crises section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (UN/NGO) → [Beneficiaries]. Some technical assistance may involve additional layer: FCDO → Intermediary (e.g., Stand-By Partnership) → Implementer.
how_efficiency.quote: "Programme includes life-saving humanitarian support focusing on a multi-sector approach; an Internal Risk Facility enabling rapid response to sudden onset crises; and enabling actions and technical assistance to improve the overall humanitarian response." (D0006248.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Discontinue regional programming (NOT RECOMMENDED)
Option 2: Separate humanitarian business cases for each context (NOT RECOMMENDED)
Option 3: Separate business cases for (i) preparedness; (ii) sudden onset response; (iii) protracted crises (NOT RECOMMENDED)
Option 4: One combined business case (RECOMMENDED - CHOSEN OPTION)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The combined business case (Option 4) was chosen because it: 1) Enables rapid response without increasing humanitarian capacity; 2) Reduces administrative burden for FCDO and partners; 3) Maximizes learning across responses; 4) Provides mechanism for sudden onset crises to transition into protracted support; 5) Improves coherence across the portfolio; 6) Allows multi-year financing for better VFM.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transaction costs for multiple business cases (Options 2 & 3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Single business case reduces administrative burden and improves efficiency

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in response time for separate business cases
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Combined case with IRF enables rapid mobilization

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Artificial delineation between crisis types (Option 3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Combined approach recognizes that sudden onset and protracted crises often co-occur

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited IRF scale (£9.2m ceiling) may require future amendments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Decision tree ensures only highest-priority crises access IRF; programme extensions can be sought if needed

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing diverse crises under one business case
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear decision criteria and intervention tables guide response selection

why_rationale.quote: "This approach would enable the UK to respond rapidly in many contexts without having to increase humanitarian capacity. It reduces administration for FCDO and implementing partners by reducing the number of agreements... A mechanism that enables sudden onset emergency responses to transition into protracted crisis responses is efficient and maximises opportunities for learning." (D0003594.odt, Option 4 recommendation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating context severely constrains partner selection: 1) In CAR, only partners with proven ability to operate in active conflict zones are considered; 2) In Eritrea, limited information and government restrictions mean only partners with existing access can deliver; 3) Climate risks require partners with disaster preparedness expertise; 4) Conflict dynamics in Cameroon limit partners to those acceptable to both government and non-state armed groups.
q27_constraints_detail: Active conflict in CAR limits to partners with conflict zone experience
Eritrea's closed political context restricts to partners with government acceptance
Cameroon's Anglophone crisis requires partners acceptable to both sides
Climate vulnerability demands partners with disaster response capacity
Weak institutions in many countries necessitate partners who can navigate bureaucratic challenges
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (direct service delivery + system strengthening) determine the hybrid delivery structure: 1) Multi-year grants for protracted crises enable predictable financing for service delivery; 2) IRF mechanism provides flexibility for rapid response; 3) Technical assistance component supports system strengthening; 4) Regional approach enables cross-border coordination for complex crises like Sudan refugee flows.
q28_linkages: Multi-year funding for protracted crises → enables partner retention and institutional memory
IRF mechanism → facilitates rapid response to sudden onset crises
Technical assistance component → supports system-wide reforms and preparedness
Regional scope → allows coherent response to cross-border crises (e.g., Sudan refugee flows)
Flexibility between components → enables adaptation to evolving needs
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses several equity-efficiency tradeoffs: 1) Speed vs. inclusion: The IRF enables rapid response but has limited funds (£9.2m), potentially excluding some vulnerable groups; 2) Northern expertise vs. local ownership: Technical assistance relies on UK/UN expertise while aiming to support localisation; 3) Cost vs. reach: Operating in high-risk environments like CAR increases costs but is necessary to reach most vulnerable populations; 4) Standardization vs. context adaptation: Regional approach improves efficiency but requires balancing standardized processes with context-specific needs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Rapid IRF responses (efficiency) vs. limited funds potentially excluding some needs (equity)
Northern technical expertise (efficiency) vs. localisation commitments (equity)
High costs of FCAS operations (efficiency) vs. reaching most vulnerable (equity)
Standardized regional processes (efficiency) vs. context-specific adaptation (equity)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The severe risk profile (FCAS contexts) drives intensive management: 1) All interventions require formal approval processes; 2) Partners undergo enhanced due diligence; 3) IRF activations involve multiple stakeholder consultations; 4) High-risk responses require Ministerial approval for amounts over £5m; 5) Continuous monitoring of safeguarding and aid diversion risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles through: 1) Technical assistance components that embed UK expertise within partner operations; 2) Support for system-wide AAP projects that require partners to implement accountability mechanisms; 3) Preparedness funding that builds partners' early warning and response capacities; 4) Localisation support that gradually increases Southern partners' roles in decision-making.
intersections.quote: "The programme will work through trusted partners with strong controls who have been assessed for their ability to manage risk, including losses, and on the mitigation measures they have in place." (S30138115.odt, Risk section)

key_programme_risks: Inability to respond to emerging crises due to IRF funding limits (only £30,000 remaining before replenishment)
Safeguarding incidents or aid diversion in high-risk FCAS contexts
Reputational damage from failed responses in visible crises
Partner capacity limitations in complex operating environments
Climate shocks creating unpredictable spikes in need
Political instability disrupting programme delivery (e.g., coups, conflict escalation)
Inflation and high food/fuel prices increasing response costs
Limited humanitarian access in conflict zones (e.g., Cameroon, CAR)
Data limitations hindering needs assessment in closed contexts (e.g., Eritrea)
Coordination challenges in multi-country regional responses

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: IRF funding limits preventing crisis response
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IRF replenishment approved (£9.17m addition); programme extensions can be sought if needed
Enhanced due diligence of partners; zero tolerance policy; strong partner controls
Robust decision criteria for IRF activation; Ministerial approval for high-risk interventions
Continuity of existing suppliers prioritized; technical assistance to build capacity
Preparedness component; climate data integration; flexible funding
Regional approach allows cross-border adaptation; constant context monitoring
Multi-year funding provides cost visibility; VFM assessments throughout
Work with partners experienced in access negotiation; adaptive programming
Use of proxy data; partner networks for information gathering
Clear FCDO leadership; standardized reporting; donor coordination

fcas_specific_lessons: Multi-year funding is essential in protracted crises for partner retention and efficiency (lesson from SHOCARR)
Flexibility must be built into budgets to respond to evolving FCAS dynamics
Technical assistance and embedded experts significantly improve response quality in complex environments
System-wide Accountability to Affected Persons (AAP) requires multi-year support in FCAS contexts
Regional approaches are necessary for cross-border crises (e.g., Sudan refugee flows, desert locusts)
Localisation is challenging but possible through country-based pooled funds in FCAS contexts
Early intervention in FCAS saves lives and reduces future costs (ROI of £1.50 for every £1 spent on preparedness)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The design incorporated lessons from: 1) Africa Humanitarian Response Fund (AHRF) Phase I - need for both large-scale and small/medium response capacity; 2) SHOCARR programme - importance of multi-year funding in protracted crises; 3) Desert locust response - value of regional approaches for cross-border crises; 4) Stand-By Partnerships - effectiveness of embedded technical expertise; 5) Cash transfer programming in CAR - VFM of market-based approaches in FCAS contexts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design adaptations based on learning: 1) Combined protracted and sudden onset components in single business case (from AHRF Phase I lessons); 2) Increased flexibility between components; 3) Expanded technical assistance role; 4) Regional scope extension to include North Africa (Libya/Egypt) for Sudan response; 5) IRF replenishment mechanism based on usage patterns; 6) Stronger emphasis on system-wide AAP projects; 7) Climate risk integration into preparedness component.
risks_lessons.quote: "The design of this programme has been informed by the lessons learnt during the first phase of the Africa Humanitarian Response Fund (AHRF) as well as the Supporting Humanitarian Operations in Central African Republic and the Region (SHOCARR) business cases: The programmes should be able to implement large scale responses as well as small to medium operations... Multi-year programming improves the VFM of operations but a proportion of the budget should be kept flexible to respond to changing needs." (D0003594.odt, Lessons Learnt)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme is designed to leverage core funding to humanitarian agencies and complement UK contributions to global pooled funds such as UN CERF, enabling greater UK visibility and influencing where pooled funds allocations are insufficient.
financial_details.quote: "The revised total programme budget will be £92.5m, including up to £9.2m IRF." (S30138115.odt, Budget section)

metadata.programme_name: Climate, Environment and Nature (CLEAN) helpdesk

quote.programme_name: "The CLEAN helpdesk will build on and succeed the Climate Mainstreaming Facility (CMF) with new risk additional dedicated resource to progress Paris alignment of ODA." (D0005097.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "AMP Start Date: April 2023", "AMP End Date: April 2026" (D0005097.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: April 2023", "AMP End Date: April 2026"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The CLEAN helpdesk is designed to provide technical assistance (TA) and capacity building to support FCDO teams in mainstreaming climate, environment, and nature (CEN) considerations into ODA programming. It also aims to ensure Paris Alignment (PA) compliance, nature-proofing, and improved reporting of International Climate Finance (ICF). The programme includes a monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) component to track progress and share lessons.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This business case seeks approval to develop a new helpdesk and technical assistance (TA) facility to support programme teams with capacity for climate, environment and nature mainstreaming." (D0005097.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: High demand met for CEN TA on climate mainstreaming, ICF, and Paris alignment and nature-proofing
PA fully embedded in FCDO ODA programming
Greater use of existing TA offers by programme teams due to enhanced awareness, convenience, and accessibility to wider CEN facilities
Improved efficiency and coordination between existing helpdesks, eventually informing a greater awareness of needs and gaps in new CEN TA/evidence generation facilities
Increased level of in-house expertise through knowledge curation activities and establishing links with Centres of Excellence and the International Academy
Stronger cases in CEN programming on NP as well as wider areas, including gender equality, disability inclusion, and social inclusion as the gateway develops over time
PA integration progress tracked, monitored, and strengthened across FCDO programming
Organisational needs of C&N TA across FCDO strategically monitored, enabling the ability to directly feed learning to wider C&N TA facilities about where needs are greatest
Regular implementation of lessons learned and dynamic adjustments to CANH to meet evolving needs of C&N programme teams over time
what_objectives.summary: The CLEAN helpdesk aims to provide a one-stop-shop gateway for climate, environment, and nature (CEN) technical assistance, ensuring FCDO programmes are Paris-aligned, nature-proofed, and capable of reporting on International Climate Finance (ICF). It builds on the Climate Mainstreaming Facility (CMF) and introduces new components like a MEL system and a centralised gateway to improve coordination and uptake of CEN support.

quote.objectives: "The CLEAN helpdesk will build on and succeed the Climate Mainstreaming Facility (CMF) with new risk additional dedicated resource to progress Paris alignment of ODA." (D0005097.odt, Programme summary)
quote.outputs: "The programme is expected to deliver the following key outputs..." (D0005097.odt, Outputs)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is assessed as moderate risk, primarily due to operational risks associated with the gateway function and the complexity of coordinating multiple CEN technical assistance facilities. The risk is mitigated through governance structures and monitoring.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0005097.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates within the constraints of FCDO's Programme Operating Framework (PrOF) Rule 5, which requires Paris Alignment and nature-proofing of all ODA. The need for technical assistance arises from limited in-house capacity and the complexity of integrating climate, environment, and nature considerations into programming.

quote.constraints: "Successfully delivering these commitments will require climate and nature to be fully integrated throughout all FCDO and ODA programming and associated upstream policies." (D0005097.odt, Organisational Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains strategic oversight and decision-making power, with the delivery partner (a non-profit organisation) managing day-to-day operations and technical assistance provision. The gateway function will coordinate with existing CEN facilities, but ultimate governance and oversight remain with FCDO.

mentorship

development of practitioner resources
