quote.partners: "The gateway function will develop productive collaborations with FCDO’s International Academy and newly proposed Centres of Excellence (CoEs), as well as other relevant development sector TA facilities." (D0005097.odt, Programme Purpose and Activities)
quote.capacity_building: "Expanding capacity for mainstreaming will enable FCDO to keep ratcheting Paris alignment ambition up... This will include collaboration with development sectors and associated cadres and TA facilities, to develop practitioner resources and materials to support CEN capabilities and decision making." (D0005097.odt, Programme Purpose and Activities)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will be delivered through an Accountable Grant (AG) mechanism, which allows for flexibility in how the technical assistance facility develops over time and enables lower day rates for consultants, as non-profit organisations typically apply no or lower mark-ups.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The CLEAN helpdesk will operate as a centralised platform (gateway) that triages CEN-related requests and connects officials to the appropriate support. The delivery partner will manage the gateway, MEL component, and technical assistance provision, while FCDO retains strategic oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection of a non-profit delivery partner is favoured due to their existing experience with FCDO, lower day rates, and the ability to quickly operationalise the helpdesk. An open competition is not feasible due to the high specialism required and the need for institutional knowledge from the previous CMF programme.

quote.funding_instrument: "An Accountable Grant (AG) mechanism is favoured over a commercial contract to utilise the breadth of climate and nature experience of the not-for-profit sector, allow flexibility in how the technical assistance facility will develop over time and enable lower day rates for consultants." (D0005097.odt, Proposed Delivery Mechanism)
quote.partner_selection: "Although holding institutional knowledge and learning externally is second-best to internal FCDO staff with the expertise, a delivery partner will be sought that already holds considerable experience of working with FCDO." (D0005097.odt, Proposed Delivery Mechanism)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: An ECED-led governance board will oversee the programme, ensuring that the gateway function meets expectations and that collaboration between different TA offers is actively managed. The board will include representatives from relevant CEN facilities and will review performance quarterly.

quote.governance: "An ECED-led governance board will ensure that expectations of the gateway are suitably met. This governance structure will be finalised through implementation." (D0005097.odt, Governance and Management Arrangements)
quote.oversight: "The overall programme is assessed as moderate risk. Risks will be reviewed quarterly with the supplier as part of the wider programme delivery review." (D0005097.odt, Risk)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components if demand exceeds supply or if certain elements (e.g., the gateway function) are not delivering value for money. Adjustments would require approval and would be considered during quarterly and annual reviews.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The MEL component will track progress and inform dynamic adjustments to the programme. If certain activities are not achieving intended impacts, resources can be reallocated or the programme can pivot to new priorities, such as ratcheting up Paris alignment ambitions post-2023.

quote.flexibility: "If demand significantly exceeds supply, future funding options will be explored to scale up this programme." (D0005097.odt, Financial Arrangements)
quote.adaptive_management: "The MEL component will track and monitor FCDO’s progress towards Paris Alignment of its Official Development Assistance (ODA), as well as tracking the success of the facility and monitoring service uptake." (D0005097.odt, Programme Purpose and Activities)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partner (non-profit organisation) → Technical Experts/Roster Consultants

quote.budget: "An initial budget of £4m, spread over three years is outlined as a starting point." (D0005097.odt, Inputs/Partners)
quote.payment_structure: "FCDO will disburse funds quarterly and in arrears on receipt and approval of a quarterly invoice and report." (D0005097.odt, Disbursement Arrangements)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (CMF ends in March 2023 without replacement)
Option 2: CMF+ (enhanced TA services with minimal remodelling)
Option 3: CLEAN (enhanced TA + gateway + mainstreaming expansion + MEL)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 (CLEAN) was chosen because it comprehensively addresses FCDO's evolving needs for Paris Alignment, nature-proofing, and CEN mainstreaming. It introduces a centralised gateway to improve coordination and uptake of existing TA facilities, expands capacity for upstream policy integration, and includes a robust MEL component to track progress and inform adaptive management. This option scored highest in a comparative analysis across impact, efficiency, evidence/learning, and agility criteria.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: CLEAN incentivises under-resourcing of in-house capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monitor requests and ensure a clear plan for directing resources towards capability activities. Only go beyond 15 days of support in exceptional circumstances.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The gateway may be too complex for a non-profit delivery partner
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Encourage consortia proposals to ensure collective skills; work closely with the partner during inception to develop a fit-for-purpose management framework; monitor performance closely and adjust if necessary.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Demand for CEN TA may be overestimated, leading to underutilisation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Conduct multiple uptake activities to raise awareness; use MEL to track demand; consider targeting strategic priorities proactively if demand is low.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The programme may fail to increase in-house capabilities, increasing reliance on TA
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Link with the International Academy and CoEs to contribute to organisational learning; design MEL metrics to monitor capability shifts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Improved PA principles at business case stage may not manifest at implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Review compliance with PA during annual programme reviews; use MEL to track progress and inform process amendments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Uncertainty in ODA budget available for ECED and CLEAN
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use an Accountable Grant mechanism to minimise delays; monitor budget availability and adjust programme scope if necessary.

quote.alternatives: "Option 3 scores the highest overall through this comparative analysis... It dropped points in recognition of the need to rationalise the new Nature Facility within the one-stop-shop concept and because it will take longer to operationalise." (D0005097.odt, Feasible options)
quote.rationale: "Option 3 is the most comprehensive vision for how CLEAN can meet current CEN TA needs... The Gateway will act as an easy access one-stop-shop for all CEN advice and technical support." (D0005097.odt, Feasible options)
quote.vfm: "Economy: average £ rate of consultants (tracked against FCDO benchmark rate); Efficiency: # requests received and fulfilled, # requests triaged; Effectiveness: # BCs supported by CANH that are subsequently approved; Equity: # Posts supported which have no other access to a climate adviser." (D0005097.odt, Monitoring and evaluation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and FCDO's central role in ODA programming constrain partner selection to organisations with existing experience working with FCDO and the ability to quickly operationalise a complex, multi-faceted technical assistance platform. The need for institutional knowledge from the CMF further limits potential partners to those already familiar with FCDO systems and processes.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for rapid operationalisation post-CMF closure (March 2023)
Requirement for institutional knowledge of FCDO systems
Complexity of coordinating multiple existing CEN TA facilities
Need to align with FCDO's PrOF Rule 5 and ICF reporting requirements
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to provide comprehensive CEN mainstreaming support—including Paris Alignment, nature-proofing, and ICF reporting—determines the platform-based delivery structure. The one-stop-shop gateway is designed to address the piecemeal nature of existing TA facilities and improve coordination, while the MEL component ensures progress can be tracked and lessons shared across FCDO.
q28_linkages: Comprehensive CEN support needs → Platform/gateway structure
Paris Alignment and nature-proofing requirements → Dedicated TA capacity and MEL component
Need for coordination among existing facilities → Gateway triage function
Learning and adaptive management needs → MEL component and knowledge repository
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between ensuring broad accessibility to CEN support (equity) and maintaining efficiency through a centralised gateway. For example, the helpdesk aims to be easily accessible to posts without embedded C&E advisors (equity) while also reducing duplication and transaction costs (efficiency). The inclusion of social development expertise in the technical roster further balances these goals by ensuring marginalised groups are considered in all advice.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Broad accessibility vs. centralised coordination (gateway design)
Inclusive support for posts without C&E advisors vs. efficiency gains from triage
Social inclusion requirements vs. rapid delivery of technical advice
Open access to knowledge vs. managing intellectual property and data sharing
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile—driven by operational complexities in the gateway function—results in quarterly oversight and a governance board to manage relationships between TA facilities. This intensity is designed to mitigate risks associated with coordinating a platform of multiple partners while ensuring flexibility to adapt as needed.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The core objective of capacity building shapes the roles of both the delivery partner and FCDO. The partner is responsible for knowledge curation, developing practitioner resources, and linking with CoEs to strengthen in-house capabilities, while FCDO's oversight ensures these activities align with broader organisational learning goals.

quote.where_who: "The success of the CMF has generated significant institutional knowledge and working experience in this space, which will be a driving factor in deciding FCDO’s award of a new AG for CLEAN delivery." (D0005097.odt, Proposed Delivery Mechanism)
quote.what_how: "The Gateway will act as an easy access one-stop-shop for all CEN advice and technical support... This will bring coherence and coordination, reducing transaction costs for officials and increasing traffic to under-utilised programmes." (D0005097.odt, Programme Purpose and Activities)
quote.equity_efficiency: "The supplier framework will require: A demonstrable commitment to equality and social inclusion... This social development expertise will similarly include other factors of marginalisation in analysis and advice." (D0005097.odt, Gender Equality and Social Inclusion)

key_programme_risks: CLEAN incentivises under-resourcing of in-house capacity
The gateway will be too complex for a non-profit delivery partner and will not perform as anticipated
Demand for CEN TA may be overestimated and CLEAN underutilised as a result
The programme will fail to sufficiently increase in-house capabilities and FCDO will become more reliant on TA capacity as a result
Improved PA principles at BC stage may not manifest into improvements at the implementation phase if they are not robustly defined and monitorable
Uncertainty in the ODA budget available for ECED and within that available for the CLEAN programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: CLEAN incentivises under-resourcing of in-house capacity
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Monitor requests, only going beyond 15 days in exceptional and verified circumstances; monitor organisational CEN capacity through internal resourcing processes; ensure a clear plan for directing increasing resource towards capabilities activities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The gateway will be too complex for a non-profit delivery partner and will not perform as anticipated
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Encourage consortia proposals to ensure collective skills; work closely with the delivery partner during inception to develop a fit-for-purpose management framework; monitor performance and adjust if necessary.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Demand for CEN TA may be overestimated and CLEAN underutilised as a result
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Conduct multiple uptake activities to raise awareness; use MEL to track demand; consider proactive targeting of strategic priorities if demand is low.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The programme will fail to sufficiently increase in-house capabilities and FCDO will become more reliant on TA capacity as a result
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Link with the International Academy and CoEs to contribute to organisational learning; design MEL metrics to monitor capability shifts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Improved PA principles at BC stage may not manifest into improvements at the implementation phase if they are not robustly defined and monitorable
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Review compliance with PA during annual programme reviews; use MEL to track progress and inform process amendments; broaden mainstreaming resource for CEN integration into upstream ODA policies.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Uncertainty in the ODA budget available for ECED and within that available for the CLEAN programme
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use an Accountable Grant mechanism to minimise delays; monitor budget availability and adjust programme scope if necessary.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the CMF informed the design of CLEAN, including the need for a more front-facing, open-access platform that prioritises ease of use. The CMF's success in delivering desk-based TA remotely during COVID-19 demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach. Key lessons included the importance of rapid same-day mini-queries, minimising administrative barriers, and ongoing awareness-raising activities to maintain organisational engagement.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The CLEAN helpdesk incorporates several design changes based on CMF lessons: 1) a gateway function to improve coordination and reduce duplication; 2) same-day mini-queries for quick knowledge access; 3) a focus on ease-of-use to broaden the user base; 4) multiple awareness-raising activities to ensure uptake; 5) a MEL component to track progress and inform adaptive management; 6) explicit integration of social inclusion and gender equality in all activities.

quote.lessons: "A report on lessons learned by the Knowledge for Development (K4D) helpdesk (2022)... has strongly informed the design of our preferred option... the CLEAN helpdesk will introduce rapid same day mini queries based on the insight that offering a quick and easily accessed basic knowledge service is key to service uptake." (D0005097.odt, Evidence Underpinning Preferred Option)
quote.design_changes: "The CLEAN helpdesk will build out from the CMF delivery model to provide a more comprehensive user-focused service... From the introduction of same day mini queries to make existing research, knowledge and good practice quickly available, to 15-day assignments for more technical tasks." (D0005097.odt, Programme Purpose and Activities)

quote.budget: "An initial budget of £4m, spread over three years is outlined as a starting point... This is an uplift on the current funding of the CMF to account for the new Paris alignment capacity, the increased service delivery expectations and to fund the critical gatekeeping function and online website and open access knowledge repository." (D0005097.odt, Inputs/Partners)
quote.breakdown: "Table 2. Indicative spending across CLEAN components (£ millions): Direct TA (£3.0m), Gateway (£0.6m), MEL (£0.4m)." (D0005097.odt, Inputs/Partners)

metadata.programme_name: South Sudan Peacebuilding Programme (SSPP)
metadata.quote: The South Sudan Peacebuilding Programme (SSPP) will be a central tool for delivering the UK’s peace and stability objectives in South Sudan. (D0006152.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "ODA: £20 million (£5m per year / 4 years)" (D0006152.odt, Programme Value)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SSPP combines implementation research (testing peacebuilding interventions), capacity building (strengthening community conflict resolution capabilities), policy influence (informing UK and regional peace agreement implementation), and service delivery (direct support to peace dialogues and monitoring mechanisms).
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will: Build the capabilities of communities, including women, in conflict hotspots to manage, reduce, and prevent violent conflict in increasingly inclusive ways; Deploy technical experts to the peace agreement and ceasefire monitoring mechanisms to strengthen their capabilities to spur regional action to implement the peace agreement; and Produce bespoke, demand-driven conflict and political economy analysis to inform UK policy and programming in South Sudan." (D0006152.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: National stability enhanced through effective diplomatic engagement and use of levers to increase and sustain momentum to implement the peace agreement in full preventing a return to nationwide violence
Sub-national violence reduced in target hotspots, along with enhanced South Sudanese capacity to manage conflicts without violence
Local communities in target conflict hotspots better able to jointly interrupt and prevent cycles of violence in increasingly inclusive and climate-sensitive ways

Key regional guarantors (including the AU, Uganda, and Sudan) increasingly take actions that incentivise influential South Sudanese elites to drive implementation of, and stop undermining, the peace agreement
BEJ conflict policy and programming increasingly fit-for-purpose and conflict sensitive, informed by a deeper, more evidence-based understanding of the local context
Technical assistance to RJMEC and CTSAMVM to strengthen their capabilities to monitor and verify ceasefire and peace agreement implementation
Bespoke, demand-driven conflict and political economy analysis to inform UK policy and programming
Support to implementation of local peace agreements and GESI- and climate-sensitive interventions addressing socio-economic drivers of conflict
what_objectives.summary: SSPP aims to reduce inter-communal violence and support implementation of South Sudan's 2018 peace agreement through three interlinked components: local peacebuilding, technical assistance to monitoring mechanisms, and conflict analysis to inform policy. The programme combines community-level interventions with national/regional political engagement.
what_objectives.quote: "SSPP will contribute to the following intended impact: Inter-communal violence is reduced, supported by and enhancing progress in the implementation of priority provisions of the 2018 peace agreement." (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: South Sudan is described as the fourth most fragile country in the world (2021 Fragile States Index) with ongoing violent conflict, weak governance, and humanitarian crises. The programme itself is rated as 'Major' risk.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0006152.odt, metadata) and "According to the 2021 Fragile States Index, South Sudan is currently the fourth most fragile country in world" (D0006152.odt, Strategic fit)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit access to conflict hotspots; political economy factors (elite manipulation of conflicts) undermine peacebuilding; weak institutions hinder implementation of peace agreements; climate risks (flooding) exacerbate displacement and resource conflicts; data limitations affect monitoring and analysis.
where_context.quote: "South Sudan’s local conflicts aren’t just local—they are linked to national political dynamics... driven and are driven by political competition between elites at the centre" (D0006152.odt, Background) and "Unprecedented levels of flooding over the past two years... have exacerbated this further reinforcing the vicious cycle of violence, displacement, and economic deprivation" (D0006152.odt, The politicisation of local conflict)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The British Embassy Juba (BEJ) acts as both the programme’s commissioning agent and an implementer, with decision-making power centralized in the UK-funded structure. Local communities and South Sudanese partners are engaged as beneficiaries and participants but not as equal decision-makers.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (community conflict resolution capabilities)
mentorship (technical experts deployed to RJMEC and CTSAMVM)
institutional strengthening (support to local peace governance structures)
gender and social inclusion (GESI-sensitive interventions)

partner_organizations.name: Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC)
partner_organizations.role: peace agreement monitoring body (technical assistance recipient)

partner_organizations.name: Ceasefire and Transitional Security Arrangements Monitoring and Verification Mechanism (CTSAMVM)
partner_organizations.role: ceasefire monitoring body (technical assistance recipient)

partner_organizations.name: Local communities in conflict hotspots (e.g., Western Equatoria, Warrap, Jonglei)
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries and participants in peacebuilding activities

partner_organizations.name: Conflict and Political Economy Analysis Fund (CAPAF) experts
partner_organizations.role: researchers/analysts (demand-driven analysis)

partner_organizations.name: Regional guarantors (AU, Uganda, Sudan, IGAD)
partner_organizations.role: political engagement targets

who_partners.quote: "BEJ acting as both the programme’s commissioning agent as well as an implementer itself" (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme) and "The programme will: Build the capabilities of communities, including women, in conflict hotspots to manage, reduce, and prevent violent conflict" (D0006152.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of technical assistance deployments (experts seconded to RJMEC/CTSAMVM), direct grants/contracts for local peacebuilding activities, and a demand-driven analysis fund (CAPAF) for bespoke research. The UK’s role in the Troika provides political leverage alongside financial instruments.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: BEJ acts as the central fund manager, commissioning three interlinked components: 1) local peacebuilding (community-led), 2) technical assistance to RJMEC/CTSAMVM, and 3) the CAPAF analysis fund. Each component has distinct delivery partners but is coordinated under BEJ’s oversight.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not applicable (direct secondments and pre-selected partners)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The UK’s membership in the Troika and existing relationships with RJMEC/CTSAMVM enable direct technical assistance deployments. Local partners are selected based on their role in conflict hotspots and alignment with UK priorities, not through open competition.
how_mechanism.quote: "The UK has seconded advisors to both bodies since 2018... Without UK support to CTSAMVM and RJMEC, they would effectively not be able to deliver" (D0006152.odt, Problem 2) and "BEJ acting as both the programme’s commissioning agent as well as an implementer itself" (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is integrated into the South Sudan Country Plan and overseen by the South Sudan Country Board (chaired by the Head of Mission), with additional approvals required from the East Africa Department and Director for East and Central Africa. The Director General for Africa and Latin America provides final approval.
how_governance.quote: "I can confirm that this business case was approved by the South Sudan country board which is chaired by the Head of Mission. It will subsequently be shared with the Head of the East Africa Department and the Director for East and Central Africa before final approval by the Director General for Africa and Latin America." (D0006152.odt, Department/Country Office confirmation of review processes) and "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0006152.odt, metadata)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can likely be reallocated between components (e.g., shifting resources from analysis to local peacebuilding if conflicts escalate), but this would require approval from BEJ/FCDO given the high-risk context and intensive oversight.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The CAPAF component is explicitly demand-driven, allowing for iterative analysis to inform adjustments. The programme emphasizes "iterative and demand-driven political economy and conflict analysis" and notes that components are "closely coordinated and mutually-supportive," suggesting adaptive management is built into the design.
how_flexibility.quote: "Underpinned by iterative and demand-driven political economy and conflict analysis, the programme’s different components will be closely coordinated and mutually-supportive." (D0006152.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending) and "The CAPAF will enable BEJ to commission and access bespoke, demand-driven analysis to inform and shape the design and delivery of components 1 and 2 as well as broader UK policy and programming in South Sudan." (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BEJ (fund manager/implementer) → [Component 1: local communities/NGOs; Component 2: RJMEC/CTSAMVM; Component 3: CAPAF experts]. BEJ acts as both commissioner and implementer, reducing layers.
how_efficiency.quote: "ODA: £20 million (£5m per year / 4 years)" (D0006152.odt, Programme Value) and "BEJ acting as both the programme’s commissioning agent as well as an implementer itself" (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen to leverage the UK’s unique position as a Troika member with direct access to peace agreement monitoring bodies (RJMEC/CTSAMVM) and to combine political influence with technical/financial support. The mixed structure (local peacebuilding + national monitoring + analysis) addresses the interlinked local-national drivers of conflict in South Sudan, while BEJ’s dual role as commissioner/implementer ensures alignment with UK diplomatic priorities.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (leveraging existing UK influence in Troika to maximize impact)
risk-mitigation (direct oversight through BEJ reduces risks in fragile context)
experience (building on POF’s success in local conflict analysis)
partner-capacity (technical assistance to RJMEC/CTSAMVM fills critical gaps)
equity (explicit focus on women, marginalized groups, and inclusive peacebuilding)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on BEJ’s dual role as commissioner/implementer may create conflicts of interest or limit local ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with local communities and regional guarantors (AU, Uganda, Sudan) to ensure buy-in and complementary roles.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Technical assistance to RJMEC/CTSAMVM may not translate into political will for peace agreement implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s Troika membership and bilateral engagement with Sudan/Uganda are used to steer regional action and incentivize compliance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Demand-driven analysis (CAPAF) could lead to fragmented or ad-hoc priorities without strategic coherence.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: CAPAF is explicitly linked to informing components 1 and 2, with BEJ ensuring alignment with overall programme objectives.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (reducing violence and supporting peace agreement implementation)
efficiency (leveraging existing UK influence and Troika role)
why_rationale.quote: "The UK is uniquely well placed to contribute to conflict reduction and prevention in South Sudan. As part of the Troika (UK, US, Norway), the UK has high profile access to key power brokers in South Sudan and the region beyond other partners... Through the flagship Peacebuilding Opportunities Fund (POF) programme (2019-22, £3.7m), BEJ has gained unique understanding of the drivers and dynamics of local conflicts in South Sudan." (D0006152.odt, UK comparative advantage) and "SSPP has been specifically designed to complement and be complemented by UK diplomatic and political work to, with others, incentivise South Sudanese authorities to implement the peace agreement." (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to entities with existing access to conflict hotspots (e.g., local communities, RJMEC/CTSAMVM) and requires UK-led oversight due to high risks. Security constraints and elite manipulation of conflicts necessitate trusted intermediaries (e.g., Troika members, regional guarantors) rather than open competitions.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict direct implementation by international actors, requiring local partners.
Political economy constraints (elite manipulation) demand technical assistance to monitoring bodies with regional legitimacy (RJMEC/CTSAMVM).
Weak institutions limit the pool of capable Southern partners, increasing reliance on UK/BEJ management.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address both local and national drivers of conflict (inter-communal violence + peace agreement implementation) determines the mixed delivery structure: local peacebuilding (component 1) targets communities, technical assistance (component 2) targets national/regional bodies, and CAPAF (component 3) bridges both levels with analysis.
q28_linkages: Local peacebuilding (component 1) requires national/regional political engagement (component 2) to address elite manipulation of conflicts.
Demand-driven analysis (CAPAF) informs both local interventions and diplomatic strategies, ensuring coherence.
UK’s Troika role enables direct technical assistance to RJMEC/CTSAMVM, which is critical for monitoring peace agreement compliance.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (inclusive, GESI-sensitive peacebuilding) with efficiency (leveraging UK’s Troika influence for rapid political engagement). Trade-offs include: 1) Time-intensive community-led processes vs. urgency of conflict reduction; 2) Local ownership vs. UK/BEJ oversight requirements in a high-risk context; 3) Broad inclusion of marginalized groups vs. focused impact in hotspots.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed-vs-inclusion: Community-led peacebuilding (component 1) may slow delivery but is necessary for sustainability.
expertise-vs-ownership: UK technical experts (component 2) ensure monitoring capacity but may limit Southern ownership.
cost-vs-reach: Intensive oversight (e.g., embedded advisors) increases costs but is justified by the FCAS context.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating and FCAS context justify intensive oversight (e.g., BEJ’s dual role, Troika leverage) and adaptive management (e.g., demand-driven CAPAF) to mitigate instability.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme: local communities receive conflict resolution training (component 1); RJMEC/CTSAMVM receive technical assistance (component 2); and CAPAF strengthens evidence-based policymaking. Southern partners’ roles are shaped by their capacity gaps (e.g., RJMEC’s need for strategic political expertise).
intersections.quote: "The contrast between the signing of the peace agreement and the rising levels of local conflicts has obfuscated the links between the two... The solution to local conflict lies partly at the national level, in building a more inclusive and functional political settlement." (D0006152.odt, The problem to be addressed) and "By operating at both the local and national level, SSPP will enable the UK to more effectively address the drivers and impacts of conflict in South Sudan at both levels, which, as demonstrated above, are inextricably inter-linked." (D0006152.odt, Overview of the programme)

key_programme_risks: Elite resistance to peace agreement implementation, undermining local and national stability.
Escalation of inter-communal violence in hotspots despite programme interventions.
Limited political will among regional guarantors (AU, Uganda, Sudan) to enforce compliance.
Climate shocks (e.g., flooding) exacerbating displacement and resource conflicts.
Weak institutional capacity of RJMEC/CTSAMVM limiting monitoring effectiveness.
Safeguarding risks for women and marginalized groups in conflict-affected communities.
Over-reliance on UK/BEJ oversight creating dependency rather than local ownership.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Elite resistance to peace agreement implementation
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK diplomatic engagement with regional guarantors (Sudan, Uganda) and Troika leverage to incentivize compliance; technical assistance to RJMEC to improve monitoring and reporting.
Community-led peacebuilding with GESI-sensitive and climate-adaptive interventions; support to local peace agreements and socio-economic dividends to build trust.
Strategic communications and outreach by RJMEC (supported by UK advisors) to raise awareness and pressure.
Integration of climate-sensitive livelihoods support and natural resource management into peace processes; monitoring of flood risks in programme areas.
Continued UK secondment of technical advisors (e.g., Ceasefire Verification, Gender and Civil Affairs, Security, Strategic Communications).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Safeguarding risks for women and marginalized groups
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded Gender Advisor in CTSAMVM; GESI-sensitive design in all components; consultation with women’s groups and organizations of persons with disabilities.
Capacity building for local communities and monitoring bodies; iterative analysis to inform adaptive management.

fcas_specific_lessons: Local conflicts are inextricably linked to national political dynamics; solutions require multi-level engagement.
Elite manipulation of inter-communal conflicts demands both local resilience-building and national/regional political pressure.
In FCAS contexts, technical assistance to monitoring bodies must be paired with diplomatic leverage to drive compliance.
Climate adaptation must be integrated into peacebuilding to address resource-based conflicts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from the Peacebuilding Opportunities Fund (POF, 2019–22), which demonstrated the value of granular local conflict analysis and strong relationships with conflict actors. POF’s success in Jonglei and Rumbek informed SSPP’s community-led approach. The collapse of the 2015 ARCSS also highlighted the need for sustained regional engagement and elite incentives.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: SSPP’s three-component structure (local + national + analysis) directly addresses the failure of past agreements to link local and national levels. The inclusion of climate-sensitive livelihoods and GESI considerations reflects lessons on the drivers of inter-communal violence. The demand-driven CAPAF replaces ad-hoc research in previous programmes.
risks_lessons.quote: "The process of creating the RTGoNU and state governments, which were meant to incorporate power-sharing, has actually institutionalised the divisions and power disparities of the conflict—bringing them into the government rather than resolving them." (D0006152.odt, Institutionalised divisions) and "The POF has established itself as one of few internationally-funded programmes that has a deep, granular understanding of the local conflict systems in which it works, including by having built strong relationships with key local conflict actors and communities." (D0006152.odt, UK comparative advantage)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages the UK’s existing influence as a Troika member and donor to RJMEC/CTSAMVM, ensuring continued operation of these bodies and signaling commitment to the peace process. This political leverage complements financial contributions.
financial_details.quote: "Donors include Canada, China, the European Union, Ireland, Japan, Norway, the UK, and the US, and contributions cover salaries of ceasefire monitors, support staff, and technical advisers." (D0006152.odt, Problem 2) and "ODA: £20 million (£5m per year / 4 years)" (D0006152.odt, Programme Value)

metadata.programme_name: 12 for 12 Initiative (Girls’ Education Private Sector partnership)

quote.programme_name: "The 12 for 12 Initiative will set out to address the challenge of the skills deficit amongst marginalised adolescent girls, and the pressing need to diversify education financing." (D0003320.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "Start Date: January 2022", "End Date: December 2025" (D0003320.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: January 2022", "End Date: December 2025"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The 12 for 12 Initiative combines **implementation research** (testing/scaling interventions for adolescent girls' skills development), **financing mechanism** (leveraging private sector funding), and **service delivery** (direct provision of skills training and employment readiness). It aims to address the skills deficit among marginalized adolescent girls while diversifying education financing through public-private partnerships.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The 12 for 12 Initiative will set out to address the challenge of the skills deficit amongst marginalised adolescent girls, and the pressing need to diversify education financing. The programme will address both challenges by creating a new partnership with 12 leading private sector companies to support adolescent girls secure the skills they need to transition successfully into the labour force." (D0003320.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 40 million additional out-of-school girls in school by 2026 (G7 target contribution)
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 40 million girls

q3_expected_outputs.output: 20 million additional girls able to read by age 10 by 2026 (G7 target contribution)
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: 20 million girls

q3_expected_outputs.output: High-quality, industry-relevant skills training (e.g., STEM, digital certificates)
Qualifications and digital certificates for in-demand roles
Improved labour force participation of adolescent girls
Policy change to support girls’ education-to-employment transitions
Scaling of successful interventions through challenge funds
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: Up to 8 grants of £1.5-2 million each

q3_expected_outputs.output: Digital skills development via UNICEF’s Generation Unlimited ‘Passport to Earning’ platform
q3_expected_outputs.quantitative: Platform to reach young people aged 15–24

q3_expected_outputs.output: Mentorship and work experience opportunities (e.g., PwC staff time)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve economic productivity and labour force participation of adolescent girls (13–24 years) by providing skills training, digital learning, and employment linkages, while leveraging £9m in private sector co-funding. It aligns with G7 targets for girls’ education and the UK’s Girls’ Education Action Plan.

quote.objectives: "The overall impact of the programme will be to increase the economic productivity and labour force participation of adolescent girls, with strong alignment to the ToC underpinning the Girls Education KPIs." (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)
quote.alignment: "12 for 12 is closely aligned with key FCDO strategic priorities. It will: Contribute to the G7-agreed girls’ education global target (getting 40 million more girls in school in the next 5 years)... Contribute to achievement of UK G7 presidency policy objectives on innovative finance that leverages private sector finance to maximise ODA." (D0003320.odt, The programme is aligned to all three key pillars)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is rated 'moderate' risk due to operational challenges in low- and lower-middle-income countries, including gender-based barriers, COVID-19 impacts, and private sector coordination risks. However, it avoids fragile/conflict-affected states (FCAS).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0003320.odt, Summary Sheet) and "12 for 12 will not operate in fragile and conflict affected states." (D0003320.odt, Conflict and Fragility)
q6_contextual_constraints: digital divide (limited internet access for girls)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: COVID-19 has exacerbated dropouts (e.g., 400% increase in pregnancies among 10–14-year-olds in Uganda), while digital exclusion limits remote learning access. Social norms and care burdens disproportionately affect girls’ ability to participate in training or employment. Private sector engagement requires aligning corporate priorities with development goals.

quote.covid_impact: "2.5 million additional child marriages are expected in the next five years and over 1 million adolescent pregnancies in the next 12 months... In Uganda, among girls aged 10-14 years, incidence of pregnancies increased by nearly 400 percent—from 290 in March to 1,353 in September 2020." (D0003320.odt, The scale of the challenge)
quote.digital_divide: "In the world’s least developed countries, men are 52% more likely to have access to the internet than women... In many contexts, boys have better access to virtual communication and digital technologies than girls." (D0003320.odt, Digital access and social inclusion)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains central management and decision-making authority, with private sector partners contributing resources but operating under FCDO-designed frameworks. Southern partners (e.g., UNICEF/GenU) implement components but follow FCDO/private sector priorities.
q10_capacity_building_details: mentorship (e.g., PwC staff time)
digital skills training (via GenU Passport to Earning)
curriculum development with industry partners
teacher training (pedagogical support)
policy advocacy for skills recognition

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Lead funder and programme designer

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF’s Generation Unlimited (GenU)
partner_organizations.role: Host of ‘Passport to Earning’ digital platform; implementation partner

partner_organizations.name: Private Sector Partners (12 companies)
roles: Skills training provision (e.g., Microsoft technology platforms)

partner_organizations.name: Local education providers (TBD via challenge funds)
partner_organizations.role: Sub-grantees for skills training delivery

quote.structure: "The programme will combine the financial resources, experience, and networks of the private sector with the policy, programme, and operational expertise of FCDO to deliver on the UK’s commitment to stand up for 12 years of quality education for girls." (D0003320.odt, Our response)
quote.private_sector_roles: "Private sector partners engaged in initial consultation have underscored the value of this senior UK political leadership in girls’ education agenda as helpful in securing additional external financing for education." (D0003320.odt, Private Sector contributions)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **partnership agreements** with private sector companies (co-financing) and **competitive grants** (Challenge Fund) for local implementers. UNICEF’s GenU platform operates under a **framework agreement** with FCDO.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO centrally manages the programme with a **hub-and-spoke model**: (1) A **Challenge Fund** awards grants to local providers via competitive calls; (2) **GenU’s Passport to Earning** platform delivers digital skills; (3) Private sector partners co-design and co-finance interventions. Governance includes partnership agreements with each company and UNICEF.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Private sector partners were selected through **direct engagement by the Prime Minister’s Special Envoy for Girls’ Education**, prioritizing companies with existing commitments to girls’ education and alignment with FCDO priorities. Challenge Fund grantees will be selected via **open competitive calls** in target countries.

quote.selection: "To date, the Prime Minister’s Special Envoy for Girls’ Education has been able to secure a commitment from private sector partners including Unilever, Microsoft, Accenture, Pearson plc, Standard Chartered, United Bank of Africa, Generation Unlimited and Price Waterhouse Coopers (PwC)." (D0003320.odt, Our response)
quote.challenge_fund: "A competitive grant fund: Awarding up to 8 grants of between £1.5-2 million each (via a competitive process) in an initial two geographies." (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will establish **partnership agreements** with each private sector partner and UNICEF, including accountability frameworks for contributions. A **central hub** (likely within FCDO’s EdGE Directorate) will oversee the Challenge Fund and GenU platform, with **in-country advisers** adapting delivery. Technical oversight is implied via FCDO’s Education Hub of Excellence.

quote.governance: "There will also be a partnership agreement in place with each partner to ensure that there is an accountability framework and reporting structure which tracks each partner’s contribution against their original commitment." (D0003320.odt, Private Sector contributions)
quote.hub_role: "The Spending Review Capping Paper calls for the establishment of an Education Hub of Excellence in FCDO. The hub will be a source of good practice... 12 for 12 will not only be able to use this hub of excellence but will be able to feed into it as programme case studies and research emerge." (D0003320.odt, Linking FCDO’s work on girls’ education)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between **Challenge Fund grantees** based on performance, but requires FCDO approval. The **Passport to Earning** platform allows scalable digital delivery, while private sector in-kind contributions (e.g., Microsoft technology) offer flexibility in resource use.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes **learning and scaling**: initial pilots in 2 countries will inform expansion, and the Challenge Fund’s open calls allow adaptation to emerging skills needs. However, major shifts (e.g., adding countries) require FCDO sign-off.

quote.flexibility: "The overall aim of the initial pilot projects will be the establishment of creative initiatives that (over time) will provide opportunities for testing and learning from the most successful projects, with a view to further scaling." (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)
quote.adaptive: "This function [central hub] should facilitate a greater level of adaptive programming, allowing us to target investment and scale up programme activity that demonstrates the greatest potential." (D0003320.odt, Appraisal of Options)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **UNICEF/GenU platform & private sector partners** → **local education providers (Challenge Fund grantees)** → adolescent girls

quote.layers: "Both of these components [Challenge Fund and Passport to Earning] will be supported by newly created partnerships with 12 leading private sector companies co-investing with the FCDO." (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)
quote.payments: "The overall aim of the initial pilot projects will be the establishment of creative initiatives that (over time) will provide opportunities for testing and learning..." (implies milestone-based disbursements) (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue existing FCDO girls’ education programmes (e.g., Girls’ Education Challenge) without new skills-focused investments or private sector engagement.
Direct funding to expand existing FCDO country education portfolios, but without private sector co-financing or central coordination.
Establish a FCDO-led hub with private sector co-investment, combining Challenge Fund grants and GenU’s digital platform.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **centrally managed PPP** was selected for its ability to: (1) **leverage private sector financing** (£9m FCDO unlocks £9m private sector); (2) **scale innovations** via competitive grants and digital platforms; (3) **ensure quality assurance** through FCDO’s central hub; (4) **align with G7 targets** for girls’ education; and (5) **build on existing partnerships** (e.g., UNICEF/GenU). Country-led options lacked private sector engagement, while ‘do nothing’ failed to address skills gaps.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage ratio of 1:1 with private sector)
speed (rapid startup via existing GenU infrastructure)
risk mitigation (central oversight of private sector contributions)
alignment with UK political priorities (G7 presidency)
scalability (potential to expand from 2 to 10+ countries)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector partners fail to deliver on in-kind commitments (e.g., Microsoft platforms, PwC mentorship).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partnership agreements with accountability frameworks and reporting structures to track contributions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Challenge Fund grantees lack capacity to deliver quality training.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Central hub provides technical assistance and quality assurance; lessons from Girls’ Education Challenge applied.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Digital platform (Passport to Earning) excludes girls without connectivity.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Blended online/low-no-tech solutions and partnerships with local providers for offline access.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-centralization limits country ownership.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: In-country advisers adapt delivery; programme design informed by local gender/skills data.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (central hub reduces duplication; digital platform scales cost-effectively)
equity (targeting marginalized adolescent girls, disability inclusion)

quote.rationale: "This option [centrally managed PPP] provides the strongest basis for meeting the FCDO’s increased ambitions on education and the pressing need to diversify education financing, including securing stronger contributions from the private sector." (D0003320.odt, Summary of option appraisal)
quote.leverage: "A £9 million commitment from FCDO will unlock a further £9 million (USD 12 million) contribution from private sector partners (USD 7 million already pledged), meaning a potential programme resource pool of up to £18 million." (D0003320.odt, Private Sector contributions)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **multi-country scope** and focus on marginalized adolescent girls constrain partner selection to organizations with: (1) **global/regional reach** (e.g., UNICEF, multinational corporations); (2) **experience in LMICs** (e.g., Pearson’s digital resources for low-connectivity settings); (3) **gender-transformative approaches** (e.g., PwC’s mentorship models). Local partners must navigate **social norms** (e.g., early marriage) and **weak skills ecosystems** (e.g., lack of accredited vocational training).
q27_constraints_detail: Private sector partners must operate in FCDO priority countries with ‘strategic fit’ (e.g., existing corporate presence).
Local grantees need capacity to deliver **gender-sensitive** and **disability-inclusive** training.
Digital partners (e.g., Microsoft) must address the **digital divide** (e.g., 19% broadband access in low-income countries).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **skills deficit objective** drives the **two-component structure**: (1) **Challenge Fund** tests localized, industry-relevant training (e.g., STEM, apprenticeships) where formal education fails; (2) **Passport to Earning** scales digital skills for hard-to-reach girls. The **private sector financing goal** necessitates **co-design with corporations** (e.g., Unilever’s supply chain linkages). **Gender barriers** (e.g., unpaid care work) require **blended online/offline delivery** and **mentorship models**.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Private sector co-funding (1:1 match) via partnership agreements.
Challenge Fund grants for localized, demand-driven skills training.
GenU’s Passport to Earning platform with low-no-tech alternatives.
Mentorship (PwC) and role models to challenge stereotypes.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting out-of-school girls, disability inclusion) with **efficiency** (central hub, digital scaling). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid digital scaling risks excluding girls without connectivity (mitigated by blended approaches). (2) **Corporate priorities vs. local needs**: Private sector partners (e.g., Microsoft) may prioritize tech skills over contextual relevance (addressed via country-specific Challenge Funds). (3) **Cost vs. reach**: High-touch mentorship (e.g., PwC) is resource-intensive but critical for overcoming gender barriers.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Digital platform efficiency (scaling to millions) vs. equity (excluding offline girls).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Blended online/offline models and local partner networks.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Private sector’s preference for cash contributions (easier to track) vs. in-kind value (e.g., Microsoft platforms).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Quantifiable in-kind valuation requirements in partnership agreements.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Central quality assurance vs. local adaptation.
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: In-country advisers tailor delivery within FCDO frameworks.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** drives **milestone-based oversight**: (1) Private sector contributions are tracked via formal agreements; (2) Challenge Fund grantees undergo due diligence; (3) Digital partners must demonstrate disability/inclusion compliance. **FCAS exclusion** reduces security risks but limits reach to conflict zones where girls’ education needs are acute.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles: (1) **Private sector** provides mentorship (PwC) and curriculum (Pearson) to strengthen local training quality; (2) **GenU platform** upskills local providers in digital delivery; (3) **Challenge Fund** includes TA for grantees on gender-inclusive pedagogy. Southern partners (e.g., local NGOs) deliver training but rely on Northern/FCDO **technical backstopping**.

quote.equity_efficiency: "Digital learning initiatives can be designed to be inclusive so that they provide marginalised groups, including adolescent girls, the support to access the available tools and platforms." (D0003320.odt, Digital access and social inclusion)
quote.capacity_roles: "Non-financial contributions, such as mentoring or work experience opportunities, can be incredibly valuable and make a significant contribution towards the objectives of the programme." (D0003320.odt, Private Sector contributions)

key_programme_risks: Private sector partners fail to meet co-financing commitments (cash or in-kind).
Challenge Fund grantees lack capacity to deliver quality, gender-sensitive training.
Digital platform excludes girls without internet access or digital literacy.
COVID-19 exacerbates dropouts (e.g., early marriage, pregnancies).
Social norms limit girls’ participation in training/employment.
Weak labour market absorption of skilled girls post-training.
Over-centralization limits country ownership and adaptation.
Reputational risk if private sector partners face controversies (e.g., labour practices).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Partnership agreements with quantifiable in-kind valuation and reporting requirements.
Central hub provides technical assistance; lessons from Girls’ Education Challenge applied.
Blended online/offline solutions; local partners facilitate access.
Targeted outreach to out-of-school girls; flexible training schedules.
Mentorship and community engagement (e.g., role models for parents).
Industry-aligned curriculum design; private sector employment pipelines.

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid operating in FCAS due to heightened safeguarding risks (e.g., sexual exploitation, child marriage).
Lessons from GEC on adapting to conflict contexts (e.g., Nepal’s Sisters for Sisters) inform safeguarding standards.

from_GEC: Importance of **gender-sensitive pedagogy** and **community engagement** to overcome social norms.
**Mentorship** (e.g., Nepal’s Sisters for Sisters) effectively reduces early marriage.
Need for **flexible funding** to adapt to crises (e.g., COVID-19 school closures).
from_Skills_for_Prosperity: Central quality assurance improves **skills recognition** but must balance local adaptation.
**Industry partnerships** (e.g., STEM employers) strengthen employment transitions.
from_digital_programmes: **Blended approaches** (online + offline) critical for equity in low-connectivity settings.
Platforms like GenU must **prioritize low-no-tech solutions** for marginalized girls.

design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **disability inclusion** requirements (vs. GEC’s limited focus).
Explicit **climate resilience** components (e.g., green skills training) based on FCDO’s 2021 guidance.
**Safeguarding standards** strengthened post-GEC (e.g., mandatory policies for all partners).
**Private sector co-financing** model adopted to address COVID-19 funding gaps (vs. traditional ODA).

quote.lessons: "Lessons from the earlier Girls’ Education Challenge will also be applied in the design of the call for proposals and grantee selection." (D0003320.odt, Option 3: Centrally managed public-private partnership)
quote.adaptations: "12 for 12 will differentiate itself from previous FCDO programmes... by innovatively using a challenge fund approach in seeking interventions specific to in-demand skills, including digital and STEM-related." (D0003320.odt, How will 12 for 12 address this problem?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £9m FCDO commitment unlocks an additional £9m (USD 12m) from private sector partners, doubling the programme’s resource pool to £18m. USD 7m is already pledged.

quote.leverage: "A £9 million commitment from FCDO will unlock a further £9 million (USD 12 million) contribution from private sector partners (USD 7 million already pledged), meaning a potential programme resource pool of up to £18 million." (D0003320.odt, Private Sector contributions)
quote.allocation: "The programme will invest in an initial two countries and directly [via Challenge Fund grants]... In addition, via the Public Private Youth Partnership (PPYP) platform, UNICEF’s Generation Unlimited ‘Passport to Earning’, the programme will reach a wider number of countries." (D0003320.odt, Our response)

metadata.programme_name: Sustainable Blue Economies Programme (SBE)
metadata.quote: "This programme aims to enhance the resilience of ODA-eligible SIDS and their economies to the impacts of climate change and economic shocks, including through better ocean management, poverty reduction/improved livelihoods and greater use of nature-based solutions." (D0001294.odt, Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 1 June 2022", "AMP End Date: 31 March 2028" (D0001294.odt, Programme metadata)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening SIDS' ocean governance and blue economy capabilities), implementation research (testing nature-based solutions and revenue models), and service delivery (direct support for policy implementation and community projects). It also includes financing mechanisms to unlock climate finance for marine conservation.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme aims to enhance the resilience of ODA-eligible SIDS and their economies... through better ocean management, poverty reduction/improved livelihoods and greater use of nature-based solutions... This Programme will boost blue economy planning and community implementation support, as well as research the feasibility of revenue opportunities from nature-based solutions such as carbon offset schemes." (D0001294.odt, Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Marine policy frameworks developed (e.g., "support for broad policy framework endorsed at the highest level of government")
15.5m GBP for direct government implementation support
5m GBP for environmental policy/planning/research
10m GBP Social Challenge Fund for community projects
Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) processes established
Nature-based solutions piloted (e.g., carbon offset schemes, Payments for Ecosystem Services)
Virtual ocean platforms for regional coordination (exploratory)
Training for 35 ODA-eligible SIDS on ocean governance
Improved access to climate finance for SIDS (e.g., "enable SIDS to gain access to the global funds that are currently available")
Reduction in illegal fishing through strengthened enforcement
Protected marine areas expanded (area targets TBA during mobilisation)
5:1 return on investment in sustainable ocean economy (cited from High-Level Panel analysis)
what_objectives.summary: The SBE programme aims to transform SIDS' economic resilience by transitioning to sustainable blue economies, addressing both climate adaptation and poverty through direct capacity supplementation, research into nature-based revenue models, and community-level implementation support.
what_objectives.quote: "The anticipated impact of the programme will be that SIDS have more resilient development pathways, are better adapted to climate change, and can protect and restore the ocean whilst using its resources sustainably." (D0001294.odt, Strategic Case)

countries_regions: All 35 ODA-eligible Small Island Developing States (SIDS)

regional_groupings: Pacific SIDS (e.g., Tonga, Fiji, Solomon Islands)
AIS group (Atlantic, Indian Ocean, South China Sea)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: SIDS face extreme vulnerability to climate shocks (e.g., hurricanes causing 225% GDP loss in Dominica) and economic fragility (e.g., 50% output losses during COVID-19), but the programme itself is classified as "moderate risk" due to mitigations like direct capacity supplementation and regional coordination.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0001294.odt, Programme metadata); "SIDS suffered average output losses of 50% and were economically worst hit by the pandemic" (D0001294.odt, Summary)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (e.g., "fragmented and uncoordinated ocean governance systems")
climate risks (e.g., "sea level rise, tropical cyclones, coral bleaching")
data limitations (e.g., "significant scientific gaps related to data, information, and ocean/seabed mapping")
regulatory (e.g., "complex approval processes to secure finance")
political economy (e.g., "low social capital due to marginalisation of affected groups")
infrastructure (e.g., "limited domestic research and evidence functions")
capacity gaps (e.g., "SIDS lack technical capability for environmental management")
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints force the programme to adopt direct capacity supplementation (e.g., UK experts delivering activities) rather than traditional capacity development, and to create virtual platforms to streamline fragmented regional bodies. Climate risks require nature-based solutions to be prioritised, while weak institutions necessitate embedded advisory roles.
where_context.quote: "Our approach recognises the limited success of traditional capacity ‘development’ programmes in SIDS over the last thirty years. We propose in-country capacity ‘supplementation’—where UK support directly delivers some of the required activities." (D0001294.odt, Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight and approval authority, with Southern partners (SIDS governments/regional bodies) implementing components under direct UK supplementation. Decision-making for technical priorities (e.g., nature-based solutions) is shared but relies on UK-provided capacity.
q10_capacity_building_details: Direct capacity supplementation (UK experts embedded in SIDS ministries)
Training on Marine Spatial Planning (MSP)
Support for ocean governance policy frameworks
Technical assistance for climate finance access
Community-level skills development via Social Challenge Fund
Regional coordination platforms (e.g., virtual ocean platforms)
Scientific data collection and mapping (e.g., bathymetric, habitat data)

partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiaries and implementers of capacity supplementation

partner_organizations.name: Pacific Islands Forum (PIF)
partner_organizations.role: Regional coordination for Pacific SIDS

partner_organizations.name: Caribbean Community (CARICOM)
partner_organizations.role: Regional policy alignment and fisheries management

partner_organizations.role: Ocean acidification and habitat research

partner_organizations.name: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS)

partner_organizations.name: Commonwealth Marine Economies Programme (CME)
partner_organizations.role: Lessons integration and technical backstopping
