partner_organizations.role: protection consortium lead (originally); multi-donor fund management (proposed in 2024 addendum)

partner_organizations.name: Cash Consortium for Sudan
partner_organizations.role: cash-based assistance delivery

partner_organizations.name: Palladium
partner_organizations.role: Enabling Facility implementation (technical support, data, monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs and mutual aid groups
partner_organizations.role: frontline service delivery in hard-to-reach areas; testing new partnerships for localisation

partner_organizations.name: International NGO Safety Organisation (INSO)
partner_organizations.role: supporting NGO capacity to manage insecurity (proposed in 2024 addendum)

partner_organizations.name: Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs)
partner_organizations.role: community-led response in areas where international actors cannot reach

who_partners.quote: "The flexibility designed into SHPR (since reinforced), has allowed British Office Sudan to adapt to the evolving context and explore new partnerships. The intended outcome and impact of the programme have remained consistent, and all partners set out in the original Business Case remain part of the portfolio." (D0007322.odt, Changes)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs), Accountable Grant Agreements (AGAs), and commercial contracts (e.g., for consultants under the Enabling Facility). Funding is channeled through direct partnerships with UN agencies, INGOs, and local actors, as well as pooled funds like the Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The British Office Sudan manages the programme directly, with a flexible, adaptive approach that allows for diversifying partnerships based on access and context. Partners include UN agencies, INGOs, and local actors, with new relationships added as needed (e.g., DRC multi-donor fund, mutual aid groups). The Enabling Facility provides technical surge support, and the Internal Risk Facility (IRF) allows for rapid reallocation of funds.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on proven track records in Sudan’s challenging environment, existing relationships with FCDO, and ability to deliver in high-risk contexts. The programme prioritizes flexibility and speed, which aligns with direct awards to trusted partners rather than competitive processes.
how_mechanism.quote: "Implementing partners will likely include trusted partners currently delivering UK Aid humanitarian and development funding (e.g., DRC, ICRC, WFP, UNICEF) and may include others not currently partnering with BEK but highly respected and well established in the sector, such as Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) and Save the Children." (D0002801.odt, Programme Delivery)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: For pooled funds like the Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF), sub-awards are allocated by the fund’s governance mechanisms (e.g., UN-led clusters). For direct partnerships (e.g., UNICEF, WFP), sub-awards are managed by the partner according to their internal procedures, with FCDO oversight.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: The programme undergoes regular monitoring, including third-party verification through the Sudan Independent Monitoring and Analysis Programme (SIMAP), due diligence refreshes, and risk management escalations. The British Office Sudan actively advocates for humanitarian access and holds partners accountable for response quality.
how_governance.quote: "The launch of the Sudan Independent Monitoring and Analysis Programme (SIMAP) in April 2024 has enhanced FCDO’s oversight and risk management of SHPR, and will provide third-party verification of activities and results, supporting FCDO’s zero-tolerance approach to cases of fraud and safeguarding." (D0007322.odt, Risk)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes a £30m Internal Risk Facility (IRF) to absorb underspends and address underfunded needs. The 2024 addendum emphasizes adaptability to "test and diversify a range of partnerships and ways of working," including reallocating funds to new partners like mutual aid groups or local responders.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to adapt to evolving risks, access constraints, and humanitarian needs. The Theory of Change was revised in 2024 to reflect a broader range of activities and partners, and the programme leverages flexibility to respond to spikes in need (e.g., famine declarations, conflict escalations).
how_flexibility.quote: "The flexibility built into SHPR, including through the IRF, has allowed British Office Sudan to adapt to the evolving context, challenges, and needs, exploring new partnerships for delivery and mechanisms to support the broader response and humanitarian architecture." (D0005343.odt, Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., UNICEF, WFP, ICRC, SHF, DRC) → [End beneficiaries]. Some partners (e.g., SHF) may add an additional layer for sub-grants to local NGOs.
how_efficiency.quote: "New partnerships will require new funding agreements. Given the likely partners, these are expected to be MoUs and Accountable Grants, though small-scale contracts continue to be possible (e.g., of consultants) under the Enabling Facility." (D0007322.odt, Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (discounted: would fail to meet UK commitments and increase suffering)
Multi-sectoral preparedness and response with resilience focus (not recommended: mixed evidence on VfM for short-term resilience in humanitarian contexts)
Focus on development outcomes (discounted: political uncertainty and high ongoing humanitarian needs)
Multi-sectoral preparedness and response (RECOMMENDED: best VfM, aligns with evidence on cash transfers, nutrition, and protection)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed delivery model was chosen for its flexibility, ability to respond to sudden-onset crises (e.g., famine, conflict spikes), and adaptability to access constraints. The programme prioritizes: (1) **Value for Money**: Evidence shows cash transfers and community-based nutrition interventions are cost-effective; (2) **Risk Mitigation**: Diversifying partners (UN, INGOs, local actors) spreads risk in a volatile context; (3) **Speed and Scale**: Direct awards to trusted partners enable rapid response; (4) **Equity**: Localisation efforts (e.g., SHF grants to Sudanese NGOs, support to mutual aid groups) aim to reach marginalized populations.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial and fiduciary risks (e.g., fraud, aid diversion in high-risk areas)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence refreshes, third-party monitoring (SIMAP), and zero-tolerance policies for fraud. Escalation to Directors for risks outside risk appetite.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risks (e.g., protection of beneficiaries in conflict zones)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced due diligence, third-party monitoring, and adherence to FCDO safeguarding standards. Two safeguarding risks are currently escalated to Directors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Access constraints (e.g., bureaucratic restrictions, insecurity, looting of aid)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversifying partnerships to include local actors with better access; advocacy for humanitarian access; flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., IRF, SHF).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner capacity limitations (e.g., weak local NGO sector)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strengthening local NGOs through SHF grants, secondments, and technical support (e.g., Enabling Facility).

why_rationale.quote: "Option 2 [multi-sectoral preparedness and response] presents greater benefits across nutrition and protection but does not attempt to systematically build resilience. There is limited evidence, from BEK’s previous humanitarian programme and the literature, of the ability of small-scale resilience interventions to improve people’s outcomes as part of a humanitarian response. [...] Given a constant monetary cost for each of the two options, Option 2 is expected to save more lives and provide more focus on improving the humanitarian response and therefore more strongly meet the objectives of this programme than Option 3." (D0002801.odt, Options Appraisal)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The conflict and access constraints in Sudan (e.g., bureaucratic restrictions, insecurity, looting) limit the ability of international partners (UN agencies, INGOs) to operate in certain areas, necessitating partnerships with local NGOs, mutual aid groups, and community-led responders. The politicized environment also requires partners with strong negotiation skills and existing relationships with authorities.
q27_constraints_detail: Bureaucratic restrictions (e.g., HAC monitoring of NGO recruitment, visas, travel permits)
Insecurity and looting of humanitarian warehouses
Politicized aid access (e.g., SAF controlling famine data and border crossings)
Limited infrastructure (e.g., poor roads, damaged WASH facilities)
Weak local NGO capacity (requires investment to meet Grand Bargain localisation goals)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, large-scale humanitarian response** (food, nutrition, protection) drives the use of **trusted, high-capacity partners** (UNICEF, WFP, ICRC) for immediate delivery, while the **localisation agenda** and **access constraints** push for diversification into local NGOs and mutual aid groups. The **flexibility** required by the conflict context (e.g., IRF, adaptive programming) shapes the open partnership structure.
q28_linkages: Life-saving objectives (e.g., treating malnutrition) → Direct partnerships with UNICEF/WFP for speed and scale.
Protection and localisation goals → Support to SHF and local NGOs to reach marginalized groups.
System strengthening (e.g., data, coordination) → Enabling Facility and secondments to UN agencies.
Conflict sensitivity → Conflict Sensitivity Facility (CSF) integration and DRC-led protection consortium.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (e.g., using large UN agencies for rapid scale-up) with **equity** (e.g., funding local NGOs through SHF, testing mutual aid groups). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: International partners can deliver quickly but may struggle with access, while local actors reach more people but require capacity building; (2) **Cost vs. Reach**: Cash transfers are cost-effective but require robust monitoring to prevent diversion; (3) **Expertise vs. Ownership**: Northern-led partners bring technical skills, but Southern-led approaches are critical for sustainability and trust.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (UN/INGO delivery) vs. inclusion (local NGO access)
Cost-effectiveness (cash transfers) vs. risk management (fraud prevention)
Northern expertise (e.g., ICRC hospitals) vs. Southern ownership (e.g., mutual aid groups)
Scale (WFP food assistance) vs. tailored responses (community-led protection)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Severe** risk profile (conflict, famine, access constraints) justifies **intensive oversight** (e.g., SIMAP monitoring, due diligence refreshes, embedded advisors) and **flexible management** (e.g., IRF, adaptive programming). High risks also drive the diversification of partners to mitigate delivery failures.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded across the programme: (1) **Local NGOs** receive SHF grants and technical support to strengthen their role in delivery; (2) **UN agencies** benefit from secondments to fill critical gaps; (3) **Mutual aid groups** (proposed in 2024) would test direct community-led response models, with FCDO providing oversight and learning support.
intersections.quote: "The parties to the conflict understand how to manipulate the international humanitarian aid architecture to obstruct, delay and deny aid to people in need. Access is strictly controlled whether through bureaucratic and administrative impediments. [...] As a result, we have begun diversifying our partnerships to deliver aid in different ways and with different value add (and consequent trade-offs)." (D0007322.odt, Detailed information)

key_programme_risks: Humanitarian access restrictions (bureaucratic and security-related)
Famine and escalating food insecurity (e.g., Zamzam IDP camp)
Aid diversion and looting of warehouses
Weak local NGO capacity and safeguarding risks
Politicization of humanitarian data (e.g., SAF controlling famine assessments)
Financial and fiduciary risks (fraud, misappropriation in high-risk areas)
Protection risks (SGBV, exploitation of beneficiaries)
Climate hazards (flooding, drought) exacerbating displacement and food insecurity
Volatile political and security environment (e.g., SAF-RSF conflict, border closures)
Partner fatigue or withdrawal due to operating challenges

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversify partnerships to include local actors with better access; advocate for access through UN and diplomatic channels; use flexible funding (IRF, SHF) to adapt to constraints.
Scale up food assistance (WFP, SHF) and nutrition services (UNICEF); monitor early warning systems; support local response capacities (e.g., ERRs).
Third-party monitoring (SIMAP); due diligence refreshes; zero-tolerance policies; secure supply chains.
Strengthen through SHF grants, technical support, and mentorship (e.g., Protection Consortium, Enabling Facility).
Work with independent assessors (e.g., Famine Review Committee); advocate for transparent, evidence-based needs assessments.
Enhanced due diligence; SIMAP verification; escalation of high-risk cases to Directors; regular compliance checks.
Safeguarding risk assessments for all interventions; third-party monitoring; adherence to IASC GBV guidelines; community-based protection approaches.
Integrate climate risk assessments into programming; support shock-responsive interventions (e.g., cash for drought-affected areas).
Conflict sensitivity training (via CSF); adaptive programming; secondments to UN for coordination; real-time risk assessments.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexibility is critical in FCAS: The IRF and adaptive programming allowed rapid response to the 2023 conflict escalation and famine declarations.
Localisation improves access: Local NGOs and ERRs often reached populations that international actors could not, though they required capacity support.
Conflict sensitivity must be embedded: Partners received training on avoiding unintended harm (e.g., elite capture, exacerbating tensions).
Pooled funds (e.g., SHF) enable agile responses: The SHF’s ability to double contributions to community-led organisations in 2024 demonstrated value in FCAS.
Data is politicized: Independent verification (e.g., SIMAP, Famine Review Committee) is essential for credible needs assessments.
Cash transfers require robust controls: While cost-effective, cash programmes in Sudan faced safeguarding and diversion risks, necessitating intensive monitoring.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2023 Annual Review (score: A) highlighted that: (1) **Diversification of partners** improved reach in access-constrained areas; (2) **Flexible funding** (IRF, SHF) enabled rapid adaptation to spikes in need; (3) **Local actors** (e.g., grassroots organisations) delivered faster in some contexts but required capacity building; (4) **UN agencies** provided scale but faced bureaucratic delays; (5) **Protection and gender equality** outcomes were strengthened by community-based approaches and safeguarding measures.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2024 addenda introduced: (1) **Expanded localisation** (testing mutual aid groups, ERRs); (2) **New partnerships** (e.g., DRC multi-donor fund, INSO for security management); (3) **Reinforced enabling environment** (addressing misinformation, hate speech); (4) **Extended timeframe** (to March 2026) to allow for learning and adaptation; (5) **Increased budget** (from £90m to £199.4m) to match escalating needs.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons have been learned on the need for a broad range of partners to deliver in a highly access-constrained environment. UN agencies and international NGOs faced different types of access constraints, while local, grassroots organisations may sometimes offer greatest access to populations in need, but at a much smaller scale. The flexibility built into SHPR [...] has allowed British Office Sudan to adapt to the evolving context, challenges, and needs, exploring new partnerships for delivery." (D0005343.odt, Changes)

financial_details.quote: "Approved budget: £139.9m of which £8m is from the Internal Risk Facility. Amount already spent: £120.2m (of which £8m from Internal Risk Facility). Amount of cost extension: £62m. Revised BC total: £199.4m." (D0007322.odt, Budget)

metadata.programme_name: Good Governance Fund (GGF) Eastern Neighbourhood – Phase Three
metadata.quote: "The Good Governance Fund (GGF) Phase 3 will deliver demand-led support to governance reforms that allow open societies and economies to flourish. The GGF will focus on improving democratic and economic governance, primarily through strategically targeted technical assistance." (D0001555.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: April 2022", "End Date: March 2025" (D0001555.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GGF Phase 3 delivers **technical assistance** (capacity building) to support **governance and economic reforms** (implementation research) while aiming to **prevent democratic backsliding** (policy influence) and **strengthen UK partnerships** (financing mechanism). It combines capacity-building with strategic policy engagement and flexible funding mechanisms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The GGF will deliver interventions on a flexible basis, based on identified needs and/or requests from government counterparts or civil society in beneficiary countries in support of governance and economic reforms. This will support delivery and seek to prevent/reverse democratic backsliding." (D0001555.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Enhanced capacity of government institutions, parliament, civil society, and media to protect/demand/drive/reform governance (e.g., "Government institutions, parliament, civil society and media have enhanced capacity")
Adoption of GESI-sensitive legislation, policies, and regulations (e.g., "Critical GESI-sensitive/transformative legislation, policy, regulations, strategies")
Strengthened UK dialogue with governments and civil society (e.g., "Expanded and strengthened UK dialogue and relationships")
Improved private/public dialogue platforms (e.g., "strengthened private/public dialogue platforms")
15% of programme spend targeted at gender-transformative interventions (EECAD’s Gender Roadmap)
Pilot projects in Azerbaijan focusing on economic diversification (£150,000 in FY2023-24)
what_objectives.summary: The GGF provides **demand-led technical assistance** to Eastern Neighbourhood countries (Armenia, Georgia, Moldova, and now Azerbaijan) to improve democratic governance, economic resilience, and UK strategic partnerships. It focuses on **adaptive, conflict-sensitive interventions** that respond to local reform priorities while mitigating risks of democratic backsliding and malign influence.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will support delivery of reforms and/or seek to prevent/reverse democratic backsliding. GGF is part of an integrated portfolio of programmes operating in the EECA region and supports the delivery of four NSC strategies and the Integrated Review." (D0001555.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The region faces **protracted conflicts** (Nagorno-Karabakh, Transnistria), **Russian malign influence**, **democratic backsliding**, and **weak institutions**. Azerbaijan’s inclusion adds complexity due to its **authoritarian governance** and **restrictions on civil society**.
where_context.q5_source: "Unresolved protracted conflicts (Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Nagorno Karabakh and Transnistria) have the potential to re-surface... leaving the region vulnerable to malign influence." (D0001555.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending) && "Azerbaijan’s political alignment [has] moved further away from Russia, but grant funding to civil society must go through central government approval." (D0004845.odt, Azerbaijan-specific considerations)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: 1) **Conflict**: Protracted disputes undermine stability and reform traction. 2) **Regulatory**: Azerbaijan requires government approval for civil society grants, limiting partner options. 3) **Political Economy**: Vested interests (oligarchs, Russia-aligned actors) hinder reforms. 4) **Data**: Limited evidence base in "difficult operating environments" (D0004845.odt). 5) **Security**: Hybrid threats from Russia and risk of violent conflict recurrence.
where_context.quote: "The nature of the GGF means that we sometimes work in difficult operating environments where there is a narrow evidence base and a limited choice of partners." (D0004845.odt, Risk) && "Unresolved conflicts... have the potential to re-surface, leaving the region vulnerable to malign influence." (D0001555.odt, Rationale)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO and UK-based advisers drive **strategic priorities** and **project approvals**, while local embassies and partners implement. Decision-making is centralized in the UK with input from in-country teams.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to government institutions
mentoring and learning-by-doing (vs formal training)
support to civil society for demand-side accountability
gender and social inclusion (GESI) analysis for all projects
political economy analysis (PEA) to inform interventions

partner_organizations.role: Development Partner (technical assistance and lending)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Development Partner (policy reform and trust funds)

partner_organizations.role: Bilateral donor (coordination and alignment)

partner_organizations.name: European Union (EU)
partner_organizations.role: Bilateral donor (complementary programming)

partner_organizations.name: Local Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partners (demand-side reforms and advocacy)

partner_organizations.name: National Democratic Institute (NDI)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance provider (democratic governance)

partner_organizations.name: Expert Advisory Call-down Service (EACDS)
partner_organizations.role: Framework for rapid technical support (replaced in 2022)

partner_organizations.name: Embassy-based teams (Tbilisi hub)
partner_organizations.role: Programme management and political engagement

who_partners.quote: "The GGF currently uses three delivery mechanisms: Development Partnerships (multilaterals/IFIs), a Managed Fund for Technical Assistance (commercial supplier), and a Strategic Support Fund (CSOs/think tanks)." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of options) && "FCDO will support and work with implementing partners to utilise GESI analysis to identify programme adjustments." (D0001555.odt, Gender Equality Act compliance)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: 1) **Development Partnerships**: Block funding to multilaterals (e.g., World Bank, EBRD) for large-scale reforms. 2) **Managed Fund**: Competitive grants/contracts for technical assistance (min £3m threshold for cost-efficiency). 3) **Strategic Support Fund**: Direct grants to CSOs for demand-side reforms. 4) **Framework Agreements**: Pre-approved commercial contracts (e.g., EACDS) for rapid deployment.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Regional hub in **Tbilisi** coordinates across countries, with **FCDO advisers** providing technical oversight. Embassies identify priorities, while **implementing partners** (multilaterals, CSOs, commercial suppliers) deliver projects. The **Strategic Support Fund** and **Managed Fund** operate as semi-autonomous mechanisms with FCDO approval gates.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: 1) **Development Partners**: Direct awards to pre-vetted multilaterals (e.g., World Bank) for efficiency. 2) **Managed Fund/Strategic Support Fund**: Competitive processes for CSOs/commercial partners, with **political economy analysis** guiding selection. 3) **Framework Agreements**: Pre-approved suppliers (e.g., EACDS) for speed. **Demand-driven criteria** prioritize alignment with UK/FCDO strategies and local reform agendas.
how_mechanism.quote: "Development Partnerships fund larger projects with the UK’s key strategic partners in-country... Strategic Support Fund will focus on the demand-side of reform, increasing and catalysing civil society’s ability to demand reform." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of options) && "The use of an FCDO Framework Agreement would require staff resource at Post level." (D0004845.odt, Implementation approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Programme Board** (comprising FCDO, embassies, and advisers) oversees strategic direction, while **Post Programme Boards** approve individual projects. **Annual reviews** and **political economy updates** inform adaptations. For Azerbaijan, additional safeguarding checks are required due to regulatory constraints.
how_governance.quote: "Firm oversight and monitoring will ensure a demand-led approach focused on strategic priorities... Regular (at least annual) updates to political economy analysis." (D0001555.odt, Key risks) && "All agreements will be subject to review of performance, value for money, changes in context and relevance." (D0004845.odt, Implementation approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be **scaled up/down** between countries or sectors based on **political momentum** and **emerging priorities**, but requires **FCDO approval** and alignment with **NSC strategies**. The **Managed Fund** allows rapid reallocation for time-sensitive interventions.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses **"adaptive management"** with **quarterly reviews** and **political economy updates** to adjust priorities. **Window-of-opportunity** responses (e.g., post-election reforms) are built into the design, but major shifts require **Programme Board sign-off**.
how_flexibility.quote: "The GGF is designed to address this through an ability to respond to evolving priorities, step in rapidly, scale up or scale down as necessary." (D0001555.odt, Why technical assistance) && "Projects will be identified and approved based on... political will/political economy analysis that shows broad support for reform." (D0004845.odt, Implementation approach)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Delivery Mechanism (e.g., Managed Fund/Development Partnership)** → **Implementing Partner (e.g., EBRD/CSO)** → **End Beneficiary (e.g., government ministry/civil society)**
how_efficiency.quote: "The Managed Fund... would require a minimum level of projects to achieve VfM (ca £3m)." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of options) && "All projects within GGF are expected to take due consideration of gender and will align with requirements for gender marking." (D0004845.odt, Expected results)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Do Nothing (no GGF programming)
Option B: Refreshed (continue Phase 2 mechanisms with lessons learned)
Option C: Development Partnerships Only (focus on multilaterals)
Option D: Focused (mix of Development Partnerships + Strategic Support Fund + Framework Agreements)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: **Option D (Focused)** was selected for its **balance of flexibility and sustainability**. It retains **responsive mechanisms** (e.g., Strategic Support Fund) while leveraging **multilateral partnerships** for scale. The **Framework Agreement** replaces the Managed Fund for efficiency, and the **reduced number of projects** improves oversight. This aligns with **Integrated Review** priorities and **lessons from Phase 2** (e.g., need for clearer purpose per mechanism).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Proliferation of small, low-impact programmes (undermining strategic focus)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear criteria for GGF support (results/value for money) and limiting project numbers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak programme management (delays, poor coordination)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Deliver chain mapping, political economy analysis, and firm oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supply-led portfolios (misalignment with demand)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand-driven approval process with embassy validation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud/corruption in reform programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence, safeguarding checks, and conflict sensitivity tools.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced UK visibility in multilateral channels
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strategic engagement with multilaterals and civil society implementers.

why_rationale.quote: "RECOMMENDED OPTION: Option D: Focused. A focus on Development Partnerships, the potential use of an FCDO Framework Agreement (rather than the Managed Fund) and more focused Strategic Support Fund would be more manageable... This would enable a more balanced approach to reform." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of options) && "The GGF’s adaptive working was identified as a critical contributory factor to success in its second phase." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of evidence)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: **Regulatory environment** in Azerbaijan limits partners to government-approved CSOs or commercial contracts. **Conflict sensitivity** requires vetting partners in Armenia/Georgia/Moldova to avoid exacerbating tensions. **Russian influence** necessitates working with pro-reform actors aligned with UK values.
q27_constraints_detail: Azerbaijan: Government approval required for CSO grants → restricts to commercial contracts or multilaterals.
Armenia/Georgia/Moldova: Protracted conflicts → partners must be conflict-sensitive.
Region-wide: Russian malign influence → partners vetted for alignment with democratic values.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: **Demand-led technical assistance** requires **flexible mechanisms** (e.g., Managed Fund for rapid response). **Political economy focus** necessitates **embedded advisers** and **local partner networks**. **Conflict sensitivity** mandates **adaptive management** and **safeguarding protocols**.
q28_linkages: Objective: *Prevent democratic backsliding* → Mechanism: **Strategic Support Fund for CSOs** to demand accountability.
Objective: *Economic resilience* → Mechanism: **Development Partnerships with IFIs** for sectoral reforms.
Objective: *UK influence* → Mechanism: **Framework Agreements** for rapid, high-profile interventions.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions between **speed** (using pre-approved frameworks) and **inclusion** (ensuring marginalized groups benefit). **Gender transformative goals** (15% spend) compete with **rapid deployment** needs. **Local ownership** (Southern-led reforms) vs. **UK strategic priorities** (Northern oversight).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. Inclusion: Framework Agreements enable rapid response but may bypass local CSOs.
Expertise vs. Ownership: Northern technical assistance risks crowding out Southern capacity.
Cost vs. Reach: Fewer, larger projects (Option D) improve efficiency but reduce geographic coverage.
intersections.risk_affects_management: **High-risk FCAS context** → **Intensive oversight** (quarterly reviews, embedded advisers). **Conflict sensitivity** → **Additional screening layers** for partners/projects. **Azerbaijan’s regulatory risks** → **Stricter due diligence** for commercial contracts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) **Multilaterals** (EBRD/World Bank) receive TA to **improve reform delivery**. 2) **CSOs** are funded to **demand accountability** (Strategic Support Fund). 3) **Government institutions** get **mentoring/learning-by-doing** to sustain reforms post-GGF.
intersections.quote: "The nature of the GGF means that we sometimes work in difficult operating environments where there is a narrow evidence base and a limited choice of partners." (D0004845.odt, Risk) && "GGF interventions address the foundational causes of instability and support the ‘building blocks’ of stability including fair power structures, effective and legitimate institutions and inclusive economic development." (D0001555.odt, Conflict sensitivity)

key_programme_risks: Democratic backsliding in target countries (e.g., media restrictions, emergency measures)
Russian malign influence undermining reforms (e.g., energy leverage, disinformation)
Weak institutional capacity limiting reform absorption
Corruption diverting funds or capturing reforms
Conflict recurrence (e.g., Nagorno-Karabakh, Transnistria)
Economic shocks (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine war spillover)
Overambitious reform plans raising unrealistic expectations
Limited civil society space (especially in Azerbaijan)
Donor fatigue or misalignment reducing leverage
UK reputational risk if reforms stall or backslide

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Clear criteria for GGF support (results/value for money) and limiting project numbers.
Delivery chain mapping, political economy analysis, and firm oversight.
Demand-driven approval process with embassy validation.
Due diligence, safeguarding checks, and conflict sensitivity tools.
Focus on countries with demonstrated reform commitment; early warning systems via embassies.
Conflict analysis and adaptive programming (e.g., scaling down in crisis).
Robust safeguarding protocols and partner vetting (assessed as low risk).
Strategic engagement with multilaterals and civil society implementers.
Use commercial contracts or multilaterals; focus on economic reforms with government buy-in.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Conflict sensitivity is critical**: GGF uses proportional screening and ongoing adjustments for all interventions.
**Political economy analysis is non-negotiable**: Annual updates required to adapt to shifting power dynamics.
**Local demand drives sustainability**: Phase 2 showed that supply-driven TA failed; Phase 3 prioritizes buy-in.
**Windows of opportunity are fleeting**: 85% of economic reforms occur within 15 months of a government change (World Bank 2007).
**Resilience requires economic diversification**: Azerbaijan’s oil dependence highlights vulnerability to shocks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Sustainability gaps**: Phase 2 achieved outputs but struggled with outcome-level change due to **political turnover**. Phase 3 strengthens **incentives and handover plans**. 2) **CSO engagement works**: Demand-side projects (e.g., election monitoring) had **higher traction**. 3) **Multilateral leverage**: Trust funds influenced World Bank lending (e.g., gender strategies). 4) **Adaptive management pays off**: Rapid response to **COVID-19 democratic rollbacks** preserved gains. 5) **UK political capital matters**: Diplomatic engagement **unlocked reforms** (e.g., Georgia’s tax model).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Fewer, larger projects** (Option D) to improve strategic focus. 2) **Stronger sustainability plans** (mentoring, institutional support). 3) **Explicit conflict sensitivity tools** (screening, trade-off analysis). 4) **Gender transformative target** (15% spend). 5) **Framework Agreements** replace Managed Fund for efficiency. 6) **Azerbaijan pilot** tests economic reforms in a new context.
risks_lessons.quote: "The GGF’s adaptive working was identified as a critical contributory factor to success in its second phase." (D0001555.odt, Assessment of evidence) && "The PCR assessed that while output targets have been achieved, the programme did not fully meet all outcome targets due to an ‘implementation gap’... Sustainability has therefore been identified as an area that requires further attention." (D0001555.odt, GGF Historic Performance)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: GGF influences **World Bank/EBRD lending** (e.g., Trust Funds adjust Bank operations) and **catalyses other donor funding** (e.g., USAID, EU alignment). In Azerbaijan, pilot aims to **unlock longer-term reforms** with minimal ODA spend (£150k).
financial_details.quote: "The programme budget is £38,000,000 subject to FCDO-wide allocations processes... A pilot project in Azerbaijan... is expected to spend approx. £150,000." (D0004845.odt, Additional support) && "GGF Phase III funding will return to previous levels of funding for multiple years." (D0001555.odt, Programme Value)

metadata.programme_name: Ukraine Good Governance Fund – Phase Three
metadata.duration_text: The GGF Phase Three will be delivered via complementary delivery mechanisms, each of which have their own commercial approach. Outcome level targets are expected to be delivered within the life of the programme (April 2025)
metadata.quote: "Working in tandem with our diplomatic, defence, and trade levers, the GGF will provide flexible and technical assistance that can be mobilised quickly to enable economic and governance reform in Ukraine." (D0003138.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Outcome level targets are expected to be delivered within the life of the programme (April 2025)" (D0003138.odt, Theory of Change)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GGF provides technical assistance to support governance and economic reforms in Ukraine, focusing on capacity building, policy influence, and implementation research. It aims to strengthen institutions, reduce corruption, and enhance trade opportunities with the UK, while also supporting civil society to demand reforms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The GGF will provide flexible and technical assistance that can be mobilised quickly to enable economic and governance reform in Ukraine. Its overall objectives will be to support: an open society based on rule of law; effective, transparent, and accountable institutions; and economic reforms that create a more inclusive and rules-based economy, enhancing trade opportunities with the UK." (D0003138.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Government institutions, parliament, and/or civil society have enhanced capacity to protect, demand, drive, influence, or implement reforms
Government, institutions, parliament, and/or civil society have enhanced capacity to address gender equality and social inclusion issues
Critical legislation, policy, regulations, strategies, and implementation plans designed and adopted and supported in implementation
Expanded and strengthened UK dialogue and relationships/collaboration with government, like-minded actors, and civil society
Technical assistance approaches tested and evidence and learning informs programming
Rule of law and anti-corruption institutions are more independent and effective, reducing corruption and impunity
Ukraine adopts and implements liberalising reforms that create a more inclusive and rules-based economy (enhancing trade opportunities with the UK)
Citizens (including women and girls), civil society, and businesses are better equipped to demand reform, engage politically, and hold government to account
what_objectives.summary: The GGF aims to strengthen Ukraine's governance and economic systems through technical assistance, focusing on anti-corruption, rule of law, and economic reforms to enhance trade with the UK and build resilience against malign influences.
what_objectives.quote: "The impact that GGF aims to contribute to alongside wider government and partner efforts is: an open Ukraine with stronger rule of law, more effective, transparent, and accountable institutions, an economy that is competitive, inclusive, and rules-based, and greater resilience against malign influences." (D0003138.odt, Theory of Change)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is described as facing hybrid warfare from Russia, with ongoing conflict in the east and significant political and economic instability. The overall programme risk is assessed as 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: "Since 2014, Russia has been engaged in hybrid warfare in Ukraine, supporting proxies in the east of the country, promoting a wide range of disinformation narratives, and working to undermine political and economic reform." (D0003138.odt, Context) and "The overall risk is assessed as Major." (D0003138.odt, Key Risks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The conflict in eastern Ukraine and Russian hybrid warfare create security risks and undermine reform efforts. Corruption and vested interests resist reforms, while weak institutions limit implementation capacity.
where_context.quote: "Ukraine remains vulnerable to internal shocks and external aggression – either of which could reverse recent progress." (D0003138.odt, Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO and British Embassy Kyiv lead decision-making, with Ukrainian partners primarily as implementers and beneficiaries of technical assistance.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
institutional strengthening
support to civil society organizations

partner_organizations.name: USAID
partner_organizations.role: co-funder and partner in projects like TAPAS

partner_organizations.name: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU)
partner_organizations.role: recipient of technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: development partner

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: development partner

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: recipients of Strategic Support Fund grants

partner_organizations.name: Think tanks and private sector associations
partner_organizations.role: recipients of Strategic Support Fund grants

who_partners.quote: "The GGF currently uses three strands to deliver its goals: Strand I: Development Partnerships, funding larger projects with key partners (such as USAID), multilaterals such as the UN, and International Financial Institutions (IFIs) such as the World Bank and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)." (D0003138.odt, Strands or Mechanisms)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The GGF uses a combination of grants (Strategic Support Fund), contracts (Managed Fund), and development partnerships with IFIs and multilaterals. The Managed Fund is a competitively tendered mechanism for technical assistance, while the Strategic Support Fund provides grants to CSOs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through three strands: Development Partnerships (with IFIs/multilaterals), a Managed Fund (contracted to an external supplier), and a Strategic Support Fund (grants to CSOs). The British Embassy Kyiv plays a critical role in identifying priorities and maintaining relationships.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Managed Fund is contracted to an external supplier, with efforts to increase competition and reduce overhead costs. Development Partners are chosen based on strategic alignment and past performance.
how_mechanism.quote: "The commercially driven Managed Fund is a competitively tendered mechanism, which is currently funded by Ukraine CSSF for financial year 2021-22. This route to market followed extensive engagement with PCD and early market engagement with potential suppliers." (D0003138.odt, Options for Delivery)

how_governance.quote: "The GGF will track and compare operational costs to benchmark rates to keep fees low. However, this linear approach is unlikely to capture the complexity and the uncertainty of operating in Ukraine. Past evidence shows that in such contexts better results are delivered when we engage on not only reforms that have a probability of success, but projects that adapt and learn as they go forward." (D0003138.odt, Value for Money)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between projects based on progress and emerging opportunities, but major reallocations require approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The GGF emphasizes adaptive management, allowing for adjustments based on political momentum and reform opportunities. This includes scaling up effective projects and reducing less effective ones.
how_flexibility.quote: "Should things change, we are also able to adjust the projects by scaling up more effective elements whilst scaling down others." (D0003138.odt, Key Risks)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → External Supplier (Managed Fund) → Ukrainian Government/CSOs; or FCDO → Development Partners (IFIs/USAID) → Ukrainian Government/CSOs
how_efficiency.quote: "The commercially driven Managed Fund is a competitively tendered mechanism, which is currently funded by Ukraine CSSF for financial year 2021-22." (D0003138.odt, Options for Delivery)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing: no GGF programming in Ukraine but continued lobbying on governance and economic reforms as part of regular business

Refreshed GGF: use of the same strands/delivery mechanisms (IFIs/multilaterals, Managed Fund (MF), and Strategic Support Fund (SSF)) as GGF Phase Two but applying lessons learned from the Project Completion Review, including refining priority themes

Development Partnerships only: fewer projects delivered only via Development Partnerships, including multilaterals, the UN, the IFIs and other major development actors such as NDI. This option would end the Managed Fund and the Strategic Support Fund

Focussed GGF: this option would retain the Development Partnerships strand as well as the Strategic Support Fund, but would see the Managed Fund removed and instead use an FCDO Framework Agreement for specific technical support. Change of SRO and PRO from London to Post
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The 'Refreshed GGF' (Option B) was chosen because it maintains the UK's relationships, access, and influence in Ukraine while retaining flexibility and responsiveness. This approach has been successful in the past and allows the UK to support emerging reform opportunities quickly.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management costs due to retaining three mechanisms (Development Partnerships, Managed Fund, Strategic Support Fund)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on reducing overhead costs and improving value for money through negotiation and streamlined processes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of unique position as the most flexible and rapid donor if the Managed Fund is removed (as in Option D)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Retaining the Managed Fund ensures continued flexibility and responsiveness.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced ability to respond quickly to government requests if relying only on Development Partnerships (Option C)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Retaining the Managed Fund and Strategic Support Fund ensures rapid response capability.

why_rationale.quote: "The preferred option is Option B: Refreshed GGF. As the appraisal of options demonstrates, this option offers clear benefits to our objectives in Ukraine. In particular, it would help strengthen relationships and enhance the UK’s access and influence, whilst also allowing us to retain our flexibility and responsiveness – something that has been of particular value in supporting reform in a fast-moving environment such as Ukraine." (D0003138.odt, The preferred option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The conflict and political instability in Ukraine limit the pool of potential partners to those with experience operating in FCAS environments. Security risks and corruption also constrain which organizations can effectively deliver technical assistance.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in eastern Ukraine limits access to certain regions
Corruption and vested interests resist reforms, requiring partners with strong anti-corruption credentials
Political instability requires partners who can adapt quickly to changing priorities
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid, flexible technical assistance to support emerging reform opportunities determines the use of a Managed Fund and Strategic Support Fund. The focus on both supply-side (government) and demand-side (civil society) reforms requires a mixed delivery structure with multiple strands.
q28_linkages: Flexible technical assistance is needed to respond to fast-moving reform opportunities (Managed Fund)
Longer-term structural reforms require partnerships with IFIs and multilaterals (Development Partnerships)
Civil society engagement requires grant-based support (Strategic Support Fund)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the need to balance rapid delivery (efficiency) with inclusive partnerships (equity). For example, the Strategic Support Fund focuses on smaller CSOs to ensure inclusivity, while the Managed Fund allows for quick disbursement of technical assistance to government reformers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed of response (Managed Fund) vs. inclusivity (Strategic Support Fund for smaller CSOs)
Scalability (Development Partnerships with IFIs) vs. local ownership (direct support to Ukrainian institutions)
Flexibility (adaptive management) vs. sustainability (longer-term institutional strengthening)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk environment (FCAS) requires intensive oversight and adaptive management to mitigate risks such as political shocks or reform reversals. This increases management costs but is necessary for effective delivery.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with technical assistance designed to transfer skills and knowledge to Ukrainian institutions. This shapes partner roles, as local organizations are expected to take on increasing responsibility over time.
intersections.quote: "The GGF will be agile and responsive – able to provide technical assistance in areas that advance reform and/or to respond to the opportunities that emerge in Ukraine’s fast-moving political environment." (D0003138.odt, Why technical assistance to economic and governance reform?)

key_programme_risks: Political or economic shocks negatively impacting the reform agenda
Over-ambitious reform plans that cannot be delivered, raising expectations or undermining trust in government
Reform being prevented or undone by vested interests
Instability and/or violence
Proliferation of small, low-impact programmes
Poor programme management
Supply-led portfolios (the ‘principal agent problem’)
Failure to deliver adaptive programming
Fraud or corruption in the programme
Safeguarding risks
Inadvertent negative contribution to conflict dynamics

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Ongoing assessment and monitoring of political and conflict dynamics, with adjustments to the portfolio as needed.
International engagement to make Government of Ukraine strategies and reform initiatives more realistic and attainable.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reform being prevented or undone by vested interests
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Political engagement and technical assistance to defend institutions and advance reforms.
Keep the number of programmes proportionate to staffing capacity and focus on high-impact areas.
Risk monitoring and management strategies, with a focus on proportional programme management resources.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fraud or corruption in the programme
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Internal controls, due diligence, audits, and spot checks.
Conflict sensitivity screening and adherence to safeguarding policies.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible and responsive technical assistance is critical in FCAS environments where reform opportunities emerge and disappear quickly.
Sustained engagement and adaptive management are necessary to navigate political uncertainty and resistance from vested interests.
Building local capacity and ownership is essential for sustainability in fragile contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases of the GGF have demonstrated the value of a demand-driven approach, with projects aligned to government priorities and political momentum. The programme has also learned the importance of focusing on implementation (not just policy design) and sustainability, including through mentoring and institutional support. The Midline Evaluation and Project Completion Review highlighted the need to strengthen incentives for implementation and to address the 'implementation gap' where policies are designed but not fully executed.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The refreshed GGF (Phase Three) incorporates lessons from previous phases, including a continued focus on adaptive management, stronger emphasis on sustainability and implementation, and refined priority themes. The programme will also aim to improve gender sensitivity and conflict sensitivity in its interventions.
risks_lessons.quote: "There is evidence of an ‘implementation gap’, arising due to outputs like reformed policies, new laws and procedures not always having moved to the implementation stage. Sustainability has been identified as an area that requires further attention, including by strengthening incentives during programme design and delivery." (D0003138.odt, Option B: Refreshed GGF with existing mechanisms)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The GGF has influenced larger sums of funding from other donors, such as through trust funds with IFIs. For example, GGF support helped shape the economic transformation strategy for Ukraine’s eastern conflict-affected regions, which directed much larger volumes of Government of Ukraine spending.
financial_details.quote: "At this level of funding, the GGF in Ukraine will retain the full range of delivery mechanisms, allowing the UK to be a responsive and flexible partner and quickly support emerging reform opportunities, providing technical assistance and capacity-building in critical sectors." (D0003138.odt, What will the UK Deliver to meet this Need?)

metadata.programme_name: Western Balkans – Freedom and Resilience Programme
metadata.quote: The Freedom and Resilience Programme will comprise a portfolio of interventions in three areas: reconciliation and peacebuilding in conflict-affected communities; empowering women and girls and tackling CRSV and gender-based violence; and strengthening government capacity, transparency and accountability. (D0003956.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The Freedom and Resilience Programme will be a three-year (2022-25) programme of support spending up to £30m (D0003956.odt, What will the UK deliver?)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions and skills), implementation research (testing and scaling interventions), and service delivery (direct support to conflict-affected communities). It focuses on governance reform, peacebuilding, and gender equality, with a strong emphasis on addressing structural issues like corruption, conflict legacies, and gender-based violence.
what_objectives.q1_source: The Freedom and Resilience Programme will comprise a portfolio of interventions in three areas: reconciliation and peacebuilding in conflict-affected communities; empowering women and girls and tackling CRSV and gender-based violence; and strengthening government capacity, transparency and accountability. (D0003956.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Improved reconciliation and peacebuilding outcomes for conflict-affected communities, with a focus on building connections across conflict divides and strengthening access to transitional justice processes
Empowerment of women and girls through tackling CRSV, GBV, and promoting women’s meaningful participation in decision-making processes
More transparent and accountable governance through building state capacity and strengthening civil society
Support for regional cooperation on war crimes prosecution and missing persons cases
Strengthened capacity of domestic institutions to handle evidence, including for cases of CRSV
Increased political access and influence for the UK in the Western Balkans region
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to enhance stability, resilience, and democratic governance in the Western Balkans by addressing conflict legacies, empowering women and girls, and strengthening government transparency and accountability. It builds on previous UK programming and aligns with the UK's International Development Strategy.
what_objectives.quote: The Freedom and Resilience Programme will complement the CSSF programmes by addressing the longer-term, structural issues across the region, including ethno-nationalist division, gender discrimination and gender-based violence, and a lack of transparency and accountability in government, which create the vulnerabilities that hostile state actors and organised crime groups exploit. (D0003956.odt, Why should the UK address this need?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The Western Balkans region is described as fragile with ongoing risks of instability, including ethno-nationalist divisions, weak governance, and external malign influences. The document explicitly states the risk category as 'Major' and notes vulnerabilities to political or economic shocks, reform resistance, and deteriorating public support.
where_context.q5_source: The risk category is Major. We do not expect to work outside of the FCDO risk appetite statement. (D0003956.odt, Risks and assurances)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The region's fragility is exacerbated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, creating energy and food crises. Political instability (e.g., secessionist moves in Bosnia and Herzegovina, tensions between Kosovo and Serbia) and weak trust in institutions limit reform progress. Gender inequality and ethnic divisions further complicate delivery, while the need for energy transition adds pressure on governments.
where_context.quote: Stability remains fragile, Serious and Organised Crime (SOC) that affects the UK is a major problem, and weak governance and geopolitical competition risk outcomes that are profoundly against our interests. (D0003956.odt, Portfolio/Business/Country Plan Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU) in the UK manages funds centrally, with Posts (embassies) bidding for project interventions. Decision-making power rests with the WBPU and FCDO, though country-led priorities are considered.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
institutional strengthening
support for regional cooperation (e.g., war crimes prosecution, missing persons)
technical assistance for governance reform
civil society empowerment

partner_organizations.name: Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU)
partner_organizations.role: Central programme management and fund allocation

partner_organizations.name: UK Embassies (Posts) in WB6 countries
partner_organizations.role: Identify priority areas, bid for funds, and engage with local stakeholders
partner_organizations.location: Western Balkans (Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia)

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Institutions (IFIs) (e.g., World Bank, EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Potential implementing partners for governance and economic reforms

partner_organizations.name: UN Agencies (e.g., UNDP, IRMCT)
partner_organizations.role: Support for transitional justice, war crimes prosecution, and missing persons

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs and civil society organizations
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of community-level interventions, especially on gender equality and reconciliation

partner_organizations.name: Host governments in WB6 countries
partner_organizations.role: Co-design and implementation of reforms, with political buy-in

partner_organizations.name: EU, USAID, GIZ
partner_organizations.role: Coordination and potential co-funding for aligned priorities

who_partners.quote: Programming will be country-led, with Posts able to bid for funds in support of projects in line with their priorities. (D0003956.odt, What will the UK deliver?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a flexible fund model where UK Embassies (Posts) bid for project interventions. Funds are managed centrally by the Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU), with a portfolio approach allowing for grants, contracts, and partnerships depending on the intervention.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The WBPU acts as a central fund manager, overseeing a portfolio of interventions across the WB6. Posts submit bids for country-specific projects, which are assessed against priorities and evidence. Regional or multi-country projects are also considered for cross-border issues.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Posts (UK Embassies) bid for funds based on country priorities, with proposals ranked against strategic objectives, likely impact, and political buy-in. This ensures alignment with UK goals while allowing country-level flexibility. The WBPU and senior officials provide oversight to avoid proliferation of small or ineffective programmes.
how_mechanism.quote: The Western Balkans Regional Strategy Board agreed that funds should be managed centrally by the Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU), as opposed to devolving them to Posts to be allocated and managed at that level. (D0003956.odt, How have we assessed the options?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Western Balkans Programme Board and Western Balkans Portfolio Board review and approve the programme. The Director Europe serves as the Portfolio SRO. Country-level Theories of Change and regular political economy analyses guide decision-making, with oversight from senior FCDO officials and diplomatic missions.
how_governance.quote: I can confirm the Business Case has been reviewed and approved by the Western Balkans Programme Board and Western Balkans Portfolio Board. Director Europe, Portfolio SRO. (D0003956.odt, Department/Country Office confirmation of review processes)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects based on priority setting and oversight from senior officials, but this requires alignment with country-level Theories of Change and strategic priorities. The programme allows for adaptive management to scale up effective elements or adjust to challenges.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes adaptive programming, with regular updates to political economy analyses and results frameworks to check progress and encourage adaptation. Firm oversight ensures a demand-led approach focused on strategic priorities, with robust systems for evidence and feedback.
how_flexibility.quote: Regular (at least annual) updates to political economy analysis (including by implementing partners) and updates to results frameworks will help to check progress and encourage adaptation. (D0003956.odt, Risks and assurances)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU) → Implementing partners (Posts, NGOs, multilateral organizations)
how_efficiency.quote: The Western Balkans Programme Unit (WBPU) will manage funds centrally, with Posts bidding for project interventions. (D0003956.odt, What will the UK deliver?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Limited countries (focus on 3-4 WB6 countries, e.g., BiH, Kosovo, Serbia)
Option B: Focused themes (select only one theme: conflict resolution OR governance/opens societies, with gender mainstreamed)
Option C: Flexible fund (retain wider remit with bidding process across all WB6 countries and themes)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option C (Flexible Fund) was chosen because it allows the programme to address HMG’s broad objectives across all WB6 countries while tailoring interventions to country contexts. It builds on the success of previous programmes (GGF and Stability Programme) and offers the best balance of effectiveness, equity, and flexibility. The approach enables political access and influence while mitigating risks of scattered outputs through economies of scale.
q25_decision_factors: experience from previous programmes (GGF, Stability Programme)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of disparate or thinly spread activity due to large number of projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Development of clear criteria for support, linked to NSC strategies and country-level Theories of Change, to avoid proliferation of small/ineffective programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak programme management due to insufficient capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of central programme management team (WBPU) with advisers and finance/corporate staff to reduce burden on Posts; robust systems for evidence and feedback.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of buy-in for reform and failure to deliver adaptive programming
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular updates to political economy analysis and results frameworks; firm oversight to ensure demand-led approach.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of partner organizations being involved in fraud and corruption
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence on all partners; delivery chain mapping and political economy analysis to mitigate fraud risks.

why_rationale.quote: Option C: Flexible Fund [...] has the best chance of meeting HMG’s broad objectives in the WB6. It would enable us to build on previous successes through the GGF and Stability Programme. (D0003956.odt, Preferred option)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The fragile and politically complex context of the Western Balkans limits partner selection to reliable international partners and trusted local NGOs with robust control mechanisms. The need for conflict sensitivity and regional cooperation (e.g., on war crimes or missing persons) requires partners with cross-border experience and credibility.
q27_constraints_detail: Political instability (e.g., secessionist moves in BiH, Kosovo-Serbia tensions) limits engagement with certain government actors
Weak governance and corruption risks require vetting of local partners
Ethnic divisions necessitate inclusive partner selection to avoid exacerbating conflicts
Dependence on Russian energy creates economic vulnerabilities affecting partner stability
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (reconciliation, gender equality, governance) require a flexible fund structure to tailor interventions to country-specific needs. The regional scope of issues like war crimes and missing persons necessitates multi-country projects, while governance reforms often require bilateral, country-led approaches.
q28_linkages: Regional issues (e.g., war crimes, missing persons) → Multi-country projects managed centrally by WBPU
Country-specific governance reforms → Bilateral projects led by Posts with local partners
Gender equality and CRSV → Mixed delivery (local NGOs for community work, multilateral partners for policy influence)
Conflict sensitivity → Requires adaptive management and conflict advisers embedded in delivery
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., standalone workstream on women and girls, inclusion of all WB6 countries) with efficiency (e.g., central management by WBPU to reduce transaction costs). The flexible fund model allows for tailored interventions but risks scattered outputs, which is mitigated by clear criteria and oversight.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Inclusion of all WB6 countries (equity) vs. higher transaction costs (efficiency)
Standalone gender workstream (equity) vs. potential duplication with mainstreaming efforts
Country-led priorities (equity) vs. need for regional coherence (efficiency)
Adaptive programming (equity) vs. risk of inconsistent quality (efficiency)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk profile leads to intensive oversight, including regular political economy analyses, embedded conflict advisers, and milestone-based reviews. The need to mitigate risks of fraud, instability, and reform resistance drives the central management structure and demand-led approach.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with technical assistance and mentoring designed to transfer skills to local institutions (e.g., prosecutors’ offices, civil society). The programme emphasizes sustainability through institutional support and learning-by-doing, which shapes partner roles to include co-design and gradual handover.
intersections.quote: The Freedom and Resilience Programme will complement the CSSF programmes by addressing the longer-term, structural issues across the region, including ethno-nationalist division, gender discrimination and gender-based violence, and a lack of transparency and accountability in government. (D0003956.odt, Why should the UK address this need?)

key_programme_risks: Political or economic shocks disrupting delivery
Reform hindered by vested interests (political, business, civil society, media)
Deteriorating conditions undermining public support for reform
Interventions failing to deliver required impact
Weak programme management due to capacity constraints
Supply-led proposals misaligned with demand
Lack of buy-in for reform
Partner organizations involved in fraud/corruption
Risk of aid diversion to terrorist groups (assessed as low)
Safeguarding risks (assessed as low)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Ensure FRP operates where there is commitment to progress and reform, with reliable partners. Use political economy analysis to refine focus and monitor performance.
Work with engaged partners and beneficiaries; use political economy analysis to shape portfolios and agree projects.
Strategic guidance and priority setting from senior officials; clear criteria for support linked to NSC strategies.
Central team of programme managers, advisers, and finance/corporate staff to reduce burden on Posts; robust systems for evidence/feedback.
Due diligence on all partners; delivery chain mapping and political economy analysis.
Regular updates to political economy analysis; adaptive programming to respond to challenges.
Delivery through reliable international partners and trusted local NGOs with robust control mechanisms.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity must be central to design and delivery, with dedicated advisers and tailored guidance.
Regional cooperation is essential for issues like war crimes and missing persons, requiring multi-country approaches.
Adaptive management is critical in FCAS contexts, with tolerance for unpredictability and occasional failure.
Sustained engagement with national institutions builds trust and identifies political openings for reform.
Inclusive programming (e.g., gender, minorities) is necessary to address root causes of conflict and instability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous programmes (GGF, Stability Programme) demonstrated the importance of demand-driven, politically informed solutions; capacity transfer (not substitution); and iterative, adaptive approaches. The GGF’s success in leveraging World Bank funds (USD 700m) showed the value of catalytic UK support. Lessons include the need for realistic timelines, sustained engagement, and alignment with host governments’ international commitments.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from CSSF to FCDO baseline for conflict resolution programming due to CSSF’s narrower remit.
Greater focus on sustainability in governance interventions, addressing the 'implementation gap' from GGF.
Stronger emphasis on conflict sensitivity and regional cooperation, informed by Stability Programme evaluations.
Inclusion of a standalone workstream on women and girls, building on previous gender programming.
Use of central management (WBPU) to ensure coherence and reduce burden on Posts, based on GGF/Stability Programme experience.
risks_lessons.quote: The GGF consistently scored an A in Annual Reviews. It was most successful in policy and delivery reform. Technical assistance provided under the GGF was generally assessed to be relevant, well-targeted and of high-quality. (D0003956.odt, Evidence from the GGF and Stability Programme)

co_funding_partners.partner: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The GGF leveraged over USD 700 million from the World Bank during its activities, demonstrating the catalytic effect of UK support. (D0003956.odt, Evidence from the GGF and Stability Programme)
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: up to £30m 2022-2025. (D0003956.odt, Programme Value)

metadata.programme_name: Building Resilience, Inclusion and Diversity through Girls' Education (BRIDGE)
metadata.quote: "BRIDGEsupportstheGovernmentofJordan(GoJ)providequalityeducationtothemostmarginalisedchildren,includingrefugees,throughacombinationoffinancialaidandtechnicalassistance." (D0006692.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original projects start and end dates: 31 Aug 2022 to 31 Dec 2025" and "New project end date (if applicable): 31 Oct 2026" (D0006692.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: BRIDGE combines financing mechanisms (channeling funds through AAI and UNICEF) with service delivery (direct provision of education services to vulnerable children) and capacity building (strengthening MoE systems). It also includes implementation research elements through the ERICC programme.
what_objectives.q1_source: "BRIDGEsupportstheGovernmentofJordan(GoJ)providequalityeducationtothemostmarginalisedchildren,includingrefugees,throughacombinationoffinancialaidandtechnicalassistance." (D0006692.odt, Summary Information) AND "The programme (BRIDGE) will continue the UK’s leading strategic role in the education sector in Jordan. It will combine work to catalyse national reforms with delivering a more inclusive, quality education system that delivers on the Jordan Compact commitment and provision of education for vulnerable girls and boys so that no child is left behind." (D0003448.odt, Impact and Outcome We Expect to Achieve)
q3_expected_outputs: 152,583 refugee students receive textbooks and have their tuition fees paid (AAI)
360 learning support teachers and 147 multi-disciplinary teachers receive salaries (AAI)
204 dropout centres and 72 catch-up centres remain open (AAI)
4,452 children with disabilities supported with transportation (AAI)
34,000+ students (51% female) in 51 camp schools and 29 KG2 centres (UNICEF)
3,600 students (50% female) access early childhood education in camps (UNICEF)
608 Syrian refugee adolescents access NFE in camps (UNICEF)
7,500 females benefit from menstrual health and hygiene (UNICEF)
1,500 students with disabilities receive assistive devices/transport (UNICEF)
1,300 Syrian community members engaged as volunteers (UNICEF)
5,000 children benefit from school-based violence prevention (UNICEF)
300+ teachers/community health volunteers trained on harm reduction (UNICEF)
Data on out-of-school children generated and analysed (UNICEF)
Evidence-based Social and Behaviour Change framework on drug use prevention (UNICEF)
MoE capacity strengthened for data utilization and inclusive education (TA)
National Inclusive Education Strategy and Gender Equality Strategy targets met (System Strengthening)
what_objectives.summary: BRIDGE aims to improve access to quality, inclusive education for 190,000+ vulnerable children (95,000+ girls) in Jordan, including refugees and children with disabilities, while strengthening the public education system's resilience and inclusion through financial aid (AAI/UNICEF) and technical assistance to the Ministry of Education.
what_objectives.quote: "Through a three-year up to £30m programme, BRIDGE will champion the UK’s commitment for every girl to receive 12 years of quality education. This investment in human capital is essential for building Jordan’s economic development and stability." (D0003448.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Jordan is classified as a Fragile and Conflict-Affected State (FCAS) due to its high refugee population (28% of total population), economic fragility, and regional instability risks. The document explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" but contextual evidence points to FCAS classification.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0003448.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Jordan has made significant improvements in education access over the past two decades. However, rapid population growth and the influx of Syrian and other refugees has put unprecedented strain on the system... This has created challenges for basic service delivery and deteriorating quality has created growing dissatisfaction with the state that could contribute to unrest." (D0003448.odt, Country Context and Need for an Intervention)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The refugee crisis (2.9M refugees, 28% of population) strains public services like education, while economic stagnation (2.4% avg growth since 2010) and high unemployment (23.3%, 52% for youth) limit GoJ's ability to fund education reforms. School closures during COVID-19 (nearly 2 years) exacerbated learning poverty, with girls and refugees most affected. Weak MoE capacity for data utilization and parallel systems for refugee education create coordination challenges.
where_context.quote: "Jordan’s struggling economy is now its biggest risk to stability... Public finances remain weak because of a range of exemptions and loopholes offered to the workforce. Such unsustainable economic and fiscal practices and dependencies hamper its macroeconomic growth and its economic stability." (D0003448.odt, Country Context) AND "The provision of quality education is a benchmark for judging the effectiveness of the GoJ, along with public sector jobs, public security and healthcare. Most Jordanians see education as a purely public good and expect a quality and inclusive service from their government. Failure in this space undermines public confidence in the state and is damaging to long-term stability." (D0003448.odt, Jordan’s Education System)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is co-led by FCDO (funding/strategic oversight) and MoE (implementation), with joint decision-making through the AAI Donor Coordination Unit and Education Development Partner Group (EDPG). UNICEF and other donors participate in governance structures, but MoE retains operational control.
q10_capacity_building_details: Teacher training on inclusive pedagogy (92,000 teachers targeted)
Awareness-raising for MoE staff on gender-sensitive approaches (22,000 staff)
Strengthening MoE’s Special Education Unit and Gender Equality Unit
Support for MoE’s Research and Evidence Department
Technical Assistance to Donor Coordination Unit (DCU) within MoE
Training for school leaders on inclusive education
Parent communication campaigns on gender-sensitive pedagogy
Support for MoE’s financial planning and budgeting systems

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Education (MoE), Jordan
