partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer; manages AAI funds, school operations, and national reforms

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF Jordan
partner_organizations.role: New partner for camp school operations, assistive devices, and studies on out-of-school children/drug use

partner_organizations.name: Accelerated Access Initiative (AAI) Donors
partner_organizations.role: Multi-donor pool (UK, Germany, EU, US, Canada, Norway, Australia) providing financial aid for refugee education

partner_organizations.name: Education Development Partner Group (EDPG)
partner_organizations.role: Coordination platform for donors and MoE (UK co-chairs with Germany)

partner_organizations.name: Education Research in Conflict and Crisis (ERICC)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support/helpdesk for evidence generation (centrally managed by FCDO)

partner_organizations.name: British Embassy Amman
partner_organizations.role: Programme oversight, safeguarding, and strategic direction

who_partners.quote: "The UK will ensure that the AAI programme and support to the multi-donor JFA avoid the development of a parallel system for M&E, budgeting, financial management and procurement." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "The UK’s leadership since launching AAI in London 2016 has been highly effective in providing the MoE with the finance needed to deliver." (D0003448.odt, Why Should the UK Engage?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: BRIDGE uses (1) **financial aid** through the multi-donor Joint Financing Agreement (JFA) under AAI (off-budget, earmarked for refugee education costs), (2) **direct contribution agreement** with UNICEF for camp operations, and (3) **technical assistance** via embedded advisors and ERICC helpdesk. Funds flow through GoJ systems (MoE) with strict accountability measures.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through: (1) AAI’s multi-donor JFA (UK as lead donor), (2) MoE’s Donor Coordination Unit (DCU) for implementation, (3) EDPG for sector-wide coordination (UK co-chairs), and (4) direct FCDO oversight via the Education Programme Manager and embedded roles. UNICEF operates under a separate contribution agreement but aligns with AAI targets.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: MoE is the mandated government body for education in Jordan, and UNICEF was selected due to its existing role in camp school operations and technical capacity. The UK’s leadership in AAI since 2016 and trust built with GoJ justified direct funding continuation.
how_mechanism.quote: "The multi-donor Joint Financing Agreement (JFA) is an innovative financing modality that provides financial aid to the MoE... By using Jordan’s education system, rather than parallel non-state systems, and by requiring strict standards of financial accountability, UK aid is supporting capacity-building while mitigating fiduciary risks." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "A new contribution agreement will be developed between UNICEF and FCDO to formally endorse the additional activities." (D0006692.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: AAI is governed by: (1) **Donor Coordination Unit (DCU)** within MoE (staffed by UK-funded roles), (2) **Education Development Partner Group (EDPG)** co-chaired by UK and Germany, and (3) **local programme steering committee** for the World Bank’s P4R loan (where UK has a seat). UNICEF activities are overseen via a separate project document with FCDO.
how_governance.quote: "The UK will ensure that the AAI programme and support to the multi-donor JFA avoid the development of a parallel system for M&E, budgeting, financial management and procurement... Having a seat on the local programme steering committee will allow us to continue ensuring essential reforms benefit all students, focusing on girls and refugees." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "The monitoring plan will include regular school and site visits to assess progress and monitor the implementation of the programme. Detailed quarterly progress and financial reports will be obtained from the MoE, with the support of the programme-funded role." (D0006692.odt, Monitoring and Reporting)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reprofiled between AAI and UNICEF components (e.g., £9m shifted from TA to financial aid/UNICEF in the addendum), but requires FCDO approval. The flexible TA pool allows strategic reallocation based on emerging needs, subject to governance review.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an **iterative approach** with annual reviews to adjust priorities. The addendum itself reflects adaptive management, adding UNICEF support and drug prevention studies in response to emerging risks (camp school closures, rising drug abuse). ERICC helpdesk provides on-demand technical support for new challenges.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexible TA will continue, enabling strategic use as needed... The programme-funded officer will work closely with the MoE and the FCDO programme manager to ensure effective delivery and oversight of UK investment and will help manage risks to delivery, VfM, and UK reputation as a donor." (D0006692.odt, Flexible Technical Assistance) AND "The theory of change will be updated to incorporate the additional activities outlined in this addendum." (D0006692.odt, Key Changes to the Original Business Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) MoE/UNICEF (implementers) → end beneficiaries. The embedded programme-funded role at MoE reduces layers for AAI components.
how_efficiency.quote: "Detailed quarterly progress and financial reports will be obtained from the MoE... The FCDO programme team will review these reports, gather feedback from donors, and ensure that all questions and comments are addressed with the MoE." (D0006692.odt, Monitoring and Reporting) AND "Financial aid to AAI will continue as per the current Joint Financing Agreement and bilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with GoJ until 31st August 2026." (D0006692.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: No new funding (£0m) – Scale back UK commitment, rely on existing RAMP programme and GCFF loan extension.
Option 2: Non-budget support financial aid only (£22m) – Expand AAI focus on access/inclusion without technical assistance.
Option 3: Mixed model of financial aid + technical assistance (£30m) – Selected option combining AAI, UNICEF support, and TA for system strengthening.
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed model (Option 3, later adjusted to £39.9m) was chosen to: (1) **maintain UK leadership** in the Jordan Compact and refugee education response, (2) **address both access and quality** through combined financial aid (AAI/UNICEF) and technical assistance, (3) **mitigate risks** of GoJ reducing refugee education support due to fiscal pressures, and (4) **leverage multi-donor coordination** to maximize impact. The addendum further justified increasing AAI funding and adding UNICEF to prevent camp school closures and respond to new risks (drug abuse, out-of-school children).
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (preventing rollback on refugee access)
past experience (UK’s successful AAI leadership since 2016)
partner capacity (MoE’s limited ability to absorb camp costs without support)
flexibility (need to adapt to COVID-19 learning losses and new crises)
equity (targeting most marginalized, including girls and children with disabilities)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial mismanagement in AAI/UNICEF funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Enhanced due diligence checks on UNICEF and MoE; compliance with UK terrorism financing legislation; simple delivery chains.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complementary funding gaps for UNICEF activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early identification of shortfalls and prioritization exercises; diplomatic leverage to secure EU/German/Swiss co-funding.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MoE capacity gaps in managing AAI (e.g., delays, weak reporting)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme-funded officer embedded in MoE for oversight; Technical Assistance to strengthen Donor Coordination Unit.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding incidents with vulnerable children
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UNICEF’s robust safeguarding measures; mandatory training/vetting; UK reporting guidelines and intervention protocols.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political decisions undermining delivery (e.g., volunteer work permits)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diplomatic leverage from UK and AAI donors; demand-driven research to align with MoE priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Currency fluctuations/inflation affecting costs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monitoring through quarterly financial reports; flexible TA to address emerging needs.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3: Expand focus on equity and inclusion through a mixed model of financial aid and technical assistance maximising UK investments to deliver a more inclusive, quality education system (£30m), alongside continued GCFF focus as above... This option was selected as it allows the UK to maintain its leadership role in the education sector, deliver on the Jordan Compact commitments, and address both access and quality issues." (D0003448.odt, What Needs to Be Done?) AND "Increasing annual financial aid to the MoE under AAI to £7m and extending the BRIDGE timeline... will mitigate against the risk that further education services to the refugees are reduced and demonstrate to the GoJ the UK’s continued commitment to the Jordan Compact." (D0006692.odt, Why Should We Do This?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Jordan’s FCAS context and refugee crisis constrain partner selection to entities with: (1) **legal mandate** to operate in camps (e.g., UNICEF), (2) **trusted relationships** with GoJ (MoE as primary partner), and (3) **capacity to navigate complex donor coordination** (e.g., EDPG structure). The high dependency on external funding (28% of population are refugees) limits GoJ’s ability to absorb costs, necessitating off-budget modalities like AAI.
q27_constraints_detail: GoJ’s fiscal constraints require off-budget donor financing (AAI model).
Camp operations legally require UNICEF’s involvement due to their existing mandate.
MoE’s weak capacity necessitates embedded TA and donor coordination units.
Refugee status limits partner options to those with humanitarian access (e.g., UN agencies).
Political sensitivity around refugee issues requires trusted donors (UK’s historical leadership).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (financing + service delivery + system strengthening) determine the **hybrid structure**: (1) **Financial aid** flows through AAI’s multi-donor JFA to address access/inclusion, (2) **UNICEF partnership** ensures camp operations (direct service delivery), and (3) **Technical Assistance** (embedded roles/ERICC) targets system strengthening. The need for **rapid response** (e.g., camp school closures) justifies direct UNICEF funding, while **long-term reforms** use MoE-led modalities.
q28_linkages: Financing mechanism (AAI) → addresses access for 190,000+ vulnerable children (WHAT) → requires multi-donor pool and MoE implementation (HOW).
Service delivery (UNICEF camps) → responds to immediate risk of 35,000 children losing education (WHAT) → necessitates direct contribution agreement (HOW).
System strengthening (TA) → targets MoE’s weak data capacity (WHAT) → uses embedded advisors and ERICC helpdesk (HOW).
Equity focus (girls/disabilities) → requires gender-sensitive pedagogy and assistive devices (WHAT) → delivered via AAI funds + UNICEF (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The addendum explicitly highlights tensions between: (1) **equity** (targeting most marginalized in camps) vs. **efficiency** (higher costs for camp operations), and (2) **speed** (urgent UNICEF support to prevent closures) vs. **sustainability** (long-term MoE capacity building). The decision to fund UNICEF directly for camps (despite parallel systems) reflects a trade-off favoring immediate equity over long-term integration.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Equity vs. Cost: Camp schools serve the most vulnerable but are more expensive per child than host community schools.
Speed vs. Ownership: Direct UNICEF funding ensures rapid response but reduces MoE’s operational control over camps.
Inclusion vs. Scale: Targeting children with disabilities (assistive devices) adds complexity but aligns with ‘leave no one behind’ principles.
Flexibility vs. Accountability: Reprofiling funds from TA to UNICEF increases adaptability but requires additional oversight.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate-high risk profile** (FCAS, fiscal instability, refugee dependencies) drives **intensive oversight**: quarterly financial reports, embedded programme-funded roles at MoE, and steering committee participation. Safeguarding risks (vulnerable populations) necessitate mandatory partner vetting and incident reporting protocols.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: MoE’s **limited capacity** shapes the delivery structure by: (1) requiring **embedded TA** (programme-funded officer for AAI oversight), (2) justifying **donor coordination units** (DCU within MoE), and (3) necessitating **simplified funding modalities** (JFA’s earmarked financial aid). UNICEF’s role expands due to MoE’s inability to absorb camp costs.
intersections.quote: "The UK’s leadership since launching AAI in London 2016 has been highly effective in providing the MoE with the finance needed to deliver... The multi-donor JFA modality has also proven uniquely successful in leveraging additional humanitarian and development finance for the GoJ." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "MoE’s limited capacity to absorb camp costs (despite 2023 agreements) led to near-closure of 51 schools in January 2024, risking 35,000 children’s education. This justified direct UNICEF funding in the addendum." (D0006692.odt, Why Should We Do This?) AND "The programme will deliver against the campaign goal on Humanitarian, Inclusion and Protection in the Business and Country Plan (BCP) for Jordan... supporting the most vulnerable in humanitarian contexts." (D0006692.odt, Legislation)

key_programme_risks: GoJ reducing refugee education support due to fiscal pressures (e.g., 2023 camp school transition failure).
Learning poverty exacerbated by COVID-19 (1.2 years of learning loss, girls/refugees hardest hit).
MoE’s weak capacity for data utilization and financial management (e.g., delays in AAI reporting).
Safeguarding vulnerabilities among refugee children (sexual exploitation, child labour, early marriage).
Parallel systems for refugee education undermining sustainability (e.g., UNICEF camp schools vs. MoE host schools).
Currency fluctuations and inflation increasing costs (e.g., rising commodity prices post-Ukraine war).
Political decisions disrupting delivery (e.g., work permit restrictions for Syrian volunteers).
Drug abuse among youth escalating post-Gaza crisis (new risk identified in addendum).
Donor fatigue reducing complementary funding (e.g., EU’s temporary emergency funding for camps).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Increase AAI funding to £7m/year and extend BRIDGE timeline to 2026; demonstrate UK’s long-term commitment to Jordan Compact.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: MoE capacity gaps in AAI management
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embed programme-funded officer in MoE for oversight; provide TA to strengthen Donor Coordination Unit.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Camp school closures (35,000 children at risk)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Direct UNICEF funding for camp operations; secure co-funding from EU/Germany/Swiss.
Expand catch-up education and remedial support via AAI; align with new Education Sector Plan (ESP).
UNICEF’s robust safeguarding policies; mandatory partner vetting; UK incident reporting protocols.
Ensure AAI/UNICEF activities align with ESP; avoid duplicate M&E systems; transition planning for camp schools.
Develop evidence-based Social and Behaviour Change framework; train teachers/community volunteers on harm reduction.
UK diplomatic leverage to secure multi-donor commitments; prioritize high-impact activities (e.g., assistive devices).

fcas_specific_lessons: Off-budget modalities (e.g., AAI’s JFA) are critical in FCAS contexts where GoJ cannot absorb costs into national budgets.
Donor coordination platforms (e.g., EDPG) prevent fragmentation in refugee responses but require strong leadership (UK’s role as co-chair).
Embedded TA roles (e.g., programme-funded officer in MoE) bridge capacity gaps without creating parallel structures.
Flexible funding (e.g., reprofiling TA to UNICEF) allows rapid response to emerging crises (e.g., camp closures, drug abuse).
Long-term donor commitments (e.g., Jordan Compact) are essential to maintain GoJ’s political will for refugee inclusion.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases (e.g., AAI 2016–2020) showed that: (1) **earmarked financial aid** (JFA model) effectively leverages multi-donor funding, (2) **MoE’s capacity limits** require embedded support (e.g., delays in AAI Phase 1 due to weak DCU), and (3) **parallel systems** (e.g., UNICEF camps) create sustainability risks but are necessary for equity. The 2023 AAI Annual Review recommended shifting from TA to direct financial aid due to MoE’s absorption challenges.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addendum reflects key adaptations: (1) **Shift from TA to financial aid** (£9m reprofiled to AAI/UNICEF) due to MoE’s limited capacity to utilize TA effectively. (2) **Addition of UNICEF component** to address camp school crisis (lesson from failed 2023 transition). (3) **Extension to October 2026** to align with ESP launch and AAI’s 3rd year. (4) **New focus on drug abuse** in response to post-Gaza crisis trends. (5) **Reduced TA facility** based on 2023 Annual Review recommendations.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learnt (from the first and existing phase of JFA) indicate that this option is expected to require higher levels of programme management from the UK to oversee the programme implementation as well as recruited Technical Assistance to capacity build the Donor Coordination Unit within the MoE (DCU)." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "The 2023/24 BRIDGE Annual Review recommended that procurement of the TA Facility will not proceed, and the planned resources of £9m will be redistributed within the programme to provide additional financial aid (for AAI) and to provide direct support to UNICEF." (D0006692.odt, Flexible Technical Assistance) AND "The transition [of camp schools] is now considered unfeasible until there is a substantial increase in multi-year funding." (D0006692.odt, Why Should We Do This?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The AAI multi-donor JFA has leveraged £190m+ in grant finance for refugee education since 2016, with UK contributions catalyzing commitments from Germany, EU, US, and others. The addendum’s UNICEF component secured provisional co-funding from EU, Switzerland, and Germany for camp operations.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue-focused: Primarily covers operational costs (teacher salaries, textbooks, school operations) and technical assistance, with no major capital infrastructure mentioned.
financial_details.quote: "The UK’s leadership since launching AAI in London 2016 has been highly effective in providing the MoE with the finance needed to deliver (AAI has provided the MoE with £190m of grant finance including £85m from the JFA (£49m from the UK) 2016–2020)." (D0003448.odt, Option 2) AND "The UK will continue in a leadership role on AAI coordination, working with Germany, the EU, the US, Canada, Norway, and Australia to secure funding for Year 2 and Year 3 of AAI." (D0006692.odt, Partnerships) AND "£9.9m of additional financing (and reprofiling £9m of funding previously earmarked for technical assistance) will enable us to provide: a new total of £14 million as financial aid towards AAI; up to £4.7 million contribution to UNICEF; and a £200,000 reserve for flexible technical support." (D0006692.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Congo Basin Forest Action (CBFA) Programme
metadata.primary_sector: environmental conservation / climate change / sustainable development

quote.text: The Programme will address the primary driver of deforestation across the Congo Basin—small-scale agricultural practices. This will be achieved by working directly with local communities to support a transition away from unsustainable practices, whilst ensuring economic livelihoods are secured.

duration_source.text: Programme Value: £90m (2024-31)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The CBFA Programme combines implementation research (testing sustainable livelihood interventions), capacity building (strengthening local forest governance), and service delivery (direct support to forest-dependent communities). It aims to reduce deforestation by transitioning small-scale farmers to sustainable practices while securing economic benefits, with a strong focus on co-design with local communities.

q1_source.text: The Programme will address the primary driver of deforestation... by working directly with local communities to support a transition away from unsustainable practices... Co-design and co-ownership at its core... Innovative piloting alongside traditional activities as part of a multi-pronged, holistic approach...

q3_expected_outputs.output: Sustainable livelihood alternatives for 80 million forest-dependent people
Reduced deforestation in active forest frontiers (unprotected zones)
Strengthened community forest rights and management capacities
Evidence base on best practices for forests and development
Monitoring, Evaluation & Learning (MEL) system for adaptive management
Pilot innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., PES, carbon markets)

what_objectives.summary: CBFA is a £90m, 7-year programme addressing Congo Basin deforestation by co-designing sustainable livelihoods with local communities, strengthening forest governance, and piloting innovative finance—while building an evidence base for scalable solutions.

quote.text: Innovative piloting alongside traditional activities as part of a multi-pronged, holistic approach to develop an evidence base of best practice on forests and development across the Congo Basin... Efforts will be focused on areas of active deforestation as a result of human activity—primarily unprotected forest frontier zones where local populations are encroaching on the forest for economic reasons.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with extreme fragility (DRC, CAR), conflict, weak governance, and corruption. The World Bank lists DRC and CAR as 'extremely fragile' and 'conflict-affected,' with pervasive institutional challenges hindering development efforts.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Major... Congo Basin countries score amongst the lowest on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index... DRC and CAR are classified as 'extremely fragile' and in conflict by the World Bank (2023).
q5_source.source: D0005764.odt, Overall programme risk rating; Table 3

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and corruption undermine governance interventions; unclear land tenure discourages sustainable investment; climate shocks (e.g., droughts) threaten agricultural livelihoods; and limited institutional capacity hampers monitoring and enforcement. Road expansion, while economically beneficial, accelerates deforestation by opening previously inaccessible areas.

quote.text: Weak governance continues to undermine many domestic and international interventions across the region... Laws and policies governing natural resource exploitation and management may lack coherence and often are not enforced, while powerful vested interests are able to influence land use allocations... The overarching lack of clarity in forest & land use rights... disincentivises long-term investment in sustainable management.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes 'co-design and co-ownership' with local communities, but the lead institution (FCDO) and component structures (e.g., Central African Forest Initiative) suggest Northern decision-making dominance. Local communities are framed as 'key partners' in design, but governance details are not explicit.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for community forest management
support for simple management plans (SMPs)
linking communities to markets (NTFPs, carbon credits)
strengthening local monitoring/transparency systems
piloting innovative finance (PES, ITMOs)

partner_organizations.name: Central African Forest Initiative (CAFI)
partner_organizations.role: Component 3 lead (regional policy coordination)

partner_organizations.name: Local communities (DRC, RoC, Cameroon, Gabon)
partner_organizations.role: Co-design and implementation of forest management practices

partner_organizations.name: Congo Basin Forests Partnership (CBFP)
partner_organizations.role: Regional coordination platform

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and NGOs
partner_organizations.role: Implementation support and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Research institutions (e.g., CIFOR, IIED)
partner_organizations.role: Evidence generation and MEL

quote.text: Co-design and co-ownership at its core. This means ensuring local communities form a key part of the design of programme activities... CBFA Partners Facility (Component 2) will support a range of partners, including CSOs, research institutions, and private sector actors, to deliver innovative pilots.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (AG) for components like the CBFA Partners Facility, direct contracts for implementation (e.g., Component 1: Forests for Local Communities), and partnerships with multilateral initiatives (e.g., CAFI). The MEL component suggests performance-based funding elements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: CBFA is structured into 4 components with distinct delivery models: (1) direct implementation with communities, (2) a competitive Partners Facility for CSOs/NGOs, (3) multilateral coordination via CAFI, and (4) a centralized MEL system. This hybrid approach allows flexibility in partner selection per component.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Component 1 (local communities) likely uses direct engagement; Component 2 (Partners Facility) implies competitive calls for CSOs/NGOs; Component 3 (CAFI) is pre-existing. The rationale emphasizes local ownership (Component 1) and innovation (Component 2).

quote.text: Component 1 – Forests for Local Communities: Direct work with communities... Component 2 – CBFA Partners Facility: Will support a range of partners through a competitive process... Component 3 – Central African Forest Initiative: Leverages existing CAFI structures.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions a 'governance structure' with roles for FCDO, implementing partners, and local communities (Section E.i), but explicit composition is not detailed. The MEL component (Component 4) suggests embedded oversight.

quote.text: Governance Approaches & Objectives: The programme will establish a governance structure to oversee delivery, with roles for FCDO, partners, and communities (Section E.i)... Monitoring, Evaluation & Learning (Component 4) will track performance against milestones.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The phased approach allows adjustments between components based on evidence (e.g., scaling successful pilots). However, Component 3 (CAFI) and Component 1 (local communities) may have fixed allocations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The MEL component (Section B.vi) is designed to enable 'adaptive management,' with annual reviews to adjust interventions based on community feedback and pilot results. The programme explicitly notes it will not force practices that reduce income.

quote.text: A phased approach to targeted support will allow the programme to support evidence-building in the initial stage... MEL will play a key role in... proactively tracking performance to ensure economic benefits to local communities... CBFA will not force individuals to adopt alternative practices if it reduces their income.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Component leads (e.g., CAFI, Partners Facility manager) → Local implementers (communities/CSOs). The MEL component adds a cross-cutting oversight layer.

quote.text: Payments and Performance Management: Funds will be disbursed against milestones (Section C.iv)... The programme’s multi-component structure includes direct implementation, a partners facility, and multilateral coordination.

q24_alternatives_considered: Fortress conservation (protected areas excluding humans) – ruled out due to lack of local buy-in and governance challenges
Pure top-down policy interventions – rejected for failing to address local livelihood needs
Standalone community forestry – limited by weak legal frameworks and capacity gaps
Large-scale industrial reforms – deemed ineffective for smallholder-driven deforestation
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality was selected to (1) address the primary driver of deforestation (small-scale agriculture) through direct community engagement (Component 1), (2) foster innovation via competitive partnerships (Component 2), (3) leverage existing regional platforms (CAFI, Component 3), and (4) ensure adaptive learning (MEL, Component 4). This balances local ownership with scalable solutions, mitigating risks of past failures (e.g., lack of co-design).
q25_decision_factors: experience (builds on UK’s COP26 forest pledges and FGMC programme)
partner-capacity (local communities + CSOs for implementation; CAFI for policy)
equity (co-design with Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities - IPLCs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Local partner capacity gaps may delay implementation (Component 1)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded training and simplified management plans (SMPs) for communities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Competitive Partners Facility (Component 2) may exclude smaller CSOs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted outreach to local NGOs and phased funding to build capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: CAFI coordination (Component 3) may face bureaucratic delays
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage existing CAFI secretariat and align with their workflows.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MEL system (Component 4) could become overly centralized
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Decentralized data collection with community involvement.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (co-design for local relevance, MEL for adaptation)

quote.text: A UK-funded and managed intervention centred on fortress conservation... was considered and ruled out... The programme’s multi-component approach ensures flexibility to adjust based on evidence... Co-design reduces risk of activities failing post-funding... CBFA validates UK’s COP26 pledges on forests and IPLCs.
quote.source: D0005764.odt, Section A.iii (Intervention Opportunities); B.ii (Programme Approach)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context (conflict, corruption, weak institutions) limits partner selection to organizations with existing regional presence (e.g., CAFI, CBFP) and necessitates community co-design to ensure local buy-in. Security risks in DRC/CAR restrict field operations to stable zones, while tenure insecurity requires partners with legal expertise (e.g., for Component 1).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in DRC/CAR → excludes partners without security protocols
Corruption → requires partners with transparent financial systems
Weak land tenure → prioritizes partners with legal/advocacy experience
Limited research capacity → relies on Northern institutions (e.g., CIFOR) for MEL
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address small-scale deforestation (WHAT) drives the mixed delivery structure (HOW): direct community engagement (Component 1) for livelihood alternatives, competitive partnerships (Component 2) for innovation, and CAFI (Component 3) for policy alignment. The MEL component (WHAT) enables adaptive management (HOW).
q28_linkages: Small-scale agriculture focus → requires grassroots partners (Component 1)
Innovation pilots → necessitates competitive Partners Facility (Component 2)
Regional policy gaps → leverages CAFI (Component 3)
Evidence needs → embedded MEL system (Component 4)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (co-design with IPLCs, gender inclusion) against efficiency (phased pilots, competitive funding). Trade-offs include: (1) time-intensive co-design vs. rapid scaling, (2) local capacity building vs. immediate results, and (3) decentralized MEL vs. standardized data.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed-vs-inclusion: Co-design slows implementation but ensures local ownership
expertise-vs-ownership: Northern MEL support vs. Southern-led data collection
cost-vs-reach: Competitive Partners Facility may exclude smaller CSOs but ensures value for money
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk rating (FCAS, corruption) justifies intensive oversight (milestone-based payments, MEL tracking) and adaptive management (annual reviews). High fragility in DRC/CAR requires embedded safeguards (e.g., community grievance mechanisms).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: communities lead forest management (Component 1) after training; CSOs (Component 2) must demonstrate innovation + local reach; and CAFI (Component 3) provides policy expertise. MEL (Component 4) strengthens all partners’ adaptive capacities.

quote.text: Effective localisation of ownership reduces the risk of activities failing once programme funding ends... The programme’s structure reflects the need to balance local priorities with regional coordination... Weak governance and corruption necessitate robust monitoring and community-led transparency mechanisms.
quote.source: D0005764.odt, Programme summary; Section A.ii (The Problem); E.i (Governance)

key_programme_risks: Local disillusionment with past programmes (lack of co-design)
Weak governance undermining tenure reforms (Component 1)
Corruption siphoning funds (especially in DRC/CAR)
Climate shocks (droughts) threatening agricultural alternatives
Market failures limiting economic incentives for sustainable practices
Conflict disrupting field operations (DRC/CAR)
Overlapping land concessions creating legal conflicts
Limited MEL capacity in Southern institutions

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Co-design workshops and community-led MEL.
Align with ongoing tenure reforms (e.g., DRC’s 50,000ha community forests) and pilot transparent systems.
Milestone-based payments, third-party audits, and community oversight.
Diversify livelihood options (NTFPs, agroforestry) and climate-resilient crops.
Pilot PES and carbon credit schemes (Component 2) to create economic incentives.
Focus on stable zones; partner with conflict-sensitive organizations.
Support customary tenure recognition and mediation mechanisms.
Pair Southern institutions with Northern research partners (e.g., CIFOR).

fcas_specific_lessons: Past programmes failed due to top-down designs; CBFA prioritizes co-ownership.
In DRC, decentralized forest rights (50,000ha) show promise but require capacity building.
Conflict zones need flexible, non-permanent structures (e.g., mobile MEL teams).
Corruption risks demand community-led transparency (e.g., public fund-tracking).
Fragile states benefit from phased, adaptive approaches (e.g., pilot → scale).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 ICAI review highlighted inconsistent community consultation in UK aid programmes. CBFA addresses this via mandatory co-design. Lessons from Yangambi (DRC) and REDD+ in RoC show that lasting impact requires economic benefits to communities—hence the focus on livelihoods (Component 1) and innovative finance (Component 2).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Mandatory co-design workshops (vs. ad-hoc consultation in past programmes).
Phased funding to test interventions before scaling (unlike previous 'big push' approaches).
Explicit focus on women’s tenure rights (addressing gender gaps in land ownership).
MEL system with community feedback loops (vs. donor-only evaluations).
Flexible component structure to adapt to local contexts (e.g., conflict zones).

quote.text: Past programmes struggled due to limited co-design and lack of long-term funding... The 2021 ICAI review concluded that consultation with communities during programme design is inconsistent. CBFA’s adaptive management and MEL components directly address these gaps... Lessons from Yangambi and REDD+ in RoC demonstrate that economic benefits must reach communities for sustainability.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize additional funding through innovative finance mechanisms (e.g., carbon credits, PES) and align with CAFI’s existing resources, but explicit leverage targets are not stated.

quote.text: Programme Value: £90m (2024-31)... CBFA is funded through International Climate Finance... The programme will leverage partnerships with CAFI and pilot market-based mechanisms (e.g., PES, carbon credits) to sustain impacts post-funding.
quote.source: D0005764.odt, Programme summary; Section D.i (Financial Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SIMAP is designed to strengthen the effectiveness of UK policy and programme delivery in Sudan by providing independent monitoring, analysis, and capacity building. It combines evidence generation (through research and data collection), capacity building (for implementing partners), and policy influence (to inform UK and international decision-making). The programme does not directly deliver services or develop technology but supports better implementation of existing interventions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "SIMAP will strengthen the effectiveness of the UK’s policy and programme portfolio in Sudan through providing timely, objective information on delivery and contextual developments to inform decision-making in a fluid operating environment." (D0006084.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.summary: SIMAP is a cross-portfolio monitoring and analysis programme that generates evidence through field visits, compliance checks, and research, while simultaneously building partner capacity and informing UK policy. It operates as a flexible facility to respond to emerging priorities in Sudan’s fragile context.

quote.objectives: "The programme will have three core outcomes: 1) Assurance & Capacity Building; 2) Learning & Innovation; 3) Strategy & Analysis." (D0006084.odt, Programme summary)
quote.outputs: "Indicative activities include: Activity verification, Expenditure verification, Results verification, Policy compliance assessments, Beneficiary feedback, MEL Capacity Assessments, Contextual/thematic monitoring reports, Action learning research." (D0006082.odt, Table 3: Indicative Programme Activities)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sudan is ranked the 8th most fragile state globally (Fragile States Index 2021) and faces protracted conflict, economic crisis, and climate vulnerability. The 2021 military coup disrupted the political transition, exacerbating humanitarian needs and restricting international access.
where_context.q5_source: "Sudan is considered the 8th most fragile country in the world... Sudan is further the sixth most climate-vulnerable country in the world." (D0006082.odt, Context and need for intervention)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks and government travel restrictions limit HMG staff’s ability to monitor programmes outside Khartoum. Poor transport infrastructure and climate shocks (floods/droughts) disrupt field access. Host government permissions are required for all monitoring activities, creating delays. Data reliability is compromised by weak institutional capacity and conflict-induced displacement.

quote.constraints: "Due to a combination of security risks, host government restrictions on travel for foreign nationals, and logistical constraints arising from Sudan’s vast, remote geography, HMG staff face obstacles to monitoring programmes and meeting with interlocutors outside Khartoum." (D0006082.odt, Context and need for intervention)
quote.climate: "Sudan is... the sixth most climate-vulnerable country in the world and regularly faces significant climate shocks in the form of floods and droughts." (D0006082.odt, Context and need for intervention)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The commercial supplier (OPM, UK-based) holds primary decision-making authority for programme delivery, with Sudanese sub-contractors providing field expertise. FCDO retains strategic oversight through the steering board and contract management.
q10_capacity_building_details: MEL capacity assessments for implementing partners
targeted technical assistance (e.g., safeguarding training, data systems)
inclusive supplier teams (gender/ethnic balance)
learning strategy to synthesize evidence for FCDO and partners

quote.partners: "A large share of BEK’s implementing partners in Sudan are UN agencies, presenting an opportunity for the programme to influence system-level changes." (D0006082.odt, Intended beneficiaries)
quote.capacity: "MEL Capacity Assessments and Technical Assistance: Field and/or desk-based assessments of implementing partners’ MEL capacity... tailored technical assistance to help partners act on findings." (D0006082.odt, Table 3)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: A commercial contract with a fixed budget (£7.5m) and performance-based deliverables. FCDO specifies requirements in Terms of Reference and holds the supplier accountable for outputs, with provisions for contract exit if performance is inadequate. Payments are milestone-based.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: OPM (lead supplier) manages a consortium of sub-contractors, with FCDO oversight through a steering board. The programme includes a project-funded G7 Adviser embedded in the British Office Sudan team to bridge policy and implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Commercial suppliers were prioritized due to their established track record in similar FCDO programmes (e.g., Somalia, Syria) and the nascent state of the Sudanese MEL market. The Early Market Engagement event confirmed strong private sector capability.

quote.instrument: "Commercial suppliers are the most common providers in other FCDO portfolio monitoring programmes... with programme reviews confirming the private sector has a good range of suppliers with the skills and expertise required." (D0006082.odt, Delivery routes)
quote.selection: "The Early Market Engagement (EME) event conducted in February 2022... attracted strong interest from commercial suppliers (95% of registrations were from private sector organisations)." (D0006082.odt, Delivery routes)
quote.structure: "The programme will be delivered through a commercial contract, deploying a team of thematic and contextual experts... likely a consortium with one lead supplier." (D0006084.odt, Programme summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The steering board includes FCDO’s Results & Evidence Adviser, the SRO (Alice Motion), and programme leads. It sets strategic priorities and reviews supplier performance. The G7 Adviser (project-funded post) links implementation to policy engagement.

quote.governance: "Central oversight of all evaluations by BEK’s Results & Evidence Adviser and the programme steering board could help to ensure alignment with the FCDO’s Evaluation Strategy and Policy." (D0006082.odt, Option 4)
quote.oversight: "The supplier will work with BEK during the inception phase to design a learning strategy... including mapping key audiences, their information needs, and a schedule of events (e.g., workshops, debriefs)." (D0006082.odt, Option 3)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities (e.g., monitoring visits, research commissions) with FCDO approval, but the contract specifies core deliverables. The programme’s ‘flexible, cross-cutting nature’ allows adaptation to emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an inception phase to align activities with evolving FCDO priorities. Research topics and field visit locations can be adjusted based on contextual changes (e.g., conflict, humanitarian needs), but requires steering board sign-off.

quote.flexibility: "The programme will be designed to be flexible to the evolving information and analysis needs of BEK’s policy and programme portfolio over its five-year length." (D0006082.odt, Indicative activities)
quote.adaptive: "The exact number, location and focus of site visits will be based on a sampling process agreed between the supplier and BEK during the inception phase." (D0006082.odt, Option 3)

quote.layers: "The programme will be delivered through a commercial contract, deploying a team of thematic and contextual experts." (D0006084.odt, Programme summary)

Centralized cross-portfolio monitoring with flexible research facility.
Add a centralized evaluation function to the monitoring programme.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The centralized independent monitoring programme (Option 3) was selected for its ability to: (1) provide comprehensive oversight across the entire portfolio (vs. fragmented programme-level approaches); (2) achieve economies of scale through a single contract; (3) offer flexibility to respond to emerging priorities; and (4) build on lessons from similar FCDO programmes in Somalia/Syria. The evaluation facility (Option 4) was rejected due to higher management burden and risk of diverting focus from rapid analysis.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (3% of ODA budget vs. 5% HMT recommendation)
risk mitigation (centralized oversight in FCAS context)
partner capacity (nascent MEL market required commercial expertise)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier unable to access priority locations due to security/political restrictions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible fieldwork planning with local sub-contractors; adaptive management protocols.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor supplier relationship management with implementing partners (e.g., UN agencies)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong contractual requirements for stakeholder engagement; FCDO oversight of supplier performance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited absorptive capacity within BEK to utilize monitoring outputs
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Learning strategy with tailored products (e.g., 1-page briefs); embedded G7 Adviser to bridge research and policy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market nascence leading to insufficient skilled suppliers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Consortium model with lead supplier (OPM) and local sub-contractors; early market engagement confirmed capability.

quote.alternatives: "Option 3 (Recommended) – Independent monitoring and analysis programme focused on Sudan bilateral policy and programme portfolio... For a modest investment (~3% of annual ODA spend), this option would provide comprehensive oversight of how aid is being delivered across the FCDO’s bilateral programme portfolio in Sudan." (D0006082.odt, Options Appraisal)
quote.rationale: "This option would include a central budget and management structure for all evaluations undertaken utilising funds from the BEK bilateral ODA portfolio in Sudan... Central oversight would help to ensure alignment with the FCDO’s Evaluation Strategy and Policy." (D0006082.odt, Option 4)
quote.risks: "The largest risks associated with the programme are: (i) deterioration in the security and/or political situation restricting the supplier’s ability to access sites across Sudan; (ii) the nascence of the supplier market... (iii) the supplier managing relationships with implementing partners poorly." (D0006082.odt, Risk)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Sudan’s FCAS context constrains partner selection to commercial suppliers with: (1) proven ability to navigate access restrictions (e.g., government permissions, security risks); (2) existing relationships with UN agencies (major implementing partners); and (3) capacity to deploy diverse, locally trusted field teams. Multilateral partners were dismissed due to conflicts of interest (80% of ODA delivered through UN agencies) and lack of market interest.
q27_constraints_detail: security risks limit field access to commercial actors with local networks
government restrictions require suppliers experienced in Sudanese regulatory environment
nascent MEL market excludes most local NGOs/CSOs (only 5% of EME participants)
UN conflicts of interest preclude their role as monitors
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **real-time, cross-portfolio oversight** determines the centralized consortium structure, while the **flexibility requirement** (responding to Sudan’s volatile context) necessitates a commercial contract with adaptive management clauses. The **capacity-building objective** (for UN/INGO partners) shapes the inclusion of technical assistance in the supplier’s scope.
q28_linkages: cross-portfolio scope → consortium model (vs. single implementer)
rapid feedback needs → commercial contract (vs. grant)
UN/INGO capacity gaps → embedded technical assistance
FCAS risks → supplier selection criteria (local access, security protocols)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid research turnaround (1-month delivery) limits deep community engagement, mitigated by targeted female enumerator recruitment. (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern-led supplier (OPM) ensures technical quality but requires proactive measures (e.g., Sudanese sub-contractors, G7 Adviser) to embed local perspectives. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Commercial rates enable robust oversight but reduce funds available for direct Southern partner capacity building.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: rapid research (1-month delivery) vs. inclusive beneficiary consultation
q29_tradeoffs_detail.mitigation: targeted recruitment of female/marginalized enumerators; safeguarding protocols

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern supplier expertise (OPM) vs. Southern ownership
q29_tradeoffs_detail.mitigation: Sudanese sub-contractors; G7 Adviser embedded in BOS

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: commercial contract costs vs. budget for local capacity building
q29_tradeoffs_detail.mitigation: technical assistance included in supplier scope; 3% ODA budget allocation

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk FCAS context** increases oversight intensity: milestone-based reporting, embedded G7 Adviser, and supplier performance levers (contract exit clauses). Conversely, **supplier market nascence** limits management flexibility, requiring upfront investment in inception phases and partner relationship-building.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme’s capacity-building objectives directly shape partner roles: (1) **UN agencies** (primary implementers) receive technical assistance to improve MEL systems; (2) **Sudanese sub-contractors** are prioritized for fieldwork to ensure contextual relevance; (3) **G7 Adviser** bridges policy and implementation to enhance absorptive capacity.

quote.constraints: "Due to a combination of security risks, host government restrictions on travel for foreign nationals, and logistical constraints... HMG staff face obstacles to monitoring programmes outside Khartoum. Posts with similar size ODA portfolios... utilise independent monitoring to manage fiduciary, safeguarding, and delivery risks." (D0006082.odt, Context and need for intervention)
quote.linkages: "The programme will be delivered through a commercial contract, deploying a team of thematic and contextual experts to undertake activities with three aims: (i) improving assurance... (ii) enabling more innovative policy... (iii) increasing access to outcome-focused analysis." (D0006082.odt, Programme summary)
quote.tradeoffs: "The programme will ensure that an inclusive supplier team is recruited, which will help ensure that women and marginalised groups are given equitable voice in programme activities... The programme will be implemented in line with FCDO’s Inclusive Data Charter Action Plan." (D0006082.odt, Gender Equality)
quote.risk_management: "Risk management will follow established internal practices and escalation mechanisms, including reporting into the Sudan Country Board and Directors... The programme itself will play a key role in providing assurance over the delivery of the rest of FCDO Sudan’s policy and programme portfolio." (D0006082.odt, Risk)

key_programme_risks.risk: Deterioration in security/political situation restricting supplier access to field sites
Nascent supplier market leading to insufficient skilled/diverse staff
Poor supplier relationship management with implementing partners (e.g., UN agencies)
Limited absorptive capacity within BEK to utilize monitoring outputs
Reputational damage to FCDO if supplier performs poorly
Fraud or fund diversion in high-risk settings
Conflict sensitivity: unintended exacerbation of tensions through programming

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible fieldwork planning with local sub-contractors; adaptive sampling processes; remote data collection where possible.
Consortium model with established lead supplier (OPM) and local partners; early market engagement confirmed capability.
Contractual requirements for supplier relationship management; technical assistance to align with UN systems.
Learning strategy with tailored products (1-page briefs, workshops); embedded G7 Adviser.
Expenditure verification activities; supplier compliance checks (Terrorism Act 2000, Proceeds of Crime Act 2002).
Policy compliance assessments; beneficiary feedback mechanisms to identify unintended harm.

fcas_specific_lessons: Independent monitoring is critical in FCAS to compensate for limited donor field access (evidence from Somalia/Syria).
Local sub-contractors are essential for navigating access restrictions and cultural barriers (lesson from Sudan pilot).
Flexible, randomized site selection deters fraud in high-risk environments (Somalia review).
UN agency resistance to external monitoring requires proactive relationship management (Pakistan experience).
Rapid research facilities must balance speed with conflict sensitivity (Syria programme).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Sudan pilot (2022) demonstrated that: (1) robust inception phases with partner visits are critical for alignment; (2) female enumerators improve access in conservative areas; (3) adaptive fieldwork management is necessary for volatile contexts. Somalia/Yemen programmes showed that centralized monitoring improves risk management and learning across portfolios.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added G7 Adviser post (addendum) to strengthen policy-research linkage and UN engagement.
Increased focus on safeguarding and gender inclusion in monitoring teams (pilot lesson).
Flexible contract clauses to allow activity reallocation (FCAS adaptability).
Technical assistance component added to address partner capacity gaps (UN/INGO feedback).

quote.risks: "The overall risk profile for the programme is Moderate. The largest risks associated with the programme are: (i) deterioration in the security and/or political situation restricting the supplier’s ability to access sites across Sudan; (ii) the nascence of the supplier market... (iii) the supplier managing relationships with implementing partners poorly." (D0006082.odt, Risk)
quote.lessons: "Lessons from the [Sudan pilot] include: (i) planning for a robust inception phase, including visits to implementing partners... (ii) including targeted, additional effort to recruit female staff for fieldwork teams... (iii) ensuring management of fieldwork is kept highly adaptable." (D0006082.odt, Evidence for intervention)
quote.design_changes: "The introduction of a G7 Human Development Adviser will bolster the capacity within the British Office Sudan and be complimentary to SIMAP in enhancing oversight of FCDO programmes... The role will be instrumental in SIMAP’s ambition to play a leadership role on collaboration and evaluation of a broader range of external partners." (D0006084.odt, Changes)

quote.budget: "Original programme budget: £7,500,000.00" (D0006084.odt, Detailed information)
quote.costs: "The year 1 cost of this project-funded role is estimated to be £186,864... with the ongoing costs estimated to be £151,006 per year." (D0006084.odt, Budget)
quote.vfm: "The total anticipated cost of the business case represents 3% of FCDO Sudan’s 2020/21 budget. This level of investment is similar to that of other FCDO independent monitoring programmes." (D0006082.odt, Summary Value for Money Statement)

metadata.programme_name: Ethiopia Crises to Resilience (EC2R) 2021/22–2024/25
metadata.quote: "EC2R is a flexible £240 million programme which will i) provide multi-sector humanitarian assistance to meet the needs of Ethiopia’s most vulnerable populations; ii) support poor households so they are better able to withstand disasters and shocks; and iii) invest in the humanitarian systems so it is able to identify risks and respond early and cost-effectively." (D0002694.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 31/01/2022" and "AMP End Date: 31/03/2025" (D0002694.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The EC2R programme delivers multi-sector humanitarian assistance (nutrition, health, WASH, protection, education) directly to vulnerable populations in Ethiopia, while also investing in resilience-building and humanitarian system strengthening. It combines emergency response with longer-term system improvements.
what_objectives.q1_source: "EC2R is a flexible £240 million programme which will i) provide multi-sector humanitarian assistance to meet the needs of Ethiopia’s most vulnerable populations; ii) support poor households so they are better able to withstand disasters and shocks; and iii) invest in the humanitarian systems so it is able to identify risks and respond early and cost-effectively." (D0002694.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 480,000 women and girls reached with UK-funded GBV response and sexual/reproductive health services
At least 400,000 mothers and children reached with UK-funded nutrition assistance
300,000 people with access to water, sanitation, and hygiene services
At least 300,000 people reached annually with UK-funded humanitarian cash/social protection assistance
50,000 girls and boys provided with access to emergency education each year
At least 300,000 people supported annually to cope with effects of climate change
Humanitarian system improvements (preparedness, coordination, early response)
what_objectives.summary: EC2R combines emergency humanitarian service delivery with investments to strengthen household resilience and humanitarian systems in Ethiopia, focusing on sectors where the UK has comparative advantage (nutrition, protection, education, WASH) and where needs are most acute.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will be delivered by UN agencies, NGO partners, and World Bank managed support to the Government of Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP)." (D0002694.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia is experiencing active conflict (Tigray war, Oromia violence), severe drought (worst in 40 years), economic crisis (38% inflation), and institutional fragility with over 30 million people needing humanitarian assistance - the largest crisis globally.
where_context.q5_source: "Almost 30 million people are currently in need of humanitarian assistance in Ethiopia, more than any other country in the world. There is a significant risk the situation may deteriorate further due to conflict in many parts of the country, a ‘once in 40 years’ drought in the Horn of Africa, and an economic crisis exacerbated by the Russia-Ukraine conflict." (D0002694.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Humanitarian access is severely restricted (e.g., "de facto blockade" of Tigray with <15% of required aid reaching the region), government-imposed restrictions on NGOs/UN (visa delays, expulsions), weak coordination between government and international systems, and inadequate data sharing. The operating environment is described as "extremely restrictive" with significant gaps in humanitarian data due to weak systems and government approval requirements.
where_context.quote: "Humanitarian operations have also been hindered by an extremely restrictive operating environment: in 2021 two major international NGOs were suspended and 7 senior UN staff members were expelled; many organisations have faced difficulties obtaining visas and work permits for staff; and there are significant restrictions on the import and movement of humanitarian supplies and communications equipment." (D0002694.odt, Humanitarian Response Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority over programme design, funding allocations, and strategic direction, with implementation delegated to UN agencies, NGOs, and World Bank. The document emphasizes UK "comparative advantage" and policy influence as key drivers.
q10_capacity_building_details: support to Government of Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP) to improve resilience and shock responsiveness
investments in humanitarian system preparedness (logistics, data, coordination)
training and support for partners on conflict-sensitivity and safeguarding
technical assistance to improve targeting and service delivery in hard-to-reach areas

partner_organizations.name: UN agencies (UNICEF, WFP, WHO, UNOCHA)
partner_organizations.role: direct implementation of humanitarian services (nutrition, health, WASH, protection)

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs
partner_organizations.role: last-mile delivery in conflict-affected areas, protection services, accountability to affected populations

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: management of Trust Fund for Government of Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ethiopia (via PSNP)
partner_organizations.role: implementation of rural social protection and resilience programmes

who_partners.quote: "Delivery Option 3: Portfolio partnership with World Bank, UN operational organisations and NGOs: in this option, the UK would use a portfolio approach to manage risk and maximise impact. We would work with the best performing UN agencies from our current humanitarian portfolio and a limited number of NGO partners in areas where the UN performs poorly (e.g. protection and accountability to affected populations)." (D0002694.odt, Delivery Options Appraisal)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Funding will be delivered through a combination of Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs), Accountable Grant Agreements (AGAs), and Administrative Agreements (AAs) with UN agencies, NGOs, and the World Bank. This provides flexibility to adapt to the volatile operating environment while maintaining accountability.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO will manage a portfolio of partners (UN agencies, NGOs, World Bank) with distinct roles: UN for scale and normative functions, NGOs for local access and specialized services, and World Bank for government systems. The structure allows for dynamic allocation of funds across channels based on context changes.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (selection based on performance in previous programmes)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The restricted approach was chosen due to the urgent humanitarian needs, challenging operating environment, and need for partners with established field presence. Open competition was deemed impractical given the protracted bureaucratic process for new entrants in Ethiopia.
how_mechanism.quote: "We have developed our commercial approach on the basis of market research and advice from FCDO commercial advisers. There are only a limited number of organisations who would be able to deliver EC2R’s objectives due to the challenging operating environment in Ethiopia and the governance of the humanitarian sector." (D0002694.odt, Commercial approach)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will be governed by a partnership principles framework and overseen through regular risk management processes. High-level decisions (e.g., shifts between emergency response and resilience-building) will be informed by the British Embassy Addis Ababa country plan and programme governance structures.
how_governance.quote: "The programme will ultimately only be successful if we can work in a cross-Embassy and cross-government manner with our key allies... This demonstrates that whilst they are not directly funded by the business case, we rely heavily on a joined-up approach between political engagement and programme interventions." (D0002694.odt, ONE HMG Approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes a £40 million internal risk facility and is designed to allow reallocation between components (e.g., emergency response vs resilience) based on contextual shifts. Funds can be moved between UN/NGO/World Bank channels as needed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes conflict-sensitivity and flexibility to respond to sudden emergencies. Adjustments will be made through regular risk management processes, with the ability to scale up emergency assistance or shift away from government channels if access deteriorates. The British Embassy’s country plan will guide adaptations.
how_flexibility.quote: "EC2R will give us a flexible portfolio of delivery channels that we can use to respond to a range of scenarios... We have built in additional safeguards and capabilities to better manage the risk of working in conflict-affected areas. Our aspiration is that during programme implementation we will focus increasingly on resilience building and partnering with the Government of Ethiopia to develop more sustainable systems. But, if needed, the programme also allows us to scale-up our emergency assistance and move away from Government channels." (D0002694.odt, Case for FCDO Intervention)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UN/NGOs/World Bank) → End Beneficiaries. The document notes that MoUs/AGAs are used to reduce layers compared to contract modalities.
how_efficiency.quote: "MoUs/AGAs provide more agility than contract modalities to scale up or down in a timely manner in response to changing needs." (D0002694.odt, Commercial approach)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Not to invest at all (counterfactual - rejected due to humanitarian imperative)
Option 2: Scale up existing basic services and humanitarian programmes (rejected due to lack of conflict-sensitivity and agility)
Option 3: Design a new multi-sector humanitarian and resilience programme (CHOSEN - provides flexibility for protracted crises)
Delivery Option 1: Partnership with NGOs only (rejected due to scale limitations and access risks)
Delivery Option 2: Partnership with UN only (rejected due to lack of local insight and government influence)
Delivery Option 3: Portfolio partnership with World Bank, UN, and NGOs (CHOSEN - balances scale, local access, and system influence)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed portfolio approach (Option 3/Delivery Option 3) was selected for its flexibility to operate in Ethiopia’s volatile context, ability to leverage the strengths of different partners (UN scale, NGO local access, World Bank government systems), and capacity to adapt to both climate and conflict shocks. It allows the UK to maintain influence over humanitarian policy while delivering services in hard-to-reach areas.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (value for money through complementary partner strengths)
risk-mitigation (diversified delivery channels reduce exposure to access restrictions)
experience (builds on lessons from previous UK programmes like BRE)
partner-capacity (uses best-performing partners from current portfolio)
flexibility (adaptive to sudden emergencies and changing needs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Increased complexity and management burden for FCDO due to multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Managed by coinciding EC2R mobilization with closure of other programmes, reducing overall number of partners compared to FY2021/22, and using portfolio approach to balance workload.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Higher administrative costs from managing UN/World Bank overheads
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Offset by cost-effectiveness of PSNP system and economies of scale in UN procurement, with limited scope to negotiate overheads acknowledged.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential for aid diversion or instrumentalization in conflict areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong safeguarding risk assessments, third-party monitoring, and conflict-sensitivity training for partners. Clear vulnerability-based targeting criteria.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (reducing input costs through preparedness investments)
efficiency (improving response time and targeting accuracy)
effectiveness (meeting SPHERE standards and reducing mortality/morbidity)
equity (reaching hard-to-access populations and vulnerable groups)
why_rationale.quote: "Delivery option 3 is considered the most appropriate option. It is the most flexible and agile which is critical given the uncertain operating context in Ethiopia. Partnering both with NGOs who are direct implementers and closer to affected populations and with the UN and the World Bank who have normative functions and partnerships with Government means we can link delivery and understanding of the situation on the ground with humanitarian policy direction." (D0002694.odt, Delivery Options Appraisal)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating environment in Ethiopia severely limits partner selection: NGOs face suspension risks and government restrictions, UN agencies struggle with access in conflict zones, and new entrants cannot establish operations quickly due to bureaucratic hurdles. This forces reliance on established partners despite their limitations.
q27_constraints_detail: NGOs face higher risk of operational constraints (suspensions, visa delays) than UN agencies
UN agencies have struggled to adapt to complex security environments and meet needs of specific communities
Government-imposed restrictions limit ability to work in non-government-controlled areas
Protracted bureaucratic processes prevent new organizations from entering the market
Humanitarian data gaps and weak coordination systems hinder effective targeting
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for multi-sector humanitarian response (nutrition, health, WASH, protection, education) in a conflict-affected context requires a mixed delivery structure: UN agencies for scale and normative functions, NGOs for local access and specialized services, and World Bank for government systems. The volatile environment demands flexibility to shift between emergency response and resilience-building.
q28_linkages: Multi-sector needs → Portfolio approach with complementary partner strengths
Conflict sensitivity → Diversified channels to mitigate access risks
Resilience focus → Integration of World Bank/PSNP for sustainable systems
Hard-to-reach areas → NGO partnerships for last-mile delivery
System strengthening → UN coordination roles and humanitarian reform priorities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive partnerships and rapid delivery, noting that: 1) Working only through NGOs would provide better local insight but lack scale and system influence, 2) Relying solely on UN agencies would improve coordination but reduce field-level adaptability, and 3) Direct government funding (via PSNP) is cost-effective but cannot operate in conflict-affected areas. The chosen portfolio approach balances these trade-offs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Local insight (NGOs) vs. scale (UN) - resolved through mixed portfolio
Speed (established partners) vs. competition (limited new entrants) - resolved via restricted selection
Government systems (cost-effective) vs. conflict access (NGOs) - resolved by parallel channels
Flexibility (adaptive management) vs. oversight (management burden) - mitigated through risk facility and governance structures
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context (conflict, drought, economic crisis) drives intensive oversight needs: milestone-based management, embedded safeguarding, third-party monitoring, and adaptive governance structures. The programme includes a £40m risk facility and regular risk assessments to address the volatile environment.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: UN agencies lead system-wide coordination and large-scale service delivery, NGOs provide localized, conflict-sensitive services, and the World Bank strengthens government systems (PSNP). Technical assistance focuses on improving preparedness, data systems, and resilience capabilities across all partners.
intersections.quote: "Partnering both with NGOs who are direct implementers and closer to affected populations and with the UN and the World Bank who have normative functions and partnerships with Government means we can link delivery and understanding of the situation on the ground with humanitarian policy direction." (D0002694.odt, Delivery Options Appraisal)

key_programme_risks: Deterioration in humanitarian access (e.g., expanded blockade, new conflict fronts)
Failure of rain seasons leading to deepened famine conditions
Hyperinflation reducing purchasing power of assistance
Government restrictions on humanitarian operations (visa denials, expulsions, supply chain limits)
Aid diversion or instrumentalization by conflict parties
Weak coordination between international and national humanitarian systems
Underfunding of critical sectors (protection, education) by other donors
Climate shocks (floods, droughts) overwhelming response capacity
Displacement crises straining service delivery in host communities
Economic collapse limiting government’s ability to complement humanitarian efforts

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible portfolio allows shift between government/non-government channels; funding for humanitarian security experts; high-level advocacy with Government of Ethiopia.
Investments in strategic stockpiles (e.g., RUTF), climate-resilient WASH infrastructure, and early warning systems; partnerships with FAO/WFP for anticipatory action.
Use of cash transfers where markets function; regular adjustments to targeting criteria; focus on in-kind assistance for critical supplies.
Diversified partner base (UN/NGOs); diplomatic engagement on operating environment; third-party monitoring in restricted areas.
Safeguarding risk assessments for all interventions; vulnerability-based targeting; third-party monitoring in high-risk areas.
UK seat on Humanitarian Country Team; investments in data systems and joint planning; support to EDRMC (national disaster agency).
UK focus on neglected sectors (protection, education); advocacy with other donors; proof-of-concept for innovative financing.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict-sensitivity is critical: previous programmes struggled to adapt to rapidly evolving conflict dynamics, requiring real-time adjustments to targeting and delivery channels.
Local partnerships are essential for access: NGOs with established community trust can operate in areas where UN agencies are restricted.
Government systems have limits in conflict zones: PSNP cannot operate in non-government-controlled areas, requiring parallel humanitarian channels.
Humanitarian-diplomatic coordination is vital: UK’s dual role as a major donor and political actor (e.g., on peace talks) must be leveraged to address access constraints.

Preparedness saves lives and money: Investments in stockpiles, early warning, and resilient infrastructure generate high returns in FCAS contexts (e.g., £1 spent on preparedness saves £1.5-2.6 in response costs).
Cash transfers work where markets function: Evidence from Ethiopia shows cash is more efficient than in-kind aid in accessible areas, but requires market monitoring.
Protection risks spike in displacement: GBV and child protection needs must be integrated from the start, not treated as add-ons.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Building Resilience in Ethiopia (BRE) programme (2016-2022) demonstrated that: 1) Government-led safety nets (PSNP) are cost-effective but cannot reach conflict-affected areas, 2) UN agencies excel at scale but struggle with localization, 3) NGOs provide critical access but lack system-wide influence, and 4) flexibility to shift between emergency and resilience modes is essential in protracted crises. EC2R builds on these lessons by combining all three channels in a single portfolio.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations include: 1) Adding a £40m internal risk facility for rapid reallocation, 2) Expanding protection and education components (previously underfunded), 3) Strengthening conflict-sensitivity safeguards, 4) Investing in humanitarian preparedness (e.g., RUTF stockpiles, WASH infrastructure), and 5) Formalizing adaptive management processes linked to Embassy country plans.
risks_lessons.quote: "The experience of the last two years has demonstrated the importance of flexibility and conflict-sensitivity in our approach in Ethiopia. The trajectory is uncertain: there are some promising signs with the recent cessation of hostilities in the Northern Ethiopia conflict, but localised conflict is spreading in other parts of the country. EC2R will give us a flexible portfolio of delivery channels that we can use to respond to a range of scenarios." (D0002694.odt, Case for FCDO Intervention)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to crowd in other donors (e.g., G7, Gulf Cooperation Council) by demonstrating innovative approaches (e.g., WASH infrastructure investments, humanitarian cash models) and generating evidence on cost-effective interventions. Specific leverage targets are not quantified.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both revenue spending (humanitarian services, cash transfers) and capital investments (e.g., WASH infrastructure rehabilitation, strategic stockpiles). Explicit split not provided, but enabling investments (£31.5m) and internal risk facility (£40m) suggest ~30% for systemic/capital components.
financial_details.quote: "The total cost of FCDO support is up to £240 million over 3.5 years... The expected profile of spending (including use of £40 million internal risk facility) is: 21/22: £22m, 22/23: £40m, 23/24: £79m, 24/25: £99m."
