(D0002694.odt, Economic appraisal of the preferred option)

metadata.programme_name: Maternal and Newborn Health and Rights Programme
metadata.duration_text: 10 years with initial funding for 6 years approved
metadata.quote: "The programme will contribute to lower global maternal and newborn mortality, using three distinct mechanisms aimed at filling critical global gaps in support." (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "the business case is written for 10 years with initial funding for 6 years approved." (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening local midwifery associations and grassroots advocacy), policy influence (nurturing a global 'Birth Justice' movement), and service delivery (supporting emergency transport systems for pregnant women). It aims to reduce maternal and newborn mortality by addressing systemic gaps in care, advocacy, and transport.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will contribute to lower global maternal and newborn mortality, using three distinct mechanisms aimed at filling critical global gaps in support." (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Number of grassroots organisations identified and small grants for MNH advocacy given
Number of local midwifery associations capacity strengthened and number of advocacy activities carried out
M-Mama programme fully set up in Kenya, creating a national emergency referral system
Monitoring, evaluation and learning systems set up by each partner
Advocacy actions carried out through small grants and resulting changes
Global Birth Justice movement forming
Advocacy and leadership actions carried out by local midwifery associations
Number of women transported by M-mama programme, maternal and newborn outcomes of those transported, and trends
Early lessons learnt and best practice documented across all components

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce maternal and newborn mortality by strengthening local systems, advocacy, and emergency transport, focusing on marginalized groups and building sustainable local capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will strategically use funding to support the three priority areas that have been identified as global gaps." (D0006509.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in countries with high maternal mortality and fragile health systems, but the overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak health systems, conflict, and climate change exacerbate maternal/newborn mortality, while poor transport infrastructure and social norms (e.g., disrespect in care) deter women from seeking services. Political neglect of MNH advocacy limits systemic change.
where_context.quote: "Most deaths now occur in humanitarian crises, due to disruption to the health system and the huge difficulties women face in reaching facilities." (D0006509.odt, Causes of Deaths)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Local midwifery associations and grassroots organizations (Southern partners) will lead advocacy and service delivery, with technical support from global partners like Global Fund for Women and ICM. Decision-making for grants and priorities rests with local movement committees.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening local midwifery associations (financial sustainability, advocacy, leadership)
Small grants and technical support for grassroots organizations
Training on advocacy, policy influence, and movement-building
Support for emergency transport system setup (e.g., M-mama in Kenya)

partner_organizations.name: Global Fund for Women (GFW)
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager for grassroots advocacy component; provides grants and technical support to local organizations

partner_organizations.name: International Confederation of Midwives (ICM)
partner_organizations.role: Strengthens local midwifery associations in Kenya, Malawi, and Pakistan; provides advocacy training and policy support

partner_organizations.name: White Ribbon Alliance (WRA)
partner_organizations.role: Potential partner for MNH advocacy (considered but not selected)

partner_organizations.name: Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (PMNCH)
partner_organizations.role: Existing UK partner for high-level advocacy (considered but not selected for grassroots focus)

partner_organizations.name: Local midwifery associations (e.g., in Kenya, Malawi, Pakistan)
partner_organizations.role: Implement advocacy, training, and service delivery at country level

partner_organizations.name: Local grassroots organizations (unspecified)
partner_organizations.role: Receive small grants for MNH advocacy and movement-building

partner_organizations.name: Kenyan government (M-mama programme)
partner_organizations.role: Implements national emergency transport system for pregnant women

who_partners.quote: "FCDO could support GFW to start a new stream of their work on MNH/Birth Justice, combining advocacy with small grants to grassroots organisations." (D0006509.odt, Stage two: Appraisal of delivery options)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core funding to Global Fund for Women (GFW) and ICM for grant-making and capacity building; direct grants to local organizations for advocacy; and block funding for the M-mama transport system in Kenya.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: GFW acts as the fund manager for the grassroots advocacy component, disbursing small grants to local organizations and providing technical support. ICM manages midwifery association strengthening, while the M-mama transport system is implemented by the Kenyan government with FCDO support.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: GFW and ICM were selected based on their existing networks, experience in movement-building, and ability to reach marginalized groups. The appraisal process compared them against alternatives (e.g., PMNCH, IPPF) and scored GFW highest for its grassroots focus and local capacity-strengthening approach.
how_mechanism.quote: "The result of this appraisal concludes that support to Global Fund for Women is the strongest option." (D0006509.odt, Table 1: Options for advocacy component)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: GFW’s movement committee (comprising local grassroots organizations) prioritizes grants and strategies. ICM’s governance involves national midwifery associations and global policy linkages. FCDO retains oversight but delegates day-to-day management to partners.
how_governance.quote: "The movement committee is responsible for determining grant-making priorities, resources needed, and how resources should be distributed." (D0006509.odt, GFW’s approach)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between components with approval, given the programme’s adaptive design (e.g., lesson-learning for scale-up). The 10-year framework allows for iterative changes based on early outcomes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes learning and scaling up successful approaches. For example, transport interventions may expand to other countries if the Kenyan model proves effective. Grassroots advocacy priorities will evolve based on local movement committees’ decisions.
how_flexibility.quote: "The business case is written for ten years of support although only six years of funding will initially be approved. This long time reflects the ‘patient development’ approach needed for this type of programme." (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Fund Manager (GFW/ICM) → Local Implementers (grassroots organizations/midwifery associations) → End Beneficiaries (women/newborns)
how_efficiency.quote: "Monitoring, evaluation and learning systems set up by each partner." (D0006509.odt, Expected outputs)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Increased funding to PMNCH for grassroots advocacy
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: PMNCH lacks direct grassroots grant-making capacity and cannot easily earmark funds for specific countries.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Funding IPPF to start a new MNH small grants mechanism
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: IPPF lacks experience in MNH and would need to build new networks, delaying impact.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Supporting White Ribbon Alliance (WRA) for advocacy
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: WRA’s structure is less equipped for direct grant-making to marginalized groups.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Supporting UNFPA’s Maternal Health Thematic Fund (MHTF) for midwifery
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: MHTF’s broad focus and government-level work would dilute impact on local associations.
Gaps in midwifery, advocacy, and transport would persist, worsening maternal/newborn outcomes.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: GFW and ICM were selected for their proven ability to strengthen local capacity, reach marginalized groups, and align with the programme’s rights-based, movement-building approach. GFW’s flexible, movement-led model and ICM’s focus on midwifery associations address critical gaps identified in the scoping assessment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited reach of nascent grassroots movements in some countries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GFW’s landscaping phase will identify and strengthen existing local networks before scaling up.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of midwifery associations without government support
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ICM’s focus on financial sustainability and advocacy for policy change (e.g., salary retention).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on local transport infrastructure (e.g., M-mama in Kenya)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot phase with lesson-learning to adapt to other contexts (e.g., Malawi, Lesotho).

why_rationale.quote: "The programme will provide value for money by supporting local organisations and local systems with the aim of lesson learning for scale up to other countries." (D0006509.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on EPD flagship countries (many with weak health systems, conflict, or climate vulnerability) limits partner selection to organizations with existing local presence and adaptability (e.g., GFW’s experience in fragile contexts).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict/humanitarian crises in flagship countries require partners with rapid-response capacity.
Climate change impacts (e.g., heat stress, extreme weather) demand resilient health systems, favoring partners like GFW with environmental advocacy experience.
Weak midwifery associations in some countries necessitate ICM’s targeted support for governance and advocacy.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to address **three distinct gaps** (grassroots advocacy, midwifery capacity, emergency transport) shapes the mixed delivery structure: GFW for advocacy, ICM for midwifery, and direct government support for transport. The rights-based, movement-building objective requires decentralized, local-led implementation.
q28_linkages: Grassroots advocacy (Component 1) links to midwifery strengthening (Component 2) by amplifying demands for respectful care and policy change.
Emergency transport (Component 3) complements advocacy by removing physical barriers to care, addressing the ‘second delay’ in the Thaddeus and Maine model.
Local midwifery associations (Component 2) feed into global policy platforms (e.g., PMNCH) to scale up lessons.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly prioritizes equity (targeting adolescents, disabled women, and conflict-affected groups) over efficiency, accepting higher transaction costs for small grants and localized interventions. For example, GFW’s movement-led approach requires extensive landscaping and capacity-building but ensures marginalized voices shape priorities.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Movement-building (e.g., Birth Justice) takes time but ensures sustainable, locally owned advocacy.
Small grants to grassroots organizations are less cost-efficient than bulk funding to multilaterals but critical for equity.
GFW/ICM provide technical support but cede decision-making to local movement committees.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk profile allows for milestone-based oversight rather than intensive monitoring, with flexibility to adapt to local contexts (e.g., adjusting transport models based on pilot results).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: GFW strengthens grassroots organizations’ ability to advocate, ICM builds midwifery associations’ policy influence, and the M-mama component tests scalable transport solutions.
intersections.quote: "The programme will focus on strengthening local alliances and organisations to allow women to demand and access better quality care for themselves and their babies." (D0006509.odt, Programme results)

key_programme_risks: Stalled progress on maternal/newborn mortality (SDG 3.1/3.2) due to systemic gaps in advocacy, midwifery, and transport.
Disrespect/abuse in maternity care deterring women from seeking services (prevalence 15–98%).
Climate change and conflict exacerbating health system fragility in flagship countries.
Limited sustainability of midwifery associations without government salary support.
Potential duplication or fragmentation of grassroots efforts without coordination.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: GFW’s movement-led approach consolidates disparate efforts and links to global platforms (e.g., PMNCH).
ICM’s focus on resource mobilization and governance systems (e.g., in Kenya, Malawi, Pakistan).
Pilot in Kenya with lesson-learning for adaptation to other countries (e.g., Malawi, Lesotho).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Exclusion of marginalized groups (e.g., disabled women, adolescents)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Explicit targeting in grant criteria and advocacy priorities (e.g., GFW’s movement committee composition).

fcas_specific_lessons: Humanitarian crises require flexible, rapid-response transport and advocacy models (e.g., M-mama’s driver networks).
Climate-resilient health systems must integrate maternal/newborn needs (e.g., heat stress increasing preterm labor).
In FCAS, grassroots movements need protected civic space to operate (GFW’s participatory decision-making mitigates this).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past FCDO programmes (e.g., Women’s Rights Organisations Programme) showed that small grants to grassroots groups are effective for policy influence but require long-term support. The SRHR Grassroots Programme demonstrated the need for movement-building to sustain advocacy gains.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 10-year timeframe and adaptive management (e.g., scaling transport based on Kenyan pilot) reflect lessons on the need for ‘patient development’ in complex contexts.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learnt from other FCDO grassroots programmes, such as the Women’s Rights Organisations programme have shown that grassroots work is best done by organisations that have the contacts and the systems in place." (D0006509.odt, Stage two: Appraisal of delivery options)

financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: £5.83 million for 6 years (business case is written for 10 years to 2034 with further approval of funding required in 2030)." (D0006509.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: Portfolio Risk Assurance Programme III (PRAP III)

quote.text: The Portfolio Risk Assurance Programme III (PRAP III) will strengthen the Pakistan Network’s ability to identify, manage and address governance, management, financial, safeguarding risks, and help improve Value for Money (VFM) at programme level in a challenging external risk environment.

duration_source.text: The programme will be delivered through a consortium of an international commercial partner with strong presence in country and in collaboration with a national NGO. [...] The programme budget is up to £2 Million over five years.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PRAP III is designed to provide assurance, advisory support, and capacity building to improve risk management, safeguarding, and value for money across FCDO's Pakistan portfolio. It combines elements of capacity building (strengthening implementing partners' systems), advisory support (technical assistance on risk management), and assurance (independent reviews of high-risk programmes).

q1_source.text: The programme will focus on assurance, by playing an advisory role, building capacity of implementing partners and developing tools to mitigate risks for all Official Development Assistance (ODA) and non-ODA programmes including those funded through the Conflict, Stability and Security Fund (CSSF) and, in due course, the Integrated Security Fund (ISF).

q3_expected_outputs.output: Specialist reviews of high-risk programme elements
q3_expected_outputs.target: 41 reviews conducted in PRAP II (baseline for PRAP III)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Cash flow tracking exercises
q3_expected_outputs.target: e.g., £50m Financial Inclusion Programme review costing £25,000

q3_expected_outputs.output: Capacity building for FCDO staff and implementing partners
q3_expected_outputs.target: Training sessions on risk management, VFM, and safeguarding

q3_expected_outputs.output: Value for Money (VFM) reviews
q3_expected_outputs.target: Sample-based reviews of technical assistance programmes

q3_expected_outputs.output: Safeguarding policy implementation support
q3_expected_outputs.target: Periodic reviews for programmes focusing on women/girls, minorities

q3_expected_outputs.output: Demand-driven technical assistance
q3_expected_outputs.target: 13 demand-driven requests responded to in PRAP II (2021-2022)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Tools for risk identification/management
q3_expected_outputs.target: Development of VFM indicator bank and safeguarding tools

what_objectives.summary: PRAP III aims to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of FCDO's £400m Pakistan portfolio by reducing exposure to fraud/corruption risks, ensuring safeguarding policies are implemented, and enhancing VFM measurement. It provides independent assurance through specialist reviews while building local capacity to sustain improvements.

quote.text: The intended impact of the programme is ‘Improved efficiency and effectiveness of FCDO's bilateral programmes (including CSSF) in Pakistan’, and the intended outcomes of the programme are: 1) Improved risk management of BHC Islamabad programmes; 2) Improved understanding, measurement, and management of value for money within the portfolio.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Pakistan ranks 140/180 on Transparency International's Corruption Perception Index (2022), with systemic corruption across public services, procurement, and senior officials. The country faces economic instability (30%+ inflation), recent floods causing £30bn damage, and security risks limiting access to programme sites. Safeguarding risks are elevated due to gender inequality (ranked 145/146 on WEF Gender Gap Index) and displacement crises.

q5_source.text: Transparency International ranked Pakistan 140 out of 180 countries in the Corruption Perception Index 2022. [...] Pakistan is characterised by high levels of violence and insecurity, poverty, inequality, and deteriorating human rights which makes it a complex environment in terms of safeguarding and reporting.
q5_source.source: S3014776.odt, A. Context and need for a FCDO intervention

q6_constraints_impact.security: Limits FCDO staff access to programme sites in some regions, requiring local partners for reviews (e.g., 'access to geographic locations which are not accessible for the FCDO staff').
q6_constraints_impact.corruption: Systemic corruption in procurement and public finance increases risk of aid diversion, requiring enhanced controls (e.g., 'widespread corruption can act as a drag on the delivery of most of HMG’s objectives').
q6_constraints_impact.economic instability: Inflation (>30%) and flood damages (£30bn) increase financial burdens on beneficiaries and fraud risks (e.g., 'economic crisis [...] has put immense financial burden on masses to meet their needs, increasing fraud and corruption risks').
q6_constraints_impact.safeguarding: Gender inequality and displacement (664,000 in camps) heighten risks of abuse/exploitation, requiring tailored safeguarding measures (e.g., 'more vulnerable to abuse, sexual and physical violence and exploitation').

quote.text: The complexity of operating context for the FCDO’s bilateral programme in Pakistan has increased significantly due to COVID-19, ODA cuts, staff turnover, massive floods, deteriorating economic situation, and difficulties in directly monitoring programmes in some parts of the country due to security concerns.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Programme Effectiveness and Transparency (PET) Team (FCDO) + International Commercial Supplier + National NGO
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The international commercial supplier leads technical reviews (e.g., financial audits, VFM analysis) while the national NGO leads safeguarding work, with FCDO's PET Team managing the consortium. Decision-making is shared: FCDO approves workplans, but implementing partners design/deliver reviews and capacity-building activities.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for FCDO staff on interpreting financial/assurance reports
Workshops for implementing partners on risk management and safeguarding
Development of tools (e.g., VFM indicator bank, safeguarding checklists)
Mentorship through demand-driven technical assistance
Lesson-learning sessions to promote standardisation

partner_organizations.name: Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) - PET Team
partner_organizations.role: Programme management and oversight

partner_organizations.name: International Commercial Supplier (TBD via procurement)
partner_organizations.role: Lead specialist reviews (financial audits, VFM analysis, cash flow tracking), technical advisory

partner_organizations.name: National NGO Partner (TBD via procurement)
partner_organizations.role: Safeguarding reviews, capacity building for local partners, community engagement

partner_organizations.name: Implementing Partners (FCDO-funded programmes)
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of reviews/capacity building; include CSSF/ISF grantees and ODA implementers

quote.text: The preferred option is Option 2: Independent Programme. [...] The model of an international commercial supplier in partnership with a national NGO is the preferred model. This should ensure impartial and consistent professional integrity of the reviews and protection of the partners, given the sensitivity of the work.
quote.source: S3014776.odt, Option 2: Independent Programme & Delivery Approach

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO will sign a commercial contract with a consortium (international supplier + national NGO) to deliver specialist reviews, capacity building, and advisory services. Payments are milestone-based, with funds disbursed in arrears upon delivery of agreed outputs (e.g., review reports, training sessions).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Programme Effectiveness and Transparency (PET) Team at FCDO’s Pakistan office will manage the consortium contract, with a single point of contact for the supplier. The consortium combines an international commercial partner (for technical reviews) and a national NGO (for safeguarding/capacity building), ensuring both global expertise and local access.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition is required to comply with FCDO procurement rules and ensure value for money. The Early Market Engagement (EME) session will test delivery options, but the final selection will prioritise: 1) technical expertise in risk assurance/VFM/safeguarding; 2) demonstrated ability to operate across Pakistan; 3) established partnership with a national NGO; and 4) cost transparency (open-book accounting).

quote.text: A competitive bidding process through a suitable framework agreement. In absence of a suitable framework agreement, we plan to run an open OJEU procurement process. [...] The investment for this programme will be up to £2m for five years. Competitive tendering the service requirements will drive added value for the programme investment and comply with the legislative requirements of the Commercial Directorate.

The programme will be managed within the Programme Effectiveness and Transparency (PET) Team. [...] The supplier will be required to build the capacity of BHC staff in interpreting these statements and called upon on an ad hoc basis to support programme staff. [...] Continuation from each review point will be contingent on supplier performance, programme results, satisfactory work plans and a continuing VfM rationale.
quote.source: S3014776.odt, The proposed response & Contract Management

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The contract includes breakpoints to adapt to changes (e.g., scale up/down) and allows workplan/budget amendments within the agreed scope. Annual reviews assess continuing VfM rationale, enabling reallocation between components (e.g., risk management vs. safeguarding) if priorities shift.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a rolling workplan agreed annually with FCDO, with monthly updates. Demand-driven technical assistance (e.g., 13 requests in PRAP II) allows responsiveness to emerging risks, but major shifts require FCDO approval during contract reviews.

quote.text: The contract will have adequate provision for variation in form of break points to adapt to changes that occur during the life of the programme, including scale up and down. [...] The contract will have a provision to extend the contract for another two years if there are any unmet needs and funds are still available.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Consortium (International Supplier + National NGO) → Implementing Partners (no sub-grantees).

quote.text: The programme funds will be disbursed to the programme partner in arrears in accordance with an agreed work plan and payment schedule. [...] The contract will move to a hybrid contract with some costs paid on an input basis, but majority of payments made against successful delivery of quality outputs.
quote.source: S3014776.odt, Flow of funds & Contract Management

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Discontinue PRAP after Phase II, relying on existing FCDO tools (FRAs, audits, due diligence) without a dedicated assurance facility.
Integrate specialist reviews into individual programmes, managed separately by each programme team with no central coordination.
Partner with a multilateral (e.g., UNOPS) to conduct reviews, though conflict-of-interest risks were noted.
Use an Accountable Grant Agreement with an INGO/NGO, but lacked expertise for financial/VFM reviews.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The independent consortium model (Option 2) was selected because: 1) **Value for Money**: Centralised management reduces transaction costs (vs. embedded) and avoids duplication (e.g., 'one central contract [...] saving programme teams substantial time'); 2) **Risk Mitigation**: Provides consistent standards across the portfolio (vs. embedded's fragmented approach) and specialist skills unavailable in-house (e.g., 'all 41 reviews commissioned by PRAP II [...] required specialised skills'); 3) **Flexibility**: Allows demand-driven support (e.g., 13 TA requests in PRAP II) while maintaining FCDO oversight; 4) **Local Access**: National NGO partner enables reviews in insecure areas (e.g., 'access to geographic locations which are not accessible for FCDO staff'); 5) **Learning**: Promotes standardisation and lesson-sharing across programmes (vs. siloed embedded reviews).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from uncovering fiduciary/safeguarding failures
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monthly risk reviews and escalation protocols aligned with FCDO’s Risk Management Policy; sensitive findings elevated to senior management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier conflict of interest (e.g., if also implementing FCDO programmes)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Contractual requirement to declare conflicts; procurement process excludes organisations delivering FCDO-funded programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited supplier base for specialised services in Pakistan
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early Market Engagement (EME) to test feasibility; hybrid contract (input + output-based payments) to attract quality bidders.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Cost escalation due to inflation/currency fluctuations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Payment-by-results model; benchmarking against FCDO rates; annual budget reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in procurement (e.g., OJEU process)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Exploring framework agreements; fallback to open competition if needed.

quote.text: Option 2 is preferred as it provides the best chance for the optimum use of specialist resources, while still being flexible enough to allow programme teams and the office as a whole to guide when and how these resources are used. It also offers excellent value for money to have one central contract in place to provide assurance and demand driven specialist reviews across BHC. [...] The independent programme will enable the dedicated BHC team to effectively manage the work of the supplier, learning continuously and improving how the facility works.
quote.source: S3014776.odt, The preferred option is Option 2

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk context in Pakistan (security restrictions, corruption, safeguarding risks) directly shapes partner selection: 1) **Security**: FCDO staff cannot access many programme sites, requiring a national NGO partner with local presence ('access to geographic locations which are not accessible for FCDO staff'); 2) **Corruption**: Need for an independent, impartial supplier to avoid conflicts of interest (e.g., 'ensuring impartial and consistent professional integrity of the reviews'); 3) **Safeguarding**: National NGO leads safeguarding work due to cultural/linguistic expertise in sensitive areas (e.g., gender-based violence, child protection).
q27_constraints_detail: Security restrictions limit FCDO’s direct monitoring, necessitating local partners for fieldwork.
Corruption risks require suppliers with no ties to government or implementing partners to ensure independence.
Safeguarding complexities (e.g., gender inequality, displacement) demand partners with contextual expertise.
Economic instability (inflation, flood recovery) increases need for flexible, demand-driven support.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (assurance + capacity building + advisory) drive the consortium structure: 1) **Assurance Needs**: Independent reviews require an international supplier with audit/VFM expertise (e.g., 'specialist reviews of the highest risk elements'); 2) **Capacity Building**: National NGO partner delivers training/mentorship to local implementers (e.g., 'build the capacity of implementing partners'); 3) **Flexibility**: Demand-driven TA and rolling workplans reflect the need to adapt to emerging risks (e.g., 'occasional demand-based expertise that cannot be precisely forecast').
q28_linkages: Specialist reviews (WHAT) → Consortium’s international supplier (HOW).
Safeguarding support (WHAT) → National NGO’s local expertise (HOW).
VFM measurement (WHAT) → Hybrid payment structure (input + output-based) (HOW).
Demand-driven TA (WHAT) → Annual workplan flexibility (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: 1) **Local Partnerships vs. Speed**: Using a national NGO ensures cultural appropriateness in safeguarding but may slow procurement (e.g., 'it will take longer to complete this procurement process'); 2) **Specialist Skills vs. Cost**: International expertise for VFM/audit reviews increases costs but is deemed necessary for quality (e.g., 'required specialised skills and expertise that were not available in-house'); 3) **Inclusive Reviews vs. Access**: Prioritising programmes in insecure areas (e.g., CSSF policing projects) balances equity with higher delivery risks.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: National NGO ensures safeguarding reviews are culturally appropriate but adds a layer to consortium management.
International auditors provide rigorous VFM analysis but at higher rates than local alternatives.
Demand-driven support meets emerging needs but requires adaptive contract management.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk context (FCAS) intensifies oversight: 1) **Monthly Risk Reviews**: More frequent than typical annual checks due to corruption/safeguarding risks; 2) **Embedded Quality Assurance**: PET Team’s central role ensures consistency across reviews (vs. light-touch in stable contexts); 3) **Breakpoints**: Contract allows rapid reallocation of funds if risks materialise (e.g., fraud cases).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: 1) **Implementing Partners**: Reviews identify gaps (e.g., '9 areas for improvement' in SNG Programme II), with partners required to address findings; 2) **FCDO Staff**: Training on interpreting audits/VFM reports builds in-house skills for long-term sustainability; 3) **National NGO**: Leads safeguarding capacity-building for local organisations, ensuring policies are cascaded to sub-partners.

quote.text: The complexity of operating context for the FCDO’s bilateral programme in Pakistan has increased significantly due to COVID-19, ODA cuts, staff turnover, massive floods, deteriorating economic situation, and difficulties in directly monitoring programmes in some parts of the country due to security concerns. [...] The programme will help build capacity across BHC programmes to measure the VfM and report on it, which will contribute directly to achieving the intended impact of the programme.
quote.source: S3014776.odt, Option 1: Counterfactual & B. Impact and Outcome

key_programme_risks.risk: Fraud/corruption in programme delivery
Safeguarding failures (e.g., SEAH, exploitation of beneficiaries)
Reputational damage to FCDO from uncovered risks
Supplier underperformance or conflicts of interest
Limited access to programme sites due to security
Economic instability increasing fraud risks (e.g., inflation-driven diversion)
Inconsistent VFM measurement across programmes

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Specialist reviews (e.g., cash flow tracking), enhanced due diligence, and Counter Aid Diversion Action Plan. Example: £25,000 review of £50m Financial Inclusion Programme identified control weaknesses.
Periodic safeguarding reviews by national NGO, training for partners, and enhanced due diligence (e.g., 'support the implementation of safeguarding policies by delivery partners').
Monthly risk monitoring, escalation protocols, and proactive disclosure of findings to senior management.
Contractual disclosure requirements and exclusion of suppliers implementing FCDO programmes.
National NGO partner conducts fieldwork in insecure areas; remote reviews where possible.
Rolling workplans to adapt to inflation; hybrid payment model to control costs.
VFM indicator bank and standardised tools developed in Year 1; sample-based reviews to align approaches.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from PRAP II: Timely risk identification (e.g., 'baseline reviews helped identify risks early') is critical in FCAS where risks evolve rapidly (e.g., post-flood displacement).
Adaptation to security constraints: PRAP II’s spot checks and remote reviews were effective where FCDO staff couldn’t access sites.
Conflict sensitivity: Reviews must account for political drivers of corruption (e.g., 'political patronage [...] commonplace') to avoid destabilising local power dynamics.
Local partnership models: National NGOs are essential for safeguarding in conservative areas (e.g., gender-based violence programmes).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: PRAP II (2016–2022) demonstrated that: 1) **Early Risk Identification**: Baseline reviews resolved 39/59 high risks, with 19 showing ongoing progress. 2) **Capacity Building Works**: Partners conducted quality due diligence in-house post-training. 3) **Demand for Assurance Persists**: Even with staff capacity-building, teams requested PRAP support until the programme ended. 4) **VFM Gaps**: Sample review of 4 TA programmes revealed inconsistent indicator tracking. 5) **Cost Efficiency**: Reviews cost 0.05–0.06% of programme budgets (e.g., £23k for £36m SNG Programme).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: PRAP III expands support to CSSF/ISF programmes (previously ODA-only) and adds: 1) **VFM Focus**: Dedicated reviews and indicator bank to address PRAP II’s findings on inconsistent measurement. 2) **Safeguarding Component**: Standalone workstream (£0.4m) responding to gender inequality and displacement risks. 3) **Hybrid Contract**: Shifts from input-based to output-based payments to improve accountability. 4) **Breakpoints**: Formalises flexibility to scale up/down based on annual reviews.

quote.text: One of the key lessons learnt from PRAP II is that timely identification of risks not only offers the opportunity to safeguard funds but also helps ensure value for money. [...] The lessons from the PRAP II clearly highlight the need to have a quality assurance mechanism in place to ensure a consistent application of value for money frameworks across the full range of the FCDO’s development work. [...] PRAP II also identified the need to build the capacity of the delivery partners to manage safeguarding risks.

The programme budget is up to £2 Million over five years. [...] The programme will have two main components, one focusing on overall risk management and VFM (estimated value £1.6m) and a second component focusing on safeguarding support (estimated value £0.4m). [...] The programme will be funded from programme resources (RDEL).

metadata.programme_name: Multilateral Core/Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights – ‘United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Core Funding 2022–2025’
metadata.quote: "To support the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) to advance the empowerment of all women and girls through sexual and reproductive health and rights for all, including increasing access to contraception, enabling women to have healthy pregnancies and safe births, and protecting women and girls from harm." (D0004635.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 20/01/2022-30/09/2025" (D0004635.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (direct provision of SRHR services), financing mechanism (core funding to UNFPA), and policy influence (advancing global norms on SRHR). It supports UNFPA's operational work in fragile contexts while also funding its normative role in setting global standards.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UNFPA is a key partner for the UK in the delivery of life-saving reproductive health services and supplies, including in fragile and conflict affected contexts. [...] Core funding enables UNFPA to operate in fragile contexts and provides the agency with the flexibility to respond to crises when they hit." (D0002977.odt, Strategic Case)
q3_expected_outputs: 255 million couple years of contraceptives provided (2018-2021 baseline)
71.4 million unintended pregnancies prevented (2018-2021 baseline)
200,000 maternal deaths averted (2018-2021 baseline)
570,000 girls saved from FGM (2018-2021 baseline)
Support for 50,000 pregnant women in Gaza crisis (2023 extension)
Distribution of reproductive health kits to 18,000+ births in Gaza (2023 extension)
Psychosocial support for GBV survivors in OPTs (2023 extension)
Strengthened data systems integrating population changes by 2025
Improved SRHR integration into universal health coverage policies by 2025
Enhanced capacity of 150 UNFPA country offices to deliver SRHR services
what_objectives.summary: The programme provides flexible core funding to UNFPA to deliver its 2022-2025 Strategic Plan, focusing on three transformative results: ending unmet need for family planning, ending preventable maternal deaths, and ending gender-based violence. The 2023 addendum extends support to address acute SRHR needs in the Occupied Palestinian Territories crisis.
what_objectives.quote: "This business case (2022-2025) runs parallel to UNFPA's Strategic Plan 2022-25, [...] focusing on critical pathways and the strategies necessary to accelerate the achievement of three transformative results [...] (a) ending the unmet need for family planning; (b) ending preventable maternal deaths; and (c) ending gender-based violence and harmful practices." (D0002977.odt, Strategic Plan)

countries_regions: Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPTs) - specific focus in 2023 addendum
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) including Gaza where 85% of the population is displaced and 13 of 36 hospitals are functional. The addendum explicitly addresses conflict-related sexual violence and humanitarian access challenges.
where_context.q5_source: "The crisis in the OPTs has had a severe impact on the entire population of Gaza, and on populations in the West Bank where the situation remains critical. [...] Securing easy access for women and girls to comprehensive health services, including sexual and reproductive health services is of key importance." (D0004635.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)
q6_contextual_constraints: infrastructure (destroyed health facilities - only 13/36 hospitals functional in Gaza)
weak institutions (health systems collapse in Gaza)
data limitations (challenges monitoring in conflict zones)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The Gaza conflict has destroyed 65% of hospitals, displaced 85% of the population, and created severe water/sanitation shortages that particularly affect pregnant women (50,000 currently pregnant with 15% needing emergency obstetric care). Humanitarian access is "incredibly challenging" with only limited truck convoys able to deliver supplies.
where_context.quote: "Access of humanitarian aid into Gaza remains incredibly challenging. UNFPA are taking all possible measures to ensure assistance goes to the people who need it. [...] There were an estimated 50,000 pregnant women in Gaza at the start of the crisis. [...] 13 out of the 36 hospitals in the Gaza strip are functional and providing limited services." (D0004635.odt, Implementation Approach)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UNFPA's Executive Board (where UK has voting rights) sets strategic direction, while country-level implementation is led by UNFPA's 150 country offices. The UK influences priorities through its Executive Board membership and core funding allocations.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training of medical professionals including midwives
Strengthening national health systems for family planning commodity allocation
Support to governments on SRHR policy frameworks
Youth leadership programmes (e.g., Youth Advocacy Panel in OPTs)
Psychosocial support training for GBV survivors
Disability inclusion strategy implementation

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer and recipient of core funding
partner_organizations.location: Multilateral (HQ in New York, 150 country offices)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Health (OPTs)
partner_organizations.role: Local service delivery partner (receives SRH kits and supplies)

partner_organizations.name: Safe Spaces (OPTs)
partner_organizations.role: GBV response and psychosocial support provider

partner_organizations.name: Youth-led organizations (OPTs)
partner_organizations.role: Psychosocial support for adolescents in refugee camps

partner_organizations.name: Palestine Adolescent Health Coalition
partner_organizations.role: Advocacy and service coordination for adolescent health

partner_organizations.name: Health Cluster (OPTs)
partner_organizations.role: Coordination platform co-led by UNFPA

partner_organizations.name: GBV Sub-Cluster
partner_organizations.role: Gender-based violence coordination led by UNFPA

who_partners.quote: "UNFPA has 150 offices worldwide with over 4000 personnel. [...] UNFPA is an essential part of the international system for humanitarian and development aid. It has the legitimacy to work in politically sensitive contexts where national governments are not welcome." (D0002977.odt, UNFPA Background)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides voluntary core contributions (up to £8m/year) through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with UNFPA. Core funding gives UNFPA full flexibility to allocate resources according to its Strategic Plan priorities, including crisis response. The 2023 addendum adds £4.25m for OPTs through a contribution arrangement.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNFPA manages all funds through its global structure (150 country offices + HQ). The UK's SRHR team in FCDO oversees the partnership through Executive Board representation and annual strategic dialogues. No sub-awards are mentioned - UNFPA implements directly or through its vetted partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNFPA is the designated UN agency for SRHR with a unique mandate. The UK has been a core donor for decades, and stopping funding would "signal a significant shift in the UK's support for UNFPA's role on SRHR" (D0002977.odt). The addendum extends to OPTs due to UNFPA's established presence there since 1986.
how_mechanism.quote: "UNFPA has been a longstanding partner to the UK for the operational and normative strengthening of women's and girls' sexual and reproductive health and rights. [...] Core funding enables UNFPA to operate in fragile contexts and provides the agency with the flexibility to respond to crises when they hit." (D0002977.odt, UK Partnership)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: UNFPA's Executive Board (where UK holds a seat) provides oversight. The UK engages through: 1) Annual Ministerial/Director-General dialogues; 2) Quarterly Executive Board meetings; 3) UN Effectiveness Network monitoring; 4) FCDO's SRHR team management (1/3 FTE PRO + 1/2 FTE SRO).
how_governance.quote: "The programme will be managed by the Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) team within FCDO's Human Development Department. [...] The Deputy Director, Head of Human Development Department, will lead the overarching relationship with UNFPA and will engage with UNFPA's senior leadership team in person at least annually." (D0002977.odt, FCDO Management and Governance)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core funding allows UNFPA to allocate resources globally according to emerging needs. The 2023 addendum demonstrates this flexibility by reallocating £4.25m to OPTs crisis response without requiring a new business case.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: UNFPA's Strategic Plan 2022-25 includes six accelerators for adaptive management: human rights-based approaches, innovation, partnerships, data, leaving no one behind, and resilience. The UK influences priorities through Executive Board engagement and can adjust funding allocations annually.
how_flexibility.quote: "Core funding enables UNFPA to operate in fragile contexts and provides the agency with the flexibility to respond to crises when they hit. [...] This addendum creates additional support to a critically needed SRHR response to the crisis unfolding in the OPTs." (D0004635.odt, Objective of Cost Extension)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNFPA (HQ/country offices) → [vetted local partners in OPTs]. The addendum specifies UNFPA works with "pre-crisis network of vetted partners" for Gaza delivery.
how_efficiency.quote: "The UK's investment to UNFPA will be structured through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and UNFPA for up to £24 million over a three-year period. [...] Disbursement Date: December 2022 - Up to £8,000,000; December 2023 - Up to £8,000,000; December 2024 - Up to £8,000,000." (D0002977.odt, Budget)

q24_alternatives_considered: Stopping core funding entirely
Reducing core funding from 2021 levels (£8m → lower amount)
Continuing core funding at £8m/year (selected option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Continuing core funding was selected to: 1) Maintain UK influence on UNFPA's Executive Board; 2) Signal continued commitment to SRHR globally; 3) Enable rapid crisis response (demonstrated by 2023 OPTs addendum); 4) Leverage UNFPA's unique mandate in politically sensitive contexts; 5) Avoid reputational damage from reducing support during fiscal pressure.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (core funding leverages £2.53 additional resources per £1 contributed)
risk-mitigation (maintaining Executive Board seat for influence)
partner-capacity (UNFPA's established presence in 150 countries including FCAS)
speed (core funding enables immediate crisis response)
flexibility (allows reallocation to emerging priorities like OPTs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of Executive Board seat if core funding stops/reduces
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain £8m/year contribution to retain influence and voting rights

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced ability to respond to crises without flexible core funding
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Core funding structure preserved to enable rapid reallocation (e.g., OPTs addendum)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Perceived UK retreat from SRHR leadership if funding cuts continue
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Public commitment maintained through stable multi-year funding

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Inefficient use of core funds if UNFPA priorities diverge from UK interests
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual Executive Board engagement and results tracking through IRRF framework

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging £2.53 additional funds per £1 core contribution)
effectiveness (alignment with UK's Women and Girls Strategy and EPD commitments)
equity (prioritizing furthest behind including in FCAS like OPTs)
why_rationale.quote: "Stopping core funding to the agency would signal a significant shift in the UK's support for UNFPA's role on SRHR, and the UK's broader policy position on SRHR and this will reverberate globally. [...] Providing an £8m per annum core contribution will bolster the organisational structure that supports these results and UNFPA's focus, allowing the UK to retain its influential voice within UNFPA and the UN Development System." (D0002977.odt, Options Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in OPTs (active conflict, hospital destruction, 85% displacement) necessitates using UNFPA due to its: 1) Established presence since 1986; 2) Vetted partner networks; 3) Health Cluster leadership; 4) GBV Sub-Cluster coordination role. Local NGOs lack capacity to deliver at scale in this environment.
q27_constraints_detail: Active conflict limits partner options to those with existing access (UNFPA's 38 years in OPTs)
Destroyed infrastructure requires partners with logistics capacity (UNFPA's supply chains)
GBV sensitivity requires specialized expertise (UNFPA's global GBV AoR leadership)
Humanitarian access restrictions favor multilateral actors with UN privileges
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both normative work (global SRHR standards) and operational delivery (FCAS service provision) determines the multilateral core funding approach. UNFPA's dual mandate requires flexible funding that supports both policy influence (e.g., ICPD forums) and direct service delivery (e.g., RH kits in Gaza).
q28_linkages: Global normative goals (three zeros) → require core funding for unrestricted use
FCAS service delivery → requires UNFPA's existing country office infrastructure
Humanitarian response needs → require pre-positioned supplies and rapid reallocation
Policy influence objectives → require Executive Board membership maintained through core contributions
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The documents explicitly discuss balancing: 1) Speed vs. inclusion (rapid OPTs response through established UNFPA partners vs. local ownership); 2) Global reach vs. country-specific needs (core funding flexibility vs. earmarked OPTs addendum); 3) Normative leadership vs. service delivery (UNFPA's dual role requires both).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Using UNFPA's existing systems enables rapid Gaza response but limits local NGO involvement
Equity: Core funding reaches furthest behind but gives UNFPA HQ control over allocations
Speed: Pre-vetted partners enable immediate delivery but may exclude newer local actors
Scale: UNFPA's global infrastructure ensures broad impact but with higher overhead costs
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context (Gaza) increases oversight intensity through: 1) Monthly risk monitoring meetings; 2) Direct FCDO engagement with UNFPA's surge personnel; 3) Enhanced PSEAH monitoring due to conflict-related GBV risks; 4) Humanitarian licence requirements for counter-terrorism compliance.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: UNFPA's capacity building activities (midwife training, youth leadership programmes) are designed to transition service delivery to local systems over time, while maintaining UNFPA's normative leadership role. The OPTs addendum shows this through support to Ministry of Health systems alongside direct service provision.
intersections.quote: "In fragile and conflict affected contexts like Gaza, UNFPA's established presence and vetted partner networks are critical for delivery. The addendum leverages UNFPA's 38 years of operations in OPTs to ensure life-saving SRH services reach those most in need, while building local capacity through Ministry of Health engagement and youth programmes." (D0004635.odt, Implementation Approach)

key_programme_risks: Critical mass of Member States not prioritizing core funding (Severe/Possible)
Operating environment deterioration in FCAS (Moderate/Possible)
UNFPA mandate threatened by SRHR backlash (Severe/Possible)
UNFPA insufficiently prioritizing UK policy interests (Major/Unlikely)
Weak UNFPA human resources in humanitarian contexts (Major/Possible)
Poor UN reform progress undermining efficiency (Moderate/Unlikely)
Resistance to comprehensive SRHR within UNFPA (Major/Possible)
FCDO capacity constraints for programme management (Moderate/Unlikely)
ODA pauses affecting disbursement (Major/Possible)
Fraud and PSEAH risks (Major/Possible)
Inadequate environmental/social safeguards (Major/Possible)
Access restrictions in Gaza (Severe/Likely - addendum-specific)
Supply chain disruptions for RH commodities (Severe/Likely - addendum-specific)
Conflict-related sexual violence increasing GBV caseloads (Severe/Likely - addendum-specific)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain £8m/year core funding to retain voting rights and strategic engagement
Leverage UNFPA's pre-crisis vetted partners and surge personnel deployments
Use Executive Board position to build coalitions with like-minded states
Enhanced due diligence through Central Assurance Assessments and UNFPA's PSEAH focal point network
Pre-positioned reproductive health kits and coordination with Health Cluster
Prepare business case justifications for timely disbursements
Bilateral engagement on leadership appointments and HR process reviews

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-existing partner networks are critical for rapid response (UNFPA's 38-year OPTs presence enabled immediate crisis action)
Health Cluster coordination mechanisms must be established before crises (UNFPA's co-leadership of RH Working Group facilitated OPTs response)
Local capacity building should be embedded in humanitarian responses (youth volunteers and midwife training in OPTs)
Flexible funding instruments are essential for FCAS (core funding enabled immediate OPTs reallocation)
GBV services must be integrated from crisis outset (UNFPA's GBV Sub-Cluster provided immediate response framework)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 funding cuts to UNFPA created "significant efforts at the partnership level to demonstrate continued commitment" (D0002977.odt). This informed the 2022-25 design to: 1) Maintain stable multi-year funding; 2) Preserve Executive Board influence; 3) Use addendums for crisis response rather than new business cases.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Shift from Payment by Results (2017-21) to flexible core funding (2022-25) based on ICAI recommendations; 2) Added explicit FCAS focus in addendum design; 3) Enhanced PSEAH monitoring for high-risk environments; 4) Integrated climate adaptation into programming following UNFPA's 2021 Environmental Efficiency Strategy.
risks_lessons.quote: "The absence of UK core funding would undermine UNFPA's ability to act as a delivery partner for FCDO's multi-bi programmes. Core funding means that UNFPA can maintain its presence at the country and regional level, be present in conflict and fragile affected states and respond to emerging crises as they develop. [...] By only providing earmarked programme funding to UNFPA, we would shift to a service delivery relationship that would undermine our prioritization of women and girls." (D0002977.odt, Options Analysis)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UNFPA estimates that for each £1 of core resources, an average of £2.53 of other resources are mobilised (2021 data).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Core funding is primarily revenue (programme activities: £238m staffing, £74m contracted services, £70m supplies in 2021). Institutional budget covers management costs through cost recovery mechanisms.
financial_details.quote:
"Core resources are the foundation for all UNFPA programmes and are especially important for the leave no one behind agenda and ability of UNFPA to reach the furthest behind first. [...] For each dollar of core resources raised in 2021, an average of $2.53 of other resources were mobilised." (D0002977.odt, Core Funding)

"The UK's investment to UNFPA will be structured through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and UNFPA for up to £24 million over a three-year period [...] with an additional £4.25m for OPTs crisis response." (D0002977.odt/D0004635.odt, Budget)

metadata.programme_name: UK–South Africa Skills for Work Programme

quote.text: The programme will support a more productive and equitable vocational skills system in South Africa, improving livelihoods of disadvantaged groups.

duration_source.text: AMP Start: 1 July 2023; AMP End: 31 March 2027

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening South Africa's vocational skills system), policy influence (supporting the Presidential Youth Employment Intervention and Just Energy Transition), and service delivery (direct skilling initiatives for marginalised groups). It aims to improve youth employment and support South Africa's economic transition through skills development.

q1_source.text: The programme will: Fund technical assistance to the Office of the Presidency to build capacity within the Presidential Youth Employment Intervention (PYEI)... Fund quality, technical education and vocational training and skills development in priority industries... Fund direct skilling and initiatives targeted at improving access to employment of marginalised groups...

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened youth employment and skills strategies/policies adopted for productive jobs in South Africa
Increased capability and capacity in South Africa's system for just transition through strengthened qualifications, curricula, pedagogy, and skilling
Increased access for women and girls to employment, income, and business growth opportunities
Piloting (green) re-skilling models in key geographies (e.g., Mpumalanga and Free State)
Technical assistance to the Office of the Presidency to support the National Pathway Management Network
Direct skilling initiatives for 3 million+ NEET youth (indirect target, based on context)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 3 million (contextual reference to NEET youth in 2022)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen South Africa's vocational skills system to drive inclusive economic growth, particularly supporting the Just Energy Transition and improving employment opportunities for marginalised groups, especially women and girls.

quote.text: The programme will help to strengthen South Africa’s skills system, through policy advice; and contribute to higher youth employment in productive jobs, especially for women.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting South Africa's stable but unequal economic context, with high unemployment and institutional challenges. The risk is mitigated by strong political backing (e.g., Presidential Youth Employment Intervention) and established UK-South Africa partnerships.

q5_source.text: Overall risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Structural constraints in the economy (e.g., lack of jobs in labour-intensive sectors) and weak education/vocational training systems limit youth employment opportunities. Spatial inequality concentrates poverty in disadvantaged areas, exacerbating access challenges. Labour market mismatches mean technical graduates often don't secure jobs in their trained fields, reinforcing inequalities.

quote.text: Despite national policy focus, education and vocational training systems are failing to deliver the skills needed to support sustained growth, productivity and deliver skilled jobs. Over 3 million young people were not in employment, education or training (NEET) in 2022. Structural constraints in the economy mean a lack of jobs in labour-intensive sectors. Where growth and demand for labour does occur, young people lack the experience and skills to capitalise on job opportunities.
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Why the intervention is needed?

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) retains decision-making authority, with South African partners (e.g., Presidency, DHET) involved in implementation but not leading strategic decisions. The programme is designed and overseen by the British High Commission South Africa (BHC).
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to the Presidency and government departments
lecturer training in TVET colleges
curriculum and qualification framework development
work placement and pathway-to-employment programmes
entrepreneurship and leadership training for marginalised groups

partner_organizations.name: Office of the Presidency (South Africa)
partner_organizations.role: Primary government partner; recipient of technical assistance for the Presidential Youth Employment Intervention (PYEI)

partner_organizations.name: Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET)
partner_organizations.role: Key stakeholder for skills policy and TVET system reforms

partner_organizations.name: Department of Basic Education
partner_organizations.role: Partner for education-to-employment pathways

partner_organizations.name: Department of Labour
partner_organizations.role: Stakeholder for labour market alignment

partner_organizations.name: TVET Colleges
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partners for vocational training and green skills development

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (industry bodies)
partner_organizations.role: Partners for curriculum development, work placements, and sector skills planning

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery partners for direct skilling initiatives (via Accountable Grants)

partner_organizations.name: British High Commission South Africa (BHC)
partner_organizations.role: Programme management and oversight

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral agencies (e.g., World Bank, UNDP, GIZ)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-financing or alignment partners (not direct implementers)

quote.text: The programme has three Components: Component 1: Procured through a mini-competition using an FCDO Framework... Components 2, 3: Delivery partners will be procured through Accountable Grant arrangements or Memoranda of Understanding (MoU).
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Delivery Mechanism and Implementation Partners

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Component 1 uses a **contract** (via FCDO Framework mini-competition) for technical assistance to the Presidency. Components 2 and 3 use **Accountable Grants** or **Memoranda of Understanding (MoU)** for skills delivery and gender-focused interventions. This hybrid approach allows flexibility for policy influence (contracts) and direct service delivery (grants).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by the British High Commission (BHC) with multiple delivery partners: (1) a commercial supplier (via FCDO Framework) for technical assistance, (2) CSOs or multilateral agencies (via Accountable Grants/MoUs) for skills training, and (3) government/private sector for implementation. Partners are selected based on technical expertise and existing stakeholder relationships.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Component 1 uses a **restricted competition** (FCDO Framework mini-competition) for speed and existing supplier relationships. Components 2–3 use **direct awards** (Accountable Grants/MoUs) to leverage pre-existing partnerships with CSOs and industry bodies, ensuring alignment with South African priorities and rapid mobilisation. The rationale emphasises technical capability, stakeholder relationships, and value for money.

quote.text: Option 6: Work with multiple delivery partners... This option reflects our assessment that there does not seem to be a single supplier of any type which could implement all the components set out in the strategic case. This option would also allow us to have a flexible approach to implementation... We envisage deploying a combination of accountable grants and a contract (locally sourced or via the International Multidisciplinary Development Framework).

The SRO will ensure that funds are disbursed in accordance with the signed agreements and contracts, and on the basis of agreed milestones and performance indicators... The PRO will ensure financial reporting and monitoring (monthly and quarterly) in accordance with defined Work plans, budget forecasts, output definitions and milestones for payment milestones and against agreed expenditure.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between components based on performance and evolving circumstances, but require approval. The programme budget table shows indicative forecasts that 'will likely change during implementation.'
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for calibration of activities based on labour market analysis and stakeholder feedback. Monthly meetings assess delivery risks and determine adjustments needed, particularly for green skills and gender components.

quote.text: We will adjust activities, and forecast spend, as needed under each component in light of performance and evolving circumstances... Monthly meetings with partners will assess delivery risk and determine any calibration needed.
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Programme Code and Risk Mitigation sections

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partners (commercial supplier/CSOs) → End beneficiaries (no sub-grantees mentioned).

quote.text: Management costs—Programme management costs are targeted at less than 10% of total costs... Payment milestones and against agreed expenditure.
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Value for Money and Programme Code sections

q24_alternatives_considered: Do Nothing (rejected: no material impact)
Partner with a bilateral donor (rejected: no single donor covered all components)
Partner with a multilateral institution (rejected: high overheads, risk of lost UK influence)
Partner with a commercial supplier (rejected: no single supplier had all required expertise)
Partner with a Civil Society Organisation (rejected: no single CSO had all capabilities)
Work with multiple delivery partners (selected: flexible, leverages complementary strengths)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **multiple delivery partners** option was chosen because no single organisation had the technical expertise, stakeholder relationships, and capacity to deliver all three components (policy influence, green skills, and gender equity). This approach allows flexibility to respond to changes in South Africa/UK circumstances, leverages pre-existing partnerships (e.g., with GIZ, World Bank), and maximises UK added value by combining commercial contracts (for technical assistance) with grants (for direct skilling).
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (avoiding over-reliance on one partner)
flexibility to adapt to political/economic changes

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Co-ordination challenges between multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular engagement frameworks with visible targets/dashboards; formalised roles and obligations via contracts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of UK influence/visibility when working with multilaterals or bilaterals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain open dialogue with partners (e.g., GIZ, World Bank) to ensure alignment with UK priorities; SRO to consider bilateral/multilateral agreements if needed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in partner mobilisation due to complex procurement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use pre-approved HMG framework suppliers to reduce procurement time; leverage existing relationships (e.g., with PYEI, DHET).

vfm_criteria_used: equity (targets for women/girls and disadvantaged groups)

quote.text: Option 6: Work with multiple delivery partners... This option would also allow us to have a flexible approach to implementation (pace, content, and scale of funding), to respond to changes in South Africa (or UK) circumstances... We envisage deploying a combination of accountable grants and a contract (locally sourced or via the International Multidisciplinary Development Framework).

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: South Africa’s **political economy** and **institutional fragmentation** limit partner selection to organisations with: (1) **existing relationships** with the Presidency/DHET (critical for policy influence), (2) **local presence** in priority geographies (e.g., Mpumalanga, Free State for green skills), and (3) **capacity to navigate labour market mismatches**. The legacy of apartheid and spatial inequality also require partners with **township economy expertise** and **gender-inclusive approaches**.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for **Presidential-level access** (only partners with existing DHET/PYEI relationships considered)
Requirement for **local delivery capacity** in coal-dependent regions (Mpumalanga, Free State)
**Labour market volatility** demands partners with real-time sector intelligence
**Gender norms** necessitate partners with safeguarding and women’s economic empowerment expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **three-tiered objective** (system-level policy influence, institutional green skills development, individual-level equity interventions) directly shapes the **mixed delivery structure**: (1) **Contracts** for technical assistance to government (Component 1) ensure policy alignment with UK priorities; (2) **Accountable Grants** for CSOs (Components 2–3) enable flexible, locally led skilling; (3) **Multi-partner approach** mitigates risk of over-reliance on any single actor, given the complexity of South Africa’s skills ecosystem.
q28_linkages: **Policy influence objective** → **Contract modality** (FCDO Framework for Presidency support)
**Green skills pivot** → **CSO/private sector grants** (for agile sector-specific training)
**Gender equity focus** → **Targeted MoUs** (with women-led organisations)
**Just Energy Transition alignment** → **Co-ordination with JETP partners** (e.g., World Bank)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs are discussed: (1) **Higher costs for marginalised groups**: The programme acknowledges that supporting disadvantaged youth (e.g., women, township economies) incurs higher transaction costs but justifies this as necessary for equity. (2) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct skilling for NEET youth is prioritised over slower systemic reforms to address urgent unemployment. (3) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: UK technical assistance (e.g., for PYEI) is balanced with local implementation (e.g., TVET colleges) to combine global best practices with context relevance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: **Cost vs. reach**: "Supporting disadvantaged young people often incurs higher costs" but is deemed essential for equity (e.g., township-focused interventions).

**Policy influence vs. direct delivery**: Technical assistance to government (Component 1) is low-cost but high-risk if political will wanes; direct skilling (Components 2–3) has higher transaction costs but tangible impact.
**Speed vs. sustainability**: Rapid mobilisation via existing partners (e.g., GIZ) is prioritised over building new local capacity, which would take longer.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (political, labour market, and delivery risks) drives **milestone-based oversight** with monthly partner reviews. High-risk areas (e.g., labour market volatility, academic disruptions) trigger **intensive monitoring** (e.g., dashboards for pathway management networks).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles: (1) **TVET colleges** receive lecturer training and curriculum support to sustain green skills; (2) **CSOs** are selected based on their ability to deliver **entrepreneurship training** for women; (3) **Private sector** partners co-develop qualifications to ensure market relevance. The programme avoids standalone capacity-building activities, integrating them into delivery mechanisms.

quote.text: The programme will build assets, skills and resources for marginalised groups, and strengthen visibility, voice and representation... Sector-based expertise and analysis of skills needs will be available through close co-ordination and involvement with development of Sector Skills Masterplans.
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Programme summary and Delivery Mechanism

Change in departmental/political leadership disrupting partnerships
Labour market challenges reducing work placement opportunities
Employability interventions not being market-responsive (especially in new green sectors)
Ecosystem-level partnerships failing to deliver as planned
Academic disruptions (e.g., student protests) affecting course delivery
Safeguarding risks for women/girls in education programmes
Green skills training not aligning with Just Energy Transition job demands
Co-ordination failures between multiple delivery partners

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political will: Drop in SA government commitment
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Sustain political engagement with PYEI, DHET, and provincial administrations; focus on PSET system protection.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delivery risk: Change in leadership impacts partnerships
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Monitor leadership changes; work with GoSA counterparts and partners to ensure continuity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delivery risk: Labour market challenges reduce placements
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use employability mapping tools; embed labour market intelligence; include entrepreneurship training.
Sector-specific advocacy with industry; monthly risk calibration meetings; pilot green re-skilling models.
Framework for regular partner engagements with visible targets/dashboards; due diligence on partner capacity.
Careful selection of education institutions; assess funding pressures, attendance records, and disruption history.
Identify incident management/escalation pathways; mandatory safeguarding risk reporting.
Co-ordinate with JETP International Partners Group; scale M&E systems at municipal level.
Formalise roles/responsibilities via contracts; maintain open dialogue with bilaterals/multilaterals.

fcas_specific_lessons: In **high-inequality contexts** like South Africa, skills programmes must explicitly target **spatial disparities** (e.g., township economies) and **gender segregation** (e.g., women in male-dominated sectors) to avoid reinforcing inequalities.
**Political economy risks** require embedding interventions within **Presidential-level initiatives** (e.g., PYEI) to ensure sustainability across election cycles.
**Labour market mismatches** demand real-time sector intelligence and **adaptive training models** (e.g., pivoting to Electric Vehicles in automotive sector).
**Legacy of apartheid** necessitates **equity-focused delivery** (e.g., prioritising black women, low-income youth) but increases transaction costs.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Skills for Prosperity programme (2020–2023)** demonstrated that: (1) **Industry-education partnerships** (e.g., automotive sector collaborations) improve curriculum relevance and employment outcomes; (2) **Presidential backing** (via PYEI) amplifies impact and policy adoption; (3) **Blended teaching** (virtual + in-person) is more effective than fully virtual training; (4) **Gender-targeted interventions** yield higher returns (e.g., women in male-dominated sectors earn 3x more); (5) **Donor co-ordination** (e.g., Youth Employment Development Partners’ Forum) avoids duplication and strengthens influence.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Based on prior lessons, this programme: (1) **Pivots to green skills** (aligning with Just Energy Transition); (2) **Deepens gender focus** (explicit targets for women/girls); (3) **Uses multiple delivery partners** (mitigating single-point failure risk); (4) **Embeds labour market intelligence** in training design; (5) **Includes entrepreneurship pathways** (addressing formal job shortages).

quote.text: Key findings [from Skills for Prosperity] included: Importance of working directly with industry/sector bodies and education institutions... Value of collaboration and co-ordination with wider donor community... In 2020, the President launched the Presidential Youth Employment Intervention (PYEI) to address chronic youth unemployment... The previous programme provided extensive technical assistance to the PYEI to design new financing and pilot models in marginalised areas... This positioned the UK as a trusted partner.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will actively seek co-funding opportunities as part of intervention design, particularly for green skills and women-focused components. Co-funding also helps demonstrate demand (e.g., via student fees or private company sponsorships).
