quote.text: Programme management costs are targeted at less than 10% of total costs... The programme budget is £5m, RDEL... Component 1: £1.2m (TA to Presidency); Components 2–3: £1.9m each (green skills and women/girls).
quote.source: D0005562.odt, Value for Money and Programme Forecast sections

metadata.programme_name: UK–South Africa Urban Resilience Programme

quote.text: The Urban Resilience Programme will fund technical assistance (TA) for inclusive, sustainable and climate-resilient economic development in South African cities.

duration_source.text: The South Africa Country Plan is a 3-5 year strategy outlining the UK’s priorities to help South Africa recover from COVID...

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening sub-national governments' technical capabilities), policy influence (supporting national policy implementation), and implementation research (testing urban governance and economic development interventions). It focuses on inclusive, sustainable urban economic development with climate resilience as a core component.

q1_source.text: The programme will: support national policy implementation to improve infrastructure and enable economic development; enhance technical capabilities within sub-national governments to guarantee inclusive development locally; and improve institutional efficiency, access to reliable public services and sustainable revenue generation in intermediate cities.

q3_expected_outputs: strategies for urban governance, spatial planning and economic development (building on Future Cities)
improved technical capabilities in sub-national governments
enhanced institutional efficiency and sustainable revenue generation in intermediate cities
data-based solutions for urban governance and management
economic development and infrastructure plans for green recovery and just transition
spatial and economic reconfiguration of township economies
support to National Framework for Local Economic Development (LED) implementation
peer-to-peer learning networks for knowledge dissemination
improved access to reliable public services for marginalised groups
gender-sensitive urban planning (e.g., safe mobility options)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to drive inclusive, climate-resilient urban economic development in South Africa by strengthening sub-national governance, implementing national urban policies, and fostering equitable access to opportunities. It builds on the successes of the Future Cities programme while expanding support to intermediate cities and townships.

quote.text: The programme will build on the learning and achievements of Future Cities, which successfully delivered strategies for urban governance, spatial planning and economic development in Durban/eThekwini, Johannesburg and Cape Town.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The document explicitly states an "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" and highlights challenges like political instability, weak local government capacity, and climate vulnerabilities, but does not classify South Africa as FCAS or high-risk.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak municipal capacity and political instability (e.g., coalition governments in metros) hinder service delivery and policy implementation. Climate risks (floods/droughts) disrupt economic recovery, while spatial inequalities and poor infrastructure limit equitable development. Data gaps and regulatory fragmentation further complicate urban planning and revenue generation.

quote.text: Declining service delivery, corruption and overall poor health of the economy is causing civil discontent with rising number of protests... Many municipalities... continue to be poorly managed and dysfunctional... constant threat from climate change... is preventing most city economies from recovering to pre-pandemic levels.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (DCoG)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes South African ownership (e.g., alignment with National Development Plan and LED Framework) while leveraging UK technical expertise. Decision-making is shared, with DCoG and SALGA leading implementation and the UK providing technical assistance and funding. The hybrid delivery model (Option 3) explicitly includes Southern-led components (e.g., peer-to-peer learning networks).
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to sub-national governments for urban planning and LED
institutional strengthening (e.g., embedding data tools in municipal systems)
training for municipal officials on climate-resilient infrastructure and revenue generation
mentorship through peer-to-peer learning networks (DCoG/SALGA)
community engagement methodologies for inclusive development
gender equity and social inclusion (GESI) planning

partner_organizations.name: Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (DCoG)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementing partner; provides technical assistance to intermediate cities

partner_organizations.name: South African Local Government Association (SALGA)
partner_organizations.role: co-implementer; supports LED and municipal capacity building

partner_organizations.name: National Treasury (Cities Support Programme)
partner_organizations.role: collaborator on municipal finance and economic planning

partner_organizations.name: British High Commission (BHC) South Africa
partner_organizations.role: programme oversight, stakeholder coordination, and strategic alignment with UK-SA Country Plan

partner_organizations.name: Swiss Economic Cooperation Organisation (SECO)
partner_organizations.role: development partner; co-funding for LED initiatives

partner_organizations.name: European Union
partner_organizations.role: development partner; potential co-funder

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: development partner; potential collaborator on municipal finance

partner_organizations.name: Intermediate City Municipalities (ICMs)
partner_organizations.role: direct beneficiaries; recipients of technical assistance for LED and resilience

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: complementary implementers; support community engagement and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: Metropolitan Municipalities (eThekwini, Johannesburg, Cape Town)
partner_organizations.role: secondary beneficiaries; knowledge-sharing hubs

quote.text: The programme will partner with DCoG and SALGA to provide technical assistance on LED to intermediate cities... These outputs and partnerships are also well aligned with the UK in SA country plan by... expanding South Africa’s economic sectors to create opportunities for international investment.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Assessment of interventions and the UK’s comparative advantage

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use a **hybrid model (Option 3)** combining: 1) **Accountable Grants** for civil society-led interventions, 2) **commercial contracts** with private sector suppliers for technical assistance, and 3) **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** with multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, EU). This allows flexibility to fund diverse activities while maintaining oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme will operate through a **diversified portfolio** with multiple delivery routes: 1) direct technical assistance to selected cities, 2) policy-based partnerships with national/provincial governments (e.g., DCoG, National Treasury), and 3) project-based collaborations with metros and intermediate cities. The BHC will manage stakeholder relationships and monitor progress, while DCoG will cascade lessons through intergovernmental forums.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The hybrid model (Option 3) was chosen for its **flexibility, risk diversification, and value for money**. It allows the programme to: 1) adapt to emerging priorities (e.g., climate shocks), 2) leverage both non-profit and private sector expertise, and 3) spread fiduciary risk across suppliers. Open contracting was rejected due to delays, while sole-source options lacked scalability.

quote.text: We judge the hybrid option (Option 3) to be the most suitable delivery model to implement the programme in line with the strategic case. The main challenge of this option is potential resource constraint and risk of losing cohesiveness, which will have to be actively managed to minimise risk to delivery... This modality will also make provision for cost economy as activities can be costed in relation to the risk to delivery.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will be overseen by the **BHC South Africa Portfolio Committee and Country Board**, with implementation reviewed quarterly. A **formal agreement with DCoG** will frame technical assistance to intermediate cities, and **bilateral MoUs with national departments** (e.g., National Treasury) will ensure policy alignment. The hybrid delivery model requires BHC to manage multiple supplier relationships and stakeholder engagements.

quote.text: Reviewed by BHC South Africa Portfolio Committee and Country Board... The BHC programme team will review progress against these plans quarterly and identify adjustments as necessary.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Summary Sheet and Gender Equality section

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be shifted between suppliers or interventions **with BHC approval**, particularly to address fiduciary risks or poor outcomes. The hybrid model allows budget adjustments to prioritize emerging needs (e.g., climate adaptation) but requires active management to avoid cohesiveness loss.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adapt to **shifting UK/SA priorities, beneficiary demands, or crises** (e.g., health emergencies, weather extremes) by reallocating resources or reprioritizing interventions. However, changes require BHC endorsement and may involve exit costs for underperforming suppliers.

quote.text: Flexibility for BHC to fund civil society organisation-led proposals where aligned with programme strategic case. Agility for BHC to shift budget to different suppliers with due consideration to exit costs... in case of fiduciary risk or poor outcomes experienced with another supplier.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → BHC South Africa (management) → Implementing Partners (DCoG/SALGA/CSOs/private suppliers) → End beneficiaries (municipalities/communities). The hybrid model reduces layers by avoiding multilateral intermediaries.

quote.text: The hybrid deliverymodality (Option 3) will provide cost efficiency through adaptive delivery mechanisms and a mix of service providers (non-profit and private sector expertise)... This modality will also make provision for cost economy as activities can be costed in relation to the risk to delivery.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Table 3: Delivery Options and Value for Money section

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Approach 1: Direct Technical Assistance to 2-3 cities
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Bilateral partnerships with individual municipalities (e.g., metros). Risk: poor vertical coordination and limited scalability.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Approach 2: Diversified partnerships (policy + project-based)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Combination of national/provincial policy partnerships and metro-level projects. Risk: high coordination burden on BHC.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Approach 3: Do nothing
q24_alternatives_considered.description: No further UK support; rely on policy diplomacy. Risk: dilution of past achievements and reputational damage.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Option 1: Accountable Grants only
q24_alternatives_considered.description: High flexibility but risk of coherence loss and fiduciary gaps.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Option 2: HMG framework supplier/open contracting
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Limited flexibility and potential overhead costs; poor VfM for diverse needs.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Option 3: Hybrid model (mix of grants, contracts, MoUs)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Highest flexibility and VfM; allows adaptive responses to risks and priorities.

q24_alternatives_considered.name: Option 4: MoU with multilateral
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Low flexibility and limited oversight of impact.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **hybrid delivery model (Option 3)** was selected for its **balance of flexibility, risk management, and value for money**. It allows the programme to: 1) **adapt to emerging priorities** (e.g., climate shocks, political economy shifts), 2) **leverage diverse expertise** (non-profits, private sector, multilaterals), 3) **spread fiduciary risk** across suppliers, and 4) **scale impact** through peer-to-peer learning. The model also aligns with the UK’s strategic goals of building resilient economies and green recovery while mitigating risks of poor coordination (a flaw in Approach 1).
q25_decision_factors: lessons from Future Cities (need for vertical coordination)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Resource constraints and loss of cohesiveness
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active management by BHC to minimise delivery risks; limited number of Accountable Grants within management capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor intergovernmental coordination (national vs. local)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Formal agreement with DCoG to cascade lessons and embed reforms across municipalities; use of DCoG’s convening power.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks with non-profits lacking HMG experience
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence before funding; diversified portfolio to spread risk.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Information asymmetry between cities and national government
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Cross-government ownership mechanisms; regular monitoring by BHC.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (balanced ODA spend across metros and intermediate cities)

quote.text: We therefore judge that the most cost effective, risk adjusted and impactful option is to build a diversified portfolio of projects and policy partnerships with South African stakeholders (Approach 2)... The assessment of these options also underscores the importance for programme impact of: differentiated design and delivery approach to beneficiary needs; formalised mechanisms for documenting and disseminating knowledge and learning; [and] cross-government ownership and capability within partner government to sustain technical outputs.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Assessment of Technical Assistance Approaches

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **political economy and institutional weaknesses** in South Africa limit partner selection to entities with **strong government endorsement** (e.g., DCoG, SALGA) and **proven capacity** to navigate municipal dysfunction. Intermediate cities’ low technical capabilities require partners with **adaptive delivery models** (e.g., hybrid grants/contracts) and **vertical coordination mechanisms** (e.g., DCoG’s regional approach). Climate and social volatility further restrict options to those with **disaster response expertise** and **community trust**.
q27_constraints_detail: weak municipal capacity → need for partners with institutional strengthening expertise (e.g., DCoG)
political instability (coalition governments) → requires partners with government relations (e.g., SALGA)
climate risks → necessitates partners with adaptation/mitigation experience (e.g., UKPACT, CLIC)
data limitations → prioritizes partners with data-driven decision tools (e.g., Future Cities legacy)
regulatory fragmentation → favors partners aligned with national frameworks (e.g., LED, IUDF)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for inclusive economic development and climate resilience** drives the **hybrid, multi-layered delivery structure**: 1) **Policy influence objectives** → require partnerships with national/provincial governments (e.g., DCoG, National Treasury). 2) **Capacity building for intermediate cities** → necessitates technical assistance via accountable grants and embedded tools. 3) **Scaling lessons from metros** → demands peer-to-peer networks and knowledge-sharing platforms (e.g., SALGA). 4) **Adaptive management** → shaped by the programme’s focus on **responding to shocks** (climate, economic).
q28_linkages: inclusive LED goals → hybrid model to reach both metros and intermediate cities
climate resilience priorities → partnerships with adaptation experts (e.g., UKPACT)
gender equity (GESI) → embedded capacity building in all interventions
township economy focus → direct TA to sub-national governments for spatial reconfiguration
national policy alignment (NDP, IUDF) → MoUs with DCoG/Treasury for vertical coordination
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (e.g., targeting marginalised groups in townships/intermediate cities) with **efficiency** (e.g., leveraging existing metro relationships for scalability). Trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct TA to fewer cities (Approach 1) would be faster but less equitable; the hybrid model prioritizes broader reach. 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: UK technical leadership risks overshadowing local agency, mitigated by DCoG/SALGA co-implementation. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Supporting intermediate cities (higher poverty) reduces economies of scale but aligns with SDG10 (reduced inequalities).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: metros (efficient) vs. intermediate cities (equitable) → hybrid model balances both
UK expertise (efficient) vs. local ownership (equitable) → joint decision-making with DCoG
direct TA (targeted) vs. peer learning (scalable) → combines both for cohesion
rapid delivery (fewer partners) vs. inclusive partnerships (diverse stakeholders) → managed via BHC oversight
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (political instability, climate shocks) necessitates **quarterly oversight** and **adaptive management**. High-risk areas (e.g., intermediate cities with weak capacity) receive **embedded support** (e.g., DCoG-led TA), while stable metros (e.g., Cape Town) allow for **lighter-touch partnerships** (e.g., knowledge-sharing).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) **DCoG/SALGA** lead institutional strengthening (e.g., LED frameworks, data tools). 2) **Metros** serve as hubs for peer learning, cascading capacity to intermediate cities. 3) **CSOs** complement government efforts in community engagement. 4) **Private suppliers** provide niche technical expertise (e.g., climate adaptation) where government capacity is lacking.

quote.text: The programme will partner with DCoG and SALGA to provide technical assistance on LED to intermediate cities... Supporting inclusive urban development will also strengthen the role of South African cities in achieving gender equality... The programme’s methodology will emphasise the critical importance of sustainable finance and effective participatory planning with whole-of-society approach.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Assessment of interventions and Table 1: Key National Urban Policies

key_programme_risks: Poor intergovernmental coordination (national vs. local)
Limited municipal capacity to absorb technical assistance
Political instability (coalition governments in metros)
Climate shocks disrupting implementation (floods/droughts)
Fiduciary risks with non-profit partners
Reputational risk if past achievements (Future Cities) are not sustained
Economic volatility reducing public/private investment
Social unrest due to service delivery protests
Data gaps hindering evidence-based planning
Overlap/duplication with other donor programmes (e.g., EU, World Bank)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Formal agreement with DCoG to cascade lessons; cross-government ownership mechanisms.
Differentiated TA approaches; embedded data tools for sustainability.
BHC stakeholder management; alignment with District Development Model.
Flexible budget reallocation; focus on climate-resilient infrastructure.
Due diligence for non-profits; diversified supplier portfolio.
Continuity with Future Cities legacy; quarterly progress reviews.
Support for economic diversification (e.g., JETP alignment).
Community engagement methodologies; inclusive service delivery.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from **Future Cities**: Institutionalising technical outputs (e.g., data tools in Cape Town) ensures sustainability.
**Climate adaptation**: Post-KwaZulu-Natal floods, programmes must integrate ecological infrastructure and disaster response.
**Political economy**: Coalition governments in metros (e.g., Johannesburg) require conflict-sensitive engagement.
**Township economies**: Spatial integration and value chain access are critical for reducing inequality (per UNU-WIDER/WIEGO).
**Local ownership**: NFLED implementation fails without vertical alignment (national → provincial → local).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **Future Cities programme** demonstrated that: 1) **Embedding data tools** in municipal systems (e.g., Cape Town) maximizes sustainability. 2) **Community engagement** (e.g., Soweto-Johannesburg relations) improves public trust. 3) **Institutionalisation of outputs** (e.g., organisational strategies for data-driven decision-making) is critical for long-term impact. 4) **Cross-departmental coordination** on infrastructure projects enhances governance. However, **scaling beyond metros** requires formal knowledge-sharing mechanisms (a gap in Future Cities).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Expanded geographic focus**: Shift from only metros (Future Cities) to include **intermediate cities** and townships. 2) **Hybrid delivery model**: Adopted to address **scalability limitations** of direct TA (Approach 1). 3) **Climate integration**: Explicit focus on **adaptation/mitigation** (e.g., JETP alignment) based on recent flood/drought impacts. 4) **GESI mainstreaming**: Added **gender-sensitive urban planning** (e.g., safe mobility) as a core component. 5) **Peer learning networks**: Introduced to **disseminate metro lessons** to intermediate cities (addressing Future Cities’ scalability gap).

quote.text: Future Cities delivered technical outputs and capacity building support... However, the absence of a formal agreement for knowledge sharing and capacity building with provincial and national governments may result in poor vertical coordination... The programme could achieve better value for money by expanding technical support to other cities and provinces... We judge the hybrid option (Option 3) to be the most suitable delivery model to implement the programme in line with the strategic case.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Box 1: Future Cities and Table 3: Delivery Options

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **unlock public and private investment** in urban infrastructure by creating a conducive environment for LED. Potential leverage includes: 1) **National Treasury’s Cities Support Programme** (co-funding for municipal finance). 2) **JETP alignment** (mobilizing climate finance for just transition). 3) **Peer-to-peer networks** (scaling impact without additional ODA).

quote.text: Programme Value: up to £8m... The programme will build on existing relationships with Durban and Cape Town in data and technology, infrastructure and climate adaptation, thereby leveraging institutional memory. This will ensure cost effectiveness and efficiency given prior experience with municipal structures and leadership.
quote.source: D0003225.odt, Summary Sheet and Value for Money section

metadata.programme_name: UK-South Africa Health System Strengthening Partnership
metadata.quote: "This programme will support the delivery of the UK-South Africa Strategic Health Partnership." (D0004318.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The programme will start in August 2023 and run until August 2027." (D0004318.odt, Mobilisation)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening health systems, technical assistance), policy influence (supporting Universal Health Coverage reforms), and service delivery improvements (primary healthcare, access to medicines). It also includes elements of implementation research (pandemic preparedness systems) and financing mechanisms (technical assistance contracts).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support South Africa’s goal to achieve Universal Health Coverage, thereby helping to address gender and other inequalities. Programme activities will complement the broader UK–South Africa partnership and collaboration on health priorities internationally." (D0004318.odt, Summary Sheet)
q3_expected_outputs: Improved oversight and governance with focus on hospital management and quality of care (Health Ombuds/Parliamentary Health Committee twinning)
Strengthened access to medicines and medical products (establishment of South Africa’s first Health Technology Assessment unit)
Enhanced primary healthcare capacity (training and building skills of general practitioners)
Improved Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights (increased access to safe abortion for young people and women in rural areas)
Increased regulatory capacity (SAPHRA achieving WHO maturity Level 4)
Established national integrated monitoring systems for disease surveillance
Technical assistance to national and provincial departments of health, hospitals, and primary healthcare facilities
Institutional partnerships between UK and South African health institutions for knowledge exchange
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen South Africa’s health systems to achieve Universal Health Coverage by 2030, while enhancing pandemic preparedness and addressing gender inequalities in health access. It focuses on governance, primary healthcare, regulatory systems, and sexual/reproductive health rights through technical assistance and institutional partnerships.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will provide £5m to strengthen South Africa’s health systems, support it to achieve Universal Health Coverage, and drive collaboration on pandemic preparedness." (D0004318.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as "moderate" risk, reflecting operational challenges in South Africa’s health system (e.g., weak governance, corruption, medico-legal suits) but without active conflict or extreme fragility.
where_context.q5_source: "Programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004318.odt, Summary Sheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak hospital governance, lack of accountability, and poor disciplinary procedures impair service delivery. The two-tier health system (overburdened public vs. well-resourced private) creates inequities. Medico-legal suits drain health budgets, and climate change increases health threats. Data systems need strengthening for effective disease surveillance.
where_context.quote: "The public health care system faces major challenges across primary, secondary and tertiary levels... including variable leadership and management skills; lack of accountability; poor disciplinary procedures and corruption; poor staff attitudes and absenteeism." (D0004318.odt, Why is the intervention needed?)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is jointly designed and overseen by UK and South African institutions, with decision-making shared through steering committees and institutional partnerships. UK institutions provide technical expertise, while South African partners lead implementation and adaptation to local context.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and skill-building for general practitioners (primary healthcare capacity)
mentorship and knowledge exchange through institutional partnerships (e.g., NHS Consortium, UK NICE, MHRA)
technical assistance to South African health departments and hospitals
regulatory capacity building (e.g., supporting SAPHRA to achieve WHO Maturity Level 4)
establishment of new units (e.g., Health Technology Assessment unit)

partner_organizations.name: British High Commission (BHC) South Africa
partner_organizations.role: Programme management, oversight, and coordination

partner_organizations.name: National Department of Health (NDoH), South Africa
partner_organizations.role: Primary government counterpart, strategic direction

partner_organizations.name: Provincial Governments (South Africa)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation at provincial level

partner_organizations.name: NHS Consortium (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance, knowledge exchange, and capacity building

partner_organizations.name: UK Health Ombuds
partner_organizations.role: Twinning with South African Health Ombuds for governance and quality oversight

partner_organizations.name: UK NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence)
partner_organizations.role: Health Technology Assessment support

partner_organizations.name: MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, UK)
partner_organizations.role: Regulatory capacity building (e.g., supporting SAPHRA)

partner_organizations.name: UK Health Security Agency
partner_organizations.role: Disease surveillance and pandemic preparedness

partner_organizations.name: Royal College of GPs (UK)
partner_organizations.role: Health professional development (primary healthcare training)

partner_organizations.name: South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAPHRA)
partner_organizations.role: Regulatory capacity building (target: WHO Maturity Level 4)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organisations (SRHR focus)
partner_organizations.role: Service delivery and advocacy for sexual/reproductive health and rights

partner_organizations.name: Private sector consultants (local and international)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance and short-term expertise

who_partners.quote: "The programme will draw extensively on the NHS Consortium... Key UK institutions involved include Health Ombuds (healthcare quality); UK NICE (health technology assessment); MHRA (regulatory environment); UK Health Security Agency (disease surveillance); and the Royal College of GPs (health professional development)." (D0004318.odt, What outcomes will the programme achieve?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with UK health institutions and international organizations, commercial contracts with private sector technical assistance providers, short-term contracts with local consultants, and Accountable Grants (AGs) with civil society organizations. This mix allows for flexibility in engaging different types of expertise and partners.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by the British High Commission (BHC) South Africa, which coordinates multiple implementing partners (UK institutions, local consultants, CSOs) through separate agreements (MoUs, contracts, grants). A steering committee with South African government stakeholders provides strategic oversight, while the BHC Programme Team handles day-to-day administration and partner coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The programme uses a mix of direct partnerships (MoUs with UK institutions like NHS Consortium) and competitive processes for commercial contracts and grants. Direct partnerships leverage existing relationships and expertise (e.g., NHS’s experience with South Africa’s health system), while competitive processes ensure value for money for technical assistance and local consultancies.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will use a mix of delivery mechanisms including: Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with UK Health institutions... commercial contracts with an international private sector technical assistance provider... Accountable Grants (AGs) with a civil society organisation." (D0004318.odt, Commercial Approach and Requirement)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A steering committee/working group with key stakeholders from the National Department of Health (NDoH) will be established during the inception phase. This committee will oversee progress, provide strategic direction, and meet at least six-monthly. It operates within the broader UK-South Africa Health Partnership governance structure.
how_governance.quote: "The Programme Team will meet implementing partners either monthly or quarterly to review progress, financials and manage operational matters... The Programme Team will review programme performance annually against the logical framework." (D0004318.odt, Governance Arrangements and Performance)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, as the programme uses a mix of delivery partners and adaptive management. The BHC Programme Team will review progress quarterly and adjust budgets/forecasts as needed, with break clauses in agreements to accommodate changes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes regular review points to assess feasibility and risks, with flexibility built into agreements to adapt to policy shifts or evolving priorities. The inception phase allows for finalizing the logical framework and performance indicators based on initial assessments.
how_flexibility.quote: "Ensure that the programme activities have the buy-in of senior officials as well ministers. Build in flexibility to allow for adaptation in response to future policy shifts." (D0004318.odt, External Risks) && "The Programme Team will review progress, agree any adjustments or mitigations, through structured programme management meetings at least quarterly." (D0004318.odt, Performance)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (UK institutions/CSOs/consultants) → End beneficiaries (South African health facilities, patients). The BHC Programme Team manages partners directly without additional intermediary layers.
how_efficiency.quote: "The Programme Team will ensure that funds are disbursed in accordance with the signed agreements and contracts and in line with agreed milestones and performance indicators." (D0004318.odt, Monitoring, Reporting and Accounting for Funds)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Single UK health institution (e.g., NHS)
Option 2: Single technical assistance provider (private sector or international organisation)
Option 3: Single Civil Society Organisation (CSO)
Option 4: Multiple delivery partners (preferred)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 (multiple delivery partners) was chosen for its ability to: 1) access a broad range of expertise for each programme component; 2) build and deepen relationships across all UK-South Africa health partnership priorities; 3) respond flexibly to evolving needs; and 4) achieve better value for money by spreading costs and risks across mechanisms. This approach leverages existing partnerships (e.g., NHS-South Africa) while allowing for competitive selection of technical providers.
q25_decision_factors: flexibility to adapt to evolving priorities

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of coordination between implementing partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Include requirements in terms of reference/agreements for partners to coordinate, with KPIs tied to collaboration. Arrange regular meetings with all partners.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Too many programme components/delivery partners make programme difficult to manage
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Source partners with strong programme management capacity. Use review points to assess component benefits and streamline delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of funds flow from partner to end use (fiduciary risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Maintain thorough financial/contract management practices, including due diligence assessments (DDA) and regular supplier reporting on disbursements.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 4... enables access to range of relevant expertise and experience for each specific deliverable of the programme... allows for different delivery mechanisms to strengthen the UK-SA Health Partnership across all priority areas... cost, procurement, efficiency and risks to be adequately spread across the various delivery options." (D0004318.odt, Figure 2: Summary appraisal of delivery options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The weak institutional capacity and governance challenges in South Africa’s public health system (e.g., corruption, lack of accountability, medico-legal risks) necessitate partnerships with UK institutions (e.g., NHS, MHRA) to provide technical expertise and oversight. The two-tier health system (public vs. private) also requires tailored partnerships to address inequities, such as focusing on primary healthcare in underserved areas.
q27_constraints_detail: Weak public sector governance requires external technical assistance for hospital management and regulatory systems.
High medico-legal risks limit local capacity to manage health service delivery without support.
Unequal distribution of health workers (urban vs. rural) necessitates targeted partnerships for primary healthcare training.
Regulatory capacity gaps (e.g., SAPHRA’s need to reach WHO Maturity Level 4) require UK expertise (e.g., MHRA).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (health system strengthening, UHC, pandemic preparedness, SRHR) require a diverse delivery structure: institutional partnerships for knowledge exchange (e.g., NHS-South Africa twinning), technical assistance contracts for specialized tasks (e.g., regulatory capacity), and grants for civil society engagement (e.g., SRHR services). The need for both rapid mobilization (e.g., disease surveillance) and long-term capacity building (e.g., primary healthcare training) shapes the use of multiple, flexible mechanisms.
q28_linkages: Health system strengthening goals → Institutional partnerships (e.g., NHS Consortium) for sustained knowledge exchange.
Pandemic preparedness needs → Technical assistance contracts with regulatory and surveillance experts (e.g., UKHSA, MHRA).
SRHR and equity objectives → Accountable Grants to civil society for service delivery in rural areas.
Flexibility requirements → Mixed delivery options to adapt to policy shifts (e.g., NHI implementation).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., targeting rural women for SRHR services, addressing public-private health disparities) with efficiency (e.g., leveraging UK expertise to avoid reinventing systems). For example, while direct service delivery (e.g., safe abortion access) is resource-intensive, it is prioritized to reduce maternal mortality inequalities. The use of UK institutions (e.g., NHS) provides cost-effective technical assistance but requires mitigation to ensure local ownership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid mobilization through existing UK-SA partnerships (e.g., NHS) accelerates delivery but requires effort to ensure South African leadership.
Expertise vs. ownership: UK regulatory expertise (e.g., MHRA) strengthens systems quickly but risks limiting local capacity development if not paired with mentorship.
Cost vs. reach: Targeting rural and underserved populations (e.g., SRHR) increases per-beneficiary costs but aligns with equity goals.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., governance weaknesses, political shifts) drives intensive oversight mechanisms, such as quarterly partner reviews, milestone-based payments, and a steering committee with South African government stakeholders. Fiduciary risks (e.g., fund mismanagement) are mitigated through strict financial controls and due diligence assessments.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: UK institutions (e.g., NHS, NICE) provide technical mentorship, while South African partners (e.g., NDoH, SAPHRA) lead implementation and institutionalize reforms. For example, the Health Technology Assessment unit will be South African-led but developed with UK NICE’s support, ensuring skills transfer.
intersections.quote: "The programme will provide technical assistance and knowledge exchange between UK and South African health institutions... to improve oversight and governance with a focus on hospital management and quality of care; strengthen access to medicines... enhance primary healthcare capacity; [and] build an enabling environment for Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights." (D0004318.odt, Programme summary) && "Option 4 allows for different delivery mechanisms to strengthen the UK-SA Health Partnership across all priority areas... spreading cost, procurement, efficiency and risks." (D0004318.odt, Figure 2)

key_programme_risks: NHI contestation impacts programme delivery (political risk)
Change in political leadership disrupts continuity
Changes in ODA allocation reduce funding
Lack of coordination between implementing partners
Too many programme components make management difficult
Fiduciary risk: misdirection of funds from partners to end use
Safeguarding: recipients of programme harmed (SEAH risks)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on health system strengthening using international best practice. Use review points to assess intervention feasibility.
Ensure buy-in from senior officials and ministers. Build flexibility to adapt to policy shifts.
Deploy adaptive delivery model to manage risks from ODA/budget cuts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of coordination between implementing partners
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Include coordination requirements in terms of reference/KPIs. Hold regular partner meetings.
Select partners with strong programme management capacity. Use reviews to streamline components.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fiduciary risk: funds flow from partner to end use
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain thorough financial/contract management. Require delivery chain transparency and regular audits.
Enforce FCDO-aligned SEAH policies across delivery chains. Require supplier training/awareness workshops and direct reporting to FCDO.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous UK collaboration (e.g., Better Health Programme) demonstrated that small investments in policy development (e.g., Non-Communicable Diseases strategy) and systems (e.g., Electronic Vaccination Data System) can yield significant, sustainable impacts. The importance of aligning with national priorities (e.g., NHI) and leveraging UK-SA institutional partnerships was reaffirmed.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme builds on the Better Health Programme’s success by expanding institutional partnerships (e.g., NHS Consortium) and focusing on areas with proven impact (e.g., health technology assessment, primary care training). The mixed delivery model addresses past challenges with flexibility and coordination.
risks_lessons.quote: "Previous UK collaboration with South Africa demonstrated that a small investment can achieve a significant outcome in support of South Africa’s health policy reforms. For example, the UK helped South Africa to develop and embed its National Policy on Non-Communicable Diseases; and to establish the Electronic Vaccination Data System." (D0004318.odt, Evidence Base) && "The programme will draw extensively on the NHS Consortium... to ensure mutual learning and systems strengthening sustained beyond the programme lifetime." (D0004318.odt, What outcomes will the programme achieve?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will seek opportunities to promote private sector investment in South Africa’s health system (e.g., infrastructure, manufacturing capacity), though no specific leverage targets are stated.
financial_details.quote: "The programme’s budget is £5 million over 4 years from the UK bilateral ODA budget for South Africa." (D0004318.odt, Budget) && "Forecast spend is anticipated as follows: Year 1 (2023/24): £800k; Year 2: £1.5m; Year 3: £1.5m; Year 4: £1.2m." (D0004318.odt, Budget table)

metadata.programme_name: Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning for Yemen (MERLY)
metadata.quote: The proposed Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning for Yemen (MERLY) programme will support the Yemen Office Network (YON) to deliver, monitor, and evaluate results against the Country Business Plan. (D0006551.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The MERLY programme is proposed for a value of up to £15 million, delivered over up to five years. (D0006551.odt, Affordability section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: MERLY is designed to provide independent oversight, assurance, and evidence generation to improve the effectiveness of UK support in Yemen. It combines monitoring, evaluation, research, and learning (MERL) to inform strategic decisions, enhance accountability, and drive value for money across both humanitarian and development activities.
what_objectives.q1_source: The MERLY programme will operate cohesively across the YON Campaign Goals. It will enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of UK support by supporting connectivity across the portfolio and diplomatic activities. (D0006551.odt, Programme Fit)
q3_expected_outputs: Third-party monitoring (TPM) and verification via remote and in-person methods (e.g., satellite data, call centres, field visits)
Assessments of partner capability and compliance (e.g., M&E systems, safeguarding, fraud, accountability)
Quality research and analysis (e.g., thematic reports, context monitoring, scenario development)
Holistic monitoring of non-programmatic activities (e.g., stakeholder mapping, policy briefs)
Programme support (e.g., Due Diligence Assessments, Annual Reviews, logframes)
Cross-office support (e.g., impact evaluations, risk assessments, information management)
Learning products and events for YON and partners
what_objectives.summary: MERLY aims to strengthen the evidence base for UK interventions in Yemen, ensuring programmes are impactful, aligned with strategic goals, and offer value for money through adaptive, whole-of-office MERL support.
what_objectives.quote: MERLY will be designed and contracted to be adaptive, so that activities can be reprioritised should the context or portfolio needs change. (D0006551.odt, Programme Fit)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Yemen is a fragile country with fractured governance, ranked 174/180 on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, and has been in conflict since 2015. The UK has no permanent in-country presence due to security risks.
where_context.q5_source: Yemen is a fragile country with fractured governance structures. It is rated as highly corrupt and ranked 174 of 180 countries in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index. (D0006551.odt, Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The conflict and security risks limit FCDO’s ability to monitor activities in person, requiring reliance on trusted suppliers for third-party monitoring. Authorities impose restrictive permissions for field access, delaying data collection and verification.
where_context.quote: Due to the security risks, FCDO has not been based in Yemen since 2015. The context is fluid and fragmented. It is extremely challenging to deliver and verify results. (D0006551.odt, MERL for Yemen)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The lead Supplier (likely UK-based) will manage the consortium, including local Yemeni partners, with FCDO retaining oversight through the SRO/PRO and Steering Committee. Decision-making rests with the Supplier and FCDO, with local partners in delivery roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: Assessing partner M&E systems and safeguarding approaches
Providing recommendations for improving feedback mechanisms
Building relationships with Yemeni partners to reduce FCDO intervention needs
Potential MERL capacity-building for partner government departments (limited scope)

partner_organizations.name: Lead Supplier (TBD via procurement)
partner_organizations.role: Consortium manager; responsible for delivering MERL services, subcontracting local partners, and ensuring quality

partner_organizations.name: Local Yemeni partners (TBD)
partner_organizations.role: Support field monitoring, data collection, and context analysis; part of Supplier’s downstream consortium

partner_organizations.name: Yemen Office Network (YON)
partner_organizations.role: Client and beneficiary; provides strategic direction via Steering Committee and SRO/PRO

who_partners.quote: It is anticipated that MERLY will be awarded to a lead Supplier, responsible for securing and managing a supporting downstream consortium capable of delivering against YON’s MERL needs. (D0006551.odt, Single Agreement)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: MERLY will be procured via a commercial contract (likely through the Global Evaluation and Monitoring Framework Agreement, GEMFA Lot 3). This allows FCDO to retain control over deliverables, performance metrics, and adaptive management while leveraging pre-qualified suppliers.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A lead Supplier manages a fixed consortium of subcontractors (including local Yemeni partners) to deliver MERL services. The Supplier reports to FCDO’s SRO/PRO and Steering Committee, with no open competition for sub-awards during implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Using GEMFA Lot 3 (a pre-qualified framework) mitigates procurement delays and risks, as suppliers have already undergone compliance checks. Open competition via a commercial tender is an alternative if framework options are unsuitable.
how_mechanism.quote: MERLY could be procured via the Global Evaluation and Monitoring Framework Agreement (GEMFA) Lot 3 – Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning High Value Lot. (D0006551.odt, Procurement Pathways)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Steering Committee includes representatives from all YON Sections (Humanitarian, Economy, Political, CSSF, Defence) and the Supplier. It meets quarterly to set direction, balance priorities, and review deliverables. The SRO/PRO chairs and escalates to senior Programme Heads as needed.
how_governance.quote: The Steering Committee will contain representation from each of YON’s Sections. It will set direction, facilitate collaboration and coherence, and balance priorities from across YON. (D0006551.odt, Governance and Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reprioritized between activities if context or portfolio needs change, subject to Steering Committee approval and contract amendments. The programme is designed to be adaptive but requires formal review for major shifts.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: MERLY’s workplan and activities can be adjusted via the Steering Committee, which assesses evolving needs (e.g., new conflict dynamics, humanitarian priorities). The Supplier must demonstrate flexibility in responding to YON’s strategic shifts.
how_flexibility.quote: MERLY will be designed and contracted to be adaptive, so that activities can be reprioritised should the context or portfolio needs change. (D0006551.odt, Programme Fit)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Supplier (consortium manager) → Local Yemeni subcontractors/partners
how_efficiency.quote: The MERLY Supplier costs will be paid in arrears, following review and approval by the YON SRO/PRO. [...] The Supplier will be required to provide an invoice with a financial report detailing the breakdown of regular and deliverables costs. (D0006551.odt, Payment, Monitoring, Reporting and Risk)

q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Non-compliant with FCDO Programme Operating Framework (PrOF) Rule #20, which mandates monitoring for all programmes.
Would require duplicate MERL components across programmes, increasing management burden, reducing economies of scale, and fragmenting messaging.
Still fragmented; insufficient capacity in YON to manage multiple MERL facilities, with risks of duplication and lack of cross-office coherence.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The cross-office MERL model was selected for its ability to: (1) achieve economies of scale by consolidating services under one contract; (2) enhance coherence across YON’s diplomatic and development activities; (3) reduce management burden on YON staff; (4) provide a portfolio-wide perspective to identify risks/opportunities; and (5) improve value for money by avoiding duplicated costs (e.g., multiple TPM providers).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (economies of scale, reduced duplication)
past experience (lessons from IMEDA, Nepal PMEL, Somalia MESH)
partner capacity (lead Supplier manages local partners, reducing FCDO workload)
flexibility (adaptive design to respond to context changes)
equity (single procurement enables diverse partnerships, including Yemeni organizations)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier underperformance could have office-wide impact due to centralized delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Competitive procurement process, robust KPIs, and strong SRO/PRO oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of engagement from YON teams could delay activities or limit learning integration.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Supplier integration (e.g., co-location, regular Steering Committee meetings) and visible senior-level support.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Yemeni authorities’ restrictive permissions could delay data collection.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible workplan and leveraging Supplier’s local partnerships to navigate access constraints.

why_rationale.quote: A cross-office MERL programme for YON will facilitate coherence and alignment. [...] Procuring a single MERL programme offers better value for money and will facilitate the achievement of economies-of-scale benefits. (D0006551.odt, Multi-Criteria Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Yemen limits partner selection to organizations with: (1) proven ability to operate in high-risk environments; (2) existing local networks to navigate access restrictions; (3) capacity for remote monitoring (e.g., satellite data, call centres). FCDO’s lack of in-country presence requires reliance on trusted suppliers with Yemeni partnerships.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks prevent FCDO from direct in-country management, necessitating local partners for fieldwork.
Authorities’ restrictive permissions require suppliers with established relationships to obtain field access.
Data poverty and fragmented governance demand partners with contextual expertise and innovative methods (e.g., satellite analysis).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **whole-of-office MERL** (covering diplomatic, humanitarian, and development activities) drives the **consortium structure**, as no single organization could deliver all required services (e.g., TPM, policy analysis, climate risk assessment). The **adaptive design** reflects the **fluid context**, requiring a flexible Supplier able to reprioritize activities.
q28_linkages: Portfolio-wide objectives (e.g., peacebuilding, humanitarian response) → Require a **centralized MERL hub** to avoid silos and ensure coherence.
Need for real-time data (e.g., famine early warnings, conflict monitoring) → Demands **local partnerships** and **technological innovation** (e.g., satellite data).
Risk of fragmented messaging → Necessitates a **single Supplier** to consolidate external communications.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses balancing: (1) **Efficiency** (consolidating MERL under one Supplier to reduce costs) vs. **Equity** (ensuring Yemeni organizations can participate despite exclusivity risks). Mitigations include mandating local partnerships in the SoR and avoiding exclusivity clauses.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Economies of scale (single Supplier) vs. risk of excluding smaller Yemeni organizations → Mitigated by requiring diverse subcontractors.
Northern expertise (lead Supplier) vs. local ownership → Addressed by embedding Yemeni partners in delivery and decision-making.
Speed (pre-qualified framework) vs. inclusivity (open competition) → Balanced by using GEMFA (pre-vetted but diverse suppliers).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk FCAS context** increases oversight intensity: quarterly Steering Committee reviews, embedded Supplier integration (e.g., co-location), and adaptive management clauses to respond to access shocks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded to **reduce FCDO’s management burden** (e.g., training partners on M&E systems) and **strengthen local ownership** (e.g., Yemeni partners lead field data collection).
intersections.quote: The cross-office MERL programme will assess, collate and disseminate learning, reducing the burden upon FCDO Yemen while improving the office’s knowledge, skills and capability. (D0006551.odt, Multi-Criteria Analysis)

key_programme_risks: Supplier underperformance due to complex, multi-year delivery demands.
Lack of engagement from YON teams limiting learning integration.
Yemeni authorities’ restrictions delaying data collection/verification.
Context deterioration (e.g., conflict escalation) disrupting field access.
Fragmented stakeholder coordination weakening UK influence.
Variation in MERL standards across programmes if not centrally managed.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Competitive procurement with pre-qualified suppliers (e.g., GEMFA), robust KPIs, and break clauses for non-delivery.
Steering Committee with Section representatives, co-location of Supplier team, and visible senior-level support.
Flexible workplan, local partnerships, and leveraging Supplier’s existing permissions.
Adaptive design with reprioritization clauses and scenario planning.
Centralized assurance function and independent oversight to maintain credibility.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, **local partnerships are critical** for access and ground-truthing (lesson from IMEDA’s satellite analysis and community engagement).
**Flexible contracts** are essential to adapt to fluid conflicts (e.g., IMEDA’s fuel analysis informed diplomatic shifts).
**Consolidated MERL** reduces donor fragmentation, a common issue in Yemen’s humanitarian response.
Technology (e.g., satellite data, call centres) can mitigate **data poverty** but requires local validation.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from IMEDA (predecessor programme) include: (1) MERL services must be **procured multi-year** to embed learning; (2) **Visible senior support** is needed to drive integration; (3) **Information management** must be innovative to ensure uptake; (4) **Supplier co-location** improves collaboration (e.g., Nepal PMEL).
design_changes_based_on_learning: MERLY includes a **3-month handover/inception phase** (vs. IMEDA’s direct start) to ensure smooth transition.
Explicit **climate mainstreaming** requirement added (unlike IMEDA) to align with FCDO’s Strategic Framework.
**Supplier integration** (e.g., co-location, Steering Committee role) strengthened based on IMEDA’s engagement challenges.
**Gender and inclusion** made a ‘significant’ objective (vs. ad-hoc in IMEDA) per the 2014 Gender Equality Act.
risks_lessons.quote: Driving improvements in MERL across the portfolio [...] takes time to embed. MERL services should be procured and planned across multiple years. (D0006551.odt, Key lessons from existing programmes)

financial_details.quote: The MERLY programme is proposed for a value of up to £15 million, delivered over up to five years. (D0006551.odt, Affordability)

metadata.programme_name: UKPACT (Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions)
metadata.duration_text: five-years covering the period April 2022 to March 2027
metadata.quote: "UKPACT (Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions) was established in 2018 as a pilot to test a new delivery model to support delivery of Paris Agreement commitments." (D0005236.odt, Executive Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Build on current delivery phase and continue UKPACT for a further five-years covering the period April 2022 to March 2027" (D0005236.odt, Executive Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: UKPACT is a demand-led capacity building programme that provides technical assistance to support climate transitions in high-emission countries. It combines capacity building, policy influence, and financing mechanisms to accelerate emissions reductions and green growth. The programme leverages UK expertise to support partner countries in implementing climate policies, mobilizing private finance, and building institutional capacity.
what_objectives.q1_source: "UKPACT delivers focused, context-specific support to drive transformational change in these countries’ emissions. Reflecting the rapidly changing operating context, UKPACT deploys a flexible and dynamic delivery model that anticipates changes in partner countries (e.g. changes in policy priorities)." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.1.3)
q3_expected_outputs: 30,866 key individuals trained (90% rated training as useful)
25 recommendations proposed for policies, legislation, and regulation
13 recommendations proposed for relevant actions to reduce CO2 emissions
64 knowledge products developed
35 communication products disseminated
26 climate-related networks created or strengthened
US$174.4m finance accessed or leveraged
US$695.2m finances invested in support of reduced carbon emissions
6 recommendations implemented for reduced carbon emissions
what_objectives.summary: UKPACT aims to accelerate climate transitions in high-emission countries through technical assistance, capacity building, and policy support. It focuses on reducing emissions, fostering green growth, and enhancing climate resilience while leveraging UK expertise and diplomatic influence.
what_objectives.quote: "UKPACT aims to: Support delivery of the UK’s international commitments under the 2015 Paris Agreement, by providing capacity building technical assistance to countries with potential for high emissions reduction, to accelerate the green transition, mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change and alleviate poverty." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.1.3)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in middle-income countries with varying political and economic stability. While not classified as FCAS, risks include political changes, economic volatility, and potential misalignment with partner country priorities. The Gateway Review rated delivery confidence as 'Amber', indicating significant issues requiring management attention.
where_context.q5_source: "The Review Team found widespread evidence of a passionate team and leaders who are committed to achieving the UKPACT outcomes. UKPACT is transitioning from policy and strategy development to operationalisation and delivery. In light of this transition a number of processes and plans need to be developed, refined, and embedded to assure outcomes are realised and demonstrable." (D0005260.odt, Gateway Review)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political changes in partner countries can disrupt programme alignment and delivery. Regulatory environments may limit the effectiveness of interventions, while weak institutions can hinder the adoption and sustainability of programme outputs. Climate risks and data limitations affect monitoring and evaluation efforts.
where_context.quote: "The programme’s delivery has improved to a ‘positive’ evidence rating. Key achievements in this area include output delivery on time and to quality expectations, positive output complementarity, and ongoing support for output adoption." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.1)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy (BEIS)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making power rests primarily with BEIS and FCDO teams in the UK, with in-country teams providing contextual insight and facilitating stakeholder engagement. The hybrid model includes embedded staff in British embassies, but strategic direction and approvals are managed from London.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
peer-to-peer skill shares
long-term secondments
institutional strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Palladium
partner_organizations.role: Delivery Partner for Country Programmes & Communications

partner_organizations.name: ICF Consulting
partner_organizations.role: Delivery Partner for Green Recovery Challenge Fund

partner_organizations.name: PA Consulting
partner_organizations.role: Delivery Partner for Skill Shares & Secondments

partner_organizations.name: Oxford Policy Management (OPM)
partner_organizations.role: Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) Partner

partner_organizations.name: Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing Partner in Colombia

partner_organizations.name: British Embassies
partner_organizations.role: In-country teams for stakeholder engagement and programme coordination

who_partners.quote: "The UKPACT deliverymodel currently sees roughly half the team embedded in British embassies. This hybrid model has been tested in Mexico, Colombia, China, and has expanded into a number of further countries (Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria, South Africa, and Brazil)." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.6)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: UKPACT uses a combination of grants, contracts, and secondments. Grants are awarded to implementing partners for project delivery, contracts are used for delivery partners managing programme components, and secondments involve placing UK experts in partner country institutions for capacity building.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UKPACT operates through a hybrid model combining BEIS staff in London, teams embedded in British embassies, and contracted delivery partners. The platform integrates multiple components (Country Programmes, Green Recovery Challenge Fund, Skill Shares & Secondments) with a central MEL function, allowing for coordinated delivery across countries and sectors.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The open competition for implementing partners ensures that projects are demand-led and aligned with UKPACT's strategic priorities. It allows for the selection of partners with the most relevant expertise and local knowledge to deliver context-specific interventions.
how_mechanism.quote: "The delivery partner contracts expire from September 2022. The shape of the future delivery model is not elaborated in this EBC and is yet to be determined. UKPACT is undergoing a ‘Delivery Model Assessment’ (DMA), a Cabinet Office facilitated activity to advise on the most efficient and best value delivery model." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.6)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The UKPACT Programme Board provides strategic oversight, with decision-making delegated to component leads and in-country teams. The Board includes representatives from BEIS, FCDO, and delivery partners, ensuring alignment with UK government priorities and adaptive management.
how_governance.quote: "Project governance: The UKPACT Programme Board provides strategic oversight of the programme, with decision-making delegated to the lowest appropriate level. The Board is chaired by the UKPACT SRO and includes representatives from BEIS, FCDO, and the delivery partners." (D0005236.odt, Section 6.2)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, allowing UKPACT to respond to emerging opportunities or changes in partner country priorities. The hybrid model supports flexibility in funding distribution across countries and sectors.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: UKPACT employs an adaptive management approach, with annual reviews and a dedicated MEL function to inform adjustments in programme priorities. Changes require approval from the Programme Board to ensure alignment with strategic objectives.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme’s delivery has improved to a ‘positive’ evidence rating. Key achievements in this area include output delivery on time and to quality expectations, positive output complementarity, and ongoing support for output adoption." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.1)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO/BEIS → Delivery Partners → Implementing Partners/Sub-grantees
how_efficiency.quote: "In BEIS, internal requirement costs are covered by the wider ICF ODA programme budget and those outlined here are in addition to the £340m funding that is proposed in this business case. Under all modelled scenarios the programme’s internal staff requirement is forecast to cost ~4-5% of total programme cost." (D0005236.odt, Section 5.1.1)

q24_alternatives_considered: in-house delivery
totally outsourced
new institution
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid model was chosen for its ability to combine the strengths of in-house expertise with the flexibility and specialized skills of delivery partners. This approach maximizes value for money by leveraging economies of scale, ensures responsiveness to partner country demands, and maintains UK government oversight while allowing for adaptive management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity in coordinating multiple delivery partners and components may lead to inefficiencies or misalignment.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear roles and responsibilities are defined for all partners, with robust governance structures and regular coordination meetings to ensure strategic alignment and avoid duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on delivery partners for critical functions (e.g., MEL, communications) may limit UKPACT’s ability to adapt quickly to changing priorities.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme includes a dedicated in-house team to oversee delivery partners and ensure that adaptive management is embedded in all components. Contracts include provisions for flexibility and responsive adjustments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High management costs associated with the hybrid model could reduce funds available for direct delivery.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Management costs are closely monitored and benchmarked against similar programmes to ensure they remain within acceptable limits (~11% of total budget). Efficiencies are sought through shared services and economies of scale.

why_rationale.quote: "The hybrid delivery model – roles and responsibilities: UKPACT operates through a combination delivery model that brings together teams in London, teams located in British embassies and contracted delivery partners with staff around the globe." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.6)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country scope and varying risk profiles of partner countries constrain partner selection to organizations with proven experience in complex environments. Political and economic instability in some countries limits the pool of potential partners to those with strong local networks and adaptive capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: political instability in partner countries
regulatory barriers to foreign organizations
need for local expertise and networks
ODA eligibility requirements
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The demand-led and capacity-building objectives of UKPACT determine its hybrid delivery structure, which combines in-house strategic oversight with decentralized implementation. This allows for responsive, context-specific interventions while maintaining coherence with UK government priorities.
q28_linkages: demand-led approach requires flexible, localized delivery partners
capacity-building objectives necessitate embedded teams and long-term engagements
policy influence goals drive the need for strong government relationships and diplomatic leverage
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive partnerships and rapid delivery, particularly in balancing the use of UK expertise with local ownership. Efforts to localize delivery (e.g., through regional rosters of experts) are weighed against the need for specialized technical skills that may not be available in-country.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of delivery vs. inclusive partner selection
UK expertise vs. Southern ownership
cost efficiency vs. equitable benefit distribution
standardized approaches vs. context-specific adaptations
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of partner countries influences the intensity of oversight, with more frequent monitoring and adaptive management in higher-risk contexts. This includes embedded advisors in some countries and milestone-based reviews to ensure alignment with programme objectives.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by emphasizing co-creation and knowledge transfer. Implementing partners are expected to work closely with in-country teams to ensure skills and institutional strengthening are central to all interventions, not just standalone activities.
intersections.quote: "The UKPACT model of establishing and working through deep and strategic partnerships with target countries consciously aligns with and complements the following positions and priorities: Building partner government capacity to be more informed recipients of aid from multilateral development banks/organisations (e.g. World Bank) that the UK contributes to." (D0005236.odt, Section 2.2.2)

key_programme_risks: Political changes in partner countries disrupting programme alignment
Economic volatility affecting partner country priorities and funding availability
Regulatory barriers limiting intervention effectiveness
Weak institutions hindering adoption and sustainability of outputs
Data limitations affecting monitoring and evaluation
Complexity in coordinating multiple delivery partners leading to inefficiencies
Dependence on delivery partners for critical functions limiting adaptability
High management costs reducing funds for direct delivery
Reputational risks from perceived misalignment with partner country priorities
Currency and fraud risks in financial management

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political changes in partner countries disrupting programme alignment
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded teams in British embassies maintain strong government relationships and adapt to changing priorities. The flexible delivery model allows for rapid reorientation of activities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Economic volatility affecting partner country priorities and funding availability
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Multi-year funding commitments and diverse country portfolio balance risks. Regular reviews ensure alignment with evolving country contexts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Complexity in coordinating multiple delivery partners leading to inefficiencies
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Clear governance structures and defined roles/responsibilities for all partners. Regular coordination meetings and a central Programme Management Hub ensure strategic alignment.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: High management costs reducing funds for direct delivery
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Management costs are benchmarked and monitored to remain within 11% of total budget. Shared services and economies of scale improve efficiency.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Currency and fraud risks in financial management
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Robust financial controls, including multi-layered approvals and audits. Payments are made in arrears with strict due diligence processes.

fcas_specific_lessons: While UKPACT does not operate in FCAS, lessons from similar contexts emphasize the need for adaptive programming and strong local partnerships to navigate political and economic instability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The initial phase of UKPACT demonstrated the importance of multi-year funding for sustainability and transformational change. The programme adapted successfully to COVID-19 by shifting to virtual delivery and refocusing on green recovery. Key lessons include the need for longer project timeframes, clearer MEL processes, and stronger integration of gender and social inclusion (GESI) objectives.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The extension phase incorporates multi-year project funding, enhanced MEL systems with dedicated evaluations, and a greater focus on GESI. The delivery model has been adjusted to include more in-country staff and regional expert rosters to improve localization and responsiveness.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learned from current funding round: Grant Agreements: Lessons learned and changes adopted: Over-programming: The results from this evaluation confirm those reported in the first evaluation in that the programme’s design is largely demand-driven and responsive to local contexts through collaborative processes and stakeholder engagement." (D0005236.odt, Section 5.7)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: US$695.2 million finances invested in support of reduced carbon emissions; US$174.4 million finance accessed or leveraged through UKPACT interventions
financial_details.quote: "The £340m funding sought will straddle spending periods... Total: £340m" (D0005236.odt, Section 5.1.1)

metadata.programme_name: Ukraine Humanitarian Response Programme
metadata.quote: This programme extension will continue to respond to humanitarian needs by supporting life-saving interventions and protection for the most vulnerable and at-risk populations, including women and children, people with disabilities, older people, institutionalised populations, people near and in hard-to-reach areas (this includes non-government-controlled areas and areas close to the frontlines), refugees and those who have been internally displaced. (D0006054.odt, Overview)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: 6 March 2022 – 31 March 2023; New project end date (if applicable): 31 March 2024 (D0006054.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers life-saving humanitarian assistance and protection to vulnerable populations affected by the war in Ukraine. It focuses on providing food, shelter, health, WASH, cash, and protection services, particularly to women, children, people with disabilities, and other marginalized groups.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme extension will continue to respond to humanitarian needs by supporting life-saving interventions and protection for the most vulnerable and at-risk populations, including women and children, people with disabilities, older people, institutionalised populations, people near and in hard-to-reach areas (this includes non-government-controlled areas and areas close to the frontlines), refugees and those who have been internally displaced. (D0006054.odt, Overview)
q3_expected_outputs: 11.5 million people targeted with humanitarian assistance (food, shelter, WASH, cash, protection) in Ukraine (D0006054.odt, Expected Results)
Support to 90,000 vulnerable families in Moldova with cash transfers (D0006054.odt, Expected Results)
