quote.lessons: "Whilst the Tayari approach was found to be effective, it has not been systematically scaled up by different counties due to the decentralised approach, and lack of development partner support." (D0005957.odt, Why ECE?)
quote.fcas: "The programme will leverage other partner investments, to strategically respond to climate-related education challenges." (D0005957.odt, Climate and Environment)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages existing investments: 1) **Deris Wanaag** (£Xm, FCDO-funded) for security/stability in Wajir/Mandera; 2) **CREST** (£3m, FCDO-funded) for climate resilience; 3) **HSNP** (GoK-funded) for poverty mitigation. No new co-funding is secured, but alignment with these programmes reduces duplication.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Revenue-focused: The programme funds **technical assistance** (non-capital) and **operational costs** (e.g., teacher training, materials). Capital investments (e.g., classroom construction) are excluded, as the document notes: "Capital and recurrent costs should be met by government not by external programming."

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £4.95 million" (D0005957.odt, Metadata section)
quote.leverage: "The programme will leverage the UK-funded Deris Wanaag programme investments, to support the cross-border ECE schools in Wajir and Mandera." (D0005957.odt, Education-Security Nexus)
quote.capital: "Capital and recurrent costs should be met by government not by external programming." (D0005957.odt, Potential Programme Interventions)

metadata.programme_name: Kenya Institutional Strengthening Programme (KISP)

quote.programme_name: "The UK will deliver up to £14m over five years to support Kenyan institutions to erode incentives and opportunities for corruption and improve trust in Kenya’s political system." (S30150512.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "The UK will deliver up to £14m over five years" (S30150512.odt, Programme summary)
quote.sector: "This programme supports Kenya Country Plan (2023–2025) delivery and achievements against campaign goal (6) on Open Societies, Democracy and Human Rights, where the UK aims to support the evolution of Effective Institutions and to promote Transparency and Accountability to tackle corruption and reduce illicit finance." (S30150512.odt, Country Plan Summary)

metadata.duration_source: "The UK will deliver up to £14m over five years to support Kenyan institutions to erode incentives and opportunities for corruption and improve trust in Kenya’s political system." (S30150512.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: KISP combines capacity building (strengthening government institutions and accountability systems), policy influence (supporting electoral reforms and anti-corruption frameworks), and implementation research (testing adaptive approaches to reduce corruption and illicit finance). The programme also includes evidence generation through political economy analyses and iterative learning.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The UK will deliver up to £14m over five years to support Kenyan institutions to erode incentives and opportunities for corruption and improve trust in Kenya’s political system. This will be achieved through strengthening government institutions and systems of accountability, enhancing skills and resources that will enable political parties and politicians to focus on policies that improve the daily life of Kenyan citizens and working with citizens to hold leaders accountable." (S30150512.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened legal & policy frameworks, processes that tackle corruption & illicit finance
Improved governance & integrity of electoral processes & practices
Civil Society (incl. private sector) increasingly mobilised & empowered to engage in policy making and hold those with power to account
Politicians and political parties have increased access & are able to use better quality evidence to understand voters & their preferences
Reduced opportunities and incentives for corruption and illicit finance in Kenya's political system (long-term impact)
Kenya's political system increasingly utilises an issue-based politics model where policy benefits the broader public (long-term impact)
Compliance rates of the beneficial ownership register increased (indicating improved behaviour within private actors)
Public officers declare interests and wealth in a register (indicating improved behaviour in public institutions)
Campaign finance regulations enacted and implemented
At least 5 main political parties and their leadership prioritise clear and consistent policy-oriented agenda (as evidenced by their party manifestos and policies)

what_objectives.summary: KISP aims to reduce corruption and illicit finance in Kenya’s political system by strengthening institutions, improving electoral integrity, and shifting politics from ethnic/clientelist to issue-based models. It uses an adaptive approach to test, learn, and refine interventions based on real-time evidence.

quote.objectives: "The expected impact of the programme is: Reduced corruption and illicit finance in Kenya’s political system." (S30150512.odt, Proposed UK Intervention)
quote.approach: "An adaptive approach and high-risk tolerance of KISP will allow the programme to move at pace, proactively respond to contextual changes and opportunities, and develop interventions as illicit finance and political corruption risks alter." (S30150512.odt, What is the rationale for UK International Development spending?)
quote.outputs: "Outputs: Strengthened legal & policy frameworks, processes that tackle corruption & illicit finance; Improved governance & integrity of electoral processes & practices; Civil Society (incl. private sector) increasingly mobilised & empowered to engage in policy making and hold those with power to account; Politicians and political parties have increased access & are able to use better quality evidence to understand voters & their preferences." (S30150512.odt, Proposed UK Intervention)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Kenya suffers from systemic corruption (CPI score 32/100, ranking 121/180), political violence during elections, and high debt-to-GDP ratio (66%, exceeding the 55% sustainability threshold). The programme is rated 'Major' risk, reflecting complex political economy challenges and potential resistance to reforms.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (S30150512.odt, Summary Sheet) && "Kenya suffers from deeply rooted, systemic corruption that results in loss of public funds, increasing debt, poor service delivery and reducing Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)." (S30150512.odt, What is the rationale for UK International Development spending?)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Systemic corruption and weak institutions undermine service delivery and public trust, while ethnic/clientelist politics and high election costs perpetuate inequality. Regulatory loopholes enable illicit finance, and debt crowds out development spending. Political violence during elections risks destabilizing reforms.

quote.constraints: "Kenya suffers from endemic corruption [...] A score below 50 signals serious public sector corruption." (S30150512.odt, Why UK intervention is needed) && "The cost of politics in Kenya [...] surpasses both Africa’s average of $4.50 and the global average of $2.10." (S30150512.odt, Corruption and illicit finance are symbiotic with politics) && "Kenya’s debt-to-GDP ratio is almost 66%, compared to a sustainability threshold of 55% enshrined in law." (S30150512.odt, Why UK intervention is needed)
quote.impact: "Corruption and illicit finance are symbiotic with politics: Kenya’s elections are one of the most expensive globally [...] it deepens both regional and vertical inequality between the wealthy and the poor and fosters ethnic distrust which works against investment in public services." (S30150512.odt, Corruption and illicit finance are symbiotic with politics)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic oversight and adaptive management authority, with Kenyan institutions (e.g., IEBC, EACC) as implementation partners. Decision-making on programme adjustments rests with FCDO’s Development Director and High Commission in Nairobi.

training for electoral commissioners and public servants
support for civil society coalitions (e.g., media, private sector)
behaviour change interventions for political parties
change management strategies for e-Government Procurement adoption

q24_alternatives_considered: Traditional supply-side governance reforms (rejected due to assumption that government may be disinterested or hostile)
Pure demand-side approaches (e.g., civil society campaigns; rejected due to limited evidence of effectiveness)
Standalone electoral support (rejected for not addressing systemic drivers of corruption)
Technical assistance alone (rejected as insufficient; per UK International Development White Paper 2023)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The adaptive, politically informed approach was chosen because: 1) Kenya’s context is highly dynamic and resistant to linear interventions; 2) Past FCDO programmes (e.g., KAP, DDP) showed that rigid designs fail in corrupt, clientelist systems; 3) The UK’s comparative advantage lies in its ability to take risks and combine diplomatic and development levers; 4) The White Paper (2023) emphasizes resilience-building over compliance-focused technical assistance.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (adaptive approaches avoid wasted spend on ineffective activities)
risk mitigation (flexibility allows response to political shocks)
past experience (lessons from DAP, DDP, KAP programmes)
partner capacity (leveraging trusted relationships with IEBC, EACC, etc.)
equity (targeting marginalized groups like youth and women)

q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on ‘windows of opportunity’ (e.g., post-election reforms, citizen mobilisation); build coalitions with reform-minded actors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Convene partners to align objectives; leverage UK’s diplomatic influence for coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High-risk tolerance leading to failure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: 'Fail fast, learn quickly' culture with systematic risk analysis and theory refinement.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Kenya’s high-risk political economy (ethnic clientelism, elite capture) limits partner selection to institutions with reform-minded leadership (e.g., IEBC post-2022) and civil society groups with credibility. The FATF grey-listing and IMF conditions create urgency but also require partners with technical capacity to navigate compliance (e.g., Auditor General’s Office).
q27_constraints_detail: Elite resistance to anti-corruption reforms
Weak capacity in oversight institutions (e.g., EACC)
Ethnic/political fragmentation complicating coalition-building
Regulatory loopholes enabling illicit finance (e.g., real estate, legal sector)
High cost of politics disincentivizing issue-based candidates
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to tackle **systemic** corruption (not just symptoms) requires a mixed delivery structure: Component A (institutional strengthening) uses traditional capacity-building contracts, while Component B (issue-based politics) tests innovative, adaptive grants for civil society and political parties. The reserve fund (Component C) addresses the unpredictability of reform windows.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Component A’s technical assistance to financial regulators + Component C’s reserve for emergent AML/CFT opportunities
Component B’s adaptive grants to youth networks (e.g., Gen Z) and think tanks, linked to Component A’s electoral integrity work
Embedded capacity building (Component A) + evidence generation (Component B) to shift incentives

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (rapid testing via Component C’s reserve fund) with equity (targeting youth, women, and marginalized groups in Component B). However, the adaptive approach prioritizes **speed** (3-6 monthly reviews) over deep inclusion, risking that some groups (e.g., rural poor) may be underserved if their issues don’t align with emergent opportunities.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Adaptive 3-6 monthly cycles may exclude slower-moving stakeholders (e.g., rural CSOs) if their priorities don’t align with rapid learning.
Targeting ‘coalitions for change’ (e.g., reform-minded politicians) risks sidelining broader citizen engagement.
UK-led adaptive management may limit Kenyan partners’ control over strategic pivots.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight (milestone-based reviews, embedded political economy analysis) and justifies the high-flexibility reserve fund (Component C). The FATF grey-listing and debt crisis increase scrutiny of financial management, requiring tighter FCDO approvals for fund reallocation.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak institutional capacity in Kenyan partners (e.g., IEBC’s post-2022 credibility issues) shapes the programme’s focus on **embedded** capacity building (e.g., change management for e-Government Procurement) and coalition-building (e.g., media + private sector for illicit finance). The UK’s role as convener (e.g., with World Bank/EU) compensates for local coordination gaps.

key_programme_risks: Resistance from political elites benefiting from corruption
Limited absorptive capacity in Kenyan institutions (e.g., IEBC, EACC)
Ethnic/clientelist norms undermining issue-based politics
FATF grey-listing deadlines creating implementation pressure
Debt crisis crowding out reform priorities
Youth protests (Gen Z) escalating into violence or co-optation
Overlap with other donors (EU, World Bank) leading to duplication
Adaptive approach failing to deliver tangible results in 5-year timeframe
Weak enforcement of new laws (e.g., campaign finance regulations)
Backsliding on electoral integrity gains post-2022

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Thinking and Working Politically (TWP) to identify and engage reform-minded actors; build coalitions with private sector and media to shift incentives.
Embedded technical assistance (e.g., for e-Government Procurement); pilot interventions with iterative learning.
Component B’s focus on issue-based politics, using data (e.g., citizen policy preferences) to counter ethnic appeals.
Prioritize AML/CFT compliance in Component A; leverage UK’s diplomatic influence for extensions if needed.
Align with IMF-supported reforms; frame anti-corruption as critical for debt sustainability.
Engage Gen Z networks early (Component B); support peaceful channels for accountability demands.
Convene World Bank/EU to align programmes; focus on UK’s niche (political corruption drivers).
Regular 3-6 monthly reviews; reserve fund (Component C) for course correction.
Strengthen diagonal accountability (media, CSOs) to pressure compliance.
Sustain IEBC’s post-2022 gains via induction training and operational support.

fcas_specific_lessons: Elections are processes, not events—early engagement is critical (lesson from DDP/KESP).
Technical assistance alone is insufficient; must pair with political economy analysis (per UK White Paper 2023).
Elite capture requires ‘working with the grain’ while testing windows for reform (e.g., post-election moments).
Youth mobilisation (e.g., Gen Z protests) can create reform opportunities but risks co-optation or violence.
FATF grey-listing can catalyse reforms if paired with targeted support (e.g., beneficial ownership registers).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past FCDO programmes (DAP, DDP, KAP) showed that: 1) Electoral support must address **systemic** drivers of corruption (e.g., campaign finance), not just logistics; 2) Civil society ‘demand-side’ approaches have limited impact without supply-side reforms; 3) Adaptive programming requires **local political analysis** and risk tolerance; 4) UK’s diplomatic + development levers are most effective when aligned (e.g., NADCO mediation post-2022 elections).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: KISP incorporates: 1) A **reserve fund** (Component C) for emergent opportunities (missing in KAP); 2) Explicit **behaviour change** focus (COM-B framework) to address social norms (gap in DDP); 3) **Issue-based politics** testing (Component B) to shift clientelist dynamics; 4) **Coalition-building** across government/private sector/CSOs (lesson from DAP’s siloed approach).

metadata.programme_name: Reforming the United Nations System – Humanitarian (RUSH)
metadata.quote: This business case provides £324m of unearmarked core funding over a period of three years (Financial Years 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26). (D0003586.odt, Financial Case)
metadata.duration_source: This business case provides £324m of unearmarked core funding over a period of three years (Financial Years 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to five UN humanitarian agencies to deliver life-saving assistance while driving systemic reforms. It combines financing (70% unearmarked core funding) with performance incentives (30% Payment-by-Results) to improve humanitarian response quality, transparency, and accountability. The focus is on both immediate service delivery (saving lives) and long-term system strengthening (reform agenda).
what_objectives.q1_source: This core funding is the most effective way of supporting these agencies to provide life-saving humanitarian assistance, rapidly and at scale. It will also enhance the value-for-money of FCDO bilateral humanitarian programmes, cement UK influence at these agencies and in the wider multilateral system, and drive priority humanitarian reforms including early and anticipatory action, enhanced quality and transparency of data, protection of the most vulnerable, accountability to affected populations, and inclusion in humanitarian response. (D0003586.odt, Summary Sheet)
q3_expected_outputs: Life-saving humanitarian assistance delivered rapidly and at scale (no specific quantitative target mentioned)
Enhanced value-for-money of FCDO bilateral humanitarian programmes
Driven priority humanitarian reforms: early/anticipatory action, data quality/transparency, protection of vulnerable groups, accountability to affected populations, inclusion
Strengthened UK influence in UN agencies and wider multilateral system
Improved coordination between UN humanitarian agencies (e.g., cash programming, joint needs assessments)
70% unearmarked core funding for flexible response, 30% Payment-by-Results (PbR) for reform incentives
Progress on UK priorities: gender equality, disability inclusion, safeguarding, climate resilience, anticipatory action
Maintenance of UK as top-10 donor for each agency, preserving governance influence
what_objectives.summary: The programme provides flexible core funding to UN humanitarian agencies to deliver immediate life-saving aid while incentivizing systemic reforms through a Payment-by-Results mechanism, aligning with UK's strategic priorities in humanitarian response, gender equality, and climate resilience.
what_objectives.quote: To provide core funding to five humanitarian agencies of the United Nations (UN). This core funding is the most effective way of supporting these agencies to provide life-saving humanitarian assistance, rapidly and at scale. (D0003586.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The document explicitly states the programme operates in high-risk contexts including conflict zones (Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen, Ukraine) and FCAS (Fragile and Conflict-Affected States), with significant challenges like terrorism risks, aid diversion, and safeguarding vulnerabilities. The overall programme risk rating is classified as 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major. (D0003586.odt, Summary Sheet) && In high-and very high-risk countries, FCDO country programmes are very heavily reliant on multilaterals for humanitarian delivery. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security and conflict limit access to affected populations, requiring reliance on UN agencies with neutrality/legitimacy. Terrorism risks necessitate strict counter-financing controls. Climate change exacerbates food insecurity and displacement. Data limitations affect needs assessments and targeting. Weak institutions in FCAS reduce local capacity to respond without multilateral support.
where_context.quote: Conflict and crises are increasingly trapping marginalised people, in particular women and girls, in cycles of vulnerability... Humanitarian funding has not kept up with rising need, and the humanitarian system is under significant pressure. (D0003586.odt, Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations (five agencies: OCHA, WFP, UNHCR, UNICEF, IOM)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) sets strategic priorities, performance indicators, and retains governance influence through executive board seats and PbR mechanisms. UN agencies implement operations but must align with UK-driven reform agendas and reporting requirements.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening agencies' anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., replicating CERF models)
Improving data quality/transparency (disaggregation for vulnerable populations)
Enhancing protection/inclusion strategies (PSEA standards, gender mainstreaming)
Building local NGO roles in coordination structures (via PbR indicators)
Safeguarding training and victim-centred approaches (IASC PSEA Strategy 2022-2026)
Climate resilience and adaptive social protection systems

partner_organizations.role: Food security and nutrition interventions, including anticipatory action

partner_organizations.role: Protection and assistance to refugees and internally displaced persons

who_partners.quote: These agencies, together with the Red Cross Movement (to which we provide core funding through a separate business case), are the backbone of the international humanitarian system, and an incomparable channel for delivery of humanitarian assistance at scale globally. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** with each UN agency, combining **70% unearmarked core funding** (flexible, multi-year) with **30% Payment-by-Results (PbR)** tranches contingent on achieving pre-agreed reform milestones. Core funding supports central agency budgets and operations, while PbR incentivizes specific UK priorities (e.g., anticipatory action, gender inclusion).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO’s **Humanitarian Partnerships and Systems Performance (HPSP) team** manages the programme centrally, negotiating MoUs and monitoring performance. Agencies operate independently but report jointly on PbR indicators. Quarterly inter-agency meetings and annual reviews facilitate coordination. FCDO retains governance influence via executive board seats and policy advocacy.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The five UN agencies were selected based on their **mandates as the backbone of the humanitarian system**, proven capacity to deliver at scale, and alignment with UK strategic priorities. The business case explicitly states this is a continuation of a previous high-performing programme (scored A+), with no competition mentioned.
how_mechanism.quote: This Business Case will work alongside those which provide core funding to the Red Cross Movement and the Central Emergency Response Fund... These agencies... are the backbone of the international humanitarian system. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: FCDO convenes **quarterly inter-agency meetings** and an **annual roundtable** to review PbR progress. Agencies submit joint reports on collaborative indicators. FCDO also engages through **UN executive boards** (e.g., WFP, UNHCR, UNICEF) and donor forums (e.g., OCHA Donor Support Group). The **Humanitarian Engagement Cell** within FCDO strategically influences agency policies.
how_governance.quote: Progress will be regularly monitored by Institutional Leads and the programme team at internal quarterly Portfolio Boards... FCDO will also arrange quarterly meetings with all of the agencies to discuss performance... Urgent issues will be raised and escalated via senior engagement. (D0003586.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The **70% unearmarked core funding** can be reallocated by agencies according to need, but the **30% PbR tranche** is contingent on meeting specific milestones. Underperformance may lead to deductions of up to 30%. Reallocation between agencies or major shifts require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: PbR indicators are negotiated annually, allowing adjustments to reflect emerging priorities (e.g., climate resilience, anticipatory action). However, changes require agreement between FCDO and agencies. The programme includes a **Humanitarian Engagement Cell** to capitalize on institutional influence for policy adaptation.
how_flexibility.quote: Indicators will be defined in the business case log frame to capture and measure progress... The precise indicators and shape of the PbR agreement will be negotiated in parallel to the development of this Business Case. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN Agencies (no sub-grantees mentioned; agencies implement directly or through their existing partners).
how_efficiency.quote: Non-PbR payments are likely to be made in August each year, with PbR payments released in October, subject to satisfactory performance. (D0003586.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: 1. ‘Do nothing’ counterfactual (no core funding to UN agencies)
2. 30% PbR component (70% unearmarked, 30% PbR - **preferred option**)
3. 0% PbR component (100% unearmarked funding)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **70/30 split** was chosen to balance **flexibility** (allowing agencies to respond rapidly to crises) with **accountability** (driving UK reform priorities). Evidence from the previous programme (scored A+) showed PbR incentivized collaboration and progress on joint milestones (e.g., cash programming, needs assessments). The option aligns with **Grand Bargain commitments** (70% unearmarked) while adding UK-specific priorities like anticipatory action and climate resilience.
q25_decision_factors: partner-capacity (agencies’ proven ability to deliver at scale)
equity (inclusion of marginalized groups via PbR indicators)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Agencies may prioritize existing programmes over UK reform priorities (e.g., anticipatory action not covered by Grand Bargain)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: PbR indicators are carefully negotiated to incentivize actions agencies ‘would not otherwise have carried out.’ Financial penalties (up to 30% deductions) enforce compliance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced UK burden share (4-5% vs previous 8%) may limit influence
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage technical expertise, governance seats (e.g., executive boards), and policy advocacy to maintain influence despite lower funding levels.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: PbR reporting burdens could divert agency resources
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use existing data sources and avoid creating new reporting requirements; focus on fewer, measurable indicators.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (core funding enables bulk procurement and anticipatory action)
effectiveness (PbR drives reforms like data transparency and protection strategies)
equity (targeted inclusion of women, girls, and disabled populations)
why_rationale.quote: Option 2 [70/30 split]... allows us to exercise a substantive and credible incentive that allows FCDO to drive reforms and demonstrate impact, without jeopardising our influence and relationships or hampering agency delivery capabilities. (D0003586.odt, Options Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **high-risk, conflict-affected contexts** (e.g., Afghanistan, Syria, Ukraine) constrain partner selection to UN agencies due to their **neutrality, legitimacy, and access** in areas where other actors cannot operate. Local NGOs or governments often lack capacity or security clearance to deliver aid independently.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict zones require partners with **humanitarian access negotiation skills** (e.g., OCHA’s role in advocacy)
Counter-terrorism regulations limit funding to certain regions/groups, necessitating UN agencies’ risk management systems
Climate-induced crises (e.g., famines) demand partners with **global logistics capacity** (e.g., WFP’s supply chains)
Weak local institutions in FCAS increase reliance on **multilateral coordination** (e.g., IOM’s migration management)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rapid, large-scale response** determines the use of **core funding** (70% unearmarked) to UN agencies, while the **reform agenda** (e.g., anticipatory action, gender inclusion) shapes the **PbR mechanism** (30%). The mix ensures agencies can act flexibly in crises while being held accountable to UK priorities.
q28_linkages: **Global reach requirement** → Multilateral partners (UN agencies) as implementers
**Systemic reform goals** → PbR indicators to drive collaboration (e.g., joint needs assessments)
**FCAS constraints** → Core funding to preserve agencies’ field presence for rapid scale-up
**Climate/anticipatory action focus** → PbR targets on early warning systems and resilience-building
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between **efficiency** (rapid delivery via UN agencies) and **equity** (inclusion of local actors). For example: PbR indicators incentivize agencies to **strengthen local NGO roles in coordination**, but core funding still flows primarily to multilateral bodies. Safeguarding risks (e.g., SEAH) are mitigated through **centralized UN systems**, potentially sidelining community-led accountability mechanisms.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: **Unearmarked core funding** enables rapid response but may bypass local partners in decision-making.
Expertise vs. ownership: UN agencies lead on **technical standards** (e.g., gender markers) while local women’s groups have limited influence over strategic priorities.
Cost vs. reach: **Bulk procurement** by agencies reduces costs but may exclude smaller, Southern suppliers.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight**: quarterly performance reviews, embedded safeguarding monitors, and executive board engagement. High-risk contexts (e.g., terrorism, FCAS) require **additional assurance mechanisms** (e.g., Central Assurance Assessments, counter-financing clauses in MoUs).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded in PbR indicators**, shaping partners’ roles: agencies must demonstrate progress on **localization** (e.g., including women-led orgs in planning) and **institutional strengthening** (e.g., anticipatory action frameworks) to unlock PbR funds. This shifts their role from implementers to **system convenors**.
intersections.quote: In high-and very high-risk countries, FCDO country programmes are very heavily reliant on multilaterals for humanitarian delivery—who are often the only actors with the neutrality, legitimacy, access, capacity and risk management processes to be trusted to deliver value-for-money interventions, rapidly and at scale in conflict environments. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: Reduced UK burden share (4-5%) may diminish influence over agency strategies
Agencies deprioritizing UK-specific reforms (e.g., anticipatory action) not covered by Grand Bargain
PbR indicators creating perverse incentives (e.g., focusing on measurable outputs over systemic change)
Safeguarding incidents (SEAH) in high-risk contexts despite improved UN policies
Climate shocks outpacing agencies’ adaptive capacity
Fraud/aid diversion in conflict zones with proscribed terrorist groups
Underperformance leading to PbR fund withholding and reputational damage
Fragmentation if agencies compete for ‘market share’ rather than collaborating

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reduced influence due to lower funding levels
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Leverage **governance seats** (e.g., executive boards), **policy advocacy**, and **technical expertise** to maintain influence. Use PbR to demonstrate tangible UK impact.
Negotiate PbR indicators that incentivize **‘additional’ actions** agencies wouldn’t otherwise take. Align with existing commitments (e.g., Grand Bargain) to reduce resistance.

Require compliance with **IASC PSEA Strategy 2022-2026**, including victim-centred approaches and organizational culture change. Monitor via **quarterly Portfolio Boards** and agency executive boards.
Include **counter-terrorism financing clauses** in MoUs. Conduct **Central Assurance Assessments** and require agencies to report credible allegations immediately.
PbR indicators focus on **anticipatory action frameworks** and climate resilience. Use FCDO’s **HEW early warning system** to monitor risks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Core funding is critical to **preserve agencies’ field presence** in FCAS for rapid scale-up (e.g., Afghanistan, Ukraine).
In FCAS, **UN agencies are often the only actors** with access, requiring reliance on multilaterals despite localization goals.
**Payment-by-Results must account for FCAS volatility**—indicators should balance ambition with feasibility in unstable contexts.
Safeguarding risks are heightened in FCAS; **victim-centred approaches** and local capacity-building are essential.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
The **2020 Annual Review** of the predecessor programme (scored A+) highlighted: 
- PbR drove **collaboration** (e.g., 186% surpass on cash programming targets) and **joint needs assessments** (79% of HRPs met standards).
- **Flexible core funding** enabled rapid responses to unpredictable crises (e.g., COVID-19, Afghanistan).
- **Lessons applied**: Fewer, more measurable PbR indicators; alignment with Grand Bargain commitments; avoiding new reporting burdens.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **PbR indicators**: Reduced in number, focused on **critical bottlenecks** (e.g., anticipatory action, data transparency).
2. **Policy alignment**: Indicators linked to **Grand Bargain** and **UK Humanitarian Framework** (3Ps: Prevent, Prioritise, Protect).
3. **Monitoring**: Triangulate agency reporting with **FCDO country office data** to verify results.
4. **Climate focus**: Added **anticipatory action** and resilience indicators to PbR.
5. **Localization**: PbR now incentivizes **strengthening local NGO roles** in coordination structures.
risks_lessons.quote: The previous iteration of this business case... was a high-performing programme, scoring an A+ in its most recent Annual Review... PbR-driven progress toward then-DFID’s reform goals was ‘broadly positive,’ with particular success regarding the humanitarian-development nexus and Joint Needs Assessment. (D0003586.odt, Strategic Case)

financial_details.quote: This business case provides £324m of unearmarked core funding over a period of three years... The funding will be split into two tranches; 70% is unearmarked... with a 30% Payment by Results tranche. (D0003586.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: UK Support to Financing of Recovery from Economic Emergency in Ukraine (FREE Ukraine)
metadata.duration_text: Expected to be 2052, but dependent on maturity and terms agreed for guaranteed lending to Ukraine
metadata.primary_sector: Multi-sectoral (economic recovery, fiscal support, social protection)
metadata.quote: "The UK will provide fiscal support to the Government of Ukraine through a £74m grant to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund and up to $450m in guarantees of World Bank lending to Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Expected to be 2052, but dependent on maturity and terms agreed for guaranteed lending to Ukraine." (D0005254.odt, New project end date)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides fiscal support to Ukraine through guarantees and grants to the World Bank, enabling the Bank to increase lending volumes and disburse funds rapidly. This is a financing mechanism designed to address Ukraine's urgent budgetary needs during the war, ensuring macroeconomic stability and continuation of essential services.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The UK will provide fiscal support to the Government of Ukraine through a £74m grant to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund and up to $450m in guarantees of World Bank lending to Ukraine. The guarantees will enable the IBRD to lend more than it would otherwise do so to Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Reduced financing gap for the Ukrainian Government (target: up to $550m additional affordable financing initially, later expanded to ~£2.5bn in guarantees)
Maintenance of essential payments (e.g., pensions, state salaries)
Support for macroeconomic stability in Ukraine
Direct budget support to the Government of Ukraine via World Bank disbursements
Coverage of 80%+ of total pension costs (August 2022 data)
Support for social protection, energy, and health expenditures
Reduction in monetary financing (evidenced by IMF observation of decline from Q3 2022)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to provide rapid fiscal support to Ukraine during the war by leveraging World Bank mechanisms, ensuring the government can maintain essential services and macroeconomic stability. It combines guarantees (to unlock additional World Bank lending) with direct grants to maximize impact.
what_objectives.quote: "The intended impact of the programme is to support the macroeconomic stability of Ukraine, support the Ukrainian state to continue to function and alleviate suffering in the face of the invasion." (D0005248.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is experiencing active conflict (Russian invasion), economic collapse, and institutional strain. The documents explicitly note the "extraordinary" and "major" risks due to war, including potential default, protracted conflict, and economic instability.
where_context.q5_source: "The risks associated with the programme are assessed as major. However the context in Ukraine is extraordinary and the economic and political consequences of not acting rapidly significantly outweigh these risks." (D0005248.odt, Risk section) && "On 24 February 2022, Russia launched a large-scale invasion of Ukraine which is ongoing." (D0005248.odt, Context)
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (Government of Ukraine under severe strain)
political economy (international sanctions, capital market access restricted)
infrastructure (destruction of key infrastructure like schools/hospitals)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The war has led to a financing gap of $11-12bn (2022), with Ukraine unable to access affordable finance. The conflict has destroyed infrastructure, displaced populations, and created urgent humanitarian needs, while also limiting the government's ability to borrow domestically or internationally. The programme design (e.g., World Bank disbursements) explicitly accounts for these constraints by providing rapid, flexible support.
where_context.quote: "The immediate economic impacts on the Ukrainian economy are unprecedented... Ukraine’s financing gap is large and growing, and the Government has been unable to access international capital markets reliably and affordably." (D0005248.odt, Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, IBRD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (a Northern-led multilateral) designs and manages the financing operations, disburses funds, and monitors use. The UK (FCDO) provides guarantees/grants but defers to World Bank processes for implementation. The Government of Ukraine receives funds but has limited decision-making power over the mechanism design.

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (IBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer: designs financing operations, disburses funds, monitors use, and manages guarantees/grants on behalf of the UK

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ukraine (Ministry of Finance)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient: receives disbursed funds for budget support and essential services

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Funder: provides guarantees and grants, oversees risk management, and approves high-level strategy

partner_organizations.name: HMT (HM Treasury)
partner_organizations.role: Approver: signs off on contingent liabilities and budgetary implications

partner_organizations.name: IMF (International Monetary Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Advisor: assesses debt sustainability and macroeconomic stability (influences guarantee terms)

partner_organizations.name: PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers)
partner_organizations.role: Auditor: conducts verification of PEACE programme expenditures (e.g., March–August 2022)

partner_organizations.name: G7 and other donors (US, EU, Japan, etc.)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers: contribute to World Bank trust funds alongside the UK

who_partners.quote: "The World Bank will act as administrator for the guarantee arrangement and grant financing flowing through the MDTF and will monitor and manage the risks on our behalf, in accordance with their own policies and procedures." (D0005248.odt, Assurances) && "The UK will provide fiscal support to the Government of Ukraine through a £74m grant to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund and up to $450m in guarantees of World Bank lending to Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses two instruments: (1) **Guarantees**: Contingent liabilities where the UK promises to cover World Bank losses if Ukraine defaults on IBRD loans. These unlock additional lending without upfront costs. (2) **Grants**: Direct contributions to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) for immediate budget support. Both instruments are channeled through the World Bank’s existing systems.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank manages all operational aspects: disbursement, monitoring, and reporting. FCDO provides oversight and approval for guarantees but relies on the Bank’s systems for implementation. The Government of Ukraine receives funds but follows World Bank-approved expenditure rules (e.g., PEACE programme’s retroactive reimbursement model).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its existing relationship with Ukraine, preferred creditor status, rapid disbursement capability, and robust safeguards. The documents emphasize the need for speed and coordination, which precluded competitive processes. The UK’s prior experience with World Bank guarantees (e.g., Egypt, Iraq) also informed this choice.
how_mechanism.quote: "Aligning support to World Bank financing can provide rapid and coordinated financial assistance in a single package, limiting administrative burdens for the Government of Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, Rationale) && "The World Bank will act as administrator for the guarantee arrangement and grant financing..." (D0005248.odt, Assurances)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Financial Transactions Steering Board (FTSB)** (a sub-committee of FCDO’s Investment and Delivery Committee) oversees guarantee risks. The **SRO (Senior Responsible Owner)** in FCDO monitors default risks and reports to FCDO’s Finance Directorate. The **World Bank Board** approves loans covered by guarantees. Ministerial approval is required for guarantee issuance, and Parliamentary approval is sought via Departmental Minutes.
how_governance.quote: "The Financial Transactions Steering Board will provide oversight of the guarantee, in line with the recent update on the governance of guarantees." (D0005248.odt, Management arrangements) && "The SRO will lead on monitoring the risk of default regularly and through a formal annual process involving carrying out a Default Risk Assessment (DRA)." (D0005248.odt, Management arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Guarantees can be issued for different World Bank operations (e.g., DPLs or IPFs) as long as they are additional to the Bank’s original lending plans. The SRO decides which loans to guarantee in consultation with FCDO and HMT. However, once a guarantee is issued for a specific loan, funds cannot be reallocated.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme retains flexibility to adjust the type of World Bank financing supported (e.g., shifting from DPLs to IPFs in later addendums). New guarantees require approval from FCDO, HMT, and Parliament, with input from the IMF on debt sustainability. The World Bank’s incremental approach allows for adjustments based on Ukraine’s evolving needs.
how_flexibility.quote: "The SRO, in consultation with IFID and UKDEL, will decide which World Bank loans to guarantee." (D0005248.odt, Approval process) && "The UK will only issue a guarantee to the World Bank that if it supports financing that is additional to the Bank’s own lending plans." (D0005248.odt, Theory of Change)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank → Government of Ukraine (no sub-grantees; World Bank disburses directly to designated GoU bank accounts)
how_efficiency.quote: "The World Bank will disburse funds directly into designated bank accounts for specific purposes related to the financing agreement." (D0005248.odt, Assurances) && "IPF disbursements will be tranched and used to reimburse eligible expenditures, mitigating fiduciary risks." (D0005251.odt, Approach to implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Guarantee MDB commitments (selected option)
Guarantee Eurobond issuance (rejected due to high risk and lack of framework)
Grant finance only (rejected due to lower volume of support)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The guarantee mechanism was chosen for three key reasons: (1) **Volume**: It unlocks significantly more financing (up to $450m initially, later expanded) than grants alone. (2) **Risk management**: The World Bank’s preferred creditor status reduces the likelihood of default, and the UK only pays if Ukraine defaults after 180 days. (3) **Speed and coordination**: Aligning with the World Bank leverages existing systems, reduces administrative burdens for Ukraine, and signals international support. The grant component was added to provide immediate liquidity.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (guarantees provide 4-5x leverage per £1 of contingent liability)
experience (UK’s prior guarantees with World Bank for Egypt/Iraq)
flexibility (ability to adjust guarantee terms as needs evolve)
equity (support reaches vulnerable populations via social protection)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Financial risk: Ukraine defaults on World Bank loans, triggering UK guarantee payments (estimated £31m/year max under baseline).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: World Bank’s preferred creditor status and incremental lending approach reduce default likelihood. FCDO monitors exchange rate and interest rate risks and maintains RAME provisions for probable defaults.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delivery risk: Conflict escalation worsens economic crisis, increasing financing needs beyond commitments.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK retains flexibility to issue guarantees for additional World Bank operations. Coordination with G7 partners aims to fill gaps collectively.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risk: Misuse of funds by Government of Ukraine.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: World Bank disburses to designated accounts for specific purposes (e.g., pensions, salaries). PEACE programme uses retroactive reimbursement with PwC verification. Exclusion lists prohibit military expenditures.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk: UK perceived as not doing enough or guarantee terms seen as unfavorable.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Transparency in guarantee terms and coordination with G7 partners. No fees charged to Ukraine for guarantees to avoid criticism.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exchange rate risk: GBP depreciation increases cost of USD/EUR-denominated guarantees.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO accepts and monitors risk; guarantees denominated in loan currency (EUR/USD) to match World Bank lending. Stress scenarios model 15% GBP depreciation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Interest rate risk: Rising global rates increase UK’s contingent liability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO models stress scenarios (e.g., SOFR/EURIBOR rising to 20-year Treasury/Bund rates). No hedging due to HMT guidelines and cost inefficiency.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (guarantees have no upfront cost; grants leverage World Bank’s low overhead)
efficiency (World Bank’s existing systems reduce administrative burdens)
effectiveness (direct budget support maintains essential services)
equity (funds prioritize social protection for vulnerable groups)
why_rationale.quote: "A UK guarantee to support additional MDB lending to Ukraine represents good value for money given the broader context and political imperative to provide fiscal support to Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, VfM Statement) && "The guarantee has no up-front cost and therefore does not present immediate trade-offs with other spending programmes." (D0005248.odt, VfM Measures)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context (active war, economic collapse) limits partner selection to multilaterals with rapid disbursement capabilities and robust safeguards. The World Bank was chosen over alternatives like EBRD or direct Eurobond guarantees due to its existing Ukraine portfolio, preferred creditor status, and ability to operate under conflict conditions. The documents explicitly note that "the context in Ukraine is extraordinary," requiring partners who can manage major risks and disburse funds quickly.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict restricts access to domestic/international capital markets (rules out commercial lending options)
Weak institutions limit direct budget support (rules out bilateral grants to GoU)
Urgent needs require rapid disbursement (rules out slow-moving or untested partners)
Fiduciary risks necessitate trusted intermediaries (rules out partners without robust safeguards)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, large-scale fiscal support** (WHAT) directly shapes the **multilateral guarantee/grant mechanism** (HOW). The programme’s objectives—macroeconomic stability and essential services—require: (1) **Volume**: Only multilaterals like the World Bank can disburse at scale. (2) **Speed**: Existing World Bank pipelines (e.g., DPLs/IPFs) enable faster delivery than new instruments. (3) **Risk management**: The World Bank’s PCS and safeguards mitigate default/fiduciary risks, which are critical given Ukraine’s FCAS status. The shift from DPLs to IPFs in later addendums reflects a trade-off between fiscal flexibility and fiduciary control.
q28_linkages: Large financing gap (WHAT) → Need for leverage → Guarantees chosen over grants (HOW)
Urgent disbursement (WHAT) → Use of existing World Bank pipelines (HOW)
High fiduciary risks (WHERE) → Retroactive reimbursement model (HOW)
Preferred creditor status (WHO) → Lower risk premiums for guarantees (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The documents explicitly discuss tensions between **speed/efficiency** and **equity/inclusion**: (1) **World Bank’s systems prioritize rapid disbursement** (efficiency) but limit GoU’s discretion over fund use (equity). (2) **Guarantees leverage Northern multilateral expertise** (efficiency) but reduce Southern ownership (equity). (3) **PEACE programme’s retroactive reimbursement** balances fiduciary control (efficiency) with coverage of social protection (equity). The UK accepts these trade-offs as justified by the "no regrets" imperative of supporting Ukraine during war.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: World Bank’s rapid disbursement limits GoU’s input on expenditure priorities.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led World Bank designs mechanisms; GoU implements with limited decision-making power.
Cost vs. reach: Grant financing (£74m) has high opportunity cost but ensures immediate impact for vulnerable groups.
Flexibility vs. control: IPFs offer more predictability than DPLs but reduce fiscal flexibility for GoU.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **major/FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight**: (1) **Default risk monitoring**: Annual DRAs, real-time World Bank communication, and RAME provisions. (2) **Exchange/interest rate stress testing**: Regular modeling of 15% GBP depreciation or rate hikes. (3) **Fiduciary safeguards**: PwC audits, designated bank accounts, and exclusion lists. The documents state that "the risks... are mitigated by safeguards put in place by the World Bank," but the extraordinary context justifies higher management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **World Bank’s capacity** (robust safeguards, PCS, rapid disbursement) enables it to act as the **sole implementer**, while the **GoU’s constrained capacity** (war, institutional strain) limits its role to recipient. The UK/FCDO focuses on **high-level oversight** (approvals, risk monitoring) rather than delivery, deferring to the Bank’s systems. The documents note that "the World Bank will disburse funds directly into designated bank accounts," reflecting this division of roles based on capacity.
intersections.quote: "The risks associated with the programme are assessed as major. However the context in Ukraine is extraordinary and the economic and political consequences of not acting rapidly significantly outweigh these risks." (D0005248.odt, Risk) && "Providing support through the World Bank ensures that World Bank monitoring and reporting processes are followed. It also reduces the associated administrative burden for both the UK and the Government of Ukraine." (D0005251.odt, Approach to implementation)

key_programme_risks: Ukraine defaults on World Bank loans, triggering UK guarantee payments (financial risk)
Conflict escalation increases financing gap beyond donor commitments (delivery risk)
Exchange rate depreciation (GBP/USD/EUR) increases contingent liability costs (financial risk)
Interest rate rises increase UK’s exposure (financial risk)
Misuse of funds by Government of Ukraine (fiduciary risk)
World Bank financing fails to meet UK standards on sanctions (reputational risk)
Protracted conflict delays economic recovery, reducing impact (political risk)
Debt sustainability concerns limit further non-concessional lending (financial risk)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: World Bank’s preferred creditor status; incremental lending approach; RAME provisions for probable defaults; stress-testing exchange/interest rates.
Flexible guarantee structure to support additional World Bank operations; coordination with G7 partners to fill gaps.
Guarantees denominated in loan currency (EUR/USD); regular monitoring; stress scenarios modeling 15% GBP depreciation.
Stress scenarios (SOFR/EURIBOR rising to 20-year rates); no hedging per HMT guidelines.
PEACE programme’s retroactive reimbursement; PwC audits; designated bank accounts; exclusion lists for ineligible expenditures (e.g., military).
World Bank’s safeguard policies; direct disbursement to designated accounts for specific purposes.
Close coordination with IMF on Ukraine’s debt carrying capacity; prioritization of concessional lending where possible.

fcas_specific_lessons: Preferred creditor status is critical in FCAS contexts to reduce default risks (World Bank’s PCS justified guarantee approach).
Rapid disbursement mechanisms (e.g., S-DPLs, IPFs) are essential in crises but require trade-offs with fiduciary control (retroactive reimbursement model adopted).
Stress-testing for exchange/interest rate volatility is necessary in economically unstable environments (15% GBP depreciation scenario included).
Donor coordination (G7+) is vital to fill financing gaps that exceed individual countries’ capacities (UK’s guarantees leveraged broader support).
Flexible instruments (guarantees vs. grants) allow adaptation to evolving needs (shift from DPLs to IPFs in later phases).
In FCAS, reputational risks of inaction outweigh financial risks of guarantees ("no regrets" basis for approval).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The UK’s prior experience with World Bank guarantees (e.g., Egypt, Iraq, Jordan) informed the design: (1) **No fees charged** to avoid reputational risks (lesson from earlier guarantees). (2) **Stress-testing** incorporated based on past exposure to exchange/interest rate fluctuations. (3) **Incremental lending approach** adopted to manage exposure limits (mirroring Egypt/Iraq structures). The documents note that "the UK has previous experience in providing guarantees to support additional IBRD lending to Egypt, India, Iraq and Jordan."
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. **Shift from DPLs to IPFs**: Later addendums replaced Development Policy Loans (DPLs) with Investment Project Financing (IPFs) to improve predictability and fiduciary controls while retaining flexibility. 2. **Debt sustainability checks**: Added IMF coordination to assess Ukraine’s debt carrying capacity before issuing new guarantees. 3. **Expanded guarantee volume**: Increased from $450m to ~$2.5bn in response to escalating financing gaps (from $11-12bn in 2022 to $39.5-49bn in 2023). 4. **Currency alignment**: Later guarantees denominated in USD (not EUR) to match World Bank lending terms.
risks_lessons.quote: "The proposed financing modality for the UK-guaranteed World Bank lending has changed from a Development Policy Loan (DPL) to Investment Project Financing (IPF)... IPF provides slightly less fiscal flexibility... but will provide more predictability." (D0005249.odt, Key changes) && "We are working closely with the World Bank and the IMF to ensure that further UK guarantee support is implemented sustainably." (D0005251.odt, Key changes)

co_funding_partners.partner: G7 and other donors (US, EU, Japan, etc.)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s guarantees unlock ~5x additional World Bank lending: £74m in grants + ~£2.5bn in guarantees (contingent) mobilized ~$3bn+ in total World Bank financing to Ukraine. The programme also catalyzed broader donor support, with the World Bank’s PEACE mechanism expanding to include non-G7 countries (e.g., Austria, Netherlands, Sweden).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme is entirely revenue-based (no capital expenditures). Funds support recurrent expenditures (salaries, pensions, social protection) and budgetary gaps, with no infrastructure or asset creation.
financial_details.quote: "The total financial support provided to Ukraine through this programme will be a fiscal grant of £74m (RDEL) and up to approximately £2.5bn in guarantee." (D0005254.odt, Additional support) && "The UK’s £74m grant contribution to a World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) in support of an IBRD DPL for Ukraine." (D0005248.odt, What support will the UK provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Investing in the humanitarian capability of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and British Red Cross (BRC) enabling quick and effective responses to humanitarian crises

quote.programme_name: "Title: Investing in the humanitarian capability of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and British Red Cross (BRC) enabling quick and effective responses to humanitarian crises" (D0001354.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "The UK will provide three years of unearmarked core funding to the IFRC and BRC." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £39 million" (D0001354.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "The UK will provide three years of unearmarked core funding to the IFRC and BRC." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening IFRC and National Societies' preparedness and response capabilities), service delivery (direct humanitarian assistance), and financing mechanism (core funding to enable rapid responses). It focuses on improving the effectiveness of the Red Cross Movement in delivering life-saving assistance while building resilience and anticipatory action capabilities.
what_objectives.q1_source: "To support the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to assist those most vulnerable in contexts of natural disasters, mass population movement, health and food crises and to cope with the effects of climate change." (D0001354.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: delivery of more effective life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable, rapidly and at scale
better prepared and coordinated National Societies that can prevent or anticipate future humanitarian crises through improved early and anticipatory action
stronger, more sustainable and accountable Red Cross partners able to maximise the impact of bilateral FCDO and wider humanitarian resources
percentage of IFRC-supported operations applying minimum standards for protection, gender and inclusion in emergencies
number of people reached by protection, gender and inclusion programming
number of National Societies with a PSEA Policy and Action Plan to enforce prevention and support survivors
q3_expected_outputs.target: 150 National Societies by 2025

q3_expected_outputs.output: number of BRC-supported National Societies that integrate and institutionalise minimum operating standards for PSEA in their policies, operations and procedures

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the humanitarian capability of the IFRC and BRC to deliver rapid, effective responses to crises while improving accountability, inclusion, and anticipatory action across the Red Cross Movement. It combines core funding with performance incentives to drive organizational improvements.

quote.objectives: "delivery of more effective life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable, rapidly and at scale; better prepared and coordinated National Societies that can prevent or anticipate future humanitarian crises through improved early and anticipatory action; stronger, more sustainable and accountable Red Cross partners able to maximise the impact of bilateral FCDO and wider humanitarian resources to deliver value-for-money interventions in crises worldwide." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)
quote.approach: "This programme is designed to support the IFRC and BRC, and by extension the wider National Society network, to assist the most vulnerable in contexts of natural and man-made disasters, conflict, mass population movement and health and food crises, as well as cope with the effects of climate change." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in high-risk environments where National Societies deliver preparedness activities and emergency responses, often in contexts with complex fiduciary, safeguarding, and reputational risks. The overall programme risk rating is classified as 'major'.
where_context.q5_source: "The risks associated with this programme are considered 'major' overall. This is in line with the risk appetite of the FCDO for a humanitarian programme and reflects the risk level of the predecessor programme." (D0001354.odt, Risk)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The IFRC and National Societies operate in environments with significant security, safeguarding, and fiduciary risks, which complicate the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Conflict and climate change exacerbate vulnerabilities, particularly for marginalized groups such as women, girls, and people with disabilities.

quote.risk: "The IFRC and National Societies operate in high-risk environments delivering preparedness activities and emergency responses. These are often contexts which present complex fiduciary, safeguarding and reputational risks." (D0001354.odt, Risk)
quote.constraints: "Conflict and crises disproportionately affect marginalised peoples such as women and girls and people with disabilities, trapping them in cycles of worsening vulnerability." (D0001354.odt, Background - Global humanitarian context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The IFRC (multilateral) and BRC (UK-based) lead decision-making, with National Societies (Southern partners) implementing programmes under their coordination and capacity-building support. The BRC and IFRC provide strategic direction, oversight, and funding to National Societies.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on gender and diversity inclusion
support for National Societies to develop and adopt PSEA policies
improved National Society preparedness and coordination
strengthening accountability and feedback mechanisms
technical support for anticipatory action and early warning systems

partner_organizations.name: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
partner_organizations.role: coordination of National Societies, global representation, capacity building, and emergency response

partner_organizations.name: British Red Cross (BRC)
partner_organizations.role: strategic partner to IFRC, capacity building for National Societies, auxiliary to UK Government, donor to the Movement

partner_organizations.name: 192 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
partner_organizations.role: local implementation of humanitarian responses, auxiliary to their governments, first responders in crises

quote.structure: "The IFRC is largest humanitarian network in the world comprising 14 million volunteers and Red Cross/Red Crescent National Societies in 192 countries." (D0001354.odt, Programme summary)
quote.capacity_building: "UK funding will promote improvements in Red Cross agencies’ transparency, accountability and risk management, including the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), contributing to a more effective and efficient humanitarian system that delivers better for the most vulnerable." (D0001354.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)
quote.decision_power: "The IFRC represents National Societies in global forums and coordinates their actions in disasters of international concern and humanitarian emergencies. It also helps to build the capacities of National Societies." (D0001354.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme provides unearmarked, multi-year core funding to the IFRC (£9m/year) and BRC (£2m/year) to strengthen their humanitarian capabilities. This includes a Payment by Results (PbR) component (30% of funds) tied to pre-agreed targets for organizational improvements, such as PSEA, accountability, and anticipatory action.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The IFRC and BRC manage their respective components of the programme, with the IFRC coordinating National Societies globally and the BRC providing targeted support to selected National Societies. The FCDO retains oversight through annual reviews, quarterly discussions, and the PbR mechanism.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The IFRC and BRC were selected based on their unique mandate as part of the Red Cross Movement, their global reach, and their established track record as effective humanitarian partners. The business case states there is 'no comparable channel' for the proposed core funding, given the Movement's distinctive role in the humanitarian system.

quote.instrument: "The UK will provide three years of unearmarked core funding to the IFRC and BRC. This builds on the recommendation in the Project Completion Report (PCR) for the previous core funding programme, which gave the programme an overall score of 'A', that predictable and flexible multi-year funding is important to enable partners to achieve value-for-money efficiencies." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)
quote.selection: "Given the IFRC and BRC’s comparative advantages set out in the Strategic Case, namely their worldwide presence and record of delivery, there is no comparable channel for the proposed core funding component of this programme." (D0001354.odt, Strategic decisions)

quote.management: "The IFRC and BRC will deliver the two programme components, with FCDO oversight through annual reviews and quarterly discussions." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)
quote.oversight: "The programme will continue the UK’s innovative payment by results (PBR) approach, under which 30% of funds are conditional upon attainment of pre-agreed targets designed to incentivise achievement of results most important for the successful delivery of the programme’s Theory of Change." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes an Internal Risk Facility (IRF) of up to £6m (£2m/year) to respond to unforeseen humanitarian spikes. While core funding is largely unearmarked, the IRF allows for rapid reallocation to crises where FCDO has limited presence, subject to FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The PbR targets and IRF allow for adjustments based on emerging needs, but significant changes require FCDO agreement. The programme is designed to be adaptive to crises, with the IRF enabling faster responses to new or deteriorating situations.

quote.reallocation: "This programme also proposes to include an Internal Risk Facility (IRF) with a ceiling of £6 million that could be drawn on to support IFRC-led/funded National Society responses. An IRF is a contingency mechanism within a Business Case that can be deployed to support an unforeseen shock or spike in humanitarian need." (D0001354.odt, Internal Risk Facility)
quote.adaptive: "The IRF will allow the UK to respond with greater flexibility through the IFRC and National Societies to new humanitarian crises in contexts with minimal FCDO capacity such as the Caribbean and Indo-Pacific." (D0001354.odt, Internal Risk Facility)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IFRC/BRC → National Societies (end implementers)

quote.layers: "The IFRC directly implements the majority of its programmes through the IFRC regional and country offices, National Societies, as well as the ICRC." (D0001354.odt, Review of IFRC)
quote.payment: "The programme will continue the UK’s innovative payment by results (PBR) approach, under which 30% of funds are conditional upon attainment of pre-agreed targets." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)

q24_alternatives_considered.option: £33m funding for the IFRC and BRC channelled bilaterally instead of as core funding
q24_alternatives_considered.assessment: Limited evidence; would reduce flexibility and UK influence over Movement-wide improvements.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Core funding to the IFRC and BRC with 0% PBR
q24_alternatives_considered.assessment: Medium/limited evidence; lacks incentives for organizational improvements.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Core funding to the IFRC and BRC with 30% PBR
q24_alternatives_considered.assessment: Medium/strong evidence; aligns with past success in driving reforms.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Core funding to the IFRC and BRC with 30% PBR and establishment of an Internal Risk Facility (IRF)
q24_alternatives_considered.assessment: Medium/strong evidence; combines core funding with flexibility for rapid crisis response.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 (core funding with 30% PBR + IRF) was chosen because it maximizes value for money by combining predictable multi-year funding with performance incentives and flexibility to respond to crises. The IRF enables rapid disbursement in underfunded or hard-to-reach contexts, while the PBR mechanism ensures accountability for key improvements (e.g., PSEA, anticipatory action). This aligns with the UK’s ambition to drive a more effective humanitarian system (IDS 2022) and builds on lessons from previous programmes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: National Societies may not fully embrace or sustain improvements funded by the programme, limiting impact.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The PBR mechanism incentivizes adoption of reforms, and the IFRC/BRC will provide targeted capacity-building support. Progress is monitored through quarterly discussions and annual reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays or inefficiencies in disbursing IRF funds could limit rapid response.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The IRF is designed as a contingency mechanism with pre-agreed criteria for activation, reducing administrative delays. Lessons from DFID’s Somalia IRF (2017) inform its design.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on IFRC/BRC for oversight of National Societies may lead to gaps in accountability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The PBR targets include strengthening IFRC’s central assurance functions, and FCDO conducts regular Central Assurance Assessments of the Movement.

quote.why_chosen: "Option 4 is recommended. This is assessed as the best option to meet the stated objectives whilst ensuring maximum impact for FCDO resources and sustained UK influence. This option is expected to deliver maximum value for money (VfM), supporting the proposed shifts outlined in the theory of change." (D0001354.odt, Conclusion of appraisal)
quote.risks: "The results achieved on this agenda will depend on i) the ability of IFRC to influence the processes and approaches of National Societies, and ii) the corresponding willingness of National Societies to embrace the opportunities offered through FCDO’s core investment." (D0001354.odt, Building on lessons learned)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global, high-risk operating environment (conflict, climate change, weak institutions) necessitates partners with a permanent local presence and auxiliary status to governments. This limits viable implementers to the Red Cross Movement, as National Societies are uniquely positioned to operate in restrictive contexts where other NGOs or UN agencies may face access challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with legal mandate and neutrality to operate in conflict zones (e.g., National Societies’ auxiliary status)
Requirement for rapid response capabilities in climate-vulnerable regions (e.g., IFRC’s DREF for early action)
Safeguarding and fiduciary risks in fragile contexts demand robust oversight (e.g., PSEA standards)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—delivering life-saving assistance at scale, improving anticipatory action, and strengthening accountability—require a decentralized but coordinated structure. The IFRC’s federated model (global Secretariat + National Societies) is uniquely suited to balance local responsiveness with global standards, while the PBR mechanism ensures alignment with UK priorities (e.g., PSEA, inclusion).
q28_linkages: Global-local model (IFRC + National Societies) enables rapid, localized responses while maintaining accountability to UK standards.
PbR targets (e.g., PSEA, gender inclusion) directly address UK policy priorities (IDS 2022, Grand Bargain 2.0).
IRF complements core funding by filling gaps in underfunded crises, aligning with the ‘Prevent’ pillar of the UK Humanitarian Framework.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
The programme explicitly balances efficiency (rapid, large-scale responses via IFRC/BRC) with equity (targeted support for marginalized groups). For example: 
- **Speed vs. inclusion**: The IRF enables quick disbursements but includes targets for gender and disability inclusion in programming.
- **Global standards vs. local adaptation**: PbR incentivizes Movement-wide improvements (e.g., PSEA policies) while allowing National Societies to adapt approaches to their contexts.
- **Cost vs. reach**: Core funding prioritizes National Societies in high-need countries, even where FCDO has no presence, accepting higher oversight costs for greater impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed of response (IRF) vs. ensuring inclusion of vulnerable groups (disaggregated data targets)
Centralized oversight (IFRC/BRC) vs. National Societies’ local autonomy
Cost of PBR monitoring vs. value of driving organizational reforms
intersections.risk_affects_management:
The ‘major’ risk profile (high-risk environments, safeguarding concerns) justifies intensive oversight mechanisms: 
- **PbR**: 30% of funds tied to performance targets (e.g., PSEA, accountability) to mitigate reputational and fiduciary risks.
- **Quarterly reviews**: More frequent than annual to address dynamic crises.
- **IRF safeguards**: Pre-agreed activation criteria to prevent misuse in volatile contexts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity-building objectives (e.g., National Society preparedness, PSEA standards) define partner roles: 
- **IFRC**: Leads coordination, sets global standards, and monitors National Societies.
- **BRC**: Provides technical support (e.g., cash programming, CEA) to weaker National Societies.
- **National Societies**: Implement programmes with increasing responsibility as their capacity grows (e.g., anticipatory action pilots).

quote.where_who: "The IFRC and National Societies operate in high-risk environments delivering preparedness activities and emergency responses. These are often contexts which present complex fiduciary, safeguarding and reputational risks." (D0001354.odt, Risk)
quote.what_how: "The programme is designed to support the IFRC and BRC, and by extension the wider National Society network, to assist the most vulnerable in contexts of natural and man-made disasters... through improved early and anticipatory action." (D0001354.odt, Theory of Change and how this programme will deliver results)
quote.equity_efficiency: "By putting beneficiary and population accountability at the forefront, including through a focus on the specific needs of women, girls and people with disabilities, the investments under this Business Case will build on previous Movement funding streams to continue to strengthen the Movement focus on equity." (D0001354.odt, Value for Money - Equity)

key_programme_risks: National Societies may not fully adopt or sustain improvements (e.g., PSEA policies, anticipatory action) funded by the programme.
Delays in IRF activation could limit rapid response to spikes in humanitarian need.
Safeguarding incidents (SEAH) could damage reputation and effectiveness, particularly in high-risk contexts.
