who_partners.quote: "The UK guarantee would be to AfDB lending of $1bn to South Africa... The UK would agree the projects covered by the guarantee with the AfDB." (D0006477.odt, Designing the guarantee: options appraisal) AND "The programme will be managed by the British High Commission (BHC) in South Africa. The Just Energy Transition working group, formed of a mixture of technical and policy experts, chaired by the Deputy High Commissioner, will oversee the programme." (D0004749.odt, Governance)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a mix of funding instruments including a guarantee agreement with AfDB (contingent liability), accountable grants with non-profits, commercial contracts with private entities, and memoranda of understanding with multilaterals. The guarantee enables AfDB to lend up to $1bn to South Africa for JETP projects, while grants and contracts support technical assistance and project preparation.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a partnership between FCDO, AfDB, and the South African government. FCDO South Africa engages with AfDB on project selection and monitors risk, while AfDB administers loans and pursues recoveries. A Just Energy Transition working group in South Africa oversees day-to-day delivery, with technical and policy experts providing input.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The selection of AfDB as the primary partner is based on its existing lending portfolio in South Africa, strong relationship with the South African government, and ability to manage risk. The use of a framework agreement (IMDP) for other partners allows for flexibility and leverages pre-approved suppliers to maximize efficiency and value for money.
how_mechanism.quote: "The programme will use a mix of modalities for implementation: Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with multilaterals; Accountable Grants (AGs) with non-profit organisations; and possibly a commercial contract with a private entity." (D0004749.odt, Commercial Approach and Requirement) AND "The UK through FCDO will guarantee AfDB investment lending of $1bn to South Africa... The UK guarantee would be to AfDB lending of $1bn to South Africa." (D0006477.odt, Term of UK Guarantee)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Just Energy Transition working group in South Africa, chaired by the Deputy High Commissioner, oversees the programme and decides which proposals to support. The group includes technical and policy experts and meets weekly. For the guarantee, FCDO South Africa engages with AfDB on project selection, and a Memorandum of Understanding outlines the agreed scope and criteria for projects.
how_governance.quote: "The programme will be managed by the British High Commission (BHC) in South Africa. The Just Energy Transition working group, formed of a mixture of technical and policy experts, chaired by the Deputy High Commissioner, will oversee the programme and decide, using the above criteria, and suitability, which proposals to support as discrete projects." (D0004749.odt, Governance) AND "FCDO South Africa will engage with the AfDB country team about all proposed lending operations enabled by the Guarantee, to ensure they meet the criteria to be agreed with AfDB." (D0006477.odt, Management Arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be shifted between components (within RDEL and CDEL constraints) to achieve best value for money, but significant changes require approval. The programme is designed to be flexible to respond to strategic needs as they arise, with adaptive programming and break clauses included in contracts.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses adaptive management with review points and break/scale-up/down clauses in contracts. Task orders allow for adjustments based on emerging evidence and political risks, particularly in dealing with municipalities.
how_flexibility.quote: "Flexibility would be needed to shift between components (working within RDEL and CDEL constraints) so as to achieve best value for money and results." (D0006341.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?) AND "The contract includes break clauses (before the next spending review and in 2027) and uses adaptive programming – Task Orders with review points and break/scale up and scale down elements in them to manage the political risk of dealing with municipalities in particular." (D0006341.odt, Commercial and Management Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → AfDB/Implementing Partners → End Beneficiaries (municipalities, SMEs, communities)
how_efficiency.quote: "The total budget is up to £5m, all programme RDEL/CDEL... BHCSouthAfrica will agree a budget for each project." (D0004749.odt, Budget and Cost Drivers) AND "The contract includes break clauses... and uses adaptive programming – Task Orders with review points..." (D0006341.odt, Commercial and Management Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: scaling up existing grant support (ruled out due to budget constraints and scale of financing gap)
working through alternative Multilateral Development Banks (ruled out as they don’t face lending constraints in South Africa)
providing alternative forms of support to AfDB (ruled out as capital increases require payments from all shareholders)
doing nothing (ruled out as it would damage UK’s reputation and South Africa’s ability to finance JETP)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The guarantee to AfDB was chosen because it enables additional lending at below-market rates, leverages AfDB’s existing relationship with South Africa, and provides flexibility to support a range of projects aligned with JETP priorities. The mixed delivery structure (grants, contracts, MOUs) allows for responsiveness to emerging needs while maintaining value for money and risk management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of default by South Africa on AfDB loans, triggering UK guarantee payments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: AfDB’s Preferred Creditor Status reduces likelihood of default; UK will monitor risk quarterly and has structured the guarantee with pro-rata risk sharing and a 180-day grace period before calls.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political resistance to coal plant closures and energy reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with communities and unions to demonstrate job creation and economic benefits; adaptive programming to respond to political economy challenges.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited capacity in South African municipalities to deliver projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on ‘learning by doing’ with technical assistance embedded in project preparation; avoid standalone training due to high staff turnover.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Corruption and mismanagement in Eskom and other entities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of supervised procurement mechanisms, involvement of South African Treasury, and regular reporting on corruption risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations increasing UK exposure
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monitor exchange rate risk regularly; structure guarantee to account for long maturity and gradual disbursement.

why_rationale.quote: "We judge the proposed guarantee is economical because it will increase AfDB lending at a very low administrative and most likely financial cost (see Financial case) to the UK... We assess efficiency by considering how much additional AfDB lending capacity the guarantee unlocks. This is par: $1bn guarantee enables $1bn of new and additional lending capacity." (D0006477.odt, Value for Money) AND "The programme will use a mix of modalities for implementation: Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with multilaterals; Accountable Grants (AGs) with non-profit organisations; and possibly a commercial contract with a private entity. This approach is to ensure we can remain flexible in response to the changing needs and opportunities throughout the Just Energy Transition programme." (D0004749.odt, Commercial Approach and Requirement)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political and institutional context in South Africa constrains partner selection by requiring partners with strong local relationships and technical capacity to navigate complex stakeholders (e.g., Eskom, municipalities, unions). The need for social acceptance of coal plant closures also necessitates partners who can engage effectively with communities and demonstrate tangible benefits.
q27_constraints_detail: resistance from coal-dependent communities and unions
limited capacity in municipalities and local institutions
corruption risks in state-owned enterprises like Eskom
need for partners with existing networks in South Africa
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for flexible, demand-driven support to respond to emerging JETP priorities (e.g., project preparation, SME investments, policy reforms) determines the mixed delivery structure. The combination of financing mechanisms, technical assistance, and capacity building is designed to address both the energy transition and the 'Just' elements (jobs, livelihoods) simultaneously.
q28_linkages: financing mechanisms (guarantee, CDEL) enable large-scale infrastructure projects while grants support SMEs and community livelihoods
technical assistance embedded in project preparation builds capacity in municipalities and national institutions
adaptive management allows for shifts between components (e.g., project prep vs. transformational change) based on political and practical issues
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between the need for rapid, large-scale infrastructure investments (efficiency) and the requirement to ensure inclusive, equitable outcomes (e.g., job creation in coal regions, community engagement). The use of performance-based contracts and blended finance aims to balance these objectives by incentivizing private sector efficiency while targeting social benefits.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed of infrastructure delivery vs. inclusive community consultation
large-scale AfDB loans vs. targeted grants for SMEs and livelihoods
Northern expertise (e.g., AfDB, UK consultants) vs. local ownership and capacity building
cost of technical assistance vs. reach of benefits to marginalized groups
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk profile (political, institutional, corruption) necessitates intensive oversight, including quarterly risk reviews, adaptive programming, and embedded technical assistance. The management structure is designed to mitigate risks through joint decision-making (FCDO, AfDB, South African government) and flexible funding reallocation.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme through technical assistance to municipalities and national institutions, with a focus on 'learning by doing' rather than standalone training. Partners like AfDB and consultants are selected for their ability to transfer skills and build local capacity during project implementation.
intersections.quote: "The programme will be managed by the British High Commission (BHC) in South Africa. The Just Energy Transition working group... will oversee the programme and decide... which proposals to support as discrete projects." (D0004749.odt, Governance) AND "The UK guarantee would be to AfDB lending of $1bn to South Africa... The UK would agree the projects covered by the guarantee with the AfDB." (D0006477.odt, Designing the guarantee: options appraisal) AND "Flexibility would be needed to shift between components (working within RDEL and CDEL constraints) so as to achieve best value for money and results." (D0006341.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

key_programme_risks: Political environment acting as a barrier to meaningful change
Domestic challenges in South Africa distracting from Just Transition priorities
Insufficient UK and South African staff and technical capacity to deliver impact
Policy advice and research not being acted on by the South African government
Lack of coherence of projects with existing JET work in South Africa
Risk of funds not flowing from partners to end use (fiduciary risk)
Recipients of programmes being harmed (safeguarding risk)
Default by South Africa on AfDB loans triggering UK guarantee payments
Exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations increasing UK exposure
Corruption and mismanagement in Eskom and other South African entities
Limited pipeline of investable projects in South Africa
High staff turnover in municipalities limiting capacity building effectiveness

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political environment acting as a barrier to meaningful change
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Ensure areas of work are fully demand-driven and have sufficient buy-in from UK and South African counterparts; use adaptive and flexible programme mechanisms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Domestic challenges in South Africa distracting from Just Transition priorities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Create a true partnership between UK and South Africa with engagement from the beginning; use adaptive and flexible programme mechanisms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient UK and South African staff and technical capacity
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support capacity through technical assistance where needed; choose policy areas intentionally based on capacity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Policy advice and research not acted on by South African government
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strong engagement with South African government on the 'so what' from policy research; political analysis supports each project selection.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of coherence with existing JET work
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Advanced stakeholder coordination and mapping to ensure join-up and complementarity.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fiduciary risk (funds flow from partner to end use)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Supply chain will be developed during inception to assess risks and identify mitigations; monitored quarterly.
Rigorous safeguarding approach with mandatory reporting, risk registers, and monitoring through monthly engagement.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Default by South Africa on AfDB loans
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: AfDB’s Preferred Creditor Status and graduated sanctions policy reduce risk; UK will monitor exchange rate and interest rate risks regularly.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Corruption in Eskom and South African entities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use supervised procurement mechanisms and involve South African Treasury; require reporting from AfDB on corruption risks.
Focus on project preparation to develop bankable projects; leverage AfDB’s experience and technical assistance.
Avoid standalone training; focus on 'learning by doing' and embedding technical assistance in project delivery.

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for adaptive programming to respond to political and institutional volatility
Importance of embedding technical assistance to build capacity in weak institutions
Use of performance-based contracts to incentivize private sector efficiency while targeting social outcomes
Leveraging multilateral partners (e.g., AfDB) to manage sovereign risk and provide concessional finance
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous experience with PPP capacity building in South Africa showed limited success due to staff turnover and scattered responsibility across agencies. The current programme avoids standalone training and focuses on institutional stability (e.g., National Treasury) and 'learning by doing.' Evidence from non-revenue water projects globally demonstrates the cost-effectiveness of performance-based contracts, which are being applied in this programme.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates adaptive management with review points, break clauses, and task orders to respond to emerging risks and opportunities. The focus on project preparation and blended finance reflects lessons about the need for bankable projects and risk-sharing mechanisms in South Africa’s context.
risks_lessons.quote: "The key risks are set out in Figure 2 above... The programme team will refine and update this at least every six months, or more frequently as needed, during programme implementation." (D0004749.odt, Risk) AND "The UK guarantee would be to AfDB lending of $1bn to South Africa... The AfDB’s practice is to follow a graduated approach using reminders, incentives and sanctions when dealing with clients with overdue debt service." (D0006477.odt, Guarantee Recoveries) AND "The programme will use a mix of modalities for implementation... This approach is to ensure we can remain flexible in response to the changing needs and opportunities." (D0004749.odt, Commercial Approach and Requirement)

co_funding_partners.partner: International Partners Group (IPG: UK, US, Germany, France, EU, Netherlands, Denmark)
British International Investment (BII) and Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG)
Other development partners (e.g., World Bank, German Development Bank KfW, French Development Agency AFD)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK guarantee to AfDB is expected to unlock $1bn in additional lending to South Africa, which will catalyze further private and public investment in the JETP. The programme aims to mobilize $200m in climate finance by 2027, with an additional $500m in private finance envisaged.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both capital expenditures (e.g., infrastructure projects, SME investments) and revenue expenditures (e.g., technical assistance, capacity building). The guarantee covers principal and interest repayments on AfDB loans, while grants and contracts support project preparation and transformational change.
financial_details.quote: "The cost extension would finance: continued technical assistance for the investment project pipeline... additional transformational change work... potential CDEL – for the Just side of the transition – primarily for blending... a programme funded adviser." (D0006341.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?) AND "The UK through FCDO will guarantee AfDB investment lending of $1bn to South Africa... The guarantee has no DEL cost unless called." (D0006477.odt, Programme Value) AND "The total budget is up to £5m, all programme RDEL/CDEL... The Programme does not involve financial aid to governments." (D0004749.odt, Budget and Cost Drivers)

metadata.programme_name: ACTION (Accelerating Climate Transition and Innovation) Rwanda

quote.programme_summary: "ACTION Rwanda will build the climate resilience of the most vulnerable to climate shocks, delivering UK International Climate Finance (ICF) commitments to support Rwanda’s Nationally Determined Contribution." (D0006187.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "AMPEndDate: 01/04/2029" and "AMPStartDate: 2024" (D0006187.odt, Programme details)

metadata.duration_source: "Programme Value: up to £15 million over 5 years (100% ICF contribution)" (D0006187.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ACTION Rwanda combines financing (direct financial aid through Intego Facility), capacity building (technical assistance to government agencies), evidence generation (MERL component), and implementation research (testing adaptation solutions). It aims to build climate resilience while strengthening institutional capacity and generating transferable lessons.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ACTION Rwanda will build the climate resilience of the most vulnerable to climate shocks, delivering UK International Climate Finance (ICF) commitments... It will use a multi-component approach that delivers technical assistance to support catalytic change, invests in Monitoring, Evidence, Research and Learning (MERL) to improve programming, and enhances a Rwandan public sector facility (Intego) to invest in sustainable infrastructure..." (D0006187.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: GoR technical assistance requests responded to in a timely and effective manner
Intego facility replenished and functioning as an effective public sector financing facility
Increased connections made to other HMG programming demonstrating a cohesive UK approach
Research published that informs policy on national planning and public sector (with BCRs of 4.1 assumed)
Number of people supported to better adapt to climate change effects (ICF KPI1)
Amount of public finance mobilised (ICF KPI11)
Transformational impact scorecard (ICF KPI15)
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers UK climate finance commitments through three components: 1) technical assistance to strengthen Rwandan institutions, 2) MERL to generate evidence on effective adaptation, and 3) direct financial aid via the Intego Facility to fund public sector climate resilience projects. It targets systemic change in climate governance while demonstrating measurable resilience outcomes.

quote.objectives: "ACTION Rwanda programme delivers on a key international development priority for the UK to tackle climate change and protect nature... It will use a multi-component approach to galvanise public action on climate change..." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.outputs: "Outputs: GoR technical assistance requests responded to in a timely and effective manner; Intego facility replenished and functioning as an effective public sector financing facility... Research published that informs policy on national planning and public sector" (D0006187.odt, Programme Impact and Outcomes)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The document explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006187.odt). Rwanda is classified as a Least Developed Country with significant climate vulnerability (2.5% GDP loss projected by 2050) but has stable governance institutions and a track record of climate action (e.g., Rwanda Green Fund).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006187.odt, Programme details)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate risks (floods/droughts) directly threaten programme outcomes, requiring adaptive management. Institutional constraints in sectors like agriculture limit absorption capacity for funds. Data gaps (e.g., on local climate impacts) hinder evidence-based planning. Regulatory barriers were noted for carbon market development (Component 5 was discounted due to limited FCDO expertise).

quote.climate_risks: "Extreme climate events like flooding and droughts are increasing in Rwanda... The cost of inaction on adapting to the realities of climate change in Rwanda are simply too high." (D0006187.odt, Context and Challenges)
quote.institutional: "The need for FCDO intervention: Investing in climate adaptation and resilience can reduce the economic costs of climate change in Rwanda over the next 20 years... Delivering effective adaptation is challenging, and its efficiency and effectiveness can be enhanced by institutional strengthening, capacity building and technical assistance." (D0006187.odt, The need for FCDO intervention)
quote.data: "There is still a relatively low global evidence base on adaptation programming, and a need for better evidence and learning." (D0006187.odt, The need for FCDO intervention)
quote.regulatory: "For Component 5, FCDO has limited comparative advantage on carbon markets in Rwanda (despite CMPs including Ci-Dev working regionally), with other development partners possessing greater technical expertise..." (D0006187.odt, The options for FCDO intervention)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Rwanda (GoR) via Rwanda Green Fund (RGF)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Government of Rwanda (GoR) retains decision-making authority over technical assistance requests, Intego facility priorities, and MERL focus areas. FCDO provides funding and strategic oversight but defers to GoR institutions for operational decisions, as evidenced by the demand-led TA approach and direct financing to RGF.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to GoR agencies (e.g., MINECOFIN, RGF)
institutional strengthening of RGF’s M&E and inclusion expertise
training for public sector climate planning (e.g., NST2 integration)
MERL component to build evidence for adaptive learning
support for climate governance coordination across ministries

partner_organizations.name: Rwanda Green Fund (RGF)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner; manages Intego Facility and receives direct financial aid

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning (MINECOFIN)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of technical assistance for climate mainstreaming in national planning

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Environment (MoE)
partner_organizations.role: Policy coordination and NDC implementation support

partner_organizations.name: District governments
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries of Intego Facility funding for local adaptation projects

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Kigali
partner_organizations.role: Funding and strategic oversight; technical backstopping

partner_organizations.name: Met Office
partner_organizations.role: Provider of climate data/weather patterns (complementary programme)

partner_organizations.name: Scottish Government
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder of climate justice programming (aligned with ACTION)

quote.southern_led: "ACTION Rwanda programme delivers on a key international development priority... It will use a multi-component approach to galvanise public action on climate change... Component 3 provides direct adaptation support to public sector institutions and builds on the UK’s strong previous track record." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.capacity_building: "Capacity building – including technical assistance and institutional strengthening – is a high potential adaptation ‘Best Buy’... We will use a flexible and demand-led approach to target TA where it is most needed: whether to RGF, MINECOFIN or another GoR entity to improve the enabling environment and progress delivery towards Rwanda’s NDCs." (D0006187.odt, Component 1. Technical Assistance)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) **direct financial aid** (block funding to RGF’s Intego Facility for public sector projects), 2) **technical assistance contracts** (likely competitive grants or framework agreements for TA providers), and 3) **MERL grants** (flexible funding for research/learning activities). The Intego Facility operates as a multi-donor trust fund with proposal-based disbursements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO provides funding and high-level oversight, while the Government of Rwanda (via RGF and line ministries) manages day-to-day delivery. Technical assistance and MERL components are demand-driven, with priorities set jointly but led by GoR. The Intego Facility uses a proposal-based system for sub-awards to districts/public bodies.
how_mechanism.q14_partner_selection_method: direct award (for RGF); restricted competition (for TA/MERL)
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (for TA/MERL); direct award to RGF
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: RGF was selected via direct award due to FCDO’s long-standing partnership (including prior £20m capitalisation) and its role as Rwanda’s national climate fund. TA/MERL providers are likely selected through restricted competition based on FCDO’s framework agreements, given the demand-led and flexible nature of these components.

quote.funding_instruments: "Component 3. Direct Financial Aid for Adaptation: The final component provides direct financial aid for adaptation, aligned to key priorities in the NDC in the climate resilience space. This would include targeting adaptation to the most vulnerable and providing support to the RGF through the Intego (NDC) Facility." (D0006187.odt, Component 3)
quote.rfg_role: "The RGF is now moving to a new phase, maturing to deliver through distinct public and private sector windows, to assist with the financing of the updated NDC. This will require a further evolution of finance and programming." (D0006187.odt, The Rwanda Green Fund)
quote.ta_selection: "We will use a flexible and demand-led approach to target TA where it is most needed: whether to RGF, MINECOFIN or another GoR entity..." (D0006187.odt, Component 1)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The RGF Board of Directors oversees the Intego Facility, with FCDO represented alongside other donors. Technical decisions for TA/MERL are made jointly between FCDO and GoR, while Intego sub-awards use a proposal review process involving both RGF and FCDO input. The document notes: "Intego facility replenished and functioning as an effective public sector financing facility, with links made to other donors and technical assistance offers to the extent possible."

quote.governance: "Reporting from Rwanda Green Fund through its formal structures, including Auditor General reporting, Board of Directors reporting and specific partner reporting on the impact of the Intego facility" (D0006187.odt, Programme Impact and Outcomes)
quote.oversight: "We will carry out independent monitoring using the MERL component to verify results on a periodic basis, aligning reviews with independent audits of other development partners to the extent possible." (D0006187.odt, Programme Impact and Outcomes)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the TA and MERL components can be reallocated based on demand (e.g., shifting focus between ministries or research topics), but Intego Facility funds are earmarked for public sector adaptation projects via proposal rounds. Major reallocations between components would require approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The TA and MERL components use a demand-led approach, allowing priorities to adjust annually based on GoR needs and emerging evidence. The MERL component explicitly includes "deep dives into unlocking financing for hard-to-reach sectors" as an adaptive feature. However, significant shifts (e.g., adding new sectors) would require FCDO approval.

quote.flexibility: "Decision B: Within components 1 & 2 should the TA and MERL (a) have a medium term (2- or 3-year plan) set out in advance, or (b) be more flexible with short-term (e.g., 6 month) priorities agreed and then delivered?" (D0006187.odt, Decisions within ACTION programme components)
quote.adaptive_merl: "Examples of activities under this demand-driven component will include: technical dialogues to unlock complex adaptation issues, research into what works and why in the public resilience space, and lessons sharing with others..." (D0006187.odt, Component 2. MERL)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Government of Rwanda (RGF/line ministries) → [end beneficiaries: districts/communities]. The MERL component may add a third layer if external researchers are commissioned.

quote.layers: "ACTION will further complement a broad set of FCDO centrally managed programmes... utilising latest weather pattern data from the Met Office project; and crucially finding synergies between Intego and Ireme Invest..." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.payments: "The Facility [Intego] works through proposal rounds to provide public sector financing for key districts and public sector bodies to deliver on the adaptation priorities outlined within Rwanda’s NDCs." (D0006187.odt, Component 3)

q24_alternatives_considered: Component 1 only (TA to government agencies)
Component 2 only (MERL/research)
Component 3 only (direct support to RGF)
Component 4 (support to Ireme Invest private sector facility) - discounted due to overlap with existing UK support
Component 5 (carbon market facility) - discounted due to limited FCDO expertise
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (Components 1+2+3) was selected to: 1) **leverage FCDO’s comparative advantage** in technical assistance and direct financing (via prior RGF engagement), 2) **address multiple adaptation barriers** (policy, evidence, finance access) simultaneously, 3) **align with Rwanda’s NDC priorities** (which require both institutional strengthening and project funding), and 4) **balance flexibility with accountability** through demand-led TA/MERL and structured Intego financing.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (high BCRs for TA/capacity building)
risk mitigation (direct funding to trusted RGF partner)
partner capacity (RGF’s fiduciary strength and NDC alignment)
flexibility (demand-led TA/MERL to adapt to emerging needs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on RGF’s institutional capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fiduciary risk assessments and targeted TA to strengthen RGF’s governance (e.g., gender/safeguarding expertise). The 2023 assessment identified gaps, with recommendations adopted by multiple donors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MERL component explicitly links TA and Intego outcomes, with joint monitoring frameworks. "Increased connections made to other HMG programming that demonstrates a cohesive UK approach."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Demand-led TA/MERL leading to misalignment with UK priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual joint planning sessions between FCDO and GoR to align TA/MERL focus with both NDC and UK climate goals.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (BCRs of 4.1 assumed for Intego; >10:1 for TA)
economy (leveraging existing RGF platform to reduce setup costs)
equity (targeting vulnerable groups via Intego’s public sector focus)

quote.rationale: "Having consulted with GoR, analysed other development partners’ activities, and assessed FCDO’s comparative programming advantages, it is recommended that the ACTION programme will work on a combination of Components 1, 2 and 3..." (D0006187.odt, The options for FCDO intervention)
quote.vfm: "Capacity building and institutional strengthening is generally reported as being extremely effective... Some international reviews have identified high economic benefits... reporting results of >10:1..." (D0006187.odt, Assessment of the three ACTION components)
quote.risks: "We have already identified a number of gaps within RGF’s operations and governance arrangements (for example, needing a greater level of gender, social inclusion and safeguarding expertise) through our latest fiduciary risk assessment (2023)..." (D0006187.odt, Gender Equality and Social Inclusion)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Rwanda’s **moderate risk profile** (climate vulnerability + institutional strengths) shaped partner selection by: 1) **limiting eligibility to entities with strong fiduciary systems** (hence RGF’s central role), 2) **requiring local embeddedness** (TA providers must have existing GoR relationships), and 3) **prioritizing public sector partners** (due to weak private sector absorption capacity for climate finance). The document notes: "ACTION will focus on building on previous successes and further bolstering the capacity of GoR to meet own climate ambitions through this programme."
q27_constraints_detail: Fiduciary requirements (RGF selected due to its UN-awarded governance standards)
Local presence (TA providers must engage directly with ministries/districts)
Public sector focus (private sector component Ireme Invest handled separately due to capacity gaps)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (financing + capacity building + evidence) necessitated a **multi-component structure**: 1) **Direct financing** (Component 3) was tied to RGF’s Intego Facility to ensure alignment with NDC priorities, 2) **TA** (Component 1) was designed as demand-led to address governance barriers identified in the NDC, and 3) **MERL** (Component 2) was embedded to generate evidence on what works, given the "low global evidence base on adaptation programming." The document states: "We have drawn on the lessons learned from previous... programmes to design a new adaptation programme that helps address the challenges outlined above."
q28_linkages: NDC implementation gaps → TA component (Component 1) to strengthen coordination
Evidence gaps → MERL component (Component 2) for adaptive learning
Finance access barriers → Intego Facility (Component 3) for direct support
Cross-cutting gender/safeguarding needs → Integrated into all components via GESI goals
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions were noted between: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: The demand-led TA/MERL components prioritize GoR ownership but risk excluding marginalized groups (e.g., women, LGBTQI+) without targeted outreach. The document admits: "Additional consultation with vulnerable groups representatives were not conducted due to ACTION’s focus on strengthening national level systems... and the risk that this might set undue expectations of direct support to the CSOs." 2) **Scale vs. localization**: The Intego Facility targets district-level projects but relies on public sector absorption capacity, which varies geographically. 3) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern technical experts (e.g., for MERL) are used to ensure rigor, but the programme commits to "push GoR to be more responsive to vulnerable community needs."

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Demand-led components risk bypassing CSOs/vulnerable groups; mitigation via GESI goals and donor coordination.
Intego Facility uses proposal rounds to balance national priorities with local needs, but absorption capacity limits reach.
MERL component combines international research standards with Rwandan leadership (e.g., showcasing lessons at COP).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk rating** drives **milestone-based oversight** (e.g., periodic MERL reviews aligned with RGF audits) and **embedded safeguards** (e.g., fiduciary assessments for Intego). The document notes: "We will carry out independent monitoring using the MERL component to verify results on a periodic basis, aligning reviews with independent audits of other development partners." High-risk areas (e.g., gender inclusion gaps in RGF) trigger **intensive technical assistance** (Component 1).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: 1) RGF’s role expanded from fund manager to **technical leader** via TA (e.g., M&E systems, NDC alignment), 2) Line ministries (e.g., MINECOFIN) **co-design TA priorities** based on capacity needs, and 3) Districts **implement Intego projects** with embedded learning (MERL). The programme explicitly links capacity gains to role evolution: "Technical assistance and capacity-building efforts enhance the GoR’s ability to plan, react, and adapt to climate impacts."

quote.context_partners: "ACTION will focus on building on previous successes and further bolstering the capacity of GoR to meet own climate ambitions through this programme... Working through this Facility [Intego] will enable the increased domestic capability of the GoR to respond to the scale of the adaptation challenge." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.objectives_structure: "ACTION will address three key problems (barriers) to adaptation: 1) Policy and governance barriers... 2) Information failures around what works... 3) The need to channel adaptation finance to the most vulnerable." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.equity_tradeoffs: "The British High Commission in Kigali’s GESI analysis points to individual and community vulnerabilities in Rwanda based on six characteristics: gender, age, disability, LGBTQI+, refugee status and historically marginalised persons... We will continue to use our understanding of vulnerabilities to press the Government of Rwanda to be more inclusive." (D0006187.odt, Gender Equality and Social Inclusion)
quote.capacity_roles: "Component 1. Technical Assistance: In recent years, our technical assistance to the GoR... has helped to strengthen Rwanda’s climate coordination, national planning and delivery towards NDCs... We will use a flexible and demand-led approach to target TA where it is most needed." (D0006187.odt, Component 1)

key_programme_risks: Political will for climate commitments may wane due to competing priorities (e.g., youth employment, poverty reduction).
RGF’s absorption capacity for Intego funds may limit scaling.
Climate shocks (floods/droughts) could disrupt implementation or increase humanitarian needs.
Gender/social inclusion gaps in RGF operations may persist without targeted TA.
Fragmentation between ACTION components and other UK/Rwandan climate programmes.
Low global evidence on adaptation may hinder MERL component’s ability to generate actionable lessons.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political will for climate commitments may wane
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Align TA/MERL with NST2 and Vision 2050 priorities; use MERL to demonstrate economic benefits of adaptation (e.g., BCRs).
Targeted TA to strengthen RGF’s fiduciary systems; phased disbursements via Intego proposal rounds.
Intego Facility includes contingency funding for disaster response; MERL tracks climate impact on delivery.
GESI goals embedded in all components; joint donor pressure on RGF to adopt safeguarding recommendations.
MERL component explicitly links ACTION to other UK programmes (e.g., Ireme Invest, Met Office data).
MERL component prioritizes "what works" research; partnerships with LSE/Grantham Institute for rigorous methods.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from prior FCDO-RGF collaboration (2020 Programme Completion Review) highlighted the need for **flexible TA** to respond to evolving GoR priorities.
Rwanda’s **moderate risk profile** (stable governance but high climate vulnerability) demonstrated that **institutional strengthening** (e.g., RGF’s M&E systems) must precede large-scale financing.
The **demand-led approach** (from prior governance programmes) was adopted to ensure GoR ownership but required **embedded safeguards** (e.g., GESI audits) to mitigate exclusion risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **Technical Assistance**: Prior FCDO TA to RGF (e.g., for NST2 climate integration) showed that **embedded advisors** (vs. external consultants) improved uptake. 2) **Financing**: The RGF’s evolution from a single window to public/private sectors (Ireme Invest/Intego) demonstrated the need for **phased, adaptive funding mechanisms**. 3) **MERL**: Previous climate programmes in Rwanda lacked robust learning components; ACTION’s MERL was designed to fill this gap by **linking research to policy cycles** (e.g., NDC revisions).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Component 1 (TA)**: Shifted from pre-defined workplans to **demand-led priorities** based on lessons from rigid prior programmes. 2) **Component 3 (Intego)**: Added **explicit links to Ireme Invest** (private sector facility) to avoid duplication with existing UK support. 3) **Gender/Safeguarding**: Expanded GESI goals in all components after 2023 fiduciary assessments revealed gaps in RGF’s inclusion practices. 4) **MERL Flexibility**: Included **adaptive research topics** (e.g., cost of inaction studies) to respond to emerging evidence needs.

quote.risks: "Assumptions underpinning this Theory of Change include: Political will to meet Rwanda’s climate commitments remains strong... Rwanda’s governance and institutions responsible for carrying out their environmental obligations remain strong..." (D0006187.odt, Theory of Change)
quote.lessons: "We have drawn on the lessons learned from previous and existing programmes to design a new adaptation programme that helps address the challenges outlined above... Lessons include bolstering support for strong climate governance and leadership from Government of Rwanda institutions." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.design_changes: "ACTION will further complement a broad set of FCDO centrally managed programmes... crucially finding synergies between Intego and Ireme Invest – Rwanda’s private sector climate finance facility supported by the UK through its support for the Taskforce on Access to Climate Finance." (D0006187.odt, The ACTION Rwanda programme)
quote.fcas: "The RGF is now moving to a new phase, maturing to deliver through distinct public and private sector windows... This will require a further evolution of finance and programming." (D0006187.odt, The Rwanda Green Fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The Intego Facility is a multi-partner fund with a strong pipeline to absorb additional donor funding. RGF has historically mobilised $250m+ in public/private climate finance from initial donor capital (including UK’s £20m). ACTION’s £15m is expected to crowd in further co-financing via the Facility’s proposal rounds.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The majority of funds are revenue (for TA/MERL and Intego operating costs), but a portion of Intego Facility funds may support capital investments (e.g., climate-resilient infrastructure projects at district level).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £15 million over 5 years (100% ICF contribution)" (D0006187.odt, Programme summary)
quote.leverage: "Since its inception, the RGF has used donor funding (including the UK’s initial £20m capitalisation) to mobilise over $250m in public and private climate finance." (D0006187.odt, The Rwanda Green Fund)
quote.south_funding: "ACTION will provide direct financial aid for adaptation, aligned to key priorities in the NDC in the climate resilience space. This would include targeting adaptation to the most vulnerable and providing support to the RGF through the Intego (NDC) Facility." (D0006187.odt, Component 3)

metadata.programme_name: Powering Sierra Leone’s Hospitals
metadata.quote: "The programme was approved in July 2022 with a budget of £4.95 million intended to cover a single round of solar system installations in medical facilities, followed by two years working with the Government of Sierra Leone on a country-wide plan for solar Operations and Maintenance (O&M) and directly funding O&M for the systems we had installed during this period." (S30152612.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: 22/7/2022-31/3/2025 (current end date 30/6/2025)" and "New programme end date (if applicable): 31/3/2026" (S30152612.odt, Detailed information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **service delivery** (installing solar energy systems in hospitals) and **implementation research** (testing and scaling solar solutions for health facilities). It also includes **capacity building** (training engineers, developing O&M systems) and **financing mechanism** (funding O&M for sustainability).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This intervention will provide reliable solar power to the largest maternity and children’s hospitals in Sierra Leone and two off-grid regional hospitals... The programme will work with the Government of Sierra Leone to establish a sustainable maintenance regime." (D0003681.odt, Programme summary) AND "The cost extension will allow the scaling up of a successful intervention to provide solar energy systems to improve energy supply to, and health outcomes delivered by, public health facilities in Sierra Leone." (D0005919.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)
q3_expected_outputs: 17 hospital solar systems installed (including 5 original + 12 additional)
25 Community Health Centre solar systems installed
Reliable 24/7 power supply for ~7 million people (2m original + 5m additional)
Reduction in preventable deaths of women and children during childbirth
12 female engineers trained (co-financed with SEforALL)
Sector-wide O&M strategy developed for solar systems in health facilities
Energy audits and designs for 12 hospitals and 25 CHCs
Operations and maintenance support for all systems until March 2026
Data collection on healthcare benefits and reduced diesel generator usage
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers solar energy systems to hospitals and health centres in Sierra Leone to improve maternal/child health outcomes, while building local capacity for O&M and testing scalable models for health facility electrification.
what_objectives.quote: "The major impact of additional funding being an increase in the number of facilities supported... There will be additional engagement with wider policy and regulatory issues including a sector wide operations and maintenance regime for solar energy systems." (D0005919.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Sierra Leone is categorized as a **severe risk** environment with high fraud potential and weak public sector maintenance capacity. The 2023 elections and COVID-19 supply chain disruptions are explicitly noted as major risks.
where_context.q5_source: "The fiduciary environment in Sierra Leone is categorised as severe risk." (D0003681.odt, Availability of funds) AND "Sierra Leone is a high-risk environment for fraud and mismanagement." (D0003681.odt, Fiduciary Risk)
q6_contextual_constraints: infrastructure (unreliable grid, lack of transmission lines)
weak institutions (poor public sector maintenance record)
regulatory (lack of payment security instruments for private sector)
climate (not explicitly mentioned but implied in off-grid energy needs)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Unreliable power amplifies other health system constraints (e.g., night-time deliveries with candlelight, failed sterilization, delayed surgeries). Weak maintenance capacity risks system sustainability. Election periods may disrupt implementation timelines.
where_context.quote: "Their regular electricity supply was a frequently cited challenge relating to hospital infrastructure in both urban and rural areas, and affects many other aspects of the surgical system... Power outages can have devastating consequences for the intubated surgical patient or the intensive care unit patient." (D0003681.odt, Programme summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: SEforALL (multilateral/Northern-led) designs and implements systems with Sierra Leonean government input. Downstream EPC contractors (likely local) handle installation, but strategic decisions (site selection, O&M models) are led by SEforALL/FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training of 12 female engineers
development of sector-wide O&M strategy with Ministry of Health
private sector maintenance contracts to build local capacity
knowledge transfer through installation supervision

partner_organizations.name: Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer (Tier 1)

partner_organizations.name: Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contractors
partner_organizations.role: Downstream installation partners (Tier 2)

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Health and Sanitation (MoHS), Sierra Leone
partner_organizations.role: Client and government counterpart

partner_organizations.name: Crown Agents
partner_organizations.role: Data collection on healthcare benefits

partner_organizations.name: The Susan Thompson Trust (US NGO)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Koidu Hospital installation

partner_organizations.name: Partners in Health (US NGO)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for Koidu Hospital installation

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Planned funder for future O&M regime

who_partners.quote: "SEforALL is an international organisation... with a track record globally in the use of solar to improve health care delivery... They have collaborated with the World Health Organisation and Powering Africa to produce much of the evidence base of powering healthcare in Africa." (D0005919.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is an **Accountable Grant** to SEforALL (via UNOPS), with **co-financing** from US NGOs for specific sites. The grant covers capital costs, O&M, and capacity building, with milestone-based disbursements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO contracts SEforALL as the sole Tier 1 implementer, which then subcontracts EPC firms (Tier 2) for installation. A **Programme Steering Committee (PSC)** chaired by MoHS oversees strategic decisions, with FCDO and SEforALL as core members.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: SEforALL was selected based on **prior successful delivery** of the initial phase, **global expertise** in solar-for-health, and **existing relationships** with FCDO/UNOPS. Their role in COP28 and WHO collaborations also justified direct continuation.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO has used SEforALL previously to undertake studies... and have been impressed by their technical capacity and the effectiveness of their partner engagement... The intention to continue delivering through SEforALL reflects their strong performance in delivering the initial installations." (D0005919.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Programme Steering Committee (PSC)** is chaired by the Ministry of Health and Sanitation (MoHS) and includes FCDO, SEforALL, and other stakeholders (e.g., Ministry of Energy). It meets monthly to oversee milestones and results, with FCDO retaining approval authority for financial disbursements.
how_governance.quote: "The PSC will be chaired by the Ministry of Health and Sanitation and comprise of the FCDO, lead implementer and other relevant actors... These will occur on a monthly basis, alongside other bilateral engagements." (D0003681.odt, Stakeholder Engagement) AND "FCDO will monitor sites through regular site visits... and scrutinize partner forecasts against activities on a monthly basis." (D0003681.odt, Risk Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between sites (e.g., Koidu Hospital redesign) but require FCDO approval. The cost extension explicitly repurposes £528k from other programmes (Invest Salone, Saving Lives) to cover O&M gaps.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme adapted to **unplanned energy demand increases** (e.g., hospitals adding equipment post-installation) and **land allocation conflicts** (Koidu Hospital). O&M strategies were revised based on lessons from initial installations.
how_flexibility.quote: "Lessons learned have included a faster than anticipated increase in energy demand as partners increased investment in equipment more quickly than expected once the power supply became reliable." (S30152612.odt, Changes) AND "The cost extension will provide O&M cover for the 17 hospitals we funded through to March 2026... This will protect the value of installation warranties." (S30152612.odt, Implementation)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → SEforALL (Tier 1) → EPC contractors (Tier 2) → subcontractors (e.g., for customs clearing)
how_efficiency.quote: "Management cost (~5%): £0.24m in 2022/23... The lead implementer will provide quarterly financial and progress reports to FCDO." (D0003681.odt, Availability of funds) AND "Payments are made against agreed milestones in the activity schedule and financial plan." (D0003681.odt, Supplier Performance)

q24_alternatives_considered: Financing agreement with World Bank/AfDB (rejected due to timeliness/value for money)
Commercial tender for EPC contractors (rejected due to lack of local capacity and time constraints)
Direct FCDO procurement (rejected due to lack of in-house solar expertise)
Hybrid solar-diesel systems (rejected under UK fossil fuel policy)
Grid extension (rejected as infeasible/costly for remote hospitals)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: SEforALL was chosen for **proven delivery** (successful initial phase), **technical expertise** (lithium-ion batteries, health-sector solar), **speed** (avoiding tender delays), and **alignment with UK priorities** (Ayrton Fund demonstrator). The accountable grant model allowed flexible adaptation (e.g., Koidu redesign) while maintaining FCDO oversight.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (SEforALL’s lower lifetime energy costs vs diesel)
experience (prior work in Uganda/Ghana and with WHO)
equity (female engineer training, local EPC contractors)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier performance risk (delays by EPC contractors)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular site monitoring by FCDO, Clerk of Works, and KPIs (e.g., % systems with signed maintenance contracts).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud in high-risk environment (Sierra Leone)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence on SEforALL, financial thresholds (±5% variance), and explicit fraud liability clauses in contracts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of O&M post-handover
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Lithium-ion batteries (10-year warranties), private sector contracts, and World Bank transition plan.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Election-related disruptions (2023)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Geographical balance in site selection and accelerated timelines to complete installations pre-election.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 [SEforALL grant] is preferred in terms of effectiveness, timeliness and sustainability... Their strong performance in delivering the initial installations [and] leading role globally in the use of solar to improve health care delivery." (D0005919.odt, What is the approach to implementation?) AND "The choice for stand-alone generation is between diesel generators and solar. There is significant and increasing evidence that solar energy offers the better value for money solution in off-grid locations in Africa." (D0003681.odt, Appraisal of Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limited partner options to organizations with **existing Sierra Leone presence** (e.g., SEforALL via UNOPS/RESL) and **experience in high-risk environments**. Local EPC contractors were required due to **logistical challenges** (port delays, customs) and **security risks** (theft of equipment).
q27_constraints_detail: Fraud risk excluded direct cash transfers to government
Weak maintenance capacity necessitated private sector O&M contracts
Election timelines accelerated implementation to avoid disruptions
Supply chain delays required buffer stocks and port relationship management
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rapid, large-scale installations** (17 hospitals + 25 CHCs) required a **centralized implementer** (SEforALL) with subcontracted EPC firms. **O&M sustainability goals** shaped the hub-and-spoke model and private sector engagement. **Health equity focus** (maternal/child outcomes) prioritized referral hospitals over smaller clinics.
q28_linkages: Service delivery scale → Closed consortium structure (SEforALL + EPC firms)
O&M sustainability → Private sector contracts and World Bank transition
FCAS risks → Intensive oversight (monthly PSC, site visits)
Gender equity → Female engineer training component
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs included: **speed vs. inclusion** (direct award to SEforALL accelerated delivery but limited local ownership); **cost vs. reach** (lithium-ion batteries increased upfront costs but reduced long-term O&M burdens); **expertise vs. capacity building** (Northern-led design with embedded training for Sierra Leonean engineers).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Direct award to SEforALL sacrificed competitive pricing for speed
Lithium-ion batteries prioritized long-term reliability over cheaper lead-acid options
Hub-and-spoke O&M model balanced efficiency (centralized hubs) with equity (covering remote CHCs)
Female engineer training added costs but addressed gender gaps in technical roles
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **severe fiduciary risk** in Sierra Leone led to **intensive oversight** (monthly financial reviews, site spot-checks) and **restrictive payment structures** (milestone-based, ±5% variance thresholds). Political risks (elections) accelerated timelines to front-load installations.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited local **technical capacity** (e.g., no prior lithium-ion experience) required SEforALL to lead design/procurement, while **EPC contractors** (Tier 2) handled installation. O&M training for MoHS staff was embedded to transition to government-led maintenance by 2026.
intersections.quote: "The fiduciary environment in Sierra Leone is categorised as severe risk... FCDO will apply due diligence on partners prior to signing a funding agreement and will closely monitor project implementation." (D0003681.odt, Availability of funds) AND "The intention to continue delivering through SEforALL reflects their strong performance... but also their leading role globally in the use of solar to improve health care delivery." (D0005919.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

key_programme_risks: Supply chain delays (COVID-19, Freetown port)
Election-related violence/disruptions (June 2023)
Fraud/theft (cables, batteries)
GoSL failure to fund O&M post-handover
Underestimated energy demand (hospitals adding equipment)
Land allocation conflicts (Koidu Hospital)
Safeguarding incidents (SEAH, child labour)
Private sector O&M contractor capacity gaps
World Bank O&M programme delays (now expected 2026)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Accelerated procurement routes, port relationship management, buffer timelines.
Front-loaded installations, geographical balance in site selection, supplier contingency plans.
Secured battery containers, safeguarding clauses, financial thresholds, due diligence on partners.
Lithium-ion batteries (10-year warranties), private sector contracts, World Bank transition plan.
Flexible system designs, additional capacity at Masanga Hospital.
Redesign for adjacent land, co-funding from US NGOs.
SEAH due diligence, local safeguarding officers, training for contractors.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Local partnerships are critical**: Leveraged existing RESL mini-grid operators for maintenance networks.
**Flexible designs needed**: Energy demand grew faster than anticipated as reliable power enabled equipment upgrades.
**Security investments pay off**: Secured containers and roof-mounted panels reduced theft at Masanga Hospital.
**Political timing matters**: Election cycles required accelerated implementation to avoid disruptions.
**Private sector can fill gaps**: O&M contracts bridged public sector capacity limitations.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The initial phase (2022–23) revealed: 1) **Underestimated O&M needs** (now central to design), 2) **Rapid equipment uptake** post-electrification (led to demand spikes), 3) **Effectiveness of lithium-ion** (Masanga Hospital system operational since 2018), 4) **Importance of private sector** (RESL mini-grid operators provided maintenance models).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Expanded O&M funding from 2 to 5 years; 2) Added CHCs to scale impact; 3) Developed hub-and-spoke O&M model; 4) Increased system capacities (e.g., Koidu redesign); 5) Embedded female engineer training.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learned have included a faster than anticipated increase in energy demand as partners increased investment in equipment more quickly than expected once the power supply became reliable... Work on O&M should have been more central to the original programme design." (S30152612.odt, Changes) AND "The combination of health sector and solar energy experience in Sierra Leone gives the UK comparative advantage for implementation of a solar solution supporting hospitals." (D0003681.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme mobilized **£300k in co-funding** for Koidu Hospital from US NGOs and is positioned to transition O&M costs to the **World Bank’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy programme** (expected 2026). As a **Country Demonstrator for the UK’s £1bn Ayrton Fund**, it also generates lessons for wider clean energy investments.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: ~90% capital (solar system installations) / 10% revenue (O&M, capacity building). Initial phase: £4.51m capital, £0.18m O&M. Extension added £15m for additional systems + O&M.
financial_details.quote: "The total programme value will be classified as International Climate Fund (ICF) expenditure... A portion of the proposed funding will be available for system maintenance for a period of two years prior to formal handing over to the MoHS." (D0003681.odt, Availability of funds) AND "The cost extension will provide O&M cover for the 17 hospitals we funded through to March 2026." (S30152612.odt, Implementation)

metadata.programme_name: Priorities for Universal Health Coverage: Realising Cost-Effective Health Services for Everyone (PURCHASE)

quote.programme_name: "Priorities for Universal Health Coverage: Realising Cost-Effective Health Services for Everyone (PURCHASE)" (D0004306.odt, Title section)
quote.duration: "PURCHASE will be a three-year programme from 2023-2026" (D0004306.odt, The way forward section)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: Up to £4.25m" (D0004306.odt, Summary Sheet section)

metadata.duration_source: "PURCHASE will be a three-year programme from 2023-2026" (D0004306.odt, The way forward section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: PURCHASE combines capacity building (strengthening regional/national institutions for priority-setting), policy influence (advocacy for UHC financing), and implementation research (testing priority-setting frameworks). The core focus is on institutionalizing evidence-based decision-making to improve allocative efficiency in health budgets.
what_objectives.q1_source: "PURCHASE will fund: advocacy and engagement on the goal of UHC and, strengthen regional leadership, technical capacity and partnerships for better decision-making in health across Africa to help governments prioritise this agenda and make better decisions, informed by robust evidence, on how to get more health for their money and accelerate progress towards the goal of universal health coverage." (D0004306.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: strengthened regional leadership and technical capacity for priority-setting
development of continental frameworks on priority-setting (Africa CDC)
3-4 countries receiving direct support for priority-setting processes
q3_expected_outputs.target: 3-4 countries

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased political commitment to UHC at regional/national levels
evidence-informed health benefit packages designed/implemented
regional hubs established (West and East Africa)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 2 hubs

q3_expected_outputs.output: advocacy products/events promoting UHC (£400,000 allocation)

what_objectives.summary: PURCHASE aims to institutionalize evidence-based priority-setting for health budgets in Africa, combining advocacy to mobilize political commitment with technical support to strengthen regional/national capacity for allocative efficiency. The programme focuses on both demand (political leadership) and supply (institutional frameworks) sides of priority-setting.

quote.objectives: "PURCHASE will focus on (1) generating political commitment to investing better in health and increasing demand for evidence that informs priority setting and (2) strengthening regional and national institutional capacity to generate and use this evidence to inform priority setting in health budgets." (D0004306.odt, The way forward section)
quote.outputs: "This will deliver benefits across populations, with an intention to see accelerated access for more vulnerable and marginalised groups to essential quality health services, without financial hardship." (D0004306.odt, Programme summary section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a context of constrained fiscal space and technical inefficiencies in African health systems, but without active conflict or extreme fragility. The risk is categorized as 'moderate' due to institutional capacity gaps rather than security threats.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004306.odt, Summary Sheet section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Technical inefficiencies in African health systems (e.g., leakage, corruption, inefficient service delivery) are estimated to have lost ~$23 billion in 2019. Data limitations hinder evidence-based decision-making, while fiscal constraints (e.g., debt servicing > healthcare spending in 62 countries) limit resource allocation. These constraints necessitate adaptive priority-setting frameworks and regional coordination.

quote.constraints: "It has been estimated that technical inefficiencies in health systems in the region means that almost $US23 billion of expenditure in 2019 was lost to the health sector." (D0004306.odt, Context section)
quote.fiscal: "The number of countries spending more on external public debt servicing than healthcare increased from 34 to 62 over the last decade." (D0004306.odt, Context section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Africa CDC retains strategic and technical decision-making authority, with FCDO providing funding alignment. The programme explicitly adopts a 'patient development approach' to respond to locally owned priorities, with regional institutions (e.g., Africa CDC) enhancing sustainability.
q10_capacity_building_details: institutional strengthening (Africa CDC Health Economics Programme)
training on health technology assessment (HTA)
mentorship for priority-setting processes
development of regional hubs (West/East Africa)
co-production of evidence with academic/policy actors
peer-to-peer learning networks (e.g., AfroHTA)
