metadata.programme_name: Iraq Catalytic Economic Diversification (ICED) Programme

quote.text: This programme seeks to catalyse economic development and diversification in Iraq, focussing on creating a thriving private sector and removing barriers to entrepreneurship.

duration_source.text: AMP Start Date: April 2023; AMP End Date: March 2028

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening private sector and financial institutions), policy influence (supporting government economic reforms), implementation research (testing interventions for SME support), and service delivery (direct financing and training to SMEs). It aims to catalyse economic diversification in Iraq by addressing macro-level reforms, meso-level financial sector improvements, and micro-level SME support.

q1_source.text: This programme seeks to catalyse economic development and diversification in Iraq, focussing on creating a thriving private sector and removing barriers to entrepreneurship. It will cover both Federal Iraq and KRI. It does this at macro, meso and micro levels: Macro-Technical Assistance facility focussed on supporting the Government of Iraq’s economic reform initiatives; Meso–Support directly to the financial sector, through multilaterals, to increase access to credit for businesses and deepen the financial sector; Micro–Support directly to small and medium enterprises (SMEs), through an SME facility, providing mindset training, investment coordination and direct capital (investment and cash transfer).

q3_expected_outputs.output: Technical assistance ventures with Government of Iraq (GoI)
Technical assistance ventures with financial institutions
Guarantees on SME lending
Cash transfers to SMEs
Loans to SMEs
Equity investments in SMEs
Mindset training sessions for SMEs
New private sector jobs created
Improvement in Iraq’s private sector credit/GDP ratio

what_objectives.summary: The ICED Programme aims to catalyse economic diversification in Iraq by improving the private sector operating environment, increasing access to capital, and strengthening economic governance. It operates at macro (government reforms), meso (financial sector support), and micro (direct SME support) levels, with explicit focus on gender equality and climate adaptation.

quote.text: Through improving the business environment and creating better functioning markets the programme aims to mobilise investment (both domestic and foreign), in particular commercial capital for non-oil sectors.

countries_regions: Iraq (Federal Iraq and Kurdistan Region of Iraq - KRI)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as 'moderate' risk, reflecting Iraq's fragile context with significant economic and political challenges, including high unemployment, weak institutions, and oil dependency. However, the programme is designed to mitigate these risks through flexible delivery and strong oversight.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security restrictions limit FCDO staff movement, requiring third-party monitoring. Political economy challenges (e.g., rent-seeking, corruption) necessitate flexible, adaptive programming. Weak financial institutions constrain private sector access to credit (only 10% of GDP). High youth unemployment (24%) and female unemployment (33%) exacerbate social instability. Climate risks (e.g., water scarcity) are integrated into economic diversification efforts.

quote.text: The private sector in particular is underdeveloped, due to a combination of regulatory and financial constraints, and endemic corruption. [...] Iraq’s ease of doing business and corruption are in the bottom 10% globally. [...] Without a thriving private sector Iraq risks significant instability – this is an existential threat to Iraq.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority, with input from in-country advisers (Economic, Climate, Conflict) and the Country Board. Implementing partners (e.g., IFC, national NGOs) execute delivery but require FCDO approval for major decisions (e.g., TA ventures, sub-awards).
q10_capacity_building_details: mindset training for SMEs
technical assistance to financial institutions (governance, risk management, SME finance)
skills development for Iraqi labour force
institutional strengthening of Government of Iraq (GoI) economic institutions

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of financial sector facility (meso component): technical assistance to banks, risk-sharing guarantees, and access to credit for SMEs

partner_organizations.name: Commercial supplier (TBD via competitive tender)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of Technical Assistance (TA) facility (macro component): supporting GoI economic reforms

partner_organizations.name: National NGO(s) (TBD via competitive process)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of SME facility (micro component): mindset training, investment coordination, direct capital to SMEs

partner_organizations.name: Third-party monitoring provider (TBD)
partner_organizations.role: Independent monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) to assess performance and risks

partner_organizations.name: Work and Opportunities for Women (WOW) Helpdesk
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support on gender equality integration across components

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Iraq Climate Adviser
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support on climate change integration (e.g., green finance windows)

quote.text: This programme will be delivered through three components: 1) Macro – a Technical Assistance facility delivered through a commercial contract; 2) Meso – a Financial Sector facility delivered through the IFC; 3) Micro – an SME facility delivered through a national NGO. [...] The programme will be built on principles of partnership, whereby local actors views and input will be taken into account on equal terms at all stages of design and implementation.
quote.source: D0003397.odt, Proposed approach and Partnership principles

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses multiple instruments: 1) **Commercial contract** for the TA facility (macro) to ensure flexibility and accountability; 2) **Administration Agreement (AA)** with IFC for the financial sector facility (meso) to leverage multilateral expertise; 3) **Commercial contract or accountable grant** for the SME facility (micro) to engage national NGOs; 4) **Commercial contract** for MEL/third-party monitoring. Each instrument is tailored to the component’s needs (e.g., IFC’s AA reduces FCDO administrative burden).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme combines: 1) **Direct FCDO management** of the TA facility (via commercial supplier); 2) **Multilateral management** of the financial sector facility (IFC via AA); 3) **NGO-led delivery** of the SME facility (with FCDO oversight); and 4) **Independent third-party monitoring**. FCDO retains strategic oversight through the Country Board and annual reviews, while partners manage day-to-day operations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition is used to ensure value for money, local relevance, and technical capacity. For the TA and SME facilities, Early Market Stakeholder Engagement (EMSE) events will identify potential suppliers before competitive tenders. IFC was selected via direct award for the financial sector facility due to its unmatched in-country expertise and track record in Iraq.

quote.text: FCDO will run a competitive process to find the supplier [for TA and SME facilities], inviting all those with experience of providing economic-focussed TA in Iraq. [...] For component two, IFC are the only partner in Iraq with significant experience of working across the GoI, public and private banks, and directly with the private sector. [...] FCDO will run Early Market Stakeholder Engagement events (EMSEs), followed by a call for proposals.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **Country Board** (with input from FCDO’s Economic, Climate, and Conflict Advisers) approves criteria for TA proposals and reviews performance. **IFC’s internal governance** manages the financial sector facility, while **FCDO programme team** oversees the TA and SME facilities. **Third-party monitoring** provides independent assurance. Annual reviews inform funding reallocation.

quote.text: The criteria of all three components will be developed in conjunction with the Work and Opportunities for Women (WOW) Helpdesk to ensure best practice. [...] The programme will be managed through regular meetings and steering committees [with IFC]. [...] Active third-party monitoring and evaluation will allow understanding of what is working and what is not, as well as if programme outcomes are being met; with component financings scaling up and down accordingly.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components annually based on performance (e.g., scaling up effective interventions). The Annual Review process, informed by MEL data, drives these decisions. For example, underperforming components may receive reduced funding, while successful ones (e.g., IFC’s financial sector work) could be expanded.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **adaptive management** through: 1) Flexible TA facility to respond to GoI priorities; 2) Annual reviews to adjust component focus/financing; 3) Third-party monitoring to identify emerging risks/opportunities; 4) Scalable components (e.g., IFC can leverage private finance if demand grows). Political economy analysis shapes real-time adjustments.

quote.text: Flexibility to scale up components that are performing well (and scale down those that are facing blockages) will help ensure greater value for money and delivery against core objectives. [...] Funds can be re-allocated by the programme team between components over the years, to reflect implementation requirements and partner performance.
quote.source: D0003397.odt, Why rationale and Financial Case

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., IFC/NGO/commercial supplier) → End beneficiaries (GoI/financial institutions/SMEs). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned beyond the primary partners.

quote.text: FCDO will ask the commercial partner to develop budget proposals for all TA requests and check that it is engaging only key staff at the right level. [...] IFC’s programme management systems are strong; and its procurement processes for externally contracted work are robust and will drive-down costs through commercial competition. [...] Payment structures will be tied to deliverables (e.g., TA ventures completed, SMEs trained).
quote.source: D0003397.odt, Commercial Case and Value for Money

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rely on advocacy only)
Multilateral multi-donor trust fund (e.g., World Bank’s I3RF or UN-coordinated fund)
Macro component only (TA facility)
Meso component only (financial sector facility)
Micro component only (SME facility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen:
The **hybrid delivery model (Option 6)** was chosen for its **flexibility**, **value for money (VFM)**, and **comprehensive impact** across all objectives (macro/meso/micro). Key reasons:

1. **Risk mitigation**: A single-component approach (Options 3–5) risked failure if that component underperformed (e.g., TA alone couldn’t address financial sector weaknesses). The hybrid model diversifies risk.

2. **Flexibility**: Allows scaling of components based on performance (e.g., IFC’s financial sector work can expand if effective).

3. **Leverage**: IFC’s multilateral status mobilizes private finance; commercial TA suppliers ensure accountability.

4. **Local relevance**: National NGOs deliver SME support with contextual understanding.

5. **Past experience**: Lessons from World Bank’s I3RF (poor flexibility) and UK’s TAFFI (successful flexible TA) informed the design.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (IFC’s expertise, NGO local knowledge)
flexibility to adapt to political economy
speed of delivery (TA facility can respond quickly to GoI requests)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High transactional/management costs due to multiple components (TA + IFC + NGO + MEL)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Streamlined procurement (e.g., EMSE events, framework agreements) and leveraging IFC’s existing systems to reduce FCDO administrative burden.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges between components (e.g., TA reforms not aligning with IFC’s financial sector work)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular steering committees, integrated MEL, and FCDO’s central oversight role to ensure coherence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IFC’s limited flexibility compared to commercial suppliers (e.g., slower response to GoI priorities)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Complementary TA facility (commercial supplier) provides agility; IFC focuses on systemic financial sector changes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: National NGOs may lack capacity for scale-up in SME facility
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Phased rollout with close FCDO monitoring; focus on established NGOs with existing SME networks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy risks (e.g., GoI lack of buy-in for reforms)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible TA facility to seize reform windows; demonstration effects (e.g., SME job creation) to build political will.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (competitive procurement, leveraging IFC’s economies of scale)
efficiency (targeted TA vs. large-scale financing; IFC’s existing relationships)
effectiveness (hybrid model addresses all programme objectives)
equity (gender/climate windows in all components; focus on marginalized areas)

quote.text: Option 6: Delivery across Micro, Meso and Macro components is the preferred option. This offers flexibility, value for money, and achieves impact across all programme objectives (macro reform, financial sector and SME support). It also has strong alignment with wider HMG objectives. [...] A solely multilateral approach was considered. However, learning lessons from the World Bank’s Iraq Reform, Reconstruction and Recovery Fund (I3RF) programme this was viewed as too risky; delivery and results have been mixed and faced challenges. Diversifying delivery of programme outcomes [...] mitigates against the risk that one component doesn’t perform.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who:
Iraq’s **fragile context** constrains partner selection in three ways:

1. **Security risks** limit FCDO’s ability to manage delivery directly, necessitating local partners (e.g., national NGOs for SME support) and third-party monitoring.

2. **Weak institutions** require multilateral expertise (e.g., IFC for financial sector reforms) and flexible TA providers who can navigate political economy challenges.

3. **Regulatory/corruption barriers** favor partners with existing in-country networks (e.g., IFC’s relationships with Iraqi banks) and robust due diligence (e.g., commercial suppliers for TA).
q27_constraints_detail: Security restrictions → reliance on local NGOs and third-party monitors
Political economy volatility → need for flexible, adaptive partners (e.g., commercial TA suppliers)
Weak financial institutions → requirement for IFC’s technical expertise
Corruption risks → enhanced due diligence for all partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how:
The programme’s **multi-level objectives** (macro/meso/micro) directly shape the **delivery structure**:

1. **Macro (GoI reforms)** → **Commercial TA facility**: Requires agility to respond to political windows and technical expertise to influence policy (e.g., public financial management).

2. **Meso (financial sector)** → **IFC Administration Agreement**: Needs systemic leverage (e.g., guarantees to unlock private lending) and multilateral credibility to engage banks.

3. **Micro (SMEs)** → **National NGO delivery**: Demands local trust, contextual knowledge, and ability to reach marginalized groups (e.g., women-led businesses).

4. **Cross-cutting (gender/climate)** → **Embedded windows in all components**: Ensures equity is not siloed but integrated into delivery mechanisms.
q28_linkages: Macro reforms (TA) → requires **flexible, high-expertise partner** (commercial supplier) to navigate GoI politics
Financial sector deepening → requires **multilateral with banking relationships** (IFC) to mobilize private finance
SME support → requires **local NGOs** with grassroots networks to deliver training/finance
Gender/climate focus → requires **embedded criteria** in all partner contracts (e.g., WOW Helpdesk input)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs:
Explicit trade-offs are discussed:

1. **Local ownership vs. speed**: Using national NGOs for SME support prioritizes local relevance and equity but may reduce efficiency (e.g., higher transaction costs, slower scale-up) compared to international providers.

2. **Multilateral expertise vs. flexibility**: IFC offers unmatched financial sector expertise but is less nimble than commercial TA suppliers in responding to GoI priorities.

3. **Gender/climate integration vs. cost**: Dedicated windows for women-led and green businesses add complexity (e.g., separate MEL requirements) but are deemed essential for equity.

4. **Direct delivery vs. catalytic effects**: SME grants/loans (direct service) are balanced with TA/IFC components (systemic change) to ensure both immediate impact and long-term sustainability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Local NGOs (equity) vs. international providers (efficiency)
IFC (expertise) vs. commercial suppliers (flexibility)
Gender/climate windows (equity) vs. simplified delivery (cost)
Direct SME financing (immediate impact) vs. systemic reforms (long-term change)
intersections.risk_affects_management:
Iraq’s **moderate risk profile** (fragility, corruption, political volatility) drives **intensive oversight**:
- **Third-party monitoring** mandated due to security restrictions.
- **Annual reviews** replace lighter-touch approaches to enable rapid reallocation of funds.
- **FCDO’s central role** in TA approvals (vs. delegated authority) reflects political economy risks.
- **IFC’s fiduciary standards** reduce FCDO’s administrative burden while mitigating financial risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles:
Capacity building is **embedded** in partner roles:
- **IFC**: Builds financial institution capacity (e.g., governance, SME lending systems) as core to its delivery.
- **TA facility**: Strengthens GoI institutions (e.g., public financial management) through targeted technical assistance.
- **SME NGOs**: Provide mindset training and business skills to entrepreneurs, with a focus on women and youth.
- **WOW Helpdesk/Climate Adviser**: Shape partner criteria to ensure capacity building aligns with equity goals.

quote.text: The programme will be built on principles of partnership, whereby local actors views and input will be taken into account on equal terms at all stages of design and implementation. [...] A solely multilateral approach was considered. However, learning lessons from the World Bank’s I3RF [...] this was viewed as too risky; delivery and results have been mixed and faced challenges. Diversifying delivery [...] mitigates against the risk that one component doesn’t perform. [...] The programme will improve the private sector to growth and jobs for those excluded from the current rent-seeking political settlement.
quote.source: D0003397.odt, Partnership principles and Conclusion of options analysis

key_programme_risks: GoI lack of political will for economic reforms (e.g., resistance to reducing public sector bloat)
Security constraints limiting FCDO oversight and partner movement
Corruption undermining financial sector reforms or SME financing
Oil price volatility disrupting fiscal space for reforms
Weak SME absorption capacity for financing/training
Coordinating multiple components (TA + IFC + NGO) creating management burdens
IFC or NGO underperformance due to contextual challenges
Gender/climate windows not reaching intended beneficiaries (e.g., women in conservative areas)
Migration dynamics (e.g., irregular migration from marginalized areas) affecting target geographies
Global oil demand decline accelerating faster than Iraq’s diversification

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible TA facility to seize reform windows; demonstration effects (e.g., SME job creation) to build buy-in; FCDO’s development diplomacy to lobby senior officials.
Third-party monitoring for independent verification; reliance on local NGOs with existing networks; remote management where possible.
IFC’s robust fiduciary standards; enhanced due diligence for all partners; transparent guarantee mechanisms for SME lending.
Diversification focus (non-oil sectors); fiscal space analysis integrated into TA reforms.
Phased rollout with pilot testing; mindset training to prepare entrepreneurs; NGO selection based on proven SME engagement.
Integrated MEL system; regular steering committees; FCDO’s central oversight role to align components.
Annual reviews to reallocate funds; break clauses in agreements; third-party monitoring to flag issues early.
Criteria developed with WOW Helpdesk/Climate Adviser; disaggregated MEL data; targeted outreach in conservative areas.
Year 1–2 focus on migration-prone areas with evaluation to assess efficacy; flexible geography targeting.
Urgency in diversification efforts; climate-adaptation focus in SME/green finance windows.

fcas_specific_lessons: Flexible, adaptive programming is critical in fragile contexts (e.g., TAFFI’s success in responding to political economy shifts).
Local partners (e.g., national NGOs) are essential for reach but require robust capacity assessment and support.
Multilateral platforms (e.g., I3RF) can struggle with flexibility; hybrid models (e.g., ICED) balance systemic leverage with agility.
Demonstration effects (e.g., visible SME job creation) are powerful for building political will in rentier economies.
Third-party monitoring is non-negotiable in high-risk environments to verify results and mitigate fraud.
Gender and climate objectives must be **embedded** in all components to avoid being sidelined in crisis contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
Lessons from **TAFFI (CSSF-funded TA facility)** and **World Bank’s I3RF** shaped ICED’s design:

1. **TAFFI**: Proved that flexible, demand-driven TA can deliver results in Iraq’s political economy. ICED replicates this model for its macro component.

2. **I3RF**: Showed that multilateral trust funds can face bottlenecks (e.g., slow disbursement, limited flexibility). ICED avoids this by diversifying delivery mechanisms.

3. **SME support programmes**: Highlighted the need for **mindset training** alongside financing to shift labour force mentality away from public sector jobs.

4. **Gender programmes**: Demonstrated that **dedicated windows** (e.g., for women-led businesses) are more effective than mainstreaming alone in conservative contexts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
Explicit design adaptations include:
- **Hybrid delivery model** (vs. sole multilateral approach) to mitigate I3RF’s flexibility risks.
- **Embedded gender/climate windows** in all components (not standalone) to ensure integration.
- **Phased SME support** with Year 1–2 focus on migration-prone areas, informed by TAFFI’s adaptive lessons.
- **Third-party monitoring** as a core component (not add-on), reflecting FCAS accountability needs.
- **Annual fund reallocation** mechanism to address underperformance, learned from I3RF’s disbursement delays.

quote.text: A solely multilateral approach was considered. However, learning lessons from the World Bank’s Iraq Reform, Reconstruction and Recovery Fund (I3RF) programme this was viewed as too risky; delivery and results have been mixed and faced challenges. [...] The UK’s Technical Assistance Financing Facility for Iraq (TAFFI) uses a similar operating model and has been effective in delivering results within the complicated political economy. ICED would seek to replicate this through this TA component. [...] Active third-party monitoring and evaluation will allow understanding of what is working and what is not, as well as if programme outcomes are being met; with component financings scaling up and down accordingly.
quote.source: D0003397.odt, Conclusion of options analysis and MEL section

financial_details.leverage_achieved: IFC’s financial sector facility will leverage private finance through portfolio guarantees, mobilizing significantly more than the £6m FCDO contribution. For example, small-scale UK ODA will unlock "much higher volumes of private finance to businesses" (exact leverage ratio not specified).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: All spend is **revenue** (Resource Departmental Expenditure Limit - RDEL); no capital expenditure (CDEL) is planned.

component_breakdown.delivery_mechanism: Commercial contract or accountable grant to national NGO

component_breakdown.component: Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) + Third-Party Monitoring (TPM)

quote.text: The programme is expected to spend primarily through IFC in the first year, with the TA and SME facilities having to undergo ESMEs and call for proposals, followed by a longer mobilisation period. [...] Support to all components is easily scalable depending on budget availability. [...] We expect to allocate approximately 43% of the budget for the TA facility. [...] The IFC Financial Sector Deepening Facility is expected to account for roughly 33% of the total budget. [...] The SME facility is expected to account for roughly 18% of the total budget.

metadata.programme_name: Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises Phase III (EiEPC III)

quote.programme_name: "Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises Phase III (EiEPC III)" (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £90 million" (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)
quote.duration: "AMP Start Date: 01/03/2023", "AMP End Date: 31/03/2027" (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)
quote.sector: "Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises" (D0005046.odt, Title)

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01/03/2023", "AMP End Date: 31/03/2027"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing (channeling £80m through Education Cannot Wait), capacity building (boosting FCDO technical capability), and implementation research (investing in thematic partnerships to test interventions). It aims to deliver education services in crisis settings while reforming the international system for better coordination and funding.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The next phase of our programming will build on these achievements and deliver on the International Development Strategy’s commitments on girls’ education, humanitarian support, and climate change by: Funding Education Cannot Wait (ECW) to directly support 20 million children... Boosting access to FCDO technical capability... Investing in thematic partnerships with organisations..." (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 20 million children (60% girls, 10% with disabilities) reached with ECW support
£1.25 billion raised by ECW over 2023–2026 (UK contribution as catalyst)
Improved literacy/numeracy outcomes in ECW-supported programmes (new target)
Better coordination of education support for crisis-affected children (target TBA)
Policy/guidance on education-climate links (for COP27)
Reformed ECW with clearer value proposition in global education architecture

what_objectives.summary: EiEPC III is a £90m programme to fund Education Cannot Wait (ECW) as the primary global mechanism for delivering education in emergencies, while strengthening FCDO’s technical capacity and investing in thematic partnerships to address gaps in climate resilience, refugee integration, and disability inclusion. It aims to reach 20 million crisis-affected children (60% girls) and catalyse £1.25bn in total ECW funding by 2026.

quote.objectives: "This programme will be the third phase of UK EiEPC programming. EiEPC phases I and II have helped to establish ECW as a leading global fund for EiEPC and strengthened the UK’s own EiEPC policy and programming. The next phase... will deliver on the International Development Strategy’s commitments on girls’ education, humanitarian, and climate change by: Making a core contribution to ECW (£80m)... Boosting access to FCDO’s technical capability... Investing in UK thematic partnerships (£9m)..." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.outputs: "Number of children and adolescents reached with ECW support - target 20 million of whom 60% are girls and 10% have a disability" (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates exclusively in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), with explicit references to protracted crises, armed conflict, and humanitarian emergencies. The document states: "The risk rating for the programme is Major. EiEPC will operate in contexts that have been severely disrupted by COVID-19... and work in contexts with high degrees of complexity."
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" and "EiEPC will operate in contexts... with high degrees of complexity" (D0005046.odt, Assurances)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit access to conflict zones (e.g., Rohingya camps in Bangladesh have government restrictions). Weak institutions in host countries (e.g., Chad, DRC) hinder integration of refugees into national education systems. Climate shocks disrupt schooling (e.g., 40 million children/year affected by extreme weather). Data limitations make it difficult to track learning outcomes: "Lessthan 10% of grantees have solid evidence on safety and protection, and only 20% of MYRPs can report any changes in learning." Language barriers and socio-cultural norms (e.g., girls’ attendance in Myanmar curriculum rollout) further complicate delivery.

quote.constraints: "In Cox’s Bazar... the planned roll-out of the Myanmar Curriculum to this age group is likely to be slow due to a lack of teachers, widespread government restrictions, and socio-cultural attitudes limiting girls’ attendance at school." (D0005046.odt, Box 4)
quote.data: "Lessthan 10% of grantees have solid evidence on safety and protection, and only 20% of MYRPs can report any changes in learning." (D0005046.odt, Box 5)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with ECW’s Executive Committee (multilateral) and FCDO (UK), with Southern partners (e.g., local NGOs, host governments) primarily as implementers. The document notes: "FCDO can complement ECW operations with political buttressing in-country," implying a top-down structure.
q10_capacity_building_details: surge support to FCDO posts during crises
strengthening ECW’s Secretariat
technical assistance to local education groups (LEGs)
training for humanitarian clusters
disability inclusion guidance (via ECW’s Policy Framework)

quote.structure: "The programme will focus on delivering through an investment in ECW alongside smaller investments in UK thematic partnerships and FCDO capacity." (D0005046.odt, What will the programme deliver?)
quote.capacity: "Boosting access to FCDO’s technical capability across education, humanitarian, and conflict sectors (£1 million) to provide i) surge support to posts in the event of a crisis... and ii) strengthen ECW’s Secretariat." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.southern_roles: "We have also been discussing with UNICEF how to improve the coordination of the humanitarian response in affected countries, particularly in situations where the lines between development and humanitarian action are blurred... and with UNHCR on how to make faster progress on getting refugees integrated into host government schools." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses: 1) **Core funding** to ECW (£80m) as a multilateral trust fund; 2) **Grants** for UK thematic partnerships (£9m); and 3) **Block funding** for FCDO technical capacity (£1m). ECW operates with three funding windows: First Emergency Response (FER) for rapid crises, Multi-Year Resilience Programmes (MYRP) for protracted crises, and an Acceleration Facility (AF) for innovation.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: ECW acts as a global platform coordinating multiple implementers (UN agencies, NGOs, host governments) through competitive calls. FCDO provides core funding and political oversight, while thematic partnerships are managed separately. The structure is described as: "ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly."
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ECW’s partners are selected through a mix of: 1) **Pre-qualified implementers** (e.g., UNICEF, Save the Children as cluster leads); 2) **Competitive calls** for the Acceleration Facility; and 3) **Direct awards** to host governments/LEGs in protracted crises. The rationale emphasizes speed and existing capacity: "Responding on a case-by-case would be transaction heavy and inefficient."

quote.instrument: "Making a core contribution to ECW (£80m)... Investing in UK thematic partnerships (£9m)... Boosting access to FCDO’s technical capability (£1m)." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.structure: "ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly... Coordination with host government is frequently difficult and by working with humanitarian actors, ECW offers an alternative channel." (D0005046.odt, Box 8)
quote.selection: "The FER is one of three ECW funding modalities and provides an immediate and rapid response to education needs in sudden onset emergencies... MYRPs are for funding education in protracted crises... AF is focused on innovation." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: ECW is governed by an **Executive Committee** (ExCom) with donor representatives (including FCDO) and a **High-Level Steering Group** (HLSG). The UK works through these structures to influence reforms: "We are working with our partners on ECW’s ExCom to deliver on a set of ECW reform priorities." FCDO also conducts **Annual Reviews** to monitor progress.

quote.governance: "We are working with our partners on ECW’s ExCom to deliver on a set of ECW reform priorities which has been informed by the recommendations from three evaluations commissioned by ECW." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.oversight: "Progress will be tracked annually through the log frame... If ECW consistently fails to meet agreed reform targets, the UK will retain the option to reconsider our committed level of funding." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within ECW can be reallocated between crises (e.g., Ukraine response), but major shifts require ExCom approval. The UK retains the option to reduce funding if ECW underperforms: "If ECW consistently fails to meet agreed reform targets, the UK will retain the option to reconsider our committed level of funding."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: ECW’s Strategic Plan (2023–2026) includes adaptive mechanisms: "ECW is reviewing its priorities and portfolio as it develops its next four-year Strategic Plan... The plan will be launched at the Transforming Education Summit (TES) in September." The UK’s thematic partnerships allow for testing new approaches (e.g., climate-education links).

quote.reallocation: "The UK will retain the option to reconsider our committed level of funding [if targets are missed]." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.adaptive: "ECW is reviewing its priorities and portfolio as it develops its next four-year Strategic Plan (2023–2026)... We are working with our partners on ECW’s ExCom to deliver on a set of ECW reform priorities." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ECW (fund manager) → Implementing partners (UNICEF, NGOs, LEGs) → End beneficiaries (children). The document notes: "ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly," implying a layered structure.

quote.layers: "ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly... Not all FCDO posts have the capacity to respond – ECW is an effective delivery channel in these circumstances." (D0005046.odt, Box 8)
quote.payment: "Progress will be tracked annually through the log frame... UK reform priorities are identified in table 4 below together with key performance indicators. These will be monitored through ECW’s Annual work plan and FCDO’s Annual Review process." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to FCDO country posts (rejected due to capacity gaps: "Not all FCDO posts have the capacity to respond")
Direct grants to INGOs (rejected as "transaction heavy and inefficient")
World Bank-led mechanisms (complementary but limited to state institutions: "development instruments can be too focused on supporting state institutions")
Global Partnership for Education (GPE) alone (rejected due to overlap; UK "has taken a leadership role with donors across the two funds [ECW and GPE] to improve collaboration")
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: ECW was chosen for its **speed**, **global reach**, and **specialization in crises**: "Crises are complex and ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly." The mixed modality (ECW + thematic partnerships + FCDO capacity) addresses gaps in **localization** (via partnerships), **climate resilience** (new priority), and **systemic reform** (ECW’s role in global architecture).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with GPE leading to duplication
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK has taken a "leadership role with donors across the two funds to improve collaboration" and secured closer working in Afghanistan/Myanmar responses.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: ECW’s limited capacity to drive reforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will monitor reform KPIs annually and "retain the option to reconsider funding" if targets are missed. Thematic partnerships (£9m) will address gaps where ECW lacks capacity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak coordination between humanitarian and development actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Investment in FCDO technical capability (£1m) to "provide surge support to posts... to coordinate and influence international efforts."

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited Southern ownership in ECW governance
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Engagement with local actors via LEGs and "discussions with UNICEF on how to improve coordination... particularly in the nexus [humanitarian-development blur]."

quote.why_chosen: "Crises are complex and ECW provides a platform for bringing together education technical expertise which can be deployed to respond quickly. Not all FCDO posts have the capacity to respond – ECW is an effective delivery channel in these circumstances... Responding on a case-by-case would be transaction heavy and inefficient." (D0005046.odt, Box 8)
quote.risks: "There is some overlap in mandates between the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and ECW... The UK has taken a leadership role with donors across the two funds to improve collaboration." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)
quote.vfm: "UK reform priorities are identified in table 4... These will be monitored through ECW’s Annual work plan and FCDO’s Annual Review process... If ECW consistently fails to meet agreed reform targets, the UK will retain the option to reconsider our committed level of funding." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with **humanitarian access** and **rapid-response capacity**. For example: "In Cox’s Bazar... education in the camps is delivered primarily by humanitarian non-state actors" due to government restrictions. Local NGOs (e.g., in Syria or DRC) are often excluded from cluster leadership due to perceived capacity gaps: "There are challenges in making faster progress [on localization]... inequities in terms of experience, capacity and resourcing of international actors."
q27_constraints_detail: Government restrictions on NGO operations (e.g., Bangladesh, Myanmar)
Limited local NGO capacity for cluster coordination (ODI 2020 study)
Security risks excluding Southern partners from high-threat areas
Donor preferences for multilateral channels (e.g., ECW over bilateral)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for rapid response** drives the choice of ECW’s platform model ("respond quickly" to sudden crises), while the **gap in climate-education links** necessitates thematic partnerships (£9m). The **complexity of protracted crises** requires a mixed structure: "The international community does not always have the right modalities to work in the grey area between humanitarian support and development... ECW offers an alternative channel."
q28_linkages: Rapid response needs → ECW’s FER window ("immediate and rapid response to education needs in sudden onset emergencies")
Systemic reform goals → Core funding to ECW + ExCom engagement
Climate priorities → Thematic partnerships (separate from ECW)
Localization gaps → FCDO technical surge support (£1m)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between **speed** and **inclusion**: "Responding on a case-by-case would be transaction heavy and inefficient" (justifying ECW’s platform), but notes that this risks sidelining local actors. The **£1m for FCDO capacity** aims to balance this by improving coordination with Southern partners. On climate, there’s a trade-off between **global advocacy** (e.g., COP27 guidance) and **local adaptation**: "Much greater attention is needed to the impacts of the climate crisis on education... but the evidence base is nascent."
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (ECW platform) vs. localization (limited Southern leadership in governance)
Global reach (ECW) vs. context-specific adaptation (thematic partnerships)
Efficiency (core funding) vs. equity (earmarked funds for Sahel girls)
Humanitarian focus (ECW) vs. development needs (LEG coordination gaps)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **Major risk rating** drives **intensive oversight**: annual reviews, reform KPIs, and the threat to reduce funding if ECW underperforms. In FCAS contexts, "FCDO will work closely with country Posts... to ensure programmes are guided by in-depth local knowledge," implying higher management intensity where risks are acute.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** in the structure: the £1m for FCDO technical capability enables posts to "coordinate and influence international efforts," while ECW’s AF window funds local innovation. However, Southern partners’ roles remain largely implementational: "The role and commitment of national government [is] a critical enabling factor, but this was often raised alongside inequities in experience, capacity and resourcing."

quote.where_who: "In Cox’s Bazar... education in the camps is delivered primarily by humanitarian non-state actors, is of low quality, and reaches only around half those who need it... Finding durable solutions under these conditions is extremely challenging." (D0005046.odt, Box 4)
quote.what_how: "The international community does not always have the right modalities to work in the grey area between humanitarian support and development... ECW offers an alternative channel." (D0005046.odt, What more needs to be done)
quote.tradeoffs: "Responding on a case-by-case would be transaction heavy and inefficient... There are challenges in making faster progress [on localization]... inequities in terms of experience, capacity and resourcing of international actors." (D0005046.odt, Box 8 and 200428_synthesis_report.pdf)
quote.risk_management: "The risk rating for the programme is Major. EiEPC will operate in contexts that have been severely disrupted by COVID-19... By working closely with country Posts... we will ensure programmes are guided by in-depth local knowledge." (D0005046.odt, Assurances)
quote.capacity_roles: "Boosting access to FCDO’s technical capability... to provide surge support to posts in the event of a crisis to coordinate and influence international efforts... The role and commitment of national government [is] a critical enabling factor." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond? and Box 6)

key_programme_risks: Chronic underfunding of EiEPC (only 22% of 2021 appeals met)
Weak data on learning outcomes in crises (<10% of grantees track safety/protection)
Limited Southern ownership in ECW governance (ODI 2020 study)
Overlap between ECW and GPE mandates causing duplication
Climate shocks disrupting education (40m children/year affected)
Protection risks for children (GBV, trafficking, child labour in crises)
Host government restrictions (e.g., Rohingya education in Bangladesh)
Short-term humanitarian funding cycles misaligned with protracted crises
Low transition rates from emergency to formal education

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK’s £80m core contribution to ECW aims to catalyse £1.25bn total funding. Advocacy for increased donor commitments via the Safe Schools Declaration and TES replenishment event.
ECW’s 2023–2026 Strategic Plan prioritizes improved M&E; UK’s Data for Foundational Learning Programme includes an EiEPC focus.
£1m for FCDO technical capacity to support localization; engagement with LEGs and national governments in protracted crises.
UK-led donor collaboration to clarify roles (e.g., GPE for state institutions, ECW for non-state actors).
Thematic partnerships (£9m) to pilot climate-resilient education models; new FCDO guidance for COP27.
Safeguarding policies embedded in all partnerships; ECW’s disability inclusion framework; focus on safe learning spaces.
Political engagement by FCDO posts (e.g., Rohingya curriculum negotiations in Bangladesh).
ECW’s MYRP window provides multi-year funding; UK advocacy for sustained support in protracted crises.

fcas_specific_lessons: Localization requires **long-term investment in national systems**: "The role and commitment of national government [is] a critical enabling factor" (Box 6).

Humanitarian-development **nexus challenges** persist: "In situations where the lines between development and humanitarian action are blurred" (e.g., Afghanistan), coordination mechanisms must be adaptive.
**Non-state actors** are essential in FCAS: "Education in the [Rohingya] camps is delivered primarily by humanitarian non-state actors" due to government restrictions.
Data systems must be **conflict-sensitive**: "Capturing completion, transition and holistic learning for those affected by conflict and crisis is more challenging" (Box 5).
Climate adaptation requires **context-specific approaches**: "The evidence base on the links between education and climate change is nascent but growing."
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase I-II of EiEPC established ECW as a global fund but revealed gaps in: 1) **localization** (limited Southern leadership); 2) **climate integration** (new priority for Phase III); 3) **disability inclusion** (ECW’s 2022 Policy Framework addresses this); 4) **transition from emergency to formal education** (<60% transition rates). The UK’s £9m thematic partnerships directly respond to these gaps.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1. **Added climate focus**: New thematic partnerships and COP27 guidance. 2. **Stronger localization**: £1m for FCDO technical capacity to support posts in engaging local actors. 3. **Disability inclusion**: ECW’s 2022 Policy Framework and UK’s requirement to disaggregate data by disability. 4. **Flexible funding**: AF window for innovation (e.g., climate-resilient schools). 5. **Explicit reform targets**: KPIs for ECW’s coordination with GPE/World Bank.

quote.risks: "Only 22% of [2021] appeals for EiEPC were met... Lessthan 10% of grantees have solid evidence on safety and protection." (D0005046.odt, What more needs to be done)
quote.lessons: "EiEPC phases I and II have helped to establish ECW as a leading global fund for EiEPC... The next phase will build on these achievements and deliver on... climate change by investing in thematic partnerships." (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)
quote.design_changes: "The UK’s new Data for Foundational Learning Programme includes an EiEPC focus... We are interrogating the 20 million [children reached] figure with ECW to check it is feasible and achievable." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s £80m core contribution to ECW aims to catalyse £1.25bn in total funding for 2023–2026. Previous UK funding helped ECW leverage additional support (e.g., USAID in the Sahel).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £90 million" (D0005046.odt, Programme summary)
quote.allocation: "Making a core contribution to ECW (£80m)... Boosting access to FCDO’s technical capability (£1m)... Investing in UK thematic partnerships (£9m)." (D0005046.odt, How will the UK respond?)
quote.leverage: "ECW has the ambition to raise $1.5 billion (£1.25 billion) over the period of the coming Strategic Plan and to reach 20 million crisis affected children and adolescents." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)
quote.previous_leverage: "Since 2019 earmarked funding for the Sahel region... has helped leverage additional support to the region from other donors, such as USAID." (D0005046.odt, How has the UK responded?)

metadata.programme_name: Delivery Solutions Hub

quote.text: The Centre for Delivery aims to inspire, empower and equip FCDO staff to achieve real-world impact by building a more capable organisation that embraces evidence, learning, innovation, creativity, empowered accountability, and informed decision making.

duration_source.text: AMP Start Date: 1 April 2023; AMP End Date: 31 March 2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening FCDO's programme design and delivery capabilities) with evidence generation (research to identify best practices and lessons) and implementation research (testing adaptive approaches). It aims to improve programme effectiveness through better design, monitoring, and learning systems.

q1_source.text: The interventions funded by this programme will strengthen the evidence base and reach of the support the Solutions Hub can provide to the design, delivery, and review of programmes. [...] This will enable the Hub to have a catalytic role and more equitable reach, promoting more efficient and effective approaches to design and delivery of individual programmes within FCDO’s portfolio.
q1_source.source: D0003516.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending

q3_expected_outputs.output: Resource bank of advice/evidence developed for programme teams
Guidance on Annual Reviews and Programme Completion Reviews refined
Training/drop-in clinics on programme design and review practices
Research reports synthesizing lessons from FCDO programmes
Strengthened linkages between programmes and delivery networks
Improved capability of FCDO teams in adaptive programme design

what_objectives.summary: The Solutions Hub aims to transform FCDO's programme delivery by embedding evidence-based practices, reducing bureaucracy, and building internal capacity through a mix of in-house expertise and external research. It focuses on improving design quality, portfolio coherence, and outcome tracking across FCDO's global programmes.

quote.text: The intended outcome of the Hub will be to contribute to the improved quality, efficiency & effectiveness of design, delivery, and review of policy programmes across the FCDO by: [...] Outcome 1: Improving quality of programmes designed, drawing on evidence and with a focus on effective implementation.
quote.source: D0003516.odt, Proposed impact & outcome of the Solutions Hub

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is classified as 'Minor' risk and focuses on internal capacity building within FCDO systems rather than direct implementation in fragile contexts. The primary risks relate to organizational change management rather than external operational risks.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Minor

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The merger of DFID and FCO created variation in programming capability across the organization. Limited cognitive bandwidth and institutional memory gaps constrain the adoption of new practices. Internal data systems require synthesis and cleaning before analysis can be conducted effectively.

quote.text: The merger of the Department for International Development and the Foreign Commonwealth Office also widens the variation of skills and project/programming capability within the new organisation. [...] Cognitive bandwidth refers to the natural limits of our focus and attention: we cannot notice everything, remember everything or calculate everything.

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) - Centre for Delivery
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Core Team and in-house delivery advisors (all UK-based) will drive the strategic direction, research priorities, and capacity-building support. External experts will be commissioned for specific analytical tasks but won't have decision-making authority over programme direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on adaptive programme design
mentorship through embedded advisors
knowledge management systems
constructive challenge during programme reviews
tailored support for Posts with limited programming capacity

partner_organizations.name: External research consultants (various)
partner_organizations.role: Conduct targeted research and analysis; produce case studies and guidance documents

partner_organizations.name: In-house delivery advisors (potential future roles)
partner_organizations.role: Embed lessons, provide tailored training, and support programme teams

partner_organizations.name: FCDO programme teams (internal)
partner_organizations.role: Primary beneficiaries of Hub support; implement programme improvements

partner_organizations.name: Centre for Delivery's Core Team
partner_organizations.role: Strategic leadership, coordination, and quality assurance

quote.text: The optimal model for the programme would combine external expertise with in-house delivery expertise, to provide training, accompaniment, and capacity building - helping the organisation take forward lessons, drive changes in behaviour and embed good practice.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme will use a combination of accountable grants to non-profits, contracts procured through FCDO framework agreements, and potentially direct procurement for specialized expertise. Initial phase relies heavily on external contracts due to workforce constraints.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Centre for Delivery's Solutions Hub Core Team (existing FCDO staff) will manage all programme activities, with external experts contracted for specific research tasks. No consortium or partnership structure is established - all delivery flows through FCDO's internal systems.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: External experts will be selected through existing FCDO framework agreements or direct procurement when frameworks don't meet needs. This approach balances speed with value-for-money considerations, leveraging pre-approved suppliers where possible.

quote.text: Outsourced delivery: the Programme Responsible Owner (PRO) in agreement with the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) will determine the route to market and funding mechanism for each research and analytical project. In many cases, we anticipate that the Hub will use a combination of grants to non-profit organisations and drawdown from FCDO framework agreements.
quote.source: D0003516.odt, Route to market & funding mechanism

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Core Team reports through FCDO's existing management structures to the Programme Co-ordination, Learning and Improvement pillar lead (A1/Grade 6) and ultimately to the Centre for Delivery's Senior Leadership Team. No external governance bodies are established.

quote.text: The Core Team and in-house delivery advisors [...] will determine before any recruitment campaign, the duration of any appointment, nature of the contract [...] and what happens to in-house delivery staff when the programme comes to an end - with proper consideration given to FCDO's contingent liability and duty of care to such personnel in line with FCDO HR requirements.
quote.source: D0003516.odt, Route to market & funding mechanism

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between research topics based on emerging needs identified through Core Team engagements, but requires approval through FCDO's internal processes. The programme is designed with decision points to revisit delivery options if in-house capacity becomes available.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs a staggered approach where research priorities are adjusted based on real-time feedback from programme teams. External research contracts will be commissioned in phases to respond to identified gaps, with the Core Team determining key issues that emerge.

quote.text: Commitment to fund external expertise will be short term, with decision points where the Core Team looks at what the key issues are that have come up through its interactions with programme teams, and commission further work externally to address them.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → External contractors/researchers (no additional layers as all work is either done by Core Team or directly contracted experts)

quote.text: The performancerequirements and frameworks (where appropriate) for each research and analytical project commissioned will be outlined in a Terms of Reference agreed by the SRO and the A1/grade 6 PCLIPillar lead, prior to the signing of any funding agreement.

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing scenario (maintain Core Team only)
Option 1: Targeted outsourced delivery (Core Team + external experts)
Option 2: Combination of in-house delivery expertise and targeted outsourcing (preferred but not immediately feasible)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (targeted outsourced delivery) was selected as the initial approach because: 1) In-house delivery roles require uplifts to FCDO's workforce spending target which haven't been approved by HMTreasury; 2) External expertise provides immediate access to specialized skills not available in-house; 3) It allows flexibility to adjust priorities based on emerging needs while building the evidence base. The programme will transition to Option 2 if workforce constraints are resolved.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited organizational capacity to embed learning from external experts due to lack of in-house delivery roles
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Staggered implementation with decision points to introduce in-house elements when feasible; Core Team will prioritize knowledge management and dissemination activities

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: External consultants may lack understanding of FCDO's internal systems and incentives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Core Team will provide clear briefs and steer research to ensure relevance; in-house advisors will be added later to bridge this gap

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Programme management burden from coordinating multiple external contracts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of framework agreements to streamline procurement; phased approach to contracting

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential delay in achieving transformational change without in-house capacity building
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus initial external research on generating actionable, easy-to-absorb guidance; build institutional memory through documentation

quote.text: Delivery option 2 is likely to represent the most cost-effective approach, with the Core Team and in-house delivery experts being better able to drive a shift in culture and behaviour around design and delivery, increasing overall levels of assurance around programme quality. [...] However, the programme will proceed with delivery option 1 focussed on targeted outsourced delivery, until such time as in-house delivery becomes feasible.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The internal FCDO context (post-merger capability variations and workforce constraints) limits the ability to use in-house delivery experts initially, forcing reliance on external contractors despite their limitations in driving organizational change.
q27_constraints_detail: Workforce spending targets prevent immediate hiring of in-house advisors
Variation in programming skills across merged DFID/FCO staff requires tailored support
Cognitive bandwidth limits constrain how much new information staff can absorb
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both rapid evidence generation (to inform current programme designs) and long-term capacity building (to embed cultural change) requires a hybrid delivery model that can initially outsource research while planning for future in-house embedding of lessons.
q28_linkages: Complex programme designs requiring adaptive approaches → Need for external expertise in innovative delivery models
Goal of reducing approval times → Requires both process improvements (external analysis) and staff capability building (future in-house roles)
Portfolio coherence objectives → Necessitates centralized coordination (Core Team) with decentralized implementation support
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) The efficiency of using external experts (faster access to specialized skills) versus the equity benefits of building internal capacity (more sustainable organizational change); 2) The need for equitable reach across all FCDO teams versus the efficiency of focusing on high-priority programmes first.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed (external experts) vs sustainability (in-house capacity)
specialized skills (external) vs organizational knowledge (internal)
broad reach vs targeted impact
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Minor' risk rating enables a relatively light-touch management approach focused on milestone delivery rather than intensive oversight, though the need for cultural change requires more engaged support than typical research contracts.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The limited initial capacity (only Core Team) shapes the phased approach where external experts generate evidence first, which will later be embedded by in-house advisors when capacity allows. This creates a clear division between research production and capacity building roles.

quote.text: The optimal model for the programme would combine external expertise with in-house delivery expertise, to provide training, accompaniment, and capacity building - helping the organisation take forward lessons, drive changes in behaviour and embed good practice. Should in-house delivery not be feasible, bought-in expertise will be used.

key_programme_risks: In-house delivery capacity limited by workforce constraints
External consultants may not fully understand FCDO's internal systems
Programme teams may not have capacity to absorb new approaches
Risk of generating evidence that isn't effectively used
Potential for new approaches to create additional bureaucratic burden
Difficulty in changing entrenched program design practices
Limited institutional memory due to staff turnover

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: In-house delivery capacity limited by workforce constraints
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proceed initially with external expertise (Option 1) while negotiating workforce spending uplifts; staggered approach to introduce in-house elements later

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: External consultants may not fully understand FCDO's internal systems
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Core Team provides detailed briefs and steers research; future in-house advisors will validate and contextualize findings

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Programme teams may not have capacity to absorb new approaches
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on producing 'easy to absorb' guidance; provide tailored support to teams with limited capacity

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Risk of generating evidence that isn't effectively used
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Build resource bank that's directly tied to programme teams' needs; use in-house advisors to embed lessons

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Potential for new approaches to create additional bureaucratic burden
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Design interventions to reduce complexity; focus on streamlining existing processes

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Difficulty in changing entrenched program design practices
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use constructive challenge approach; leverage Senior Leadership Team support

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous reviews (2018 DFID analysis) showed common programme design weaknesses including: weak theories of change, optimism bias in success estimation, poor use of evidence, and lack of focus on delivery mechanisms. These findings directly shaped the Hub's focus areas.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates: 1) Explicit focus on addressing optimism bias through constructive challenge; 2) Emphasis on 'how' delivery will occur, not just 'why' programmes exist; 3) Requirements for outcome-focused monitoring; 4) Adaptive management approaches to respond to geopolitical changes.

quote.text: An internal review of business cases for Official Development Assistance (ODA) programmes in the former Department for International Development in 2018 found that: Some theories of change were weak, with poor use of evidence; Design placed more emphasis on the 'why' of the programme, less on 'what' it will deliver, and very little on 'how' it would deliver; Design teams tended to have some optimism bias in estimating the likelihood of success.
Programme Value: £660k (FY23/24: £110k; FY24/25: £300k; and a provisional £250k for FY25/26 - dependent on future SR settlements)

metadata.programme_name: Global Health Security Research & Development Programme
metadata.quote: D0004243.odt, Key Information section
metadata.duration_source: "Start and end dates: January 2023–December 2027" (D0004243.odt, Key Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines technology development (vaccines, diagnostics, treatments), capacity building (equitable partnerships with LMICs), and evidence generation (research to inform policy). It focuses on preparing for, preventing, and responding to disease outbreaks with epidemic/pandemic potential.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The GHSR&D business case is for R&D investment to prepare for, prevent and respond rapidly to disease outbreaks with epidemic or pandemic potential, benefiting vulnerable populations, and building sustainable and equitable R&D partnerships with LMIC organisations." (D0004243.odt, Detailed information)
q3_expected_outputs: 5–10 new affordable vaccines, diagnostics and treatments developed and available for up to 10 priority diseases
Equitable partnerships and capacity developed with LMICs, including a Science & Technology partnership offer for emerging science powers (e.g., Vietnam, South Africa, Kenya, Senegal)
Evidence generation and use to shape policy
Multiple UK institutions contributing to the Centre of Research
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to accelerate the development of affordable health technologies for LMICs, reduce vaccine development timelines to <100 days, and establish collaborative research partnerships to strengthen global health security.
what_objectives.quote: D0004243.odt, Detailed information

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme focuses on LMICs with high outbreak risks and complex operating environments, including weak health systems and capacity constraints.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall Risk Rating: Major" (D0004243.odt, Key Information)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme requires strong health systems for product delivery (supported through bilateral programmes) and relies on partnerships with governments and manufacturing partners in LMICs to address capacity gaps.
where_context.quote: D0004243.odt, Detailed information

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes collaborative partnerships with LMIC organizations, including joint research and decision-making through platforms like the Centre of Research and pooled funds with donors like Wellcome Trust and BMGF.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
institutional strengthening
research grants
collaborative research partnerships

partner_organizations.role: Product development partnership for vaccines

partner_organizations.name: Wellcome Trust
partner_organizations.role: Co-donor for pooled funds and joint platforms

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-donor for pooled funds and joint platforms
