quote.budget: "Programme Value: £4.95m" (D0006532.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Supporting the Pandemic Fund (SPF)
metadata.quote: "The UK will play a leading role in building global resilience against threats to human health for a safer and more prosperous world, ensuring we are harnessing xHMG capabilities to deliver the global health aims of the Integrated Review and the International Development Strategy." (D0003174.odt, Summary Sheet)
metadata.duration_source: "AMPEndDate: May2025" (D0003174.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides seed funding to the Pandemic Fund, a Financial Intermediary Fund hosted by the World Bank, to support pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response (PPR) in low- and middle-income countries (L/MICs). The goal is to leverage UK influence to shape the fund's design and ensure investments are targeted effectively, while catalyzing broader international and domestic financing for PPR.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme provides early seed funding towards the Pandemic Fund – a new Financial Intermediary Fund for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response hosted by the World Bank." (D0003174.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened national laboratory systems to detect pathogens of epidemic potential
Improved surveillance systems for early detection of disease outbreaks
Enhanced country capacity to implement mass vaccinations and risk communication
Establishment of coherent response structures for health emergencies
Increased domestic resource investment in public health and PPR in L/MICs
Improved Joint External Evaluation (JEE) and SPAR scores in beneficiary countries
Leverage of over $1.5bn in financing for pandemic preparedness through UK's £25m contribution
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce the health, social, and economic impacts of disease outbreaks in L/MICs by investing in pandemic PPR, while ensuring the UK retains influence in global health governance and leverages significant additional financing.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will do this through targeted investments in pandemic PPR that allow countries to better detect, contain and respond to disease outbreaks." (D0003174.odt, Expected impacts and outcomes)

countries_regions: global (focus on low- and middle-income countries)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's risk rating is assessed as moderate due to concerns about the Pandemic Fund's nascent stage and lack of a track record, which could affect the quality of proposals and value for money (VfM). However, the fund works through established implementing entities with strong relationships with the UK.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme’s risk rating is assessed as moderate. The main programme risk relates to concerns that Pandemic Fund investments offer weak value for money if they are poorly targeted or if the proposals it receives are of a poor quality." (D0003174.odt, Risk)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak health systems in L/MICs limit the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks. Climate change increases zoonotic disease risks, and under-investment in PPR has left critical gaps in laboratory capacity, surveillance, and workforce skills. Environmental degradation heightens pandemic risks by increasing human-animal contact.
where_context.quote: "Environmental degradation is a key risk in increasing the likelihood of future pandemics, bringing animal and humans into greater contact and heightening the risk of disease crossovers." (D0003174.odt, Climate and Environment)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Pandemic Fund (hosted by the World Bank)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Pandemic Fund Board, which includes donor constituencies (e.g., UK as part of a donor group), makes decisions. Implementing entities (e.g., UN agencies, MDBs) deliver programmes in L/MICs, but the document does not explicitly clarify the balance of decision-making power between Northern and Southern actors.
q10_capacity_building_details: Strengthening national laboratory systems
Training health workforce in surveillance and response
Building domestic resource mobilization for PPR
Supporting One Health platforms (e.g., multisectoral coordination)
Upskilling local staff for health emergency response

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Host of the Pandemic Fund and Trustee

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Technical support and seconded staff to the Pandemic Fund Secretariat

partner_organizations.name: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
partner_organizations.role: Accredited Implementing Entity

partner_organizations.name: Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
partner_organizations.role: Accredited Implementing Entity

partner_organizations.name: Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI)
partner_organizations.role: Accredited Implementing Entity

partner_organizations.name: Low- and middle-income country governments
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and co-investors in PPR projects

partner_organizations.name: UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF, FAO, OIE)
partner_organizations.role: Potential Implementing Entities

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)
partner_organizations.role: Potential Implementing Entities

who_partners.quote: "The Pandemic Fund will work through established implementing entities, many of whom the UK already has a strong relationship and who offer a track record of cost effectiveness." (D0003174.odt, Risk)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK's contribution is governed by a Contribution Agreement (CA) with the World Bank, which acts as Trustee for the Pandemic Fund. The CA outlines financial and management terms but is not legally binding. Funds are pooled and allocated by the Pandemic Fund Board, with no earmarking by donors.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The Pandemic Fund is managed by a Secretariat (World Bank and WHO staff) and overseen by a Governing Board with donor and beneficiary representation. Implementing Entities (e.g., UN agencies, MDBs) deliver projects in L/MICs based on competitive calls for proposals. The UK participates in a donor constituency on the Board.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO will contribute up to £25m to the Pandemic Fund as announced by former Prime Minister Johnson at the G7 leaders’ meeting in June 2022. This contribution represents ~1.9% of the total contributions announced to date (approx. $1.6bn) for the Pandemic Fund." (D0003174.odt, Financial Details)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Pandemic Fund Governing Board includes donor constituencies (e.g., UK as part of a group) and beneficiary representatives. Decisions on funding allocations are made collectively, with technical input from a Technical Advisory Panel (10/21 members are women). The Board approves calls for proposals and evaluates bids based on criteria including VfM and equity.
how_governance.quote: "The Governing Board will consider the scope and needs of the call [for proposals] as well as future plans, including any replenishment strategy once designed. The Board can only agree to issue a CfP on the basis of Currently Available Resources and Indicative Expected Resources as reported by the Trustee." (D0003174.odt, Payment in Advance of Need Assessment)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are pooled and allocated by the Board based on proposals, but reallocation between projects requires Board approval. The UK can influence priorities through its Board constituency but cannot earmark funds.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The Pandemic Fund's results framework is still evolving, and the UK will push for adaptive management through Board engagement. The first call for proposals (2023) will focus on "Detect" capacities (e.g., surveillance, laboratories), but future rounds may adjust priorities based on emerging gaps.
how_flexibility.quote: "The PF is still developing an overarching results framework which will set specific targets for its headline impacts and outcomes." (D0003174.odt, Expected impacts and outcomes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Pandemic Fund Secretariat (World Bank/WHO) → Implementing Entities (e.g., Gavi, Global Fund) → L/MIC beneficiaries
how_efficiency.quote: "The other major cost category is the operating expenses of the Secretariat, which are estimated to be $3.825m to cover setup and running costs for the period July 2022–July 2023, which should represent around 1% of the first call for proposals from implementing countries." (D0003174.odt, Financial Details)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: FCDO does not provide funding for the Pandemic Fund and leverages existing UK investments to deliver PPR objectives.
Option 2: FCDO provides a moderate contribution (£25m) to the Pandemic Fund (selected).
Option 3: FCDO provides a large contribution (>£50m) to the Pandemic Fund.
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (£25m) was selected to balance influence and risk. A larger contribution (Option 3) would increase UK influence but also the risk of poor VfM given the Fund's nascent stage. Option 1 was rejected because it would limit the UK's ability to shape global PPR coordination and miss the opportunity to leverage £25m into over $1.5bn of financing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak VfM if Pandemic Fund investments are poorly targeted or proposals are of low quality.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will work with the Board to develop robust VfM policies and assessment criteria for bids, leveraging relationships with established implementing entities (e.g., World Bank, Gavi).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UK influence may be limited as an alternate seat holder in a donor constituency.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will use its development expertise to promote strategic objectives (e.g., health systems strengthening, equity) and build consensus within its constituency.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in disbursement or fund absorption due to the Fund's new processes.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will engage early to shape Secretariat policies and ensure timely calls for proposals, with the first £10m disbursed in 2022/23 to secure Board membership.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 2 is selected as the preferred option, as it was assessed that the potential downside VfM risks associated with Option 3 were too great to justify the additional benefits it offered, particularly given wider ODA & financial pressures." (D0003174.odt, Appraisal of Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on L/MICs constrain partner selection to multilateral entities (e.g., UN agencies, MDBs) with existing capacity to operate in fragile contexts. Weak national institutions in L/MICs necessitate reliance on international implementing entities, though the Fund aims to catalyze domestic investment over time.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited capacity of L/MIC governments to directly manage funds
Need for multilateral entities with experience in FCAS contexts
Dependence on established partners (e.g., World Bank, WHO) to ensure VfM
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The financing mechanism objective (leveraging £25m to influence a $1.5bn+ fund) determines the multilateral delivery structure. The need for global coordination and equity requires a Board with donor and beneficiary representation, while the focus on PPR capacities (e.g., surveillance, laboratories) shapes the selection of technical implementing entities.
q28_linkages: Global public good benefits → multilateral governance structure
Focus on L/MICs → reliance on UN/MDB implementing entities
Equity goals → Technical Advisory Panel with gender balance (10/21 women)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between efficiency (rapid disbursement through established entities) and equity (ensuring benefits reach marginalized groups). For example, the UK will push for disaggregated data on beneficiaries by gender and disability, though this may add complexity to monitoring.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (using existing multilateral partners) vs. inclusion (ensuring local ownership)
Efficiency (pooled funding) vs. equity (targeting vulnerable groups in L/MICs)
Global coordination (donor-led Board) vs. country ownership (L/MIC representation)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to milestone-based oversight (e.g., Board approval of calls for proposals) and active UK engagement to shape VfM policies, rather than light-touch management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, with implementing entities required to upskill local health workforces (e.g., surveillance, laboratory systems) and strengthen domestic institutions. The UK will advocate for proposals that include training and institutional support as part of PPR investments.
intersections.quote: "The UK will prioritise using this seed funding to work with other Board members to develop a strategy to crowd in support from other actors, recognising the strain on international ODA budgets. We will also emphasise how the Fund should catalyse domestic financing." (D0003174.odt, Fits with UK priorities)

key_programme_risks: Pandemic Fund investments may offer weak VfM if poorly targeted or proposals are low quality.
UK influence may be diluted as an alternate seat holder in a donor constituency.
Delays in fund absorption due to nascent Secretariat processes.
Future pandemics may emerge that are difficult to contain (e.g., respiratory viruses).
Political and social determinants of pandemic response (e.g., government decision-making, inequities) may limit impact.
Fragmentation in global health architecture could undermine coordination.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Weak VfM from Pandemic Fund investments.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will work with the Board to develop robust VfM policies and assessment criteria, leveraging relationships with implementing entities (e.g., World Bank, Gavi) that have strong track records.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited UK influence on the Board.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will use its development expertise to build consensus within its constituency and advocate for strategic priorities (e.g., health systems, equity).
Early engagement to shape Secretariat policies and ensure timely calls for proposals, with £10m disbursed in 2022/23 to secure Board membership.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Future pandemics may be difficult to contain.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on upstream investments (e.g., surveillance, One Health) to detect and respond early, while advocating for complementary improvements in vaccine/therapeutic access.
UK will promote coherence on the Board, ensuring PF investments align with existing systems (e.g., IHR, WHO) and avoid duplication.

fcas_specific_lessons: Weak health systems in FCAS contexts require investments in core public health functions (e.g., surveillance, laboratories) to detect and respond to outbreaks.
Environmental degradation in fragile settings increases zoonotic disease risks, necessitating One Health approaches.
Previous outbreaks (e.g., Ebola in West Africa) demonstrated that delayed detection and response in FCAS can prolong epidemics.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from COVID-19 and earlier outbreaks (e.g., SARS, Ebola) highlight the need for: 1) Stronger surveillance systems to detect pathogens early; 2) Integrated health systems that can pivot to respond to emergencies; 3) Sustainable financing mechanisms to avoid "panic and neglect" cycles. Programmes like REDISSE (World Bank) and TDDAP (FCDO) demonstrated that investments in laboratory capacity and One Health platforms improved COVID-19 response readiness.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The Pandemic Fund was designed to address gaps identified in previous PPR financing, including: 1) Catalytic funding to incentivize domestic investment; 2) Focus on upstream capacities (e.g., detection) rather than reactive response; 3) Coordination with existing architectures (e.g., IHR, WHO). The UK’s role reflects lessons on the need for donor influence to shape fund priorities.
risks_lessons.quote: "The number of disease threats is on the rise, with the WHO recognising more than 1,300 epidemic events since 2011... In 2022, experts estimated that there are at least 10,000 virus species able to infect humans, mostly circulating silently in wild mammals." (D0003174.odt, Context)

co_funding_partners.partner: G7 and G20 countries (20+ sovereign donors)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK's £25m contribution is part of a pooled fund expected to exceed $1.5bn (£1.2bn), leveraging over 50x the UK's investment. The fund aims to catalyze additional domestic and international financing for PPR.
financial_details.quote: "Through a moderate, £25m investment, the UK can leverage its world-leading health and development expertise to maximise the potential impact of over $1.5bn in financing for pandemic preparedness." (D0003174.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

metadata.programme_name: South Sudan Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience Programme (SSHARP)
metadata.quote: "The South Sudan Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience Programme (SSHARP) will spend up to £300 million over four years to tackle protracted humanitarian crisis needs and drivers in South Sudan." (D0006100.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "The South Sudan Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience programme will spend up to £300 million over four years" (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SSHARP is a **service delivery** programme (direct humanitarian assistance) combined with **implementation research** (testing integrated humanitarian-resilience approaches) and **capacity building** (strengthening local systems). It focuses on saving lives through emergency aid while simultaneously building resilience to reduce long-term dependency, with explicit testing of new approaches like cash programming and conflict-sensitive delivery.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Providing life saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable people in South Sudan and where possible strengthening their resilience to conflict, climate and economic shocks is a priority within the UK approach in South Sudan. This programme will directly contribute to meeting these needs, as part of the international humanitarian response." (D0006100.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "SSHARP will help deliver UK climate ambitions... delivering assistance in a principled manner, at a minimum doing no harm, as well as proactively identifying opportunities to build resilience to climate change." (D0006100.odt, Strategic Case)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 1 million people reached annually
q3_expected_outputs.details: through emergency humanitarian response, resilient livelihoods support, and protection interventions

q3_expected_outputs.output: strengthened resilience to conflict and climate shocks
q3_expected_outputs.details: in vulnerable communities via livelihoods, early warning systems, and climate-adapted infrastructure

q3_expected_outputs.output: more effective and efficient humanitarian response
q3_expected_outputs.details: through improved coordination, cash programming, and conflict-sensitive analysis

q3_expected_outputs.output: evidence generation
q3_expected_outputs.details: on what works in fragile states, including climate-risk data and gender-responsive cash transfers

q3_expected_outputs.output: policy influence
q3_expected_outputs.details: pushing Government of South Sudan to invest in basic services and improve humanitarian access

what_objectives.summary: SSHARP integrates emergency humanitarian aid with longer-term resilience-building, testing adaptive approaches (e.g., cash transfers, conflict-sensitive programming) while generating evidence to inform policy. The dual focus on immediate needs and systemic change reflects a shift from short-term relief to sustainable solutions in a protracted crisis.
what_objectives.quote: "SSHARP will directly contribute to meeting [humanitarian] needs... as part of the international humanitarian response... [and] strengthen resilience to conflict and climate shocks." (D0006100.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "A key shift in implementation under SSHARP will be integration of resilience and livelihood programming in areas of high humanitarian need, supporting greater integration between humanitarian-development-peace actors." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: South Sudan is classified as the world’s **third most fragile state** (Fragile States Index 2023), with **active conflict**, **extreme food insecurity** (63% of population in crisis), and **state collapse** (ranked last on Human Development Index). The programme operates in a context of **subnational violence**, **climate shocks**, and **near-total impunity for aid worker attacks** (210 killed since independence).
where_context.q5_source: "South Sudan is the world’s third most fragile state and ranks last out of 191 countries in the UN Human Development Index... Multiple violent conflicts, a deteriorating economy, and vulnerability to climate-driven shocks mean that South Sudan remains caught in a fragility trap." (D0006100.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "South Sudan remains one of the most dangerous places in the world to be an aid worker with 210 killed since Independence." (D0006100.odt, South Sudan context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit aid worker access (e.g., 210 deaths since independence) and force prioritization of life-saving over development. Weak institutions and elite capture undermine service delivery, while climate shocks (flooding/drought) destroy livelihoods. Regulatory barriers (e.g., bureaucratic impediments, informal taxation) and data gaps (e.g., lack of transparent government spending) hinder coordination. Political economy dynamics—such as elite manipulation of patronagenetworks—distort aid effectiveness and local ownership.
where_context.quote: "The Government of South Sudan’s inability and apparent unwillingness to contain conflict and violence... has significantly eroded people’s livelihood options and coping capacity... Increasingly the international community is calling on the government to meet the needs of its citizens and to strengthen accountability." (D0006100.odt, South Sudan context) AND "Humanitarian needs are increasing across the country year on year, yet the available resources from the international community are decreasing. This requires tough prioritisation which in itself is causing local tension." (D0006100.odt, South Sudan context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic control (e.g., budget allocation, programme adjustments) while implementing partners (UN agencies, INGOs, and local NGOs) deliver services. Local actors are engaged as sub-contractors or beneficiaries, with limited decision-making authority over programme design or funding flows.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for local NGOs on conflict sensitivity and gender-responsive cash programming
institutional strengthening of Government of South Sudan ministries (e.g., humanitarian affairs, disaster management)
mentorship for national actors on resilience programming (e.g., climate-adapted livelihoods)
inclusion of local partners in humanitarian coordination platforms

partner_organizations.name: United Nations agencies (e.g., WFP, UNICEF, UNHCR)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (service delivery)

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs (e.g., humanitarian consortia)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (emergency response, resilience-building)

partner_organizations.name: Local/national NGOs
partner_organizations.role: sub-contractor (community-level delivery, accountability mechanisms)

partner_organizations.name: Government of South Sudan (e.g., Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs)
partner_organizations.role: coordination and policy counterpart (limited direct implementation)

who_partners.quote: "We will work with partners, developing synergies with their financing and securing backing for humanitarian diplomacy efforts... SSHARP will support priorities in the FCDO International Women and Girls Strategy and Disability Inclusion and Rights Strategy, ensuring programmes... work with and for crisis-affected women and girls." (D0006100.odt, Strategic Case) AND "SSHARP will contribute to the UK’s International Climate Finance (ICF) targets, primarily through interventions to strengthen resilience and livelihoods, including climate-adapted infrastructure for flood management." (D0006100.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core funding is allocated via **grants** to UN agencies/INGOs, with **block funding** for resilience components and an **Internal Risk Facility (IRF)** (up to 10% of budget) for emergency scale-ups. The IRF allows reallocation from FCDO central reserves or underspends within the Africa Directorate, enabling rapid response to spikes in need.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as the **funding manager**, with implementation delegated to a **diverse pool of pre-qualified partners** (UN, INGOs, local NGOs). Partners operate under framework agreements with flexibility to adapt activities within defined outcomes. The British Embassy Juba provides **strategic oversight** and diplomatic leverage, while technical coordination occurs through sectoral clusters (e.g., food security, GBV).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are pre-selected based on **technical capacity**, **contextual expertise**, and **alignment with UK priorities** (e.g., gender equality, climate resilience). The use of framework agreements enables rapid deployment in a volatile environment while maintaining accountability. Past performance in South Sudan (e.g., under HARISS programme) is a key criterion.
how_mechanism.quote: "The British Embassy Juba has a strong track record in the humanitarian donor community, primarily due to its technical capacity and capability... the humanitarian advisers are well respected, leading policy debates with donor, UN and NGO partners." (D0006100.odt, UK response to date) AND "SSHARP will be implemented alongside UK diplomatic and policy engagement... We will work with partners, developing synergies with their financing." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Partners have autonomy to allocate funds to sub-contractors (e.g., local NGOs) within agreed sectoral outcomes, but must comply with FCDO safeguarding and conflict-sensitivity requirements. Reallocations between core components require FCDO approval.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **Country Board** (chaired by the British Ambassador) provides high-level oversight, with technical input from a **Humanitarian Donor Group** (led by FCDO) and sectoral **UN clusters**. The **Internal Risk Facility (IRF)** governance includes FCDO Africa Directorate approval for drawdowns. Local partners are represented in coordination platforms but lack voting rights on strategic decisions.
how_governance.q18_oversight_intensity_details: FCDO conducts **quarterly reviews** of financial/operational progress, with **annual deep dives** on adaptive programming. Embedded advisors in Juba monitor conflict sensitivity and gender inclusion. The IRF triggers additional scrutiny for emergency reallocations.
how_governance.quote: "Kobi Bentley, Development Director, British Embassy Juba... confirms that this Business Case has gone through the appropriate review and assurance channels: my own QA, HMA approval via Country Board, QAU, and IADC." (D0006100.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "The framework for implementing adaptive programming (Annex B) includes managing flex in relation to any required changes in the scope of the programme." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core budgets are fixed annually, but **adaptable funding** (confirmed in-year) and the **IRF (10%)** allow reallocation for emergencies. Geographic or thematic shifts require Country Board approval, with prioritization guided by real-time needs assessments (e.g., IPC food security data).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses a **pre-defined adaptive framework** (Annex B) to adjust activities based on: (1) **conflict dynamics** (e.g., sudden violence), (2) **climate shocks** (e.g., flooding), (3) **government policy changes**, and (4) **partner performance**. Annual reviews flex between humanitarian response and resilience-building, with a bias toward **cash programming** and **localization** where feasible.
how_flexibility.quote: "SSHARP will need ability to flex its scope given South Sudan’s unpredictable operating environment... SSHARP may need to flex in terms of geography and between humanitarian response and more sustainable resilience efforts." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION) AND "A framework for implementing adaptive programming has been developed to manage flex in relation to any required changes in the scope of the programme (Annex B)." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **UN/INGO prime partners** → **local NGO sub-contractors** → end beneficiaries. The British Embassy Juba acts as an intermediate layer for strategic oversight but does not directly implement.
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: Disbursements are tied to **output delivery** (e.g., number of people reached, resilience indicators met) with **quarterly tranches**. The IRF uses **reimbursement** for emergency scale-ups, while core funding follows **pre-agreed milestones** in partner contracts.
how_efficiency.quote: "The main budget for SSHARP is split into core and adaptable components... Core budgets will be confirmed annually prior to the start of the financial year but the adaptable budget may only be confirmed in-year/quarter 3." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

q24_alternatives_considered: Direct FCDO implementation (rejected due to lack of operational capacity in South Sudan)
Single-prime contractor (rejected due to need for multi-sectoral expertise)
Pure humanitarian response (rejected for failing to address root causes of fragility)
Development-only focus (rejected as premature given ongoing conflict)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **mixed partnership model** was selected to balance **speed** (leveraging existing UN/INGO frameworks), **flexibility** (adaptive funding for shocks), and **localization** (embedded capacity building). The **open partnership structure** allows rapid scaling via pre-qualified actors while the **IRF** mitigates volatility. Past UK programmes (e.g., HARISS) demonstrated that **integrated humanitarian-resilience approaches** reduce aid dependency more effectively than siloed interventions.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (cost-efficiency of UN/INGO frameworks vs. direct delivery)
risk-mitigation (diversified partners reduce single-point failure risk)
flexibility (IRF and adaptable budgets for shocks)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Elite capture of funds via patronagenetworks
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Conflict-sensitivity analysis embedded in all partner agreements; transparent reporting requirements; FCDO approval for sub-awards over £500k.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap/duplication with other donors due to vertical programming
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Area-based coordination with UN clusters; joint donor messaging on prioritization; pushing for ‘One UN’ approach.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner absorption capacity limits adaptive programming
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year funding for core partners; pre-agreed flexibility parameters in contracts; annual capability assessments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government obstruction (e.g., bureaucratic delays, informal taxation)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diplomatic engagement via Troika (UK/US/Norway); public advocacy on humanitarian access; contingency plans for parallel delivery.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing UN/INGO systems to reduce overhead)
efficiency (cash programming to lower transaction costs)
effectiveness (integrated resilience outcomes vs. standalone humanitarian aid)
equity (gender and disability inclusion markers; 50%+ of funds targeting women/girls)
why_rationale.quote: "The UK’s ability to think, position itself, and work across humanitarian, development, peacebuilding, climate, gender, and political spaces is one of our comparative advantages in South Sudan... SSHARP will enable the UK to maintain a leading role on humanitarian and resilience programming, policy and diplomacy." (D0006100.odt, Strategic Case) AND "A key shift in implementation under SSHARP will be integration of resilience and livelihood programming in areas of high humanitarian need, supporting greater integration between humanitarian-development-peace actors." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** restricts partner selection to actors with **high risk tolerance** (e.g., UN agencies with security protocols) and **existing in-country presence**. Local NGOs are engaged only where they have **demonstrated neutrality** in conflict zones, while government partners are limited to **non-sensitive sectors** (e.g., disaster management) due to corruption risks. The **climate shocks** and **subnational violence** require partners with **rapid-response capacity**, excluding smaller or less experienced organizations.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks → exclusion of partners without UN-level security protocols
Elite capture → avoidance of direct government funding for service delivery
Data gaps → reliance on partners with existing monitoring systems (e.g., WFP’s food security data)
Regulatory barriers → preference for multilateral actors who can navigate bureaucratic impediments
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **integrated humanitarian-resilience objective** drives the **open partnership model** (needing both emergency responders and development actors) and **adaptive management framework** (to toggle between relief and recovery). The **focus on women/girls** mandates partners with **GBV specialization**, while **climate resilience** requires actors with **environmental expertise**. The **cash programming priority** shapes payment structures (milestone-based disbursements tied to output data).
q28_linkages: Resilience outcomes → need for multi-year partner agreements (not short-term contracts)
Conflict sensitivity → embedded advisors in governance structure
Gender targets → mandatory GBV prevention components in all partner ToRs
Climate adaptation → requirement for partners to use UK Met Office data in programming
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) **Localization vs. speed**: "We will identify ways to better incentivise our partners to ensure equitable partnerships with national NGOs and local actors" (D0006100.odt) but acknowledge that "tough prioritisation... is causing local tension" (D0006100.odt). (2) **Gender inclusion vs. cost**: Gender-transformative cash programming is prioritized despite "limited evidence from humanitarian contexts" (D0006100.odt) and higher transaction costs. (3) **Resilience vs. relief**: Shifting funds to long-term livelihoods risks underfunding immediate needs in a "protracted crisis" (D0006100.odt).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Pre-qualified partners enable rapid response but limit opportunities for new local actors.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led technical assistance is embedded to meet climate/gender standards, reducing Southern autonomy.
Cost vs. reach: Cash programming increases efficiency but requires market functionality absent in some areas.
Flexibility vs. accountability: Adaptive budgets improve responsiveness but complicate auditing.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight** (quarterly reviews, embedded conflict advisors) and **restricted partner selection** (excluding high-risk local actors). The **high risk of elite capture** mandates **milestone-based payments** and **FCDO approval for sub-awards**. Conversely, the **need for rapid adaptation** (e.g., to climate shocks) justifies the **IRF’s light-touch governance** for emergency funds.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Partners with **stronger local networks** (e.g., national NGOs) are tasked with **community-level delivery** and **accountability mechanisms**, while **international actors** lead **technical design** and **donor coordination**. The **conflict-sensitivity capacity** of partners determines their role in **peacebuilding linkages** (e.g., only those with mediation experience can implement integrated HDP activities).
intersections.quote: "The UK’s ability to think, position itself, and work across humanitarian, development, peacebuilding, climate, gender, and political spaces is one of our comparative advantages in South Sudan... SSHARP will build on experience from previous programming and policy engagement and will apply learning and innovate." (D0006100.odt, Strategic Case) AND "We will continue to work with partners, developing synergies with their financing and securing backing for humanitarian diplomacy efforts." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

key_programme_risks: Elite manipulation of aid for political gain (e.g., diversion of resources to patronagenetworks)
Escalation of subnational violence disrupting implementation (e.g., Jonglei, Upper Nile)
Climate shocks (flooding/drought) overwhelming resilience interventions
Government obstruction (e.g., bureaucratic delays, informal taxation on aid)
Donor fatigue leading to underfunding of critical gaps (e.g., 54% HRP funding gap in 2023)
Overlap/duplication with parallel donor programmes reducing efficiency
Partner absorption capacity limiting adaptive programming
Gender backlash in conservative areas resisting women’s empowerment activities

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Conflict-sensitivity analysis in all partner agreements; transparent reporting; FCDO approval for high-value sub-awards; diplomatic pressure via Troika.
Real-time security monitoring; pre-positioned stocks; contingency plans for remote management; IRF for rapid reallocation.
Climate-adapted infrastructure (e.g., flood barriers); early warning systems linked to adaptive budgets; multi-year funding for livelihoods.
High-level diplomatic engagement; public advocacy on access; parallel delivery channels where needed.
Coordinated donor messaging; evidence-based advocacy on gaps; leveraging UK’s convening role in Troika.
Area-based planning; joint needs assessments; pushing for ‘One UN’ approach.
Multi-year core funding; capability assessments; mentorship for local NGOs.
Community engagement strategies; male allyship programmes; phased rollout of sensitive activities.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from HARISS/BRACE-II: Multi-year funding improves resilience outcomes but requires **flexible milestones** to adapt to shocks.
Conflict sensitivity must be **embedded in partner selection**, not just a reporting requirement.
**Cash programming** reduces transaction costs but requires **market assessments** to avoid inflationary effects.
**Localization** in FCAS contexts needs **phased approaches**—direct funding to local actors only after capacity assessments.
Diplomatic leverage is critical to **mitigate government obstruction** (e.g., Troika statements on access).
**Area-based strategies** reduce duplication but require **stronger donor coordination** to succeed.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **HARISS programme (2015–2023, £787m)** demonstrated that: (1) **Integrated humanitarian-resilience programming** reduces aid dependency more than siloed approaches; (2) **Cash transfers** improve efficiency but need **gender-sensitive design** to avoid exclusion; (3) **Multi-year funding** enables partners to plan for resilience but requires **adaptive management frameworks** to handle volatility. The **BRACE-II programme (2015–2023, £48m)** showed that **livelihoods support in non-conflict areas** can be sustainable but struggles in **high-violence zones** without peacebuilding linkages.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from **separate humanitarian/resilience programmes** (HARISS/BRACE-II) to **geographically integrated delivery** under SSHARP.
Expanded **Internal Risk Facility (IRF)** (from ad-hoc in HARISS to 10% of budget) for rapid reallocation.
**Mandatory conflict-sensitivity analysis** in all partner agreements (previously optional).
**Gender-transformative cash programming** (beyond gender-blind transfers in HARISS).
Stronger **diplomatic-policy linkage** (e.g., Troika coordination on access, unlike previous bilateral advocacy).
**Area-based planning** to replace vertical sectoral programmes and reduce overlap.
risks_lessons.quote: "The Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience in South Sudan (HARISS) programme... marked a shift from short-term assistance to more flexible, longer-term approaches. These principles are now a cornerstone of the UK Humanitarian Reform agenda." (D0006100.odt, UK response to date) AND "A key shift in implementation under SSHARP will be integration of resilience and livelihood programming in areas of high humanitarian need, supporting greater integration between humanitarian-development-peace actors." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION) AND "The unintended consequences of humanitarian action in South Sudan... [include] protracted aid dependency... A self-critical awareness of these dynamics will continue to underpin our policy and programming." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on **revenue expenditure** (e.g., cash transfers, service delivery) with limited **capital investments** (e.g., climate-adapted infrastructure for flood management). No explicit split provided.
financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: Up to £300m over four years." (D0006100.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "The main budget for SSHARP is split into core and adaptable components, all of which is affordable on the current published ODA allocation for South Sudan." (D0006100.odt, PROPOSED UK INTERVENTION)

metadata.programme_name: Core contribution to the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women)

quote.text: "To support UN Women in implementation of its triple mandate, encompassing normative support, UN system coordination and operational activities, to achieve gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls and support achievement of 2030 Agenda."

duration_source.text: "This business case seeks approval for a total budget of £9.9m in FYs 2022/23 to 2024/5."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme supports UN Women's triple mandate through **normative work** (policy influence), **operational activities** (service delivery/capacity building), and **UN system coordination** (financing mechanism). It combines evidence generation (e.g., gender statistics), policy advocacy (e.g., SDG5 mainstreaming), and direct implementation (e.g., humanitarian responses).

q1_source.text: "To support UN Women in implementation of its triple mandate, encompassing **normative support**, **UN system coordination** and **operational activities**, to achieve gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls and support achievement of 2030 Agenda."

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened global norms and standards for gender equality
Coordination across the UN system for gender mainstreaming
Application of global norms into national legislation/policies
q3_expected_outputs.target: 57 countries supported on tackling discriminatory norms (2018–2021 example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Training in political leadership skills
q3_expected_outputs.target: 35,000 women trained (2018–2021 example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Support to countries implementing gender action plans
q3_expected_outputs.target: 41 countries (2018–2021 example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved services for survivors of gender-based violence
q3_expected_outputs.target: 69 countries (2018–2021 example), benefitting 2.7 billion women

q3_expected_outputs.output: Women, Peace and Security Action Plans agreed
q3_expected_outputs.target: 99 countries/territories (2018–2021 example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Humanitarian services provided to women
q3_expected_outputs.target: 1.9 million women (2018–2021 example)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Production of gender statistics and sex-disaggregated data
Advocacy for women’s equitable access to services/resources

what_objectives.summary: The programme provides **core funding** to UN Women to deliver its **triple mandate** (normative, coordination, operational) globally. It focuses on **gender equality**, **women’s empowerment**, and **SDG5**, with outputs ranging from policy influence (e.g., global norms) to direct service delivery (e.g., humanitarian support) and systemic change (e.g., UN coordination).

quote.source: D0005222.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?
quote.text: "Core funding to UNW directly supports delivery of the UK’s objectives on women and girls... UN Women is a key partner for the UK on women’s political and economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls... It leverages its global normative intergovernmental role and provides technical support to Member States to strengthen development of global norms and standards on gender equality."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in **fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS)** where UN Women works, but the overall risk is assessed as **moderate and within FCDO’s risk appetite**. Risks include fraud, SEAH, and operational challenges, but UN Women has governance frameworks and audit processes in place.

q5_source.text: "The programme is within the FCDO risk appetite... The risks of this programme are considered **moderate** and within FCDO’s risk appetite."

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and humanitarian emergencies **disproportionately impact women and girls**, increasing risks of gender-based violence, limited access to sexual/reproductive health services, and economic exclusion. UN Women’s work in **FCAS** requires adaptive responses to **protracted crises** (e.g., Ukraine, where 90% of refugees are women/children). Climate change and biodiversity loss also **exacerbate gendered vulnerabilities**, particularly in LDCs and SIDS.

quote.text: "Conflict... and humanitarian emergencies are protracted and have devastating outcomes for women and girls... Women and girls are 14 times more likely than men to die during climate-related disasters... Women have been 1.8 times more vulnerable to the pandemic’s impact than men."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UN Women’s **Executive Board** (where the UK holds a seat as a top donor) sets strategic direction, while **country offices** (often in LMICs) implement programmes. Decision-making is **centralized** at HQ/Board level, with **delegated authority** to regional/country offices. Southern partners (e.g., women’s organizations) are engaged as **beneficiaries/stakeholders** but do not hold governance roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., 35,000 women in political leadership skills)
institutional strengthening (e.g., supporting 41 countries to implement gender action plans)
technical assistance (e.g., advising 44 countries on women’s economic empowerment policies)
normative support (e.g., global standards for ending violence against women)
coordination platforms (e.g., linking UN system, CSOs, private sector)

partner_organizations.role: Collaborators for gender mainstreaming

quote.source: D0005222.odt, How UK support will be used
quote.text: "Core funding underpins UNW’s operational capacity and expertise... It is the most flexible resource for UNW and is pooled with that of other donors and deployed to deliver the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022-2025... UNW targets their support to the most vulnerable women and girls, who experience multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides **unearmarked core funding** to UN Women, which is **pooled with other donors’ contributions** and allocated flexibly to support the **UN Women Strategic Plan 2022–2025**. This funding is **not tied to specific projects/countries**, enabling UN Women to use it for **normative work, coordination, and operational activities** (e.g., humanitarian responses, policy advocacy).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UN Women operates as a **UN entity** with a **centralized governance structure** (Executive Board) and **decentralized implementation** through regional/country offices. The **UK (FCDO)** sits on the Executive Board, providing oversight, while UN Women manages day-to-day delivery. **No consortium or sub-awards** are involved; funds flow directly to UN Women’s global system.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UN Women is the **lead UN agency for gender equality**, and the UK has been a **top donor since its formation**. The **2019 Funding Compact** commits member states to provide core funding to multilateral agencies. The UK’s seat on the **Executive Board** is tied to its donor status, ensuring influence over strategic direction.

quote.source: D0005222.odt, How UK support will be used
quote.text: "Core funding to UNW helps ensure that UK aid to the UN which is focused on our top development and humanitarian priorities can be deployed in a gender responsive manner... The UK has been a top donor to UNW since its formation."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The **UN Women Executive Board** is the governing body, comprising **41 member states** (including the UK). It provides **intergovernmental oversight**, approves policies/budgets, and meets **three times yearly**. Decisions are made by **consensus**. The UK participates in **strategic dialogues** and **bilateral engagement** to influence priorities.

quote.text: "The Executive Board is the governing body of UNW, providing intergovernmental support and oversight to the organisation... It comprises 41 members... and meets three times each calendar year... Executive Board sessions are held at the United Nations headquarters in New York."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core funding is **not earmarked** and can be reallocated across **normative, coordination, or operational activities** as needed. UN Women can deploy funds to **emerging crises** (e.g., humanitarian responses) or **strategic priorities** (e.g., policy advocacy) without donor approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: UN Women can **adapt priorities** in response to **global/regional needs** (e.g., COVID-19, Ukraine conflict) or **strategic opportunities** (e.g., intergovernmental processes like the Commission on the Status of Women). The **Strategic Plan 2022–2025** provides a framework, but core funding allows **real-time adjustments**.

quote.source: D0005222.odt, How UK support will be used
quote.text: "Core funding... is the most flexible resource for UNW and is pooled with that of other donors and deployed to deliver the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022-2025... In crisis and humanitarian situations which require rapid responses, it is used to ensure that interventions are designed from the outset to take into consideration the needs of women and girls."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **UN Women (HQ/regional/country offices)** → **end beneficiaries** (women/girls, governments, CSOs). No additional intermediaries are involved.

quote.text: "Financial forecasting, tracking and payments will be maintained in FCDO’s Aid Management Platform and Hera in accordance with PrOF Rule requirements."

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Would reduce UK influence on UN Women’s Executive Board, undermine the UK’s role as a champion for women/girls, and risk ceding space to less progressive countries.
Would further decrease the UK’s core-to-non-core funding ratio (already below the 30% target) and weaken UN Women’s operational capacity.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Continue core funding within envelope agreed by Ministers (£3.3m/year)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Maintains UK’s seat on the Executive Board, supports UN Women’s mandate, and aligns with the **2019 Funding Compact** commitments.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Continuing core funding was selected to: 1) **retain UK influence** on UN Women’s strategic direction via the Executive Board; 2) **support flexible, rapid responses** (e.g., humanitarian crises); 3) **fulfill multilateral commitments** (Funding Compact); 4) **leverage UN Women’s unique mandate** as the lead UN agency for gender equality; and 5) **ensure value for money** by pooling resources with other donors.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (economies of scale via pooled funding)
partner-capacity (UN Women’s global reach and expertise)
strategic alignment (supports UK’s International Development Strategy)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Critical mass of Member States do not prioritize core funding to UN Women
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with other Member States to encourage prioritization of core funding, including through Strategic Funding Dialogues at Executive Boards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN Women insufficiently prioritizes delivery of key FCDO policy priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with other Member States to monitor strategic plan results, including through the midterm review (June 2024).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak human resources systems in UN Women lead to ineffective Country Representatives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Improve accountability of leadership selection through bilateral engagement and Executive Board opportunities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN Women does not make good progress on UN reform, undermining efficiency/effectiveness
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continued engagement at the Executive Boards with other Member States and bilaterally.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN Women does not effectively work across the UN system to mainstream gender equality
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Consistent messaging on the importance of linking up with other UN agencies and activities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary: UN Women has insufficient capacity to prevent/detect fraud or inadequate risk management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Due diligence via central assurance assessments; ongoing monitoring through Executive Board; appropriate provisions in MoU.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (high output delivery via UN Women’s global network)
effectiveness (alignment with SDG5 and UK development priorities)
equity (focus on intersectional discrimination and ‘leave no one behind’)

quote.text: "Retaining a viable level of core funding to UN Women is important for the UK’s reputation within the UN Development System and will provide results against the Foreign Secretary’s priorities... Core funding also enables UNW to achieve the greatest impact for women and girls by securing expert staff who can scale up proven solutions."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: UN Women’s **global mandate** requires engagement with **diverse stakeholders** (governments, CSOs, private sector) across **FCAS and non-FCAS contexts**, but **fragility and conflict** limit the ability of some Southern partners to lead implementation. The **Executive Board’s composition** (41 member states) ensures Northern donors (e.g., UK) retain governance influence, while **country offices** adapt to local constraints (e.g., security, weak institutions).
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict/humanitarian crises require rapid, flexible responses (constraining long-term planning)
Weak institutions in programme countries limit local ownership (necessitating UN Women’s technical leadership)
Political economy risks (e.g., gender equality backlash) affect partner selection (prioritizing ‘like-minded’ actors)
Climate/environmental risks disproportionately affect women in LDCs/SIDS (shaping geographic focus)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: UN Women’s **triple mandate** (normative, coordination, operational) necessitates a **multilateral, flexible funding mechanism** (core funding). The need for **global standards** (e.g., SDG5) requires a **centralized governance structure** (Executive Board), while **country-level adaptation** demands **decentralized implementation** (regional/country offices). The **mixed objectives** (policy influence + service delivery) are enabled by **pooled, unearmarked funds**.
q28_linkages: Global normative work → **centralized governance** (Executive Board)
Country-level implementation → **decentralized offices** with local partnerships
Flexible crisis response → **core funding mechanism** (no earmarking)
UN system coordination → **multilateral structure** (collaboration with UNDP/UNFPA/UNICEF)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (targeting women/girls facing intersectional discrimination) with **efficiency** (leveraging UN Women’s global scale). Trade-offs include: 1) **Northern-led governance** (Executive Board) vs. **Southern implementation** (country offices); 2) **flexible core funding** (enabling rapid responses) vs. **accountability risks** (e.g., fraud); 3) **broad mandate** (normative + operational) vs. **focused impact**.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Core funding enables **rapid humanitarian responses** but may bypass local CSOs in decision-making.
Expertise vs. ownership: UN Women’s **technical leadership** ensures quality but limits Southern partner control.
Cost vs. reach: **Pooled multilateral funding** reduces transaction costs but dilutes donor attribution.
Global norms vs. local adaptation: **Standardized approaches** (e.g., SDG5) may not fully align with context-specific needs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (fraud, SEAH, operational challenges) justifies **milestone-based oversight** (Executive Board reviews) and **embedded safeguards** (e.g., MoU provisions). **FCAS contexts** increase risk, prompting **adaptive management** (e.g., real-time reallocation of core funds).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: UN Women’s **capacity building** (e.g., training 35,000 women in leadership) enables Southern partners to **implement programmes**, but **governance roles** remain with Northern donors (e.g., UK on Executive Board). **Technical assistance** (e.g., policy advice to 44 countries) strengthens local institutions without transferring decision-making power.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **2016 Central Assurance Assessment** identified weaknesses in UN Women’s **risk management**, **fraud detection**, and **strategic planning**, leading to improvements in governance frameworks. The **2017–18 MOPAN assessment** highlighted needs for **transparency in resource allocation** and **consistent country-level coordination**, which informed the **2022–25 Strategic Plan**. **Budget surpluses** (e.g., $107m in 2021) prompted UN Women to develop an **action plan** for better resource deployment (e.g., pivot to field offices).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Stronger risk management**: UN Women developed an **action plan** to reduce budget surpluses and improve internal governance. 2) **Enhanced safeguarding**: Following MOPAN findings, UN Women updated **SEAH policies**, though tracking mechanisms remain weak. 3) **Flexible core funding**: Retained to address **FCAS needs** (e.g., humanitarian crises) and **global priorities** (e.g., SDG5). 4) **Executive Board engagement**: UK uses its seat to push for **transparency** and **UN reform**.

metadata.programme_name: Security and Stabilisation Programme
metadata.quote: "This programme aims to increase UK effectiveness in preventing or reducing conflict through a) the application of stabilisation principles and b) applying security sector reform (SSR) best practice." (D0007302.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: August 2022-March 2023 (later extended to March 2025)" and "New programme end date (if applicable): 31/03/2026" (D0007302.odt, Detailed information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines policy influence (developing UK guidance on stabilisation and SSR), capacity building (strengthening HMG expertise), and implementation research (testing interventions in priority geographies). It also includes direct advisory support to countries like Ukraine.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme aims to increase UK effectiveness in preventing or reducing conflict through a) the application of stabilisation principles and b) applying security sector reform (SSR) best practice. This includes developing and advocating for the UK’s governance and human rights-centred approach on stabilisation, SSR, disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR), sharing our outputs with the international community for the benefit of those living in conflict-affected countries." (D0007302.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Refreshed, published UK approach to stabilisation (policy output)
Expanded evidence base underpinning stabilisation policy (research output)
Advice delivered to, and lessons derived from HMG stabilisation interventions in priority contexts (implementation support)
Consultations on stabilisation policy held with key international partners (policy influence)
Refreshed, central policy on SSR, including political economy analysis (policy output)
Advice provided to support and guide SSR in a number of key countries (technical assistance)
Advisory support provided to key multilateral partners (international engagement)
Sustained support by an expert from the Civilian Stabilisation Group (CSG) to BE Kyiv on Ukraine SSR (country-specific output)
Funding a member of an expert group on NATO’s Southern neighbourhood (international influence)
what_objectives.summary: The programme develops UK policy guidance on stabilisation and SSR while providing technical assistance to priority countries (notably Ukraine) and engaging international partners to strengthen global approaches to conflict prevention.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme was initially allocated £350,000 (FY 2022/23). This amendment proposes an additional £500,000 for FY 2023/24 and £650,000 for FY 2024/25, totalling a proposed business case value of up to £1.5m." (D0004520.odt, Summary Information)

countries_regions: Fragile and Conflict Affected States (FCAS) - general focus
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates exclusively in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) with active conflicts (e.g., Ukraine) and post-conflict reconstruction contexts. The documents repeatedly emphasize conflict sensitivity and the challenges of working in unstable environments.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme is designed to contribute to conflict management and resolution. Activities will be focused in conflict affected geographies where the injection of resources may exacerbate conflict dynamics." (D0004517.odt, Conflict and Fragility) AND "The programme’s involvement in conflict-affected contexts... will allow the team to continually monitor risks in this evolving environment." (D0004520.odt, Risk management)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit physical access and require conflict-sensitive approaches. Political economy constraints affect SSR interventions due to the highly politicized nature of security sectors in conflict contexts. Weak institutions in FCAS require tailored capacity building. Data limitations in conflict zones challenge evidence-based programming.
where_context.quote: "In situations of conflict, control and composition of the security sector is highly political and closely tied to conflict and power dynamics, and hence frequently at the heart of political contestation." (D0004517.odt, SSR section) AND "Conflict sensitivity will be central to the policy and practice guidance developed with the support of the Programme." (D0004517.odt, Conflict and Fragility)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO/SSD retains full strategic and operational control over programme design, partner selection, and resource allocation. Southern partners (e.g., Ukrainian government, NATO experts) receive technical assistance but do not co-lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: Deployment of Deployable Civilian Experts (DCEs) to build in-country capacity (e.g., Ukraine SSR support)
Training package development for SSR
Knowledge sharing through international networks (e.g., NATO Expert Group)
Mentorship via long-term expert embeddings

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of contracts (for DCE deployments via Palladium), accountable grants (for research/data analysis), and potential MoUs with international partners (e.g., NATO). The CSG roster operates under a framework agreement.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FCDO's SSD manages the programme directly, with operational support from Palladium for DCE deployments. No consortium or platform structure is used; partnerships are bilateral and project-specific.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Civilian Stabilisation Group (CSG) roster of 500+ pre-vetted experts was chosen for speed and proven track record in conflict zones. Palladium was selected as the commercial partner to manage the roster due to existing contracts with OCSM.
how_mechanism.quote: "The procurement of technical experts will be done primarily through the HEROS Programme and the performance of the supplier managed through existing arrangements." (D0004517.odt, Commercial Case) AND "All experts are Deployable Civilian Experts (DCEs) recruited from the Civilian Stabilisation Group (CSG), a roster of 500+ consultants... managed by OCSM’s Operations Team alongside our commercial partner, Palladium." (D0004520.odt, Programme activities to date)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A Programme Delivery Board (PDB) provides oversight and approves key decisions. The Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) leads strategic direction, supported by a Programme Responsible Officer (PRO) for day-to-day management.
how_governance.quote: "A Programme Delivery Board (PDB) will provide overall governance and approve key decisions. The SRO will lead on strategic/technical direction and supported by a PRO, who will lead on day-to-day management, including compliance." (D0004517.odt, Management Case) AND "The programme team will continue to meet with relevant partners regularly to discuss progress and risk dynamics, in line with current practices on the programme. These discussions will continue to feed into an overall programme risk matrix stored on AMP, and will guide how we continue to deliver future activities." (D0004520.odt, Risk management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within the same financial year with PDB approval, but the programme operates under annual budget constraints. The Inception Phase allowed testing of different interventions before scaling up.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The Theory of Change is treated as a 'living document' with quarterly strategy testing sessions. Adjustments require PDB approval but are encouraged based on emerging evidence. The programme uses 'contribution analysis' to link activities to outcomes in complex environments.
how_flexibility.quote: "The Theory of Change will remain as a ‘living’ document for the programme... the programme team will frequently (every quarter) run strategy testing sessions which will look at the assumptions and change pathways in the ToC and consider the evidence emerging from implementation." (D0004517.odt, Theory of Change) AND "Adaptation will be informed by evidence communicated through intervention leads in quarterly progress reports and driven by the PDB." (D0004517.odt, Management Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Palladium/CSG (for DCE deployments) → End experts. For direct FCDO-managed activities (e.g., policy development), only 1 layer exists.
how_efficiency.quote: "A significant portion of the Programme’s funds will be spent on DCEs via the HEROS Programme and via other established FCDO Programmes, where there are already well-established and tested financial management arrangements in place." (D0004517.odt, Financial Case) AND "Intervention leads will be responsible for ensuring deliverables meet the required standard in line with ToRs before payment is made and that no payments are made in advance of need." (D0004517.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Add-on to existing OCSM programmes (e.g., HEROs, ISSAT) - rejected due to limited innovation and flexibility
Option 2: Fully outsourced to a commercial service provider - rejected due to procurement delays and lack of strategic alignment
Option 3: In-house management with blended delivery (preferred) - chosen for flexibility and control
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The blended in-house model was selected to (1) maintain strategic control over policy development, (2) enable rapid, flexible responses to emerging conflicts (e.g., Ukraine), (3) leverage existing CSG expertise while allowing niche external inputs, and (4) avoid the 4-month procurement delays of full outsourcing. The model also supports adaptive management through quarterly reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on CSG/Palladium for DCE deployments may limit access to niche expertise not on the roster.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Supplementary recruitment channels and international partnerships (e.g., NATO, RUSI) are used for specialized needs.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: HEROS Programme absorptive capacity may be exceeded by SSD demand.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Detailed forward planning with Palladium to align demand with supply.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sensitive contexts (e.g., Ukraine) require thorough vetting of experts, causing delays.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early drafting of ToRs and pre-deployment briefings to streamline clearance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: In-house management may lack programme management expertise initially.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging existing OCSM processes and upskilling core staff.

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 provides broader scope for accessing and testing capabilities within the limited time available during this short Inception Phase... This blended delivery model will have several additional benefits, not least the flexibility to source the right expertise to tackle specific highly technical problems." (D0004517.odt, Appraisal Case) AND "In-house delivery is assessed to be the most cost-effective means of implementing this Inception Phase." (D0004517.odt, Value for Money)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with proven conflict sensitivity expertise and security clearances. Physical access constraints in active conflict zones (e.g., Ukraine) restrict partnerships to entities already operating in-country or with remote capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Security clearances required for all deployed experts
Need for conflict-sensitive approaches narrows partner pool
Rapidly changing conflict dynamics (e.g., Ukraine) require partners with adaptive capacity
Multilateral partners (e.g., NATO) prioritized for their existing FCAS engagement
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both policy influence (e.g., SSR guidance) and rapid crisis response (e.g., Ukraine support) drives the blended delivery model. Policy development requires in-house control, while technical assistance benefits from CSG's deployable experts.
q28_linkages: Policy objectives (e.g., SSR framework) → require in-house management for HMG alignment
Implementation needs (e.g., Ukraine SSR) → leverage CSG's rapid deployment capability
International influence goals → necessitate partnerships with multilaterals (NATO, OSCE)
Evidence-generation requirements → use of accountable grants for research
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern expertise (CSG/DCEs) with Southern ownership by embedding experts in local institutions (e.g., Ukrainian government). However, decision-making remains Northern-led for strategic coherence. The use of pre-existing rosters (CSG) prioritizes speed over competitive Southern partner selection.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: CSG roster enables rapid deployment but limits local partner diversity
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern experts lead SSR design while building Southern capacity
Cost vs. reach: In-house management reduces overheads but may limit grassroots engagement
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS risk profile drives intensive oversight (quarterly PDB reviews, monthly progress meetings) and adaptive management (living Theory of Change). Conflict sensitivity requirements increase monitoring burdens but are deemed essential for VFM.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme's capacity-building focus (e.g., DCE embeddings in Ukraine) directly informs partner roles, with Southern institutions receiving tailored support while Northern partners (FCDO/CSG) retain strategic control.
intersections.quote: "The programme is planning to make a significant investment in piloting and testing of application of stabilisation and SSR activity, to achieve better impact in tackling some of the most unstable environments and violent and protracted conflicts in the world." (D0004517.odt, Risk Management) AND "The programme will allow us to engage key experts and academics to support this engagement at key moments and in key international fora." (D0004520.odt, Partnerships)

key_programme_risks: Over-reliance on CSG/Palladium limiting access to niche expertise
Delays in DCE deployments due to vetting requirements in sensitive contexts
Absorptive capacity constraints within HEROS Programme
In-house management inexperience hindering delivery
Rapidly evolving conflict dynamics (e.g., Ukraine) disrupting planned activities
Difficulty in attributing impact in complex multi-donor environments
Limited budget flexibility due to annual ODA constraints
Safeguarding risks in conflict-affected geographies

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: CSG/Palladium absorptive capacity exceeded by demand
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Detailed forward planning with Palladium to align demand with supply and explore supplementary recruitment channels.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Delays in expert deployments due to security vetting
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Early drafting of ToRs and pre-deployment briefings to streamline clearance processes.
Leveraging existing OCSM processes and targeted upskilling of core staff.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Difficulty demonstrating additionality in busy donor landscapes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Stakeholder mapping to weave causal links from programme activities to observed changes.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Budget slippage due to ODA payment freezes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Front-loading spending in Q2/Q3 and deferring lower-priority activities.
Context-specific data/analysis and adherence to FCDO safeguarding policies.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity must be central to all interventions, with locally relevant data driving adaptations
Political economy analysis is critical for SSR interventions due to the politicized nature of security sectors
Flexible funding mechanisms are essential to respond to rapidly changing conflict dynamics
International partnerships (e.g., NATO) amplify impact but require alignment with HMG priorities
Embedded experts (e.g., in Ukraine) provide continuity amid instability
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from UK interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and Syria, emphasizing the need for: (1) politically led (not technical) SSR approaches, (2) integrated civil-military stabilisation strategies, and (3) adaptive programming based on real-time learning. The 2019 UK Stabilisation Guide and DFID’s 2016 Building Stability Framework provide foundational knowledge.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme evolved from an initial focus on DCE deployments to include: (1) direct policy development (SSR/stabilisation guidance), (2) expanded international partnerships (NATO, OSCE), and (3) a shift toward higher-value, catalytic projects in FY 2025/26 based on Annual Review recommendations.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons learned to date include: Embedding core programme management processes and streamlining programme activities to further simplify management while increasing strategic impact; Finalising programme activities early in the financial year to maximise opportunity to identify impactful activities and full utilisation of funds." (D0007302.odt, Changes) AND "The UK’s experience and learning in this area has been hard-earned, particularly from interventions in Iraq and Afghanistan, but equally from multiple other contexts, including Libya, Syria, Somalia, South Sudan, DRC, Mali and Nepal." (D0004517.odt, Strategic Case)
