metadata.programme_name: Catalysing Private Finance for Adaptation and Resilience
metadata.primary_sector: Private Finance for Adaptation and Resilience

quote.text: The programme will focus on developing methodologies and metrics to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience, addressing the evidence gaps on suitable financial vehicles and investment frameworks, piloting this work in a climate-vulnerable country context to demonstrate a framework for enhanced investment in systemic resilience, and scaling and disseminating these learnings through public-private partnerships.

metadata.duration_source: This business case will run for three years from 2023/2024–2025/2026, noting that spending for activities post 2024/25 is dependent on the resource allocation round that will follow the next Spending Review.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (developing methodologies and metrics), technology development (tools for climate risk assessment), capacity building (enhancing public-private coordination), and implementation research (piloting frameworks in Jamaica). It also includes a financing mechanism component to catalyse private investment.
what_objectives.q1_source: Given the low baseline on private investment in adaptation and resilience and the need to better understand how to overcome the barriers, this programme will focus on: developing methodologies and metrics to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience, addressing the evidence gaps on suitable financial vehicles and investment frameworks, piloting this work in a climate-vulnerable country context to demonstrate a framework for enhanced investment in systemic resilience, and scaling and disseminating these learnings through public-private partnerships.
q3_expected_outputs: Methodologies and metrics to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience
Evidence on suitable financial vehicles and investment frameworks
A framework for investment in systemic resilience piloted in Jamaica
Scaled and disseminated learnings through public-private partnerships
Improved data and information supporting investment in adaptation and resilience projects at country and asset/portfolio level
Adaptation and resilience/systemic risk data incorporated into decision-making by public and private institutions in Jamaica
Financial instruments, investment vehicles, and business models to deliver viable, bankable investments in adaptation and resilience
Increased private finance mobilised (GBP) - ICF KPI 12
Number of people supported to better adapt to the effects of climate change - ICF KPI 1
Number of people with improved (climate) resilience - ICF KPI 3
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to catalyse private finance for climate adaptation and resilience by addressing key barriers through evidence generation, tool development, capacity building, and piloting interventions in Jamaica, with a focus on systemic resilience and scalable solutions.

quote.text: The programme will focus on: developing methodologies and metrics to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience, addressing the evidence gaps on suitable financial vehicles and investment frameworks, piloting this work in a climate-vulnerable country context to demonstrate a framework for enhanced investment in systemic resilience, and scaling and disseminating these learnings through public-private partnerships.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting the complexity of catalysing private finance in climate-vulnerable contexts but without the extreme fragility or conflict conditions of FCAS environments.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
q6_contextual_constraints: lack of revenue sources for adaptation investments
lack of data and metrics to accurately price risk and capture benefits of adaptation
poor enabling environments for climate resilience
data limitations on climate risk and vulnerability
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: These constraints create significant barriers to private investment in adaptation and resilience, necessitating public finance interventions to de-risk investments and improve the enabling environment. For example, the lack of revenue sources means many adaptation projects cannot attract private finance without innovative revenue models, while limited data makes it difficult to price risk accurately.

quote.text: Private investment for adaptation and resilience is constrained by a set of barriers, including lack of business models with clear revenue sources, lack of a pipeline of bankable projects, lack of data to accurately price risk and measure adaptation benefits/impacts and limited public/private coordination resulting in poor enabling environments.

For example, the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs), a Southern-led regional body, plays a key role in the Jamaica pilot, while Northern institutions like the Global Infrastructure Hub (GIH) and Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC) lead on metrics and methodologies.

development of tools and methodologies to enhance private sector understanding of climate risks
support for early-stage project developers to build a pipeline of bankable adaptation projects
institutional strengthening through public-private partnerships and coordination platforms

quote.text: The CCRI Legacy Programme provides the coordinating framework between the private sector, public policymakers and donors to advance this. The Global Infrastructure Hub (GIH) will take forward the secretariat and responsibility of work on systemic resilience metrics and financial instruments... The Caribbean Community Centre on Climate Change (5Cs) is a regional body with a mandate from CARICOM to support the Caribbean on climate finance.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, What is the UK’s offer in this space? and Proposed intervention sections

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (for GIH and IIGCC), a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with 5Cs, and a Flexible Fund for convening and influence activities. Accountable Grants are performance-based agreements with strict reporting and audit requirements, while the MoU outlines collaborative arrangements for the Jamaica pilot.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through the CCRI Legacy Partnership, a multi-stakeholder platform that includes GIH (secretariat), IIGCC, 5Cs, ARIC, and other public/private partners. GIH provides overall strategic governance and convening power, while component leads (e.g., IIGCC for PCRAM 2.0, 5Cs for Jamaica pilot) manage specific workstreams. FCDO retains oversight through accountable grant agreements and a Flexible Fund.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their existing roles in the CCRI Legacy Programme and prior FCDO-supported work (e.g., GIH’s history as CCRI’s trusted partner, IIGCC’s expertise in climate risk methodologies, and 5Cs’ mandate from CARICOM). The business case emphasizes the need for continuity and leveraging established relationships to ensure rapid implementation and private sector buy-in.

quote.text: GIH was a trusted partner of CCRI up until CCRI transitioned to a Legacy Partnership... This close working relationship means GIH understands CCRI’s previous mandate and is best placed to provide overall strategic governance to the Legacy Partnership Programme. IIGCC are well positioned to deliver PCRAM 2.0... They are one of the largest membership organisations for investor collaboration on climate change... The 5Cs, supported by the University of Oxford, has provided a draft proposal to the FCDO to deliver the next steps of the work previously supported by the FCDO.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, Accountable Grant and MoU sections

how_governance.q17_governance_details: GIH’s Legacy Advisory Board, composed of private sector organizations, provides governance and strategic leadership to the CCRI Legacy Partnership. FCDO retains oversight through accountable grant agreements, which include reporting and audit requirements. For sub-awards, GIH and IIGCC are responsible for ensuring due diligence and safeguarding checks.

quote.text: The accountable grant will outline all reporting and audit requirements. A due diligence assessment is being carried out and only on completion would FCDO enter into an agreement with GIH. GIH will be responsible for ensuring that due diligence and safeguarding checks are undertaken for any subgrantees as delivery partners to the funding... We will use a three-person Procurement Board to ensure a rigorous assessment of Value for Money (VfM) when agreeing Accountable Grants and MoUs for all grants.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, particularly through the Flexible Fund, which is designed to support emerging work and convening opportunities. However, core component budgets (e.g., GIH, IIGCC, 5Cs) are pre-allocated based on the Theory of Change.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme adopts a ‘pilot, learn and apply’ approach, with a strong Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) component to test assumptions in the Theory of Change. Adjustments to priorities can be made based on lessons learned, subject to FCDO approval. The Flexible Fund provides additional agility to respond to emerging opportunities (e.g., COP28 dialogues).

quote.text: This programme will take a ‘pilot, learn and apply’ approach, with learnings applicable for any subsequent phase... The Flexible Fund would be used to support an initial COP28 dialogue on private finance for adaptation and resilience and a follow-up event in 2024, as well as subsequent interventions that would enhance high-level progress.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, How will this be monitored? and Flexible Fund sections

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (GIH, IIGCC, 5Cs) → End users (e.g., Jamaica government, private investors). There is no explicit sub-grantee layer beyond the primary partners.

quote.text: The accountable grant will outline all reporting and audit requirements... The contracted agency is required to provide a detailed cost breakdown as part of the accountable grant process. We will benchmark costs against previous accountable grants for similar services.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: FCDO would not continue to fund CCRI or ARIC, relying instead on influencing MDBs/DFIs through shareholder channels. This was rejected due to poor value for money and failure to capitalize on UK convening power.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Catalyse private finance at system level (preferred option)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Address barriers through methodologies, evidence-building, country pilot, and public-private partnerships. Chosen for its systemic approach, cost-effectiveness, and alignment with UK leadership in climate finance.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The systemic approach was selected for its potential to deliver stronger value for money by improving the enabling environment for private finance (rather than relying on expensive, project-level concessional financing). It leverages the UK’s convening power post-COP26/G7 Presidency and builds on existing partnerships (CCRI, ARIC) to ensure rapid implementation and private sector adoption. The modality also allows for flexibility through the Flexible Fund and adaptive management via the MEL component.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (systemic vs. project-level interventions)
equity (focus on climate-vulnerable SIDS like Jamaica)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low private sector engagement in tool development
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: GIH and IIGCC will use their convening power to ensure private sector leadership in designing metrics and financial products. The Legacy Advisory Board (private sector-led) will provide oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited adoption of tools/methodologies by investors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pilot testing in Jamaica and dissemination through ARIC/DFI networks to demonstrate feasibility and scalability. IIGCC’s extensive membership (400+ investors) will socialize tools.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to replicate Jamaica pilot in other countries
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible Fund will support regional dissemination (e.g., Caribbean SIDS). Partnership with IDB/IMF provides pathways for scaling via their country platforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient leverage of UK’s MDB/DFI shareholdings
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will use the programme’s evidence base to advocate for MDB reforms (e.g., World Bank’s ‘liveable planet’ objective) and influence DFI strategies through ARIC.

quote.text: Option 2: Catalyse private finance by addressing barriers through a systemic approach to improve the enabling environment and strengthen public-private partnerships... This systemic intervention provides better VfM to address barriers to investment than to influence MDBs at a project level. It is also a more impactful approach than relying solely on influencing through shareholder channels... Option 2 allows us to capitalise on the UK’s perceived leadership in this area following our COP26 Presidency and 2021 G7 Presidency.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on climate-vulnerable SIDS (e.g., Jamaica) and the need for localized climate risk data constrain partner selection to organizations with regional expertise and credibility. For example, 5Cs was chosen due to its CARICOM mandate and prior work on the J-SRAT tool, while GIH’s global convening power is essential for scaling solutions beyond the Caribbean.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with existing relationships in Jamaica/Caribbean (e.g., 5Cs’ CARICOM mandate)
Requirement for organizations capable of bridging public-private gaps in fragile contexts (e.g., GIH’s G20-backed infrastructure focus)
Limited pool of institutions with expertise in systemic climate risk assessment for SIDS
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (evidence generation, tool development, piloting, scaling) necessitate a platform-based delivery structure. For example: 1) The need to develop globally applicable metrics requires a multilateral convener (GIH); 2) Pilot testing in Jamaica demands a regional implementer (5Cs) with government trust; 3) Scaling through DFIs/MDBs is enabled by ARIC’s coalition structure.
q28_linkages: Global metrics development (GIH/IIGCC) → Local pilot testing (5Cs in Jamaica) → Regional/Global scaling (ARIC/DFIs)
Private sector engagement (Legacy Advisory Board) → Tool adoption (investor uptake of PCRAM 2.0)
Flexible Fund → Adaptive management (responding to emerging opportunities like COP28)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly acknowledges tensions between inclusive partnerships and rapid delivery. For example: 1) The direct award to GIH/IIGCC prioritizes speed and private sector buy-in over open competition; 2) The Jamaica pilot’s regional focus (Caribbean SIDS) balances depth of impact with the need for replicable models; 3) The Flexible Fund allows for agile responses to high-level dialogues but risks diluting focus on core components.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to GIH/IIGCC accelerate implementation but limit opportunities for new Southern-led partners.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern institutions (GIH, IIGCC) lead on metrics development, while Southern partners (5Cs) implement pilots.
Cost vs. reach: The £3.2m budget prioritizes systemic tools over direct project financing, trading immediate impact for long-term scalability.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk rating justifies milestone-based oversight (e.g., accountable grant reporting requirements) and the use of a Procurement Board to scrutinize VfM. High-risk components (e.g., Flexible Fund) are counterbalanced by FCDO approval processes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: 1) 5Cs’ mandate includes strengthening Jamaica’s planning institutions; 2) GIH’s convening power is leveraged to build private sector capacity; 3) ARIC’s DFI coordination aims to enhance MDB/DFI absorptive capacity for adaptation finance.

quote.text: The programme will tackle these barriers by developing methodologies and metrics to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience... The pilots sit within a country platform approach, which includes development of a Project Preparation Facility (PPF) focused on Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) by IDB... The Flexible Fund would support convening of governments, private sector, experts and MDBs/DFIs at COP meetings, and other influencing moments.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, Proposed intervention and Flexible Fund sections

key_programme_risks: Low baseline of private investment in adaptation and resilience
Limited adoption of new metrics/tools by investors and governments
Failure to demonstrate scalability beyond Jamaica pilot
Insufficient leverage of MDB/DFI shareholdings to drive systemic change
Data gaps persisting despite new methodologies
Political or economic instability in Jamaica/Caribbean affecting pilot implementation
Private sector disengagement from Legacy Partnership

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low private sector engagement in tool development
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: GIH and IIGCC will use their convening power and membership networks (e.g., 400+ IIGCC investors) to ensure private sector leadership in designing metrics and financial products. The Legacy Advisory Board (private sector-led) will provide oversight.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited adoption of tools/methodologies by investors
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pilot testing in Jamaica and dissemination through ARIC/DFI networks to demonstrate feasibility. IIGCC will socialize PCRAM 2.0 among its membership and CCRI Legacy Partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to replicate Jamaica pilot in other countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible Fund will support regional dissemination (e.g., Caribbean SIDS). Partnership with IDB/IMF provides pathways for scaling via their country platforms (e.g., Egypt pilot by EBRD).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient leverage of UK’s MDB/DFI shareholdings
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will use programme evidence to advocate for MDB reforms (e.g., World Bank’s ‘liveable planet’ objective) and influence DFI strategies through ARIC and the Flexible Fund’s convening activities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Data gaps persisting despite new methodologies
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Integration of J-SRAT tool into Jamaica’s national planning systems and collaboration with University of Oxford to ensure data quality. PCRAM 2.0 will be tested on investor portfolios to refine risk assessment.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political or economic instability in Jamaica/Caribbean
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Close coordination with IMF’s Resilience and Sustainability Facility and IDB’s PPF to align with Jamaica’s macroeconomic stability efforts. 5Cs’ CARICOM mandate provides regional legitimacy.

fcas_specific_lessons: While Jamaica is not classified as FCAS, the programme applies lessons from FCAS contexts by focusing on systemic resilience and public-private coordination, which are critical in fragile environments. The J-SRAT tool’s integration into national planning mirrors approaches used in post-disaster recovery settings.
The emphasis on ‘bankable’ projects and revenue models (e.g., land value capture) reflects lessons from FCAS on the need for innovative financing to attract private investment in high-risk contexts.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on prior FCDO support for CCRI (2019–2023), which demonstrated the value of systemic resilience metrics and country platform approaches (e.g., Jamaica pilot). Key lessons include: 1) The need for private sector co-creation of tools to ensure adoption; 2) The importance of embedding risk assessment in national planning (e.g., J-SRAT’s integration into Jamaica’s PIOJ); 3) The role of MDBs/DFIs in de-risking investments through guarantees and concessional finance.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The shift from CCRI to the Legacy Programme reflects lessons on the need for sustained coordination post-initial funding. The inclusion of a Flexible Fund addresses gaps in high-level political dialogue identified in earlier phases. The Jamaica pilot’s expansion to include a prioritized investment plan responds to feedback on the need for actionable project pipelines.

quote.text: Earlier this year, CCRI transitioned its activities over to a set of not-for-profit partners under the CCRI Legacy Programme. However, funding is limited and there is further work to do to complete and disseminate the country pilot and develop the tools, metrics, and research on financial vehicles needed to improve the investment case for adaptation and resilience... The CCRI Legacy Programme provides the coordinating framework between the private sector, public policymakers and donors to advance this.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, What is the UK’s offer in this space?

co_funding_partners.partner: Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC) members
Adaptation and Resilience Investors Collaborative (ARIC) DFIs
Global Infrastructure Hub (GIH) private sector members (in-kind contributions)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s contribution to ARIC is expected to leverage 10–12 times co-funding from other DFI members. GIH’s work will mobilize private sector in-kind support for tool development. The Jamaica pilot aims to crowd in private investment through coordination with IMF/IDB facilities.

quote.text: The UK’s contribution to ARIC will leverage 10-12 times co-funding from other members... Donor support is only needed for the non-commercial components. In addition, the UK’s contribution to ARIC will leverage 10-12 times co-funding from other members... The Flexible Fund will provide a degree of agility to pursue emerging work that would facilitate meeting the overall objectives articulated in the Theory of Change.
quote.source: D0005811.odt, Economic Appraisal and Flexible Fund sections

metadata.programme_name: Women and Girls Health: The Ending Preventable Deaths of Mothers, Babies and Children support programme
metadata.quote: "This programme will run from 2023 to 2030 to provide technical assistance (TA) to FCDO country and central teams to complement all UK investments, policy and diplomacy efforts that support the manifesto commitment to End the Preventable Deaths of mothers, babies and children by 2030 (EPD)." (D0003323.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "This programme will run from 2023 to 2030 to provide technical assistance (TA) to FCDO country and central teams to complement all UK investments, policy and diplomacy efforts that support the manifesto commitment to End the Preventable Deaths of mothers, babies and children by 2030 (EPD)."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides technical assistance (TA) to strengthen health systems, influence policy, and build capacity in 11 flagship countries to reduce maternal, newborn, and child mortality. It combines policy influence, capacity building, and implementation support to achieve the UK's Ending Preventable Deaths (EPD) goals by 2030.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will run from 2023 to 2030 to provide technical assistance (TA) to FCDO country and central teams to complement all UK investments, policy and diplomacy efforts that support the manifesto commitment to End the Preventable Deaths of mothers, babies and children by 2030 (EPD)."
q3_expected_outputs: 5-10% reduction in maternal, newborn, and child mortality in 11 countries by 2025
5% improvement in a set of key indicators compiled into a ‘Universal Health Coverage Index’ in the same countries
Increased government commitment and capability on EPD, measured through strengthened institutions, policy reforms, improved coordination, and greater use of evidence
EPD plans developed and implemented in flagship countries
Strategic use of flexible funding to further EPD aims
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce preventable deaths of mothers, babies, and children by 2030 through technical assistance that strengthens health systems, influences policy, and builds capacity in 11 flagship countries.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will contribute to the overall FCDO EPD approach that aims to reduce the maternal, newborn and child mortality through increased country commitment and capability on EPD." (D0003323.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS) such as South Sudan, Somalia, and Yemen, but the overall risk rating is classified as 'Moderate' due to mitigation strategies and FCDO's experience in these contexts.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall programme risk rating: Moderate." (D0003323.odt, Risk)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states where health systems are weak, political economy challenges are significant, and climate risks threaten progress. These constraints require flexible, adaptive approaches to technical assistance and policy influence.
where_context.quote: "Most deaths now occur in fragile and conflict affected settings and amongst the most marginalised people." (D0003323.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO (UK-based) manages the programme and makes key decisions, though local experts and country offices provide input and guidance. Technical assistance is designed to be context-specific and delivered by local experts where possible.
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
institutional strengthening
policy influence support

partner_organizations.name: FCDO country offices (11 flagship countries)
partner_organizations.role: technical oversight and guidance

partner_organizations.name: Local experts (consultants)
partner_organizations.role: delivery of technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: Consultancy firms (via EACDS and IMDP frameworks)
partner_organizations.role: hiring and management of consultants

partner_organizations.name: Governments of flagship countries
partner_organizations.role: policy and implementation partners

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral partners (e.g., WHO, UNICEF, World Bank)
partner_organizations.role: collaboration and alignment

who_partners.quote: "The TA will be from local experts as much as possible, be context specific and designed to work hand in hand with the existing UK portfolio, in strong partnership with country governments and in close collaboration with other development partners." (D0003323.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of framework agreements (EACDS and IMDP) for hiring consultants, programme-funded in-house roles, and flexible funding for catalytic activities. Payments are milestone-based and managed centrally by the EPD Hub.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed centrally by the EPD Hub within FCDO's Human Development Department. The Hub oversees the hiring of consultants (via framework agreements), in-house roles, and the allocation of flexible funds. Country offices provide technical oversight, while a lead consultancy firm handles administrative and stewardship functions.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The use of existing FCDO framework agreements (EACDS and IMDP) allows for rapid mobilization of consultants, streamlined procurement, and pre-vetted suppliers. This approach balances speed, cost-efficiency, and quality assurance.
how_mechanism.quote: "FCDO has two existing consultancy frameworks that can be used to hire long and short-term consultants. Expert Advisory Call Down Service (EACDS) can be used for work under £1m, lasting less than 1 year whilst International Multi-Disciplinary Programme (IMDP) can be used for work up to £12m, lasting multiple years." (D0003323.odt, Hiring of long and short-term consultants)

how_governance.quote: "The programme will be managed by one Senior Responsible Officer (25%) and one Programme Responsible Officer (50%) with technical inputs from a senior health adviser (15%). They will carry out the mini-competition among the frameworks and/or the hiring of the in-house roles eventually. They will also be the point of contact for the lead agency for all TA activities, meeting formally every quarter to discuss." (D0003323.odt, Governance and management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between countries or technical areas based on emerging needs, but this requires approval from the EPD Hub and alignment with the programme's strategic goals. A strategic flexible fund (10% of budget) is set aside for catalytic activities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with annual reviews and bottleneck analyses informing adjustments. Technical assistance can be redirected based on changing country contexts or UK priorities, but this requires approval from the SRO/PRO and EPD Hub.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will be flexible enough to address those underlying, neglected and persistent issues to support the core UK EPD influencing and investment work, providing excellent value for money." (D0003323.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Consultancy Firm → Country-based Consultants/In-house Roles
how_efficiency.quote: "The lead agency for the long and short-term TA will be paid quarterly in arrears after receiving a financial report outlining which consultancies have taken place, for how long and for what purpose." (D0003323.odt, Financial Management)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (not viable due to reduced FCDO health footprint)
Technical assistance funding managed by flagship country offices (less strategic coherence)
Technical assistance managed centrally (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The central management option (Option 3) was chosen for its ability to provide strategic coherence across flagship countries, better value for money through streamlined procurement, flexibility to respond to UK priorities, and stronger lesson-learning. It also reduces the administrative burden on country offices while maintaining local context specificity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The delivery of large amounts of TA to 11 countries—short and long term—is too difficult to manage
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The stewardship function of the consultancy firms will help mitigate this risk by carrying out the administration around the TA.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: The right skills of people delivering TA cannot be found (or extensive delays affect credibility/timeliness)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The framework agreements include a large range of organisations, widening the scope of finding the right people. In addition, FCDO will use its own extensive network to identify consultants.

why_rationale.quote: "Based on this assessment, Option 3 is the preferred option." (D0003323.odt, Appraisal 1: Options for TA delivery modalities)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS) such as South Sudan, Somalia, and Yemen, which limits the pool of available partners and requires specialized expertise in conflict-sensitive approaches. Local ownership is prioritized, but security and political constraints may necessitate regional or international consultants in some cases.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks in FCAS limit in-country presence of international staff
Weak institutions require long-term capacity building rather than short-term fixes
Political economy challenges necessitate adaptive, context-specific approaches
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s focus on policy influence, health systems strengthening, and equity (EPD pillars) requires a flexible, multi-modal delivery structure. Technical assistance must be both long-term (for institutional strengthening) and short-term (for targeted expertise), with central management ensuring coherence across countries and sectors.
q28_linkages: Policy influence goals → need for embedded, long-term TA to build government relationships
Health systems strengthening → requires both technical expertise (short-term consultants) and institutional support (long-term TA)
Equity focus → necessity for local experts and context-specific approaches
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery (efficiency) and inclusive partnerships (equity). For example, using local experts enhances ownership but may slow down mobilization compared to international consultants. The flexible fund (10%) balances these trade-offs by allowing catalytic, equity-focused activities without sacrificing overall efficiency.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Local expertise vs. speed of mobilization
Long-term capacity building vs. short-term results
Central management (coherence) vs. country-led flexibility
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (with FCAS elements) leads to quarterly oversight, embedded safeguarding measures, and adaptive management structures (e.g., annual reviews, bottleneck analyses). High-risk contexts like South Sudan require more intensive stewardship and political economy analysis.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles through mentorship, institutional strengthening, and co-design of TA. Local experts are prioritized for delivery, while FCDO and consultancy firms provide backstopping and quality assurance.
intersections.quote: "The TA will be from local experts as much as possible, be context specific and designed to work hand in hand with the existing UK portfolio, in strong partnership with country governments and in close collaboration with other development partners." (D0003323.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

key_programme_risks: EPD does not stay on the agenda for FCDO in health, and the TA input is not backed up with senior buy-in.
EPD supporting programmes are too small to make the TA effective.
The right skills of people delivering TA cannot be found (or extensive delays affect credibility/timeliness).
The delivery of large amounts of TA to 11 countries—short and long term—is too difficult to manage.
The outputs do not lead to the outcomes wanted due to external factors (complex political economy, geopolitics, crises, conflict, pandemics, etc.).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: EPD does not stay on the agenda for FCDO in health, and the TA input is not backed up with senior buy-in.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: EPD is now in all key health strategies, including the Global Health Strategic Framework, Africa Strategy, IDS, and likely in Women and Girls. Minister Mitchell is now the EPD Champion.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: EPD supporting programmes are too small to make the TA effective.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO is moving to more of an influencing and innovations approach as well as investments—EPD fits with this. The bottleneck analysis will ensure the programme focuses on the right areas.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The right skills of people delivering TA cannot be found (or extensive delays affect credibility/timeliness).
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The framework agreements include a large range of organisations, widening the scope of finding the right people. FCDO will use its own extensive network to identify consultants.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The delivery of large amounts of TA to 11 countries—short and long term—is too difficult to manage.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The stewardship function of the consultancy firms will help mitigate this risk by carrying out the administration around the TA.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: The outputs do not lead to the outcomes wanted due to external factors (complex political economy, geopolitics, crises, conflict, pandemics, etc.).
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of political economy analyses and the flexibility of approach, tailored to the changing context, will mitigate this to some extent. Some outcomes will strengthen a country’s response to a crisis, so may be beneficial.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, TA must strengthen links between humanitarian and development efforts through a health systems approach.
Long-term TA is essential in fragile states to tackle deep, intractable issues and build resilient institutions.
Flexibility and adaptive management are critical to respond to rapidly changing contexts (e.g., conflict, climate shocks).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past DFID/FCDO health programmes showed that effective TA requires mutual accountability, local ownership, and responsiveness to partner needs. Inflexible theories of change and poorly defined activities hamper long-term impact. Continuity of staff and strategic use of flexible funding were key success factors.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates annual reviews, bottleneck analyses, and a flexible fund (10%) to adapt to lessons. It also prioritizes local experts and context-specific approaches based on past experience with capacity substitution risks.
risks_lessons.quote: "Historically many TA examples have been supportive of a particular aid programme, not designed to build long-term capacity, have been poorly coordinated and have defaulted into capacity substitution." (D0003323.odt, The evidence for Technical Assistance)

financial_details.quote: "The approximate budget of this programme is up to £15m of Overseas Development Assistance, RDEL over three years." (D0003323.odt, Financial Management)

metadata.programme_name: International Finance Facility for Education (IFFEd)
metadata.duration_text: September 2023 to September 2044 (guarantee term of 23 years - average repayment maturity of 18 years and 5 year replenishment period)

quote.text: IFFEd is a new, innovative instrument that will use donor guarantees and grants to unlock significant concessional finance for education in Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMICs).

duration_source.text: AMP Start Date: September 2023 (TBC, depending on BC approval) ... AMP End Date: September 2044 (guarantee term of 23 years - average repayment maturity of 18 years and 5 year replenishment period)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: IFFEd is an innovative financing instrument designed to unlock significant concessional finance for education in Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) by leveraging donor guarantees and grants. It aims to address the gap in education aid architecture by working through Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) to provide affordable loans, thereby multiplying donor cash investments up to seven times.

q1_source.text: IFFEd is a new, innovative instrument that will use donor guarantees and grants to unlock significant concessional finance for education in Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMICs). ... IFFEd is much more effective than traditional grant finance because it will unlock up to seven times donors’ cash investments in affordable loans.

q3_expected_outputs.output: additional concessional MDB education finance
q3_expected_outputs.target: $980 million in the initial phase, aiming for $10 billion by 2030

q3_expected_outputs.output: expanded educational opportunities for marginalized children and youth
q3_expected_outputs.target: focus on girls, the poorest, disabled, and forcibly displaced children

q3_expected_outputs.output: improved quality of education and learning at scale
q3_expected_outputs.target: focus on foundational skills (literacy, numeracy, socio-emotional skills)

q3_expected_outputs.output: increased prioritization of education among IFFEd-supported governments
contribution to achievement of SDG4 in eligible countries
q3_expected_outputs.target: proportion of children achieving minimum proficiency and completing primary/secondary education

what_objectives.summary: IFFEd is a financing mechanism that leverages donor guarantees and grants to unlock concessional loans for education in LMICs, aiming to address the learning crisis by expanding access and improving learning outcomes, particularly for marginalized groups.

quote.text: IFFEd will unlock up to seven times donors’ cash investment in concessional financing. It will provide a new, attractive offer to LMICs, a new opportunity for a closer partnership with MDBs on education, and an opportunity for further UK leadership on girls’ education and innovative financing.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting the innovative nature of the financing mechanism and the need to mobilize sufficient donor commitments, but with mitigations in place through MDB involvement and governance structures.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

q6_contextual_constraints: low demand for non-concessional education loans
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: LMICs face suppressed demand for education loans due to long payback periods and higher non-concessional rates, while MDBs lack sufficient resources to address the scale of education financing needs. Climate risks exacerbate vulnerabilities, particularly for girls, and the learning poverty crisis affects 70% of children in LMICs post-COVID-19.

quote.text: LMICs are unable to access suitable education financing at the scale required. ... Non-concessional MDB borrowing costs are higher than the very generous lending terms offered to the MDBs’ poorest member countries, but they remain considerably below market rates. One reason for this is the long time it takes for education investments to generate returns. ... The current generation of students are at risk of losing up to 21 trillion in lifetime earnings in present value, or the equivalent of 17% of today’s global GDP.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, The rationale for IFFEd / The global learning and skills crisis

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: IFFEd is governed by a Board with representation from sovereign donors (including the UK), LMICs, MDBs, and civil society. Decision-making is shared among these stakeholders, with the UK having a Board seat as a major contributor.
q10_capacity_building_details: support to MDBs to expand education lending capacity
technical dialogue between donors, LMICs, and MDBs on education investments
evidence-based guidance through the Committee on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships
alignment with global evidence base (e.g., 'Smart Buys' from Global Education Evidence and Advisory Panel)

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Participating MDB; approved involvement in April 2023; will channel IFFEd funds to eligible Asian countries

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: Participating MDB; expected to approve involvement in Autumn 2023; will focus on TVET and higher education in Africa

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Major donor; provides guarantees and grants; Board seat; influences programming expectations

partner_organizations.name: Government of Sweden
partner_organizations.role: Donor; committed $200m guarantee (signed August 2023)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Canada
partner_organizations.role: Donor; likely to provide $18.75m in grants (potentially as paid-in capital)

partner_organizations.name: Global Partnership for Education (GPE)
partner_organizations.role: Partner; will co-finance pilot programmes in Asia with IFFEd loans

partner_organizations.name: Atlassian Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Philanthropic donor; committed $1.5m in seed capital

partner_organizations.name: Jacobs Foundation
partner_organizations.role: Philanthropic donor; committed $1.2m in seed capital

partner_organizations.name: Eligible LMIC Governments
partner_organizations.role: Recipient countries; will receive IFFEd-supported loans and grants for education projects
partner_organizations.location: LMICs (30 countries across Asia and Africa)

quote.text: IFFEd will convene sovereign donors, private and philanthropic donors, LMICs, and the MDBs to discuss education financing in LMICs under a formal governance structure. ... The Facility will ensure that MDBs regularly discuss their pipeline of education projects and scale up where their comparative advantage lies.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, How IFFEd works / IFFEd’s governance structure

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: IFFEd combines (1) **guarantees** (contingent commitments from donors, with 15% paid-in capital to secure a AAA credit rating) and (2) **grants** (10% of loan amounts to buy down loan costs and make them concessional). These instruments are used to provide portfolio support to MDBs, enabling them to expand lending for education in LMICs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IFFEd is structured as an independent facility hosted in Switzerland, with a Board (including donor representatives like the UK), a High-Level Advisory Group, and a Committee on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships. The MDBs (ADB, AfDB) implement education projects in eligible countries, while IFFEd provides financial guarantees and grants to incentivize lending.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The MDBs (ADB and AfDB) were selected based on their existing relationships with LMICs, ability to leverage resources, and comparative advantage in education financing. Eligible LMICs are determined by GNI per capita and access to non-concessional MDB lending.

quote.text: IFFEd’s financial innovation is enabling the participating MDBs to expand their total lending capacity for education by insuring their entire loan portfolio against the risk of late payment. ... The participating MDBs are currently the ADB and AfDB, though other MDBs can be included at a later point, subject to approval by the IFFEd Board.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, How IFFEd works / Where will IFFEd work

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: IFFEd-supported projects are developed through dialogue between MDBs and eligible LMICs, aligned with country education strategies and IFFEd’s programming expectations. Proposals are approved by the IFFEd Board.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The IFFEd Board includes representatives from contributing donors (e.g., UK, Sweden), MDBs, and potentially LMICs/civil society. A **Committee on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships** provides multi-stakeholder expertise to guide investments. The UK will have a Board seat and aims to include an FCDO Education Adviser on the Committee.

quote.text: The Facility will ensure that MDBs regularly discuss their pipeline of education projects and scale up where their comparative advantage lies. ... The Committee [on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships] will develop a guidance note at the beginning of each IFFEd replenishment period (of five years) elaborating on the eligibility criteria for IFFEd investments.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to MDBs based on demand from eligible LMICs and alignment with IFFEd’s programming expectations. Reallocation between MDBs or countries would require Board approval and demonstration of additionality.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: IFFEd’s programming expectations (e.g., focus on foundational learning, inclusion, climate) are set for each 5-year replenishment period but can be adjusted by the Board based on emerging evidence or country needs. The Committee on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships provides adaptive guidance.

quote.text: The determination of which countries will receive IFFEd support will be undertaken through each MDB’s dialogue with eligible countries and an exploration of how IFFEd funding could support the country’s strategic education objectives, aligned to IFFEd’s programming expectations. ... The Committee will develop a guidance note at the beginning of each IFFEd replenishment period ... elaborating on the eligibility criteria for IFFEd investments.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, Where will IFFEd work / IFFEd’s governance structure

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IFFEd (Board/Secretariat) → Participating MDBs (ADB/AfDB) → LMIC Governments/Implementers
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: The UK’s guarantee contribution includes (1) **upfront paid-in capital** ($18m/£15m, 15% of the $120m guarantee) and (2) **contingent liability** ($102m/£85m, 85%). Grants (£80m) are disbursed over 4 years (£20m/year) to buy down loan costs. MDBs receive portfolio support to expand lending.

quote.text: A guarantee of $120m (£100m), of which: $18m (£15m) CDEL paid-in capital (15% of the guarantee); Up to $102m (£85m) CDEL contingent liability if the guarantee is called. ... An RDEL grant of up to £80m (up to £20m per year over four years).

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Terminate the initiative due to insufficient donor commitments.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Persevere with the $500m guarantee target for launch
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Wait until the original $500m guarantee target is met, risking further delays.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Proceed with a smaller guarantee of $245m (current commitments)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Launch IFFEd with existing donor pledges ($245m guarantee + $98m grants) to unlock $980m in loans, then scale up later.
Rejected as insufficient to address the scale of LMIC education financing needs.
Would increase lending capacity but not target education specifically or offer concessional terms.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **smaller launch model (Option 3: $245m guarantee)** was chosen to (1) **avoid IFFEd failure** after years of development, (2) **prove the concept** with a viable multiplier (4x), and (3) **catalyze further donor commitments** by demonstrating results. The UK’s leadership and the innovative leverage ratio (1:7) made this a strategic use of ODA despite high opportunity costs.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (7x leverage of donor cash)
partner capacity (MDBs’ ability to scale lending)
speed (urgency of the learning crisis post-COVID-19)
equity (focus on marginalized groups in LMICs)
UK leadership (reputation in global education financing)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to attract further donors after launch
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The smaller model is designed to prove the concept and create momentum. The UK will lobby other donors (e.g., Canada, Netherlands) to join post-launch.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Credit rating agencies lose confidence due to lower donor commitments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The 15% paid-in capital ratio is maintained even with the smaller guarantee, supporting the AAA rating. The UK’s £15m paid-in capital signals commitment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: MDBs do not prioritize education lending despite IFFEd support
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFFEd’s governance includes a Committee to monitor MDB pipelines and incentivize lending through concessional terms (10% grant element).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: LMICs do not demand education loans even with concessional terms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Eligibility criteria require countries to demonstrate commitment to SDG4 and domestic education budget increases. IFFEd will work with countries already expressing public support (e.g., Indonesia, Pakistan, Egypt).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (low management costs via MDB implementation)
effectiveness (focus on learning outcomes and marginalized groups)
equity (targeting girls, disabled, and poorest children)

quote.text: Option 3 (proceeding with what we have, which is a smaller guarantee of $245m) is the preferred and recommended option. ... It is the option that makes it likely that IFFEd will be established, and failure avoided. ... IFFEd makes donor grants go further. $1 of grant financing alongside guarantees can unlock $7 of concessional education financing. ... The bigger prize is for IFFEd to make a major contribution to the education financing gap in LMICs.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, Discussion of options and preferred option

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **LMIC context** constrains partner selection in two ways: (1) **Eligibility is limited to countries with GNI per capita below the LMIC threshold and access to non-concessional MDB lending**, excluding poorer LICs (covered by other funds) and richer MICs. (2) **MDB participation is determined by their existing relationships with LMICs** (e.g., ADB for Asia, AfDB for Africa) and their sectoral focus (e.g., AfDB does not work on primary/secondary education).
q27_constraints_detail: GNI per capita ceiling (LMIC threshold)
Access to non-concessional MDB lending (excludes LICs)
MDBs’ geographic mandates (ADB for Asia, AfDB for Africa)
MDBs’ sectoral priorities (AfDB focuses on TVET/higher education, not basic education)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **financing mechanism objective** (leveraging donor guarantees/grants) determines the **multilateral delivery structure** because: (1) **MDBs are uniquely positioned to leverage capital markets** and provide long-term lending at scale; (2) **LMICs prefer MDBs over bilateral donors** due to fewer conditions; (3) **Portfolio support requires a AAA-rated intermediary** (IFFEd) to insure MDB loan portfolios.

q28_linkages.mechanism: MDBs’ ability to leverage guarantees into multiples of lending (4x target)
10% grant element to buy down loan costs, managed through IFFEd’s grant window
Governance structure (Board + Committee) to oversee MDB pipelines and alignment with global evidence

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between **efficiency (leverage)** and **equity (targeting marginalized groups)**: (1) **Broad eligibility (30 LMICs) vs. deep impact**: IFFEd could spread funds thinly across many countries, but programming expectations prioritize marginalized groups (girls, disabled, poorest). (2) **MDB comparative advantage vs. education focus**: The AfDB’s strength in TVET/higher education may divert funds from basic education, but FCDO accepts this as a trade-off for scaling skills financing.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: IFFEd’s 7x leverage ratio maximizes finance but requires broad country eligibility. Equity is addressed by programming expectations (e.g., 10% of projects must focus on marginalized groups).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Speed (rapid launch) vs. inclusion (waiting for more donors)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Option 3 (smaller launch) prioritizes speed to prove the model, accepting lower initial impact but aiming to attract more donors later.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: MDB sectoral focus vs. FCDO priorities
q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: AfDB’s focus on TVET/higher education (not basic education) is accepted to align with its comparative advantage, though FCDO’s priority is foundational learning.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., donor commitment uncertainty, MDB demand) leads to **milestone-based oversight** with regular Board reviews and a 5-year replenishment cycle to adjust strategies. The Committee on Education Results provides additional technical scrutiny.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in IFFEd’s structure: (1) **MDBs** receive portfolio support to expand education lending capacity; (2) **LMICs** must demonstrate capacity to sustain MDB debt and align with SDG4; (3) **IFFEd’s Committee** provides evidence-based guidance to all partners.

quote.text: The determination of which countries will receive IFFEd support will be undertaken through each MDB’s dialogue with eligible countries and an exploration of how IFFEd funding could support the country’s strategic education objectives, aligned to IFFEd’s programming expectations. ... The Committee [on Education Results, Innovations and Partnerships] will develop a guidance note at the beginning of each IFFEd replenishment period ... elaborating on the eligibility criteria for IFFEd investments.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, Where will IFFEd work / IFFEd’s governance structure

key_programme_risks: Insufficient donor commitments to meet the $500m guarantee target (mitigated by proceeding with $245m)
Credit rating agencies downgrading IFFEd due to lower-than-planned guarantees (mitigated by maintaining 15% paid-in capital)
MDBs not prioritizing education lending despite IFFEd support (mitigated by governance oversight and concessional terms)
LMICs not demanding education loans even with concessional terms (mitigated by eligibility criteria requiring SDG4 commitment)
Failure to attract further donors post-launch (mitigated by UK lobbying and proof-of-concept results)
Climate and conflict risks disrupting education systems in LMICs (mitigated by programming expectations on resilience)
Learning poverty persisting despite increased financing (mitigated by focus on evidence-based interventions)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: IFFEd fails to launch due to insufficient donor commitments
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proceed with a smaller $245m guarantee to establish the facility and demonstrate results, which can attract further donors. The UK will lead lobbying efforts post-launch.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: MDBs do not expand education lending as intended
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IFFEd’s governance includes a Committee to monitor MDB pipelines and incentivize lending through concessional terms (10% grant element). Eligibility criteria require MDBs to demonstrate additionality.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: LMICs do not use IFFEd funds effectively
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Countries must have a credible education sector plan aligned with SDG4 and commit to increasing domestic education budgets. IFFEd will coordinate with other education funds (e.g., GPE) to avoid duplication.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Credit rating agencies lose confidence in IFFEd
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain the 15% paid-in capital ratio even with the smaller guarantee. The UK’s £15m paid-in capital signals strong donor commitment.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: IFFEd does not reach marginalized groups
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Programming expectations require a focus on girls, disabled children, and the poorest. Results data will be disaggregated by gender and disability.

fcas_specific_lessons: LMICs with fragile contexts (e.g., conflict, climate vulnerability) require flexible financing and resilience-focused education investments. IFFEd’s programming expectations include climate-smart education systems and support for displaced children.
In FCAS, demand for education loans may be lower due to perceived risks. IFFEd’s concessional terms and grants aim to mitigate this.
Coordination with Education Cannot Wait (ECW) ensures alignment with education-in-emergencies responses in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2019-20 attempt to launch IFFEd failed due to insufficient donor commitments and the World Bank’s withdrawal during COVID-19. Lessons learned include: (1) **Start smaller** to prove the concept before scaling; (2) **Secure anchor donors** (UK, Sweden) to build credibility; (3) **Align with MDBs’ comparative advantages** (e.g., ADB for basic education, AfDB for TVET). The 2023 design reflects these adjustments, including a lower launch threshold ($245m vs. $500m) and a step-wise scaling plan.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key changes from the 2019 design: (1) Reduced launch target from $1bn to $500m (now further to $245m); (2) Added a **step-wise scaling approach** to prove the model before replenishment; (3) Strengthened governance with a **Committee on Education Results** to ensure quality; (4) Explicit **programming expectations** on foundational learning, inclusion, and climate resilience; (5) **Hosted in Switzerland** (neutral ground) with interim Board leadership.

quote.text: IFFEd mobilisation paused in 2020, due to lack of other donor commitment in the context of the Covid-19 crisis and World Bank’s subsequent withdrawal. It re-started in 2022. ... Partners agreed that Switzerland would host IFFEd. It was agreed that IFFEd would launch with a smaller minimum number of partners and funding committed, in order to prove the concept before later scaling up. ... The UK committed £750,000 in seed funding ... to help IFFEd launch in 2023/24.

leverage_achieved.description: IFFEd’s $245m guarantee (including $37m paid-in capital) will unlock $980m in MDB loans (4x multiplier). With $98m in grants (10% of loans), the total concessional financing unlocked is $980m, achieving a 7x unlocking ratio on donor cash ($140m cash + $208m contingent).

capital_vs_revenue_split.description: The UK’s contribution includes (1) **capital**: $18m (£15m) paid-in capital for the guarantee (15% of $120m); (2) **revenue**: £80m in grants disbursed over 4 years (£20m/year). The $102m (£85m) contingent liability is not disbursed upfront.

quote.text: A guarantee of $120m (£100m), of which: $18m (£15m) CDEL paid-in capital (15% of the guarantee); Up to $102m (£85m) CDEL contingent liability if the guarantee is called. ... An RDEL grant of up to £80m (up to £20m per year over four years). ... The target for launching IFFEd in 2023/24 is for donors to provide guarantees of $500m (of which $75m is paid-in) and $200m in grant contributions. This would lead to $2bn of additional finance through the MDBs (a multiplier of 4). ... We are proposing a step-wise approach for mobilising IFFEd over the next year, starting with $245m in operational guarantees and $98m in grants to unlock $980m of concessional financing.
quote.source: D0005760.odt, Programme Value / How IFFEd works

metadata.programme_name: Emerging Market Climate Action Fund (EMCAF)
metadata.duration_text: The Fund is entered into for a fixed term of 17 years from the final closing date, currently planned for November 2023, meaning an end date of November 2040, subject to early termination.

quote.programme_name: "Title: Emerging Market Climate Action Fund (EMCAF)" (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)
quote.duration: "The Fund is entered into for a fixed term of 17 years from the final closing date, currently planned for November 2023, meaning an end date of November 2040, subject to early termination." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
quote.sector: "Sector: Climate mitigation, adaptation and environment" (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)

metadata.duration_source: "The Fund is entered into for a fixed term of 17 years from the final closing date, currently planned for November 2023, meaning an end date of November 2040, subject to early termination."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: EMCAF is a blended finance vehicle designed to unlock private capital for climate mitigation, adaptation, and environment (A&E) projects in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs). It operates as a public-private investment fund, leveraging senior investment through junior equity contributions from public and impact investors, with the goal of demonstrating the commercial viability of climate finance, particularly in adaptation and resilience (A&R).
what_objectives.q1_source: "FCDO will invest up to £9m (in EUR equivalent) into EMCAF, a public-private investment vehicle, directly unlocking up to £18m senior investment into the top fund with further leverage at sub-fund and investment levels. This blended finance vehicle will invest in new business models, technologies and infrastructure which deliver climate mitigation, adaptation and environment (A&E) projects in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs), aiding their transitions to low carbon and climate resilient economies." (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)
q3_expected_outputs: Unlock up to £18m senior investment with FCDO’s £9m contribution (leverage ratio of 1:2)
Invest in 12-15 funds by 2026, supporting 150+ projects
Achieve emissions reductions of 51 million tonnes CO2 over 28 years
Install 91 GWh of clean energy capacity
Target 19% of investments in Adaptation and Environment (A&E) funds
Mobilize private capital for climate adaptation and resilience in EMDEs
Develop market exposure to climate investment through knowledge-sharing and public communications (10+ efforts during investment period)
Generate lessons on A&R investment models for wider market dissemination
what_objectives.summary: EMCAF aims to catalyze private investment in climate projects in EMDEs by providing junior equity to leverage senior capital, with a focus on demonstrating the commercial viability of adaptation and resilience (A&R) investments. It targets a 19% allocation to A&E funds and seeks to influence market practices through knowledge-sharing and policy learning.

quote.objectives: "This blended finance vehicle will invest in new business models, technologies and infrastructure which deliver climate mitigation, adaptation and environment (A&E) projects in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs), aiding their transitions to low carbon and climate resilient economies." (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)
quote.outputs: "By then, EMCAF will be expected to have, and hold, a portfolio of 12 to 15 investments, supporting the financing of 150+ projects." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)

countries_regions: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) recipient list countries
70% of investments in Low-Income Countries (LICs) and Lower-Middle Income Countries (LMICs)
Focus on Africa (e.g., ARCH Cold Chain Solutions Fund in East Africa), Asia, and other EMDEs
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting the challenges of unlocking private investment in adaptation and resilience (A&R) in EMDEs, where such investments are traditionally underfunded and perceived as risky. The fund-of-funds structure and reliance on commercial investors introduce financial risks, but these are mitigated by the track records of Allianz Global Investors (AGI) and the European Investment Bank (EIB).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)
q6_contextual_constraints: limited private investment in adaptation and resilience (A&R) due to perceived high risks and low returns
lack of track record for A&R investments in EMDEs
difficulty in pricing climate risks or opportunities in A&R infrastructure
regulatory and market barriers to mainstreaming A&R investments
climate hazards exacerbating investment needs but public finance alone insufficient
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The limited private investment in A&R is attributed to the inability to price climate risks, lack of revenue streams for nature-based solutions, and traditional public-sector delivery of such services. This constrains the pipeline of bankable A&R projects and requires blended finance to de-risk investments. EMCAF addresses this by providing junior equity to crowd in senior private capital and demonstrating commercial viability.

quote.constraints: "A&R attracts limited private finance in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) as a result of factors that include: the inability to price climate risks or opportunities into investments or A&R infrastructure (e.g. water or flood management infrastructure) and services (e.g. weather forecasting, disaster relief services)." (D0004321.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Allianz Global Investors (AGI) and European Investment Bank (EIB)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with the Fund Manager (AGI, based in the City of London) and the Investment Advisor (EIB). FCDO, as a junior limited partner, has influence through the Investor Advisory Committee (IAC) but no direct control over investment decisions. The General Partner (AGI) and EIB originate and approve investments, with FCDO providing strategic guidance on A&R priorities.
q10_capacity_building_details: AGI and EIB will support and advise sub-fund managers, particularly first-time managers, to build regional expertise and develop novel business models.
EMCAF will coach managers of sub-funds it invests in, deepening climate-focused fund management industries in EMDEs.
Knowledge-sharing on A&R investment models through public communications and case studies to build market capacity.

partner_organizations.name: Allianz Global Investors (AGI)
partner_organizations.role: Fund Manager and General Partner; responsible for fund administration, financial management, risk management, impact monitoring, and reporting.

partner_organizations.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
partner_organizations.role: Investment Advisor; responsible for sourcing and due diligence of investment opportunities, including E&S standards compliance.

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Junior Limited Partner; provides £9m junior equity to leverage senior capital and influences fund strategy on A&R through the Investor Advisory Committee (IAC).

partner_organizations.name: German Government
partner_organizations.role: Junior equity investor (€25m committed).

partner_organizations.name: Luxembourg Government
partner_organizations.role: Junior equity investor (€15m committed).

partner_organizations.name: Nordic Development Fund
partner_organizations.role: Junior equity investor (€15m committed).

partner_organizations.name: Senior Private Investors
partner_organizations.role: Provide senior equity (€400m committed as of 2023), unlocked by junior capital from public/impact investors.

partner_organizations.name: Sub-Fund Managers (e.g., ARCH Cold Chain Solutions, Alcazar Energy Partners II)
partner_organizations.role: Receive EMCAF investments to implement climate projects in EMDEs; supported by AGI/EIB for capacity building.

quote.structure: "Managed by Allianz Global Investors (AGI) supported by the European Investment Bank (EIB), EMCAF will put into practice the strategic objectives of the Partnership for Investment and Infrastructure (PII) announced at the UK-chaired G7 at Carbis Bay." (D0004321.odt, BusinessCaseSummarySheet)
quote.decision_power: "As a junior limited partner, FCDO will sit on the Investor Advisory Committee (IAC), providing an opportunity to influence the decision-making process. The IAC meets bi-annually, providing advice, guidance, and overall supervision of operation of the Fund and compliance with the Limited Partnership Agreement." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
quote.capacity_building: "AGI will support and advise investees, in particular first-time managers, but will remain distant from management decisions." (D0004321.odt, Commercial Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO will invest as a Limited Partner in EMCAF through a Limited Partnership Agreement (LPA), Subscription Agreement, and Side Letter. The fund operates as a blended finance vehicle, where FCDO’s junior equity (up to £9m) unlocks senior private investment (£18m+) at a 1:2 ratio. Returns are distributed via a waterfall structure prioritizing senior investors, with FCDO’s capital at first-loss risk.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: EMCAF is structured as a fund-of-funds, with Allianz Global Investors (AGI) as the General Partner (GP) and Fund Manager, and the European Investment Bank (EIB) as the Investment Advisor. AGI handles financial and risk management, while EIB sources and conducts due diligence on investments. FCDO participates as a junior Limited Partner with influence via the Investor Advisory Committee (IAC).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (direct selection of AGI and EIB based on track record)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: AGI and EIB were selected due to their established expertise in climate finance and fund management. AGI’s commercial network and EIB’s pipeline of climate investments in EMDEs were deemed critical for achieving EMCAF’s objectives. The G7’s Partnership for Infrastructure and Investment (PII) also endorsed EMCAF as a flagship initiative, further justifying the selection.

quote.instrument: "FCDO will enter into four agreements with the Fund. These are; the Limited Partnership Agreement, Offering Memorandum, Subscription Agreement, and Side Letter." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
quote.structure: "EMCAF is a blended public-private fund-of-funds which provides early-stage equity financing to climate funds in EMDEs." (D0004321.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.selection: "AGI has launched 3 impact investment vehicles with combined committed capital of more than EUR 900m [...] EIB has a strong track record sourcing and developing climate investment opportunities in EMDEs." (D0004321.odt, Commercial Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Investor Advisory Committee (IAC) meets bi-annually to provide advice and oversight of the Fund’s operations and compliance with the Limited Partnership Agreement (LPA). The IAC includes FCDO as a member, allowing it to influence strategic decisions, though ultimate investment authority rests with the General Partner (AGI) and Investment Advisor (EIB).

quote.governance: "The IAC meets bi-annually, providing advice, guidance, and overall supervision of operation of the Fund and compliance with the Limited Partnership Agreement." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
quote.oversight: "FCDO will receive quarterly management reports, including unaudited financial statements, and annual detailed management reports, including environmental and social impact reporting and audited financial statements." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are committed to EMCAF under a fixed-term partnership agreement, and reallocation between investments is determined by the General Partner (AGI) and Investment Advisor (EIB). FCDO, as a limited partner, cannot unilaterally reallocate funds but can influence strategic priorities through the IAC.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: While FCDO can advocate for A&R priorities through the IAC, the fund’s investment strategy is largely predetermined by the LPA. Adjustments to the 19% A&E target or sectoral focus would require consensus among limited partners and the GP, making mid-programme shifts difficult.

quote.flexibility: "The partnership is closed-ended, meaning that once FCDO commits funding, it will not have an option to withdraw and retrieve funding until the partnership terminates." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
quote.adjustment: "FCDO has set an internal programme target for EMCAF to invest 19% of its investment capital into ‘adaptation and environment’ (A&E) funds [...] We will use that target to track EMCAF’s A&E investment activities and softly influence the Fund Managers." (D0004321.odt, Strategic Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → EMCAF (Fund Manager: AGI + Investment Advisor: EIB) → Sub-Funds/Platforms → End Projects

quote.layers: "A fund-of-funds structure allows EMCAF to access regional expertise via downstream fund managers in regions with specialist funds or platforms." (D0004321.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.payment: "Capital commitments can be called during this period [investment period: 2021-2026]." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (counterfactual: no investment in EMCAF)
Another party (e.g., British International Investment - BII) investing on FCDO’s behalf
Fund existing HMG programmes (e.g., PIDG, CP3)
FCDO invests directly in EMCAF (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Direct investment in EMCAF was chosen because it allows FCDO to: (1) leverage significant senior private capital (1:2 ratio) with limited ODA; (2) influence a mainstream commercial fund (AGI) to prioritize A&R, demonstrating market viability; (3) gain governance rights through the IAC to shape fund strategy; (4) build on the track records of AGI and EIB in climate finance; and (5) align with the G7’s Partnership for Infrastructure and Investment (PII) for global credibility. Alternative options (e.g., BII or existing programmes) were rejected as they lacked the scale, commercial reach, or strategic alignment with PII.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (commercial expertise of AGI, EIB’s climate pipeline)
strategic alignment (G7 PII, UK climate finance commitments)
market influence (demonstrating A&R viability to mainstream investors)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited control over investment decisions
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO’s seat on the Investor Advisory Committee (IAC) provides strategic influence, and side letters can set internal targets (e.g., 19% A&E allocation) to guide the fund manager.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: First-loss capital erosion if fund underperforms
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: AGI’s base-case scenario assumes a 2% IRR return, with historical EIB fund performance (3-5.5% returns) providing confidence. The diversified portfolio and commercial lens applied by AGI further reduce risk.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low private investor interest in A&R sectors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Blended finance structure de-risks investments, and FCDO’s junior capital catalyzes senior investment. Knowledge-sharing and case studies will demonstrate A&R commercial viability to attract future private capital.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fund-of-funds fees reducing value for money
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fees (0.4-0.6% for AGI/EIB) are benchmarked against similar HMG programmes (e.g., CP3) and deemed reasonable given the commercial expertise and leverage achieved.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leverage of senior capital at 1:2 ratio)
efficiency (low management fees relative to leverage)
equity (70% of investments in LICs/LMICs, gender-responsive investments)

quote.alternatives: "FCDO conducted a qualitative multi-criteria analysis of these options. [...] Direct investment, C is the most proportionate for this type of intervention considering funding available. This is therefore the preferred option." (D0004321.odt, Appraisal Case)
quote.rationale: "Investing in EMCAF as a PII vehicle supports International Development Strategy delivery. FCDO will exercise leadership to increase EMCAF’s impact on climate adaptation and resilience." (D0004321.odt, Strategic Case)
quote.risks: "FCDO’s funding as junior equity will operate as first-loss capital, so may be eroded if the Fund is not achieving strong returns." (D0004321.odt, Financial Case)
