Financial access (Component 3) is designed to scale the business models developed in Component 2
MEL (Component 4) ensures adaptive management across all components based on real-time learning
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting women-headed businesses, indigenous populations, and marginalized groups) with efficiency (focusing on peri-urban areas with better infrastructure and market access). There is tension between the cost of reaching remote, high-need areas and the programme's ability to deliver at scale.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Rapid delivery is prioritized in peri-urban zones, potentially excluding more remote rural populations
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led commercial suppliers provide technical expertise, while efforts are made to build local capacity through sub-contracting and training
Cost vs. reach: High transaction costs in DRC limit the number of direct beneficiaries, requiring careful targeting to maximize impact
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'Major' risk rating drives intensive oversight, including third-party monitoring, regular field visits by FCDO staff, and embedded safeguarding measures. The FCAS context requires real-time risk management and escalation pathways.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded across components: technical assistance to GoDRC (Component 1), training for agri-SMEs (Component 2), and financial literacy for banks (Component 3). Partners are selected based on their ability to strengthen local systems while delivering immediate results.
intersections.quote: The programme will focus on peri-urban areas surrounding major and medium cities: Kinshasa, Kisangani, Goma, Bukavu... This is to mitigate access challenges from insecurity and leverage existing market infrastructure. (D0006253.odt, GG geographic focus)... We will expect the lead supplier to work with and sub-contract to organisations in DRC who have the ability, the local knowledge and the language skills to deliver in DRC. (D0006253.odt, Value for Money Assessment)

key_programme_risks: Political instability and conflict disrupting programme activities
Weak governance and corruption undermining policy reforms (Component 1)
Limited absorptive capacity of agri-SMEs and financial institutions (Components 2 and 3)
Climate change exacerbating food insecurity and deforestation pressures
ICF eligibility risks if activities shift away from climate focus
Fraud and corruption in financial flows to private sector partners
Security risks limiting access to target geographic areas
Low adoption of climate-smart practices post-intervention

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Robust conflict sensitivity analysis, avoiding high-risk areas, and flexible activity planning to adapt to changing contexts.
Working with reform-minded champions in GoDRC, third-party monitoring, and transparent financial tracking.
Technical assistance embedded in all components, phased support to build local capacity, and targeting peri-urban areas with better infrastructure.
Clear principles for ICF ambition, climate screening for all activities, and focus on climate-smart value chains.
Third-party monitoring, FCDO field visits, and safeguarding due diligence for all partners.
Geographic targeting to avoid conflict hotspots and contingency planning for remote delivery.
Results-based payments, post-intervention monitoring, and linking support to measurable income improvements.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict sensitivity must be integrated from design through delivery, with continuous context monitoring
Local ownership is critical; external partners must work through trusted local intermediaries
Flexible funding mechanisms are essential to adapt to rapidly changing security and political conditions
Safeguarding requires explicit attention to indigenous populations and marginalized groups who are disproportionately affected by conflict and climate change
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from FCDO's £91.6m Private Sector Development (PSD) programme (ELAN and ESSOR, 2012-2022), including: 1) The need for a stronger climate resilience focus; 2) The importance of integrating policy, private sector, and financial support; 3) The effectiveness of technical assistance paired with financial incentives; and 4) The challenges of government-led extension services in DRC.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Explicit focus on climate-smart agriculture (unlike PSD, which had a broader private sector mandate)
Deeper integration of policy (Component 1) with private sector support (Components 2 and 3)
Targeted technical assistance to financial institutions to overcome the 0.9% GDP lending rate to SMEs
Embedded MEL system to address PSD's limitations in tracking long-term impact
Stronger safeguarding and conflict sensitivity measures based on DRC's FCAS context
risks_lessons.quote: The GG programme incorporates evidence from BEK’s £91.6 million Private Sector Development (PSD) programme consisting of ELAN and ESSOR (2012-2022)... There will be a more explicit focus on improved climate resilience, productivity, and/or mitigation as recommended in an analysis of the ELAN component of the PSD. (D0006253.odt, Annex A)... The programme will take a robust approach to conflict sensitivity, reinforcing the principle of ‘do no harm’... Such analysis is necessary for identifying how programme design will impact on different groups. (D0006253.odt, Conflict, fragility and stability)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to mobilize private finance (ICF KPI 12) through incentives to lenders and investors, though specific leverage targets are not quantified in the document.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes capital departmental expenditure limits (CDEL) to attract additional private finance, particularly in Component 3 (financial access).
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: £38m... This programme will support the development of a climate-smart agricultural sector in DRC... 80% [of programme spend] will be counted as ICF. (D0006253.odt, Programme summary and ICF Alignment)... provide start-up capital (capital departmental expenditure limits (CDEL)) to attract additional private finance. (D0006253.odt, Component 3 description)

metadata.programme_name: UK Contribution to the Reserve Account of the IMF’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)

quote.text: The RST is a lending instrument that provides affordable, long-term finance to vulnerable countries. Loans disbursed via the RST will have a maturity of 20 years with a grace period of 10.5 years.

duration_source.text:
Start Date: April 2023
End Date: March 2025

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is a financial contribution to the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST), which provides long-term concessional lending to vulnerable countries to address macroeconomically critical challenges like climate change, energy resilience, and pandemic preparedness. The UK's contribution unlocks significant SDR lending capacity (£2.3bn) for development objectives.

q1_source.text: The IMF’s RST is a new lending facility to support low and middle-income countries foster resilience to macroeconomically-critical challenges including climate change, energy resilience, and pandemic preparedness, through long-term concessional lending.

q3_expected_outputs.output: £2.3bn of SDR lending unlocked for vulnerable countries
Strengthened public financial management related to climate change/pandemics in borrowing countries
Countries with RST programmes more resilient to climate variability and pandemic risk
Reduced economic and human loss during crises (climate/pandemic)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to bolster the IMF's RST by contributing up to £50m to its Reserve Account, enabling the UK to on-lend £2.3bn in SDRs to vulnerable countries. This supports long-term macroeconomic resilience through policy reforms addressing climate change and pandemic preparedness.

quote.text: A contribution of up to £50m to the Reserve Account of the RST will enable the UK to on-lend 1.8bn (£2bn) of our SDRs; every pound of ODA into the Reserve Account unlocks the equivalent to £40 of UK lending in support of our development objectives.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The IMF is assessed as a low-risk partner with strong central systems and processes. The overall programme risk rating is 'Minor'.

q5_source.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is a low-risk partner for FCDO. It has strong central systems and processes, with extensive oversight mechanisms and carries no unacceptable fiduciary or reputational risks.

q6_contextual_constraints: limited fiscal space in vulnerable countries
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Developing countries face compounding crises (food/fuel price shocks, climate disasters, pandemic recovery) that limit fiscal space for long-term resilience investments. The RST aims to address these constraints by providing affordable long-term finance.

quote.text: Developing and emerging economies have emerged from the Covid pandemic with significant and permanent economic losses, reversing decades of development gains. In addition, the world is now facing overlapping fiscal, terms of trade and financial crises, that are compounding the challenges facing developing countries.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The IMF Executive Board (where the UK has a single seat with 4.03% voting power) approves all RST programmes and investment strategies. The UK influences decisions but does not unilaterally control them.
q10_capacity_building_details: policy reform support (e.g., climate budget tagging, fiscal risk management)
technical assistance through IMF staff collaboration with national authorities
institutional strengthening via macroeconomic policy dialogue

partner_organizations.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
partner_organizations.role: Trustee and administrator of the RST; designs and implements lending programmes

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Collaborates with IMF on RST programme design (e.g., climate/pandemic reforms)

partner_organizations.name: UK HM Treasury (HMT)
partner_organizations.role: Manages UK's SDR holdings and loan contributions to RST

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Administers the £50m grant contribution to the RST Reserve Account

quote.text: The IMF is the legal trustee of the RST, and thus is responsible for conducting its operations. The IMF has a proven track record of lending operations.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme combines: (1) a **grant** (up to £50m to the RST Reserve Account) to manage credit risk, and (2) **SDR loans** (£2.3bn on-lent to the RST Loan Account) from the UK's foreign exchange reserves. The grant is ODA-eligible; the loans are not.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The IMF administers the RST as a trustee, with oversight by its Executive Board (where the UK has a seat). The UK's contribution is governed by agreements between HMT/FCDO and the IMF. IMF staff design programmes with borrowing countries, supported by the World Bank and other partners.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (IMF is the sole multilateral trustee for the RST)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The IMF was selected due to its mandate, expertise in macroeconomic lending, and existing infrastructure for concessional finance (e.g., PRGT). The RST was established by IMF membership, including the UK, during the UK's G7 Presidency in 2021.

quote.text: The IMF is the legal trustee of the RST, and thus is responsible for conducting its operations. The UK has a strong historical record of contributing to IMF Trusts.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The IMF Executive Board oversees the RST, with the UK represented by a single seat (4.03% voting power). The Board approves all lending programmes, investment strategies, and financial reports. The UK influences decisions through its Board representation and bilateral engagement with IMF management.

quote.text: The IMF Executive Board is regularly updated on financial operations, including on the IMF investment strategy, income position, and through reviews of its concessional lending facilities. Papers for these Board discussions are circulated to HMT and FCDO officials via the UK’s Delegation to the IMF.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The £50m grant is a one-off contribution to the RST Reserve Account, which is invested in liquid assets per IMF rules. Funds cannot be reallocated; they serve as a credit buffer for the RST's lending operations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The RST's policy focus (e.g., climate vs. pandemic preparedness) is set by the IMF Executive Board. While individual country programmes are tailored, the UK cannot unilaterally adjust the Trust's strategic priorities. The IMF may expand the RST's scope over time (e.g., to include more pandemic-related reforms) with Board approval.

quote.text: The RST’s mandate focuses on climate resilience and pandemic preparedness, but the IMF may develop programmes to bolster pandemic preparedness in the future, alongside climate-focused reforms.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IMF (as trustee and implementer). The IMF directly disburses loans to borrowing countries; no additional sub-grantees are involved.

quote.text: The payment will be one payment to the IMF’s RST Reserve Account alongside or promptly after the overall contribution agreement is made effective.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Bilateral programmes in FCDO countries: providing £50m in concessional lending directly to countries for climate/pandemic reforms.
Multilateral action: UK contribution to the RST Reserve Account (preferred option).
Counterfactual (do nothing): RST continues without UK support.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option B (RST contribution) was selected for its **leverage** (1:40 ratio of SDR lending unlocked per £1 grant), **scale** (£2.3bn lending vs. £50m bilateral), **expertise** (IMF's macroeconomic policy dialogue with countries), and **alignment** with UK G7 commitments. The multilateral approach also spreads risk and catalyses additional donor contributions.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (IMF's expertise in macroeconomic lending)
speed (RST already operational with 4 pilot programmes)
strategic alignment (delivers on UK G7 2021 Presidency pledges)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Credit Risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IMF requires RST borrowers to have an Upper Credit Tranche (UCT) programme in place, ensuring commitment to sound governance and economic reform. Debt sustainability analyses are conducted for all RST applicants.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Investment Strategy Risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IMF Executive Board scrutinises the RST’s investment strategy, ensuring Reserve Account funds are invested in liquid, high-quality assets. UK officials monitor compliance via the Board.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Governance Risk (misuse of funds by borrowing countries)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: RST programmes require UCT-quality IMF programmes with governance/anti-corruption conditionality. Disbursements are tranched and subject to Board review.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (low management costs via IMF systems)

quote.text: Option B is assessed as being higher impact and lower cost than the other options considered for contributing to the macroeconomic sustainability, climate resilience, and pandemic resilience of developing countries.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope** and **multilateral nature** of the RST constrain partner selection to the IMF, as it is the sole trustee with the mandate and infrastructure to administer SDR-based lending facilities. The need for **credit safeguards** (e.g., Reserve Account buffers) further limits alternatives to institutions with the IMF's risk management capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Only the IMF can legally administer SDR-based trusts (per its Articles of Agreement).
The RST’s financial architecture requires simultaneous contributions to Loan, Deposit, and Reserve Accounts, which only the IMF can manage.
Vulnerable countries’ limited fiscal space necessitates concessional lending at scale, which bilateral programmes cannot match.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **financing mechanism objective** (unlocking £2.3bn in SDR lending) determines the **multilateral delivery structure**, as only the IMF can on-lend SDRs. The **policy reform focus** (climate/pandemic resilience) shapes the IMF’s programme design role, requiring its macroeconomic expertise and collaboration with the World Bank.
q28_linkages: Financing goal (SDR on-lending) → Multilateral partner (IMF as SDR administrator).
Policy reform focus (macroeconomic conditionality) → IMF’s role in programme design and monitoring.
Global reach objective → IMF’s membership and existing relationships with 190+ countries.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between **efficiency** (leveraging IMF systems for rapid, large-scale lending) and **equity** (ensuring funds reach the most vulnerable). The RST’s tiered interest rates and eligibility criteria (prioritising LICs and vulnerable MICs) address equity, while the 1:40 leverage ratio ensures efficiency. The UK accepts **indirect control** (via IMF Board oversight) as a trade-off for scale and risk mitigation.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: The RST’s existing infrastructure enables rapid disbursement (4 programmes approved in first 4 months), but limits the UK’s ability to tailor programmes to specific bilateral priorities.

IMF’s macroeconomic expertise ensures high-quality reforms, but Southern partners (borrowing countries) have limited influence over Trust-wide policies, which are set by the IMF Board (where Northern countries hold majority voting power).
The £50m grant unlocks £2.3bn in lending (high leverage), but the UK has no direct control over how funds are used at the country level—decisions are made by the IMF and borrowing governments.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **low-risk profile** of the IMF as a partner enables **light-touch day-to-day management** by FCDO/HMT, with oversight focused on strategic Board-level engagement rather than operational micromanagement. The ‘Minor’ programme risk rating justifies this approach.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The IMF’s **existing capacity** in macroeconomic lending and risk management shapes its role as the sole implementer, while the UK’s **limited in-house capacity** for bilateral macro-critical reforms (noted in Option A’s disadvantages) reinforces the rationale for multilateral delivery.

quote.text: The disadvantage of [Option A: bilateral programmes] is increased delivery risk due to a lack of comparable experience in the sectors of macro-critical climate change and pandemic-based reform, and FCDO staff time involved in management and coordination imposing significant administrative and cost burdens.

key_programme_risks.risk: Credit Risk
key_programme_risks.description: RST loans perform badly, leading to significant arrears/defaults. The Reserve Account (including UK’s £50m) would absorb losses, depleting the buffer.

key_programme_risks.risk: Investment Strategy Risk
key_programme_risks.description: IMF’s investment of Reserve Account funds in poor-performing assets generates sustained losses, reducing the Trust’s financial safeguards.

key_programme_risks.risk: Governance Risk
key_programme_risks.description: Borrowing countries misuse RST funds or fail to implement reforms, diminishing programme efficacy.

key_programme_risks.risk: Political Risk
key_programme_risks.description: RST programmes are approved for countries under UK sanctions, creating reputational or legal conflicts.

key_programme_risks.risk: Exchange Rate Risk
key_programme_risks.description: GBP depreciation against the SDR before the £50m payment is made, increasing the cost to the UK (mitigated by securing approval for up to £50m).

key_programme_risks.risk: Demand-Supply Mismatch
key_programme_risks.description: High demand for RST financing (SDR22bn) outstrips pledged resources (SDR15bn), limiting the number of countries that can benefit.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IMF requires RST borrowers to have an Upper Credit Tranche (UCT) programme in place, ensuring commitment to sound governance. Debt sustainability analyses are mandatory for eligibility.
IMF Executive Board scrutinises the RST’s investment strategy quarterly. Assets are limited to high-quality, liquid instruments (e.g., BIS deposits, government debt with BBB+ ratings).
RST programmes are disbursed in tranches, conditional on reform implementation. The IMF Board can halt disbursements if programmes go off-track.
UK officials will vote on RST programmes at the IMF Board in line with UK sanctions regimes. The IMF’s majority-voting system aligns with UK allies.
FCDO secured approval for up to £50m to cover potential GBP depreciation against the SDR before payment.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The business case cites the UK’s **positive experience** with previous IMF Trusts (e.g., Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust) as evidence of the IMF’s strong safeguards and efficient administration. The IMF’s **Central Assurance Assessment (2022)** confirmed it as a ‘low-risk partner’ with robust systems.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The RST’s design incorporates lessons from earlier IMF facilities, including: (1) **tiered interest rates** to differentiate concessionality by country income level; (2) **policy conditionality** tied to disbursements to ensure reform implementation; and (3) **a Reserve Account** to absorb credit losses (a feature strengthened based on past Trust experiences).

quote.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is a low-risk partner for FCDO. It has strong central systems and processes, with extensive oversight mechanisms and carries no unacceptable fiduciary or reputational risks. It implements its lending operations and capacity development activities in-house and has strong internal administrative and programme management capacity.

leverage_achieved.description: The UK’s £50m grant to the Reserve Account unlocks £2.3bn in SDR lending to vulnerable countries (a 1:40 leverage ratio). The total UK contribution to the RST is SDR2.5bn (£2.8bn), composed of:

components.description: SDR loans on-lent to borrowing countries.
Generates investment income for the RST.
Grant contribution to absorb credit losses and preserve SDR reserve asset status.

capital_vs_revenue_split.description: The £50m grant is a **capital contribution** to the RST’s Reserve Account (classified as ODA-eligible with a 100% grant coefficient). The SDR loans (£2.3bn) are **non-ODA** and do not count against the UK’s aid budget.

quote.text: The OECD DAC confirmed in December 2022 that the IMF RST is ODA-eligible with a 100% ODA coefficient on grant contributions. The DAC also confirmed that SDR loans do not generate any ODA, so just the grant part is ODA.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) as the primary instrument, combining core budget support (unrestricted transfers to SHG's consolidated fund) with ring-fenced allocations for specific priorities. Payments are made in tranches based on agreed schedules and evidence of need.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO and SHG operate as equal partners under a jointly agreed MoU, with regular monitoring through financial aid missions and monthly meetings. SHG maintains operational control while FCDO provides oversight and technical support. The structure includes embedded technical cooperation posts within SHG.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: St Helena Government is the sole legitimate governing body for the territory, and the UK has a legal obligation under Article 73 of the UN Charter to provide financial assistance to its Overseas Territories. The direct award reflects this constitutional relationship.

quote.instrument: "a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between FCDO and the SHG will be used to structure the aid disbursements... The Financial Aid process will be implemented in accordance with the FCDO’s Programme Operating Framework." (D0005573.odt, Summary of Disbursement Process)
quote.structure: "FCDO provides funding to SHG, which decides on allocations through its own democratic and legislative processes... This approach has lower transaction costs than a project-based approach and gives SHG greater ownership." (D0005573.odt, Option 3: Budget Support)
quote.selection: "The UK has a responsibility under Article 73 of the UN Charter to meet the reasonable assistance needs of those living in the Overseas Territories (OTs) where financial self-sufficiency is not yet possible." (D0005573.odt, Overview)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The governance structure includes: 1) Regular financial monitoring meetings between FCDO and SHG; 2) Annual Financial Aid Missions for in-depth reviews; 3) Joint agreement on reforms and priorities documented in the MoU; 4) Technical advisory support through embedded posts. The St Helena Programme Manager (FCDO) acts as Programme Responsible Owner with oversight from the Senior Responsible Owner.

quote.day_to_day: "The St Helena Programme Manager will be Programme Responsible Owner (PRO) for the implementation of the programme... Coordinates team on budget support programme design, implementation, monitoring, risk management and budget management." (D0005573.odt, Roles and Responsibilities)

quote.oversight: "The FCDO will scrutinise monthly and quarterly budgets to ensure good public financial management (PFM) and strengthen the value for money of SHG’s spending decisions." (D0005573.odt, Option 3: Budget Support)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, following the process outlined in Paragraph 38a of the MoU amendment. Reallocation requires written agreement and must align with the programme's strategic objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Priorities can be adjusted through the annual Financial Aid Mission process and quarterly strategy meetings. Changes require joint agreement between FCDO and SHG and are documented in updated MoUs. The programme includes a reforms and priorities workstream that is regularly reviewed.

quote.reallocation: "The Government should only submit payment claims to the FCDO for expenditure it has incurred... Where the Government believes an exception to this approach is required... this should be highlighted and agreed in writing with the FCDO." (D0005364.odt, Paragraph 38a)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: St Helena's small island context and limited local capacity constrain partner selection to primarily involve SHG as the sole implementing partner, with technical support provided through embedded international experts. small population base (4,500 inhabitants)
geographic isolation
lack of competitive local service providers
high dependence on international technical expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's dual objectives of meeting immediate service needs while supporting sustainable development determine the mixed delivery structure. Core budget support addresses essential services while ring-fenced funds target specific development priorities like tourism. The need for both flexibility (to respond to changing needs) and accountability (for UK taxpayer funds) shapes the governance arrangements with regular monitoring and joint decision-making.
q28_linkages: Core budget support → meets essential service needs (health, education, social services)
Ring-fenced tourism fund → supports sustainable economic development
Embedded technical cooperation → builds capacity while ensuring service delivery
Regular financial missions → balance flexibility with accountability
Outcome framework → aligns short-term spending with long-term development goals
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity considerations (supporting vulnerable populations, gender equality, disability inclusion) with efficiency needs (cost control, value for money). This is evident in the ring-fenced allocations for social services and tourism development, as well as the monitoring of disaggregated data by gender, ethnicity, and disability.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: inclusive service delivery (equity) vs. cost containment (efficiency)
local ownership (equity) vs. international technical standards (efficiency)
comprehensive needs coverage (equity) vs. focused impact measurement (efficiency)
long-term capacity building (equity) vs. short-term service delivery (efficiency)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile results in intensive oversight through monthly financial meetings, quarterly strategy reviews, and annual financial aid missions. This management intensity is designed to mitigate risks associated with SHG's limited capacity and the programme's significant budget while maintaining flexibility for adaptive management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles through embedded technical cooperation posts that both deliver immediate services and transfer skills to local staff. The gradual approach to building SHG's capacity influences the programme's phased increase in local decision-making authority and the focus on succession planning.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: RAIN combines capacity building (strengthening government systems for climate resilience), policy influence (supporting Nepal’s National Adaptation Plan and climate finance access), implementation research (testing early warning systems and anticipatory action), and service delivery (community-level resilience interventions). (D0005656.odt, Programme summary)

quote.objective: "By supporting effective investments in climate adaptation and mitigation, resilience, disaster risk management and adaptive and shock-responsive social protection, RAIN will prevent humanitarian need. (D0005656.odt, Strategic Fit and Rationale)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal ranks 10th globally for climate vulnerability (2000–2019) and faces cascading hazards (e.g., earthquakes triggering landslides/floods), weak institutional capacity post-federalization, and political instability. The programme’s risk rating is classified as ‘Major’ by FCDO.
where_context.q5_source: "Nepal is one of the countries most affected by climate change, ranking number 10 over the period 2000-2019 in terms of vulnerability." (D0005656.odt, CONTEXT) && "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0005656.odt, Programme summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Federalization has led to unclear roles across government tiers, limited fiscal/human resources at local levels, and fragmented social protection systems. Climate hazards (e.g., GLOFs, earthquakes) exacerbate vulnerability, while donor projects often overwhelm local governments. Lack of integrated data systems hampers disaster response and social protection delivery.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grants (for technical assistance and community interventions), an Internal Risk Facility (£3.5m for large-scale shocks), and catalytic co-financing to leverage additional climate funds. The climate finance component includes support for accessing multilateral funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: RAIN will operate through multiple implementing partners (international, national, local) collaborating under a shared outcomes framework. A Strategic Learning Unit will coordinate across components, and a GESI Advisory Group will oversee inclusion. BEK retains oversight but emphasizes local ownership.

quote.funding: "RAIN will include... (ii) unlock additional climate finance and (iii) support early action and adaptation efforts at community level (iv) make social protection systems more adaptive and shock-responsive." (D0005656.odt, Programme summary) && "BEK is transitioning away from providing support to small and medium-scale disasters. This IRF could be activated to enable BEK to help respond to a large scale (for Nepal) shock if the GoN requests assistance." (D0005656.odt, Programme focus and components)
quote.structure: "The programme will offer the following interlinked components. It is important to note that RAIN envisages a combination of implementing partners who will be expected to collaborate, share learning and work towards shared outcomes." (D0005656.odt, Programme focus and components)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A GESI Advisory Group (comprising activists and academics) will advise on inclusion, while a Strategic Learning Unit will coordinate across components. BEK’s risk advisory group oversees programme risks, and partnerships with GoN are formalized via Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs).

quote.governance: "Establish a GESI Advisory Group, made up of prominent GESI activists, thought leaders and academics to advise on RAIN objectives and act as a challenge function." (D0005656.odt, Textbox 1) && "A BEK risk advisory group has been established to continually support BEK in adopting best practice from the Centre and improve how risk management is observed and discussed across BEK." (D0005656.odt, Risk)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with BEK approval, particularly for climate finance mobilization and early action. The Internal Risk Facility (£3.5m) allows rapid response to large-scale shocks if requested by GoN.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes strategic learning and continuous review of the Theory of Change. Components will adapt based on evidence (e.g., shifting from projectized LAPAs to mainstreaming climate resilience in local plans).

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (consortium of international/national/local orgs) → Communities. No explicit sub-grantee layer mentioned.

q24_alternatives_considered: Projectized Local Adaptation Plans of Action (LAPAs) (rejected for lack of sustainability)
Standalone social protection or climate finance programmes (rejected for fragmentation risk)
Short-term humanitarian response (rejected; RAIN focuses on long-term resilience)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed modality (technical assistance + finance + community action) was selected to: (1) address systemic gaps in Nepal’s climate governance (e.g., weak inter-governmental coordination); (2) leverage FCDO’s comparative advantage in policy influence and inclusion; (3) build on 13 years of UK-Nepal climate collaboration; and (4) align with Nepal’s GRID framework for integrated development. The open partnership structure enables localization while retaining FCDO oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overwhelming local governments with multiple donor requirements
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Co-creation with GoN, embedded technical assistance, and capacity-building for local ownership. Strategic Learning Unit to harmonize donor efforts.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation between climate finance, DRM, and social protection components
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Interlinked components with shared outcomes, GESI Advisory Group, and cross-component learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in accessing international climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Dedicated support to GoN for application processes and alternative financing mechanisms.

quote.alternatives: "While the LAPA projects have benefited vulnerable communities, the approach was found to be too projectized and lacking sustainability once funding ended." (D0005656.odt, UK Response to Date)
quote.rationale: "RAIN will build on and protect the gains of 13 years of UK support to Nepal on climate change adaptation and mitigation, disaster resilience, and humanitarian preparedness and response." (D0005656.odt, Strategic Fit and Rationale) && "The programme will maximise central investments and make strong connections to UK Centres of Expertise in climate change, disaster risk management and social protection." (D0005656.odt, Strategic Fit and Rationale)
quote.risks: "Donor implemented projects (which often introduced different types of plans and tools to address the same challenges) often overwhelm local governments who lack the resources to coordinate and monitor these activities." (D0005656.odt, Current challenges)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s federalization process and weak local capacity constrain partner selection to organizations with: (1) experience navigating decentralized governance; (2) ability to work across all three tiers of government; and (3) existing trust relationships with local communities. The high climate risk profile also necessitates partners with disaster response expertise.
q27_constraints_detail: Uneven progress in decentralization limits partner options to those who can bridge federal/provincial/local gaps
Frequent staff turnover in government requires partners with embedded capacity-building expertise
Cascading hazards (e.g., earthquakes → landslides) demand partners with multi-hazard DRM experience
Social exclusion (e.g., Dalits, persons with disabilities) requires partners with strong GESI track records
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **systems strengthening** (not just project delivery) shapes the open partnership structure, while the focus on **inclusion** drives the GESI Advisory Group and local CSO engagement. The **climate finance mobilization** objective necessitates links to multilateral actors (e.g., Green Climate Fund, World Bank).
q28_linkages: Systems strengthening objective → Open partnership with multiple tiers of government and local actors
Inclusion focus → GESI Advisory Group and direct funding to CSOs/Women’s Rights Organizations
Climate finance goals → Collaboration with MDBs (e.g., ADB, World Bank) and technical support for GCF access
Early action emphasis → Continued support to Start Fund Nepal (transitioning by 2026)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid climate finance mobilization risks bypassing marginalized groups, mitigated by GESI targeting; (2) **Local ownership vs. technical expertise**: Embedded TA balances GoN leadership with FCDO-backed capacity; (3) **Scaling vs. tailoring**: Standardized early warning systems must adapt to diverse hazards (e.g., floods in Terai vs. GLOFs in mountains).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Prioritizing Dalits/women with disabilities may slow rollout but aligns with ‘leave no one behind’ principles
Local CSO partnerships increase transaction costs but improve relevance and trust
Multi-hazard approaches (vs. single-hazard) require more complex coordination but address cascading risks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight (e.g., BEK risk advisory group, continuous ToC reviews) and adaptive management (e.g., flexible reallocation between components). Political instability and climate hazards necessitate embedded learning systems.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Weak local government capacity shifts partners into **co-implementation** roles (not just advisory), with technical assistance embedded in ministries. CSOs are prioritized for their community reach, while MDBs are engaged for financing leverage.

quote.constraints: "Local governments also have insufficient fiscal and human resources skills and capacities. New and restructured staff face new systems and procedures that are not fully established and internalized yet." (D0005656.odt, Current challenges) && "The programme will focus on BEK’s three priority provinces: Madesh, Karnali and Lumbini... Each province has a different starting point and specific challenges." (D0005656.odt, Geographical targeting)
quote.tradeoffs: "The focus on early action will help to build the resilience and adaptive capacity of social excluded communities to natural hazards at the provincial and local level... tailored early warning and evacuation messages that considers gender, disability and SEAH." (D0005656.odt, Textbox 1) && "A mix of strategies will be used by partners (including taking into sectoral vulnerability and poverty)." (D0005656.odt, Geographical targeting)
quote.capacity: "Having embedded staff within the government systems, experts stationed outside the ministries to provide technical advice or a mix of both is required to deliver activities on behalf, together with or in some cases for the government, given the lack of technical capabilities." (D0005656.odt, UK Response to Date)

key_programme_risks: Weak inter-governmental coordination undermining climate adaptation planning
Limited fiscal space at local levels restricting resilience investments
Exclusion of marginalized groups (e.g., Dalits, persons with disabilities) from interventions
Delays in accessing international climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund)
Cascading hazards (e.g., earthquake → landslide → flood) overwhelming response systems
Staff turnover in government disrupting capacity-building efforts
Donor fragmentation leading to duplicated or conflicting priorities
Negative coping strategies (e.g., high-interest loans, child labor) during shocks

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Technical assistance to all three tiers of government; Strategic Learning Unit to harmonize efforts; GESI Advisory Group to ensure inclusion.
Support for mainstreaming climate adaptation into local budgets; catalytic co-financing to leverage additional funds.
Targeted interventions for women, Dalits, and persons with disabilities; GESI analysis and Advisory Group; disaggregated data collection.
Dedicated support to GoN for GCF applications; exploration of alternative financing mechanisms (e.g., ADB, World Bank).
Multi-hazard early warning systems (linked to REAP/EWS4ALL); adaptive social protection for rapid response.
Embedded technical assistance; patient, long-term capacity-building approach.
Co-creation with GoN; Strategic Learning Unit to align donor activities.
Shock-responsive social protection; early action to reduce asset loss; SEAH safeguarding measures.

fcas_specific_lessons: Federalization requires **patience and trust-building**—local governments need time to absorb new roles/responsibilities.
**Embedded TA** is critical in FCAS contexts where institutional capacity is nascent.
**Local CSOs** are essential for reaching excluded groups but require capacity support to avoid overburdening.
**Flexible financing** (e.g., Internal Risk Facility) is needed to respond to unpredictable shocks.
**GESI mainstreaming** must be explicit in FCAS to counter structural exclusions (e.g., caste, disability).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past programmes (e.g., LAPAs, Post-Earthquake Reconstruction) showed that: (1) **Projectized approaches** lack sustainability; (2) **Local ownership** requires co-creation, even if slower; (3) **Inclusion** must be proactive (e.g., targeting Dalits in reconstruction); (4) **Multi-year programming** is needed for resilience; (5) **Synergies between programmes** (e.g., CSD and SDR) must be intentionally designed.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Shift from projectized LAPAs to **mainstreaming climate resilience in local development plans**.
Explicit **GESI targeting** (vs. ad-hoc inclusion) with Advisory Group oversight.
**Adaptive management** framework to refine ToC annually based on evidence.
Longer-term **patient development** approach (6-year duration) to allow systemic change.
Integration of **Start Fund Nepal** for phased humanitarian-to-resilience transition.

quote.risks: "Roles and responsibilities are not fully and clearly delineated across three levels of governments in the disaster risk management space." (D0005656.odt, Current challenges) && "The poor and most marginalized groups who lack the resources to adapt are often disproportionately affected and more likely to resort to negative coping strategies." (D0005656.odt, CONTEXT)
quote.lessons: "It is critical to work with all three tiers of government and local partners to ensure local ownership, coherence and sustainability. Co-creation with the government takes longer but is essential to maximise government ownership." (D0005656.odt, UK Response to Date) && "While the LAPA projects have benefited vulnerable communities, the approach was found to be too projectized and lacking sustainability once funding ended." (D0005656.odt, UK Response to Date)
quote.design_changes: "In the final phase of this support and going forward under RAIN, we will shift to a mainstreaming approach focusing on making local annual and multi-year development plans climate (and disaster) resilient." (D0005656.odt, UK Response to Date)

co_funding_partners.partner: Multilateral Development Banks (e.g., World Bank, ADB)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: RAIN aims to unlock additional climate finance to address Nepal’s $47.4 billion adaptation gap (2020–2050), with £3.5m Internal Risk Facility for large-scale shocks. Links to CARA programme (FCDO-funded) and GRID framework (World Bank/UK) for co-financing.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £38.5m (including £3.5m unfunded Internal Risk Facility)." (D0005656.odt, Programme summary)
quote.leverage: "The NAP has assessed the need for $47.4 billion in adaptation investment until 2050... RAIN will support the GoN to access this funding." (D0005656.odt, Current challenges) && "RAIN will collaborate with and complement the regional Climate Action for a Resilient Asia (CARA) programme." (D0005656.odt, Strategic Fit and Rationale)

metadata.programme_name: UK Humanitarian Support in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (FY2022-2026)
metadata.duration_text: Start Date: 04 July 2023, End Date: 31 March 2025
metadata.quote: "The aim of the ‘UK Humanitarian Support in the OPTs’ programme is to improve the resilience of households in the OPTs to mitigate the consequences of the protracted protection crisis; save lives during rapid onset emergencies; and prevent a further deterioration in the humanitarian situation until a more durable political solution is reached." (D0005034.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: 04 July 2023, End Date: 31 March 2025" (D0005034.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides direct humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPTs), focusing on food security, health, shelter, WASH, and protection. It aims to save lives during emergencies and improve household resilience in a protracted crisis context.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The aim of the ‘UK Humanitarian Support in the OPTs’ programme is to improve the resilience of households in the OPTs to mitigate the consequences of the protracted protection crisis; save lives during rapid onset emergencies; and prevent a further deterioration in the humanitarian situation until a more durable political solution is reached." (D0005034.odt, SUMMARY INFORMATION)
q3_expected_outputs: Provide food security support to 44,610 people (WFP)
Provide multi-sectoral support (protection, nutrition, WASH, MHPSS) to 77,556 people (UNICEF)
Support 17,948 people through multi-sectoral interventions via OCHA pooled fund
Improve access to essential WASH services and shelter supplies for 140,000 people (ICRC)
Provide emergency healthcare to 62,435 people (WHO)
Support basic needs (food, water, sanitation, health, protection, education) for 22,000 displaced people (UNRWA)
Deliver Core Relief Items (CRIs) to meet immediate needs of civilians in Gaza
Support humanitarian access and coordination through OCHA and UNOPS
Provide child-sensitive cash assistance to vulnerable households in Gaza (UNICEF)
Capacity building for Egyptian Red Crescent Society (ERCS) in cargo handling and management
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers life-saving humanitarian assistance across multiple sectors (food, health, shelter, WASH, protection) through trusted multilateral partners, with a focus on vulnerable groups including women, children, and displaced populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
what_objectives.quote: "The UK’s humanitarian response for Gaza will concentrate on food security, health and nutrition, shelter and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), alongside cross-cutting issues of access and protection and working through cash-based interventions where possible." (D0005034.odt, Sectors)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in an active conflict zone with severe movement restrictions, airstrikes, and high risks of aid diversion. The risk profile is explicitly categorized as 'major' with significant operational challenges due to ongoing hostilities between Israel and Palestinian armed groups.
where_context.q5_source: "The business case operates in an extremely challenging, high-risk environment. Risks have increased substantially since October 7th and continue to increase. It assumes Israeli movement, airstrikes and access restrictions will continue to limit the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and that there will be spikes in need resulting from conflict. The risks to the success of the programme are major, with risks of actual or perceived diversion of humanitarian aid." (D0005034.odt, Risks and Safeguarding)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints (airstrikes, movement restrictions) limit humanitarian access and delivery of aid. Infrastructure damage (power plants, water systems) disrupts essential services. Regulatory and political economy challenges include Israeli restrictions on imports, Hamas-imposed taxes, and internal Palestinian divisions. Weak institutions and conflict exacerbate coordination difficulties and increase risks of aid diversion.
where_context.quote: "The humanitarian situation in Gaza continues to deteriorate... Israeli movement, airstrikes and access restrictions will continue to limit the delivery of humanitarian assistance... The risks to the success of the programme are major, with risks of actual or perceived diversion of humanitarian aid." (D0005034.odt, Humanitarian Situation and Risks and Safeguarding)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The BCGJ Humanitarian, Emergencies and Refugees Team manages the programme and makes funding decisions, with implementation carried out by multilateral partners (UN agencies, Red Cross/Crescent societies) and regional actors.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to UN agencies via Standby Partnerships
Support to Egyptian Red Crescent Society (ERCS) for cargo handling and management
Training and deployment of humanitarian advisory expertise
Capacity building for local NGOs through OCHA's pooled fund

who_partners.quote: "The business case will be managed by the BCG Jerusalem’s Humanitarian, Emergencies and Refugees Team. We will directly fund four multilateral partners (OCHA, UNICEF, UNRWA, and ICRC) with whom we already hold trusted relationships and broaden our multilateral partners to include World Food Programme and the British Red Cross." (D0005034.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of funding instruments: Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with multilateral partners (e.g., UN agencies), direct grants to organizations like the British Red Cross, and framework agreements for technical assistance (e.g., Standby Partnerships). Core Relief Items (CRIs) are managed through inter-departmental coordination with UK government bodies (MoD, DHSC).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The BCG Jerusalem’s Humanitarian, Emergencies and Refugees Team manages the programme, with direct funding to multilateral partners (UN agencies, Red Cross/Crescent societies) and coordination through OCHA’s pooled fund. Technical support is provided via Standby Partnerships and UK government departments (MoD, DHSC) for CRIs.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on proven capacity to deliver at scale in high-risk environments, existing trusted relationships with FCDO, and alignment with UK humanitarian priorities. The urgent nature of the crisis and need for rapid response justified direct awards to pre-vetted partners.
how_mechanism.quote: "The approach is informed by the Humanitarian Response Strategy which has been developed jointly by BCG Jerusalem and the Humanitarian Response Group. Humanitarian aid will continue to be provided on the basis of need. Our delivery partners all have strong mechanisms to provide assurances that aid is reaching the most vulnerable and to minimise risks of aid diversion." (D0005034.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Funding allocations to sub-partners (e.g., through OCHA’s pooled fund) are managed jointly by OCHA’s Advisory Board and the Humanitarian Coordinator, with FCDO input via its Observer Member status on the Board.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: OCHA’s Humanitarian Fund (HF) is governed by an Advisory Board (AB) that advises the Humanitarian Coordinator (HC) on fund allocations. The AB includes donor representatives (FCDO is an Observer Member) and meets at least four times a year. Final decision-making authority rests with the HC.
how_governance.quote: "The Humanitarian Coordinator (HC) agrees the strategy for the use of the Fund and ensures it delivers on its key objectives and is managed in accordance with the Global Guidelines. The HC is supported by an Advisory Board (AB), which advises the HC on the allocation of funds, and by the OCHA Head of Office (HoO) and OCHA Humanitarian Financing Unit (HFU)." (D0005032.odt, Delivery mechanism)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme retains significant unallocated funds (e.g., £7.5m in D0005033.odt) for flexible reallocation based on evolving needs. Ministers have delegated authority to senior officials for rapid reallocation decisions, and the business case explicitly emphasizes embedding ‘flexibility’ in the approach.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach, with regular reviews to adjust priorities based on the evolving context. Changes require Ministerial approval but are designed to enable rapid response to crises (e.g., reallocation of underspend in D0005033.odt).
how_flexibility.quote: "The Foreign Secretary asked for FCDO to ensure that ‘flexibility’ was embedded in our approach... We will retain at least £20m for added flexibility and ensure a strong pace to our humanitarian response." (D0005031.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral partners (e.g., OCHA, UNICEF) → Local NGOs (via pooled funds). For CRIs: FCDO → UK government departments (MoD/DHSC) → UNRWA/ERCS.
how_efficiency.quote: "The business case will be managed by the BCG Jerusalem’s Humanitarian, Emergencies and Refugees Team. We will directly fund four multilateral partners (UNRWA, OCHA, UNICEF, UNOPS) with whom we already hold trusted relationships." (D0005031.odt, What is the approach to implementation?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (rejected due to high reputational and operational risks)
Multi-year support to OCHA’s Humanitarian Fund only (rejected in favor of a diversified portfolio)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The multilateral, flexible funding mechanism was chosen to enable rapid response in a high-risk, volatile environment. It leverages trusted partnerships with UN agencies and Red Cross/Crescent societies, which have proven capacity to deliver at scale despite access constraints. The approach balances efficiency (via pooled funds) with the need for direct oversight in a context of high aid diversion risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion due to complex operating environment and multiple layers of sub-partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust due diligence, deliverychain mapping, and third-party monitoring. Partners are required to implement beneficiary verification and post-distribution monitoring.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Access restrictions limiting delivery of CRIs and medical supplies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pre-positioning of supplies in Cyprus and coordination with Egyptian Red Crescent. Contingency planning for alternative routes (e.g., Jordanian land corridor).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overstretched partner capacity (e.g., ERCS, UNRWA) affecting efficiency
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted capacity-building support (e.g., funding for ERCS cargo handling) and deployment of technical advisors via Standby Partnerships.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from perceived or actual association with controversial actors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strict adherence to UK sanctions lists, vetting of partners against UN Security Council resolutions, and transparent reporting on fund flows.

why_rationale.quote: "The business case addendum is a direct response to the humanitarian needs following the escalation in conflict between Israel and Gaza... The objectives of the business case addendum are: To increase the value of the business case by up to £30 million... To provide additional funding to (existing and new) partners to address the most urgent humanitarian needs." (D0005031.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk, conflict-affected context limits partner selection to organizations with proven capacity to operate under severe access restrictions and complex political dynamics. Local NGOs are primarily engaged through OCHA’s pooled fund due to their vulnerability to Israeli designation as ‘terror organizations’ and operational constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: Israeli restrictions on movement and imports (e.g., dual-use items)
Hamas-imposed taxes and audits on INGOs in Gaza
Risk of partner designation as ‘terror organizations’ by Israeli authorities
Limited operational space for local NGOs due to Israeli and Hamas restrictions
High security risks for international staff deployment
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid, large-scale delivery of life-saving assistance (food, health, shelter) determines the multilateral structure, as UN agencies and Red Cross/Crescent societies are best placed to operate at scale in Gaza. The focus on cash-based interventions and CRIs shapes the use of pooled funds (OCHA) and direct procurement (MoD/DHSC).
q28_linkages: Multilateral partners (UNICEF, WFP) selected for their sectoral expertise (health, food security) and ability to deliver at scale in Gaza
Pooled funds (OCHA HF) used to diversify partnerships and reach local NGOs, aligning with the goal of inclusive response
Direct procurement of CRIs via UK government departments (MoD/DHSC) linked to the need for rapid, high-volume deliveries
Technical assistance (Standby Partnerships) supports coordination and capacity building, addressing cross-cutting access and protection challenges
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (via multilateral partners and pooled funds) with equity considerations, such as targeting women-headed households, persons with disabilities, and marginalized communities. However, the reliance on large UN agencies and Red Cross/Crescent societies—while efficient—limits direct funding to local actors, creating a tension with localization goals.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Use of multilateral partners (UNICEF, WFP) for rapid, large-scale delivery vs. Equity: Limited direct funding to local NGOs due to risk and capacity constraints
Speed: Direct awards to pre-vetted partners for quick disbursement vs. Inclusion: Reduced opportunities for new or smaller local actors to access funds
Expertise: Northern-led technical assistance (Standby Partnerships) vs. Ownership: Limited decision-making power for Southern partners in programme design
Cost: Pooled funds reduce transaction costs vs. Reach: Local NGOs may face barriers in accessing pooled fund mechanisms due to Israeli restrictions
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘major’ risk profile (FCAS context) drives intensive oversight, including embedded advisors (Standby Partnerships), regular risk reviews, and direct FCDO involvement in partner selection and fund reallocation decisions. The high risk of aid diversion necessitates layered safeguards (due diligence, third-party monitoring, beneficiary verification).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles to address contextual constraints. For example, ERCS receives funding to strengthen cargo handling capacity, while UN agencies are supported via Standby Partnerships to enhance coordination and technical expertise. Local NGOs are engaged primarily through OCHA’s pooled fund, which provides indirect capacity support.
intersections.quote: "The business case operates in a challenging, high-risk environment. It assumes Israeli movement, airstrikes and access restrictions will continue to limit the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and that there will be spikes in need resulting from conflict." (D0005031.odt, Risks and Safeguarding)

key_programme_risks: Actual or perceived diversion of humanitarian aid (major risk)
Israeli movement and access restrictions limiting aid delivery
Spikes in humanitarian need due to ongoing conflict
Overstretched partner capacity (e.g., ERCS, UNRWA)
Reputational risks from association with controversial actors
Operational risks in Gaza (e.g., damage to health facilities, attacks on humanitarian workers)
Logistical challenges in delivering CRIs (e.g., border closures, Israeli permissions)
Protection risks for vulnerable groups (women, children, persons with disabilities)
Shrinkage of humanitarian space due to Israeli designation of NGOs as ‘terror organizations’
Coordination challenges among multiple actors in a complex response

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Robust due diligence, deliverychain mapping, third-party monitoring, and beneficiary verification. Partners are vetted against UK/UN/EU/US sanctions lists.
Pre-positioning of CRIs, coordination with Egyptian Red Crescent, and advocacy for humanitarian access. Exploration of alternative routes (e.g., Jordanian land corridor).
Targeted capacity-building support (e.g., ERCS cargo handling, UNOPS Access Support Unit). Deployment of technical advisors via Standby Partnerships.
Strict adherence to UK sanctions lists and transparent reporting. Regular engagement with Israeli authorities to ensure compliance with access protocols.
Gender-responsive programming, MHPSS services, and targeted support for women, children, and persons with disabilities. Safeguarding measures embedded in all partner agreements.
Use of pooled funds (OCHA HF) to channel support to local NGOs indirectly. Advocacy for respect of International Humanitarian Law (IHL).

fcas_specific_lessons: Enhanced due diligence and safeguarding measures are critical in FCAS contexts, particularly for aid diversion risks.
Flexibility in funding mechanisms (e.g., unallocated contingencies) is essential to respond to rapidly evolving crises.
Localization efforts must be balanced with risk management; pooled funds can serve as a bridge to local actors in high-risk environments.
Technical assistance and capacity building should be embedded in partner roles to address systemic constraints (e.g., access, coordination).
Direct engagement with regional actors (e.g., Jordan, Egypt) can facilitate humanitarian access where multilateral channels are constrained.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases highlighted the need for multi-year predictable funding to address chronic humanitarian needs in the OPTs. Lessons included the value of cash-based programming for dignity and efficiency, the importance of coordination to reduce fragmentation, and the necessity of integrating protection (especially MHPSS) into sectoral responses. The 2021 escalation reinforced the need for rapid, flexible mechanisms to respond to spikes in demand.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporated lessons by: (1) expanding cash-based interventions based on beneficiary preferences, (2) strengthening MHPSS components in response to rising psychosocial needs, (3) increasing flexibility in funding (e.g., £20m contingency in D0005031.odt), and (4) diversifying partners to include regional actors (e.g., Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation) with better access to Gaza.
risks_lessons.quote: "The current programme continues to operate in a complex and volatile environment. However, some of the previously identified risks in the original Business Case have materialized and new risks have been identified due to the Gaza conflict and new interventions proposed." (D0005034.odt, Risk Overview)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages multilateral partnerships (UN agencies, Red Cross/Crescent) to mobilize additional resources and coordinate with other donors. For example, UK funding to OCHA’s pooled fund is matched by contributions from Germany, Belgium, and other donors, amplifying the impact of UK aid.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily focuses on revenue expenditure (e.g., food aid, medical supplies, cash transfers) but includes capital elements such as Core Relief Items (CRIs) like tents, water filters, and armoured vehicles. CRIs are procured via UK government departments (MoD, DHSC) and pre-positioned for rapid deployment.
financial_details.quote: "The UK will provide an additional £30M to this business case, which brings the total value of the business case to £51M between July 2023 and Dec 2026... We will retain at least £20m for added flexibility and ensure a strong pace to our humanitarian response." (D0005031.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?)

metadata.programme_name: Ukraine Resilience and Energy Security (URES)
metadata.quote: "Established in 2022 with an initial funding ceiling of £80m, the Ukraine Resilience and Energy Security programme ("URES") is BE Kyiv’s sole energy-focused aid and development programme, and main vehicle of support for this critical sector." (D0006340.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: 1 March 2022 – 31st March 2025, with an o-cost extension approved by HMT to 31 March 2026. New project end date (if applicable): 31st March 2028." (D0006340.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: URES combines emergency relief (generators, repairs), financing mechanisms (blended finance for private sector), capacity building (technical assistance), and innovation support (challenge fund). It aims to restore energy access during war while laying foundations for a greener, more resilient energy sector post-war.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Short-term, the programme aims to restore Ukrainians’ access to power by providing energy companies with equipment needed to effect repairs and provide resilience for energy infrastructure in the face of targeted Russian aerial strikes. Longer-term, URES aims to lay the groundwork for a more resilient, independent, and greener energy sector post-war." (D0006340.odt, What is the project’s purpose?)
q3_expected_outputs: 850+ generators supplied to Ukraine (already delivered)
150 hybrid solar and fully solar devices for social facilities (already delivered)
4 high voltage auto-transformers, 3 regulating transformers, 47 surge arresters, 46 voltage transformers (already delivered)
High-grade gabions for physical protection of 25% of high-priority energy infrastructure (already delivered)
9 industrial research pilots and 4 innovative studies developed through UK-Ukraine partnerships
£12m UK ODA unlocking £29m (£12m concessional debt + £17m private co-funding) for biogas/biofuel facilities
Full implementation plan for Government’s Energy Strategy to 2050 with 4 bankable projects
Development of Ukraine’s National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) adopted July 2024
Support to 1-4 private sector investments at 3-4x leverage ratio
16 energy innovation feasibility studies and 8 pilots funded
2-4 diagnostics completed and 3-6 reforms progressed in renewable energy sector
what_objectives.summary: URES delivers immediate energy resilience through equipment and repairs while simultaneously investing in private sector resilience, innovation, and reforms to enable Ukraine’s green energy transition and EU accession.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme’s primary stated outcome is: ‘Ukraine is able to continue to provide energy to uninterruptible customers throughout the war and strengthen its resilience to Russian aggression’." (D0006340.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is experiencing active conflict with Russia, including targeted attacks on energy infrastructure (50% damaged in early 2023), blackouts affecting millions, and ongoing missile/drone strikes. The World Bank estimates $10.6 billion in energy sector damage as of December 2023.
where_context.q5_source: "Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, the importance of energy security for Ukraine has become all the more pronounced, with Russia targeting energy infrastructure with drones and missiles in Winters 2022/2023 and 2023/2024. 50% of energy transmission was damaged, destroyed or under occupation in early 2023." (D0006340.odt, Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints require rapid adaptation to attacks (e.g., 22 March 2024 attack used 151 weapons targeting all levels of the energy system). Regulatory barriers include feed-in tariff issues that stalled renewable investment. Political economy challenges include vested interests in state-owned enterprises. Infrastructure damage (e.g., Kakhovka Dam breach) disrupts both energy and agricultural sectors.
where_context.quote: "Russian onslaughts are hard to predict and have the potential to significantly increase the scale and severity of emergency needs in the energy sector in the short-to-medium term. Growing needs in the energy sector look set to deepen recovery challenges, particularly for the most vulnerable and marginalised groups." (D0006340.odt, Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains ultimate decision-making authority, though the programme emphasizes Government of Ukraine (GoU) buy-in and demand-led technical assistance. Key strategic decisions (e.g., fund allocations between components) are made via in-country governance structures chaired by HM Ambassador.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to Ministry of Energy’s Rapid Response Unit
Support for Green Transition Office (independent advisory unit at Ministry of Economy)
Training on green skills (e.g., renewable energy installation courses for women)
Knowledge transfer through Innovate Ukraine challenge fund (pairing UK/Ukr institutions)
Reform support for energy market liberalization and EU alignment
Institutional strengthening for decentralized energy planning

partner_organizations.name: Energy Community Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: Primary channel for emergency repairs (Ukraine Energy Support Fund); pooled multi-donor trust fund administrator

partner_organizations.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
partner_organizations.role: Blended finance for private sector resilience (Economic Resilience Action platform); co-financing clean energy projects

partner_organizations.name: Innovate UK
partner_organizations.role: Challenge fund implementation (Innovate Ukraine Green Energy Competition); accelerator support for pilots

partner_organizations.name: DiXi Group
partner_organizations.role: Ukrainian NGO; third-party monitoring and local coordination

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Energy (Ukraine)
partner_organizations.role: Primary government counterpart; demand-led technical assistance recipient

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Economy (Ukraine)
partner_organizations.role: Houses Green Transition Office; NECP implementation lead

partner_organizations.name: Ukrenergo (Ukraine’s grid operator)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of repair equipment and resilience support

partner_organizations.name: Oxford University
partner_organizations.role: Green hydrogen study (Component 3)

partner_organizations.name: UK Climate Change Committee
partner_organizations.role: Advisory support for Green Transition Office design

who_partners.quote: "The UK has been recognised by the Ministry of Energy as the ‘first partner on the ground’ delivering 856 generators for Ukraine in its hour of need in Spring 2022." (D0006340.odt, Delivery to date)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: URES uses: (1) Grants for emergency support (Component 1); (2) Capital Development Grant Financing blended with IFC loans for private sector (Component 2); (3) Challenge fund grants for innovation (Component 3); and (4) RDEL for technical assistance (Component 4). The £20m stand-alone disbursement to Energy Community in May 2024 was retrospectively accounted for under the addendum.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: URES operates as a flexible platform with four components (emergency support, private sector resilience, innovation, technical assistance) managed centrally by FCDO Kyiv. Each component has dedicated delivery partners (e.g., Energy Community for Component 1, IFC for Component 2) but retains flexibility to reallocate funds between components annually based on need.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on pre-existing relationships (e.g., Energy Community’s established Ukraine Energy Support Fund), specialized expertise (e.g., IFC’s Economic Resilience Action platform), and demand from Government of Ukraine. For innovation, an open competition was used for challenge fund applicants, but core partners were directly awarded based on proven track records.
how_mechanism.quote: "We have assessed options on offer and remain convinced that IFC [is] the most impactful channel for building business-led renewable generation capacity and stimulating investment in low-carbon private sector projects during the war." (D0006340.odt, Component 2)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Decisions on annual fund allocations between components are made via in-country governance structures chaired by HM Ambassador to Ukraine. The programme’s Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) participates in Embassy Delivery Groups (Humanitarian, Economic Stability, Early Recovery and Reconstruction). Technical oversight for components is provided by respective partners (e.g., IFC for private sector, Innovate UK for challenge fund).
how_governance.quote: "A decision will be taken each year via relevant in-country governance structures on the split on emergency needs versus private sector resilience, with the team retaining the option of directing spend to private sector resilience if it appears that the more urgent needs have been met." (D0006340.odt, Contingency)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated annually between the four components (emergency support, private sector resilience, innovation, technical assistance) based on evolving needs. For example, the £20m committed to Energy Community in May 2024 was not originally budgeted but was retrospectively approved. The programme retains a £24m/year flexible envelope to respond to either emergency needs or private sector support.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach with annual reviews to adjust component allocations. For example, if attacks intensify, more funds can shift to emergency repairs; if conditions improve, focus can pivot to reconstruction and innovation. The Innovate Ukraine challenge fund allows for open competition to identify emerging priorities.
how_flexibility.quote: "This does not imply that the programme will not provide VfM for the UK taxpayer... Rather, it implies that a pre-defined fixed plan would have a higher likelihood of failure and lead to greater wastage of resource if the envelope for each component were set in stone." (D0004311.odt, Assessing Value for Money)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partners (e.g., Energy Community, IFC, Innovate UK) → End Beneficiaries (Ukrainian energy companies, private sector, research institutions). The programme avoids additional layers by using direct channels like the Energy Community’s pooled fund (100% of contributions go to impact with no admin fees).
how_efficiency.quote: "The Energy Community’s Ukraine Energy Support Fund offers better Value for Money on costs grounds as there are no admin charges or overheads charged for this facility so 100% of UK contribution can be used for impact." (D0004311.odt, Output 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: Contribute to the Energy Community Ukraine Energy Support Fund (selected)
Support wider IFI investments in recovery (e.g., World Bank URTF)
Establish a UK-led delivery unit for energy sector recovery
Launch a portfolio of clean energy market-shaping interventions
Provide flexible technical assistance on regulatory reforms
Refocus ODA toward supporting refugees in the region (rejected)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The mixed platform approach was selected to balance (1) **speed** (using proven channels like Energy Community for rapid repairs), (2) **flexibility** (annual reallocation between components), (3) **leverage** (IFC’s ability to mobilize 3-4x private co-financing), and (4) **alignment with GoU priorities** (demand-led technical assistance). The programme avoids creating parallel systems by working through existing platforms (e.g., G7+ Clean Energy Partnership).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Aid diversion in high-corruption environment (Ukraine ranks 122/180 on Corruption Perceptions Index)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Third-party monitoring of generator distribution; Thomson Reuters World-Check for contractor vetting; planned external audit of Energy Community fund with Germany.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other donors in crowded energy sector
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Horizon-scanning via Dixi Group; niche focus (e.g., physical protection advisory, cogeneration units other donors avoid); coordination through G7+ Clean Energy Partnership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector reluctance to invest during active conflict
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFC’s first-loss guarantees (e.g., £15m UK grant de-risked £30m IFC loan for biogas project); piloting new financial instruments to crowd in commercial investors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Innovation pilots not scaling due to war disruptions
