q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Accelerator component to link grantees with follow-on funding (e.g., World Bank CIFs, Ukraine Reconstruction Sovereign Bonds); mapping of ‘hand-off’ funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Technical assistance not absorbed due to GoU capacity constraints
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Rationalizing TA partners to 5 core organizations; embedding UK secondee in British Embassy for 6+ months; focusing on high-priority reforms (e.g., Guaranteed Buyer liquidity issues).

why_rationale.quote: "Opting to support via [IFC ERA] was a key recommendation of FCDO’s Quality Assurance Unit (QAU) when it reviewed the original URES Business Case in 2023." (D0006340.odt, Component 2)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The active conflict and FCAS context constrain partner selection to organizations with (1) **in-country presence** (e.g., Energy Community’s Kyiv office), (2) **rapid procurement capabilities** (e.g., IFC’s pre-approved supplier networks), and (3) **risk appetite** (e.g., willingness to operate in conflict zones). Local Ukrainian NGOs (e.g., DiXi Group) are prioritized for monitoring due to access, while multilateral partners (e.g., EBRD, World Bank) are avoided for emergency repairs due to slower disbursement processes.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks limit field visits and physical oversight, requiring reliance on Ukrainian partners for distribution (e.g., Ministry of Energy for generators).
Regulatory barriers (e.g., feed-in tariff arrears) necessitate partners with reform expertise (e.g., IFC for private sector de-risking).
Infrastructure damage requires partners with logistics capacity (e.g., Energy Community’s pre-positioned spare parts).
Political economy constraints (vested interests in state-owned enterprises) demand partners with diplomatic leverage (e.g., FCDO’s convening role in G7+).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **dual objective** of immediate resilience and long-term green transition shapes the mixed delivery structure: (1) **Emergency needs** → Channeled through Energy Community’s pooled fund for speed and absorption capacity; (2) **Private sector resilience** → IFC’s blended finance to crowd in commercial investors; (3) **Innovation** → Open competition via Innovate UK to identify local priorities; (4) **Reforms** → Demand-led TA facility to align with GoU’s EU accession agenda.
q28_linkages: Urgent repair needs → Pooled fund mechanism (Component 1) for rapid absorption.
Green transition goals → IFC’s ERA platform (Component 2) to leverage private capital for renewables.
Local innovation gaps → Challenge fund (Component 3) with accelerator to scale pilots.
EU accession reforms → Flexible TA facility (Component 4) tied to NECP milestones.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to multilaterals (e.g., Energy Community) enable rapid repairs but limit local ownership; mitigated by seconding UK staff to Ukrainian ministries. (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern leadership**: UK-led innovation fund pairs with Ukrainian institutions to build capacity. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Hybrid solar devices target vulnerable groups (IDPs, elderly) despite higher per-unit costs than centralized repairs.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Generators were sourced from UK suppliers for speed, though local procurement could have built Ukrainian industrial capacity.
IFC’s ERA platform prioritizes large agribusinesses (e.g., 28,000 employees) over SMEs for scalability, though Component 3 targets smaller innovators.
Technical assistance focuses on national-level reforms (e.g., NECP) but includes regional pilots (e.g., coal-mining transition) to address inequities.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS context** increases oversight intensity: (1) **Third-party monitoring** for all Component 1 deliveries; (2) **Embedded advisors** (e.g., UK secondee to Energy Community); (3) **Milestone-based payments** for IFC/Innovate UK; (4) **Annual reallocation decisions** via in-country governance structures.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles: (1) **Energy Community** receives a part-time UK secondee to strengthen fund management; (2) **Innovate UK** must include knowledge transfer to Ukrainian innovation bodies; (3) **IFC** provides advisory services alongside financing to drive reforms; (4) **DiXi Group** builds local NGO capacity for monitoring.
intersections.quote: "The programme’s combined approach to grant funding for repairs to state-owned grid assets in addition to Development Capital for private sector resilience (with the ability to scale back one in favour of the other) is illustrative [of adapting to context]." (D0006340.odt, Why this modality?)

key_programme_risks: Continued Russian attacks on energy infrastructure outpacing repair capacity (e.g., 22 March 2024 attack used 151 weapons).
Private sector investment stalling due to war uncertainty (IFC pipeline has $700m+ unfunded needs).
GoU reform fatigue or capacity constraints delaying NECP implementation.
Innovation pilots failing to scale without follow-on funding (only 13 of 29 fundable projects progressed in Round 1).
Corruption or aid diversion in high-risk procurement (e.g., generators, transformers).
Overlap with other donors leading to duplication (mitigated via G7+ coordination).
Energy sector skills gap hindering green transition (e.g., lack of trained technicians for renewables).
Decentralized generation not integrating with centralized grid post-war.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible £24m/year envelope to surge emergency support; physical protection advisory (e.g., gabions for 25% of high-priority sites); coordination with GoU’s Rapid Response Unit.
IFC first-loss guarantees (e.g., £15m UK grant unlocked £52m total investment); piloting new financial instruments; focusing on energy-intensive sectors (e.g., agribusiness) with export potential.
Aligning TA with EU Ukraine Facility milestones (e.g., NECP adoption); embedding UK advisors in ministries; rationalizing TA to 5 core partners.
Accelerator component to link grantees with follow-on funds (e.g., World Bank CIFs); requiring UK-Ukraine institutional partnerships for Round 2.
Third-party monitoring of all Component 1 deliveries; Thomson Reuters World-Check for contractors; external audit of Energy Community fund with Germany.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Rapid disbursement channels** are critical: Energy Community’s pooled fund (no admin fees) outperformed World Bank mechanisms in speed.
**Physical protection** of infrastructure (e.g., gabions) must complement repairs in active conflict zones.
**Decentralized coordination** (e.g., GoU’s Rapid Response Unit) is more effective than donor-led structures during crises.
**Blended finance** (e.g., IFC ERA) can crowd in private capital even during war, but requires first-loss guarantees.
**Localization** of monitoring (e.g., DiXi Group) improves aid effectiveness in high-risk environments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 1 demonstrated that: (1) **Flexibility between components** is essential (e.g., pivoting from repairs to innovation during 2023 lull in attacks); (2) **UK’s early-mover advantage** (e.g., first to deliver generators in 2022) builds long-term trust with GoU; (3) **Demand-led TA** (e.g., Guaranteed Buyer reforms) has higher uptake than donor-driven agendas; (4) **Innovation competitions** reveal untapped local capacity (29 fundable projects vs. 13 funded in Round 1).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Phase 2 adjustments include: (1) **Tighter engagement with local governments** in innovation competitions; (2) **Expanded scope for energy efficiency and green buildings**; (3) **Deeper knowledge transfer** to Ukrainian innovation bodies; (4) **Regional focus on coal-mining areas** for just transition; (5) **Rationalized TA partners** from 9 to 5 core organizations.
risks_lessons.quote: "The enthusiastic market response to the call for bids to our Innovate Ukraine Green Energy Challenge Fund, as well as the quality of those bids (projects considered of a fundable quality had a total value of over £25m, far exceeding the initial £10m envelope), is testament to the programme’s strategic fit with the local context and needs profile." (D0006340.odt, Delivery to date)

co_funding_partners.partner: Germany (joint audit of Energy Community fund)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Component 2 (private sector resilience) achieved a 1:2 ratio of UK grant to IFC balance sheet lending (e.g., £15m UK grant unlocked £30m IFC loan, catalyzing £22m private co-financing for a total £52m investment). The programme aims to mobilize 3-4x private capital across all Component 2 investments.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The £230m budget includes: (1) **Capital expenditures** (e.g., generators, transformers, gabions via Component 1; biogas facility upgrades via Component 2); (2) **Revenue expenditures** (e.g., technical assistance, innovation grants, programme management). The addendum notes that Component 1 (emergency support) is largely capital, while Components 3-4 are revenue.
financial_details.quote: "The £12m ($15m) UK ODA [in Component 2] unlocked a further £29m (£12m concessional debt and £17m co-funding from the private sector) for the upgrade and expansion of biomass to biogas and biofuel facilities." (D0006340.odt, Delivery to date)

metadata.programme_name: Data for Development - Unleashing the Data Dividend

quote.text: This business case will deliver the Technology and Analysis Directorate Business Plan goal to "Maintain and build the UK’s reputation/visible leadership as a leader of the international data and statistics agenda for sustainable development."

duration_source.text:
AMP Start Date: 24 Oct 2023
AMPEnd Date: 31 March 2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening national data systems), technology development (integrating innovative data tools), and policy influence (positioning the UK as a global leader in data for development). It aims to improve decision-making for SDGs by enhancing data availability, quality, and use.

q1_source.text: The aim of this programme is to empower decision making and accountability by improving the coverage, quality and use of data on and for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The programme will leverage the UK’s technical expertise and reputation as a global leader in data to deliver a well-functioning, coordinated international data system, and to work with national Governments to strengthen data systems, integrate innovative data, tools and methods, and create a culture of evidence-based decision making.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased availability, accessibility, coverage, and quality of data
Improved capacity of users to make effective use of data
Strengthened cultures of data for decision-making
Number/proportion of SDG indicators with available data (proxy for strength of national data systems)
Financial investment in data and statistics (proxy for government and donor demand for data)
Statistical Performance Index (SPI) for low- and middle-income countries
Use of statistics in national planning documents
Output storylines demonstrating higher-level results of specific outputs
Impact storylines demonstrating use of data to inform decisions linked to the SDGs

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen data systems globally and nationally to accelerate progress on the SDGs, leveraging the UK’s expertise to improve data-driven decision-making and accountability.

quote.text: This programme positions the UK at the centre of global data initiatives, supporting countries to achieve the SDGs by placing our priorities and values at the core of international efforts and mitigating the impact of malign actors.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The overall programme risk rating is classified as 'Minor' in the document, indicating a low-risk profile. The programme operates globally but focuses on strengthening data systems rather than direct service delivery in fragile contexts.

q5_source.text:
Overall programme risk rating:
Minor

q6_constraints_impact.weak institutions: Low-income countries perform poorly on data sources and infrastructure parameters, limiting their ability to produce and use quality data. Only 25% of countries in sub-Saharan Africa and fewer than two-thirds in Asia have fully funded national statistical plans.
q6_constraints_impact.data limitations: There are persistent challenges in securing timely data across all 169 SDG targets, with significant gaps in geographic coverage, timeliness, and disaggregation. For 9 of the 17 SDGs, only around half of the 193 countries have published internationally comparable data since 2015.
q6_constraints_impact.regulatory: Legal and regulatory frameworks are weak, creating barriers to public-private data sharing and the use of new data sources. There is a lack of common standards for data interoperability.
q6_constraints_impact.infrastructure: Limited digital infrastructure and technical capacity in low-income countries hinder data collection, analysis, and dissemination. Only 20% of individuals in low-income countries used the internet in 2021, compared to 49% in lower-middle-income countries.
q6_constraints_impact.political economy: Underinvestment by governments and donors in national statistical systems is a key constraint. Competing priorities often take precedence over data system strengthening.

quote.text: A key constraint on the development of country data systems is insufficient investment. This includes underinvestment by governments and donors. Limited resources and competing demands hinder investment in data systems, as more pressing and visible priorities take precedence.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO (UK) leads the programme design, partner selection, and overall strategic direction. Implementing partners, including international and Southern-based organizations, deliver outputs under FCDO’s oversight and alignment with the Cape Town Global Action Plan (CTGAP).
q10_capacity_building_details: training
mentorship
institutional strengthening
technical support
knowledge sharing

partner_organizations.name: Global Partnership for Sustainable Development Data (GPSDD)
partner_organizations.role: International system programming; strengthening data ecosystems and multi-stakeholder partnerships

partner_organizations.name: PARIS21
partner_organizations.role: International system programming; coordination and strategic leadership on data for sustainable development

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD)
partner_organizations.role: International system programming; dissemination and use of sustainable development data

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (Global Data Facility)
partner_organizations.role: International system programming; innovation and modernization of national statistical systems

partner_organizations.name: Flowminder
partner_organizations.role: Targeted country-level programming; geospatial data and mobile phone data for development

partner_organizations.name: WorldPop
partner_organizations.role: Targeted country-level programming; geospatial approaches for population and health data

quote.text: We have selected six implementing partners to deliver results. The main outputs that the partners will deliver are described below. They are weighted against the relevance of their work under the five output areas.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of core funding for international partners (e.g., GPSDD, PARIS21) and targeted grants/contracts for country-level implementers (e.g., Flowminder, WorldPop). Core funding supports strategic alignment with UK priorities, while targeted funding delivers specific outputs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme brings multiple implementing partners under a single business case, with FCDO providing overarching management. Partners collaborate under the Cape Town Global Action Plan (CTGAP) framework, with shared outcomes but individual delivery responsibilities. A partner forum facilitates coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their established roles in the international data ecosystem, alignment with the CTGAP, and proven track records in delivering data for development outcomes. The selection leverages existing relationships and complementary expertise.

quote.text: We have selected four international partners, GPSDD, PARIS21, UNSD and the World Bank as they form the core of the international statistical system. [...] We have selected two partners to deliver targeted country results, Flowminder and WorldPop due to their ability to deliver high standards of support in the modernisation of national data systems.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme uses a partner forum to facilitate collaboration and shared learning. While no formal steering committee is mentioned, FCDO retains oversight through annual reviews and milestone-based progress assessments. Implementing partners are required to deliver against agreed output milestones, with FCDO conducting course corrections if results fall short.

quote.text: Progress against output milestones will be scored annually and an overall output score will be used to assess the performance of the programme. [...] Ultimately, the programme is only successful if it delivers against the outcome and impact, to which the implementing partners contribute.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between partners or activities within the hybrid approach, but this requires FCDO approval and alignment with the overarching Theory of Change. The multi-phase design includes a review at the end of Phase 1 to adapt Phase 2 based on lessons learned.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an independent review toward the end of Phase 1 to assess effectiveness and adapt Phase 2. Partners can adjust activities in response to emerging needs, but major shifts require FCDO approval to ensure alignment with UK priorities.

quote.text: The use of a multi-phase approach provides a break point at which FCDO can test the effectiveness of the multi-partner model and its ongoing relevance to FCDO priorities. An independent review will be conducted toward the end of Phase 1. The review will identify what is working well and how the programme could be adapted to improve its effectiveness in Phase 2.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (e.g., GPSDD, WorldPop) → End users (national governments, civil society). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned beyond the six core partners.

quote.text: Bringing implementing partners together under one business case can also improve FCDO efficiencies and effectiveness. It reduces administrative costs by simplifying the annual reporting process and improves efficiencies and the ability to communicate our approach to data for development by bringing learning and experience together in one place.
quote.source: D0005101.odt, Summary Value for Money Statement

q24_alternatives_considered.description: FCDO would not use ODA funding for data for development programming, limiting UK influence and credibility.
ODA funding invested in international initiatives to improve data outcomes globally, with limited country-level targeting.
ODA funding invested in country-level partnerships to achieve targeted data outcomes, with limited international influence.
Combines international and national programming to balance global leadership with country-level impact.

q25_why_chosen.rationale: The hybrid approach (Option 4) was chosen because it provides opportunities for global leadership and influencing of international data standards while delivering targeted results aligned with UK policy priorities. It maximizes value for money by creating linkages between partners, avoiding duplication, and enabling adaptive management. The approach also allows FCDO to respond to emerging needs and align with the UK International Development Strategy and other national strategies.
evidence: The hybrid approach presents good value for money by combining global influence with country-level credibility.
It reduces administrative costs and improves efficiency by consolidating partners under one business case.
The multi-phase design allows for mid-programme adaptation based on independent reviews.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing a hybrid model with multiple partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Active programme management by FCDO, including a common risk matrix, annual milestone reviews, and a partner forum to facilitate collaboration. An independent review at the end of Phase 1 will assess effectiveness and adapt Phase 2.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential duplication or misalignment between international and national activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners are required to align with the Cape Town Global Action Plan (CTGAP) and deliver against shared outcomes. FCDO will monitor for overlaps and encourage complementary approaches.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited FCDO control over partner-delivered activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Output milestones and annual scoring will track partner performance. FCDO retains the ability to reframe the programme or adjust funding if results fall short.

quote.text: Option 4, a hybrid approach of international system programming and national programming is the preferred option. This will provide opportunities for global leadership and the influencing of international standards on data and boosts our credibility through the delivery of targeted results aligned with UK policy in priority countries. [...] It provides an agile mechanism by which the UK can support the core of the international system, and also deliver priorities and generate results and evidence at a national level.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope and focus on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) constrain partner selection to organizations with proven experience in data-poor environments and existing relationships with national governments. Partners must demonstrate the ability to navigate weak institutional contexts, regulatory barriers, and limited digital infrastructure.

q27_constraints_detail.constraint: Weak national statistical systems in LMICs
q27_constraints_detail.impact: Partners must have expertise in institutional strengthening and capacity building to address gaps in data sources, infrastructure, and human resources.

q27_constraints_detail.constraint: Regulatory and legal barriers to data sharing
q27_constraints_detail.impact: Partners like GPSDD and World Bank are selected for their experience in addressing legal barriers to public-private data sharing and promoting open data standards.

q27_constraints_detail.constraint: Limited digital infrastructure in target countries
q27_constraints_detail.impact: Partners like Flowminder and WorldPop are chosen for their geospatial and mobile data expertise, which can operate in low-connectivity environments.

intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (global influence + country-level impact) determine the hybrid delivery structure. The need to strengthen both international data standards and national data systems requires a combination of core funding for global partners (e.g., UNSD, PARIS21) and targeted grants for country-level implementers (e.g., Flowminder). The Theory of Change explicitly links global coordination (CTGAP) with national capacity building.

q28_linkages.mechanism: Core funding for GPSDD, PARIS21, and UNSD to shape global initiatives and embed UK principles in international guidance.
Targeted partnerships with Flowminder and WorldPop to modernize national data systems in priority countries.
Capacity building embedded in all partner activities, with a focus on disaggregated data to ensure vulnerable groups are visible.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses the tension between inclusive data systems and efficient delivery. For example, the programme prioritizes disaggregated data to "make the invisible visible" (e.g., women, disabled populations), which requires additional resources for data collection and analysis. However, the hybrid model aims to balance this by leveraging partners’ existing networks and avoiding duplication.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: The programme commits to increasing the availability of disaggregated data (e.g., by gender, disability) to inform policy for vulnerable groups. This is acknowledged as resource-intensive but justified by its impact on equity and programme effectiveness.

The hybrid approach balances UK leadership in global data standards with the need for country-specific adaptations. While core funding ensures alignment with UK priorities, targeted country programming allows for local responsiveness.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s ‘minor’ risk rating enables a milestone-based oversight approach rather than intensive management. However, the complexity of the hybrid model increases coordination demands, leading to active programme management by FCDO and annual partner performance reviews.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles to include training, mentorship, and institutional strengthening. For example, PARIS21 and GPSDD focus on strategic leadership and multi-stakeholder partnerships, while Flowminder and WorldPop provide technical support to modernize national systems. Partners are selected based on their ability to deliver both capacity-building outputs and higher-level outcomes.

quote.text: The programme will leverage the UK’s technical expertise and reputation as a global leader in data to deliver a well-functioning, coordinated international data system, and to work with national Governments to strengthen data systems, integrate innovative data, tools and methods, and create a culture of evidence-based decision making.

key_programme_risks.risk: Insufficient investment in national statistical systems by governments and donors
Limited technical capacity in LMICs to adopt innovative data methods
Weak legal and regulatory frameworks for data sharing and privacy
Potential misuse of data or lack of ethical standards in data collection/analysis
Duplication or misalignment between international and national partner activities
Low demand for data use among decision-makers due to political or institutional biases

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient investment in national statistical systems
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme will advocate for increased funding for data systems and work with partners to develop resource mobilization strategies. It will also demonstrate the economic returns of data investment (e.g., $32 for every $1 spent).

Capacity building is embedded in all partner activities, including training, mentorship, and the integration of user-friendly tools (e.g., dashboards, e-learning platforms). Partners like WorldPop and Flowminder will provide hands-on technical support.

The programme will support partners in addressing legal barriers to data sharing, promoting open data standards, and developing guidelines for ethical data use. UNSD and World Bank will lead on regulatory reforms.
Partners will promote data confidentiality, security, and ethics through training and the adoption of international standards (e.g., Data Values Manifesto). Safeguarding policies will be enforced.
The programme will use the CTGAP framework to align partner activities and encourage complementary approaches. A partner forum and annual reviews will identify overlaps and gaps.

The programme will work to cultivate a culture of data-driven decision-making by demonstrating the value of data through impact storylines, advocacy, and incentives (e.g., public scorecards, mandatory use of data in strategies).

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS or high-risk contexts, the programme will prioritize partnerships with organizations that have existing relationships with national governments and experience in conflict-sensitive data collection (e.g., World Bank’s work in Somalia, South Sudan).

Lessons from previous FCDO programmes (e.g., Nigeria’s polio eradication) highlight the importance of integrating marginalized populations into data systems to ensure no one is left behind. This will be applied in fragile settings.
The programme will use geospatial and mobile data to fill gaps in traditional data sources in FCAS, where censuses or surveys may be incomplete or outdated.

lessons_from_previous.lesson: Past FCDO investments in data for development (e.g., Nigeria’s demographic data for vaccination campaigns) demonstrate that integrating missing populations into data systems can lead to significant development outcomes (e.g., polio eradication). The programme builds on this by focusing on inclusive data and disaggregation.
evidence: FCDO investment in demographic data to map populations missing from official statistics in Nigeria delivered better access to vaccination campaigns, contributing to the eradication of wild polio (WHO, 2020).

Collaboration between partners (e.g., Flowminder and World Bank) in Somalia and South Sudan successfully produced poverty maps using mobile phone data, demonstrating the value of public-private data integration.

design_changes_based_on_learning.change: The hybrid model (combining international and national programming) was adopted based on lessons from past FCDO programmes, which showed that both global influence and country-level delivery are needed to achieve sustainable impact. The multi-phase design with an independent review after Phase 1 was also added to enable adaptive management.
design_changes_based_on_learning.evidence: Evidence from a broad range of FCDO-funded programmes over the past decade has shown that both ‘international system programming’ and ‘national system programming’ can deliver outputs under the Theory of Change. The hybrid approach was chosen to maximize strengths of both models.

quote.text: Evidence from a broad range of FCDO-funded programmes over the past decade has shown that both the ‘international system programming’ (option 2) and the ‘national system programming’ (option 3) can both deliver output results under the theory of change which lead to outcomes and impacts. [...] The hybrid approach (Option 4) provides the best of providing strong positioning to provide international influencing along with credible understanding and experience of delivery at the national level.

metadata.programme_name: Moldova Resilience Programme (MRP) - M-GROW Trust Fund
metadata.duration_text: AMP Start Date: Oct 2023, AMP End Date: 31/03/2026

quote.text: The UK’s portfolio in Moldova supports reform through the Good Governance Fund and Conflict Stability and Security Fund, as well as through recent humanitarian programming on Social Protection. This new programme of £9M (delivered through World Bank) will provide key support to meet Moldova’s emerging critical needs and help strengthen broader resilience, responding to the recent shocks.

duration_source.text: AMP Start Date: Oct 2023, AMP End Date: 31/03/2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling £9M through the World Bank's M-GROW Trust Fund) with capacity building (technical assistance for policy reforms, institutional strengthening) and implementation research (testing resilience-building approaches). It aims to support Moldova's economic and governance reforms while responding to immediate shocks from Russia's war in Ukraine.

q1_source.text: The proposed programme will deliver against the Foreign Secretary’s commitment made in Moldova in March 2023 to further support the resilience of Moldova, particularly its governance and economic reforms, including the energy sector. This programme supports wider efforts to help deliver on that commitment and helps the Moldovan economy and society to be more resilient to the effects of crisis and the shock caused by Russia’s war in Ukraine.

q3_expected_outputs: Government of Moldova supported to make critical new investment and expand existing projects to boost competitiveness and expand green, resilient and inclusive development
Government of Moldova’s technical and operational implementation capacity enhanced
Government of Moldova carries out reforms towards regional integration into Europe
Government of Moldova has relevant data, analytics and capacity to conduct institutional strengthening for EU accession readiness
Increased opportunities for formal employment (specific targets not quantified)
Improved human capital development (specific targets not quantified)
Increased resilience to climate change and crisis (specific targets not quantified)
Support for 600,000 vulnerable energy households (under rejected Option 1, not selected approach)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to build Moldova's long-term resilience to economic shocks and malign influence through a £9M contribution to the World Bank's M-GROW Trust Fund, focusing on formal employment, human capital development, and climate resilience while supporting EU accession reforms.

quote.text: The overall impact of the programme would be the Moldovan economy and society are more resilient to the effects to shocks generally but particularly those caused by Russia’s war in Ukraine. This could be seen through increased opportunities for formal employment, improved human capital and increased resilience to climate change and crisis.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Moldova faces compounded crises from Russia's war in Ukraine (792,000 refugees hosted), energy price shocks (168% electricity price increases), political instability (pro-Russian protests), and institutional fragility (high corruption, weak democracy). The country is classified as highly vulnerable to external shocks with a history of natural disasters and economic contraction (-5.9% GDP in 2022).

q5_source.text: Moldova is likely to be one of the economies that is feeling the worst effects of the current crisis given its proximity and close connections to Russia and Ukraine and the innate vulnerabilities of being a small landlocked economy... The war has also led to a decline in foreign direct investment inflows disrupted trade and logistic links and dwindling remittances from Ukraine and Russia.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The war in Ukraine has disrupted trade routes, caused energy price spikes (168% for electricity), and created refugee pressures (109,000 remaining). Political polarization (pro-Russian vs pro-EU factions) threatens reform momentum. Institutional capacity is strained by multiple crises (COVID, drought, war), limiting ability to implement reforms. Energy infrastructure remains vulnerable due to dependence on Russian-controlled Transnistria for 70-90% of electricity.

quote.text: The Moldovan government faces significant challenges in a context where governments are often short lived. Moldova is likely to be one of the economies that is feeling the worst effects of the current crisis given its proximity and close connections to Russia and Ukraine and the innate vulnerabilities of being a small landlocked economy.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led multilateral) and Government of Moldova co-chair the Partnership Council, but the UK as a founding member has significant influence in shaping priorities. Day-to-day management rests with the World Bank's Country Management Unit.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for policy reforms
institutional strengthening for EU accession
training for government officials
digitalization support
systems for social protection targeting
health management capacity
climate resilience planning

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Trust Fund manager and implementer

partner_organizations.name: Government of Moldova
partner_organizations.role: co-chair of Partnership Council, beneficiary

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funder, founding member of Partnership Council

quote.text: The UK will be a founding member of the PC. Decisions of the PC would be made by consensus during meetings or by virtual 'no-objection' between meetings... The PC would be responsible for ensuring that M-GROW efficiently and effectively supports Moldova to implement its Country Partnership Framework (CPF) goals.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK will contribute £9M to the World Bank's M-GROW Multi-Donor Trust Fund through a standard Administrative Agreement (MoU). Funds are pooled with other donors and managed by the World Bank according to the Trust Fund's governance structure, with the UK having a seat on the Partnership Council.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The M-GROW Trust Fund is governed by a Partnership Council (PC) co-chaired by the World Bank and Government of Moldova, with donor members including the UK. Day-to-day management is handled by the World Bank's Country Management Unit (CMU) which acts as the Trust Fund's secretariat. The UK will receive quarterly reports and participate in annual PC meetings.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its established presence in Moldova, proven track record with Trust Funds, and ability to quickly mobilize resources. The urgency of Moldova's needs and the Bank's existing Country Partnership Framework made it the preferred partner over alternatives like UNDP.

quote.text: Given the urgency and scale of the needs, the most viable option is to use established multilateral partners, therefore no early market engagement or commercial tender will be suitable for this support... The World Bank option best improves Moldova’s outcomes to shocks that the country is most likely to face as it contributes to improving resilience more broadly.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Partnership Council (PC) serves as the high-level governance body, with the Government of Moldova and World Bank as co-chairs and development partners (including UK) as members. Decisions are made by consensus. The PC is responsible for: (i) endorsing Annual Work Plans and Budgets; (ii) reviewing Annual Financial and Progress Reports; and (iii) providing guidance on the results framework. The World Bank's Country Management Unit acts as secretariat.

quote.text: The PC will meet annually at the invitation of the Co-Chairs... In addition to this formal governance structure, the Post and Programme team will meet with the World Bank’s local team at least monthly to ensure that projects are on track and remain effective and efficient... The World Bank will provide quarterly reviews, specific to FCDO contribution.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities within the Trust Fund's broad pillars (investment support and institutional strengthening) with Partnership Council approval. The flexible design allows adaptation to emerging needs, but major shifts would require consensus among donors.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an adaptive management approach with annual reviews and the ability to adjust activities based on evolving country circumstances. The Theory of Change will be periodically reviewed and updated through consultation with the Partnership Council. The World Bank's systematic country diagnostics inform ongoing prioritization.

quote.text: A high-level theory of change has been developed for the M-GROW Umbrella Trust Fund. This will be further refined and updated through consultation with the Trust Fund Partnership Council... It will also be subject to periodic reviews to ensure the programme can adapt to evolving country circumstances and needs.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (Trust Fund manager) → Government of Moldova/implementing entities

quote.text: We expect to pay the full amount in a single tranche, in line with FCDO-WBG agreements that funding to Trust Funds must be paid in advance (not in advance of need) so that the Bank can create the projects once donor funding is received... The operational cost of using the World Bank as an implementing partner will be 5% of the programme cost... There will be a separate Programme Management budget line for the Trust Fund, which we expect to be around 1% in line with current Trust Funds with the Bank in the region.

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Energy Vulnerability Reduction Fund (EVRF) with UNDP - Focused on immediate energy poverty relief through targeted payments and efficiency vouchers
Option 2: World Bank M-GROW Trust Fund - Broader resilience-building through technical assistance, policy reforms, and capacity building (SELECTED)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The World Bank option was selected because it: 1) Aligns with the Foreign Secretary's commitment to bolster Moldova's broader resilience against Russian hybrid aggression; 2) Moves beyond immediate energy shocks to address systemic vulnerabilities; 3) Offers better value for money (5% vs 10% operational costs) and potential to crowd in additional donors; 4) Provides flexibility to adapt to evolving needs; and 5) Leverages the World Bank's established presence and technical expertise in Moldova.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of control over fund allocation due to multilateral pooling
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK's founding member status on the Partnership Council ensures influence over strategic decisions and activity selection. The UK will nominate its spend to Technical Assistance activities aligned with its Theory of Change.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in Trust Fund establishment affecting timely delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early engagement as a founding member allows the UK to shape the fund's creation. The programme is designed to initiate activities by October 2023 with a results framework finalized by December 2023.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: World Bank's operational costs (5% + 1% management fee) reducing funds available for direct activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The 6% total overhead is benchmarked as competitive compared to alternatives like UNDP (10%). The Bank's economies of scale and ability to leverage additional funding justify the costs.

quote.text: Option 2 with the World Bank dominates across all criteria. In terms value the World Bank provides greater potential benefits over a large range of resilience activities and at a lower operational fee. The World Bank option also addresses a broader set of resilience risks... The preferred option was selected using a multi-criteria decision analysis and considered: Value for Money (benefits exceeding cost); Enhancing Moldova’s Resilience to shocks; improving opportunities for better climate outcomes; and delivering inclusive outcomes.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Moldova's FCAS context and urgent needs constrained partner selection to established multilaterals with existing in-country presence. The political sensitivity of energy sector reforms (given Russian influence) and the need for rapid disbursement ruled out new or local partners in favor of the World Bank's neutral, high-capacity platform.
q27_constraints_detail: Urgent timeline required partners with existing operational capacity in Moldova
Energy sector's geopolitical sensitivity necessitated a politically neutral implementer
Need for financial leverage favored multilaterals that could crowd in additional donors
Weak local institutional capacity made direct government implementation unfeasible
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's dual focus on immediate shock response and long-term resilience building required a flexible, multi-component mechanism. The World Bank's Trust Fund model was selected because it could: 1) Channel funds quickly for urgent needs; 2) Support both investment projects and capacity building; 3) Adapt to evolving priorities through its governance structure; and 4) Align with Moldova's EU accession reforms.
q28_linkages: Broad resilience objectives → Required multilateral platform capable of cross-sectoral work
Need for policy influence → Necessitated partner with government relationships (World Bank)
Urgency of energy crisis → Demanded existing implementation mechanisms
EU accession focus → Required partner with experience in institutional strengthening
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery and inclusive outcomes, particularly regarding: 1) The rejection of UNDP's EVRF option (which had immediate poverty impacts) in favor of the World Bank's longer-term resilience approach; 2) The balance between technical assistance for government capacity (equity) and the need for quick disbursement (efficiency); 3) The tradeoff between World Bank's 6% overhead costs and its ability to deliver at scale.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: World Bank option prioritized systemic resilience over UNDP's immediate poverty relief
Northern expertise vs local ownership: World Bank's technical leadership balanced with Government of Moldova's co-chair role
Cost vs reach: Higher World Bank overhead (6%) justified by its leverage potential and implementation capacity
Flexibility vs control: Pooled fund model enabled adaptation but reduced UK's direct control over allocations
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context led to intensive oversight arrangements including: 1) Monthly meetings between FCDO and World Bank local teams; 2) Quarterly progress reviews; 3) Annual Partnership Council meetings with consensus-based decision making; 4) Embedded risk management tools in the AMP system. The management intensity is explicitly calibrated to the 'moderate' risk rating and the need to respond to a dynamic context.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme's core capacity building objectives directly shaped partner roles: 1) The World Bank was selected for its technical assistance capabilities; 2) The Government of Moldova's co-chair role in the Partnership Council was designed to build its institutional leadership; 3) Technical advisors from FCDO (economists, governance experts) are embedded to support knowledge transfer; 4) The Trust Fund's focus on 'higher risk activities that lead to significant learning' reflects a capacity-building approach.

quote.text: The World Bank option also addresses a broader set of resilience risks... Although both options score similarly in terms of opportunities for better climate outcomes the World Bank scores better in terms of better inclusive outcomes (providing the World Bank option is carefully managed)... The UK will be well placed to help shape the programme, ensuring our funding is used for practical results-oriented projects in line with our values and the NSIG Strategy.

key_programme_risks: Political instability in Moldova disrupting reform momentum (Possible/Severe)
Government absorption capacity limiting programme effectiveness (Possible/Moderate)
Spillover effects from Ukraine war creating new shocks (Possible/Severe)
Energy price volatility affecting economic stability (Likely/Severe)
Donor coordination challenges in multi-partner Trust Fund (Possible/Moderate)
Implementation delays due to complex World Bank procedures (Possible/Moderate)
Corruption risks affecting fund allocation (Possible/Moderate)
Climate change exacerbating agricultural vulnerabilities (Likely/Moderate)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political instability in Moldova disrupting reform momentum
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The Bank is a politically neutral organisation whose work could continue despite changes in government. The UK will use its position on the Partnership Council to ensure a long-term approach is taken to project interventions to ensure sustainability despite disruption.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Government absorption capacity limiting programme effectiveness
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The UK will continue to use diplomatic relationships to ensure the Government focuses on the Bank projects. Technical assistance is explicitly designed to build implementation capacity. Early scoping showed government commitment to reform areas.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Energy price volatility affecting economic stability
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme supports diversification of energy sources and efficiency improvements. The Trust Fund's flexible design allows reallocation to emerging energy needs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Donor coordination challenges in multi-partner Trust Fund
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The Partnership Council structure with consensus-based decision making ensures aligned priorities. The World Bank's secretariat manages coordination.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Implementation delays due to complex World Bank procedures
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Monthly check-ins between FCDO and World Bank local teams to monitor progress. The UK's founding member status allows influence over timelines.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Good Governance Fund show that well-targeted technical assistance in areas government prioritizes achieves results (Ecorys 2021 evaluation)
Experience demonstrates that capacity building must be paired with political engagement to sustain reforms in fragile contexts
Previous energy crises in Moldova highlight the need for both immediate relief and systemic resilience building
The importance of donor coordination in FCAS contexts to avoid duplication and maximize impact
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The midline evaluation of the Good Governance Fund (Ecorys 2021) demonstrated that technical assistance focused on government-prioritized areas achieves measurable results in FCAS contexts. This informed the M-GROW design's emphasis on aligning with Moldova's reform commitments and using flexible TA modalities.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: 1) A results framework that will be adapted based on periodic reviews; 2) Explicit focus on 'higher risk activities that lead to significant learning'; 3) Quarterly monitoring to enable real-time adjustments; 4) A Theory of Change that will be refined through consultation with the Partnership Council.

quote.text: Evidence from implementation of the Good Governance Fund in the region demonstrates that well targeted technical assistance focused on areas that the government is prioritising will achieve results... The high-level ToC rests on the following key assumptions... The programme will use the FCDO 4E framework (equity, effectiveness, efficiency, and economy) to inform the VFM statement.

co_funding_partners.partner: Other donors to M-GROW Trust Fund (not specified)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK's £9M contribution (7% of the total $155M target) is expected to help mobilize the full Trust Fund amount. The World Bank's involvement is anticipated to attract additional donor contributions through its convening power.

quote.text: The operational cost of using the World Bank as an implementing partner will be 5% of the programme cost... There will be a separate Programme Management budget line for the Trust Fund, which we expect to be around 1% in line with current Trust Funds with the Bank in the region... By becoming an early mover with around 7% of total planned investment, the UK will be well placed to help shape the programme.

metadata.programme_name: ASEAN-UK Women Peace and Security (WPS) Programme

quote.text: The programme will promote women’s participation in conflict prevention, resolution and recovery. It will also support ASEAN to become a knowledge hub on WPS and lead the advancement of the WPS agenda in the region.

duration_source.text: Original project start and end dates: June 2023–March 2026

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening ASEAN institutions and Member States on WPS), policy influence (advancing normative frameworks and regional policies), and implementation research (testing and scaling innovative approaches to WPS). It also includes service delivery elements through technical assistance and training.

q1_source.text: The programme will focus on advancing normative frameworks for WPS, capacity building and exchange of knowledge and good practices at the ASEAN regional level, as well as supporting country-level policy implementation, including supporting further WPS National Action Plan (NAP) development.

q3_expected_outputs.output: ASEAN Secretariat, sectoral bodies and institutions have increased access to gender and WPS expertise to develop regional policies on WPS and related frameworks
ASEAN sectoral bodies and institutions and non-state actors have strengthened capacity to implement the WPS agenda

A regional platform for cooperation and advocacy among ASEAN Member States, sectoral bodies, and institutions as well as civil society and women organizations is strengthened to promote good practices and evidence on WPS

ASEAN Member States and non-state actors have increased knowledge and capacity to develop, implement and monitor WPS policy frameworks and test and upscale innovative approaches to implementing WPS agenda and conflict prevention at the national level
Technical support to establish a coordination, monitoring, reporting, evaluation and implementation structure for the Regional Plan of Action (RPA)
Training/capacity building workshops to strengthen the capacity of IPR/AWPR and sectoral bodies
Support to the development of Cambodia’s first National Action Plan (NAP) on WPS
Technical assistance and raising awareness in Lao PDR and Malaysia on WPS and NAP development
Support to implement the second generation of the NAP on WPS in Timor-Leste

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda in ASEAN by building institutional capacity, advancing normative frameworks, and supporting national-level implementation of WPS policies. It focuses on promoting women’s participation in peace processes, preventing violence against women, and fostering social cohesion in the region.

quote.text: The programme will promote women’s participation in conflict prevention, resolution and recovery. It will also support ASEAN to become a knowledge hub on WPS and lead the advancement of the WPS agenda in the region.

countries_regions: ASEAN Member States (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with areas affected by protracted conflicts, fragility, and disaster-proneness, but the overall risk rating is assessed as moderate. This is due to the involvement of established partners like UN Women and ASEAN-IPR, which have existing mechanisms for risk management.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The ASEAN region includes areas affected by protracted conflicts and fragility, which disproportionately impact women and girls. Climate change increases the risk of extreme weather events, exacerbating gender inequalities and vulnerabilities. Weak institutions and political economy factors may hinder the implementation of WPS policies at national and regional levels.

quote.text: ASEAN is a highly diverse region which includes areas affected by protracted conflicts and fragility. Women and girls bear the greatest impact of these conflicts, whilst still not having their full voice and leadership recognised in policy decision making processes. [...] Climate change is likely to increase the risks of conflict and fragility in SE Asia as well as increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is delivered through UN Women and ASEAN-IPR, both of which are regional entities with strong legitimacy and decision-making power within ASEAN. The ASEAN Secretariat and Member States play a central role in shaping and implementing the programme, indicating a Southern-led approach.
q10_capacity_building_details: training/capacity building workshops for ASEAN sectoral bodies and government stakeholders
technical assistance to build capacity of women’s organizations and networks
support to develop and implement National Action Plans (NAPs) on WPS
mentorship and knowledge exchange through regional platforms and dialogues

partner_organizations.name: UN Women
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementing partner for regional and national activities, including capacity building, technical assistance, and policy development
partner_organizations.location: South (Indonesia Country Office with regional coverage)

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN-IPR)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of WPS training programmes for mid-level government officials from ASEAN Member States

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: Coordination and facilitation of engagement with ASEAN Advisory Group on WPS

partner_organizations.name: Governments of ASEAN Member States (AMS)
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiaries and participants in training, policy development, and implementation of WPS agendas

partner_organizations.name: Civil society organizations and women’s networks
partner_organizations.role: Capacity building, advocacy, and engagement in WPS processes

partner_organizations.name: Government of Timor-Leste
partner_organizations.role: Observer state receiving technical assistance for WPS NAP implementation

quote.text: For this option, FCDO will partner with two organisations that are already working on WPS with ASEAN, namely UN Women and the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation. The advantage with supporting these two initiatives is that they are both undertaking recognised ASEAN WPS activities.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a Contribution Arrangement with UN Women and a Grant Agreement with ASEAN-IPR. These instruments provide structured funding while allowing flexibility for capacity building and technical assistance activities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed by a Programme Lead in the UK Mission to ASEAN, supported by advisers from the Indo-Pacific Regional Department and Gender and Conflict Policy Team. UN Women and ASEAN-IPR deliver activities independently but in coordination with ASEAN bodies and Member States.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UN Women and ASEAN-IPR were selected due to their existing work on WPS in ASEAN, recognized legitimacy with Member States, and ability to reduce transaction costs by building on ongoing initiatives. An open bid process was considered but rejected due to risks of non-approval by ASEAN and lengthy negotiations.

quote.text: For this option, FCDO will partner with two organisations that are already working on WPS with ASEAN, namely UN Women and the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation. The advantage with supporting these two initiatives is that they are both undertaking recognised ASEAN WPS activities. Additional funding from the UK will increase the scale and scope of these programmes.
Following standard FCDO practice, the FCDO SRO and Programme Manager for this programme will review the risk matrix every quarter.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, as evidenced by the cost extension to support additional in-country activities in Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, and Timor-Leste.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has demonstrated adaptive management by responding to increased demand from ASEAN Member States for localization of the WPS agenda, leading to a cost extension for additional technical assistance and capacity building.

quote.text: The aim of the cost extension is to maximise the outcomes and impact of the existing ASEAN-UK WPS programme, by expanding and enhancing AMS in-country activities, which, at the same time, supports the implementation of regional policy frameworks on the WPS agenda.
quote.source: D0005865.odt, What is the objective of the cost extension or other changes?

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UN Women/ASEAN-IPR → end beneficiaries (ASEAN Member States, civil society, women’s organizations)

quote.text: The funding agreements for both organisations will set payment schedules and the schedule for financial reporting.

q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: The signed ASEAN-UK Plan of Action makes a commitment to support women, peace and security in ASEAN, as does the UK National Action Plan on WPS. For this reason, doing nothing on ASEAN on WPS and security is not a viable option.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Open bid for external bidders to implement the programme
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: An open bid process could generate innovative approaches but carries risks of selecting suppliers not approved by ASEAN or requiring lengthy negotiations with the ASEAN Secretariat. This option was rejected due to these risks.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option of partnering with UN Women and ASEAN-IPR was chosen due to their existing work on WPS in ASEAN, recognized legitimacy with Member States, and ability to reduce transaction costs by building on ongoing initiatives. This approach offers good value for money and aligns with the UK’s strategic priorities in the region.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of political resistance or lack of approval from ASEAN for new partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: By working with existing, ASEAN-approved partners (UN Women and ASEAN-IPR), the programme mitigates the risk of non-approval or delays in implementation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of low attendance or connectivity issues in training programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ASEAN-IPR requested funding for in-person training to address issues encountered during online delivery, such as attendance and internet connectivity problems.

quote.text: The advantage with supporting these two initiatives is that they are both undertaking recognised ASEAN WPS activities. Additional funding from the UK will increase the scale and scope of these programmes. It also offers good value for money for the UK in reducing the transaction costs that would be required to set up a new WPS ASEAN programme.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The ASEAN context, which includes diverse political systems and varying levels of institutional capacity, constrains partner selection to organizations that are already recognized and approved by ASEAN. This limits the programme to working with UN Women and ASEAN-IPR, both of which have established legitimacy and relationships with ASEAN Member States.
q27_constraints_detail: ASEAN approval requirements for partners
Need for regional legitimacy and acceptance
Diverse political and institutional landscapes across Member States
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—such as advancing normative frameworks, building institutional capacity, and supporting national-level implementation—determine the delivery structure. The need for regional coordination and legitimacy necessitates partnerships with multilateral and regional organizations (UN Women and ASEAN-IPR), while the focus on national-level activities requires flexible, country-specific technical assistance.
q28_linkages: Regional policy frameworks (e.g., ASEAN Regional Plan of Action on WPS) require multilateral partners for coordination and advocacy.
National-level implementation (e.g., development of NAPs) requires in-country partners with local expertise and relationships.
Capacity building and training necessitate partners with existing networks and credibility among ASEAN stakeholders.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between inclusive partnerships and efficient delivery. While working with established partners like UN Women and ASEAN-IPR ensures efficiency and legitimacy, it may limit opportunities for newer or smaller organizations to participate. The focus on capacity building for women’s organizations and civil society aims to address equity by empowering local actors, though this requires additional resources and time.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (working with established partners) vs. inclusion (limiting opportunities for new organizations)
Speed (building on existing initiatives) vs. reach (ensuring all Member States and observer countries benefit)
Northern expertise (FCDO oversight) vs. Southern ownership (ASEAN-led implementation and decision-making)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile of the programme influences the oversight intensity, with quarterly reviews by FCDO to monitor progress and mitigate risks. The involvement of established partners like UN Women and ASEAN-IPR, which have their own risk management strategies, allows for a balanced approach that avoids overly intensive oversight while ensuring accountability.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective of the programme, shaping the roles of partners like UN Women and ASEAN-IPR to focus on training, technical assistance, and institutional strengthening. This ensures that ASEAN Member States and civil society organizations are equipped to implement WPS agendas independently, fostering long-term sustainability.

quote.text: The programme will focus on advancing normative frameworks for WPS, capacity building and exchange of knowledge and good practices at the ASEAN regional level, as well as supporting country-level policy implementation, including supporting further WPS National Action Plan (NAP) development.

key_programme_risks: Political resistance or lack of commitment from ASEAN Member States
Low participation or engagement in training and capacity building activities
Connectivity and attendance issues in virtual training programmes
Limited institutional capacity in some Member States to implement WPS agendas
Risk of funds being misused for non-intended purposes (e.g., terrorism financing)
Challenges in ensuring inclusion of women with disabilities in WPS activities

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Political resistance or lack of commitment from ASEAN Member States
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme builds on existing political commitments (e.g., ASEAN Regional Plan of Action on WPS) and works with recognized partners (UN Women, ASEAN-IPR) to ensure legitimacy and buy-in. Regular engagement with senior decision-makers and advocacy efforts are included to maintain momentum.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low participation or engagement in training and capacity building activities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: ASEAN-IPR shifted from online to in-person training to improve attendance and engagement. The programme also includes tailored capacity building for specific stakeholders, such as women’s organizations and civil society.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Connectivity and attendance issues in virtual training programmes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Funding was allocated for in-person training courses to address connectivity and participation challenges encountered during online delivery.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited institutional capacity in some Member States to implement WPS agendas
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: The programme includes technical assistance and capacity building at both regional and national levels, with a focus on supporting the development of National Action Plans (NAPs) and localization of the Regional Plan of Action (RPA).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Risk of funds being misused for non-intended purposes (e.g., terrorism financing)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UN Women and ASEAN-IPR follow robust financial procedures, including audits and compliance checks. FCDO monitors these processes to ensure funds are used appropriately, particularly when supporting women’s rights organizations.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Challenges in ensuring inclusion of women with disabilities in WPS activities
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will engage with programme partners to highlight the challenges faced by women with disabilities in conflict situations and explore opportunities to enhance inclusivity in programme activities.

fcas_specific_lessons: The programme recognizes that women and girls in FCAS (Fragile and Conflict-Affected Settings) within ASEAN, such as Myanmar and areas with protracted conflicts, face disproportionate impacts. Lessons from similar initiatives emphasize the need for gender-responsive conflict analysis and inclusive peacebuilding processes.

Climate change is identified as a cross-cutting risk that exacerbates fragility and conflict in the region. The programme integrates climate-related security issues into WPS frameworks to address these challenges.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous UK cooperation with UN Women in Vietnam to organize international conferences on WPS National Action Plans (NAPs) demonstrated the value of regional dialogues and capacity building. This experience informed the design of the current programme, which includes similar activities at a larger scale.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The shift from online to in-person training for ASEAN-IPR’s WPS courses was a direct response to lessons learned about low attendance and connectivity issues during virtual sessions. Additionally, the cost extension to support in-country activities in Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, and Timor-Leste reflects the programme’s adaptive response to increased demand and successful early implementation.

quote.text: ASEAN-IPR delivered the modules online last year which came across issues relating to attendance and internet connectivity. Therefore, they asked the UK to fund an in-person two-week delivery of the training this year in Bangkok.
quote.source: D0004175.odt, ASEAN-IPR Training Programmes on WPS

co_funding_partners.partner: Government of the Republic of Korea

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages co-funding from Canada and the Republic of Korea, which support the same UN Women project. This enhances the scale and impact of the programme without additional UK resources.

quote.text: The UK’s contribution of £2.7m, the UN Women project 'Empowering Women for Sustainable Peace' is currently directed to regional-level activities and in-country activities for five AMS: Indonesia, The Philippines, Thailand, Viet Nam, Timor-Leste. [...] The proposed activities are estimated to cost around £355,500. However, due to a reduction of £170,000 in the required commitment to ASEAN-IPR from the original business case, the cost extension needed for the whole programme is £190,000.
quote.source: D0005865.odt, What is the additional and total support the UK will provide?

metadata.programme_name: Empowering Palestinian Institutions and Civil Society (EPICS)
metadata.quote: "EPICS aims to improve the viability, legitimacy and inclusion of governance and service delivery, to protect and support civic space, and to empower women, in the OPTs." (D0003842.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 1 May 2023; AMP End Date: 30 March 2031" (D0003842.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: EPICS combines capacity building (strengthening PA institutions and civil society), policy influence (supporting governance reforms and accountability), and service delivery (protecting civic space and empowering women). It uses technical assistance to improve PA financial viability and service provision while funding CSOs to hold duty-bearers accountable and promote women's rights.
what_objectives.q1_source: "EPICS aims to improve the viability, legitimacy and inclusion of governance and service delivery, to protect and support civic space, and to empower women, in the OPTs. It will provide technical assistance to PA institutions across governance sectors... EPICS will protect and support Palestinian civic space by supporting CSOs to hold the PA and other local duty bearers to account for governance and service delivery." (D0003842.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Strengthened systems and capacities for public financial management and tax (Output 1)
Strengthened systems, processes, and capacities for transparency, accountability, and inclusion (Output 2)
Civil Society Organisations more capable of conducting outreach and holding PA and other local duty bearers to account (Output 3)
Civil Society Organisations have active coalitions promoting women's rights through dialogue and advocacy (Output 4)
Improved PA finances, better directed toward equitable provision of quality public services (Outcome 1)
Improved accountability for governance and service delivery in the OPTs (Outcome 2)
Better protected and more vibrant civic space (Outcome 3)
Greater empowerment and inclusion of women (Outcome 4)
what_objectives.summary: EPICS is a £35m, 8-year governance programme designed to strengthen Palestinian Authority (PA) institutions, protect civic space, and empower women through technical assistance, civil society support, and coalition-building. It responds to the PA's fiscal crisis, legitimacy deficit, and threats to civil society in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPTs).
what_objectives.quote: "EPICS will provide technical assistance to PA institutions across a range of governance sectors... EPICS will protect and support Palestinian civic space by supporting CSOs to hold the PA and other local duty bearers to account... EPICS will work to strengthen women’s empowerment, primarily through supporting local and grassroots organisations to advocate and build capacity." (D0003842.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The OPTs are characterized by ongoing conflict, occupation, and institutional fragility. The PA faces a serious fiscal crisis, declining legitimacy, and risks of collapse, while civil society is under threat from both the PA and Israeli authorities. The overall programme risk rating is 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0003842.odt, Summary Sheet) and "The PA is in serious crisis, and widely seen as being unable to protect Palestinians, deliver sovereignty or safeguard human rights. Stability in the West Bank is deteriorating... PA collapse would likely entail extensive violence, put at risk basic services... and create a vacuum that extremist groups would take advantage of." (D0003842.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The Israeli occupation restricts PA authority to 18% of the West Bank (Area A) and limits its operations in Gaza and East Jerusalem. Movement restrictions, fiscal crises (e.g., Israeli deductions from clearance revenues), and political divisions between Hamas and Fatah undermine PA viability. Civil society faces repression from the PA, Hamas, and Israel, including arbitrary arrests, cyber-crime laws, and NGO designations as 'terrorist organizations'.
where_context.quote: "The PA’s operating environment is shaped by the Israeli occupation of the West Bank, heavy restrictions on movement and access into Gaza... The PA is only able to exercise authority in limited geographic areas... Palestinian civil society... is under threat, both from the Government of Israel and from the PA itself." (D0003842.odt, Context sections)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO retains decision-making authority through a Programme Board responsible for approving interventions. Palestinian CSOs and PA institutions are implementing partners but do not lead strategic decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to PA institutions (e.g., public financial management, tax collection)
support to CSOs to hold PA accountable and engage with citizens
coalition-building among women’s rights organizations
training and advisory support embedded in PA ministries

partner_organizations.name: Palestinian Authority (PA) institutions
partner_organizations.role: recipient of technical assistance (e.g., Ministry of Finance, Centre of Government)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: implementer of Transparency, Evidence and Accountability (TEA) programme

partner_organizations.name: Palestinian Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: sub-grantees for civic space protection and women’s empowerment

partner_organizations.name: International NGOs
partner_organizations.role: accountable grant agreement holders (potential sub-grantors to local CSOs)

partner_organizations.name: Technical assistance suppliers (e.g., for PFM, MERL)
partner_organizations.role: contractors providing embedded advisors and monitoring services

partner_organizations.name: UK-based Governance Advisor (new component in addendum)
partner_organizations.role: external engagement lead for PA reform and donor coordination

who_partners.quote: "EPICS will be delivered through four components: (a) a contract with a supplier for monitoring, evaluation, research and learning; (b) a contract with a technical assistance supplier; (c) a Contribution Agreement with UNDP; and (d) Accountable Grant Agreements with NGOs/CSOs." (D0003842.odt, Options) and "A Programme Board will be responsible for making decisions on starting, modifying and terminating interventions." (D0003842.odt, Option 3)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: EPICS uses a combination of contracts (for technical assistance and MERL), contribution agreements (with UNDP), and accountable grants (to NGOs/CSOs). This allows flexibility to fund both institutional support and civil society activities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a Programme Board that oversees multiple components: technical assistance contracts, UNDP contribution agreements, and grants to CSOs. This structure enables adaptive responses to reform opportunities or setbacks.
how_mechanism.quote: "Option 3 (recommended): A flexible governance programme, able to fund a broad set of interventions... This option can be delivered by four components: (a) a contract with a supplier for monitoring, evaluation, research and learning; (b) a contract with a technical assistance supplier; (c) a contribution agreement with UNDP; and (d) accountable grant agreement(s) with NGOs/CSOs." (D0003842.odt, Options)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Accountable Grant Agreements with NGOs/CSOs allow sub-granting to other Palestinian CSOs, but this requires FCDO permission.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: A Programme Board is explicitly mentioned as responsible for decision-making on interventions. The addendum also introduces a UK-based Governance Advisor to lead external engagement and support the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO).
