risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past technical assistance in India (e.g., support for Insolvency Code implementation, PPP frameworks) demonstrated that success requires: (1) close collaboration with clients from initiation to recommendations; (2) sustained follow-up post-task completion; (3) demand-driven, targeted assistance. The programme builds on these lessons by embedding capacity building and strategic partnerships.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates flexible delivery plans, regular reviews, and adaptive management to respond to emerging issues—lessons from past rigid structures. It also prioritizes areas where UK has proven credibility (e.g., financial sector reforms) and avoids sectors with low political will.
risks_lessons.quote: "The effectiveness of technical assistance (TA) has been mixed... Key parameters that influenced success are as follows: the technical quality of Economic and Sector Work (ESW) and Technical Assistance (TA) influenced their effectiveness; close collaboration with clients... was important for ESW and TA to be effective; sustained follow-up after the completion of the tasks... was important for effectiveness. The model envisaged for this programme... is well aligned with these findings." (D0004524.odt, Strategic Case) and "Risk Register: The programme has identified 7 risks across 5 categories... The risk register will be regularly monitored and updated on a monthly basis." (D0004524.odt, Risks)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme expects to mobilize additional private sector capital (e.g., through green bonds and City of London investments) and align with India’s $1.9 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline, though specific leverage targets are not quantified.
financial_details.quote: "The business case is for up to £4.5 million, but ODA budgets only for 2023/24 have been confirmed, of which £1.5 million ODA funding in 2023/24 has been internally allocated for technical cooperation... Going forward, the team also expects to access partial funding from... Non-ODA (allocation of £1.25m in FY2023/24 confirmed); Centres of Expertise (£1m allocation for FY2023/24 confirmed)." (D0004524.odt, Financial Case) and "The programme will provide up to £1.5m ODA in technical cooperation in 2023/24, with funding allocations for the following two years to be confirmed, subject to a maximum of £4.5 million over 3 years." (D0004524.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: UK-Central Asia Green Inclusive Growth Fund (GIG)
metadata.quote: The programme will directly contribute to the Central Asia NSIG Strategy, providing key activities under the Prosperity pillar to create more open, resilient, and internationally integrated economies benefiting Central Asia’s citizens (D0005878.odt, Programme summary).
metadata.duration_source: AMP Start Date: 12/07/2023; AMP End Date: 30/05/2029 (D0005878.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: GIG is a financing mechanism (establishing Central Asia’s first SME private equity/venture capital fund) combined with capacity building (business development services for SMEs) and policy influence (technical assistance for regulatory reforms). It aims to drive green, inclusive economic growth by investing in SMEs while improving their capability and the enabling environment.
what_objectives.q1_source: GIG will drive Central Asia’s independence, economic resilience, and support inclusion by developing and investing in the region’s small and medium enterprises (SME). To do this, GIG will establish Central Asia’s first SME private equity/venture capital fund (PE/VC), investing in high-potential firms, providing much needed green finance to support Central Asia’s green transition. (D0005878.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 2,200 firms trained across the region (D0005878.odt, Component 1)
8,500 new, sustainable, and green jobs created (D0005878.odt, Expected Impact and Results)
Establishment of Central Asia’s first SME private equity/venture capital fund (D0005878.odt, Programme summary)
£9m development capital grant to establish a SME equity investment finance facility (D0005878.odt, Component 2)
Policy/regulatory changes to enable PE/VC funds in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan (D0005878.odt, Component 3)
Emission reductions due to supported firm activity (D0005878.odt, Expected Impact and Results)
Total funding leveraged by FCDO (public and private) (D0005878.odt, Expected Impact and Results)
what_objectives.summary: GIG aims to create a vibrant SME sector in Central Asia through a mix of direct investment, capacity building, and policy reforms to drive green, inclusive economic growth and reduce dependency on Russia/China.
what_objectives.quote: Through SME-led growth, the economies of Central Asia will be diversified which will promote their resilience and sovereignty. (D0005878.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: Turkmenistan (limited inclusion due to data constraints)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Central Asia is described as having undiversified economies heavily dependent on Russia/China, with weak private sectors, political economy challenges, and exposure to climate risks. The programme itself is rated as 'Major' risk.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major (D0005878.odt, Summary Sheet); The region finds itself at a crossroads... the depth of Russia’s ties, combined with the region’s undiversified economies presents challenges. (D0005878.odt, Context)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory (lack of PE/VC regulations in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan)
weak institutions (low SME management capacity, poor policy environment)
data limitations (Turkmenistan lacks reliable economic data)
climate risks (flooding expected to reduce GDP by 1.3% by 2060)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Regulatory gaps prevent PE/VC funds from operating in 3/5 countries; state dominance stunts private sector growth; climate change threatens agriculture (20% of Tajikistan’s GDP); and reliance on Russian remittances (up to 50.9% of Tajikistan’s GDP) creates vulnerability to external shocks.
where_context.quote: Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan are lacking a full sweep of policy and regulatory changes to enable private equity investments... existing funds are domiciled outside of these countries. (D0005878.odt, Lack of investment of growth finance in the region)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains oversight and approval authority, with local implementers delivering components. The Fund of Funds (FoF) manager (likely international) will have investment decision-making power, while local firms receive capacity building.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (2,200 firms trained in business development)
mentorship (specialized support for green/women-led businesses)
institutional strengthening (policy/regulatory reforms for PE/VC enabling environment)
business advisory services (demand-led BDS modules)

partner_organizations.name: Astana International Financial Center (AIFC)
partner_organizations.role: Potential domicile for the Fund of Funds (FoF)

partner_organizations.name: Highland Capital, Sturgeon Capital, MOST Ventures
partner_organizations.role: Existing VC funds active in Central Asia (potential sub-partners)

partner_organizations.name: Local SMEs (2,200 firms)
partner_organizations.role: Direct beneficiaries of training and investment

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan
partner_organizations.role: Policy/regulatory counterparts for Component 3

partner_organizations.name: EIP (Enterprise and Innovation Programme) graduates
partner_organizations.role: Potential pipeline for GIG investments

who_partners.quote: GIG’s interventions form part of UK’s wider ODA offer in Central Asia, and complements existing bilateral programmes... (D0005878.odt, Proposed programme)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: £7m for business development services (likely grants/contracts); £9m as a development capital grant to establish a Fund of Funds (FoF) for equity investments; £2m for policy/technical assistance (grants). The FoF will make equity/quasi-equity investments in SMEs on market/near-market terms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FoF will be managed by a selected fund manager (likely international) with sub-funds/funds in Central Asia. Component 1 (BDS) and Component 3 (policy) will have dedicated implementers per country, but the FoF operates regionally. FCDO retains oversight.
how_mechanism.quote: It will be the first such FoF model created in Central Asia and aims to be a key driver of expanding PE/VC in the region. (D0005878.odt, Component 2)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: FCDO will establish governance and oversight during inception, but post-implementation, the FoF will operate independently. No steering committee or board is explicitly mentioned.
how_governance.quote: Over the five years of implementation, FCDO will establish appropriate governance and oversight of the SME financing facility so that after this BC ends and FCDO’s active role ends, the facility will continue investing in SMEs... (D0005878.odt, Component 2)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Components are country-adapted, and the policy facility (Component 3) is designed to be flexible to address emerging bottlenecks. However, core allocations (£7m BDS, £9m FoF, £2m policy) are fixed.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The policy facility (Component 3) can pick up specific issues identified during implementation. The BDS component will use demand-led assessments to inform new modules.
how_flexibility.quote: By design, this facility [Component 3] will remain flexible as the programme begins, picking up specific issues identified during the implementation of components i.) and ii.). (D0005878.odt, Component 3)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → FoF Manager (international) → Local Funds/SMEs; FCDO → Country Implementers (BDS/Policy) → SMEs
how_efficiency.quote: FCDO’s £9m is expected to achieve at least leverage 1:1 from the selected FoF manager... (D0005878.odt, Component 2)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The FoF model was chosen to address the critical gap in risk capital for SMEs (only £150-155m invested in 5,000 startups over 5 years) and to demonstrate proof-of-concept for PE/VC in Central Asia. The mixed approach (BDS + FoF + policy) reflects lessons from EIP, which showed demand for both capacity building and financing.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (leverage 1:1 private capital; revolving fund for sustainability)
risk-mitigation (diversified portfolio to offset high failure risk of SMEs)
experience (builds on EIP’s success with 831 businesses trained)
partner-capacity (uses AIFC’s regulatory environment in Kazakhstan)
equity (targets women-led businesses and marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High failure rate of SME investments in a nascent PE/VC market
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Portfolio approach and revolving fund to sustain impact; technical assistance to improve SME capacity

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory barriers in Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan/Uzbekistan preventing FoF operations
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: £2m policy component to address bottlenecks; domiciling FoF in Kazakhstan (AIFC) as a workaround

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited local capacity to manage equity investments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Capacity building for local fund managers and SMEs; partnership with existing VC funds (Highland, Sturgeon, MOST)

why_rationale.quote: GIG is closely aligned with the International Development Strategy... Plans to create PE/VC funds with trusted IFIs and local implementers will enable engagement with financial intermediation... (D0005878.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Regulatory gaps in Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan/Uzbekistan limit the domiciling of funds locally, requiring the FoF to be based in Kazakhstan (AIFC). Political economy constraints (state dominance, elite capture) necessitate partnerships with trusted IFIs and gradual introduction of chargeable BDS services to ensure sustainability.
q27_constraints_detail: No PE/VC regulations in 3/5 countries → FoF domiciled in Kazakhstan
State-dominated economies → Need for IFI partnerships to ensure market credibility
Weak SME management capacity → Embedded training/mentorship in BDS component
Data limitations (Turkmenistan) → Exclusion from some activities
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to combine financing (addressing the £150-155m gap for 5,000 startups) with capacity building (only 19.3% of SMEs innovate) and policy reform (no PE/VC regulations) drives the three-component structure (BDS + FoF + Policy). The regional scope requires a FoF model to operate across currencies/borders.
q28_linkages: Financing gap (WHAT) → FoF structure (HOW) to pool and leverage capital
Low SME innovation (WHAT) → BDS component (HOW) with training/mentorship
Regulatory barriers (WHERE) → Policy component (HOW) to enable FoF operations
Green transition goal (WHAT) → Specialist green business advisory (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (FoF model for leverage/scale) with equity (targeting women-led businesses, rural areas, and returning migrants). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher transaction costs for small-ticket investments (£15k–£500k) to reach underserved SMEs; (2) Gradual introduction of chargeable BDS services to ensure sustainability while maintaining accessibility.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed-vs-inclusion: Demand-led BDS design may slow rollout but ensures relevance
expertise-vs-ownership: International FoF manager provides expertise, but local funds/implementers retain delivery roles
cost-vs-reach: Small-ticket investments (£15k–£500k) increase reach but reduce economies of scale
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight during inception (FCDO establishes governance) but allows for lighter-touch management post-implementation via the revolving FoF structure.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Low local capacity for PE/VC management necessitates: (1) International FoF manager; (2) Embedded BDS training; (3) Policy component to build enabling environment. Local partners (SMEs, governments) are primarily recipients of capacity building.
intersections.quote: The knowledge and relationships gained will create a platform for future British Investment Partnership (BII) projects in the region... (D0005878.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

key_programme_risks: High failure rate of SME investments in an untested PE/VC market
Regulatory barriers in 3/5 countries preventing FoF operations
Political economy risks (state dominance, elite capture)
Climate change impacts on agriculture (20% of Tajikistan’s GDP)
Dependency on Russian remittances (up to 50.9% of GDP in Tajikistan)
Limited local capacity to absorb equity investments
Potential market distortion from state-owned enterprises
Exchange rate volatility affecting cross-border investments

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Portfolio diversification; revolving fund structure; technical assistance to improve SME resilience
Domiciling FoF in Kazakhstan (AIFC); £2m policy component for reforms
Partnership with existing VC funds (Highland, Sturgeon); embedded training
Focus on green businesses; support for climate-resilient sectors (e.g., agri-tech)
Job creation to absorb returning migrants; support for migrant-led businesses

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for flexible policy components to adapt to regulatory gaps
Importance of local partnerships to navigate political economy constraints
Gradual introduction of market-based services (e.g., chargeable BDS) to avoid dependency
Leveraging multilateral platforms (e.g., AIFC) to mitigate country-specific risks
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: EIP (2019–2024) demonstrated strong demand for BDS (831 businesses trained, 65% women-led) but identified financing as a critical gap. Key lessons: (1) Need to complement capacity building with financing; (2) Importance of inclusion-targeting; (3) Value of demand-led, sector-agnostic training; (4) Later-stage partnerships with donors expanded reach.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added financing component (FoF) to address EIP’s missed opportunity
Expanded geographic scope beyond Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan to all Central Asia
Included policy component to tackle regulatory barriers identified in EIP
Enhanced inclusion focus (women, youth, migrants) based on EIP’s gender outcomes
risks_lessons.quote: Lack of financing for the highest potential graduates was a possible missed opportunity under EIP... Not offering financing to the firms with the highest potential may represent a missed opportunity to deepen EIP’s job creation and wider impact. (D0005878.odt, Lessons from EIP)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: 1:1 minimum leverage expected from FoF manager; additional private sector leverage at fund level (D0005878.odt, Component 2)
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: £9m capital (FoF grant); £7m revenue (BDS); £2m revenue (policy)
financial_details.quote: FCDO’s £9m is expected to achieve at least leverage 1:1 from the selected FoF manager, doubling the financing available for innovative SMEs... (D0005878.odt, Component 2)

metadata.programme_name: Chevening Scholarships Programme
metadata.duration_text: Covering period from the start FY22/23 to the end FY27/28

quote.text: "Chevening is the FCDO’s flagship international scholarship programme for future global leaders. It supports exceptional scholars from 160 countries and territories around the world with fully funded master’s degrees at top UK universities."

duration_source.text: "Covering period from the start FY22/23 to the end FY27/28."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The Chevening Scholarships Programme is a capacity-building initiative that provides fully funded master’s degrees and fellowships to future global leaders. It aims to enhance the UK’s influence and diplomatic ability, increase trade and business links, and support development in target countries. The programme combines elements of capacity building, policy influence, and service delivery through scholarships and fellowships.

q1_source.text: "Chevening is one of the UK’s most important soft-power instruments. With an established reputation as a world-leading, global scholarships programme, Chevening creates lasting positive relationships with future leaders, influencers and decision-makers across the world."

q3_expected_outputs.output: 55,000 alumni with strong affinity to the UK
1,400 scholarships per year
200 fellowships per year
110 active Chevening alumni associations worldwide
£1 billion net additional Gross Value Added to the UK economy (1983-2015)
£314 million additional investment in the UK (1983-2015)
96% of funding supports scholars from ODA-eligible countries
11,000 users on the Chevening alumni engagement platform (Q3 2022)

what_objectives.summary: The Chevening Scholarships Programme is a strategic, long-term investment in human capital that enhances the UK’s global influence, fosters trade and business links, and supports development in target countries. It achieves this through fully funded scholarships and fellowships for future leaders, creating a global network of alumni who advocate for the UK and drive positive change in their home countries.

quote.text: "Chevening is a long-term, strategic investment in human capital – by harnessing the expertise and resources of the UK’s world-leading Higher Education (HE) sector, it invests in the academic development of young leaders and supports them to achieve positions of influence later in their professional careers."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme has an overall risk rating of 'Minor' and operates in a wide range of countries, including stable and developing contexts. The risk is managed through established processes and a strong alumni network that supports the UK’s diplomatic and development goals.

q5_source.text: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor"

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme requires scholars to travel by air, which poses some environmental risks, though this is considered acceptable for a long-term educational experience. Political and economic instability in some target countries may affect the selection and return of scholars, but the programme’s global reach and established processes mitigate these risks.

quote.text: "The Chevening programme represents some risk in terms of direct impact on environmental protection and climate, given the requirement for awardees to travel by air to the UK and return home at the end of the programme."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO, based in the UK, holds decision-making power over the programme’s strategic direction, budget allocation, and overall management. Posts (UK missions overseas) are responsible for selecting scholars based on local priorities, but final decisions and programme governance rest with the FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on equality, diversity, and consent for scholars and fellows
welfare support and events programme for scholars in the UK
alumni engagement activities, including the Chevening Alumni Programme Fund (CAPF)
partnerships with universities and organizations to co-fund scholarships and provide in-kind benefits
disability support, including additional funding and reasonable adjustments

partner_organizations.name: Chevening Secretariat (contracted provider)
partner_organizations.role: administration of the programme, including communications, scholar selection, placement, and alumni engagement

partner_organizations.name: UK Universities
partner_organizations.role: host scholars and fellows, provide tuition fee waivers and in-kind benefits, deliver fellowship programmes

partner_organizations.name: Corporate Partners (e.g., charities, businesses, governments)
partner_organizations.role: co-fund scholar places, typically covering 50% of the cost of their scholars

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Posts (Embassies, High Commissions, Consulates)
partner_organizations.role: select scholars based on local priorities, engage with alumni, and promote the programme

partner_organizations.name: Universities Wales
partner_organizations.role: partnership to promote Welsh universities in India, Vietnam, and Canada

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: collaboration on promoting UK universities through the "StudyUK" initiative

quote.text: "Chevening is administered via a contracted provider, white-labelled as the Chevening Secretariat. The current contract is performing effectively, with a new contract for 2023-27 finding further opportunities to build on success and find further opportunities for innovation and greater VfM."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The Chevening programme is delivered through a contracted service provider (Chevening Secretariat), which manages all administrative aspects of the programme, including communications, scholar selection, placement, and alumni engagement. The contract is awarded through an open competition process and is subject to Public Contract Regulations.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a central ‘hub and spoke’ model, with the UK-based Chevening Secretariat (contractor) working closely with the FCDO in London and at Posts overseas. This model ensures efficient and rigorous delivery, with the Secretariat handling day-to-day operations and the FCDO providing oversight and strategic direction.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The open competition for the administration contract is designed to drive better value for money and ensure the selection of a capable and cost-competitive supplier. This approach aligns with Public Contract Regulations and the programme’s category strategy, allowing the FCDO to leverage market interest and innovation.

quote.text: "Historically, all procurement relating to Scholarship programmes has sat under FCDO (previously FCO) Commercial (Corporate). Commercial (Corporate) governance is such that approach and spend are approved by the FCDO Commercial Assurance Board, Operations Committee and CO/HMT (as required)."

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Scholarships and fellowships are allocated based on a country-specific formula that considers the Register of British Interests (30%), population size (30%), programme success (20%), and a discretionary Directorate element (20%). Posts select scholars based on local priorities, but the overall budget and allocation are approved by the FCDO.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Chevening Programme Board scrutinizes the risk register at least quarterly. The Board includes representatives from the FCDO and the contracted provider, ensuring oversight and alignment with strategic priorities. The 2023-2027 administration contract also includes requirements for the delivery partner to adhere to FCDO policies on safeguarding, equality, and environmental impact.

quote.text: "Chevening reviews and updates its risk register at least quarterly, when it is scrutinised by the Chevening Programme Board."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme allows for some flexibility in budget allocation through the discretionary Directorate element (20% of the award budget), which Geographic Directors can use to align with geostrategic priorities. However, significant changes to the contract scope or value would require re-running the tender process, as per Public Contract Regulations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme can adjust priorities through the annual allocation process, where Posts and Geographic Directors can realign funding based on evolving strategic needs. However, material changes to the contract (e.g., scope or budget) require approval from the FCDO and potentially HMT, which may involve re-running the procurement process.

quote.text: "Strong consideration has been given to the context of (a) the ongoing retender of the joint Chevening and Marshall Administration Contract and anticipated award in Spring 2023, and (b) Spending Review Settlement. As such, options that would result in material change to the 2023–2027 administration contract (e.g. value of the contractor scope of the services), have not been proposed."

q21_management_costs_source.text: "The value of the administration services contract has historically been less than 10% of the total programme budget, which we have sought to maintain in the 2023-2027 contract through introduction of a price cap."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Chevening Secretariat (contractor) → Scholars/Fellows. The Secretariat acts as the primary implementer, with Posts (FCDO overseas missions) playing a key role in scholar selection and engagement.

quote.text: "The supplier to strive to achieve the best value for money in all purchases required under the contract, including use of procurement processes that are proportionate to the size and risk of the spend."

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Delivery through a contracted service provider (joint Chevening and Marshall)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue to run the Chevening programme in approximately 160 countries, with administration services provided by a delivery contractor. This option includes consolidating the Chevening and Marshall programmes under a single contract to achieve efficiencies.

Bring the administration of the Chevening programme in-house, employing internal FCDO resources to manage the programme. This would require a significant increase in headcount and the development of new systems and capabilities.
Wind down the programme, which would result in significant reputational risk and diminished soft power influence for the UK.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (delivery through a contracted service provider) was recommended because it offers the best value for money (VfM) in delivering key outcomes related to economics, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. This option recognizes the programme’s current achievements and responds to recommendations for continuous improvement in programme design and management. It also aligns with Public Contract Regulations, the programme’s category strategy, and the interests of the supply market. The consolidation of Chevening and Marshall programmes under a single contract is expected to drive further efficiencies and innovation.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (avoiding reputational and operational risks associated with in-house delivery or programme wind-down)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Changes in supplier leading to disruption of service delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Include an appropriate transition/mobilisation period (6 months) in the contract to ensure smooth handover between suppliers.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of clarity by the supplier on each programme’s needs and discrete identity (Chevening vs. Marshall)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Design the contract with discrete requirements, evaluation panels, and contract management structures to maintain the unique identity and needs of each programme.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial and legal risk if material changes are made to the contract post-award
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Incorporate flexibility and scalability within the contract design to allow for reasonable adjustments (e.g., changes in cohort size or budget drawdown) without requiring a full retender.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational impact on FCDO’s relationship with potential implementing partners if the tender is re-run
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ensure the Business Case is presented to the Investment Appraisal and Delivery Committee (IADC) as soon as possible to avoid delays and reputational damage.

quote.text: "Option 1 is recommended based on offering the best VfM to deliver key outcomes with regards to economics, efficiencies, and cost effectiveness. The option both recognises the current achievements of the Chevening programme, and responds to recommendations for continuous improvement in programme design and management."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope of the programme (operating in 160 countries and territories) requires a delivery structure that can manage diverse and complex operational environments. This necessitates a centralized administration model (Chevening Secretariat) to ensure consistency, efficiency, and compliance across regions, while allowing Posts to tailor engagement and selection to local contexts.
q27_constraints_detail: The need to operate in both stable and fragile contexts requires robust risk management and safeguarding policies, which are best handled by a specialized contractor with experience in global programme delivery.

The requirement to maintain a prestigious and consistent global brand (Chevening) necessitates centralized management of communications, selection, and alumni engagement, which would be difficult to achieve through a decentralized or in-house model.

The programme’s reliance on partnerships with UK universities and corporate sponsors requires a dedicated team to manage these relationships effectively, which is facilitated by the contracted Secretariat.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—enhancing the UK’s influence, increasing trade and business links, and supporting development—require a delivery structure that can build and maintain long-term relationships with alumni, universities, and partners. The ‘hub and spoke’ model (central Secretariat + Posts) is designed to balance global consistency with local adaptability, ensuring that scholars are selected based on both UK priorities and local development needs.
q28_linkages: The goal of enhancing UK influence and diplomatic ability is supported by the Secretariat’s centralized alumni engagement and partnership management, which ensures a cohesive global network of Chevening alumni.

The objective of increasing trade and business links is facilitated by the Secretariat’s ability to leverage corporate partnerships and promote the UK’s higher education sector globally, in collaboration with Posts and the British Council.

The development objective is operationalized through the country-specific allocation formula and Post-led scholar selection, which ensures that scholarships align with local development priorities and contribute to sustainable outcomes.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency through its scholar selection process, which prioritizes merit and leadership potential while ensuring diversity and inclusion. For example, the programme provides additional support for scholars with disabilities and aims to reach marginalized groups within countries. However, the efficiency of centralized administration (e.g., through the Secretariat) is prioritized to maintain cost-effectiveness and scalability, which may limit the extent of localized adaptability.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.description: The use of a single contracted provider (Chevening Secretariat) ensures efficiency and consistency but may reduce the ability of Posts to fully tailor the programme to ultra-local needs without approval from the centre.

Maintaining Chevening’s reputation as a prestigious, world-leading scholarship programme requires rigorous selection criteria, which may inadvertently exclude candidates from the most marginalized backgrounds who lack access to quality undergraduate education or professional networks.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Cost efficiency vs. alumni engagement depth
q29_tradeoffs_detail.description: The programme invests in alumni engagement platforms and events to sustain long-term relationships, but budget constraints (e.g., flat-cash settlement) may limit the depth or frequency of these activities, particularly in lower-priority countries.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s low overall risk rating (‘Minor’) allows for a quarterly oversight intensity through the Chevening Programme Board, rather than more intensive or embedded management. However, risks specific to the contracted delivery model (e.g., supplier changes or lack of clarity on programme needs) necessitate robust contract management and transition planning to mitigate potential disruptions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The programme’s capacity-building objectives—such as training scholars on equality, diversity, and consent, and providing welfare support—shape the roles of the Chevening Secretariat and Posts. The Secretariat is responsible for delivering these components centrally (e.g., through pre-departure services and UK-based events), while Posts focus on local engagement and scholar selection, ensuring that capacity-building is both standardized and contextually relevant.

quote.text: "Chevening is a long-term, strategic investment in human capital – by harnessing the expertise and resources of the UK’s world-leading Higher Education (HE) sector, it invests in the academic development of young leaders and supports them to achieve positions of influence later in their professional careers."

key_programme_risks.risk: Reputational risk to the UK if the programme is perceived as diminishing in scale or quality
key_programme_risks.description: Reductions in the scale of Chevening could negatively impact diplomatic relations if perceived as signalling a diminution of the UK’s interest in or commitment to affected regions.

key_programme_risks.risk: Financial sustainability due to flat-cash settlement and inflation
key_programme_risks.description: The flat-cash settlement across the Spending Review period represents a decrease in real terms, as costs are subject to high levels of inflation in the UK. This may limit the programme’s ability to maintain current levels of scholarships and engagement.

key_programme_risks.risk: Supplier performance and transition risks
key_programme_risks.description: Changes in the contracted supplier could disrupt service delivery if insufficient transition time is allowed. The programme mitigates this through a 6-month mobilisation period and robust contract management.

key_programme_risks.risk: Environmental impact of scholar travel
key_programme_risks.description: The requirement for scholars to travel by air to the UK and return home contributes to the programme’s carbon footprint. The 2023-2027 contract includes requirements to reduce climate and environmental impact, such as exploring digital engagement alternatives.

key_programme_risks.risk: Equality and safeguarding risks
key_programme_risks.description: The programme must ensure that scholars and fellows are protected from harm and discrimination. This is addressed through safeguarding training, a Code of Conduct, and disciplinary policies.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk from perceived diminution of the programme
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Maintain the programme’s global reach and prestige through consistent funding levels (where possible) and proactive communication about its strategic value. The 2023-2027 contract includes flexibility to adjust cohort sizes based on budget availability.

The contract includes a price cap to control administration costs (less than 10% of the total budget) and explores efficiencies through consolidation with the Marshall programme. Partnership income (£13m/year) is also leveraged to offset budget pressures.

The contract includes a 6-month mobilisation period to ensure smooth transitions between suppliers. The Secretariat is also required to maintain detailed documentation and knowledge transfer processes.

The 2023-2027 contract requires the delivery partner to reduce the programme’s climate and environmental impact, including exploring digital and virtual engagement alternatives (e.g., online interviews).

All scholars and fellows receive training on equality, diversity, and consent. The Secretariat has a safeguarding policy, disciplinary framework, and reporting mechanisms to address misconduct. The contract also requires the supplier to embed equality and accessibility into programme design.

fcas_specific_lessons: The programme operates in a range of contexts, including fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS), where scholar safety and return may be at risk. Lessons include the importance of robust welfare support and flexible policies (e.g., pregnancy and maternity provisions) to ensure scholars can complete their studies even in challenging environments.

In FCAS, Posts play a critical role in selecting scholars who are well-positioned to contribute to local development and stability. The programme’s requirement for scholars to return home for at least two years helps mitigate brain drain and supports long-term recovery.

The programme’s global reach includes small island developing states and disputed territories, where traditional recruitment channels may be limited. The Secretariat’s centralized communications and outreach efforts help ensure these regions are not overlooked.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme has been running for 40 years, during which it has refined its delivery model to balance efficiency with impact. Key lessons include the value of a centralized administration model (Chevening Secretariat) for maintaining consistency and brand prestige, while allowing Posts to tailor engagement to local priorities. The introduction of fellowships (2005, 2014) and partnerships with universities and corporate sponsors has expanded the programme’s reach and value for money. The 2010 budget cut demonstrated the importance of flexible contract design to accommodate changes in funding levels without disrupting core operations.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2023-2027 contract incorporates several design changes based on past learning, including: (1) consolidation with the Marshall programme to achieve efficiencies; (2) a price cap to control administration costs; (3) increased focus on partnership income to leverage additional funding; (4) stronger requirements for safeguarding, equality, and environmental sustainability; and (5) greater flexibility to adjust cohort sizes and budget allocations in response to changing priorities or financial constraints.

quote.text: "The delivery route is well-established, with current programme management conducted through a central ‘hub and spoke’ model, with a UK-based ‘Chevening Secretariat’ (the Contractor) working closely and effectively with the FCDO both in London and at Post. This model has been found to be efficient and rigorous by internal audits, post and key stakeholders."

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme leverages £13 million annually in partnership income, equivalent to 18% additional benefit. This includes £3.3 million in direct income from corporate partners and £9.1 million in in-kind benefits from university fee waivers. For every £1 invested in Chevening, an estimated £1.38 of economic benefit is generated for the UK.

quote.text: "Chevening has a total annual budget of £59.4m for 2022/23, of which 97% is ODA and 3% is non-ODA. FCDO funding is supplemented by partnership income, which for 21/22 came to £3.5m (budgeted at £3.3m p/a from FY22/23 onwards) in direct income and £9.1m of in-kind benefit from university fee waivers."

metadata.programme_name: UK guarantee support to The Asian Development Bank’s Innovative Financing Facility for Climate in Asia and the Pacific (IFCAP)
metadata.quote: "The proposed $300m UK guarantee to support ADB’s new IFCAP initiative is closely aligned with the FCDO/UK policy priorities and wider HMG programmatic work within the region." (D0006596.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "AMPEndDate: Approximately 2049." (D0006596.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes a $300m UK guarantee to the Asian Development Bank's Innovative Financing Facility for Climate in Asia and the Pacific (IFCAP), unlocking up to $1.8bn of additional climate finance for middle-income countries in the Indo-Pacific region. It aims to scale climate finance through a multi-donor mechanism that leverages ADB's balance sheet to increase lending capacity for climate mitigation and adaptation projects.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The proposed $300m UK guarantee to support ADB’s new IFCAP initiative is closely aligned with the FCDO/UK policy priorities and wider HMG programmatic work within the region. It will mobilise a large volume of climate finance, focused on both adaptation and mitigation, for countries in the Indo-Pacific region." (D0006596.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Unlock $1.8bn of additional climate finance from ADB for middle-income countries in Asia and the Pacific
Enable ADB to exceed its $100bn climate finance ambition for 2019-2030 (reaching $100bn-$113bn)
Two-thirds of IFCAP climate finance directed towards adaptation and resilience investments
Support climate-vulnerable countries including Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and fragile states
Strengthen ADB's climate policies, including Paris Alignment by 2025 and nature mainstreaming
what_objectives.summary: The programme leverages a UK guarantee to catalyze significant climate finance through ADB's IFCAP mechanism, focusing on both mitigation and adaptation in climate-vulnerable countries while strengthening ADB's climate policies and institutional capacity.
what_objectives.quote: "Through IFCAP, development partners will be able to contribute a combination of grants and guarantees to the ADB, which will unlock new climate-focused lending from the Bank. The proposed $300m UK guarantee to support IFCAP would unlock up to $1.8bn of additional, affordable climate finance from the ADB for middle-income countries in Asia and the Pacific." (D0006596.odt, Programme summary)

countries_regions: Specifically: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Philippines, Uzbekistan, Nepal, Georgia, Vietnam, Cambodia, Mongolia, Papua New Guinea, Thailand, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Timor-Leste, Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Bhutan, Lao PDR, Solomon Islands, Maldives, Fiji, Palau, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Tonga, Samoa
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk in the business case, reflecting a balanced assessment of financial risks (e.g., 42% chance of >£100m demand on the UK guarantee) and the stable institutional framework of ADB as a AAA-rated multilateral development bank.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006596.odt, SummarySheet)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate risks (e.g., extreme weather, sea-level rise) directly threaten development gains and increase financing needs for adaptation. Weak institutions in some countries (e.g., fragile states like Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea) may affect absorption capacity for climate finance. Debt sustainability concerns limit borrowing capacity for some countries (e.g., Pakistan, Sri Lanka), requiring concessional terms. Political economy challenges (e.g., coal dependency in Indonesia, Vietnam) may slow energy transition investments.
where_context.quote: "Climate change and environmental degradation acutely threaten development gains in the Indo-Pacific region. Estimates suggest that in East Asia and the Pacific, 7.5 million more people could fall below the extreme poverty line due to climate change by 2030, while the equivalent figure for South Asia is 35.7 million." (D0006596.odt, The Problem Statement)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: ADB (a multilateral institution with Northern shareholders like the UK, US, and Japan) retains decision-making authority over the unlocked funds, though the UK and other donors provide strategic oversight through IFCAP's governance structure. The UK's influence is proportional to its financial contribution (e.g., 10% of guarantees = 10% of loss-sharing).
q10_capacity_building_details: Supporting ADB's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) development and implementation
Strengthening ADB's climate co-benefits methodology and nature mainstreaming
Promoting Paris Alignment by 2025 and climate-resilient debt clauses
Technical assistance for project pipeline development (e.g., through PIDG partnership)
Knowledge-sharing on safeguards and gender/disability inclusion

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and recipient of the guarantee; responsible for unlocking and disbursing climate finance

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Primary funder ($300m guarantee) and strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: United States
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner (expected to be a large guarantor)

partner_organizations.name: Japan
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner (expected to be a large guarantor + grant funding)

partner_organizations.name: South Korea
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner ($100m guarantee committed)

partner_organizations.name: Sweden
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner (smaller guarantor, experienced in guarantees)

partner_organizations.name: Denmark
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner (smaller guarantor)

partner_organizations.name: Italy
partner_organizations.role: Founding partner (expected commitment from new climate fund)

partner_organizations.name: Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG)
partner_organizations.role: Technical assistance and upstream support for project pipeline

who_partners.quote: "The Founding Partners of IFCAP are expected to be the US, Japan, Korea, Sweden, Denmark, Italy, and the UK. The US and Japan are expected to be the largest guarantors of IFCAP." (D0006596.odt, The proposed intervention)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides a $300m (£232m) portfolio guarantee to ADB's IFCAP mechanism. This first-loss guarantee protects ADB against defaults on a reference portfolio of loans to 29 countries, enabling ADB to unlock $4 of new climate finance for every $1 guaranteed. The guarantee is contingent—ODA is only scored if called (expected loss ~£136m).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IFCAP is governed by ADB with annual meetings of guarantor partners for strategic oversight. No project-by-project approval is required. The UK and other donors share losses pro-rata based on their guarantee contributions. ADB retains full operational control over lending decisions, while donors influence strategic priorities (e.g., adaptation focus, exclusion of wealthier borrowers).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (ADB is the sole multilateral partner for IFCAP)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: ADB was selected due to its established role as the largest MDB in Asia-Pacific, its AAA credit rating, and its alignment with UK climate and development priorities. The IFCAP mechanism was co-designed with ADB and other donors to maximize leverage and scale.
how_mechanism.quote: "A $300m UK guarantee contribution to the ADB’s new Innovative Financing Facility for Climate in Asia and the Pacific (IFCAP). Through IFCAP, which the ADB launched at its May 2023 Annual Meeting, development partners can provide grants and/or guarantees to the ADB to enhance the Bank’s climate finance capacity." (D0006596.odt, The proposed intervention)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Guarantors meet annually to oversee IFCAP and provide strategic steer. ADB manages day-to-day operations and lending decisions. The UK and other donors influence priorities through the IFCAP design (e.g., adaptation focus, country exclusions) and loss-sharing arrangements.
how_governance.quote: "Achieved. Simple administrative structure obtained: guarantors will meet once, annually, to oversee IFCAP and provide strategic steers. No project-by-project approval, not lots of new overhead burdens or carve-outs." (D0006596.odt, Table 4 – Progress on design considerations)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are tied to ADB's climate finance portfolio, with country allocations determined by ADB's lending policies. The reference portfolio (29 countries) is fixed, though the exact composition may evolve. Reallocation between mitigation/adaptation is possible within ADB's strategic priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Strategic priorities (e.g., adaptation focus) are set at the IFCAP design stage and can only be adjusted through annual guarantor meetings. ADB retains flexibility in project selection within the agreed climate finance framework.
how_flexibility.quote: "The reference portfolio describes the risks that the IFCAP will take off the ADB balance sheet, it does not dictate where the new climate finance unlocked by IFCAP will be targeted." (D0006596.odt, The proposed intervention)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → ADB (implementer) → end recipients (countries/projects). No additional intermediaries are involved in the guarantee mechanism.
how_efficiency.quote: "A guarantee worth up to $300m. The guarantee has no DEL cost unless called. The expected loss from the guarantee is approximately £136m." (D0006596.odt, SummarySheet)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing
Support bilateral/multi-donor International Climate Finance projects
General Capital Increase (GCI) at ADB
Multiple single-country MDB guarantees (e.g., like India/Indonesia JETP guarantees)
IFCAP portfolio guarantee (selected option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: IFCAP was chosen for its scale (unlocking $1.8bn vs. $1bn-$2bn for single-country guarantees), efficiency (low administrative burden, high leverage of $4:$1), and alignment with UK priorities (regional focus, adaptation emphasis, multilateral leadership). It complements existing UK guarantees (e.g., JETPs) while avoiding upfront ODA costs (contingent liability only).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (high leverage, low admin costs)
risk mitigation (ADB's AAA rating, first-loss structure)
past experience (success with Room to Run guarantee for AfDB)
partner capacity (ADB's strong regional presence and climate finance track record)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High expected loss (~£136m) due to first-loss structure and risky reference portfolio (e.g., Pakistan, Nepal).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversification across 29 countries and risk-sharing with other guarantors (UK bears pro-rata share). ADB retains second-loss position.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Moral hazard: ADB may take on riskier loans knowing guarantees are in place.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: ADB remains exposed to losses beyond the guarantee cap (~$2.5bn total). UK pushed for ADB to retain skin in the game.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited UK control over unlocked funds (ADB decides lending allocations).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strategic design of IFCAP to exclude wealthier borrowers (China, Malaysia) and prioritize adaptation. Annual guarantor meetings for oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other UK climate programmes (e.g., JETPs, CARA).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IFCAP focuses on middle-income countries and adaptation, complementing mitigation-focused JETPs and grant-based CARA.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency ($4 unlocked per $1 guaranteed, minimal admin)
effectiveness (scale of climate finance, alignment with Paris goals)
equity (focus on vulnerable countries and adaptation)
why_rationale.quote: "On balance, we conclude that IFCAP is the best way to unlock additional high quality climate finance for the Indo-Pacific region at scale. [...] A portfolio guarantee mechanism, such as IFCAP, is better suited to deliver greater scale and leverage across multiple countries and multiple sectors." (D0006596.odt, Options Appraisal)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Indo-Pacific's climate vulnerability and middle-income status constrain partner selection to ADB (as the dominant regional MDB) and limit direct UK bilateral engagement (due to ODA eligibility rules). The need for scale and speed favors multilateral mechanisms over bilateral programmes.
q27_constraints_detail: ODA rules restrict UK grants to low-income countries, making guarantees the only viable instrument for middle-income Indo-Pacific nations.
ADB's regional mandate and AAA rating make it the sole feasible multilateral partner for large-scale climate finance.
Climate risks (e.g., flooding, heatwaves) necessitate ADB's technical expertise in resilience projects.
Fragility in some countries (e.g., Pakistan, Timor-Leste) requires ADB's safeguards and risk management capacity.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to mobilize large-scale climate finance ($1.8bn) for both mitigation and adaptation determines the use of a portfolio guarantee (vs. project-specific grants). The regional scope (29 countries) and ADB's balance sheet constraints necessitate a first-loss structure to maximize leverage ($4:$1).
q28_linkages: Scale objective ($1.8bn) → Portfolio guarantee (not bilateral projects)
Adaptation focus → ADB's regional expertise and safeguards
Middle-income target → Guarantee (not grants) to avoid ODA trade-offs
Speed → Existing ADB mechanisms (not new capital increases)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The design explicitly balances efficiency (high leverage, low admin) with equity (adaptation focus, vulnerable country targeting). Trade-offs include: (1) First-loss structure increases risk but unlocks more finance; (2) ADB-led implementation ensures scale but limits UK control; (3) Regional focus achieves breadth but may dilute country-specific impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion: Rapid scale-up through ADB may bypass local civil society engagement.
expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led ADB retains decision-making power over Southern recipients.
cost vs. reach: High leverage ($4:$1) comes with higher risk (~42% chance of >£100m demand).
adaptation vs. mitigation: Two-thirds focus on adaptation reduces funds for high-impact mitigation projects.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The 'moderate' risk profile (with high financial risk from the guarantee) leads to light-touch oversight (annual meetings) but requires robust ADB safeguards and UK influence on strategic priorities (e.g., adaptation focus).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: ADB's strong climate finance capacity enables it to manage the guarantee, while UK/FCDO provides strategic oversight and pushes for reforms (e.g., Paris Alignment, nature mainstreaming). PIDG's technical assistance addresses pipeline constraints.
intersections.quote: "The UK has provided more MDB guarantees than any other Development Partner [...] and FCDO expertise has played a leading role in shaping the final structure of the IFCAP mechanism." (D0006596.odt, Box 3: UK Experience using MDB guarantees)

key_programme_risks: Financial risk: 42% chance of >£100m demand on the UK guarantee; 72% chance of >£50m demand.
Moral hazard: ADB may take on riskier loans due to guarantee protection.
Additionality: Risk that unlocked finance replaces (rather than adds to) ADB's existing climate lending.
Debt sustainability: New lending could exacerbate debt risks in vulnerable countries (e.g., Pakistan, Sri Lanka).
Implementation capacity: ADB's ability to scale climate projects quickly without compromising quality.
Geopolitical risks: Tensions in the region (e.g., China-India) may affect project selection or implementation.
Climate risks: Increasing extreme weather events may raise project costs or reduce effectiveness.
Safeguards: Weak enforcement in some countries could lead to environmental or social harm.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Diversified reference portfolio (29 countries) and pro-rata loss-sharing with other guarantors. ADB retains second-loss position.
ADB exposed to losses beyond the guarantee cap (~$2.5bn). UK pushed for ADB skin in the game.
IFCAP designed to expand ADB's climate finance from $100bn to $100bn-$115bn. UK secured commitments to exceed targets even in worst-case scenarios.
Blended finance terms for vulnerable countries (e.g., 25-year loans, 5-year grace periods). Exclusion of wealthier borrowers (China, Malaysia).
ADB's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) includes scaling up staff and technical resources. Partnership with PIDG for project pipeline support.
Explicit alignment among IFCAP partners (US, Japan, UK, etc.) on targeting vulnerable countries. UK ensured wealthier/geopolitically sensitive countries (e.g., China) are excluded.
Focus on adaptation and resilience projects (two-thirds of IFCAP funds). ADB's safeguards and climate-proofing standards.
UK lobbying for stronger ADB safeguards (e.g., SEAH policies, disability inclusion). ADB's ongoing safeguards review (2024 completion).

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from ADB's engagement in fragile states (e.g., Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea) highlight the need for flexible financing terms (e.g., longer grace periods) and upstream technical assistance.
Experience with Small Island Developing States (SIDS) in the Pacific demonstrates the importance of climate-resilient debt clauses and disaster risk financing.
UK's previous guarantees (e.g., Room to Run for AfDB) showed that portfolio guarantees can effectively scale finance in FCAS without exacerbating debt risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The UK's experience with the Room to Run guarantee for the African Development Bank (AfDB) demonstrated that portfolio guarantees can mobilize $1bn-$2bn of additional lending with minimal administrative burden. This informed IFCAP's design, including the first-loss structure and annual oversight model. Lessons on moral hazard from Room to Run led to ADB's retained second-loss position in IFCAP.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: IFCAP's design incorporated several lessons: (1) Pro-rata loss-sharing (vs. UK bearing full risk in Room to Run); (2) Explicit adaptation focus (addressing gaps in previous guarantees); (3) Annual guarantor meetings (balancing oversight and efficiency); (4) Exclusion of wealthier borrowers (avoiding criticism from Room to Run).
risks_lessons.quote: "The UK’s leadership on providing guarantees to the MDBs has had a demonstration effect. Other guarantors, including Japan and the US are now committing MDB guarantees for the first time." (D0006596.odt, Box 3: UK Experience using MDB guarantees)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: $4 of new climate finance unlocked for every $1 guaranteed. Total expected leverage: $1.8bn from UK's $300m (£232m) guarantee, with potential for $10bn-$15bn mobilized through IFCAP with all partners.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The $300m guarantee is a contingent liability (capital risk), not revenue expenditure. Expected loss is ~£136m (45% of guarantee value), with no upfront ODA cost unless called.
financial_details.quote: "The guarantee has no DEL cost unless called. The expected loss from the guarantee is approximately £136m." (D0006596.odt, SummarySheet)

metadata.programme_name: The Global Financing Facility for Women, Children and Adolescents - Phase 3

quote.text: "This programme will enable low- and lower-middle-income countries (LMIC) to invest in primary health care systems that deliver for women, children and adolescents."

duration_source.source: D0006423.odt, AMP Start Date and AMP End Date fields
duration_source.text: "AMP Start Date: April 2025", "AMP End Date: March 2030"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme channels UK Official Development Assistance (ODA) into the Global Financing Facility (GFF), a multi-donor trust fund housed within the World Bank. Its core purpose is to catalyze financing for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH-N) in 36 low- and lower-middle-income countries, leveraging World Bank loans and domestic resources to strengthen health systems and deliver essential services.

q1_source.text: "UK ODA will be invested in the Global Financing Facility, a country-led partnership, housed within the World Bank and launched in 2015 to improve Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH-N)."

q3_expected_outputs.output: 70 million more women, children, and adolescents accessing essential life-saving health services by 2030
27 out of 36 current partner countries receiving a second round of support
7 new countries joining the GFF
£100m UK ODA unlocking $8bn in World Bank/IDA financing for women, children, and adolescent health
Expansion of access to family planning and contraceptive services for more than 25 million additional adolescents, girls, and women by 2025
Integration of comprehensive SRHR services as a core part of national health systems in at least 20 additional countries by 2025
Advancement of legal and policy reforms in 10 countries to create more opportunities for women, girls, and adolescents to access SRHR services by 2025
96 million pregnant women with 4+ antenatal care visits (achieved to date)
103 million women with safe delivery care (achieved to date)
500 million users of modern contraceptives, with more than 187 million unintended pregnancies averted (achieved to date)

what_objectives.summary: The GFF Phase 3 aims to scale up financing for RMNCAH-N in LMICs by leveraging World Bank loans and domestic resources, with a focus on strengthening primary health care systems, expanding access to essential services (e.g., antenatal care, contraceptives, skilled delivery), and advancing gender equity and SRHR. The UK’s £100m investment is designed to catalyze $8bn in additional financing, reaching 70 million more women, children, and adolescents by 2030.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending section
quote.text: "This programme will drive forward the UK commitments on Ending Preventable Deaths of Mothers, Babies and Children, and wider priorities on Global Health... Its focus, increasing the amount and efficiency of RMNCAH-N financing, including from other donors, World Bank loans and domestic resources, fills a niche not covered by others in health."

countries_regions: 36 current partner countries (27 receiving second-round support)
Flagship EPD countries for FCDO: Ethiopia, DRC, Sierra Leone, South Sudan, Somalia, Kenya, Malawi, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Nigeria
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in 14 FCAS, including some of the most complex emergency contexts (e.g., Afghanistan, Myanmar), where 60% of preventable maternal deaths and 45% of preventable newborn deaths occur. The overall programme risk rating is classified as 'Major' in the business case.

q5_source.source: D0006423.odt, Overall programme risk rating field and FCAS section
q5_source.text: "Overall programme risk rating: Major", "60% of preventable maternal deaths and 45% of preventable newborn deaths occur in [fragile and conflict-affected] settings."

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and fragility disrupt health service delivery and increase vulnerability to diseases (e.g., malaria, undernutrition). Economic downturns (post-COVID-19, Russia-Ukraine war) reduce fiscal space for health spending, while climate change exacerbates health burdens (e.g., heat stress, water-borne diseases). Opposition to SRHR, including safe abortion and comprehensive sexuality education, undermines progress in adolescent health. Weak health systems and data limitations hinder monitoring and service quality.

quote.text: "Multiple crises—COVID-19, economic, climate and conflict and the rollback on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) threaten progress... In FCAS, 60% of preventable maternal deaths and 45% of preventable newborn deaths occur."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The GFF is housed within the World Bank (a Northern-led institution), and its governance mechanisms (Trust Fund Committee, Investors Group) are dominated by Northern donors, including the UK. While the model is 'country-led' in principle, implementation relies heavily on World Bank systems and processes, with limited independence for Southern partners in decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to countries for investment case development and resource tracking
Support to strengthen health financing systems (e.g., public financial management, expenditure tracking)
Training for civil society organizations (CSOs) on budget advocacy and accountability
SRHR fellows embedded in World Bank regional offices to mainstream SRHR
Flexible technical assistance for health system reforms (e.g., human resources for health, quality of care)

partner_organizations.name: Global Financing Facility (GFF)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager (multi-donor trust fund within the World Bank)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Host institution for GFF; provides IDA/IBRD loans linked to GFF grants; implements programmes at country level

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Major donor; sits on GFF governance bodies (Trust Fund Committee, Investors Group); co-leads donor group

partner_organizations.name: Country governments (36 LMICs)
partner_organizations.role: Develop and implement country-led investment cases; receive GFF/WB funding

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and youth networks
partner_organizations.role: Engage in country platforms; hold governments accountable; receive capacity-building support

partner_organizations.name: UN agencies (UNFPA, UNICEF, WHO)
partner_organizations.role: Technical partners; collaborate on alignment and multisectoral working (e.g., UNFPA partnership on SRHR)

partner_organizations.name: Other Global Health Initiatives (GHIs: Global Fund, GAVI)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary funding and technical support in GFF countries

partner_organizations.name: Private sector (e.g., IFC in Kenya)
partner_organizations.role: Limited engagement; pilot projects like AMEF in Kenya to support private health providers

quote.source: D0006423.odt, How does the GFF address these needs? section
quote.text: "The GFF is a country-led, multi-donor trust fund housed within the World Bank... GFF funds are linked to World Bank IDA or IBRD loans and both are usually delivered together."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK’s £100m ODA is channeled into the GFF, a multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) within the World Bank. GFF grants are strategically linked to World Bank IDA/IBRD loans (ratio of 1:7.3), creating incentives for countries to allocate more loan funds to health. The mechanism combines grant funding (GFF) with concessional loans (World Bank) and domestic resources, all aligned to country-led investment cases.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The GFF operates as a lean secretariat embedded in the World Bank, with liaison officers in 35 countries. Governance includes a Trust Fund Committee (donors) and an Investors Group (broader stakeholders). Implementation is decentralized: countries develop investment cases with multi-stakeholder platforms (CSOs, government, partners), while the World Bank manages loan/grant disbursement and technical assistance.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The GFF was selected as the UK’s existing strategic partner for RMNCAH-N financing, with a proven track record of leveraging World Bank loans and aligning with UK priorities (e.g., ending preventable deaths, SRHR, health systems strengthening). The UK has influenced the GFF since its inception and co-leads its donor group.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Is the GFF strategic for the UK? section
quote.text: "The UK has been involved with the GFF since its inception and started funding in 2018. We sit on both governance mechanisms... and co-lead the GFF donor group."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The GFF is governed by: 1) a **Trust Fund Committee** (donors, including the UK), which oversees financial and strategic decisions; 2) an **Investors Group** (broader stakeholders, including GHIs and CSOs), which provides technical guidance; and 3) **country platforms** (multi-stakeholder groups at national level). The UK proposes to add FCDO advisors to quality-assure investment cases and improve alignment at country level.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Is the GFF strategic for the UK? and How does the GFF address these needs? sections
quote.text: "The UK... sits on both governance mechanisms, the donor Trust Fund Committee and the broader Investors Group... The GFF works at two levels: Level 1 with development partners in countries, and Level 2 intensively with the World Bank."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are earmarked for RMNCAH-N but can be reallocated across technical areas (e.g., SRHR, nutrition, health systems) based on country priorities identified in investment cases. However, reallocation requires alignment with World Bank loan conditions and GFF strategic pillars. The UK’s £18m tranche is contingent on defined reforms.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The GFF’s country-led investment cases can be adjusted to reflect changing priorities (e.g., COVID-19 response, climate resilience), but modifications require approval from the World Bank and GFF governance bodies. The UK’s technical advisory support (£2m) aims to improve adaptability at country level.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Programme Value and How does the GFF address these needs? sections
quote.text: "£80m will be committed to the GFF straight away with another £18m committed on completion of defined reforms... The investment case activities should be prioritised based on the resources available."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → GFF Secretariat (World Bank) → Country Implementation (government/CSOs/partners). The GFF’s lean structure embeds liaison officers in countries but relies on World Bank systems for disbursement.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, How does the GFF address these needs? section
quote.text: "The GFF grant funding is strategically linked to much larger World Bank IDA/IBRD loans... The grants incentivise countries to allocate a greater share of IDA/IBRD loans to health."

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral funding to individual countries (rejected due to limited leverage and fragmentation)
Direct funding to other GHIs (e.g., Global Fund, GAVI) (rejected as GFF fills a niche in health financing and systems strengthening)
Standalone UK-managed trust fund (rejected due to higher transaction costs and lower World Bank leverage)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The GFF was selected for its **comparative advantage** in leveraging World Bank loans (1:7.3 ratio) and domestic resources, its alignment with UK priorities (EPD, SRHR, health systems), and its country-led, multisectoral approach. The UK’s existing influence within GFF governance and the mechanism’s track record in catalyzing $6.30 in additional funding per $1 of GFF grants were decisive factors.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (leverage ratio of 1:7.3 with World Bank loans)
risk mitigation (GFF’s embeddedness in World Bank reduces fiduciary risks)
partner capacity (GFF’s technical assistance and country platforms)
strategic alignment (fits UK’s Global Health Framework and Women/Girls Strategy)
equity (focus on marginalized populations and FCAS)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on World Bank systems limits GFF’s independence and ability to drive reforms.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proposed reforms include a more formal GFF-World Bank relationship, increased GFF country presence, and clearer articulation of GFF’s value addition. The UK will fund advisors to improve alignment at country level.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak alignment of non-GFF funding to investment cases due to limited coordination.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strengthen use of the Investors Group for global-level alignment discussions, improve communication with core donors in-country, and embed SRHR fellows in World Bank offices.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited domestic resource mobilization (DRM) beyond World Bank loans.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Introduce DRM key performance indicators, focus on efficiency (e.g., frontline service funding), and use RMET tool to track expenditures.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Insufficient focus on sensitive SRHR areas (e.g., safe abortion) despite rhetorical commitments.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Push for inclusion of SRHR DLIs in World Bank programmes, use Development Policy Financing instruments for legal reforms, and increase funding to CSOs/youth networks (minimum $3m/year).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of transparency on GFF’s ‘behind-the-scenes’ value addition.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Develop Country Engagement Frameworks, improve dissemination of implementation progress, and increase regular communication with donors.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (results in RMNCAH-N indicators, e.g., 70% of long-term partner countries show improvements)
equity (focus on marginalized groups, FCAS, and gender-responsive data)

quote.source: D0006423.odt, What is the GFF’s Comparative Advantage? and Why was THIS modality chosen? sections
quote.text: "The GFF’s focus on domestic resource mobilisation to strengthen health systems around country priorities complements investments through the Global Fund... Each GFF dollar is associated with $6.30 funding aligned to the investment case from other donors."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context (14/36 countries) limits partner selection to organizations with strong risk management capacities (e.g., World Bank, UN agencies). Conflict and weak institutions reduce the pool of viable Southern implementers, increasing reliance on multilateral intermediaries. For example, in Zimbabwe (no IDA financing), the GFF must adopt a more strategic approach to justify engagement.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS environments restrict partnerships to entities with conflict-sensitive expertise (e.g., World Bank’s FCAS instruments).
Weak public financial management in LMICs necessitates World Bank-led fiduciary oversight, limiting direct funding to Southern CSOs.
Opposition to SRHR in conservative contexts requires careful selection of local partners (e.g., youth networks vs. government ministries).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s **financing mechanism** objective (leveraging World Bank loans) dictates the **multilateral delivery structure** (GFF within WB). The need to influence **health systems strengthening** and **SRHR** requires embedded technical assistance (e.g., SRHR fellows in WB offices) and country-level advisors. The **FCAS risk profile** drives the use of World Bank instruments (e.g., Development Policy Financing for legal reforms).

q28_linkages.objective: Leverage World Bank loans for RMNCAH-N
q28_linkages.mechanism: Multi-donor trust fund (GFF) housed within the World Bank, with grants linked to IDA/IBRD loans.
Technical assistance for health financing reforms, performance-based payments (DLIs), and on-budget support via country systems.
Embedded SRHR fellows in World Bank offices; use of Development Policy Financing for legal reforms (e.g., pregnant girls’ education in Niger).
Country platforms with multi-stakeholder engagement (CSOs, donors, government) and joint working with other GHIs (e.g., Global Fund in DRC).

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between **inclusive partnerships** (e.g., CSO engagement) and **rapid delivery** (e.g., World Bank’s fiduciary requirements). Key trade-offs include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: World Bank systems enable quick disbursement but limit direct CSO funding; 2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: GFF’s lean structure reduces costs but relies on World Bank staff, risking limited local influence; 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Pooled funding improves efficiency but may dilute focus on marginalized groups (e.g., adolescents, disabled women).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: World Bank’s fiduciary systems ensure rapid disbursement but restrict direct funding to Southern CSOs, requiring intermediaries (e.g., NGO host partners for CSO coordination).
GFF’s reliance on World Bank staff and Northern-led governance (Trust Fund Committee) limits Southern partners’ decision-making power, despite ‘country-led’ rhetoric.
The 1:7.3 leverage ratio with World Bank loans maximizes funding but may prioritize loan conditions over equity-focused interventions (e.g., safe abortion, disability-inclusive services).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** (due to FCAS contexts) drives **intensive oversight**: milestone-based disbursement, embedded advisors (proposed UK technical support), and regular Investors Group reviews. In high-risk settings (e.g., Afghanistan), the GFF adopts more strategic, light-touch approaches to justify engagement.
