intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building (e.g., RMET tool, CSO training) enables Southern partners to engage in **budget advocacy** and **alignment processes**, but structural constraints (e.g., World Bank’s limited transparency) hinder full participation. For example, CSOs trained in budget advocacy can influence national plans but lack decision-making power in GFF governance.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Emerging areas for improvement/reform and Strengthening the partnership model sections
quote.text: "The GFF’s ability to do more across sectors is dependent on a successful replenishment... The GFF is reconsidering the positioning of the liaison officer role... Communication with other health partners is highly variable."

key_programme_risks: Stalled progress on SDG health targets due to COVID-19, economic crises, and SRHR rollbacks.
Over-reliance on World Bank systems limits GFF’s independence and reform influence.
Weak domestic resource mobilization (DRM) beyond World Bank loans.
Limited alignment of non-GFF funding to investment cases.
Insufficient focus on sensitive SRHR areas (e.g., safe abortion) despite commitments.
Fragmented coordination with UN agencies (WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF) at country level.
Climate change exacerbating health burdens (e.g., undernutrition, heat stress) without adequate adaptation in health systems.
Political opposition to gender equity and SRHR in conservative contexts.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on resilience-building in health systems (e.g., climate-adaptive PHC, emergency preparedness) and prioritize high-impact interventions (e.g., neonatal resuscitation, family planning).
Push for a more formal GFF-World Bank relationship, increased GFF country presence, and use of a wider range of WB instruments (e.g., DPF for policy reforms).
Introduce DRM key performance indicators, use RMET tool for expenditure tracking, and incentivize efficient spending (e.g., frontline services).
Strengthen Investors Group discussions on alignment, improve communication with core donors in-country, and use pooled funding (e.g., Tanzania, Pakistan).
Embed SRHR fellows in World Bank offices, include SRHR DLIs in WB programmes, and increase CSO/youth funding ($3m/year).
Develop strategic partnerships with UN agencies (e.g., UNFPA on SRHR) and clarify roles in country platforms.
Integrate climate resilience into health programmes (e.g., WASH in health facilities, early warning systems) and train healthcare workers on climate adaptation.
Use Development Policy Financing for legal reforms (e.g., pregnant girls’ education in Niger) and support local advocacy networks.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, **health financing must prioritize flexibility** (e.g., emergency funds, adaptive DLIs) due to volatile contexts.
**Pooled funding** (e.g., in Pakistan, DRC) improves alignment and reduces duplication in fragile settings.
**Legal reforms** (e.g., keeping girls in school) are critical but require careful sequencing to avoid backlash.
**CSO engagement** is essential for reaching marginalized groups but needs protection in conflict zones (e.g., via NGO host partners).
**World Bank instruments** (e.g., DPF) can be used for policy changes (e.g., SRHR) but require strong donor coordination to mitigate risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Phase 2 of the GFF showed success in leveraging World Bank loans and improving RMNCAH-N indicators (e.g., 70% of long-term partners reported progress) but highlighted challenges in **domestic resource mobilization**, **alignment of non-GFF funding**, and **transparency on GFF’s value addition**. The need for **country-level advisors** and **strengthened partnership models** was identified as critical for Phase 3.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Allocation of £2m for UK technical advisory support to improve investment case quality and alignment.
Proposal for FCDO advisors to work with HQ and country teams to influence World Bank programme design.
Increased focus on **expenditure tracking** (not just resource mapping) to identify funding gaps.
Stronger use of the **Investors Group** for global-level alignment discussions and quality assurance.
Embedding **SRHR fellows** in World Bank regional offices to mainstream SRHR.
Development of **Country Engagement Frameworks** to clarify GFF’s role and value addition.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, What results has the GFF achieved so far? and Emerging areas for improvement sections
quote.text: "Phase 2 of the programme has shown areas of success as well as areas that can be improved... The GFF is reconsidering the positioning of the liaison officer role... More emphasis needs to be placed on expenditure tracking as opposed to just mapping."

co_funding_partners.leverage: £1 GFF grant linked to £7.30 in World Bank funds (1:7.3 ratio)
£1 GFF grant linked to £6.30 from other partners (1:6.3 ratio)
GFF catalyzes increased domestic spending on RMNCAH-N (evidence weaker; focus of Phase 3 reforms)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £100m UK investment is expected to unlock $8bn in World Bank/IDA financing for RMNCAH-N, of which $2bn is additional. Historically, every £1 committed to GFF has leveraged £7.30 in World Bank funds and £6.30 from other partners.

quote.source: D0006423.odt, Programme Value and What results has the GFF achieved so far? sections
quote.text: "This business case requests £100m. £80m will be committed to the GFF straight away with another £18m committed on completion of defined reforms and £2m set aside to provide extra technical advisory support to FCDO... Every $1 in GFF is linked to US$7.30 in World Bank funds and $6.3 in funds from other partners."

metadata.programme_name: Rebuilding insurance markets in Ukraine
metadata.quote: The UK is now seeking to scale a complementary war risk insurance initiative, the Ukraine Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF), being developed by the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). (D0006924.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: Original project start and end dates: November 2023/November 2024; New project end date (if applicable): March 2029 (D0006924.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling funds to de-risk investments) with market shaping (rebuilding insurance markets) and implementation research (testing insurance models). It aims to leverage private sector investment in Ukraine's economic recovery by providing war risk insurance through multilateral partners (MIGA and EBRD).
what_objectives.q1_source: "Leveraging the contribution of the private sector is one of the core pillars of the UK’s strategy for supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery." (D0006923.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Guarantees issued through MIGA's SURE Trust Fund
q3_expected_outputs.target: £100m+ worth of guarantees in medium to long term (1:5.5 leverage ratio)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Insurance policies underwritten by EBRD's URGF
q3_expected_outputs.target: >€1.3bn of assets insured by 2028

q3_expected_outputs.output: Private capital crowded in
q3_expected_outputs.target: 85% private sector participation share by 2028

q3_expected_outputs.output: Jobs supported
q3_expected_outputs.target: Gender-disaggregated data on direct jobs (temporary and permanent)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Technical assistance for capacity building
q3_expected_outputs.target: ~5% of UK's contribution to MIGA

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to rebuild Ukraine's insurance markets by providing war risk coverage through two complementary mechanisms: MIGA's SURE Trust Fund (for foreign investors) and EBRD's URGF (for local businesses), thereby crowding in private capital for economic recovery.
what_objectives.quote: "The principal objectives of the URGF are: to expand the provision of war risks and related insurance cover available to businesses in Ukraine on a sustainable basis; and to crowd in private risk capital from insurers and reinsurers and remedy a market failure." (D0006924.odt, Expected Results)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is in active conflict with Russia since February 2022, with significant economic contraction (30% in 2022) and elevated political/military risks that deter private investment. The insurance market has collapsed due to war exclusions by commercial providers.
where_context.q5_source: "The lack of war risk insurance puts a significant drag on economic activity and is a key blocker for private trade and investment activity, especially at the scale required to meet Ukraine’s substantial recovery and reconstruction needs." (D0006923.odt, Strategic Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Commercial insurers have withdrawn all coverage for Ukraine due to war risks, creating a market failure. Regulatory requirements (e.g., EBRD's prudential liquidity rules) and weak local insurance infrastructure limit the speed of market rebuilding. Ongoing conflict disrupts supply chains and increases operational risks for investors.
where_context.quote: "The commercial and political risks faced by international and local businesses and investors while the war is ongoing are very significant... De-risking mechanisms, including insurance, blended finance and technical assistance will have a critical role to play to mobilise private finance in support of Ukraine’s early recovery." (D0006923.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with MIGA/EBRD (Northern multilateral institutions) and the UK (as a donor on governing councils). Ukrainian entities (e.g., Ministry of Economy) are consulted but do not have voting power on fund allocation.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for project due diligence (MIGA)
support to local insurers for underwriting/claims management (EBRD)
coordination with Ukrainian Ministry of Economy

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA)
partner_organizations.role: Administrator of SURE Trust Fund; underwrites political risk guarantees

partner_organizations.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Manager of Ukraine Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF); contracts reinsurance brokers

partner_organizations.name: Ukraine Ministry of Economy
partner_organizations.role: Key government interlocutor; coordinates with FCDO/EBRD

partner_organizations.name: Lloyd’s of London/AON/Vienna Insurance Group (VIG)
partner_organizations.role: Commercial insurers exploring non-war peril coverage (market-building)

partner_organizations.name: Local Ukrainian insurers (unnamed)
partner_organizations.role: Issue policies and manage claims under URGF

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Donor; sits on MIGA SURETF Governing Council and EBRD URGF oversight

who_partners.quote: "The UK will join the Governing Council for the SURE Trust Fund and will therefore be able to exert a level of decision-making authority on how the Trust Fund allocates funding." (D0006923.odt, Governance of SURE Trust Fund)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK provides grant funding to two multilateral trust funds: (1) MIGA's SURE Trust Fund (£20m one-off grant for risk capital), and (2) EBRD's URGF (£5m grant for operational expenses). Both instruments use blended finance: donor grants leverage multilateral balance sheets and private reinsurance.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: MIGA and EBRD act as fund managers/administrators. MIGA's SURETF has a Governing Council (with UK representation) for strategic oversight, while EBRD's URGF will use a dedicated 'war insurance sub-account' under its Crisis Response Special Fund. Day-to-day operations are delegated to specialized teams (e.g., MIGA underwriting, EBRD-contracted insurance brokers).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: MIGA and EBRD were selected based on their existing mandates for conflict-affected economies, specialized expertise in political risk insurance, and ability to leverage multilateral balance sheets. The UK had prior experience with MIGA's CAEF Trust Fund (2014–2033).
how_mechanism.quote: "Supporting MIGA’s facility, compared with alternative facilities from IFIs or the commercial sector, will present strong Value-for-Money (VfM) credentials... MIGA will charge a one-off, administrative fee equal to 1% of the total commitment made." (D0006923.odt, Rationale for Using MIGA)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: MIGA SURETF: Governing Council with UK representation (non-voting on individual deals but can influence sectoral allocation). EBRD URGF: Oversight via CRSF-Ukraine Window, with annual audited financial statements. Both structures include World Bank/EBRD internal approvals (e.g., MIGA's Project Review Council).
how_governance.quote: "The Governing Council will provide high-level guidance, direction and advice to the MSP Program, including reviewing the progress, impact, and evaluation reports of MSP Trust Funds. It will meet at least annually to review the progress, impact, and evaluation reports of the Trust Fund." (D0006923.odt, Governance of SURE Trust Fund)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within SURETF/URGF can be recycled as guarantees expire, but reallocation between sectors requires Governing Council consensus. The UK can influence sectoral priorities (e.g., agribusiness vs. energy) but not individual projects.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: MIGA/EBRD can adjust underwriting criteria in response to market conditions (e.g., reinsurance availability), but strategic shifts require donor consultation. The URGF's 'incorporated cell' structure allows for expansion into new asset classes (e.g., warehousing, agricultural machinery) post-2025.
how_flexibility.quote: "The risk-sharing percentage attributable to SURE would be revisited when reinsurance market conditions improve, likely at the time when Ukraine enters a stabilized reconstruction phase." (D0006923.odt, Option 4: SURE Trust Fund)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → MIGA/EBRD (fund managers) → [local insurers/brokers for URGF]
how_efficiency.quote: "MIGA will charge a one-off, administrative fee equal to 1% of the total commitment made, to act as the SURETF’s Administrator." (D0006923.odt, Rationale for Using MIGA)

q24_alternatives_considered: Doing nothing (rejected due to reputational risks and missed catalytic opportunity)
Leaving it to commercial insurance industry (rejected as market failure persists)
UK Export Finance (UKEF) (rejected due to limited UK content requirement and lack of scale)
EBRD’s Ukraine Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF) (initially deferred; now adopted as complementary)
Support to MIGA’s SURE Trust Fund (selected as primary vehicle)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: MIGA was chosen for its (1) immediate pipeline of deals, (2) high leverage ratio (1:5.5 to 1:14), (3) robust governance (tried-and-tested trust fund model), (4) cost efficiency (1% management fee vs. >7% for private contractors), and (5) ability to blend donor funds with its balance sheet. EBRD's URGF was added to address the gap in local insurance market development, complementing MIGA's focus on foreign investors.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lower-than-expected leverage ratios in SURETF
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will challenge MIGA's assumptions via Governing Council; leverage figures based on actual Ukraine pipeline data.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited pipeline of investment opportunities delays impact
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MIGA confirms £410m demand from financial sector; UK/DBT will promote SURETF to UK businesses.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High claims drain SURETF corpus
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: MIGA's financial prudence guidelines and rigorous underwriting; preference for high-quality projects.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: URGF fails to attract sufficient private reinsurers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: EBRD's guarantee backstop (€110m Risk Capital Pool) and phased expansion into new asset classes.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited UK influence over project selection
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK sits on Governing Councils and can veto sectoral allocations; results framework enables performance challenges.

why_rationale.quote: "By routing our support through the multi-donor trust fund, we are using a proven instrument, that leverages MIGA’s expertise and brings in other donors and industry players." (D0006923.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to multilaterals (MIGA/EBRD) due to (1) commercial insurers' withdrawal from Ukraine, (2) need for balance sheet strength to absorb war risks, and (3) regulatory requirements for reinsurance (e.g., EBRD's prudential liquidity rules). Local Ukrainian insurers lack capital to underwrite risks independently.
q27_constraints_detail: Commercial insurers exclude Ukraine from global policies (war risk)
Local insurance market is "relatively small and insufficiently capitalised" (D0006923.odt)
Reinsurers require donor guarantees to participate (EBRD's €110m Risk Capital Pool)
Ukrainian regulatory environment necessitates multilateral intermediation
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to (1) de-risk both foreign and local investments and (2) crowd in private capital determines the two-pronged structure: MIGA (foreign investors) + EBRD (local businesses). The scale of reconstruction needs (US$411bn) and the urgency of early recovery require leveraged instruments (trust funds) rather than direct grants.
q28_linkages: Foreign investor focus → MIGA's SURETF (global political risk insurance expertise)
Local market development → EBRD's URGF (local insurer capacity building)
Blended finance need → Multilateral balance sheets (MIGA/EBRD) + donor grants (UK/Norway/US)
Speed requirement → Existing platforms (SURETF/CRSF) vs. new entities
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly trades some equity (Northern-led multilaterals) for efficiency (leverage ratios, speed). Trade-offs include: (1) UK influence over project selection is limited to sectoral guidance (not individual deals), and (2) local insurers play an operational role (underwriting/claims) but lack decision-making power over URGF strategy.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards to MIGA/EBRD enable rapid deployment but sideline local ownership.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern multilaterals manage risks/underwriting; Ukrainian partners implement but don’t govern.
Cost vs. reach: 1% management fee (efficient) but requires accepting multilateral overhead structures.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context increases oversight intensity (quarterly reviews, Governing Council) and limits flexibility in fund reallocation (e.g., claims may drain corpus). MIGA's prudential guidelines constrain underwriting to higher-quality projects, reducing risk but potentially limiting reach.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded but targeted: (1) MIGA's TA component (5% of UK contribution) focuses on due diligence/project development, and (2) EBRD's URGF includes training for local insurers on underwriting/claims. Southern partners' roles are operational (e.g., claims management) rather than strategic.
intersections.quote: "The lack of war risk insurance puts a significant drag on economic activity and is a key blocker for private trade and investment activity... De-risking mechanisms... will have a critical role to play to mobilise private finance." (D0006923.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks.risk: Insufficient pipeline of investment opportunities limits immediate impact (Delivery)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: MIGA confirms £410m demand from financial sector; UK/DBT to promote SURETF to businesses.

key_programme_risks.risk: Higher-than-expected claims drain trust fund corpus (Delivery/Financing)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: MIGA's financial prudence guidelines; preference for high-quality projects.

key_programme_risks.risk: URGF fails to achieve breakeven by 2028 (Financing)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: EBRD's €110m Risk Capital Pool backstop; phased expansion into new asset classes.

key_programme_risks.risk: Limited demonstration effect on commercial insurance market (Context)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: UK will promote URGF/MIGA to global reinsurers via G7+ platforms.

key_programme_risks.risk: Projects funded have limited development impact (Delivery)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: KPIs on jobs creation; learning from MIGA's CAEF facility.

key_programme_risks.risk: Reputational damage if UK-backed projects misalign with objectives (Safeguarding)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: MIGA's integrity due diligence; EBRD's Project Accountability Mechanism.

key_programme_risks.risk: Regulatory changes in Ukraine disrupt operations (Context)
key_programme_risks.mitigation: Close coordination with Ministry of Economy; EBRD's compliance team.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK will challenge MIGA's assumptions via Governing Council; leverage based on actual pipeline data.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: URGF does not attract private reinsurers
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: EBRD's guarantee backstop (€110m) and demonstration effect through initial underwriting.
MIGA's 30-year track record (10 claims paid out of 900 projects); EBRD's 24% loss ratio target.

fcas_specific_lessons: Blended finance is essential in FCAS to crowd in private capital (MIGA's 1:5.5 leverage).
Local insurance markets require capacity building before they can absorb risk (EBRD's URGF model).
Multilateral intermediation reduces fiduciary risks in high-corruption environments (MIGA's integrity due diligence).
Flexible instruments (recyclable guarantees) are critical for long-term FCAS engagement.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from MIGA's Conflict-Affected and Fragile Economies Facility (CAFEF, 2014–2033) informed SURETF design: (1) 1:12–1:14 long-term leverage ratios are achievable; (2) rigorous underwriting reduces claims (10 paid out of 900 projects); (3) technical assistance improves project quality.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The URGF was added post-2023 to address the gap in local insurance market development, complementing MIGA's focus on foreign investors. The £5m grant structure reflects lessons from EBRD's CRSF-Ukraine Window (established July 2022).
risks_lessons.quote: "MIGA’s past performance on guarantees suggests a leverage ratio of up to 1:12 to 1:14 for donors... In over 900 projects supported by MIGA over a 30-year period, only 10 claims have been paid out." (D0006923.odt, Rationale for Using MIGA)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £20m to MIGA SURETF expected to unlock £100m+ in guarantees (1:5.5 ratio); £5m to EBRD URGF targets €1.3bn in insured assets by 2028 (1:260 ratio). Combined donor contributions (£80m+ to SURETF) aim to catalyse ~£400m in guarantees.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: MIGA SURETF: 95% CDEL (risk capital for guarantees), 5% RDEL (technical assistance). EBRD URGF: 100% RDEL (operational expenses).
financial_details.quote: "The UK’s contribution of £20m can be expected to provide more than £100m worth of guarantees in the medium to long-term, thus enabling reconstruction support far greater than the original sum of the contribution." (D0006923.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Tanzania Health Resilience Programme (THRP)

quote.text: The programme aims to build a more resilient and sustainable health system, that effectively reduces preventable deaths and tackles major disease outbreaks, and makes progress towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030.

metadata.duration_source: AMPEndDate: 31 March 2029; AMPStartDate: 01 April 2024

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines health system strengthening (capacity building) with direct service delivery (implementation) and policy influence. It aims to improve primary healthcare services, strengthen disease surveillance, and enhance data use for decision-making, while also addressing maternal, newborn, and child health outcomes.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme aims to build a more resilient and sustainable health system, that effectively reduces preventable deaths and tackles major disease outbreaks, and makes progress towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030. It will increase the access, quality and equity of life-saving primary health care services by strengthening health systems that support the ending preventable deaths of mothers, newborns, and children (EPD). It will improve Tanzania’s capacity to prevent, detect and respond to health threats by supporting integrated disease surveillance and a stronger initial response to outbreaks. Finally, it will facilitate the use of data to inform decision towards more equitable health outcomes.
q3_expected_outputs: Improved access, quality and equity of life-saving reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services
Strengthened and sustainable delivery of health services, including more transparent and accountable resource allocation and use
Improved quality and quantity of staffing
Better family planning commodities market intelligence, affordability and uptake
Improved sector accountability
Improved prevention, detection and response to health threats
Increased political commitment to comply with International Health Regulations
Progress towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030
what_objectives.summary: THRP is a strategic, long-term programme designed to strengthen Tanzania's health system resilience, reduce preventable deaths, and improve health security through integrated primary healthcare, disease surveillance, and data-driven decision-making.

quote.text: The programme will support Tanzania to regain momentum towards achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030 as measured by a change in Tanzania’s UHC index.
quote.source: D0005963.odt, Proposed programme: Impact and Expected Outcomes

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting Tanzania's status as a lower-middle-income country with health system challenges but without active conflict or extreme fragility.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak health systems, inadequate human resources (70% staffing gaps in primary care), poor data quality for logistics, and climate vulnerabilities (e.g., disease outbreaks like Marburg) constrain service delivery. Political pressures and donor fragmentation also affect resource allocation and policy decisions.

quote.text: Tanzania’s health system constraints undermine the ability to meet international health regulations and implement comprehensive epidemic preparedness and response (EPR) measures. The recent Joint External Evaluation (JEE) supported by WHO in 2023 highlighted health system gaps including the lack of integration of between routine surveillance systems and the laboratory surveillance system, inadequate capacity for risk assessment at subnational level and inadequate workforce surge during public health emergencies.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes collaboration with the Government of Tanzania (GoT) through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), with shared decision-making in health sector reforms. The UK provides technical assistance and funding, while GoT leads implementation and policy direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., for health workers in emergency obstetric care)
institutional strengthening (e.g., supporting the National Public Health Institute)
mentorship (e.g., improving data use for decision-making)
system reforms (e.g., Universal Health Insurance implementation)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania (Ministry of Health)
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner and policy leader

partner_organizations.name: World Health Organization (WHO) Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: Technical support for health security and surveillance

partner_organizations.name: Health Basket Fund (HBF) donors (Canada, Denmark, Ireland, Switzerland, South Korea, UNFPA, UNICEF, World Bank)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers through pooled funding mechanism

partner_organizations.name: US Government (USAID, CDC)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary programme implementers (e.g., health security, family planning)

partner_organizations.name: Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and Women's Rights Organizations (WROs)
partner_organizations.role: Community engagement and advocacy

quote.text: The programme strengthens UK’s convening power, voice and influence in the health sector and complements UK investments through the global institutions (such as The Global Fund, GAVI Vaccine Alliance, Global Financing Facility), and supports strategic partnerships with other partners in the country such as the USAID, Ireland, World Bank, Canada, WHO, CDC, UNICEF, Switzerland etc.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of Accountable Grants (AG) and direct funding to the Government of Tanzania through mechanisms like the Health Basket Fund (HBF). The MoU with the Ministry of Health formalizes the partnership, ensuring alignment with national priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a multi-stakeholder approach, leveraging the Health Basket Fund (a pooled funding mechanism) and direct collaboration with the Ministry of Health. The UK provides technical assistance and funding, while implementation is led by GoT with support from WHO, CSOs, and other donors.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Government of Tanzania is the primary partner due to the programme's alignment with national health strategies (e.g., Health Sector Strategic Plan V) and the existing MoU between UK and Tanzania. The Health Basket Fund and other partners were pre-selected based on their established roles in Tanzania's health sector.

quote.text: The UK’s historical cooperation in health was cemented through an MoU with the Ministry of Health in May 2023. The MoU sets out four goals that the health partnership will focus on: 1) Stronger health systems for UHC and EPD; 2) Improved capacity for health security; 3) Trade and investment on healthcare; and 4) Research collaborations and exchanges.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is governed through the Health Sector Strategic Plan V (HSSPV) and the Health Basket Fund (HBF) mechanisms, which include multi-donor oversight. The UK, as Chair of the Development Partners Group (DPG) for Health, ensures alignment with other donors and the Government of Tanzania.

quote.text: BHC Dar es Salaam currently Chairs the Development Partners Group and is an Outgoing Chair for DPG-Health group. Through those seats, maximum alignment with other funders is ensured and we leverage other donors’ resources and share risks.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated within the programme's three pillars (health security, ending preventable deaths, health system strengthening) but require approval for significant shifts. The programme includes a small crisis reserve (£1m) for rapid deployment during health emergencies.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in response to emerging health threats (e.g., disease outbreaks) or policy opportunities (e.g., Universal Health Insurance implementation), but changes require approval from the UK and GoT.

quote.text: The health security support will involve both technical assistance (£2m) and a small crisis reserve provision of up to £1m to be rapidly deployed in a health emergency.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Government of Tanzania (Ministry of Health) → Implementation (health facilities, CSOs, etc.). The Health Basket Fund adds a pooled layer but is managed jointly.

quote.text: Pooling funds at the health facility level empowers health facilities to plan and budget efficiently according to the local needs (evidence-based planning) and catalyses increased accountability and transparency.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 1: A standalone programme targeted on maternal, newborn and child health
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Focused on direct service delivery for maternal and newborn health, with limited system strengthening.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 2: Health system strengthening approach in primary healthcare, with a priority focus on maternal, newborn and child health outcomes
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Shifted from direct service delivery to system-wide reforms, influencing government priorities like Universal Health Insurance.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Option 3: A combined programme approach to support health system strengthening for ending preventable deaths of women, newborn and children, and an additional focus on health security
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Integrated health system strengthening with health security, including a crisis reserve for emergencies.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected because it aligns with both UK and Tanzania’s strategic priorities (e.g., Global Health Framework, Health Sector Strategic Plan V), creates synergies between Universal Health Coverage and health security, and positions the UK as a core partner in Tanzania’s health reforms. It also maximizes value for money by leveraging existing investments (e.g., Global Fund, GAVI) and addressing systemic constraints (e.g., staffing gaps, disease surveillance).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Funding may be spread too thinly across the three pillars (health security, ending preventable deaths, and health system strengthening), reducing impact.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritize interventions explicitly linked to evidence and focus on foundational reforms that other donors can build upon.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Increased management and overhead costs due to the wider range of health interventions and partners.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage existing platforms (e.g., Health Basket Fund) and technical assistance to streamline coordination.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on sustained government and donor financing to implement reforms, which the UK can influence but not dictate.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use UK’s convening power (e.g., DPG Chair role) to align donors and advocate for predictable financing.

quote.text: Option 3 scores most highly from a strategic, impact, equity, and VFM perspective. It is also the option that provides co-benefits of bringing Universal Health Coverage and health security together and increases UK’s ability to influence the Government on key health sector reforms.
quote.source: D0005963.odt, Assessing each option against agreed criteria

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Tanzania’s weak health infrastructure (e.g., 70% staffing gaps in primary care, poor data systems) and political economy constraints (e.g., donor fragmentation, administrative-boundary-based resource allocation) limit the pool of capable implementing partners. The Government of Tanzania is the default lead due to sovereignty, but its capacity gaps necessitate technical support from multilateral partners (e.g., WHO) and donors (e.g., UK, USAID).
q27_constraints_detail: Limited local capacity to manage complex health system reforms without external technical assistance.
Donor fragmentation (80% of donor support spent off-budget) reduces efficiency and requires pooled mechanisms like the Health Basket Fund.
Regulatory barriers (e.g., rigid procurement policies) limit private sector engagement in commodity supply chains.
Climate and disease risks (e.g., Marburg outbreaks) demand rapid-response capabilities that local systems lack.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (health system strengthening + health security + service delivery) require a hybrid delivery structure. Direct service delivery (e.g., maternal health) is channeled through GoT systems, while system-wide reforms (e.g., surveillance, UHC) leverage multilateral platforms (e.g., WHO, HBF) for coordination. The need for rapid crisis response (e.g., disease outbreaks) justifies the small reserve fund and embedded technical assistance.
q28_linkages: Health security goals → Technical assistance from WHO/CDC and crisis reserve fund.
UHC and equity objectives → Pooled funding (HBF) and GoT-led implementation to ensure inclusivity.
System strengthening → Capacity building for MoH and integration with existing programmes (e.g., Scaling Up Family Planning).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (e.g., targeting rural/poor populations through primary healthcare strengthening) with efficiency (e.g., using pooled funds to reduce transaction costs). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Rapid outbreak response may bypass slower community engagement processes. (2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern technical assistance (e.g., WHO) is needed for complex reforms, but risks undermining local leadership. (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Expanding services to remote areas increases costs but is critical for leaving no one behind.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Pooling funds through HBF improves efficiency but requires ceding some control to GoT and other donors.
Prioritizing health security (e.g., outbreak response) may divert resources from routine services, affecting equity.
Embedding capacity building in system reforms takes longer but ensures sustainability vs. short-term service delivery.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., weak systems, disease threats) justifies intensive oversight through milestone-based management and embedded advisors (e.g., UK technical assistance to MoH). The Joint External Evaluation (JEE) gaps necessitate stronger coordination mechanisms, hence the emphasis on the National Public Health Institute and DPG alignment.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to the programme, with partners’ roles designed to address specific gaps: (1) **GoT** leads policy and implementation but receives technical support for reforms (e.g., UHI, surveillance). (2) **WHO/CDC** provide health security expertise. (3) **CSOs/WROs** focus on community engagement and equity. (4) **Donors (UK, USAID)** align funding and advocacy through platforms like HBF.

quote.text: The programme will support the gathering and use of data to inform decision making and resource allocation to deliver more equitable health outcomes. [...] The programme will adhere with the Equality Act, following the need to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations between different people when carrying out their activities.

key_programme_risks: Inadequate human resources for health (70% gaps in primary care) undermining service delivery.
Poor data quality in logistics systems leading to stockouts or expiries of essential commodities.
Fragmented donor financing (80% off-budget) reducing efficiency and coordination.
Climate and disease vulnerabilities (e.g., Marburg, malaria) straining health system resilience.
Slow progress on Universal Health Coverage (UHC index of 43 vs. LMIC average of 58).
Limited private sector contribution to commodity markets due to policy barriers.
Delays in disbursement of Health Basket Funds affecting facility-level planning.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Human resource gaps (70% in primary care)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Support GoT’s National Accelerated Plan for Acquisition of Human Resources and community health worker programmes. Provide targeted training (e.g., emergency obstetric care).

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor logistics data quality (21% of reports rejected)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strengthen electronic Logistics Management Information System (eLMIS) and bottom-up quantification for commodity forecasting.
Leverage Health Basket Fund for pooled financing and align donors through DPG-Health Chair role.
Establish crisis reserve fund (£1m) and support National Public Health Institute for coordinated surveillance/response.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Slow UHC progress (index 43 vs. target 60 by 2030)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on primary healthcare expansion and Universal Health Insurance implementation, with UK technical assistance.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Private sector barriers in commodity markets
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Advocate for policy reforms (e.g., market shaping) and engage private-not-for-profit providers.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from Marburg outbreak (2023): Community-based surveillance systems must be strengthened to detect outbreaks earlier (18-day delay in reporting).
Health Basket Fund mid-term review (2019): Delayed disbursements from Ministry of Finance impede facility-level planning; solutions include co-mingling funds with government allocations.
Joint External Evaluation (2023): Tanzania’s weak subnational risk assessment capacity requires targeted technical assistance, not just funding.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous UK programmes (e.g., Scaling Up Family Planning) demonstrated that: (1) **Pooled funding (HBF) improves accountability** but requires capacity building at facility level. (2) **Technical assistance must be demand-driven** to avoid parallel systems. (3) **Policy influencing (e.g., for SRHR) is more effective when linked to national priorities** (e.g., demographic dividend). (4) **Crisis reserves enable rapid response** but need clear triggers to avoid misuse.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) A **small crisis reserve** (£1m) based on Marburg response lessons. (2) **Explicit focus on data quality** (e.g., eLMIS) to address logistics gaps. (3) **Alignment with GoT’s Universal Health Insurance Act (2023)** to ensure sustainability. (4) **Integration of health security and UHC objectives** to avoid siloed approaches.

quote.text: The Marburg outbreak further revealed gaps in community-based surveillance systems as it took over 18 days of community transmission (7 cases and 5 deaths) before the health facilities reported the ‘unknown illness’ to the regional authorities.

Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria

It also aligns with the Health Basket Fund, which has disbursed over $1 billion since 1999 and contributes 8–10% of total health expenditures in Tanzania.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: LIFE-AR is a financing mechanism that channels climate adaptation funds to local levels while simultaneously building institutional capacity and influencing global climate finance architecture. It combines implementation research (testing locally-led adaptation models) with capacity building (strengthening local governance) and policy influence (advocating for systemic changes in climate finance).
what_objectives.q1_source: UK funding of LIFEAR will contribute to: 1. Establishing a LIFEAR global platform which will engage donors, advocating on behalf of the initiative and the LDC Group and influencing the international climate finance architecture; 2. Provide support to LIFEAR frontrunner countries [...] to enhance National and local governance structures and delivery mechanisms to enable finance flows to support demand-led local actions; 3. Establishing a community of evidence and practice to promote south to south peer learning and support adaptive management.
q3_expected_outputs: National platforms established in 6+ countries
70% of climate finance reaching local levels in participating countries

Community of practice for peer learning across LDCs
Global advocacy platform influencing climate finance architecture
Evidence base on locally-led adaptation effectiveness
what_objectives.summary: LIFE-AR aims to transform climate adaptation by shifting decision-making and finance to local actors in Least Developed Countries, demonstrating a proof-of-concept for channeling ≥70% of climate funds to local levels while building governance systems and global advocacy for systemic change.

quote.text: This will build the adaptive capacity of up to 4.5 million men, women and children in up to 12 countries and will lay the foundation for scaling up across all least developed countries, ultimately reaching a potential population of nearly 1 billion of the world's poorest people.

countries_regions: (potential expansion to all 46 Least Developed Countries)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in climate-vulnerable LDCs with governance challenges but has existing UK-supported mechanisms (like Devolved Climate Finance) and LDC ownership structures to mitigate risks. The business case explicitly states "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate".
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
q6_contextual_constraints: complex accreditation processes for global funds
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: LDCs face barriers in accessing global climate funds (e.g., GCF accreditation requires proving legal capacity and institutional systems). Traditional funding models silo climate finance in environment ministries, excluding local voices. Short-term projects fail to address structural needs for long-term adaptation.

quote.text: LIFEAR is a unique initiative, owned by LDCs, set up to change this [lack of local finance access] [...] Countries will develop tailored mechanisms to channel up to 70% of all climate funds available to that country, to local levels supporting community-prioritised investments in climate action.
quote.source: D0004546.odt, Programme summary and LDC Vision sections

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The £12M UK contribution is provided as core funding to the LIFEAR platform, which then acts as a financing mechanism to channel funds to frontrunner countries. Countries use these funds to establish national systems that can access additional climate finance (e.g., GCF, Adaptation Fund) and allocate ≥70% to local levels. The instrument combines grant funding with technical assistance and advocacy.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: LIFEAR operates as a multi-donor platform with an LDC-chaired Board and Technical Advisory Committee. A third-party managing agent (selected via mutual agreement) provides coordination support. Frontrunner countries implement locally through national platforms, with peer learning facilitated across the LDC group. The UK participates in governance but does not control implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: LIFEAR was selected as the "best fit" against Locally Led Adaptation (LLA) Principles due to its LDC ownership, existing progress in 6 frontrunner countries, and alignment with the UK’s COP26 adaptation commitments. The initiative builds on prior UK-supported programmes (e.g., BRACED) and offers a scalable model for all LDCs.

quote.text: Therefore, we recommend that the option to be taken forward in this Business Case is maintaining and increasing support for the currently supported LIFEAR initiative [...] LIFEAR is designed and articulated as catalysing and enabling enhanced access to all major climate finance instruments [...] rather than as a funding source in its own right.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The LIFEAR Board is chaired by an LDC nominee (2022: Senegal’s Ministry of Environment) and includes donor representatives (e.g., UK/FCDO). A Technical Advisory Committee provides additional oversight. Frontrunner countries have autonomy to design local mechanisms, with peer accountability through the LDC group.

quote.text: LIFEAR has been delivered by a third-party managing agent mutually agreed with, and supported by, donors and overseen by a board chaired by an LDC nominee [...] on which the UK (FCDO) as a donor sits.
quote.source: D0004546.odt, The Preferred Option - LIFEAR section

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between frontrunner countries based on demand and performance, but require Board approval. The 70% local allocation target provides a fixed parameter, while country-specific mechanisms allow adaptation to context.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: LIFEAR emphasizes adaptive management through peer learning and south-to-south exchanges. The programme is designed to evolve based on lessons from frontrunner countries, with flexibility to adjust national mechanisms as long as the 70% local finance target is met. Monitoring systems are being developed to support iterative learning.

quote.text: LIFEAR is still developing its MEL system. Learning across the LDCs predicated on south-to-south peer to peer processes so building in adaptability and flexibility. LIFEAR also aiming to integrate adaptative programming to allow flexibility in changing circumstances.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → LIFEAR platform (managing agent) → Frontrunner country governments → Local communities/CBOs

quote.text: LIFEAR has been delivered by a third-party managing agent mutually agreed with, and supported by, donors and overseen by a board chaired by an LDC nominee [...] Countries will develop tailored mechanisms to channel up to 70% of all climate funds available to that country, to local levels...
quote.source: D0004546.odt, The Preferred Option - LIFEAR section

q24_alternatives_considered: Do Nothing (counterfactual)
Deliver through Green Climate Fund (GCF)
Deliver through Global Environment Facility (GEF) instruments (SCCF, LDCF, SGP)
Deliver through Adaptation Fund
Replicate BRACED programme
Channel through IMF Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: LIFEAR was selected as the best fit against the **Principles for Locally Led Adaptation** (LLA), scoring highest in the appraisal (31/40) for its alignment with devolved decision-making, equity, and long-term institutional capacity building. Key factors included: (1) **LDC ownership** (addressing power imbalances in climate finance); (2) **scalability** (potential to reach 1 billion people across all LDCs); (3) **complementarity** with existing UK commitments (COP26 adaptation goals); (4) **proof of concept** (building on BRACED/Devolved Climate Finance lessons); and (5) **catalytic potential** to unlock larger climate finance flows (e.g., GCF, Adaptation Fund) for local use.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited donor commitment to long-term, predictable funding (LIFEAR relies on shifting from project-based to strategic finance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s £12M commitment signals confidence; LIFEAR’s Board will advocate for additional donors. The initiative’s design allows phased scaling based on available funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: LDC capacity constraints in managing devolved funds (e.g., governance, fiduciary risks)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Built-in capacity building (e.g., national platforms, peer learning) and technical assistance from the managing agent. Lessons from BRACED/DCF inform risk management.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political resistance to shifting power to local levels (national governments may resist devolution)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: LDC ownership and south-to-south advocacy reduce Northern imposition risks. Frontrunner countries self-select, ensuring buy-in.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges across multiple climate funds (GCF, Adaptation Fund, etc.)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: LIFEAR’s global platform is designed to harmonize requirements and advocate for simplified access (e.g., Enhanced Direct Access).

quote.text: The closest fit to realising the Principles for Locally Led Adaptation in practice is the LIFEAR initiative. [...] Despite the high risk nature of this approach, returns from investment have the potential to be transformative – an investment of £10M has the ultimate potential to unlock the doors for LDCs to access and effectively use larger streams of less accessible international climate finance.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on **Least Developed Countries (LDCs)**—which face weak institutional capacity, complex climate finance accreditation processes, and political economy barriers—directly shapes partner selection. LIFEAR’s **LDC-owned structure** was chosen because traditional Northern-led models (e.g., GCF accreditation) exclude local actors. The **fragile contexts** in many LDCs (e.g., Burkina Faso, The Gambia) require partners with deep local roots, favoring community-based organizations over international consultants.
q27_constraints_detail: GCF accreditation barriers limit LDC access to funds, necessitating LIFEAR’s Enhanced Direct Access advocacy
Project-based funding models (e.g., GEF SGP) are misaligned with LDCs’ need for **strategic, long-term finance**
Weak local governance in some LDCs requires **embedded capacity building** rather than arms-length grants
Climate vulnerability (e.g., floods, droughts) demands **adaptive, demand-led mechanisms** that Northern partners cannot design alone
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **goal of channeling 70% of climate finance to local levels** drives the **platform-based delivery structure**, as no single organization could achieve this alone. The need for **south-to-south learning** (to avoid Northern expertise dominance) explains the peer-learning design. **Advocacy for systemic change** (e.g., GCF reform) requires a **multi-donor platform** with LDC leadership to credibility challenge global norms.
q28_linkages: 70% local finance target → **devolved governance structure** (national platforms + community mechanisms)
LDC ownership principle → **Board chaired by LDC nominee** (not donor-led)
Need for adaptive management → **peer learning networks** (not rigid Northern TA)
Global advocacy goal → **multi-donor platform** (not bilateral project)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly acknowledges tensions between **equity** (local ownership, inclusive processes) and **efficiency** (speed, cost-effectiveness): (1) **Local decision-making** slows disbursement compared to Northern-led models but ensures relevance; (2) **Peer learning** replaces cheaper Northern technical assistance but builds sustainable capacity; (3) **70% local allocation** reduces overhead for international intermediaries but requires upfront investment in LDC systems. The document argues these trade-offs are justified by **long-term effectiveness** (e.g., reduced climate vulnerability).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: "Devolving power to local actors increases awareness of and investment in adaptation which can lead to longer-term and more effective adaptation outcomes" (slower but more sustainable)
Expertise vs. ownership: "Traditional technical assistance models remain [...] northern-led (at associated high costs and limited effectiveness)" vs. LIFEAR’s south-to-south approach
Cost vs. reach: Upfront capacity-building costs enable access to "larger streams of less accessible international climate finance"
Flexibility vs. accountability: Adaptive programming requires "robust monitoring and learning systems" to balance responsiveness with results
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (LDC fragility, governance challenges) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and a **joint secretariat** (LDC + donor) rather than light-touch management. High climate vulnerability increases the need for **adaptive management**, while weak institutions necessitate **embedded capacity building** (e.g., national platforms).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **capacity-building core objective** directly shapes partner roles: (1) **Frontrunner countries** co-design mechanisms (not just implement); (2) **Local CBOs/NGOs** allocate funds (not just receive them); (3) **LDC Board** sets global advocacy priorities (not donors). This contrasts with traditional models where Northern partners control design and Southern partners execute.

quote.text: The major climate finance instruments [...] will need to reform their systems and allocation processes to allow less arduous accreditation for the more fragile and vulnerable states from the least developed countries. [...] LIFEAR is designed and articulated as catalysing and enabling enhanced access to all major climate finance instruments [...] rather than as a funding source in its own right.
quote.source: D0004546.odt, Appraisal of options and Background sections

key_programme_risks: Limited donor commitment to long-term, predictable funding (affects LIFEAR’s scaling)
LDC capacity constraints in managing devolved funds (fiduciary, governance risks)
Political resistance to devolution within LDC governments
Coordinating across fragmented climate finance instruments (GCF, Adaptation Fund, etc.)
Global economic crises (e.g., cost of living) reducing climate finance availability
Climate shocks disrupting implementation (e.g., floods, droughts in target countries)
Ensuring meaningful inclusion of marginalized groups (women, youth, indigenous peoples)
Balancing upward donor accountability with downward community accountability

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK’s £12M anchor funding; LIFEAR Board advocacy; phased scaling based on results
Embedded capacity building (national platforms, peer learning); technical assistance from managing agent; lessons from BRACED/DCF
LDC ownership model; self-selection of frontrunner countries; south-to-south advocacy
LIFEAR’s global platform to harmonize requirements; advocacy for Enhanced Direct Access
Adaptive programming; flexible finance mechanisms; community-led prioritization
Gender and social inclusion policies; mandatory stakeholder consultation; targeted outreach

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from **BRACED programme (2013–2019)** in Kenya showed that **county-level climate funds** with participatory design led to higher ownership and relevance (e.g., "strong sense of community ownership").
Experience with **Devolved Climate Finance (DCF)** in East/West Africa demonstrated that **local governance structures** can effectively channel funds but require upfront investment in systems.
**Enhanced Direct Access (EDA)** pilots (e.g., Namibia, Antigua & Barbuda) proved that simplified accreditation increases local access but needs scaling.
Post-COVID recovery highlighted the need for **long-term, predictable funding** (not project-based) to address structural vulnerabilities in FCAS.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Prior UK-supported programmes (BRACED, DCF) showed that: (1) **Local ownership** increases effectiveness (e.g., Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds had high community engagement); (2) **Peer learning** accelerates adaptation (e.g., DCF’s cross-country exchanges); (3) **Flexible finance** is critical in fragile contexts (rigid projects fail to respond to shocks); (4) **Advocacy for systemic change** (e.g., GCF reform) must complement local action.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: LIFEAR’s design incorporates lessons by: (1) **mandating 70% local allocation** (vs. BRACED’s ~10%); (2) **focusing on national platforms** (not just projects); (3) **prioritizing south-to-south learning** (reducing Northern TA costs); (4) **linking to global advocacy** (e.g., GCF/Adaptation Fund reform). The shift from BRACED’s "participatory" to LIFEAR’s **"locally led"** model reflects deeper devolution of power.

quote.text: Experience from the former BRACED programme [...] from Kenya shows that the institutional/governance structure and decision-making processes of the Kenya County Climate Change Funds (CCCF) are leading to some significant benefits. These include a strong sense of community ownership of the investments, and the active involvement by the beneficiaries of CCCF investments in the development of project proposals, the construction works and in the day-to-day management of the investments.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £12M UK investment aims to catalyze larger climate finance flows by: (1) Enabling LDCs to access GCF/Adaptation Fund resources (potentially hundreds of millions); (2) Demonstrating proof-of-concept to attract additional donors; (3) Reducing transaction costs for local actors. The business case states this could ultimately unlock finance for nearly 1 billion people in LDCs.

quote.text: This will build the adaptive capacity of up to 4.5 million men, women and children in up to 12 countries and will lay the foundation for scaling up across all least developed countries, ultimately reaching a potential population of nearly 1 billion of the world’s poorest people.

q12_instrument_explanation.text: The UK will fund R2R through an Accountable Grant Agreement with Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors (RPA), the administrative host. RPA manages funds on behalf of the Climate Champions Team, with payments tied to biannual reviews of progress against KPIs. No funds flow directly to downstream partners; RPA covers all legal/financial administration.

q13_structure_description.text: R2R operates as an open partnership platform under the UNFCCC’s Marrakech Partnership. The Climate Champions Team (secretariat) coordinates activities, while partners (NSAs) implement resilience commitments independently. Governance is provided by a Committee with High-Level Champions, UNFCCC, and RPA. The structure leverages existing NSA networks rather than creating new entities.

q14_selection_rationale.text: The High-Level Champions approached FCDO with an unsolicited proposal. Given R2R’s unique mandate from the UNFCCC and its established track record (e.g., 64 partners, 2.9B people reached), a competitive process was deemed unnecessary. The proposal was assessed as value-for-money, and setting up a new vehicle would be costlier and less effective.

quote.text: The High-Level Champions originally approached FCDO with an unsolicited funding proposal for R2R. [...] Therefore, this funding qualifies for delivery through an Accountable Grant Agreement.

q17_governance_details.text: Governance is provided by a **Governance Committee (GC)** composed of: the two serving High-Level Champions, UNFCCC Executive Secretary, COP Presidency representatives, and RPA. The GC meets biannually to approve budgets, policies, and key personnel. A **Marrakech Partnership Leadership Council** provides strategic advice, and a **Coordination Group** (HLC offices, UNFCCC, Climate Champions Team) meets weekly/monthly for operational oversight. FCDO engages quarterly to review progress.

quote.text: The [Coordination] group shall meet on a weekly basis to ensure aligned support to the HLCs, information flow and provide updates regarding delivery; and in an Operations Review Meeting on a monthly basis to provide operational review and oversight.

q19_reallocation_details.text: Flexibility to reallocate funds between R2R’s 6 priorities is retained, but requires alignment with the work plan. The budget is indicative and will be confirmed via a detailed work plan post-approval. Major reallocations would likely require GC approval.

q20_adaptive_management_details.text: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with annual reviews assessing progress against KPIs (e.g., partner recruitment, finance mobilized). The High-Level Champions can adjust strategic priorities in consultation with the GC, but core goals (e.g., 4B people by 2030) are fixed. The Expert Review Group provides ongoing advice on improving the campaign’s effectiveness.
