intersections.risk_affects_management: High-risk contexts (e.g., Gaza, Libya) result in intensive oversight, including milestone-based reporting, due diligence assessments, and embedded advisory support (e.g., HSOT deployments).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in partner roles, with technical experts (e.g., Gender in Humanitarian Action Coordinator in Libya) deployed to strengthen local systems and ensure sustainable delivery.
intersections.quote: The Programme will look to leverage MRD expertise to support posts with limited humanitarian capacity and use the Crisis Reserve Fund to deliver interventions. (D0004273.odt, PROPOSED INTERVENTION)

key_programme_risks: Delays in mobilizing technical expertise due to limited in-country capacity (e.g., Libya, Morocco)
Funding gaps for new crises due to reliance on Crisis Reserve Fund
Security risks limiting access to crisis-affected areas (e.g., Gaza, Al-Kufra)
Reputational risks from operating in politically sensitive contexts (e.g., Israel/Gaza)
Aid diversion in high-risk areas (e.g., Gaza, Syria)
Negative local perceptions of refugee-focused support (e.g., Al-Kufra)
Reliance on downstream partners reducing oversight (e.g., PUI in Libya)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of HSOT advisory support and standby partnerships for rapid deployment.
Unfunded allocation of £4.4m and ability to seek additional funds from MENA baseline or Crisis Reserve Fund.
Use of local CSOs for delivery and pre-positioned supplies.
Neutral language in DEC appeal and ring-fencing of FCDO funds for ODA-eligible locations.
Enhanced due diligence on partners and monitoring through central risk management.
Design of programmes to benefit both refugees and host communities, with communications reflecting overall benefits.
Due diligence on partner oversight capabilities and regular engagement to monitor risks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-positioned technical expertise (e.g., HSOT) is critical for rapid response in FCAS contexts.
Local CSOs are essential for delivery in high-risk areas (e.g., Al-Kufra, Gaza).
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., Crisis Reserve Fund) enable adaptation to evolving crises.
Enhanced due diligence is required for partners operating in proscribed group areas (e.g., Gaza).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous responses in Libya and Morocco demonstrated the need for pre-approved funding and technical capacity to avoid delays. The three-year regional programme was designed to address these lessons by establishing a flexible framework for future crises.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme includes an unfunded allocation (£4.4m) and standby partnerships to enable faster mobilization of expertise, addressing delays experienced in Libya/Morocco responses.
risks_lessons.quote: The mobilisation of advisory support through HSOT meant that the UK has been able to deliver an effective response, however final allocations were not agreed until over a month after the crises in Libya and Morocco. (D0004273.odt, UK RESPONSE AND CAPACITY)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The DEC MENA Humanitarian Appeal is expected to raise £30-40m from the UK public, with the UK government contributing £10m in Aid Match funding. This leverages public donations to scale up NGO responses in Lebanon, Gaza, and Syria.
financial_details.quote: The full £10m [for DEC] will be spent this financial year. (D0007172.odt, INFORMATION)

metadata.programme_name: CHOICES [Commodity Options, Equity and Supply] for Reproductive Health

quote.text: The CHOICES programme will be part of a comprehensive approach to addressing SRHR barriers through a portfolio of SRHR investments aiming to support the full range of conditions required for SRHR access at global, regional and country level, and in humanitarian settings.

metadata.duration_source: AMP Start Date: 01/04/2025; AMP End Date: 31/03/2030

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CHOICES combines financing mechanisms (replenishment to UNFPA Supplies and a market-shaping accelerator) with implementation research (testing new product introductions) and capacity building (strengthening government systems). It aims to transform SRH markets while delivering direct commodity access.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme includes two main components: a replenishment to UNFPA Supplies alongside an innovative accelerator to transform SRH markets... The Accelerator will build government capacity and support national market stewardship...
q3_expected_outputs: 21 million women and girls reached with contraceptives (2022 UNFPA Supplies baseline)
8 million unintended pregnancies averted annually (UNFPA Supplies impact)
170,000 maternal and child deaths prevented annually (UNFPA Supplies impact)
300,000 hormonal IUD units procured since 2021 (market shaping example)
40+ countries with DMPA-SC self-injectable introduced (product innovation)
16 countries with family planning integrated into Essential Package of Health Services (systems strengthening)
$13.3 million mobilized in domestic resources through Match Fund (sustainability)
56% of women in 68 countries able to make SRHR decisions (rights outcome)
what_objectives.summary: CHOICES aims to simultaneously expand access to SRH commodities through UNFPA Supplies while transforming markets through an accelerator that builds government capacity, introduces innovative products, and strengthens health systems for long-term sustainability.

quote.text: The programme includes two main components: a replenishment to UNFPA Supplies alongside an new and highly innovative accelerator to transform SRH markets, driven by national ownership for long term sustainability.

countries_regions: fragile and conflict-affected states (34 of 48 countries in 2022)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in 34 fragile/conflict-affected states where 60% of preventable maternal deaths occur. Climate change, political rollbacks on women's rights, and supply chain disruptions are explicitly noted as high-risk factors.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major... 60 percent of preventable maternal mortality deaths take place in settings of conflict, displacement and natural disasters...
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (limited government capacity for market stewardship)
climate risks (disproportionate impact on women's health)
regulatory (small market sizes deter supplier registration)
supply chain (weak last-mile distribution in rural areas)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political sensitivities around SRHR limit domestic financing transitions. Fragmented private sector procurement creates price/quality variations. Climate events disrupt supply chains while increasing SRHR risks (e.g., 27% higher stunting risk with short birth intervals). In FCAS, 507 women/girls die daily from pregnancy complications.

quote.text: In fragile and conflict-affected states... women and girls often face significantly increased risk of unwanted pregnancy, gender-based violence, and maternal mortality... 60 percent of preventable maternal mortality deaths take place in these settings.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes national ownership with government-led demand shaping (e.g., Kenya's hormonal IUD rollout) while FCDO provides strategic oversight. UNFPA's constituency-based Steering Committee includes donor voting rights, but country-level decisions are government-driven.
q10_capacity_building_details: government capacity for market stewardship (e.g., Nigeria's coordination mechanism)
health worker training (5,000+ trained on hormonal IUD)
supply chain management (eLMIS training for 3,000+ providers)
product introduction support (e.g., Zambia's Levoplant integration)
co-financing mechanisms (Match Fund to mobilize domestic resources)
policy integration (family planning in national health insurance schemes)

partner_organizations.name: UNFPA
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer for Supplies component; global commodity procurement and health systems strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI)
partner_organizations.role: Market shaping technical assistance (Best Practices grant model)

partner_organizations.name: Global South governments
partner_organizations.role: Co-financing and national ownership (e.g., 44 Compact agreements signed)

partner_organizations.name: Reproductive Health Supplies Coalition (RHSC)
partner_organizations.role: Convening and advocacy for market coordination

partner_organizations.name: Social Marketing Organizations (SMOs)
partner_organizations.role: Private sector distribution channels (serve ~50% of women in LMICs)

partner_organizations.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for market shaping initiatives (e.g., SEMA)

partner_organizations.name: Children's Investment Fund Foundation (CIFF)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder for market shaping (e.g., SEMA)

partner_organizations.name: Global Financing Facility (GFF)
partner_organizations.role: Alignment partner for UHC integration

quote.text: The Accelerator will build government capacity and support national market stewardship to strengthen global and country markets... UNFPA Supplies has spearheaded initiatives to generate domestic resources, including a Match Fund that mobilized $13.3 million across 16 countries.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: UNFPA Supplies uses a replenishment model (block funding) while the Accelerator employs technical assistance grants (e.g., CHAI's Best Practices grant). Both are governed by partnership agreements with performance-based milestones.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNFPA Supplies operates through a constituency-based Steering Committee with donor voting rights (including FCDO) and specialized subcommittees. The Accelerator uses a fund manager model (FCDO-managed) with country-level technical assistance providers.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: direct award (UNFPA as existing multilateral partner)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNFPA's role as the "world's largest provider of SRH commodities" and existing FCDO partnership justified direct award. CHAI was selected for market shaping based on proven results from the Best Practices grant under RH Supplies.

quote.text: The UK's investment in UNFPA Supplies continues to deliver impressive results. As the world's largest provider of SRH commodities... the programme has dramatically increased access to SRH supplies in 54 of the world's poorest countries.

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: UNFPA's Steering Committee approves country allocations using a needs-based categorization model (MCPR, maternal mortality, economic status). The Accelerator uses FCDO-managed competitive calls for technical assistance.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: UNFPA Supplies: Constituency-based Steering Committee with donor voting rights (FCDO holds a seat) and specialized subcommittees (e.g., for procurement, HSS). Accelerator: FCDO programme board with ad-hoc participation from GFF/UNITAID.
how_governance.q18_oversight_details: UNFPA Supplies uses annual in-country assessments tied to commodity delivery performance. The Accelerator employs quarterly reviews against product introduction milestones (e.g., hormonal IUD rollout targets).

quote.text: The programme has embarked on an ambitious reform journey, including the launch of a dramatically improved governance and operational model... a constituency-based Steering Committee and specialised subcommittees that provide FCDO with much stronger visibility and assurance.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: UNFPA Supplies uses a needs-based allocation model allowing shifts between countries (e.g., 2021 categorization reform). The Accelerator has flexible funding for country priorities but requires FCDO approval for major reallocations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Country introduction plans can be adjusted based on demand (e.g., Tanzania's hormonal IUD pilot). New products can be added via the Catalytic Opportunities Fund ($4.9M allocated to 21 proposals).

quote.text: The programme launched a new approach to budget allocation that saw countries categorised based on their modern contraceptive prevalence rate, maternal mortality ratio and economic status... providing a fair way to ensure countries with highest needs receive most funding.
quote.source: D0007228.odt, Box 1: UNFPA Supplies - Driving Equitable Access

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNFPA/CHAI (implementers) → [government health systems for last-mile delivery]. No additional sub-grantee layers documented.
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: UNFPA Supplies payments tied to commodity delivery milestones (75% on-time delivery in 2021). Accelerator uses output-based payments (e.g., per health worker trained).

quote.text: In 2021, at least 75% of commodity orders were delivered on time in 39 out of 48 programme countries... UNFPA Supplies has maintained low average shipping costs (4-6% of commodity purchases).

q24_alternatives_considered: standalone market manager (SEMA model - rejected due to donor consensus failures)
bilateral country programmes (rejected for lack of scale)
pure commodity financing (rejected for missing market transformation)
global procurement only (rejected for ignoring country-level barriers)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The dual-component model was selected to balance (1) immediate commodity access via UNFPA's proven procurement scale with (2) long-term market transformation through country-owned stewardship. Lessons from RH Supplies showed that commodity funding alone couldn't address systemic barriers like weak supply chains or private sector fragmentation.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (UNFPA's $2.62 per CYP vs country procurement costs)
experience (UNFPA's 54-country footprint; CHAI's Best Practices success)
flexibility (Catalytic Opportunities Fund for emerging needs)
equity (64% rural facilities stocked vs 21% in 2021)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination failures (SEMA collapse)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO-managed Accelerator with ad-hoc partner participation (GFF/UNITAID) to avoid standalone entity risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Market distortion from large procurements
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand aggregation paired with price transparency (UNFPA's competitive pricing) and supplier diversification.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Government absorption capacity limits
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Gradual co-financing transitions (Match Fund) and embedded TA (e.g., Kenya's training modules).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FCAS implementation challenges
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Humanitarian preparedness strategies in 14 countries; refugee-inclusive rollout plans.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (75% on-time deliveries; 380K hormonal IUDs procured)
equity (64% rural stocking rate; disability-inclusive guidelines)

quote.text: While pooled, global procurement of SRH products represents excellent value for money, there is a wider set of barriers that complicate product access... Market shaping activities 'accelerate' the impact of large-scale commodity procurement by securing better prices and allowing countries to buy newer products.
quote.source: D0007228.odt, Why fund market shaping interventions?

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: FCAS contexts limit partner options to organizations with humanitarian expertise (e.g., UNFPA's 34 FCAS operations). Political sensitivities around SRHR exclude some local partners, requiring multilateral intermediaries.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict zones require partners with humanitarian supply chain expertise (e.g., UNFPA's emergency kits).
Rollbacks on abortion rights limit engagement with certain government agencies.
Small market sizes in LMICs deter commercial suppliers, necessitating donor-backed intermediaries.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both immediate commodity access (UNFPA's replenishment) and systemic change (Accelerator's TA) drove the dual-structure design. Product innovation goals (e.g., hormonal IUD introduction) required flexible funding mechanisms like the Catalytic Opportunities Fund.
q28_linkages: Market transformation objective → Accelerator's country-level TA structure
Commodity access goal → UNFPA's global procurement model
Equity focus → embedded capacity building for marginalized groups
Sustainability aim → co-financing mechanisms (Match Fund/Compacts)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions between (1) rapid scale via UNFPA's centralized procurement and (2) inclusive market development requiring localized TA. The programme addresses this via: (a) earmarked funds for fragile states, (b) private sector engagement for last-mile reach, and (c) self-care products (DMPA-SC) to overcome stigma barriers.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: UNFPA's bulk procurement enables $2.62/CYP but risks bypassing local suppliers; mitigated via supplier diversification targets.
Expertise vs ownership: Northern TA (CHAI) accelerates introductions (e.g., hormonal IUD) while building Southern capacity (5,000+ health workers trained).
Cost vs reach: Private sector channels (serving 50% of women) have higher prices; addressed via price negotiations (e.g., EC costs reduced 7x).
intersections.risk_affects_management: High FCAS risk profile drives intensive oversight (quarterly reviews in conflict zones) and embedded advisors (e.g., last-mile tracking systems). Stable countries use lighter-touch milestone checks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Countries with strong stewardship (e.g., Kenya) lead product introductions, while fragile states (e.g., Yemen) receive direct TA. The Match Fund's $13.3M mobilization shows how capacity building enables co-financing transitions.

quote.text: The programme's work on health systems strengthening is central to these efforts and has been bolstered by the shift to tying HSS technical assistance to annual in-country assessments... In Kenya, stronger government leadership saw hormonal IUD rolled out to 32% of facilities in 2 months.

key_programme_risks: Political rollbacks on SRHR rights (e.g., 11 countries reduced budgets in 2021)
Supply chain disruptions (COVID-19 increased shipping costs to 10%)
Manufacturer concentration (e.g., 2 suppliers for hormonal IUDs)
FCAS implementation (60% of maternal deaths occur in conflict zones)
Domestic financing transitions (only 4 countries spent >80% of SRH budgets in 2021)
Climate change impacts (increased SRHR risks during extreme weather)
Anti-rights group opposition (well-funded campaigns in 60+ countries)
Product stockouts (rural facilities had only 21% stock rates in 2021)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Foreign Secretary's SRHR campaign and civil society partnerships to counter opposition.
Regional warehousing and last-mile tracking systems (eLMIS for 3,000+ providers).
Supplier diversification (e.g., new quality-assured MA combipack manufacturers).
Humanitarian preparedness strategies in 14 countries; refugee-inclusive rollouts.
Match Fund ($13.3M mobilized) and Compact agreements (44 signed).
Heat-stable products (e.g., carbetocin) and disaster-resilient supply chains.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, co-financing requires conflict-sensitive approaches (e.g., Yemen/Djibouti/CAR contributions).
Humanitarian settings need pre-positioned stocks (17 countries received emergency kits in 2022).
Local partners in FCAS require additional TA (e.g., Central African Republic's first-time contributions).
Refugee populations must be explicitly included in rollout plans (e.g., Rwanda's 98% combipack coverage).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: RH Supplies taught that (1) standalone market managers fail without donor consensus (SEMA collapse), (2) country ownership requires flexible TA (Best Practices grant success), and (3) governance reforms must include donor voting rights (UNFPA Steering Committee changes). The 50% ODA cut in 2021 caused reputational damage, prompting the new needs-based allocation model.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added GHI seat to UNFPA Steering Committee for better alignment.
Shifted from product donation to co-financing (44 Compact agreements).
Expanded Catalytic Opportunities Fund based on Best Practices grant success.
Integrated climate-resilient products (e.g., heat-stable carbetocin).
Embedded equity metrics (e.g., rural stock rates increased from 21% to 64%).

quote.text: The failure of SEMA to be viable shows the challenges of building a high-performing new institution against a backdrop of significant donor change... A key obstacle was securing consensus among donors on programme priorities.
quote.source: D0007228.odt, Box 2: Key learnings from Track 2

co_funding_partners.co_financing_mechanism: Compact agreements and Match Fund ($13.3M mobilized)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: $13.3M in domestic resources mobilized through Match Fund; $30.7M government expenditure on contraceptives in 2022 (up from $21.2M). Every $1 invested generates $8.40 in returns by 2035 (UNFPA estimate).

quote.text: By 2023, 44 governments had signed Compact agreements with UNFPA, formalising their commitment to share the cost of programme-funded commodities... Government expenditure on contraceptives totalled US$30.7 million in 2022 compared with US$21.2 million the previous year.
quote.source: D0007228.odt, Donor investments in SRH products

metadata.programme_name: BEJ Open Societies Enabling Fund (OSEF)

quote.programme_name: "BEJ Open Societies Enabling Fund (OSEF)" (D0004818.odt, Summary Information)
quote.duration: "Original project start and end dates: April 2023-March 2025" (D0004818.odt, Summary Information)
quote.sector: "promote UK values and interests through supporting a transparent, healthy democracy with a vibrant and protected civil society and strong protections for human rights" (D0004818.odt, Information)

metadata.duration_source: "Original project start and end dates: April 2023-March 2025" (D0004818.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling funds to civil society), capacity building (strengthening civil society organizations), and policy influence (supporting legal reforms and electoral transparency). It funds activities to protect human rights, promote media freedom, and tackle modern slavery during Indonesia's politically volatile election period.
what_objectives.q1_source: "this programme will contribute to the Human Development strand of the CBP. Funding will support Indonesia’s civil society in responding to threats to civil liberties ahead of the February 2024 Election..." (D0004817.odt, Programme summary) AND "The British Embassy Jakarta Open Societies Enabling Fund (BEJ OSEF) aims to promote UK values and interests through supporting a transparent, healthy democracy with a vibrant and protected civil society and strong protections for human rights." (D0004818.odt, Information)
q3_expected_outputs: Supporting relationship building with local CSOs that promote and protect Indonesia’s open society and democracy
Defending UK-Indonesia shared values as reflected in various human rights treaties and other documents, including protecting the freedom of religion and belief, media freedom and anti-discrimination
Contributing to the creation of a conducive environment for human rights defenders to carry out their work, including from particularly marginalised and minority groups
Building public resilience against narratives that attack Indonesia’s open society
Supporting legal reform measures to ensure that the letter and implementation reflect the UK-Indonesia shared values and human rights commitments
Technological tool to boost transparency and integrity of the 2024 elections (mobile application for crowd-sourced monitoring of electoral results)
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds Indonesian civil society organizations to protect human rights, promote media freedom, and support legal reforms during the 2024 election period, with a focus on minority rights and electoral transparency.

quote.objectives: "Supporting civil society in responding to threats to civil liberties ahead of the February 2024 Election, as well as to rule of law dynamics that may positively or adversely impact Indonesia’s vibrant democracy" (D0004817.odt, Programme summary)
quote.outputs: "The additional funding will allow BEJ to support a leading, well-regarded civil society partner to deliver a technological tool that will boost the transparency and integrity of the series of elections in Indonesia in 2024." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Indonesia is categorized as a "flawed democracy" with declining civic freedoms (Freedom House score 58/100 in 2023). The programme operates in a politically febrile period with risks to human rights defenders, but the overall programme risk rating is classified as "Minor".
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Minor" (D0004817.odt, Summary Sheet) AND "Indonesia is categorised as a 'flawed democracy' by the Economist Intelligence Unit... Freedom House ratings for political rights and civil liberties saw the country’s score fall to 58/100 in 2023" (D0004817.odt, Context)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The shrinking civic space and legal reforms (e.g., new Criminal Code) create challenges for civil society operations. Human rights defenders face harassment, SLAPP lawsuits, and physical threats, particularly in politically charged periods like elections. The programme must navigate these constraints while supporting advocacy and legal reforms.

quote.constraints: "Indonesia’s laws and regulations either due to the letter or the interpretation have been used to silence peaceful expressions" (D0004817.odt, Theory of Change) AND "Methods of attacks also vary, including by using criminal and civil justice system to administer SLAPP (strategic lawsuit against public participation), cyber attacks and physical violence or threats." (D0004817.odt, Context)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The British Embassy Jakarta (BEJ) Political Section manages the fund, selects partners, and oversees all projects. Indonesian civil society organizations implement activities but do not have decision-making authority over fund allocation or strategic direction.
q10_capacity_building_details: monthly monitoring and capacity-building sessions for partners
assistance with risk registers and safeguarding
programme-funded AO position to provide closer support to partners
six-monthly partners’ meetings to identify collaboration opportunities

partner_organizations.name: NETGRIT
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partner for electoral transparency tool (mobile application for crowd-sourced election monitoring)

partner_organizations.name: Unnamed civil society organizations (6 selected for 2023-24)
partner_organizations.role: Implementing partners for human rights, minority protection, and legal reform activities

partner_organizations.name: KUHP reform coalition (mentioned as example)
partner_organizations.role: Advocacy for criminal law reform (not directly funded but referenced as key actor)

quote.partners: "OSEF’s primary aim to support civic freedoms and human rights defence work in Indonesia... six projects that will aim to deliver impact to human rights defence work in western and eastern Indonesia, empower and protect youth, women, and girls, and sexual and religious minorities." (D0004818.odt, Program-funded AO Position)
quote.selection: "The selection of six projects... has resulted in the selection of six projects that will aim to deliver impact to human rights defence work in western and eastern Indonesia" (D0004818.odt, Program-funded AO Position)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses accountable grants to fund civil society projects. Grants are disbursed on a reimbursement basis, with six-monthly financial and substantive reports required. The fund operates as a flexible enabling mechanism to respond to emerging needs, particularly during the election period.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The British Embassy Jakarta (BEJ) Political Team manages the fund directly, with support from the Development Management Unit (DMU). An AO-level staff position is funded by the programme to provide day-to-day oversight, monitoring, and capacity building for grantees. No intermediary organization is used; BEJ acts as the fund manager.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: For the initial six projects, a bidding process was used, but the selection was limited to pre-identified civil society actors committed to human rights. The electoral transparency tool (NETGRIT) was selected via direct award due to its unique expertise and time sensitivity, in accordance with FCDO rules for sole-source procurement when no alternative exists.

quote.instrument: "The bidding process will be done for FY2023-2024, with a maximum of six approved projects." (D0004817.odt, Management Case) AND "The FCDO funding will be used to build the digital assets and fund related activities... to support its deployment; costs (and therefore value for money) are therefore straightforward to assess." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)
quote.selection: "After conducting due diligence process with our selected partners, we have also found that the projects require closer, monthly monitoring..." (D0004818.odt, Program-funded AO Position) AND "The project would be implemented with NETGRIT without a competitive process, in accordance with the relevant rules and guidance." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)

quote.governance: "The programme board will assign a programme officer for each selected project, the Assistant Political Officer as the PRO and the Political Counsellor as the SRO." (D0004817.odt, Management Case) AND "Quarterly reporting and progress meetings will be held with the partner to discuss progress, forecasts, challenges and risks." (D0004817.odt, Management Case)
quote.oversight: "Organizing monthly meetings with partners to track progress, including financial expenditure... Assisting in maintaining each OSEF project’s risk register..." (D0004818.odt, Program-funded AO Position)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects with approval, particularly to respond to emerging needs during the 2024 election period. The programme is designed to be flexible, with ad-hoc arrangements possible for urgent initiatives in 2024.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments to respond to political dynamics, such as the 2024 election. New initiatives can be funded without a bidding process if situational dynamics require it, as long as they align with the fund’s objectives.

quote.flexibility: "For FY 2024-2025, consideration will be made to either finance continuation to the 2023-2024 funded projects or funding a particularly urgent initiative without bidding, depending on the situational dynamics at the time." (D0004817.odt, Management Case) AND "The additional funding will allow BEJ to support... a particularly urgent initiative... to promote electoral transparency and integrity." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (BEJ Political Team) → Civil Society Implementing Partners (no intermediary layer; BEJ manages directly).

quote.layers: "The programme will be managed through the British Embassy Jakarta Political Team, drawing on the Development Management Unit for guidance and support where necessary." (D0004817.odt, Management Case)
quote.payment: "To the extent that is possible, the fund will be disbursed on reimbursement basis, thus compelling six monthly financial and substantive report to ensure expenses are reimbursed." (D0004817.odt, Management Case)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option A: Project delivered by one appointed civil society grant administrator through bidding process
Option B: Project delivered by a number of local civil society organisations through bidding process (smaller grants)
Option C: A number of trusted civil society organisations are invited to carry out select projects they champion that are in line with the open society fund’s objectives
Option D: Do nothing
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option B (multiple local CSOs through bidding) was initially preferred for its value for money and ability to spread risk across actors. However, the final approach combines elements of Options B and C: a restricted competition for six projects plus a direct award to NETGRIT for the electoral tool. This hybrid model balances risk diversification with the need for rapid, credible action during the election period.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Increased administrative burden for BEJ if managing multiple small grants
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limiting the number of partnerships per year, drawing on wider resources, and engaging DMU to streamline processes. Hiring an AO-level staff to assist with monitoring.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of financial irregularities with longer reporting chains if using a single grant administrator
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Avoided by not using Option A; instead, BEJ manages grants directly with quarterly reports and reimbursement-based disbursements.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Poor programme delivery due to political momentum leaving partners preoccupied
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular communication with partners to anticipate delays and adjust timelines.

quote.alternatives: "From the four options above, option B is the preferred choice as it is the most likely to deliver the desired outcomes with the most VFM." (D0004817.odt, Appraisal)
quote.rationale: "The project would be implemented with NETGRIT without a competitive process, in accordance with the relevant rules and guidance... No organisation would therefore be able to carry out the project as effectively or credibly." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)
quote.vfm: "Economy: Supporting civil society partners in affecting legislative change and ensuring implementation of laws that are in line with open society values is a proven effective method in Indonesia... Efficiency: Civil society organizations... will be able to serve as a policy bridge and work on the realisation of changes sought in a resources-efficient manner." (D0004817.odt, Economy/Efficiency)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The politically febrile context in Indonesia, including legal restrictions (e.g., new Criminal Code) and risks to human rights defenders, limits partner selection to organizations with proven track records in navigating these constraints. Smaller or less established CSOs may lack the capacity or credibility to operate safely, leading BEJ to prioritize well-regarded actors like NETGRIT.
q27_constraints_detail: Legal risks (e.g., Criminal Code articles criminalizing cohabitation or defamation) require partners with legal expertise to avoid backlash.
Political sensitivity during elections necessitates partners with nationwide credibility (e.g., NETGRIT’s links to the Electoral Commission).
Safeguarding risks for vulnerable groups (e.g., women HRDs, religious minorities) require partners with robust protection mechanisms.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid, flexible responses to election-related threats (e.g., democratic backsliding, disinformation) shapes the delivery structure. This includes: (1) a fund manager model (BEJ) to enable quick reallocation of resources, (2) direct awards for time-sensitive initiatives (NETGRIT’s electoral tool), and (3) embedded capacity building to ensure partners can adapt to emerging risks.
q28_linkages: Responsive approach (WHAT) → Fund manager model (HOW) to allow ad-hoc adjustments during elections.
Legal reform objectives (WHAT) → Selection of partners with legislative advocacy experience (WHO).
Protection of minority rights (WHAT) → Direct oversight by BEJ to mitigate safeguarding risks (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (inclusive support for marginalized groups) with efficiency (rapid delivery during elections). For example: (1) The electoral tool (NETGRIT) was directly awarded for speed, potentially excluding other CSOs. (2) Capacity building is embedded to ensure smaller partners can meet safeguarding standards, adding administrative costs but improving inclusivity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct award to NETGRIT prioritizes credibility and timeliness over open competition.
Cost vs. reach: Hiring an AO for oversight increases management costs but enables support for a broader range of partners.
Risk aversion vs. innovation: Restricted competition for grants reduces financial risks but may limit engagement with newer CSOs.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (shrinking civic space, election volatility) justifies intensive oversight (monthly meetings, risk registers) and a reimbursement-based payment structure to detect irregularities early. The programme’s ‘Minor’ risk rating allows for flexibility but requires close monitoring due to the political context.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) Partners must demonstrate safeguarding and financial management capacity to receive grants. (2) The AO position is explicitly tasked with providing ‘capacity building in several areas especially on risk register and safeguarding’ (D0004818.odt), shaping how partners engage with the fund.

quote.constraints: "The shrinking civic space for civil society participation in Indonesian governance issues... impacts Indonesia’s democratic gains since 1998." (D0004817.odt, Programme summary) AND "The origin of this project is an unsolicited approach by... NETGRIT... No organisation would therefore be able to carry out the project as effectively or credibly." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)
quote.tradeoffs: "This will constitute significantly less money than commissioning a larger organization to manage OSEF..." (D0004818.odt, Program-funded AO Position) AND "The selection of established, well-respected implementing partners will help mitigate all these risks." (D0004817.odt, Risk)

key_programme_risks: Unavailability of budget due to pressures on ODA
Increased safeguarding risks due to working with politically vulnerable groups
Poor programme delivery due to political momentum leaving partners preoccupied
Lack of programme supervision due to lack of human resources at the Embassy
Weak financial management by partners
Poor integration with other Embassy programmes
Election-related disinformation or manipulation undermining democratic processes
Backlash against human rights defenders during politically charged periods

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Unavailability of budget due to pressures on ODA
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased programme approach, with future components dependent on budget availability.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Increased safeguarding risks due to working with politically vulnerable groups
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Thorough Due Diligence Assessments and regular safeguarding check-ins with implementing partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor programme delivery due to political momentum leaving partners preoccupied
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular communication with partners to anticipate and discuss how to respond to undue delays.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of programme supervision due to lack of human resources at the Embassy
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Limiting number of partnerships each year, ensuring processes are thorough but proportionate, and hiring an AO-level staff for oversight.
Quarterly reports to detect fraud or mismanagement early; reimbursement-based disbursements; selection of established partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Poor integration with other Embassy programmes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Consulting internal Embassy stakeholders and inviting key individuals to progress meetings.
Supporting NETGRIT’s electoral transparency tool to provide independent monitoring of results.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS-like contexts (e.g., Indonesia’s flawed democracy), civil society requires both financial support and protection mechanisms (e.g., legal safeguards, crisis response networks).
Electoral periods in volatile democracies necessitate agile funding mechanisms to respond to emerging threats (e.g., direct awards for time-sensitive tools).
Embedded capacity building is critical to mitigate risks for partners operating in high-risk environments (e.g., monthly safeguarding check-ins).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past civil society advocacy in Indonesia (e.g., Anti-Sexual Violence Law, Migrant Worker Protection Law) demonstrates that sustained, well-coordinated efforts can achieve legislative change. The programme builds on this by supporting coalitions with legal expertise (e.g., KUHP reform coalition).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addition of the AO position and direct award to NETGRIT were introduced based on: (1) the need for closer partner monitoring (identified during due diligence), and (2) the time-sensitive opportunity to address election integrity gaps.

quote.risks: "Risk: Unavailability of budget due to pressures on ODA. Mitigated by a phased programme approach..." (D0004817.odt, Risk) AND "The origin of this project is an unsolicited approach by... NETGRIT... There is significant need for this project. Actors across Indonesia’s political system... are open in their concern about democratic backsliding in Indonesia." (D0004818.odt, Increased funding limit to promote electoral transparency and integrity)
quote.lessons: "Supporting civil society’s efforts will also assist in ensuring the recent legal developments and reform agenda will be implemented in a manner that reflects UK-Indonesia shared values... Some key examples of this are the enactment of Law on Migrant Worker Protection and the Anti-Sexual Violence Law." (D0004817.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

quote.budget: "The committed OSEF funds for the period of April 2023-March 2025 is £600,000. This amendment seek to increase the funding by £80,000, making the total funding £680,000." (D0004818.odt, Summary Information)
quote.allocation: "The grants offered will be a minimum of £50,000 and maximum £150,000 per annum, making a maximum of six small grants to be administered each year." (D0004817.odt, Timing)

metadata.programme_name: DIAL Nepal: Development Influencing And Learning in Nepal
metadata.quote: The proposed facility supports development influencing and learning, enabling the British Embassy in Kathmandu (BEK) to respond to strategic opportunities. It promotes innovation and influencing as part of BEK’s international development portfolio, with a focus on subnational engagement. (D0005977.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: DIAL Nepal will be active for up to three years from August 2023 (D0005977.odt, "DIAL Nepal will allow BEK to respond to short-term opportunities...")

what_objectives.q1_explanation: DIAL Nepal is a financing mechanism that enables policy influence and capacity building through small projects. It supports BEK staff to fund interventions that build relationships and influence policy reforms, particularly at subnational levels, while incorporating learning on adaptive policy influencing.
what_objectives.q1_source: "DIAL Nepal enables BEK staff members to submit funding proposals for small projects to support key interlocutors... Proposals will centre on building relationships and influencing policy reforms for development impact, in line with BEK’s campaign goals." (D0005977.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Alliances and influencers of development-related reform convened and enabled
Learning on effective policy influencing incorporated into BEK’s ways of working and programmes
Initiatives funded through DIAL Nepal will contribute to long-term policy outcomes (e.g., poverty alleviation, good governance, green growth)
what_objectives.summary: DIAL Nepal is a responsive facility designed to fund small projects that build strategic relationships and influence policy reforms, with a focus on subnational engagement and learning on adaptive approaches.
what_objectives.quote: "The overall outcome for DIAL Nepal is improved engagement with key interlocutors to deliver reforms critical to poverty alleviation, good governance, and green growth." (D0005977.odt, Intended policy objectives)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as moderate risk due to the limited scale of the programme and close engagement of BEK, though safeguarding risks are judged as moderate.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall risk rating: Moderate" and "Safeguarding risks are judged to be moderate, given the limited scale of the programme and close engagement of BEK." (D0005977.odt, Risk rating and Safeguarding sections)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme aims to address BEK’s limited agility in responding to strategic interventions, particularly at subnational levels, due to weak institutional capacity and political economy challenges. Climate risks are also a focus, given Nepal’s vulnerability to disasters and climate change.
where_context.quote: "Under its existing portfolio, BEK’s agility and responsiveness to immediate, strategic interventions has been limited. This has undermined BEK’s ability to build strategic relationships and influence policy reforms that are important for Nepal’s development trajectory, especially at subnational level." (D0005977.odt, Context issues)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making power rests with BEK (a UK institution), though implementation involves local stakeholders and provincial engagement units. The Delivery Board, chaired by the Development Director (UK), oversees all funding decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (via learning on adaptive policy influencing)
institutional strengthening (supporting provincial/local government engagement)

partner_organizations.name: British Embassy Kathmandu (BEK)
partner_organizations.role: Lead institution and fund manager

partner_organizations.name: Provincial Engagement Units (within BEK)
partner_organizations.role: Support implementation and local engagement

partner_organizations.name: Implementing partners (suppliers/contractors)
partner_organizations.role: Deliver specific projects as approved by BEK

who_partners.quote: "DIAL Nepal will be managed by BEK’s E&K Hub under the strategic leadership of the Development Director and with oversight from the Delivery Board." (D0005977.odt, Governance arrangements)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: DIAL Nepal uses a combination of contracts (for implementing partners) and internal BEK funding mechanisms (for staff-led proposals). Payments are milestone-based or reimbursable, depending on the agreement with suppliers.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: BEK’s Evidence and Knowledge (E&K) Hub manages the facility, with oversight from the Delivery Board. Individual projects are led by BEK staff or contracted suppliers, but all decisions and funds flow through BEK.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: For procurements up to £25,000, a competitive process is recommended but not mandatory; decisions to sole-source must be justified. Larger projects (up to £250,000) require more elaborate proposals but are still managed within BEK’s framework. This balances speed with accountability.
how_mechanism.quote: "For procurements up to £25,000, a competitive process is not mandatory but is recommended; decisions not to competitively procure should be justified." (D0005977.odt, Procurement guidance)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Delivery Board, chaired by the Development Director, oversees all funding decisions. It includes representation from BEK’s campaign goal leads and is described as BEK’s "most inclusive decision-making body." Small proposals (up to £30k) can be approved via a written procedure, while larger ones require a dedicated meeting.
how_governance.quote: "The Delivery Board (chaired by the Development Director) will decide on the proposals... Financial performance reports will be scrutinised to ensure funds are being properly accounted for and used for intended purposes." (D0005977.odt, Governance and Financial risks sections)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects, but each proposal must align with BEK’s campaign goals and be approved by the Delivery Board. The facility is designed to be adaptive but within a structured framework.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme explicitly incorporates learning on adaptive policy influencing. Proposals must include a commitment to integrating lessons into wider programmes, and the Delivery Board can adjust timelines or procedures as needed.
how_flexibility.quote: "DIAL Nepal will incentivise learning on agile and adaptive policy influencing as an explicit objective in each approved project... The DD and Delivery Board can amend this procedure and/or timeline on a needs basis." (D0005977.odt, Rationale and Proposal process sections)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (BEK) → Implementing partner/supplier. BEK manages the facility directly, with suppliers contracted for specific projects.
how_efficiency.quote: "Payments will not be made in advance of need... funds will be disbursed on receipt of a valid invoice supported by a breakdown of expenditure in line with the agreed workplan, budget and cost drivers." (D0005977.odt, Financial risks section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Relying solely on existing programmes (rejected due to limited agility)
De-incentivizing programmes from responding to influencing opportunities (avoided by making DIAL a complementary facility)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: DIAL Nepal was chosen to address BEK’s limited agility in responding to strategic opportunities, particularly at subnational levels. It complements existing programmes by providing a flexible, rapid-response mechanism for policy influencing while ensuring alignment with BEK’s campaign goals. The modality balances speed (via streamlined procurement) with accountability (via Delivery Board oversight).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented, dispersed, and uncoordinated funding of ad hoc requests may not improve BEK’s relationships or influencing capability.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ensure clear focus on BEK’s focal provinces and priority areas; decision-making by the Delivery Board; thought leadership role of the Development Director.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Disproportionate programme management pressure on E&K and wider office.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use of Smaller Projects design (per PRoF) to reduce burden; teams requesting funds manage their own projects; possible procurement of a procurement agent.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: De-incentivizing programmes to become more adaptive and focused on policy influencing.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limited size of DIAL Nepal; requirement to assess programmes as the first port of call; integrate lessons into programme adaptations.

why_rationale.quote: "The need to establish a separate facility to support influencing is part of the ambition of BEK to be more adaptive and responsive, and through that better at influencing policies of provincial and local governments." (D0005977.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The subnational focus (provincial/local government engagement) shapes partner selection, as projects must align with BEK’s focal provinces and prioritize local interlocutors. This limits partners to those with strong subnational presence or relationships.
q27_constraints_detail: Geographic focus on BEK’s focal provinces
Requirement for provincial/local government engagement
Need for partners with existing subnational relationships
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The goal of policy influencing at subnational levels determines the delivery structure: a flexible, BEK-managed facility with rapid-response funding windows and decentralized implementation by provincial units or local partners.
q28_linkages: Policy influencing objective → Need for agile, small-scale funding → DIAL’s two funding windows (£25k and £250k)
Subnational focus → Requirement for provincial engagement units → Decentralized project management
Learning on adaptive influencing → Embedded in proposal templates and Delivery Board oversight
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (streamlined procurement, rapid response) with equity (inclusive Delivery Board, GESI requirements, subnational focus). For example, while competitive procurement is not mandatory for small grants, proposals must demonstrate gender equality and inclusion.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed (rapid funding windows) vs inclusion (GESI requirements)
Centralized oversight (Delivery Board) vs decentralized implementation (provincial units)
Flexibility (adaptive management) vs accountability (milestone-based payments)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to milestone-based oversight and a structured governance process (Delivery Board), with safeguarding and financial risks mitigated through due diligence and regular reporting.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building (e.g., learning on adaptive influencing) is embedded in the roles of implementing partners, who must integrate lessons into their work. Provincial engagement units also play a key role in bridging national and local capacity.
intersections.quote: "DIAL Nepal will allow BEK to respond to short-term opportunities to influence key interlocutors and/or decisions, prioritising provincial and local government in BEK’s focal provinces... Proposals will centre on building relationships and influencing policy reforms for development impact." (D0005977.odt, Programme summary and Rationale sections)

key_programme_risks: Fragmented, uncoordinated funding undermining BEK’s influencing capability
Disproportionate management pressure on BEK teams
De-incentivizing programmes from adapting to policy influencing opportunities
Safeguarding risks (moderate, due to limited scale and close BEK engagement)
Financial risks (fraud, misuse of funds)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Clear focus on focal provinces; Delivery Board oversight; alignment with campaign goals.
Use of Smaller Projects design; procurement agent; monitoring of workload.
Limited DIAL size; requirement to exhaust programme options first.
Due diligence for partners; adherence to UK Government Safeguarding Standards.
Reimbursement-based payments; regular financial reports; zero-tolerance for fraud.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from the Nepal Influencing Pilot (NEIP, 2022–2023) and the TA Research Fund under the PCU informed DIAL’s design, particularly the need for clear decision-making procedures, empowered governance, and a higher risk appetite with robust mitigation measures.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: DIAL incorporates NEIP’s guide to influencing strategies, systematic planning/monitoring/evaluation, and a focus on subnational engagement (transitioning from PCUs to provincial facilities). It also adopts a higher risk appetite, accepting that not all interventions will succeed.
risks_lessons.quote: "Lessons from a previous facility, the TA research fund under the PCU, are that a clear decision-making procedure, clarity of purpose and an empowered governance structure are critical to success. A higher risk appetite that puts in place robust mitigation measures but accepts that not all interventions will be successful is important." (D0005977.odt, Context issues)

financial_details.quote: "DIAL Nepal will have a budget of GBP 2 million for a period of up to three years." (D0005977.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Humanitarian Access in Nigeria (SHAN) Programme

quote.text: The programme will finance the delivery of key assets to enhance humanitarian access, including uninterrupted supply of electricity from renewable sources to eight deep-field humanitarian hubs that enable access of humanitarian workers to approximately 1.3m internally displaced persons (IDPs) and the construction of cargo, storage and fuel facilities that streamline operations and facilitate efficient transportation of relief goods and essential humanitarian aid...
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Programme summary and Theory of Change sections

metadata.duration_source: The programme will be executed over 15 months with an initial mobilisation period of three months for detailed scoping, agreement of bid specifications and selection of key suppliers by the contracted partners followed by a 12-month core delivery period.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: SHAN aims to improve humanitarian access in northeast Nigeria by investing in critical infrastructure: solar installations at humanitarian hubs and upgraded aviation facilities. The programme directly provides enabling services (safe housing, offices, connectivity, and reliable air transport) to humanitarian workers reaching vulnerable populations in remote areas.
what_objectives.q1_source: The humanitarian response in northeast Nigeria targets 6m people with live-saving support in a difficult environment. This programme proposes two capital investments which will bolster access, improve efficiency and strengthen the operational delivery of the humanitarian response to ongoing humanitarian needs through: Solar installations in Humanitarian Hubs which provide humanitarian workers with safe housing, offices and connectivity in remote areas. Improved aviation infrastructure to increase the operational capacity, reliability, and efficiency of humanitarian transport...

q3_expected_outputs.output: Solarisation of eight humanitarian hubs
q3_expected_outputs.target: 8 hubs serving approximately 1.3 million IDPs

q3_expected_outputs.output: Upgraded aviation infrastructure (fuel storage, cargo, passenger facilities)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Improved reliability for 51,300 passengers and 205 tonnes of cargo transported annually (2022 baseline)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Reduction in diesel fuel costs
q3_expected_outputs.target: 76% reduction in carbon footprint (655 tonnes CO2e/year) and cost savings equivalent to 690,000 litres of diesel fuel annually

q3_expected_outputs.output: Enhanced operational efficiency
q3_expected_outputs.target: Fewer cancelled flights and improved passenger/cargo processing at Maiduguri airport

what_objectives.summary: SHAN delivers critical infrastructure to sustain humanitarian operations in northeast Nigeria's conflict-affected areas, focusing on renewable energy solutions and aviation logistics to maintain access to 1.3 million IDPs in 'extremely hard-to-reach' locations.

quote.text: The programme will finance the delivery of key assets to enhance humanitarian access, including uninterrupted supply of electricity from renewable sources to eight deep-field humanitarian hubs that enable access of humanitarian workers to approximately 1.3m internally displaced persons (IDPs) and the construction of cargo, storage and fuel facilities that streamline operations...

countries_regions: Nigeria (Northeast region, specifically Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The operating environment in North-East Nigeria remains extremely volatile and fluid. The security situation continues to deteriorate, humanitarian needs are increasing, and the negative impacts of the macroeconomic crisis are significant. 8.3 million people require humanitarian assistance, with 1-1.2 million in 'extremely hard-to-reach' areas where aid workers face regular security threats.
where_context.q5_source: 8.3m people require humanitarian assistance in North-East Nigeria, with 6m people targeted with live-saving support. Between 1 and 1.2 million people are in areas currently classified as ‘extremely-hard-to-reach’ for humanitarian actors. The operating environment is fragile: compromised by insecurity and lack of access. The safety of aid workers is regularly threatened...
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security threats limit road access to 1.2 million people in 'extremely hard-to-reach' areas, forcing reliance on costly air transport. Diesel fuel shortages (prices tripled in past year) and regulatory hurdles for construction permits delay infrastructure projects. The macroeconomic crisis (inflation, currency risks) increases procurement costs for solar panels and aviation fuel. Weak government capacity in conflict zones requires UN agencies to manage all logistics.

quote.text: The operating environment is fragile: compromised by insecurity and lack of access. The safety of aid workers is regularly threatened and reaching populations in deep field locations is expensive and reliant on helicopter transport... Diesel fuel prices have tripled in Nigeria during the last year and account for 30% of the total operational budget of the Humanitarian Hubs.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO (UK) sets strategic priorities and approves all financial decisions; UN agencies (IOM/UNHAS) implement with technical oversight from their global HQs. Nigerian government has regulatory approval roles but no implementation authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: Deployment of a NORCAP Energy Expert (60% time) to support IOM with solar system design and procurement
Training for national NGO staff on hub operations and maintenance
Knowledge transfer through joint monitoring with Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority

partner_organizations.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of solarisation for 8 humanitarian hubs; hub management
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (global HQ in Geneva, operations in Nigeria)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS), managed by World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Upgrades to aviation infrastructure (fuel storage, cargo/passenger facilities)
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (global HQ in Rome, operations in Nigeria)

partner_organizations.name: Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)/NORCAP
partner_organizations.role: Technical support for solar energy systems (60% of an Energy Expert's time)

partner_organizations.name: Federal Aviation Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCA)
partner_organizations.role: Regulatory approvals and oversight

quote.text: FCDO has pre-selected two partners with sufficient capacities to deliver on the Theory of Change. The partners are: the International Organization for Migration (IOM) currently operating the eight (8) humanitarian hubs in the Northeast region of Nigeria... and the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS), managed by the World Food Programme (WFP)... No other partners in the complex operating environment of North-East Nigeria are available with appropriate reach, footprint, mandate or expertise to deliver these investments.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Primary instrument is Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with IOM and UNHAS, supplemented by a Contribution Agreement with WFP (aligned with global framework). Payments are milestone-based with 7% overhead for eligible costs. Co-funding from USAID and ECHO (£893k) is channeled through IOM.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO Nigeria manages two parallel MoUs with IOM and UNHAS, each with dedicated project teams. Monthly review meetings and quarterly progress reports align activities. Technical oversight comes from FCDO's Humanitarian and Resilience Team (HART) and the Integrated Strategy and Delivery Unit (ISDU). Steering Committees for Humanitarian Hubs and UNHAS provide multi-stakeholder coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were pre-selected based on (1) sole service provision (IOM operates all 8 hubs; UNHAS is the only humanitarian air service), (2) existing long-term relationships with FCDO, (3) proven track records in Nigeria's FCAS context, and (4) government endorsements. The document states: 'No other partners... are available with appropriate reach, footprint, mandate or expertise.'

quote.text: FCDO has pre-selected two partners with sufficient capacities to deliver on the Theory of Change... Based on a detailed review of the humanitarian response, delivery context and relative competencies, FCDO has pre-selected two partners... No other partners in the complex operating environment of North-East Nigeria are available with appropriate reach, footprint, mandate or expertise to deliver these investments.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Two Steering Committees exist: (1) Humanitarian Hubs Steering Committee and (2) Humanitarian Air Service Steering Committee. Both include FCDO, implementing partners (IOM/UNHAS), and service users (NGOs, other UN agencies). Decisions on operational delivery and risk management are made collectively, with FCDO retaining financial approval authority.

quote.text: The HART team will also work closely with the Steering Committees for both the Humanitarian Hubs and the Humanitarian Air Service for the operational delivery and management of the programme... Monthly review meetings to assess the partners’ performance against set delivery criteria... Quarterly review meetings and tracking of recommendations from the DDAs will be implemented.
quote.source: D0006183.odt, FCDO Programme Governance and Delivery Partners’ Governance sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Reallocation between the two outputs (solar hubs vs aviation) requires SRO approval. Within each output, partners have flexibility to adjust budgets during the 12-month delivery phase, provided milestones are met. The document notes: 'changes would take place within the approved budget ceiling, based on clear and rigorous evidence and subject to approval from the SRO.'
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a 3-month mobilisation phase for 'detailed scoping, agreement of bid specifications and selection of key suppliers,' allowing adjustments before core delivery. Quarterly reviews assess whether to 'continue, stop, or change the intervention design/approach.' However, major changes require Development Director approval.

quote.text: The programme will be executed over 15 months with an initial mobilisation period of three months for detailed scoping, agreement of bid specifications and selection of key suppliers... We will ensure internal communications/advocacy on funding is clear as to the imperative on maintaining agreed payment levels and disbursement schedules. FCDONigeria will be the principal financier of both outputs however... if necessary, changes would take place within the approved budget ceiling, based on clear and rigorous evidence and subject to approval from the SRO.
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Delivery Route and Financial Details sections

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (IOM/UNHAS) → Subcontractors (e.g., solar panel suppliers, construction firms). No further sub-grantees are mentioned.

quote.text: Payments will be made based on requests submitted by the partners based on a narrative justification and expenditure reporting accompanying the request... This will be reviewed by the PRO and programme manager... Accountability for final approval will lie with the Development Director. Partners will be spending 'directly' (i.e., spending money themselves) through procurements and 'indirectly' (i.e., through contracted suppliers/vendors).
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Reporting and Financial Risk Management sections

q24_alternatives_considered: Investment in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure in primary health centres, schools and learning centres
More ambitious aviation infrastructure programmes including construction of landing pads for helicopters
'Do nothing' option (continuing with diesel generators and existing aviation facilities)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The selected modality (direct awards to IOM/UNHAS via MoUs) was chosen because: (1) **Alignment**: Both partners are already central to FCDO's existing humanitarian architecture (IOM manages all 8 hubs; UNHAS is the sole air service provider). (2) **Risk Mitigation**: Their long-standing presence in Nigeria's FCAS context reduces delivery risks compared to new entrants. (3) **Speed**: Pre-existing relationships and infrastructure allow rapid mobilisation (15-month timeline). (4) **Value for Money**: Solar investments will offset diesel costs within 5 years, and aviation upgrades reduce flight cancellations. (5) **Equity**: Hubs provide subsidised access to national NGOs, ensuring local actors benefit.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud in procurement-heavy infrastructure programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners must provide Delivery Chain Risk Mappings; FCDO conducts spot checks on subcontractors; payments linked to audited expenditure reports; whistleblowing policies required.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slippages due to technical/procurement delays in FCAS context
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Monthly review meetings to track progress; Gantt charts for task dependencies; 3-month mobilisation phase for detailed planning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Regulatory hurdles from Nigerian aviation authorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage partners' existing relationships with FAAN/NCA; initial positive feedback already secured; long-term asset handover to authorities planned.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Inflationary pressures on construction materials
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Prioritise domestic procurement to reduce transport costs; scale economies for solar installations; VfM negotiations during mobilisation.

quote.text: Other options considered in the design phase of this business case included investment of available capital funding in water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure in primary health centres, schools and learning centres... These were discounted as being i) less aligned to the Theory of Change of FCDO’s existing humanitarian programming in northeast Nigeria... and ii) a larger programme with higher risks of not being delivered in a short timeframe. A ‘do nothing’ option remains feasible, however would mean that current costs for fuel would need to continue to run the humanitarian hubs... The investment options chosen both enhance the capacity of the humanitarian response to reach current priority locations with goods and people, substantially support common services across the existing humanitarian portfolio...
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Other Options Considered and Value for Money sections

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in northeast Nigeria constrains partner selection to UN agencies with (1) existing security protocols for high-risk areas, (2) government-approved mandates to operate in conflict zones, and (3) logistical capacity to manage air/road blockades. The document states: 'No other partners in the complex operating environment of North-East Nigeria are available with appropriate reach, footprint, mandate or expertise to deliver these investments.' National NGOs lack the scale for capital-intensive infrastructure, and private contractors cannot navigate the regulatory/security environment.
q27_constraints_detail: Security threats limit partners to those with armed escorts and UN privileges
Government requires UN agencies for large-scale infrastructure approvals
Local contractors lack capacity for solar/aviation technical standards
Donor coordination mechanisms (e.g., North-East Donor Group) favour multilateral implementers
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, large-scale infrastructure** in a **high-risk environment** determines the delivery structure: (1) **Capital intensity** requires partners with existing asset management experience (IOM's hubs; UNHAS's aviation fleet). (2) **Security constraints** necessitate UN agencies with negotiated access to conflict zones. (3) **Time sensitivity** (15-month delivery) precludes open competitions or capacity-building for new partners. The direct award to IOM/UNHAS via MoUs reflects the **implementation urgency** over inclusive partnership models.
q28_linkages: Solar hubs require partners with existing hub management mandates (IOM's sole role)
Aviation upgrades need the only operational air service provider (UNHAS)
FCAS context demands partners with pre-negotiated government/armed group access
Short timeline (15 months) excludes complex consortium arrangements
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly acknowledges trade-offs between **efficiency** (rapid delivery via UN agencies) and **local ownership**: (1) **Northern expertise**: NORCAP (Norwegian) provides technical solar support, while Nigerian firms are subcontractors. (2) **Cost vs. reach**: Solar investments prioritise hubs serving 1.3m IDPs over dispersed WASH projects. (3) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Direct awards to IOM/UNHAS exclude local NGOs from decision-making, though they access subsidised hub services. Mitigation includes training for national NGO staff on hub operations.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Direct awards to UN agencies enable 15-month delivery but limit Nigerian NGO control over infrastructure.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern technical expertise vs. Southern capacity
q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: NORCAP Energy Expert (Norwegian) leads solar design, with 'training for national NGO staff' as mitigation.
Hubs in 8 locations prioritise operational efficiency over broader geographic coverage.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **severe risk rating** (FCAS + fiduciary risks) drives **intensive oversight**: (1) Monthly reviews replace annual reporting. (2) Milestone-based payments (not upfront) with expenditure audits. (3) Embedded FCDO advisors in Steering Committees. (4) Delivery Chain Risk Mappings required for all subcontractors. The document states: 'Because of the nature of capital programmes in Nigeria the fiduciary risk is high... we will ensure that reporting includes sufficient detail to assess fiduciary risk.'
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity constraints shape partner roles through: (1) **IOM's technical gap**: NORCAP deploys an Energy Expert (60% time) to compensate for limited in-house solar expertise. (2) **UNHAS's procurement limits**: WFP/UNDP technical departments support engineering quality. (3) **Local contractor exclusion**: International firms lead construction due to 'lack of local capacity for large-scale solar/aviation works' (implied in risk mitigation strategies).

quote.text: The operating environment in Nigeria remains extremely volatile and fluid, which presents severe exposure to fraud and aid diversion... The fiduciary environment of delivery is high risk with significant potential for fraud or aid diversion especially on a procurement-heavy infrastructure programme such as SHAN... No other partners in the complex operating environment of North-East Nigeria are available with appropriate reach, footprint, mandate or expertise to deliver these investments... The complexity of the programme and the delivery approach... makes this a credible risk. We will work to agree detailed work plans, have a full mitigation strategy for task dependencies, have regular update meetings to track progress...
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Risk Management and Delivery Route sections

key_programme_risks: Deteriorating security in Northeast Nigeria reducing humanitarian access
Macroeconomic crisis (inflation, fuel price tripling) increasing procurement costs
Regulatory delays from Nigerian aviation authorities (FAAN/NCA)
Fraud in procurement chains (solar panels, construction materials)
Partner capacity gaps in solar/aviation technical standards
Currency exchange risks (naira volatility)
Aid diversion in conflict zones
Poor estimation of budgets leading to cost overruns
Delays in supplier contracting during mobilisation phase
Failure to secure government approvals for aviation fuel storage

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Flexible delivery plans; partners' experienced security teams; adaptive use of air assets.
Delivery Chain Risk Mappings; spot checks on subcontractors; audited expenditure reports; 7% overhead cap.
Leverage partners' existing relationships with FAAN/NCA; early communication of plans.
Prioritise domestic procurement; scale economies for solar; VfM negotiations during mobilisation.
NORCAP Energy Expert deployment; WFP/UNDP technical support for UNHAS.
Budget contingencies; quarterly financial reviews to adjust for exchange rates.
UN zero-tolerance policies; FCDO spot checks; whistleblowing mechanisms.

fcas_specific_lessons: Use of solar power reduces reliance on diesel (target of fuel theft and price volatility in conflict zones)
UNHAS's integrated humanitarian terminal at Maiduguri airport improves coordination during security incidents
IOM's hub model provides 'safe accommodation and offices' in areas where NGOs cannot operate independently
Pre-positioning fuel storage mitigates supply chain disruptions during road blockades
Steering Committees with donor/NGO participation improve information-sharing in fluid contexts
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from NENTAD (2017-22) and HARP (2022-25) programmes inform SHAN's design: (1) **Hub sustainability**: Solarisation builds on IOM's existing hub management since 2017. (2) **Aviation reliability**: UNHAS's track record in conflict zones (e.g., South Sudan, CAR) validates the infrastructure approach. (3) **Localisation limits**: Previous attempts to engage local contractors for capital works faced 'quality and timeline issues,' leading to international firm preference. (4) **Risk management**: DDAs and monthly reviews were added after NENTAD faced procurement delays.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: SHAN incorporates: (1) **Shorter timeline** (15 months vs NENTAD's 5 years) to mitigate FCAS volatility. (2) **Milestone-based payments** (replacing NENTAD's annual disbursements). (3) **Explicit climate alignment** (solar focus) responding to HARP's carbon footprint critiques. (4) **Technical advisers** (NORCAP) addressing NENTAD's solar design gaps.

quote.text: Lessons and best practices applied in RDEL programming will guide this team’s management of SHAN... During previous and ongoing partnerships with FCDO Nigeria, both partners demonstrated the controls and processes necessary to manage financial and compliance risks...
