The complexity of the programme and the delivery approach (including leasing of solar panels, and multi-construction by UNHAS) makes this a credible risk. We will work to agree detailed work plans, have a full mitigation strategy for task dependencies... FCDO has developed a CDEL cost eligibility guidance for partners, and we will work to organise inception meetings to clarify points in the guidance...
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Delivery Route and Risk Management sections

co_funding_partners.partner: European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Co-funding of £893k from USAID/ECHO for Output 1 (solar hubs), representing ~8% of total budget. The programme also enables cost recovery mechanisms for hub/aviation operations, though specific leverage figures are not quantified.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: 100% capital expenditure (CDEL). The programme finances infrastructure assets (solar systems, aviation facilities) with no revenue components.

quote.text: SHAN has a proposed budget of £11 million... All costs on SHAN will count solely as CDEL... FCDO Nigeria will be the principal financier of both outputs however Output 1 will be co-funded by the USAID Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance and European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO) with a sum of approx. £893k... Core cost drivers of the programme are principally related to input costs of the infrastructure improvements... FCDO will also pay overhead costs of 7% where the overheads are reasonable and attributable to the creation of the infrastructural works...
quote.source: D0006183.odt, Proposed Budget and Sources of Funding sections

metadata.programme_name: Promoting Women and Girls’ Education in ASEAN
metadata.quote: This programme will help to improve the learning outcomes, agency and freedoms of women and girls and other left-behind groups across the full range of countries in ASEAN, spanning Low, Lower and Upper Middle-Income countries, in line with the commitments we have made to ASEAN as a Dialogue Partner. (D0006832.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: Programme Value: £30m (over 5 years) (D0006832.odt, Programme summary); AMP Start Date: April 2023; AMP End Date: March 2028 (D0006832.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines **capacity building** (strengthening education systems and regional partnerships), **policy influence** (supporting reforms and regional policy dialogue), **implementation research** (piloting evidence-based interventions), and **service delivery** (direct technical assistance to improve learning outcomes). It focuses on generating and using evidence to inform education policies while delivering tangible improvements in foundational learning, digital skills, and gender inclusion.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will deploy technical advice to support regional partnerships and reform initiatives that can influence and multiply domestic and multilateral education finance. [...] It will provide technical assistance, capacity building and evidence assessment to help ASEAN Member States (AMS) design and implement more cost-effective measures to address the foundational learning crisis. (D0006832.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: AMS participation in robust regional learning assessments (e.g., SEA-PLM 2024)
Enhanced data systems and advocacy for out-of-school children and youth (OOSCY), particularly girls and children with disabilities
Gender-specific barriers to digital skills and employment overcome in key sectors (STEM, green economy)
AMS access to timely expertise on EdTech investments for inclusive learning
Accelerated progress toward global objectives: 40 million more girls in school and 20 million learning to read by 2026
q3_expected_outputs.target: 40 million girls in school; 20 million reading by age 10 (global targets)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy uptake of cost-effective interventions for foundational learning (aligned with GEEAP "Smart Buys")
Pilot programmes for marginalised groups (girls, disabled children) in IAI countries (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve foundational learning outcomes for girls and marginalised groups in ASEAN through technical assistance, regional policy influence, and targeted interventions in digital skills, EdTech, and inclusive education. It aligns with UK global commitments on girls' education (40M in school/20M reading by 2026) and ASEAN’s education priorities, using evidence-based approaches to scale cost-effective solutions.
what_objectives.quote: The programme’s intended impact is: Improved foundational learning outcomes for girls and boys in ASEAN, with enhanced education and skills training systems that are responsive to the demands of marginalised girls, women and disadvantaged groups. (D0006832.odt, Expected outcome and impact)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The risk rating is 'Moderate' due to FCDO’s limited recent experience in ASEAN’s public education sector, post-COVID-19 disruptions, and the diversity of ASEAN Member States (AMS) in terms of income levels, political economies, and education system maturity. Myanmar’s conflict and fragility add complexity, while regional coordination challenges (e.g., aligning with ‘ASEAN ways of working’) are noted.
where_context.q5_source: The risk rating for the programme is ‘Moderate’. FCDO has comparatively limited recent experience working in the public education sector in most AMS and the full extent of COVID-19 disruption in basic education and skills sub-sectors is not yet known. (D0006832.odt, Risk)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (diverse AMS priorities and ‘ASEAN ways of working’)
conflict (Myanmar’s ongoing conflict and military regime)
weak institutions (limited education system capacity in CLMV countries)
data limitations (lack of disaggregated data on marginalised groups)
climate risks (ASEAN’s high vulnerability to climate shocks, e.g., Myanmar #2, Philippines #4 in Global Climate Risk Index)
regulatory (language and labour market restrictions limit cross-border skills mobility)
post-COVID-19 learning losses (140M Southeast Asian children affected, 27M waited >1 year to return to school)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The **political economy** constraints require aligning with ASEAN’s consensus-based decision-making, which may slow reforms. **Conflict in Myanmar** limits direct engagement with the regime, requiring non-state actor partnerships. **Weak institutions** in CLMV countries necessitate capacity-building focus. **Climate risks** disrupt education provision (e.g., school closures from floods/droughts), while **digital divides** exclude marginalised groups from EdTech solutions. **Post-COVID-19 learning losses** exacerbate existing inequalities, particularly for girls and disabled children.
where_context.quote: Alignment with ASEAN ways of working and the geographic and socio-economic diversity between AMS may prove challenging. [...] The ongoing conflict in Myanmar is worsening its situation. [...] Over 140 million Southeast Asian children have experienced learning losses, over 27 million children were waiting for more than a year to return to their classrooms. (D0006832.odt, Risk and Situation Analysis on COVID-19)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: FCDO (UK) in partnership with ASEAN Secretariat (ASEC) and ASEAN Member States (AMS)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme will be **jointly designed and delivered** through formal governance mechanisms with ASEC, AMS, and UK officials. Decision-making involves **ASEAN sectoral bodies** (e.g., SEAMEO) and **AMS governments**, with FCDO providing technical expertise. The ‘ASEAN centrality’ principle ensures AMS leadership in priority-setting, while UK brings global evidence (e.g., GEEAP).
q10_capacity_building_details: Technical assistance to AMS for education system reforms (e.g., SEA-PLM data use)
Training for AMS officials on EdTech strategies and digital transformation
Pilot programmes for inclusive education (e.g., screening tools for children with disabilities)
Knowledge exchange platforms to share best practices across AMS
Support for Timor-Leste’s ASEAN accession capacity building
Gender-sensitive skills training for marginalised adolescent girls

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Secretariat (ASEC)
partner_organizations.role: Coordinating body for regional accreditation and governance; aligns programme with ASEAN blueprints (e.g., ASEAN Work Plan on Education 2021-2025)

partner_organizations.name: Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Organisation (SEAMEO)
partner_organizations.role: Regional technical partner for learning assessments (e.g., SEA-PLM 2024) and knowledge exchange

partner_organizations.name: ASEAN Member States (AMS) governments
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of national interventions; policy uptake and data provision

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: Support for English language, girls’ education, and TVET/higher education mobility (existing programmes)

partner_organizations.name: Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel (GEEAP)
partner_organizations.role: Evidence-based advisory on cost-effective interventions (e.g., ‘Smart Buys’ for learning)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF/UNESCO/ILO
partner_organizations.role: Technical cooperation on inclusive education and EdTech (e.g., data disaggregation for children with disabilities)

partner_organizations.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
partner_organizations.role: Complementary financing for education sector (e.g., via International Financing Facility for Education)

partner_organizations.name: Education Commission (Asia Hub)
partner_organizations.role: Regional knowledge hub for education transformation (chaired by UNSG Envoy for Education)

partner_organizations.name: UK Education Centre of Expertise / EdTech Hub
partner_organizations.role: Technical advisory on EdTech and adaptive learning solutions

partner_organizations.name: Non-state actors in Myanmar
partner_organizations.role: Direct assistance to Myanmar people (bypassing military regime)

who_partners.quote: This programme will be run as a joint ASEAN-UK cooperation project, with UK Government officials and the programming implementing partners working closely with ASEC, AMS and the relevant ASEAN Sectoral Bodies throughout. [...] The programme will aim to strengthen ASEAN-UK relationships and draw on the relative strengths of both parties to maximise programme impact. (D0006832.odt, ASEAN-UK Dialogue Partner Relationship)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a **combination of instruments**: (1) **Technical Assistance (TA) contracts** for evidence generation and advisory services (e.g., GEEAP, EdTech Hub); (2) **Partnership Agreements** with ASEC/SEAMEO for regional coordination; (3) **Grants or MOUs** with AMS governments for pilot interventions. Non-ODA funds may be used for Singapore/Brunei engagement. The UK’s **International Financing Facility for Education (IFFEd)** is mentioned as a complementary financing mechanism.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a **multi-layered partnership model**: (1) **Strategic oversight** by FCDO and ASEC; (2) **Regional coordination** via SEAMEO and ASEAN sectoral bodies; (3) **Country-level implementation** through AMS governments and local partners. Technical working groups (e.g., IAI Task Force) will guide priority-setting, while UK-based entities (e.g., EdTech Hub) provide backstopping.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on **pre-existing relationships** (e.g., ASEC, SEAMEO, British Council) and **alignment with ASEAN accreditation requirements**. The programme builds on UK’s prior engagements (e.g., Skills for Prosperity in Malaysia/Philippines/Indonesia) and leverages multilateral platforms (e.g., GEEAP, ADB) to ensure credibility and regional buy-in. Competitive processes are not mentioned; selection prioritises **ASEAN centrality** and **UK strategic partnerships**.
how_mechanism.quote: The programme will be accredited by ASEAN so that it can be formally recognised as a contribution to the ASEAN-UK Plan of Action. Requirements for ASEAN accreditation are: [...] Be endorsed by either the relevant ASEAN sectoral body/ASEAN body or the Committee of Permanent Representatives (CPR), or both. (D0006832.odt, ASEAN Ways of Working)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A **formal programme governance mechanism** will include: (1) **ASEAN sectoral bodies** (e.g., SEAMEO, IAI Task Force); (2) **FCDO and UKASEAN country posts**; (3) **Technical Working Groups** for each priority area (e.g., foundational learning, EdTech). Decisions on sub-awards and pilots will require **joint approval** from AMS and FCDO, with ASEC facilitating regional alignment. The **ASEAN-UK Joint Consultative Committee (JCC)** is referenced for high-level oversight.
how_governance.quote: This will be done through the formal programme governance mechanisms (see management case below) and through the joint design and delivery of various programme activities. (D0006832.odt, ASEAN-UK Dialogue Partner Relationship)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated **between thematic areas** (e.g., foundational learning, EdTech) with **joint approval** from FCDO and ASEAN bodies, but **country-specific allocations** (e.g., IAI focus) are likely fixed. The programme’s **portfolio approach** allows adaptation based on early implementation lessons (e.g., shifting focus from skills to EdTech if demand is higher).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs **adaptive management** through: (1) **Agile pilot testing** (e.g., proof-of-concept interventions for marginalised groups); (2) **Annual reviews** of regional priorities (e.g., ASEAN Work Plan updates); (3) **Flexibility to respond to emerging needs** (e.g., Timor-Leste’s accession, post-COVID-19 recovery). Adjustments require **ASEC/FCDO endorsement** and alignment with ASEAN blueprints.
how_flexibility.quote: Option 5’s inter-connected thematic focus that is backed by a range of global and locally contextual studies offers stronger supporting evidence than focusing on many of the possible priority single issues considered. [...] The approach of directing limited resources and expertise to enhance AMS service delivery [...] allows adaptation and flex to adjust focus. (D0006832.odt, Discussion of Feasible Options)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → **Regional partners (ASEC/SEAMEO)** → **Country-level implementers (AMS governments/NGOs)** → **End beneficiaries (schools, marginalised groups)**. The British Council and EdTech Hub may add sub-layers for specific components.
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will utilise technical assistance (TA) and evidence to work with AMS to scope conducive enabling environments, identify opportunities and adapt evidence-based interventions. (D0006832.odt, Example Activities)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Continue current UK engagement on trade/investment in private education and English language, with lighter-touch skills/TVET support.
Provide financial contribution to an ASEC-administered trust fund or UN/multilateral agency with generic priority areas.
Allocate resources to 7 ODA-eligible AMS based on population/human development indices, designing separate bilateral interventions.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Focus on a Signature Priority Regional Issue
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Select one specific theme (e.g., disability inclusion, EdTech) for deep regional/national engagement with proof-of-concept pilots.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Regional Partnerships across Mutually Agreed Priority Themes (CHOSEN)
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Develop limited thematic partnerships (foundational learning, EdTech, skills, inclusion) combining regional policy uptake with demand-based AMS support.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 (**Regional Partnerships across Priority Themes**) was selected because it: (1) **Aligns with ASEAN accreditation requirements** (addresses multiple PoA commitments: 3.2, 3.4, 4.4.2); (2) **Balances strategic fit** for both UK (IDS, Women & Girls Strategy) and ASEAN (Education Work Plan 2021-2025); (3) **Mitigates risk** by focusing on 4 interconnected themes (vs. over-reach in Option 2 or fragmentation in Option 3); (4) **Leverages existing UK assets** (e.g., GEEAP, EdTech Hub, Skills for Prosperity lessons); (5) **Allows adaptability** through a portfolio approach, enabling shifts between themes based on early evidence.
q25_decision_factors: equity (focus on marginalised girls and IAI countries)
value for money (building on existing UK investments like S4P)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity of managing 4 thematic areas across 10 diverse AMS
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Judicious selection of implementation partners with regional/national capabilities; phased rollout with pilot testing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: ASEC’s limited programme implementation capacity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO embedded advisors and technical working groups to support ASEC; focus on ASEC’s strengths in coordination vs. direct delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Misalignment with ‘ASEAN ways of working’ (consensus-based decision-making)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Formal accreditation process and endorsement by ASEAN sectoral bodies; joint design with AMS from inception.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other ASEAN-UK programmes (e.g., economic integration, health)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear delineation of education focus; coordination through ASEAN-UK Joint Consultative Committee (JCC).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Myanmar’s conflict limiting direct engagement
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Funds channeled through non-state actors; technical assistance designed to bypass military regime.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (targeting IAI countries and marginalised groups)
economy (leveraging existing platforms like SEAMEO, EdTech Hub)
why_rationale.quote: Option 5: Regional Partnerships across Mutually Agreed Priority Themes [...] is judged to be slightly favourable as it also takes a portfolio approach, allowing adaptation and flex to adjust focus from initial entry points where early implementation and the political economy suggest more traction, influence and outcomes can be realised. (D0006832.odt, Discussion of Feasible Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **ASEAN context** constrains partner selection by requiring: (1) **ASEAN accreditation**, which mandates engagement with **all 10 AMS** (including non-ODA-eligible Singapore/Brunei) and alignment with ASEAN blueprints; (2) **ASEAN centrality**, limiting Northern-led decision-making and necessitating endorsement by ASEAN sectoral bodies; (3) **Myanmar’s conflict**, restricting partnerships to non-state actors; (4) **Diverse AMS capacities**, requiring tailored technical assistance (e.g., IAI countries need more intensive support).
q27_constraints_detail: ASEAN accreditation rules (must engage all AMS and avoid bilateral dominance)
Myanmar’s military regime (precludes direct government partnerships)
Timor-Leste’s prospective membership (requires capacity-building inclusion)
ASEAN’s consensus-based decision-making (slower reforms, need for regional buy-in)
ODA eligibility constraints (Singapore/Brunei require non-ODA funds)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **programme’s objectives** (foundational learning, EdTech, skills, inclusion) determine a **multi-layered delivery structure**: (1) **Regional policy influence** (via ASEC/SEAMEO) for cross-cutting themes like EdTech; (2) **Country-specific TA** (via AMS governments) for contextualised interventions (e.g., IAI pilots); (3) **Global evidence hubs** (GEEAP, EdTech Hub) to ensure cost-effective solutions. The **mixed delivery structure** (consortium + platform) reflects the need to balance **regional coordination** (ASEAN priorities) with **local adaptation** (AMS diversity).

q28_linkages.mechanism: Regional assessments (SEA-PLM) + country-level TA for AMS to design interventions
IAI Task Force-led pilots with local OPDs (Organisations of Persons with Disabilities)
Partnerships with industry and ASEAN Labour Ministers for gender-sensitive TVET
ASEC-endorsed regional strategy with country-level adaptation support

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses trade-offs between **equity** (reaching marginalised girls, IAI countries) and **efficiency** (scaling cost-effective interventions). Key tensions include: (1) **Inclusion vs. speed**: Disaggregated data collection for children with disabilities slows implementation but is critical for equity; (2) **Local ownership vs. global expertise**: AMS leadership in priority-setting may conflict with UK’s evidence-based ‘Smart Buys’; (3) **Breadth vs. depth**: Covering 10 AMS risks shallow engagement, but focusing only on IAI countries would undermine ASEAN centrality. The **portfolio approach** (Option 5) was chosen to balance these trade-offs by allowing adaptive focus shifts.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Inclusion (disaggregated data for disabled girls) vs. speed (delays in pilot rollout)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Phased data strengthening with initial focus on IAI countries

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: ASEAN centrality (consensus-based decisions) vs. agility (slow reforms)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Embedded FCDO advisors to facilitate alignment

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Global evidence (GEEAP ‘Smart Buys’) vs. local context (AMS priorities)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Joint design of interventions with AMS technical working groups

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Breadth (10 AMS) vs. depth (limited resources per country)
q29_tradeoffs_detail.resolution: Tiered support: intensive for IAI, lighter-touch for upper-MICs

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (diverse AMS, post-COVID disruptions, Myanmar conflict) drives **milestone-based oversight** with embedded advisors. High-risk areas (e.g., Myanmar, EdTech cybersecurity) trigger **intensive monitoring**, while lower-risk components (e.g., SEA-PLM support) use **light-touch reviews**. The **ASEAN accreditation requirement** adds a layer of regional governance, increasing coordination complexity but mitigating fiduciary risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: (1) **ASEC/SEAMEO** focus on regional coordination (leveraging their convening power); (2) **AMS governments** lead national implementation (building systemic capacity); (3) **UK entities** (GEEAP, EdTech Hub) provide backstopping (transferring global knowledge). The **IAI Task Force** exemplifies this: AMS lead priority-setting, while UK/FCDO provide TA to strengthen data systems.
intersections.quote: The programme will assist ASEC, SEAMEO and ASEAN developing nations to develop strategic initiatives and scale interventions with promise to improve student progression and learning outcomes. [...] Embedding these principles into policy dialogue, strategic planning and industry partnerships will aim to provide a coherent UK entry point. (D0006832.odt, How can the UK Support ASEAN to Tackle the Learning Crisis and Gender Inequality?)

key_programme_risks: Limited FCDO experience in ASEAN’s public education sector (mitigated by partnering with SEAMEO/ASEC)
Post-COVID-19 learning losses and school closures (addressed via GEEAP’s RAPID framework for recovery)
Myanmar’s conflict restricting engagement (non-state actor partnerships prioritised)
Digital divides excluding marginalised groups (gender-sensitive EdTech strategies planned)
ASEAN’s consensus-based decision-making slowing reforms (embedded advisors to facilitate alignment)
Weak data systems for tracking marginalised groups (pilots for disability-inclusive data tools)
Climate shocks disrupting education provision (resilience-building integrated into curriculum support)
Overlap with other ASEAN-UK programmes (coordination via JCC)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: FCDO’s limited recent experience in ASEAN education
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Leverage SEAMEO’s regional expertise and GEEAP’s global evidence; embed advisors in ASEC.
Channel funds through non-state actors; focus on direct support to Myanmar people.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: ASEAN’s diverse AMS capacities leading to fragmented outcomes
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Tiered support model: intensive for IAI countries, lighter-touch for upper-MICs.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Digital divides excluding girls and disabled children
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Gender-audits of EdTech tools; pilot offline/low-tech solutions for remote areas.
Phase activities with early wins (e.g., SEA-PLM 2024) to build momentum.
Integrate disaster risk resilience into school infrastructure TA and curriculum.

fcas_specific_lessons: In Myanmar, **avoid benefiting the military regime** by channeling funds through non-state actors (e.g., ethnic education providers, CSOs).
Use **conflict-sensitive education approaches** (e.g., portable credentials for displaced students).
Prioritise **psychosocial support** in post-conflict areas to address trauma barriers to learning.
Leverage **cross-border education networks** (e.g., with Thailand) for Myanmar’s displaced populations.

lessons_from_previous.lesson: Need for **stronger AMS ownership** to sustain reforms; S4P’s delivery challenges highlighted the importance of aligning with national TVET strategies.
**Equitable access** and **teacher support** are critical for learning outcomes; Vietnam’s model of disadvantaged student inclusion will inform regional dialogue.
**Rapid, evidence-based interventions** (e.g., catch-up classes) can mitigate learning losses; ASEAN adaptation of GEEAP’s RAPID framework planned.

lessons_from_previous.source: British Council’s light-touch engagement in Cambodia/Laos
lessons_from_previous.lesson: **Deeper partnerships** are needed for systemic change; programme will build on but intensify prior engagements.

design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **Timor-Leste capacity-building** following ASEAN’s request for pre-accession support.
Incorporated **climate resilience** into education TA after recognizing ASEAN’s high climate vulnerability (e.g., Myanmar #2 in Global Climate Risk Index).
Expanded **disability inclusion** focus based on lessons from Cambodia/Laos pilots (e.g., Washington Group data tools).
Adopted **portfolio approach** (Option 5) to allow adaptive shifts between themes, addressing risks of over-reach in earlier options.
risks_lessons.quote: The programme will draw from the UK’s extensive domestic and international experience of doing similar work in the past, including in Africa and the Asia-Pacific, drawing lessons learnt from the programmes and knowledge base of partners such as the British Council, the Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel (GEEAP), the Department for Education (DfE), and the EdTech Hub. (D0006832.odt, How can the UK Support ASEAN to Tackle the Learning Crisis and Gender Inequality?)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **multiply domestic and multilateral education finance** by providing technical advice that influences AMS and donor spending. Complementary financing expected from ADB’s **International Financing Facility for Education (IFFEd)** for lower-MIC AMS.
financial_details.quote: It will deploy technical advice to support regional partnerships and reform initiatives that can influence and multiply domestic and multilateral education finance. (D0006832.odt, Programme summary)

metadata.programme_name: Productive Social Safety Net Programme in Tanzania Phase II & III

quote.text: The UK will provide up to £30m from 2024/25 to 2028/29 targeting the poorest 15% of Tanzanian households...

duration_source.text: The UK will provide up to £30m from 2024/25 to 2028/29...

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines service delivery (cash transfers, public works), capacity building (institutional strengthening, technical assistance), and financing mechanism (co-financing with World Bank and other donors). It aims to reduce poverty, improve resilience to climate shocks, and strengthen Tanzania's national social protection system.

q1_source.text: The UK will provide up to £30m from 2024/25 to 2028/29 targeting the poorest 15% of Tanzanian households to increase their resilience to economic, food and climate shocks, increase their consumption and improve health and education outcomes for their children. [...] The programme will have the following anticipated results: [...] A stronger national social protection mechanism (PSSN III) which is more (i) climate-sensitive, (ii) shock-responsive, and (iii) sustainably financed via a government-owned plan that includes increased domestic funding.

q3_expected_outputs.output: 5 million extremely poor people (of which UK support covers 215,000 people) improve their incomes, food consumption and resilience to shocks
Vulnerable communities better able to mitigate against climate change via flood defences, irrigation, drought-resistant crops and climate-smart farming practices
A stronger national social protection mechanism (PSSN III) which is more climate-sensitive, shock-responsive, and sustainably financed
Approximately one million poor households or 5 million extremely poor people with reduced income poverty and improved food consumption
Beneficiary households and communities supported to better cope with the effect of climate change and other livelihood shocks
Beneficiary households have more diversified, non-farm incomes and capital assets
Improved education and healthcare attendance for children and adolescent girls and boys from extremely poor households

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce extreme poverty and vulnerability in Tanzania through a combination of cash transfers, public works, and institutional strengthening of the national social protection system, with a strong focus on climate resilience and human capital development.

quote.text: The UK will provide up to £30m from 2024/25 to 2028/29 targeting the poorest 15% of Tanzanian households to increase their resilience to economic, food and climate shocks, increase their consumption and improve health and education outcomes for their children.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as 'moderate' risk, reflecting Tanzania's stable political environment but significant development challenges, including high poverty rates, climate vulnerability, and institutional capacity constraints.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak institutions and limited domestic revenue mobilization constrain the government's ability to finance and sustain social protection programmes. Climate risks (droughts, floods) exacerbate poverty and food insecurity, while data limitations affect targeting and monitoring of beneficiaries. Low tax-to-GDP ratio (13.3%) limits fiscal space for social spending.

quote.text: Tanzania’s tax to GDP ratio of 13.3% is below the expected 15% for lower middle income countries. Low domestic revenue mobilization has led to low overall public expenditure with the most pronounced gap observed in social spending. [...] Climate change is undermining peoples’ resilience and increasing poverty. Most people involved in agriculture depend on rain-fed irrigation. Climate shocks and unpredictable rain patterns coupled with limited financial buffers impede peoples’ ability to adapt to shocks, leading to increasing food insecurity and income losses.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The Government of Tanzania (GoURT) leads the programme design and implementation through TASAF, with technical and financial support from the UK and other donors. Decision-making is embedded within Tanzanian institutions, with donor coordination mechanisms in place.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to strengthen PSSN III design and implementation
support to develop a medium-term expenditure framework for social protection
institutional strengthening of TASAF and national social protection systems
training and gender-sensitive measures to improve programme delivery

partner_organizations.name: Tanzania Social Action Fund (TASAF)
partner_organizations.role: implementing agency for PSSN programme, manages cash transfers, public works, and livelihood components

partner_organizations.name: Government of the United Republic of Tanzania (GoURT)
partner_organizations.role: programme owner, provides policy framework and partial financing (in-kind and cash contributions)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: main financier via IDA loan ($650 million for PSSN II), oversees implementation alongside GoURT

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: potential implementer for CashPlus and climate-sensitive components (Options 2 and 3)

partner_organizations.name: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funding and technical assistance provider, donor coordination

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Sweden, Norway, United States, Ireland, OPEC, Global Fund)
partner_organizations.role: co-financiers of PSSN programme

quote.text: Implemented by the Tanzania Social Action Fund (TASAF), PSSN activities include a Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) to supplement the incomes of extremely poor households (HH). [...] The UK has supported 5 years (2015-2020) of PSSN phase I (PSSN I) and 1 year (2023) of PSSN phase II (PSSN II) with a contribution of £112,322,798. [...] The Government of Tanzania (GoURT) is committed to PSSN objectives and social policy more broadly, including establishing and strengthening social protection institutions.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Social Protection as a Response / Lessons from previous support

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of core funding (pooled with other donors) and earmarked financing for specific components (e.g., CashPlus for adolescents or climate-sensitive social protection). Funds are channeled through TASAF, with technical assistance delivered via contracts or MoUs.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme is managed through a multi-donor governance mechanism chaired by the World Bank, with TASAF as the implementing agency. Technical working groups co-chaired by TASAF and donors support coordination. The UK's technical assistance will be delivered via contracts or MoUs to support PSSN III design and implementation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TASAF is the established implementing agency for PSSN, with a proven track record. The World Bank leads the donor consortium, and the UK's technical assistance will build on existing partnerships. For Options 2 and 3 (CashPlus and climate-sensitive components), a multilateral organization like UNICEF may be directly awarded based on prior experience with pilot programmes.

quote.text: Funding for the implementation of the core PSSN programme is pooled with contributions from several development partners. The World Bank is the main financier of the programme through an IDA loan and oversees the implementation of the PSSN programme alongside the Government of Tanzania. [...] Alldelivery options include direct procurement of technical assistance delivered through contracts or an MoU. [...] Option 2: BHCTanzania would provide earmarked financing to PSSN Phase III to support a subset of beneficiaries, to prevent deterioration of their human capital and break the intergenerational transfer of poverty. [...] Option 3: This entails the adoption of an ambitious, climate-sensitive social protection mechanism providing non-variable transfers to PSSN households and expanding into new, climate-stressed communities.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: A donor governance mechanism is in place, chaired by the World Bank with a rotating co-chair. Technical working groups co-chaired by TASAF and donor partners support resource management, joint monitoring, and policy dialogues. The National Steering Committee (NSC) oversees PSSN implementation at the national level.

quote.text: A donor governance mechanism is in place, chaired by the World Bank with a rotating co-chair. Technical working groups co-chaired by the Tanzanian Social Action Fund (TASAF) and donor partners support more coordinated resource management, joint monitoring, and policy dialogues, reducing the conflicting demands on TASAF by different donors. [...] The National Steering Committee (NSC) provides oversight and strategic direction for the PSSN programme.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Lessons from previous support / Options for Delivery

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within the core PSSN programme can be reallocated between components (e.g., cash transfers, public works) with donor approval, but earmarked funds (Options 2 and 3) are tied to specific beneficiaries or objectives. The shock-responsive component in Option 3 allows for scaling up transfers during emergencies.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a shock-responsive approach in PSSN III, allowing for temporary scaling of cash transfers during climate or economic shocks. Technical assistance will support adaptive management, including climate-sensitive targeting and early warning systems. However, major changes require approval from the donor governance mechanism.

quote.text: Making PSSN an adaptive and shock responsive mechanism, will strengthen PSSN’s ability to protect populations against shocks. [...] PSSN phase III is considering inclusion of a shock responsive approach to enhance its targeting of the most insecure and climate stressed. [...] The forward looking, pre-emptive, reactive and scalable safety net is designed to use climate information to identify an approaching climate/drought shock and either increase cash payments to current beneficiary households or expand payments to a larger target group within the area experiencing the shock.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Lessons from previous support / Option 3

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TASAF (implementing partner) → beneficiaries. For Options 2 and 3, an additional layer is added: FCDO → multilateral organization (e.g., UNICEF) → TASAF → beneficiaries.

quote.text: Administration costs remain constant at 11 percent based on the history of programme implementation. [...] Funding for the implementation of the core PSSN programme is pooled with contributions from several development partners. [...] The multilateral organisation will design and manage the programme and work with PSSN to disburse humanitarian cash transfers through TASAF structures.

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Core financing of the national Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN) Phases II and III programme
Option 2: Earmarked financing to PSSN Phase III to support a subset of beneficiaries (adolescent girls and boys)
Option 3: Earmarked financing to the national PSSN–Phase III programme to support an ambitious, climate-sensitive social protection mechanism
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (core financing) was chosen as the primary modality because it aligns with the UK's long-term support to PSSN, leverages existing systems (TASAF, World Bank oversight), and ensures economies of scale. It also allows for integrated delivery of cash transfers, public works, and institutional strengthening. Options 2 and 3 were considered for targeted interventions (adolescents, climate resilience) but involve higher administrative costs and complexity.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (Option 1 leverages existing systems and pooled funding)
risk mitigation (established governance and implementation structures)
strategic alignment (supports Tanzania's National Social Protection Policy)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: High administrative costs for earmarked options (Options 2 and 3)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Limit earmarked components to 25% of total costs and integrate with core PSSN systems to reduce duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordination challenges among multiple donors
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use existing donor governance mechanism and technical working groups co-chaired by TASAF to align priorities and reduce conflicting demands.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited government capacity to absorb increased financing
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Provide technical assistance to strengthen TASAF's financial management and medium-term expenditure planning, including a phased increase in domestic contributions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Climate shocks disrupting programme delivery
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Incorporate shock-responsive components in PSSN III, including early warning systems and scalable transfers, with support from multilateral partners for implementation.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (administration costs at 11%, below regional averages)
effectiveness (proven impact on poverty reduction and resilience)
equity (targeting the poorest 15% of households, with gender-sensitive measures)

quote.text: Option 1: Core funding to elements of the PSSN phase II (1 year) and phase III (3 years), namely the management, financing, and payment of the conditional cash transfers (CCT) including a non-variable disability grant; green public works (PW) for beneficiaries with labour capacity and livelihood grants to enable beneficiaries to initiate and manage more sustainable income generating activities. [...] Option 2 and 3 are likely to include TA to deliver cash plus or climate sensitive social protection, but will result in higher administration costs (assume costs for this component increase to 25%). [...] The programme will have the following anticipated results: [...] A stronger national social protection mechanism (PSSN III) which is more (i) climate-sensitive, (ii) shock-responsive, and (iii) sustainably financed via a government-owned plan that includes increased domestic funding.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Options for Delivery / Programme summary

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Tanzania's moderate risk profile and weak institutional capacity constrain partner selection to organizations with existing in-country presence and experience (e.g., TASAF, World Bank, UNICEF). The need for climate resilience and shock responsiveness requires partners with technical expertise in adaptive social protection, limiting options to multilateral agencies or specialized NGOs.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited fiscal space requires reliance on established implementers (TASAF) with donor financing
Climate vulnerability necessitates partners with adaptive management experience (e.g., UNICEF for shock-responsive components)
Weak data systems favor partners with existing beneficiary registries and monitoring tools
Gender and disability inclusion requirements limit partners to those with proven inclusive approaches
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's mixed objectives (service delivery + capacity building + financing) determine a hybrid delivery structure: core funding for scalable cash transfers (Option 1) and earmarked funds for targeted interventions (Options 2 and 3). The need for climate resilience and shock responsiveness drives the inclusion of adaptive components (e.g., early warning systems) managed by multilaterals.
q28_linkages: Service delivery objectives (cash transfers, public works) → require TASAF's implementation capacity and World Bank oversight
Capacity building objectives (institutional strengthening) → necessitate embedded technical assistance via contracts/MoUs
Climate resilience objectives → demand multilateral partners (e.g., UNICEF) for specialized adaptive components
Financing mechanism objectives → pooled funding structure to leverage donor contributions
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between inclusive targeting (reaching the poorest 15%) and administrative efficiency. For example: (1) Earmarked options (Options 2 and 3) increase costs but improve equity for adolescents or climate-vulnerable groups; (2) Shock-responsive components add complexity but enhance resilience for the most vulnerable; (3) Gender-sensitive measures (e.g., cash to women) empower beneficiaries but may increase domestic conflict risks.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Earmarked financing (Options 2/3) increases administrative costs (25% vs. 11%) but targets specific vulnerable groups (adolescents, climate-affected communities)
Shock-responsive components improve equity during crises but require additional oversight and partner capacity
Gender-targeted transfers (to women) enhance empowerment but risk increasing household conflicts or women's time poverty
Pooled funding (Option 1) maximizes efficiency but may dilute focus on niche objectives like climate adaptation
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (climate shocks, institutional weaknesses) justifies intensive oversight, including annual fiduciary risk assessments, embedded gender focal points, and a multilateral-managed shock-responsive component. The World Bank's leadership in the donor governance mechanism mitigates financial risks, while technical working groups address operational challenges.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is a core objective, shaping partner roles as follows: (1) TASAF receives technical assistance to strengthen financial management and climate-sensitive targeting; (2) Multilateral partners (e.g., UNICEF) are tasked with delivering specialized components (CashPlus, climate adaptation) due to their technical expertise; (3) The UK's role focuses on financing and high-level policy dialogue, avoiding direct implementation.

quote.text: The UK will work with the GoURT and other donor partners to achieve the following impacts and outcomes. [...] Option 2: Earmarking funding will result in higher administration costs: assume costs for this component increase to 25%. [...] Option 3: Earmarking funding will result in higher administration costs, assume costs for this component increase to 25%. [...] The programme will also achieve sustainability through the operationalisation of the National Social Protection Policy as it will provide the institutional, legal, and administrative framework around social protection in Tanzania and formally anchor TASAF and PSSN in the country’s government structures. [...] The forward looking, pre-emptive, reactive and scalable safety net is designed to use climate information to identify an approaching climate/drought shock and either increase cash payments to current beneficiary households or expand payments to a larger target group.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Expected PSSN Impact and Outcomes / Options for Delivery

key_programme_risks: Limited graduation from poverty due to small transfer sizes and inflation erosion
Low domestic financing for social protection (only $3m/year from government)
Climate shocks disrupting livelihoods and programme delivery
Weak supply-side services (health, education) limiting impact of conditional transfers
Gender-based violence or domestic conflict from women-managed cash transfers
Fiduciary risks in fund disbursement through TASAF
Coordinating multiple donors with divergent priorities
Limited capacity of local government to manage shock-responsive components

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Complement cash transfers with livelihood grants, public works, and technical assistance to diversify incomes. Advocate for transfer size adjustments to account for inflation.
Support development of a medium-term expenditure framework and advocate for increased government allocations to social protection. Provide technical assistance to broaden the tax base.
Incorporate shock-responsive components in PSSN III, including early warning systems and scalable transfers. Strengthen climate data use and anticipatory action plans with multilateral partners.
Coordinate with health and education ministries to align conditionalities with service improvements. Use technical working groups to address cross-sectoral challenges.
Implement gender training for staff, establish senior gender focal points, and monitor impacts through community sessions. Use savings groups to mitigate women's time poverty.
Conduct annual audits and fiduciary risk assessments. Use financial flow arrangements through the Central Bank to reduce mismanagement risks. Report suspicions to FCDO’s counter-fraud unit.
Maintain the donor governance mechanism chaired by the World Bank and technical working groups co-chaired by TASAF to align priorities and reduce conflicting demands.
Provide technical assistance to strengthen district emergency response plans and climate trigger systems. Partner with multilaterals (e.g., UNICEF) to build local capacity.

fcas_specific_lessons: Tanzania's moderate risk profile requires adaptive social protection mechanisms to respond to climate and economic shocks, which disproportionately affect the poor.
Pooled funding and multilateral oversight (World Bank) are critical in FCAS contexts to mitigate fiduciary and coordination risks.
Shock-responsive components must be designed with local government capacity constraints in mind, using multilaterals for technical support.
Gender and disability inclusion are essential in FCAS to address compounded vulnerabilities but require careful implementation to avoid unintended harms (e.g., GBV).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases of PSSN demonstrated strong cost efficiencies (administration costs at 11%) and impacts on poverty reduction (10% reduction in extreme poverty among beneficiaries) but limited graduation from the programme (only 1.5% of households). Key lessons include: (1) Cash transfers must be complemented with livelihood support and shock-responsive components; (2) Supply-side constraints (health, education) limit the effectiveness of conditionalities; (3) Donor coordination mechanisms reduce implementation burdens on TASAF; (4) Climate-sensitive targeting improves resilience but requires robust data systems.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: PSSN III incorporates several design changes based on lessons: (1) Addition of a shock-responsive component to address climate and economic shocks; (2) Expanded focus on climate-sensitive targeting and green public works; (3) Technical assistance to develop a medium-term expenditure framework for sustainable financing; (4) Strengthened gender and disability inclusion measures (e.g., disability grants, gender action plan); (5) Pilot innovations like CashPlus for adolescents to break intergenerational poverty.

quote.text: Lessons from previous support to social protection and the PSSN programme: Longer term investment is needed to support households to sustainably exit chronic poverty. [...] Supply side assessment and inter-ministerial coordination must be incorporated from the start. [...] Donor coordination is essential to manage the multiple demands on implementing partners. [...] Making PSSN an adaptive and shock responsive mechanism, will strengthen PSSN’s ability to protect populations against shocks. [...] The programme will also achieve sustainability through the operationalisation of the National Social Protection Policy as it will provide the institutional, legal, and administrative framework around social protection in Tanzania. [...] The forward looking, pre-emptive, reactive and scalable safety net is designed to use climate information to identify an approaching climate/drought shock and either increase cash payments to current beneficiary households or expand payments to a larger target group.
quote.source: D0006216.odt, Lessons from previous support / Options for Delivery

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK's £30m contribution leverages a total PSSN II budget of $890m (£650m from World Bank IDA loan + bilateral grants). The programme is designed to catalyze increased domestic financing for social protection in Tanzania.

quote.text: Programme Value: £30 million. [...] The total cost of PSSN II is $890 million of which the Government of Tanzania is financing $650 million through the IDA loan. [...] Administration costs remain constant at 11 percent based on the history of programme implementation. [...] The Government of Tanzania’s priority is to consolidate and strengthen the effectiveness of the PSSN as a safety net that builds human capital and helps extremely poor households move into sustainable livelihoods.

metadata.programme_name: Growth Research Platform (GRP)
metadata.quote: The Growth Research Platform (GRP) will consolidate three existing research programmes on economic growth in developing countries and add a new policy response pillar. (D0005467.odt, Title: Growth Research Platform (GRP))
metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 17/10/23; AMP End Date: 04/04/2029" (D0005467.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The GRP consolidates three existing research programmes (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) and adds a new Policy Response Window (PRW) to generate evidence on economic growth, structural transformation, private enterprise development, and conflict economics. It aims to inform policy decisions, build capacity among Southern researchers, and facilitate uptake of research findings through synthesis products like VoxDev Lits. The programme directly supports FCDO's International Development Strategy by providing evidence for investment decisions and policy reforms in developing countries.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Growth Research Platform (GRP) will consolidate three existing research programmes on economic growth in developing countries and add a new policy response pillar." (D0005467.odt, Title: Growth Research Platform (GRP)) AND "The programme will benefit developing country policymakers, the development community, and ultimately the poor, through better evidenced economic policy and programme decisions, leading to more sustainable growth outcomes and job creation." (D0005467.odt, Title: Growth Research Platform (GRP))
q3_expected_outputs: High-quality, policy-relevant research on structural transformation, private enterprise development, and conflict economics (4 pillars: STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE, PRW)
VoxDev Lits (wiki-inspired literature reviews) and Policy Insight papers for policymakers (expansion of existing 7 themes to comprehensive coverage)
Responsive, short-term research and expert advice through the Policy Response Window (ODA and non-ODA)
Capacity building for Southern researchers (training, mentorship, research grants, institutional partnerships)
Synthesis products and uptake activities (in-country events, policy blogs, social media engagement)
Evidence to support BII and other DFIs in investment decisions (e.g., spillover effects, climate impacts)
Gender-disaggregated data and analysis across all research themes
what_objectives.summary: The GRP generates rigorous economic research to inform FCDO and partner country policies, while building local research capacity and ensuring evidence uptake through responsive policy windows and synthesis products. It combines long-term research agendas (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) with demand-driven policy support (PRW).
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver new, operationally relevant evidence on firms, productivity, structural transformation and economic growth. Uptake will mean more evidence-based – and therefore effective – investments, growth policies and interventions by FCDO and its country partners." (D0005467.odt, Outputs, outcome and impact)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where 50% of extreme poverty is projected to be concentrated by 2045, but mitigates risks through established partnerships (CEPR) and adaptive management. The overall risk rating is assessed as 'moderate' with specific risks flagged for ReCIPE (new programme) and PRW (new component).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall, the GRP is within FCDO tolerances and would provisionally be regarded as ‘moderate’." (D0005467.odt, Risk) AND "Poverty is over-time becoming heavily concentrated in fragile states - by 2045, around half of extremely poor people worldwide are projected to live in countries that are recurrently fragile." (D0005467.odt, ReCIPE)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory barriers (e.g., trade policies, industrial policy design)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and fragility limit data collection and policy implementation, while weak institutions in low-income countries (LICs) constrain private sector development. Climate vulnerability exacerbates economic instability, particularly in agriculture-dependent economies. Gender inequality increases conflict risk, requiring tailored interventions. Data gaps in FCAS hinder causal analysis of economic-conflict linkages.
where_context.quote: "The challenges of the global market play a strong role; trade, capital flows, and foreign direct investment have not worked in favour of these countries. In particular, competition from East Asia has made the middle-income countries less competitive in the global market." (D0005467.odt, STEG) AND "Existing research often relies on monitoring reports and qualitative research, hence our understanding of causal relationships in this field remains weak." (D0005467.odt, ReCIPE)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: CEPR (UK-based) manages the platform, research agendas, and sub-awards, with Southern researchers engaged as sub-grantees and through capacity-building initiatives. Decision-making rests with CEPR's academic leadership and FCDO oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: Dedicated calls for LIC and early-career researchers
Mentorship and match-making programmes
Training workshops (e.g., IMF training on structural transformation)
Research grants for Southern institutions (e.g., African Centre for Economic Transformation - ACET)
Co-authorship opportunities with Northern researchers
Inception phase consultations to integrate local priorities

partner_organizations.name: Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR)
partner_organizations.role: Platform manager, research commissioning, synthesis products, policy engagement

partner_organizations.name: British International Investment (BII)
partner_organizations.role: Collaborator on private enterprise development research (PEDL), investment decision support

partner_organizations.name: International Growth Centre (IGC)
partner_organizations.role: Policy uptake partner, country office network for engagement

partner_organizations.name: African Centre for Economic Transformation (ACET)
partner_organizations.role: Southern research partner, capacity building

partner_organizations.name: Southern researchers (LIC-based institutions)
partner_organizations.role: Research implementation, local context expertise, co-authorship

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Country Offices and Centres of Expertise
partner_organizations.role: Demand articulation, policy uptake, in-country engagement

partner_organizations.name: Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) and Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)
partner_organizations.role: End-users of research (e.g., World Bank, IMF, Regional Development Banks)

who_partners.quote: "CEPR will be asked to develop a new GRP capacity building strategy which can be taken forward under each of the research areas in a coordinated manner." (D0005467.odt, Capacity Development) AND "The GRP presents an opportunity to build on the lessons learned through these initiatives and to further support southern capacity." (D0005467.odt, Capacity Development)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The GRP uses a combination of block funding for existing programmes (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) and competitive grants for new research under the Policy Response Window (PRW). CEPR acts as a fund manager, re-granting to researchers through open calls and responsive expertise mechanisms. The instrument blends core funding for platform operations with project-specific awards.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: CEPR operates as a central platform manager, overseeing four research pillars (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE, PRW) with dedicated academic leadership for each. Research is commissioned through competitive calls, while the PRW provides demand-driven responsive expertise. FCDO retains oversight via approvals and annual reviews, but day-to-day management is delegated to CEPR.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: CEPR uses open, competitive research calls with peer review to ensure quality and policy relevance. This builds on the existing STEG and PEDL models, which have established credibility through rigorous selection processes. The approach balances academic excellence with operational relevance.
how_mechanism.quote: "Quality threshold for research managed by academic leadership. Competitive open research calls. Selections subject to peer review." (D0005467.odt, Summary of Key Risks) AND "CEPR will develop an easy-access interface where they will be able to respond to ToRs identifying research/evidence demands." (D0005467.odt, Policy Response Window)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Each research pillar (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) has its own steering committee with academic and policy representatives. The GRP will nest these into an overarching log frame, with CEPR providing consolidated oversight. FCDO retains approval rights for major decisions (e.g., budget reallocations).
how_governance.quote: "CEPR will be asked to update the Theory of Change and develop a full log frame during the first year of the platform. It is anticipated that STEG, PEDL and ReCIPE will each have their own log frames which will then be nested into an overarching GRP log frame." (D0005467.odt, Outputs, outcome and impact) AND "Performance and adherence will be monitored through the Programme Management Meetings and Annual Reviews." (D0005467.odt, Public Sector Equality Duty)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between pillars with FCDO approval, as evidenced by the £18m new funding request (£10m STEG, £3m PEDL, £5m PRW). The platform design allows for adaptive management, but major shifts require formal review.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Research priorities can be adjusted through the Policy Response Window (PRW) and during the ReCIPE inception phase (9 months for agenda refinement). The platform includes mechanisms for responsive expertise and synthesis updates (e.g., VoxDev Lits), but structural changes require FCDO sign-off.
how_flexibility.quote: "The types of question ReCIPE will investigate include: [list]... During the inception phase ReCIPE will consult with all existing FCDO funded conflict programmes to ensure value added." (D0005467.odt, ReCIPE) AND "The policy response window will also have options for Non-ODA work." (D0005467.odt, Title: Growth Research Platform (GRP))

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → CEPR (platform manager) → end researchers (no additional intermediary layers explicitly described)
how_efficiency.quote: "Programme Value: Total=£39m, made up of £38m of ODA and £1m of non-ODA. £21m of the funding is previously approved, £18m is seeking approval." (D0005467.odt, SummarySheet)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The platform model was chosen to consolidate three existing programmes (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) under a single management structure, reducing transaction costs and improving coherence. CEPR's established network and track record with FCDO (through STEG/PEDL) provided confidence in their ability to deliver high-quality, policy-relevant research. The addition of the Policy Response Window (PRW) addresses demand for flexible, short-term expertise while maintaining rigorous academic oversight.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (consolidation reduces management costs)
risk mitigation (CEPR's proven capacity to manage complex research)
partner capacity (CEPR's global academic network and IFI links)
flexibility (PRW allows responsive support to FCDO country offices)
effectiveness (synthesis products like VoxDev Lits enhance uptake)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Wide scope of GRP causes difficulty in maintaining coherence and engaging top researchers across silos
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong academic research leadership for each pillar (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE, PRW) with oversight to achieve balance. Continuation of individual programme management groups (PMGs) and log frames.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Research is poor quality or not policy-relevant
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quality threshold managed by academic leadership; competitive open calls with peer review; impact plans with specified policy engagement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of availability/willingness of researchers with sufficient skills for ReCIPE and PRW
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Inception phase to develop research community via network meetings and high-profile events. Focus on early-career researchers through small grants.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of ability to engage high-level decision-makers
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage CEPR's existing links with IFIs (IMF, World Bank) and FCDO Centres of Expertise. Use IGC country offices for in-country engagement.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (policy relevance through FCDO/CoE demand articulation)
equity (Southern researcher inclusion and capacity building)
why_rationale.quote: "Bringing these separate research programmes into one platform will improve coherence of the three research themes while also generating efficiencies in the management of the programme on both the FCDO and CEPR sides." (D0005467.odt, What will the programme do?) AND "CEPR has a wide network of researchers across a very broad range of economic issues. The PRW will give FCDO full access to these researchers together with the ability to respond to any emerging economic and growth-related issue." (D0005467.odt, Policy Response Window)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The focus on fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) limits partner selection to organizations with proven experience in high-risk environments (e.g., CEPR's existing work in FCAS through ReCIPE). Local research capacity constraints necessitate Northern-led management with embedded Southern researcher inclusion.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS environments require partners with conflict-sensitive research methodologies
Data limitations in FCAS demand partners skilled in innovative data collection
Weak institutions in LICs/FCAS necessitate capacity-building components in partner roles
Gender inequality in target regions requires partners with gender expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for both long-term structural research (STEG, PEDL) and demand-driven policy support (PRW) shapes the platform's dual structure, combining competitive research calls with responsive expertise mechanisms. The synthesis requirement (VoxDev Lits) drives the centralization under CEPR for coherence.
q28_linkages: Long-term research agendas (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) → competitive grants with peer review
Short-term policy demands (PRW) → responsive expertise interface
Evidence synthesis needs → centralized platform management by CEPR
Southern researcher inclusion → dedicated capacity-building strategy
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances Northern efficiency (CEPR's established systems) with Southern equity (dedicated LIC researcher funding and mentorship). The platform design accepts higher transaction costs for capacity building (e.g., inception phases, training) to ensure local ownership and relevance.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Inception phases for ReCIPE/PRW delay start but improve local relevance
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern academic leadership ensures quality but limits Southern decision-making
Cost vs. reach: Capacity-building components increase budget but expand Southern participation
Flexibility vs. coherence: PRW allows responsiveness but risks fragmentation without strong synthesis
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (FCAS focus) increases oversight intensity, with milestone-based reviews and FCDO approval requirements for fund reallocations. Conflict-sensitive contexts demand adaptive management structures (e.g., ReCIPE's 9-month inception phase).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles by requiring CEPR to develop a dedicated GRP capacity strategy, including Southern researcher grants, mentorship, and institutional partnerships (e.g., ACET). Southern researchers are positioned as co-implementers rather than mere beneficiaries.
intersections.quote: "The GRP will work closely with the new ‘UK Centres of Expertise’, feeding in evidence and responding to requests for expert academic advice." (D0005467.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending) AND "Developing southern research capacity and fostering lasting links between ‘southern’ and ‘northern’ researchers has been an important aim of the existing STEG and PEDL programmes." (D0005467.odt, Capacity Development)

key_programme_risks: Wide scope causes difficulty in maintaining coherence and engaging top researchers (moderate likelihood, major impact)
Research quality or policy relevance is insufficient (possible likelihood, major impact)
Unavailability of skilled researchers for ReCIPE/PRW (moderate for ReCIPE, minor for STEG/PEDL)
Inability to engage high-level decision-makers (possible likelihood, major impact)
Adverse political economy blocks good policy decisions (likely, major impact)
External/political shocks disrupt implementation (likely in FCAS, major impact)
Terrorism financing risk in fragile contexts (low but monitored)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Wide scope causes difficulty in maintaining coherence
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strong academic leadership for each pillar; continuation of individual PMGs and log frames nested under GRP.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Research is poor quality or not policy-relevant
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Competitive open calls with peer review; impact plans requiring policy engagement.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of researcher availability for ReCIPE/PRW
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Inception phase to build research community; focus on early-career researchers.
Leverage CEPR's IFI links (IMF, World Bank) and IGC country offices.
Develop rigorous understanding of local political economy; use Country Office knowledge.
Compliance checks at review meetings; OSJA Guidance for fragile contexts.

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict and economic growth have bidirectional relationships requiring adaptive research designs
Qualitative data dominance in FCAS necessitates mixed-methods approaches
Local researcher inclusion is critical for accessing fragile contexts
Inception phases are essential for agenda-setting in high-risk environments
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: STEG and PEDL demonstrated that: 1) Competitive calls with policy engagement criteria improve uptake; 2) Synthesis products (VoxDev Lits) enhance influence; 3) Northern-Southern co-authorship strengthens relevance; 4) IFI partnerships (e.g., BII, World Bank) expand reach. ReCIPE builds on these by adding conflict-sensitive methodologies.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The GRP consolidates previously separate programmes (STEG, PEDL, ReCIPE) into a single platform to improve coherence and reduce management costs. The new Policy Response Window (PRW) addresses demand for flexible expertise, while expanded VoxDev Lits respond to calls for accessible synthesis. Capacity-building components were strengthened based on STEG/PEDL experiences.
risks_lessons.quote: "Both PEDL and STEG have developed large, decentralised networks of researchers linked into policy practitioners... This relatively low-cost intervention has significantly enhanced STEG’s reach and influence." (D0005467.odt, Examples of impact) AND "ReCIPE will fund a body of high-quality, rigorous and policy-relevant research to better inform economic policymaking in fragile and conflict affected states." (D0005467.odt, ReCIPE)

financial_details.quote: "Programme Value: Total=£39m, made up of £38m of ODA and £1m of non-ODA. £21m of the funding is previously approved, £18m is seeking approval." (D0005467.odt, SummarySheet) AND "The programme will benefit developing country policymakers, the development community, and ultimately the poor, through better evidenced economic policy and programme decisions." (D0005467.odt, Title: Growth Research Platform (GRP))

metadata.programme_name: AgDevCo Ventures - targeting early-stage African enterprises in the agriculture sector to scale up activities (400140)

quote.text: "FCDO will provide design funds and seed capital for AgDevCo Ventures, which will target early-stage investment into small and medium sized enterprises in the African agriculture sector requiring $1m to $4m of capital."

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: 01/03/2024", "AMP End Date: 31/03/2035" (D0006681.odt, Metadata section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme establishes AgDevCo Ventures as a new subsidiary to provide patient capital (equity-like and mezzanine finance) to early-stage African agribusinesses that struggle to access traditional financing. It aims to catalyze private investment by de-risking early-stage ventures through first-loss capital, while embedding technical assistance to improve business viability. The goal is to transform Africa's food systems by scaling SMEs that contribute to food security, climate resilience, and economic opportunities for marginalized groups (women, youth, black Africans).
what_objectives.q1_source: "FCDO’s funding will target the absence of certain types of capital (including equity-like and structures which are a hybrid of debt and equity i.e. mezzanine finance) to support early-stage African agribusinesses... This kind of capital that is able to take greater risk over a longer investment and impact return time horizon... is scarce and makes it difficult for new agribusinesses to expand." (D0006681.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 10-15 early-stage agribusinesses invested in over 5 years
Leverage at least £17.857 million in private co-financing (total £42.857 million mobilized)
q3_expected_outputs.target: £17,857,143 co-financing leveraged

q3_expected_outputs.output: 30% of investee businesses owned/managed by women (up from current 24%)
50% of investee businesses meeting Black Ownership and Leadership Development (BOLD) criteria (up from current 30%)
Increase in food and nutrition security through scaled agribusiness operations
3,968,923 GBP in FTE income generated by 2036
124,422,850 GBP in smallholder farmer income generated by 2036
Improved resilience to climate change through adoption of climate-smart technologies
Increased cross-border agricultural trade

what_objectives.summary: The programme creates a dedicated financing vehicle (AgDevCo Ventures) to fill the critical gap in early-stage agribusiness financing in Africa, combining patient capital with technical assistance to scale SMEs that enhance food security, climate adaptation, and inclusive economic growth. It explicitly targets systemic barriers like lack of equity-like finance and gender disparities in agribusiness ownership.

quote.text: "The targeted approach of Ventures, is expected to contribute to the following development outcomes: [...] Increase availability of foods and services essential for food and nutrition security; Increase income and jobs in food & agriculture sector; Improve long term viability of investee businesses; Increase agricultural cross border trade; Increase adaptation and resilience to climate change; Increase government revenues from agribusinesses/products; Inclusion, gender equality and women’s economic empowerment."

countries_regions: Primary focus: East Africa (with potential expansion to other regions)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in Sub-Saharan Africa, which faces compounded risks from conflict, climate shocks (e.g., droughts, floods), economic instability, and weak institutional capacity. The document explicitly rates the programme's risk as 'Major' due to these contextual challenges, which affect both the viability of agribusinesses and the stability of investments.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0006681.odt, Metadata) and "The changing future context for Africa’s food demands [...] driven by war, conflict and climate change and further exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic pushing even more people into hunger." (D0006681.odt, Context section)
q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory barriers (land ownership disputes, trade restrictions)
market inefficiencies (fragmented smallholder systems, high transaction costs)
limited access to finance (high cost of capital, lack of collateral)
low productivity (yield growth decline, underuse of inputs)
political economy risks (corruption, politically exposed persons)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: These constraints collectively hinder agribusiness growth by increasing costs (e.g., transport costs 5x higher than global benchmarks), reducing productivity (African fertilizer use at 10-20 kg/hectare vs. 150+ kg/hectare in EU/US/China), and creating investment delays (e.g., land disputes causing 5+ year delays). Climate risks exacerbate food insecurity, while weak infrastructure and regulatory barriers limit market access for smallholders.

quote.text: "Africa’s record transport and logistics costs make it uncompetitive to move food around the continent. Africa’s storage and transport costs are up to five times higher than world benchmarks [...] Lack of investment in fertiliser coupled with record fertiliser prices are putting further pressure on Africa’s food production [...] Market inefficiencies are exacerbated due to the small land holdings and fragmented farming system in Africa."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with AgDevCo Ltd's UK-based Board (with FCDO as a shareholder via AgDevCo Holdings), though the Ventures subsidiary will have a dedicated African investment team based in Nairobi. The Investment Committee includes AgDevCo executives and non-executives with African agribusiness experience, but ultimate governance remains with the UK-registered entity.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for investee SMEs (agronomic, business management, financial reporting)
gender-sensitive business development support
climate-smart technology adoption training
market linkage facilitation (e.g., cold chain, processing)
board-level governance support for women-led businesses
incubation for early-stage ventures (e.g., financial systems, sales agreements)

partner_organizations.name: AgDevCo Ltd
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and fund manager (via Ventures subsidiary)
