where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Ageing infrastructure and outdated agreements hinder regional cooperation; climate impacts exacerbate water/energy scarcity; Russian/Chinese influence creates political constraints for reform; weak institutions limit implementation capacity for climate adaptation.
where_context.quote: "Legacy Soviet transboundary water/energy agreements are outdated... infrastructure is on the verge of collapse... The region is exposed to climate risks... Energysystems are failing as Central Asia’s population increases... fuelshortages and rising prices are driving internal protests and increasing pressure from Russia." (D0004791.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: World Bank (Central Asia Water and Energy Programme - CAWEP)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (Northern-led multilateral) manages the regional trust fund with FCDO oversight. Southern partners (Central Asian governments/CSOs) receive technical assistance but decision-making rests with the Bank/FCDO for Component 1. Component 2 allows some Southern input through demand-led flexible funds.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for regional water/energy governance
capacity strengthening for national/sub-national institutions
training on climate resilience/adaptation measures
support for evidence-based policy development
twinning arrangements and knowledge exchange platforms
community-level capacity building for vulnerable groups

partner_organizations.name: World Bank (CAWEP Phase 4)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer for Component 1 (regional water/energy)

partner_organizations.name: United Nations agencies (TBC)
partner_organizations.role: potential manager for Component 2 flexible fund

partner_organizations.name: NGOs with regional reach (TBC)
partner_organizations.role: potential implementer for Component 2 (community-level)

partner_organizations.name: Central Asian governments
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries/recipients of technical assistance

partner_organizations.name: UN Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE)
partner_organizations.role: specialist expertise provider

partner_organizations.name: OECD
partner_organizations.role: specialist expertise provider

partner_organizations.name: USAID/GIZ/Swiss Development Cooperation
partner_organizations.role: like-minded donors for coordination

partner_organizations.name: Civil society organizations
partner_organizations.role: local implementation partners (limited market)

who_partners.quote: "For Component 1, we will work regional organisation like the World Bank, UN agencies and multilateral organisations working at the regional level... For Component 2, we will work with government, civil society and international partners using a flexible fund." (D0004791.odt, Delivery arrangements)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Component 1 uses a Trust Fund via Standard Administrative Agreement with World Bank (multi-donor mechanism). Component 2 will use either: 1) accountable grants with NGOs, 2) MOUs with UN agencies, or 3) commercial contracts with suppliers, managed through a flexible fund.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Component 1 operates through the World Bank's established CAWEP trust fund with FCDO as contributor. Component 2 creates a demand-led flexible fund managed by either a UN agency, NGO, or commercial supplier, allowing adaptive responses to emerging needs. The programme combines regional coordination with bilateral flexibility.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: Component 1: direct award to World Bank; Component 2: early market engagement with restricted competition among pre-identified partners
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: World Bank selected for Component 1 due to its "uniquely placed" regional convening power and existing CAWEP platform. Component 2 partners will be chosen based on: 1) experience with catalytic climate funds, 2) understanding of political economy, 3) ability to work with marginalized groups, and 4) local expertise - with selection through consultations during inception phase.
how_mechanism.quote: "The World Bank is uniquely placed to deliver the level of water and energy programming and is a proven partner with an ability to convene government as well as other donors... For Component 2... we will conduct an early market engagement and consult government stakeholders, international NGOs, regional civil society organisations and multilateral partners." (D0004791.odt, Administrative arrangements/Scoping phase)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Component 1: World Bank's CAWEP has an Advisory Committee (AC) that oversees the trust fund, with annual reporting to FCDO. Component 2: Governance structure for the flexible fund will be designed early 2024 with Portfolio Board input, likely including a joint decision-making mechanism for sub-awards.
how_governance.quote: "A workplan for the FY23/4 has been agreed in consultation with FCDO... Administrative costs... will be monitored over the life of the programme, with a report to the Advisory Committee (AC) covering this each year... The fund’s strategy and delivery route will be developed and discussed with the Portfolio Board." (D0004791.odt, Administrative arrangements/Fund management options)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between Component 1 (regional) and Component 2 (national/sub-national) after Year 1 review, but requires Portfolio Board approval. Component 2's flexible fund allows responsive adjustments within its climate governance/adaptation focus.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed as adaptive: Year 1 focuses on scoping partners for Component 2; the flexible fund can respond to emerging opportunities/risks; and the balance between regional/national programming will be reviewed annually. Technical assistance can be redirected based on demand.
how_flexibility.quote: "CEW-CA is designed as an adaptive programme... we will review partnerships and balance of spend between region/national/sub-national priorities after the first year of operation and adapt our approach where appropriate... The flexible fund... will allow us to target funds in a responsive and adaptive way." (D0004791.odt, FY24/5 programme closure)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank (Component 1); FCDO → Fund Manager (UN/NGO/commercial) → sub-grantees (Component 2)
how_efficiency.quote: "During FY23/24 the Bank will deduct from the Trust Fund and retain for its own account a fee equal to 12% of the amount for Bank-executed activities... The Bank is subject to a Central Assurance Assessment (CAA) process... Payment will be milestone-based with deliverables tied to workplan." (D0004791.odt, Administrative costs)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (no dedicated climate programme)
Option 2: Deliver a standalone bilateral UK programme (high visibility but limited leverage)
Option 3: Work through regional/national/sub-national development partners (RECOMMENDED)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 3 was selected for its ability to: 1) leverage World Bank's regional convening power and IFI investments; 2) maintain flexibility through a dedicated fund; 3) achieve better value for money (3:1 benefit-cost ratio estimated); 4) deliver systemic change through regional coordination while allowing national adaptation; and 5) reinforce relationships with like-minded donors (Swiss, USAID, EU).
q25_decision_factors: value for money (Option 3 scored highest on VfM criteria)
risk mitigation (multilateral partners reduce implementation risks)
partner capacity (World Bank's embedded regional teams)
equity (ability to target marginalized groups through flexible fund)
speed (avoids 1-year procurement delay of standalone programme)
influence (ability to shape regional discourse through IFIs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on World Bank's priorities may limit UK's strategic influence in Component 1
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO retains oversight through Advisory Committee and can redirect Component 2 funds

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexible fund in Component 2 may face delays in partner identification
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Early market engagement and scoping phase during Year 1 to pre-qualify partners

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Coordinating between multilateral (Component 1) and bilateral (Component 2) approaches creates complexity
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Portfolio Board will align strategies and monitor synergies

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy constraints in Central Asia may limit reform implementation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Technical assistance focuses on catalytic interventions with high government demand

why_rationale.quote: "Option 3 delivers: high value for money; strong climate mitigation and adaptation outcomes; regional resilience and reduced dependence on Russia; wider influence with development partners; and inclusive development outcomes... This approach would maintain flexibility through a dedicated fund that would respond to emerging opportunities and risks." (D0004791.odt, Summary of options and assessment)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS-like context (Russian/Chinese influence, Taliban instability, water conflicts) limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) strong regional political navigation skills (e.g., World Bank's embedded teams); 2) ability to work across Central Asian governments despite tensions; and 3) experience in conflict-sensitive programming. Local CSOs are noted as having limited capacity.
q27_constraints_detail: Russian malign influence requires partners with diplomatic leverage
Transboundary water conflicts necessitate neutral conveners (e.g., World Bank)
Ageing infrastructure demands partners with engineering/technical expertise
Climate urgency prioritizes partners with adaptive management experience
Weak local CSO market limits direct Southern implementation
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The transboundary nature of water/energy issues (WHAT) mandates a regional platform (World Bank CAWEP) for Component 1, while the need for targeted community adaptation (WHAT) requires flexible bilateral mechanisms (Component 2 fund). The mix of policy influence (regional) and implementation (local) objectives shapes the two-component structure.
q28_linkages: Regional water/energy goals → multilateral trust fund (Component 1)
National/sub-national climate adaptation → flexible bilateral fund (Component 2)
Need for policy coherence → World Bank's convening role
Vulnerable community focus → demand-led NGO/CSO partnerships
Climate science gaps → embedded research in both components
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicitly discussed: The programme balances efficiency (leveraging World Bank's existing platforms) with equity (flexible fund targeting women/marginalized groups). Trade-offs include: 1) using multilateral partners for speed vs. building local CSO capacity; 2) regional coordination benefits vs. ensuring country-specific adaptation; and 3) World Bank's 12% overhead vs. its ability to unlock larger IFI investments.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: World Bank's 12% management fee vs. its ability to leverage 3:1 additional funding
Regional platform efficiency vs. need for localized community adaptation
Rapid IFI delivery vs. time needed to build Southern institutional capacity
Standardized multilateral approaches vs. tailored gender/inclusion interventions
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (geopolitical/climate/infrastructure risks) justifies milestone-based oversight with annual reviews, while the adaptive design allows reallocation of funds between components based on emerging risks (e.g., Afghanistan spillover, Russian pressure).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The weak institutional capacity in Central Asia shapes partner roles by: 1) positioning World Bank as primary implementer for complex regional coordination; 2) using Component 2's flexible fund to build local CSO capacity gradually; and 3) embedding capacity building as a core objective across both components.
intersections.quote: "The challenging and shifting geopolitical context is driving a strong desire across the region for broader international partnerships... Our comparative advantage lies in using funding flexibly to support small, but catalytic investments... The UK also has a competitive edge in institution building and forging enduring development partnerships." (D0004791.odt, Case for UK support)

key_programme_risks: Geopolitical risks from Russian malign influence and Chinese strategic investments
Climate-induced water conflicts exacerbating regional tensions
Ageing Soviet infrastructure collapse threatening energy/water systems
Limited local CSO capacity hindering community-level implementation
Population growth (36.9% by 2050) outpacing resource availability
Fossil fuel subsidies distorting energy transition incentives
Talent migration from rural areas increasing vulnerability
Afghanistan instability creating security/refugee pressures
Data gaps limiting evidence-based climate planning
Policy resistance to decarbonization from fossil-fuel dependent economies

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Promote regional energy trading to reduce dependence; align with EU/US strategies
Strengthen transboundary governance through CAWEP; support conflict-sensitive programming
Prioritize technical assistance for critical system upgrades; leverage IFI investments
Use flexible fund to gradually build local partner capabilities; twin with international NGOs
Focus on most vulnerable communities; integrate early warning systems
Demand-led technical assistance; demonstrate economic benefits of transition

fcas_specific_lessons: Need for conflict-sensitive water/energy programming in post-Soviet contexts
Importance of neutral conveners (e.g., World Bank) in high-tension regions
Value of flexible funds to respond to sudden crises (e.g., Afghanistan spillover)
Critical role of diplomatic development approaches in FCAS-adjacent areas
Lessons from CAWEP Phase 3 on balancing regional cooperation with national sovereignty concerns
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Builds on UK support to earlier CAWEP phases and CASA-1000 programme, which established the UK as a key partner in Central Asia’s water/energy development. Lessons include: 1) importance of long-term patient partnerships; 2) need to align with government incentives; and 3) value of small catalytic investments to leverage larger IFI funds.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The two-component structure (regional + flexible fund) reflects lessons about needing both systemic coordination and localized adaptation. The adaptive management approach responds to past challenges with rigid programmes in dynamic contexts.
risks_lessons.quote: "CEW-CA builds on previous and current UK support in Central Asia, including UK support to earlier phases of CAWEP and the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA-1000) programme, which established the UK as a key partner in Central Asia’s water and energy development... The UK’s role as a convening power makes it well placed to deliver on regional climate, energy and water issues." (D0004791.odt, Strategic fit)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme expects to leverage additional IFI investments at a 3:1 ratio (£3 of additional funding for every £1 of UK ODA). World Bank's CAWEP platform provides access to larger regional investments.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Year 1 focuses on revenue activities (technical assistance, capacity building) with potential capital investments (infrastructure) in later years through unlocked finance.
financial_details.quote: "During FY23/24 the Bank will deduct from the Trust Fund and retain for its own account a fee equal to 12% of the amount for Bank-executed activities... Upto £12m of ODA will contribute to regional water and energy security outcomes... Upto £6.3m of ICF will be focussed on delivering climate outcomes... The remainder of funds would support programme funded posts and MEL." (D0004791.odt, Commercial arrangements)

metadata.programme_name: Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) - Early Action and Resilience Transformation in Humanitarianism (EARTH)

quote.programme_name: "Title: Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) - Early Action and Resilience Transformation in Humanitarianism (EARTH)" (D0005252.odt, Title section)
quote.duration: "AMP Start Date: December 2023 (4 financial years) AMP End Date: April 2027" (D0005252.odt, Summary Sheet)
quote.sector: "Country/Region or Sector: Global; Humanitarian" (D0005252.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.duration_source: "AMP Start Date: December 2023 (4 financial years) AMP End Date: April 2027" (D0005252.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanism (channeling funds through FAO's SFERA), service delivery (emergency agricultural interventions), and capacity building (strengthening resilience and data systems). It aims to protect agricultural livelihoods and reduce future humanitarian needs by funding anticipatory and early action interventions, while also supporting food security analysis tools like the IPC.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will invest in the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the UN’s (FAO) emergency and resilience activities across the humanitarian-development nexus to protect communities at risk from climate-driven food insecurity by supporting agricultural livelihoods and localised food production... It will do this by providing earmarked funding to FAO’s humanitarian interventions funding mechanism—the ‘Special Fund for Emergency and Resilience Activities’ (SFERA)... UK contributions will be earmarked to support FAO’s ‘El Niño Anticipatory Action and Response Plan’... and the Integrated Food Security Classification (IPC)" (D0005252.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Emergency agricultural interventions delivered
q3_expected_outputs.target: 4.8 million people supported via El Niño Response Plan (2023-2024)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Climate-adaptive action plans funded
q3_expected_outputs.target: Annual allocations for climate mitigation via SFERA (Years 2-4)

q3_expected_outputs.output: IPC food security knowledge products maintained
q3_expected_outputs.target: Coverage of 30+ countries (baseline) with option to expand to 40

q3_expected_outputs.output: Resilience of agricultural communities strengthened
q3_expected_outputs.target: Reduction in future humanitarian caseloads (qualitative)

q3_expected_outputs.output: UK diplomatic influence enhanced
q3_expected_outputs.target: Membership in SFERA donor group and IPC Steering Committee

what_objectives.summary: The programme channels UK funding through FAO's SFERA mechanism to deliver anticipatory agricultural interventions (seeds, tools, training) during climate crises like El Niño, while simultaneously maintaining the IPC's global food security analysis capacity. It aims to reduce acute food insecurity, build long-term resilience, and position the UK as a leader in climate-adaptive humanitarian action.

quote.objectives: "The overarching goal of this programme is to help protect the lives and livelihoods of vulnerable populations at risk from climate-driven food insecurity across current, and future, humanitarian crises worldwide. It will do this by investing in FAO’s humanitarian interventions funding mechanism—the SFERA—to deliver targeted and emergency climate-adaptive agricultural interventions which help support sustainable local food production and build more shock-resilient agricultural communities." (D0005252.odt, What this programme will do)
quote.outputs: "Provide UK funds to support FAO’s anticipatory and early action agricultural interventions to mitigate the impact of breaking climate threats on global food security, including El Niño (via FAO’s emergency funding mechanism—the SFERA)... Promote UK leadership, influence, and a more holistic approach to the UN humanitarian system on food security issues... Signal UK support for expert food security knowledge products and analysis" (D0005252.odt, Programme objectives)

countries_regions: 34 prioritised countries affected by El Niño (2023-2024)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in climate-vulnerable regions facing acute food insecurity, conflict, and economic instability. The document explicitly states an 'Overall programme risk rating: Major' due to the intersection of climate shocks, humanitarian crises, and systemic funding gaps.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" (D0005252.odt, Summary Sheet) && "The climate crisis is a multiplier of threats. It exacerbates humanitarian needs, increases the risk of conflict, triggers displacement, exacerbates food insecurity and threatens public health. weak institutions (need for capacity building in local systems)
data limitations (gaps in food security analysis without IPC funding)
funding gaps (humanitarian system underfunded at 35% coverage in 2023)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate shocks reduce agricultural yields and disrupt local food systems, while underfunding limits the ability to pre-position resources. Conflict and economic instability exacerbate food insecurity, and weak data systems (e.g., IPC funding shortfalls) hinder targeted interventions. The document notes that only 4% of humanitarian funds currently support agricultural livelihoods despite two-thirds of food-insecure populations relying on agriculture.

institutional strengthening (local agricultural systems, early warning networks)
knowledge products (IPC food security analysis tools)
infrastructure development (e.g., pre-positioning agricultural inputs)

(D0005252.odt, Why UK investment in climate adaptive food security programming is needed)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **earmarked contributions** to FAO’s SFERA funding mechanism (a pooled fund for humanitarian interventions) and **direct funding** to the IPC Global Support Unit. SFERA allows flexible allocations across three windows: working capital, revolving fund, and programme funds (earmarked/softly earmarked). The UK’s contribution is split between SFERA (£12m) and IPC (£4.5m) over 4 years.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FAO’s Office for Emergencies and Resilience (OER) in Rome manages the SFERA fund centrally, with technical oversight of country-level interventions. The IPC Global Support Unit (GSU), also based in FAO HQ, manages food security analysis. The UK’s funding is channeled through these central mechanisms, with FAO responsible for allocation to country offices and partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: FAO is a longstanding UK partner with a UN mandate for food security and agricultural livelihoods. The business case highlights FAO’s "proven track record" in anticipatory action and its comparative advantage in delivering climate-adaptive programmes across the humanitarian-development nexus. The SFERA mechanism was selected for its ability to rapidly disburse funds for time-sensitive interventions like El Niño response.

quote.instrument: "This programme will provide earmarked funding to FAO’s humanitarian interventions funding mechanism—the ‘Special Fund for Emergency and Resilience Activities’ (SFERA)... UK contributions will be earmarked to support FAO’s ‘El Niño Anticipatory Action and Response Plan’... and the Integrated Food Security Classification (IPC)." (D0005252.odt, Programme summary)
quote.selection: "The FAO is a longstanding and trusted UK and FCDO partner, who has the UN mandate to deliver anticipatory and early action agricultural interventions across the humanitarian-development nexus. It has a proven track record of delivering quality climate adaptive programming across the nexus through its widespread global network of country offices." (D0005252.odt, Why the FCDO should fund the OER SFERA and the IPC)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: FAO’s OER governs SFERA allocations through its Anticipatory Action Donor Group (which meets quarterly) and technical committees. The UK’s contribution grants access to this group, allowing influence over strategic priorities. The IPC Steering Committee (where the UK holds a seat) oversees food security analysis standards.

quote.governance: "The UK would be granted membership to existing groups, such as the SFERA donor group which meets quarterly. The UK would also be empowered to establish new donor work strands, with a particular focus on improving SFERA’s advocacy strategy to attract more funding." (D0005252.odt, Why the FCDO should fund the OER SFERA and the IPC)
quote.oversight: "During this programme’s inception phase, we will also explore the possibility of providing a UK contribution to the Global Network Against Food Crises (GNAFC) donor consortium... The OER will also be at liberty to choose to allocate UK funding into DIEM’s food security research and early-warning systems via the SFERA funding mechanism." (D0005252.odt, How does this programme link with the wider portfolio of FCDO?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within SFERA can be reallocated between climate-adaptive action plans (Years 2-4) based on emerging needs, but the initial £3m for El Niño (Year 1) is earmarked. The OER has discretion to allocate UK funds to DIEM’s research or other SFERA windows (e.g., Anticipatory Action).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes an inception phase to explore additional engagements (e.g., Global Network Against Food Crises). FAO can adjust intervention priorities based on updated risk analyses (e.g., El Niño impacts) but requires alignment with SFERA’s technical governance.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → FAO (OER/SFERA or IPC GSU) → Country offices/partners. The document does not detail sub-grantees beyond FAO’s country-level networks.

quote.layers: "FAO’s humanitarian programmes can be funded by donors in two ways: at country level bilaterally or via the SFERA funding channel, managed by FAO’s humanitarian and livelihoods assistance arm, The Office for Emergencies and Resilience (OER) based in FAO Rome Headquarters (HQ)." (D0005252.odt, About FAO’s Office for Emergencies and Resilience)
quote.payment: "The OER updates its humanitarian action plans in accordance with new assessments and data on an ongoing basis, such as its ‘El Niño Response Plan’, which is now in its second publication since August 2023." (D0005252.odt, About FAO’s Office for Emergencies and Resilience)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: No additional UK funding to FAO/SFERA or IPC. Risks increased food insecurity and missed diplomatic opportunities.
£16.5m to WFP for emergency food aid. Aligns with UK’s humanitarian mandate but does not address root causes (e.g., climate-adaptive agriculture).
£16.5m to UN Central Emergency Response Fund. Only ~£240k would reach FAO; no direct support for anticipatory action or IPC.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The SFERA/IPC modality was selected for its **proven cost-effectiveness** (FAO’s ROI of $6 per $1 invested), **speed** (SFERA’s rapid response capacity), and **alignment with UK priorities** (climate adaptation, anticipatory action, and food security leadership). FAO’s technical expertise in agricultural livelihoods and its mandate across the humanitarian-development nexus were deemed critical for sustainable impact, unlike WFP’s focus on emergency food aid or CERF’s limited FAO allocations.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (FAO’s $6 ROI vs WFP’s higher food aid costs)
risk mitigation (SFERA’s pre-positioned funds for climate shocks)
partner capacity (FAO’s global network and technical expertise in agriculture)
speed (SFERA’s rapid disbursement vs CERF’s slower UN-wide allocations)
equity (IPC’s impartial data for fair resource targeting)
strategic influence (UK’s seat in SFERA donor group and IPC Steering Committee)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Underfunding of SFERA limits impact
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s £3m annual contribution (Years 2-4) signals donor confidence to attract additional funding. The business case notes that Norway, Belgium, and Sweden are major SFERA donors, suggesting a stable funding environment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IPC funding gap reduces data quality
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK’s £1.5m/year to IPC GSU maintains coverage of 30+ countries, preventing a scale-back to only 10 crises. This ensures continued evidence for FCDO’s targeting decisions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FAO’s centralised management may delay local adaptation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SFERA’s country-level windows and OER’s technical assistance to field offices aim to balance global priorities with local needs. The El Niño Response Plan is updated bi-annually based on new data.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging FAO’s existing systems to reduce overhead)
efficiency (SFERA’s rapid disbursement vs traditional humanitarian cycles)
effectiveness (FAO’s track record in reducing food insecurity caseloads)
equity (IPC’s impartial analysis for fair resource allocation)

quote.rationale: "FAO’s institutional comparative advantage (and UK investment appeal) is its technical capability and capacity to simultaneously address, mitigate and prevent threats to global food security by focusing on the delivery of localised agricultural interventions... FAO’s emergency interventions help to meet humanitarian needs in the immediate aftermath of crisis, while building resilience to withstand future shocks, thereby reducing the scale of future needs." (D0005252.odt, Why the FCDO should fund the OER SFERA and the IPC)
quote.vfm: "In 2022, with just $598 million, FAO’s emergency programmes enabled 23 million people in 29 countries to produce their own food, resulting in a remarkable Return-On-Investment (ROI) of $6 for every dollar (USD) supplied." (D0005252.odt, Why UK investment in climate adaptive food security programming is needed)
quote.risks: "FAO is facing a significant shortfall in humanitarian funding. The agency requested $2.4bn in FY2023/24, of which 15% has so far been received... FAO’s ‘El Niño Response Plan’ requires $160 million to support around 4.8 million people in 34 prioritised countries... As of January 2024, SFERA’s cash balance across all its accounts stood at approximately $50 million (USD)." (D0005252.odt, A overview of FAO humanitarian, SFERA and IPC funding levels)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s **global scope** and focus on **climate-vulnerable, conflict-affected regions** (e.g., Eastern Africa, Asia-Pacific) necessitate a **multilateral partner** (FAO) with existing country offices and technical expertise in FCAS contexts. Local NGOs or governments lack the capacity to deliver anticipatory action at scale, while bilateral agencies cannot match FAO’s mandate or speed via SFERA.
q27_constraints_detail: Climate shocks (El Niño) require pre-positioned agricultural inputs, favoring FAO’s global supply chains over local actors.
Conflict and fragility in target regions (e.g., South Sudan, Somalia) limit the operational presence of smaller partners.
Need for impartial data (IPC) in politically sensitive contexts requires a UN-hosted mechanism.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **anticipatory action objective** (mitigating climate shocks before they escalate) drives the choice of **SFERA’s rapid-disbursement mechanism**, while the **need for impartial food security data** necessitates funding the **IPC’s multilateral governance structure**. FAO’s dual humanitarian-development mandate aligns with the programme’s goal of bridging emergency response and resilience-building.
q28_linkages: Anticipatory action → SFERA’s pre-allocated funding windows for time-sensitive interventions (e.g., El Niño).
Resilience-building → FAO’s country offices and local partners for long-term capacity development.
Data-driven targeting → IPC’s consensus-based analysis to prioritise interventions.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between **rapid delivery** (via FAO’s centralised SFERA system) and **local ownership** (limited direct funding to Southern partners). It prioritises efficiency (SFERA’s ROI and speed) but mitigates equity risks by: (1) earmarking funds for LMICs/FCAS, (2) supporting IPC’s impartial data to guide fair allocations, and (3) building local agricultural capacity through FAO’s country offices.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: SFERA’s centralised management enables rapid response but limits direct Southern partner control over funds. Mitigation: FAO’s country offices and local partners implement interventions.
FAO (HQ in Rome) designs Anticipatory Action plans, while local actors deliver them. Mitigation: Capacity building for local agricultural systems is a core objective.
Standardised SFERA interventions may not fully align with local contexts. Mitigation: OER provides technical assistance to country offices for adaptation.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** (due to climate shocks, funding gaps, and conflict) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and FAO’s centralised management. The business case notes that SFERA’s flexible windows allow reallocation to underfunded crises, while IPC data helps target high-risk regions.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded in the delivery structure**: FAO’s OER provides technical assistance to country offices, while IPC funding strengthens local data systems. The programme explicitly links **Southern partners’ roles** (e.g., delivering seeds/tools) to **capacity outcomes** (e.g., climate-adaptive farming training).

quote.context_partner: "The OER was established in 2016 to ‘save lives, save livelihoods and transform lives’ by supporting the in-country delivery of anticipatory action and early action agricultural interventions in humanitarian crises. It has oversight of all FAO humanitarian assistance programmes globally and provides technical assistance to FAO’s country offices." (D0005252.odt, About FAO’s Office for Emergencies and Resilience)
quote.objectives_structure: "The SFERA funding channel provides FAO with flexible funding to facilitate its timely response to humanitarian crises... FAO’s interventions have been proven to reduce reliance on short-term food aid provided by WFP." (D0005252.odt, Why the FCDO should fund the OER SFERA and the IPC)
quote.tradeoffs: "FAO’s emergency interventions help to meet humanitarian needs in the immediate aftermath of crisis, while building resilience to withstand future shocks, thereby reducing the scale of future needs... The IPC is used by donors, UN agencies, NGOs, and the international community to understand acute and chronic food insecurity needs, prioritise geographies, make large-scale funding decisions, and inform political and diplomatic engagements." (D0005252.odt, Why the FCDO should fund the OER SFERA and the IPC)

key_programme_risks: Underfunding of SFERA limits FAO’s ability to scale anticipatory action (current $50m balance vs $315m annual need).
IPC funding gap reduces coverage from 30+ to 10 countries, undermining evidence-based targeting.
Climate shocks (El Niño) exacerbate food insecurity beyond planned intervention capacity.
Conflict or political instability in target regions disrupts implementation.
Donor fatigue or shifting priorities reduce complementary funding to SFERA/IPC.
FAO’s centralised management may delay local adaptation of interventions.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK’s £3m/year contribution (Years 2-4) signals donor confidence to attract co-funding. Business case notes that Norway, Belgium, and Sweden are major SFERA donors, suggesting a stable environment.
UK’s £1.5m/year maintains coverage of 30+ countries, preventing scale-back. IPC’s Steering Committee (where UK holds a seat) oversees prioritisation.
SFERA’s Anticipatory Action window pre-positions funds for scalable responses. FAO’s El Niño plan targets 4.8m people but can adjust based on real-time data.
FAO’s country offices in FCAS regions (e.g., South Sudan, Somalia) have existing partnerships with local actors for adaptive implementation.
UK’s diplomatic engagement via SFERA donor group and IPC Steering Committee aims to mobilise additional resources.

fcas_specific_lessons: Pre-positioning agricultural inputs (seeds, tools) ahead of planting seasons is critical in FCAS where supply chains are fragile. FAO’s 2022 programmes reached 23m people in 29 countries using this approach.
Localising interventions through FAO’s country offices improves acceptance in conflict zones. The business case highlights FAO’s work in Somalia and South Sudan as examples.
Bundling emergency aid (e.g., seeds) with resilience training (e.g., climate-adaptive techniques) reduces long-term dependency in protracted crises.
IPC data is essential for neutral needs assessment in politically sensitive FCAS contexts, where access for other actors may be restricted.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The business case cites USAID’s 2018 study in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Somalia, which found that **anticipatory action is up to 3x more cost-effective than post-disaster response**. It also references FAO’s 2022 ROI of $6 per $1 invested in emergency agricultural programmes, demonstrating the efficiency of this approach compared to traditional food aid.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Inception phase added to explore contributions to the Global Network Against Food Crises (GNAFC), based on lessons about the need for multi-donor coordination.
Flexible SFERA allocations (Years 2-4) designed to adapt to emerging climate threats, informed by IPC’s real-time data.
Explicit focus on **climate-adaptive** agricultural inputs (e.g., drought-resistant seeds) based on evidence of their higher ROI in FCAS contexts.

quote.risks: "FAO is facing a significant shortfall in humanitarian funding. The agency requested $2.4bn in FY2023/24, of which 15% has so far been received... As of January 2024, SFERA’s cash balance across all its accounts stood at approximately $50 million (USD)." (D0005252.odt, A overview of FAO humanitarian, SFERA and IPC funding levels)
quote.lessons: "USAID has found that acting ahead of emergencies by utilising resilience interventions can be up to three times as cost-effective as traditional humanitarian aid after the fact." (D0005252.odt, Why UK investment in climate adaptive food security programming is needed) && "In 2022, with just $598 million, FAO’s emergency programmes enabled 23 million people in 29 countries to produce their own food, resulting in a remarkable Return-On-Investment (ROI) of $6 for every dollar (USD) supplied." (D0005252.odt, Why UK investment in climate adaptive food security programming is needed)

(D0005252.odt, How does this programme link with the wider portfolio of FCDO?)

quote.programme_name: "Enhanced Water Leadership in a Changing Climate" (Document: D0006380.odt, Title section)
quote.duration: "Enhanced Water Leadership in a Changing Climate will deepen the UK’s engagement and influence in water security, sanitation and hygiene over 4 years from April 2024." (Document: D0006380.odt, Programme summary section)

metadata.duration_source: "Enhanced Water Leadership in a Changing Climate will deepen the UK’s engagement and influence in water security, sanitation and hygiene over 4 years from April 2024."

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines policy influence (inspiring political leaders to prioritize WASH), capacity building (strengthening governance and finance systems), and financing mechanism (mobilizing climate finance and private investment). It focuses on accelerating access to resilient WASH services in low- and lower-middle-income countries by reinforcing global platforms like SWA, JMP, and the World Bank’s Water Global Practice.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Enhanced Water Leadership in a Changing Climate will deepen the UK’s engagement and influence in water security, sanitation and hygiene... Its entry point is an existing programme, Global Water Leadership in a Changing Climate... Building on Global Water Leadership, the new programme has a sharper focus on governance, accountability and finance, reinvigorating sector leadership with just seven years left to deliver the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)." (Document: D0006380.odt, Programme summary section)

q3_expected_outputs.output: National commitments to accelerate progress on WASH by at least 20 low- and lower-middle-income countries
Water Security and Climate Adaptation Global Challenge programme operationalised in at least 8 countries
High-quality data and evidence on WASH systems produced by JMP, GLAAS, and World Bank
Technical support provided to at least 30 low- and lower-middle-income countries
Partnerships with development banks and private investors mobilised to secure new finance
Progressive reduction in preventable deaths of mothers, children, and infants caused by WASH-related infections

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to accelerate progress toward SDG6 by strengthening political leadership, improving sector governance and finance, and mobilizing climate finance for resilient WASH services. It builds on existing platforms (SWA, JMP, World Bank) to drive systemic change in low- and lower-middle-income countries.

quote.objectives: "The programme’s focus on supporting national political leadership to prioritise water security, sanitation and hygiene is critical, given the overriding need to overhaul sector performance and attract private investment needed to deliver reliable, resilient and inclusive WASH services." (Document: D0006380.odt, Rationale section)

SWA convenes high-level political dialogues, JMP/GLAAS generate data and evidence, and WGP provides technical assistance. FCDO coordinates across these platforms but does not manage day-to-day operations.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their track record and existing relationships with FCDO. SWA, JMP, and WGP are long-standing platforms with proven impact in the WASH sector, reducing the need for competitive selection.

The World Bank’s WGP is guided by its Donor Council and Global Challenge Programme leadership. FCDO participates in these structures but does not lead them.

quote.oversight: "Risks will be reviewed every quarter with mitigation measures introduced as necessary, ensuring that the residual risk levels are maintained within HDD’s risk appetite." (Document: D0006380.odt, Risk management section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to predefined components (SWA, JMP, WGP) but can be adjusted within these components based on performance reviews. Major reallocations between components would require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in technical support and policy focus based on emerging evidence (e.g., climate resilience indicators). However, significant changes require approval from FCDO and partner governance bodies.

quote.flexibility: "The programme will reinforce our policy initiatives, our diplomatic engagement and complementary programmes... ensuring the new programme can quickly dock into place." (Document: D0006380.odt, Programme linkages section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral partners (SWA/JMP/WGP) → National governments/implementers

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £16.9m (ICF 45%)" (Document: D0006380.odt, Metadata section)
quote.layers: "The programme’s outputs will be delivered through three components, involving established partners..." (Document: D0006380.odt, Programme delivery section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Continue supporting only JMP, SWA, and WGP (existing components)
Option 2: Add GLAAS to the existing components (chosen option)
Do-nothing counterfactual: Rely on national governments without global platform support
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 (including GLAAS) was selected to strengthen the evidence base for sector reform and climate resilience. GLAAS provides critical data on WASH systems and finance, complementing JMP’s service monitoring and SWA’s political engagement. The combined approach maximizes the UK’s influence across data, policy, and finance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partner failure to attract sufficient resources
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will monitor financial sustainability and provide diplomatic support to mobilize co-funding.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited collaboration between partners (e.g., WGP and SWA)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular joint reviews and FCDO-facilitated coordination mechanisms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor fatigue or shifting priorities (e.g., pandemics, economic crises)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Diversified donor base and alignment with global priorities (e.g., climate adaptation).

quote.alternatives: "Option 1 is based on the three components currently supported through Global Water Leadership programme: JMP, SWA and the World Bank’s Water Global Practice... Option 2 adds GLAAS... to Option 1." (Document: D0006380.odt, Identification of options section)
quote.rationale: "GLAAS provides decision makers with information on national WASH systems, focusing on governance, finance, capacity building and the use of information... 95% of participating governments reported using GLAAS data to inform decision-making." (Document: D0006380.odt, GLAAS assessment section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s focus on low- and lower-middle-income countries with weak WASH systems limits partner selection to organizations with existing regional presence and multilateral legitimacy (e.g., SWA, WHO, World Bank). Local NGOs or private sector actors are not directly engaged due to capacity constraints and risk profiles.
q27_constraints_detail: weak institutional capacity in target countries
need for multilateral legitimacy to influence governments
climate vulnerability requiring technical expertise
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—political leadership, evidence generation, and finance mobilization—require a platform-based approach. SWA is needed for high-level advocacy, JMP/GLAAS for data, and WGP for technical/financial leverage. Direct service delivery is avoided in favor of systemic change.
q28_linkages: Political leadership (SWA) → requires convening power and accountability mechanisms
Evidence generation (JMP/GLAAS) → needs multilateral credibility for global data
Finance mobilization (WGP) → depends on World Bank’s lending instruments
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme prioritizes equity (focus on poorest countries, gender inclusion) over efficiency (higher transaction costs of multilateral platforms). Trade-offs include slower decision-making in exchange for broader legitimacy and Southern ownership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs. inclusion (multilateral processes take longer but ensure broad buy-in)
Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership (technical leadership by WHO/World Bank balanced with national commitments)
cost vs. reach (higher overheads for global platforms but wider impact)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (e.g., political instability, financial sustainability) justifies milestone-based oversight and quarterly risk reviews. High-risk contexts (e.g., fragile states) would trigger more intensive management.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in all components: SWA strengthens political leadership, JMP/GLAAS build data analysis skills, and WGP enhances financial/technical capacity. Southern partners (governments) co-lead these processes.

quote.constraints: "The programme’s focus on supporting national political leadership to prioritise water security... is critical, given the overriding need to overhaul sector performance and attract private investment." (Document: D0006380.odt, Rationale section)
quote.tradeoffs: "SWA has unique convening power in the sector... WGP is known for the high quality of its technical outputs and thought leadership... JMP processes are well established, leading to the efficient production of outputs." (Document: D0006380.odt, Partner assessments section)

key_programme_risks: One or more partners fail to attract sufficient financial resources
Partners fail to collaborate effectively (e.g., WGP and SWA)
Major pandemic or global recession diverts government attention from WASH
UNICEF ends its hosting arrangement with SWA
Safeguarding issues among implementing partners
Government partner implicated in human rights abuses
Climate change exacerbates water scarcity, undermining progress
Corruption in WASH sector finance

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: FCDO will use diplomatic leverage to mobilize co-funding and monitor financial health.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited collaboration between WGP and SWA
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Regular joint reviews and FCDO-facilitated coordination.
Advocacy to maintain WASH as a priority in crisis responses.
Contingency planning for alternative hosting arrangements.
Enhanced due diligence and monitoring of partner policies.
Integration of climate resilience indicators and adaptive programming.

fcas_specific_lessons: In fragile contexts, focus on institutional arrangements to unlock public finance (e.g., South Sudan compact).
Use high-level political champions (e.g., Head of State Initiative) to sustain momentum.
Blend climate finance with traditional WASH funding to address compounded risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases (Global Water Leadership) demonstrated the value of combining political advocacy (SWA), data (JMP), and finance (WGP). Lessons include the need for stronger accountability mechanisms and deeper engagement with development banks.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Sharper focus on governance, accountability, and finance (vs. earlier service delivery approach).
Added GLAAS to strengthen evidence on sector systems and climate resilience.
Expanded climate finance mobilization through World Bank’s Global Challenge Programme.

quote.risks: "Risks will be reviewed every quarter with mitigation measures introduced as necessary, ensuring that the residual risk levels are maintained within HDD’s risk appetite." (Document: D0006380.odt, Risk management section)
quote.lessons: "Learning lessons from our previous support to the sector, this new programme will reinforce global mechanisms designed to inspire political leaders to prioritise water security, sanitation and hygiene." (Document: D0006380.odt, Programme summary section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to crowd in additional finance, including climate finance and private investment, by improving the bankability of WASH projects. WGP alone influenced $13.2 billion in World Bank water investments in 2023.

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £16.9m (ICF 45%)" (Document: D0006380.odt, Metadata section)
quote.leverage: "WGP reports to have directly influenced $13.2bn of World Bank investments in the water sector, over 60% of which was channelled to low and lower-middle income countries." (Document: D0006380.odt, WGP assessment section)
