who_partners.quote: "FCDO’s contribution (proposed at least £30m of £38m business case) will continue the work and extend these networks and labs further, including into more countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. [...] IDRC has a proven track record in delivering global research programmes using a ‘grants plus’ model—whereby IDRC staff are mentors and advisors to the research programme, not only funders." (D0006995.odt, Option 4: Delivery through IDRC)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of grant funding (through IDRC's 'grants plus' model), partnership agreements (with BMGF, USAID, GIZ), and potential public-private partnerships (e.g., 'GAVI for compute' initiative). IDRC acts as a fund manager distributing grants to Southern research institutions while providing mentorship and advisory support.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IDRC serves as the central fund manager and research broker, with FCDO providing strategic oversight. The structure includes: 1) Regional research hubs (African universities) managing local implementation; 2) Thematic networks (policy, innovation, scaling) with specialized partners; 3) A coalition of donors (FCDO, BMGF, USAID) coordinating funding; and 4) Private sector partners (Google, Microsoft) contributing in-kind resources. The model emphasizes Southern leadership with Northern partners providing complementary expertise and funding.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IDRC was selected based on its proven track record in delivering similar AI-for-development programmes (AI4D Africa since 2020), established grants management systems, alignment with UK priorities, and ability to leverage existing research networks in Africa. The selection emphasizes continuity with ongoing work rather than competitive bidding.
how_mechanism.quote: "Through conversations with other donors and key AI stakeholders, FCDO identified IDRC as the organisation with the greatest wealth of knowledge and implementing activity in the AI for development space. [...] IDRC launched AI4D Africa in 2020 [...] representing the predominant ‘AI-first’ international development ecosystem support programme." (D0006995.odt, Option 4: Delivery through IDRC)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme is governed by a funders' coalition including FCDO, IDRC, BMGF, and USAID, with IDRC managing day-to-day operations. A steering committee approach is implied through references to "coordinated funding" and "shared vision" among partners. The African Union and ASEAN institutions provide regional policy oversight, while technical advisory groups are mentioned for specific pillars (e.g., AI safety research).
how_governance.quote: "FCDO’s contribution [...] has already unlocked further investment from IDRC on AI4D in Africa, as the Board of Governors recently approved a briefing on the partnership and has committed to investing £6.6m and is expected to help catalyse other co-ordinated support from donors, foundations and the private sector, around a shared vision." (D0006995.odt, Option 4: Delivery through IDRC)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme includes break clauses to manage spending risks and reserves funding for emerging issues. While the core pillars are fixed, there is flexibility to adjust allocations between geographic regions (Africa vs. Indo-Pacific) and specific activities within pillars based on partner contributions and learning.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme emphasizes agility in a fast-evolving field, with reserved funding for emerging opportunities and a design phase for the Indo-Pacific expansion to refine objectives. Adjustments require approval from the funders' coalition, particularly for major shifts in geographic or thematic focus.
how_flexibility.quote: "In a fast-evolving field, the programme will need to be agile and adaptive, including by reserving funding for emerging issues and opportunities." (D0006995.odt, Vision for crowding in complementary efforts) AND "Break clauses are built into the programme to manage the risk of spending beyond FY27/28 for the last two years of the programme." (D0006996.odt, Additional support)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IDRC (fund manager) → Southern research institutions/innovation networks → end beneficiaries (researchers, policymakers, communities). The structure includes an additional coalition layer for donor coordination.
how_efficiency.quote: "IDRC has a proven track record in delivering global research programmes using a ‘grants plus’ model—whereby IDRC staff are mentors and advisors to the research programme, not only funders." (D0006995.odt, Option 4: Delivery through IDRC)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (counterfactual)
Leverage existing FCDO programming (light-touch approach)
Fund existing multilateral work (UNESCO IRCAI)
Set up a wholly new FCDO-owned programme (commercial procurement)
Deliver through IDRC (recommended approach)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The IDRC-led approach was chosen for five key reasons: 1) **Proven track record**: IDRC's successful management of AI4D Africa since 2020 with strong results; 2) **Southern leadership**: Alignment with the programme's goal of Global South ownership; 3) **Efficiency**: Existing grants management systems and research networks reduce startup costs; 4) **Leverage**: Ability to catalyze additional funding from other donors (BMGF, USAID) through a shared vision; 5) **Flexibility**: IDRC's 'grants plus' model allows for adaptive management in a fast-evolving field.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (IDRC's no management fee to FCDO)
risk mitigation (proven systems for grants management)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited FCDO engagement in day-to-day delivery may reduce learning opportunities for UK policy
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Structured knowledge-sharing mechanisms between IDRC and FCDO, with FCDO representation in governance bodies

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other donor programmes (e.g., GIZ Fair Forward) could create duplication
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proactive coordination with complementary initiatives and clear division of labor (e.g., AI4D focusing on research/innovation while GIZ leads on policy dialogue)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Private sector partners (Google, Microsoft) may prioritize commercial interests over development goals
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear memoranda of understanding with safeguards for responsible AI and development alignment

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Southern institutions may lack capacity to manage large-scale grants
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IDRC's 'grants plus' model provides mentorship and capacity building alongside funding

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging existing IDRC systems to reduce costs)
efficiency (catalyzing £1 of external funding for every £1 of FCDO investment)
effectiveness (focus on scalable AI solutions with measurable SDG impact)
equity (explicit targets for women, people with disabilities, and marginalized groups)
why_rationale.quote: "IDRC has a proven track record in delivering global research programmes using a ‘grants plus’ model [...] IDRC staff are mentors and advisors to the research programme, not only funders. [...] FCDO’s contribution [...] has already unlocked further investment from IDRC on AI4D in Africa." (D0006995.odt, Option 4: Delivery through IDRC) AND "Building multi-stakeholder partnerships with other development stakeholders will be critical for meeting the speed and scale of the challenge that AI poses for developing countries." (D0006995.odt, Vision for crowding in complementary efforts)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The operating context in Sub-Saharan Africa and Indo-Pacific directly shapes partner selection: 1) **Data limitations** require partners with existing datasets or data collection capacity (e.g., Lacuna Fund, GSMA); 2) **Language barriers** necessitate partnerships with local linguistic experts (e.g., Masakhane for African languages, SEA-LION for Asian languages); 3) **Weak institutions** favor partners with governance experience (e.g., IDRC's policy hubs, ASEAN for regional coordination); 4) **Digital divide** prioritizes partners with inclusive approaches (e.g., GSMA's Mobile for Development); 5) **Climate vulnerability** leads to partnerships with climate-focused organizations (e.g., EdTech Hub for climate-smart education).
q27_constraints_detail: Data scarcity → Requires partners with data generation capacity (Lacuna Fund, mobile operators)
Language diversity → Needs linguistic research networks (Masakhane, SEA-LION)
Institutional weakness → Favors partners with governance expertise (IDRC, ASEAN)
Digital exclusion → Prioritizes inclusive tech partners (GSMA, assistive tech organizations)
Climate risks → Demands climate-resilient AI applications (EdTech Hub, agricultural partners)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's mixed objectives (research + capacity building + innovation + policy) require a networked delivery structure: 1) **Research goals** → Need academic partners (universities, think tanks) managed through grants; 2) **Capacity building** → Requires mentorship-intensive models (IDRC's 'grants plus'); 3) **Innovation scaling** → Demands private sector engagement (Google, Microsoft for compute); 4) **Policy influence** → Necessitates government partnerships (African Union, ASEAN); 5) **Inclusion targets** → Mandates civil society collaboration (disability organizations, women's networks). The fund manager model (IDRC) was chosen to coordinate these diverse activities while maintaining Southern leadership.
q28_linkages: Evidence generation → Academic partnerships with grant management (IDRC model)
Talent development → University networks with mentorship (post-graduate hubs)
Data infrastructure → Multi-donor data funds (Lacuna Fund collaboration)
Innovation scaling → Private sector accelerators with milestone funding
Policy influence → Regional bodies with technical advisory groups (AU, ASEAN)
Inclusion targets → Civil society co-design with participatory methods
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses three key trade-offs: 1) **Speed vs. Inclusion**: The rapid pace of AI development creates pressure to deliver quickly, but the programme prioritizes inclusive design (e.g., expanding datasets to include marginalized groups) which may slow implementation; 2) **Northern Expertise vs. Southern Ownership**: While Northern partners (IDRC, BMGF) provide efficient systems and funding, the programme structures governance to ensure Southern institutions lead research and innovation; 3) **Cost vs. Reach**: Developing locally-relevant AI (e.g., language models for 46 African languages) is more expensive than using existing Western tools but necessary for equitable impact. The 'grants plus' model attempts to balance these by combining Northern funding with Southern leadership.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. Inclusion: "The programme will need to be agile and adaptive [...] while ensuring gender, disability and inclusion are core elements" (D0006995.odt)
Expertise vs. Ownership: "Place leadership of this research in the hands of AI leaders and researchers in the Global South" despite using Northern fund manager (D0006995.odt)
Cost vs. Reach: "Developing locally-relevant machine-learning ready datasets" for 46 African languages increases costs but is essential for inclusion (D0006996.odt)
Flexibility vs. Accountability: Reserved funding for emerging issues requires robust governance to prevent mission creep (D0006995.odt)
Scale vs. Depth: "Few developing countries have developed venture capital markets" making scaling difficult without compromising local relevance (D0006995.odt)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives several management intensity choices: 1) **Major risks** (harm from irresponsible AI, deepened inequality) → Require milestone-based oversight with break clauses; 2) **Political risks** (state capture, information disorder) → Mandate policy research with government engagement; 3) **Economic risks** (job displacement) → Necessitate labor market monitoring; 4) **Social risks** (exclusion of women/PwDs) → Lead to dedicated inclusion targets with separate reporting. The management structure balances these risks with the need for adaptability in a fast-changing field.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives directly shape partner roles through: 1) **Research Hubs**: Universities receive grants plus mentorship to develop both AI skills and institutional research capacity; 2) **Innovation Networks**: Startups get seed funding combined with business development support; 3) **Policy Institutions**: Think tanks receive funding tied to policy engagement targets; 4) **Civil Society**: Disability and women's organizations are embedded in programme design and monitoring. The 'grants plus' model explicitly links funding to capacity development outcomes.
intersections.quote: "The programme will strengthen African AI ecosystems to develop and apply AI responsibly with investments across: AI policy and governance research; AI talent and skills; machine-learning ready datasets; AI innovation; scaling AI impact. All of the above activities will have a strong focus on responsible AI and on gender and inclusion." (D0006995.odt, Programme summary) AND "IDRC has a proven track record in delivering global research programmes using a ‘grants plus’ model—whereby IDRC staff are mentors and advisors to the research programme, not only funders." (D0006995.odt, Option 4)

AI innovations privileging elites over marginalized groups (D0006995.odt, Risks)
Data limitations preventing development of locally relevant AI (D0006995.odt, Gap 2)

AI-enabled cybercrime or biological misuse (D0006995.odt, Technological risks)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to adopt responsible AI principles
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Funding research on AI safety and governance; establishing policy observatories; requiring ethical review boards for all funded projects
Explicit inclusion targets (gender, disability, marginalized languages); participatory design methods; monitoring differential impacts
Investing in machine-learning ready datasets; partnering with Lacuna Fund; liberating private data through responsible sharing mechanisms
Supporting independent policy research hubs; multi-stakeholder governance; transparency requirements for public-private partnerships
Expanding training datasets to include marginalized groups; requiring bias audits; funding research on fair AI
Targeted funding for women/PwD inclusion; mobile-based solutions; digital literacy components
Research on AI safety; partnerships with cybersecurity experts; ethical guidelines for high-risk applications
Climate impact assessments for AI projects; promoting energy-efficient models; offset requirements
Legal support for researchers; clear data ownership agreements; exploring open-source models
'GAVI for compute' initiative to reduce costs; cloud credit partnerships; local data center investments
Dedicated scaling pillar with financing partnerships; milestone-based funding for growth-stage innovations
Regional policy research centers; engagement with ASEAN on AI governance; sector-specific standards development
Gender-transformative AI applications; targeted skills development for women; monitoring gendered impacts

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS contexts, AI applications must prioritize conflict sensitivity (e.g., misinformation risks in election periods)
Weak state capacity requires non-state partners (universities, civil society) for service delivery
Data scarcity in FCAS necessitates alternative approaches (e.g., synthetic data, mobile operator partnerships)
Humanitarian applications need rapid deployment mechanisms while maintaining ethical safeguards
Post-conflict settings offer opportunities for leapfrogging but require trauma-informed design
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: 1) **From IDRC's AI4D Africa**: The importance of grassroots AI communities (e.g., Deep Learning Indaba) and avoiding donor-driven approaches that stifle local innovation; 2) **From FCDO's digital programmes**: Mobile operators as key partners for data and reach in low-connectivity areas; 3) **From health AI pilots**: The need for regulatory sandboxes to test innovations safely; 4) **From climate AI**: Local data is critical for relevant applications (e.g., crop models using regional weather data); 5) **From gender programmes**: Separate targets for women's participation are necessary to overcome structural barriers.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) Added explicit focus on generative AI following its rapid advancement; 2) Expanded to Indo-Pacific based on successful Africa model; 3) Increased emphasis on scaling mechanisms after identifying 1% AI funding in African tech investments; 4) Strengthened inclusion components after gender/disability gap analysis; 5) Added 'GAVI for compute' concept to address cost barriers; 6) Incorporated climate AI as a cross-cutting theme based on regional vulnerabilities.
risks_lessons.quote: "A gap analysis of FCDO research investments on AI has revealed three key gaps that this programme would help to fill: developing AI capability and skills; local data as a fundamental pre-requisite; and research on safely managing the political, social and economic risks posed by AI in developing countries." (D0006995.odt, The development challenge) AND "The programme has also been welcomed by the AI community in Africa, with representatives of universities, civil society, startups, governments, international organisations and industry from across the continent convening in Accra in February 2024 to inform the programme’s activities." (D0006996.odt, Development challenge)

co_funding_partners.partner: Potential additional partners (Australia, Germany, Republic of Korea, France)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme has catalyzed approximately £80m in aligned investments including: £38m (FCDO) + £6.6m (IDRC) + $20m (BMGF) + contributions from USAID, GIZ, and private sector (Google, Microsoft). The 'GAVI for compute' initiative aims to match donor funding with private sector in-kind contributions.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme includes both revenue spending (research grants, operational costs) and capital investments (dataset development, compute infrastructure). At least 10% of the Indo-Pacific funding is classified as International Climate Finance (ICF).
financial_details.quote: "The UK will provide up to an additional £20m over 2024-2029, taking the total programme budget to £58m. [...] The additional funding will be allocated from within FCDO Research and Evidence Directorate’s ODA CDELR&D budget. [...] Upto £2m of the additional funding will be used to leverage more affordable access to compute for AI research and innovation for development impact across Africa and the Indo-Pacific." (D0006996.odt, Additional support) AND "FCDO’s contribution [...] has already unlocked further investment from IDRC on AI4D in Africa, as the Board of Governors recently approved a briefing on the partnership and has committed to investing £6.6m and is expected to help catalyse other co-ordinated support from donors, foundations and the private sector." (D0006995.odt, Option 4)

metadata.programme_name: Climate & Health Research Programme (CHIRP)

quote.text: This programme will add high quality evidence in the field of climate and health, with a focus on generating implementable solutions in LMICs...

duration_source.text:
AMP Start Date: May 2024
AMPEnd Date: 31st March 2029

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research to create new knowledge) with capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills) and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions). It focuses on generating actionable evidence for climate-resilient primary healthcare systems while building LMIC research capacity and learning from climate-related disasters.

q1_source.text: This programme will add high quality evidence in the field of climate and health... with a focus on generating implementable solutions in LMICs... The programme will address a critical and increasingly urgent research gap... Supporting the development of a strong and actionable evidence base for delivering climate resilient primary health care systems. Generating robust evidence on the health co-benefits of climate investments. Supporting learning from climate related disasters for health systems.
q1_source.source: D0007318.odt, Programme summary and What we will invest in

q3_expected_outputs.output: High quality evidence on the health benefits of key climate interventions
New knowledge on responsive climate and health data and information systems in primary healthcare settings
Evidence on what is needed to ensure a skilled, resilient, and responsive health workforce
Policies and services for better care and resilience in primary health systems
Evidence on health system preparedness, disaster response, and learning from climate-related disasters
Strengthened capacity and increased involvement of LMIC individuals, organisations, and networks in climate and health research
Effective knowledge brokering activities that drive translation of research into practical improvements
Establishment of a world-leading Research Centre for Climate and Health Impact and Learning
Up to five regional research hubs led by LMIC organisations
q3_expected_outputs.target: at least 3

what_objectives.summary: CHIRP aims to generate actionable evidence on climate-resilient health systems while building LMIC research capacity and learning from climate disasters. It combines research, capacity strengthening, and policy influence to address the urgent gap in climate-health interventions.

quote.text: The programme will address a critical and increasingly urgent research gap, with a focus on the following three pillars, and has been designed to be scalable so it can match need and ambition: 1) Supporting the development of a strong and actionable evidence base for delivering climate resilient primary health care systems; 2) Generating robust evidence on the health co-benefits of climate investments; 3) Supporting learning from climate related disasters for health systems.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme has a moderate residual risk rating, with risks associated with research delivery in complex environments but with established mitigation measures. The document explicitly states: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate."

q5_source.text:
Overall programme risk rating:
Moderate

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The programme notes limited evidence on climate-resilient primary healthcare in LMICs, weak health system preparedness for climate impacts, and the need to build research capacity in Southern institutions. Climate risks directly affect health systems and research delivery, while political and institutional constraints may limit policy uptake.

quote.text: Health systems are under prepared for the impacts of climate change and are unlikely to have the resilience and resources available to respond appropriately... There is a dearth of evidence on how to deliver climate resilient PHC, specifically interventions that will contribute to health systems strengthening... There is limited research focusing on the role of primary healthcare, an essential component in the delivery of climate resilient health systems; we need to better understand the health impacts of climate interventions to maximise benefits to health... There is a lack of capacity in LMIC researchers to deliver research in this field.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, The case for action and What we will invest in

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Research Centre for Climate and Health Impact and Learning (with regional hubs led by LMIC organisations)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme explicitly prioritizes LMIC research leadership, with regional hubs led by Southern institutions and a focus on equitable partnerships. Decision-making for research priorities and implementation will be driven by LMIC-led hubs and local researchers, though some technical oversight may involve Northern partners (e.g., IDRC for Pillar 1).
q10_capacity_building_details: training and mentorship for LMIC researchers
sub-grants to Southern institutions
regional hubs led by LMIC organisations to strengthen networks
inception grants to build local engagement and research skills
knowledge brokering to support research uptake

partner_organizations.name: Canadian International Development Research Centre (IDRC)
partner_organizations.role: Co-funder and manager for Pillar 1 (Building Climate Resilience), responsible for regional hubs and sub-grants

partner_organizations.name: LMIC-led regional research hubs (5 planned, at least 3 confirmed)
partner_organizations.role: Lead research implementation, capacity strengthening, and knowledge brokering in their regions
partner_organizations.location: LMICs (West/Central Africa, East/Southern Africa, Asia, Latin America/Caribbean, Middle East/North Africa)

partner_organizations.name: Local research teams (sub-grantees)
partner_organizations.role: Conduct context-specific research under regional hubs or direct commissions

partner_organizations.name: Expert research management team (Pillar 2)
partner_organizations.role: Lead selection and oversight of health co-benefits studies, methodological innovation, and capacity strengthening

partner_organizations.name: Local governments and communities
partner_organizations.role: Engaged in research design and implementation to ensure buy-in and relevance

partner_organizations.name: Alliance on Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH)
partner_organizations.role: Platform for sharing findings and advocacy, co-convened by UK government

quote.text: The preferred approach identified through the appraisal process, which centres LMIC research leadership, means that under this business case we will establish a world-leading Research Centre for Climate and Health Impact and Learning, as well as up to five regional research hubs (notethat there will be at least 3) which will be led by LMIC organisations and champion climate and health research excellence and strengthen capacity through their networks... If we partner with IDRC, we will launch a joint research programme... The hubs would be led by LMIC institutions or consortia from within those regions with technical expertise in climate and health, capacity to sub-grant, and a track record of managing research programmes.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Options for the Building Climate Resilience Pillar and How was the partner selected?

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: 1) A partnership agreement with IDRC for Pillar 1 (co-funded, joint management); 2) Direct commissions or competitive grants for Pillars 2 and 3, with an expert research management team overseeing sub-awards. The structure allows for both block funding (to regional hubs) and milestone-based payments (for specific studies).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Pillar 1 operates as a decentralized network of LMIC-led regional hubs managed jointly with IDRC, while Pillars 2 and 3 use a hybrid model: an expert team commissions and oversees individual studies (Pillar 2) or country-specific implementations (Pillar 3). This balances centralized quality control with localized delivery.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: For Pillar 1, IDRC was selected via direct partnership due to aligned priorities, existing relationships (e.g., CLARE programme), and complementary funding. For Pillars 2 and 3, an expert team will use competitive processes to select studies, ensuring methodological rigor and local relevance. The rationale emphasizes leveraging IDRC’s management capacity (reducing FCDO burden) and ensuring LMIC leadership.

quote.text: Option 1.3 – Partnership with the Canadian International Development Research Centre (IDRC): We have started exploring a potential partnership with IDRC that would build off the foundations established by the successful joint Climate, Adaptation, and Resilience (CLARE) research programme... The preferred approach is Option 1.3, working in partnership with IDRC... For Pillar 2, Option 2.3 – Commission an expert research management team: Under this model, one institution or consortium would be selected at the outset for their deep expertise in climate and health research methodologies. They would lead the project selection but would then commission and manage the individual studies... The preferred approach is Option 2.3, commissioning an expert research management team.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: For Pillar 1, IDRC will manage agreements with regional hubs and support delivery, with FCDO providing oversight. Pillars 2 and 3 will use an expert research management team to oversee sub-awards, with FCDO approval for major decisions. The programme also links to ATACH (WHO-hosted) for broader coordination.

quote.text: IDRC would have responsibility for managing the agreements with the hubs and supporting them to deliver... The hubs would then run regional funding calls focused on... The [expert] team would be responsible for capability strengthening, quality assurance, and feeding in lessons and findings to wider strategic discussions... Risks will be reviewed every quarter with mitigation measures introduced as necessary.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Options appraisal and Risk sections

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between studies within pillars (e.g., shifting resources to higher-impact projects), but reallocation between the three pillars requires approval due to their distinct objectives. The regional hub model (Pillar 1) allows flexibility in responding to local priorities.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be adaptive, with quarterly risk reviews and the ability to adjust research foci based on emerging evidence or context changes (e.g., new climate disasters). However, major shifts require FCDO approval, and the Theory of Change assumes stability in multi-year commitments.

quote.text: Risks will be reviewed every quarter with mitigation measures introduced as necessary... The programme has a moderate residual risk rating... We assume that through careful selection criteria and inception grants, we will be able to select projects with strong local community and appropriate government engagement, which will make them more likely to be relevant and have impact... The programme has been designed to be scalable so it can match need and ambition.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Risk and Theory of Change sections

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IDRC/Expert Management Team → Regional Hubs/Sub-grantees → End Researchers (for Pillar 1); FCDO → Expert Team → Local Research Teams (for Pillars 2 and 3).

quote.text: IDRC would have responsibility for managing the agreements with the hubs and supporting them to deliver... The hubs would then run regional funding calls... [For Pillar 2,] the expert team would commission and manage the individual studies... This approach would require compromise [but] would allow overheads to be minimised.

alternatives: Directly commission a portfolio of studies (Option 1.1)
Commission one research team to conduct all studies (Option 2.2)
Commission an expert research management team (Option 2.3, selected)
Not explicitly detailed, but implies localized implementation with global sharing

q24_alternatives_considered.overall: Considered using the Research Commissioning Centre (RCC) but rejected due to desire for closer relationships with delivery partners and niche skills.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The partnership with IDRC (Pillar 1) was chosen for its value for money (leveraging CAD 10M co-funding), reduced management burden on FCDO, global reach, and alignment with LMIC leadership goals. The expert management team (Pillar 2) was selected to balance methodological rigor with local engagement, while minimizing FCDO overheads. Both approaches prioritize LMIC capacity strengthening and adaptive learning, addressing the urgent need for evidence while mitigating risks through established partners.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (IDRC’s experience with CLARE programme)
speed (rapid evidence generation for climate emergency)
equity (LMIC research leadership and local engagement)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Partnership risks with IDRC (e.g., shifting government priorities over the funding period).
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong historical alignment with IDRC and shared commitment to climate-health research; robust procedures for oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Decentralized hub model (Pillar 1) may lead to variability in research quality or oversight.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IDRC’s established quality control mechanisms and support to hubs; inception grants to ensure local engagement.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Expert team (Pillar 2) adds overhead costs, reducing direct funding for studies.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Offset by gains in methodological leadership, quality assurance, and capacity strengthening.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited FCDO internal capacity to manage multiple small contracts if direct commissioning were used.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Avoided by selecting partnership and expert team models to reduce management burden.

vfm_criteria_used: equity (prioritizing LMIC leadership and local relevance)

quote.text: Option 1.3 [IDRC partnership] would provide excellent value for money; in addition to leveraging additional funding, IDRC would manage the grants and most of the programme management, which would both reduce overheads for FCDO and require relatively light FCDO resourcing... This approach would allow the pillar to have a global reach... Both FCDO and IDRC are committed to empowering LMIC researchers... Option 2.3 [expert team] would be relatively light management for FCDO... It would mean that experts would be engaged in the identification and selection of the projects... It would build in clear mandates for quality assurance (to ensure rigour), methodological leadership, and strengthening capability.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The multi-country/LMIC focus and moderate risk profile constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) Experience operating in LMICs and fragile contexts; 2) Capacity to manage decentralized hubs (for Pillar 1); 3) Ability to engage local communities and governments effectively. The need for climate-health expertise further limits the pool to institutions with technical skills in both domains, favoring established Northern-Southern partnerships (e.g., IDRC’s CLARE network).
q27_constraints_detail: Limited LMIC research capacity in climate-health nexus
Need for partners with experience in fragile contexts (moderate risk rating)
Requirement for regional coverage (multi-country scope)
Local government buy-in as a prerequisite for impact
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (evidence generation + capacity building + policy influence) drive its hybrid delivery structure: 1) **Pillar 1’s** focus on scalable, locally relevant evidence necessitates decentralized hubs led by LMIC institutions; 2) **Pillar 2’s** need for methodological rigor and comparability across studies requires centralized oversight by an expert team; 3) **Pillar 3’s** disaster-learning goal demands flexible, context-specific implementations with global knowledge-sharing mechanisms. The urgency of the climate crisis further justifies adaptive management and rapid evidence translation.

q28_linkages.objective: Generating actionable evidence for climate-resilient PHC
q28_linkages.mechanism_link: → Decentralized regional hubs (Pillar 1) to ensure local relevance and scalability; expert team (Pillar 2) to standardize methods across contexts.
→ LMIC-led hubs with sub-granting authority; inception grants for local engagement; embedded capacity-building in all pillars.

q28_linkages.objective: Policy influence and climate finance leverage
q28_linkages.mechanism_link: → Partnership with IDRC (credibility) and ATACH (advocacy platform); focus on mature, scalable interventions (Pillar 2).
→ Country-specific implementations (Pillar 3) with global knowledge-sharing to balance context specificity and wider applicability.

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly grapples with tensions between: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: The urgency of the climate crisis demands rapid evidence generation, but the programme prioritizes LMIC leadership and local engagement (e.g., inception grants), which may slow initial delivery; 2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: While IDRC (a Northern institution) manages Pillar 1, the hubs and sub-grants are LMIC-led, and capacity strengthening is a core objective; 3) **Global reach vs. depth**: The regional hub model (Pillar 1) balances breadth (covering multiple climates/contexts) with depth (strong local engagement in selected countries).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Urgent need for climate-health evidence conflicts with time required for equitable partnerships and local engagement (mitigated via inception grants and regional hubs).
Northern partners (IDRC, expert team) provide methodological rigor and management capacity, while LMIC institutions lead implementation and decision-making (e.g., hubs sub-granting to local teams).
Pillar 2’s expert team ensures methodological consistency across studies, while Pillar 1’s hubs adapt research to regional contexts.
Expert team (Pillar 2) adds overhead but enables higher-quality evaluations; regional hubs (Pillar 1) reduce per-country costs while expanding geographic coverage.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s **moderate risk rating** drives a **milestone-based oversight** approach with quarterly risk reviews. Decentralized delivery (e.g., LMIC-led hubs) is paired with robust quality control (via IDRC and expert teams) to mitigate risks of variable research standards. In fragile contexts, additional safeguards (e.g., inception grants for government/community buy-in) are embedded to ensure relevance and uptake.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives directly shape partner roles: 1) **Regional hubs** (Pillar 1) are designed as both implementers and capacity-strengtheners, with mandates to sub-grant and mentor local teams; 2) **Expert team** (Pillar 2) includes capability strengthening as a core function, ensuring evaluations build LMIC skills; 3) **Local researchers** are positioned as co-leads in study design/implementation, not just data collectors. The programme’s Theory of Change assumes that strengthening Southern capacity will improve evidence quality and policy impact.

quote.text: Strengthening and championing LMIC research leadership – in order to develop a thriving research community, and ensure that research is locally-relevant, the focus must be on strengthening the capacity of LMIC researchers to conduct climate and health research in their own countries... Building capacity and partnerships to research solutions for climate and health will create a strong base of researchers globally who can bid for future research funding in this space... The focus should be on generating actionable evidence that can catalyse access to other investment... Strong local community engagement – additionally, in order to identify appropriate and locally-relevant solutions, it is not sufficient to work with local researchers but there must also be active engagement with the local communities from the outset.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Theory of Change and Options appraisal

key_programme_risks: Limited evidence base for climate-resilient primary healthcare in LMICs
Weak health system preparedness for climate impacts
Risk of climate-related disasters disrupting research delivery
Potential misalignment between global climate policies and local health priorities
Capacity constraints in LMIC researchers to lead complex studies
Political or institutional barriers to policy uptake (e.g., climate denial in some governments)
Overlap or duplication with other climate-health funders (e.g., Wellcome Trust)
Carbon footprint of research activities undermining programme goals
Shifting government priorities (UK or partner countries) during implementation
Economic pressures reducing LMIC investments in health/climate adaptation

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited evidence base for climate-resilient PHC
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Focus on generating actionable evidence through targeted pillars; leverage existing FCDO programmes (e.g., climate-resilient health systems policy programme) for synergies.
Design interventions to align with ongoing health system reforms; use inception grants to ensure local buy-in and relevance.
Build flexibility into research designs (e.g., adaptive management); include disaster learning as a core pillar (Pillar 3).
Strong local community and government engagement from outset; regional hubs to tailor research to context.
Embed capacity strengthening in all pillars (e.g., regional hubs, expert team mentorship); use inception grants to build skills.
Select countries with demonstrated demand (e.g., Pakistan, Nigeria); work through multilateral platforms (e.g., ATACH) for advocacy.
Coordinate with Wellcome Trust and others to fill gaps; join UK Funders Group for Climate and Health.
Require partners to minimize travel emissions; ensure programme is 100% ICF-eligible.
Leverage IDRC’s stable funding and management; diversify country portfolio to reduce dependency on any single partner.
Generate evidence to support climate finance applications; highlight co-benefits (e.g., health gains from climate investments).

fcas_specific_lessons: In conflict-affected or high-risk settings (e.g., Somalia, Chad, Syria), avoid direct government engagement if climate denial or instability is present; use multilateral platforms or civil society partners instead.
Prioritize resilient supply chains and decentralized service delivery in fragile contexts, as climate shocks may exacerbate existing vulnerabilities.
Ensure research designs in FCAS include rapid learning mechanisms to adapt to changing security or access constraints.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on lessons from the **CLARE programme** (IDRC-FCDO partnership), which demonstrated the effectiveness of: 1) Regional hubs for balancing global reach with local relevance; 2) Co-funding to reduce management burdens; 3) Strong quality control mechanisms for decentralized research. The **Lancet Pathfinder Commission** also informed the focus on health co-benefits of climate interventions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: 1) **Decentralized hub model** (Pillar 1) adopted from CLARE to ensure LMIC leadership while maintaining oversight; 2) **Expert team for Pillar 2** added to address methodological gaps identified in earlier climate-health evaluations; 3) **Disaster learning pillar (Pillar 3)** included to fill a gap in post-event evidence generation, informed by gaps in post-disaster health system responses.

quote.text: We have a strong relationship with [IDRC], and both are, and historically have been, well aligned on our approaches and priorities... The decentralised regional hub model also comes with some risks around oversight and research quality, but IDRC has robust procedures for managing these... Risks will be reviewed every quarter with mitigation measures introduced as necessary... The programme has been designed to be scalable so it can match need and ambition... We assume that through careful selection criteria and inception grants, we will be able to select projects with strong local community and appropriate government engagement, which will make them more likely to be relevant and have impact.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Options appraisal and Risk sections

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The partnership with IDRC leverages approximately CAD 10 million (~£6M), bringing the total for Pillar 1 to ~£16M (from FCDO’s £10M). This reduces FCDO’s management burden and expands geographic reach.

quote.text: If we partner with IDRC, we will launch a joint research programme, leveraging approximately CAD 10 million in additional funding from IDRC (bringing the total budget to approx. £16 million)... Programme Value: Up to £20 million.
quote.source: D0007318.odt, Programme summary and Options appraisal

metadata.programme_name: Development & Open Societies – Support to Bond and the UK Alliance

quote.text: The programme will ensure that Bond can act as a catalyst for the UK’s INGO sector to meet challenges and seize opportunities in delivering the SDGs.

metadata.duration_source: The programme will run from 1st April 2024 to 31 March 2027 with a budget of £3.6 million.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme primarily focuses on **capacity building** (strengthening the UK INGO sector) and **policy influence** (supporting advocacy and sector transformation), with elements of **financing mechanism** (channeling funds to Bond and UK Alliance). It aims to enhance the sector's ability to deliver SDGs through networking, data-driven approaches, safeguarding, and geographic transformation.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme will ensure that Bond can act as a catalyst for the UK’s INGO sector to meet challenges and seize opportunities in delivering the SDGs. It will fund Bond’s core offer, enabling it to invest in its unique networking function, while also supporting specific projects on data, safeguarding, technological and geographic transformation, and supporting regional UK networks through the UK Alliance.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Convening the sector on policy and advocacy in the UK and at key international moments
Building a coherent, dynamic, and more data-driven sector, agile and equipped for the future
Sustaining dynamic working groups that support policy development, operational excellence, and cross-sector learning in UK INGOs
Improving the sector’s safeguarding response

q3_expected_outputs.output: Supporting sector transformation (e.g., becoming actively locally-led and anti-racist)
Support to the UK Alliance (CADA, HCA, SIDA, SIDCN, SWIDN)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Reserved funds for emerging issues (e.g., safeguarding crises, Afghanistan, Gaza responses)

where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Minor.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an **accountable grant** to Bond, which includes both **flexible core funding** (for networking and adaptive activities) and **ring-fenced project funding** (for specific initiatives like data, safeguarding, and sector transformation). FCDO retains oversight through quarterly reviews, financial reporting, and a break clause. The Civil Society and Civic Space Department (CSCSD) in FCDO manages the programme with support from an embedded advisor (0.5 FTE).
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Bond is the **only recognized UK-wide network** for international development CSOs, with a 30-year track record of convening the sector. The business case argues that no alternative supplier could deliver the same scope efficiently, given Bond’s unique role and existing relationships with FCDO.

quote.text: Bond is the only general, UK-wide network organisation for international development CSOs and, as such, there is not a viable alternative supplier capable of delivering the work defined in the appraisal case. [...] Given the specific context for the relationship between the FCDO and domestic networks, a bespoke approach is needed.
quote.source: D0006039.odt, Value for Money and Why deliver through Bond and UK Alliance networks?

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: Bond allocates funds to UK Alliance members based on approved proposals, with FCDO oversight through quarterly reviews and financial reporting. Sub-grantees must align with milestones for payments.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: No formal steering committee or board is mentioned. Oversight is managed by FCDO’s Civil Society and Civic Space Department (CSCSD) through quarterly reviews, financial reports, and a break clause assessment in 2025. Bond attends quarterly reviews, and UK Alliance partners may also participate.

quote.text: Oversight of the programme will be managed and controlled by CSCSD. [...] Bond will attend quarterly review meetings with FCDO and there will also be the opportunity for UK Alliance partners to attend. [...] The programme will include an official break clause in September 2025 to allow CSCSD the opportunity to review and assess performance and relevance of programme.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core funding (36% of budget) is flexible for Bond’s adaptive activities, while project-specific funds (e.g., data, safeguarding) are ring-fenced. A reserved pot (£368,000) allows reallocation for emerging issues (e.g., crises like Afghanistan/Gaza) with FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a **break clause in September 2025** for FCDO to assess performance and adjust priorities. Bond’s core funding allows responsiveness to sector needs, while project funds require FCDO alignment. The reserved £368,000 enables rapid response to unforeseen challenges.

quote.text: We will reserve £368,000 within the programme in order to allow Bond and the FCDO to respond to emerging issues within the sector. [...] The programme will include an official break clause in September 2025 to allow CSCSD the opportunity to review and assess performance and relevance of programme.
quote.source: D0006039.odt, What will the programme do? and Governance

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Bond (fund manager) → UK Alliance networks (sub-grantees). No further layers to end beneficiaries (UK INGOs).
how_efficiency.q23_payment_details: Payments are made in advance up to three months (but not in advance of need), tied to a results framework and quarterly forecasts. PrOF Rule 25 requires justification for advance payments.

quote.text: Payment will be in advance up to three months (but not in advance of need). In accordance with PrOF Rule 25, this will require a written justification and VfM explanation to be accepted and form part of the arrangement.

q24_alternatives_considered: Procuring advisory roles externally (through consultants) – rejected as lower value for money
Rolling Bond funding into a new central civil society funding vehicle – rejected due to timing and bespoke needs for domestic networks
Seeking alternative providers to replicate Bond’s convening role – rejected as prohibitively expensive and inefficient
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Bond was chosen due to its **unique position as the sole UK-wide INGO network**, with 30 years of trust and relationships in the sector. The **direct award** modality was justified by: (1) **value for money** (Bond’s existing infrastructure reduces costs), (2) **risk mitigation** (proven track record with FCDO), (3) **speed** (avoiding delays from competitive processes), and (4) **equity** (ensuring small and regional INGOs are included). The mixed funding (core + project) balances flexibility with accountability.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (Bond’s convening power and sector trust)
speed (urgent need to respond to sector challenges)
equity (inclusion of small and regional INGOs)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud or misuse of funds (Low likelihood, High impact)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Bond required to submit detailed forecasts, rigorous fund breakdowns, and notify FCDO of fraudulent activity. Due Diligence Assessment (DDA) conducted prior to funding.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Inability of Bond to adapt to changing contexts (Low likelihood, Medium impact)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular engagement with FCDO departments and quarterly reviews to assess deliverables. Unrestricted core funding enables pivoting to emerging priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Failure to maximize income from other streams (Medium likelihood, High impact)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Quarterly meetings to monitor income streams and agile approach to unrestricted income generation (e.g., online events).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding incidents (Low likelihood, High impact)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Compliance with FCDO safeguarding rules, incident reporting measures, and proactive monitoring through the central FCDO Safeguarding Unit.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (proven impact on sector capacity and safeguarding)
equity (inclusion of small, regional, and diverse INGOs)

quote.text: Network and membership organisations are crucial in ensuring – and are also bellwethers for – the health of complex and diverse sectors. [...] Bond is the only general, UK-wide network organisation for international development CSOs and, as such, there is not a viable alternative supplier capable of delivering the work defined in the appraisal case. [...] The approach of Bond and the UK Alliance will achieve outputs efficiently by enabling them to strengthen their existing working models which are already delivering.
quote.source: D0006039.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending and Value for Money

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **UK domestic context** constrains partner selection to organizations with established credibility and reach across the UK’s devolved nations. Bond’s unique role as the **only UK-wide INGO network** and its regional alliances (UK Alliance) are explicitly cited as non-replicable by other partners, limiting alternatives.
q27_constraints_detail: Regulatory environment (FCDO funding rules favor established UK-based partners)
Geographic reach (need for coverage across UK nations and regions)
Sector trust (Bond’s 30-year history as a convenor is irreplaceable)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for sector-wide convening and rapid adaptation** (e.g., responding to safeguarding crises or public sentiment shifts) determines the **fund manager model**, where Bond’s core funding enables flexibility. The **mixed funding structure** (core + projects) reflects the dual objectives of **long-term capacity building** (core) and **targeted transformations** (projects like data and anti-racism).
q28_linkages: Sector convening (WHAT) → Fund manager model (HOW) to leverage Bond’s networks
Adaptive needs (WHAT) → Flexible core funding + reserved pot (HOW)
Regional inclusion (WHAT) → UK Alliance sub-grants (HOW)
Safeguarding improvements (WHAT) → Ring-fenced project funds + FCDO oversight (HOW)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **equity** (inclusion of small/micro INGOs via UK Alliance) with **efficiency** (centralized fund management through Bond). Trade-offs include:

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Direct award to Bond enables rapid response but limits competition (potentially excluding innovative newcomers).
UK-led networks (Bond/UK Alliance) drive sector transformation, but Southern partners’ influence is indirect (e.g., through locally-led guides rather than governance).
Funding regional networks (UK Alliance) increases costs but ensures equity for smaller INGOs outside London.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **low-risk profile** (Minor rating) enables **light-touch oversight** (quarterly reviews) rather than intensive management. However, reputational risks (e.g., safeguarding, fraud) trigger **specific controls** (e.g., DDA, PrOF compliance).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Bond’s **capacity as a convenor** shapes its role as fund manager, while UK Alliance members’ **regional expertise** determines their implementation focus (e.g., SWIDN for South-West England). Southern partners’ capacity is addressed through **sector transformation projects** (e.g., anti-racism tools) but not governance roles.

quote.text: Bond and the UK Alliance, as the principal networks for INGOs across the UK, are the only organisations that can credibly represent the whole INGO UK sector, bringing together the knowledge and on-the-ground experience of their members. [...] The ability of Bond and the UK Alliance to convene and unite the sector allows them to achieve greater impact on collaborative advocacy, shared learning, collective strategising and problem solving. [...] Without infrastructure bodies the sector would lack direction and support.
quote.source: D0006039.odt, Why deliver through Bond and UK Alliance networks?

key_programme_risks: Damaging safeguarding incidents (Low likelihood, High impact)
Fraud or misuse of funds (Low likelihood, High impact)
Inability of Bond to adapt to changing contexts (Low likelihood, Medium impact)
Failure to maximize income from other streams (Medium likelihood, High impact)
Reduction in sector trust or public support for aid (linked to media landscape)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proactive monitoring, compliance with FCDO safeguarding rules, and incident reporting mechanisms. Bond’s existing safeguarding working groups and FCDO Safeguarding Unit oversight.
Detailed financial forecasts, Due Diligence Assessment (DDA), and PrOF compliance. Bond must notify FCDO of any fraudulent activity.
Quarterly reviews, unrestricted core funding for flexibility, and FCDO engagement to assess emerging priorities.
Agile income generation (e.g., online events), monitoring through quarterly meetings, and diversified revenue (membership fees, other donors).

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **UK Aid Connect (2017–2024)** informed this design, including:

lessons_details.lesson: Importance of **flexible core funding** to enable adaptive responses (e.g., safeguarding crises).
lessons_details.application: 36% of budget allocated to core activities with unrestricted use.

lessons_details.lesson: Need for **robust financial controls** after past incidents.
lessons_details.application: DDA, PrOF compliance, and quarterly forecasting introduced.

lessons_details.lesson: **Sector convening power** of Bond during crises (e.g., Covid-19, Afghanistan).
lessons_details.application: Reserved £368,000 pot for emerging issues and break clause for reassessment.

lessons_details.lesson: Value of **regional networks** (UK Alliance) for equity.
lessons_details.application: 20% of budget ring-fenced for UK Alliance members.

risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme **retains Bond’s core funding flexibility** (unlike UK Aid Connect’s project-focused approach) and **adds explicit safeguarding and anti-racism components** based on past sector challenges. The **break clause (2025)** and **reserved funds** were introduced to address lessons on adaptive management.

quote.text: The new Bond arrangement is being designed to deliver both defined core activities using flexible funding and also specific, ring-fenced projects on data, safeguarding, technological and geographic transformation [...] We will retain the flexibility to decide whether Bond funding should be rolled into any future programming at the break clause point, depending on the extent to which new programming can meet these specific needs. [...] Bond was also recognised for its significant contribution to safeguarding in the International Development Committee’s 2019 report ‘Sexual Exploitation in the Sector.’
quote.source: D0006039.odt, What will the programme do? and lessons from UK Aid Connect

co_funding_partners.partner: Bond’s other revenue streams (membership subscriptions, Gates Foundation, etc.)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Bond’s total revenue for FY24/25 is ~£9 million (FCDO contribution is ~30%), indicating leverage of additional funds from membership fees, Gates Foundation, and other donors.

quote.text: The FCDO contribution runs in parallel with Bond’s other revenue streams from other donors as well as membership subscriptions and income-generating activities. These are a mixture of restricted and unrestricted funds which includes contribution from the Gates Foundation and other contributions on the restricted side and then membership funds and other contributions which fall just under £3m for FY24/25, leaving FCDO contribution approximately 30% of total revenue.

metadata.programme_name: Twiyubakire Governance Programme

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Programme summary
quote.text: "Twiyubakire will support more efficient, effective and accountable policy responses and service delivery in Rwanda."

metadata.duration_source: "upto £35m over 5 years" (D0006283.odt, Programme Value section) and "AMP Start Date: 21/11/2024; AMP End Date: 21/11/2029" (D0006283.odt, Dates section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: Twiyubakire combines financial aid to strengthen government systems (capacity building), technical assistance for policy implementation (policy influence), and civil society grants for accountability (implementation research). The programme aims to improve local governance, decentralisation, and citizen participation through a multi-component approach.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Twiyubakire will support more efficient, effective and accountable policy responses and service delivery in Rwanda. Through non-budget support financial aid to Ministry of Economic Planning and Finance (MINECOFFIN), and the Ministry of Local Government (MINALOC), we will strengthen local government systems and build local government capacity, supporting Rwanda’s vision for decentralisation." (D0006283.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Local Government policies and systems strengthened (e.g., decentralisation policies, M&E, planning, tax systems)
Human Resource and institutional capacity in decentralised entities strengthened (e.g., district spending decisions, procurement, citizen participation)
Capacity of CSOs, citizens, and non-state actors strengthened (4-6 medium-sized CSOs; engagement in budget cycles and accountability)
q3_expected_outputs.target: 4-6 CSOs

q3_expected_outputs.output: Policy making, implementation, and coordination in GoR institutions strengthened (technical assistance, evidence generation, political economy analysis)
Accelerated and more inclusive socio-economic development at district level (overall impact)
More efficient, effective, and accountable policy responses and service delivery at local level (overall outcome)

what_objectives.summary: Twiyubakire is a £35m governance programme (2024-2029) designed to strengthen Rwanda’s decentralisation, local government capacity, and citizen accountability through financial aid, technical assistance, and CSO grants. It builds on 20 years of UK governance support in Rwanda, aiming to deliver cross-sectoral impacts in education, climate, and economic growth.

quote.name: D0006283.odt, What will Twiyubakire deliver?
quote.text: "Twiyubakire will deliver a multi-component programme that combines financial aid, technical assistance, and civil society support... The programme will contribute towards the following impact: accelerated and more inclusive socio-economic development at the district level."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Rwanda is classified as 'moderate risk' in the document, with a stable governance system post-1994 but facing complex challenges in decentralisation, local capacity gaps, and political economy dynamics. The programme acknowledges risks related to policy implementation and sustainability.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006283.odt, Programme Value section)
q6_contextual_constraints: data limitations (M&E weaknesses, lack of integrated systems)
infrastructure (limited IT tools for local governance)
climate risks (environmental degradation from poorly monitored projects)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Constraints affect service delivery quality, citizen engagement effectiveness, and local government accountability. For example, weak M&E systems led to environmental degradation in resettlement projects (Auditor General Report, 2024), and low salaries cause high staff turnover at local levels (68% of positions filled in some districts).

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Background and challenge
quote.text: "The nature of Rwanda’s challenges is becoming more complex, and reform has slowed down recently, particularly at local level... Limited government capacity at the local level, including cell, sector, and district levels... These capacity challenges risk undermining the quality of local systems to deliver services to citizens."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains strategic control and approval authority (e.g., annual Partnership Principles assessments, issue selection criteria), while Rwandan government (MINECOFFIN, MINALOC) and local CSOs implement components. Decision-making is shared but ultimately overseen by FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to government (M&E, planning, procurement)
embedded programme-funded advisors in MINECOFFIN/MINALOC
CSO grants for institutional strengthening (4-6 medium-sized CSOs)
training for local leaders in participatory planning
evidence-based advocacy support for non-state actors
HR management reforms at local level

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Economic Planning and Finance (MINECOFFIN), Rwanda
partner_organizations.role: Primary recipient of financial aid; implementation of decentralisation policies and PFM reforms

partner_organizations.name: Ministry of Local Government (MINALOC), Rwanda
partner_organizations.role: Strengthening local government capacity and citizen participation systems

partner_organizations.name: Commercial Provider (TAF manager)
partner_organizations.role: Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) management, including short-term/embedded TA and policy research

partner_organizations.name: NGO (CSO grants manager)
partner_organizations.role: Management of civil society sub-grants for accountability and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: 4-6 medium-sized Rwandan CSOs
partner_organizations.role: Local governance transparency, evidence-based advocacy, and citizen engagement

partner_organizations.name: National Women Council, National Youth Council, National Council of Persons with Disabilities
partner_organizations.role: Citizen participation platforms (existing structures for engagement)

partner_organizations.name: Private sector actors
partner_organizations.role: Policy dialogue partner (e.g., joint advocacy on economic issues like property tax)

quote.name: D0006283.odt, How we will deliver Twiyubakire
quote.text: "Twiyubakire will use a range of delivery mechanisms to maximise entry points across issues... support will include technical assistance (short-term and embedded) in policy development, policy implementation, and coordination; evidence generation to support policy advocacy work with GoR; dissemination of existing research findings to government decision makers."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **non-budget support financial aid** to MINECOFFIN/MINALOC (for structural reforms), **grants to CSOs** (for accountability), and **technical assistance contracts** (for policy implementation support). Financial aid is tied to Rwanda’s Sector Strategic Plans (SSPs) and subject to annual Partnership Principles compliance reviews.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO oversees the programme with two parallel delivery mechanisms: (1) a **commercial provider** managing the Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) and (2) an **NGO** managing CSO sub-grants. This dual structure aims to balance flexibility (commercial provider) with local ownership (NGO/CSOs). A Programme Funded Advisor is embedded in MINECOFIN/MINALOC for cross-ministry coordination.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The business case appraised two options (Option 1: single commercial provider for both TAF and CSO grants; Option 2: split between commercial provider for TAF and NGO for CSO grants). Option 2 was preferred for its "increased likelihood of sustaining results beyond the programme" due to NGO’s local relationships and lower profit motives. No open competition details are provided, suggesting a restricted process based on prior experience in Rwanda.

quote.name: D0006283.odt, How we will deliver Twiyubakire & Option 2 analysis
quote.text: "Option 2: Twiyubakire is delivered through financial aid, a non-governmental organisation (NGO) delivers the civil society grants, and a commercial provider manages the TAF (preferred)... This dual approach retains the benefits of the commercial provider (flexibility, adaptability) while mitigating the risks of local knowledge and intervention sustainability."

quote.name: D0006283.odt, How we will deliver Twiyubakire
quote.text: "Embedding monitoring and evaluation as a core part of the programme (as opposed to a separate function) will continuously generate learning and evidence that directly informs outputs... Ongoing engagement with key stakeholders including the government and civil society will ensure the programme remains aligned with the most relevant and impactful priorities."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between components based on political economy analysis and emerging priorities, but require alignment with GoR’s Sector Strategic Plans (SSPs) and FCDO approval. The adaptive programming approach allows for "real-time data and evidence to support informed decision making and timely adjustments."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme integrates adaptive management through: (1) ongoing political economy analysis to inform entry points; (2) real-time MEL data to adjust interventions; (3) issue-based approach (rather than pre-set themes) to align with GoR priorities; and (4) annual Partnership Principles assessments to ensure compliance. Specific issues (e.g., school feeding, climate resilience) will be selected during mobilisation based on feasibility and demand.

quote.name: D0006283.odt, How we will deliver Twiyubakire
quote.text: "Adaptive programming will enhance programme outcomes... Embedding monitoring and evaluation as a core part of the programme... will continuously generate learning and evidence that directly informs outputs... Given Rwanda’s commitment to evidence-based policy development, this adaptive approach will strengthen Twiyubakire’s ability to engage effectively on key issues."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → (1) Commercial Provider (TAF) / NGO (CSO grants) → (2) Rwandan CSOs/local government entities → (3) Citizens/end beneficiaries

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Option 2 analysis
quote.text: "This approach will require additional management and coordination from FCDO to ensure complementarity across outputs. However, a competent NGO and commercial provider would reduce the overall programme management needed, allowing the team to focus on other strategic aspects."

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Single commercial provider delivers both Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) and CSO grants
Option 2 (preferred): Commercial provider for TAF + NGO for CSO grants
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 2 was selected for its **higher sustainability** (NGOs’ long-term presence in Rwanda), **local ownership** (NGOs’ trusted relationships with CSOs/government), and **cost-effectiveness** (mitigating commercial providers’ profit margins). It balances the commercial provider’s flexibility with NGO’s contextual expertise, addressing risks of limited local knowledge in Option 1.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (cost-effectiveness of dual approach)
partner capacity (NGOs’ existing networks vs commercial providers’ adaptability)
flexibility (commercial providers’ responsiveness to policy shifts)
local ownership (NGOs’ ability to engage CSOs meaningfully)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited coherence between TAF (commercial provider) and CSO grants (NGO) due to separate management
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO coordination role to ensure complementarity; aligning TA thematic windows with CSO grant focus areas

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Performance management challenges with NGO (accountable grants have fewer levers than commercial contracts)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear results framework linked to GoR’s SSPs; annual Partnership Principles assessments

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Commercial provider’s lack of local governance context (e.g., PFM systems, CSO dynamics)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded Programme Funded Advisor in MINECOFIN/MINALOC; NGO’s local knowledge to inform TA design

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sustainability of interventions post-programme (commercial provider’s profit focus)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: NGO’s long-term presence in Rwanda; capacity building for local CSOs/government

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (balancing commercial provider costs with NGO’s local expertise)
sustainability (NGO’s ability to sustain results beyond programme)

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Analysis of Option 2
quote.text: "This dual approach retains the benefits of the commercial provider (flexibility, adaptability) while mitigating the risks of local knowledge and intervention sustainability. As NGOs and CSOs have been operating in Rwanda for a long time, they have developed key relationships with GoR and have important local knowledge to enhance delivery... There is an increased likelihood of sustaining results beyond the lifetime of the programme."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Rwanda’s **centralised governance history** and **limited local capacity** constrain partner selection to organisations with: (1) deep contextual knowledge (e.g., NGOs with existing CSO networks); (2) ability to navigate political economy (e.g., commercial providers with adaptive programming experience); and (3) willingness to work within GoR’s decentralisation framework. The **high turnover of local officials** (due to low salaries) and **weak M&E systems** necessitate partners who can provide embedded support (e.g., Programme Funded Advisors).
q27_constraints_detail: Centralised governance legacy limits decentralisation progress, requiring partners who can bridge national-local gaps
Local skill gaps (e.g., procurement, M&E) demand capacity-building-focused partners
Political economy dynamics (e.g., national priorities overriding local needs) require partners skilled in constructive dialogue
High staff turnover at local level necessitates partners with HR reform experience
Weak feedback loops between citizens and government need partners who can strengthen accountability mechanisms
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **multi-component objectives** (policy strengthening + capacity building + accountability) determine the **mixed delivery structure**: (1) **Financial aid** for structural reforms (aligned with GoR’s SSPs); (2) **Technical Assistance** for implementation support (flexible, adaptive); and (3) **CSO grants** for bottom-up accountability (locally led). The **issue-based approach** (rather than pre-set themes) shapes the open partnership model, allowing responsiveness to GoR priorities.
q28_linkages: Decentralisation policy implementation (Output 1) → requires embedded TA (commercial provider) + local government capacity building (Output 2)
Citizen engagement (Output 3) → needs CSO grants (NGO-managed) + evidence generation (TAF-supported research)
Cross-sectoral impacts (e.g., education, climate) → demand coordination between TAF (policy) and CSO grants (advocacy)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: (1) **Speed vs inclusion**: Rapid policy implementation (e.g., decentralisation) risks excluding marginalised groups (e.g., youth, persons with disabilities) if citizen participation forums are not adapted (e.g., timing, accessibility). (2) **Northern expertise vs local ownership**: Commercial providers offer technical efficiency but may lack contextual nuance, while NGOs ensure local relevance but require more management. (3) **Cost vs reach**: Sub-grants to 4-6 CSOs balance depth of support against broader coverage.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (commercial provider’s adaptability) vs equity (NGO’s focus on marginalised groups)
Speed of reform (GoR’s decentralisation timeline) vs meaningful citizen engagement (time-consuming dialogue processes)
Technical rigor (TAF’s evidence generation) vs local applicability (CSOs’ advocacy priorities)
Cost-effectiveness (limited number of CSO grants) vs inclusive representation (need to engage diverse voices)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., policy implementation delays, local capacity gaps) drives **milestone-based oversight** with embedded MEL. High-risk areas (e.g., fiscal decentralisation, CSO sustainability) receive intensive support (e.g., Programme Funded Advisors in ministries), while lower-risk components (e.g., TA for M&E systems) allow more partner flexibility.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: (1) **Commercial provider** focuses on technical capacity (e.g., PFM systems, M&E tools) for government; (2) **NGO** strengthens CSO institutional capacity (e.g., research, advocacy skills); and (3) **Embedded advisors** (in MINECOFIN/MINALOC) bridge national-local gaps. The **‘one-size-fits-all’ district resourcing** issue is addressed by tailoring TA to local needs (e.g., procurement training where gaps are identified).

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Background and challenge & How we will deliver
quote.text: "The above issues are exacerbated by limited government capacity at the local level... Twiyubakire will use a range of delivery mechanisms to maximise entry points across issues... Embedding monitoring and evaluation as a core part of the programme will continuously generate learning and evidence that directly informs outputs."

key_programme_risks: Slow or inconsistent implementation of decentralisation policies (e.g., Fiscal and Financial Decentralisation Policy not fully operationalised)
Limited local government capacity (e.g., 68% of district positions filled; high turnover due to low salaries)
Weak citizen engagement mechanisms (e.g., rushed consultations, national priorities overriding local needs)
Sustainability of interventions post-2029 (e.g., commercial provider’s profit-driven approach)
Political economy resistance to reform (e.g., central ministries reluctant to cede control to districts)
Coherence between TAF and CSO grants (risk of siloed delivery in Option 2 structure)
Fraud/corruption in decentralised systems (e.g., school feeding procurement issues)
Climate and environmental risks (e.g., resettlement projects causing degradation due to weak M&E)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Embedded Programme Funded Advisor in MINECOFIN/MINALOC; alignment with Prime Minister’s 2024 order on sectoral decentralisation
Technical assistance for M&E/planning systems; HR management reforms; on-the-job coaching (lessons from SPARC)
