CSO grants for evidence-based advocacy; strengthening Joint Action Development Forums; inclusive participation mechanisms (e.g., timing of Inekozo abaturage)
NGO-led CSO grants (long-term local presence); capacity building for local CSOs; linking interventions to GoR’s SSPs
Political economy analysis to identify entry points; issue-based approach to align with GoR priorities
FCDO coordination role; thematic alignment of TA and grants; shared MEL framework
Strengthening e-procurement and e-payment systems (e.g., School Data Management System upgrades)
Integrating climate considerations into M&E systems; supporting districts’ resource mobilisation strategies

fcas_specific_lessons: **Adaptive programming** is critical in FCAS contexts: Twiyubakire’s design builds on SPARC’s success in adjusting to Rwanda’s evolving governance priorities (e.g., shifting from central PFM reforms to local-level focus).

**Embedded advisors** work better than external consultants: Lessons from Ikiraro Cy’iterambere (Building Bridges) showed that early relationship-building with government is essential to avoid misperceptions.

**Issue-based advocacy** trumps normative approaches: Past failures (e.g., Building Bridges) assumed donor priorities would align with GoR’s; Twiyubakire instead starts with GoR’s SSPs and selects issues collaboratively.
**Local ownership mitigates FCAS risks**: The dual NGO/commercial provider model addresses sustainability risks identified in previous programmes by leveraging local CSO networks.
**Real-time MEL is non-negotiable**: In FCAS, delays in learning can derail reforms; Twiyubakire embeds MEL as a core function (not separate) to enable rapid adjustments.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous UK programmes (e.g., SPARC, INKI) demonstrated that: (1) **Coaching and on-the-job training** effectively strengthen local capacity (e.g., districts achieving clean audits); (2) **Policy uptake requires political traction**—evidence alone is insufficient (e.g., Imihigo evaluations led to systemic changes only when aligned with GoR’s priorities); (3) **CSO-government coalitions** can influence policy (e.g., property tax revision in 2019 due to joint CSO/private sector advocacy); and (4) **Digital tools** improve transparency and efficiency (e.g., School Data Management System became the primary source for education statistics).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Twiyubakire’s design incorporates: (1) **Adaptive issue selection** (unlike SPARC’s pre-set themes); (2) **Embedded MEL** (addressing SPARC’s separate MEL function); (3) **Dual delivery structure** (mitigating Building Bridges’ lack of local ownership); (4) **Explicit focus on marginalised groups** (learning from FCDO’s 2022 inclusion analysis); and (5) **Cross-ministry advisors** (responding to siloed implementation in past programmes).

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Why should the UK intervene? & How we will deliver
quote.text: "Programmes that have failed to do this [combine evidence with political analysis] have faced challenges in delivering their intended impact. E.g. The Ikiraro Cy’iterambere (Building Bridges) failed to build the necessary relationships early on in programme design, contributing to misperceptions about the programme’s intentions and blockages to delivery... Twiyubakire will take an issue-based approach instead, bringing together demand and supply side stakeholders on the same governance issues."

quote.name: D0006283.odt, Programme Value
quote.text: "Programme Value: upto £35m over 5 years"

metadata.programme_name: Support to TradeMark East Africa – Strategy 2 (STS2)
metadata.quote: The programme aims to increase sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa by increasing East Africa’s trade with the region and the rest of the world. (D0006850.odt, Programme Summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: July 2017", "End Date: June 2023" (D0006850.odt, Programme Summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing trade facilitation interventions), capacity building (strengthening trade institutions and private sector skills), policy influence (supporting regulatory reforms), and service delivery (improving trade infrastructure). It aims to reduce trade barriers while building export capacity and inclusive trade systems.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will (i) invest in improving the efficiency and capacity of transport, logistics and trade infrastructure at key port and border points; (ii) invest in systems to improve trading standards, reduce non-tariff barriers and enhance transparency in trade processes; (iii) improve the regulatory and policy environment for trade; and (iv) support private sector advocacy for trade competitiveness, the export capacity of East African businesses and the greater participation of women and small and growing businesses in trade." (D0006850.odt, Programme Summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 0.6% additional GDP growth in East Africa
1.8 million fewer people living below $2/day poverty line
$1.1 billion additional government revenue (excluding grants)
$600 million net added total trade volume
1.1% increase in trade growth rate above trend
$200 million net added exports from EAC to rest of world
1.9% increase in export growth rate
$100 million net added intra-EAC exports
1.3% increase in intra-EAC export growth
Reduction in time to move/clear goods through Mombasa Port from 11 days (2011) to 3.8 days (2017)
50% reduction in cost of clearing containers destined for Uganda
32% reduction in cost of clearing containers destined for Rwanda
80% reduction in crossing times at Busia border post
74% reduction in average testing time for 80 most traded goods
59% reduction in testing costs for harmonized standards
Increase in trade of harmonized goods from $0.86bn (2010) to over $2bn (2014)
Development of 7 logistics hubs (Kigali, Busia, Jinja, Gulu, Kampala, SAGCOT, Mombasa)
250 women traders able to trade within AfCFTA
100 women-owned businesses certified along specific value chains
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to reduce trade barriers and enhance private sector markets through infrastructure improvements, regulatory reforms, and targeted support to women and SMEs, with measurable economic growth and poverty reduction targets.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme will deliver the following results. At an impact level: Increased sustainable and shared prosperity in East Africa, by contributing to an additional 0.6% growth in East African gross domestic product (GDP) above trend; by helping to reduce the number of people living below the poverty line ($2/day) by 1.8 million; and by helping increase government revenue excluding grants by an additional $1.1 billion." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with political economy challenges and infrastructure constraints, but has strong alignment with regional integration priorities and established partnerships. The overall risk is assessed as moderate and fitting DFID's risk appetite.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006850.odt, Programme Summary) and "The largest risks will be those associated with procurement and with the political economy, and are well managed." (D0006850.odt, Programme Summary)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy (alignment challenges across EAC states)
weak institutions (capacity gaps in customs/standards bureaus)
conflict (South Sudan instability affecting trade corridors)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Poor infrastructure at Mombasa Port adds up to 40% to trade costs and causes delays (11 days in 2011 reduced to 5 days by 2017). Non-tariff barriers and regulatory misalignment reduce intra-EAC trade potential. Political economy factors require adaptive approaches to reforms, particularly in Tanzania and South Sudan.
where_context.quote: "Trade remains constrained by a wide range of barriers... poor infrastructure... tariffs (which have not fallen uniformly across the East African Community) and non-tariff barriers... regulatory barriers to trade, especially for staples, along the whole supply chain need to be removed to advance food security and growth." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) and "The poor performance of logistics means that EAC states remain largely excluded from global value chains." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is governed by a TMEA Council comprising all donors (including DFID/FCDO), with the Head of DFID Kenya chairing as SRO. Day-to-day management and implementation decisions are led by TMEA (African-led), while strategic oversight involves joint donor-TMEA structures.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to customs/standards bureaus
training for SMEs on standards compliance
gender audits and advisory roles within TMEA
support for women cross-border traders (e.g., 250 women trained on AfCFTA)
institutional strengthening of EAC Secretariat and national trade agencies
development of logistics hubs with private sector participation

partner_organizations.name: TradeMark East Africa (TMEA)/TradeMark Africa (TMA)
partner_organizations.role: primary implementer (technical assistance, infrastructure investments, policy dialogue)

partner_organizations.name: East African Community (EAC) Secretariat
partner_organizations.role: regional policy coordination and harmonization

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Ports Authority (KPA)
partner_organizations.role: port infrastructure upgrades and efficiency improvements

partner_organizations.name: Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA)
partner_organizations.role: customs modernization and Single Window system

partner_organizations.name: Uganda Revenue Authority
partner_organizations.role: Electronic Cargo Tracking System implementation

partner_organizations.name: Government of Rwanda
partner_organizations.role: Lake Kivu port development and trade facilitation

partner_organizations.name: Government of Tanzania
partner_organizations.role: Dar es Salaam port improvements and SPS reforms

partner_organizations.name: East Africa Business Council (EABC)
partner_organizations.role: private sector advocacy and NTB monitoring

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: co-financing (e.g., $345m for Dar Port, $600m planned for transport)

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: co-financing for border posts (e.g., Moyale)

partner_organizations.name: DFID/FCDO (UK)
partner_organizations.role: major funder and strategic oversight (SRO role)

partner_organizations.name: Other donors (Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Netherlands, USA)
partner_organizations.role: co-financing through TMEA platform

who_partners.quote: "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase. Each DFID office will assign an SRO to oversee their respective country/regional support, and the Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (D0006850.odt, Quality Assurance) and "TMEA, initially set up by DFID, has attracted 7 other donors, has raised over £450 million (now the largest aid for trade facility globally) and works closely with governments, private sector and civil society in the EAC to reduce barriers to and costs of trade." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of block funding to TMEA (for regional/technical components) and direct contracts for capital investments (e.g., port infrastructure). DFID/FCDO provides core funding to TMEA as a not-for-profit company, while leveraging additional donor contributions through the TMEA platform.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: TMEA operates as a multi-donor platform with a governing Council (all donors), country-level SROs (DFID offices), and technical implementation teams. The Head of DFID Kenya chairs the TMEA Council, providing strategic oversight while TMEA manages day-to-day delivery through country offices and thematic clusters.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: N/A (TMEA was established by DFID in 2010 and expanded with other donors)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: TMEA was created by DFID as a dedicated vehicle for trade facilitation in East Africa, with a proven track record from Strategy 1 (2011-2017). The platform model allows for donor coordination, regional integration, and leveraging of additional funding (£450m+ raised from 7 other donors).
how_mechanism.quote: "DFID created TradeMark East Africa (TMEA) in 2010 to tackle these problems in East Africa. This programme is an extension of DFID’s support provided under TMEA’s Strategy 1 (2011-2017), recognising the progress it has already made and opportunities to build momentum." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) and "TMEA, initially set up by DFID, has attracted 7 other donors, has raised over £450 million (now the largest aid for trade facility globally)..." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The TMEA Council (comprising all donors, chaired by Head of DFID Kenya) provides strategic oversight. Country-level SROs (DFID offices) oversee regional/country components. Technical advisory groups support thematic areas (e.g., standards, SPS, gender).
how_governance.quote: "Programme management and advisory support will remain the same as the first phase. Each DFID office will assign an SRO to oversee their respective country/regional support, and the Head of DFID Kenya, who currently chairs the TMEA Council (comprising all TMEA donors) will remain as overall SRO for DFID’s engagement with TMEA." (D0006850.odt, Quality Assurance) and "A mid-term review... will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed and use any unspent budget beyond the spending review timeline." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with approval, particularly for emerging priorities like export capacity support. The programme uses a phased approach (e.g., logistics hubs) to apply lessons learned. Mid-term reviews are required for significant reallocations.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme has "in-built flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context," particularly for newer components like export capability support. A phased approach to logistics hubs ensures lessons are applied iteratively. The mid-term review process allows for adjustments based on evidence.
how_flexibility.quote: "There is in-built flexibility to learn and adjust to changes in context, particularly with regard to newer components on export capability support. The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (D0006850.odt, Flexibility) and "As the programme may spend beyond the current spending review period, progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review, proposed work-plans and budgets, which will form the basis for seeking HMT approval to proceed." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → TMEA (platform) → [sub-contractors/partners for specific components]. TMEA acts as both implementer and fund manager, reducing layers.
how_efficiency.quote: "Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions including technical assistance and development of regulatory/policy frameworks... and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) implies a results-based allocation, and "progression of programme delivery will be subject to acceptance of a mid-term review..." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) suggests milestone dependency.

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (counterfactual - no further DFID support)
Option 2: Focus on 1-2 of the 3 Strategy 1 areas in more depth
Option 3: Continue all Strategy 1 focus areas without expansion
Option 4: Expand TMEA’s remit beyond trade/logistics (e.g., broader business climate reforms)
Option 5 (Preferred): Continue all Strategy 1 areas AND add export capacity support
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 5 was selected because evidence shows that trade facilitation interventions are most effective when combined with supply-side support (export capacity building). The mixed approach addresses both demand (trade barriers) and supply (productive capacity) constraints, with explicit targets for women/SME inclusion. The TMEA platform model leverages existing donor coordination and regional integration structures.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (Option 5 maximizes impact per £ by combining infrastructure and capacity building)
risk-mitigation (moderate risk profile managed through phased implementation)
experience (lessons from Strategy 1 show complementary interventions enhance impact)
partner-capacity (TMEA’s established regional presence and donor trust)
flexibility (phased logistics hubs allow iterative learning)
equity (explicit focus on women and SMEs in export support)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overstretch of TMEA’s capacity if expanding beyond core trade/logistics (Option 4 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Option 5 maintains focus on "core" trade facilitation while adding targeted export capacity support, avoiding mission creep. TMEA divided work into "core" and "non-core" to manage scope.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Donor coordination challenges in multi-donor platform
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Established TMEA Council with DFID/FCDO chairing, and country-level SROs to ensure alignment. Clear division of labor with World Bank/AfDB on infrastructure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political economy barriers to regional integration (e.g., Tanzania’s resistance)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Politically aware technical assistance and phased reforms. PEA analysis informs adaptive approaches to national contexts.

vfm_criteria_used: economy (leveraging £450m+ from other donors through TMEA platform)
efficiency (phased implementation reduces waste; milestone-based payments)
effectiveness (complementary interventions shown to enhance impact)
equity (explicit gender and SME targets with 74% of cross-border traders being women)
why_rationale.quote: "Option 5 (Preferred Option): Do all of the previous focus areas from Strategy 1 and support export capacity... It is a direct response to DFID’s learning to date... that trade facilitation interventions which improve infrastructure are the most effective in increasing trade volumes and reducing trade costs... however, complementing interventions that seek to reduce the cost of trade with those that seek to improve the local export capacity significantly enhance the impact of trade facilitation programmes." (D0006850.odt, Summary of Options) and "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (D0006850.odt, Flexibility)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The East African context constrains partner selection to organizations with: (1) regional presence/legitimacy (e.g., TMEA’s EAC-wide offices), (2) ability to navigate political economy of integration (e.g., EAC Secretariat’s convening power), and (3) technical capacity for cross-border work (e.g., customs/standards bureaus in multiple countries). Conflict in South Sudan and regulatory fragmentation limit engagement with some actors.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for EAC-wide operational presence (rules out single-country implementers)
Requirements for political savvy to navigate national interests within regional integration
Capacity to work in FCAS contexts (e.g., South Sudan, DRC borders)
Ability to leverage multi-donor funding (TMEA’s £450m+ platform model)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The mixed objectives (infrastructure + policy + capacity building) require a platform structure (TMEA) that can: (1) manage capital investments (ports/borders), (2) provide technical assistance (standards/SPS), and (3) convene public-private dialogue. The need for regional coordination and donor alignment makes a single-implementer model impractical.
q28_linkages: Regional scope → Platform delivery model (TMEA’s multi-country structure)
Infrastructure + policy objectives → Mixed funding instruments (block grants for TA, contracts for capital works)
Gender/SME inclusion → Embedded capacity building (e.g., women trader programmes within logistics hubs)
Phased learning → Adaptive management structure (mid-term reviews, iterative hub development)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (e.g., leveraging TMEA’s existing platform to reduce transaction costs) with equity (e.g., targeting 74% women cross-border traders through dedicated channels at borders, storage facilities, and training). The logistics hubs design includes "afocus on the inclusion of women and small businesses" despite potential trade-offs in speed or scale.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Phased hub development slows rollout but ensures women/SME participation (e.g., Kigali hub’s focus on women-led agro-businesses).
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern technical assistance (e.g., for customs IT systems) paired with Southern-led implementation (TMEA/EAC Secretariat).
Cost vs. reach: Higher upfront costs for gender-inclusive infrastructure (e.g., sanitation at border posts) justified by poverty impact (1.8m fewer people below $2/day).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (political economy, procurement) leads to milestone-based oversight and phased implementation, particularly for capital-intensive components (ports, hubs). High-risk areas (e.g., South Sudan) receive targeted, smaller-scale interventions (e.g., Gulu hub contingent on peace).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) TMEA’s expanded gender team (adviser + screening mechanisms) ensures mainstreaming; (2) EAC Secretariat’s strengthened standards committees enable regional harmonization; (3) Private sector advocacy roles (e.g., EABC) are paired with TA to improve evidence-based engagement.
intersections.quote: "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes... Special attention will be paid to the needs and capacities of women, who are in the majority amongst informal cross-border traders." (D0006850.odt, Option 5) and "TMEA has also initiated various specific interventions that target the benefits of trade equally for both men and women... through support to informal cross-border trade (dominated by women)." (D0006850.odt, Gender Equality Act Compliance)

key_programme_risks: Procurement delays (e.g., port contractor mobilization in Rwanda)
Political economy barriers to regional integration (e.g., Tanzania’s resistance to reforms)
Sustainability of reforms post-DFID exit (e.g., customs efficiency gains)
Conflict disruption (e.g., South Sudan affecting Northern Corridor trade)
Gender backlash (e.g., sexual harassment at borders despite sensitization)
Climate risks (e.g., Lake Kivu port infrastructure vulnerable to environmental changes)
Donor coordination challenges in multi-partner platform
Overstretch of TMEA’s capacity with expanded remit (export support)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phased implementation with contractor performance milestones; parallel technical assistance to strengthen public sector project management (e.g., Tanzania Port Authority).
Politically aware technical assistance; PEA-informed engagement strategies; focus on "quick wins" (e.g., OSBPs) to build momentum.

TMEA’s sustainability strategy includes reducing donor reliance through development capital instruments and encouraging EAC governments/private sector to finance reforms. Capacity building embedded in all components (e.g., customs TA, gender adviser roles).
Contingency planning for South Sudan routes; smaller, flexible interventions (e.g., Gulu hub scaled to context).
Gender audits of all interventions; dedicated women trader programmes (e.g., 250 trained on AfCFTA); sensitization for customs administrators.
Green Port policies (e.g., Dar es Salaam); climate-resilient design for Lake Kivu ports.
TMEA Council with DFID chair; clear division of labor (e.g., World Bank handles large-scale port infrastructure, TMEA focuses on efficiency/TA).
Option 5 limits expansion to "core" trade facilitation + targeted export support; phased hub development; mid-term review to assess capacity.

fcas_specific_lessons: In South Sudan, small-scale, flexible interventions (e.g., Gulu hub) are prioritized over large infrastructure, with humanitarian trade corridors integrated where possible.
For DRC/Rwanda border trade, ferry services on Lake Kivu reduce reliance on conflict-affected road routes.
In fragile settings, focus on "quick wins" (e.g., simplified trade regimes for informal traders) builds trust for larger reforms.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Strategy 1 (2011-2017) showed that: (1) Infrastructure improvements (e.g., Mombasa Port time reduction from 11 to 5 days) have the highest trade impact; (2) Complementary supply-side support (e.g., standards harmonization + SME training) enhances sustainability; (3) Women’s informal trade (74% of cross-border trade) requires dedicated channels/facilities; (4) Regional political economy requires adaptive, phased approaches (e.g., Tanzania’s variable engagement).
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added export capacity component (Option 5) based on evidence that supply-side constraints limit trade growth.
Phased logistics hubs design to apply lessons iteratively (vs. Strategy 1’s corridor-focused approach).
Stronger gender mainstreaming (Gender Audit, adviser roles) after Strategy 1’s ad-hoc gender activities.
Enhanced ICT focus (e.g., TLIP platform) based on Strategy 1’s success with digital customs systems.
Targeted support for informal traders (e.g., cross-border markets, low-cost storage) addressing Strategy 1’s gap in reaching micro-traders.
risks_lessons.quote: "Box 1: Summary of lessons from TMEA Strategy 1... Evidence is context-specific, but unequivocal that trade facilitation interventions which improve infrastructure are the most effective in increasing trade volumes and reducing trade costs, followed by reforms that improve customs efficiency and then reforms improving the regulatory/business environment... There is need for more evidence to deepen understanding of channels and linkages in trade facilitation programmes... Tradeliberalisation can have short-term negative impacts on select groups..." (D0006850.odt, Box 1) and "The programme will adopt a phased approach to developing the ‘logistics hubs’ ensuring that lessons learnt are applied to improve outcomes." (D0006850.odt, Flexibility)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: TMEA platform has attracted over £450 million from 7 other donors, making it the largest aid-for-trade facility globally. DFID’s £229m leveraged ~£90m from other donors in Strategy 2 (total £319m). World Bank co-financing includes $345m for Dar Port and $600m planned for transport corridors.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: Roughly half the budget supports "soft" interventions (technical assistance, policy reforms) and half supports capital investments (infrastructure, ICT systems).
financial_details.quote: "DFID will provide £229 million overall towards TMEA’s Strategy 2 over 6 years... of which £42 million has already been approved in previous Business Cases. A further £187 million in additional funding will be added, and all funds will be used in a coherent approach across the region." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) and "Roughly half of the resources will support soft interventions including technical assistance and development of regulatory/policy frameworks... and the balance will support public and private stakeholders to address infrastructure related constraints." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary) and "TMEA, initially set up by DFID, has attracted 7 other donors, has raised over £450 million (now the largest aid for trade facility globally)..." (D0006850.odt, Intervention Summary)

metadata.programme_name: Humanitarian Diplomacy Fund (HDF)

quote.text: The Humanitarian Diplomacy Fund will provide a vehicle for Humanitarian Department (HD) to reinvigorate UK thought-leadership in shaping the future of the international humanitarian system.

duration_source.text: Programme Value: Up to £4.5m (£1.5m FY24/25; £1.5m FY25/26; £1.5m FY26/27)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The HDF is designed to support three key objectives: (1) provision of humanitarian data and evidence to stakeholders, (2) convening international and national stakeholders on humanitarian issues, and (3) piloting transformational humanitarian practices. It combines elements of policy influence, evidence generation, and implementation research to strengthen the humanitarian system.

q1_source.text: The Humanitarian Diplomacy Fund will invest small amounts of funding to enable the UK to deliver projects focused on (i) Provision of humanitarian data and evidence to a wider audience of key stakeholders (ii) Convening of international and national stakeholders on key humanitarian issues, through engagement in initiatives to drive forward reform and (iii) Piloting of activities that could be transformational to humanitarian practice.
q1_source.source: D0006022.odt, The rationale for UK Aid spending

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened humanitarian policy based on evidence
Strengthened consensus on humanitarian issues, and delivery of shared initiatives in the UK and globally
Utilisation of lessons from innovative humanitarian pilots, ensuring best practice informs future approaches
Convening events (e.g., Wilton Park forums)
Pilot projects (e.g., cash assistance integration, AI in humanitarian response)

what_objectives.summary: The HDF aims to reinvigorate UK leadership in humanitarian diplomacy by funding data provision, stakeholder convening, and pilot projects to improve humanitarian practice and policy.

quote.text: HDF will support a limited range of outputs which contribute to the delivery of the outcomes, aligned with the objectives in the Humanitarian Framework, namely: Protect, Prioritise, Prevent.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a high-need humanitarian context with complex crises but is assessed as moderate risk due to its focus on diplomacy and thought leadership rather than direct service delivery in fragile environments.

q5_source.text: Risk associated with this programme is moderate.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The global humanitarian system is under strain due to unpredictable and complex crises, which may limit the ability to prioritize and respond effectively. The HDF aims to address systemic challenges through diplomacy and reform rather than direct crisis response.

quote.text: With crises expected to become more unpredictable and more complex globally, we can expect an increased strain on an already stretched international humanitarian system, despite efforts to prioritise responses.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making power rests with FCDO HD, with project proposals submitted by FCDO policy leads and approved by the HD Delivery Board. Southern partners may be involved in project delivery but not in strategic decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (through convening events)
knowledge sharing (dissemination of evidence and lessons)
pilot projects (testing innovative approaches with partners)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Arms-Length Bodies
partner_organizations.role: potential implementing partner

partner_organizations.name: Multilateral Agencies (e.g., UN, Red Cross)
partner_organizations.role: potential implementing partner via MoUs/framework agreements

partner_organizations.name: Not-for-Profit Organisations
partner_organizations.role: potential grantee for accountable grants

partner_organizations.name: Wilton Park
partner_organizations.role: convening partner for events

partner_organizations.name: K4DD (Knowledge, Evidence and Learning for Development)
partner_organizations.role: evidence provider for project selection

quote.text: The programme will support the delivery of the following goals in HMFD’s Business Plan: World-leading humanitarian diplomacy, securing better protection for the most vulnerable, unblocking access, safeguarding International Humanitarian Law, and making tangible progress against the underlying drivers of humanitarian crisis.
quote.source: D0006022.odt, Strategic scope of the programme

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The HDF will use accountable grants, MoUs/framework agreements, and direct contracts with partners. Grants will be used for not-for-profit projects, while MoUs and contracts will be used for multilateral and arms-length bodies.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The HDF is managed by FCDO’s Humanitarian Department (HD), with a Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and Programme Responsible Officer (PRO) overseeing project selection, funding, and monitoring. Projects are proposed by FCDO policy leads and approved by the HD Delivery Board.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Direct awards are preferred for Year 1 to ensure alignment with HD’s strategic objectives and efficient use of resources. This avoids the administrative burden of open competitions for a small fund. Mixed approaches (direct awards + competitive bidding) may be considered in later years.

quote.text: Option 2 would work through the FCDO’s arms-length bodies, as well as working through multilateral agencies and partners through MoUs or framework agreements, based on proposals received from project leads that would deliver HDF’s objectives.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The HD Delivery Board (comprising the Senior Management Team) reviews and approves project proposals quarterly. The Board includes the Head of HD, SRO, PRO, and policy leads. Ad-hoc boards can be convened for urgent proposals.

quote.text: All proposals will be shared with the HD Delivery Board, which occurs on a quarterly basis (with the option of ad-hoc Boards when required) with recommendations for decision.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects within the annual budget, subject to approval by the SRO/PRO and Delivery Board. Flexibility is built into the programme to respond to emerging priorities, but reallocation requires justification and alignment with HDF objectives.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in response to emerging crises or new evidence, but changes must be approved by the Delivery Board. Annual reviews and quarterly check-ins enable adaptive management.

quote.text: The programme will respond flexibly to priorities and ensure work can be supplied by the most suitable organisations, depending on FCDO’s requirements.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., multilateral agency, NGO, or arms-length body). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned, so the structure is relatively flat.

quote.text: Invoices and payment requests will be reviewed by the PRO, who will ensure that outputs have been met and that financial reports meet FCDO requirements.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: HD would not take action to deliver humanitarian diplomacy objectives through a standalone fund, reducing UK influence.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Deliver through existing programmes within HD
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Incorporate HDF objectives into existing HD programmes, but this risks diluting focus and increasing administrative burden.
Create a dedicated funding vehicle (HDF) to pursue strategic interventions efficiently.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: A new standalone programme (Option 3) was chosen because it provides a dedicated funding vehicle to deliver humanitarian diplomacy objectives without altering existing programmes. It offers greater flexibility, efficiency, and control over strategic interventions, while avoiding the risks of diluting other programmes or missing opportunities for UK leadership.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Competing priorities of other Member States and global actors may challenge HDF’s ability to drive change.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Careful design of the programme to ensure appropriate ambition; selection of high-impact interventions; focus on implementation and follow-up.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Budget may be insufficient to fund catalytic interventions.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust selection process to maximize impact from available funds.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of high-quality proposals may limit achievement of outcomes.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Effective promotion of HDF within HD and FCDO to ensure a strong pipeline of proposals.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Emerging crises may deprioritize HDF.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Design programme to maximize impact with minimal resources; use annual reviews to build evidence for continuation.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Devolved project management may reduce oversight of performance.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear roles and reporting requirements; quarterly check-ins and risk escalation protocols.

quote.text: Option 3 presents the best option to ensure that FCDO can deliver a more coherent humanitarian response which reinvigorates UK leadership in shaping the future of the international humanitarian system.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global humanitarian context (e.g., complex crises, stretched systems) necessitates a focus on partners with existing capacity to deliver quickly and effectively. This may limit opportunities for newer or smaller Southern partners without established track records.
q27_constraints_detail: High humanitarian needs require prioritization of experienced partners.
Stretched systems limit capacity for extensive partner onboarding.
Focus on diplomacy and thought leadership favors partners with global influence (e.g., multilaterals, established NGOs).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The HDF’s objectives (data provision, convening, piloting) require a flexible, responsive delivery structure. Direct awards and accountable grants are used to ensure alignment with strategic priorities, while the fund manager model allows for quick approval of high-priority projects.
q28_linkages: Data provision objective → requires partnerships with research/evidence organizations (e.g., K4DD).
Convening objective → necessitates partnerships with forums like Wilton Park.
Piloting objective → requires agile funding mechanisms for innovative projects.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme acknowledges tensions between inclusivity (e.g., engaging diverse stakeholders) and efficiency (e.g., limiting partner numbers to manage administrative burden). The direct award approach prioritizes speed and alignment with UK objectives but may reduce opportunities for Southern-led proposals.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct awards enable quick action but may exclude smaller or less-connected partners.
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern-led convening ensures high-quality events but may limit Southern leadership.
Cost vs. reach: Limited budget requires prioritization, potentially reducing the number of funded projects.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to quarterly oversight and structured escalation protocols. High-risk activities (e.g., piloting in fragile contexts) would require additional safeguards, but the programme’s focus on diplomacy reduces exposure to operational risks.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded through pilot projects and convening events, which aim to strengthen partners’ ability to contribute to humanitarian reform. However, decision-making remains with FCDO, limiting Southern partners to implementation roles.

quote.text: The programme will support the delivery of the following goals in HMFD’s Business Plan: World-leading humanitarian diplomacy, securing better protection for the most vulnerable, unblocking access, safeguarding International Humanitarian Law, and making tangible progress against the underlying drivers of humanitarian crisis.
quote.source: D0006022.odt, Strategic scope of the programme

key_programme_risks: Competing priorities of other global actors may limit HDF’s influence.
Insufficient budget to fund catalytic interventions.
Lack of high-quality proposals may restrict outcomes.
Emerging crises could deprioritize HDF resources.
Devolved project management may reduce oversight of performance.
Reputational risk if HDF fails to deliver visible impact.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Competing priorities of other Member States and global actors, challenge ability of the HDF to drive the level of change/influence envisaged.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Careful design of programme to ensure appropriate level of ambition; careful selection of funded interventions to maximise potential impact; ensuring project teams are focused on impact through implementation and afterwards.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Budget for the HDF is insufficient to fund the level of catalytic interventions to achieve the impacts sought.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Careful selection of funded proposals to ensure the maximum impact is achieved from available budget.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Success of the HDF is contingent upon a suitable spread of good quality proposals. If that does not materialise, there is a risk that the full breadth of the intended outcomes are not achieved.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Effective promotion of the HDF amongst HD (and other parts of FCDO if eligible to bid) to ensure good spread proposals; robust selection process of proposals to ensure good quality and a suitable spread of initiatives are funded.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Emerging crises necessitate HD to prioritise staff and programme resource, leading to the de-prioritisation of the HDF, and reduction in available resource for the HDF.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Design of programme to maximise impact with minimum resource and staff management capacity; strong annual reviews and reviews of the projects further build the evidence base and strengthen the case for the continuation of the HDF.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Project management of funded proposals is devolved to FCDO teams that bid for funding. The Programme SRO/PRO may lack a direct line of sight of performance of individual proposals (from which project leads are required to escalate) and therefore may not spot emerging risks or performance issues of the programme in a timely fashion.
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Clear allocation of roles and responsibilities between programme team and individual project teams; clear reporting requirements on project teams including quarterly check ins as well as a requirement to raise any risks they believe may affect the performance/outcome of the project in a timely manner and provide appropriate resolutions, and to immediately escalate any risks that are outside of appetite.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from the Grand Bargain highlight the value of convening stakeholders to drive systemic change (e.g., cash assistance, localisation).
Pilot projects (e.g., Women’s Refugee Commission’s IPV case management) demonstrate the importance of testing innovations in real-world settings.
The need for adaptive management in response to unpredictable crises is emphasized.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The Humanitarian Policy Fund (HPF) completion review identified constraints due to lack of programme management resource, which limited scope and ambition. HDF addresses this by requiring project proposals to demonstrate management capacity upfront and ensuring sufficient oversight through the PRO/SRO structure.
design_changes_based_on_learning: HDF includes explicit requirements for project management capacity in proposals, unlike HPF.
Quarterly reviews and a structured governance board (Delivery Board) were introduced to improve oversight.
Flexibility is built into the programme to respond to emerging priorities, informed by HPF’s rigid structure.

quote.text: The Humanitarian Policy Fund (HPF) was a HD programme that concluded in 2022. The aim of the HPF was to fund analysis and pilots to build the evidence base for existing and future UK priorities in humanitarian policy and programming. The programme completion review (PCR) of the fund includes valuable lessons which have been applied to HDF, including the constraints caused by a lack of programme management resource, which ultimately limited the scope and ambition of what could be delivered by the fund.
Programme Value: Up to £4.5m (£1.5m FY24/25; £1.5m FY25/26; £1.5m FY26/27).

metadata.programme_name: Eliminating Lymphatic Filariasis in Africa (ELFA)

quote.programme_name: "EliminatingLymphaticFilariasisinAfrica(ELFA)" (D0006462.odt, Title section)
quote.duration: "1st September 2024 to 31st March 2027" (D0007449.odt, Original programme start and end dates)
quote.sector: "Diseases of Poverty, Global Health" (D0006462.odt, Country/Region or Sector)

metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: 1st September 2024 to 31st March 2027" (D0007449.odt, Detailed information section)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The ELFA programme combines service delivery (MDA, surgeries, DMDI care), capacity building (health system strengthening, training), and implementation research (disease mapping, surveillance). It directly supports elimination of lymphatic filariasis while strengthening health systems for sustainability.
what_objectives.q1_source: "Programme activities will include disease mapping, treatment, surgeries and supportive care to treat long-term symptoms, capacity building for sustainability, plus support for elimination processes." (D0006462.odt, Programmesummary)
q3_expected_outputs: 6 million people reached with river blindness MDA in Benin (D0007449.odt)
Hydrocoele surgeries delivered (quantity not specified)
DMDI services scaled up across programme countries (D0006462.odt)
16 million Ivermectin pills utilized before expiry (D0007449.odt)
Health facility assessments completed in multiple countries (D0006462.odt)
Social behaviour change initiatives implemented (D0006462.odt)
Operational Framework for Supporting LF Patient Care developed (D0007449.odt)
Two hydrocoele master surgeon trainings conducted (D0007449.odt)
National NTD master plans supported (D0006462.odt)
Supply chain management systems strengthened (D0006462.odt)
Lab capacity development in target countries (D0006462.odt)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to eliminate lymphatic filariasis (and now river blindness) in Africa by 2030 through direct service delivery, health system strengthening, and technical support to national programmes, while contributing to the broader Reaching the Last Mile Fund initiative.

quote.objectives: "The ELFA programme will be implemented in countries that are close to eliminating lymphatic filariasis (LF), supporting them with this important step and beyond. Programme activities will include disease mapping, treatment, surgeries and supportive care to treat long-term symptoms, capacity building for sustainability, plus support for elimination processes." (D0006462.odt, Programmesummary)
quote.expansion: "The proposed change is to broaden the scope of the programme beyond just the NTD lymphatic filariasis to include activities in support of the elimination of river blindness (onchocerciasis)" (D0007449.odt, Changes section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in multiple African countries including FCAS contexts (e.g., South Sudan, DRC, Chad) with challenges of weak health systems, conflict risks, and implementation difficulties. The overall risk rating is assessed as moderate with major risks in strategy/context and programme delivery categories.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall risk rating of the programme is moderate" (D0006462.odt, Overall programme risk rating) and "Strategy & Context, plus Programme Delivery are considered to be major risks due to the countries where the programme will operate and the challenges of implementation on the ground" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security issues affect implementation in countries like South Sudan and DRC; weak health systems limit service delivery capacity; climate change threatens disease resurgence; data gaps hinder surveillance; and political instability in some countries creates operational challenges. The programme must adapt to these constraints through flexible approaches and local partnerships.

quote.constraints: "Climate change is likely to affect the range and (re)emergence of multiple NTDs... There is a need for improved surveillance and monitoring to identify areas at risk" (D0006462.odt, Future trends) and "The programme will be implemented in countries in the African region that are close to eliminating LF, supporting them with this important step and beyond" (D0006462.odt, Countries and activities)
quote.risk_evidence: "Strategy & Context, plus Programme Delivery are considered to be major risks due to the countries where the programme will operate and the challenges of implementation on the ground" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Sightsavers (UK-based) serves as consortium lead with decision-making authority over sub-grants to Southern partners (The Carter Center, END Fund) and national partners, though implementation is country-led through Ministries of Health. The governance structure (donor steering committee) is also Northern-dominated.
q10_capacity_building_details: training of healthcare professionals for DMDI services
surgical capacity building at district hospitals
health worker training for quality care
supply chain management strengthening
lab capacity development
Leave No One Behind approaches
social behaviour change initiatives
local partner capacity building (where needs identified)

quote.structure: "Sightsavers will act as a consortium lead for the ELFA programme, sub-granting to other RLMF partners (The Carter Center and The End Fund) where appropriate and to national partners" (D0006462.odt, Partner Procurement capability)
quote.capacity: "Strengthening national programmes to improve the provision of quality hydrocoele surgeries and lymphoedema care through the primary health care system... training health workers to provide quality care" (D0006462.odt, Proposed activities)
quote.decision_power: "The donor steering committee comprises large donors plus external representatives (e.g. WHO, USAID) and is responsible for funding decisions, identifying priorities, monitoring progress on elimination" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an Accountable Grant (AG) with Sightsavers, which provides flexibility to adapt to evolving epidemiology and risks while maintaining FCDO oversight. The AG is non-legally enforceable but includes clauses on FCDO requirements for reporting, fraud prevention, and aid diversion. Payments are made in arrears based on quarterly financial reports.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Sightsavers serves as consortium lead, managing sub-grants to The Carter Center, The END Fund, and national partners. The Reaching the Last Mile Fund (RLMF) provides overarching coordination through a donor steering committee (with Gates Foundation, UAE, USAID, WHO) and three working groups (country engagement, systems strengthening, technical support). FCDO engages directly with Sightsavers and the RLMF secretariat.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Sightsavers was selected due to its "high level of technical expertise in NTDs," "extensive network of country offices," and "long history of work on NTDs" including previous successful partnerships with FCDO (e.g., ASCEND programme). The business case states that "a competitive process to securing a partner would [not] offer benefits" given Sightsavers' comparative advantage.

quote.instrument: "An AG would support the partnership approach to this work and would enable the programme to adapt more effectively and efficiently... AGs have previously been used with Sightsavers (and other partners) to deliver similar size and complexity of programmes, with great success" (D0006462.odt, Learning and evaluation)
quote.selection: "We do not believe a competitive process to securing a partner would offer benefits, given Sightsavers' comparative advantage in this sector... Sightsavers consistently scored highly in its programme annual reviews and delivered substantial outputs with impact, sustainability and good VfM" (D0006462.odt, Learning and evaluation)
quote.structure: "Sightsavers will act as a consortium lead for the ELFA programme, sub-granting to other RLMF partners (The Carter Center and The End Fund)... The donor steering committee comprises large donors plus external representatives (e.g. WHO, USAID)" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The RLMF donor steering committee includes major donors (UAE, Gates Foundation, CIFF, USAID) and external representatives (WHO). It is responsible for funding decisions, priority-setting, and monitoring progress. Three working groups (country engagement, systems strengthening, technical support) report to the steering committee. Sightsavers provides quarterly reports to FCDO and biannual reports to the RLMF donor group.

quote.governance: "The donor steering committee comprises large donors plus external representatives (e.g. WHO, USAID) and is responsible for funding decisions, identifying priorities, monitoring progress on elimination, and supporting resource mobilisation and advocacy" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
quote.oversight: "Reporting by all implementing partners will be biannual to the central RLMF donor group. Sightsavers will also provide quarterly reports to FCDO" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
quote.sub_awards: "Sightsavers will develop a full delivery chain map for programme implementation, which will be reviewed by the central programme team and relevant country offices to ensure compliance with local rules" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities/countries with FCDO approval, as demonstrated by the £400k underspend from Year 1 being repurposed for the Benin river blindness MDA. However, major reallocations require programme amendments (e.g., the Benin MDA addition was classified as a 'significant' change but not requiring full re-approval).
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs adaptive management to respond to evolving epidemiology (e.g., climate change impacts on LF transmission), funding gaps (e.g., USAID withdrawal), and country progress. The Accountable Grant structure and regular quarterly reviews enable course corrections, as seen with the Benin MDA addition. However, significant changes require FCDO approval.

quote.reallocation: "The use of these funds for the MDA will mean there will be correspondingly less funding for other DMDI activities in fy25-26... we judge supporting the Benin MDA to be sufficiently high priority... to justify this" (D0007449.odt, Changes)
quote.adaptive: "Given the uncertainties, contingencies, and risks associated with progress towards elimination, the ELFA programme will need to take a flexible approach to delivery to achieve the best results and VfM" (D0006462.odt, ELFA programme approach)
quote.approval: "The change is not so material as to require programme re-approval" (D0007449.odt, Changes)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Sightsavers (consortium lead) → [The Carter Center/END Fund/National Partners] → Ministries of Health/Community Implementers

quote.layers: "Sightsavers will act as a consortium lead for the ELFA programme, sub-granting to other RLMF partners (The Carter Center and The End Fund) where appropriate and to national partners" (D0006462.odt, Partner Procurement capability)
quote.payments: "Payment to Sightsavers will be made in arrears subject to detailed financial reports provided prior to payment" (D0006462.odt, Cost Drivers and commercial risk)
quote.budget: "Programme Value: £15 million" (D0006462.odt, Programme Value)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Core funding to RLMF (pooled fund - discarded due to reduced oversight)
Option 2: Sightsavers as direct partner (proposed option)
Option 3: The Carter Center (TCC) as partner (less FCDO experience)
Option 4: The END Fund as partner (limited FCDO experience)
Do nothing (discarded due to strategic decision to contribute to NTD programming)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Sightsavers was chosen due to its "high level of technical expertise in NTDs," "extensive network of country offices," and proven track record with FCDO (e.g., ASCEND programme). The Accountable Grant modality was selected for its flexibility to adapt to risks and evolving epidemiology, while the consortium structure leverages RLMF's existing coordination platforms for efficiency. The direct funding approach ensures clear accountability and alignment with UK development strategies.
q25_decision_factors: partner capacity (Sightsavers' expertise and country presence)
strategic alignment (UK's contribution to RLMF's AfricaFree initiative)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced FCDO control over sub-awards to The Carter Center/END Fund
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Sightsavers conducts due diligence for all partners and maintains oversight; FCDO reviews delivery chain maps

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex coordination among RLMF's three implementing partners
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: RLMF's governance structure (steering committee + working groups) ensures alignment; Sightsavers leads systems strengthening workstream

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Flexibility of Accountable Grant could lead to mission drift
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Regular quarterly reviews and annual FCDO assessments maintain focus on elimination goals

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Dependence on Sightsavers' financial systems for £15m programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO's prior due diligence assessments and Sightsavers' robust Financial Management Framework

quote.why_chosen: "Sightsavers is the proposed option for this programme, primarily due to their experience in LF programmes and strong working relationship developed through previous NTD programmes, including the ASCEND programme" (D0006462.odt, Options considered for delivery)
quote.vfm: "Economy: The main cost drivers... Sightsavers can track cost drivers to ensure economical use of inputs... Efficiency: The ELFA programme will work through existing processes and structures... Effectiveness: Programme activities will be based on international norms and frameworks... Equity: Leaving no one behind is a principle of the programme" (D0006462.odt, Value for money)
quote.risks: "The main cost drivers for this programme include programme activities (procurement of DMDI equipment, providing training for key personnel)... Sightsavers will develop a full delivery chain map for programme implementation, which will be reviewed by the central programme team" (D0006462.odt, Cost Drivers and commercial risk)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme's multi-country scope in Africa—including FCAS contexts (e.g., South Sudan, DRC) and least developed countries—constrains partner selection to organizations with: (1) extensive in-country presence (Sightsavers' country offices), (2) experience navigating fragile contexts, and (3) existing relationships with Ministries of Health. The need for rapid response to gaps (e.g., USAID withdrawal in Benin) further limits options to partners already embedded in RLMF structures.
q27_constraints_detail: FCAS contexts require partners with conflict-sensitive approaches
Weak health systems necessitate partners with capacity-building expertise
Multi-country scope demands partners with regional networks
USAID funding gaps require agile partners able to repurpose resources quickly
WHO validation processes require partners with technical alignment
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme's mixed objectives (elimination + health systems strengthening) determine its consortium structure: (1) **Service delivery** (MDA, surgeries) requires Sightsavers' technical expertise and country offices; (2) **Systems strengthening** leverages RLMF's existing working groups; (3) **Flexibility needs** (adapting to climate change, funding gaps) justify the Accountable Grant modality; and (4) **Equity goals** (Leave No One Behind) shape sub-granting to local NGO/CSO partners.
q28_linkages: MDA delivery → requires Sightsavers' drug distribution experience (ASCEND legacy)
DMDI scale-up → necessitates consortium with Carter Center/END Fund for technical support
Health system integration → aligns with RLMF's systems strengthening workstream
Climate adaptation → demands flexible AG structure for responsive programming
FCAS operations → requires embedded safeguarding/duty-of-care policies
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: The Benin MDA repurposing prioritized rapid action over planned DMDI activities to prevent drug expiry and disease resurgence; (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: Sightsavers (UK) leads decision-making while Ministries of Health implement, with capacity-building mitigations; (3) **Cost vs. reach**: Pooling funds through RLMF achieves economies of scale but reduces FCDO's direct control over allocations.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Benin MDA repurposing (speed) reduced funds for DMDI activities (inclusion)
Sightsavers' consortium lead role (expertise) centralizes some decision-making (ownership)
RLMF pooled funding (efficiency) limits FCDO's oversight of sub-awards (control)
Standardized MDA protocols (efficiency) vs. localized adaptation needs (equity)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme's moderate-high risk profile (FCAS contexts, implementation challenges) drives intensive oversight mechanisms: quarterly FCDO-Sightsavers meetings, biannual RLMF donor reports, and embedded safeguarding policies. The Accountable Grant's flexibility is balanced by strict financial reporting requirements (payments in arrears).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives shape partner roles through: (1) Sightsavers' sub-grants to national NGO/CSOs including capacity assessments; (2) The Carter Center's technical support workstream strengthening Ministries of Health; and (3) RLMF's systems strengthening group focusing on sustainable skills transfer (e.g., hydrocoele surgery training).

quote.where_who: "The programme will be implemented in countries in the African region that are close to eliminating LF, supporting them with this important step and beyond... Sightsavers has an extensive network of country offices" (D0006462.odt, Countries and activities & Options considered for delivery)
quote.what_how: "The goal of the new programme is to contribute to broader efforts of the elimination of LF as a public health problem at the country level... The programme will work to well-established principles and guidelines, with the aim of elimination of LF" (D0006462.odt, ELFA programme approach)
quote.tradeoffs: "The use of these funds for the MDA will mean there will be correspondingly less funding for other DMDI activities in fy25-26... we judge supporting the Benin MDA to be sufficiently high priority... to justify this" (D0007449.odt, Changes)
quote.risk_management: "Strategy & Context, plus Programme Delivery are considered to be major risks due to the countries where the programme will operate and the challenges of implementation on the ground... We would look to work with relevant UK Embassy/High Commission contacts in these countries to help monitor and manage these risks" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
quote.capacity_roles: "Sightsavers will provide grants to Ministries of Health in some countries, and to national NGO/CSO implementing partners in all countries... Sightsavers applies Minimum Partnership Criteria to all partners at the outset of granting agreements, a thorough due diligence process, and local partner capacity building where specific needs are identified" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)

key_programme_risks: Disruption to Benin's river blindness elimination progress if MDA not funded (D0007449.odt)
Logistical complexity of delivering preventive chemotherapy to 6 million people in 51 areas (D0007449.odt)
Expire of 16 million Ivermectin pills if not utilized (D0007449.odt)
Strategy and context risks (major) due to FCAS operating environments (D0006462.odt)
Programme delivery risks (major) from implementation challenges on the ground (D0006462.odt)
Climate change impacting LF transmission patterns and elimination progress (D0006462.odt)
Data gaps in LMICs underestimating NTD burden (D0006462.odt)
Potential resurgence of LF if surveillance systems are weak post-MDA (D0006462.odt)
Dependence on donated drugs (supply chain vulnerabilities) (D0006462.odt)
Safeguarding risks in fragile contexts (D0006462.odt)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Disruption to Benin's river blindness elimination
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Repurpose £400k underspend to fund MDA, coordinating with Gates-led re-prioritization process (D0007449.odt)
Leverage Sightsavers' prior MDA experience in Benin (2005-2018) and existing Government of Benin relationships; coordinate with former implementer (FHI360) (D0007449.odt)
Accelerate MDA implementation between March-May 2025 to utilize drugs before July expiry (D0007449.odt)
Engage UK Embassies/High Commissions for local monitoring; use Sightsavers' country offices with national staff (D0006462.odt)
Flexible programme design to adapt to changing transmission patterns; strengthened surveillance systems (D0006462.odt)
Invest in health system strengthening (lab capacity, data systems) and post-validation surveillance planning (D0006462.odt)
Strengthen supply chain management systems and buffer stocks; diversify suppliers (D0006462.odt)
Apply Sightsavers' safeguarding policies and local partner due diligence; regular FCDO reviews (D0006462.odt)

fcas_specific_lessons: Leverage existing country offices with national staff for FCAS operations (Sightsavers model)
Coordinate with UK Embassies/High Commissions for local risk monitoring
Prioritize flexible funding mechanisms (Accountable Grants) for adaptive management
Invest in local partner capacity building to mitigate weak institutional contexts
Use regional training hubs to overcome travel/security constraints in conflict zones
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The ASCEND programme demonstrated that: (1) Integrating NTD care into primary health systems improves sustainability; (2) Regional approaches (e.g., bulk procurement, cross-country training) enhance efficiency; (3) Strong M&E frameworks are critical for validation processes; and (4) Local ownership (via Ministry of Health leadership) accelerates elimination. These lessons shaped ELFA's health system strengthening focus and consortium structure.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: ELFA incorporated ASCEND's: (1) Leave No One Behind toolkit; (2) Social Behaviour Change Communication protocols; (3) Standard Operating Procedures for supply chain management; and (4) emphasis on national NTD master plans. The Benin MDA addition also reflects adaptive learning from USAID's funding withdrawal.

quote.risks: "The main risks are under strategy and context and programme delivery which are assessed to be major reflecting the countries where the programme will be operating and the challenges of implementation on the ground" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
quote.mitigations: "Sightsavers will develop a full delivery chain map for programme implementation, which will be reviewed by the central programme team and relevant country offices to ensure compliance with local rules" (D0006462.odt, Management Case)
quote.lessons: "ASCEND had a strong focus on sustainability through health systems strengthening... It also supported the development of national NTD master plans and of improved systems and skills in partner countries" (D0006462.odt, ELFA programme approach)
quote.design_changes: "The programme will build on long established relationships with national stakeholders to provide technical expertise and guidance, programme management support and resourcing to support delivery in line with the national NTD roadmaps" (D0006462.odt, Countries and activities)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The £15m FCDO contribution leverages the RLMF's $500m AfricaFree initiative, which includes $350m in new pledges secured at COP28 (2023). The programme also utilizes donated drugs (e.g., 16 million Ivermectin pills for Benin MDA) and benefits from RLMF's existing coordination structures.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget includes £300,000 (2%) for capital expenditure (e.g., DMDI equipment) across the programme lifetime, with the remainder allocated to revenue activities (MDA, surgeries, training, etc.).

quote.budget: "Programme Value: £15 million" (D0006462.odt, Programme Value) and "The first £5 million is agreed and the remaining £10 million is subject to the next spending review" (D0006462.odt, Cost Drivers and commercial risk)
quote.leverage: "The recent expansion of RLMF (2.0) aims to increase this commitment to $500 million towards its 'AfricaFree Initiative' to eliminate lymphatic filariasis (LF) and river blindness... New pledges totalling $350m were secured in December 2023 at COP28" (D0006462.odt, Reaching the Last Mile Fund)
quote.co_funding: "RLMF is a priority for the UAE government. Supporting the initiative broadens joint UK-UAE development cooperation... RLMF is managed by the Gates Foundation and Reaching the Last Mile" (D0006462.odt, Reaching the Last Mile Fund)

metadata.programme_name: Global Compactson Refugees and Migration Programme (GCP)
metadata.quote: "This programme is strengthening the multilateral architecture of migration and displacement management by supporting instruments that put into practice the objectives of the Global Compact on Migration (GCM) and the Global Compact on Refugees (GCR)." (D0006138.odt, Summary Information)
metadata.duration_source: "New project end date: FY24/25, FY25/26, FY26/27" (D0006138.odt, Summary Information)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines financing mechanisms (funding Multi-Partner Trust Funds) with policy influence (supporting implementation of the Global Compacts on Migration and Refugees) and service delivery (inclusion of refugee children in national education systems). It also includes capacity building through technical assistance and advocacy.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The Global Compactson Refugees and Migration Programme (GCP) seeks to strengthen the multilateral architecture of migration and displacement management by supporting instruments that put into practice the objectives of the Global Compactson Migration and Refugees. Primary activities will be the funding of two Multi-Partner Trust Funds – one focusing on interventions to promote safer, more orderly, and regular migration. The second will support inclusion of refugee children in to national education systems." (D0006137.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Funding of two Multi-Partner Trust Funds (one for migration, one for refugee education)
Inclusion of refugee children in national education systems (targeting 10 million IDPs on pathways to solutions by end of 2024)
Support for 15 pledges announced by the UK at the 2023 Global Refugee Forum
Technical assistance to refugee-host governments for education integration
Advocacy grants to national NGOs for gender equality in nationality laws
Support for meaningful refugee participation in policy-making
33 additional programmes under MMPTF once further resources are available
7.5 million beneficiaries reached through GCFF (including 3.9 million refugees and 1.6 million host community members)
Development of a Legal Atlas on gender discrimination in nationality laws
Convening of a youth summit and global multi-stakeholder summit
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen multilateral migration and displacement management through funding trust funds, technical assistance, and advocacy, with a focus on refugee education, gender equality, and solutions for internally displaced people.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme is an inclusive instrument to further the implementation of the GCM and GCR and progress related SDGs. Through funding – and in one case co-initiating – thematic Multi-Partner Trust Funds, UK Aid can facilitate cooperation on migration and displacement, shift policy discussions, and motivate and test new innovative approaches." (D0006137.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in complex migration and displacement contexts with political sensitivities, but uses trusted multilateral partners to manage risks. The overall risk rating is explicitly stated as moderate.
where_context.q5_source: "The overall programme risk rating is moderate; risk will be closely monitored and managed throughout the programme lifecycle." (D0006137.odt, Risk section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Political tensions in transit countries and conflict-driven displacement create operational challenges. Climate change exacerbates displacement risks, while weak institutions in host countries limit service delivery capacity.
where_context.quote: "Human mobility, both voluntary and forced, is at record levels and migration is a permanent feature of the global economy... Drivers of human mobility are complex... Recent rises in forced displacement have been driven by conflict in Ukraine, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Myanmar, drought, floods and insecurity in Somalia, and the prolonged humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan." (D0006137.odt, Global Context)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: United Nations (various agencies including UNDP, UNHCR, World Bank)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making occurs through multilateral steering committees where the UK participates but does not unilaterally control. For example, the MMPTF steering committee includes rotating member states, and the GCFF steering committee includes both donor and recipient countries.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to host governments for refugee education integration
advocacy grants to national NGOs for gender equality campaigns
support for UN system coordination on internal displacement
development of a Legal Atlas on gender discrimination

partner_organizations.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
partner_organizations.role: Fund manager for MMPTF and IDSF

partner_organizations.name: UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
partner_organizations.role: Implementation partner for refugee education and solutions for IDPs

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Manager of GCFF and INSPIRE Trust Fund for refugee education

partner_organizations.name: Women’s Refugee Commission
partner_organizations.role: Implementation of gender equality in nationality laws project

partner_organizations.name: Office of the UN Special Adviser on Solutions to Internal Displacement
partner_organizations.role: Coordination of IDP solutions

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank
partner_organizations.role: Potential funding window for Rome Process

partner_organizations.name: National NGOs (various countries)
partner_organizations.role: Local implementation of gender equality and refugee participation projects

who_partners.quote: "The programme is also designed to fund a range of activities aimed at implementing UK pledges made at the 2023 Global Refugee Forum... Through funding – and in one case co-initiating – thematic Multi-Partner Trust Funds, UK Aid can facilitate cooperation on migration and displacement." (D0006137.odt, Programme summary)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of accountable grants with NGO partners (for gender equality and refugee participation projects) and Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with multilateral agencies (UNDP, World Bank, UNOCHA) for trust fund contributions. The MoUs are amended to include new funding allocations.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Implementation is primarily managed through existing multilateral trust funds (MMPTF, IDSF, GCFF) with their own steering committees. The UK participates in these committees (e.g., MMPTF steering committee, GCFF steering committee) but does not unilaterally control them. Bilateral components (e.g., gender equality projects) use accountable grant agreements with NGOs.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on existing relationships and alignment with programme objectives. For example, the World Bank and UNHCR were natural choices for the refugee education pledge due to their co-sponsorship of the INSPIRE Trust Fund, while UNDP manages the MMPTF and IDSF as established pooled funds.
how_mechanism.quote: "Upon approval of this business case addendum we will agree an amendment to the existing MoUs with UNDP for funding to the MMPTF... The UK is an existing donor to the MMPTF and engages with the fund’s steering committee." (D0006138.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The MMPTF, IDSF, and GCFF each have steering committees with rotating membership that include donor countries (like the UK), recipient countries, and multilateral agencies. For example, the GCFF steering committee is co-chaired by one donor and one recipient country, while the MMPTF steering committee includes UN entities and contributing donors on a rotating basis.
how_governance.quote: "The UK will attend the quarterly steering committee meetings at Deputy-Director level... We will hold bi-annual meetings with the MMPTF fund manager (with further ad-hoc meetings as needed) to monitor and review progress." (D0006138.odt, Approach to Implementation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds within each trust fund (MMPTF, IDSF, GCFF) can be reallocated among approved projects, but transfers between funds or major strategic shifts require approval. The initial projects were agreed on a single-year basis with potential for extension based on results.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for extensions of initial one-year projects based on performance, and the UK can influence fund directions through steering committee participation.
