However, major changes would require approval through the existing governance structures of each trust fund.
how_flexibility.quote: "Projectshavebeenagreedinitiallyonasingleyearbasis,butmaybeextendeddependingonsuccessfuldeliveryofresults." (D0006138.odt, Assurances)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral Trust Fund (MMPTF/IDSF/GCFF) → Implementing partners (e.g., UN agencies, World Bank, national NGOs). For bilateral components: FCDO → NGO implementer.
how_efficiency.quote: "All partners are required to provide us with regular reports, which will also be used to inform the programme’s Annual Reviews (ARs) and Project Completion Report (PCR)." (D0006138.odt, Approach to Implementation)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (maintain existing £350k/year to MMPTF with no new activities)
Option 2: Multilateral delivery only (all funds through existing trust funds)
Option 3: Direct bilateral delivery (in-house FCDO management or fund manager)
Option 4: Combined multilateral and bilateral delivery (preferred option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The combined approach (Option 4) was chosen because it balances the allocative efficiency and global public good provision of multilateral channels with the flexibility and UK alignment of bilateral components. Multilateral funds provide economies of scale and signal UK commitment to global compacts, while bilateral elements ensure delivery on specific UK pledges (e.g., refugee education).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lack of flexibility in multilateral funds may limit alignment with UK pledges
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Use bilateral components for UK-specific priorities while leveraging multilaterals for broader impact

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk if UK fails to deliver on GRF pledges
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Direct bilateral funding for pledge-related activities (e.g., refugee education) alongside multilateral contributions

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Administrative burden of managing multiple trust funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leverage existing MoUs and steering committee participation rather than creating new structures

why_rationale.quote: "Option4simultaneouslyenablesgreateralignmenttoUKobjectiveswhilealsoensuringtheintegrityofsystemsrequiredintheprovisionofglobalpublicgoodsinthiscontext... Thisrelevanceandstrengthacrossoutcomessuggestthatoption4isthemostcost-effective." (D0006137.odt, Recommendation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The political sensitivity of migration issues in transit countries (e.g., high migrant tensions) makes multilateral channels preferable for implementation, as they can absorb operational risks and diffuse local political concerns that might limit bilateral partners.
q27_constraints_detail: Political tensions in transit countries limit bilateral engagement
Conflict and fragility in host countries (e.g., Chad, Somalia) require multilateral expertise
Need for global coordination on migration compacts favors multilateral partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to deliver on specific UK pledges (e.g., refugee education) requires bilateral components for direct control, while the global public good nature of migration governance favors multilateral channels for efficiency and cooperation.
q28_linkages: UK’s co-sponsorship of the INSPIRE Trust Fund → bilateral-through-multilateral delivery for refugee education
Global nature of GCM/GCR implementation → multilateral trust funds for broad impact
Need for localised responses (e.g., gender equality in nationality laws) → grants to national NGOs
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (using existing multilateral funds with economies of scale) with equity considerations (e.g., gender markers in MMPTF, inclusion of refugee-led organizations). The choice to fund both global trust funds and local NGOs reflects a trade-off between reach and targeted impact.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Multilateral funds (efficient but less flexible) vs bilateral grants (targeted but higher transaction costs)
Global coordination (broad impact) vs local ownership (context-specific solutions)
Speed of delivery (using existing funds) vs depth of engagement (capacity building for Southern partners)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile leads to quarterly oversight through steering committees and regular reporting, with more intensive management for bilateral components (e.g., NGO grants) where the UK has direct accountability for pledge delivery.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme through technical assistance (e.g., INSPIRE’s support to host governments) and grants to national NGOs, which shapes partner roles by enabling local actors to implement global commitments.
intersections.quote: "Multilaterals have a comparative advantage in selecting beneficiaries through needs-based criteria due to their extensive networks and expertise... However, UK pledges in the GRF are likely to require considerable funding on specific issues. Given the reputational and cooperative implications of failing to deliver on pledges, a level of discretionary funding through bilateral channels would be useful." (D0006137.odt, Full appraisal of delivery options)

key_programme_risks: Failure to deliver on UK’s Global Refugee Forum pledges (reputational risk)
Limited flexibility in multilateral funds restricting alignment with UK priorities
Operational risks in fragile contexts (e.g., Somalia, Libya)
Administrative burden of managing multiple trust funds and partners
Uncertainty around the Rome Process funding window
Potential for aid diversion in high-risk countries
Limited evidence of success for the newly established IDSF

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to deliver on GRF pledges
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Direct bilateral funding for pledge-related projects (e.g., refugee education) alongside multilateral contributions
Use combined delivery model (Option 4) with bilateral components for UK-specific priorities
Leverage multilateral partners (e.g., UN agencies) with experience in FCAS environments
Use existing MoUs and steering committee structures rather than creating new mechanisms
Engage at Director General level in the steering group and seek clarity on the African Development Bank funding window
Conduct due diligence assessments on all partners and include safeguarding clauses in MoUs/grants
Monitor closely through steering committee participation and regular reporting

fcas_specific_lessons: Use of multilateral partners to manage risks in fragile contexts (e.g., UN agencies for IDP solutions in Somalia, Yemen)
Importance of localised responses (e.g., grants to national NGOs for gender equality campaigns)
Need for flexible funding to adapt to changing FCAS conditions (e.g., single-year project agreements with potential extensions)
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on the UK’s existing engagement with the MMPTF, where previous contributions (£350k/year) demonstrated the value of pooled funding for migration programmes. The decision to increase funding to £500k/year reflects positive experience with the fund’s management and alignment with UK priorities.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The addendum expands the programme from £3.25m to £24.25m based on the Foreign Secretary’s approval, extending activities from one to three years and adding new components (IDSF, GCFF, Rome Process) to address upstream drivers of irregular migration. This reflects learning about the need for sustained, multi-year engagement to achieve impact in migration and displacement.
risks_lessons.quote: "The programme’s moderate risk rating contrasts with CSSF Migration programme’s high-risk rating and helps ensure we have a balanced risk profile across the Migration Department’s wider programme portfolio." (D0006137.odt, Risk section)

co_funding_partners.partner: African Development Bank (Rome Process funding window)
Other donors to MMPTF/IDSF/GCFF (e.g., Germany, Canada)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The GCFF leverages initial donor financing to unlock additional concessional loans from Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs). For example, the UK’s £8m contribution to GCFF will enable recipient countries to borrow larger amounts for refugee-hosting projects. The MMPTF has already mobilised $57.5m from other donors.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The GCFF provides concessional financing (capital) for infrastructure and long-term projects, while other components (e.g., refugee education, gender equality grants) are revenue-based for service delivery and advocacy.
financial_details.quote: "The GCFF lends concessional finance to middle-income countries hosting large numbers of refugees, provided those funds will have a positive impact on refugees and host communities. Donors, including the UK, provide initial financing that leverages additional financing from Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)." (D0006138.odt, Global Concessional Financing Facility)

metadata.programme_name: Ukraine–Foundations for Infrastructure and Recovery (FIRE)
metadata.quote: "This programme lays the foundations for a robust approach to infrastructure identification, appraisal, project preparation, design and delivery in support of Ukraine’s reconstruction." (D0007263.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "This business case has been designed to be of short duration (up to 18 months)" (D0007263.odt, Development of this business case and its successor)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (training on 5CM methodology and BIM), technology development (establishing a Digital Construction Office), and policy influence (promoting standardized project preparation methodologies). It aims to strengthen Ukraine's infrastructure planning and delivery systems for post-war reconstruction.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme lays the foundations for a robust approach to infrastructure identification, appraisal, project preparation, design and delivery in support of Ukraine’s reconstruction." (D0007263.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: 5CM methodology adapted for Ukraine context
Training programme developed for national, regional, and local government levels
q3_expected_outputs.target: 300 officials

q3_expected_outputs.output: Training in 5CM rolled out by supplier
5CM alignment to DREAM (Ukraine's digital reconstruction management system)
Business cases developed using 5CM
Technical Assistance (TA) facility established for GoU infrastructure stakeholders
End of phase 2 report with recommendations for scaling up digital construction
q3_expected_outputs.target: July 2025

q3_expected_outputs.output: Upskilled SARDI team with requisite knowledge and skills for Digital Construction Office (DCO)
Introduction of BIM/digital construction into projects
q3_expected_outputs.target: 3 projects

q3_expected_outputs.output: Design of a more formal project preparation facility
Multi-year business case developed

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to institutionalize UK best practices in infrastructure project preparation (5CM methodology) and digital construction (BIM) within Ukraine's government systems, while providing technical assistance to build capacity for reconstruction planning.
what_objectives.quote: "The programme aims to be catalytic in moving Ukraine towards global best practice approaches to infrastructure identification, appraisal, project preparation and delivery before sub-optimal practices become embedded." (D0007263.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is in an active conflict situation with Russia, facing significant institutional fragmentation, capacity constraints, and coordination challenges among multiple donors. The RDNA3 report highlights US$152 billion in direct damage and US$499 billion in economic losses due to the war.
where_context.q5_source: "It is now two years since Russia illegally invaded Ukraine... Damage continues to be concentrated in Donetska, Kharkivska, Luhanska, Zaporizka, Khersonska, and Kyivska oblasts." (D0007263.odt, Background to Ukraine–damage and needs)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The ongoing war creates security risks for personnel and project sites. Weak institutional capacity at national and sub-national levels limits absorption of reconstruction funds. Fragmented donor coordination risks duplication. The decentralized governance structure complicates standardized approach implementation. Damage to existing infrastructure creates baseline challenges for new construction.
where_context.quote: "The scale of the challenge is enormous, and delivery of this agenda is made even more challenging by complex and at times fragmented institutional architecture for reconstruction and infrastructure; the decentralised governance structure of Ukraine; financial and capacity constraints at all levels of government; and the on-going challenges for GoU of co-ordinating a wide range of partners with different interests and approaches in reconstruction and reforms." (D0007263.odt, Background to Ukraine–damage and needs)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK's IPA leads on methodology development, training design, and technical standards (5CM and BIM), while Ukrainian partners (SARDI, MoR) implement with advisory support. Decision-making on programme adaptation rests with FCDO/IPA based on Ukrainian feedback.
q10_capacity_building_details: training in 5CM methodology (300 officials targeted)
training in BIM/digital construction
mentorship through technical assistance facility
institutional strengthening of SARDI and MoR
strategic advice on agency structure and processes

partner_organizations.name: Infrastructure and Projects Authority (IPA)
partner_organizations.role: Lead technical partner for 5CM and BIM implementation; training delivery; strategic advice

partner_organizations.name: Connected Places Catapult (CPC)
partner_organizations.role: BIM/digital construction technical support; DCO establishment

partner_organizations.name: State Agency for Restoration and Development of Infrastructure (SARDI)
partner_organizations.role: Primary Ukrainian implementing partner; capacity building recipient

partner_organizations.name: Ministry for Restoration (MoR)
partner_organizations.role: Policy alignment; strategic oversight; TA facility user

partner_organizations.name: PWC Ukraine
partner_organizations.role: Local training provider (anticipated contractor)

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-funder for future Project Preparation Facility

partner_organizations.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
partner_organizations.role: Potential co-funder for future Project Preparation Facility

who_partners.quote: "IPA will be the key delivery partner for output 1, and they will provide both strategic and direct inputs to the development of the 5CM and the training of partners in Ukraine... IPA offers the UK government’s international best-practice approach for developing public and PPP infrastructure projects." (D0007263.odt, Commercial Case - Output 1)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of: 1) Direct contracts with UK entities (IPA, CPC) via framework agreements; 2) A managed Technical Assistance facility for on-demand expertise; and 3) Potential future co-funding through multilateral partners (World Bank, EIB) for scaled-up facilities. Existing MOUs between FCDO/IPA and Ukrainian agencies provide the cooperation framework.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the overall programme with IPA as the primary implementer for 5CM/BIM components. A supplier-managed Technical Assistance facility provides flexible expertise on demand. Local training providers (e.g., PWC Ukraine) deliver scaled-up capacity building under FCDO-approved frameworks.
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: not stated (existing Green Cities and Infrastructure Centre of Expertise framework used)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The use of existing framework agreements (e.g., with PWC Ukraine) enables rapid mobilization. IPA and CPC were selected based on their status as UK government centers of expertise in infrastructure and digital construction, with proven international experience in 5CM and BIM implementation.
how_mechanism.quote: "In addition to the support of IPA, we anticipate the need to deliver training locally and at scale to the GOU. To deliver this, FCDO plan to contract a local training provider (likely PWC Ukraine) through the existing framework agreement held by the Green Cities and Infrastructure Centre of Expertise." (D0007263.odt, Commercial Case - Output 1)

how_governance.quote: "A payment mechanism will be agreed with the mon approval of this business case, in time to start delivery, within the two months following approval." (D0007263.odt, Commercial Case - Output 1)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The Technical Assistance facility allows flexible allocation to emerging priorities, but core 5CM/BIM components have fixed budgets. Reallocation between major workstreams would require FCDO approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a scoping phase for a multi-year follow-on business case, allowing adjustments based on GoU feedback and emerging needs. The TA facility provides built-in flexibility to address new technical assistance requests.
how_flexibility.quote: "This business case has been designed to be of short duration (up to 18 months) to achieve two objectives: 1) To provide [and continue] rapid support to pressing requests from the Government of Ukraine... 2) To provide the time needed to scope out long-term support through a multi-year business case." (D0007263.odt, Development of this business case and its successor)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (IPA/CPC) → Ukrainian Government Agencies (SARDI/MoR). The TA facility adds a third layer for specific expertise requests.
how_efficiency.quote: "Separate terms of reference for consultants working on this programme will be developed including milestone-based payments or payments by results where appropriate." (D0007263.odt, Commercial Case)

q24_alternatives_considered.description: FCDO exits current reconstruction support entirely. Discarded due to reputational risks and loss of momentum.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Do-nothing now but scope and design a multi-year business case
q24_alternatives_considered.description: Pause current activities to develop a 4-year strategy. Discarded due to risk of losing existing progress and missing immediate capacity-building opportunities.
Combine responsive support to GoU needs with parallel design of a long-term strategy. Chosen for balancing urgency with strategic planning.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The selected modality balances immediate capacity-building needs (5CM training, BIM pilot) with long-term strategic planning (multi-year BC design). It leverages UK's comparative advantage in infrastructure expertise while maintaining flexibility to adapt to Ukraine's evolving reconstruction priorities. The use of existing framework agreements enables rapid deployment.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: GoU fails to adopt 5CM methodology as policy
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong advocacy campaign and continued training in follow-on BC; demonstrate value through pilot projects

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low uptake of BIM/digital construction approaches
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Close collaboration with GoU to tailor to priority projects; leverage international standards (ISO 19650) credibility

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented donor coordination undermines standardization efforts
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Align with existing GoU initiatives (DREAM, PIM roadmap) and advocate for common business case approaches with IFIs

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Staff turnover in Ukrainian agencies disrupts capacity building
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Focus on institutionalizing methodologies rather than individual training; develop training materials in Ukrainian

why_rationale.quote: "Option iii-(supporting immediate requests+design)–recognises that there is more in-depth work needed by FCDO to develop a longer-term more strategic plan for infrastructure in the form of a multi-year business case... But while this is undertaken, FCDO can provide targeted support to MoR and SARDI through the output areas set out in para 50–output areas 1-3 helping to set the foundations for recovery and our future business case." (D0007263.odt, Options Analysis)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) Proven experience in conflict-affected environments; 2) Ability to operate under security constraints; 3) Existing relationships with Ukrainian government agencies. Local partners must navigate institutional fragmentation and capacity gaps.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict field operations and site visits
Weak institutional capacity requires intensive hands-on support rather than arm's-length partnerships
Donor coordination challenges necessitate partners with multilateral experience (e.g., IPA's relationships with WB, EIB)
Language barriers favor partners with Ukrainian-language capabilities or translation support
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for rapid standardization of project preparation methodologies (5CM) drives the choice of a closed consortium led by UK centers of expertise (IPA, CPC) with existing frameworks. The requirement for flexible technical assistance to address diverse capacity gaps leads to the TA facility design. BIM's technical complexity necessitates phased implementation with pilot projects.
q28_linkages: Standardization objective → Closed consortium with methodology experts (IPA)
Capacity gaps → Technical Assistance facility with on-demand expertise
Digital transformation → Phased BIM implementation with DCO establishment
Decentralized needs → Training rollout at national/regional/local levels
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) Rapid deployment of UK methodologies vs. local adaptation needs; 2) Standardization requirements vs. decentralized implementation realities; 3) Immediate capacity building vs. long-term institutionalization. The 18-month duration reflects a compromise to demonstrate quick wins while designing a more inclusive long-term approach.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Use of pre-existing UK methodologies (5CM, BIM) enables quick deployment but requires adaptation to Ukrainian context to ensure ownership
Northern-led technical leadership (IPA/CPC) provides global best practices but risks limited local decision-making without strong capacity transfer
Push for common business case approaches (5CM) must balance with diverse donor requirements and sub-national variations

intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context increases oversight intensity (milestone-based payments, regular progress reviews) and favors embedded advisory roles over arm's-length funding. High fragmentation risk drives more centralized coordination through IPA despite decentralized implementation needs.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Identified capacity gaps in SARDI/MoR (project management, PPP expertise, procurement) directly shape the TA facility design and the focus on institutional strengthening. The programme assigns UK partners to lead technical components (5CM, BIM) while building Ukrainian capacity to eventually take over.
intersections.quote: "Encouraging the GoU to improve its systems of project preparation and digital construction management now, to globally recognised standards, will enable it to make effective use of the resources currently available for reconstruction and be better positioned for scaling up delivery of infrastructure projects when conditions improve." (D0007263.odt, Strategic Case)

key_programme_risks: GoU fails to adopt 5CM as standard methodology
Low institutional uptake of BIM/digital construction
Staff turnover in Ukrainian agencies disrupts capacity building
Donor fragmentation undermines standardization efforts
Security situation limits field implementation
Political changes (e.g., ministerial reshuffles) alter priorities
Overemphasis on short-term results at expense of long-term reform
Limited absorptive capacity for reconstruction funds
Misalignment between national strategies and sub-national needs
Insufficient buy-in from Multilateral Development Banks for 5CM approach

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: GoU fails to adopt 5CM as standard methodology
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Pilot demonstrations with high-visibility projects; advocacy through PIM working group; alignment with DREAM system; continued training in follow-on BC

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low institutional uptake of BIM/digital construction
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Phase 3 focuses on organizational-level training and DCO establishment; leverage ISO 19650 international standards; integrate with DREAM platform
Institutionalize methodologies through policy adoption; develop Ukrainian-language materials; train broader cohort of officials (300 targeted)
Coordinate with WB/EIB on Project Preparation Facility; advocate for common approaches in donor forums; align with GoU's PIM roadmap
Focus on national-level systems and digital tools; prioritize areas under Ukrainian control; build remote capacity where possible

fcas_specific_lessons: Conflict contexts require flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., TA facility) to respond to changing priorities
Capacity building must balance immediate needs with long-term institutional development
Standardization efforts need strong government champions to navigate fragmented systems
Digital tools (BIM, DREAM) can mitigate physical access constraints
Donor coordination platforms are essential to avoid duplication in reconstruction
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Initial GGF-funded phase demonstrated strong GoU demand for 5CM training and institutional advice. The positive feedback from senior officials who attended UK training validated the approach but highlighted need for practical application support. Lessons included: 1) Importance of Ukrainian-language materials; 2) Need to balance theoretical training with project-based learning; 3) Value of high-level political buy-in (MOU with SARDI/MoR).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 18-month duration was selected to allow time for scoping a more adaptive multi-year programme. The TA facility was added to address ad-hoc technical needs identified in initial phase. BIM implementation was structured in phases (discovery → DCO establishment → scaling) based on GoU's digital maturity. Training targets were expanded from central to regional/local levels based on decentralization needs.
risks_lessons.quote: "The business case has been designed to be of short duration (up to 18 months) to achieve two objectives: 1) To provide [and continue] rapid support to pressing requests from the Government of Ukraine to build capacity to deliver infrastructure in support of Ukraine’s sustainable reconstruction... 2) To provide the time needed to scope out long-term support through a multi-year business case." (D0007263.odt, Development of this business case and its successor)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to catalyze adoption of standardized project preparation methodologies that will unlock larger reconstruction funding from Multilateral Development Banks. Successful implementation could increase the pipeline of 'bankable' projects eligible for IFI financing.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The budget primarily supports revenue expenditures (training, technical assistance, advisory services) rather than capital investments in physical infrastructure. Capital expenditures would be included in potential follow-on phases.
financial_details.quote: "This intervention is expected to cost £4.7m. The main cost drivers are fee rates of consultants and running training events." (D0007263.odt, Costs of intervention and drivers)

metadata.programme_name: Ensuring Minerals Enable Responsible Growth (EMERGE)
metadata.quote: This programme will spend up to £3.015 million over 2 years (Sept 2024-Sept 2026) to bolster efforts by African governments to optimise social and economic development benefits for their citizens from the minerals sector. (D0006409.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: This programme will spend up to £3.015 million over 2 years (Sept 2024-Sept 2026)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills), policy influence (informing policy decisions), and implementation research (testing/scaling interventions) to improve governance of critical minerals in Africa. It focuses on increasing value addition opportunities, enhancing revenue mobilisation, and improving mineral sector governance through anti-corruption efforts and international standards.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will spend up to £3.015 million over 2 years (Sept 2024-Sept 2026) to bolster efforts by African governments to optimise social and economic development benefits for their citizens from the minerals sector. [...] This will be achieved by supporting the development of value addition opportunities; enhancing revenue mobilisation; empowering effective oversight; and improving international standards and anti-corruption efforts. (D0006409.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Producercountrygovernmentssupportedorinfluencedtoimprovepoliciesandpracticeoncriticalmineralgoodgovernance
Intra-regionalbodiessupportedtoincreasetradeandvalueadditionopportunitiesincriticalmineralsupplychains
Relevantglobalentitiessupportedorinfluencedtostrengthencriticalmineralgovernancepoliciesandtheirresponsibleimplementation
SupportingthedevelopmentofacoherentnationalstrategyforcriticalmineralsgovernanceinDRC
SupportingCSOsandmediatoadvancetransparencyandapplyNRGI’scorruptiondiagnostictoolinGhana
Buildingoninitialadvicetogovernmentontheimplementationofthe2022MiningandMineralsActinUganda
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen critical mineral governance in Africa (DRC, Ghana, Uganda) by improving policies, enhancing revenue mobilisation, and promoting value addition, while also influencing international standards and anti-corruption efforts. It combines capacity building, policy influence, and implementation research to achieve sustainable and inclusive economic growth.
what_objectives.quote: The programme aims to focus on increasing value addition opportunities, enhancing revenue mobilisation, and improving mineral sector governance – including through promoting adherence with international standards and anti-corruption efforts – in order to accelerate sustainable development in mineral-rich countries. (D0006409.odt, What the programme will deliver)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is 'moderate,' reflecting challenges in governance, corruption, and weak institutions in the target countries, which are resource-rich but face significant poverty and institutional constraints.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate (D0006409.odt, Risk rating)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak governance and corruption in the mining sector (e.g., DRC scores 36/100 in NRGI’s Resource Governance Index) hinder revenue mobilisation and value addition. Regulatory gaps (e.g., Uganda’s Mining and Minerals Act 2022 lacks clarity on fiscal regimes) and limited stakeholder consultation (e.g., Ghana’s lithium deals) create risks of missed opportunities and supply chain disruptions. Artisanal mining and informal sector activities (e.g., 20% of DRC’s cobalt production) exacerbate environmental damage and social conflicts.
where_context.quote: DRC mining governance is weak, scoring the lowest (36/100) in NRGI’s 2021 Resource Governance Index. [...] On cobalt, where artisanal mining represents 20% of the production, corruption and human rights abuses erode DRC’s reputation and increase concerns about sustainable supply. (D0006409.odt, DRC country focus)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme emphasizes multi-stakeholder engagement, including government agencies, civil society, private sector, and community representatives in decision-making processes (e.g., Expert Group meetings in DRC, citizen awareness dialogues in Ghana). NRGI, as the implementer, facilitates these processes but does not unilaterally control decisions.
q10_capacity_building_details: training for policymakers and civil society (e.g., NRGI’s corruption diagnostic tool)
technical assistance to governments (e.g., fiscal regime design in Ghana)
institutional strengthening (e.g., supporting oversight roles for civil society in DRC)
advocacy and awareness dialogues (e.g., citizen engagement in Uganda)
multi-stakeholder convenings (e.g., regional coordination on DRC-Zambia battery value chains)

partner_organizations.name: Natural Resource Governance Institute (NRGI)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (with country offices in DRC, Ghana, Uganda)

partner_organizations.name: Government of DRC (e.g., ACTEDD, ARECOMS, EGC)
partner_organizations.role: local partner (policy implementation)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ghana (Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources)
partner_organizations.role: local partner (policy implementation)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Uganda (Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development)
partner_organizations.role: local partner (policy implementation)

partner_organizations.name: Civil society organizations (CSOs) in DRC, Ghana, Uganda
partner_organizations.role: oversight and advocacy

partner_organizations.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_organizations.role: technical assistance collaborator

partner_organizations.name: OECD, EITI, International Energy Agency (IEA)
partner_organizations.role: global standards and advocacy partners

who_partners.quote: NRGI will leverage their long-standing knowledge of mining governance to help countries seize the opportunities for rising demand for critical minerals and to avoid the pitfalls of previous mining booms. [...] NRGI will also work to translate evolving global governance norms into action within producing countries and support national and local efforts to apply and adapt international accountability systems. (D0006409.odt, Option 1: Support a singular specialist organisation)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme is structured as a direct grant to NRGI, with FCDO providing upfront funding for a 2-year period (£1.015m in FY2024/25 and £2m in FY2025/26). The grant supports NRGI’s existing work streams, with flexibility to adapt activities based on stakeholder engagement and emerging priorities.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: NRGI acts as the sole implementer, managing day-to-day delivery in collaboration with local government agencies, civil society, and regional bodies. FCDO provides oversight through annual reviews and milestone-based reporting, but operational decisions are delegated to NRGI and its in-country partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: NRGI was selected based on its proven track record in delivering similar programmes (e.g., RTPEED, which scored A/A+ in annual reviews) and its deep expertise in natural resource governance in the target countries. The business case highlights NRGI’s existing relationships with governments and civil society in DRC, Ghana, and Uganda as a key rationale for direct award.
how_mechanism.quote: Partnering with NRGI will enable them to put their previous country strategy work into action, focusing on ensuring these strategies are implemented successfully in selected countries. [...] RTPEED was a high performing programme, consistently scoring A in its annual reviews (AR) 2016-2020 and A+ in 2020. (D0006409.odt, Option 1: Support a singular specialist organisation)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: NRGI allocates funds to local stakeholders (e.g., CSOs, government agencies) based on programme priorities and multi-stakeholder agreements. Sub-awards are used for activities like corruption diagnostics, policy dialogues, and capacity-building workshops, with NRGI retaining oversight.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme establishes Expert Group meetings in each country (composed of government, civil society, private sector, and community representatives) to guide strategy development. NRGI also participates in global platforms like the NRGI/OECD/EITI Expert Group on Preventing Corruption in Transition Mineral Supply Chains for cross-cutting governance.
how_governance.quote: The programme will leverage and build on NRGI’s existing work in Africa and globally in year one. [...] Supporting the development of a coherent national strategy for critical minerals governance by convening and supporting Expert Group meetings (composed of representatives from key government agencies, civil society, private sector and community representatives). (D0006409.odt, What the programme will deliver)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between countries or activities within the approved budget envelope, subject to FCDO approval. The programme design allows for adjustments based on learning from the first year and stakeholder consultations, but major shifts require FCDO sign-off.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme employs an adaptive management approach, with activities in Years 2-3 shaped by lessons from Year 1 and stakeholder feedback. For example, Uganda’s focus on the National Mining Company’s governance structure was not initially detailed but will be developed based on early implementation insights.
how_flexibility.quote: The precise elaboration of project activities and priorities for future years will be shaped by the learning and progress of the project in the first financial year, and in consultation with key stakeholders including FCDO and NRGI’s national and international partners. (D0006409.odt, Future years)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → NRGI (implementer) → Local partners (government/CSOs). NRGI sub-contracts with local stakeholders but retains direct management responsibility.
how_efficiency.quote: We anticipate spending up to £1.015 million of financial support under Option 1 in Financial Year One, and a further £2m in Financial Year Two. (D0006409.odt, Breakdown of Financial Costs Under Option 1)

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Support a singular partner (NRGI) to improve critical minerals governance in target countries
Option 2: Support multiple partners for a composite critical minerals programme (e.g., NRGI + EITI + third-party contractor)
Option 3: Counterfactual – FCDO commits no new EDPD budget to the programme
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 1 (single partner) was chosen for its simplicity, lower transaction costs, and NRGI’s proven track record in the target countries. The business case emphasizes NRGI’s existing relationships with governments and civil society, which reduce start-up delays and align with FCDO’s strategic goals for responsible mineral governance. Option 2 was deemed more complex and costly, while Option 3 risked reputational damage and missed opportunities for UK influence.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (lower overhead for Option 1)
risk mitigation (NRGI’s local expertise reduces implementation risks)
past experience (NRGI’s success with RTPEED programme)
partner capacity (NRGI’s established networks in DRC, Ghana, Uganda)
equity (Option 1’s focus on local stakeholder engagement)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single partner (NRGI) could limit diversity of approaches or create bottlenecks if NRGI faces operational challenges.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO’s milestone-based oversight and annual reviews ensure accountability. NRGI’s multi-stakeholder governance structures (e.g., Expert Groups) mitigate single-point failure risks.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited competition in partner selection might reduce innovation or value for money.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: NRGI’s strong track record (e.g., RTPEED’s A+ ratings) and adaptive management approach justify direct award. The programme’s focus on learning and stakeholder feedback allows for course correction.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (NRGI’s proven impact in similar contexts)
why_rationale.quote: Option 1 has the overall impact aims to drive systemic change and equitable benefits from the responsible scale-up of critical minerals in Africa, and to enhance responsible business practices in international transition minerals supply chains. [...] Partnering with NRGI will enable them to put their previous country strategy work into action, focusing on ensuring these strategies are implemented successfully in selected countries. (D0006409.odt, Option 1: Support a singular specialist organisation)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk context in DRC (e.g., weak governance, corruption) and regulatory gaps in Uganda/Ghana limit the pool of capable local partners. NRGI’s established presence and trust with governments/CSOs in these countries were critical for selection, as few other organizations have the required expertise and relationships to navigate these constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: DRC’s weak governance (scoring 36/100 in NRGI’s index) requires partners with deep local knowledge to engage effectively with state actors like ACTEDD and EGC.
Uganda’s incomplete Mining and Minerals Act 2022 necessitates partners who can provide technical assistance on fiscal regimes and environmental safeguards.
Ghana’s civil society concerns about lithium deals demand partners skilled in transparency and multi-stakeholder dialogue.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (policy influence, capacity building, implementation research) require a delivery structure that combines NRGI’s global standards expertise with localized, adaptive engagement. The single-partner model was chosen to balance top-down governance improvements (e.g., anti-corruption laws) with bottom-up stakeholder empowerment (e.g., CSO oversight training).
q28_linkages: Policy influence goals → Need for NRGI’s participation in global platforms (e.g., OECD/EITI Expert Groups) to shape international standards.
Capacity building objectives → Requirement for embedded training and mentorship, necessitating NRGI’s in-country presence.
Implementation research → Adaptive management structure to test and scale interventions (e.g., DRC’s variable royalties modelling).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The business case explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery and inclusive partnerships. For example, the direct award to NRGI (efficiency) was balanced by requiring multi-stakeholder Expert Groups (equity) in each country. The programme also prioritizes local content and beneficiation (e.g., Ghana’s Green Minerals Policy) despite potential short-term delays, reflecting a trade-off between speed and equitable outcomes.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct award to NRGI accelerates implementation but risks limiting diverse perspectives; mitigated by mandatory CSO/community representation in governance structures.
Expertise vs. ownership: NRGI’s technical leadership (e.g., corruption diagnostics) is paired with capacity-building for local actors to ensure long-term ownership.
Cost vs. reach: Focus on 3 countries (DRC, Ghana, Uganda) balances depth of engagement with geographic coverage, acknowledging trade-offs in regional scalability.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘moderate’ risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., annual reviews) and adaptive management. For example, DRC’s corruption risks necessitate embedded anti-corruption tools and frequent stakeholder check-ins, while Uganda’s nascent mining sector requires flexible technical assistance to address emerging gaps in the Mining and Minerals Act.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building objectives directly shape partner roles: NRGI provides technical training (e.g., fiscal regime design in Ghana), while local CSOs and government agencies take on increasingly active roles in oversight and policy implementation over time. The programme’s phased approach (e.g., Year 1 scoping → Years 2-3 implementation) reflects this gradual capacity transfer.
intersections.quote: The programme will leverage and build on NRGI’s existing work in Africa and globally in year one. [...] Supporting the development of a coherent national strategy for critical minerals governance by convening and supporting Expert Group meetings (composed of representatives from key government agencies, civil society, private sector and community representatives). (D0006409.odt, What the programme will deliver)

key_programme_risks: Weak governance in DRC (e.g., corruption in cobalt supply chains) could undermine revenue mobilisation and value addition efforts.
Regulatory gaps in Uganda’s Mining and Minerals Act 2022 may lead to inconsistent implementation or investor disputes.
Limited civil society capacity in Ghana to monitor lithium deals could result in opaque contracting processes.
Geopolitical tensions over critical minerals (e.g., DRC-Zambia battery value chain competition) may disrupt regional coordination.
Failure to align with international ESG standards could reduce investor confidence and supply chain resilience.
Climate and environmental risks (e.g., artisanal mining damage in Uganda) may trigger community conflicts or regulatory backlash.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: NRGI will support the implementation of the 2022 anti-corruption law, including beneficial ownership training, and apply corruption diagnostic tools to mineral value chains. Multi-stakeholder Expert Groups will enhance oversight.
Technical assistance to the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development on fiscal regimes, environmental safeguards, and National Mining Company governance.
Training for CSOs and media on transparency tools (e.g., NRGI’s corruption diagnostic) and quarterly engagement with the Minister of Lands and Natural Resources.
Regional convenings on DRC-Zambia battery value chains, aligned with AfCFTA and Lobito Corridor initiatives, to harmonize policies and reduce trade barriers.
NRGI will work with OECD/EITI to strengthen global governance norms and incorporate African producer perspectives into consumer-country policies (e.g., EU CBAM).
Socio-environmental impact assessments and community beneficiation schemes (e.g., Ghana’s Mineral Development Fund reforms) to address local grievances.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from DRC’s Mining Sector Reform programme (2012–2019) highlight the need for sustained CSO engagement to improve transparency, even in high-risk contexts.
Ghana’s experience with oil revenue management frameworks (lacking equivalent provisions for mining) underscores the importance of tailored fiscal regimes for critical minerals.
Uganda’s ASM sector challenges demonstrate the need for gradual formalization to avoid displacing livelihoods while improving governance.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The RTPEED programme (2015–2019) showed that concerted support for strategy implementation (not just design) is critical for success. Key lessons included: (1) Focus on closing implementation gaps (e.g., DRC’s suspended mining operations due to ESG failures). (2) CSO engagement is essential for unlocking governance improvements (e.g., DRC’s transparency gains). (3) Regional coordination (e.g., DRC-Zambia battery plans) must align with national priorities to avoid conflicts.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The EMERGE programme incorporates RTPEED’s lessons by: (1) Prioritizing implementation support over strategy development (e.g., DRC’s anti-corruption law rollout). (2) Embedding CSO capacity-building as a core objective (e.g., Ghana’s lithium sector transparency). (3) Adding explicit regional coordination components (e.g., DRC-Zambia value chains) to address previous silos.
risks_lessons.quote: The Releasing the Transformational Potential of Extractives for Economic Development (RTPEED) project [...] highlighted the critical role of resource governance in helping countries translate oil, gas and mineral wealth into better quality of life for citizens. Major lessons learned through RTPEED include the need for concerted support and focus on implementation gaps. (D0006409.odt, Why the UK should intervene)

financial_details.quote: We anticipate spending up to £1.015 million of financial support under Option 1 in Financial Year One, and a further £2m in Financial Year Two. (D0006409.odt, Breakdown of Financial Costs Under Option 1)

metadata.programme_name: Accelerating Education Attainment in Central Asia for Resilience (AEAR–CA)
metadata.quote: The UK will spend up to £5 million over the next three years to establish the AEAR-CA. (D0006221.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The UK will spend up to £5 million over the next three years to establish the AEAR-CA.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (improving teacher competency, educational quality assurance systems), service delivery (English language development, textbook provision), and implementation research (piloting interventions and testing hypotheses about English language impact). It aims to strengthen education systems while directly addressing gaps in English proficiency and inclusive education.
what_objectives.q1_source: The UK will apply the UK’s comparative advantage of education expertise to: (i) identify catalytic gaps in educational provision and provide targeted support for equitable and quality education, particularly augmenting support to UNICEF as lead on GPE; (ii) provide systemic support to: improve teacher competency; educational quality assurance systems; and English language development across the region with the British Council and Voluntary Services Overseas (VSO); (iii) promote a XHMG UK education offer built on evidence/learning, with education (including English language skills) being an enabler for economic/social development and a counterbalance to Russian influence in the region. (D0006221.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Improved teacher competency in English language proficiency and pedagogical skills
Strengthened educational quality assurance systems (including assessment frameworks)
Provision of English language textbooks for Kyrgyzstan
Scholarships for marginalized women/girls in higher education
Enhanced coordination of education projects to reduce aid fragmentation
Increased English language proficiency among students (targeting B2 CEFR levels)
Improved learning outcomes in reading and numeracy
Establishment of school improvement systems and inclusive education practices
Policy development informed by programme data and evidence
what_objectives.summary: AEAR-CA aims to catalyze systemic improvements in Central Asia's education sector by focusing on teacher quality, English language proficiency, inclusive education, and coordination of donor efforts, while countering Russian influence and promoting economic resilience.
what_objectives.quote: Education is the bedrock of pluralistic societies. It plays a crucial role in economic and social development and building resilience. [...] The programme will specifically work on 4 interrelated components: (1) Improve the quality of teachers; (2) Establish/Strengthen links between the UK and Central Asia Higher Education Institutions; (3) Need-based support to strengthen individual country Quality Assurance Systems; (4) Build capacities of government structures responsible to coordinate education projects/programmes to tackle aid fragmentation. (D0006221.odt, Business case summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The region is described as volatile with security risks (Afghanistan instability, Russian influence, water resource tensions), weak institutions, and corruption risks in education systems. The programme risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Major'.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Major. (D0006221.odt, SummarySheet) [...] The security situation in the region at times remain volatile. (D0006221.odt, Cost elements section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security volatility increases administrative costs and risks to implementation. Weak regulatory frameworks and corruption undermine education quality and assessment systems. Rural-urban disparities and disability access gaps limit equitable education delivery. Russian linguistic dominance creates barriers for English language adoption, while limited data on learning outcomes hampers evidence-based reforms.
where_context.quote: Central Asia is a pivotal region for advancing UK interests in the world. The region sits within Russia’s so-called sphere of influence, with strong ties through security, trade, investment, and remittances. [...] The shifting geopolitical context offers a crossroads for the UK’s engagement and development offer. [...] Development pathways vary across the region and poverty rates remain persistently high in rural areas. [...] National examinations have historically been undermined by a lack of consistent administration, or marking, as well as a lack of anonymity and transparency of process. (D0006221.odt, Business case summary)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains oversight and approval authority, with UK-based organizations (British Council, UNICEF, Aga Khan Foundation) leading implementation. Local partners (e.g., University of Central Asia) play operational roles but decision-making remains with Northern institutions.
q10_capacity_building_details: Improvement in Initial English Language Teacher Education (IELTE) programmes
Continuous Professional Development (CPD) for teachers and civil servants
Mentorship and coaching for teachers
Training for higher education officials in English proficiency
Scholarships for marginalized women/girls
Support for inclusive education strategies and policies

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: Lead on accelerating English language learning; teacher training; textbook provision
partner_organizations.location: UK (with regional offices in Central Asia)

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Assessment and school improvement systems; quality assurance; working with Aga Khan Foundation

partner_organizations.name: Aga Khan Foundation (AKF)
partner_organizations.role: Expanding education opportunities; higher education linkages; sub-awards to VSO and University of Central Asia

partner_organizations.name: Voluntary Services Overseas (VSO)
partner_organizations.role: Teacher training and deployment of volunteers

partner_organizations.name: University of Central Asia (UCA)
partner_organizations.role: Higher education training and scholarships

partner_organizations.name: University of Sussex
partner_organizations.role: Partnership with National Girls Teacher Training College in Almaty

who_partners.quote: All three delivery partners have a longstanding presence in Central Asia with well-established field offices and partnerships with relevant government authorities to facilitate delivery with a sustainable impact. (D0006221.odt, Procurement route section) [...] The programme will allow BC to share their considerable experience with other countries in the region to deliver training to teachers. (D0006221.odt, Efficiency section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of instruments: (1) Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the British Council; (2) Contribution Arrangement with UNICEF under FCDO’s broader framework; (3) Accountable Grant Arrangement with Aga Khan Foundation; and (4) FCDO-recruited programme-funded posts for management oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO manages the programme through a closed consortium of pre-selected partners (British Council, UNICEF, Aga Khan Foundation) with defined roles. Each partner leads specific components, with FCDO retaining oversight through programme-funded posts and regular reviews. The structure is designed to leverage existing relationships and local presence.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on their longstanding presence in Central Asia, existing frameworks with FCDO, and specialized expertise in education. The document states: "All three delivery partners have a longstanding presence in Central Asia with well-established field offices and partnerships with relevant government authorities."
how_mechanism.quote: The FCDO also holds strong global relationships with all three organisations with negotiated global MoUs and framework arrangements already in place. (D0006221.odt, Procurement route section) [...] The following three Options have been evaluated: [...] Option A: A flexible facility with a focus on improving English language provision and influencing wider educational reforms, via assistance to IFIs and strategic delivery partners like the British Council, UNICEF, and Aga Khan Development Network, including VSO & the University of Central Asia (UCA). (D0006221.odt, Options Appraisal)

how_governance.q16_sub_award_allocation_details: Selected organisations (e.g., Aga Khan Foundation) will manage sub-awards to VSO and UCA, but FCDO must approve these arrangements. The document states: "Selected organisations will be expected to conduct enhanced due diligence assessments of their downstream implementing partners before FCDO will enter into a funding agreement with them."
how_governance.quote: Performance of partners against different components will be managed as set out in the Management Case. The FCDO team will ensure funding commitments are only made to organisations capable of delivering quality interventions and services within Central Asia’s context fostering programme sustainability. [...] Work plans and associated KPIs/milestones will be mutually agreed by FCDO and respective partners for each quarter of implementation linking to the logical framework. (D0006221.odt, Delivery Modalities section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components based on lessons learned during the inception phase and annual reviews, but this requires FCDO approval. The programme includes a break clause allowing adjustments at review points.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The first year acts as a pilot, with interventions scaled up, down, or adjusted based on lessons learned. The programme includes a break clause at regular review points to respond to implementation experience or spending reviews. Adjustments require satisfactory performance against KPIs.
how_flexibility.quote: The first year will act as pilot for interventions, to then scale up, down or to adjust interventions as resources permit and based on lessons learned. (D0006221.odt, Option A) [...] FCDO will incorporate a break clause into all delivery arrangements thereby giving FCDO the option to invoke a break at or after inception, at regular review points (in the case of underperformance against agreed Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in two subsequent performance reviews). (D0006221.odt, Programme Delivery Cycle)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partners (British Council/UNICEF/AKF) → End Beneficiaries (teachers, students, institutions). Some components involve a third layer (e.g., AKF → VSO/UCA).
how_efficiency.quote: Work plans and associated KPIs/milestones will be mutually agreed by FCDO and respective partners for each quarter of implementation linking to the logical framework. For each individual milestone, means of verification will be set out and agreed as part of this process. (D0006221.odt, Delivery Modalities section) [...] Fee and direct expenses: Management fees and salary costs of technical experts; and costs for direct expenses to education and systems strengthening interventions are likely to constitute more than 80% of the programme budget. (D0006221.odt, Cost elements section)

q24_alternatives_considered: Establish a flexible 1-year pilot facility to test multiple organisations’ capabilities, with a focus on education reform and English language provision (with potential to scale up).
Increase existing contributions into larger multilateral-led donor programmes.
Do nothing further; continue to support education through the UK’s contribution to the Global Partnership of Education (GPE) and English language training through ISF.
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option A (flexible facility) was chosen for its ability to: (1) drive sustainable, systems-level interventions aligned with UK priorities; (2) leverage existing partnerships for rapid scaling; (3) tailor approaches to country contexts; (4) crowd in additional funding; and (5) maintain high UK visibility. The rationale emphasizes flexibility, catalytic impact, and alignment with Central Asian governments’ education strategies.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complexity in coordinating across multiple partners adds risk, especially given the brief pilot window.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO’s risk appetite must incorporate these conditions; robust MEL framework and regular reviews will manage implementation challenges.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: English language provision outcomes at the classroom level have a less comprehensive evidence base.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme will closely monitor outcomes and explore undertaking a randomised control trial during the pilot to generate evidence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Effective management from FCDO is necessary but may be challenged by election-related delays.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The programme includes a break clause to adapt to spending review decisions and a phased approach to scale interventions based on learning.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Uncertain future funding may limit long-term success after the pilot.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The flexible design allows for adjustments based on available resources, and the pilot phase will demonstrate value to secure continued support.

why_rationale.quote: On the balance of these cases, our preferred option is A. With a focus on English language provision, the flexible facility with a consortia of delivery partners will bring substantial expertise as well as the ability to leverage existing relationships and local partnerships, that delivers outcomes mutually beneficial in enhancing regional educational capabilities and meeting UK objectives. (D0006221.odt, Options Appraisal) [...] The programme will also partner with FCDO research Centrally Managed Programmes (CMPs) among others to test the hypothesis whether where English language is promoted it enables the school community to make overall improvements. (D0006221.odt, Business case summary)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The geopolitical context (Russian influence, security risks) and weak institutional capacity in Central Asia limit partner selection to organizations with established regional presence and government relationships. The document states: "All three delivery partners have a longstanding presence in Central Asia with well-established field offices and partnerships with relevant government authorities to facilitate delivery with a sustainable impact."
q27_constraints_detail: Security volatility requires partners with risk management experience.
Russian linguistic dominance necessitates partners skilled in navigating language transitions.
Weak education institutions demand partners with systems-strengthening expertise.
Government preferences for English language training favor partners like the British Council with proven methodologies.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s focus on systemic education reform (teacher quality, assessments, coordination) determines the need for a consortium structure with specialized partners. English language objectives drive the inclusion of the British Council, while quality assurance goals require UNICEF’s expertise. The mixed delivery approach (pilot + scaling) reflects the need to test interventions before broader implementation.
q28_linkages: Teacher quality improvements → Requires British Council’s pedagogical expertise and VSO’s volunteer deployment.
English language focus → Necessitates textbook provision and higher education linkages (UCA/Sussex University).
Aid coordination → Demands a central management role for FCDO to align donor efforts.
Pilot phase → Enables adaptive management to refine interventions based on evidence.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses tensions between rapid delivery and inclusion, noting that: (1) English language training risks crowding out foundational learning for marginalized groups; (2) Urban-rural disparities require targeted interventions that may slow overall progress; (3) Scholarships for women/girls are prioritized despite potential delays in broader systemic reforms. The document states: "There are risks related to English language crowding out resources and time for foundational learning and exacerbating inequalities."
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Pilot phase allows testing but may delay full-scale implementation.
Expertise vs ownership: Northern partners lead delivery, limiting Southern institutional ownership.
Cost vs reach: High-quality teacher training (e.g., coaching/mentoring) is resource-intensive but critical for equity.
English focus vs foundational skills: Risk of prioritizing English over basic literacy/numeracy in resource-constrained settings.
intersections.risk_affects_management: The ‘Major’ risk rating drives intensive oversight, including quarterly reviews, embedded safeguarding measures, and a break clause for underperformance. The document notes: "FCDO’s risk appetite must be sufficient to incorporate these conditions."
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is core to partner roles: (1) British Council focuses on teacher training to address low English proficiency; (2) UNICEF leads quality assurance to strengthen weak systems; (3) AKF/VSO deploy volunteers to fill local gaps. Partners’ capacity determines their ability to absorb sub-awards (e.g., AKF managing VSO/UCA).
intersections.quote: The programme will specifically work on 4 interrelated components [...] Combined, the above activities will increase the capacity of the CA national education systems to undertake measurable improvement in the quality and inclusiveness of teaching and learning. (D0006221.odt, Business case summary) [...] There are risks related to English language crowding out resources and time for foundational learning and exacerbating inequalities which would need to be assessed. (D0006221.odt, English language Evidence section)

key_programme_risks: Security volatility in Central Asia disrupting implementation.
Low English proficiency among teachers limiting programme impact.
Weak education institutions undermining systemic reforms.
Corruption in examination systems affecting credibility of assessments.
Russian influence countering UK education objectives.
Uncertain UK funding post-election delaying or reducing programme scope.
Duplication of efforts with other donors (e.g., GPE, World Bank).
Limited evidence base for English language interventions at classroom level.
Child protection and SEAH risks in education programming.
Exchange rate fluctuations impacting budget stability.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Security assessments and costing included in bids; FCDO’s risk appetite adjusted for regional conditions.
Targeted CPD, mentoring, and revised IELTE programmes; action research to test interventions.
Systems-strengthening focus (e.g., quality assurance, school inspections) with UNICEF/AKF.
Support for transparent assessment frameworks and anonymity in testing.
Promote English as a counterbalance; diversify information sources to reduce disinformation.
Phased approach with break clauses; demonstrate value to secure future resources.
Coordinate with GPE/World Bank; focus on catalytic gaps (e.g., English language).
Pilot phase with randomised control trials; action research with research CMPs.
Rigorous due diligence, GESI analysis, SEAH prevention integrated into design.
Budget based on sterling commitments; partners manage local currency risks.

fcas_specific_lessons: Leverage existing partner relationships to navigate volatile contexts (e.g., British Council’s regional presence).
Prioritize systems-strengthening to address institutional weaknesses (e.g., quality assurance with UNICEF).
Use pilot phases to test interventions before scaling in high-risk environments.
Integrate safeguarding and GESI analysis upfront to mitigate FCAS-specific risks (e.g., SEAH, corruption).
Align with national education strategies to ensure government buy-in and sustainability.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The document references lessons from Kenya’s Tusome literacy programme, which demonstrated that high-level buy-in and pedagogical improvements (e.g., teaching at the right level) are critical for success. It also notes that additional inputs alone (e.g., textbooks) without pedagogical changes are ineffective (‘bad buys’).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates: (1) a pilot phase to test and adapt interventions; (2) action research to address evidence gaps; (3) break clauses for flexibility; and (4) a focus on teacher quality based on global evidence (e.g., Kenya’s 30% improvement with pedagogical reforms).
risks_lessons.quote: One mistake that many systems make is to assume that simply investing more in inputs at the margin, without improving how they are used or for whom, will improve learning. [...] Studies in many different settings have found that additional inputs alone, used in support of ‘business as usual,’ without improving how they are being used, are not effective and are ‘bad buys.’ (D0006221.odt, Evidence and Value for Money section) [...] The programme will also partner with FCDO research Centrally Managed Programmes (CMPs) among others to test the hypothesis whether where English language is promoted it enables the school community to make overall improvements. (D0006221.odt, Business case summary)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Potential co-financing from Tajikistan’s Ministry of Finance for women’s scholarships; crowding in of additional English language support from target countries (e.g., VSO volunteer deployment). The British Council’s expanded presence may attract further funding.
financial_details.quote: Fee and direct expenses: Management fees and salary costs of technical experts; and costs for direct expenses to education and systems strengthening interventions are likely to constitute more than 80% of the programme budget. (D0006221.odt, Cost elements section) [...] The Government of Tajikistan may co-finance support for women participants from Tajikistan in accordance with an offer from the Minister of Finance. (D0006221.odt, Component 2)

metadata.programme_name: Empowering Survivors of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Sexual Harassment (ES-SEAH)

quote.programme_name: "Empowering Survivors of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Sexual Harassment (ES-SEAH)" (D0006390.odt, Title)
quote.duration: "up to £15m over 5 years" (D0006390.odt, Programme summary)
quote.sector: "Ending violence against women and girls" (D0006390.odt, Input Sector Code)

metadata.duration_source: "up to £15m over 5 years across multiple countries" (D0006390.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: ES-SEAH combines implementation research (testing survivor-centred reporting mechanisms), capacity building (strengthening WROs and UN systems), and service delivery (direct support to survivors). The programme explicitly aims to generate evidence on 'what works' while simultaneously delivering survivor support and strengthening institutional responses.
what_objectives.q1_source: "ES-SEAH will provide up to £15m over 5 years... with the aim of increasing reporting of SEAH perpetrated by aid actors and strengthening survivor-centred responses" and "Build the evidence base on ‘what works’ for a survivor-centred approach" (D0006390.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Improved survivor-centred support aligned with IASC Principles and UN OVRA’s Victims’ Rights Statement
Enhanced evidence base on supporting SEAH survivors (via participatory action research)
Increased SEAH reporting through accessible, context-appropriate mechanisms
Global public goods (guidance, tools) to inform wider safeguarding sector
Strengthened capacity of 3-5 Women’s Rights Organisations (WROs) to handle SEAH cases
q3_expected_outputs.target: 3-5 countries

q3_expected_outputs.output: Support to UN mechanisms (OVRA/Trust Fund) for survivor-centred responses

what_objectives.summary: ES-SEAH aims to simultaneously test and scale survivor-centred reporting mechanisms, build capacity of local WROs and UN systems, and generate actionable evidence to inform global safeguarding practices. The programme bridges research, implementation, and institutional strengthening.

quote.objectives: "The 3 components of the ES-SEAH programme will be: Component 1: Engaging Women’s Rights Organisations... Component 2: Improving the evidence-base... Component 3: Addressing the rights and dignity of victims-survivors of SEAH committed by UN personnel" (D0006390.odt, Programme components)
quote.mixed_approach: "Participatory action research will be undertaken to develop the best way to deliver a survivor-centred response" and "WROs will work closely with PSEA Networks... to hold aid agencies to account" (D0006390.odt, Components 1-2)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in contexts with chronic under-reporting of SEAH due to power imbalances, weak institutional responses, and risks of retaliation against survivors. The overall programme risk rating is explicitly categorized as 'Major' in the document.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Major" and "SEAH remains grossly under-reported, due to factors such as poor reporting mechanisms and responses that are not survivor-centred" (D0006390.odt, Context sections)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Under-reporting is driven by fear of retaliation (security), lack of trust in aid agencies (weak institutions), harmful social norms (political economy), and inaccessible reporting channels (language/data). In FCAS contexts, survivors face heightened risks of community backlash and loss of aid if they report abuses. Digital reporting mechanisms exclude marginalized groups (e.g., women with disabilities).

quote.constraints: "Retaliation can also be experienced from the community (‘We will beat her if she speaks out to an organisation… we will lose all aid’)" and "Reporting mechanisms can be highly inaccessible for the most marginalised... women with disabilities have particular difficulty" (D0006390.odt, Context: Under-reporting)
quote.FCAS: "The lack of awareness that SEAH is a form of violence... contributes to under-reporting. Communities where harmful social norms and gender-based violence are already prevalent are more likely to normalise behaviours that should be reported" (D0006390.odt, Context: Under-reporting)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The lead supplier (potentially Northern-based) will manage the programme, but WROs (Southern-based) will co-design interventions and have representation in governance. Decision-making is structured to include survivor feedback and local WRO input, with FCDO oversight.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for WROs on SEAH case handling
Technical assistance to align with IASC survivor-centred principles
Research capacity for participatory action research
Institutional strengthening of UN mechanisms (e.g., OVRA)
Mentorship via lead supplier’s in-country presence

partner_organizations.name: Lead Supplier (consortium)
partner_organizations.role: Programme management, capacity building, research coordination

partner_organizations.name: 3-5 Women’s Rights Organisations (WROs)
partner_organizations.role: Survivor support, community engagement, local reporting mechanisms

partner_organizations.name: UN Office of the Victims’ Rights Advocate (OVRA)
partner_organizations.role: UN-wide survivor support, rights advocacy, justice facilitation

partner_organizations.name: UN Trust Fund for Survivors of SEA
partner_organizations.role: Funding mechanism for survivor-centred projects

partner_organizations.name: PSEA Networks (where existing)
partner_organizations.role: Coordination with aid agencies, accountability

quote.structure: "Option C: Fund one lead supplier (to deliver components 1 and 2) and UN partners (component 3)" (D0006390.odt, Appraisal of options)
quote.partnership: "The lead supplier will be expected to contract an independent evaluation... WROs will work closely with PSEA Networks... to hold aid agencies to account" (D0006390.odt, Components 1-2)
quote.capacity: "The lead supplier will build the capacity of WROs to be a more effective reporting channel for SEAH complaints and to provide a survivor-centred response" (D0006390.odt, Option C)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Components 1-2 will use a **contract** with a lead supplier (open competition) to manage WROs and research. Component 3 will use **Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)** with UN agencies (OVRA/Trust Fund). The contract includes performance-based payments, while UN funding follows multi-donor trust fund mechanisms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: A lead supplier (consortium) will sub-contract WROs and research partners, with FCDO oversight. UN components will be managed via direct MoUs. The structure allows for adaptive management, with quarterly reviews and a survivor feedback panel.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The pre-market survey showed strong interest from both NGOs and private sector (50/50 split), with 64% preferring a consortium approach. Open competition was chosen to drive value for money and ensure technical expertise in SEAH survivor support and research.

quote.instrument: "Components 1 and 2 will be delivered through one open contract... A procurement competition will be used to drive Value for Money" and "Component 3 will be delivered through... MoUs with the relevant UN agencies" (D0006390.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.selection: "The EME survey ran in May 2024. Of the 14 suppliers who expressed an interest to lead ES-SEAH, 64% indicated a consortia approach would be their preferred approach" (D0006390.odt, Commercial Case)
