how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme will have: 1) A **Steering Committee** for the evaluation (with FCDO, EQUALS, and 10% of an FCDO Evaluation Advisor’s time); 2) **Quarterly progress meetings** with partners (including WROs and UN); 3) A **survivor feedback panel** for oversight of global public goods; 4) **Safeguarding Unit Programme Board** (meeting every 4-6 weeks) for compliance and risk management.

quote.governance: "The FCDO will be on an evaluation Steering Committee... The Committee will develop the ToR, assess bids and oversee the supplier’s draft and final reports" and "Quarterly progress meetings will be held with partners... The ES-SEAH programme team will convene on a quarterly basis" (D0006390.odt, MEL and Management sections)
quote.oversight: "The SRO will be responsible for escalating any risks outside of appetite to the Safeguarding Unit’s Deputy Director... Arisk register will be kept for the programme, which will be reviewed at least quarterly" (D0006390.odt, Risk Management)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components with FCDO approval, particularly between Components 1-2 (WROs/research) and Component 3 (UN mechanisms). The document notes: "If our scoping of further UN mechanisms... leads to our understanding that other mechanisms would not be in alignment with the UK’s goals... we may decide to scale back the ES-SEAH budget, or put more into components 1 and 2."
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses **participatory action research** to continuously inform implementation. The log frame will be reviewed regularly based on research findings, and a **review clause** is included for mid-programme adjustments. Survivors’ feedback is embedded in reporting.

quote.flexibility: "There will be flexibility in how the budget is allocated... This approach also allows flexibility related to the availability of ODA in future years" (D0006390.odt, Financial Case)
quote.adaptive: "The log frame will be reviewed at regular intervals based on action research findings... We will require that victim-survivor feedback is included in reporting" (D0006390.odt, MEL section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Supplier (consortium) → WROs/Research Sub-contractors → Survivors/Communities

quote.layers: "The lead supplier will be expected to set up, or already have a presence in, the 3-5 countries... It will oversee research that brings together learning from across all countries" (D0006390.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.payments: "Payments will be made in advance for UN agencies and in arrears for the lead supplier delivering components 1 and 2" (D0006390.odt, Financial Management)

q24_alternatives_considered.reason_discounted: Would undermine UK’s safeguarding leadership and leave gaps in survivor support.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: B: Fund individual WROs, research supplier, and UN partners directly
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_discounted: High management burden for FCDO; risk of fragmented learning; WROs may lack capacity to influence aid agencies alone.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: C: Fund one lead supplier (components 1-2) and UN partners (component 3) (RECOMMENDED)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_selected: Balances efficiency (single contract) with adaptability (consortium approach); enables global public goods creation; leverages existing UN partnerships.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option C was selected for its **value for money** (lower FCDO management burden), **risk mitigation** (lead supplier builds WRO capacity), **flexibility** (adaptive research), and **equity** (survivor-centred design with local WROs). The consortium model allows testing approaches across diverse contexts while generating scalable evidence.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FCDO criticised for not funding WROs directly
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strong partnership principles based on mutual respect; lead supplier must engage WROs in decision-making.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lead supplier may lack influence over aid agencies’ responses
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Select supplier with proven track record in safeguarding; use action research to adapt approaches.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UN mechanisms fail to drive systemic change
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Fund only mechanisms showing progress (e.g., OVRA’s Victims’ Rights Statement); work with UNSG’s Special Coordinator for SEA.

quote.rationale: "Option C... allows for a more robust way to gather learning on ‘what works’ and the creation of global public goods... This approach is less burdensome for the FCDO to manage" (D0006390.odt, Appraisal of options)
quote.vfm: "To ensure ES-SEAH represents VfM under Option C, we will expect partners to report at least annually against VfM indicators" (D0006390.odt, Value for Money statement)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme’s multi-country, high-risk contexts (e.g., DRC, FCAS) constrain partner selection to organizations with: 1) **in-country presence** (to mitigate security risks for WROs); 2) **experience in GBV/SEAH** (to navigate harmful social norms); 3) **trust of marginalized groups** (e.g., women with disabilities, LGBT+). The lead supplier must have local roots or establish in-country offices to support WROs facing community backlash.
q27_constraints_detail: WROs must be embedded in communities to avoid retaliation risks (e.g., ‘we will lose all aid’ threats).
Partners need capacity to handle digital exclusion (e.g., non-digital reporting for women with disabilities).
UN mechanisms must align with UK priorities, limiting options to OVRA/Trust Fund due to their survivor-centred mandates.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **implementation research** objective (testing reporting mechanisms) requires a **consortium structure** to: 1) standardize approaches across countries for comparability; 2) embed research within delivery (via sub-contracted researchers); 3) enable rapid course-correction. The **survivor-centred focus** necessitates WROs as sub-partners (not direct grantees) to ensure safeguarding oversight by the lead supplier.
q28_linkages: Participatory action research (WHAT) → Consortium with research sub-contractors (HOW).
Need for local trust (WHAT) → WROs as sub-partners with lead supplier support (HOW).
Global public goods (WHAT) → Steering Committee with survivor panel (HOW).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Directly funding WROs (Option B) would be faster but risked fragmented learning; the consortium (Option C) adds a layer but ensures standardization. 2) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern lead supplier provides technical safeguarding expertise, while WROs ensure local legitimacy—requiring explicit partnership principles. 3) **Cost vs. reach**: Digital reporting is cheaper but excludes marginalized groups, necessitating hybrid mechanisms (e.g., trusted intermediaries + hotlines).

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Consortium layer (efficiency cost) vs. standardized learning (equity gain).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.example: Option C’s lead supplier adds management costs but enables cross-country comparisons.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Northern technical leadership (expertise) vs. Southern decision-making (ownership).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.example: Lead supplier designs MEL framework, but WROs co-develop community engagement strategies.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.tradeoff: Rapid scale-up (speed) vs. survivor feedback loops (inclusion).
q29_tradeoffs_detail.example: Inception phase delays implementation but ensures interventions are trauma-informed.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **‘Major’ risk rating** drives **intensive oversight**: quarterly risk register reviews, embedded survivor feedback panels, and FCDO presence on the evaluation Steering Committee. High-risk contexts (e.g., retaliation against WROs) require **in-country lead supplier presence** and **real-time adaptive management** (e.g., adjusting reporting mechanisms if hotlines fail).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **core to partner roles**: WROs are selected for their GBV expertise but receive **technical training** on SEAH-specific protocols (e.g., IASC principles). The lead supplier’s role includes **mentoring WROs** to handle aid agency perpetrators, while UN partners (OVRA) focus on **systemic capacity** (e.g., disseminating the Victims’ Rights Statement).

quote.where_who: "The S2S programme highlighted that it is important for the lead supplier to have an in-country presence. It is not easy for WROs to support victim-survivors of SEAH when perpetrated by aid agency staff from ‘powerful’/large/international organisations" (D0006390.odt, Commercial Case)
quote.what_how: "Participatory action research will be undertaken to develop the best way to deliver a survivor-centred response... Research will also be undertaken to test ‘what works’ for effective reporting mechanisms" (D0006390.odt, Component 2)
quote.tradeoffs: "Having a lead supplier oversee WROs... allows for a more robust way to gather learning on ‘what works’... [but] the FCDO could be criticised for not funding WROs directly" (D0006390.odt, Option C)

key_programme_risks.risk: Rollback of women’s rights undermines WROs’ ability to operate.
ES-SEAH fails to influence aid agencies on survivor-centred responses due to power dynamics.
UN mechanisms (e.g., OVRA) lack leverage to drive systemic change across UN entities.
Funds mismanaged or fraud committed by partners/sub-partners.
Poor capacity-building of WROs leads to re-traumatization of survivors.
WROs face community backlash (e.g., threats, aid cuts) for reporting SEAH.
Research findings are ignored or disputed by implementing partners.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Lead supplier works in-country with WROs; FCDO embassies undertake proactive mitigation.
Action research flexes approaches; evaluation generates evidence for advocacy.
Fund only high-performing mechanisms (e.g., OVRA); engage UNSG’s Special Coordinator.
Due diligence on partners; quarterly risk reviews; FCDO financial oversight.
Work with WROs having proven GBV/SEAH experience; prioritize survivor feedback.
Posts engaged from start; lead supplier provides in-country support.
Steering Committee co-designs research; FCDO on evaluation committee.

fcas_specific_lessons: In FCAS, **community engagement is critical** to prevent SEAH and encourage reporting (e.g., DRC study showed men’s support increases women’s reporting).
**Local intermediaries** (WROs) are essential where aid agencies are distrusted; direct reporting to agencies risks retaliation.
**Hybrid reporting mechanisms** (trusted individuals + hotlines) work better than digital-only in low-literacy/conflict zones.
**Economic dependencies** (e.g., fear of losing aid) must be addressed via confidential channels and survivor support funds.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **S2S programme (2022–2024)** revealed: 1) Independent reporting mechanisms alone are ineffective without aid agency accountability. 2) WROs struggle to influence agencies due to power imbalances. 3) Survivors prefer reporting to trusted women over hotlines. 4) UN Trust Fund reviews are needed to ensure alignment with survivor needs.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added **lead supplier in-country presence** to mitigate WRO risks (vs. S2S’s remote support).
Included **survivor feedback panels** in governance (absent in S2S).
**Action research** embedded in delivery (vs. S2S’s separate research).
Flexible budget allocation between components (S2S had fixed silos).
Explicit **partnership principles** for WRO engagement (addressing S2S’s power imbalance issues).

quote.S2S_lessons: "S2S demonstrated that independent mechanisms for reporting SEAH can be ineffective... If an independent reporting mechanism gets SEAH reports and informs the relevant aid agency, they have no lines of accountability to make the aid agency respond" (D0006390.odt, FCDO programming to date)
quote.FCAS: "A small-scale study in DRC found that engaging men can also support SEAH reporting, as ‘when a man is supportive, a woman will be more likely to report SEAH’" (D0006390.odt, Context: Community engagement)
quote.design_changes: "The S2S programme highlighted that it is important for the lead supplier to have an in-country presence... We have used the same model for S2S, engaging FCDO Malawi, which has been invaluable" (D0006390.odt, Management section)

quote.budget: "The Business case is seeking approval for up to £15m over a five-year period (August 2024 to August 2029)" (D0006390.odt, Financial Case)
quote.allocation: "A proposed breakdown of the £15m programme budget is £11m to a lead supplier to deliver components 1 and 2 (inclusive of an evaluation), and £4m to UN mechanisms" (D0006390.odt, Financial Case)
quote.flexibility: "There will be flexibility in how the budget is allocated... we may decide to scale back the ES-SEAH budget, or put more into components 1 and 2 if they show strong promise" (D0006390.odt, Financial Case)

metadata.programme_name: Central Asia Small Project Programme
metadata.quote: "This programme will provide the mechanism for embassies to develop small projects to further the aims of the Country Business Plans and develop learning to support wider programming initiatives, with the overall aims of supporting development in the region and helping to develop UK influence and soft power." (D0006430.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Programme Start Date: 1/05/2024", "Programme End Date: 30/04/2027" (D0006430.odt, Metadata)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme serves as a financing mechanism for small projects that support Country Business Plans across Central Asia, while also generating learning for wider programming. It combines capacity building (e.g., training parliamentarians, supporting civil society), policy influence (e.g., monitoring foreign agent legislation), and service delivery (e.g., women’s shelters, youth inclusion in tech).
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will provide the mechanism for embassies to develop small projects to further the aims of the Country Business Plans and develop learning to support wider programming initiatives, with the overall aims of supporting development in the region and helping to develop UK influence and soft power." (D0006430.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Building capacity of parliamentarians to hold government to account
Monitoring impact of foreign agent legislation and building evidence for international lobbying
Support to civil society to survive restrictive legislation
Improved inclusion of youth, women, and people with disabilities in sport
Increased involvement of women and youth in the technology sector
Dialogue between Human Rights NGOs and government supported
Biodiversity protected alongside economic growth
Stronger links to the UK via John Smith Trust fellowships
Pilot projects generating lessons for future scale-up
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds small, high-impact projects aligned with Country Business Plans to strengthen governance, resilience, and UK influence in Central Asia, while testing innovative approaches for potential scale-up.
what_objectives.quote: "The projects in the programme will support the Country Business plans in the region as well as objectives of the Russia strategy. They will work alongside existing programmes, providing a more flexible way for embassies to support small initiatives that can have high impact in terms of increasing the visibility of the embassy as well as supporting smaller organisations or one-off activities." (D0006430.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The region faces geopolitical volatility (Russia’s declining influence, Taliban in Afghanistan), weak governance, shrinking civic space, and economic vulnerability to Russian exposure (e.g., 30% of Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan GDP from Russian remittances). Climate risks and gender inequality exacerbate instability.
where_context.q5_source: "Central Asia is increasingly exposed to new and developing security risks following the Taliban takeover of neighbouring Afghanistan, the declining role of Russia as a security guarantor and the diminishing viability of Russian-led multilateral initiatives." (D0006430.odt, Context issues)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Restrictive legislation limits civil society operations; Russian disinformation risks reputational harm; weak state capacity complicates service delivery; and climate vulnerability (e.g., water/energy insecurity) threatens stability. Gender norms and shrinking civic space further constrain inclusive programming.
where_context.quote: "Weak state capacity and corruption remain areas for concern across the region. There is also a trend of restrictions in civic space and media freedom according to global indices (Freedom House 2023)." (D0006430.odt, Governance)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO/embassies retain approval authority for all projects, with delegated accountability to Heads of Mission (HMAs) in-country. Local partners implement but do not set strategic priorities.
q10_capacity_building_details: Training for project leads on due diligence, safeguarding, and gender inclusion
Support to civil society survival under restrictive laws
John Smith Trust fellowships for mid-career professionals
Gender equality marker assessments for all projects
Washington Group Questions for disability-inclusive data

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Projects use **accountable grants** (for CSOs/NGOs) and **contracts** (for think tanks, academics, private sector). Funds are disbursed via FCDO’s existing frameworks (e.g., CSSF, Global Development Delivery Framework) or direct agreements, with payments typically milestone-based or in arrears.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: FCDO acts as fund manager, with embassies selecting partners via **proportionate processes** (direct awards for small projects, competitive bids for larger ones). Posts can use pre-approved frameworks or local knowledge to identify implementers. No closed consortium; partners vary by project.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: For projects **under £10,000**, direct awards based on local staff knowledge; **£10,000–£100,000** requires low-value due diligence; **over £100,000** demands full competitive processes. Framework agreements (e.g., CSSF) enable rapid selection of pre-vetted suppliers.
how_mechanism.quote: "Each Post will be empowered to run its own processes to collect bids or approach partners, including commercial processes in line with latest commercial guidance. For post with limited funding, delivery partners are expected to be selected based on the knowledge of local staff and UKB working in country." (D0006430.odt, Delivery partners)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: Multi-layered governance: **Post Project Boards (PPB)** (chaired by HMAs) approve projects; **Central Asia Strategy Board (CASB)** reviews risks/spend; **PARG (Programme Assurance and Risk Group)** provides advisory support. SRO (Tim Smart) and PRO (PARG) oversee programme-wide compliance.
how_governance.quote: "Proposals will come to Post Project Boards (PPB) for review and approval by HMA. Risk escalation will be done via the PPB and CASB as needed." (D0006430.odt, Governance arrangements)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: SRO can reallocate funds **between countries** mid-year based on spend rates (reviewed at 6-month mark), but requires justification. Underspend can be rolled over or reallocated to other EECAD programmes.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Projects can pilot new approaches, but adjustments require Post Board approval. Annual reviews inform shifts in Year 2/3 priorities. Strategic coherence is maintained via CA Strategy Board.
how_flexibility.quote: "The Programme SRO will have discretion to move spending between countries within the year based on spend rates. A review of country level spend rates and progress towards results would be conducted at the 6-month mark to inform a discussion at the Central Asia Strategy board." (D0006430.odt, Criteria for project selection)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (no sub-grantees permitted; direct delivery only).
how_efficiency.quote: "Payments will be disbursed in accordance with schedules in agreement documents. Some partners may require payments in advance, and justification for this will be set out to the PRO for approval on a case-by-case basis." (D0006430.odt, Financial risks)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **flexible small-project model** was selected to: 1) **complement** larger ODA programmes by testing innovative approaches; 2) **mitigate risk** via modest project sizes (max £250k); 3) **respond rapidly** to local opportunities (e.g., civil society needs); and 4) **build UK influence** through visible, high-impact initiatives. The mixed instrument approach (grants/contracts) balances speed (direct awards for small projects) with rigor (competitive bids for larger ones).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited project management capacity at embassies (staff juggling projects alongside day jobs)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: HMAs must confirm adequate resourcing pre-approval; PARG provides training/guidance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational harm from Russian disinformation targeting UK-funded activities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Clear communication strategies; discretionary funding (e.g., third-party channels).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fraud/aid diversion due to limited oversight of small projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Payment in arrears/milestones; low-value due diligence for £10k–£100k projects.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Administrative burden from multiple small projects
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Proportionate processes (e.g., simplified templates for <£10k); PARG support.

why_rationale.quote: "A key driver of VFM that is common across Posts are likely to be the cost of consultants. Posts will be responsible for using the most appropriate selection processes (including competitive processes) to ensure VFM." (D0006430.odt, Value for money)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context** limits partner selection to organizations with: 1) **local legitimacy** (to avoid disinformation risks); 2) **capacity to navigate restrictive laws** (e.g., foreign agent legislation); and 3) **existing embassy relationships** (due to due diligence constraints). Direct government funding is avoided due to weak institutions.
q27_constraints_detail: Russian disinformation risks → preference for low-profile or third-party-channeled funding
Restrictive NGO laws → reliance on pre-vetted frameworks (e.g., CSSF) or trusted local CSOs
Weak state capacity → avoidance of government systems for fund disbursement
Gender norms → need for discrete women’s rights projects (e.g., shelters via local partners)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **diverse project types** (policy influence vs. service delivery) shape delivery structures: 1) **Advocacy projects** (e.g., monitoring legislation) use **contracts** with think tanks for rapid, expert-led outputs; 2) **Community-focused projects** (e.g., women’s inclusion in tech) use **grants** to local CSOs for flexibility; 3) **Pilot projects** leverage **framework agreements** (e.g., CSSF) for speed.
q28_linkages: Policy influence objectives → contracts with Northern/Southern think tanks
Service delivery objectives → grants to local CSOs/NGOs
Capacity building objectives → John Smith Trust fellowships (UK-managed)
Risky contexts (e.g., Turkmenistan) → pre-approved framework suppliers
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tensions include: 1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Competitive processes for larger projects (>£100k) may exclude smaller local organizations; 2) **Cost vs. reach**: Administrative costs capped at 10%, limiting support for remote/rural areas; 3) **Expertise vs. ownership**: Northern contractors (e.g., for climate analysis) may lack local contextual knowledge.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency: Competitive bids for >£100k projects → smaller local NGOs may lack capacity to compete
Equity: Gender equality marker requirements → additional reporting burden for partners
Risk: Payment in arrears → cash flow challenges for Southern CSOs
intersections.risk_affects_management: High-risk contexts (e.g., Tajikistan’s weak governance) trigger **intensive oversight** for larger projects (full due diligence, milestone payments) but **light-touch** for small projects (<£10k: background checks only).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Local partners with **limited capacity** (e.g., rural CSOs) are restricted to smaller grants with embedded safeguarding training, while **higher-capacity** organizations (e.g., international NGOs) can access larger contracts.
intersections.quote: "For the smallest projects, under £10,000, initial background checks will be undertaken, and some physical checks that the work has been done. [...] For projects between £10,000 and £100,000 the low value due diligence assessment template will need to be completed prior to disbursement of funding." (D0006430.odt, Due diligence)

key_programme_risks: Fraud/aid diversion due to limited embassy capacity to monitor small projects
Reputational damage from Russian disinformation targeting UK-funded activities
Poor project quality due to staff managing projects alongside day jobs
Safeguarding incidents in diverse, high-risk contexts
Strategic misalignment if UK/Central Asia priorities shift (e.g., post-election)
Underspend due to absorption capacity limits at posts
Climate-related disruptions to project delivery

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Limit project size to £250k max; payments in arrears/milestone-based; random receipt checks.
Clear communication strategies; discretionary funding channels; due diligence on partners’ media profiles.
HMA confirmation of adequate staffing pre-approval; PARG training/guidance.
Mandatory SEAH policy reviews; safeguarding training for project leads; reporting hotline.
Annual reviews by CA Strategy Board; small project sizes limit exposure.
6-month spend review; SRO can reallocate funds between countries.

fcas_specific_lessons: Avoid direct government funding due to corruption/weak systems; use CSO/NGO channels.
In conflict-affected areas (e.g., Tajikistan-Afghanistan border), prioritize flexible, short-term projects.
Disinformation risks require **pre-emptive** communication (e.g., embedding UK messaging in local media).
Gender projects must navigate **traditional norms** via discrete partnerships (e.g., women’s shelters through trusted local orgs).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: No explicit lessons from prior phases mentioned, but the **John Smith Trust** model (fellowships for mid-career professionals) is cited as a successful approach to build UK links.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The **proportionate due diligence** tiers (£10k/£100k thresholds) and **payment in arrears** default were introduced to balance risk and efficiency based on past FCDO small-project programmes.
risks_lessons.quote: "The current context provides an ideal opportunity to reinforce HMG political engagement and messaging on wider UK Government objectives in the region including building stability, fostering open and inclusive societies, tackling traditional gender norms, countering Serious and Organised Crime (SOC), enhancing prosperity and building resilience to State Threats." (D0006430.odt, Context issues)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme is a financing mechanism that supports small projects to achieve Country Business Plan objectives, including capacity building (e.g., training parliamentarians), policy influence (e.g., monitoring foreign agent legislation), and service delivery (e.g., supporting civil society survival). It also pilots new initiatives to generate learning for wider programming.

q1_source.source: Document: D0006431.odt, What are the intended policy objectives/outcomes for the programme?
q1_source.text: "The projects in the programme will support the Country Business plans in the region as well as LOE7 of the Russia strategy. Increased involvement of women and youth in the technology sector
Supporting dialogue between Human Rights NGOs and the government
Protecting biodiversity for protected habitats alongside economic growth

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The volatile political context (e.g., Russian influence, restrictive legislation) limits partner selection to trusted local CSOs or pre-approved frameworks. Weak state capacity requires reliance on embassies for oversight, reducing options for direct funding to government entities.
q27_constraints_detail: Russian disinformation risks misrepresenting embassy activities, limiting public-facing partners.
Restrictive civic space laws (e.g., foreign agent legislation) require partners with legal resilience.
Corruption risks necessitate robust due diligence, favoring established organizations.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **small, agile projects** (WHAT) drives the **decentralized, embassy-led structure** (HOW), with light-touch oversight for low-value grants. Policy influence objectives (e.g., lobbying on foreign agent laws) require **contracts with think tanks**, while capacity-building (e.g., civil society support) uses **grants to CSOs**.

metadata.programme_name: Ethiopia Education Transformation Programme (EETP) support through Financial Aid and Technical Assistance
metadata.quote: "This programme will help Ethiopia protect education gains to date, and level up regions with poor education outcomes, through a focus on equity, including girls, other marginalised groups and developing regions." (D0007590.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Start Date: April 24", "AMPEndDate: April29" (D0007590.odt, SummarySheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines implementation research (testing/scaling interventions like Teaching at the Right Level), capacity building (strengthening school leadership and teacher training systems), and service delivery (direct support to marginalized regions). It also includes a financing mechanism through Financial Aid to the government's education transformation plan.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The programme will build the long-term capability of Ethiopia’s education system, by working through government systems to improve foundational learning." and "The programme will work hand in hand with the Ethiopia Crisis to Resilience (EC2R) programme’s education component which operates in crisis-affected and post-crisis areas." (D0007590.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: Improved educational attendance and learning for over 1 million children (50% girls) at primary and secondary levels
Building skills of 125,000 teachers and school leaders (based on GEQIP-E achievements)
Conducive learning environments for girls and children with disabilities (supporting 24,000+ children with disabilities)
Reduction in dropout rates by 15% and repetition rates by 5% at primary level (based on GEQIP-E results)
Improved transition rates to secondary school through targeted interventions
Enhanced school leadership systems at national, regional, and local levels
Strengthened data collection, research, and evidence-based decision making in the education system
Integration of 70% of refugee secondary school pupils into work/TVET opportunities (through GoE pledge support)
Pilot of Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) approach for marginalized groups
Improved English language teaching capacity and materials
Expansion of pre-primary education (O-classes) with focus on rural/pastoral areas
Development of inclusive education resource centers (IERCs) for children with disabilities
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to protect Ethiopia's education gains while addressing persistent inequities through a dual approach of Financial Aid (85%) to support system-wide reforms and Technical Assistance (15%) to catalyze transformative changes in teaching quality, school leadership, and inclusion - particularly for girls and marginalized regions.
what_objectives.quote: "This programme will help Ethiopia protect education gains to date, and to level up regions with poor education outcomes and educational inequity. This will be achieved through a focus on equity, including girls, targeting other marginalised groups, and developing regions; and a focus on improving learning outcomes, particularly foundational learning, and the transition to secondary school." (D0007590.odt, This programme section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ethiopia faces multiple overlapping crises including armed conflict (3.9 million children unable to attend school in Amhara due to conflict), climate-induced shocks (1.6 million children's education disrupted by drought), and COVID-19 recovery challenges. The education system has suffered extensive damage with over 11,300 schools damaged/destroyed between 2020-2022.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall, more than 11,300 schools were damaged or destroyed as a result of conflict between 2020 and 2022 in Afar, Amhara, Oromia, and Tigray" and "In Amhara, in October 2023 the Regional Education Bureau reported that out of the 6 million eligible children, approximately 3.9 million primary and secondary students are unable to attend school this academic year due to the ongoing conflict" (D0007590.odt, Education in Ethiopia section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security constraints limit access to conflict-affected regions (3.9M children out of school in Amhara). Infrastructure limitations include damaged schools (11,300+ damaged) and lack of secondary schools (1:10 primary-to-secondary ratio vs 1:3 in Kenya). Weak institutions are evident in flawed teacher licensing processes and limited EMIS usage (only 76% of schools). Climate risks disrupt education (1.6M children affected by drought). Data limitations affect monitoring in pastoralist communities. Political economy challenges include regional budget variations and inflation reducing real-term education spending by 23.2%.
where_context.quote: "The stalled progress since 2019 has been caused by unpredictable and adjacent crises across the country. These include conflict and instability, climate-induced shocks and the residual impacts of Covid-19 and associated lockdowns." and "A number of studies identified the negative impact of the pandemic on access to education, particularly on equitable access... Children with disabilities saw the most limited access to education opportunities during school closures." (D0007590.odt, Education in Ethiopia section)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: Government of Ethiopia (Ministry of Education) with FCDO
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme operates through government systems with FCDO providing both financial aid (through multi-donor trust funds) and technical assistance. Decision-making is shared between MoE (leading implementation) and FCDO (providing oversight and technical guidance), with regional education bureaus having operational authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: School leadership training (building on TARGET programme)
Teacher professional development (focus on English language, structured pedagogy, and Teaching at the Right Level)
Institutional strengthening of Regional Education Boards (REBs)
Data collection and EMIS system improvements
Inclusive education resource centers (IERCs) for children with disabilities
Girls' clubs and gender-sensitive school improvement programmes
Pre-service teacher training curriculum reforms
Public expenditure review and education financing strategy development

partner_organizations.role: Primary implementing partner and recipient of Financial Aid

partner_organizations.name: Regional Education Boards (REBs)
partner_organizations.role: Regional implementation and oversight

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Parallel Education Transformation Operation for Learning (ETOL) programme with aligned objectives

partner_organizations.role: Complementary funding for textbooks and school infrastructure

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF
partner_organizations.role: Early childhood development support and education in emergencies

partner_organizations.role: Current Technical Assistance provider through TARGET programme (likely to continue)

who_partners.quote: "Our bilateral education programme works directly with government and is long-standing and appreciated element of our bilateral relationship" and "The UK's education programme works directly with government and is long-standing and appreciated element of our bilateral relationship, in turn contributing to our efforts to promote peace" (D0007590.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses Financial Aid (85%) channeled through a multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) aligned with the government's Education Transformation Plan, combined with Technical Assistance (15%) delivered through competitive procurement. The FA follows a payment-by-results mechanism with Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs), while TA provides catalytic support for system reforms.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through government systems with FCDO providing oversight. Implementation involves MoE at national level, REBs at regional level, and schools at local level. Technical Assistance will be delivered by a supplier selected through open competition, working alongside government structures. The programme includes an insourced role for additional management capacity.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Market engagement activities have been completed for the Technical Assistance component, suggesting a competitive procurement process to select the most capable supplier. The rationale emphasizes the need for specialized expertise to complement Financial Aid investments and drive system-wide transformation.
how_mechanism.quote: "We expect the technical assistance component to be delivered via a competitive open procurement. Market engagement activities have been completed" (D0007590.odt, Modality section) and "Our TA will be designed to best support FA investments... unlock FA investments to deliver the maximum results against UK education priorities" (D0007590.odt, Technical Assistance section)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The programme mentions a Technical Working Group for education and an Education in Emergencies Steering Committee. Decision-making involves joint oversight between FCDO and MoE, with regional adaptations managed through REBs. The insourced role will provide additional management capacity for crisis-affected regions.
how_governance.quote: "Detailed oversight will be required to understand how education is operating in crisis-affected regions. This will add management oversight requirements to the programme, and we are this is part of the reason we are including an insourced role in this business case." (D0007590.odt, Education in emergencies section) and "The programme will have different interventions by regions to respond to crises, rather than a 'one-size-fits-all' approach" (D0007590.odt, This programme section)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme allows for different interventions by region to respond to crises, suggesting some flexibility in fund allocation between components. However, the Financial Aid component follows pre-agreed DLIs, and major reallocations would likely require approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes adaptive elements such as region-specific interventions for crisis response and the ability to adjust Technical Assistance focus areas based on emerging needs. The insourced role provides additional capacity for management oversight in changing contexts. However, significant changes would require approval through the governance structure.
how_flexibility.quote: "The programme will have different interventions by regions to respond to crises, rather than a 'one-size-fits-all' approach in the GEQIP-E programme" (D0007590.odt, This programme section) and "We will deliver the majority of the programme through financial aid. As this programme will work through and strengthen government systems, it will operate in areas where the Government of Ethiopia is working to deliver its own ambitious Education Sector Plan targets" (D0007590.odt, Modality section)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Government of Ethiopia (MoE/REBs) → Schools/Implementation Partners (with Technical Assistance provider working across layers)
how_efficiency.quote: "The FA and TA split in option 3 is proposed because under the previous phase of the programme a split of 85%-15% worked well and helped to maximise investments to deliver the maximum results" (D0007590.odt, Figure 6 caption) and "Most Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLI's) of the Payment for Results programme have been met" (D0007590.odt, Learnings from GEQIP-E section)

q24_alternatives_considered: FA only (100% Financial Aid with no TA component)
TA only (100% Technical Assistance with no FA contribution)
FATA combined (85% FA and 15% TA - selected option)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The combined FA/TA approach (85/15 split) was chosen because it balances direct support to beneficiaries through government systems with catalytic technical assistance to drive system-wide reforms. This model proved successful in the previous GEQIP-E programme, delivering substantial results while working through government structures. The split maximizes investments to deliver results while maintaining influence over reform priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Investments in FA may not be efficient without TA support, potentially limiting beneficiary reach
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Including 15% TA component to catalyze and guide FA investments, ensuring they deliver maximum results against UK priorities

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Working on TA in isolation from FA may result in disconnect between reform efforts and government/donor approaches
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Integrated FA/TA approach with TA designed to directly support and enhance FA investments

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Increased management and transaction costs for FCDO with combined approach
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Leveraging existing government systems and including insourced role to manage additional oversight requirements, particularly for crisis-affected regions

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: FA spending tends to be less innovative and struggles to reach children outside formal education system
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Targeted TA interventions focusing on marginalized groups and innovative approaches like Teaching at the Right Level

why_rationale.quote: "The FA and TA split in option 3 is proposed because under the previous phase of the programme a split of 85%-15% worked well and helped to maximise investments to deliver the maximum results. We want to encourage the TA provider to work in a catalytic way rather than focus excessively on parallel delivery of support" (D0007590.odt, Figure 6 caption) and "Our TA will unlock FA investments to deliver the maximum results against UK education priorities" (D0007590.odt, Technical Assistance section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with existing presence and capacity to operate in conflict-affected regions. Security constraints in areas like Amhara (3.9M children out of school) and Somali region (500,000 children out of school due to drought) require partners with specialized crisis response capabilities. Weak institutional capacity at regional level necessitates partners who can work effectively with REBs despite varying budget allocations and implementation challenges.
q27_constraints_detail: Conflict in Amhara, Tigray, and Oromia regions limits access for many international partners
Drought in Somali region requires partners with emergency education expertise
Regional budget variations (some regions are 'cash-strapped') affect partner ability to work effectively across all areas
Limited EMIS usage (only 76% of schools) constrains data-driven partner selection
Teacher licensing challenges require partners with capacity to work on systemic reforms
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The focus on foundational learning and equity objectives (particularly for girls and marginalized regions) determines the need for: 1) A government-led delivery structure to ensure national coverage, 2) Technical Assistance to address specific bottlenecks like teacher quality and school leadership, 3) Flexible regional interventions to respond to varied contexts, and 4) Parallel humanitarian programming for crisis-affected areas outside government control.
q28_linkages: Foundational learning focus → Requires structured pedagogy approaches → Determines need for TA component with specialized expertise
Equity objectives (girls, disabilities, rural areas) → Requires targeted interventions → Shapes regional adaptation mechanism in delivery structure
System strengthening goal → Requires government partnership → Determines FA modality working through MoE systems
Crisis response needs → Requires flexible funding → Shapes 85/15 FA/TA split with capacity for reallocation
Teacher quality bottlenecks → Requires specialized TA → Determines focus areas for competitive procurement
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between: 1) Reaching marginalized groups (equity) vs. achieving economies of scale (efficiency) - addressed through targeted TA interventions alongside system-wide FA; 2) Northern expertise in structured pedagogy vs. Southern ownership - mitigated through capacity building of Ethiopian institutions; 3) Immediate crisis response vs. long-term system building - balanced through parallel humanitarian programming (EC2R) and development funding.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Urban vs rural disparities: "Regression analysis shows that rural children in both grades perform poorly compared to their urban counterparts... effort focusing on rural areas needs to be strengthened" (equity) vs. "The expansion of preschools is taking place largely in urban areas" (efficiency)

Specialized TA vs government ownership: "Our TA will be designed to best support FA investments" (efficiency) vs. "ensuring the college education training is informed by the TARGET's experience" (local capacity building)

Immediate crisis needs vs long-term reform: "Parallel humanitarian programming... will address education needs for crisis-affected populations" (responsiveness) vs. "this programme will help Ethiopia protect education gains to date" (sustainability)

Innovative approaches vs system constraints: "FA spending tends to be less innovative" (system limitations) vs. "TA interventions focusing on marginalized groups and innovative approaches" (targeted impact)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk FCAS context increases management intensity through: 1) Additional oversight requirements for crisis-affected regions, 2) Inclusion of an insourced role to manage complex regional adaptations, 3) Milestone-based oversight rather than light-touch management, and 4) Detailed monitoring of different regional interventions rather than a standardized approach.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building objectives shape partner roles by: 1) Requiring TA providers to have expertise in school leadership training and teacher professional development, 2) Embedding capacity strengthening within government systems (MoE, REBs, teacher training colleges), 3) Including institutional strengthening as a core TA component rather than standalone activity, and 4) Designing TA to be catalytic for FA investments rather than parallel delivery.
intersections.quote: "The programme will have different interventions by regions to respond to crises, rather than a 'one-size-fits-all' approach in the GEQIP-E programme. Detailed oversight will be required to understand how education is operating in crisis-affected regions. This will add management oversight requirements to the programme" (D0007590.odt, This programme section) and "Our TA will unlock FA investments to deliver the maximum results against UK education priorities... providing additional expertise in the areas under the ETOL programme" (D0007590.odt, Technical Assistance section)

key_programme_risks: Learning losses due to COVID-19 and conflict disrupting education continuity
Wide gaps between emerging regions and others in textbook access and learning environments
Limited expansion of preschools in rural/pastoral areas despite urban progress
Persistent urban-rural disparities in learning outcomes
Teacher quality bottlenecks (only 6% of teachers have expected content knowledge)
Low secondary school transition rates (only 3% passed university entrance exams)
Weak school leadership systems affecting education quality
Limited data collection and EMIS usage (only 76% of schools)
Climate shocks disrupting education (1.6M children affected by drought)
Conflict displacing children (3.9M out of school in Amhara)
Inflation reducing real-term education spending by 23.2%
Limited contingency spending capacity in government systems for crisis response

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Learning losses from COVID-19 and conflict
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Teaching at the Right Level pilot and catch-up interventions for marginalized groups, integrated psychosocial support in schools
Targeted grants for marginalized regions, different interventions by region rather than one-size-fits-all approach

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited preschool expansion in rural areas
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Explicit focus on improving access to preschool in rural and pastoral areas through TA component
Structured pedagogy approaches, teacher professional development focused on English language and foundational learning
Improved English language teaching and school leadership systems to better prepare students
Digitalization of EMIS system with focus on disaggregated data including for children with disabilities
Climate-smart infrastructure, shock-responsive systems, and integration with humanitarian programming
Parallel humanitarian programming through EC2R for non-government controlled areas
Focus on efficiency improvements and leveraging multilateral funding (GPE, World Bank)
Including insourced role for additional management capacity and flexible TA funding

fcas_specific_lessons: Education in emergencies programming must include protection and psychosocial support elements
As crises become protracted, focus must shift to reintegrating young people into mainstream education
National systems need capacity to respond to children who have missed school due to crises
Mainstreaming psychosocial training for teachers and 'teaching at the right level' approaches helps crisis-affected children
Humanitarian system cannot reach all out-of-school children - development funding must build system resilience
School grants and contingency funding mechanisms are needed to respond to shocks
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: GEQIP-E demonstrated that: 1) Payment-by-results mechanisms can deliver significant improvements (reduced dropout rates by 15%); 2) School grants empower local decision-making but need sufficient per-capita amounts; 3) Girls' clubs and gender-sensitive programmes improve retention; 4) System-wide improvements require sustained focus on rural/disadvantaged areas; 5) Teacher quality and 'time on task' remain key bottlenecks; 6) Digital tools and real-time data collection improve planning; 7) Regional variations in capacity require tailored support approaches.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key design changes include: 1) Moving from one-size-fits-all to region-specific interventions; 2) Adding an insourced role for crisis management oversight; 3) Explicit focus on rural preschool expansion; 4) Teaching at the Right Level pilot to address learning poverty; 5) Strengthened focus on school leadership systems; 6) Enhanced data disaggregation requirements; 7) Integration with humanitarian programming; 8) Increased flexibility in TA component to respond to emerging needs.
risks_lessons.quote: "GEQIP-E was not implemented as planned due to the dual shocks of COVID-19 and the conflict in 2020. As a result, learning losses were reported over the programme period. Greater effort and increased resources will be needed to counter the negative effects on learning outcomes" (D0007590.odt, Learnings from GEQIP-E section) and "The programme will have different interventions by regions to respond to crises, rather than a 'one-size-fits-all' approach in the GEQIP-E programme" (D0007590.odt, This programme section)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme expects to leverage over $500 million from multilateral sources (World Bank IDA and GPE grants) over the next 5 years, aligned with the Ethiopia Education Transformation Plan. The UK's TA programme success has already triggered commitments from other donors to scale up school leadership interventions.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses primarily on revenue expenditures (teacher training, school grants, technical assistance) with limited capital expenditure mentioned (some school rehabilitation/construction expected through GPE programmes in underserved areas).
financial_details.quote: "The World Bank is developing its new programme of IDA support and the GPE Board is expected to sign off a set of grants in early 2024. Taken together, these multilaterals could bring over $500 million to the sector over the next 5 years" (D0007590.odt, Future direction for development assistance section) and "The FA and TA split in option 3 is proposed because under the previous phase of the programme a split of 85%-15% worked well and helped to maximise investments to deliver the maximum results" (D0007590.odt, Figure 6 caption)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening the Global Architecture for Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Sexual Abuse, and Sexual Harassment (GA-PSEAH)

quote.text: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years to support and develop global architecture to improve protection from sexual exploitation, sexual abuse, and sexual harassment (PSEAH) in humanitarian, development and peace settings.

duration_source.text: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening PSEAH standards and tools), technology development (creating global public goods like the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme), policy influence (driving up international standards), and implementation research (piloting new approaches). It also includes financing mechanisms to support coordination and dialogue.

q1_source.text: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years to support and develop global architecture to improve protection from sexual exploitation, sexual abuse, and sexual harassment (PSEAH) in humanitarian, development and peace settings. Key priorities are to: Scale up, pilot and implement PSEAH global tools, cross sector initiatives and approaches; Support PSEAH coordination and multi stakeholder dialogue to address common challenges and to improve collective action; Seek the PSEAH tools and ‘global public goods’ of the future through research and pilots to address critical gaps in evidence on what works to prevent and respond to SEAH in different contexts.

q3_expected_outputs.output: PSEAH global tools (e.g., Misconduct Disclosure Scheme, PSEAH Index, Data Harmonisation Tool)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Scaled-up and sustained (e.g., Misconduct Disclosure Scheme grew from 2.7k to 50k vetting checks 2019-2023)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Cross-sector coordination mechanisms (e.g., PSEA-CAP, Common Approach to Protection from SEAH)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Structured support for ongoing PSEAH coordination and multi-stakeholder dialogue

q3_expected_outputs.output: Research and pilot studies on effective PSEAH approaches
q3_expected_outputs.target: Address critical gaps in evidence (e.g., organisational culture change, sustainable resourcing models)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Training and capacity-building (e.g., Investigation Qualification Training Scheme)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Focus on training women and staff in low-income countries

q3_expected_outputs.output: Global public goods (e.g., online platforms, harmonised reporting schemes)
q3_expected_outputs.target: Open-access tools for public use (e.g., CAPSEAH, RSH)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen global PSEAH architecture by sustaining existing tools, fostering coordination, and piloting innovative solutions to prevent and respond to SEAH in humanitarian, development, and peace settings. It builds on the UK’s leadership role post-2018 Safeguarding Summit and aligns with the 2023 International Development White Paper.

quote.source: D0007015.odt, What is the rationale for UK Aid spending?
quote.text: This programme will allow the UK to support and improve cross sector PSEAH standards and practices and so protect the integrity and delivery of FCDO, UK and wider HDP work. It will underpin and build on the UK’s strong reputation as a credible and influential leader in PSEAH and deliver on our ongoing commitment to harness our global convening power to drive up standards, best practice and coherence on PSEAH.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in humanitarian, development, and peace settings where SEAH risks are heightened by conflict, climate change, and instability. The overall programme risk rating is assessed as 'Moderate' with manageable risks proportionate to the potential high returns in preventing SEAH.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate

q6_contextual_constraints: varying maturity of standards across sectors
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Rising conflict and climate change increase SEAH risks, while underreporting and resource gaps hinder effective response. The programme must adapt to evolving risks in contexts where HDP needs overlap and interact, requiring coordinated international action.

quote.text: Rising conflict, climate change and other causes of instability increase the risk of SEAH and the need for countries, organisations and individuals to adapt to evolving SEAH risks in contexts where HDP needs, work and organisations evolve, overlap and interact.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO Safeguarding Unit (UK-based) manages strategic direction, partner selection, and funding allocation. Southern partners (e.g., regional RSH hubs, national organisations) implement activities but decision-making remains with FCDO.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (e.g., Investigation Qualification Training Scheme for staff in low-income countries)
mentorship (e.g., support to national organisations via HQAI Facilitation Fund)
institutional strengthening (e.g., certifying organisations against Core Humanitarian Standard)
knowledge-sharing (e.g., RSH regional hubs, CAPSEAH platform)

partner_organizations.name: Core Humanitarian Standard Alliance (CHS Alliance)
partner_organizations.role: Delivers PSEAH Index, Misconduct Disclosure Scheme, and data harmonisation tools

partner_organizations.name: Humanitarian Quality Assurance Initiative (HQAI)
partner_organizations.role: Certifies organisations against CHS and assesses PSEAH compliance

partner_organizations.name: Safeguarding Resource and Support Hub (RSH)
partner_organizations.role: Provides regional capacity-building and hosts CAPSEAH platform

partner_organizations.name: UN PSEA-CAP
partner_organizations.role: Pooled fund for PSEA coordinators in high-risk emergencies

partner_organizations.name: UK Safeguarding Leads Network (SLN)
partner_organizations.role: Coordinates private sector engagement on PSEAH

partner_organizations.name: Wilton Park
partner_organizations.role: Hosts cross-sector dialogues (e.g., on sustainable resourcing)

partner_organizations.name: National/local organisations (via HQAI Facilitation Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Build capacity to meet CHS standards

quote.text: The proposed programme will sustain and scale-up cross sector tools supporting international standards, vetting and data which were developed under the successful Safeguarding Innovation and Engagement programme, and are now evolving into PSEAH global public goods. Using the Common Approach to Protection from SEAH as an anchor for dialogue and collective action it will also provide structured support for ongoing targeted PSEAH coordination and multi-stakeholder dialogue to improve coherence of PSEAH approaches, and support research, innovation and pilots to seek the PSEAH tools of the future.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of **Accountable Grants**, **MOUs**, and **contracts** (for research/consultancy). Core funding supports global public goods (e.g., CHS Alliance, HQAI), while flexible instruments (grants/contracts) fund innovation and pilots. Pooled funds (e.g., PSEA-CAP) are also utilized.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The FCDO Safeguarding Unit manages strategic direction and selects partners based on expertise. Delivery is decentralized across multiple partners (CHS Alliance, HQAI, RSH, UN, etc.), with FCDO overseeing coherence. The structure allows for agile engagement with new partners as opportunities arise.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on **expertise in PSEAH**, alignment with global standards, and ability to convene stakeholders. The programme builds on existing relationships (e.g., CHS Alliance, HQAI) from the predecessor programme, with new partners added through consultation with the sector. Framework agreements (e.g., FCDO’s Global Development Delivery Framework) are used for speed and VfM.

quote.text: The programme will be flexible so that it can respond to ideas, innovations and opportunities as they arise. [...] Selection criteria for new projects and activities will be set in close collaboration with programme advisers and SGU senior leadership to ensure robust prioritisation alongside the flex and ambition needed to test new approaches. [...] For each component, Safeguarding Unit will ensure PrOF guidance is followed, especially around effective management, protection of vulnerable populations, and seeking the best VfM. We will use MOUs and Accountable Grants and explore pooled instruments (MOUs/AGs) to test more sustainable collective funding models.

The SRO is ultimately accountable for the expenditure of funds against this business case. The PRO will work closely with the SRO to ensure the programme expenditure is in line with budgets and project work plans, and is compliant with the PrOF rules. [...] Payments will mostly be made in arrears upon successful delivery but payments may be made in advance where there is clear justification. [...] FCDO will undertake occasional spot checks, supervisory field visits and annual reviews.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components to respond to emerging opportunities or constraints. For example, if budget constraints occur, resources can be targeted to core tools while scaling back new research.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to adapt to new challenges (e.g., scaling back innovations if they don’t deliver). Research priorities will be finalized in Year 1, allowing for alignment with emerging evidence. Break clauses in funding agreements enable adjustments.

quote.text: The programme is designed to be flexible to meet new challenges and priorities as the safeguarding agenda develops or changes, and also to ensure we can halt support for innovations that do not deliver as hoped. [...] If wider budget or other capacity constraints occur over the life of the programme, its flexibility means that we will be able to target resources on the core tools and engagement that others across the international system rely on, while scaling back support for new research and innovations.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing partners (e.g., CHS Alliance, HQAI, RSH). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned beyond these direct partners.

quote.text: Payments will mostly be made in arrears upon successful delivery but payments may be made in advance where there is clear justification and approval in line with PrOF rules. [...] All payments will be based on performance against log frame milestones, contractual/MoU criteria being met, and evidence of funding need.

q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: Would undermine UK’s reputation as a PSEAH leader, risk losing progress since 2018, and require FCDO to replicate tools internally (less efficient).

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Outsource to an overarching delivery partner
q24_alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: No international partner currently has the capacity/credibility to convene the sector. High governance costs and uncertainty around buy-in from stakeholders.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Manage in-house with flexible partner selection (CHOSEN)
q24_alternatives_considered.rationale: Leverages FCDO’s convening power, builds on existing relationships, and allows agile response to sector needs. Maximizes VfM by sustaining proven tools while testing innovations.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The in-house management model was selected to **maintain UK leadership** in PSEAH, **build on proven tools** (e.g., CHS Alliance, HQAI), and **enable flexibility** to adapt to emerging evidence. It balances risk (by sustaining core tools) with innovation (through pilots) and ensures alignment with UK priorities (e.g., 2023 White Paper). The approach also maximizes VfM by leveraging small UK funds to influence global standards.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on UK funding may create dependency, risking gaps if UK support ends.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO will fund mechanisms that promote cross-sector buy-in (e.g., CAPSEAH) and develop exit strategies/contingency plans. Co-funding from other donors will be sought to reduce burden-sharing.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex management of multiple partners/workstreams may reduce coherence or duplicate efforts.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: SGU will oversee all components, coordinate closely with partners, and use tools like CAPSEAH to align approaches. Quarterly reviews will monitor duplication.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: New innovations may fail to gain sector buy-in or prove ineffective.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Flexible funding allows scaling back underperforming pilots. Only innovations with strong sectoral interest and VfM will be supported.

quote.source: D0007015.odt, Summary appraisal of programme options
quote.text: The programme is unique in the PSEAH sector, as the only programme with a flexible approach to enable multiple cross-sector, multi stakeholder projects through engagement, buy-in and endorsement with different implementing partners. [...] The recommendation from the appraisal case is to establish a source of flexible funding capable of supporting a range of partners according to their expertise and ability to help achieve programme objectives.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **global scope** and **cross-sector nature** of PSEAH require partners with **multilateral convening power** (e.g., CHS Alliance, UN) and **technical expertise** (e.g., HQAI, RSH). Local partners are engaged primarily through capacity-building mechanisms (e.g., HQAI Facilitation Fund) rather than direct leadership roles, due to the need for standardized global tools.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with **global reach** (limits to multilateral/INGOs)
Requirement for **alignment with international standards** (excludes partners without PSEAH expertise)
**Language/data barriers** in LMICs addressed via regional hubs (e.g., RSH)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (sustaining tools + innovation + coordination) necessitate a **flexible, multi-partner structure**. Core tools (e.g., Misconduct Disclosure Scheme) require predictable funding (MOUs/core grants), while innovation needs agile instruments (grants/contracts). The **global public goods focus** drives open-access delivery models (e.g., CAPSEAH platform).
q28_linkages: Sustaining **global tools** → Requires **multilateral partners** (CHS Alliance, HQAI) with existing sectoral buy-in.
Piloting **innovations** → Needs **flexible funding** (grants/contracts) and **diverse partners** (researchers, NGOs).
**Coordination** objective → Demands **UN/multilateral platforms** (PSEA-CAP, CSSG) for cross-sector dialogue.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **global efficiency** (standardized tools like the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme) with **equity** (e.g., training investigators in LMICs, disaggregated data for vulnerable groups). Tensions include:

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Framework agreements enable rapid partner selection but may favour established (often Northern) organisations over local actors.
Tools like the PSEAH Index are global, but regional hubs (e.g., RSH) adapt guidance for local contexts.
Core funding for global tools (60% of budget) limits resources for LMIC-specific innovations, though pilots target gaps like child/LGBT+/disability safeguarding.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., reputational risks from underperforming tools) drives **milestone-based oversight** and **quarterly reviews**. High-risk innovations are managed via flexible funding and break clauses.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is **embedded** in tool delivery (e.g., HQAI certifies organisations, RSH strengthens regional hubs). Southern partners (e.g., national NGOs) are primarily **implementers** rather than strategic decision-makers, reflecting current capacity gaps in PSEAH leadership.

quote.text: The programme will seek to engage partners who have expertise and credibility in this area and are best placed to deliver projects and convene others. [...] The programme will request partners consider risk to [vulnerable] groups and to monitor that interventions do not have adverse impacts. [...] While there is growing consensus about where sustained and scaled-up investment is needed to support and further develop the global architecture that underpins PSEAH efforts, [...] there is also a continuing need for dialogue and coordination (and a growing need for engagement with national governments from developing countries).

key_programme_risks.risk: Delivery risk: Projects fail to deliver or gain sector buy-in.
Financial/sustainability risk: Global architecture becomes dependent on UK funding without alternative resourcing.
Reputational risk: UK seen as deprioritising PSEAH if funding cuts occur abruptly.
Geopolitical risk: Rollback of women’s rights reduces international commitment to PSEAH.
Coherence risk: Multiple workstreams lead to duplication or lack of coordination.
Fraud risk: Funds mismanaged or used for non-aligned activities.
Equity risk: Activities fail to adequately target vulnerable groups (e.g., women, disabled persons).

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Quarterly reviews and reflection points to assess progress; flexible funding to scale back underperforming innovations.
Develop exit strategies/contingency plans; seek co-funding from other donors; promote cross-sector buy-in for tools.
Communicate UK’s long-term commitment; use break clauses to phase out support gradually.
Engage like-minded donors and multilateral missions to sustain momentum; tactically protect PSEAH as a priority.
SGU oversees all components; use CAPSEAH as an anchor for dialogue; coordinate with partners to reduce duplication.
Due diligence assessments for all partners; robust financial oversight; milestone-based payments; annual audits.
Engage key stakeholders (e.g., disability experts) in design; disaggregate data; monitor for adverse impacts.

fcas_specific_lessons: SEAH risks are heightened in **conflict and climate-affected settings**, requiring adaptive tools (e.g., SEA-RORisk Overview Composite Index).
**Underreporting** and **weak institutions** in FCAS contexts necessitate harmonised data tools and local capacity-building.
Lessons from **previous crises** (e.g., 2018 Safeguarding Summit) show that **cross-sector coordination** is critical but challenging in fragile states.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous:
The predecessor **Safeguarding Innovation and Engagement Programme (2018–2024)** demonstrated that: 
1. **Global tools** (e.g., Misconduct Disclosure Scheme) gain traction when backed by core funding and multilateral endorsement. 
2. **Regional hubs** (e.g., RSH) effectively adapt global standards to local contexts. 
3. **Flexible funding** allows testing of innovations (e.g., SEA-RORisk Index) while sustaining proven tools. 
4. **Donor coordination** (e.g., via CSSG) is essential to avoid duplication but requires active UK leadership.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
1. **Sustained core funding** for tools like the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme (previously ad-hoc). 
2. **Structured dialogue mechanisms** (e.g., CAPSEAH) to replace informal coordination. 
3. **Explicit focus on equity** (e.g., training women investigators in LMICs, disaggregated data). 
4. **Break clauses** added to funding agreements for adaptive management. 
5. **Piloting of resourcing models** (e.g., via CAPSEAH working groups) to address sustainability gaps identified in previous phase.

quote.source: D0007015.odt, Evidence Base & Risks and risk appetite
quote.text: The proposed programme will sustain and scale-up cross sector tools supporting international standards, vetting and data which were developed under the successful Safeguarding Innovation and Engagement programme. [...] The programme is designed to be flexible to meet new challenges and priorities as the safeguarding agenda develops or changes. [...] Lessons from the Innovation and Engagement Programme include the need for predictable core funding for tools like the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme, which grew from 2.7k to 50k vetting checks (2019–2023), and the importance of regional hubs (e.g., RSH) to adapt global standards locally.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will **actively engage other donors** to contribute to pooled funds (e.g., PSEA-CAP) and co-fund projects, reducing UK burden share. Global public goods (e.g., CAPSEAH, RSH) are designed for **long-term sectoral use beyond UK funding**.

quote.source: D0007015.odt, Value for Money & Budget Breakdown
quote.text: The bulk of programme funding (over 60%) will go to organisations that are delivering global tools developed under the Innovation and Engagement Programme. [...] Enabling the creation of open access, sustainable ‘global public goods’ means the programme benefits are not just limited to its lifetime. [...] FCDO will also actively engage with other donors and funders to encourage engagement and contributions to support project initiatives, in order to reduce UK burden share and build their long-term sustainability.

metadata.programme_name: Building organisational capability to safeguard against sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment

quote.text: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years across multiple countries...

metadata.duration_source: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years across multiple countries, with the aim of building organisational capability in the aid sector and strengthening safeguards against sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (strengthening organisational safeguarding capabilities) with implementation research (testing and scaling prevention/response approaches) and financing mechanisms (dedicated capability fund). It aims to both build capability in less-resourced organisations AND generate evidence on what works in SEAH prevention.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years across multiple countries, with the aim of building organisational capability in the aid sector and strengthening safeguards against sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH). Keypriorities are: Supporting less-resourced organisations in the sector to reach international SEAH safeguarding standards through a direct capability-building programme; Investing in pioneering capability-building initiatives to drive up prevention and response practices and standards through a dedicated capability fund
q3_expected_outputs: Improved and sustainable capacity and capability to effectively hardwire safeguarding SEAH within organisations (contributing to a shift in organisational culture and strengthened accountability)
Widespread, rooted endorsement of SEAH safeguarding beyond 'donor compliance' (with networks across the sector engaging in more inclusive dialogue)
Contextualised and accessible evidence and learning on what works on building organisational capability and to prevent and respond to SEAH in the sector
1.2 million individuals reached via community-led communication raising activities (from previous ICOF fund example)
Free quality training, resources, support and good practice accessible to less-resourced CSOs
Key insights, lessons and evidence disseminated which address gaps in evidence
Continuation of essential, unique sector services and offers which address prevention and/or response to SEAH
Small-scale pilot activities by organisations developing innovative solutions
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to build organisational capability to prevent SEAH in the aid sector through direct support to less-resourced CSOs (Component 1) and a dedicated capability fund for innovative prevention/response initiatives (Component 2), while generating evidence on effective approaches.

quote.text: This programme will provide up to £20m over 5 years across multiple countries, with the aim of building organisational capability in the aid sector and strengthening safeguards against sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH).

countries_regions: FCDO countries/regions with highest risk from SEAH perspective
Targeted primarily at small NGOs in developing countries
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'. The context involves high-risk environments where SEAH is prevalent due to power imbalances and weak protection systems, but the programme itself is designed with mitigation measures.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
