where_context.q6_constraints_impact: High-risk contexts present heightened opportunities for perpetrators to commit SEAH, with persisting inequalities and power imbalances making certain groups more vulnerable. Under-reporting is perpetuated by fear and lack of trust in reporting systems, and there is currently no systematic data on SEAH prevalence across the sector. These constraints require tailored, contextualised approaches and strong safeguarding measures.

quote.text: The relationship between aid provider and recipient is often rooted in unequal power dynamics. This can drive vulnerability to SEAH if power is abused. Evidence shows that high risk contexts present heightened opportunities for perpetrators to commit SEAH. Persisting inequalities and power imbalances mean that certain groups of people can be more vulnerable to SEAH being perpetrated against them... SEAH is intrinsically sensitive and both under-reported and often undocumented. Under-reporting is also perpetuated where there is fear and lack of trust in reporting systems. There is currently no systematic data on the prevalence of SEAH across the sector...

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO/SGU retains strategic oversight and decision-making for both components, with Component 1 delivered by a lead supplier (likely Northern-based) and Component 2 managed in-house by SGU. Local partners (Southern CSOs) receive support but decision-making remains with FCDO/SGU and the lead supplier.
q10_capacity_building_details: training (free quality training for less-resourced CSOs)
mentorship (support and good practice sharing)
institutional strengthening (building capability to reach international safeguarding standards)
peer learning (coordinated stakeholder engagement to amplify voices and share lessons)
technical assistance (direct support to CSOs via lead supplier)

partner_organizations.name: Lead Supplier (Component 1)
partner_organizations.role: Delivery of capability-building programme for less-resourced CSOs; management of sub-contractors and regional hubs

partner_organizations.name: Sub-contractors (Component 1)
partner_organizations.role: Provide specific expertise (e.g., supporting vulnerable groups, national/localknowledge)

partner_organizations.name: Less-resourced CSOs (target beneficiaries)
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of capability-building support and training
partner_organizations.location: LMICs (FCDO priority countries/regions with highest SEAH risk)

partner_organizations.name: FCDO Safeguarding Unit (SGU)
partner_organizations.role: In-house management of Component 2 (capability fund); strategic oversight of entire programme

partner_organizations.name: Partners for Component 2 initiatives
partner_organizations.role: Recipients of small-scale grants for innovative SEAH prevention/response activities
partner_organizations.location: Global (open to all, with potential for wide impact)

partner_organizations.name: Existing sector platforms (e.g., RSH, HQAI, CHS Alliance)
partner_organizations.role: Potential collaborators/co-funders for aligned initiatives

quote.text: We recommend option 4. In this option, FCDO would continue to use the same delivery model for Component 1, a programme to support less-resourced CSOs as we do not have the capacity to do this in-house. For Component 2, the Safeguarding Unit would set up dedicated programme fund which it would manage in-house... Under Component 1 (Contract to a lead supplier) suppliers will propose their preferred model during the procurement process... For component 2: The fund will be managed in-house and therefore an SRO and HEO PRO from within the Safeguarding Unit will oversee the day-to-day programme management of the fund.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Component 1 uses a contract with a lead supplier (competitive procurement), while Component 2 uses a mix of Accountable Grants (AGs), Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs), and potentially low-value contracts for technical assistance, managed in-house by FCDO's Safeguarding Unit.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Component 1: Closed consortium led by a principal supplier with sub-contractors, overseen by FCDO/SGU. Component 2: Fund manager model with FCDO/SGU managing competitive calls and direct awards in-house. The structure combines contractual delivery (Component 1) with flexible, demand-led funding (Component 2).
how_mechanism.q14_competition_ratio: 24:1 (24 suppliers expressed interest to lead Component 1)
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Open competition was chosen to ensure value for money, sector-wide buy-in, and access to diverse expertise. The Early Market Engagement (EME) survey indicated strong supplier interest (100% preference for consortium-style delivery), and competitive procurement aligns with FCDO's standard practice for large programmes. For Component 2, in-house management allows FCDO to retain strategic control and responsiveness.

quote.text: Through fair and open competition, we will procure a lead supplier to deliver this programme... The EME survey ran in May 2024. Of the 24 suppliers who expressed an interest to lead the programme 100% indicated a preference towards a partnership consortium-style delivery model... We recommend option 4... For Component 2, the Safeguarding Unit would set up dedicated programme fund which it would manage in-house.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: For Component 1, FCDO/SGU provides strategic direction via governance boards, with the lead supplier managing day-to-day delivery. For Component 2, SGU manages the fund in-house with internal oversight. No formal steering committee or external board is mentioned; governance is retained within FCDO structures.

quote.text: The contract will receive strong strategic direction from FCDO, including through ensuring the Safeguarding Units sit on any strategic governance boards... Supplier performance will be managed through performance criteria, including key performance indicators (KPIs)... For component 2: The fund will be managed in-house and therefore an SRO and HEO PRO from within the Safeguarding Unit will oversee the day-to-day programme management of the fund.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Component 1 has built-in flexibility to scale services over time, and Component 2's fund allows for adjustments to project budgets. However, reallocation between Components requires approval, and the programme is designed to respond to emerging evidence while maintaining strategic focus.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme incorporates continuous learning (e.g., using RSH evaluation findings) and allows for small-scale experimentation. Component 2's in-house fund enables responsive, demand-led activities, but adjustments must align with FCDO priorities and are subject to internal oversight.

quote.text: The programme is expected to generate evidence and learning on what works in the course of its work, and to disseminate these sector-wide... Enables small-scale experimentation and adaptation in key priority areas... The flexible nature of the programme will help to scale the resources, targeting them where the need and potential impact is greatest... We will build in flexibility to the programme, so that the learning generated during the programme continuously informs implementation.
quote.source: D0007560.odt, Proposed programme components and Recommendations

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Lead Supplier (Component 1); FCDO → Direct grantees (Component 2). For Component 1, sub-contractors add a third layer (FCDO → Lead Supplier → Sub-contractors → CSOs).

quote.text: A robust KPI-linked payment mechanism and programme flexibility will allow the FCDO SRO and Commercial Lead to manage performance effectively... Payments will not be made in advance of need and will be made in arrears, as standard. This will be agreed in advance between FCDO and suppliers. Each disbursement will be conditional on specific delivery milestones being met.
quote.source: D0007560.odt, Monitoring, reporting, and accounting for funds

q24_alternatives_considered: Option 1: Do nothing (FCDO stops direct delivery/funding post-March 2025)
Option 2: Outsource entire programme to a single lead supplier
Option 3: Two separate programme components, each contracted to preferred lead suppliers
Option 4: Mixed model - Component 1 contracted to lead supplier; Component 2 managed in-house (CHOSEN OPTION)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Option 4 was selected for its balance of value for money, strategic control, and flexibility. Contracting Component 1 ensures specialist delivery for CSO capacity building, while in-house management of Component 2 allows FCDO to retain oversight, align with priorities, and respond nimbly to emerging needs. This model avoids the risks of supplier-led fragmentation (Option 2) or complex multi-contract governance (Option 3), and builds on successful past approaches (e.g., RSH, ICOF).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Supplier lack of alignment with FCDO priorities (Option 2 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Chose mixed model (Option 4) to retain FCDO oversight for Component 2 and strategic direction for Component 1.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Complex governance with multiple suppliers (Option 3 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Avoided by selecting a single lead supplier for Component 1 and in-house management for Component 2.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reduced responsiveness with fully outsourced model (Option 2 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: In-house fund (Component 2) enables agile, demand-led support aligned with FCDO priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmented portfolio with supplier-led investments (Option 2 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: FCDO retains control over Component 2 funding decisions to ensure coherence and VfM.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Gap in support for less-resourced CSOs (Option 1 risk)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme explicitly targets CSOs with free resources and direct support via Component 1.

quote.text: We recommend option 4... This would put the Safeguarding Unit in a better position to: Achieve best value for money, with appropriate balance between components of governance and oversight and appropriate expertise... Catalyse the sector in improving safeguarding standards by continuing to invest in both critical and new and innovative capability building activities... Balance opportunistic and demand-led activity with a strategic focus on FCDO- and HMG-wide priorities... Facilitate collaboration internally and across a range of external actors... The table below provides a summary appraisal of programme options against four categories: Responsive; SGU Oversight; Strategic Impact; Cost.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The programme targets FCDO countries/regions with highest SEAH risk, which shapes partner selection toward local CSOs in these contexts. The need for contextualised, accessible support (e.g., translated materials, local hubs) requires partners with regional expertise, limiting options to those with existing footprints or ability to establish them quickly.
q27_constraints_detail: High-risk contexts require partners with safeguarding expertise and local trust
Need for translated/accessible materials limits partners to those with multilingual capacity
Focus on less-resourced CSOs requires suppliers with experience supporting small, underfunded organisations
Digital services must be globally accessible, constraining technical platforms/partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The dual objectives of capability building (Component 1) and innovative funding (Component 2) directly shape the mixed delivery structure. Component 1's standardised training/support for CSOs suits a contracted supplier model, while Component 2's flexible, demand-led grants require in-house management for strategic alignment.
q28_linkages: CSO capability building → Lead supplier with sub-contractors for scalable, standardised support
Innovative prevention/response → In-house fund for agile, priority-aligned grants
Evidence generation → Both components feed into sector-wide learning, requiring coordination
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity (targeting less-resourced CSOs in high-risk contexts) with efficiency (using competitive procurement and in-house fund management). Trade-offs include: (1) Higher transaction costs for inclusive partnerships (e.g., sub-contractors for vulnerable groups) vs. speed of delivery; (2) Local leadership priorities vs. standardised safeguarding approaches; (3) Free resources for CSOs vs. sustainability of support post-programme.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs inclusion: Competitive procurement may favour established suppliers over local organisations, though sub-contracting mitigates this
Expertise vs ownership: Northern lead supplier provides technical quality, while local hubs/sub-contractors ensure contextual relevance
Cost vs reach: Free resources for CSOs maximise access but require significant programme subsidy
Standardisation vs adaptation: Core training materials ensure consistency, while local hubs allow for contextualisation
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile drives milestone-based oversight (e.g., quarterly reports, KPI-linked payments) and embedded safeguarding measures (e.g., due diligence for sub-awards). High-risk contexts (e.g., FCAS regions) would trigger more intensive management, but the programme's moderate rating allows for a balanced approach.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is the core objective, shaping partner roles as follows: (1) Lead supplier focuses on delivering training/technical assistance to CSOs; (2) Sub-contractors provide specialised support (e.g., for disabled persons, children); (3) Component 2 fund targets innovative approaches to fill evidence gaps. Partners are selected based on their ability to strengthen organisational capability, not just deliver outputs.

quote.text: Determining which regions to focus support on will be considered as part of the market engagement phase. But we expect to continue to identify countries/regions with highest SEAH risk using key data sources... We will seek to continue to provide support to less-resourced CSOs in particular, but seek to continue an approach which would provide free, online resources relevant sector-wide... The programme is expected to generate evidence and learning on what works in the course of its work, and to disseminate these sector-wide... We will likely draw on the FCDO’s Global Development Delivery (GDD) Framework Agreement... to enable organisations with specific knowledge supporting particular vulnerable groups (children, people with disabilities) and with specific contextual expertise (e.g. national, local knowledge) to engage with this programme.
quote.source: D0007560.odt, Proposed programme components and Programme delivery

key_programme_risks: Gap in support for less-resourced CSOs if programme stops (Option 1 risk)
Reputational damage to UK/FCDO for failing to deliver on SEAH commitments
Supplier misalignment with FCDO priorities (Option 2 risk)
Fragmented investments with outsourced model (Option 2 risk)
Complex governance with multiple suppliers (Option 3 risk)
Reduced responsiveness with fully contracted approach
Under-reporting of SEAH due to fear/lack of trust in systems
Lack of systematic data on SEAH prevalence hindering targeting
High-risk contexts increasing vulnerability to SEAH
Potential harm to beneficiaries if safeguarding measures fail

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Selected Option 4 to continue direct support via Component 1 and flexible funding via Component 2.
Programme aligns with UK's 2020 SEAH Strategy and international commitments (e.g., CAPSEAH).
FCDO provides strong strategic direction and sits on governance boards; in-house management of Component 2 retains control.
Single lead supplier for Component 1 and FCDO-managed fund for Component 2 ensure coherence.
Community-led awareness raising and victim-survivor centred reporting mechanisms (e.g., ICOF model).
Programme includes evidence generation and dissemination as a core output.
Targeted support to regions with highest SEAH risk; contextualised approaches via local hubs.
Due diligence assessments, zero-tolerance fraud policy, robust financial reporting, and FCDO Counter-Fraud Team oversight.

fcas_specific_lessons: Local leadership is vital for effective support in FCAS contexts (lesson from RSH programme).
Contextualised offers are critical in protracted crises (e.g., RSH hubs in Yemen, Ethiopia).
Reactive hubs can address emerging crises (e.g., Eastern Europe Hub for Ukraine response).
National networks of PSEAH specialists enable joint capacity building (ICVA finding).
Community-led communication raises awareness effectively in high-risk settings (ICOF model).
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The RSH programme demonstrated that free, contextualised support for less-resourced CSOs is effective and in demand, with strong uptake in priority countries. The ICOF fund showed that small grants for community-led awareness raising significantly increase SEAH reporting. HQAI's certification model proved that independent assessment can drive up standards. Lessons include: (1) Free resources are essential for CSOs; (2) Local hubs enhance contextual relevance; (3) Peer learning and national networks amplify impact; (4) Victim-survivor centred approaches increase reporting.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme builds on RSH's success by continuing free resources and national hubs, adopts ICOF's community-led awareness model, and incorporates HQAI's certification approach. Changes include: (1) Explicit focus on less-resourced CSOs; (2) Mixed delivery model (contract + in-house fund) for balance of standardisation and flexibility; (3) Stronger emphasis on local leadership and contextualisation; (4) Integration of victim-survivor centred reporting mechanisms.

quote.text: The Safeguarding Resource and Support Hub (RSH) capability programme has been successfully providing free support to aid organisations to strengthen their measures against SEAH... Since its creation in 2020, the programme has consistently met or exceeded expectations... The Interagency PSEA Community Outreach and Communication Fund (ICOF) 2020-2023... attracted strong interest with over 5,000 applications from NGOs worldwide... 87% of the projects resulted in a significant increase in awareness of SEA and 85% reported an increase in reporting of SEAH incidents following the awareness campaigns... We will seek to build on lessons from the Resource and Support Hub in providing deeply contextualised support... Determining which regions to focus support on will be considered as part of the market engagement phase... We expect to continue to identify countries/regions with highest SEAH risk using key data sources (for example, the SEA-RO Index and alignment with SGU wider programming priority areas).
quote.source: D0007560.odt, Context and Proposed programme components

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme will seek co-funding from other donors (e.g., DEC for Türkiye-Syria hub) and encourages wider donor contributions to maximise impact. Previous RSH programming attracted co-funding for short-term regional hubs (e.g., post-earthquake in Türkiye-Syria).

quote.text: This Business Case seeks approval for up to £20m over a five-year period, starting from autumn 2024 to March 2030... Some elements of our previous capability-building programme (the Resource and Support Hub) was provided via co-funding from wider donors (for example, a short-term regional hub was established in Türkiye-Syria with funding provided by DEC to support in the aftermath of the earthquake). We will continue to take a flexible approach to the programme and seek additional funding and co-funding investment from other sources.
quote.source: D0007560.odt, Financial details and Programme delivery

metadata.programme_name: Climate Resilience in the Sahel Programme (CRiSP)
metadata.duration_text: The programme is structured in two phases: phase 1 (2024-26) and phase 2 (2026-28).
metadata.quote: The Climate Resilience in the Sahel Programme (CRiSP) will support progress across all three objectives, making the most significant contribution to (ii) and (iii-b). The programme will also directly contribute to delivering Goal 2 (Delivering a cleaner greener planet) of the Business Plan for West Africa, Sahel, Sudan and South Sudan. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: The programme is structured in two phases: phase 1 (2024-26) will be delivered by the World Food Programme in eastern Chad (on the border with Sudan) and eastern Mauritania (on the border with Mali) and will inform potential scale up, geographic expansion in the Sahel or adaptation in phase 2 (2026-28). (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: CRiSP combines **implementation research** (testing nature-based solutions in protracted crises), **service delivery** (direct ecosystem restoration and livelihood support), and **capacity building** (strengthening local resilience and policy integration). It aims to bridge humanitarian-development-peacebuilding (HDP) nexus gaps while generating evidence on what works in fragile contexts.
what_objectives.q1_source: The programme will help refugees and host communities in areas where land degradation exacerbates food insecurity, to restore and manage their ecosystems, in order to increase the natural capital essential to their subsistence and livelihood. [...] CRiSP will make an important contribution to meeting the UK’s current £11.6 billion target for international climate finance (ICF) [...] and demonstrate how people-centred, complementary approaches [...] can respond to immediate needs while also building long-term resilience. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Cash and food assistance for over 30,000 households (Phase 1)
Increased access to natural resources (land and water) for refugees, IDPs, and host communities
Over 30,000 participants and their households supported to better adapt to climate change (ICF KPI1)
tCO2 mitigation through land restoration (ICF KPI6, Phase 2)
Restoration of ecosystem function (ICF KPI10, Phase 2)
Land restored and under sustainable management practices (ICF KPI17, Phase 2)
Proof of concept to unlock and leverage climate finance in protracted crises (KPI11)
Lessons learnt and evidence generated to inform the Resilience and Adaptation Fund (RAF) and FCDO’s work on climate resilience in humanitarian contexts

what_objectives.summary: CRiSP aims to reduce reliance on humanitarian assistance in the Sahel’s protracted crises by restoring ecosystems and building climate resilience through nature-based solutions (NbS), while generating evidence to inform UK policy and climate finance strategies. It directly addresses the ‘missing middle’ between emergency aid and long-term development.
what_objectives.quote: The programme will tackle the environmental root causes of food insecurity and contribute to restoring ecosystem function to enable long-term resilience for people and nature. [...] It will reduce reliance on humanitarian assistance for people in protracted crisis in the Sahel by promoting complementary approaches at the intersection of climate, nature, humanitarian and peace interventions. (D0006552.odt, The solution)

countries_regions.region: Hodh Ech Chargui (HEC) region (border with Mali)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The Sahel is characterized by **protracted conflict, weak governance, and extreme climate vulnerability**, with Chad and Mauritania hosting large refugee populations in climate hotspots. The UK’s Sahel Strategy explicitly highlights climate resilience as central to addressing fragility.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: **Moderate** [...] The Sahel has been identified as one of the regions where climate change is most likely to undermine security and trigger violent conflict. (D0006552.odt, Summary Sheet and The problem)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Security risks limit FCDO staff access; weak institutions hinder coordination of adaptation efforts; conflict disrupts transhumance and land governance; climate shocks (droughts/floods) exacerbate food insecurity; political instability (e.g., coups) reduces multilateral funding; and lack of climate data impedes evidence-based planning.
where_context.quote: State institutions are overwhelmed and unable to envision and coordinate adaptation efforts. [...] Climate adaptation measures [...] largely rest on the people themselves. [...] The region is comparatively overlooked by development and climate institutions that have historically been risk- and shock-averse. (D0006552.odt, The problem)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The **FCDO designs the programme framework and selects partners**, while WFP (multilateral) implements Phase 1. Local communities and governments are consulted but do not lead decision-making.
q10_capacity_building_details: training on sustainable land management (SLM) and ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA)
mentorship for local stakeholders on climate-resilient practices
institutional strengthening of government systems for land governance
community participation in land rehabilitation to empower women and marginalized groups

partner_organizations.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
partner_organizations.role: Phase 1 implementing partner (2024-26)
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (headquartered in Rome, operations in Chad/Mauritania)

partner_organizations.name: Local governments (Chad/Mauritania)
partner_organizations.role: consulted for alignment with national climate strategies; limited implementation role

partner_organizations.name: Host communities and refugees
partner_organizations.role: beneficiaries and participants in ecosystem restoration

who_partners.quote: The programme will engage with governments, partners and communities to identify ways to improve pathways to change in a given context. It will promote local leadership, drawing on local knowledge and expertise [...] while ensuring our approach will be gender-responsive and conflict-sensitive. (D0006552.odt, The solution)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: FCDO will contract the **World Food Programme (WFP)** for Phase 1 delivery (2024-26) using standard FCDO templates, with due diligence checks. The contract includes iterative learning and adaptive management clauses.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Phase 1 is delivered by **WFP as sole implementer** under FCDO contract, with FCDO oversight. Phase 2 (2026-28) may expand to additional partners based on Phase 1 lessons.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: WFP was selected due to its **existing operational presence in Chad/Mauritania**, experience in food security-climate nexus programming, and alignment with FCDO’s strategic priorities for the Sahel.
how_mechanism.quote: Phase 1 (2024-26) will be delivered by the **World Food Programme** in eastern Chad and eastern Mauritania. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)

how_governance.quote: The programme will take an **iterative and adaptive approach**, investing in existing context-specific solutions as a platform for the UK to learn, engage with resilience stakeholders and demonstrate how people-centred approaches [...] can respond to immediate needs while also building long-term resilience. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be adjusted between components **with FCDO approval**, as the programme is designed to ‘flex up or down’ in line with future allocations and learning from Phase 1.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme uses an **iterative approach** with embedded learning loops. Partners have autonomy to test and refine interventions, with FCDO providing oversight based on evidence. The Centre for Delivery (CfD) Solutions Hub will support experimentation.
how_flexibility.quote: The programme is designed to be **flexible and agile** so it can flex up or down, in line with future allocations. [...] We will ensure our learning informs other innovative work in the climate-humanitarian nexus including through the RAF community of practice. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary and Why the UK?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → WFP (implementer) → [communities/governments as sub-partners]
how_efficiency.quote: The programme will take an **iterative and adaptive approach**, investing in existing context-specific solutions [...] delivered with governments and communities. (D0006552.odt, Programme summary)

q24_alternatives_considered: Expanding existing humanitarian programmes (e.g., SHAPP) to include resilience components
Bilateral partnerships with Sahelian governments (rejected due to weak institutional capacity)
Multilateral climate funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund) – deemed too slow for protracted crises
Local NGO consortia (limited by operational risks in FCAS contexts)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The **WFP-led contract model** was selected for its **speed of deployment in FCAS contexts**, **existing operational footprint in target areas**, and **alignment with FCDO’s strategic priorities** (climate-humanitarian nexus). The direct award to WFP mitigates risks of partner failure in fragile settings while enabling adaptive learning.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (WFP’s economies of scale in food security-climate programming)
risk-mitigation (WFP’s experience in Chad/Mauritania’s high-risk environments)
partner-capacity (WFP’s ability to integrate NbS with humanitarian aid)
flexibility (iterative design to adjust to shocks)
equity (focus on women/girls and displaced populations)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a single implementer (WFP) may limit local ownership and innovation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded learning loops and community co-design to ensure local voices shape interventions.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: WFP’s humanitarian mandate may conflict with long-term resilience goals.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Explicit focus on **ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA)** and alignment with national climate strategies (NDCs/NAPs).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political instability in Chad/Mauritania could disrupt implementation.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Geographic focus on **accessible areas** with conducive political conditions (per Sahel Regional Board criteria).

vfm_criteria_used: economy (cost-effective use of WFP’s existing infrastructure)
effectiveness (evidence generation for RAF and ICF strategies)
equity (targeting women, refugees, and host communities)
why_rationale.quote: The UK is piloting approaches to land governance and climate resilience to reduce conflict over natural resources in Mali and Niger through the JASS programme. [...] CRiSP would build on the FCDO’s extensive natural-resource experience in forestry, agriculture, land management, pastoralism and water sectors. (D0006552.odt, Why the UK?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The **FCAS context limits partner selection to organizations with existing operational presence** (e.g., WFP) due to security risks, weak institutions, and donor aversion to fragile states. Local NGOs lack capacity for large-scale resilience programming, while multilaterals offer risk mitigation but may dilute local ownership.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict FCDO’s ability to manage implementation directly
Weak government capacity necessitates reliance on international partners
Donor risk aversion reduces funding options for local actors
Climate finance blind spots exclude protracted crisis contexts from vertical funds
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for integrated HDP nexus solutions** drives the choice of a **single-implementer model (WFP)** to bridge humanitarian-climate gaps, while the **focus on nature-based solutions (NbS)** requires a partner with both environmental and food security expertise. Iterative learning demands **adaptive management structures**.
q28_linkages: HDP nexus goal → WFP’s dual mandate (humanitarian + resilience)
NbS focus → Need for partner with ecosystem restoration experience
FCAS context → Direct award to minimize implementation risks
Evidence generation → Embedded learning loops and CfD Solutions Hub support
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly acknowledges tensions between **rapid delivery (efficiency)** and **local ownership (equity)**, opting for WFP’s efficiency while embedding community participation and gender-responsive design. The **direct award to a multilateral** prioritizes speed over competitive selection but includes safeguards for inclusivity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Direct award to WFP enables quick start but limits local partner diversity
Expertise vs. ownership: Northern/multilateral leadership ensures technical quality but risks sidelining Southern institutions
Cost vs. reach: Milestone-based payments control costs but may constrain adaptive responses to shocks
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **FCAS risk profile** drives **intensive oversight** (milestone-based reporting, conflict-sensitivity frameworks) and **restricted partner selection** (only organizations with proven FCAS experience). Adaptive management is used to offset high environmental and political volatility.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is **embedded** to address weak local institutional capacity, with WFP responsible for **training communities in SLM/EbA** while FCDO focuses on **policy integration** (e.g., aligning with NDCs/NAPs). Women and girls are prioritized for empowerment through land rehabilitation activities.
intersections.quote: The absence or lack of operational capacity of established adaptation, resilience and environmental actors [in FCAS] means we must improve collaboration across development, humanitarian, climate and peacebuilding actors. [...] Working on land rehabilitation issues presents a risk of ‘doing harm’ if the programme is insufficiently conflict-sensitive. (D0006552.odt, The solution and What others are doing)

key_programme_risks: Climate shocks (droughts/floods) may undermine resilience gains in target areas
Political instability in Chad/Mauritania could disrupt implementation or access
Conflict over land/water resources between host communities and refugees
Limited climate finance reaching protracted crisis contexts
Over-reliance on WFP may create dependency and limit local innovation
Gender-based violence risks in displacement settings
Weak government capacity to sustain interventions post-programme

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use of **climate-resilient NbS** (e.g., drought-resistant species, water harvesting) and iterative adaptation based on Met Office projections.
Focus on **geographically stable areas** (per Sahel Regional Board criteria) and maintain flexibility to relocate activities.
**Conflict-sensitivity frameworks** integrated into programme design, with community co-management of restored land.
Generate evidence to **unlock RAF and other ICF streams** for protracted crises; align with national climate strategies (NDCs/NAPs).
Gender-responsive safeguarding measures, including **women-led land rehabilitation** and safe access to natural resources.

fcas_specific_lessons: Protracted crises require **integrated HDP approaches**—humanitarian aid alone cannot address root causes (land degradation, climate shocks).
In FCAS, **adaptive management is critical** to respond to rapidly changing political and environmental conditions.
**Local leadership must be embedded** to ensure interventions are context-specific and sustainable, but external partners (e.g., WFP) are needed to mitigate implementation risks.
Climate finance **rarely reaches FCAS contexts**—programmes must proactively bridge this gap through innovative partnerships.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from **BRACED (2014-19)** and **SPARC (2020-25)** highlight the need for: 1) **context-specific solutions** (no one-size-fits-all in the Sahel); 2) **mid-delivery adaptability** to political/environmental shocks; 3) **linking and layering** complementary interventions (e.g., cash-for-work with land restoration).
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: CRiSP incorporates **iterative phases** (Phase 1 learning informs Phase 2 scale-up) and **integrated landscape management (ILM)** to address BRACED/SPARC findings on siloed approaches. The **HDP nexus focus** responds to lessons on the failure of standalone humanitarian or development programmes in FCAS.
risks_lessons.quote: The BRACED programme demonstrated that climate resilience programmes work best when following four principles: linking and layering, responding and adapting to rapidly changing circumstances, including the most vulnerable, and scaling and embedding into local policies. [...] The SPARC programme highlighted that **context is paramount**—solutions to similar issues may look very different across regional boundaries. (D0006552.odt, What the UK is doing)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The programme aims to **unlock additional climate finance** for protracted crises by demonstrating proof of concept for the **Resilience and Adaptation Fund (RAF)** and influencing ICF4 allocations. Success in Phase 1 could leverage further funding for Phase 2 (2026-28).
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme focuses on **revenue expenditures** (cash/food assistance, training, ecosystem restoration activities) with potential **capital co-benefits** (e.g., restored land as natural infrastructure).
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: **£19.5m** [...] The programme will help refugees and host communities in areas where land degradation exacerbates food insecurity, to restore and manage their ecosystems. (D0006552.odt, Summary Sheet)

metadata.programme_name: Ukraine Economic Stabilisation Programme

quote.text: HMGovernment will guarantee $3bn in World Bank lending to the Government of Ukraine over 2024-27.

duration_source.text: This will support the financing of the Government of Ukraine's budget, by increasing the amount that the World Bank can lend to Ukraine. [...] The package marks a shift from ad-hoc unpredictable funding to structured multi-year assistance, tied to the broader objectives of creating the conditions to win the peace through recovery, reform and growth.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides loan guarantees to the World Bank to enable increased lending to Ukraine, addressing its fiscal gap and supporting macroeconomic stability. It shifts from ad-hoc funding to structured multi-year assistance, facilitating predictable fiscal support for Ukraine's war and recovery efforts.

q1_source.text: This will support the financing of the Government of Ukraine's budget, by increasing the amount that the World Bank can lend to Ukraine. [...] The support represents the UK's contribution to a wider financing commitment from international donors which helped unlock Ukraine's IMF programme in March 2023, effective for four years.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Upto $3bn in fiscal support provided via World Bank lending
Regular and predictable disbursement of tranches
Portion of social protection or public services supported
Portion of civil servant wages supported
Ukraine passes IMF review points (quarterly; yearly)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to provide predictable fiscal support to Ukraine through World Bank loan guarantees, ensuring macroeconomic stability and safeguarding essential public services during and after the war. It aligns with Ukraine's IMF programme and supports early recovery and reform efforts.

quote.text: The core objective of UK guarantee support for Ukraine remains unchanged. However, a longer war combined with Ukraine’s IMF programme means it is now necessary to do so over the medium-term (up to 2027) while targeting our priority of ‘Winning the Peace’: Delivering fiscal assistance that supports Ukraine’s macroeconomic stability and safeguards the provision of essential services and; Integrating complementary assistance that helps support the conditions for early recovery where possible.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is in an active war with Russia, facing catastrophic economic impacts including a 30% GDP decline in 2022, loss of 30% of its labour force, and significant physical damage to infrastructure. The fiscal gap expanded to $42bn in 2022 due to defence expenditures and revenue shortfalls.

q5_source.text: On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a large-scale invasion of Ukraine which has had a catastrophic impact on the Ukrainian economy. In 2022, Ukrainian GDP fell by nearly 30% and the World Bank estimates that the national poverty rate increased from 5.5% to 24.2%. [...] The war has also caused significant physical damage to Ukraine’s buildings and infrastructure, with the World Bank estimating reconstruction costs of $411bn (March 2023; World Bank).

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The war has severely constrained Ukraine's fiscal capacity, with defence spending consuming nearly half of government expenditures (48% since March 2022). The loss of 30% of the labour force and occupied territories has reduced revenue, while monetary financing (a last resort) risks macroeconomic instability. Institutional capacity is stretched, complicating the absorption of international support.

quote.text: One of the most direct threats to Ukraine’s economic security post-invasion has been to its public finances. The Government of Ukraine (GoU) was at risk of being unable to fully finance the defence of the country and provide essential public services, which would have undermined its war effort and potentially precipitated a wider economic collapse. [...] With a large increase in spending driven by defence pressures, Ukraine’s fiscal gap expanded to $42bn (NBU) in 2022.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The World Bank (a Northern-led multilateral institution) manages the lending and disbursement processes, with the UK providing guarantees and oversight. Ukraine (GoU) is the recipient but does not have decision-making power over the guarantee structure or World Bank operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for social protection reforms
support for Ukraine’s reform agenda (judicial, anti-corruption, business environment)
joint programme work with World Bank on governance and early recovery

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: Lending institution and administrator of UK guarantees; disburses funds to Ukraine

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ukraine (GoU)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of World Bank lending; implements budget expenditures

partner_organizations.name: FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office)
partner_organizations.role: Provider of loan guarantees; oversees programme alignment with UK priorities

partner_organizations.name: IMF (International Monetary Fund)
partner_organizations.role: Sets macroeconomic framework and conditions for Ukraine’s fiscal support

partner_organizations.name: British Embassy Kyiv
partner_organizations.role: Local coordination and monitoring

quote.text: The deliverypartner for this programme is the World Bank. Cooperation on Ukraine has deepened in response to the war, with the UK having committed a large portion of its guarantee capacity to World Bank lending. [...] The World Bank will act as administrator for the guarantee arrangement and will monitor and manage risks on our behalf, in accordance with their own policies and procedures.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The primary instrument is a **loan guarantee** (up to $3bn) provided by the UK to the World Bank, enabling the Bank to lend additional funds to Ukraine. This is complemented by **technical assistance grants** (up to £3m) for joint UK-World Bank programming on social protection and reform. The guarantees are structured as contingent liabilities, with no upfront cost to the UK unless Ukraine defaults.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The World Bank administers the guarantee and manages disbursements to Ukraine, while the FCDO oversees alignment with UK priorities. The British Embassy Kyiv supports local coordination. The structure leverages the World Bank’s existing PEACE programme (Public Expenditures for Administrative Capacity Endurance in Ukraine) and may expand to include new instruments like Development Policy Operations (DPOs) or framework projects.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The World Bank was selected due to its established role as a trusted intermediary for Ukraine, its AAA credit rating (enabling low-cost lending), and its existing PEACE programme, which has successfully disbursed UK-guaranteed funds since the war began. The UK’s shareholder status in the World Bank also facilitates close oversight.

quote.text: The UK has neither an agreed framework to provide sovereign guarantees nor a direct sovereign lending capability. [...] The World Bank has performed strongly as a delivery partner in this regard, working effectively and flexibly to disburse all guaranteed lending to Ukraine since the war began consistent with UK objectives in Ukraine.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The World Bank manages day-to-day operations, while the FCDO monitors progress through annual reviews and IMF programme benchmarks. No formal steering committee or board is mentioned; oversight relies on the World Bank’s internal governance and the UK’s shareholder influence.

quote.text: The World Bank will act as administrator for the guarantee arrangement and will monitor and manage risks on our behalf, in accordance with their own policies and procedures. [...] The FCDO’s Annual Review found that the IBRD’s financial accountability policies and practices are robust.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are structured as annual tranches (up to $1bn/year), with flexibility to adjust the number and size of tranches based on evolving conditions. However, reallocation between instruments (e.g., from PEACE to a new DPO) would require approval and alignment with IMF constraints.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in instrument mix (e.g., shifting from budget support to early recovery projects) if Ukraine’s needs evolve, but changes must align with the IMF programme’s phased approach and G7 donor coordination. Technical assistance priorities (e.g., social protection vs. governance reforms) can also be refined over the first 12 months.

quote.text: We propose provisionally earmarking up to £3m for new technical assistance funding to support World Bank and FCDO programming in Ukraine subject to additional approvals led by the programme SRO. [...] It is possible that loan guarantees could facilitate World Bank instruments and complementary technical assistance that helps to deliver against these areas.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → World Bank → Government of Ukraine (GoU)

quote.text: The structure of existing World Bank support, which operates on a reimbursement basis, helps to mitigate the fiduciary risk. The World Bank will continue to disburse funding into designated bank accounts related to the specified purposes of the financing.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Providing grants into a World Bank multi-donor trust fund (MDTF). Scored highly on IMF alignment but deemed unaffordable due to ODA scarcity.
Combining guarantees with grants to improve lending terms (e.g., matching EU’s 0% interest loans). Requires prohibitive ODA amounts (e.g., £1.71bn for EU-equivalent terms).
Direct UK lending to Ukraine (up to $3bn). Rulled out due to lack of UK sovereign lending capability, high upfront ODA costs, and no Preferred Creditor Status.
Rejected as it would break G7 unity and risk undermining Ukraine’s IMF programme and war effort.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Loan guarantees were selected as the most **value-for-money** option, enabling the UK to leverage its AAA-rated World Bank partnership to unlock $3bn in lending **without upfront costs**. This approach aligns with the IMF programme’s phased support, avoids opportunity costs from ODA cuts, and maintains G7 burden-sharing. The World Bank’s strong governance and existing PEACE programme mitigate fiduciary risks.
q25_decision_factors: risk mitigation (World Bank’s AAA rating and Preferred Creditor Status)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Moral hazard
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: World Bank’s incentive to avoid defaults (to protect its Preferred Creditor Status) and 180-day non-payment threshold before guarantees are called. UK monitors this closely.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Contingent liability risk
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Guarantees are structured as contingent liabilities (£4.1bn estimated exposure), with no upfront ODA cost unless Ukraine defaults. The UK’s preferred recovery option is to let the World Bank pursue repayments.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Non-concessional lending caps under IMF programme
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Annual tranches are capped at $1bn and aligned with IMF’s non-concessional funding limits. Flexibility to adjust instrument mix if conditions worsen.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fiduciary risk in new instruments
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Ongoing monitoring of commercial risks, especially if supporting capital expenditure (e.g., framework projects). World Bank’s reimbursement system and audit processes mitigate misuse.

quote.text: Overall, we conclude that providing up to $3bn more in IBRD loan guarantees to support Ukraine’s fiscal needs represents the best value for money method of providing fiscal support at scale over the course of the IMF programme. [...] IBRD loan guarantee efficiency is demonstrated through the lending capacity unlocked; each $1bn guarantee enables further $1bn of new lending.
quote.source: D0007382.odt, Value for Money of preferred fiscal support option section

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Ukraine’s **FCAS context** (active war, weak institutions, and fiscal collapse) constrains partner selection to **multilateral institutions with strong governance** (e.g., World Bank). The UK cannot provide direct budget support or sovereign loans due to lack of frameworks, and Ukrainian institutions lack the capacity to manage large-scale, flexible funding independently.
q27_constraints_detail: Ukraine’s **credit downgrade** post-invasion limits its access to capital markets, necessitating multilateral intermediaries.
**Weak institutional capacity** in Ukraine (e.g., stretched Ministry of Finance) requires trusted partners like the World Bank to administer funds.
**G7 coordination requirements**** limit unilateral UK actions, favoring multilateral channels for burden-sharing.
**IMF programme constraints**** (e.g., non-concessional lending caps) shape the choice of instruments (e.g., IBRD guarantees over grants).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **need for predictable, large-scale fiscal support** (WHAT) drives the choice of **loan guarantees** (HOW), as they unlock World Bank lending without upfront ODA costs. The **shift to medium-term support** (2024–2027) also necessitates a **flexible instrument mix** (e.g., PEACE for budget support + potential DPOs for reforms) to align with Ukraine’s evolving recovery needs.
q28_linkages: **Fiscal stability objective** → Loan guarantees (scalable, no upfront cost) over grants (unaffordable).
**Early recovery focus** → Potential use of framework projects (capital expenditure) alongside budget support.
**IMF alignment** → Tranche structure (≤$1bn/year) matches IMF’s annual non-concessional caps.
**Social protection priorities** → Technical assistance grants complement guarantees to strengthen systems.
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between **efficiency** (speed, scale) and **equity** (inclusive recovery):

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: **Loan guarantees** enable rapid, large-scale disbursements but risk **bypassing local ownership** (World Bank-led). Technical assistance (e.g., social protection reforms) mitigates this by embedding UK priorities in GoU systems.

The UK provides **non-concessional IBRD guarantees** (less generous than EU/US grants) to meet its **G7 burden-sharing commitment**, balancing cost (no upfront ODA) with equity (Ukraine’s debt sustainability).
While the programme allows **instrument adjustments** (e.g., shifting to DPOs), these must align with **IMF constraints** and **World Bank board cycles**, limiting agility.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk FCAS context** (default risk, protracted war) necessitates **intensive oversight** via the World Bank’s reimbursement systems, IMF reviews, and FCDO annual audits. Moral hazard risks are mitigated by the World Bank’s **Preferred Creditor Status incentives** and 180-day default threshold.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: The **World Bank’s capacity** (AAA rating, existing PEACE programme) enables it to **administer guarantees and disburse funds**, while the **GoU’s limited capacity** restricts its role to expenditure implementation. Technical assistance aims to **strengthen GoU systems** (e.g., social protection, anti-corruption) for longer-term ownership.

quote.text: The UK has neither an agreed framework to provide sovereign guarantees nor a direct sovereign lending capability. [...] The World Bank has performed strongly as a delivery partner in this regard, working effectively and flexibly to disburse all guaranteed lending to Ukraine since the war began consistent with UK objectives in Ukraine.

key_programme_risks.risk: Ukraine default
key_programme_risks.description: Non-repayment of World Bank loans would trigger UK guarantee liabilities (up to £4.1bn).

key_programme_risks.risk: Prolonged war
key_programme_risks.description: If the conflict extends beyond mid-2024 (IMF baseline assumption), Ukraine’s fiscal gap may exceed committed G7 support, requiring additional concessions or debt relief.

key_programme_risks.risk: Macroeconomic instability
key_programme_risks.description: Inflation or exchange rate volatility could increase Ukraine’s debt burden, affecting repayment capacity.

key_programme_risks.risk: Reform backsliding
key_programme_risks.description: Failure to implement IMF benchmarks (e.g., anti-corruption, governance) could halt disbursements.

key_programme_risks.risk: Fiduciary risks in new instruments
key_programme_risks.description: Expanding beyond PEACE to capital expenditure (e.g., framework projects) may introduce corruption or mismanagement risks.

key_programme_risks.risk: G7 unity fractures
key_programme_risks.description: If other donors renege on commitments, the UK’s $3bn may become insufficient to close the fiscal gap.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: World Bank’s Preferred Creditor Status incentivizes repayment; 180-day grace period before guarantees are called; UK’s preferred recovery option is to let the World Bank pursue repayments.
Flexible tranche structure (≤$1bn/year) allows adjustments. Blended finance or grants can be reconsidered if the IMF’s downside scenario materializes.
IMF programme includes inflation targets and exchange rate monitoring. World Bank’s reimbursement system ensures funds are used for designated purposes.
IMF’s phased approach ties disbursements to benchmarks. UK technical assistance supports GoU reform delivery (e.g., anti-corruption via TAPAS project).
World Bank’s safeguards (audits, fraud detection) and FCDO’s annual reviews. New instruments require additional approvals.
UK’s $3bn commitment is part of a collective $115bn G7 pledge. Regular G7 coordination and IMF reviews monitor burden-sharing.

fcas_specific_lessons: **Lesson 1**: In FCAS contexts, **multilateral guarantees** are more effective than bilateral loans due to Preferred Creditor Status and risk-sharing.
**Lesson 2**: **Reimbursement-based disbursements** (vs. upfront grants) reduce fiduciary risks in weak institutional environments.
**Lesson 3**: **Phased IMF programmes** (stabilization → reform) provide a structured framework for donor coordination in active conflicts.
**Lesson 4**: **Technical assistance must complement fiscal support** to address systemic gaps (e.g., social protection targeting) exposed by crises.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The **FREE Ukraine programme** (2022–2023) demonstrated that: (1) **World Bank guarantees** can be disbursed rapidly and at scale during war; (2) **PEACE programme’s reimbursement model** effectively mitigates corruption risks; (3) **Donor coordination** (G7+IMF) is critical to unlocking large-scale support. The new programme builds on these lessons by expanding the guarantee volume ($3bn vs. $2bn) and integrating technical assistance for early recovery.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Key adaptations include: (1) **Longer-term horizon** (2024–2027 vs. annual addendums under FREE); (2) **Flexible instrument mix** (potential DPOs/framework projects alongside PEACE); (3) **Explicit technical assistance budget** (£2–3m) to address social protection and governance gaps identified during FREE.

quote.text: The UK’s previous fiscal support is set out in the Financing of Recovery from Economic Emergency in Ukraine (FREE Ukraine) business case (March 2022). The scale of UK support under FREE Ukraine has been increased three times through business case addendums to approximately $1bn/annum in loan guarantees in 2022 and 2023. [...] The original business case also provided £99m in grants through the World Bank’s Multi-donor Trust Fund and for Ukraine’s armed forces.
quote.source: D0007382.odt, UK support up to the IMF programme section

co_funding_partners.role: Lending institution (mobilizes $3bn in loans backed by UK guarantees)
Provides $15.6bn in lending and coordinates $115bn G7 donor package
Collective $115bn fiscal support commitment (UK’s $3bn is part of this)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s $3bn (£2.4bn) guarantee unlocks $3bn in World Bank lending, creating a **1:1 leverage ratio**. This is part of a broader $115bn G7 package that enabled Ukraine’s IMF programme.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The programme primarily supports **revenue expenditures** (e.g., social protection, civil servant salaries) via budget support. Potential **capital expenditures** (e.g., infrastructure) may be included later through framework projects, but these are not the primary focus.

quote.text: The UK will provide a guarantee covering up to $3bn (£2.4bn) of World Bank lending to Ukraine, plus associated interest repayments. This will create an estimated contingent liability of £4.1bn. [...] The loan guarantees will be recorded as contingent liabilities on the FCDO’s balance sheet that would only result in ODA expenditure if Ukraine were to default on a loan and the guarantee were to be called.

metadata.programme_name: Hybrid Capital contribution to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)
metadata.quote: The UK’s £100m contribution will mean an extra £800m to £1000m in lending. This will support work in areas discussed in paragraph A9. (S4003064.odt, Strategic Case)
metadata.duration_source: Hybrid Capital can be leveraged ten times over ten years if the UK chooses to waive its coupon and advise the Bank to direct its saving to IBRD General Reserves. (S4003064.odt, Appraisal Case)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides hybrid capital to the IBRD to unlock additional lending capacity for middle-income countries (MICs) to address global challenges like climate change, pandemics, and fragility. It leverages the UK's contribution 10x to generate £800m-£1bn in new financing over a decade.
what_objectives.q1_source: The main outcome of this hybrid capital contribution will be an increase in IBRD support to Middle Income Countries. The UK’s £100m contribution will mean an extra £800m to £1000m in lending. (S4003064.odt, Expected Impacts)
q3_expected_outputs: £800m-£1bn in additional IBRD lending over 10 years
45% of lending with climate co-benefits (equivalent to ~£360m-£450m)
Support for 8 global challenges: climate mitigation/adaptation, digital enablement, energy access, food security, fragility, pandemic preparedness, biodiversity, water security
Potential coverage of 6.4 million tCO2 equivalent GHG reductions annually (based on FY23 results)
Support for 67.9 million people under social safety nets (FY23 benchmark)
what_objectives.summary: The programme scales up IBRD's financial capacity to address urgent global challenges through a hybrid capital instrument that multiplies UK funding 10x, with explicit targets for climate action and global public goods.
what_objectives.quote: To meet the SDGs and tackle climate change we must work with middle income countries (MICs)... The World Bank Group is one of the UK's most important development partners... A 'bigger' bank, delivered through... unlocking higher IBRD lending. (S4003064.odt, Strategic Case)

countries_regions: Specific focus on countries with high climate vulnerability (e.g., China 30% CO2, India 7.62%, Indonesia 1.96%)
Fragile and conflict-affected states (FCS) where IBRD operates
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: IBRD operates in MICs with stable credit ratings (AAA) but faces risks from climate vulnerability, fragility, and pandemic threats. The Bank has strengthened its crisis toolkit (e.g., Climate Resilient Debt Clauses) to mitigate these risks.
where_context.q5_source: Climate change is not the only global challenge... the recent coronavirus pandemic has shown we need to invest more in global health security... IBRD plays a critical role in supporting countries during conflicts and crises. (S4003064.odt, Strategic Case)
q6_contextual_constraints: political economy barriers to reform in MDBs
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Debt limits and climate vulnerabilities in MICs reduce their ability to access affordable finance; IBRD's hybrid capital model addresses this by providing below-market-rate lending for global public goods. Political barriers slow MDB reform processes (e.g., capital increase negotiations take 'several years').
where_context.quote: An increasing number of countries are in severe debt and unable to access affordable finance to grow their economies... The boost to IBRD lending from the 2018 capital increase and early CAF measures has already happened. Without additional measures IBRD lending commitments will remain flat. (S4003064.odt, Strategic Case)

who_partners.lead_institution_name: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The IBRD is governed by its Board of Executive Directors where shareholder countries (primarily Northern) hold decision-making power. The UK, as a major shareholder, influences reforms and capital increases but MICs have limited voting rights proportional to their shares.
q10_capacity_building_details: Support for MICs to decouple carbon emissions from economic growth (technical assistance)
Strengthening crisis preparedness through Climate Resilient Debt Clauses (CRDCs)
Knowledge sharing on '3i strategy' (investment, infusion, innovation) for escaping middle-income traps
Institutional strengthening for disability inclusion and gender equality in IBRD operations

partner_organizations.name: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)
partner_organizations.role: Primary recipient and implementer of hybrid capital; leverages funds 10x for MIC lending

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Funder and strategic influencer; pushes for IBRD reforms and allocation priorities

partner_organizations.name: G7 countries (Belgium, Denmark, Latvia, Netherlands, Norway)
partner_organizations.role: Co-financiers of hybrid capital; collective pledges unlock $70bn in IBRD lending

partner_organizations.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)
partner_organizations.role: Partner for exposure exchanges and guarantees (e.g., $1bn guarantee for IBRD loans)

partner_organizations.name: Middle-Income Country governments
partner_organizations.role: Borrowers of IBRD loans; implement climate, health, and fragility projects

who_partners.quote: The UK has been a leading partner in GFS reform: pushing MDBs to 'stretch their balance sheets'... pioneered the use of innovations such as guarantees... The UK’s commitment and payment of its hybrid capital contribution will increase pressure on other donors to follow through. (S4003064.odt, Strategic Case)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The £100m hybrid capital combines debt and equity features: it is a perpetual debt instrument with equity credit (100% recognized by credit ratings agencies) that pays a waivable coupon. It can later convert to paid-in capital during a general capital increase.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IBRD manages the hybrid capital through its existing AAA-rated balance sheet, leveraging it 10x via capital markets borrowing. The UK allocates its contribution to IBRD's Global Solutions Accelerator Platform (GSAP) for targeted global challenges.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IBRD is the largest MDB with a proven leverage model (10x) and alignment with UK priorities. The hybrid capital instrument was designed specifically for IBRD's capital structure and risk appetite, as validated by the G20 CAF Review.
how_mechanism.quote: Hybrid Capital is a way for shareholders to provide additional capital to the MDBs outside of normal capital increases... IBRD has designed its hybrid capital structure to receive 100% equity credit from the CRAs. (S4003064.odt, What is hybrid capital)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: IBRD's Board of Executive Directors oversees capital allocations and lending decisions. The UK, as a shareholder, participates in Board discussions but does not micromanage project-level decisions.
how_governance.quote: FCDO regularly reviews the IBRD’s proposed projects to seek to ensure full compliance and can raise concerns at the Board if we believe the World Bank is falling short... (S4003064.odt, Compliance with UK legislation)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are allocated to IBRD's GSAP but can be reallocated within the 8 global challenge areas. The hybrid capital's coupon savings can be directed to specific initiatives (e.g., CRDC fees) with UK input.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The UK can recommend changes to coupon allocation (e.g., to Livable Planet Fund or CRDC subsidies) but structural changes require IBRD Board approval. The GSAP has a 7-year sunset clause allowing reallocation.
how_flexibility.quote: We could consider earmarking the coupon to be used in other ways in the Bank... Any earmarking of the coupon would expire upon conversion of the hybrid capital to paid-in capital. (S4003064.odt, Appraisal Case)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IBRD → MIC borrowers (no additional intermediaries)
how_efficiency.quote: In addition to approval for £100m – we will need up to £140,000 for set up and maintenance fees... The UK’s £100m contribution will mean an extra £800m to £1000m in lending. (S4003064.odt, The proposed intervention)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do nothing (discounted due to urgent SDG/climate financing gaps)
General capital increase only (discounted due to slow negotiation timeline)
Portfolio Guarantee Platform (discounted due to lower leverage ratio of 6x vs 10x)
Commercial hybrid capital (discounted due to higher borrowing costs for MICs)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Hybrid capital was selected for its speed (unilateral, no lengthy negotiations), high leverage (10x), and ability to act as a 'downpayment' on a future general capital increase while pushing IBRD to implement CAF reforms. It aligns with the UK's 'twin track' approach of scaling IBRD quickly while advocating for longer-term reforms.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Lower leverage if coupon is not waived (8x vs 10x)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK commits to waive the coupon to maximize ODA scoring and leverage.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: IBRD may not allocate GSAP funds to UK priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: UK will recommend coupon savings be used for Climate Resilient Debt Clauses, aligning with existing UK advocacy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Conversion to paid-in capital at future GCI reduces UK's negotiating power
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Hybrid capital is sized at 50% of benchmark (£100m vs £220m) to retain influence for GCI negotiations.

why_rationale.quote: On balance, we conclude that a hybrid capital contribution is the best way for the UK to enable increased lending volumes for the IBRD fast... This makes it a highly effective way to increase MDB financing capacity, bringing financing forward given urgent present needs. (S4003064.odt, Appraisal Case)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: IBRD's focus on MICs (WHERE) limits partner selection (WHO) to countries with sufficient creditworthiness to borrow from IBRD, excluding the poorest LICs that rely on IDA. The GSAP's global challenges framework further narrows eligibility to countries facing cross-border risks (e.g., climate-vulnerable MICs).
q27_constraints_detail: MIC creditworthiness requirements exclude many LICs
GSAP's 8 global challenges prioritize countries with cross-border externalities
IBRD's AAA rating depends on shareholder backing, limiting non-traditional partners
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need to scale climate finance and global public goods (WHAT) drives the choice of hybrid capital (HOW) due to its speed and leverage. The 45% climate co-benefit target shapes the GSAP allocation mechanism, while the £800m-£1bn lending goal determines the £100m UK contribution size.
q28_linkages: 45% climate target → GSAP allocation for climate mitigation/adaptation
Urgent SDG financing gap → Hybrid capital's 10x leverage model
MIC focus → IBRD's non-concessional lending instruments
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly discusses tensions between (1) maximizing leverage (efficiency) by allocating to IBRD's general reserves vs. targeting global challenges (equity) via GSAP, and (2) waiving the coupon for full ODA scoring (equity) vs. using it to subsidize CRDCs (efficiency in crisis response).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: General reserves (10x leverage) vs. GSAP (8x leverage but targeted equity)
Coupon waiver (full ODA) vs. coupon use for CRDC subsidies (targeted impact)
Speed of hybrid capital (unilateral) vs. reform influence of general capital increase (multilateral)
intersections.risk_affects_management: IBRD's moderate risk profile (climate/fragility exposure) justifies milestone-based oversight (e.g., GSAP's 7-year sunset clause) rather than intensive management, while the AAA rating enables light-touch financial controls.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: IBRD's strong existing capacity (AAA rating, leverage model) allows it to absorb hybrid capital without additional implementation layers, while MICs' limited capacity drives the embedded technical assistance (e.g., 3i strategy support).
intersections.quote: Allocating to IBRD’s general reserve would boost core resources... However, we recommend allocating the UK’s hybrid capital contribution to the GSAP, as it would recognise the need to scale up MDB support to deliver on these pressing global challenges... (S4003064.odt, Appraisal Case)

key_programme_risks: IBRD lending may not reach the poorest within MICs (equity risk)
GSAP fragmentation could reduce IBRD's operational flexibility
Hybrid capital conversion at GCI may limit UK's negotiating leverage
MIC debt sustainability could worsen, increasing IBRD's non-performing loans
Climate co-benefit targets (45%) may not be met if MICs prioritize economic growth over decarbonization

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: IBRD lending may not reach the poorest within MICs
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IBRD targets 70% of non-crisis lending to below-GDI countries and offers lowest pricing to vulnerable groups (small states, FCS, IDA blends).
7-year sunset clause allows reallocation to general reserves; broad global challenges focus avoids over-specialization.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Hybrid capital conversion reducing UK leverage
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: UK contribution sized at 50% of benchmark (£100m vs £220m) to retain influence for GCI negotiations.
IBRD's AAA rating and prudent E/L ratio (19%) mitigate default risks; CRDCs provide payment pauses during crises.

fcas_specific_lessons: IBRD has quadrupled financing to fragile states over the past decade, with FCS share of portfolio doubling from 2016–2021.
Climate Resilient Debt Clauses (CRDCs) were developed based on FCAS experiences to pause repayments during disasters.
The World Bank's FCS strategy emphasizes state legitimacy and regional stability, lessons applied to IBRD's MIC engagements.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2018 IBRD capital increase demonstrated that shareholder contributions can be leveraged 10x over a decade, but negotiations took years. The G20 CAF Review showed that balance sheet reforms (e.g., E/L ratio reduction to 19%) could unlock hundreds of billions without new paid-in capital, informing the hybrid capital design.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Hybrid capital designed to receive 100% equity credit (vs. AfDB's 130bps premium for commercial hybrid capital).
GSAP includes a 7-year sunset clause to prevent permanent fragmentation, addressing MOPAN's concerns about 'cascade' approach implementation.
Coupon waiver structure aligns with OECD DAC's ODA scoring rules, ensuring full grant equivalent recognition.
risks_lessons.quote: The World Bank has been helping developing countries respond to health, social and economic impacts of Covid-19... Financing to the poorest, fragile and conflict affected countries has quadrupled over the past decade... (S4003064.odt, Expected Impacts)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: £100m UK contribution leverages £800m–£1bn in IBRD lending over 10 years (10x if coupon waived; 8x if directed to specific initiatives). Collective donor pledges unlock $70bn in IBRD lending.
financial_details.capital_vs_revenue_split: The £100m is capital expenditure (hybrid capital instrument) that generates revenue streams for IBRD via loan repayments over 10+ years. The coupon waiver (revenue foregone) is ~$7.1m/year at full disbursement.
financial_details.quote: For each dollar in capital, IBRD can hold more than 5 dollars in outstanding loans and guarantees... an additional dollar in capital can increase IBRD’s financing capacity by up 10 dollars over a period of 10 years. (S4003064.odt, Box 4: IBRD’s Leveraging Model)

metadata.programme_name: Trade Centre of Expertise – Evidence and Innovation Programme

quote.text: The Trade Centre of Expertise-Evidence and Innovation Programme accompanies the Trade Centre of Expertise Programme and will improve the use of evidence across HMG’s Aid for Trade (AFT) Portfolio through targeted research and evidence, and coherent and effective Monitoring, Reporting, Evaluation and Learning.

duration_source.text:
AMP Start Date: July 2024
AMPEndDate: March 2030

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines evidence generation (research to create new knowledge) with policy influence (informing policy decisions) and capacity building (strengthening institutions/skills). It aims to improve the use of evidence across HMG’s Aid for Trade Portfolio through targeted research, monitoring, evaluation, and learning, while also driving forward improvements in evidence and data to influence development partners and partner governments.

q1_source.text: The Trade Centre of Expertise-Evidence and Innovation Programme accompanies the Trade Centre of Expertise Programme and will improve the use of evidence across HMG’s Aid for Trade (AFT) Portfolio through targeted research and evidence, and coherent and effective Monitoring, Reporting, Evaluation and Learning. It will aim to increase HMG and international understanding of what works in Trade for Development policy, driving forward improvements in evidence and data and use this to influence the policies of development partners and partner governments.

q3_expected_outputs.output: longitudinal study to measure the long-term impacts of the new Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS)
study focused on measuring the benefits of the services provisions in the UK-CARIFORUM EPA
Trade COE MREL approach including a first-year Process Evaluation and a fourth-year in-depth Trade COE Impact and Value for Money evaluation
design and maintenance of a central Trade COE website
scoping assessment reports for potential Trade COE support to developing country partners
support to the global good services data project proposed by the World Bank and the WTO
portfolio of strategic internal evidence projects (1 large, 1 medium, 3 small) and MREL projects for the main Trade COE
strategic communications and engagements (1 large and 1 small event)

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to improve the use of evidence in Trade for Development policy and programmes, focusing on both internal HMG needs and global evidence gaps. It will deliver a mix of long-term research projects, responsive policy-led projects, and strategic communications to drive evidence-based decision-making.

quote.text: The programme will aim to increase HMG and international understanding of what works in Trade for Development policy, driving forward improvements in evidence and data and use this to influence the policies of development partners and partner governments.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The overall programme risk rating is classified as 'Minor', indicating a low-risk profile. This is based on the nature of the programme, which focuses on evidence generation and strategic communications rather than direct implementation in high-risk environments.

q5_source.text: Overall programme risk rating: Minor

q6_contextual_constraints: compliance with sustainability and environmental requirements
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Developing countries face challenges such as poor quality and incomplete data, especially in services trade, which limits the ability to measure the impact of policy or programme interventions. Non-tariff barriers, compliance issues, and weak capabilities in international trade further constrain their participation in global trade systems.

quote.text: Evidence Gaps: Poor quality and incomplete data, especially in specific policy areas such as services trade, mean we do not always know what trade is happening, or can measure the impact of policy or programme interventions.

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The FCDO (UK-based) retains decision-making power over the programme's strategic direction, project approvals, and overall governance.
