Southern partners (e.g., World Bank, WTO) are engaged as implementers or collaborators but do not have primary decision-making authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and mentorship through evidence projects
institutional strengthening via MREL support
knowledge sharing through strategic communications and engagement activities

partner_organizations.name: World Bank
partner_organizations.role: implementer (global good services data project)

partner_organizations.name: World Trade Organization (WTO)
partner_organizations.role: collaborator (global good services data project)

partner_organizations.name: Global Development Delivery (GDD) Framework suppliers
partner_organizations.role: deliverypartner (Evidence and Learning Facility)

partner_organizations.name: Trade COE Hub (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: programme management and coordination

quote.text: The programme will be led by the evidence team within the UK-based Trade for Development team in the Trade and Economic Security Directorate.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses a combination of funding instruments: 1) Accountable Grants and Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) for the Global Evidence Fund Window, 2) a framework agreement (Global Development Delivery Framework) for the Evidence and Learning Facility, and 3) programme-funded roles (FCDO staff) for the Trade COE Hub functions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme combines a central FCDO-managed Trade COE Hub with an externally delivered Evidence and Learning Facility (via GDD framework) and a Global Evidence Fund Window (via MoUs/grants). The Hub coordinates overall strategy and MREL, while the Facility provides responsive support and the Fund Window focuses on global evidence projects.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The Global Development Delivery (GDD) Framework was chosen for its ability to offer a broad range of capable delivery partners with relevant experience, while allowing the programme to start quickly. The framework's competitive bidding process is expected to drive value for money.

quote.text: The Global Development Delivery (GDD) Framework will be used to procure a delivery partner for this delivery element. This offers a balance between a broad offer of capable delivery partners with relevant experience and the ability to get the programme started this financial year.

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Trade COE Board serves as the governance body, with approval authority for projects over a certain value (e.g., £0.5m). The Board includes representation from the Trade for Development team and other relevant HMG stakeholders. Day-to-day management is shared between the FCDO Trade COE Hub and the Evidence and Learning Facility delivery partner.

quote.text: The approval decision will be made by the Technical Assistance Facility Manager in accordance with the strategic priorities set by the management board and the SRO and in consultation with the Regional Leads for Africa and Asia. Approval of project over a certain value (e.g. £0.5m) will remain with the management board.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between components to respond to demand from Posts and changing circumstances, but budget transfers require approval at the appropriate governance level and are actioned on HERA in line with the budgeting timetable.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme is designed to be responsive to FCDO programme and policy evidence needs, with the ability to adapt work according to externalities (e.g., trade-disrupting events). The hybrid delivery model allows for adjustments in project focus, though major changes require governance approval.

quote.text: The allocation of funds between different components will be flexible, in part to respond to demand from Posts, and the scope of individual activities will be reviewed (and where necessary adjusted) on at least an annual basis to maximise impact through adapting to learning and any changing circumstances.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Delivery Partner (Evidence and Learning Facility or Global Evidence Fund implementers). For programme-funded roles, the layer is just FCDO (no intermediary).

quote.text: Payments will be released following receipt of accurate invoices and deliverables.
quote.source: D0005776.odt, Expenditure Monitoring, Reporting and Accountability

q24_alternatives_considered: Support long-term projects of global value only
Support bespoke, responsive projects tied to policy needs only
Focus on frontier issues (think-tank role) only
Provide strategic communications and engagement activities only
Provide direct MREL/impact support across portfolio only
Act as Shop-Front for the broader Trade COE only
Combination of some or all of the above
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The hybrid approach was chosen to balance global evidence needs with internal policy responsiveness. This model allows the programme to deliver both long-term, high-impact global projects (via the Global Evidence Fund) and responsive, policy-driven projects (via the Evidence and Learning Facility), while embedding coordination and MREL functions within the Trade COE Hub. The combination maximizes flexibility, value for money, and the ability to influence both HMG and global trade policy.
q25_decision_factors: past experience (lessons from FCDO evidence programmes)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Risk of not securing quality proposals through the GDD framework call
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated via early market engagement with framework delivery partners, which offered reassurance of interest and allowed suppliers to prepare supply chains for the outlined timeframe.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited ability to influence delivery of projects under the World Bank Umbrella Facility
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Managed by including a ‘preference’ in the Administrative Arrangement to indicate areas of strongest interest and through regular direct engagement with project leads.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Potential lack of internal capacity for programme-funded roles
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: If suitable internal candidates are unavailable, the delivery partner may be asked to deliver the entire ‘Shop-Front’ function.

quote.text: The hybrid approach, that combines the two options above and includes a programme funded role(s) to lead the Shop-Front element as part of a Trade COE Hub, thereby embedding expertise and evidence into the team.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The global scope of the programme requires partners with the ability to operate across multiple regions and engage with international organizations (e.g., World Bank, WTO). This limits partner selection to organizations with established global networks, multilateral experience, and the capacity to manage complex, multi-country evidence projects.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for partners with global reach and multilateral experience
Requirement for partners capable of delivering in developing countries and LDCs
Capacity to engage with high-level stakeholders (e.g., WTO, World Bank)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s mixed objectives (global evidence generation + internal policy support) directly shape its hybrid delivery structure. The need for long-term global evidence projects necessitates the Global Evidence Fund Window, while the requirement for responsive, policy-linked projects drives the Evidence and Learning Facility. The Shop-Front function is embedded in the Trade COE Hub to ensure coordination across the portfolio.
q28_linkages: Global evidence gaps → Global Evidence Fund Window (long-term projects)
Internal policy needs → Evidence and Learning Facility (responsive projects)
Portfolio coordination needs → Shop-Front function in Trade COE Hub
MREL requirements → Centralized MREL function within the Hub
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly discusses the tension between delivering high-quality, inclusive evidence (equity) and the need for rapid, cost-effective responses to policy demands (efficiency). For example, the decision to limit focus on frontier issues (which scored lower in the appraisal) reflects a trade-off between innovative, long-term research and immediate policy relevance. Additionally, the programme emphasizes the importance of disaggregating data by gender and marginalized groups, which may require additional resources but is critical for equity.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Innovation (frontier issues) vs. policy relevance (responsive projects)
Global evidence needs vs. internal HMG priorities
Inclusive data collection (disaggregation) vs. cost/efficiency
Long-term research impact vs. short-term policy demands
intersections.risk_affects_management: The programme’s low overall risk rating ('Minor') allows for a more flexible and less intensive management approach, with quarterly oversight rather than embedded advisors. However, specific risks (e.g., partner performance, fund diversion) are managed through structured governance, due diligence, and performance-based incentives.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded throughout the programme, particularly in the MREL and Shop-Front functions, which are designed to strengthen the internal evidence base and improve the use of data across the Aid for Trade portfolio. The programme-funded roles (Engagement Manager, Monitoring and Learning Lead) are explicitly tasked with building and coordinating this capacity within the Trade COE Hub.

quote.text: The programme will aim to increase HMG and international understanding of what works in Trade for Development policy, driving forward improvements in evidence and data and use this to influence the policies of development partners and partner governments.

key_programme_risks: Failure to secure quality proposals through the GDD framework
Limited influence over World Bank Umbrella Facility project delivery
Insufficient internal capacity for programme-funded roles
Low utilization of the Shop-Front function by Posts
Inadequate integration of gender and inclusion considerations in evidence projects
Financial risks (exchange rate fluctuations, unspent funds)
Fraud and corruption risks in partner organizations

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Failure to secure quality proposals through the GDD framework
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Early market engagement with suppliers to test proposals and confirm interest; competitive bidding process to drive value for money.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited influence over World Bank Umbrella Facility project delivery
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Include a ‘preference’ in the Administrative Arrangement and maintain regular engagement with project leads.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Insufficient internal capacity for programme-funded roles
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Consider asking the delivery partner to deliver the entire Shop-Front function if internal candidates are unavailable.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low utilization of the Shop-Front function by Posts
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proactive engagement and marketing by the Trade COE to Posts, including a website with guidance and request forms.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Inadequate integration of gender and inclusion considerations
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Explicit requirement to disaggregate data by gender and marginalized groups in all projects; KPIs to incentivize inclusive evidence.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Financial risks (exchange rate fluctuations, unspent funds)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Contracts denominated in GBP; regular financial forecasting and adherence to FCDO spending targets.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Fraud and corruption risks in partner organizations
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Due diligence checks prior to partner appointment; zero-tolerance approach to fraud; regular audits and reviews.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from previous FCDO evidence programmes highlight the benefits of: 1) structuring programmes as funds rather than direct institutional funding to allow flexibility, 2) collaboration between policymakers and researchers to increase the likelihood of research leading to change, 3) cross-project learning and quality review processes, and 4) integration of inclusion (e.g., gender) considerations. The programme design incorporates these lessons, particularly in the hybrid approach and emphasis on strategic communications.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The hybrid delivery model (combining a responsive facility, global fund, and embedded roles) was explicitly chosen based on lessons from past programmes, which showed that a mix of long-term and responsive funding mechanisms maximizes impact. The inclusion of a Shop-Front function and centralized MREL support also reflects learning about the need for coordination and evidence use across portfolios.

quote.text: Programmes structured as a fund rather than direct funding to institutions allow for greater flexibility and responsiveness. However, funding through institutions is generally better at measuring outcomes and impact over longer time periods. Collaboration between policymakers and researchers on the research approach leads to significantly greater likelihood of the research leading to change.
The total indicative budget for the programme is up to £25 million. This will be primarily ODA RDEL but we will scope opportunities to use non-ODA funding where appropriate.

metadata.programme_name: Future-fit Food Policy Fund (FFPF)
metadata.duration_text: Programme Start Date: 23/12/2024, Programme End Date: 03/03/2026

quote.text: "The purpose of the Future-fit Food Policy Fund (FFPF) is to enable the Global Food Security, Agriculture and Land department (GFALD) to support strategic, time-bound international action to tackle hunger and extreme poverty..."

duration_source.text: "Programme Start Date: 23/12/2024", "Programme End Date: 03/03/2026"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The FFPF is a financing mechanism that supports both policy influence (e.g., shaping the Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty) and evidence generation (e.g., analytical work to inform future FCDO food security programming). It also includes catalytic interventions to improve global food system governance.

q1_source.source: Document: D0007242.odt, Programme summary and Key outcomes sections
q1_source.text: "The purpose of the Future-fit Food Policy Fund (FFPF) is to enable... support strategic, time-bound international action to tackle hunger... and to support policy and analytical work that will inform the design of the next phase of GFALD sustainable food (and nutrition) security programming."

q3_expected_outputs.output: implementation of an effective Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty (GAHP)
analytical and policy work on (geo)politics of food and land
analytical work on agrifood productivity (soil health, fertiliser use, seeds, livestock, value chains)
global food security data partnerships
nutrition improvement strategies (supply vs demand interventions, crop diversification)
strategies to reduce gender gaps in agriculture
coherence in global financing for food system transformation
design of a new GFALD central programme on food security

what_objectives.summary: The FFPF aims to catalyze global policy coherence and generate evidence to inform future UK food security programming, with a focus on reducing hunger and poverty through strategic interventions in the international food system.

quote.text: "Key outcomes include: The implementation of an effective Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty... Analytical and policy work to advance policy thinking and impact..."

countries_regions: global (with focus on LMICs and FCAS)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme's overall risk rating is assessed as 'Moderate' and is stated to be within GFALD’s and HMFD’s risk appetite. The context involves fragmented international systems and policy tensions, but no FCAS-specific risks are highlighted.

q5_source.source: Document: D0007242.odt, Overall risk rating section

metadata.programme_name: Catalytic Activities Supporting Climate and Disaster Resilience in the Caribbean (CASCaDe)

quote.text: "This programme will enable a range of tactical activities to support the achievement of UK’s Caribbean disaster and climate resilience objectives..."

metadata.duration_source: "Programme Start Date: September 2024", "Programme End Date: March 2028"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (technical assistance to address gaps), implementation research (innovative solutions and testing replicability), and financing mechanism (funding through multilateral institutions/NGOs). It focuses on catalytic activities that boost sustainability of regional initiatives and incentivize climate/disaster resilience actions.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will enable a range of tactical activities to support the achievement of UK’s Caribbean disaster and climate resilience objectives, specifically work that contributes to boosting sustainability of regional initiatives, offers innovative solutions, technical assistance to address capacity gaps or incentivises others to act." (S4003706.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: evidence of effectiveness shared (transformational change element)
capacity and capability increased (through technical assistance)
innovation or replicability demonstrated
scalability support provided
sustainability actions implemented
disaster risk-reduction measures strengthened (e.g., early warning systems)
climate-resilient infrastructure supported
regional initiatives made more sustainable
climate/disaster finance flows increased to the region
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen Caribbean climate and disaster resilience through catalytic, small-scale projects that complement larger initiatives. It focuses on transformational change by addressing capacity gaps, promoting innovation, and ensuring sustainability of resilience efforts.

quote.text: "Strengthened regional climate and disaster resilience and biodiversity, through bilateral partnership and multilateral/global advocacy, as well as greater flows of climate or disaster finance to the region. We will do this by supporting key elements of transformational change viz: evidence of effectiveness shared; capacity and capability increased; innovation or replicability; scalability support; sustainability actions."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a disaster-prone region with high vulnerability to climate change and natural hazards. The overall risk rating is assessed as 'moderate' after mitigation, with specific risks related to disaster impacts, limited institutional capacity, and political engagement.
where_context.q5_source: "The programme is assessed to carry moderate risks after mitigation." and "Caribbean states are seven times more likely to be hit by natural disasters than larger states, and the estimated cost of damages is six times higher." (S4003706.odt, Risk section and context)
q6_contextual_constraints: climate risks (high vulnerability to natural disasters and climate change)
weak institutions (small size governments with limited capacity)
political economy (limited engagement/cooperation from partner governments)
data limitations (need for better planning to address long-term climate impacts)
supply chain challenges (dependency on imports for many states)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Disaster events can delay implementation by impacting partner capacity. Small administrations struggle to absorb complex projects, requiring enabling mechanisms. Limited staff availability (often with multiple responsibilities) and global supply chain dependencies create operational bottlenecks.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, Strategic Case and Risks sections
quote.text: "Capacity of small administrations to absorb and deliver project aims especially if onerous or complex so ensuring enabling mechanisms which respond to bottlenecks..." and "global supply chain challenges given large dependency on imports for many states"

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Decision-making rests with the FCDO-governed Programme Board (chaired by the Caribbean Development Director), with input from UK High Commissioners and regional advisers. Southern partners (e.g., PAHO, CDEMA) implement projects but do not lead governance.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to address capacity gaps
support to regional institutions (e.g., CARICOM agencies)
training/mentorship through project implementation (e.g., 'Smart' healthcare facilities rollout)
institutional strengthening (e.g., disaster management agencies)

quote.source: S4003706.odt, How will delivery partners be selected? section
quote.text: "Delivery partners will be drawn from local and regional institutions, UN agencies or NGOs that have a strong track record of performance in the region or are mandated agencies of CARICOM." and "The programme will be governed by a Programme Board that will select/agree projects... chaired by the Development Director."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses multiple instruments: Accountable Grant Agreements (for NGOs), Memoranda of Understanding (for UN/multilateral agencies), Development Partnership Agreements (with bilateral donors), and potential drawdowns from HQ-managed programmes (e.g., Centres of Expertise).
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: The programme operates through a flexible, project-based structure where multiple partners (NGOs, UN agencies, CARICOM bodies) can be engaged for specific initiatives. A Programme Board oversees selection and progress, but implementation is decentralized to partners.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners are selected based on pre-existing relationships, strong track records in the region, and alignment with programme criteria (e.g., PAHO and CDEMA have "a long history of implementing FCDO projects successfully"). No open competition is mentioned; selection is driven by strategic fit and prior performance.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, How will delivery partners be selected? section
quote.text: "We have identified two potential projects for the first year through partner discussions and evaluations of recently completed projects. Both potential partners have a long history of implementing FCDO projects successfully in the region."

how_governance.q15_day_to_day_details: The Programme Manager (Climate Change Team) oversees implementation and liaises with partners, while the SRO (Caribbean Climate and Disaster Resilience Adviser) ensures high-level delivery. FCDO regional staff also participate in monitoring.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Programme Board includes the Caribbean Development Director (Chair), SRO, Head of Climate and Disaster Risk Management Team, UK High Commissioners, and other CDT leaders. Decisions are made by consensus, with at least 50% core membership required. The Board reviews projects, risks, and progress quarterly.

quote.text: "The programme will be governed by a Programme Board that will select/agree projects... The Board will meet at a minimum, quarterly and will comprise of the following core members: Caribbean Climate and Disaster Resilience Adviser (SRO), Caribbean Development Director (Chair), Head of Climate and Disaster Risk Management Team (alternate chair), UK High Commissioners in region..."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between projects if approved by the Programme Board, especially for multi-year extensions (e.g., increasing a project from £250k to £500k if it demonstrates better value for money). However, this requires justification and formal approval.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments in response to natural disasters or emerging needs, with flexibility built into implementation plans. Changes require Programme Board approval and are subject to risk reassessment.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, Appraisal Case and Risks sections
quote.text: "if warranted and agreed by the Programme Board, the amount may be increased to no more than £500,000 per project, if the overall risk is deemed minor." and "Build in flexibility to cater for impacts of natural disasters on implementation and business disruption"

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Implementing Partner (e.g., PAHO, CDEMA, NGOs). No sub-grantees are explicitly mentioned, though some projects may involve multiple implementers with a lead organization.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, How will you manage financial risks? section
quote.text: "Funding will be disbursed when FCDO is satisfied that appropriate systems are in place to track expenditure, and not in advance of need. Subsequent disbursements will not be made until the previous tranche is accounted for satisfactorily."

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen for its flexibility to support small, catalytic projects that complement larger programmes, and its ability to respond quickly to regional needs. The direct award approach leverages trusted partners (e.g., PAHO, CDEMA) with proven track records, reducing implementation risks in a high-vulnerability context.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (value for money from disaster risk reduction investments)
risk-mitigation (using partners with strong regional experience)
flexibility (ability to adapt to disasters and emerging needs)
equity (focus on inclusive resilience for marginalized groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Over-reliance on a small pool of pre-selected partners may limit innovation or competition.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: The Programme Board includes diverse stakeholders (High Commissioners, advisers) to review and challenge partner selections. Regular monitoring and spot checks ensure accountability.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Direct awards without competition may raise perceptions of favoritism or reduce value for money.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners are selected based on rigorous due diligence (DDA process) and prior performance. Value for money is assessed against benchmarks and the 4Es framework.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, Appraisal Case and Strategic Case sections
quote.text: "The entire programme is built around achieving value for money and it is known that investment in disaster risk reduction... is cost effective." and "The programme will allow for smaller, catalytic initiatives to be supported that complement our longer-term programme of work in the region."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Caribbean’s high disaster risk and small institutional capacity limit partner selection to organizations with regional mandates (e.g., CARICOM agencies) or proven resilience expertise. Local NGOs must demonstrate ability to manage complex projects despite resource constraints.
q27_constraints_detail: disaster vulnerability (partners must have contingency plans for interruptions)
institutional capacity (only organizations with strong track records are eligible)
geographic focus (partners must operate regionally, not single-country)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for transformational change (e.g., innovation, scalability) drives the open partnership structure, allowing diverse implementers (NGOs, UN, private sector) to propose solutions. The focus on catalytic activities requires flexible, small-scale funding mechanisms (e.g., grants under £250k).
q28_linkages: transformational change goals → open partnership structure (to enable innovation)
regional resilience objectives → use of CARICOM-mandated agencies (for alignment)
capacity-building needs → embedded technical assistance (via trusted partners)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances efficiency (using pre-vetted partners for speed) with equity (ensuring vulnerable groups benefit). For example, while direct awards to PAHO/CDEMA may limit competition, these partners have deep regional roots and can target marginalized communities effectively.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: speed vs inclusion (direct awards to trusted partners accelerate delivery but may exclude newer organizations)
expertise vs ownership (Northern-led governance ensures standards but may limit Southern decision-making)
cost vs reach (administrative costs are minimized, but small project sizes may limit scale)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (disaster vulnerability, weak institutions) necessitates quarterly oversight by the Programme Board and regular partner checks (e.g., site visits, spot checks). High disaster risk justifies flexible implementation plans and contingency buffers.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is embedded in partner roles (e.g., PAHO’s ‘Smart’ healthcare project includes training for local staff). Partners are selected based on their ability to strengthen institutional resilience, not just deliver outputs.

quote.source: S4003706.odt, Strategic Case and How will delivery partners be selected? sections
quote.text: "Weak inclusion approaches and limited use of nature-based solutions... Small size governments or institutions that require technical assistance support." and "Delivery partners will be drawn from local and regional institutions... that have a strong track record of performance in the region or are mandated agencies of CARICOM."

key_programme_risks: Lack of sustained engagement from partner governments (political risk)
Natural disasters disrupting implementation (contextual risk)
Skills/technical assistance mismatch (operational risk)
Limited capacity of local partners causing delays (institutional risk)
Fraud or fiduciary issues (reputational risk)
Safeguarding incidents (social risk)
Reduction in FCDO resources (financial risk)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Lack of expected and/or sustained engagement from partner Governments
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Proactively engage with governments to address concerns; use regional FCDO network for advocacy; build coalitions around issue areas.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Natural disaster impacts a Caribbean beneficiary country significantly
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Build flexibility into implementation plans; explore opportunities arising from disaster response.
Ensure strong understanding of needs; select partners with good track records; monitor activities closely.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Limited capacity of local partners leads to delays
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Select best-fit partners; monitor implementation pace; support partners to adapt with innovative solutions.
Disbursements made after expenditure scrutiny; partners given FCDO Fraud Policy information; regular monitoring and spot checks.
Ensure partners implement safeguarding policies; agree communications/training on FCDO standards.
Communicate UK offer as more than money; plan activities with scalable budgets.

fcas_specific_lessons: In disaster-prone contexts, flexibility in implementation timelines is critical to accommodate interruptions.
Small administrations require enabling mechanisms (e.g., simplified reporting) to absorb projects effectively.
Regional bodies (e.g., CARICOM) are essential for coordination but may face capacity constraints during crises.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Past FCDO projects in the Caribbean (e.g., with PAHO/CDEMA) demonstrated that trusted partners with regional mandates can deliver effectively despite contextual challenges. The need for technical assistance and innovative solutions was highlighted in the FCDO Caribbean Growth and Resilience Diagnostic 2023.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme incorporates flexibility for disaster-related delays and focuses on catalytic, smaller projects (under £250k) to complement larger initiatives, addressing past lessons about absorption capacity.

quote.text: "The programme is assessed to carry moderate risks after mitigation... effective mitigating actions can reduce these risks to acceptable levels. The team will work closely with the respective implementing partners to develop robust risk monitoring arrangements."

quote.source: S4003706.odt, Outline the total budget section
quote.text: "The total budget of £2.0m is expected to be split equally over four financial years, up to £0.5m per year... The funding will be allocated from the FCDO Caribbean Development Team programme (R-DEL) budget and will be tagged as 100% ICF International Climate Finance (ICF)."

metadata.programme_name: One Caribbean

quote.text: "Programmesummary:TopromotesustainabledevelopmentintheCaribbeanthroughstrengthening(a)climateresilience;(b)citizensecurity;(c)privatesectorengagement;and(d)foodsecurity."

duration_source.text: "AMPStartDate: 25/03/2025", "AMPEndDate: 31/07/2029"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme aims to promote sustainable development in the Caribbean by addressing four key pillars: climate resilience, citizen security, private sector engagement, and food security. It combines capacity building, policy influence, financing mechanisms, and implementation research to achieve systemic reforms and resilience in the region.

q1_source.text: "TopromotesustainabledevelopmentintheCaribbeanthroughstrengthening(a)climateresilience;(b)citizensecurity;(c)privatesectorengagement;and(d)foodsecurity."

q3_expected_outputs.output: Climate-resilient infrastructure projects (e.g., health, education, water facilities)
Enhanced disaster risk management strategies and instruments
Skills and pathway programmes for at-risk youth
Private sector projects financed with climate adaptation focus
Reduced intra-regional trade barriers for agricultural goods
q3_expected_outputs.target: 25% reduction in CARICOM’s food import bill by 2025

q3_expected_outputs.output: Increased local food production and productivity
Regional collaborations on crime prevention
Cybersecurity policy and incident response frameworks

what_objectives.summary: The programme is a multi-sectoral initiative designed to build resilience, inclusivity, and prosperity in the Caribbean by addressing climate vulnerability, citizen insecurity, private sector constraints, and food insecurity through regional solutions.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Intended programme impact, outcomes and activities
quote.text: "The intended impact is for a more resilient, inclusive, safe and prosperous region, with fewer persons in or at risk of backsliding into poverty."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in a region with high vulnerability to climate shocks, economic instability, and institutional weaknesses, but is not classified as FCAS. The overall programme risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'.

q5_source.text: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate"

q6_contextual_constraints: regulatory barriers (e.g., high CARICOM tariffs on agricultural goods)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The small scale of Caribbean countries limits their ability to absorb shocks or implement large-scale projects. High costs and regulatory barriers (e.g., 30-40% tariffs on agricultural goods) hinder trade and food security, while climate vulnerability exacerbates economic and social instability. Institutional weaknesses constrain effective project design and implementation.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: The Challenges and Opportunities
quote.text: "Many Caribbean SIDS face common challenges that are holding back sustainable development. These challenges include their small scale, high vulnerability to climate and economic shocks, low institutional capacity, dependency upon tourism or in some cases commodity revenues, exceptionally high communication, energy and transportation costs, and poor quality and quantity of infrastructure."

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (as a donor and IDB shareholder) has significant influence over strategic direction through the Steering Committee and IDB Board representation, while IDB (a multilateral institution with regional offices) leads implementation. Decision-making is shared, with IDB managing day-to-day delivery and the UK shaping priorities via governance structures.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance for climate resilience and disaster risk management
skills programmes for at-risk youth (crime prevention)
support for private sector project preparation and investment readiness
institutional strengthening for food security and trade policy harmonization

partner_organizations.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementing partner (direct implementation in 6 borrowing member countries; indirect via CDB in Eastern Caribbean)

partner_organizations.name: Caribbean Development Bank (CDB)
partner_organizations.role: Downstream implementing partner for Eastern Caribbean countries (via agreement with IDB)

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: Donor and strategic oversight (Steering Committee, Board representation)

partner_organizations.name: Governments of Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Guyana, Jamaica, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary countries (direct implementation)

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Feasible Options / Option 2
quote.text: "IDB is the biggest multilateral financier in the Caribbean by lending volumes and has over 50 years of a successful partnership with the region. [...] IDB has deep in-house expertise in each of the areas as well as offices in 6 countries in the region and excellent working relationships for access and getting things done."

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK will contribute £5m to the IDB’s One Caribbean Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) via a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). The MDTF pools donor resources, with IDB managing disbursements and implementation according to a pre-agreed results framework. The UK’s funds will be earmarked for ODA-eligible countries.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IDB executes the programme through its MDTF, with a Steering Committee (including FCDO) overseeing strategic direction. IDB, IDB Lab, and IDB Invest manage operations under their respective policies, with CDB acting as a financial agent for Eastern Caribbean countries. FCDO retains oversight via the Steering Committee and Board representation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IDB was selected due to its unmatched regional expertise, existing ‘One Caribbean’ framework (aligned with UK priorities), ability to leverage co-funding, and established delivery capacity across all four programme pillars. No private sector or other multilateral partner had comparable breadth and depth of expertise in the region.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Feasible Options / Option 2
quote.text: "IDB is the biggest multilateral financier in the Caribbean by lending volumes and has over 50 years of a successful partnership with the region. [...] For the reasons set out above and the ability to effectively mitigate the risks identified above, this is our preferred option."

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The One Caribbean MDTF Steering Committee includes IDB and donors (e.g., FCDO), meeting semi-annually to review progress, prioritize interventions, and ensure complementarity with other initiatives. The Committee approves procedures and oversees the fund’s strategic direction. FCDO’s funds are earmarked for ODA-eligible countries, and an Operating Manual details rules for the Committee and fund framework.

quote.text: "IDB and donors will constitute a Steering Committee that meets semi-annually. [...] The Steering Committee will meet periodically to review the status of the MDTF, pipeline of potential operations, and to consult with stakeholders and experts, among other activities."

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between pillars/activities within the MDTF framework, subject to Steering Committee approval. The UK’s funds are earmarked for ODA-eligible countries, limiting flexibility to non-ODA countries. Reallocation requires alignment with the results framework and donor agreements.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme allows for adjustments to priorities via the Steering Committee, which reviews progress semi-annually and can reprioritize interventions. The Theory of Change and results framework are designed to evolve during implementation, but changes require donor consensus.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Theory of Change
quote.text: "The theory of change will be further developed with the implementing partner and form part of the operating manual. The ToC development will include developing clear causal pathways and setting out the necessary assumptions for impact."

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IDB (MDTF manager) → [end beneficiaries/governments]. CDB acts as a financial agent for Eastern Caribbean countries but is not an additional layer for most activities.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Financial Management / Disbursement profile
quote.text: "FCDO funds will be disbursed in a one-off payment to launch the One Caribbean fund. There is a 5% administrative fee on the commitment which will be deducted from this."

q24_alternatives_considered.option: Implement through existing FCDO ODA programmes
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: Existing programmes (e.g., UKCIF, SOCAP) are either too narrow in scope, focused on specific countries (e.g., Jamaica), or lack capacity to address food security. Expanding them would require significant time and still leave gaps.

q24_alternatives_considered.option: New programme implemented by other regional partners (UN/CARICOM agencies)
q24_alternatives_considered.reason_rejected: No single UN or CARICOM agency had the depth and breadth of expertise across all four pillars (climate, security, private sector, food). A coalition was not feasible due to lack of an obvious lead.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: IDB was chosen for its unparalleled regional expertise, existing ‘One Caribbean’ framework (aligned with UK priorities), ability to leverage £1 of UK funding into £5+ of total investment (including IDB’s $20m commitment and co-funding from other donors), and capacity to deliver across all four pillars. The UK’s early contribution positions it to shape the initiative’s direction and demonstrate leadership in SIDS support.
q25_decision_factors: value for money (economies of scale, leverage of £1:£5+)
risk mitigation (IDB’s established regional presence and safeguards)
partner capacity (IDB’s 6 regional offices and multi-sector expertise)
speed (existing IDB initiatives enable rapid mobilization)
strategic influence (UK as first donor can earmark funds and shape priorities)
equity (IDB’s inclusive approach and focus on vulnerable groups)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Loss of control over fund allocation (multi-donor trust fund)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Mitigated by UK membership on the Steering Committee and earmarking funds for ODA-eligible countries.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow delivery when CDB is downstream partner
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: IDB and FCDO will closely monitor CDB-implemented projects, with Directors pushing for governance reforms via the IDB Board.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Duplication with other UK/FCDO programmes (e.g., Compete Caribbean)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Steering Committee will prioritize interventions to avoid overlap, with FCDO Caribbean leads ensuring complementarity.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: ODA eligibility of funds (IDB members include non-ODA countries)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Written assurances from IDB and FCDO oversight to ring-fence funds for ODA-eligible countries.

vfm_criteria_used: efficiency (IDB’s regional offices and economies of scale)
effectiveness (aligned with UK/FCDO priorities and regional needs)
equity (focus on vulnerable groups and inclusive growth)

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Feasible Options / Option 2
quote.text: "The UK would become the first donor to One Caribbean and in doing so would give us considerable scope to both earmark our funds to priority UK activities under each of the pillars, shape the future direction and evolution of ‘One Caribbean’ (including influencing IDB’s wider related initiatives) as well as demonstrate to the region/other partners that the UK remains a strong modern partner for SIDS within the multilateral system."

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Caribbean’s small scale, institutional weaknesses, and high vulnerability to climate/economic shocks limit the pool of potential implementing partners. Few organizations have the regional breadth, multi-sector expertise, and delivery capacity required to address all four pillars (climate, security, private sector, food). This constrained the selection to IDB, which has deep regional roots and a holistic ‘whole of bank’ approach.
q27_constraints_detail: Limited number of partners with multi-sector expertise across climate, security, private sector, and food
Need for partners with established regional offices and government relationships (due to weak institutions)
Requirement for partners capable of leveraging private/other donor funds (due to resource constraints)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s multi-sectoral objectives (climate resilience, citizen security, private sector development, food security) necessitated a delivery structure with: (1) **breadth of expertise** (only IDB had this across all pillars), (2) **regional reach** (IDB’s 6 offices and CDB partnership), and (3) **ability to leverage co-funding** (IDB’s $20m commitment and donor mobilization). The mixed financing mechanism (MDTF) was chosen to pool resources while allowing the UK to earmark funds for priorities.

q28_linkages.how_link: Required a partner with technical capacity for infrastructure projects and disaster risk financing (IDB’s existing Project Preparation Facility and CDB partnership).
Needed a partner with governance expertise and ability to work across countries (IDB’s regional offices and justice sector experience).
Demanded a partner with blended finance tools (IDB Invest) and project preparation support (IDB’s PPF).
Required agricultural trade and productivity expertise (IDB’s regional focus and FAO partnerships).

intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document explicitly notes tensions between **inclusive partnerships** (e.g., ensuring benefits reach vulnerable groups like at-risk youth and rural populations) and **rapid delivery** (e.g., leveraging IDB’s existing systems for speed). For example: (1) **Earmarking funds for ODA-eligible countries** ensures equity but limits flexibility; (2) **Using IDB’s regional offices** balances local ownership with efficiency; (3) **Steering Committee oversight** adds governance layers but ensures inclusive prioritization.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: IDB’s existing initiatives enable rapid mobilization, but the Steering Committee’s semi-annual reviews ensure vulnerable groups (e.g., at-risk youth, rural populations) are prioritized.
UK shapes strategic direction via the Steering Committee and IDB Board, while IDB’s regional offices and CDB partnership ensure local implementation.
The 5% administrative fee is justified by IDB’s ability to leverage £1 of UK funding into £5+ of total investment (including co-funding).

intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (e.g., climate vulnerability, institutional weaknesses) justifies **milestone-based oversight** (semi-annual Steering Committee meetings) and **embedded safeguards** (IDB’s Office of Institutional Integrity, environmental/social policies). High-risk areas (e.g., safeguarding, fiduciary risks) receive intensive monitoring (e.g., annual audits, fraud reporting to FCDO’s Counter Fraud Service).
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded in the programme’s design, with IDB’s role explicitly including **technical assistance** (e.g., for disaster risk management, private sector project preparation) and **institutional strengthening** (e.g., social registries, cybersecurity policies). This shapes partner roles by: (1) Positioning IDB as both implementer and capacity builder; (2) Enabling governments to take on more complex projects over time; (3) Ensuring sustainability through local ownership (e.g., skills programmes for at-risk youth).

quote.text: "Inclusive and equitable in approach – Although data is limited, it is clear that the challenges are impacting different socio-economic groups differently and thus an implementing partner must have an in-depth understanding of the socio-economic characteristics of populations in the region, able to identify those most in need and provide services that directly benefit them."

key_programme_risks.risk: Impending hurricane season threatens programme delivery
Failure to raise additional funds from other donors/partners
Duplication of support with other UK/FCDO programmes (e.g., Compete Caribbean)
Funds not spent as intended (fiduciary risk)
Slow delivery by CDB (downstream partner for Eastern Caribbean)
UK ODA funds used for non-ODA-eligible countries
Poor performance of One Caribbean with UK association (reputational risk)
Beneficiaries subject to abuse/harassment (safeguarding risk)

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Impending hurricane season threatens programme delivery
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: IDB has an established regional presence, experience with hurricane contexts, and contingency plans for continued delivery.

IDB’s Office of Resource Mobilization is actively pursuing multi-donor leads. The UK’s early contribution is expected to catalyze other donors (e.g., Canada, US, Japan). IDB has committed $20m of its own resources.
FCDO Caribbean will coordinate with IFID and UK representatives at IDB to avoid overlap. The Steering Committee will prioritize high-impact, non-duplicative interventions.

FCDO will utilize the MDTF Steering Committee, annual financial audits, and IDB’s robust fiduciary policies to ensure oversight. IDB’s procedures include fraud reporting to FCDO’s Counter Fraud Service.
UK Directors on the IDB Board will advocate for governance/operational reforms at CDB. FCDO will closely monitor CDB-implemented projects.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UK ODA funds used for non-ODA-eligible countries
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Written assurances from IDB and FCDO oversight to earmark funds for ODA-eligible countries. Operating Manual will exclude MDTF results attributable to non-ODA countries.
IDB was selected for its strong regional reputation and delivery capacity. FCDO will monitor progress via the Steering Committee and annual reviews.
IDB has safeguarding policies, including gender-based violence prevention and reporting mechanisms. The Office of Institutional Integrity investigates incidents, with updates to FCDO.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from UKCIF (UK Caribbean Infrastructure Fund) highlight the need for **leveraging private finance** and **project preparation support** to address institutional weaknesses in the region.
Experience with CCRIF (Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility) demonstrates the value of **regional risk-pooling mechanisms** for climate-vulnerable SIDS.
Post-hurricane recovery efforts (e.g., Dominica’s CREAD) underscore the importance of **pre-positioned financing** and **local institutional capacity** for resilient infrastructure.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous FCDO programmes (e.g., UKCIF, SOCAP, Violence Prevention Partnership) revealed: (1) The critical role of **project preparation facilities** in attracting private investment; (2) The need for **regional solutions** to address common challenges (e.g., crime, climate); (3) The importance of **gender-responsive and socially inclusive** design, particularly for citizen security interventions. The new programme builds on these by embedding technical assistance and leveraging IDB’s regional platforms.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The programme design incorporates: (1) A **Project Preparation Facility** (Pillar 3) to address private sector investment barriers identified in UKCIF; (2) **Regional trade policy harmonization** (Pillar 4) to reduce barriers highlighted in the FCDO Growth Diagnostic; (3) **Explicit safeguarding measures** (e.g., gender-based violence prevention) based on lessons from SOCAP; (4) **Blended finance mechanisms** to catalyze private sector engagement, a gap noted in the Caribbean Thematic Evaluation (2024).

quote.text: "The programme benefits from covering a range of sectors and issues which previous (and current) FCDO programmes have worked on. Accordingly, lessons learnt will inform the detailed design and implementation of this programme’s activities."

co_funding_partners.note: IDB’s own resources committed to the One Caribbean initiative.

co_funding_partners.partner: Other donors (expected: Canada, Qatar, US, Japan)
co_funding_partners.note: IDB is in conversations with these donors; UK’s early contribution aims to catalyze their engagement.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s £5m contribution is expected to leverage at least £20m+ in total funding (including IDB’s $20m and co-funding from other donors), achieving a leverage ratio of at least 1:4. IDB’s ability to pool resources and utilize its ‘whole of bank’ approach (IDB, IDB Lab, IDB Invest) further maximizes economies of scale.

quote.source: Document: D0007283.odt, Section: Value for Money for the preferred option
quote.text: "Funds will be subject to a 5% administrative fee on the committed amount. [...] IDB operates within set and benchmarked cost parameters established and monitored by the Board (which the UK is represented at). Its significant size also enables it to pool resources, leverage funds and maximise economies of scale thus achieving better VfM."

quote.budget: "Programme Value: up to £25m" (D0006506.odt, Summary Sheet)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines capacity building (technical assistance to governments and businesses), policy influence (economic reforms and climate finance access), and implementation research (testing interventions like women's economic empowerment models). It also includes a financing mechanism component through direct support to firms.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will support inclusive economic growth and build economic resilience in the Caribbean, enabling the region to better respond to economic and climate shocks. There are four pillars: 1) small-medium business development; 2) macroeconomic and debt sustainability; 3) women’s economic empowerment; 4) strategic, inclusive economic development interventions on policy themes including green finance and data." (D0006506.odt, Programme summary)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Direct and indirect jobs created (including for women and vulnerable groups)
Increased productivity (e.g., revenues) and exports from Caribbean firms (including women-led firms)
Additional concessional finance (e.g., from MDBs/IMF) and climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund) leveraged
q3_expected_outputs.target: 30%-50% of programme finance counted as International Climate Finance (ICF)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Economic, inclusive, and climate-aligned reforms submitted and legislated through parliament
Increased government revenues (e.g., from tax-related technical assistance)
Number of success stories reflecting capacity strengthening at government and regional level
Increased business development capacity for SMEs (including in climate-smart agriculture and blue/green economy)
Business-friendly and gender-responsive economic reforms drafted
Women-led businesses supported to grow and trade
q3_expected_outputs.target: 47% of firms supported in previous phase were women-owned (Compete Caribbean Phase II)

q3_expected_outputs.output: Regional institutions receiving technical assistance to support private sector adaptation to climate change

what_objectives.summary: The EDC programme aims to drive inclusive economic growth and resilience in the Caribbean through four pillars: SME development, macroeconomic stability, women's economic empowerment, and strategic policy interventions. It combines technical assistance, direct business support, and policy reforms to address structural constraints like debt, climate vulnerability, and gender inequality.

quote.objectives: "This programme will directly contribute to the Foreign Secretary’s priorities of accelerating sustainable and inclusive investment and growth in the global south and unlocking climate finance; and the Development Minister’s priorities: supporting economic transformation, tackling unsustainable debt, empowering women and girls and unlocking climate finance." (D0006506.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
quote.outputs: "Indicative Intermediate Outcome indicators to be measured include: [...] Outcome 1: Direct and Indirect jobs created, including for women and vulnerable groups; Outcome 2: Increased productivity (e.g. revenues) and exports from Caribbean firms, including women-led firms." (D0006506.odt, Outcomes section)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The region faces acute vulnerability to climate shocks (e.g., hurricanes causing 200%+ GDP damage) and economic volatility due to tourism dependence, but has stable democratic governance and high human development indicators. The programme explicitly rates overall risk as 'Moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006506.odt, Summary Sheet) && "Caribbean SIDS face underlying structural constraints [...] vulnerability to economic and climate shocks (the Caribbean is the region most at risk of climate change and natural disasters)" (D0006506.odt, Context section)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Climate shocks (e.g., Hurricane Beryl destroying 98-100% of infrastructure on some islands) and economic dependence on tourism (15% GDP contraction during COVID-19) create instability. Weak public financial management and limited private sector competitiveness hinder growth, while small market sizes and high transport/energy costs (e.g., electricity at USD$0.25-$0.40/kWh) reduce productivity. Data gaps (e.g., lack of real-time population data) impair disaster response.

quote.constraints: "Caribbean SIDS face underlying structural constraints that have had a sustained, limiting effect on development. Constraints include small scale, vulnerability to economic and climate shocks [...] and generally low capacity in both the public and private sectors." (D0006506.odt, Context section)
quote.climate_impact: "Hurricane Beryl [...] destroyed 98-100% of houses and infrastructure on the tiny islands of Carriacou, Union and Canouan (in Grenada and the Grenadines)." (D0006506.odt, Climate risks section)
quote.economic_volatility: "The English-speaking, tourist-dependent Caribbean economies contracted by 15% on average [during COVID-19], compared to -3.9% for advanced economies." (D0006506.odt, Economic shocks section)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The UK (FCDO) sets strategic priorities and allocates funds to multilateral partners (IMF, IADB), which then implement activities. Southern governments and businesses receive technical assistance but have limited decision-making power over programme design.
q10_capacity_building_details: technical assistance to governments (e.g., debt management, PFM)
business advisory support to SMEs
training for women entrepreneurs
institutional strengthening (e.g., regional statistical capacity)
mentorship and networking for women-led businesses

quote.partners: "Implementing partners include the IMF and the Inter-American Development Bank. Caribbean governments will benefit through technical assistance, the Caribbean private sector, including small and women-led businesses, through business advisory support, finance and in-kind support." (D0006506.odt, Programme summary)
quote.capacity_building: "The UK will offer much needed technical assistance to support countries to implement key economic reforms and embed systems that promote economic stability, sound public finances and create an enabling environment for private sector-led inclusive growth." (D0006506.odt, UK Support section)
quote.decision_power: "The UK will provide £25m, mainly in the form of technical assistance to support governments and businesses in the Caribbean to implement reforms and systems [...]" (D0006506.odt, UK Support section)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses **block funding** for multilateral trust funds (CARTAC Phase VI and Compete Caribbean Plus) and **grants/contracts** for direct support to firms (Pillars 3 & 4). The UK contributes to multi-donor trust funds managed by the IMF and IADB, with additional flexible funding for strategic interventions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Pillars 1 and 2 are implemented through existing multilateral trust funds (CARTAC Phase VI and Compete Caribbean Plus), with the UK as a donor alongside other governments. Pillars 3 and 4 will use a fund manager model for flexible allocations. Governance includes steering committees (e.g., CARTAC Steering Committee) with UK representation.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: The IMF and IADB were selected based on their established regional presence, technical expertise, and existing trust fund mechanisms (CARTAC Phase VI and Compete Caribbean Plus). The UK is leveraging these platforms to avoid duplication and benefit from economies of scale.

quote.instrument: "Pillar One: Caribbean Regional Technical Assistance Centre - CARTAC (Phase VI) - A multi-donor trust fund, for core macroeconomic technical assistance, implemented by the IMF. The UK will provide approximately 13% or £7.5m out of the planned budget of USD$76m/£58.5m [...] Pillar Two: Compete Caribbean Plus Programme (‘CompetePlus’) - A private sector development programme, co-financed with the Government of Canada and the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB)." (D0006506.odt, Pillar descriptions)
quote.selection: "The UK will provide £25m, mainly in the form of technical assistance to support governments and businesses in the Caribbean to implement reforms and systems that promote economic stability [...] EDC will also provide some financial or in-kind support (such as technology upgrades) to firms and entrepreneurs to grow their businesses." (D0006506.odt, UK Support section)
quote.governance: "CARTAC is co-funded with the Government of Canada, the EU, the Netherlands, the ECCB, the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), USAID and China. The UK will remain a key voice on the Steering Committee going forward." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: CARTAC Phase VI has a Steering Committee with donor representatives (including the UK), Caribbean governments, and the IMF. Compete Caribbean Plus has a similar multi-donor governance structure. Pillar 4 (strategic fund) will use a demand-driven allocation process overseen by FCDO.

quote.day_to_day: "CARTAC provides demand-led, short-term technical assistance and capacity building to governments in the region for core economic policy making to improve macroeconomic sustainability." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)
quote.sub_awards: "Pillar Four: Inclusive Economic Development Strategic Fund - a £4m fund that will provide flexible funding that can be quickly programmed in response to unanticipated challenges or opportunities that deliver toward EDC’s theory of change." (D0006506.odt, Pillar Four description)
quote.governance: "CARTAC Phase VI is co-funded with [...] the UK will remain a key voice on the Steering Committee going forward." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description) && "The UK will provide £25m, mainly in the form of technical assistance [...] Governance arrangements for all pillars are outlined in the Management Case." (D0006506.odt, UK Support section)
quote.oversight: "CARTAC consistently scored ‘A’s for their outputs in previous annual reviews completed under the previous programme." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Pillar 4 (£4m strategic fund) is explicitly designed for flexible reallocation to respond to unanticipated needs. Pillars 1 and 2 (CARTAC and Compete Caribbean Plus) have predefined work programmes but allow adjustments through their steering committees.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a dedicated strategic fund (Pillar 4) for adaptive management. CARTAC and Compete Caribbean Plus use demand-led technical assistance models, allowing priorities to shift based on country needs, subject to donor approval.

quote.reallocation: "Pillar Four: Inclusive Economic Development Strategic Fund - a £4m fund that will provide flexible funding that can be quickly programmed in response to unanticipated challenges or opportunities that deliver toward EDC’s theory of change." (D0006506.odt, Pillar Four description)
quote.adaptive: "CARTAC provides demand-led, short-term technical assistance [...] Prioritisation was informed by member country surveys, Steering Committee members and development partners regarding the anticipated Capacity Development needs for 2024-29." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → Multilateral implementers (IMF/IADB) → End beneficiaries (governments/businesses). Pillar 4 may add a fund manager layer.

quote.layers: "Implementing partners include the IMF and the Inter-American Development Bank. Caribbean governments will benefit through technical assistance, the Caribbean private sector [...] through business advisory support." (D0006506.odt, Programme summary)
quote.payment: "CARTAC provides demand-led, short-term technical assistance [...]" (implies milestone-based delivery) (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)

q24_alternatives_considered: Bilateral technical assistance (rejected due to lack of scale)
Standalone UK-managed funds (rejected due to higher transaction costs)
Direct grants to governments (rejected due to absorption capacity limits)
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The multilateral trust fund model was chosen for its **scalability** (leveraging existing platforms like CARTAC and Compete Caribbean Plus), **risk mitigation** (IMF/IADB have strong regional track records), and **efficiency** (avoiding duplication of systems). The UK’s prior experience with these partners and their alignment with Caribbean governments’ priorities also drove the decision.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Limited country ownership due to multilateral intermediation
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Demand-led technical assistance models (e.g., CARTAC’s country surveys) and UK representation on steering committees to align priorities.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Slow disbursement from trust funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Pillar 4’s flexible fund for rapid response, and milestone-based payments for Pillars 1-3.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Overlap with other donor programmes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Coordination through regional steering committees and alignment with Caribbean Development Strategy.

quote.alternatives: "The UK is well-positioned to deliver this programme, building on an established economic development portfolio in the Caribbean, and collaboration with key multilateral and bilateral development partners." (implies rejection of standalone bilateral approach) (D0006506.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)
quote.rationale: "This programme will directly contribute to the Foreign Secretary’s priorities [...] The UK is well-positioned to deliver this programme, building on an established economic development portfolio in the Caribbean, and collaboration with key multilateral and bilateral development partners." (D0006506.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending) && "CARTAC Phase VI is co-funded with [...] The UK will remain a key voice on the Steering Committee going forward." (D0006506.odt, Pillar One description)
quote.risks: "Going forward the evaluators suggested further work to improve impact and sustainability, by the partner governments, particularly their commitment of financial and people resources to deliver." (D0006506.odt, CARTAC Evaluation section)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The Caribbean’s **small market sizes**, **climate vulnerability**, and **limited institutional capacity** constrain partner selection to multilateral organizations (IMF/IADB) with regional expertise. Local firms and governments lack the capacity to manage large-scale technical assistance directly, necessitating intermediation.
q27_constraints_detail: Small market sizes limit the pool of qualified local implementers.
High climate risk requires partners with disaster resilience expertise (e.g., IMF’s CARTAC).
Weak public financial management systems necessitate multilateral oversight.
Data gaps (e.g., real-time population data) require partners with statistical capacity (e.g., World Bank).
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **mixed objectives** (macroeconomic stability + private sector growth + gender inclusion) require a **multi-pillar structure**: Pillars 1-2 use multilateral trust funds for technical assistance, while Pillars 3-4 use flexible funds for targeted interventions. The need for **regional integration** (e.g., OECS coordination) shapes the choice of partners like the IADB.
q28_linkages: Macroeconomic stability goals → Multilateral trust funds (IMF CARTAC) for debt/PFM reforms.
Private sector development → IADB’s Compete Caribbean Plus for firm-level support.
Women’s empowerment → Flexible fund (Pillar 3) to address gender-specific barriers.
Climate resilience → Cross-cutting theme requiring both policy reforms (Pillar 1) and firm-level adaptation (Pillar 2).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances **efficiency** (using existing multilateral platforms) with **equity** (e.g., 47% of Compete Caribbean Plus firms supported were women-owned). Trade-offs include: (1) **Speed vs. inclusion**: Multilateral processes may slow disbursement but ensure broader reach. (2) **Northern expertise vs. Southern ownership**: IMF/IADB lead implementation, but Pillar 3 prioritizes women-led businesses.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Efficiency (multilateral trust funds) vs. country ownership (limited local decision-making).
Scale (regional programmes) vs. tailoring (flexible Pillar 4 fund for country-specific needs).
Technical expertise (IMF/IADB) vs. local knowledge (e.g., women’s business networks).
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate risk profile** (climate shocks, debt distress) justifies **milestone-based oversight** and **flexible funding** (Pillar 4). High climate risk increases the need for adaptive management, while debt vulnerabilities require IMF-led fiscal monitoring.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Limited Southern capacity (e.g., "low government capacity and low private sector competitiveness") shifts implementation to multilaterals, but capacity building (e.g., PFM reforms, women’s entrepreneurship training) is embedded to strengthen local ownership over time.

quote.context_constrains: "Caribbean SIDS face underlying structural constraints [...] vulnerability to economic and climate shocks (the Caribbean is the region most at risk of climate change and natural disasters), and generally low capacity in both the public and private sectors." (D0006506.odt, Context section)
quote.objectives_shape_delivery: "This programme will support inclusive economic growth and build economic resilience in the Caribbean, enabling the region to better respond to economic and climate shocks. There are four pillars: 1) small-medium business development [...] 2) macroeconomic and debt sustainability [...]" (D0006506.odt, Programme summary)
quote.tradeoffs: "Gender and inclusion will be mainstreamed through all of CompetePlus’ work; for example, in the previous phase, 47% of the firms supported were women-owned." (D0006506.odt, Pillar Two description) && "The UK will provide £25m, mainly in the form of technical assistance to support governments and businesses [...]" (D0006506.odt, UK Support section)
quote.risk_management: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006506.odt, Summary Sheet) && "Pillar Four: Inclusive Economic Development Strategic Fund - a £4m fund that will provide flexible funding that can be quickly programmed in response to unanticipated challenges or opportunities." (D0006506.odt, Pillar Four description)

key_programme_risks: Limited country absorption capacity for technical assistance
Climate shocks derailing economic reforms (e.g., hurricanes, pandemics)
Debt distress in target countries (e.g., Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines)
Overlap with other donor programmes leading to duplication
Slow disbursement from multilateral trust funds
Gender norms limiting women’s economic participation
Political economy barriers to reform implementation

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Demand-led technical assistance (CARTAC) and embedded advisors to build local capacity.
Flexible Pillar 4 fund for rapid response and climate-proofing of infrastructure investments.
IMF-led debt sustainability analyses and fiscal buffers through PFM reforms.
Coordination via regional steering committees and alignment with Caribbean Development Strategy.
Pillar 4’s £4m strategic fund for quick programming.
Targeted Pillar 3 interventions (e.g., finance access, mentorship for women-led businesses).

fcas_specific_lessons: Small island states require layered disaster risk finance (e.g., Jamaica’s post-Beryl insurance payouts).
Debt-for-climate swaps (e.g., Belize’s marine protection swap) can create fiscal space.
Regional integration (e.g., OECS) helps pool resources for resilience.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Previous phases of **CARTAC** and **Compete Caribbean Plus** demonstrated strong output delivery (consistent ‘A’ ratings) but highlighted needs for: (1) **better impact monitoring**, (2) **sustainability planning** (e.g., government resource commitments), and (3) **gender mainstreaming**. The UK’s past support for statistical capacity (e.g., OECS Living Conditions Surveys) will be expanded.
design_changes_based_on_learning: Added Pillar 4 (flexible fund) to address slow adaptive capacity in previous phases.
Increased focus on women’s economic empowerment (Pillar 3) based on Compete Caribbean Plus’s success (47% women-owned firms supported).
Stronger emphasis on climate finance leverage (30-50% of programme counted as ICF).

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers direct English Language Training (ELT) to Ukrainian civil servants engaged in EU and NATO accession negotiations and reforms. It combines immediate service provision with longer-term capacity building for sustainable ELT systems in Ukraine.
what_objectives.q1_source: This programme, which will be delivered by the British Council, will provide English Language Training (ELT) for civil servants working on EU and NATO accession negotiations and reforms, and is expected to improve the English language skills of up to 1400 officials in its first year.
q3_expected_outputs: Course completion rates (disaggregated by teaching methodology)
Post-training test scores of participants higher than pre-training test scores (disaggregated by teaching methodology)
Action plan on how to improve GoU teaching of English to Civil Servants
1400 individuals provided with English language training in the first year
Improved English language proficiency and communication skills of Ukrainian civil servants in the global arena
Increased capability within the Government of Ukraine to deliver training programmes in ELT
what_objectives.summary: The programme delivers ELT to Ukrainian civil servants to support EU/NATO accession while building sustainable ELT capacity in government institutions.
what_objectives.quote: The programme will provide English Language Training (ELT) for civil servants working on EU and NATO accession negotiations and reforms (D0007519.odt, Programme summary)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Ukraine is in active conflict since February 2022, with most participants and teachers living in a war-torn country, requiring war sensitivity training for teachers.
where_context.q5_source: Most-if not all-participants and teachers have been living in a war-torn country since Feb 2022, which will have taken a psychological toll on them.
q6_contextual_constraints: limited access to platforms in Kyiv
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The war context creates psychological stress for participants and teachers, limits physical access to delivery platforms, and strains government resources that could otherwise support language training. Civil servants are already overloaded with recovery efforts, making consistent attendance challenging.
where_context.quote: The delivery of teaching services to adults in a work context means safeguarding risks for this programme are low. [...] Most-if not all-participants and teachers have been living in a war-torn country since Feb 2022 (D0007519.odt, Risk sections)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The British Council (UK-based) designs and delivers the programme with oversight from FCDO/BE Kyiv, while Ukrainian institutions (GoU) are recipients of training and capacity building. The Programme Board includes GoU representatives but ultimate decision-making rests with FCDO and British Council.
q10_capacity_building_details: Direct ELT for 1400+ civil servants in Year 1
Consultancy to assess GoU capability for long-term ELT teaching (Year 1)
Investment in sustainable ELT systems and Ukrainian institutional capacity (Years 2-3)
Training for teachers including war-sensitivity modules
EDI (Equality, Diversity, Inclusion) training integrated into courses

partner_organizations.name: British Council
partner_organizations.role: Primary implementer (design, delivery, and capacity building)

partner_organizations.name: Government of Ukraine (GoU) - Cabinet of Ministers
partner_organizations.role: Beneficiary and partner (provides participants, signs cooperation agreements)
