metadata.programme_name: BIOT voluntary returns and reintegration
metadata.quote: A tailored package of support to incentivise the voluntary return of irregular migrants currently on BIOT. (D0007553.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: ProgrammeValue: upto £300,000 over three years (D0007553.odt, Programme summary) \n ProgrammeStartDate: 02/10/2024 \n ProgrammeEndDate: 02/10/2027

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers a tailored support package to incentivise and facilitate the safe voluntary return and reintegration of migrants from the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) to Sri Lanka. It addresses urgent safeguarding risks and litigation costs by providing financial support, accommodation, education, training, and employment assistance.
what_objectives.q1_source: To incentivise and facilitate the safe voluntary return and reintegration of migrants to Sri Lanka. (D0007553.odt, Intended policy objectives) \n A tailored package of support to incentivise the voluntary return of irregular migrants currently on BIOT. The proposed package [...] includes initial financial support, accommodation, education, training and employment support. (D0007553.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: safe voluntary return of up to 10 migrants (planning assumption)
reintegration support (financial, accommodation, education, training, employment) for returnees in Sri Lanka
reduction in safeguarding risks for vulnerable migrants (children, victims of abuse, individuals with medical needs)
cost savings for the UK (current annual cost of ~£50m for migrants remaining on BIOT)
what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to deliver a voluntary return and reintegration package for irregular migrants stranded on BIOT, addressing humanitarian, legal, and financial pressures through direct service provision.
what_objectives.quote: The situation requires an urgent solution because: [...] There are significant safeguarding risks to some of the migrants (especially children). [...] There is an ongoing cost to the UK of circa £50m per annum while the migrants remain on BIOT. (D0007553.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The context involves vulnerable migrants (including children and victims of abuse) in a militarized, uninhabited island with no permanent facilities, alongside ongoing litigation and political sensitivities around forced returns. The programme notes "significant safeguarding risks" and potential reputational risks from legal disputes.
where_context.q5_source: There are significant safeguarding risks to some of the migrants (especially children). Two migrants have been convicted of sexual offences against children and vulnerable women [...] (D0007553.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending) \n Overall risk rating: Minor (D0007553.odt, Metadata) \n We face mounting litigation from the migrants, in multiple courts and against multiple defendants [...] (D0007553.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Migrants are housed in a camp within US military facilities on an uninhabited island with no permanent habitation, creating extreme living conditions. The lack of local institutions on BIOT and the sensitive political context (e.g., Sri Lankan authorities potentially viewing returnees as suspects) constrain delivery. Data protection is critical due to allegations of abuse and ongoing legal cases.
where_context.quote: They are housed in a camp within sensitive US military facilities on an island with no permanent habitation. (D0007553.odt, Rationale for FCDO spending) \n It is possible that the Sri Lankan authorities may see returnees as suspect and push for information on them [...] (D0007553.odt, Risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: FCDO retains full decision-making authority, with IRARA (a UK-based NGO) implementing the programme in Sri Lanka under FCDO oversight. The selection of IRARA was based on Home Office due diligence and their global track record, not local ownership.
q10_capacity_building_details: reintegration support (education, training, employment assistance) for returnees
financial management and reporting capacity for IRARA’s local team in Sri Lanka

partner_organizations.name: IRARA (International Rescue and Relief Association)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner (delivery of reintegration services in Sri Lanka)
partner_organizations.location: North (UK-based, with operations in Sri Lanka)

partner_organizations.name: Home Office
partner_organizations.role: trusted provider selection (due diligence on IRARA)

who_partners.quote: IRARA have a strong track record and have successfully managed complex reintegration processes worldwide based on the same approach. (D0007553.odt, Risks) \n FCDO is relying on Due Diligence of IRARA carried out by the Home Office. (D0007553.odt, How will the programme manage risk)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The FCDO will contract IRARA under a time-bound agreement with upfront and milestone-based payments. The contract includes financial reviews and proof-of-spend requirements before quarterly payments are released. This is framed as a "Trusted Provider" arrangement, leveraging IRARA’s existing framework with the Home Office.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: IRARA is the sole implementer, reporting directly to FCDO’s Migration Department. The programme is managed by a small FCDO team (SRO: Greg Houston; Project Officer: Ian Ball) with no consortium or sub-awards. Oversight includes monthly financial reviews and regular progress meetings.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: IRARA was selected as a "Trusted Provider" based on prior competitive tendering by the Home Office for its Returns Reintegration Programme. The urgency of the Ministerial priority and IRARA’s existing capacity in Sri Lanka justified direct award without further competition. FCDO relied on Home Office due diligence.
how_mechanism.quote: Following a competitive tender exercise to identify the most appropriate reintegration delivery providers across priority returns countries, the Home Office selected IRARA and two other main organisations to deliver these services. (D0007553.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?) \n IRARA were selected as a Trusted Partner able to operate at the speed required for this urgent Ministerial priority. (D0007553.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

how_governance.quote: The SRO is Greg Houston and the Project Officer is Ian Ball. Migration Department has significant experience of managing project delivery [...] (D0007553.odt, Governance arrangements) \n Monthly project and financial reviews will be undertaken by the project team [...] (D0007553.odt, How will financial risks be managed?)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds are tied to the number of migrants accepting the offer, with no explicit provision for reallocating between components. The budget is structured as a fixed cost per migrant, and unspent funds in one quarter are not carried forward.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme’s scope is narrowly defined (voluntary returns and reintegration) with no mention of adaptive management. Changes would require FCDO approval, but the focus on speed and Ministerial priority suggests limited flexibility.
how_flexibility.quote: The planning assumptions assume 10 migrants will accept the offer but it is likely to be fewer than that so costs are likely to be lower. (D0007553.odt, Outline the total budget) \n No additional payments will be issued where IRARA may have funds remaining ahead of each subsequent quarter. (D0007553.odt, How will financial risks be managed?)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → IRARA (implementer) → end beneficiaries (migrants). No sub-grantees or additional layers are mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: An initial one-month upfront (25%) payment will be made, followed by quarterly payments in advance over the subsequent period of the contract. (D0007553.odt, How will financial risks be managed?)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen due to (1) **urgency** (Ministerial priority to address safeguarding risks and litigation costs quickly), (2) **partner capacity** (IRARA’s existing framework with the Home Office and on-the-ground presence in Sri Lanka), (3) **risk mitigation** (relying on a Trusted Provider with a proven track record in complex reintegration), and (4) **value for money** (negotiated cost reductions and milestone-based payments).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low uptake by migrants, incurring costs without achieving returns
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Costs are tied to the number of participants; planning assumes 10 migrants but expects fewer, reducing financial exposure.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk from perceived interaction with ongoing legal disputes
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Comms plan to explain the rationale and nature of the project, alongside strong project oversight.

why_rationale.quote: IRARA have agreed cost reductions for both fixed costs and the cost per migrant as part of our negotiations with them. (D0007553.odt, How will value for money be delivered?) \n IRARA were selected as a Trusted Partner able to operate at the speed required for this urgent Ministerial priority. (D0007553.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The remote, militarized context of BIOT and the urgency of safeguarding risks constrained partner selection to organizations with (1) **existing frameworks** (IRARA’s Home Office contract), (2) **rapid deployment capacity** (on-the-ground presence in Sri Lanka), and (3) **experience in complex reintegration** (including handling sensitive data protection needs for victims of abuse). Local Sri Lankan partners were not considered due to time constraints and political sensitivities.
q27_constraints_detail: urgency (Ministerial priority for quick action)
remote/militarized operating environment (no local institutions on BIOT)
political sensitivity (Sri Lankan authorities’ potential suspicion of returnees)
safeguarding risks (need for trusted providers with robust data protection)
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The **service-delivery objective** (direct reintegration support) determined a **single-implementer structure** (no consortium) to ensure speed and accountability. The need for **confidentiality** (due to abuse allegations) and **flexibility** (unknown number of participants) shaped the **milestone-based payment** approach.
q28_linkages: Direct service delivery → Single-implementer contract (no sub-awards)
Urgency → Trusted Provider (IRARA) selected via direct award
Safeguarding risks → Emphasis on data protection and financial controls
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **high-risk context** (safeguarding, litigation, political sensitivity) led to **intensive oversight** (monthly financial reviews, proof-of-spend requirements) despite the programme’s small size. The "Minor" overall risk rating contrasts with the detailed mitigation measures, suggesting risk aversion drives management intensity.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: IRARA’s **existing capacity** in Sri Lanka and prior experience with Tamil returnees enabled their role as sole implementer, but the programme does not include capacity building for local Sri Lankan institutions, reflecting a focus on immediate delivery over long-term ownership.
intersections.quote: The project will be scrutinised by the SRO. (D0007553.odt, How will the programme manage risk) \n IRARA have a strong track record and have successfully managed complex reintegration processes worldwide [...] (D0007553.odt, Risks)

key_programme_risks: Low uptake by migrants (fewer than 10 accepting the offer)
Safeguarding risks if Sri Lankan authorities target returnees as suspects
Reputational damage from perceived links to ongoing legal disputes
Financial loss if costs are incurred without achieving returns
Data protection breaches given sensitive information on abuse victims

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Budget planning assumes 10 migrants but expects fewer, reducing financial exposure. Costs are tied to actual participants.
IRARA’s robust approach to data protection.
Comms plan to explain the project’s rationale and nature, alongside strong oversight.
Monthly financial reviews, proof-of-spend requirements, and no advance payments if funds remain from prior quarters.

risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The programme builds on IRARA’s prior experience delivering similar reintegration services for the Home Office in 11 priority countries, including complex cases involving Tamil returnees. The use of a Trusted Provider framework reflects lessons from past successful collaborations.
risks_lessons.quote: IRARA have a strong track record and have successfully managed complex reintegration processes worldwide based on the same approach. (D0007553.odt, Risks) \n Following a competitive tender exercise [...] the Home Office selected IRARA and two other main organisations to deliver these services. (D0007553.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

financial_details.quote: ProgrammeValue: upto £300,000 over three years (D0007553.odt, Programme summary) \n Migration Department has the funding available, drawn from a recent uplift to upstream migration funding. (D0007553.odt, Outline the total budget)

metadata.programme_name: Preparations for the FFD4 conference – a pivotal moment for the SDGs and mobilising finance

quote.text: "A programme to support engagement for the fourth Financing for Development (FFD4) conference and its outcomes, with a focus on Global South partners... This programme will provide flexible and demand-led support for a range of activities that will contribute to achieving successful FFD4 outcomes in line with UK objectives."

metadata.duration_source: "Programme Start Date: 1 February 2025", "Programme End Date: 1 August 2025"

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme combines policy influence (shaping FFD4 outcomes), capacity building (supporting CSO participation), and financing mechanism (channeling flexible funds to partners). It aims to accelerate SDG financing through strategic engagement and research support.
what_objectives.q1_source: "This programme will provide flexible and demand-led support for a range of activities that will contribute to achieving successful FFD4 outcomes in line with UK objectives. These activities will include commissioning quick pieces of research on key FFD4 topics, organising events with key stakeholders... and support for partners, particularly Civil Society Organisations, to meaningfully participate in key FFD4 preparatory events and processes."
q3_expected_outputs: Commissioned research on key FFD4 topics (no quantitative target)
Events/workshops with stakeholders (e.g., roundtables, cross-stakeholder knowledge exchanges)
Support for CSO participation in FFD4 preparatory events (costs covered for attendance)
Synthesis of evidence on financing for development policy issues
Demonstration of UK leadership on Global South priorities (qualitative outcome)
what_objectives.summary: The programme supports UK engagement in FFD4 through research, stakeholder events, and CSO participation, aiming to influence global financing policies for SDGs and reform of the international financial system.

quote.text: "The programme will likely support the following broad types of activities: Supporting meaningful engagement from partners, particularly Civil Society Organisations... Structured engagement and policy dialogues to influence key FFD4 policy and reform agendas... Research and analysis to build or synthesise evidence base on critical financing for development policy issues."

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme is categorized as moderate risk due to potential logistical challenges (e.g., conference attendance, participant engagement) and the short timeframe for delivery, but operates in a stable multilateral context (UN-led conference).
where_context.q5_source: "Overall risk rating: Moderate" and "We judge that financial risk associated with this project is moderate. metadata.programme_name: RIVA (Rights, Inclusion, Voice and Agency) Nepal
metadata.primary_sector: gender equality, disability and social inclusion (GEDSI)

quote.text: The RIVA programme (£4.98m, October 23–March 28) will empower women, girls, and excluded groups in Nepal to understand and claim their Rights individually and collectively...

metadata.duration_source: The RIVA programme (£4.98m, October 23–March 28)...

what_objectives.q1_explanation: RIVA combines capacity building (strengthening WROs/CSOs), financing mechanism (flexible multi-year grants), and implementation research (testing social norm change approaches). It focuses on empowering marginalized groups to claim rights and participate in policy-making while also providing technical assistance for GEDSI mainstreaming across FCDO's portfolio.
what_objectives.q1_source: RIVA will strengthen the capacities of diverse and intersecting Women Rights Organisations (WROs) and Civil Society Organisation’s (CSOs) through the provision of flexible, multi-year funding and catalytic enabling grants. [...] It will help foster an enabling environment in Nepal, increasing collectivisation and exchange between organisations to support movement building and social norm change [...] RIVA will provide strategic demand-led TA to mainstream GEDSI effectively across BEK’s portfolio...
q3_expected_outputs: Empowered women, girls, and excluded groups to understand/claim rights (collective/individual)
Increased participation of marginalized groups in inclusive policy-making (national/local levels)
Stronger voice/agency for excluded groups to advance GEDSI
Strengthened capacities of 10+ WROs/CSOs via flexible multi-year funding (£4.98m total)
Enabling environment for movement building/social norm change in 3 priority provinces
Strategic TA to mainstream GEDSI across BEK’s £XXm portfolio
Support to GoN’s 16th Periodic Plan/SDGs (SDG1, SDG5, SDG10) implementation
Contribution to FCDO’s 80% gender equality requirement (OECD Gender Equality Marker ‘Principal’ score)
Generation of intersectional data/evidence on GEDSI in Nepal
what_objectives.summary: RIVA aims to transform structural inequalities in Nepal by empowering excluded groups (women, Dalits, LGBT+, persons with disabilities) through flexible funding to local WROs/CSOs, movement-building support, and technical assistance to embed GEDSI across FCDO’s Nepal portfolio, while generating evidence on what works for inclusive development.

quote.text: RIVA will empower women, girls, and excluded groups in Nepal to understand and claim their Rights individually and collectively, participate in Inclusive policy-making and implementation, and have a stronger Voice and Agency at both national and local levels to advance Gender Equality, Disability and Social Inclusion (GEDSI)... It will help foster an enabling environment in Nepal, increasing collectivisation and exchange between organisations to support movement building and social norm change...

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Nepal is post-conflict (2006 Peace Accord) with persistent social exclusion, weak GEDSI policy implementation, and climate vulnerability, but has stable democratic institutions and progressive legal frameworks. The programme’s risk rating is explicitly stated as 'Moderate'.
where_context.q5_source: Overall programme risk rating: Moderate
q6_contextual_constraints: weak institutions (GEDSI policy implementation gaps across federal/provincial/local government)
political economy (elite capture, caste/ethnic hierarchies, patriarchal norms)
conflict legacy (post-2006 Maoist war divisions, marginalized group grievances)
climate risks (disaster vulnerability for excluded groups)
data limitations (lack of intersectional disaggregated data)
shrinking civic space (CSO self-censorship, government co-optation)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Weak GEDSI implementation hinders service delivery to excluded groups; regulatory pressures limit CSO advocacy; caste/ethnic discrimination and patriarchal norms create barriers for women’s participation; climate risks disproportionately affect marginalized communities; data gaps prevent targeted interventions.

quote.text: Despite having relatively progressive Constitution (2015) and laws [...] implementation is hindered by a lack of inclusive planning, decision-making, and institutional mechanisms [...] Deep-rooted bureaucratic practices systematically prioritise seniority and rank, perpetuating dominance of certain demographics [...] Numerous GEDSI policies have been developed, and many GEDSI trainings delivered to government officials, but it is not clear how effective these are or to what extent GEDSI commitments have been reflected in sectoral policies and budgets.
quote.source: D0006262.odt, Challenge 2: GEDSI policies, laws and frameworks are poorly implemented

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: Local WROs/CSOs set priorities and receive multi-year core funding; FCDO provides strategic oversight and TA. Decision-making on grants and movement-building is devolved to Nepali organizations.
q10_capacity_building_details: multi-year flexible funding for WROs/CSOs
catalytic enabling grants for movement building
governance/leadership training
financial management (budgeting, fundraising)
strategic planning support
advocacy/communications skills
digital/ICT training
legal/compliance support (safeguarding, risk management)
self-care/collective care for activists
peer-led mentorship and network strengthening

partner_organizations.role: Primary implementers (receive flexible grants, lead movement building)

partner_organizations.role: Co-implementers (advocacy, social norm change, policy engagement)

partner_organizations.role: Strategic oversight, TA provider, convenor

quote.text: RIVA will strengthen the capacities of diverse and intersecting Women Rights Organisations (WROs) and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) through the provision of flexible, multi-year funding and catalytic enabling grants [...] BEK recognises that locally led WROs and CSOs should be at the heart of setting development priorities in their communities [...] RIVA will help to promote and consolidate the UK’s role as a champion and convenor of gender equality, social inclusion and the rights of women and girls and excluded groups in Nepal.

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core funding (flexible multi-year grants to WROs/CSOs) combined with catalytic grants for movement building and demand-led technical assistance (TA) for GEDSI mainstreaming. The programme uses a ‘fund manager’ model where local organizations receive unrestricted funds to set their own priorities, complemented by targeted TA.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: RIVA operates as a funding platform with three components: 1) flexible grants to WROs/CSOs, 2) movement-building support (collectivization, exchanges), and 3) strategic TA for GEDSI mainstreaming across BEK’s portfolio. Local organizations lead implementation, with BEK providing oversight and TA.

quote.text: RIVA will strengthen the capacities of diverse and intersecting Women Rights Organisations (WROs) and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) through the provision of flexible, multi-year funding and catalytic enabling grants. It will help foster an enabling environment in Nepal, increasing collectivisation and exchange between organisations to support movement building and social norm change [...] RIVA will provide strategic demand-led TA to mainstream GEDSI effectively across BEK’s portfolio...

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The BEK Country Board approved the business case (23/10/2024), suggesting oversight by a senior governance body. Day-to-day management is devolved to WROs/CSOs, with BEK providing strategic guidance and TA.

quote.text: Date of Approval of Business Case: 23/10/2024 [...] Name and role of Approver: Pippa Bird–Development Director/Rob Fenn–HMA, BEK Country Board [...] RIVA will provide strategic demand-led TA to mainstream GEDSI effectively across BEK’s portfolio...

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Multi-year core funding allows WROs/CSOs to reallocate funds based on emerging priorities. Catalytic grants support adaptive movement-building.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Demand-led TA and movement-building components enable responsiveness to local context changes, with BEK oversight for strategic alignment.

quote.text: RIVA will strengthen the capacities of diverse and intersecting Women Rights Organisations (WROs) and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) through the provision of flexible, multi-year funding and catalytic enabling grants [...] RIVA will provide strategic demand-led TA to mainstream GEDSI effectively...

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → WROs/CSOs (direct funding to local organizations with BEK oversight/TA).

quote.text: The RIVA programme (£4.98m, October 23–March 28)...

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The platform model was selected to: 1) Address systemic exclusion by empowering local WROs/CSOs to set priorities (localization agenda); 2) Provide flexible, long-term funding to counter shrinking civic space and donor fragmentation; 3) Combine core funding with TA to build sustainable movements; 4) Align with FCDO’s Women and Girls Strategy (2023-2030) and Disability Inclusion Strategy by centering marginalized voices; 5) Generate evidence on intersectional approaches to GEDSI.
q25_decision_factors: vfm (flexible funding reduces administrative costs for donors/CSOs)
risk-mitigation (multi-year core funding builds resilience against shrinking civic space)
experience (lessons from FCDO’s £38m Equality Fund for WROs)
partner-capacity (addresses gaps in financial management, advocacy, and movement-building)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Political capture of CSOs/WROs by elites or government
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Multi-year core funding to reduce donor dependency; peer-led capacity building on safeguarding and advocacy.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Fragmentation of civil society due to competition for resources
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Catalytic grants for collectivization/exchange; movement-building support to foster alliances.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak absorption capacity of local organizations for flexible funds
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Embedded TA on financial management; phased disbursement with mentorship.

vfm_criteria_used: effectiveness (intersectional approach targets root causes of exclusion)

quote.text: RIVA will promote localisation and local leadership agenda in Nepal by building women’s and marginalised groups’ voice, capacity for advocacy and social change and through emphasising that locally led WROs and CSOs should set development priorities [...] RIVA will deliver on the FCDO policies including Indo-Pacific Strategic Framework; FCDO Women and Girls Strategy (2023-2030) [...] Providing ‘core support’ or unrestricted/unearmarked funding to civil society is ‘the most development-effective type of support, with advantages such as flexibility, predictability, administrative efficiency, ownership and accountability’ (OECD 2020).
quote.source: D0006262.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending & OECD reference

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: Nepal’s regulatory environment (CSO restrictions, donor dependency) and caste/ethnic hierarchies limit which organizations can access funding and decision-making spaces. Shrinking civic space and elite capture risk sidelining grassroots WROs, necessitating flexible, long-term support to build resilience.
q27_constraints_detail: CSO regulations favor established (often urban/higher-caste) organizations, excluding grassroots groups
Donor fragmentation creates competition, undermining collectivization
Patriarchal norms limit women-led organizations’ access to networks/resources
Post-conflict political economy risks co-optation of CSOs by parties/elites
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **intersectional** GEDSI outcomes (addressing caste, ethnicity, disability, LGBT+ exclusion) requires a **platform model** that: 1) Channels core funds directly to diverse WROs/CSOs (not just women-focused); 2) Supports movement-building across identities (e.g., Dalit women, LGBT+ groups); 3) Provides TA to mainstream intersectionality in BEK’s portfolio.
q28_linkages: Intersectional exclusion → Platform funding (to reach Dalit women, LGBT+, persons with disabilities)
Social norm change → Movement-building grants (collectivization across provinces)
GEDSI mainstreaming → Demand-led TA (embedded in BEK’s £XXm portfolio)
Localization → Multi-year core funding (reduces donor dependency)
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: Explicit tension between **rapid delivery** (e.g., short-term projects) and **inclusive partnerships** (e.g., multi-year core funding for grassroots WROs). The programme prioritizes equity by accepting higher transaction costs for flexible funding and movement-building, citing OECD evidence that core support yields longer-term impact despite slower disbursement.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Speed vs. inclusion: Multi-year grants to grassroots WROs take longer to disburse but build sustainable capacity
Expertise vs. ownership: BEK provides TA but defers priority-setting to local organizations
Cost vs. reach: Flexible funding has higher administrative costs but reduces fragmentation
Risk vs. innovation: Core funding to new WROs carries fiduciary risk but enables testing intersectional approaches
intersections.risk_affects_management: Nepal’s ‘Moderate’ risk profile (post-conflict, weak GEDSI implementation) justifies **milestone-based oversight** with embedded safeguarding TA, while flexible funding mitigates civic space risks by reducing CSO dependency on short-term donor agendas.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity gaps in financial management/advocacy among WROs/CSOs necessitate **peer-led TA and mentorship**, shaping roles: local organizations lead implementation, while BEK/FCDO provide backstopping. This builds on lessons from FCDO’s Equality Fund, where Southern-led fund management strengthened ownership.

quote.text: Achieving transformative GEDSI outcomes in Nepal is challenged by limited financial and institutional resources, short-term donor-driven, projectized support for women’s and civil society organisations and networks in Nepal [...] WROs and CSOs require diverse capacity-building support to enhance their effectiveness and sustainability [...] Providing ‘core support’ or unrestricted/unearmarked funding to civil society is ‘the most development-effective type of support’ (OECD 2020), with advantages such as flexibility, predictability, administrative efficiency, ownership and accountability.

key_programme_risks: Elite capture of CSO/WRO funds or agendas
Backlash against gender/LGBT+ rights from conservative groups
Weak absorption capacity of local organizations for flexible funds
Fragmentation of civil society due to competition
Government restrictions on CSO advocacy spaces
Climate disasters disrupting implementation in rural areas
Low participation of most excluded groups (e.g., Dalit women with disabilities)
Safeguarding risks in movement-building activities

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Targeted outreach to grassroots WROs; intersectional analysis in partner selection; peer accountability mechanisms.
Alliances with progressive government actors (e.g., Ministry of Women); legal TA to navigate restrictions.
Phased funding with mentorship; embedded financial management TA.
Catalytic grants for collectivization; provincial exchange platforms.
Multi-year core funding to reduce donor dependency; advocacy for CSO enabling environment.

fcas_specific_lessons: Post-conflict contexts require **intersectional** approaches (caste, ethnicity, gender) to avoid exacerbating divisions (lesson from Nepal’s Civil War).
Flexible funding is critical in FCAS to adapt to political shifts (e.g., Maoist-led federalism).
Localization must address **power imbalances** within civil society (e.g., urban vs. rural WROs).
Movement-building in FCAS needs **safeguarding** against co-optation by armed groups/parties.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: Lessons from FCDO’s £38m Equality Fund (Southern-led fund management) and Enabling State Programme (2001–2014) highlight: 1) Core funding strengthens CSO resilience; 2) Peer-led TA is more effective than Northern experts; 3) Intersectional data is critical for FCAS; 4) Long-term support is needed to counter pushback against rights.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: RIVA incorporates: 1) **Multi-year core funding** (vs. projectized grants); 2) **Demand-led TA** (vs. top-down training); 3) **Explicit intersectional focus** (Dalit women, LGBT+, persons with disabilities); 4) **Movement-building component** (lesson from fragmented civil society).

quote.text: A £38m Centrally Managed FCDO programme supports women’s rights organisations and movements, recognising their vital role in gender equality and rights protection [...] Key lessons from the CMP have been incorporated into the design of RIVA [...] Nearly two decades later, Nepal’s civil society faces challenges such as perceptions of political bias, partisanship, and heavy reliance on external donor funding [...] To regain public trust, CSOs must become more transparent, strengthen monitoring and evaluation systems, and build stronger coalitions.
quote.source: D0006262.odt, Financing and Capacity Build Support & Civil Society in Nepal
