partner_organizations.name: Somaliland Development Fund (SDF)
partner_organizations.role: Coordinating platform (mentioned as complementary)

who_partners.quote: By setting up an Accountable Grant with NIMD as the implementing partner the UK will be able to deliver the recommended support package. (D0007431.odt, DELIVERY ROUTE OPTIONS)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The programme uses an **Accountable Grant** to NIMD, which operates as a pass-through mechanism for UK funds. NIMD sub-contracts NGOs and media outlets while managing direct technical support to NEC. The grant includes milestone-based disbursements with FCDO oversight.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: NIMD serves as the sole contractor, managing all sub-awards (NGOs, media) and technical advisers. FCDO retains direct oversight via quarterly reviews and embedded monitoring. No consortium or joint decision-making bodies are established.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Urgent timeline (elections in November 2024) and limited supplier market in Somaliland justified direct award to NIMD, which had pre-existing relationships with NEC and prior UK-funded experience. A 2024 commercial process for election observers received zero bids, demonstrating market constraints.
how_mechanism.quote: We propose to single source an implementing partner who has been identified as the only possible supplier of this requirement given the urgency of the delivery and existing knowledge of the market. (D0007431.odt, DELIVERY ROUTE OPTIONS)

how_governance.quote: The Programme Team will have regular engagement with implementing partners where they will evaluate both project and financial performance of the projects. On a quarterly basis the implementing partner will provide a performance report. (D0007431.odt, DELIVERY PARTNER PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Savings from Component 1 (e.g., training/voter education) can be reallocated to post-election activities (Component 2) with FCDO approval. The budget includes an 8% admin contingency for adjustments.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: Post-election scoping (Component 2) allows some flexibility to respond to the election outcome, but core election-support activities (Component 1) are fixed. A 'small amount' can pivot to demand-side interventions if gaps are identified.
how_flexibility.quote: There are likely to be some savings in the components, which we will use for post-election purposes, including evaluation. [...] if we judge that more is needed to support the demand side of elections, we will have the ability to pivot a small amount of support. (D0007431.odt, ECONOMIC APPRAISAL / Package of Technical Support and Post-Election Support)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → NIMD (implementing partner) → [NGOs/media/sub-contractors]
how_efficiency.quote: Admin Cost 8% [...] Payments will be made in accordance with terms of the FCDO PrOF – monthly in arrears for administrative costs and mixed of monthly in arrears and pre-payment for activities. (D0007431.odt, FUNDING TYPES AND BUDGET / EXPENDITURE MONITORING)

q24_alternatives_considered: Do Nothing
Provision of Technical Advisers only
Package of Technical Support (including advisers) and post-elections scoping on reform opportunities [preferred option]
Package of Technical Support and longer-term, multi-year governance support
Package of Technical Support and demand side interventions
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option (Technical Support + Post-Election Scoping) was selected for its balance of **speed** (urgent election timeline), **value for money** (leveraging existing NIMD relationships), and **strategic impact** (bridging elections to governance reforms). Sole-sourcing NIMD reduced transaction costs in a constrained supplier market, while the two-component structure allowed flexibility to adapt post-election.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: NIMD’s limited in-country capacity could affect delivery quality
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Robust due diligence assessment of NIMD’s local capacity, with action plans for gaps. (D0007431.odt, COMMERCIAL RISKS)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Delays in FCDO approval processes could push back programme start
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Programme team to aim to meet all required deadlines to ensure timely approvals. (D0007431.odt, COMMERCIAL RISKS)

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Sole-sourcing may limit competitive pricing
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Rates benchmarked against NEC’s own budget and market standards; savings redirected to post-election activities. (D0007431.odt, ECONOMIC APPRAISAL)

why_rationale.quote: This approach would be consistent with the Theory of Change and allows for delivery of the higher-level outcomes and impact that this programme seeks. [...] It would address both the technical and financial constraints that the NEC faces in delivering elections. (D0007431.odt, Assessment of Feasible Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The FCAS context in Somaliland constrained partner selection to organizations with **existing in-country presence** and **trusted NEC relationships**. Limited local supplier capacity (e.g., zero bids for a 2024 election observer tender) and urgent timelines forced reliance on NIMD despite its Northern HQ.
q27_constraints_detail: Urgent election timeline (November 2024) precluded open competition
No local suppliers with required technical expertise (prior commercial process received zero bids)
Security risks required partners with established Somaliland operations
NEC’s weak capacity necessitated partners with prior institutional relationships
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The need for **rapid, large-scale training** (5,500+ polling staff) and **voter education at scale** (1.2M voters) drove the choice of a **single implementer (NIMD) with sub-contracting authority** to NGOs/media. Post-election reform scoping required **embedded advisers** due to the political sensitivity of engaging with ministries.
q28_linkages: Large-scale training outputs → sole implementer with sub-contracting model
Post-election policy influence → embedded advisers in BoH/ministries
Urgent timeline → sole-source procurement
NEC capacity gaps → technical advisers + supply-chain support
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly trades **speed/efficiency** (sole-sourcing NIMD, limited competition) for **equity** (geographic reach to minority clans, gender-inclusive training). Voter education materials are tailored for marginalized groups, but the tight timeline limits participatory design processes.
q29_tradeoffs_detail: sole-sourcing NIMD (efficiency) vs. open competition (equity)
rapid training rollout (speed) vs. localized material adaptation (inclusion)
embedded UK advisers (expertise) vs. Somaliland-led reform ownership (sustainability)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The **moderate-high risk profile** (election delays, conflict) justified **intensive oversight** (quarterly reviews, embedded monitoring) and **milestone-based payments** to ensure NEC readiness. Political risks elevated the need for FCDO diplomatic engagement alongside technical support.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: NEC’s **limited operational capacity** shaped NIMD’s role as a **hands-on implementer** (managing training, voter education, and supply chains) rather than a purely advisory partner. Post-election, advisers are embedded in ministries to **compensate for weak public-sector reform skills**.
intersections.quote: Given the extreme short timelines we are working to, it is necessary to find the most appropriate implementing partner who is well-positioned to deliver. Existing knowledge of the market has led us to identify through a single source. (D0007431.odt, DELIVERY ROUTE OPTIONS)

key_programme_risks: Elections delayed for political, security, or technical reasons (Medium/High)
Re-emergence of conflict (e.g., Las Anod, clan violence) disrupting elections (Medium/High)
UK support perceived as interfering in elections (Medium/Low)
NEC commissioners resign or NEC is disbanded (Low/High)
Freedom of expression crackdown by government (Medium/Low)
Al-Shabaab (AS) attacks (Low/Medium)
Fraud or misuse of funds (Medium/High)
Lack of technical/budgeting capacity from partners (Medium/High)

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Use programme to support technical readiness; diplomatic levers to hold president accountable; escalate via Democratisation Steering Committee (DSC). (D0007431.odt, RISK REGISTER)
Work with NEC to assess feasibility of allowing registered voters in conflict areas to vote elsewhere; stop direct support if authorities violate rights. (D0007431.odt, RISK REGISTER)
Deliver support via NEC (independent institution); agree communications with NEC on specifying UK role. (D0007431.odt, RISK REGISTER)
Due diligence on partners’ internal controls; separate tracking of FCDO funds; spot checks and evidence requirements for invoices. (D0007431.odt, EXPENDITURE MONITORING)
Assess whether support could continue under new commissioners. (D0007431.odt, RISK REGISTER)

fcas_specific_lessons: Prior UK support to Puntland elections (2024) demonstrated the need for **conflict-sensitive voter education** and **domestic observer missions** to build credibility.
Somaliland’s **clan-based exclusions** require targeted outreach to minority groups in voter education.
**Post-election violence risks** (e.g., 2021 disputes) necessitate pre-agreed response plans with NEC.
**Limited local supplier markets** in FCAS contexts justify sole-sourcing to partners with existing relationships.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 Somaliland elections (UK support: £2M) showed that **international technical support improved NEC credibility** but **local ownership of core functions (e.g., salaries, equipment) remained weak**. The 2024 Puntland district elections (USD 500K) proved that **voter education and domestic observers** reduce contestation but require **early planning** to avoid delays.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: Shifted focus from **core NEC funding** (2021) to **targeted technical support** (2024) for training/voter education, where UK adds most value. Added **post-election reform scoping** to capitalize on political momentum, addressing prior gaps in linking elections to governance gains.
risks_lessons.quote: In 2021, the UK provided almost £2m as part of a USD 3.4m joint-donor programme to the NEC [...] The UK also supported an International Observer Mission (£210k). Since then, the NEC Commissioners have changed and the presidential elections were delayed [...] The UK has since been instrumental, alongside others, in pressing for these elections to be held in a timely fashion. (D0007431.odt, WHAT HAS BEEN DONE TO DATE)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: Potential co-financing to increase total programme value from £2.5M (UK) to £5M (with partners). (D0007431.odt, Programme Value)
financial_details.quote: Programme Value: Up to £2.5m UK funding and potential for other partners to co-finance up to a total programme value of £5m. [...] Admin Cost 8% (£200,800). (D0007431.odt, Programme Value / FUNDING TYPES AND BUDGET)

metadata.programme_name: Small ODA Projects – BE Nouakchott
metadata.quote: "Post proposes to use the International Programme Fund allocation of £84,500 in FY24-25 to fund two projects that support delivery of business plan objectives." (D0007438.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Programme Start Date: 01/09/2024", "Programme End Date: 28/02/2025" (D0007438.odt, Programme details)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme delivers two concrete projects: 1) improving weapons/ammunition management and security in Dakhlet-Nouadhibou, and 2) providing sustainable solar-powered drinking water access to 5,280 inhabitants in Ziwas village. Both are direct service interventions addressing security and basic needs.
what_objectives.q1_source: "The first project will contribute to strengthening the internal control of weapons in Mauritania... The second project aims to improve access to drinking water in the village of Ziwas in the Assaba Region to 5280 inhabitants..." (D0007438.odt, Programme summary)
q3_expected_outputs: 5,280 inhabitants gaining access to drinking water (2,746 women)
379 school students (222 girls) with improved learning conditions
temporary employment generated during water infrastructure implementation
improved sanitation and health conditions in Ziwas village
enhanced security of weapons stockpiles in Dakhlet-Nouadhibou
trained personnel in weapons/ammunition management
reduced illegal cross-border flows of ammunition
income-generating activities enabled (especially for women)
reduced gender-based violence risk through decreased water collection time
what_objectives.summary: The programme combines security interventions (weapons management) with basic service delivery (water access) to address Mauritania's dual challenges of regional instability and climate resilience.
what_objectives.quote: "Reducing conflict and building security is a priority in Mauritania... Supporting sustainable and inclusive economic growth and a cleaner, greener and more climate resilient Sahel..." (D0007438.odt, Intended policy objectives)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Mauritania faces risks from regional instability (Mali spillover), non-state armed groups, and unplanned explosions at munitions sites. The document explicitly mentions "considerable risk of proliferation and use of ammunition by non-state-armed-group active in the Sahel region."
where_context.q5_source: "Mauritania also faces a considerable risk of proliferation and use of ammunition by non-state-armed-group active in the Sahel region, posing a real security challenge..." (D0007438.odt, Portfolio/Business/Country Plan Summary)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Remote areas with difficult access pose logistical challenges for delivery. Extreme desert conditions and obsolete infrastructure near populated areas increase risks of unplanned explosions. Proximity to Western Sahara conflict affects mine/cluster munition contamination.
where_context.quote: "Low risk of non-delivery in time due to activities taking place in remote areas, with difficult access, posing a logistical challenge." (D0007438.odt, Risks)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The British Embassy Nouakchott (FCDO) holds decision-making authority as both SRO (Guy Harrison, HM Ambassador) and PRO (Fatimetou Moctar, Deputy Development Director). Implementing partners execute but do not appear to have strategic decision-making roles.
q10_capacity_building_details: training personnel in weapons/ammunition management
raising awareness within security forces
gender-balanced teams in risk education activities
community resilience building through water infrastructure

partner_organizations.name: Mines Advisory Group (MAG)
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner for weapons/ammunition management project

partner_organizations.name: World Vision International
partner_organizations.role: implementing partner for safe drinking water project

who_partners.quote: "Partners will be selected by the PRO and HoM through scoping on the basis of clear ability delivery criteria and alignment of project proposals with Post business plan objectives." (D0007438.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Funding arrangements will vary between Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and Accountable Grant Agreement depending on the registration status of the partner. This suggests a combination of formal contracts and less rigid agreements.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: Each project has a single designated implementing partner (MAG for security, World Vision for water) with direct oversight by the British Embassy Nouakchott. There is no consortium or platform structure.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: Partners were selected based on "clear ability delivery criteria and alignment with Post business plan objectives" and are described as "trusted partners of the FCDO" with prior due diligence assessments.
how_mechanism.quote: "Funding arrangements will vary between Memorandum of Understanding and Accountable Grant Agreement depending on the registration status of the partner." (D0007438.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Deputy Development Director (PRO) manages programme delivery and both PRO/SRO hold accountability. No steering committee or board is mentioned; governance is embedded within the Embassy structure.
how_governance.quote: "Project delivery will be monitored through regular communication with the implementing partners on progress, site and field visits where possible and an end-of-project report." (D0007438.odt, Monitoring and Reporting)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: The programme funds two fixed projects with specific budgets (£9,500 and £75,000). No mention of flexibility to reallocate between components.
how_flexibility.quote: "Project 1: Safe Drinking Water for Ziwas in Assaba Region - Value: £9,500", "Project 2: Improving Safety and Security for Weapons and Ammunitions Management - Value: £75,000" (D0007438.odt, Budget details)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO (British Embassy Nouakchott) → Implementing Partner (MAG/World Vision) → Beneficiaries. No sub-grantees or additional layers mentioned.
how_efficiency.quote: "Financial risks will be managed by: Receiving receipts for the work delivered. Conducting site visits and attending events organised as part of the programme." (D0007438.odt, How will you manage financial risks?)

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The modality was chosen based on: 1) Trusted partnerships with proven FCDO implementers (MAG/World Vision), 2) Alignment with Post business plan objectives, and 3) Proportionate processes for small ODA projects as per FCDO guidance.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Low risk of non-delivery due to logistical challenges in remote areas
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Partners have mobilised all resources needed for timely delivery.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risks (sexual exploitation, abuse, harassment)
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Implementing partners have strict zero-tolerance policies implemented at every stage.

why_rationale.quote: "Partners will be selected by the PRO and HoM through scoping on the basis of clear ability delivery criteria and alignment of project proposals with Post business plan objectives." (D0007438.odt, How will delivery partners be selected?)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The remote and high-risk operating environment (Dakhlet-Nouadhibou's security challenges and Assaba's remote access) limits partner selection to organizations with established presence and logistical capacity in Mauritania. This excludes newer or less-experienced actors.
q27_constraints_detail: need for partners with existing Mauritania operations
capacity to work in remote/conflict-affected areas
experience with FCDO safeguarding/compliance requirements
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The direct service delivery objectives (water access and weapons security) require specialized implementers: World Vision for community-based infrastructure and MAG for mine/weapons expertise. This determines the single-implementer-per-project structure.
q28_linkages: water project → needs partner with WASH and solar energy expertise → World Vision selected
weapons project → needs mine action and security sector experience → MAG selected
intersections.risk_affects_management: The FCAS context and "minor" risk rating result in milestone-based oversight rather than intensive management. Site visits and receipt verification are used as proportionate controls.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity building is embedded within service delivery: training security forces on weapons management and enabling income-generation through water access. Partners' existing gender/inclusion policies shape their implementation roles.
intersections.quote: "The two partners implementing project part of the programme are trusted partners of the FCDO, which have both received funding from different FCDO-funds and have due diligence assessments in place." (D0007438.odt, How will the programme manage the risk associated with delivery through each partner?)

key_programme_risks: Logistical challenges in remote areas delaying delivery
Safeguarding incidents (sexual exploitation, abuse, harassment)
Reputational risk from non-delivery
Low community participation (mitigated as 'very low risk')

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Low risk of non-delivery in time due to logistical challenges
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Partners have mobilised all resources needed for timely delivery.
Project implementing partners have strict zero-tolerance policies and approaches to sexual abuse, harassment and bullying implemented at every stage of project delivery.
Mitigated through partner resource mobilisation and Embassy oversight.

fcas_specific_lessons: Use of trusted partners with FCAS experience (MAG/World Vision) to navigate security and access challenges
Embedded gender and conflict-sensitive approaches in mine action work
Proportionate oversight (milestone-based) balanced with operational flexibility
risks_lessons.quote: "Mitigation risks are in place to manage the identified minor risks and any potential impact." (D0007438.odt, How will the programme manage the risk associated with delivery through each partner?)

financial_details.quote: "The total budget of the programme for the financial year 2024/2025 is £84,500 from the International Programme Fund." (D0007438.odt, Outline the total budget)

metadata.programme_name: Strengthening Human Rights Compliance of the Multinational Security Support Mission to Haiti

quote.text: This Programme, implemented by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), will help the MSS achieve its objectives by i) building the capacity of mission personnel to prevent, identify, investigate, report, and follow up on human rights violations, gender-based violence, and sexual exploitation and abuse; ii) advancing human rights protection of Haitian local communities and civil society; and iii) strengthening the capacity of Haitian rule of law entities collaborating with the MSS, such as the police, judiciary and prison administration, to conduct operations in accordance with international human rights standards.

duration_source.text: This would take the form of a ring-fenced one-year programme providing £5m for this purpose.

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme focuses on strengthening the human rights compliance of the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission in Haiti by building the capacity of mission personnel, Haitian civil society, and rule of law entities. It aims to prevent, identify, and address human rights violations, gender-based violence, and sexual exploitation and abuse, while fostering trust and accountability.

q1_source.text: The Programme, implemented by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), will help the MSS achieve its objectives by i) building the capacity of mission personnel to prevent, identify, investigate, report, and follow up on human rights violations, gender-based violence, and sexual exploitation and abuse; ii) advancing human rights protection of Haitian local communities and civil society; and iii) strengthening the capacity of Haitian rule of law entities collaborating with the MSS, such as the police, judiciary and prison administration, to conduct operations in accordance with international human rights standards.

q3_expected_outputs.output: Strengthened capacity of MSS mission personnel to implement the human rights compliance framework
Empowered civil society human rights actors engaged in prevention, documentation, and reporting of human rights violations
Strengthened capacity of Haitian rule of law entities (police, judiciary, prison administration) to operate in accordance with human rights standards
Prevention and investigation of human rights violations, including gender-based violence (GBV) and sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA)
Training of key local and international groups (commanding officers, local human rights actors, UN Integrated Office in Haiti)
Implementation of the UN Human Rights Compliance Framework

what_objectives.summary: The programme aims to strengthen human rights compliance within the MSS mission in Haiti by building the capacity of security personnel, civil society, and rule of law institutions to prevent and address human rights violations, particularly gender-based violence and sexual exploitation. It seeks to foster trust between the mission and local communities while ensuring operations align with international human rights standards.

quote.text: By achieving these complementary outcomes, human rights violations, GBV, and SEA will be prevented and the MSS and the HNP will start to gain the trust of the local population. In addition, civil society human rights actors will have a role in decreasing the risk of abuses linked to HNP operations supported by the MSS mission, and Haitian rule of law entities will have stronger capacity to conduct their operations in accordance with human rights standards.

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: Haiti is experiencing extreme gang violence, political instability, and a collapsed healthcare system, with 578,074 internally displaced persons and widespread human rights abuses. The operating environment is classified as 'major' risk due to the potential for further instability and violence.

q5_source.text: The operating environment in Haiti is high risk due to widespread gang violence and lack of state control. The risks associated with the MSS are also high given the potential for failure if, for example, the mission generates unintended consequences and thus further instability and violence. These risks are described in more detail in the approved Programme Overseas Security and Justice Assistance (OSJA) form.

where_context.q6_constraints_impact: The security situation in Haiti is dire, with gang violence controlling 80% of Port-au-Prince and critical infrastructure under attack. Weak institutions, such as a collapsed healthcare system and a judiciary with low capacity, hinder service delivery. Political instability and natural disasters exacerbate the crisis, while climate risks (hurricanes, floods, earthquakes) further strain the already fragile state.

quote.text: Haiti’s deteriorating security situation has resulted in 578,074 internally displaced persons (IDPs), of which 200,000 are children... The country’s healthcare system is close to collapse... In the capital Port-au-Prince, only 18% of health facilities are fully functional... Gang violence has soared. Documented abuses include targeted killings; mass rapes; kidnappings; the forced recruitment, exploitation and trafficking of children by gangs; deliberate attacks against human rights defenders, journalists, and state officials...

who_partners.lead_institution_name: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)
who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: The programme is led by OHCHR, a UN agency, with decision-making power centralized within its international structure. Local Haitian partners (civil society, rule of law entities) are recipients of capacity-building activities but do not hold primary decision-making authority.
q10_capacity_building_details: training of MSS mission personnel on human rights compliance
training of Haitian rule of law entities (police, judiciary, prison administration)
training and empowerment of civil society human rights actors
mentorship through OHCHR’s oversight and compliance framework
institutional strengthening of Haitian rule of law entities

partner_organizations.name: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)
partner_organizations.role: Lead implementer and technical partner

partner_organizations.name: Multinational Security Support (MSS) Mission
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of capacity-building support

partner_organizations.name: Haitian National Police (HNP)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of capacity-building support

partner_organizations.name: Haitian Judiciary and Prison Administration
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of capacity-building support

partner_organizations.name: Haitian Civil Society Organizations
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of training and empowerment

partner_organizations.name: Local NGOs (sub-grantees)
partner_organizations.role: Recipient of grants for workshops and community engagement

quote.text: OHCHR will support the MSS mission to apply the UN comprehensive Human Rights Compliance Framework to all aspects of its operations in Haiti to prevent violations and abuse. With OHCHR’s oversight, the UN system in Haiti will also adhere to the UN Human Rights Due Diligence Policy (HRDDP).
quote.source: D0006504.odt, MSS Human Rights Compliance section

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: The UK will provide a direct financial contribution of £5 million to OHCHR, earmarked for activities related to human rights compliance within the MSS mission. The funds will cover staff, training, and operational costs over one year, with payments released in two tranches based on progress reviews.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: OHCHR is the sole implementer, responsible for all programme activities, including training, monitoring, and reporting. The Caribbean Development Team (CDT) within FCDO will oversee the programme, with support from the British Embassy in Santo Domingo and UK Missions to the UN in Geneva and New York.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: OHCHR is the only international partner with the mandate, expertise, and on-the-ground presence to implement the programme. It is explicitly authorized by UN Security Council Resolution 2699 to cooperate with the MSS mission and has a proven track record in similar contexts (e.g., the Sahel).

quote.text: OHCHR is the only international partner with the capability to implement the Programme and manage the funds in accordance with UK policies. In addition, OHCHR is the best choice of partner because i) they are mandated by the UNSC to cooperate with the MSS; ii) they are already on the ground working in Haiti with direct access to the MSS commander; iii) they have a proven track record of providing human rights support in other countries with UK funding...
quote.source: D0006504.odt, Why was THIS modality chosen? section

how_governance.q16_sub_award_details: OHCHR will allocate grants to local NGOs for workshops and community engagement, with approximately 3% of the total budget (£140,318) earmarked for this purpose.
how_governance.q17_governance_details: The Caribbean Development Team (CDT) within FCDO will provide oversight, including regular monitoring meetings and reviews. A Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) from CDT will dedicate 30% of their time to the programme, supported by a Programme Responsible Officer (PRO) and a Programme Manager. OHCHR will report progress through annual reports and financial statements, with additional oversight from the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services and the Joint Inspection Unit.

quote.text: CDT, in collaboration with BE Santo Domingo, will provide oversight of OHCHR activities, including frequent monitoring meetings and reviews, and represent the UK in the donor technical working group. The Programme team will monitor progress through the annual report from OHCHR as well as attend regular meetings to discuss results, risks and challenges.

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Funds can be reallocated between activities based on emerging needs, but significant changes require FCDO approval. The programme is designed to be demand-driven and responsive to the dynamic security situation in Haiti.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: The programme includes a delivery plan that will be assessed quarterly and revised to reflect changes in the operating environment. Adjustments to priorities or activities require approval from FCDO, particularly if they impact the log frame or results framework.

quote.text: A delivery plan will be developed within the first quarter, for programme implementation and will be assessed at each quarter thereafter and be the main tool for programme activity management. The delivery plan will incorporate an activity plan as well as a mechanism for monitoring the risks, issues and delivery challenges as well as changes to the log frame/results framework.

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → OHCHR (implementer) → Local NGOs (sub-grantees for workshops).

quote.text: FCDO will make a £2.5 million payment in November/December. Upon a satisfactory expenditure review and progress against log frame targets in February/March 2025, the second payment will be released.

q24_alternatives_considered.description: Direct funding to OHCHR to implement the UN Human Rights Compliance Framework and support the MSS mission.
No UK intervention, leaving the MSS mission without dedicated human rights oversight.

why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: The preferred option was chosen because OHCHR is the only partner with the mandate, expertise, and on-the-ground presence to implement the programme effectively. It aligns with UN Security Council resolutions, leverages OHCHR’s proven track record (e.g., in the Sahel), and addresses critical gaps in human rights compliance within the MSS mission. The 'Do Nothing' option risks reputational damage to the UK and the MSS, as well as increased human rights violations due to lack of oversight.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk: The compliance mechanism fails to address violations by the MSS or HNP, eroding trust in the UK as the key donor.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continuous monitoring by the SRO and Deputy Head of Mission (DHM) in Santo Domingo, with regular briefings from OHCHR and participation in donor technical working groups. The SRO will track allegations of human rights violations and ensure due process is followed.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Reputational risk: OHCHR and the UK are blamed for impeding MSS activities if the programme is perceived as restricting operational efficacy.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Strategic communications by OHCHR to clarify the programme’s objectives and differentiate it from the MSS mission. Communications will emphasize the integration of human rights compliance as a tool to enhance mission legitimacy and effectiveness.

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Safeguarding risk: Incidents of violence or abuse occur during programme delivery, affecting staff, partners, or beneficiaries.
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: OHCHR’s robust safeguarding policies, including training on human rights, child protection, and gender-based violence. The programme will also monitor and report on safeguarding incidents, with the SRO raising concerns directly with OHCHR if issues arise.

quote.text: Option 1 is this appraisal case’s preferred option, and would see a UK contribution cover the cost of UN staff and support activities under the OHCHR’s mandate. This aims to produce several outcomes detailed in the Theory of Changes set out in paragraph 43, including the prevention, and investigation of human rights violations... The importance of human rights monitoring in conflict zones, especially in fragile states like Haiti, is well-documented... OHCHR has the expertise in this area, having provided similar oversight in conflict-prone regions through its monitoring, reporting, and investigative functions.

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: The high-risk operating environment in Haiti, characterized by gang violence, weak institutions, and political instability, limits partner selection to organizations with existing on-the-ground presence and security protocols. OHCHR was chosen because it is already operational in Haiti and has direct access to the MSS mission leadership, reducing implementation risks.
q27_constraints_detail: Security risks restrict the number of viable partners to those with established operations in Haiti.
Weak institutional capacity in Haiti necessitates a lead partner (OHCHR) with strong technical expertise and international backing.
Political instability and gang control require a partner that can navigate complex stakeholder relationships and maintain neutrality.
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: The programme’s objectives—strengthening human rights compliance, preventing GBV/SEA, and building trust—require a delivery structure that combines technical expertise (OHCHR) with local engagement (Haitian civil society and rule of law entities). The multilateral approach was chosen to ensure alignment with UN mandates and leverage OHCHR’s existing frameworks (e.g., Human Rights Compliance Framework).
q28_linkages: The need for a robust compliance mechanism (WHAT) necessitates a single, specialized implementer (OHCHR) with a proven track record (HOW).
Capacity-building objectives (WHAT) shape the inclusion of Haitian rule of law entities and civil society as direct beneficiaries (WHO).
The focus on human rights monitoring and reporting (WHAT) requires a partner with investigative and oversight capabilities (OHCHR’s mandate).
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The programme explicitly balances equity and efficiency by integrating gender specialists into the OHCHR team and adopting participatory approaches with civil society. While this may slow initial implementation (e.g., coordinating with diverse local actors), it is deemed essential for long-term effectiveness and sustainability. The document notes that "inclusive human rights frameworks and data practices aim to build trust and legitimacy among local communities," which may require additional resources but is critical for mission success.

q29_tradeoffs_detail.detail: Engaging civil society and marginalized groups (e.g., women, IDPs) may delay rapid deployment but is necessary to ensure the programme addresses the needs of vulnerable populations and builds local trust.
OHCHR’s international expertise is prioritized for compliance and oversight, but the programme includes capacity-building for Haitian institutions to foster long-term ownership and sustainability.
Direct funding to OHCHR (a multilateral with economies of scale) is balanced with grants to local NGOs to ensure community-level impact, though this adds complexity to financial management.

intersections.risk_affects_management: The high-risk environment in Haiti (gang violence, weak institutions) necessitates intensive oversight, including regular briefings, donor coordination, and real-time monitoring of human rights violations. The management structure (e.g., SRO dedication, quarterly reviews) is designed to mitigate reputational and safeguarding risks associated with operating in a FCAS context.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: Capacity-building is a core objective, shaping the roles of Haitian partners (rule of law entities, civil society) as recipients of training and mentorship. OHCHR’s role as the lead implementer is justified by its capacity to deliver technical assistance, while local actors are positioned to apply learning and sustain outcomes post-programme.

quote.text: Given the current situation on the ground, limited options are available to support the MSS. This results in long-list options appraisal not being possible, with the only viable option for use of ODA funds being to strengthen the human rights compliance of the MSS in support of the OHCHR... OHCHR will support the MSS mission to apply the UN comprehensive Human Rights Compliance Framework to all aspects of its operations in Haiti to prevent violations and abuse.
quote.source: D0006504.odt, Options and MSS Human Rights Compliance sections

key_programme_risks.risk: Reputational risk: Failure of the compliance mechanism to address violations by the MSS or HNP, eroding trust in the UK as the key donor.
Reputational risk: OHCHR and the UK are perceived as impeding MSS operations, leading to backlash from mission leaders or contributing nations.
Safeguarding risk: Incidents of violence, GBV, or SEA occur during programme delivery, affecting staff, partners, or beneficiaries.
Operational risk: The MSS mission fails to achieve its security objectives, leading to further instability in Haiti and the wider Caribbean region.
Financial risk: Aid diversion or mismanagement of funds due to the volatile operating environment.
Political risk: Changes in Haiti’s transitional government or international support for the MSS mission disrupt programme implementation.

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Continuous monitoring by the SRO and DHM in Santo Domingo, with regular updates from OHCHR and participation in donor technical working groups. The SRO will track allegations of human rights violations and ensure due process is applied to perpetrators.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Reputational risk (perceived impedance of MSS operations)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Strategic communications by OHCHR to clarify the programme’s role in enhancing mission legitimacy and effectiveness. Communications will emphasize that human rights compliance is a tool to build trust with local communities.

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Safeguarding risk (incidents of violence or abuse)
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Implementation of OHCHR’s safeguarding policies, including training on human rights, GBV, and SEA. The programme will monitor and report incidents, with the SRO escalating concerns to OHCHR leadership as needed.

The programme is designed to complement the MSS mission by addressing human rights compliance, which is critical for long-term stability. OHCHR’s oversight aims to improve mission accountability and reduce the risk of unintended consequences.

Funds are disbursed directly to OHCHR, a UN agency with robust financial controls. A due diligence assessment (DDA) of OHCHR will be conducted before funding is released, and expenditures will be monitored through regular financial reports.

fcas_specific_lessons: Lessons from past UN peacekeeping missions in Haiti (e.g., MINUSTAH) highlight the need for robust human rights oversight to prevent abuses and reputational damage. The programme incorporates these lessons by mandating OHCHR’s compliance framework and public reporting mechanisms.

The use of the UN Human Rights Compliance Framework, previously tested in the Sahel, demonstrates the value of adaptive, context-specific tools for FCAS environments. The framework’s pillars (e.g., training, accountability, community engagement) are tailored to Haiti’s challenges.

The programme emphasizes the importance of local trust and legitimacy in FCAS contexts, integrating civil society engagement and strategic communications to address historical skepticism toward international interventions.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The OHCHR’s prior implementation of the Human Rights Compliance Framework with the G5 Sahel Joint Force (2018–2020) provided evidence of its effectiveness in improving accountability and reducing human rights violations. An EU evaluation concluded that the framework "systematically addressed all aspects of the JF’s operations" and was "highly relevant in strengthening the capacity of beneficiaries." This experience informed the design of the Haiti programme, particularly the focus on training, monitoring, and community engagement.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning:
The programme incorporates the following adaptations based on lessons from the Sahel and past Haiti missions: 
1. **Mandatory public reporting**: Unlike previous missions where abuses went underreported, the programme requires transparent reporting of human rights violations to build accountability.
2. **Civil society integration**: Direct engagement with Haitian civil society to monitor and document abuses, addressing gaps in local ownership from past interventions.
3. **Gender and disability inclusion**: Explicit focus on GBV/SEA and the needs of vulnerable groups (e.g., IDPs, women, people with disabilities), reflecting critiques of past missions’ failures to address these issues.
4. **Adaptive management**: Quarterly reviews and a flexible delivery plan to respond to Haiti’s dynamic security environment, a lesson from the Sahel where rigid structures hindered responsiveness.

quote.text: The EU Evaluation (2023) of this work concluded 'The implementation of the project within the JF has been highly relevant in strengthening the capacity of many beneficiaries, armed forces, magistrates and civil society organizations, and in providing a framework for the actions of the members of the JF to protect the population.'... The project design demonstrated in-depth human rights expertise and international humanitarian law (IHL) understanding, and the CF that forms the core of the project was appropriate to address the need for the JF to fulfil its HR and IHL obligations.
quote.source: D0006504.odt, MSS Human Rights Compliance section

co_funding_partners.note: The US has committed $360m to the MSS mission overall, not specifically to this programme.
Canada has donated $63.4m to the MSS mission overall.
France has contributed €3m to the MSS mission overall.
Spain has contributed €3m to the MSS mission overall.

financial_details.leverage_achieved: The UK’s £5m contribution to OHCHR is part of a broader international effort to fund the MSS mission, which has a total estimated cost of $600m for one year. While the UK funds are earmarked specifically for human rights compliance, they complement larger contributions from the US, Canada, and other donors, enhancing the overall mission’s legitimacy and effectiveness.

metadata.programme_name: 2024 Core funding to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
metadata.duration_text: December 2024 to December 2025 (with one-year cost extension to December 2026)
metadata.primary_sector: global development (health, education, humanitarian, WASH, child protection, social protection)
metadata.quote: "Support to UNICEF will directly contribute to the implementation of its 2022-2025 Strategic Plan" (S4005355.odt, Programme summary)
metadata.duration_source: "Original programme start and end dates: December 2024 to December 2025" and "The objective of this one-year cost extension is to support implementation of UNICEF’s Strategic Plan 2022-2025 in Financial Year 2025/26" (S4005355.odt, Changes)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to UNICEF to implement its 2022-2025 Strategic Plan across five goal areas: child survival/thriving, education, protection, WASH/climate, and social protection. It combines service delivery (e.g., vaccines, education access), capacity building (e.g., strengthening health systems), policy influence (e.g., normative leadership on girls' education), and financing mechanism (flexible core funds pooled with other donors).
what_objectives.q1_source: "Core funding is provided to UNICEF to implement its mandate as agreed by global forums including the General Assembly. Core funding provides an organisational backbone and is necessary for the presence of agencies at global, regional and country levels" (D0006397.odt, How UK support will be used)
q3_expected_outputs: 210 million children reached with services for early detection/treatment of child wasting (2023)
6.2 million doses of malaria vaccine delivered to seven African countries (2023)
132.9 million children vaccinated against measles (2023)
400 million children vaccinated against polio (2023)
9.3 million children treated for severe wasting (2024)
26 million out-of-school children/adolescents gained education access (2024)
18 million people gained access to basic sanitation services (2024)
33 million gained access to safe water (2024)
21 million gained access to basic hygiene (2024)
Ending all forms of malnutrition in children (Strategic Plan goal)
Universal access to safe drinking water (Strategic Plan goal)
76% birth registration rates achieved (2023)
37.7 million displaced children in crisis settings accessed education (2023)
34.7 million children/parents received mental health support (2023)
5.4 million people used climate-resilient water systems (2023)
7,500 schools and 3,000 health facilities provided with WASH services (2023)
what_objectives.summary: The programme funds UNICEF's global operations to deliver life-saving services (health, nutrition, education, protection, WASH) to children in 190 countries, with a focus on fragile/humanitarian contexts and systemic change through policy leadership and capacity strengthening.
what_objectives.quote: "OverthedurationofthisBusinessCase,theUKwillcontributetowardsthedeliveryofanumberofkeyobjectives,including: Endingallformsofmalnutritioninchildren; Ensuringthatallgirlsandboyscompletefree,equitableandqualityprimaryandsecondaryeducation; [...] Strengtheningresilienceandadaptivecapacitytoclimaterelatedhazards" (D0006397.odt, What will the programme deliver)

countries_regions: Middle East and North Africa (Sudan, Syria, Gaza)
where_context.q5_risk_evidence: UNICEF operates in 190 countries including fragile/humanitarian settings (e.g., Gaza, Sudan, Haiti) with high child vulnerability. The FCDO's 2021 Central Assurance Assessment rated UNICEF as 'moderate risk' due to complex operating environments but strong crisis response capabilities.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0006397.odt, Summary Sheet) and "FCDO’s March 2021 Central Assurance Assessment of UNICEF had an overall rating of moderate" (D0006397.odt, Risks)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and climate change have thrown SDG progress off-track, with children bearing the brunt: 1 billion children live in 'extremely high-risk' climate zones, 400 million in conflict areas, and 2/3 of child-related SDGs unlikely to be met. UNICEF's dual mandate requires operating in high-risk environments (e.g., Gaza, Afghanistan) where other agencies cannot.
where_context.quote: "Conflict, natural disaster, and climate change, combined with Covid-19 recovery has thrown progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) off track. Children are likely to bear the brunt of this [...] Currently over one billion children, almost half of the global child population, live in regions that are ‘extremely high-risk’ from the impact of climate change" (D0006397.odt, Why UK support is needed)

who_partners.q9_north_south_decision_power: UNICEF's Executive Board (36 member states including UK) sets policies and approves programmes, while country offices implement with local governments. The UK has a governance role via its Executive Board seat but no direct control over Southern operations.
q10_capacity_building_details: training and deploying emergency teams
strengthening health systems for pandemic preparedness
building capacity to respond to violence/exploitation
empowering communities on WASH/hygiene
supporting governments to implement social protection systems
disability-inclusive policy advocacy
mental health service investments

partner_organizations.role: implementation, normative leadership, global coordination
partner_organizations.location: multilateral (HQ in New York, 190 country offices)

partner_organizations.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
partner_organizations.role: funding, governance via Executive Board seat, strategic oversight

partner_organizations.name: UNICEF Executive Board (36 member states)
partner_organizations.role: governance, policy approval, budget oversight

partner_organizations.name: National governments (190 countries)
partner_organizations.role: programme implementation, policy alignment

partner_organizations.name: Civil society organizations (CSOs)
partner_organizations.role: service delivery, advocacy (mentioned in Theory of Change)

partner_organizations.role: coordination, joint programmes (e.g., global programme to end child marriage)

who_partners.quote: "UNICEF is mandated by the United Nations General Assembly to advocate for the protection of children's rights [...] It is the only UN agency with a dual development and humanitarian mandate and works in more than 190 countries and territories" (D0006397.odt, Why UK support is needed)

how_mechanism.q12_instrument_explanation: Core (regular) funding is unearmarked, flexible money pooled with other donors to support UNICEF's global operations and Strategic Plan. It underpins UNICEF's organizational capacity across 190 countries, enabling rapid crisis response and long-term programming without donor restrictions.
how_mechanism.q13_structure_description: UNICEF manages funds centrally via its Executive Board-governed system, with FCDO providing oversight through its Board seat. Country offices implement programmes in partnership with national governments, while FCDO's Scholarships, Tertiary Education and Partnerships (STEP) department monitors the UK's contribution.
how_mechanism.q14_selection_rationale: UNICEF is the only UN agency with a dual humanitarian/development mandate for children, and the UK has been a long-standing core funder. The selection reflects UNICEF's unique global reach, neutrality, and proven track record in fragile contexts where bilateral donors cannot operate.
how_mechanism.quote: "Core funding is provided to UNICEF to implement its mandate as agreed by global forums including the General Assembly [...] It allows agencies to provide substantive leadership around goals, advocacy, and policy work" (D0006397.odt, How UK support will be used)

how_governance.q17_governance_details: UNICEF's Executive Board (36 member states) provides intergovernmental oversight, approving policies, country programmes, and budgets. The UK participates via its Board seat, with additional bilateral engagement. The Board meets three times yearly (February, June, September) at UN HQ in New York.
how_governance.quote: "Executive Board is the governing body of UNICEF, providing intergovernmental support and oversight to the organisation [...] It comprises 36 members including the UK, representing the five regional groups of Member States at the United Nations" (D0006397.odt, UNICEF Executive Board)

how_flexibility.q19_reallocation_details: Core funds are unearmarked and can be allocated flexibly across UNICEF's Strategic Plan goals, regions, or crises as needed. The 2023 example shows nearly half of core funds went to the Middle East/North Africa for Gaza/Sudan responses, demonstrating adaptive reallocation.
how_flexibility.q20_adaptive_management_details: UNICEF can shift priorities in response to emerging crises (e.g., Gaza, Turkey earthquake) or strategic needs (e.g., climate resilience) without donor approval, as core funds are not earmarked for specific projects. The UK influences priorities via its Executive Board role but does not control allocations.
how_flexibility.quote: "Core funding provides two main functions to the UK: influencing agencies in line with UK priorities; and supporting the mandated ‘business as usual’ of agencies which supports the delivery of UK bilateral funding [...] It provides agencies with the funds to undertake programme design that helps to attract resources from other donors" (D0006397.odt, How UK support will be used)

how_efficiency.q22_layers_description: FCDO → UNICEF (central) → UNICEF country offices/local partners
how_efficiency.quote: "A new MoU with UNICEF will be agreed internally and negotiated following approval of the business case. The business case will be attached to the MoU and will be the primary means for setting out our expectations for funding" (D0006397.odt, How is FCDO Funding Delivered?)

q24_alternatives_considered: Stop core funding (shift to bilateral or alternative multilateral agency)
Continue core funding at £16m/year
why_rationale.q25_why_chosen: Continuing core funding was chosen to maintain the UK's influence within UNICEF and the UN system, leverage UNICEF's unique mandate/neutrality in fragile contexts, and ensure predictable support for global child rights. Stopping funding would risk ceding influence to rivals like China and undermine UK-delivered multi-bi programmes (e.g., GFATM, COVAX).

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Critical mass of other Member States does not prioritise core funding to UNICEF
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with other Member States to encourage prioritisation of core funding, including through the Strategic Funding Dialogues at Executive Boards

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Mandate of UNICEF comes under threat from non-like-minded member states with attempts to roll back progressive policies
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Continue to engage with UNICEF at all levels on these issues, working with like-minded, middle-ground and conservative member states

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: UNICEF insufficiently prioritises delivery of key FCDO policy priorities
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Work with other Member States to monitor strategic plan results, including through midterm review

q26_modality_specific_risks.risk: Weak human resources systems in UNICEF lead to ineffective Country Representatives
q26_modality_specific_risks.mitigation: Improve accountability of leadership selection through bilateral engagement and Executive Board opportunities

why_rationale.quote: "Retaining a viable level of core funding to UNICEF is critical to the UK’s reputation within the UN Development and Humanitarian System and will provide high-profile results against the Foreign Secretary’s priorities [...] Stopping core funding would mean that the UK would be unlikely to have a seat on the Executive Board in future years. This would reduce our influence over UNICEF’s strategic direction and programme performance" (D0006397.odt, Options)

intersections.q27_where_constrains_who: UNICEF's mandate to operate in 190 countries—including fragile/conflict states (e.g., Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan) where few other agencies can work—limits partner selection to organizations with global reach, neutrality, and rapid-response capacity. The UK cannot deliver bilaterally in these contexts, making UNICEF a necessary partner despite governance risks.
q27_constraints_detail: Need for neutrality/legitimacy in conflict zones
Requirement for rapid crisis response (e.g., Gaza, Turkey earthquake)
Operational presence in 190 countries including FCAS
Ability to work with national governments in fragile states
intersections.q28_what_determines_how: UNICEF's dual humanitarian/development mandate and the need for flexible, unearmarked funds to respond to unpredictable crises (e.g., pandemics, conflicts, climate disasters) necessitate a core funding mechanism. The global scope and normative leadership goals (e.g., SDG advocacy, girls' education) require a multilateral structure with country-level implementation.
q28_linkages: Global child rights mandate → multilateral delivery structure
Need for crisis agility → core funding instrument
Normative leadership (e.g., SDGs) → Executive Board governance
Service delivery in 190 countries → decentralized implementation with central oversight
intersections.q29_equity_vs_efficiency_tradeoffs: The document highlights tensions between (1) UNICEF's need for flexible core funds to respond equitably to crises worldwide and (2) donor demands for efficiency/oversight; and (3) the trade-off between UNICEF's global mandate (requiring multilateral governance) and the UK's desire to influence specific priorities (e.g., girls' education).
q29_tradeoffs_detail: Flexible core funding (equity) vs. donor earmarking demands (efficiency)
Global mandate (inclusivity) vs. UK priority alignment (focus)
Rapid crisis response (speed) vs. governance oversight (control)
Multilateral decision-making (legitimacy) vs. bilateral influence (strategic alignment)
intersections.risk_affects_management: The moderate risk profile (due to FCAS operations) leads to milestone-based oversight via the Executive Board and annual reviews, rather than light-touch management. High-risk contexts (e.g., Gaza, Sudan) require tolerating inherent risks while monitoring for significant changes.
intersections.capacity_shapes_roles: UNICEF's capacity building for national governments (e.g., health systems, social protection) enables decentralized implementation, while its global technical expertise (e.g., vaccine procurement, WASH) justifies its lead role over local partners.
intersections.quote: "UNICEF’s ability to respond quickly to a crisis, considerable access to vulnerable populations, strong staff expertise in technical areas, and good procurement management processes" (D0006397.odt, Risks) and "Core funding provides two main functions to the UK: influencing agencies in line with UK priorities; and supporting the mandated ‘business as usual’ of agencies" (D0006397.odt, How UK support will be used)

UNICEF insufficiently prioritizing UK policy goals

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Critical mass of other Member States does not prioritise core funding to UNICEF
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work with other Member States to encourage prioritisation of core funding, including through the Strategic Funding Dialogues at Executive Boards

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Operating environment significantly deteriorates, substantially affecting commitment and ability of UNICEF and FCDO to deliver the results sought
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Inherent risk that will need to be largely tolerated. However, we will monitor for any significant change in the operating environment

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Mandate of UNICEF comes under threat from non-like-minded member states with attempts to roll back progressive policies and programming in areas such as climate, humanitarian and women and girls’ rights
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Continue to engage with UNICEF at all levels on these issues, working with like-minded, middle-ground and conservative member states

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Work with other Member States to monitor strategic plan results including through midterm review (presented to the Executive Board June 2024) to ensure targets continue to be suitably ambitious

risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Improve accountability of leadership selection through bilateral engagement and Executive Board opportunities. Use central assurance assessment to review HR processes and provide recommendations to the agency

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNICEF do not make good progress on UN reform, undermining efficiency and effectiveness
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Continued engagement at the Executive Boards and bilaterally. Engagement in-country to monitor effectiveness and reform implementation, via the UN Effectiveness Network

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: ODA pauses impact the distribution schedule of the funding
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: STEP follow government guidance and prepare business case with justification for the need to pay on time

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: UNICEF has insufficient capacity to prevent, detect, investigate and sanction fraudulent activity, or inadequate risk management, oversight and assurance arrangements
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: Due diligence undertaken of UNICEF through central assurance assessments. Ongoing monitoring of agency performance through Executive Board, and negotiation of decision language to press for improvements where required. Appropriate provisions incorporated into MoU

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: Partner agencies lack appropriate social and environmental safeguards, leading to funding being used for purposes that inadvertently cause harm
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: MoU agreed by FCDO and UNICEF has strong safeguarding commitments

risk_mitigation_pairs.risk: STEP lacks sufficient capacity and capability to effectively manage the programme
risk_mitigation_pairs.mitigation: STEP operates flexibly to lend oversight support across the team as needed. Arrangements established with other FCDO departments to supply additional advisory inputs required

fcas_specific_lessons: UNICEF's ability to operate in FCAS (e.g., Afghanistan, Gaza, Sudan) where bilateral donors cannot is critical for reaching children in extreme vulnerability.
Core funding enables rapid response to FCAS crises (e.g., 2023 allocations to Gaza/Sudan) without delays for donor approval.
FCAS contexts require tolerating higher residual risks (e.g., 'Severe/Possible' for mandate threats) while maintaining oversight.
Lessons from Sudan/Haiti highlight need for UNICEF to strengthen local partnerships in FCAS to mitigate access risks.
risks_lessons.lessons_from_previous: The 2021 Central Assurance Assessment and MOPAN review highlighted UNICEF's strengths in crisis response, access to vulnerable populations, and technical expertise, while noting challenges in HR systems and UN reform progress. The 2023 results (e.g., 210M children reached for malnutrition services) demonstrate the impact of core funding in scaling proven solutions.
risks_lessons.design_changes_based_on_learning: The 2024 Business Case Addendum extends funding to align with UNICEF's Strategic Plan 2022-2025 end date, incorporating lessons on fiscal challenges and DEI risks. The UK is engaging in UNICEF's 2026-2029 Strategic Plan development to address these issues.
risks_lessons.quote: "Given UNICEF’s proven track record, and our assessment of their processes and policies, the risks of this programme are considered moderate and well within FCDO’s risk appetite" (D0006397.odt, Risks) and "SincetheoriginalBusinessCasewasapproved,wehaveseenasignificantdeclineinoverallODAfundingtoUNICEFandtheUNsystem" (S4005355.odt, Risk)

co_funding_partners.partner: Other UNICEF core donors (36 Executive Board members)

financial_details.leverage_achieved: UNICEF's 2023 core funding supported: £183m in UK bilateral (non-core) funding leveraged; $5.2 billion in supplies/services procured globally; partnerships with Gavi, WHO, and Africa CDC for vaccine distribution (e.g., mpox, malaria). Core funds also attract additional donor resources by demonstrating UNICEF's operational capacity.
financial_details.quote: "The UK’s £16m core funding payment will put the UK as the third largest G7 core funding donor to UNICEF behind the US ($137m) and Germany ($76.1m)" (D0006397.odt, Why UNICEF?) and "UNICEF procured $5.2 billion worth of supplies and services for children in 162 countries and areas achieving savings of $74.8m" (D0006397.odt, Value for Money)

what_objectives.q1_explanation: The programme provides core funding to UNDP to strengthen its institutional capacity and deliver systemic solutions across climate, gender, democracy, and crisis prevention. It combines financing mechanism (channeling flexible funds), capacity building (strengthening UNDP's operational presence), and service delivery (direct support in 170 countries).
what_objectives.q1_source: "To support UNDP in its delivery of Agenda 2030 and the Paris Agreement in challenging and complex circumstances. Across its wide portfolio, to support the strengthening of UNDP as an institution and the development and delivery of systemic solutions to climate, gender and equality, democracy, and crisis prevention and peacekeeping goals." what_objectives.summary: The programme provides predictable core funding to UNDP to strengthen its global operational capacity, enabling rapid crisis response, systemic development solutions, and progress toward Agenda 2030/SDGs across 170 countries.
what_objectives.quote: "Core funding to UNDP supports delivery of the UK’s objectives across governmental priorities... investing in UNDP not only helps get help fast to those who need it, it helps deliver our UN reform agenda through strengthening a UN agency with a wide global presence." (D0007348.odt, Rationale for UK Aid spending)

countries_regions: Specific focus on fragile contexts (e.g., Gaza, Ukraine, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Lake Chad Basin, Liptako-Gourma)
Least Developed Countries (79% of UNDP's Accelerator Labs)

where_context.q5_risk_evidence: The programme operates in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) where UNDP spends 50% of its resources, but the overall programme risk rating is assessed as 'moderate' due to UNDP's established systems and decentralized presence.
where_context.q5_source: "Overall programme risk rating: Moderate" (D0007348.odt, Summary Sheet) and "UNDP spends 50% of its total resources in fragile contexts, investing in all 60 countries defined as fragile by the OECD." (D0007348.odt, Advancing UK policy priorities - Peacebuilding)
where_context.q6_constraints_impact: Conflict and fragility require rapid, flexible responses (e.g., Gaza waste management, Ukraine recovery) while UN procedural constraints (e.g., Executive Board negotiations, immunities) limit FCDO's direct control over fund allocation. Climate risks and weak institutions in programme countries demand adaptive programming.

Core funding to UNDP will help expand the UK’s reach, allowing UNDP to provide support in countries and regions where the UK does not have a significant development presence." Country-level delivery is highly decentralized (93% of UNDP workforce based in-country).

supporting national partners on gender equality (e.g., Equanomics initiative with 60 economists deployed)
building resilience in fragile states (e.g., early recovery programmes in Gaza, Ukraine)
technical advisory support (e.g., electoral assistance, climate NDCs)
